https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9q9.title: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9q9.text:
"Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat.

Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dart of movement.

Eluding us is the numbat, a rare Australian marsupial which could be the love-child of a chipmunk and an anteater.

Numbats were once populous across the bottom half of the continent, but Dryandra Woodland – in the south-western corner of Australia – is one of the few places they remain.

As we slowly roll along bush tracks, researchers explain how this annual trip helps plot the species' survival.

Classified as endangered until this month, numbats have been bouncing back. This team's efforts have seen them scratched off the international red list of threatened species - a rare glimmer of hope in a country facing an extinction emergency.

This part of Australia is the front line of that crisis: a last stand for many species driven to the brink by feral pests, disease, urban development, habitat destruction and climate change.

Winging over our car at one point is the endangered Carnaby's cockatoo. On an island just off the coast is one of the last surviving pockets of the world's rarest marsupial, the Gilbert's potoroo. Diving in the sapphire waters around it is the increasingly scarce Australian sea lion.

Australia has long been celebrated as a nature haven, home to some of the world's most unique plant and animal species. More than 80% cannot be found anywhere else.

But it has arguably become the extinction capital of the world, losing roughly four species every decade - and the decline is only worsening.

Dedicated volunteers and under-funded conservationists have been slowing the army of increasing threats, but experts fear that without urgent action and political courage, the biodiversity Australia says it loves is headed for a bloodbath.

"It's not even a case of imagining it, it's happening in front of our own eyes," Professor Euan Ritchie tells the BBC.

If spotting a rare creature in the wild wasn't challenging enough, the numbat is a squirrel-sized camouflage connoisseur, explains Dr Tony Friend, the godfather of conservation in the state of Western Australia.

"They just slept in today," jokes Rob McLean, president of the Numbat Taskforce, a volunteer group which makes a lot of Tony's thinly-resourced work possible.

For two weeks each spring, as the young start venturing from their burrows, this team drives a daily circuit and records every numbat spotted. They log GPS coordinates, measure the distance to the road, and use a complicated equation to estimate the density of the animals in these woods and, from that, broader population health.

One person sits in concentrated silence at each window, another perched in the back of the pick-up truck, ducking for the occasional limb branching from trees which rise around us.

Through the trunks, we get the occasional glimpse of the razed farmland which tightly fences this pocket of protected woodland. On the side of one trail is a machine which detects and sprays feral cats and foxes with poison, another reminder of the perils numbats face.

"This year's been a bit of a feast," Rob admits.

For hours on end, we cruise around, seeing parrots, wallabies, a goanna and a couple of echidnas - but no numbats.

Tony arrived at Dryandra back in the 80s to find a numbat population fewer than 50. Many of the culprits then were the same as those still driving extinctions across the nation today.

Swathes of critical habitat are being cleared for development or industries like farming, mining and timber.

Leaving a trail of destruction in their wake are introduced pests: fire ants, cane toads, rabbits, foxes, feral cats.

Invasive weeds like lantana are choking the Australian bush, chlamydia has sent koalas to the edge of existence across much of the country, while the skin-eating chytrid fungus has caused seven frog extinctions here and counting.

The changing climate is creating unliveable conditions for some species, like native flying foxes which are dropping out of trees in their thousands due to extreme temperatures.

For others it is eliminating their food or their homes.

Climate change is also driving natural disasters which fry and drown both plants and animals with now frightening regularity.

The infamous Black Summer bushfires of 2019-20, for example, killed an estimated three billion animals. The successive years of record-breaking flooding which followed were so widespread it's impossible to estimate the impact on wildlife.

Many species once abundant across the continent are now isolated to increasingly small and disjointed patches, each impact compounding and leaving them more vulnerable to the next.

There are small, yet determined, efforts to slow the momentum of decline.

As a young numbat scoffs his breakfast – custard with "termite sprinkles" – at Perth Zoo, a keeper explains how this stud's upcoming release at Dryandra will help boost genetic diversity.

"When you get that feedback: your babies have got babies, it's very satisfying," Vicki Power says.

Breeding programmes like this have also made setting up additional populations of an array of threatened species possible.

But many cannot survive in the true wild, where large-scale predator control remains an endless battle, and are instead sent to fenced nature reserves, themselves high-maintenance undertakings facing problems like in-breeding and overpopulation.

Habitat protection or restoration projects have been ramping up, but they are not keeping pace with destruction, particularly in the most critical areas.

Scientists are also trying to fight disease, though that's an expensive and laborious endeavour, which for most species buys only a little more time. Others are preserving genetic material in case we ever work out how to resurrect species from the dead.

Scientists agree that we're living though the world's sixth mass extinction event, the first caused by humans. But Australia is at the front of this trend.

It leads the world in mammal extinctions, and medals when it comes to the loss of other species classes too.

"Despite Australia being one of the wealthiest countries per capita in the world and having more than its fair share of world-leading scientists… we have a truly awful record of conserving species," Ritchie says.

"And things aren't getting better."

The Australian government's official extinctions list sits at 67, but researchers are confident at least 100 plant and animal species have been lost forever.

They suspect the true figure is far higher. The country is still discovering species which have already been wiped out.

Though the rate of extinction in Australia has stayed stable, at around four per decade, the number of threatened species is still climbing quickly, and the deterioration of many is only gathering speed.

This trajectory has some scary flow-on effects, experts warn. Australia's biodiversity "underpins everything", ecologist Jack Pascoe says.

Think food production, tourism, construction – much of the economy. Potential scientific breakthroughs could be stymied: in medicine, agriculture and even climate change adaptation. And for First Nations Australians, the decline also threatens their culture.

"We think of ourselves as custodians of all life on Earth… so there's a much more personal and social feeling of loss that comes when these things are not doing well or we lose them forever," Pascoe, a man from the Yuin Aboriginal nation, says.

Though environment protection is a state responsibility, the federal government oversees matters of national importance.

Labor took office in 2022, promising no new extinctions under its watch, and it has sought to make nature protection a defining feature of its second term.

"It's well understood that nature is facing many challenges in the world today, both here in Australia, and overseas… we are losing biodiversity at an alarming rate," Environment Minister Murray Watt told the BBC in a statement.

His party has significantly increased Australia's emissions reduction efforts and massively boosted renewable energy projects. There is some praise for their work on drawing critically endangered mammals back from the brink. And the passage of revamped environment laws last year was heralded as the most significant reform in a generation.

The country also has an ambitious goal to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.

But there's limited optimism that this will be a real turning point.

The new laws are only the scaffolding of change. The substance of it is still being worked out – in the form of National Environmental Standards (NES) and a federal watchdog to enforce them.

And many in the sector say the problem is not so much the regulatory tools available, but rather the political will to use them.

Successive governments have failed to adequately protect the environment over the past 30 years, Australia's longest serving environment minister tells the BBC.

​​That includes his own administration. "We should have done more too," says Robert Hill, who lead the last major reforms in 1999 under John Howard's conservative coalition.

Many of the challenges of his era still haunt leaders today.

The nation's wealth has largely been built off the back of its natural resources – often at the expense of the environment. Those riches still underpin the economy and help fund government spending on essentials like healthcare and housing.

Then there's the added pressure applied by industry and the competing interests of states - whose stake in regulatory controls blurs the lines of accountability and increases bureaucratic hurdles.

These battles leave even the toughest environmental advocates within governments bruised.

For example, the Albanese government last year rushed through laws protecting salmon farming after lobbying by Tasmanian state officials, silencing opposition from within and ignoring advice from its own department concerning the impact of the A$1.4bn (£733m; $989m) industry on the survival of the Maugean Skate, an endangered ray.

"The axe falls on the environmental outcome if there's the alternative of an economic one," Hill says.

"Even if [the federal government] does want to act, it's still got to have the political strength to turn its aspirations into reality."

There is also a belief that greater regulation alone will achieve little.

Too much conservation work currently relies on philanthropists' cash and devoted volunteers, those in the sector say, and much more languishes on the to-do list due to a lack of money.

The federal government directly spends about A$700m on nature protection, a fraction of the A$33bn – or 1% of GDP – conservationists say it should be. That is an eyebrow-raising figure, people like Paul Elton concede, but one they argue is reasonable.

According to his research – which the government disputes – more than A$26bn is still being spent on subsidies for things like mining, intensive agriculture or fuel despite Australia signing global pledges to wind them back.

"For every dollar the government is spending on positive biodiversity conservation action, there's A$26 being spent on subsidies that are causing harm to nature," he tells the BBC.

"That's a pretty stark imbalance."

Minister Watt didn't directly respond to questions about conservationists' demands, but said: "We remain committed to long-term environmental recovery, in partnership with state and local governments, community and environmental groups."

Though public sentiment is shifting, there's scepticism the government will prioritise the environment amid competing demands and compounding crises until voters force them to do so.

"The community will say to you, we should spend a lot of money on the environment. And then if you say, 'Well, what are you prepared to sacrifice to ensure that funding base?', then they're no longer interested," Hill says.

In the face of so many challenges and what they see as little progress, advocates admit it's hard to hang on to hope.

"We know what the problems are. We know how to address them. We know when we spend money on the environment, it pays back many times over," Ritchie, a mammal ecologist, says.

"It's like being a doctor and seeing all these sick people in the community and you know how to fix them, but no one will let you do that."

Small wins, like the future of the numbat, keep them fighting.

There are now around 3,000 nationwide, and in Dryandra numbers have increased ten-fold. The animal has recently been taken off the international endangered species list and is now classified as near-threatened.

It takes five hours, but finally synchronised cries of excitement come from the driver's seat and the back of the pick-up truck. The cause of the commotion stands frozen and alert at the end of a hollowing log.

"It's not a competition," Rob says. Chuckling, he points at his rival spotter: "But I beat him by a second."

The dam has broken. Over the next little while we see eight numbats, including two pairs of babies, blinking at us in the dusky light.

This year's full count, Tony later tells me, is one of the best yet.

"But I remind people they're not out of the woods yet," Tony says.

The relief at the numbat's revival is tempered by worry this will make it harder to access the funding and support needed to cement those gains.

The woylie, or brush-tailed bettong, is a cautionary tale. It recovered slightly and was taken off the threatened list only to be added again a decade later, in a worse state.

"We can't walk away," Tony says, "and say 'no, they're fine,' you know?"

"It's got to be accepted that continued work is needed to keep that animal on the planet."

The country is still discovering species which have already been wiped out. The numbat has been taken off the international endangered species list and is now classified as near

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2el.title: How a schoolteacher's son became Kashmir's first India Test cricketer
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2el.text:
"You play with so many cricket stars. Why don't you take selfies with them?"

Bilal Ahmad Dar once asked his young cousin, Auqib Nabi.

Auqib smiled and replied: "One day I will reach a place where they will want to take selfies with me."

Years later, that prediction has come true.

On Monday, the 29-year-old all-rounder became the first cricketer from Jammu and Kashmir to earn an India Test call-up after replacing Jasprit Bumrah in the squad for the two-match series against Sri Lanka, which starts on 15 August.

For a region where conflict, harsh winters and limited infrastructure have long restricted sporting opportunities, Auqib's selection is being seen as a landmark moment.

Raised in a small village in Baramulla district, Auqib grew up playing on local grounds with little infrastructure and few opportunities. His father, Ghulam Nabi Dar, a schoolteacher, initially wanted him to concentrate on academics and become a doctor.

"There was no scope in cricket. We used to think playing sport was a waste of time, so I insisted that Auqib focused on his studies," Ghulam says.

But Auqib's persistence eventually changed his father's mind.

"After seeing his passion for cricket, I accepted it. I realised that, as a parent and a teacher, I shouldn't force him to do something he didn't want to do. I started supporting him."

Auqib's childhood friend, Junaid Dar, remembers growing up in an environment where professional cricket barely seemed possible.

"Auqib was obsessed with cricket from childhood. I used to ask him, 'Why are you doing all this? There's no future in it.' We came from a place where there was no concept of playing sport professionally and hardly any infrastructure."

To pursue his dream, Auqib regularly travelled around 70km (43 miles) to Srinagar to practise on proper cricket pitches. He did not even own a pair of spike shoes when he attended his first cricket trials.

But his work ethic never changed, his cousin Bilal says.

"Auqib is very hardworking and consistent. He knows how to fight obstacles and make a way for himself.

"He would wake up early to go to the gym and then practise for the rest of the day. He did that almost every day for 10 years."

His breakthrough came in 2020 when he made his Ranji Trophy (India's top domestic tournament) debut for Jammu and Kashmir, taking a five-wicket haul against Jharkhand.

Former India all-rounder Parvez Rasool, Jammu and Kashmir's first international cricketer and Auqib's long-time captain, says one quality always stood out.

"I have followed Auqib's progress for a long time, and what stands out about him is his work ethic and discipline."

Success, however, did not come overnight. Auqib claimed 44 wickets during the 2024-25 Ranji Trophy season, finishing as the competition's leading fast bowler, but remained largely outside the national conversation.

"When you do well but don't get recognition, it hurts," his father says.

"But we should never lose hope. Hope is what keeps the world intact. I always believed his time would come."

The following season, Auqib produced one of the finest bowling campaigns in recent Ranji Trophy history, taking 60 wickets in 10 matches to finish as the tournament's leading wicket-taker and help Jammu and Kashmir win their maiden Ranji Trophy title after a wait of 67 years.

Those performances earned him an 84m rupees (£730,000; $982,000) Indian Premier League (IPL) contract with Delhi Capitals. Although opportunities in the IPL were limited, his red-ball exploits had already caught the attention of India's selectors.

For Rasool, Auqib's Test call-up carries significance far beyond one player.

"Playing Test cricket is the ultimate dream for any cricketer. It was my dream too. Seeing Auqib earn that call-up fills me with immense pride.

"In a way, it feels like a dream many of us in Jammu and Kashmir carried has finally been realised through him. It is a historic moment not just for Auqib and his family, but for cricket across the region."

He believes Auqib's journey is remarkable not just because he reached the Indian team, but because of where he came from.

"Making it to the Indian team is incredibly difficult for any player, but the challenge is even greater when you come from Jammu and Kashmir. For years, we have had limited infrastructure, fewer opportunities and many obstacles that players from other parts of the country don't necessarily face.

"To reach this level, you need exceptional consistency, mental strength and the determination to keep believing in yourself. Auqib has shown all of those qualities, which is why this achievement is so special."

Jammu and Kashmir became affiliated with the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) in 1957, yet the region still has only two major cricket stadiums, both with limited facilities. Long winters, heavy snowfall and decades of conflict have further slowed cricket's development.

"This is a landmark moment for cricket in Jammu and Kashmir," Rasool says.

"For a long time, people questioned whether someone from our region could make it to India's Test team. Auqib has answered that question. His selection shows players from Jammu and Kashmir can compete with the best if they are given the opportunity."

He believes Auqib's journey will inspire a new generation.

"When I started playing, there weren't many role models from Jammu and Kashmir. Today, things are changing.

"Auqib becoming the first player from the region to earn an India Test call-up will give countless youngsters the belief that they can dream big too. His journey proves that no matter where you come from or what challenges you face, hard work and perseverance can take you to the highest level."

Back in Baramulla, Ghulam Nabi now finds himself recognised everywhere he goes.

"People come up to me, hug me and say, 'This is Auqib's father.'

"It makes me immensely proud."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2el.summary: Auqib Nabi is the first cricketer from Jammu and Kashmir to earn an India Test call-up. The 29-year-old all-rounder replaced Jasprit Bumrah in the squad for the two-match series against Ghulam Nabi.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gy.title: The phone book that led us to Assad's spy chief in hiding
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gy.text:
In an abandoned luxury apartment in the Syrian capital Damascus, armed men dressed in military fatigues sifted through designer clothes and documents.

Scattered across the living room floor, under a sparkling crystal chandelier, were dozens of photos of the same slender man in different settings - sitting at his desk, even playing in the snow. And multiple prints of the same image, showing him smiling warmly as he shook the hand of ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad.

The man was not instantly recognisable, but gold medals and gilded certificates piled nearby were inscribed with the name Hussam Luka.

Known as "The Spider", Luka was one of Assad's top henchmen, accused of orchestrating atrocities and systematic torture, and sanctioned by the UK, US and European Union.

As head of Syria's most powerful civilian intelligence agency, Luka was among the most feared men in the country. But much of his work was conducted from the shadows.

Like others in the regime, Luka seemingly vanished overnight in December 2024 when Assad was toppled, leaving a trail of unanswered questions and demands for justice that many fear will never be realised.

In his apartment, days after Assad's fall, we watched the rebels looking for clues as to where he might have gone.

In the corner of the living room, on a console table, was an unremarkable-looking notebook.

Inside, in scribbled blue handwriting, we found dozens of names - from shopkeepers and doctors, to military officials and people with the Luka family name.

Could these contacts help us learn more about The Spider and his crimes, or even help us to track him down?

At one time, Luka's own phone number was hard to avoid - in the early days of the Syrian civil war, it had been spray-painted on walls around the central city of Homs.

The conflict was sparked by Assad's brutal crushing of a pro-democracy uprising in 2011 - a war in which hundreds of thousands of people would go on to be killed.

Luka was a local head of the Political Security Directorate, one of Assad's main intelligence agencies, and had been given the task of wresting the city from the rebels.

At the time, rebel-held areas in Homs were under siege by the government, and residents were struggling to access food and medicine. Several people, including former rebel fighter Motaz al-Zaydi, told us they had resorted to eating rats.

Al-Zaydi remembers Luka's name and phone number appearing on a wall in his neighbourhood, and said the message began to spread that those wanting to flee the fighting could phone the number for safe passage.

Some are believed to have been granted safe transit out of the city by Luka, but others who called the number were never seen or heard from again, according to several people we spoke to, including al-Zaydi.

Many told us they referred to Luka as "The Spider" because of his vast web of allies and informants, including some embedded in rebel groups. "He was everywhere," Homs residents told us. Al-Zaydi described Luka as an "evil genius" and "a fox of a man".

But his most egregious action in the city, many argue, was his alleged involvement in the so-called Eid Massacre, known by some as the Children's Massacre, which the US noted when sanctioning him.

It was the Muslim holiday of Eid al-Adha in September 2015, and Mohammed Towakatli's seven-year-old, Wael, was gardening in the playground he had set up in the al-Waer neighbourhood.

At 17:10, just after the power ration had kicked in, Mohammed remembers the strike hitting.

As Mohammed walked around the park earlier this year, now planted with rows of saplings, he recalled the names of the children killed and the games they had been playing at the time, gesturing to the places where he had found their bodies, including that of Wael.

"They were tiny children," he said with tears in his eyes. "The ground here was painted red with blood."

Twenty-eight people were killed, including 17 children and four women, according to the Syrian Network for Human Rights.

Luka, according to a Syrian activist group, and a pro-opposition newspaper at the time, was responsible for the regime's selection of targets in the area that day.

His actions in Homs earned him a promotion, and by the time of the regime's collapse he ran the General Security Directorate (GSD) intelligence agency, making him one of the most powerful people in the country.

The government security services could target anyone - from opposition fighters, journalists, doctors, or rights activists, to people believed to be opposed in any form to the Assad government.

Those arrested were detained in Syria's political prisons, including Sednaya in Damascus - a facility so notorious it was dubbed the "human slaughterhouse". Many imprisoned there were never seen again.

As head of the GSD, Luka had strategic control over Syria's detention policies, and his personnel would monitor communications to and from Sednaya.

There are widespread calls across Syrian society on social media for former senior officials to be held accountable. Some also say the new Syrian government is not doing enough to bring these people to justice.

Syria's Attorney General, Hassan al-Turba, told the BBC the government had launched a lawsuit against Luka, accusing him of "premeditated murder, torture, and death resulting from torture".

"A warrant has been circulated domestically and we are working on circulating it internationally as well," he said, adding the administration was working to track the location and seek the extradition of Luka and other missing senior regime officials.

As he continues to grieve for his son, Mohammed told the BBC he wanted Luka, alongside other senior regime officials, to be returned to Syria and executed.

"They look like humans but have no humanity in them at all," he said.

We had taken photos of every page of the book we discovered in Luka's apartment and, back in London, began testing every one of its 155 numbers - aware that many people close to the regime would have fled or gone to ground. Fifty-one numbers appeared to be operational.

We then called these again in order of their apparent importance to Luka, starting with military commanders and relatives.

Every call was unsuccessful. Anyone who answered simply hung up when we explained who we were and what we wanted - or denied knowing Luka or his family, or even being the people listed in the book.

So a BBC reporter, whose own name was once on a GSD wanted list while Luka ran the agency, headed to Syria to try in person.

Many of those listed in the phone book were doctors, so our reporter began booking medical appointments with some of them as a way to meet them.

A doctor in Aleppo reluctantly acknowledged he had treated Luka, but then ordered our journalist to leave and returned his consultation fee.

Our reporter then booked an appointment with another doctor in the phone book, this time based in Damascus. This doctor revealed he had once accompanied Luka's mother on a medical trip to Russia, but was reluctant to give us any more information, other than to vaguely direct us to a pharmacy belonging to one of Luka's daughters.

Locals said she, too, had not been seen since December 2024.

For months we drew a blank in our hunt for Luka.

And then we had our first breakthrough.

One of those listed in the book, who we tried calling again, finally answered the phone.

He had been the guard for Luka's apartment block, he told us, and eventually agreed to give us the number for someone he said had been Luka's personal bodyguard - a man we are calling Mahmoud.

It took weeks to secure an interview with Mahmoud. Meetings would be scheduled but he would not show up, or he would request a meeting in a private space such as a car or apartment, which our reporter judged too much of a risk.

They eventually met at a hotel one night, just before midnight. Broad-shouldered and physically imposing, Mahmoud seemed to be considering every answer carefully before he spoke.

He told us he was angry with Luka for leaving him behind when the regime fell. As word had spread in December 2024 that Assad's rule was on the brink of collapse - with rebels advancing on the capital - Luka had said he would stay and defend Damascus, Mahmoud told us. But by the early hours of the next morning, Luka had disappeared, taking a large sum of money with him from the office safe, Mahmoud said.

Mahmoud refused to share any contact details for Luka or his family, but did give us a number for Luka's driver, who he believed had driven the former spy chief out of the capital that night.

This man proved even harder to reach.

When he answered the phone, his voice was nervous and unsteady. He repeatedly insisted he was just a driver, and knew nothing of Luka's activities. Multiple meetings with us were never kept, and eventually he stopped replying.

We turned our attention to Luka's possible escape routes, including neighbouring Lebanon - where the Iran-backed group Hezbollah had close links with the Assad regime.

One senior source in the Lebanese government told us he understood Luka had passed through Lebanon on a "good Russian passport but with a different name", before flying out to Russia.

We managed to find a man, now based in Lebanon, whose name was listed in Luka's contacts book, but under a number that no longer worked. He is one of many wanted by the new Syrian government, because of his close association with the Assad regime.

This man, who we cannot identify, said he had a number for Luka.

We saw it, and realised it had a Russian country code.

Russia was a key backer of the Assad regime, and in the days after his fall, Assad released a statement confirming that he had fled there. Many of his inner circle were believed to have followed him.

Back in Luka's apartment in Damascus, we had found clues that Luka also had strong links to Moscow - awards from Russia's foreign spy service, and even a New Year's card addressed to him from a senior Russian official.

Now, the Russian telephone number for him suggested we finally had proof that he was - as we had predicted - in Russia.

We wanted to verify that this number really was Luka's.

So a few days later, with us present, the man agreed to put the person he said was Hussam Luka on speakerphone, and ask him questions which we believed only Luka would know the answer to, based on information we had gathered during our investigation.

The voice on the other end of the phone sounded confused, but answered the questions instantly and correctly.

He refused, however, to speak to us directly.

But our contact later agreed to call Luka again and allow us to try to interview him.

The same voice answered, and we introduced ourselves, explaining that we had questions about serious allegations relating to massacres and torture committed by the former regime official.

"I can't take any risk talking on the phone in the position I'm in," Luka said, his tone anxious.

Asked if Russia was blocking him from talking, Luka said: "I cannot talk. I can't explain. You have to understand."

When asked if he would meet us outside Russia, he said: "It's difficult."

He then hung up the phone.

We later obtained a second number which we were told was also for Luka - this time registered in Syria and linked to social media and messaging apps which he appeared to be still using.

Over a period of a day, the BBC was able to locate him in two ​suburban areas on the outskirts of the Russian capital, Moscow.

The locations seemed far removed from the luxurious lifestyle Assad is reported to be leading in exile in Russia, and to the life Luka himself once led in Syria.

We knew we could not approach him in person in Russia, where Assad's henchmen are shielded from international journalists and police, so we decided to try putting our allegations to him over the phone once again.

We rang the number and the same voice as before answered, the line crackly.

He asked who was calling, and when told it was the BBC, he immediately hung up.

We sent a message over WhatsApp, asking for his response to the many allegations against him, but he did not reply.

Confirmation that Luka is in Moscow is difficult news for those in Syria seeking justice. Russia is highly unlikely to extradite officials from the regime that it long supported.

The Russian government did not respond to BBC requests for comment about Luka's presence there, or whether it would ever consider an extradition request.

Back in Homs, Mohammed says he will never let go of the hope that Luka, and other senior members of the Assad regime, will one day face justice.

"[I am] angry at all those who were with the regime and its security apparatus… They were all against us," he says.

"Wael was just a seven-year-old child… All he cared about was playing and having fun."

Additional reporting by Riam Dalati, Ghaith Solh and Abigail Akerman
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gy.summary: Hussam Luka was one of Assad's top henchmen, accused of orchestrating atrocities. Luka's most egregious action in Homs was alleged involvement in the so-called Eid Massacre. Lukas is a former regime official in Moscow, Russia, where he is a ex-regulator.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3r0.title: 'I ran because I knew I would die': Russian drones target medics in Ukraine
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3r0.text:
Inna Lytvynenko always puts on her bright orange body armour when she's out on an emergency call.

Last July, the paramedic was sent out in Kherson to treat a woman injured in a Russian drone attack, when an FPV drone smashed into her ambulance.

Seconds later, she heard a buzzing sound in the sky. Another drone was flying straight towards her, fast.

"I panicked. I grabbed my trauma bag and started running," she recalls. "I shouted and screamed. I knew that if I stopped, I would die."

After chasing her for about 10 minutes, the drone flew away. Lytvynenko was quickly picked up by police.

But what she called the "safari hunting" continued. Drones hit two more vehicles that arrived to take the injured woman to hospital. Hours later, a third police car finally managed to get her out.

After another "safari" attack earlier this week, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called to put greater pressure on Russia in order to stop deliberate "hunting attacks" on civilians.

Hospitals and ambulances in Ukraine are increasingly coming under Russian drone and missile attack, even though, according to the international rules of war known as the Geneva Conventions, they must be protected by all parties to the conflict.

"This is a new normality, which should not be the normality," says Dr Jarno Habicht, the World Health Organization's (WHO) representative in Ukraine.

The WHO has registered 3,118 attacks on healthcare since the start of the Russian invasion in February 2022. "That's two cases per day," Habicht says.

Since 2023 the number of attacks on healthcare has steadily grown. In 2024 it went up by 30%. Last year there was another 20% increase. This trend is expected to continue this year.

A recent Doctors Without Borders (MSF) report says that Russia systematically and often deliberately targets Ukrainian medical facilities. The frequency of attacks on healthcare suggests that they are "a sustained feature of the war rather than an episodic consequence of large scale offensives," the report said.

Last month Russian missiles hit a hospital in Kherson, badly damaging the building and killing one doctor.

Hospital director Olena Tymoshenko believes it was a targeted attack. "It wasn't just one missile, there were three missiles that hit the hospital within a few minutes from each other. It cannot be an accident," she told the BBC.

Contains disturbing scenes.

Moscow also often uses a "double-tap" tactic, when they target the same location twice within a short period of time. Many believe that the second attack is deliberately aimed at first responders who arrive at the scene of the initial strike to rescue survivors.

During a recent massive Russian air attack on Kyiv, seven people were killed, including a police officer and a volunteer, after a second strike on the same location.

And lately Russian forces have been also targeting warehouses of humanitarian organisations. Last month alone, warehouses of three UN agencies, including the WHO, were damaged during air strikes. According to Habicht, the organisation shares coordinates of its facilities with both Moscow and Kyiv specifically in order to protect them from strikes.

While missile and drone strikes can be indiscriminate, first-person view (FPV) drone strikes are almost always intentional. A drone pilot can see the target in a live feed from the drone's camera. So when it hits an ambulance, it has to be on purpose, says Robin Meldrum, MSF country coordinator in Ukraine.

Dr Inna Lytvynenko says that she was wearing a uniform identifying her as a medical worker. The ambulance was also clearly marked. So, she believes the drone operator consciously chose to target them.

According to the WHO, strikes on ambulances make up 20% of all attacks on Ukraine's healthcare system, which suggests these are part of a calculated strategy.

The result of such sustained attacks is that the civilian population close to the frontline are getting increasingly cut off from health services.

The majority of people left in these areas are elderly people who often chronic diseases. Even if they survive air strikes and shelling, without medication and occasional check-ups they face a slow death.

And ambulances may not be able to reach them if the risks are high.

Lytvynenko and her colleagues constantly monitor social media to learn about threats.

"It's really scary," she says. "Every time when we take a patient to hospital, we just pray. These drones can appear from anywhere, they can even get through anti-drone nets."

In some cases, police are dispatched instead of ambulances.

Since the danger zone where FPV drones operate is growing – as both Ukraine and Russia develop drones with greater and greater ranges – mobile clinics run by various health organisations have had to shift their operations further and further away from the frontline.

"Two years ago, we could go up to 5-8km (3.1-5 miles) from the frontline," says Meldrum. "Now we won't go anywhere within 30km and this distance keeps growing."

Over the past 18 months, MSF stopped regular visits to about 80 villages near the front where they had provided health services, says Meldrum. And recently it has paused ambulance services in Sloviansk, a major city in eastern Ukraine.

"It doesn't feel like we're protected in this environment, and in the way that Russia is conducting the war," Meldrum says.

"We don't feel that the rules of war are being respected."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz05.title: He's been frozen on Everest for 30 years, now 'Green Boots' may finally be coming home
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz05.text:
For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit.

The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since.

Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body – arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain.

Warning: This story contains a picture of a dead body.

They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home.

"On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC.

"When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'"

The night before he left to be part of a historic Indian expedition on Everest, Morup sat with his wife at his home in Ladakh, an Indian-administered territory in another part of the Himalayas.

He made her a promise: that he would come back a hero and make his country proud.

"He asked me to take care of the kids and come to the airport to greet him on his return," Konchak Yangskit told the BBC at her home.

A lance naik, or lance corporal, in the Indo Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), the force guarding much of India's border with China, 48-year-old Morup was no stranger to Himalayan trekking.

But Yangskit says she had a strange sense of foreboding that night: "I wondered if I was ever going to see him again."

Morup was one of six climbers on the ITBP expedition attempting to reach the top of Everest – which lies on the border between Nepal and the Chinese-governed territory of Tibet.

Most climbers choose to ascend from the Nepalese side, but Morup's crew wanted to write their names into the history books as the first Indian expedition to do it from the treacherous Chinese side.

Three out of six members of the expedition turned back due to a snowstorm, but Morup and two others - Tsewang Smanla and Tsewang Paljor – kept struggling, all the way up to the 8,849m summit.

Disaster, a blizzard, struck as they descended and killed all three.

Like many of the more than 300 people who have died in the Everest region since records began a century ago, their bodies remain on the mountain.

Two have never been found, but the third body - that of "Green Boots" - has been lying frozen in the snow for three decades at an altitude of 8,500 metres.

For years, it was assumed that "Green Boots" was another member of the expedition, Tsewang Paljor.

But testimony from surviving members of the 1996 expedition and the location of the last radio contact with the climbers have now led authorities to believe the remains belong to Morup.

An ITBP official, speaking anonymously because he is not authorised to speak to the media, told BBC News Hindi that Morup's clothes and climbing gear helped officials identify the body in recent years.

Since then, they've been plotting how to get their comrade home so they can confirm his identity beyond doubt through DNA testing and offer his family a semblance of closure.

"We never forgot him. It was only a matter of time," the ITBP official said.

Retrieving those who have died on the mountain is a dangerous, gruelling task, and, up until the past decade, very rare.

Many of the bodies, like Morup's, are in what climbers call Everest's death zone – where temperatures can plunge to -40C and oxygen levels are about a third of those at sea level.

"The weather and snow conditions are going to be crucial," said Tshiring Jangbu Sherpa, a prominent Nepalese mountaineer who has taken part in other recovery missions.

"The north side has fewer crevasses, but it is riskier. If something bad happens from the Nepalese side, you get quickly evacuated by helicopter. But there is no such system from the Chinese side," he told BBC Hindi.

The Chinese side of the peak – where Green Boots' body is – is steeper and doesn't have the same support structures as the southern slope, which is another complicating factor, Sherpa sources have told BBC News Nepali.

"It's really tough to get that body down even in popular spring season, let alone the autumn [which has more unpredictable weather]. That's the simple reason it is still there for so many years," mountaineering guide Pemba Ongchu Sherpa said.

"There would need to be 10 to 12 climbers who are capable of making summits, just to fix [support] ropes to reach that point."

Green Boots will also have to be physically carried down to an altitude where it can be collected by a helicopter, or possibly yaks, and transported back to an airport – a job which also requires huge manpower.

Sherpas say bodies shrouded in iced-up climbing gear often weigh several times the average man and are frequently frozen into awkward positions, making bringing them down the challenging terrain even more treacherous. The remains may also begin defrosting and decomposing once they reach lower altitudes.

The start of the descent with the body would be the most difficult, Indian climber Kuntal Joisher told BBC Nepali.

"It's going to be very, very risky endeavour. It's extremely steep ground with lots of rock. Logistically, this [first] 1000m is going to be a humungous challenge."

"The main thing is to not put Sherpa lives at risk for a dead body."

All of this makes for a hugely expensive recovery mission – experts say even the most straightforward ones cost between $40,000 and $80,000, a sum beyond the means of most families.

It is more common for local teams to move people who have died out of view on the mountain: like explorer Francys Arsentiev, dubbed the Sleeping Beauty of Everest, who in 2007 was moved to a more private final resting place on Everest almost a decade after she died.

But the ITBP – which is funding the recovery operation – wants Morup's body to be returned by September, and is looking for mountain rescue Sherpa groups who could do the job.

Once returned to India, the body will undergo DNA testing and, if confirmed to be Morup, his remains will be given back to his family.

For years, Morup's family back in Ladakh have struggled to come to terms with his disappearance.

Now around 75, Yangskit struggles to recall even the day she was married. But the days after the tragedy remain etched in her mind.

"I only knew there was a storm on the mountain. Even though we organised cremation prayers at home, my heart refused to believe he had died," she says with tears rolling down her face.

"I didn't see his dead body, so it was difficult for me to believe it."

All that remains of Morup today are his medals and trophies, a couple of old photos from his mountain adventures – and, most importantly, a certificate from the Chinese government which states that at 17:30 on 10 May 1996, Morup reached the top of Everest.

If the recovery mission is successful, Morup's son Punchok Dorjai told the BBC that the family would hold a funeral for him near the Martyrs Park in Ladakh's capital Leh.

"My father gave his life for the country and he should be remembered as a martyr," Dorjai said, adding that his teammates who perished deserve the same title.

The family will also proudly save a symbol of Morup's legacy at their home, to go alongside his summit certification, he said: "We are planning to keep the Green Boots."

Additional reporting by Pradeep Bashyal, BBC News Nepali
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz05.summary: Dorje Morup was one of six climbers on the ITBP expedition to reach the top of Everest. He died in 1996, but his body has been lying frozen in the snow for 30 years. The body is believed to be that of a third body that Kuntal Joisher says would be the most difficult.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgl.title: Scale of devastation shocks US city's fire-seasoned residents
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgl.text:
Last year, Chris Matthews was forced to flee with his family of five after a brushfire threatened their home in Spokane, Washington.

That evacuation lasted only a few hours. So when an ominous column of dark smoke raced towards him last Saturday, and he and his family were evacuated again, he expected he'd be back home soon.

Instead, he returned to find nothing but smouldering ruins.

"All of us thought we were going to be able to get back to our houses," he recalls. "And we didn't think it'd be a situation where we were going to lose our homes or anything like that."

Smoke and fires are a normal occurrence here in the US Pacific Northwest every summer, as residents wait for the autumn rains to arrive. Small evacuations are not unexpected. But the scale of this year's fires in Spokane is unprecedented.

Kira Townsend, 39, says she realised the immense danger when word came that the fire had jumped over the river, which normally acts as a barrier protecting the city from fires.

"It's never jumped the river like that, and just roared up the hill that fast," she says.

Nearly a quarter of the city population – 65,000 people – were forced to evacuate since the fires began. For those whose homes did not burn down, officials say it may be weeks before it is safe to return to their neighbourhoods.

Miraculously, there have been no deaths or major injuries reported from the fires.

Matthew Kincanon, 31, fled for his life as the fire entered his neighbourhood of Prosperity Lane on Saturday night. He returned 12 hours later to discover that there was nothing left.

"As soon as I stepped out of the car I threw up," he says. "I felt sick. I couldn't control it. I just lost it. It hit me all at once," he says.

While firefighters battle three large fires around the city that remain less than 40% contained, the recovery effort is beginning for people who have lost everything.

"We have two fronts going at the same time. We're actively fighting the fire and trying to put that out. But we're also starting recovering for folks that have lost their homes," City Councilman Zack Zappone, who grew up in the devastated Indian Trails neighbourhood, tells the BBC.

"There just a lot of uncertainty and frustrations and difficultness," he says at a city shelter, describing the tensions in the city.

Chrissy Goodrich's voice cracks in anger as she calls on people to do everything they can to prevent more wildfires. She echoes warnings from officials, who say that innocent activities like mowing your lawn could ignite a fire.

"People have got to use their brains," she says.

"Stop doing things that are gonna cause sparks. I can't believe someone was mowing."

"So many people have lost their houses, and people are just being so stupid," she adds.

She and her 73-year-old father, Scott Hansen still ride their mountain bikes through burned-out neighbourhoods to get groceries back to home, which is in the mandatory evacuation zone.

Like many Spokane residents, he expressed surprise at how easily the fire breached the river.

"The winds were too strong," he says. "It just blew over the river like it wasn't even there."

Anger has intensified since police charged a local man, who has allegedly confessed to sparking one of the fires.

"I was so happy they got him. It's just not right," says lifelong resident Susan Crouch, 70, who previously lost her home to wildfire.

The fires this summer, she adds, "are the worst Spokane has ever had".

Local media reported that he had previously been questioned for arson, and had a prior conviction for killing his own father in Arizona in 2010.

The suspect, Aaron Farinacci, 37, has not yet entered a plea, and a judge has ordered him to undergo a mental competency evaluation.

According to investigators, he specifically chose a dry, windy day, in the hopes of sparking a large fire. More dry windy days are in the forecast.

Matthews, who lost his house, is now urging his neighbours to prepare for the worst. In retrospect, he says he wishes he had a generator that he could have used to power a sprinkler system around the property after the electricity went out.

"For future reference, and for everyone else – take it seriously. Don't assume past historical times are what's going to happen in the future as well."

His wife, Melissa Matthews, says she feels a sense of "closure" to discover that the blaze that destroyed her home may have been set intentionally by a man who is now accused of arson.

"It brought a little bit of closure," she says, adding: "That sounds weird to say."

Chris adds: "Knowing that a person did this, as opposed to it being a natural thing that happened, it just does feel a little bit comforting for some reason."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgl.summary: Spokane, Washington, has been hit by three large fires this summer. Nearly a quarter of the city population – 65,000 people – were forced to evacuate since the fires began. Residents say they are still struggling to recover from the fires. A local man has been charged with arson in the fires and ordered to undergo a mental evaluation.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c07r.title: I was standing in front of my teacher when she was shot, Thai pupil says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c07r.text:
On Friday morning, as the final classes of the week were under way, panicked students began streaming out of a prestigious school just outside Bangkok.

Inside, police say, a 14-year-old boy had opened fire.

"I was standing in front of the teacher when she was shot," a shaken seventh grader tells the BBC, near the gates of Debsirin School in Nonthaburi. "She was talking to me when [the gunman] showed up."

Still in her uniform, with her mother by her side, she explains how the shooter stalked from room to room.

Authorities say he killed five teachers and injured 23 people - including fellow pupils - before turning the weapon on himself. Earlier, he had gunned down his grandparents.

"I had to climb over the school fence to escape with other friends," the girl, who the BBC is not naming, continues.

Her mother says the girl thought she might die. "[She said] 'I thought I'd never see you again'."

One 18-year-old student told Reuters he initially thought firecrackers were going off.

"I didn't think it was a gun at first," he said. "There were many shots: bang bang bang. Then it went quiet. Then it started again."

Metres from the school gates, paramedics loaded the wounded into ambulances and rushed them to hospital, as milling crowds hugged and cried.

Rescue worker Kiatikhun Verapongpradith rushed to the scene after hearing children as young as 12 had been hurt.

"I saw students who had been shot, some in the arm, some in the back, some in the chest. So I rushed to help get them to the hospital first," the 47-year-old rescue worker told Reuters news agency.

One grieving teacher told the BBC his friend was among the dead.

"She was my age. We went to this school together as students. Then we both became teachers at this school," the 31-year-old, who declined to give his name, said.

It is early days in the investigation and police haven't said anything about a motive.

They believe the 9mm handgun the shooter used belonged to his grandfather. Forensic officers found the gunman's shots to be "quite accurate", with several hitting "vital spots" on victims' bodies.

Others are filling some of the gaps. A teacher at the school has said the shooter was a good student - not aggressive and with good grades - and education authorities have described him as an avid gamer.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said study pressures may have played a role.

"We learned that his grandmother was a teacher and she might have been strict with him. From what the police gathered from his close friend, they knew he was quite stressed about it."

It is clear authorities will have many questions to answer in the coming days - many of them about what change this crime must trigger.

This is Thailand's deadliest mass shooting in years - and the second at a school this year.

In February, a head teacher and a female student were shot by an 18-year-old gunman during a school siege in southern Thailand.

Four years ago, a 34-year-old in the eastern Nong Bua Lamphu province killed 37 people, most of them preschoolers, in a shooting and stabbing at a nursery.

These crimes have resurfaced questions about gun control in the country.

"This shouldn't have happened," the boyfriend of one of the killed teachers told reporters, clearly distressed and trying to hold back tears.

More than seven million people are believed to own guns in the country, one of the highest rates of ownership in the world. Of those, more than one million are unlicensed owners.

While there are restrictions on gun licences in Thailand, people can still acquire the weapons - legally or illegally - with relative ease.

There is a thriving black market, aided by Thailand's porous land borders with four other nations. Problems with corruption and loose regulation in the police and military have seen weapons end up in the wrong hands.

Prime Minister Anutin said he had tightened regulations when he was interior minister three years ago - suspending new gun permits.

But gun crime remains rife, with deaths from gunshots among the highest in the region. And some in the community are calling for greater action.

"An act of violence in an educational institution, which should be one of the safest places in our society, serves as a stark reminder for Thai society to seriously and systematically review gun control measures," Natthaphong Ruengpanyawut, leader of the People's Party - an opposition party - wrote in a Facebook post.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgd.title: German airport drone-bomb: Could Russia be involved?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgd.text:
As Germany investigates how a drone loaded with explosives reached a runway at Leipzig airport, there is renewed talk in Europe of hybrid war.

The interior minister is warning of a "new level of danger" from an attack that "may involve foreign powers".

There is no proof at this stage to link the flying bomb directly to Russia, which denies any role. But as well as the means and the motive, Moscow does have form.

The BBC has seen details of the investigation into a plot in 2024 in which Russian-linked proxies in Poland and Lithuania not only handled drones and explosives but also delivered them to Germany.

The quadcopter was discovered at Leipzig airport late on Tuesday night, forcing one runway into lockdown as a bomb disposal robot rolled into action.

On the tarmac close by were several Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes, stripes along their enormous bodies in the blue and yellow of the country's flag. One reads, "Be Brave Like Kherson", the southern city now on the frontline of Russia's invasion.

Pictures published by German media suggest the drone was a relatively small device which airport staff spotted "floating" between the Ukrainian planes.

Around the same time, a DHL cargo plane collided with an "unidentified object" as it pulled up into the sky, unable to land in Leipzig.

Teams are still working to establish whether that was a second drone.

They are also trying to trace who launched the devices and why.

A previous Russian-backed plot involving Leipzig airport could provide clues.

In 2024, a parcel containing a sophisticated incendiary device caught fire at the airport's DHL hub shortly before it was loaded onto a plane. Similar packages then ignited in the UK and Poland, causing extensive damage.

A group of men are currently on trial in both Lithuania and Poland, where prosecutors believe they were part of a substantial network of proxies recruited by Russian military intelligence.

But there was a subplot that has been little discussed before.

Last September, Lithuanian prosecutors said that investigators had also seized RDX explosives meant for "other terrorist attacks". The amount was significant: equivalent to 6kg of TNT.

"Some of the devices were manufactured to intensify the blast," the prosecutor added.

The BBC has since had access to case documents that describe how several of the men on trial were paid to transport those explosives around Europe, concealed in cans of sweetcorn and chopped tomatoes. The detonators were hidden inside headphone sets.

The suspects also handled drone parts and the case talks specifically of attachments, suitable for holding a bomb.

Prosecutors allege that some of the items were brought into the EU from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.

Almost two dozen suspects have been charged with terror offences, but with the men's handlers still at large, believed to be in Russia, it is not clear whether the entire network was disbanded or all the hidden material found.

While there is no evidence of a link to the Leipzig drone bomb, the 2024 plot certainly highlights the potential.

One of the suspects charged in Poland, a Ukrainian called Vladyslav D., described in detail to investigators how he made multiple long car trips in July 2024 following instructions from someone he knew as "Warrior".

He has since pleaded not guilty in court.

One message sent him to the edge of a Lithuanian forest where he found a carrier bag containing "three or four packs of headphones", soggy with rain.

He had already collected two cans of corn "lightly covered with soil" from another location, telling investigators he had no idea what was inside.

He was ordered to leave the headphones many hours' drive away in Poland where he noticed "a guy on a bicycle" collect them from beside the road.

For another assignment he received a pin for a location inside a Lithuanian cemetery and was told to dig beneath some plastic flowers. He quickly uncovered a bin bag wrapped in brown tape.

"Inside were drone components: small plastic propellers, I think four pieces," Vladyslav told investigators.

These items were to be left by a road in central Poland for pick-up.

Finally there was a trip to Germany where he was given the code to access a hostel room in Dusseldorf. He was instructed to leave the drones and other items inside.

The intended targets were never revealed.

In statements to investigators, Vladyslav D. said he was paid more than $2,000 (£1,487) in cryptocurrency for his efforts. His motive was clear.

And what about the Leipzig case?

Few details about the drone bomb are yet public.

Some German sources report that the explosive was Semtex, which contains RDX - the explosive found in the food cans in a Lithuanian cemetery.

We do not know how much the drone found at the airport was carrying and the physical damage may have been limited.

"The drone casing, if it was metal, might have put a hole in the plane but just a blast wave probably would just have dented it unless they put some fragmentation inside," explosives expert Professor Jackie Akhavan of Cranfield University explained.

But if Russia was behind this, its aim was more likely to sow fear.

Andrei Soldatov, an expert on Russia's intelligence agencies, said it "makes sense" to suspect Moscow, pointing to a clear pattern of sabotage and hostile activity, from arson attacks on facilities supporting Ukraine to drones over sensitive sites in Europe.

Germany is one of Kyiv's biggest suppliers of military aid.

"It's a message. You get something like that [bomb] into one of the biggest European airports and you send the message that, 'Guys, we can do that. Remember'," Soldatov explained.

"You hint to the adversary that you might cause a really big problem: that tomorrow might be more serious."

And the potential motive? Moscow is under intense pressure from Ukraine's long-scale drone attacks, he said, and the fact that Russian President Vladimir Putin "has been humiliated, repeatedly".

"We are aware of the incident, which the German authorities continue to investigate," a Nato official told the BBC.

Antonov Airlines has also been cautious so far in its response.

The firm supplies planes for certain Nato operations but declined to say whether that includes military support for Ukraine.

Asked whether the Ukrainian planes might have been targeted, a spokeswoman in Kyiv told the BBC: "We are not making any such assumptions…We don't know what this drone was or why it was there."

But Russia watchers are clear.

"This is Russian interference," said John Lough of the New Eurasian Strategies (NEST) Centre. "It's all part of undermining support for Ukraine by pointing to the dangers of escalation and, frankly, scaring the German authorities."

He sees high potential for a surge in such hybrid attacks now because Ukraine has "changed the balance" of the war.

"My expectation is that such activity will increase quite sharply over the coming months. I think it's a dangerous moment."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr7k.title: Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr7k.text:
Warning: This story contains details some may find distressing

A 17-year-old Sudanese girl holds a young child in her arms with a heavy calm that belies her age and the concerns she has for his future.

"This son of mine has no father, no birth certificate and no national number," Amira, whose name has been changed to protect her identity, tells the BBC.

Looking down at him, she speaks slowly as if still trying to grasp the details of what has happened to her since the civil war erupted in Sudan.

She and her family used to live in the eastern neighbourhoods of el-Fasher, a city that came under siege from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been in a brutal power struggle with the military since April 2023.

El-Fasher was the army's last stronghold in the western region of Darfur until it fell to the RSF and allied Arab militias after 18 months last October.

For the tens of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city, it was a nightmare – with constant bombardment, clashes and suffering from a lack of food.

In the end Amira and her family decided to flee early in 2025, desperate to find a safer area.

But as they snuck out on a road south-west of the city, she says she was abducted by three armed men from the RSF and held captive.

"They blindfolded me and took me to the Tabit area south of el-Fasher. I was locked in a room for two months, and every day one of them raped me in turn," she recounts in a low voice

After weeks in captivity, she discovered she was pregnant and became very sick.

Amira says when the men wanted to get rid of her, they dropped her near the area she had been captured.

It was with the help of other people fleeing el-Fasher that she was taken to receive medical help.

Months later, at a humanitarian hub that was not under RSF control, she gave birth at a hospital run by the International Medical Corps.

There she received some support from a Sudanese aid organisation - the Nada Al-Azhar Foundation for Disaster Prevention and Sustainable Development (Nada).

The group was also able to find her family, who had made it to a camp where hundreds of thousands of people from el-Fasher have sought refuge.

It was a huge relief for them all to be reunited, but the family still face challenges - one being that eight months after giving birth, Amira has been unable to register her son's birth.

"Even getting a birth notification from the hospital requires information that doesn't exist," says Amira, explaining that she is unable to provide any details about the child's father.

Without this she cannot organise any official recognition of the baby's legal identity.

"I can't get him vaccinated, or enrol him in nursery or school," she says.

"I'm afraid for his future because he isn't registered at all. My economic situation is very difficult, and I can't afford his treatment or care. I can't even go to work for fear of being exposed to violence again."

According to Nada, Amira's story is not an isolated case, but part of a reality repeated in areas experiencing conflict across Sudan.

This is because many children are being born in complex circumstances, often without the knowledge of the father - meaning their births cannot be registered, explains Abu Bakr Yousif Yaqoub, Nada's director of protection programmes.

"Registering a child requires identity information, a national number and a birth certificate. But when the father is absent or unknown, it becomes extremely difficult," he tells the BBC from el-Fasher.

"The mother is often alone, and sometimes she herself is still a child who needs care, which limits her ability to care for her baby.

"There are also health challenges related to the lack of follow-up on essential vaccinations, which begin at birth and continue through the child's early years."

He warns that this situation does not just affect a child's early years but extends to their future education and as an adult being able to travel or obtain official documents.

It is not easy to obtain data about the number of children that have been born as a result of rape in Sudan.

According to Nada's director general, Shaza Ahmed, this comes down to social stigma as the true numbers are not recorded.

"Women who experience such assaults do not feel comfortable reporting them," she tells the BBC, speaking from Port Sudan, an army-held city in the east of Sudan.

"Unfortunately, most of the mothers of these children are themselves children - girls under the age of 18. Therefore, they cannot make the decision to go officially to court or the police, as they need a guardian to accompany them."

She notes that 90% of the cases recorded by her organisation involve families refusing to allow official reporting of the sexual assaults that led to pregnancy.

"As a Sudanese woman, my greatest fear and concern for children born as a result of rape is that we are facing a whole generation that will live under stigma, danger and fear," Ahmed says.

"These children will not receive respect from society, their well-being will not be truly protected, and above all, they will not have access to services or their rights."

For Ahmed they are not being treated as if they are "fully human", even though Sudanese law does grant all children the right to obtain an identity.

Sudanese lawyer Majida Idris explains that the Child Act of 2010 allows for the registration of children born outside marriage.

But it relies on the mother being willing to file a report that she has been assaulted - because this kick starts the registration process.

Once reported, the case is then referred to social services for documentation, before being sent to the civil registry, where the child is registered under the mother's name and given a full legal name according to procedures.

However, Idris says that the reality during war is completely different, especially in Darfur, where the ongoing conflict has led to the collapse of civil services and the shutdown of civil registry offices, leaving thousands of children unregistered.

"The absence of documents does not just mean the absence of a piece of paper - it means denying the child access to education, healthcare and legal recognition," she tells the BBC.

The lawyer says it is imperative to reactivate civil registry offices in accessible areas and intensify legal efforts to ensure children obtain their right to identity and legal recognition.

Amira and her child remain in Darfur - and therefore in administrative limbo.

Her mother admits that the lack of paperwork for her grandson is a worry.

Yet for the moment the family is overwhelmed with gratitude to have found one another again.

Amira has also been offered emotional and psychological support sessions and other advice by Nada - which is a comfort to the family.

"I was so extremely worried until I found her. I hadn't been eating or drinking," Amira's mother told the BBC.

"The reunion was like a miracle from God. To see our daughter back sitting among us is a gift and blessing that could not be thanked enough for."

She was held captive for two months and raped by the men, who then dropped her near the area she had been captured. She gave birth to her son at a hospital run by the International Medical Corps.
