https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0qv.title: Wildfire damage could take hundreds of years to recover from, experts say
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0qv.text:
It could be hundreds of years before habitats destroyed by wildfires in Wales recover, an environment watchdog has said.

Nick Thomas, from Natural Resources Wales (NRW), said if soil had been incinerated in upland areas rich in peat, which grows at about a millimetre a year, it could take centuries for the vegetation to come back.

He expects 2026 to be the worst year Wales has ever experienced.

As well as damage to natural habitats and animal life, Thomas warned loss of soil could increase flood risks, because it no longer acted as a "sponge" holding water on high ground.

Wales has witnessed huge wildfires this summer, including one major incident and the evacuation of a village in Conwy county.

In the Rhinogydd mountain range in Gwynedd, which is home to a National Nature Reserve and a Special Area of Conservation, a blaze burned for nearly two weeks and affected over 2,000 acres.

Both fires were visible from space.

Meanwhile, a fire in Blaenavon, Torfaen, could be smelt as far away as Cardiff.

Although fewer wildfires were reported in the second half of July in England and Wales compared with 2025, Thomas said: "This year seems to have been worse, I would say, than any of the ones I can remember.

"I would expect this to probably be the worst year for wildfires perhaps we've ever had."

While some areas will recover quite quickly - potentially within a couple of years - he said: "It all depends on how deep the fire goes.

"If a fire burns into the soil and incinerates the soil... then you've lost hundreds of years worth of soil.

"So it's going to take hundreds of years really for that vegetation to come back in a similar way to what it was."

Thomas said a large wildfire on Mynydd Llantysilio near Llangollen, Denbighshire, in 2018 had incinerated about 10cm (4in) of peat in some areas.

Eight years on, there is still no heather in large patches.

The mountain also saw a "big upsurge" in heather beetles this year - possibly linked to milder winters. The beetles stripped plants of their leaves and left combustible woody stems, he said.

"It's kind of all part of the vicious circle which is associated with climate change."

While it may be months before the full scale of the devastation this year is known, Thomas said the situation was "very frightening".

"It is really worrying because there is so much moorland, heathland in Wales, and forest, which can easily be set on fire. So, we need to be doing more to address that," he said.

Management of moors and heaths to "reduce the fuel loads" could help, he said, as well as grazing, but: "The public can do so much because they're all started by people basically."

Bird protection charity RSPB Cymru said it was also devastated to see the impact of wildfires, which "can have significant impact on breeding birds and fragile habitats that can take years to fully recover".

Julian Thompson, who has been warden of Pensychnant Conservation Centre for 36 years, said the soil had turned to dust "right down to the rock" after the nature reserve had lost about one-third of its 150 acres during the wildfire in July.

While fires have been used for centuries as a way of managing the mountainside, Thompson said controlled burning was usually done in the winter.

"This fire, being in the summer in the middle of a drought, was so intense that it's burnt away the soil. There is no organic matter left."

He added: "Things like the snakes, adders, reptiles, they can not escape, so they will be destroyed.

"All the invertebrates will be destroyed.

"There are a number of very rare moths which occur there, in particular two - the Ashworth's Rustic and the Weaver's Wave - which occur in the mountains of Snowdonia and Meirionyddshire and nowhere else.

"This is the best-known place for them. So on our land... they will have been destroyed."

The moths would survive in some surrounding areas, he said, but their habitat is "diminished".

"Nature is quite resilient, but it can't cope with catastrophes on this scale over and over again. It won't keep on coming back."

The Pensychnant reserve is supported by volunteers who help preserve and run the centre, including Gwyndaf Pritchard, from Dwygyfylchi.

He said it had been a special place for the community and that the loss of wildlife had been "tragic".

"We've talked about it for years and years, but now climate change is here and we have to start to respect the countryside and we have to be in a position to actually stop these fires happening again," he said.

Evie Roberts, a silversmith who teaches jewellery-making at the centre, said people needed to be educated about the dangers of discarding bottles or cigarettes, which could cause fires.

"Your actions can have devastating effects and I think that education for people is vital to stop this," she said.

"There's a new fire every week at the moment, and there's so much of our land damaged."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0qv.summary: Natural Resources Wales says it could take centuries to recover from wildfires. Wildfires have destroyed peat in upland areas rich in peat, which grows at a millimetre a year. The loss of soil could increase flood risks, because it no longer acted as a "sponge" holding water on high ground.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr59.title: Drone warnings and sheltering in airports as South Korea battles historic heatwave
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr59.text:
South Korean authorities are deploying drones to issue heat warnings to farmers while residents are taking shelter in airports, as the country battles an unprecedented heatwave.

President Lee Jae Myung has ordered public agencies to mobilise all available resources to deal with the extreme heat, which he has called a "national disaster".

Temperatures in the south soared to a record 42.5C (108.5F) earlier this week.

At least 23 people have died from heat-related illnesses in the country so far this year, while nearly 2,500 have visited emergency rooms for heat-related conditions since mid-May, authorities say.

"Heatwave conditions once seen only in foreign news reports have now become our reality," Lee said on Thursday.

Some local governments have deployed trucks to parks, markets and bus stops to distribute chilled bottled waters for free.

In the southern city of Yangsan, where the mercury hit a historic high of 42.5C on Sunday, fleets of sprinkler trucks have been roaming the streets, spraying water onto sun-baked roads.

Meanwhile in rural areas such as North Gyeongsang province, local authorities are deploying drones attached with loudspeakers and thermal imaging cameras to protect its farmers, many of whom are also elderly.

The drones hover over the farmers, broadcasting warnings such as "it's hot, you need to go inside" to remind them to take breaks and cool down.

Most outdoor activities have been cancelled on the advice of the national weather agency. These include the daily changing-of-the-guard ceremony at Seoul's Gyeongbokgung Palace.

The national baseball organisation has also called off all scheduled games for the week.

These cancellations come after a 23-year-old spectator collapsed at a game in Incheon on Tuesday, reportedly due to dehydration and low blood pressure brought on by the heat.

Amid the scorching temperatures, South Korea's air-conditioned airports – including its largest in Incheon – have become a refuge for some vulnerable communities, including the homeless and the elderly.

Photographs on local media show people lying on benches and platforms, using towels as makeshift blankets.

One visitor sheltering in Seoul's Gimpo airport told The Korea Times it is a "perfect place to rest without spending any money".

"I come here from time to time with my friends whenever the weather gets too hot," he said.

Meanwhile a mobile app developed by an undergraduate to direct people to the shadiest walking paths has gained traction online, particularly among students.

Geuneulro, named after the Korean term for "shaded road", takes into account the positions of the sun and shadows cast by buildings and trees to recommend the most shaded routes through the city.

"This summer has become so hot that I feel like meat on the grill," the app's developer Yoo Min-jun told BBC Korean.

Yoo said he came up with the app after struggling with commuting in the heat. "The fact that it has resonated with so many people shows that many are struggling.

"That makes me worry because they say it will only get hotter in the future. I hope this prompts more to pay attention to climate change," the 23-year-old said.

Climate experts have said the extreme heat could ease starting this weekend, with daytime highs falling to around 36C, but the hot weather could continue.

Earlier this week, Seoul's meteorological administration forecast a 50% probability that temperatures in September and October could continue trending higher than average.

With reporting by Emily Choi and Kim Hyojung in Seoul

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqjx.title: South Korea space agency shares Moon images after SpaceX rocket debris crash
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqjx.text:
South Korea's space agency has released images that show the Moon after part of a SpaceX rocket crashed into its surface on Wednesday.

The Korean AeroSpace Administration (KASA) said lunar orbiter Danubri captured images after the impact, which it shared alongside photos of what the Moon's surface looked like before the crash.

Rocket debris struck the Moon at around 06:35 GMT on Wednesday, according to the South Korean space agency.

SpaceX has said the impact was not intentional.

Re-usable Falcon 9 rockets were designed to allow part of the rocket to return to Earth (the upper stage) and other sections to be shed in space. SpaceX has used this type of rocket on several missions.

The empty upper stage of this Falcon 9 rocket, which scientists predicted would hit the Moon at a speed of about 5,400mph (8,700km/h), is about the size of a five-storey building and weighs approximately 4,000kg (630st) on Earth.

The short, dramatic flash created when the rocket part hit the Moon would have been hard to catch by amateur astronomers even with high-end telescopes, but larger observatories - including Seoul's space agency - are analysing the information.

While the impact did not pose any danger to Earth, Matt Bothwell, astronomer at the University of Cambridge, raised concerns about space debris.

"Space is getting more and more crowded," he said, as each year "we launch more stuff into space".

"It could feasibly be within a few decades that it's actually quite hard to get past Earth's orbit because space is so crowded," Bothwell warned.

This Falcon 9 was in orbit since January last year, when it blasted off from Florida.

The same booster section from the January 2025 mission is due to set off on its 18th flight on 10 August. SpaceX says the mission hopes to launch 29 Starlink satellites to low-Earth orbit.

The rocket that blasted from Florida last January was carrying two lunar landers into space.

Its job was to fire the upper stage hard enough to send both of the landers out of Earth's orbit and onto a path towards the Moon.

The spent stage was left drifting in a long, looping orbit that swung out towards the Moon and back again.

Over the next 18 months, the gentle gravitational tug of the Earth, Moon and Sun, along with light from the Sun, gave it a faint push.

Astronomers tracking the rocket part eventually worked out that those small nudges had put it on a course towards the Moon, and it was picking up speed every day.

The impact on Wednesday happened in broad daylight for many parts of the world, but the tiny flash it produced would have been far too faint to see, even through a telescope.

The impact was not intentional, but the impact was caused by a SpaceX rocket part. The rocket was carrying two lunar landers into space last January.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8dn.text:
When Derrick Bowler and his wife moved to Trimingham on the Norfolk coast they thought they would leave the village "feet first" after being told they had 100 years before their "dream home" would be lost to the sea.

The couple moved to the village in 2011 with Bowler's wife hoping to replicate her fond memories of going to the beach every day when she lived in Cape Town, South Africa.

Over the past 20 years dozens of properties in the village have become uninhabitable in a battle of man versus nature with the most recent home demolished in May 2024.

"We've had to revise our opinions and our thoughts because of the coastal erosion, but it's not something we think about every day - you would go mad otherwise," he said.

Built in 1780, the Bowlers' home was sold to the couple as the "house of their dreams".

In recent years Bowler said North Norfolk District Council told them the property was expected to be a victim of coastal erosion in about 20 years' time.

When they first moved in, he said there was a 45-degree slope you could walk down to access the water's edge, however now, it looks as if "a giant has taken two big bites" out of the cliff.

He said: "In comparison to the inhabitants of Hemsby and Happisburgh, we are so lucky. We don't think about it too much."

However, the couple try to not worry about the threat of erosion for "peace of mind".

He said: "If we worry about that, we will never get a night's sleep. Let's just enjoy it while we can and when the time comes we'll have to find something else."

However he knows it is a fight that cannot be won, adding: "Even if I was to win the Euro Lottery, you still can't stop what's happening from happening.

"Everything has a lifespan. We might be able to pass it on to Liz's children but we'll just have to see."

Instead of fighting the erosion, villagers have introduced their own mitigating measures to give their properties and livelihoods a better chance against the inevitable.

Terry Brown moved to the village 17 years ago and bought his home knowing where it could end up.

Back then, the village hall was only expected to last up to 20 years so villagers set to build a new one.

While the cliff at the back of the hall has "barely receded", Brown said it was important to act before it was too late.

"We've got to make sure this village has a future and is able to roll back and continue to be," he said.

Despite Trimingham being a part of Norfolk Coast Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, Brown believed building social housing ready for homeowners who lose their properties to the sea would help future-proof the village.

He said: "Nobody knows how quickly it's going to go. You come here because you like what you've got. You like the surroundings, you like being able to get on the beach, you like the people that live around you.

"You've got to be on your toes. We've had little movement through this part of the village but you could wake up tomorrow morning and suddenly you're faced with something quite dramatic."

Alex Ponting, the operation manager for the MacKenzie Hotel Group, said it would be "foolish" to build anything in the village.

Two years ago, five mobile sea view lodges were built on the grounds of the Sea Marge Hotel at Overstrand, near Cromer.

Ponting said: "We have done this purposefully as we are concerned about coastal erosion.

"These five lodges were built off site and transported… if you take down the wooden cladding you can unbolt them and they are reusable somewhere else."

He said in the 30 years the hotel has been there, the threat of coastal erosion has been constant.

"We are very lucky here that there has been very little degradation of our coastal point but to the right and to the left of us there has been some erosion so we had no choice," he said.

Along the coast £1m is being spent on reinforcing the sea wall at Overstrand in the hope of giving the village's properties another 30 to 40 years.

Harry Blathwayt, portfolio holder for coast at North Norfolk District Council, said: "Overstrand is a remarkably vibrant and economically viable community so we can actually say, 'we need to expend this money' because this is what we are protecting.

Blathwayt said the sea level has been rising more rapidly than predicted about 50 years ago, however the strategy is to put infrastructure in place now to make sure homeowners were prepared for the eventuality.

He said: "I would say there should be a level of concern. Everyone should know the risks they face, but there isn't anything to stay awake about at night.

"[Residents] can thrive. It's not a survival issue, it's how we best thrive and how North Norfolk District Council can support people thriving in this community."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c89n.title: Waste company owner is a 'woman in a man's world'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c89n.text:
The owner of a waste collection company that distributes reusable items to deserving causes said she was "a woman in a man's world".

Sandra McCluskey, who lives in Bedfordshire but operates in the Milton Keynes area, said she had been "warned" about getting involved in the industry but wanted to reduce the amount of waste sent to landfill or left by the roadside.

She first tried to make a waste clearance business work a few years ago, but the Covid pandemic made it difficult. Once the masks had been packed away and the crisis was over, she set about creating "The Firm".

"I've been warned a couple of times that it's definitely a man's world and I shouldn't be involved," she said.

"Just because I'm a woman, it doesn't mean that I can't do the job efficiently," she added.

Across the country, only 19% of the waste management workforce is female, according to data from the Chartered Institute of Wastes Management.

McCluskey's own life experiences have, she believes, contributed to her desire to help vulnerable people by passing on useful waste: "I was homeless myself, I've suffered hardship, I've been on benefits, I've lost my son, I'm a single parent now and I've seen things.

"I could see how things could help people - mattresses for single mums, or dishwashers or washing machines, clothes for the homeless, bottled water from event clearances."

There have been hurdles along the way, and she said bricks were thrown through a window at her house after she "made a strong stand" against a company she believed did not have the correct licences to operate.

She continued: "As registered waste carriers, we're being undercut by unlicensed people who aren't being responsible about where the waste goes, and that's why there's so much fly-tipping."

Milton Keynes has seen fly-tipping fall by more than a quarter over the past five years, but the city council believes "there is much more to do".

"Being a woman, I do have that bit of emotional attachment as well to the fact that I would like to see greener spaces and stronger communities."

She feels that responsible carriers often get "tarred with the same brush" as unauthorised companies, even though she is paying out for licences, insurances and tip fees.

For McCluskey, the reward comes in the face of those who receive items that someone else has thrown away.

"If you can see a child of maybe five who's never had a scooter in their life, and I've managed to give that child a scooter through a donation I picked up in a tonne bag, and it hasn't ended up on the side of the road, and it's made someone really happy, I believe that's a really good thing to do," she said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czrj.title: Couple turning inherited farm into nature site
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czrj.text:
A couple who inherited an 80-acre (32-hectare) farm are turning it into a wildlife restoration project in a bid to preserve its future.

Jessie Roper's father Jim Parkin ran Greenbank Farm near Cockermouth, in Cumbria, but despite growing up there, she had little farming experience and left for university in Manchester about 12 years ago.

But when her dad died suddenly in 2023, the 32-year-old said she "couldn't really face anyone else having it" so decided to move back to take over operations with her husband Joe Roper.

The 33-year-old said he had never been on a farm before but believed the project would have had his late father-in-law's approval.

"It was quite hard work, adjusting to life on the farm, we also had the worst winter that year when we moved back, I don't think it stopped raining for about four months," Joe said.

During that winter, the farmhouse's cellar flooded, the pipes froze and "the tractor just decided to go kaput".

"It was like, 'oh god, what have we done?'"

Jessie said her dad was across the running of the farm "and then suddenly he's gone".

"It's not as if he gave a handover," she added.

Greenbank had produced dairy and beef in its past, she said.

Before Jessie's dad died, he was renting fields out to a local shepherd, which is still bringing in income now.

"I couldn't really face anyone else having it, so selling it was out of the question," Jessie said.

"We just kind of thought if we went back, if we had turned into full-time traditional farmers, it just wasn't really for us."

Through their research, Jessie and Joe came across biodiversity organisation Environment Bank which is helping the couple transform the land.

The 30-year nature recovery project will see grazing animals used to help restore habitats.

Senior land manager at Environment Bank Anne Gray said: "Traditional summer hay cuts and cattle grazing will be the long-term management mechanism for the site.

"Nature recovery projects like this are important because the UK has experienced significant biodiversity loss over many decades.

"For many, it provides a secure, diversified source of income that allows them to invest in the long-term future of their land, while continuing to play an important role in managing the countryside, supporting wider environmental outcomes, and supporting the rural economy."

The financial security was a major factor for Jessie and Joe in their decision.

Environment Bank gives Greenbank Farm lease payments as well as paying the couple to help manage the land through the livestock grazing and hay cutting.

"One of the main things for us is that it's 30 years of guaranteed income," Jessie said.

"With farming, you just never know what's going to happen.

"If we solely rely on producing haylage, we could have a really bad year of rain like we did a few years ago - we produced rubbish haylage to be honest so we didn't really make that much in terms of profit.

"It's like a diversification project for us."

Similar projects have faced opposition in the past and Jessie admits other farmers in the area were sceptical.

"We're like the guinea pig of the area," she said.

But Joe said he thought his late father-in-law would have been on board with the plan.

"Jim really loved nature," Joe said.

"So it's kind of like a bit of a nod to him as well, like it's nice to do something with the land that he would approve of."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1d1.title: Monkey sanctuary shuts after more than 60 years
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1d1.text:
A monkey sanctuary has closed after more than 60 years after plans for a buyer fell through.

Wild Futures said on its social media and website the park, near Looe, in Cornwall, had started to develop "structural issues" which made it unfit for purpose and no longer suitable as a long-term sanctuary.

The charity, which was established in 1964, said it had already started the process of rehoming monkeys to selected sanctuaries and organisations, and that their welfare remained its "top priority".

Wild Futures said it thought it had found a buyer to help improve the the site after it was put on the market in June 2025. However, after six months of negotiations, plans had fallen through, it said.

"We do not believe it would be responsible to invest hundreds of thousands of pounds into a site that is no longer suitable for the sanctuary's long-term future, and whose ongoing maintenance now far surpasses the financial resources we have available to us," said Sarah Hanson, the charity's director.

"As such, we have made the difficult decision to direct funds towards securing a safe future for the monkeys."

The charity said an emergency appeal would be launched to help cover the "significant costs" of safely rehoming every monkey.

In March 2025, it announced it would close to the public for the rest of the year because of financial struggles.

Wild Futures said the sanctuary began when it started rescuing woolly monkeys from the pet trade.

"We are proud that we were the first Global Federation of Animal Sanctuaries accredited wildlife sanctuary in Europe, and we educated hundreds of thousands of visitors on animal welfare, conservation, and the need for a ban," it said.

"While we feel deep sadness at the closure of the sanctuary, we are filled with hope for the future and the next chapter of Wild Futures, as there is still important work to be done."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c1e1v0.title: 1999: Solar eclipse experienced from Alderney
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c1e1v0.text:
Archive footage from 1999 looking back at the total eclipse of the sun from Alderney.

Hundreds of astronomers were among those who travelled to Alderney in the Channel Islands to view the eclipse on 11 August 1999.

Cloud cover meant it was not the perfect spectacle, but many viewers said the cloud cover made watching easier.

The next eclipse to be viewed from the Channel Islands will be a partial solar eclipse when about 94% of the sun will be covered by the moon and will peak at 19:17 BST on Wednesday 12 August.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd69.title: What it's like to chase solar eclipses around the world
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd69.text:
On Wednesday, parts of Europe will be plunged into daytime darkness as the moon passes in front of the sun, temporarily blocking its light and casting a shadow across the continent.

For many of us, it will be a once-in-a-lifetime experience. But for some, following eclipses has become something of an addiction.

Armed with two high-spec cameras, a specialist telescope and a drone, Mark Griffiths has spent two days driving from Cheshire to Galicia - one of the best places to view the eclipse - to record the event.

It's a hobby that started six years ago, when he went to Shetland to see the northern lights - though the weather was so dreary he "didn't see anything".

But it didn't put him off and he soon found he couldn't stop. He loved the thrill of witnessing and capturing the sky's most spectacular events.

He's since filmed the northern lights numerous times - he goes to Iceland once a month and leads tour groups there - and has photographed various auroras, eclipses and bioluminescence.

But this is his first total solar eclipse.

"I kept wanting more," he says, and Europe's first total solar eclipse for more than 25 years is "like what the World Cup is to football" for enthusiasts like him.

"I'll be honest, it's like an addiction now," he tells me.

I'm speaking to him the day after he's finished his marathon drive from England, across France and into Spain. He only paused to take photos of the night sky and rest for a few hours in Bordeaux. "I'm quite sleep deprived."

The path of total eclipse begins at the tip of Siberia before curving round the Arctic Ocean and crossing parts of Greenland and Iceland.

It then proceeds across a stretch of the northern Atlantic Ocean before reaching northern Spain and finishing in the Mediterranean. Other parts of Europe will see a partial eclipse.

The total eclipse is only expected to last a couple of minutes for people who watch it, but that doesn't deter eclipse hunters from crossing continents to witness it.

Samantha Phillips-Brown and her husband Gregory have flown to Iceland and hired a camper van so they can drive to a remote area to see it.

This will be the second solar eclipse they've witnessed.

It was the awe-inspiring power of the first one they saw, near their home in upstate New York in 2023, that convinced them to travel for this one. They booked their flights and van more than a year ago.

"It was such a phenomenal experience to see the Sun start going dark and hear, suddenly, the birds stop chirping," recalls Samantha. "It's just a very strange experience."

Gregory thinks of how Iceland's first settlers must have felt witnessing such a phenomena more than a millennium ago, a time of mythological rather than scientific explanation.

"They really didn't know what was happening, didn't know how long it was going to last... it must have been quite terrifying for them, in a way."

They are spending the days before the eclipse driving round eastern parts of Iceland to go hiking and camping.

The path of totality crosses the western part of Iceland and they hope to find a spot in the Westfjords peninsula to witness it.

Although they've heard rumours of roads being closed to stop too many people overwhelming the area, so are keen to get there a couple of days before the spectacle.

Samantha, who her husband describes as an "obsessive travel planner", is all over the Facebook groups and social media pages being used by eclipse hunters to share information and advice.

She's expecting a good turnout given the number of eclipse glasses she's seen people with in Iceland. "They're really trying to prepare everybody," she says.

"What I expect, as we start inching westward, is we're going to see more and more of them."

Andrew Wills is also going to an island to see the eclipse, albeit a much warmer one: Majorca.

He's travelling with his wife and his dad, who is 90. Father and son witnessed Europe's last total solar eclipse together in 1999 while stood atop St Agnes Beacon in Cornwall.

The landmark, believed by some to be a Bronze Age bowl barrow, offers panoramic views across the Cornish countryside and out to the Atlantic. It was a cloudy day, remembers Andrew.

"We didn't see the shadow rushing across the sea towards us, though we did see the dawn appearing and it getting closer very quickly," he says. "It was awe-inspiring."

He has high hopes for a clearer day in Majorca where he has booked a villa near the town of Andraitx, located in the west of the island.

Andrew has earmarked a spot nearby he hopes will give a good view across the sea. Their location in the path of totality means the eclipse will likely happen low on the horizon.

"We're going to take a couple of camping chairs with us, so Dad can sit if we can get there an hour or so before."

The islands of Majorca and Menorca will be the last places on land to view the eclipse before the Sun sets and the shadow disappears.

Eclipses have fascinated Andrew ever since he saw his first in St Agnes all those years ago.

"We live on a planet where we have this amazing coincidence. Where the Sun is 400 times bigger than the moon but the moon is 400 times closer.

"And so when the moon passes in front of the Sun and between Earth, it casts this perfect shadow."

It made him appreciate the delicacy of life on our planet in the way astronomer Carl Sagan once did when speaking of the Pale Blue Dot photograph.

"We are tiny little specks in a huge vast area of nothingness," says Andrew. "We're amazingly lucky to be alive."

The moon will temporarily block the sun and cast a shadow across the continent. The path of totality begins at the tip of Siberia before curving round the Arctic Ocean and crossing parts of Greenland and Iceland.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c86n.title: What can we see during the partial solar eclipse?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c86n.text:
A partial solar eclipse is set to be visible across the South West and Channel Islands on Wednesday evening.

The entire event is set to last about one hour and 50 minutes, starting at about 18:20 BST and finishing by 20:10.

But what is a solar eclipse and just what is expected to happen?

The cosmic event requires the sun, the moon and the earth to be in a perfect alignment.

When this happens, the moon casts two types of shadows.

The team at the National Space Centre said the main event of this year's total solar eclipse will be visible in a giant arc moving across from northern Russia to Greenland, Iceland, Spain and northern Portugal.

They said although the "arc of totality - the path the eclipse shadow takes - misses us here in the UK, we will still get to see over 90% of the sun covered by the moon".

The next full solar eclipse in the UK is due to take place in 64 years, on 23 September 2090.

Guernsey-based Dr Jean Dean, fellow of the Royal Astronomical Society, said nature would alter its behaviour as the eclipse progresses.

She said: "First contact is when the edge of the moon touches the edge of the sun and after first contact, you will very quickly see the moon start to bite the sun.

"A little while after this, you should start to notice a slight change in temperature and the sky starting to darken.

"As the maximum approaches, nature will begin to respond. Birds will fall silent and nyctinastic plants (plants that open their leaves during the day and close them at night) such as clovers, dandelions and daises will close.

"Nature will then return to normal, the sky will lighten and the temperature will rise slightly."

Plymouth Astronomical Society chairman Chris Cooke said the darkness brought by the eclipse would be "eerie".

He said: "I've been chasing eclipses as long as I can really, as much as my wife would allow me to do.

"All my holidays are eclipse chasing holidays.

"So what's coming up in August is not a total eclipse from the UK, it's a partial, but this partial is where the the moon will block out the sun almost fully, but not quite.

"It's the darkest partial solar eclipse since 1999 and things will get a bit eerie."

People watching the eclipse have been urged to avoid looking directly at the sun without the right protection.

Following the 1999 total solar eclipse, the Royal College of Ophthalmologists reported about 70 cases of people experiencing vision problems after watching the eclipse.

The college said about 40% of those people had looked at it for less than a minute.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has issued a warning and said the sun would appear dimmer than usual, which would make it easier to look at directly, which result in damage to eyesight.

The agency recommended the use of eclipse glasses and handheld solar viewers, providing they were genuine models.

The UKHSA also suggested alternatives such as a pinhole viewer, watching the sun's image projected through a colander or the gaps between tree leaves, or projecting the sun's image onto a sheet of paper using a simple pinhole projector.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c980.title: What you need to know about the solar eclipse over Yorkshire
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c980.text:
People across Yorkshire and the UK have a chance to witness the most dramatic solar eclipse in nearly three decades on 12 August.

Up to 95% of the sun will slowly disappear behind the moon between 18:00 and 20:15 BST - the first time such coverage has been seen since 1999's total eclipse.

While there will be smaller solar eclipses in the coming years, including one next August, the next total eclipse will not take place until 23 September 2090.

Weather permitting, astronomers say the natural spectacle promises to be a "very, very special" event - so, here's what you need to know about how and where to safely watch it unfold.

According to Neil Sanders, astronomer at Go Stargazing and co-founder of UK Eclipse, the event on Wednesday is an unmissable occasion.

"These aren't rare events, but they are uncommon," he said.

"They happen almost yearly. But what's very, very special about this one is the amount of coverage."

The path of the eclipse shadow means this year the UK won't see a total eclipse, but in Yorkshire and the North-East the sun will be about 92% obscured, he explained.

"What's really cool about it is that, certainly when you're using eclipse glasses, you can actually see the movement that's happening in our solar system.

"You are looking at the movement of the moon as it goes around the earth. It's one of these very rare events when you can see the solar system in action."

Other countries, such as parts of Spain and Portugal, will enjoy the spectacle of a total eclipse this year.

Chris Higgins, a retired scientist and volunteer at Lime Tree Observatory and Planetarium in Grewelthorpe, North Yorkshire, added it is still "certainly worth" seeing it from the UK.

"It's quite significant. It's not the greatest prize, a total eclipse, but it is a partial eclipse of almost nine-tenths of the sun's disk," he said.

"It's a natural phenomenon that will have been witnessed by humanity forever, so it's something that will inspire people."

It is very important to enjoy the eclipse safely to avoid damaging your eyes.

You must never look at the sun directly with the naked eye, Sanders explained, and follow proper guidance for safely viewing the eclipse.

Eclipse glasses offer protection - legitimate pairs will have safety certification 'ISO 12312-2' or 'ISO 12312-2:2015' printed somewhere on the glasses, according to The Royal Observatory Greenwich.

Regular sunglasses do not provide adequate protection as "they don't block out the harmful rays of sunlight" - with this eclipse, 8% of the sun's surface will still be visible, Sanders said.

Alternative methods for safely viewing the eclipse include, using a solar telescope, which are being offered to look through as part of local astronomical society viewing events, or making a pinhole projector, which projects an indirect image of the sun onto a surface through a tiny hole.

Household objects with small holes, such as a colander, can be used to make the projector, Higgins added.

The Royal Observatory in Greenwich are also live streaming the event so people can watch from the comfort of their own home.

The best way to view the eclipse is at an elevated location with a clear view to the west, because the sun and moon will be dipping to the horizon ahead of sunset.

The sun will be very low in the western sky, which could be a bit of an issue for Yorkshire, Higgins said.

"If we were a west coast county, we could all go to the beach and then we'd have a nice low horizon and we could watch it," he said.

"So you need to find a vantage point where your horizon looking west is clear of any obstructions such as trees."

According to BBC climate correspondent Paul Hudson, the moon should begin blocking the sun between approximately 18:12 and 18:19 BST.

The peak of the eclipse will occur about an hour later, with the whole event ending just after 20:00, before the sun finally sets.

Don't panic if it seems as though nothing is happening straight away, Higgins added, and even cloudy weather doesn't spell disaster.

"It's not suddenly going to whiz past and you'll miss it. It's worth waiting around just in case the clouds move on."

There are a number of community events happening across Yorkshire to mark the occasion:

Yorkshire has experienced plenty of warm, clear nights for many weeks now - perfect for stargazing - or eclipse-spotting.

It looks like 12 August is shaping up to follow that trend, according to Hudson.

"At the moment, the forecast for Wednesday couldn't be better," he said.

"It will be a hot day with plenty of sunshine, although as the event begins there may be some high cloud towards the western horizon where the eclipse will take place."

However, this is unlikely to be thick enough to obscure the sun, he added.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq6d.title: All of England's rivers and lakes polluted with chemicals, officials say
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq6d.text:
England's rivers, lakes and coastal waters remain in a challenging state with only around one in seven classed as being in good ecological condition, according to the first comprehensive assessment of their health in six years.

And no single waterway passed a separate test by the regulator for chemical pollution.

The Environment Agency (EA) said this is because legacy substances, such as heavy metals, and so-called 'forever chemicals', are building up.

Its chair acknowledged the country's waterways were "below standards" but said it was increasing enforcement action to tackle other issues like sewage spills.

Data from the EA shows that while 15% of rivers are classed as good, fewer than 7% of lakes reached that level.

The biggest individual problem is phosphate - a nutrient from sewage and farm runoff - with around half of rivers still exceeding safe levels.

Despite a record £22bn earmarked for water company environmental improvements by 2030, the overall picture has changed little since 2019.

The government is on course to miss its legally binding target of restoring 77% of England's waters to good ecological status by 2027 - a goal the environmental watchdog, the Office for Environmental Protection, has warned will be missed by a "considerable margin".

It's now investigating both the government and the Environment Agency over possible rule breaches.

Environment Secretary Angela Eagle said the figures "underline the need for wholesale change across the water sector".

She pointed to new laws the government has introduced to hold water companies to account and record investment. "We will drive forward a system that puts the public interest first," she said.

Water UK, which represents the water companies, said it was spending record amounts of money on improving the country's waterways.

"Water companies are investing £22bn in environmental improvements by 2030. This will help to secure our water supplies, support economic growth and end sewage entering our rivers and seas."

Other types of pollution affecting England's water bodies include petrol, garden pesticides and contaminated water running off roads picking up microplastics and chemicals.

The regulator said some chemicals are challenging to tackle as they do not easily break down, and begin to accumulate.

But Prof Penny Johnes, a leading water quality scientist at the University of Bristol, told the BBC it was also a "failure to regulate effectively" the new chemicals entering rivers.

She pointed to 'forever chemicals' known as PFAS and antibiotics, many of which are not routinely monitored.

There are currently 23 enforcement notices against water companies requiring them to lower the levels of PFAS to reduce the danger to human health.

Water UK has called for PFAS use to be banned to limit their build-up and reduce water treatment costs, but the chemicals are currently used in thousands of products, from school uniforms to medical devices.

The Environment Agency stressed that this year's data could not be directly compared with 2019 because it had changed its methods.

In particular, it said the steep fall in the number of lakes ranked as good - down about half from 2019 - largely reflected a change in how its experts now assess them, rather than a genuine decline in their condition.

Its chair, Alan Lovell, has acknowledged that too many water bodies were "still not achieving the standards we want to see", adding that the agency was "transforming our enforcement work" with its largest ever workforce.

But Prof Johnes said the true picture was almost certainly worse than the classifications suggested.

The scheme was "not fit for purpose", she said, measuring too few pollutants too infrequently, and missing nitrogen and other substances scientists have long understood to be driving rivers' decline.

The findings come as much of England sits in official drought, with rivers running low and more than 20 million people facing hosepipe bans.

Lower flows can concentrate the very pollution the new data is designed to track, leaving fish and other aquatic life exposed to more dangerous levels.

Climate change is expected to bring drier and hotter summers which could further exacerbate this issue.

Asked directly whether England's waters were healthier than six or seven years ago, Prof Johnes said: "No, definitely not."

Much of the debate about the state of England's waters has centred on water companies and the sewage they release into rivers.

But campaigners and scientists also point to agriculture as an equally large source of pollution - one that attracts far less public attention.

Erica Popplewell, of the campaign group River Action, said some farming, particularly intensive poultry units - vast sheds housing hundreds of thousands of birds - were a growing threat to rivers such as the Wye and Severn.

"There's a lot of poo that comes out of the chickens," she said. "If it goes straight into a river, it causes eutrophication. The whole ecology of the river is damaged, and the river is dying." She called on the government to tackle sewage and farming "with the same urgency".

The National Farmers' Union of England and Wales urged the government and the Environment Agency to prioritise working with farmers with targeted investment.

"These results demonstrate the need for continued action from every sector across the water supply chain, and farming is no exception, but the underlying indicators do show that the health of many waterways in England is encouraging, which is a positive foundation to build on," NFU deputy president Paul Tomkins said in a statement.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c78g.title: Rhine falls to record low levels as drought strains Europe's rivers
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c78g.text:
The River Rhine has fallen to record low levels in several locations in Germany and the Netherlands as prolonged heatwaves continue across Europe.

Last week, levels were measured in Cologne in western Germany and in Lobith, where the Rhine crosses from Germany into the Netherlands, that were lower than at any point since records began.

Other major European rivers with important transport, industrial and agricultural functions have also seen record low levels, including the Danube, which flows through 10 countries, and Italy's Po river.

Drought conditions remained stable and critical in most of Europe and worsened in central-western Europe in mid-July, according to the EU's Drought Observatories.

Renewed heatwave conditions are due to continue for at least another week, pushing temperatures above 40C in many central and southern European countries.

Germany's Low Water Information System (NIWIS) said that 44% of the Rhine measuring stations and 78% of those on the Danube had recorded extremely low water levels at the end of July.

The Rhine - which starts in the Swiss Alps and empties in the North Sea - is one of Europe's busiest waterways. Decreasing water levels have sparked concerns about the economic fallout of having to limit navigation and shipping.

On Friday, the navigable water depth at the chokepoint of Kaub near Koblenz hit the 2018 record low of 25cm, before recovering slightly on Monday.

The Kaub gauging station in western Germany is a key indicator of navigability on the Rhine because it measures how heavily cargo vessels can be loaded. Low water levels measured there can severely restrict inland shipping.

Martin Wolters of the Rhine Waterways and Shipping Authority told German outlet WDR that although shipping on the Rhine was unlikely to be suspended altogether, precautions would have to be taken, such as spreading out cargo among more vessels to make them less heavy.

In time, this can result in higher transport costs and supply bottlenecks, Wolters said.

"There comes a time when loads are too small to be worthwhile or vessel owners are worried about damaging their ships," one commodity trader told Reuters.

Last week, the waters of the Danube fell to the lowest levels for 30 years in several countries, including Serbia and Romania, leaving Hungary's only nuclear power plant on the brink of shutting down.

The facility is operating at a reduced capacity and officials are monitoring whether it may need to be taken offline completely.

The drought of the Danube is also causing serious disruption to power supplies in Serbia and Romania.

Serbia cut output at its coal-fired power plants due to the lack of water disrupting cooling systems, while Romania carried out a controlled explosion on a large rock on the banks of the Danube to increase waterflow to the Cernavoda nuclear power plant.

Two car plants in Romania run by Dacia and Ford have agreed to halt production for more than a fortnight to reduce electricity consumption.

Italy's longest river, the Po, hit a historic low near the northern city of Cremona in late July. Authorities raised the drought alert level to "high" across the entire Po Valley, while experts have issued warnings about potential disruption to the drinking water supply.

Lower river flows at the mouth of the Po have also pushed saltwater from the sea into the riverbed, disrupting the ecosystem and causing serious issues for farmers who use water from the Po to irrigate their crops.

A recent study by scientists at the World Weather Attribution group found that there had been no clear long-term trend towards lower rainfall across much of Europe.

But the researchers said that human-caused climate change was increasing evaporation of moisture through higher temperatures, making drought conditions more likely.

The hot, dry weather also increased the demand for water for household, agricultural and industrial use.

Prolonged periods of drought can also affect the water levels of lakes, impacting availability of freshwater resources.

The EU's Copernicus climate service said the 2022 drought in Europe contributed to increased wildfire activity - which in turn drove higher than average carbon emissions.

Additional reporting by Mark Poynting

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr7k.title: Italy putting nearly all major cities on highest heat alert
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr7k.text:
Italy is putting nearly all of its major cities on the highest "red" alert for high temperatures, as a new heatwave grips the country.

Health officials say 19 cities from north to south - including the capital Rome, Milan, Venice and Naples - are already at red alert, and by Monday all but two cities will be.

Temperatures hit mid-30s C in many places on Saturday, and authorities are warning of risks to even healthy and active people - not just groups including the elderly, very young children and people with chronic illnesses.

The warnings come as several European nations battle devastating wildfires after a succession of heatwaves that have created favourable conditions for blazes.

In its latest heatwave bulletin published on Saturday, the Italian health ministry says that by Monday, some 25 of the country's 27 major cities will be on red alert.

It says it expects only two - Reggio Calabria in the southern tip of Italy's "boot" and Messina, facing it across on the island of Sicily - to be on the second-highest "amber" alert.

The ministry urges residents in the affected areas to avoid exposure to heat and direct sunlight during the hottest hours between 11:00 and 18:00, stay indoors and drink plenty of fluids.

The extreme heat is being caused by a subtropical anticyclone from North Africa that is now strengthening over the Mediterranean.

Meanwhile, firefighters in Greece, France, Portugal and Spain are still tackling blazes spanning thousands of hectares.

In France, some 2,500 people were evacuated in the south-eastern Var region on Friday evening after a blaze - which had been contained for several days - reignited, local officials said.

But a massive fire in the south-western Gironde region is now under control, and some 200,000 local evacuated residents have been able to return to their homes.

In Greece, hundreds of people - mostly tourists - have been evacuated by sea from a coastal town of Viotia hemmed in by one of the many wildfires raging across the country.

And in Spain, more than 200,000 hectares of land has burnt in 2026 - roughly five times above the average by this point in the year - while the burnt land in Portugal is also higher than usual, EU data shows.

Climate change is driving up temperatures around the world, and Europe is the fastest warming continent, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service.

This is causing increased summer heatwaves, greater pressure on Europe's water supply, and more intense wildfires.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdep.title: First dinosaur bone from Antarctica found in a drawer
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdep.text:
An unassuming-looking fossil that spent 40 years lying forgotten in a drawer has turned out to be the first dinosaur bone ever found in Antarctica.

The specimen was unearthed in 1985, but the team that discovered it was not sure what it was - so it was stored away in the geology collection of the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) in Cambridge.

Now the fossil has been studied by palaeontologists who have confirmed that it is a tail bone from a type of dinosaur called a Titanosaur - this group contained the largest dinosaurs to ever walk the Earth.

The discovery helps to reveal more about how these beasts lived in a part of the world where the fossil record is sparse.

Dr Mark Evans, the collections manager at BAS, recently spotted the fossil amongst thousands of specimens brought back from expeditions to Antarctica over the decades.

"It's only when you start thinking 'what's in this drawer', that sometimes you come across something and you think, 'Ah, this looks interesting'," he said.

The specimen was originally collected on James Ross Island and its discovery was recorded in a field notebook kept by geologist Dr Mike Thomson.

Alongside a tiny, neat sketch of the fossil dated 9 December 1985 he has written "vertebra of large reptile", noting it was about 10cm wide.

Evans says the team that found it probably thought the fossil belonged to a marine reptile.

But as soon as he saw it, Evans realised the vertebra looked very dinosaur-like. And the date of its discovery meant it would have been the first dinosaur fossil found on the continent.

He called in Prof Paul Barrett from the Natural History Museum (NHM) to confirm his discovery.

"Although it's not too much to look at, it actually has a really distinctive shape," Barrett told us, holding the fossil in his hands.

He pointed to a hollow on one end of the fossil and then turned it over to reveal a rounded bump at the other. The vertebrae line up to create a series of ball-and-socket joints running from head to tail.

"As soon as I saw it, I knew what we were dealing with… it was a dead cert we were dealing with a Titanosaur," he said. "This is a combination of features that's completely unique to these types of dinosaurs."

More than 100 species of Titanosaur have now been identified around the world.

All are four-legged plant eaters, with very long necks that helped them reach up into trees and long counter-balancing tails. The very biggest Titanosaurs were more than 115ft (35m) long and weighed about 60 tonnes.

From the size of this tail bone, the scientists estimate the Antarctic Titanosaur was about 23ft (7m) in length.

"Maybe it was a juvenile dinosaur, or maybe it was a genuinely small one - one that was actually bucking the trend for the rest of the group as a smaller adult," explained Barrett.

This dinosaur would have lived 82 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous Period when Antarctica was very different from how it is today. It would have been covered in lush forest, providing ample food for the plant-eating beast.

The long-forgotten fossil now holds an important place in the history of exploration in Antarctica. Other dinosaur fossils have been found in this remote part of the world in the years after 1985 - but not very many.

Antarctica is a challenging place for palaeontologists to work and the ice conceals the prehistoric record in the rock beneath.

"It shows that an area that we now think is really uninhabitable was once actually very habitable and had this huge cast of characters living on it," explained Barrett.

"It's helping us to work out how they fitted into these broader ecosystems at the very bottom of the world about 80 million years ago."

A paper on the discovery has been published in the journal Acta Palaeontologica Polonica.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy5d.title: How the UK's extreme heat is shifting the conversation about air-con
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy5d.text:
Mandy Bourne lives with her 80-year-old mum in a top-floor social housing flat in the West Midlands. Both struggle with health conditions exacerbated by the recent heatwaves.

For Mandy, temperature shifts can trigger flare-ups of her chronic lung condition. "I've got COPD and sometimes I can't breathe," she explains.

Across the UK, solid brick homes like theirs quietly absorb heat the way they have for decades. Charged-up walls radiate warmth back into rooms that never get the chance to cool.

Mandy says she is constantly reaching for her inhaler as her flat overheats. "It's red hot in the flat. The sun is just beaming in."

That retained warmth can push night-time temperatures in urban centres up to 7C higher than the surrounding countryside. This is the urban heat island effect and it is at its most dangerous in the early hours when bodies need cooler air and cannot find it. Modelling of a previous West Midlands heatwave by researchers from the University of Birmingham reached the bleak conclusion that the heat island impact alone accounted for roughly half the 130 heat-related deaths.

Jo Shields, head of sustainability for Mandy's housing association Walsall Housing Group, known as whg - which owns 23,000 homes across Walsall and the Midlands - hears the same complaint time and again. "The heat gain stays within the concrete or the brick," she says, "so the night-time cooling becomes harder".

Last summer, as the region baked, the residents of Ellum Pointe - a whg scheme for the over-55s - began telling their landlords they simply could not cool their flats. The response was improvised.

"We took the community room, closed all the windows and doors, and we put a mobile air-conditioning unit in there," Shields says. "And basically, we created an internal cool room." She likens it to the warm spaces opened during the pandemic for people who couldn't afford to heat their homes.

Shields' job has previously focused on decarbonising - reducing the emissions from the housing stock - but she now has to balance those pressures with the need to adapt homes to rising heat. Across the country, landlords are facing similar choices.

As Britain enters a new kind of summer, with homes built to trap warmth and heatwaves intensifying, two questions loom: should we embrace air conditioning despite its costs and consequences, and how much should we spend on adapting homes versus cutting carbon?

For 40 years, wealthy countries have focused heavily on cutting the carbon emissions that cause climate change, known as mitigation. Adaptation such as designing housing so it is more resilient to hotter temperatures and installing air conditioning has not always had the same focus.

Reducing emissions was seen as morally right because richer nations produced most of the gases that have warmed the planet. And with that focus came a funding imbalance.

In 2023, $1.8tn was given to mitigation, while adaptation did not secure even 5% of that – it scraped $65bn globally.

Spending too much on adaption was seen by many as giving up on the fight against climate change. But this mainstream view has now been challenged.

In a memo published last year, Bill Gates - a man who has poured billions into clean technology - argued that the climate movement's "doomsday" fixation on temperature targets had diverted money from the things that most improve lives in a warming world.

Climate change is serious, he wrote, but "will not lead to humanity's demise". Governments, he added, should be investing in cooling for the countries that need it.

The publication sparked backlash from climate scientists who accused Gates of making arguments based on "false dichotomies" - pitting mitigation and adaptation against each other.

Some, including US President Donald Trump, saw it as sign that the billionaire was "finally" supporting the belief that climate change was a hoax.

Gates insisted he was not arguing against cutting emissions, but rather for spending money where it saves the most suffering.

The row that followed exposed the real fault line that's coming to the surface this summer: not whether to cut carbon or adapt to the heat – but how much to spend on each.

There's another reason that muddies the waters and helps explain why cutting carbon became the prime focus – it was investable. Heat pumps and EVs can be sold. Spending on shade, ventilation and cooler hospitals and homes all produce little in the way of bankable returns - even if it reduces costs of climate change long term.

Baroness Brown - also known as the engineer Julia King, who chairs the adaptation committee of the government's Climate Change Committee - argues this imbalance is written into UK law.

Under the Climate Change Act, the mitigation half of her committee recommends legally binding carbon budgets that ministers must deliver and are marked on every year.

Adaptation has no such teeth: the government writes its own risk assessment and its own plans.

"Essentially, the government writes an essay, and our job is to say, is it doing the things it said would do in its essay. It's not actually to say, are these things any good."

Her committee has spent, she says, "almost 20 years pulling our hair out" - but this year has been different. With exquisite timing it produced a report just as the first heatwave was striking Britain in May - urging lawmakers to set hard adaptation targets.

"We've actually looked at the difference that providing some sort of support with cooling for the 30% of most vulnerable homes, and cooling in our hospitals, [with] preventive care visits. The modelling we've done suggests that that would reduce 40% of the increase in heat-related deaths that are predicted for 2050."

"We're saying these are the actions that can make a big difference."

One of the most controversial ideas in the report is on air conditioning. Right now, only 5% or so of English homes have a cooling unit. The Committee recommends fitting these devices in hospitals and care homes within 10 years, and schools in 25 years.

This goes against years of government advice that passive cooling was the preferred method - using shade, ventilation and other design features to bring down temperatures, not mechanical means.

Prof Mat Santamouris from the University of New South Wales, is the world's most-cited researcher on urban overheating.

Machines, he argues, should be the last line of defence: reflective roofing alone, in one of his studies, dragged indoor temperatures from around 43C towards 30C, while a ceiling fan gives comfort for a fraction of the cost.

Putting up unshaded glass towers in cities, he says, is "crazy". "We cannot air-condition our way out of climate change."

Santamouris is scathing about who is driving the air con demand - the industry, he says, is "extremely powerful" – adding that passive cooling adds its own economic growth, as money is spent on plumbers and builders.

Against him stand those who think Britain's hostility to cooling has curdled into a type of masochism.

David Lawrence, of the Centre for British Progress think tank, puts it plainly: we don't tell people to insulate their homes in winter and then skip the radiators. So why insist shade and shutters are enough in summer?

He points out that air conditioning is standard now in offices, hotels and shops, "but we don't expect it for schools and hospitals - which is kind of odd, because those are places where millions of people are every day", and where heat measurably dents concentration, learning and health.

This dispute over the pros and cons of the technology is becoming political.

Some London councils, following a planning "cooling hierarchy", say low-energy ways of keeping homes cool should be prioritised over air conditioning and in a small number of cases have ordered property owners to remove them; the Conservative front bench calls it "dark ages" miserabilism; other MPs and political commentators demand an "air-con revolution".

Since April, in England and Wales the Boiler Upgrade Scheme has offered £2,500 towards a reversible air-air heat pump: a machine that warms a home in winter and cools it in summer. It is, in all but name, Britain's first air-conditioning subsidy - but it is badged as a heat pump, and only worth a third of the £7,500 for a heating-only model.

Such has been the silence around this grant, that in its first month only around 45 households claimed it. By comparison, the numbers claiming a heating-only model ran into the thousands.

In Scotland homeowners can also get a £7,500 grant for a heat pump via its Home Energy scheme - but for air-air versions that could offer cooling there is no funding at all. And in Northern Ireland there is no universal heat pump grant offered for households.

Under the terms of the England and Wales scheme, some people cannot apply at all. It is closed to social housing and new builds - which many argue shuts out the very people most exposed.

Take Woolwich, in south-east London, where a resident called Keisha says her top-floor flat reaches 43C in a heatwave.

She calls the building "inhumane"; she and around twenty neighbours in Canada Court and Clifton Lodge are taking their landlord, the housing association PA Housing, to court over homes they say are unfit to live in.

Even the landlord half-concedes the ground: its chief executive accepts that a growing number of residents face "uncomfortably warm temperatures … due to the changing climate", in homes "designed to keep heat in rather than keep them cool".

Keisha is exactly the tenant the state's new cooling grant might have been written for. But as a social tenant, she is barred from it.

Baroness Brown's committee finds the most deprived neighbourhoods are more than seven times as likely to be badly exposed to heat.

The government had a long-running scheme for supporting upgrades to social housing - ECO - but it will close after this year over reports of "cowboy" installations. The replacement scheme, if it continues under the new government, will not start until next year.

There is a cruel physics beneath the financial unfairness.

Air conditioning doesn't destroy heat, it moves it - out of the flat and into the street, where, Santamouris says, it warms the air your neighbours breathe and drives up the demand for still more cooling, by about a third in his studies of Sydney.

The machines keeping the financially comfortable cool make everyone else's nights worse; and as wealthier households cool their rooms, the rest fall further behind. A thermal divide, opening street by street.

And it lands on the electricity grid at the worst possible moment.

The electricity demand for cooling peaks on still, hot evenings - just as the wind drops and solar fades, leaving gas to supply the extra energy. In so doing, further greenhouse gas emissions are generated, adding bit by bit to the climate change effect – the very one driving the temperatures and the demand for air conditioning.

And the same heat that drives the demand also weakens the supply: gas turbines lose output as the air warms, and in June several UK plants had to be turned down.

But such is the scale of the heat that people are voting with their wallets - demand for portable air con units is through the roof, regardless of grants and the environment.

The evidence from experts is that we should not go down this road.

Santamouris and Baroness Brown reach for the same answer: passive cooling first, machines where genuinely needed, clean power behind them, and the lesson that France learned painfully in the deadly heatwave of 2003 - the vulnerable protected rather than left to improvise.

Cooling every home by machine would strain the grid and warm the streets, hampering the effort to slow the warming that drives the demand.

In Tokyo, Santamouris says, so many air conditioners now pump their waste heat into the air that the exhaust alone generates heat that's measured at close to a thousand watts of warming on every square metre - as much energy as falls from the sky at midday. "It's another sun," he adds with emphasis, "another sun."

"It's not the same in London. But if we continue in the same way, in some years we will have the same results."

The heat of this year and last, and the prospects of it being repeated, is a future Jo Shields is upset by.

"It's our survival," she says. Most days, she tries to bury the thought of it - "because otherwise it terrifies me."

Meanwhile, Mandy says she is grateful that the new community room with its air conditioning is providing some immediate respite for her and her mum.

"We sit there all day with it on, it helps so much I want one in my flat."
