https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c89n.title: How a former GB Olympian curbed his porn problem - and the signs and steps to recovery
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c89n.text:
Former Team GB diver Freddie Woodward was a teenager when he realised he had a problem with porn.

"Every time I sat down to revise, all I wanted to do was open those sites," he revealed.

By age 12, he was regularly visiting what he calls "hardcore" sites. As his career progressed - which included representing his country in the Olympics - he was watching adult content several times a day.

Now aged 30, the Olympian has told the BBC how he eventually curbed his habit by shifting his mindset.

"You can't be the person who is trying to quit porn. You have to be someone who doesn't watch porn, and that takes a lot of work," he said.

So how can you spot when a porn habit has become unhealthy, and how can you tackle it?

Although it has become a common phrase, "porn addiction" is not an officially recognised condition in its own right.

"We know a lot of people have a problem with porn," explains sex and relationship psychotherapist Silva Neves, who says the matter has become more prevalent among clients at his private practice.

But experts are divided as to whether it is a true "addiction" – like someone might experience with drugs, for example – and how best to deal with it.

Researcher Campbell Ince, from Australia's Monash University, says the vast majority of clinicians now agree people can suffer from "problematic porn use", but there is still a lot to figure out about its causes and treatments.

This means there is no definitive list of symptoms or treatments available to those worried they may be addicted.

Some clinicians approach it as a compulsive sexual behaviour disorder, a condition recognised by the World Health Organization.

This is sexual behaviour that "feels out of control, is causing significant distress, and despite repeated attempts to control it, they can't," explains psychotherapist Dr Paula Hall, who works privately at the Laurel Centre, a sex and porn addiction centre, and also runs a not-for-profit service.

The NHS does say it is possible to be addicted to "just about anything", including sex.

So what are the markers of an unhealthy porn habit? Neves says it's "not about the frequency or duration, it's about the damage to your life".

That might be arriving late to work because you were up all night watching porn, prioritising it above commitments to your loved ones, or watching it in the office, he says.

Other crucial questions to ask yourself are whether you can actually cut back or adjust your habit when you try, and whether you carry on watching despite enjoying it less and less, adds Ince, whose research focuses on problematic porn use.

For Craig, who describes himself as a recovering addict, it was this loss of control which marked a turning point during the Covid-19 pandemic, when he was in his mid-thirties.

"I don't think it ever became a huge issue for me until lockdown, where that extra pressure, extra isolation, just compounded the issue.

"I didn't know how to get it to loosen its grip on me," he recalls.

Ince cautions that many people may feel distress about their porn use for social, moral or religious reasons – but that this does not necessarily mean your habit is out of control.

"Someone could be watching porn for five minutes, three times a week – and because they have a lot of shame, they think 'I'm an addict'," agrees Neves.

"But then there might be someone who watches it every day and thinks it's fine."

Hall similarly encourages clients to "get away from the idea of 'I'm either an addict or I'm not'", and focus instead on how much it is affecting things like your studies and relationships.

TV presenter Ore Oduba last year spoke publicly about his 30-year-long porn addiction which began at the age of nine – saying it had been "destroying my life from the inside out".

"It was the thing from a very early age that I was running to as a response to a lot of trauma", he told the We Need to Talk podcast last year, before curbing the habit.

It is not clear what might cause such behaviour, as experts say much more research is needed.

"The scientific examination is certainly accelerating, but there is a very long way to go," Ince says.

It might begin as something which gives you a break from other issues in your life, says Hall, such as a stressful career or relationship breakdown.

There may also be "predisposing factors", such as trauma, issues from early childhood, or negative self-belief, that can make it harder to curb your use, she says.

Craig, now 40, says porn became a "tool to turn to for every one of life's ups and downs".

He remembers feeling he was "broken, that there was no way out", before recovery helped him to think differently.

Hall also points to the impact of the digital environment and people becoming "addicted by design" through algorithms.

Both she and Neves say AI-generated porn is making matters worse by enabling people to create "exactly what they want and need", as Neves describes it.

If you are worried about your porn use, Ince recommends seeking out support from a qualified and experienced professional.

A registered psychologist can be particularly helpful because they may consider your mental health more broadly, "and we know that co-occurring mental health problems are more or less the rule, rather than the exception", he says.

This was the case for Craig, who did not realise his porn use may be unhealthy until he started therapy for his mental health.

"Porn addiction was like a contributing factor," he came to learn.

His therapist suggested he join a 12-step programme for sex addiction – a recovery model created by Alcoholics Anonymous – which he credits for his recovery.

"I didn't necessarily find it easy and straightforward to step away from my addiction. I feel I'm in a good place now, but also acknowledge the fact it's one day at a time."

There is currently no central, dedicated NHS service for those struggling with their porn use – although some local services offer support, and you can talk to your GP. This means treatment will more likely come from private practitioners, support groups or online self-help.

Ince suggests doing thorough research to find the right fit for you, and cautions against using online resources which may offer generic advice.

Some practitioners will help clients towards cutting out porn altogether, while others will help people "integrate it into their lives in a way that is functional," says Neves.

Seeking to understand any underlying factors will be a crucial part of treatment, says Hall.

There are some practical steps you can take yourself, she says, such as placing blocking software on your device.

She also advises recognising when you might feel more susceptible to using porn – which, for some, can be when you are stressed or alone – and planning ahead for what you might do instead.

But she says there should ultimately be more support on the NHS, particularly early intervention before porn can take over a person's life.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care said: "It is troubling to hear accounts of individuals becoming addicted to pornography at such a young age.

"It reinforces the importance of the online safety laws we have put in place to prevent children from accessing harmful content."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c89n.summary: Freddie Woodward was a teenager when he realised he had a problem with porn. He was watching porn several times a day as a professional diver. Now aged 30, he has told the BBC how he eventually curbed his habit by shifting his mindset. Experts are divided as to whether it is a true "addiction"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y3.title: Artificial Intelligence used to design brand new viruses
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y3.text:
Artificial Intelligence has been used to design brand new viruses that are fully functional and can replicate in the laboratory, say US researchers.

It is the first time whole genomes have been successfully designed by AI.

The resulting 16 novel viruses were created to infect bacteria and pose no threat to people.

The breakthrough has been labelled a "very significant turning point" in science that could unlock a new era for treating disease. But experts have also warned AI-designed viruses raise "urgent" safety and security concerns.

AI tools are rapidly advancing and have already been used to design new antibiotics.

But that is relatively simple compared with designing a new viable virus from scratch.

"This is a next step in the complexity that's designable by generative AI, this is the first time generative AI has been used to design a complete genome, it's something that can replicate and have other functions inside cells… this was new territory for us," Brian Hie, assistant professor at Stanford University, told the BBC.

The technology works similarly to large language models, like ChatGPT, which predict sequences of text.

In this instance the AI models, known as Evo1 and Evo2, predict the language of life rather than words.

The AI models were trained on genetic codes from viruses, bacteria, plants and people.

They were then refined to produce a type of virus, known as a bacteriophage, which infect only specific species of bacteria.

The Stanford researchers picked the most promising 302 AI designs and synthesised them in the lab. Of these, 16 proved effective at killing E. coli bacteria.

Samuel King, a PhD student in the lab, said they realised the phage were working in the early hours of the morning.

The phage were placed on petri dishes growing a layer of bacteria on them and the scientists waited for signs their new viruses were enjoying the feast.

"We were starting to see these clear spots and it was just extremely exciting," says King. When the results were shared with the wider team "the room spontaneously burst into applause", Hie recalls.

Developing new phage could lead to new ways of treating infections that have become resistant to antibiotics.

But the breakthrough also points to the ability of AI to design new biology that goes beyond the natural world – what is known as synthetic biology.

Hie argues this has the potential to "massively improve human health" by developing new drugs and therapies.

But concerns have already been raised that the same technology could be used maliciously to create new diseases.

In a commentary accompanying the publication in the journal Science, Dr Thomas Inglesby and Dr Moritz Hanke from the Center for Health Security at Johns Hopkins University wrote that the findings raise "urgent biosafety and biosecurity questions".

They said it was no longer a question of "whether generative viral genome design will exist" but whether it can be used without "enabling serious harm".

For example, they said new viruses with the potential to cause disease "should not be pursued".

The researchers themselves took steps to maximise safety. They excluded viruses that could infect complex organisms from the training database, performed the research on phage rather than viruses that infect people and it all took place in a secure laboratory.

Hie argues even existing safeguards go a long way towards "ensuring that the technology is used for good".

Viruses are not alive and it would take another significant leap for AI to generate living organisms.

The genetic code of the phage is around 5,400 base pairs (letters) long. The smallest genome of a living cell is around 500,000 base pairs. The human genome is three billion base pairs.

Hie says "it would probably be a lot of work, but not impossible" to attempt some simple organisms and they were "definitely interested in working towards" that.

Prof Marc Güell, from the synthetic biology lab at Pompeu Fabra University in Spain, said the study was a "very significant turning point" because for the "first time in history, we are beginning to design biology on a computer".

He said it "allows us to dream of exciting possibilities for tackling humanity's greatest challenges" such as developing phages to tackle disease, enzymes to treat genetic disorders and antibodies that could be used in immunotherapy.

Prof Patrick Cai, chair of synthetic genomics at the Manchester Institute of Biotechnology, said the study was an "important milestone".

"The significance extends far beyond phages – it suggests that genome language models are beginning to learn the design principles encoded by evolution, opening the door to AI-assisted genome writing."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gk.title: NHS must plan for heatwaves like it does for winter, health secretary says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gk.text:
The NHS must prepare for the effects of heatwaves each year in the same way that it plans for cold weather in the winter, the health secretary has said.

Yvette Cooper said there had been a "big increase" in people attending A&Es because of the effect of hot weather this summer. Meanwhile, some hospitals have reported disruption due to key equipment failing in the heat.

In an interview with LBC Radio, Cooper called on people to look out for the elderly and other vulnerable people as well as urging better planning by the NHS.

It comes as Union released testimonies from ambulance workers describing the difficult and "vile" conditions they have had to work in.

The UK registered its 34th day of temperatures reaching 30C (86F) or higher in a calendar year on Tuesday, equalling the record set in 1995.

Forecasts suggest that this record is likely to be beaten as early as next week, with some suggesting the potential for a sixth heatwave to develop. Yellow heat warnings are already in place in some areas.

Every year the NHS sets out detailed plans for winter, including measures to cope with increases in patients.

Speaking about the recent heatwaves, England's health secretary, who also gave an interview to the Guardian newspaper on the topic, said: "I spoke to A&E staff who were telling me that they've had a big increase in patients coming into A&E linked to the heat in a way that you would normally only see in the winter.

"So I've been clear: the NHS has to make sure we are preparing for summer pressures now in the same way we prepare for winter.

"What it means is making sure that you've got plans in place to respond to higher numbers of people coming in to A&E, for example, who are vulnerable because of the heat, and that you've got the arrangements in place to make sure people can then be returned from hospital as swiftly as possible.

"But it also needs much stronger prevention - we know that it's the elderly and vulnerable who are at risk when you have these heatwaves."

The call was echoed by Unison, which represents ambulance workers.

The union said emergency workers have been working in some very difficult conditions this summer.

Unison said its members had reported being sent out in ambulances in stifling heat with faulty or no air conditioning, and often with limited access to drinking water or toilet facilities.

It said this has occurred during shifts where staff have queued for hours outside hospitals to hand over patients in stifling temperatures.

One ambulance technician from Birmingham told the union working in the heat was "vile".

"We have one uniform whether it's minus 10 or 30 degrees. You're sweating even when you're just driving. We then go into hot care homes and houses.

"Doing CPR for 40 minutes in the heat is ten-times harder. Then you simply move on to the next job. I could have cried during my last shift. I often think, I can't do this again."

Unison ambulance national officer Sharan Bandesha said it was time for a re-think.

"Ambulance services have well-established plans for winter. It's increasingly clear they're needed for summer too.

As well as reports of a surge of patients being brought in for heat-related conditions, hospitals have reported problems with equipment, including scanners and IT systems, and difficult working conditions for staff, particularly at some of the older sites.

Alongside the risk of dehydration and heatstroke, a bout of extreme heat raises the chances of complications from chronic conditions like advanced heart, kidney and respiratory failure.

In a preliminary assessment last month, the UK Health Security Agency said there were an estimated 2,877 heat-related deaths during the May and June heatwaves, almost double the figure for the whole of last year.

And it said that it was "likely that 2026 could see the highest number of heat-associated deaths on record", surpassing the number in 2022 when the agency started studying them.

Some hospitals have reported disruption due to key equipment failing in the heat. UK registered its 34th day of temperatures reaching 30C (86F) or higher in a calendar year on Tuesday.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cpd7.title: Walk-in mental health centres to open in banks and libraries across England
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cpd7.text:
People in England needing immediate care for mental health problems will be able to access specialist walk-in hubs close to their home, the government is promising.

Ministers have set out plans to create a network of nearly 200 community mental health centres and mental health A&Es by 2029.

The aim is to give those experiencing a mental health crisis or significant distress somewhere to go to get help when they need it - with plans to open dozens of the hubs in high street locations like banks and libraries.

One in five people struggle with their mental health and thousands of people turn up at A&E when they get to crisis point because they cannot find help elsewhere.

The government believes its plans, which build on pilots that have been run over recent years, will help tackle this issue and ensure people receive expert care when they need it.

The government said there will be 100 new community mental health centres opened in a variety of locations, from libraries and banks. Some will be set up in new buildings.

They will bring together existing teams of nurses, therapists and support workers.

Many of the hubs are expected to be open seven days a week and some will have short-stay bed facilities.

Six areas have trialled the approach since 2024.

The government is also pledging to set up another 59 dedicated mental health A&Es, on top of the 23 which are already operational. Many will be attached to existing A&Es.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "Nobody should be left to struggle with their mental health alone. But every day, thousands of people are waiting months for help, then finding the only door open to them is a busy A&E.

"These new centres will be a lifeline for so many," he said.

"They will bring NHS services closer to home, making it easier to get support before problems get worse and ensuring those in crisis get the right care in the right place."

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper added: "This is how we can turn the tide on mental ill health - preventing more people from reaching crisis, cutting waits for care, and building an NHS which is there for everyone when they need it.”

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Cooper said there would be a "continual programme" of rolling out these mental health centres - with the first ones set to open this autumn.

"It will take a bit of time in some areas but 100 right across the country I think will make a real difference to getting people mental health support early," she said, adding that "prevention can be much more effective to provide healthcare".

She said the government has already increased mental health staffing, but said "what these services are going to be doing is bringing together existing teams of staff to work together in a different way".

The chief executive of the Centre for Mental Health, Andy Bell, said he welcomed the announcement on the whole - although was concerned that the mental health emergency departments had not been properly tested yet.

He also said children and young people, who will be able to use these services, needed their own dedicated hubs.

But he said he was "delighted" that the government was taking action on mental health after it had been neglected by successive governments for too long.

"This must now be backed up by investment, most crucially in the workforce needed to provide effective mental health care," he said.

Stephen Jones, of the Royal College of Nursing, said he agreed investment in staff would be crucial if the new centres were going to cope with demand.

"More services closer to people's homes are a crucial step towards more humane care," he said.

But he added: "To succeed, both will need specialist mental health nurses at the centre."

The Department of Health said that the initiative is backed by £343m and the first sites will open in autumn this year, with "further facilities following from March 2027".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cpd7.summary: Ministers have set out plans to create a network of nearly 200 community mental health centres and mental health A&Es. One in five people struggle with their mental health and thousands turn up at A&E when they get to crisis point. Government believes its plans will help tackle this issue and ensure people receive expert care when they need it.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgj.title: Sunshine to meal times: How to beat jet lag
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgj.text:
Many will have experienced it – that feeling at 3pm when all you want to do is go to bed and sleep like a log.

Or, finding yourself wide awake at 3am, brain whirring and no prospect of sleep.

Jet lag - the world's most annoying holiday souvenir – is the price we pay for flying off around the globe on travels or holidays.

So how does it work, and what can you do about it?

Jet lag is what you feel when local time changes abruptly, but your body clock is playing catch up, says Dr Nina Rzechorzek, who leads research at the University of Cambridge on human brain temperature, sleep, and circadian rhythms.

"After rapid travel across several time zones, your internal biological time initially stays aligned with home while you are trying to sleep, eat, and function on destination time.

"That mismatch can cause disturbed sleep, daytime sleepiness, poor concentration, irritability, reduced performance, and digestive problems," she says.

And jet lag is closely linked to what are called our circadian rhythms – the body's internal body clock.

"Almost all the cells in our body maintain their own 24-hour clock, which are synchronised by a master clock in the brain," explains Dr Anna Edmondson, of the Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge.

"The master clock is set to environmental timing cues, one of the most important cues being daily cycles in sunlight and darkness. However, if the timing of the sunlight/darkness cycles suddenly change (you fly far east or west), then it takes several days for the master clock to adjust to the new time, leading to jet lag.

"So effectively, it's like your body is still stuck in the timezone of where you've just flown from."

The direction of travel also makes a difference, says Rzechorzek.

"Travelling east is often harder, because most people find it easier to shift their clock later than earlier. That quirk is partly because the average human internal cycle is slightly longer than 24 hours, giving us a modest natural bias towards delaying rather than advancing our timing."

So what can we do about it?

Well the bad news is there's no cure, but it is possible to mitigate it.

"There are many ways to set the clock that we can control, including light, food, and exercise," says Dr Tatiana Wilson, another circadian researcher at Newnham College, Cambridge University.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce85.title: Half of vaccines are binned - 'fridge-free' versions could change that
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce85.text:
Vaccines that do not need to be kept cool in a fridge have been successfully trialled in patients for the first time, say UK scientists.

Currently, most vaccines need to be refrigerated or frozen - but around half are wasted each year, mainly because they become unusable after getting too hot or too cold.

In the trial, which involved 60 volunteers, company Stablepharma converted a liquid tetanus-diphtheria vaccine into a "fridge-free" version by keeping it as a dry powder for a year at room temperature before mixing it with water and injecting it.

Vaccines often need strict temperature control during storage and transportation, from the moment of manufacture up until being injected into a patient's arm.

This practice is known as the "cold chain" and is especially challenging in the poorest and most remote parts of the world or in war zones, where fridges may be scarce and electricity unreliable.

The UK's National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) has been testing the new "fridge-free" approach.

The new technology is inspired by resurrection plants, which dry out and appear dead during a drought, before springing back to life when it rains.

The plants produce large amounts of a sugar called trehalose, which stabilises the plant's cells during a drought.

The trial dried out the tetanus-diphtheria vaccine with trehalose to protect its vital components.

Prof Saul Faust, the director of the NIHR Clinical Research Facility in Southampton, said it gave "equivalent" immune responses to the conventional vaccine as well as being "safe and well tolerated" in the early stage studies.

Faust added: "This obviously has potential to remove cold chain dependence, reduce wastage and improve access."

A larger trial involving 160 people is already due to start in the coming months.

This would be the final stage of research as the original vaccine is already approved and licensed so there is no requirement to perform large-stage trials needed for a novel vaccine.

The studies are being done to meet the World Health Organization's (WHO) goal of a vaccine that survives at 30C and 75% relative humidity.

But the research team say separate data shows the components of their vaccine also survive cycling between temperatures of -20C and +40C. That could mean the vaccine being viable after transport in a cold aircraft hold and then in the back of a truck in the heat.

There is not one single reason vaccines are wasted and disposed of, but the WHO estimates this is the fate of half of all vaccines globally. This can include damage in transport, passing the expiration date, and unused doses from multi-dose vials, but a major factor are failures in the cold chain.

Prof Sir Jonathan Van-Tam, the former deputy chief medical officer for England and an advisor to Stablepharma, used to work in remote field clinics.

"I can remember taking out vaccines in cool boxes… doing that on really inhospitable roads where one couldn't predict getting from A to B in a short period of time and there was always this nervousness about maintaining the cold chain in time to get the vaccines into arms of waiting children."

The new mRNA vaccine could not be adapted using this approach, but many current vaccines could be stabilised with the sugar trehalose.

It could also work for some medicines – such as monoclonal antibodies – which need to be kept in a fridge.

Prof Tuck Seng Wong is the director of the UK-Southeast Asia Vaccine Manufacturing Research Hub but was not involved in the study. He said it was "very exciting" and a "significant breakthrough in UK science".

But added there were still "several areas" that still needed investigation, including how stable the vaccines are when the temperature is regularly fluctuating and how well the vaccines perform in both larger and more ethnically diverse groups of people.

The findings have been published in eClinicalMedicine, part of the Lancet group of journals.

Ephrem Tekle Lemango, the associate director of immunization at Unicef, said immunisation was a "life-saving service that depends on refrigeration" so "this innovation could help us vaccinate more children and pave the way for a future of fridge-free vaccines".

Dr Bruce Roser, the founder of Stablepharma, said: "Reliable and safe fridge-free vaccines could be a game-changer for global health - helping life-saving vaccines reach millions more people, wherever they live, and making immunisation programmes more sustainable, reliable and equitable for future generations."

The vaccine could be used to stabilise the sugar trehalose, which stabilises the plant's cells during a dry period.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cnvn.title: From flip flops to fisherman's sandals: How to look after your feet this summer
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cnvn.text:
Flip-flops have always been a popular solution to sweaty, uncomfortable feet in scorching weather - and now they've had a revamp.

The most stylish way to wear them this summer is with a kitten heel, according to fashion expert and trend forecaster Angela Baidoo.

"It's not a high heel and it's really kind of easy to just slip in and slip out of," she says.

However, heel or not, the flip-flop has earned itself a bad rap for lack of support and damaging our feet. Is that fair?

"In terms of arch support and joint support, it's not the best style, but people are investing a bit more, getting their flip-flops customised, because it's something that is just so easy to wear," Baidoo says.

Podiatrist Dr Helen Branthwaite, who is also chief clinical adviser at the Royal College of Podiatry, says it's "not accurate" to say flip-flops are bad.

The problem comes if you go straight from wearing a very structured shoe to wearing flip-flops a lot, she explains. It means your foot is under more strain than normal, which makes you more prone to injury.

"The foot does start to change shape and tends to splay a little bit over time," says Branthwaite.

"A good analogy is if you were to wear a corset all the time and then took the corset off, everything would sort of all hang out, so to speak."

So what are the stylish and comfortable alternatives?

Baidoo suggests a more supportive flip-flop, such as a FitFlop, which is sturdier and contoured - a world away from the flat and thin flip-flops that have been cut from a big sheet of foam.

Sliders are out and Crocs are in for Gen Z, she says. They might be "anti-fashion shoes" but they're "really comfy" and designed "orthopaedically" with footbed sandals like Birkenstocks offering the same advantages.

The wooden clog is also making a comeback. It's worn by doctors and chefs on their feet all day. Scholl slider mules are the original orthopaedic shoe, Baidoo says - and admits she once had a pair in pink suede.

Wedges are another option in the heat. "When I speak to some of my friends and some of my clients who work in the plus-size category, the wedge actually provides a form of comfortable footwear. And it provides a nice kind of silhouette for the ankle. You've got the support all the way through the shoe."

You could always opt for the fisherman-style sandal, which looks like something a history teacher might have worn in the 1970s. With socks.

"Men can wear it as an alternative to a loafer. It's not as casual as a flip-flop, which might not be suitable for certain environments. It's a really cool kind of style to adopt for women too," Baidoo says.

So what about the trend for wearing minimalist barefoot shoes? It's all about easing into them, says Branthwaite. In other words, don't buy a pair and then decide to go on a 5-mile hike.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd9w.title: Top-rated mental health trust asked to save £24m
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd9w.text:
A mental health trust rated "outstanding" by the health watchdog says it has to make £24.1m in savings this year — about 2% of its budget.

East London NHS Foundation Trust (ELFT) provides mental health and community health services for about 1.8 million people across east London and Bedfordshire.

Like other NHS trusts, ELFT is required to meet annual financial and efficiency targets. Up to 330 posts from a workforce of 6,000 could be affected by any cuts and a union said patients would "feel the consequences".

A spokesperson said the trust had "a responsibility to live within its means" and was working to deliver the required efficiencies while "protecting the quality and safety of care".

The trust plans to redesign nine front-line services for the financial year 2026-27 including child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS), addiction services, adult mental health crisis and community services, and talking therapies.

Some 40 posts could go through reduced spending on temporary staff, while a smaller number of posts are expected to be lost from non-clinical and corporate services.

Last year, ELFT made £37m in what it described as efficiency savings.

The union Unite told the BBC it planned to ballot members on strike action over the way the changes were being implemented.

Regional union officer Gary Boodhna said: "You cannot take 5% of the workforce out of an NHS trust and pretend it will not affect services.

"Staff are already stretched to breaking point. Our members know how hard it is to keep services running with the resources they have now.

"Cutting hundreds more jobs will only pile more pressure on to those who remain and patients will inevitably feel the consequences."

The trust said providing "safe and compassionate care" was at the "heart of what we do".

Apsana Begum, Labour MP for Poplar & Limehouse in east London, said she had written to the trust to express her fears.

"At this moment, the focus could have been on how NHS funding is restored and how there can be parity between the quality and level of care for physical health and mental health," she said.

"I am concerned that these cuts are particularly targeted towards mental health care services that are of equal importance to patients."

More from Bedfordshire:

The trust has a strong national reputation, being one of a small number of NHS organisations to hold the highest rating from the Care Quality Commission.

Managers from ELFT have previously been placed in charge of other struggling organisations, including Norfolk & Suffolk NHS Foundation Trust.

An ELFT spokesperson said: "Like all NHS providers, we have a responsibility to live within our means so that we can continue to provide high-quality care to the communities we serve.

"Our approach is clinically led and focused on meeting the needs of our service users.

"We are working closely with our trade unions, colleagues and partners to identify the most effective and sustainable way to deliver the efficiencies required of us, while protecting the quality and safety of care."

A Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) spokesperson said: "This government is dedicated to transforming the quality and sustainability of NHS services, including for those who need mental health support."

The DHSE said the government was due to invest a record £16.1bn in mental health services in England in 2026-27 compared with £15.7bn in 2025-26.

It said it would publish a mental health plan later this year setting out how services would respond earlier and reduce waiting times.

NHS England has been contacted for comment.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgv.title: Breast cancer checks missing most women under 50 who are at risk, says study
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgv.text:
NHS criteria for screening women under 50 for breast cancer are too narrow and missing up to 95% of those at higher risk of developing the disease, researchers have warned.

The current guidelines - set by the National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (Nice) - focus solely on inherited genes and not other factors such as lifestyle, they found.

Older women are offered routine mammogram scans to check their breasts, but under 50s do not get any breast screening unless they have a strong family history of the disease.

Using a new risk assessment tool, a study published in the British Journal of Cancer identified eight times as many women in this age group who developed breast cancer.

In England, guidance from Nice recommends GPs ask about family history if a woman is worried that she might have a higher risk of breast cancer, and sometimes if they are over 35 and using an oral contraceptive pill or considering taking hormone replacement therapy (HRT).

About one in seven women develops breast cancer in their lifetime, yet only 5-10% of cases are linked to inherited genes.

Hormones have been linked to a slightly increased risk of breast cancer, although larger risk factors include alcohol intake and obesity.

Breast cancer is a leading cause of death in women under 50 in the UK.

Most cases - 96% - are in women over 40, while 25% are in women over 75.

Men can get breast cancer too, with about 420 new cases every year in the UK.

Natasha Finch was diagnosed with an aggressive breast cancer at just 23 despite having no known risk factors.

She has since become an advocate for breast cancer awareness and wants young women to take symptoms seriously.

"I'm six years on and still here, still winning. Going to the GP was scary, but I'm so glad I went when I did — because if I hadn't, who knows?"

"I just want to advocate for girls."

This study, by a team from Cambridge University and the Institute of Cancer Research, looks at how to predict breast cancer risk in younger women.

They used a risk calculator called Boadicea that combines factors such as family history, lifestyle, reproductive history and genetic information to give a risk score.

If all women under 50 were to have this done, they estimate about a quarter (26.5%) would be categorised as at above-average risk and referred for further assessment.

This would include a third of women under 50 (34.8%) who develop breast cancer within 10 years.

By comparison, the current Nice criteria would result in 1.4% of women under 50 being referred for further assessment, which would include just 4.4% of those women who develop breast cancer.

A main reason for the disparity, the researchers say, is because three-quarters of women (73%) under 50 who develop breast cancer within a decade have no family history of breast cancer - the key criterion in the Nice guidelines.

Lead researcher Dr Juliet Usher-Smith said the NHS should review the criteria in the light of the findings, but acknowledged referring more people would add to workloads and could cause some women unnecessary checks and anxiety.

Dr Sowmiya Moorthie, from the charity Cancer Research UK which funded the work, said: "Any changes must be accessible and equitable, taking into consideration the anxiety that extra referrals might cause for women."

Several breast cancer risk calculators like Boadicea already exist and none are perfect.

Nice said it welcomed the findings and recognised the potential of such multifactorial risk assessment tools but said the current evidence did not warrant a change to its breast cancer guidelines.

The NHS breast cancer screening programme - which advises the NHS for all four nations - is regularly evaluated by the UK National Screening Committee.

The four UK nations run broadly comparable breast screening programmes.

Like most high income countries, women are first invited at 50 and then every three years - though there are some variations.

For example, Sweden, begin screening at the age of 40, while others, including Australia and Canada, offer mammograms every two years rather than every three.

The UK's screening programme aims to balance detecting cancer early while minimising the downsides of screening, such as false positives, overdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment, and ensuring the programme remains cost effective.

All women are encouraged to know what looks and feels normal or usual for them and to see a doctor if they notice any changes.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgv.summary: NHS guidelines focus solely on inherited genes and not other factors such as lifestyle. Older women are offered routine mammogram scans but under 50s do not get any breast screening. Study identified eight times as many women in this age group who developed breast cancer.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c86n.title: Woman has pioneering womb surgery to fix 'miracle' baby with intestines outside its body
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c86n.text:
Doctors have used ground-breaking surgery on an unborn baby to successfully correct a birth defect while he was still inside the womb.

His mother, Maisie Savage, from London, was operated on by doctors in the US while she was 26 weeks pregnant.

Baby Theo, who is now five months old and thriving, had gastroschisis, where the belly button does not develop properly, causing the intestines to grow externally.

Doctors partially exposed his mother's womb and then gently pushed his organs back inside his abdomen using keyhole surgery.

He was the third baby in the world to benefit from the first-of-its-kind clinical trial.

Maisie, 29, and Theo's father, Josh French, 36, both teachers, say they are incredibly relieved by the success of the pioneering surgery.

"He's a little miracle, isn't he?" Maisie told BBC News.

But they both know things could have been very different.

The serious birth defect affects one in 3,000 UK babies each year. In the best-case scenarios, babies can require weeks in intensive care and nutritional feeding through a tube or IV and corrective surgery.

For the most complex cases, like Theo's, outcomes are far more serious with up to six months in neonatal intensive care, multiple surgeries, IV nutritional feeding for up to two years, and a possible intestinal transplant.

Even with the highest level of medical care, one in 10 babies will die.

Theo's parents initially had no idea anything was wrong with their unborn child.

"Going towards a 20-week scan, we were purely just excited to have an image of our baby," said Josh. "We didn't know he was going to be a 'he' at the time."

Josh said discovering Theo had gastroschisis had been a shock and "incredibly scary".

At 24 weeks gestation, specialist doctors at London's Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH) had been preparing expectant parents Maisie and Josh for what the first six months of Theo's life were going to look like.

However, after discovering he had the more serious condition of complex gastroschisis, doctors referred him to Texas Children's Hospital, in Houston.

There, a team of foetal and paediatric surgeons, led by Dr Michael Belfort, had been leading a first-of-its-kind clinical trial to repair complex gastroschisis before birth.

Belfort, the clinical lead on the trial, had previously pioneered a similar surgical procedure in the womb on babies with spina bifida.

Maisie was told she would have to travel to Texas straight away and remain there for the rest of her pregnancy. "It was a huge decision," she said.

As part of the trial she first had to travel to Leuven Hospital, in Belgium, where specialists needed to give Maisie a Botox injection through her womb into Theo's abdominal wall, to relax the muscles to make the repair easier.

The family then flew to Texas where the operation was performed in November last year, 26 weeks into the pregnancy.

Josh said he had had an agonising wait while doctors had operated on Maisie. "The length of that day, it felt like a week," he said. "The waiting and just not knowing exactly what was going on at each and every stage."

Maisie's womb was partially exposed to position the uterus and baby, the amniotic fluid was drained and replaced with carbon dioxide (CO2) gas to expand the operating space. Using keyhole surgery, Theo's organs were then gently pushed back inside his abdomen, which was stitched closed.

Maisie was left with a scar, twice the size of a C-section incision. But unlike other women who are recovering from a C-section, she still had a baby to grow inside her for another 14 weeks.

She said Theo would often kick inside her, hitting her scar and causing her pain. "It was a hard recovery," Maisie said. "But, it was worth it."

The operation was a complete success and Theo was carried to term and born in February by vaginal delivery in Texas.

Belfort, obstetrician and gynaecologist-in-chief at Texas Children's Hospital, said he and his team are very happy with the results so far.

"The mother, the baby, the surgery, the time of the surgery, the fact that we had zero complications during the foetal surgery and after the foetal surgery, just remarkable."

If the trial is a success, Paolo de Coppi, professor of paediatric surgery at GOSH and head of stem cells and regenerative medicine at University College London, would perform the procedure in the UK.

"We hope that we will be able to offer this to patients in a larger scale very soon," he said.

Belfort is excited about the partnership and said Texas Children's and GOSH working together will be a formidable team.

And Belfort is already looking ahead to what he can do next.

"The inside of the uterus is now a new surgical space for innovation," he said. "And spina bifida and gastroschisis are just two, but I believe that we could actually do certain cardiac surgeries in utero, and I think we can also do some lung surgeries in utero."

Back home in London, Maisie said Theo is doing amazingly.

"Everything they did just completely reversed what could have been a really horrible start to his life and he's just the best. He's a completely normal baby essentially."

"We both feel incredibly fortunate," Josh said. "The impact that they've had on us as a family is incredible. They made us feel so welcome from the team at Great Ormond Street to Dr Belfort and the team.

"Whilst we were over there, the level of care was amazing, and they made a very traumatic time of our lives so much easier, and we've got this little man - we couldn't be happier."

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd69.title: What your summer reading list says about you
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd69.text:
You've been dreaming about that summer break on the sun lounger, book in one hand and drink in the other, for months. Now the dash to the airport gate, train station or hours-long drive is all that stands in your way.

But what does the book you've just shoved in your suitcase say about you?

"It's definitely not a random choice," says Edgar Dubourg, a cognitive scientist at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris. "Your reading list is basically a map of your personality.

"When you pick a thriller or romance or horror or science fiction you're not escaping your psychology, in a way, you're really feeling very intuitive and very old parts of your brain.

"Fiction isn't inventing new emotions in you. It's pressing on those pre-existing motivations like instincts."

Studies have shown that our book choices can subconsciously reveal important parts of our personality - including what gives us pleasure and what makes us feel emotion.

Research by Dr Valerie van Mulukom, a senior lecturer in psychology at Oxford Brookes University, suggests that our inner anxieties (or what she calls existential insecurities) determine which book we pick from the shelf.

During her study, she used how often someone might engage with a certain genre to match it up with one of the following four clusters:

But what do they mean? And how do they match up with our own anxieties?

If, like me, you're big on crime novels, then this suggests you're concerned with - or intrigued by - threat and danger.

This isn't just limited to old-fashioned detective novels or psychological thrillers, but can be anything from true crime and spy stories to supernatural horrors like the works of Stephen King's books.

The UK bestseller lists have a range of titles that sit in the "threat and danger" category defined by the research, including:

Meanwhile, if lustful romance is more your thing (very much not mine), then your insecurities are more likely to be about your relationships, both romantic and platonic, and your thoughts on social status and reputation.

The UK bestseller lists have a range of titles that sit in the "everyday life and human relationships" category defined by the research, including:

At the opposite end, someone who likes science fiction or fantasy novels tends to be more concerned with the state of the world.

If you're spending your summer holiday finally reading the Game of Thrones novels, known for mixing political intrigue and medieval battles with tales of dragons and undead armies, then you're likely to be someone who worries about climate change or the threat of war.

The UK bestseller lists have a range of titles that sit in the "epic other-world adventures" category defined by the research, including:

For me, holiday reading is serious work. On my last trip abroad, I took eight books for a three-week holiday, ranging from Frank Herbert's sci-fi epic Dune to James Ellroy's noir throwback The Black Dahlia.

But not everyone likes disappearing off into fictional worlds. What if autobiographies or books about history are more your thing?

Dr Dubourg says it is narratives that are important, not necessarily whether they're fact or fiction.

"Everybody consumes narratives, be it in the form of actual news, of anecdotes, of stories that people tell in neighbourhoods."

The UK bestseller lists have a range of titles that sit in the "facts and history" category defined by the research, including:

So next time you pick up a book, what you think is just something vaguely interesting might actually make up an important part of your psychology.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgv.title: Holidaymakers warned about 'explosive diarrhoea' cyclospora parasite infection
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgv.text:
UK holidaymakers are being warned about a nasty infectious disease called cyclosporiasis that can cause explosive diarrhoea, after a sharp rise in cases.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said 67 cases have been reported since April, with many of them among travellers returning from Mexico.

It comes amid an outbreak in the US that has infected more than 18,000 people across 45 states. The source hasn't been identified yet and there have been no reported deaths.

The illness is caused by a parasite, cyclospora, that can contaminate food like salads, herbs and soft fruits. It doesn't naturally occur in the UK and there is no risk of spread from person to person, experts stress.

Between 30 April and 15 July 2026, 30 cases have been reported in England, 27 in Scotland and 10 in Wales, according to the UKHSA.

Of the 52 cases with travel information available, 48 reported having travelled to Mexico, with many saying they had stayed in either the white sand beach resort area of Riviera Maya, or slightly north of there in coastal Cancún.

The UKHSA said those affected reported staying in "a range of different hotels and consuming a variety of different food and drink within their resort as part of an all-inclusive holiday package".

There are ongoing investigations and monitoring of the situation.

People can protect themselves while away by following good food and water hygiene measures, including drinking bottled water and eating thoroughly cooked food, even when staying in high-end all-inclusive resorts.

Experts also advise people avoid certain foods such as fresh uncooked berries and herbs, unpeeled fruit and salad items.

Some who have been struck by it describe having to use the toilet up to 20 times a day, due to the frequent and explosive nature of the watery diarrhoea that's the main symptom.

The intestinal illness has recently affected thousands of people in the US.

Nick Palmiter, who is 29 and from Monroe County in Michigan, told the BBC he experienced feeling constant pressure and bubbling, "almost like you have a balloon in your stomach".

Although most cases resolve on their own, antibiotics can be given to treat severe or prolonged infections.

The UKHSA said it anticipates there will be more cases linked to increased summer travel to Mexico and possibly the US too.

Dr Philip Veal from the agency said: "If you develop symptoms after returning from travel, such as watery diarrhoea, loss of appetite, weight loss, stomach cramps or pain, bloating, increased wind, nausea, fatigue or other flu-like symptoms, please seek medical attention and inform your healthcare professional of your travel history."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2d.title: I went for a full body MOT and the results came as a shock
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2d.text:
I don't mind having my photo taken - triple checked and filtered for Instagram - but 70 cameras pointing at me while I'm down to my knickers is a bit daunting.

A robotic voice tells me to stay still and close my eyes as I stand in a huge curved scanner while classical music plays in the background.

With a flash of light, 2,000 photographs are taken of my body, in the hope of capturing every mark, freckle and mole to analyse for different skin cancers.

This full-body scan is happening at a sci-fi-style clinic in Manchester city centre, with me wearing a dressing gown and hexagon-shaped rubber slippers. The millions of data points collected will create a 3D avatar of my body using AI.

Over the past two years, the market for health MOTs has boomed, with people willing to pay hundreds, or even thousands, for them, and companies such as Prenuvo, Ezra and Neko Health raising millions in venture capital.

While Prenuvo and Ezra offer a whole-body MRI scan, I've opted for Neko Health, which doesn't delve quite as deeply, and comes with a more modest £299 price tag. There are currently 100,000 people on its waiting list.

I will be screened for a range of different conditions, including skin cancer, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, eye conditions like glaucoma, as well as kidney and blood disorders.

I don't have any symptoms, but what if they do find something? More on that later.

The body scan industry sees itself as a new frontier in healthcare, preventing disease before it has a chance to fully appear. But there is scepticism about how beneficial these scans really are for otherwise healthy patients.

My socials are inundated with videos of enthusiastic clients filming themselves in scan machines, getting their bloods taken and testing their grip strength.

Hjalmar Nilsonne, one of the founders of Neko Health, wants to see this preventative treatment available for every individual, not just those who can afford to pay for it.

"While medicine has progressed so much over the past century, primary care is still very basic. Why wait until we see symptoms?" Nilsonne says. "The data is super clear - prevention is preferable to cure."

However, GPs and doctors in the wider NHS are more sceptical, with NHS England warning that the popularity of these scans is leading to more "over-diagnosis, unnecessary investigations and avoidable anxiety".

As well as having a scan myself, I've spoken to two women who had very different experiences.

Annabel Mason-Thompson went for a Neko Health scan in September last year, knowing she had a suspicious-looking mark on her back - but it wasn't flagged by the technology.

"I felt a bit let down if I'm honest," the 50-year-old says. "Their AI scanner failed to pick up any of my four cancerous lesions.

"It was only when I went into the doctor's room after the scan and I pointed out my red mark did they take a look at it."

Further examination confirmed the mark was suspicious, so Neko Health contacted Annabel to say she would need treatment and wrote a letter to her private dermatologist to say the "lesion requires evaluation with a view to possible excision".

Her dermatologist found three more cancerous marks which needed urgent treatment.

"Luckily," she says, "they were all slow-growing basal cell carcinomas. I had to have two cut out and two taken off via cryotherapy."

Neko Health says "member safety and clinical excellence are at the heart of everything" it does. The company said its clinical team did identify a "lesion of concern" and it was reviewed by two of its dermatologists before a referral was made for potential treatment.

"We know that no one system is foolproof," Nilsonne says, "which is why we have multiple lenses - it is crucial that the technology and human expertise work together."

His company's latest data shows that of the 4,362 scans carried out on clients who visited Neko Health's Stockholm headquarters last year, 1.2% discovered life-threatening conditions such as melanoma and leukaemia. A further 4% spotted significant health conditions that required further treatment, and 1.2% flagged conditions that could be reversed such as pre-diabetic blood sugar levels.

While the figures are not representative of the population and only account for those who can afford to pay for this kind of preventive healthcare, Nilsonne says this is an indicator of how medicine should look in the future.

But GPs disagree. Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs (RCGP), says they haven't seen "convincing evidence" private broad screening tests "improve health outcomes".

She says the results from these private scans can also place an additional strain on the NHS as clients come back for further tests and potential treatment, even "where the findings prove to be clinically insignificant".

Mehvish says nothing could have prepared her for what she was told after her full body scan. She left Birmingham's Neko Health clinic with a life-changing diagnosis.

"I expected to feel relief," the 33-year-old says. "Instead, I was told that I had a rare form of diabetes."

After her long-term blood sugar levels came back very high, she had another blood test which confirmed she had suspected diabetes.

She was referred back to her GP, who sent her for an urgent hospital appointment the same day, and was diagnosed with Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA), a type of diabetes which bridges both type 1 and type 2.

Like type 1, it is an autoimmune condition that attacks the body's pancreatic cells, but it also shares traits with type 2 because it can progress slowly and, depending on the stage of the condition, it can initially be managed with diet and exercise.

"I didn't have any of the symptoms," Mehvish says, "It was difficult to get my head round it - how could I have this condition and not know about it?"

But she says the early, unexpected intervention "saved my life".

Now she injects insulin twice a day, monitors what she eats, and despite missing the spontaneity of her old life, is learning to adapt to her new one.

"I feel so much better, more clarity, less brain fog and I feel so much more balanced."

After my own scan, I'm feeling slightly out of balance. I've been told I have 3,311 skin markings - compared to the average Neko Health client's 845. Three need extra review by the company's dermatologist in Sweden.

"But I don't have any big moles or markings," I say during the post-scan consultation with a doctor. It's my freckles, I'm told, and having freckles puts me at higher risk of skin cancer.

Having felt confident I would get a clean bill of health - especially when it comes to my skin - I was a bit unnerved to discover that I'd need to have extra tests.

As well as the three suspicious-looking moles that needed further attention, I also discovered I have an unusual heart rate. The trace from the electrocardiogram (ECG) highlighted an extra wave, known as a bifid P wave, which was referred to Neko Health's in-house cardiologist for review. Thankfully, it came back all clear.

A few days later, I received a follow-up text to say there were no abnormal skin changes that required treatment.

I am one of thousands of clients who has had something flagged as a potential issue, then later found no further treatment was required. Some doctors say this causes unnecessary anxiety and that patients should only rely on national screening programmes through the NHS.

Dr Stephen Harden, president of the Royal Society of Radiologists, points to the technology used in the NHS, which targets "specific areas" like the breasts, bowel or cervix, and which he says may be more reliable than a whole-body scan.

But former health minister Steve Brine, who acts as an advisor to a preventative healthcare company, says precautionary scans like the one I had "fit the direction of travel of how people are approaching their health".

"Change is afoot across the NHS - prevention is a huge policy area," Brine says. "We want to identify people's problems before they become patients, so these scans could well become a part of our future healthcare and primary care needs to adapt."

As for me? I was told my heart age was four years younger than my actual age, and on the whole, I was in tip-top health. But I've also learned a valuable lesson - that I could be more at risk of skin cancer because of my freckles.

So, thanks to my time in the scanner, I am now far more enthusiastic about lathering sunscreen all over my body - rather than only on my face.

It is an immune system that attacks pancreatic cell cells, but it also shares traits with type 2. The condition can progress slowly and can be managed with diet and exercise.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd0x.title: Obesity rates have doubled in England since 1993 - what's going on?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd0x.text:
If England's obesity rates were still the same as 1993 there would be seven million fewer adults living with obesity.

There are 14 million adults classified as obese, despite successive governments launching 14 separate obesity strategies over the past three decades.

It's clear something isn't working, so what's behind the increase?

And can anything be done about it?

According to new analysis by the King's Fund, 15% of England's adult population - those aged 16 and over - in 1993 was obese, with rates achieving a record high of 30% in 2024.

Their analysis suggests obesity rates are rising fastest in 16-to-24 year-olds, with 18% classified as obese or severely obese in 2024 compared with just 6% in 1993.

Accounting for population change, this means there are now one million young adults living with obesity in England - 700,000 more than if rates had not risen over the past three decades.

Dave Buck, senior fellow for public health at the King's Fund, called this rise "clearly worrying" and says governments have "talked the talk, but not sufficiently walked the walk" in addressing obesity rates.

"This analysis shows the scale of the failure to take the necessary action on tackling this obesity timebomb," he added.

There are several factors behind the rise in obesity, including changes in eating habits and food prices over the last 30 years.

Service industry - or "white collar" jobs - take a larger share of the economy and there has been a decline in traditional manufacturing and other "blue collar" work such as manual labour.

This means more people are in sedentary office jobs so spend more time sitting down than moving around.

Food prices have also fallen since the 1990s, partly because of increased competition between the major supermarkets alongside an increase in fast food outlets and home delivery.

Buck told the BBC that these changes mean it's "far easier to over-consume or consume in ways that add to our weight".

"With things like deliveries, it's very easy and convenient now to click a button and you get a takeaway at your door, so we're making it much easier to have high fat, high salt and high sugar foods."

Takeaways high in fats, salt and sugar are more widely available in areas of high deprivation where people are at higher risk of obesity.

Less healthy foods in supermarkets are also cheaper than they were three decades ago, while there have been several cost-of-living crises in recent years.

Obesity can be a risk factor for several chronic conditions including type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure, osteoarthritis and some cancers.

Reports estimate obesity and being overweight costs the UK economy approximately £126bn per year, including £12bn to the NHS - roughly 7% of its annual budget.

Since 1992 - the year before data on obesity in England was first collected - 14 national obesity strategies have been published.

Campaigners argue progress has been too slow and calls for further intervention have increased in recent years.

Tony Blair's government introduced a ban on junk food advertising during children's TV programmes - although some campaigners were calling for a wider ban - while Gordon Brown launched a strategy aiming to reverse the "rising tide of obesity" after becoming prime minister in 2007.

The Conservative government introduced a UK-wide levy on high-sugar soft drinks in 2018, causing several manufacturers to cut sugar levels in their products so that they fell below the levy threshold.

During his final weeks in office in 2016, then-Prime Minister David Cameron considered banning "buy one get one free" deals for unhealthy products in supermarkets and restricting TV ads for junk food and other high sugar products.

Although both Theresa May and Boris Johnson argued at times for further action, Cameron's ideas were not followed up, partly due to the pandemic which delayed plans further, and afterwards when ministers argued restrictions on such deals would be unfair on shoppers due to surging inflation.

In January this year, the Labour government introduced a ban on junk food advertising before 21:00 on television and at any time online after almost a decade of consideration.

Further plans to crack down on the sale of unhealthy food items are still yet to come into effect despite being first pledged by Labour in 2024, while a recent select committee report urged ministers to do more like stopping fast food outlets opening close to schools.

Weight loss drugs such as GLP1s are increasingly being used to treat obesity, though only adults with a BMI of at least 35 and who have at least one pre-existing weight-related health condition qualify for Wegovy on the NHS.

People with cardiovascular disease who are classed as overweight, but not quite obese, can also be given the drug, while Mounjaro has been available from specialist NHS weight-loss clinics in England and Wales since March 2025.

Many people chose to buy these drugs privately.

A new weight loss pill from Wegovy is now available to buy privately from High Street and online pharmacies in the UK - but is not yet on the NHS.

The Department of Health and Social Care says weight loss jabs are only one part of a broader plan.

It says tackling the promotion of less healthy food and drink, increasing exercise and encouraging people to eat healthier options are all important for addressing obesity.

Earlier this year, England's Chief Medical Officer Prof Sir Chris Whitty said it would be a "societal failure" if medicating people for life was our only answer to obesity.

He says the lessons are there in other countries, such as France, which have kept obesity levels stable.

Now the question is what do we want to learn?

There are now one million young adults living with obesity in England - 700,000 more than if rates had not risen. There have been 14 different obesity strategies in England since 1992.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0qv.title: There's a reason child vaccination rates are falling - and it's not social media
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0qv.text:
Twenty-week-old Grayson easily could have become one of the tens of thousands of British babies left unvaccinated against polio.

His mother, Lily, agrees with the principle of immunisation. But overwhelmed by the early weeks of motherhood, and suffering from post-partum depression after a traumatic birth, she was daunted by the prospect of a long journey to a doctor's surgery. "I've been through the trenches, awake all night. You don't want to leave the house, or go to a different town."

Weeks ticked by, and eventually Grayson missed the polio and diphtheria jabs he was supposed to get at eight weeks old. By that point he was officially classed by the NHS as "overdue" for vaccination; effectively, he was on his GP's naughty list.

Then Lily realised there was a clinic practically on her doorstep - at a location she hadn't expected.

That clinic - in Keighley, West Yorkshire - runs from a vacant retail unit at the Airedale shopping centre, a 1960s-era precinct that locals say has fallen on hard times in recent years, with plenty of empty, boarded-up units. The staff who created the clinic thought: why not use one of those vacant units to administer vaccines?

"This was an empty shop; there was nothing here, the windows were all blacked out," Flora Jennings, a local charity coordinator, tells me over the sound of a baby's laughter, on the morning I visit the clinic.

It's an imaginative solution to a national problem. Over the last 15 years, childhood vaccination rates have fallen across Britain. The share of five-year-olds in England who have received a four-in-one jab (which protects against viruses like polio and tetanus) is now 81%, down from 89% in 2014. About 84% have received both of their recommended MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) jabs, down from 88% a decade ago.

"If you just look at the generalised population, the decline doesn't look horrific," says Prof Dan Hungerford, an epidemiologist at the University of Liverpool who gave evidence to Parliament on this topic. "But if you compare us to other nations, particularly our European neighbours, we are one of the worst-performing countries in terms of getting early-life vaccinations to children."

Politicians are now asking how Britain - the country of Edward Jenner, the "father of immunology" - could have allowed its immunisation rates to drop so low, and what could fix it.

One Labour MP on the Health Committee has gone further, telling the BBC that it's time to consider a policy that's commonplace in some countries, but still something of a taboo in Britain: mandatory childhood immunisations.

Before the 1800s, between 40% and 50% of children in Europe died before their 15th birthday. Now, in Britain that number is well below 1%, according to the UN.

Scientists broadly agree that vaccines were key to this improvement.

"Along with clean water and sanitation, immunisations have had a profound impact on keeping children alive," says Ben Kasstan-Dabush, a lecturer in global health policy at the University of Edinburgh.

And that's why some find it so worrying that Britain's rates have slipped. Last year alone saw measles outbreaks in parts of Birmingham, Bristol, and north London; so far this year, two children in England have died of the disease.

In January, MPs on the Health Committee described the backslide as "national disgrace".

Some blame the rise of misinformation on social media. Last year, a group of American scientists found that reading just one anti-vax Facebook comment about the HPV jab - given to teenagers - was enough to make some parents hesitate.

But all of the public health experts who spoke to the BBC said that whilst anti-vax social media sentiment plays its part, they don't think it's the main reason immunisation rates have slipped.

Instead, they point to something more mundane: they think that parents of young children simply have fewer face-to-face contacts with medical professionals than they did 10 or 15 years ago.

Beccy Baird, a senior fellow at the King's Fund think tank, says that despite colourful media reporting around "anti-vaxxers", most parents who turn down vaccination are not ideologically opposed to it. Convenience plays a big role, she says; vaccination rates are highest when parents regularly interact with medics, who can remind them to get their children jabbed and tell them exactly where to do it.

And those interactions have become rarer. England has seen a 45% decline over the last decade in the number of health visitors (nurses and midwives who treat young children at their home), according to BBC analysis. It's part of a health visitor's job to remind parents about vaccines and, in some cases, administer jabs directly.

And over roughly the same period, the number of fully trained GPs in England struggled to keep up with rising patient demand, according to British Medical Association data; while the Nuffield Trust think tank suggests that patients have become less likely to see the same GP on repeated visits - meaning families don't build trusted relationships with doctors they recognise.

"Those touch points have become fewer," says Kasstan-Dabush.

At Keighley's shopping centre, inside the vaccination clinic, nurses are passing around biscuits.

"The kitchen's there, the playpen's there," says Jennings as she points to a soft-play where parents can leave children while their siblings are vaccinated. "I wanted it to be really inviting, almost like you're walking into someone's home."

The idea of opening a vaccination clinic inside a town centre shopping arcade seemed odd to some of the staff when it was first suggested.

Now, they say it's key to the clinic's success. "We need to make it simple, we need to put services where people come," says Jennings. It means they can catch casual shoppers who "pop their head around the door" and decide on a whim to get their child vaccinated.

"We're right in the centre. And down here it's flat, so you don't have to push a pram up a hill." She says some parents simply won't attend a clinic if it involves more than one bus.

And in the families come. Over the morning, the clinic vaccinates 10 infants, some of whom are classed by the NHS as "overdue". In many cases, the parents actually turn up to use a different service, like baby weighing, but once they are inside, lead GP Dr Zoyah Hussain gently suggests an immunisation - and most parents say yes.

"I do get a lot of questions… 'why do we need to give them jabs?', 'why don't we just let nature manage itself?'," Hussain says.

There's Lily, the 18-year-old who finally gets her son Grayson his polio and diphtheria jabs. And there's Keeley, an assistant in a ceramics shop, who arrives with her baby Luca, and is impressed by the clinic's convenience, with no need for an 08:00 phone call or complicated online form. "It's easy-peasy," she says.

Most of the young mothers have come across online anti-vax posts. "I see these things on Facebook where it's like, don't give your child vaccines because it's got ADHD in them," says Lily. Indeed, Hussain says she still hears parents asking if the MMR jab causes autism, a full 28 years after a link was suggested in a now-discredited paper by the former doctor Andrew Wakefield.

The clinic - which serves a relatively poor community - has vaccinated hundreds of infants since 2023, helping to boost coverage in an area that's historically had a low rate of immunisations. As of March this year, 88% of the children registered with Modality AWC (the GP practice that runs the clinic) now receive their first MMR dose by the age of 18 months, up from 78% three years ago.

"We are bucking that national trend," says Bill Graham, a senior administrator at the practice.

So what can be done about falling vaccination rates across the rest of the country?

One option is to emulate the Keighley model, and open walk-in clinics in vacant retail units. Jennings argues there are crumbling shopping centres all over the country, hit by online shopping, that could do the job.

Baird, from the King's Fund, agrees that vaccination works best when it's carried out in small, easy-to-access local venues - like shopping centres - rather than large, intimidating vaccine hubs that might involve a long journey. In a paper, she studied the roll-out of Covid vaccines in Gloucestershire - and found that "vaccines delivered locally through… familiar community venues - instead of mass-vaccination centres - made access easier, more trusted".

She says: "If you put it in Tesco car park, people will get it."

But some experts are sceptical. Whilst schemes like Keighley's can help on the margins, they say, at the national level a much bigger answer is needed. Hungerford says that child poverty is a key driver of vaccine refusal; parents who have to worry about bills often don't have the brain space to think about immunisations, he says.

And some are pushing for more radical solutions.

Labour MP Paulette Hamilton, a former nurse who was recently interim chair of Parliament's Health Committee, tells the BBC it's time for a "national conversation" on whether child vaccinations should be "opt out" rather than "opt in" (though she stresses she is not speaking on behalf of the committee).

"We were a country that was free of some of these childhood illnesses, and now it's just getting really bad," she says. "The conversation should be about, do you get a small payment [for getting your child vaccinated]? Do you make it mandatory, so you opt out rather than opt in? Is it that we need more education?."

She didn't specify what an "opt out" policy would look like, but various US states already do it. In Texas, a child needs certain vaccinations to attend school, unless their parent fills out a government-issued form explaining a moral, religious, or medical exemption. Supporters say these policies capture the "casual refuseniks" - people who aren't particularly opposed to vaccination, but simply don't make the effort to get their child jabbed.

Other places go further. In Germany, parents can be fined if their children aren't jabbed against measles. Under Australia's "no jab, no pay" policy, parents who refuse immunisations are denied certain benefits.

But those tough, coercive policies leave some uncomfortable. "Mandatory vaccination has been steered away from in the UK for good reason," says Hungerford. For one thing, he thinks, "you risk excluding vulnerable people from things like childcare."

Others say that barring unvaccinated children from school is only likely to alienate their parents further from healthcare, amplifying their mistrust of authority.

At the Keighley shopping centre, Bill Graham says he doesn't think a mandatory approach would work in his corner of Yorkshire. "I think it destroys trust. Healthcare in Britain is based on trust. Maybe the trust isn't quite where it was again 10, 15 years ago, but we're not going to build that up by mandating healthcare."

All that said, experts stress that there's still a degree of mystery about Britain's vaccination problem.

Some parents who refuse jabs simply won't say why - and they're the same groups (poor, lower levels of educational attainment) who are hard to reach via surveys.

This becomes apparent towards the end of my morning at the clinic, when a couple in their thirties arrive to have their baby weighed. Hussain quickly notices that their 23-week-old hasn't had any of his recommended jabs - and asks if they might consider it. The couple glance at each other and quietly shake their heads.

They don't give a reason, and they turn down my request for an interview (the only parents who do so).

Still, Hussain hopes their conversation might have planted a seed. "I've sent her some information. Giving them a platform to speak about their concerns can help.

"It's not us forcing it on anyone. This is a choice."
