https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8x2.title: India wants to join the strawberry superpowers
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8x2.text:
In the west of India, the mountainous region of Mahabaleshwar is home to most of India's strawberry farms.

Around 85% of India's strawberry cultivation happens there.

An altitude of more than 1,000m (3,280ft) gifts the region a long cool growing season between November and March.

In addition, light, well-drained soil is well-suited to strawberry cultivation.

But that doesn't mean farmers have an easy life - it's a labour intensive and risky way to make a living.

"If you have a field full of strawberries and sudden heavy rains hit, the entire crop is ruined and we have to bear massive losses," says Sheetal Danavle who, with her husband, grows strawberries on half of their three-acre farm.

Strawberry plants have to be replaced every season and are not grown from seed. Instead, farmers buy young plants from suppliers. For Danavle, on her small farm, that's an outlay of $2,500 (£1,900) every year.

"If the season goes well, you can earn double your investment. But the climate makes it a huge gamble," she says.

Thousands of farmers grow strawberries across the Mahabaleshwar region, making the fruit one of the most profitable horticultural crops in western India.

Despite that success the industry still relies on varieties that are imported from California, Florida, Italy and Spain, as no one in India has developed a domestic plant.

It can take 10 to 15 years for breeders in the US and Europe to develop a top quality fruit and they patent their varieties.

"We import the certified mother plant from the breeder abroad," says Nelson Sequeira, the founder and director of Tara Farms Fresh, a licensed strawberry propagator.

Once imported the plants have to go through a government quarantine, before they are planted in a nursery. There the mother plant produces daughter plants and those are then sold to farmers.

"One single imported mother plant becomes an engine. That single mother plant will shoot out runners to yield an average of 20 daughter plants - with some advanced growers pushing that up to 30 or 40," says Sequeira.

It's a high-tech and precision operation.

"The plants do not touch the ground. We use large industrial pipes split completely in half to form long, rounded gutter containers," Sequeira explains.

"Instead of soil, we pack these containers with a specialized coco-peat substrate derived entirely from coconut husk. We then integrate a highly precise drip-irrigation and fogging system to control micro-climates."

Sequeira and other propagators rely on mother plants from abroad - for now.

But work at Mahatma Phule Krishi Vidyapeeth (MPKV), an agricultural university in Maharashtra, might change that.

MPKV has partnered with the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) on a breeding experiment.

Researchers are using controlled, low-dose gamma irradiation on plant tissues to induce stable genetic mutations.

"The goal is to fast-track the development of India's first indigenous, climate-resilient strawberry cultivar that matches the large fruit size and firm texture of foreign varieties while natively tolerating Indian heatwaves," says Dr Darshan Shashank Kadam, assistant professor of Horticulture at MPKV.

He admits it could be a long process, with results perhaps in 10 or 15 years. But in the near term they are helping farmers in other ways.

"We are developing scientific packages of practices for farmers. We have already standardised planting schedules, fertiliser recommendations and growth regulator applications specifically for Mahabaleshwar conditions," he says.

Large farms with more resources are investing in new technology.

Ketan Yashwant Sodha, is the founder and CEO of Berry Fresh Agrotech. He started with traditional open-field farming, but was frustrated by losses caused by the weather.

"For the past 10 years, it has consistently rained in India during our peak season - November, December, and the first week of January. When you are in an open field and your plantation is at its absolute peak, a single rain will ruin your entire crop," he says.

So in 2022, he started to experiment with hydroponics, a type of covered cultivation that does not use soil and tightly controls water, nutrients, light, and temperature.

His early results were not encouraging.

"I suffered immense losses and failed multiple times," Sodha says.

"The soil is forgiving; hydroponics does not forgive. If you make a mistake today, you will wake up tomorrow morning to a disaster - and the recovery time in hydroponics takes twice as long as soil."

But the lessons learned from those mistakes are paying off.

"We have trailed 19 different varieties, including rare Japanese ones, and we are the only ones in India trailing a specific Netherlands variety this season."

Sodha says that limiting each plant to 75ml of water a day produces "rich, highly concentrated sugars and aromas instead of water-logged, bland fruits".

His team also runs what he calls regular "blood work" on the crops, which involves laboratory testing of the leaves and petioles (the stalks attaching leaves to the stems) to measure exact nutrient uptake. That way he knows exactly which nutrients and chemicals need to go into the water supply.

And by using a semi-open polyhouse, strawberries can grow the whole year round. "It's not a seasonal fruit for us," Sodha says.

Now he is ready to scale-up.

"We have built the trial facility, written the SOPs (standard operating procedures), and designed the farm manual. We are talking to investors to expand to a five-acre facility that will accommodate 200,000 plants."

Krishan Bhilare's family has been farming strawberries for generations in Mahabaleshwar.

He can remember when the first American varieties were planted in 1992 and being amazed at the size of the fruit.

Bhilare is part of a Farmer Producer Organisation (FPO) network. They have installed towers at four strategic locations across their land. The towers monitor weather conditions.

The system employs AI, which uses the weather data to pinpoint when rain will strike. Farmers can then be advised to delay spraying their crops, so expensive chemicals are not just washed away.

The FPO is also building vertical towers, where strawberries can be grown on a coco-peat substrate, five layers deep.

"By stacking five pots into a single vertical tower, we can scale our density from 25,000 plants to 125,000 plants per acre. We are effectively multiplying our production footprint by five times on the exact same piece of land," says Bhilare.

But such investments are either beyond small farms, or a huge risk.

In 2017, Danavle and her husband experimented with hydroponic strawberry farming.

"The experiment was 100% successful and the fruits we grew were entirely organic. It saved us a lot of labour, the workers didn't have to constantly bend down or prune, and it saved us a lot of money on medicines and field manure."

But they were unlucky - a massive cyclone hit Mahabaleshwar that year.

"The cyclone completely knocked down our entire hydroponic setup. Then we did not have the courage to set it up again."

So, Sheetal went back to the traditional method of growing strawberries, but with a twist.

"I took help of social media. I post videos of how one can grow strawberries and invite tourists to visit my strawberry farm, learn and pick the fruit. They directly now buy from the farm. This has helped, cut the middle man, and make more profit. So, now I am an influencer and entrepreneur."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0jl.title: The Chinese robot army transforming the UK's retail industry
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0jl.text:
Every time you click "buy" on an online order, the chances are that your purchase starts getting processed within minutes.

Increasingly, the journey starts with a squat silver floor robot gliding beneath a storage rack, lifting a shelf and carrying it across a warehouse to a waiting worker.

At Geek+'s factory in the eastern Chinese city of Hefei, which the BBC visited, fleets of the robots are built and tested before being shipped to warehouses around the world.

Some of Britain's biggest retailers - including Tesco, Asda and Next - now use the company's technology.

By automating these repetitive journeys, Geek+ says retailers can increase picking speeds, store more goods in spaces that are hard to reach for humans, and reduce errors.

Unlike traditional warehouse automation, which relies on fixed conveyor systems and permanent infrastructure, autonomous mobile robots can be deployed simply using QR code floor markers and safety fencing.

Geek+, which listed in Hong Kong last year in one of the biggest robotics share sales of 2025, has become the world's largest supplier of autonomous mobile robots.

The UK has struggled with weak productivity growth for more than a decade, and economists say wider adoption of robotics will be essential if businesses are to become more efficient.

In its 2026 report SME Technology Adoption in the United Kingdom, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) said technologies like robotics would be key to improving productivity.

According to the OECD, Britain's low adoption of robotics is "surprising" given its manufacturing heritage, noting that while UK firms have embraced mature digital technologies, they lag behind in robotics and automation.

That presents an opportunity for companies such as Geek+. The UK has one of Europe's largest e-commerce and logistics sectors, but many warehouses are still in the early stages of automation.

Britain has already become Geek+'s biggest European market, with UK partner MotionTech deploying more than 2,000 robots across 10 warehouse sites.

"Customers want fast deployable solutions," says Barry Pemberton, Account Director at MotionTech. "They want high volume, high storage, fast picking... ultimately on a smaller footprint with a reduced headcount."

"We seem to have a very big shortage of labour in the UK at the moment. These technologies are really important to keep businesses thriving and meet demand."

The Trades Union Congress (TUC), which represents almost 6 million UK workers, says robotics should be used to raise productivity and improve jobs, rather than simply cut labour costs.

In its response to the government's consultation on a new AI and innovation strategy, it urged ministers to ensure workers are involved in decisions about automation and that employers invest in retraining.

"Working with technologists, workers and unions can help steer the UK's research and innovation towards workers' priorities for automation... avoiding job-cutting, low-productivity automation," the TUC said in its report.

Robotics has become a strategic priority for Beijing under President Xi Jinping's drive to develop what he calls "new quality productive forces".

With China's working-age population shrinking, policymakers increasingly see automation as essential to boosting productivity and maintaining the country's manufacturing advantage.

"The robotics story builds directly on China's electric vehicle ecosystem," says Kyle Chan, a researcher at the Brookings Institution.

Batteries, electric motors, cameras, sensors and semiconductors developed for electric vehicles (EVs) are increasingly being used across China's robotics sector, creating what he describes as "overlapping industrial ecosystems".

One company leading that crossover is Chinese EV maker XPeng, which unveiled its humanoid robot, Iron, last year.

Founder He Xiaopeng says he no longer sees XPeng simply as a carmaker.

"We want XPeng to be a high-tech company," he told the BBC. "In the future, any car company will transform into a car and robotics company."

Analysts say China's robotics push could follow a similar path as its global EV success, with local players using manufacturing prowess, dense supplier networks and rapid product development to establish an early lead.

"China is deliberately trying to build on some of those strengths," says Chan. "As it reaches into new areas, from humanoid robots to industrial robots to delivery robots."

Tesla is pursuing a similar vision with its Optimus robot, which Elon Musk has said could eventually become a bigger business than carmaking.

But China's ambitions to dominate the global robotics industry was dealt a blow this week when the US banned the import of new foreign-made advanced robots, citing national security.

The Chinese embassy in Washington responded to the move by saying that Beijing has long opposed the US' "politicising" of trade issues and sanctions based on "groundless pretexts".

The Chinese-made robots now operating in British warehouses are designed to solve the problem of moving goods. Geek+ says the company's next goal is to automate everything else.

"We are working on... end-to-end unmanned warehouse solutions," says Yanyu Liu, head of communications at Geek+.

That means automating picking, handling and eventually packing goods.

Across China, companies including AgiBot and Unitree are investing billions in humanoid robots.

But the business case for humanoids is less clear than it is for today's warehouse robots. If wheeled robots move goods cheaply, reliably and efficiently or robots with just arms can do the other automated tasks, what problem does a humanoid solve?

Developers say factories, hospitals and offices have all been designed around people, and so they may eventually be able to work in different environments without the need to redesign workplaces around automation.

But experts and developers alike agree that the current technology is not yet suitable for some repetitive tasks that require more dexterity.

"I don't think [humanoids] will change the landscape of the types of technology or the automation that's going to be put into place," says Pemberton. "They're definitely going to be complementary."

Chinese companies already account for the vast majority of global humanoid deployments, but it may be years before they are commonplace in warehouses.

For Britain, where productivity pressures and labour shortages are driving demand for automation, the country's warehouses are becoming an early testing ground for China's next major technology export.

Additional reporting by Jaltson Akkanath Chummar
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0jl.summary: Robotic firms are increasingly using technology to build and transport robots to warehouses. Geek+ is the world's largest supplier of autonomous mobile robots. The UK has struggled with weak productivity growth for more than a decade.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62q.title: How cow showers and fans help farmers keep cattle cool
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62q.text:
Dairy farmers are installing "cow showers" and giant cooling fans as hotter, drier summers become more common and an official drought has been declared.

Extreme heat has cut milk production by up to 20% and farmers are spending thousands of pounds to keep their cattle cool and protect milk yields.

Sarah Godwin's family have invested £15,000 in a ventilation and sprinkler system at their farm near Chippenham, Wiltshire, to help their animals cope with the "nearly continuous heatwave we are living through".

Professor Nicola Cannon from the Royal Agricultural University (RAU) in Cirencester says drought-hit grassland is also forcing many farmers to use winter feed earlier than planned.

On a dairy farm near Swindon, Sam Woolford presses a switch on the wall of the milking parlour and 10 industrial-scale fans whirr into life.

"It's like a wind tunnel in here," he says.

It blows my hair back, like I'm riding a motorbike at speed.

The cows like it too, it seems, and crucially, they linger in the milking parlour, clearly cool and relaxed.

The system helps keep cattle comfortable during hot weather, but farmers say it cannot eliminate all of the effects of prolonged heat.

"Milk production is down by 20%," Prof Cannon says.

She explains that "cows feel stressed just as humans feel stressed when it's really hot and, as a response to that, their milk productivity goes down.

"So farmers are trying to help their cows, by putting in big fans, or sprinkler systems, to just try and cool animals down."

Experts say prolonged dry weather is now becoming a regular challenge for dairy farms, leaving grass scorched, cattle heat-stressed and farmers relying on winter feed months earlier than planned.

"What we used to think of as extreme weather, we increasingly consider as normal." says Mike Kendon, a climate scientist at the Met Office.

In Somerset, farmers have described this as the worst drought in 50 years, leaving crops struggling.

"Look at this stemmy nonsense," says Woolford, holding a bunch of thin grass towards me.

"There's no leaf to it, they don't get any nutritional quality from this rubbish."

His family have farmed dairy cows just outside Swindon for five generations.

They have seen hot summers and wet ones, but now Woolford, aged 20, and his dad and grandad have noticed a permanent change in the weather.

"We're praying it's not going to become the new norm," he says.

"But it looks like it will recur.

"It's really tough. The cows don't enjoy it, we're down on milk production by 20%, we just need some rain for the grass."

"Basically, soils are parched," explains Prof Cannon.

"There's people quoting 38, 39 days without rainfall now.

"We call that 'permanent wilting point'. Grass can't rebound after grazing, or after cutting for hay or silage."

Woolford's cows still come out into the fields in the morning, but by midday they are back in the barns, sheltering from the sun and eating feedstocks that should have been saved for the winter.

Last year this was news; this year, it is standard practice across west country dairy farming.

Down the road near Chippenham, Godwin's family have gone a step further, installing a network of what they call 'cow showers'- sprinklers that douse the cattle with cool water.

"Farming has got very hard recently," Godwin says.

"It seems like one long heatwave this summer."

The whole system cost £15,000 and "a lot of elbow grease and hard work" to install but it is not unique.

Even ice cream producers are having a tough time.

Just north of Bath, Marshfield Farm churns out some of the West Country's best-known ice creams using milk from its own herd.

Rory Hawkins helps manage the herd that produces all the milk.

"The summers are getting hotter, which is great for the ice cream sales," he explains.

"But it affects the cows with heat stress, and we lose a lot of milk through the hotter summers now."

Hawkins, 27, is one of three children working in the family business.

Speaking to him and Woolford, aged just 20, I wonder why they would commit to a life in dairy farming.

All the Met Office experts agree that these hot summers will be more common, grass will be harder to grow, cows will need cooling down.

"I love working outside, helping look after the animals," Hawkins says.

"Weather is changing, but we just have to crack on with it."

Woolford agrees it is the "variety" of farm work that keeps him interested.

On his farm, I also meet Lara Browne, whose family run a farm near Trowbridge.

"You just have to make the best of the situation, and make your farm as resilient as you can," she says.

While many in their 20s often worry about the changing climate, these young farmers seem determined just to change the way they farm, and get on with it.

"I've not got any kids," Browne says, "but I feel like I'm already farming for the next generation."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62q.summary: Extreme heat has cut milk production by up to 20% and farmers are spending thousands of pounds to keep their cattle cool. Experts say prolonged dry weather is now a regular challenge for dairy farms. Experts agree that hot summers will be more common, more common.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czxe.title: Shop selling second-hand school uniforms for £5
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czxe.text:
An east London charity shop where parents can pick up school uniforms for £5 is helping with the rising cost of living, users have said.

This is the eighth year that S.M.I.L.E. London & Essex, which "provides support to families facing poverty, homelessness, and hardship", runs the swap shop for uniforms from its premises in Romford.

Parent Sandra Koli, on a visit to the shop, told BBC London: "It helps me not to be anxious, because the price is really affordable so I don't have to worry too much.

"This is the right time for it, because by the end of August it will be really crowded and much more expensive - so I can relax and enjoy my summer until the school starts."

Maria Quaife, from S.M.I.L.E. London and Essex, told BBC London: "We've got 1,000 items of school uniform - branded and generic uniform - (from) across Havering, Barking and Dagenham.

"Families can come in, donate items that don't fit their kids any more and grab as much new uniform as their family needs for only £5.

"We tend to get about 500 children coming through our doors each year and it's been getting more and more every year unfortunately because of the cost of living.

"But a new school uniform can cost around £300-400 per child. We're saving families locally thousands of pounds."

The shop also stocks a selection of shoes and football boots at a reduced price.

According to the Department for Education, the average total expenditure on school uniform, based on the items required in the school year 2023/24, was just under £250 and PE kit cost just under £140.

Ishtiaq Khan, also visiting the shop, explained that he has six children.

He said: "Three of them are still going to school. Otherwise, it could have been very much more difficult for us or a struggle for us. But due to this, all arrangements and the provisions, we say that it is one of the very satisfying experiences that we are here to do all these things for the children."

The swap shop is open to all and runs until 22 August. People may also make donations of back to school packs for disadvantaged families.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0qv.title: Jeweller 'priced out' of Christmas market stall this year
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0qv.text:
When silversmith Alex Healy was planning her return to work after maternity leave, the first date she hoped to add to her diary was Liverpool's Christmas market, an event where she had sold jewellery since 2021.

However, due to a change in operator and a rise in costs, Alex said this would be the first winter she would not be renting a stall and she and other traders were being "priced out".

A new company, Underbelly, has taken over this year, and Alex said the cost of running a stall had doubled.

Liverpool City Council, which awarded the tender to Underbelly to run the event at St George's Hall, said the markets offered a "cost-effective way for traders to showcase and sell their products". It added the new operator would manage their own trader arrangements independently. Underbelly has been asked for comment.

Alex, 37, said selling her jewellery at the Christmas market on St George's Plateau for the past five years had been a "really great place to be". She said the friendship between traders had created "a community, family feel".

Alex said she paid £6,780 including VAT and electricity to rent a chalet for the six-week market last year. She said the total cost of renting a chalet this year had risen to just under £14,000 before additional charges.

She said that, under the terms of a new contract, traders would be expected to pay additional charges for water and grey waste, chiller and storage space, and energy supply.

Alex said it felt like she and other traders were being "priced out" of an event that had previously been run by a smaller, local company. She added "I feel like Liverpool council have just treated us not even as a second thought really."

She said despite trying to take time off with her new baby, she had still been preparing for the market, as it usually provided 80% of her Christmas market income. She added that her business, Pare de Bijoux, might not survive if she could not afford to be part of the event.

A Liverpool City Council spokesperson said: "The operators at St George's Hall and Pier Head manage their own trader arrangements independently, however Liverpool Markets will once again be organising festive pop-up markets in locations across the city during the Christmas period." They added that these markets were "Designed to support local and independent businesses" and would offer a "cost-effective way for traders to showcase and sell their products."

A Christmas market has taken place on St George's Plateau in Liverpool for a decade.

Global events company Underbelly won the tender to operate the event earlier this year. The company already manages two festive events in central London.

The company said it would bring a new outdoor ice-skating experience, 'Skate St George's', to the city-centre landmark.

Ed Bartlam, co-founder of Underbelly, said: "Set against the magnificent backdrop of St George's Hall, we're looking forward to working with the local community to create a new seasonal highlight that complements Liverpool's festive calendar."

The company did not respond to a request for a specific comment to address the concerns over the rise in costs for vendors.

Liverpool council said the city's Christmas Markets attract more than 500,000 visitors each year and deliver "a significant economic boost to the city."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yr.title: Mums hope school uniform swap will help families
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yr.text:
A free school uniform swap has been set up by two mums who want to help stop families from "forking out" on "expensive" clothing.

Bex and Faye created the Tavistock Uniform Swap Shop in Devon where people could donate clothing their children had outgrown along with having a selection of new items as well.

A stall at Tavistock Library was set up on Thursday where they received three "huge boxes" of uniforms from lost property at local schools, as well as half a dozen bags from the community.

Bex said a lot of parents and guardians were "in the same situation" and she and Faye hoped it would help people financially while also stopping clothes being thrown away.

Donations in Tavistock included branded and unbranded jumpers, shirts, skirts, dresses, wet weather clothing, shoes, lunchboxes and trousers.

Bex and Faye, who have been friends for 10 years, said people who visited were "shocked" everything was free and they did not have to make a donation to do a swap.

Bex, who works at a nursery in Tavistock, said: "We are all in the same situation, it doesn't matter if you're working full-time, things are really expensive and if we can save on something like this, then let's do it."

In September, a new law from the Department for Education will be introduced on branded school items in England.

It means parents and guardians will not have to buy more than three branded items, plus a tie for children in secondary school.

The government decided to create the law after it was estimated a quarter of secondary schools still had four or more items on its list last year.

Bex said it was "relief" there was at least a limit on the branded items, but it depended on what items the school or establishment chose.

"I think in the long run, if the cost of living keeps going up, we are going to need to push for there to be less and less uniforms with logos, but it will definitely help," Bex said.

Mum-of-two Faye said the price of uniform depended on the school and what their rules were around branded items, but some school uniforms could set a family back about £60 per child.

She said the swap event helped families from having to "fork out" on uniforms.

The retail supervisor said: "Children lose their uniforms or it gets dirty, so you're often having to re-buy stuff throughout the year.

"But at least this way it helps with the cost for families not worrying so much about how they're going to get their school uniforms for their children."

Bex said it was also a sustainable way to re-use clothing that would otherwise be thrown in the bin.

She said her daughter's dresses and labelled items still had "so much wear left in them", but they were too small.

"It's great places like the recycling centres take clothing, but that doesn't go back to families again," Bex said.

"I think it's really important, particularly the grey trousers, the dresses and the whites to be reused because they're all universal and any school can use them."

Faye and Bex said the event in Tavistock had been a "success" as more than half the uniform they started with had been taken and they received lots of messages asking when the next swap would be.

They hope to run another event towards the end of the summer holidays.

The pair added if they received good feedback, they would make it an annual event.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2d.title: Hospital staff work in pubs to balance cost pressure
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2d.text:
Staff at a Kent hospital have said they pick up shifts in pubs to balance cost pressures caused by increased parking charges and wage cuts.

The cost of parking at Gillingham's Medway Maritime Hospital for one day increased from £9.20 to £15 at the start of August, while in May bank shift wages were reduced by 20%, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.

One midwife, who wished to remain anonymous, said the increased costs had led many to consider their positions.

Siobhan Callanan, interim chief executive of Medway NHS Foundation Trust, said: "While we are unable to provide free parking for all colleagues, eligible staff can apply for an on-site parking permit to use designated staff parking areas."

The midwife said that she had to budget £250 a month to travel into work.

"They're kicking us whilst we're down, and I could get more as a cleaner. Some of us are doing cash-in-hand work in pubs," she said.

"It sounds ridiculous. How can you be such a qualified professional, but you're getting more money pulling pints behind a bar?"

The trust said that all income from the car parks went firstly towards maintenance and then "directly into patient care and services".

Reducing bank shift wages caused more than financial issues, the midwife added.

"We're short-staffed, we're asking people to work outside of their specialties," she said.

Medway Council deputy leader Teresa Murray said he wanted to meet with leadership about this issue.

"The hospital has a £47m deficit and this is their decision to make, but overall, this is not making anything any better," she said.

Callanan added: "We understand that any increase in parking charges is difficult for patients and visitors.

"A range of parking concessions remain available for eligible patients and visitors and the hospital is well served by public transport links.

"Our staff are highly valued and we remain committed to supporting them wherever possible."

Free off-site parking and a shuttle bus service is available to all staff, she added.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yz.title: The homeowners selling up for a life on the water
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yz.text:
The cost of living crisis is well documented and for many people a mortgage is a millstone around their necks - but a growing number have chosen to cut costs by swapping their houses for a narrowboat.

The BBC took to the waterside in Leeds to find out how it's worked out for some of them.

Ken Tracey, 57, sold his house in Suffolk in 2022, citing the need for "a change in life".

"The cost of the house, it was really tricky to keep up with everything, keep the payments going," he says.

"I've not got a mortgage any more, but I own this, so it's safe."

However, he admits there are "swings and roundabouts" to his new lifestyle.

Alongside trying to save money, Ken says he bought the boat to "live an adventure" - but admits he had not realised how difficult boat life would sometimes be.

"You're not really prepared for it at the start - things like winter are a different thing.

"You've got to deal with a whole load of things that you wouldn't have to deal with if you're in a house. And then travelling around, you've got to solve problems every day."

He described life on a narrowboat as "not a land of health and safety" and warned: "Locks are dangerous places".

"This is technology that's a couple of hundred years old now and you can see that in some places," he claimed.

It also took him more than 18 months to "get to grips" with steering the boat.

"It takes weeks and weeks of bumping into things, scraping along the side of things, before you can work out the best way to steer it."

Ken spent £75,000 on his boat and a further £20,000 on unforeseen maintenance.

However, he still feels the decision was the right one.

"I wouldn't necessarily choose the same path to get here - but I like being here," he says.

"It's amazing, it's genuinely amazing."

Ken is not the only person to have opted for a new life on the water.

The Canal and River Trust says that, post-Covid, our waterways have increasingly become "places of dwelling".

According to the Trust's annual Boaters' Survey for 2026, in Yorkshire and the North East just over a third of respondents (34%) said they used their boat as a permanent home - compared to 27% in 2025.

Just under half (49%) of respondents in Yorkshire and the North East said they used their boat as a temporary home.

After holidaying on narrowboats, Andy Brown said it was "a fairly easy decision" for him and his wife to move into one post-retirement.

Before they retired, their son died, which they say also influenced their decision to make the move.

"I'm sure he would have loved to have done all this so he's always at the back of our thoughts wherever we are and wherever we go," Andy says.

They traded their life at home in Edinburgh and have been living on board for around two and a half years since having the narrowboat built for them.

"It's been fantastic," says Andy.

"It slows you down and you get to see places you just wouldn't see in a car. We've seen places we just never would have dreamed of stopping at before."

He says the Leeds Liverpool canal is among his highlights, as was "skirting along the southern edge of the [Yorkshire] Dales."

Though a significant downsize from a house, Andy says it's not necessarily much cheaper.

"It's probably a bit cheaper than living in a house, but not significantly so," he says.

Ken Marshall, from Wakefield, has owned his boat Willow for about eight years. Two years ago, he decided to sell up his house and move on board full time.

"There's struggles involved living on a boat, but I enjoy it," he says.

Moored up in Leeds city centre's Granary Wharf, with his son on board for a few weeks, Ken says he still feels a sense of community despite not having permanent neighbours.

"I find in general that that people you know are very open to talking and helping," he says.

Now working part-time, Ken says he has "no regrets whatsoever" about his decision to sell his house and move onto the water.

One of the main things he bears in mind when deciding where to moor up is ensuring he can get to and from work from there.

Ken says his favourite thing about moving onboard is being able to choose your surroundings.

"I like being here in the city centre, but then I also like to be able to get back into somewhere quiet, where you're surrounded by fields and nature."

Eric Wilson is new to the waters. He has been living on his narrowboat for just over a month after cashing in his pension to make the move.

He says he found the transition "easy enough", but travelling around is difficult.

"I was supposed to be living the dream, but it's not turned out that way really," Eric explains.

"I was expecting to go off and travel the canal network, but I tried doing a couple of locks and it's too hard for me now.

"I think you've got to be fit, really," he admits.

Eric is hoping to get used to locks and steering so he is able to travel the network in his new home.

Alex Hennessy, the national boating manager at the Canal and River Trust, urges anyone considering a life on the water to "do [their] homework".

"There are so many great hire boat operators across our network and it's a great way to get a flavour of what life is like on the water," he adds.

"I would certainly recommend trying a hire boat holiday first, and you can gradually build it from there."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8e2.title: Why Gen Z are planning for life without a state pension
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8e2.text:
Joel has finally landed his first graduate engineering job after several years of lower‑paid roles. He's in his early 20s, lives with his parents and works in London. But instead of splashing the extra cash, or saving up for holidays or a house deposit, he's decided to squirrel more of it away into his workplace pension.

The reason? He doesn't think he'll get any kind of state pension. Like Joel, around half of Gen Z (those born from 1997–2012) say they don't expect the state pension to exist by the time they retire. It's pretty stark to hear, but growing up with constant headlines about an ageing population, a proportionally smaller working-age population, and the pressure that government finances are under, Joel thinks it's his generation that will suffer.

"I don't believe that I'll be a recipient of a state pension. I know a lot of people my age don't think they're going to be... There just won't be enough money," he says.

Retirement has always felt distant when you're in your 20s - something to think about later. But what's emerging among today's under‑30s is something different: not just distance, but doubt.

"It just mathematically doesn't make sense… There has to get to a point where that state pension is taking up too much of the budget and can't exist in the way that it exists right now," Joel says.

The state pension age is shifting. At the start of April, the age at which you receive it began to gradually creep up, rising from 66 years to 67 years by March 2028. It's due to go up again in 20 years' time to 68, though that might happen earlier as the government has an ongoing independent review.

That's a frustration for 27-year-old retail manager Connor, who got in touch via BBC Your Voice, because he says "the goalpost keeps moving". "At the minute I'll be 68 by the time I can retire, but I do think I'll be probably closer to 75, if I'm honest."

More than 13 million people - 19% of the population - are currently of state pension age. By 2050, even with the state pension age rising to 68, that group is projected to exceed 15 million people, nearly a quarter of the population, with numbers projected to climb towards 17 million by the 2070s. In other words, there will be lots more people qualifying for the state pension, and fewer working people, as a proportion, paying taxes into the pot to cover the bill.

At the same time, almost half of working‑age adults are not paying into a private pension pot. That means many will be relying solely on the state pension for their retirement income - and with relative poverty rates among pensioners now at 14%, we can already see how difficult that can be.

Experts warn that if a whole generation stops believing the state pension will be there, it could push people towards more risky investments, prompt overly restrictive behaviour, or lead others not to save at all.

So, are we heading towards a major pension crisis for many in Gen Z? And if we are, might the Gen Z generation end up redefining what retirement looks like?

For those hitting the state pension milestone today, as long as they've made 35 years of National Insurance contributions, they're entitled to £241.30 a week.

That amount rises each year to help people keep pace with rising living costs. Since 2011, pension increases have been guaranteed by the triple lock - which means the rise will either match the rate of inflation, average earnings or 2.5% - whichever is higher.

But in recent weeks, several organisations have called for the rules to be rewritten.

The centre-left Resolution Foundation think tank has argued for scrapping the triple lock, saying that continuing to prioritise the incomes of pensioners over working-age adults and children would be unfair.

Meanwhile, the Tony Blair Institute (TBI), a think tank set up by the former prime minister, takes things a step further and has called for the whole state pension to be scrapped and replaced with a new "Lifespan Fund". Thomas Smith, director of economic policy at the TBI, argued: "Britain's state pension system was built for a different era. We can't keep pouring money into a system that is increasingly unaffordable."

It suggests scrapping the triple lock and allowing people to access some of their state pension early if they need it because of redundancy and frequent job changes.

That's an idea that might appeal to Connor in Chesterfield. He's facing redundancy from his job at a global cosmetics firm, and the ability to draw down a small amount - effectively a withdrawal from his future state pension - might tide him through.

"There's not that many jobs out there at the minute, unfortunately. I still live at home with my parents luckily, but I pay board to them. I still have a car payment, I still have my insurance to pay."

But former pensions minister Steve Webb argues those changes would be "a huge backward step". He says the benefit of the current system is its simplicity which shouldn't be replaced with "something fiendishly complex and highly intrusive, which would take many decades to implement in full."

The government says it has committed to the triple lock for the rest of this parliament, and that the Pensions Commission, an independent body set up to review the regime for UK private pensions, is examining "how we can ensure secure retirements for tomorrow's pensioners".

It's likely that those in their 20s will not have a triple‑locked pension. That means living on the state pension alone will become more difficult, as its value may rise more slowly than the cost of food, travel, clothing and household bills.

For those who doubt the triple lock will endure, the debate often shifts to how the state pension can be sustained at all. One idea that regularly surfaces is means‑testing. In some ways it already is: very low‑income pensioners can receive an additional benefit called Pension Credit. But 24‑year‑old Joel believes that for the state pension to survive, the choices may need to be more radical.

"I don't think a means-tested state pension is necessarily a bad thing. But it would be a bad thing if it only applies to people in 50 years and not now when we should be saving some of that money."

Engineer Joel is one of life's squirrels. His fear about the future of the state pension means he's doubling-down on his private pension. He contacted BBC Your Voice because he feels that consecutive governments have sheltered current pensioners, leaving the consequences for his generation to face.

"I'm going to have to increase the amount of my paycheck that goes into a private pension, which obviously isn't good with cost of living through the roof," he says.

The scale of what younger workers may need to save adds to that anxiety for some. Investment company Rathbones estimates that a single person retiring today at 65 (with the state pension) may need around £796,000 in savings to fund a "comfortable retirement". If the state pension remains, a 25‑year‑old today would need a pot of around £1.68m to retire comfortably as a single person. Without the state pension, the figure for Gen Z jumps to more than £2.4m.

Against this backdrop, Joel says many of his friends are considering opting out of private and workplace pensions altogether and investing independently instead, mostly in "crypto or index funds and things like that.

"There's a sense, whether it's right or wrong, that that's more secure than putting it in a pension where they're also going to take a chip on top."

It's possible that individual investment choices could earn more than a pension scheme, but it's a big gamble.

Behavioural economics suggests that when people lose trust in a system, they tend to either opt out entirely or over‑compensate. Both can be problematic. Saving extra in a private pension may limit current life options, but opting out can leave many with riskier retirement savings, or indeed none at all.

In central Manchester, 23‑year‑old Ashleigh agrees with Joel that the state pension is unlikely to be coming her way: "At this rate I don't think anyone's ever going to retire, I think everyone will just have to fend for themselves in the end."

But as someone on a lower income, her pension choices are less squirrel‑like. When working for a big retailer, she says that she chose to stop contributing to her employer's auto-enrolment pension.

"I opted out of it. I need the money now." She explains: "I'd rather save for a house and then at least I have something to show for it".

Some experts warn that the gap between rich and poor in retirement could widen significantly for this generation.

Dr Suzy Morrissey, deputy director at the Pensions Policy Institute (PPI), believes that alongside how much Gen Z save privately, another factor will widen the divide: far more of them will be renting.

"Renting in retirement increases your chances of pensioner poverty, and they do face challenges to save, as younger people, that previous generations didn't face when they were at the same age," she says. "If we have people paying rent in retirement who don't have large pension pots to cover those expenses, then that equals higher risk of pensioner poverty."

But Morrissey sees a silver lining: pensions auto-enrollment, the system that automatically puts most employees into a workplace pension unless they opt out. If they've been employees, "they will have spent their working life contributing into a pension pot, and they will be the first generation that will have spent their whole life doing that."

It'll be a backstop for many, but the minimum contribution rate is unlikely to be enough for a comfortable retirement. It's not automatic for the self-employed and people like Ashleigh have opted out because of immediate financial pressures, so it looks like plenty won't see the benefit of that silver lining.

For some, the response to an uncertain future is to focus on the present.

Lauren, from Hull, says: "Money always comes back, time doesn't. The world is so vast, we shouldn't wait till the last 10/20 years of our lives to go out and see it!"

At 24, she's about to take six months off from her job as a business coordinator. She's one of a growing number planning to take regular career breaks, or "grown-up gap years", which many are terming "mini retirement". HSBC's 2025 UK survey found that 63% of Gen Z plan to take at least one mini‑retirement, compared with 32% of Gen X and 13% of Boomers.

"The majority of my friends don't pay into pensions and instead decide to take their whole wage [after taxes] and spend it how they see fit. A large proportion goes on travels or holidays," says Lauren.

"I currently don't pay into a pension, actually I never have. I'd way rather have my money now and use it to live life," she says.

But there's a warning for Gen Z from the experience of the Waspi women - hundreds of thousands born in the 1950s who campaigners say have suffered because of poorly communicated rises in the state pension age. Their financial shock shows that costs may only become clear when it's too late to course-correct.

If Gen Z's suspicions are right, and the state pension becomes a less dependable part of income in later life, then more will have to take a totally different approach to retirement, savings and life choices to navigate the new landscape.

Additional reporting: Kris Bramwell and Harriet Whitehead

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0l5.title: Andy Burnham to embark on cost of living tour through the UK
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0l5.text:
The prime minister is set to announce "a series of measures to make life easier" for those struggling with the cost of living in the coming days, Downing Street says.

No 10 says Andy Burnham's plans are to "give people some room to breathe". He will also focus on ways of "improving high streets" as he embarks on a tour of the UK.

But the government is facing continued pressure over its early release scheme for prisoners in England and Wales – with criticism of the fact that two of PC Andrew Harper's killers will be eligible from next year.

Burnham is also likely to face pressure for more action on the cost of living – although significant interventions are unlikely before October's Budget.

Even then, Chancellor John Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" – which will limit how much the government has to spend.

The prime minister has been on holiday this week, but Downing Street said he would be in "listening mode" in the coming days as he tours the UK's nations and regions and works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

A spokesman for the prime minister said: "He thinks Westminster has got used to telling people that everyday hassles – like hidden pricing and consumers being ripped off – must be accepted as part of life.

"He doesn't think that's right. That's why he's going to start rolling out a series of pro-consumer cost of living measures to give people some room to breathe."

The spokesman added: "He's also going to be kicking off his summer tour around the country, getting out of Westminster and meeting people where they are.

"The prime minister is going to be in listening mode to help inform his 10-year plan to bring back hope and make Britain better off."

There are, though, likely to be continued questions about the forthcoming early release scheme, due to start in October.

One of Burnham's first acts in Downing Street was to order a review which limited the range of people who would be eligible.

But those convicted of manslaughter will still qualify for the scheme – including two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper.

The prime minister has faced calls from PC Harper's family, former senior police officers and opposition politicians for them to be denied early release.

But he has said he cannot go any further without risking prison capacity. Downing Street said on Saturday night that position remained unchanged, despite reports the prime minister could revisit the case.

Despite early release schemes having been in place for England and Wales since late 2023 under the previous Conservative government, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has warned the prison population could overtake capacity as soon as this November.

The latest figures for England and Wales, recorded on 23 August, showed the prison population was at 86,495 - more than 97% of useable capacity.

On the cost of living plans, the Conservatives said the government's "tax hikes and red tape are hammering our high streets".

Shadow chancellor Mel Stride said: "This is breathtaking hypocrisy from Burnham… they are forcing businesses to close, destroying jobs and driving up prices for the public.

"Meanwhile, Labour are plotting to release dangerous criminals onto our streets, leaving people feeling unsafe in their communities."

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper said struggling high street businesses "need more than a new PM embarking on a vanity tour this summer".

She said the PM should adopt the Lib Dem plan for high streets: "That means reversing the damaging jobs tax, delivering an emergency VAT cut for hospitality, replacing broken business rates and cracking down on the ghost landlords leaving our shop fronts vacant."

Reform UK's economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "If Andy Burnham wants to help people with the cost of living, he should scrap the green levies and taxes on energy bills and rule out tax rises at the Budget."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0l5.summary: Andy Burnham will announce plans to "give people some room to breathe" No 10 says he will be in "listening mode" as he tours the UK's nations and regions. But the government is facing pressure over early release scheme for prisoners in England and Wales.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8en.title: Streeting 'sickened' by sex abuse claims at Army college
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8en.text:
Warning: This article contains sexual language and details of sexual assault

Wes Streeting has said he is "absolutely sickened" by reports of rape and sexual abuse of young female recruits at the Army Foundation College (AFC) in Harrogate.

Four women told the BBC they were sexually assaulted and harassed while attending the North Yorkshire college, and described a culture of misogyny and sexual violence.

The defence secretary said he would be "looking in detail specifically at what's gone wrong at Harrogate, but also looking more broadly at how we lead a programme of culture change across our armed forces and across defence."

The Army said "unacceptable and criminal behaviour has absolutely no place in our armed forces" and urged victims and witnesses to come forward.

AFC is the largest military training establishment for under-19s in the UK and it receives all the Army's 16-year-old recruits.

North Yorkshire Police told the BBC in a response to a Freedom of Information Act request it had received 16 reports of sexual offences linked to the college in the year to June, including allegations of exposure, voyeurism and sexual assault.

No information was included on whether the reports had led to prosecutions.

A total of 176 complaints of inappropriate sexual behaviour at the college were made between January 2018 and June 2025, according to Ministry of Defence (MoD) data.

The women, whose names have been changed to protect their identities, all attended AFC over the last five years.

One woman, Tilly, told the BBC she was 17 when she was raped at AFC by several fellow soldiers who invited her into their room.

"They started taking my clothes off and then this led to them doing stuff I didn't consent to.

"And then I was raped… by multiple junior soldiers, same age as me. It went on for hours. I felt like a piece of meat."

Streeting said he sympathised with the women who had been "badly failed", and praised them for speaking up.

"We have a duty to uphold the very highest standards in uniform and to treat every woman with the dignity and respect she deserves.

"I don't want anyone who has the ambition and talent to join our armed forces to be deterred, so it's contingent on us to make sure that we've got our act together," he added.

Another woman's story was shared with the BBC by her mother, who said her daughter Amy was sexually assaulted and subjected to almost daily sexual harassment during her training.

Because the lock to Amy's room was not working, her mother said "she found herself sleeping across the door to stop male soldiers coming in".

Another woman, who said she was sexually assaulted and harassed at AFC, described how misogynistic attitudes and behaviour of staff rubbed off on some of the male teenagers.

She recalled one of the instructors saying: "It's all about the pussy and how much of it you can get."

The MoD told the BBC that the college "welcomes external scrutiny and challenge".

It said that AFC had in the last year "hosted the safeguarding bodies, parliamentarians, the Children's Commissioner's office and the Armed Forces Commissioner, as well as receiving an outstanding report from Ofsted".

Earlier this week, Sarah Atherton, former MP for Wrexham, told the BBC that public confidence in the college could "only be restored through an independent inquiry".

Atherton, who previously served in the Army's Intelligence Corps, led a 2021 government review into the experiences of women in the armed forces.

Emma Lewell MP said: "If this was any other school or residential environment for children, it would have been closed down."

The Children's Commissioner for England Dame Rachel de Souza said she would ensure the "appalling attacks" were investigated and "those responsible, including for failing to safeguard these girls, are held to account".

She said all children living away from home had a right to contact her team for support, and that she would make sure all girls at AFC could do so.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8en.summary: Army Foundation College in Harrogate received 16 reports of sexual offences in the year to June. Four women told the BBC they were sexually assaulted and harassed at the college. The Army said "unacceptable and criminal behaviour has absolutely no place in our armed forces"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdew.title: Prisoner release row proving to be Burnham's first big test as PM
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdew.text:
Three weeks into his premiership, Andy Burnham has "hit bumps in the road" in the estimation of one long-serving Labour MP with the row over the early release of some prisoners from jail.

His political opponents are already sharpening their attacks, believing they have found an issue with which to discomfit a new prime minister early in his time in office who had, until now, displayed a pretty deft political touch.

Conservative Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: "This the most important decision Andy Burnham has made since he became prime minister and he's got it wrong."

For Labour MPs, however, this week has shown Burnham is prepared to confront difficult choices and take decisions which, as he said in his first speech in Downing Street, are "more about problem solving than point scoring".

Burnham's first two weeks in the job were pretty problem free, with a succession of announcements, from a cap on bus fares to a determination to overhaul of social care, along with a blitz of social media videos, all designed to portray a more relaxed PM with a focus on everyday issues.

The overcrowding crisis in our prisons has presented him with a dilemma for which there are only unpalatable choices.

Crucially too, they are some of the first difficult choices Burnham has had to make in office.

The issue long predates his arrival in Downing Street. In 2023, with space in jails on the verge of running out, the last Conservative government started releasing prisoners 18 days early. That was only a temporary fix.

Just days after becoming prime minister in July 2024, Sir Keir Starmer had to contemplate a more far-reaching prisoner release scheme, saying "it is shocking for our country to have got into a state where we have too many prisoners and not enough prison places".

In January this year, Sir Keir's government passed the Sentencing Act under which several thousand prisoners will be released early starting this autumn, including some convicted of very serious crimes.

Andy Burnham, aware of how sensitive this would be, immediately ordered a review.

His frustration was evident when he announced he was removing some categories of prisoner from early release, rapists and child sex offenders among them, but not others.

"The truth is I wanted to go even further," he said, "I have pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do".

The Conservatives seized on the fact that his decisions mean that among those still being let out early will be some who committed grooming-related crimes as well as some killers, including those of PC Andrew Harper.

"The Labour government has made mistake after mistake on this early release scheme," said Chris Philp.

"Despite our warnings in Parliament, they initially planned to release rapists and dangerous criminals.

"But, even after Andy Burnham's review, it turns out they still plan to release cop-killers and men involved in the grooming gang scandal early. It's an insult to PC Harper's family and many other victims."

Up against Sir Keir, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch managed to find issues she could use to force him on to the back foot and into what turned out to be a damaging series of policy shifts. She has seized on the early releases to do try to do the same with his successor.

A first sign of that came when Burnham had to "personally intervene" this week, his spokesperson said, to order officials to find out how many people convicted of grooming-related offences might still be getting early release.

That came after Badenoch highlighted the issue in an open letter to him.

The Conservatives are now considering how they can keep the pressure up when parliament returns in September.

They will aim to place Labour MPs in an uncomfortable position if the issue can be debated in the Commons.

Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy has called on the government to introduce "emergency primary legislation as soon as Parliament returns in September," as he says that is the only way to permanently exclude "killers - like the killers of PC Harper - child abusers and grooming gang members from early release".

For now, Labour MPs are off on their summer breaks.

"There is no point in bemoaning what is going on" one says phlegmatically, "Andy Burnham's inherited this vexed issue that our jails are full, it's in the nature of being PM.".

"I have every confidence in him. Over all the years Andy Burnham has never been fearful of speaking to victims directly," adds the MP who has served on the justice select committee.

But they added: "We need to have an honest conversation about who we are sending to jail as we don't have the spaces to accommodate everyone we are sending."

Another MP, from the left of the party, said Labour members still felt overwhelmingly positive about their new leader despite the row over prisoner releases.

"They don't believe he has a magic wand. I don't blame him for the overcrowding crisis and I don't think voters do".

And the MP added "at least we have a recognisably Labour government. It feels like we are in play again, with a second chance to make a difference, maybe even to win a second term".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdew.summary: Andy Burnham has "hit bumps in the road" in the estimation of one long-serving Labour MP. His political opponents are sharpening their attacks on the issue. The overcrowding crisis in our prisons has presented him with a dilemma for which there are only unpalatable choices.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd69.title: Conservatives pledge to ban foreign nationals from social housing
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd69.text:
The Conservatives have said they would end the provision of social housing for foreign nationals in England if they win power at the next election.

The party said ending new tenancies for all foreign nationals, as well as current tenancies for couples where neither person is a UK, Irish or EU citizen, would free up an estimated 228,144 homes for British families.

The Conservatives said Labour had "lost control of immigration" and British families had been left sitting on housing waiting lists as a result.

But Labour said the policy was an "unserious, unworkable proposal, copied from Reform, that does nothing to tackle the housing crisis the Tories themselves created".

In June, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said he would make it a requirement for foreign national tenants to find private accommodation within three months or face possible deportation if his party won power.

Under the Tory proposals, ineligible tenants would be expected to move out of their homes within six months.

Any single person currently living in social housing who is not a UK, Irish or EU citizen would lose their social home. This includes those with or without children.

Couples, where neither of them are UK or EU citizens, and they do not have EU settled status, will also lose their entitlement.

Anyone with EU settled status would not be evicted.

For future tenancies, UK nationals and those with EU settled status would be eligible but any new EU citizens without settled status would not be.

Foreign nationals with settled status, refugee status, or specific humanitarian protections can currently qualify for social housing.

Asylum seekers are not eligible for social housing, unless in exceptional circumstances such as domestic abuse cases.

Social housing, usually provided by housing associations or local councils, is typically cheaper and more secure than privately rented homes.

When they were last in government in 2024, the Conservatives were considering plans to make it a requirement for foreign nationals to have to live in the UK for 10 years before qualifying for social housing.

There are 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists, as of March 2025, the latest government figures.

The vast majority of social housing lettings are given to single people.

In 2024-25, most lead tenants of new social lettings, the person in whose name the social home is rented, were UK nationals - 89% or 233,000 tenants.

In the same period, 2.3% of new lettings were given to refugees - 800 refugees were UK nationals, while the remaining 3,900 were non-UK nationals.

The most common nationality of refugees in a new social letting was Afghanistan with the second most common being Ukraine.

Conservative shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said: "Making Britain your home should be earned by working, paying tax and integrating.

"It should not come with a free ride on the benefits system. Britain cannot be a cash machine for the world.

"Labour has lost control of immigration and lost control of the welfare bill, and it is British families picking up the bill and sitting on waiting lists."

Labour's Housing Secretary Angela Rayner said the Conservative policy would primarily affect refugees and long-term UK residents who had contributed to the country, while also leaving more families at risk of homelessness.

"No amount of headline-chasing, or following Reform to the extremes, can hide the damage the Tories did to our housing system," she said, adding: "This unserious, unworkable proposal, copied from Reform, would do nothing to tackle the housing crisis the Tories themselves created."

Housing and homelessness charity Shelter said there were already strict rules on eligibility for social housing and accommodation was not handed out to people on arrival.

"These divisive plans would brutally kick people out of their homes, including thousands of families and pensioners who have lived in them for decades," chief executive Sarah Elliott said.

"The housing emergency is caused by successive governments failure to build enough genuinely affordable social homes - not by who accesses social housing."

Reform UK's home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf said the Conservatives were trying to copy his party's policy but accused them of not going far enough as their proposed ban does not include those with EU settled status.

"Incredibly, Kemi Badenoch's new policy is to allow tens of thousands of foreign nationals from the EU to occupy British social housing funded by British taxpayers," he said.

"Reform UK will ensure British social housing is strictly for British citizens."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwy4.title: Badenoch pens letter to Clacton ahead of by-election
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwy4.text:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has vowed to "put forward a serious candidate" to run in a coastal by-election if a standards investigation leads to another one.

Voters in Clacton in Essex are due to go to the polls on Thursday after Nigel Farage stood down as an MP, triggering a by-election that he will stand in.

Reform UK's leader will be one of 34 candidates on the lengthy ballot paper, although Labour, the Conservatives, Liberal Democrats and Greens are not putting up candidates, claiming the resignation is a stunt with no bearing on the inquiry.

In a letter "to the people of Clacton", Badenoch wrote: "Nigel Farage has called this by-election not to help you, but to help himself."

Farage was being investigated by the parliamentary standards commissioner Daniel Greenberg over a £5m gift from cryptocurrency tycoon Christopher Harborne, which he received before taking his seat in the House of Commons.

The investigation was looking into whether he should have declared the money when he arrived in Parliament.

But it was suspended on his resignation and is likely to resume if he wins the by-election, which he is billing as a public vote on the issue of his honesty.

If he is found to have broken the rules and a suspension of more than 10 days is imposed, it could trigger a recall petition and the prospect of Farage losing his seat, forcing another public vote.

Badenoch wrote: "Mr Farage wants the people of Clacton to settle his problems for him.

"He wants to point to you and say, 'even after the £5m scandal, Clacton still chose me'.

"The people of Clacton are entitled to ask why someone would donate Nigel Farage that kind of money".

The Reform leader has said the money was an "unconditional gift".

Farage previously said the money was for his security, given to him "with the knowledge that the state in this country has never, ever wanted to help" with his personal protection.

Badenoch, who is the North West Essex MP, continued: "When the proper process has run its course and there is a genuine contest, we will be there.

"I will put forward a serious candidate who understands that representing Clacton is a job — someone who turns up, listens, holds meetings and works for the people who live here.

"When the real choice comes, the Conservatives will be there and I hope we can earn your support."

Farage's opponents in Clacton include Count Binface, actor-turned-politician Laurence Fox, and three candidates from the Official Monster Raving Loony Party – Nick The Incredible Flying Brick, its leader Alan "Howling Laud" Hope and Baron Von Thunderclap.

A spokesperson for Reform UK said: "If Kemi Badenoch and the Conservatives truly had any respect for democracy they would have stood a candidate in this by-election.

"The truth is that the Tories have turned their backs on the people of Clacton by refusing to put up a candidate. It's the latest in a long list of betrayals.

"Voters here have the chance to send a resounding message to the Tories and the rest of the failing political establishment by voting for Nigel Farage and Reform next Thursday."

The constituency includes the towns of Clacton-on-Sea, Frinton-on-Sea and Walton-on-the-Naze, as well as villages stretching inland to Frating, Tendring, Wix and Little Oakley.

A full list of the 34 candidates is available here.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyv.title: Government criticised over plastic spill response
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyv.text:
Andy Burnham has pledged to be the prime minister for the North. But volunteers cleaning up a major plastic spill on the north-east of England coast say his government's treatment of the "disaster", which they say lacks urgency, does not support that claim.

"This should be declared a national emergency," says campaigner Olly Armstrong who believes, if the spill had happened further south, it would have been treated differently.

Armstrong, from North Shields in North Tyneside, is one of thousands of volunteers who have spent weeks clearing beaches of millions of plastic pellets that washed into the River Tyne and the North Sea following a collision between two ships at the Port of Tyne.

"We're in an emergency situation," he says, adding he is surviving on a few hours sleep a night while orchestrating the response.

"The North often feels it's ignored and I know now is the time to prove the North matters," he says. "Andy Burnham has declared he is the prime minister of the North as well as London. Now is the time to prove it."

The government has been approached for comment on whether Burnham might get involved but meanwhile has said the Environment Agency has been "on this from the start, supporting partners, and is now stepping up its work on the ground".

The environment secretary had also spoken to North East Mayor Kim McGuinness "to discuss the response and next steps", a spokesperson said.

The collision between the Wind Orca, a 100-metre (328ft) tall wind turbine installation vessel, and the berthed container ship, BG Orange, on 19 July resulted in a gantry crane on the quayside collapsing onto the ship.

Some of the containers on the BG Orange were full of nurdles - pre-production plastic pellets, about the size of a lentil, which are used as the raw material to manufacture nearly all everyday plastic goods.

When the containers were damaged these tiny pieces of plastic spilled into the water and eventually washed up on beaches. Videos have emerged of birds appearing to eat them, while other footage shows dead birds floating amid pools of the plastic.

"We have acted," Armstrong says. "We want to see those with power in the government to act quickly to put legislation in place so this doesn't happen again."

Labour councillor Josephine Mudzingwa, who represents the badly affected North Shields ward, says volunteers need "money, boats and people on the ground".

"We need central government to get involved, we need more people in the boats actually clearing the nurdles," she says. "Every day we get loads of nurdles everywhere. I come here at 0600 in the morning and leave at 1900 at night.

"Please, Andy Burnham, you promised you are going to be looking north. We need you for this emergency."

"If something like this happened on the River Thames they'd have been on it within hours," says fellow volunteer Dave Shaw, also from North Shields.

"Up here they're just not bothered at all.

"This should be declared a national disaster, because that's exactly what it is."

Labour mayor Kim McGuinness says "the government haven't done enough" and accuses the Environment Agency of being "absent".

She says she spoke directly to Environment Secretary Angela Eagle to demand more clean-up support this week and was told she "would look at it".

"We've been in touch with government throughout this, with agencies throughout this, trying to convene people to pull them together," she said.

"There has been a direct lack of action from the centre."

The Environment Agency, responding on behalf of the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, says it has been "actively involved from the outset" and is "working closely" with local authorities, the Port of Tyne and other groups.

"We have increased monitoring along the affected coastline, including deploying our coastal patrol vessels and drones to identify where nurdles have accumulated so response teams can target their efforts where they are needed most," it says.

It says it will also support local authorities in recovering costs.

McGuinness suggests the response from local and national organisations has not been joined-up and this has delayed the clean-up.

"Everyone has been able to pass the buck," she says. "That should not be how it is. We should be able to convene everyone and direct them to do something about it."

She says she was "completely outraged" at the spillage and the speed of the subsequent clean-up.

"I don't have, as unbelievable as it is as mayor of this region, any power to fix this problem, but it doesn't mean I haven't shoved my nose in," she says.

Since the comments, Marine Minister Stephen Morgan said he chaired a meeting with local authorities and agencies earlier to "better understand the challenges they face and help to ensure cleanup happens as quickly and effectively as possible".

"People in the North East rightly expect a strong, coordinated response to this incident," he said.

The Port of Tyne denies it acted slowly.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce3q.title: Illegal working arrests double in two years, Home Office says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce3q.text:
Arrests of migrants working illegally in the UK have doubled since Labour has been in government, the Home Office has said.

It said more than 17,000 arrests had been made since July 2024, a 122% increase on the previous two years, with a record number of immigration raids and arrests in the last six months.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: "This surge in enforcement activity takes us to the highest level in British history. Illegal workers and rogue employers have nowhere to hide."

Reform UK said Labour was "insulting the intelligence of the British public" with these new figures.

The number of people arrested during immigration raids on businesses was increasing before Labour took office in July 2024.

According to the figures, since then there has been a 50% rise in individuals being returned to their home countries, a total of 2,357.

Immigration raids in the first six months of this year increased to 7,270, a 31% increase on the same period last year, leading to 4,756 arrests, a 20% rise.

The highest arrest rates were in London, the West Midlands and South West England.

Some 1,256 arrests were made in the capital, up 32% on the same period in 2025.

Meanwhile, 701 arrests were made in the West Midlands and 693 in the South West - a 22% and 44% increase respectively.

Employers, including those in the beauty, retail and hospitality sectors, have been hit with £74m worth of civil penalties so far this year.

Opposition parties have warned that opportunities to work illegally in the UK act as a pull factor for migrants, encouraging people to cross the Channel in small boats.

Reform UK announced on Thursday it would pay members of the public for tip-offs that lead to successful prosecutions of High Street shops employing illegal workers.

The party pledged to fine large firms up to 10% of their global revenues and make chief executives and directors criminally liable for illegal working.

Responding to the new figures, Reform's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said: "The British public can see the scourge of illegal working growing all around them. Labour is only insulting their intelligence by claiming it is not."

The Home Office says it is already increasing penalties for companies hiring illegal workers.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said earlier this year that "illegal working is booming because Labour have turned Britain into a soft touch".

Companies have a legal responsibility to verify that people they employ directly have the right to work in the UK. For agency workers, the responsibility lies with the agency to conduct the relevant checks.

From 1 October, employers caught hiring illegal workers in the gig economy, such as delivery riders, could face fines of up to £60,000 per illegal worker or five years in prison.
