https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd69.title: The serial candidates standing against Farage in the Clacton by-election
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd69.text:
A record number of candidates are standing in next week's Clacton by-election, but some names on the ballot will be more familiar than others.

As the main parties are not standing against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, the 33 other candidates on the ballot are either from smaller political parties or are standing as independents.

Nine of these names have already appeared on multiple ballot papers elsewhere in the UK, including Reclaim Party leader Laurence Fox and satirical candidates Count Binface and Howling Laud Hope.

BBC Verify has taken a look at the serial candidates who have decided to stand in Clacton, how they have fared in previous elections, and whether they have ever won enough votes to save their £500 parliamentary - or £10,000 London mayor - deposits.

The Clacton by-election takes place on 13 August, and because there are a total of 34 people contesting the seat it means people in the constituency will be casting their votes on what is understood to be the longest ballot paper in British electoral history.

Using confirmed parliamentary records, we found nine candidates standing against Farage who have stood at least twice before in Westminster parliamentary or London mayoral elections.

They are: Rejoin EU candidate John Stevens, Social Democratic Party leader William Clouston, Reclaim leader Laurence Fox, independent Joseph 77, Count Binface, independent Andy Erlam, and three candidates from the Monster Raving Loony Party - leader Howling Laud Hope, Nick the Incredible Flying Brick and Baron Von Thunderclap.

UK electoral law does not prevent a registered political party from fielding more than one candidate in a parliamentary by-election. Each candidate must have a valid nomination and be authorised by the party's nominating officer.

Nigel Farage has previously stood in seven parliamentary contests since 1994, and successfully became an MP for Clacton in the 2024 general election.

Parliamentary candidates do not have to be from the area they want to stand in to appear on the ballot, but they do have to be nominated by 10 people who live in the constituency.

A £500 deposit is also required to validate their candidacy, which they only get back if they achieve more than 5% of the vote share.

Mayoral elections have stricter eligibility rules. For example, in London candidates must either live, work or be registered to vote in the capital, or rent or own a property in the city. They must also get at least 10 nominations from each London borough and at least 10 from the City of London, and win more than 5% of the vote share to have their £10,000 deposit returned.

Howling Laud Hope, the leader of the Official Monster Raving Loony Party, has previously stood in 37 parliamentary elections since 1983.

Real name Alan Hope, the party leader challenged David Cameron's seat when he was elected prime minister in 2010, and stood against former prime minister Theresa May in the 2017 general election.

He gained his highest share of the vote in the 2011 Leicester South by-election, which was held by Labour. Hope finished last of five candidates, with 553 votes, or 1.6%.

He has never won enough votes to get back a £500 parliamentary deposit.

Previous attempts: 37

Nick the Incredible Flying Brick, whose real name is Nick Delves, has previously stood for the Official Monster Raving Loony Party in 13 parliamentary contests.

He stood against former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer in the 2024 general election, but his highest share of the vote came in West Derbyshire at the 2001 general election, when the Conservatives held the seat. He finished fifth of six candidates with 472 votes, or 0.9% of all votes.

Like Hope, he has never won enough votes to get back a £500 parliamentary deposit.

Previous attempts: 13

Tom Darwood, who stands under the name Joseph 77, has previously contested eight parliamentary elections.

The strongest of those runs came in Southend West in Essex at the 2019 general election. He received 574 votes, or 1.2%, in a seat held by the Conservatives.

Darwood has never won enough votes to get back a £500 parliamentary deposit.

Count Binface is the satirical alter ego of comedian Jon Harvey, who has previously stood in four parliamentary elections and two London mayoral elections.

As Count Binface, Harvey has been on the same ballot as two sitting prime ministers during a general election - Boris Johnson in 2019 and Rishi Sunak in 2024 - and separately stood as a different character, Lord Buckethead, against Theresa May in Maidenhead in 2017.

In 2023 Count Binface stood in the Uxbridge and South Ruislip by-election after Johnson resigned as an MP, and in June this year he stood against now prime minister Andy Burnham in the Makerfield by-election.

His best parliamentary result came in the Richmond and Northallerton vote against Sunak in the 2024 general election. He gained 308 votes - 0.6% of the total share - and finished sixth out of 13 candidates.

He has not previously won enough votes to get back any of his deposits.

Baron Von Thunderclap - real name Peter Berry - is the third Official Monster Raving Loony Party candidate on the ballot. He previously stood in six parliamentary elections.

The Clacton contest is his first parliamentary by-election however, and his first parliamentary race outside Mid Sussex. His strongest turnout was during the 2001 general election, when he received 601 votes, or 1.3% of the vote share. He finished fifth out of five candidates and the Conservatives held the seat.

He has never won enough votes to get back a £500 parliamentary deposit.

Former Conservative MEP John Stevens, who is standing for the Rejoin EU Party, has previously appeared on the ballot in four parliamentary elections.

His best result came as an independent in Buckingham in the 2010 general election, when he challenged then speaker of the House of Commons John Bercow. The main parties do not usually stand against the Speaker in a general election, and Stevens finished second of 11 candidates with 10,331 votes, a 21.4% vote share. Farage also challenged Bercow for the seat that year and came third.

It means Stevens is the only Clacton candidate to have stood against and won more votes than Farage in a parliamentary contest. Stevens also gained enough votes to qualify to have his deposit returned.

William Clouston, the leader of the Social Democratic Party, previously stood in three parliamentary elections.

His best result came in Durham North West, in the 2001 general election, when Labour held the seat. Clouston, standing as a Conservative, finished second of four candidates with 8,193 votes, or 20.9% of the vote share.

This was enough votes to retain his £500 parliamentary deposit.

Andy Erlam has previously contested three parliamentary elections.

His best run was in Bexleyheath in London at the 1983 general election. He received 7,560 votes, or 17.1%, in a seat held by the Conservatives.

Erlam won enough votes to get back two of his parliamentary deposits.

Actor turned right-wing commentator Laurence Fox, of the Reclaim Party, has previously stood in one parliamentary by-election and one London mayoral election.

His only parliamentary contest before Clacton was the 2023 Uxbridge and South Ruislip by-election. Fox finished fourth out of 17 candidates. The Conservatives held the seat, while Fox received 714 votes, or a 2.3% share of the vote.

He did not win enough votes to get back either of his deposits.

For this analysis, the BBC counted previous UK House of Commons elections dating back to 1955, by-elections to 1983 and Mayor of London records to 2000. Results prior to this are not included in the analysis.

The current Clacton contest counts towards the three-contest threshold to be included in the analysis.

Local council elections, local and combined-authority mayoral elections, devolved legislatures, European Parliament elections and London Assembly elections were excluded.

Official records do not track individual candidates over time and there can be discrepancies where individuals are recorded under different variations on their name, aliases, or for different parties across their careers.

Correction 6 August 2026: This article has been amended to include details found through historical data where candidate names and political parties were recorded inconsistently. We have updated the text and graphics relating to William Clouston and Joseph 77 to add one more election each to their totals, and added an additional candidate to our analysis, Andy Erlam, who met the threshold for inclusion.

What claims do you want BBC Verify to investigate?

Main parties are not standing against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage. The 33 other candidates on the ballot are either from smaller political parties or are standing as independents.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj9d.title: Sturgeon's criticisms of Swinney reveal tensions in SNP ranks
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj9d.text:
He was her loyal deputy for almost a decade - a trusted ally through the highs and lows of Nicola Sturgeon's tenure as first minister.

From her fallout with Alex Salmond to the Covid pandemic and gender self-ID, John Swinney was right there next to her.

Even in the wake of Peter Murrell's conviction for embezzlement of SNP funds, he resisted criticising Sturgeon's oversight of the party's governance during her time as leader.

In fact, Swinney's support has been so steadfast, Sturgeon once described him as the most important person in her life outside of her family.

It therefore came as something of a surprise when the former first minister chose to criticise the current first minister in the new foreword to her autobiography.

Giving her views on the recent Holyrood election, Sturgeon wrote there was "a lack of vision or big picture thinking" when it came the SNP's campaign.

She went on to say that while the outcome was "an outstanding result" for the party after 19 years in government, there were lessons to be learned.

In her view, the SNP was lucky the Scottish Greens did not stand in more constituencies, suggesting that had they done so, they could have eaten into John Swinney's 58-seat tally.

It was the Greens, Sturgeon said, who'd come closest to "injecting a sense of hope for the future" into the campaign.

In what could be seen as a nod to issues like trans rights and climate change, she said the party had the courage to stand up for what it believed in.

And she added it would be a "massive electoral blunder" for the SNP to "soften" its left-of-centre environmentalist credentials, a reference perhaps to the party's shifting position on oil and gas.

Of course, Sturgeon would be well aware of the headlines such comments would generate, and some have suggested she's simply attempting to garner more publicity.

But her intervention has provoked a bit of a backlash among former colleagues and has raised some questions around the current first minister's approach going forward.

There have long been rumours about the state of the Swinney-Sturgeon friendship.

Relations are understood to have cooled in the last couple of years, as the Scottish government moved away from some elements of the Sturgeon agenda.

After the SNP's poor results in the 2024 general election, Sturgeon publicly blamed a lack of focus on independence.

This time around, she said the party had "rightly put Scottish independence centrally as an objective but didn't always bring alive the opportunities it offers for people in a tangible sense".

Asked about her most recent comments during a ministerial visit on Wednesday, Swinney was characteristically restrained.

He said it was important for people to express their views and described working with Sturgeon as a "great privilege", adding that he was now enjoying having his own mandate to govern.

Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth said her former boss and friend was "entitled to her opinion", but was clear that she didn't share it.

Economy Secretary Stephen Flynn told the BBC it was important that former first ministers share their views, but added that the election result had produced an "emphatic mandate" for Swinney that spoke for itself.

Some of his cabinet colleagues - including those once closely allied to Sturgeon - were more pointed in their responses.

Education Secretary Mairi McAllan - a former Sturgeon protégé - said the claims were "nonsense".

And Health Secretary Angela Constance said she was "incorrect", describing Swinney as the best first minister yet - remarks seen as a dig at Sturgeon.

Of course, it's the cabinet's collective job to be loyal to the current boss. But such sharp rebukes may well suggest the former first minister's standing in the party has shrunk.

Indeed, there is frustration within parts of the SNP that she has sought to criticise, without acknowledging her own role in some of its recent difficulties.

One party figure said she would do well to remember her own irritation at Alex Salmond's backseat driving when she replaced him at the top of the party.

Others have been quoting Clement Attlee, recommending "a period of silence".

Some believe Swinney can and should now take the opportunity to more publicly distance himself from the Sturgeon era, given he now has his own mandate to govern.

That may be easier said than done, especially if his predecessor is unable to resist future political interventions.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj9d.summary: John Swinney was Nicola Sturgeon's loyal deputy for almost a decade. He was a trusted ally through the highs and lows of her tenure as first minister. But he resisted criticising Sturgeon's oversight of the party's governance during her time as leader.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c86n.title: Why there's a row about standing up while drinking in central London
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c86n.text:
It has been claimed so-called vertical drinking is under threat in the heart of London's West End.

In short: standing up to have a drink, often outside.

The borough of Westminster has more licensed venues than anywhere else in the UK with about 500 pubs, bars and wine bars, and roughly 1,750 cafes and restaurants.

It follows a report on page three of Thursday's Guardian newspaper, headlined "Time at the bar? Council accused of trying to stop pubs being pubs with 'no standing' plan". The headline in its online version of the story has since been tweaked.

By 1 October, Westminster City Council (WCC) needs to update its current licensing policy - drawn up in 2021.

It has therefore published draft proposals as part of a consultation which closes on Sunday, which the Guardian report was based on.

In the draft plans, WCC said it wanted to "discourage excessive drunkenness and encourage the provision of more seating in premises that serve alcohol for people to sit and enjoy a drink and order food by table service in place of open bar space that caters for high volume vertical drinking".

One policy is to refuse pub, bar, fast food or music venue licences in an area known as the "West End cumulative impact zone": an area roughly between Oxford Street and Trafalgar Square, taking in Leicester Square and Soho.

"The introduction of measures to reduce the extent of, or to remove opportunities for, vertical drinking could address the underlying reasons for the policy," the document reads.

The guidance suggests applicants for new licences should aim for "a predominantly seated operation with fixed seating", alongside waiter service replacing vertical drinking and restrictions on customers consuming alcohol while standing.

WCC insists there is no plan to ban pub-goers in Soho from drinking while standing up, branding reporting of anything of that nature "utterly ludicrous", and on Friday afternoon it published a "myth-busting" response to the proposals.

Tim Barnes, WCC deputy leader and cabinet member for growth and planning, said: "There is no plan, and never has been, to ban drinking while standing up in a Westminster pub.

"Suggesting otherwise is a wilful misreading of the policy proposals with clauses taken out of context.

"We want people to go out in the West End and have a good time. Our guidance is simply about encouraging venues to manage their customers so people don't pack on to pavements or excessive drinking doesn't disturb others passing by."

Responding to the Conservative council's consultation, a spokesperson for the government said: "Busy pubs full of people talking to each other is not a public nuisance, it is British life and it is thousands of jobs.

"Soho did not become world famous by taking last orders early, switching the lights off at 10 o'clock."

While the Labour mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, said that you "can't run a world-famous nightlife district with a village-hall mindset".

A Conservative Party spokesperson called for WCC to strike a balance between the needs of the night-time economy and residents' concerns.

A spokesperson for Soho Business Alliance, which represents businesses in the area, said WCC "don't want the late-night economy" and accused it of "trying to reduce the capacities in these venues".

They added: "It's been like that for years where people are standing and drinking, it's not causing crime, it's not causing issues.

"It's them trying to change the nature of Soho and it's quite sad that they've gone to such lengths to sanitise the area."

Local community organisation, the Soho Society, has previously stated that "alcohol-related harm, including risks to women and vulnerable people at night, must be considered" in decisions on licensing.

The group has previously expressed concern about "the unmanaged cumulative impact of a high concentration of licensed premises in a small area on Soho's whole ecosystem", including crime, anti-social behaviour, public safety concerns, public nuisance and disruption to the area's day-to-day functioning.

Council wants to ban vertical drinking in area known as the West End cumulative impact zone. Council says it wants to encourage more seating in premises that serve alcohol. Soho Business Alliance says it doesn't want late-night economy.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9q9.title: Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9q9.text:
The senior investigating officer in the PC Andrew Harper case has told BBC Breakfast he is "appalled" that two of the killers will become eligible for early release.

PC Harper, 28, from Wallingford, Oxfordshire, died from catastrophic injuries in 2019 when he was dragged behind the getaway car of three teenagers who had fled the scene of a quad bike theft.

Two of his killers – Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers – will be eligible for early release next year under revised government plans to tackle prison overcrowding.

Stuart Blaik, who investigated the killing, said it was "particularly hard to understand" their case for early release and said police officers were shocked at the prospect.

PC Harper's widow, Lissie Harper, has been among a growing number calling for Cole and Bowers to be denied early release from prison.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC on Friday that early release is "not okay" - adding that no government should have been put in the position of having to deal with limited prison capacity.

Contains flashing images.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".

The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.

Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.

The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.

Streeting said the government is taking the issue "extremely seriously".

"We should never have been put in a position where prisons across the country were so full-to-bursting that any government, let alone this government, had to contemplate the early release of people from serious convictions that have led to being in prison in the first place.

"We're not pretending this is okay."

He pointed to "strong controls" and supervision that will be in place for people released into the community and added that the government is "determined" to build more prison places and is looking carefully into the exemptions under the scheme.

In an earlier statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, former Det Sup Blaik said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.

He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case", Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early.

"Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

"I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.

Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.

But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.

An average of 150 people a year are sentenced at crown court for manslaughter with an average term of nine years. That means that in any given year there are hundreds of these offenders in jail. If they were all kept in, that would eat into the available spare beds - a number that is declining despite the massive prison-building programme.

If the government were to try to differentiate between different types of manslaughter offenders based on the specific nature of the crime they committed, that could be legally complex to deliver - and may in turn face serious legal challenges from prisoners who find their release dates changed.

Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.

They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.

PC Harper and Lissie had been married for just a month when he was killed in the line of duty.

On Thursday, the police officer's widow said she "will not give up" and hoped people would share a petition calling for his killers to be denied early release from prison.

She said: "Hopefully we can make the current government come to their senses and realise we cannot put people like this back on our streets.

"Justice should mean justice and serving the sentence given."

Thames Valley Police Federation chair Aileen O'Connor began the petition this week.

"My ask is that the prime minister, the home secretary and everybody else in government gets on the right side of this and does the right thing and makes the changes that keep the two killers behind bars," she said.

"We have been working closely with Chief Constable Jason Hogg and Police and Crime Commissioner Matthew Barber from the outset on this.

"We are all united in our frustration and dismay at the government's ridiculous plans when it comes to releasing from prison early the killers of police officers."

The government said it was trying to avoid running out of prison spaces as soon as October this year.

The justice secretary Alex Norris previously said about 1,000 prisoners would now not be released early following the revision to the scheme.

"If we drew it any wider we would have a prison capacity crisis," said Norris.

Prisoners released on licence, he said, would be subject to "very significant controls on their lives" and victims would be consulted.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9q9.summary: Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers will be eligible for early release next year. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting says early release is "not okay" and says no government should have been put in the position of having to have to release 1,000 prisoners.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c77g.title: Sir Keir Starmer made misleading defence spending claim, watchdog says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c77g.text:
Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, the Wales Office and the Ministry of Defence (MoD) used misleading figures about how much the country would spend on defence, a watchdog has said.

In March Sir Keir told MPs that ministers were increasing defence spending by £270bn. The two other departments later repeated similar claims in June.

But the UK Statistics Authority say that is wrong, as the figure is the proposed overall amount the government plans to spend between 2025 and 2029. The Wales Office deleted a post on X that had contained the claim.

A UK government spokesperson said: "We have previously acknowledged this phrasing and took immediate steps to ensure it was not replicated."

Downing Street and Sir Keir's office said they had nothing to add. The authority said steps taken by the Wales Office and the MoD should reduce the risk of the claim being made again in future.

Sir Keir resigned from Downing Street in July, when he was succeeded by Andy Burnham.

In March Sir Keir told the House of Commons liaison committee: "We have already committed to 2.5% in 2027, and we will hit that. That means that, in this Parliament, we will spend £270bn more on defence than we would otherwise have done."

Similar claims were made by an MoD spokesman in June, and by the Wales Office X account, which said on 3 June: "The UK government is increasing defence spending by £270bn over this Parliament to strengthen our national security."

BBC Wales was told that the figure originated in the MoD, rather than the Wales Office, which was led by the then-Welsh secretary Jo Stevens at the time.

The Wales Office, which is a part of the UK government, oversees the system of devolution and aims to be a voice for Wales within Westminster.

In a letter to Tory shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge, UK Statistics Authority's interim chair, Penny Young, said: "We agree that it is incorrect and misleading to describe the £270bn as an increase in defence spending over the course of this Parliament, or to describe it as an extra £270bn.

"The £270bn represents the proposed overall spending on defence over the lifetime of the current Parliament, from 2025-26 to 2028-29."

According to the letter, the Wales Office told the authority the figure used "was a mistake and was amended as soon as it was noticed".

"In addition, Wales Office has told us it has reviewed its press office lines in relation to this topic, and its quality assurance process for press lines, to ensure that this mistake is not replicated elsewhere," Young said.

She added: "The MoD has taken steps to ensure that future communications use precise and consistent language when presenting defence spending figures."

Conservative Shadow Wales Secretary Mims Davies MP said: "At a time of growing global instability, the public deserves honesty and transparency about our defence budget.

"Labour ministers and civil servants in the Wales Office should be setting out the facts, not presenting figures in a way that risks misleading people."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c77g.summary: Former PM Sir Keir Starmer told MPs that ministers were increasing defence spending by £270bn. Wales Office deleted post on X that had contained the claim. UK Statistics Authority says figure is proposed overall amount the government plans to spend between 2025 and 2029.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy4k.title: Ex neo-Nazi activist withdraws as Tory election candidate
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy4k.text:
A former neo-Nazi selected by the Conservatives to fight a council election next year has pulled out after a backlash against his candidacy.

Joshua Bonehill-Paine was convicted of racially harassing Jewish former Labour MP Luciana Berger in 2016, while already serving a separate jail sentence for sharing antisemitic posts.

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch had defended the decision to select him as a candidate for the new Somerset Council seat of Crewkerne South, saying he had been rehabilitated and her party "believes in second chances".

But Bonehill-Paine said he had now withdrawn his candidacy, and had been offered a position as an anti-extremism adviser to the party.

In a social media post, he said the position with the Conservative Party's Culture and Integration Commission would focus on advising on how to prevent young men from being radicalised.

Berger, who now sits as Baroness Berger in the House of Lords, described the appointment as an "insult," adding that making him a party adviser was "no better than allowing him to stand as a council candidate".

The position as an anti-extremism adviser to the party is unpaid, the BBC understands.

Bonehill-Paine spent three years in prison after he was jailed in 2015 for posting antisemitic material ahead of a planned neo-Nazi rally. He was convicted of racially harassing then-Labour MP Berger the following year.

He has described his past views as "indefensible" and says he has spent years opposing antisemitism since leaving prison in 2018.

But the party's decision to pick him for the Somerset seat sparked a huge political backlash, with Jewish groups declining the offer from Bonehill-Paine of a meeting.

The criticism of his candidacy from Jewish groups made Bonehill-Paine's decision to step down feel increasingly inevitable.

There are likely to be questions about Badenoch's judgement in this case after her decision to defend him so publicly raised eyebrows in Westminster.

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Bonehill-Payne "should never have been a candidate ... given the harassment that he visited on Luciana Berger, a colleague and a friend of mine".

"[The] Conservative Party should answer for why he was a candidate in the first place and also for any future activities he might be undertaking on behalf of the Conservative Party," he said.

Baroness Berger, who attended court at the OId Bailey in London to give evidence in Bonehill-Paine's trial, has said his past behaviour fell "very, very short" of the standard required to stand for public office.

Speaking earlier, she said Bonehill-Paine's harassment "affected my life in lots of different ways because of the volume of the material that he was disseminating and putting out, the extremity of it in terms of just frankly how shocking and awful it was".

"It was very difficult just being in court and having to give evidence at that time, I was over six months pregnant," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

In sentencing remarks, the judge said it was "difficult to envisage a worse case than this of racially aggravated harassment of this kind", adding Bonehill-Paine had "sat in the dock smirking throughout the trial" and had "plainly enjoyed" Baroness Berger's discomfort.

In his social media post, Bonehill-Paine said his local election candidacy would prompt opposition parties to "spend all their time focusing on my past rather than the work I'm doing today".

"Rather than standing as a local council candidate, I believe that my experience is better used supporting Kemi Badenoch in her ongoing mission to combat the antisemitism and extremism that is dividing our nation," he added.

In a blog post earlier for ConservativeHome, he said his anti-extremism work had included delivering training sessions and seminars for institutions including universities, schools, colleges, and probation services.

In a social media post, Badenoch said: "While I am sad that Joshua feels he won't be given the space to explain his position and represent his community, I am glad he is going to work with me and the party on tackling radicalisation."

"If we are going to stop extremism and antisemitism we are going to need help from those people who were part of the problem, but have now changed and are being part of the solution," she added.

"Piling on them and trying to get them cancelled may be sport for other parties, but this is a different Conservative Party."

But Reform UK hit out at Badenoch's decision to offer him the adviser role, with a spokesman saying it "beggars belief" and was "alarming news for the Jewish community in Britain".

Adam Dance, Liberal Democrat MP for Yeovil, said Bonehill-Paine's withdrawal was "the right outcome, but it should never have got to this point".

He said: "What's most concerning now is Kemi Badenoch's response – she has not accepted her party got this wrong, and instead frames legitimate concern about antisemitism as 'piling on'. That is a troubling message to send."

The Board of Deputies of British Jews welcomed his withdrawal as a council candidate, adding: "We continue to urge all parties to use their vetting to ensure a robust stance on racism and discrimination, including antisemitism."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy4k.summary: Joshua Bonehill-Paine was convicted of racially harassing former Labour MP Luciana Berger. He was already serving a separate jail sentence for sharing antisemitic posts. Bonehill Paine said he had withdrawn his candidacy and had been offered a position as an anti-extremism adviser. Tory leader Kemi Badenoch

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy07.title: SNP write-off value of Murrell motorhome in party accounts
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy07.text:
The SNP has written-off the cost of the motorhome bought for £124,550 by former chief executive Peter Murrell before his conviction for embezzling party funds.

Accounts published by the Electoral Commission show the value of the luxury Niesmann and Bischoff vehicle had been removed from its books.

The balance sheet, which covers 2025, showed Murrell was still owed £60,000 from a loan he gave the party in 2021.

It also detailed SNP membership had fallen below 51,000, and was down about 5,000 from the previous year's figures.

First minister John Swinney said the accounts proved the SNP remained in a position of "formidable financial strength".

About £1.7m of the SNP's income last year came from membership fees, according to the accounts.

Independent auditors also suggested the party's manual journal entries and related party transactions remained at "heightened risk of fraud".

The party had a cash surplus of £509,903, a huge rise from a near £400,000 deficit the previous year following a redundancy push in 2024.

However, the figures do not include the run-up to the Holyrood election in May.

Murrell pled guilty to embezzling more than £400,000 from the SNP earlier this year.

The motorhome, bought in late 2020, was initially claimed to have been purchased to be used by the party as a campaigning tool.

The vehicle was driven a short distance from being picked up in Rosyth, Fife, to the home of Murrell's mother in Dunfermline, where it was parked until being seized by officers.

His estranged wife and former First Minister Nicola Sturgeon has repeatedly insisted she was unaware of the existence of the motorhome.

The motorhome was listed as having a value of £100,790 on 1 January 2024.

That had dropped by more than half to £41,284 by 31 December of the same year, according to the accounts.

Sturgeon was initially arrested during Operation Branchform, the name given to the Police Scotland investigation into SNP finances, before being told she would not face charges.

Murrell loaned the party £60,000 in 2021. That figure remains in the accounts, but the party said Murrell had not "formally requested" the sum to be paid back.

It is unclear whether it will have to be repaid.

The party has said it will seek to "recover from the guilty party the full amount embezzled" at a proceeds of crime hearing, which is due to take place next month.

Posting on X, Swinney said: "The publication of the SNP's accounts today shows that at the end of 2025 the party was in a position of formidable financial strength, having made a surplus of more than £500,000 over the year.

"The rebuilding of the party's finances allowed us to run a well-resourced campaign that took our positive message to every community in Scotland and made a major contribution to our historic election victory."

Craig Hoy, the Scottish Conservatives' finance spokesman, said the accounts raised "further serious questions".

"The fact they still technically owe the crooked Peter Murrell £60,000 is astonishing and eyebrows will also be raised at auditors highlighting the party still has a heightened risk of fraud," he said.

"Their infamous campervan has now met its demise having more than halved in value after being Murrell's most expensive criminal purchase.

"Questions remain over that, including Sturgeon's remarkable claims that she was unaware of it being parked in her mother-in-law's driveway."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy07.summary: Peter Murrell was convicted of embezzling party funds in May. The former chief executive bought the motorhome for £124,550 in 2020. Accounts show the value of the luxury Niesmann and Bischoff vehicle had been removed from its books. The accounts show Murrell still owed £60,000 from

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3r0.title: Referrals to Prevent anti-terror scheme at record high
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3r0.text:
Nearly 10,000 people were referred to the government's anti-terrorism scheme, Prevent, in the year to September 2025, Home Office figures show, a record number for the programme.

Figures show 10,293 referrals were made in England and Wales for 9,957 people - up by 39% from the previous 12 months and the highest number in a single year since records began in 2015.

Where the age is known, 393 referrals were for children under 10, the largest proportion concerned 11 to 15-year-olds at 36%, followed by 16 to 17 year-olds at 13% of referrals.

The Home Office said the spike was in part due to "heightened public awareness of Prevent" after the Southport attacks in July 2024, where a teenager killed three girls at a dance class.

Axel Rudakubana was 17-years-old when he stabbed 11 children and two adults, killing nine-year-old Alice da Silva Aguiar, seven-year-old Elsie Dot Stancombe, and six-year-old Bebe King at a Taylor Swift–themed yoga and dance workshop.

Rudakubana was referred to Prevent on three occasions between 2019 and 2021 due to his interest in terrorist attacks and school shootings, but there was no evidence of a fixed ideology or motivation.

A government review found that his case was closed "prematurely", and that counter terrorism officers staffing the Prevent scheme had "sufficient information" to escalate Rudakubana's case to the next stage - known as Channel - which would have included enhanced monitoring for those deemed at risk of radicalisation.

The Home Office said the Southport attacks may have also led to a 117% increase in referrals discussed at a Channel panel, rising from 997 to 2,159.

It also cited a major review from last year led by Lord David Anderson KC, which found an increase in Prevent referrals from January to March 2025 during Rudakubana's trial.

The Home Office said it was possible that "a number of operational and policy changes and improvements, along with associated training rolled out" may have also had an impact on referrals.

Tim Jacques, the government's Independent Prevent Commissioner, said greater awareness about the scheme "isn't a bad thing", but "the system wasn't set up for the problem it's currently dealing with".

He told BBC Radio 4's World At One programme that the "online world" has become "massive factor in what we see in these referral statistics".

"The role of the online world and online influence, and how people with some grievance, some sense of fascination in violence can find communities that will echo those beliefs and develop those beliefs is a phenomenon... which is relatively new," he said.

Thursday's figures show that 20% of the total referrals were because of concerns over extreme right-wing ideology - an increase from 1,480 to 2,103 in the previous 12 months - while 8% of referrals concerned Islamist extremism.

A further 8% of referrals concerned fascination with extreme violence or mass casualty attacks, 1% concerned Incel extremism, and 0.3% concerned left-wing extremism.

More than half of the referrals (56%) were for individuals with no identified ideology.

The Home Office also published data showing the ethnicity of those referred to Prevent.

This is not mandatory and can be left blank, and only 5,315 (52%) referrals included the data.

Of these referrals, 68% were white, 18% were Asian, 8% were black, while 7% were listed as "other".

Prevent, which forms a key part of the UK's counter-terror strategy, places a legal duty on public bodies to identify people who may turn to extremism.

The Home Office figures are for England and Wales. Scotland reports its referral figures separately.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3r0.summary: 10,293 people referred to Prevent in England and Wales for 9,957 people in the year to September 2025. The Home Office said the spike was in part due to "heightened public awareness of Prevent" The number of referrals was up 39% from the previous 12 months.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg5l.title: Burnham orders review of grooming gang early releases
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg5l.text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has ordered an "urgent" review to identify any grooming gang members who may be eligible to be freed from jail under the government's early release scheme.

The announcement comes after Tory leader Kemi Badenoch raised concerns that child sex offenders could leave jail well before the end of their sentences.

She pointed out that indecent assault was not included in the list of offences that the government said would be excluded from the early release scheme.

Five men convicted of indecent assault as part of a historical grooming-gang case in Bradford are among the prisoners whose offences were not included in the list of exclusions.

The prime minister's spokesperson said Burnham had asked the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) to "conduct an in-depth review of cases to ensure that grooming cases were identified".

"This work is happening urgently," Burnham's spokesperson said.

"This is extremely important to the PM and he has personally intervened to ensure everything possible is being done so that vile groomers are dealt with in the way their victims deserve."

It is understood that at this stage the review will only seek to identify offenders who might be released early.

The government has not confirmed whether the review will lead to the prevention of any early releases of offenders convicted of grooming-related crimes.

Badenoch described the intervention as "another U-turn secured" and "another review from Burnham following my letter".

The government is planning to release about 5,000 offenders in England and Wales early in an effort to make space in overcrowded jails.

Burnham launched a review of the scheme after he became prime minister and this week he announced that some prisoners convicted of rape, serious child sex and other grooming offences would barred from early release.

But in a letter, Badenoch said many more types of offenders - including those convicted of sexually assaulting children - could be freed early.

"On Tuesday, you told the country that those convicted of grooming offences would be excluded," she wrote. "Your own government has now put in writing that some of these men will be released early anyway."

Highlighting that indecent assault was not excluded from the early release scheme, Badenoch said "many cases of child sex abuse committed before 2004 were charged this way, including Rotherham and Rochdale".

Badenoch branded this a "betrayal of victims", and urged Burnham to publish the full list of offences that remain eligible for early release.

Under changes made by Burnham, people sentenced for rape, serious child sex and grooming offences will now not be eligible for early release from October.

But some prisoners who are not excluded could be freed after serving a third of their total custodial sentence rather than after 40% or 50% of their term.

Burnham said he had wanted to exclude more offenders, but prison overcrowding prevented this.

The prime minister said making more prisoners exempt was not possible without the prison system collapsing and putting the public "at much greater risk".

The prison population in England and Wales on 3 August was 86,495, which was 97% of useable capacity.

The number of places in jails in England and Wales has not kept pace with the significant rise in the prison population in recent decades under successive governments.

There are cases of offenders who were convicted of indecent assault under section 14 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1956.

These sections of the 1956 Act were not included in the government's list of exclusions, suggesting prisoners convicted of these crimes could qualify for the early release scheme.

Five men who were jailed in October 2005, after being convicted of indecent assault for abusing a teenage girl in Bradford in the early 2000s, could be eligible for early release under the scheme.

In December 2024, Ajaz Karim was jailed for 21 months after he was convicted of indecent assault for sexually abusing a 13-year-old girl at the school where he was a sports coach.

In another case, Shahid Hussain was jailed for eight years in September 2024, after he was convicted of indecently assaulting a 14-year-old girl in Rotherham in 2003.

The government has not yet confirmed exactly which offenders will be released.

The mother of PC Andrew Harper also said she was "devastated" to learn two men jailed after her son was killed will still be eligible for early release.

PC Harper, 28, was killed in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

His family previously said they had received a letter from the Ministry of Justice confirming that two of the offenders could be included in the early release scheme.

Earlier this week, Justice Secretary Alex Norris apologised to families affected by the early release scheme, saying they were "carrying the can from previous failures".

The justice secretary said about 5,000 extra releases will take place in 10 batches from October - down from about 6,000 before the revision.

The changes are due to be phased in, beginning with prisoners serving sentences of fewer than 575 days, going up to inmates jailed for 12 years or more being eligible for early release in June 2027.

The number of individuals released each time will depend on the prison population, which the government says will evolve between now and implementation.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg5l.summary: Andy Burnham has ordered an "urgent" review of the scheme to identify any grooming gang members. The PM has asked the Ministry of Justice to conduct an in-depth review of cases. The government has not confirmed whether the review will lead to early releases of offenders convicted of grooming-related crimes.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3r0.title: All schools in England to get pupil attendance targets, government says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3r0.text:
Every mainstream state school in England will be given their own target to improve pupil attendance, the government has confirmed.

Schools will also be encouraged to offer more clubs and activities on Fridays, to improve attendance at the end of the week.

It comes as official attendance data, published on Thursday, suggested school absence rates in England remained above pre-pandemic levels, with nearly one in five pupils missing at least 10% of school in the 2025/26 academic year.

Education minister Paul Waugh said the new attendance targets would take each school's local challenges into account, but that "every school has a role to play to improve attendance".

Before the Covid pandemic, when many schools closed to pupils for significant periods of time, attendance rates at English mainstream state schools regularly stayed above 95%, but schools have struggled to get back to those rates in the years since.

Thursday's figures suggested an overall attendance rate of 93% for 2025/26, a slight decrease on the previous year. That includes both authorised absences, such as illness, and unauthorised absences, which is when pupils miss school without permission or a valid reason.

The rates of persistent absence have doubled since the pandemic. A pupil is described as persistently absent if they miss at least 10% of school sessions.

In 2018/19, persistent absence rates for England state schools were around 10%, while the most recent data showed it was at 19% in 2025/26.

Pupils on free school meals and those with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) were also still more likely to be absent from school than their peers.

Many mainstream schools in England were given attendance targets specific to their school in a widespread trial last year, but on Thursday the Department for Education (DfE) confirmed that every school would be getting their own target and that it would be monitored for the first time.

The BBC understands there will be no immediate penalties for schools who miss their attendance targets, but that the DfE will get in touch with schools that are off-track to make sure they are aware and taking action.

Schools could then be pointed towards best practice guidance, or encouraged to join with other schools in a local behaviour and attendance hub.

The regulator Ofsted already considers a schools' overall attendance rates in their inspections.

In an opinion piece published in The Independent newspaper on Thursday, newly-appointed education minister Paul Waugh said the latest attendance stats showed "progress has slowed over the past year", and that the government's response needed to be "broader, smarter and more ambitious".

Schools have been promised access to more data tools in the coming year to help them analyse individual pupils' attendance records, Waugh said, so they can identify concerns earlier and be "intervening more quickly when pupils begin to drift away from regular attendance".

Fridays are "becoming a particular weak spot for attendance", he added, and said he would be investigating why pupil illness absences are regularly significantly higher at the end of each week.

He called on schools to put on interesting clubs and enrichment sessions on Fridays "so every child stays engaged right through to the end of the week".

Paul Whiteman, general secretary of schools leaders' union NAHT, said Thursday's attendance data showed "just how hard it is to drive absence rates back down to pre-pandemic levels".

"Schools already go above and beyond in encouraging attendance, but it isn't a problem that they can solve alone or that government targets will fix," he said.

"The issue often has roots beyond the classroom, from illness and mental health challenges to poverty and unmet special educational needs."

He said it highlighted the importance of the government's upcoming reforms to the SEND system in England.

The data released on Thursday also showed that nearly 12% of pupils missed school in the week beginning Monday 22 June, when an exceptional heatwave was affecting parts of England, leading to the highest absence rate of the year.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3r0.summary: Every mainstream state school in England will be given their own target to improve attendance. Education minister Paul Waugh says every school has a role to play to improve Attendance. Schools will also be encouraged to offer more clubs and activities on Fridays to improve attendance.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1e1.title: Miliband says reopening Strait of Hormuz 'essential' as he meets Rubio
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1e1.text:
Reopening the Strait of Hormuz is essential to bringing down the cost of living in the UK, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said as he met his US counterpart Marco Rubio.

The Labour minister is in Washington for his first official one-on-one meeting with Rubio.

The pair were expected to discuss the war in Ukraine and the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

Miliband was invited to the US capital by Rubio after they met on the sidelines of a foreign ministers' summit in the Philippines, where the former Labour leader made his debut as foreign secretary.

The White House was reported to be concerned about Prime Minister Andy Burnham's decision to hand Miliband the Foreign Office brief, given his previous criticism of US President Donald Trump as a racist and a misogynist.

When asked by the BBC if the comments would hinder his working relationship with the Trump administration, Miliband said they would not and had not been mentioned during a 90-minute meeting.

Miliband said the "productive" discussion had focused on Iran, support for Ukraine, and "how we can work towards relieving the terrible suffering we are seeing in Gaza and have a two-state solution for the security of the Israeli and Palestinian people".

Trump is also a trenchant opponent of wind farms and supports the opening up North Sea oil and use of fossil fuels, whereas in his former role as UK energy secretary, Miliband championed net zero and renewables.

Burnham has signalled a shift in North Sea oil policy, earning praise from the Oval Office, but the dynamic between Miliband and Rubio was set to be closely watched.

Last month, Washington's top diplomat in London, Warren Stephens, said Miliband had been "wrong" in 2016 to call Trump "a racist, misogynistic self-confessed groper" and added "hopefully his views have changed".

Following their meeting, US state department spokesman Tommy Pigott said: "The two discussed the importance of Europe taking on a greater role in its own security.

"They reiterated their shared commitment to safe transit in the Strait of Hormuz and ensuring Iran never develops or obtains a nuclear weapon."

In a statement after the meeting, Miliband thanked Rubio for a "warm, productive meeting" and said he was "hopeful" that the Strait may be re-opened.

"The number one priority for this government is to tackle the cost of living crisis that people are facing and my job as foreign secretary most immediately is to work with our closest ally the United States on getting a lasting ceasefire in relation to the Iran war.

"We are working night and day to make that happen - that was a large part of our discussions today - I am hopeful that this may happen, but we are not there yet."

He added: "People should be in no doubt, I know as foreign secretary that the British people are worried about what's happened to petrol prices, diesel prices, energy bills, and the single biggest thing we can do is get that ceasefire in relation to Iran."

The strategic sea route, which had been open before the US and Israel launched the war in February, has been a flashpoint in the Middle East conflict and disruption to trade has driven up fuel and food prices.

Miliband added: "We also discussed standing together with Ukraine in the face of Putin's war, and spoke about the intolerable situation in Gaza and the urgent need to address the humanitarian situation there, as we work towards a lasting peace for Palestinians and Israelis."

Miliband will be taking the UK's seat on the World Bank board, so he will also meet its president Ajay Banga during his visit to discuss development, climate change and strengthening global resilience

Separately on Wednesday, new Defence Secretary Wes Streeting visited Ukraine for the first time since he started in the role.

He met President Volodymyr Zelensky at the National Security Defence Council meeting in Kyiv earlier today, which is a meeting with all the military and civil officials and ministers in government.

In a post on Telegram, Zelensky said he and Streeting discussed how London and Kyiv could jointly protect people who face "ballistic threats" from Russia.

He said: "We discussed how the UK could help Ukraine better protect our cities and communities from such ballistic threats - both bilaterally and multilaterally - just as it has done many times before by helping secure supplies of scarce defensive equipment.

"In particular, we discussed opportunities to establish co-production of certain types of weaponry, as both the UK and Ukraine possess strong battle-proven capabilities.

"We also discussed sanctions against Russian enterprises involved in the production of ballistic missiles."

He added: "I am grateful to the United Kingdom, His Majesty, the Prime Minister, and the British people for their unwavering support."

Miliband said he was "hopeful" that the Strait of Hormuz may be re-opened. The pair were expected to discuss the war in Ukraine and the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvg9.title: Burnham failing public over heat threats, says Green leader
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvg9.text:
Zack Polanski has accused Labour of a "dereliction of duty" in the face of this summer's heatwaves, as he urged Andy Burnham to take further action in response to recent wildfires and droughts.

In a speech, the Green Party leader said the threat to public health and food supplies posed the "biggest threat to this country since the Second World War".

Record temperatures in recent months showed the need for immediate measures, he said, such as publicly accessible "cool spaces" and financial support to help households heatproof their homes.

But Labour criticised the Greens' record on reservoirs and clean energy projects, accusing them of "repeatedly" opposing new developments.

This summer has been exceptionally dry and hot, with temperatures setting numerous records and drought conditions leaving water supplies under strain and prompting warnings from farmers about the impact on food supplies.

Speaking in central London, Polanksi said higher temperatures were posing a "threat to our way of life" on multiple fronts, whilst footage of wildfires across Europe were "frankly apocalyptic".

He called on Burnham, who entered Downing Street two weeks ago, to show greater urgency in response to high temperatures, as he criticised him for not holding an emergency government Cobra meeting on the issue.

"Extreme weather is now the new normal – and without action, the impact on the people of this country will be unimaginably grave," he said.

The leader of the Green Party of England and Wales added: "The response from our government is to pretend none of this is happening.

"It's an astonishing dereliction of duty from those whose first responsibility is to keep us safe".

Among the immediate measures suggested by Polanksi were freely accessible cool spaces in "every local area". He has previously cited a need for such zones in schools, hospitals and care homes.

Polanksi also renewed his call for Burnham's government to block new oil and gas drilling licences, and block the development of the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields in Scotland.

He also called for a new strategy to prevent wildfires following a series of blazes in various areas this summer, including "firefighting helicopters where needed".

And he argued that the need to prevent future droughts justified his party's longstanding policy of taking the water sector in England back into public ownership, arguing it would increase investment in new reservoirs.

However, Labour said the Greens had "repeatedly opposed plans for new reservoirs and clean energy projects" at a local level, which "makes it harder to achieve what they say they want".

The party cited previous calls from Green councillors for a public inquiry into a planned mega-reservoir in Oxfordshire, and objections from local Greens to the size of solar farms planned in Norfolk.

"If Zack Polanski wants to tackle the climate crisis, he should start by telling his fellow Green Party politicians that actions speak louder than words," a Labour spokesperson added.

"The Labour government will crack on with delivering these vital upgrades. The Greens should get on board."

Burnham has said he wants all parts of the UK to take "greater public control" of the water sector, although he has stopped short of calling for all water companies in England to be fully renationalised.

He has suggested a new model for the sector could emulate Greater Manchester's bus network, where private operators bid to run services on a franchise basis, with local authorities controlling fares, timetables and routes.

However, he is yet to spell out what an equivalent model for water would mean in practice.

He says the threat to public health and food supplies posed the "biggest threat to this country since the Second World War" Polanksi also calls for the government to block oil and gas drilling licences. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g3.title: New £215,000 council CEO was reality show winner
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g3.text:
A businessman who won a reality television show is due to take on the £215,000 a year job as a council chief executive.

Dennis Bacon, who has a wide-ranging background in adult social care, has been chosen to take charge of Reform UK-led Norfolk County Council.

He also runs a bed and breakfast in Norwich and last year was crowned winner on an episode of Channel 4's Four in a Bed.

The final decision on his appointment still requires the normal pre-employment checks and sign-off from full council, which is due to meet next week.

Bacon's appointment comes after Tom McCabe suddenly quit the post shortly after Reform took control of the authority in May.

Alongside his hospitality ventures, Bacon spent 19 years as chairman of the Norfolk Independent Care Association, which supports more than 600 organisations and 11,000 staff in the adult social care industry, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.

The 63-year-old has also sat on the Norfolk and Waveney Sustainability and Transformation Partnership – a network of local NHS organisations and councils, and previously was given an Outstanding Leadership in Public Services award by the county council.

Last year, he emerged as winner on Four in a Bed, where B&B owners compete against each other to be named best host.

More stories from Norfolk

"We were impressed with Dennis's commercial and public sector experience," said David Bick, the Reform leader of the council.

He added Bacon was determined to "ensure value for money and quality services for the residents of Norfolk".

Final interviews for the role were conducted this week.

According to a council report, 49 people applied for the job.

However, the process has been criticised by opposition leaders, who accused Reform of running the recruitment with "extreme haste".

The post was advertised for 24 days, which some argued was too short a window.

Kay Mason Billig, the former leader of the council and current leader of the Conservatives, also raised concerns that her party had no representation on the cross party panel.

If the appointment is approved by the council, Bacon is expected to start on 7 September.

He has a wide-ranging background in adult social care and hospitality ventures. Last year he won a reality TV show, Four in a Bed, where B&B owners compete against each other to be named best host.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ye.title: Student loan repayment rates an 'unsustainable burden', chancellor told
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ye.text:
More than 120 MPs and peers have asked the chancellor to carry out an "urgent review" of the student loan repayment system.

An open letter coordinated by the campaign group Rethink Repayment says the current set-up places an "unsustainable burden on the next generation of workers".

Among the cross-party signatories are MPs with their own Plan 2 student loans, which have come under particular scrutiny this year.

Last week, Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the interest rate on those loans was "egregious" and the issue was at the top of her in-tray.

Current and former students have different student loan plans depending on where they live in the UK and when they went to university.

The letter to Chancellor John Healey does not specify a particular plan signatories would like to be reformed, nor does it name a particular nation.

However, the debate has centred around Plan 2 loans, which were taken out by students in England between September 2012 and July 2023 and are still issued in Wales. Graduates pay back what they earn above the repayment threshold at a rate of 9%.

The letter says that "successive governments' adjustments to repayment thresholds – together with high interest and marginal tax rates – are placing an unsustainable burden on the next generation of workers".

It says many middle-income graduates "see less than half of any hard-earned pay rise due to a combination of income tax, national insurance and student loan repayments".

It adds: "We are united in the belief that the current repayment framework requires urgent review... to ensure it is fair, sustainable, and supportive of aspiration."

The letter refers to a decision taken last November by then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves to freeze the Plan 2 repayment threshold at £29,385 between 2027 and 2030, instead of allowing it to rise with inflation.

The change would result in students starting to repay their loans sooner than they would otherwise have done, and their rising salaries leading to greater repayments.

Campaigners want that decision to be reversed – a call echoed by the Treasury select committee in a report following its inquiry into student loans last month.

The committee's report referenced a BBC investigation which found the government compared Plan 2 student loan repayments to £30-a-month phone contracts in promotional presentations to teenagers a decade ago.

This was "inaccurate for higher earners", the report said, and "amounted to mis-selling".

Laura Trott, shadow education secretary for the Conservatives, and Munira Wilson, education spokeswoman for the Liberal Democrats, are among MPs who have signed the letter.

Tom Gordon, Liberal Democrat MP for Harrogate and Knaresborough, also signed the letter and told the BBC he could not "see an end in sight" to his own Plan 2 student loan repayments. Instead, he said he expected his debt to be written off after 30 years in line with the repayment terms.

"If someone earning an MP's salary still isn't likely to repay their student loan in full, what chance does someone on a much lower income have?" Gordon asked, adding it was "an issue of fairness".

"Governments have changed the repayment terms and increased interest rates after people had already signed up," he said.

"No bank or mortgage lender could retrospectively rewrite the terms of a loan like that. It simply wouldn't be allowed. So why should the government be able to do it?"

Oliver Gardner, founder of Rethink Repayment, said the letter showed "the student loans crisis" was not "a partisan issue".

"We believe that now is the time to create a system that is fair and that unshackles millions of graduates from mountains of student loan debt," he said.

A Department for Education spokesperson said: "We know the system we inherited is broken and unfair, and some graduates feel the weight of this more strongly.

"We want to make sure the student loans system works better for everyone and are considering our response to the Treasury Committee's inquiry."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ye.summary: More than 120 MPs and peers have signed open letter to Chancellor John Healey. They say current set-up places an "unsustainable burden on the next generation of workers" Campaigners want the Chancellor to carry out an "urgent review" of the student loan repayment system.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czjl.title: Government to function as normal while Burnham on holiday, No 10 says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czjl.text:
Andy Burnham's government will continue to function normally while the new prime minister is away on holiday, Downing Street has said.

Burnham is taking a break from his day-to-day duties to spend time with his family, after entering No 10 two weeks ago.

His official spokesman has said he will remain in direct contact with officials and continue to hold meetings while away from Downing Street.

But Reform UK's chairman Lee Anderson has criticised Burnham for going on holiday so soon after taking office, saying: "This isn't a prime minister that's serious about leading."

He accused the new prime minister of having "bunked off" after "dropping a number of unfunded commitments and overseeing over 2,000 illegal migrants breaking into our country", in reference to a raft of policy announcements made in Burnham's first two weeks.

But Justice Secretary Alex Norris defended Burnham's decision.

"The prime minister is having a few days away with his family," he told Sky News on Tuesday.

"He will be in constant contact with his office. I mean, I might gently say that I've spoken to him virtually every day since I joined the cabinet, and I suspect that won't change."

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she would not criticise Burnham for taking a holiday so soon into the job, but insisted he should have recalled Parliament after becoming prime minister in order to face scrutiny from MPs.

"Andy Burnham was running away from Parliament - he can't run away forever, I'm not going to be giving him a holiday when we come back in September," she told reporters on Tuesday.

Burnham's holiday, the location of which is not known, follows a blitz of announcements during his first two weeks in office.

This included a cut to VAT on household electricity bills and business rate cuts for pubs, reinstating a £2 bus fare cap in England and holding initial cross-party talks on social care reform.

He has also established a "No 10 North" base in Manchester, and announced plans to allocate English city mayors a share of income tax in exchange for grant funding from central government.

Burnham's last public appearance came over the weekend when he visited Dover in Kent, where he pledged to be "relentless" in curbing the number of people arriving in the UK on small boats.

The former mayor of Greater Manchester will hope his holiday will be more successful than that of former prime minister Gordon Brown in 2007.

Around six weeks after becoming prime minister, Brown travelled to Dorset for a break with his family.

But he had to cut his trip short after a matter of hours after an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease was reported among cattle in England.

He called an emergency Cobra meeting and worked from Chequers, the prime minister's official country residence, instead.

Burnham's predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, had planned to go abroad for a holiday in August 2024, a month after entering No 10.

But he had to cancel his plans due to riots and unrest in towns and cities across the UK in the wake of the deaths of three girls in the Southport attack.

His first holiday abroad came in December that year, when he flew to Madeira.

David Cameron frequently stayed in Cornwall with his wife Samantha, holidaying there every summer while in No 10.

Polzeath, a seaside village in the north of the county, was one of their favourite holiday spots.

The former Conservative prime minister and his wife gave their youngest daughter Florence a middle name of Endellion in honour of the Cornish area where they were staying before she was born in 2010.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czjl.summary: Andy Burnham is taking a break from his day-to-day duties to spend time with his family. His official spokesman says he will remain in direct contact with officials and continue to hold meetings. Reform UK's chairman Lee Anderson says Burnham has "bunked off"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2g.title: Reform Facebook page accuses Plaid minister of using husband's death for political gain
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2g.text:
A local Reform Facebook page for a Senedd constituency criticised a Plaid Cymru minister for discussing a family tragedy in a newspaper interview.

Two Reform MSs from the same area both distanced themselves from the social media comment, which accused Siân Gwenllian of using her experience as a "card for political gain".

The housing and local government minister brought up four children as a single parent after her husband, Dafydd, died from cancer in 1999.

Plaid said the comment was "vile". Reform's James Evans called it "totally unacceptable".

A Reform UK spokesman said: "This is not a London HQ or Senedd Group office account."

Evans' colleague Iain McIntosh also distanced himself from the now-deleted comment, which was made by Reform UK Brycheiniog Tawe Nedd on Facebook, and said he had asked for it to be deleted.

It is not clear who runs the account. Evans said he was not sure who ran the page and was investigating.

Both Evans and McIntosh are Reform MSs for the Brycheiniog Tawe Nedd area.

In a profile for WalesOnline, Gwenllian said of her husband's death: "It was a very difficult time for me but it taught me so much about myself. It taught me to have empathy, that really grew during that time.

"I can empathise with lots of people in vulnerable situations but it also taught me, 'gosh, well, if I can do that, I can do anything'."

The article was posted to a WalesOnline Facebook account, which highlighted the tragedy in the headline.

In the comments on the post, the Reform branch account said: "We have all had family tragedies, but we don't use it as a card for political gain."

That prompted Plaid Cymru MS, Beca Brown, to reply: "What a vile comment.

"There are politicians in all parties - including your own - who have personal experiences that reflect those of their constituents.

"Sharing those experiences publicly makes others who have suffered similarly feel less alone, and it can bring people together and shine a light on the suffering of others."

A Plaid Cymru spokesperson told BBC Wales: "The Reform UK Brycheiniog Tawe Nedd page must reflect on their disgusting comment - and as the local Reform MS, James Evans should condemn such an abhorrent statement."

The account describes itself as the "official Facebook page of Reform UK Brycheiniog Tawe Nedd, covering the areas of Brecon, Radnor and Cwm Tawe, with Neath and Swansea East".

Evans told BBC Wales: "These comments are totally unacceptable."

He said neither he nor his branch chairman had been aware that the comment had been posted, and that both he and the local branch would "totally distance ourselves" from the message.

"We've got a new branch chair. We're not fully aware of who is the admin of the page," he said.

"If we knew who the admin of the page was, these comments would be removed.

"We're doing an investigation to find out.

"Politicians are right to highlight personal experiences and it's not right that this comment was made about a fellow member of the Senedd."

McIntosh told BBC Wales that he was also distancing himself from the comment.

"I have asked the admins to remove the message," he said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2g.summary: Plaid Cymru minister James Evans called it "totally unacceptable" Two Reform MSs from the same area distanced themselves from the comment. The comment was made by Reform UK Brycheiniog Tawe Nedd's Brycheine Nedd branch.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2j.title: Burnham not actively considering Epstein inquiry, No 10 says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2j.text:
Andy Burnham is not actively considering holding a public inquiry into the UK activities of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, Downing Street has said.

It comes after Victims Minister Alex Davies-Jones told BBC Newsnight the prime minister was "looking into" the possibility of an inquiry into the alleged actions of Epstein and the former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed.

The prime minister has agreed to meet Epstein's victims.

Davies-Jones resigned from former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government in May, later accusing his government of failing to listen to Epstein's survivors.

She was reappointed as victims minister when Burnham took office.

The confusion in government thinking came after Davies-Jones told BBC Newsnight on Tuesday evening that she had discussed holding a public inquiry into the alleged behaviour of Epstein and Al Fayed with the prime minister and cabinet secretary Dame Antonia Romeo during her re-appointment.

Asked whether an inquiry was now possible, Davies-Jones said: "We are looking at this, we are reviewing what is possible. Again, same with Harrods survivors."

She added: "I have been assured that the prime minister is taking this very seriously.

"He will meet with those victims and he is looking at what is possible, now he has access to all of the information as prime minister to see what action we can take."

After resigning in May, Davies-Jones told the Commons in June that people whose lives were devastated by Epstein's abuse have too often been reduced to a footnote.

Asked what assurances or guarantees she had asked from Burnham in relation to the survivors when he re-appointed her to government, the minister said: "I did have those discussions with the prime minister before he became the prime minister."

"He agreed to meet with the Epstein victims," she continued, adding that Burnham "has assured me that he will meet them now he's prime minister and will work with us to look at systemic change across the system for all victims."

BBC Newsnight understands that as Burnham was finalising plans to become prime minister, he was sent a document by leading Labour campaigners on Violence Against Women and Girls.

It contained a key suggestion: to hold a full public inquiry into the UK activities of Epstein, the alleged behaviour of the late Harrods boss Mohamed Al Fayed and into allegations in a BBC Panorama and Times investigation that West Ham co-owner David Sullivan preyed on women.

David Sullivan has described the claims as false. He said he was "absolutely not the person the media has decided to paint me as".

The document called for an "impunity" inquiry to ask how powerful men were able to carry out the alleged behaviour.

On Epstein, the document calls for a focus on UK borders, asking how he was able to fly in and out of UK military bases on his private jet, often with allegedly trafficked women. Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown highlighted this issue in February.

Davies-Jones is understood to be familiar with the Labour document.
