https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2j.summary: Victims Minister Alex Davies-Jones says PM is looking into possibility of inquiry into Epstein's alleged actions. She says she had discussed the possibility of a public inquiry into the alleged actions of Epstein and the former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2v.title: Police chief considers joining legal action over PC Harper killers' early release
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2v.text:
The chief constable of Thames Valley Police says he will consider joining legal action to block the release of two of PC Andrew Harper's killers.

Chief Constable Jason Hogg told the BBC he was in talks with the Police Federation of England and Wales over the matter, adding public opinion on their potential release was "overwhelming".

PC Harper, who served with Thames Valley, was killed in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

The two passengers in the car, Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, were sentenced in 2020 to 13 years for manslaughter and could apply for early release after serving half of their sentences.

The driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, received a 16-year sentence and is not eligible for early release.

Speaking on the Today programme, Thames Valley Police chief Jason Hogg urged the government to reconsider its position.

Only prisoners convicted of murder, rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from the scheme in England and Wales - while those convicted of manslaughter remain eligible.

"I fully understand the challenges around the crisis in the prison system," he said.

"But the decision made and where that line has been drawn, I do not believe that people responsible for taking the life of another citizen in our country should be released early."

He said: "I was informed yesterday that the Police Federation are considering legal action, I am in discussions with the Police Federation with regards to this matter".

Asked whether this meant he would join them, he said: "I think we need to get some legal advice in relation to this. This is something I certainly would consider."

Following PC Harper's death and a campaign by his widow Lissie, Parliament passed "Harper's Law", which gives mandatory life sentences to the killers of emergency services workers. It also doubles the maximum penalty from 12 months to two years for those who assault police or other emergency workers.

But the new rules - introduced in 2022 - did not apply retrospectively to the sentencing of PC Harper's killers, and so do not prevent them from being released early.

Hogg said: "The law isn't retrospective and we all understand that, but the fact that they are released early simply seems perverse."

Aileen O'Connor, branch chairman of Thames Valley Police Federation told BBC Breakfast her organisation was exploring whether legal action was an option.

"If it is an avenue we can explore then I'll get behind that 110%," she said.

As for what shape a potential legal challenge might take, she said: "Ultimately that's for the specialists, the barristers and those in that legal sector to make that decision whether there is a challenge there.

"If there is a challenge then we will look to take that challenge."

Sentencing minister Jake Richards told the BBC it would be wrong to pick out individual cases and block two of PC Harper's killers from early release.

Although the government had reviewed what sentences would be excluded from the early release scheme, he confirmed "manslaughter is not one of those offences".

On Wednesday the Ministry of Justice released a new list of exclusions that will be exempt from the early release scheme.

It said rapists, as well as criminals sentenced for child sex offences and grooming and conspiracy offences for these crimes, will no longer be eligible to leave prison early.

Murderers and terrorists were already not eligible for the early release scheme.

Richards said: "It would be wrong to pick out individual cases within different offending cohorts. That wouldn't be right. It wouldn't be lawful either. So it is correct that those two individuals will be subject to the new regime from October".

Any legal challenge would have to be heard in the High Court, where ministerial decisions are reviewed.

Judges would have to be convinced that the government's choice of who gets out and who remains inside was either totally unlawful because they did not have the power to decide - or so irrational that it failed a legal test for reasonable decision-making.

Crucially, judges do not rule against a minister just because they do not like the choice they have made - there has to be a clear legal flaw in how they went about it.

Met Police commissioner Mark Rowley said the PC Harper case has had "a chilling effect on the confidence of police officers when they see a justice system that's not prepared to support their bravery".

On Tuesday Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the government wanted to go further but warned that a prison capacity crisis would be likely if fewer prisoners were allowed early release.

Norris apologised to families who would be affected by the early release scheme and stressed that the government wanted to go further "but we cannot".

"We have to make this decision, we've been able to make some changes to it, but we have to have the rest of the sentencing act changes otherwise we run out of prison places in November and that can't happen," he said.

The justice secretary said 5,000 extra releases will take place in 10 batches from October.

Approximately 1,000 prisoners will now not be released early following the revision to the scheme, he clarified.

The government also announced an extra £10m will go to front-line victim support services, including a new national helpline.

Additional reporting by home and legal correspondent Dominic Casciani
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2v.summary: Thames Valley Police chief Jason Hogg says he is in talks with the Police Federation of England and Wales. He says he will consider legal action to block the release of two of PC Andrew Harper's killers. PC Harper was killed in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62v.title: What could happen to prisoner early release scheme now?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62v.text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has changed the incoming early release scheme for some prisoners in England and Wales amid huge political and public pressure to rethink the scheme.

His decision to exclude rapists and some other offenders from the plans comes after the widow of PC Andrew Harper described two of his three killers being freed earlier than had been expected as "deplorable".

Under the new Sentencing Act, set to come into force in September, some 6,000 criminals had been due to be released at varying stages - the aim being to ease overcrowding that has caused chaos across prisons and the courts.

Earlier this year Parliament voted through the Sentencing Act 2026 to radically reform the rules governing the sentencing and management of prisoners.

This was part of Sir Keir Starmer's government's plan to tackle the unprecedented crisis of overcrowded jails it had inherited: quite simply, if the prisons ran out of cells - as was nearly the case in late 2024 - the police and courts would be unable to lock up newly caught criminals.

Police would not be able to charge suspects. Trials would have to be stopped. Judges would not be able to sentence criminals to years in prison.

It would be unprecedented in modern Britain.

One part of the plan means many jailed offenders on fixed terms will leave prison after serving just a third of their term behind bars, rather than at the halfway point which has long been the law.

Leaving prison does not mean they are free: release on licence includes strict conditions and often an electric tag or curfews to monitor whereabouts - although recent figures show thousands of people required to have a tag did not have one.

The plan had been that from 2 September, the first prisoners to benefit from the scheme were those serving up to 19 months. Offenders serving longer fixed-term sentences would become eligible for the scheme month-by-month.

That roll-out has now been delayed. Burnham says the scheme should exclude rapists, serious sexual offenders against children and those guilty of grooming gang related crimes. There will be a "presumption" that all offenders are tagged.

So that means that prison governors and probation officers must put plans on ice - and start rethinking who gets out and when.

This is where it gets really complicated. The government wants the new plan operational by October.

Ministers can use their powers to lay down new rules - but Parliament can intervene in such direct orders - and that raises the possibility of a clash with the opposition over who to exclude from early release. Last October, when the plan was going through Parliament, the Tories attempted to amend it to exclude the very groups who will now be kept inside.

So whatever the wording of the new orders triggering the release plan, it may not be plain sailing.

Initially up to 6,000 offenders were to benefit from the scheme, but it's unclear now how many will still be released because ministers have not published the draft of the new rules which specifically lists the offences that will be excluded.

While politicians and the public roughly understand the aim, this lack of clarity has caused a huge problem for prison governors.

They must tell offenders their release dates.

The Prison Governors Association says its members are unclear how many prisoners will now need their sentences to be recalculated again and who will remain in prison.

"We don't know if it is tens, hundreds or thousands that will be excluded," it said in a statement.

Knowing the date means governors can plan how they are using cells for other inmates - and it helps inmates prepare better for release through resettlement and rehabilitation - including making sure they have a bed for the first critical nights.

A safe bed means a better shot at going straight and getting a job.

Anything that makes it harder to resettle an offender increases the chance they will break the law again and return to prison - and that in turn means more overcrowding and the chances of rehabilitation diminish.

In 2019 the 28-year-old officer was killed when he was dragged down a road in Berkshire after getting caught in a strap attached to the back of a car that teenage burglary suspects were using to flee the scene.

Henry Long, 18 at the time, was the driver and the jury did not convict him of murder because it was not sure he knew he was dragging the officer along as he drove off.

But he, Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole, both 17 at the time, were all convicted of manslaughter - which means causing an unlawful death, without necessarily intending to do so.

They were all jailed in 2020.

Long was jailed for 16 years. It would have been 24 had he not admitted manslaughter.

The sentencing judge said he would serve 10 years and eight months of that in a cell before he could be released on licence.

Bowers and Cole were told they would serve two thirds of their 13 years in custody and the rest on licence in the community.

Release on licence is baked into sentencing laws in the UK and comparable countries. It means an offender leaves prison but is not free of their sentence - they are subject to restrictions and conditions on their life which can include electronic tag monitoring of their movements and curfews.

If an offender breaks the conditions, they can be sent back behind bars.

Bowers and Cole were in a category of criminals who were told by their trial judge they would spend two-thirds of their sentence in jail.

But that was changed under the new rules which meant they could leave at the halfway point of their term. That remains the case - they are unaffected by Labour's U-turn to exclude some groups of prisoners. If the government sticks to the original release timetable for most prisoners, they will become eligible from after next June.

No. His more severe sentence is unaffected by any of the new rules under the original or revised plan. He still has at least another four years of prison walls to look at.

Almost certainly. The prison population today is about 86,500 and there are about 2,400 spare places.

That headroom is reducing monthly despite the government pushing ahead with building 14,000 extra cells. By 2030 officials think there will be around 100,000 in prison - but it could be more than that.

Worst-case scenario? The government begins to run out of space in 2029 unless this new plan to manage and monitor more offenders in the community is a success.

Sir Keir's government sold its reforms as "prison outside of prison", but there are widespread and genuine concerns across criminal justice that the Probation Service, which has been rocked by a series of disastrous reorganisations in the last 15 years, is still not fully resourced and able to deal with all the risks.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62v.summary: Andy Burnham has changed the early release scheme for some prisoners in England and Wales. It comes amid huge political and public pressure to rethink the scheme. It is part of the government's plan to tackle the unprecedented crisis of overcrowded jails.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz97.title: Greens review social media operation as Polanski row rumbles on
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz97.text:
The Green Party of England and Wales is reviewing its social media operation which has been central to its surge in popularity over the past year, sources have told the BBC.

They insist it is not connected to the backlash to Zack Polanski this week after he re-posted a photo of a man wearing a t-shirt with an image of a guillotine and the slogan "we're only making plans for Nigel" - seen as being a reference to Nigel Farage.

But that incident has raised questions about whether it is sustainable for the Green Party leader to manage his own social media channels, with one party figure calling it an "avoidable mistake" and that Polanski "should have said sorry" for it.

In an interview with BBC Newsnight, Polanski repeatedly refused to apologise for "an inadvertent mistake" but acknowledged he needed to "be better on social media".

"I just didn't look carefully enough and I accepted it, as soon as I was aware of what happened I unaccepted it and took it down," he said.

Like other high profile figures on social media, Polanski receives a lot of material from other users seeking re-posts. But unlike most political leaders in the UK, he still manages his own accounts, rather than handing control to party staffers.

This may allow him to appear spontaneous and authentic - both valuable commodities on social media - but it comes with risks.

The current row began after Polanski shared a single post on Instagram that contained a carousel of 20 pictures.

The re-post was shared to Polanski's 713,000 followers, because he accepted a request to tag him as a collaborator, which on the platform makes him a "co-author," placing it on his page and into his followers' feeds.

Polanski said he had not noticed the offending image among the others on the post.

According to him, he had accepted collaborator tags for eight other posts from the same event in Bristol alone.

Reform UK leader Farage claimed the t-shirt amounted to incitement to murder and his party reported it to the police.

Neither the Metropolitan Police nor Avon and Somerset Police say the incident meets the threshold for further action.

But the political row has continued with Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick calling Polanski a "nasty piece of work", at a news conference earlier on Thursday.

Inside the Green Party, there has been some criticism of Polanski's behaviour online.

He has attracted positive and negative attention for the rate at which he posts, comments, likes and replies across multiple platforms including X, Bluesky, Facebook and Instagram.

And this is not the first time a quick reaction has attracted controversy; last month he had to apologise to police after posting about their response to the Golders Green attack.

One senior party source said it was clear that due diligence had not been done on Polanski's social media output, and that moving forwards he needs "tight controls" to stay credible, while keeping a similar tone of engagement with his followers.

They pointed out that the speed and number of Polanski's interactions came with a "small upside" but a "colossal downside", and with the latest incident he had "shot himself in the foot at precisely the wrong time".

It comes as recent polling suggests the Green Party has lost ground to Labour, following Andy Burnham's election as Labour leader, and down from a peak earlier this year.

They added their concerns about a wider problem with the party's vetting on social media and of candidates, including around antisemitic posts in recent months.

Several candidates in recent elections have stood down over their social media activity, with two candidates arrested during May's local elections, and another suspended after being elected.

But Green Party peer and former deputy mayor of London Baroness Jones said the criticism of Polanski's Instagram re-post seemed to be "mainly from our opponents, not internal discussions".

She said that her party leader had "made a mistake", adding "we've all done it and got flak."

But she added: "His online presence is what makes him relatable".

Along with relatability, comes popularity: Polanski is the second-most followed UK leader on Instagram after Nigel Farage. The Greens surpassed other parties to become the most popular on the platform this year.

It is also seen as where a good portion of their voters spend time, as they are the most popular party among the under-30s, according to pollsters YouGov.

One party source said there had been discussions among councillors and activists about whether Polanski was "too online".

"Is he just too online? Is he doing it all himself? Where's the professionalisation here, given the level the party's now grown to, and what people expect of us?" they said.

"There's got to be more checks and balances" the source added.

A separate party source confirmed there was a review going on internally into the party's social media operation, but would not be drawn on whether that meant changing who had oversight of Polanski's posts.

"We are looking at our processes and systems in this area," they said.

"Obviously Zack is really active on social media. It is how we have grown our reach and our membership."

Until around a year ago the party's entire social media team consisted of one full-time employee.

That has now gone up to three or four and may increase further following the review.

"We have expanded hugely as a party and we are looking at how we work," the source said.

"As part of that we are looking at what we might do to support and beef up our social media team."

They said the coverage of the Instagram re-post row had been "deeply irritating" but added that the review was not directly linked to that incident.

But it remains to be seen how much longer Polanski can retain control of his accounts before handing over the passwords to party staffers.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz97.summary: Green Party of England and Wales reviewing its social media operation. Party sources say it is not connected to the backlash to Zack Polanski's re-post.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj4k.title: Andy Burnham wants to fix social care - what are the options?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj4k.text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants major reform of the social care system in England, calling the current situation "bad for everybody".

In a speech at a care home on Wednesday he announced that cross-party talks involving the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats would start later.

Burnham also said he had asked Baroness Casey - who is carrying out a review of social care - to bring forward her report by a year. She will now set out her recommendations in 2027.

He confirmed that her review will also look at the question of how to pay for any reforms.

BBC Verify has looked at four options for approaching reform and how much they could cost.

Some people face extremely high costs for care at the end of their life.

It has been estimated that around one in seven people aged 65 and over face lifetime care costs of more than £100,000.

One proposal is to cap these costs with the government picking up the bill above a certain cash threshold.

In 2011 a commission headed by the economist Andrew Dilnot proposed a lifetime cap of £35,000.

Dilnot estimated his proposed reforms would cost between £1.3bn and £2.2bn a year. The cost today would be higher due to inflation and the ageing population.

The Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government, led by David Cameron, accepted Dilnot's recommendations.

But after the 2015 general election, which delivered a Conservative majority, Cameron delayed the implementation of the cap to 2020 over what he said were pressures on the public finances.

In 2017, when Theresa May was in No 10, the Conservatives' general election manifesto proposed a different way to reform social care.

This would have included the value of an individual's home in the means test used to decide what state funding they could get for care in their own homes.

It did not, initially, include any cap on lifetime care costs, with the manifesto saying this was more "equitable" than the Dilnot plan.

The May plan was branded a "dementia tax" by opponents and eventually dropped.

In England people can currently qualify for local authority financial support in a residential care home if all their assets - including their home - are worth less than £23,250.

This is known as a means test - where the level of financial support a person gets is based on the value of their assets and savings.

Some have suggested this threshold should be raised significantly so that many more people would qualify for means-tested support.

Boris Johnson's Conservative government in 2021 planned to raise the means test threshold to £100,000.

The annual cost of Johnson's reforms would have been £1.8bn a year over three years - although this was expected to rise over time as more people qualified.

The Johnson government planned a new Health and Social Care levy to pay for the package, but this was eventually scrapped by his Conservative successors as prime minister, because they wanted to keep taxes down.

An alternative approach is to ensure that everyone who is eligible, based on their needs, should get state-funded personal care that is free at the point of use.

This would be provided free regardless of an individual's means and whether it was received by an elderly person in their own house or a residential care home.

Scotland has implemented such a system.

However, it's important to note that personal care takes in things like helping frail elderly people wash and dress and go to the toilet.

But it does not include accommodation, food and everyday living costs which are subject to means testing.

The Health Foundation think tank estimates that implementing a Scottish-style system in England would cost £7.5bn a year by 2036.

Like Scotland, Japan and Germany have systems which base entitlement to personal social care mainly on people's care needs rather than their ability to pay.

Japan and Germany though have a mandatory long-term care insurance system which is funded through contributions from workers and employers.

Both countries also do not usually cover the full cost of personal care so individuals are responsible for some of the expenses.

Some have suggested that the government should set up a national care service in England, similar in ambition to the NHS.

This would mean all personal care would be free at the point of use while establishing national standards and care entitlement criteria.

The Health Foundation has estimated the cost of creating a universal and comprehensive social care system in England would be around £19bn a year extra by 2036.

When Andy Burnham was health secretary in Gordon Brown's Labour government in 2010 he produced a plan for a national care service.

It was suggested this would be paid for through a compulsory contribution from people's estates after they'd died.

But the idea was branded a "death tax" by Labour's opponents. The party lost the 2010 general election and its proposals went no further.

In the 2024 general election Labour again proposed a "national care service" without providing details or how it would be funded.

And after the election then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer effectively kicked the issue into the long grass by commissioning Louise Casey to investigate social care reform and report back in 2028.

It's worth bearing in mind that these four approaches above are not mutually exclusive.

Previous reform proposals have often combined more than one of them - such as a cap on lifetime costs and a more generous means test.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj4k.summary: Andy Burnham has asked Baroness Casey to bring forward her report by a year. She will now set out her recommendations in 2027. A cap on lifetime costs and a more generous means test are both possible.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce8l.title: 'Every day I'm just winging it': The families hoping for social care reform
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce8l.text:
Andy Burnham has pledged to reform the adult social care system in England, meeting the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats to try to find "common ground" on the issue.

He wants an independent review of care to be brought forward by a year to 2027, as well as major reforms to pay and conditions for staff and the creation of a national care service.

But the prime minister said "difficult decisions" would have to be made on tax to fund sustainable change, adding that in an "ideal world" no-one should have to sell their home to pay for care.

BBC Your Voice has been speaking to families affected by what they see as shortfalls in the system.

Emma Riley has been caring for her mother Carol, who has dementia, since she lost her father 18 months ago.

"She's a cracking lady, still with a sense of humour but she's living with this awful condition," said Riley, from Manchester.

She is paying £34 an hour for a care company to come to the house three times a week, which she describes as a "huge chunk of money" although she is happy with the level of care.

Riley wants to keep her mum in the family home, but the caring commitments affect her job as a dental nurse.

She started applying to the local council for funding to support her mother at home at the beginning of the year, but six months on, she is still waiting for a final decision.

"It's not the social worker's fault, it is just the caseload," she said.

Riley called for more communication to help her navigate the system, adding: "I'm blindly going through it at the moment.

"Every day I'm just winging it but there's a human being upstairs."

Riley said she heard the prime minister's speech and it had left her feeling "quietly confident".

Burnham has announced that a review of social care by veteran Whitehall troubleshooter Baroness Casey would now be published next summer.

"I do think Baroness Casey will make the changes we need," Riley added.

Lisa Greenwood, from Halifax, West Yorkshire, said she would be supportive of the prime minister if he managed to change how the care sector operates.

"It does need changing and hopefully it will get better," she said.

Greenwood said her family is having to make "some very tough decisions" in caring for her mother, Mavis, who is 90 and in local respite care.

It is costing £1,305 a week, something Greenwood says the family "cannot sustain".

She said they now face the prospect of having to sell her mother's home, describing this as "very distressing".

Greenwood backs Burnham's proposal to increase pay in the sector and suggests it will help attract more staff.

"Carers do need to be paid more," she said. "There are some fantastic people doing the job on little wages."

Greenwood told the BBC's Your Voice that both her parents had worked "all their lives saving for the future".

"Yet here we are in a situation of stress not knowing how we are going to continue with mum in the home," she added.

"We can't give up our jobs, we need to work to pay our bills."

Sophie Daniels was 16 when her father died in 2024 as a result of stage 4 glioblastoma, a highly aggressive brain tumour.

The 18-year-old felt that there was a lack of support for her family. Along with her mother and sister, she looked after her father at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire, as "social care provision was incredibly limited".

Daniels said: "We hardly had any help and we were left to figure things out ourselves.

"Thankfully, charities helped us with that but towards the end my mum had to give up work to care for my dad."

She said that one of the biggest practical challenges her family faced was a lack of a lifting service to help him move around the house.

"He fell fairly frequently and a lack of lifting service meant that our dad was forced to either wait for hours on the floor for an ambulance or for us to try and use techniques to pull my dad up."

Steve West, from Wakefield, West Yorkshire, cared for his mother for many years before taking the difficult decision to place her in a care home. She died earlier this year.

West, 64, said he was "frustrated hearing the same issues that need fixing being discussed by each new government".

Listening to the prime minister's speech, he said that a proposed national care service "could give focus, but its remit needs to be confirmed".

"I think a cross-party approach would be a benefit as the plans would take a few terms of parliament at least and then to maintain the benefits for years to come," he added.

He said when caring for his mother, the biggest challenge was "knowing who to speak to" and "dealing with several health bodies", sometimes having to repeat her medical history several times.

"She got progressively worse and I remember one time sitting in a car park for an hour-and-a-half trying to get an emergency social worker," he said, adding that "having a system that is unified would be a massive help".

West believes the prime minister "needs to focus on one or two big-ticket items - those that will have the biggest impact".

He said if relatives caring for loved ones were paid at similar rates to private companies, "perhaps more people would feel they were able to provide support" as they would not be negatively impacted by cutting work hours or leaving their jobs.

Jeanette Barry from Essex was married to her husband John for 42 years before he was diagnosed with dementia in 2018.

The former policeman was moved to a local care home as his needs became more complex.

"At one point he was roaming the streets at night because he thought he was still on duty," said Barry.

"I couldn't keep him in the house, so at 2am or 3am I was having to follow him to make sure he was alright."

She paid £2,000 a month in care home fees out of her husband's police pension, on top of local authority funding, although she didn't "begrudge a penny of that money" as he was well looked after.

She says she was told by one social worker that she would have to remortgage her house or her husband would be moved to another care home, but he was later reassessed and qualified for more financial support.

"I had to think twice before putting my heating on," she says. "It was a horrible, terrible time for the family."

Barry, whose husband died two years ago, said she doesn't have much faith in politicians to make the social care system work, but noted the prime minister has experience of the matter as his father has Alzheimer's.

"They all make promises but then they never do anything," she said.

"I have slightly more confidence in Andy Burnham because he has personal experience of dementia but how is he going to pay for it?"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c24y.title: How a rise in ADHD benefits claims is adding to welfare spending challenge
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c24y.text:
Andy Burnham, who is expected to become prime minister in a matter of weeks, has said he wants to get the UK's benefits bill down by encouraging more people into work.

The total bill for working age sickness and disability benefits has been increasing rapidly since 2020. It currently stands at £58bn and has been projected to rise to £78bn by 2030, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

More than 100,000 people with ADHD as their main condition now receive Personal Independence Payments (Pip), the latest government figures show, an increase of 40% in these cases since Labour came to power two years ago.

It comes as an interim report into Pip by Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms says it is "not fit for purpose" and argues a sweeping overhaul of the assessment system is needed.

BBC Verify has been looking into the official figures around Pip claims and the wider numbers on the working-age welfare bill.

Pip is the working age benefit which helps individuals deal with the extra costs of having a physical or mental health condition or disability.

It was introduced in 2013 as a replacement for Disability Living Allowance (DLA).

You do not have to be out of work to claim Pip and it does not come with requirements to seek work.

People currently receive between £1,580 and £10,120 per year depending on the severity of their condition.

Official figures show total Pip claims in England and Wales now stand at 4 million, up from 3.6 million when Labour took power, an increase of around 400,000.

The overall rise in claimants continues an earlier upward trend that was clear under the previous Conservative government.

A growing share of new Pip claims since the 2020 pandemic have been related to mental health or neurodevelopmental conditions, with the share of total claims related to ADHD, autism, depression or anxiety rising from around 16.5% in 2020 to 24% in 2026.

The latest official statistics show the number of people claiming Pip with ADHD as their main condition was around 100,000 in April.

Just over half of these were aged 16 to 24.

That is up from around 70,000 when Labour took office in July 2024, an increase of 30,000 over that time.

An initial independent review for the Department of Health and Social Care this year found that the increase in people diagnosed with ADHD was likely due to a combination of factors from an improved recognition of the condition to more people seeking help and changing expectations of support.

It also stated that "where access to support is closely linked to diagnosis, demand for diagnostic assessment may increase".

Pip is the fastest growing part of the total working age sickness and disability bill, which was £58 billion in 2025.

That's roughly the same size as the budget for schools in England, which will be £66bn in 2027.

The Office for Budget Responsibility, the official forecaster, expects the total sickness and disability bill - which includes Pip and the health-related element of Universal Credit - to rise to £78 billion in cash terms by 2030.

The overall share of GDP spent on all non-pensioner welfare has actually fallen since 2010.

This decline reflects real-terms cuts to working-age benefits during the austerity years after the 2010 general election, including cuts to housing benefit and to elements of Universal Credit.

The OBR projects that this overall non-pensioner welfare bill as a share of GDP will remain broadly steady in the coming years rather than increasing sharply.

Some policy analysts argue that cuts to the welfare system since 2010 may have created a counterproductive incentive for people to claim sickness and disability benefits instead of other forms of support.

The previous Conservative government said it was necessary to cut welfare spending to help reduce the budget deficit.

Many experts agree that reform of parts of the working age welfare system is needed, but warn that is important to bear the overall context in mind too.

A government spokesperson said: "We inherited a broken welfare system and we are fixing it - a package of measures already coming into effect will save nearly £2 billion by the end of the decade, and the Timms Review, working with disabled people and their representative organisations, is looking at how to make Pip fit and fair for the future."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp8l.title: How the leasehold revolution could transform neighbourly relations
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp8l.text:
When Sally, 74, bought her two-bedroom flat in 2021, she hoped it would be the home she could peacefully retire in.

But she says buying a leasehold home has led to terrible stress.

There are around five million leaseholders in England and Wales. Sally is one of over 1,000 people the BBC spoke to in an attempt to understand the pressures on leaseholders. Most said that fast rising service changes and ground rent costs make them feel they have little control over their own homes.

When she moved into her London flat, Sally says service charges were around £2,600 a year. One year, they totalled more than £5,400.

"That was a really bad year. Me and my fellow owners were very stressed and anxious. There were tears and I remember us talking about how we were going to pay."

Now, the government wants to fundamentally change how flats are owned.

Under its Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, new leasehold flats will be banned and replaced with commonhold, a system where residents collectively own and manage their buildings.

"The people who should own buildings, and who should exercise control over their management, shared facilities and related costs are not third-party landlords but the people who live in flats within them and who have a direct stake in their upkeep," said Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook, in a speech in April.

Freeholders argue that the English Housing Survey suggests 93% of leaseholders living in flats are satisfied with being an owner occupier (the survey doesn't ask specifically about being a leaseholder).

Despite this, the government is introducing reforms widely seen as the biggest shake-up of home ownership in decades.

But as commonhold moves closer to becoming the default for new-build flats, questions remain over whether it can avoid creating a new set of challenges for homeowners. And can a system that has existed for centuries really be replaced - or will a whole new set of problems emerge?

To understand the complexities of today's leasehold system, described by many, including Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook, as "feudal", we have to go back almost 1,000 years.

In the Middle Ages, William the Conqueror took control of England's land and granted parts of it to loyal nobles, who leased it to others for a fixed term.

While today's leasehold system is very different, critics argue the basic principle remains the same - homeowners pay for the right to occupy land they do not fully own.

For almost 60 years, successive governments have tried to reform it, with one alternative repeatedly put forward: commonhold.

It was first introduced into law under Tony Blair's government in 2004, but developers have rarely chosen it. According to the Land Registry, there are only 18 commonhold developments in England.

Commonhold is a type of home ownership where flat owners have a share in running their building. There is no freeholder, and residents vote on decisions about shared spaces and maintenance. Homeowners are expected to pay into a reserve fund and either manage the property themselves or appoint a managing agent.

Nick Hopkins, Professor of Land Law at UCL and specialist adviser to the House of Commons Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee - the group of MPs scrutinising the draft Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill - says that after years of looking into the issue he is "convinced" commonhold is the right direction for the government to go in.

He says flat owners would still have to pay towards the upkeep of their building, but they would have "much more autonomy" over decision-making under the proposals.

John Bartholomew, 81, and his wife have lived in one of England's commonhold developments, in Somerset, for around 12 years.

The development consists of two blocks of flats and five town houses. They have an annual general meeting and come together to discuss issues such as the shared car park.

He says he has been lucky to live in a place where people agree on the work that needs to be done.

"If a renegade came in, we might struggle," he says.

"If we want something done, we have to agree that part of the fee will be put to that purpose, like the repainting of the sheds."

Freeholders argue that they act as "stewards" of buildings.

They point to research by the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS), which they say suggests Scotland's commonhold-like system has created "major hurdles" in carrying out essential building maintenance, with 28% of buildings in critical disrepair.

Similar concerns were raised in evidence to MPs scrutinising the draft legislation.

Mari Knowles, a landlord and tenant lawyer, told the Select Committee there was a risk of a "stalemate situation" where residents may not agree on paying for maintenance and investment in a building.

She said she had worked with resident-managed buildings that "traditionally have not paid into the reserve fund... now the buildings are severely dilapidated, and they are all looking at five-figure or six-figure bills."

Under the leasehold system, the freeholder appoints a managing agent to maintain and service the common parts of a building. Flat owners are then given the bills.

Leaseholders are also legally obliged to pay ground rent - a fee paid for the land beneath their building - to the freeholder. Depending on the terms of the lease, the amount can either double at fixed intervals or increase in line with inflation, which can make a property harder to sell, mortgage or remortgage.

Freeholds can be bought and sold between investors who do not live in the building, and sometimes not even in the country, meaning the English system of flat ownership has become "financialised", according to Hopkins.

He believes a move to commonhold would change that, ensuring "the only financial interest in the block is with those living in it."

Under the proposed plans, ground rents will also be capped at £250 before falling to a "peppercorn" rate - effectively zero - after 40 years. In a debate in Parliament on Thursday, a number of MPs called for that process to be sped up - and described ground rents as "money for nothing".

Freeholders say this overlooks the long-term oversight and legal accountability they provide, including maintaining buildings and acting as an independent party when disputes arise.

The BBC wrote to all of the groups that run commonhold developments in England and Wales, and not all described a harmonious way of living.

One resident described commonhold as a "nightmare".

He says one flat owner has refused to pay towards maintenance and other residents now have to pay more to cover that share. The collective is now £10,000 in debt.

"The government is pushing commonhold forward, but it's not the way to go. It's terrible - a disaster."

Due to the ongoing dispute, the man did not want to be named for this article, but said the leasehold system would have offered more protection in his case because, "if a leaseholder doesn't pay there is something in the contract that will say 'you forfeit the lease'. With commonhold, that doesn't happen, so the payments fall on everyone else."

A freeholder can seek to repossess someone's home if a leaseholder doesn't pay service charges, something that will also be abolished under the reforms. In a commonhold, disputes between owners must be resolved through the courts. Under the changes, in the most extreme cases, homeowners who refuse to pay could be forced to sell their home to settle debt.

Hopkins accepts that commonhold is "not a panacea for everything that can go wrong when you own a flat," but says it is "the right legal basis to have to deal with the issues that can go wrong".

He says commonhold will require "a bit of a cultural change" and that people will need to view themselves as "stewards" of their building.

One of the main arguments from Hopkins and many others is that commonhold, or similar forms of ownership, already work in much of the rest of the world.

Dr Cathy Sherry, Professor at Macquarie Law School in Australia, has studied property law and ownership across the world. She agrees there is no perfect way of owning buildings but believes England and Wales should move to commonhold.

Australia uses a system known as strata, which Sherry describes as a form of commonhold similar to the condominium model used in the United States and other countries.

"The reason why we have strata and condominiums is ex-British colonies were settled by people, the working class of Scotland, England, Wales and Ireland, and they actively did not want the emergence of a landed aristocracy."

Sherry, who was also a technical adviser to the Law Commission's review of commonhold, describes leasehold as "deeply unfair".

She says the Australian system is "much better than leasehold" because ownership and building management are set out in legislation, rather than relying on millions of different leases.

Under the government's proposals, there would also be standard rules around how commonhold buildings are managed.

The Residential Freehold Association (RFA) argue the picture is more complicated.

They point to research from Your Strata Property suggesting only 30% of committee members in Australia's strata system considered themselves "very knowledgeable" about strata law, while 70% admitted to having limited or no confidence in their legal understanding.

They argue this can result in poor governance, legal non-compliance and deferred maintenance - all risks in collectively owned building

Although commonhold has been an option for developers for more than 20 years, they have continued to build leasehold blocks. One reason was reluctance from lenders to provide mortgages for commonhold properties because they were seen as an untested risk.

John Bartholomew says that when he tried to draw equity from his home he was told: "We don't lend to commonhold."

He believes one of the biggest challenges is getting institutions to treat commonhold owners "like any other householders" rather than "second or third-class citizens".

Charles Roe, former Director of Mortgages at UK Finance, which represents around 120 mortgage lenders, told MPs in March that estate agents, valuers, surveyors and conveyancers would all need to be brought up to speed, and that the transition for consumers and the industry would be a "big piece of work".

He said lenders' main concern is what happens when existing leasehold buildings convert to commonhold.

And that is arguably the most complex part of the government's plans.

Campaigners are calling for "commonhold now" and a select committee report released in May called for the government to "go further and faster". But Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook has sought to manage expectations.

In April he said the "outright and immediate abolition of the leasehold system in England and Wales" would be "almost certainly impossible".

Converting a block to commonhold means transferring ownership from the freeholder to the residents, and how existing freeholders should be compensated is disputed.

The previous government tried to make buying a share of freehold cheaper through the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024. But those changes were challenged in the courts by freeholders, who argued the reforms breached their human rights.

The government won that case, but the decision is now under appeal.

Barrister Dr Douglas Maxwell told MPs it was "almost inevitable" that further legal challenges would be brought under human rights law once the new legislation is introduced.

Meanwhile, court battles could slow attempts to make it easier for residents to convert their buildings.

Despite what has happened in Australia and other countries, there is no direct comparison for dismantling a leasehold system on the scale of England and Wales.

Scotland did not so much reform leasehold as remove a much smaller version of it.

Ken Gerber, a solicitor in Glasgow, explains that most residential properties in Scotland are already owned outright after a feudal-style system of land ownership was abolished in 2000. Long leases were automatically converted to ownership in 2015.

But he says the scale was very different. In 2006 there were around 2,500 long leases in Scotland - roughly 2% of all residential properties.

"Leasehold in England is much, much more common than in Scotland," he says.

Scottish landlords were entitled to compensation, but Gerber says it was relatively modest. "It was roughly 40 times the amount of annual rent. But it was only leases where the rent was less than £100 a year."

The compensation likely to be sought by English freeholders would be far greater.

On Scotland's current system, which has similarities to commonhold, Gerber says it "generally works".

"You'll always find one that doesn't want to stump up their money... that can be a problem," he says.

Most of the experts agreed there is no perfect system where multiple people share responsibility for a building.

Hopkins believes commonhold will happen, regardless of further legal challenges. "The judicial review failed at first instance and failed quite comprehensively. A lot of the arguments, I think, have really been lost."

He says there is now broad political support for reform.

Former housing secretaries Angela Rayner and Michael Gove both backed reform when giving evidence together to MPs. The Liberal Democrats and Greens also support commonhold, while Reform UK has stopped short of supporting the complete abolition of leasehold.

A spokesperson at the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said their reforms would "transform the experience of flat ownership in England by giving homeowners "more power and control over high costs".

Professor Sherry accepts that "stuff can be tricky, but it's workable".

"Commonhold is better because I don't believe that people who don't live in homes should own the underlying land and get the benefits that flow from that."

Whether that vision becomes reality now depends on politics as much as policy.

The likely next prime minister, Andy Burnham, has previously expressed support for leasehold reform, but who he appoints as housing secretary will matter. With the draft bill described as "technical and long", there is still a long way to go before the manifesto pledge comes to fruition.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g4.title: Sir John Curtice: The 'Burnham bounce' is real but it's not massive
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g4.text:
The consistent message of the opinion polls since the new prime minister walked into Downing Street almost a fortnight ago is that Labour is enjoying a "Burnham bounce". And this has now been confirmed by the party's convincing victory in Thursday's Greater Manchester mayoral by-election.

Polls conducted in the last week put Labour on average in the mid 20s. It is the party's highest standing since the beginning of last year and compares to their rating of 19% in late June when Sir Keir Starmer announced he was standing down.

But with Reform polling only narrowly behind Labour, Burnham's party still has a long way to go before it can face the prospect of fighting a general election with confidence.

The Burnham boost is far from unprecedented.

All but one of the recent mid-term changes of prime minister have been followed by an increase in the popularity of the incumbent government. Support for Labour rose by seven points after Gordon Brown replaced Tony Blair in 2007, while the Conservatives enjoyed a six-point bounce when Boris Johnson took over from Theresa May in 2019. Only Liz Truss' arrival in Downing Street in 2022 – which was overshadowed by the death shortly thereafter of Queen Elizabeth II – failed to give her party a boost.

We should also bear in mind the depth of the electoral hole that Burnham has inherited as Labour leader. The 19% at which Labour stood when Sir Keir resigned was the lowest poll rating passed on by any prime minister departing mid-term – even lower than the 23% bequeathed by Liz Truss when she resigned after just 45 days in office.

Against that backdrop, it would have been very surprising indeed if the replacement of the deeply unpopular Sir Keir by the relatively popular Burnham had not given Labour a short-term boost. However, even after Burnham's bounce, his party's poll average is still the lowest for any newly minted mid-term PM, while the party is still well adrift in the polls of the (relatively low) 35% it won at the 2024 general election.

That said, Labour's victory in Thursday's Manchester mayoral by-election was convincing. True, Labour's 47% share of the first preference vote was well down on the 63% that Burnham secured in the last mayoral contest shortly before the 2024 general election. However, not only did it represent a near doubling of the 24% that Labour registered across the region in May's local elections, but also it was even four points up on Labour's tally locally in the 2024 general election – and thus a much better performance than would have been anticipated from even the latest national polling.

But with still no more than a narrow lead over Reform, it is unsurprising Burnham has ruled out an early election. In any event, Reform's displacement from first place in the polls for the first time in over a year appears to owe more to its own difficulties than it does to Labour's new-found popularity.

Reform has been dogged in recent weeks by questions about the legality of the source of some of its funding and about whether Farage should have declared to the Commons authorities some of the funding he received before being elected an MP. Following these allegations, Farage announced on 7 July that he was standing down and putting himself again before the voters of his Clacton constituency in a by-election now scheduled for 13 August.

This move appears to have backfired. Immediately before Farage's announcement, Reform's average poll rating stood at 27%. In the polls conducted immediately after Farage's announcement, it fell by three points to 24%, the level at which it still stands now, and the lowest it has been for 15 months. At the same time, Farage's personal poll ratings are now the worst they have been since he returned as Reform's leader during the 2024 election campaign.

In the Manchester by-election, Reform's share of the first preference vote was nine point down on its tally across the region in May's local elections. As in the Makerfield by-election, the party seemingly suffered from the advance made by Rupert Lowe's breakaway from Reform, Restore Britain, which won nearly 9% of the Manchester vote, outpolling the Conservatives in the process.

But for Reform's difficulties, the "Burnham bounce" would probably have been insufficient to put Labour in the lead in the national polls.

The principal source of that bounce has been clawing voters back from the Greens and the Liberal Democrats, both of whom have suffered a two-point drop since Burnham's uncontested victory in the Labour leadership contest. For the Greens – much of whose increased support in recent months came from disappointed 2024 Labour voters – the change of prime minister has proven particularly damaging. The Greens' current 11% tally is as much as four points adrift of where it was when Sir Keir announced he was leaving.

When he resigned, 14% of Labour's 2024 election voters said they would now back the Greens. That figure is now 9%.

Winning back former Labour voters has generally been a key component of the Burnham bounce. Overall, 67% of those who voted Labour in 2024 now say they would vote for the party, compared to 57% when Sir Keir indicated he was leaving Downing Street.

Following Farage's difficulties, Labour is also now losing fewer of its 2024 voters to Reform. But the same is true of the Conservatives, whose loss of support to Reform in the polls during this Parliament has always been much greater than that suffered by Labour. Far from suffering from a Burnham bounce, Kemi Badenoch's party has edged up to 20% in the polls for the first time since last spring.

Burnham's arrival has given Labour new hope. But despite having overtaken Reform in the polls, the new Labour leader still has to prove he can win back the working class pro-Brexit voters that Labour once regarded as its core vote but who now form the heart of support for Reform.

To do this – and put Labour on course for victory in 2029 - Burnham needs to deliver on the policy challenges facing his government, which remain as formidable as those that beset Sir Keir. Labour's prospects at the next election will ultimately depend on whether voters have come to believe that what he has said he will do is actually happening.

John Curtice is a professor of politics at Strathclyde University and senior fellow at the National Centre for Social Research and The UK in a Changing Europe

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cglj6x.text:
Devon is bracing itself for a council shake-up, made up of four new authorities responsible for everything from leisure centres and planning to recycling.

The plan, set to kick-in in 2028, is expected to cost about £70m, with those behind it saying it will save £400m over 10 years.

Critics, however, say that is unlikely - and residents will have to wait and see what the impact on their council tax bills will be.

You can check how the changes will affect you with Devon County Council's postcode checker on their website.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq56.title: Zendaya saw me on the red carpet and her jaw dropped - I'm still in shock
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq56.text:
"I can't zip this! Mummm?"

This was 29-year-old Zainab Jiwa, calling out for help squeezing into a corset while filming a "get-ready-with-me" TikTok video. It's a scene many 20-somethings still living at home will relate to.

The difference is, Zainab was on her way to the recent London premiere of The Odyssey, one of the summer's biggest blockbusters.

She was invited there as a guest and says she caught the eye of Hollywood megastar Zendaya, thanks to her custom look: a striking gold gown complete with a hood.

"She just walked past, and she saw me there. Her jaw just dropped, so did mine," Zainab tells me.

"It was just a stare-off for a minute, and she was like, 'Oh my god, amazing, amazing,' and then she just walked off."

"I’m still in shock,” she adds. “The thought of her noticing my outfit blew my mind."

The interaction went viral with 19m TikTok views. Her phone blew up.

While Zendaya has been ruling the red carpets with high-fashion "method dressing" – where stars match outfits to a film's themes – Zainab is perhaps proving that independent creators like her can give Hollywood a run for its money.

Zainab, who is Muslim and wears a hijab, is also often one of the only people covering her hair at premieres, but she says finding ways to incorporate modest wear is part of the fun.

"Even though you're covered, you can still find a way to be on theme.”

Arriving for our interview at BBC Broadcasting House this week, her look was on-point in an olive shirt, tie, and brooches. "I put in effort today," she says.

She's a self-confessed fashion addict. "From the womb," she says, when I ask her when her passion started.

Her other love is film - but she initially kept that as a hobby. Still, she posted videos on social media for fun about her favourite films and outfits inspired by them.

Soon, major studios took notice. Disney was first, offering her a junket interview for the series Moon Knight, where she got to interview the stars.

"I thought it was a scam,” she says. “I can’t watch that back. I was NOT good.”

Today, Zainab is a full-time creator and presenter, interviewing A-listers such as Denzel Washington, Paul Mescal, Tom Hiddleston and Zendaya herself – while decked head to toe in outfits paying homage to the films.

She's one of many digital content creators on the red carpet, with others including Chicken Shop Date’s Amelia Dimoldenberg, Reece Feldman and social media personality Jake Shane.

It's not always easy. Sometimes, Zainab gets invites to premieres the night before, meaning a mad rush to sort her look before travelling to the event - often by public transport (“and I look ridiculous”).

She works with a range of designers and brands, but says she also keeps costs down by reusing items as much as possible.

Her outfits are purposely bold, allowing her to "break the ice" with stars. For House of the Dragon season two, she wore a red gown by a student designer featuring three faces wearing hijabs.

"I'm a bit extra, but I like to add culture in everything I do," she says.

For Spider-Man: Brand New Day, she customised her look with spiderweb henna. For Gladiator II, she wore gold armour.

She admits she has worried whether dressing modestly will make it harder for her to succeed in this industry, but she finds pleasure in it too.

"I have a fun time working around the fact that I cover my hair or I cover my arms," she says. "I'd call it halalify the look. I'd always say, ‘'but how do I halalify this?'"

"I enjoy that bit the most because it shows there's no restriction really here."

But while Zainab spends much of her time rubbing shoulders with Hollywood royalty, home life in Harrow, north-west London is completely different.

"Oh my god, my house is chaos," she laughs. Storage space is at a premium, and outfits often end up "shoved somewhere".

She has a cat, siblings who often pop in, and parents who are frequently enlisted for wardrobe emergencies.

Despite it not being the career trajectory they’d expected for their daughter, Zainab says her parents are now "so supportive".

With 660,000 followers on TikTok and close to 400,000 on Instagram, she's becoming a key content creator in this field. But she also faces criticism - including from some who claim her outfits are not modest enough.

"There's always hate in this industry," she says.

But she adds: "For every negative comment, there's so many positive ones.

"If I'm doing it to inspire other people, or entertain other people, or educate other people, if that's still happening, then I really don't care about the rest."

For now though, Zainab is swept up in enjoying a string of blockbusters.

"The summer's felt good for film - I think it's exciting," she says.

"And there's loads more coming. We've got Dune. We've got Doomsday," she says.

"I love film and TV. I think it's a really fun way to build community," she adds. "I'm just a fan. At the end of the day, I'm just a fan."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cewr.title: Madonna pays tribute to 'genius, otherworldly' producer William Orbit
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cewr.text:
Madonna has paid tribute to her regular collaborator and acclaimed music producer William Orbit, who died last month at the age of 69.

"You pressed a magic button inside of me and I fell into a galaxy of unrealised dreams," the pop superstar wrote on Instagram on Saturday. "Your music gave me a magic carpet to fly on and I visited many places."

Orbit's family announced "with profound sadness" on Friday that the Grammy-winning producer died at home on 23 July. No cause of death was given.

The British producer, whose real name was William Wainwright, helped reinvigorate Madonna's career in 1998 with Ray of Light, an album that blended electronic dance music and ambient techno with pop and trip-hop.

With its genre-bending sound, Ray of Light went on to win three Grammy Awards and is still considered by many to be the Queen of Pop's greatest record.

"I had an epiphany when I met you and started working with you," Madonna wrote in her post, alongside a video of herself standing beside Orbit to accept a Grammy Award. It also includes clips of the music videos and work she and Orbit created together.

Madonna said Orbit inspired her to sing and write in ways she never had before, without caring if her words "made sense or not".

"In many ways you were my Ray of Light - as was my daughter Lola who was born around this time," the singer wrote.

At the time she began working with Orbit, Madonna said she was beginning a new chapter, and Orbit stayed by her side with his "genius way of hearing music".

"The studio was often church-like and I would sit in silence, waiting for your ideas to explode out of your keyboard or your guitar and then I would run with them," she wrote. "I miss those days."

In addition to Ray of Light, Orbit also worked with Madonna on her 2000 album Music and produced several tracks for her 2012 album work MDNA.

The London-born producer was also renowned and sought-after for his production work, collaborating with artists from across the music world including Blur, Pink, U2, All Saints, Robbie Williams and Britney Spears.

"You were so otherworldly. So singular," Madonna wrote in her tribute.

The pop star said even though she worked with other producers over the years, she never forgot Orbit and "the magical time we spent together".

"I was so lucky to have known you and fallen down the rabbit hole with you."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cewr.summary: Madonna pays tribute to her regular collaborator and acclaimed music producer William Orbit. The British producer died at home on July 23 at the age of 69. The pop star says she never forgot Orbit and "the magical time we spent together"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2v.title: Banksy works cost public almost £150,000
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2v.text:
Three artworks by street artist Banksy have cost taxpayers almost £150,000 in cleaning operations and security so far, with the bill expected to rise.

The largest single cost relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in September 2025, where removal efforts and security have so far cost more than £85,000.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) says it has spent £50,000 trying to remove paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building in Carey Street. A further £35,300 was spent on overtime and security costs.

The spending was disclosed to the BBC through Freedom of Information requests and is likely to reignite debate over whether Banksy's work is vandalism or valuable public art.

Banksy, who emerged from Bristol's graffiti scene in the 1990s and became one of the world's most famous street artists, is known for murals and installations that often appear overnight and attract large crowds.

The latest costs relate to a mural depicting a judge in a wig battering a protester with his gavel, which appeared on the Royal Courts of Justice in London on 8 September 2025.

Banksy claimed the image as his own work, by posting it on his website and Instagram account.

A HM Courts and Tribunals Service (HMCTS) spokesperson said: "The Royal Courts of Justice is a listed building and HMCTS are obliged to maintain its original character."

The Metropolitan Police have confirmed: "On Monday, 8 September officers received a report of criminal damage to the side of the Royal Courts of Justice.

"At this time, no arrests have been made and the investigation remains ongoing."

Court staff barricaded off the area and guarded it. Attempts to clean off the mural began immediately.

But the fact he has painted on an historic court has divided opinion.

Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy said: "It's outrageous that tens of thousands of pounds of taxpayers' money – maybe more – will have to be spent cleaning up after Banksy, who seems to believe he has a right to deface public buildings with impunity.

"Our courts are a national symbol of justice and the rule of law.

"Banksy's vandalism should be stopped and he should foot the bill for the costs he imposes on others."

However, art critic Estelle Lovatt defended Banksy's work and pointed to the benefits for tourism: "Some people visit Buckingham Palace and others visit Banksy's art.

"His work brings people together in a way that politics can divide us. He's like the Pied Piper or a town crier.

"It can be intimidating if a mural appears on your building, in terms of the crowds, but he makes art accessible because there's no gallery fee."

It's not the first time Banksy has painted on a listed building.

His early works in Bristol included a mural of a man hanging from a window, on a Georgian house.

First attempts to scrub off the paint on the court were not completely successful, so contractors have been on site using "laser technology".

Westminster City Council will have to inspect the wall and if the removal is deemed incomplete, another cleaning method will have to be used.

As a final option, the affected stonework may have to be removed and replaced.

A Listed Building Consent (LBC) application has been submitted for the installation of railings across the wall that Banksy targeted.

If approval is granted then the costs to install the railings are not yet known.

The court mural is not the first of Banksy's works to create costs for public bodies.

In April, a statue of a man carrying a flag appeared in Waterloo Place near Trafalgar Square.

The flag covers the man's face and he appears to be about to step and fall from the plinth.

Banksy claimed responsibility with a video on Instagram showing the night-time installation.

Westminster City Council, which owns the land, says it had no prior knowledge of the statue.

The authority said it had spent almost £60,000 on safety barriers, administration and paying for a security guard to keep watch over it.

In response to a Freedom of Information request, Westminster Council said: "Ownership of the statue now sits with the council as landowner.

"The council has notified the artist's agent that it is reviewing options for the short, medium and long term."

The BBC has asked for more clarification on this statement.

In August 2024, Banksy painted piranha fish on a City of London Police sentry box.

The sentry box had been installed in the 1990s as part of security measures introduced after IRA attacks in the City of London.

After Banksy painted it, the box was removed at a cost of £2,200 and was never replaced.

It was put in storage and is due to be displayed at the London Museum when it reopens in November.

The works are a reminder of Banksy's continuing influence more than three decades after he first became known in Bristol, where surviving murals remain among the city's best-known tourist attractions.
