https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cre4.title: Kellie Bright to leave EastEnders after 13 years
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cre4.text:
EastEnders star Kellie Bright is to leave the soap after playing one of its key characters, Linda Carter, for 13 years.

She arrived in Albert Square with on-screen husband Mick, portrayed by Danny Dyer, when they became the new owners of the Queen Vic pub.

Carter's matriarch character has been central to major storylines including plots about murder, sexual assault and alcoholism.

Bright said she made the "tough decision" to leave more than a year ago but "happily" agreed to stay on to be part of an "exciting storyline".

The BBC has promised "unmissable drama" before her on-screen exit, which is said to be a "while away" yet.

Executive producer Ben Wadey described the actor as being "the beating heart of EastEnders" and said she had become "a classic EastEnders icon".

Viewers have seen the much-loved character at the heart of many emotional storylines including in 2014 when she was raped by her brother-in-law Dean Wicks.

More than 7m people watched the episode which prompted dozens of complaints. The sexual assualt led to long-running story arc about family conflict and trauma.

In 2022, Linda Carter's husband vanished into the sea trying to save Janine Butcher. The soap followed her as she grieved and began to navigate life as a single mother.

She was also at the centre of the 2023 Christmas Day episode where she stabbed Keanu Taylor to death to save the life of her friend Sharon Watts, played by Letitia Dean.

More recently, the character opened a B&B and had several romances.

"I will miss my friends and colleagues hugely, but I am looking forward to my next chapter and spending more time with my wonderful boys," Bright said, referring to her husband and three sons.

Bright appeared on Strictly Come Dancing in 2015, and has starred in films including Ali G Indahouse in 2002 and 2005's Kinky Boots.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cre4.summary: Kellie Bright will leave EastEnders after 13 years on the soap. She arrived in Albert Square with on-screen husband Mick when they became new owners of Queen Vic pub. The BBC has promised "unmissable drama" before her exit, which is said to be "while away" yet.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy9w.title: Strictly dancers Ola and James Jordan separate after 23 years of marriage
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy9w.text:
Former Strictly Come Dancing stars James and Ola Jordan have confirmed they have separated after more than 20 years of marriage.

The former professional dancers were regulars on the show for several series after first featuring in 2006.

The couple in a statement said they were "taking some time apart as we work through very difficult personal challenges".

"This has been an incredibly painful and emotional journey for us both and it certainly wasn't an easy decision," they said in a joint post shared on their Instagram accounts.

The couple said James had moved out the family home some time ago and they "don't know exactly what the future holds".

"Right now, more than anything we ask for kindness, empathy and a little privacy as we work through this as a family."

The couple's manager Vickie White had prevously said in a statement: "It is with great sadness that I can confirm that James and Ola began a trial separation some time ago

"Their shared priority remains co-parenting their daughter, Ella, and they are committed to putting her wellbeing first.

"They would greatly appreciate your understanding as they navigate this difficult time."

Ola Jordan won the Open Polish Championship in 1999 when she was 17 years old and became James' dance partner shortly afterwards in March 2000.

She moved to England a month later and the pair got married in October 2003.

James appeared on Strictly from 2006 to 2013 while Ola appeared on the show until 2015.

Ola's celebrity partners included wildlife presenter Steve Backshall and Welsh sprinter Iwan Thomas, while James danced with former international gymnast and broadcaster Gabby Logan, as well as The One Show presenter Alex Jones.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy9w.summary: James and Ola Jordan have separated after more than 20 years of marriage. The couple said they were "taking some time apart as we work through very difficult personal challenges" The former professional dancers were regulars on the show for several series after first appearing in 2006.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn4n.title: Campaigners call for Jared Leto's concerts to be cancelled after criminal sexual conduct claims
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn4n.text:
Warning: Contains graphic details of alleged sexual offences and misconduct, as well as strong language

Women's safety campaigners are calling for Thirty Seconds to Mars' upcoming concerts in the UK to be cancelled after frontman Jared Leto was accused of criminal sexual conduct.

A BBC investigation published last week heard from four women who have accused the US musician and actor of behaviour which includes sexual assault and grooming.

The alleged offences took place in the 2000s and 2010s when the women were teenagers and Leto was in his 30s and 40s. He is now 54.

The musician - who strongly denies the claims - is currently scheduled to perform with his band at two of the UK's biggest arenas next April.

The End Violence Against Women coalition and domestic abuse charity Women's Aid have told BBC Newsbeat they have concerns about the upcoming events in London and Manchester - urging organisers not to go ahead with them.

BBC Newsbeat has contacted the promoters, venues and the band for comment, but has not received any responses.

A spokesperson for Women's Aid told Newsbeat it is "troubling to hear that UK concerts are still planned to go ahead that will put an alleged abuser in the spotlight".

"In light of the very serious allegations of criminal sexual conduct, we would urge organisers to put safety over profit and avoid platforming figures like this."

Janaya Walker, interim director of the End Violence Against Women Coalition, said she backed the charity's call.

"I think it really is about putting people over profit in this instance, and particularly women and girls' safety," she said.

Walker said tickets still being sold for Thirty Seconds to Mars' upcoming concerts at London's The O2 and Manchester Co-Op Live was "really worrying".

"Particularly for victims and survivors of violence against women and girls, they'll be seeing these reports and then seeing that things are moving forward seemingly without any consequence," she said.

"I think that will cause a huge amount of alarm and frustration and anger."

Walker said the coalition wants the industry to consider whether platforming groups and individuals "sends a message" about whether they "condone particular forms of behaviour".

"And that's the choice that I think is in front of them."

US rock band Thirty Seconds to Mars, known for hit songs including The Kill, This is War and Kings And Queens, was formed by Leto and his brother Shannon in the late 1990s.

They began touring in the 2000s and progressed to headlining major arenas around the world.

As part of the BBC documentary Jared Leto: Hollywood's Dark Secret, two men who worked with Leto's band for many years recall how uncomfortable staff felt about the way Leto would interact with teenage girls.

One alleges that crew members were instructed to invite young girls backstage after they would join Leto on stage at gigs.

Another says at one point there would typically be about two girls a day stopping by to see Leto at a house where the band was working.

Among those who have accused Leto is ex-model Alex, who says her agency was invited to a Thirty Seconds to Mars' concert at London's O2 arena in 2013.

She says she was later invited to an after-party by Leto's female assistant and, although she was 19 at the time, she says to protect herself she "felt the need" to pretend to be younger when she met Leto.

She says she told him she was 17, and that Leto, then 41, replied: "Age is just a number, and anyway, we're in Europe."

Alex says one of Leto's assistants encouraged her to go to another party at a nearby hotel later, but only Leto was in the room when she arrived.

When she asked Leto if she could sleep on the chaise longue in the room, Alex says the star responded by saying that, if she did, she would wake up "with a dick in her ass".

Alex says she tried to dismiss what happened, but she now believes the hotel encounter had been "all planned out".

In total, 10 women have spoken to the BBC documentary, with nine of them sharing their stories publicly for the first time.

Despite repeated attempts to contact Jared Leto before publication of the original story, he did not respond to the allegations put to him by the BBC.

After the story was published, Leto said in a statement released by his representatives to the BBC: "I have never sexually assaulted anyone in my entire life. These claims are absolutely and categorically false".

Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn4n.summary: Women's safety campaigners call for concerts in UK to be cancelled after Jared Leto accused of sexual offences. Four women have accused Leto of sexual assault and grooming. The US musician is currently scheduled to perform with his band at two of the UK's biggest arenas next April.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg5l.title: Siân Phillips to step back from acting aged 93 after memory issues
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg5l.text:
One of Wales' most celebrated actresses, Dame Siân Phillips, is stepping back from full-scale stage acting after experiencing memory issues during rehearsals.

The 93-year-old made the decision after struggling to remember her lines while preparing for a recent production, according to The Times.

However, Phillips said she would continue performing in smaller projects, including a production with Michael Sheen's Welsh National Theatre next year.

Her career has spanned more than 80 years across stage, television and film.

Phillips told The Times she decided to stop taking on major stage productions after struggling to remember her lines during rehearsals for Atonement at Chichester Festival Theatre earlier this year.

According to the newspaper, she said she would continue performing in her show It's All Greek and is also due to appear in Samuel Beckett's Rockaby for Michael Sheen's Welsh National Theatre next year.

Born in Betws, near Ammanford, Carmarthenshire, in 1933, Phillips grew up speaking Welsh before learning English by listening to the radio.

She began performing as a child, appearing on Welsh-language radio from the age of 11, before studying at the University of Wales and later winning a scholarship to the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art.

She performed in radio productions such as The Archers and an adaptation of John le Carre's Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy, opposite Sir Alec Guinness.

Before her acting career took off, she worked for BBC Wales as a bilingual announcer and newsreader.

Phillips went on to become one of Britain's most acclaimed actresses, appearing in productions including Doctor Who, Calendar Girls, Dune, and I, Claudius.

She won a Bafta for her portrayal of Livia in the BBC's I, Claudius and received a Tony Award nomination for playing the title role in Marlene.

She was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in 2000 for services to drama, and then a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire (DBE) in 2016.

She struggled to remember her lines during rehearsals for Atonement at Chichester Festival Theatre. She said she would continue performing in smaller projects, including a production with Michael Sheen's

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0m7.title: Amanda Knox defends Fringe comedy show after claims it will 'trivialise violence'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0m7.text:
Amanda Knox, who was convicted and later acquitted of murdering British student Meredith Kercher in Italy in 2007, has defended her solo comedy show following calls for it to be cancelled.

The sold-out show called Cartwheel, which Knox will perform at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, discusses motherhood and how she will explain the case to her daughter.

Knox told the BBC she is not the first person to use comedy to talk about traumatic events and said her material focuses on "how the world is unsafe and unfair towards women".

But Stephanie Kercher, the victim's sister, said she is concerned it will "normalise and trivialise" violence against women, and Meredith, in particular.

Speaking on BBC Breakfast, Stephanie Kercher, said: "What I would say [to Knox] is to think about the family here, think about her friends and to turn the tables if it was your sister that this had happened to, because I know you have a sister as well."

Responding to the comments, Knox said: "The interesting irony of that is that my daughter is a huge motivation for me doing this show.

"It's about how the world is unsafe and unfair towards women and what it means to raise a daughter in that world, knowing how bad it can be.

"If they [Kercher's family] saw my show, they would recognise that."

A petition against the show, set up by a friend of Meredith, has been signed by nearly 5,000 people.

It states the show disrespects her memory and risks making light of such a harrowing event.

Stephanie Kercher added she did not believe Meredith would find these topics of any comedic value.

She said: "Our family's pain is immense. I can't explain to you how much pain our family have been through, and also we're talking two decades later now, this pain.

"I think that if it was a generic theme, as many comedy shows are, even when they're pushing the boundaries, it would be different.

"Because this is associated with an individual case and individual person, I think that's where the worry lies here for me, because who else is this going to then open up this opportunity for?"

But Knox told BBC Scotland News she does not downplay the seriousness of the case and is respectful in her approach.

"I hope people will honestly engage in my work and recognise the deep heart and sensitivity that I bring to it as I tell a very personal story," she said.

The comedy show is set to run over 11 days in the Gilded Balloon Teviot.

Its title Cartwheel references a story that once claimed Knox did cartwheels in the police station after her British roommate's death.

She said the cartwheel becomes a metaphor throughout the show.

"It is about acknowledging that bad things happen in life which will turn you upside down," Knox said.

"But it's also about not letting that arrest your momentum because the only way you can land on your feet is through those difficult experiences."

Knox added she would love to have an open and honest conversation with Kercher's family but claimed she has never had the opportunity.

"It would be incredible for them to see me for who I really am instead of the idea that was delivered to them by people in bad hands," she said.

Tony Lankester, director of the Fringe Society, said the festival is no stranger to controversy and it is a platform for free speech.

"It's the nature of an open access platform," he told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast.

"When you open up your stages and invite people in to tell their stories without censorship, any curation and without trying to control the content ahead of time, you're inevitably going to end up staging things that cause discomfort and push the boundaries."

Lankester added the line in terms of what is acceptable is the law, which he claimed is clear.

"If anyone wants to use the Fringe to break the law, to incite violence or to embark on hate speech, that is our red line and we would intervene," he said.

"For us, the baseline principle is it is a platform for free speech and some people may not regard it as being in good taste but we cannot apply that criteria because who decides that?"

He said the decision as to whether the comedy show goes ahead lies with the venue and Knox, herself.

Since Meredith Kercher's death, Knox has written two books about her imprisonment and served as an executive producer on the biographical drama The Twisted Tale of Amanda Knox.

Now 39, she is married with two children and lives in Washington state.

Knox, from Seattle, and Kercher, from Surrey, were both exchange students sharing a house in the university town of Perugia.

Alongside her then-boyfriend, Raffaele Sollecito, Knox was arrested on suspicion of murdering Kercher, 21, who was found dead in their house.

Her throat had been cut and she had been sexually assaulted.

Knox was found guilty and spent four years in an Italian prison before she and Sollecito were acquitted through an appeal.

She returned home to the US in 2011.

A retrial in 2014 reinstated Knox and Sollecito's convictions but Italy's top appeals court finally overturned them in 2015.

Ivory Coast-born Rudy Guede served 13 years of a 16-year sentence for Kercher's murder after his fingerprints were found at the scene.

The court ruled he did not act alone but after Knox and Sollecito were acquitted, no other accomplices were convicted.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0m7.summary: Knox will perform at Edinburgh Festival Fringe on Friday night. She will discuss motherhood and how she will explain the case to her daughter. Meredith Kercher's sister Stephanie Ker Knox and Sollecito were acquitted after they were acquitted. No other accomplices were convicted of any crimes.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0l5.title: Singer Self Esteem to make cinematic debut in film set in 1980s
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0l5.text:
Singer Self Esteem has landed her first major movie role, starring in a film set in 1980s Wales.

The coming of age story, Mountain, directed by Celyn Jones, was filmed in his home town of Holyhead, on Anglesey.

Peter Mullan, Iwan Rheon and Seth Isaac Thomas will star alongside Rebecca Lucy Taylor, who goes by the stage name Self Esteem.

The film tells the story of a neglected young boy in 1980s Wales, looking for friendship and community when he meets a man living alone on a mountain.

Jones said filming the project, which wrapped earlier this year, had been "an emotional and spiritual homecoming".

Self Esteem, known for her hit tracks Focus Is Power and I Do This All The Time, is no stranger to commanding both the stage and screen.

The pop star performed in the hit London West End musical, Cabaret in 2023, and the revival of David Hare's 1975 play, Teeth 'n' Smiles, earlier this year.

She also took on roles in the Sky Comedy series Smothered and Sky TV drama I Hate Suzie.

Speaking to Variety following the project's announcement, Jones said he was "honoured to bring a world class team, on both sides of the camera" to north Wales.

Despite telling a fictional tale, Jones said the project feels "deeply personal" to him, with "emotional themes and humour that many can relate to".

"I'm really looking forward to bringing it to life and sharing the cinematic beauty of home with the world."

Peter Mullan, who previously worked with Jones on psychological thriller The Vanishing, said: "When I read the script, I emailed Celyn and said: 'You made me cry, I'm in!'

"It will be great for us to work together again and in such a beautiful part of the world too."

An official release date for Mountain has not yet been announced.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0l5.summary: Mountain is directed by Celyn Jones and filmed in his home town of Holyhead, on Anglesey. Peter Mullan, Iwan Rheon and Seth Isaac Thomas will star alongside Rebecca Lucy Taylor. The film tells the story of a neglected young boy in 1980s Wales.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx7.title: Nadia Sawalha threatens ITV with legal action over Loose Women removal
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx7.text:
Loose Women panellist Nadia Sawalha has threatened to take legal action against ITV, claiming the network dropped her for speaking out in support of Palestinian rights.

A legal organisation representing her has sent a pre-action letter to ITV, claiming the broadcaster "subjected Nadia to direct discrimination, indirect discrimination and harassment because of her protected philosophical beliefs".

In an Instagram video, Sawalha said she had become "the target of an escalating campaign of smears, complaints, hostile media coverage and targeted calls to have me removed from Loose Women".

She added: "Since then, ITV have taken me on and off Loose Women a number of times." BBC News has asked ITV for comment.

The presenter said she "began speaking publicly in support of Palestine in December 2023", two months after the 7 October Hamas attacks on Israel and Israel's subsequent military campaign in Gaza.

She said she was "speaking out against brutal oppression", but her critics have accused her of promoting false claims and conspiracies about Israel and Jewish people.

A group of Jewish executives in the entertainment industry recently sent a dossier to ITV, urging the channel not to reinstate her, citing what they called "repeated examples of conspiratorial rhetoric, inflammatory commentary, disinformation, and antisemitic discourse".

Sawalha said she hadn't had a chance to see the document and answer the accusations, but has denied antisemitism.

Two newspapers that previously accused Sawalha and her husband of antisemitism and supporting terrorism have since issued apologies and paid damages to the couple.

In her video on Thursday, Sawalha said she had "mostly been told" by ITV that "the reason for [my removal] was, and I quote, 'It's all a bit noisy out there for us'."

The controversy, she alleges, prompted ITV to remove her on repeated occasions from the line-up of its long-running lunchtime programme.

"ITV have continued to take me on and off Loose Women, forever changing the goalposts whilst also saying they couldn't guarantee they wouldn't take me off again as it would depend on what was said," she said.

Sawalha added that she was "hired for being an opinionated woman on a discussion show and I've never brought up or spoken about Palestine directly on the show".

The presenter also said she wanted to express "how sad I am that it's got to this - believe me, I have appealed to ITV's hearts and minds, but to no avail".

The European Legal Support Center (ELSC), which supports pro-Palestinian cases, has written to ITV on her behalf, alleging she has been discriminated against because of her "anti-Zionist beliefs, which are protected under the Equality Act 2010".

Sawalha has appeared regularly on the daytime panel show, which sees four female media personalities discuss topical subjects, since 2013.

She also had an earlier stint on the panel between 1999 and 2002, shortly after playing Annie Palmer in EastEnders.

Her other TV credits include Casualty and The Bill, and she is also a former winner of Celebrity MasterChef.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx7.summary: Nadia Sawalha has threatened to take legal action against ITV over her removal from Loose Women. She says she was dropped for speaking out in support of Palestinian rights. The BBC News has asked ITV for comment.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clye.title: Comedian Mo Gilligan says Gavin & Stacey brings back 'fond memories' of holidays at Barry Island
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clye.text:
Comedian and TV presenter Mo Gilligan says watching episodes of Gavin & Stacey reminds him of his visits to Barry Island during his childhood.

His mother grew up in the town in the Vale of Glamorgan, although her father originally settled in Grangetown, Cardiff, after leaving Jamaica.

Gilligan said he still visited family in the area, adding he and fellow comedians performed a gig to help with fundraising to safeguard the future of Cadoxton Conservative Club in February.

"I've got very fond memories of spending six-week holidays there," he said.

"It holds a huge place in my heart so it's always important that I'm making sure I'm still present."

Gilligan, a judge on popular ITV series The Masked Singer, recalled spending days on the beach and riding the log flume at the fun park as well playing the penny arcade machines.

He told BBC Radio Wales' Lucy Owen that he was pleased Gavin & Stacey had put the resort on the map although the show did not have the same "connection" that he remembered from his youth.

Gilligan said that, if series co-writer James Corden had written him in to the series as a "random black cousin", people would have been "mad confused".

"They'd be like 'how, how are you in this?", adding people seemed surprised to learn about his Welsh connections as he grew up in London.

He also said he enjoyed returning to perform in Cardiff because it had a "really good vibe".

"Getting to go back to some of those places that always show me a lot of love is really important and there's no better place to perform than Cardiff," he added.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clye.summary: Mo Gilligan says he still visits family in Cardiff and has fond memories of Barry Island. The comedian says he was pleased Gavin & Stacey had put the resort on the map. He says he enjoyed returning to Cardiff because it had a "really good vibe"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cewr.title: Stephen Bear jailed for harassing ex-partner Georgia Harrison
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cewr.text:
Reality TV contestant Stephen Bear is back in prison after admitting breaching a restraining order that banned him from posting online about ex-partner Georgia Harrison.

The order was imposed when Bear was jailed in 2023 after he filmed and shared a video of the pair having sex on OnlyFans and WhatsApp without Harrison's knowledge.

The 36-year-old was told not to post or incite comments on social media about that case or Harrison but did so multiple times in 2025 while she was pregnant.

In a statement read to Chelmsford Crown Court, the Love Island star and campaigner said Bear's online presence left her "feeling petrified" and she feared for her safety. He was jailed for 16 months.

Bear, of Walthamstow, east London, admitted the charge of harassment – breaching of a restraining order, at a previous hearing in June.

Judge Christopher Morgan, who presided over the original trial in 2023, said Bear's posts and videos in 2025 were "to ensure the maximum harm [was] caused to Georgia Harrison".

"You knew all of that was untrue, and yet you posted it," he said.

"You left Miss Harrison, I'm afraid, at the mercy of any individual who had aligned themselves with your lies."

In addition to the prison sentence, the judge extended the restraining order to stop Bear from contacting Harrison's mother and her friend, which remains in place until a new order is imposed.

After serving half his original sentence, Bear was released from prison, but between 1 March 2025 and 21 July 2025 began posting on Instagram, TikTok, X, YouTube and Facebook about the case and Harrison.

The court heard these were "consistently posted messages of the most abhorrent and harmful type".

Addressing Bear, the judge said: "What you did in that three to four-month period is simply victim-blaming."

Harrison did not attend court, but the prosecution read out a statement in which she described feeling isolated, exposed and unsafe, and asked for the restraining order to be extended.

She said the significant stress had made her worry about her unborn child and caused her to "spiral" on some occasions.

"I shut him out of my mind for a long time and it's not fair that he's managed to crawl his way back in," she said.

Bear arrived for Thursday's sentencing with his wife, who is eight months pregnant.

As he walked in to court, he refused to answer questions but gave a thumbs-up and said: "Wish me luck guys. See you soon, hopefully."

As his barrister spoke about why there should be a reduced sentence, Bear appeared to briefly cry.

He shook his head as he was taken away to begin another prison term.

Senior crown prosecutor Andrew Young said Bear "used his platforms to amplify abuse and encourage others to target" Harrison.

The Crown Prosecution Service said Bear had looked to cast doubt on his convictions, including by alleging Harrison and her mother had conspired to pervert the course of justice.

He also created an online petition seeking support for a retrial.

Young added: "No woman should be made to live in fear because someone refuses to accept the restrictions placed on them by a court."

In a separate statement released through Essex Police following sentencing, Harrison said she was grateful to the force because it "took me seriously when so many women in my position are overlooked".

"They treated this as the serious crime it is – not a celebrity story. It is a real offence against a real person," she said.

"They built the case properly, they stayed with it, and when the order was breached, they acted instead of shrugging. From the messages I get every day, I know how rare that still is.

"If every force treated this the way Essex Police did, thousands of women would feel safer today."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cewr.summary: Stephen Bear jailed for 16 months for breaching restraining order in 2023. He was jailed for a year after posting video of him and ex-partner Georgia Harrison. Judge said he was not allowed to post or incite comments about the case. He also banned him from contacting Harrison's mother and her friend.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn4n.title: TikTok star Sydney Towle, who shared her cancer journey online, dies aged 26
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn4n.text:
Sydney Towle, a popular social media influencer who shared her experience living with a rare, aggressive form of cancer, has died at the age of 26.

Towle's family announced her death, from complications related to bile duct cancer that had spread to other parts of her body, on her social media accounts on Thursday.

"Syd went peacefully last night after an almost three-year-long battle with cholangiocarcinoma," her brother Austin said in a video message, alongside their mother, on TikTok.

Towle, who was moved to hospice care earlier this week, had over a million followers on TikTok and over 200,000 on Instagram.

She spent the last three years chronicling her daily life as a young person going through chemotherapy and living with cancer, with all its hopes, joys and struggles. She had been living in New York City at the time of her death.

"We are so proud of how hard Sydney fought and for sharing her journey with so many people," Towle's family said in a statement.

"She wanted to raise awareness for rare cancers and was passionate about promoting self-advocacy. We will continue her legacy and honour her in every way we can."

Following the announcement of her death, thousands of followers posted messages on Towle's social media accounts paying tribute to her and sending well wishes to her family.

"Sweet angel. Fly high," actress Alyssa Milano commented. "Praying for all who loved her. She is really something special."

"You were such a bright light and will be missed," one person wrote on Instagram, while another said: "How lucky we all are to have found you on the internet. Thank you for sharing yourself and your story."

In May, Towle posted a series of videos from the hospital where she was receiving treatment for complications related to her cancer.

She shared that her cancer had spread to her peritoneum, a membrane that lines the abdominal and pelvic cavities and protects internal organs.

On 19 May, she posted a video of herself, sitting beside her mother in the hospital, in which she said her oncologist had told her he would no longer treat her cancer, recommending she begin end-of-life care. Towle said she would not accept this and vowed to continue fighting, choosing instead to switch to another specialist.

Despite her illness, she expressed fervent optimism and joy for life on her social media accounts. She often posted videos of herself dancing, getting ready, and having fun with friends.

She recently fulfilled her dream of modelling, walking in a swimsuit for The Chemo Club x Post Swim show at Miami Swim Week.

"Rich in life because my friends choose to spend a Saturday fundraising for cancer research," Towle wrote in a post in March.

"Go get a pint of Ben and Jerry's, watch your favourite movie, remember that life is good and bad things happen sometimes but that doesn't make it a bad life," Towle wrote in another post last year.

Towle was not shy about showing her stomach, where she had a hepatic artery pump implanted, on social media.

"I have only recently started seeing the resilience and beauty in this body," she wrote in a post last year, alongside photos of herself in a swimsuit. "Scars that remind me of how far I've come. And I'm reminded that dreams only end when you allow them to."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn4n.summary: Sydney Towle, 26, has died from complications related to bile duct cancer. She had been living in New York City at the time of her death. Towle had over a million followers on TikTok and over 200,000 on Instagram. She was moved to hospice care earlier this week.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwye.title: Judge grants Trump's request to delay handing financial records to BBC
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwye.text:
A judge has granted Donald Trump's request to delay handing over financial records to the BBC as part of his $10bn (£7.4bn) lawsuit against the broadcaster.

The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the 2021 Capitol riots.

The BBC has asked for some of Trump's financial records in relation to his argument that the documentary damaged the president's business interests.

A judge granted that request in July and the first documents were due to be filed on Thursday, but another judge has now agreed to an emergency motion filed by Trump's lawyers earlier this week to pause the disclosure.

The president's legal team said disclosure of the financial records would cause him "irreparable harm".

They argued that no such revelations should be made until the court rules on an objection to the order requiring the disclosure.

Trump has also recently asked to amend his main case, which his lawyers said would make the document release unnecessary.

The president has asked for his central complaint against the BBC to be amended so it no longer claims the documentary damaged his brands and businesses. His lawyers have asked that the case is amended to claim for damages for "the reputational injury to the President, full stop".

In a ruling on Thursday, the judge said the order for financial information disclosure would be paused until the amendment question is resolved.

The BBC had said Trump's request for a delay to disclosure was "a transparent effort to evade this court's clear and direct order and to continue to avoid the discovery obligations that the plaintiff took on when he chose to file this lawsuit".

"In fact, this is just the latest in [Trump's] months-long refusal to provide documents, sworn answers to interrogatories, deposition dates, any meaningful information to support his pursuit of $10bn from the BBC for a documentary the BBC never aired in the United States."

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The BBC has apologised for an editing error that gave "the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action".

However, the BBC has asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the programme doesn't meet the legal criteria for defamation and wasn't made available on its US platforms.

Last month, Trump's lawyers admitted they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service, as they had originally claimed, or on BBC.com, BBC Select or through US broadcasters.

Trump also recently agreed to drop the BBC's commercial arm BBC Studios from his lawsuit, after the BBC argued the company had "no role in creating or producing the documentary".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly5.title: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back - and 'a bit more real'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly5.text:
It's Saturday afternoon and I've nearly fallen at the first hurdle – I've left my digital camera battery on charge at home.

Forgive me, I last took this camera out with me 15 years ago on a family holiday to the Canary Islands.

Take two. Now with the charged battery in hand, I'm taking my digital camera to a DJ set as an experiment.

It's because older technology is having a bit of a moment – social media is full of people talking about why they're going back to basics with the likes of digital cameras, wired headphones and early MP3 players.

Sales of iPods and Walkman portable audio players in the UK on eBay increased by nearly 50% in 2025, the online marketplace told us, while searches for iPod minis on the platform have increased by 48% over the last year.

Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on the dancefloor.

The mere sight of us pulling out the camera and squinting through its tiny viewfinder draws attention – "I've not seen one of these in years", a man remarks.

He's right – digital cameras had their heyday in the late 1990s and early 2000s, just before smartphones took off.

There are currently 42 million active film camera users globally, more than a third of these aged 18–30 and largely influenced by social media trends, according to a market research report last year.

So why, when we're surrounded by more advanced tech here in 2026, are they seemingly making a resurgence?

For Lily Redman, a 26-year-old content creator from South Wales, digital cameras "capture a quality that my phone just can't replicate".

She's been taking one on nights out and to concerts and feels the flash on her phone "is grainy and too high definition" compared to the "more smooth" finished product on a digital camera.

"I think people are looking for a bit of grit or something that feels a bit more real," she says.

That may also explain why low exposure photos taken on iPhones and Androids – where people dodge ready-made filters to artificially crank down the exposure setting and produce a darker image – are also popular on socials right now.

With digital cameras offering an element of surprise when you plug in the memory card reader to your computer at home, digital cameras capture a moment in time.

"If I look back at photos my mum took when I was two, they look so old but when I look at photos I took five years ago, they look like they were taken yesterday," says Redman.

"Phone photos have warped our perception of time."

It's not just digital cameras returning from the archives (or a dusty cupboard), but early MP3 devices like iPods too.

According to refurbished tech website Backmarket, iPods are "driving the trend" in sales of older MP3 devices with a 48% increase in sales between 2024 and 2025, with demand for MP3 and MP4 players "accelerating further into 2026".

Cheri Sanih, 30, runs a Tumblr account about older technology which she says has gained thousands of followers recently.

As she scrolls through the music library on her mint green iPod, filled with album artwork from 15 to 20 years ago, childhood memories of receiving one as a Christmas present come flooding back.

For her, it's all about nostalgically "wanting to remember simpler times"; being able to "bury into escapism".

Sanih points out how her "phone is always getting notifications and sometimes I just want to be outside, blissfully listening to music".

She thinks iPods have become popular again because of their "beautiful design" and the way the music player is "the first bit of technology really catering to humans with a less cluttered user interface".

And speaking of back to basics, wired headphones are perhaps as simple as you can get, but again proving popular online.

These are now a daily staple for 23-year-old Monique Wellman-Mason from Bristol, who grew tired of losing her wireless earbuds.

"Every single time I get them out my bag I spend two minutes trying to detangle them which is a bit of a pain," she jokes, "but at the same time I love that they have a microphone and I'm [always] connected to my phone".

She tells the BBC that the clear mic is useful for her job as a social media manager and she enjoys being able to "spark that nostalgia", while another positive is wired earphones are "really cheap" at about £20.

Monique made the switch from bluetooth wireless to wired earphones a few months back and says she hasn't returned to the former since.

"Technology only goes up and we're always looking for the quickest thing but this is a step back in a way – I love it," she says.

Whether it's digital cameras, iPods or wired earphones, does a renewed love for early-digital gadgets among some young people tell us something more?

It's been on the mind of Andrew Przybylski, professor of technology and human behaviour at the University of Oxford.

Underpinning a fondness for more basic tech is "people's desire on a very deep level to be in control of their experiences," he argues.

He says the modern digital world often leaves us inflicted by decision paralysis - the inability to choose because there are so many options.

When a new series comes out, he explains, "binge watching it automatically" often feels like a decision that is made for us.

In contrast, when you choose to turn on a digital camera and play with its settings or add an album to your iPod library "you move towards something you want versus it coming at you".

Andrew says "people want more than to just rent the things [and experiences] they're passionate about" and that buying your own music or taking your own pictures creates a sense of connection.

He references Xbox's server outage in late July, in which users couldn't play games even if they owned the discs and how "nobody liked that".

"Imagine if a book worked that way," he adds.

Additional reporting by Amy Walker.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly5.summary: Digital cameras are becoming more popular with young people in the UK and around the world. iPods and Walkman portable audio players are also popular online. New series is a new series of series on Xbox.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdew.title: Lauryn Hill and Wyclef ‘in an amazing place’ as fans hope for new Fugees album after 30 years
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdew.text:
Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean have raised hopes of the Fugees making their first new album in nearly three decades, with Hill saying the band have gone through "an incredible healing process".

The group have not released a studio album since The Score in 1996, which was one of the defining albums of its generation, featuring the hits Ready or Not, Fu-Gee-La and Killing Me Softly.

The pair have reunited on stage a number of times in recent years and spoke to BBC News ahead of a major concert in Milton Keynes on Friday to mark the album's 30th anniversary.

Jean said they are "in an amazing place", and broke into song during the interview to celebrate that he is "back with my bandmate".

The renewed bond between the two was evident during the interview. When asked about the possibility of a new album, Jean began by restating the question, "Will there be music in the future?", and Hill chimed in: "Absolutely."

Jean continued: "All I can tell you is, man, we're in God's hands,” before singing: “I’m back with my bandmate!

"So we're in an amazing place. I think the energy is very important."

He suggested they would continue "projecting that love" to the world.

Hill added: "There was an incredible healing process that happened with us as a band and as bandmates, and as you said we just want to showcase that and give some of that energy to the world as well."

The comments will fuel hopes of a full Fugees reunion, although neither artist confirmed that a new album is currently being recorded.

The group's third member, Pras Michel, is currently serving a prison sentence in the United States following his conviction in a federal lobbying and fraud case.

Hill and Jean were speaking ahead of Diaspora Calling! By Ms. Lauryn Hill, a one-day festival that will make its UK debut at the Milton Keynes National Bowl on Friday.

The event will feature performances from Hill, Jean, Erykah Badu, Giggs, Fireboy DML, YG Marley and Zion Marley, with comedian Dave Chappelle hosting.

Reflecting on the anniversary of The Score, Jean said the Fugees' ambitions had always extended beyond music.

"I remember saying from a very young age, we're not going to do music, we're going to be a movement," he said.

He said the themes explored by the group three decades ago remain as relevant as ever.

"When you talk about the idea of refugees, look where we are today. We were saying these things 30 years ago. It was never just about us – it was always about the movement."

Hill said the Fugees themselves embodied the idea behind Diaspora Calling.

"Our different places of origin came together to unite culture, reflect culture and show people how beautiful, powerful and resourceful that culture is," she said.

Earlier in the day, Hill and Jean surprised fans with a pop-up appearance in London's Piccadilly Circus, performing an a cappella rendition of Ready or Not.

Hill said London was the natural place to launch the festival.

"There's so much of the diaspora in London," she said. "So many people are represented here. It felt like a full-circle moment for us."

Hill and Jean also offered advice to young musicians navigating an industry increasingly driven by algorithms and viral success.

Jean said many emerging artists were no longer chasing online fame.

"The kids are saying, 'I don't want to be on TikTok like that. I don't want to be on Instagram. I'm not trying to go viral. I just need people to listen to my music and engage with my music.'"

Hill encouraged artists to remain patient and focus on their craft.

"Art is not gone yet," she said. "Patience is a virtue. You want it in 30 seconds, but it isn't going to happen in 30 seconds.

"If you keep coming together with a positive plan and saying, 'We want to be heard,' then you'll be heard. Find like-minded individuals."

She added: "Respect your audience, respect yourself."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c39e.title: 'Put your phone down': K-pop band weighs in on concert etiquette
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c39e.text:
Kicking off their global tour in the South Korean city of Incheon, the five members of K-pop boy band Cortis saunter onto stage in casual, streetwear-inspired outfits, exuding an effortlessly cool vibe.

"Put your phone down," one of the members bellows. Piercing screams erupt. A sea of illuminated screens flickers back.

"I told you, put your phone down," he repeats, louder this time.

Some fans do just that, but the packed stadium vibrates harder with cheers as thousands of phones stay in the air.

It's hard to say how serious this theatrical command is.

"Put your phone down" is also the name of Cortis's ongoing concert tour, which started in Incheon on 18 July and will head to cities like New York and Los Angeles before returning to Seoul later this month.

The refrain reflects a message the band has long pushed: that fans should stop watching concerts through six-inch screens and engage with their performances in real life.

It's drawn mixed reactions from their fandom: fan-filmed content is a valuable social currency in K-pop.

Park Ji-yeon, for one, could not bring herself to stop recording Cortis's performances. The 22-year-old had specially rented a new, top-tier smartphone for both days of the Cortis concert just so she could film in the highest quality.

"I was standing right at the front, and I couldn't bring myself to put my phone down because I don't know if I'll ever get this opportunity again," she tells the BBC.

"I usually film concerts because I know a lot of those memories will fade as soon as I leave the venue."

While fans like Park continued to film, some heeded the band's call. Kim Ga-eun, 25, who was seated in the amphitheatre-style venue, saw it all.

"People in the back of the standing section were having a great time dancing together. I thought that really reflected the intention behind the concert," she says.

Cortis has had a whirlwind year since debuting last year under record label BigHit Music - part of the company that created pop sensation BTS. Most of its members are teenagers. The oldest of the group, James, is just 20 years old.

Their music videos have each amassed millions of views. Over the weekend they performed at Lollapalooza, the famed music festival in Chicago.

The band's name, Cortis, is derived from the phrase "colour outside the lines", which according to their record label is meant to encapsulate the band's free spirit and refusal to conform to societal rules - which, in this case, appears to include telling fans to resist the temptation of the phone camera.

They join a prominent wave of artists around the world who have been advocating the same.

Singers like Phoebe Bridgers and Alicia Keys have required their concert attendees to use lock pouches - sealed bags that allow people to hold on to their phones without being able to access them.

Few have gone as far as British rock group Suede, whose frontman Brett Anderson leapt over a barricade during a 2023 performance in Singapore to grab at fans' phones.

Billie Eilish, who has defended filming as a way for fans to relive precious memories after a show, gently cooed to her front row audience during a performance in Amsterdam: "Put your phone down, I'm right here."

Even BTS, K-pop's golden boys, have made similar requests. "Stop looking at your phone screen. Just look at me," BTS member Jungkook teased the audience at one concert.

"From the artists' perspective, interacting with fans is a really important part of performing, so I think they want people to focus more on that than on their phones," Park says of Cortis's anti-mobile rallying cry.

After all, fancams - zoomed-in videos focusing on a single celebrity - are a prized currency in K-pop communities. Once shared online, people meticulously study the choreography in them and delight in catching subtle movements and expressions by their favourite band members. These clips live on as fodder for collective swooning and fan-made montages.

And this is why Cortis's incessant calls to for people to put their phones down have rubbed some the wrong way - in a fan culture that's obsessed with capturing every moment. After the first day of their concert, disgruntled comments emerged online among fans.

"I spent over one million won ($700; £520) attending both days," Park says, referring to the sum of not just concert tickets but also additional expenses like transport and accommodation.

"I think a lot of fans spent similar amounts of money, so constantly hearing them asking us to put our phones down made some fans even more frustrated."

These murmurs appear to have reached Cortis, who fans say dialled down their message on the second day of the concert.

"On the first day, the message felt more like, 'Let's put our phones down and have fun together.' On the second day, it changed slightly to, 'We understand why you want to film, so let's just make sure we enjoy ourselves together,'" Kim recalls.

"They said filming was okay, but they wanted us to enjoy the concert together, and that 'Put Your Phone Down' was more of a mindset."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyl.title: Charli XCX on lying, Love Island and life post-Brat
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyl.text:
"Was that the truth, or was it a lie?"

This is the question posed by Radio 1's Jack Saunders to Charli XCX about an answer she gave in their last interview.

The Apple singer previously told the presenter that she hadn't started making any new music - when in fact she was putting the finishing touches to her new album, Music, Fashion, Film.

"Yeah, it was a lie," says Charli.

"I'd finished the record pretty much," she tells Saunders during a special performance at the BBC's Maida Vale studios.

"So I was just lying to your face basically.

"I knew when I said yes to Reading and Leeds it was going to be about this next album."

But why do artists feel they need to keep their plans under wraps, and is there pressure to do so?

Released in July, Music, Fashion, Film follow's Charli XCX's huge hit album, Brat.

The record became a cultural phenomenon, used in Kamala Harris' 2024 presidential campaign and even resulted in Collins English Dictionary updating its definition of Brat.

So why keep her much anticipated follow-up quiet?

Publicist Josh Moss tells BBC Newsbeat that at the early stages of a campaign, artists won't be giving much away.

"What people don't realise is that there's so much planning and strategy that goes into an album roll out," says Moss, who has represented artists like Maisie Peters, Bruno Mars and SOMBR.

"At a time where attention spans have shortened, artists want to sustain excitement pre and post release.

"One of the best ways to do that is through drip-feeding information."

So is it all just harmless fun, or is this a case of artists being more cautious?

Maria Veronese runs media training company Mediapro and says Charli XCX's method may not be a surprise to her fans.

"She's fun, she's Brat and it's what we expect of her really," says Veronese.

"It's what her fan base loves her for."

She says a lot of people who use media training, do so because they're nervous about saying things they don't want to.

"We just help them go through all of those scenarios.

"Talk about bridging techniques, and what they can say instead of things they don't want to say, so we're not telling them to lie."

During her interview with Jack Saunders, Charli XCX also discussed the process of getting the album cover together for Music, Fashion, Film.

It contains a black-and-white photo of Velvet Underground musician John Cale, fashion heavyweight Marc Jacobs, and film director Martin Scorsese.

"I will say it was an absolute nightmare," says the singer.

"We were really down to the day before that deadline and you know, they're busy guys," she says.

"I felt it was one of those moments where I was like this is a once in a lifetime moment, this is probably never going to happen again.

"It was really sweet and overwhelming."

And she wanted this album to feel like something new and different.

"The way that Music, Fashion, Film sounds was like a very sort of deliberate response to the way that Brat sounds.

"They're sort of polar opposites."

After the overwhelming success of Brat, does Charli feel like she can have a 'normal' life?

"I can't just sort of go home and like unplug and be like a different person," she tells Saunders.

"Apart from when I'm watching Love Island.

"I will say, that is my one time where I'm like, I'm actually off now.

"I'm not thinking about fonts or whatever."

But she wouldn't want things to be any different.

"I love the life that I have, I wouldn't change it for anything else."

You can watch the full Charli XCX performance on BBC iPlayer.

Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyl.summary: Charli XCX's new album, Music, Fashion, Film, was released in July. The Apple singer previously told Jack Saunders that she hadn't started making new music. But why do artists feel they need to keep their plans under wraps?

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y0.title: Kate Nash on Irish history, heritage and covering Sinéad O'Connor
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y0.text:
Singer-songwriter Kate Nash believes many English people are disconnected from parts of their own history, and her latest single is an attempt to start a conversation about why.

She has recorded a cover of Famine, Sinéad O'Connor's 1994 song about one of Ireland's darkest periods, using it to explore wider questions about how Britain's role in the famine is remembered.

For Nash, the project was also deeply personal.

Born in London to an Irish mother, she attended a Catholic school, spent childhood holidays in the Republic of Ireland and the first instrument she learned was the tin whistle, despite long claiming it was the piano.

Revisiting the song more than three decades later, Nash said she was struck not only by its message, but by her little knowledge of the subject matter.

"Sinéad gave me the whole history lesson that school never gave me, that I didn't really get at home either," Nash told BBC News NI ahead of a performance in Belfast as part of this year's Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann fringe programme.

She is quick to clarify what she means when she says English people do not know their own history.

"When I'm saying the English don't know their history, I'm also English.

"So I'm saying, I don't know my history… and I want to learn."

Nash's debut album Made of Bricks came out in 2007 and spawned her biggest hit, Foundations.

She's since released four more studio albums, including 9 Sad Symphonies in 2024.

While working in the United States more than a decade ago, Kate met music producer Kool Kojak and was encouraged to explore her Irish heritage through music.

After O'Connor's death in 2023, he suggested recording Famine.

"I was like, 'oh my God, that's so audacious, only an American could suggest that'," Nash said.

"But then I thought, why not?

"The tradition of covering old folk songs, passing music through is really important. And the more people that cover that song really the better, because you can bring that message, the education, to a new audience."

Rather than simply replicate the original, Nash rewrote parts of the song and added a new verse reflecting her own experience of dual identity.

"England doesn't take responsibility for destruction that it's caused, for its empire and now commonwealth, they left us uninformed", she sings, echoing wider debates about how Britain's imperial past is taught and remembered.

Enda Delaney, professor of modern history and director of research at the Edinburgh Futures Institute, believes Nash's point of view is "fair comment".

Unlike in the Republic of Ireland, he said, Anglo-Irish history is not routinely taught to English students, creating a gap in public understanding.

"The fact that one million people died in a part of the United Kingdom, which of course Ireland was in the 1840s... there isn't a really good knowledge of the context in which those terrible events occurred."

He said there should be greater emphasis on Irish history in schools and pointed to growing interest in the subject at university level.

"When you've got two societies which are so closely located to each other and so deeply intertwined, it's really important that both Irish people and British people understand those shared points of history."

Nash said she had discussed the issue with educators and believes they need more support.

"There's a lot of pressure on teachers… they need to be empowered to teach difficult topics," she said.

"Sometimes they rely on lessons they've already developed because they don't have time or resources to introduce new material."

The Department for Education, which oversees the curriculum in English maintained schools, said Ireland and the UK "have a uniquely shared history, relevant not just to the millions of British citizens of Irish descent but the country as a whole".

"The national curriculum provides a core frame within which teachers can take the opportunity to teach about Britain and Ireland in the 19th Century, including the Great Famine," a spokesperson told BBC News NI.

A revitalised curriculum "will go further to strengthen pupils' understanding", they added.

"This will give teachers a clear framework to bring in a wide range of topics, including those that are challenging or uncomfortable."

More than one million people died during the Irish famine between 1845 and 1852, when Ireland was part of the United Kingdom, and about two million emigrated over the following decade.

It was triggered by potato blight which spread across Europe.

In 1997, Tony Blair issued a landmark statement, acknowledging that the British government failed the Irish people during this time.

However it later emerged it was neither written, nor approved by him.

That debate sits at the centre of both O'Connor's and Nash's interpretation of Famine.

Robert Tombs, professor emeritus at the University of Cambridge and founding editor of History Reclaimed, argued the British government relief efforts should be judged against the economic realities of the 1840s.

"If the Irish famine were to be taught, it should counter the myth that it was caused or aggravated by Britain," he said.

While Irish farmers did export some food to Britain, "it was dwarfed by the amount being brought in for distribution by the UK government", he added.

As ministers grappled with high food prices and moved to repeal the Corn Laws, (tariffs on grain that kept the price of bread artificially high), the government, led by Sir Robert Peel, imported large quantities of maize and expanded relief schemes that at one stage fed about three million people a day.

However, the maize proved difficult to mill and distribute.

The UK Parliament has acknowledged the next government led by Lord John Russell "did not handle the famine effectively".

Direct food distribution programmes were dismantled and legislation was introduced to place the financial onus for famine relief on Irish landowners, who in turn attempted to save money by ejecting tenants.

"It is possible to say that more could have been done, but there was a serious risk of financial meltdown," Tombs reasoned.

He has suggested that history should be approached through "careful interpretation of complex evidence", rather than political narratives.

Nash's exploration of Irish history also places her in a long tradition of second-generation Irish artists examining their heritage.

Prof Sean Campbell, whose research focuses on popular culture and the Irish diaspora in Britain, said artists including Kevin Rowland, the frontman of Dexy's Midnight Runners, Shane MacGowan and members of Oasis had done the same.

Campbell explained that second-generation Irish identity is often misunderstood, with artistic expressions of that heritage frequently provoking mixed reactions.

Artists he said, did not simply "decide to become Irish".

"They grew up feeling Irish. It was just an organic sense of identity."

But of the many second-generation, political pop efforts, he said Nash's recent recording stands out for being so "overt".

"She's tackling one of the really big issues in Anglo-Irish politics and history," he said.

"It's quite a brave thing to do."

Nash believes that while many people in England engage with Irish culture, they are avoiding harder conversations about history.

"For English people, it's really important to appreciate more than just the food and the culture and the Guinness," she said.

"We need history, we need context, we need to understand things."

Kate Nash performs at The Mac in Belfast on 6 August as part of the fringe programme for the Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y0.summary: Kate Nash has recorded a cover of Sinéad O'Connor's Famine, Sinéads O' Connor's 1994 song. She says she was struck by her little knowledge of the subject matter. She has also rewrote parts of the song and added a new verse reflecting her own experience of dual identity.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3ek.title: Ariana Grande has had enough of body comments, but 'scrutiny' will linger
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3ek.text:
Three years ago, Ariana Grande made a plea for people not to comment about her body.

Responding in a TikTok video to comments about her weight and figure, the pop star and actress told fans there were "many different ways to look healthy and beautiful".

Three years on, and the social media speculation about her body and her health has continued. After "endless, ongoing public scrutiny", the star's spokesperson released a statement saying she "will be taking a step back from visibility" at the end of her current tour.

"She looks forward to finishing the tour and ending it on a high note, both healthily and happily," the statement stressed, "and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny."

It follows the release of her eighth studio album Petal and the graphic video for its title track on Friday.

The song refers to the pressures of fame, and the video shows Grande as a starlet who tries out for a group of talent scouts, dressing as a variety of different pop star personas. None are deemed good enough.

The men initially inform her that it "couldn't hurt" to lose some weight, among other things, before they tell the final persona that they miss "the way you used to be".

She then murders them all with a chainsaw.

"I wrote [this album] from a place that I don't usually, which was like an unfiltered rage," she has said.

Whatever the message, her appearance is the thing that has attracted the most attention, and with many on social media saying the scrutiny comes from genuine concern. The comments and screengrabs flooded social media over the weekend.

The top comment under the Petal video on YouTube said: "It's not about wanting the old Ariana back. It's about wanting her to be healthy."

One fan wrote on X that she "has become so thin that people are genuinely concerned".

Her loyal fans sent their support, making #Weloveyouariana trend on social media. Some criticised those who were focusing on her body. "No-one has the right to comment on anyone else's body or appearance," a user wrote.

Music journalist Sophie Williams told BBC Radio 5 Live that the "constant commentary around her has really, really elevated over the weekend as she's been promoting new music".

"So we're led to think in part that that [commentary] has brought us to this decision," she said.

Grande is scheduled to continue the Eternal Sunshine Tour in Chicago this week before 10 dates at London's O2 arena, where the tour will finish on 1 September.

Her "step back" means she will no longer star in Stephen Sondheim's stage musical Sunday in the Park with George opposite her Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey at London's Barbican in 2027.

Grande has lived for more than 15 years - half her life - in the spotlight.

"I've been doing this in front of the public and been a specimen in a petri dish since I was 16 or 17, so I have heard it all," Grande told an interviewer during the press tour for the first Wicked film in 2024.

"I've heard every version of it, of what's wrong with me. And then you fix it, and then it's wrong for different reasons. But that's everything from – even just the simplest thing – your appearance, you know?

"It's hard to protect yourself from that noise."

Grande began singing at the age of eight and made her name as a teenage actress in Nickelodeon sitcom Victorious and its spin-off, Sam & Cat.

Since releasing her debut single in 2011, she has scored 10 US number one hits and earned 20 Grammy Award nominations, winning three times.

She has also made a successful move into acting, earning an Oscar nomination in 2025 for Wicked.

But she has also experienced some difficult times.

In 2017, 22 people were killed in a suicide bomb attack outside her concert at Manchester Arena.

The following year, she said she was dealing with symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and that she wanted to "not be afraid" but added: "The truth is, it's scary. It's scary going anywhere. You look at places differently."

When her ex-boyfriend, rapper Mac Miller, died in 2018, she later spoke about her "all-consuming" grief.

Her relationships and break-ups have never been far from the headlines, including with comedian Pete Davidson, estate agent Dalton Gomez, her married Wicked co-star Ethan Slater, and former backing dancer Ricky Alvarez.

In another new song, Oh Well, she says an unnamed ex or exes can "all go to hell".

Elsewhere, she has also spoken about having depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and has called for mandatory therapy for child stars.

This summer, she launched the Brighter Days Ahead Foundation, a mental health initiative to support groups including the crew and performers on her current tour.

"A lot of people perhaps forget that she's been famous for nearly 15 years, and she has a unique story in that she sadly lived out a lot of trauma in the public eye," Williams says.

"As fans and those working in music, all that we can do is wish her well," she told BBC News

In Grande's video appeal in 2023, she said that even if concerned onlookers thought they were "saying something good or well-intentioned" about someone's appearance and wellbeing, they should think twice.

"I think we should be gentler and less comfortable commenting on people's bodies, no matter what."

The star also told fans that the period when they considered her to have looked the healthiest was in fact a time when she was on antidepressants while also drinking and eating poorly, so it was, in fact, "the unhealthiest version of my body".

"Healthy can look different," she said. "You never know what someone is going through, so even if you are coming from a loving place and a caring place, that person probably is working on it or has a support system that they are working on it with."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crrv.title: 'I did my first book signing in a police custody suite'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crrv.text:
For former lawyer turned crime writer Steve Cavanagh, addressing a court room jury is not a world away from writing a compelling novel. Indeed the idea for his first book came to him while he was cross-examining a witness.

"I kind of conned them into revealing that they were lying and it hit me then that con artists and trial lawyers have all the same skills," he said.

The idea sparked something in Cavanagh, who has just released his tenth novel about the conman turned lawyer Eddie Flynn.

The Northern Irish author has now sold more than five million books globally and has appeared on the Sunday Times bestseller list.

Cavanagh's home, near Lisburn, is busy. His daughter pops in to say hello, Muffin the dog is looking for someone to throw a ball, he's not long back from a US tour promoting his last book and he's packing to leave the following day for a UK book tour.

It's something he never really thought would happen when he was working as a solicitor.

He grew up on Palestine Street in south Belfast, went to school in Ballynahinch, then onto Belfast tech before going to uni in Dublin.

He only started writing in his mid 30s, after his mum died.

Cavanagh said she was the only one who ever really encouraged him to write so he wrote his first book for her.

His surname is Mearns, but he used Cavanagh, his mother's maiden name as a tribute to her. It was also easier to separate the practising solicitor from the author.

Cavanagh sais that "every word is a weapon in a courtroom".

"I thought con artists and trial lawyers all have skills which are perfectly allowed: misdirection, distraction, persuasion, manipulation," he said.

"I thought that would be a good idea for a character, someone who had all those skills as a conman, who then becomes a lawyer and that's be an interesting character to write about."

That led to the birth of his character Eddie Flynn, a lawyer based in New York, aided by his associates Harry Ford, Melissa Bloch, Gabriel Lake and a dog named after Clarence Darrow, another inspiration of Cavanagh's.

It wasn't an easy start for Cavanagh, who was rejected by more than 50 agents before getting representation for the Eddie Flynn series and securing the first book deal.

He recalls publication day for his first book, The Defence. He was representing a client in a police station in County Down when one of the police officers said he'd heard he had released a book.

"I went in and did the interview and by the time I came out the old custody sergeant had been to Eason's and bought it, so I did my first signing in Bangor custody suite."

While the first book won awards, it didn't sell particularly well and it was only when Thirteen, the novel which Cavanagh describes as having changed his life, was released did things really take off.

He believes this was down to the books gripping tag line: "The serial killer isn't on trial, he's on the jury."

Readers took to it and in 2019 he was able to stop working as a solicitor to focus on writing.

He's written 10 Eddie Flynn books and a few stand-alone thrillers.

Author of The Housemaid, Freida McFadden, recently posted on Facebook about his thriller Kill for Me, Kill for You, saying it is "one of the best thrillers I've ever read".

"It's not often that I read a book where all the twists and turns are perfectly executed, but this is one of them. It's kind of a masterpiece, in my humble opinion," she said.

It's high praise from the hottest author around at the moment and Cavanagh is quick to return the compliment and also talk about other local authors who he thinks people should be reading.

Cavanagh has touched on a number of themes in his books. In Two Kinds of Stranger, he looks at a TikToker who has shared so much of her life online that she's become an easy target for a criminal mastermind.

In his latest book, One Of Us is Guilty, we meet the billionaire Vanderpool family and are immersed in a gruesome murder.

Patrick Vanderpool, who is running for governor, and his wife Vanessa are both in the firing line for the murder but Patrick's father Julian controls half of New York so will anyone really have to pay?

Cavanagh said he wanted to look at extreme power and wealth in America the influence of multi billionaires.

"I write about law and a lawyer, and increasingly these days, laws don't matter to some people," he said.

He is critical of AI companies.

"That entire technology is almost based entirely on piracy. They have scraped millions of books and the government's doing nothing.

"It's almost the more powerful you are, the more you can get away with."

For Cavanagh, this is a world away from his working class upbringing in Belfast.

He plans to take a break from Eddie Flynn for now, he has a standalone book in mind and has been asked by the Conan Doyle estate to write a short Sherlock Holmes story for a collection in the Autumn.

But he wants to reassure fans that Eddie Flynn will be back and hasn't been beaten yet.
