https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy8e.title: Why Love Island fans are choosing the US edition: 'They actually fancy each other'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy8e.text:
What's your dream Love Island series on paper?

Some watch for the heartwarming romances, like Molly-Mae Hague and Tommy Fury falling for each other back in 2019, while others prefer intense dramas - we see you 2022 winners Ekin-Su Cülcüloğlu and Davide Sanclimenti.

Others tune in for exciting challenges like Snog, Marry, Pie or the ones which literally send heart rates soaring.

For most, it's a mix of all of the above, and it's a balance TV producers have been trying to strike for years with the original UK series, as well as a host of spin-offs and international editions.

It's no secret that Love Island UK linear viewing figures have dropped from their 2019 heyday, with streaming and social media becoming more of a focus.

Across the pond the US edition has been reaching new heights, with the latest eighth series ranked as the number one reality show for five weeks in the States across all streaming platforms, according to its streamer Peacock.

It also had an injection of star power as US celebrity fans, including Lizzo, Demi Lovato and Kesha, sent messages of support to the finalists, while rapper Megan Thee Stallion has become a regular guest.

BBC Newsbeat has been speaking to fans, commentators and an ex-Islander to see what they feel the UK edition could learn from the US version to regain its spark.

The 13th series of the UK show ended on Monday, with Julia Majchrzak and Lorenzo Alessi crowned the winners.

The final drew in an average audience of 1.1m viewers across all devices, including streaming, according to its broadcaster ITV, but this was a notable drop from last year's, which had an overnight audience of 1.3m.

By comparison, series five in 2019 broke the show's viewing records with 6m tuning in to an episode post Casa Amor, and that year's final had the highest average audience to date.

However, ITV say this 2019 figure was a consolidated number reached once it "had received all the data post final" and said it does not yet have an "equitable" figure for series 13.

According to the network, more than 60% of its audience now engage with the show through streaming and the latest series, as well as its companion shows Aftersun and The Debrief, have had more than 180 million streams on ITVX.

Content creator Sarel, known for her Love Island debriefs to her 1.2m followers on TikTok, feels the biggest issue with the most recent UK series is "there hasn't been much love" between the couples, so she wasn't rooting for anyone at the end.

And while she knows people watch it for the drama and conversations it sparks, she thinks those are just "added extras" and the romances should be at the centre of the show.

"I want somebody to fall in love. I love stories where we get the butterfly moments," she says.

"Where you had your Indiyah [Polack] and your Dami [Hope] when they ran to each other, or you had couples like Molly-Mae and Tommy."

She thinks that's an aspect which the US version has been getting right, as it feels like "everyone who is in there actually fancies one another" and there is "no box" they have to fit into.

Someone from the UK who chose to go on the US version is Aaron Evans, but this wasn't his first reality series as he was one of three winners on the first series of The Traitors UK.

He feels the US edition's success is helped by having "fresh eyes" on the format and the show having "so much social media presence", which makes it "highly engaging".

Stats given to Newsbeat by TikTok - which called Love Island "one of the most influential entertainment franchises" on the app - suggest he's not wrong.

During the latest series, the hashtag #LoveIsland was mentioned in 123,000 posts in the UK, with #LoveIslandUK featuring in 88,000.

While in the US, #LoveIsland appeared in 1.09m posts and #LoveIslandUSA was tagged in 502,000 posts.

That said, the US population is nearly five times the size of the UK's.

US entertainment journalist Carly Thomas says executive producers have told her they look for ways to "bring in the US audience", be that through social media, challenges and the islanders they choose.

"I think for the US audience, we love to just relate and connect with people," Thomas, who works for The Hollywood Reporter, says.

She also feels the US edition wants to "push the limits" of the islanders with intense challenges and viewers "love to see how far they'll go", including rapper Megan Thee Stallion hosting one which saw them sit on cakes and throw them at each other.

Love Island USA has not been all smooth sailing, though.

Contestants in last year's series faced relentless online bullying which forced the show to broadcast a statement saying it does not tolerate "cyberbullying, harassment or hate". The show insists it takes duty of care seriously.

The US version runs for six weeks once a year, while the UK summer edition typically airs across eight weeks.

There is also now an additional series in the UK throughout the year, with a winter edition airing in 2020 and 2023, which has now been succeeded by All Stars.

The finale of the third All Stars version, which sees ex-islanders return to the villa, attracted about 910,000 viewers earlier this year.

During the most recent UK series, producers tried to get hearts racing, and TikTok numbers up, by introducing some new twists.

A few islanders were summoned for a sleepover at a different villa before Casa Amor, and for the first time, only three couples were in the final after two pairs got dramatically dumped.

Some fans have appreciated the changes, while others, like Sarel, feel they didn't land.

Love Island superfan Dami Amoo, who has watched every episode of the UK, US and All Star editions, says the UK series is starting to feel "overproduced".

"I do think it's been on a steady decline because they're trying to give us what we want, but then they're overdoing it and then they're taking away the classic [elements]."

She thinks this may have been due to budget constraints, but missed the islanders going on exciting dates and taking part in "fun activities or games" where you see their personalities more.

Amoo, 28, also thinks you can really see the impact of investment in the US version, which was aired almost simultaneously with the latest UK edition.

"They've invested so much into the props, the games and all of these brands are part of the actual production," she says.

"Whereas the UK version, it seems like they're just on an island somewhere just doing it on their own.

"You don't get a lot of hype, we don't get British celebrities contributing to the discussions."

The US edition has been able to bring in revenue by becoming a major space for advertising, with numerous content partners and more than 1,000 media partners, according to Peacock.

Evans isn't surprised by the US version capitalising on brand partnerships, saying "everything's bigger, everything's brighter, everything's just very American".

So as the sun sets on another run of Love Island series, what could UK producers do ahead of the next launch?

Superfan Dami thinks "they should really get some real fans in the production room".

"The people that do the debriefs online, people who engage on Twitter, they should get us in a room and we tell them what we really, really want."

An ITV spokesperson told Newsbeat "reaction of the fans is at the heart of the show as seen in public votes and including opinions as part of the challenges".

They added Love Island UK "continues to wield huge cultural relevance, both in the UK and in the USA" and to date it has had "over 2bn streams on ITVX and remains the biggest 16-34 show in commercial television".

Additional reporting by BBC Newsbeat reporters Srosh Khan and Jack Gray.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwye.title: Spider-Man fans hail Brand New Day as Holland's best yet
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwye.text:
Fans have been queuing outside cinemas to catch the latest Spider-Man film, with many hailing it as a spectacular return for the web-slinging superhero.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day marks Tom Holland's fourth standalone adventure as the protagonist and hero Peter Parker.

Picking up after the events of Spider-Man: No Way Home, the film follows Parker as he devotes his time to protecting New York City while adjusting to a life in which everyone, including his closest friends, has forgotten who he is.

The fourth Spider-Man film is director Destin Daniel Cretton's second project in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), having previously been at the helm of Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings.

Appearing together in the same film for a second time this summer, Holland reprises the role alongside his wife Zendaya, who stars once again as MJ.

There is also a return for Jon Bernthal's Punisher, making his first appearance in an MCU feature film, and an introduction to the MCU for Sadie Sink, whose role in the plot has been kept firmly under wraps.

The reviews from critics have been largely positive.

Many critics have welcomed the film-makers' decision to scale back from the multiverse seen in No Way Home, in favour of a more personal, character-centred story.

The Telegraph's Robbie Collin called it "the best Spider-Man film since the Tobey Maguire era", and praised the relationship between Holland and Zendaya, who create a "real yearning and perplexity" that we have not seen previously in the dynamic between their characters.

In his review for The Wrap, William Bibbiani described it as the strongest entry in Holland's Spider-Man series, applauding its emotional focus and character-driven storytelling, and praising its "wonderful, propulsive quality".

Meanwhile, Empire's John Nugent awarded the film four stars, declaring the web-slinging hero is "still Marvel's ace in the pack", and in its five-star review The Standard said the film had "verve, intelligence and above all, heart".

However, others have been more reserved.

The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw declared that Zendaya "saves this film" from "silliness and the generic déjà vu overfamiliarity that is always threatening to sink it".

This opinion was supported by David Rooney in the Hollywood Reporter, who wrote that the film "chugs along satisfyingly even with the occasional patch of sluggishness and the usual overly convoluted plot contortions".

He adds: "As much as the movie revels in the thrill of Spidey swinging between skyscrapers with erratic command of his shooters, the more intimate scenes with MJ and Ned are what supplies the emotional charge."

Danny Leigh of the Financial Times awarded the film three stars, praising the chemistry between Holland and Zendaya but criticising the film's insistence on falling back on CGI-heavy action sequences.

But that is just what the critics say. What do audiences think?

Fresh from a screening of the film, Sam said "I have been a Spider-Man fan since I was six years old, but it's only in the last decade I have really got into it, all because of these films".

He called Brand New Day his favourite film of Holland's tenure, praising him for the "most mature performance" as the character to date.

Kimberly agreed, but said while Holland does a "fantastic job" she still has a soft spot for "the OG" Tobey Maguire.

Maguire played the role in three movies directed by Sam Raimi from 2002 to 2007.

Spidey fan Joe praised Holland's handling of the famous character over the years, saying his version of Spider-Man has "shown his progression" over the years.

"Half his life he has been doing this character. He's handled it very well."

Asked how he felt about Holland one day leaving the franchise, he said: "I hope not! I think we still have a lot more to see from him."

Clutching her Spider-Man popcorn bucket, Danika was more open to the idea of a passing of the baton, saying Zendaya and Holland have "had a good run" so she would not be disappointed "as long as they end the characters in a good way."

She said Zendaya's acting in particular was "amazing," and labelled Brand New Day as "the most comic accurate Spider-Man movie".

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is poised to become one of Marvel's most successful movies at the box office, and Sony will be hoping to emulate the returns of Holland's previous outing, Spider-Man: No Way Home.

Released in 2021, the film benefited massively from the return of previous Spider-Man actors Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield and went on to gross $1.9 bn (£1.4bn) worldwide.

Holland and Zendaya were just 20 and 19 years old, respectively, when they first met in 2016 on the set of Spider-Man: Homecoming, during the movie's casting and initial production.

Ten years and multiple other blockbusters later, there is an ever-growing speculation that their futures now lie away from the MCU.

Speaking on the Happy Sad Confused podcast with Josh Horowitz, Holland hinted that a new chapter was on the horizon, albeit not clarifying when.

"It's going to change, for sure", he said.

"There is a whole plan that we have been working on since, I would say, Spider-Man No Way Home.

"I have a really clear vision to the passing on of the baton, and I think it is really exciting."

As for Zendaya, she has hinted previously that she is planning on taking a career break at the end of 2026, after a busy schedule that included the promotion of her films The Drama, The Odyssey, Spider-Man: Brand New Day and Dune: Part Three.

Earlier this year Zendaya told Elle that "I think that after this, I'm going to have to take a little bit of a break".

She backed this notion up when asked about her future plans by Entertainment Tonight at the NYC premiere of The Odyssey, replying, "Oh, girl, nothing. Just mind my business!".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwye.summary: Tom Holland returns to the Spider-Man franchise as Peter Parker. The film follows the events of the previous film, No Way Home. The fourth Spider- man film is director Destin Daniel Cretton's second project in the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8rn.title: British girl band FLO 'want it all' - and they're confident they will get it
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8rn.text:
"It's kind of been like a bit of a crash course in making music," says Stella Quaresma of making FLO's second album, Therapy at the Club.

After entering the music industry as teenagers, the British girl band say they grew to trust their own instincts during six months making their new record.

Formed of Quaresma, Jorja Douglas and Renée Downer, they first broke through in 2022 with the track Cardboard Box and have since won Best R&B/Soul Act at the 2026 MOBO Awards.

The group have more than five million monthly Spotify listeners and 1.2 million TikTok followers.

The campaign around their second album has included a NPR Tiny Desk performance viewed over a million times and appearances on high-profile US podcasts, helping reintroduce them stateside.

"It felt like we went to university and graduated with honours," Quaresma adds.

For their latest album, the group say they became more involved than ever before in every stage of the album's creation, from songwriting and vocal arrangements to production decisions.

"Sometimes you walk away from a session and people are surprised that you contributed, that you had ideas," says Douglas.

Quaresma suggests that's partly because when FLO first entered the industry, they leaned on the experience of the writers and producers around them.

"In the past we'd kind of been okay with that," she says. "But now we really don't need that kind of crutch."

For Downer, that greater creative control has resulted in FLO's most authentic record yet.

"We're definitely a lot more grown up. We've been a lot more involved, so this really is the best reflection of us at this point in time," she says.

Love has always been central to FLO's music, but on this album they explore its messier realities, with nights out providing the backdrop for stories of heartbreak, healing and friendship.

"So go ahead and kiss who you wanna / whatever the trauma / If you ever fall out of love / try therapy at the club," they sing on the title track.

Quaresma says the title came to represent the role friends can play during difficult moments.

"It's the idea that you're having the worst time of your life, but your friends are saying, 'No, you're coming out, you're going to dance and forget about it for a second.'"

While R&B remains at the heart of FLO's sound, they say they also aimed to push further into pop on their second album.

Quaresma says making Therapy at the Club taught her "how fun it is to really blend genres and to delve more into making pop music to make really big songs".

One example is Remedied, co-written with Grammy-winning songwriter Amy Allen, who has worked with pop stars Sabrina Carpenter and Tate McRae.

When making their Grammy-nominated debut album, Access All Areas, the FLO trio wrote songs together - but for Therapy at the Club, they wrote separately before bringing ideas back to one another.

Quaresma says this process helped them appreciate one another's strengths in a new way.

"You don't fully get to appreciate each other's talents when you're writing in a room of 10 people. To go away and write songs, then show each other what we'd made, was really special," she says.

That approach also extended to the album's collaborations. One of just two guest appearances on the record is Sex in Peace, their second collaboration with rising British R&B singer kwn. Quaresma wrote the song before bringing it to the rest of the group.

Downer says working with kwn has become a natural fit.

"We work really well with kwn when it comes to sexy R&B, so it felt right to send it to her and see if she'd do a verse," she says.

"She sent it back really quickly. We had no notes. We loved it."

FLO's ambition doesn't stop with the music. Live performance is never far from their minds, with choreography, visuals and music videos all considered throughout the album-making process.

"As we elevate everywhere else in our career, with the vocals, the music, the appearance, we also want to elevate the music videos and the dance," Douglas explains.

The demanding schedule has meant long rehearsal days and little sleep, but Douglas says it's worth it.

"This is the most thrilling, entertaining, fulfilling job we could have ever asked for."

Asked what success looks like over the next year, the trio don't hesitate.

"We want it all," Quaresma says.

Douglas nods in agreement before adding: "We want the shows, we want the numbers, we want the awards, we want the love and we want the success."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8rn.summary: FLO's second album, Therapy at the Club, is out on September 26. The British girl band have more than five million monthly Spotify listeners and 1.2 million TikTok followers. The group have more to do with their music, with choreography, visuals and music videos all considered throughout the album-making process.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c78g.title: Glasgow gets starring role in Spider-Man: Brand New Day film
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c78g.text:
Any comic book fan knows that Spider-Man's secret identity is Peter Parker, a science nerd who gained superhero powers after being bitten by a radioactive spider.

But in the latest installment from the Marvel cinematic universe, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Parker - played by Tom Holland - is not the only star in disguise.

The action takes place in New York City but much of the movie, which premiered in London this week, was filmed more than 3,000 miles away in Glasgow.

Filming almost brought the city centre to a halt last summer, when fans gathered to watch Holland in an action sequence in full superhero mode.

Parts of the nearby Merchant City were also dressed up to resemble the Big Apple.

It was the latest in a long line of Hollywood blockbusters to have been filmed in the city in recent years.

And next month Glasgow is expected to double as Gotham City, when filming starts on the sequel to The Batman.

Screen Scotland said the Victorian architecture, wide avenues and grid layout make it an "incredibly versatile stand-in" for many US cities.

Filmmaker Destin Daniel Cretton praised Scotland as a filming destination during an interview at the premiere on Wednesday.

"I love Scotland," he told Press Association.

"I got to go to Scotland first ages ago with a short film to the Edinburgh Film Festival and I fell in love with that place."

The 37-year-old added: "When we shot in Glasgow, that was our first day shooting and that was just such an energising way to start.

"We had thousands of people show up who are cheering us on and getting excited and feeling that energy which was really a wonderful way to start."

Asked about what would draw him back to Scotland, Cretton said: "The people. The people in Glasgow, in particular, were so warm and welcoming and fun and knew how to party and have a good time.

"It was a really wonderful experience."

Producer Amy Pascal said "everything about Scotland is great" and that it was "wonderful to make movies in the real places".

The film follows Parker as he navigates his new life four years on from the events of the last film, 2021's Spider-Man: No Way Home, which saw a spell cast to make the world forget his real identity so he can save the universe.

His romance with MJ (Zendaya) and his friendship with Ned Leeds (Jacob Batalon) have also been erased from civilians' minds, leaving a lonely Peter to continue his crime-fighting in secret while his friends experience life at university.

Screen Scotland, which supports Scotland's film and TV industry, said: "It's fantastic to see Spiderman: Brand New Day hitting our screens.

"As we can already see from the trailer, Glasgow has a starring role, as the city once again seamlessly doubles for New York.

"Glasgow's grid layout, wide avenues and Victorian architecture make it an incredibly versatile stand-in for many US cities including New York and Philadelphia and Spiderman: Brand New Day is the latest example of the scale of production the city can accommodate."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c78g.summary: Spider-Man: Brand New Day, starring Tom Holland, is the latest in a long line of Hollywood blockbusters to be filmed in Glasgow. The action takes place in New York City but much of the movie was filmed in the city. The film premiered in London this week and was filmed more than 3,000 miles away

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c05q.title: Cambridge to review process for hiring senior academics after Jason Arday resignation
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c05q.text:
The University of Cambridge will review its process for appointing senior academics following the resignation of Jason Arday in the midst of a plagiarism row.

The institution said findings from an investigation into the education professor's academic qualifications and appointments would "feed into" a new review on the appointment process for senior academic roles.

The Jesus College fellow has also faced accusations of fabricating or exaggerating elements of his CV. He has defended himself and his work, with attention now turning to Cambridge's handling of concerns and his upcoming memoir.

News of the review comes after a group of academics called for an independent probe into his appointment.

Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge and among those calling for an independent inquiry, said the university was facing "massive reputational damage" over the affair.

"This is reputational damage that has upset colleagues across disciplines, across the political spectrum," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.

"I've been quite struck by the number of people who are very upset by what has happened. So I don't think it is an option for Cambridge to just sweep this under the carpet and not take any action at all."

Gopal said the university should not be "marking its own homework", adding that the group of academics of which she is a part had suggested a mix of senior academics at Cambridge and elsewhere to conduct an investigation.

Cambridge said on Friday that it was "fully aware of the public commentary and concerns" and would "continue to investigate the circumstances around Jason Arday's appointment and tenure". A spokesperson declined to comment further.

It previously announced an investigation into "new information" about Arday's academic qualifications and appointments on Wednesday, having already said it was looking into allegations of plagiarism.

Jesus College welcomed the appointments review, saying Arday's role as fellow there had been "contingent on his university position".

"We rely on the university to do checks on academic credentials for its appointments," a spokeswoman added.

The University of Glasgow, where Arday worked for just over a year before moving to Cambridge, has commissioned its own review of his appointment.

"Jason Arday was employed as Professor of Sociology of Education at the University of Glasgow, from January 2022 to March 2023," a statement said.

"The Principal has commissioned a review of the appointment with the aim of understanding all the facts and learning lessons for the future."

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash against his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

He highlighted that plagiarism detection software had found several tracts of Arday's PhD dissertation to be copied verbatim or lightly rephrased from prior academic works by other authors.

Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU), which awarded Arday's PhD, has said it investigated the allegations of plagiarism last year and dismissed them, saying they were likely the result of "honest and reasonable error".

It told the BBC on Friday that its position remains unchanged in light of recent events and that his PhD "still stands".

Cofnas also noted that a retired professor had previously raised concerns about Arday's subsequent academic articles, which led to two journals issuing correction notes, and raised questions about some of his claimed achievements, including extensive marathon running and raising millions for charity.

Several universities at which Arday claimed on his CV to have had academic positions have since denied him having those roles.

The controversy has attracted a range of opinions, including within academia, about whether he had been scrutinised unfairly because of his race.

Arday has admitted errors in his work but denied plagiarism, saying his autism and a lack of adequate supervision early in his academic career may have contributed to those mistakes. He also denied lying about his achievements.

He said his decision to step down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me", which he has previously said were "racially motivated".

Gopal said universities were "being targeted in particular by a lazy and false division between academic excellence and diversity and equality on campus", which was "really part of culture wars rather than any part of university life".

She and her colleagues found it "unusual" that Arday had been appointed to a "very senior, very prestigious" post early in his career - and that he had been put forward in the media with "frankly a bit of a target on his back".

Gopal also said any investigation should review "whether the university was involved in any way or any level with efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations".

This came after it emerged the Metropolitan Police investigated Times Higher Education (THE) reporter Jack Grove over a complaint of harassment after he contacted Arday concerning allegations of plagiarism last year.

The Telegraph also reported that Arday hired law firm Carter-Ruck to send a letter to THE which implied that the "apparent attack" on Arday might be "racially motivated".

The Met closed the case and Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley apologised for the investigation, telling LBC on Thursday that the complaint should have been "screened out earlier on as not requiring investigation".

Among the claims by Arday that have been viewed as outlandish is one, made in an interview with the Guardian, that he was paid "1.4 million" for his memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things, due to be released next week. He did not specify the currency.

While not inconceivable, publishing insiders cast doubt on a figure such as Arday being able to attract such a large advance payment.

Publisher Simon & Schuster has said it plans to press ahead with the publication despite the controversy surrounding Arday.

But the Atlantic reported on Thursday that there were discrepancies between an advance copy of the memoir and the proposal for the book from 2024 it had obtained.

Among the differences, the magazine said the proposal gave his suicide attempt as happening before the Covid pandemic, whereas in the memoir it occurred during, and that the proposal detailed Arday being hit by a car as a teenager before "miraculously" reawakening, an episode omitted from the finished book.

It comes after the Telegraph reported that Arday had claimed to have already published a book entitled Being Young, Black and Male: Challenging the Dominant Discourse.

Palgrave Macmillan, which was attributed to its publication, told the newspaper it had accepted a proposal for the book but did not publish it.

The BBC has contacted Simon & Schuster and the Good Law Project, which has publicly represented Arday during the plagiarism row, for comment.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c05q.summary: University of Glasgow has commissioned its own review of Jason Arday's appointment. University of Cambridge says it is "fully aware of the public commentary and concerns"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgje.title: How parents and pupils took on 'cruel', 'authoritarian' schools - and won
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgje.text:
To avoid getting into trouble, 14-year-old Amelia says she decided to stop drinking water at school so she would not need the toilet.

Her school, Camborne Science and International Academy in Cornwall, had introduced strict disciplinary policies, which included limiting toilet visits during classes, according to pupils and former teachers.

New discipline rules were implemented when the school was taken over in January 2024 by the Athena Learning Trust, which runs six secondary schools in Devon and Cornwall.

Amelia's mother, Kayley, believes these strict policies resulted in her daughter becoming ill from a series of serious infections caused by not drinking.

Hundreds of parents, including Kayley, have campaigned against the way Athena runs its schools.

Across Devon and Cornwall, there have been public meetings, school-gate protests and online petitions. Local MPs and councillors have also backed concerned parents.

The opposition to Athena now appears to have paid off - with the trust announcing last month that it was planning to disband and transfer all its schools to other trusts.

It said that trustees had "listened carefully to feedback" and recognised the "clear need for change".

BBC Panorama has spoken to nearly 100 pupils, parents and former teachers from Athena schools, who say levels of discipline went too far. Many pupils and parents queued to talk to us at two town hall meetings we arranged.

The way the schools had been run was "authoritarian" and "cruel", some said.

"You're constantly scared you're going to do something wrong," one student with ADHD told us, while a former music teacher said the strict discipline had meant his lessons were taught in silence.

Athena is not the only academy trust that has enforced strict discipline.

There are those who argue that education built on tough discipline and high expectations can benefit pupils - and exam results at Athena-run schools have improved.

About 20% of the school day in England is lost to bad behaviour, the government says.

The benefits of a "high level of strictness" is that students understand what is expected of them, says the government advisor on behaviour in schools in England, Tom Bennett.

Commenting generally, rather than on individual academies, he told us that pupils soon realise they have to get into the habit of meeting expectations.

However, there is growing concern that punitive disciplinary practices at some schools in England are damaging children.

Athena's secondary schools are attended by about 6,500 children. In the past three years, more than 500 children have left to be educated at home, according to Cornwall and Devon county councils.

Amelia is one of them.

While at Camborne, Amelia would often come home with the bottle of water she had left with in the morning still full.

When Kayley asked Amelia why, she says her daughter would reply that she had not drunk anything all day, "so I wouldn't need to go to the toilet".

Camborne has strict rules around toilet visits during lessons.

Pupils were not allowed to go to the toilet in the first or last 15 minutes of a lesson, and were only allowed to go in the middle of a lesson at the teacher's discretion, pupils and former teachers told us.

On school days, Amelia would only drink after school and in the evening. Kayley believes her daughter's fear of breaking the rules ended up making her ill.

"She's now on antibiotics, she's had water infections, she has got scarring on her kidneys because of this," Kayley says.

Amelia says her time at Camborne "makes me feel ill, even thinking of it".

Athena told Panorama that staff work hard to "support children to remain in education" and "support access to toilets during lessons" through professional staff judgement.

Academies are independent, state-funded schools, that receive their funding directly from central government, rather than through a local authority. They have independent control over their own admissions, curriculum and staff pay.

There are no academy trusts in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, but more than 80% of secondary schools in England are now run by them.

Multi-academy trusts like Athena oversee a network of schools. Athena's reports from the regulator, Ofsted, have mostly been positive.

Brian Maywood used to be the head of Launceston College in north Cornwall and was an English teacher there when Athena took over.

Initially he welcomed the trust's highly disciplined approach, and was pleased the school was "moving into a new way of learning".

But his opinion quickly shifted, he says, once he witnessed how the children were treated, calling it a "dictatorship".

The way students were spoken to at times "made me really, really uncomfortable", he adds.

He left the school last summer because of these reasons, he says.

It was the same for the former head of art, Estelle Pears.

"There is discipline and then there is being oppressed," she says. "It sounds dramatic, but that's what it became.

"If you're frightened of moving a pencil on a desk because you will get a sanction, that's beyond discipline."

Former Athena teachers who spoke to Panorama said they were forced to uphold the strict rules by the trust and that some made little sense.

Ieuan Horgan says his music lessons had to be taught in silence.

"At the start of the lesson, I would go through how to play the musical notation, and then the lesson would just be silent focus on trying to learn this musical notation," he says.

"They pushed for 100% distraction and disruption-free lessons - and 100% silent focus - in a music lesson."

Pupils have told Panorama they could be punished for minor offences and Bethany, who has just finished her GCSEs at Camborne, describes the strict and regimented approach as "demoralising" and "like you're being talked to like you were a primary school kid".

Athena schools have a two-strike policy: a warning for one mistake, sent out of the class for the second. Students then go to what is called "reflection" - a room where they work in silence from workbooks.

At Launceston College there were about 1,000 cases a month of pupils being sent to "reflection" rooms between September 2025 and March 2026, according to figures released by the trust.

Athena says reflection rooms are "supervised environments" where "students continue their learning independently".

It says it does not have a rigid two strikes policy and the "vast majority of students spend little or no time in these spaces". Students are not normally punished for isolated minor issues, it adds.

Some parents say children with special educational needs and disabilities are disproportionately affected by Athena's strict policies.

April, whose son Jack has special educational needs and has just finished his GCSEs at Ilfracombe Academy, says he was sent to reflection countless times.

He could not cope with the regimented environment, she says.

"Just to look out the window to refocus, that's not harming any of the other children or their education within the room - but that's enough to be sent out, because that's him not focusing on the teacher."

Jack was also suspended - sent home from school - dozens of times. He is far from alone.

The suspension rate at Ilfracombe Academy was almost five times higher than the average in England, according to government figures for 2023 to 2025. At Camborne, it was about five times higher than the average and three times higher at Launceston, according to the same figures.

Athena says suspensions are reserved for "serious or repeated breaches of behaviour expectations" and that rates have fallen significantly in the past year.

April and Jack's concerns were echoed at our town-hall events. More than half of the dozens of parents and pupils who turned up were concerned about the impact on students with special educational needs.

Finn, a student at Camborne with ADHD, says it was a difficult environment for neurodiverse pupils. "You're constantly scared that you're going to do something wrong," he says.

Faye, whose son has special educational needs and attends Pool Academy, says he had spent 96 hours in reflection the past school year. "Day in, day out, he feels like he's failing," she says.

And Zara says her autistic daughter Hannah, who has hearing difficulties and attends Ilfracombe Academy, was repeatedly removed from class because her needs were not recognised.

"Behaviour is just put down to persistent defiance and bad behaviour, and they're punished for it," she says. "It's never recognised as being linked to their disabilities."

Athena told us that children with special educational needs are "not routinely sanctioned for behaviours associated with their needs".

A lot of the anger we heard in Devon and Cornwall is, we were told, down to the lack of accountability.

Academy trusts do not have any supervision from local councils, meaning only central government can intervene.

One of the biggest weaknesses of the trust system is that it complicates the complaints process, says education journalist Laura McInerney, who co-founded Teacher Tapp, an app designed to track educators' wellbeing, classroom practices, and opinions on education policy.

If parents are not satisfied with a specific school's response, she says, they have to contact the trust, which could be miles way, and which "you may or may not hear from in anything other than a letter".

The government says parents can take complaints about academy trusts to the Department for Education.

Across England, there is growing concern about punitive disciplinary practices in schools.

The BBC's File on 4 Investigates recently found that a school in Wakefield, West Yorkshire, put a pupil in an isolation booth away from the classroom for more than half an academic year.

A safeguarding review last year also found an east London school's zero-tolerance policy involved pupils being routinely humiliated by shouting and prioritised control above all else, leaving some children with lasting psychological harm.

A team at law firm Leigh Day is now investigating potential legal claims on behalf of 50 families who believe their children may have been subjected to excessive or inappropriate disciplinary measures while at school.

However, there are many who argue that education built on tough discipline and high expectations can benefit pupils.

The government's advisor on behaviour, Tom Bennett, told us that discipline is vital, including for children with special educational needs.

"If you've got, for example, ADHD or an anxiety disorder, what you need more than anybody else is a calm, safe, dignified environment. Otherwise, you'll be massively distracted by the environment round about you," Bennett says.

In Devon and Cornwall, parents appear to have won in their campaign against Athena.

In May, the head of the trust, who implemented the tough discipline, resigned.

Last month, the trust announced it was planning to disband.

In a statement, Athena said it had "listened carefully" and recognised the "clear need for change". It said it would work with the Department for Education to "identify alternative trusts" to which the schools could transfer.

Until then, Athena will keep running the schools.

The Department for Education told Panorama the allegations about Athena are "serious and concerning" and that it is "taking robust action to make sure the trust improves" ahead of the schools transferring.

The trust is now "subject to enhanced monitoring" to make sure its "approach to pupil behaviour is reasonable and proportionate", it says.

Bethany says the school has caused "incredible harm".

"They need to change the way that they're thinking they can teach students as a one-size-fits-all."
