after newsletter promotion

Since then they have suffered with their mental health and undergone panic attacks as they wait for the decision of the court.

Their lawyer, who requested not to be named for security reasons, said the Belovs are very likely to be at risk if they are deported to Russia. Nikita’s work history will also put them at risk, the lawyer said. In a previous role he said he had access to confidential government information.

While it has long been difficult to get asylum in Finland, the lawyer said that recent changes on the border and to asylum procedure, including reduced access to legal aid, has made it even harder. “It’s even more difficult to get refugee status, even with clear political opinion showing. We really have to fight these cases to get the status that was earlier easier to get.”

The political activist and Putin critic Bill Browder, who is the head of the Global Magnitsky Justice Campaign, said the case is “a defining test of Europe’s commitment to protecting those who have risked everything to oppose Putin’s war”.

Browder, whose friend and lawyer Sergei Magnitsky died at the hands of Putin’s regime, added: “If people who refused to support aggression, openly opposed the regime, and now face persecution are denied protection, it could create a dangerous precedent that discourages others from taking a stand against authoritarianism.”

A Finnish immigration service spokesperson said it could not comment on individual cases.

Antti Lehtinen, the director of the department for international protection, which is part of the Finnish immigration service, added: “The situation of each applicant is assessed individually, taking into account their personal circumstances.

“For example, opposition to the war in Ukraine and related activities may constitute grounds for persecution based on political opinion. If we assess that a person’s political opinion or activities place them at risk of persecution or serious harm in Russia, they will be granted international protection.”

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Warning of increased activity as patrols spent 21 days in July shadowing Moscow’s ships in Dover Strait and North Sea

The Royal Navy has warned of increasing Russian activity around the UK’s waters after it spent 21 days in July monitoring Moscow’s ships.

Naval operations to monitor Russian vessels increased by 25% last month compared with the previous year, with warships making repeated voyages through the strait of Dover and the North Sea.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Offshore patrol vessels HMS Tyne, HMS Mersey and HMS Severn, alongside Wildcat helicopters from 815 Naval Air Squadron and Merlin submarine-hunting aircraft, were deployed throughout the month to shadow Russian frigates Neustrashimy and Admiral Grigorovich, which are tasked with escorting so-called “shadow fleet” tankers.

Last month, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in its annual report that Royal Navy vessels had been “activated” 116 times in the year to March 2026, shadowing 61 Russian warships and 28 merchant vessels around the UK’s waters.

This reflected a 30% increase in Russian naval activity over the previous two years and included operations to deter the spy ship Yantar, which was spotted near undersea cables off Scotland last November.

Vladimir Putin has been accused of using the Kremlin’s shadow fleet of ageing vessels to evade international sanctions on its oil and fund the war in Ukraine.

The increase in Russian naval activity follows the seizure of the tanker Smyrtos by Royal Marines in June, the first time British troops have directly boarded a shadow fleet vessel.

The MoD said the diversion of ships from Russia to escort shadow fleet vessels meant the country was “using up valuable operational capacity to constantly guard cargo”.

The UK has already imposed sanctions on more than 500 vessels, and Russia’s oil and gas revenues fell by 24% year on year in 2025.

HMS Tyne was also tasked with monitoring the Neustrashimy as it carried out a live-firing exercise outside British and French waters on 20 July.

Another ship, the frigate HMS Somerset, has been involved in monitoring Russian activity in the North Atlantic as part of a four-month Nato deployment searching for submarines, alongside helicopters from the Navy’s Fleet Air Arm.

Somerset’s commanding officer, Cmdr Matt Millyard, said on Saturday: “This deployment demonstrates exactly what the Royal Navy exists to do: protect the UK and our allies from wherever our interests are threatened.

“I am immensely proud of every single member of the ship’s company for what we have achieved over the past four months.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: The Bond effect? How MI6 fascinates spy watchers around the world
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Britain’s spooks take quiet satisfaction from survey ranking Secret Intelligence Service Europe’s top espionage agency

M
I6 has the swagger of James Bond; its French equivalent, DGSE, the complexities of the television drama Le Bureau. The film and TV shows may be fictional, but a survey run by a French magazine that placed the British spy agency above the French as No 1 across all of Europe this week is not.

L’Express, a news weekly, conducted a Eurovision-style poll of 60 current and former spies from across the continent, plus the CIA and Israel’s Mossad. Each was asked to rank their top five foreign intelligence agencies, in secret, naturally enough. MI6 was first with 251 points ahead of DGSE on 169, with other agencies trailing behind.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The result did not surprise Alexandra Saviana, a deputy editor at the publication, specialising in defence and intelligence, but the margin of victory did. “It is a huge point gap,” she said, reflecting the opinions of insiders and allies, 17 of whom are or were agency chiefs in a interconnected, covert ecosystem.

At MI6’s headquarters in Vauxhall, London, there has been no sign of a public reaction from its chief, Blaise Metreweli. But there is a quiet satisfaction at the unexpected verdict, not least because the agency values how it is perceived by both allies and adversaries. “Reputation matters a lot in the espionage game,” said a former Whitehall insider.

“British spies fascinate Europe, and beyond,” L’Express explained in its cover story. Saviana added that MI6’s success in the poll was principally down to its record in recruiting and running high-level human sources over generations: a focus on human intelligence in an era dominated by technology, intercepts and satellite monitoring.

“The British have the ability to play the long game, to bet on sources over 10 years, a bit like the Russians,” a former French DGSE spy told the magazine, adding “and they have a penchant for underhand tactics” without revealing what they meant.

One ex-spy voiced scepticism about the survey and added that a human intelligence service such as MI6 was only as good as the high-value agents on its books. Under Richard Moore, MI6’s previous chief, there were worries that it no longer had enough. Others, including Saviana, accept that greater credit might have been given to MI6’s sister agency, the signals intelligence experts at GCHQ, but it was not in the poll.

MI6’s reputation among its peers, the French publication said, was built on “long standing tradition”, including recruiting cold war assets, most notably the KGB’s Oleg Gordievsky, a double agent through late 1970s and early 80s, who helped convince Margaret Thatcher to take Mikhail Gorbachev seriously before he had to be dramatically smuggled into Finland in 1985, his cover finally blown.

Not every mole evaded capture. Alireza Akbari, a former Iranian deputy defence minister who had become a British citizen, was arrested on a return to Iran in 2019 and executed in 2023. Prior to his death, he confessed to being an MI6 agent. Though the confessions appeared coerced, spies from a number of countries indicated he was the person who had passed on the existence of the Fordow nuclear enrichment site in 2008.

In the run-up to the 2003 Iraq war, MI6 was accused of simplistically supporting the case for war, promoting what turned out to be false sources, claiming that Iraq’s leader, Saddam Hussein, could attack UK targets within “45 minutes”, and relied on one source who described supposed chemical weapons devices that were remarkably similar to one in the Hollywood movie The Rock. It was a low point.

L’Express argued that MI6 had rehabilitated itself in the run-up to the Ukraine war in February 2022, correctly warning in conjunction with the CIA that Russia was about to invade, while French and German counterparts were sceptical up until the last minute, having misjudged the situation. The chief of the German BND agency even flew into Kyiv the day before the invasion, seemingly unprepared.

It reflects MI6’s close and longstanding relationship with the CIA, part of the wider Five Eyes arrangements for intelligence sharing, between the US, UK, Australia, Canada and New Zealand, that are the envy of continental Europe, even allowing for the complexities posed by Donald Trump’s chaotic presidency. “Every other country wants to say they are the sixth eye,” Saviana said.

Fiction also has its advantages. Gordon Corera, a co-presenter of The Rest is Classified podcast, recalled that a former MI6 chief once told him a story of a young officer going somewhere far flung, not knowing whether the person he was trying to cultivate spoke English. “As he walked into the room the contact extended his hand and said: ‘Hello, Mr Bond.’ The former chief remarked: ‘I doubt if he would have received such a warm welcome if he’d been from the Belgian secret service.’”

Each was asked to rank their top five foreign intelligence agencies, in secret, naturally enough. MI6 was first with 251 points ahead of DGSE on 169, with other agencies trailing behind.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Nazi shipwrecks emerge from the depths as Europe’s Danube dries up
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Oliver Holmes
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Unexploded ordnance and a military motorcycle also recovered following record heat and drought conditions

Record-low water levels in the Danube have exposed remnants of Europe’s Nazi past, with dozens of second world war ships emerging from the riverbed during an intense drought.

In the middle of the river on the Serbian and Romanian border, a broken-up hull was visible on a sandbank that is normally underwater. Other vessels were partly submerged, some still believed to be laden with weapons.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The ships were part of Adolf Hitler’s Black Sea fleet that the German military deliberately sank towards the end of the war to slow down the Soviet advance. Historians say up to 200 German warships were scuttled in this way in September 1944. But Nazi Germany did not surrender until the following year in May 1945.

The ships have been revealed during previous droughts only to disappear again as water levels rose along the second-longest river in Europe. The Serbian government has tried in the past to remove the wrecks, but most remain in place owing to the explosives they carried.

Other second world war remnants have been found in other parts of the river, including a German military motorcycle in Budapest, Hungary.

In Slovakia, police recovered an unexploded British 1,543lb (700kg) bomb. Police said authorities loaded it on to a “specially modified firefighter vehicle with a sand bed, which ensured its safe transport” and took it to a 5-metre deep pit to detonate it.

In 1944, Britain’s Royal Air Force mined the river to disrupt enemy troops.

The Danube, which flows through 10 countries, has become increasingly difficult to navigate as low water levels create dangerous conditions. Prolonged droughts have left major European rivers at significantly lower water levels than is typical for the time of year, creating an energy crisis as many power plants rely on their natural water supply for cooling.

Sign up to Down to Earth

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

Intense summer heat and continuing drought conditions are being supercharged by the escalating human-caused climate crisis.

Temperature records have been broken in several countries across central and eastern Europe as the extreme weather that has caused wildfires and droughts across the continent continues.

Slovakia, Austria and Hungary registered record temperatures this week. On Thursday, the Slovakian hydrometeorological agency said a new national record of 42C (108F) had been reached in the village of Dolné Plachtince.

The Associated Press contributed to this report

The Serbian government has tried to remove the wrecks but most remain in place owing to the explosives they carried.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/a.title: High divers take the plunge in Paris for a new test of reclaimed Seine’s water
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/a.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/a.text:
European Aquatics Championships taking place in city

Threat to water quality tested two years after Games

Paris is staging its first high-diving competition in the Seine, with athletes launching themselves from a 20-metre platform in front of the Eiffel Tower – a spectacular new test of the city’s effort to reclaim its river for sport. The event on the Pont de Bir-Hakeim has also exposed the fragility of that ambition.

Organisers suspended training on Thursday when traces of hydrocarbons were detected upstream. By Friday, the French Swimming Federation said the affected area had been treated, allowing athletes to return to the water and the event to proceed as planned. High diving concludes on Saturday with the final two rounds and medal events, while the broader European Aquatics Championships run through to 16 August.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“There are things that are within our control and there are uncertainties that are inevitably linked to any outdoor activity,” said Maxime Sauvage, the Paris deputy mayor in charge of sports, sports facilities and equal access to sport. Among the things within the city’s control, he said, are the massive investments made before the 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games to make the river safe for swimming, such as work to prevent sewage from flowing directly into the Seine to improvements in stormwater management.

“There is always a small risk, but that is also part of what makes outdoor events special,” he said. “When they work, it is magical.”

Hundreds of people gathered along the banks on Friday to watch the divers. Some stopped during their lunch break, while others stumbled across the competition by chance. Among them was Rebecca Kapogiannis, a 45-year-old visitor from London, Ontario, who was visiting Paris with her daughter to celebrate her graduation. Her daughter had even packed a bathing suit in case she got the chance to swim in the Seine.

“We just headed down to the [Eiffel] Tower today and thought we would walk along the Seine and stumbled upon this and thought it was a really cool activity to watch,” she said. “I was not expecting a competition to take place in the Seine, but it’s such a cool use of this water that runs right through the city.”

For Cynthia Matz, who was visiting with her husband, Sean, the setting was part of the draw. She said they probably would not have sought out the competition had it been held inside. “Anybody can go. I don’t have to know anything about diving. I can just say: ‘This is really cool to see’. Having it out in public, people will just stop and go, ‘huh, what’s going on?’ and stop and spend some time and enjoy it.”

That ability to stumble across elite sport in the middle of the city reflects a broader transformation Paris officials have been pushing for years: turning the Seine from a river associated largely with commerce, transport and tourism into a place where people can also swim, play and compete.

Sign up to The Hotspot

A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis

after newsletter promotion

The 38th European Aquatics Championships mark the centenary of the inaugural championships, held in Budapest. For Paris, they are a return of another kind: the capital last hosted the event in 1931. More than 1,000 athletes are competing in five disciplines: swimming, diving, artistic swimming, open-water swimming and high diving.

The Seine is hosting the open-water swimming and high diving, placing the river back at the centre of a major international sporting event two years after the Paris Oympics. Swimming in the Seine was banned in 1923 because of pollution and the dangers of river traffic. Public swimming returned in 2025, after Paris and its partners mobilised €1.4bn to make the river swimmable, an effort accelerated by the Olympics.

For many French people, making the Seine clean enough for swimming again seemed a distant dream. But images of athletes competing – and now residents swimming – in the river have become almost familiar. “Paris is not just a postcard image, it is also a magnificent sporting venue,” said Sauvage.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Iran issues tough demands to reopen strait of Hormuz as deal still out of reach
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Guardian staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Tehran urges US to ‘correct its behaviour’ as UAE says one of its ships targeted by Iranian missile

Iran has issued tough new demands for reopening the strait of Hormuz, while the United Arab Emirates said one of its ships was targeted by an Iranian missile, as a deal to open the strategic waterway remained out of reach on Saturday.

Iran’s politburo-like body known as the supreme national security council said the strait of Hormuz will not open until the United States “corrects its behaviour”, and its state broadcaster published a statement from the council’s secretary, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who is also a commander in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The US must never threaten Iran again, the statement said, and must permanently end the war with Iran and its armed allies in the region. The US must lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports and withdraw its military from the area. It also must “completely compensate” Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and “unconditionally” release frozen assets.

There was no immediate comment from the US, which has wanted an acceptable deal on the strait before ending the blockade. According to the interim deal signed in June, a schedule to end sanctions and a plan for compensation would be part of the final deal, and negotiations would address frozen assets.

The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said on Saturday that they were close to reaching an agreement on navigation, “specifically the determination of a transit route”. But the waterway’s reopening is contingent on other conditions, he said, in remarks shared on social media, and blamed the situation on what he called the US violation of the interim deal.

Oman, which is mediating and has made relatively few comments on the talks, said in a statement on Saturday that the discussions were continuing “in a positive and constructive atmosphere”, and condemned attacks on ships on the strait.

Iran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait and wants to charge users for passage, repeatedly attacking ships it accuses of attempting to circumvent its preferred route.

The US opposes any Iranian tolls in the strait, though the June deal allows Tehran to hammer out arrangements for the “future administration” of Hormuz in conjunction with fellow coastal state Oman.

The 60-day period to negotiate a final deal will end in just over a week but could be extended.

Iran has said it was close to reaching a separate deal with Oman to manage the strait, which runs between the two countries.

Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian, a relative moderate, said he believed now was the best time for an agreement.

“There is cohesion, strength, and unity in the country, and as far as I know, Iran is considered victorious and powerful in this war,” Iranian news agencies quoted him as saying.

Continued attacks in the strait, which was free to sail through before the war, led to the collapse of an April ceasefire, and mediators have since urged both sides to return to the terms of the June memorandum.

The strait, which is crucial to global supplies of oil and natural gas, had been considered an international waterway before the war. Ship transits remain low.

Meanwhile, a vessel owned by Abu Dhabi’s state-owned Adnoc oil and gas company was attacked while sailing through the strait of Hormuz, Emirati authorities said earlier on Saturday. The foreign ministry said Iran fired the missile as part of attacks on commercial shipping.

Adnoc said in a statement that there were no casualties following the attack early on Saturday. The company said more than a dozen of its vessels have been attacked by missiles and drones while using the strait since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February. One crew member has been killed and 20 others wounded, it said.

Adnoc did not elaborate on the location of the attack or any damage.

Later, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre said a vessel east of the town of Khasab, Oman had been struck by a projectile that caused a fire that was put out, and the vessel and crew were safe. It was not clear whether this was the Adnoc incident.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.summary: Tehran urges US to ‘correct its behaviour’ as UAE says one of its ships was targeted by Iranian missile. The US must lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports and withdraw its military from the area. The United Arab Emirates says one ship was targeted as a deal to open the strategic waterway remained out of reach

https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.title: Bluster and backdown have turned Iran war into Trump’s own Groundhog Day
https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.author: Robert Tait in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.text:
The US president’s profound ignorance of his enemy has led to an impotent cycle of empty threats, analysts say

Being the subject of mockery may be the most intense of all Donald Trump’s known aversions.

Yet more than five months after embarking on a war of choice against Iran, the US president risks attracting ridicule as he struggles to secure a military victory – while repeatedly threatening devastating bombardment against the Tehran regime, only to back down on the pretext of renewed negotiations.

Critics suggest the ultimatum-climbdown sequence has acquired a Groundhog Day quality. By one count, he has adopted the same tactic seven times since launching the war in tandem with Israel on 28 February.

Last weekend saw the latest episode, as Trump told reporters onboard Air Force One that he had suddenly called off “a massive” attack that he said would have been “the biggest since world war two” after an appeal from US allies and because “I think there’s a deal”.

Despite negotiations between Iran and Oman over shipping in the strait of Hormuz, no deal has thus far materialized, and the strategically vital waterway – conduit to a fifth of the world’s oil supply before the war – remains closed.

The pattern resembled one that unfolded on a string of other occasions – including Trump’s memorably dire threat in April that Iranian “civilization will die tonight” unless Tehran capitulated to his demands only to retreat at the 11th hour and agree to a ceasefire.

The US president has also claimed multiple times that the US has “virtually” won the war and that Iran’s regime was clamoring for a deal.

Increasingly, such claims are prompting ridicule.

A recent CNN montage showed 14 separate pieces of footage dating back to March, with Trump insisting peace was at hand because Iran’s leaders “want to make a deal” after being supposedly rendered militarily impotent – assertions belied by a continuing Iranian ability to inflict damage on US and allied targets in the Middle East.

The veteran British journalist and commentator Andrew Neil pilloried Trump’s boasts as worthy of the Nobel peace prize he is known to covet.

“He, in the past five months, has brought peace to the Iran war eight times,” Neil said sarcastically on Times Radio. “What more do you have to do to merit a Nobel peace prize?”

He added: “We waste our time even analyzing it, because it’s either meaningless, or he’s done a U-turn on it within 24 hours … You might as well read the shipping forecasts.”

Trump’s wildly zigzagging messaging on the war betrays an absence of strategy and a profound ignorance of his enemy, analysts say – and threatens to deliver an electoral disaster in November’s US congressional midterms.

Mehrzad Boroujerdi, vice-provost and a political scientist at Missouri Science and Technology University, believes the US president’s failure to understand the individuals leading Iran’s authoritarian Islamic system has misled him into a dead end of ineffective and counterproductive threats.

“One of the most terrible mistakes that Trump made was invoking this type of a language,” said Boroujerdi, who argued that regimes who come into being through mass revolutions such as the one in 1979 that swept Iranian revolutionaries to power are much harder to topple than other governments.

“First, these are not people who are going to bend the knee,” he said. “Second, you have just killed the top of their leadership (including the former supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei). Their psychology is only an invitation for Trump to become more aggressive.”

Boroujerdi made it his life’s mission to understand the motivations of the men inside the Islamic regime after his father, Malek-Mohammad Boroujerdi, a senior executive with the national oil company, was assassinated by an Islamist guerrilla group in December 1978, on the eve of the revolution that overthrew the western-backed monarch, Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.

He kept his personal stake in scrutinizing the regime under wraps, lest it be seen as impairing the impartiality of his academic studies

Nearly half a century later, key members of the group, the Mansouroun, occupy some of the regime’s most sensitive military posts. They include Mohammad Baqer Zolqadr, secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, and Mohsen Rezaei, the founding commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, who is now military adviser to the present supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, whose father was killed in an Israeli military strike at the start of the war.

Having compiled over two decades a vast database of about 2,700 members of the country’s elite, Boroujerdi has co-authored a 900-page book, Post Revolutionary Iran: A Political Handbook, that puts its political leadership under the microscope.

Understanding it helps to explain how the outwardly ramshackle regime has withstood US hostility, international sanctions, diplomatic isolation and periods of war over 47 years all while staying resilient, he argued.

“I have looked at their nepotism ties, who is connected to whom,” said Boroujerdi. “These are folks who came from very modest backgrounds. They are predominantly the sons of farmers, peasants. And then secondly, clerics, who basically enjoyed social mobility thanks to the revolution.

“These were mister nobodies who became mister somebodies thanks to the revolution. And therefore, their attachment to this system and wanting to defend this system makes absolute sense because they owe everything they have currently, their whole career, to what this revolution has given them.

“If we want to understand Iran’s resilience, its performance, we need to better understand the psychology and upbringing of these individuals. But that requires serious work that the political class in Washington isn’t necessarily interested in.”

Having not undertaken such work, Trump has been reduced to railing in frustration at a regime whose defiance is a source of confusion and bewilderment to him.

After a ceasefire agreed in June collapsed over differing interpretations of a memorandum of understanding Trump had signed in the Palace of Versailles, he shocked fellow attenders at last month’s Nato summit in Ankara by calling Iran’s leaders “scum”.

“All they do is make me angry,” he told reporters, while also calling their behavior “unbelievably duplicitous”.

Such incomprehension means Trump’s pattern of ultimately unfulfilled blood-curdling threats is likely to continue, according to Boroujerdi. Other seasoned Iran observers agree.

Ali Vaez, the International Crisis Group’s deputy program director for the Middle East and north Africa, called explaining Trump’s approach in strategic terms “an impossible task” and lamented what he called the lack of a clear policy process in the current administration.

But he also said Iran’s leaders had strengthened their negotiating position in the strait of Hormuz since the collapse of the June ceasefire, while triggering a painful debate in Washington about military choices after recent strikes on a US base in Jordan that killed three US service personnel.

The possibilities for a renewed military onslaught against Iranian targets are believed to be limited because of concerns that US missile and interceptor stockpiles have become depleted.

Trump’s approach “boils down to his frustration that he really doesn’t have any good military options in front of him”, suggested Vaez. “A lot of it is emotional reactions, like when he does a deal with Iran that produces a political backlash, even among Republicans.

“That criticism gets under his skin, so he tries to extract better terms from Iran by bombing them. But when he ends up in an even worse position, he returns to the negotiating table and tries to pursue a diplomatic solution.

“This war started based on a lot of misguided assumptions, which are a clear reminder that half the battle is understanding your enemy – and clearly, President Trump and his administration didn’t understand the enemy.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Israel indicts settler over death of Palestinian activist who worked on No Other Land
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Yinon Levy charged with manslaughter in first exception this decade to culture of impunity for Israelis who kill Palestinians in the occupied West Bank

Prosecutors in Israel have indicted an extremist settler for shooting a Palestinian activist last July, the first attempt this decade to hold an Israeli responsible for killing a Palestinian in the occupied West Bank.

Yinon Levy, who was under western sanctions, is charged with manslaughter over the death of Awdeh Hathaleen, an English teacher and peace activist. In his last moments, Hathaleen filmed the settler drawing his weapon and opening fire towards him.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Hathaleen’s family said Levy should have been charged with first-degree murder over the well-documented attack in the village of Umm al-Khair.

Reckless manslaughter carries a maximum prison sentence of 12 years, far less then murder.

“This was not an accident,” said his cousin Tarek Hathaleen. “Yinon Levy must be held fully accountable for Awdeh’s killing.”

The charges nevertheless represented a “significant development”, Hathaleen added, after years of near-total impunity for Israelis who attack Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Israeli settlers and soldiers have killed more than 1,500 Palestinians this decade, according to rights group B’tselem. Levy is the first person indicted over any of those deaths.

Military prosecutors last brought charges over a 2019 shooting of a young man who stopped to help victims of a traffic accidentThe last time civilian prosecutors brought charges was in 2018 over the killing of a mother of eight, hit by a rock as she was driving.

Settler violence and ethnic cleansing has surged in the occupied West Bank over the past three years, supported by far-right Israeli cabinet ministers who hold security, defence and finance portfolios.

Levy’s indictment over one of the highest-profile killings in that period does not represent a policy shift for Israel, rights groups said.

Hathaleen had worked on No Other Land, the Oscar-winning documentary about his community’s decades-long struggle against the Israeli state and settlers, to stay in their homes and lands in the south Hebron hills.

“It’s important to see this killing as part of an ongoing and systematic situation in the West Bank,” said Ziv Stahl, executive director of Yesh Din, an Israeli rights and advocacy organisation.

“I don’t think these charges are an indication of increased law enforcement or accountability. It is more likely due to the fact that [Awdeh Hathaleen] was a well-known activist and the case got a lot of media exposure and public critique. It’s more about an appearance of law enforcement, rather than actual law enforcement.”

Levy, who was under sanctions for violence against Palestinians by the UK, EU, Canada and Australia at the time of the attack, was briefly detained last year but police released him after three days under house arrest.

He spent the last year free and continued establishing illegal outposts in the occupied West Bank, said Yair Dvir, spokesperson for B’tselem.

“The decision to indict Yinon Levy is the exception that proves the rule,” Dvir said. “The impunity Israel grants to soldiers and settlers who harm Palestinians is not a failure of the system – it is a central component of a policy designed to allow the violence to continue and escalate.”

The culture of impunity spurred the former Israeli prime minister Ehud Olmert to call for the International Criminal Court to bring charges against “Jewish terrorists”, saying intervention was needed to halt the violence.

Levy is also charged with armed trespassing and malicious property damage in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair.

Before Hathaleen was shot, another settler drove a bulldozer through Palestinian land, destroying trees and property. When a resident approached and asked him to stop, the driver knocked the man down with the bulldozer blade.

Even if the case goes to trial, any verdict could be many years away, and Israeli judges have a record of lenient treatment of Israelis who attack Palestinians.

The Israeli soldier who shot 23-year-old Ahmad Manasrah dead in 2019 pleaded guilty to the equivalent of negligent homicide and was sentenced to three months community service for the killing. He has not been publicly named.

Eight years after a 2018 attack that killed 47 year-old Aisha Rabi, an Israeli court ruled that a settler had thrown the stone that killed her.

Judges did not hand down a conviction or sentence, instead ordering a review because the man, who was not named, was 16 at the time of the attack. No further details have been made public.

Hathaleen’s family say they will continue to fight for Levy to face full trial. “Justice requires more than simply bringing a charge,” said Tarek Hathaleen. “Awdeh was not only my cousin. He was my childhood friend and someone very dear to me. His absence has left a pain that will never go away.”

Sufian Taha contributed reporting
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.summary: Yinon Levy charged with manslaughter over death of Awdeh Hathaleen. In his last moments, Hathalean filmed settler drawing weapon and opening fire towards him. He was under western sanctions for violence against Palestinians by the UK, EU, Canada and Australia at the time of the attack.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Iran plots to deal Trump a blow in midterms by keeping him entangled in war
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
By dragging out talks, Tehran aims to damage the US president politically – but some fear a bruised and weakened Trump could lash back

Tehran has set out a protracted negotiating timetable designed to keep Donald Trump embroiled in the Iran conflict until the midterm elections, in the hope of inflicting the same ruinous blow on his presidency as Jimmy Carter suffered over the 1979-81 US embassy hostage crisis.

For many inside Iran, inflicting meaningful revenge on Trump is a legitimate and self-standing war aim, reflected in the mood of those attending the funeral of the supreme leader Ali Khamenei where demands for retribution were ubiquitous.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

While Iranian officials since the 1979 Islamic revolution have never trusted the US, that animus is now also directed personally towards Trump. He not only tore up the painfully negotiated nuclear deal in 2018, but he sanctioned the assassination of the military leader Qassem Suleimani and twice involved Iran in negotiations on its nuclear programme only to launch wars against it. He shows no remorse for the killing of the country’s supreme leader, or for the attempt on the life of Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian.

As the countdown to November’s midterms begins, what could be Trump’s political demise has become a subject of obsessive speculation in Tehran. Iranian media track the US president’s waning ratings, attributing the decline to the war’s unpopularity and high oil prices. The changing politics of the Democrats is minutely examined.

But the focus on the midterms became more obvious this week when the deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, told the official IRNA news agency that after agreeing a route for commercial shipping through the strait of Hormuz, it would take two to four months to reach the second phase of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme. The original plan – to commence the nuclear phase of the talks within 30 days of signing June’s memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the US – had been jettisoned by the Trump administration, Gharibabadi said.

To get to that second stage, he laid out an obstacle course including the lifting of sanctions, the end of the US blockade of Iranian ports, the unfreezing of Iranian assets and new commitments on non-belligerence in a process that could last well beyond the midterms.

If Tehran gets its way on this timetable, Trump will be going to the polls with no Iranian commitment on nuclear weapons, only a hefty economic bill for a failed war. “This raises the very likely scenario of continued cycles of conflict between the US and Tehran over the strait,” said Jason Brodsky from United against a Nuclear Iran, an advocate of the war. “There won’t be any true quiet before the midterm elections – Tehran has no interest in giving this to the Trump administration … It will continue to play games.”

Mehr News, an agency close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, published a piece saying Iran had given Trump a major dilemma. “Continuing the war could increase political and economic pressure on the government and exacerbate the decline in his popularity. On the other hand, backing down, or moving towards reducing tensions, could also be interpreted by some of Trump’s supporters as a retreat from his campaign slogans,” it said.

From this perspective, the outcome of this war will not be played out on the battlefield, but at the ballot box. The agency suggested the outcome could affect the course of American domestic and foreign policy for years to come.

Few in Iran take Trump’s statements at face value. But his denials that the midterms affect his Iran strategy are treated with special scepticism. Iranian media point to comments from Marc Zell, chair of Republicans Overseas Israel, who has said: “It’s all about the midterms … the American public simply is tired of war and the administration is navigating the pre-election waters adroitly in order to avoid a Democratic takeover of Congress.”

Such remarks fuel the debate inside Iran about how much the midterms should be part of Iran’s calculus. Some believe the loss of Congress will inhibit Trump or lead to his impeachment; at the very least, it may mark the end of the war’s funding. Mostafa Zahrani, a former Iranian diplomat, argued electoral defeat “will make it inevitable that Trump will not be able to go back to war and will take the negotiations seriously”.

Others such as Nasser Hadian, a professor of international relations at Tehran University, disagree, advocating cashing in on Iran’s victories now rather than waiting for Trump to become weaker. “If he loses, he’ll have less incentive to reach an agreement with Iran, because in that case he’ll be weakened, and Israel and others will find it much easier to attack him – something they don’t dare do now,” he said. “Those who say we should wait for the midterm elections have no understanding of politics in America.”

Iran’s pleasure in seeing Trump defeated would indeed be reduced if he felt he had nothing left to lose, but its diplomats overall believe the US president’s freedom to act will be constrained by the unpopularity of more conflict and by Republican presidential candidates’ anxiety to wrap this up. Trump would also be at risk of seeing his whole second term consumed by a disastrous war.

Sign up to First Thing

Our US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

The bigger question is what Iran itself wants to achieve. Agreeing to keep the dispute simmering until November is not an answer to that question – one that Iranians are better at debating than resolving.

Pezeshkian, working in alliance with Mohammad Ghalibaf, the chief negotiator, repeatedly says he does not want endless war, and insists that almost all the supreme national security council concur. He still has faith in the MoU, saying it should be the cornerstone of Iran’s foreign policy.

But the conservative newspaper Kayhan describes the memorandum as worthless since the US always breaks its commitments. “Accordingly, officials should know that the strait of Hormuz is not a bargaining chip and should not be opened as a passage for America,” it said.

Both hardliners and moderates envision the war leading to a new regional security architecture. But the hardliners put the emphasis on America’s expulsion and see this as something less to be negotiated and more to be enforced using control of the entry points to the strait of Hormuz as a lever to close US bases.

Pezeshkian says he sees a place for legitimate US investment in Iran, while the former foreign minister Javad Zarif, in an essay this week, argued Iran in “a post-polar era would benefit from not depending solely on Russia and China in future”.

If Iran developed “a balanced and multifaceted foreign policy”, Tehran would not be forced into relationships based on necessity, he wrote. “Continuing uncontrolled tensions with the United States not only imposes direct costs on Iran, but also makes it more difficult for other countries, even close partners such as China and Russia, to cooperate with Iran.”

Just as Trump cannot resolve from one sentence to the next what he thinks of Iran, nor can Iran agree what it thinks it can get from America.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.summary: Iran wants the US to leave the country until November. Iran wants to achieve what it wants to do with the US. The dispute has been simmering for months.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.title: Iran says a deal with Oman to reopen the strait of Hormuz is close to being finalised – as it happened
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.author: Lucy Campbell, Vivian Ho and Taz Ali
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text:
Welcome to our live coverage of the latest in the ongoing Middle East crisis.

Iran said a deal with Oman to reopen the strait of Hormuz is close to being finalised, with reports suggesting Tehran would have control over ships entering the Gulf through the strategic waterway.

Both countries, which sit on opposite ends of the narrow strait, have been engaged in talks to jointly manage the key shipping route, which has been effectively closed since the start of the war in February. Iran has insisted the strait would not operate as it did before the conflict, as an open international waterway that carried about a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply, as it seeks greater control over the flow of maritime traffic through the channel. Several media reports, citing sources familiar with the talks, suggest Oman would oversee outbound shipping through the strait.

But despite reports of potentially one of the biggest concessions yet to Iran, Reuters news agency said Iranian sources ⁠rejected US President Donald Trump’s claims that a deal to reopen the strait was imminent, saying important details ​were still to be agreed.

“The concession has already been made regarding some form of control over Hormuz,” one of the sources said.

Iran has also said that reopening the strait would hinge on the US lifting its blockade of Iranian ports.

Trump told Fox News earlier this week that talks over the strait were “moving along nicely”, adding that the strait “is going to be open very soon”.

There were three days of talks in Rome, the second of which was cut short after Israel resumed heavy strikes on southern Lebanon on Wednesday, accusing Hezbollah of violating the fragile ceasefire agreement initially agreed upon on 26 June.

But as the United Nations and local authorities have noted, Israel had continued to launch periodic airstrikes, shelling, and demolitions in the areas of southern Lebanon it’s occupying, despite the truce, killing more than 350 people.

The renewed Israeli attacks came as hundreds thousands of displaced people had begun returning to their homes in southern Lebanon, only to be forced to flee again under new orders from the IDF.

Dhaka accuses India of giving platform to a ‘convicted genocider’ by allowing Sheikh Hasina to address journalists

Bangladesh has lashed out at India for allowing the ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina to address journalists in New Delhi, plunging already strained bilateral relations to a fresh low.

Dhaka accused India of giving a platform to a fugitive it labelled a “convicted genocider” and of undermining efforts to repair ties, after Hasina vowed to return to Bangladesh in December despite facing a death sentence on charges of “crimes against humanity”.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The angry response late on Wednesday came hours after Hasina, speaking on the second anniversary of the massive student-led uprising that led to her flight to India, declared: “Whatever fate awaits me, I will return to my people.”

Bangladesh’s foreign ministry said it was “outraged” Hasina had been allowed to participate in the event, where it said she and her allies launched “venomous vitriol” against Bangladesh and its people.

“This interaction by Hasina on Indian soil stands as an affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh,” the ministry said. Dhaka also renewed its demands for India to extradite Hasina.

India earlier distanced itself from the news conference – Hasina’s first since fleeing Bangladesh in 2024, saying it had no role in organising it and would not endorse any political views voiced.

Hasina said she was ready to face whatever fate awaited her in Bangladesh, where her Awami League party is now banned. “They may put me in a cell. They may kill me. Anything may happen, but I still have to go,” the 78-year-old said via audio link.

“My life moved beyond calculations of personal safety long ago.”

After 15 years in power, Hasina fled to India in 2024 following weeks of student-led protests. Her government was accused of misusing state institutions to entrench its hold on power and stamp out dissent, including through the killing of opposition activists.

In her speech, she dismissed criminal cases against her as politically motivated and accused Bangladesh’s new government, led by Tarique Rahman, of economic mismanagement, political repression and persecution of her supporters.

Hasina was sentenced in absentia to death by hanging over her government’s deadly crackdown on the uprising. She said she wanted to return in December because it marked Bangladesh’s “month of victory”, commemorating Pakistan’s defeat in the 1971 independence war.

She claimed thousands of Awami League activists had been killed or jailed since her downfall.

Her son Sajeeb Wazed Joy stoked the diplomatic row by extolling India’s hospitality. “She’s being treated very well and has been provided with the full services and security accorded to a head of state,” he said. “Prime Minister Modi’s government has shown her the utmost respect.”

Hasina was joined at the event by Shakib Al Hasan, a former national cricket captain. Hours later unidentified attackers hurled petrol bombs and smashed windows at his home in Bangladesh, but no one was hurt, police said. Shakib, elected to parliament as an Awami League candidate, has remained outside Bangladesh since Hasina’s overthrow.

Tarun Tejpal, ex-editor of Tehelka magazine, was initially acquitted in 2021 in case that drew nationwide attention

An Indian court has sentenced a high-profile former editor of an investigative news magazine to 10 years in prison after convicting him of raping a junior colleague, overturning his acquittal in a case that drew nationwide attention.

Tarun Tejpal, 63, the founder and former editor of Tehelka magazine, was accused of raping a journalist in the lift of a five-star hotel in the western coastal state of Goa during an event in November 2013. He was arrested and spent seven months in jail until the supreme court granted him bail.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

A court in Goa acquitted Tejpal of charges including rape, sexual harassment and wrongful restraint in 2021.

The government of Goa challenged the acquittal before the Bombay high court, which set aside the trial court’s verdict and sentenced him to 10 years in jail on Thursday.

“He has been convicted to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment. He has been given two weeks’ time to surrender,” the police investigator Sunita Sawant, who led the case against Tejpal, told reporters.

The court also ordered him to pay a £3,900 fine, he said.

Tejpal, 63, said he would challenge the conviction in the supreme court.

He had initially blamed the assault on “a lapse of judgement” but later alleged the case against him was part of a vendetta by the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) government in Goa.

“For the past 13 years, they have been pursuing me as a part of a political vendetta,” he said after conviction.

Sawant told reporters: “This is a sentence where a girl has stood up for her rights … so this judgment is very important for women who are working in any sector.”

The case emerged at a time when India’s handling of sexual assault cases was under intense scrutiny after the gang-rape and murder of a 23-year-old student on a Delhi bus in December 2012.

That attack triggered nationwide protests and international outrage, and prompted the government to strengthen the country’s rape laws.

Tejpal’s case severely damaged the authority and credibility of Tehelka, which had historically championed women’s rights and social justice.

The magazine continues to operate under new leadership, but it has failed to regain the influence it had before the 2013 case.

In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

Sheikh Hasina plans a December comeback two years after being ousted in a bloody uprising led by students

Bangladesh’s ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina has vowed to return home by the end of the year, even though she faces a death sentence.

“They may put me in a cell. They may kill me. Anything may happen, but still I have to go,” said Hasina, two years after a student-led uprising toppled her government.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Hasina, 78, who has lived under tight security in India since fleeing Dhaka, said on Wednesday she would return in December – Bangladesh’s “month of victory”, marking the defeat of Pakistani forces in the 1971 war of independence.

“Whatever fate awaits me, I will return to my people,” the former Awami League leader told a news conference at the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia in Delhi, speaking via audio link.

Her son, Sajeeb Wazed Joy, told the news conference she was being treated well in exile.

“She is staying with the full services and security of a head of state,” he said. “Prime minister [Narendra] Modi’s government has shown her the utmost respect, and for that I am eternally grateful.”

India officially distanced itself from the news conference, saying it had no role in organising it and did not endorse the political views expressed.

India has been walking a diplomatic tightrope over Hasina, who was one of its closest regional allies. Bilateral ties have deteriorated sharply since her downfall and India has been seeking to mend relations with Bangladesh while resisting demands for her extradition.

Hasina’s flight ended more than 15 years of increasingly authoritarian Awami League rule. The Bangladesh Nationalist party, led by Tarique Rahman, the son of the former prime minister Khaleda Zia, swept to power earlier this year in an election that barred the Awami League. The government has said Hasina would probably be arrested the moment she set foot in Bangladesh.

Last November, Bangladesh’s international crimes tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over the violent suppression of the protests. The demonstrations began over government-job quotas and snowballed into a mass movement against Hasina’s government.

The UN estimates up to 1,400 people may have died. Hasina’s supporters say the death toll was about 800. She has rejected the court’s verdict as politically motivated and said the execution threat would not change her plans.

Hasina was imprisoned several times during her fierce rivalry with Zia, who died in 2025. The two women traded claims of using corruption cases and arrests against each other in a “Battle of the Begums”, an honorific title for a senior woman.

Bangladesh has prohibited domestic media from broadcasting or publishing Hasina’s statements. She has demanded that the ban on the Awami League be lifted, political prisoners be released and “false cases” against party activists be dropped.

Claiming Bangladesh is sinking into lawlessness and economic ruin, she accuses the new government of trying to erase the country’s secular character.

The government has been grappling with high inflation and sluggish economic growth while blaming many of the country’s problems on alleged corruption and mismanagement during Hasina’s years in power.

She was ousted in a bloody uprising led by students led by the Awami League. She faces a death sentence for crimes against humanity over the violent suppression of the protests.

Rules brought in soon after killing of dozens of protesters, news of which was reported only by overseas outlets

Pakistani authorities have imposed severe new restrictions on international media, including barring them from reporting in most of the country, in a move that has provoked a significant backlash from journalist organisations.

According to the new rules anyone, including Pakistani nationals, should seek permission first if they want to report from anywhere in Pakistan except three cities – Islamabad, Karachi and Lahore.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Pakistan is ranked 153 out of 180 on the World Press Freedom Index. Successive regimes there have imposed restrictions and censorship on local media. But this is the first time they have put restrictions on international media.

The sudden announcement of new rules came after the killing of dozens of protesters in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, which was only reported by international media.

Al Jazeera’s website was restricted in Pakistan after it reported on the bloody protests and the news that people were boycotting regional elections from Muzaffarabad, the capital of Pakistan’s Kashmir.

Pakistan’s information ministry derided Al Jazeera’s reporting as “yellow journalism”, a derogatory term used for sensationalised reporting.

Authorities have not publicly announced a ban of the news website, but it remains inaccessible without a VPN.

The BBC reported from Pakistan-administered Kashmir and quoted protesters and people who accused Pakistani security forces of firing at unarmed protesters. Pakistani authorities issued a strongly worded denial and asked all journalists to immediately leave Kashmir.

The new rules, which the ministry of information called the Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines 2026, do not specify a timeframe for how long it would take for journalists to be granted permission to report.

Nasir Zaidi, a former general secretary at the Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists and a senior journalist, said that international media has been objectively reporting on protest movements, crackdowns on opposition parties and the repressive political situation in Pakistan.

“For decades, various governments have always tried to kill the news and they failed because of the reporting of international media and now it came up with these repressive rules to curb the movement of journalists. They don’t want the truth to be reported,” said Zaidi.

The government denies that the new rules are a blanket restriction on the movement of journalists or constrict media.

Zaidi, who was subjected to public flogging during the military dictatorship of Gen Zia ul-Haq for raising his voice for media rights, said that he had never witnessed such times before.

“Despite the fact I have worked during martial laws, but, such curbs and restrictions on international media were unseen. It is worse than martial law,” he added.

According to the new guidelines, the accreditation and registration is mandatory for international media outlets and journalists in the country.

The new rules also state that journalists can lose their accreditation for “acts against ideology, sovereignty, security or public order of Pakistan”.

Legal experts and journalists have said that these stipulations are vague and difficult to interpret.

“Pakistan is sending a very wrong message to the world with all these rules curbing free speech and freedom of international media,” said Zaidi.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.summary: Pakistani authorities have imposed severe new restrictions on international media. The new rules do not specify a timeframe for how long it would take for journalists to be granted permission to report. The move has provoked a significant backlash from journalist organisations.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Pakistan precinct suspends all 78 officers and staff over alleged rape at police station
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Haroon Janjua in Islamabad
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Lahore police official says all personnel were responsible for preventing and reporting any wrongdoing at station

The alleged rape of a 20-year-old woman with learning disabilities in a police station in Lahore, Pakistan, has prompted authorities to suspend all 78 police officers and staff at the precinct, in one of the country’s biggest ever disciplinary actions against its police force.

The woman alleges that an assistant sub-inspector apprehended her, took her to Ghaziabad police station and raped her in a room on the second floor. The woman’s family said she disappeared on the street, before returning home in tears and stating that she had been sexually assaulted at the station.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The accused officer has been arrested and is now facing a criminal investigation for rape. All 78 police officials and staff members of Lahore’s Ghaziabad police station were suspended on Tuesday.

Lahore’s deputy inspector general of police (operations), Faisal Kamran, told the Guardian that the officers were suspended because, under police rules, all personnel were responsible for preventing and reporting any wrongdoing within the station and they had failed to do so.

“No officer questioned why the assistant sub-inspector had brought the woman to the station without any female police personnel present,” Kamran said.

“I suspended all 78 police officials, and the gender crime wing is investigating the case, and we will dismiss the culprits, and we will ensure the safety of all police stations in the city,” he added.

The case has sparked outrage in Pakistan, where rights groups have long claimed many women are reluctant to report sexual violence because of stigma and a lack of confidence in law enforcement. Allegations of misconduct by police officers have further eroded public trust, activists say.

“This is an extremely disturbing incident and reflects the longstanding lack of accountability within the police,” said Farzana Bari, a women’s rights activist. “It is a stark example of the abuse of power. Allegations of police misconduct and custodial rape are not new, and we have seen such cases over the years.

“We campaigned relentlessly in the 1990s for women’s police stations because survivors often did not feel safe reporting abuse to male officers. While the police’s record on protecting women remains poor, the fact that this case has been reported offers some hope that justice will be served.”

Convictions for rape remain rare despite legal reforms in recent years. The Sustainable Social Development Organisation said the national conviction rate was about 0.5% in 2024, while official data showed the rate in Punjab, where the incident occurred, was 4% in 2025.

Rights groups attribute the low rates to weak investigations, poor evidence collection, delays in prosecutions and the stigma surrounding sexual violence.

According to police data, there were more than 20,000 crimes against women in Punjab province in the first half of 2026, up from the same period in 2025.

“Unless state institutions are held accountable, such crimes will continue. What is needed is structural reform and stronger oversight to ensure justice for ordinary people,” Bari said.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.summary: All 78 police officers and staff members of Ghaziabad police station in Lahore, Pakistan, were suspended on Tuesday. Alleged rape of 20-year-old woman with learning disabilities in police station. Woman's family said she disappeared on the street, before returning home in tears and stating she had been sexually assaulted at the station

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Andy Burham to tour Britain in effort to reconnect government with public
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Raphael Boyd
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
PM expected to announce policies to tackle cost of living and indicate intent to help improve country’s high streets

Andy Burnham is to undertake a national tour this coming week as he aims to improve the government’s connection with the British public during his premiership.

The prime minister is expected to announce a set of policies that will help people financially as many struggle with the cost of living, as well as indicate his intent to improve high streets across the country.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Burnham has previously given the public “breathing space” since succeeding Keir Starmer in the role last month, but is said to be in “listening mode” as he tours Britain and pushes his “10-year plan to bring back hope”.

While an official itinerary has yet to be released by Downing Street, the prime minister is expected to visit areas where Labour has lost support in the last decade, as well as areas hit by declining industry.

Port Talbot in south Wales, which is home to the largest steelworks in the UK, is likely to be one of the stops given the closure of its final blast furnace in 2024.

A spokesperson for Burnham said: “He thinks Westminster has got used to telling people that everyday hassles – like hidden pricing and consumers being ripped off – must be accepted as part of life. He doesn’t think that’s right. That’s why he’s going to start rolling out a series of pro-consumer cost of living measures to give people some room to breathe.”

With the fallout of the Iran war keeping inflation higher than expected, the cost of living remains a big concern among the public. A poll published by Ipsos at the end of July found 30% of people listed the economy as a leading concern while 22% listed inflation or prices specifically.

But opposition figures have accused Burnham of “tinkering” with his announcements. The shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, accused the prime minister of “breathtaking hypocrisy”and claimed that Labour was “hammering our high streets” by forcing businesses to close with the party’s “red tape” policies.

The Tory MP also accused the government of “plotting to release dangerous criminals on to our streets”.

Stride added: “If Burnham is really serious about cutting the cost of living, he should adopt our plan for stronger high streets – including scrapping business rates for thousands of high street firms. And if he wants people to feel proud of the places where they live, he should scrap his disastrous plans to let vile criminals walk free.”

Reform UK’s Treasury spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, said Burnham should scrap green levies and taxes on energy bills. He added: “It’s high time the Labour party cut the ballooning benefits bill so we can relieve pressure on the hard-working majority that hold our country together.”

The Liberal Democrats’ Treasury spokesperson, Daisy Cooper, echoed Stride’s criticisms regarding bureaucracy and accused the prime minister of “embarking on a vanity tour this summer”.
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.summary: Andy Burnham expected to announce policies to tackle cost of living and indicate intent to improve high streets. PM expected to visit areas where Labour has lost support in the last decade.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Home Office ‘error’ leaves Italian man’s wife with no right to stay in UK
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Lisa O’Carroll
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Man is told he should not have been granted settled status so he can no longer sponsor Brazilian wife to remain

A 33-year-old Italian engineer who has been in London since 2018 has been plunged into a battle with the Home Office after officials told him they made a mistake allowing him to stay in the UK after Brexit.

Fabio, who initially came to London to finish his doctorate and who has built a successful career working on energy and climate change, says he is shocked by the development as he has not broken any rules since Brexit.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

He was given settled status under the EU settlement scheme, permanent residency given to qualifying EU citizens after five years in the UK.

The Home Office has now told him this was “in error” – and his wife, who he has been with since arriving in the UK, now has no right to remain as a qualifying family member of someone with settled status.

While officials told him he could remain in the UK as they would not be removing his settled status, despite their claim to have made a mistake, the consequence of their error is that his wife now has no right to be in the country with him.

“It was quite devastating for both of us. We have been here for a long time. We have done everything by the book, and we’ve always felt very welcome here and I always thought this is somewhere I could grow my career.

“It is so upsetting and frustrating to know that we are now in this vulnerable position just as we were thinking of building a family, buying a place for ourselves. Now all our plans must stop,” he said.

Fabio, whose name has been changed, is one of more than at least 100 individuals who have been contacted by the Home Office to say an “error” had been made in awarding them status under the EU settlement scheme.

The Home Office wrote to him in April as part of a review that appears to have been triggered by his Brazilian wife’s application for status under the EU settlement scheme.

He too was born in Brazil but is an Italian dual national by birth and provided a certificate to demonstrate this from the Italian consulate in his settled status application.

Officials have now told him the evidence of his Italian citizenship was “insufficient”, and they needed proof that he was Italian before the Brexit cut-off date of 31 December 2020.

“It has therefore been decided that, on the basis of the information and evidence currently available, your settled status under the EU settlement scheme was granted in error,” the Home Office said.

It added he was no longer “relevant EEA citizen” and he would therefore not be able to sponsor a family member, his wife, to remain in the UK.

Catherine Barnard, professor of EU law at the University of Cambridge, said she was astonished by his case, which suggested the Home Office was creating a two-tier system.

“This appears to be contrary to the withdrawal agreement on the basis of which his rights were granted. The Home Office cannot punish him by saying he has only second-class rights and, in particular, that he doesn’t have family rights so long as he retains settled status,” she said.

She points to article 13 (4) of chapter two of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, which states “the host state may not impose any limitations or conditions for obtaining, retaining or losing residence rights”.

The Home Office has contacted at least 100 people, but possibly many more, to tell them they made “an error” in awarding status.

Monique Hawkins, acting chief executive of the3million, said stripping people of rights in such a way would affect “whole families” as people faced a “cliff-edge loss of their rights” without any of the “proportionality assessment” required under the withdrawal agreement.

The Independent Monitoring Authority, the statutory body set up to implement the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, has also said it is worried that the Home Office moves “may be incompatible with the EU withdrawal agreement”.

It has written to the Home Office to raise “discretionary decisions” about the original applications for post-Brexit residency being made by caseworkers revisiting historic decisions.

It has asked any EU citizen who is experiencing difficulties to contact them.

Mala Savjani, partner at Wilson Solicitors in London, which is acting for Fabio, said it was “not clear why” the government was “targeting EU nationals who have dual nationality”.

She added: “In order to come to its conclusions, the Home Office is having to make, sometimes unverified, assertions about complex areas of other EU member states’ nationality laws. It is not evident what the policy objective is.”

The Home Office said: “It is longstanding government policy that we do not routinely comment on individual cases.”

However, officials said the case was “not a breach of the withdrawal agreement” and “those who have been granted EU settlement scheme (EUSS) status in error are not withdrawal agreement beneficiaries and, unless they can [provide] evidence they meet the requirements for that status, have no basis of qualification under the EUSS”.
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.summary: Italian engineer Fabio, 33, has been in London since 2018 and has been working on energy and climate change. He was given settled status under the EU settlement scheme. But he was told he could remain in the UK as they would not be removing his settled status. https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/a.title: Where are the Ugandan boxers? Four are latest athletes to vanish after UK sports events
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/a.author: Robyn Vinter
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/a.text:
Team manager has ‘no idea’ why they disappeared, after reports one of Commonwealth Games athletes said they intended to claim asylum

Y
ears of arduous preparation and training had come to fruition and the pressure was finally lifted. After competing for their country in the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, athletes from Uganda were afforded a couple of days’ sightseeing time before catching their plane home on Tuesday.

But when the flight took off, there were four empty seats.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Only two of the team of six boxers returned to Uganda. Ibrahim Kemis, Emily Nakalema, Angel Katushabe and the captain, Nuhu Batte, were missing.

One of the athletes reportedly told the Ugandan news website NBS Sport they were intending to claim asylum in the UK where there are better training facilities. But the team manager for the Ugandan Commonwealth Games team told the BBC he had “absolutely no idea” what basis they would have for an asylum claim in the UK.

“It’s nothing political, it’s nothing to do with gender or something [like that] – I have absolutely no idea why they would be doing that,” said the team’s chef de mission, Godwin Kayangwe.

The first indication something was amiss was that their phones were turned off – against the rules of the Ugandan team camp, as athletes need permission to come and go. And then they vanished.

The Guardian understands the foursome were initially taken in by a boxing gym in Glasgow but are no longer in Scotland. The owner of the gym did not respond to queries about the missing boxers.

Kayangwe hoped they would make the “right decision” and return to Uganda.

The Pakistani boxer Qudratullah was also missing, having not joined his teammates on the flight home. He was not in his room when officials went to search for him.

The events have been the subject of gossip in the boxing world, with rumours abound that the Ugandans had paid money to a Scottish coach to help them disappear. One man involved in boxing, who did not want to be named, said he believed there was “something very, very suspicious going on” and that their location was a closely guarded secret..

Police Scotland said it had received reports of athletes not returning home and that it was working with the Home Office to assess the situation.

A Glasgow 2026 spokesperson said the organisers were working closely with authorities – including Police Scotland, Border Force and UK Visas & Immigration – to ensure that 3,000 athletes from 74 nations and territories could safely and securely participate.

This is not the first time athletes have disappeared after tournaments in the UK. The Home Office carries out enhanced checks on participants before big sporting events, due to how prevalent it is.

It is estimated 27 people did not leave after the Manchester Commonwealth Games in 2002, 66 after Glasgow 2014, and 17 after Birmingham in 2022. After the 2012 Olympics in London, several athletes chose to stay. Tribunal decisions from asylum applications show a number of people, including athletes from Cameroon and Sudan, and the Ethiopian Olympic flag bearer, all attempted to claim asylum in the UK.

The stories go back decades. More than 600 former East German athletes defected before the fall of the Berlin Wall, some of them exposing compulsory doping going on in their home country.

Pete Carvill, a boxing commentator and author, said there were many examples of boxers not going back to their home countries because it was possible to have a more lucrative career elsewhere.

“Most of the guys who do defect don’t make the best of the opportunity,” he said. “They leave behind the discipline of their amateur programmes and usually end up with lifestyle issues.”

He said they often “put weight on that is hard to take off, they begin drinking and partying, they stop training. A lot of them also get taken advantage of, signing contracts that they don’t understand and blowing the purses that they receive.”

There are examples of athletes who have stayed in the UK after big tournaments facing legal trouble. Last year, Philip Pariyo, a Ugandan rugby player who claimed asylum after the 2014 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, was imprisoned for raping a woman in Cardiff. A team Pakistan boxer, Nazeer Ullah Khan, was convicted of harassing a woman he met while working in a kebab shop after failing to return to his home country when the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham ended.

There are far more success stories, however. Many athletes have made a life in the UK and had families, and some still compete. Eritrean-born Weynay Ghebresilasie was the fastest Scottish man at the London Marathon this year, having claimed asylum and settled in Glasgow after the 2012 Olympics.

Cyrille Tchatchet, a Cameroonian-born weightlifter, won a silver medal for Team GB at the Commonwealth Games last week, 12 years after he refused to go back to his home country.

He disappeared after the 2014 Games, sleeping rough and eventually being granted refugee status in 2016. He told the BBC: “I remember talking to [my mum] when I left the Commonwealth village. I told her I didn’t have a place to go and she was very concerned.”

Tchatchet, who now works as a nurse in the West Midlands, said: “Going back to Glasgow, competing and actually winning a silver medal … I’m very, very proud and honoured to have been given this opportunity to represent England.”
