They were supposed to claim asylum in the UK where there are better training facilities. But they were not allowed to go and go, and their phones were turned off. They are believed to have been taken in by a boxing gym in Glasgow but are no longer

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: AI push is putting banks at mercy of tech firms, warns Moody’s
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Finance sector will gain from the tech but it will need substantial investment and create risks, says rating agency

The rating agency Moody’s has said the race to adopt AI is putting big banks at the mercy of a small group of Silicon Valley firms, leaving them vulnerable to widespread outages and price gouging by profit-hungry tech bosses.

The financial sector’s efforts to integrate AI into day-to-day operations will eventually cut costs and increase revenues across the City and Wall Street, Moody’s said.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

But that will require “substantial investments”, and with so many rivals racing towards the same goal, many of those benefits will end up being “competed away”.

AI will also create bigger risks around data privacy, cybersecurity, fraud and so-called “deposit flight”, as well as an overdependence on a small number of tech firms, the rating agency warned.

That will raise concerns for bosses across the financial sector. More than 75% of City companies now use AI, according to a UK Treasury select committee report published in January, with insurers and international banks among the biggest adopters. They are mostly using it to automate administrative tasks or even help with core operations, including processing insurance claims and assessing customers’ creditworthiness.

“The reliance of most financial firms on a relatively small set of foundation AI model and cloud computing providers risks creating a systemic dependency,” the Moody’s report said.

“This is because a model outage at one major provider could potentially spread quickly across customers and sectors. As AI adoption deepens, regulators may increase their focus on operational resilience and third-party concentration in the AI model stack.”

The AI race also risked creating “vendor dependence risk”, Moody’s said, meaning that “a set of dominant AI model and infrastructure providers could, over time, exert control over the price of AI services”. That issue is likely to emerge as the bosses of loss-making generative AI companies, including the ChatGPT creator OpenAI and the Claude owner Anthropic, come under pressure to deliver profits for investors.

“While this could pose credit risks to financial firms, they would nevertheless retain control over key assets, including proprietary data,” Moody’s said. Many big banks and insurers also have longstanding experience negotiating down tech contracts, and may be using open-source AI models, and striking key partnerships, to try to offset “dependency risks”.

Lloyds Banking Group’s chief executive, Charlie Nunn, recently doubled down on AI investment plans with a £13bn strategy that would involve using the technology to lure new business, improve efficiency and increase payouts for shareholders.

That will involve £2bn of cost cuts, which Nunn said would affect staff. “That is going to impact work. It is going to require us to continue to reskill people and hire new people, but that’s been my history for 30-odd years in financial services.”

Moody’s acknowledged the potential blow to some staff, who could be deemed replaceable as a result of new tech. Its report said there was a 20% chance that, by 2030, AI will be able to do the work of a “solid mid-level employee”.

For banks, AI might also make it easier for customers to switch to accounts offering higher interest rates, creating the possibility that large chunks of cash could be moved at short notice. “In this context, depositors’ trust in the institution and the resilience and stability of deposit funding are critical,” Moody’s said.

Financial sector's efforts to integrate AI into day-to-day operations will eventually cut costs and increase revenues. But that will require ‘substantial investments’ and many benefits will end up being ‘competed away’

https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/au.title: Sweet, soft and strong: TikTok turns Japanese milk bread into latest UK food craze
https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/au.author: Sarah Marsh Consumer affairs correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/au.text:
Natto toast, fresh fruit sandwiches and soufflé pancakes all part of growing interest in east Asian cuisine

Golden brown and glistening with melted butter, a tray of freshly baked bread fills the screen in a TikTok video. The camera lingers on the glossy tops before one bun is gently pulled apart, revealing a cloud-soft interior.

The clip is one of countless videos of Japanese milk buns that have racked up millions of views and thousands of comments and shares, helping to propel the pillowy rolls into UK supermarkets.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Japanese milk bread (shokupan) and buns are having a viral moment. The lightly sweet, fine-crumbed yeast breads trace their roots to a bakery tradition introduced to Japan through western contact, but modern Japanese milk bread evolved during the 20th century as bakers adapted European techniques to local tastes.

They are far from the only Japanese food to find global fame on social media. Japan’s deep-fried sandwiches have inspired queues around the block, while fluffy soufflé pancakes, delicate crepes and Japan’s distinctive fruit sando – fresh fruit and cream layered between slices of soft milk bread – have all found devoted followings online and beyond.

The growing appetite for Japanese cuisine is being reflected in supermarkets. Waitrose says sales of Miso Tasty ramen paste are up 41% compared with last year, while sales of Miso Tasty soup paste have increased by 22%.

But it is the rise of milk bread that Emilie Wolfman, the world foods product developer at Waitrose, said was “one of the most exciting food trends we’ve seen cross over from social media into mainstream kitchens”. Searches for “Japanese milk buns” on Waitrose’s website have risen by 617% over the past month, while sales are up 27% over the same period.

As well as their viral success online, Wolfman attributes the growing popularity of milk buns to “London’s cult burger restaurants and east Asian bakeries”.

Black Bear Burger, a London-based chain, has built a loyal following by serving its smash burgers and crispy fried chicken in soft milk buns. In London’s Chinatown, Bun House showcases Cantonese-style baked milk buns with both savoury and sweet fillings.

Outside the capital, Tomás Gormley, the chef-patron of Scottish fine dining restaurant Cardinal, said it opened with milk buns on the menu. “My first pastry chef, Mia, developed an incredible recipe that we still use today. We switch to sourdough every now and then to keep things interesting but always seem to end up back at the milk buns,” he said.

Gormley believes part of the appeal to chefs is how quickly and easily they can be made. “I have all the time in the world for slow-fermented sourdoughs and overnight focaccias, but logistically a bread you can bash out in a couple of hours is a winner in the kitchen,” he said. “It’s also usually less butter-heavy than the French equivalent, brioche, which helps with costs, but also with balancing a menu and how much a guest can really eat over the course of a tasting menu, in my case.”

Michael Booth, the author of Sushi and Beyond and The Meaning of Rice, said Japanese cuisine’s “huge focus on presentation, aesthetics” and social media were a perfect match, with the country having been ahead of the curve for at least a decade. “I can remember visiting a restaurant in Kyoto that was specifically tailored to presenting its food for social media,” he added.

Recipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every week

after newsletter promotion

Booth said he became “totally obsessed” with milk buns and Japanese baked goods when he first visited Japan in the 1990s. “They had long ago mastered that super-light crumb.”

The MasterChef winner and restaurateur Tim Anderson notes the huge variety of milk breads available in Japan, which range from mildly milky and sweet to those rich with eggs, butter, cream and honey that are more akin to brioche. “I think if British bakeries and supermarkets are trying to nail what makes milk bread special they should focus on the yudane and gluten development, which are what give milk bread its unique combination of strength and softness,” he added.

Anderson said he would recommend using it to make natto toast, which features fermented soya beans under a layer of crisp melted cheese. Failing that, it works well for an egg sandwich, or “pizza toast is fantastic”.

He added that in the US at the moment it was “peach and tomato season”, both of which would pair well with it. “A toasted nut butter and peach jam sandwich would be exquisite,” he said.

Use it with tomatoes in a bacon, lettuce and tomato sandwich with Kewpie mayo, thick-cut streaky bacon, iceberg lettuce and the best-quality tomatoes you can get,which should be “sliced thick, patted dry and pre-seasoned with sea salt and MSG [monosodium glutamate]”.
https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/au.summary: Japanese milk breads are having a viral moment in UK supermarkets. The lightly sweet, fine-crumbed yeast breads trace their roots to a bakery tradition introduced to Japan through western contact. They are far from the only Japanese food to find global fame on social media.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Plastics contamination an ‘overlooked’ concern in food waste schemes, experts say
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Ushika Kidd
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Researchers find microplastics can persist in compost, leaching into agricultural soils

Plastic contamination should be a central concern in efforts to deal with food waste, which campaigners call one of the most overlooked problems of the climate crisis, researchers have said.

This is despite the fact that, as the chef, author and activist Max La Manna puts it, food waste management is “one of the few climate problems where everyone wins”.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

About one-third of all food produced worldwide is wasted each year, according to UN data. In the US, 40% of food waste goes to landfill, where it creates 30m metric tonnes of CO2 equivalent a year – more than Cuba’s total annual CO2 emissions in 2024, which amounted to 24.4m tonnes.

A new study, published in Nature Food, used life-cycle analysis modelling to compare the impacts – in terms of climate, nutrient pollution and plastic contamination – of different food-waste management scenarios.

The authors, based at the University of Vermont, compared the annual climate impacts of landfilled food waste with the climate impact of alternative recycling pathways and found that diverting food waste from landfill would reduce climate impacts by between 89% and 99%.

These non-landfill scenarios could also reduce nutrient pollution in water bodies – a process called eutrophication that occurs when excess nutrients result in algal blooms.

But the researchers also said that microplastics can persist in compost, which could lead to 20,000 tonnes contaminating US agricultural soils each year. To date, no study has looked at the “plastic pollution footprint” of different food-waste management strategies at national scale.

Kate Porterfield, the lead author, said the method was comparable to working out a “carbon footprint of a product or process”. Essentially, the researchers looked at the process of managing food waste and “tall[ied] up what the carbon emissions are across all of those life-cycle stages”, she said.

Porterfield said the large proportion of wasted food still in packaging “goes bad before it even reaches the consumer”. One approach to recycling food waste is using a mechanical “depacker”; the packaging then goes to landfill, while food waste goes to “beneficial reuse, like composting or anaerobic digestion”.

However, they found that even if plastic separation technologies were 99% efficient, diverting food waste from landfill could still increase microplastic pollution in soil by an order of magnitude. “Any time where you’re diverting food waste, there is a risk of microplastic pollution” because “people aren’t perfect, machines aren’t perfect, and all of our food these days is packaged in plastic”.

The US state of Vermont has “one of the most ambitious” state organics-diversion mandates in the US, according to the co-author Eric Roy.

The state’s Universal Recycling Law has been fully effective from 2020 and requires food waste to be diverted from landfill. This applies to all households and means food scraps are banned from bins.

The authors said their findings provided an effective evaluation of the possible countrywide scale-up of such regulations and pointed to the need for “more attention to the plastics issue” from the outset of creating these policies.

Phil Holtam, a co-founder and director of the food waste social enterprise Sussex Surplus, said there was “a little bit of a misconception that [plastic packaging] is unnecessary”, and that it was a “necessary tradeoff”, essential to extending the shelf life of fresh produce, particularly for smallholder farms.

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

“That’s where the tension lies because as environmentalists we want to reduce food waste but we also want to prevent needless use of plastics.”

La Manna, who has worked with farmers in the UK and also witnessed food waste working in a Michelin-starred restaurant in New York, said consumer expectations of perfect-looking food were shaping what produce even made it to store shelves and adding to the waste problem. “Some of it may be misshapen, wonky, slightly cosmetically imperfect … [which is] challenging for supermarkets because they believe consumers want a perfect cucumber.

“We’re allowing ‘perfect’ to become this enemy of good.”

Roy underlined that in institutions such as schools, there “may be some well-intentioned rules that actually create challenges in moving away from highly packaged foods” because “food safety is always going to be a number one concern”.

Porterfield said that, ultimately, to reduce plastic contamination food waste management systems needed to be “as easy as possible to make it mindless for people to separate things efficiently”.

This included addressing the phenomenon of “wish recycling”, said Roy, where people put non-recyclable items in recycling in the hope they will be recycled.

He advised “old-school environmentalism” to reduce litter overall: “buy in bulk”, “make every effort to separate” – and “if in doubt, put it in the landfill stream”.

They found diverting food waste from landfill would reduce climate impacts by between 89% and 99%. The researchers also said that microplastic pollution can persist.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Pilots of helicopter that crashed while fighting Utah wildfire confirmed dead, officials say
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Officials did not identify the pilots but said they were employed by Helicopter Transport Services, which was contracted by US Forest Service

Two helicopter pilots who crashed while they were fighting a wildfire in Utah have died, officials confirmed Saturday. The pilots were killed when their Sikorsky Skycrane helicopter went down Friday morning, according to the Sevier County Sheriff.

The helicopter was among those fighting a fire in the Fishlake National Forest. The crash ignited a new fire that spread to connect with the existing blaze, which has now scorched nearly 174 square miles (nearly 451skm).

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Officials did not identify the pilots but said they were employed by Helicopter Transport Services, which was contracted by the US Forest Service.

Initially officials said they were unable to reach the crash site because of the fire. Then, on Saturday, crews were able to enter the area and confirmed the deaths, according to the Sevier County sheriff and coroner.

Widemouth 2 has swept through more than 114,600 acres (46,400 hectares) and was 24% contained, as of Saturday. That figure marked a jump from early on Friday, where the fire’s scope was reported as reaching more than 105,000 acres, according to state data.

The chopper’s crash ignited a new blaze, state authorities said at a news conference on Friday evening. The accident site is within the fire’s perimeter.

“Ground resources attempted to respond immediately, but access to the scene was compromised by the emergent fire,” the US Forest Service wrote in a Saturday statement. “Without a safety zone, the Incident Management Team determined not to place lives at risk until the area is deemed safe.”

Federal officials had advised the public to refrain from speculating on the nature of the crash, as search-and-rescue teams waited for fire conditions to subside to safer levels.

Investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) were en route to Richfield, a city roughly 160 miles (250km) south of Salt Lake City, as of Friday. When they are able to reach the crash site, they will document the scene, before retrieving the aircraft.

It will probably take the NTSB a year or more to determine the cause.

The western US states have faced a deadly wildfire season. In June, three firefighters died, as they battled a blaze along the Colorado-Utah border. A fourth firefighter later died from burn injuries sustained during the emergency response.

The crash ignited a new fire that has scorched nearly 174 square miles (nearly 451skm) Officials did not identify the pilots but said they were employed by Helicopter Transport Services.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Super El Niño’ could bring wet winter and flooding to western US, climate scientists warn
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Weather system tied to warming sea surface expected to intensify in fall and winter, persisting until early spring 2027

El Niño, a recurring climate phenomenon marked by above-average sea surface temperatures, when changes in wind patterns allow warmer water to spread across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, could spell a wet winter for portions of the western and south-eastern US, climate models show. Coastal areas may be at elevated risk of flooding, experts warn.

Climate scientists predict this year’s “super” El Niño, a label assigned when sea surface temperatures climb by at least 2C, will be the strongest of the century. The weather system is expected to intensify in the fall and winter, persisting until early spring 2027, according to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa).

Not signed in before? Create a free account

California has a 70%-100% chance of experiencing above-average rainfall along its coast, according to a model from the European center for medium-range forecasts.

“El Niño is never going to guarantee any particular outcome in any California winter,” Daniel Swain, the UCLA climate scientist, noted at a virtual El Niño town hall hosted by the California state senator Mike McGuire this week. But, he added, a weather event as strong as the one being currently predicted shifts the odds in favor of a wet winter: “That will likely affect and increase the likelihood of coastal flooding, particularly during strong storm events or during king tide events.”

California has been devastated by El Niños in the past.

A 1982-83 weather system destroyed 33 oceanfront homes and damaged 3,000 other residences, according to the California coastal commission. In a 1997-98 El Niño, California experienced massive flooding and 17 storm-related deaths. In more recent history, during the El Niño winter of 2015-16, state officials reported record coastal erosion on California beaches.

“With less beach in front of the coastline, the waves will have even greater impact on the shoreline with more likelihood of flooding and undercutting of cliffs,” said Mark Merrifield of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, at McGuire’s town hall.

El Niño is not expected to completely erase drought in the US south-west, where some reservoirs are at an all-time low. “It would have to be exceptionally wet,” Dr Joel Lisonbee, senior associate scientist at the Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences at the University of Colorado Boulder, told the Guardian in June. “That would also mean flooding, and the destruction and potential loss of life that comes along with that.”

Swathes of the US Gulf coast and east coast, stretching from Florida up to the mid-Atlantic region, are facing similar high odds of increased precipitation.

During El Niño years, central and south Florida has historically experienced more severe weather with more tornadoes and flood events, according to Noaa. In a 1998 El Niño winter, an outbreak of unusually strong tornadoes in that region led to 42 deaths and more than $100m in damage.

Experts warn that not every El Niño behaves the same, nor does it affect different geographical regions in the same way. Some have fueled hurricanes and heavy precipitation, while others have triggered extreme heat and drought.

While this is “a natural cycle”, Merrifield said at the town hall, the potential effects of a temporary sea-level rise in California from the super El Niño also “gives us a bit of a stress test of what the state is likely to experience with future climate change”.

“The El Niño, I think, is a good opportunity to sort of see where our vulnerabilities are throughout the state and what we can do to prepare,” Merrifield added, “and it also is a sobering look at what we can expect with climate change.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Hunter Biden talks about how his father’s cancer has spread and is causing him pain
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Joe Biden’s prostate cancer is reportedly ‘debilitating’, even as ex-president continues to speak out on public issues

Former US president Joe Biden’s prostate cancer has spread to other parts of his body and is causing him pain, even as he continues to speak out on public issues, his son Hunter said in an interview.

In a wide-ranging interview with the BBC broadcast late on Friday, Hunter Biden grew emotional as he discussed his father’s condition, describing it as very sad to watch.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further,” he said. “It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects.”

Joe Biden, 83, was the oldest man to serve as US president and his age was a source of concern for much of his four years in office. He and his White House advisers have faced intense criticism for allegedly concealing the extent of his health issues, especially after he was forced to abandon his bid for re-election after a disastrous debate with his eventual successor, Donald Trump.

The former president revealed his cancer diagnosis in May of last year, less than four months after he left the White House.

Hunter Biden said the diagnosis had been tough on the family.

“It’s really sad to watch,” Biden said. “The only thing that I’d say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good.”

But Biden said his father remains “out there”, speaking publicly about the issues that are important to him.

“He’s still doing his thing,” he said. “He so believes in this country.”

Biden also expressed gratitude for the pardon his father granted him because if he had not, Trump would have sought retribution against him, he said. But he also acknowledged that it was not good for the former president’s legacy or the American people.

“It is something that is easily criticized and for good reason,” Biden said. “All I know is that I’m grateful he did it for me, and all I can say to anybody out there is, what would you have thought of my dad if he did not do that for me?”

Joe Biden will publish a memoir, Promise Me, America, after the midterm elections.

The Associated Press contributed reporting
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Joe Biden's prostate cancer is reportedly 'debilitating' in his body, his son Hunter said. The former president revealed his cancer diagnosis in May of last year, less than four months after he left the White House.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.title: Blanche confirmation allows Trump to continue ‘pervasive, breathtaking corruption’, says Schumer – as it happened
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.author: Victoria Bekiempis (now); Yohannes Lowe, Emily Mackay (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text:
The Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, has said Senate Republicans have “handed Trump an excuse on a silver platter” to continue his “pervasive, breathtaking corruption” by confirming Todd Blanche as attorney general

“If you want to wipe out corruption, you can’t have the president’s personal attorney as the attorney general. You don’t need a PhD in political science to know that,” he wrote in a post on X.

“Todd Blanche has no intention of stopping Trump’s corruption. He advanced his career enabling it. Every senator who voted to confirm him has now branded themselves as an enabler, too.”

Schumer said Senate Democrats will continue to resist the Trump administration’s “assault on the rule of law and undermining of democratic values”.

All Democrats voted against Blanche’s nomination to lead the Justice Department on a permanent basis, with a wide spectrum of lawmakers saying he was unfit for the role and would do the president’s bidding.

We’re wrapping our live politics coverage for the day. Here’s the top political news:

The US Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as attorney general. Blanche, who was deputy attorney general prior to former AG Pam Bondi’s ouster, previously served as Donald Trump’s criminal defense attorney. Blanche won the confirmation by a 50-49 vote early Saturday morning. Just two Republican senators, Maine’s Susan Collins and Alaska’s Lisa Murkowski, voted against him.

Blanche was confirmed despite facing intense criticism for his handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files. Remember: Trump’s Department of Justice was required by bipartisan legislation to disclose all files related to Epstein by 19 December, with redactions only in extremely limited circumstances. While some files were disclosed on this deadline, many were released after the congressionally mandated cutoff. Blanche’s rollout has also been criticized for redacting information that should have been public–-while disclosing survivors’ names.

US Senators started their five-week recess this morning after handing Trump a major win with Blanche’s confirmation. But, GOP senators managed to go on recess without meeting some of Trump’s demands--including passage of the Save America Act. This proposed legislation would restrict voting across the US. Trump had pushed for senators to postpone their recess to green-light this act, but they reportedly told Trump portions of it would be included in a Republican budget package.

It’s not just Blanche--dozens of Trump nominees were confirmed by the Senate early Saturday morning. Senate Republicans pushed through a resolution confirming more than 70 Trump picks for role such as ambassadors, judges, and US attorneys.

Among the early morning votes pushed through the US Senate by Republicans before dawn was a resolution to confirm a slate of 71 of Donald Trump’s picks to serve in a variety of roles, including as ambassadors, US attorneys, judges and senior staff at federal agencies.

One of the nominees confirmed this way was P Wells Griffith, a former Republican campaign operative and Trump aide who was the senior director for international energy and environment on the National Security Council in 2019.

As of today, Griffith is now a US ambassador, representing the United States at the International Atomic Energy Agency in Vienna. The IAEA played a key role in verifying Iran’s compliance with the nuclear deal negotiated during the Obama administration, which Trump withdrew from during his first term, and could be similarly important should a new nuclear deal with Iran be struck by the Trump administration.

During the impeachment inquiry over Trump’s pressure campaign against Ukraine in 2019, Fiona Hill, the NSC’s Russia expert during Trump’s first term, testified that Griffith was present at a July 2019 meeting with Ukrainian officials in which John Bolton, then Trump’s national security adviser, discovered that other US officials had secretly pressed Ukraine to open a sham investigation of Joe Biden.

Griffith refused to testify to the House impeachment inquiry, defying a subpoena.

Pete Buttigieg called for unity among Democrats on Friday during a rally in Michigan, saying “the stakes are high, and people from around the country, people from around the world, are watching” to see if Democrats can win the swing state.

Buttigieg’s remarks, reported by Politico, came during a planned event that involved Michigan’s statewide Democratic ticket. Buttigieg ran for president in 2020 and is considered a possible Democratic contender for 2028.

Michigan Democrats must hold onto their Senate seat if Democrats want to regain control of the Senate. And while Michigan has long been a battleground state, residents voted for Donald Trump in the last two elections, Politico noted.

“We’re going to win because we know what it means to focus on what’s at stake, to lock arms as allies after a spirited primary, to pull together in common cause,” Buttigieg said.

Buttigieg remained neutral during Michigan’s Senate primary, which exposed deep schisms within the Democratic party. Abdul El-Sayed won against the US representative Haley Stevens on Tuesday and is up against the Republican representative Mike Rogers in the general election.

El-Sayed needs to attract moderate and establishment Democrats to win, Politico said, with the GOP noting a potential opportunity to attract some Democrats.

“Wherever you sit, in this big tent of ours, and it is a big tent, but whatever corner of that tent you think of as home, there is a set of things, and I mean big, big things, where we agree with each other, we agree with most Michiganders, and Washington and Lansing Republicans disagree with us,” Buttigieg reportedly said. “That’s what’s at stake right now, and it’s not all about left, right and center, Democrat and Republican.”

El-Sayed also called for coming together.

“In the spirit of unity, in the spirit of the work, in the spirit of coming together, I want to thank both of my colleagues who ran, Haley Stevens and Mallory McMorrow, for an incredible race,” he reportedly said. “Their incredible public service in the state of Michigan, and I cannot wait to see what both of them will do next.”

“They don’t know who we fight for,” he also said, referring to Republicans. “We fight for the families barely able to put their groceries in the cart and check out, we fight for the mom who’s worried about the childcare she needs to be able to work a job that barely pays enough, we fight for the folks who are afraid about what happens if they get sick. We fight for each other, and we don’t back down.”

A former Republican strategist thinks that “this might be the year” that Democrats beat the GOP in a race for statewide office in Texas.

Joseph Moreno’s comment came during an interview with Jake Tapper on CNN’s The Lead. Tapper questioned Moreno about the Texas state representative James Talarico besting the GOP state attorney general Ken Paxton 47-45% in recent polling.

“It surprises me, and it worries me a little bit, Jake. Normally, I would say, ‘I’m not worried about this,’ right? It’s been 30 years since a Democrat won statewide office in Texas,” Moreno remarked, according to the Hill.

Paxton beat the incumbent senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary after receiving Donald Trump’s endorsement. Talarico bested the Democrat representative Jasmine Crockett during the primary, his victory boosted by Democratic leaders, according to the Hill.

“The problem is, here’s what happens – in 2024, the Republican was up by 2%, wins by 8%. In 2020, Cornyn was up 10%, wins by 10%,” Moreno said. “Now, you’ve got Talarico even, or maybe even ahead of Paxton.”

“I hate to say it, this might be the year for Democrats in Texas,” Moreno also remarked.

US senators kicked off their five-week recess early on Saturday after delivering Donald Trump a major victory – but punting several of the president’s demands.

Senators confirmed Trump’s pick for US attorney general, Todd Blanche. They green-lighted a broad Russian sanctions package to help Ukraine and approved a deal to fund the federal government through early December, as to avoid a shutdown, according to the Associated Press.

But the Senate did not advance Trump’s Save America Act, which would place restrictions on voting across the US, prior to their break. Trump had pushed senators to remain in session so they could approve this proof-of-citizenship voting legislation.

According to the AP, GOP senators pitched an alternative plan to Trump late on Friday. Under the Republican senators’ proposal, they would push for approval of some portions of this bill “as part of a broader GOP budget package to fund the Iran war and replenish the Pentagon when they return to work in September”.

Joe Biden’s prostate cancer has spread throughout his body, causing the former president great pain, his son Hunter Biden said during an interview broadcast Friday.

“The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further,” Hunter Biden said in a sit-down with the BBC. “It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects.”

“It’s really sad to watch,” Hunter Biden also said. “The only thing that I’d say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good.”

Biden, now 83, disclosed his prostate cancer diagnosis in May 2025, just months after he departed the White House. As the oldest president in US history, Biden’s age was routinely the target of his political opponents.

Biden and his staff have also been criticized for purportedly hiding his health problems. This criticism came to a crux following a devastating debate against Donald Trump that prompted calls for him to step out of the presidential race.

Biden abandoned his run and his vice-president, Kamala Harris, became the Democratic candidate. Donald Trump bested Harris in the election and he is serving a second term as president.

Hunter Biden noted that his father has not stepped back from public life, discussing issues that matter to him.

“He’s still doing his thing,” Hunter Biden said. “He so believes in this country.”

Hunter Biden also remarked that he was “the most privileged person there is” after Joe Biden pardoned him. He felt that the pardon was “not good” for the nation, his father’s legacy or the US constitution.

But, Hunter Biden said, he did not discuss the pardon beforehand with his father. He told the BBC that his dad did so – despite vowing not to intervene in Hunter’s criminal cases – out of fear that Donald Trump would go after him.

With reporting from the Associated Press

Democrats instigated a government shutdown last year when they refused to approve funding bills without an agreement to extend subsidies for Affordable Care Act health plans. That led to the longest funding lapse in US history, but ultimately no agreement to keep the cost offsets going after the shutdown ended 43 days later.

Some government agencies shut down again briefly earlier this year after Democrats held up a funding bill for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in protest of the killings by federal agents of two US citizens in Minneapolis during an intensive immigration enforcement drive.

While an agreement was reached to resolve that blockade, the two parties did not agree on funding DHS for weeks, as Democrats held out for reforms to immigration enforcement operations.

The US Senate on Friday passed a government funding bill that will prevent a shutdown through the midterm elections, though it still must be approved by the House of Representatives.

The continuing resolution (CR) passed by a 90-6 vote will keep the government running at its current funding levels until 11 December, more than a month past the midterms in which Democrats are hoping to regain control of Congress and block Donald Trump’s legislative agenda for the final two years of his presidency.

The measure’s passage signals a recognition by both parties that they would prefer to avoid a messy battle over federal spending in the weeks leading up to the 3 November vote.

The government will shut down after 30 September if new funding is not approved, and the Republican Senate appropriations committee chair, Susan Collins, called the CR “a major step toward averting a damaging shutdown that only harms vital programs and federal workers”, and noted it makes no major changes to funding levels.

Although Donald Trump has not yet commented directly on Todd Blanche’s confirmation as attorney general, he has taken to his platform Truth Social to post a screenshot from an account on X that refers to Lisa Murkowski, the Republican Alaska senator, as a “traitor”.

Murkowski was one of only two Republicans, along with Maine’s Susan Collins, to vote against Blanche.

The US embassy in London is offering grants of up to half a million dollars for new “public education” programmes in what has been criticised as interference in British domestic politics.

Using language that the pro-Trump Maga movement has sought to appropriate, a funding notice identifies a goal of fostering a “national conversation” about “shared civilizational values” underpinning US-UK ties. Priority will go to applicants aiming to celebrate “freedom of speech” and “limited government”.

It comes after senior Trump officials voiced sharp criticism of British authorities and repeated misinformation on a range of fronts including abortion and digital regulation, and allied with European far-right movements in attacks on hate speech and immigration policies.

Adding to Chuck Schumer’s comments, New Mexico’s Democratic representative Melanie Stansbury said the confirmation of Todd Blanche as attorney general represents a “dark moment” for the nation’s traditional system of checks and balances.

She said this is because the justice department “is being weaponized for retribution, shielding the administration from accountability, and actively obstructing the Epstein case.”

“There is no doubt that these 50 votes will go down in history. To every survivor and every person who cares about justice: this is not the end. We will continue fighting to hold them accountable,” Stanbsury added in her post on X, in reference to the concerns raised about Blanche’s handling of the release of Jeffrey Epstein-related documents.

The US constitution’s creation of the three branches of government, with the legislative branch being the third, was intended to ensure checks and balances so that no branch had too much power.

The system, however, has come under severe strain during the Trump administration, with presidential power aggressively expanded and the president accused of usurping powers reserved for the legislature.

The Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, has said Senate Republicans have “handed Trump an excuse on a silver platter” to continue his “pervasive, breathtaking corruption” by confirming Todd Blanche as attorney general

“If you want to wipe out corruption, you can’t have the president’s personal attorney as the attorney general. You don’t need a PhD in political science to know that,” he wrote in a post on X.

“Todd Blanche has no intention of stopping Trump’s corruption. He advanced his career enabling it. Every senator who voted to confirm him has now branded themselves as an enabler, too.”

Schumer said Senate Democrats will continue to resist the Trump administration’s “assault on the rule of law and undermining of democratic values”.

All Democrats voted against Blanche’s nomination to lead the Justice Department on a permanent basis, with a wide spectrum of lawmakers saying he was unfit for the role and would do the president’s bidding.

Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana said he was undecided about whether to vote to confirm Todd Blanche as the attorney general as late as last Wednesday.

“I’ve got to be convinced that he is an attorney general who just happens to have once been President Trump’s personal attorney, as opposed to President Trump’s personal attorney who is now the attorney general,” he said in a radio interview. “I think there’s a big difference between the two.”

In what was a major win for Donald Trump, Cassidy soon got in line with the president’s wishes as he brushed off his concerns about Blanche’s independence and cast the deciding vote in the acting attorney general’s favour.

Here is a video of Cassidy, who has had a strained relationship with the president, explaining his vote on the Senate floor on Friday:

Todd Blanche faced heavy criticism for the department’s sloppy rollout of files related to Jeffrey Epstein, which redacted information that should not have been redacted and left unredacted the names of victims that should have been kept private.

During his confirmation hearing, Blanche refused to personally meet with Epstein victims, then agreed to do so. The survivors said they received few answers from Blanche during the meeting.

Blanche, who left a lucrative partnership to represent Trump in 2023, has been at the center of the president’s attempt to bend the federal government to his will. Scores of career justice department attorneys have left the agency under his leadership. Department lawyers have been rebuked by judges across the US for making misrepresentations to the court.

Blanche has also been at the center of Trump’s efforts to use the justice department to punish political rivals. During his tenure as both the deputy attorney general and acting attorney general, the department has indicted former FBI director James Comey twice, New York attorney general Letitia James, the non-profit Southern Poverty Law Center – all in cases that exerts see as thin.

It has also tried to bring criminal charges against two Democratic senators, Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and Mark Kelly of Arizona, and used its investigative powers to try to get leverage over Jerome Powell, the former chair of the Federal Reserve.

The US Senate has narrowly confirmed Todd Blanche as attorney general, installing Donald Trump’s former defense lawyer as the nation’s top law enforcement official.

Blanche was confirmed by a vote of 50-49 early on Saturday morning, with only two Republican senators – Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska – having voted against him, joining all the chamber’s Democrats in opposing the nomination.

He said he was “deeply honored” to be confirmed as the new attorney general, thanking Trump for the “trust and confidence” that has been placed in him.

Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who was among earlier Republican holdouts, cast the deciding vote in Blanche’s favor. Explaining his decision on the senate floor on Friday, he said:

Mr Blanche is not perfect, and he will tell you this, but the choice is not between perfection and Mr Blanche.

It is between Mr Blanche and another acting attorney general who may not run the department effectively under President Trump and who indeed may not be as good as Mr Blanche.

Blanche has been serving as the acting attorney general since the president fired Pam Bondi, another Trump loyalist, in April.

However, there was a lengthy delay to Blanche’s confirmation amid concerns he could use the department to go after Trump’s political adversaries as attorney general.

Blanche faced pushback from Republican senators over the department’s deal to create a $1.8bn so-called “anti-weaponization fund” and to give the president, his sons, and business tax immunity, as my colleague notes in this story.

“The attorney general is supposed to be the people’s lawyer,” Senator Dick Durbin, the ranking Democrat on the Senate judiciary committee, said on Tuesday.

“Mr Blanche continues to operate as the president’s personal lawyer, treating the justice department like a law firm serving one client: the president.”

But despite these concerns, Blanche’s confirmation was narrowly confirmed after a late-night session ran over into the early hours of Saturday ahead of a planned five-week Senate recess.

The Senate majority leader, John Thune, Trump and Senate conservatives reached a deal last night to postpone a vote on a budget resolution and defer action on a significant portion of the SAVE America Act until after the break.

Trump had demanded that senators stay in session to pass a strict proof-of-citizenship voting bill before the summer recess.

Instead, Republican senators who had brought the chamber to a standstill spoke to Trump late in the evening about an alternative plan: they would try again to approve elements of the voting bill as part of a broader GOP budget package to fund the Iran war and replenish the Pentagon when they return to work in September.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘They kidnapped a hard-working kid off our streets’: the gardener seized by ICE – and the New York town fighting back
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Alex Hannaford
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Gerson Turcios was 17 when he fled violence in Honduras to build a new life in the US. Six years later, he was mowing lawns in his home town of Rhinebeck when immigration officers took him. Within hours, friends, neighbours and local celebrities sprang into action. Could they stop his deportation?

G
erson Turcios didn’t recognise the men standing next to a couple of dark SUVs outside his house one July afternoon last year. He figured they were lost and approached to see if he could help. A slim 23-year-old with short dark hair and big brown eyes, Turcios had just finished work mowing lawns in the pretty town of Rhinebeck, in New York’s Hudson Valley. The men asked if he knew someone called Jimmy – he did, but Jimmy hadn’t lived in the small, white weatherboard house with Turcios, his brother and his brother’s girlfriend for a while.

The men noted Turcios’s accent and asked where he was from. Turcios didn’t answer, so one took out his phone and snapped a photograph. The next thing Turcios knew, he was in handcuffs in the back of one of the SUVs and on his way to an ICE processing centre in Newburgh, New York, then on to a detention centre.

Mass deportation has been the defining mission of Donald Trump’s second presidency. In the year since he took office, ICE – United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement – has deported nearly a quarter of a million people from inside the US (half a million including from its borders) as part of an immigration crackdown. These forceful apprehensions, which have in some cases resulted in fatal shootings of potential deportees and bystanders, have resulted in protests – and sparked international outrage. Behind the statistics, though, are stories of hope and perseverance; of young immigrants who risked everything crossing rivers and deserts to build lives, start businesses and put down roots in communities that are now fighting to keep them.

Back then, as he was shackled and led to his cell, sure he was about to be deported back to Honduras, Turcios – an immigrant who had made a terrifying journey as a teenager, fleeing violence there – had no idea that his community in Rhinebeck was already mobilising; that they would raise tens of thousands of dollars in days, galvanise support from Hollywood actors and film-makers who also called the town home, and even recruit the lawyer who essentially wrote the book on stopping ICE deportations around the nation to represent him.

I’d moved to Rhinebeck with my own family from Texas during the pandemic, drawn to the bucolic countryside and good schools. Our own daughter now walks the same high school hallways Turcios once did. For me, and a lot of other people who call this small town home, Turcios’s arrest was personal.

“Well, it’s happened,” wrote actor Griffin Dunne on Instagram. “ICE has come to my beloved Dutchess County and kidnapped a hard working kid with his own local lawn care business, and without a criminal record, off our tranquil streets.” But he added, “This is only the beginning.” Dunne, who has a home in Rhinebeck, told his followers that the community had started a war chest to defend Turcios. “Our pressure has brought about a hearing for Gerson at 11:00 tomorrow morning at Thurgood Marshall Courthouse for those who wish to show support. To my Rhinebeck neighbors, a bus will leave from Tops [grocery store] at 7:00 am.”

S
ix years earlier, around 9pm on a freezing December night, Turcios and three other migrants had stood by the southern banks of the Rio Grande river in Mexico, looking across into Texas as flames torched the desert brush behind them; Mexican soldiers had set it alight to flush them out.

With nowhere left to go, Turcios turned to the others. “We are right here,” he told them. “The other side is the United States.” Another boy checked that everyone was able to swim – they were – but all Gerson could think about was alligators, which had occasionally been known to inhabit the Rio Grande.

The four boys jumped into the black water together, fighting the current as it pushed them downstream. Along that stretch, near McAllen, Texas, the width of the Rio Grande ranges from 45 to 90 meters. Finally, soaking wet, they scrambled up a concrete wall on the US side. They ran through scrubland until headlights appeared behind them, then three German shepherds. A heavier boy was dragged down by the dogs as he scaled a fence; the others scattered. Turcios sprinted until three cars boxed him in and US immigration officers emerged with guns drawn. “If you keep running,” they shouted, “we’re gonna shoot your legs.” Turcios stopped, put his hands up, then fell to his knees and felt a boot between his shoulder blades as they threw him to the ground and handcuffed him. He had spent six weeks on a journey that had nearly broken him. Against all odds, he had made it across the river. And now he’d been caught.

In 2019, during the first Trump administration, an adult detained by Border Patrol crossing into the US was increasingly likely to be sent back to Mexico to wait for their immigration case to be heard. Turcios, though, was under 18, and the law dictated he be taken to refugee resettlement housing for minors. Turcios stayed at a facility in Long Island for almost a month until his brother, Henoch, and Henoch’s girlfriend, Yorleny Weigel, were allowed to pick him up and return to Weigel’s home in Rhinebeck.

Henoch had come to the US in 2017 via a tortuous route, and Turcios hadn’t seen him for six years. Their first stop was a Wendy’s fast food joint for a burger – “So big,” Turcios now recalls, “I didn’t know how to eat it.”

He would have to wait for the government to notify him of his first immigration hearing, but soon the Covid pandemic would throw the courts into chaos, with some hearings postponed indefinitely and others rescheduled then postponed again, leaving Turcios in limbo.

Weigel showed Turcios his room, then drove him across the river to a big outlet store in the city of Kingston to buy clothes. He spoke no English, so Weigel registered him with a county language integration programme and with the local high school. In the summer of 2020, ahead of the start of the school year, he was introduced to Anna Lawson, who would be one of his classmates. Lawson was in advanced Spanish and, as Covid was still forcing people to meet virtually, they spoke regularly over Zoom. “He is a really lovely, positive person,” Lawson says. “He’d often be sitting outside, talking about how much he enjoyed Rhinebeck.”

On the first day of school, Turcios was afraid he’d be arrested by the police officer who sat outside in his car for an hour each morning as kids entered the building – just under half of US state schools have police patrol on campus – but after his first day, that fear passed. “After that I wasn’t afraid. I was excited,” he says. “But I didn’t speak any English at all.” Turcios immediately hit it off with his classmates. Brendan Dougherty shared a study hall with him. “Gerson is a very sociable guy, so it wasn’t difficult to strike up a conversation with him,” Dougherty says. “And his English progressed very quickly. Each day we’d go outside and play basketball.”

Turcios finished high school in the early summer of 2022 and began working in the kitchen of a local French restaurant and, in his spare time, for a crew that did landscaping and house maintenance, and mowed lawns. One of his first clients was Jenny Friedberg, a creative director and producer who had moved up to Rhinebeck from the city during the pandemic. Turcios and the maintenance crew painted her basement in Brooklyn, and excavated 24in of bedrock under her barn in Rhinebeck. “Whatever they did, Gerson was always there,” Friedberg says. “He was the youngest of the crew, the smiliest, the most helpful, and my favourite.”

In the summer of 2025, Turcios left the restaurant and went to work full-time with the crew. At 7.30pm on 18 July 2025, Friedberg’s phone rang. It was Carlos, Turcios’s boss. Turcios had been detained by ICE, he told her, and he didn’t know what to do.

Friedberg made several calls that evening. The first was to Luciano Valdivia, a local restaurateur and president of Rhinebeck’s chamber of commerce. The next was to Amanda Miller, a local attorney. Then John Reinish, a political communications strategist she knew. Within 24 hours, they’d set up a Spotfund, an online fundraising platform, to raise money for Turcios’s legal battle. Miller called Gregory Copeland, a law school friend who had pioneered legal strategies to stop ICE deportations and had also moved to Rhinebeck.

Copeland was a nationally recognised civil rights and immigration attorney, and co-founder of the Rapid Defense Network, a non-profit providing pro bono legal support to immigrants facing deportation. He was also the subject of the documentary Guerrilla Habeas, which looked at the legal strategy it employed to stop deportations at the last moment. That strategy hinged on filing habeas corpus petitions, which empower federal judges to compel the authorities to justify detentions, a power enshrined in the constitution. Doing this forces cases out of immigration courts and into federal court, where due process can be properly considered and immigrants have a fairer shot at justice.

Miller says Copeland had experience fighting “the biggest machine there is – the federal government”. But since his move to Rhinebeck, he had stopped practising civil rights and immigration law, and had turned his attention to estate planning for clients. Still, Miller knew there was no one better to help Turcios.

“It wasn’t clear to me immediately that I would help him, but I went into triage mode, gathering information and figuring out what our options were,” Copeland says. As soon as Copeland got Turcios’s “A-Number” – the alien registration number assigned by the US Department of Homeland Security to non-citizens– he could check his status in the system. He discovered that, years earlier, Turcios had been ordered deported “in absentia” for missing a hearing. During Covid, courts repeatedly moved locations; Turcios missed a notice despite living at the same address he’d always provided.

Copeland knew it was now vital to get the Rhinebeck community to show up for him. “If you consider what the government evaluates when justifying someone’s detention, it’s whether they’re a danger to the community and a flight risk,” Copeland says. “The community is typically not going to show up for a dangerous person. And you’re less of a flight risk if there’s a strong community around you.”

It was a matter of urgency to identify where Turcios was being taken and where he was going next. Copeland says it’s not an exact science, but after working these cases as long as he had, you get a feel for it. A red flag was if he had been sent to Louisiana, a staging location for deportations – at this point, he had not. However, Turcios had been detained with his passport – another red flag. “[The government] needs two things to remove you: a travel document and a final order of removal,” Copeland says. “They need something to show who you are because in immigration court one of the first things they need to establish is that you’re not a citizen.” If an immigrant picked up by ICE doesn’t have a travel document on them, that buys their attorneys more time.

Meanwhile, Valdivia asked Leah Conklin, another resident who worked in international criminal justice reform, to get involved. Within days of Turcios’s arrest, a crack team was coming together, but time was of the essence. “One of the reasons they make arrests on Friday, I think, is because you can’t catch up,” Valdivia says, “and if you don’t know where they’re going, you don’t know how to stop it.”

Copeland was looking at the online detainee locator system, trying to get a feel for where Turcios was moving – through which processing centre; which detention centre. In New York state, if you are taken to Federal Plaza in Manhattan and then your location “goes dark”, that’s an indicator you could be bound for a deportation flight. “It’s very relevant for filing a habeas petition,” Copeland says, “because you have to file where they’re detained.” If you don’t know where your client is, you can’t file and they can be deported. “So it’s a game they’re playing – hiding the person.”

Conklin had been calling around law firms but found it impossible to get a lawyer quickly enough. On Sunday, Copeland agreed to take on Turcios’s case himself. “I had created the Rapid Defense Network because there’s a small window in which you have to do this. It’s like a death penalty case: you have to strike while the iron’s hot or you’re dead.” By that evening, with Miller’s help, Copeland had filed an emergency petition on Turcios’s behalf, seeking a stay to allow him to consult with lawyers and challenge his removal order. Conklin says that the community came together in record time.

Valdivia messaged some other Rhinebeck residents he knew could amplify Turcios’s story. He called Dunne, the actor and writer who had starred in An American Werewolf in London and After Hours, and whom Valdivia counted as a friend. He texted film-maker Andrew Jarecki, who donated, as did actor Paul Rudd, who co-owns a sweet shop in Rhinebeck and lives there with his family. Word spread. Other contributions came in from all over the US and beyond.

Dunne began posting about Turcios’s case on social media. “It was the first time I’ve ever used Instagram without kind of being embarrassed about self-promotion because I had a movie coming out,” he says. “It made sense to me for the first time. I was just struck by the inhumanity and the contagion of cruelty.”

Friedberg says that when Turcios was arrested, she had a reckoning with herself: “This sort of recognition of how we don’t often know the people that have been working for us or near us for years.” She had never asked about Turcios’s story.

T
urcios spent his early childhood in the small town of Balfate on Honduras’s northern coast. His father, Juan, raised cattle. Irma, his mother, gave birth to 10 children. The disappearance of his eldest brother, Amilcar, is one of Turcios’s earliest memories. He was four when his brother went missing after travelling by boat to Roatán, a Honduran island, to seek a better life. Of the five people who made the trip, authorities recovered the bodies of three. Amilcar and the boat’s captain were never found. Turcios’s family never learned the truth; they suspect it had something to do with organised crime, but they’ve come to accept that Amilcar is dead.

While there has been a drop in violent crime in the last couple of years, historically Honduras has been one of the most dangerous countries in the world, with gangs vying for control of drugs and extortion rackets. A decade ago, it frequently topped global lists of the highest murder rates in non-war zone countries, fuelled by its position as a major transit hub for South American cocaine heading to the US.

“My mother was afraid, so she decided we should move from that place where she lost her son,” Turcios says. The family relocated to just outside the large city of San Pedro Sula and stayed there for nine years. Turcios went to school, but eventually they sold up and moved to a house in the mountains. It was beautiful, he says, but dangerous; you could never be sure which was more deadly – the criminal gangs who stole livestock, or the venomous snakes and other wildlife.

They had 10 cows to tend and a few horses, and they began constructing their own house. Laundry was done in a small stream and cooking over fire. Walking to the city took nine hours, over mountain passes; Turcios recalls jumping on his father’s shoulders to cross rivers.

By the time Turcios moved to the mountains, his brother Henoch had already migrated to the US. Henoch says he travelled from Honduras, across Mexico by train, without any money and had to beg for food. He spent three months in Monterrey, where he almost had to have his left hand amputated due to an infection. A friend helped him pay for the medication – the same friend would eventually take in Henoch in Rhinebeck. After he’d recovered enough, he hitched a ride on a train to the border town of Sonoyta, then spent 22 days walking through the southern desert into Arizona. He says he nearly died after spending weeks without eating, surviving on nothing but water.

Eventually, Turcios’s parents decided to move back to town as they wanted his younger sisters, aged eight and 10, to go to school, and to be nearer to a hospital in case they got sick. Turcios stayed in the mountains, living alone for six months so his father wouldn’t have to sell his animals, but he was an hour away by foot from the nearest house. His father gave him a gun for safety and most nights he’d lie awake, clutching it, and listening to the cries of animals in the wilderness.

After the 16-year-old son of his nearest neighbour was murdered over drugs, Turcios’s siblings decided it was time for him to leave Honduras. One day, when visiting his sister in town, he was told that the following morning a man would arrive who would help him cross into Mexico and travel to the US to join his brother. “I didn’t have a future in Honduras,” he says. “If you wanted to go to college, you had to pay a lot of money and my parents couldn’t afford it. And I knew if I went to the United States I would learn how to speak English and it would be better for me.”

Two days later he was travelling across Guatemala by bus and car, under the “care” of a coyote – a people smuggler he had paid 12,000 Honduran pesos, the equivalent of about £350 – or, as he recalls, the amount he’d received for a cow he’d sold five days earlier. Turcios had been told the back route through the mountains would keep him safe. He, his coyote and a group of other migrants moved only at night, but safety proved elusive. At a bus stop in Guatemala, armed officers boarded and ordered passengers to strip. Turcios had hidden his money in his sock, out of sight. The coyote paid the officers off and they kept moving. Hours later, another police stop. This time the driver was pulled from the van, kicked and beaten while officers held a pistol to his head. Only when the driver produced 25,000 Mexican pesos (about £1,000) did they relent.

After 16 nights in a safe house, one migrant demanded better treatment from the people smugglers and that they get moving. Three strangers dragged him outside and he never returned.

The journey took a month and a half. In early December, Turcios and his closest companion, Antonio, were roused at midnight and, together with four others, were packed into a van and dumped in desolate brush. Turcios and Antonio were from the same state in Honduras but hadn’t known each other before. The others were from different countries – El Salvador, Guatemala, Mexico. “I was 17. Antonio was 28 and like my older brother,” Turcios says. “His wife and kid had moved to the US a year before and lived in Georgia, so he was trying to reunite with them.”

A guide led them through darkness for 30 minutes. By 3am they had joined 40 others alongside the Rio Grande, shivering in the winter cold. The border was not unguarded. Helicopters buzzed low, forcing them to hide in the grassland and scrub. Mexican army troops encircled them, weapons raised, setting fire to the surrounding brush to flush out the remaining migrants, most of whom fled into the night. Turcios surrendered his pesos and ran. Then, it was time to cross.

After his capture, the US Border Patrol officers took Turcios to a room with a table and two chairs. An officer accused him of being an adult; of running drugs across the border. Turcios told them he was 17, that he had never muled drugs, and that he had gone three days without sleep or food. He produced his birth certificate, which they took and never returned. A doctor arrived, checked his teeth, and confirmed his age. Then the officers stopped yelling, moved him to a cell full of boys his age or younger, and gave him two cookies and a bottle of Kool-Aid – the best meal he had eaten in weeks.

Two days later, he was given new clothes, a jacket for the cold, and told he was flying to New York. It was his first time on a plane, his first time seeing “ice fall from the sky”, as it was snowing that day in New York City. After 26 days in a Long Island shelter, showering each morning and night, and attending a little school inside the facility, he was met by Henoch and Weigel, who drove down from Rhinebeck to collect him.

S
ix months after Turcios was detained outside his home in Rhinebeck, the campaign to help him had shifted from emergency response to sustained pressure. On a freezing Tuesday afternoon in January, more than 100 students walked out of Rhinebeck’s middle and high schools as part of nationwide anti-ICE protests, defying district policies that required parental permission to leave campus.

My daughter, Scout, then 14, helped organise the walkout, and I watched from the edge of the park as she stood on a podium and told the crowd how ICE had taken a Rhinebeck High School alumnus who had done nothing but contribute to the community and how his detention had affected everyone.

Turcios has been shuffled between detention facilities across three states – New York, New Jersey and Louisiana – seemingly at random. Last August he was taken to the Alexandria Staging Facility in Louisiana, a factory for deportation flights. One morning he was led on to a plane bound for Honduras, but guards pulled him off just before departure after Copeland and other lawyers working on his case won a stay of removal. Over the next 48 hours, Turcios watched as 50 other migrants left the United States, before he was driven back to the detention facility.

In June Turcios had his second court hearing; unlike the first, this one he was required to attend. Dunne says he couldn’t get out of his head the picture of this boy in ankle chains, flanked by guards, looking over at his friends and supporters in the public gallery. “And when he gave us a wave it was just heartbreaking.”

It also brought up traumatic memories. Back in 1982, Dunne’s younger sister, Dominique, died after being strangled by her ex-boyfriend. “The last time I was in a courtroom was over 40 years ago, representing my sister who had been murdered,” he says. “I attended the trial every day … and every day felt like a situation where the system fails you. Seeing Gerson really, really shook me and I thought about things I hadn’t thought about in a long time – that feeling of helplessness.”

On 18 July 2026 Turcios had been in detention for a full year. His fundraiser has reached more than $130,000 in donations from 1,121 different people, but his legal fight continues. After nine years living in Rhinebeck, Henoch self-deported back to Honduras. He says that, given what was happening to Latino people in the US under the Trump administration, he decided it was better to return. “Having to start over here in Honduras is tough, but it has to be done,” he tells me. Today he works on a cattle farm. Henoch’s former girlfriend, Yorleny Weigel, still lives in Rhinebeck.

She misses Turcios. “I used to take him everywhere with me. People thought he was my son. I’d tell them he wasn’t, but in the end I just gave up and went with it. He loved to go dancing; he’d try to dance but he wasn’t very good.” She talks to Turcios most nights on the phone. “He’s changed,” she says. “He doesn’t want to admit it, but I think it’s breaking him a little bit.”

Today, now aged 24, Turcios is housed in the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn – the same building in which former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and Luigi Mangione, accused of murdering UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York City, are awaiting trial. Immigration detainees are kept separate, but are in the same facility.

Turcios says he’s locked in his cell three times a day but allowed out for breakfast, lunch and dinner, and a few hours’ recreation – playing cards, watching TV. “There are four telephones in the unit and we need to line up to use them,” he says. “Sometimes there are eight people waiting and you don’t get to make a call.”

He says the food is bad – breakfast is a packet of milk and a muffin; lunch is pasta with meat that is “old or cold and flavourless”; dinner is mashed potato, spinach and occasionally chicken. “We don’t see sunshine,” he says. “There is a small room where we play basketball and there’s a big opening like a cage, with no glass, and we can see a little piece of the sky.” He speaks to his parents, Irma and Juan, once a week, but calls are expensive – $10 to call Honduras.

Turcios often thinks about how Trump campaigned on deporting all criminal undocumented immigrants. “But the criminals are on the outside,” he says. “And inside, most of these people here with me just came to the United States to work, to try to build our lives and make things better.”

He wants to return to his home in Rhinebeck. “I knew the community was full of incredible, nice people,” Turcios says. “I never expected everyone would get together to help me out. I was so surprised and happy.”

Turcios’s lawyers are challenging his prolonged detention – under a supreme court ruling, the government may detain someone it wants to deport who has a final order of removal for 90 days; between 90 and 180 days, it must show special justification to keep holding them; and after 180 days, it must prove they are “wildly dangerous”. Copeland says this is a level that even a history of gang-related homicide has in the past failed to meet. He argues that Turcios should have been released by October, roughly 90 days into his detention, and that ICE failed to properly notify him of a custody review hearing. In addition, Copeland is pursuing Turcios’s claim for asylum in the US.

Meanwhile, Turcios’s high school friend Anna Lawson, who recently graduated from McGill University in Canada and is taking a gap year before starting law school, is in disbelief that Turcios has been identified by her government as someone who doesn’t belong here. “Gerson is someone who is a benefit to our community and has only enriched it and helped people. I think the American dream really does live in him. He is such an embodiment of what it’s supposed to mean.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Eric Berger
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
State’s attorney general says scammers have made off with more than $100m in past two years

Scammers in New York have been using gold bars to steal money from victims, primarily older adults, and made off with more than $100m over the past two years, the state’s attorney general announced on Friday.

The scheme starts with victims receiving a fake pop-up message that states their computer or financial account has been compromised, the press release stated. The message includes a phone number to call, and when people do, the scammers convince the victims to provide remote access to their computers, which allows them to access their financial information or online bank accounts.

The victims are then directed to someone posing as law enforcement who tells them that their accounts have been compromised. To protect their money, the person says, they must withdraw it and purchase gold bars or coins and then turn them over to the authorities.

The scammers tell the victims not to discuss the breach with anyone and then send couriers to collect the gold.

“Targeting older adults with seemingly legitimate claims that their life savings are in immediate danger is flat-out cruel,” the state attorney general, Letitia James, said. “Seniors deserve to live comfortably without fear of losing their hard-earned savings to a manipulative scam. I am urging all New Yorkers to beware of these gold bar scams and report suspicious messages related to this scam to my office.”

The scam is not unique to New York. Victims in Hawaii, Maine, Washington DC and Wisconsin have reported the same thing happening to them.

In one case in July, scammers targeted an 85-year-old man in DC by email and phone claiming to be US federal agents, and told him his money was at risk and to protect it by buying gold, ABC-7 News in DC reported. When the victim tried to purchase $200,000 in gold from a dealer, the seller recognized the scam and alerted law enforcement.

The investigators then arrested the suspects when they arrived at the victim’s home to collect the gold.

The attorney general instructed the public not to call a number provided in a pop-up, text or email and not to provide anyone they don’t know remote access to their computer.

Individuals also should not provide money from a bank account at the urging of someone over the phone.
