https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Ed Pilkington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Dr Mark Fowler assisted in the failed execution of a Tennessee prisoner. Physicians are meant to heal patients - why is he working in the death chamber?

Mark Fowler, a physician with 25 years’ experience, stepped beneath the bright lights and approached the middle-aged man lying on a gurney. Around him, people in medical gowns prepared needles and sterile tubing.

It had all the appearances of a hospital setting.

Fowler had been called in to help establish an IV line through which the 57-year-old man, Tony Carruthers, would be injected with pharmaceutical drugs. The team had struggled to find a vein, so Fowler was summoned to set a central line – an intravenous catheter inserted into the major vein below the collarbone.

First, he had to numb the area where he would cut Carruthers with a scalpel and then pierce the vein with a large needle. But before he applied the lidocaine, he asked the IV team if “the patient” was allergic.

It was a strange choice of words. Carruthers was not a patient, and the room was not an OR.

Fowler had entered the death chamber at Riverbend maximum security prison in Nashville, Tennessee. Carruthers, condemned to death for a triple murder in 1994 for which there was no forensic evidence and over which he has always maintained his innocence, was forcibly strapped to the gurney.

The tube Fowler was attempting to insert would pipe the sedative pentobarbital at a lethally high dose.

Standing just a few feet away inside the chamber was Carruthers’ lawyer, Maria DeLiberato, a senior counsel at the ACLU’s capital punishment project.

She heard the doctor’s description of her client, and recoiled.

“He called Tony ‘the patient’,” she said. “And he was trying to kill him.”

Mark Walton Fowler, 68, of Union City, Tennessee, is an exceedingly rare breed: a doctor who signed up to participate in executions, and whose identity has become public.

In most cases, execution physicians are shielded by ironclad secrecy laws, allowing them to carry out their controversial work shrouded in anonymity.

Fowler has not been so lucky. He was identified, paradoxically, by the Tennessee department of corrections. A warden inadvertently let slip his name as he announced the death by lethal injection of another death row prisoner, Byron Black, 69, last August.

The public disclosure has clearly inconvenienced Fowler. Two months after his name was released, he was subpoenaed by lawyers acting for prisoners challenging the constitutionality of Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol.

In the course of the deposition, an irritated Fowler scolded his inquisitors.

“I certainly hope your office will handle this responsibly,” he chided, “and that I won’t be reading about myself in the Nashville Banner or the Guardian.”

Before Fowler could read about himself in the Guardian, I called him on his cell phone. He declined to respond to a list of detailed questions, but he did say that this was “a private situation. The inmate is entitled to privacy. The lawyers are churning up a lot of nonsense, and I don’t want to discuss it.”

The inconvenient truth, however, is that Fowler’s situation is no longer private. It has erupted into public debate about the death penalty and Tennessee’s record in applying it.

The botched procedure placed Carruthers in his own rare category: people who have survived an execution attempt.

Fowler was unable to secure the central line, and after Carruthers had spent an hour and 15 minutes being repeatedly pierced by Fowler and the IV team in his arms, feet and shoulder, the execution was called off.

Next Thursday, Tennessee is scheduled to execute Darrell Hines also by lethal injection. The prisoner, 65, who was convicted of a 1985 murder, is in poor health, having suffered multiple strokes that have left him partially paralyzed.

Hines’s lawyers have argued in court filings that if Fowler were to be allowed back into the death chamber for what would be his fifth execution, the same botched procedure endured by Carruthers would probably be repeated. They alleged that there would be “an intolerable risk that [Hines] will experience severe suffering due to the … use of insufficiently qualified medical personnel”.

On Thursday, the Tennessee supreme court denied a motion that would have obliged the state to disclose whether the physician will be on duty next week. That means he is now likely to disappear back into the shadows.

At a more fundamental level, Fowler’s unmasking has laid bare the ethical conundrum at the heart of lethal injections, America’s killing technique of choice for the past 44 years. From its inception, the protocol has been wrapped in the swaddling clothes of medicine.

It was billed as the humane answer to the primitive brutality of the electric chair or the firing squad. But to meet such claims, death penalty states have had to persuade doctors to participate – and there’s the rub.

For 2,500 years doctors have operated under the Hippocratic Oath, with its soaring edict: “Do no harm.” The following line of the oath is less well known, but for these purposes even more instructive: “To please no one will I prescribe a deadly drug, nor give advice which may cause his death.”

In 1980, two years before Charles Brooks in Texas became the first prisoner to be killed by lethal injection in the US, the American Medical Association issued a clear prohibition: “A physician must not participate in a legally authorized execution.”

As Corinna Lain has chronicled in her book, Secrets of the Killing State, that has whittled down the field of physicians available to death penalty states to a rump of those Lain calls the “dissenters” – doctors ethically flexible or contrarian enough to bring their white coats and healing arts into the death chamber.

And as we now know from the warden’s slip of the tongue, Fowler is one of them.

The road that led Fowler to Riverbend, Tennessee is long and winding. He studied public administration at the University of Tennessee (UT), then went into law.

Long before he became involved in executions, Fowler spent three years as a public defender. He even represented several capital defendants, managing in each case to persuade the jury to spare his client a death sentence.

Around 1994 Fowler made a dramatic career switch, retraining to become a doctor at the UT Memphis college of medicine. The yearbook of his 1999 graduating class shows him wearing a gown and glasses, smiling broadly. His appearance chimes with the description given by someone who has worked alongside Fowler: “He looks like the kind of fella who goes on fishing trips in Alabama and drinks beer.”

In a quarter century of medical practice Fowler has tried his hand at several different aspects of the profession. For the first decade or so he worked as an ER physician, then as a family doctor. Today, most of his income comes through numerous medical directorships, including of weight loss and aesthetic clinics, and a wound care facility.

There have been controversies along the way. In the deposition he said his employment ended at Centurion, the company that provides healthcare services to Tennessee’s prisons, after he engaged colleagues in a conversation about a transgender prisoner in a women’s prison in Connecticut whom he claimed had impregnated two other women.

We don’t know precisely what Fowler said, but it was provocative enough to inspire a formal complaint from the prison psychiatrist who overheard it.

Fowler writes occasional opinion columns for his local newspaper, the Union City Daily Messenger, that are reproduced by the conservative blog the Patriot Post. The articles give a glimpse into his staunchly rightwing, Trumpian worldview – a way of thinking whose proponents often advocate for the death penalty and have proposed reverting to older, brutal methods such as “firing squads”.

After Renee Good and Alex Pretti were shot dead in Minneapolis in January by federal officers amid Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, Fowler wrote that they had been “killed because they and others were violent and/or reckless” (neither victim engaged the officials in violence).

In February he penned a column that accused liberals of condoning violence. He wrote that “liberal logic” dictated that “Christian conservatives must be shut out of public discourse by killing them (Charlie Kirk)”.

In a column from June 2025 he addressed his previous life as a public defender. “I managed a number of death penalty cases in my career. None got the death penalty, although two cases come to mind where it was surely warranted,” he wrote.

In the same article, he recognised that there could be lapses in a criminal justice system in which overzealous prosecutors, “corrupt police”, and “prosecution-oriented judges” can be thrown together. The result can be that “the constitutional protections intended to protect individuals from erroneous convictions are watered down to nothing”.

In the course of last October’s deposition, Fowler related how he came to sign up as Tennessee’s execution doctor. Under the state’s official protocol, he is assigned the responsibility for setting a central line if necessary, and at the end of the procedure he must determine that the prisoner is dead.

Fowler said that he was a friend of the state’s previous death penalty physician. In 2018, “he asked me to accompany him to an execution so that I might take over when he retired.”

That rather bland narrative illuminates little as to motive. Could it be the money? During the deposition it was revealed that Fowler is paid $3,000 for every execution he attends, well below what he might command in other states such as Oklahoma ($15,000) and Arizona ($18,000).

When asked about the payments, Fowler grew tetchy. “I don’t wish to read about myself in the newspaper saying, ‘This bloodthirsty coward doctor gets money for doing this.’ I get paid for the time and effort of going.”

Further insight can be gleaned from an interview he gave NBC News shortly after the failed Carruthers execution. “Every attempt was made to minimize the defendant’s discomfort,” Fowler said. “No one wants Carruthers to suffer.”

But Carruthers’ lawyers say that what they witnessed was alarming. Maria DeLiberato, present in the chamber, was struck that from the moment Fowler entered the room, he took charge.

“Once he came in, it was clear that he was taking over the direction of everything. He was very assertive. ‘Take his socks off,’ he said.”

Fowler began jabbing Carruthers in his left foot, seeking a vein. After about 15 minutes he admitted defeat and refocused his efforts on the much more difficult challenge of securing a central line under the prisoner’s clavicle.

At this point, alarm bells began ringing for DeLiberato and her attorney colleagues. In his deposition, Fowler had said that the last time he had attempted a central line was back in his ER days, about 13 years previously.

The procedure is complicated and fraught with potential mishaps. To be adroit at setting a central line you have to refresh your abilities regularly.

“Nobody should be doing a dangerous procedure such as a central line unless they do it routinely and frequently, so that their skills are maintained,” said John Greer, a retired physician. Greer was among 50 medical experts who wrote a joint letter to Tennessee’s Republican governor, Bill Lee, lamenting the involvement of medical professionals in state executions.

Kit Thomas, the deputy chief of Nashville’s capital habeas unit, was present at the deposition when Fowler revealed the long hiatus in him placing central lines. She was also on hand to give real-time legal advice as the Carruthers execution was proceeding.

When she received a call from DeLiberato saying that Fowler was about to attempt a central line, she went into instant overdrive. “We knew the last time he had set a central line was 13 years ago, so we said, ‘Object! He’s not qualified!’”

DeLiberato did just that. She rushed back into the death chamber, where Fowler was crouched over Carruthers, and objected to the warden that the doctor was unqualified for the job.

“Yes, I am qualified,” Fowler snapped back.

At which point the warden said: “Doctor, do your job.”

Fowler went ahead and cut Carruthers’ skin. DeLiberato is still haunted by what she witnessed next.

“Tony was moaning and groaning in a guttural way that I can still hear. It sounded like agony, and I could see blood slowly seeping out of the puncture.”

Despite the terrible scene, Fowler remained preternaturally calm. DeLiberato said: “He was dispassionate. He didn’t say anything. He didn’t try to reassure anyone.”

The doctor struggled to set up a central line for 16 minutes, as “the patient” groaned “it hurts, it hurts”.

Not able to do what he had been hired to do, he had to concede defeat a second time.

The execution was called off, and Carruthers was sent back to his cell. DeLiberato visited him there about an hour later.

In a declaration she filed for the courts she recalled that the prisoner was “sweaty, pale, tearful, and he seemed to be in shock and pain. He could barely stand or walk.”

Carruthers looked up at DeLiberato and told her Fowler “was hurting me, and knew he was hurting me”.

The Guardian sent Fowler an email and text message detailing how Carruthers had accused him of inflicting suffering. The doctor did not reply.

With days to go to Tennessee’s next scheduled lethal injection, the enigma of the execution doctor is looming large. Carruthers’ sister, Tonya Hervey, has filed a complaint against Fowler with state health authorities alleging he violated medical ethics and caused her brother excruciating pain.

For Kit Thomas, who is a part of the legal team representing Darrell Hines as he prepares to go to his death next Thursday, the revelation of Fowler’s involvement has given us “a peek behind the curtain”. What it showed us, she said, was that the department of corrections was drawing on “unqualified physicians” who were “willing to engage in killing people for $3,000 a pop”.

DeLiberato remains deeply disturbed by what she witnessed, standing just a few feet away as the doctor worked on her client. She believes it should make us all think twice about the asserted humanity of lethal injections.

“They want to make this a medical procedure, but it’s not. It’s premeditated murder. There’s really no way to kill a person humanely, with or without a doctor. What I witnessed was torture.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.summary: Dr Mark Fowler, 68, of Union City, Tennessee, was a physician who signed up to participate in executions. He was named by a warden who accidentally let slip his name as he announced the death by lethal Tennessee's execution doctor.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Who’s winning New York City’s war on rats: rodents or trash bins?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Edward Helmore in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
City on track to record fewest reported rat sightings since pandemic as Mamdani’s ‘containerization’ program brings bins to boroughs

Is New York finally winning its war on rats? Or are New Yorkers’ vermin neighbors merely adapting to changing circumstances and, at least in some neighborhoods, staying out of sight?

With an estimated one rat for every three people, New York’s long-running rat war is in a period of uneasy detente.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Last week Bloomberg reported that New York is on track to record the fewest reported rat sightings since the pandemic, down 22% in the first seven months of 2026 compared to a year earlier, a drop attributed to a “war on rats” campaign initiated by former mayor Eric Adams.

The city’s population had spiked during the Coivd pandemic when rats flourished unchecked due to uncollected trash, an increase in take-out and delivery food, and outdoor dining sheds that provided snacks and refuge.

As mayor, Adams was fixated on rats. His administration posted an advertisement for a “rat czar” that would require applicants to be “highly motivated and somewhat bloodthirsty” and possessed of both “stamina and stagecraft” and a “swashbuckling attitude, crafty humor and general aura of badassery”.

When Adams appointed Kathleen Corradi to the post in early 2023, he said sagely: “Rats impact how you feel about the city you’re in … many of us live in communities where rats think they run the city.”

The measures Adams’ instituted included “Rat Pack” teams, a bin program that Adams called the city’s “trash revolution” requiring trash cans throughout the five boroughs to reduce household waste left on the streets for collection in plastic trash bags.

During his tenure, Adams ordered the formation of specialized teams to tackle the estimated 600,000 rats that live in the city’s street tree beds. Thousands live in holes in the city parks, venturing out only at night to feed on trash.

All businesses and low-density residential buildings, producers of around 70% of the city’s trash, were required to containerize in 2024. Full containerization of the city’s trash is expected to be complete by 2031.

Leading rodentologist Robert Corrigan said he felt “very positive” about the containerization effort. He told Bloomberg that garbage is a rat’s favorite food and lids on trash cans are “the true hero of rat management”.

The first concerted effort to tackle the issue came in late 2022 when Adams and then-Sanitation commissioner Jessica Tisch launched a “Get Stuff Clean” initiative, cleaning up neglected areas and combatting litter. Tisch was asked if a sanitation department flyer featuring a travel influencer rat with a suitcase was too cute. Tisch said the point was to get people’s attention.

“Everyone that knows me, they know one thing: I hate rats,” Adams told reporters when the city narrowed the window when trash can be put out on the curb. He acknowledged that he’d be branded a murderer. “Well, you know what? We’re going to kill rats.”

The current mayor, Zohran Mamdani, does not appear to share Adams obsession with rats. He dropped the “rat czar” position but has expanded the city’s “containerization” program to six districts, bringing oversize “Empire Bins” to 25,000 new residences. The city is set to lose 30,000 parking spots as a result, alongside a city council proposal threatening up to 300,000 spots.

“In the wealthiest city in the wealthiest nation in the history of the world, no New Yorker should have their sidewalks covered in garbage. By finishing the job on containerization, we will ensure New York City’s streets remain the envy of the world,” said Mamdani said in April.

But is it really as simple as that? Not all of the city’s neighborhoods have seen the same improvements. West Harlem, which as been fully containerized since June 2025, reported rat sightings fell 34% in the first seven months of 2026 compared with last year.

Though overall rat sightings are down so far this year, it’s not uniform across community districts. Parts of Brooklyn’s Dumbo and Brooklyn Heights are down 48%. But the gentrified East Village, Lower East Side and parts of Chinatown have seen a 37% surge in rodent reports compared to this time last year.

Overall numbers of rats, or rat sightings, have dropped, but they are not below pre-Covid levels, suggesting that the New Yorker’s furry frenemies are still very much in situ despite the loss of Covid dining sheds and easy-to-access refuse.

Gil Bloom of Standard Pest Management, a company that consults for local and federal government agencies, says rat sightings dropped to a record low in 2019. “Covid rearranged the topography and rats went wild. They were running around horribly once we had these food shacks up all around the city and the population skyrocketed.”

Bloom says the city’s rat population has certainly gone down with trash containerization, but warns it would be unwise to declare victory given the adaptability of rodents. “We have to consider who our adversary is,” he says. “They’re still in the underground and catch spaces of the city.”

With some trash still in bags, and the time between trash being left out and collected, rats “have reset their clocks. They know when the trash is going out. People litter. There are food and fruit stands. There’s still enough food around for rodents to survive.”

While the visibility of rats has been reduced that doesn’t necessarily reflect the total number. New Yorkers relationship to rats, like many attributes of city life, is psychological bordering on metaphysical. “If they’re out at night and people don’t see them is it still a rat? It’s still a rat, but no one is seeing it,” Bloom says.

The East Village has older buildings, the large Tompkins Square Park and city infrastructure in disrepair below ground. Plus it has a younger population more likely to be out at night. Parks don’t used rodenticide because of the hawks and birds, but use traps with liquid nitrogen to freeze the holes.

The variables are endless, Bloom says.

“Rats are burrowing animals and in a city with limited earth and space, a rat is going to find you. We’ve learned over the last 15 or 20 years that a rats’ range is much greater than we previously thought,” he says. “ Rats only require one ounce of food and water a day, they don’t need a whole sandwich.

“So there’s a direction toward control, and the numbers are down to pre-Covid levels. But pre-Covid there were still a lot of rats, so no one is saying, ‘Hey, there’s no rats,’”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The number of rats has been reduced, but it doesn't necessarily reflect the total number of rodents. The city’s population had spiked during the Coivd pandemic when rats flourished unchecked due to uncollected trash.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Lion saved as cub from Ukraine war and brought to US battles rare fungal disease
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Richard Luscombe
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Four-year-old Taras, who now resides at a Minnesota sanctuary, was diagnosed with an often fatal infection

A lion that escaped the war in Ukraine after being found as a four-month-old cub inside a duffel bag at Odesa railway station is facing an even greater battle for survival in his new home in Minnesota from a rare and often fatal fungal disease.

Taras; his two sisters, Lesya and Stefania; and an unrelated, slightly older cub from Kyiv named Prada were brought to the US in November 2022 by the Wildcat Sanctuary, a secluded private reserve near Sandstone, Minnesota, that arranged their rescue with the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW).

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

An American veterinarian working in Ukraine’s capital, which was under sporadic attack from Russian missiles and drones, evacuated them from Kyiv to safety in Poland, a 36-hour land journey, where they awaited import permits for the US.

Now aged four, Taras was an energetic head of the Ukrainian pride until May, when veterinarians noticed he was sluggish and off his food. Numerous tests, including a 180-mile (290km) round trip for an expensive scan and lung biopsy at a specialist clinic in Minneapolis, diagnosed blastomycosis, a non-contagious fungal infection usually contracted from soil.

The condition was blamed in the death of a white tiger called Ginger at a wildlife sanctuary in Wisconsin in June. Also known as Gilchrist’s disease, it is often fatal in humans and animals if not caught early and treated.

Tammy Thies, the sanctuary’s founder and chief executive, said Taras responded well to intensive treatment, including twice-daily injections of extra-strength antifungal medication through an IV line in the early weeks, and had rejoined his pride.

But he still requires oral medicine twice a day, she said, and it could be weeks or months before sanctuary staff could be confident he was out of the woods.

“He was in a fight for his life,” she said. “Usually when big cats are diagnosed with blastomycosis, it’s when they’re showing respiratory distress, and by that time the disease is so advanced that even the aggressive antifungal medication can be life-threatening. There’s a very low chance of survival.

“The specialist told us he had a guarded prognosis, and when I asked: ‘Does he have a 30% chance?’, they all just looked at me and looked at their feet. We knew this was going to be an uphill battle, and we might not be able to save him.”

Thies said Taras’s survival was his “second miracle”, after escaping the Ukraine war with his siblings.

“Everybody we reached out to just told us they were sorry and not to be optimistic,” she said. “We’re just really grateful for the staff and the vet team that found this early, before he was showing breathing symptoms, because I don’t think we could have saved him.”

His reunion with his sisters was emotional. “He wanted to be with his family, so we started with one play date with a sister at a time,” she said.

“We were concerned that after being away for weeks they could pick on him [but] there was so much nuzzling going on, and so much rolling around on each other, the pride welcomed him with open arms, and they’ve been inseparable ever since.”

Even so, Taras needs to be separated twice, every day, so his pride members do not steal his food with the medication in it.

The lions’ origin is impossible to know, Thies said, but they were likely taken from their mother after birth and destined to become part of the illegal but lucrative international trade in exotic animals, at least until the start of the war thwarted the smugglers’ plans.

“As borders were getting shut down and checkpoints set up, a lot of these traffickers were dumping the animals versus trying to smuggle them across the border to sell them,” she said.

“It was just devastating after all he went through, after this lion had fought so hard and come out so much stronger, to then get a diagnosis of a fungal disease in his lungs, and to know he might not make it.

“That was the hardest for us. He has a fight on his hands but still has a lot of life to live, and we were all going to come together and fight for him.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Senate passes funding bill to prevent shutdown through US midterms
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Chris Stein in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Bill must still be approved by House but would keep government running at current funding levels

The US Senate on Friday passed a government funding bill that will prevent a shutdown through the midterm elections, though it still must be approved by the House of Representatives.

The continuing resolution (CR) passed by a 90-6 vote will keep the government running at its current funding levels until 11 December, more than a month past the midterms in which Democrats are hoping to regain control of Congress and block Donald Trump’s legislative agenda for the final two years of his presidency.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The measure’s passage signals a recognition by both parties that they would prefer to avoid a messy battle over federal spending in the weeks leading up to the 3 November vote.

The government will shut down after 30 September if new funding is not approved, and the Republican Senate appropriations committee chair, Susan Collins, called the CR “a major step toward averting a damaging shutdown that only harms vital programs and federal workers”, and noted it makes no major changes to funding levels.

The House had last month approved a different CR that would continue funding until 4 December. It is unclear which bill will ultimately be adopted – the House is on recess until the end of the month, and senators were expected to leave Washington DC for their break following the vote.

Patty Murray, the top Democrat on the Senate appropriations committee, said the House’s bill had “several major issues” that the Senate’s version addressed. It would block until 11 December a new rule by the White House office of management and budget that Democrats fear would allow the Trump administration to cancel grants at any time for any reason. The Senate CR also closes what Murray called a “loophole” in the House bill that would have allowed the White House to take money meant for other purposes and give it to the border patrol.

“Today’s CR gives us the breathing room necessary to work out a budget that helps make life more affordable to working families and reins in Trump’s rampant chaos, his rampant corruption,” the Democratic minority leader, Chuck Schumer, said ahead of the vote.

Democrats instigated a government shutdown last year when they refused to approve funding bills without an agreement to extend subsidies for Affordable Care Act health plans. That led to the longest funding lapse in US history, but ultimately no agreement to keep the cost offsets going after the shutdown ended 43 days later.

Some government agencies shut down again briefly earlier this year after Democrats held up a funding bill for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in protest of the killings by federal agents of two US citizens in Minneapolis during an intensive immigration enforcement drive.

While an agreement was reached to resolve that blockade, the two parties did not agree on funding DHS for weeks, as Democrats held out for reforms to immigration enforcement operations.

A bipartisan agreement was reached to fund the department operations exclusive of the agencies involved in Trump’s mass deportation push, then Republicans passed a party-line bill that allocated funding to Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection for the duration of Trump’s presidency, with no reforms to immigration enforcement.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Prosecutor fired over blogposts critical of Trump sues US justice department
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Will Rosenzweig’s defunct blog was publicized online by conservative pundit who tagged senior DoJ officials

A federal prosecutor fired last year over critical comments he had written as a private citizen about Donald Trump sued the justice department on Friday, saying his termination violated his first amendment rights.

Will Rosenzweig was two weeks away from trying a multimillion-dollar Medicare fraud case when a blog he had written years earlier covering a broad range of topics was publicized online by a conservative political commentator who also included a screenshot of Rosenzweig’s LinkedIn account and tagged senior justice department officials.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Less than three hours after the post, the lawsuit says, Rosenzweig received an email signed by then attorney general Pam Bondi informing him that he had been fired. The news came as Rosenzweig was out of town with his family observing the Jewish holiday of Rosh Hashana.

The September 2025 termination was part of a sweeping personnel purge over the last year-and-a-half inside the justice department, which has fired prosecutors who worked on investigations into Trump and others seen as being against the administration’s efforts.

A lawsuit filed in federal court in Miami, where Rosenzweig worked as a federal prosecutor for five years, seeks reinstatement to the job as well as backpay and a court order declaring his firing unlawful.

The complaint says Rosenzweig was a highly respected prosecutor who received “consistent praise and awards” and was so highly valued in his office that he was told just weeks before his firing that he would be getting a special parking spot due to his performance.

“Will Rosenzweig was an excellent prosecutor who returned millions of dollars to the taxpayers by prosecuting healthcare fraud cases,” said a statement from his lawyers, Margaret Donovan, Daniel Fridman and Adam Fels.

“Yet the Department of Justice fired him on the eve of trial because, years ago as a private citizen, he published criticisms of President Trump. Since the current Department of Justice will not stand up for the first amendment and the American people, we will. We look forward to vindicating Will’s rights in court.”

The blog Rosenzweig had maintained had been defunct for more than six years at the time of his firing and included his thoughts on travel, sports and other “apolitical, anodyne topics” in addition to critical observations about Trump and other political candidates, the lawsuit says.

The conservative commentator Natalie Winters, who has a large online following, characterized Rosenzweig as “a rogue Trump hater” as she posted screenshots of some of his political musings, according to the complaint, which characterizes the firing as a direct assault on Rosenzweig’s free-speech rights.

“The department’s conduct rests on a single premise: a citizen must forever refrain from criticizing the government and its leaders to remain eligible to serve it,” the lawsuit says.

“That rule would force every American who might one day serve to choose between speaking freely now and working for the government later. Conditioning public employment on political loyalty, where a party card rather than merit opens the door to a government job, is a way of life in Havana and Caracas. It has no place here.”

A justice department spokesperson declined to comment, citing pending litigation.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US Senate passes Russia sanctions bill championed by Lindsey Graham
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Chris Stein
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Late senator spent final days of his life working to advance bill that will now head to the House after 86-11 Senate vote

By a large, bipartisan margin, the US Senate on Friday approved a bill intended to punish Russia and countries that buy its petroleum exports over the invasion of Ukraine, capping a legislative push that was spurred by the death of its champion, the Republican senator Lindsey Graham.

The measure, renamed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia Act in honor of the late senator’s work on the issue, was approved by an 86-11 vote. Rand Paul of Kentucky was the sole Republican to oppose the legislation, together with 10 Democrats.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The bill would impose new sanctions and visa bans on Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, and top military commanders, as well as put tariffs of up to 500% on the country’s exports. It would also allow Donald Trump to impose levies of up to 100% on goods from countries that are the top five importers of Russian oil and gas.

The proposal was a top priority for Graham, a Republican senator from South Carolina who spent the final days of his life working to advance it. But the effort had became mired in months of negotiations between the White House and Senate leadership.

After Graham’s sudden death last month at the age of 71 following a trip to Kyiv, party leaders announced an agreement to get the bill through the chamber and honor his legacy as an ally of Ukraine. The Senate took the first step toward advancing it last month, on the day of Graham’s funeral, with Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, watching from the chamber.

“This bill forces those primary countries keeping Russia’s economy afloat to make a simple yet critical choice – a choice between doing business with America or buying cheap Russian energy,” said Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister who was appointed to his seat after his death.

Graham, who presided over the Senate and announced the bill’s passage, added: “This legislation tells Russia’s customers that the United States of America will not sit by while they fund Putin’s assault.”

The measure was a relatively rare bipartisan accomplishment ahead of November’s midterm elections, where Democrats hope to channel voter sentiment against Trump to regain control of Congress.

“By imposing steep sanctions that will further drain the Kremlin’s war chest, Congress is delivering an important reminder to Putin and his allies that this is a losing war and authoritarianism will never go unchallenged,” said Chuck Schumer, the minority leader.

“I urge Trump to use these sanctions to hit Putin where it hurts. Continuing to appease Putin won’t work.”

After the vote, Zelenskyy thanked the US Senate, writing on X that the bill’s advancement “certainly helps increase pressure ⁠on the aggressor ​to bring ​this insane Russian ​war against ​our ‌independence and ​our ​people to an end”.

Ursula ⁠von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, also cheered the Senate’s action. “Together, let us drain Russia’s ​means to continue a war it cannot win,” she wrote on X. “With hard-hitting, complementary ⁠sanctions, Europe and the United ​States can ​once again ​show what historic ​partners can ‌achieve when ​we ​act together.”

The measure now heads to the House of Representatives, which may consider once it returns from recess at the end of August.

Some Democrats have warned that the bill would give Trump new tariff powers at a time when he has put such levies at the center of his trade policy. Paul and Democratic senator Ron Wyden had offered an amendment that would have stripped some of the new tariff authority from the text, but the Senate rejected it by a 32-64 vote.

“This bill gives him so much discretion that Trump can ultimately decide what countries to tariff, or what countries to exempt. And he can modify tariffs at his will,” said Wyden, who voted against the bill.

“Trump can pick and choose even more countries to tariff every 180 days, but there is no mechanism in this bill for Congress to roll back these tariffs,” he continued.

“If Congress passes this bill, members will be condoning the tariff chaos of the last year and a half – and inviting more.”

Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee, and Don Beyer, the senior Democrat on the joint economic committee, criticized the legislation for creating “sweeping new tariff authorities that the president could weaponize with abandon, as he has repeatedly done in the past”.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Trump renews bid to fire Fed governor Lisa Cook despite supreme court ruling
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Gaya Gupta
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
White House continues to target Cook despite decision from justices that upheld Federal Reserve’s independence

Donald Trump is attempting once again to oust the US Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook over allegations of mortgage fraud, despite a recent US supreme court decision that upheld the central bank’s independence.

Cook reportedly received a letter from the White House this week that provided notice, in accordance to the supreme court’s June ruling, that Trump was “considering removing” her from her Fed position over the same claims of mortgage fraud that he levied against her last summer.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The letter, first reported by ABC News, accused Cook of falling “well short of the standard” required of a sitting Fed governor and requested she provide a written response to the allegations within three weeks.

The supreme court in June ruled 5-4 that Cook was entitled to stay on as Fed governor while she fights the president’s allegations, writing in its majority opinion that Trump “failed to afford Cook the procedural protections to which she was entitled by statute”.

“Without such protections, she could not properly dispute the charges the president laid against her,” the justices said.

In response to the White House’s letter, one of Cook’s lawyers, Abbe D Lowell, called the allegations “as baseless now as they were a year ago when President Trump tried to remove Governor Cook and interfere with the independence of the Federal Reserve”.

“No matter what President Trump tries to do next, this much is clear under the facts and Supreme Court precedent – there is no valid cause for removing Governor Cook,” Lowell said in a statement. “As we did before, we will challenge this latest pretext and preserve her position and the historic role of the Fed.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Cook was appointed by Joe Biden in 2022 to a 14-year term that will end in 2038. She is the first Black woman to serve as a Fed governor. Before she joined the Fed, she served on Barack Obama’s council of economic advisers and has taught at Harvard University and Stanford University.

Trump first abruptly fired Cook last August in an unprecedented attack on the central bank’s independence. The White House accused her of wrongly designating two separate properties in Georgia and Michigan as her primary residence and failing to report rental income on her Atlanta property for two years. Cook denied the allegations and sued the Trump administration for firing her without cause or proper procedure.

Cook and her legal team have maintained that the claims of mortgage fraud are based on “inadvertent” paperwork errors and that the administration is “cherrypicking” facts.

Cook’s firing and ongoing legal battles also coincided with Trump’s attacks on the Fed for not lowering rates. Cook, along with then Fed chair, Jerome Powell, had backed the central bank’s decision not to lower rates, which drew the ire of the White House. Trump called Powell “too stupid and too political” and launched a justice department investigation into his renovations of the Fed’s headquarters in Washington, which has since been dropped.

The Fed is now under the leadership of Kevin Warsh, a Trump pick who had previously shown favor towards cutting rates. Warsh has maintained that he will make decisions based on economic data, not the will of the president, and has made it his mission to fight the country’s heightened inflation, which typically is addressed by rate hikes.

“We’re an independent central bank,” he said in response to questioning from Democratic House members at a hearing in July. “We’re honored to be independent.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Democratic party needs to do more than represent wealthy progressives | Dustin Guastella
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Dustin Guastella
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
New research shows that a class gap on the left threatens any winning coalition – but there are ways to address it

D
ebates on the left are typically framed as a division between moderates and progressives, with the two sides wrestling over how best to form a governing coalition. Yet, in many ways, this divide obscures a much bigger fault line: the class divide. The fact is, many of the Democratic party’s ideological factions consist almost exclusively of college-educated professionals. As a result, the priorities of this class tend to dominate the party’s appeals. The priorities of working-class voters, meanwhile, are an afterthought.

A new report from Jared Abbott, the director of the Center for Working Class Politics, and Joan Williams, author of Outclassed: How the Left Lost the Working Class and How to Win Them Back, looks at ways to bridge the yawning class divide that threatens the possibility of forming a winning coalition.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

They developed an original survey to explore the various attitude “gaps” between the broad working class (defined as non-college educated, middle income workers) and the liberal upper middle class (Democratic-leaning college graduates with a household income in the top 25%).

The resulting report, titled The Left’s Coalition Crisis: Understanding the Massive Divide Between Working Class and College Educated Voters, and How to Bridge it, is, according to the authors, “the most comprehensive review available to date” of class-based political attitudes across a number of issue areas.

The first thing to note about the gaps between the educated upper middle class and the working class is that the latter overwhelmingly prioritize economic issues, while the former lean toward cultural ones.

Of the top 12 political priorities listed by working-class respondents, 11 are economic concerns. The only non-economic issue prized by the working class was a desire to lower the crime rate. Meanwhile, educated upper-income respondents rated cultural and symbolic issues over economic concerns. Of their top 12 priorities, only six were economic. They also rate abstract ideals over concrete, material ones. Educated voters prioritized “resisting authoritarianism” above “protecting social security” and “ending racism” above “protecting Medicaid”.

On an issue by issue basis, the largest gaps that Abbott and Williams found were along culture, climate, crime and immigration issues. That is, the very issues many college-educated liberals have built their political identities around. Maybe that wouldn’t be such a problem if these issues were largely downplayed by Democratic party leaders, in favor of shared economic grievances. But that’s hardly the case.

Not only do the cultural priorities of the privileged fail to speak to working-class voters’ economic frustrations, but, because Democratic party primaries are dominated by educated upper-income voters, these appeals have come to define liberalism itself.

No doubt, the surest way to get a huge cheer at a liberal political rally is to simply mention racism or authoritarianism. Bonus points if you bravely proclaim your unwillingness to “throw X group under the bus”. Such rhetorical gestures have the added benefit of committing candidates to nothing in particular, and thus never threaten potential rich donors.

You might say, so what? Who cares if candidates say some throwaway lines about the “marginalized” at a campaign rally; what’s the harm?

As Abbott and Williams demonstrate, signaling allegiance to such political priorities is far from costless. Embracing the values and slogans of the privileged tells working-class voters that you are either aloof to, or ignorant of, their priorities.

And worse, that you don’t respect working people as political actors. As the authors note, college graduates in Europe and the United States “are more biased against the less-educated than any other stigmatized group”, including racial, religious, and sexual minorities. Blue-collar workers can sense liberal condescension in smarmy injunctions to “be kind”, and they resent what they perceive as upper-class attempts to morally re-educate them.

It gets worse. Even if upper-income progressives steer clear of cultural condescension, their economic priorities are also class-bound. While working-class voters prioritize jobs, wages and economic growth, the educated knowledge workers are mainly concerned with high costs. This, too, is a function of the latter’s relatively privileged class position.

Despite recent wage erosion, the college-educated set still make much more than their non-college educated counterparts – between 60% and 80% more on average. This wage premium, combined with our K-shaped economy, means that the well-educated and well-heeled, those in the top 20% of the income hierarchy, now drive nearly 60% of all consumer spending.

For many educated, upper-income voters – especially those in corporate careers – the defining feature of their economic lives is consuming, not producing. As such, they are extremely sensitive to price increases.

Working-class voters are too, but for very different reasons. It’s the devaluing of work that drives their frustrations. As the authors point out, for the working class, and especially for blue-collar workers, it’s work, not consumption, that defines their lives.

But long-term wage stagnation, and the disappearance of good stable jobs, has meant that essential goods have become even more difficult to afford. Here, globalization plays a major role. And, on that issue, the data show yet another chasm between the popular classes.

While some liberal appeals to “affordability” emphasize the need to scrap tariffs and embrace more liberal immigration rules in order to broaden consumer demand (and lower the agricultural wage-bill), working-class voters are rightly skeptical of these solutions.

Restrictions on trade and immigration represent efforts to address the long neglected problems of wage stagnation. Free-trade has devastated the working class, shuttering thousands of factories and sinking many into drug-addiction and despair. At the same time, mass migration has eroded the wage packet for manual workers. For them, addressing affordability must mean policies that speak to the essentially place-bound character of blue-collar life.

While professional-class status is portable – effectively equivalent in London, New York, Paris or Washington DC – working-class status is not so liquid. Seniority in a job or trade is not typically a transferrable credential. For these reasons place-loyalty matters a great deal to working-class people.

On the other hand, globalization and the growth of “knowledge work” has supercharged select high-income metro areas, where many professionals live and where progressives thrive. Democrats now represent nine of the top 10 highest-income congressional districts in the country.

The truth is, educated upper-income voters, be they progressive or moderate, largely benefit from low-wage immigrant labor and cheap foreign goods. Contrary to the place-based loyalty of blue collar workers, they prize their status as global-citizens and cosmopolitan consumers.

Navigating these tensions isn’t easy, but Abbott and Williams did find a number of issues that could serve as a foundation for a progressive program of popular-class unity.

Getting it right means addressing both the wage and the price side of the affordability equation, downgrading the cultural priorities of the privileged (including on abortion and transgender issues), and grappling with the tension between globalist affinities and local loyalty.

By focusing only on those issues that win more than two-thirds of support from both working-class and educated upper-middle-class respondents, they propose a political program with the following planks: allow Medicare to negotiate lower prescription drug prices, protect and improve social security, spend $150bn on infrastructure, expand Medicaid, ratchet up education spending, and raise the minimum wage.

That’s a great start. But it could be improved by an even greater emphasis on working-class priorities. We need new trade rules, revitalized national industry and real pro-labor immigration reform that can help right the wrongs of globalism.

We ought to advocate expansive and generous policies that emphasize the importance of family life. Why not make giving birth entirely free, implement national paid-parental leave, and provide affordable childcare?

And finally, we need to make expanding and improving badly underfunded local police and fire departments a national priority in order to make every neighborhood and community safe. Such priorities speak directly to felt needs and they signal a genuine political attempt at reorganizing politics around working-class demands, rather than the preferences of the professionals.

Putting working-class priorities first will no doubt result in political tensions. Flashpoints around gender, immigration and even class itself, will break out. Getting through those fights will be necessary if progressives ever hope to expand their coalition by reaching into the working class.

Plus, who knows, maybe professional-class progressives could learn a thing or two from their working-class counterparts.

Dustin Guastella is a research associate at the Center for Working Class Politics and the director of operations for Teamsters Local 623. He is a Guardian US columnist

The authors found that the top priorities of the working class are economic concerns. Democrats now represent nine of the top 10 highest-income congressional districts in the country.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Rest assured, the new CDC director thinks ‘abortion surveillance’ is essential | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
An exchange between Dr Erica Schwartz and Senator Josh Hawley during her confirmation hearing is alarming

R
obert F Kennedy Jr’s new cooking show isn’t the only big news out of the public health world this week. On Wednesday, Dr Erica Schwartz was confirmed by the US Senate as director ‌of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), making her the first Black woman to hold the position. This is the first time in almost a year that the agency has had a permanent leader; the previous director, Susan Monarez, only lasted 29 days before she was ousted for butting heads with RFK about US vaccine policies. Translation: she was a little too keen on following accepted science for the Trump administration.

So is Schwartz an RFK-approved vaccine skeptic who thinks you can cure cancer by praying to trees? Surprisingly: no. Schwartz, who served as deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first term, actually has government experience and a public health background. During her confirmation hearing in July, she walked a careful tightrope when asked about her stance towards vaccines. Schwartz said she “will never betray the science” but also dodged questions about how she would handle pressure from Kennedy.

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

But don’t breathe a sigh of relief quite yet. During that same confirmation hearing, Schwartz made some chilling remarks about abortion surveillance when quizzed on the issue by Missouri senator Josh Hawley, an anti-abortion lawmaker who wants to ban the abortion pill mifepristone nationwide.

“The CDC collects data on abortions that are committed in the United States of America through a system called the Abortion Reporting System,” Hawley said when asking Schwartz whether she would commit to collecting detailed data on abortions. “This system is voluntary, and so a number of states, not coincidentally large blue states, do not turn over any data, so that it’s difficult to get a picture of just how many abortions and under what circumstances are committed in this country. We do know the numbers are going way up.”

“Senator, you have my commitment,” Schwartz replied. “Abortion surveillance is absolutely a critical component of what the CDC is currently doing.”

“I also want to make sure that certain states are not conflating emergency services and hiding abortions in that emergency services case definition,” she added. “We need to make sure we’re pulling out true abortions and making sure that we’re really having clear case definitions regarding abortions so the data is actually accurate.”

“Tremendous,” Hawley replied. He seemed very happy with her response.

If you are concerned about the growing criminalization of abortion and surveillance of pregnant women in the US, then absolutely nothing about this is tremendous. I’ve quoted the majority of the exchange between Hawley and Schwartz instead of paraphrasing it, because the choice of language is so alarming. First, look at the way in which Hawley frames the issue. He talks about abortions being committed: a loaded word which makes you think of murder. (Imagine it in another medical context: I’m having a mammogram committed tomorrow!) Then he insinuates that blue states are hiding abortion data for nefarious reasons. As it is, 44 states plus Washington DC have some form of mandated abortion reporting, according to the Guttmacher Institute, and there is no evidence that these states are hiding anything. New York is an outlier in that it only requires abortion reporting when a patient makes a request related to the disposition of the fetus’s remains. Which seems like a sensible policy that protects the privacy of people who have had abortions.

Now look at Schwartz’s reply. Why would abortion surveillance be “a critical component” of what the CDC is doing? Data collection around abortions can serve legitimate purposes, sure, but isn’t it rather more important for the CDC to be, I dunno, controlling and preventing diseases? Her reference to “true abortions” (as opposed to fake ones?) and to states “hiding abortions” is also worrying. Pregnant people are already dying preventable deaths because providers in states with abortion bans are terrified of treating them. This sort of language from the CDC director is going to make the situation even worse.

Donald Trump has called Schwartz “a STAR”. If her exchange with Hawley is anything to go by, however, she seems to be yet another stooge: happy to facilitate the Trump administration’s anti-abortion agenda and politicization of public health.

“Erica Schwartz’s testimony … should alarm everyone who believes private medical decisions belong to patients, not politicians,” Mini Timmaraju, the president and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All, said in a statement. She added that, under the Trump administration, “abortion surveillance could be expanded or weaponized to collect more intrusive information, spread disinformation about reproductive health care, and support efforts to investigate or criminalize patients and providers”.

As activists and experts have repeatedly said, overturning Roe v Wade was just the beginning of the new war on reproductive rights in the US – a war facilitated by an unprecedented network of surveillance technology. The convicted felon in the White House seems intent on treating every pregnant woman as a potential criminal.

During a private call with religious groups, the acting attorney general, Todd Blanche, said efforts to reverse the Biden administration’s efforts to protect abortion were “taking longer than we want”. He seemed to suggest that the administration was working to restrict access to abortion pills and said: “We don’t have complete victory yet, but we will have victory, and victory will be soon, and it will be permanent.” Blanche has faced a rocky road to confirmation as attorney general. The bad news is that the government’s anti-abortion agenda will continue whether he gets the role or not.

That’s according to a new ruling by the state’s supreme court. No doubt they’ll soon be forced to report abortions, though!

“If you’ll notice, women don’t method act because we have things to take care of,” Taylor-Joy said in an interview promoting her new Apple TV show Lucky (which is extremely good, by the way). Back in 2024, Natalie Portman similarly described method acting as a “luxury women can’t afford”. She added: “I don’t think that children or partners would be very understanding of, you know, me making everyone call me ‘Jackie Kennedy’ all the time.”

More than a million people watched Towle navigate her cholangiocarcinoma, a rare cancer of the bile ducts. She raised awareness of the disease and built community. However, because the internet is often toxic, she was also accused by trolls of exaggerating or even faking her cancer. It even got to a point where Towle’s doctor had to confirm to the New York Times that she had stage 4 cancer.

This is not some unfortunate byproduct of war; it is by design. Last year, a UN report found that Israel’s systemic attacks on women’s healthcare in Gaza amount to “genocidal acts”. The report noted that Israel’s destruction of maternity wards, an IVF clinic and control on essential supplies into Gaza “destroyed in part the reproductive capacity of Palestinians in Gaza as a group”.

A cat called Toast Malone survived a fire that destroyed an apartment complex in Utah by hiding in a closet for three days. Toast did not get burned, and has now been reunited with their family. Now they’re the toast of the town.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Parenting is hard. Should we let AI do it for us? | Dave Schilling
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Dave Schilling
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Tech companies offer eye-movement trackers, personalized podcasts and ‘optimized nap predictions’. Who actually needs this?

W
hat job in our world is less lucrative than being a parent? A Hollywood internship? Volunteering at a soup kitchen? Professional writer? Parenting is the only job you have to pay money to do. Lots of money. Lodging, clothes, food, school, Pokémon cards – it really adds up. And it’s getting worse. According to the tech industry, I have to strap my drooling offspring to a computer in order to ensure the baby’s survival.

Parents are being offered life-altering advancements in artificial intelligence that purport to make this taxing endeavor a tiny bit easier. OpenAI is suggesting its latest products can make child-rearing more efficient: its boss, Sam Altman, suggests generating a podcast about your kid’s life that you can listen to in the morning on the way to school. How entertaining would a podcast “that talks about one kid’s soccer game that afternoon, one kid’s upcoming birthday, some news, etc” actually be? “Jimmy needs to work on his dribbling.” Great. I think he knows already. He’s not going to be the next Messi, so how about we switch back to music?

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Presumably, this idea renders the need for conversation moot. The computer already knows everything about our lives and has now regurgitated it into digital mush delivered by a generically cheery voice. But why I would find it helpful to have a machine reiterate information I have at my disposal already is a grand mystery even Philip Marlowe couldn’t solve. I’m a functioning, alive adult human being. This is like giving me an extra tooth with the promise that I can chew my food faster.

But what about the eight to 10 hours a day when your child has the gift of blissful solitude? Surely, they can’t be left alone at bedtime, lest they swallow a Hot Wheels car or open your favorite jar of loose razor blades. That’s where Nanit comes in – a startup that promises the kind of 24-hour surveillance that would make the Department of Homeland Security salivate. Nanit sells a camera and monitor set that observes your kid during sleep, tracking eye movements, “sleep efficiency”, and breathing patterns. Nanit’s rival, a company called Owlet, attaches a pulse oximetry tracker to your child’s foot through a sock. That’s not quite hooking your kid up to a terminal from the novel Neuromancer, but it feels like a decent first step in that direction. An app called Huckleberry offers “optimized nap predictions” and a chatbot assistant.

Of course, all of this costs money. A Nanit kit is $474, plus $100 a year in subscription fees. Owlet’s robo-sock is $300. Huckleberry’s app is free, but its nap predictions, like expert sports betting advice, will cost you. For $120, you can be told when your kid might go to sleep. I doubt there’s a money-back guarantee if they get it wrong, and the kid ends up spilling Legos all over the floor instead of going to bed.

These services promise to save lives by identifying health issues early in a child’s development. Nanit claims it offers more sleep and peace of mind, so parents can move their babies into their own rooms, thereby giving mom and dad a chance to go back to having regular intercourse. Yes, Nanit has looked into parents’ sex habits, too. If you went back to when I was married, you’d find there wasn’t much to look into.

None of this is anything people actually need to be parents. Babies need food, toys, diapers and a regular bath. Those all cost money. If I have to choose between saving for my son’s college and a spreadsheet with a bunch of biometric data, I’m skipping the spreadsheet. I realize, of course, these products are not for me. I don’t have an unlimited supply of disposable income. I have to prioritize and be practical. These devices are for people who optimize every single shred of their daily lives, thinking it will protect them from the reality of failure, illness and death. I’m sorry to report that a $400 camera isn’t going to fix any of that.

Society has been trying to offer solutions to solve the conundrum of parenting for decades: self-help books, classes, the legendary (and expensive) Snoo crib that shakes your child like it’s a gin martini until it stops crying. In every case, these aids cost money, turning parenting into a lucrative sector of the economy. If you can’t afford these modern “miracles”, where can you turn?

Parenting is hard, and we all need help. But there was a time when grandparents lived with their kids and grandkids, or at least lived close enough to help. I grant that the idea of living with my mother is akin to pitching a tent next to a cave filled with grizzly bears, but I’d do that before I got an AI-powered camera system to take a video of my kid sleeping. The best part of extended family childcare is that people can do something an AI can never do. It can teach children about someone besides themselves.

Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: President Xi never wastes a good crisis. As Iran, Ukraine and Palestine distract the world, he tightens his grip | Simon Tisdall
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Simon Tisdall
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Ever the strategist, the Chinese leader is taking the offensive, both abroad and at home. That’s bad news for global order, and minorities in his country

I
magine what would happen if a British prime minister in London told the Scots they could not have their own parliament, national football team or fly the saltire. Or if the Welsh were told their language and poetry were banned and must no longer be taught in schools. The ensuing uproar would probably destroy the United Kingdom. Yet that’s exactly what Xi Jinping, China’s communist emperor, is telling the roughly 125 million members of the 55 ethnic and religious minorities who together comprise about 9% of the country’s (majority Han Chinese) population.

Xi claims his sinicisation policy, embodied in a new “ethnic unity” law, will boost national identity and integration and, by expanding compulsory use of the Mandarin language, improve life and work prospects. Minorities should “hug tightly like pomegranate seeds” to build a strong, united China, he says. But Tibetans, Mongolians, Uyghurs and others who value their separate language and customs fiercely object to what they see as forced assimilation into a conformist, intolerant monoculture dominated by the Communist party’s tunnel vision. For them, it’s ethnic cleansing by another name.

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

The new law has been condemned, though not too loudly, by western governments and more vociferously by rights organisations such as Amnesty International. The death of Lobga Rangzen, a Free Tibet activist who set himself on fire in protest outside the UN in New York last month, briefly drew international attention. But such tragedies are not new. Wholesale repression in Tibet and brutal “re-education” camps in Xinjiang are but two longstanding aspects of Xi’s intensifying nationwide war on dissent, difference and diversity. The law and its harsh penalties, which extend to Chinese citizens based abroad, adds legal weight to existing efforts to enforce his and the party’s will (much the same thing these days) by creating a politically compliant, cowed population that dare not answer back.

A debilitating fatalism has taken hold in the west about China’s behaviour, whether it involves persecution of minorities, evisceration of democracy in Hong Kong, vindictive prosecutions of pro-democracy activists such as the former Apple Daily publisher Jimmy Lai, or vicious suppression of independent Christian churches and “unapproved” religious groups. It’s as though Xi’s China is now seen as simply too big, too economically powerful and too militarily threatening to influence, let alone contain or control. When China’s internal affairs are the issue, it’s easier to steer clear. Awkwardly balancing trade against security, and culpably silent on human rights, Britain is far from alone among western democracies in failing to articulate a coherent China policy.

But Xi’s increasingly aggressive, uncompromising policies are not confined to domestic matters. In power for nearly 15 years, Xi, 73, is growing ever more confident and abrasive in pursuit of his international legacy bucket list: establishing China as the dominant global power, relegating the US to second place and making his country the essential hub of a new multipolar security, economic and diplomatic order. His legacy list includes a takeover of Taiwan before he stands down, and unchallenged supremacy across the Asia-Pacific region. It all points one way: to Xi’s coronation as the greatest Chinese leader since Mao Zedong.

With the 21st party congress approaching, 2027 could be a big year for Xi – and he is already getting his ducks in a row. His dictatorship looks unassailable. Top regime cadres, meeting this week in secretive conclave at the Beidaihe seaside resort in Hebei province, are expected to endorse his redoubled drive to enforce loyalty and discipline in the ranks – the official phrase is “sustained advancement of full and rigorous party self-governance”. The Beidaihe gathering, and another meeting due in October, come amid almost Stalinist purges of senior political and military figures.

Signs of a more assertive international posture are everywhere. In recent months, China has stoked nationalist tensions with Japan and deliberately provoked the Philippines in disputed areas of the South China Sea. Its intimidation of Taiwan is unceasing. This week, Japan’s latest defence white paper singled out China as presenting “an unprecedented strategic challenge” and warned the threat was moving closer to home. Admiral Samuel Paparo, head of US Pacific Command, fired a broadside at China’s “coercive actions” in pursuit, he said, of regional dominance.

Xi is now actively challenging the US and the west on several other fronts. China is reportedly planning to provide Iran with up to 400 shoulder-fired missiles and new air defence systems. It is already materially assisting Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. And an emboldened Beijing is deploying the sort of trade weapons beloved of Donald Trump. Last year it restricted exports of vital rare earth minerals, to Washington’s great alarm. Only this week, China hit back at Trump’s new tariffs by blocking sales of drone technology.

Xi’s ever more bullish stance owes much to Trump’s trashing of the post-1945 global order, disdain for international law and national sovereignty (as seen in Venezuela and Greenland), and strained relations with traditional allies such as Japan, South Korea and European Nato countries. Many now view the US as an unreliable partner. For China, Trump’s shifting focus away from Asia and towards the western hemisphere is a golden opportunity to be exploited while it lasts. That may be one reason why Xi has taken the unusual step of agreeing to visit Trump in Washington next month, so soon after their May meeting in Beijing.

The main focus of the summit is expected to be artificial intelligence, amid US worries that it is in danger of losing the AI race. According to Chinese commentators, at least, Trump asked for the meeting after China agreed AI partnerships with 28 countries, mostly from the global south. AI is “probably the biggest thing anybody’s ever seen”, Trump said last month. “Whoever wins that race is probably going to win, period.” By which he presumably means, win the 21st century’s superpower crown.

The summit is likely to confirm the impression left by the last one: that Xi, outmanoeuvring Trump on Asia-Pacific security and Taiwan, accumulating geopolitical clout, and winning trade and tech wars, is well on the way to fulfilling his ambition of gaining the upper hand over the US. Yet in the end, Xi is still an unelected autocrat, a thug in a suit who relies on force to stay in power. He’s failing to deliver economically and, as in India and elsewhere, young urban Chinese may not tolerate his old-school brand of suffocating authoritarianism indefinitely. Who knows? Perhaps his ethnic unity law may ultimately prove a step too far – as it certainly would in Britain.

All should be on their guard. Xi, no friend of the west, may be morphing into an outright enemy while all eyes are on Iran, Gaza and Ukraine. Symbolically if not yet physically, a dangerously unconstrained Xi is shutting the door on peaceful coexistence at home and abroad.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Trump is laying waste to the agency that keeps hospital patients safe | Robert B Shpiner
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Robert B Shpiner
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Few have heard of the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, but it has saved tens of thousands of lives and billions of dollars

W
hen I started my training in 1980, we accepted an arithmetic that would now be indefensible. Central lines, the catheters we threaded into the great veins of the critically ill, became infected, and some of those patients died. We recorded the deaths as complications. Almost no one thought of them as preventable, because no one had yet done the slow work of proving they were.

That work got done, and federal money paid for it. Beginning in 2008, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, a small arm of the health department, funded a national effort in more than a thousand adult intensive care units: a checklist, a sterile insertion protocol, and a unit culture in which a nurse could stop a surgeon. Central-line bloodstream infections fell by 41%, from 1.915 to 1.133 per 1,000 catheter days. The agency estimates that effort alone averted between 290 and 605 deaths. Across its wider work on hospital-acquired harm, AHRQ’s own accounting credits 20,500 deaths prevented and $7.7bn saved in the four years from 2014 to 2017. Hardly any of my patients have heard of the agency. That was always rather the point.
