But Arkansas is uniquely restrained, with lawmakers in the state banning datacenters. Activists have been passing out handbills calling on the neighborhood to attend the quorum court, the Arkansas equivalent of a county commission, to register objections.

https://www.theguardian.com/media/ng-int.title: ‘I have an ego that needs to be put in check’: ex-Gawker editor AJ Daulerio on life after addiction
https://www.theguardian.com/media/ng-int.author: John McDermott
https://www.theguardian.com/media/ng-int.text:
After his fall from grace, media’s former enfant terrible is now sober and helping others with his addiction recovery newsletter and podcast, The Small Bow

Every other Tuesday, AJ Daulerio wakes up at 5.30am and meditates for five to 20 minutes before beginning his multistep daily journaling protocol: reading a selection from a poetry anthology, then a passage from one of his daily wisdom readers (his go-to is a heavily annotated copy of Leo Tolstoy’s A Calendar of Wisdom); writing his Fear of the Day and gratitude list, then sharing his spiritual takeaway in a note to his three kids.

After a banana and coffee, Daulerio trains Brazilian jujitsu before hitting a 9.45am meditation at Besant Lodge – a community center just below the Hollywood sign that once served as a meeting place for mid-century mystics – immediately followed by him leading a recovery meeting of his own through Zoom.

He goes to personal therapy at 11.15am, picks up his kids in the afternoon and spends the rest of the evening with them and his wife, giving him just a few hours at night to work on his advice column for Slate and the two books he’s writing.

This is in addition to emotional sobriety step work (cultivating inner peace after the drinking stops) on Zoom on Wednesday nights, an Adult Children of Alcoholics meeting every Friday morning, Alcoholics Anonymous on Sundays, couples therapy every other week, and a quarterly meeting with his psychiatrist to refine his cocktail of psychotropic medications, including a mood stabilizer (Lamictal) and an antipsychotic (Zyprexa), to treat his bipolar disorder.

“I have an ego that needs to be put in check all the time,” Daulerio tells me. “Half of my recovery is dedicated to that.”

Daulerio celebrated 10 years of sobriety this July, a joyous capstone to a tumultuous decade-plus that saw Daulerio go from digital media visionary as editor of Gawker to broke, disgraced and the man most responsible for the site’s demise.

Daulerio has re-emerged in recent years, again as a media innovator – not as the cutthroat, traffic-obsessed editor reputation he garnered at Gawker, but as the gentle, deeply pensive and contrite author of The Small Bow, the newsletter he created in 2018 to chronicle his recovery from drug and alcohol addiction, and his attempts to reclaim his life as a changed man.

Today Daulerio maintains a rigorous recovery regimen to battle the twin demons that once fueled his self-destructive impulses: the lonesomeness that led him to seek companionship in dive bars among other strange drunks, and the ego that convinced him he had it all under control, despite signs to the opposite.

Daulerio has built a devout following by writing about his recovery program in unsparingly honest, vulnerable first-person essays in The Small Bow, and he now wants to grow the company into a multiplatform media company that provides wisdom and guidance to people struggling with addictions of all kinds.

But therein lies Daulerio’s existential dilemma: how to build a successful media business without sacrificing the spiritual practice that made his second act possible.

“It’s something I have to get comfortable with and better at, because I do believe in what we’re doing,” Daulerio says between bites of his cheeseburger. “I know there’s a good way of self-promoting, I’m just wary of my intentions a lot of the time.”

One needs a certain amount of irrational self-confidence to start any business, especially in print media, an industry that has been in steady decline since Daulerio first became a journalist in 2000. Then there’s the self-promotion required to grow a business, even as it risks inflating the ego that fueled his fall from grace and that he’s worked so hard to keep in check.

That The Small Bow is built almost entirely around Daulerio’s personal experience makes this all the more difficult.

In Daulerio’s favor is his unmatched skill at growing digital media properties. It’s what propelled him to success as the editor of the now defunct Gawker Media – and also what led to his and the company’s downfall.

The Small Bow uses lots of religious iconography in its branding: pen and colored pencil illustrations of demons and angels drawn by Edith Zimmerman, a writer and artist who has also found sobriety – and they serve as an easy metaphor for the tension between Daulerio’s professional ambitions and his personal recovery: the demon whispering in one ear to revert to his old tricks and grow The Small Bow by any means necessary, and the angel whispering in the other to preserve what’s made The Small Bow so resonant with readers undergoing their own struggles.

“How do you sell something that is supposed to be genuine?” he asks me rhetorically. As with his sobriety, all he can do is forge ahead and attempt to achieve this seemingly irreconcilable balancing act, one day at a time. “What are the other options?”

The last 10 years of Daulerio’s life have been an exercise in being humbled. Few figures in recent history have had their rise and fall scrutinized as intensely by the media. His exploits have been the subject of two Netflix documentaries, glossy magazine profiles, and countless reports and thought pieces on sound journalistic practice and the limits of first amendment freedoms.

But long before he was media’s enfant terrible, he was one of the most promising young talents in 2000s digital journalism.

Daulerio started in journalism in 1998, covering city council meetings for the East Brunswick Sentinel in New Jersey. His initial dream was to be a music producer – he was simultaneously interning at a recording studio – or, saving that, a music critic. But he quickly exhibited a preternatural talent for landing scoops, a skill that would become his MO as he ascended the highest echelons of the digital publishing industry.

“I had the ability to get people to tell me things they weren’t supposed to,” Daulerio says. “Because I didn’t have strict deadlines, I could hang out with the council members.” A former college classmate of Daulerio’s worked the same beat for a competing newspaper, and Daulerio delighted in beating him to stories. “I loved it. I was weirdly competitive in a way that’s good for reporting. I’ve never been competitive in anything else.”

Despite being a diehard Philly sports fan, Daulerio was a feckless athlete himself, much to the embarrassment of his father (a topic Daulerio frequently visits in his Small Bow columns). “I grew up playing sports, but I never knew how to win. In the journalism world, I knew how to win.”

Daulerio shuffled through writing and editing gigs in New York and Philadelphia – including stints at the trade publications Bond Buyer and American Lawyer Media; men’s lifestyle newsletter Thrillist; and Philadelphia magazine – before landing a senior editor job at Deadspin, Gawker’s sports vertical, in 2008. Just months later, he was promoted to editor for the entire site.

Then Daulerio published photos of former New York Jets quarterback Brett Favre’s penis, and his life trajectory was forever altered.

In August 2010, Daulerio published a Deadspin post alleging that Favre had sent lewd voicemails and pictures of his penis to the Jets sideline reporter Jenn Sterger. Two months later, Daulerio published the illicit photos, purportedly from Favre, in a video montage, with Favre’s voicemails providing the soundtrack.

The story generated millions of page views for Deadspin and months of headlines across the wider sports media ecosystem, cementing the three-person sports blog as a player on the national stage and Daulerio as a fearless journalist on the vanguard of a new era of digital journalism. “So many NFL reporters had known about [Favre’s behavior] the whole time and wouldn’t cover it,” Daulerio says. (Favre admitted to leaving the voicemails but denied sending lewd photos.)

Professional and personal accolades showered over Daulerio. He did the Today show (while drunk, stoned and on Adderall). Nick Denton, Gawker Media’s founder and CEO, rewarded Daulerio with a raise, three more Deadspin staff writers and a freelance budget.

Daulerio was spotlighted in a GQ profile and became a star of the New York City media scene. “A friend of mine from high school came to a Gawker office rooftop party,” Daulerio recalls. “He watched me walk into this place and he was like, ‘I feel like I’m with Don Corleone.’”

It was the success and recognition Daulerio had always coveted. He had dreamed about having his glossy portrait photo featured in Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list. And yet all the attention – and criticism – made him uncomfortable. “I did not like my full-time job to be a punching bag for all the heels on the internet,” he says. “On the other hand, I had been treading water for 10 years in online journalism, and now I had attention and career options.” After the GQ story, “there was no reversing who I was.”

As he climbed the ranks of the media industry, Daulerio was also feeding a drinking habit that would land him in rehab. He drank six nights a week, rotating through a familiar circuit of bars near work in the Bowery (Congee Village, Professor Thom’s) and, on weekends, in Williamsburg (Dardy Bar). Some Saturdays he would post up at a bar at 11am, down 10 beers and five shots, stay until close and then do cocaine with his newly formed friends. “I would just live in these places,” Daulerio says. “I was a binger. I would go to a bar on Thursday and come out of it on Monday … There was never really a plan other than to stay for as long as I possibly could.”

Drinking was a way to treat the “free-floating loneliness” Daulerio had lived with since he was a child, he says. “It was fun to do cocaine with strangers until 4.30 in the morning. That felt like home to me … It would be silly to blame [my addiction] on anything other than I never felt normal or at ease, and I’m always battling that and probably always will.”

He was one of the most successful editors in the burgeoning digital publishing industry, but he couldn’t afford an apartment because his credit was so bad. He bounced between friends’ couches.

His cavalier editorial philosophy came under fire at the same time. To critics, Gawker became emblematic of a new wave of digital journalists who prioritized the almighty click and page view without any consideration for journalistic ethics or basic human decency.

Publishing the Favre story, for instance, meant burning Sterger, the recipient of the reportedly unsolicited “dong shots” (Daulerio’s words), who had explicitly asked to not be included in the story. (Daulerio bought the photos and voicemails from a third party for $12,000.) He even published Sterger’s request to leave her out of it.

Daulerio now says he wishes he had broken the Favre scoop without mentioning her.

Later, when the Gawker empire imploded, a narrative emerged that Daulerio’s alcohol and drug use was largely to blame for the editorial decisions that led to its collapse, a premise Daulerio wholly rejects. “A lot of good things were happening when things were bad,” he says.

Such as Deadspin’s immense growth. In just three years under Daulerio’s tenure, Deadspin’s traffic tripled, as the site continued to break raunchy, irreverent scoops – former New York Jets head coach Rex Ryan filming foot fetish videos starring his wife; photos of Texas Rangers outfielder Josh Hamilton drunk and shirtless, licking whipped cream off a woman’s breasts in a Tempe, Arizona, bar, despite supposedly being sober; and ESPN Horndog Dossier, a collection of unconfirmed rumors about rampant illicit sexual behavior at “the Worldwide Leader in Sports”.

There was even some genuine investigative reporting mixed in with the scuzzy gossip, such as leaked financial documents exposing the creative accounting techniques that Major League Baseball franchises employ to boost profits.

Denton named Daulerio editor of Gawker.com, Gawker Media’s flagship site, in late 2011. The following fall, Daulerio approved publication of a sex tape starring the professional wrestler Hulk Hogan. Hogan filed an invasion of privacy lawsuit against Gawker just two weeks later, a legal action that would bankrupt Gawker and force its sale, and temporarily ruin Daulerio’s life and career. (It was later revealed that Hogan’s suit was financed by the billionaire venture capitalist Peter Thiel, who harbored a grudge against Gawker Media ever since it outed him as gay in 2007.)

Hogan won a $140m judgment in March 2016 against Gawker, including $100,000 in punitive damages for Daulerio, a verdict that was largely blamed on Daulerio and his callous editorial ethos. (Gawker settled with Hogan for $31m, and Daulerio didn’t have to pay the $100,000.)

During the trial, Hogan’s attorneys brought up how Daulerio once published a separate sex tape of two people who were not public figures, and how Daulerio initially dismissed the woman in the video when she requested its removal. (Daulerio implored her to “not make a big deal out of this”.)

The post was eventually deleted, and Daulerio says publishing it was the most regrettable moment of his career.

The most damning moment in the trial was when Hogan’s attorneys showed the courtroom a videotaped deposition of Daulerio from October 2013, in which a Hogan attorney asked Daulerio: “Can you imagine a situation where a celebrity sex tape would not be newsworthy?”

“If they were a child,” Daulerio replied.

The lawyer pushed: “Under what age?”

The exchange sent “a palpable sense of shock” through the courtroom, according to the New York Times. There were audible gasps and groans. Daulerio says the comment was a sarcastic joke, “a defense mechanism” after getting frustrated with the interrogation, but it supported the plaintiff’s portrayal of Daulerio as a heartless gossip-peddler who trafficked in the sordid details of people’s personal lives, even when they had zero news value.

Adding to Daulerio’s embarrassment, the trial revealed he had a net worth of negative $35,000. The court froze the $1,500 he had in his bank account. The 2017 Netflix documentary Nobody Speak: Trials of the Free Press about the Hogan trial opens with Daulerio laughing as he reads a bank email informing him a $230m hold had been placed on his bank account.

Daulerio can’t recall how he felt during the trial. He dissociated. “It was so big and overwhelming, I just felt like I was a character in this thing,” he says. The only part of the experience he can latch on to is the photo of him from the New York Times article. “I feel like I know what that expression is: really helpless, but also in trouble.”

As Daulerio’s professional life was put on trial, he was also trying to get sober. He first entered rehab in August 2015, seven months before the trial began, but quickly relapsed. “Two months later, I was back at it pretty hardcore,” he says.

Daulerio fully committed to sobriety on 15 July 2016, a month after Gawker filed for bankruptcy and put itself up for sale. “July 15, 2016, was simply the day I decided to stop resisting and give up the warped idea that I could do my own modified version of sobriety, something akin to what I liked to call ‘advanced moderation’,” he wrote in a recent Small Bow essay about his 10th anniversary of sobriety.

What Daulerio still longed for in his early days of recovery was a way to process the experience the best way he knew how: through writing.

The first piece Daulerio published after the trial was a 2017 first-person essay about his fraught relationship with his father for the now shuttered men’s publication Mel.

The piece had the pugnacious writing that made Deadspin so popular; Daulerio opens the essay recounting a physical fight with his father. But it also had the emotional vulnerability of an adult man trying to heal his daddy issues, told through the prism of past Father’s Days. (I was a staff writer at Mel at that time, but did not work with Daulerio).

“The piece was masculinity and neuroses laid bare, not in a self-pitying, ‘woe is me’ way, but in a curious way,” former Mel editor-in-chief Josh Schollmeyer says. “If there’s any difference between the pre- and post-trial AJ, it’s AJ falling in love with his own mythology versus being who he really is, which is a master storyteller. That humility was apparent from the jump.”

The naked confessional style would become The Small Bow’s signature. In the newsletter, Daulerio recounts his various sobriety efforts – AA meetings, therapy, meditation, psychiatry, stoicism, Buddhism – in oftentimes painful, but always heartfelt honesty.

Earlier this year, he wrote about moving his elderly mother into an assisted living facility in Florida near where he went to rehab. He also frequently writes about the spiritual blessings of being a family man; Daulerio and screenwriter Julieanne Smolinski married in 2018, and they have three children together in Los Angeles.

Some of the most powerful Small Bow entries are about Daulerio making amends – steps eight and nine in 12-step programs – to those he wronged during his years actively in addiction, such as making peace with Sterger.

In a January 2020 essay, Daulerio revealed he and Sterger incidentally reconnected when he adopted a dog for his growing family. Sterger just so happened to work at the dog shelter Smolinski emailed, resulting in Daulerio and Sterger meeting at the LA diner House of Pies.

She admitted that there are still uncomfortable days and awkward moments stemming from the Favre ordeal. There’s still a version of her that exists in the internet’s memory hole where she will never be a real person; she’s just a plot point without context, without skin. But the thing that I did was more vicious. You see, I knew she was a real person – and I did what I did anyway. I didn’t care if I destroyed her. That’s just the type of person I was back then.

I don’t remember how long we actually talked, but I remember we both walked out of there a little relieved like we’d both just found a therapist who finally understood the excavation tools required to break new ground. Some hurts were still unreachable, though. Time takes time.

Sterger agreed to meet him out of curiosity: she wanted to understand why Daulerio betrayed her wishes and upended her life. “I found a guy that had looked at himself in the mirror and really done a lot of hard work on himself – really examined why he had done the things that he had done, and realized the hurt that he had caused people,” Sterger says.

The two got along so well that they developed the unlikeliest of friendships. “He has been through the level of public shame that I have,” Sterger says. “Few people have experienced that.” Sterger later appeared on The Small Bow podcast, where she and Daulerio publicly buried the hatchet.

“There’s a concept in recovery of a living amends,” Daulerio says. When a direct amends might inflict even more pain on the injured party, addicts in recovery are instructed to atone by simply living a good life. “The Small Bow is a living amends for whatever version of me came before on the internet.”

The newsletter has amassed 20,000 subscribers – about 2,000 of them paid, making him $72,000 a year – including some celebrities that have embraced the publication as a platform to discuss their own sobriety.

Fans of the CBS talkshow The Talk and the Barstool Sports podcast Pardon My Take know Jerry O’Connell as a happy-go-lucky actor with a goofy sense of humor, but on The Small Bow podcast in April, O’Connell revealed he’s been in recovery from alcoholism for 13 years.

Going public about his sobriety took some convincing. O’Connell got sober under the old-school AA mentality that treats anonymity as sacrosanct – “it’s right there in the title,” he says – but made an exception because Daulerio had been so important to his own recovery. The two connected during the pandemic over their shared sobriety after O’Connell, a longtime Deadspin fan, reached out.

“AJ has a new-school way of thinking, and that’s why this venture is interesting,” O’Connell says of Daulerio’s willingness to bare it all. “This is all uncharted territory.”

“I was publicly drunk, so being publicly sober makes sense to me, and I like to talk about the many methods I go about to stay that way,” Daulerio recently wrote in The Small Bow. “But recovery is a personal thing – how someone chooses to do it isn’t my business.”

Actor and documentarian Alex Winter has a routine meetup with Daulerio at House of Pies, where they discuss recovery and fatherhood. Winter, too, discussed his recovery on an episode of The Small Bow, the only time he has appeared on a recovery podcast.

“I’ve always bristled a little bit at these kinds of recovery-forward podcasts,” Winter says. “I always worry about people getting very enthusiastic about getting sober. … Recovery is delicate. It’s fragile. So I just feel for the people who expose themselves that way and hope that they’re OK.” What separates Daulerio, Winter says, is his radical candor. “He’s very self-effacing in a way that is honest, not trying to win brownie points by being self-effacing.”

The day after Hogan died last July, Daulerio penned a Small Bow essay partially thanking the Hulkster for body-slamming his life and career. “Without that experience, there is no Small Bow, probably,” Daulerio says. “That’s how I choose to think about it.”

“Iforgot to brush my teeth,” Daulerio announces to The Small Bow production team, as he prepares to tape a new episode.

Between fatherhood and his recovery routine, Daulerio’s is more structured than ever, but chaos seeps in at times. After nearly three decades as a writer, he still gets bothered by commenters. He recently sent a snarky email response to a reader who criticized one of his Slate advice columns.

A current focus in his recovery is on improving his sleep. A night owl, Daulerio typically gets only five hours of sleep a night, staying up until the wee hours to watch violent action movies, often starring Jason Statham. He has started using a sleep mask and soothing ASMR sounds to help lull him into slumber.

The podcast is integral to Daulerio’s strategy for growing The Small Bow. His larger vision is something akin to a trade magazine for the recovery industry. He wants to sell subscriptions to recovery facilities – hospitals, clinics, rehabs, halfway houses – whose patients would then be able to access, and even contribute to, The Small Bow’s archive of addiction-related content. “A farm system for The Small Bow,” he says, not unlike how Gawker recruited the wittiest contributors in its comments section to become paid staff writers.

Daulerio piloted such a program with Divided Sky, the Ludlow, Vermont, drug rehab facility co-founded by the Phish frontman Trey Anastasio, whose appearance on The Small Bow podcast is the show’s most popular to date.

As The Small Bow has attracted more contributors, its scope has widened to include a broader array of addictions and mental health issues: sex, shopping, gambling, weed, depression, bipolar disorder. The internet itself.

Today’s podcast taping is with writer Ryan O’Connell, who’s promoting his essay collection, Inspiration Porn – a welcome development for Daulerio, who wants The Small Bow to be a requisite stop on the memoir promotion circuit. Daulerio’s own books, a compilation of essays about recovery called The Small Book, a play on AA’s Big Book, and a memoir about his life post-Gawker trial, are scheduled to publish in 2027.

Ryan O’Connell’s relationship with alcohol falls into the expanded definition of sobriety. He never hit “rock bottom” because he quit before he could get there. “It’s the only substance you get shamed for quitting,” he says. “What I want to create a dialogue about is: you can stop drinking just because you don’t like it. AJ is expanding recovery conversations to be about so much more.”

I ask Daulerio what success looks like to him now. On a personal level, it’s spending quality time with his family, the spiritual opposite of when he would stay out all night to avoid going home.

Professionally, success means rediscovering his love of writing, doing it consistently, and serving the recovery community he’s cultivated.

“I’m never going to have the notoriety I had, but I really enjoy what I do know and learning how to write again,” he says. “It’s the best work I’ve ever done.”
https://www.theguardian.com/media/ng-int.summary: AJ Daulerio is a former Gawker editor and Gawker editor. He is now a sober and helping others with his addiction recovery newsletter and podcast, The Small Bow. Daulerserio published photos of former New York Jets quarterback Brett Favre's penis in 2010.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Exclusive: Major Republican fundraiser winning contracts from Trump administration, emails reveal
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Aram Roston in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Palmer Luckey has donated $5.9m to Republicans and bundled more, while reaping billions in Pentagon contracts

W
ealthy Republicans on the west coast received an emailed invitation in July to an upcoming fundraiser titled “Keep the Senate”. The email, obtained by the Guardian, described the event as a “private roundtable and dinner with the National Republican Senatorial Committee” where donors can pledge $50,000 for seats at the head table, and mingle with legislative heavy hitters from Capitol Hill including the Senator majority leader, John Thune, and Mike Rogers, who is running for Senate in Michigan with Donald Trump’s endorsement.

One of the organizers listed on the invite was the defense industry tycoon Palmer Luckey, the 33-year-old co-founder of sprawling weapons manufacturer Anduril Industries.

The invitation is one of dozens of emails obtained by the Guardian that unravel Luckey’s vast Maga political fundraising over the last seven years.

A longtime GOP donor and activist who spoke on condition he not be identified in order to preserve his political relationships said Luckey was now the “godfather of Republican fundraising on the west coast”.

“If you’re raising campaign money in California, you have to go to Palmer Luckey,” he said. “Luckey is the top tier. There are others who are important below him but no one at his level.”

Anduril, launched just nine years ago, has emerged as a major military contractor for the Trump administration, working on contracts for everything from drones to autonomous jet fighters to space-based interceptors.

In March, the US army awarded a $20bn sole-source contract to Anduril for a variety of drones it sells, though it is not clear which of its weapons systems are operational or have been deployed for combat in US operations.

Anduril, though it is not widely known as a space contractor, announced in May it would work, with a team of other companies, on what may be the mother of all contracting opportunities offered by the Trump administration, the so-called “Golden Dome” anti-missile space-based interceptor effort. Estimates for the Golden Dome range between $185bn and $1.2tn.

Much of Anduril’s PR sparkle comes from Luckey. He’s a media darling, profiled on 60 Minutes and in the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times, which called him the “It Guy of the booming defense-technology industry”.

His offbeat, relaxed attire – colorful Hawaiian shirts, a chin puff goatee, cargo shorts and flip-flops – counterintuitively makes him seem more credible.

Luckey is treated by many in the defense industry as a technology prophet and futurist who often holds forth on what he believes to be the true nature of warfare. For example, he told Axios that future wars will be fought in a “subterranean domain”, under the earth’s crust, in underground conflicts.

Anduril’s success in winning huge contracts has blossomed with little attention paid to the central role Luckey plays as a donor and fundraising “bundler” for the Republican party. Bundlers hold large fundraisers for candidates or campaign committees and political action groups, and curate high-dollar invitation lists for those events.

The emails obtained by the Guardian shed light on Palmer Luckey’s vast GOP political fundraising efforts and activism over the last 10 years.

Palmer declined an interview for this piece, writing, “I am not going to help you guys make money,” and did not respond to a detailed list of questions.

OpenSecrets, a non-profit that tracks campaign donations, says Federal Election Commission (FEC) records show that Luckey has donated $5.9m to Republicans since 2017. While that is a tremendous amount of money for one person to give to politicians, it does not put him in the order of, say, Miriam Adelson, the widow of Sheldon Adelson, who has forked over $100m to Trump’s campaign in 2024.

Luckey doesn’t have her wealth. His real value to GOP politicians exceeds his own donations. He hosts and organizes fundraising events and campaigns for Republicans from the president all the way down to state races.

“If you become a bundler, it just multiplies your influence,” said Brendan Glavin of OpenSecrets. “It makes you a more important person. You’re bringing in not just your money. You’re bringing other people’s money. It integrates you in the campaign and makes you more important to the candidate than just a donor.”

Behind the scenes, Luckey has reached a position in campaign finance and politics that rivals his influence in military contracting, according to two GOP fundraising figures.

The emails, which are a partial list of invitations, show that Luckey has held fundraisers over the last seven years for at least 20 Republican politicians, ranging from Trump to a California attorney general candidate.

Just as Luckey has emerged as a major fundraiser on the right, his co-founder, Anduril’s CEO, Palantir veteran Brian Schimpf, became a major donor to Democratic causes, albeit on a far smaller scale. So, in time-honored tradition, Anduril’s management ends up donating to both sides of the political aisle, though the vast majority goes towards the GOP. FEC records show Schimpf’s donations at $1.16m over the same period that Luckey gave $5.9m.

An Anduril official emailed the Guardian: “It shouldn’t surprise anyone that two executives at the same company have different political views. Like millions of Americans, Brian and Palmer don’t share identical political views.”

Luckey first became famous in tech before he could legally drink. At 20, in 2012, he launched a Kickstarter that raised more than $2m for a virtual reality gaming headset he said he was building first in his parents’ garage. It was a Silicon Valley Cinderella narrative. Two years later, Facebook became the prince at the ball and paid him $2bn for the company. In 2016, after four years of hype, the first Oculus Rift headset started getting shipped to consumers.

And then, quickly, Luckey seemed to flame out in scandal. The Daily Beast revealed he’d been secretly funding a group dedicated to “shitposting” negative memes about Hillary Clinton.

“We know Hillary Clinton is corrupt, a warmonger, a freedom-stripper. Not the good kind you see dancing in bikinis on Independence Day, the bad kind that strips freedom from citizens and grants it to donors,” Luckey had written, under the pseudonym Nimblerichman, on Reddit.

The disclosure had an immense impact, at least for a time. Eight months later Luckey left Facebook, and he later portrayed himself in interviews as simply being canceled for giving money to Republicans, ignoring the main criticisms over the group’s crude and underhanded tactics.

after newsletter promotion

Luckey left Facebook with immense wealth, and in April 2017, just four months after Trump’s first inauguration, he founded Anduril.

His partners in the venture came from the Peter Thiel-backed Palantir, a company that had long had success in federal contracting through major lobbying and PR battles.

In June of 2017, his company just two months old, Luckey gave his first ever actual campaign finance donation, to Ted Cruz, the senator from Texas. Looking at his subsequent donations, it appears that the dam broke for him. Palmer gave 25 more times to political committees and legislators that year alone, FEC records show, and he has donated on more than a thousand occasions, or, on average, about 100 times every year.

In the emails shared with the Guardian, the very first fundraising event Luckey co-hosted took place in August of 2017, two months after his donation to Ted Cruz. It was a major effort, and would include GOP House members such as Ken Calvert, Duncan Hunter, Darrell Issa, Devin Nunes, Dana Rohrabacher and Kevin McCarthy.

Then in November, in a separate email chain, Palmer’s name came up again, for the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC). A congressional aide named Jason Pitkin wrote to a party official: “we are going to be asking people for $33,900 for the NRCC and then after the first of the year we can ask them for $101,700.”

Pitkin noted that congressman Rohrabacher had introduced Luckey to Kevin McCarthy, then the powerful House majority leader, “at a Private meeting”.

“As you can see by the attached invitation,” Pitkin said, “Palmer is hosting an event for Dana [Rohrabacher] On December 15th. Our understanding is that Palmer was going to contribute $100,000 for the CA Victory event. Please let us know how much more Palmer can give to the NRCC.”

Pitkin did not respond to emailed questions.

In July of 2020, just three years after its creation, Anduril won its first mammoth contract from the first Trump administration. Customs and Border Protection awarded the young company a contract estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars for surveillance towers on the border.

And in that period it was clear that Luckey had hit the most senior levels of political access. On 6 October, the emails show, Luckey and his wife hosted Trump himself at a lunch at their waterfront mansion. The stakes were high and so were the tickets. Donors were told that $150,000 would get access to the round table, a VIP reception and event, and a photo op with the president.

During the Biden years, Anduril still maintained its business efforts targeting US national security, and still won contracts. It went on a major acquisition binge, buying up drone companies across the country.

And Luckey’s fundraising for the GOP continued. The records obtained by the Guardian show that after 2021, Luckey hosted fundraisers for key figures including Tom Cotton, the head of the Senate intelligence committee; Rick Scott, the Republican senator from Florida; Ken Calvert, then the influential ranking member of the House’s defense appropriations subcommittee; and Mike Waltz, now Trump’s UN ambassador and briefly his national security adviser.

Luckey also hosted another event for a future Trump official: a $50,000-a-plate fundraiser in June 2022 for Mehmet Oz, who would later join the Trump administration. That event became scandalous when Jezebel reported the fundraiser incorporated a speech by Oz in front of a car that once belonged to Adolf Hitler. Jezebel pointed out that Luckey’s sister is married to Maga firebrand Matt Gaetz, then a congressman from Florida.

Now that Trump is president, Anduril appears to be taking its turn at the table of the major contractors, amid Lockheed Martin, Raytheon and General Dynamics.

Certainly it has raised extraordinary money. In the latest round, led by Thrive Capital, controlled by Jared Kushner’s brother Joshua, it raised $5bn in venture capital.

Anduril says in Trump’s first year in office it doubled its revenue – a growth rate of 100%, but still only reached $2.2bn for 2025, which is barely a blip in the Pentagon’s trillion-dollar budget.

Still, the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has twice toured Anduril factories. “Palmer and everyone, thank you so much,” he said last December as he visited Anduril’s factory in Costa Mesa, California, at a giant former industrial site where the Los Angeles Times was once printed. The Anduril factory was “foundational” to the new Pentagon, Hegseth said. On that tour, Hegseth donned a special helmet designed by Anduril.

A soldier wearing the helmet would be able to see the outside world not through his eyes but through sensors, as a kind of virtual or “augmented” reality, just like the old Oculus Rift headset Palmer Luckey made his fortune on.

In his speech, Hegseth referred to “that cool helmet I just saw that the army might be wearing eventually”.

'Most people don’t want pervert glasses that can film us without our consent,' said a spokesperson from activist group Everyone Hates Elon. The group has launched a series of guerilla adverts deriding non-consensual filming by the glasses as well as an email campaign encouraging people to legally object to being filmed by Meta glasses under general data protection regulations, which over 20,000 people have signed.

Rights groups have warned that the glasses threaten the right to privacy, while countries such as Germany are reportedly considering a ban.

And while Meta’s safety guidelines say smart glasses should not be used for 'harassment, infringing on privacy rights, or capturing sensitive information', women have taken to social media to share their stories of being filmed by men without their consent.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Stock market turmoil sheds stark light on the opaque AI economy
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Aisha Down, Dan Milmo and Graeme Wearden
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Investors scramble to make sense of a shock Chinese challenge to the dominance of western chipmakers

Even for the rollercoaster world of AI, last week was particularly volatile as investors scrambled to keep up with developments that threatened the dominance of the largest western chipmakers.

It began with a double whammy. On Monday, the Chinese memory chipmaker CXMT floated on the Shanghai stock market, soaring by 466% in value to 3.3tn yuan (£365bn).

That same day, it was reported that China had developed its own tools to carry out deep-ultraviolet lithography, a technique essential to the computer chip supply chain over which the Dutch company ASML had held a monopoly.

AI-linked shares, particularly chipmakers, dropped around the world, sending many indices sliding. South Korea’s main share index, the Kospi, fell 11.5% on Tuesday and a further 6% on Wednesday, dragged down by its two biggest companies – the semiconductor maker SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics.

On Thursday, the main US tech index, the Nasdaq, fell into correction territory at one point after dropping more than 10% from its recent high, before easing back. Nvidia lost more than 5% by Thursday evening, by which time it had been overtaken by Apple as the world’s largest listed company.

The next day there was a big rebound, when strong financial results from Amazon and Microsoft calmed traders’ nerves. The Kospi jumped nearly 20% – although the week’s slump still means it recorded its worst month since the height of the global financial crisis in October 2008.

So, what exactly do these advances mean, and why have they got western investors so jittery?

CXMT’s debut is impressive. But the company is arguably more of a boon to the global AI economy than a threat. It makes dynamic random-access memory (Dram) chips, which store the data that other AI chips draw on for their calculations.

There is a global shortage of Dram chips, which is why phones and computers are expected to get far more expensive. Crucially, they are not graphics processing units (GPUs) – which are the key chips and the “brains” in an AI system.

This means, put simply, that CXMT is not a threat to GPU maker Nvidia, the biggest company in the AI economy and the only one making a profit on AI. They produce complementary, not competing goods.

The Chinese company could be a threat to SK Hynix and Micron, which do make memory chips. However, Alvin Nguyen, an analyst at the research firm Forrester, said the sell-off in these shares was an “overreaction” given that the global memory chip shortage is likely to continue until 2030.

“SK Hynix, Micron, others, they can’t produce enough memory chips to begin with … the demand keeps growing even higher,” Nguyen said.

A more serious concern could be the news that China can make the lithography tools. These are essentially extremely precise lasers that allow chipmakers to etch the thinnest lines in the world into wafers of silicon.

Until now, only ASML could manufacture such machines. If this week’s reports are correct, Beijing could – in theory – produce GPUs that rival Nvidia’s. This would spell trouble for the world’s biggest company, and therefore Wall Street. But a serious competitor is still years away.

“Fabs [semiconductor fabrication plants], as I know them, still take years to develop,” said Nguyen.

Mark Boost, the chief executive of the UK cloud company Civo, agreed. “Investors are overreacting to the short-term threat,” he said. “Manufacturing a handful of [deep-ultraviolet] machines is a massive symbolic victory, but not a commercial replacement for ASML overnight.

“Fabs run on efficiency and yield, and until these Chinese tools can match western reliability, ASML’s global dominance remains structurally safe outside mainland China.”

Long term, this week’s advances are gamechanging for the AI economy, although in many ways they should have been predictable. Given US export controls, China has had little choice but to develop domestic capabilities.

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at IG, an online share trading company, said: “These Chinese chip companies appear poised to do to the big chipmakers what they have done to steel, automobiles and a host of other industries, namely undercut them and outcompete them on price.”

It may be that last week’s correction is an overreaction – but also a reasonable response to a circular and extremely opaque AI economy that rests heavily on the fate of a single company, Nvidia.

Its shares are gradually creeping up again, although they are still below what they were last week. A contributing factor to the investor skittishness appears to be yet another circular, opaque deal.

Last Sunday, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia was considering providing a $250bn (£186bn) backstop to OpenAI for a large datacentre project. This comes roughly half a year after a $100bn deal between the two companies fell apart.

It was a significant factor in Nvidia’s decline over the week, according to Morningstar. The anxiety that underlies this is that the company has become the “central bank of AI” – holding up vast parts of the economy, and the global stock market, in ways that most people, investors included, do not understand.

Many believe that it cannot last. What is on the other side is less clear.

“Nvidia knows the gravy train’s going to run out,” Nguyen said. “Everybody’s waiting for them to fall apart. I don’t know that they will because what they do still has value … at some point in the future, they’ll no longer be one of the most valuable companies in the world. Maybe … they’ll be worth only $2tn. It’s still pretty good.”

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/a.title: EA Sports FC 27: what does the next instalment of the world’s biggest football game have in store?
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/a.author: Steve Boxer
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/a.text:
The all-conquering franchise’s revamps are technically impressive, its transfers more true to life – and its new grassroots social hub is surprising fun

A
s if the world wasn’t sufficiently football-obsessed, it’s time to prepare for the arrival of its biggest football video game. EA Sports FC 27 (the franchise that used to be Fifa – what better time to no longer be Fifa-branded?) is due to be released on 25 September. I just spent two intense days in Vancouver, where the EA FC games are made, playing FC 27 and talking to its developers.

With an annual franchise such as EA FC, it helps to have something fresh to entice regular fans, and FC 27 has a whole new element, entitled the Grounds. It’s a physical hub-type area, similar to the City as seen in 2K’s recent NBA 2K basketball games, but much more pleasant to frequent, split as it is into areas inspired by British, French and Argentinian street-football culture.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The Grounds provides a new physical home for an existing element of EA FC: Clubs, its casual online mode in which you control a single player and play matches closer to kickabouts than real-world football, but beyond that, it has plenty of other activities and distractions.

I spent about an hour in the Grounds, and found it more enjoyable than expected. Among its buildings are playing areas, whose entrances act as lobbies where you can choose to play against random people or to set up a custom game with your FC 27-owning friends. Each playing area hosts a specific type of game, and the Grounds has a map that you can teleport around.

It rewards exploration: I encountered targets that could be smashed by spawning a football and drop-kicking it, some of which were clumped into mini-games. Its games offered clever twists on the Clubs blueprint. In one 3v3 game, target areas appeared for short periods, and if I scored from one, I got a bonus goal for my side. And one game based on dodgeball gave its players three lives, which they would lose if others successfully kicked a ball at them.

The Grounds should prove popular: it has been tastefully and cleverly constructed and will no doubt expand as new game-types are added. You could also envisage it, in future years, hosting a narrative mode along the line of the Journey from Fifa 17 to 19.

FC 26 marked a mission by EA Sports to improve the franchise’s responsiveness by enacting a surprising number of changes to its fundamental gameplay, and that process continues apace in FC 27.

Although anyone who played FC 26 will testify that those efforts actually caused some new problems, such as an annoying tendency for defensive interceptions to bounce back weirdly into the path of forwards. EA Sports, according to gameplay design director Kantcho Doskov, took radical action to eliminate such aberrations: “We had to completely strip out the existing system for interceptions and build a new one from scratch. We spent six months doing that.”

Via a build that let me play Champions League games between a limited number of teams, I found that to be a worthwhile exercise: those defensive bounce-backs were blissfully absent. But an awful lot more was also in evidence in FC 27 on the gameplay revamp front.

Much of this – perhaps counterintuitively at a time when AI is worming its way ever deeper into all our lives – involved paring back the in-game AI. That’s certainly the case for the defensive AI: whereas previously, defenders would rush towards the ball, getting pulled out of position and opening up annoying gaps, FC 27 now gives much more manual control over defensive jockeying, movement and tackles.

Crossing, previously AI-assisted, has been revamped in FC 27, leaving it up to me to get the direction and weight of cross right, then giving me more of a chance to position my centre-forward correctly. The AI controlling forward players, meanwhile, has been improved, so that off-the-ball players now move much more helpfully, allowing pass-and-move sequences, and they are much better at staying onside.

I was also impressed by revamped two-stage corner and free-kick systems. But FC 27, gameplay-wise, achieves what FC 26 set out to, this time with no evident anomalies, and feels more responsive to your inputs than any of its predecessors.

FC 27’s Career Mode, in which you get to play out your fantasies of managing your favourite team, has also been extensively revamped – primarily with a view towards making its transfer system more like the one that operates in the real world, and to force you to do more actual management.

The headline means of doing the latter is called Dynamic OVR. OVR is simply jargon for any player’s all-important overall rating; where previously OVRs remained constant, in FC 27’s Career Mode they will go up and down depending on form, fitness and general happiness. Thus, you will have to rest your best players over the course of a long season, but you may also be able to buy players cheaply with artificially low OVRs if, say, they are coming back from injury.

Pete O’Donnell, FC 27’s Career Mode game director, explains how the game’s transfer system has been modernised: “Previously, you could do things instantly, which was good for a game but was not very realistic. We looked at how clubs interact with each other, how they do the deals themselves, and we spoke to scouts and directors of football. Then it was about extracting the fun bits of those jobs.”

The new system will back you up with more data; now each player will have an xTV (Expected Transfer Value) rating, which should speed negotiations. FC 27 will also reflect clubs’ real-life transfer policies, according to O’Donnell, with clubs’ boards requesting that you sign certain players. Press conferences in FC 27 will force you to make decisions that will please some players and annoy others, and 20 Unexpected Events have been added to Career Mode.

FC 27’s Ultimate Transfer (FUT) mode, the hardcore card-based system that provides a home for most of FC’s loot box action, will have a new headline feature in the form of a Gallery, which will showcase all the players and card-sets collected, rather than just first 11s.

EA Sports says it has also “streamlined” FUT’s previously impenetrable Squad-Based Challenges (SBC) system, and has made a tweak designed to avert stalemates, which affected the latter stages in FUT in FC 26, by restricting plus-level FUT players to three, rather than five, play-styles. But the nature of FUT – which develops over a long period post-launch – means that it will take a while to ascertain whether those changes prove effective.

There will be another major change to FC 27 that has nothing to do with how it plays: because it contains microtransactions, it will now be rated 16+ rather than the previous 3+, after a policy change at age-rating organisation Pegi. Given the game’s enthusiastic young and teenage audience, we asked EA Sports’ top brass to comment, but they blandly responded: “While the game functionally remains the same, this has resulted in a new Pegi age rating. It marks a change in the way we are giving the information to players and parents.”

Beyond Pegi’s European jurisdiction, the game will be rated E for Everybody. But in the UK, parents should think hard about letting youngsters play a 16-rated game. If they are worried about their offspring racking up huge bills for FUT transactions, the good news is that a new Ultimate Plus Edition of the game, which includes loads of stuff that would previously have cost in-game currency, will go on sale. But the bad news is it costs £139.99 and will only be available as a pre-order before 31 August.

EA Sports FC 27 is out on 25 September on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, and PC. It will also launch on PS4, Xbox One, and Switch, but without some features, such as the new Grounds mode.

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/a.title: Pony Island 2 Panda Circus: gallop out of hell in this phantasmagorical follow-up to 2016’s indie hit
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/a.author: Ignas Vieversys
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/a.text:
Daniel Mullins explains how he plans to follow up his quirky classic without losing what made it stand out in the first place

G
litchy aesthetics. Literally collapsing menu boxes. The game taunting you by “possessing” your Steam friends. Technical tricks of this nature may sound gimmicky in 2026, but they felt excitingly unorthodox a decade ago, when Pony Island came out to critical acclaim.

Fans of Daniel Mullins, the celebrated indie developer of Inscryption, will be forgiven for forgetting that Pony Island 2: Panda Circus is in active development. After all, it’s been almost three years since the announcement – and a full decade since it was first teased as an Easter egg in Pony Island’s ARG (Alternate Reality Game) – with only a single trailer and a bunch of tunes from the soundtrack released to the public.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

While the announcement trailer teases the return of endless-runner sequences and glitchy menus, Panda Circus is seemingly a far bigger and more complicated project than its predecessor; hence the 3D landscapes, pixel art JRPG sequences and even apparent nods to games such as The Case of the Golden Idol. Which is why Mullins claims that, at least in terms of gameplay variety, Panda Circus is closer to The Hex and Inscryption than the original game.

“[Pony Island 2] is multifaceted in its gameplay and wide-ranging in its influences. But this time the disparate game systems are united by more common elements,” he says, referencing the drag-and-drop “hacking” puzzle. “That simple premise was extended into an endless amount of blocks and holes of various descriptions.”

The plot sees a historical warrior who was slain on his crusade and was damned to hell, where he’s tormented by a video games-making Lucifer. This comically morbid tale “is the strongest link to its predecessor” from a narrative standpoint – although, we’re told, this warrior won’t be Theodore (Pony Island’s protagonist), but a different ancient crusader.

In the gameplay that we do get to glimpse in the trailer, the player and his furry companion are traversing through the top-down map, visiting villages and places of interest. It plays like “Oregon Trail through medieval China”, Mullins says after I mention noticing hunger and thirst bars. All this is happening while you’re being tormented by lordly King Yan, the Chinese god of death, played by voice actor SungWon Cho in lavish full-motion interludes.

Other sections promise different mythological themes and menacing deities – an overarching structure that will be familiar to those who played Inscryption. Then there is the Earth Prison, a three-dimensional hub that our hell-bound protagonist can explore, accessing different chapters by using what seems to be a mythical USB stick.

If the devil is truly in the details, Mullins gives him plenty of places to hide: Panda Circus seems to be brimming with them. “There is an almost unmanageable number of bespoke, one-off game systems,” he says. “It’s too big to fit in my mind now and that is a new challenge.”

The indie dev admits he would have “been troubled” if he knew just how long it would take to make Panda Circus – even with a handpicked team of collaborators. “I’m very lucky because it was a total chance that we started working together,” Mullins says about composer Jonah Senzel, whom he has worked with ever since the original Pony Island. “He turned out to be a genius.”

after newsletter promotion

While Mullins shies away from showing any new piece of gameplay, Panda Circus, now in its “final stretch” phase of development, is undergoing private beta. As for the release date: “it may become public knowledge soon,” he hints coyly.

Bombastic boss battles, an ARG that will see fans dissecting previous games with archaeological zeal (“I bet they’ll crack it in a couple weeks,” Mullins quips), and meta moments that wink at you cheekily are all to be expected from the developer’s most ambitious project to date.

“All the time has gone into making a big game that’s just downright turgid with secrets. There are worlds within worlds and layers upon layers.” Another classic Mullins joint, then, and we couldn’t be more ready.

Pony Island 2: Panda Circus is in development for PC with plans for Linux/Mac “not long after”.

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/a.title: Nazis and Happy Feet collide in Penguin Colony, a psychological horror game set at the world’s end
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/a.author: Sarah Thwaites
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/a.text:
Explore Antarctica as a flightless bird – and dodge some earthly monsters – in this surreal adaptation of HP Lovecraft

W
hile watching the 2006 animated film Happy Feet with his daughter, Origame Digital founder Naphtali Faulkner noticed something interesting. “[In the movie], they see the digger fall into the ocean, and it has an almost eldritch quality,” he says. Over time, and with plenty of iteration, Faulkner’s inspirations coalesced, from HP Lovecraft to the 1982 version of The Thing and the works of David Lynch. “I’m a big fan of horror that sits in your head rather than in your stomach,” says Faulkner.

In Penguin Colony, players body-switch between species of flightless birds, piecing together cryptic cosmic clues as they tail a Nazi expedition to Antarctica. In the process, Origame Digital draws on Lovecraft’s novella At the Mountains of Madness. “I’d always wanted to do a creature that’s a manifestation of colonial thought, energy and power, and the idea of it resting and then regrowing,” says Faulkner. “I was looking through the history of Lovecraft and him being a gigantic racist, and this idea of the Nazis sort of came out,” he adds.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The visual style of Penguin Colony pays homage to the low-poly aesthetics of the PS2, a period Faulkner calls romantic, owing to the era’s limited technical capabilities, which led to impressionist designs. “We’re not a rich studio,” he says. “There was just a games crash; publishers aren’t funding anything, everyone seems to be out of money. So why don’t we make something very cheap to make?” It started with the game’s isolated setting, followed by a decision to have humans in the game appear as soldiers; their uniform bodies could be duplicated with only their heads swapped out. “Repetition pays its weight in gold sometimes because you aren’t having to be so meticulous. You can paint with broad strokes and really build something out.”

Penguin Colony’s Antarctic setting is predominantly open-world, allowing Origame Digital to hide enigmatic notes, photographs and soundbites across the frigid tundra. “We wanted to play into the Lovecraftian fear of the unknown,” Faulkner says. As such, instead of relying on a user interface, players are guided by their intuition.

This stylistic choice was also inspired by Dark Souls director Hidetaka Miyazaki, whose intentional vagueness evokes a distinctly pre-internet sense of discovery. “Certain things are in an alien language that players will need to decipher if they want to know what’s being said,” says Faulkner. By investigating, players also emulate the Nazi expedition’s archaeological activity. “[Later] you’ll come across some hieroglyphics, and we’ve made sure those image files contain no metadata, so players will actually have to look at them and try to decipher what it’s saying in context.”

This cryptic touch isn’t the only homage to FromSoftware. Penguin Colony features an insight system comparable to Bloodborne, which lets players interpret the game’s otherworldly aspects with greater clarity based on how they play. “I don’t want to spoil exactly what,” adds Faulkner. “But, in a dark area, if you have enough insight, you can hear something walking around behind you.”

Despite its surreal surroundings, Penguin Colony’s narrative draws on real history. “I did my research on this group called the Ahnenerbe, which was tasked with finding the Spear of Destiny and other Christian artefacts,” says Faulkner. “Nazi relic hunting went all around the world,” he continues. “They would find things with barely any connection to anything, and invent histories that don’t actually exist, and that was used as their justification for the colonial annexation of Europe.”

It’s a confronting topic, but Faulkner feels this kind of conversation belongs in games, especially since they are one of the few art forms in which audience participation is mandatory. He recalls a conversation with his mentor about playing in the grey, where you place ideas side by side and explore the feelings they can evoke. “There are people out there who, the moment you say colonisation, freak out and start stomping their feet. [That’s] not my audience … I think of it like this: if this game reaches someone who hadn’t thought about this [topic] before and they change the way they think about it, just a little bit, then it was worth it.”

Penguin Colony is coming soon to PC and Nintendo Switch 2.

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/a.title: Metroid at 40: happy birthday to Samus Aran, gaming’s greatest badass and my personal heroine
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/a.author: Maddy Myers
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/a.text:
Being a woman who loves video games has often felt lonely, like being on a hostile planet – but Metroid’s female space hunter has been with me all the way

I
t’s 1986, and you’re playing a brand-new game. (You’re in Japan in this scenario, by the way; the game in question, Metroid, won’t come to North America and Europe until later.) Anyway, this new game has you in its grip. You are a lone astronaut exploring a hostile alien planet full of ancient, mysterious structures. This astronaut looks human enough – but this distinctly alien place is full of objects that power up their spacesuit’s capabilities. Each new ability allows you to explore a new area, and as you do, you realise that the entirety of the planetary base you’re exploring is one, massive, interconnected maze. Whoa.

Hours later, you finally defeat Mother Brain and set off a timed self-destruct sequence. Upon your escape, you’re treated to an endgame screen: the little astronaut faces you as text on screen implores you to “pray for peace in space”.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

But then, the astronaut’s suit starts flashing rapidly – pink, green, orange. Suddenly, the suit disappears. What remains is … a woman! And a hot one, at that. Her pixelated hourglass figure has been lovingly rendered; her low-cut red leotard matches the dot of red lipstick that denotes her mouth. She’s looking right at you, the player, and she’s waving, as if to say, Congratulations, big boy! And if you beat the game even faster, I’ll strip down to just a bikini.

This reveal lacked the consideration that a woman or girl might be the one playing the game. (The concept of a queer female player was also almost certainly not on any developer’s mind, either.) By 1986, video games were already “for boys”. As reporter Tracey Lien outlined in her extensive feature on how and when video game marketing shifted towards targeting boys, the video game crash of 1983 was followed by a marketing reset for several companies. The Nintendo Entertainment System, on which Metroid made its debut to non-Japanese audiences, “was targeted toward boys under 10. If you look at the Super NES five years later, it starts targeting boys ages 10-15,” Jesse Divnich, former vice president of insights and analysis for Electronic Entertainment Design and Research, told Lien.

The reveal of Samus Aran’s red bikini demonstrated that, in 1986 at least, if a game was going to have a female protagonist, she needed to be presented as a sex object to be enjoyed by the (presumed male, straight) player. That trend continued … for decades, unfortunately. But Samus Aran herself complicated the narrative. Sure, she was wearing increasingly skimpy outfits underneath that battle suit, but she also had spent the entire game up to that point performing extraordinarily badass feats. Well, technically, you – the player! – had performed them, as her. You were her, after all. Metroid tried to make you forget that, right at the end, by having her present herself to you as an object. But prior to that moment; she had been you, and you had been her, with all the personhood that implies.

It’s hard not to project personality traits on to the largely blank slate that is Samus. She must be fearless, venturing into space completely alone. She must be intelligent; she’s mapping out this entire mazelike structure as she goes along. She must be devoted, determined, working for herself alone as a bounty hunter – a solitary job. The instruction booklet says that Samus “is the greatest of all the space hunters and has successfully completed numerous missions that everybody thought were absolutely impossible”. This is the hyper-competent hero whose space boots you’re stepping into, and yeah, once again, she’s a woman.

It’s for all of these reasons that I love the original Metroid so much. Its design and concept, iterated and improved upon in its sequels, would go on to inspire countless other games (and one of gaming’s most famous genre terms). I always enjoy environmental puzzles and exploration in games, but it’s Samus Aran herself that I truly love – the version of Samus I created in my own head, as I played these games and projected myself on to her.

Just like Samus Aran, I am 40 years old. My birthday is just one month prior to hers; I appreciate that I did not have to live in this world for very long without her. Because, like Samus, my journey has often been a lonely one. I didn’t start playing Metroid games until I was 21 and had just gone through a bad breakup; we had shared an apartment, and now suddenly, I was living alone. At that time, I was a college student and an unpaid intern at the Boston Phoenix, and I had yet to get any of my article pitches approved. I had been playing video games ever since getting a Game Boy as a young child, but I had mostly played games with male characters in them. After all, that’s what video games were, most of the time. But I always knew there were some exceptions, like Lara Croft in the Tomb Raider series, or Jade in Beyond Good and Evil. And of course, Samus Aran in Metroid.

In a post-breakup depressive fugue, I rented and played through a bunch of Metroid games, totally out of order. Like a baby bird seeking her mother – or more relevantly, like a baby Metroid – I glommed on to Samus Aran with a fervour that has yet to really end. I began to seek out other games with female characters, and spaces online where other female gamers and queer gamers hung out. Through these spaces, I learned what feminism actually was (turns out, it’s not “hating men,” as I had been assuming prior to that point). Starting out as a video games journalist, I clung on to this small community I found.

Writing about games as a queer woman in the 2000s and 2010s came with a lot of harassment and blowback. Often I felt very alone – but I would tell myself I was like Samus Aran, on a hostile planet. I kept on going, kept on exploring, kept on building up my abilities. After all, like Samus on Zebes, the hostile place I was exploring was also actually my home. I had a right to be there. Those space pirates – or the bigots sending me death threats, whatever – did not belong. The blank slate of Samus, especially in the earliest Metroid games, let me infuse as much of myself and my own personality into her journey as I wanted.

There have been many Metroid games since, some of which have depicted versions of Samus with a bit more personality. Most notoriously, Metroid: Other M serves up a fearful and traumatised Samus who refuses to question Galactic Federation orders, even when those orders make no sense and put her in danger. This version of the character clashed so heavily with many players’ perceptions of her that it has since become something like a shared trauma for the Metroid fandom. I thought the game was so bad that the only solution for Metroid going forward would be a full reboot.

But that’s not what happened. Instead, fully seven years after Other M, we got Samus Returns, MercurySteam’s 2017 remake of Metroid 2. It was a reminder of the power of the original Metroid games – Metroid, Metroid 2, and Super Metroid. (These games actually make up a trilogy, albeit with a minimalist narrative.) It was a reminder of the Samus I remembered and loved: fearless, intelligent, devoted, determined. And unlike in Other M, whose camera’s gaze was unafraid to slide slowly over Samus Aran’s clingy zero suit, Samus Returns was not objectifying Samus or distancing her from the player. It was much easier to remember, instead, that Samus is you.

You should want to be Samus Aran. You can’t even help it, right? She’s just so fucking cool! And that part at the end of the first few Metroid games where she performs for you as a sex object is not, really, the important part; it’s dissonant, actually, a fourth-wall breaking moment that doesn’t reflect the core of what Metroid is. The important part is the whole rest of the game, where you get to be Samus – who happens to be a woman. And a person, just like you.
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/a.summary: The game is a reminder of the power of the original Metroid games – Metroid, Metroid 2, and Super Metroid. The game has a new character who is a woman who is not a man.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: China’s tech advances are causing chaos from Silicon Valley to the White House
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Nick Robins-Early
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
New AI models, advanced robots and specialty computer chips are unsettling markets and the US tech industry

O
ver the past month, a series of advancements in China’s artificial intelligence, chip manufacturing and robotics technologies have rattled financial markets, caused divisions among US tech moguls and left the Trump administration scrambling to respond.

Silicon Valley has long pointed to China’s tech industry as a competitive threat and used its growth as rationale for why US firms should not face regulatory oversight that could slow them down. In recent weeks, however, China’s progress has pushed US tech CEOs past vague warnings and into open disagreement over how to address Chinese-made products upending their industry.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The most immediate threat to Silicon Valley’s status quo has come from a series of Chinese-made open-source, open-weight AI models that are free to download and use. The models, such as Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, are powerful enough to compete in some applications with proprietary and comparatively expensive AI products from OpenAI and Anthropic.

The emergence of China’s open-source AI alternatives has caused divisions in both the White House and US tech industry over whether to oppose or embrace these new models. On one side are chip manufacturers who see revenue opportunities from increased AI usage and tech companies concerned about OpenAI and Anthropic’s growing dominance in the AI industry. On the other is Anthropic and OpenAI, which face profit pressures from open source models and argue that Chinese-made models pose security risks.

The White House is similarly divided, historically hawkish on China’s tech industry but wary of blocking low-cost AI models that American businesses have come to rely on. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent suggested in recent weeks that the US could sanction Chinese AI firms over alleged intellectual property theft from American companies, while commerce secretary Howard Lutnick has received letters from tech-startup founders asking him not to cut off access to open models.

Amid reports that the Trump administration was considering banning or limiting the use of China’s open source models, a swath of prominent big tech companies including Microsoft, Nvidia, Palantir and Meta also recently published a letter urging lawmakers to refrain from putting restrictions on open models. Additionally, Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang went to Capitol Hill on Tuesday to meet with Democratic and Republican party leaders to lobby in support of open models.

While facing heat from China and other tech companies, OpenAI and Anthropic revealed in recent weeks that their AI models went rogue during cybersecurity tests and hacked into outside organizations. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman visited lawmakers and administration officials this week to discuss controls on AI following the incident. That forced Donald Trump to field questions about whether he would put more safety restrictions on AI development.

“We have to be careful in both ways. We don’t want to restrict them when all of a sudden we come in second to China,” Trump said, adding: “I know many of these people. I don’t want to restrict them from doing great work.”

While the Trump administration debates potential safety controls and limits on Chinese-made AI models, it took tangible action this week against China’s increasingly prominent robotics industry. The Federal Communications Commission announced on Tuesday a ban on humanoid robots from China over what it alleged was an unacceptable national security risk.

China’s humanoid robots from companies such as Unitree have been the subject of numerous viral videos this year, showcasing their ability to dance or interact with people when programmed to do so. The FCC alleged that the robots could also steal data or surveil US citizens, as well as threaten US manufacturing and supply chains.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

The FCC’s decision further escalates the US competition with China over emerging technologies and comes as fears over China’s tech have shifted financial markets. A report from the Information this week stating that China had begun mass production of specialty chips key to the AI boom spurred a stock selloff that erased $1tn in market value from other chip manufacturers.

As Chinese-made tech advancements increasingly begin to rival their US counterparts, Silicon Valley’s divisions could intensify, markets could become more skittish and the Trump administration could face more pressure over how to counter China’s influence.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Silicon Valley donations make Colorado Democratic primary one of state’s most expensive
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Dara Kerr
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Manny Rutinel’s House campaign draws millions from big tech as pro- and anti-AI factions spar over regulation

Political groups funded by top tech executives have been homing in on one local race in Colorado, as the state’s Democratic primary vote gets under way on Tuesday. Democrat Manny Rutinel, who’s running in the competitive eighth congressional district for a seat in the House, has seen his campaign boosted with at least $2m in donations from committees led by the former Google CEO Eric Schmidt and crypto billionaire Chris Larsen.

Rutinel is a progressive candidate running against former state representative and centrist Democrat Shannon Bird. During his campaign, he has focused on his Latino heritage and centered his platform around affordability and regulating Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Technology and artificial intelligence are not topics he’s publicly waded into, but when he was a state representative, he supported two bills aimed at putting guardrails on AI, according to Axios. Bird, conversely, opposed a bill to regulate AI, saying it would restrain innovation in the state.

Political spending on Rutinel’s campaign has made it one of the most expensive races in Colorado, outpacing other district and Senate races. The two top Super Pacs funded by tech dollars, which contributed to Rutinel’s campaign, are Somos Pac and You Can Push Back.

Schmidt and his wife, Wendy, donated $2m to the Somos Pac, which supports Latino voter engagement, which then gave $1.3m to Rutinel’s campaign, according to Axios. You Can Push Back, which is entirely funded by the crypto mogul Larsen, donated nearly $1m to the Colorado lawmaker’s campaign. Rutinel also received millions in donations from Super Pacs focused on Latino candidates.

Another chunk of funding for Rutinel came from individual employees from top AI and tech firms, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta. Rutinel has received more than $265,000 from these donations, according to a campaign finance tracker created by the publication Transformer. Anthropic employees were the largest group of givers, with 57 people donating nearly $162,000 combined.

This race in Colorado serves as an example of a stark rift that is forming among big tech donors. One cohort is throwing money behind candidates seen as lenient on AI regulations, while the other is backing political hopefuls who indicate they will rein in the breakneck growth of the technology.

The donations to Rutinel’s campaign come after a showdown in a local congressional race in New York last week, where pro- and anti-AI groups spent a combined $24m to either oppose or support the Democratic candidate Alex Bores, a member of the state assembly who sponsored an AI safety bill. Similar scenarios played out during the primaries in North Carolina and California.

Rutinel’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
