Zachariah understands why people might find it difficult at first. “It’s very unnatural. You might put your phone in the living room while you work in the kitchen, but here you’re seeing it locked behind what is essentially a gate that you can’t access,” he says. But when people leave, they often say they would like to have their own phone lockbox, or tell him that they’re going to try to not look at their device until they get home. “It’s kind of sad that we have to literally lock our phones away. But people really crave that time.”

This is true for Jarred Laros, 31, who lives in Essex and has been a regular at the Offline Project since it launched. One of the first events he went to was a “paint and sip” evening, where an artist taught everyone how to paint a landscape scene with mountains, a river and a sunset. People sat around a table together, working on their canvases while having drinks and snacks, and getting to know each other. “I liked the idea of getting off my phone and being more intentional with how I’m spending my time. I would never try to teach myself how to paint, but doing that in a community setting is very easy-going. The conversation flows.”

Laros runs his own business, and spends a lot of time on his devices. “I’m always glued to a screen, whether it’s my iPad, my MacBook, my phone, or all three at the same time,” he says. “Outside of work, there’s the doomscroll that you succumb to. I go on Instagram without intending to. Half an hour later, I’m, like, ‘What am I still doing on this app?’ My average daily screen time is seven and a half hours. My relationship with my phone is not what I want it to be.”

The Offline Project is part of a new wave of digital detox communities that host events to give people time away from screens. It’s not hard to understand the appeal: adults in the UK now spend an average of four and a half hours online a day, and most of that is on their phones, according to Ofcom’s 2025 Online Nation report.

In 2025, the annual TouchPoints survey by the Institute of Practitioners in Advertising found that British adults were spending more time on their phones than watching TV for the first time. The government has recently announced that in spring 2027 it will bring in a social media ban for under-16s, which will include platforms like Instagram, TikTok and YouTube. When the news was announced, a teenage girl went viral when asked by a news reporter how she would spend all her newfound free time. Her answer? “Stare at a wall.”

Thankfully, if you want a break from your phone, there are plenty of things to do that are much more engaging. As our lives are becoming ever-more online, people are starting to push back against the hold that technology has on us. Sick of looking out at a sea of screens, some musicians are enforcing a no phones policy at their gigs. Bob Dylan’s 2025 UK and Ireland tour, Fred Again’s gigs at Alexandra Palace in February, and Harry Styles’s one-off gig in Manchester in March this year all had rules against using phones. It’s happening at comedy events, too – phones were placed in locked pouches at Sarah Silverman’s London Palladium gig last year, and Russell Howard’s current Don’t Tell the Algorithm tour promises “no phones, no distractions, just humans and jokes”.

According to data from Eventbrite, attendance at phone-free events in 2024 to 2025 increased by 121% globally. At broadcaster and DJ Annie Mac’s club night Before Midnight, stickers are placed on phone cameras so you can’t take photos or videos. “It reminds people to be in the moment. You’re only going to get so much satisfaction out of blurred videos with distorted sound, or dark, fuzzy photos,” she says. “Nightclubs are traditionally places where you go to feel a sense of freedom – to be whoever you want to be. They’re meant to be dark for that dual sense of losing yourself and finding yourself at the same time. Phones inhibit both of those things.”

While some are seeking out pockets of time at events and venues where they can escape their smartphones, others are going one step further and ditching them altogether. Cody Ramone, 31, from Derby, was using an old flip phone from 2015 until the pandemic, when life became more online than ever and he needed a smartphone again. In 2024, he switched back to a “dumb phone”. “I got tired of all the notifications and being constantly online,” he says.

Abandoning his smartphone has been transformative and given him time for more enriching activities. “I get bored more. Being bored is what drives you to try new things, pick up an old hobby, or think creatively. My attention span has improved, so I read more and spend more time doing creative hobbies, like crochet. I call people or hang out with them more often,” he says.

What is it that makes our phones so addictive? “Digital media activates the same reward pathway as drugs and alcohol, releasing dopamine, our reward neurotransmitter, in a key area of the reward pathway in the brain,” says Anna Lembke, professor of psychiatry at Stanford University School of Medicine and the author of Dopamine Nation. “Moving images are like catnip for the mammalian brain, leading to video-chaining, akin to ‘chain smoking’. Once we begin, it’s hard to stop, even when we want to.”

The more time we spend on our phones, the more we become “desensitised to what we are seeing” and look for more “potent rewards to recreate that original experience of pleasure”, says Lembke. “At the same time, we lose our ability to take joy in other more modest rewards, like watching a sunset, sharing a meal with friends, or reading a good book. We spend more time scrolling alone. We become increasingly dissatisfied and lonely.”

While that might sound like a bleak state of affairs, the good news is that it doesn’t have to be this way. With the rise of phone-free experiences, it’s possible to detach yourself from your device, even if it’s temporarily. “Part of having a healthier relationship with technology must include discrete periods of time when we are not using it, and instead fully present and interacting with the people and the world around us,” says Lembke. “This means creating collective spaces where we come together device-free.”

From off-grid, tech-free cabins to the pubs where devices aren’t allowed, these are the places to escape your phone in the UK.

Set up in Amsterdam in 2024 by friends Jordy van Bennekom, Valentijn Klok and Ilya Kneppelhout, the Offline Club has 14 chapters in cities across 10 countries, including London and Bristol in the UK. Events start with everyone putting their devices in the “phone hotel”, a lockable metal box with slots. For the first hour, there’s music playing but no talking, and everyone does their own thing. For the second hour, people are encouraged to chat.

The demand for these kinds of events is growing. In London there’s the Switch Off – quiet, phone-free sessions for women where they can journal, collage or read a book – while the Offline Project hosts screen-free walks, talks and workshops. Logging Off Club is a UK initiative – with local groups in London, Bristol, Brighton, Southampton, Cambridge and the New Forest – that has now expanded to Sydney, Mexico City and Winnipeg.

In Bath, friends Nicola MacDonald and Laura Hughes started the Digital Detox Club in early 2025. They host events every two months at The Den cafe in Bath – phones go into the “tech motel” on arrival, and the pair provide optional activities like board games, journalling and crafts. “We’ve been struck by the diversity of attendees, from university students to retirees, which suggests this isn’t a niche concern,” says MacDonald. “It reflects a broader cultural fatigue with constant connectivity.”

If you’re trying to spend less time on your phone, a craft class does some of the work for you by keeping your hands busy. But there are specifically phone‑free classes, too. Native Hands offers basketry, pottery and bushcraft sessions, held outside in an ancient woodland in Sussex. At Curious House in East Sussex, classes range from basket weaving to portrait painting. All sessions start with a mindful breathing exercise to help people switch off.

In November last year, Dan Palmer launched Airplane Mode – a monthly phone-free event at his organic restaurant and natural wine bar, Eat Your Greens, in Leeds. The free events include workshops hosted by local creatives, doing things like painting, collage and origami.

Rather than locking phones away in a safe, they use a swear jar system. “Every time I catch anyone on their phone, I fine them 50p,” Palmer says. “All the fines go to a charity called Positive Action for Refugees and Asylum Seekers. So far, I’ve issued three fines – and one of them was for me! No one wants to be on their phones when they have something more interesting to do.”

The idea of using your hands to make something tangible rather than doomscrolling is what inspired Nadia Butt from Inner Canvas to host art sessions for women at her home in Reading without the distraction of screens. “The screen-free element is at the heart of the sessions,” she says. “We treat it like a ritual. At the start of each session, phones are silenced and placed in a box. I call it the ‘phone spa’. Framing it as something collective removes the anxiety around it.”

Spas are all about relaxing and switching off, but often these spaces aren’t phone-free. That is changing, though, with some spas now enforcing phone bans. The Bath Thermae Spa has a strict no phones policy – guests must put devices in a lockable pouch that’s kept in their locker. At Careys Manor in the New Forest, there’s a digital detox spa break, which includes relaxing treatments, a complimentary journal and a phone amnesty box in the room.

Phones have been banned at the Bothy at Heckfield Place, Hampshire, since it launched in 2023. “Seeing someone on their phone in a space dedicated to restoration felt out of alignment. You are there to be with yourself, to listen inwardly, to slow down,” says the spa operations director, Reka Seres-Erdei.

It’s not just at spas – as sauna culture rapidly grows, many people are finding these spaces offer a welcome break from technology. Ryan Haynes, 34, is a regular at London’s Community Sauna Baths, which has locations in Camberwell, Hackney Wick, Stratford, Walthamstow and Peckham. You can’t take your phone into the sauna, but you’re allowed to take photos outside, although they are considering a phone ban throughout.

Haynes’s Wednesday morning sauna session is “non-negotiable” for him. “All of my best ideas in the past two years have been while sitting in a sauna. Everyone needs to slow down to hear what’s going on in their brain,” he says.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

As an independent bookshop owner and a sauna enthusiast, Kelly Wickson had an inspired idea last year: a book club in a sauna. Wickson owns Chapter 34 in Shoreham-by-Sea on the Sussex coast, and hosts the sauna book club once a month at the Nomadic Sauna on Kingston Beach. Creating a phone-free space was a big part of it, and the sauna conveniently ticks that box. “It will ruin your phone; you’ve got no choice,” she says.

The books are always 250 pages or less, and there’s no commitment to go every month. Phones are left in waterproof tubs outside the sauna. The book club is an hour long, and they go in and out of the sauna throughout, with some having a quick dip in the sea during breaks. Wickson has been amazed at how popular it is. “We do it on a Friday evening and it sells out,” she says.

While a book club in a sauna is particularly unusual, people increasingly value being given the time and space to switch off and read. This is the thinking behind Silent Book Club, where one of the mottoes is: “Put down your phone, pick up a book.” It’s a global network with about 2,000 chapters in more than 60 countries, and there are almost 150 in the UK and Ireland.

When Camille Jetzer and James Nasmyth opened the Roses of Elagabalus in Dalston, east London, last year, they knew they wanted to minimise phone use. They refer to it as a “clubhouse” – there’s a bar, restaurant, dancing and cabaret. “The idea of having no phones is that you would walk into the Roses, leave the outside world behind and enter this fantasy world where you can just enjoy the moment,” Jetzer says.

When you arrive at the Roses, a host explains that there’s no photography, and places a sticker over your phone camera. There are also reminders on the menus. “It’s a ‘you were there or you missed it’ situation,” Jetzer says, who has also noticed their regular punters reminding new visitors about the rule.

While phones aren’t locked away, Jetzer says the stickers on cameras mean they are used less. “It creates an environment where phones are less desired. In a dream world, we’d lock away the phones. That’s maybe next year’s project,” she says.

Elsewhere in London, Esmeralda’s Mayfair and the Spy Bar at Raffles London at the OWO both put stickers on phone cameras. In 2019, Samuel Smith’s pubs brought in a rule that customers couldn’t use phones or laptops in their establishments, of which there are more than 200 across the country. At the Barrel at Bude in Cornwall, anyone who breaks its no phones rule has to donate £1, which goes to local charities. In Herne Bay in Kent, the Butchers Arms has been a phone-free zone since it opened in 2005 – there are no signs needed to enforce it, says owner Martyn Hillier. “A disgruntled look from other customers is enough. If that doesn’t work we all start saying, ‘Rhubarb, rhubarb, rhubarb’, louder and louder until they realise they can’t converse any more.”

In Woking, Kim and Mike Jarred run Beyond the Screen, a monthly phone-free social at their local pub the Olive Tree. They set it up in March 2025 after talking about how they could model good phone habits for their teenage sons. They provide activities like puzzles and conversation starters, but mostly people just sit and chat. “Pubs are closing down and we’re just staying in our houses with our phones in front of our faces rather than getting out and meeting people. We’re human beings, and we need to connect with each other. Phones are getting in the way of that,” Kim says.

“Nights out now can feel like content creation exercises. We wanted to remove that layer entirely and return the focus to the room,” says James Hutchins, co-founder of Manchester club Amber’s. It opened in December 2024 and has a no-photo, no‑video policy, with stickers placed over phone cameras. “If people are seen taking photos or videos inside the club, they are politely asked to leave,” Hutchins says.

Amber’s is part of a growing trend in UK clubs, as more venues are making their dancefloors a phone‑free space. The policy is used at both Fold and Fabric in London, Lakota and sister venue Moon Club in Bristol, and Doppler Studio in Leicester. Some clubs ban phones completely. At Offgrid, a monthly day party at House Party in Soho, London, co‑founded by Stormzy, phones are sealed in a locked pouch. At her club night Before Midnight, Annie Mac has noticed a palpable shift in atmosphere – something she experienced during the first phone‑free Before Midnight event at the Warehouse Project in Manchester. “People were more present and louder. They whooped, they hollered, they whistled. They reacted to the tunes in a visceral way.”

In 2019, Hector Hughes was working for a tech startup in London and feeling burnt out. “I ended up at a silent retreat at a Buddhist temple on top of a mountain in the Himalayas. When you got there, they took your phone off you. I spent 10 days cut off from the outside world. It was a revelation,” says Hughes.

He came back from that trip, quit his job and started setting up Unplugged – off-grid cabins in the UK where you lock your phone away. It launched in the summer of 2020; there are now 60 digital detox cabins around the country (and they have expanded to Catalonia, too). The phone-free element is self‑policed, but each cabin has a lock box with a padlock, and the key is in a sealed envelope. They provide a Polaroid camera, a map and an old-school Nokia phone in case of emergencies. Hughes says that Unplugged’s customers often return for regular stays and go on to make changes in their daily lives, like having phone-free date nights or drastically cutting down their screen time.

If you like the idea of escaping to an off-grid cabin and ditching your phone, there are various options around the UK. Unyoked’s cabins run on solar power, have no wifi and often no phone signal – there’s a “spice signal”, from mild to extra spicy, to set expectations for how remote a cabin feels, and how long it might take to walk to one. They also have Brick devices, which help you block certain apps from your phone for a set amount of time. Similarly, Shacks’ cabins are off-grid with no wifi, and lockboxes for phones.

Alternatively, you could look for a remote cottage with no wifi and limited or no phone signal, like the Cottage in the Clouds in the middle of the Lake District national park, or Woodcock Cabin in the Cambrian mountains in Wales. If you want to escape dry land, too, Lilypod in Devon is a floating retreat with three solar-powered eco pods built on a platform next to a lake, where there’s no TV, wifi or phone signal, but there are board games, beanbags and a king-sized bed.

Florence Achery, founder of Yoga Retreats and More, launched her “Retreat like it’s 1999” digital detox breaks, in Lancashire and Cumbria, in 2023. A recent guest enjoyed the break from her devices so much that she forgot to pack her laptop and phone when she left. “I had to WhatsApp the guest she was travelling with to get them to pick up her stuff,” Achery says.

On arrival, guests hand over their devices before spending the next few days sharing meals together, going on long walks, doing yoga and star gazing. “They’re in charge, not their phones,” says Achery, who gives her guests a battery-powered alarm clock to take home, to encourage them to keep phones out of their bedrooms. She has also launched a parent and teen digital detox retreat to help younger people to change their relationship with technology.

At its 223-hectare (550-acre) estate on the River Dart in Devon, the Sharpham Trust hosts retreats focused on mindfulness and connecting to nature; guests are encouraged to switch off their phones.

And, in Suffolk, sisters Lauretta and Sharon Gavin host regular phone-free retreats at the Detox Barn, where guests enjoy vegan food, yoga, sound baths and countryside walks. “For many people it’s a huge relief to step away from their phones for 48 hours,” Lauretta says. “People open up, share stories and properly connect.”
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.summary: Offline Project has been running events in London since August 2025. The Digital Detox Club is a UK initiative that has now expanded to Sydney, Mexico City and Winnipeg.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.title: One of UK’s best fossil collections sold overseas in ‘loss to the nation’
https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.text:
Exclusive: Lack of funds left British museums unable pay eight-figure sum for collection, which went to Abu Dhabi institution

Britain’s Jurassic gold rush: the fossil hunters chasing fortunes on Dorset’s beaches

One of the most important collections of UK Jurassic fossils ever compiled has been sold to a museum in Abu Dhabi, the Guardian can reveal, in what British experts have described as a loss for the nation.

The collection, which was amassed by a private fossil collector, consisted of 318 specimens, including ichthyosaurs, fish and crustaceans among other creatures, some of which could be new species.

The fossils were initially offered for purchase to the Natural History Museum (NHM) in London and to Amgueddfa Cymru (Museum Wales) for what was described by one source as an “eight-figure sum”.

Neither institution bought the collection, with both citing a lack of funding. An email seen by the Guardian suggested the NHM had “no money at all” for acquisitions.

One curator said that while there had long been a hope that the collection could be kept in the UK, it also posed issues around storage space, curatorial time and packaging materials.

“I don’t blame the collectors at all. That’s all they can do. They can’t sit on these things forever,” the curator said, adding that the issue was expected to occur again and again as collectors get older and look for a suitable home for their life’s work.

“Whose responsibility is it to fund our heritage and the preservation of our heritage? Because otherwise it could get lost,” they added.

The extensive collection is understood to come from a sequence of rocks known as the Lower Lias, from Lyme Regis, Charmouth, and the south-west of the UK.

It was compiled by Chris Moore, a private Dorset-based collector with experience of hunting fossils in the area. In emails seen by the Guardian the collection is described as “stunning”.

Some countries, including Mongolia and Brazil, consider all fossils found in those countries in recent decades to be property of the state – a situation that has led to international disputes over repatriation of fossils housed abroad. However, this is not the case in the UK.

Richard Butler, a professor of palaebiology at the University of Birmingham who was not involved in the sale, said the collection was of national significance. “This is one of the most important collections of fossils ever made on the world-famous Jurassic Coast of Dorset. It would have been wonderful to see these fossils on display and engaging the public in a UK museum.”

He added: “This sale raises important questions about whether more should be done to preserve important and irreplaceable natural heritage such as this for the benefit of the UK public.”

In the United Arab Emirates, the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi confirmed it had bought a collection from Moore, which went on display in November 2025. A spokesperson for the museum said the Lower Jurassic rocks of the UK preserved some of the best examples of marine life from when what is now the Dorset coast was roughly at the same latitude as north Africa.

“All natural history museums around the world tell this story, often using fossils from multiple countries to help narrate their journey through time. If we are to tell a 4.2bn-year story of the evolution of life on Earth, all museums must travel both spatially and temporally with their collections,” the spokesperson said.

“A large majority of the Chris Moore collection is already on public display in the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi in the Mesozoic Gallery (Age of Dinosaurs Gallery).”

Lyme Regis is part of the Jurassic Coast, a Unesco world heritage site, that is rich with fossils that date back to between 200m and 145m years ago. The area has a long history of private fossil collecting, with notable figures including Mary Anning – a pioneering palaeontologist and fossil dealer whose triumphs included the discovery of the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaurus in 1823.

While approaches vary across the UK nations, modern fossil collectors along England’s Jurassic Coast are encouraged to follow the west Dorset fossil collecting code and the Undercliffs national nature reserve fossil collecting code.

Fossils initially belong to the owner of the land on which they are found, legal ownership is typical transferred to collectors who adhere to such codes and recording schemes – a situation that reflects the valuable role collectors are deemed to have in finding fossils that might otherwise never be recovered.

But while highly valuable archeological finds turned up by activities such as metal detecting can be classified as treasure – and therefore must be reported to the relevant authorities within 14 days of discovery – the same is not true for fossils, even those deemed to be key scientifically important fossils, known as category 1.

According to the west Dorset fossil collecting code of conduct, collectors “who intend to sell or otherwise dispose of their category 1 specimens must first offer them to UK registered museums for a period of six months. If no purchase has been agreed by this time, the collector will be free to offer the specimen elsewhere.”

However, such codes are not legally binding and even if followed, as Moore did, fossils found in the UK can be sold by collectors to private individuals, museums or other buyers – including those overseas. Moore was approached for comment.

According to the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DDCMS), only objects that are over 50 years old and are manufactured or produced require an individual cultural property export licence, and there are no export requirements specific to the sale of fossils.

A quick search of online marketplaces reveals a plethora of fossils, with small ammonites selling for as little as a few pounds.

But some fossils can also fetch colossal sums: in 2020, Stan the T rex, now also housed at the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, was sold for a then record-breaking $31.8m (£23.6m), while in July this year another T rex skeleton nicknamed Gus was sold at Sotheby’s for $50.1m.

These figures are far beyond the budget of most museums, with such specimens instead snapped up by private buyers – including business people and celebrities. Among those known to have bought dinosaur fossils are the actors Leonardo DiCaprio, Nicolas Cage and Russell Crowe – although Cage later returned the rare dinosaur skull he had bought to Mongolia, after it emerged it had been illegally removed from the country.

Fossils have also become popular on social media, with hunters using platforms such as TikTok to share videos of themselves cracking open rocks in a “fossil or no fossil?” reveal. Some accounts have several million followers.

Finding a fossil is only the first step on the road to a sale: as the NHM in London notes, painstaking mechanical and chemical preparation is needed to turn it one into a museum-grade exhibit. Only dedicated fossil hunters have the tools and skills to prepare fossils – and Moore is among them.

Many experts support the status quo for fossil collecting and sales, arguing that a ban on collecting would mean many important specimens would remain undiscovered and could result in a black-market for fossils – rather than allowing collectors to work with academics.

There is no suggestion the sale of the Moore collection to the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi has broken any rules.

Yet Dr Erin Maxwell, an expert in Early Jurassic marine vertebrates based at the State Museum of Natural History in Stuttgart said the sale was a blow. “Such a sale in my opinion represents a loss to the UK, as fossils represent part of the natural [or] cultural heritage of the region and country from which they originate.

“The loss is somewhat offset by the fact that these fossils are going to a museum rather than into the collection of a wealthy individual.”

Maxwell added that there were other options for countries such as the UK where fossils are not automatically considered property of the state.

“I think it is important for the state to have the right of first refusal on acquiring the collection on an at-cost basis prior to export – rather than the currently grossly inflated market price,” she said. “However, if the state declines, then sale to a foreign museum is a best-case scenario.”

Phil Davidson, a palaeontologist at Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre in Dorset, said the priority was that fossil specimens of key scientific interest were in public collections, such as museums, so they could be described by teams of international experts, noting most scientific journals did not allow specimens to be described if they were within a private collection.

“All the researchers I have talked to have said the same thing: the location of where the museum collection is housed is secondary,” Davidson said.

“Countless specimens of scientific importance are housed outside their country of origin. Often this was because the specific researchers are based in other countries, or that they do not have the capacity or need to focus on other pressing priorities”.

Davidson also stressed the importance of keeping the Moore collection together, adding the specimens come from a world heritage site “and this heritage is for everyone and not limited to lines on a map”.
https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.summary: The collection was amassed by a private fossil collector in Dorset. Neither museums bought the collection, with both citing a lack of funding. Only objects that are over 50 years old and are manufactured or produced require an individual cultural property export licence.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Where in the UK will get the best view of the solar eclipse?
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Rachel Hall
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
When, where and how to get the optimal view of the first solar eclipse to be visible across the country this century

For the first time this century, people across the UK will be able to see an almost total solar eclipse in the evening sky on Wednesday.

A solar eclipse occurs when the moon moves between the sun and the Earth, blocking the sun’s light either partly or fully. This year, people in the UK and Ireland will see 90-96% of the sun covered by the moon for the first time since 1999 – and it’s their last chance until 2081.

Across north-western Europe, people will see about 88-95% coverage, while spectators in parts of Greenland, Iceland and northern Spain will see a total eclipse for up to two minutes and 18 seconds in duration.

In the UK, viewers in the west will see the most of the sun obscured: 95% in Plymouth, 93.2% in Cardiff and 93.1% in Belfast. Spectators in Manchester will see 91.9% and Londoners will catch 91.4%. Farther north and east people will see smaller proportions, with Edinburgh at 90.7%, Newcastle at 90.2%. Shetland will have the lowest coverage at 88%.

Royal Observatory Greenwich astronomer Jess Lee said that these are small differences, and all “will still be impressive sights”. She recommended finding hills with clear views to the west, for example Parliament Hill, Alexandra Palace or Primrose Hill in London, or rooftop venues.

Because the eclipse takes place in August, there’s a stronger chance of clear skies. Tom Morgan, a Met Office meteorologist, said it was too early to be confident, but “given the summer we’ve had a lot of the UK will have reasonable viewing conditions”.

At present, there is a higher risk of thick cloud and rain in Scotland and Northern Ireland, while the clearest skies are likely to be towards the south and the east of the UK. “For many it’ll be quite a spectacular and rare event,” he said.

For Scotland’s astronomer royal, Catherine Heymans, keeping an eye on the clouds is the secret to scoring the best view, since these could partly or entirely obscure the eclipse.

“I plan to check the Met Office’s fantastic online cloud cover forecast as we get closer to the day. I’m ready to hop on a train north, south, east or west to find some cloud-free skies,” she said.

Getting to a high point with a clear view of the horizon also helps. “I’d recommend a dress rehearsal in the days before. If you can’t see the sun from your planned viewing spot at 7.30pm because your view is blocked by a hill or a house, then you’ll want to find yourself a different location for the real event,” Heymans added.

The most important thing, she stressed, is to wear eclipse glasses and avoid looking directly at the sun.

During an eclipse, the sun appears dimmer, making it easier to look at directly. However, solar radiation can still reach and damage the retina, often without causing any pain, so viewers may not realise harm is occurring until it’s too late.

Following the 1999 total solar eclipse, the Royal College of Ophthalmologists reported about 70 cases of people experiencing vision problems after watching the eclipse.

The UK Health Security Agency advises that there are two safe approaches: specialist eclipse viewers or indirect viewing methods.

Eclipse glasses or handheld solar viewers must be genuine and sold by a reputable retailer, and should have specially designed filters that meet the international safety standard ISO 12312-2:2015(E), and no scratches, tearing or damage to the lens. Old pairs may not be reusable and sunglasses should never be used.

Indirect view methods include viewing the sun’s image projected through a colander or the gaps between tree leaves on to white paper, or using a pinhole pierced in one sheet of card and projected on to another.

Sarah Crowther, an astronomer at the University of Manchester, said it was important to remember that the solar eclipse would take place at different times across the UK.

It starts at about 6.08pm in Edinburgh and Glasgow, 6.10pm in Belfast, 6.13pm in Manchester and Liverpool, 6.15pm in Birmingham, 6.17pm in London and 6.18pm in Cornwall. Maximum eclipse follows roughly an hour later, ending about 8pm.

People might observe the surrounding area going quiet during the solar eclipse, “when animals think it is night because it is darker, which gives a sense of calm. And then there’s an awakening as it gets light again, birds think it is dawn so there could be a dawn chorus,” said Crowther.

She added: “I think many people feel a sense of awe when they see an eclipse. It can put the vast scales of the solar system into some kind of perspective.”

It's their last chance to see an almost total solar eclipse in the evening sky on Wednesday. People in the west will see the most of the solar eclipse: 95% in Plymouth, 93.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Spanish mountain village braces for astrotourists lured by total solar eclipse
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Sam Jones in Somosierra
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Somosierra will be prime spot to view celestial alignment on 12 August, an event that poses logistical challenges

Little stirs in the mountains above Somosierra beyond the wind that lashes the flat peaks, the cows that graze on parched grass and the sun that beats down on the abandoned aerodrome where generations of glider pilots learned to ride air currents alongside squadrons of vultures and red kites.

But all this stillness will disappear, albeit temporarily, on the evening of 12 August, when swathes of northern and eastern Spain and the Balearic islands experience a total solar eclipse, the likes of which has not been seen here for more than 120 years.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The rare celestial alignment has suddenly turned Somosierra – a small village that sits at an altitude of 1,440 metres where the northernmost reaches of the Madrid region fade into neighbouring Castilla y León and Castilla-La Mancha – into a prime astrotourist destination. No site as close to the Spanish capital will enjoy what Somosierra will: one minute and 29 seconds of pure, clear-skied total eclipse.

Awe-inspiring as the event promises to be, however, it has thrown up all sorts of unexpected but pressing questions for the village and its 93 inhabitants.

With as many as 2,000 visitors expected, where will everyone park? Will there be enough water? And, last but not least, how many batches of paella will the local restaurant need to prepare for the invasion of hungry sky-gazers?

“The fact that we’ve been selected as the best place in the Madrid region to watch the eclipse has led to a huge amount of media and social media coverage,” said Somosierra council’s tourism manager, Irma López Muñoz, as she looked out across the eclipse observation site, a 10-minute drive up past the village.

“That’s generated a lot of interest among people in Madrid – and some from abroad. So we’re anticipating a large influx of visitors because it is a unique event that hasn’t been seen for over 100 years.”

Even before the recent massive wildfires broke out to the west of Madrid, Somosierra council was thinking about how to minimise risk factors on the day of the eclipse and has been coordinating its efforts with police and civil protection authorities.

Although the village council has offered 400 official registration slots, it believes five times as many people could turn up on the day.

“We’re very close to a major European capital with a huge population, and many people are going to come without seeking out information beforehand,” added López. “That’s beyond our control. We can’t predict that someone might be watching television and say, ‘Well, I’m going to make some sandwiches and go see the eclipse with my children.’”

With that in mind, the council is scrambling to recruit and educate volunteers to help steward events on 12 August. It recently hired El Nocturnario, a company of astrotourism experts, to deliver a day’s training to the volunteers who had gathered in Somosierra’s tiny cultural centre to learn about the joys and dangers of eclipses.

One of the volunteers, María Gradaille, said she was delighted to help out with what she called “a once-in-a-lifetime event and a historic scientific milestone”. She was also grateful for the knowledge and the tips she had picked up at the training session.

“I’ve learned so much about the eclipse,” she said. “I didn’t know it could burn your eyes so badly or just how dangerous it can be.”

after newsletter promotion

According to Sarai de la Hoz, one of El Nocturnario’s co-founders, local and regional authorities around Spain are belatedly beginning to wake up the potential benefits of all things astronomical. The looming total solar eclipse will be followed by a six-minute-long “eclipse of the century” in August next year, and by a spectacular “ring of fire eclipse” in January 2028.

Little wonder, then, that the Spanish government has set up a special committee to oversee the trio of eclipses. As the government spokesperson Elma Saiz Delgado pointed out on Tuesday, the events will put Spain “at the centre of global astronomical observation and astrotourism”. This first eclipse alone is expected to attract 446,000 additional visitors in a year when tourist numbers in Spain could pass the 100-million mark for the first time. The event is also forecast to bring in an extra €342m (£292m) in tourist revenue.

“When we started talking about the eclipse a year ago, people kind of thought we were mad. They were like: ‘It’s not going to be that big a deal’ and: ‘Not that many people will come,’” said De la Hoz, “But as time’s gone by and the authorities have realised what’s to come, we’re been getting calls from people who need our help.”

While much of the training she and her colleagues provide is about eclipses and how to watch one safely, the classes also involve a lot of logistics and organisation: “How’s the event going to be organised; who’s going to liaise with the local police and the civil protection authorities, and how will you deal with parking and people at the venue?”

Authorities in the Balearics, which are bracing for huge numbers of extra visitors, have already announced that restrictions will be introduced on 20 main roads across Mallorca, Ibiza, Menorca and Formentera from 3pm until 9pm on the day of the eclipse to prevent gridlock.

Practicalities of a rather different nature are on the mind of Yolanda Cerezo, who has run the Hotel Restaurante El Puerto de Somosierra for the past 26 years. Sitting on the shady terrace of the hotel and restaurant, Cerezo pondered the possibility of a tenfold increase in the 200 to 300 customers she would normally serve on a busy day.

“We’ve had some big one-day events and parties, but we’ve never seen this kind of volume,” she said. “The eclipse is going to be a long day, but we have to make the most of it. We’re not going to see another day like it, are we? It’ll be unique.”

Cerezo, who also caters events, is hoping to get the necessary licences to set up a stall and a bar at the observation site. If she succeeds, she will need to hire another eight or nine people to supplement the restaurant’s regular workforce of nine people. Menu-wise, she’s thinking lamb stew, paella and an assortment of hot and cold sandwiches, all of which can be prepared in the hotel kitchen and driven up the mountain.

“If I do a massive paella and it runs out, I’ll ring down to my people in the kitchen here and they’ll prepare another one and bring it up,” she said. “We can’t leave people stuck halfway up a mountain with nothing to eat.”

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: E-scooters far more dangerous than motorbikes or cycles, analysis suggests
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Ian Sample Science editor
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Study of accidents in England and Wales shows e-scooter riders three times more likely to suffer traumatic brain injury than bikers

Electric scooter riders are three times more likely to suffer traumatic brain injuries than motorcyclists, according to an analysis of accidents in England and Wales – which found women were particularly at risk of serious harm.

Brain injuries accounted for more than a third of adult injuries on e-scooters, but riders also sustained more internal organ and blood vessel damage than did motorcyclists or pedal cyclists, the study found.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The government has backed trials of rental e-scooters in England since 2020, but an additional 1m or so e-scooters are privately owned in the UK. These cannot legally be used on public roads, paths or cycle lanes, but police forces across the country have confiscated thousands because their owners were breaking the law.

The accident analysis reveals that women were involved in about a third more collisions than men – and were more than twice as likely to report severe injuries. Children were also at risk with, 16% of e-scooter injuries in under 18s.

The findings have led to calls to make e-scooters more stable and safer, especially for women who suffer more chest injuries because the handlebars are typically set at a height for men. Mandatory safety training and making helmets compulsory would also help, experts said.

David Bodansky, a consultant hand, trauma and orthopaedic surgeon at Chelsea and Westminster hospital NHS foundation trust, turned to the national major trauma registry to analyse injuries from e-scooter, motorbike and bicycle collisions in 18 cities in England and Wales between 2020 and 2022.

He found e-scooter riders were more than three times as likely to suffer traumatic brain injury or blood vessel damage and 1.5 times more likely to injure internal organs than motorbike riders, and they fared worse than cyclists for these injuries. Their risk of bone fractures was lower, however, than cyclists or motorcyclists.

The data shed no light on why e-scooters are involved in so many accidents, but Bodansky believes that design is a factor. “They’ve got very small wheels and it’s very easy to jam one of those into a pothole. You’ll then go head over heels over the front and land on your head,” he said. Less than 6% of e-scooter riders reported wearing a helmet, according to the study, in Scientific Reports.

While some previous work found women were more likely to ride e-scooters on the pavement, other research saw no sex differences. In a 2024 study, Dr Petya Ventsislavova, senior lecturer in transport psychology at Nottingham Trent University, found more than half of e-scooter riders rode on pavements, and with another person at the same time, while men reported using their phones and shooting red lights more than did women.

“These figures highlight the urgent need for comprehensive legislation governing private e-scooters,” said Ventsislavova. The legislation should clarify not only where and how e-scooters can be used but also include mandatory safety training, she said.

“Unlike cars and motorcycles, e-scooters were introduced without any requirement for formal training, despite being motorised vehicles,” she said. “E-scooters handle very differently from bicycles. Riders stand upright, have a higher centre of gravity, use more sensitive steering, and are more vulnerable to sudden stops caused by small wheels striking kerbs, potholes or road debris. These characteristics make them inherently less stable and contribute to the severity of injuries when crashes occur.”

A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “These are concerning findings, and our thoughts are with anyone who has been injured on our roads. Road safety is our top priority, which is why our e-scooter trials are testing their use in a controlled environment now, before updating the law to ensure they can be used safely more widely.”

Brain injuries accounted for more than a third of adult injuries on e- scooter. Riders also sustained more internal organ and blood vessel damage than motorcyclists.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: ‘Spectral lines’ and a giant plume: what science saw when the SpaceX rocket hit the moon
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Mark Saunokonoko and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Sodium and lithium gas was detected in a plume thought to span tens of kilometres, created when part of a SpaceX rocket crashed into the lunar surface

A telescope in Chile has captured evidence of the impact caused by part of a SpaceX rocket slamming into the moon while travelling at 8,690km/h (5,400mph).

The European Southern Observatory’s (ESO) Very Large Telescope observed “spectral lines” – a colourful illustration of sodium and lithium gas – in the plume of lunar dust stirred up by the impact.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The ESO telescope recorded these “chemical fingerprints” of the plume, which were visible for five to 10 minutes, the observatory said. The plume measured a few tens of kilometres in size, according to Carl Schmidt, an astronomer from Boston University’s Center for Space Physics.

Benjamin Fernando of Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico, said earlier the collision could provide valuable data for future seismic experiments, and assessing “hazards from artificial space debris impacts”. Nasa hopes to soon establish a sustained human presence on the Moon, making it critical to better understand space debris in lunar orbit.

The impact occurred near the moon’s terminator line, or the boundary of its shadow between the sunlit side and its far side. Similar to past objects that have hit the moon, the rocket stage kicked ​up a plume of lunar dust that was briefly illuminated by sunlight, but difficult to spot ‌with the naked eye from Earth.

Numerous satellites were orbiting the moon but none were in the right place at the right time to witness the crash, which occurred about 6.35am GMT on Wednesday. The piece of the rocket was the height of a five-storey building and weighed four tonnes.

Nasa and its Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter probe and South Korea’s Pathfinder Lunar Orbiter are planning to take images of the site after impact, which may show the wreckage of the rocket, but it could take days to receive that information.

However, the manner in which the impact plume ‌interacted with the sunlight allowed astronomers to glean some clues about its composition.

The sodium gas in the spectra is believed to have originated from the lunar soil, while the traces of lithium may have come from ‌the rocket stage itself, Schmidt said.

“This observation did not go perfectly and this is a very crude analysis, but I wanted to share something quickly, and we can say more about these results in time,” he said.

Dr Sara Webb, an Australian astrophysicist at Swinburne University, said the tremendous force of the crash would have gouged out a “massive” new crater, probably 20 metres (65 feet) in diameter and five metres deep.

A vast plume was anticipated, Webb said, but “what we didn’t expect was how hard it was going to be to see this impact. We had multiple telescopes and eyes on the moon watching it, and nobody caught clear imagery or shots of it actually hitting.”

The Falcon 9 rocket from Elon Musk’s SpaceX launched in January 2025 carrying two lunar landers. Its booster returned to Earth, but the upper stage stayed in space to push the landers onward.

The rocket stage was just one of tens of thousands of pieces of “space junk” orbiting Earth. The moon routinely weathers impact from space debris including meteoroids. However, artificial collisions are less common.

With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

The plume was created when part of a SpaceX rocket crashed into the lunar surface. The impact occurred near the moon’s terminator line, or the boundary of its shadow between the sunlit side and its far side.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Unprecedented images may explain one of greatest mysteries of the sun
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Ian Sample Science editor
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Highest-ever resolution pictures of our star could help show why its corona is millions of degrees hotter than its surface

Golden bands and swirling vortices have been spotted on the sun in the most detailed images ever captured of the turbulent surface of our home star.

Astronomers observed the sun with the Inouye solar telescope in Hawaii, the world’s most powerful solar telescope, and saw new features smaller than 20km (12 miles) across in a magnetically active region close to a sun spot.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The unprecedented pictures show processes on the surface that are likely to explain the decades-long mystery of why the corona, the sun’s outer atmosphere, is millions of degrees hotter than its surface.

“These are the highest spatial resolution images of the solar surface ever acquired,” said Dr Friedrich Wöger, a senior scientist at the US National Solar Observatory, which operates the telescope near the summit of the Haleakalā volcano, on the island of Maui.

Previous observations with the telescope found the sun’s surface to be a patchwork of granular structures each about the size of France. Those images picked out details as small as 30km across, but the latest are right at the limit of the telescope’s capability.

“My first reaction was: ‘Wow, how can we see such tiny, fine-scale structures on the sun?” said Dr David Kuridze, an astronomer on the team. “This is something we have never seen before in any solar observations.”

In the latest images, the small whirlpool-like structures on the sun’s surface were identified as signatures of what scientists call Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities (KHIs). These form when fast-moving plasma slides past slower moving fluid, creating shear at the interface. This sets up small disturbances in the sun’s plasma that grow into spiralling vortices that look like breaking waves.

Scientists have seen KHIs in lakes and oceans, and in cloud formations on Earth, and even in the atmospheres of Jupiter and Saturn, but have never confirmed their existence on the sun. The details of the findings are published in Nature.

Explosive events on the sun, from solar flares and jets to coronal mass ejections, are powered by extreme, fluctuating magnetic fields in the star. The explosions can cause widespread disruption on Earth, taking out power grids, satellites, GPS positioning and global communications.

The magnetic fields are generated by the movement of hot, charged plasma in the sun, but the physics isn’t fully understood. Astronomers know that magnetic field lines can twist around each other like braided hair, creating tension that is suddenly released when the tangled lines break. What is less clear is what starts the process. The swirling vortices are now a key culprit, explaining why the field lines become braided in the first place, and perhaps why the sun’s corona is heated to a few million degrees while the surface is a mere 6,000C.

“This could solve this biggest mystery of the last half a century for solar physics and astrophysics,” said Kuridze. “When you have this instability in the system, it is very easy to cascade the energy into smaller scales. And at some point, it just dissipates as a heat. This could make hot coronas, hot outer atmospheres of the sun and similar stars.”

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Study finds three midlife health factors that could delay dementia for 13 years
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Research suggests addressing risk factors for poor cardiovascular health between the ages of 45 and 65 could help reduce risk of cognitive decline

Scientists claim to have identified three health measures in middle age that can ward off dementia for more than a decade.

Having normal blood pressure, no type 2 diabetes, and not smoking between the ages of 45 and 65 were associated with almost 13 additional years, on average, of dementia-free life, a study shows.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The research also suggested that, no matter how many risk factors people had, women lived longer without dementia than men, and that white people had more dementia-free years than black people.

The findings were published in the medical journal Neurology.

Researchers from NYU Langone Health analysed data from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (Aric) study, which began in 1986 and followed Americans for decades into late life, measuring midlife vascular risk factors and dementia.

In the new analysis, researchers looked at 12,409 people with an average age of 56 who were free of dementia. Participants were assessed for three risk factors: high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and smoking. They were then followed for about three decades, with an average follow-up of 26 years.

During that time, 3,008 developed dementia and 5,238 died without developing the condition.

Those who had none of the three risk factors lived without developing dementia almost 13 years longer than those who had all three.

Those with no diabetes, no high blood pressure and who did not smoke at the start of the study had an average of 30.1 more years free of dementia, the study found.

Meanwhile, those with one risk factor had an extra 26.3 years, those with two had 21 years, and those with three had just over 17 years.

“Our findings argue that people need to actively avert these factors in midlife as a strategy for preserving brain health for more than a decade,” said senior investigator Dr Josef Coresh, director of the Optimal Aging Institute at NYU Langone.

“Hopefully, these results will encourage people to stop smoking and watch their vascular health closely from age 45 on.”

The number of people living with dementia globally is forecast to nearly triple to 153 million by 2050. But experts believe almost half of dementia cases worldwide could be prevented or delayed.

Previous research has suggested that addressing 14 modifiable risk factors, starting in childhood and continuing throughout life, could prevent or delay 45% of dementia cases, even as people live longer.

The NYU Langone study said the three factors it identified “often emerge in midlife” and “exert lasting effects on neurodegenerative pathology”, underscoring the critical importance of early identification and management.

Dr Jacqui Hanley, head of research funding at Alzheimer’s Research UK, who was not involved with the research, said: “Rather than focusing only on the chances of developing dementia, this study asks a question that matters to people: how long can we expect to live free from dementia?

“This approach gives a meaningful picture of how midlife health may shape the number of years we spend living free from dementia, while also recognising that high blood pressure, diabetes and smoking are linked to a higher likelihood of dementia as well as a greater risk of dying earlier from other conditions.

“These findings emphasise why it’s so important to look after your heart health as well as your brain health.”

Hanley said everyone should take practical steps, including staying physically active, not smoking, and managing conditions such as high blood pressure and diabetes.

“While there is no guaranteed way to prevent dementia, research, including this study, suggests that addressing risk factors for poor cardiovascular health may also help reduce the risk of cognitive decline and dementia.”

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: SpaceX rocket thought to have crashed into the moon in unintentional collision
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Oliver Holmes
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Four-tonne piece of SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket believed to have hit lunar surface on Wednesday at 5,400mph

A four-tonne piece of a discarded SpaceX rocket that has been floating in space since last year is believed to have unintentionally crashed into the moon at high speed, in a collision that posed no danger to Earth but was expected to blast out a new lunar crater.

The object, the height of a five-storey building, was part of the SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket that launched two commercial lunar landers, one from the US and one from Japan, towards the moon in January 2025.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

The rocket body ⁠was due to hit the moon about 6.35am BST, crashing into its surface at 5,400mph (8,690 km/h). The impact was predicted to kick up a miles-long plume of lunar dust that, although illuminated by sunlight, would be difficult ⁠to spot with the naked eye from Earth.

Professional and amateur astronomers using high-quality telescopes and cameras were not able to confirm the impact on Wednesday, possibly because the impact site was close to the visible edges of the moon.

US and South Korean lunar satellites will be positioned to photograph the site after impact but it may take days to receive that information.

Nasa said the impact was expected to create a crater about 60ft (18 metres) wide and 12ft (4 metres) deep and throw dust and rock outward as ejecta.

The space agency said it would look for opportunities to image the site, with any data collected helping scientists “better understand artificial impacts and their exploration implications”.

The Nasa spokesperson Jimi Russell said on Tuesday: “The impact poses no danger to Earth and Nasa scientists are planning to collect lunar data from the event and refine techniques for tracking objects in space.”

Such rocket parts, known as stages, ‌typically fall back into Earth’s atmosphere and burn up or plunge into the ocean after boosting the rocket’s payload to a precise spot in orbit.

But ‌because the January 2025 lunar lander mission required more thrust than missions closer to Earth, the rocket’s second stage remained in space, floating aimlessly among thousands of other pieces of space junk that active satellites must steer clear of.

It was not until this year that astronomers determined that the rocket stage, which had dumped its remaining fuel and could not be controlled, was on an orbital trajectory ending at the moon.

Julianna Scheiman, SpaceX’s ‌director of Nasa science and Dragon spacecraft programmes, told reporters on Monday: “What has happened is essentially a mixture of solar activity and gravity forces have put it on a path toward the moon.”

Bill Gray, the creator of a widely used piece of astronomy software who published a report ​on the stage’s impact in April, said: “This may be of some – probably minor – scientific interest, and we may learn some things from it.

“It doesn’t present any danger to anyone, though it does highlight a certain carelessness about how leftover space hardware [space junk] is disposed of.”

While tens of thousands of pieces of space junk – defunct satellites, discarded rocket parts and debris from rocket launches – are increasingly crowding Earth’s orbit, human-made impacts on the moon are relatively rare.

Multiple US and Soviet spacecraft intentionally or accidentally crashed into the moon during the 20th-century space race. More recently, a Chinese rocket stage crashed into the moon in March 2022 after completing a lunar test mission. In 2009, Nasa intentionally crashed a rocket stage into the moon to study the plume of lunar material kicked up by the impact.

Several spacecraft intended to land ⁠softly on the moon in recent years have crashed instead, including Russia’s Luna-25 mission in 2023 and India’s ​Chandrayaan-2 lander mission in 2019.

Israel’s Beresheet lander also crashed in 2019. Among the Israeli lander’s payloads were tiny ​tardigrades, microscopic animals known for surviving ‌radiation and other harsh ​environments, which may still be ​on the surface.

Scheiman said Nasa and SpaceX were discussing ways to prevent future lunar impacts.

The SpaceX rocket​ carried two lunar landers ​f​or the 2025 mission, successfully launching them towards the moon. ​One, named Blue Ghost, was made by the US company Firefly Aerospace a​nd achieved a​ soft landing on the moon’s north-eastern near side to conduct tests, including analysing lunar soil.

A second, 2-metre lander, made by the Japanese company ispace and containing a small robotic rover, crashed on final descent.

On Tuesday, SpaceX reported a smaller loss than Wall Street had expected, along with a surge in revenue, in its first quarterly report as a public company. Despite this, shares tumbled as investors remained sceptical about the company’s ability to deliver on its lofty promises.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: AI-generated stories rated better quality than human-written ones, study finds
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Researcher says simpler writing by AI is easier to read and digest, but this does not mean human authors are obsolete

From Homer’s Odyssey to Agatha Christie’s crime fiction, humans have produced plenty of tales to grace the bookshelf. But research suggests artificial intelligence may now be providing some competition.

In a study published in the journal Judgment and Decision Making, 1,682 adults were asked to read one of six short stories, three of which were written by humans and three by ChatGPT. Each AI story had a similar theme to one of the human-authored works.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The team told participants whether their story was written by a human or AI, but this information was not always correct. The researchers then asked participants to rate how absorbing and engaging they found the story, and its quality.

Participants who read an AI-generated story rated it as more absorbing and of higher quality than those who read a story written by a human. However, participants gave higher ratings to stories they had been told were written by people.

Dr Deena Skolnick Weisberg, a senior author of the research from Villanova University in Pennsylvania, said: “AI systems can already generate short stories that are seen as being at least as good as – if not better than – human-written stories. We should update our views of AI’s abilities accordingly.”

However, Weisberg, who is herself a creative writer, said that did not mean writing should be left to AI, noting that novels produced by tech were probably going to be different from those written by humans.

“We may need to make room for AI-generated novels, and for AI/human co-written novels, but that doesn’t mean that there’s no longer space for us to appreciate the process of human creativity,” she said.

“Humans write as a form of creative self-expression or to challenge ourselves, or to make sense of our experiences. The fact that AI can generate human-like stories doesn’t change any of that.”

The results also suggest attitudes to AI matter: participants with more positive attitudes toward AI gave higher ratings to stories they were told were produced by ChatGPT than those with a less positive outlook.

The researchers carried out two further experiments in which 905 adults were given two of the six short stories – both on the same theme and only one of which was penned by a person. They were then asked to guess which was written by a human and which by AI.

In one experiment, about 40% guessed correctly, a result that is worse than chance, while in the other experiment 52% guessed correctly.

“There is no general evidence that participants were able to distinguish human-written from AI-generated stories,” the authors write.

The researchers found that while participants’ self-reported expertise with fiction was not linked to how accurately they guessed, greater expertise with AI systems was.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

“AI writing has a particular style that we can learn to recognise with practice – just as we can learn to recognise different human authors’ unique styles,” Weisberg said.

Weisberg suggested that the preference for stories labelled as being written by humans was linked to a desire for authenticity, but that people actually preferred AI-generated stories because they were easier to read and digest.

However, Luke Kennard, a professor of film and creative writing at the University of Birmingham, who was not involved in the work, emphasised that AI was highly contentious.

“Because we’re human, we tend to personify AI and imagine it as some kind of glowing robot with a benign and neutral face, when it’s really just predictive code based on a massive stolen database of actual writing, physically based in vast, expensive and destructive datacentres with catastrophic repercussions for the surrounding communities,” he said.

Kennard also stressed that AI was not a “tool” similar to spellcheck or a thesaurus, but an existential threat.

“Of course it’s capable of spitting out a coherent and even enjoyable poem with the right prompting and finessing. Given that it’s been trained on thousands of years of human work, it would be embarrassing if it wasn’t,” he said. “I suppose the question we should be asking is: is it worth it? And the answer is absolutely, categorically, it is not.”

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Children using social media at younger age appear to do worse in school tests
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Ian Sample Science editor
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Pupils who open accounts aged 11 to 12 score lower in some subjects than those who wait a few years, study finds

Children who open social media accounts at the start of secondary school appear to perform worse in tests than those who delay, with researchers suspecting that the constant checking for updates is a major distraction for many students.

Pupils who opened their first social media account aged 11 to 12 scored lower in mathematics and reading tests than those who waited a few years, with scores at age 16 differing between the groups by the equivalent of about six months of learning, the study found.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The work does not prove social media is to blame, but the researchers took account of many other factors that could skew the results, such as the students’ academic performance before they had social media, their family structure and parents’ education.

“I think we now know there is a problem and that it’s a complex problem, to do with how these platforms are built,” said Dr Marco Gui, the first author on the study at the University of Milano-Bicocca in Italy. “Our research shows that at least during pre-adolescence, these social media are problematic.”

Gui and his colleagues analysed surveys on the social media habits of more than 5,000 Italian schoolchildren and their results in standardised maths, Italian and English exams. When tested at age 13 to 14, those who had opened their first social media account at 11 or 12 scored worse than those who waited until at least 14 years old. The score gap at age 15 to 16 remained the same for Italian and widened for maths.

Writing in Nature Human Behaviour, the researchers say the difference in scores is roughly equivalent to the early adopters falling behind by six months of schooling. Put another way, the benefit to those who delayed social media was about half that achieved with intensive and costly tutoring.

While a performance gap was evident for maths and Italian, there was no impact on English, which the students were learning as a foreign language, possibly because so much social media is in English, providing “incidental exposure and practice”, the researchers said.

One of the best predictors of the performance gap was how often children picked up their phones throughout the day and night, suggesting that constantly checking social media was at least partly to blame.

“We speculate that one of the mechanisms is the continuous state of alert that social media used on a smartphone exerts on minors’ lives. The continuous need to check messages, to see if something is happening in the online world, why you are engaged in something in the physical world you have around you,” Gui said. “This means being less present in the physical space of the family or the house. And from a cognitive point of view, it could mean being less engaged in something that takes time, as homework can for a student of that age.”

The study comes as the UK is poised to introduce a social media ban for under-16s, following Australia which brought in its own ban last year. While Gui favours an age limit on social media, he said a ban was an “emergency policy” and that work was needed to make the platforms themselves safer and less addictive. “For pre-adolescents we have to work on diminishing the social relevance of these environments,” he said.

Dennis Ougrin, a professor of child and adolescent psychiatry at Queen Mary University of London, said the work added to growing evidence that the age at which young people first engaged with social media may affect their educational development. “The message for parents, educators and policymakers is not necessarily to ban social media, but to support young people in developing healthy habits when interacting with social media,” he said.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Is your ill fate bad luck or a curse? You could ask Ted Lasso, but why not consider the psychology | Helen Pilcher
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Helen Pilcher
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The hit TV show confirms that sports lore is rife with powerful hexes. But there’s really nothing mystical about the dread and self-doubt they can induce

A
s the new season of Ted Lasso started, I was reminded of one of the show’s stranger storylines. When Dani “Football is life!” Rojas gets injured, his teammates blame the incident on a curse said to haunt the treatment room.

Absurd? Perhaps. But sports curses aren’t just fictional plot devices. Football is fertile ground for stories of mysterious forces, blamed for everything from missed penalties to decades of failure.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Take Mayo’s Gaelic football team. After they won the All-Ireland title in 1951, the story goes that a local priest cursed them, declaring they would not win another final until every member of that team had died. Over the next 75 years, Mayo reached 11 more finals – and lost them all. Paddy Prendergast, the last surviving member of the 1951 squad, died in 2021. Then Mayo made it to the final again last month and won. This prompted the Canadian prime minister Mark Carney, who has family ties to Mayo, to announce on X: “The curse is broken.”

Birmingham City – a team close to my heart – has its own curse story. The club is said to have endured decades of disappointment after a 100-year hex was placed on its home ground in 1906. And this year, Harry Kane missed a close-range chance in England’s Fifa World Cup match against Ghana, shortly after a “witch-doctor” claimed to have cast a spell on him. Coincidence?

There are, of course, many possible explanations. Maybe supernatural forces really were at work. Maybe the teams had bad luck, made tactical errors or were simply beaten by better opponents. Or maybe, once the curse became part of the team’s folklore, it acquired a life of its own. In this scenario, it doesn’t matter whether the “spells” were ever cast, or whether players personally believed in them. What matters is that the idea gained a cultural foothold. Retold by fans, journalists and commentators, the stories shaped expectations about what might happen next. And expectations can have very real effects.

Psychology has a name for the power of negative expectations: the nocebo effect. The phenomenon is best known in medicine. A person takes a placebo pill but is warned it may cause side-effects. Often, they experience them anyway. The symptoms are real, even though the tablet isn’t causing them. The same principle can play out in sport. Philip Hurst and colleagues at Canterbury Christ Church University have shown that when runners are given an inert supplement but told it will negatively affect their sprint performance, they run slower. Give them the same supplement but tell them it will improve their performance, it has little effect. This hints that in sport, negative expectations may have more of an impact than positive ones.

Now, imagine a football player walking on to the pitch. The trigger hardly matters. A “curse”, a run of defeats or a teammate’s throwaway comment can all plant a seed of doubt. After that, every misplaced pass, heavy touch or missed chance can seem like proof that something is off. Confidence falters. A game that once felt instinctive becomes something to overthink, until doubt itself starts to undermine performance.

What begins in one player’s mind can also become a team-wide narrative. Players absorb cues from team members, supporters, critics and the media, quietly internalising the atmosphere that surrounds a team. Psychologists call this social contagion: the spread of emotions, behaviours and beliefs through groups. Over time, these shared beliefs can become part of a team’s identity, shaping how it responds under pressure. The result is a feedback loop: the story shapes expectations, expectations shape behaviour, and behaviour can appear to confirm the original story. The question is: how do you break the cycle?

Perhaps we can learn a thing or two from Ted Lasso and the real-life managers who faced similar scenarios. Lasso’s solution was a late-night cleansing ritual, with players throwing treasured possessions into a container which he set alight. Meanwhile Birmingham City’s Barry Fry tried a more “fluid” approach, by urinating on the pitch’s four corners.

Whether these rituals had any mystical power is beside the point. Their value was psychological. They created a reset – a chance for the team to draw a line under the past and start expecting a brighter future. For Mayo, that reset has finally arrived. The next generation of players and supporters will inherit a different memory – not of the final they could never win, but of the one they finally did. As former Mayo player Colm Boyle put it after their victory: “The shackles are off.” The curse may only have been a story, but now Mayo can tell a different one.

Helen Pilcher is a science writer and author of Life Changing: How Humans Are Altering Life on Earth and This Book May Cause Side Effects
