https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Rise in adulterated sexual enhancement supplements could mean users are getting stiffed | Antiviral
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Often sold as ‘herbal’ solutions for sexual prowess, research has found many supplements are cut with prescription medications that could harm the people who take them

Read more in the Antiviral series

S
exual enhancement supplements have always been a bit of a joke: you walk into a supplement store (or chuck a search into Google) and voilà – hilariously titled drugs that supposedly give you the sexual prowess of a god await you. All you have to do is pop a little pill and your flagging stamina or general lack of desire will disappear.

But like all things that sound too good to be true, is there any evidence these supplements work – and could they be doing more harm than good?

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Sexual enhancement supplements are usually sold as “natural” products containing various herbal ingredients.

There are horny goat weed pills, touted as a way to support sexual function and energy because the plant contains a protein which may increase blood flow to your genitals. There are various pun-titled candies with everything from royal jelly – a product of bees created to feed the queen – to various types of honey, coffee, ginseng and more in them. And there are supplements that appear almost identical to normal multivitamins, presumably because vitamins are generally important to good health and therefore must improve your sex life as well.

But as recent Therapeutic Goods Administration testing reveals, many of the products available to buy in retail stores and online have been found to be adulterated with prescription medications such as sildenafil, commonly sold as Viagra, and tadalafil, sold under the brand name Cialis. These are common erectile dysfunction medications that require a prescription from a GP to avoid harmful side effects.

As a general rule, there is no evidence to support the fact that ingredients like goat weed or royal jelly can improve sexual performance. But the problem is, when supplements are adulterated with prescription medications, the products can become quite dangerous. In 2007, Cialis was discovered in a herbal supplement for men in Australia and was ordered to be withdrawn from the market, with the TGA warning the product could have “serious health consequences, especially for patients with existing medical conditions such as heart problems, or persons at risk of stroke”.

And it’s not just a problem in Australia – there are worldwide concerns that prescription medications are readily being added to supplements. This problem is only getting bigger due to the proliferation of the online supplements hidden market thanks to influencers spruiking the products on social media.

Dr Ian Musgrave, a molecular pharmacologist from the University of Adelaide, says the products are being adulterated because people want an effective supplement and “prescription drugs work”.

“Adding pharmaceutical drugs to herbal preparations with marginal efficacy … provides for a readily marketable product” that can be illicitly sold as effective “herbal” or “natural” remedies.

But these prescription drugs carry significant risks when taken without the advice of a doctor. Many of them work by influencing how blood flows around your body, which means that when combined with other medications they can cause extreme low blood pressure and other heart issues.

This isn’t an issue if you’re prescribed the pills by your doctor, who will carefully go through the potential problems with you before you use the medication, but can be a huge problem if you don’t know that you’re taking it. For example, combining Viagra and chest pain medications can cause really serious health problems.

The fact that there are supplements being sold on our shelves and online with potential hidden ingredients decades after the problem first emerged is concerning. Dr Musgrave says that part of the problem is that it is very hard to regulate the online illicit supplements market.

“Border Force is vigilant for unapproved medical products, along with illicit drugs, but the supplement market is very fluid, and the types and forms of supplements vary continuously”. He said it would require a “significant expansion” in both monitoring and personnel to ensure that we are safe from adulterated products.

Buying supplements online without a prescription can be potentially dangerous. Purchasing products in a chemist reduces the risk of adulteration, especially if products carry an AUST L number on them, which means they are registered with the TGA. But the best advice is to always see your doctor first before taking supplements – even if they claim to be “natural”.

Dr Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz is an epidemiologist and science communicator and a senior research fellow at the University of Wollongong

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on the Lovell telescope: budget cuts to physics are bad science and worse politics | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Funders have picked a damaging fight with scientists and the public. They should reconsider their plans

T
he iconic Lovell telescope, housed at the Jodrell Bank Observatory in Cheshire, has always expanded our view of the universe – from tracking the Sputnik launch in 1957 to its current contributions to the study of dark matter. It is now threatened with closure after it was announced that government funding will not continue past March 2028. The projected savings are just £2.8m a year.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

This is just the latest in a rolling package of cuts from the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC) – which disperses government funding to particle, astro and nuclear physics, among other disciplines – aimed at saving about £160m over the next four years. The STFC has insisted that the measures are a result of cost overruns. That may be true, but it is hard not to see this as part of a larger shift in what kind of science the government funds and prioritises, and what areas it allows to wither.

There is no doubt that physics is expensive. From telescopes to synchrotron beams, its instruments are increasingly large-scale and power-hungry. And scientists are not immune to the cost of living crisis. If households are feeling the pinch of electricity costs, just imagine getting the monthly bill for a particle accelerator. However, UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), of which the STFC is a subsidiary, has just gone through a revamp of its funding model, one that clearly prioritises economic growth and measureable outcomes. Looking across the programmes cut, which include international collaborations with other telescope arrays and the Cern facility in Switzerland, many scientists believe that long-term, fundamental research is under specific threat.

The UKRI and STFC have not helped the situation by badly misreading the politics. In a session at the House of Lords earlier this month, the UKRI chief, Ian Chapman, seemed surprised by the scientists’ “hyperbolic” reaction, and noted that they “feel that they have been cut” when, in fact, overall physics funding has increased. But scientists have reason to feel slighted when valued ongoing projects and collaborations – rather than future plans – are axed, and when what appear to be relatively small cost savings (the UKRI budget will be £10bn by 2030) fall on their shoulders. There are shades of the departed Starmer government in this saga: the UKRI wants to tell a big story about science funding going up, but instead is mired in a row over a fairly minor sum that has angered scientists and sections of the public. One does not have to be an astronomer to know that optics matter.

The UKRI and STFC are technically arm’s‑length bodies, but it hasn’t escaped notice that the ministers who set its funding priorities, Liz Kendall and Patrick Vallance, are no longer in office, while Andy Burnham has abolished the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. It would seem a good time for the current course to be reconsidered, whether by the funding councils or the new government itself.

There is a conversation to be had about what research we fund with limited resources, and the balance between so-called blue sky projects and those expected to yield commercial returns. But when physicists warn that the UK could lose a “generation of scientists” to these cuts – in one of the few fields in which we can credibly claim to be world-leading – they should be heeded. It’s time to refocus, and look again.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/audi.title: Revisited: Saunas and cold plunges, where does the evidence stand? – podcast
https://www.theguardian.com/science/audi.author: Presented by Madeleine Finlay with Ian Sample; sound design by Joel Cox; executive producer Ellie Bury
https://www.theguardian.com/science/audi.text:
Saunas and cold plunge pools are popping up everywhere in the UK, bringing fiery heat and icy cold to a beach, city farm or park near you. Their users will be ready with all the reasons why it’s good for both the mind and the body. But what’s the evidence for the benefits of sauna and cold plunge? https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Britain’s Jurassic gold rush: the fossil hunters chasing fortunes on Dorset’s beaches
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Social media and soaring prices are fuelling a fossil-hunting boom, with rare discoveries worth thousands of pounds

One of UK’s best fossil collections sold overseas in ‘loss to the nation’

Bent double at the waist, Martin Curtis combs a stretch of a Dorset beach with the concentration of a man searching for a lost cufflink or wedding ring.

The search is meticulous – and with good reason. What he hopes to find could be far more valuable than an errant piece of jewellery. Curtis is searching instead for the telltale spiral of an ammonite, the star-shaped rod of a crinoid or rocks of a particular shape and colour that suggests there is something very special inside. He is hunting fossils.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Along Charmouth beach and elsewhere on the Jurassic Coast, families with children, seasoned collectors and lone day-trippers peer intently at the ground in search of traces of creatures that lived 190m years ago. While some are here for fun, a growing number are here for business.

That growing professional interest reflects the rising popularity and value of Jurassic fossils, creating a thriving marketplace that has made some collectors social media celebrities and others very wealthy.

A Guardian investigation this week revealed that one of Britain’s most significant collections of Jurassic fossils was recently sold to a museum in Abu Dhabi for what is believed to be an eight-figure sum.

The collection, amassed by the private fossil collector Chris Moore, included 318 specimens, some of which may represent species previously unknown to science. The sale was described by some experts as a loss for the nation.

Yet while British museums lacked the funds to acquire Moore’s collection, wealthy institutions in the Gulf did not. For the fossil hunters combing Charmouth beach, it is another reason to scrutinise every promising item of unusual shape, colour and texture.

Fossil hunting – and the industry that has grown around it – is not a modern pursuit. Perhaps England’s best-known fossil hunter and dealer, Mary Anning, was born at nearby Lyme Regis in 1799 and made breathtaking discoveries along this coastline, including the first complete plesiosaur skeleton – a huge long-necked marine reptile that lived during the Jurassic period before becoming extinct alongside most dinosaurs 66m years ago.

Anning has not been forgotten. Her name and image are everywhere, from information boards along the seafront to the colourful Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre overlooking the beach. Here, fossil collecting is largely encouraged.

“On the rapidly eroding West Dorset coast, fossil collecting is essential if specimens, some of which may be of great scientific value, are to be saved from damage or destruction by the sea,” notes the West Dorset fossil collecting code of conduct.

And just as Anning sold many of her discoveries, fossils are still bought and sold today. Downstairs is a shop where small ammonites can be picked up for a few pounds, while larger specimens, painstakingly prepared within their surrounding rock, sell for several hundred. Provided hunters follow the code of conduct, ownership of fossils passes to the finder.

“Professional collectors have the most time, are able to react quickly to events that uncover the fossils – ie: storms and landslides – and have a great deal of local knowledge. But they need to sell their finds in order to earn a living,” the code notes.

It is easy to understand how fossil hunting becomes addictive. As we comb the beach, Curtis points to a smooth, brown, bullet-shaped object: the fossilised remains of a squid-like creature known as a belemnite.

“That belemnite’s 190m years old. And we are the only three people to ever see that creature,” he says.

A little later, I spot a sparkling curve nestled among the pebbles and prise out a tiny ammonite, glittering with iron pyrite. It is the size of a penny and, though it is probably worth very little, I feel as if I have won the lottery.

As a professional guide and fossil hunter, Curtis knows these beaches intimately. “I spent a lot of my childhood on the beach with my father, finding fossils a bit further down the coast that way in Kimmeridge,” he says.

As an adult, he returned to the coastline while caring for his eldest daughter. “I could take her out on the beach, walk along for two hours looking for fossils [while she was] fast asleep in the backpack,” he says.

He later turned his hobby into a business, using his mountain leader qualifications to run guided fossil walks and selling specimens he has painstakingly revealed from the surrounding rock using air chisels and iron-powder air abrasion.

“I’m a big ammonite fan. They are my favourite fossils, and I’ve got loads of rocks at home with some really nice big special ammonites in, waiting to be prepared,” he says.

Progressing along the beach, we pass the remnants of huge mudslides, where it is clear there are many for whom fossil collecting is a more than a casual pastime. Hammers are swung, chunks of sticky mud broken apart and carefully examined. This is fossil hunting in earnest.

Curtis says TikTok and Instagram have transformed the activity in recent years. Social media is awash with videos of fossil hunters cracking open rocks on Britain’s beaches.

“It’s really changed the scope of fossil hunting down here. It’s now making it a lot harder because it’s introducing a lot more people to fossil hunting. I’ve been running walks here for 10 years now and the change [during that time] is quite significant,” he says, adding that the influx of fossil hunters during Covid staycations accelerated the trend.

Curtis believes parts of the coastline are being over-collected. “The erosion rate is struggling to keep up with the amount of people on the beach, because of the conditions,” he says, noting that fresh material is not being exposed quickly enough. And when new material does appear, word spreads quickly on social media. “So even on a[good day], there’s going to be twice as many people here.”

Competition among professional fossil hunters is intense, with experts keeping an eye on one another as they inspect new falls and vie for the finest discoveries. It is perhaps not surprising that rare finds or beautifully prepared specimens can command substantial sums.

“As fossil hunters, [when] we come to the beach, we are collecting to try to earn money. Maybe selling a few bits … online. But generally, we are collecting for ourselves. And if we find anything good, we keep it,” Curtis says.

Some fossil hunters have amassed remarkable collections. Figures such as Moore have become big names in the fossil-hunting world, with his specimens displayed in museums locally and beyond, and counting David Attenborough among his friends.

The recent sale has cemented Moore’s status as one of the Jurassic Coast’s leading collectors. But his collection is unlikely to be the last to leave Britain. As the country’s professional fossil hunters grow older, more private collections are likely to be in need of new homes.

Perhaps unsurprisingly for a man used to handling relics from millennia gone-by, Curtis is philosophical about his friend’s collection being sold overseas. “It’s always sad when things like that go abroad” said Curtis, adding that Moore had worked hard on his collection. “The key thing is it’s being enjoyed by someone,” he said. “It’s all well and good having a good collection, but it’s no good stuck in a box somewhere.”

There is a striking irony here. The remains of creatures that have been hidden in these shores for 190m years are now being sold to countries whose modern wealth is derived from plumbing their own oily depths.

Yet down on the beach in Dorset, the international marketplace feels a long way away. For Curtis, size isn’t everything – it’s all about the next swirl in the sand. “[A discovery] doesn’t have to be big. It just generally needs to be special. And the more you get into fossil hunting, the fussier you become,” he says.

One of Britain's most significant collections of Jurassic fossils was recently sold to a museum in Abu Dhabi. Social media is awash with videos of fossil hunters cracking open rocks on Britain's beaches.

How many ways are there to fill a 3×3 grid with positive whole numbers such that the product of the numbers in each row and each column is 30?

[Each of the nine cells in the grid has a whole number in it. When you multiply the three numbers in each row, and in every column, the answer is 30. The three numbers in each row or column do not have to be three different numbers.]

Alex said: “I like this puzzle because the key idea is to look at the prime factors of the numbers and realize that the arrangements of each prime factor (2, 3, 5) can be considered independently. This clean separation into different parts is one of my favourite aspects about maths.”

The first thing to notice is that 30 = 2 x 3 x 5.

So, every row and column must include a 2, a 3 and a 5.

There are six ways to have a single 2 in every row and column. (3 ways to choose the 2 in first row, 2 ways to choose the 2 in second row in a different column, and 1 way to choose the last 2 in the third row, so 3 × 2 × 1 = 6). Here they are:

Similarly there are 6 ways to choose the placement of 3s and the placement of 5s.

Each full grid is a unique placement of 2s, 3s and 5s. Therefore there are 6 × 6 × 6 = 216 ways to fill the grid.

For example, here is one way to combine 2s, 3s and 5s.

These placements produce the full grid below, which is constructed by placing each number in the correct cell. If there is more than one number per cell you multiply them, and if there are no numbers, you put a 1.

There are 216 ways to combine the 2s, 3s and 5s in this way.

I hope you enjoyed today’s puzzle. Thanks to Alex and best of luck for in your mathematical career!

I’ll be back in two weeks.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump faces calls for windfall tax on big oil’s profits from Iran war
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Dharna Noor
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
US president’s complaint industry ‘making too much money’ comes after his policies boosted corporations

Donald Trump’s statement that oil companies have made “too much money” from the Iran war has angered environmentalists, who say that his policies were designed to benefit those very corporations. If he really believes his own claims, he should impose a windfall profits tax, advocates say.

“Trump’s declaration that big oil is ‘making too much money’ belies his accommodation and giveaways to the industry that have enabled its price-gouging – not to mention his disaster of a war of choice against Iran,” said Tyson Slocum, energy program director at the consumer advocacy non-profit Public Citizen. “But like a broken clock that’s correct twice a day, the president is right that oil companies are ‘making too much money’, which means Trump should endorse a windfall profits tax.”

ExxonMobil and Chevron on Friday both reported windfall profits for the second quarter of the year. Chevron said its earnings soared nearly 400% to $12bn, while Exxon’s profits more than doubled to $14.5bn. On Monday evening, Trump took aim at those gains, saying the companies “ought to give some of that back to the public”.

“They’re making too much money based on a shortage,” he told reporters at the White House. “I don’t like it.”

Not long ago, however, Trump was celebrating the fact that the war on Iran, which he launched with Israel in February, has pushed up gas prices. “When oil prices go up, we make a lot of money,” he said on social media in March.

Earlier that month, Trump claimed that Iran’s shutdown of the major shipping route the strait of Hormuz “doesn’t really affect” the US the way it does “other countries” because it is the top global crude producer, and because just a small portion of the country’s oil imports comes from the Persian Gulf. But oil prices are influenced by global markets and supply chains, experts have noted.

Trump has also relentlessly boosted oil and gas interests while in office. In 2024, he reportedly met with more than 20 oil bosses, seeking $1bn in campaign donations from their industry and promising if elected to remove dozens of environmental regulations.

While he did not manage to get to that $1bn figure, he did obtain record contributions from the sector. Since re-entering the White House last year he has eased dozens of restrictions and regulations on fossil fuel expansion, exempted fossil fuel producers from environmental rules, and signed an executive order last year directing the attorney general to prioritize blocking climate lawsuits targeting oil majors.

“We shouldn’t be surprised that the same companies that struck a $1bn quid pro quo to help elect Trump in exchange for delivering on their policy wishlist are now cashing in on his anti-consumer agenda,” said Lena Moffitt, executive director of climate advocacy group Evergreen Action.

Trump has also personally invested in major oil companies. According to his 2025 financial disclosure, he increased his personal energy portfolio last year, placing between $3m and $12m in ExxonMobil stock and between $1.25m and $6m in Chevron stock, Politico first reported, indicating he may be benefiting from the two companies’ windfall profits.

As oil companies have reaped billions from the Iran war’s impact on fossil fuel prices, the Rhode Island senator Sheldon Whitehouse and California congressman Ro Khanna have proposed taxing big oil’s windfall profits from the Iran war-fueled crisis, saying proceeds from that tax should go to American families who are paying more for fuel.

Reached for comment, a White House spokesperson, Taylor Rogers, said: “President Trump’s energy dominance agenda is successfully unleashing reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources.

“The President’s main priority has been and always will be lowering gas prices for Americans,” Rogers added. “Allowing the oil and gas industry to ‘DRILL, BABY, DRILL’ is imperative to driving down prices.”

American families have paid more than $78bn more at the pump since the start of the Iran war, according to a Brown University tracker. And a recent analysis from the environmental advocacy group Climate Power and liberal thinktank Center for American Progress Action Fund found that Trump’s policies have cost the average American family $285 more at the pump.

In addition to supporting a windfall profits tax, Trump should work to limit fossil fuel exports “as they contribute to higher prices for Americans and fatter profits for industry”, said Slocum. Khanna in April introduced legislation aimed at banning the export of gasoline during price spikes.

But Trump officials say they have no intention of considering restrictions on fossil fuel exports.

“While the President and his entire energy team have taken several actions to mitigate temporary disruptions to the energy market, the Administration has been quite clear: there is no plan to implement restrictions on oil and gas exports,” said Rogers.

Earlier this week, dozens of US advocacy groups led by environmental organization Food and Water Watch called on congressional leaders to ban on fossil fuel exports and impose a windfall profits tax on oil majors.

“There are concrete ways to fight back against the fossil fuel industry and their insatiable profiteering,” the letter says.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Accused arsonist studied how to maximize Washington wildfire’s harm, police say
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Court documents allege Aaron Farinacci, who faces slew of arson charges, set 25 fires in Spokane area over past year

The 37-year-old man accused of sparking a devastating fire in Washington allegedly studied how to maximize the blaze’s destruction and was responsible for setting 25 other fires in the Spokane area over the past year, according to a court affidavit.

Aaron Farinacci, who faces a slew of arson charges, is accused of starting the Old Trails fire, which began on 1 August and is still burning – one of three “Spokane complex” fires that have scorched hundreds of homes and displaced thousands of residents.

The other two fires were also started by people, though not necessarily deliberately, investigators have said. They remain under investigation.

Farinacci allegedly knew Spokane county was under a “red flag warning”, an advisory the National Weather Service issues when low humidity and powerful winds raise the risk of hazardous fire conditions.

According to court documents, Farinacci lit a homemade ignition device and placed it in grass on 1 August, reasoning that, with the strong gusts of wind he observed, if he started a fire it “was gonna get bad”.

Three individuals observed Farinacci in the vicinity of the fire. When questioned by police about the witnesses’s statements, Farinacci initially denied being responsible for the blaze.

If confronted by police, Farinacci said he planned to draw a knife so they would shoot him, but instead settled instead on feigning innocence, the affidavit stated.

Farinacci told investigators he viewed fire as “powerful” and “beautiful” and said it spurred “a kind of rebirth”. He researched the arsonist John Leonard Orr, a former fire captain who sparked roughly over 2,000 fires in southern California, court records show.

He also told investigators he allegedly set five fires in the span of 24 hours in 2025 to overwhelm the capacity of fire suppression efforts.

Farinacci was arraigned in court on Thursday, where a Spokane county superior court judge increased his bond to $2m. He was initially being held on a $1m bond.

Farinacci has run into trouble with law enforcement before. In 2012, he pleaded guilty to manslaughter and aggravated assault after fatally shooting his father, Maricopa county court records show.

He told investigators that he had recently been struggling with “life issues” after the birth of his son in 2025.

As of Wednesday, the Old Trails fire was 5% contained, according to data from the National Interagency Fire Center.

The wildfires raging in the US Pacific north-west are blanketing the region with thick smoke and delivering some of the world’s worst air quality.

In portions of central and eastern Washington and Oregon, sensors detected air quality indexes reaching above 200, which is categorized as “very unhealthy”.

In the Seattle area, the smoke is expected to clear up by Friday, according to the Washington department of ecology, but poor air quality may persist to the east in Spokane. An air quality advisory issued by Oregon officials for the Portland area is expected to be lifted on Thursday evening.

In Washington, there are 16 uncontained wildfires burning more than 672 sq miles (1,740 sq km) and being fought by more than 7,000 fire personnel, said Thomas Kyle-Milward, a spokesperson for the Washington department of natural resources.

“We’re looking down the barrel at one of the worst fire seasons in state history,” he said.

Firefighters have taken advantage of cooler weather to begin getting a handle on wildfires that have displaced tens of thousands of people. But hotter, drier and breezier days lie ahead.

Officials said firefighters had established containment lines around the perimeters of all three fires affecting Spokane and that they were focused on reinforcing those lines. Temperatures were expected to climb from the 80s into the upper 90s, with less humidity, late this week.

Associated Press contributed reporting

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Agreement with RWE is fifth deal Trump team has made with energy companies, offering payouts to give up projects

The German energy company RWE has reached a $1.22bn deal with the US government to relinquish its offshore wind leases and instead redirect funds towards fossil fuel investments.

The agreement marks the fifth deal the Donald Trump administration has struck with energy companies, offering payouts in exchange for abandoning renewable energy projects and redirecting investment towards fossil fuels.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

This latest deal takes it to almost $4bn of taxpayer money spent on killing offshore wind projects.

Announcing the deal with the US interior department on Thursday, RWE said it had agreed to give up its offshore wind leases off the coasts of New York, California and Louisiana.

“After careful consideration, it was determined there is no path forward to permit these projects in the US for the foreseeable future,” the company said, referring to the leases it initially secured with a “long-term commitment to develop offshore wind capacity”.

RWE paid $1.1bn for its New York lease in a 2022 auction held by the Joe Biden administration, while its leases in Louisiana and California cost a combined $163m, Reuters reports.

“The settlement resolves RWE US Offshore’s legal claims and provides $1.22 billion in settlement funds,” RWE continued, adding that the deal would allow it to “direct resources toward energy projects that can be advanced with certainty.”

As part of the agreement, RWE will spend $900m to acquire a 16% stake in an unnamed Louisiana liquified natural gas (LNG) project. The company said the settlement proceeds would be used to fund construction of the terminal.

RWE has also signed a $300m turbine reservation agreement under which it will develop a pipeline of 15 natural gas peaker plants across the country.

The interior secretary, Doug Burgum, hailed the deal, saying on Thursday: “We welcome RWE’s agreement and voluntary investment in projects that strengthen our nation’s energy security, provide dependable baseload power, and help keep electricity affordable for hardworking Americans today while supporting our country’s long-term energy future.”

The RWE agreement appears to be the largest deal the Trump administration has struck with an energy company to kill clean energy projects. Earlier agreements with other companies, including TotalEnergies and Duke Energy, amounted to $2.7bn in taxpayer money.

Following the Trump administration’s $928m deal with French energy company TotalEnergies to cancel its offshore wind lease off the coast of New York, seven states, including New York, sued the administration over what the New York attorney general, Letitia James, described as a “sham deal” and “illegal agreement”.

The administration has also spent up to $1.1bn to boost coal, a move critics argue is “fattening the wallets of his cronies” while raising working Americans’ energy bills, particularly as the US’s war on Iran drives up fuel prices.

At the same time, the federal government is seeking to slash public input periods for fossil fuel drilling on federal lands while shifting more of the financial risks of cleanup to taxpayers.

Meanwhile, a report released last fall by the Environmental Integrity Project found that every fully operational LNG facility in the US had violated federal pollution limits in recent years.

According to the non-profit research organization, violations included the discharge of illegal amounts of bacteria, zinc, oil and other pollutants into waterways, as well as failures of terminal managers to submit monitoring reports for waterway discharge.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Lucy Campbell
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Burmese pythons are an invasive species in the Everglades, and the challenge is part of initiative to remove them

The winner of this year’s annual Florida Python Challenge hunted down and eliminated 96 invasive Burmese pythons from the Everglades national park, as part of an initiative to remove hundreds of the snakes from the area every year.

The challenge invites hunters to participate in 10 days of capturing and humanely euthanizing as many of the invasive snakes as possible across eight designated hunting locations, with the winner taking home a cash prize of $10,000. The event is hosted by Florida fish, wildlife and conservation (FWC), the south Florida water management district, the National Park Service and others.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

This year’s competition drew 907 participants from 30 US states, as well as Canada and Vietnam. The winner, Tom Rahill, harvested 96 Burmese pythons, all from the Everglades. A python hunter by trade, Rahill founded an organization called SwampApes in Broward county that takes veterans suffering from PTSD on python hunts in Florida’s wetlands.

In comments reported by Naples Daily News, Rahill told an FWC meeting in Panama City on Wednesday: “I was on a mission to get one of our veterans a big snake. I did it. And we wrestled this thing … The veteran was just over the moon.”

Once that was achieved, he said he went deeper into the Everglades, where he found the 96 snakes. Over the course of 10 days in July, 280 snakes in total were removed. Before the competition began, 1,400 pythons had been taken out this year.

The challenge also awards several other cash prizes, including $1,000 for the longest python killed, which this year went to Rahm Levinson, who hunted a snake measuring 16ft 5in.

Burmese pythons are native to south-east Asia, and have wreaked havoc since they were first found in the Everglades ecosystem in the 1990s, consuming resources and wiping out a significant portion of the area’s native wildlife. The apex predators are incredibly hard to detect, contributing to the population ballooning to a number that conservative estimates put in the tens of thousands.

Females can lay dozens of eggs, sometimes up to 100 annually, and although many hatchlings do not survive to adulthood, there are fears the pythons are reproducing faster than they can be caught. The annual challenge is therefore now held during the summer hatching season in a bid to boost the number captured.

Aimed at raising public awareness of invasive species, and getting the public involved in conservation and efforts to protect the Everglades ecosystem by controlling the number of Burmese pythons, the event has seen more than 1,600 of the snakes removed from the area since 2017. Combined with FWC contractors, who hunt the reptiles year-round, that figure rises to more than 19,000 snakes removed since 2017.

Sarah Funck, program coordinator at the FWC, told Wednesday’s meeting that there is no “silver bullet” to solve Florida’s python invasion, but stressed that the elimination of just one python “is a win for Florida’s native wildlife”.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The winner of this year’s annual Florida Python Challenge hunted down and eliminated 96 invasive Burmese pythons from the Everglades national park. The winner, Tom Rahill, harvested 96 Burmies python, all from the area. The annual challenge is now held during the summer hatching season

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Drought and record heat have forced the Norfolk and Suffolk league to move kick-off to the end of August as the ground is deemed too dangerous to play on

This summer’s record drought has forced a football league to delay the start of its season because “rock hard” pitches are a danger to its players.

The 2026/27 season in the Anglian Combination League of 85 amateur teams in Norfolk and Suffolk was due to start next weekend.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

But on Friday after an urgent meeting, the league’s board announced it had unanimously decided to postpone the start of the season until the end of August, because most of the clubs’ pitches are dried out and too dangerous to play on.

It said a number of pre-season friendlies have had to be cancelled because of the drought and matches that have gone ahead have led to “many injuries”.

In a statement addressed to all leagues clubs, players and officials, it confirmed the start of the season will be delayed until 29 August.

“The rationale behind this decision is to protect the welfare of players, officials and all associated with the match day, in what has been the driest and hottest July since records began in 1836,” the league chair, Dale Brown, said in the statement. “Most of our league clubs pitches are grass and the ground conditions are extremely dry and pitches rock hard.”

Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning

after newsletter promotion

Brown added: “This was a very difficult decision to reach and one that will not please all clubs.”

The league’s decision comes after a series of record-breaking heat waves and exceptionally low rainfall have left much of England and Wales visibly parched and the ground as hard as concrete.

Record temperatures were experienced in May and June, and July was the driest month since records began. A drought was declared in half of England last month with many water companies imposing hosepipe bans. Such a ban by Anglian Water which covers Norfolk and Suffolk, has been in force since 11 July.

Aerial images have shown dried out parks and sports fields devoid of any signs of green, with the exception of golf clubs, some sports clubs, and private schools who enjoy controversial exemptions from hosepipe bans.

The Met Office forecasts another heatwave next week, with temperatures set to reach 36C in parts of East Anglia and south-east England by next Thursday. There is no sign of much-needed rain, although humidity is expected to increase next week.

The FA does not hold figures on the number of leagues that have been forced to postpone the start of next season because of the drought. It said it was a matter of individual leagues and county football associations.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: US is ‘using Mexico as a garbage sink’ leading to ‘toxic crisis’, UN expert says
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Verónica García de León and Erin McCormick
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Marcos Orellana, a special rapporteur, found lax environmental standards and lack of oversight allowed pollution to accumulate

Revealed: Mexico’s industrial boomtown is making goods for the US. Residents say they’re ‘breathing poison’

Mexico is facing a “toxic crisis” and has become a “garbage sink” for the US, exposing Mexican communities to dangerous pollution, a UN expert has warned.

In an interview with the Guardian and Quinto Elemento Lab, an investigative outlet, Marcos Orellana, an environmental specialist, said pollutants ranging from imported waste to dangerous pesticides were affecting people’s right to live healthy lives.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Orellana, whose title is UN special rapporteur on toxics and human rights, conducted an 11-day investigative mission in Mexico last month to learn about toxic threats facing its population. He said he found lax environmental standards and a lack of oversight, which have allowed pollution to accumulate over the years.

“Where standards are weak, what you get is legalized pollution,” he said, adding that imports of hazardous and plastic waste from the United States were worsening the situation.

“US overconsumption and economic activity are using Mexico as a garbage sink.”

The rapporteur said there were more than 1,000 contaminated locations officially recorded in Mexico’s National Inventory of Contaminated Sites, many of which he said had become “sacrifice zones”, where diseases such as cancer, and medical events such as miscarriages, were normalized.

In a preliminary report summarizing his visit, he cited factories spewing hazardous waste into the Atoyac River in Puebla, huge industrial pig farms contaminating drinking water on the Yucatan peninsula and a decade-old mining chemical spill that continued to affect health in communities around the Sonora River.

He said many of these situations left residents struggling with dire health effects.

“As I heard during one meeting: living in a sacrifice zone means losing the right to die of old age,” he wrote.

He cited one place he visited, the industrial corridor of Tula in the central Mexican state of Hidalgo, where steel plants, cement factories and petrochemical facilities operate near a river polluted by industrial waste and untreated sewage from Mexico City. He said proposals to bring in additional waste for recycling would only add to an already devastating environmental burden on communities there.

Meanwhile, companies are not held responsible for preventing, mitigating and repairing the damage, he said.

The result, he said, was the “legalized poisoning of people”.

The rapporteur highlighted the influx of plastic waste from the United States. He said once this waste crosses the border, there is often little clarity about its final destinations. In addition, he said he was concerned that microscopic plastic particles had been detected in rivers such as the Tecate in Baja California, the Atoyac in Puebla and the Jamapa in Veracruz.

Government records show the US ships hundreds of thousands of tons of hazardous waste to Mexico each year, including lead-acid car batteries, as well as common scrap such as plastic, paper and metal for recycling. Environmental groups have questioned whether the country is equipped to handle all this without it leading to pollution.

Residents in Monterrey, which serves as a US manufacturing hub and suffers some of the worst air pollution in North America, welcomed the rapporteur’s calls for more attention to the health of Mexico’s people.

María Enríquez, a mother and activist in Monterrey, who co-founded the environmental group Comité Ecológico Integral, warned that poor air quality has become part of daily life in the city, and residents suffer from rhinitis, eye irritation and asthma attacks.

“We have learned to live sick, especially with respiratory illnesses,” she said.

Guadalupe Rodríguez, director of a network of childcare centers in Monterrey, agreed, saying children in her nursery program were also affected.

“Families consider it normal for children to have constant coughing,” said Rodríguez. She called on the government to do more to enforce Mexico’s constitutional guarantee of a healthy living environment, especially for the most vulnerable. “If they are not protected, the right to health is not being guaranteed.”

The rapporteur’s visit, at the invitation of the Mexican government, comes at a time when toxic and hazardous waste are coming under increasing scrutiny in the country.

In Monterrey, residents have been demanding government action to reduce heavy metal pollution, much of it emitted in the air by factories that are manufacturing goods for the US or recycling hazardous US waste.

Already, officials in President Claudia Sheinbaum’s administration have acknowledged that regulatory standards, such as rules for how much pollution factories can emit, are out of date, and have announced plans to strengthen them.

In an interview, Mariana Boy Tamborrell, Mexico’s federal attorney for environmental protection, said her agency had reached a regulatory “turning point”, and would start requiring industries to remediate environmental damage they caused. Her agency is rolling out a new air monitoring system to detect emissions coming from specific facilities, starting in an industrial corridor of Monterrey.

“Then there will be no room for ‘it wasn’t me,’” she said. “We will be able to clearly identify the source.”

The rapporteur said Mexico could adopt restrictions on the import of hazardous waste as a measure to address part of the crisis. He noted that some countries had chosen to ban such imports to avoid becoming destinations for international waste, without undermining their participation in global trade.

Waldo Fernández, a Mexican senator, has already introduced legislation to more strictly regulate imports of waste into Mexico for recycling. The law would prohibit importing waste if it has greater environmental impacts in Mexico than allowed in its country of origin.

Mexico “must not become a dumping ground for toxic waste or a recipient of pollution under commercial pressures”, said Fernández.

The rapporteur also said the upcoming review of the free trade agreement between Mexico, the US and Canada represented an opportunity to strengthen environmental standards and their enforcement.

If they did not, “economic pressure will worsen the toxic crisis”, he said.
