https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Union calls for robust review of OBR over fears it holds back economic growth
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Heather Stewart
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
TUC will urge John Healey to order ‘root and branch’ assessment of watchdog amid claims its forecasts downplay investment benefits

The TUC is urging the new chancellor, John Healey, to order a “root and branch” review of the Office for Budget Responsibility, claiming the forecaster’s approach holds back investment.

With Andy Burnham promising “good growth in every postcode”, the union umbrella body is calling on Healey to use his first budget on 28 October to re-examine the assessments of the watchdog.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

In particular, it accuses the OBR of downplaying the benefits of public investment, by assuming it “crowds out” private capital – an approach disputed by some economists.

Paul Nowak, the TUC’s general secretary, said: “For too long, the OBR has been a millstone preventing good growth across the country.

“The world has moved on from the self-defeating logic of austerity, but the OBR models still bake in its false assumptions. Only a root and branch review can bring the OBR into the modern economic mainstream.”

The TUC’s critique echoes calls for a restructuring of the independent forecaster from a range of thinktanks and campaign groups, including Progress, from the right of the Labour party, and the leftwing New Economics Foundation.

Louisa Dollimore, of the Good Growth Foundation thinktank, previously called the body “a backseat driver with out-of-date maps” that “obstructs long-term planning and investment at a moment when Britain needs both”.

Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, recently picked economics professor Jonathan Haskel as the next chair of the OBR, after the resignation of Richard Hughes last December, after the OBR inadvertently published details of the budget in advance.

Haskel, a former member of the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee, will have to oversee a new economic forecast to inform this year’s budget.

He told MPs on the Treasury select committee last month that he was more pessimistic about the outlook than some other experts. “My ⁠forecast would be in the medium term of somewhat higher interest rates and weaker GDP growth than ​most are expecting,” he said.

Haskel also told the committee in a public hearing that Britain was “not in a very good fiscal position”.

The TUC is also calling on the chancellor to beef up investment bodies such as the National Wealth Fund (NWF), to take advantage of flexibility built into the fiscal rules.

Reeves revised the rules so that government borrowing does not count against Treasury targets if it is matched by a financial asset – such as a share in a company or a loan.

The TUC says this should allow for significant additional investment by government-backed institutions including the NWF and the National Housing Bank.

The NWF invests in infrastructure projects and backs British businesses, in an effort to boost growth and “crowd in” private investors.

Sign up to Business Today

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

The TUC is calling on the government to change the NWF’s mandate to allow it to pick investments that could take as long as 15 years to generate a return in order to widen the pool of suitable projects.

Nowak said: “Amid global economic turmoil, Labour has delivered the second fastest growth in the G7. That’s partly down to the government’s fiscal rules that rightly allow more borrowing for investment.

“But the government needs to do more to release the handbrake. An ambitious application of the existing fiscal rules and a wider mandate for the National Wealth Fund can reindustrialise Britain.”

Some economists have raised concerns about the potential impact on the bond market of increased borrowing. On Friday, the consultancy firm Oxford Economics said: “The UK’s fiscal position is poor, while there’s an underlying wariness about the new PM’s commitment to fiscal sustainability.

“While Healey has been saying all the right things, it’s what the new administration does that will be key. If the first move is to loosen policy, despite no underlying improvement in the public finances, that risks sending a signal that markets won’t like.”

A Treasury spokesperson said: “Fiscal discipline is the bedrock of economic stability and national security.

“The chancellor and prime minister are in lockstep that the government will meet the fiscal rules, with a buffer against uncertainty – and that includes getting debt down.

“As has always been the case, the chancellor will set out decisions at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on proposals.”
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.summary: TUC wants John Healey to order 'root and branch' review of Office for Budget Responsibility. Union umbrella body accuses OBR of downplaying benefits of public investment.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Thetford residents remain on edge after days of ‘mob rule’ over asylum plans
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Ben Quinn Political correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
People voice frustration with officials’ failure to engage with community over placement of asylum seekers in area

A smashed window pane and some broken eggshells on a footpath were some of the tell-tale signs of events that took place this week on a residential street at the edge of Thetford.

On Friday afternoon it was not hard to find local people with a sense of foreboding after the latest disorder in the Norfolk market town which has seen crowds attempt to break into properties believed to be housing asylum seekers.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“The main concern is safety, the proximity of children and that people just have not been consulted about this,” said Jenny Hollis, a former councillor, who indicated the proximity of a local school and nursery to a – now seemingly vacant – house on the targeted street in the north of the town.

“Thetford is a small town where people know each other, but if you are putting young men who people know nothing about into an area, sometimes in the dark of night, then it will be a cause of concern,” she said in reference to asylum seekers.

For three nights, Thetford was the scene of protests and disorder, with police officers being subjected to violence, windows smashed, fences broken and people attempting to break into a residential property, police said.

However, after unrest which the local MP said had “put Thetford back decades”, there was also deep unease among residents and others about the prospect of racism poisoning local relations, fuelled by disinformation and the role of the far right in seeking to exploit tensions.

“I have lived here for more than a decade and have come to call it home,” said a woman, originally from eastern Europe, around the corner from where the latest unrest took place. “The people are lovely, but last week was the first time that my partner was shouted at by someone who derided him as a ‘migrant’.”

Amid chants of “We want them out” from a crowd of up to 200 people on the targeted street on Wednesday night, a male police officer was hit by a brick and a female colleague was seriously bitten, Norfolk constabulary said. The number of arrests in connection with disorder in different parts of the town had risen to six as of Friday.

Asylum seekers had been removed from properties on Thursday for their safety, according to the police, and there was no answer at a number of homes believed to have been used for that purpose when the Guardian visited.

“I have HMOs [houses of multiple occupancy] with asylum seekers in them on both sides of my house,” said one man. They had tended to keep to themselves, he said, but he had concerns about tensions in the area and what it would do to property prices.

The three nights of disorder threaten to become the spark for the type of anti-immigration tensions that boiled over last year around a hotel outside the Essex town of Epping and spread elsewhere.

If the unrest in Thetford is different, however, it is that it marks the first time HMOs in England have become the target of concerted and organised anger.

Terry Jermy, the MP for South West Norfolk and a rare Labour presence in what has traditionally been a Conservative-leaning region, has criticised what he described as a lack of engagement by the Home Office, and given voice to people’s unease that cheaper, working-class areas have been chosen as the location for housing asylum seekers in HMOs.

“The lack of engagement both with the community and elected officials has been a huge concern, along with the apparent lack of a strategy, in terms of a cohesive plan, but also to close down rumours and the spread of misinformation,” said Jermy.

“I have been happy to acknowledge people’s concerns and support peaceful protest but what we have seen over the last few days is outright criminality, mob rule and vigilante-style antics which go way beyond the rule of law. These people – and in many cases I’m talking about those who have travelled to Thetford – claim to be proud to be British, but to be proud to be British is to support the rule of law.”

Criticism has persisted over the use of HMOs and the choice of locations to house asylum seekers, with protesters in Thetford targeting a list of houses believed to be used by Serco, a company that has a multimillion pound contract with the Home Office.

Sign up to Headlines UK

Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning

after newsletter promotion

Social media accounts operated by prominent far-right activists, including Stephen Yaxley-Lennon – who calls himself Tommy Robinson – have disseminated footage from the protests. In one clip, a man can be seen directing crowds to an address where he said there were “invaders”, a term used by Robinson and others.

In answer to the allegation it had mishandled its contract, a spokesperson for Serco said it worked under the direction of the Home Office, which tells it the number of people it expects to house in local authority areas based on overall national levels of demand.

The Home Office has insisted the use of “large sites” is a key part of its strategy, and said the population of asylum seekers in hotels fell by 35% in the past year and by 63% from the peak of 56,000 in 2023.

Figures from Reform UK have taken a prominent interest in the opposition to the use of HMOs.

Scott Hussey, a member of the cabinet on Reform-controlled Norfolk county council, was at the scene on Friday, and said residents were frustrated at seeing their town being turned into “a dumping ground for illegal immigrants”.

He said his understanding from meeting with the Home Office was that more HMOs were going to be sited in Thetford,and that this would add to tensions over proposals to use a nearby RAF base to house asylum seekers.

Those who protested in Thetford this week included participants in a regular protest outside RAF Barnham, outside the town. Plans to house 3,750 migrants at the former base were revealed in June.

Anna Turley, the minister for border security and asylum, said on GB News on Friday that people had a right to protest but that the disorder in Thetford had been “horrendous”.

“What we’ve seen is spilling over into violence, which is just not acceptable,” she said. “Nobody should feel harassed, intimidated or threatened in their home, and certainly we shouldn’t see our emergency workers and our police attacked in the way that we have seen.”
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.summary: Thetford was the scene of protests and disorder this week. Residents are frustrated at seeing their town being turned into ‘a dumping ground for illegal immigrants’

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: A ‘Keminaissance’ for the Tories is wishful thinking – Badenoch’s Reform-lite summer will only end one way | Jonathan Freedland
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Jonathan Freedland
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Hiring a convicted antisemite as an adviser; rabble rousing at a time of violent unrest. She is still in a race to the bottom and making too many mistakes

T
he Keminaissance will be delayed. For nearly a year, Conservative optimists and a clutch of supportive pundits have been forecasting an upturn in the fortunes of Kemi Badenoch, confident that her party will emerge from the crater it fell into in 2024, overtake Reform UK to become once again the main party of the right and, who knows, maybe, with a following wind, even push Labour aside and return to government. Every sign of strength from the Tory leader – a robust conference speech here, a viral clip on social media there – has been hailed as evidence of the coming Keminaissance. On the evidence of the past week or so, we will have to wait a little longer.

It’s quite true that Badenoch’s personal ratings are better than those of her party. True, too, that she ended a long losing streak when the Tories won a Westminster seat at the Aberdeen South byelection in June. But there is a more recent election result that should temper the boosters’ enthusiasm, along with a series of decisions that confirm that, when it comes to both strategy and judgment, Badenoch is badly lacking.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Start with that contest from a week ago. For many, the standout fact of the byelection to replace Andy Burnham as mayor of Greater Manchester was that Reform came a very poor second, taking just 21% of the vote to Labour’s 47%. It was indeed a crushing defeat for Nigel Farage’s party, which a matter of weeks earlier had talked up its chances of winning the mayoralty.

But run your finger further down the vote tally until it finally reaches the Conservative candidate on a mere 7.7%. In all the previous mayoral contests in Greater Manchester, the Tories were in second place. This time they were fifth, behind Restore Britain, a party of the hard right that has become home to all manner of racists and white supremacists.

A Tory result that bad among such a large electorate suggests not merely that Badenoch is making slow progress, but that she is moving her party backwards. When it comes to challenging Labour, other parties are either level with the Conservatives or ahead of them. In that context, it seems an undeserved compliment to call Kemi Badenoch the leader of the opposition.

Her strategic response to this competition on the right has been to move towards her rivals, hoping to blunt the appeal of the nationalist populist parties by matching their offer. The latest step came late on Thursday with, as the Telegraph billed it, a Tory “promise to end council housing for foreigners”. Badenoch’s pledge is to evict almost 230,000 non-EU foreign national households from their homes.

Never mind that many of those turfed out will include people who, while not UK citizens, have been living, working and paying taxes in Britain for years, while others will be refugees fleeing war and persecution. Never mind that, once evicted, those families, including their children, will be rendered homeless, leaving local councils with the choice of either abandoning them to the streets or providing (much costlier) emergency accommodation. Never mind that it’s unclear who exactly would identify and locate these families, unless Badenoch plans to create a British equivalent of ICE, mounting raids, snatching terrified people from their cars and throwing them into detention. Never mind all that; Badenoch doesn’t care.

So much for the policy; now consider the timing. The Tory leader decided the right moment to demand foreigners be kicked out of their homes was as the Norfolk town of Thetford entered its third night of violence and disorder, triggered by a mob surrounding the accommodation of suspected asylum seekers, some in the crowd trying to force their way in, as others threw rocks and chanted: “We want them out.” Into this tinderbox of a situation walked the Conservative party leader, clutching a petrol can.

Just a day or two earlier, she had been defending the selection as a Somerset council candidate of Joshua Bonehill-Paine, a man who has served long jail sentences for, among other things, a sustained campaign of antisemitic harassment and abuse of the Jewish former MP Luciana Berger, a campaign that saw Berger branded an “evil money-grabber”, her face superimposed on the body of a rat and photographs of her doctored into multiple, sexualised images.

Badenoch argued that Bonehill-Paine had renounced his past as a self-described “nationalist, fascist, theorist and supporter of white rights” and now works to prevent others succumbing to what he calls the disease of antisemitism. In April, he published a lengthy account of how he had come to see Jews as the malign, all-powerful “force operating behind events”, a text that contains some useful insights. (Among them, as my colleague Rafael Behr has pointed out, is an arresting admission by Bonehill-Paine that, though then a full-strength neo-Nazi, he “welcomed Jeremy Corbyn’s election as Labour leader”, which should give pause to those who, at the time, so adamantly dismissed Jewish fears that Corbyn was a draw to those who hate Jews.)

Though candid, the essay is not wholly reassuring. For one thing, it contains no apology to Berger or any of Bonehill-Paine’s other victims. For another, he explains that what changed him was reading the Bible and coming to realise that Jews are “God’s chosen people”. I suspect few Jews will find comfort in that. Instead, they will worry that the would-be politician has traded antisemitism for philosemitism, which means he still singles out “the Jews” rather than seeing Jews as regular people, with the right to be as ordinary and flawed as anyone else.

Still, even if Bonehill-Paine’s disavowal of his past were wholly convincing and he should be regarded as fully rehabilitated, that doesn’t make it obvious that he is acceptable for public office. The bar for that is higher, a point Badenoch herself implicitly conceded when she hinted that Bonehill-Paine would not have cleared the threshold to become an MP. Serving as a councillor was different, she explained, as he would be responsible for nothing more than “parking and bins” – thereby, and at a stroke, insulting the many thousands of Conservatives who devote themselves to public service in their local communities.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Bonehill-Paine eventually withdrew his candidacy, but that did not draw a line under the episode. In her stubbornness, the Tory leader said the former neo-Nazi would now serve the party as an adviser, thereby giving him a role on the very national level she had earlier said was off-limits. Worsening matters still further, the shadow cabinet member Claire Coutinho posted that, while, “Luciana and others are unable to forgive Joshua, I do,” attributing this vicarious generosity of hers to her Catholic faith, and so, doubtless unconsciously, reinforcing that age-old trope of the forgiving Christian and the vengeful Jew.

What a mess to have made in just a few days. If it were only tactical blunders and in-the-moment misjudgments, one might be more, er, forgiving. But the flaw is strategic. Badenoch has chosen to fight a race to the bottom against Reform, but it is a race she can never win. Farage will always be willing to go further. Take that latest proposal on housing. She would give foreign nationals six months to get out of their homes; Reform promises to boot them out in three. The penny has still not dropped that in a contest of Reform v Reform Lite, the real thing will always have the edge.

All the while, as Badenoch chases after Farage supporters, moderate Tory voters grow more disenchanted. There may be room for ex-fascists in Conservative ranks, but the leader will allow no place for Conservatives who support net zero targets and do not want the UK to leave the European convention on human rights. The result is that those “blue wall”, southern Tories who defected to the Lib Dems in 2024 have every reason not to come back.

So, yes, Kemi Badenoch may score a win now and then; she’s bound to land the odd blow on Burnham when normal hostilities resume in September. But a Keminaissance? For the Tories, it looks like the dark ages have a while to run yet.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Bonehill-Paine's disavowal of his past was not convincing, says Jonathan Freedland. But he says he still singles out ‘the Jews’ rather than seeing Jews as regular people.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: It must be tricky for Nige to remember what’s what. It’s so hideously complicated | John  Crace
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: John Crace
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
I can’t pass up the moment the Reform leader celebrates his byelection victory against ‘the establishment’ – a man with a dustbin on his head

You would have thought that after 35 years of writing for the Guardian I would have mastered some of the basics of holiday protocol by now. Apparently not. While I had remembered to let the newsdesk know I wouldn’t be writing the political sketch for two weeks, it had completely slipped my mind to inform the Saturday editor. So rather than leave her with the headache of an empty page, you’re getting an extra dose of me this week. And, in truth, I don’t mind because, for what is a usually empty August, there’s an awful lot still going on. I’ve even told the newsdesk that I’d like to write next Friday as I can’t pass up the moment Nigel Farage celebrates his byelection victory against the “establishment”, AKA a comedian with a dustbin on his head. This summer has been quite the reckoning for Reform. First some excellent investigative reporting from the Guardian and the Sunday Times, followed by even some of the party’s most loyal followers in the Spectator and the Telegraph beginning to turn. We will know the game is up when GB News begins to have doubts about Nige. It can only be a matter of time.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

This time last year, Reform was dominating the polls and setting the news agenda with weekly press conferences. Now it’s as if Nige has placed himself in a witness protection programme as he tries to avoid anyone asking about his financial arrangements. There again, it must be tricky for Nige to remember what’s what as it all seems so hideously complicated. There’s the £5m from Thai crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne that was first a gift to spend on Ferraris, then to pay for his security and now could be a downpayment on the £1m per year Nige said he would need to make it worth his while to return to full-time politics. Then there are funds travelling from various offshore bank accounts from George Cottrell – the boy who liked to call Nige “Daddy” – to his mum, Fiona, and then on to Dicky Tice. Some of which – no one is quite sure which – seemed to end up in Reform’s bank accounts. Nor can Nige even quite remember when he did decide he was politically active despite owning a majority share in Reform. Confusion doesn’t seem to begin to cover this. Nige still has a week to get his story straight for the Clacton voters.

What with one thing and another – first Jill’s cancer and then breaking her shoulder – it’s looking unlikely we will be making it to Minneapolis to see our daughter, Anna, and her husband, Robert, for a second year. . Instead they have come to visit us for a week, so we have been trying to plan fun things to do in London. Today, given Robert is American, we thought we should all go to see the exhibition to mark the 250th anniversary of American independence at the British Museum.

Truly, five minutes that none of us will get back. I’m trying to be generous to the museum here. Perhaps the trustees and curators have become so obsessed with not tearing the Bayeux Tapestry to shreds that they completely took their eye off the ball. Because this exhibition was an embarrassment. A darkened room with just four items on display. A peace medal made by Paul Revere. A tomahawk that doubled as a peace pipe and had been given to a British general. A wampum belt that had been made by Native Americans. All of which looked like they had been dug out of the museum’s storage department as an afterthought.

Then the piece de resistance: a facsimile of a declaration of independence, complete with a notice saying that the original, which is kept in Chichester, would be on display in September. Thanks for nothing.

What was the British Museum thinking? You’d have been disappointed if any of that had been on display at your local library. I guarantee that anyone coming to my house to see the ceramics I have collected over the years would have had a better time.

No one wants to kick a man when he’s down, but I can’t help thinking that Jason Arday – the professor of sociology who has just resigned from the University of Cambridge – has been badly let down by his former employer. Surely someone must have thought of putting his PhD thesis through a plagiarism detector before offering him a job? The most alarming thing about Arday is that he seems clearly unwell. A fantasist who makes it hard to take almost anything he says as the truth. The list is seemingly endless: his claim to be a world-class athlete who once ran 600 miles in six days, or saying he had been part of the epic TV documentary series Seven Up. A programme that has been watched by millions of people over the years.

Somehow, though, Cambridge managed to overlook all this and more. The greater the fable, the more the university defended him. And in the process it has done far more damage to him than if it had quietly and systematically gone through the evidence and declined to offer him a professorship. Thanks for applying, but no thanks.

Worse still, Cambridge has done a huge disservice to other academics of colour because it has opened the gateway to rightwing critics who will now claim that many other professors at other universities got their jobs on a nod and a wink. Jason has a book coming out later this month. If Simon & Schuster has any thought for its own credibility and Arday’s wellbeing it will quietly announce the book has been delayed “indefinitely”.

Maybe there’s something in theair, but Kemi Badenoch seems to be having a bit of a moment. Having appeared on the Political Currency podcast this week to accuse Reform of “woke” politics and to rubbish Andy Burnham for having done nothing of any value – er, it’s only been two weeks and he’s already promised to solve social care. I guess there’s no pleasing some people.

Badenoch has now nailed herself to the cross of defending the former neo-nazi Joshua Bonehill-Paine, who was jailed for harassing the Jewish Labour MP Luciana Berger. In Badenoch’s view, Bonehill-Paine is a reformed man and deserved a second chance to serve as a Tory councillor because all he would be doing was sorting out the “bin collections”. Bonehill-Paine clearly had second thoughts when some of his CV turned out to be nearly as creative as Jason Arday’s and he withdrew as a Conservative candidate. Only for Kemi to appoint him as a Tory special adviser.

Now I’m all for second chances. But Badenoch didn’t seem to think the Labour cabinet minister Lou Haigh deserved rehabilitation to atone for her phone fraud: a conviction that predated Joshua’s by many years. As far as Badenoch was concerned, Haigh still had to repay her debt to society. It’s also curious to know what is and isn’t acceptable in today’s Tory party. A bit of previous for antisemitism and Hitler loving? Just fine. Believing in net zero and the European convention on human rights, not so much. Grant Shapps has been banned from standing as a Tory MP because he happens to believe in the climate crisis. There again, maybe Kemi understands her party better than most. The columnist Tim Stanley caused huge waves in the Telegraph by writing that maybe climate change was true after all, and got 9,000 comments of complaint. All for saying what 99.9% of the rest of us know to be true.

It’s been hard to keep up with the excesses and moral corruption of the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino. As I write, various football bodies and national organisations have expressed their lack of confidence in him but for the time being he appears to be just about hanging on to his job. Maybe he will even ride this one out. But it has struck me that one person has remained silent throughout the scandal: David Beckham. For the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, Beckham was paid millions to be a Fifa ambassador. His one contribution was to say he hadn’t spotted any gay people being persecuted. Top detective work from DB. This time round in the US, David seemed content being an unofficial ambassador, there to be filmed sitting in the VIP seats wearing a suit and looking miserable most of the time as he notched up another £24m that he doesn’t need in advert endorsements. He seemed to be Infantino’s mute puppet. He said nothing when Gianni devalued Fifa by awarding Donald Trump a peace prize. He said nothing when Gianni introduced hydration breaks and extended the half-time interval during the final. He said nothing when Gianni bowed to Trump’s demand to overturn Folarin Balogun’s red card. And he has said nothing while Gianni has tried to sell off stakes and reinvent the competition as an even fatter cash cow. It all feels so sad. A mini tragedy. David used to be almost a national treasure. Someone who appeared to have both a sense of what is right and wrong and also a good sense of humour. Now he just appears to be obsessed with wealth and status. Over the last few months, he could have been a voice for the country, speaking up against the commercialisation and obvious corruption of Infantino’s regime. We would all have loved him for it. Instead he has trashed his brand by being complicit. The only obvious reason for his silence is that either he doesn’t think Infantino has done anything wrong, or he just isn’t bothered as long as the cash keeps coming. It would be nice to be proved wrong. We want our Becks back.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: How divided is the UK really? Here’s a way to find out | Brendan Cox
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Brendan Cox
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Social media-fuelled riots and fractured politics make us feel more divided than ever, but is that so? Our study hopes to reveal what bring us together – and pushes us apart

Take part in the National Conversation

Brendan Cox is co-founder of the Together Coalition, which acts as the secretariat for the Independent Commission on Community and Cohesion

W
hen my late wife Jo Cox was killed by a far-right extremist 10 years ago, the phrase “more in common”, taken from her maiden speech in parliament, became a rallying cry against extremism and division.

The phrase succinctly articulated that, no matter our differences, we have more in common than that which divides us.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

In the decade since, that solidarity has faded. But it hasn’t just faded as time has elapsed: it has been replaced by a cynicism and a polarisation that it’s hard to overstate.

In an era of hostile states, algorithms designed to incite rage and collapsing community institutions, repeating the mantra that we have “more in common” is no longer enough. It’s time we mapped out that common ground.

Because what we have in common matters. It’s the strength of our connections that defines what we are willing to commit to each other. It determines the strength of our democracy and is the basis of social solidarity. It defines everything from our commitment to the welfare state to our ability to fight wars and defend ourselves.

So it’s pretty remarkable that we haven’t mapped the strength and nature of those connections. I guess we have taken them for granted in the past. Yet with a digital environment that now actively seeks to escalate, exacerbate and exaggerate our divisions, that complacency is no longer an option.

That’s where the Independent Commission on Community and Cohesion comes in, a cross-party group co-chaired by former Conservative chancellor Sajid Javid and former Labour MP Jon Cruddas. Central to the commission’s work is the National Conversation, a project with Oxford University to build the best picture we have ever had of what we have in common, what connects us, what divides us, and the kind of country we want to build together.

In any other era, that kind of national research exercise would have been prohibitively expensive. You would have needed thousands of researchers interviewing members of the public, classifying and coding responses, before trying to summarise the millions of data points.

AI makes this kind of exercise possible at scale for the first time. It means as part of the survey you can leave a 60-second voice note on your vision for the country. It means you can identify places on a map that bring you together or write open text. Our ability to gather all this information means the national conversation will provide the richest ever snapshot of what future we want to build together.

Our hope is that the results will help provide us all with a common understanding of our connections, perhaps some reassurance and a chance to play back to our country what vision connects us still.

But its insights will only be a strong as its inputs. Which is why I’m asking you to take just a few minutes to share your vision of the country you want to see. We’ll be publishing the results in a few months. Thousands of others have already joined the conversation but every voice that takes part deepens the insights and adds richness to our understanding of the nature of our connections.

In future, we hope the National Conversation will become an institution like the census – not answering who we are and where we live, but the country talking about what unites us. We’d like you to be part of the start of this journey by adding your voice today. Because in a world that is trying to tear us apart, the least we can all do is speak up for the future we want to see.

Brendan Cox is co-founder of the Together Coalition, which acts as the secretariat for the Independent Commission on Community and Cohesion

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: As a Tory, I say things are looking up. Farage is fading, and the looming threat to No 10 is called Kemi | Simon Hart
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Simon Hart
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
My party has seen difficult times – but with a few canny moves the leader is finally cutting through, and there are clear signs of recovery

Something is afoot. The bookies can feel it. “Badenoch overtakes Farage as favourite to be next prime minister,” was the word from betting website William Hill this week.

Let me tell you what is happening. This is a challenging political time. Even today, there is controversy for Kemi Badenoch to deal with. But as a Conservative it seems to me that in the past few tumultuous weeks, she has shown many of the qualities necessary in a party leader: to appear easy-going and humorous; to craft a style that teases her opponents rather than being snide or unkind; and to do this all confidently enough to leave sceptics thinking that she really could be the next prime minister.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

This easygoing style was frustrating for Keir Starmer. Badenoch’s riposte to his defence of his economic record – “if it’s all going so fine, why is he resigning?” – was spontaneous, humorous and deadly. The opposition cheered, the government benches stared at their feet. And this style will soon challenge Andy Burnham once MPs actually get the chance to cross-question him on his deluge of summer announcements. “Not being Starmer” may work in the dog days of August, but that won’t last long.

Burnham has been fortunate: few prime ministers have had such a gentle induction into life at the top. But the interaction between Badenoch’s fluency (which is about pitch perfect at the moment) and Burnham’s northern mateyness (which is also going down surprisingly well) is about to become more intense and take on new significance. Badenoch is being careful to avoid being cast as a more digestible version of Nigel Farage or the sort of Tory relic that voters grew weary of. If she can keep that up, her chances of stripping Burnham of his “fancy that, little old me in No 10” veneer are all the more possible.

Look at Badenoch’s recent comments about net zero and climate change – “Climate change is real. The net zero plans are not. They are a political fiction” – and then on social care (an offer of support but only if the PM rules out tax rises), and you see something of her calculus on the issue of risk versus opportunity. Are those statements an admission that the Conservative party hasn’t really changed at all, or evidence of a party leader offering a clarity rarely revealed in public?

Most leaders yearn for something that gives them an edge over their opposition, but Badenoch seeks distinctiveness from her predecessors too. Tony Blair did that by amending Clause four , whereas David Cameron stared down the Tory faithful on the question of same-sex marriage. This made them different – and therefore, to a wider electorate, electable. Badenoch follows that tradition by being questioning but not a climate denier, and by not slating Burnham’s social care plans in advance of their proper exposure.

Comparisons with Margaret Thatcher are always a risk, such is the sacred nature of her legacy in Tory circles, but I think some of her political skills are evident in Badenoch: never closing off avenues of opportunity, making it clear what the overall ambition looks like, and persuading MPs and the public why that ambition is worth some pain along the way. That’s hard in opposition. It can’t all be achieved by opposing for opposing’s sake.

Badenoch’s challenge is to reassure voters in leafy home counties – just as much as the “red wall” voters – that the Conservatives can be trusted again. Policies must be “conservative”, that is, driven by a philosophical belief that business is generally successful despite the state, not because of it. The tax regime must be based on funding public services, not by punishing success or constraining choice.

​The faces and voices of ​our politicians matter too, which is why every single Conservative candidate has had to reapply to be considered for election and sign up to the party’s flagship plans. It’s why the controversial approval of the former convicted racist Joshua Bonehill-Paine to stand for his local council in Somerset was big news. Badenoch’s “judgment call” to let him stand, as she explained it, relied entirely on the fact that his approval extended only to his local area, and that since his conviction he has embarked on a Home Office-sponsored mission to educate people on the perils of radicalisation. In other words, contrition played its part in her decision. Amid a deal of uproar, Bonehill-Paine himself stood down on Wednesday, but Badenoch has now asked him to be an adviser to the party’s culture and integration commission. Again, a distinctive strategy. Whether the public thinks the matter was handled well, only time will tell.

But there is method there, for mo​st pertinent ​to any Tory leader is Thatcher’s absolute conviction that the job is to set out the case and trust that public opinion will positively reflect it, rather than testing public opinion with a view to aping it. ​Badenoch, it seems, understand​s that.

I’m not getting too excited. The Conservatives’ polling position is running at about 20% (YouGov recently put Reform UK at 23%, Labour at 22% and the Conservatives at 19%. Survation: Reform 24%, Labour 26%, Conservatives 21%). That’s a little way off celebration territory.

after newsletter promotion

But with Labour now level-pegging with Reform, or having overtaken it, I can’t help wondering when we will see the inevitable Reform meltdown. Many Tory defectors jumped ship to Reform, thinking their voyage back to relevance looked smoother under Captain Farage, but now​, with his vessel heading for the icebergs, the ructions within Reform will surely begin in earnest. There is opportunity for us in that.

Badenoch’s own poll ratings are climbing too. They are better now than at any recent stage, and a lot healthier than Nigel Farage’s. Does that matter? Indeed it does. It may seem odd that the party leader and the party itself poll quite differently, but history does throw up examples of “catchup”, when people warm to the leader before that warmth extends to the party they lead. In the unbelievably time-limited windows of opportunity that most leaders get, that means Badenoch has to be different, amusing, professional, relaxed and penetrative. She also has to be unflappable – and there, the signs are promising. So far so good.

Simon Hart was Conservative government chief whip from 2022 to 2024, and is the author of Ungovernable, the political diaries of a chief whip

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on mental health: the new secretary of state should make it a priority | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Parity for people with physical and psychological ailments has been promised for years. New neighbourhood clinics are a step in the right direction

T
he rise in children and young people with mental health problems makes this week’s announcement of a new network of community clinics in England particularly welcome. A&E departments have recorded an increase in difficult-to-manage symptoms including aggression and hallucinations. New specialist walk-in mental health services should take some of the pressure off. The bringing forward of a deadline for ending out-of-area acute placements, and a pledge to reduce waiting times for children, are also positive.

Declining mental health was among the key themes of Alan Milburn’s interim report on young people and work. It is a big factor behind the rise in claims for illness and disability benefits. Children’s anxiety and other psychological difficulties are also among the many challenges facing schools. Recent years have seen steep rises in emotionally based school avoidance, as well as in autism and neurodiversity.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

But while concerns about mental health are shared across government, they have not been prominent in policies put forward by the department where you might expect them to feature most: health. Partly, that is due to other pressing issues including social care and enormous hospital waiting-lists. Partly, it is because ministers have been waiting for a review led by Prof Peter Fonagy into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism. Its recommendations are expected soon, and will feed into an upcoming strategy. In her first interview with the Guardian as health secretary, Yvette Cooper focused on maternity services and the need to prepare for future heatwaves. But the commitment to expand community mental health points to a welcome recognition that this should be an area of focus too.

Parity between mental and physical healthcare became a policy goal in 2011, with the launch of a No Health Without Mental Health initiative. Efforts to stress the importance of psychological wellbeing, and its interconnectedness with physical health, long predate that. The commitment made in last year’s 10-year health strategy to shift resources gradually away from acute hospitals and towards community services would seem to dovetail with this balanced, holistic outlook. But one year on from its launch, experts including Siva Anandaciva, of the King’s Fund, have raised doubts about “whether the NHS really will be committed to the fundamental shift away from hospital care that the health plan proposed”. This week it was revealed that one mental health trust, in east London, is planning to make £25m of cuts. Mental health is not ringfenced within NHS budgets, and as a proportion of overall health spending fell from 9.0% of the total in 2023/24 to 8.78% in 2024/25.

The reasons for the lower priority placed on mental health, compared with physical diseases and injuries, are complex, and reflect cultural as well as structural factors to do with the way that the NHS is organised. Socioeconomic determinants of poor mental health including incomes, work and housing, are outside Ms Cooper’s remit. But the disparities in access to treatment are irrational and unjust. Severe depression and anxiety are highly debilitating conditions. Expectations about waiting times and treatment options need to be clarified.

There are no easy fixes in a system as complicated as the NHS. It is not clear where the new neighbourhood centres fit in existing plans – or who will staff them. But providing that further details are produced in due course, the shift in focus that they signal should be supported.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: By day five of my labour, I didn’t want an ‘ideal birth’. I only wanted to survive | Natalie Morris
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Natalie Morris
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Yvette Cooper’s maternity reforms must change a system that too often fails women when they’re at their most vulnerable

O
n the third day of being in labour with my first child, I entered a new state of being. It was time to dig deep. This is what I had learned in all the childbirth classes. As long as I remained calm, breathed as instructed, moaned through the pain, things would happen as they were meant to. My body knew what it was doing. Only, it didn’t.

On the fourth day, I started to beg. This wasn’t right. Despite contraction after relentless contraction, I wasn’t dilating. I hadn’t slept, I couldn’t even sit down. I needed help. And still, they waited. For what, I never understood.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

When Yvette Cooper told the Guardian this week that women must not “feel pressurised” to have “an ideal birth experience”, it was a relief to hear her name this all-too-common phenomenon in which maternity staff are reluctant – or refusing – to escalate. But Cooper’s characterisation of the problem is not the full picture. The harm here is not just in women being nudged towards a certain kind of birth experience, but in a culture that can completely override women’s physical and psychological safety in favour of a low-intervention ideal.

Half of Britain’s maternal deaths are considered preventable, and low-intervention births are the ideal for a reason. Midwife-led care usually results in better outcomes for healthy women with straightforward pregnancies – lower risk of infection and severe bleeds, and quicker recovery. In 2024-25, 45% of all hospital deliveries in England (542,235 total births) were performed via caesarean section – it was the first time C-sections outnumbered unassisted natural vaginal births. (Another 11% needed extra support through instruments such as forceps.) There is a natural, and warranted, cautiousness about the over-medicalisation of birth, which can lead to avoidable complications, and leave women who would prefer a natural birth feeling pressured to take a different route. But we can’t ignore that there are also structural forces at play here: lower intervention also translates to lower cost for an overstretched, under-resourced system. One midwife told me explicitly that they would have admitted me to the labour ward earlier if there had been a bed.

Of course most first-time mothers would choose the lowest possible intervention if they could. I had hoped to float blissfully in a birthing pool under the soft glow of fairy lights. But when it comes to the messy, unpredictable, dangerous act of bringing new life into the world, the concept of choice can quickly be revealed as a fallacy. By day five of my labour, I was not thinking about my birth plan. I was not thinking about very much at all. My only focus was survival.

The demographic of people giving birth today looks nothing like it did 30 years ago. The average age of a mother in England and Wales is now 31, a figure that has been creeping up since records began. There is something deeply flawed about a system that pushes quite so strongly for low-intervention births despite the fact that mothers over 30 are more likely to require a higher level of medical involvement. Almost half of UK women aged 30-39 have caesareans, and for those over 40, it is now the most common way to give birth. Yet the narrative of an “ideal birth” persists, leaving women who end up needing more help wondering where they went wrong. Maternity practices must reflect this reality, or risk perpetuating a cycle that leaves women at risk and then pushes the blame back on to them.

After the best part of a week, I was eventually wheeled down for an emergency C-section. Even then, it wasn’t the desperate pleas from my husband and me that finally spurred action, it was the fact that my baby started showing signs of distress. The doctors who greeted us displayed clear consternation that I had been left in that state for so long, a factor that probably played a part in my child developing an irregular heartbeat. The ideal birth narrative – that low-intervention, midwife-led care is always best – has hardened into institutional bias, amid a system in which women’s choices about their medical care are too often sidelined.

In one of her first acts as health secretary, Cooper said she intends to reintroduce binding national maternity standards. They will include ending the postcode lottery for levels of care, and tackling racial inequalities that have meant worse outcomes for poorer and for black and Asian women. Her promises sound reassuring, but we have heard similar things before. What’s needed is a fundamental cultural shift so that women’s voices are treated as clinical evidence, not background noise.

There is a deep-rooted disconnect in NHS maternity units. Between the needs of patients and the people treating them, and between different parts of the system itself. When midwife-led care and obstetric intervention are positioned in opposition, rather than as complementary approaches, escalation can be perceived as failure instead of necessary care. And in that gap, women at their most vulnerable have their pain minimised and their instincts questioned, sometimes to the point that risk becomes life-threatening.

Trauma is a brutal introduction to motherhood, and one that is all too common. For me and thousands of other mothers, our births could have gone so differently if we had only been heard. My ideal birth is not defined by candlelight or calm breathing. It is one where I am listened to, believed and responded to in time. One that both my baby and I survive at any cost.

Natalie Morris is the author of Mixed/Other: Explorations of Multiraciality in Modern Britain

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: I knew Rod Liddle and hated what he became. He would have wanted me to say so | Zoe Williams
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Zoe Williams
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
A man who prized blunt speaking has been selectively eulogised. There’s a balance between decency and honesty: I’m sad he caused such harm

A
s tributes poured in for Rod Liddle, the Sunday Times and Sun columnist who has died at the age of 66, they were markedly coy and sanitised. Paradoxically, those were the exact deficiencies obituaries praised Liddle for avoiding – they said he shot from the hip and ruffled feathers, remorselessly attacked the liberal establishment and was ebullient. Michael Gove called him “special and brave”. But brave in the face of what? Attacked the liberal establishment how?

This delicacy was particularly noticeable in a segment on Radio 4’s Today programme, of which Liddle was editor in the 90s, between Justin Webb and Amol Rajan. “If there was a golden thread that connected the person you saw back then with the person of a few weeks ago,” Webb said, “it was a distrust of authority.” But Liddle’s targets as a columnist were not the authorities. Often they were Muslims and immigrants, transgender people and chronic illness sufferers, African-Caribbean men from Harlesden. He did not attack the establishment, he attacked the marginalised, constantly.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

There is sometimes a dilemma in how we process death. Decently, we seek not to speak ill of the dead, and certainly one hopes to never increase the grief of those who loved them. But does that mean we are also duty-bound not to discuss more uncomfortable issues? Here I feel the dilemma.

I was friends with Rod Liddle in the 90s. He was a different Rod then. The principal target of his satire was himself. He would lampoon guys having affairs, guys who were a shambles, guys who had run out of road. If there was any ethno-caricaturing, it read as a footnote to a worldview in which nobody was more ridiculous than he, Rod Liddle. This carried on into his collection of short stories, Too Beautiful for You (2003), in which the most memorable escapade was a man getting into a train crash, after seeing his mistress, rushing across a field carrying his severed arm so that he could get to a hospital without blowing his alibi, and realising as he bleeds out that he must actually really love his wife.

In 1983, he was a member of the Socialist Workers party and by 1990, a researcher for the Labour party, but what made him seem left-left, rather than centre left, didn’t have a membership card. It was the self-parody coupled with an overall dishevelment that conveyed a deep-seated humanity and pluralism: “I’m a mess, you’re a mess, let’s get out of this mess together.” I know that is maddeningly unspecific, but I also know that anyone on the left will get what I mean.

So his transformation into an attack dog for the race-baiting right was painful to watch, if not exactly unprecedented. On Tuesday, sociologist Will Davies characterised this post-68 type, “drawn to norm-breaching, moving via adolescent rebellion, punk, revolutionary socialism and eventually ending up at racism, because by the 21st century that was the most efficient transgression still on offer”. The rightwing media will pay absolutely top dollar for a big-name left-to-right defector.

Peter York, in his book A Dead Cat on Your Table, examines the nexus of rightwing thinktanks, the mainstream right and “alt-right” media to argue that what we call “culture wars” aren’t ideological, they’re about hegemonic capture in the service of capital. Depressingly, it does work: GB News, which hedge-funder Paul Marshall hosed money at, to widespread ridicule, now secures higher average audiences than Sky News or BBC News. Arguably, the greater victory is that all we ever talk about is what GB News wants to talk about.

One thing the obituaries did mention was Liddle’s feud with Yasmin Alibhai-Brown – “they loathed each other,” Justin Webb said, then, later he asked: “Deep down, did he really? There was no loathing in Rod that I could ever divine.” But “feud” is doing some heavy lifting there: Liddle attacked Alibhai-Brown constantly in his columns, for opinions which many of us hold but seemed unaccountably more obnoxious to him coming from her. This culminated in a clash on Channel 4 in 2014, after which the then Conservative MP Michael Fabricant, tweeted that he might have ended up punching Alibhai-Brown in the throat.

Liddle the Today editor, listening to much of the discussion, would have said, “what the fuck are you playing at, trying to describe this outrageous character without naming any of his outrages?” Not least as they are so easy to Google – the time he said he couldn’t have been a teacher because he would have ended up shagging the children, “right in there, on day one”; the endless attacks on Muslims, arguing that it was the faith itself, not unhinged individuals, that drove terrorism, that the 2019 election should be held on a day when “Muslims are forbidden to do anything on pain of hell” to suppress their vote. The editor Liddle of the 90s would have also said: “You can’t have two blokes on the radio, explaining why whipping up racist misogyny is fine so long as, underneath, you have a heart of gold.” Not because of diversity and whatnot, but because it’s just not cricket.

after newsletter promotion

One of the last times I saw Liddle was a couple of months ago when we were both on Sky News. He looked really different, because he had COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease). I asked him how he was and he said “depressed”, and I asked why, but I was just being tactful, because it was obvious why. My mum died with COPD last year, and by the time your face goes grey, life is pretty horrible, like drowning in air. “I’m no longer priapic,” he replied.

I felt ineffably sad; that privately, his persona was still the same, standing there with his arm hanging off, insisting that the first thing he would do, once he got it sewed back on, was get a hard-on; sad at the pantomime of it, cartoon prejudices with real-life consequences, trotted out on command, funded by people with mountains of money who wish society ill; sad about the empathy and solidarity that had once built a collective firewall against hate-for-fun, which had been slowly extinguished.

In fact, I wanted to start crying but I’d just had my makeup done, so we went on air and argued about Andy Burnham in Makerfield, and he said he would only win it if he “sorted out” immigration. I won’t miss Rod Liddle, but I miss the person he was when the world was different, and I miss that different world.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/ng-i.title: The night Belfast burned: how the Northern Ireland race riots unfolded
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/ng-i.author: Hannah Al-Othman and Rory Carroll in Belfast
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/ng-i.text:
A horrific knife attack on a street in June sparked another summer’s night of racial violence, stoked by loyalist groups. How did the unrest erupt – and why do many fear it will happen again?

Shortly after 10.30pm on Monday 8 June, as a summer twilight lingered over Belfast, a horrific scene unfolded on Kinnaird Avenue: a man straddled and repeatedly stabbed a figure lying on the ground in a bloody assault that ended only after onlookers intervened.

Others captured the drama on cameraphones and uploaded the footage to social media. Once seen, the grainy images were hard to forget, and by dawn on Tuesday 9 June they were ricocheting around X, WhatsApp, Facebook, Telegram and other platforms.

Many commentators highlighted one aspect: the assailant was black, the victim white.

Police had a suspect in custody – he was initially identified as a refugee from Somalia, later corrected to Sudan – but this did not stem a cascade of outrage. What, commentators demanded to know, about other foreign men of “military age” in Northern Ireland? Had they been “vetted”? What “alien culture” had they imported?

By 9.30am a message – an exhortation – was being widely shared. “All business to close at 5.30pm tonight. No excuses.” It listed 25 locations around Northern Ireland for people to gather at 7pm. “Please forward [to] all men of the age of 18 and over. Wear dark clothing … and be prepared to fight or be arrested.”

It was an invitation to a pogrom.

Far-right agitators, such as Elon Musk and Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, known by his alias Tommy Robinson, amplified calls to protest, and those interventions were prominent in the coverage that followed.

Through a combination of interviews with witnesses and people who responded to the unrest, on-the-ground reporting in loyalist strongholds and at far-right rallies in Northern Ireland, and analysis of messages sent by figures connected to the extreme right, the Guardian has established the most complete picture yet of how a single incident of horrific violence precipitated the crisis. And it suggests that organisers in Belfast needed no encouragement or direction. This was their show.

Drawing on previous eruptions of violence – this was to be the third consecutive summer of racial disturbances in Northern Ireland – the organisers issued further instructions: leave mobile phones at home and deactivate dashcams and doorbell cameras.

By early afternoon, schools were sending children home, public transport was halting and steel shutters were clanging down over foreign-owned barber shops, supermarkets and other businesses.

As families sat down for dinner, crowds gathered at designated roundabouts and intersections in loyalist areas across the city.

At about 7.30pm a woman with a megaphone on the Shankill Road recited the Lord’s Prayer to several hundred people, some draped in union flags. They marched through terraced sidestreets and halted outside the home of a Romanian family. A nearby Black family, anticipating trouble, had already fled and asked neighbours to move their car.

The Romanian family’s windows had been “put out” twice before, but the family had refused to leave. The previous night’s stabbing had nothing to do with the Romanians but somehow alchemised into what one woman in the crowd called “the last straw”.

Dozens of boys and men wearing hoods and masks surged forward. Some launched bricks through windows, others shoved fireworks through the letterbox. A woman inside, visible to the crowd, watched helplessly as her home came under attack. The family’s car went up in flames, then men in balaclavas broke down the door.

Women and children in the mob observed proceedings. “There’s wee girls inside,” said one. In contrast to race riots in England and Belfast in 2024, and in Ballymena last year, the violence was not recorded or streamed on mobile phones. A teenage boy who ignored the injunction against filming was dragged aside and chastised.

Similar scenes played out across Belfast. In the east of the city, families from Ukraine, Romania, Poland and Sudan left. Properties and vehicles, including a Glider bus, were set ablaze and plumes of smoke rose into the night.

On arterial roads and by roundabouts, crowds lit bins and set up roadblocks to question and intimidate suspected foreigners. In Sandy Row, central Belfast, Ethiopian and Chinese residents fled and arsonists burned a Syrian supermarket. On Crumlin Road, in the west, Ugandan health workers and Nigerian families sought refuge. In some places the police were absent or stayed back and it was left to community volunteers to navigate the mobs and escort families to safety.

At around 10pm the violence abated and crowds began to disperse. Some whooped in jubilation, others surveyed the smouldering debris with satisfaction. A point, they said, had been made. Rain began to fall, helping emergency crews to douse the embers of gutted homes and vehicles.

The riot should not have come as a surprise. Northern Ireland was primed for it. “We could see it coming,” said Daniel Holder, the director of the Committee on the Administration of Justice (CAJ), a Belfast-based advocacy group. “It wasn’t unprecedented, it was an escalation of an existing pattern.”

An escalation, and a learning curve. Drawing on lessons from 2024 and 2025, the agitators refined their methods to hit more targets and reduce the chance of arrest.

Far-right allies in England and the US were taking notes. Enrique Tarrio, the former head of the militant US group Proud Boys, recently visited and interviewed activists for a documentary. And last month, the Advance UK-affiliated YouTuber Sarah White was streaming multiple events in Northern Ireland, including an Orange Order march and an anti-migrant protest in Portrush.

The Northern Ireland “model” is not necessarily transferable. It has taken a unique mix – the legacy of the Troubles, xenophobia, social media platforms and state acquiescence – to create the toxic climate.

Until the 1998 Good Friday agreement the region was almost entirely white and native-born. As sectarian violence eased, immigrants trickled in. By the 2021 census, 3.4% of the population was from a minority ethnic background – small compared with 19% in England, but the sight of people from Africa, Asia and the Middle East still came as a jolt.

Many immigrants settled in working-class loyalist areas where the population was declining, property was cheaper – and paramilitary groups endured. Despite a state-sponsored “transitioning” process, the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) and Ulster Defence Association (UDA) split into sub-groups that continued to deal drugs and coercively control communities.

“Peace” walls between Catholic and Protestant neighbourhoods still stand, underlining the persistence of traditional sectarian divisions, but the waning IRA threat weakened loyalist paramilitaries’ claims to be community defenders, prompting them to seek a new bogeyman to justify their existence.

“Loyalism has always been a reactionary ideology based on keeping out ‘foreign’ influence,” said Stephen Millar, an academic and author of Performing Paramilitarism: Loyalist Songs, Conflict, and Culture War in Northern Ireland. “The pivot from [opposing] Irish nationalism to anti-migrant rhetoric is, to some extent, internally consistent, and serves to keep loyalism ‘relevant’, trading one form of racism for another.”

Sporadic attacks and harassment against minority ethnic families – paint bombs, smashed windows, “locals only” graffiti, threatening posters – have proliferated over the past decade, especially in County Antrim, where healthcare workers from Africa were among those targeted.

That turned out to be the warm-up for a full-scale riot in Belfast in August 2024 – a copycat response to mayhem in England after the killing of three girls in Southport. Then in June 2025, Ballymena, 25 miles outside Belfast, erupted after two Roma teenagers were charged with rape (the charges were later dropped).

June’s eruption completed a grim summer hat-trick.

Jon Boutcher, the chief constable of the Police Service Northern Ireland (PSNI), said the overall picture of paramilitary involvement in the most recent trouble was “inconsistent” but that paramilitaries were present.

However, many say the police have been slow to recognise, at least in public, the role of paramilitary groups in controlling the violence. Holder said: “To anyone on the ground, that was very obvious from the start.”

The UDA and UVF are fractured. Some factions urged restraint – that is partly credited with keeping Ballymena calm this summer – but independent observers say other factions orchestrated much of the violence. Firefighters had no doubt about paramilitary influence and sought permission from their leaders before tackling blazes, sources said.

The ferrying of teenagers to and from flashpoints was further evidence of orchestration, said Chris Quinn, Northern Ireland’s children’s commissioner. “There’s been a long history of child criminal coercion and child criminal exploitation.”

Such children should not escape legal consequences but they too were victims, said Quinn. Some heeded the call to riot to service debts, including drug debts, he said. Another source, a youth worker, said paramilitary groups paid boys £100 to join the rioting.

Instead of Catholics, it was now people of colour in the crosshairs of loyalist groups, said Michaela Rafferty, of Anaka, a women’s group that helped escort besieged families to safety. “There has been a sectarian element, obviously, through our years of Troubles and violence. Now that focus has kind of moved to brown and black people.”

AI-generated anti-Islam murals have appeared in loyalist strongholds such as Moygashel and Newtownabbey. “Islam is Heathen, Islam is Satanic — A New Evil Has Arisen,” says one, “Not welcome, not wanted, not here,” says another.

Agitators have refined their methods. Most rioters in Ballymena last year wore masks or hoods but footage uploaded by participants and onlookers helped police identify and charge dozens of rioters. The lesson was not lost on the recent rioters in Belfast – they banned filming and made greater efforts to conceal identifying details, such as tattoos.

Through trial and error they also discovered that without a galvanising incident, such as a brutal crime allegedly committed by a foreigner, calls for mass mobilisation tended to flop, and this punctured morale.

Instead, they set up online community groups and joined existing ones to drip-feed anti-foreigner sentiment, said Dessie Donnelly of rabble.coop, a Belfast-based tech cooperative that tracks online xenophobia. “Ballymena was a watershed. You had loads of groups springing up online and a far-right network emerging.”

Before the most recent riot, posts about dark-skinned men in parks, and foreigners moving into houses of multiple occupation (HMO) on particular streets, proliferated. The tactic distilled Islamophobia to a hyper-local level, said Donnelly. “It prepares people for when there is an animating event.”

Activists in Belfast, Bangor, Coleraine, Derry, Newtownabbey, Portadown and other towns formed online “clusters” that shared and amplified posts and infiltrated online forums for loyalist bonfires and marching bands, said a researcher with Accountability Project Northern Ireland, a group that monitors online hate.

Last summer, the watchdog noticed that a Portadown-based Facebook group was circulating a screenshot of council-owned HMO properties – a ready-made hitlist of addresses that rioters used in June.

Burgeoning attacks – in the year to 31 March, police recorded 2,367 race incidents and 1,507 race crimes, the highest on record – created a sense of foreboding as summer approached, said Naomi Green, the Northern Ireland-based assistant secretary general of the Muslim Council of Britain (MCB). “We thought it was going to get quite scary very quickly, and it did.”

A week before the riot, anti-racism organisations convened an emergency meeting in Belfast because they feared trouble, said Holder. The marching season loomed and there was “a huge buildup” of racist activism on- and offline, he said. “For a third successive summer, it was waiting on an excuse.”

The attack at Kinnaird Avenue provided the spark. For foreigners who had been previously targeted there was a sense of inevitability, on the afternoon of 9 June, to what came next. “We’ve been sharing the same messages all day: go home early, stay inside, don’t go out,” Mohammed Mahmoud, 39, said as a crowd gathered near his Sandy Row grocery store.

The violence that night gave way to an eerie calm the next day. Central Belfast was like a ghost town, with most businesses remaining shut in expectation of fresh strife. A familiar message duly began to circulate on social media. “All business to close … wear dark clothing.”

In fact, Belfast remained largely quiet on the night of 10 June but in Glengormley, 7 miles north, a mob tried to march on the Chimney Corner hotel, which had been used to house asylum seekers, and fought against police in riot gear. The crowd hurled bricks and rocks, lit bonfires in the street and torched a vacant house. Police used water cannon and plastic bullets to drive them back.

Around 11pm the violence dwindled and stopped, as if someone had turned off a tap. That was the last disturbance in June. But in some ways the aftermath has been just as troubling.

In a poll by the thinktank More in Common, 8% of people in Northern Ireland said it was justified to burn migrants out of their homes and 11% agreed with intimidating them out of an area. Forty-one per cent said they sometimes feel like a stranger in their own country and three-quarters worry about asylum seekers entering Northern Ireland.

Conleth Burns, the associate director and Ireland lead for More In Common, said polling in England showed similar results. “You’ve got a similar number of people in lots of societies who think that this level of violence against migrants is justified.”

Northern Ireland, however, has far fewer foreigners and people of colour than England, which shows that even small numbers can have an outsized impact, said Burns. Most people expressed concern about immigration, racism and violence, he added. “People don’t see [those views] as being contradictory.”

The Institute for Strategic Dialogue, which tracks extremism and misinformation, said the unrest turbo-charged far-right activism online. Posts that promoted claims of anti-white police bias surged to more than 200,000 in the first two weeks of June compared with 104,000 in the whole of May, it said in a report published this week.

The main parties at Stormont strongly condemned the violence but critics say the executive failed to prepare for the crisis.

“This was the third time in two years,” said Donnelly. “They should have known something would happen, it was building up.”

Even though the Police Service of Northern Ireland had struggled to contain unrest in previous years it was still under-resourced, said Donnelly. “There was no acknowledgment that immigrants had been systematically attacked twice and that it would happen again.”

Holder said Stormont’s response had downplayed the gravity of the crisis. “You’d expect a racist pogrom to be the key issue for the institutions to deal with over the summer, and putting in emergency measures to prevent that happening again. But no, there’s no sense of urgency.”

Liz Griffith, the head of migration justice at the Northern Ireland Law Centre, said the devolved government had failed to update anti-racism legislation and downgraded a long-awaited policy document.

The strategy now focused on “race relations”, which Griffith said was “a discredited term now; it is woefully out of date and has been out of date since the 1970s”.

“It’s as if this was to do with somehow the relationships of people not getting on with each other,” Holder said. “That the people having the brick put through their window need to improve their relationship with those putting the brick through the window.”

The Stormont executive had failed to bring forward hate crime and race equality laws in line with the rest of the UK.

“The law in itself does not prevent racism but it’s the bedrock on which all your other initiatives rest,” Griffith said. “It’s been updated in England, Scotland and Wales, and ours is just antiquated. There’s constant talk of consultation after consultation to update this legislation, but it has just got stuck, it’s never moved.”

In the face of this inaction, many want Andy Burnham, the new prime minister, to step in. “Unless Westminster intervenes at this point and ensures that there are protections, and legal protections, and consequences for some of this behaviour, unless there is some accountability here, it’s going to continue,” Green said.

Many migrants and refugees think another eruption is likely but some try to remain optimistic. Suleiman Abdulahi, the founder and director of Horn of Africa People’s Aid Northern Ireland, has endured many attacks and reported 12 of them, most recently on 26 June. None have resulted in a prosecution but he did not wish to condemn his adopted home. “I’m not saying the Northern Ireland people – the majority – are racist. The majority are hospitable.”
