https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Kemi Badenoch’s weird week: defence of ex-neo-Nazi raises questions over Tory direction
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Alexandra Topping and Jessica Elgot
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Some in party are delighted by leader’s tack rightwards but opponents have savoured latest Conservative controversy

T
here was a moment in the middle of this week when a news alert raised eyebrows among the politically committed. It read: “Kemi Badenoch: Former neo-Nazi candidate would just be sorting out bins.” It was a collection of words that might prompt palpitations in the most sanguine of communications professionals, followed by panicked advice that retreat was necessary. But as a deeply weird week for the Conservative party came to a close on Friday, its leader appeared adamant she would hold the line.

With Badenoch accused of aping Reform UK on policy and purging centrists from her party in recent weeks, her decision to stand by a man who was jailed after creating sexualised images of a Jewish MP and calling her a “rodent” has prompted concerns about the leader of the opposition’s political antennae and the Tories’ wider strategy.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

On Monday it emerged that Joshua Bonehill-Paine, a former neo-Nazi activist convicted of the sexist and antisemitic harassment of the Labour peer Luciana Berger, had been selected as a Conservative candidate for a local election in Somerset.

A little over 48 hours later, Bonehill-Paine – creator of pro-right viral AI clips that often depict politicians on the left in an ugly light – withdrew his candidacy, saying Badenoch had instead asked him to become an adviser to the party’s culture and integration commission, focusing on how young men become radicalised.

As pressure mounted, Badenoch said she was “sad” that Bonehill-Paine felt he “won’t be given the space to explain his position and represent his community”, chastising those who had called her judgment into question.

“Piling on [people who have changed] and trying to get them cancelled may be sport for other parties,” she wrote on social media. “But this is a different Conservative party.”

Her stance has left some in her party delighted by her persistent pugilism but others scratching their heads and looking to the door. For opponents, it has been a moment to savour, with Reform saying her support “beggars belief”, while locally focused Liberal Democrats delighted in criticising Badenoch’s insistence that as a councillor Bonehill-Paine would only have been “looking at parking, sorting out bins”.

The embrace of Bonehill-Paine has come at a critical moment in Badenoch’s leadership. Last month she embarked on a purge of the Conservative parliamentary party, writing in the Telegraph that it was “not a retirement home for failed politicians” and warning that anyone who supported net zero targets or Britain’s membership of the European convention on human rights (ECHR) would be blocked from standing as a candidate in the next election.

The former minister Gavin Barwell lost the whip, and another former cabinet member, Grant Shapps, was blocked from standing again for the party. Sources said multiple Reform members had been blocked from joining the party. “To do that while welcoming this chap has definitely raised a few eyebrows,” one source said.

The purge had left many young Tories and centrists politically homeless, said the former Tory activist Cody Butler, who resigned last weekend as chair of the One Nation Conservative Network and left the party. He said centrists, members worried about the climate crisis and conservation, and remainers – those who Margaret Thatcher may have referred to as “Wets” – were “running out of road”.

“We keep hearing the parliamentary party has never been more united,” Butler said. “But I think the real truth is the arsonists have taken control, and they’re trying to set the great oak tree of Toryism alight.”

Badenoch also announced this week that a Conservative government would evict foreign nationals with leave to remain from social housing, prompting Reform’s Zia Yusuf to accuse her of trying to copy his party’s policy, and the homelessness charity Shelter to warn the policy would “drive up homelessness and put extreme pressure on councils”.

Despite the private worries of some in the Tory party, delight in Badenoch’s unabashed tack rightwards is not difficult to find among the rank and file. “It’s going down really well,” said one MP. “The party thinks Kemi is doing brilliantly.”

A senior Conservative adviser said the party was being clear on what it believed and why. “At the last election, voters would tell us they didn’t know what the party stood for. Kemi is changing that,” they said.

But rightwingers are not the only ones enjoying the ride. Labour sources said they had been looking on and reaching for the popcorn this week. “Just as you think Kemi might finally be sorting out their tent, she spends a week focused on totally irrelevant nonsense,” said one. “Nothing trumps a person’s instincts and hers are just wrong.”

In the yellow corner, gleeful Lib Dems point out that under Badenoch the Tories seem to be showing little interest in taking back any of the 60 seats they lost directly to their party in 2024 as part of a drubbing in which the Conservatives shed a record 251 seats.

Once the near unchallenged flagbearer of middle England, the Conservatives now have zero MPs in Oxfordshire, for the first time since 1777. A committed leftwing hiker could walk from Land’s End to London without passing through a Tory constituency. Despite Badenoch’s insistence that the May local elections showed “the Conservatives are coming back”, the party lost about 500 councillors in England and ceded control of three local authorities. Even now, the Tories are skittering along at 19% of the vote, compared with Reform on 24 and Labour on 23, according to Politico’s poll of polls.

A senior Lib Dem source said: “It was widely expected that the Conservatives were at their lowest ebb in 2024 and would quickly start making progress. In fact, it’s us that have taken loads off them rather than the other way round.

“Whether it is [on] fighting for more action on the climate or defending human rights, the Conservatives sound more like Nigel Farage than former leaders who were popular with middle England. It is genuinely giving us the biggest opportunity against them we have ever had.”

Given current polling – and the results of the 2024 election in which the Conservatives lost about a third of their votes to Reform – attempting to woo those who voted for Farage was logical, said the pollster John Curtice. “The Tories are in a pretty dire state but not quite as dire as they were a few months ago,” he said. “By my calculation, they are now losing around 17% of those votes to Farage.”

Polling indicates Badenoch’s personal approval rating is on the up: a YouGov poll last month put her net favourability at -11, the highest of any Conservative leader in more than five years.

Curtice said the Tories were facing a dilemma: whether to try to build a more centrist coalition with the voters who had stuck with the party, or try to win back Reform voters. “But in [Reform] voters’ minds they are the party who failed to deliver Brexit properly and who created the Boris wave,” he said. “And the more fundamental problem is not to do with ideology, it’s to do with competence. Partygate trashed their ethical reputation, and [Liz] Truss trashed their reputation on the economy.”

Robert Hayward, a Conservative peer and polling analyst, played down the theory that Badenoch was increasingly moving the Conservatives to the right but said she would have to adapt against a Labour party under Andy Burnham.

Asked where it currently looked as if the Conservatives would gain seats on their current trajectory, Hayward was candid. “I don’t think that is very clear as yet, and that’s a major challenge to the party,” he said.

“But it’s a problem for everyone. People’s allegiance to any political party is weaker now than at any moment during my lifetime. Who knows where we’ll be in December 2026, never mind on the eve of a general election.”

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: What can Dublin teach us? Milburn goes on a quest to solve youth jobs crisis
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
The former UK minister discovers how apprenticeships and support networks helped slash Ireland’s Neet rate

English primary schools to be told to identify children at risk of future unemployment

A
lan Milburn is guiding a metal loop along the serpentine wire of an electrical buzzer game as he explains the challenge of Britain’s youth jobs crisis. “We have got more than a million young people not in education, employment or training (Neet). Crisis is an over-used word – but this is a crisis.”

On a fact-finding trip to Dublin, the former UK cabinet minister is being shown around an Irish Rail training facility. He tells the apprentices who rigged up the game that, while things are bad in Britain, Ireland is on the right track.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“It’s about half the rate here, it’s fallen very rapidly. And we want to try to work out, what is that? Why? There’s something going on; maybe there’s something you guys have been doing that we haven’t?”

Alyx Tobin, one of the hi-vis clad trainees, chips in: “Hopefully we can get to the bottom of it together?”

Over the past decade, Ireland has achieved the fastest reduction in Neet rates anywhere in the EU, from 14.3% in 2015 to 6.1% last year. That compares with a rise from 11.1% to 12.8% in the UK. Romania is the only EU country with a higher rate.

As he prepares to publish a report into the crisis for the UK government this autumn, Milburn has brought a delegation of officials, charity leaders, industry bosses and the mayor of South Yorkshire, Oliver Coppard, with him on the trip across the Irish sea.

“We’re here really to understand what the secret sauce is,” he says.

“The life chances of young people here are being transformed. You don’t have to go far – to the outskirts of Dublin – before you find huge pockets of deprivation and poverty. So nobody here would say, ‘We’ve got it solved.’ But there is definitely something different that we can learn from.”

Back home, Andy Burnham has made tackling Britain’s youth jobs crisis a top priority, using his first weeks as prime minister to launch a series of measures to boost technical education and apprenticeships.

Labour is also preparing for a fresh attempt at welfare reform amid concerns about the £125bn annual cost to the economy and public finances from the rise in youth worklessness.

Under Keir Starmer, the government set targets to eradicate long-term youth unemployment and launched jobs programmes, grants and guarantees aimed at helping young adults to get into work.

However, business leaders argue Labour has made matters worse through tax increases, a rising minimum wage, and plans to strengthen workers’ rights. Employers have also faced other rising costs and weak consumer demand amid the cost of living crisis.

In Ireland, part of the reason for the youth jobs turnaround is down to its economic recovery from the 2008 financial crisis.

The country was among the biggest global casualties as the implosion of a property market bubble triggered a 10% crash in the economy in a single year and drove unemployment to 16% by 2012. Youth joblessness peaked at almost 30%, while many left to work abroad amid the 2010s eurozone debt crisis.

Corey Farrell’s father was among many who left for the UK when his job as a mechanic at German airline Lufthansa was put at risk. “When that shut down here, he got sniped to go over,” says the Irish Rail apprentice. “He’s worked over there ever since. I was only six at the time.”

Since then, the economy has bounced back, in part fuelled by big US tech companies taking advantage of low taxes. The country is “100% through the worst”, Farrell says. If anything, things have gone too far the other way as living costs surge. “You can see it more than anything else in how expensive everything here is.”

Milburn recognises Ireland’s progress is partly driven by economic factors. Still, Britain could still learn a few policy lessons.

At St Seton’s secondary school, to the west of central Dublin, teachers tell the former Labour cabinet minister that they get extra money from the Irish government to support children at risk of poverty, social exclusion and educational disadvantage.

Funded under the “DEIS” (delivering equal opportunity in schools) programme, there is a big focus on technical education and helping students to prepare to enter the world of work.

Sitting in the staff room, the school’s principal, Sarah Green, and its career and guidance counsellor, Cheryl Keeler, explain they are agnostic about whether a student progresses to university. Getting a job is more important.

Work experience is graded as part of the curriculum, while pupils have an opportunity to take a “transition year” (TY) before studying for either an academic or vocational leaving certificate (equivalent to A-levels or the international baccalaureate). As an optional scheme, the TY has no curriculum and typically involves work experience and careers guidance, but core subjects have to be covered in some form for two hours a week.

Calum, a student at the school, took a Chinese course for 10 weeks. After completing his applied leaving certificate, from September he will start as an apprentice for Diageo at Dublin’s celebrated St James’s Gate Guinness brewery. “It was easy thanks to the school,” he says.

In Britain, Burnham is pushing to advance the parity of esteem between academic and technical education routes. Last month he announced a new £4,500 per year per household bursary to support the take-up of apprenticeships.

At Irish Rail, the apprentices say they feel they are on the fast track while their friends at university struggle with debt. Even so, Alyx Tobin says the reputation of apprenticeships in Ireland is similar to Britain.

“If you performed above average you were guided towards college as the main option. It was like, if you did an apprenticeship you weren’t smart enough to go to college,” she says. “But I think that’s a stigma that absolutely has to be dismantled as soon as possible.

“Some of the smartest people I’ve ever met are in apprenticeships, and some of the most dithering you meet could be in college.”

At a youth centre in the north Dublin suburb of Ballymun, one of the city’s most deprived neighbourhoods, Milburn pulls on a plastic apron over his Paul Smith polo shirt to bake fairy cakes with local children.

The Reco Central Youth Facility is buzzing in the school summer holidays, as a place where young people can engage in activities. It also provides mental health counselling, careers guidance and job support.

Geraldine Comerford, the manager, says the hub works with other organisations to support the community. “You can’t work in isolation. People need so many different areas.”

Milburn says the Reco shows what Britain is missing out on. Since the 2010s Tory austerity drive, spending on youth services in England has been cut by 73%. Thousands of publicly run youth clubs have shut. Meanwhile, analysis shows children from poorer backgrounds where a youth club closed performed almost 12% worse in exams at age 16.

As part of the recommendations for his final report Milburn will call on the government to drastically boost the level of youth support, with schools expected to help identify and help pupils most at risk of becoming Neet.

“We have got to get upstream because this country, and young people, are paying the price of failure.”

With exam stress fuelling a rise in mental illness, and school attainment an indicator of Neet risk, the concern is that pushing children to sit academic qualifications, alongside cuts to youth support, the health service and jobs schemes all risk the creation of a lost generation of young people.

Dr Sarah Hughes, boss of the mental health charity Mind, also on Milburn’s fact-finding trip, says: “In the UK we use the language of kids being ‘hard to reach’ all the time. The kids are not hard to reach, it is us that are hard to reach. We have literally turned it on our head.”

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Healey urged to be bold on borrowing in first test of Burnham’s growth pledge
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Heather Stewart
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Some want the chancellor to exploit newly flexible fiscal rules – others want a more creative approach, such as borrowing from markets

With just 12 weeks to go until his first budget, new chancellor John Healey is seeking ways to ramp up public investment, without busting the Treasury’s fiscal rules – and some economists are urging him to be bold.

As he settles into No 11 Downing Street, the former defence secretary’s most immediate challenges concern day-to-day government spending.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

These include the need to pay for Andy Burnham’s VAT cut on energy bills and to fill the £5bn funding gap in the defence investment plan left by his predecessor Rachel Reeves – which helped prompt Healey’s resignation earlier this year.

Healey could opt to meet these costs through tax changes – with a bank windfall levy back on the agenda, for example – or by ordering Whitehall departments to penny-pinch elsewhere.

It will help that Reeves bequeathed him significant “headroom” against the rules, £24bn at the time of her spring forecast, which is unlikely to have been completely eroded by the impact of the Iran war.

But separately from these short-term pressures, Healey’s boss has made clear that he wants to see a step-change in long-term investment in infrastructure and housing, to meet his promise of growth in every postcode.

One way to fund some of that additional investment may be to exploit what Burnham called “any flexibility” in the existing fiscal rules. The chancellor told the Times there was “scope for more and more rapid investment”.

Reeves, now a humble backbencher, made a historic change to the way debt is defined under those rules. It means extra borrowing doesn’t count against the Treasury’s target if the government uses it to acquire a financial asset. That can mean a stake in a company, or a loan, for example.

Reeves used the new definition, known in Treasury parlance as public sector net financial liabilities (PSNFL – pronounced “persnuffle”), to promise a significant increase in public borrowing, but economists have argued for some time that the Treasury could go further.

A recent paper by the Resolution Foundation thinktank argued that the “PuFins” – public financial institutions, which include the National Wealth Fund, British Business Bank and National Housing Bank – could borrow up to an additional £9bn a year, without breaching the fiscal rules.

The Starmer government had already expanded these bodies, giving them additional capital, but the thinktank urged Burnham to go further.

Lord Jim O’Neill, the former Goldman Sachs chief economist who has been mooted as a possible Burnham adviser, has also suggested there could be scope within the rules to borrow more for infrastructure projects – and suggested creating a new independent agency to assess which should be supported.

Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) cautions that the question of whether there is flexibility within the rules may not be the best one to ask.

“People are getting a little bit hung up on the fiscal rules. I think they should stick to them, for credibility reasons. But if the government increases borrowing, it is still borrowing: it will still put up borrowing costs and increase debt, creating more problems for the future.

“The real, meatier question is: ‘What is the substantive case for that investment? Is that a good thing to be investing in?’” she adds.

Some experts argue for a more creative approach, however. Thomas Aubrey, of the Bennett school of public policy at Cambridge University, says: “If you really want to move the needle, which seems to be what Andy Burnham is implying in speeches, then the PSNFL stuff is just not going to be enough.”

after newsletter promotion

Instead, he argues that public corporations, such as the development corporation for Greater Cambridge that Reeves announced earlier this year, should be allowed to borrow directly from markets. “You could do that with energy, water, large-scale public infrastructure projects, housing,. The UK is one of the only major economies that doesn’t have a deep market for public corporation debt.”

Interest rates would be higher than for direct government borrowing, he argues, where there is a Treasury guarantee – but the trade-off would be significantly more scope for long-term investment.

And he argues the buyers of such debt, including pension funds keen to match their liabilities, would be distinct from those that now buy government bonds, or gilts – so the Treasury would not be cannibalising existing demand.

“There is no shortage of capital for projects with detailed costings, credible revenue forecasts and hypothecated income streams,” he argued in a recent policy note for the Centre for Cities thinktank.

The UK’s borrowing costs are already higher than many other large economies, and Treasury officials would likely caution Healey against anything that might unsettle the gilt markets.

Aubrey suggests other Whitehall departments have previously shown interest in allowing public corporations to borrow – but it has always been blocked by the Treasury, which would have to agree to classify their debts as separate from government borrowing.

The approach urged by Aubrey chimes with proposals from Burnham-adjacent thinktank Mainstream. The PM’s right-hand woman Louise Haigh also pointed to proposals for public corporations to be allowed to borrow directly, in a piece she wrote for leftwing publication Renewal, earlier this year.

How to boost investment is just one of a slew of economic questions facing Healey and the prime minister in the next few critical months, but it is perhaps the one most central to Burnham’s projects of devolution and reindustrialisation – and an early test of how radical the new administration will be.

https://www.theguardian.com/music/ng-int.title: Is it OK to talk about Ariana Grande’s body? There is no right answer
https://www.theguardian.com/music/ng-int.author: Emma Madden
https://www.theguardian.com/music/ng-int.text:
I wish I could say that expressing concern for the pop star’s health is helpful – but I know from experience it’s not that simple

The last time I opened X, a photo of Ariana Grande leaning over in a low-cut black dress, clavicle showing, was at the top of the feed. The post read: “hey @grok make Ariana Grande healthy and fat”.

Images of celebrities at their most skeletal regularly rise to the top of social feeds because they generate enormous, dissenting engagement. Social media platforms have made half-hearted efforts to suppress explicit pro-eating disorder content; Instagram and TikTok redirect searches for “thinspo” toward support resources. Yet over the past couple weeks, Grande has sent users into a frenzy that outstrips the platforms’ attempts.

The screenshot the user posted was taken from Grande’s music video for Petal, the title track from her latest album. Grande and her team have not said that she lives with any kind of eating disorder. Nevertheless, promotion for Petal has been thoroughly overshadowed by discussion of the singer’s ultra-thin body.

Other replies to the screenshot ranged from vicious attacks on Grande and other users’ bodies, to earnest, almost desperate pleas for empathy. Having lived with an eating disorder as a teenager, I recognize in these reactions a familiar pattern. People often respond to the visibly suffering body with a visceral pity intertwined with a kind of disgust. Whether that response actually protects anyone, or instead solidifies the very dynamics it seeks to resist, is a question worth returning to.

Those of us who have lived through eating disorders and are witnessing this news cycle feel compelled to offer our own interpretations – to explain what this moment means, and to argue for the “right” way to speak about it. But precisely because disordered eating is so idiosyncratic and so forceful, there may be no single correct language for confronting it. The only honest response may be to acknowledge its contradictions.

In the case of Grande, all of the prayers, best wishes and outcries so far haven’t provoked the public response so many have hoped for. Instead, it appears to have pushed her in the opposite direction. Over the weekend, just days after the release of Petal, a representative told People magazine that Grande would be “taking a step back from visibility” after her current tour, cancelling future promotional plans and withdrawing from an upcoming West End revival of Sunday in the Park With George. At a recent concert, Grande explained to fans that stepping back from the spotlight was something she had planned “a long time ago” and that it came from a “thoughtful and empowered place”.

If this were a case of disordered eating, a retreat from public life might seem like a positive step towards recovery. But I know from experience that someone who is suffering can mistake isolation for self-preservation. The cruelty of an eating disorder is how easily it convinces you that it is the only thing standing between you and a world trying to take control away from you.

Concerns over Grande’s body have hovered since the beginning of her teenage acting career. In 2013, the year she released her debut album, Yours Truly, she took to her old Tumblr account – which has itself been accused of “pro-ana” content, or content promoting disordered eating – to address “the rumors going around.” In a blogpost she wrote that reports of “this whole ‘eating disorder thing’” had been “a bit blown out of proportion”.

“Yes, I lost a bit of weight last year,” she continued. “It’s because I stopped eating junk food and started making healthy choices. I was happy with the way I was before and I’m still happy now! Just healthier!”

More than a decade later, she made much the same point in a TikTok after people posted side-by-side photos of her during the Wicked press tour and the years when she acted on the Nickelodeon show Victorious. “The body you’ve been comparing my current body to was the unhealthiest version of my body,” she said in April 2023. “I was on a lot of antidepressants and drinking on them.”

Her response reminded me of something the singer Fiona Apple said in 2013, after years of speculation about her weight. While performing on stage, Apple exploded at a heckler who shouted: “get healthy”. “I’m healthy and I shouldn’t even have to say any of that,” Apple told Pitchfork the next day. “What makes me unhealthy and puts me in danger is that kind of scrutiny itself.”

Avoiding scrutiny can become part of an eating disorder itself. I know this because I suffered for many years with bulimia, and I now realize my years spent hiding in the bathroom after every meal was an attempt to withdraw from any kind of outside opinion. When friends hugged me and recoiled at the touch of my bones, that only influenced me to raise the wall between myself and the rest of the world. It was an untenable and, frankly, devastating attempt to cope with the terror of puberty, trying all I could to stay both in control and independent of my body and its radical changes.

On several levels, disordered eating is built on irreconcilable tensions. It requires relentless self-control while submitting to an all-consuming fixation. In seeking to disappear, the thin body only becomes a spectacle of morbid curiosity. What usually begins as an effort to master the self soon becomes an act of self-destruction. The confused discourse surrounding Grande’s weight mirrors the paradox. Every word feels stuck in place, because we don’t yet have a cultural script capable of holding all these ambiguities.

It is obvious and true that the bodies of female celebrities are uniquely surveilled. It’s why Billie Eilish resisted that surveillance by wearing oversized clothing and criticizing the public’s sense of entitlement to judge her body – a tactic Grande employed, too, in 2018, a year after the devastating Manchester Arena bombing.

For much of the 2010s, the body positivity movement supplied a simple injunction against prying eyes: don’t comment on women’s bodies. It corrected for the smarmy and misogynistic tabloid treatment of celebrities in the aughts, discouraging public discussion of other people’s bodies as intrusive, harmful and unnecessary.

But it might have been an overcorrection. Grande’s appearance presents a case where that consensus no longer feels entirely adequate, or ethically tenable. But it’s complicated. Two feminist arguments are at odds. The first is that women should not have to submit their bodies to public interpretation or explanation. The second is that eating disorders thrive in secrecy and denial. We do not want a culture that treats visible suffering – and conversations around them – as too taboo to acknowledge.

After all, Grande has long featured in thinspo Pinterest boards. On private pro-ana message boards, users have found recognition in her public statements. “The whole ‘don’t worry about me’ and ‘the old me was sad and unhealthy’ sounds like people responding to an intervention lol,” one user wrote. On the pro-ana internet, Grande’s body is both hailed as aspirational and a huge trigger. In eating-disorder recovery Reddit communities, users describe her as the reason for their “relapse”, putting them back into the mindset of their illness. Beneath the now widely circulated photograph of Grande bending over, users in the underground X community known as EDTwt have openly compared themselves to her body and wondered how they might achieve a similar appearance.

More broadly, her body has also become a proxy on to which wider cultural anxieties are projected. In a moment of GLP-1 drugs reinstating the aspiration of thinness, body positivity in retreat, bonesmashing still on the up, and Maga tradwives once again moralizing fatness, fears about the return of aughts-era anorexia have settled on to Grande herself. Whether or not those fears belong to her alone is almost beside the point. Her body has become the site through which the culture argues with itself.

She is hardly the first celebrity on to whom those anxieties have been projected. From Karen Carpenter’s collapse from starvation at her parent’s home in 1983 to the many stars who have since publicly disclosed eating disorders – including Demi Lovato, Taylor Swift and Kesha – it is almost assumed that a significant portion of the female entertainment industry has, or has had, some form of eating disorder. The illness is simultaneously embedded within ordinary culture and yet treated as an aberration whenever it becomes visible.

The desire to resolve those contradictions might even keep us at the distance the illness relies on, allowing us to imagine that a single correct response will absolve us of having to deal with it in the first place. Instead we could try broadening our concern towards the millions living with eating disorders by petitioning to improve a medical system that has so often failed them; insurers that routinely deny care if the patient’s BMI is anything other than extremely emaciated; and clinicians who still stigmatize the illness.

Grande’s visibility isn’t moving down the feed. People are continuing to debate it, defend it, plead for us to find another way to talk about it. But ultimately, another person’s physical and mental reality is out of our control; no one person’s recovery can be crowdsourced. If only it were all as simple as Grok editing Grande into health.

In the US, help is available at nationaleatingdisorders.org or by calling ANAD’s eating disorders hotline at 800-375-7767. In the UK, Beat can be contacted on 0808-801-0677. In Australia, the Butterfly Foundation is at 1800 33 4673. Other international helplines can be found at Eating Disorder Hope

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Wasted medicine in England could fill 75 swimming pools a year, pharmacy group says
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Nadeem Badshah
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Industry body calls for more regular reviews of repeat prescriptions to tackle ‘growing problem’

The amount of wasted medicines thrown away in England in one year could fill 75 swimming pools, according to a pharmacy group.

The National Pharmacy Association (NPA) estimated that 3,400 tonnes of partly used medicines were disposed of in England in 2024-25.

The organisation, which analysed data from regional health bodies, also estimated that the problem costs the NHS at least £480m annually.

Olivier Picard, chair of the NPA, said: “Wasted medicines cost the NHS significant sums of money every year that could be invested in better services for patients.

“More than this, wasting medicines can have environmental and health consequences, and we can do much more to tackle this growing problem.

“As soon as a medicine leaves a pharmacy, even if it is not used and is unopened, it must be disposed of, so it is important patients only get medicines they are sure they will use.”

The NPA, which represents 6,000 independent community pharmacies in the UK, called for patients with several repeat prescriptions to have more reviews so that medicines that were no longer needed could be identified.

It also urged the public not to “over order” medicine.

Picard added: “We are urging patients only to request medicines if they really need them when ordering repeat prescriptions.

“As well as this, patients who are prescribed multiple medicines should have these more regularly reviewed to ensure they are being fully utilised.

“If a patient has any concerns about their medicines, they should speak to their pharmacist who can help them get the most out of their medicines.”

Dr Rasha Abdelsalam Elshenawy, a senior lecturer at the University of Hertfordshire, said surplus medicines “aren’t only a financial and environmental problem – it’s a patient safety and resistance problem”.

She added: “Leftover antibiotics kept at home are often taken later without medical advice, which fuels antimicrobial resistance, one of the biggest threats to modern medicine.

“Regular medication reviews and only ordering what is needed protects patients, the NHS and the environment.”

An NHS England spokesperson said it had taken action to ensure people could better manage their prescriptions on their mobile phones through the NHS app, including repeat prescriptions.

“We know there is more to do, which is why several local NHS services are running campaigns to reduce medicines waste, alongside wider efforts to optimise medicines use that have also seen the total number of dependency-forming medications prescribed fall over the last decade,” they added.

In June, health leaders warned that Britons were facing some of the “most severe” shortages of NHS medicines on record, including common painkillers, epilepsy drugs and HRT.

The NPA and the Royal College of GPs highlighted long-lasting supply issues affecting Estradot, a hormone replacement therapy (HRT) medicine used by menopausal women, and Creon, a drug taken by people with pancreatic cancer and cystic fibrosis to help them digest food.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Millions in England face longer waits for mental health care as NHS providers plan cuts
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Exclusive: Seven in 10 survey respondents expect services to be reduced or shut, while more than half anticipate job losses

Millions of adults and children in England face being forced to wait longer for mental health care, with more than two-thirds of NHS providers planning to cut services and half expected to axe jobs, the Guardian can reveal.

With mental health services already under extraordinary pressure amid soaring demand for support, experts warned the proposed cuts – drawn up by trusts to plug holes in their finances – would also have “significant” consequences for the wider NHS, the economy and public services.

Key services such as child and adolescent mental health care, talking therapies, addiction support, help for adults undergoing a mental health crisis and community programmes, including those for ethnic minorities and low-income groups, are among those that may be affected.

Seven in 10 (68%) NHS trusts providing mental health services are likely to reduce or shut some of their services in 2026-27, according to the results of a national survey conducted by the NHS Alliance and seen by the Guardian.

Of respondents, 59% said they expect to freeze vacancies, with more than half (57%) likely to cut the number of clinical staff they employ this year.

Earlier this week, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, announced plans to create a network of nearly 200 community mental health centres and mental health A&Es by 2029. Writing on LinkedIn, he said: “These services will make it much easier for people to get the right support, at the right time, in the right place.”

Mental health charities welcomed the ambition but said if funding for staff and services was being cut, meaningful improvements to care would be “impossible”.

One of the NHS mental health trusts affected, East London foundation trust, plans to cut a wide range of services and axe hundreds of jobs to close a £25m hole in its finances, the Guardian reported on Monday.

NHS mental health professionals at other trusts said similar plans were being drawn up where they work. They fear the cuts will strip back services so much that they will not be able to properly perform their duties or guarantee safe care in their areas.

An NHS consultant psychiatrist, speaking on condition of anonymity, said: “This is not an isolated example in east London. Many mental health trusts are in a similar, if not worse, situation and are responding in similar ways through cutting jobs and compromising service delivery.”

A mental health service manager at a third NHS mental health trust said: “Many mental health trusts are in a similar position. They have faced declining funding for the last couple of years alongside cost reduction targets.”

Alex Stewart, assistant director of the NHS Alliance’s mental health network, said: “Mental health services are coming under extraordinary pressure as a result of rapidly rising demand for care and very tough financial conditions.

“Despite this, we see many examples of innovation and great care which give real grounds for hope. But it’s increasingly evident that the trade-offs and difficult decisions over jobs and services which we warned about are making their mark.

“Mental health leaders face particular pressures when finances are tight because a higher proportion of their expenditure goes on staff.”

Sign up to First Edition

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

The NHS Alliance survey, conducted in March before the new financial year, revealed widespread concerns about the need to make record efficiency savings in 2026-27.

There were also concerns among the 37 NHS mental health providers responding to the poll that the focus on balancing the books would impede progress on providing more care outside hospital settings and increasing preventive mental health care.

One NHS mental health trust leader told the survey there was “no investment for mental health community services” and their teams were “under resourced” to manage the rise in demand.

Stewart said: “We welcome recent announcements on capital funding for community mental health centres and the confirmation of targets to improve access to mental health care. But in the face of rising demand, the share of national NHS spend on mental health is expected to reduce for the third year in a row.

“It is essential that mental health investment is not allowed to fall behind, as the consequences of underfunding mental health for the wider NHS, the economy and public services will be significant.”

Tom Pollard, the head of policy, public affairs and campaigns at Mind, said the results of the survey showed “the huge uphill battle we face” to save mental health services in England and ensure everyone could access high-quality care.

He said: “The government set out a welcome ambition to move towards a more open access model of support through neighbourhood mental health centres. But if funding for staff and services is being cut, meaningful improvements to the mental health system will be impossible.”

Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the trade union Unite, said: “We cannot balance the books on the backs of the most vulnerable in society and by underfunding mental health provision you simply kick the can down the road and it costs more in the long term.

“Our members at health trusts across the country are outraged at attempts to cut jobs and services and will be fighting back with the full support of their union.”

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “As well as investing a record £16.1bn into mental health services this year, we have recruited more than 8,500 additional mental health workers since this government came into office, and only this week, we announced the rollout of 159 new NHS mental health facilities across England, backed by £343m in funding.

“Later this year, our mental health strategy will outline how we plan to future-proof the mental health system, including responding earlier and reducing waiting times for support.”

Experts warn proposed cuts would have'significant' consequences for wider NHS, economy and public services. Department of Health and Social Care has invested £16.1bn in mental health services this year.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Let’s all get on board with travel etiquette | Letters
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Readers add to a guide for handling tricky situations on public transport

Re your article on travel etiquette (The ultimate guide to travel etiquette: how to handle 36 tricky situations, from manspreaders to smelly armpits, 4 August), it’s totally wrong to advise people not to give up seats for a woman any more. Women could be menstruating, in the first trimester of pregnancy (the most exhausting time, and not one you advertise with badges saying “Baby on board”), perimenopausal, menopausal or have endometriosis (excruciating pain). Women live with a level of pain and discomfort as routine, for much of their lives. Yes, of course men can be suffering with specific ailments at specific times, but it is not part and parcel of being a man. Gentlemen, please just do it.
Helen Walker
London

To your list of dubious travel behaviours, I’d like to add constant sniffing and its more guttural and nauseating relation, snorting. It seems that handkerchiefs, tissues and even the concept of blowing your nose have gone out of fashion. I am frequently nauseated by this on planes and trains, and if I don’t have headphones with me I have to resort to blocking my ears. I have not yet had the courage to speak to a culprit (although I have often been tempted to pass them a tissue).
Judith Milburn
Hartlepool, County Durham

I enjoyed your guide to travel etiquette. It was very sensible and reflective of our modern society. I had to smile at the guidance for offering your seat to elderly people – as a man in my mid-50s who is (happily) fit and healthy, I always have to remind myself that people offering me a seat aren’t commenting on my physical state, they are just being kind to a stranger.

Given the increasing incidence of harassment on public transport, particularly of women, it might be helpful to give some guidance as to what to do if you see someone being harassed – that’s a tricky balance of ensuring the safety of yourself and those around you, but it is (sadly) a reflection of the times.

However, you didn’t go into enough detail about one of my biggest bugbears – people who insist on keeping their backpacks on on crowded buses and tubes where standing space is at a premium. It’s frustrating, and occasionally very problematic, when people aren’t aware that the space they’re taking up by keeping the backpack on is much larger than their unencumbered body. As they move or turn they bump into whatever you’re holding, and it reduces the opportunity for others to join the service.

It’s a simple rule: take the backpack off and have it at your feet – always – to avoid encroaching on other people’s personal space and to free up space for others. Or maybe my middle-aged grumpiness is just getting the better of me on this one.Peter AntolikLondon

Recently, after a three day-visit to London, I returned home to Devon and jokingly complained that Londoners constantly made me feel old. Every journey I made on public transport, someone offered me a seat. On two occasions a woman offered me a helping hand as I descended the stairs on a bus. I am a six-foot, healthy 80-year-old and can easily manage to stand for a short journey but, as my wife pointed out, it is much nicer to smile and accept the offers. On another bus, a woman offered to move so that my wife and I could sit together. In conclusion, I felt I should point out that Londoners, in my experience, do not really need much of your advice. They already have an embarrassment of politeness riches and made me feel much happier about the human race.Paul WesleyTotnes, Devon

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Why are ultra-processed food firms panicking and suing? Because they know time is running out | Felicity Lawrence
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Felicity Lawrence
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
As the harm caused by their products becomes more evident, manufacturers are resorting to denial and lawsuits to keep regulation at bay

I
t is rare for people to drop dead holding the incriminating packaging, but there is no longer any serious doubt that consuming a diet of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) risks a catalogue of life-shortening illnesses from heart disease and stroke to diabetes and cancer. Because these diseases are degenerative over time, the food and drink industry has been able to argue for decades that its UPFs are fine in moderation. It would have us believe that there is no such thing as a “junk” individual food, only poor diets overall, and that its products therefore should not be subject to any restrictions.

Just as with climate breakdown and smoking, the science on harm caused by foods high in fat, salt and sugar is now settled, but the industry continues to deny and distract to delay action. Two weeks ago, a new report highlighted the lengths to which big food has gone to stop governments implementing policies that would tackle the global crisis of diet-related disease.

Since 2010, it and its lobby groups have brought 235 lawsuits against governments. More than a third of cases where the plaintiff was identifiable were filed by top global brands, led by Coca-Cola, PepsiCo and Mondelēz. The cases add up to 595 years of litigation, according to the investigative group Lighthouse Reports, which has been monitoring the trend around the globe alongside academics, the Guardian and other media outlets.

The litigation strategy is cynical but effective and Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director general of the World Health Organization, is damning. “Litigation has been used to oppose or weaken public health measures on obesity and unhealthy diets,” he said. “These delays cost countries billions in healthcare and legal expenses and create a regulatory chill that deters governments from adopting vital protections.”

Protections are much needed. Around the world more than 1 billion people live with obesity and a further 2 billion are overweight. In many countries, including the UK, US and Australia, UPFs have become staples, and make up half the average diet.

​Hence the industry manoevres. Faced with mounting ​worldwide concern, ​it can no longer hold back the tide of evidence any more than fossil fuel or tobacco companies can, but like those sectors, it hopes to tie governments up for a few years more while it protects its profits, even if that takes us to a tipping point at which state health services are overwhelmed.

As with fossil fuels and tobacco, the problem is existential for the food industry. Although manufacturers say they are making their food and drinks healthier, the bald truth is that the economic structure of the agrifood system means that is not possible in any real sense. Manufacturers of UPFs take cheap commodity crops, most often corn, soya and sugar cane and sugar beet, and break them down into their constituent parts. These crops are cheap because governments, especially in the US and EU, have long subsidised farmers, who are a powerful voting lobby, to produce surpluses of them. Farm subsidies and exports of food surplus have been a plank in US geopolitical strategy since the end of the second world war. Donald Trump in fact increased support to farmers in the US in his One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025.

Separated into processed parts – bulk oils, proteins, sugars, and starches – these cheap commodity crops are stripped of the fibre and many of the vitamins, minerals and other micronutrients we need for health. But they can be reconstituted as “added value” processed foods, with the help of flavouring, colouring and texturising additives to replace what has been lost, or sold as high-value animal feed for the world’s ever-growing intensive livestock industry. Unlike minimally processed foods such as perishable fruits and vegetables, they don’t go off and have the advantage of a long shelf life.

My general rule of thumb however, is that added shareholder value is in inverse proportion to human nutritional value. The arrival of anti-obesity drugs has seen the industry tacitly admit it. As people taking GLP-1 weight-loss drugs find their appetites shrinking, they are buying fewer UPFs. Retailers have developed “nutrient-dense” but calorie light meals in response, for a premium, as if meals should be anything but nutrient dense as a matter of course.

The fact is we need to stop eating UPFs in any significant amount, just as we need to leave oil in the ground and give up smoking. The more the public realises that, the greater the industry’s need to keep marketing to us and block any government attempts to help us make better choices. It is no coincidence that the majority of lawsuits brought or threatened by the top food and drink companies occur in countries that have been in the vanguard of identifying the harm from UPFs, such as Brazil, or in restricting them, such as Mexico with its sugary drink taxes.

In the UK it was Kellogg’s that sued the secretary of state for health in 2021 over plans to control promotions on foods high in fat, salt or sugar (HFSS), including many of its breakfast cereals. Its UK marketing company argued in the high court that the health secretary was acting beyond his powers and that such controls breached its rights under the Human Rights Act (by assault on its right to freedom of commercial expression and on its companies’ “goodwill” monetary value). Tellingly, its lawyers cited case law involving British American Tobacco. They also pleaded that, although more than half of its breakfast cereals fell foul of the HFSS limits thanks to their ingredients, if you took into account the milk people ate with its products, they looked much healthier. Kellogg’s lost its case, with Mr Justice Linden, the trial judge, noting that mixing a high-sugar breakfast cereal with milk does not “alter the fact that it is high in sugar”. But in losing, Kellogg’s tied up considerable government time and resource.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

It would be transformative if governments across the world switched distorting agricultural subsidies away from corn, soya and sugar, crops which are also associated with ecological destruction. They could support greater local production of healthy fruit and vegetables instead. Negotiating global agreement seems overwhelmingly daunting, with individual states having few levers to pull.

But there is also a lesson here and it is that, as with so much policy, small battles patiently won do make a difference. Curbs on promotion – clearer labelling, no two-for-one offers, no end-of-aisle positioning – may seem small fry, but the fact that the industry and its lobbying groups choose to fight costly delaying litigation shows these incremental changes do have an effect. Manufacturers are right to see government action as a threat. It needs to be.

Felicity Lawrence is a former Guardian special correspondent, and is author of Not on the Label: What Really Goes Into the Food on Your Plate
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.summary: The science on harm caused by foods high in fat, salt and sugar is now settled. Since 2010, it and its lobby groups have brought 235 lawsuits against governments. Kellogg's argued that health secretary was acting beyond his powers.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/a.title: Thirst by John Robins audiobook review – an ex-drinker’s darkly funny journey
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/a.author: Fiona Sturges
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/a.text:
The comedian and broadcaster narrates the heartfelt and at times self-lacerating account of his relationship with alcohol

A
memoir chronicling the comic and broadcaster John Robins’s life in alcohol and his subsequent path to sobriety, Thirst is structured around the drinks that changed his life. There’s the bottle of Jacob’s Creek wine left out on a kitchen worktop which he helped himself to at the age of seven, secreting it into his orange juice, and the beer given to him at scout camp which he drank alone. There’s also his stomach-churning recreation, while on a comedy tour of Australia, of the white russians drunk by the Dude in The Big Lebowski using a gallon of milk, a litre of vodka and a bottle of Kahlua.

As an adult, Robins, who is best known for his shows on Radio X and on BBC5 Live, romanticised pubs, which he saw as places of peacefulness and refuge. He even co-hosted the podcast The Moon Under Water where he invited guests to describe their ideal pub. Robins reveals that what kept him drinking for so long was the lie that he was in control. That he could, on occasion, get through a Dry January convinced him he couldn’t be an addict, although he got a wakeup call when a GP told him to “sort your fucking life out”.

Robins is our narrator and his reading, much like his prose, is heartfelt, darkly funny, sometimes self-lacerating and full of sage advice born from bruising experience. Currently sober, he must now grapple with the depression from which alcohol was shielding him. “I can thank alcohol for trying to step in,” he notes “but remind it that its services are no longer required, that I’ll take it from here.”
