https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: The mRNA technology behind Moderna’s Covid vaccine reaches the flu
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The mFlusiva vaccine for older people is first made with mRNA platform key to ending coronavirus pandemic

The Food and Drug Administration has approved a new kind of flu vaccine for older people, the first made with the same mRNA technology that was key to ending the Covid-19 pandemic, Moderna, the manufacturer, said.

The shot, named mFlusiva, is intended for adults aged 50 or older. Other brands of flu shots already have begun arriving in pharmacies ahead of fall vaccination season, and Moderna said late on Wednesday that it expected some of its new version to be available soon at select retailers.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

While there already are multiple flu vaccine options in the US, including three specifically recommended for people age 65 or older, tens of thousands of Americans die from influenza every year and older adults are among the most vulnerable.

Flu vaccines must be updated annually to best match circulating strains of the virus. Vaccines made with the Nobel prize-winning mRNA technology are faster to manufacturer than other types, and experts say this additional option might help if the shape-shifting flu virus mutates in a way that requires suddenly brewing new doses.

Moderna, which is based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, said the FDA granted full approval for mFlusiva’s use in people ages 50 to 64, based on a study of 40,000 people that found the new shot reduced flu cases by about 27% compared with another routinely used flu vaccine brand. For people 65 or older, the biotech and pharmaceutical company said the FDA granted what’s called accelerated approval for the shot – based on a smaller study showing it generated a strong immune response compared with an existing high-dose vaccine for seniors – while it conducts an additional postmarketing study.

Moderna’s data showed no major safety issues although the shot did cause some temporary reactions including injection site pain, fever, headache, tiredness and aches that occurred somewhat more than with today’s flu shots.

The FDA action comes after a highly unusual public dispute over mFlusiva earlier this year. A then top FDA official blocked the company’s application, a sign of the agency’s heightened vaccine scrutiny under the health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr. Days later, the agency changed course after Moderna publicly challenged the ruling – and in June a panel of independent advisers to the FDA unanimously recommended the vaccine’s approval.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The mFlusiva vaccine is intended for adults aged 50 or older. It is the first made with the same mRNA technology that was key to ending the Covid-19 pandemic.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: ‘It can make you psychotic or give you a cardiac arrest’: why are so many children vaping the ‘prison drug’ spice?
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Amy Fleming
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Parents and teachers worry about the number of kids who vape cannabis. But many of them are using something far more dangerous – without even realising it

I
bumped into an old acquaintance the other day. Updating me on his children’s ages, he said, with an eyeroll of resignation: “My daughter’s 15 now; just found a cannabis vape in her room.” It’s an increasingly common and concerning situation for parents – with no way of telling if a vape does in fact contain weed (which comes with its own risks, just like vaping tobacco) or something much worse.

Instead of the natural cannabinoids THC or CBD, these vapes can contain a much cheaper substitute: the “prison drug” spice. Last year scientists from the University of Bath analysed 1,923 vapes that had been confiscated from children in 114 schools in England, and found that 13% contained spice. In London and Lancashire it was 25%. And this is among vapes of all kinds, nicotine included, not just those that purported to contain cannabis. As for vapes labelled as containing THC, CBD or cannabis, when the drug-testing service Wedinos (part of Public Health Wales) examined 297 samples received in the year up to March 2025, it found that 39% contained spice.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Chris Pudney, professor of applied biochemistry at the University of Bath, said researchers also found that these vapes are “overtly and blatantly available on the major social media platforms”, which hold huge sway over young people. A recent report for ITV’s Good Morning Britain featured a boy who was incredulous that, at the age of 12, he had become addicted to spice vapes advertised on social media as THC – which he “bought for a tenner” – and ended up in a coma with a collapsed lung.

Scientists aren’t allowed to buy drugs from dealers to test them, so to get an idea of how many supposedly THC products advertised on social media contain spice, Pudney used his experience with testing vapes seized by schools to “visually triage” them (more on how to spot a spice-containing vape later) and estimated that 68% of those bought via TikTok contained spice, compared with 12% bought via Facebook.

If, as a concerned adult, you look up spice on the internet, it’s hard not to panic. You will find a heartbreaking BBC News clip about the drug turning users in north Wales into “zombies”, along with reports of it causing deaths among homeless and prison populations. “It’s not considered a drug like heroin that causes a lot of death,” says Pudney, and is not to be confused with the mass killer fentanyl and other, even stronger, emerging synthetic opioids. But, he says, “it can have acute health outcomes, depending on dosage”.

Spice has a dissociative affect, “so it makes you feel like you’re not in your body – which is why you can imagine people who are in prison or homeless like it – but it can also make you psychotic and potentially make you aggressive and give you a hypertensive crisis. At the worst end, it can give you seizures or cause a cardiac arrest.” There’s also a risk of serious accidents arising as a result of being incapacitated, which can easily happen because the effects can come on fast and strong.

Spice isn’t one drug – it’s a catch-all name for a range of chemicals that are often referred to as synthetic cannabinoids. “I think over 250 have now been recorded,” says Pudney. New variations were developed in quick succession as existing versions were made illegal, “in the same way we’re seeing with synthetic opioids at the moment, that are changing all the time,” he says. “The Psychoactive Substances Act [2016] was there to stop that sort of whack-a-mole. We now ban things based on a whole class of molecules, so all synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists fall under the Psychoactive Substances Act.”

Cannabis itself was often viewed as a fairly harmless entry-level illegal drug in the 1990s. But in this century, a type of high-potency cannabis called skunk became the norm. Cultivated for a very high concentration of THC (the chemical that makes you feel stoned and potentially paranoid), it has barely any of the more calming CBD. Smoking lots of skunk in adolescence can increase the risk of psychotic illness fivefold, according to a paper in the BMJ.

It’s wrong, says Pudney, to view spice as synthetic cannabis. Where the THC in natural cannabis partially binds to certain receptors in cells, spice binds much more strongly to them. “It’s what’s called a full agonist, so it has a much stronger effect, and the structure of the molecule is completely different.” How does it compare to high-dose THC as found in skunk? “There is no comparison,” he says. “It’s vastly more harmful than cannabis.” In 2015, the Global Drugs Survey found that the risk of needing emergency medical treatment when using spice was 30 times greater than when using skunk.

“There are relatively regular media reports of children collapsing in school after vaping spice,” says Pudney. Spice is also addictive. “When you’re addicted to a really strong drug like spice, you simply don’t have any choices left in your life,” says Pudney. “Kids start stealing from their parents. When you’re addicted to a drug like that, it puts you in the pocket of the drug dealer. So my real concern is that spice is so remarkably addictive that it places people, young people who are already vulnerable, in very risky situations.” As with most poor health outcomes, those affected by poverty, trauma and lack of family support are at far greater risk.

Spice flew through the prison system because it was easily smuggled in, soaked on to paper that could then be smoked without incriminating odours. Similarly, it can be vaped in school without detection. “When we’re speaking to schools about it, they’ve got absolutely no idea if this is just a normal vape or a spice vape,” says Annabelle Johnson, of the health and social care charity Change Grow Live. “That’s one of the reasons why we’re finding so much of it in school.”

Jack Spicer, senior lecturer in criminology at University of Bath, has been speaking to young people who use spice as part of his own research. “The spice vapes have no real smell,” he says. “This makes it easier for children to use them and become addicted.” Spicer says this cautiously, “not wanting to overstate it and whip up a moral panic around it. But, at the same time, there are legitimate reasons to be concerned.”

Spice is cheap and easy to produce, and there is serious money to be made from it. Most forms in the UK are made from one of two molecules, says Pudney, and kits containing the components for these can be bought from China. Approximately £1,000 to £1,500 will get you enough to make a kilogram of spice – “but if you can sell it all in vape liquid, it will be worth about £1m”.

It’s in the last three to five years that vape devices have become “the new method of consumption” for children, says Chris Henniker, children and young people’s cluster manager for Change Grow Live. Originally, he’d hear of THC vapes being bought for £30 to £40. “Then we started to hear more and more young people saying they were buying ‘THC vapes’ for £10, £15. And then we started to hear these anecdotal adverse reactions, people being hospitalised.”

Once it became clear that these supposed THC vapes were spice vapes, usage died down among young people, “because there was a lot of stigma attached to spice use,” says Henniker. More recently, however, he says that young people haven’t seemed as concerned about the stigma. “They were willing to throw caution to the wind and see what happens. A number of them will try to ensure that it is THC they’re using, buying from what they have classed as trusted sources, but we also know there are a significant number of young people who are just buying whatever is being sold, with the hope it’s THC, but if it’s not, it’s not: ‘And we’re still going to use it anyway.’”

Some concerned teens buy cheap urine tests online that claim to identify spice once you’ve taken it. However, Pudney, who first developed his test for prison use, says “there’s no urine test you can buy on the market that’s going to be accurate for picking up spice.” Vape testing can’t be carried out locally, says Henniker. The only way to define what’s inside vapes is to send them for laboratory testing.

Having tested so many at the University of Bath, Pudney has some guidelines for recognising spice v cannabis in a vape in the first instance. Along with the often telltale pricing mentioned above, “you can know very easily whether it’s a THC vape because it will stink of cannabis, whereas spice vapes don’t smell of anything other than vape liquid,” he says.

Much of what’s sold on social media comes in unlabelled vape liquid refill bottles, and there’s a “high chance” that what you’re buying is spice, says Pudney. His analysis found that spice doesn’t tend to get mixed with genuine THC; it’s usually one or the other.

Dealers will often post menus of cannabis vape options alongside their other products. Spicer says you often see branded vapes “mimicking the legitimate ones that are being sold in jurisdictions where they are legal, in the US and Canada. Most young people are pretty alive to the fact that they probably aren’t legit, but still, in some way, buy into the branding. There’s some sort of materialism around it.”

Clarissa (not her real name), 21, from the north-west of England, who vapes THC in the evening because she feels it helps manage her panic attacks, says she can tell the difference by the effect of the drug. “With normal THC, you get the munchies and you’re still aware of what’s going on. But with the synthetic ones, it makes you very zombie-ish. It makes it very easy to fall asleep and it can take away your appetite.” In the past, she disposed of these, but recently she has been keeping them, to use if she can’t sleep. “I don’t use them on nights when I know I’ve got work the next day. I only use it on the weekends when I’m really struggling to sleep, and I use the THC on weeknights.” She works full-time and says she’s never had problems with spice: “But I know I’m taking a risk, whereas kids don’t know that they’re buying that.”

She has friends who knowingly use spice vapes more frequently and “struggle with tiredness”. When one went cold turkey, she vomited for days “and she had headaches”, Clarissa says.

Spice is so lucrative that dealers will always find ways to reach children, but Pudney is campaigning for more action to be taken about the presence of vapes on social media. Under the Online Safety Act, tech firms are required to tackle this themselves, but drug content still slips through the net. Pudney and his colleagues presented their findings to MPs in November 2025 during Evidence Week – an event set up eight years ago in Westminster to discuss how evidence is used and scrutinised – but gaining traction for further action is frustratingly slow. He has called for Ofcom to penalise social media firms for failing to uphold their duty. “If the regulator won’t enforce the law, we end up in the situation we’re in at the moment,” he says. “They haven’t found the evidence we’ve provided sufficient to warrant them taking any action. So we’re having a continuous dialogue with them.”

Meta – the owner of platforms including Facebook and Instagram – didn’t respond to the Guardian’s invitation to comment, but according to TikTok, 99.8% of all the videos removed from the platform for violating its “policies on regulated goods and services” were taken down before anyone had reported them. An Ofcom spokesperson said: “We’ve been pressing tech firms on what they’re doing to comply with their duties, and we’ve shown we’ll take action where companies fall short. Insights from academics like Prof Pudney are crucial to our work in enforcing the act, and we remain open to receiving further evidence on this matter.”

Meanwhile, says Pudney, “very vulnerable young people are at risk.”
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.summary: Vape devices have become ‘the new method of consumption’ for children, says Chris Henniker. Ofcom has called for more action to be taken about the presence of vapes on social media.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: NHS must prepare for annual summer heat pressures, says Yvette Cooper
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Jessica Elgot, Alexandra Topping and Fiona Harvey
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Health secretary says global heating means UK hospitals and GPs will have to prepare for summer as well as winter peaks of demand

Adapting to global heating: which UK public services are struggling in hot weather?

The NHS has been warned to prepare for potential annual summer crises caused by extreme heat with the same pressures as winter, as heatwaves caused by the climate crisis become routine in the UK.

The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said NHS staff were feeling A&E pressures that would normally be expected only during flu season – and said the government would use major investment in NHS infrastructure to tackle the health service’s resilience to high summer temperatures.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Doctors and other medical professionals have warned of the impact that repeated heatwaves are having on the NHS in England, including advice from the Royal College of GPs to cancel surgeries in extreme weather. Radiotherapy machines and MRI scanners have failed in hot weather, wards have overheated and cooling units serving hospitals have broken down.

England is on track to record its highest number of heat-related deaths this summer, with an estimated 2,877 people dying in the May and June heatwaves.

Summers are likely to become increasingly hot in the future, with temperatures topping 40C likely to become more frequent instead of being outliers as the climate crisis takes further hold.

Cooper told the Guardian that rising global temperatures were causing challenges for the NHS that it had not encountered before. “This is a new thing for the NHS to have to deal with. There is a remarkable determination of the NHS to respond, but we need much greater resilience.”

She said that in her new role as health secretary she had visited her local A&E in Yorkshire where staff described the overcrowding caused by heatwaves. “It would be normal during the winter weeks and months, but not in the summer, to have the very high attendances that they have had,” she said.

She said she had discussed a public health awareness campaign with the chief medical officer, Sir Chris Whitty, warning people to look out for elderly relatives and those with young babies to ensure they were coping in the heat.

Climate change meant “some immediate acute responses”, Cooper said, adding: “I’ve been clear we now need to prepare for summer pressures in the way that the NHS for a long time has prepared for winter pressures.

“We need a much clearer assessment now of what that means, what the pressures are going to be, what management needs to be in place to cope.”

The Climate Change Committee, the government’s statutory advisers on net zero, published a landmark report in May warning that the UK’s infrastructure was not built for such a climate, and calling for all hospitals and care homes to have air conditioning within the next decade, with all schools to follow by 2050. The CCC advised the government to plan for at least 2C of global heating by 2050, and potentially further rises.

Farmers this summer have also warned about how the extreme temperatures caused by the climate crisis were affecting the UK’s food security and ability to cope with drought.

No 10 said that improving the UK’s resilience to extreme heat was high on the agenda of the government – including building more reservoirs – saying the focus on tackling climate change must be on “practical resilience alongside cutting emissions”.

Cooper said that she and Whitty agreed there needed to be more public information about who was most at risk from extreme heat, because of the “distressing” number of heat deaths.

“There is a need for all of us to look out for our elderly neighbours and family members in the heat of summer, exactly as you would if it was freezing cold weather and you would be checking on elderly family members or relatives. We need to do the same thing now, in the summer, in the heatwaves and also for the very young.”

She said that cooling hospitals and other facilities would be a key part of the major investment in NHS infrastructure. “That is a new thing we are now having to address and to plan for. That obviously takes time as well to address that. But it is one of the things that’s being looked at now as part of the capital programme,” she said.

The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, told a press conference in London on Wednesday that tackling the climate crisis should be higher on the agenda. “I think we need to sit with that reality: 3,000 people have died because of extreme heat,” he said.

“The scenes we have seen play out on our television screens are frankly apocalyptic. And yet the response from our government is to pretend none of this is happening. It’s an astonishing dereliction of duty from those whose first responsibility is to keep us safe.”

The Royal College of Physicians’ clinical vice-president, Dr Hilary Williams, has said the NHS currently had very little built-in resilience to cope with extreme heat. “The impact of heatwaves on staff cannot be overstated,” she said. “There is a sense of foreboding when we see the weather forecast, because we know what is to come, and there is very little staff can do.”

The government has also been urged by MPs to do more to allow people to cool their own homes. More than 50 MPs have written to the UK’s certification agencies to urge them to speed up a process to get air conditioning on to the boiler upgrade scheme, which offers grants for replacing gas boilers with greener alternatives like heat pumps.

Despite the government expanding the scheme to air-coolers last year, accreditation agencies have not yet given a stamp of approval.

“If people worried about a future of extreme temperatures know they can get a heat pump which will also act as air conditioning they will be more motivated to make the switch – that’s good news for energy bills and the planet,” said Alistair Strathern, the Labour MP for Hitchin, who organised the letter. “The agencies accrediting this scheme just really need to get on with it now.”

July was the driest month ever recorded in southern England, with no significant rainfall expected in the area for some time.

The summer has already seen two record-breaking heatwaves in May and June, fuelling drought and wildfires. About 23 million people across England and Wales are under a hosepipe ban.

The National Farmers’ Union warned earlier this week that Britain could face shortages of certain foods after punishing drought in parts of England. Farms across the country were affected by floods over the winter, making planting extremely difficult.

This year’s El Niño, fuelled by global heating, is also supercharging temperatures: the World Meteorological Organisation confirmed this week that the weather system developing in the Pacific was likely to be unusually strong.

Andy Burnham has been criticised for failing to mention the climate crisis, net zero or the drought and heatwaves in his first weeks in No 10 – though he has promised the government will ramp up efforts to improve the state’s resilience.

A spokesperson for the prime minister said: “We recognise that climate change is already affecting communities across the country, through extreme heat, drought and pressure on food production. That’s why we’re focused on practical resilience alongside cutting emissions.”

He said the government would put “record investment in water infrastructure, including new reservoirs, while backing farmers to improve water security and strengthen the resilience of British food production.

“Planning reforms are also making it easier to deliver on-farm infrastructure, including reservoirs and other productivity improvements.”
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.summary: Health secretary Yvette Cooper says NHS staff are feeling A&E pressures. England is on track to record its highest number of heat-related deaths this summer. July was the driest month ever recorded in southern England.

Six additional states caught up in investigation after Michigan reported first two US deaths linked to disease

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reportedly expanded the scope of the largest known cyclosporiasis outbreak to more states, including Arkansas and Missouri.

A spokesperson from Arkansas’s health department confirmed the outbreak expansion to their state in a statement to the Guardian: “Arkansas is one of the states the CDC is adding to the multi-state outbreak for cyclosporiasis.”

The Missouri health department also confirmed the state’s “involvement in this multistate outbreak”, a spokesperson told the Guardian.

The alleged expansion also includes Iowa, Nebraska, New Hampshire and North Carolina, according to the Washington Post.

On Wednesday, a New Hampshire health department spokesperson told the Guardian: “New Hampshire DHHS has identified residents exposed to recalled lettuce and has launched a cyclosporiasis webpage that includes information on infections linked to recalled food. The DHHS cyclosporiasis webpage related to the multistate outbreak is updated each Tuesday by 12.00pm.”

The Guardian has contacted the CDC and the health departments of Iowa, Nebraskaand North Carolina.

As of 28 July, the CDC had recorded 6,707 laboratory-confirmed cases of cyclosporiasis, along with approximately 11,500 suspected cases awaiting confirmation. Cases have been reported in 45 states since May, although most of the suspected cases have been concentrated in Michigan and Ohio.

The disease is a form of food poisoning originating from Cyclospora cayetanensis, a microscopic parasite that causes symptoms including diarrhea, appetite loss, bloating, extreme fatigue, low-grade fever, stomach cramps, nausea and vomiting.

Cyclosporiasis spreads through the fecal-oral route, most commonly by consuming contaminated food or water. Symptoms typically begin about a week after infection, and without treatment can last anywhere from a few days to a month or longer, according to the CDC. Those with symptoms are advised to stay well hydrated.

Although the Food and Drug Administration is still investigating six cyclosporiasis outbreaks, it has identified iceberg lettuce produced by Taylor Farms de Mexico as the source of one outbreak. In response, Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled lettuce distributed to restaurants in 27 states and grocery stores in 15 states.

On 24 July, the CDC announced that the outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce had expanded to four additional states – Illinois, Kansas, Oklahoma and Pennsylvania. As of that date, illnesses associated with the outbreak had been reported in nine states: Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia.

Michigan – the state hardest hit by the outbreak, with health officials reporting 11,234 outbreak-linked cases – on Monday reported the first two US deaths linked to the disease since the outbreak began.

The CDC has warned the public to not eat recalled Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce, and to contact healthcare providers if cyclosporiasis symptoms are experienced.

https://www.theguardian.com/fashion/ng-i.title: ‘So destructive’: women are paying for face scans that tell them what cosmetic procedures to get
https://www.theguardian.com/fashion/ng-i.author: Laura O'Connor
https://www.theguardian.com/fashion/ng-i.text:
‘Looksmaxxing’ culture has led to the rise of facial analysis services – but experts warn they aren’t backed by science and can be harmful to users

Danielle, 37, didn’t always have issues with body image: she used to be a model and recalls receiving positive attention from men. However, when two years of unemployment plunged her into a period of financial insecurity, her confidence faded. “It was easy to wonder, if I was prettier, if some of my features were different, would that help?” she said.

So, when Danielle saw videos on TikTok about a “facial analysis” service that claimed it could provide her with “science-backed” glow-up advice, she bought it without hesitation. Three-hundred and thirty dollars later, after sending in selfies to be analyzed, Danielle received her personalized 30-page report from the company Qoves.

Qoves scored everything from Danielle’s ear shape to the femininity of her features. It recommended she get a rhinoplasty, a lower blepharoplasty, a canthopexy, chin implants and a malarplasty. Additionally: microblading, lash enhancements, filler in her temples and cheeks, a mixture of filler and Botox in her chin and jaw, and Botox around her mouth.

Danielle, who now works in tech in Colorado, is delaying any cosmetic surgery until she pays off the credit card debt accrued from her two years without a paycheck; once it is, she is interested in traveling to Mexico for procedures on her nose and eyelids. She also recently consulted a Botox and filler injector.

Qoves states that attractive people “get better treatment everywhere, from the hospital to the courtroom” and claims it is easier for them to find jobs and earn money. There is some truth to this: the “halo effect” is a documented phenomenon of good-looking people being perceived as smarter and more sociable than their average-looking counterparts, and studies have linked attractiveness to better pay. For Danielle, who asked to go by first name only for privacy, this promised material advantage was a selling point: “It gave me a motivation that I didn’t have in the past, which was seeing it as potentially helping my career and financial security.”

Plastic surgery and nonsurgical cosmetic enhancements such as Botox have unambiguously increased in popularity over the past two decades, to the point that the aesthetics of bought beauty have become inescapable on social media. This has opened the door for “looksmaxxing” influencers, who take fixation with appearance to the extreme. Coalescing around the language of science and “self-improvement”, looksmaxxers claim that attractiveness can be quantified – that individual features should be analyzed and empirically scored, and physical improvements are made where necessary. The ultimate goal is to achieve “facial harmony”, or the ideal proportions of nose, eyes and other features in relationship to one another.

Now, a slew of facial analysis services are benefitting from the looksmaxxing ethos, capitalizing on people’s insecurities about appearance under the guise of helping them become their best selves. Qoves, which Danielle used, cites peer-reviewed research to lend credibility to its idea of quantifiable beauty. It provides analyses for men and women, and for $150 recommends “nonsurgical” changes, such as injectables, with an optional $180 upgrade for surgical recommendations. Cheaper tools such as Facemaxify and Epica use AI to score the components of a user’s face against an opaque metric of facial harmony. In addition to recommending expensive procedures, the services often offer paid subscriptions. Epica’s specialty is skin and makeup plans for women, and it directs users to affiliate links for cosmetics and grooming products.

“I do believe that the standard I’ve acquired for what’s beautiful is impossible to achieve without spending thousands of dollars,” Danielle said, noting that her confidence decreased when she started using TikTok. “All of the people that I look at [on social media] and think are beautiful have gotten plastic surgery.”

Océane, 25, discovered Qoves via one of its beauty videos on YouTube, where it has more than 1m subscribers. Self-image was a longstanding concern for her: “I’ve always loved beauty, makeup and physical appearance, but I’ve never really liked my own image. I was always put down by my parents,” she said. “My mom wanted to pay for a nose job for me when I turned 18.” At school, kids bullied her. “They called me a dolphin because of my nose.”

Océane, who lives in France, paid an additional $80 for express delivery and received her results from Qoves in two days. It provided her a sense of relief: the report didn’t recommend any changes to her nose and otherwise “confirmed what I already knew about my flaws”, she said.

Dr Tracy Vaillancourt is a professor of psychology at the University of Ottawa and one of the many scholars Qoves cites in promotional materials. She expressed concern about the negative psychological impact of facial analysis services on self-esteem. “This is what women are most insecure about: their appearance,” she said. “There are going to be some who are told they look better than they thought and that’s great. Is that really going to be sustained over time?” In other words, can a service that emphasizes appearance as a metric of self-worth ever provide someone with lasting peace of mind, or does it perpetuate a cycle of self-criticism?

Moreover, though Qoves and Epica limit their services to adults aged 18 and up, the age restrictions are easy for minors to bypass. Qoves users are expected to self-report issues with self-image, with few guardrails in place to deter anyone with body dysmorphia disorder before they are presented with a menu of their flaws. “You can circumvent that so easily, it’s just going to give them the appearance of due diligence and making sure they’re not exploiting people who are vulnerable – but ultimately, they will be exploiting people who are vulnerable,” Vaillaincourt said. “These sorts of things are so destructive to people who have body dysmorphia, dysphoria, a history of eating disorders and people with low self-esteem.”

Qoves referenced Vaillancourt’s work in a video called The Cost of Being Too Pretty to show that beautiful women face jealousy from others. But Vaillancourt isn’t a scholar of beauty: she researches bullying, mental health and violence prevention. Though Qoves correctly interpreted her research on physical appearance and hostility, she is uneasy about research like hers being used for paid services like Qoves, that she believes have the capacity to harm women’s mental health.

Beyond Vaillancourt’s research, the applications of “science” used to back up these facial analysis services are shaky at best.

Qoves breaks down customers’ features based on “masculine and feminine facial qualities”, it explains in a video referencing a 2018 bulletin in the journal Frontiers of Psychology. Dr Justin Mogilski, psychology professor at the University of South Carolina Salkehatchie, co-authored the bulletin. However, his research was a limited view of how a group of primarily college-aged Americans perceived certain features as masculine or feminine.

“Do findings like mine generalize to every single population that makes up the world or a country? Or within every context where the attractiveness of a given feature can vary based on local ecology or culture? They do not,” Mogilski said. “So, would I make suggestions [for facial enhancements] based on our or anyone else’s data? I would not.”

Some services do not make any pretense of considering location or cultural standards in how they quantify beauty. On its website, Epica reports a commitment to diversity and inclusion, though it is unclear how its methodology reflects this – particularly as AI tools are increasingly criticized for perpetuating racial bias. Qoves insists its analyses are appropriate for all ethnicities, and says it will “consider unique facial traits and characteristics common to your demographic” when creating a report. In reality, as some people have pointed out online, its promotional materials often replicate Eurocentric conceptions of beauty: slim noses and large, double-lidded eyes for women, for example. As one person commented on a Qoves video breaking down Bangladeshi women’s faces: “What’s shown here seems to reflect a beauty ideal rather than the real diversity of Bangladeshi women.”

The lack of transparency around the methods and metrics the services use to measure attractiveness is its own issue. “These services owe it to their clients and themselves – if they want to be seen as credible – to be able to demonstrate scientifically” what their methods are, said Dr Mitch Brown, an assistant professor of psychological science at the University of Arkansas who has studied the science of attraction for over a decade. According to experts such as Brown, the available literature on attractiveness is too heterogenous, making any universal, population-wide generalizations questionable. And, even if we know certain features are deemed as attractive by a specific community, are these findings lasting enough to justify changing one’s appearance? Are they sound enough to support a paid service’s recommendation?

“I don’t think the science is anywhere clear enough to do that. I would caution anyone against that,” Brown said.

In an email to the Guardian, Epic said: “We are unable to disclose proprietary information regarding our algorithmic methodologies, technical frameworks, or internal product development details.” It continued: “We continually review and refine our platform to ensure our services provide a supportive, fair and positive experience for all users.”

Qoves did not respond to a request for comment.

Ipurchased my own report with Qoves and uploaded my selfies to Epica to see what these tools really offered.

For Qoves, I was asked to check boxes confirming that I did not have “concerns related to body dysmorphic disorder” and would be comfortable receiving weight loss recommendations, and then asked to upload pictures of my face and side profile.

A couple of days later, Qoves presented me with an 18-tab analysis of each of my features, along with a 16-page “aesthetic protocol”, complete with a disturbing mockup of what my face would look like should I implement its recommendations: a healthy dose of lip filler, makeup and the overly tweezed eyebrows I sported in 10th grade.

For Epica, I was asked: how often do I use makeup? Do I want more control over my appearance? Instantly, I received a “skin health” score of 61%, with uneven texture highlighted as the main concern and a flood of serums advertised across my screen to fix it. I then moved to my couch, retook a selfie in the new lighting, and saw my skin health score jump to 81%.

Before receiving these reports, I had never considered whether my mouth was upturned or wide, or whether or not Botox at my ripe age of 26 would be beneficial. I had not considered “dark feminine” makeup styles as being my look. But now I found myself second-guessing what I saw in the mirror. Just how downturned did my mouth really look to those around me? How would Botox or a haul of new makeup change features I hadn’t previously been concerned about?

The language of looksmaxxing was in my head, and I didn’t like it.

“Ultimately, there are going to be implications for mental health,” Vaillancourt said, “and it’s going to be about social comparison: never feeling good enough, never achieving enough.”

In the UK, the charity Mind is available on 0300 123 3393 and Childline on 0800 1111. In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Women must not be put under pressure to have ‘ideal birth’, says Yvette Cooper
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Jessica Elgot
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Exclusive: New health secretary promises root-and-branch reform after damning maternity scandals

Women should not feel pressurised into experiencing an “ideal birth”, the new health secretary, Yvette Cooper, has said, promising a root-and-branch reform of standards after several damning maternity scandals.

Cooper, who returns to the department 27 years after she was the minister for public health under Tony Blair, said maternity and child health would be a major focus in the role, where she will also be expected to implement significant reforms to social care.

In an interview with the Guardian, she said the culture change should address any pressure on women to have a particular kind of birth experience, after families have repeatedly raised the alarm about an unwillingness by some maternity units to escalate interventions because of a desire for more natural births.

“I would worry about any mum feeling pressurised that there is somehow a kind of an ideal birth experience to live up to when it’s always different in every case, and you have to follow the evidence, you have to have informed choice,” she said.

In one of her first acts as health secretary, Cooper said she intended to re-introduce binding national maternity standards, which were dismantled under the early Conservative NHS reforms and replaced with fragmented trust-by-trust practices.

The standards, to be drafted by a new maternity taskforce, would have five key aims. They include ending the postcode lottery for levels of care, and tackling racial inequalities that have meant worse outcomes for deprived areas, in particular for black and Asian women. They will also make patient experience part of the measurement of standards and have targets that will give early warning of underperformance before a major scandal develops.

Cooper, who was the first minister to take maternity leave, as a junior health minister in the early 2000s, said she had found the reports of maternity scandals “traumatic” to read and that it was clear systemic change was needed.

“We’ve always said the NHS is about the cradle to the grave. I want to make it a personal crusade to put the cradle back at the heart of the NHS, and to have much more focus around maternity and child health, the very beginning of a family’s life, making that much more central to the priorities of the NHS, giving it the priority that it really deserves.”

Cooper said that there had been discussions for the past two decades about how maternity services could better listen to mothers’ needs. But she said on returning to the department, it felt clear that emphasis had been lost.

“It feels incomprehensible that we could be in this situation in the 2020s. I went back to look at some of the things that we’d done 25 years ago. And what did strike me was how much we were talking then about women and families being at the centre of care and about listening to women’s views.

“It is really shocking and distressing feeling that has somehow been lost in some of the maternity units where actually it should be the central issue. I had a direct interest. I was pregnant at the time. But I am really struck by it now, just feeling like there is this big gap in the priorities that the NHS has been focused on,” she said.

Cooper added she was determined to provide a robust response to the two major independent inquiries into maternity failings – Donna Ockenden’s reports into major trust-level failures in Shrewsbury and Telford and at Nottingham, alongside Valerie Amos’s national investigation into England’s maternity system.

Both highlighted systemic clinical errors, understaffing and toxic institutional cultures, revealing that hundreds of infant and maternal deaths were directly attributable to a refusal to listen to mothers and a defensive impulse toward institutional cover-ups.

Amos’s review, in particular, has faced significant backlash including the resignation of one expert adviser over the lack of explicit warnings about “normal birth ideology” – and over Amos’s central recommendation for a new statutory maternity commissioner, which families said would lack meaningful independence.

Cooper said she was committed to introducing a commissioner. “In the end, the most important people in the maternity services are the mothers, babies, the families. But the point of having a maternity commissioner is to make sure that those issues are championed as part of an NHS,” she said.

She said she was clear about the need to tackle an oppositional culture in some trusts between doctors and midwives – and how they approached levels of intervention in birth.

“The thing that struck me most was the sense of women feeling they weren’t being listened to … And I think that probably does go back to issues around culture,” she said.

Cooper, until recently foreign secretary, said she was prepared for a tough fight in the health role as she sought to implement Andy Burnham’s social care reforms – saying she was committed to putting in place a national care service, announced by the prime minister last week.

A longstanding ally of the former prime minister, Keir Starmer, and a former leadership rival of Burnham’s in 2015, Cooper said she believed the change of prime minister had been necessary.

“Of course it’s not easy. I really did not think it was possible to win the election when I came back into the shadow cabinet in 2022. It’s only because of what Keir did that we managed to win.

“But we had very difficult local election results … we have to respond to that. But I think we’ve got a sense of energy now.

“All of the things that Andy wants to focus on and drive are also just very much the things that that people are concerned about across the country.”

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: Cockroach protests: parents of Indian students who took their own lives reveal pressure of leaked exam papers and resits
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Cheena Kapoor
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
The number of student suicides in the country has risen steeply in the past 10 years and many families blame education system mismanagement as a contributing factor

W
hen the Indian government announced the resignation of its education minister in late July after weeks of protest, there were widespread celebrations. Students from across the country had joined the mass demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janta party amid growing resentment over repeated examination cancellations and question paper leaks.

The pressure of exams in the country has only increased in recent years. The number of student suicides rose from 8,068 in 2014, to 14,488 in 2024 – an increase of roughly 80% – according to the Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India report released by the country’s National Crime Records Bureau. After family problems, failure in examinations has been listed as the leading cause of suicides among students.

For families who say they lost their children to education system mismanagement and examination scandals, watching the protest scenes unfold on television came with mixed feelings. Some were happy that future students may be spared the same fate; others questioned why it had taken so long.

The Guardian spoke to four families about what happened to their children and how they feel today.

Anshika Pandey, the eldest of twin sisters and four siblings, was, her father says, the calmest, quietest and most responsible member of the family. Revision books still lie neatly stacked, bags and accreditation cards hang from the nails where they were last placed. Her ambition was to be a doctor in the community where she lived, to be able to help the “poor people in need of medical care” some day.

Pandey studied for more than 12 hours every day, worked part-time at a store for nearly six hours and slept no more than five hours each night.

This year’s national eligibility cum entrance test (Neet) to gain entrance to medical training was her third attempt at becoming a doctor. After sitting the exam on 3 May, she was hopeful. But on 12 May she learned that the exam had been leaked for the second year in a row and there would be a resit.

“Anshika was deeply hurt. She had been hoping to enter college this year and was happy with the exam she had taken. Still, after cancellation, when I tried to console her, all she lamented was how could she hope to give another good exam,” says her father, Indradhar Pandey, a cab driver in Delhi.

Anshika remained calm and performed her household duties and engaged with everyone normally. But two days later, on 14 May, when everyone had left for work and her twin sister and younger brother were napping, she hanged herself.

Anshika’s dream had been to move her family, especially her siblings, from the slum where they lived. Her younger sister, Pragati, hopes to fulfil that dream and reminisces about how the two sisters had talked about it several times.

Anshika’s sketches and positive messages and mantra chants on the walls of their home, which she wrote to motivate herself, are now the memories her family is refusing to let go of.

Before leaving the house on the morning of 25 October 2024, Sufi Shaheen straightened her hair and put on her favourite jeans. As she left, she asked her mother for 10 rupees (8p), unlike other days when she would ask for 100. Then she headed for her joint entrance examination (Jee) lesson.

Her mother, Sultana Khatoon, asked her why she was leaving the house on an empty stomach. Shaheen replied she would be back soon. Twenty minutes later, she jumped from the seventh floor of a tutoring centre, about a mile away from her home.

It has been almost two years since she died, but Khatoon has not recovered from that day. She is being treated for severe depression and bouts of headaches.

“She was my only daughter of the four children and more like a friend. Every time I stepped out of the house, she would help me get ready. Even though she was deeply passionate about studying and becoming an engineer, she also loved dressing up and made everyone in the house do it too,” says Khatoon, as she looks through her daughter’s school photos.

Living with her parents and three brothers on her father’s modest income as a technical engineer, Shaheen had dreamed of becoming a software engineer and “excelling even more than the boys in her community”, says her mother.

A quick learner and highly motivated, Shaheen taught herself to draw and paint, and even learned to speak Japanese and Korean. But she had been stressed for several months and feared not being able to clear her second attempt at the national engineering entrance exam in January 2025.

When India’s National Testing Agency made changes to the Jee exam syllabus, Shaheen couldn’t sleep for days. She remained stressed, cried when talking to her brother and her best friend on the phone, and wrote a note to her parents in which she apologised and asked her younger brother, Masoom, to make their dreams come true.

“Almost two years later, Masoom was ranked 188th in the whole of India in his CUET [common university entrance test]. But we do not have Shaheen to celebrate this with,” says Khatoon.

Niha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern India

after newsletter promotion

“Even God will not be able to stop me from becoming a doctor this year,” were 22-year-old Pradeep Mahich’s words to his father right after his Neet exam on 3 May. This was his fourth attempt and, most importantly, he felt confident. But the announcement of the exam paper leak and resit broke his heart.

No one in the family had ever “dreamt so big”, says Pradeep’s father, Rajesh Kumar, a farmer in Rajasthan’s Sikar district. Kumar sold a large part of his farmland and took a loan of 11 lakhs (£8,600) under the farmer’s crop loan schemes.

“Sikar, the main coaching hub for Neet, is only an hour and a half from our village. My eldest daughter, Babita, who was preparing to join the police, and my son were both studying in Sikar, renting an apartment. This was his fourth year of tutoring, and the money from selling the land and the loan was slowly being consumed. I would send monthly expenses of £250 and Pradeep’s annual tutoring fees of £4,000, asking them not to worry about money and focus on his studies,” says Kumar.

“Pradeep had told me, ‘Papa, we will do a big celebration before I go to college. And one day I’ll return to serve the people of the village,’” says Kumar.

On 15 May, as he did every day, Kumar sent milk and curd to his two children on a bus that goes to Sikar; Pradeep came to pick it up at 9.30am then went home and told his sister he would help prepare lunch. But when his sister was showering, he hanged himself. She has taken a break from her studies and returned home.

Seeing students protesting on his television screen, Kumar says he is relieved that the eduction minister has gone but says there should be a proper investigation so that “no family suffers the same fate that we did”.

S Anitha belonged to an underprivileged lower caste, or Dalit, community from Tamil Nadu’s Ariyalur district. Born to a daily wage labourer, her mother died when she was seven, leaving her grandparents to raise her.

As a teenager, she decided she wanted to become a doctor. “At such a tender age, she was so focused that we used to feel proud of her,” says her brother, Manirathinam. “She knew what she wanted and never distracted herself with anything else. She never asked for any clothes, jewellery or food – her focus was clear and she knew the circumstances.”

She scored a perfect 100 in physics and chemistry at school and was offered a place to study aeronautical engineering at the state’s technological institute. But when she could not even meet the cut-off marks in the Neet exam, she realised that she had been studying a different syllabus.

Tamil Nadu had already criticised the national government for imposing an all-India examination – “disrupting the federal structure” – because it had a different education system. As a result, the state was exempted from Neet in 2016, but not in 2017, the year Anitha sat the exam.

When the supreme court ruled on 22 August 2017 that admissions to medical school would be based only on the Neet exam, she lost hope. On 1 September, Anitha hanged herself in her grandparents’ home. Her suicide became the subject of a public debate and led to widespread protests across the state and even in Delhi.

Her brother took part in last month’s protests in the capital and, while happy about the Indian education minister’s resignation in July, argues that all exams should become state-run, rather than by central government, as not everyone can afford the hefty tutoring fees needed to sit the Neet exam.

He now runs a free library and education centre in Anitha’s name.

In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org, or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/ng-int.title: ‘I hate what AI is doing to the minds and happiness of the young’: Katherine Rundell on the view from the classroom
https://www.theguardian.com/books/ng-int.author: Katherine Rundell
https://www.theguardian.com/books/ng-int.text:
Education is at a crossroads, argues the author and academic. Should we embrace new technology in the name of efficiency, or is it time to fight back?

If you set out to design from scratch a tool to facilitate authoritarian rule, it would look exactly like AI. You would cherish it for its ability to destabilise our shared reality and its creation of disinformation on a scale unprecedented in human history. With it you need no armies of typists and artists to spread your propaganda. It can enable mass surveillance and thereby put shackles on those who seek to resist you. Its lethal autonomous weapons systems can perfect and normalise remote killing. It will turbocharge inequality; it is already facilitating a breathtaking shift of power and wealth from the hands of the many to the hands of a tiny number of men who – to put it in terms for which I can’t be sued – seem to hold dangerously damaged views about the value and dignity of human life.

AI could be a magnificent thing. It could revolutionise medicine, speed the cure of cancer, assist disabled people, transform the way we are able to understand data, democratise access to the law, bolster disaster early warning systems and uncover hitherto unimagined truths about the Earth’s ecosystems. But if it ends up in the hands of crooks and despots that will be completely irrelevant.

Most of all, if you were a would-be autocrat, you would love the way that large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Claude and Google’s Gemini have thrown a grenade into thousands of years of teaching and learning: the way they threaten to upend our ability to think with the robust clarity that is needed in emergencies of justice. I write fiction for children and I hold a fellowship at Oxford University, so I spend a lot of time working with, and for, young people. I’ve seen first-hand the way that generative AI has already infiltrated young people’s lives. I’ve seen, at the same time, how it has thrown stark and urgent light on how fundamental books and reading are to our shared understanding of who we are, and to our democracy.

There are many things I hate unequivocally about AI. I hate that it can make counterfeit people; computer-generated humans that risk destabilising our entire civilisation. I hate that much of AI’s LLMs were built on an illegal pillage of human labour. I hate the environmental catastrophe that AI brings with it: the yearly electrical demand of AI-optimised data centres is predicted, by the end of this decade, to exceed that of the whole of Japan. I hate that it may be the factor that tips the Earth’s ecosystems into irreparable chaos.

And I hate what it is doing to the minds, and the happiness, of the young. Going into schools, I meet thousands of children a year and every day I become more certain that, if justice for all is to be our organising principle, AI is not for children and not for young people. It risks becoming an iron curtain that comes down between a young person and their potential for thinking, for experiment and conquering frustration, for stamina and for invention – and thereby, between the young people and their freedom. It risks halting learning before it can take flight.

Studies show, over and over, that when we engage in AI-assisted learning we give up sooner. One found that after just “10 minutes of AI-assisted problem-solving, people who lost access to the AI performed worse and gave up more frequently than those who never used it”. An MIT study showed that test groups who used ChatGPT had the lowest brain activity and “consistently underperformed at neural, linguistic, and behavioural levels”. We undergo not just cognitive offloading, but cognitive surrender: we forget what was possible.

Children, we have known for a long time, take deeper meaning from text on paper than on screen, in part because we’re tactile creatures and the brain is also of the body; but we are now living through a surge of ed tech driving learning increasingly online, such that my teenage goddaughter tells me that almost every single member of her class is using ChatGPT to do their homework. More, the work they produce in AI’s greasy little fluent voice is often mistaken by young people themselves for their own mastery. If the work a child produces is no longer an indicator of their understanding, we have put them in a situation that makes them vulnerable to their desire for speed and to their anxiety about looking stupid; we risk becoming the unwitting thieves of our children’s intellectual clarity.

Those who work in ed tech promise that it will liberate teachers and create one-to-one learning experiences for children from disadvantaged backgrounds. Certainly, AI teaching will be cheaper than teaching assistants. But we know that the second it becomes possible for an institution to achieve an end cheaply – even if it’s far worse – there is immense pressure from above to do so. I think it’s more likely that the rich schools will follow the lead of Sweden, which has taken a strong swerve towards non‑tech‑based learning, and Norway, which just all but banned AI in elementary classrooms – while poorer schools are left to make ever-greater use of LLM technology.

AI, we’re told, will make learning more efficient. But is that what we dream of for our kids – an efficient childhood? To write an efficient story, sing an efficient song? An adequate teacher is not only teaching about Henry VIII; they’re teaching your child how to read a human character. A good teacher is showing them how to shape an argument, how to command an audience, how to tell jokes, how to pass on knowledge. A great teacher is showing your child what it is to love. They are teaching your child how to be human. A computer will only teach your child how to be a computer.

At its most bleak, constant interaction with humanised tech risks killing children. The idea of a vulnerable adolescent holding what feels like a conversation with a computer’s sycophantic, confident, almost-human voice fills me with dread. Sewell Setzer III was 14 when he died by suicide, encouraged by the chatbot to which he was obsessively typing, which told him: “come home to me”.

The most obvious objection to my loathing of AI in the classroom and in childhood is this: AI is coming, and they need to learn how to use it or be left behind. But the tech of today looks nothing like it will in five or even two years’ time: it’s the equivalent of selling your child’s intellectual liberty in exchange for a penny-farthing bicycle. I asked a contact who is the president of a billion-dollar tech enterprise, what would you teach your sons? He said he wouldn’t teach his children to use AI, because it will prepare them for nothing. He would teach them the humanities. Teach them who we are, who we have been, what we can make. The FT’s Gillian Tett reported that a senior financier’s New York firm now seeks out humanities students, because “AI-native” Stem graduates are entering the job market with “alarmingly shallow ideas”.

At the university level, teaching staff across the country were already feeling the extraordinary impact of the ubiquity of a decade of smartphones on the brilliant young developing mind. Students were already arriving having read dramatically fewer books, less able to parse complex text; and now the advent of LLMs has changed everything. It has always been the case, of course, that students don’t do all the work they’re assigned. I absolutely didn’t. But this is different. It was always very possible to write an essay about Paradise Lost without having read Paradise Lost. This is the first time it is possible to create an essay about Paradise Lost without having read the essay you just “wrote”. This is the first time in history that sentences do not need to have humans behind them.

Professor Paul Musgrave of Georgetown University writes in his Substack Systematic Hatreds: “One could, in general, rely on many to most students to attempt to read many to most pages of many to most assignments – and to understand a like proportion of what they have read. In smaller courses, the difference in the quality of course discussion where 70% of the students have done 50% of the readings and one in which 20% have done 10% of the readings is obvious in the same way that a cold Coke tastes different than lukewarm spit. The former is no chablis, but it is more palatable.”

Many students want to resist, but the temptation is great, and some start to feel they’re being penalised for their honesty. I tell the students I meet: imagine you’re an Olympic athlete. You set out to sprint the 3km across London, from Clapham to Balham. You know if you take the bus, it will be faster. But you also know that the point was never being in Clapham or Balham; they’re very similar: they both have a nice Pizza Express. It was the strength you built, the speed and knowledge of your body that you gained. A student’s essay on Macbeth has no value as a product. It’s what you learned in the reading and writing that created it – the swiftness and resilience and suppleness of thinking you built, along with the knowledge gained of a literary marvel, of something quicksilver and unsummarisable – that was the point. So you can’t collaborate with AI in the same way you can’t collaborate with a bus. And you cannot learn to think without a climbing frame of facts and ideas and texts to move around in.

But we can no longer guarantee that the work students give us is the product of their own minds. Friends at universities around the UK optimistically tell me that they can tell when their students are handing in AI-generated work. But I think we can’t, not from written work alone; for myself, I’m only sure that I can tell when a young person is using AI badly. A friend who teaches maths at a London university told me his students are handing in essays without deleting AI’s jaunty “Happy to help!” at the start. You don’t have to be Sherlock Holmes. But I think an AI essay edited over the course of a day could pass as original, and, in a world in which young people are under extraordinary stress, we should not be shocked if many gave in to that temptation. My colleagues in academia – particularly those in law, where a lack of genuine understanding is catastrophic for justice, and philosophy and English, where the irreducible text itself is the thing – are full of fury at the inertia of our political class. MPs have been largely silent on the threat to our capacity to think independently, boldly and confidently – which is, ultimately, a threat to democracy.

What is the answer? I don’t think the commonly suggested solutions of spoken vivas and weekly exams can be the sole answer in the humanities, because the essay isn’t an arbitrary method of testing or certification: it is a hundreds-of-years-old method of thinking. To write is not just to transcribe the mind’s ideas; it’s a form of transformation, turning a nascent, half-built thought into something sturdier, tougher, sharper. EM Forster wrote: “How do I know what I think until I see what I say?”

I do not know what the answer is, but I do know that it’s not to give up. The young mind is a spectacular thing. To waste its beauty and strength would be a dereliction of the trust the young are asked to put in the old. To wrap AI into the art of learning when we have overwhelming proof of the harm it does to developing minds is feeding snake oil to the people we should cherish most. We already have counterfeit AI people infiltrating our media: we must not risk sending out young people into a hard world armed only with counterfeit knowledge. We should treat it with the same urgency with which we would treat a wildfire.

There are many young people who are furious at the influx of AI slop and tech chaos into their lives, who have asked me over the last year, how do we resist? I tell them that I think, for the young, knowledge and imagination are together the first site of resistance. And that by reading books (and talking about what they have loved reading so that it becomes a community, rather than purely private, act) they can begin their fight.

I talk a great deal about reading for pleasure; I’ve written elsewhere about the necessity of pleasure in the classroom, and why it is not an optional extra but the hallmark of true education. We must find ways to show children that reading gives you access to an inexhaustible source of delight. But I worry, too, that we are limiting the meaning of the word pleasure. Learning is a strange and discomfiting experience; it’s a struggle and a frustration, and epiphanies are rare. It is not always pleasure in its easiest sense.

So I think we also need to talk to young people about reading to outrun and outfight injustice. Reading to get faster, swifter and tougher; to develop powers of scrutiny and criticism and huge creative imagination. Reading human work to insist that we are human. Reading for liberation and emancipation; reading for intellectual freedom, and to have the strength to fight in the arenas of the mind, because when we let a computer think for us, we put a gun to the head of civilisation.

There are dark days ahead. If we are to fight against those with untold financial wealth, we will need untold intellectual wealth. We will need tough-minded people; people with stamina, a huge range of knowledge, and an ability to see wide and far enough to understand in real time what is being done to us. Reading for pleasure and delight are vital – but alongside that and even more urgently: reading for power.

Katherine Rundell’s latest children’s book, Impossible Creatures: The Neverfear, will be published by Bloomsbury on 27 August

Group calls for ‘thorough and transparent investigation’ of hiring of professor who resigned after his claims came under scrutiny

The University of Cambridge has announced a review into the way it vets and hires senior academic staff in an effort to fend off external and internal criticism of its appointment of Jason Arday as a professor.

But a group of Cambridge academics quickly rejected the university’s response, saying: “We strongly believe that a thorough and transparent investigation into the wider circumstances of this damaging episode is essential.”

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Arday resigned earlier this week after mounting scepticism over his personal and professional claims, three-and-a-half years after he was acclaimed as Cambridge’s youngest black professor with a life story of educational disadvantage, including being unable to speak until the age of 11.

Cambridge sources said that university and college leaders had hoped Arday’s resignation would end the controversy. But internal anger has continued to grow over his appointment process and the threats to the university’s black staff from toxic media commentary.

In a statement issued on Friday, Cambridge said: “Jason Arday has resigned from his post at the university with immediate effect. Regardless of this, and for clarification, the university will continue to investigate the circumstances around Jason Arday’s appointment and tenure.

“The findings will feed into a review of the process for the appointment of senior academic roles. In addition, and as previously stated, the university’s research policy committee will review the misconduct in research policy.”

The Guardian revealed on Thursday that Cambridge academics were demanding the university carry out a thorough investigation.

The letter sent on Friday to Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, highlights the “toxic and frequently racist commentary” that has accompanied much of the online and media coverage, adding: “These manifestly false claims have the potential to set back the modest progress Cambridge has made in addressing historical underrepresentation, and to deter any Black academic from applying for or accepting a position at the university in the future.”

Prentice became vice-chancellor of Cambridge in July 2023, after Arday’s appointment earlier that year.

The letter states: “We therefore ask that you appoint an independent body comprising senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge to address these issues, with a clear timeline for completing its work and a commitment to share its findings with the university and the public.”

The nearly 100 signatories are senior professors and Cambridge academics, including Suchitra Sebastian, a professor of physics, and Mónica Figueroa, a professor of sociology, as well as Timothy Gowers, a past winner of the Fields medal for mathematics. Other prominent names include Nicholas Guyatt, a professor of North American history, Mary Laven, a professor of early modern history, Anuj Dawar, a professor of logic, and Clair Wills, the King Edward VII professor of English literature.

The signatories want an independent investigation into the circumstances of Arday’s appointment, and any risk assessment made by the university’s management “when crafting a media narrative focusing on his youth, his race, and his transformative potential”.

It also wants details of the university’s handling of allegations of academic misconduct against Arday, including whether the university was involved in efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations.

The university has denied supporting Arday’s efforts to stop publication of critical coverage in the Times Higher magazine last year, or funding his use of lawyers.

The signatories also call for an evaluation of the “enormous damage this episode has done to people of colour within and beyond the Cambridge academic community, and what can be done immediately to reassure them – and the wider public – that anti-racism and academic integrity at Cambridge are both essential and mutually reinforcing.”

However, Cambridge’s Jesus College – where Arday was a fellow – has said it will drop its previously announced plans to carry out a parallel “process” to the university’s investigation first revealed on Wednesday evening.

A message to staff from Sonita Alleyne, the college’s master, said: “Because Professor Arday’s college fellowship was contingent on his university appointment, his resignation brought his fellowship to an end. The college’s acceptance of his resignation concludes the process announced in last night’s statement.

“This is a very difficult time for Professor Arday and his family. As he requested in his resignation letter, we hope that they are now afforded peace and privacy.”

One Cambridge academic said the message showed that the university wanted to “draw a line” under the affair in the hope that it would subside.

Arday’s resignation on Wednesday followed intense media scrutiny, beginning with accusations of plagiarism and followed by questions over a string of his claims ranging from endurance running and charity fundraising to confrontations with masked assailants.

Cambridge initially defended Arday as “the victim of a vile campaign” before announcing that it would conduct an internal investigation of “new information” regarding Arday, who then resigned shortly after.

On Friday night, the University of Glasgow said it would review its past appointment of Arday as a professor.

A university spokesperson said: “Jason Arday was employed as professor of sociology of education at the University of Glasgow, from January 2022 to March 2023.

“He left the university to take up his role as professorial chair at the University of Cambridge.

“The principal has commissioned a review of the appointment with the aim of understanding all the facts and learning lessons for the future.”
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.summary: Group calls for 'thorough and transparent investigation' of hiring of professor who resigned after his claims came under scrutiny. University of Glasgow's new professor will take up professorial chair role from January 2022 to March 2023.
