https://www.zdnet.com/article/what-to-ex.text:
Wi-Fi 7 adoption in the US quadrupled in a year - is it time to upgrade?

Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google.

This Wednesday, Google will announce its new smartphone lineup: the Pixel 11 series. Hot on the heels of Samsung's latest (very successful) foldables, Google will follow up with refreshes to its own: the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, along with the Pixel 11 Pro, XL, and base model at its "Made by Google" event in New York.

Also: Is the new (pricier) Pixel 11 series still a good value compared to Samsung's Galaxy phones?

Based on preliminary information, it looks like the 11 series will feature incremental upgrades to the processor, camera, and storage, and Google seems to be doing away with the low-end configuration with 128GB of storage. On top of this, prices will likely go up for the higher-end models, putting the new starting price at $899 for the base 256GB model.

Apart from phones, Google will likely announce its new smartwatch -- the Pixel Watch 5, following up last year's device with a better battery and upgraded chip. We're also potentially looking at a new Bluetooth tracking device to rival Apple's AirTag -- potentially with support for Google's Find Hub network.

Google takes a different approach from Apple's annual iPhone event, as it's in the evening, after product announcements officialy drop that morning.

Made by Google will be August 12th at 3 p.m. PST (6 p.m. EST), and will be livestreamed on YouTube at this link.

Google Pixel 10 Pro and Pro XL

Google's new Pixel 11 lineup includes the base model, the Pixel 11 Pro, the Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold, all of which will likely be incremental upgrades from last year's Pixel 10. Instead of leaps forward in design, we'll likely get slightly better processor performance with the Tensor G6 chipset, the usual range of improvements to the camera, and a focus on new features.

There is one big design change, however, and that's a new LED light module on the phone's camera bar, as teased on Google's Pixel store landing page, and reported by 9to5 Google. According to leaks, it's called the "HiLite", and resembles the rainbow motif associated with Gemini, particularly when interacting with the AI model or when it's "thinking."

Also: The new Pixel 11 isn't enough to make me give up my Pixel 9 Pro - here's why

It could also illuminate different colors based on notification or when the phone is charging, for example. Similar lights have been done on phones before, like on OnePlus devices, for example, which use "edge lighting" around the display for different notifications.

We also have some idea of pricing based on an Amazon leak as reported by Android Authority last month, putting the base Pixel 11 with 256GB of storage at $899 -- and doing away with the 128GB model altogether. The Pixel 11 will likely feature the same-sized 6.3-inch OLED display with 120Hz refresh, 4,985mAh battery, and 13MP front-facing camera.

On the high end, it looks like the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold breaks the $2,000 mark for the 1TB version with 16GB of RAM, featuring 120Hz refresh, a 6.5-inch OLED display, and a 4,750mAh battery. Interestingly, it doesn't appear to support Wi-Fi 7 in the leaked specs.

The Pixel Watch 5 should offer some upgrades to the smartwatch family, including a slightly bigger battery capacity across watches and an accelerated version of the Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 chip within the device. Rumors suggest the Pixel Watch 5 will have double the storage of the Watch 4 -- I'd imagine this is for all the Gemini Intelligence features it's packing into the device. With the advent of Wear OS 7, the smartwatch becomes more contextually aware and agentic.

Also: Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 vs. Google Pixel Watch 4: I compared both Android flagships, here's what I prefer

Leaker MyMobiles reported that a Loss of Pulse Detection feature could arrive on the Watch 5, as well. In promotional material, Google boasts the smartwatch as having its "most complete wellness tracking features".

The 41mm watch will likely start at $399 with the opportunity to add LTE for an extra $100, and the 45mm starts $429, according to a leaked specs sheet. You can expect the same IP68 and 5ATM durability ratings, as the case and display are the same from generation to generation.

Google has lots of room for its own line of tracking devices, as currently the Android ecosystem has tons of options. We could be getting one soon, if leaks from 9to5Google are correct. The oblong Bluetooth tracker will likely support Google's Find Hub network and (hopefully) support Ultra-Wideband for high-precision location tracking -- one of the features that sets Apple's AirTags apart from competitors.

Google announced its next-gen laptop lineup merging ChromeOS and Android earlier this spring, but we haven't heard a whole lot since then. At the time, Google said it would launch the new laptops in the fall, so it's likely we could get some news (or a teaser for an upcoming event).

Also: First look at Googlebook: A premium Chromebook alternative for Android users

The new Googlebook lineup isn't a replacement for Google's existing Chromebooks (thankfully -- as I've reviewed some fantastic models over the last year), but a premium expansion of the lineup that promises better integration with Android mobile devices with its integrated OS.

Everyone is releasing their own pair of smart glasses, and Google has been on that train for a while now. After all, it threw its hat in the ring years ago with the (in)famous Google Glass device over ten years ago.

Also: I wore Google's XR glasses, and they already beat my Ray-Ban Meta in 3 ways
In 2025, we saw Google's XR glasses with Gemini support, in-lens displays, cameras, and mics up close, but not much has happened since then in terms of developments. Following suit with Samsung's forthcoming Galaxy glasses, it's likely Google will tease its own Android XR glasses, potentially with a launch date this year.

Chargers are the lifeblood of modern tech, and things have moved along a lot since the days of the small USB-A wall wart that could push out half an amp of power. Nowadays, we want a charger that has multiple ports and can handle hundreds of watts of output.

Also: Duress passcodes explained: How they work and why they can land you in court

Handling all that power means that there's a lot of effort put into safety and cooling, so modern chargers have a lot of technology built into them to handle this. Then there's the issue of keeping the user in the loop. When you're charging multiple devices, it's good to keep an eye on whether everything is charging as it should.

After all, you might have used a damaged cable or one that's not as fast as it should be.

You need less of a charger and more of a charging station or, if you want to be fancy, a charging computer. And this is exactly what the Satechi ChargeView 240W charger brings to your desk. I've had a chance to go hands-on with this charger before its official release date.

A sleek and stylish 6-port USB-C desktop charger that can power two laptops simultaneously or a handful of your smaller gadgets.

The ChargeView 240W is a follow-on from the smaller 4-port ChargeView 140W, and it carries forward everything that was good about the 140W version and brings even more to the table.

Also: The 7 tech travel hacks I swear by - after years of learning the hard way

A problem I have with many high-power desktop chargers is that they are big, brick-like lumps that loom over your desk. Take the Ugreen Nexode 500W charger, a huge charger with a colossal power output. It's a big, heavy, hulking gray brick. It looks great in a lab-style or industrial setting -- or on my desk, where it's among all the other clutter -- but there's nothing stylish about it.

I love the Ugreen Nexode 500W charger, but it's a big, gray brick.

Also, while the Nexode 500W is a very capable charger, able to squeeze out more than twice the power of the ChargeView 240W, it has nothing in the way of an interface. There's a light on it to show that it's on, and there are a bunch of ports.

I've plenty of stories of plugging things into this charger only to find that they didn't charge because I'd done something dumb, like not plugging the cable in right, or I'd charged something at super-slow speeds because I'd used some scabby old cable off my desk.

Where the ChargeView 240W excels is that it has a display that shows real-time data for each port. The display can be configured to show the power output for each port separately or the combined power output for all the ports.

But, and this is something some other makers would learn from, the display powers down after a minute of inactivity, only powering up again when you plug something in or press the button. So, you don't have a screen facing you all the time (I know how my eye is drawn to any screen in the room, no matter how small).

The charger can be used either horizontally or vertically on the desk, and the included stand works great in both orientations. You can switch the orientation of the display using the little button on the top of the unit -- yes, a physical button, so you're not having to mess about with a touchscreen.

There are a lot of companies out there that can make a decent charger, but so many just don't want to put in the extra effort to make an excellent product.

There are six USB ports on the ChargeView 240W, and all of them are USB-C, so this is a charger built for modern workloads. But if you have the odd USB-A charging cable that you still need to use, you can always use an adapter.

Also: You've been using your power bank wrong, and airline rules make that obvious

The six USB-C ports are arranged into three banks of two. The first two are capable of 140W max, the second pair can deliver up to 100W max, and the final two can deliver up to 30W max. When you use more than one port, the charger will output the maximum power that each device can take, up to the charger's overall 240W maximum.

So, for example, you can have a MacBook pulling 140W from the first port and another laptop drawing 100W from the second, or you can have six devices all connected at once, with the first two ports handling up to 70W apiece, the next two ports handling 30W each, and the last two handling up to 20W each.

If you're 100% USB-C or you have an adapter, this charger has you covered.

I've tested all the outputs, and the charger has no problem at all delivering full power.

And since I know that people will ask, yes, 70W is only half of the 140W that a modern laptop can draw, but it's enough for charging and keeping a laptop topped up during a working day.

Satechi has also packed this charger with the latest charging tech, with the two high-power ports supporting Power Delivery 3.2, a protocol that supports AVS (Adjustable Voltage Supply) alongside PPS (Programmable Power Supply).

Without boring you with the technical details, what this means is that no matter what device you plug into the charger, you get the best, fastest, and safest charge possible. It also means that it supports the fastest charging possible for the latest iPhone.

The remaining four ports all support Power Delivery 3.0 PPS, making them ideal for all your other power-hungry devices.

As with all modern chargers that have to negotiate power transfer speeds, when you plug in a new device to charge, it's normal for charging to be temporarily interrupted for a few seconds. I know this worries a lot of people, but rest assured that everything is working the way it should.

The other thing that I get asked about a lot when it comes to chargers is heat. And given that I know just how hot some chargers can get, I understand why people worry about this.

Also: I tested a 4TB quantum-resistant USB drive - but you don't have to spend $3000 for this much security

Yes, but it's nothing to worry about.

Yes, I've had periods where the charger got warm, but there was never anything to worry about, and it seems very well engineered to dissipate heat generated by the internal power supply and charging circuitry (as long as you don't do something dumb like bury it under a pile of papers or throw a duvet over it).

But even if it gets warm, it has three built-in modes that allow it to throttle charging to cool the unit down.

I'm very impressed by this charger, but if you allow me to be annoyingly nitpicky for a moment, there are a couple of things that I'd change. I'd love to be able to keep the display on all the time (I know my eyes would be drawn to it, but it's cool as long as it's not used on a nightstand), and I'd also like to see real-time internal temperature readings, again, just because that would be cool.

The ChargeView 240W isn't without competition, but I've not reviewed anything that overlaps it completely. Ugreen has the Nexode Pro 300W, an 8-port charger (this has six USB-C ports, one USB-A port, and a DC port that I never hear much call for) for $170, and Anker has the 6-port Prime Charging Station (four USB-C ports and two USB-A ports) for $150.

I find the interfaces for both of these busier, either making use of multiple buttons or a knob, and neither can be set vertically. But these do offer different port layouts, so one might suit you better.

The Satechi ChargeView 240 is currently available for preorder and will be released August 11. It's priced at $150, which is competitive for a charger of this caliber and with this feature set.

Don't need six ports? Pick up the baby 4-port version for $100, which gives you a pair of 140W max ports (one supporting PD 3.2 with AVS and the other PD 3.1 with PPS) and another pair of 40W max ports (both supporting PD 3.1 with PPS).

For those with a more modest number of gadgets, this will be enough and will save you a good chunk of change (to spend on some decent cables, perhaps?).

Just a week ago, a T-Mobile outage affected thousands of customers nationwide, and depending on your choice of words when conversing with a service representative, you were compensated anywhere from $10 to $80 in bill credits. Fun, right?

Had I still been a part of the magenta family, I likely would've experienced the frustration of my in-laws, who were outside a concert venue that day, waiting to regain any bit of signal to validate their tickets in the 90-degree weather.

Also: Hit by T-Mobile's outage? You can get up to $80 in credit - here's how

Instead, I had already switched to Mint, a smaller but more humble conglomerate, after more than a decade as a T-Mobile customer. The decision was easy, and the lower price wasn't the only reason. Here's why you should probably change, too.

When it comes to picking a mobile service provider, big carriers like T-Mobile, Verizon, and AT&T seem like the obvious choices. The extensive marketing budgets, from billboard ads to celebrity cameos in TV commercials, the BOGO phone offers, and the switch-now deals are hard to ignore. The thousands of neon-lit stores don't make things easier.

Also: How I use Samsung's secret Wi-Fi menu to seriously improve my connectivity

But those same deals and promotions are what lock you in, whether it's a three-year contract that charges you fees if you decide to terminate things (this is in the fine print, but how many people are actually reading it?), the "bill credits" that can be viewed as free money or compensation but really only exist to retain your membership, or the inability to unlock your phone until months, if not years, after consistent usage.

Between these commitments, customers often incur hidden fees. Some examples I've seen on my past bills include:

I stuck with T-Mobile for more than a decade because of the convenience (and the thought that switching away would be inconvenient). Through all the random fees, payment plans, and occasional network outages, I also found it easy to swing by a local store whenever I needed help setting up a device or switching to another.

Also: Wi-Fi 7 adoption in the US quadrupled in a year - is it time to upgrade?

My plan also included the weekly freebies via the T-Life (formerly T-Mobile Tuesdays) app, such as $5 movie tickets and free photo prints (which came in handy for printing wedding photos for family and friends). There was also the discounted Netflix subscription, which brought the monthly price of an ever-expensive service down to $5.

But ultimately, the perks didn't equate to the higher cost I was paying for my service, even if it was grandfathered in from years ago.

Those same benefits certainly didn't outweigh the added costs of being forced onto the new Experience More plan when T-Mobile pushed the migration on me back in June. As confirmed by The Mobile Report, T-Mobile began forcing legacy customers onto newer, more expensive plans this summer, including folks like me who were on Simple Choice plans. Here's a breakdown of how things would change.

$140/month (with AutoPay)

(Added on top of base rate; typically $5 to $10 extra per line, depending on local tax)

(Added on top; includes $4.49/line Telco fee, local taxes, and surcharges)

Basic Unlimited, capped at 3GB of high-speed data

(Data may be deprioritized during network congestion)

Unlimited Premium 5G/LTE

(No speed deprioritization or throttling, regardless of usage)

While the increased hotspot bandwidth and faster cellular speeds looked beneficial on paper, I realized (and confirmed) that I spend most of my days connected to Wi-Fi anyway, so the perks of paying $60 more per month weren't worth it.

Also: I compared Google's pricier Pixel 11 series to Samsung's Galaxy lineup - here's the better value now

On top of this, the enhanced trade-in values read to me as a play to encourage more installment plans. Given how frequently I switch phones, I'd rather not deal with the longer-term commitments.

The main reason I switched to Mint was that the service uses the same 5G and LTE networks as T-Mobile. After all, my issues with the latter had more to do with excessive payments and benefits. If I could pay significantly less (roughly $20 per month now, down from the potential $140) for basically the same amount of data usage, then why not?

The migration was surprisingly swift, with my wife's number and mine transferring easily after a few minutes on the phone with a customer service representative. Converting to eSIM a few years ago made moments like this feel so futuristic -- and worth it.

Also: You're charging your phone all wrong: 6 common myths, debunked

Funny enough, the customer service interaction is also the biggest downside of switching from a big carrier to a smaller one. Unlike T-Mobile, Mint does not have physical stores across the country, so your best bet for payments, SIM issues, and other inquiries is to reach out to the company via phone or virtual chat agent.

Being a smaller carrier also means its service is deprioritized in congested spaces like sports arenas and concert venues. You'll still get service, but uploading that snippet onto your social media page may take a few seconds longer.

Also: Your phone doesn't block SIM swapping attacks by default: Turn on these carrier settings now

Perhaps these limitations will be more of a pain point for me in the future, but for now, they're ones that I'll gladly shoulder if it means I'm getting the same, if not more reliable, cellular service for significantly less money.

Consumers are catching on to the fact that not every generational upgrade to their favorite tech can be life-changing. Instead, companies are forced to improve their products little by little.

I've thought about this a lot as I tested the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9. It arrives with a few improvements under the hood: a new processor, some additional health metrics, and a longer battery on the 40mm device.

Also: Galaxy Watch 9 vs. Galaxy Watch 8: I've compared both models, here's my advice

It isn't a groundbreaking smartwatch, but it's great for a first-time buyer, with upgrades that point to the future Samsung aims to create through its wearables. The question is whether those upgrades are as helpful to users today as they will be when the next generation of wearables arrives.

The Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 arrives with a bigger battery, a few more health metrics to track through the Samsung Health app, and a new processor, the Snapdragon Wear Elite. You probably won't need to upgrade from the Galaxy Watch 7 or 8 just yet, unless you want more use per charge. This is a great first smartwatch for Android users, specifically those with a Samsung phone.

One of the goals of the Snapdragon Wear Elite chip is to divest in the smartphone as the center of the personal device ecosystem, adding instead several different AI-powered wearables that integrate and work together. "Intelligent eyewear represents that next step," Samsung's press release says, hinting at smart glasses to come -- something we've been watching closely now for over a year.

Also: How Qualcomm's new wearables chipset could spell the end of smartphone dominance

It would follow then that Samsung's forthcoming smart glasses will work with the Galaxy Watch 9 to summarize what wearers see, read and translate information, contextualize content, and activate gestures recorded by the watch, making the Galaxy Watch 9 a crucial component in its smart glasses' ecosystem integration (and maybe one of the reasons why its taking so long to launch). In fact, the intelligent eyewear will operate through voice activation and gestures, but those gestures are activated through the Galaxy Watch 9.

I love working out with the Galaxy Watch 9. It's mighty good at what you're buying it for: counting steps, tracking your exercise, and delivering post-workout encouragement. The bright, 3,000-nit super AMOLED screen is easy to see between weight-training reps, and the bevy of new health-tracking features means there's always lots to look at.

The Galaxy Watch 9 ships with Google's Wear OS 7 and Samsung's One UI 9 Watch, including features like Heart Health Score, Fitness Index, and Daily Cardio Load. They offer a nice blend of short-term and long-term insights, allowing me to check daily cardio load to see if I'm getting my steps in, and then checking Heart Health Score just how those daily changes evolve into a longitudinal metric.

Also: I went running with the Galaxy Watch 9 in London, and it taught me something new

It's accurate, too. I put the Galaxy Watch 9's heart-rate monitor to the test during a recent Stairmaster workout and compared that data to the gold standard heart rate monitoring chest strap, the Polar H10. What I found surprised me: the Galaxy Watch 9's average heart rate for the workout was within 3 beats per minute of the Polar H10's, and the max heart rate was within 1 bpm of the Polar H10. That's stellar agreement. The Polar H10 measured around 8.3 calories burned per minute, while the Galaxy Watch 9 measured 7.9.

The Galaxy Watch 9's hydration guidance is also helpful on runs, buzzing you with a reminder to hydrate based on your energy exertion. While it may seem intuitive, I can imagine this feature being useful for cardio warriors spending hours in the sun training for a marathon or casual users who tend to forget to hydrate.

Samsung said the watch will last you around 30 hours with the smartwatch's always on display enabled, and that's exactly what my testing proved during the first week of wear. The watch was charged at 98% at 9:33a.m. on July 27 and depleted to 2% at 9:15 p.m. on July 28. This puts the watch's run time at around 36 hours and 30 minutes.

The Galaxy Watch 9 lives up to its 390 mAh battery claims, but I'm still wishing for a faster-charging device, especially after testing the Pixel Watch 4, whose battery was replenished in around 45 minutes. It takes the Galaxy Watch 9 around an hour and 20 minutes to recharge from 0%. That's too much time to wait.

Also: Galaxy Watch 9 vs. Galaxy Watch 8: I've compared both models, here's my advice

You might not have an issue wearing this watch, but my small wrists did. Its silicon band felt heavy, sticky, and clingy around my wrist, and toggling between the two adjustment holes either made the watch too tight or too loose. The fixed loops that hold the strap in place regularly move, so the strap has ended up flying free as I run or go about my day. I've never liked a silicon watch band and would highly suggest buying an additional watch band built to wick water and be a little more comfortable to wear around the clock.

Samsung doesn't skimp on quantifiable health scores. Take Vitals, one of many new health metrics scored on the Samsung Health app, for example. It monitors a selection of biomarkers the watch already records, including resting heart rate, heart rate variability, respiration rate, and blood oxygen, to detect deviations (or illness) from a person's baseline.

Also: I wore the Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for a week - it's a true Apple Watch Ultra 3 rival

In fact, the app delivers tons of scores: one for sleep, sleep apnea, energy, heart health, cardio load, antioxidant levels, and metabolic health. I am still left wondering, after several days testing these features, how this groundswell of graded health data will result in my own behavior changes.

Right now, it just feels like more data to parse through with no core focus. This is where an AI health coach or agent would be most useful. I can see how Samsung is laying the groundwork for an intelligent tool with these metrics (and testing a health coach of its own in beta), but the contextual layer is currently missing. In its absence, users are left with a bevy of numbers and ratings.

I'd recommend the Galaxy Watch 9 to first-time smartwatch users. It's easy to navigate, tracks every possible metric you'd want, and is a functional, everyday smartwatch. I can't say I enjoyed sleeping with the watch, though. And I'd recommend buying a different band if you plan to wear the watch 24/7, as the one that comes in the box is too airtight and impermeable for my liking.

Also: Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 vs. Google Pixel Watch 4: I compared both Android flagships, here's what I prefer

But I'd highly suggest buying this watch for exercise tracking and general health purposes, especially if you want a smartwatch that can take messages and phone calls and pose as a smartphone for your wrist. The battery boost sweetens the deal, making this a smartwatch you can wear for over a day before its next charge.

Samsung's latest flagship smartwatch does all the big stuff well: exercise tracking, sleep monitoring, with both short- and long-term health insights. The battery lasts more than a day, and you can use those 36 hours of device time to gain insights into your daily and historic cardio trends, understand your blood pressure, and potentially improve your sleep. The Galaxy Watch 9 is worth its asking price, and is a great general purpose health-tracking companion.

Marshall's Stanmore line of speakers has been my reliable music partner for six years now. I like playing songs on my mains-powered Stanmore II more than any other speaker. It runs in the background when I'm working, chilling, or just existing at home. So, I was more than excited to see if the latest model, the new Stanmore IV, was worth the upgrade.

Also: Marshall Stanmore IV vs. Sonos Era 300: I tested both to find the ultimate home speaker

The fourth-gen speaker promised a more immersive experience with deeper bass and a wider soundstage, along with a more repairable design. I have now been testing it for a month, and am glad to report that it stands true to most of those promises.

The Marshall Stanmore IV is still a Bluetooth-only speaker, lacking Wi-Fi or voice assistant support, unlike other smart speakers in its price range. However, it is the signature Marshall design, sound, and overall experience that'll sway you away from the smart options and toward an analog-first approach. But is it really worth the $430 price tag? Allow me to answer.

The Stanmore IV may lack modern smart feature speakers, but its design, sound, and longevity appeal to those looking for a hassle-free analog experience.

The Stanmore IV features Marshall's signature look, packed in a more repairable wooden cabinet measuring 13.78 x 7.99 x 7.28 inches and weighing 8.81lbs. As a mains-powered speaker, it is meant to be kept in a single place, plugged into an outlet. It is big, but unlike other home speakers, the Stanmore blends into your room's interior. It doesn't look like an odd gadget sitting on a shelf.

Like its predecessor, the Stanmore IV has a faux-leather-clad exterior, a brass speaker grille, and golden accents, along with a large Marshall logo at the front. These design elements give it a classy, timeless look, which would complement any living space.

Marshall's physical controls offer satisfying, analog feedback that I miss on the Sonos Era 300.

On top, you get three physical knobs to adjust the volume, treble, and bass. They are paired with a power switch, Source button (to toggle between RCA, Bluetooth, and Aux), a playback control button (to play/pause or go to previous/next track), and an all-new M button. The multifunction M button can be customized through the Marshall app, where you'll find options to switch between your saved EQ presets or open a Spotify playlist with Spotify Tap. Plus, the red LED indicators are now brighter and more legible than before.

Also: I tested Sonos' new beta features on iOS and Android - how to opt in and what to expect

This control system feels like the perfect mix of analog and digital. There's something more satisfying about the physical feedback of knobs, buttons, and switches, which can't be replicated by vibrations on digital buttons. Marshall's use of buttons and knobs means you don't have to take out your phone to change the EQ, volume, and source settings. It is simply a more joyful experience.

My Marshall Stanmore II (left) has its ports located on the back, whereas the Stanmore IV (right) has a cleaner look and has shifted its controls to the bottom.

Marshall has also worked on tidying up the design. All ports, except the 3.5mm Aux port on top, have been moved to the speaker's underside, whereas on the Stanmore II, they were on the back.

This shift in port locations allows you to place the Stanmore IV flush against a wall, or if it is on an open shelf, it'll look tidier from the back. It is also more repairable than before. You can swap out the front grille, knobs, feet, and the iconic logo, should they get damaged.

I compared the latest-generation Stanmore IV to my Stanmore II, and it sounded better than ever. It is clearer, louder, and has a bigger soundstage. The new Marshall speaker uses two 0.75-inch tweeters with 25W of amplification and a 5-inch sub with 60W of amplification to deliver big, booming bass.

Also: Marshall's first soundbar rocks as a mainstream alternative - Here's my take

I listened to all kinds of genres, and the Marshall Stanmore IV delivers an all-around pleasing experience. It offers deep bass without fatiguing your ears. The lower frequencies have a thumping impact while remaining clear, without sacrificing mids.

Rock songs have excellent instrument separation, where you can hear the drumbeat alongside the energy of electric guitars. The treble sounds controlled and vibrant at all volumes, with minimal distortion even when you crank it up. And none of it affects the vocal clarity. I enjoyed listening to acoustic music as much as I enjoyed rock.

Also: Sennheiser Momentum 5 vs. Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3: I tested both, and one wins nearly every metric

For the better part of my testing, I had my Marshall Stanmore IV connected to the Vivo X300 Ultra (for higher-res LDAC) and iPhone 17 Pro Max. For the most part, I couldn't tell the difference between the two sources. However, I did notice vocals on the LDAC codec sounded slightly more detailed and had more space.

Overall, the Stanmore IV sounds as energetic as before, but with better tonal accuracy, deeper bass, and a broader soundstage.

The Stanmore IV can be paired with your phone via the new Marshall app. It enables over-the-air updates and customization options, and offers nifty features to deliver a better experience.

The app allows you to adjust the brightness of the LED indicators, use placement compensation to optimize the speaker's audio output based on its position, and save up to three EQ presets with a five-band equalizer. You can also customize the M button to your preference here.

Also: Google Home vs. Sonos Era 100: I used both smart speakers, here's what I recommend

Marshall has also added Aurcast support to its new Stanmore IV and Action IV speakers. This means you can finally connect a Stanmore speaker to an Acton, Woburn, or other supported Marshall speaker for a multi-room experience. Earlier, you could only stack a Stanmore with a Stanmore or a Woburn with a Woburn. I'm glad this is now an option.

However, I'm disappointed that you'll need a $300 Marshall Heddon streaming hub to connect the Stanmore IV to its predecessor or to the Marshall Heston soundbars. Additionally, the lack of Auracast support for connecting to speakers from other manufacturers is a major drawback. Unfortunately, if you have a Stanmore II like me, you can't connect it to Marshall's latest home speakers.

I also wish Marshall had included Wi-Fi support in its new generation of home speakers. I'd like to connect my speaker to the home network and cast songs via AirPlay -- not for quality but for a no-interruption experience. On Bluetooth, my music pauses when I'm scrolling through social media, and a video starts playing. If there were Wi-Fi support, this disruption wouldn't have happened, and I could have continued using my phone without worrying about a random noise interrupting my music.

At $430, the Marshall Stanmore IV is not the most affordable speaker on the market. It directly competes with a smarter $479 Sonos Era 300, which has Wi-Fi support and voice assistant capabilities. However, it doesn't have the same timeless, classy look as the new Marshall speaker.

Despite the price tag, the Stanmore IV remains an easy recommendation because of its timeless design and excellent sound combination.

The Stanmore IV's faux-leather exterior with golden accents would easily fit into any living space, and its strong bass, paired with vibrant highs and clear vocals on a wide, room-filling soundstage, would please every listener. If my experience with the Stanmore II is any indication, this speaker is built to last, and a more repairable design only instills more confidence. If you don't need smart features, the Marshall Stanmore IV is the best home speaker you can buy in its price range.

https://www.zdnet.com/article/your-phone.title: Your phone doesn't block SIM swapping attacks by default: Turn on these carrier settings now
https://www.zdnet.com/article/your-phone.text:
In recent years, SIM swapping attacks have increased, prompting the mobile industry to try to combat them more effectively.

SIM swapping is a type of fraud in which a scammer transfers your mobile phone number to a SIM in their own device. By intercepting calls or texts sent to your phone, they can capture two-factor authentication codes and other information intended for you. From there, the attacker can take over not only your mobile account but also other accounts that rely on authentication.

Also: The shadowy SIM farms behind those incessant scam texts - and how to stay safe

SIM swapping attacks can play out in a couple of different ways. A scammer may be able to convince the mobile carrier to transfer the SIM to a new device by pretending to be you. Criminals have also offered money to employees at such carriers as Verizon and T-Mobile, tempting them to perform SIM swaps.

The three major US carriers -- AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon -- all offer their own tools to protect your account from SIM swapping scams. I subscribe to Verizon on my main iPhone and T-Mobile and AT&T on my test and backup phones, so I've used these security settings for all three. Here's how to protect yourself from these types of attacks across all three carriers.

Verizon offers two safeguards against SIM swapping attacks. SIM Protection prevents unauthorized SIM or device changes on your phone number unless you disable the setting. Number Lock blocks any unauthorized swaps of your mobile phone number. I've turned on both and would advise all Verizon subscribers to do the same.

Also: Still using a physical SIM? This $25 kit brings eSIM to your old phone - here's how

SIM swapping attacksTo set these up, sign in to your account at the Verizon website or through the My Verizon app for iOS or Android.

If you're using the website, select Account at the top of the screen. On the Account page, click Account overview. Next, select Profile and settings. Under the Security section on the left, click the link for SIM Protection. Turn on SIM Protection for each line in your plan, and then click the Save Changes button.

If you're going through the My Verizon app, go to the Me screen and tap Profile and settings at the top. Swipe down to the Security section and tap SIM Protection. Turn on the setting for all your lines.

To turn on Number Lock on the website or in the My Verizon app, go back to the previous screen after enabling SIM Protection. In the Security section, select the link for Number Lock. Turn on Number Lock for the lines you wish to lock. On the website, be sure to click Save Changes.

Also: 14 secret phone codes that unlock hidden features on your Android and iPhone

Verizon offers other security settings worth investigating. You can set up and use a passkey instead of a password. The secret question option lets you choose a question and answer to help Verizon reps confirm your identity if you call to request a change. The Voice ID feature analyzes your speaking voice to verify your identity when you call.

T-Mobile's SIM Protection aims to thwart unauthorized number transfers. To enable this, sign in to your account at the My T-Mobile website. Click the My T-Mobile button at the upper left and select My Profile. On your profile page, select SIM Protection. Turn on the switch for your number and any other lines you wish to protect. Check the box for "I agree to these conditions," and then click Save Changes.

Also: How to easily add a backup carrier to your phone - for free or cheap

AT&T offers a setting called Wireless Account Lock, which prevents unauthorized account changes, billing updates, and wireless number transfers.

Also: Lock down your AT&T account to prevent SIM swapping attacks - here's how

To set this up, you'll have to install and use the AT&T app for iOS or Android. Fire up the app and make sure you're signed in to your account. Tap the person icon at the upper right. Swipe down the screen and tap the setting for Wireless Account Lock. To confirm your action, swipe across your phone in the highlighted area. A message notifies you that your account has been locked.

If you ever need to disable the account lock to modify your account or phone number, return to the same screen and tap the Unlock Account button.

Seven years of folding phone innovation have led Samsung to finally embrace a wide-format design with its new Galaxy Z Fold 8. The compact, BlackBerry-esque phone unfolds into a mini tablet, with aspect ratios that feel more natural than its taller Fold 8 Ultra sibling. This isn't the first time we've seen a shorter, wider folding phone, but this is indeed the first time it appeals to a wider audience.

Also: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is so good, I don't see the point of flip phones any more

Samsung's all-new form factor debuts amid mounting rumors of a palm-sized foldable iPhone Ultra, and isn't free of shortcomings. However, the fun, practical design outweighs all weaknesses. Since its launch at Galaxy Unpacked, I've used the Fold 8 for 10 days, and unexpectedly, it hasn't lost its charm yet.

I'm still amazed by how comfortable it is to type on the cover screen or how comfortably it fits my pocket. This is, in a way, the compact phone I've been waiting for.

Amazon's latest foldable is finally ready for mainstream appeal.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 borrows the best of different foldables and packages it in one palm-sized device

I was skeptical about the usability of a short and wide cover screen, but I've found it to be the perfect combination of novelty and practicality. In fact, the 5.5-inch AMOLED panel has been my go-to reading companion, thanks to its 10:16 aspect ratio.

From browsing in Chrome to reading in the Kindle or NYT app, I haven't once felt forced to unfold my Fold 8 for better readability. I've also been typing on it (with both hands) more than expected. Unlike flip phones, you can see the conversation while typing your message. The keyboard takes up about half the screen, but it leaves plenty of room for unbothered messaging without feeling cramped.

I wish I had more digital magazines to read on this phone.

The comfortable in-hand feel is also made possible by the slim and light design. As a matter of fact, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is Samsung's lightest Z Fold phone at 201 grams (versus the 215g Fold 8 Ultra and 214g S26 Ultra). Plus, it is just 4.5mm thick when unfolded and 9.7mm when closed. It doesn't feel any thicker than a regular slab phone. And that's not even the best part.

Its true uniqueness lies in its versatility. It unfolds into a 7.6-inch mini tablet with a 4:3 aspect ratio, which is more natural in everyday tasks than traditional book-style foldables' squarish 8-inch screens.

Fold 8's 4:3 folding screen is much better than traditional book-style foldables' squarish aspect ratio for video consumption.

I open the Fold 8 when I want to watch video content. Everything from YouTube videos to movie watching in Netflix or Prime Video is better than other tall folding phones. A 4:3 screen means you get less letterboxing (black borders on top and bottom) when watching videos.

Instagram Reels interface on the cover screen (left) vs. on the folding screen (right).

It's the vertical videos (TikTok, Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts) that require adjustment. Instagram downloads in the tablet version, which pushes the like, comment, and share buttons to the black border on the right side (on both the cover screen and inner display) for better reel watchability. Personally, I like it, but it might be an adjustment for anyone used to the mobile app UI.

The big canvas is also great for reading, but that punch-hole selfie camera is unexpectedly more bothersome on this phone. It cuts off words on the right edge of the screen. You can always rotate it so the camera is positioned on the side of your right palm, but it sometimes interferes with the auto brightness. I wish Samsung had positioned it in the corner or found a way to add an under-display camera.

It did improve the multitasking experience, however, with One UI 9 (based on Android 17). It feels more intuitive, natural and easy to use. The Fold 8 can run three apps side by side, but that's not ideal. I found myself multitasking more often 90:10 split-screen between two apps.

It is smoother and more intuitive to multitask on the Fold 8 than before.

For instance, I had Chrome (for research) and Google Docs (to type) set side by side. When researching, I could easily maximize Chrome's screen space by sliding the middle bar and pushing Docs to cover (roughly) 10% of the screen, and vice versa when I wanted to type. This was hardly as buttery smooth on previous versions.

Also: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra vs. Motorola Razr Fold: Which premium foldable should you get?

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is different than other book-style foldables in a way that it doesn't force you to adjust to its design quirks. Instead, it adapts to your usage more naturally.

Samsung uses a "Flex Titanium" technology in its folding display structure, which helps with durability, slimness and minimizing the crease. It combines a titanium-alloy film with an enhanced titanium plate to strengthen the display and "refine the way the device opens."

All this is to say that the crease is definitely more subtle, and the phone pops open after a certain angle, giving you a more natural unfolding experience. However, Samsung has removed Flex mode on the hinge, so you can't prop up the Fold 8 like its Ultra sibling to watch videos. The Tent mode on its cover screen is a fair substitute.

Tent mode on Galaxy Z Fold 8.

As for the crease, it has been minimized to an extent that you can't feel it when running your finger over it. You can still spot it in some lighting situations but it is a non-issue and won't distract you from on-screen content.

An even bigger upgrade comes in the form of anti-reflective coating. Samsung claims that the reflectivity on the Fold 8's inner screen has been reduced by 50% (versus the Fold 7).

Also: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 vs. Z Flip 8: How Samsung's two new foldables compare

It is the upgrade I've wanted since the Fold 6 days, and I'm glad the Korean phone maker finally listened. In practical usage, this means the folding screen is much more legible in direct light than its predecessor. I could navigate on Maps, see the camera viewfinder clearly, and browse in the Delhi sun without any issues. It's also in part thanks to the higher brightness levels (3,000 nits vs. 2,600 nits on the Fold 7).

The crease is a non-issue on Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8

Like last year, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is rated IP48 for dust and water resistance. This means it can survive freshwater submersion but isn't resistant to small dust particles like pocket lint. While this is in line with most foldable phones, the Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold and Honor Magic V6 offer a dust-tight design with their IP68 ratings. I hope Samsung adopts it for its next generation of Z series phones.

You need to change the default settings to get the most out of this dual-camera setup.

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 has one less camera than the Fold 8 Ultra and a lower-resolution main sensor. It has a dual camera system consisting of a 50MP main camera and another 50MP ultrawide angle sensor.

I'm not a fan of Samsung's default processing, but it has improved in the last year, and there are ways to extract the best from what you have. I took most of my photos in 50MP mode, which gives you more details than the default mode.

Over the last year, Samsung has improved its processing for sunset shots.

However, you miss out on certain features like the ability to add a filter style, which is hard to understand because I'd rather have these styles applied to a higher resolution photo than 12MP shots.

I also like the rich contrast and details on ultrawide photos. They look better than my Fold 7's ultrawide shots.

As for videos, they aren't sharp and get noisy once you zoom in on your scene. Every time I wanted to zoom in on a subject in videos, I wished this phone had a telephoto camera. And this leads me to another gripe - the camera position, again.

The Fold 8's cameras are located in a vertical camera module, but I think it'd have been better to have a horizontal layout (ultrawide on top of the main camera) because I kept getting my finger in 1x shots. I have big hands, and I'm assuming people with smaller hands won't have to readjust their grip so often. However, it bothered me enough to stand out in my camera experience.

Samsung's new wide-fold houses the same chip that powers its Galaxy S26 Ultra and Fold 8 Ultra - the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy processor. It is paired with 12GB of RAM for the 256GB and 512GB storage variants and 16GB of RAM with 1TB of storage. In my day-to-day usage, the phone ran smoothly with no issues at all.

However, it tends to struggle under certain scenarios, like gaming for 30 minutes or more. Samsung says that it has reworked the internals to create more space for heat dissipation, which should result in better thermal management. But the Fold 8 gets warm to touch under sustained workloads. Other than that, you won't find any major misses here. From multitasking to camera processing, everything is smooth and fast.

Also: I've been using the Galaxy Z Fold 8 for two weeks - these two accessories perfect the experience

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 also received a big battery upgrade. It packs a 4,800mAh cell with support for 45-watt fast charging. This might not look like a big deal, but the Fold 7 had a 4,400mah battery capacity and the new Z series is the first lineup of Samsung smartphones to feature high-density silicon-carbon anode batteries. In real-world usage, it delivers an all-day battery life without breaking a sweat.

Qi2.2 magnets are useful for attaching magnetic accessories and getting the perfect alignment on a wireless charger. You'll need to add a case on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 to get this functionality.

In my testing period, I've consistently used my Fold 8 to take calls, scroll through Reddit, Instagram, answer messages on WhatsApp, video call my niece, take photos, and read. I consistently got more than eight hours of screen time. This isn't the Oppo Find N6 or Honor Magic V6, but I didn't have to charge it twice a day (like my Fold 7). And when you do need to charge, it goes from 10% to 75% within 30 minutes.

Also: Amazon will give you a $350 gift card when you buy a new Samsung phone - here's what to know

While the Galaxy Z Fold 8 supports 20-watt fast charging, it doesn't have built-in magnets. You'll need to purchase a Qi2-compatible case, or you'll be left figuring out the perfect alignment on a wireless charger half of the time. In my opinion, the absence of magnets for another year is a big miss. I don't want to ruin Fold 8's marvelous piece of engineering by slapping a case on it; it's a tough phone, built to withstand drops, and I'd like to add magnetic accessories like a kickstand or power bank on it without needing a case.

My FanCam can be useful in some scenarios.

The new Samsung foldables run One UI 9 based on Android 17 and they have a few new AI features worth talking about.

This is the most fun new AI feature. If you shoot a video where your subject is with a few other people, you can choose to track them with AI to make it look like the camera was following them. You can also adjust the aspect ratio, but it will degrade the video quality. Samsung suggests you take 4K videos if you plan on using My FanCam.

It works like Magic Cue for Google Pixel phones. It suggests actions based on your on-screen content. For instance, if someone sends me a message asking for availability on a specific date, the Fold 8 will show a popup to open the Calendar. Once you tap on it, it pulls up the Calendar on half of the screen. It sounds good in theory, but like Magic Cue, Now Nudge doesn't work all the time.

Apart from these two features, I haven't proactively used any of the generative AI stuff. I hardly ever use the AI Eraser in my photos, but when I need it, Samsung does surprisingly well to detect, delete, and fill in the details. I mostly use it to delete annoying elements in my selfies, like dustbins and signboards.

Also: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra vs. Google Pixel Fold 10 Pro: You can't lose, but here's my surprise pick

Regarding other AI features, I wish Samsung and Google would stop forcing use cases that don't exist to sell their unreliable AI. I'm glad this phone doesn't need any of it to make a case for its $1,900 price tag.

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is one of the most expensive folding phones on the market, but it is also one of the best mix of fun and practicality. At $1,900, I'd expect my device to have a dedicated camera for optical zoom and iron out the misses from previous generation products (like the lack of Qi2.2 magnets). But despite this, it's easy to recommend. I haven't had this much fun using a phone in a long time.

Also: I went hands-on with the Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8, but it's not the upgrade I expected

The new Samsung smartphone is built for most people. It combines flip pocketability and fold usability in a wider design that's ideal for video consumption -- not just for reading. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 adapts to your usage instead of asking you to adjust to its design. It is a refreshing take on a relatively new concept, and I'm all for it.

If your usage involves reading, watching videos, and browsing the web - and you have the budget for it -- the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the best folding phone out there right now.

Its refreshing new design is both practical and pocketable, and it feels like the fold for everyone -- not just power users. While it has its own limitations, and its $1,900 price tag is not exactly what I'd call "affordable", the new Fold 8 redefines what you can do on a foldable phone.

https://www.zdnet.com/article/i-read-mic.title: I read Microsoft's Windows 11 'quality' progress report - and the subtext says it all
https://www.zdnet.com/article/i-read-mic.text:
Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google.

Earlier this year, Microsoft Windows boss Pavan Davuluri wrote an open letter addressed to the Windows Insider community but really aimed at a much larger cohort of frustrated Windows enthusiasts and power users.

That post laid out a laundry list of improvements that would be coming to Windows: more control over updates, a "more intentional" approach to AI, more attention to performance and reliability, and some enhancements to the user experience that customers have been complaining about for five solid years.

Also: Microsoft announces sweeping Windows changes - but no apologies

"We're listening to customer feedback" was the ostensible message, but the subtext was really a confession that Microsoft had been ignoring customer feedback for years. And last week, we got an update on that admission.

As I pointed out more than three years ago, Microsoft has focused all its energy on turning Windows into a billboard for the company's other products and services: more promotions, more nudges, more cross-selling, more pressure to use a Microsoft account, more hooks to subscription-based services, and more "recommended" content. The bottom line is that Windows has become increasingly annoying, not by accident but by design, with monetization as the end goal.

Also: If Microsoft really wants to fix Windows 11, it should do these four things ASAP

The turn toward "improving Windows quality" represents a belated recognition of that reality. "The team and I have spent a great deal of time analyzing your feedback," Davuluri said. "What came through was the voice of people who care deeply about Windows and want it to be better."

Davuluri shared a progress report last week. It wasn't so much a list of successes as a summary of work in progress.

If you've been testing Windows Insider builds, you've seen some of the changes, but the rest of us won't see anything for months. (The smart money says early October.) Others are vague and impossible to quantify, like this summary of performance work:

[W]e've steadily been introducing several improvements to the memory efficiency of Windows, from taking advantage of a more efficient memory allocator to reduce overhead across apps and components, continued tuning of WinUI 3 so that apps built on it use less memory by design, as well as driving efficiencies across Chromium and Webview2 components when they appear in the operating system ... Boot and logon times are also improved.

Also: Windows Search just got a faster, cleaner overhaul - how to try it today

Sounds great, right? Except none of those boasts are accompanied by a single benchmark. No measurement of any kind. Without numbers that outsiders can confirm for themselves, it's just hand-waving.

Collectively, the entire list adds up to an admission that Microsoft has been seriously neglecting Windows fundamentals for years.

Take a look, for example, at the description of improvements in Windows Hello: "It's part of our broader focus on the everyday experiences that should just work." This implies that many of those everyday experiences aren't "just working."

Another example: "[E]xperiences like Start, File Explorer, Search, and Snipping Tool are faster and more responsive. Our focus has been on improving these experiences, so they are responsive, free of stutters and delays, and customers enjoy a reliable experience every time."

The improvements to File Explorer include "foundational architecture enhancements designed to improve responsiveness and reliability across launch and navigation. We've addressed long-standing feedback about Home, including unstable transitions and blurry thumbnails. We also made updates to address File Explorer reliability, readability, and usability across the Address Bar, file size formatting, keyboard navigation, and renaming..."

Also: Why your Windows installation files keep getting bigger - AI is filling up smaller drives

Those are all tasks that any serious Windows user performs every day, using a basic tool that has been part of Windows forever. Windows 11 isn't some newfangled product that was just released. It has been generally available for nearly five years. The fact that the company is only now getting around to fixing multiple longstanding issues with responsiveness, reliability, stability, and usability in File Explorer is an admission that core parts of the user experience simply haven't been working properly.

Anyway, Microsoft says it's doing great, and it's expanding its focus to include some more areas: a "faster and more efficient out-of-box experience," refinements to parental controls, and improvements to make voice "more natural and fluid to interact across the apps you use every day."

And, most significantly, "Memory optimization for 8GB and above - Reducing Windows memory footprint to deliver a fast and responsive Windows experience across the PCs customers use every day." Again, this has been one of the loudest complaints about Windows 11 since day 1.

Don't get me wrong. I applaud this effort. This is the first time in many years that I can recall a senior member of the Windows leadership team talking about the things people use a Windows PC for instead of promoting whatever irrelevant feature the marketing team wants highlighted. Remember mixed reality and Paint 3D? Remember Cortana? Remember when you were going to be able to run Android apps on your Windows 11 PC? All of those features were hyped to the moon, and they're all gone now.

Also: Microsoft goes all in on new AI-powered Windows security strategy - what it means for you

I was actually encouraged to see that AI got only a passing mention in this progress report, and then only in the context of integrating those features where they're most useful. The focus right now seems to be on the accumulation of unfinished and neglected features that have made Windows increasingly irritating to use.

The big question now is whether Microsoft's top management has the willingness to continue shifting resources to this core work instead of spending those dollars on new AI-based features. The company's history suggests that removing annoyances is easy when it puts its mind to it. Resisting the urge to add new annoyances is much harder.

https://www.zdnet.com/article/google-pri.title: I compared Google's pricier Pixel 11 series to Samsung's Galaxy lineup - here's the better value now
https://www.zdnet.com/article/google-pri.text:
Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google.

Google's Pixel phones have, for quite some time, been premium enough to compete with Samsung's best phones, but they were usually a bit cheaper. That made overlooking any performance or hardware gaps very easy.

But the Pixel 11 series will be different.

Also: Google's new Pixel 11 series drops next week - what we know from leaks

Based on reported pricing, Google might charge Samsung-level prices for its next phones. The hardware still sounds competitive, according to what's leaked and known so far, but the Pixel value proposition is now more about the software than the lower price.

Google has confirmed that its next generation of Pixel devices will arrive during a Made by Google event on Aug. 12 at 6 p.m. ET. Preorders are expected to open that day, while reports suggest an Aug. 20 retail release.

Also: You're charging your phone all wrong: 6 common myths, debunked

Samsung's latest phones, the Galaxy S26, S26+, and S26 Ultra, were announced Feb. 25 and released March 11. Samsung unveiled the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Z Flip 8 on July 22, with availability on Aug. 7.

A recent leak reported by The Verge and others claimed the Pixel 11 will cost $899.

Meanwhile, the Pixel 11 Pro will be $1,099, the Pixel 11 Pro XL will be $1,299, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold will be $1,899. That's a $100 increase for the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro, although they are expected to double their starting storage from 128GB to 256GB. The Pixel 11 Pro XL and Pro Fold, however, would cost $100 more while retaining the same 256GB starting capacity.

Also: Own a Pixel? You can add device protection now for $5/month

Those new prices almost perfectly mirror Samsung's current lineup.

The 256GB Galaxy S26 starts at $899.99, the S26+ costs $1,099.99, and the S26 Ultra starts at $1,299.99. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 costs $1,899.99, while the bigger Fold 8 Ultra starts at $2,099.99.

Keep in mind that until Google makes everything official, specifications and prices remain rumors.

OK, here's a basic spec sheet for Samsung's latest Galaxy series:

Now compare that to Pixel 11. It will reportedly use Google's Tensor G6 processor. These chips are optimized for AI and computational photography, which, for the end user, typically means excellent photos and clever features. Samsung's Snapdragon, on the other hand, is known for its performance, its ability to power more capable cameras, and faster charging.

Also: The new Pixel 11 isn't enough to make me give up my Pixel 9 Pro - here's why

The standard Pixel 11 is thought to have a 6.3-inch OLED display and three rear cameras, while the Pro models might offer upgraded LTPO displays and better wide, ultrawide, and telephoto cameras. The Pixel 11 Pro XL will likely be 6.8 inches in size.

As for charging, rumors for the Pixel 11 battery indicate a base capacity of around 4,985mAh, up to 30 hours of battery life, and fast charging speeds that can reportedly reach a 55% charge in about 30 minutes using matching 30W to 45W USB-C adapters.

The foldable comparison is more interesting. If the rumored $1,899 price is true, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold will cost essentially the same as the Z Fold 8. Samsung's model offers a 7.6-inch folding display, two 50MP rear cameras, a 4,800mAh battery, and a light 201g design. The last I saw, Google's new foldable will have an 8-inch inner screen and a 6.4-inch outer display.

The battery is said to be around 4,800mAh.

The thing is, unless someone is a real tech nerd, differences in camera, display, and battery sizes aren't necessarily the biggest concern. Most premium phones offer comparable hardware for the average person. I tend to care more about the software experience, and I wonder how many others feel the same way. I want a pure, feature-rich Android experience.

In my opinion, the Pixel's value shouldn't be measured entirely by processor speeds, camera counts, and fast-charging capabilities. Android is a major part of the equation. Since Google controls both Pixel hardware and Android, it typically designs features around its own phones and delivers major Android updates and Pixel Drops to them quickly.

Also: I've been using the Galaxy Z Fold 8 - these accessories perfect it

For example, Android 17 rolled out first to the Pixel 6 and newer devices in June, bringing productivity upgrades such as floating App Bubbles, stronger security protections, Screen Reactions, improved gaming features for foldables, and built-in parental controls.

Alongside Android 17, the June Pixel Drop brought custom Take a Message greetings, Gemini Omni video creation, Lyria 3 music generation, Voice Translate for the Pixel 10a, broader Quick Share compatibility with AirDrop, and expanded Magic Cue support.

Samsung phones don't get Pixel Drops. Those are just for Pixel devices, bringing features such as Call Screen, Magic Cue, Take a Message, and Camera Coach. Many of these exclusives are powered by Google's Tensor chips, which also enable excellent computational photography tools. One example is Best Take. It combines multiple frames to produce a group photo.

But Samsung is typically among the first manufacturers to receive major Android updates. When Android 17 launched, Google said other eligible devices would get it throughout 2026. Samsung also layers One UI and its own apps and services on top of Android. Features such as DeX and Knox security do add value, but other additions may feel like bloat. I prefer Google's cleaner approach.

To be clear, Google loads Pixel devices with its Workspace apps and services, but most Android phone owners probably use at least one or two Google apps. You can also easily delete most of them from your phone. Purchasing an eligible Pixel device usually includes six or 12 months of Google AI Pro and additional Google One storage, too, depending on the model and current promotion.

Simply put, if the latest AI and software features, including Gemini and Google's own services, matter most, Pixel devices should be among the first considered. If hardware matters more, including having the highest-end specifications available, Samsung often wins that side of the comparison. We'll know more, of course, when the Pixel 11 debuts next week.

I think so, but the Pixel is no longer a cheaper alternative to Galaxy devices.

Samsung is known for exceptional hardware, while Pixel is about a purer Android experience, frequent updates, computational photography, and early or exclusive access to Google's newest features. That's the real value.

Also: Google's Pixel 10a is the affordable iPhone alternative I've wanted

Who cares about another $100 for the Pixel 11 series? The price difference between Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel devices was never huge to begin with, and most people are already firmly team Samsung or team Pixel.

Longtime Galaxy owners likely won't switch now, if the leaked Pixel 11 prices prove accurate. As for longtime Pixel users, the real question is whether this year's changes are worth the upgrade. But that's a different story.

https://www.zdnet.com/article/apple-rush.title: Apple rushes out emergency fix for screen sharing flaw on Macs - update ASAP
https://www.zdnet.com/article/apple-rush.text:
Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google.

Apple has pushed out new updates for MacOS Tahoe, Sonoma, and Sequoia in light of a serious security vulnerability.

Also: Why Apple's iOS 26.6 is worth installing (it's not just for the 91 security fixes)

Released on Thursday, the updates for all three systems patch a flaw that could allow an attacker to exploit the Screen Sharing feature to access and control your Mac.

The updates are available in three different versions, depending on which OS you run -- MacOS Tahoe 26.6.1, MacOS Sonoma 14.8.9, and MacOS Sequoia 15.7.9.

Also: Older iPhones have an unfixable security flaw - why it can't be patched and the models affected

To install the update, head to System Settings, select General, and then click Software Update. Allow the update to appear, and then click the Update Now button to install it.

Since these updates were unexpected, Apple must have considered the flaw serious enough to warrant an immediate fix. And that certainly seems to be the case. The description on the support pages says that an attacker may be able to authenticate to Screen Sharing without valid credentials.

Also: These two critical Mac security features are off by default - how to turn them on and why you should

The ability to remotely connect to another Mac has long been built into MacOS. But the current iteration of the Screen Sharing app was introduced in 2023 with MacOS Sonoma. Using this tool, you're able to access and control another Mac on your network. But to do this, you must supply a valid username and password.

Based on the description of the vulnerability, an attacker could bypass the normally required authentication and gain control of your Mac without your permission or authorization. From there, they could easily view your personal files, tamper with Mac features and settings, install malware, and even enlist your system in a botnet from which to target other computers.

Also: The best antivirus software to protect your computer in 2026

For such an attack to succeed on a home or protected network, the hacker would first need to gain that initial access. But on a public and unprotected network, that access would be easy enough to pull off.

Apple didn't indicate that the flaw had been exploited in any known attacks. But the potential is there, which is why you should install the update ASAP.

Today is a sad day for Android enthusiasts. OnePlus has officially ceased operations across North America and Europe. It will no longer launch new smartphones or restock existing models in either region. The company first announced the decision to leave on July 16 over on its Community blog. OnePlus states that this move is the result of a "proactive global strategy adjustment" and also thanks its customers for their years of support. As part of the shutdown, the official Community app and website will go offline on August 16 at 11:59 p.m. EST. The final smartphone released in these markets was the OnePlus 15.

Since July 16, the OnePlus 15 has been available for purchase on the company's official website, but it has since sold out, along with nearly every other product in the catalog. As of this writing, only eight items are still available for purchase:

So, it's just a bunch of accessories. You can still find OnePlus phones on sale through third-party retailers. Amazon, for example, still has the OnePlus 15R for $699. Keep in mind that the remaining stock is limited. Once those devices sell out, they're gone forever, leaving the secondhand markets like eBay as your only option.

The reason for the brand's exit from these regions is unclear, beyond the vague phrase "strategy adjustment." There is a lot of speculation online. Some people believe the exit is due to the ongoing global RAM shortage; maybe OnePlus couldn't get the components it needs for the phones. Bloomberg, in a recent report, said the decision is related to stiff competition from phone giants, such as Samsung and Apple, as OnePlus struggled to gain market momentum. Others point to geopolitical tensions between the United States and Canada.

Also: 5 ways I speed up my Android phone beyond clearing system cache - all for free

Regardless of what happened, one question lingers on everybody's mind.

If you're worried that your OnePlus is about to become obsolete overnight, don't be. In a recent Notice of Business Adjustment, OnePlus said customers in affected regions will continue to receive promised software updates, security patches, and customer support until a device's end-of-service date. As an example, the OnePlus 15 is set to receive four years of updates. Your warranty will remain valid, and you can repair your device through the company's official service network.

Also: How long should you keep your phone for? I did the math - it's likely not what you think

Arguably, the biggest change is the end of the operating system, OxygenOS. OnePlus is retiring the system globally in favor of parent company Oppo's ColorOS. ColorOS 17 is slated to be the next major update. The system promises to bring a smoother software experience and better performance. Oppo hasn't announced a release date for the new OS, although it could be soon. OnePlus has launched a closed beta program for ColorOS 17 for OnePlus 15 users in India.

ColorOS 17 is not mandatory. OnePlus stated that users will have the option to switch. If you do switch, you can roll back to OxygenOS. However, there is a catch, as "specific rollback versions available will be subject to future official announcements." This statement means the rollback may differ from your initial OxygenOS build.

OnePlus isn't disappearing entirely. Following its exit from North America and Europe, the company will narrow its focus to China and India. However, as noted in the Bloomberg report mentioned earlier, that strategy may not be permanent, as the brand reportedly plans to exit India in 2027. OnePlus also isn't finished making phones. Recent leaks suggested the OnePlus 16 is currently in development.

Also: Slow Android phone? My 4-step refresh routine can speed it up fast

Determined fans may try to import the OnePlus 16 and connect the device to a local carrier. Unfortunately, that approach may not work. Carrier support isn't guaranteed, as they can choose which smartphones from around the world they will provide service to. AT&T has a BYOD (bring-your-own-device) program that lets you add any phone to the network, meaning the connection might work, but I have my doubts.

If you were planning to buy a OnePlus phone, you'll now have to look elsewhere. Lucky for you, I have plenty of suggestions.

My top recommendation is Nothing. Founded by OnePlus co-founder Carl Pei, the company has carved out a similar niche by delivering premium mobile devices at a competitive price. They stand out even further with their unique user interface and eye-catching designs. Models like the Nothing Phone (4a) Pro feel like a spiritual successor to early OnePlus devices. They offer a similar streamlined experience to the one that made people fall in love with OnePlus in the first place.

Nothing Phone 4a Pro in silver.

Motorola is another strong choice if value is a top priority. I've reviewed several Motorola models over the past couple of years, and they've impressed me with their great balance of performance and battery. For recommendations, check out the 2025 Razr Edge and 2026 Moto G Play. If you want a more luxurious Motorola device, I suggest the 2026 Razr Ultra.

Also: I've been using the Galaxy Z Fold 8 for two weeks - these two accessories perfect the experience

For people wanting to spend more, Samsung and Apple remain the premium options. Both brands offer industry-leading cameras, top-notch hardware, and mature ecosystems packed with great accessories. The Galaxy S26 Ultra is the best choice if you want to stay with Android, while the iPhone 17 Pro is the best way to experience iOS.

As someone who's used OnePlus phones for years, I am very disappointed. I currently own the OnePlus 13R, and before that, I used the Nord N20. I loved both. The devices consistently delivered strong performance, housed high-quality cameras, and had great battery lives. With OnePlus leaving the market, Android buyers have fewer choices than before.

I plan to use my OnePlus 13R until its final firmware update. After that, I'm not sure where to go. Samsung seems like the obvious choice, but I've never been a fan of how much bloat is a part of the Galaxy experience. I could see myself switching to an iPhone, but I think my next phone will be a Motorola. As stated, I have been consistently impressed by Motorola devices recently. If that streak continues, I'll probably get whatever Razr model comes out in 2030.

https://www.zdnet.com/article/what-do-cy.text:
