https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: High LDL rising globally while associated mortality falls
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

The number of adults with elevated LDL increased from 2.5 billion in 1990 to 4.6 billion in 2023, with 6% of all global deaths attributable to high LDL in 2023, according to study findings published in JAMA.

Although age-standardized deaths and disability-adjusted life-years associated with elevated LDL decreased since 1990, the LDL burden shifted and now affects more middle-income countries, researchers reported.

“LDL is one of the most established, modifiable drivers of ASCVD, yet most data track population lipid trends in isolation from actual outcomes,” Christian Razo, PhD, acting assistant professor in the department of health metrics sciences at the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation and University of Washington, told Healio. “We wanted to quantify the ischemic heart disease and stroke burden attributable to elevated LDL globally and identify where that burden is growing fastest and why.

“LDL’s causal role has been settled for decades, and there are well-known, effective lifestyle and medical interventions available. Despite decades of knowledge, surveillance, testing and treatment still aren’t reaching most people at risk,” Razo told Healio. “The findings function less as a discovery and more as a measurement of a known, preventable problem that isn’t being acted on at the scale the evidence has demanded for years.”

For the present study, the Global Burden of Disease 2023 LDL Cholesterol Collaborators used data from 204 countries and territories to estimate population-level LDL exposure, data from 806 studies across 161 countries to calculate mean LDL levels and data from 38 randomized trials to assess relative risk for ischemic heart disease and stroke related to elevated LDL.

Trends from 1990 to 2023 in LDL burden and its impact on mortality and DALYs were reported.

During that time, the global number of adults aged at least 25 years with LDL of 54 mg/dL or higher increased from approximately 2.5 billion to 4.6 billion, according to the study.

Researchers reported that countries with the lowest age-standardized mean LDL levels — less than 80 mg/dL — included Burkina Faso, Lesotho, Somalia and Rwanda. Countries with the highest age-standardized mean LDL levels — more than 135 mg/dL — included Serbia, Slovenia, Russia, Norway and Austria.

From 1990 to 2023, sharp increases in age-standardized mean LDL were reported in countries with low LDL levels at baseline, such as São Tomé and Príncipe, Cameroon and Bangladesh, whereas consistent declines in LDL levels were observed in several high sociodemographic index countries such as Belgium, the Netherlands, Norway, Finland, Germany, Switzerland and Sweden.

In 2023, elevated LDL accounted for 3.6 million deaths, or 6% of global mortality, and 90.7 million DALYs; however, rates of age-standardized death decreased 45.6% and rates of age-standardized DALYs decreased 39.5% since 1990, according to the study.

“Our results can be used to inform regional- and country-level policies that strengthen surveillance systems and position primary care as the delivery point for cholesterol screening and treatment,” Razo told Healio. “They also can serve as a benchmark. Country- and region-level breakdowns show where health systems are losing ground, whether from rising exposure, an aging population or stalled care quality or other factors, compared against similar peers rather than the global average. That specificity can guide where to prioritize resources, from promoting lifestyle interventions to expanding healthcare and treatment access.”

After omitting risk related to other modifiable risk factors, researchers reported that DALY rates associated with elevated LDL shifted toward middle-sociodemographic areas since 1990.

“The larger shift needed is from treating CVD after it presents to catching cardiometabolic risk decades earlier, starting with baseline lipid screening in childhood rather than waiting for a first cardiac event,” Razo told Healio. “Because obesity, high BP, high fasting plasma glucose and high LDL often coexist in the same patients, health systems also need combined approaches that screen for and manage these risk factors jointly, rather than in isolation.”

Christian Razo, PhD, is acting assistant professor in the department of health metrics sciences at the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation and University of Washington. Razo can be reached at razoc@uw.edu.

GBD 2023 LDL Cholesterol Collaborators. JAMA. 2026;doi:10.1001/jama.2026.8628.

Disclosures: Razo reports no relevant financial disclosures. Please see the study for all other authors’ relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/hematology-o.title: Patients comfortable with AI-created portal messages
https://www.healio.com/news/hematology-o.author: Josh Friedman
https://www.healio.com/news/hematology-o.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Many patients report high comfort with health systems using AI-written portal messages, noting it gets them information quickly and reduces clinician workload.

Their comfort comes with caveats, though. Patients want both clinician oversight and transparency that AI is being used.

“Pretty much everyone in our sample recognized that this could be a helpful tool,” Kellie Owens, PhD, assistant professor in the department of population health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine, told Healio.

“[However], patients were very clear that they see AI not as something they wanted to replace human judgment or involvement, but something they wanted to work hand-in-hand, to make clinicians’ work easier, to automate the things that can be automated, but still very much seeing the ultimate responsibility lying on the clinician to provide good care.”

Healio previously reported that annual patient-authored portal messages across 2,000 hospitals and 40,000 clinics increased 153% between 2020 and 2025.

Clinicians and staff authored 3.25 billion messages during that time.

Prior research has shown that the increase in portal communication has contributed to both clinician burnout and dissatisfaction, according to study background.

Many health care practices and institutions have started using AI to compose messages to patients to reduce clinician workload.

Healio previously reported on a survey of nearly 1,500 participants that showed significantly higher satisfaction with AI-generated responses than human-written ones. However, patients also had significantly higher satisfaction if they found out messages came from clinicians instead of AI.

Participants viewed vignettes of low-, medium- and high-risk messages, ranging from prescription refills to medication side effects to seeing lab results that could provoke concerns.

“We wanted to do a follow-up to that survey, to chat with patients to try to understand why we saw these results,” Owens said. “One of the benefits of qualitative research is being able to dive more deeply into why patients feel the way they do about AI integration, what it might mean for patient-provider relationships, what it might mean for their trust levels with their health care institutions, and ways that AI can help them in their health care journey.”

The study included 40 participants from the previous survey (75% women; 35% Black; 32.5% white; 25% aged 55-64 years).

Perspectives on portal messaging preferences, comfort with AI responses, message content and tone, and disclosure expectations served as primary endpoints.

Most interviewees reported portal messaging served a “transactional” purpose, researchers described.

The portal provides patients a pathway to get information, have questions answered or finish administrative tasks.

They expect to use the portal to manage their clinical needs in a quick, concise way.

“It doesn’t really need to be very personal. It just needs to be quick and to the point. ... You see that I’m having issues, and how do I address them?” one participant said.

“I came in with a naive assumption that the purpose of these chats with your clinician online is that you want to have some sort of human-to-human connection about something meaningful in your health care,” Owens said. “What we found is that’s not really how folks use these online tools.”

Even patients who expressed lower comfort with AI overall had minimal issues with AI in this context.

One participant noted AI reduces “personal touch” and they expressed concern over “losing” contact with their clinician. The interviewee did not have a problem with the transactional approach in the portal, though.

“I’m only looking for [a personal touch] in person, not online. ... that’s online ... it’s a machine, so I don’t expect the interpersonal,” they said.

Participants reported high comfort with AI-drafted communication across message types.

“I was surprised,” Owens said. “Even in our higher medical severity examples, like, ‘I’m worried about this mass found on imaging, what can you tell me about it?’ Folks still were mostly OK with AI being used in the drafting of those messages. The AI-drafted message didn’t say, ‘We think you have cancer.’ It said something like, ‘Here’s a little bit more detail about what this might mean. Let’s have a conversation in person or please call our office, here’s how you can schedule an appointment.’”

However, most interviewees described their comfort as conditional on clinician oversight.

“I feel like if AI can generate a message that the doctors feel comfortable with, and it answers all the questions that the patients have, it’s a win for both the doctors and for the patients, because we’re going to get responded to quicker because they’re not having to sit there and generate a message from scratch and AI is going to help them to keep things moving and flowing quicker,” one participant said.

“I think as long as there’s an indication ... that somebody reviewed it before they sent it, that alleviates any fears,” added another.

Viewpoints on message content and empathy varied considerably. Some participants preferred short responses with no personal touch. Others preferred empathy and a “customer service” tone, researchers wrote.

“I usually just want to get an answer. I don’t need all of the extra stuff. I’m not expecting [empathy] that I might expect if I were in the office with my doctor directly, but from just messaging ... I don’t need the empathy. I don’t need ‘I’m sorry that you’re feeling this way’ or anything like that. I just want the answers at that point,” one participant said.

“I really liked kindness and leading with kindness,” another said.

In general, interviewees preferred shorter responses to low-risk messages and longer responses to higher-risk queries.

All participants agreed that transparency was important. However, the way in which systems disclosed use of AI did not matter.

“Patients are very clear that transparency is helpful,” Owens said.

Researchers acknowledged study limitations, including the small sample size.

Owens noted several areas of future research regarding AI use in the portal and overall, beginning with how to disclose AI use “appropriately.”

Owens also wants to see additional research on how much time clinicians are saving when using AI tools.

“If you are ultimately responsible for assessing the quality and content of an AI-generated summary in an electronic health record, is that saving time for you, or are you spending just as much time with the editing and review than you might if you were just taking your own notes?” Owens asked. “We’ve seen some minor time savings, and maybe as the tech gets better and folks become more comfortable with it, we’ll see greater efficiency there.

“I also want to track whether they’re actually going in and editing. Are they spotting when there is a problem? If they’re not, then it’s a little bit more disingenuous to say that these are truly clinician-reviewed messages.”

Owens described herself as “nervous” when discussing whether future AI iterations could tailor messages based on individual patient preference.

“I’m certainly interested in studies where people try to mimic the tone that a patient wants to see how that works, but I would be nervous about whether the tools are good enough, whether patient preferences are stable enough to get that right,” she said. “Instead, we could potentially change tone and content based on the question that the patient asks. It would still be stable across individuals, but if you’re asking about a quick medication refill, you can have a different tone than for some of these higher medical severity questions.”

Owens also highlighted the importance of continued monitoring and maintenance of AI systems.

Teva Brender, MD, resident physician at UCSF, and Elizabeth Dzeng, MD, PhD, MPH, associate professor of medicine at UCSF, agreed in an accompanying editorial in JAMA Network Open.

“Patients’ perspectives — informed by their experiences with AI in health care and in their personal and professional lives — will continue to evolve as social norms adapt to rapid technological change,” they wrote. “One can imagine a not-too-distant future where disclosing AI’s role in portal messaging will feel as superfluous as disclosing the use of spell check. All studies exploring patients’ views on AI in medicine should therefore be understood as key snapshots in time: provisional, not permanent.”

Kellie Owens, PhD, can be reached at kellie.owens@nyulangone.org.

Owens K, et al. JAMA Netw Open. 2026;doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.22463.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: PREVENT improves CV risk prediction in Native Americans
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

SCOTTSDALE, Ariz. — The PREVENT equations predict risk for cardiovascular disease, atherosclerotic CVD and heart failure in Native Americans better than earlier models, researchers reported.

At the American Society for Preventive Cardiology (ASPC) Congress on CVD Prevention, Mohan Satish, MD, postdoctoral fellow in cardiovascular diseases at NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital and Weill Cornell Medicine, presented findings validating the PREVENT equations in Native Americans, who were included in the “other” race/ethnicity category in the development of the PREVENT equations due to low representation. Satish won the award for best oral abstract on the first day of the ASPC Congress.

“There’s a disproportionate prevalence of cardiometabolic risks, specifically current tobacco smoking and diabetes among American Indians, contributing to their burden of cardiovascular disease at the very top of their causes of death, much like other race/ethnic subgroups, in addition to diabetic deaths overall in this population,” Satish said during a presentation. “We have made strides with the PREVENT equations with the incorporation of more cardiometabolic risk, but we have an unknown representation of American Indians in their development, and likewise in subsequent validation efforts, often pooled within this other race and ethnicity subgroup. So we took it upon ourselves to ask the question about how this would work within this understudied cohort of individuals within the Strong Heart Study.”

The Strong Heart Study is a prospective cohort of Native American participants from 12 tribes or communities in Arizona, North Dakota, Oklahoma and South Dakota, in which original participants were recruited from 1989 to 1991 and family members were recruited from 2001 to 2003, Satish said during the presentation, noting that the cohort has been used to validate previous risk tools, but only for coronary heart disease, with one producing a C-statistic of 0.73 in women and 0.71 in men.

For the present validation effort, the researchers analyzed data from 3,613 participants (median age, 56 years; 1,382 men) free from CV events at baseline, of whom 40.5% had hypertension, 85.7% had dyslipidemia, 53.2% had obesity, 31.4% had diabetes, 4.5% had chronic kidney disease and 36.5% were current smokers.

The 10-year cumulative incidence of CVD was 8.2%, the 10-year cumulative incidence of ASCVD was 5.5% and the 10-year cumulative incidence of HF was 4.6%, Satish said.

The model for total CVD had good discrimination and adequate calibration with some overestimation in men (Harrell’s C-statistic, 0.783 overall, 0.739 in men, 0.808 in women), the model for ASCVD had good discrimination and adequate calibration with some underfitting in women (Harrell’s C-statistic, 0.777 overall, 0.76 in men, 0.786 in women) and the model for HF had better discrimination and calibration than those for total CVD or ASCVD (Harrell’s C-statistic, 0.805 overall, 0.77 in men, 0.831 in women), Satish said.

“We didn’t look at the enhanced PREVENT models that incorporate urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio or HbA1c,” Satish said during the presentation. “But having said that, it demonstrates very nice predictive performance compared to what we had before for both total CVD, ASCVD and heart failure compared to the prior models. Hopefully with some additional work to address the high prevalence (13%) of individuals with extreme risk factor values that precluded risk calculation (eg, BMI > 40 kg/m2), we can present an opportunity for broadly applying some of the primary prevention efforts that we have discussed for quite some time now in this historically understudied population.”

Satish M, et al. Abstract S202. Presented at: American Society for Preventive Cardiology Congress on CVD Prevention; July 31-Aug. 2, 2026; Scottsdale, Ariz.

Disclosures: Satish reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.author: Lucas Laboy; Michael Greger, MD; Michelle L. Tollefson, MD, FACOG, FACLM, DipABLM
https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Clinicians should look for supporting evidence when answering questions about the latest nutrition trends or providing dietary recommendations, according to Michael Greger, MD, FACLM.

“You don’t want to change your clinical practice based on one study,” Greger said during a Healio Community webinar. “We want overwhelming evidence of benefit before we recommend it.”

In the webinar, Michelle Tollefson, MD, FACLM, an OB/GYN and professor in the department of health professions at Metropolitan State University of Denver, spoke with Greger, a founding member and fellow of the American College of Lifestyle Medicine, and physician author, about various nutritional questions that clinicians may hear when counseling patients.

When asked what physicians may underemphasize in obesity counseling, Greger said calorie counts are not just about what you eat, but how and when.

“One hundred calories of chickpeas has a different impact than 100 calories of chicken or chiclets based on their ... impacts on things like absorption, appetite [and] our microbiomes,” he said. “The same number of calories ... at a different time of day, in a different meal distribution, or even after different amounts of sleep can translate into different amounts of body fat.”

When considering ultraprocessed foods vs. plant-based choices and alternatives, clinicians should ask “compared to what,” Greger said.

“[It’s] the most important question in the field of nutrition,” Greger said. “Are plant-based milks and meats healthy? Well, compared to the animal products that they were designed to replace? Absolutely. Though whole plant foods would be even better.”

When making dietary decisions, a “single swap” can make a difference, Greger said.

“Swapping even just one serving of plant-based meat a day nationwide could prevent more than 100,000 cases [of] heart disease, stroke and cancer in the U.S. every year,” he said.

The best dietary changes to improve health and longevity are the simplest ones, according to Greger.

“One needn’t make drastic changes,” Greger said. “Even these basic, common sense lifestyle factors can mean literally living a decade longer. Not smoking, not being obese, regular exercise, more fruits and vegetables. Just those four — and it’s never too late.”

Tollefson and Greger also discussed studies and randomized controlled trials exploring how nutritional choices may impact cognitive health, mood and depression, and chronic pain. They also discuss how to personalize nutritional choices by focusing on specific markers, such as LDL, to move away from proinflammatory diets.

To catch future conversations like this with physician authors on Healio Community, register here or join the Healio Community Food is Medicine group.

Greger M, et al. Clinician to Clinician with Dr. Greger: A Conversation About Health with Michelle Tollefson, MD, FACLM, and Michael Greger, MD, FACLM. Healio Community webinar. July 21, 2026.

Disclosures: Greger and Tollefson report no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.title: Tirzepatide reduces heart risks in real-world setting
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.author: Michael Monostra
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Tirzepatide reduced risk for major adverse cardiovascular events among adults with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, according to real-world data published in The BMJ.

As Healio previously reported, the SURPASS-CVOT trial found tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Eli Lilly) conferred a similar reduction in risk for CV events as dulaglutide (Trulicity, Eli Lilly) among adults with type 2 diabetes and atherosclerotic CVD. In a new study using data from two national claims databases in the U.S., researchers compared CV outcomes among adults using tirzepatide with those using the DPP-IV inhibitor sitagliptin (Januvia, Merck).

“The recent CV outcomes trial, SURPASS-CVOT, established that tirzepatide was noninferior to dulaglutide, but it did not directly quantify the CV benefit of adding tirzepatide to contemporary standard care,” Nils Krüger, MD, MPH, physician data scientist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, told Healio. “This matters because clinicians and patients often want to know not only how tirzepatide compares with another active treatment, but also how much benefit they might expect from initiating it.”

Researchers collected data from the Optum Clinformatics and Merative MarketScan databases of adults aged at least 40 years with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic CVD from May 2022 to May 2025. Propensity score matching was used to compare 7,442 adults receiving tirzepatide with an equal number of people using sitagliptin. Sitagliptin was used as a placebo proxy because it has been shown to have no effect, beneficial or harmful, on CV outcomes, the researchers wrote.

The primary outcome was major adverse CV events, which were a composite of myocardial infarction, stroke and all-cause mortality. An expanding composite outcome consisting of MI, stroke, coronary revascularization and unstable angina was also assessed.

During a mean on-treatment follow-up of 182 days, 1-year risk for a major adverse CV event was 2.9% with tirzepatide and 4.4% with sitagliptin. Adults receiving tirzepatide had reduced risk for major adverse CV events compared with those receiving sitagliptin (HR = 0.68; 95% CI, 0.58-0.8).

Tirzepatide was associated with lower risk for MI (HR = 0.67; 95% CI, 0.52-0.87) and all-cause mortality (HR = 0.55; 95% CI, 0.42-0.72) compared with sitagliptin. There was no difference in ischemic stroke risk.

In analysis of the expanded composite endpoint, tirzepatide was associated with lower risk for major adverse CV events than sitagliptin (HR = 0.92; 95% CI, 0.85-0.99).

“For patients with type 2 diabetes and established CVD, the findings support viewing tirzepatide as more than a glucose- or weight-lowering treatment,” Krüger said. “Its potential CV benefit can be discussed in absolute terms during shared decision-making.”

Adults receiving tirzepatide had lower risk for infection-related mortality than those using sitagliptin (HR = 0.4; 95% CI, 0.26-0.61). Tirzepatide also reduced risk for infections leading to hospital admission (HR = 0.64; 95% CI, 0.55-0.75), infections in any care setting (HR = 0.83; 95% CI, 0.78-0.87) and urinary tract infections (HR = 0.83; 95% CI, 0.76-0.91) compared with sitagliptin.

“This is an intriguing signal that warrants further investigation and points to additional benefits of incretin-based therapies beyond their established metabolic effects,” Krüger said of the reduced infections risk with tirzepatide.

According to Krüger, longer-term studies are needed to better assess CV benefit with tirzepatide.

“Future research should also disentangle atherosclerotic from nonatherosclerotic mechanisms, and determine how much of the reduction in mortality may be related to fewer serious infections,” Krüger said.

Nils Krüger, MD, MPH, is a physician data scientist in the division of pharmacoepidemiology and pharmacoeconomics, department of medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School; and resident physician in the department of cardiology at TUM University Hospital German Heart Center at Technical University of Munich in Germany. Krüger can be reached at nkruger1@bwh.harvard.edu or LinkedIn @nilskruger.

Krüger N, et al. BMJ. 2026;doi:10.1136/bmj-2026-100011.

Disclosures: Krüger reports no relevant financial disclosures. Please see the study for all other authors’ relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: Avoiding three risk factors extends life without dementia
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Andrew (Drew) Rhoades
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Not smoking, having normal BP and no diabetes may extend life without dementia by almost 13 years, a new study in Neurology Open Access shows.

“Our findings support prevention of risk factors developing in midlife as a strategy for delaying the onset of dementia and maintaining brain health,” Josef Coresh, MD, PhD, a professor at NYU Grossman School of Medicine, said in a press release. “Finding ways to prevent or delay dementia is crucial as the population ages as treatments remain limited.”

Healio previously reported that addressing over a dozen risk factors, including depression, hypertension, obesity, vision loss and physical inactivity, could prevent or delay nearly half of dementia cases globally.

Prior studies assessing vascular health risk factors for dementia “have largely focused on etiologic associations or cumulative risk metrics, which do not directly capture how vascular health shapes the timing and duration of dementia-free survival years,” Coresh and colleagues wrote.

The researchers assessed 12,409 participants (56% women, 25.2% Black) from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study, who were free of dementia at age 55 years and were followed over a median 26.3 years.

During that follow-up period, 3,008 participants developed dementia and 5,238 died free of dementia.

Three risk factors — current smoking, hypertension and diabetes — increased the risk for dementia (HR = 2.69; 95% CI, 1.94-3.73) and death without dementia (HR = 5.61; 95% CI, 4.67-6.74) vs. zero risk factors.

“Dementia-free survival years, which quantifies the expected duration of life lived cognitively intact,” decreased with more risk factors, dropping from 30.1 years (95% CI, 29.9-30.4) for zero risk factors to 26.3 years (95% CI, 26.1-26.6) for one risk factor, 21 years (95% CI, 20.5-21.4) for two risk factors and 17.5 years (95% CI, 16.3-18.7) for three factors, Coresh and colleagues reported.

Multiple biological mechanisms, “including chronic cerebrovascular injury, neuroinflammation triggered by vascular damages through hypertension and diabetes, and cumulative oxidative stress resulting from smoking,” may explain the associations, they added.

The outcomes varied for different populations. Women with three risk factors lived longer without dementia vs. men (18.1 vs. 16.6 years) and Black participants had fewer dementia-free survival years vs. white participants (16 vs. 19.6 years).

“Women more often reach older ages and, therefore, experience many cases of late-onset dementia,” Coresh said in the release.

Coresh and colleagues acknowledged that limiting their assessment to three vascular risk factors “rather than a comprehensive cardiometabolic profile ... may not fully reflect clinical risk assessment but allows transparent translation of vascular burden into time-based outcomes.”

“Hopefully these results will help encourage people to stop smoking, manage their blood sugar and manage their BP in midlife,” Coresh said in the release. “Of course, other healthy habits such as eating better and being more active are also important.”

Hu J, et al. Neurology. 2026;doi:10.1212/WN9.0000000000000152.

Disclosures: Coresh and colleagues report no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/pediatrics/2.title: Senate confirms Schwartz as CDC director
https://www.healio.com/news/pediatrics/2.author: Sara Kellner
https://www.healio.com/news/pediatrics/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Erica Schwartz, MD, JD, MPH, will become the first full-time director of the CDC in nearly 1 year after senators confirmed her to the post on Wednesday, largely along party lines.

Senators voted 51-44 in favor of Schwartz’s confirmation, with all Republicans voting “yea” and all Democrats except Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., voting “nay.”

Five senators — two Democrats and three Republicans — did not vote. Kaine was also the only Democrat who voted in support of her nomination in committee last week.

Schwartz served as deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first presidential term. She spent 24 years as an occupational medicine physician in the U.S. Navy and Coast Guard and was the U.S. Coast Guard’s chief medical officer and director of health, safety and work life from 2015 to 2019.

She will take the reins of a public health agency that has been without a permanent director since Susan Monarez, PhD, was fired last August after less than a month on the job.

During Schwartz’s nomination hearing, she told senators that her goal as CDC director would be to restore trust in public health institutions and modernize the CDC's response to infectious disease outbreaks.

Schwartz also said she would “lead with integrity” and would not betray science.

Paul A. Offit, MD, director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, told Healio after her nomination hearing that he was not convinced by her statements.

For more on the nomination process and reaction to Schwartz’s hearing, check out our collection of healthcare policy stories.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Large language models fail to produce adequate diet plans for patients with hypertension
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

SCOTTSDALE, Ariz. — A new feasibility study found significant safety and quality gaps in AI-generated meal plans for hypertension, according to findings presented at the American Society for Preventive Cardiology Congress on CVD Prevention.

Vijaya Parameswaran, MS, PhD, RD, postdoctoral fellow at Stanford Prevention Research Center, Stanford University School of Medicine, and colleagues compared the performance of three large language models (LLMs) with those of a dietitian at devising a 1-week meal plan for two hypothetical patients with hypertension, one an American omnivore and one an Indian vegetarian. Parameswaran won the Best Early Career Abstract award at the meeting.

“Because of the public health and our healthcare system, we are not able to provide the nutrition care our population needs,” Parameswaran said during a presentation. “In parallel, there is growing enthusiasm around large language models in nutrition care. But before we deploy these models in the patients with chronic disease, we must think about whether these are safe, accurate and appropriate. And that’s what our study decided to evaluate. We show that these models are not there yet.”

The researchers compared diet plans generated by three LLMs — Claude 3.7, GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 — with one generated by a dietitian in terms of adherence to Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) nutrition guidelines and culturally specific patient dietary needs.

The plans were evaluated for acceptability, defined as expected tastiness, preparation appropriateness, cultural appropriateness and image appeal; harm potential, defined as excess saturated fat, excess sodium and calorie imbalance; and accuracy, defined as DASH concordance, nutrition prescription concordance and U.S. Department of Agriculture identifier concordance, Parameswaran said during the presentation.

Expected tastiness and preparation appropriateness scores for all three LLMs were inferior to those of the dietitian (P < .05 for all), whereas for cultural appropriateness, DeepSeek-R1 was inferior to the dietitian (OR = 0.33; 95% CI, 0.15-0.71; P = .005) and the others were numerically worse, and for image appeal, GPT-4o (OR = 0.34; 95% CI, 0.18-0.63; P < .001) and DeepSeek-R1 (OR = 0.25; 95% CI, 0.13-0.45; P < .001) were inferior to the dietitian and Claude 3.7 was numerically worse, according to the researchers.

The dietitian vastly outperformed the LLMs on DASH score (American omnivore, 9 vs. 2.4 to 3.1; Indian vegetarian, 7 vs. 1.9 to 4.1), nutrition prescription score (American omnivore, 7/7 vs. 3/7 to 4/7; Indian vegetarian, 7/7 vs. 2/7 to 3/7), mean daily harm score (American omnivore, 0 vs. 0.57 to 1; Indian vegetarian, 0 vs. 1.57 to 1.71) and days with any harm (American omnivore, 0/7 vs. 3/7 to 6/7; Indian vegetarian, 0/7 vs. 7/7), Parameswaran and colleagues found.

For the concordance performance, “the large language models ... were to share an identifier if they used it to retrieve nutrition information from the USDA’s database,” Parameswaran said. “The concordance with this was very low and concerning because it was clear that all the identifiers that the GPT model generated were made up. And there was low concordance [for] both Claude and DeepSeek.”

“LLMs’ role in therapeutic meal planning should be limited to expert-facing suggestions, at least for now, in their current form, until safety and guideline adherence can be consistently established,” Parameswaran said during the presentation. “Once guidelines, concordance and safety can be established ... with good pre- and post-processing, we will be able to get there.”

Parameswaran V, et al. Early career research presentations. Presented at: American Society for Preventive Cardiology Congress on CVD Prevention; July 31-Aug. 2, 2026; Scottsdale, Ariz.

Disclosures: Parameswaran reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/dermatology/.title: 5-step action plan aims to bridge psoriasis, metabolic disease gap
https://www.healio.com/news/dermatology/.author: Gabrielle M. Grasso
https://www.healio.com/news/dermatology/.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

The International Psoriasis Council has released a list of five recommendations for prioritized action items that will help dermatologists incorporate metabolic disease considerations into psoriasis care.

Researchers attending the 2025 International Psoriasis Council Think Tank symposium identified metabolic disease management as the primary unmet need and future priority of psoriasis treatment, according to a summary paper published in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. Based on feedback from more than 150 survey responses from dermatologists, the five finalized action items are:

These recommendations highlight the shifting understanding of psoriatic disease among physicians, according to Joel M. Gelfand, MD, MSCE, FAAD, Healio Dermatology’s Chief Medical Editor and one of the paper’s authors.

“The modern view of psoriasis is that it is a systemic inflammatory metabolic disease,” Gelfand told Healio. “The International Psoriasis Council has prioritized key areas of action and research to address the rapidly developing data in this area that has important implications for clinical practice.”

The authors called the priorities a “practical roadmap” that will help promote multidisciplinary collaboration, identify cardiometabolic risk factors early and spur more targeted research, particularly for younger patients who may not receive timely follow-up care.

During the council’s symposium, dermatologists reported that psoriasis is associated with elevated risks for metabolic and cardiovascular diseases, with psoriasis severity levels directly impacting these odds, according to the paper. Obesity can similarly impact psoriasis severity as well as the effectiveness of psoriasis therapies, according to the authors.

“Mendelian randomization studies show obesity/visceral adiposity and CVD risk contribute to psoriasis pathogenesis,” the authors wrote. “Adiposity should be considered a primary target of effective psoriasis therapy in overweight or obese patients.”

Genetic studies and clinical observations have demonstrated that GLP-1 receptor agonists, initially approved for type 2 diabetes, can protect against psoriatic disease, suggesting combination treatment with biologics may improve patient outcomes, according to the authors.

“Dermatologists, rather than acting as primary care providers, are well-positioned to screen for increased metabolic risk in psoriasis patients by leveraging the frequent dermatology visits these patients already attend,” the authors wrote. “Subsequent coordination with other specialties would increase preventative benefit.”

Joel M. Gelfand, MD, MSCE, FAAD, is the James J. Leyden Professor of Clinical Investigation and professor of dermatology and epidemiology at University of Pennsylvania’s Perelman School of Medicine and Healio Dermatology’s Chief Medical Editor. Gelfand can be reached at dermatology@healio.com.

Strober BE, et al. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2026;doi:10.1016/j.jaad.2026.07.066.

Disclosures: Gelfand reports having financial relationships with multiple drug and device companies. Please see the summary paper for all other authors’ relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: AI photo-based calorie-tracking tools underestimate them by 33%
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Emma Bascom
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. — Many individuals use AI-powered calorie-tracking apps as a tool for weight loss, but these apps may underestimate the calories in the meals, according to research presented at the annual NUTRITION meeting.

“Photo-based calorie tracking apps are very popular, especially for people trying to manage their health or lose weight,” Aaron Hengist, PhD, a postdoctoral visiting fellow with the intramural program of the NIH’s National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, said in a press release “However, the accuracy of many of these apps has not been thoroughly evaluated. Our study helps address this question by looking at whether these apps can reliably estimate calories.”

For the controlled feeding study, the researchers prepared 102 nutrient-controlled meals using national food composition tables. They used four commercially available apps — Appediet, Cal AI, Lose It! and MyFitnessPal — to analyze pictures of the meals. Then, they compared the differences in macronutrient and energy content between the food composition tables and apps with paired t tests.

“By using meals prepared in a tightly controlled metabolic kitchen, we were able to compare the apps’ estimates against a precise reference,” Hengist said in the release. “This kind of direct, high-quality comparison hasn’t been available before.”

Hengist and colleagues found that the AI photograph-based features in these apps underestimated meals’ energy content by about 33%, which they said is “similar to previously reported underestimation using self-report diet assessment methods.” Each app underestimated the mean energy content slightly differently: Appediet by 252 kcal (95% CI, 295 to 210), MyFitnessPal by 327 kcal (95% CI, 385 to 269), Lose It! by 333 kcal (95% CI, 383 to 282) and Cal AI by 345 kcal (95% CI, 392 to 296). However, Lose It! and MyFitnessPal both were able to approximate the energy content of higher energy meals more accurately than lower energy meals.

Additionally, two apps — Lose It! and Cal AI — both underestimated carbohydrates by about 14 g, and all the apps underestimated fat content by 30 g.

The researchers wrote that future work should evaluate the “utility of photograph-based AI to decrease the burden of traditional diet assessment methods.”

“People using a photo-based tracking app without adjusting the portions or entering the amounts of food should take the results with a grain of salt,” Hengist said in the release. “These apps tend to underestimate calories, especially from fats, so what they actually ate is likely higher than what the app shows.”

These findings are important, but they are not entirely surprising. Decades of nutrition research have shown that accurately measuring dietary intake is one of the field’s greatest challenges, and this study suggests that AI-powered photo tracking has not yet eliminated that problem. The investigators strengthened the study by comparing four commercial apps against meals prepared in a tightly controlled metabolic kitchen, providing a high-quality reference standard. Across all four apps, energy intake was underestimated by roughly one-third, with particularly large underestimation of fat intake. Interestingly, carbohydrate estimates were more consistent than estimates for fat or overall energy, although two of the four apps still significantly underestimated carbohydrate intake. This suggests the apps perform better for some nutrients than others, but there is still room for improvement.

The greater concern isn’t simply that the estimates are imperfect — it’s that they consistently underestimate energy intake. For people trying to closely match calorie goals, this kind of systematic bias is more consequential than random error. Random error might overestimate calories one day and underestimate the next, roughly balancing out. But because these apps consistently underestimate energy intake, someone relying on them is likely eating more than they think at every meal — an error that compounds over time and works against, rather than for, weight management goals.

In short, AI may make dietary tracking easier, but it does not eliminate one of nutrition science’s oldest challenges: accurately measuring what people actually eat.

For clinicians, I don’t think the message is to discourage patients from using these apps. Rather, it’s to set appropriate expectations. These tools are probably best viewed as behavior-change aids rather than precision nutrition instruments. They can increase awareness, reduce the burden of food logging and support healthier habits, but patients should recognize that calorie and fat estimates may be systematically underestimated, particularly if they rely solely on a photograph without reviewing or adjusting the results.

The relatively more consistent carbohydrate estimates suggest these apps may provide more reliable information for carbohydrate tracking than for total energy or fat intake, although they should not be assumed to provide precise carbohydrate estimates either. The investigators also noted preliminary follow-up findings suggesting underestimation may be greater for higher-fat, lower-carbohydrate meals, meaning patients following ketogenic or other low-carbohydrate, high-fat diets should be especially cautious when interpreting the results. More broadly, when dietary assessment needs to be highly accurate — such as during medical nutrition therapy, sports nutrition or management of conditions where energy intake is closely monitored — these apps should complement, not replace, individualized nutrition assessment.

One important distinction is that this study evaluated measurement accuracy, not whether these apps improve health outcomes. Those are related but separate questions. An app doesn’t have to estimate every calorie perfectly to be clinically valuable if it helps people consistently make healthier food choices or adhere to dietary recommendations over time.

To me, the most important question isn’t whether an app counts every calorie perfectly. It’s whether it helps people build healthier eating habits that last.

Finally, because these findings are being presented as a conference abstract, they should be considered preliminary until the full study has undergone peer review.

Charles O, et al. Photograph-based AI features in calorie-tracking apps underestimate energy content of meals. Presented at: NUTRITION; July 25-28, 2026; National Harbor, Md.

Disclosures: Hengist reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: One in 10 US mothers experienced gestational hypertension in 2024
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Rates of gestational hypertension among U.S. mothers increased from 2016 to 2024 with varying differences emerging by race, age and BMI, according to study findings published in National Vital Statistics Reports.

Overall, the rate of gestational hypertension increased 73% in the U.S., and was most common in mothers of non-Hispanic Native American or Alaska Native and non-Hispanic Black race, mothers aged at least 40 years and mothers with obesity, according to Elizabeth C.W. Gregory, MPH, a health scientist at the CDC National Center for Health Statistics.

“Hypertensive disorders in pregnancy, which include chronic hypertension, chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia, gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, and eclampsia, are common pregnancy complications and are among the leading causes of maternal morbidity and mortality in the United States,” Gregory wrote. “This report describes overall trends in gestational hypertension from 2016, the first year for which national data are available based on the 2003 revision of the U.S. Standard Certificate of Live Birth (which includes race data consistent with the 1997 Office of Management and Budget standards and data to calculate body mass index), through 2024.”

A gestational hypertension notation was added to U.S. birth certificates in 1989. For the present analysis, Gregory used data from all births registered in the U.S. from 2016 to 2024 to calculate the overall rate of gestational hypertension and rates of gestational hypertension by maternal race, age, BMI, plurality and state of residence, according to the study methods.

Gregory observed that the rate of gestational hypertension increased 73%, rising from 6% in 2016 to 10.4% in 2024.

The lowest rate of gestational hypertension in 2024 was in Asian non-Hispanic individuals (7.1%), followed by Hispanic, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, white, Black and American Indian/Alaska Native subgroups (13.2%), according to the study. However, the rate of increase between 2016 and 2024 was highest in Asian mothers (103%), and every race/ethnicity subgroup had an increase of at least 66%, Gregory wrote.

In both 2016 and 2024, women aged at least 40 years had higher rates of gestational hypertension (2016, 8.2%; 2024, 12.2%) than women from other age groups, Gregory wrote.

Rates of gestational hypertension increased as maternal BMI increased, a pattern that was similar in both 2016 and 2024, according to the study.

In addition, rates of gestational hypertension were nearly twofold greater among those with twin or higher-order multiple birth compared with those with a singleton birth. This pattern was also similar in both 2016 and 2024, Gregory reported.

Rates of gestational hypertension increased in all U.S. states between 2016 and 2024, with the smallest increase of 21% observed in Idaho and the largest increase of 144% occurring in Hawaii, according to the study. The 2024 gestational hypertension rates were lowest in New Jersey (6.9%) and highest in Louisiana (14.6%), Gregory wrote.

“A primary advantage of birth certificate data is that information is collected on all women giving birth in the United States each year, allowing for analysis of both national trends and trends for smaller population groups, such as Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander subgroups,” Gregory wrote. “However, gestational hypertension is most likely underreported on the birth certificate. Despite potential reporting issues, trends and patterns in gestational hypertension observed in this report are consistent with known risk factors and findings from other studies and provide opportunities to examine gestational hypertension among all women giving birth in the United States.”

Sadly, I was not surprised by this study. As a cardiologist who specializes in CVD in pregnancy, I have questioned current published statistics as being underestimated and outdated. The numbers reported in this study help confirm the staggering trends we have been seeing in our day-to-day practices.

Another important takeaway is the universal and significant increase in gestational hypertension across all ages, races and BMI categories. For all women, regardless of their demographics or clinical risk, there was a significant increase in gestational hypertension. Historically, there was a phenotype of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy that trended with known risk factors such as obesity, advanced age, chronic hypertension and plurality. It now seems that we are seeing a new and different disease phenotype, across all demographics and even in women with no risk factors. There is something more going on here that we are missing that explain these changing trends.

Unfortunately, I agree with the authors that even these contemporary data are likely an underestimate of the true problem. Here at Atlantic Health, we recently reviewed data from 2024-2025 which showed hypertensive disorders of pregnancy rates as high as 18%.

Accurate and contemporary data is the key. These data can help drive funding and development of programs to identify and treat these women. Many women go underrecognized and undertreated due to lack of standardization and guidelines for management and treatment. While these data bring attention to the problem, we desperately need studies to understand the “why” — why are we seeing a 73% increase in gestational hypertension? If we can uncover this mystery, we can move toward preventing gestational hypertension and its complications.

Lastly, we need more widespread programs focused on the transition from pregnancy to postpartum care and beyond.  Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy not only increase the risk for maternal morbidity and mortality; they are a major risk factor for future CVD. We must not miss the window of opportunity to identify these women, educate them and create systems of care to manage and prevent their future CV risk.

Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy is an epidemic that is not getting enough attention. Although there is local variation, this crisis deserves national attention and resources to understand, address and reverse these trends. We must also look locally and internally at our own health systems. Local forces such as social determinants of health and access to healthcare must be understood and addressed. I fear that this is just the tip of the iceberg and that over time these trends will only continue to grow unless we act quickly to understand and address this epidemic.

Gregory ECW. Natl Vital Stat Rep. 2026;doi:10.15620/cdc/252456.

Disclosures: Gregory reports being an employee of the CDC.

https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.title: Off-label testosterone use may raise cardiovascular risk for men
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.author: Michael Monostra
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Men prescribed testosterone therapy despite no symptoms of hypogonadism have higher risk for major adverse cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality than men with hypogonadism using testosterone therapy, researchers reported.

In an analysis of data from the TriNetX global collaborative network published in eBioMedicine, researchers found risks for several CV events with testosterone therapy varied based on each person’s medical profile at initiation. Hatim Kerniss, MD, physician and researcher at University Hospital Frankfurt in Germany, said the findings shed light on the importance of screening men for hypogonadism prior to prescribing testosterone.

“[Testosterone] treatment should not be regarded as a general intervention for aging-related symptoms, fatigue, reduced vitality or physical performance without adequate diagnostic evaluation,” Kerniss told Healio. “Our results also support assessment and optimization of CV risk factors before treatment and careful follow-up, including monitoring of hematocrit and emerging CV symptoms.”

Kerniss and colleagues conducted a retrospective cohort study of men aged 30 to 75 years prescribed testosterone therapy beginning in 2006. Men were considered to have hypogonadism if they had at least one symptom of testicular hypofunction, total testosterone concentration of 300 ng/dL or less or free testosterone of 60 pg/mL or lower. The primary outcome was major adverse CV events, which was a composite of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, cardiac arrest and all-cause mortality.

Researchers used propensity score matching to pair 113,554 men with hypogonadism using testosterone with 113,554 men prescribed testosterone without hypogonadism.

Men without hypogonadism had higher risk for major adverse CV events than those with hypogonadism (HR = 1.51; 95% CI, 1.46-1.56; P < .001). Those without hypogonadism also had increased risk for all-cause mortality (HR = 1.9; 95% CI, 1.8-2; P < .001), ischemic stroke (HR = 1.23; 95% CI, 1.14-1.33; P < .001), MI (HR = 1.1; 95% CI, 1.02-1.17; P = .008), cardiac arrest (HR = 1.41; 95% CI, 1.23-1.61; P < .001), heart failure (HR = 1.32; 95% CI, 1.26-1.39; P < .001) and pulmonary embolism (HR = 1.15; 95% CI, 1.05-1.25; P = .002).

Median follow-up for men with hypogonadism was 1,448 days compared with 697 days for those without hypogonadism. In sensitivity analysis limiting follow-up to 2 years, men prescribed testosterone without hypogonadism continued to have increased risk for all outcomes except for MI and pulmonary embolism compared with those with hypogonadism.

In analysis of racial-ethnic subgroups, Asian men without hypogonadism had the highest increased risk for major adverse CV events (HR = 2.39) and all-cause mortality (HR = 2.98) compared with those with hypogonadism. Black men without hypogonadism had the lowest increased risk for major adverse CV events (HR = 1.31) and all-cause mortality (HR = 1.51) than those with hypogonadism (log-rank P for all < .0001). Kerniss said it was surprising to see Asian men having the highest risk for both outcomes.

“They raise important questions about whether differences in biological susceptibility, body composition, pharmacokinetics, prescribing patterns or residual confounding may influence CV risk and warrant confirmation in dedicated studies involving Asian populations,” Kerniss said.

Large prospective registry studies and real-world target-trial emulations should be conducted to confirm the findings as well as conduct more detailed analysis, Kerniss said.

“Particular attention should be paid to treatment dose and formulation, achieved testosterone levels, hematocrit changes, duration of exposure and CV risk profiles,” Kerniss said. “The pronounced signals observed in Asian men should also be examined in dedicated studies to determine whether they reflect biological susceptibility, treatment patterns or residual confounding.”

Hatim Kerniss, MD, is a physician and researcher in the department of cardiology at University Hospital Frankfurt and at the Lübeck Institute of Experimental Dermatology at University of Lübeck in Germany. Kerniss can be reached at kerniss@med.uni-frankfurt.de or LinkedIn @HatimKernissMD.

Kerniss H, et al. EBioMedicine. 2026;doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106373.

Purpose-built for physicians

U.S. News & World Report released its 2026-2027 Best Hospitals rankings Tuesday.

This year’s edition features 505 hospitals across 49 states and Washington, D.C. “that have demonstrated superior patient outcomes for a variety of common procedures and conditions,” according to a press release.

“U.S. News’ performance-driven metrics ensure American families can confidently find and choose high-quality care, often right in their own communities,” Ben Harder, U.S. News’ chief of health analysis and managing editor, said in the release.

Harder added that this edition also includes four new regional specialty rankings, including cancer; rehabilitation; cardiology, heart and vascular surgery; and orthopedics.

Listed in no particular order, the hospitals ranked or tied for first in major metropolitan areas with five or more best hospitals include:

Twenty hospitals were named to the Best Hospitals Honor Roll, which in alphabetical order include:

The hospitals ranked first across specialties are:

A Mayo Clinic representative told Healio that its recognition “reflects the dedication, expertise and collaboration of our staff and care teams. It also reflects their shared commitment to quality, compassion and putting patients at the center of everything we do. We are grateful to our staff, whose work helps Mayo Clinic deliver exceptional care and advance the future of healthcare.”

Glenn I. Fishman, MD, director of the Leon H. Charney Division of Cardiology at NYU Langone Health, said their ranking as the leading hospital in cardiovascular health “reflects years of investment in multidisciplinary cardiovascular care, where clinical excellence, innovation and research work together to improve patient outcomes.”

“Sustaining a ranking like this requires not only expertise across every aspect of heart and vascular care, but the ability to deliver that care at scale while continuing to raise the bar,” he told Healio.

Glenn I. Fishman, MD, can be reached at primarycare@healio.com.

https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.title: Medication burden on dialysis rose between 2003 and 2024
https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.author: Lucas Laboy
https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Medication burden for patients on dialysis has increased significantly between 2003 and 2024, according to study data published in Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology.

Higher medication burden is linked to increased risks for adverse drug reactions, worsened adherence and higher hospitalization and mortality rates, according to Harold J. Manley, PharmD, FASN, FCCP, senior pharmacy director at Dialysis Clinic Inc., and colleagues. Previous research on medication burden in dialysis populations has been limited by short study timeframes, the researchers wrote.

“Knowledge of patient medication burden may inform the need for possible deprescribing, to reduce patient burden and financial burden,” Manley and colleagues wrote.

In a point-prevalent analysis, the researchers assessed changes in medication burden and regimen complexity for 82,549 adults (mean age, 62 years; 44% women; 49% white) on hemodialysis (88%) or peritoneal dialysis (12%) at a Dialysis Clinic facility between 2003 and 2024. They defined medication burden in four categories:

Results showed significant increases in all four categories, according to the researchers.

The number of medications prescribed per patient-day increased from 13.4 to 15.9 (mean yearly rate increase, 0.23; 95% confidence level [CL], 0.22-0.24), pill burden increased from 18.1 to 18.6 per patient per year (mean yearly rate increase, 0.16; 95% CL, 0.15-0.17) and MRCI score increased from 29.3 to 35 (mean yearly rate of increase, 0.54; 95% CL, 0.53-0.56).

Major polypharmacy prevalence increased from 77% to 87%, with odds for major polypharmacy rising each year by 5.1% (95% CL, 4.9%-5.4%).

In addition, mean number of medications, polypharmacy prevalence and MRCI score were greater for patients using PD vs. hemodialysis, whereas mean pill burden was lower, according to the researchers.

Prescriptions for CVD and mineral and metabolic bone disease contributed most to the increased medication burden, the researchers wrote.

Overall, the findings suggest patients using hemodialysis or PD have been prescribed a greater number of medications, experienced higher rates of polypharmacy and face increasingly complex medication regimens, according to the researchers.

“Among dialysis patients in the United States, a progressive increase in polypharmacy and medication regimen complexity index over the past 22 years was observed,” Manley and colleagues wrote. “This change was driven chiefly by cardiovascular and diabetes medications. Conversely, pill burden declined modestly over the past decade, although it remains very high in this patient population.”

Manley and colleagues quantified what those of us caring for patients on dialysis witness every day: Most of our patients do not know their medicines or why they are on them, and neither do their physicians.

Our patients see many physicians across a disparate health system that communicates poorly. As we are always pressed for time, each of us focuses on what our own specialty is involved with. Nobody owns the whole list. The result is here in the data: close to 16 medications a day, and the situation is getting worse.

Guideline-directed medical therapy, which helps us translate research into practice, gives us a sense of accomplishment. However, it is changing us into machines that follow algorithms with no thinking and no soul. As the authors note, most guideline-directed medical therapy regimens were tested in cleaner populations and in trials that excluded patients on dialysis. Complexity is more than pill counts. Phosphate binders, for example, demand strict timing with meals, and I always worry that they may affect absorption of other medications. Combination pills, which are meant to help, make it harder to adjust the dose of one component, so we end up preferring the separate components, and the lists grow longer.

The result is patients with poor quality of life, either suffering through hidden adverse effects as they try to adhere to these medicines or living with the risks of nonadherence to important drugs. Polypharmacy is associated with nonadherence, hospitalizations and mortality (Oosting IJ, et al. Kidney360. 2024;doi:10.34067/KID.0000000000000447).

Deprescribing is what we really need, but it is not easy. It requires experience, time, connections with other physicians and the willingness to stop each medicine with little expected benefit while ensuring the patient is not harmed. Early work, which the authors review, shows this can be done safely, and patients welcome it.

I would like to see research define the ideal set of medications for the profiles we actually treat: patients on dialysis with diabetes, heart failure and low blood pressure vs. the young dialysis patient with diabetes and hypertension; those with poor nutrition vs. those with a great appetite prone to high phosphorus; and those with limited life expectancy vs. those expecting a transplant soon. These profiles are different, and the fact that their comorbidity lists carry the same entities does not mean their needs are the same.

Who will fund these studies, and who will conduct them, remain open questions. In this era of advanced machine learning, we have the opportunity to combine the input of different specialties across different organizations and design smart advice for each of these profiles, instead of relying on what was developed for the isolated clean profiles of clinical trials.

This will be a different paradigm from how we currently practice, and it needs the support of funders, researchers and dialysis organizations. Only then can our prescriptions serve what matters most: helping patients achieve their own goals and live better lives while prolonging life and reducing hospitalizations and wasteful practice.

Manley HJ, et al. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2026;doi:10.2215/CJN.0000001114.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Safe levels of caffeine do not harm heart health
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby; Gregory M. Marcus, MD, MAS
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Caffeine, the most commonly consumed drug in the world, may have heart-healthy benefits when consumed below certain levels and may even help prevent diabetes, according to a new American Heart Association scientific statement.

As Healio previously reported, prior research has shown various health benefits related to coffee intake, including a link to less atrial fibrillation recurrence in those with AF; anti-inflammatory benefits; and reductions in LDL with certain coffee filters.

In light of the literature, the American Heart Association issued a scientific statement, published in Circulation, detailing the relationship between caffeine intake and cardiometabolic health as well as recommendations for maximum daily intake for healthy individuals.

Gregory M. Marcus, MD, MAS, chair of the statement writing committee, and colleagues wrote that up to 400 mg, or five 8 oz cups of coffee, per day, was safe for most healthy adults and consumption may lower risk for developing diabetes.

The statement delineates the relationship between caffeine intake and CV risk factors and CVDs including arrhythmias, coronary artery disease, heart failure and stroke as well as the pharmacologic mechanism by which caffeine interacts with the cardiometabolic system.

Healio spoke with Marcus, who is a cardiologist and Endowed Professor of Atrial Fibrillation Research in the division of cardiology at the University of California, San Francisco, about the impact of caffeine on heart health; whether the type of caffeine impacts this relationship; and whether there exists any patient population who should avoid caffeine intake.

Healio: What was the motivation to publish this statement?

Marcus: Rigorous research on the topic of caffeine and CVD has been growing recently, now with randomized trials among ambulatory populations consuming common caffeinated substances — not just relying on small, laboratory-based trials of pure caffeine, for example — and a formal statement summarizing research on the subject had not previously been produced.

Healio: What are some of the common concerns you hear from patients regarding their caffeine intake?

Marcus: Many of patients that I see in my arrhythmia clinic have been told to stop caffeine consumption even though they had not actually experienced any problems with it. Many are delighted to learn that it is reasonable to drink their caffeinated coffee, assuming they had not noticed adverse consequences of it.

Healio: By what mechanism does caffeine affect CV health?

Marcus: One of the reasons caffeine is interesting to study and yet hard to summarize is because it has protean effects. Caffeine does not act on the CV system via only one mechanism, and in fact can influence different CVDs in different ways. Caffeine can amplify the effects of the sympathetic nervous system, or adrenaline, it can dilate some blood vessels as well as parts of airways in the lungs, and it can have diuretic effects leading to loss of fluid and likely salt via more urination. While caffeine does not reduce the need for sleep, it can reduce the sensation of sleepiness by blocking a naturally occurring substances in our bodies called adenosine. As an example of how none of these effects are simple, we also know that high-dose adenosine administered for medical purposes can trigger atrial fibrillation, hence blocking adenosine receptors may be one way that caffeine might protect against this common heart rhythm disturbance.

Healio: Why might caffeine intake lower diabetes risk?

Marcus: The mechanisms by which caffeine might lower diabetes risk are unclear. Short randomized trials have failed to demonstrate acute effects on lowering blood glucose, suggesting that, if indeed the observational data that those who consume caffeinated coffee experience a lower risk for diabetes is true, it is likely due to more chronic effects. There is some evidence that caffeinated coffee in particular may have beneficial effects on the liver, which in turn may have favorable effects on glucose metabolism. We found in a randomized trial of days assigned to caffeinated coffee vs. avoidance among participants wearing Fitbits, participants took an average of 1,000 more steps per day when exposed to caffeinated coffee. Therefore, these observed beneficial effects related to diabetes might be because caffeine motivates people to be more physically active.

Healio: Does the form of caffeine intake matter with regard to its cardiovascular benefit (eg, coffee vs. energy drinks vs. espresso)?

Marcus: Head-to-head studies on different forms of caffeine are rare to nonexistent. The great majority of the research demonstrating potential beneficial effects seems to be when studying caffeinated coffee. It is therefore important to emphasize that, in general, it can be difficult to disambiguate effects that might be related to caffeine per se vs. other constituents in coffee. Data regarding energy drinks are quite scant, but what limited data that is available suggests these high-dose and synthetic caffeinated products may actually be harmful to the heart, particularly in increasing risks of potentially dangerous heart rhythm disturbances and HF.

Healio: Does the brewing method matter (eg, drip vs. French press vs. pour-over)?

Marcus: There is fairly strong evidence that unfiltered coffee may raise cholesterol, whereas filtered coffee, such as drip coffee or after using a paper filter, removes the compounds from coffee that raise cholesterol.

Healio: If people are only drinking one cup of coffee per day, could they increase their intake to improve heart health?

Marcus: There is no evidence to demonstrate that increasing one’s caffeine consumption leads to improved health.

Healio: Is there a population who might consider reducing caffeine intake for CV benefit?

Marcus: A small randomized trial did suggest that caffeinated coffee may increase the frequency of premature ventricular contractions. While this is deserving of more study, those who are either bothered by these early beats or who have a very high burden of these beats — which has been associated with the development of HF — should at least experiment with reducing their caffeine intake.

Healio: Anything else you would like to mention?

Marcus: The best evidence regarding consumption of this common substance comes from curiosity-driven, investigator-initiated and often government-funded research. So all the taxpayers in the U.S. should be recognized for contributing to these data. But there is much left to learn and almost certainly underlying truths that, once uncovered, might substantially enhance the health of literally tens if not hundreds of millions of people. The best way to uncover those truths is by supporting this sort of unbiased research.

Gregory M. Marcus, MD, MAS, can be reached at greg.marcus@ucsf.edu or X @gregorymmarcus.

https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.title: GLP-1s reduce C-reactive protein among adults without diabetes
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.author: Michael Monostra
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Incretin-based medications lower high-sensitivity C-reactive protein levels among adults with a range of cardiometabolic conditions, researchers reported at the International Congress on Obesity.

“Clinicians should be aware that when prescribing semaglutide (Wegovy, Novo Nordisk) or tirzepatide (Zepbound, Eli Lilly) for weight management, they may also meaningfully reduce their patients’ inflammatory burden, which has independent prognostic value for cardiovascular risk,” Mario Cesar Torres-Chávez, MD, research assistant at Instituto Nacional de Cardiología Ignacio Chávez in Mexico City, told Healio. “This is particularly relevant for patients with elevated baseline high-sensitivity C-reactive protein who are already at higher CV risk.”

Torres-Chávez and colleagues conducted a meta-analysis of 10 randomized controlled trials assessing changes in inflammatory biomarkers for adults without diabetes using GLP-1s. Change in high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) was the primary outcome.

There were 23,652 adults included in the trials. Those receiving incretin-based therapy had a 45% greater decrease in hsCRP than those receiving placebo (P < .0001).

There was significant heterogeneity (I2 = 71.1%) in the findings, which Torres-Chávez said was fully explained by clinical phenotype.

“It was really interesting to see that the clinical phenotype fully accounted for the differences we observed across studies,” Torres-Chávez said. “When we looked closer at whether patients had obesity-related conditions, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction or established cardiovascular disease, the differences between studies disappeared completely. This suggests that the anti-inflammatory response can be predicted based on the patient’s underlying condition, which is quite encouraging.”

Adults with obesity and weight-related comorbidities had a 48% greater decrease in hsCRP with incretin-based therapy compared with placebo. Those with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) receiving semaglutide or tirzepatide had a 38% larger reduction in hsCRP than those receiving placebo. Similarly, adults with established CVD had a 38% greater decrease in hsCRP if they received an incretin-based drug compared with placebo.

There was no difference in hsCRP change when semaglutide was compared with tirzepatide. Torres-Chávez said the lack of difference between the drugs “raises some intriguing questions” about whether the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide agonism seen in tirzepatide has an impact on anti-inflammatory markers.

Torres-Chávez said the biggest question moving forward is to determine whether change in hsCRP is caused by the medication or weight loss itself. He added that more research is needed to examine how incretin-based drugs affect other inflammatory biomarkers.

“Longer-term studies are important to see if the anti-inflammatory effects last and if they lead to real reductions in CV events through these inflammation-specific pathways,” Torres-Chávez said.

Mario Cesar Torres-Chávez, MD, can be reached at ctorres92@uabc.edu.mx; LinkedIn @MarioCesarTorresChavez; X @MarioCTorresMD.

Torres-Chávez MC, et al. Effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists in high-sensitivity C-reactive protein in adults without diabetes: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Presented at: International Congress on Obesity; July 15-17, 2026; Mexico City.

Disclosures: Torres-Chavez reports no relevant financial disclosures.
