Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at military commitments for Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey; a mass shooting in Thailand; and Colombia’s new right-wing president.

Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey inked a joint defense pact on Friday, concluding nearly a year of negotiations aimed at countering aggressive military posturing in the Middle East. Dubbed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, the alliance will act as a NATO-style mutual defense pact that consolidates the power and influence of three regional heavyweights.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at military commitments for Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey; a mass shooting in Thailand; and Colombia’s new right-wing president.

Sign up to receive World Brief in your inbox every weekday.

Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey inked a joint defense pact on Friday, concluding nearly a year of negotiations aimed at countering aggressive military posturing in the Middle East. Dubbed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, the alliance will act as a NATO-style mutual defense pact that consolidates the power and influence of three regional heavyweights.

According to a trilateral statement, “the agreement is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression, and stipulates that any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all.” Although Egypt participated in early talks, Cairo was not mentioned as a participant in Friday’s deal. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan all attended the signing in Mecca, Saudi Arabia—Islam’s holiest city.

Military cooperation among the three Sunni Muslim-majority nations is nothing new. For decades, Pakistan has provided Saudi forces with training and technical aid, Islamabad and Ankara have previously exchanged warships and training aircraft, and Riyadh has repeatedly purchased Turkish drones. Last month, Pakistan and Turkey also backed a Saudi-proposed maritime defense coalition that would help protect regional shipping routes and prevent global supply chains from being held hostage during war.

But just how far the joint defense pact will go remains unclear. The three nations do not have a history of eagerly providing military support; last September, Pakistan signed a mutual defense deal with Saudi Arabia. However, Islamabad has not responded militarily to Iran’s recent attacks on the kingdom, and it has downplayed suggestions that its nuclear capabilities might be extended to allies.

Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim nation in the world, but it is not the only one bringing something to the table. Turkey has NATO’s second-largest military and is known for its extensive (and profitable) defense industry. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia is one of the world’s top oil exporters and recently signed a pact with the United States to begin development of a civilian nuclear program.

All three regional powers are expected to leverage these assets to counter worsening security in the Middle East. Erdogan stressed on Friday that the pact is not aimed at one particular country, and Riyadh expressed similarly placatory sentiments. Friday’s agreement “does not represent an effort to establish a military axis or a sectarian bloc. Nor is it linked to any nuclear ambitions or arms race, rather it is focused on building sustainable capabilities,” Rayed Krimly, Saudi deputy minister for public diplomacy, posted on X.

But experts suspect that the deal is likely a direct response to Iranian and Israeli military maneuvers.

Until now, Turkey and Pakistan have avoided getting directly involved in the Iran war despite both sharing land borders with Iran. Saudi Arabia also initially sought non-involvement; however, long-standing tensions with the Iran-backed Houthis in neighboring Yemen drew the kingdom into active conflict, and in late July, Saudi and U.S. forces launched joint strikes on Iran-backed militias in Iraq.

In public, Iranian officials appear unimpressed. “The Saudis should know that a paper agreement with Turkey and Pakistan will not bring them security, just as years of one-sided milking by the Americans did not bring them security,” Ebrahim Rezaei, an Iranian politician, wrote on X. “Change your policies so that you do not have to #BegForSecurity from others.”

Turkey and Israel, meanwhile, have increasingly found themselves in each other’s rhetorical crosshairs. In July, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan described Israel as a “burden that humanity can no longer bear”—remarks that Israeli officials interpreted as a call for genocide. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other prominent political figures in the country have painted Turkey as the new Iran and warned of an “emerging radical Sunni axis.” This new defense pact is likely to further inflame such fears.

Israel has yet to respond to Friday’s signing.

Deadly school shooting. A mass shooting at a high school in Thailand on Friday killed at least six people and injured more than 20 others, with nine in critical condition. The youngest victim was 12 years old. Earlier that morning, the suspected shooter, age 14, also killed his grandparents in their home. Local officials confirmed that the perpetrator killed himself before authorities could apprehend him and that the situation is “now under control.”

Thailand has one of the highest gun ownership rates in Asia, second only to Pakistan. In 2017, more than 10.3 million firearms were owned by civilians (or around 15 guns per every 100 people). The country also has the second-highest rate of gun homicides in Southeast Asia after the Philippines. Thailand’s deadliest mass shooting occurred in 2022, when 36 people—including 24 children—were killed at a childcare center.

“When I became prime minister, one of my to-do things was to issue a new law regarding weapons, and it is still in the process,” Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters on Friday, adding that “the new ​law will only allow government officials on duty to carry guns.” Thai government officials and law enforcement are allowed to buy as many firearms as they want at a discounted rate, and few regulations are in place to prevent individuals from then selling those weapons on the black market.

Colombia’s new leader. Conservative outsider Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as Colombia’s new president on Friday. Rather than hold the ceremony in Bogotá, though, de la Espriella chose to be inaugurated in the southwestern city of Cali, symbolizing his hard-line approach to crime. Cali has become known for its high homicide rate, rampant gang violence, and drug-trafficking networks.

One of the key pledges of de la Espriella’s campaign was to tackle violent crime. He criticized outgoing President Gustavo Petro’s policy of negotiating with armed groups, and he dismissed the efficacy of a previous peace agreement with the now-defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC). Dissident rebel groups have emerged in the vacuum left by FARC, particularly the National Liberation Army, which has seized on FARC’s absence to fight for greater territorial control.

Among de la Espriella’s other ambitions, the right-wing businessman and lawyer aims to revive the country’s oil and gas sector, build mega-prisons, eliminate wealth taxes, and roll back many benefits established under the previous administration. He is the latest in a slew of far-right leaders to clinch electoral victories across Latin America, several of whom attended de la Espriella’s inauguration.

Ebola infections. The number of confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo surpassed 4,000 for the first, according to government data, with deaths exceeding 1,850 individuals. Experts believe that the epidemic, which has been recorded in five Congolese provinces, is the second-largest and fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record. A Science report published last month estimated that the virus broke out at least four months before it was officially detected.

Ebola is “spreading at an alarming and unprecedented rate,” Doctors Without Borders said in a statement this week. And the response “is still not reaching communities quickly enough to break transmission chains.” On Wednesday, World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged local authorities to prioritize support for health care responders.

The largest Ebola outbreak occurred between 2014 and 2016, when more than 28,000 cases and around 11,000 deaths were detected across West Africa. Health officials believe that the current outbreak is being exacerbated by poor infrastructure in rural communities, mining-related movement, and rebel conflict.

Several capybaras strolled into a legislative building in Cuiabá, Brazil, last week, surprising lawmakers preparing for a scheduled vote. The adorable rodents, known for their sociability and chill demeanor, are native to South America, with many living in the wildlife park located next to the Cuiabá facility. “They show up here quite often, so we’ve gotten used to seeing them,” staffer Nayara Bueno said. Unlike their human counterparts, they’re usually not visiting lawmakers to file a complaint.

The moment that my friend decided she wanted to leave China came one day in 2018, on a busy street in Beijing.

A born-and-bred Beijinger with a well-paying job at an international company, she was riding in a taxi when she saw a man lying at a bus stop, apparently having a seizure. Several people stood nearby, but no one checked on him. My friend felt compelled to get out of the taxi and called an ambulance. During the roughly 15 minutes that she waited, many people passed, but no one stopped. A boy walking by asked his father, “Dad, what is happening to him?” His father hurried him away and told him not to meddle in other people’s business.

The moment that my friend decided she wanted to leave China came one day in 2018, on a busy street in Beijing.

A born-and-bred Beijinger with a well-paying job at an international company, she was riding in a taxi when she saw a man lying at a bus stop, apparently having a seizure. Several people stood nearby, but no one checked on him. My friend felt compelled to get out of the taxi and called an ambulance. During the roughly 15 minutes that she waited, many people passed, but no one stopped. A boy walking by asked his father, “Dad, what is happening to him?” His father hurried him away and told him not to meddle in other people’s business.

The next day, she began looking for ways to leave and eventually applied for a transfer to one of the company’s U.S. offices.

Of course, not everyone in China would react this way. There are plenty of tales of strangers selflessly coming to the aid of others. But I have heard enough stories like the one told by my friend, who now lives in Washington, D.C., to say that the indifference and mistrust pervading public life play a significant role in some people’s decision to leave—even when they have privileged and prosperous lives in China.

News about China’s dominance in clean energy and electric vehicles, along with its advances in artificial intelligence and robotics, can make the country sound like the obvious place for ambitious Chinese elites to thrive. Carefully selected videos of gleaming cities, efficient delivery networks, and rapidly developing industries project the image of a society hurtling toward a bright future.

Meanwhile, state propaganda portrays the United States as a declining empire beset by police violence, crime, and racism. The contrast is not entirely invented: Whenever I am stuck on yet another delayed Amtrak train, I think about how much faster and more punctual the journey would be in China.

Left: 
				Trains move along the tracks at Union Station in Washington on Nov. 9, 2021.
				  Right: 
				An aerial photo of high-speed trains at Nanjing South Railway Station in Nanjing, China, on June 30.

And yet, people still want to leave. The desire became so widespread that internet users coined the term runxue—“runology,” or the study of how to “run” from China—in the early 2020s. When I ask my Chinese friends why they moved to the United States or other Western countries, few begin with “freedom” and “democracy.” After all, most people are not preoccupied with politics. Instead, they mention small experiences: strangers who smile at them or offer assistance; neighbors who greet and socialize with one another; and professional relationships that do not depend on deciphering hidden motives and cultivating personal connections.

Distrust among strangers has long been a feature of Chinese society. Studies show that people often feel strong obligations toward family, friends, and other people within their personal circles while extending markedly weaker trust to unfamiliar people. But this does not mean that Chinese people lack compassion. Periodic nationwide uproars over the mistreatment of the vulnerable often reveal precisely the opposite.

Protesters demand justice for the dog Wang Wang in London on Aug. 1. Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images

Last month, the torture and killing of Wang Wang, a stray dog, by a group of boys in Guangdong province provoked widespread grief and outrage. People raised money, purchased billboards condemning animal cruelty, and demanded stronger animal welfare protections. A similar outpouring of concern occurred in 2022, when a video showing a mother of eight confined by the neck in a freezing shed in Jiangsu province went viral. Millions demanded to know who she was, whether she had been trafficked, and why local authorities had failed to protect her.

Yet compassion expressed collectively often does not translate into helping a stranger face to face. When confronted with someone in distress, many people hesitate—because they fear being deceived or exploited.

Consider pengci, or “touching porcelain”—the practice of staging or exaggerating an accident to extort compensation. Perhaps the most influential case was that of Peng Yu in 2007. Peng, a young man in Nanjing, said he had helped an elderly woman who had fallen near a bus stop, but the woman accused him of knocking her down, and a court ordered him to pay compensation. In the following years, numerous stories, often with murky details, circulated about alleged good Samaritans falsely accused by the people they had assisted.

                China Launches New Crackdown on Organized Crime            


    
    	From local gangs to sand mafias, Beijing keeps running into the same problems.    	    


        
        China Brief    
        |
        
    
    James Palmer

From local gangs to sand mafias, Beijing keeps running into the same problems.

Public anxiety over the risks of helping strangers became so widespread that, in 2017, the government adopted a national good Samaritan provision shielding people from civil liability for harm inadvertently caused while voluntarily providing emergency assistance. Local governments have also offered financial rewards and official honors to those recognized for “acting courageously for a just cause” (jianyi yongwei). National ceremonies celebrate good Samaritans, while official campaigns urge citizens to “show compassion” (xian aixin) and spread “positive energy”(zheng nengliang).

These measures can be helpful, but it is hard to manufacture care and trust through slogans, prizes, and televised ceremonies. Stories of help to others bringing negative consequences spread rapidly because they touch a fear that remains deeply rooted. In 2023, for example, a Shanghai man surnamed Chai stopped an elderly woman from falling backward on a subway escalator. She escaped injury, but he fractured his heel, incurred medical expenses, and missed three weeks of work. When local authorities sought to recognize him for bravery, the woman refused to confirm that he had rescued her. He ultimately sued her to obtain compensation.

Real trust in society can grow only when rules are predictable and applied equally, wrongdoing can be exposed, and perpetrators are held accountable. It requires confidence that, when disputes arise, the police and courts will pursue the truth rather than protect the powerful and well-connected or suppress embarrassing stories. That confidence is missing under the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) rule, where preserving social stability takes precedence over justice, political connections can buy impunity, and the party itself stands above the law.

Real trust also requires a free civil society. As Robert Putnam famously observed, neighborhood groups, charities, professional associations, women’s organizations, and religious communities give strangers opportunities to connect, cooperate, and care for one another. Yet the CCP regards such independent organizations as a threat.

Changsha Funeng founder Cheng Yuan (right) and his wife, Shi Minglei (left), in an undated photo. Shi Minglei

Changsha Funeng, for example, was an organization that advocated for migrant workers and people facing discrimination because of disabilities and chronic illnesses. In 2019, authorities shut it down and arrested its founder Cheng Yuan, later sentencing him to five years in prison for “subversion.” Across China, independent organizations serving vulnerable communities have been shuttered or forced under party control.

In the cases of both the stray dog Wang Wang and the chained woman, rather than allowing public compassion to develop into sustained solidarity with the vulnerable, authorities censored discussions, removed petitions, and obstructed independent efforts to investigate the cases or advocate for change.

To encourage socially approved behavior and discourage misconduct, authorities instead have increasingly turned to surveillance technology. China has built the world’s most extensive surveillance apparatus, with facial recognition cameras blanketing streets and public transportation while police collect phone, biometric, and other personal data. Yet while cameras can help deter people from staging a pengci scam and reassure good Samaritans that they can prove their innocence if falsely accused, they cannot build trust between strangers. And the same surveillance system that watches criminals also watches human rights activists, journalists, and religious believers.

Surveillance cameras are seen near a portrait of Mao Zedong in Beijing on May 15.Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images

By nearly eliminating civil society, the CCP has helped create an increasingly atomized social world. People inhabit crowded cities and communicate constantly through digital platforms, yet they often feel alienated and powerless inside. They may care about an abused woman, a tortured animal, or a persecuted neighbor, yet feel that there is little that they can do. Over time, helplessness can become indifference. People avert their eyes, mind their own business, and teach their children to do the same.

The CCP can make daily life efficient, orderly, and convenient—at least for the urban middle classes. It can compel people to follow rules and manufacture the appearance of social harmony. Yet it cannot engender human warmth.

People want more than material comfort and technological advancement. They want authentic relationships and communities. They want to believe that a stranger will stop when they collapse, that a neighbor will speak up when they disappear, and that joining others to help the vulnerable will foster connections instead of making them a target of the state.

That is why some members of China’s elite continue to leave even when doing so means exchanging fast trains and inexpensive delivery services for the United States’ dysfunction and disorder. They may not invoke freedom or democracy when explaining their decisions, but as the feminist slogan reminds us, the personal is political.

At time of writing, U.S. President Donald Trump’s haphazard attacks on Iran have killed 18 U.S. service members, an unknown number of Iranian civilians and military personnel, and cost tens of billions of dollars. Most importantly for everyone else on Earth, it has closed the Strait of Hormuz to international shipping.

Approximately 90 percent of traded goods are shipped by sea. Disruptions caused by a war over vitally important naval choke points are not new, nor are their calamitous economic effects. Trump’s war has catalyzed a reversion to a period before Great Britain and the United States enforced the neutrality of major global waterways in the 19th and early 20th centuries, a deliberately manufactured situation that modern Americans inherited without remembering or understanding that it was artificial, and like everything artificial, needed to be maintained.

At time of writing, U.S. President Donald Trump’s haphazard attacks on Iran have killed 18 U.S. service members, an unknown number of Iranian civilians and military personnel, and cost tens of billions of dollars. Most importantly for everyone else on Earth, it has closed the Strait of Hormuz to international shipping.

Approximately 90 percent of traded goods are shipped by sea. Disruptions caused by a war over vitally important naval choke points are not new, nor are their calamitous economic effects. Trump’s war has catalyzed a reversion to a period before Great Britain and the United States enforced the neutrality of major global waterways in the 19th and early 20th centuries, a deliberately manufactured situation that modern Americans inherited without remembering or understanding that it was artificial, and like everything artificial, needed to be maintained.

Trump’s grotesque actions do not represent the abdication of empire, as some Trump supporters from the far left and right hope, but its degeneration. Unless this failure is reversed, the world’s waterways will again become sites of brutal contention, as they have been historically.

Consider two examples: the Dardanelles, between the eastern Mediterranean and the Black Sea; and the Oresund Sound into and out of the Baltic. One exemplifies the way control over geography can make even a weak power vital to international decision-making. The other provides an example of the financial rewards of control of a shipping choke point—which becomes unsettling when applied to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and its power over Hormuz.

From 1453 and the final conquest of Constantinople (modern-day Istanbul), the Ottoman Empire controlled the entire Turkish Straits, the passage from the Mediterranean to the Black Sea including the Dardanelles and the Bosphorus. Since the Baltic exit to the open ocean was dominated by Denmark, Russia had for centuries bent toward an exit to the Mediterranean through the Turkish Straits.

As the Ottoman Empire crumbled, control of this important waterway was a recurrent aim of warfare in the eastern Mediterranean: between Russia and everyone else. After the Napoleonic wars, control over the Turkish Straits swung back and forth, eventually culminating in the Crimean War, during which a European alliance propped up the Ottomans to deny Russia control of the Bosphorus.

The Oresund connects the Baltic to the North Sea, which from the late Middle Ages onward was a vital nexus of shipping for a broad group of Northern European communities from Muscovy to England. (This contact is how Shakespeare knew enough about Russians for characters to disguise themselves as Muscovites in Love’s Labour’s Lost, for instance.) The Baltic trade was in vital but unsexy commodities like timber and wood products, hemp and flax, iron and copper, grain, beer, salt, and fish, as well as more visible luxury products like furs and amber—and after the adoption of gunpowder in Europe, firearms. From 1429, the sound was controlled by the Kalmar Union and then Denmark, and so were the lucrative sound tolls, where ships paid 1 percent to 2 percent of the cargo’s value for passage. (The closeness of this date to the fall of Constantinople is not a coincidence: Throughout Eurasia, the early modern period was characterized by the development of state power, including the ability to make war and extract revenue.)

This money went not to the embryonic Danish government—at this time, the Rigsrad, or council—but to the king of Denmark as a personal asset. In 1625, control of this independent revenue, amounting to one-eighth of Danish state income, allowed Christian IV to intervene in the Thirty Years’ War without consulting his own council, a disastrous decision for Denmark.

That raises an uncomfortable parallel in Iran: Is this money going to the Iranian government as such, or directly to the IRGC, a parallel armed force whose purpose is to maintain the theocracy? This purpose has enabled a substantial expansion of its remit: For instance, it is the IRGC, and not the regular Iranian armed forces, that controls the ballistic missiles. It is also a vast economic cartel.

Even before 2026, the IRGC was already becoming stronger at the expense of other entities within the Iranian power structure, such as the clerisy. During the U.S. attacks this year, it has rapidly consolidated power. Independent revenue would reinforce revenue from its economic operations within Iranian society and give it more funding to finance war as well as support proxies like Hamas, Hezbollah, and Shiite militias in Iraq, without input from other Iranian decision-makers. This would bring Iran closer to what I believe is one probable decay state for the Islamic Revolution: instead of a cleric-dominated Islamic republic, an IRGC-led junta.

The Turkish Straits, the Oresund, and other waterways were forced open to shipping and commerce during the 19th and early 20th centuries by the British Empire and the United States. In 1841, the London Straits Convention barred all warships from the Bosphorus, benefiting British naval power at Russia’s expense. Although dissatisfaction with the sound tolls had been brewing in Denmark itself throughout the early 19th century, the United States forced the issue when it refused to pay tolls in 1856; in response, Denmark convened a summit to establish the sound’s neutrality. The modern United States has inherited this imperial structure, which remains beneath the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which protects “innocent passage” within narrow waterways and coasts.

The Gulf needs a joint front on deterrence, engagement, and freedom of navigation.

Until this year, the United States securing international trade is how the world has functioned. Trump has thrown this away for zero gain—not even for pacifism’s sake. (In 2026 so far, he has bombed Iran, Somalia, the Caribbean and the Pacific, Iraq, Syria, Nigeria, and Venezuela.)

A world order enforced by the United States was morally unpalatable for many people on the American left. But when isolationists imagined a world without U.S. hegemony, they envisioned a world order characterized by mutual restraint without considering who might enforce this situation. As we are now seeing, the alternative to some kind of enforcement of a consistent world order is not an acephalic, mutually respectful world, but recurrent, destructive wars.

Within this more bellicose world, every single power bordering an important shipping channel is likely to remember it has a potential throat hold on the world economy, and eventually they will act accordingly. The Iranian-allied Houthis in Yemen are already attempting to contest the Bab el-Mandeb passage from the Arabian Sea to the Red Sea. If I were one of Russia’s enemies, I would be seriously contemplating the old significance of the Oresund and the Turkish Straits. If Finland and Estonia block the Gulf of Finland, Russia could not export oil through this routeor resupply Kaliningrad.

In the Iran conflict in 2026, we are confronted with the same conclusion that T.R. Fehrenbach, infantry officer and author, reached regarding the Korean War: “Americans in 1950 rediscovered something that since Hiroshima they had forgotten: you may fly over a land forever; you may bomb it, atomize it, pulverize it and wipe it clean of life—but if you desire to defend it, protect it, and keep it for civilization, you must do this on the ground, the way the Roman legions did … [in] the mud.” What decides history is the geography of earth and water, and the human beings on it.

Thomas Wright’s short, effective new book diagnoses how Donald Trump and Joe Biden’s foreign policies signal a transformed world order, albeit in different ways. Wright, who served on Biden’s National Security Council from 2022 to 2025, combines a scholar’s insight and a practitioner’s experience to shed light on a changing world. However, the book is limited by a lack of meaningful discussion about both Israel-Palestine, and the future of the Democratic Party’s foreign policy.

Wright focuses on a few major themes, the most important of which is the idea that the post-Cold War world is over. Barack Obama, he argues, was the last true “restorationist” president who tried to preserve a grand strategy based on alliances, free trade, and military supremacy. Obama was also the last president to try to integrate Russia and China into a cooperative, liberal international order—and this effort failed. Now the United States faces two major revisionist autocratic rivals that seek to weaken its global influence and assert control over their zones of the world.

Thomas Wright’s short, effective new book diagnoses how Donald Trump and Joe Biden’s foreign policies signal a transformed world order, albeit in different ways. Wright, who served on Biden’s National Security Council from 2022 to 2025, combines a scholar’s insight and a practitioner’s experience to shed light on a changing world. However, the book is limited by a lack of meaningful discussion about both Israel-Palestine, and the future of the Democratic Party’s foreign policy.

Inflection Point: Biden, Trump, and the Future World Order, Thomas Wright, Penguin, 176 pp., April 2026

Wright focuses on a few major themes, the most important of which is the idea that the post-Cold War world is over. Barack Obama, he argues, was the last true “restorationist” president who tried to preserve a grand strategy based on alliances, free trade, and military supremacy. Obama was also the last president to try to integrate Russia and China into a cooperative, liberal international order—and this effort failed. Now the United States faces two major revisionist autocratic rivals that seek to weaken its global influence and assert control over their zones of the world.

These changes, Wright argues, were well under way in Trump’s first term, if not earlier, but Trump exacerbated them with an incoherent hybrid strategy. He blasted his predecessors for overextending U.S. power and letting allies free-ride, but under the influence of his more conventional Republican policy advisors, he did not radically revise the global U.S. role.

Senior White House policy advisor Stephen Miller, left, and chief strategist Steve Bannon, center, sit with other members of the Trump administration at a news conference at the White House in Washington on Feb. 13, 2017.Mark Wilson/Getty Images

In this light, Biden’s presidency and Trump’s return to office constitute definitive inflection points from the post-Cold War world. Where some have criticized Biden as a restorationist, Wright contends that he made a series of corrections in response to an increasingly multipolar world and to the vulnerabilities exposed by the COVID-19 pandemic. He broke with the post-Cold War free trade consensus by imposing strict export controls on critical technologies like advanced microchips, expanding U.S. industrial capacity, and making the United States less vulnerable to supply-chain disruptions.

Biden also completed Trump’s withdrawal from Afghanistan, signaling an end to multiple decades of U.S. nation-building overseas. He bolstered ties to traditional U.S. allies after the first Trump term’s disruptions but did so by rallying coalitions to support partners doing the heavy lifting, as in the collective backing of Ukraine after Russia’s 2022 invasion. He also embraced strategic competition with China and Russia, in contrast to Obama’s efforts to build relationships and ease tensions with those countries. In sum, Biden’s foreign policy maintained the longstanding Democratic commitment to multilateralism and institutions while stepping back from the post-Cold War U.S. role as Atlas of the world order. He also tipped economic policy toward protectionism and re-shoring of key defense industries while acknowledging the reality of competition with revisionist powers.

Trump’s second term, Wright concludes, signifies a permanent break from the post-Cold War world and a new orientation for U.S. power. Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and other MAGA conservatives wanted to ensure that Trump’s will would not be impeded by conventional Republican advisors or bureaucratic inertia. This led to the appointment of a bizarre mix of lackeys and ideologues in his second-term cabinet, as well as a campaign to hollow out foreign policy agencies like the State Department.

In practice, this consolidation of MAGA influence over Republican foreign policy has meant aggressive and erratic U.S. behavior, including two separate military campaigns against Iran, threats against allies like Canada and Denmark, and the kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Trump has also gone harder on economic protectionism in his second term by imposing steep and arbitrary tariffs on dozens of nations. The core ethos of MAGA’s foreign policy, Wright notes, is that it is foolish for the United States to provide any public good, such as freedom of the seas or support for defense alliances like NATO, that it does not benefit from immediately and tangibly. Enlightened self-interest remains a critical part of Democratic foreign policy thinking, but it is dead and buried in Trump’s Republican Party.

The Trump administration has also aligned itself firmly with far-right parties around the world, especially in Europe, while alienating longstanding allies. The post-Cold War order is over, Wright concludes, because both Biden and Trump moved away from the idea of the United States as the linchpin of world order, although Trump’s actions have been more extreme in this regard.

A man holds up a placard with the words ‘God Bless Donald Trump’ as people take part in a far-right protest called Unite the Kingdom in London on May 16.Carl Court/Getty Images

A second major theme of Wright’s book is the growing divergence of Republican and Democratic foreign policies. The Cold War featured a strong consensus on containing communism, and the post-Cold War era featured a new consensus on U.S. leadership (if not hegemony), free trade, military interventionism, and support for key alliance systems.

However, Wright argues, hyper-polarization in the United States has affected foreign policy by pushing Republicans and Democrats ever further apart, despite some overlap on issues like protectionism. U.S. foreign policy will therefore lurch wildly when administrations change hands. Now that Trump has instilled America First as the bedrock of Republican foreign policy, this will be a permanent dynamic.

Wright concludes that this oscillation of U.S. foreign policy will make addressing every global problem harder, from preserving treaty agreements to reassuring partners and allies like Taiwan, Ukraine, and NATO. The world, especially U.S. allies, will have to adapt to this reality. This means that regional coalitions will have to take more responsibility for key challenges, even if that means pushing back on Trump’s bullying. Wright quotes Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s insight on this new condition: “We are in the midst of a rupture, not a transition,” and so “the middle powers must act together, because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu.”

                When the Democratic Recession Comes Home            


    
    	Michael McFaul wants more democracy promotion. Is now the time?    	        
            


        
        Review    
        |
        
    
    Vivek Viswanathan


    


             
                    
                
    
            
                    
        
        
        An illustration shows Joe Biden at a lecturn on a bridge spanning a chasm with two heads of Donald Trump in profile forming the base of the bridge.
    
        
        An illustration shows Joe Biden at a lecturn on a bridge spanning a chasm with two heads of Donald Trump in profile forming the base of the bridge.
    
    
        
    
                Why Biden’s Foreign Policy Fell Short            


    
    	The White House never met its own grandiose standards.    	    


        
        Essay    
        |
        
    
    Kori Schake

Michael McFaul wants more democracy promotion. Is now the time?

The White House never met its own grandiose standards.

While Inflection Point is an insightful assessment of U.S. foreign policy in the 2020s, it has less to say on what comes next. Indeed, it is at once minor but telling that Wright declines to offer a name for the new global context we now inhabit.

A larger problem is that Wright has little to say about Israel and Gaza. He is focused on great power competition and grand issues of trade, arms races, and alliances. Nonetheless, world order can be reshaped by smaller actors as well. The United States has now been deeply involved in a series of Middle Eastern wars stemming from the Oct. 7 terrorist attack on Israel. Biden failed to put any meaningful constraints on the Israeli reaction, which led not only to catastrophe in Gaza but a steady escalation of conflict in the region. Biden showed that he was stuck in a much older mentality that viewed Israel as the underdog bastion of democracy in a hostile part of the world, rather than what it has actually become: a reckless, militaristic state controlled by the far-right.

Inflection Points feels incomplete without a look at this tragic issue. Biden’s ongoing accommodation of Israel was more of a feature than a bug of Democratic foreign policy over the last several decades, as presidents such as Obama and Bill Clinton lamented Israel’s behavior but rarely responded with meaningful consequences. Now, Trump has launched an ill-considered, unprovoked attack on the Iranian regime and doubled down on the alliance with Israel. As a result, it is especially important for Democrats to think through alternatives to both Biden and Trump’s approaches to the Middle East, which have been far too similar in their failings.

The bridge linking Bandar Abbas and Kehuristan, rendered unusable in a U.S. strike, is seen in Iran’s Hormozgan province on July 19. Amir Hossein Khorgooei/Anadolu via Getty Images

A fundamental revision of the U.S.-Israeli relationship is in order, on both strategic and ethical grounds. If Democratic foreign policy experts cannot think of a new path forward in the Middle East beyond opposing Trump’s actions, then the party will be rudderless going forward. As Wright notes, Democrats are deeply divided over the Israel-Palestine issue, with the trend line moving toward the rejection of the U.S.-Israeli partnership. But he does not offer his own answer to this critical question. This reflects a larger abdication among Democratic Party elites, as exemplified by the Democratic National Committee’s failure to even mention Israel or Gaza in its autopsy of the 2024 election.

Democrats remain deeply uncertain about what role the United States should play in the world. Wright shows that the slate does not need to be wiped clean, as Biden took effective multilateral action on Ukraine, alliances, the defense industrial base, and other issues. But he was lacking in a broader vision that could counter Trump’s America First appeal. The party still desperately needs a persuasive strategy for addressing a more multipolar international system, allies whose trust in the United States has been permanently damaged, and the global reaction against liberal democracy.

In the course of a short, concise volume, Wright has conclusively demonstrated that, for all their differences, Biden and Trump moved the United States away from the key assumptions and policies of the post-Cold War system, which now appears as a roughly 25- to 30-year interim between eras of strategic competition. The message of this book is that there’s no going back. Unfortunately, it does not tell us where to go from here.

This month, we’re reading two deeply divergent takes on displacement and the pull of home, from an unnamed country in the wake of a devastating war to modern Nigeria.

Paul Yoon (Scribner, 208 pp., $28, August 2026)

This month, we’re reading two deeply divergent takes on displacement and the pull of home, from an unnamed country in the wake of a devastating war to modern Nigeria.

Paul Yoon (Scribner, 208 pp., $28, August 2026)

As many a moviegoer leaving Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey can attest, the most powerful scene in Homer’s epic is arguably a quiet one—when Odysseus returns home to Ithaca to find that his dog, Argos, has waited for him for 20 years. Upon seeing Odysseus, who cannot greet him lest he give up his disguise, Argos dies. (It’s also potentially the first moment of sentimentality in the Western tradition.) Dogs, Homer knew, unearth layers of emotion and pathos that even tales of war and human suffering cannot always access.

In Etna, Paul Yoon has tried his hand at what Nolan has called “the ultimate dog story,” reimagining the Odyssey from a canine perspective. The result is as moving and wrenching as one might expect. The novel is narrated by an ex-military dog named Etna, who was trained by Americans fighting in an unnamed Asian country as a bomb-detection and attack canine. Although the side he fought for has technically won, the country is in ruins after four years of war. As Etna sets out to attempt to find his way back to the coast he was taken from as a pup—the only reference point he has for home—he confronts what is left of this land: rubble, starvation, desolation. Few buildings still stand. Medical aid never arrives from the West. As one of the two surviving U.S. soldiers in Etna’s unit says early on, “Yeah, we sort of made a mess of things here, didn’t we?”

Etna features the spare yet emotionally rich prose of Yoon’s earlier work, along with his preoccupations with trauma and displacement. (Reading this book, I was reminded often of “Valley of the Moon,” a gorgeous story of his in the New Yorker a few years ago.) This lack of embellishment makes Etna’s recollections of the war all the more haunting. At one point, he recalls seeing his military handler die in an explosion: “the spaces appearing between parts of his body where there shouldn’t have been spaces.”

It almost feels like a paradox for a writer of such economy to have penned a wartime epic. And yet, in just 208 pages, Yoon’s novel manages to touch seemingly infinite dimensions of life amid and in the wake of great conflict, from the near-futility of rebuilding to the miracle of feeling the grass beneath your feet (or paws) again to the absurdity of corralling others—human or otherwise—to fight for a cause that is alien to them. Etna is also a reminder that, nearly 3,000 years later, a well-trodden genre has not yet been exhausted, if only one knows which perspectives to take.—Chloe Hadavas

A. Igoni Barrett (Graywolf Press, 264 pp., $17, August 2026)

As Whyteface begins, Frank Whyte is facing a struggle that most travelers know all too well: He is stuck in traffic on the way to the airport, worried about missing his plane. In his hometown of Lagos, Nigeria, “traffic could make you late to your own funeral,” writes novelist A. Igoni Barrett, who lives in the city. Frank bemoans that he did not “set off for the airport at least twelve hours before his flight.”

But after Frank’s freak-out on a packed Lagosian highway, Whyteface stops being a widely relatable travelogue. That’s because of Frank’s unique identity. Born as Furo Wariboko, a Black Nigerian man, Frank woke up one morning as an adult to discover that he had become Caucasian overnight—except for his butt, which remained Black. “His transformation hadn’t made him white, but rather a piebald creature, the in-betweener, forever yoked to his inborn blackness despite the singed branding of whiteness,” Barrett writes.

After his metamorphosis, Frank changed his name; moved from Lagos to Abuja, Nigeria’s “capitalistic capital”; and built up enough wealth to finally make his maiden voyage to Europe. Readers accompany Frank on a tri-country jaunt to Amsterdam, Oslo, and Milan—a satirical yet unsettling journey through the Schengen area. (Barrett first introduced Frank to readers with his 2016 novel Blackass, but Whyteface can be read on its own.)

Used to being the “token white face” in Nigeria, Europe is—at first—a relief for Frank. He “promenaded unnoticed among the sightseeing masses, a new experience for him.” But when he opens his mouth—“a black voice in a white face”—Frank confuses many locals. Meanwhile, fellow Nigerians whom Frank encounters are baffled to meet an “oyibo” carrying a green passport who is fluent in pidgin, asking him, “where are you really from?”

Barrett juxtaposes Frank’s relatively privileged journey to Schiphol Airport (hefty Schengen visa fees and airfare still required) with the plight of African migrants who cross the Mediterranean by boat or languish in Libyan prisons in the hopes of gaining refuge in Europe.

Because Frank is white, many Europeans do not couch their racial prejudices around him. His Airbnb host in Amsterdam calls African children whom he sees on TV “future migrants.” In Milan, Frank identifies with the “lamentation” of Black Italian soccer phenom Mario Balotelli. When Frank observes a racist attack in Oslo, he feels “as if he were witnessing an outrage against his former face … his black family.”

Fed up with Europeans complaining about African migrants, Frank notes that Americans’ and Europeans’ “inalienable rights to travel anywhere and settle everywhere had been earned over violent centuries of undocumented migration.”

Frank was once a “whining citizen” who complained endlessly about Nigeria. But by the end of his trip, he is “no longer at ease with bashing the country he called home.” He traveled to Europe in search of savoir vivre; instead, he got an inside look at the continent’s animus. In the face of frustration abroad, he starts feeling comfortable in his apparently contradictory racial and national identities—and allows others to call him by his old name again.

“Furo was learning that his becoming was the journey and that his being—not his whyteface or blackass, but rather shared humanity, shorn of tribe and gender—was always and forever the destination,” Barrett writes. “A Nigerian is still a man o, whether he’s a black or white.”—Allison Meakem

Edwidge Danticat, the great literary voice of the Haitian diaspora, returns with her first novel in over a decade, Dèy. Dutch crime queen Anya Niewierra’s breakthrough thriller, The Camino, is translated into English by Eileen Stevens. With Unprecedented Times, Malavika Kannan has written what one critic has called the “first Great American Gen Z Novel.” Family secrets loom over Louise Nealon’s portrait of Irish domestic life, Everything That Is Beautiful. Rachel Cusk, patron saint of contemporary autofiction, interrogates the cost of global stardom in Life of M.

Indian author-composer Amit Chaudhuri looks beyond the sheen of the City of Light in his novel-in-fragments, Château Rouge. A cold case is reopened in Margrét Ann Thors’ debut novel, Freyja, a thriller steeped in Icelandic folklore. With A Tender Age, Korean American novelist Chang-rae Lee offers up a new addition to the canon of Western bildungsromans. The psychological weight of geopolitics crashes down on an unreliable narrator in Awake Awake by Fiona Mozley. And Andrés Barba’s contemporary ghost story, Last Day of a Prior Life, is translated from the Spanish by Lisa Dillman.—CH

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: The region’s so-called second pink tide comes to an end, Bolivia secures a $1.9 billion IMF loan, and the United States ends deportation protections for Haitians.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: The region’s so-called second pink tide comes to an end, Bolivia secures a $1.9 billion IMF loan, and the United States ends deportation protections for Haitians.

Sign up to receive Latin America Brief in your inbox every Friday.

Right-wing lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella will be inaugurated as Colombia’s president on Friday. He replaces Gustavo Petro, the latest in a string of left-wing Latin American leaders to leave office amid the region’s broader shift toward the right.

When Petro and his ideological allies were elected in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, their victories were so widespread that many observers dubbed the phenomenon a “second pink tide,” recalling the wave of left-leaning and socialist governments that swept through Latin America from the late 1990s to the early 2010s.

The first pink tide transformed the domestic and foreign policies of many South American countries, which increasingly turned toward one another to pursue a shared agenda of regional integration.

These changes were made possible in large part by a global commodities boom that increased public revenue across the region. Social spending generally went up, income inequality declined, and access to higher education expanded. By the end of the first pink tide, South American governments were cooperating regionally on health, infrastructure, and conflict resolution.

That momentum gave way in the mid-2010s as falling commodity prices, mounting economic challenges, and high-profile corruption scandals ushered in a more volatile political period.

Across the region’s democracies, voters elected a new crop of right-wing leaders whose foreign policies deprioritized regional integration. Their tenures, however, coincided with COVID-19, and many were ousted after a single term.

That political shift gave rise to the second pink tide. By 2023, leftist governments had taken office in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, and Peru, pledging to reduce inequality at home and resurrect regional integration as a central pillar of their foreign policies. (Mexico has also been led by the leftist Morena party since 2018, though it has prioritized integration with North America over South America.)

Latin America’s second pink tide has proved to be much shorter-lived than the first. While Morena held on to Mexico’s presidency in 2024 and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva may do the same this October, their peers elsewhere have mostly exited office.

As the ideological tides shift once again, it is a good time to ask: How much, if at all, did this pink tide change the region?

Several of these governments expanded anti-poverty efforts. In Colombia, multidimensional poverty fell to a historic low under Petro, while Brazil significantly reduced food insecurity. But without the tailwind of a commodities boom, these initiatives squeezed government budgets.

What’s more, many of the period’s most visible leaders fell short on signature progressive pledges, including Petro’s plan to reduce violence by negotiating with armed groups rather than taking a militarized approach and former Chilean President Gabriel Boric’s proposal to rewrite the country’s dictatorship-era constitution.

In foreign-policy terms, regional integration survived more than thrived. Mercosur, the South American trade bloc, expanded in 2024 to admit Bolivia and signed a long-delayed deal with the European Union this year, though keeping the group intact required careful diplomacy after Argentine President Javier Milei threatened to withdraw from it.

The leaders of the second pink tide, especially in Brazil, also revived joint work on several cross-border infrastructure corridors that had been under discussion since the early 2000s—notably the Capricorn Bioceanic Corridor, which will connect ports on South America’s east and west coasts.

Advocates of these corridors argue that they are a strategic asset for South American countries to decide their own economic fate at a time when outside powers—especially the United States and China—are pushing their own agendas for the region.

Those agendas often focus on accessing the region’s commodities, with local development remaining an afterthought, said Pedro Silva Barros, the former economic affairs director for the Union of South American Nations, a now-defunct regional body established during the first pink tide.

The Capricorn Bioceanic Corridor exemplifies this distinction. It is intended to strengthen economic ties within South America itself and spur industrialization across relatively poor regions, Silva Barros said.

“The corridor is more important for connecting these countries to each other than it is for connecting them with China or another extra-regional power,” he added.

Whether ongoing integration efforts endure will depend on their ability to survive the region’s recurring ideological swings. The repeated delays to the Capricorn Bioceanic Corridor illustrate how difficult that has been in recent decades.

Still, there are signs that the latest push for regional infrastructure may outlast the second pink tide itself. Last month, Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, and Paraguay—two of which now have far-right leaders—signed an agreement to create a single aviation market. Like that of the European Union, it’s designed to make it easier for airlines based in one member country to operate in the others.

It marks another step toward a regional foreign policy shaped by South American priorities, not those of outside powers.

Friday, Aug. 7: De la Espriella is inaugurated as president of Colombia.

Sunday, Aug. 16: The official campaign advertising period begins for Brazil’s presidential election.

Delcy Rodríguez, the interim president of Venezuela, holds up a new law to reform the country’s oil industry, in Caracas on Jan. 29.Carlos Becerra/Getty Images

Venezuela’s oil revenue. More than six months after the United States removed then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and assumed responsibility for reviving the country’s oil sector, both governments have disclosed little about how the resulting revenue is being spent. A Financial Times calculation published last month found that Washington has collected more than $13 billion in Venezuelan oil revenue this year.

By April, the United States had transferred at least $3 billion to Venezuela, according to a U.S. State Department official. But U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has yet to publish the reports that it promised, and a Venezuelan government site created to provide transparency around oil revenue has disclosed only a single $300 million transfer.

While Trump administration officials have said that they hope U.S. oil companies move into the country, the largest ones have so far held back from major new investments.

Bolivia’s IMF deal. Farther south, Bolivia’s economic overhaul is showing progress. Last week, it reached a preliminary deal with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for a $1.9 billion loan. The IMF praised the country’s decision in June to move toward a more market-determined exchange rate.

The IMF endorsement is a step forward for President Rodrigo Paz after his first months in office were marked by large-scale protests. In May and June, opposition members blocked roads across major cities; 22 people died amid during the unrest, according to Bolivia’s ombudsman’s office. For now, tensions between the government and opposition groups appear to have eased.

Essay on exile. Latin America’s prestigious Gabo journalism prize—named after Gabriel García Márquez, whose foundation presents the award—recently honored Salvadoran journalists Óscar Martínez and Carlos Martínez.

The winning essay recounts their effort to remain outside the country after they were warned that President Nayib Bukele’s government was preparing to arrest them. “Preventive departures,” they write, “were always a sugar-coated euphemism for exile.”

The brothers had previously released an investigation into a secret government deal with a criminal group, featuring a series of video interviews with the gang’s leader. The brothers mused that earlier written investigations had already documented evidence of similar backroom deals, but far more people paid attention when testimony was shown “like a Netflix series.”

What is the only major U.S. oil company that stayed in Venezuela throughout Maduro’s presidency, even after its peers had left the country?

A. Chevron
B. ExxonMobil
C. ConocoPhillips
D. Occidental Petroleum

By contrast, ExxonMobil—once another major player in Venezuela’s oil industry—withdrew after the Hugo Chávez government nationalized its assets in 2007.

Haitians living in Brooklyn join local politicians, city employees, and others at an Immigrant Resource Fair and Know Your Rights Event in New York on July 28.Spencer Platt/Getty Images

Last week, hundreds of thousands of Haitians in the United States lost temporary protected status, making them newly vulnerable to deportation.

A Haitian migration official said in July that Washington told the government to expect about 250 deportees per week. At that pace, deportations of Haitians could eventually approach the more than 25,000 Venezuelans deported during Trump’s second term.

The Trump administration has argued that insecurity and political crises in both countries no longer justify protection from deportation. But while Venezuela is experiencing a moderate economic stabilization and political opening, gang violence in Haiti remains dire.

The U.S. State Department recently renewed its “do not travel” advisory for the country, suggesting that U.S. citizens who travel there should leave copies of their dental records with family members—in case their remains need to be identified.

The Trump administration supported a September 2025 U.N. Security Council decision to expand the international security mission supporting Haiti’s police in their effort to retake gang-controlled neighborhoods, including a force of up to 5,500 troops.

But almost a year later, only 1,000 troops have arrived. Gangs still control around 85 percent of the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area, a U.N. office said.

Catherine Osborn is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Latin America Brief. She is a print and radio journalist based in Rio de Janeiro. X: @cculbertosborn

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at a potential plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, Myanmar’s junta’s pursuit of political legitimacy, and domestic mining in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

An agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz remained in the works on Thursday, as mediators separately urged U.S. and Iranian officials to come to a consensus on control of the strategic waterway. With Tehran claiming that it is in the “final stage” of drafting a deal with Oman, all eyes are now on Washington to determine what happens next.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at a potential plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, Myanmar’s junta’s pursuit of political legitimacy, and domestic mining in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Sign up to receive World Brief in your inbox every weekday.

An agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz remained in the works on Thursday, as mediators separately urged U.S. and Iranian officials to come to a consensus on control of the strategic waterway. With Tehran claiming that it is in the “final stage” of drafting a deal with Oman, all eyes are now on Washington to determine what happens next.

Regional sources told Reuters that the proposed deal between the two Middle Eastern countries would give Iran oversight over all traffic entering the Persian Gulf through the strait. It is unclear how control would be defined; Tehran demands the right to board and charge commercial vessels, but Gulf mediators insist upon their right to supervise inspections and maintain that payments should be voluntary.

Either way, any level of Iranian control over the strait would mark a major geopolitical shift in Tehran’s favor, as prior to the onset of war in February, ships could pass through Hormuz freely and without facing tolls.

The 60-day framework reportedly under discussion would also require outbound traffic to pass through Omani waters rather than Iranian territory. Parties would have 30 days to begin de-mining the strait’s median lane, and ships would eventually be cleared to use this route in both directions. Analysts remain uncertain as to what extent Tehran has mined the thoroughfare and just how long it will take to clear the area for safe use.

Yet no deal has yet been reached, and previous efforts to reach a durable agreement have failed—in no small part due to confusion, misunderstanding, and differing interpretations of what exactly has been agreed to.

Signs of similar issues plaguing this latest round of negotiations arose on Thursday, with Iran’s semi-official Fars News Agency, which is closely linked to the country’s hard-line Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, publishing a purported initial draft of the Iran-Oman deal that included much more stringent restrictions on shipping through the strait: U.S. and Israeli ships would be banned from transiting the waterway, and other nations that have harmed Iran would also not be allowed to do so until they pay compensation to the country. Such terms are almost certain to be nonstarters for the United States.

Despite major diplomatic and military setbacks, U.S. President Donald Trump appears confident in Washington’s ability to win the war. “Iran, where the country has been decimated for the purpose of NOT ALLOWING IT TO EVER HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON, is going very well!” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday in a post defending the actions of U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The White House also denied reports that U.S. munitions stockpiles are running low, telling ABC News that “[w]e have far more munitions than anyone in the world, and far more than we need.”

These assurances directly contradict Trump’s past arguments that the United States can no longer provide Ukraine with Patriot interceptors because of its own focus on Iran. According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, U.S. inventories of Patriot interceptors and anti-ballistic THAAD missiles have been reduced by two-thirds and one-half, respectively, since the Iran war began.

Seeking legitimacy. The leader of Myanmar’s junta regime traveled to Thailand on Thursday to pursue political legitimacy and reengagement with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). During the two-day state visit, President Min Aung Hlaing is expected to try to convince Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul that Myanmar is a stable country working toward democracy and that its leadership should be welcomed back to the world stage.

“Myanmar has now reestablished itself on the path to democracy and is moving toward a better future,” Min Aung Hlaing said. “As the new government, we have now begun working on national stability, peace, and national reconciliation.” Anutin confirmed that the two countries are prepared to enter a “new chapter of economic cooperation that is built upon mutual trust.”

In February 2021, Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup that ousted democratically elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi. Since then, the junta has tried to establish itself as a legitimate government by holding a phased presidential election that began late last year. However, allegations of a rigged vote, deadly government crackdowns on political dissidents, and the imprisonment of Aung San Suu Kyi has stopped Min Aung Hlaing’s government from gaining the trust of Western states and ASEAN members.

Critical mining. The Democratic Republic of the Congo has banned cobalt and copper concentrate exports, Reuters reported on Thursday, though one-year export waivers may be granted on a case-by-case basis. The June 29 government order reviewed by Reuters also introduced new taxes on significant mining byproducts, affecting a wide range of minerals. The ban took effect immediately, but the tax regime has a three-month transition window.

Congo is the world’s largest cobalt supplier, Africa’s top source for copper, and a major producer of other critical minerals, such as tantalum, lithium, tin, and gold. By imposing export bans on cobalt and copper, Kinshasa is hoping to force more domestic processing and retain a greater share of the wealth; Congo’s mining sector accounts for roughly 40 percent of the country’s annual GDP.

“Resource-rich countries have been used as extractive giants,” Heidi Crebo-Rediker, who was the U.S. State Department’s first chief economist under the Obama administration, told FP’s Christina Lu in June. Many “have not seen the benefits of the extraction of many resources over many decades.”

Massive rescue operation. Nigerian authorities rescued more than 300 people who were kidnapped during a series of recent abductions in Niger and Kwara states, according to the office of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu on Wednesday. “The successful execution of this intelligence-led operation demonstrates the growing efficiency and collaboration among our security services,” Tinubu said. This was the largest single-day rescue operation carried out by Nigerian security forces in the country’s history.

Of those freed were 145 individuals abducted from Niger state and 163 people abducted from Kwara’s Woro community. Kidnapping for ransom has become a major crisis in Nigeria, with Islamist insurgents often linked to Boko Haram or Islamic State West Africa Province targeting vulnerable rural community centers, such as schools and places of worship.

These attacks have placed added pressure on Tinubu, who plans to seek reelection in January. On Tuesday, Abuja approved pay raises of up to 80 percent for Nigerian armed forces in an effort to boost troop morale. Tinubu hopes that doing so will improve citizens’ views of ongoing security efforts and reaffirm his commitment to modernizing the military.

A book on ancient Greece was returned to an Australian public library last week—a whopping 150 years late. Antiquities of Athens, first published in 1858, was recently discovered inside a sealed fireplace during home renovations. Taking inflation into account, the late fee would be around $19,500, according to the library manager. However, the library’s records of borrowers from the 1870s, which is when the book is thought to have been checked out, have been lost, so the culprits (or their descendants) are probably off the hook.

In 1415, a young European prince named Henry, who came from an obscure, foundling dynasty in what would later be known as Portugal, charged out ahead of the troops under his command during an invasion of the African mainland, at a little trading outpost called Ceuta.

The prince, who would eventually achieve fame as Henry the Navigator, was less of a hero in battle than his reckless sally would suggest, but the Portuguese land grab soon succeeded. The gambit jolted Europe with the news of a success against the Muslims of the Marinid dynasty and announced a Portuguese dynasty, the Aviz, as a new force to be reckoned with in the Christian world.

In 1415, a young European prince named Henry, who came from an obscure, foundling dynasty in what would later be known as Portugal, charged out ahead of the troops under his command during an invasion of the African mainland, at a little trading outpost called Ceuta.

The prince, who would eventually achieve fame as Henry the Navigator, was less of a hero in battle than his reckless sally would suggest, but the Portuguese land grab soon succeeded. The gambit jolted Europe with the news of a success against the Muslims of the Marinid dynasty and announced a Portuguese dynasty, the Aviz, as a new force to be reckoned with in the Christian world.

What Henry sought was not converts to Christianity, nor even so much territory to add to the Aviz realm. Rather, it was access to the huge wealth in gold that had flowed into Europe for centuries via Mediterranean Africa from points far to the south, below the Sahara Desert.

In recent days, developments in tiny Ceuta, which helped launch the Portuguese empire and the so-called Age of Exploration, have led the news again. But this time, there has been a rush in the opposite direction, with tens of thousands of citizens of Morocco and other African countries risking their lives and perishing by the dozens to use the Spanish-controlled exclave as a springboard toward more prosperous lives in wealthy Europe.

As someone who has written at length about the origins of European imperialism—and with it, the commerce and conquest in Africa that formed much of Europe’s early wealth—I have been struck by the narrow frames that many news outlets have employed to cover what has occurred in Ceuta. Much of the coverage has presented it as a simple, if grave, immigration crisis, taking the current situation on the map, and the deep historical backstory behind today’s headlines, for granted.

As I wrote in my book, Born in Blackness: Africa, Africans, and the Making of the Modern World, it is a mistake to buy into the notion that Portugal acquired its imperial possessions in Africa as “in a fit of absence of mind”—as one historian famously described British colonial conquest—with Ceuta being a mere historical relic and curio that the world should today unquestioningly accept as part of Europe.

The Aviz conquest of Ceuta followed its rivalry with Spain for control of the Canary Islands off the coast of Africa in the 14th century, where the Portuguese raided for slaves and the Spanish committed what some historians consider the first modern genocide, wiping out the native Guanche population. As with Ceuta and other islands such Madeira and the Azores, the Portuguese carried out carefully conceived ambitions to capture African gold wealth in an era that long predated both the trans-Atlantic slave traffic and Iberian efforts to discover a maritime route to Asia.

Beyond the search for gold, Portugal’s early imperialism was motivated by competition with its far larger and more powerful neighbor, Spain, which hoped to subdue and incorporate Portugal into a united Iberia. Ceuta acquired its legal status as part of Spain after a convoluted crisis of Portuguese royal succession in 1578, when a new king, another Henry—Henry the Navigator’s distant nephew—took the throne at an old age without an heir. This left Philip II of Spain, the grandson of a Portuguese king, with the strongest claim to the Portuguese crown upon Henry’s death in 1580.

Given today’s focus on Ceuta, one can’t move on here without mentioning the striking fact that Portugal’s 16th-century succession crisis resulted from a broader invasion of Morocco, which ended in disaster when King Henry’s predecessor, Sebastian I, was killed along with much of his family. Decades later, after Portugal waged a successful war to restore its own royal line, independent of Spain, the spit of Moroccan land known as Ceuta was ceded to the Spanish.

Although extended a patina of legitimacy by international law and by the recognition of Spanish sovereignty by other states, this situation is clearly a historical fluke, and one that seems unlikely to endure. Consider how fragmented and open to contestation similar relics of imperial history are in this part of the world. Almost directly across the Mediterranean sits Gibraltar, a small protrusion of land into the sea that Britain has claimed and controlled since Anglo-Dutch forces seized it during the War of Spanish Succession in 1704. Nine years later, Spain ceded it to Britain in supposed perpetuity as part of the Treaty of Utrecht.

Spain rejects Morocco’s historic and geographic arguments to rightful ownership of Ceuta, but it makes very similar claims to Gibraltar. A glance at the map quickly makes clear why Madrid and Rabat believe that they should control Gibraltar and Ceuta, respectively. (Incidentally, Gibraltar was founded as a fortified lighthouse outpost by North Africans from the Muslim Almohad empire in the 12th century, but this is a claim that Moroccans long ago quite sensibly relinquished.)

In their willingness to blame Spain, European leaders have shown they cannot be trusted on collective security.

Creating a pathway to citizenship in return for military service will help Europe stand on its own.

Continued possession of the exclave brings only a point of pride to Spaniards who are susceptible to nostalgia over the country’s puny remaining imperial possessions. In fact, policing Ceuta against the next upsurge in immigrants incurs large, ongoing fiscal costs and intra-European tensions.

Indeed, last week, much of Europe recoiled in shock and anger at the prospect of tens of thousands of Africans entering their continent by storming the beaches of Ceuta, bearing the meager possessions that they could carry. Though most had returned within 48 hours, Europe’s right-wing parties and press sensationalized what was happening for political or commercial gain, and Spain’s near-neighbor, Italy, quickly instituted the screening of people arriving from Spain to make sure that no Africans were sneaking in through Spain’s North African exclave.

My bet, though, is that Spain will gradually, and perhaps even soon, see the wisdom of abandoning its African territorial claim out of a realism that has so far eluded the British in Gibraltar. The reason for that can be summed up in one word: demographics. Africa’s population is growing more quickly than any other region, albeit a bit more slowly than projected a mere decade ago. Europe is heading in the exact opposite direction, with women in many countries—including Spain and Italy, to take two southern European examples—having roughly one child on average.

Spain’s government has taken the wisest measure of this trend that I know of in Europe, granting amnesty to many who have immigrated illegally in the past, and hitherto publicly identifying continued immigration as one of the rare available remedies for population collapse, with all of the dire economic consequences that would bring to the country.

The quick and fierce lashing out against Spain by fellow European neighbors over the momentary Ceuta crisis makes clear, though, that public opinion on the continent is easily stirred by the prospect of any big and sudden foreign influx, especially one that involves brown- and Black-skinned people.

At this point, Spain should do the right thing and restore this geopolitically insignificant territory to Morocco, closing off the possibility of it ever being used as a backdoor into the pan-European immigration zone known as Schengen.

While doing so, Spain should take the lead in the European discussion of the future of immigration to the continent—which, given its proximity, will disproportionately hinge on the future of Africa. Much of the rest of Europe clings to the delusion that the movement of peoples from Africa and elsewhere in the global south can be handled indefinitely through little more than police action. But Africans and other migrants will continue to show up in Europe in ever larger numbers no matter what. Just how many, though, will depend on what Europe does today to renovate its economic ties to the continent just to the south, making sure that prosperity spreads there, as it once did from Africa to Europe.

Howard W. French is a columnist at Foreign Policy, a professor at the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism, and a longtime foreign correspondent. His latest book is The Second Emancipation: Nkrumah, Pan-Africanism, and Global Blackness at High Tide. Bluesky: @hofrench.bsky.social X: @hofrench
