Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report, where our team has spent the last week taking turns falling sick. But don’t worry, we rallied so that we could bring you this week’s edition.

All right, here’s what’s on tap for the day: A Chinese AI conundrum in Washington, another potential Hormuz reopening, and the cost of Trump’s new battleships.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report, where our team has spent the last week taking turns falling sick. But don’t worry, we rallied so that we could bring you this week’s edition.

All right, here’s what’s on tap for the day: A Chinese AI conundrum in Washington, another potential Hormuz reopening, and the cost of Trump’s new battleships.

No, we’re not talking about the latest U.S. attempt to reach a deal with Iran (though there’s more on that below). Instead, we’re talking about Washington’s latest freakout over China’s artificial intelligence capabilities.

Many people (us included) have spent years asking the question of which of the world’s two biggest economies is winning the AI race. The latest round of soul-searching has been sparked by a model named Kimi that was created by Chinese company Moonshot AI. The chatbot’s latest version, which released in July, showed capabilities that potentially rival the top U.S. models.

The prevailing wisdom indicates a U.S. lead at the cutting edge through Silicon Valley giants such as OpenAI and Anthropic. But China’s bigger innovation may be in how Kimi, DeepSeek, and its other models are taking over the market. Most top Chinese models are open-weight, meaning that anyone can download their building blocks of data and code to create bespoke versions of the model at a much lower cost. As Rishi wrote soon after Kimi’s new model launched, it’s a form of Chinese AI-maxxing that gives countries around the world an easier entry point into an AI ecosystem than the far more expensive (and increasingly unreliable) tech stack that Washington is exporting.

The choices that countries in Africa are making, for example, are particularly instructive. According to a new report in the New York Times, developers across Kenya, Uganda, Ghana, and Nigeria are increasingly opting for Chinese AI models over U.S. ones to build everything from business and legal tools to education applications.

Even U.S. startups are largely hooked on Chinese open-weight models, which resulted in a rather quick end to the Trump administration’s debate over whether they should be banned. Trump is reportedly set to exclude open models from an upcoming AI governance framework that could subject U.S. models to government review—exempting the kinds of models that China dominates and making U.S. restrictions against them less likely. Meanwhile, the administration appears to be tinkering around the edges, with an import ban last week on new Chinese humanoid robots and a possible ban on the use of some Chinese components in U.S. data centers.

Those are among a flurry of anti-China moves from U.S. regulators in recent days, and Beijing has retaliated with its own set of export restrictions on technologies such as drones—potentially making Chinese President Xi Jinping’s anticipated September trip to meet with U.S. President Donald Trump more awkward than Trump’s Beijing trip earlier this year.

But when it comes to AI, China may be playing a different game altogether.

Table stakes. In a must-read FP essay titled “America’s Cosmic Bet on AI,” Harvard University scholar Graham Allison examines the trillions of dollars that the United States has poured into maintaining its AI lead with more advanced chips, more capable models, and acres of new (and not always popular) data centers.

China, meanwhile, is simply doing more with less—though U.S. officials and executives have accused it of stealing their technology—and proliferating good-enough models at a miniscule fraction of the cost.

“The fact that the United States’ only credible competitor in AI—China—is taking such a strikingly different path should make Americans pause and think,” Allison wrote. “China’s strategy for becoming the world leader in AI reflects its basic strategy for achieving dominance in the production of everything. In essence, as we have seen in its domination of solar panels, fast trains, 5G, consumer electronics, and now increasingly electric cars, China begins by offering a product almost as good as the alternative but at a far more affordable price.”

His chosen analogy is one that will be familiar to anyone who uses a smartphone (so, almost everyone): The closed ecosystem that Apple offers in its iPhones vs. Google’s more open and replicable Android operating system. While both of those are U.S.-made, the results speak for themselves—Android is used in 70 percent of smartphones in the world and offers twice as many apps as Apple’s iOS.

Even without worrying about the rest of the world, the disproportionate role that investment in AI is playing in the overall U.S. economy right now prompts Allison to warn (as many have) of a bubble whose bursting would have catastrophic consequences for the global economy and U.S. national security.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention will finally have a Senate-confirmed director for the first time in nearly a year after the Senate on Wednesday confirmed Trump’s nominee for the role, Dr. Erica Schwartz, in a 51-44 vote.

On Tuesday, the Senate Judiciary Committee voted to advance Trump’s nominee for attorney general, Todd Blanche, after he formally pledged to scrap the administration’s controversial anti-weaponization fund. Blanche has been serving as acting attorney general since April, but his confirmation remains far from a sure thing given the pushback surrounding his nomination and the GOP’s razor-thin majority in the Senate. A vote in the full Senate could occur as soon as this week.

It’s also been another tricky week for the FBI that Blanche’s Justice Department oversees, with FBI director Kash Patel telling Reuters that the agency has started conducting joint operations with U.S. adversaries Russia and China. Separately, an FBI agent stands accused of stealing nearly $1 million in cryptocurrency from accounts that the agency was monitoring.

What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already.

Hamas disarmament. Just days after Trump lauded a “historic” agreement for Hamas to disarm, Israel rejected the proposed framework this week. John broke down why Israel is against the U.S.-backed plan in his latest piece.

Once MOUre. Iran and Oman are close to agreeing a deal for commercial ships to transit through the Strait of Hormuz that separates both their coastlines—nearly two months after a memorandum of understanding between the United States and Iran pledged to open the crucial waterway. Under the reported terms of the deal—which Iran said the United States is not a part of—Iran would control the passageway to enter the Persian Gulf through the strait, while Oman would control the exit.

Trump, meanwhile, took to Truth Social to downplay reports that the U.S. military has depleted nearly all of its long-range missiles in the Iran war. “The U.S. has massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types,” he said, without sharing specifics. He went on to threaten “long term jail sentences” for those who leaked news of low stockpiles.

Air defense gap. Facing an intensifying Russian air campaign, Ukraine struck two oil refineries located hundreds of miles within Russian territory, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky posted on X on Thursday. The Ukrainian strikes come after Russian forces fired a barrage of missiles and drones at Kyiv on Wednesday, in a deadly attack that killed at least 17 people and wounded more than 40.

The onslaught of Russian attacks has spotlighted Kyiv’s urgent calls for more air defenses from its partners. For months, Zelensky has pleaded for more U.S. Patriot air defense missiles, which can intercept Russian ballistic missiles and which Washington has stopped donating to the country, as FP’s Alexandra Sharp has written. Making the situation even murkier, Trump recently pledged to share the technology underpinning the powerful missile system with Kyiv before swiftly backtracking on the promise.

Zelensky, for his part, has continued to sound the alarm. “Ballistic missile interceptors could have saved the lives of those killed today,” he posted on X on Wednesday. “It is very important that our partners understand that delays in supplying them, or an unwillingness to provide anti-ballistic systems, lead directly to such horrific casualties and destruction.” —FP’s Christina Lu

Members of Spain’s Civil Guard (USECIC) monitor migrants on Tarajal beach in Ceuta, Spain, on July 31. Adri Salido/Getty Images

Monday, Aug. 10: Legislative assembly elections in Pakistan-administered Kashmir are set to conclude.

Thursday, Aug. 13: Zambia holds a general election.

$275 billion—the total expected cost of the U.S. Navy’s new “Trump-class” battleship fleet, according to a report by the Congressional Budget Office.

“I’m glad he thinks I’m a lovely gentleman. A lot of people think so.”

—Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive candidate who won the Democratic nomination for Michigan’s Senate race, responding to Trump’s sarcastic use of that term to describe him in a speech on Wednesday.

What do actor John Cusack, NFL legend Brett Favre, and former U.S. Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene have in common? For the right price, you can have them record a custom video greeting for yourself or your friends. Greene—one of Trump’s previously staunch supporters who very publicly broke with him over the Epstein files and the Iran war—recently joined Cameo, a service that allows users to pay for personalized video messages from celebrities.

Israel is heading into what may be the most pivotal election in its history, but at stake this time isn’t so much its conflict with neighboring countries or its relations with the Palestinians. The core issue in this vote, slated for Oct. 27, is whether Israel will remain the liberal democracy its founders envisioned when it was established in 1948, or move even more vigorously toward a kind of illiberal regime infused by Orthodox Judaism.

After presiding over a series of center-right governments for 12 years, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took an abrupt rightward shift when he returned to power in 2022 in a coalition with far-right and ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) parties. It soon emerged that his government had two primary goals. The first was to undercut the powers of an independent judiciary and vastly increase those of elected politicians, a plan quietly built on the assumption that, as in the case in other illiberal democracies, those in power would remain so because elections would cease to be entirely free and fair. The second was to give a greater role to the Jewish religion in the public space and provide massive financial, legal, and moral support for West Bank settlers. It was accompanied by ever-bigger government handouts and increased privileges for the Haredi community, most prominently a (so far failed) effort to enshrine in law the ultra-Orthodox’s traditional exemption from military service.

Israel is heading into what may be the most pivotal election in its history, but at stake this time isn’t so much its conflict with neighboring countries or its relations with the Palestinians. The core issue in this vote, slated for Oct. 27, is whether Israel will remain the liberal democracy its founders envisioned when it was established in 1948, or move even more vigorously toward a kind of illiberal regime infused by Orthodox Judaism.

After presiding over a series of center-right governments for 12 years, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took an abrupt rightward shift when he returned to power in 2022 in a coalition with far-right and ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) parties. It soon emerged that his government had two primary goals. The first was to undercut the powers of an independent judiciary and vastly increase those of elected politicians, a plan quietly built on the assumption that, as in the case in other illiberal democracies, those in power would remain so because elections would cease to be entirely free and fair. The second was to give a greater role to the Jewish religion in the public space and provide massive financial, legal, and moral support for West Bank settlers. It was accompanied by ever-bigger government handouts and increased privileges for the Haredi community, most prominently a (so far failed) effort to enshrine in law the ultra-Orthodox’s traditional exemption from military service.

In the meantime, the government has allowed or even facilitated spiraling settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has tried with much success to turn the national police into a political tool, cracking down on anti-government protesters and giving free rein to settler attacks. Defense Minister Israel Katz has sought to do the same with the army.

Along the way, Netanyahu adopted an approach to politics designed to delegitimize the opposition and government institutions—similar to that of U.S. President Donald Trump. Although Netanyahu is less mocking and his public remarks more coherent, that is not so for his cabinet ministers, lawmakers, and social media network—which do his dirty work. He has not only cowed the opposition but also rivals inside his Likud party and government institutions ranging from the courts to the army.

The Netanyahu government’s marquee project vis-à-vis the judiciary was the plan unveiled by Justice Minister Yariv Levin just days after taking office to limit the Supreme Court’s judicial review powers, give politicians control over judicial appointments, and limit the authority of its legal advisors. The plan was never fully realized because it was met with massive street protests, court rulings striking down parts that the Knesset had approved, and the war that followed Hamas’s attack on Oct. 7, 2023. But the government never abandoned it and capped its last months in office with a legislative blitz that won Knesset approval for facets of the judicial overhaul proposal and favors to the Haredi minority.

Millions of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza have none of the rights extended to Israeli citizens. But democratic norms remain the rule inside Israel itself, despite the pressure they have come under in the past four years. If the Netanyahu government remains in power after the upcoming election, then it’s safe to assume that it will feel entirely unconstrained—much the way Trump has blown through governmental norms and conventions in his second term. After all, what could serve as better proof that Netanyahu’s plans to remake Israel have the public’s support?

Israel’s parliamentary opposition, including leftist, centrist, and right-wing parties, as well as two factions representing the Arab minority, has been largely ineffective throughout this period. It never offered a coherent alternative, nor was it able to block the government’s agenda in the Knesset. Yet as bloodless and fractious as it is, the opposition supports judicial independence, opposes the politicization of the army and police, is appalled by settler violence in the West Bank, and has no truck with Haredi privilege, like the draft exemption. An election-day victory for the opposition is the only way to stop Israel’s march to illiberal democracy.

But can it prevail in the election? The opposition’s leadership challenge seems to have been solved. Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff, has been rising steadily in the polls to the point where his Yashar party is now the biggest vote-getter among opposition parties by far. Indeed, it is running neck-and-neck with Netanyahu’s Likud. In many respects, Eisenkot is a strong candidate. He has the military credentials that many voters regard as a sine qua non for high office. He comes from a working-class, Moroccan immigrant background, which should appeal to voters with similar Middle Eastern or North African roots who traditionally vote Likud. He lost his son and two nephews in the war in Gaza. Eisenkot has kept his political stance close to his chest, but his record as chief of staff, public remarks, and party platform suggest that he is a little left of center.

That said, the opposition has two problems. The first is that Eisenkot’s meteoric rise in the polls may not reflect deep support among his voters, many of whom appear to come from the moderate right and may yet drift back to the Likud. Netanyahu is working to upgrade the Likud’s image by peppering the party’s slate with more respectable candidates than the vulgarians and yes-men that currently fill the party’s Knesset ranks. Recently, he has promised to enforce conscription of Haredim, an issue that has hurt him even among his most loyal supporters.

The second problem is that Eisenkot has pledged to include only Zionist parties in his governing coalition—rejecting Arab-led parties as potential partners. Without at least one of them, such as the more moderate Ra’am party, Eisenkot would likely fail to amass a clear-cut Knesset majority, according to polls.

Eisenkot’s rise may have maxed out the opposition’s potential to draw more votes away from the Netanyahu bloc. A poll conducted by the Jewish People Policy Institute in July found that 82 percent were already “completely” or “fairly” certain which party they were voting for. Among the rest, most were likely debating which party within the two blocs they would support, not about whether to cross lines. Like elsewhere in the world, tribal politics have grown so strong in Israel that large numbers of voters will stick to their camp, even if their leaders aren’t performing. Netanyahu’s campaign plays to that by invoking the dangerous “leftism” of his rivals.

Experts say political uncertainty makes the Trump-backed plan untenable, for now.

A new book describes the destruction of Palestinian life street by street.

Finally, there are signs that Netanyahu and his coalition plan to wage a dirty campaign. President Isaac Herzog has warned about election violence and intimidation. Others are worried that the politicized police and perhaps the Shin Bet security service will look the other way or even help the government intimidate its critics. If all else fails, Netanyahu and his allies may contest the results. It’s not clear how the opposition could stop them.

Surprisingly, the security issues that preoccupy the rest of the world (and Israelis, as well) are less likely to factor in the election. It’s not that Netanyahu’s forever wars are seen as a stunning success. Successive polls show that voters do not think the country is more secure, particularly after the Iran war. Yet, across the political spectrum, Oct. 7 has left so deep a scar that many Israelis believe the country has no choice but to pursue its enemies aggressively or risk another massacre. Their tolerance for failure is high. As a result, the opposition can only nip at the edges of Netanyahu’s policies.

Nevertheless, it is reasonable to assume that there will be some change on the security front. In Gaza, a government led by Eisenkot would no longer pursue the far right’s dreams of expelling the Palestinians and rebuilding settlements. Israel will likely end its unrelenting attacks and may even pull out its troops. Gaza’s reconstruction may move forward under a new Israeli government, if Hamas agrees to something approaching disarmament. In Lebanon, where Israel occupies a security zone in the south, the new government will face the same dilemma as the old one, namely that pulling out troops would enable Hezbollah to threaten Israel’s north. Nevertheless, the new government will likely give Trump’s peace plan a more serious try and stage at least limited withdrawals. The Iran theater is no longer Israel’s to decide on: By bringing the United States into the war, Israel has forfeited control.

In the West Bank, the wave of settler violence and settlement-building will be tamped down but not eliminated. The extremist wing of the settlement movement has become too powerful and rooted. In any case, there will be no movement toward a two-state solution. Oct. 7 buried the idea of Palestinian statehood for the foreseeable future, and neither Israel nor Trump’s Washington is interested.

David E. Rosenberg is the economics editor and a columnist for the English edition of Haaretz and the author of Israel’s Technology Economy.

High-resolution satellite imagery has never been easier to buy, or to fake. For a brief window last week, the world’s most popular digital globe, Google Earth, let users manipulate satellite images with AI to create fakes grounded in real terrain. Backlash prompted the company to roll back the feature after less than a day. But its rollout demonstrated how quickly contemporary models can churn out misinformation when the right guardrails are not in place.

Authentic imagery, meanwhile, is more available than ever. Customers’ options are rapidly expanding amid an ever-growing field of international competitors that offer similar views from low Earth orbit. But the same openness that serves as a resource for researchers and journalists also allows for more sinister uses, like Iran using commercial imagery to track U.S. troops, which can prompt governments to try to crack down on what’s available. In a world crowded with providers and rife with fakes, tomorrow’s commercial satellite imagery market will be defined more by trust than access.

High-resolution satellite imagery has never been easier to buy, or to fake. For a brief window last week, the world’s most popular digital globe, Google Earth, let users manipulate satellite images with AI to create fakes grounded in real terrain. Backlash prompted the company to roll back the feature after less than a day. But its rollout demonstrated how quickly contemporary models can churn out misinformation when the right guardrails are not in place.

Authentic imagery, meanwhile, is more available than ever. Customers’ options are rapidly expanding amid an ever-growing field of international competitors that offer similar views from low Earth orbit. But the same openness that serves as a resource for researchers and journalists also allows for more sinister uses, like Iran using commercial imagery to track U.S. troops, which can prompt governments to try to crack down on what’s available. In a world crowded with providers and rife with fakes, tomorrow’s commercial satellite imagery market will be defined more by trust than access.

Earth observation was once the exclusive domain of well-resourced governments that sent up multibillion-dollar spy satellites the size of a commercial bus. Now, these satellites can be as small as a shoebox and launched by companies, not just countries. According to the American Enterprise Institute’s Space Data Navigator, there were 848 active satellites in the year 2000. There are more than 16,000 today. Thousands of these are in orbit for Earth observation and provide a critical viewpoint for research, journalism, and humanitarian work.

Among many uses, imagery has become an essential tool in revealing human rights abuses, coordinating disaster response, surveying agricultural trends, monitoring deforestation, and tracking sea level rise. Commercial providers are so plentiful that governments can leverage satellite imagery as a public relations tool, and, in turn, the public can often check a government’s claims independently.

But that same abundance creates new risks as well. Iran needed no satellite of its own to monitor U.S. troops at Al Asad Air Base in Iraq before striking it in 2020, just a vendor with imagery to sell. Even firms like China’s MizarVision, which don’t own any satellites, can still publish annotated images of U.S. military assets. If commercial providers and vendors block sales to parts of the world, a straw purchaser can often obtain imagery by concealing who it will ultimately go to. As a result, sanctioning the firms or countries that buy satellite imagery products from Western providers will not cut off access to these images. When strikes on Iran began in 2026, for example, the U.S. government requested that American commercial satellite imagery providers stop selling photos of the region, and many curbed sales – even those who said they never received such a request. But that didn’t stop European and Chinese sources, which kept selling.

Government-requested imagery blackouts create a void filled by international providers. Now, some Chinese imagery firms proudly brag about being under U.S. sanctions as a publicity tool. As a result, the degree of shutter control over satellite images that the U.S. government could once exercise, either through legal restrictions on, or exclusive purchases of, satellite imagery is no longer possible. Cutting off access was once a feasible national security solution, but today’s proliferated imagery space means the world’s militaries must plan, act, and operate as if they are under observation.

Disinformation compounds the complexity of this space, with individual and state actors doctoring satellite imagery to further foreign-policy goals. When Russia denied its role in shooting down MH17 over Ukraine in 2014, it used deceptive satellite images to further its false claims. Social media users may also create or share such fakes to garner monetized engagement. AI has only made fakes easier to generate, creating images that are sufficiently high quality to spread rapidly online.

Deceptions like these ultimately harm all imagery providers by degrading trust in their products. As a result, commercial providers face collapsing trust from the public on one side and government restrictions on the other. Efforts to entirely shut down imagery access are not only futile but would also hinder uses of it that benefit the common good. What providers can do, however, is take steps to curb the misuse of their images.

As a first step, more companies should engage in thorough vetting for individuals who purchase the most up-to-date imagery. When it comes to satellite images, timing can matter more than resolution. An older image of an air base is suited to research; one from this morning is ideal for targeting support. This means that archival imagery should remain available, including high-resolution content essential for journalism and humanitarian efforts, alongside taxpayer-funded lower-resolution imagery from programs like the United States’ Landsat and the European Union’s Copernicus. More sensitive data, like recent high-resolution imagery and satellite tasking in conflict zones, should rest behind vetting that confirms a customer’s identity and scrutinizes end use, similar to how many financial institutions know their customers.

Vetting customers represents a more effective alternative to government-imposed blackouts, and a company that can account for who holds its most sensitive imagery has a stronger case for keeping some access flowing. After American provider Planet Labs received a request from the U.S. government for a blackout during the Iran war, it implemented a more selective distribution model that could support urgent use cases. A provider that knows its customers can do this, whereas one that sells indiscriminately can only shut off access completely to comply.

Companies can also help build trust with the public by taking visible steps to confront the manipulation and abuse of their products. In addition to vetting, providers can do better at fielding claims of misuse. A dedicated portal through which customers, and even regular social media users, can submit suspect content will help providers cut off access or publicly refute deceptions with greater speed.

George Clooney’s pioneering data project documented horrors in Sudan, but that wasn’t enough.

The United States is racing ahead where Europe, China, and India struggle.

Negotiating a new treaty to manage space seems hopeless, but a workable mechanism exists.

Communicating these actions matters, too. Imagery providers that publicize their efforts to confront misuse will maintain the public’s trust in their products, while firms that fail to do so will be missing a competitive offering. This publicity can take many forms, ranging from collaborations with journalists who report on disinformation to social media posts warning of disreputable sources. But touting their efforts to track fakes and abuse, while not revealing the method behind them, can give these firms a leg up without betraying quality-control practices.

Executives at commercial imagery companies could be reticent to draw attention to ways their products could be misused or faked, even if they are actively addressing these issues. But the reality is that deliberate misuse by bad actors and AI-fueled imagery fakes are set to bring that awareness to the public anyway.

The differentiator among imagery providers then becomes a competition of trust in process and product. A vetted customer base reassures the public that a company’s sensitive imagery rests in responsible hands. This in turn lends confidence to the imagery itself when it surfaces in media, academia, and elsewhere, because the public knows it is only available through a vetted process. There is no stopping the tide of fakes, but by establishing trust, companies can allow researchers, journalists, and the public to push back on disinformation.

Leading satellite image providers already take many important vetting and verification measures. Planet Labs screens prospective customers and runs an ethics committee. Fellow American provider Vantor supplies imagery and analysis to thousands of journalists. But these positive practices are not the norm. They vary across providers and are inconsistently rewarded by the market. The industry’s incentive structure today often rewards removing as many barriers to access as possible, and monitoring end use is discretionary. These tendencies sacrifice long-term trust for short-term sales.

As the market matures and trust gains prominence as a differentiator, providers seen as responsible and authentic sources will have the edge over competitors. Those that invest in these strategies now will lead the pack, while others that eschew them could find their products restricted by blackouts or marred by irresponsible use. With doctored or misused imagery growing more prevalent, the future of Earth observation belongs not to those with the best access, but to those seen as reliable.

Brady Africk is a research analyst specializing in open-source intelligence at the American Enterprise Institute and author of Views From Above, a satellite imagery-driven newsletter.

Conservative outsider Abelardo de la Espriella is about to be sworn in as Colombia’s new president. Gustavo Petro, the soon to be former leftist president, began his own term hoping to bring peace to the country by negotiating with a wide array of criminal and ideological armed groups under his “total peace” strategy. That approach failed. In contrast, de la Espriella has promised peace and security through a vigorous campaign of law and order, including constructing megaprisons similar to those in El Salvador.

Big swings in the approach to conflict are nothing new for Colombia, which faces multiple challenges from groups such as the Ejercito de Liberación Nacional, a longtime ideological guerrilla group that has never signed a peace accord, and the Clan del Golfo, a major cartel. The country has shown deep ambivalence between social justice and law and order approaches before. Following years of then-President Álvaro Uribe’s hard-line approach, the Colombian government painstakingly negotiated a Peace Accord with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), then the country’s main Marxist-Leninist insurgent group, which was then initially rejected by voters by a small margin in 2016 before being approved by the Colombian Congress.

Conservative outsider Abelardo de la Espriella is about to be sworn in as Colombia’s new president. Gustavo Petro, the soon to be former leftist president, began his own term hoping to bring peace to the country by negotiating with a wide array of criminal and ideological armed groups under his “total peace” strategy. That approach failed. In contrast, de la Espriella has promised peace and security through a vigorous campaign of law and order, including constructing megaprisons similar to those in El Salvador.

Big swings in the approach to conflict are nothing new for Colombia, which faces multiple challenges from groups such as the Ejercito de Liberación Nacional, a longtime ideological guerrilla group that has never signed a peace accord, and the Clan del Golfo, a major cartel. The country has shown deep ambivalence between social justice and law and order approaches before. Following years of then-President Álvaro Uribe’s hard-line approach, the Colombian government painstakingly negotiated a Peace Accord with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), then the country’s main Marxist-Leninist insurgent group, which was then initially rejected by voters by a small margin in 2016 before being approved by the Colombian Congress.

Left behind in the debate between these two extremes is what rural Colombians truly yearn for: large-scale rural development. This approach has never been tried before in earnest in Colombia, the hemisphere’s most unequal country. A truly large-scale rural development approach would be a game-changer for interrupting the coca-growing economy; bringing state presence, law, and order; and even increasing private investment into lawless areas and turning the tables on criminal groups.

Between 2021 and 2025, I was the deputy director of the large, now-closed U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) mission in Bogotá, Colombia. I also served as the U.S. Embassy lead for assisting a groundbreaking Petro administration rural infrastructure program, called Rural Roads for Total Peace. While Colombia’s leaders have generally ignored the importance of rural development, this promising Petro administration program was an exception. It contained several key lessons that, if adopted by the new administration, could rapidly scale up rural development. Doing so could be the key to reining in criminality and bringing peace to Colombia.

The evidence that rural development has consistently been left behind is compelling. The University of Notre Dame’s Kroc Institute is the official observer of Colombia’s 2016 Peace Accord, carefully measuring implementation progress and providing periodic assessments. While certain areas of the accord, such as transitional justice and greater political participation, have progressed well, the chapter dealing with rural development has not.

According to the Kroc Institute’s latest assessment, released in May 2026, the rural development chapter has achieved just 9 percent of completion, the least of any of the six chapters. Yet according to the Colombian government, the rural development chapter is by far the most expensive to implement, requiring 85 percent of the accord’s total cost. Rural development is the first chapter of the Peace Accord, speaking to its visibility and importance to millions of people in rural areas, where the FARC made its home. Its lack of implementation is why one rural woman commented to me in 2022, “The accord stayed on paper.”

Why has rural development been ignored? As a foreigner with deep experience in the region, I believe it has to do with a very Colombian way of seeing themselves. Urban Colombians will commonly speak about “the territories” to refer to rural places outside of the big cities. This phrasing is uniquely Colombian, seeming both archaic, calling back to colonial times, and binary, implying that there is the normal world and the “other.” The idea that the countryside is poor, backward, and unimprovable seems normalized for many urban Colombians.

Attitudes of urban Colombians toward their rural counterparts are a complex mix of pride; romanticism; and, at times, condescension. For instance, the classic Colombian rural hat (el sombrero vueltiao) was worn by thousands of Colombian fans attending their team’s recent men’s World Cup matches. Colombians have tremendous pride in rural culture and the beautiful countryside, often romanticizing rural life in rural-themed restaurants, filled on Sunday afternoons. Yet at the same time, perceptions of ingrained rural corruption and lack of sophistication are common as well.

My experience working with the Colombian roads authority on the rural infrastructure program encapsulated the challenge and potential for Colombia to take on rural development in a big way. In my more than 25 years working overseas in development, I had never encountered a more talented, goal-focused, and hardworking set of professionals. Yet they were surprisingly unfamiliar with rural development and working with rural people.

Despite the lack of experience, they made key program decisions in line with good rural development practices. First, the program was bottom-up, putting rural communities at the center of decision-making and implementation. Doing so ensured that the section of road chosen for improvement was the right one, leveraging local knowledge and priorities. It ensured that communities own the results. It also tended to overcome centuries of paternalism between rural citizens and the all-powerful state in Bogotá.

Second, the program leveraged well known, legally constituted entities such as Community Action Boards (Juntas de Acción Comunal, in Spanish) to implement the program, rather than something new. To the surprise of many outsiders, Colombia is a very legalistic country, so using tried-and-true methods reduced risk. The program was implemented through village committees with elected, volunteer representatives. They were legally capable of signing contracts with Colombia’s central government, providing a strong legal basis.

It’s the latest Latin American country to elect a Trump-backed leader.

Third, the program managers recognized where they lacked experience. Entities such as USAID and nongovernmental organizations commonly work on community-built infrastructure, using volunteer labor and community-led decision-making. However, this methodology was totally new for the roads authority. It quickly learned how to adapt the methodology so that it could be scaled up. Key tweaks were needed—for instance, changing from informal, volunteer labor to formal labor contracts for legal liability reasons and hiring community organizers to help the engineers work with communities.

The program wasn’t perfect. It fell victim to the fiscal crunch in the Petro administration’s second two years. Many communities were accepted by the program, but due to lack of funding, never built their roads. Recent reporting alleges that the program fell apart in its second year of operations, with too many projects started, little funding, and too little supervision, and that it was victim of vote-buying schemes led by the Ministry of Finance.

But the program debunked a commonly held belief that I often heard among urban professionals that country people would “steal all the money”—in fact, none of very detailed audits found that. Actually, community-led implementation was cheaper per kilometer than traditional contracting, as community members sought to make the most of the central government funding.

Even program critics acknowledged that of 1035 projects started in 2023, the program’s first year, 856 were completed, an astonishing 85 percent success rate for community-led infrastructure projects. And citizens in long-forgotten corners of the country felt, often for the first time, that the central government cared.

President-elect de la Espriella has a clear mandate to bring law and order to the country. Bringing a program of large-scale rural development to all of the rural places (that tended to vote for his opponent) is a tried-and-true way to knit the country together into one peaceful Colombia.

Jeremiah A. Carew was the deputy mission director of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) in Colombia from 2021 until the mission’s closing in August 2025. Over his 21-year career with USAID, he served in Peru, Afghanistan, Uganda, Vietnam, South Sudan, and Washington, D.C. He retired at the rank of counselor in the U.S. Senior Foreign Service, and his final assignment was as mission director of USAID in Somalia. He currently resides in Ecuador, where he writes on international development topics for Razón Pública in a monthly column; his work has also appeared in El Tiempo and the Foreign Service Journal.

The Black Sea’s trade corridors are at the center of the Russia-Ukraine war again, as they were from 2022 to 2023, when a Russian naval blockade stopped Ukrainian maritime exports and shook agricultural markets worldwide. The current crisis looks similar, but it’s unique in important ways, as are the alternatives to resolve it.

Understanding the conflict four years on.

On July 23, Ukraine announced that maritime transport to and from its three unoccupied Black Sea ports was effectively frozen. Russian missile and drone attacks in July alone targeted 57 Ukrainian and foreign-flagged merchant ships in ports and at sea, including Golden Leo, a Turkish-owned bulk cargo carrier sailing under the flag of Guinea-Bissau. Three Russian missiles struck it in open water off the coast of Odesa on July 19, killing 10 people; the ship sank on July 27. By then, this year’s strikes had already cut Ukraine’s grain exports by roughly a third and doubled shipping freight costs into and out of the country.

The Black Sea’s trade corridors are at the center of the Russia-Ukraine war again, as they were from 2022 to 2023, when a Russian naval blockade stopped Ukrainian maritime exports and shook agricultural markets worldwide. The current crisis looks similar, but it’s unique in important ways, as are the alternatives to resolve it.

Understanding the conflict four years on.

On July 23, Ukraine announced that maritime transport to and from its three unoccupied Black Sea ports was effectively frozen. Russian missile and drone attacks in July alone targeted 57 Ukrainian and foreign-flagged merchant ships in ports and at sea, including Golden Leo, a Turkish-owned bulk cargo carrier sailing under the flag of Guinea-Bissau. Three Russian missiles struck it in open water off the coast of Odesa on July 19, killing 10 people; the ship sank on July 27. By then, this year’s strikes had already cut Ukraine’s grain exports by roughly a third and doubled shipping freight costs into and out of the country.

As in 2022-2023, when a Russian naval blockade trapped millions of tons of Ukrainian grain and sparked a global food crisis, Ukraine’s Black Sea ports are out of business due to the attacks, even if most of the facilities are still operable. Agricultural stocks are piling up, and global grain markets are tightening. Ukraine’s agricultural sector is staring at a direct loss in export revenue between $1.5 billion and $3 ​billion this year, according to its agriculture minister. Ukraine’s Black Sea maritime corridors handle approximately 90 percent of the country’s agricultural exports, along with the lion’s share of its mining and steel products. These sectors account for three-quarters of Ukraine’s foreign-currency earnings.

This is why Ukraine urged the United Nations on July 27 to help facilitate safe transit through the Black Sea, as the U.N. temporarily succeeded in doing in 2022. Ukrainian officials accused Russia of war crimes and economic terror over attacks on civilian cargo ships and grain terminals. They argued that Russia is holding global food security hostage, just as it did four years ago. They compared Russia’s actions against food supply chains to disruptions of energy routes in the Strait of Hormuz, warning that developing nations could face hunger and rising prices.

But the current crisis is different from the previous one in key respects.

The 2022-2023 events involved Russian warships imposing a classic blockade on Ukraine’s ports, forming a cordon around the Odesa coast with vessels and mines that prevented the entry and exit of Ukrainian and foreign ships. The blockade began in late 2022, just as Ukraine was processing a record agricultural harvest from the previous year. Ukrainian silos were full, and roughly 20 million tons of grain ended up stranded. The crisis reverberated around the world, including to Africa, Asia, and the Middle East, where dozens of low-income countries rely on Ukrainian grain. Prices shot up, and although the shortage did not lead to famine, it caused hardship and food instability.

The European Union came to Ukraine’s rescue by opening maritime passages through Danube ports in Romania and Bulgaria, and by offering rail and road access to international markets through Central Europe. The deal threw a lifeline to Ukraine by enabling it to sell its goods in EU markets, including Poland, Hungary, and Slovakia. But domestic farmers in those countries struggled to compete with the sudden influx of Ukrainian produce and grains, and they protested vigorously. Politicians responded by slapping embargoes on Ukrainian agricultural goods despite EU policy to the contrary.

In July 2022, the U.N. brokered the Black Sea Grain Initiative, a safe maritime corridor for food and fertilizer exports, in exchange for easing Western sanctions on Russian food and fertilizer exports. (Russia broke the agreement less than a year later and has since regularly targeted and harassed shipping in the Black Sea corridors.)

In appealing to the U.N. again in July, Ukraine clearly hoped for a repeat intervention and used the same language. But this crisis, thus far, hasn’t triggered anything like the food market turmoil of four years ago—yet. “In February 2022, agricultural stocks in Ukraine were full,” Oleg Nivievskyi, of the Kyiv School of Economics, explained. “That’s why the impact was so heavy.” This time, however, Ukraine had already shipped its recent harvest before Russia shut down the ports, and global grain markets are relatively flush, he said.

Moreover, the impediment this time around is not a physical blockade. Russia is not obstructing ships but rather striking them, their crews, and their cargo directly. That makes the financial risk so great that merchant vessels won’t make the trip. War-risk premiums on freight rates and shipping insurance have spiked, if the latter is even available from underwriters. As a result, ship owners are citing force majeure to walk away from charters. Grain isn’t moving despite an open corridor. This is a market collapse driven by cost and risk, not a siege.

That points to possible remedies: affordable war-risk insurance—through state-backed damage compensation, for example. But the logic of this hard-nosed financial calculus raises serious ethical questions, as a similar paradigm does in the Strait of Hormuz. War-risk insurance compensates for financial loss: the vessel, the cargo, and liability payouts if crew are killed or injured. This is compensation, not protection. The insurance makes the voyage financially viable for the owner; it does nothing to reduce the physical risk to the people actually on the ship.

After oil refineries and cargo ships, Ukraine is now taking out Russian e-commerce.

In the Gulf, after hostilities knocked out commercial war-risk coverage starting in March 2026 and premiums spiked fivefold, the United States set up a $20 billion maritime reinsurance plan that covered hull, cargo, war protection, and indemnity. It’s still operating, but it hasn’t fully worked: Most shippers are still steering clear of the Gulf.

The backstop solved the insurability problem without solving the risk-to-life problem. Stephen Cotton of the International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF) summed it up: “These are not accidents, not collateral damage, these are deliberate acts against civilian workers who have no part in this conflict and no power to escape it.” No cargo, no contract, no commercial pressure is worth a seafarer’s life, the ITF underscored. “Until there is genuine, guaranteed safety, no vessel should be transiting this war zone with civilian crew aboard.”

The go-to option is the alternative routes and markets provided in 2022-2023. Some of the load can be shifted to Danube River routes in the autumn (once water levels rise from their current historic lows) and overland through Central Europe. This, of course, assumes that Central Europeans will play ball—and that is in no way assured. This time, there is no discussion of completely reopening EU markets like in 2022.

Moreover, even given good will, these corridors simply can’t absorb the roughly 2.5 to 3.5 million tons a month of capacity that Ukraine has lost from its deepwater ports. River exports on the Danube currently move around 100,000 tons a month. Truck exports, roughly, can handle another 100,000 tons a month, and rail to the western border tops out at 300,000 to 400,000 tons, according to Ukrainian sources. European ports already have their own exports to store and ship, and it’s not clear how much spare capacity they have.

“In the longer term, Ukraine has no viable substitute for its Black Sea ports,” Slawomir Matuszak, of the Warsaw-based Center for Eastern Studies, said. The Danube ports, he argued, are very small and could handle half of the Black Sea ports’ monthly capacity at best. The roads and railways through Central Europe are underprepared for Ukraine’s prodigious loads. Together, they could handle half of the Black Sea ports’ monthly capacity at best, and the alternative routes would cost Ukrainian exporters an additional $45 to $50 per ton, according to Reuters.

The picture is further complicated by Ukraine’s own strikes on Russian shipping in the Sea of Azov using one-way aerial and maritime drones. On July 10, Russia halted Kerch Strait transit after drone attacks had hit more than 100 vessels in the area, and it exported just 1.8 million metric tons of wheat in July—down around 830 percent from the same month in 2025. Russia’s busiest seaport—Novorossiysk on the Black Sea’s northeast coast—is virtually idle. Ukraine may be inflicting economic damage on Russia, but it’s also straining global grain supplies itself, even as it asks the U.N. to force Russia to stand down on humanitarian grounds—a contradiction that Kyiv didn’t acknowledge in New York.

Russia’s main grain lobby group complained on July 31, apparently with a straight face, that Ukrainian strikes on its transports could result in hunger ​in Africa and the Middle East.

Global grain markets are jittery but functional for now. “In September and October, however, there’ll be a new harvest,” Nivievskyi said. Come autumn, the world could face a food crisis every bit as severe as the one in 2022.

Paul Hockenos is a Berlin-based journalist. His recent book is Berlin Calling: A Story of Anarchy, Music, the Wall, and the Birth of the New Berlin.

For months, Hamas’s disarmament has been the biggest sticking point in the stalled Gaza peace process. Major aspects of U.S. President Donald Trump’s 20-point peace plan are contingent on Hamas giving up its weapons, and Gaza has remained in a painful limbo since a cease-fire began last October due to the impasse.

For a moment last week, it looked like change might be on the horizon as Hamas agreed to a U.S.-backed framework to lay down its arms. Last Thursday, Trump hailed the agreement, which was orchestrated by his Board of Peace and designed to bring about the full implementation of his 20-point plan, on social media as “HISTORIC” and “a monumental step toward lasting PEACE and SECURITY.” The next day, Trump said that Israel was “very happy” with the agreement.

For months, Hamas’s disarmament has been the biggest sticking point in the stalled Gaza peace process. Major aspects of U.S. President Donald Trump’s 20-point peace plan are contingent on Hamas giving up its weapons, and Gaza has remained in a painful limbo since a cease-fire began last October due to the impasse.

For a moment last week, it looked like change might be on the horizon as Hamas agreed to a U.S.-backed framework to lay down its arms. Last Thursday, Trump hailed the agreement, which was orchestrated by his Board of Peace and designed to bring about the full implementation of his 20-point plan, on social media as “HISTORIC” and “a monumental step toward lasting PEACE and SECURITY.” The next day, Trump said that Israel was “very happy” with the agreement.

But it’s evident that that’s far from the case.

In the days since, Israel has expressed strong opposition to the disarmament roadmap, citing “serious security concerns.” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanayhu said on Tuesday that Israel “did not agree” with the framework and won’t withdraw from its “current lines until Hamas is completely disarmed.” Israel has also conducted a series of airstrikes in Gaza since the plan was announced, angering the Board of Peace.

Experts told Foreign Policy that Israel’s position on the disarmament plan is extremely unlikely to change until at least after the country’s highly anticipated elections in October, which could see Netanyahu—Israel’s longest-serving prime minister—lose power.

“The problem is that politically, in Israel, and especially before elections, it’s borderline impossible for the Israeli government to accept [the plan],” said Shira Efron, the distinguished chair for Israel policy at RAND, a security think tank. “Netanyahu and this coalition promised the Israelis absolute victory.” She added that the Israeli prime minister doesn’t want to be seen as making concessions to Hamas or giving up ground in Gaza ahead of the elections.

The deal is also unpalatable to Israel because of Qatar and Turkey’s potential role in the verification mechanism. “In the Israeli minds of today, Qatar is a borderline enemy state and Turkey the same,” Efron said, emphasizing that some in Israel view Turkey as the “new Iran.”

But even if Netanyahu loses in October, experts don’t anticipate swift changes in Israel’s position. “A new government would be hard-pressed to suddenly make major concessions in Gaza,” said Julie Norman, an associate fellow with the Middle East and North Africa program at Chatham House, a London-based think tank. “That would be a difficult move for them.”


    
    
        Read More
        
                    
                
    
            
        
        
        U.S. President Donald Trump gestures as he poses next to a sign at a world leaders' summit on ending the Gaza war, amid a U.S.-brokered prisoner-hostage swap and ceasefire deal between Israel and Hamas, in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, October 13, 2025.
    
    
        
    
                Everyone Is Waiting for Trump’s Gaza Plan to Die            


    
    	The Board of Peace has been revealed to be so flawed as to be completely unworkable.    	    


        
        Analysis    
        |
        
    
    Anchal Vohra


    


             
                    
                
    
            
        
        
        Hamas militants are seen standing between two green flags while wearing all black and holding guns.
    
    
        
    
                Does the Road to Disarming Hamas Lead Through Qatar and Turkey?            


    
    	Diplomats and experts say Doha and Ankara have leverage, but it may not be enough.    	        
            


        
        Analysis    
        |
        
    
    John Haltiwanger

The Board of Peace has been revealed to be so flawed as to be completely unworkable.

Diplomats and experts say Doha and Ankara have leverage, but it may not be enough.

The disarmament framework, which provides a 14-day window to hammer out an exact timeline after all parties approve, calls for all sides to halt military operations in Gaza and ties the process to a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the territory.

But there are many reasons to believe that Israel has no intention of withdrawing from Gaza anytime soon.

Israel is currently estimated to control more than 60 percent of the coastal enclave. Israeli forces have also moved the yellow line—a military demarcation indicating the area under Israeli control—further into the territory in recent weeks. The yellow line, which was established under the Trump-backed peace deal, is supposed to be temporary. But in May, Netanyahu said that he directed the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) to expand its control of Gaza to 70 percent, in one of the many signs that Israel plans to remain for an extended period.

As Netanyahu outright rejects the plan, the Board of Peace has seemingly already backed down on the initial push for the Israeli withdrawal from Gaza to occur in concert with Hamas’s disarmament. “The withdrawal of the IDF beyond the Yellow Line will take place only once decommissioning is complete, as Hamas committed to the mediators,” the Board of Peace posted on X on Monday, the same day that its high representative for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov, met with Netanyahu in Jerusalem. The Board of Peace has essentially “reassured Israel” that it doesn’t have to “withdraw from the current yellow line,” Efron said.

The disarmament agreement calls for the process to be overseen by the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG)—a technocratic body of Palestinians that’s meant to administer Gaza under Trump’s peace plan—and for the weapons to be stored in Gaza.

Efron said that from Israel’s perspective, suggesting that Hamas’s arms should be stored in Gaza under NCAG supervision is “a joke.” Amid ongoing concerns that Hamas is taking steps to rearm and rebuild, it’s difficult for Israel to accept a process that removes it from monitoring the disarmament process, Efron said. Israel has blocked the NCAG from entering Gaza, and its 15 members remain in Cairo, which presents a significant obstacle.

The framework also states that the process will begin after the deployment of an international stabilization force (ISF). In late July, Israel reportedly offered initial approval for some form of a multinational force entering Gaza, but the ISF does not yet exist. With Israel rejecting the new disarmament framework, these key aspects of Trump’s broader peace plan are poised to remain up in the air.

At the end of the day, the details of the plan remain “hazy,” Norman said, adding that it follows a familiar pattern to “many of Trump’s diplomatic endeavors.”

“You see this initial announcement, a one-pager of bullet points, and then this idea that the rest of it will be hashed out later,” Norman said. “That hasn’t worked in other stages of Gaza or Iran or other conflicts that we’ve seen, and it doesn’t seem to be happening now.”

Nathan J. Brown, a professor of political science and international affairs at George Washington University, said that Trump’s enthusiastic announcement of the framework agreement was a “hardball tactic” as he attempts to “bully a way forward.” This development represents “noise” but “no movement,” Brown said.

Yet some experts said that the disarmament plan could serve as a roadmap toward future progress and might push the static peace process in a fresh direction.

“We can be clear-eyed about the fact that this is not going to suddenly resolve things in Gaza. Hamas is not going to bury or turn over their arms tomorrow. Israel is not going to be withdrawing anytime soon,” Norman said. “But this does change the dynamic in a way that was necessary and important.”

That’s in part because few expected Hamas to agree to disarm. The group defines itself as a resistance movement, and arms are central to its identity.

Some speculate that Hamas never expected Netanyahu to agree to the framework and that it was attempting to put the onus on Israel to make the next move, as well as shift blame to Israel for the lack of progress in Gaza.

The militant group has basically thrown “the ball to Israel’s court,” Efron said.

However strategic and calculated this move was, though, it helped “unlock” a different “dynamic and conversation,” Norman said.

The new framework also potentially offers the Board of Peace and the United States new “pressure and leverage” with the Israeli government “if they choose to use it,” Norman said, including by asking Israel to present alternatives to the plan—such as allowing the NCAG to enter Gaza if Hamas agrees to decommission its heavy weapons, for example.

Mladenov has conceded that the process is far from over, posting on X that this is “the start of the hard phase” and underscoring that this type of diplomacy is “grinding and technical work.”

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the fallout of Ukraine’s missile defense shortage, a possible deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and how SpaceX debris crashed into the moon.

Understanding the conflict four years on.

Russian forces launched an onslaught of missiles and drones at Kyiv and its surrounding area on Wednesday, killing at least 17 people, injuring around 44 others, and damaging key infrastructure for major retailers. Although Ukrainian air defenses managed to intercept nearly 90 percent of the 115 incoming drones, they failed to down a single one of the 24 ballistic missiles and four cruise missiles.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the fallout of Ukraine’s missile defense shortage, a possible deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and how SpaceX debris crashed into the moon.

Sign up to receive World Brief in your inbox every weekday.

Understanding the conflict four years on.

Russian forces launched an onslaught of missiles and drones at Kyiv and its surrounding area on Wednesday, killing at least 17 people, injuring around 44 others, and damaging key infrastructure for major retailers. Although Ukrainian air defenses managed to intercept nearly 90 percent of the 115 incoming drones, they failed to down a single one of the 24 ballistic missiles and four cruise missiles.

“Ballistic missile interceptors could have saved the lives of those killed today,” Ukrainian ​President Volodymyr Zelenskiy wrote on X. “It is very important that our partners understand that delays in supplying them, or an unwillingness to provide anti-ballistic systems, lead directly to such horrific casualties and destruction.”

For months, Zelensky has warned of Ukraine’s shortage of U.S. Patriot missiles, which are the only weapons in Kyiv’s inventory that can reliably intercept Russian ballistic missiles. With the onset of the Iran war in February, the United States has stopped providing Ukraine with these essential weapons, instead keeping the highly sought after resource for its own use.

But now, even the United States may be running out. Last week, a report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies found that the number of U.S. Patriots in stock has dropped by around 65 percent since the start of the Iran conflict. The Defense Department has requested $67 billion in supplemental funding from Congress to address this shortfall; some of these missiles take years to manufacture and deliver.

During last month’s NATO leaders’ summit, U.S. President Donald Trump tried to appease Zelensky’s appeals for aid by agreeing to give Kyiv a license to manufacture Patriot missile interceptors. But on Friday, Trump denied having done so. “It is a hard thing to give away that kind of technology,” Trump said, warning that “those people you give the technology, they could someday turn on you.” Hours later, Russian ballistic missiles killed at least nine people and injured roughly 28 others in Kyiv.

Zelensky has since shifted his attention to other potential suppliers. On Wednesday, he spoke separately with NATO chief Mark Rutte and British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting about new avenues to secure missile interceptors. He also convened his national security council to brainstorm ways to bolster anti-ballistic technologies.

“Our partners do have the missiles,” Zelensky wrote on X. “It is important that the necessary political decisions on supplies and the acceleration of production processes are ultimately made.”

But these efforts may prove to be too little, too late. European countries have failed to fast-track large-scale interceptor production over the past five years and have prioritized what technology is available for their own protection. Over the past year, NATO members have accused Russian and Ukrainian forces of launching stray drones, missiles, and aircraft into the airspaces of Denmark, Estonia, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, and Romania, among others. That includes a suspected Russian drone incursion at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport on Wednesday, which authorities believe was carrying an explosive when it collided with a cargo plane.

Back in business? Tehran and Muscat are close to finalizing a deal that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said on Wednesday. The agreement would include the creation of a temporary safe route for commercial shipping to help alleviate the global energy crisis. But this will only occur if “certain third parties do not obstruct the process,” Baghaei added, in a thinly veiled reference to the United States.

Trump has similarly foreshadowed that a deal to reopen the strait could be reached as soon as this week. “It could happen. Tomorrow or the next day,” Trump said late Tuesday. “A lot of progress has been made.” Regional sources told Axios that the 60-day framework under discussion would require inbound ships to pass through Iranian waters and outbound traffic to go through Omani territory until the median lane is cleared of all mines.

Iran and Oman sit on opposite sides of the strategic waterway, and for weeks, Tehran has only expressed interest in working with Muscat to come up with a solution for the thoroughfare. However, on Tuesday, Qatar confirmed that U.S. and Iranian negotiators are in indirect talks, and Axios reported that the current proposal does not allow Tehran to charge tolls during the 60-day period.

Lunar collision. Part of a SpaceX rocket unintentionally crashed into the moon on Wednesday. Experts maintain that the collision posed no danger to Earth and could lead to some minor scientific discoveries. However, the high-speed impact also highlighted growing concerns about the vast quantity of leftover hardware floating in lower-Earth orbit. According to NASA, more than 100 million particles of space debris larger than 1 millimeter in diameter are circling Earth, largely from satellite explosions and collisions; SpaceX makes up roughly 60 percent of all working satellites.

Such debris usually falls back into Earth’s atmosphere, but a mixture of solar activity and gravitational forces instead put this SpaceX material on track to hit the moon. Wednesday’s incident saw a school bus-sized section of a Falcon 9 rocket stage, weighing 4 metric tons, hit near the moon’s Einstein Crater at 5,400 miles per hour. Lunar collisions are rare, though China, Russia, India, Israel, and the United States have all (intentionally or otherwise) fired payloads that have struck the moon.

These incidents could pose a threat to NASA’s Artemis mission, which aims to build a lunar base and send astronauts to the moon by the end of the decade. Space debris risks hitting these assets and undermining Washington’s multibillion-dollar program.

Han Kuang drills. Taiwan on Wednesday kicked off its annual 10-day Han Kuang military exercise aimed at countering threats from China. “Our core belief and ultimate operational goal are to ensure their full-scale invasion fails,” Defense Minister Wellington Koo told reporters. Beijing does not recognize the island’s sovereignty and has never ruled out the use of force to seize control.

Taipei fears that Chinese forces will try to paralyze the country’s command-and-control centers, logistics hubs, strategic ports, and defense infrastructure. To combat these concerns, this year’s live-fire drills will involve 20,000 reservists, include fighter jet dispersals and emergency naval deployments, and incorporate a “backbrief” approach to promote better coordination between junior and senior officers. For the first time, the exercise will also slow down mobile internet speeds to test how residents might communicate if bandwidth became limited.

Beijing has not commented on Taipei’s Han Kuang event. However, on Tuesday, Chinese troops launched joint combat readiness patrols that included the deployment of 21 warplanes and nine warships near Taiwan, according to the Taiwanese Defense Ministry.

A small organ in Germany’s medieval Burchardi Church has played the world’s slowest composition for nearly 25 years, with some notes (or silences) lasting months if not longer. On Wednesday, the music took a rare turn, with the addition of an A4 pipe creating a rare chord change. Listeners who missed the shift will have to wait until Oct. 5, 2027, for the next evolution. The piece, titled “ORGAN²/ASLSP (As Slow As Possible),” is expected to conclude on Sept. 4, 2640. For those who have high hopes about their lifespan, tickets are already on sale for $3,045.
