Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: African governments try to distance themselves from Pretoria following xenophobic attacks, Spanish politicians seek to make sense of the border incident in Ceuta, and renewed clashes erupt in Ethiopia’s Tigray region.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: African governments try to distance themselves from Pretoria following xenophobic attacks, Spanish politicians seek to make sense of the border incident in Ceuta, and renewed clashes erupt in Ethiopia’s Tigray region.

Sign up to receive Africa Brief in your inbox every Wednesday.

South Africa has long been a leader of the African continent, but the country’s influence may be waning as its reputation takes a hit following widespread violent attacks on Black African migrants within its borders.

Since the end of apartheid, South Africa has experienced recurring waves of xenophobic violence, which have killed an estimated 705 people over the past two decades. There was an uptick in anti-migrant attacks in 2008, and xenophobic sentiment has worsened again this year as migrants have become scapegoats for the country’s economic woes and high unemployment rate.

The two anti-migrant groups driving this latest wave—Operation Dudula and March and March—are well funded and organized. More than 160,000 Africans have fled the country over the past two months, according to an AFP tally of repatriations by African governments.

Amid this migrant exodus, African governments have distanced themselves from the country in recent weeks, postponing high-level meetings with Pretoria, while Africans across the continent are increasingly boycotting South African cultural events.

Critics have also called into question South Africa’s reputation as a strong moral voice and advocate for the global south, particularly on human rights violations in Gaza. Since 2023, Pretoria has led a genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice.

“[P]rinciples are measured by how well governments uphold them at home, not just by what they advocate abroad,” read a recent opinion piece in the Addis Standard. “For many African migrants living in South Africa … that commitment often feels incomplete.”

Last week, Nigerian President Bola Tinubu declined to meet directly with a delegation sent by South Africa to address diplomatic tensions over the xenophobic attacks, sending the visitors to Nigeria’s minister of state for foreign affairs instead.

Ghanaian President John Mahama also delayed a visit last month from South African President Cyril Ramaphosa. Ghanaian government spokesperson Felix Kwakye Ofosu told the BBC that the visit was postponed “in view of the present climate around xenophobia.”

However, Mahama later met with a delegation, which included South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola, that Pretoria deployed to address the fallout. “We do not harbor ill will toward South Africa. However, we remain deeply concerned about the attacks,” Mahama said after the meeting. “This undermines the very spirit of African solidarity and our collective efforts toward continental integration.”

It’s not just governments that are putting pressure on South Africa. Grammy award winner Tyla removed a show in Lagos, Nigeria, from her global tour following social media campaigns calling for Nigerians to boycott her concert. Other South African artists have had their appearances at festivals in Zimbabwe and Malawi canceled following similar boycotts.

“A majority of South ​African artists perform on the continent, and many of them are seeing their gigs being ​cancelled,” South Africa’s justice minister, Mmamoloko Kubayi, said as she called for her compatriots to reject xenophobic violence. “We do believe that it can not only ​hurt the brand, but can hurt our social cohesion.”

Xenophobia in South Africa has also brought economic challenges. Already, the mass exodus of migrants has disrupted South African businesses, even though migrants make up only about 5 percent of the country’s population. For instance, Sixty60, the grocery delivery platform of African supermarket chain Shoprite, has faced a driver shortage, since around 70 percent of its drivers are foreign.

Sixty60 is just one of many South African businesses that relies heavily on migrant labor; South African drivers reportedly quit the company at nearly double the rate of their foreign peers due to drivers’ working conditions and concerns around safety.

“In lieu of open-mindedness and courage, South Africans have emulated the worst attitudes of the West toward Africans, treating them as the rankest sort of undesirables—people who have come to ‘steal’ their jobs or commit crimes,” FP’s Howard W. French wrote recently. “Over time, the effect on the country is likely to be similar to cutting off one’s nose to spite one’s face.”

Wednesday, Aug. 5: The U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee holds a briefing on the war in Sudan.

Thursday, Aug. 6: The U.N. Security Council discusses its mission in South Sudan.

Weaponized migration? More than 50,000 migrants entered Ceuta, a Spanish city on Africa’s northern coast, late last week, while more than 80 died attempting to cross. Although most migrants left within 48 hours, European countries near Spain hastened to tighten their borders in the wake of the rush. The reason behind it is still unclear, but some Spanish politicians have accused Morocco of engineering the influx over geopolitical tensions regarding Western Sahara.

Ceuta is bordered by Morocco but separated from mainland Spain by the Strait of Gibraltar. Ten days prior to the influx, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited Algiers, where he pledged to strengthen bilateral cooperation. Algeria hosts the Polisario Front, which fights for Sahrawi independence in Western Sahara, a region Morocco has claimed sovereignty over since the 1970s, when Spain withdrew from the territory. Morocco also claims sovereignty over Ceuta.

Analysts have pointed out the similarities between this episode and another migration surge in 2021, when some 10,000 migrants entered Ceuta over a period of a few days after Madrid allowed Polisario Front leader Brahim Ghali to receive COVID-19 treatment in Spain.

“The Moroccan police were shouting at us: ‘Go, go, go! Run now, run into Spain,’” one migrant who crossed into Ceuta last week told the Guardian. “Ceuta was a clear example of the ‘weaponization of immigration,’” Pol Morillas, director of Barcelona-based think tank Cidob, told the Financial Times.

Morocco’s interior ministry, however, rejected this narrative, blaming the surge instead on social media misinformation after the Spanish supreme court ruled that migrants arriving by sea could not be immediately deported. Spanish intelligence services concluded that Morocco did not plan the mass crossing but did allow it to occur. Moroccans were among the top 10 nationalities in irregular border crossings into the European Union last year and this year.

Renewed Tigray fighting. Clashes erupted in northern Ethiopia between federal forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) in the western Tigray region of Shererina over the weekend, in the latest sign that the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement that ended the country’s two-year civil war has fractured.

The escalation follows months of sporadic fighting, troop buildups, and the TPLF’s move to reinstate its prewar regional government earlier this year. Hundreds of Tigrayans fled across the border to Sudan during the fighting, even as the country faces the world’s worst humanitarian crisis in its fourth year of civil war.

Disarmament in Congo? The Democratic Republic of the Congo’s government said last week that the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), operating out of eastern Congo, has signed an agreement to disarm. The FDLR is a Hutu rebel group opposed to Rwandan President Paul Kagame, and some of its militants are linked to the 1994 Rwandan genocide.

The FDLR was a main component of the peace deal brokered by U.S. President Donald Trump last year between Rwanda and Congo. The agreement required that Rwanda withdraw its troops fighting alongside M23 rebels in Congo, while Congo root out the FDLR within its borders.

A U.N. expert report in June found that the Congolese army has continued to partner with the FDLR in fighting Rwanda-backed M23 rebels. So far, Rwandan Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe has dismissed the new disarmament agreement, saying that it is merely a delaying tactic.

Ugandan treason trial. Ugandan opposition leader Kizza Besigye remains in critical condition in the hospital after collapsing during a court hearing last Wednesday in Uganda’s capital of Kampala. His wife, UNAIDS Executive Director Winnie Byanyima, said in a social media post that Besigye was “only partially conscious” and unable to speak.

Besigye, who is 70 years old, has been in prison since late 2024 on treason charges, after he was kidnapped and transported from Nairobi, Kenya, to a military prison in Uganda. He collapsed as he was protesting the authorities’ refusal to let him proceed with his chosen defense team.

Local rights groups have petitioned the U.N. Human Rights Committee to intervene in the wake of Besigye’s health concerns, condemning the trial as a politically motivated effort by President Yoweri Museveni’s regime to crack down on dissent.

Saudi Arabia said on Thursday it had formed a coalition with neighboring nations to protect global shipping and freedom of navigation through the Red Sea, Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and Gulf of Aden as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed amid war in Iran. The group, named the Multinational Maritime Defense Alliance, counts among its members some of Saudi Arabia’s immediate Red Sea neighbors, including Egypt, Sudan, Djibouti, and Somalia.

Last month, Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen announced a naval blockade on Saudi ships moving through the Bab el-Mandeb southern gateway to the Red Sea. Although many details of the new initiative remain unknown, the partnership will include intelligence sharing and joint maritime operations.

Financing African needs. As Western aid dwindles and Chinese investment shifts to private equity, the African Development Bank (AfDB) must reinvent how it funds the continent’s own development priorities by leveraging private investment, argues Rabah Arezki in Foreign Policy.

“As large European banks have scaled back or sold their African franchises, the AfDB is the only remaining institution that can attract cross-border capital at scale,” Arezki writes. “But rather than trying to finance every project itself, the AfDB should leverage its money, convening power, and preferred creditor status to bring in private lenders alongside its own financing.”

Senegalese homophobia. In April, Senegal’s government toughened anti-LGBTQ+ laws, doubling the maximum prison term for same-sex relationships to 10 years and criminalizing any “promotion” of homosexuality.

In Foreign Policy, Yagnishsing Dawoor reviews Senegalese author Mohamed Mbougar Sarr’s prescient novel, Pure Men, in the context of the country’s increasing intolerance of queerness. The book “probes the roots of Senegalese homophobia, exploring how religious ideals combine with the myth of African heterosexual purity to sustain a culture of murderous hate,” he writes.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: Unrest in Pakistan-administered Kashmir underscores broader discontent, former Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina reiterates from exile her plans to return home this year, and a former top Afghan military official makes a threat against the Taliban regime.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: Unrest in Pakistan-administered Kashmir underscores broader discontent, former Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina reiterates from exile her plans to return home this year, and a former top Afghan military official makes a threat against the Taliban regime.

Sign up to receive South Asia Brief in your inbox every Wednesday.

Political unrest has gripped Pakistan-administered Kashmir, known as Azad Jammu and Kashmir, for two months. The situation came to a head in recent days, turning deadly as protesters and security forces clashed. The escalation coincided with local elections, which run from July 27 to Aug. 10 in a three-phase process.

Making sense of the simmering crisis has been difficult until now. Local authorities cut the internet in Pakistan-administered Kashmir in June, leading to information shortages that have been exploited by those eager to fill the gap. In an apparent attempt to exaggerate the crisis, government critics posted fake videos depicting massacres on the streets of Kashmir.

Pakistani media outlets, facing threats for covering the unrest, have mostly limited their reporting to the elections. However, this week, international correspondents entered the region and provided a clearer picture of what is happening on the ground. The news isn’t good—and it amplifies how public anger with the government is rising across Pakistan.

At the center of the crisis is the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a group formed in 2023 that initially focused its demands on high food and energy prices. The group has expanded its scope, and this year, it began calling for the removal of a constitutional clause that stipulates that 12 seats in Pakistan-administered Kashmir’s legislature be given to refugees from India-administered Kashmir.

The JAAC argues that since these refugees don’t live in Azad Jammu and Kashmir, Pakistani politicians are exploiting the seats for their own ends. After the JAAC’s demand was rejected by both the region’s government and supreme court, the situation grew more tense.

In early June, the JAAC announced a long march to the capital of Muzaffarabad, but local authorities arrested some of its leaders and banned the group. JAAC members then clashed with security forces, and the group called a general strike. The shuttering of businesses, combined with the internet shutdown, brought much of the region to a standstill.

Protests continued throughout June, and they broke out again last week during elections. Death toll estimates vary, but reports suggest at least 40 people have been killed since June. This week, the BBC spoke to families who said their loved ones were shot dead while protesting. The authorities insist that the JAAC is a terrorist group, and that force was only used against violent protesters.

Kashmir is the latest ground zero for protests against poor governance in Pakistan. In the last few years, people have railed against state repression in the provinces of Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Protesters in many parts of the country have decried the imprisonment of former Prime Minister Imran Khan and condemned what they see as a rigged election in 2024.

Now, in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, the JAAC and other protesters have vowed to push on, asserting their fight is about broader demands such as better health care and cheaper electricity, not just constitutional reform.

If these disparate movements managed to come together, then Pakistan might be the next South Asian country to experience a broad protest movement for change. But that’s unlikely given its social divisions and a repressive political environment that limits the capacity for mass mobilizations.

Still, Pakistan’s national leadership has a strong incentive to quickly resolve the crisis in Kashmir. It wants the world to focus on Islamabad’s mediation efforts in the Iran war, not its heavy-handed tactics in Kashmir. Because of Pakistan’s dispute with India over its status, Kashmir is also a critical and sensitive asset for Pakistan. (Its leaders often call it the country’s “jugular vein.”)

Ending the crisis peacefully will require dialogue—but with emotions running so high, that may be a hard sell for now.

Hasina reiterates plan to return. On Wednesday, exactly two years after fleeing the country amid mass protests against her rule, former Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina spoke virtually via audio feed at an event hosted by the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia in New Delhi. She reiterated her pledge to return to Bangladesh in December and turn herself in to legal authorities.

Last November, Hasina—who has remained in India since 2024—was sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity, charges linked to brutal crackdowns against protesters by her security forces. According to the United Nations, as many as 1,400 people may have died during the protests.

One thing that stands out is how India distanced itself from the Wednesday event. India has close ties to Hasina, but her residency there has strained bilateral ties with Bangladesh. New Delhi is keen to get the relationship back on track with the government that recently took office in Dhaka, which is led by the Bangladesh Nationalist Party—a bitter rival of Hasina’s Awami League.

As a result, India had a strong interest in signaling that it was not endorsing Hasina’s event or trying to provide her with a platform. Nonetheless, Bangladesh won’t be pleased that she was given the microphone and that her remarks were broadcasted live on YouTube.

Pakistani minister says system is broken. Last week marked a rare public admission from a senior Pakistani official about the shortcomings that have sparked protests in Kashmir and beyond. Speaking at an economic summit in Islamabad, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said the governance system has “collapsed” and lacks capacity to address the country’s problems.

Naqvi called for Pakistan’s political parties to unite around a governance reform agenda. The comments are significant for their candor but also because of who made them. Naqvi is close to army chief Asim Munir, Pakistan’s most powerful figure—suggesting that Naqvi was articulating a view that Munir at least endorses.

It’s unclear what specific reforms Naqvi is calling for, but Pakistani analysts familiar with the government’s thinking believe that one likely target is the devolution of power and resources from provincial governments to local authorities.

A constitutional amendment passed in 2010 was hailed for extending more autonomy to the provinces, seen as a democratic move that shifted control away from the central government and thus the military. But the amendment has also been faulted for not devolving authority further to the local level, where key decisions on matters of governance are implemented.

India and Pakistan exempted from new U.S. visa bond. India and Pakistan got a break this week from the Trump administration. They will not be among the countries whose citizens may be asked to make refundable deposits of up to $20,000 in order to receive B-1 (business) and B-2 (tourist) visas—a policy that went into effect on Aug. 1 and is intended to reduce overstays.

It’s unclear why the United States exempted India and Pakistan but included Bangladesh and Nepal among the 50 affected countries. It’s not a matter of doing a favor for countries on good terms with U.S. President Donald Trump: Bangladesh and Pakistan have each logged bilateral achievements with the United States in recent months, while U.S.-India ties have sputtered.

Bangladeshis and Nepalis are dealing with significant economic stress in their countries; the idea of posting a five-figure bond to visit the United States won’t be palatable for many of them.

Nearly five years since taking power in Afghanistan, one constant for the Taliban is that it has faced no organized armed resistance. There are those who would like to see the group gone, from common Afghans who reject its repressive rule to the Islamic State-Khorasan, which periodically attacks the Taliban.

But the Taliban has easily been able to maintain its hold on power in Kabul—making last weekend’s announcement by Sami Sadat, a former top Afghan military official, that his Afghanistan United Front (AUF) has taken up arms against the regime significant.

Until this point, the AUF has operated as a political opposition group. On Monday, a post on its official X account said that the group had struck the Taliban’s main police headquarters in Kandahar, Afghanistan. As the Taliban’s birthplace, the city is a symbolically significant place to carry out an initial operation.

Sadat, who has been based in northern Virginia, has sought support from the West for his movement. But the AUF faces many challenges. The Taliban remain a formidable force; to become stronger, the AUF will need the type of external backing that anti-Taliban factions enjoyed before 2001.

With the world essentially moving on from Afghanistan under Taliban rule—no matter how unsettling—the AUF will be hard-pressed to secure that support. And while Sadat has spoken of the capacity to quickly mobilize tens of thousands of recruits, many Afghans don’t want another war.

In the Print, education expert Karishma Shangvi argues that India’s Cockroach Janta Party protests provide an opening to change school entrance exams so they measure competence, not rank. “The recent protests over examination failures mean that the government now has a rare political mandate to bring substantial reforms in the entrance examination system,” she writes. “Let’s not waste it.”

In the Kathmandu Post, retired diplomat Lok Raj Baral writes that politicization has undermined Nepal’s foreign policy. Its diplomatic “initiatives have shrunk in recent years,” he writes. “The main reasons are uncalled-for mobilising rhetoric, miscalculation and a lack of objectivity in weighing the pros and cons of any decision taken at the whim of the leaders.”

A Dawn editorial contends that Pakistani security forces need better training to preempt terrorist attacks: “The gaps in training need to be filled so that security forces are able to defend themselves, gain the upper hand over violent elements, and, through better intelligence, break up their networks and thwart their attacks.”

Michael Kugelman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly South Asia Brief and a senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council. An analyst of the region for nearly two decades, he previously directed the South Asia Institute at the Wilson Center. X: @michaelkugelman

I feel bad for the Saudis. They find themselves hammered between the Iranians and the Houthis, an unhappy situation thanks in part to a feckless and mercurial U.S. president. Over the past decade, Saudi Arabia’s leaders have wanted nothing more than regional stability while they go about the business of transforming their country. For a while there, the Middle East was just stable enough for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and his advisors to dream big about a radically changed kingdom by 2030.

And then Hamas struck Israel in October 2023, kicking off a regional war. The Saudis have done everything they can to steer clear of that war—a rational response to the violence and bloodshed. And yet, Riyadh’s own lack of strategic forethought has made the country’s problems worse.

I feel bad for the Saudis. They find themselves hammered between the Iranians and the Houthis, an unhappy situation thanks in part to a feckless and mercurial U.S. president. Over the past decade, Saudi Arabia’s leaders have wanted nothing more than regional stability while they go about the business of transforming their country. For a while there, the Middle East was just stable enough for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and his advisors to dream big about a radically changed kingdom by 2030.

And then Hamas struck Israel in October 2023, kicking off a regional war. The Saudis have done everything they can to steer clear of that war—a rational response to the violence and bloodshed. And yet, Riyadh’s own lack of strategic forethought has made the country’s problems worse.

The latest escalation between Saudi Arabia and Ansar Allah (aka the Houthis)—which took place on July 13 when the Saudi Air Force allegedly bombed the runway at Sanaa International Airport—was, in a word, unnecessary, and in more words, a function of poor judgment.

Why the Saudis would start this fight is a mystery. Apparently, they were acting on behalf of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which has been concerned about violations of a U.N. arms embargo on the Houthis. The strikes on the airport were intended to prevent the landing of an Iranian Mahan Air flight conveying a Houthi delegation back from the funeral of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Mahan Air is the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) carrier of choice for supplying its friends around the region. It is reasonable to believe that the Houthis were carrying more than just pistachios and carpets back from Tehran.

Even stipulating that the flight was a violation of the Security Council resolution, it does not make a lot of sense to crater the runway in Sanaa. With all the Houthi and IRGC provocations that Riyadh has let slide in recent years, allowing the Houthis to land should have been an easy call. The war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis had effectively come to an end (even though Saudi officials privately grumble that the Iranians never lived up to their commitments, including those regarding Yemen after Riyadh normalized ties with Tehran in 2023). The risk inherent in bombing the airport seems greater than the reward. Surely the Saudis could have looked the other way.

The Houthis, for their part, did not look the other way. They responded by firing on Abha International Airport in Asir province and on oil facilities in Jazan, on the Red Sea coast near Yemen. They also laid on a blockade of Saudi shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Meanwhile, Iraqi militias aligned with Iran and the Houthis targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu and the Saudi oil processing plant at Abqaiq, which is massive and critical to global energy supplies.

To make matters worse, the Saudis are facing the Houthis alone. Regional leaders condemned the Houthi attacks and expressed solidarity with the Saudis, but none of kingdom’s Arab neighbors came forward to help. Most of them are too weak and timorous to confront the Houthi threat.

The one exception might be the United Arab Emirates, but in another moment of strategic mismanagement last December, Riyadh alienated Abu Dhabi over their joint war in Yemen. At the time, Emirati allies in Yemen known as the Southern Transitional Council (STC) took over  most of the southern part of the country and declared their intention to establish independence. The Saudis took saw it as an end-run around their efforts to reach a diplomatic and political resolution to Yemen’s yearslong crisis and preserve the country’s unity. So they bombed STC forces, drove its leadership out of the country, and demanded that the Emiratis stay out of Yemen. The folks in Abu Dhabi obliged.

I can understand why the Saudis were angry, but in their wrath, they lost sight of the big picture. The STC’s dramatic move was sure to put the Houthis and their IRGC patrons on the defensive, with southern forces right on the doorstep of Houthi-controlled areas. The Saudis claimed to be concerned about the breakup of an Arab state and the precedent that it would set. But a southern Yemen aligned with the UAE and Saudi interests against the Houthis seems like a better outcome than fruitless talks with the Houthis over Yemen’s future.

Around the same time, the Saudis made another strategic error. Rather than welcoming—or at least tolerating—Israel’s recognition of Somaliland, Saudi Arabia was a vocal opponent along with Turkey, Qatar, and Arab members of the African Union. It makes sense for the Egyptians to oppose the Israeli move because Ethiopia, which is a major rival of Egypt in the Horn of Africa, maintains strong ties with Somaliland. The Turks were opposed because Somaliland gives the Israelis a toehold in the Horn, where Turkey has been building up its presence for more than a decade. The Qataris, who are investors in Somaliland, were playing both sides as they normally do.

But the Saudi opposition did not make sense. An independent Somaliland that is aligned with Israel and affords the Israelis a presence in the country puts pressure on the Houthis and the IRGC. That should be good for Riyadh, even if Saudi Arabia could not celebrate publicly. Saudi leaders seemed too angry at the Emiratis—who they saw as in cahoots with the Israelis in Somaliland—to grasp the strategic win. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia’s allies in holding Somalia together—Turkey, Egypt, and Qatar—are unlikely to help the Saudis with their Houthi problem.

The Gulf needs a joint front on deterrence, engagement, and freedom of navigation.

The pact would erase decades of U.S. counterproliferation policy.

The fact that U.S. President Donald Trump has occupied the Oval Office during this period of Saudi misfortunate is particularly painful. The Saudis loathed President Barack Obama for his nuclear deal with Iran and worried that President Joe Biden would undercut their position with a follow-up agreement—which never materialized. In fact, Biden ended up strengthening ties with the kingdom and spent his last two years in office negotiating a bilateral security pact. Still, the Saudis (like other Persian Gulf countries) seemed very much to prefer Trump to his Democratic opponent, former Vice President Kamala Harris, because Trump allegedly gets stuff done and is good for business and investment.

And yet, when Saudi Arabia came to an agreement with the Trump administration that would give them access to nuclear technology, the president pulled the rug out from under them. A day after his secretary of energy signed the deal, Trump added a critical condition: normalization of relations with Israel. This is something that the Saudis have said they will only do after the establishment of a Palestinian state, which Israelis are unwilling to abide.

It was not the first time that Trump burned the Saudis. He broke the Carter doctrine in September 2019, when he failed to respond to Iran’s attacks on Saudi oil facilities. More recently, his entire misbegotten Operation Epic Fury has empowered Tehran at the expense of its neighbors on the western side of the Gulf. Once Trump finds a way out of the conflict, he will leave the Saudis and others to deal with the fallout.

No doubt, 2026 has been Saudi Arabia’s annus horriblis—and there are still more than four months to go. The Saudis wish they had the luxury of sealing their country off from the region’s problems, but they can’t. Riyalpolitik—the act of buying off those who might do them harm—only goes so far. To improve their position, the Saudis need to discard the principles and emotions that have driven their policymaking and develop a better sense of their strategic environment. Only then will they have a chance to shape the region, rather than letting others shape it for them.

https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/08/05/ira.author: Stephen M. Walt

If you’re an American, then you might be getting damn tired of losing wars. I know I am. And you may be asking yourself, “Why does this keep happening?” It’s an intriguing and disheartening puzzle: Although the United States has been far-and-away the world’s most powerful country for many decades, with a military whose budget and raw capabilities are unmatched, it has compiled a mostly losing record in recent history. This includes the current war with Iran, which has yet to achieve any of the Trump administration’s stated objectives and is likely to end with Iran in a significantly stronger strategic position.

Ongoing reports and analysis

Look at the list. The Korean War was a draw (more about that later). Vietnam was a clear defeat, as were the 2003 Iraq War and the “forever war” in Afghanistan. The 1999 Kosovo War was hardly a triumph, with Serbia getting better terms at the end of the war than it had been offered before the fighting began. Unless you include the occupation of the tiny island nation of Grenada in 1983 (a gross mismatch that hardly counts), then the United States’ only clear victory across these many decades was the 1991 Gulf War. Yes, I know: The United States and its allies did “win” the Cold War, an exception that proves the rule because it was a “war” that never involved a direct clash of arms with the Soviet Union.

If you’re an American, then you might be getting damn tired of losing wars. I know I am. And you may be asking yourself, “Why does this keep happening?” It’s an intriguing and disheartening puzzle: Although the United States has been far-and-away the world’s most powerful country for many decades, with a military whose budget and raw capabilities are unmatched, it has compiled a mostly losing record in recent history. This includes the current war with Iran, which has yet to achieve any of the Trump administration’s stated objectives and is likely to end with Iran in a significantly stronger strategic position.

Ongoing reports and analysis

Look at the list. The Korean War was a draw (more about that later). Vietnam was a clear defeat, as were the 2003 Iraq War and the “forever war” in Afghanistan. The 1999 Kosovo War was hardly a triumph, with Serbia getting better terms at the end of the war than it had been offered before the fighting began. Unless you include the occupation of the tiny island nation of Grenada in 1983 (a gross mismatch that hardly counts), then the United States’ only clear victory across these many decades was the 1991 Gulf War. Yes, I know: The United States and its allies did “win” the Cold War, an exception that proves the rule because it was a “war” that never involved a direct clash of arms with the Soviet Union.

Why has the United States done so poorly? It is surely not due to a lack of money, given the size of the U.S. defense budget and the willingness of Congress to vote supplemental funds whenever it is asked. It’s not a lack of firepower, as the United States remains remarkably good at blowing stuff up, even at considerable distances from its own shores. That capacity may be somewhat diminished at present, given how U.S. President Donald Trump and U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have squandered the country’s supply of advanced missiles in their foolish war on Iran, but this factor doesn’t explain why victory has been so elusive. It is not due to insufficient valor in the U.S. armed forces, which remain willing to place themselves in harm’s way, often heroically. And it is certainly not because U.S. troops lack sufficient testosterone, no matter what our hapless secretary of (losing a) war might think.

Instead, the real reasons that the United States keeps losing wars are strategic and structural. The country has been waging wars of choice that combine modest U.S. interests with extremely ambitious goals, such as trying remake a foreign society in the U.S. image. The result is that opponents tend to be much more highly resolved than Washington is, because they have far more at stake. They are fighting to survive or at least preserve their independence and autonomy, whereas, in most cases, the United States is fighting to achieve arguably desirable but ultimately less-than-vital objectives. Under these conditions, it is to be expected that opponents will be far more willing to make sacrifices than the United States is. As in most if not all asymmetric conflicts, the weaker side wins not by outright victory on the battlefield but by not losing and waiting for the stronger power to realize that pouring more soldiers and money into a quagmire just isn’t worth it.

This simple formula tells us a lot about all these recent wars. The United States was defending significant interests on the Korean Peninsula, as an uncontested Communist victory there might have affected the Cold War in Asia significantly. But China saw U.S. efforts to unify the peninsula as an existential threat, and eventually sacrificed at least 200,000 troops (and probably far more) to prevent that outcome. After three bitter years of fighting, the result was essentially a draw.

In Vietnam, the United States faced the fierce nationalism of the Vietnamese Communist movement, a force that had previously defeated French colonial power and proved impossible to extinguish. Although U.S. leaders were able to persuade Americans that preventing a Communist victory was a vital interest for some time—mostly by invoking exaggerated fears of falling dominos and lost credibility—in the end, the public turned against the seemingly endless war, forced a U.S. withdrawal, and paved the way for Hanoi’s eventual triumph.

Much of the same fate drove the unfortunate outcomes in Iraq and Afghanistan. Saddam Hussein was a serial troublemaker, but he was contained by 2003, his weapons programs were dismantled, and he had played no role whatsoever in the 9/11 terrorist attacks. Toppling him was not a vital U.S. interest, therefore, no matter what U.S. neoconservatives dreaming of transforming the Middle East into a sea of pro-American democracies might have said. Getting rid of Saddam was easy (which underscored how little danger he actually posed), but the occupying forces soon faced a powerful insurgency that was opposed to foreign domination and aided by both Iran and Syria, which had no desire to be next on Washington’s hit list. Another ambitious war of choice turned out to be a costly debacle. Sound familiar?

In Afghanistan, a combination of ignorance, idealism, and limited strategic importance ultimately doomed the U.S. war effort there. Washington had good reason to go after Osama bin Laden and his Taliban hosts, but staying there to turn Afghanistan into a Western-style democracy triggered fierce resistance from a society that fully deserved its reputation as the “graveyard of empires.” In the end, the insurgents cared more about getting the United States out than the country cared about defeating them—if that were even possible—and eventually Trump, during his first term, and then U.S. President Joe Biden pulled the plug on a conflict that had long been a pointless exercise.

The 1991 Gulf War is the obvious exception to Washington’s unimpressive record. Strictly speaking, it was also a “war of choice,” insofar as the United States could have let Iraq keep Kuwait without facing any immediate threats to its own security. But over time, Iraqi control of Kuwait and its oil revenues could have altered the balance of power in the Gulf in worrisome ways, and the George H.W. Bush administration was concerned that allowing an unopposed aggression of this sort to succeed might set a dangerous precedent. But very importantly, in this case, U.S. objectives were fully commensurate with U.S. interests. The United States and its allies expelled Iraq from Kuwait, decimated Iraq’s military power, and imposed intrusive United Nations inspections that dismantled its weapons programs. But U.S. President George H.W. Bush wisely chose not to “go to Baghdad” and topple the regime, both because doing so would have exceeded the authorization provided by the U.N. Security Council and forced the United States to occupy and govern a divided and resentful society. Because U.S. aims were aligned with U.S. interests and Bush ended the war promptly, it is rightly seen as a stunning success.

It is not easy for a superpower to get its interests and objectives aligned, however. Because the United States is so powerful and objectively so secure, there won’t be a lot of conflicts where truly vital interests are at stake and major sacrifices—such as those that Americans made during World War II—are easy to justify. At the same time, U.S. power and technological superiority also make it easy to intervene in all sorts of places and for policymakers to convince themselves that these conflicts will be easy to win. The problem, in short, is not that the United States is bad at fighting wars. The problem is that it is usually fighting the wrong wars for the wrong objectives, which undermines allied confidence in U.S. judgment and makes it harder to compete with genuine rivals like China.

Why does this keep happening, even under a president who claimed to oppose forever wars and insisted that he was the “peace candidate”? There are many reasons, but one of them is the U.S. foreign-policy elite’s continued reluctance to hold itself accountable and learn from past mistakes. A perfect illustration of this problem can be found in Robert Kagan’s recent interview with Responsible Statecraft. To his credit, Kagan has publicly criticized Trump’s war with Iran, but he has been a consistent proponent of a muscular approach to U.S. foreign policy and was one of the most prominent public advocates for the 2003 Iraq War. When asked whether that war was a mistake, he replied: “I’m not sure what the utility of admitting that it was a mistake is. It’s not going to bring anybody back to life.” He added that his main regret is that the war reduced public support for the kind of interventionist foreign policy that he favors.

Trump needs to learn the diplomatic art of losing well.

As long as a reluctance to admit errors and take responsibility remains widespread within foreign-policy circles—including much of the MAGA world at this point—Americans will have to get used to disappointment.

Kevin Warsh was handpicked to lead the world’s most important bank, with a remit from U.S. President Donald Trump to do one thing: lower interest rates. But economic reality, especially stubborn inflation, won’t allow the Federal Reserve to do that, and so it is now facing the wrath of both financial markets and the White House.

Add to that a novel, confusing, and contradictory communication style, and Warsh’s early steps as Fed chair have been less than encouraging. That is problematic when what the Fed says, almost as much as what it does, has huge implications for the United States and global economies.

Kevin Warsh was handpicked to lead the world’s most important bank, with a remit from U.S. President Donald Trump to do one thing: lower interest rates. But economic reality, especially stubborn inflation, won’t allow the Federal Reserve to do that, and so it is now facing the wrath of both financial markets and the White House.

Add to that a novel, confusing, and contradictory communication style, and Warsh’s early steps as Fed chair have been less than encouraging. That is problematic when what the Fed says, almost as much as what it does, has huge implications for the United States and global economies.

“Warsh doesn’t know how to speak coherently about monetary policy,” said Benn Steil, a senior fellow and director of international economics at the Council on Foreign Relations. “He is in a difficult position right now: He is not an economist, he never mastered the lingo, and he has been appointed by a man who wants him to take a position he has been opposed to for years.”

The central challenge facing the Fed, which was made plain in last week’s disastrous press conference and market panic, is that Warsh’s marching orders to lower interest rates to turbocharge Trump’s sluggish economy clash with two fundamental issues.

First, easy money and ignoring the risks of inflation go against everything that Warsh has preached for years, including during a prior tenure as a Federal Reserve board governor during the George W. Bush administration. Second, U.S. inflation remains stubbornly high, thanks to the Iran war, higher energy prices, and an endless onslaught of Trump administration tariffs.

U.S. inflation, as measured by the Fed’s preferred tool, personal consumption expenditures (PCE), is still running at nearly twice the central bank’s objective of 2 percent annual inflation. That was why many investors expected Warsh and the Fed to either raise interest rates slightly in last week’s monthly meeting or at least make a clear case for how the Fed is thinking about the challenge. Instead, the Federal Reserve held pat, with three of the 12 voting members advocating for higher rates.

The lack of action on inflation scared bond markets above all, sending yields on long-term U.S. government debt to nearly 20-year highs. (Yields rise when investors are selling the bonds.) Even a week later, yields remain much higher than almost any time since before the 2008-2009 financial crisis—a sign of worry over the solidity of the U.S. government’s financial stewardship.

Warsh then compounded the confusion with a press conference in which he welcomed those sky-high bond yields, arguing that the market was doing the bank’s work for it by raising borrowing costs for businesses and consumers. He also argued that the Fed should just sit back and listen to what the market thinks about the economy, rather than seeking to offer guidance on what the helmsmen think. That is not at all how the Fed has traditionally worked.

“Market participants are learning to play the ball, not the referee. And market prices will continue to respond in the direction and magnitude they see fit,” Warsh said. “This is, in my view, a change for the better, and we’re just getting started. After all, the central bank need not always and everywhere be the center of attention. I understand the desire for rolling forecasts and commentary from this committee, but for our part, we need to observe market reaction to developments direct and unfiltered.”

That is an abrupt change to the forward guidance that former Fed chairs, including the recently ousted Jerome Powell, routinely gave the market on how the Federal Reserve views the economy, what steps it is considering, and why.

“His stated objective doesn’t make any sense: ‘I want the markets to give me a signal without me telling them.’ The markets reflect what the Fed will do, not what it should do,” said David Wessel, director of the Hutchins Center on Fiscal and Monetary Policy at the Brookings Institution.

The White House risks gutting the independence of the world’s most important central bank in its quest for cheap money.

Inflation is rising and fault lines are widening on disruptions from history’s biggest energy shock.

Trump’s pick did not rattle markets, but the Fed’s future and independence remains uncertain.

“You can get away with this stuff as a congressman or even the president, but you can’t get away with incoherent rants when you are the Fed chairman,” added Wessel, who has written extensively about the Federal Reserve.

While current inflation trends may not be enough to justify rate hikes this summer, even if they remain elevated, Warsh further muddied the water and confused investors by suggesting that the Fed would look at measuring inflation differently in the future. That overhaul of the Fed analysis is in the hands of outside task forces that Warsh appointed, not career central bank officials, so it is not clear what numbers the Federal Reserve will even be looking at in a few months’ time.

“Who knows, come after next January, what we might say about strategy. I suspect the task forces might have something to add,” Warsh said at the press conference. “We’re going to deliver 2 percent inflation and not a whisper more, but to achieve that, I’m looking at a broader set of inflation data than PCE.”

That could be one way for Warsh to slither out of the anti-inflation skin he has worn for so long, but it is risky if the Fed waits too long to calibrate the economy.

“Right now, my reading is that he understands the correct monetary policy is to raise rates, and he is not doing that. I think he is inventing rosy scenarios. Right now, he is really rolling the dice,” Steil said.

All of this translates into more uncertainty for an economy that is already wrestling with uncertain consequences from an artificial intelligence investment boom, the lingering impacts of the Iran war on energy and commodity prices, and continued disruptions to trade thanks to a new raft of tariffs.

The confusion at the Fed could also have important political ramifications. Trump finally forced Powell out ahead of schedule in a bid to secure a more pliant central bank chair, and he tried to fire other Federal Reserve governors who did not hew to his demands for easy money. The worry is that the longer Warsh avoids placating Trump, the more political pressure he will come under, which could turn into additional efforts from the White House to fire Federal Reserve leads and further undermine the bank’s independence.

“Warsh spent the last 15 years saying that everybody at the Fed was wrong, and he doesn’t come with a lot of goodwill,” even without the worries about intensified political pressure, Wessel said. “He didn’t have a lot of credibility to begin with, and he hasn’t built any.”

On Aug. 1, in response to the storming of the Spanish exclave of Ceuta by more than 70,000 migrants crossing from Morocco, 22 European leaders signed a letter criticizing Spain. The unwillingness of the vast majority of the European Union’s member states to provide support to the country whose borders were breached by unarmed foreigners is an ill omen for what the continent’s reaction to an armed attack would actually look like.

In their joint letter, the leaders laid blame for the border crisis at Spain’s decision to provide a path toward regularization for irregular migrants as well as a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling, arguing that these actions provided a pull factor with implications beyond the Pyrenees. By shifting responsibility onto Madrid for what Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described as a “violation of Spain's territorial integrity,” as opposed to recognizing Spain as the country that carried the entire burden by virtue of its geography, European leaders have inadvertently weakened the potential of any new effort toward European collective defense.

On Aug. 1, in response to the storming of the Spanish exclave of Ceuta by more than 70,000 migrants crossing from Morocco, 22 European leaders signed a letter criticizing Spain. The unwillingness of the vast majority of the European Union’s member states to provide support to the country whose borders were breached by unarmed foreigners is an ill omen for what the continent’s reaction to an armed attack would actually look like.

In their joint letter, the leaders laid blame for the border crisis at Spain’s decision to provide a path toward regularization for irregular migrants as well as a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling, arguing that these actions provided a pull factor with implications beyond the Pyrenees. By shifting responsibility onto Madrid for what Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described as a “violation of Spain’s territorial integrity,” as opposed to recognizing Spain as the country that carried the entire burden by virtue of its geography, European leaders have inadvertently weakened the potential of any new effort toward European collective defense.

European leaders veered between condemnatory language and prima facie solidarity in the letter, mixing victim blaming with lip service to EU cooperation. Externally, the message serves as a disciplinary tool to bring Spain in line with the continent’s broader anti-migration stance. Domestically, the letter allows national leaders to present themselves as tough and resolute on an issue that can bring down incumbents.

However, in an effort to close ranks and fortify their positions at home, they assumed an incoherent position that will continue to sow doubt the next time that a crisis emerges. The fact that the letter was written by national leaders and addressed to the EU’s leadership further shows the limits of supranational crisis response.

Since U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to the White House last year, policymakers, think tanks, and pundits across Europe have been exploring what a post-American alliance would look like.

Sometimes dubbed a “European NATO,” the concept envisages a future in which Europeans jointly shoulder the duty of protecting their borders. It assumes that an individual state may be overwhelmed and therefore seeks to leverage pan-European cooperation so that the continent’s capacity and willingness to meet challenges will be greater than the sum of its parts. Some advocates of strategic autonomy and European integration have sought to position the European Union as the natural heir to NATO if the United States were to formally withdraw from the alliance.

All alliances, whether informal or treaty-bound, remain hypothetical until tested. Short of a war, it is impossible to know with full certainty whether commitments are worth more than the paper they are written on. The Ceuta border crisis, however, was an excellent opportunity to demonstrate how far states are willing to go when the border of an ally is violated.

A mass arrival of migration is not the same as a military invasion, but the way that leaders react in a moment of crisis still carries considerable weight. In 2020, for example, the Turkish government provoked a refugee crisis at the Greek border. European leaders condemned Ankara’s actions, but many Greek observers felt that they did not appreciate the severity of the threat to Greek sovereignty. As a result, the crisis exacerbated Greek fears that, in the advent of a direct military confrontation with Turkey, European states would find a way to blame Athens rather than coming to its aid.

Whereas the collective response to recent wildfires ravaging large swaths of the continent illustrated some of the EU’s potential, the political sensitivity around migration as well as memories of the 2015 refugee crisis resulted in European leaders sacrificing deepened cooperation in favor of short-term political convenience. Even though the EU’s Pact on Migration and Asylum took effect in June after years of negotiation, it took less than two months and one incident for European solidarity to unravel.

In the end, concern that the collapse of Ceuta’s border would lead to an uncontrolled flow of migrants to other countries proved to be unwarranted, given that it appears none of these arrivals crossed the Strait of Gibraltar. In fact, the overwhelming majority of migrants who breached Spain’s North African border returned to Morocco within 48 hours. Yet this outcome only further highlights what a strategic blunder the rest of Europe’s reaction—which the Spanish government criticized as “selfish, polarising and unlawful”—has been.

The European letter was co-organized by the Italian and Danish governments, though just a few months ago, it was Denmark that looked to its EU allies for support in order to defend Greenland from a possible annexation by the United States. Italy also made the decision to suspend the Schengen agreement and reimpose controls with Spain, even though they do not share a land border and none of the migrants that arrived in Ceuta have continued beyond Spain.

Creating a pathway to citizenship in return for military service will help Europe stand on its own.

Some 60,000 people from Morocco surged into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta.

Italy’s decision, in particular, is indicative of what a European response may look like in the face of a military attack. While NATO’s Article V does not have a suspension mechanism, it does allow each member of the alliance to make its own determination of whether to contribute and in what form. Amid ongoing Greco-Turkish maritime disputes and simmering Russo-Baltic tensions, there are no lack of potential threats to European sovereignty. Now, it is no longer unthinkable that an ally could be blamed for mismanaging its border and told this mismanagement justifies European inaction.

A “European NATO” assumes that all members are ready to make the ultimate sacrifice for one another. However, that cannot be credible when something far less dangerous than a war, which could turn nuclear, has resulted in ostracization. Cold War-era NATO was underpinned by a belief that any European conflict beyond West Berlin would drag the rest of the continent into it, along with the United States and the Soviet Union. However, as Ceuta confirms, border threats that are geographically restricted could lead to further selective application of sympathy.

Joint efforts to prop up Ukraine in the midst of its conflict with Russia have created a false self-impression among European policy elites. While it has led to increased military cooperation, the fact that Russo-Ukrainian fighting, with the exception of the occasional drone incursion, has not spilled over has meant that European Union solidarity was not truly tested. Now that it has been, its leaders failed to rise to the occasion.

The reaction to the scenes that broke out in Ceuta was, in many ways, a regression to the mean and a reaffirmation that the EU remains a collection of states. The Greek financial crisis, pandemic-era recovery efforts, and previous refugee crises were all examples that, when forced to choose between domestic concerns or finding a truly European response, leaders will almost always choose the former.

Instead of seizing upon the opportunity to demonstrate genuine cooperation, EU member states have relapsed into their habit of scapegoating. A military alliance made up of the same EU governments that failed in the face of Ceuta is unlikely to do any better in the face of greater threats.

Naman Karl-Thomas Habtom is a nonresident fellow at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft and was previously a guest researcher at the Swedish Defence University. He holds a Ph.D. from the University of Cambridge.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: This year’s El Niño might end up being the strongest in 140 years, Aung San Suu Kyi is confirmed alive by the Red Cross, and Malaysia takes an increasingly hard line on the Rohingya.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: This year’s El Niño might end up being the strongest in 140 years, Aung San Suu Kyi is confirmed alive by the Red Cross, and Malaysia takes an increasingly hard line on the Rohingya.

This year’s El Niño is underway, and it might end up being the strongest in 140 years. Southeast Asia will be hit hard.

The Asia-Pacific will be the worst-affected region, according to insurance giant Munich Re, with heat waves, drought, wildfires, and increased typhoon risk.

The region is already facing higher prices as result of the Iran war, and El Niño will only intensify that. As I have previously flagged, high food prices could lead to political instability in the region.

This year’s El Niño follows another strong El Niño event, which lasted from 2023 to 2024. Effects of that one, such as increased farmer debt, are still being felt in the region’s agricultural sector.

The effects on Southeast Asia will also be felt around the world, as the region is a major producer of staple crops.

Thailand and Vietnam are the world’s second and third-largest exporters of rice. Indonesia and Malaysia produce 85 percent of the world’s palm oil. Vietnam and Indonesia are the world’s second and fourth-largest producers of coffee. Rice and palm oil are particularly sensitive to climate anomalies. Experts have estimated that rice yields in the region could fall between 2 to 8 percent.

El Niño is predicted to last up until spring 2027, which means that effects on food supply and prices will persist into 2028.

The Philippines and Timor Leste are particularly high-risk countries, according to the World Food Program, with the main risk being droughts and floods affecting staple crops. Admittedly, these two countries are not agricultural powerhouses in the region. But Cambodia, Indonesia, Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam all face a serious drought risk, as well.

Some effects are already being felt.

Thailand received roughly 60 percent less rain than normal between January and April. The Bangkok export price for rice reached $490 per metric ton at the end of June, up 27.5 percent since the start of 2026.

Thailand’s Office of the National Water Resources has warned that the country could face a drought crisis more serious than the one in 2015, another El Niño year. Research by Krungthai, a major Thai bank, projected that El Niño could shave 0.5 percent from Thailand’s GDP in a worst-case scenario.

In neighboring Cambodia, more than 100,000 hectares of rice fields have been affected by drought, according to the government.

In the Philippines, water reserves are already showing signs of strain. El Niño and the Iran war shock could reduce rice production by 30 percent.

Indonesia has experienced drought in key population centers since June. Its Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) has indicated that El Niño is now making itself felt even more strongly. It predicted that roughly half the country will experience a longer-than-normal dry season. However, the overall impact on Indonesia may be weaker than in other countries. BMKG predicted that rice production will fall by just 2.6 percent, though eastern parts of the country are expected to be more affected.

Beyond food, though, Indonesia faces another risk. The tinder-dry environment creates a risk of massive forest fires, which will then affect Indonesia’s neighbors (mainly Singapore and Malaysia) as the choking haze drifts into their atmosphere.

In a June report, the Singapore Institute of International Affairs issued a red alert for haze risk. The last time it did this was in 2023, another El Niño year, where haze did indeed occur.

Buried in the report are some politely phrased concerns that Indonesia is in a worse situation to manage these risks than under the previous president, who pushed hard to get a handle on the issue. Strained fire-fighting budgets and an uptick in deforestation in the past two years were both flagged.

Rohingya deported to Myanmar. Last week, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced that Myanmar had agreed to accept the return of 5,000 Rohingya asylum-seekers. The deal has prompted shock given that the Rohingya would be returned to the hands of a government that committed genocide against them.

The deal comes amid an increase of anti-Rohingya sentiment in Malaysia, and it seems that the government felt pressure to respond. Notably, Anwar made the announcement at a campaign rally. (His coalition was thumped in a crucial state election this past week.)

My key question is if this heralds a shift in Malaysia’s approach to Myanmar. Until recently, it has been one of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) members, alongside Singapore and Indonesia, taking the hardest line against the Myanmar junta.

This deal could suggest a shift in approach. Anwar said the measure was possible because of “good relations with Myanmar.”

Malaysia’s increasingly hard line on the Rohingya is also prompting a clash with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR). “Current conditions do not ​support the safe and sustainable return of refugees from Myanmar,” the UNHCR said, adding that it “stands ready to engage with relevant ‌authorities on ⁠protection safeguards.”

This follows the arrest of more than 100 Rohingya refugees outside a UNHCR office in Penang last week. Malaysia’s foreign minister then suggested the organization could be stopped from operating in Malaysia unless it became stricter in issuing refugee documents.

Aung San Suu Kyi Alive. Aung San Suu Kyi met with a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross on Monday. The junta, which announced the meeting, also released a grainy photo that showed her shaking hands with resident Red Cross representative Arnaud de Baecque.

The event seems geared to lay to rest growing speculation about the health and well-being of the Nobel Peace Prize winner.

Aung San Suu Kyi was transferred from prison to house arrest in April. Kept out of the public eye since her detention during the 2021 coup, the only evidence that she was alive was a single undated photo released that month.

The timing of this week’s meeting is also significant. Junta leader Min Aung Hlaing is due to arrive in Bangkok on Thursday for an official visit as part of his increasingly successful push for diplomatic acceptance. The upcoming meeting follows a previous one between Myanmar’s foreign minister and ASEAN foreign ministers in Bangkok in mid-July.

The Red Cross has confirmed that the meeting took place. It said it was “carried out in accordance with the ICRC’s standards and procedures for visiting people deprived of liberty,” including an opportunity to speak to Aung San Suu Kyi privately.

Thailand’s Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul (L) is welcomed by Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto (R) upon his arrival at Merdeka Palace in Jakarta, Indonesia, on Aug. 3.Bay Ismoyo/AFP via Getty Images

Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul visited Indonesia in early August. At time of editing, little had been announced so any interesting developments will be summarized in next week’s newsletter.

FP’s Most Read This Week

Thailand is a U.S. treaty ally, but U.S. President Donald Trump is pushing it toward China,  Toru Takahashi argues in Nikkei Asia.

Even as Southeast Asia exports more to the United States, it is importing more than ever from China. Shay Wester explores this dynamic and the problems it poses to the new post-Trump trading system, for the Asia Society.

Out of the slums and onto the pommel horse—Nivell Rayda reports how one low-income neighborhood in Jakarta has become a hotspot for national gymnastics talent, for Channel News Asia.

In Focus: America’s AI bid in Southeast Asia

A couple weeks ago, this newsletter covered China’s bid to position itself as a leader in artificial intelligence for the world and especially Southeast Asia. The United States has its own plans and Southeast Asia, too, is a big part of them.

There are two prongs to the U.S. push. The first is Pax Silica, billed as an effort to build a secure (i.e., China-free) AI supply chain, from critical minerals to chip fabs, data centers, and AI models. The second is AI Spark, which offers support for governments to deploy U.S. AI models in the public sector. That initiative was announced in July as U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Southeast Asia.

Southeast Asia is an attractive target for these policies. The region hosts five of the 10 global economies with the best positions in semiconductor production: Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam. It also has an abundance of critical minerals.

For Pax Silica, two Southeast Asian countries—the Philippines and Singapore—have joined. In New Clark City, Philippines, there are now plans to build a high-tech hub on a 1,620-hectare site, though this has been hit by some inevitable controversies.

As for AI Spark, the details remain vague, and no countries have announced their participation yet. Analysts have suggested that U.S. AI models might be preferred for certain sensitive areas, while cheaper, open-source Chinese AI models would be attractive in areas where security is less of a concern.

As with China’s bid for AI leadership, Southeast Asia has maintained its usual wariness about getting too close to any superpower. U.S. unreliability—the sudden ban on overseas use of cutting-edge models even by allies, as an example—raises further questions about the benefits of aligning with Washington.

A particular sticking point could be the idea of digital sovereignty. ASEAN countries are very keen on the idea.

But Jacob Helberg, U.S. undersecretary of state for economic affairs and a Palantir alum, has denounced the concept as a quixotic waste of resources, arguing instead for a strong interdependent ecosystem that is implicitly U.S.-led.

The tensions around this debate were on display in a fascinating interview of Hellberg by Singapore’s permanent secretary for digital development and information, Chng Kai Fong, in May.

Ironically, to my ear, Hellberg’s proposals sound like Chinese President Xi Jinping’s on AI: a cooperative order, but one in which his country is a clear top dog.

Joseph Rachman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Southeast Asia Brief. He is a freelance journalist based in Jakarta. X: @rachman_joseph
