Moscow has significantly upped its attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent months, typically firing salvos of hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles, with Ukraine pleading for more US-made Patriot interceptors and other Western air defence systems.

Kyiv, in turn, has been firing record numbers of drones at Russia in retaliation.

After meeting with Vucic as part of a two-day trip to Serbia, the Ukrainian leader renewed calls for tougher sanctions to prevent the flow of missile parts into Russia from "almost every continent, including from our close partners".

"These components arrive, and then missiles strike people, killing children, civilians and soldiers," he said.

The Ukrainian leader said more access to interceptor missiles was needed in the face of increasing long-range strikes.

READ MORE
Zelensky seeks more missile interceptors in talks with NATO chief Rutte

Serbia remains one of the only European nations not to sanction Russia, a longtime ally of Belgrade.

Vucic, whose government continues to supply non-military aid to Ukraine, said although they had discussed the war, his government policy had not changed.

"We did not discuss any military cooperation today or at present. What will happen when the war ends is another matter," Vucic said.

Zelensky – who has toured much of the world seeking support since Russia's 2022 invasion – had not visited Serbia since he became president in 2019.

The Kremlin has accused Serbian firms of selling munitions to Ukraine, a claim Vucic has repeatedly denied.

Vucic went to Ukraine for a regional summit in 2025 and visited Kyiv this year.

He has promised assistance to Ukraine but avoided signing a formal declaration of support in the war.

The Serbian leader, on Saturday, also stressed his policy of support for Ukraine's territorial integrity remained unwavering.

The visit came after Russia launched another overnight barrage of missiles and drones, hitting mainly the capital and its surrounds.

An AFP reporter in the capital heard a dozen explosions as Ukraine's air force warned of the "threat of ballistic weapon use from the north".

Zelensky said shelling had also hit across all of frontline communities, injuring dozens while a three-year-old boy was among the dead after the strike on a village outside Kyiv.

"Four more people were hospitalised: the child's parents, his 15-year-old brother, and a neighbour who came to the family's aid and was wounded in a double-tap strike," Zelensky said in an earlier post to X.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.title: Spain imposes border checks on Italian travellers amid migrant dispute
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.text:
Spain on Saturday started border checks on travellers arriving from Italy, responding to similar measures Rome imposed following an unprecedented migrant rush into the Spanish north African enclave of Ceuta.

"I don't see a lot of the word 'diplomacy' used in these decisions, not by the Italian government, nor by the Spanish government," said one 36-year-old Italian tourist, Maria Celeste Grillo, who had just flown into Madrid.

She said she had not seen any added checks as she stepped off the plane, but found their implementation "sad".

Spain announced Friday it would proceed with the heightened controls, citing "persistent irregular migration pressure" facing Italy – deepening a row between the EU partners and NATO allies.

READ MORE
Ceuta migrant influx reignites immigration divisions in Europe

Spain's left-wing government has complained that Italy's hard-right government on July 31 unfairly imposed one month of border checks on travellers from Spain – suspending the EU's Schengen Area visa-free travel arrangements – because of the Ceuta influx.

More than 70,000 migrants had crossed from Morocco into the Ceuta enclave on July 30 and 31, though almost all of them subsequently returned to Morocco within 48 hours.

The inflow alarmed European nations, especially right-wing ones urging tougher rules on irregular migrants. However, rules for Ceuta mean migrants cannot travel onward to continental Europe without passing another layer of border checks.

Spain's interior ministry said the new checks on incoming travellers from Italy would apply until September 7.
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.summary: Spain has started border checks on travellers arriving from Italy. The measures follow an unprecedented migrant rush into the Spanish north African enclave of Ceuta. More than 70,000 migrants had crossed from Morocco into the enclave on July 30 and 31.

https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.title: Israeli troops infiltrate Lebanese army-held village and build roadblock, mayor says
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.text:
Israeli troops infiltrated a Lebanese village placed under the control of Lebanon's army as part of a June agreement, building an earthen barrier there overnight, state media and the local mayor said Saturday.

An AFP correspondent saw the barrier situated at the village's eastern entrance and blocking the road. The local authorities said it was unclear if any Israeli forces remained in the area.

"An Israeli occupation army force advanced into the village of Zawtar al-Gharbiya shortly after midnight... and erected a new earthen barrier near the town square," Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) reported.

Zawtar al-Gharbiya was one of two designated "pilot zones" where the Lebanese army was to take over as part of a US-sponsored framework agreement signed with Israel.

READ MORE
Middle East war: Lebanon, Israel and US sign framework agreement in Washington

Israel invaded south Lebanon after militant group Hezbollah entered the Middle East war on the side of its sponsor Iran in March. Israeli forces continue to occupy a broad band of territory in the south along the border.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Its invasion and widespread bombing campaign have killed more than 4,300 people, according to Lebanon's health ministry, and displaced hundreds of thousands more.

Under the June agreement, Lebanon is meant to disarm Hezbollah while Israel is supposed to gradually pull back its forces.

Beirut's army deployed to Zawtar al-Gharbiya on July 21, and roughly 50 families have since returned to the village, mayor Abed Ezzeddine told AFP.

READ MORE
Lebanese army deploys to three southern villages under US-backed security framework

Israeli troops had been present on the outskirts of the village before the deployment.

Ezzeddine said they were surprised to see the barrier in the morning, located around 100 metres from the town square.

Confirming the incident, a Lebanese military source told AFP it was a violation of the framework agreement.

READ MORE
‘The aim is to erase our identity’: How south Lebanon’s cultural heritage is going up in smoke

Lebanon and Israel had just completed their seventh round of direct negotiations in Rome on Thursday, with a Lebanese source telling AFP the Israelis refused to discuss withdrawing from more areas before making sure Beirut's military had full control over the pilot zones.

Hezbollah, which rejects the deal, refuses to surrender its weapons, and Israel still carries out intermittent strikes on southern Lebanon despite a ceasefire in place since June.

The NNA on Saturday reported artillery shelling in southern Lebanon.

Defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prévot pulled out of the Women's Tour de France ahead of Saturday's eighth and penultimate stage after feeling unwell.

The French rider's Visma-Lease a Bike team said on X that the decision to pull her out of the race was made after consultation with the team's medical staff.

Polish rider Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney was in the overall lead after taking the yellow jersey from Marlen Reusser with a brilliant solo climb to victory up Mont Ventoux on Friday.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/f.title: New Fremantle Traffic Bridge to open ahead of schedule
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/f.author: Briana Shepherd
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 11:02am

Rita Saffioti thanked the project team for working ahead of schedule. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

The new Fremantle Traffic Bridge is set to open before the end of the year.

The closure in February had been expected to last for 12 months.

Many locals and businesses say the impact has been better than expected.

The new Fremantle Traffic Bridge is set to open before the end of the year, months ahead of schedule, with many locals and businesses saying the impact of the closure has been better than expected.

In February, the 86-year-old wooden bridge was closed to allow for the construction of the new bridge, which has the same number of traffic lanes but wider pedestrian paths and a higher clearance for boats.

WA's Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti said while the closure had been expected to last for 12 months, the bridge would now reopen to road users before the end of the year.

"This is an incredible piece of infrastructure and the progress has been rapid," she said.

"The concrete deck has been completed and now the work really is about finishing the bridge, in particular the roads in and out."

The new Fremantle Traffic Bridge has a price tag of $596 million. (Supplied: WA government)

The joint state and federal government project came with an initial price tag of $430 million, updated to $596 million in the most recent state budget.

It is the first "extradosed" bridge to be built in Australia, combining both cantilevers and cable stay supports.

"We're very proud of what we're delivering and in fact it's an alignment that was supported by the community and it's enabled us not to have significant impacts to the businesses, the residential and the whole traffic movement around here," Ms Saffioti said.

The closure has left Stirling Bridge as the only traffic crossing on the western side of the Swan River.

Authorities implemented a number of changes to the local transport network to accommodate the closure, including additional train and bus services, more free parking bays for SmartRider users and increased monitoring of traffic via CCTV.

Federal member for Fremantle Josh Wilson said the local community had risen to the challenge in terms of dealing with the impact.

Josh Wilson says the project "represents the delivery of high quality, beautiful 21st century infrastructure for the next 100 years". (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

"A lot of incredible preparatory work done by the deputy premier and the people here in Western Australia from a transport coordination and public transport and local road modification point of view that meant that we were able to deal with that disruption effectively," he said.

"And I also want to credit the broader community for the way that they've supported local businesses."

MJ owns and runs a coffee shop in North Fremantle, an area particularly affected by the closure.

MJ says while there had been an impact from the bridge closure, the community had rallied around local businesses. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

"We did notice an impact, especially in the first month it [business] dropped significantly but our local community and support from our locals was magnificent; they were coming, bringing their friends; so community here, it's amazing," she said.

MJ said communication with the authorities about the bridge closure had been excellent, and she was looking forward to the reopening, hopeful it would bring more foot and bike traffic past her cafe.

"I just want to thank the community and our customers and everyone from North Fremantle for supporting me and the rest of the business," she said.

Eighty people with a special connection to the Fremantle Traffic Bridge are invited to cross it before it is demolished and rebuilt.

The deputy premier said the closure of the bridge had coincided with a significant increase in freight on rail, meaning fewer trucks on the road system.

More than a quarter of all containers from Fremantle Harbour were shipped in and out via rail in 2025–26, a new record for the state, and the highest proportion in the country.

"As part of the work we undertook before closing the bridge, we worked with logistics companies … on how we can better support them through supporting some extra capacity in their distribution warehouses to get more freight onto rail, so another big win in getting trucks off road," Ms Saffioti said.

She credited the rail freight subsidy scheme the Labor government introduced in 2017, in which a $50 subsidy is paid per 20-foot equivalent unit of cargo, for the increase.

An exact date for the opening of the new Fremantle Traffic Bridge has not yet been set but Ms Saffioti said likely before Christmas, with the day to be celebrated with a community event.

The competitors were sent to their dream destinations for week 10. (ABC iview/Race Around The World)

Elliot Constable has been crowned the winner of Race Around the World, bringing to an end 100 days on the road.

Unlike previous weeks, contestants on the ABC iview series were able to select their own destination for the reboot's finale.

For Constable, it was the favelas of Brazil.

Topping the leaderboard of six filmmakers, Constable has won the crown and funding to produce his own project for the ABC.

Catch the final films of Race Around the World 2026.

Title: Holding the Line

What's it about? In Brazil's largest favela, one father is determined to change the direction of his son's future.

Elliot's week 10 film, shot in Brazil. (ABC iview/Race Around The World: Elliot Constable)

Title: I can't see it

What's it about? On the Mongolian steppe, certain days are the best for change. Not because change happens that day, but because it's the best time to stop and recognise that it already has.

Mikaela's week 10 film, shot in Mongolia. (ABC iview/Race Around The World: Mikaela Zuiderduyn)

What's it about? From fillers to face lifts, it's never been easier to look younger, for longer. But for who?

Lucinda's week 10 film, shot in Los Angeles, USA. (ABC iview/Race Around The World: Lucinda Price)

What's it about? I get a tarot card from a fortune teller in rural Vietnam, and we learn a lot about each other in the process.

William's week 10 film, shot in Vietnam. (ABC iview/Race Around The World: William He)

What's it about? As bottom trawling devastates the ocean off Senegal, a local fisherman feels that illegal migration is the only option to turn his life around.

Jayden's week 10 film, shot in Senegal. (ABC iview/Race Around The World: Jayden O'Neill)

Title: I wish my dad was still alive

What's it about? Yang is a stay-at-home dad in China. Brought up by strict parents, Yang wants to raise his baby differently. His story is told through the eyes of a gwai lou (foreign devil).

Kate's week 10 film, shot in China. (ABC iview/Race Around The World: Kate McGuinness)

Describe yourself in three words: Artistic, poetic, magazine.

My motto for Race Around the World is: Art is subjective. Not everyone is going to like your film, so as long as you make something that you're proud of, it doesn't really matter if people don't like it.

One item that's making the suitcase no matter what: Wired headphones. There's too much travel to rely on a charged set of AirPods.

My greatest fear while overseas is: Having luggage go overboard and get wet. With all our filming gear, water is really hard to recover from.

Describe yourself in three words: Chaotic, introverted extrovert.

My motto for Race Around the World is: I always liked this saying in Portuguese, "Viva como se fosse morrer amanhã", which is like, live as if you will die tomorrow. I think you just need to enjoy every day.

One item that's making the suitcase no matter what: My glasses, but I'll lose them. I've lost three pairs of glasses in the last month.

My greatest fear while overseas is: Something happening to people that I love while I'm away.

Describe yourself in three words: Easy-going, lively, passionate.

My motto for Race Around the World is: I think this one's actually plagiarised from the big man David Attenborough, but if people don't care about something, they won't protect it, and people won't care about something they can't see.

One item that's making the suitcase no matter what: My long lens. It's a really long, stupidly heavy, big thing that no one in their right mind would want to carry when you're running around to 10 different countries.

My greatest fear while overseas is: Getting to day nine and a story having completely fallen through, or if I shot a full story with someone, and then I'm ready to submit it, and for whatever reason, the person in the story pulls the pin.

Describe yourself in three words: Bubbly, curious, unconventional.

My motto for Race Around the World is: YOLO [you only live once].

One item that's making the suitcase no matter what: A necklace that means a lot to me, that's my talisman.

My greatest fear while overseas is: The logistics. I dread not getting sleep.

Describe yourself in three words: Curious, Wollongong, humorist

My motto for Race Around the World is: Water off a duck's back.

One item that's making the suitcase no matter what: My nan's ring, that would be my lucky charm.

My greatest fear while overseas is: A misunderstanding would be really dreadful. Being Australian, I feel like we have a very good sense of humour, but it can also be a little bit different. You don't want people to think you're making fun of them, but that's sometimes how that can be interpreted.

Describe yourself in three words: Content, introspective, disorganised

My motto for Race Around the World is: Have fun.

One item that's making the suitcase no matter what: My Nintendo Switch.

My greatest fear while overseas is: My reputation for being a machine learning engineer getting tarnished by the fact that, I don't know, maybe I say something about not wanting to do it when really, I love my job.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/t.title: Taylor Swift songs removed from Donald Trump social media posts
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
World Politics

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:21am

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:35am

Taylor Swift songs have disappeared from TikTok videos supporting Donald Trump. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Some Taylor Swift songs have been removed from social media videos posted by Donald Trump's campaign and the White House.

Over the past week, the US president used two popular hits from the 36-year-old singer, who has been outspoken against conservative politics in recent years.

There has been no public statement from Swift explaining whether she personally authorised action against the videos.

Several Taylor Swift songs have been removed from social media videos posted by Donald Trump's campaign and the White House, reviving the long-running political feud between the world's biggest pop star and the US president.

The Trump campaign and White House have used several Swift tracks in TikTok videos, including songs from her more recent catalogue as well as earlier hits.

Among them was Swift's 2020 song August, used in a Team Trump video showing the president and First Lady Melania Trump watching fireworks.

The account appeared to acknowledge the provocative nature of the choice, tagging Swift and suggesting she would be "super excited" that her music had been used.

Songs from Swift's 2025 The Life of a Showgirl album had been used by Trump officials. (Supplied: Universal Music Group)

The audio has since disappeared from the post.

Other Swift songs, including Father Figure and Opalite, have also been removed from Trump-related TikTok videos, and several other tracks have disappeared from White House and campaign posts.

Some of the affected videos now display notices indicating the music is unavailable because of a copyright claim or has been made unavailable by the copyright owner.

Neither Swift nor the White House immediately responded to requests for comment. There has been no public statement from the 36-year-old singer explaining whether she personally authorised action against the videos.

The removals have attracted attention because of Swift's history with Mr Trump, who likes to use well-known pop songs to motivate his supporters.

The Village People's YMCA song has been a feature of Donald Trump rallies in recent years. (AP: Evan Vucci)

Mr Trump and his political operation have repeatedly invoked Swift, despite her opposition to him.

During the 2024 election campaign, Trump shared AI-generated images that falsely suggested Swift and some of her fans were supporting him.

Swift subsequently cited the fake images as one of the reasons she decided to make her own voting intentions clear.

The latest dispute also comes amid broader tensions between the Trump administration and musicians over the political use of their work.

Artists including Ariana Grande and Sabrina Carpenter have objected to their music being associated with Trump or his administration.

Taylor Swift became more political during the 2018 midterm elections in the US. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management)

For much of her early career, Swift carefully avoided partisan politics.

That changed dramatically in 2018 when she publicly entered the political arena ahead of the midterm elections in Tennessee, where she was registered to vote.

After Taylor Swift was called a childless cat lady for supporting Kamala Harris, it became a popular social media meme. (Supplied: Museum of Australian Democracy)

Swift endorsed Democrats Phil Bredesen for the US Senate and Jim Cooper for the House of Representatives while criticising Republican Senate candidate Marsha Blackburn.

She said she had previously been reluctant to reveal her political opinions but had changed her approach following events in her own life and in the US. Ms Blackburn ultimately defeated Mr Bredesen.

Swift became more outspoken during Mr Trump's first presidency.

In May 2020, during the unrest following the death of George Floyd, she accused Mr Trump of inflaming racial divisions and told him: "We will vote you out in November."

Beyonce (right) joined Taylor Swift in endorsing Kamala Harris ahead of the 2024 US election.     (AP Photo: Annie Mulligan)

Later that year she formally endorsed Democratic candidates Joe Biden and Kamala Harris, saying their leadership offered America an opportunity to begin a "healing process".

Her involvement intensified during the 2024 presidential campaign.

After initially remaining silent about the contest, Swift joined a long list of show-business identities in endorsing Ms Harris immediately following her September debate against Mr Trump.

Swift told her enormous Instagram following that she was supporting Ms Harris because the vice-president fought for rights and causes that she believed needed "a warrior" to champion them.

She described Ms Harris as a "steady-handed, gifted leader" and said the US could achieve more if governed by "calm and not chaos".

Donald Trump took aim at Taylor Swift on Truth Social last year. (Supplied: Truth Social/@realDonaldTrump)

She signed the endorsement "Taylor Swift, Childless Cat Lady", a pointed reference to controversial comments previously made by Mr Trump's running mate JD Vance.

Mr Trump responded furiously.

"I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!" he posted on social media shortly after her endorsement.

His attacks continued even after he defeated Ms Harris and returned to the White House.

In 2025, Mr Trump mocked Swift again, questioning whether she was still "HOT" since he had publicly declared his dislike for her.

Despite the exchanges, Swift has largely avoided commenting publicly on Mr Trump during his second term.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 9:15am

Carlton's Lily Goss kicked two goals against St Kilda. (Getty Images: AFKLW)

Carlton has begun the 2026 AFLW season with a 26-point win over St Kilda.

Carlton led by 31 points at one stage, before St Kilda threatened a fightback, followed by Carlton kicking late goals to extend the margin.

Round 1 of the AFLW season continues on Thursday, when Hawthorn hosts Melbourne.

Carlton has held off a St Kilda fightback to claim the opening win of the new AFLW season by 26 points in an entertaining game that made a case for more double header fixtures.

The Blues made the preliminary final last season and entered 2026 with high expectations.

Carlton led by as much as 31 points but withstood a fourth-quarter comeback from St Kilda before sealing the 9.12 (66) to 6.4 (40) victory.

Sunday's game was held at Docklands Stadium ahead of the men's AFL clash as one of five double headers this season.

The concept already appears a winner and will prompt calls for more alignment with the men's season.

Several thousand fans were in for the start of the game, with the crowd ticking over 10,000 just after half-time and reaching 20,455 when the attendance was officially counted in the fourth quarter.

Despite missing young dynamo Sophie McKay (calf), best and fairest winner Keeley Sherar (quad) and ruck recruit Lauren Bella (calf) through injury, the Blues were on top early.

The Saints couldn't capitalise on early centre clearance dominance and were swamped by Carlton's classy midfield.

Skipper Abbie McKay (32 disposals, nine clearances), Mimi Hill (28 disposals), Lila Keck (21 disposals, two goals) recruit Claudia Whitfort (27 touches) and Irish star Dayna Finn (22 disposals) collected plenty of the ball, while Lily Goss kicked two goals.

Young gun Poppy Scholz was the fire starter, brushing off a defender to kick the first goal, kicking 1.4 and appearing a constant threat with her athleticism and smarts.

Scholz's opener started a run of four straight Carlton goals.

Tyanna Smith was comfortably St Kilda's best, racking up 625 metres gained, eight clearances, 19 disposals and two terrific goals on the run, with support from Georgia Patrikios (27 disposals)

Amber Clarke provided a spark with two superb fourth-quarter goals.

Overwhelmed by Carlton's running power early, the Saints got a foothold in the game when recruit Sophie Butterworth nailed their first goal.

St Kilda smashed Carlton around the ball in the third term and cut the deficit to 23 at three-quarter time.

Clarke soccered through a wonderful skidding goal from a tight angle to spark St Kilda just 27 seconds into the final term, then snapped another to cut the lead to 11.

But Darcy Vescio's second goal put a dagger in St Kilda's hearts late on before Keck sealed the deal.

St Kilda's J'Noemi Anderson suffered a hamstring injury.

Mathew Buck's Carlton next host Adelaide at Princes Park while Nick Dal Santo's St Kilda travel to Geelong.

A crime scene has been set up up in southern New South Wales after a body was found in a suitcase.

Police say they were called to Wolgon Road at Oallen, about 60 kilometres south-east of Goulburn, just before 1pm.

Officers attached to the Hume police district attended and located a body in a suitcase.

The body is yet to be identified but police say it is believed to be female.

A crime scene has been established and the suitcase has been seized to undergo forensic examination, as detectives start their investigation.

In the Southern Tablelands region of NSW, the rural locality of Oallen, on the Shoalhaven River, is 109km north-east of Canberra and 254km south-west of Sydney.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/c.author: Michael Doyle
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 8:26am

Cameron Munster has had a dangerous contact charge downgraded. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Melbourne Storm five-eighth Cameron Munster has escaped suspension after his dangerous contact charge was downgraded.

The NRL match review committee initially gave Munster a grade two charge for his low tackle on Manly's Taniela Paseka, but the league says new information warranted it being classed as a grade one.

The Melbourne Storm have the bye next week in round 24, then host the Penrith Panthers in round 25.

Melbourne Storm five-eighth Cameron Munster has avoided suspension after the NRL Match Review Committee downgraded his dangerous contact charge from Saturday's win over Manly.

Munster was initially facing a week on the sidelines, and two if he unsuccessfully challenged the charge, for a low tackle at the knees of Sea Eagles prop Taniela Paseka.

The Storm star was the third man in to the tackle, targeted the legs of Paseka, and left the Manly big man in pain.

Paseka was helped from the field, and Munster was charged with a grade two dangerous contact.

Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

But the MRC has now downgraded that to a grade one, after receiving a medical report that shows Paseka's injury may not be as bad as first feared.

A statement from the NRL says new information warranted the charge being downgraded, which means Munster can cop a $750 fine for pleading guilty.

"When initially ascribing a grading to Melbourne Storm's Cameron Munster for the charge of dangerous contact, the MRC considered the contents of a medical report provided by the injured player’s club, which offered preliminary details as to the nature and extent of the injury," the NRL statement said.

"Subsequently, the match review committee has received a further report which materially alters the nature and extent of the injury suffered by the player.

"Pursuant to Rule 61 of the NRL Judiciary Code, where further expert or medical information warrants a different grading, the match review committee may authorise the match review manager to amend the grading and issue an amended notice of charge.

"Following due consideration of this report, the match review committee has reviewed the charge against Cameron Munster and, in accordance with the judiciary code, has forwarded the player an amended notice of charge for the offence of dangerous contact (grade 1)."

Munster made his return to action following a knee injury in the Storm's win over the Sea Eagles in Perth, keeping alive their very slim finals hopes.

The Storm have the bye next week, then must win their remaining three matches starting with a clash against Penrith at AAMI Park.

Even if the Storm win their remaining three matches, they will need other results to go their way.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 7:38am

Videos of several near misses have been released as a warning to pedestrians.

Adelaide's metropolitan rail lines recorded 163 near misses over the past year's reporting period – up 4 per cent.

Pedestrians accounted for 60 per cent of incidents, and cyclists for 35 per cent.

Transport officials have warned against risky behaviour and urged pedestrians to always pay attention.

Near misses across Adelaide's rail network have increased over 12 months, with one line accounting for nearly half of all reports.

Pedestrians accounted for 98, and cyclists for almost 60, of the 163 near misses reported by train drivers in data that covers the 2025-26 year.

Overall, incidents were up by 4 per cent compared to the previous period.

Almost half of the incidents took place along the Gawler line, with 72 near misses reported.

The Belair line also saw an increase, while the Seaford and Outer Harbor lines saw reductions.

Video released by the SA government shows several alarming incidents along Adelaide's rail lines, including one in which a cyclist pulled back at the last moment and another in which a pedestrian dived out of the way.

SA Transport Minister Joe Szakacs singled out distracted pedestrians as putting lives at risk.

One of the videos shows pedestrians having to jump out of the way at the last moment. (Supplied: SA Government)

"In just the short four months that I've been minister, I've seen some pretty mind-blowing CCTV footage of people [who], for any other reason, are just not paying attention," he said.

"It is a bee's whisker between them being cleaned up by a train and them getting home safely.

The minister said a passenger train takes 500 metres to stop in an emergency, and freight trains take 2 kilometres.

Train driver Ben Hemmerling said risk-taking witnessed by drivers included pedestrians pushing through automatic barriers at pedestrian crossings and mazes.

"Rather than waiting for the bells and the sounds to stop and wait for the train to pass, they push through and try to beat the train," he said.

While near misses increased along rail lines, the tram network had a 30 per cent reduction, from 165 incidents to 113.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 8:41am

Telstra says its cabling was damaged in a bushfire near Weipa on Saturday evening. (Supplied: Chad King)

A bushfire in Cape York in Far North Queensland has knocked out telecommunications for thousands of residents in the remote part of the state.

Many have been unable to make calls, including to Triple Zero (000), since Saturday evening.

Telstra confirmed a team of technicians was sent from Cairns to Weipa in Cape York on Sunday morning and is working to resolve the issue as soon as possible.

Some residents have been unable to make Triple Zero calls since Saturday evening. (Supplied: Chad King)

The telco said services were due to be restored on Sunday evening.

A spokesperson for Optus confirmed the telco was aware its customers in the area were also impacted.

"We understand how important connectivity is to our customers and apologise for the disruption," the spokesperson said.

The towns of Mapoon, Weipa, Napranum and Aurukun were among those impacted.

Telstra said its Mission River, Nanum and Rocky Point sites were also impacted.

Fixed line, ADSL and mobile services have all been affected, Telstra said,

A federal government spokesperson confirmed the Triple Zero custodian had been made aware of the outage.

"We expect telcos to work with affected communities to rectify issues as quickly as possible," the spokesperson said.

Queensland police had not been made aware of any issues contacting Triple Zero.

The Mapoon council says having one tower is not enough protection in case something goes wrong. (Supplied: Chad King)

The chief executive of the Mapoon Aboriginal Shire Council, Chad King, said the outage had impacted several towns in the area.

He said Mapoon, which is home to about 500 people, was particularly vulnerable because there was no fixed phone system, leaving people completely reliant on mobile coverage.

The council had set up additional free wi-fi on Sunday to try lessen some of the impacts.

But he was very concerned by the inability of residents to make Triple Zero calls, in what was already a remote part of the state and a long way from police and emergency services.

Mr King said it was "a genuine issue" and something he wanted the government to pay attention to.

"We're keeping a close eye on the health of our community," Mr King said.

Mr King said a single phone tower meant a "single point of failure", saying better services in the bush were needed.

He called on Telstra and the federal government to do more to increase services in remote and regional areas.

"Closing the gap target 17 is all about making sure that digital access for First Nations communities is as good as it is for other communities in our country," he said.

A spokesperson for the federal government said it was focused on bridging the digital divide for all Australians and had committed $68 million to initiatives aimed at closing it for First Nations people.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/s.author: Melissa Brown and Nicole Asher

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 7:04am

Community members have gathered in Melbourne's west to pay tribute to grocery store owner Van Viet Truong and to call for an increase in security measures. (ABC News: Nicole Asher)

Community members have rallied in Sunshine demanding tougher bail laws and a stronger police presence on local streets after the death of Van Viet Truong.

The 60-year-old died after he was allegedly bashed while trying to stop a group of teenagers suspected of stealing from a neighbouring shop.

A 15-year-old boy who was charged with manslaughter is expected to face court again later this month, while a boy and two girls have been released on bail after being charged with affray and intentionally causing serious injury.

Locals in Melbourne's west have rallied in Sunshine to demand tougher bail laws and increased police resources following the death of a beloved grocery store owner.

Van Viet Truong, 60, died in hospital on Wednesday, days after he was allegedly bashed when he tried to stop a group of teenagers suspected of stealing clothes from a nearby business.

A 15-year-old boy has been charged with manslaughter and remains in custody.

A 12-year-old boy and two 14-year-old girls have been released on bail after being charged with affray and intentionally causing serious injury.

Grocery store owner Van Viet Truong died after allegedly being bashed by a group of youths in Sunshine. (Supplied)

Today's vigil was organised by the Vietnamese Mothers in Australia Community and held in Sunshine's shopping precinct to show support for Mr Truong's family and to call for measures to protect the community from violent crime.

Although it was advertised as being non-political, speakers at the rally called on the community to take their anger about what happened to Mr Truong, and their opinions on the effectiveness of the state's bail laws, to the ballot box in November.

One woman travelled to Sunshine from Pascoe Vale, in Melbourne's north, telling the rally she had been a victim of an assault there.

She said it was shocking to think "you [could] just say goodbye to your wife, your kids, you go to work, you never come home again".

About 100 people attended the rally in Sunshine calling on the government to bolster community safety. (ABC News)

Another woman travelled in from Cobram, in regional Victoria, to support family who live in the area.

"The government needs to make stronger laws," she said.

"It used to be safer [in Sunshine]. Now I wouldn't be able to let my kids out on the street."

One speaker likened Mr Truong's death to that of Aidan Becker, who was fatally stabbed after stepping in to help a teenager who was allegedly being robbed at Mernda station in March.

Members of the Australian Vietnamese Refugee National Council gathered to pay their respects to Mr Truong.   (ABC News: Nicole Asher)

Outside Mr Truong's shop, members of the Australian Vietnamese Refugee National Council performed ceremonies to show respect to Mr Truong, his family and the community.

But the council's president, Phong Nguyen, said he did not believe it was the right time for the community rally, according to traditional beliefs.

"As a former refugee, he belonged to this community and we are very saddened by his passing and his tragic death but, as per our tradition, during this mourning period, we refrain from any other activity," he explained.

"Not that we're not concerned about safety, not that we're not concerned about the issue, but that will be for another day, another time."

Traditional ceremonies were performed outside Mr Truong's store. (ABC News: Nicole Asher)

He described Mr Truong as "one of the quiet heroes".

"They sacrifice their lives for their fellow human beings … [and] that's what life and heroes are about. We don't know them until they are there."

He pledged that his community would do all it could to ensure safety was improved.

Phong Nguyen says Mr Truong was one of the community's quiet heroes. (ABC News: Nicole Asher)

Mr Truong ran his Sunshine grocery store for more than 30 years.

Local mayor Virginia Tachos said the community continued to feel deep shock over his death.

"He'll be remembered as being one of the pioneers of that shopping precinct in Sunshine," she said.

A woman lays flowers outside Mr Truong's grocery store earlier this week. (ABC News)

Cr Tachos said the rally aimed to honour Mr Truong, but was also a chance for the community to support each other

"There's a real collective grief happening in the streets," she said.

"This anger and frustration is reflected in that."

Local mayor Virginia Tachos says the rally has given community members a chance to support each other through their grief. (ABC News: Nicole Asher)

She said violent crime had been escalating in Sunshine.

"Talking to the traders, they're really afraid every day," she said.

"A lot of staff are scared to come to work — staff from our library, our staff across the road here [at the council chambers] are also impacted by it."

Victoria Police increased the number of officers patrolling the shopping strip in the wake of Mr Truong's death.

Cr Tachos said the council was looking at installing better lighting and other security measures but was calling on the state government to permanently increase police patrols to help fight daily crime.

The council is calling for the increased police patrols introduced after Van Viet Truong's death to be permanent. (ABC News)

She said the council was also calling for the Community Connector Program, which runs in suburbs including Dandenong and Frankston, to be expanded to Sunshine.

"It's an outreach program approaching youths at stations, at places where they congregate to link them into services and supports," she said.

She said previous attempts to lobby the government for more police resources were met with claims that there were enough officers on the beat.

But Cr Tachos said she did not think there were enough.

"Until we have those programs in place to divert youth … programs that are missing here in the west, we need police presence," she said.

The local mayor says the community continues to feel deep shock at Mr Truong's death. (ABC News)

Sunshine Business Association vice-president John Girardi agreed with the mayor.

"We don't have as much of a police presence as, say, five or six years ago," he said.

Mr Girardi said the association met with police on a regular basis and had asked for an increased presence to help workers and customers feel safer.

"What I hear from business owners is [about] where there might be a minor incident that could be escalating," he said.

"The response times for the police to get out and deal with the incident — we'd like to see something done about that."

John Girardi says the police presence in the area has decreased over the past few years. (ABC News: Nicole Asher)

He said locals also felt like nothing was being done about low-level crime, such as groups regularly drinking in the streets.

He said that had led to retailers talking about bringing in their own private security guards to patrol the streets — and that some businesses had already started to.

Victoria Police said it had increased the number of officers on patrol over the past week and would be on hand to provide support and ongoing reassurance "as long as it's needed".

"The recent alleged incident in Sunshine has no doubt had a ripple effect through the entire community and has caused angst and concern in Melbourne's west," a spokesperson said in a statement.

"Police feel these concerns as well – we are as much a part of the community ourselves."

Police patrol the back streets of Sunshine after Van Viet Truong's death. (ABC News)

They acknowledged that some police stations in Melbourne's west now have reduced public counter hours, but said that allowed officers to go out on patrol.

"Put simply, our focus is on more street than station."

Opposition leader Jess Wilson attended the vigil.

"We have weak laws here in Victoria and we have a crime crisis," she said.

"People have just had enough and we can hear it behind us here today."

Victorian government frontbencher Anthony Carbines said the state government would listen to the community's concerns.

"People in the west are tired of their safety being compromised," said Mr Carbines, who until recently was the police minister in the Allan government.

"We should give thanks for the generosity and bravery of people who have stepped forward to help others and we need to make sure that they're supported."

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 5:34am

Following a large-scale search, the body of a man believed to be 32 years old has been found near North Wollongong Beach. (Supplied: Surf Life Saving NSW )

A body has been found during a search for a missing swimmer at North Wollongong.

NSW Police have not formally identified the body but believe it to be that of a 32-year-old man.

Police are appealing for anyone with information about the incident to contact Crime Stoppers.

A body believed to be that of a 32-year-old man has been found in the water near North Wollongong Beach, during a multi-agency search for the missing swimmer.

Emergency services received a call from the popular Wollongong beach, which is one of the only beaches patrolled during the winter months in the coastal city, about 10:30am.

In it, welfare concerns were raised about a swimmer who had not returned from the water, and whose belongings had been found on the beach.

It sparked a multi-agency response from NSW Police, NSW Ambulance, Marine Rescue and Surf Life Saving NSW.

Multiple agencies responded after the belongings of a swimmer who hadn't returned from the water were found on the beach. (Supplied: Surf Life Saving NSW)

A large-scale search got underway during which a body was found slightly submerged off the rock platform near the Continental Pool, about 1 kilometre south of the beach.

The body was retrieved by the searchers and NSW Police are now investigating the incident.

While they have not formally identified the body, in a statement police said they believed it to be that of a 32-year-old man.

Police have appealed to anyone with information about the incident to contact Crime Stoppers.

Surf Life Saving NSW's Illawarra duty officer Anthony Turner said emergency services did everything they could to locate the man quickly.

"It was a short search; within an hour the body was retrieved and brought back to shore by emergency services," he said.

He said it was a huge, multi-agency effort.

"Surf Life Saving deployed three inflatable rescue boats, two rescue services, jet skis, a UAV drone and the Westpac Lifesaver 21 helicopter from Sydney also attended the scene," he said.

"Marine Area Command [were] offshore and council lifeguards were on jet skis."

Police are appealing for anyone with information about the incident to contact Crime Stoppers. (Supplied: Surf Life Saving NSW)

He said the circumstances surrounding the death will be a matter for NSW Police.

"The conditions were quite favourable today for swimming and beach activities, so that'll be part of the police investigation," he said.

Mr Turner said while less fatal incidents occur during winter months compared to summer, the tragic event was, sadly, not unusual.

"A lot of incidents do happen outside the season and it just highlights how important it is, if you do go for a swim, adventure to beaches which are patrolled," he said.

"And look at the surf conditions before entering the water."

He said North Beach was patrolled between the hours of 9am and 4pm during the off-season.

Mr Turner said support will be provided to the first responders.

A report will be prepared for the coroner.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/w.author: Annabel Bowles
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
World Politics

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 5:26am

David Brat has been confirmed as the next US ambassador to Australia. (ABC News: Cameron Schwarz)

The United States has appointed a new ambassador to Australia, with the US Senate confirming David Brat for the role this weekend.

The appointment ends an almost 20-month vacancy.

Here's what we know about President Donald Trump's pick for the role and what his priorities will be in Canberra.

Mr Brat is a former economics professor who spent two terms in the US House of Representatives as a Republican.

He shot to prominence in 2014 as part of the Republicans' conservative Tea Party faction, when he ousted the party's then House leader Eric Cantor in a primary.

It was a big deal, with the New York Times calling it "one of the most stunning upsets in modern political history".

Known for his Christian nationalist views, Mr Brat has a master's degree in divinity from Princeton Theological Seminary and his most recent roles have been at the deeply religious Liberty University in Virginia.

Last year he took aim at "moral relativism" on conservative social media platform GETTR, writing "why can the majority culture, Christian, not teach its values in our K-12 schools, when the Open Society and the Marxists can??" he wrote.

"Our Christian culture must WAKE UP. We are the Majority. We created Minority Rights. But the Minority does NOT get to dictate perversion."

Mr Brat had a longstanding reputation as a free-market economist but has recently supported Mr Trump's tariffs and economic agenda, saying free trade is now impossible because US companies have "sold out" America.

Mr Brat has also long promoted the "deep state" conspiracy theories tied to the MAGA movement and behind Mr Trump's efforts to reshape parts of the US government and its intelligence arms.

David Brat is known as a conservative economist and firebrand MAGA pundit. (Reuters: Yuri Gripas)

Last year, he called the Biden administration's investigation into electoral interference a "conspiracy 1,000 times worse than Watergate".

He also accused the CIA and FBI of orchestrating a vast conspiracy to spy on "hundreds of Republican groups".

"The Strategy was clear, a threat to the entire system had emerged in the person of Donald J Trump," he wrote.

In the past, Mr Brat has opposed funding for Ukraine's defence against Russia and suggested NATO provoked Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

In 2022, he urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as a "Christian brother" to accept Russian demands in the wake of Vladimir Putin's invasion, instead of committing to a war which would "devastate" Ukraine.

The ambassador's post in Canberra sat vacant for nearly 20 months.

The US Studies Centre (USSC) says it is "not unusual" for the position to sit empty at the start of new presidencies.

Australia waited 18 months before the last ambassador's arrival and before that two years for Arthur Culvahouse, Mr Trump's pick during his first term.

However, the delay did not go unnoticed.

At Mr Brat's Senate confirmation hearing in May, the Foreign Relations Committee's top Democrat Jeanne Shaheen said she was glad the nomination had "finally" happened.

"It's delays like that that weaken American credibility with our allies," she said.

Caroline Kennedy, the daughter of former US president John F Kennedy, was the last US ambassador to Australia.

She held the role from 2022 to 2024 during Joe Biden's presidency and was focused on bedding down the AUKUS agreement, which she called an "existential investment in Australia's sovereignty".

Caroline Kennedy criticised her cousin Robert F Kennedy Jr, the current US Health Secretary, for his vaccine scepticism. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Kennedy also famously joined the Shitbox Rally, an annual charity fundraiser that involves people driving across the Australian outback in a cheap runabout.

She succeeded Mr Culvahouse, who left the position in early 2021, when Mr Trump's first term finished.

History has shown presidents have nominated people they share a personal relationship with over members of the foreign service, the USSC has said.

At his confirmation hearing, Mr Brat said his priorities in Canberra were critical minerals and commercial diplomacy, defence cooperation and partnership in the Indo-Pacific.

He said he wanted to build on the opening of the Australian market to US beef, which had been a grievance of the Trump administration, to create a "level playing field" for other US exports.

The US Senate's Foreign Relations Committee held a hearing to confirm multiple ambassador appointments in May. (ABC News: Cameron Schwarz)

He also flagged partnering with Australia's superannuation funds to "execute on plans to invest in the US" and going "full steam ahead" on AUKUS, which he called critical to "security for the South Pacific".

Mr Brat has no obvious connections to Australia, and at one point during the hearing he referred to Adelaide as "Adeline".

But he lauded Australia as a US ally, saying that "few countries are as integral to US interests as Australia", said he loved "everything" about the country and stressed that he was a "tennis fanatic".

On Friday, Washington time, the same day Mr Brat's appointment was confirmed, Mr Trump announced the Pentagon would invest $560 million into a critical minerals project in a tiny NSW town.

The Pentagon will invest more than half a billion dollars to expand an Australian critical mineral project poised to become the world's first scandium mine.

The conditional loan provides it with a right of first offer on the mine's output of scandium, which is used in the aerospace, defence and automotive sectors.

It came after Mr Trump and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese inked a $13 billion critical minerals deal late last year. Mr Brat has pledged to execute that agreement during his time in Canberra.

After Mr Brat's appointment was confirmed, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said he would find Australia to be a "warm host and good friend".

"We share his priorities of critical minerals, defence cooperation and partnership in the Indo-Pacific. Together we will strengthen the alliance in the interests of both our countries," Ms Wong said.

Nationals Leader Matt Canavan welcomed the news, calling Mr Brat an "eloquent contributor" to policy debates in the US.

"He is obviously very close to Trump and the administration, which is what you want in an ambassador," he said.

USSC director of research Jared Mondschein has shared that view.

"What you want in an ambassador, regardless of whether you share his political opinion or not, is one who can get the attention of the US president," he said.

Both sides of federal politics have welcomed David Brat's confirmation, but some commentators have been more critical. (ABC News: Top Stories)

However, outside of political circles, some commentators have been more critical. US analyst Bill Wyman described Mr Brat as an "undiplomatic person" and a MAGA political bomb thrower.

"This is not a sophisticated person. This is supposed to be a diplomatic position," he said.

He suggested Mr Trump may be "sending an ally over" to Australia's right, at a time One Nation's popularity is surging.

When previously asked whether Mr Brat was someone he could work with, Mr Albanese said he respected "the sovereignty of countries to put forward ambassadors, just as we expect our choices to be endorsed".

The US Embassy in Australia has been contacted for comment.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Mixed Martial Arts

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 4:25am

Australian UFC fighter Quillan Salkilld has continued his impressive run of form. (Getty Images: Zuffa LLC/Jeff Bottari)

Australian Quillan Salkilld has won his first UFC main event, defeating Mateusz Gamrot with a rear-naked choke in Las Vegas.

Salkilld is on a 13-fight win streak and has won his last four fights in the first round.

Salkilld says he is ready to be challenged by a fighter ranked in the UFC's lightweight top five.

The moment was not too big for Quillan Salkilld.

Making his main event debut, the Australian's run of first-round finishes continued on Saturday night local time in Las Vegas as he defeated veteran Mateusz Gamrot with a rear-naked choke at 4:25 of the first round of their non-title lightweight bout at UFC Fight Night at the UFC APEX.

Salkilld (13-1) survived a Gamrot (26-5) leg-lock during an extensive grappling exchange in the scheduled five-round fight before working to the back and locking in the finish, earning the biggest victory of his career while extending his winning streak to 13 fights.

Salkilld, who has now won his past four fights and five of his last six in the first round, called for a step up in competition after the victory.

"I think I deserve someone who's in the top five or close to it," Salkilld said.

Following the victory, the number 12-ranked Salkilld positioned himself for a match-up near the top of the lightweight division, while the number eight-ranked Gamrot absorbed a setback against one of the division's fastest-rising contenders.

Saturday's event marked the UFC's return to Las Vegas after two events abroad, in Abu Dhabi on July 25 and then Belgrade last Saturday.

In the co-main event, Diego Ferreira (20-7 MMA) landed more than 135 significant strikes across 15 minutes to earn a unanimous decision against Billy Quarantillo (18-8 MMA) in their lightweight bout.

Del Valle quickly closed the show against Elkins (29-13 MMA), spoiling the longtime veteran's final Octagon appearance while rebounding from the first loss of his career in February.

"I'm thankful for it all … don't ever give up on yourself," Elkins said following the loss.

Strawweight Alexia Thainara (15-1) utilised a relentless pace and a variety of take-downs alongside unorthodox striking to earn a unanimous decision against former strawweight contender Amanda Lemos (15-7-1), taking the cards 29-28, 29-28 and 30-27 in their all-Brazilian match-up.

Unbeaten welterweight Ty Miller (8-0 MMA) opened the main card by stopping Billy Ray Goff (9-5 MMA) via TKO 15 seconds into the third round.

Miller unleashed punches against the fence to force the stoppage, extending his perfect professional record while handing Goff his third straight defeat.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 4:20am

Donald Trump's 2025 filings indicate he made more than $US2.2 billion through ventures ostensibly run by his family. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

When it comes to American politics, Donald Trump may be more of a traditionalist than many give him credit.

Back in 1832, New York-based US senator William L Macy, defending the behaviour of president Andrew Jackson, uttered these immortal and now oft-repeated words.

"It may be, sir, that the politicians of the United States see nothing wrong in the rule that to the victor belong the spoils of the enemy."

The retort was a response to an ongoing fight between Jackson and his long-time political adversary.

An earlier effort by Mr Trump to roll back birthright citizenship was rejected by the US ‌Supreme Court in June, prompting him to ⁠call upon Congress to act.

Eight years earlier, Jackson accused his great rival John Quincy Adams of stealing the election but, after winning a decisive victory four years later, continued Adams's strategy of rewarding loyalists with plum government positions, otherwise known as the "spoils system".

Trump has always believed in his status as victor. And he's never been shy in collecting the spoils.

His most recent filings, for 2025, indicate the US president pocketed more than $US2.2 billion ($3.11 billion) last year through ventures ostensibly run by his family.

He has put his name to everything from Bibles to mobile phones and plunged into the murky world of cryptocurrency with a personal meme coin and support for stable coins, even as he committed to deregulating the industry.

But his latest initiative has raised hackles even within his own party.

A fortnight ago, the US president's company, Trump Media and Technology Group, announced plans to sell early access to his social media posts for as much as $US100,000 a month.

Ever since he resumed office last year, Trump's erratic leadership and constant backflips — often telegraphed through his social media posts — have caused huge market swings that have delivered enormous profits to a lucky few.

Senator Lisa Murkowski has spoken out against President Donald Trump's plan to sell access to his social media posts. (AP: J Scott Applewhite)

Longtime Trump critic, Republican senator Lisa Murkowski, described the latest plan as "wild", arguing the presidency should not be used as a tool for accumulating personal wealth.

Another Republican critic, Senator Bill Cassidy, who was beaten in the primary by a Trump-backed candidate a few months ago, delivered an even harsher assessment.

U.S. Senator Bill Cassidy believes President Trump's plan to sell access to his social media is "wrong". (Reuters: Chip Somodevilla)

"I think that's wrong. It's a form of buying access," he said.

Susan Collins, a Republican senator from Maine, had a simple retort: "That does not sound appropriate."

Gianni Infantino is fighting for his future.

From basking in the afterglow of the World Cup just weeks ago, the FIFA boss is barely clinging to power after he stunned the football world with an audacious bid to privatise the tournament and other key events.

European football body UEFA threatens FIFA with legal action over Gianni Infantino's failed plan to sell a stake in future World Cup profits to private investors.

Adding to the insult, the investment firm on the other side of the deal was fronted by Joshua Kushner, the brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law.

While considered inappropriate, Infantino's frolics on the World Cup podium with the president, on the heels of his embarrassing "Peace Prize" presentation to Trump in the lead-up to the tournament, drew a largely muted response.

But this latest insult attracted an incendiary backlash.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino with U.S. President Donald Trump during the World Cup trophy presentation. (REUTERS/Dylan Martinez/File Photo) (Reuters: Dylan Martinez)

Angry football associations expressed outrage at the $US4.2 billion proposal, with the European federation threatening legal action and demanding Infantino and Kushner retain all documents relating to the proposal.

Even world leaders expressed their disapproval, including new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said he has "no confidence" in the FIFA boss.

Clearly, passions run higher in football than politics, because Infantino ended up junking the plan as questions mounted about his future in football’s top job. The outrage at Trump’s dealings has been far more muted.

While Trump is facing enormous challenges in the upcoming mid-term elections, they are mostly related to the Iran war and the rising cost of fuel in the US.

Complaints about his family's business dealings at home and abroad, on a scale never before seen, have gained little traction outside the political sphere.

So far, about half a dozen firms are believed to have signed up to the plan to receive early access to presidential decrees via Truth Social. But their identities have remained under wraps.

Trump Media and Technology Group spokespeople have dismissed claims of irregularity, arguing the information is public and that other social media operations offer similar services.

But there are differences. Subscribers to the new Trump service will receive access to messages a fraction of a second before the rest of the world.

That may sound inconsequential. But in a world of high-frequency trading run by computers working off algorithms and increasingly powered by artificial intelligence, every nanosecond counts.

While other social media platforms offer similar services, they are mostly for back-end data rather than news-breaking pronouncements from a sitting president who owns 41 per cent of the company releasing the information.

The US president has regularly stated he has no control over his private companies, including the media group that his son Don Junior controls via a trust.

Donald Trump Jr (left) controls the Trump Media and Technology Group via a trust. (Reuters: Brendan McDermid)

Few experts, however, are convinced the links are adequately severed.

"I'll be blunt," Gian Luca Clementi, an economics professor at NYU Stern School of Business, told Fortune magazine.

"This is insider trading by definition."

It took barely a minute to complete.

On Monday, March 23, at 6:49am New York time, a huge volume of oil futures contracts was pushed through the market.

By 6:50am, about $US580 million worth of contracts covering Brent crude, the global benchmark, and West Texas Intermediate changed hands, sending prices into free fall, dropping from just under $US100 a barrel to $US89.

The trading volume was around nine times the normal level with precise bets on the direction of both oil and equity markets.

Within minutes, Donald Trump announced, via Truth Social: "VERY GOOD AND PRODUCTIVE CONVERSATIONS" with Tehran over a "COMPLETE AND TOTAL RESOLUTION" to hostilities.

Hours later, as has since become routine, Tehran refuted the claims and oil prices began climbing, sparking calls for an investigation into the trading.

"This appears abnormal, for sure," XAnalysts chief oil analyst Mukesh Sahdev told the BBC.

"At that time, there were no indications that any serious talks had been taking place between the US and Iran.

"So, to place so much money on oil going down raises questions."

Five months later, and the identity of those behind the trading remains a mystery.

America's corporate regulator, the Securities and Exchange Commission, has refused to confirm whether it has an active investigation underway, and it appears it has been left to the Department of Justice and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

The lack of action has stunned Democrats.

Back in April, New York congressman Ritchie Torres wrote to the SEC chair, Paul Atkins, imploring him to launch an immediate investigation.

"This occurrence may constitute one of the largest instances of insider trading in history," Torres wrote.

"Whether or not that ultimately proves to be the case, the seriousness of the allegations demands immediate transparency."

Trading off presidential statements already has gone beyond traditional financial markets, shifting to areas that allow trades on almost anything.

Kalshi and Polymarket have gone from obscure start-ups to two of the world's biggest prediction markets where users bet on yes-or-no questions spanning politics, pop culture and war.

In recent years, the rise of prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi has been used to bet on political and financial outcomes, raising concerns about the ethics of online betting and whether inside information is helping profiteers cash in on war.

A recent study by Columbia Law School and the University of Haifa has examined the blockchain ledger in search of odd trading patterns and discovered transactions generating profits of about $US143 million.

"The idea that someone would trade on national security information or information about upcoming terrorist activity — people thought that's not even possible," Joshua Mitts, a law professor at Columbia and one of the co-authors, told Bloomberg.

"Today what we're seeing in these prediction markets is that actually it is quite possible."

In the past few days, Todd Blanche, the acting head of the US Department of Justice, finalised the incredible offer made to Donald Trump and members of his extended family last May on his tax position.

Under the arrangement, Trump cannot be audited or examined by the Internal Revenue Service for any year up until May this year.

Blanche, formerly the president's personal criminal defence lawyer, wound back some of the provisions in his earlier immunity offer, negotiated in exchange for Trump dropping his $US10 billion lawsuit against the IRS.

The acting head of the US Department of Justice, Todd Blanche, was formerly President Trump's personal lawyer. (Reuters: Ken Cedeno)

But with the substantive agreements remaining, the deal has far-reaching ramifications, given such immunity has never been applied to any president in history.

According to Liz Oyer, a former Department of Justice lawyer in charge of pardons and who was sacked earlier this year, the immunity deal is incredibly valuable to the president.

"Last year alone, Donald Trump made over $US2 billion," she told MS NOW (formerly MSNBC).

"There is nothing to make him pay his taxes on that money at this point."

Oyer estimates that the immunity agreement, in addition to letting him off the hook on any previous actions with the IRS, could excuse the president from paying hundreds of millions of dollars in tax on last year's earnings.

In the meantime, questions continue to be raised about the Trump family's business arrangements with the government.

The Washington Post this week published an expose on Department of Defence contracts awarded to companies in which Eric and Donald Trump Jr have an association.

These companies had seen government contracts and other funding arrangements grow to $US3.2 billion, a more-than-threefold increase since Trump's second term.

The Trump brothers claim their investments — many in new forms of warfare and weaponry — are a patriotic commitment to creating new American jobs and defeating China in the areas of drones and AI.

They have also stressed that they have never worked in government and are passive investors with no direct control over the companies.

But the president's personal and family business dealings stand in sharp contrast to those of his predecessors.

His most recent filings run to 927 pages and include 21,000 securities transactions and massive crypto ventures.

Joe Biden managed just 13 transactions in his entire four years in office.

The store was founded in 1924 and for many years was one of the town's only retail businesses. (Supplied: Robert Harders)

A general store that has operated in WA's South West for more than a century has hosted celebrations over the weekend to mark the end of an era.

The once sleepy town of Vasse is now home to several major retail outlets, which Vasse General Store owners say has had a huge impact on their small business.

The store has had just a handful of owners over the century, who each dedicated decades of their lives to the business.

After 102 years, the South West's historic Vasse General Store is closing its doors amid staunch retail competition in the growing residential area.

The century-old business has folded, with owners blaming the arrival of major supermarket, Coles and Vasse Farmers' Market, which is majority owned by Gina Rinehart's Hancock Prospecting.

The small business has suffered with big business capitalising on the town's booming population and road traffic generated by tourists travelling to popular locations throughout the region.

The store, originally founded by the McGuiness family in 1924 and located 232 kilometres south of Perth, has had just a handful of owners who each dedicated decades of their lives to taking very special care of the community keystone.

The Vasse General Store has operated for more than a century. (Supplied: Vasse General Store)

Gloria and Neil MacDonald took carriage of the store in 2000, working diligently to keep it afloat for 26 years, choosing to finally shut up shop and retire.

"I'll probably be a bit teary … but I know that I've done the best I can and it's been a great journey," Mrs MacDonald said.

On Saturday, the Vasse General Store hosted a closing celebration, commemorating 26 years of ownership by the MacDonalds and 102 years of operation. (Supplied: Vasse General Store)

The closure comes less than two years after nearby commercial developments were completed, landing Coles, McDonald's, Vasse Village and Shell on the small business's doorstep.

She said the recent explosion of major retailers just a few hundred metres away has impacted the business.

Gloria and Neil MacDonald are set to retire after the store closes later this week. (Supplied: Vasse General Store)

She said the store still had a lot to offer that major supermarkets could not compete with.

"We got homemade cooking and … [supermarkets] don't fill the gap of the homemade cake," she said.

For much of its life, the general store was one of a handful of businesses available to Vasse residents, acting as a fuel station, post office, shop and, most importantly, a place for community members to come together.

Mrs Macdonald said acting as a sounding board for customers has long been a part of her job description.

"Things might be rough in their world and they just need a shoulder to cry on and someone that's not going to be judgemental," she said.

Gloria MacDonald says her time at the store has been full of hard work and community connection. (Supplied: Vasse General Store)

Robert Harders sold the store to the MacDonalds in 2000, after running it with his wife Glenis for 17 years.

He said it was the people he connected with that stood out most when he reflected on his time at the store.

"It's the loyalty of the people that we dealt with,' Mr Harders said.

Robert Harders, with daughter Nerolee Warhurt, owned the Vasse General Store from 1983 to 2000. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Mr Harders bought the general store in 1983, relocating his family of five from Perth to the South West, where he still lives today.

He said the store looked very different when he first set foot inside 43 years ago.

"[It had an] old wooden floor and they had the doors that picture-swing inwards and the wind used to whistle through," he said.

"They never had any debit cards or credit cards, so we used to run an account system.

"We made all the concrete on that where the fuel bows are and it still hasn't got any cracks in it so we must have done a pretty good job."

The concrete installed by the Harders Family remains at the Vasse General Store site today more than 40 years later. (Supplied)

Mr Harders's youngest daughter, Neisha Feutrill, had fond memories of her mother, who has since died, playing practical jokes in the shop.

"There's memories of her putting some pretty risque centrefolds in the milk delivery man's books," she said.

"So when he got to the next store, he opened it up and yeah, she had a really wicked sense of humour."

The Vasse General Store in the 1980s under the ownership of Robert and Glenis Harders. (ABC South West: Georgia Loney)

The Dragons beat the Sharks 24-16 in a thrilling derby victory at Kogarah, as the Knights ended the Raiders season with a 30-24 victory in Canberra.

Trailing 26-24 in the final 10 minutes of the contest, the Raiders were awarded a penalty after Dane Gagai and Corey Horsburgh tangled at a play the ball.

Instead of having a kick at goal to level the scores though, Horsburgh slapped Gagai over the head, resulting in the penalty being overturned.

Ricky Stuart was livid, calling the incident "a f***ing brain explosion".

"We should have gone 26-all and there was a brain explosion," Stuart said.

"It was a f***ing brain explosion, and we lost the opportunity."

Look away, Raiders fans. 🤬

Ricky Stuart wasn't mincing his words, labelling a "f***ing brain explosion" and a "s*** decision" as costing his side a win and a chance of playing finals. 😬

Blog: https://t.co/CqwRVT5q5J
Listen: https://t.co/VP2GGbfO5M#NRL #NRLRaidersKnights pic.twitter.com/q5WRLVURT8

Stuart was under no illusions that his forward was in the wrong, either.

"Of course it was [a sin bin]," he said.

"There was one last week. Everyone knows that, you're not allowed to do that. It's in the rules. It's been in the rules for the last many, many years."

The Raiders fans may have felt hard done by after Gagai was not sin binned earlier in the half following a tip tackle on Horsburgh, for which he was only placed on report by referee Ashley Klein.

In the late match, St George Illawarra dealt Cronulla Sutherland's top-two finals hopes a hammer blow with a spirited 24-16 victory.

The Dragons and Sharks engaged in a brutal first half. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings)

Recording only their third win of the season and just their second derby success in their last 13 against the Sharks, the Dragons are still in the hunt to avoid the wooden spoon.

Addin Fonua-Blake could face a spell on the sidelines for the Sharks, after being sin binned and placed on report for nasty shoulder charge on Dragons forward Hamish Stewart.

Jesse Ramien left the field with a suspected pectoral injury and Ronaldo Mulitalo also played out the second half under an injury cloud on a bad afternoon for the premiership aspirants.

Meanwhile, Storm halfback Cameron Munster was given a one-match ban for dangerous contact against Sea Eagles forward Taniela Paseka, only to have that overturned a couple of hours later.

Munster was charged after making contact with the side of the knee of the Sea Eagles prop as the third man into a tackle during the first half of the game, which the Storm came from behind to win.

The NRL judiciary later amended the charges after a medical report from Manly showed Paseka's injury was not as severe as it was initially thought.

Instead of a week off, Munster can now accept a $750 fine for a grade one dangerous contact charge.
