https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/w.title: Australia's 999th Wallaby on his injury-riddled road to Test debut
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 3:16am

Isaac Henry made his Wallabies debut against Japan. (Getty Images: Kenta Harada)

Isaac Henry made his rugby union Test debut for the Wallabies on Saturday against Japan.

Henry became the 999th player for the Wallabies, and came after years of injuries.

The centre played 10 minutes in Australia's 35-32 victory in Osaka.

Isaac Henry will run the prospect of fresh ink past his wife but is otherwise assured he can make a permanent Wallabies mark after a hard-earned debut in Osaka.

Named on the bench, the Queensland Reds centre was made to wait more than 70 minutes before being thrust into the action and then defending furiously in a 35-32 Saturday night defeat of Japan.

The 27-year-old became Wallaby number 999 in the process, the honour coming despite Henry enduring four major surgeries in as many years.

New Wallabies coach Les Kiss says his side will need to learn how to control their ambitions after Australia hangs on to win a frantic Test match against Japan in the Osaka heat.

"It's a great number, might have to talk to my wife about getting it tattooed," said Henry, who has his surname inked on his forearm.

A broken foot, hamstring tear and two separate knee ligament and tendon ruptures have been his biggest setbacks.

Incredibly, his six games for the Reds this season are more than he has managed in any campaign since his 2021 Super Rugby debut.

"It's been a journey … and there was a brief period where I was like 'maybe I won't get on, maybe next week'," he said of his nervous sideline wait.

Henry's patella tendon rupture in 2024 was a gruesome injury that left him sucking on the green whistle as he left the ground.

"I said [to myself], 'Right, I'm going to be back better than I was before'," he said of that setback.

"It's nice to be here … you look back at those days and think 'how good'.

"Deep down I'm stubborn; I wasn't going to quit, I wanted it too much, ever since I was a kid. And I set my mind to it."

Henry can kick off the tee and out of the hand and boasts a strong carry, good hands and a sharp football brain, according to coach Les Kiss.

Hunter Paisami impressed at No.12, while outside centre Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii set up one try but didn't have the impact he threatened to.

The debutant is confident he can thrive if given more opportunities in Townsville's Japan rematch on Saturday.

"There were points along the way that I didn't think I'd get it done, but now I've got a taste and I'm hungry for it," Henry said.

"I loved it and now I've sort of experienced that I just want more. Loved the next level, loved testing myself."

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 3:04am

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 9:56am

St Kilda has lost Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera to a hamstring injury just minutes into a must-win clash against Carlton at Docklands.

Earlier on Sunday, a debatable fourth-quarter goal from Bailey Humphrey upheld by the ARC proved to be the difference as Gold Coast claimed a 11.13 (79) to 11.11 (77) win over the GWS Giants in Canberra.

In Perth, Nick Daicos recorded 39 disposals as Collingwood locked up a top-10 spot with a 17.15 (117) to 15.8 (98) win against West Coast.

Meanwhile Carlton recorded a 9.12 (66) to 6.4 (40) win over St Kilda in the AFLW season-opener at Docklands Stadium as Abbie McKay recorded a game-high 32 disposals.

Follow all the action in our live blog.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 2:56am

Choose what information you see below by using filters

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 11:36am

Blues fans are going home very happy tonight.

And this is a team that could cause a lot of damage from the lower part of the ladder in the finals.

Josh Fraser might just be a coaching genius.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 11:27am

It takes 24 seconds after Sam Walsh bursts out of the middle and sends the pill forward, with it eventually landing in Brodie Kemp's hands in the forward pocket.

Kemp sees Mitch McGovern free in the goalsquare and handballs to him, and McGovern thumps it through from the line.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 11:19am

It's a game high 35-point lead and the broadcasters don't want you to stop watching by saying it, but there's no way back for St Kilda here.

Two down on the bench with Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera and Mason Wood both done for the night, and their forward line just isn't functioning for anyone over 190cm, with Jack Higgins and Liam Ryan looking like their only avenues to goal.

For Carlton, Francis Evans has played the game of his life across half-forward, dominating around 60-70m mark as the final kick before the shot at goal. I'm not sure I've ever seen Evans play a better game.

George Hewett (22) and Adam Cerra (21) are the leading disposal winners for the Blues while it's Bradley Hill (25) leading the field for St Kilda.

This will make it 10 wins from 12 games for the Blues under Josh Fraser, and I'm going to dare to say it - they win this and the top 10 is locked in. I can't see any other team sneaking in after the Giants dropped their game to the Suns today.

Please feel free to send your complaints to Chris De Silva if I'm wrong.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 11:14am

It's great forward pressure again from the Blues, and Jack Silvagni is done for throwing it. The Carlton fans love it!

Brodie Kemp has the free, he goes the snap, and he drills it.

It's a game-high 34-point lead.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 11:12am

Both teams are missing gettable ones here.

Meanwhile Francis Evans is having probably the best quarter in his journeyman career, he has been exceptional across half forward.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 11:02am

It's Frankie Evans who's doing the work across half forward again, taking a strong mark from an Adam Cerra bullet before turning quickly and finding Harry McKay on the lead.

McKay's kick is a beauty and never looks in doubt.

Danger zone for St Kilda now, they need an answer.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:59am

It's a big shove in the back from Marc Pittonet, and the ruckman plays dumb claiming the mark.

But that's as clear as day that it's a free kick, and Rowan Marshall kicks the set shot.

Boy did they need that.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:57am

That hurts the Saints badly! They've had all the play but on the one attacking entry the Blues have, they find Harry McKay deep in the forward pocket.

It's an impossible angle for the drop punt ... but somehow McKay finds the smallest slither of daylight and works the Sherrin through it! What a kick!

Blues back out by 28 points.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:54am

Two set shots already and a missed snap for the Saints to start the second half.

Blues yet to make it over the halfway mark.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:45am

Hello Kyle, I just realised you have stepped in for Chris - did he pull a hammy? Regardless, I would like to request a boost for the Saints in the 2nd half please....

Good to see you Mike, and yes, De Silva has been subbed out.

He's as healthy as ever but those pesky workplace rules mean I have to let him go home at some point.

Otherwise I'd have him going through the night live blogging baseball or something if I could.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:43am

I mentioned earlier I wasn't sure why Mason Wood was going down to the rooms.

It's now be confirmed he has a calf injury, and his night is done as well.

Awful news for the Saints.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:30am

A big goal from Max Hall just seconds before the siren and there's life in the Saints yet!

But that quarter was all about Carlton as their field kicking and pressure was just that little bit better than the Saints, taking their opportunities when they came.

George Hewett continues to lead the field with 20 touches and has looked dangerous when he's got them, while Adam Cerra (16 disposals) worked his way into the game across halfback.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:29am

Talor Byrne unloads a long kick which looks to be a shot at goal, but it sails wide.

Somehow Will Hayward keeps it in with a stretching mark on the boundary line!

He quickly takes the snap and converts!

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:24am

Spectacular pressure from Francis Evans who lays the tackle on the Saints defender, and wins a very delayed free kick for holding the ball.

Sam Walsh didn't have time to react to the whistle, so throws the ball on the boot and luckily it floats through!

Big break now for the Blues.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:22am

A beautiful set shot from the former Swan, the Sherrin doesn't move off the line.

That hurts the Saints. They had several opportunities to score the six minutes before that but butchered it so much that they'll be raffling a meat tray after the game.

Blues have the 20 point gap.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:19am

Maybe they all want a turn?

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:18am

He's doing sideline runs and it looks like good news for the Saints. Hill appears to be good to return.

A sigh of relief for Saints fans.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:14am

Oh this is awful for the Saints.

Bradley Hill is on the turf and pointing at his knee.

On replay, it's a non-contact injury. He's jumped high for the mark, landed a little awkwardly, and gone straight down.

He limps off the field and he's down into the rooms.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:12am

Talor Byrne kicks an absolute burner into the F50 and finds Ben Ainsworth for an uncontested mark.

He decides to go for the snap from quite a long way out, but flushes it. Great choice in the end.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/o.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Crime Prevention

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 2:57am

The Alfred Hospital in Melbourne would be among the seven hospitals to take part in the PSO trial. (Supplied: Alfred Health)

The Liberal-National Coalition has pledged to put 70 Protective Services Officers (PSOs) across seven major Victorian hospitals.

The pilot program will run for two years.

The Victorian government has criticised the plan, and says it is focused on investing in healthcare workers.

Victorians are due to head to the polls on Saturday, November 28.

Victoria's opposition has pledged to deploy dozens of armed law enforcement officers in major hospitals around the state in a bid to curb violent incidents if it wins government later this year.

The Liberal-National Coalition plan, announced ahead of the November election, would see 70 Protective Services Officers (PSOs) work across seven hospitals as part of a two-year pilot.

The role of the armed officers working in shifts across 24 hours would be to provide additional security presence, respond to serious incidents, assist with the guarding of prisoners and escort hospital staff to their vehicles.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said the trial would help those in power understand "how we can best protect our hospitals".

"PSOs will provide that security presence, working alongside existing security, integrating with them, and providing a visible deterrence around these hospitals to ensure that patients feel safe and clinicians feel safe," she said.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson announced the policy outside the Alfred Hospital. (ABC News)

She said it was not a "radical" idea.

"PSOs are on our train stations. They work on government buildings. These people are trained, they know how to de-escalate, they know how to work in an operational sense.

"Every single day in Victorian hospitals, Victoria Police are in our ED (emergency department)," she said.

"They are responding to incidents.

"This frees up our police force to ensure that our PSOs are there, they can respond quickly ... to provide that sense of security to our clinicians and our patients."

According to reports tabled in the Victorian parliament at the end of 2025, in the 2024-2025 financial year there were close to 24,000 violent incidents recorded across dozens of public health services.

PSOs were introduced in 2011 under the Liberal-National government led by Ted Bailleu, with the armed officers' roles centred on bolstering safety at railway stations.

The armed, uniformed officers have the power to apprehend, arrest, search and fine people, but only in designated areas related to public transport.

In April, the opposition also vowed to recruit 200 additional PSOs to patrol train stations across the city if elected.

That proposal, which had the support of the Police Association Victoria, was announced a month after Mernda man Aidan Becker was fatally stabbed at the railway station while trying to protect a 14-year-old boy from an alleged group robbery.

On Sunday, Minister for Medical Research Anthony Carbines announced $2 million for mRNA research under the mRNA Pipeline Victoria grant program.

On the opposition's PSO proposal, Mr Carbines accused the opposition of being "sort of obsessed" with law and order in healthcare.

"It's fascinating that the opposition are more focused about law and order in our health services than investment in nurses, investment in health workers, investment in health practitioners," he said

"That's the sort of conversation I want to have about how we invest in the people that make change in our health services that save lives, that change lives."

"That's where the investment has to go."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Ashleigh Barraclough

Topic:
Mining and Metals Industry

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 2:43am

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 5:21am

The union representing workers says the consortium's interest was conditional on the Tasmanian government waiving the pre-existing environmental liabilities at the site. (Supplied)

The union representing workers at Australia's last manganese smelter in Bell Bay, Tasmania, says there are parties interested in taking over the site.

On Monday, creditors voted to liquidate Liberty Bell Bay, leaving about 200 workers without a job after more than a year of uncertainty.

The union representing workers says the latest interest is conditional on the Tasmanian government waiving the pre-existing environmental liabilities at the site and the continuation of the existing power deal.

The union representing workers at Australia's last manganese smelter says there are parties interested in taking over the site.

Creditors on Monday voted to liquidate Liberty Bell Bay, leaving about 200 workers without a job.

Manganese is a critical component to make steel, meaning Australia no longer has sovereign steelmaking capability.

The Australian Workers' Union (AWU) said a consortium involving White Oak and OM Holdings was conditionally interested in buying the site and eventually restarting the smelter.

"The consortium has been involved in a range of discussions with private investors and they believe that they have enough private investors to recapitalise the plant," assistant branch secretary Robert Flanagan said.

Workers at the Liberty Bell Bay smelter have faced a long period of uncertainty about their futures. (ABC News)

Liberty Bell Bay stopped operations in May last year, originally citing ore supply challenges and global market volatility.

The company's owner, GFG Alliance, has been accused of moving about $200 million out of Liberty Bell Bay via inter-company loans.

Liquidator EY Parthenon believes Liberty Bell Bay was trading while insolvent for more than a year, including when the Tasmanian government granted the company a $20 million loan.

Of that, $14.5 million was used to purchase ore — which the government has since repossessed due to the failure of the company to resume operations.

The union said the consortium had established a new company to bid to take over the site.

Two of the parties involved in a previous bid are said to be involved in the latest proposal. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Corporate records show a company called TEMCO Bell Bay was registered in late June.

White Oak is listed as a shareholder, and the company director is White Oak's Kenneth Pereira.

Before the manganese smelter was bought by GFG Alliance, it was known as the Tasmanian Electro Metallurgical Company (TEMCO).

The ABC understands the consortium is not the only party interested in the site, and liquidator EY Parthenon would need to consider any proposals.

Mr Flanagan said he understood the consortium's interest was conditional on the state government waiving the pre-existing environmental liabilities at the site.

"So, the new owner would work and be responsible for any environmental impact that they have going forward, but the pre-existing environmental liabilities would not be their responsibility," he said.

On top of that, Mr Flanagan said the consortium wanted the existing power deal between Hydro Tasmania and Liberty Bell Bay transferred to them.

"So they would pay the power prices which were contracted by Liberty Bell Bay," he said.

Robert Flanagan described the proposal, from his union's perspective, as "a real phoenix opportunity". (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Resources Minister Felix Ellis said the government would have a conversation with any parties interested in the site.

He did not indicate if the government would accept the consortium's requests, but said any deal had to be in the interests of Tasmanian taxpayers.

"The government has received indication from White Oak that it is considering putting forward a proposal to EY," he said.

"We welcome [the AWU] supporting the 10-year power agreement, which was offered to White Oak as part of the administration process."

A consortium involving Adroit Capital, White Oak and OM Holdings had previously been interested in purchasing the site, until Adroit Capital pulled out of the process in June.

OM Holdings is a manganese ore and ferroalloy company operating in Australia, Malaysia, Singapore and China.

White Oak is a United States-based investment advisor and private credit firm.

Mr Flanagan said OM Holdings was interested in purchasing the ore from the Tasmanian government.

Deputy Labor leader Janie Finlay said the best outcome for workers and the Tasmanian economy would be a restart of the smelter.

"If there is an opportunity to recapitalise that site and get it back up and running again to protect those major industrials in Tasmania and to support those jobs, this government should be doing everything possible to make that happen," she said.

Janie Finlay called on the Rockliff state government to do everything in its power to see the manganese smelter restarted. (ABC News: Emily JB Smith)

Mr Flanagan said many of the smelter's workers, who are now out of a job, would like to remain in the area.

"We believe that a lot of the workers would return if that was available to them," he said.

EY Parthenon and White Oak have been approached for comment.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/c.title: Inside this street food market are signs of a crashing currency
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/c.author: Tim Swanston
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 2:40am

The plunging Indonesian rupiah is raising alarm among consumers and the government. (Reuters: Willy Kurniawan, File photo)

Indonesia's currency has fallen to historic lows against the US dollar, causing damage "in most of the economy", analysts say.

Some street food sellers have raised their prices to cover rising production costs, while others say they're seeing less foot traffic in the markets.

An economist says government policies are contributing to the decline but the government says it is "ensuring that inflation remains within a controlled range".

Over the past six months, the world has been glued to charts, gripped by the high price of oil.

But in Indonesia, there's another chart that's been causing fear and anxiety.

Indonesia's currency, the rupiah, has fallen to historic lows against the US dollar.

From September 2024, it went from about 15,000 rupiah per $US1, passing a psychological threshold of 17,000 rupiah in April this year.

It worsened through June to more than 18,000, and has stubbornly remained around that low ever since.

The rate is worse than it was during the 1998 Asian financial crisis, which sparked such severe unrest and protests that it led to the downfall of Indonesia's former authoritarian president Suharto.

And despite the war in the Middle East causing pain across Asia, some Indonesian economists say it is mostly domestic factors that have made the rupiah one of the worst-performing currencies in the region.

"The damage in most of the economy is quite severe," economist Dipo Satria Ramli said.

"Everyone is quite affected."

Street food sellers have had to raise their prices to deal with rising production costs. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

The nation's central bank, Bank Indonesia, has issued four rate rises in quick succession to try and wrangle the slide in the rupiah.

But further fears have been raised after the sudden resignation of the bank's governor, well before the end of his second term.

While the government scrambles to stabilise the currency, the crisis is inflicting a serious toll on Indonesians.

The drop in currency has been acutely felt by the nation's Tempeh makers.

Tempeh is an iconic Indonesian food made from soybeans, which are mostly imported from the United States.

It is a major source of affordable protein, but the declining rupiah has been pushing up the price of soybeans.

Ahmad Saikhu says the poor currency could lead to wide unemployment. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

Ahmad Saikhu, a long-time tempeh maker and secretary-general of a 4,000-strong producers association, said he and the members were in "total disarray".

"If this keeps going on, our family finances will become total chaos," he said.

"The government isn't really managing to control these prices, leaving grassroots producers at the bottom with their livelihoods in total disarray."

Tempeh, usually made with imported US soybeans, is becoming more expensive to produce. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

Ahmad said he and other producers have had to cut down the size of their packages, because they cannot increase the prices they sell at.

"We have to survive so we can continue supplying the protein needs of low-income people," he said.

At a street food market in Central Jakarta, the increasing cost of imports has been squeezing already low-income sellers.

Chilies, broths, and sambal, a type of spicy sauce, are commonly packaged in plastic for customers here.

But the cost of naphtha, a key petrochemical used to make plastics, has soared because supplies have been choked off with the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

The sinking currency has acted as a double-whammy, further causing the price of plastic products to surge.

"The main increase is definitely plastic," Andri, a satay seller, told the ABC.

"It's well over 50 per cent higher."

Andri has been seeing fewer customers in the markets recently. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

Andri has also noticed the market getting quieter, driven by less demand and tighter economic conditions.

"This current situation is getting pretty concerning … every one of us is taking home less money, and as for customers, there are fewer of them coming by," he said.

Another seller in the market, Syamsul, has had to raise prices at his noodle cart.

"Every day more and more goods are going up in price, while everyone's spending less," he said.

"The impact on me is pretty substantial … what choice do you have? Sometimes you just have to look for loans here and there."

Syamsul says customers have been spending less, putting a strain on vendors. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

Tens of millions of Indonesians are taking out online loans, known locally as pinjol, to help cover basic costs.

The growth in potentially risky pinjol loans has been rapid, with the amount of money borrowed growing by 25 per cent from the middle of 2025 to the middle of this year.

According to the government's financial services regulator, more than $8 trillion has been borrowed in these types of loans by tens of millions of Indonesians, mostly people aged under 35.

Economist Dipo Satria Ramli estimated "50 to 60 per cent" of the decline in the rupiah was because of domestic factors and not because of shocks from the war in the Middle East.

He said three issues were contributing to the decline: "unpredictable policies", concern over transparency and accountability, and fiscal policy.

"[Inflation] is across all different goods," Dipo said.

"At a consumer's perspective, it's eating up purchasing power."

The government says it's working to try and contain the currency drop. (Reuters: Ajeng Dinar Ulfiana)

Most people in Indonesia work in what's known as the "informal sector", which covers unregulated work, such as markets and manual labour, and typically pays low wages.

But Dipo said workers in the "formal sector", which includes corporations and government, were feeling the pain too.

In a statement, Indonesia's Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa said: "The depreciation of the rupiah is considered to be driven more by market sentiment than by changes in national economic fundamentals.

"The government, together with relevant authorities, continues to maintain financial system stability through coordination within the Financial System Stability Committee (KSSK).

"The government is ensuring that inflation remains within a controlled range."

The pain has not been localised to just the currency, with Indonesia's stock market losing almost 30 per cent this year.

The Jakarta Composite Index ranks as one of the worst-performing major equity markets in the world.

Major index provider MSCI has flagged it could downgrade Indonesia's equity market status, saying it was concerned about transparency.

Earlier this year, ratings agencies Moody's and Fitch lowered Indonesia's credit rating to negative.

Fitch Ratings said this was because of an "increasing policy uncertainty and erosion of Indonesia's policy mix consistency and credibility amid growing centralisation of policymaking authority".

On Wednesday, Indonesia's economic growth slowed to 5.3 per cent, down from 5.6 per cent earlier in the year, although it outperformed earlier predictions.

And even though the currency rate is worse than during the 1998 crisis, economists say that institutions are stronger now and the decline in the rupiah has been much more gradual this time around, allaying fears of economic-related unrest.

Across Indonesia, people are appealing for greater support.

"That's all we can do … we don't have any other way to voice our struggle.

"We're appealing to the president and the government to resolve this issue."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/b.title: Wildfire forces more than 20,000 people evacuate homes in western Canada
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 2:35am

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police direct people away from the Bald Range wildfire in Penticton. (Reuters: Paige Taylor White)

Thousands of people have been forced to flee their homes in western Canada as a fast-moving wildfire doubles in size.

British Columbia has declared a state of emergency.

The fires in Canada follow a persistent and severe heatwave across western Europe with more scorching temperatures forecast this week.

Thousands of people in western Canada have been ordered to flee a fast-moving wildfire that nearly doubled in size overnight.

A state of emergency was declared in British Columbia (BC) on Saturday, local time, after the Bald Range wildfire was burning out of control and grew rapidly to about 9,510 hectares.

Stefan Rahmstorf was holidaying in southern France when he came face to face with the climate future he has tried to fight.

Evacuation orders were in place for Summerland, Peachland and other districts west of Okanagan Lake in the province's southern interior.

The region produces most of BC's wine and is Canada's second-largest wine-producing area.

Premier David Eby told a news conference on Saturday that one fire official had likened the fire to "a bomb going off".

"He described flames on 100-foot tree, flames going 200 feet above that, and the fire creating its own weather system, which creates lightning, which then feeds on itself," Mr Eby said.

"Homes have been lost, and properties have been destroyed. Some people became trapped as conditions changed very quickly, and needed to be rescued," the premier said, adding it remained a very dynamic and threatening situation.

Summerland has a population of about 12,000 people, according to the 2021 census, and Peachland is home to about 6,500 residents.

The fire painted the skies with orange hues. (Reuters: Paige Taylor White)

A state of emergency grants the provincial government immediate access to special powers including travel restrictions and supply protections to prevent price gouging, and specific tools to coordinate rescue work.

Officials said the Bald Range wildfire triggered the largest evacuation event so far this summer and more than 20,000 people across BC have been forced to evacuate their homes.

"A lot of farms have been affected. We don't know how many structures have been lost. They're still busy fighting the fire," Summerland Mayor Doug Holmes said in a phone interview from Penticton.

"We have to brace ourselves for the worst."

Many residents left overnight, driving south to Penticton or north to Kelowna before highways began to close.

Trees burn in the Bald Range wildfire on Friday. (Reuters: BC Wildfire Service/handout)

Terry Fries of Summerland was watching a football game on Friday night when a neighbour advised him to get a bag ready as the fire grew.

"At the time, it was still farther back, and you could see it behind the hills," he said.

When BC authorities issued the evacuation order around midnight, he and his family drove about 45 kilometres north to the city of Kelowna.

By Saturday afternoon, ashes began to settle on cars and houses in nearby areas as the fire painted the skies with orange hues.

Europe's second-longest river is carrying less water than it has in decades, revealing shipwrecks and shutting down nuclear reactors.

Several Canadian provinces, including Ontario and Quebec, have battled blazes this year as hot, dry weather fuelled wildfires in dense forest areas. Firefighters from Mexico, Australia, France and New Zealand have helped combat the fires.

In BC, where hot and dry conditions have increased the risk of more fires spreading, about 1,500 firefighting personnel were battling more than 100 fires.

Fires have burned through 9.9 million acres in Canada this year, according to the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre.

The fires in Canada follow what has also been a record-breaking summer so far across western Europe, with scorching temperatures and destructive wildfires.

France and Spain have been particularly hard hit in recent weeks.

A wildfire in Niebla, Huelva, Spain, burning on August 8. (Reuters: Mikel Konate)

The extreme weather across Europe has pushed temperatures above 40 degrees Celsius in many countries, prompting health warnings for millions of people. Scientists and officials warn that such events are becoming more frequent and intense as the climate warms.

In Central Europe, Slovakia and Austria both recorded all-time high temperatures this week, at 42.2C and 41.2C.

In Italy, officials placed all its major cities under the highest heat alert on Thursday, signalling a health risk for the entire population, not only vulnerable groups.

The UK government has declared half of England, and all of Wales, as officially being in drought.

England saw its warmest June on record and the UK its second warmest, while England and Wales experienced their driest July on record, according to Met Office data.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/l.title: Love story: The grief and relief that comes with the death of your 'big love'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 2:00am

Hilda Quiroga says the death of her partner Steve Mayer was "peaceful". (Supplied: Hilda Quiroga)

Hilda Quiroga says she was "struck" by Steve Mayer from the moment they first met in Naarm/Melbourne in 2007. Hilda, who works in social services, and Steve, a barista and musician, went on to have an 18-year partnership and travel the world together, until his death at 53 through voluntary assisted dying (VAD).

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

The funny thing is I met him at a gym.

I hate gyms. He hated gyms with a passion.

But, he was the barista at a cafe in the gym and I was there signing up a client.

I noticed how kind and respectful he was towards her.

I knew nothing about him. He could have been married or gay for all I knew. But, I emailed my friend and said to him, "I have just met a man that is going to change my life."

Not long after I was off overseas by myself, but I took him with me in my mind. I wanted to tell him that day, "We're going to be travelling together mate, so get ready, get your passport ready."

We got together in February 2008 and three months later we moved in.

I was in my 30s. He was in his 30s. There's no point in wasting time.

I had been married before, but it was short. Steve just made me feel like he saw me.

I was 100 per cent sure that I'd met my soulmate. I cringe at that word, but I just knew, and we were together, inseparable from that day to the very last.

He knew all about the places that I'd been to and all the places that I wanted to go — like all the Inca ruins — because he was so well read.

He'd never had the opportunity to travel, but then when we got together, we were like this unstoppable force.

He got his passport and found his travelling legs and because we had no children, we were free to just travel, work, travel. That was us.

He wanted to go to see Machu Picchu and the Amazon and take ayahuasca and we did.

Hilda Quiroga says the couple had "incredible adventures", which included travelling to Samoa, Guatemala and Peru. (Supplied: Hilda Quiroga)

Everything changed in June 2023.

He had the results of a CT scan come back and they found a mass in his lung.

His only symptoms were that he was fatigued — which was not like Steve, who normally had the energy of a kid — and he was also sweating a lot.

A couple of days later tumours were found in his brain and elsewhere. It had already metastasised.

In September I quit my job. I had taken time off in those first months but was going to back work a little bit and it didn't feel right.

This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

I successfully applied for carer's allowance and disability support.

It was tricky, but I'm good at paperwork.

In our relationship, Steve usually took care of cooking and cleaning (mostly because I'm not great), and I took care of social engagements, finances, and personal administration.

He taught me a lot about myself, and I didn't think I could do the things that I did when he got sick.

You're a partner, but you also become a "carer".

I've never been comfortable with that word because I'm his partner, of course I'm going to do this.

But everything changes, like intimacy.

We were still very close and intimate, but that was a big deal for him because we'd always had a lovely sex life.

We still had our lovely little rituals in the morning — even at [the hospital], I'd get him the coffee, I'd get him the papers, he could do the sudoku. He would do the "diabolical" sudoku without even using a pencil.

And while he was in the worst possible place, he was still trying to look after me too.

When he vomited at home, he'd never let me clean it up. I would be dry-reaching because that's the one bodily fluid I can't handle.

Friends who would come and see him told me afterwards, that he would whisper, "take care of her."

Their last trip to Wye River, on Victoria's Great Ocean Road, in November 2024. (Supplied: Hilda Quiroga)

Steve mentioned voluntary assisted dying to his specialist about four months after being diagnosed.

It's a very legal process and then a pharmacist comes to your house with the medication.

That box of medication was here in the apartment for months.

Steve was then moved into palliative care and two weeks later during a terrible night, he said to me, "I think we're at the pointy end."

The next morning when the doctors were doing their rounds, he looked at me, I looked at him and he said to the doctor, "I've decided I want to use voluntary assisted dying today."

Right at the end it was just me, Steve's nephew, his partner and the VAD nurse.

He took his medication, swallowed it all in one go, and then had a bit of Coke because it's so vile.

Within about 20 minutes, he started to fall into unconsciousness.

I didn't cry. I just held Steve in my arms and just whispered in his ears as he passed away, because I thought he doesn't need to hear me sobbing, not now.

All I wanted him to hear was my voice saying, "It's all right, love. It's time. You're tired. It's time to rest."

He took his last breath. I listened to his heart. I loved falling asleep on his chest to hear that beautiful steady beat and it was gone.

Hilda Quiroga says Steve Mayer was a completely selfless, glorious and funny human. (Supplied: Hilda Quiroga)

I'm 18 months down the track and I still cry every day. I shed tears all over Melbourne.

[But] there's comfort in knowing he decided when he had had enough. Our apartment is just full of him. He's everywhere.

I've still got like his death T-shirt and I sleep with it every night and I haven't washed it. It's probably very unhygienic. My friend also nicked the pillow he died on and I sleep with that too.

We would hold hands when we fell asleep every night. He would tell me that he loved me every night and not just, "Love you, babe." He would turn around, face me and look me intently in the eyes and tell me how much he loved me.

Even though I've lost him and he's gone, I still feel obviously blessed and fortunate that I had that big love.

I think we all want that love and I'm a better person for meeting him. So, where there's grief, there's love.

Do you or does someone you know have a surprising or unique love story? We'd love to hear about it.

Perspective by Amy Sheehan

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/g.title: Infantino denies 'defamatory' affair claims made in British newspaper
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/g.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 1:29am

Gianni Infantino has strongly denied reports in a British newspaper that he was involved in an affair while working at UEFA. (Getty Images: Leonardo Fernández)

British newspaper The Daily Telegraph published allegations that Gianni Infantino was involved in an affair while at UEFA.

FIFA and Infantino have denied the allegations, describing them as 'categorically untrue' and 'defamatory'.

Infantino is up for re-election in March and maintains support in Africa and South America.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino, who has endured a week of scathing criticism revolving around the now shelved private investment plan for the World Cup, has been accused by a British newspaper of paying off an alleged lover while at UEFA.

According to The Daily Telegraph, the Italian-Swiss lawyer, who served as secretary general of European football's governing body from 2009 to 2016, also previously used his influence to secure a promotion for the same UEFA employee with whom he was in an intimate relationship.

Infantino has categorically denied the allegations, according to the article which was published late on Friday.

When contacted by AFP on Saturday, a FIFA spokesperson had not responded.

According to The Telegraph, which did not cite its sources, this employee received a "a six-figure sum" upon her departure – at an unspecified time – in addition to the payment of tuition fees for a business school amounting to around 45,000 British pounds ($85,900).

Gianni Infantino (right) in 2007 when he was UEFA's deputy general secretary. (Getty Images: Etsuo Hara)

When contacted by AFP, UEFA acknowledged that "a departure payment was made to the individual in question" at that time, "coupled with the payment of fees for an MBA course at a local business school".

However, it insisted "the payment was in line with the regulations that existed for departing staff at the time", before adding that "such regulations have been tightened since 2016".

Quoted by The Telegraph, a FIFA spokesperson stated that Infantino, who has been married since 2001, "strongly denies these allegations", which were "categorically untrue".

"Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory," FIFA added.

"No employee at UEFA and FIFA has ever raised a complaint regarding Infantino's behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved."

Infantino, who is standing for re-election next March, has been embroiled in a crisis since the announcement late last month of his controversial — and ultimately abandoned — plan to open up the World Cup to private investors.

He faces opposition in particular from UEFA, which on Thursday stood by its threat to boycott the World Cups, deeming the mere withdrawal of the controversial plan to be insufficient.

Following a crisis meeting in Morocco on Wednesday, FIFA apologised to its 211 member associations for mistakes in the handling of the proposal and said its leadership had reaffirmed its full support for Infantino.

The fallout has cast a shadow over Infantino's bid for a fourth term at the FIFA Congress in Morocco next year. No clear candidate to challenge him has yet emerged.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino (left) has faced criticism from President of the Football Association of Norway Lise Klaveness (right). (Getty Images: Jean Catuffe)

UEFA has said it no longer has confidence in Infantino, while Norwegian Football Federation President Lise Klaveness called for him to resign on Friday, saying he no longer had the institutional trust required to govern FIFA.

But Infantino continues to enjoy substantial support among FIFA's 211 members. The Confederation of African Football (CAF) unanimously backed his leadership on Thursday, while South America's CONMEBOL rejected any attempt to oust him that did not involve a vote of all FIFA members.

Mexico's football federation (FMF) also backed Infantino, despite its regional confederation CONCACAF having called for a "comprehensive reckoning" with his presidency.

"The FMF will neither recognise nor approve any process convened outside of that institutional framework," the Mexican federation said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/k.title: Fight continues for memorial to victims of one of WA's worst paedophiles
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/k.author: Will Corbett and Mark Bennett
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/k.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 1:04am

Maggie Dawkins detailed her experience with McKenna in her tell-all account.  (ABC Great Southern: Will Corbett)

Child sexual abuse victims are still fighting for recognition as one of Western Australia's most prolific serial paedophiles prepares to walk free after more than a decade behind bars.

Advocates say the Katanning shire's long-time inaction is "disgusting", and a formal apology needs to be issued.

Advocates are calling for other victims to come forward before Dennis John McKenna is released in November.

It has been more than a decade since serial paedophile Dennis John McKenna was convicted of some of the most horrific crimes in WA's history.

But victim-survivors and advocates say they are still waiting for proper recognition of their suffering.

McKenna abused dozens of boys in the 1970s and 80s while in charge of St Andrew's Hostel, a student boarding facility in Katanning, about 290 kilometres south-east of Perth.

Dozens of boys were sexually abused at St Andrews Hostel in Katanning.  (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

In August 2024, the education department agreed to demolish the former hostel site and fund $750,000 towards a memorial in Katanning.

A working group for the memorial wanted it placed in the town's all-ages playground, but the local shire blocked their request.

"We want that awareness of child sexual abuse out there to prevent it ever happening again," advocate Kaye Anderson said.

Three of Kaye Anderson's sons attended the hostel in the mid-80s, with the eldest two reporting acts of sexual violence against them. Neither are still alive. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer )

Ms Anderson said the working group was now considering placing the memorial outside Katanning, to avoid interaction with the local shire and ensure it has a prominent location.

Katanning Shire President Kristy D'Aprile said the council did not want to rush the project.

Kristy D'Aprile did not confirm whether she would consider a formal apology.  (ABC News: Anthony Pancia)

"Obviously it's a really sensitive issue," she said.

"We want to make the decisions, as do the working group, to ensure the best outcome for both the victims and their families, and the community of Katanning."

Ms D'Aprile said consultation with victims still living in Katanning needed to be completed, along with state government approvals.

"We have no interest in prolonging the process or prolonging the trauma of victims who live in our community, in the Great Southern or Western Australia," she said.

"We certainly will be reaching out for an update on how the state government are progressing.

"This is an issue that has been a dark cloud over Katanning for a very, very long time.

"We would like to come to a place where we can resolve our history, acknowledge our history and find a constructive way to move forward."

The 2012 inquiry into the horrors at St Andrews Hostel, led by former Supreme Court Justice Peter Blaxell, found 11 people in Katanning were complicit in McKenna's crimes.

Justice Blaxell's findings also described McKenna as "very good at grooming the community".

The child rapist had previously been recognised as a citizen of the year in 1984 before being unmasked as a sex offender, but was not removed from the shire's honour roll until 2012.

When whistleblower Maggie Dawkins took her concerns to a local councillor, she was "rebuffed and berated" for raising the allegation against McKenna.

Maggie Dawkins and Kaye Anderson. (ABC Great Southern: Will Corbett)

Both sides of WA state politics issued formal apologies in the wake of the inquiry, but the Shire of Katanning never did.

Ms Anderson said an apology was better late than never.

"How hard is it to apologise?" she asked.

Victim-survivor Todd Jefferis said the shire's failure to apologise had caused serious harm.

Todd Jefferis was one of the first to speak out against McKenna. (ABC Great Southern: Will Corbett)

"I think it's disgusting. I think it's inexcusable that they have not offered a formal and a public apology to all the victims," he said.

"Not only the victims, but the families."

Mr Jefferis said it was no longer only about the abuse.

"Katanning has an opportunity there for them to turn the page and get onto something far better than this. I think the apology is a part of that."

Cr D'Aprile acknowledged the pain suffered by victims but stopped short of confirming whether she would request the council consider a formal apology.

"We acknowledge that people within our organisation, and throughout or community, let those victims down," she said.

"If it was my own personal statement, I would absolutely be offering anything whatever those victims need to assist in their healing.

"It's a very difficult position to sit in to try and apologise for actions this council had no part in a long, long time ago."

Efforts to declared McKenna a High Risk Serious Offender (HRSO) and keep him behind bars for the rest of his life fell short last month.

A court found he would be be declared an HRSO, but could be released from prison under strict conditions.

His release could happen as soon as November 17, when McKenna completes his 15-and-a-half-year sentence.

Mr Jefferis believes there are more victims out there whose accounts could keep McKenna in jail and urged them to come forward.

Todd Jefferis, Kaye Anderson, Maggie Dawkins and Darryl Stephens. (ABC Great Southern: Will Corbett)

"It's not easy to tell someone. It's probably a really hard step to take but it is absolutely the best one you can take," he said.

"Unlike some of us boys, they are going to believe every word you say, you're going to get arms wrapped around you.

"If there's a couple lads that come out and speak now, you're going to land a massive blow on McKenna."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/s.title: Workers down tools for a second time at BHP's Port Hedland operations
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/s.author: Kimberley Putland
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-09/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 12:51am

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 7:35am

BHP says ships continued to be loaded despite industrial action at the port yesterday.  (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)

BHP workers across three unions have downed tools for 24 hours at the Port Hedland operations, while high voltage workers near Newman will strike for 12 hours.

Australian Workers' Union members also participated in a work stoppage yesterday.

Ports unions and BHP will meet with the oversight of the Fair Work Commission again on August 18.

Workers at Australia's most lucrative port operations have walked off the job for a second day, amid an escalating industrial dispute.

The partial strike action at the port yesterday descended into a full stoppage after workers were allegedly threatened with no pay by mining giant BHP.

"BHP must understand that the Combined Ports Unions will not be deterred by threats or intimidation," AWU state secretary Craig Beveridge said.

BHP's Port Hedland operations.  (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)

BHP rejected the claim, arguing the 47 work activities the AWU advised were subject to the ban on loading left employees with no work to do.

"Workplace laws are clear that we are not required to pay for the portion of an employee's work that is subject to an industrial ban," BHP said in a statement on Saturday.

Bargaining for a separate agreement, BHP high voltage workers responsible for Newman's electricity supply, about 450 kilometres inland from Port Hedland, are downing tools in a 12-hour work stoppage.

BHP said ships continued to be loaded during yesterday's stoppage.

"Vessels are being loaded, with scheduled departures subject to usual port planning and tides," a statement read.

Multiple bulk carriers could be seen departing BHP berths.

Ships being loaded with iron ore at Port Hedland on Saturday despite industrial action. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

Speaking on Saturday morning, AMWU WA secretary Steve McCartney said he expected more than a hundred workers would take part in today's industrial action.

Electrical Trades Union WA's lead north west organiser, Brant Softley, expected today's strike would have a more widespread impact on the miner.

"To my knowledge, there'll be nearly no union people going in," Mr Softley said.

"Electrical, mechanical and the ship-loading people with the AWU have skill sets that can't be learned in 5 minutes."

Brant Softley says today's strike will have a widespread impact. (ABC News: Rosemary Murphy)

When asked why unions weren't participating in a picket line, Mr Softley said unions didn't want to make a spectacle to get their point across.

Chamber of Minerals and Energy WA chief executive Aaron Morey said the strike was "hard to reconcile" with progress made in Tuesday's bargaining meeting.

"If the talks are genuinely progressing and there is a clear path to an agreement, there was no case for walking off the job," Mr Morey said.

"International investors are watching and the message the unions seem to be trying to send is that they should take their capital somewhere else.

"If that happens, every West Australian will be far worse off."

The Town of Port Hedland said it had no part to play, but acknowledged the action could cause unease.

"This is a matter between BHP, its workforce and their representatives, and the Town has no role in enterprise bargaining negotiations," chief executive Dale Stewart said.

"We recognise that many residents, businesses and community organisations have strong connections to the resources sector, and any significant industrial dispute can create uncertainty across the community."

Dale Stewart is the CEO of the Town of Port Hedland. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

WA Industrial Relations Minister Simone McGurk said if there was "a bit of give and take on both sides" she was sure an agreement could be reached.

"I urge the parties to continue to meet to reach agreement … the Pilbara is an important economic driver for our state and for our country, so of course we are keeping an eye on it closely," she said.

"And I think that it’s really worth keeping in mind, not just the immediate issues, but the need for good harmonious relationships post the agreement being reached."

While the AWU said this impact of this weekend's action was "significant", BHP said operations continued.

"With around 1200 people on site across our port facility, our priority is always continuing safe and productive operations," a statement from the miner read.

Negotiations between the unions began last October, with 11 bargaining meetings held so far failing to reach an agreement.

In July, unionised workers participated in an 8-hour strike which the ABC understands did not cause major disruptions for BHP.

Unionised workers participated in an 8-hour strike in Port Hedland in July.   (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

Unions have not ruled out further strikes, despite both the Combined Ports Unions and BHP alluding to positive progress in a bargaining meeting with the Fair Work Commission earlier this week.

BHP has committed to tabling an updated proposal at the next bargaining meeting with the Fair Work Commission on August 18.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Prime Minister Takaichi urged to recognize more hibakusha
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
NAGASAKI – Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi was urged on Sunday to officially recognize more hibakusha survivors of the Aug. 9, 1945, U.S. atomic bombing of Nagasaki.

Some people who were exposed to radiation from the bomb have not been officially recognized as hibakusha because they were outside locations designated as being in the blast zone by the government.

On Sunday, Takaichi met with representatives from groups of officially recognized and unrecognized hibakusha at a hotel in Nagasaki.

“Time is limited for us, so we seriously ask you to make a Cabinet decision on support measures for both” recognized and unrecognized survivors, Shigemitsu Tanaka, 85, head of the Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Survivors Council, told the prime minister.

In response, Takaichi said only that the government “has been providing unrecognized hibakusha with medical expense subsidies on par with aid to recognized hibakusha and will continue steadily implementing such support.”

The meeting took place after the city held earlier on Sunday an annual peace memorial ceremony marking the 81st anniversary of the atomic bombing. Takaichi was among participants of the event.

The ceremony came three days after the city of Hiroshima held its peace memorial ceremony for the 81st anniversary of the Aug. 6, 1945, U.S. atomic bombing of the city.

At the Sunday meeting, the hibakusha side also called on the prime minister to give legal status to Japan’s three nonnuclear principles — not possessing nuclear weapons, not producing them and not allowing their entry into the country.

Takaichi said, “The country is firmly upholding the three nonnuclear principles.” But she stopped short of referring to a future direction regarding the principles.

As in the previous year, participants from the group of unrecognized hibakusha were not given time to make comments.

Chiyoko Iwanaga, 90, one of the unrecognized survivors, asked Takaichi when the prime minister was leaving the meeting to “Please recognize us as hibakusha, just like the 84 people,” a group who were given official recognition in a so-called black rain lawsuit over the atomic bombing of Hiroshima.

Takaichi did not give a reply. But Iwanaga said, “The prime minister listened attentively.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.summary: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi met with groups of officially recognized and unrecognized hibakusha survivors. Takaich met with representatives from groups of recognized andrecognized hIBakusha. Takakusha side also called on the prime minister to give legal status to Japan’s three nonnuclear principles.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Indonesia seizes 1.3 tons of ketamine worth millions in major bust
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
BATAM, INDONESIA – Indonesian authorities have seized 1.3 tons of ketamine worth tens of millions of dollars from a foreign-flagged vessel, a top anti-drug official said on Sunday, in one of the country’s largest drug busts.

Authorities received intelligence in February that the MV King Sun was sailing east from Thailand towards Indonesia with “suspicious” cargo, prompting months of surveillance, National Narcotics Agency chief Suyudi Ario Seto said.

A navy warship intercepted the vessel on Thursday as it entered Indonesian territory, he said.

“On Aug. 7, the joint team found 65 sacks hidden inside the ship. After testing, the items were known to contain ketamine,” Suyudi told a news conference on the Indonesian island of Batam on Sunday.

The load of an estimated 1.3 tons was worth around 2.07 trillion rupiah ($116.2 million), he said. Authorities were still searching the boat to see if there was more.

Ketamine functions primarily as a fast-acting anaesthetic, but it is widely abused as an illicit party drug. Its distribution is tightly controlled and monitored in Indonesia.

State news agency Antara reported that the vessel was registered under a Tanzanian flag and that it was intercepted in waters around the Riau Islands province near Singapore.

Eight crew aboard the vessel — seven Myanmar nationals and a Taiwanese — have been detained, the narcotics agency said.

“We are still investigating with regards to the origin of the load, port destination, who was the sender and who was the receiver,” Suyudi said.

Indonesian authorities seized 3.37 metric tons of cannabis buds last month when they foiled a smuggling attempt from Thailand, arresting 12 suspects.

In 2021, Indonesian police busted a smuggling ring that moved 2.5 tons of methamphetamine into the country from Afghanistan, with 17 suspects arrested.

Indonesia has some of the world’s toughest anti-drug laws, including the death penalty for traffickers, but has maintained a moratorium on executions for several years.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
TAIPEI – Taiwan’s Cabinet will propose a 16% annual rise in defense ⁠spending for 2027 that will for the first time exceed 1 trillion new Taiwan dollars ($31 billion), the official Central News Agency reported Sunday, as Taipei bolsters its military.

The move will come as China, which views democratically governed Taiwan ​as its own territory, has ramped up military ‌and political pressure ‌over the past few years to assert ​its claims, which Taipei strongly rejects.

But Taiwan also faces calls from Washington to spend more on its own defense, mirroring pressure from ⁠the United States on Europe, something President Lai Ching-te has enthusiastically embraced.

The proposed budget ⁠of more than T$1.1 trillion, to be unveiled on Aug. 20, includes funding for the coast guard, veterans ​and special projects, and ⁠will — like this year — exceed 3% of gross domestic product, the Central News Agency said.

Detailed figures await ⁠the final Cabinet ​meeting, it added.

Taiwan’s government has made military ​modernization a key policy platform and has repeatedly pledged ​to spend ‌more on its defenses, including developing made-in-Taiwan submarines, given the rising threat from China.

China’s military operates almost daily around Taiwan, and holds periodic war games, the last in late December.

China ‌is also rapidly modernizing its armed forces, with new aircraft carriers, stealth fighter jets and missiles. In March, China unveiled a rise of 7% in this year’s defense spending, to 1.91 trillion yuan ($283.08 billion).

China refuses ​to ​talk to Lai, saying he is a “separatist.” He ​says only Taiwan’s people can decide their future. Taiwan is currently ⁠in the middle of its annual Han Kuang military exercises.

Watching drills in the northern city of Taoyuan on Sunday, Lai said every exercise was an accumulation of experience giving the military ​greater confidence.

“Every bit of solid preparation in peacetime adds another measure of stability and strength for our nation,” he said, in comments posted on his Facebook account.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: Scientists turn to sharks to improve hurricane predictions
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: Marta Serafinko
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
From the killer shark of “Jaws” to the tornado-tossed predators of the “Sharknado” movies, films long have portrayed sharks as objects of summer fear. But when a shark cuts through the waters off the U.S. East Coast, it now may be doing more than hunting. It may also be gathering data that helps scientists understand the potential intensity of a hurricane before it makes landfall.

University of ​Delaware researchers are testing whether sharks can serve as mobile near-real-time ocean-data observers, carrying sensors that measure ocean conditions to inform oceanographic, atmospheric and ‌climate models.

These ‌CTD tags are small electronic devices that measure ocean electrical conductivity — a metric closely related to salinity — as well ​as temperature and depth, as marine creatures to which they are attached swim and dive.

“Animal-borne sensors have been used successfully by oceanographers for years, particularly on elephant seals in polar regions where scientific observations are scarce,” said Aaron Carlisle, principal investigator and a professor in the university’s School of Marine ⁠Science and Policy.

Sharks offer a new opportunity in such research because they are abundant, widely distributed and easier to access than many protected marine mammals, Carlisle ⁠said.

Until now, shark tagging typically has tracked only where these fish travel and the habitats they use.

The University of Delaware researchers select sharks that can collect the measurements most useful for hurricane research, and favor species that surface often enough for their ​tags to transmit the information to satellites. Previous analyses identified ⁠shortfin mako sharks, blue sharks, smooth hammerheads and juvenile great white sharks as strong candidates for such research in the North Atlantic.

“We are really most interested in the heat content of the top layer of the ⁠ocean, which is known as ​the mixed layer,” Carlisle said.

“This is the part of the water column that really drives hurricane ​intensity — warmer mixed layer equals stronger hurricane — as it holds the heat that feeds hurricanes,” Carlisle added.

The tagging process begins in ​early May, when ‌highly migratory species move closer to the coast from their winter habitats further out in the Atlantic, according to Caroline Wiernicki, a University of Delaware doctoral candidate in marine science.

Researchers head 50 to 65 km offshore aboard a research vessel, deploy baited lines and wait, typically two to three hours, for a shark to take the bait, Wiernicki said.

“The tags are attached to the dorsal ‌fin. Then every time the shark fins (swims) at the surface, the tag can communicate and transmit data to the orbiting network of satellite receivers,” Carlisle said.

The tagging process itself is operated “like a pit crew” in an auto race, Carlisle said, and usually takes less than five minutes.

The tagging is carried out under institutional animal care oversight to minimize impact on the sharks. The tags are attached using materials designed to corrode and fall off over time. Each animal also ​undergoes ​a health check before release, as a stressed or harmed shark may not behave naturally, potentially biasing the data, ​Carlisle said.

Wiernicki contrasted the “absurdly dramatic” portrayals of sharks in popular culture to the tamer reality — far less dramatic than the giant great white shark that terrorized fictional ⁠Amity Island in the 1975 blockbuster “Jaws.”

“It’s more like Bob from Accounting, clocking in with the day’s temperature profiles before he heads back out,” Wiernicki said.

The project is also a far cry from the campy Sharknado film series.

“We aren’t deploying sharks in and out of waterspouts, yet,” Wiernicki joked, but added sharks can be “a lot of fun.”

If the project succeeds, the data collected by sharks could help improve ​forecasts of how strong hurricanes will be as they approach the U.S. East Coast. The information could give communities from North Carolina to Massachusetts more reliable information to increase coastal resilience to ever-strengthening storms, Wiernicki said.

Most people will never encounter a shark in the wild, Carlisle said, but many know them through frightening stereotypes.

In reality, Carlisle said, “they are amazing animals perfectly adapted to the ocean, and we can learn a huge amount from them. If we can show that sharks can help people, it’s a win-win situation.”

BEIJING – Typhoon Dolphin is set to make landfall on China’s east coast on Sunday, bringing torrential rain and powerful winds, as authorities brace for flooding and landslides across a broad swath of eastern China. Typhoon Dolphin has already swept through Okinawa Prefecture, injuring six people and ​cutting power to more than 50,000 buildings. Before its landfall in China, authorities moved offshore workers to safety, ordered ‌vessels back to ‌port and increased checks at reservoirs, mountain streams, landslide-prone areas, construction sites and tourist locations.

Dolphin will ​be the most powerful typhoon to make landfall in China so far this year.

The storm is expected to hit the coast on Sunday evening with sustained winds of up to 162 kilometers per hour (101 mph) before weakening and moving inland, ⁠China’s National Meteorological Center said. That is equal to a Category 2 storm on the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale, a storm capable of producing ⁠extensive damage to homes, trees and infrastructure.

Myanmar’s military-backed government rejected the latest call by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations for the unconditional release of ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi, saying demands to do so are interfering with the country’s judicial process.

The bloc’s calls for access to the Nobel Peace Prize laureate and the release of other detainees “carry implications for the relevant judicial process and the fundamental principles of the rule of law in a sovereign state,” the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement Saturday. Any release will only be carried out in accordance with the law, it said.

The statement comes days after coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing visited Thailand, following years of regional ostracism for Myanmar in the aftermath of the military power seizure in 2021. Last month, Myanmar’s foreign minister met ASEAN counterparts in an informal gathering that was the first in-person engagement at that level since the coup.
