https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Accused Thai school shooter had watched violent content online, police say
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
BANGKOK – The Thai teen behind a deadly school shooting ⁠outside Bangkok had an air gun confiscated by a teacher last year and had watched violent content online, police said on Sunday, as the government promised new safety protocols for schools.

As investigations continued into Friday’s ​rampage, where a 14-year-old boy allegedly shot dead his grandparents ‌at home before ‌killing another six people at his school ​before turning the gun on himself, police said the boy had used social media to learn how to use a firearm.

“According to ⁠witness interviews, the perpetrator had begun showing interest in studying the use of ⁠firearms for some time, about one to two years,” Atthapol Anusit, deputy commissioner of the Provincial Police Region ​1, told reporters.

Atthapol, who said ⁠police had so far interviewed 17 witnesses, said a knife had also been found in ⁠the boy’s bag ​and other evidence found at the crime scenes ​included a firearm, spent cartridge cases, and a personal computer.

“After ​examining ‌the PC, it was found that the child had watched social media content involving violence,” the deputy commissioner said, but added there was no evidence yet that he had practiced shooting.

He ‌said that last year a teacher had confiscated a BB gun, a type of air gun, that the boy took to school. The boy had lived with his grandparents for 12 years after his ​parents ​had separated, Atthapol said.

The Ministry of Education said it ​would develop new safety protocols over the next three months, including ⁠mental health screenings and a system to refer at-risk people to specialists, drills for emergency response plans, a drive to stamp out bullying and better detection to stop items from being ​taken into schools.

Along with those who died, more than 20 people were injured in Thailand’s worst mass shooting since 2022, which has reignited debate over firearms control in Southeast Asia’s largest gun-owning nation.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.summary: Thai teen behind deadly school shooting had air gun confiscated by teacher last year, police say. Police say he had watched violent content online and used social media to learn how to use a firearm. The government promises new safety protocols for schools.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: As Japan’s concrete jungles sizzle, urban forestry offers an all-natural fix
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: Tomoko Otake
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
On another sweltering day in Tokyo last Sunday, some residents took to the streets to meticulously measure just how hot it was.

According to the Japan Meteorological Agency, the mercury reached a high of 35.3 degrees Celsius that day.

But the reality on the ground in Nakano Ward turned out to be a bit more complex.

Temperatures under the shade of a mountain cherry tree just outside Nakano Station were slightly higher than the JMA’s data, measuring 37 C at around 1:30 p.m. On an asphalt road just a few meters outside the shaded area, however, a thermometer tied to a pole at a height of 130 centimeters showed it was 44.5 C.

Closer to the ground at a height of 50 cm — roughly shoulder height for young children on foot or seated in strollers — the temperature was even higher, at 46.7 C.

“Weather forecasts often say the highest temperature of the day is 35 C or 36 C,” says Sumiko Sasamoto, a member of Minna no Kokage @Nakano, a grassroots group set up last year to study how to increase tree cover in the ward. “But outside a tree canopy, few places are actually at that level. We are in fact walking on streets of 46 C.”

Later, at around 2 p.m., in a shaded area of a street lined with Japanese white oak trees, temperatures were in the 36 C range both at 50 cm and 130 cm. The street felt even cooler than that thanks to good wind circulation.

As extreme heat fueled by human-induced climate change drives daily highs into the upper 30s and even 40s across Japan, the presence or absence of tree canopy makes a world of difference, especially in urban areas, where asphalt roads and concrete structures absorb and radiate heat, and intensify the heat island effect.

And while experts agree that urban greening is crucial to mitigating the impact of urbanization and climate change, trees are becoming even more scarce in Japanese cities.

In Tokyo’s central 23 wards, “tree canopy cover,” the proportion of land area covered by tree crowns (branches and leaves) when viewed from above, declined from 9.2% in 2013 to 7.3% in 2022, according to a study by Kinya Shiraishi and Toru Terada, both researchers at the University of Tokyo, that was published in 2024.

Tree canopy cover has become one of the widely used metrics for measuring and setting urban greening targets around the world. Tokyo’s 7.3% is considerably lower than other global cities, such as New York (23.4%), Paris (21%), Barcelona (25%) and Melbourne (15.3%), according to data released by each city.

“Considering that Tokyo’s tree canopy cover is less than 10%, the situation is grim,” Shiraishi says.

According to the National Institute for Land and Infrastructure Management, as of 2022, the number of roadside trees was 6.29 million, down by half a million from the peak recorded in 2002.

While cities in North America and Australia commonly set numerical tree canopy cover targets, Japan has yet to adopt the benchmark. Most local governments currently use broader indicators such as “green coverage ratio,” which includes not only tree canopy but also other vegetation such as grass and shrubs, and “green ratio,” which includes even paved squares within parks and water surfaces.

“Tokyo, despite confronting rising annual average temperature and the heat island effect, has yet to incorporate urban forestry into its urban planning framework,” Shiraishi writes in the paper.

On top of providing shelter from the sun, which reduces ground surface temperatures and can keep buildings cooler, reducing energy consumption, experts point to multiple benefits of urban forestry. Unlike concrete, trees hold a lot of moisture, which, when evaporated by heat, helps cool the air. Tree crowns intercept rain and reduce stormwater runoff, preventing floods, too.

Urban trees are known to improve water quality by absorbing pollutants such as oxidized nitrogen and reactive phosphorus from rainwater, while offsetting traffic-related carbon dioxide emissions through photosynthesis and removing ozone, a key component of smog, from the atmosphere.

Furthermore, urban forestry has therapeutic effects: Shinrin-yoku (forest bathing) is known to reduce stress hormones in the blood, activate natural killer cells — a type of white blood cell — and generally improve people’s mood.

With all of these benefits in mind, why is the tree canopy decreasing?

Based on satellite imagery and land-use data, Shiraishi analyzed where and how the canopy coverage is declining in Tokyo. He discovered that, over the 10 years through 2023, tree cover fell by 38% on public land and 57% on private land.

Residential areas saw the highest percentage of tree cover loss, with single-family houses seeing drops of 39.8%, along with roads (14.7%), educational and cultural facilities (10.8%) and parks (10.4%).

Many old houses in residential districts of Tokyo used to have large gardens with trees on their premises. But with the aging of many landowners, there has been a trend toward selling land to reduce tree maintenance costs.

Shiraishi also points out that Japan’s inheritance tax rate is prohibitively high, with the maximum rate at 55%. When an occupant of a property dies, their families often have no option but to pay the tax with money gained from selling parts of their land. Since land prices are going up in Tokyo, property developers divide the land into several plots to build smaller detached homes on each, sacrificing trees in the process.

Many municipal governments in Tokyo encourage private homeowners with large trees to keep them by designating them as “protected trees” and providing pruning subsidies and other support, such as regular checkups by arborists. But such designations are not forceful enough, and owners of protected trees can fell them without punishment if they so desire.

“Urban trees are decreasing abroad as well,” Shiraishi says, noting that redevelopment pressures remain strong in many cities. Urban environments, where roadside space is very limited, also create exceedingly harsh growing conditions for trees.

“But many cities, such as New York, are trying hard to stem the decline or restore tree cover. In Japan, the legal protection of urban forestry is very weak,” he says.

To reverse the trend, Shiraishi says the government should provide more incentives for residential owners with large trees on their land to keep them. He also believes that Japan should fully embrace the concept of urban forestry, which requires a holistic, long-term approach to growing and maintaining trees, while also maximizing their value.

At the same time, the negative impact of increasing tree cover in cities should be weighed as well, he says. Some people may frown on the cost of maintaining trees or the darkness that dense canopies bring, while others may suffer from allergies. Others may also dislike having the ground covered in fallen leaves or lament the bugs and birds that are something of a package deal with trees.

“Concerns are varied, depending on individuals, communities or nations, so policies should weigh people’s views (carefully), not ignore them,” he says.

One thing he hopes to see more of in Japan is citizens’ active involvement in urban forestry management.

Kaoru Morimoto, co-founder of Minna no Kokage @Nakano, says she started the group in February 2025 after experiencing a torturously hot summer the year before and discovering that local shrine grounds shaded by trees felt much cooler.

Last year, the group’s members measured temperatures at 43 locations around the ward over two days, and found that on a hot day with a temperature of 35 C, shaded areas could be as much as 13.5 degrees cooler than areas under direct sunlight. The group submitted a report to ward officials and proposed that the ward incorporates tree canopy cover as a policy goal.

While the ward government has not adopted the group’s proposal, it has shown interest in creating a “model district” featuring roadside trees together with citizens, Morimoto says.

This year, the group hopes to increase the number of observation spots to enhance accuracy. Morimoto is asking participants to look up the species of tree that they survey through a smartphone app, and to “feel” the difference in the air in the shade and in the sun.

“Let’s get friendly with the trees,” she told a recent explanatory meeting. “You can touch, hug and place your ears up to the trees. You can also observe the animals around them.”

As Morimoto and Sasamoto continued to measure temperatures near a mountain cherry tree outside Nakano Station, several pigeons parked themselves in the shade at the tree’s roots.

It was a subtle scene, but one that showed that even Tokyo’s birds know where to go for a break on a scorching summer’s day.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.summary: Tokyo's "tree canopy cover" is one of the most widely used metrics for measuring and setting urban greening targets around the world. Tokyo's ward government wants to encourage homeowners with large trees to keep them. But such designations are not forceful enough, and owners of protected trees can fall them without punishment.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
Nearly half a century after Edward Said published his landmark book “Orientalism,” his central insight remains strikingly relevant.

Said argued that the “Orient” was often presented by Western media, academia, literature and institutions not as a collection of complex societies but as the West’s contrasting mirror image — irrational rather than rational, emotional rather than pragmatic, culturally driven rather than strategically motivated, backward rather than modern.

Japan, despite being one of the world’s most technologically advanced democracies that hosts more American troops than any other U.S. ally, has never entirely escaped the Orientalist framework. In news reporting, that framework operates through subtle narrative framing and language choices.

This handsome fellow is Oji. He’s relatively new to ARK and was given up when his aging owner, suffering from dementia, could no longer care for him.

Oji, whose name means “prince” in Japanese, is a Kishu, a Japanese breed that originated in the Kii Peninsula in the Kansai region.

Standoffish when he first arrived at ARK, Oji appeared disinterested in life in general. That, however, soon changed when he started to respond to new experiences.

His skin had been in shockingly poor condition, but regular baths soon fixed that problem. Walks introduced him to new stimuli and gave him a new take on life. He now loves walks so much it’s hard to get him to return to the shelter.

Toys also brought him closer to people. Now, he’ll bring you a toy and ask you to play. It’s very hard to say “no.” Oji will even ask for cuddles.

Still, he’s a classic Kishu. He’s a bit of a gourmet and can be surprisingly fussy about food. And though he’s still frightened of strangers, Oji does warm with time and a lot of affection.

He may be a “prince,” but Oji is just a dog wanting to be loved.

OSAKA – The No. 3 reactor at Kansai Electric Power’s Oi nuclear power plant in Fukui Prefecture stopped automatically after an alarm went off, the company said in the small hours of Sunday.

While the cause of the incident is under investigation, no leakage of radioactive substances has occurred, according to the firm.

An alarm sounded around 11:55 p.m. Saturday, indicating an abnormality in a device to generate a magnetic field at the reactor’s power generator connected to a turbine, and the power generator and the reactor stopped automatically, Kansai Electric said.

Thirty-five years will have passed in December since the start of operations at the 1.18-million-kilowatt pressurized water reactor. A regular checkup has been slated to begin in October.

In April 2000, a glitch at a device of the same kind led the power generator of the No. 2 reactor at the firm’s Mihama nuclear plant in Fukui Prefecture and the reactor to shut down automatically. The reactor is now in the process of decommissioning.

The Environment Ministry plans to draw up guidelines in fiscal 2027 to help foster reliable reuse companies so that consumers can buy and sell used items with a sense of safety.

As disputes between customers and some malicious firms have been reported, the ministry plans to encourage reuse companies to comply with laws and protect consumers through the guidelines, which will clarify standards on reliable businesses.

The Japan Reuse Affairs Association has designated Aug. 8 as Reuse Day to raise the public awareness of reuse services and established its own certification system to gain trust from consumers.

However, some businesses are operating without license, engaging in problematic practices such as charging high fees after advertising the free collection of goods or making unsolicited home visits to buy used products.

The guidelines, to be discussed by an expert panel, are expected to outline measures reuse businesses and flea market app operators should take, such as avoiding misleading expressions in advertisements and checking the quality of items. The ministry will also consider introducing a system to recognize and support good business operators.

The government aims to expand the reuse market by 30% to ¥4.6 trillion ($29.1 billion) in 2030 from an estimated ¥3.5 trillion in 2024. It will accelerate efforts to promote the healthy development of the industry with the goal of establishing a safe and reliable market by 2040.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: Half a month out, and England was a World Cup winner after all
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: Matthew Brooker
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
England bowed out in the 2026 World Cup semifinals, disappointing a nation that has waited 60 years to appear in a second final. Never mind: Time may not heal all wounds, but money is a consolation. Another near miss on the sporting field shouldn’t overshadow the financial positives for the game back home. A side effect of the riches reaped by FIFA and its main host, the U.S., may be to push some more air into the Premier League’s gravity-defying balloon.

Early signs of buoyancy include reports that a consortium backed by the family of Indian billionaire Lakshmi Mittal is in talks to buy a minority stake in Liverpool FC that would value the club at as much as $6 billion. Amazon.com Inc. founder Jeff Bezos is said to have held discussions on joining the group. Meanwhile, the transfer record for a British player has been broken twice since the tournament kicked off in June, with Morgan Rogers’ £117 million ($156 million) move to Chelsea from Aston Villa surpassing by £1 million the fee Manchester City agreed to pay for Nottingham Forest’s Elliot Anderson. Elsewhere, the Thai owners of Leicester City — which won the Premier League a decade ago but has now slipped into the third tier of English football — are exploring a sale of the club, according to the Financial Times. The motivation here might be distress more than rising valuations, but the timing nevertheless suggests opportune conditions in the World Cup’s afterglow.

The 2026 tournament was a more valuable showcase for Premier League talent than Qatar four years earlier. The league supplied a record 182 players to the competition, and its stars were among the standout performers. Spanish midfielder Rodri, of Manchester City, was named the tournament’s best player. His club teammate Erling Haaland of Norway, the Premier League’s top striker, became a cultural sensation in the U.S. not only for the goals that knocked out Brazil but also for his fashion sense. A total of 11 Premier League players took to the field for the final between Spain and Argentina, up from seven in Qatar. Other than England reaching the final, there aren’t many outcomes that would have provided a better shop window.

Early signs of buoyancy include reports that a consortium backed by the family of Indian billionaire Lakshmi Mittal is in talks to buy a minority stake in Liverpool FC.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
PENTICTON, BRITISH COLUMBIA – British Columbia declared a state of emergency on Saturday after thousands of people in the western Canadian province were ordered to flee a fast-moving wildfire that nearly doubled in size overnight.

The Bald Range wildfire was burning ​out of control and grew rapidly to about 9,500 hectares (23,500 acres), prompting evacuation orders in Summerland, Peachland and other districts west ‌of ‌Okanagan Lake in the province’s southern interior.

The region produces most of B.C.’s wine and ​is Canada’s second-largest wine-producing area. Premier David Eby told a news conference on Saturday that one fire official had likened the fire to “a bomb going off.”

“He described flames on a 100-foot tree, flames going 200 feet above that, and the fire creating ⁠its own weather system, which creates lightning, which then feeds on itself,” Eby said. “Homes have been lost, and properties have been destroyed. ⁠Some people became trapped as conditions changed very quickly, and needed to be rescued,” the premier said, adding it remained a very dynamic and threatening situation.

Summerland has a population of about 12,000 people, according to the ​2021 census, and Peachland is home to ⁠about 6,500 residents. A state of emergency grants the provincial government immediate access to special powers including travel restrictions and supply protections to prevent price gouging, and specific tools to coordinate rescue ⁠work.

Officials said the Bald Range ​wildfire triggered the largest evacuation event so far this summer and more than ​20,000 people across B.C. have been forced to evacuate their homes.

“A lot of farms have been affected. ​We don’t ‌know how many structures have been lost. They’re still busy fighting the fire,” Summerland Mayor Doug Holmes said in a phone interview from Penticton. “We have to brace ourselves for the worst.”

Many residents left overnight, driving south to Penticton or north to Kelowna before highways began to close.

Terry Fries of Summerland was watching a football ‌game on Friday night when a neighbor advised him to get a bag ready as the fire grew. “At the time, it was still farther back, and you could see it behind the hills,” he said. When B.C. authorities issued the evacuation order around midnight, he and his family drove about 45 km (28 miles) north to the city of Kelowna.

Residents recorded videos of fires by the highway ​and ​of structures burning as they evacuated. By Saturday afternoon, ashes began to settle on cars and ​houses in nearby areas as the fire painted the skies with orange hues. Summerland lost power on Saturday and issued a ⁠boil-water notice for residents.

The municipality said untreated water had entered the system after it bypassed the water treatment plant due to the wildfire.

Several Canadian provinces, including Ontario and Quebec, have battled blazes this year as hot, dry weather fueled wildfires in dense forest areas. Firefighters from Mexico, Australia, France and New Zealand have helped combat the fires.

In ​B.C., where hot and dry conditions have increased the risk of more fires spreading, about 1,500 firefighting personnel were battling more than 100 fires. The province has issued 40 evacuation orders and 49 alerts.

Fires have burned through 4 million hectares (9.9 million acres) in Canada this year, according to the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Center.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Amusement parks across Japan are raising their admission fees to offset rising labor, electricity and other costs and ease overcrowding during peak seasons.

As of last month, 32 of the 101 amusement park facilities in Japan have decided to raise ticket prices this year, according to research company Teikoku Databank.

Many facilities have adopted dynamic pricing systems, in which ticket prices vary depending on the season and day of the week.

Tokyo Disney Resort in Urayasu, Chiba Prefecture, is set to raise the maximum admission price under its dynamic pricing system from ¥10,900 ($69) to ¥11,900 for those visiting on Oct. 10, and then to ¥12,400 starting the following day. The price change will apply to both Tokyo Disneyland and Tokyo DisneySea.

Sanrio Puroland in Tama, western Tokyo, hiked its maximum ticket price by ¥1,000 to ¥6,900 on Aug. 1.

Universal Studios Japan in Osaka will introduce a system on Sept. 1 that enables it to flexibly change prices for specific days on which the park is likely to be crowded, even for days in which advance ticket sales have begun. The park is expected to raise fees mainly for holiday periods and weekends.

Visitors are having to pay more inside parks as well. Next month, Tokyo Disney Resort operator Oriental Land will increase the number of attractions covered by the Disney Premier Access paid service that enables users to book time slots for attractions and reserved seats to watch parades. It will also raise prices for some parades.

Additionally, Oriental Land will terminate the Priority Pass service, which allows visitors to reserve time slots for attractions for free, at the end of this month.

Teikoku Databank said that parks’ price hikes at a time when many consumers are grappling with inflation “pose the risk of a decrease in visitors.”

Parks should respond flexibly to the situation, such as introducing value-added tickets with benefits such as shorter waiting times, as well as separate fees for foreign visitors, rather than raising prices uniformly, Teikoku Databank said.

KUMAMOTO – Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has been increasingly utilized to assist relief efforts in the wake of a powerful earthquake in Kumamoto Prefecture late last month.

At the same time, AI is believed to have been used to create fake videos and other misinformation that were spread on social media, highlighting both the advantages and drawbacks of the technology.

Misato Kaetsu, 38, who experienced the quake in the Kumamoto town of Mifune, created an online information board using generative AI on her smartphone while at the evacuation center where she and her family had fled.

Those affected by the quake, which registered up to 7, the highest level on Japan’s seismic intensity scale, can use the site to share local information, such as the locations of reopened stores and emergency feeding stations. The service was launched just hours after the idea was conceived.

“I decided to develop (the service) because information has not reached those who need it,” Kaetsu said. “AI could not be used when powerful earthquakes struck Kumamoto 10 years ago, but ideas can now be easily turned into reality,” she said.

More than 160,000 people have already used the service, and it has assisted those affected by the disaster in rebuilding their lives.

Staff at quake-hit local governments are also using AI.

“We have used it to create meeting minutes and explanatory materials since before the earthquake, so it has become indispensable,” an official at the digital strategy promotion division of the Kumamoto Prefectural Government said. “By reducing the workload through the use of AI, we can focus on issues that require careful handling during disaster response.”

However, AI also has its downsides in times of natural disasters.

Following the latest earthquake, a fake video of an explosion at the Aeon Mall Kumamoto shopping facility in the Kumamoto town of Kashima was spread on social media. This and other fake videos are believed to have been created with AI.

The explosion at the shopping facility, which occurred shortly after the earthquake, left seven people dead.

“In the past year or two, the accuracy of generative AI has evolved dramatically, and reliability and convenience have increased,” Isao Echizen, professor of information security at the National Institute of Informatics who is well-versed in AI technology, said. “On the other hand, there is a risk of (AI) giving wrong answers, albeit at a low probability, and being abused.”

“It’s hard to tell if an image has been generated” with AI, he added. “It will be more important than ever to check whether those who post (images) are reliable sources.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Play space for children set up at Kumamoto quake shelter
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
YATSUSHIRO, KUMAMOTO PREF. – A space for children to play was set up at an evacuation shelter in Kumamoto Prefecture after a powerful earthquake on July 28 forced nurseries and after-school care services in the area to suspend operations.

In the city of Yatsushiro, which suffered significant damage from the 7.1 magnitude quake, the second-floor space of a gymnasium at a city-run junior high school serving has served as a shelter. It is now being used as a play space for children, as well. In the space, equipped with games and cardboard beds, children ranging from elementary school to high school ages gather to chat or play card games.

“I feel like things have returned to normal (when I’m here),” a 15-year-old high school girl said. A male high school student of the same age said that people are smiling more.

At the shelter, high school students are volunteering to look after younger kids. The play space was created with support from Tokyo-based nonprofit Chance For All, which supplied playing cards and board games, after evacuees called for a space to be created where kids can go to relax.

Kanta Kojima, 27, a member of the nonprofit, said he is worried about the trauma that children are experiencing. For example, instead of “playing house,” as many children do, Kojima said that he saw preschool and young elementary school children “play earthquake,” knocking over building blocks to simulate damage and saying phrases like “call an ambulance” and “give CPR.”

“They may have actually seen such scenes and emergencies,” Kojima said.

He said that playing may help kids process their emotions, as young children often struggle to express their feelings in words.

“People often say that there is no time to play in times of emergency, but playing is even more important now than before,” Kojima said.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.summary: A space for children to play was set up at an evacuation shelter in Kumamoto Prefecture after a powerful earthquake on July 28. The space was created with support from Tokyo-based nonprofit Chance For All.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/0.author: Gabrielle Doman
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/0.text:
Japan has long experimented with the role of sound in fermentation.

For centuries, sake brewers sang motosuri-uta, rhythmic work songs performed while grinding rice and preparing yeast starters. The songs synchronized the movements of brewery workers, kept them warm through the depths of winter and boosted morale. Folklore also held that workers would speak to the microorganisms in the kōji (rice inoculated with kōjikin mold), encouraging healthy fermentation.

Today, that tradition is being revisited through a scientific lens. Brewers, winemakers and food producers are experimenting with music, vibration and even words of gratitude — exploring whether what goes into fermentation can be as influential as its background soundtrack.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/0.title: ¥6,000 for shaved ice: Is luxury ‘kakigōri’ worth it?
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/0.author: Weiwen Lin
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/0.text:
In a Tokyo summer, it’s almost impossible to walk past a dessert shop display case without spotting a plastic replica of a dome of ice drizzled with colorful syrup.

Available year-round in Japan but coming to the fore only in summer, kakigōri (shaved ice) is a snowball toss of a riposte to the brutal heat now upon us. While similar dishes exist across East and Southeast Asia, Japan’s take stands out for the feathery texture of its ice, an effect achieved through the precision of ice-shaving machines.

A standard kakigōri is simply shaved ice with syrup, though some vendors offer various fillings or toppings, such as anko (adzuki bean paste), mochi and fresh fruit. It’s a refreshing combination of flavors that has earned the dessert a perennial spot as a cheap treat sold for a few hundred yen from yatai (food stalls) at matsuri (traditional festivals).

https://www.scmp.com/news/china/article/.title: Chinese boy, 9, missing after being swept away by wave as Typhoon Dolphin approached coast
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/article/.author: William Zheng
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/article/.text:
Rescuers still searching for child, who was taken across a causeway by two adults in Zhejiang when a typhoon warning was already in place

Rescuers continued searching on Sunday for a nine-year-old boy who has been missing since he was swept away by a giant wave in the eastern Chinese province of Zhejiang.

Local officials warned that high tides, rapid currents and dangerous whirlpools had made the search efforts very difficult, according to media reports.

Video footage of the moment the boy was washed out to sea has been widely circulating on Chinese social media platforms.

It showed two adults and two children frantically sprinting across a stone and cement causeway connecting the mainland to a rocky island.

As the group reached the middle of the exposed walkway, a colossal wave several metres tall smashed over the path, knocking all four to the ground.

When the surge receded, only three managed to scramble to their feet while the boy could not hold on to anything and disappeared with the waves.

A bystander could be heard shouting angrily at the surviving family members as they frantically looked over the edge.

“I already warned you it was dangerous and not to go out there!” the man yelled, urging them to return to safe ground immediately. A woman could be heard weeping hysterically in the background.

Shanghai news portal thepaper.cn reported on Sunday that local authorities had already cordoned off the coastline and constructed temporary fences, but the group apparently ignored the warning signs and entered the restricted coastal zone.

A local official told the news portal that all primary access roads to the seafront had been sealed off well in advance of the storm, but the four had entered the area through a small passageway.

The rescue teams discovered 10 other people were trapped on the offshore island. They were successfully evacuated.

A staff member at the local emergency command centre told the Xiaoxiang Morning News the search and rescue operation was still ongoing on Sunday.

But they warned that turbulent conditions at sea meant rescuers could only go to the high ground and use telescopes to look for the boy.

The incident triggered widespread anger across Chinese social media. Users overwhelmingly criticised the child’s guardians, accusing them of ignoring safety warnings and failing to hold his hand while crossing the causeway.
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/article/.summary: Nine-year-old boy swept away by giant wave in eastern Chinese province of Zhejiang. Rescuers still searching for child who was taken across causeway by two adults. Video footage of moment boy was washed out to sea has been widely circulating on Chinese social media platforms.

https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/ar.title: Moore Threads plans Hong Kong listing after posting 147% jump in first-half revenue
https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/ar.author: Howard Liu,Coco Feng
https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/ar.text:
The Chinese AI chip developer plans a listing in Hong Kong to deepen its ‘international strategic footprint’

Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) chip developer Moore Threads plans to seek a listing in Hong Kong after reporting a 147 per cent jump in first-half revenue, as the Nvidia challenger seeks fresh capital amid booming demand for home-grown computing power.

The Shanghai-listed company said on Sunday that its board had approved a plan to issue H shares and list on the main board of the Hong Kong stock exchange, a move designed to deepen the firm’s “international strategic footprint”, attract and retain talent, and “further enhance corporate governance and core competitiveness”.

Separately, the company said its revenue had reached 1.7 billion yuan (US$252 million) in the six months ended June. Its net loss narrowed to 11.6 million yuan from 271 million yuan a year earlier.

Moore Threads added that it was actively discussing listing plans with relevant parties, with further details yet to be finalised.

The listing plan adds to a bumper year for the Hong Kong stock market, which has seen a string of debuts by high-profile Chinese tech companies in recent months.

“As a global capital hub, a listing in Hong Kong will attract sustained coverage from overseas sovereign wealth funds and global technology research institutions,” said Guo Tao, an angel investor who is a member of the Chinese Association for Artificial Intelligence.

A total of 104 new companies listed in Hong Kong between January and July, almost double the figure during the same period last year, according to data from Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX).

The total funds raised through initial public offerings in the city reached HK$328 billion (US$41.8 billion) over the same period, up 154 per cent year on year.

Last month, Hong Kong saw its biggest share sale of the year so far, as Zhongji Innolight – a leading producer of optical transceivers used in AI data centres – raised HK$53.4 billion at a market capitalisation of over HK$1 trillion.

Major coming listings in the city include Shein Global Holdings – the online fast-fashion retailer – and Shenzhen Transsion Holdings, a Chinese smartphone maker with a major presence in the African market.

Transsion said last week that its application to issue up to 132 million shares had been approved by the China Securities Regulatory Commission.

If Moore Threads can list in Hong Kong, it will “substantially enhance its global industry profile”, as domestic GPUs currently have greatest recognition within the Chinese market, according to Guo, the angel investor.

Moore Threads’ surge in revenue came at a time when “the global artificial intelligence industry has entered a new phase of large-scale implementation and explosive growth since 2026”, with growing consensus in China that its “computing infrastructure must be independently controlled”, the firm said in a Sunday stock exchange filing.

The firm’s large-scale computing clusters powered by its self-developed flagship GPU, the MTT S5000, achieved 95 per cent in scaling linearity, a measurement of computing efficiency during AI model training, Moore Threads said.

The earnings put the company well on track to match earlier market projections. In April, JPMorgan cited consensus forecasts that Moore Threads would achieve annual revenue of 2.68 billion yuan in 2026, rising to 4.69 billion yuan in 2027.

JPMorgan grouped the company with a second tier of Chinese AI chip developers, alongside MetaX, Biren Technology, Iluvatar CoreX and Enflame, which still have relatively limited exposure to leading cloud providers compared with Huawei Technologies, Cambricon Technologies, Baidu’s Kunlunxin and Alibaba Group Holding’s T-Head. Alibaba owns the SCMP.

The bank said a breakthrough with major cloud customers could become a key driver of growth for these smaller players, provided they could secure sufficient supply and offer competitive system efficiency and total cost of ownership.

Moore Threads is also positioned to benefit from Beijing’s accelerating push to replace foreign technology in strategically important computing infrastructure.

Its GPUs were among the first AI processors added in May to China’s official “secure and reliable” technology assessment list, alongside products from Huawei, T-Head, Biren, Hygon Information Technology, Iluvatar CoreX and MetaX.

The certification system is widely used to support technology procurement by party and government agencies, state-owned enterprises and other state-linked customers under China’s Xinchuang localisation initiative.

Additional reporting by Ann Cao

https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.title: Iconic 1991 photo of Chinese girl symbolises thirst for knowledge, changing lives
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.author: Fran Lu
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.text:
Initiative behind photo has garnered US$3.7 billion in donations, establishing 21,000 rural schools for 7.8 million underprivileged students

A 1991 black-and-white portrait photograph has become an iconic symbol of impoverished Chinese students’ yearning for knowledge, profoundly altering the life of its subject.

The photograph, titled “I Want to Go to School,” captures a poignant moment of an eight-year-old Primary One girl studying at a rural school in central China’s Anhui province. Her bright eyes gaze ahead, radiating an insatiable thirst for learning.

Affectionately known as “Big Eyes,” the picture was taken by photojournalist Xie Hailong, who documented the evolution of Project Hope – an initiative sponsored by the Communist Youth League to assist young dropouts in impoverished areas since 1989.

Xie travelled to over 100 counties across 20 provinces in China. His photo series served to promote the project, and “Big Eyes” emerged as a symbol of its mission.

For his work, Xie received numerous accolades, including the special contribution award from the Photojournalist Society of China, and he was recognised as one of the “180 People in 180 Years of Photography” by the International Federation of Photographic Art.

The image has been included in official Chinese textbooks.

Over the past 30 years, this timeless photograph has continued to resonate with countless individuals, emphasising the critical importance of education.

According to official records, Project Hope had received nearly 25 billion yuan (US$3.7 billion) in donations, built over 21,000 rural schools, and supported 7.8 million students from underprivileged families by the end of last year.

The photograph’s protagonist, Su Mingjuan, was among the 7.8 million whose lives were transformed by the project.

Su was born into a modest peasant family that struggled to afford her tuition fees, which ranged from 60 to 70 yuan (US$9 – US$10) per term.

She remarked that she “would probably have dropped out of school if it weren’t for that photo.”

As the image gained widespread attention, people from across the country wrote her letters, and many visited her. Initially, she felt overwhelmed by the attention.

However, she soon realised that the photo represented more than just her – it embodied the spirit of Project Hope and the responsibility she carried as its subject.

She received donations from across the nation and ultimately completed her university education with the generosity of compassionate strangers.

Su has since paid this kindness forward, donating to other underprivileged students since her junior secondary school days.

In 2006, she auctioned the copyright of “Big Eyes” alongside Xie. They used the 300,000-yuan (US$45,000) proceeds to fund the construction of a school in a rural Tibetan area.

In 2018, Su established an educational fund in her name, which attracted 10 million yuan (US$1.5 million) in donations over six years, facilitating the construction of five rural schools.

In addition to her charitable endeavours, Su works full-time as a secretary for the Youth League Committee at a bank in Anhui.

In 2022, she was selected as a delegate to the 20th National Congress of the Communist Party of China (CPC).

Su expressed her commitment, stating: “I want to do my best to help children like me realise their dreams of going to school.”

Xie, on the other hand, became a photography educator, inspiring students to connect with their subjects and infuse love into their photographic creations.

https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.title: Chinese man’s 3,000km search for pen pal from 24 years ago sparks deep nostalgia
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.author: Fran Lu
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.text:
Li’s heartfelt journey resonates with many, attracting 62,000 likes and over 7,000 comments, with some describing it as ‘romantic’

A man from southern China travelled 3,000 kilometres to search for his pen pal from 24 years ago, stirring nostalgia among many for their own youth pen pals.

Li Zhicong, around 40, hails from the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region and has been working in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, for over a decade.

Recently, he journeyed 3,000 km to Inner Mongolia in northern China to find his pen pal “Ice Rain,” who wrote him a letter 24 years ago.

In 2002, when he was a third-year junior secondary school student, Li met Ice Rain, a girl in the same grade living in Arun Banner, through a chat app. He sent her a letter describing the breathtaking scenery of Guilin.

Guilin’s landscapes are renowned throughout the country and are depicted on China’s 20-yuan bill. Although Li was originally from Luchuan county and had never visited Guilin at that time, he chose to paint a vivid picture of the Guilin he imagined for his new friend.

Before long, Ice Rain replied with a letter enclosed in an envelope featuring the then-popular Taiwanese boy band F4.

In her letter, she described the vast prairie where she lived, writing: “From afar come the bleating of sheep, the mooing of cows, and the sound of galloping horses. How could one not be captivated by such vibrant scenes of life? I feel incredibly happy.”

She also invited Li to visit the grasslands, encouraged him to sample the delicious milk, and offered to teach him how to ride a horse.

Li found himself enchanted by the scenery Ice Rain depicted.

He recalled that they lost touch after he sent one final letter. As they transitioned from junior to senior secondary school, it was likely that her address changed.

Additionally, he noted that their chat app account numbers had also changed, making online reconnection impossible.

In 2023, Li undertook a self-drive journey across China and passed through Inner Mongolia. Although it was winter and he did not witness the lush grasslands he had imagined, the scenery rekindled memories of Ice Rain.

In June, he returned to Inner Mongolia with his parents, and this time they encountered the expansive prairie and the flocks and herds she had described to him.

Following that trip, Li set off on a special journey to Arun Banner to seek out Ice Rain.

In her letter, she revealed that her real name is Ding Kun, along with her birthday, school, and hobbies.

On the final day of his trip in Arun Banner, Li tracked down Ding’s junior secondary school teacher, who is surnamed Jing.

Jing shared with Li that Ding was an outgoing and talkative girl.

Li documented his journey on his social media account, which garnered 62,000 likes and over 7,000 comments. Many resonated with his experience, sharing their own stories of letter exchanges with pen pals.

“Your video reminded me of my pen pal from 30 years ago. It took a month to receive a response. Pen pals were a special way to make friends during a time when communication technologies were less developed. I miss that era,” commented one user.

Li remarked that this unique form of communication was cherished by youths born in the 1980s.

Some even found Li’s quest “romantic.”

Now a vlogger, Li stated that despite being single, he did not wish to disturb Ding’s life.

Instead, he felt content to walk through the city where Ding once lived.

He mentioned that if he could reconnect with Ding, he would like to invite her and her family to visit Guangxi at his expense.

“She was the most distant friend I made at that time. I want to honour a cherished memory of my youth,” Li expressed.

https://www.dw.com/en/study-obesity-bigg.title: Study: Obesity 'bigger cancer risk' than previously thought
https://www.dw.com/en/study-obesity-bigg.text:
A new study has found that being significantly overweight could be responsible for more cases of cancer than previously known. Abdominal fat, in particular, increases the risk of cancer — especially among women.

Being overweight or obese significantly increases the risk of developing colon cancer, breast cancer or liver cancer, and is a major risk factor for 10 other types of cancer, a new study has found.

Until recently, researchers believed that 2% to 8% of all cancer cases were attributable to excess body weight. But a new study by a team led by Hermann Brenner, an epidemiologist with the German Cancer Research Center  (DKFZ), suggests that this was a serious underestimate.

According to the study, up to 11.5% of cancers may be attributable to being overweight.

The DKFZ researchers "have not only updated existing risk estimates, but have also questioned whether the link between excess weight and cancer may have been underestimated until now," Michael Leitzmann, an epidemiologist at the University of Regensburg, told DW.

Leitzmann, who was not involved in the study, researches diet, body weight, physical activity and the development of chronic diseases at the university's Institute of Epidemiology and Prevention, and has advised German Cancer Aid.

The DKFZ team changed its research methods for the new study. Previous research used body mass index (BMI), which is calculated based on height and weight, as an indicator of excess weight. But BMI does not distinguish between fat and muscle mass, and does not provide information on how fat is distributed throughout the body.

This is important, because not all fat is the same. Fat cells that accumulate around the abdomen are more than just a passive store for excess calories, unlike those in other parts of the body. "They trigger what is known as a chronic inflammatory metabolic state," Leitzmann said.

Excess abdominal fat functions like a gland that releases various signaling molecules, known as adipokines. These travel through the bloodstream to different parts of the body, where they influence other metabolic processes — including cell growth and division, as well as the inhibition of programmed cell death. "These are all mechanisms that can contribute to the development and subsequent growth of tumors," Leitzmann said.

The DKFZ researchers therefore focused not only on BMI but also on waist circumference and the waist-to-hip ratio. Data from 458,543 women and men from the UK Biobank, which holds one of the world's biggest health datasets, were included in the study. The participants were followed for and average of 12 years, during which 50,000 new cases of cancer were identified.

The researchers wanted to rule out a potential methodological bias in previous studies: the fact that cancer can lead to weight loss even before diagnosis — that is, while it is still developing.

That suggests that previous studies failed to identify a link between obesity and cancer because the participants had already lost weight because they had developed cancer by the time they entered the study.

For this reason, the team excluded the first few years following the participants' enrollment from the analysis. Only cancer cases that occurred seven years after the start of the observation period were considered — and that made the statistical link between being overweight and cancer clearer.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The study suggests that the proportion of overweight women who develop cancer is higher than that of men, but Leitzmann urges caution when interpreting these findings. Further studies with a similar design are needed to see whether the results can be replicated.

Leitzmann offered a theory on why being overweight might have a more severe impact on women. Being overweight is blamed, among other things, for breast, uterine and ovarian cancers. "These types of cancer, which affect women, are hormone-dependent," Leitzmann said. For example, the hormone estrogen can stimulate the growth of breast cancer, and excess abdominal fat can contribute to elevated estrogen levels.

Most people are now aware that obesity increases the risk of cardiovascular disease or Type 2 diabetes, Leitzmann said. Conversely, this also means that people who lose weight also reduce their risk of heart attacks, strokes and diabetes.

Though the DKFZ study emphasizes the increased risk associated with obesity, Leitzmann said the findings were also a reason for optimism: "To me, this clearly indicates that, by preventing obesity, we will be able to make a greater contribution to cancer prevention than previously assumed."

https://www.dw.com/en/indonesia-mount-br.title: Indonesia: Mount Bromo wildfire grows, spurs park closure
https://www.dw.com/en/indonesia-mount-br.text:
Indonesian authorities have closed a popular national park until further notice. Strong winds and rough terrain are making it difficult for firefighters to extinguish the blaze.

Authorities in Indonesia closed the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in East Java until further notice on Saturday due to a wildfire that has scorched some 176 hectares (435 acres) of land on Mount Bromo since it began on Monday.

The blaze, one of several currently burning across Indonesia, has mobilized hundreds of firefighters, park rangers, police, soldiers and volunteers at one of Indonesia's most popular tourist destinations.

Helicopters and drones are in use in the air and firebreaks are being created by crews on the ground.

Officials describe the situation as challenging, pointing to high winds and rough terrain, with many areas difficult to access on steep volcanic slopes.

"These conditions make air operations important to reach areas that cannot be accessed optimally by land," one official said.

Dry conditions and winds are fueling the spread of the flames according to Indonesia's Meteorological, Climatological and Geophysical Agency.

Authorities say the fire was sparked during land clearing work.

Though fires — often illegally started by plantation owners and farmers to clear for planting — are common in the region, the current El Nino weather pattern and seasonal dry winds from Australia have combined to make this year especially prone to wildfire and drought.

Indonesia has lost more than 107,000 hectares of land to fire in the first half of 2026, over twice the area destroyed in wildfires in 2023, when the last El-Nino pattern started.

https://www.dw.com/en/india-ex-education.title: India: Ex-Education Minister Pradhan says Gen Z 'misled'
https://www.dw.com/en/india-ex-education.text:
Dharmendra Pradhan spoke for the first time since his resignation as education minister following mass protests against him. He said he "suffered" because of Gen Z, who led the protests. Follow DW for more.

Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Sunday, August 9:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereto add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

The Indian government has clarified that its real-time payment service, called Unified Payments Interface (UPI), will remain free-of-charge for consumers. It said only merchants will have to pay a "nominal" charge for some transactions.

The clarification came after the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 was passed in Lok Sabha earlier this week. The bill caused much concern over a potential charge on UPI transactions.

Earlier reports had suggested that the bill would allow the government to permit banks and payment companies to charge fees on UPI and other digital payments in the future.

Addressing the concern, the Ministry of Finance clarified that all person-to-person transactions will remain free of charge.

It however said that a limited set of merchant transactions will incur transaction charges when the MDR (Merchant Discount Rate) charges are introduced.

MDR is a fee levied on merchants by banks to help meet costs related to processing of transactions, settlement and infrastructure.

Since its introduction by the Reserve Bank of India in 2016, UPI has become one of the most popular payment methods across the country.

In 2025 alone, the UPI transaction load stood at 228.5 billion transactions in India. The total value of UPI transactions reached Rs 299.74 trillion (€2.7 trillion, $3.4 trillion).

Former Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan broke his silence for the first time since he resigned following massive youth protests.

Speaking at a ceremony on Saturday, Pradhan said: "Gen Z is our children. Some people attempted to mislead them."

Pradhan's  acknowledgment of the protests and his resignation came some 15 days after he quit as the education minister.

Pradhan said he "suffered" because of Gen Z's stubbornness but had come to realize that the new generation must be understood rather than resisted.

Speaking about his resignation, Pradhan said he had approached Prime Minister Narendra Modi and offered to resign from the Union Council of Ministers.

"The post was not important to me," Pradhan told a gathering at an event at GM University in Bhubaneswar, according to Indian news agency Press Trust of India.

Pradhan's resignation was the biggest demand made by the young protesters, led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).

The protests were triggered over exam irregularities in competitive exams, especially the NEET exam, which is a key requirement for those wishing to enter medical schools across India.

Reportedly, at least 21 students had taken their own lives after the NEET exam was cancelled because of a question paper leak. It was then held at a later date.

https://www.dw.com/en/australia-jetstar-.title: Australia: Jetstar, Qatar Airways planes almost collide on Sydney Airport tarmac
https://www.dw.com/en/australia-jetstar-.text:
A flight crew member was injured in a near-miss collision on the runway at Australia's Sydney Airport. An investigation has been launched to determine what caused the incident.

Two passenger aircraft —  a Jetstar and a Qatar Airways plane —  came close to crashing into each other on the tarmac at Australia's  busiest Sydney Airport on Sunday.

A crew member was injured and the incident has triggered a probe by the country's safety regulators.

The Jetstar A320 was taxiing for takeoff to the Gold Coast in the state of Queensland when its flight crew saw the Qatar Airways Boeing 777 —  which was being towed by an aircraft tug —  in close proximity on a crossing taxiway, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) said in a statement.

"Both aircraft were stopped abruptly", the statement said, leading to a Jestar cabin crew member moving through the cabin being injured and the connection between the 777 nose gear and aircraft tug suffering damage.

The injured crew member was treated by paramedics.

The ATSB said that investigators were gathering data from both the planes, air traffic control, and interviewing crew and tug operators to determine the cause of the near collision.

The regulator put out a call for witnesses at the airport to send in any visuals of the incident.

Jetstar —  which is a low-cost subsidiary of  Australia's national carrier Qantas — said it was also conducting its own investigation.

"Our aircraft was following ⁠instructions ​by Air Traffic Control when the ​pilots were forced to brake firmly after another aircraft came in ​close proximity," a ‌Jetstar spokesperson said.

There was no immediate statement from Qatar Airways, which is the flag carrier of Qatar.

Meanwhile, flights at Sydney Airport were experiencing delays following the incident, government agency Airservices Australia said.

Sunday's incident ⁠comes a day after Sydney Airport witnessed widespread delays ⁠sparked by Airservices Australia authorizing  "departure spacing" due to roster issues with air traffic controllers.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-germa.title: Germany news: German kidnapped in Niger released — Algeria
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-germa.text:
Algeria says a German citizen has been released after a "criminal armed group" kidnapped him in Niger for two weeks. Meanwhile, Germany is moving to counter the threats posed by drones. Follow DW.

Here is a roundup of the stories from and about Germany that are hitting the headlines on the weekend of August 8-9, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Algeria said on Saturday that a German citizen kidnapped by an armed criminal group some two weeks ago in neighboring Niger was safe and in the hands of the Algerian military.

The German national was taken in charge by the Algerian army's security services on Friday, according to a statement from the Defense Ministry shared on the official Algerian news agency.

He has now been taken on a special flight from Guezzam in the far south to the Boufarik military base near the capital Algiers, it said, adding that he was in "good health" and would be handed to German authorities "at a later date."

No details were provided on how the German national was freed.

A spokesperson for Germany's Foreign Office confirmed to the German DPA news agency that the federal government was aware of the case.

Niger, which has been under military rule since a July 2023 coup, has in the past few years been wracked by violence from jihadis linked to the al-Qaeda or the "Islamic State" (IS) terrorist groups.

Several states have lifted a rule banning most trucks from using motorways on Sundays and public holidays in view of the low river water levels currently hampering cargo vessels.

The DPA news agency reported that a number of trucks have already been sighted on motorways in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW).

The NRW transport minister, Oliver Krischer, said that "this exceptional regulation allows us to ensure that delivery chains are maintained and supply shortages are avoided."

Industrial associations have welcomed the lifting of the truck ban.

But one of Germany's main unions, Verdi, has criticized the move.

"This measure comes at the cost of employees in the transport and logistics branch and calls into question the legal protection of Sundays and public holidays as days of rest and recreation," said Uwe Köpke, who heads the union's postal services, freight forwarding and logistics department.

Lower Saxony, Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland are so far the only other states to have lifted the ban as one of the measures announced by Transport Minister Steffen Bilger last week to mitigate the economic effect of the cargo shipping shortfalls.

In NRW and Lower Saxony, the suspension of the ban is to run initially until August 31, and in Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland until September 30 at the latest.

In NRW, all trucks will also be able to use the motorways on Saturdays during the day in the current summer holidays as an exemption to an existing regulation.

New preliminary data released on Sunday has shown that German exports to China fell more than 12% year-on-year from January through June. German imports from China rose 8.9%.

That raises the trade deficit to about €55 billion ($63.6 billion) from €40 billion for the same period in 2025.

The data from the state-run agency Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI) reflects the decreasing reliance by Chinese firms on European imports.

They show that although China remains Germany's top trading partner, the Asian powerhouse is now only the ninth-biggest market for German goods, with far smaller economies like Austria and Switzerland buying more from Germany in 2026.

As recently as 2021, China was Germany's second-biggest ​export market.

The US remains Germany's single-biggest foreign market, despite a drop in German exports there amid protectionist tariffs introduced under President Donald Trump.

The CEO of arms giant Rheinmetall, Armin Papperger, has said he will not be intimidated despite the many threats that have been made to his safety.

"These jobs must be done, and anyone that can't take the pressure doesn't belong in this job," he told the DPA news agency, saying "chickening out" was no option in his field.

Pappberger, 63, who is believed to be a possible target of Russian murder plots, is under constant police protection at a level similar to that given to Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Rheinmetall is supplying large quantities of weapons to Ukraine amid the Russian invasion, potentially putting the company in Moscow's crosshairs.

Germany's domestic intelligence services recently called on employees in the defense sector to be very vigilant amid the threat of espionage and sabotage by Russian state agencies.

Germany is establishing a new drone security research facility as it seeks to counter a growing threat from UAVs that are possibly under foreign control, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has told Sunday's edition of the Bild tabloid.

"The arms race in drone technology requires dedicated research units to keep pace," he said.

He said the new center, to be established on August 18 at a German Aerospace Center (DLR) test airport in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, would develop and test technologies to protect against drones.

His remarks come after a number of incidents involving drones in the past week raised security concerns.

You can read more on Dobrindt's statements on security here.

The DW newsroom in Bonn says a warm guten Morgen to its readers as we resume our coverage of all things German on Sunday.

Concerns about national security amid a myriad of threats are featuring largely in today's headlines, with, for example, the interior minister warning of hybrid warfare after several drone incidents.

Some of those threats even target particular people, as the CEO of arms giant Rheinmetall, Armin Papperger, is experiencing.

And nature itself is also posing a security challenge, with the lack of water in the Rhine and other rivers having a widening impact on the economy and beyond.

Read on for more on these and other stories.

We are pausing our coverage as the clock is about to strike midnight here in Bonn. Join us again on Sunday, when we will update this blog with the latest news from Germany.

Sven Schulze, state premier and the CDU's candidate in the upcoming regional election in Saxony-Anhalt has slammed the AfD for its xenophobia, and underscored his state's reliance on exports and foreign workers.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's most important river is running low unusually early in the year.

Ships are still moving on the Rhine, but falling water levels are forcing many to carry lighter loads. Professor Kerstin Stahl, a hydrologist at the University of Freiburg, explains what is driving the drought and why the consequences reach far beyond shipping.

Some 10,000 people protested in the eastern German city of Plauen to call for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's resignation and for new elections to be held immediately.

While the "Unity for Germany" protest was officially independent of political parties, a local pro-democracy group warned that some of the rally's organizers are right-wing extremists.

"The event is being promoted by relevant far-right channels; on Facebook, the comments on the demonstration contain hateful remarks, and the calls to action spread antisemitic and ethno-nationalist narratives," the Alliance for Democracy, Tolerance and Civil Courage said.

Apart from the government's resignation and new elections, the protesters' 11 demands also include:

The immediate deportation of 'all convicted, criminal and illegal migrants'

A cheaper nationwide monthly travel pass, for €29 ($33.50)

Reform to public service broadcasting

Scrapping the carbon dioxide tax

Introducing a direct democracy model like in Switzerland

The protesters also chanted "We are the people," the slogan that was used at pro-democracy rallies during the peaceful revolution of 1989 in East Germany that preceded the end of the former German Democratic Republic.

Many German national flags, as well as banners of the historical Kingdom of Saxony — often used by the far-right Free Saxons party — were seen at the rally, as were blue peace flags with white doves, the German news agency dpa reported.

Around 800 people demonstrated in Berlin, calling for the Federal Constitutional Court to review political parties suspected of right-wing extremism.

Eleven such demonstrations were planned across Germany on Saturday. The "Prüf," which translates to "check" or "examine," initiative, founded by activist Nico Semsrott, is behind the rallies.

Citing a legal opinion published in late June by the Society for Civil Rights that declared the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party unconstitutional, speakers called for a corresponding review by the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe.

Many of the demonstrators' posters bore the slogan, "Examine today — protect tomorrow."

However, the Bundestag, the Bundesrat, or the federal government must file a motion to ban the party in order to initiate such a review.

In early May 2025, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution classified the AfD as a "confirmed far-right extremist movement," but suspended the designation after a legal challenge.

In February, a Cologne court said the agency can’t use the designation while the court evaluates the party’s lawsuit.

The AfD vehemently rejects accusations of extremism.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Several people were injured after a German tour bus overturned in Norway, Norwegian public broadcaster NRK reported, citing police sources.

According to the report, some 34 German tourists were on board.

Several passengers sustained minor injuries in the incident, while four were taken to hospital.

The bus was traveling to the Trondelag region of central Norway.

The bus reportedly overturned on a bend of the E6 highway and ended up lying on its side in the grass beside the road.

The cause of the accident was initially unclear.

According to NRK, no other vehicle was involved.

Six men and women from six different countries on Friday ended their 100-day stay in cramped, artificially lit isolation as part of a study to prepare future space missions to the moon, Mars and beyond.

The participants, from Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland and Portugal, are now able to return to their daily lives — following a recovery phase — after leaving the simulation facility at the German Aerospace Centre (DLR) in the western city of Cologne.

The goal of the SOLIS100 study was conducted on behalf of the European Space Agency (ESA) and aimed to investigate the effects of long-duration space missions  on health and performance.

The participants had to live from non-perishable foodstuffs and were not allowed personal contact with family or friends.
 
 Every day, they carried out scientific work, medical data collection, a strict exercise program and station maintenance.

Wolfram Weimer, the commissioner for culture and media, has become the first member of the federal government to call for FIFA President Gianni Infantino to step down.

"Infantino has seriously damaged world football with his planned sell-off of the World Cup," he told the German DPA news agency on Saturday.

"He has lost the trust of the European football community and should not stand for re-election next year," he said.

Weimer called on the German Football Federation (DFB) to show "active resistance" against Infantino.

"With its 24,000 clubs and eight million members, the DFB is the largest sports federation in the world (by individual registered members). Its voice carries weight," he said.

Infantino has faced a storm of criticism since he unveiled plans last week to sell World Cup rights to private investors for billions.

He withdrew the proposal after major protests, including a threat by UEFA to boycott the World Cup.

Two drones were sighted flying late on Thursday above a military base in Mechernich in western Germany, near the Belgian border,  authorities said on Saturday.

A German armed forces spokesperson said the drones were sighted at around 10 p.m. (2000 GMT) over the Bundeswehr base, which media say hosts personnel responsible for the maintenance of US Patriot air defense systems.

Among other things, US Patriot systems play a key role in defending Ukraine against Russian aerial attacks.

The sighting in Mechernich comes just two days after a drone carrying explosives was found near a runway at Leipzig/Halle Airport, with media saying it was discovered near several Ukrainian cargo planes.

A number of sightings of drones at sensitive sites in Germany in recent times has raised concerns about the penetration of NATO airspace by the unmanned aircraft and the possibility of hostile foreign involvement.

German government officials have not blamed any foreign countries publicly ​for the Leipzig incident, ⁠but some lawmakers have accused Russia of being behind it.

The Russian Embassy in Berlin on Friday dismissed the Leipzig event as a "fabricated provocation" and said Russia was once more being accused of hostile actions without evidence.

https://www.dw.com/en/canada-british-col.title: Canada: British Columbia declares emergency as fires spread
https://www.dw.com/en/canada-british-col.text:
More than 20,000 people have been forced from their homes by out-of-control wildfires in Canada's British Columbia, where 105 blazes are currently burning.

Canadian officials on Saturday declared a state of emergency in British Columbia after more than 20,000 people were ordered to flee a fast-moving wildfire.

Describing the intensity of the blaze, British Columbia Premier David Eby said a fire official compared it to "a bomb going off."

"He described flames on a 100-foot (30-meter) tree, flames going 200 feet above that, and the fire creating its own weather system, which creates lightning," Eby said.

"Homes have been lost, and properties have been destroyed. Some people became trapped as conditions changed very quickly, and needed to be rescued," he added.

The fire, first reported Friday evening, grew rapidly overnight, triggering widespread evacuation orders.

By Saturday, it had spread to about 9,500 hectares (23,500 acres), prompting all 12,000 residents of the Summerland district to evacuate.

The Summerland blaze is one of many fires challenging emergency crews across British Columbia.

The province has seen 70 new wildfires over the past week, and 105 are currently burning, according to British Columbia Minister of Forests Ravi Parmar.

Fires have scorched 4 million hectares in Canada in 2026, according to the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Center.

Blazes flared up in several regions, including Ontario and Quebec, this year as hot, dry conditions fueled fires in dense forest areas.

In recent years, Canada has faced a growing number of destructive wildfire seasons.

https://www.dw.com/en/fifa-warns-against.title: FIFA warns against 'concerted effort' to undermine Gianni Infantino
https://www.dw.com/en/fifa-warns-against.text:
Pressure is mounting on the FIFA president Gianni Infantino after plans to sell a stake in the World Cup collapsed and fresh allegations emerged relating to his time at UEFA.

FIFA warned against what it calls a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organization and its president, Gianni Infantino.

The statement, issued late on Saturday, comes amid a growing dispute over Infantino's leadership after the failed plan to create a subsidiary to run the men's World Cup and other events, with up to a 20% stake offered to external investors.

The proposal drew criticism from European governing body UEFA, which threatened to boycott future World Cups, as well as several national associations and senior FIFA officials, and prompted calls for Infantino to resign.

Amid the growing criticism Infantino persuaded FIFA's Board of Management to express its full support for him at a crisis meeting in Rabat, Morocco, on Wednesday.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The pressure on Infantino intensified on Friday when British newspaper the Daily Telegraph reported a six-figure sum was paid to a female employee alleged to have been in a relationship with him during his time as UEFA general secretary.

UEFA confirmed a departure payment and said it also funded her MBA course, stating both were in line with regulations at the time.

A FIFA spokesman told the Telegraph on Friday: "FIFA president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue."

Responding to the latest scrutiny, FIFA said on Saturday, without directly mentioning the Telegraph report, "recent reporting has included unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims concerning FIFA and its President."

The fallout over the shelved private investment plan has overshadowed Infantino's bid for a fourth term as FIFA president.

After this week's crisis meeting, UEFA said it no longer has confidence in him, and Norwegian FA President Lise Klaveness called for his resignation.

Despite the controversy, Infantino retains strong backing among FIFA members, with the Confederation of African Football (CAF) unanimously supporting his leadership and South American governing body CONMEBOL opposing any attempt to remove him without a vote of all member associations.

FIFA said that those who lacked the support of its member associations should not seek to achieve "allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through FIFA's established democratic processes."

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-interior-m.text:
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says attacks by foreign powers have become a constant threat to Germany. His remarks come just days after an explosive-laden drone was found at Leipzig airport.

Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt on Sunday warned that hybrid warfare attacks had become a daily threat to the country.

"We're not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," Dobrindt told the newspaper Bild am Sonntag following the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

"Espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, or covert operations by foreign powers aimed at destabilizing Germany or inflicting direct harm are a constant reality," Dobrindt said.

He also noted that the country is stepping up research into drones to address new security threats.

A new drone security research center will be established later in August at a German Aerospace Center (DLR) test airport in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, Dobrindt said.

On Saturday, Germany's armed forces confirmed that two drones had been spotted late on Thursday over a German military base in Mechernich in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia near the Belgian border.

The drones were detected at around 10 p.m. (2000 GMT) over the Bundeswehr base, a German armed forces spokesperson said.

German media reported that the base hosts personnel responsible for the maintenance of US Patriot air defense systems, which play a key role in defending Ukraine against Russian aerial attacks.

The sighting in Mechernich comes just two days after the discovery of a drone carrying explosives a Ukrainian transport plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport, an incident Dobrindt called a "hybrid attack scenario."

While German government officials have refrained from publicly blaming any foreign country over the Leipzig incident, some lawmakers have pointed fingers at Russia, which has been at war with Ukraine since ​its full-scale invasion of the country in 2022.
