https://www.dw.com/en/nigeria-marries-1-.title: Nigeria marries 1,500 couples in mass wedding
https://www.dw.com/en/nigeria-marries-1-.text:
The government describes the program as a way to support low-income families and promote social stability. Among those married were people who lost family members in violent attacks.

Some 1,500 couples got married at a mass wedding organized by Abba Kabir Yusuf, the governor of Kano state, in northern Nigeria.

The regional government described the two-day event as a way to support low-income families and promote social stability.

"The whole idea for the marriage is to help our families and we husbands who are not financially stable to marry; that's why the government is helping us get married," groom Abubakar Aliyu Musa told the Associated Press.

This is the second time Yusuf's administration has organized a mass wedding.

According to Kano's regional government, each bride received a dowry of 200,000 naira ($147, €127) and support to set up a small business.

The couples were also given household items including beds, mattresses and blankets.

The couples underwent screening and counseling before the wedding.

Governor Yusuf described the program as a "bold social intervention aimed at restoring hope and supporting dignified family life in Kano."

"The program was designed not only to assist women who might otherwise struggle to afford marriage, but also to strengthen families and promote social stability in the state," he said.

Among those who participated in the mass wedding were people who lost family members in violent attacks.

One of them was Haruna Bashir, who lost his wife and six children in an attack earlier in the year. Daurawa hailed the ceremony as a step toward Bashir "gradually returning to normal life" after having "hardly interacted with people … since the tragic incident."

Nigeria has been grappling with a major security crisis for years, particularly in the country's north, which is regularly hit by raids and attacks by Islamist insurgents and organized gangs.

Many armed groups in Nigeria also kidnap schoolchildren to demand large ransoms.

On Wednesday, the Nigerian government announced the release of 308 people who had been abducted.

https://www.dw.com/en/kosovo-pm-kurti-eg.title: Kosovo PM Kurti egged in parliament amid political crisis
https://www.dw.com/en/kosovo-pm-kurti-eg.text:
Kosovo has held three elections in over two years. Albin Kurti's ruling Vetevendosje is struggling to garner the two-thirds majority required to elect a president.

Kosovo's parliament was suspended on Saturday after an opposition lawmaker threw eggs at caretaker Prime Minister Albin Kurti.

"Shame on you!" Time Kadrijaj of the conservative opposition Alliance for the Future of Kosovo (AAK) party shouted in parliament before hurling eggs at Kurti.

In response, Kurti said that he was "happy to pay this price" if it was the cost of dialogue.

Kurti's left-wing Vetevendosje (VV) party is known for its own parliamentary disruptions, with party representatives launching tear gas in the chamber in 2018 and also on multiple occasions in 2015.

The incident comes after days of negotiations as Kurti attempts to gain enough opposition support to elect a new president amid Kosovo's broader political crisis.

The Balkan country has held three elections in over two years.

Kurti achieved his parliamentary majority with ethnic minority MPs in a December election that followed an inconclusive vote in February 2025.

His VV party's share of the vote fell from 51% to 43% in a snap election in June, but it maintained a parliamentary majority alongside ethnic minority allies.

However, Kurti requires a two-thirds majority in parliament to elect a president.

The current negotiations seem to have ground to another stalemate, with neither side having agreed to a candidate.

A constitutional deadline to elect a speaker of parliament expired on Friday. Opposition lawmakers have threatened legal action over Kurti's request for more time to negotiate.

Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008 after the 1998-99 war, which ended with Serbia's withdrawal following a NATO bombing campaign.

Kosovo has been recognized by over half of the world's countries, including the United States and most European Union countries.

Belgrade considers Kosovo to be part of Serbia.

https://www.dw.com/en/thousands-attend-p.title: Thousands attend Prague Pride parade
https://www.dw.com/en/thousands-attend-p.text:
Participants observed a minute of silence in memory of the victims of a van ramming near the CSD parade in Berlin. The march was accompanied by enhanced security measures.

Tens of thousands of people marched through Czech capital of Prague on Saturday as part of LGBTQ+ Pride celebrations.

The festival is to last for a week. The theme of this year's event is "Times are changing."

At the start of the parade, participants observed a minute of silence in memory of the victims of a van ramming near the Cristopher Street Day (CSD) parade in Berlin two weeks ago.

The July 25 attack killed one person and injured around 31 others.

The Saturday march in Prague was accompanied by enhanced security measures, including the deployment of hundreds of police officers and a de-escalation team.

Participants were also told to carry banners by hand or to use plastic poles rather than wooden poles.

"As every year, the aim of the festival is to raise awareness of LGBT+ issues, to show how this community lives in the Czech Republic and that it is still waiting for equal rights," the director of Prague Pride, Kamila Frohlichova, was cited by Germany's DPA news agency as saying.

According to police reports, there were no major incidents.

A group of counter-demonstrators also gathered along part of the march's trajectory.

The march began at Wenceslas Square in central Prague around noon (10:00 UTC/GMT) and arrived at Stvanice island in the Vltava River that passes through the city at around 2:30 p.m. local time, according to Czech media.

A musical program was held once the march reached its terminus and the festivities continued into the night.

https://www.dw.com/en/us-senate-confirms.title: US Senate confirms Trump loyalist Todd Blanche as new AG
https://www.dw.com/en/us-senate-confirms.text:
Republicans dropped their opposition and confirmed President Donald Trump's former defense lawyer to a Cabinet position. Now, Todd Blanche will act as the nation's top law enforcement officer.

The US Senate has narrowly approved President Donald Trump's nominee for the job of attorney general, making Todd Blanche the nation's top law enforcement officer in an early morning vote on Saturday.

The Republican-controlled body delivered a 50-49 vote to confirm the controversial Trump loyalist.

Louisiana Republican Bill Cassidy was the last-minute convert this time, supplying the crucial deciding vote after his colleagues Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Susan Collins of Maine jumped ship to join the chamber's Democrats in voting against Blanche's appointment.

In explaining her opposition, Murkowski said the country was in need of an attorney general "who will check the worst impulses of this administration."

On the Senate floor, Cassidy outlined his own conversion, saying he believed Blanche's relationship with Trump would make him effective at pushing back against Trump's demands.

Blanche, a former federal prosecutor who was Trump's personal defense lawyer and had been serving as acting attorney general since April, wrote on X, "I am deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me to lead the Department of Justice as our great nation's 88th attorney general."

There is great concern that Trump sees Blanche as "his lawyer," something that he has often openly expressed the need for in the position of attorney general, which is supposed to be independent.

"The attorney general is supposed to be the people's lawyer," Illinois Democratic Senator Dick Durbin said during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Tuesday.

"Mr. Blanche," added Durbin, the Committee's ranking Democrat, "continues to operate as the president's personal lawyer, treating the Justice Department like a law firm serving one client — the president."

On Saturday, Durbin said it would be a "serious mistake" to give Blanche control at the DOJ, "If there is ever a moment in history when we need an attorney general above reproach, who is clearly dedicated to ending corruption, even at the highest level of our government, it's right now."

During his time in office, Trump has often railed against attorneys general for not being aggressive enough in pursuing his agenda — most often when it is tied to retribution against his political opponents.

Jeff Sessions, Bill Barr and Pam Bondi all fell out of the president's good graces for failing to fully satisfy his legal desires.

Blanche is seen as a staunch ally who has no qualms doing the president's bidding.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Blanche previously defended Trump against criminal charges over the falsification of business records with the intent of hiding an affair with an adult movie actress, as well as another for the mishandling of classified documents in his attempt to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election.

Both cases were dropped after Trump won reelection in 2024.

During his time at the DOJ, Blanche has handled portions of the case against deceased sex offender and presidential friend Jeffrey Epstein — most prominently overseeing the release of millions of documents tied to the case, as well as the transfer of Epstein associate Ghislaine Maxwell to a more comfortable, minimum-security federal prison in Texas after he personally met with her.

Under Blanche and his predecessor Bondi, the DOJ has lost thousands of employees through firing, resignation or voluntary departure.

Blanche's candidacy was vehemently opposed by Democrats, and even some Republican lawmakers had qualms with his avoidance of forthright answers about a dubious $1.776 billion (€1.5 billion) compensation fund for presidential political allies — including those who stormed the US Capital on January 6, 2021 — accusing the federal government of unfair treatment; and DOJ directives that would see the president, his two eldest sons and the Trump Organization shielded from tax audits and penalties for life.

Two retiring Republican senators, John Cornyn (Texas) and Thom Tillis (North Carolina), had loudly proclaimed that they would vote against Blanche's appointment unless the compensation fund was dropped.

He assured them that it would be, while also saying that the Trumps' tax immunity would only be applied "retroactively" and not to future filings, clearing the way for Saturday's confirmation vote.

https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-russia-pou.title: Ukraine: Russia pounds Kyiv as Zelenskyy visits Serbia
https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-russia-pou.text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is visiting Serbia, a country that has traditionally been friendly with Moscow, as Russia strikes the Kyiv region once again.

As Russia continues its relentless bombardment of Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is making his first visit to Serbia, a European country that has maintained friendly relations with Russia despite the latter's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Zelenskyy arrived in Belgrade Friday evening and had dinner with his Serbian counterpart, Aleksandar Vucic. They met again for talks at the presidential palace on Saturday.

Later, Zelenskyy wrote on X that he and Vucic had discussed ways to strengthen infrastructure in both countries, including ports and railways, as well as economic development, reconstruction, and job creation in Ukraine and Serbia.

Representatives from both countries signed a memorandum of understanding regarding agricultural and food safety cooperation.

Zelenskyy added that the leaders also discussed the challenges of the upcoming winter in Ukraine, heavily hit by ⁠Russian attacks on energy facilities, and relations with the European Union. He also thanked Vucic for a new package of humanitarian support for Ukraine.

Vucic said that Serbia will continue to support Ukraine's independence and territorial integrity, including the territories that Russia has seized since 2014.

"You have never heard a single bad word about our country, not from Volodymyr Zelenskyy nor anyone else in Ukraine, and I am extremely grateful to our Ukrainian friends for that," Vucic said.

The remark appeared to address the fact that Ukraine refuses to recognize Kosovo's independence, which was declared in 2008. Belgrade considers Kosovo to be part of Serbia.

Vucic said he was skeptical that either Serbia or Ukraine would quickly join the European Union. However, he added that Belgrade would support Kyiv's bid.

Serbia has repeatedly refused to put sanctions on Moscow. This has angered the EU and delayed Belgrade's path to joining the bloc.

Both leaders also said their countries want to improve economic cooperation and finalize a free trade agreement by the end of the year. ​

Despite its dependence on Russian energy, Serbia has supplied nonmilitary aid to Ukraine. The Kremlin has accused Serbian firms of selling munitions to Ukraine, but Vucic has denied this claim.

Vucic traveled to Ukraine for a regional summit in 2025 and again this year. Despite pledging aid to Ukraine, he has refrained from signing a formal declaration of support for Ukraine in the war.

The meeting came after at least four people, including a child, were killed in overnight Russian air attacks on Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, and the surrounding region, officials said on Saturday.

"Last night, Russia killed three people in Pukhivka, Kyiv region, with drone strikes," Zelenskyy wrote on X. He added that the victims were a grandfather, a grandmother and their 3-year-old grandson.

Authorities said three other members of the family and a neighbor who came to their aid were hospitalized.

Ukraine's air force reported downing or intercepting 135 of the 151 drones that Russia launched overnight.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's General Staff announced that the military had attacked Russia's Ilsky and Syzran oil refineries overnight, resulting in fires at both locations.

https://www.dw.com/en/war-terror-diploma.title: War, terror, diplomacy: What if Israel takes Al-Aqsa Mosque?
https://www.dw.com/en/war-terror-diploma.text:
Reports from Jerusalem suggest that Israeli authorities are taking over one of Islam's holiest sites, the Al-Aqsa Mosque. If they do, experts say anything could happen, from war to terrorism to ending diplomatic ties.

The statement issued after this week's meeting in Jordan was blunt about what might happen next.

Israeli infringements on one of Islam's holiest sites, the Al-Aqsa Mosque in east Jerusalem, could lead to "a religious conflict with repercussions that will extend beyond the region and threaten regional and international peace and security," the foreign ministers of 10 countries belonging to the Arab League said after Wednesday's emergency meeting in Amman, Jordan. The statement was also signed by ministers from Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, and Malaysia.

Jordan's foreign minister called the meeting because of mounting evidence that the Israeli government is surreptitiously changing a decades-old agreement meant to ensure intercommunal peace at the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, an area of great religious significance to Muslims, Jews, and Christians.

"We warn that tampering with the status quo … could trigger a religious conflict that will reverberate beyond Palestine and Jordan into the whole Muslim world," Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi told the UK newspaper the Guardian before the meeting.

Israel's Foreign Ministry issued a response, saying the statement was inaccurate and Jerusalem "has never been more open and accessible to worshippers of all faiths."

Al-Aqsa is considered the third-holiest site in Islam, after Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia. The compound, also known as the Temple Mount, is also Judaism's holiest site — two Jewish temples are thought to have stood there — and it is also of significance to Christians for its biblical connections to Jesus Christ's life.

Al-Aqsa also bears a lot of political weight because the mosque is seen by many as the embodiment of Palestinian identity, a flashpoint in a city sought as the capital of any eventual Palestinian state.

Because of the site's importance, when Israel first occupied East Jerusalem in 1967, it was deemed in the interests of Israeli national security to keep allowing Muslims to worship there. Jews could only visit and would not be allowed to pray there. Instead Jewish visitors perform religious rituals at the wall below the mosque, known as the Western or Wailing Wall.

Jordan was also allowed to continue its century-old custodianship of the site, and today the mosque is administered by a religious trust called the Islamic Waqf, paid for by Jordan at about $20 million (€17 million) annually. Israeli authorities still take care of security there.

This delicate compromise is known as the "status quo." But recent reports indicate that the situation has been changing.

Residents of Jerusalem say dozens of mosque officials employed by Jordan have been prevented from entering Al-Aqsa this year.

The number of Muslim worshipers halved during 2025, according to Jerusalem-based monitors. More Jewish worshipers are being allowed in and are increasingly overtly performing rituals, something forbidden for decades, including by Jewish religious authorities. The Times of Israel reported in January that police openly let Jewish visitors take printed prayer sheets onto the site for the first time.

In June, there were also reports of an Israeli-US plan to turn the mosque area into a "multifaith center," although US Secretary of State Marco Rubio later denied any knowledge of such a plan.

This is not the first time that the governments of Muslim-majority countries and activists in Jerusalem have issued such warnings.

For decades, Jewish fringe groups, often referred to as the Temple Mount movement, have demanded that they be allowed to pray at the site. The most extremist of these groups say they want to demolish the mosque and construct a new Jewish temple.

At first they were mostly ignored, Jerusalem-based lawyer Daniel Seidemann wrote in 2025. Seidemann is the founder of Terrestrial Jerusalem, an organization that tracks such developments in the city. But, he said, that "radical fringe" has become more mainstream. "Over time, the Temple Mount movements, backed by more than 100 rabbis associated with the settler movement in the West Bank, became more visible, more vocal and more provocative," Seidemann said.

"This crisis has been decades in the making," said Omar Rahman, a fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs. "There's been an effort from religious extremists to destroy the Al-Aqsa Mosque since at least the 1980s, when plots to do that were uncovered. But those groups and those ideologies have gained more representation within the Israeli [parliament] Knesset today."

An October 2025 report by the Ir Amim Association, which focuses on Israeli-Palestinian issues in Jerusalem, found that politicians, including from within Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's national-conservative Likud party, frequently break rules around the Al-Aqsa status quo but never face consequences from authorities.

"In practice, Netanyahu allows and normalizes grave breaches of the status quo," the association reported. Yet Netanyahu "continues to declare that his government remains committed to the status quo and nothing has changed."

"It would be very unwise to make any sort of prediction," Joost Hiltermann, a special adviser for the Middle East and North Africa at the Crisis Group think tank, told DW.

But, Hiltermann said, it's essential to consider that "while the fate of Jerusalem as a city may be an overriding Palestinian concern, the fate of the holy sites of Islam in Jerusalem is an abiding global Muslim concern. Not just for the Arab world but also for the largest Muslim countries: Indonesia, Pakistan, Bangladesh. So any Israeli attempt to change the status quo would face a global backlash."

In the past, changes have led to violence. In 2000, Ariel Sharon, an Israeli right-wing opposition leader at the time, visited Al-Aqsa — an event that was seen as one reason for the Palestinian uprising known as the Second Intifada. In 2017, when Israeli authorities erected cameras and metal detectors at the site, it led to deadly protests.

One likely outcome of further infringements of the status quo would be major public protests in Muslim-majority countries. "While the Arab regimes would be reluctant to engage in any sort of confrontation with Israel, their publics will be outraged," Hiltermann said. "The regimes will have to manage that, and they will try to do so by launching vigorous criticism of Israel, not followed by any action — they've become very good at that. The same will be true for Indonesia and others. But all of them may have a hard time controlling domestic fury."

Rahman said the  consequences of further Israeli infringement would depend on how radically things changed at Al-Aqsa. "It would trigger a fairly significant reaction, but the extent of it is hard to say," he said. "It could spark a catastrophic religious war or maybe just a diplomatic reaction, or maybe it simply adds to the well of grievance against Israel," he added.

Because Al Aqsa is so important in Islam, it could also make it hard for some countries to resist an upsurge in anti-Israel feeling, even if they might want to, he adds. For example, countries like Morocco and the United Arab Emirates that normalized relations with Israel might feel forced to reverse that.

Because of Al Aqsa's significance to Palestinian identity, the Gaza-based militant group Hamas often says it is defending the mosque. Extremist groups with an Islamist background have also used defense of Al Aqsa to recruit members.

https://www.dw.com/en/bulgaria-unknown-d.title: Bulgaria: Unknown drone explodes near Romanian border
https://www.dw.com/en/bulgaria-unknown-d.text:
A drone that entered Bulgaria's airspace exploded near the Romanian border and the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline, the Bulgarian prime minister said. Bulgaria summoned the Ukrainian ambassador for consultations.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said that a drone entered Bulgaria's airspace from the north and exploded near the Romanian border on Saturday morning.

According to the prime minister, there were no casualties or damage to infrastructure, as the drone exploded in a sunflower field 100 meters from the border with Romania. He noted that neither of the two neighboring countries had detected the drone.

Radev added that the incident occurred about 1,000 meters from Bulgaria's compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine.

"We will continue to monitor the situation and strengthen surveillance. Following this incident, we will also redeploy border police anti-drone detection and countermeasure capabilities from the border with Turkey to the border with Romania," Radev said.

Speaking after an extraordinary meeting of his Cabinet's security council, Radev did not specify where the drone came from or what type it was.

However, he said it was believed the drone was carrying a significant amount of explosives given the strength of the blast and the black smoke it produced.

When asked if the drone was civilian or military, Radev said that there was photographic evidence available. However, because the drone was damaged in the explosion, it was impossible to determine its type.

After analysing the debris, the Bulgarian Defense Ministry said the drone was of a type "widely used by the Ukrainian military." According to the AFP news agency, Bulgaria also summoned the Ukrainian ambassador for consultations.

Kyiv said it was "in close contact with the Bulgarian side to clarify the circumstances" of the incident, the latest case of a drone straying into NATO airspace as Ukraine fights off Russia's invasion.

"We can say with certainty that the Ukrainian Armed Forces did not intentionally direct any assets toward Bulgaria," Ukraine's foreign ministry spokesman Georgiy Tykhyi said.

Radev said the drone was not detected in Bulgarian or Romanian airspace because such drones are difficult to detect due to their small size.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In recent months, there have been an increasing number of incidents involving drones in Eastern European countries that are both EU and NATO members and that support Ukraine in its four-and-a-half-year war against Russia's invasion.

The origin of the drone that exploded in Bulgaria and its potential connection to Russia or Ukraine are still unclear. Radev said that teams from the Bulgarian border police and the Ministry of Defense are working to determine the origin of the drone.

Bulgaria's Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said the incident would be raised at a meeting of the North Atlantic Council early next week.

Romania, which borders Ukraine, has faced frequent drone incursions, including crashes on its territory, such as a May incident in which a drone struck an apartment building.

Earlier this week in Germany, an explosive-laden drone was defused at Leipzig Airport, in what Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt called a "new level of danger."

https://www.dw.com/en/eu-holds-talks-wit.title: EU holds talks with big tech over Ceuta misinformation
https://www.dw.com/en/eu-holds-talks-wit.text:
EU digital chief Henna Virkkunen has called for closer monitoring of social media platforms moving forward, amid the spread of misinformation during the recent migrant influx at Spain's Ceuta.

EU Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy Henna Virkkunen has called on social media giants to exercise closer monitoring of their platforms for misinformation, especially "during crisis situations."

Virkkunen was referring to last week's Ceuta border crisis, which European, Spanish and Moroccan authorities say was exacerbated by the spread of misinformation on social media, including TikTok, Telegram and Meta platforms.

Commissioner Virkkunen addressed the disinformation on social media, calling for greater EU monitoring of platforms during crisis situations.

"Platforms must act decisively in keeping the integrity of the digital space, in particular during crisis situations," she wrote on X.

"Monitoring must increase, cooperation with fact-checkers to be strengthened," Virkkunen wrote after a Friday meeting with representatives from TikTok and Meta — which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.

A number of the estimated 72,000 people who stormed Ceuta from Morocco said they were attracted by false promises disseminated on social media and that they were lied to about the situation.

Spain and Morocco have also exchanged blame, with authorities in Rabat blaming a Spanish Supreme Court ruling that it says was exploited by human traffickers and misrepresented on social media.

Madrid says Morocco should have done a better job at stopping the tens of thousands of migrants who crossed the border.

In the end, Spanish authorities say 80 people were killed during the course of events.

Moroccan authorities reported that 11 people died on their side of the border.

Rights groups estimate the total number of dead at more than 140.

The situation in Ceuta and the circumstances surrounding it have added more fuel to Europe's ongoing political fight over issues related to immigration and security.

In Ceuta, migrants pointed to social media messages and videos announcing that the EU border at Ceuta was suddenly open.

Other posts informed people looking to get to the EU that accommodations would be available once they got to the Spanish territory and that they would be bused to the Spanish mainland from there.

Last week, EU member states convened an emergency meeting at which representatives mulled early-warning systems and social media monitoring as potential levers for improving the bloc's shared assessment capabilities in emerging situations.

Virkkunen said the EU would continue that discussion on Monday.

https://www.dw.com/en/when-german-cathol.title: When German Catholics and Protestants share a church
https://www.dw.com/en/when-german-cathol.text:
Each year, dozens of churches are decommissioned, demolished or repurposed in Germany. But there is a new, unique development.

From the outside, the Catholic church in Mannheim's Neuostheim district appears to be a typical 1950s church building: a relatively simple structure, nothing particularly remarkable about it. Yet St. Pius is truly unique. In this place of worship, Catholic and Protestant Christians celebrate services sharing the same space and taking turns in gathering around the same altar for Communion and the Eucharist.

"It actually began in the early 1970s," Annette Hübner, a Catholic parishioner, told DW. The 57-year-old has lived in the district with her family for more than half a century and is a member of the parish team. At the time, the parish priest of St. Pius was committed to fostering cooperation with the Protestant community and began holding ecumenical services in 1970. Then, at the end of 2009, the nearby Protestant St. Thomas Church sustained extensive water damage, and the building was found to be beyond repair.

What began as a temporary arrangement gradually evolved into a lasting solution. That lasting solution, in turn, grew into a genuine ecumenical friendship.

"It became increasingly clear that it made sense to continue working together," Hübner recalled. A banner on the facade of St. Pius proclaims: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." What may sound like a theological phrase from a Sunday sermon is part of everyday life here, on weekdays as much as on Sundays.

Catholics and Protestants under one roof: Germany is home to 65 so-called Simultankirchen (shared churches). Their joint use was mandated by secular rulers soon after the Reformation and the resulting division of the Church. In some cases, detailed regulations even specified who was allowed to enter the church and at what times. The best-known examples are Altenberg Cathedral near Cologne and St. Peter's Protestant Cathedral in the eastern German city of Bautzen in Saxony.

In hospital and airport chapels, shared use by different Christian denominations is now almost taken for granted. A similar trend, however, is increasingly emerging in ordinary parish communities. Protestant and Catholic churches in Germany's most populous state of North Rhine-Westphalia had already begun addressing the issue in 2017, during the commemorations marking the 500th anniversary of Martin Luther's Reformation.

"What If We All Moved In Together?" is the title of the Practical Guide to the Ecumenical Use of Churches and Parish Halls. The publication presents examples from the dioceses of Cologne and Aachen, as well as Essen, Münster and Paderborn.

The guide repeatedly points to the "accelerating reduction in church buildings." According to official church statistics for 2025, Germany had 24,500 Catholic and 21,100 Protestant churches, ranging from small chapels to grand cathedrals. Each year, dozens of churches are decommissioned, demolished or repurposed.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Examples of new shared church spaces can be found in both western and eastern Germany. In Schildow, on the northern outskirts of Berlin, only one church is expected to remain in use in the future: the larger and more prominent Protestant church. The Archdiocese of Berlin's press office  describes the initiative as "an ecumenical project with exemplary character." Its statement also hints at the significance of this development: "For all the ecumenical openness that is now taken for granted," the Catholic participants still remember "earlier times when even attending a Protestant church was considered a sin."

Catholic bishops in eastern Germany are quite accustomed to celebrating Mass in Protestant churches. For major occasions such as confirmations or parish anniversaries, the generally smaller Catholic churches are often unable to accommodate everyone. In such cases, their Protestant counterparts are often happy to provide the necessary space.

The German Bishops' Conference is also currently addressing the issue and plans to publish a practical guide on the subject. Here, too, the focus is on declining membership, church buildings that are no longer needed, financial constraints, and the potential for shared use.

But St. Pius in Mannheim is different. It is far more than a temporary arrangement born of necessity. Here, the two congregations have developed a deep and wide-ranging form of cooperation. Between 2020 and 2022, the church underwent extensive renovation and redesign. The place where the altar once stood is now occupied by the baptismal font, serving as a shared focal point for both churches. A new altar, crafted from red and grey stone, now stands in the nave.

"The red sandstone comes from the altar of the Protestant church, and the grey travertine from the altar of the Catholic church," Hübner explained. Both were crushed and cast together to form the new altar. Parts of its surface are completely smooth, while others remain rough, with visible grooves and fissures. "It was a beautiful symbol of the relationship between Protestants and Catholics. We want to come together. But there are still points of friction and unresolved questions."

St. Birgitta-Thomas Church in the northern German city of Kiel can likewise look back on decades of ecumenical cooperation. Since 1980, the Catholic parish of St. Birgitta and the Protestant Thomas congregation have shared both the church and the parish hall. Here, too, this "sharing" is governed by carefully defined legal arrangements.

Officially, the church belongs to the Catholic parish, while the parish hall belongs to the Protestant congregation. "But we use both parts of the complex jointly and on an equal footing," Pastor Rebekka Ulrich told DW. With a smile, she adds: "The Protestant side leased the printer, but the Catholic side uses it too."

The 36-year-old pastor sees "an incredible number of points of overlap." These include joint worship services, celebrations and ecumenical dialogue. Each year, the two denominations adopt a shared motto. A hymn of the month, selected alternately from the Protestant hymnal and the Catholic Gotteslob, is sung by the entire congregation during services.

The close partnership extends even to church music: both congregations share the same organist.  "On Sundays, he accompanies the Catholic Mass at 9:30 a.m. and then the Protestant service at 11:00 a.m." If only everything were that simple. As Ulrich explains, the steadily declining number of Catholic priests is creating growing challenges for the Catholic side.

In Mannheim, Annette Hübner described the process as a journey that was long but, in her view, well worth the effort. The number of clergy is declining in both the Catholic and Protestant churches. At the local level, services of the Word conducted without a priest or pastor are becoming increasingly common.

Even the Eastern Christian tradition has found a place here. Since 1971, Mannheim has been home to the "Eastern Church Center Cyril and Methodius," which has been based at St. Pius from the very beginning. Once a month, a Catholic liturgy is celebrated according to the Byzantine Rite. Since the renovation, the church entrance area has included a specially designed space with icons and a symbolic iconostasis. All of this exists under a single church roof.

This article was translated from German.

The Jharkhand government on Saturday held a second round of talks with various factions of the students protesting in Jharkhand over exam irregularities.

While the students said that the government heard their demands, they have decided to continue the protest until the issues are taken up with Chief Minister Hemant Soren before deciding whether to end their hunger strike.

The IMD issued a red alert for the city.

The waterlogged roads brought traffic to a standstill, especially in the adjoining Gurugram.

According to the IMD, the showers were triggered by multiple low-pressure systems passing through Delhi, southwest Uttar Pradesh and neighboring regions.

India has formally assigned names for 27 sites in the northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh, the state which Chinaalso claims.

The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 was passed with an overwhelming vote of 86-11.

India is among the world's top importers of Russian oil and gas, and its purchase of discounted Russian crudes has gone up since the Russia-Ukraine war began in 2022.

With the conflict in the Middle East disrupting energy markets, Russian crude has become an important alternative source for Indian refiners.

https://www.dw.com/en/typhoon-dolphin-hi.text:
A typhoon is lashing Japan's south, causing injuries and blackouts. It is now headed for China, where ports have been closed in preparation.

Typhoon Dolphin raged over Japan's southern regions on Saturday, causing some injuries and blackouts.

Okinawa and Amami island in Kagoshima prefecture were the areas expected to be worst affected.

The storm is expected to move on to China, making landfall along its eastern and southern ‌coast between late Sunday and early Monday, with Chinese authorities shutting down ports and ferry services ahead of the storm.

The China National Meteorological Centre Typhoon Dolphin has said Typhoon Dolphin will probably make landfall between the city of Zhoushan in Zhejiang province and the city of Fuding in Fujian province.

Zhejiang has raised its coastal typhoon alert to its highest level, while ceasing port operations and suspending 162 passenger ferry routes.

The storm is expected to bring rain and strong winds to eastern China, including parts of Shanghai, through August 12.

Some parts of eastern Zhejiang could be in for a deluge, forecasters say, with more than 600 mm (23.6 inches) of rain possible.

Ningbo ⁠Lishe ​International Airport in Zhejiang said it will stop its operations from 11:30 ​p.m. (1530 GMT) on Saturday and suspend all flights on Sunday.

Taiwan, where 63 international flights have been cancelled, is also expected to experience heavy rain in the north over the weekend.

New political friction between Taiwan and China has also arisen after Beijing ordered that ships passing through ⁠the Taiwan Strait must heed ​its traffic control instructions amid the typhoon.

Taipei has slammed Beijing's injunctions as "ridiculous," saying that Beijing has no right to restrict access to international waters.

"The unreasonable and crude statement ‌by ​the relevant Chinese Communist departments reflects an ignorance, disregard, and trampling of international order and norms. It is utterly ridiculous!" Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council said in a statement late ​on Friday.

China regards the democratically governed island as a breakaway territory of its own and also claims to own the strategic strait, a stance rejected by both Taipei and Washington.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-debates-re.title: Germany debates reintroducing mandatory civilian service
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-debates-re.text:
Social organizations are skeptical about the government's ideas for a civilian service program that youths could choose as an alternative should Germany reinstate mandatory military conscription.

Germany's constitution, the Basic Law, guarantees that no person can be forced into armed military service. Should the government reinstate mandatory conscription, a civilian-service alternative would have to be established for people who invoke their right to refuse military service on moral grounds as conscientious objectors.

Germany's federal government is making arrangements for this. The Family Affairs Ministry, led by Karin Prien, of the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), has confirmed that in recent months it reached out to 23 large associations and organizations to ask what capacities they had to offer if civilian service were reinstated. Of those, 22 indicated a general willingness to offer opportunities for civilian service participants.

Thorsten Frei, the parliamentary group leader of the center-right bloc of the CDU and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) in the Bundestag, told the German broadcasters RTL and ntv that it was "very clever and correct" for the Family Affairs Ministry to prepare in this way. However, Frei said, there are no new developments in the discussion surrounding the possible reinstatement of conscription.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

After lengthy negotiations, the coalition government of the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) agreed that military service would remain voluntary in Germany for now. Whether this remains the case will depend on how many soldiers the German armed forces, the Bundeswehr, can recruit in the coming months and years.

The goal is to increase the number of troops from 185,000 to at least 260,000 by 2030 in order to strengthen national defenses and fulfill NATO requirements. Or, as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) put it: The Bundeswehr should become the strongest conventional army in Europe.

The so-called new military service, which has been in force since the start of this year, is also expected to boost the recruitment effort. It combines improved conditions for volunteers with responsibilities applying to all 18-year-old men: They must fill out a questionnaire to answer if they would be prepared to serve in the army.

They are required to undergo medical examinations and to state whether they are interested in joining the armed forces. However, they maintain the constitutional right to refuse military service as conscientious objectors.

Even without reinstating compulsory military service, the recruitment drive is on track to reach its target for 2026, according to a June forecast by Germany's Defense Ministry. However, only about 530 young men have voluntarily signed up to the military as a direct result of the Bundeswehr questionnaire in 2026.

So, though a return to conscription is not currently expected, it remains an option for the government. Combined with civilian service, it was in place in Germany (starting in West Germany in 1956) until 2011, when it was suspended. However, it was not removed from the constitution. So, parliament can reactivate it by law if needed, for example if the country's security situation changes.

The alternative, mandatory civilian service (Zivildienst) usually involved working in a hospital or care home for several months.

This civilian service was replaced in 2011 by the Bundesfreiwilligendienst , or federal volunteer service, which is open to people of all ages and genders. Conscription only applied to men.

Major German welfare organizations have pledged their support should civilian service be relaunched. At the same time, they warn against false expectations. The general consensus is that civilian service is no fix for acute staff shortages in the social services sector. Instead of relying on obligation, the federal government should instead strengthen the optional engagement of young people.

"Our main wish is improved conditions for the voluntary services," Eva Maria Welskop-Deffaa, the president of the German Caritas Association, told the public broadcaster ARD. "And there is still a lot of room for improvement on that."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's opposition parties have also criticized a possible return to mandatory civilian service. According to the socialist Left Party, the state "should not dictate how young people spend a year of their lives," co-leader Ines Schwerdtner said. That applied to both military and civilian service. On the other side, young people should not serve as "stopgaps for a welfare state" which the government "has been systematically underfunding for years." Nursing care, emergency services and social institutions did not need "government-mandated cheap labor," Schwerdtner told the Funke media group.

In any case, the Family Affairs Ministry sees a need to revise and modernize the current civilian service law. It plans to present its proposals after Germany's summer recess.

This article was originally written in German.

https://www.dw.com/en/ceuta-spain-sets-u.title: Ceuta: Spain sets up border controls on travelers from Italy
https://www.dw.com/en/ceuta-spain-sets-u.text:
Spain had warned Italy it would impose entry checks on visitors unless Rome halts its controls by Sunday. Even though they don't share a land border, the countries entered a spat after the Ceuta border rush.

Spain's government on Friday moved to impose reciprocal entry checks on people traveling from Italy. The Spanish government had warned that it would do so unless Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's governemnt lifted the border measures it has implemented against Spain.

Italy's right-wing government announced the checks at the height of the social media panic as tens of thousands of people gained entry into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta bordering Morocco last week.

The checks are essentially symbolic, given that Ceuta is not on the European mainland and Italy and Spain do not share a land border, meaning that the vast majority of people potentially affected are tourists on planes.

Nevertheless, the issue has turned into a point of dispute between two governments of different ideological persuasions with contrasting messaging priorities on migration policy.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The border controls on Italy will go into effect from midnight ‌on ⁠Saturday ⁠until September 7, the Spanish government said. Border agents will check passport, nationality and visas for Italian passengers and visitors from other ​countries arriving from Italy.

Spain had called Italy's decision to impose checks on people arriving from Spain "unjustified, contrary to the interests of the European Union and discriminatory against ​the Spanish population."

Madrid said there was no real risk of people who overwhelmed Ceuta's border controls reaching the European mainland, let alone Italy. It pointed to the vast majority of the estimated 72,000 people returning to Morocco within days. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also drew attention to the higher numbers of irregular migrants reaching Italian than Spanish territory in recent years.

"If [Italy] fails to [remove the entry checks] before Sunday, August 9, Spain will be forced to adopt proportionate measures to protect the interests and dignity of its citizens," the government said.

Italy replied later Friday that it would not accept "ultimatums ⁠or ⁠impositions" from Madrid, and that it would maintain the suspension of Schengen rules for non-EU nationals arriving from Spain until at least August 15.

Despite Spain's objections, an array of European countries, including Germany, and the European Commission all made comments about the importance of border security to the open-border Schengen Zoneamid the public uproar. Italy was among comparatively few to go so far as to frame the issue as "suspending" Spain's Schengen status, however.

Details on precisely what checks, if any, Italy has actually implemented over the past week have been thin on the ground.

Migration analyst Gerald Knaus told DW earlier this week that the move was "pure populism" and a "completely bizarre" measure.

"They don't have a border, so it's only for a few flights," Knaus said. "It makes no sense in the high tourist season. And as Giorgia Meloni indicated, it shouldn't inconvenience travelers."

Knaus said the decision could only be understood in the context of domestic political appearances, not foreign policy realities.

"I think to understand it, you must understand that on [Meloni's] right, there is a radical right party in Italy that puts pressure on her. And so politicians everywhere in Europe, when they see these images which create fear, are looking for something to say — something to do that makes them look tough."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At least in terms of their stated positions and approaches, Italy and Spain have quite different stances on the issue of migration.

Meloni came to power in 2022 in Italy, after several years of much higher irregular migration rates and asylum applications caused in large part by the wars in Syria and Ukraine. She promised a tougher line on migration into one of the most common landing points in southern Europe.

Sanchez, meanwhile, has championed a more pro-migration stance during his two terms in office. He argues that Spain's economy needs migration and offered an amnesty and temporary residency permit process earlier this year to irregular migrants already in the country. Sanchez said it was better to grant residency and start collecting taxes than to keep people out of the formal labor market.

Migration expert Knaus, however, warned against overstating the practical differences between the two countries, saying Meloni faced similar economic requirements and was actually pursuing comparable policies — only with much less public fanfare.

"Italy is doing something very similar. Hundreds of thousands of people are brought in or are already in the country and are regularized for the Italian labour market under Giorgia Meloni," Knaus said. "And 1.6 million people were regularized under various Italian governments in the last 20 years."

https://www.dw.com/en/iceland-s-eu-vote-.title: Iceland’s EU vote: A nation divided over Europe
https://www.dw.com/en/iceland-s-eu-vote-.text:
Security concerns, control over fishing rights and rising living costs are shaping Iceland's debate over whether to restart talks on joining the European Union.

The white church stands alone in the Icelandic countryside. Wind sweeps across the Hvalfjord. Kristjan Ingolfsson, a retired bishop, lives here beside Hallgrimskirkja church in Saubaer, surrounded by silence and vast open landscapes.

But far from this quiet corner of western Iceland, the debate over Europe is heating up. At the end of August, voters will decide whether to reopen accession talks with the European Union.  The referendum is not about joining the EU immediately, but about restarting negotiations that were suspended more than a decade ago.

"[Icelandic] people are a bit different to the mainland folks, who always have to think about borders. We have no border, just the sea all around," Kristjan Ingolfsson says.

"That gives a specific feeling of freedom. And I believe that's also part of the whole discussion, that people want to be free."

Whether campaigning for or against closer ties with Brussels, many Icelanders frame the debate around the same ideas: freedom, independence, and sovereignty.

At the headquarters of the pro-European group in the capital, Reykjavik, supporters are celebrating the official launch of the campaign. The small office is packed, with volunteers spilling onto the pavement in the afternoon sun. Young people mingle with pensioners. A DJ provides music while beer and soft drinks are kept chilled in ice buckets.

At the center of it all is Snaeros Sindradottir, executive director of the 'Yes' campaign. The 34-year-old mother normally runs an art gallery, but that work is now on hold. Instead, she spends her days campaigning for a closer relationship with Europe.

The referendum is taking place at a time of growing geopolitical uncertainty.  US President Donald Trump's threats toward neighboring Greenland have become part of Iceland's debate over Europe, says Snaeros Sindradottir.

"And it's not a very comforting fact that Trump has mispronounced Greenland as Iceland on several occasions."

Iceland, with its population of about 400,000, has no standing army. Protection is provided through NATO, of which Iceland is a founding member. The country also has a bilateral defense agreement with Washington. During the Cold War, the US maintained an important military base near Reykjavik, although its permanent troop presence ended in 2006.

"I think security would definitely be increased if we enter the EU," says Snaeros Sindradottir.

"Given the situation in the United States, it would be wiser to lean [on] our true allies and friends in Europe."

Iceland is already closely tied to Europe. The country belongs to the European Economic Area (EEA), allowing free movement of goods, services, capital and people between Iceland and most EU countries, even though the island nation is not an EU member. It is also part of the passport-free Schengen zone.

Pawel Bartoszek, chairman of parliament's foreign affairs committee, points to Iceland's small and relatively volatile currency.

"It has cost us much higher inflation and interest rates compared to continental Europe," he says.

Bartoszek argues that joining the euro in the future could lower borrowing costs for households and businesses. Mortgage rates of 8 to 9% are common in Iceland, while borrowers elsewhere in Europe often pay roughly half as much.

In downtown Reykjavik, campaigners from the anti-EU movement are making the opposite case. They have set up a small table where they hand out leaflets and "No" campaign badges. Haraldur Olafsson, a physics professor, currently spends up to 12 hours a day campaigning against membership.

"We are basically here to explain to the people that being members of the European Union is a huge step away from democracy."

"We are giving power to someone else who will make rules that we cannot control," he adds.

For years, Haraldur Olafsson has campaigned against joining the EU. He is the president of the Heimssyn organization, which belongs to the 'No' camp.

The 'No' campaign's stand is quiet today. Tourists crowd the square opposite parliament, every now and then Olafsson is approached by acquaintances. This is Iceland. People know each other here.

"I do not know anybody in Iceland who fears either the Russians or the Americans," Haraldur Olafsson says.

"Really, I don't think these international matters matter a lot when it comes to local politics. The only threat comes from the European Union. The European Union is the only big power in the world that wants to govern Iceland, that wants to set the laws in Iceland and wants to pass judgment."

Supporters of EU membership reject this argument, saying that as an EU member Iceland would participate in decision-making rather than simply follow rules set elsewhere.

Iceland's thriving fishing industry is one of the foundations of the country's prosperity. That is why the debate over possible EU membership has become highly emotional, with both sides arguing over whether the European Union would gain control over Iceland's valuable marine resources.

"The European Union has nothing to say about the natural resources in Iceland — the sea, the fish," Haraldur Olafsson says.

"The European Union doesn't have the final word on energy, which is a very important natural resource for Iceland."

"The economy of Iceland is very different from the economy of Europe. The main disadvantage is that the EU would take over the administration of [our] natural resources," he argues.

Haraldur Olafsson heads down to Reykjavik's harbor. Here he meets former fisherman Agust Österby, who is standing on his wooden boat, fixing an old window frame. Österby first went to sea with his father when he was six years old. Today, he restores wooden boats.

Icelanders, he says, are stubborn and independent by nature.

"It is somehow in our genes to deal with [things] ourselves — to deal with life, the sea and the weather."

He adds: "We will never give our freedom to the European Union. We know exactly how to do things in Iceland. We don't need help from abroad."

The former fisherman says he does not think Icelanders feel threatened by anyone — not even Donald Trump.

The belief that Iceland can simply keep a low profile and avoid international pressure is something political scientist Audunn Arnorsson disagrees with. He fears the strategy "might backfire."

If Iceland were ever to face pressure similar to that experienced by Greenland from its "big brother in the West," having the possibility of EU accession could prove valuable, including access to the bloc's common customs protection.

Iceland had already begun accession negotiations once before, in 2010, following the banking and economic crisis. They were later suspended after a change in government and never resumed. Audunn Arnorsson argues that holding a referendum became the only way to break the political deadlock over whether Iceland should reopen negotiations.

Members of Iceland's parliament are also divided over whether the country should resume accession talks with the European Union. The debate cuts across traditional party lines.

Gudrun Hafsteinsdottir, leader of the opposition Independence Party, believes that a small nation like Iceland may have a bigger voice outside the European Union than inside.

"In the European Parliament, we would have approximately six seats out of 726. We are afraid that we will just disappear in this mass that the European Union is."

Smaller EU member states such as Malta, Luxembourg and Cyprus also hold the minimum allocation of six seats in the European Parliament.

For Gudrun Hafsteinsdottir, joining the EU is not the solution for strengthening Iceland's security.

"Our strength lies in NATO and our bilateral agreement with the United States of America. And we have not had any discussion from [the] American side that they want to change that agreement that we have had here in Iceland for decades."

But something else concerns the opposition leader deeply: the divisions the debate has created within families and friendships.

"We are building a wound that won't heal [for] years. We can't survive in this harsh country if we don't have solidarity between us, so that we can fight Mother Nature."

Opinion polls predict a tight race, with support for and opposition to closer EU integration running neck and neck. Both camps are now fighting for the same group: the many undecided voters who are likely to determine the result on August 29.

A 'yes' vote would not mean EU membership. It would only open accession talks — with a second referendum required before Iceland could ultimately join the bloc.

But former bishop Kristjan Ingolfsson is confident: "No matter how it turns out — we will remain one people and [it will] not build walls between us."

https://www.dw.com/en/migrant-tunnels-in.title: Migrant tunnels in Lithuania direct suspicion towards Minsk
https://www.dw.com/en/migrant-tunnels-in.text:
Lithuania's border guards have discovered tunnels through which migrants are trying to enter the country from Belarus. Analysts see them as a means to destabilize the country.

Migrants are taking a new route to enter the Baltic country Lithuania: underground tunnels. These could be yet another attempt by Belarus to foster political instability, experts say.

The country's border guards say they have found 12 such tunnels since the beginning of the year all along the Belarusian border, with a length of up to 25 meters on the Lithuanian side. They are expecting more to emerge.

Lithuania's border with Belarus is about 700 kilometers long, around 550 kilometers of which are fenced.

"We have a ground seismic system, which can detect easily when there's a high level of vibrations over a long period of time," General Rustamas Liubajevas, the commander of Lithuania's State Border Guard Service, explained to DW.

"We then wait [outside a tunnel] for the final stage of the digging and when the migrants come out, we apprehend them," he said, adding that up to 40 migrants exiting such tunnels had been arrested.

Lithuania's prosecutor's office confirmed to DW that a pre-trial investigation was under way concerning approximately 20 people suspected of illegally digging a tunnel. Possible charges also include people smuggling. Due to the investigation, no media visits are currently authorized at the sites.

Liubajevas is surprised migrants would attempt a subterranean crossing.

"It takes a lot of effort to dig a tunnel and the migrants are arrested almost immediately — at most, one small group gets through," he said.

The elaborate nature of the tunnels has led him to believe the migrants aren't working alone.

"They wouldn't be able to go through with this without logistical support from the Belarusian authorities, as they need a lot of material like wood to strengthen the tunnels' walls," he stressed, adding that Belarus seemingly wanted to "keep the level of tension at the border high."

Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenkohas denied facilitating migration flows to neighboring states. Similar migrant tunnels were discovered in the past in neighboring Poland.

Margarita Seselgyte, Director of the Institute of International Relations and Political Science at Vilnius University, seconded Liubajevas' view.

"Belarus is watching its border very closely, and the country doesn't fit in the natural migration route of migrants from Afghanistan, Iran or Sri Lanka," she told DW, adding that Minsk had to at least have turned a blind eye to any digging activity taking place near the border.

Seselgyte thus sees the tunnels as "a hybrid attack to cause anxiety in our society."

"There is no vacuum in the world of security. As Lithuania has been closing vulnerabilities and reinforcing its border fence, Belarus is now helping migrants pass beneath it," she said.

For her, Minsk is assisting its close ally Moscow. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 partly from Belarus, where it amassed troops under the pretext of military drills.

"Lithuania has been very vocal in terms of defense against Russia, both conventional and hybrid, on an EU and Nato level, and they want to silence that voice by causing chaos in our country," the political scientist said.

"The main goal is probably to weaken support for Ukraine and disrupt European unity," she added.

Linas Kojala, CEO of Vilnius-based think tank Geopolitics and Security Studies Center, noted that the tunnels were keeping the border force busy – even if only a few migrants got through.

He described the tunnels as "just another phase of the attack of weaponized migration we've been facing since 2021."

That's when tens of thousands of migrants crossed into Lithuania, Poland and Latvia from Belarus. The European Union called the events a "state-sponsored instrumentalization of migrants at the EU external border," organized by Lukashenko.

"Latvia, Poland, Lithuania and other countries have since set up external borders and we've managed to bring down illegal migration to a minimum," Kojala told DW. Lithuania's border guards registered 1652 attempts to enter the country irregularly in 2025.

But this number won't go down to zero unless Minsk deals with the problem on its side, according to Kojala. "And that's unlikely: Belarus is clearly trying to pose as many problems as possible."

Belarus would be far from the first country to use migration as a strategic tool, underlined Robert Gonzci, an analyst at the Migration Research Institute in the Hungarian capital of Budapest.

"It's a relatively low-cost, low-risk way of exerting pressure on other countries, and since the 1950s, there've been numerous documented cases of governments creating or manipulating migration flows," he wrote in an email to DW.

He added that even the Assyrian empire – which collapsed in the seventh century BC – used migration to consolidate imperial control.

Gonzci didn't rule out that autonomous smuggling networks might be behind the recently discovered tunnels, which Belarusian authorities don't fully control.

He added that Belarus and Russia have used weaponized migration to "divert Western attention from Russia's broader strategic agenda and create instability along NATO's eastern flank by fueling political and social tensions within European countries."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The states organizing such operations – often authoritarian regimes – enjoyed an inherent strategic advantage, Gonzci stressed.

"The target is usually a democratic state facing a fundamental dilemma: They must protect their sovereignty by securing their borders while simultaneously upholding their legal obligations and humanitarian commitments," he wrote.

But experts seem to agree that countries on the EU's eastern flank have been doing rather well in that respect.

"There's increasing cooperation and coordination between the Nordic and Baltic States and Poland, as these countries are facing similar challenges. And the EU Frontex mission has been sending additional equipment," Seselgyte said.

Lithuania is currently receiving technical support from neighboring countries.

"We are testing Polish scanning equipment, through which we can identify empty spaces underground. If these tools work well, we'll buy and deploy them," explained Liubajevas.
https://www.dw.com/en/migrant-tunnels-in.summary: Belarusian border guards have discovered 12 tunnels through which migrants are trying to enter Lithuania. The tunnels are believed to be part of a new attempt by Belarus to foster political instability. Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenkohas denies facilitating migration flows to neighboring states.

https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-s-zelensky.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy makes first visit to Russia-friendly Serbia
https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-s-zelensky.text:
Ukrainian President Zelenskyy is making his first visit to Serbia. His host, President Aleksandar Vucic, hopes to score points with the EU, while Zelenskyy seeks more arms from a country that remains friendly to Russia.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic have met several times in the past, often on the sidelines of multilateral conferences, and most recently on July 15, 2026, in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv.

On Friday, Zelenskyy arrived in Serbia for his first official state visit to the country.

The talks, however, are likely to require careful political balancing. Despite Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine, Serbia remains widely regarded as Europe's most pro-Russian country.

There have recently been several signs of closer ties between Belgrade and Kyiv. Ukraine's First Lady, Olena Zelenska, visited Belgrade two years ago. But a trip by the Ukrainian president has been postponed several times.

For Vucic, who has ruled Serbia with an iron fist for the past 14 years, the visit is a balancing act ahead of crucial parliamentary elections. A student-led protest movement plans to field its own electoral list, with a realistic chance of seriously challenging Vucic for the first time. The president has been accused of corruption and of exerting control over the media and judiciary.

According to opinion polls, the majority of Vucic's loyal supporters side with Russia and oppose Serbia joining the European Union. Pro-government media outlets, such as the tabloid Informer, have openly backed Moscow in the war.

Nevertheless, Vucic has portrayed Zelenskyy's trip as an ordinary state visit, saying: "We have several important issues to discuss. One is Ukraine's and Serbia's path toward Europe; the second is our bilateral and energy cooperation."

Observers expect the meeting to prove mutually beneficial. "Zelenskyy welcomes anything that comes across as a kind of slap in the face for [Russian President] Putin," political analyst and pollster Djordje Vukadinovic told DW. "That also applies to the European Union, which certainly played a role in making this meeting happen."

At the same time, Vucic wants to "present himself as being as open to cooperation as possible with the EU," especially after seeing what happened to Hungary's Viktor Orban. "Brussels still has enough carrots and sticks at its disposal in this part of the Balkans, and Vucic cannot afford to draw criticism from Brussels ahead of the next election," Vukadinovic said.

Zelenskyy may also be looking to secure Serbian munitions. Large quantities of Serbian artillery shells have already been delivered to Ukraine through intermediaries, despite Serbia's pro-Russian stance and opposition to anti-Russian sanctions. The Financial Times newspaper estimated that the value of military goods delivered to Ukraine totaled €1 billion ($1.15 billion) in 2024.

Christopher Hill, a seasoned US diplomat, who recently ended his career as ambassador to Serbia, spoke candidly about how he had brought the Ukrainian military and Serbian defense industry together.

"The US began supporting the purchase of significant quantities of Serbian ammunition, which we knew Ukraine urgently needed," Hill told German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung. Countries such as the Czech Republic and Poland officially bought the weapons before transferring them to Ukraine.

According to the newspaper, discussions are also taking place behind the scenes about building a joint drone factory using Ukrainian expertise, Serbian workers, and investment from the United Arab Emirates. Zelenskyy's team has reportedly already inspected potential locations in secret.

"Ukraine is trying to expand its circle of European partners, including those countries that have not imposed sanctions on Russia," Srdjan Majstorovic of the Belgrade-based think tank European Policy Centre told DW. "At the same time, Serbia has a defense industry whose products matter to Ukraine's war effort."

Although Serbia continues to promote the narrative of an "Orthodox brotherhood" with Russia, the Kremlin has increasingly signaled its dissatisfaction with Vucic. This is particularly evident in the context of Russian gas deliveries, one of Russia's most powerful sources of leverage.

Recently, Serbia has only been offered short-term gas contracts, which has increased economic uncertainty and undermined Vucic's economic model, which aims to attract foreign investors through cheap labor and low energy costs.

That is why some observers say Serbia is forced to flip-flop between Moscow and the EU — by far Serbia's most important trading partner.

Yet political analyst Vukadinovic disagrees. "Superficial observers categorize Vucic's moves as either 'pro-EU' or 'pro-Russia,' but both approaches are equally dishonest — Vucic is looking to spot the greatest threat and how best to benefit, with the goal of holding on to power forever."

Vucic finds himself in a precarious situation. The student protests — which began in late 2024 following the collapse of the Novi Sad train station canopy which killed 16 people — have made the outcome of the upcoming parliamentary election, expected to take place this fall, completely unpredictable. The protesters accuse the government of corruption and incompetence. Some opinion polls even place the movement in the lead.

Vucic's critics therefore fear large-scale efforts to manipulate the election, for instance, through gifts to voters, exerting pressure on public-sector employees, or "importing" voters from Republika Srpska, the Serb entity of neighboring Bosnia and Herzegovina.

EU criticism of Vucic has so far been both restrained and at times contradictory. While the European Commission has recommended moving ahead with Serbian accession negotiations, some EU member states oppose this due to concerns about democratic deficits in the Balkan country.

"It is quite possible that Zelenskyy's state visit and Serbia's cooperation with Ukraine will be used by some EU member states and the European Commission to push ahead with Serbia's accession talks, especially now that geopolitical considerations risk overshadowing rule-of-law criteria," Majstorovic said.

Yet Vucic also holds a trump card that he regularly plays to his domestic audience whenever he meets Zelenskyy on the sidelines of international summits.

Ukraine, like Russia, has never recognized the independence of the former Serbian province of Kosovo. This fact plays well with Vucic's voters.

This article was translated from German.
https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-s-zelensky.summary: Serbia's president has never recognized the independence of the former Serbian province of Kosovo. The country has never been recognized by Russia or Russia. Serbia remains widely regarded as Europe's most pro-Russian country.

https://www.dw.com/en/eco-wins-hungary-g.title: Eco wins: Hungary goes solar, marmots go viral and Rome gets an upgrade
https://www.dw.com/en/eco-wins-hungary-g.text:
From Hungary's accidental solar revolution to marmot crowdfunding and a long-overdue upgrade for Rome's big snake, good news comes in strange packages this week.

Hungary's former leader Viktor Orban called European Union climate policy a "utopian fantasy" and effectively banned wind turbines. And yet the country has quietly become Europe's solar leader, with 25% of its electricity now being being generated from the renewable energy source, ahead of sunnier countries like Spain, and Greece.

The boom was driven not by climate concern but by self-sufficiency politics and cheap subsidies. Now a 450-megawatt park, just east of Budapest, is due online by September 2026. It's set to power around 106,000 households.

When US federal funding dried up, researchers from UCLA and the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory got creative. They launched OnlyMarms: a free platform posting videos of yellow-bellied marmots eating, digging and scampering in the wild, where fans can donate to support the science.

The team has tracked individually marked marmots in Colorado since 1962, building six decades of data on family lives, social behavior and responses to environmental change — and say studying marmot hibernation could even hold clues about human aging.

Corviale, a kilometer-long brutalist housing complex outside Rome nicknamed "the big snake," was completed in the 1980s and has since fallen into decay. With summers in some parts of Italy's now averaging around 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit), life inside has become tough for its more than 4,000 residents.

But upgrades are coming: a new library doubling as a cooling shelter, more trees and energy efficiency improvements, all aimed at helping Corviale stay cool as temperatures keep rising.

Berlin-based designer Mame Khady Badji transforms discarded clothing into bold garments inspired by her Senegalese heritage, combining traditional Ndiakhass techniques with contemporary streetwear. Her creations have drawn musicians, performers and creatives — and recently appeared at Berlin Fashion Week 2026.

After moving to Germany in 2017, Badji built her label with support from Berlin's textile community. Now she's pursuing an ambitious goal: proving that recycled fashion can be both culturally rooted and commercially viable.
