https://www.dw.com/en/germany-far-right-.title: Germany: Far-right AfD extends its lead in nationwide polls
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-far-right-.text:
In the latest Sunday poll, the AfD continues to pull ahead. And more and more people are against excluding the right-wing populists from decision-making, at least on a case-by-case basis.

For the time being, there is still widespread agreement among all democratic parties in Germany: Cooperating with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) remains out of the question. However, whether this will remain the case is becoming increasingly uncertain. The established parties have so far been unable to halt the AfD's surge in the polls over recent months.

This has also been confirmed by the latest ARD-Deutschlandtrend survey conducted by the polling firm infratest-dimap. One thousand three hundred eligible voters were asked what party they would vote for if a federal election were held next Sunday, and 28% said they would vote for the AfD. This represents a one-percentage-point increase and a new record high for the AfD in the monthly polly.

In contrast, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's party, the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), and its sister party, Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU), have seen a slight decline compared to the last poll in early July while all other parties have maintained their previous levels.

In September, state elections will take place in two important eastern German states: Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In both states, the AfD leads in the polls. In Saxony-Anhalt, they are polling at 41% and might be able to govern alone, if the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) fails to cross the 5% threshhold for representation in parliament.

However, only 37% of voters across Germany are opposed to any form of cooperation with the right-wing populists while 32% believe such decisions should be made on a case-by-case basis.

A total of 27% are generally in favor of cooperating with the AfD, most of whom are AfD supporters.

What is especially interesting in the poll, however, is the contrast between East and West Germany. The AfD has its strongholds in the East, where more people than in the West are willing to fully embrace the party: 38% want to treat the party — of which several regional chapters have been categorized as far-right extremist by the domestic intelligence agency — just like any other political group. That figure roughly corresponds to the level of support for right-wing populists in the formerly socialist East Germany (GDR).

This figure also reflects the continuing shift away from "mainstream" parties. A good half of those surveyed — more than ever before in the Deutschlandtrend — support a fundamental change in German politics while only four in ten prefer isolated policy adjustments.

In other words, confidence and trust in the political system continue to wane. Forty-three percent of all respondents say they constantly feel marginalized. When this question is put to AfD supporters, that figure jumps to 70%.

The past few weeks in German politics have been marked by heated debates over proposed reforms and by a rather chaotic reshuffling of the cabinet. Even before this, approval ratings for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's policies were not high; now, only 12% believe that the new cabinet appointments will lead to better policies.

And the latest terrorist attack in Germany has also had a significant impact on people's views. On July 25, a young Islamist from Berlin drove a rental car into a crowd during the Berlin Pride celebrations, killing one woman and seriously injuring 31 people. The following day, police shot and killed the man, who had fled after carrying out the attack. This horrific event has once again drawn attention to how vulnerable Germany is to terrorist attacks.

One-third of all respondents said they are very concerned they might become victims of terrorism themselves. Now, 70% see Islamist terrorism as the greatest threat. At the end of the last decade, on the other hand, right-wing extremist terrorism was still seen by German citizens as the greatest threat.

For the ARD-Deutschlandtrend survey in August, infratest-dimap interviewed approximately 1,300 representative German citizens between August 3 and 5.

https://www.dw.com/en/testosterone-and-f.title: Testosterone and fertility: the trade-off men aren't told about
https://www.dw.com/en/testosterone-and-f.text:
Testosterone is trending in gyms, on social online and in politics. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth even wants troops screened for low testosterone. But taking supplements can shut down the body's natural production.

Making sperm is, in large part, what testosterone is for. Which is why it is ironic when a man who doesn't need it starts taking it anyway: His brain registers an unusually high level of the hormone in his blood, concludes his body has made too much, and sends the order to stop. The testes go silent and sperm production declines.

Testosterone is having a moment. It is all over social media, gym culture and wellness forums, sold by online labs, gym contacts and telehealth services. The information surrounding it ranges from oversimplified to outright dangerous. Men are taking more of it than ever, in pursuit of feeling more like men. In doing so, they may be telling their bodies to stop producing it themselves.

Here is what the science says — what testosterone does, who genuinely needs treatment, and what it can cost the men who take it without needing it.

Your body regulates testosterone the way a thermostat regulates heat. When the brain detects abnormally high levels of the hormone in the bloodstream, it sends a signal to the testes to stop producing it naturally. The testes effectively go offline, and because sperm production depends on what happens inside them, that shuts down too.

Some men who self-medicate with testosterone push their levels to more than four times the clinical lower threshold. The consequences include blood clotting disorders, cardiovascular stress, mood instability and, in some cases, irreversible fertility damage. What's sold as a shortcut to strength and libido can, unsupervised, cost a man his fertility.

Testosterone peaks during puberty, typically between 13 and 15. After that, it declines slowly for the rest of a man's life. A lower level at 40 than at 15 isn't a disorder — its aging.

The threshold that doctors use is 300 nanograms per deciliter of blood.

But this threshold comes with a condition: It must be confirmed by at least two blood tests taken at different times of the day, because levels fluctuate.

Below that number, a doctor may begin to consider treatment. Above 300, there is no clinical basis for intervention.

Before any medical treatment is considered, four key lifestyle factors should be examined: sleep, alcohol consumption, smoking and drug use, and chronic stress. Each of these has a measurable impact on testosterone levels. Addressing them may be all that's needed and carries none of the risks of hormonal therapy.

Testosterone replacement therapy, or TRT, treats a diagnosed hormonal deficiency. It's a legitimate medical procedure — involving injections, pills, creams — that works for men who need it.

But plenty of men taking it don't have that deficiency. Men with normal testosterone levels are increasingly seeking TRT out anyway, not as a treatment but as a performance enhancer. They're getting it from unregulated online labs, gym contacts and telehealth services that write prescriptions without adequate medical assessment.

Men who stop taking testosterone are likely to recover their own production within months. But not all of them. Depending on the dose and how long a man has been using, research puts the share who never recover at somewhere between one in ten and one in five.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Many men who self-administer testosterone report feeling stronger, sharper and more energetic. Some of that may reflect genuine physiological change.

A significant portion is likely the placebo effect — a well-documented human tendency to feel better when we believe we are being treated. That does not make the feeling less real. It does mean that unsupervised hormonal intervention is a high-risk gamble for a benefit that may exist entirely in one's mind.

Doctors' advice is unambiguous: Get tested, know the number, and treat everything else — the websites, the influencers, the gym contacts — as anecdote, not medicine.

A lot of men aren't waiting. Chasing peak masculinity online, they're reaching for the one substance that could tell their own bodies to stop making it.

Edited by: Kaukab Shairani

This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted. You can subscribe to the podcast here.
https://www.dw.com/en/testosterone-and-f.summary: Testosterone is trending in gyms, on social media, on Facebook and in politics. But taking supplements can shut down the body's natural production of testosterone. Men who self-medicate with testosterone push their levels to more than four times the clinical lower threshold.

https://www.dw.com/en/drought-threatens-.title: Drought threatens power supplies in Danube countries
https://www.dw.com/en/drought-threatens-.text:
Droughts, heat and falling water levels in the Danube are hitting central and southeastern Europe hard. Hungary and Romania are experiencing an energy crisis — whereas countries like Bulgaria are better prepared.

Riverbeds reduced to tiny streams, asphalt melting like butter, dried-up fields — these are currently the images of drought in Central and Southeastern Europe. The record-breaking lack of rainfall in recent months and this summer's heatwaves have caused severe damage to the region's economy and infrastructure.

In the agriculture sector, it has been clear for some time that harvests in Southeastern Europe, especially maize and sunflower crops, will be significantly below average. The heatwaves are also repeatedly disrupting road, rail and, above all, shipping transport. But, most importantly, the drought has triggered an unprecedented crisis in electricity generation in several Central and Southeastern European countries, forcing companies to halt production due to the historically low water level of the Danube.

Hungary and Romania are currently most affected by the energy crisis. Other countries bordering the Danube — Austria, Slovakia, Serbia and Bulgaria — are also suffering from low water levels, although not as severely as Hungary and Romania.

DW outlines the situation in each country and explains why, despite facing similar weather conditions, some are more severely affected than others.

No country in the region is currently as severely affected by drought and heat as Hungary. For months, there has been little or no rainfall in large parts of the country. On Wednesday, temperatures reached 43 degrees Celsius (109.4 degrees Fahrenheit) in the capital Budapest, and exceeded 40 degrees in many places across the country.

Due to the record-low water levels of the Danube, the Paks nuclear power plant south of Budapest had to largely shut down operations, as there is no longer sufficent cooling water available and the temperature of the Danube water is too high. The plant is currently operating at around 12% of its capacity. If Danube water levels continue to drop, the plant will have to be shut down completely.

Due to the energy crisis, the Hungarian government has been urging large energy consumers to conserve electricity. As a result, several car manufacturers, including Audi Gyor, oil and gas company MOL and other large companies have scaled back production. Hungary's energy crisis — the worst in decades — is so severe because of the country's unfavorable energy mix. Paks generates around 50% of the electricity produced in Hungary and about one-third of the electricity consumed. Although Hungary has significant solar energy capacity, it lacks storage facilities, has too few modern gas-fired power plants and very little wind or hydropower capacity.

Even if the Danube water levels rise significantly again, the Paks nuclear power plant cannot simply be brought back online quickly — the process takes a considerable amount of time. Therefore, Hungary's energy crisis will continue for at least several more weeks, during which the country will have to import electricity at high prices. In response to the crisis, the new government under Peter Magyar has announced a comprehensive review of Hungary's energy development strategy.

Romania is experiencing a similar, though somewhat less severe, energy crisis. The Cernavoda nuclear power plant, also located on the Danube in the southeast of the country, produces roughly one-fifth of Romania's electricity. Due to the river's exceptionally low water level, one of the plant's two 700-megawatt reactors was taken offline last week.

Southwest of the Cernavoda plant, Romanian authorities blasted a rock formation this week to divert more water into the Danube's eastern branch, where the nuclear plant is located. In addition, dozens of tons of rock were dumped into the river to channel more water into that branch.

Romania has a relatively balanced energy mix consisting of hydropower, nuclear energy, natural gas, coal and wind power. However, because hydropower accounts for around one-fifth of the country's electricity generation — primarily through the Iron Gate hydroelectric plant on the Danube — Romania is particularly vulnerable to droughts such as the current one.

Due to the energy crisis, several major companies, including Dacia and Ford Romania, have scaled back production. The government has announced that it would, if necessary, issue a decree ordering large factories to suspend production.

Romania is also among the Southeastern European countries most affected by aridification — the long-term climatic process through which regions become increasingly dry —  and desertification, as soils gradually become barren and take on desert-like characteristics.

Serbia, too, is suffering badly from drought and the Danube's low water level. Its energy mix is similarly ill-suited to prolonged dry periods. Around 65% of its electricity is generated by coal-fired power plants, while about 25% comes from hydropower.

The two Iron Gate hydropower plants are currently generating only a fraction of their average electricity output. The coal-fired power plants Kostolac A and B east of Belgrade, which rely on Danube water for cooling, have also had to cut back production.

Serbia relies heavily on the Danube as a transport route for coal and petrochemical products. However, due to the low water level, cargo vessels can currently only carry a fraction of their normal loads. Nonetheless, the energy crisis has so far not been so severe that large industrial plants have had to scale back production.

In Slovakia, some 60% of electricity is generated by nuclear power plants, with another 20% by hydropower. Unlike Hungary and Romania, Slovakia's two nuclear power plants, Bohunice and Mochovce, are located on smaller rivers and use cooling towers rather than once-through cooling systems. Once-through cooling requires large quantities of river water that are drawn from the river and then channeled back to it at a higher temperature. In contrast, cooling towers recirculate water in a closed system, releasing heat mainly through evaporation. As a result, Slovakia's nuclear plants require much less river water and are therefore less affected by the current drought.

In comparison, Slovakia's Gabcikovo hydropower on the Danube has been significantly affected by the low water level. At present, only one of its eight turbines is in operation. Electricity generation in Gabcikovo, however, is only about 12% lower compared to the same time last year. So far, Slovakia has not experienced any major industrial production stoppages.

Austria, which generates around 60% of its electricity from hydropower, has also been less severely affected than Hungary. One reason is that part of Austria's hydropower capacity comes from storage and pumped-storage plants rather than run-of-river facilities.

Run-of-river plants depend directly on the volume of water flowing through rivers, whereas storage and pumped-storage plants can generate electricity using water stored in reservoirs when needed, making them less vulnerable during prolonged heatwaves and droughts.

In addition, Austria generates some 30% of its electricity from other renewable energy sources.

Unlike in neighboring Romania, drought and heat are not yet causing an energy crisis in Bulgaria.

The country generates up to 40% of its energy through the Kozloduy nuclear power plant, which is also located on the Danube. Its cooling system, however, is better designed to operate under low-water conditions than those of Hungary's Paks plant and Cernavoda in Romania. As a result, it is currently operating at almost full capacity.

At the same time, Bulgaria depends only marginally on hydropower and has, in recent years, considerably expanded its solar and wind energy capacity.

The biggest difference to all the other countries lies in Bulgaria's large-scale battery storage facilities. The country currently has storage systems with a capacity of 3.4 gigawatts and a storage capacity of 8.6 gigawatt-hours. This storage capacity corresponds to 16% of the country's total installed power generation capacity — a figure unmatched by any other country in the world.

These storage facilities enable Bulgaria to balance supply shortages and peak demand, without relying on expensive imports. At the same time, the country is developing into a regional market leader in new energy concepts and as a hub for power grid stabilization and greater price stability in the electricity market.

This article was originally published in German.
https://www.dw.com/en/drought-threatens-.summary: Droughts, heat and falling water levels in the Danube are hitting central and southeastern Europe hard. The drought has triggered an unprecedented crisis in electricity generation in several Central and Southeastern European countries. Slovakia's nuclear plants require much less river water and are less affected by the current drought.

https://www.dw.com/en/mata-hari-celebrat.title: Mata Hari: Celebrated dancer turns WWI spy
https://www.dw.com/en/mata-hari-celebrat.text:
Mata Hari enthralled Europe's elite with her beauty and performances. Accused of spying during World War I, she faced a French firing squad in 1917.

Mata Hari was already a legend in her own lifetime. When she stepped into the Parisian limelight in 1905, she swept high society off its feet.

"She danced with veils and jewel-encrusted bustiers and almost nothing else," the Parisian press reported. "Never had anyone dared to appear unveiled before the gods with such trembling ecstasy. And what wonderful movements she made — both daring and demure at the same time."

Mata Hari had convinced audiences and the press that she was an exotic temple dancer — but the dark-haired performer was actually Dutch.

One of the hallmarks of the Belle Epoque era was a heightened fascination with cultures the Parisians deemed to be exotic. Driven by financial desperation, she exploited this demand by pretending to be Indian. To make her act more credible, she fabricated a backstory claiming to be the daughter of a highly esteemed Brahmin.

"My mother, first bayadere [dancer] of the Ranganathaswamy Temple, died at the age of fourteen, on the day I was born. After the temple priests cremated her body, they adopted me and named me Mata Hari, which means 'Eye of the Day [a Malay word, Hari means sun]."

She claimed to have learned the sacred temple dances from a young age. During her performances, one veil after another would fall away.  Later, she said, "I never danced well. The only reason people came to see me was that I was the first to dare to present myself naked to the public."

High society couldn't get enough of Mata Hari, unaware that her real name was Margaretha Geertruida Zelle and that she came from the small Dutch town of Leeuwarden.

Born on August 7, 1876, Mata Hari was the daughter of a hatmaker who had become wealthy through stock market speculation. He often spoiled his daughter with lavish gifts. For her sixth birthday, he gave her a carriage drawn by goats.

At the age of 13, Mata Hari's life of luxury ended abruptly. Her father went bankrupt and abandoned the family. Two years later, when her mother passed away, she moved in with relatives. Eventually, she met her husband through a newspaper ad: "An officer from the Dutch East Indies [now Indonesia], currently on home leave, seeks the company of a nice young woman with potential for future marriage. Financial circumstances irrelevant."

Mata Hari and John Rudolf MacLeod, a Dutch nobleman of Scottish descent who was 20 years her senior, quickly became a couple. In 1897, she accompanied her husband to the Dutch East Indies. But her dream of a happy life never materialized. Frequent arguments strained their relationship. Then, their two-year-old son was tragically poisoned to death. When the MacLeods returned to Europe in 1902, their marriage fell apart. MacLeod left Mata Hari, taking their daughter with him and refusing to pay any alimony, leaving her to fend for herself.

She began her career in Paris as a model for painters and tried her luck at the circus.  But it was her creation of the exotic stage persona Mata Hari that ultimately made her famous. She performed at prestigious venues across Europe, including Vienna and Monte Carlo, staying in luxurious hotels.  She danced at soirées hosted by the Rothschild banking family and entertained Crown Prince Wilhelm, the son of the German Emperor Wilhelm II. Her success gave her access to the highest social circles, where she formed relationships with diplomats and high-ranking military officers who paid generously for her company.

Eventually, Mata Hari's popularity began to wane. Younger dancers began imitating her, and thrill-seeking audiences in Paris moved on to the next sensation. When World War I broke out in 1914, Mata Hari could no longer sustain her luxurious lifestyle.

She accepted an offer from the German consul in the Netherlands to help pay off her debts. She was promised even more money for gathering intelligence from influential figures on the opposing side of the war. Her initial fee was 20,000 francs, a substantial sum at the time. And just like that, she became Agent H 21.

Then, when the French intelligence service approached her and offered her even more money, Mata Hari became a double agent. But she miscalculated the situation. The French had enlisted her so they could catch her spying for the Germans. At the same time, due to increasing suspicion of her activities, the British intelligence service also monitored Mata Hari as she traveled through Europe. On February 13, 1917, she was arrested.

On October 15, at the age of 41, Mata Hari was executed for high treason in the moat of the Château de Vincennes, near Paris. Eyewitnesses reported that she faced the 12-man firing squad with her head held high and even blew them a kiss. She refused to wear a blindfold and instead addressed her final words to the commander who gave the order to fire: "Thank you, monsieur!"

Mata Hari's status as a so-called master spy remains questionable. According to documents from the British intelligence service — which remained classified for several decades — any information she may have shared likely did not impact the course of World War I.

It seems that Mata Hari was used as a convenient scapegoat at a time when public enthusiasm for the war had significantly waned. And the French military court needed someone to blame. She herself denied having spied until the very end. Regardless of whether or not she was a master spy, she was undoubtedly a master of self-promotion until her last breath.

This article was originally published in German.
https://www.dw.com/en/mata-hari-celebrat.summary: Mata Hari was born in Dutch, but was born to a Dutch family. She was accused of spying during World War I, and faced a French firing squad in 1917. She became Agent H.H.H., who was accused by French military court of spying.

https://www.dw.com/en/can-un-chief-s-ini.title: Can UN chief's initiative kickstart resolution for Cyprus?
https://www.dw.com/en/can-un-chief-s-ini.text:
UN chief Antonio Guterres considers a resolution to the Cyprus issue to be vital for regional stability and has initiated a new diplomatic effort. What are the prospects for its success?

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres last week became the first UN chief to visit Cyprus in 16 years.

While there, he met the leaders of the island's two communities: Nikos Christodoulides, president of the Republic of Cyprus, and Tufan Erhurman, Turkish Cypriot leader and president of the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is only recognized by Turkey.

His aim in doing so was to determine whether the conditions exist for restarting negotiations on the Cyprus issue.

Progress on talks has remained stalled since the collapse of negotiations in Crans-Montana, Switzerland, in 2017, when the United Nations made its most comprehensive effort to broker a reunification agreement for the island.

So, why has Antonio Guterres decided to launch a new initiative now?

According to diplomatic sources, the answer lies less in developments surrounding the Cyprus issue itself and more in the rapidly changing geopolitical landscape of the wider region.

War in the Middle East, deteriorating relations between Israel and Turkey, and growing strategic competition in the Eastern Mediterranean have heightened UN concerns that the unresolved Cyprus conflict could undermine the stability of the entire region.

Guterres said as much after the joint meeting on July 29. "I do believe that a solution in Cyprus is absolutely crucial, not only to preserve the interests and the peace of the Cyprus people, but also as a factor of stability in what is becoming a dangerously unstable region," he said.

Speaking to DW, Andreas Mavroyiannis, former permanent representative of the Republic of Cyprus to the United Nations and former chief negotiator of the Greek Cypriot side, shared the same concern.

"The strengthening of relations between the Republic of Cyprus and Israel, combined with the deterioration of Israel–Turkey relations, increases the risk of the Cyprus issue being instrumentalized," he told DW.

According to Mavroyiannis, the UN secretary-general fears that Cyprus could, instead of serving as a pillar of stability in the Middle East, become increasingly entangled in regional rivalries and emerge as one of the area's most vulnerable flashpoints.

The UN is not alone in viewing the Cyprus issue through the prism of regional security. The EU has also shown increasing interest in playing a more active political role in efforts to revive the peace process.

A significant step came on July 7, when the European Commission appointed Executive Vice-President Raffaele Fitto as the EU's Special Representative for the Cyprus issue.

His mandate is to support the UN-led process and strengthen the bloc's involvement in efforts to restart negotiations.

A more active role for the EU has long been one of President Nikos Christodoulides' key policy objectives.

During Cyprus' recent presidency of the Council of the European Union, he reminded fellow European leaders that he was "the president of the only EU member state that remains under illegal military occupation."

The Cypriot government believes that the EU agenda could provide Ankara with incentives to contribute constructively to progress on the Cyprus issue.

Among the issues viewed as potential leverage are the modernization of the EU–Turkey Customs Union, visa liberalization for Turkish citizens, Turkey's participation in the EU's SAFE defense financing instrument and the prospect of gradually reviving its long-frozen EU accession process.

While Guterres' decision to announce a new informal expanded 5+1 meeting involving the two Cypriot communities, the three guarantor powers (Greece, Turkey and the UK) plus the UN was widely seen as a positive signal, he deliberately stopped short of setting a date.

Instead, he made it clear that the meeting would only be convened once sufficient progress had been made on confidence-building measures, methodology and the substance of the process.

So, it was no coincidence that he stressed upon arriving in Cyprus that "it depends obviously on the Cypriots themselves," underlining that responsibility for moving the process forward rests primarily with the two communities.

His remarks are directly linked to the lack of tangible progress on confidence-building measures.

Despite months of discussions, the two sides failed to reach agreement even on the opening of new crossing points — a step which, according to the UN Secretary-General, could have "a tangible impact on the daily lives of Cypriots," while helping to restore a minimum level of trust ahead of the next phase of negotiations.

The key question, however, extends beyond the two communities themselves and concerns Turkey's willingness to engage.

The real test for the UN is whether Ankara is prepared to return to negotiations conducted within the framework of the UN Security Council resolutions and the agreed basis of a bicommunal, bizonal federation, moving away from the two-state solution it has advocated since the collapse of the Crans-Montana talks in 2017.

So far, Turkey has made no public statement indicating such a shift. The only possible indication comes indirectly from Antonio Guterres' remark that he has "the consent of both sides and the guarantor powers to move towards another 5+1 meeting, provided there is adequate preparation."

The wording suggests that, at least procedurally, Ankara is willing to participate in another informal conference under UN auspices. Whether this also signals a substantive change in Turkey's long-standing position remains, for now, an open question.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan
https://www.dw.com/en/can-un-chief-s-ini.summary: UN chief Antonio Guterres is the first UN chief to visit Cyprus in 16 years. He is trying to determine whether the conditions exist for restarting negotiations on the Cyprus issue. The UN is not alone in viewing the Cyprus issues through the prism of regional security.

https://www.dw.com/en/afd-threatens-to-c.title: AfD threatens to cut funding for 'modern-thinking' culture
https://www.dw.com/en/afd-threatens-to-c.text:
The far-right party could win an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt's state election in September. Their cultural program denigrates Bauhaus, Holocaust remembrance culture and diversity in theater.

In upcoming state elections to be held on September 6, polls suggest the Alternative for Germany (AfD) could win an absolute majority in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Based on the far-right's cultural policy program, museums, theaters and cultural institutions in the region say that artistic freedom is one of the far-right party's targets.

The AfD has announced that artists and institutions would be required to sign a declaration pledging "not to hold in contempt Germany and its culture" if they want to obtain state funding. Many of these organizations and individuals heavily rely on these subsidies.

The AfD's interpretation of disrespect to German culture also ambiguously includes what the party calls "anti-German art."

"We declared in our government program that we no longer intend to spend public funds on promoting anti-German art," said Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, cultural policy spokesperson for the AfD parliamentary group in the state legislature, in a speech held in Saxony-Anhalt's parliament in late June.

Asked by other members of parliament to specify what that meant exactly, Tillschneider said, "Anti-German art is German art that doesn't want to be German." He mentioned as an example an opera production he had seen some years ago; the classical German composer's work was revisited through a "feminist deconstructivist" lens that didn't please him and corresponds to what he sees as "anti-German art."

"This anti-German aversion is still considered de rigueur in large parts of the theater world," he said. "We will no longer support this attitude — let me state that quite clearly."

Bauhaus, Germany's iconic architecture, art and design school founded in 1919, was forced to close under the Nazis, who considered their avant-garde ideas and their open-minded attitude to be "un-German." Bauhaus nevertheless went on to become one of design's most important movements of the 20th century; its influence is still felt worldwide. 
Today, the AfD once again sees Bauhaus as too modernist and globalist for the "patriotic cultural policy" the party envisions.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The AfD's criticism of Bauhaus picks up on criticism from 100 years ago; their wording is similar," Barbara Steiner, director of the Bauhaus Foundation, told DW.

The AfD Saxony-Anhalt's program describes Bauhaus as "a controversial school of architecture" and criticizes the current state government for putting too much emphasis on this landmark attraction in their current image campaign, titled "moderndenken" (thinking modern).

The AfD aims to adopt instead a campaign called "deutschdenken" (thinking German), which would downplay the role of Bauhaus and instead "highlight the state's significant contributions to the development of the German nation — from Henry I and Otto I to Luther, Bismarck and Nietzsche."

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) strongly rejects comparisons to the Nazi party and Adolf Hitler, often dismissing them as trivializations of Nazi crimes.

Yet in its cultural policy program, the far-right party regularly adopts the language used in Hitler's propaganda, downplays Nazi-era atrocities, challenges Germany's culture of remembrance and uses historically loaded language.

The proposed "deutschdenken" slogan is one example of this: "'Deutsch denken' refers to a speech Adolf Hitler made in 1938" — the "Reichenberger Rede," noted Steiner.

The Bauhaus is not the only cultural organization that feels threatened in Saxony-Anhalt. "As cultural practitioners, cultural initiators and artists, we can say that we are now genuinely afraid, because what's being triggered there is, in fact, the idea that art and culture must be 'German,'" Annegret Laabs, director of the Kunstmuseum Magdeburg told DW.

Laabs is a spokesperson for the initiative Kultur ist Vielfalt und Heimat, which roughly translates as "Culture is diversity and home." The initiative brings together a wide range of cultural institutions and artists from the region; they are warning in a joint statement that the AfD's plans could have far-reaching consequences for artistic freedom, historical memory, and public cultural life.

"We all know that what we do — from theaters to museums to libraries — is paid for with taxpayer money. It wouldn't exist otherwise," said Laabs.

Restricting funding based on an arbitrary definition of what constitutes "German" art basically equates to culture's demise, explains Laabs: "If we look at the bigger picture, we see that culture and art have been free for centuries and have known no boundaries — not even national ones. Wherever there are national boundaries, there is no longer any art or culture worthy of that name."

Along with threats to funding, the AfD's program also describes Germany's existing culture of Holocaust remembrance as the "perpetuation of a guilt complex" that has "blocked the possibilities for forming a stable national identity." It sees this as an "identity disorder" that needs to be "healed," by focusing on the "positive aspects of German history."

Sabine Schramm, director of Magdeburg's puppet theater, finds "it regrettable that we humans are not willing to draw conclusions from a complex history — conclusions that matter both to us as individuals and to us as a society."

She notes that throughout her 30-year career in theater, she has dealt with Germany's culture of remembrance, grappling with the horrors of Nazism on stage.

"It has always been important to me — especially in productions for young people — to tell stories that address precisely this issue: National Socialism, how it begins, and how the various elements interlock," she points out.

"I can still see myself standing on stage talking about 'resisting the beginnings' — that phrase, 'resisting the beginnings,' has become such a cliché," she says, referring to an idea Germans are deeply familiar with; after the horrors of the Nazi era, the generations that followed were urged to speak out against threats to democracy — before it's too late.

"But where, exactly, are the beginnings?" Schramm asks. "Is this the beginning, or are we still before the beginning? Are we right in the middle of it? What must I do to resist the beginnings?"

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-leipzig-ai.title: Germany: Leipzig airport drone attack sets off alarm bells
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-leipzig-ai.text:
German authorities have begun a counterterrorism ⁠investigation into a drone laden with explosives found near a Ukrainian transport plane at Leipzig Airport. It is seen as a "hybrid attack scenario."

German airports have seen hundreds of drone alerts, but this incident eclipses them all: in the middle of the night on Wednesday, airport staff at the Leipzig/Halle Airport in the eastern state of Saxony found a drone rigged with explosives on the runway.

Federal police specialists were able to defuse it using a bomb disposal robot. The incident prompted the closure of part of one of Europe's largest cargo hubs.

German media reports say that experts from Saxony state police found the package to contain the highly explosive substances PETN and Semtex, which are also used in military applications. The detonator attached to the package had apparently broken off, which prevented an explosion.

This unconfirmed information is particularly significant because the drone was found next to a plane of the Ukrainian state-owned carrier Antonov Airlines. The aircraft was reportedly loaded with military munitions that — according to reports — had just been transported from France to Leipzig and were slated for onward shipment to Ukraine.

Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt cut his vacation short to assess the situation firsthand at the scene. His initial assessment: "This represents a new threat scenario." At a press conference on Wednesday evening, he spoke only in general and vague terms regarding potential perpetrators and motives. However, Dobrindt did not rule out the possibility that "foreign powers" might be behind the incident — with the aim of unsettling Germany.

"All the speculation that is currently going on about the explosives, the construction, the question of the drone, the origin and, of course, who is behind it, is now part of the investigation," Dobrindt said.

In June, Dobrindt created a so-called Joint Center for Countering Hybrid Threats, as Germany has been on high alert for espionage, sabotage and disinformation, particularly from Russia.

Leipzig/Halle Airport is high on the priority list regarding security and, like other airports, is being equipped with technology to detect and intercept drones. At the same time, however, Dobrindt acknowledged that this is an ongoing race: "When drones are designed to bypass technology, the technology itself must be continuously upgraded," he said.

After Frankfurt am Main, Leipzig/Halle Airport is Germany's largest cargo hub. Security experts say this makes it a potential target for state-sponsored attacks. Consequently, counter-terrorism expert Hans-Jakob Schindler considers it possible that Russia could be the mastermind behind the explosive-laden drone.

For the moment, the facts remain unknown. "But given the location — where we have already seen similar disruptions that could be traced back to Russia — that would be my initial assumption," Schindler told DW.

Hybrid attacks generally refer to covert operations that do not aim for direct confrontation, but are designed to create uncertainty. These can involve a combination of various tactics such as sabotage, economic pressure, or disinformation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Earlier on Thursday, Saxony's Interior Minister Armin Schuster said that authorities are searching for parts of a possible second drone that collided with an aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport.

Drone sightings have frequently disrupted German airports, canceling flights and causing headaches for travelers. Drones are also sometimes sighted over German military installations.

In December last year, Holger Münch, the head of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), said that over 1,000 suspicious drones had been registered in 2025, which he said represented a "significant situation of danger."

Leipzig had already been the site of an attempted attack in July 2024: a container belonging to the logistics company DHL caught fire in the airport's cargo area. The cause was a package sent from the Baltic states containing an incendiary device designed — according to investigators — to detonate mid-air. At the time, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office suspected a targeted act of Russian sabotage.

This article was translated from German.
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-leipzig-ai.summary: A drone laden with explosives was found near a Ukrainian transport plane at Leipzig Airport. The incident prompted the closure of part of one of Europe's largest cargo hubs. The drone was found next to a plane of the Ukrainian state-owned carrier Antonov Airlines.

https://www.dw.com/en/how-gianni-infanti.title: How Gianni Infantino rose to rule football
https://www.dw.com/en/how-gianni-infanti.text:
Gianni Infantino is staying on as FIFA president despite growing pressure to step down. So who is football's most powerful man, why did UEFA and others turn against him, and how did he reassert his authority?

Despite strong pressure for him to resign, particularly from UEFA, Gianni Infantino convinced FIFA's Board of Management to express their full support for him following a crisis meeting in Rabat on Wednesday. It was the latest development in a crisis that began with news last week of a FIFA plan to create a subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run the men's World Cup and its other events, with a stake of up to 20% to be offered to external investors.

Giovanni Vincenzo Infantino was born on March 23, 1970, in the southwestern Swiss town of Brig to Italian parents. Many years later, as FIFA president, he would speak of the discrimination he said he experienced as he grew up for being of Italian heritage in Switzerland. Infantino studied law at the University of Fribourg, before becoming the general secretary of the International Centre for Sports Studies at the University of Neuchatel in 1997. The foundation had been established two years earlier by FIFA in partnership with the university and the city and canton of Neuchatel.

Infantino, who speaks six languages, first gained notoriety beyond Switzerland after joining UEFA, football's European governing body, in 2000. There, he would climb the corporate ladder to become the organization's general secretary in 2009. Serving under former UEFA President Michel Platini, Infantino's position kept him largely out of the public eye, but during this time his face became a familiar one to European football fans, as one of his roles was hosting the Champions League and Euros draws, broadcast live on TV.

The door to the FIFA presidency was knocked open by the 2015 FIFA corruption scandal in which several officials were indicted, seven of whom were arrested at a Zurich hotel. This came just ahead of a FIFA Congress to elect a new president. Although Sepp Blatter won reelection for a fifth term, he announced his resignation just days later. An extraordinary FIFA Congress was called for February 2016.

Infantino looked a rank outsider when he threw his hat into the ring. Platini, his boss at UEFA, was the favorite, but he withdrew his candidacy a month before the election, after both he and Blatter had been banned over ethics violations involving a dubious payment.

In the days leading up to the vote, Sheik Salman bin Ibrahim al Khalifa of Bahrain emerged as the frontrunner among the seven candidates. However, Infantino, running on a pledge to clean up what was a scandal-ridden organization, won the presidency in the second round of voting. He'd also promised to increase FIFA payments to every member association.

"We will restore the image of FIFA and the respect of FIFA, and everyone in the world will applaud us and will applaud all of you for what we'll do in FIFA in the future," Infantino told the delegates in Zurich's Hallenstadion.

Gianni Infantino has presided over a decade of unprecedented growth in revenue for FIFA, culminating in the 2026 World Cup — the first to feature 48 teams and 104 games — compared to 32 teams and 64 games in Qatar four years earlier. This was bound to generate higher revenue, but it was compounded by the dynamic pricing system FIFA introduced for the tournament. This led to sky-high prices for tickets — and FIFA went one better by getting into the secondary market  and taking a 15% cut from both buyer and seller on every transaction.

While the final revenue numbers won't be announced until FIFA publishes its annual report for 2026, the figures are expected to smash the almost $5.8 billion (€5.03 billion) the organization earned in 2022, largely from the Qatar World Cup. Infantino has spoken of a figure around double that. Others believe it could be far higher.

He says he wasn't to blame for a major talking point at the World Cup — the suspension of USA forward Folarin Balogun's red-card ban following his sending off against Bosnia in the round of 32. This followed a call by US President Donald Trump to Infantino to request a "review." Infantino insisted that an independent FIFA body had made the decision.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The hydration breaks, which effectively split games into four quarters, also didn't go over well with many football fans. Others were angry at his refusal to step in on rows over visas for traveling fans, officials and a referee from Somalia and the treatment of the Iran team in the US during the tournament.

Prior to the World Cup 2026, Infantino had made the headlines for the wrong reasons on several occasions. Among his more notable controversies were:

His problems began with the World Cup sell-off plan. UEFA sharply condemned the news within minutes — before threatening to boycott all FIFA events, including the men's and women's World Cups. After Infantino backed off the plan, UEFA doubled down, saying it had lost confidence in the "current FIFA leadership" and the "task of rebuilding trust in FIFA" had just begun. Football's European governing body also threatened action through its US lawyers over what it termed a "shabby, backroom, opaque deal."

The FIFA boss summoned senior staff members to an emergency meeting in Rabat on Wednesday. A statement issued after that meeting conceded that "mistakes made were acknowledged" in connection with the private investment plan and that the "process should have been handled differently."

It also said those present had "reaffirmed their full support" for the president and stressed that FIFA would "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation."

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-10-years-o.title: Germany: 10 years of 'Integration Act' for refugees
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-10-years-o.text:
The German Integration Act aimed to regulate the integration of recognized refugees following high levels of immigration, facilitating access to the labor market in return for integration efforts.

In early August 2016, a phrase began circulating in Germany that would shape political and societal discussions for many years to come: "the divided society."

There were still many Germans who remained committed to welcoming hundreds of thousands of refugees who had begun arriving the previous year, mainly from Syria. However, an increasing number were more skeptical of immigrants and foreigners, especially following the mass sexual assaults involving young men with immigrant backgrounds that took place in Cologne on New Year's Eve 2015–2016.

Under the leadership of Chancellor Angela Merkel, the coalition government of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)/Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) sought to calm the polarized mood in Germany by introducing an integration act , a law designed to appeal to all sides through the guiding principle of "support and challenge" ("fördern und fordern").

Some thought it offered too many giveaways; others felt it imposed too many demands.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"For someone in favor of strong regulatory policy, the integration law offered too much assistance while demanding far too little. One example is the fact that a rejected asylum application did not necessarily lead to deportation," says Holger Kolb, of the Expert Council on Integration and Migration (SVR).

"For someone very concerned with integration policy, on the other hand, the requirements were far too high, especially regarding temporary residence permits for vocational training. They believe this creates far too many obstacles to successful integration."

Providing support for new arrivals meant massively expanding integration and language courses, allowing new arrivals to enter the labor market more quickly. A vocational training permit for refugees whose individual asylum applications had been rejected, but whose home countries were still categorized as unsafe, allowed them to complete a three-year vocational training program followed by two years of employment in the field they trained in.

On the other hand, it was made obligatory to participate in language and integration courses. Sanctions were imposed in the form of welfare benefit cuts for those who refused to participate. Also, the refugees were distributed evenly across Germany to prevent over-concentration in major cities.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This "residency requirement" had a very negative impact on integration, says Herbert Brücker, head of the Research Department for Migration, Integration and International Labour Studies at the Institute for Employment Research (IAB).

"People were distributed disproportionately to economically weak regions with high unemployment. If we restrict people to regions where the economy isn't doing so well, that naturally has negative effects on labor market integration," Brücker explained.

However, he has a positive assessment of the vocational training policy, which allowed rejected refugees to finish their vocational training. He argues that it always makes sense to offer those who integrate well the prospect of staying: They put more effort into learning the language and finding employment and ultimately contribute to the social security systems.

And it turns out, integration in Germany isn't going nearly as badly as has often been claimed, says Brücker, even if refugees are entering the labor market much more slowly than other immigrants.

"Ten years later, we're now seeing employment rates of 65% to 67% — just 3% below the national average. This puts Germany at the top of the European rankings, alongside Norway. This is also due to the fact that we've offered integration courses, language programs and vocational training to actively promote integration."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Federal Ministry of the Interior and the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF) has partially scrapped plans to severely restrict free access to integration courses to only those with "good prospects of remaining in the country." Since June 2026, Ukrainians and EU citizens have once again been able to participate in the courses — including those without a secure prospect of remaining.

Brücker points out that integration courses are a relatively inexpensive tool for integration. "They increase employment rates by five to ten percentage points once people complete the course. Cutting funding for integration courses delays integration into the labor market and prolongs reliance on benefits. This doesn't save money — it actually costs us a lot of money."

Were Brücker able to refine the Integration Act, he says he would relax the residency requirement after asylum proceedings are concluded, begin integration courses just one month after arrival and expedite asylum proceedings in order to integrate people with protection status more quickly while also being able to deport those without protection status more quickly.

Kolb, however, wants to see more coordination between the federal government and the states, and a simpler regulatory framework.

The Integration Act of August 2016, he says, does not really deserve that name. "People expect the Integration Act to provide comprehensive regulations governing the integration of people who are already here," he says.

"In reality, however, the Integration Act is specifically designed for people who have come here as refugees. It would have made more sense to manage expectations better, and establish regulations that are significantly simpler."

This article was originally published in German.

Law was introduced by the coalition government of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)/Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD)

https://www.dw.com/en/why-is-russia-sell.title: Why is Russia selling its gold?
https://www.dw.com/en/why-is-russia-sell.text:
Russia has become one of the world's biggest sellers of gold over the past 12 months. It's an attempt to raise cash in the face of budget issues, but not necessarily a sign of a looming financial crisis.

Russia has sold significant volumes of its gold reserves so far in 2026 as the Kremlin seeks to raise cash to offset a big budget deficit.

The Russian Central Bank announced recently that its gold reserves stood at 73.4 million troy ounces, or 2,282 metric tons, as of the start of July. That represents a decline of around 43.5 metric tonnes since the start of 2026.

It means Russia's gold reserves are now at their lowest level since before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022.

Gold prices hit record levels earlier this year, with prices averaging around $4,800 (€4,210) per ounce in the first four months before falling back to a current level of around $4,000 per ounce. Moscow's sell-off is likely to have raised more than $5 billion.

"The fact that they're selling gold means that they're running out of other more liquid assets," Elina Ribakova, an economist with the Peterson Institute for International Economics, told DW. "So there is pressure on the deficit and also pressure on the sources to finance this deficit."

Russia's budget has been under serious strain in recent years due to its massively increased defense spending, which funds the war in Ukraine.

Earlier this year, the Financial Times reported that the country's finance ministry had warned the cabinet in a letter that overspending on the war would be at least $28 billion in 2026, with further overspends expected in 2027 and 2028. Defense spending has more than quadrupled since 2021. It totalled around 16 trillion rubles in 2025 ($204 billion; €178 billion).

Chris Weafer, a Moscow-based financial analyst with the consulting firm Macro-Advisory, says that while the Russian gold sell-off is significant, it is not a case of panic selling.

"It's an extraordinary situation, but it's a relatively normal trend," he told DW. "It doesn't represent any element of Russia going broke, running out of money, not having anything else and literally selling the household silver."

He says that the gold Russia has offloaded has mostly been sold by the country's finance ministry, via its National Welfare Fund (NWF), rather than the Russian Central Bank.

"Since early 2022, gold was one of the assets that the National Welfare Fund could buy, because US treasuries and bunds weren't available to them (as a result of sanctions following the invasion of Ukraine)."

Weafer pointed out that the asset had become a key liquid component of the fund, which, he said, was precisely what a national welfare fund is intended for: to be sold when funds are needed, particularly during difficult times. "To that extent, one can argue it is serving the intended purpose."

The fund's gold sale is intended to replenish its so-called liquid assets. Weafer estimates that the fund is worth approximately $150 billion, with around $50 billion of that being described as "liquid."

"The Kremlin doesn't want that buffer to go down because that would lead to maybe more speculation about financial crisis or economic difficulties, and it would undermine the Kremlin's geopolitical position," said Weafer.

"It likes to portray the country as being very stable and very strong, and that $50 billion of cash is an important part of that."

He says another important factor to consider is that as one of the world's biggest producers of gold, Russia can replenish stocks it has sold relatively quickly by buying from its domestic producers. Russia holds the fifth-largest reserves in the world, around the same level as China, France and Italy, and significantly behind the top two, Germany and the US.

Ribakova agrees that this offers Russia a significant buffer.

"Russia has an advantage," she said. "It does produce gold itself. So when it was worried about sanctions, it allocated part of the money into the gold purchases, which they were buying from the domestic producers."

The fact that Russia has become one of the biggest sellers of gold has raised further questions about its budget deficit and what that says about wider economic stability.

Russia's federal budget spending and deficit could exceed official plans by more than 1 trillion roubles ($12.85 billion) in 2026, according to ​recent government data. The budget deficit is currently projected to be 1.6% of GDP for 2026, which is approximately $40 billion, and could yet grow.

However, improved revenues from oil and gas, boosted by higher oil prices due to the war in Iran, has helped Moscow to offset the budget difficulties so far in 2026.

Ribakova says everything comes back to the prices and revenues Russia gets from its oil and gas, calling it the "real limit" on Moscow's capacity to finance the four-and-a-half-year-long war in Ukraine.

"Everything hinges on that," she noted. "When the oil price is high, Russia gets revenues. It's easier to borrow, its domestic financial system is healthier. If the oil price drops, say, to sixty or forty, then you immediately have a crisis."

Both she and Weafer caution that despite the obvious economic difficulties the Russian economy has at present, it can continue to fund the war for the foreseeable future by cutting back on non-defense spending.

"Putin can continue going for years in the current environment," said Ribakova. "Maybe not making any progress on the front line, which we haven't seen any progress for the last couple of years, but still being able to throw resources at the war with Ukraine."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Even if the deficit continues as is, Russia can still find the money and really won't be in any sort of a financial crisis or a weak geopolitical position over the next 12 to 24 months," said Weafer.

Yet he points to obvious longer-term damage being done to the economy and the trouble that may bring further down the tracks.

"It is creating this huge distortion in the economy and creating this longer-term negative picture that's now creating divisions in government," he said.

He added that the situation had a divide between those responsible for economic growth and the Kremlin. Their message, he said, is that the current approach could not be sustained, "if you want the economy to go back to a more normal trajectory after peace. That's the bottom line."

https://www.dw.com/en/what-s-behind-the-.title: What's behind the Algeria-Morocco rivalry?
https://www.dw.com/en/what-s-behind-the-.text:
Morocco and Algeria have been at odds for decades, chiefly over the territory of Western Sahara. But their rivalry now extends far beyond the territory.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez traveled to Algeria on July 20 for talks with Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune and Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb.

The meeting's aim was to resolve a diplomatic row that erupted between both countries in 2022 after Spain sided with Morocco's autonomy proposal to resolve the Western Sahara conflict — much to Algeria's dismay.

It is a matter of debate whether Spain's rapprochement with Algeria outraged Morocco so much that it deliberately allowed tens of thousands of migrants to storm the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, even though both countries have improved their relations enormously in recent years. Spanish daily El Pais has certainly entertained the possibility of Moroccan meddling.

"Ceuta tensions coincided with Pedro Sanchez's trip to Algeria, a regional rival of the [Moroccan] Alawite Kingdom," an opinion piece in the Spanish paper notes. The article later states that "any attempt to use immigration as a bargaining chip is unacceptable."

Moroccan interior ministry spokesperson Rachid El Khalfi has rejected such accusations, saying the incident resulted from "the malicious exploitation of the digital space," as well as "misleading information" and misinterpretations of a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling on the rights of arriving migrants.

Experts interviewed by DW say that while potentially deliberate inaction by Moroccan border guards contributed to the breach, it's unlikely the country intended to instigate such a major diplomaticincident.

The recent Ceuta incident and subsequent accusations point to the deep-seated rivalry between Algeria and Morocco. At its heart lies the conflict over Western Sahara, which began when Spain withdrew from the territory in 1975. A conflict between the Polisario Front, which fights for the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination, and Morocco ended in 1991 with a UN-brokered ceasefire. A planned referendum to allow Saharawis to determine its future has never taken place, and the UN considers it Africa's last non-self governing territory.

Morocco, relying on historical claims, considers the region an indispensable part of its own national territory, and has sought international recognition for its integration as a semi-autonomous province. Algeria, in contrast, supports Western Sahara's independence and backs the Polisario Front.The European Court of Justice ruled in 2024 that Morocco and Western Sahara are distinct territories.

The Western Sahara conflict has long since become a symbol of a deeper rivalry between Algeria and Morocco over influence in the Maghreb region, according to a paper by the Research Unit on International Security and Cooperation (UNISCI), an independent Madrid-based research group.

The dispute connects to both countries' domestic politics in the sense that Morocco regards the Western Sahara issue as a matter of territorial integrity, whereas Algeria favors self-determination as it sees itself as an anti-colonial state. This constellation means reaching a compromise in the Western Sahara conflict is becoming increasingly difficult. Indeed, the "Western Sahara conflict has evolved into a struggle for regional hegemony in the Maghreb," says UNISCI.

These tensions have hindered North Africa's economic integration for decades, according to UNISCI experts. Institutions such as the Arab Maghreb Union have been largely paralyzed, with regional economic and security projects making little progress. This diminishes the region's economic momentum and international standing, UNISCI analysts say.

The Algeria-Morocco rivalry took on added significance in 2020 when Morocco normalized relations with Israel, after Israel recognized Morocco's claims to Western Sahara.

Algeria began viewing Israel's increasingly close ties with Morocco as a threat to its own security, according to an analysis by the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank. Algeria's concern centers less on diplomatic normalization with Israel per se and more on the prospect of long-term military and intelligence cooperation, which could shift the regional balance of power to Algeria's detriment, the ICG finds.

ICG analysts describe the relationship between Algeria and Morocco as a classic security dilemma, with both states viewing own their military and foreign policy actions as defensive moves, yet perceiving the other's actions as a threat. This gives rise to a growing arms buildup and deepening mistrust, even though neither government has an interest in open war. It is precisely this logic, ICG scholars write, that makes the conflict so dangerous, as even minor incidents or miscalculations can trigger an escalation.

Their rivalry is no longer limited to the Western Sahara conflict. Indeed, the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR) writes that Morocco and Algeria's strained relationship has evolved into a broader competition for international partners and political influence that includes ties with the European Union. Both nations are striving to underscore their strategic importance to the bloc by leveraging their respective foreign policy strengths, says the ECFR.

While Morocco is positioning itself as a key partner in the areas of migration, counterterrorism and economic cooperation, Algeria is emphasizing its role as an energy supplier and security influence in the Maghreb and Sahel region.

This article was originally published in German.
https://www.dw.com/en/what-s-behind-the-.summary: Morocco and Algeria have been at odds for decades over the territory of Western Sahara. But their rivalry now extends far beyond the territory. Spain's rapprochement with Algeria outraged Morocco so much that it deliberately allowed tens of thousands of migrants to storm the Spanish exclave of Ceuta.

https://www.dw.com/en/will-russia-start-.title: Will Russia start a fresh mobilization drive?
https://www.dw.com/en/will-russia-start-.text:
Russia is preparing a new mobilization campaign to boost troop numbers, Ukrainian officials and independent Russian media outlets report. The Kremlin denies this.

Russian authorities are planning to "expand mobilization" in autumn this year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, citing intelligence services. According to Zelenskyy, Russian President Vladimir Putin is reportedly preparing to recruit additional Russian soldiers to fight in the war against Ukraine.

"He is concealing his intention behind different words and signals, but he is making preparations," Zelenskyy said. "It is important that we, together with our partners, exert sufficient pressure on Russia so that the idea of ending this aggression — the idea of peace, rather than further Russian mobilization — prevails," he added. The Ukrainian president also said Russia's army was losing more fighters at the front than it can recruit, even though Putin wants to intensify the attacks and expand the war.

Putin issued a decree in autumn 2022 launching a "partial mobilization," which remains in effect to this day, as confirmed by the presidential administration in 2023. The document, it said, "regulates additional measures necessary to ensure that the armed forces fulfill their objectives."

Independent Russian exile media outlet Verstka and Latvia-based Russian-language news portal Vaschnyje Istorii published an investigative report in late June stating that Russia's leadership was secretly "discussing mobilization" given the difficulties in recruiting new conscripts. One source quoted by Verstka said figures by Moscow's mayoral office show the city sent 1,708 people to the front in April of this year and 1,378 in May — around 1,000 fewer people than during the same period last year. This low recruitment rate reportedly continued in June as well.

Vaschnyje Istorii reported that the recruitment rate for soldiers serving on fixed-term contracts more than halved in the last quarter of 2025 compared with the same period the previous year. The outlet said the recruitment rate had dropped even further in early 2026. The news outlet also cited sources from different Russian regions revealing that the number of people applying for army contracts was falling.

Military personnel interviewed by Verstka said that contract soldiers being sent to fight this year were "unfit for combat," with many new arrivals fleeing the front lines. One conscript told the news outlet that "units are staffed at 30 to 40%, at best."

The US-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported in late July that the Kremlin is laying the groundwork for a fresh mobilization drive. ISW analysts wrote that such a move would be "a personal decision for Putin that is contingent on his personal perception of the battlefield situation and his perception of the stability and integrity of the Kremlin." They added that it "remains unclear whether or how Putin will decide to implement mobilization."

A few days ago, Verstka reported that demand for Armenian rental apartments had shot up, driven by Russian interest — just as it had in 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The outlet said rents in the Armenian capital, Yerevan, have risen by about 30% in recent months. According to the report, Russians are planning to leave the country ahead of the State Duma election, scheduled to be held from September 18 to 20.

One landlord told the outlet that in recent years most of his clients had been Russians who had already been living in Armenia for quite some time. Now, however, 80% of inquiries were from Russians who had recently moved to Armenia or were planning to relocate there.

Speaking at a press conference in late July, Russian presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov chose not to comment on Ukrainian President Zelenskyy's remarks regarding a possible new mobilization drive, saying "it is not Zelenskyy's job to talk about our plans."

Andrei Klishas, a member of the Russian Federation Council, told Russian-language media outlet RTVI in early summer 2026 that a new mobilization was not currently being discussed in the country as it was unnecessary.

Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of the Russian Security Council, dismissed rumors about a possible new mobilization, calling them "pre-election propaganda." The former Russian president also claimed that in the first half of 2026, some 200,000 people had enlisted in the Russian army.

"Of course, you can't blindly trust information provided by the Russian authorities," military expert Yan Matveyev told DW. "Information is adjusted to align with their objectives," he added, with regard to Medvedev's statements on the number of new Russian contract soldiers. That said, figures provided by Russian officials are not too far off when compared with analyses by independent researchers, Matveyev said. "Instead of Medvedev's nearly 200,000 new soldiers, that number would probably be closer to 170,000 or 180,000 over six months."

In his view, the current recruitment rate is not sufficient for Russia to secure a military victory over Ukraine. A new mobilization drive would not change that, Matveyev added. "Even if they doubled the size of their army, Russia would not be able to defeat Ukraine, but as can be seen from the statements made by Putin and his officials, that is precisely their goal."

Matveyev believes that, given the losses on the front lines, the strength of Russia's army will dwindle unless a fresh mobilization is launched. This decline, he believes, will continue slowly at first but then accelerate. "Losses are growing and will continue to rise given current trends."

This article was originally written in German.
https://www.dw.com/en/will-russia-start-.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Russian authorities are planning to "expand mobilization" in autumn this year. Russian President Vladimir Putin is reportedly preparing to recruit additional Russian soldiers to fight in the war against Ukraine. Russian media outlets report that Russia is preparing a new mobilization campaign.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-court-jail.title: Germany: Court jails far-right youth terror cell members
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-court-jail.text:
A Hamburg court has handed down stiff prison sentences to members of the far-right terrorist group "Last Wave of Defense." Politicians are warning that those drawn into extremist violence are getting younger.

The seven members and one supporter of the "Last Wave of Defense" (Letzte Verteidigungswelle) group were found guilty of crimes with the aim of bringing about the collapse of Germany's political system through attacks on migrants and "political opponents." The judge in the Hamburg Higher Regional Court said the group's name reflected their deeply racist and violent mindset. "We are the wave that washes the filth out of our country," the group had written in pamphlets.

The young men sentenced on Wednesday were aged between 14 and 21 when they committed the crimes.

They were sentenced under juvenile criminal law to youth prison terms ranging from one and a half to five years. The sentence for the youngest defendant — one and a half years in prison — was suspended. They had been charged with membership in, or support of, a terrorist organization. The convictions also covered offenses including attempted murder, arson, and dangerous bodily harm.

According to the ruling, the youths carried out an arson attack on a community cultural center in Altdöbern, a town in the eastern state of Brandenburg, in October 2024. Investigators believe the far-right group mistakenly identified the building — located in a town of only 2,300 residents — as a meeting place for left-wing activists. The building burned to the ground, resulting in property damage amounting to several hundred thousand euros.

Altdöbern's Mayor, Peter Winzer of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), told public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk (DLF) that he is still shocked by the attack: "An absolute catastrophe. Because it was a community hub — a place for culture and gatherings. Every local event took place there."

Two of the accused were found to have unsuccessfully attempted to set fire to accommodation for refugees in Schmölln in the eastern state of Thuringia, in January 2025. They also scrawled swastikas and slogans such as "foreigners out" on the facade of the facility.

According to the indictment, three members of the group had also planned an arson attack on an asylum seeker shelter in Senftenberg in Brandenburg.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Brandenburg's Interior Minister Jan Redmann of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) told DLF that he finds it particularly alarming how quickly very young people are radicalizing and banding together online. "We are also observing some surprising continuities — specifically, that the young perpetrators have relatives who had already come to the authorities' attention as right-wing extremists back in the 1990s — the era of the so-called 'baseball bat years.'"

The term "baseball bat years" refers to the period of massive attacks — primarily targeting refugees — that occurred in the territory of the former East Germany in the years immediately following reunification.

A few days after the trial began in Hamburg, federal prosecutors ordered raids on premises in the eastern states of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, but also in the western states of North Rhine-Westphalia and Schleswig-Holstein as part of an operation targeting 10 additional suspects.

In late June, two more youths were arrested in the eastern state of Thuringia as suspected members of the "Last Wave of Defense." In total, authorities estimate that the group has a membership in the "mid-double-digit range" across Germany.

This article was originally written in German.
