https://www.dw.com/en/the-hidden-problem.title: The hidden problem with small modular nuclear reactors
https://www.dw.com/en/the-hidden-problem.text:
Mini nuclear reactors are seen as a flexible energy source. Their promise: abundant energy, cheap, clean and climate-friendly with lower water use. But do the numbers add up? We look at what's behind the SMR hype.

Many politicians and tech companies are now pushing to build new nuclear power plants to meet the world's rapidly growing energy demands. Small reactors — known as Small Modular Reactors, or SMRs — are gaining momentum.

They could be built in less time and come online faster than conventional nuclear power plants. Originally developed to power submarines and aircraft carriers, SMRs largely work the same way as larger reactors.

They contain a nuclear reactor fueled by uranium, which releases enormous amounts of heat through nuclear fission. That heat turns water into steam, and the steam pressure drives turbines that generate electricity.

Companies and startups are working on a wide variety of SMR designs and concepts, but the underlying principle is similar across all of them.

One advantage over conventional nuclear stations is that mini reactors require a maximum of two hectares (around five acres) of land — roughly the size of two soccer fields. By comparison, conventional plants require up to 280 soccer fields, according to the industry.

What makes SMRs particularly attractive is their modular construction. Individual components can be mass-produced as prefabricated modules and pre-assembled off-site — much like a prefab house that simply needs to be put together once it arrives at its location.

Manufacturers promise an extremely short construction time of between one and a half to six years. Large reactors in the US can take anywhere from seven to 10 years to build.

Proponents also argue that modular units could deliver low-emission power to remote regions, where grid infrastructure is often not developed enough to handle the enormous energy output of a large conventional plant.

Those advantages are also shared by renewable energy sources like solar panels and wind turbines — without the risks that come with nuclear power.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The output of mini nuclear reactors is significantly lower than that of conventional nuclear power plants. Depending on the design, SMRs can deliver between 10 and around 200 megawatts of power, while a conventional plant generates between 1,000 and 1,600 MW.

To produce the same amount of energy as the roughly 400 high-capacity reactors currently operating worldwide, tens of thousands of small reactors would need to be built.

SMRs could offer some safety advantages: they contain less radioactive material than large reactors and would be distributed across multiple sites. This means that an accident or military strike resulting in a meltdown would not be as catastrophic as a worst-case scenario at a large reactor. Nevertheless, the consequences of an SMR accident could still be severe.

Germany's Federal Office for Radiation Protection points out that despite lower radiation levels per reactor, the overall risk posed by mini reactors could be many times higher. Replacing the output of existing nuclear plants with large numbers of smaller ones would require an enormous number of reactors worldwide — and that increases the likelihood that at least one of them will eventually suffer a serious incident.

Nuclear accidents and radiation leaks are extremely rare — but the consequences can be catastrophic. The last major nuclear accident occurred in 2011 at the Fukushima power plant in Japan, following a tsunami. Parts of the region have been contaminated for generations to come, and nearly 170,000 people were forced to flee their homes.

Part of the hype around some new mini reactors rests on the hope of extracting significantly more energy from the same amount of uranium. Some SMR models — known as "fast reactors" — could theoretically yield 60 to 70 times more energy from uranium than conventional technology, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

But the technology is still in the early stages of development and has so far played only a limited role in IAEA projections. In practice, it has barely been proven in SMRs at all. Only two SMR facilities are currently in operation worldwide — one in China and one in Russia.

Work is also underway on recycling SMR fuel rods, but that process remains largely untested. Most SMR projects continue to rely on the same conventional technology used in traditional reactors.

And the problem of radioactive waste remains unsolved — for both conventional and fast reactors. The risks this poses are already visible: at the Asse facility in Lower Saxony, Germany, a temporary storage site built in the 1970s, hundreds of barrels of intermediate-level radioactive waste are now rusting and beginning to leak. Germany has yet to establish a permanent disposal site.

In fact, no permanent repository for spent fuel or highly radioactive reactor waste is currently in operation anywhere in the world. After 20 years of construction, the Onkalo facility in Finland is set to become the first when it opens in 2026.

Another problem for nuclear power is growing water scarcity. Recent heat and drought have already forced European nations to curb nuclear output due to for cooling due to low river levels.

Because SMRs are mainly just smaller, simplified versions conventional reactors, they still use water to run and for cooling. While individual units use less water than traditional plants, clustering units could increase overall use, warn experts. Researchers are investigating the use of alternative coolants like molten salts and helium gas for newer designs.

Enthusiasm for small reactors runs high in the nuclear community. But what may look promising at first glance is, in many respects, difficult or impossible to back up with solid evidence.

Calculating the costs of a technology still in development is no easy task. Nevertheless, the German Institute for Economic Research estimates that electricity from new mini nuclear plants — even accounting for economies of scale, including construction and manufacturing — will cost at least twice as much per megawatt-hour as the already very affordable electricity generated by solar or wind power. In a worst-case scenario, the cost could be nearly eight times higher.

Adding up all the announcements, plans and strategies of major nations, a few hundred SMRs could come online in China, the US, Europe and India by 2050. But according to Germany's Federal Office for Nuclear Safety and Radiation Protection, citing figures from the nuclear industry, production would only become economically viable at a threshold of 3,000 reactors.

The international community has committed to limiting global warmingto well below 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) by the end of the century. Meeting that target requires large parts of the global economy to become climate-neutral by 2050. The EU aims to reach zero emissions by then; Germany is even targeting net negative CO2 emissions by 2050.

That means climate-friendly nuclear technology would arrive too late to meaningfully limit global warming — and its advantages would be significantly diminished as a result.

What would remain: the radiation risk, and the question of what to do with the radioactive waste.

https://www.dw.com/en/sleep-do-you-reall.title: Sleep: Do you really need eight hours of shuteye?
https://www.dw.com/en/sleep-do-you-reall.text:
Every so often we hear of high-ranking politicians or CEOs claiming to get by on very little sleep — some as little as three hours a night. If they're not natural short sleepers, chances are they're heading for trouble.

I've been having trouble sleeping — for as long as forever. Sometimes it's just a feeling. Other times, it's a fact (I know because my watch tells me). But then my watch may be part of the problem. It's constantly reminding me to get to bed on time and accosting me with poor sleep scores. It drives my anxiety through the roof, my heart races and I feel like I can't sleep. But then I still feel fine the next day. Weird.

"When you're sleep deprived, you have poor judgment," said Catia Reis, a sleep researcher at the University of Lisbon, when we spoke.

That might explain my predicament. Because even when I feel fine during the week, I oversleep at the weekend, which is a sure sign of sleep debt, she said.

Reis has studied a variety of sleep-related conditions, including the effects of jet lag and sleep deprivation among athletes.

One investigation compared levels of sleepiness among patients with sleep apnea — a condition where you stop breathing intermittently through the night — and shift workers, who work against their natural, circadian rhythm. That's our inner clock that tells us when we're wakeful or sleepy.

She compared the results from both subjective assessments made by participants and objective, clinical tests, and found a "mismatch" in people's ability to assess their own levels of sleepiness the more they were exposed to that very thing: sleepiness.

Basically, the brain stops working. And that should be concerning, given that the brain plays a central role in sleep.

When we sleep, the body performs several restorative functions: It removes toxins we have ingested through food or the atmosphere, generates new energy, and is essential for our learning and memory.

"Sleep involves many parts of the brain," said Ying-Hui Fu, a sleep researcher at the University of California San Franscisco. "Almost every disease of the brain, including neurological and psychiatric, [can be linked to] sleep problems."

On average, people need about 7.5-8.5 hours' sleep per night.

But every so often we hear about people in demanding jobs, usually politicians, boasting — or claiming credibility — by saying they rarely sleep more than a few hours; like they're ALWAYS WORKING FOR THE PEOPLE.

Most recently, it was Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi who reminded us she's slept between zero and three hours per night while in office.

As a former heavy metal drummer, you might expect a certain level of stamina from the Japanese PM. But while voluntary, habitual (or trained) sleep deprivation — if that's what it is in Takaichi's case — may be an impressive sleep-work-no-life-balance ethic, it's not a good, long-term strategy.

In the best-case scenario, a long-term "sleep debt" can cause your body to accumulate toxins, risking heart or brain disease. In the worst-case scenario, it can be fatal.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"There are only two things more important than sleep for our total health," Fu told DW. "One is air. If we don't have air, we die in a few minutes. The other is water. If we don't have water, we die in a few days. If you don't eat, you can live a couple of months. But if you don't sleep, you can probably only live for a couple of weeks."

And that goes for all animals — "if we don't sleep, we die," she said.

Natural short sleepers are the exception to the rule. They can sleep fewer than six hours per night and not only feel fine, but also actually are fine — healthy, happy and energetic. They appear to have genetic variations that allow them to thrive. Fu cited an 80-year-old natural short sleeper who competed in triathlons.

Fu and her lab found the first of these variations in the gene DEC2 and published their findings in 2009. Ten years later, they published a paper suggesting that the gene ADRB1 was also linked to Natural Short Sleeper Syndrome. Findings into the genes NPSR1, GRM1, SIK3 followed, and there are others in the pipeline.

We're calling them gene "variations" rather than "mutations" because mutations are often associated with negative health effects. But it appears that Natural Short Sleep does not risk the health issues that habitual short sleepers or sleep deprived people face.

The genes show a range of functions that sleep effects:

Each has taken years of painstaking basic — foundational — research to find and test.

"Every one of us has between 500 to 1,000 unique mutations in our genome. To know which one is causal is very difficult," said Fu.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The number of known natural short sleepers is small, but Fu says the condition is likely to be more common than research currently suggests.

Most of Fu's findings are limited families that share a gene variation. That's been for a practical, methodological reason: If three members of a family have the same variation and they all appear to be healthy on only four to six hours' sleep, then that gene variation may well be responsible, especially if it's in a gene that is known to be important for healthy sleep function. But it's early days.

"We just know that they perform better and they're healthier. And the most logical explanation for me is that their sleep function is better," said Fu.

Reis is also cautious about the state of research in this area, saying there are still too few studies into natural short sleepers.

"When we objectively test [habitual short sleepers] and we expand their sleep, we know they improve," said Reis. "But the problem is we don't have enough longitudinal studies with [natural short sleepers]."

Fu would agree. But she said it was a struggle to get the research financed.

"My goal is to help everybody get good sleep. Because if we can help everybody get good sleep, all diseases will drop," said Fu. "The entire spectrum of disease incidence would drop. Can you imagine the impact on humanity?"

https://www.dw.com/en/hungary-s-lake-vel.title: Hungary's Lake Velence is drying up
https://www.dw.com/en/hungary-s-lake-vel.text:
Hungary is feeling the heat. The country's third-largest lake is shrinking, the Danube is running low, and soaring temperatures could force the country's only nuclear power plant to shut down.

A dead fish lies half-decayed on the shore. Its eyes have been picked out by the birds.

Hungary's Lake Velence will likely experience a massive fish kill. That's because oxygen levels in the body of water are too low, according to environmental experts. This means more and more fish will suffocate.

Hungary has seen temperatures soar to 40 degrees Celsius, with barely any rain. This heat is having a major impact on the country's third-largest natural lake.

Its water has never been particularly deep, but the current situation is dire. Water levels have been recorded in Agard, on the southern shore, since 1933. It dropped to a historic low in September 2022, measuring just 53 centimeters. Yet as of today, August 4, the water level has dropped to a mere 29 centimeters (11 inches).

As long as it doesn't rain and temperatures remain hot, the water level will continue to drop every day, by half a centimeter per day on average. The water is currently evaporating at such a fast pace that there may soon be no continuous body of water left, only isolated pools. This could mark a critical tipping point for the lake.

The impact of Hungary's ongoing drought is already clearly visible. The lake has receded by dozens of meters. Ground once covered in water is now so dry that the soil is cracking. The reed belt surrounding the lake, which serves as a habitat for numerous bird species, is now largely rooted in dry soil.

But not all living creatures are suffering under the current conditions: that's evident from a constant hum in the air near the water's edge. As fish and aquatic plants find their habitats shrinking, flies, bacteria, and other decomposers take over, breaking down what the drought leaves behind.

The water shortage isn't just changing the lake — it's changing the entire region. Lake Velence is a popular tourist destination, located just 50 kilometers from Hungary's capital, Budapest. It is considered less crowded than nearby Lake Balaton.

But these days, there are barely any visitors. The remaining water has turned a brownish-green and taken on a slightly musty odor. A "No Swimming" sign has been put up, with yellow tape blocking access to the water. Five swimming spots have been closed to the public since July 23.

The Velence municipal government says the beach will only reopen once the lake's water quality improves, though it is unclear when that might happen. The persistent heat and low water levels mean the lake's water is getting warmer and warmer, leading to a growth in bacteria and blue-green algae.

The people living around the lake, who make their living in the region's tourist sector, are hard hit by the lake's falling water levels. Today, only one family is visiting the northern beach — not for swimming but sunbathing. There is a water slide, slowly rusting away, with the end of the chute not even reaching the water anymore.

Only one kiosk is open today. A woman is selling langos, Hungary's well-known fried bread, as well as ice cream and lemonade. "The slide hasn't been used for years," the saleswoman tells DW. "It really needs fixing, but who will pay for it when fewer and fewer tourists come here?" Campsites and holiday homes around the lake seem deserted, with many stores closed.

Peggy Barath works in an ice cream shop on Velence Promenade, telling DW, "We've always had a lot of tourists here." She says many visitors were from East Germany, the Czech Republic and the Netherlands. But in recent years, their numbers have been dwindling "because of the lake's low water levels."

Peggy says that the ice cream shop now focuses on cyclists rather than tourists looking to swim, as cyclists are undeterred by low water levels.

Major interventions in the region's water cycle have made the lake more vulnerable to droughts over the years. "The lakeshore has been subject to significant construction activity over the past 15 years," Zoltan Kun, president of the Hungarian Great Lakes and Wetlands Association, tells DW.

"The water management authority has focused on quickly draining excess water from the region rather than storing it using nature-based solutions. And the agricultural industry destroyed our soils, which means they are less able to absorb water."

This isn't the first time Lake Velence has dried up. When this happened in the early 1990s, the lake was replenished with water from various other sources, a solution that proved effective but also expensive and time-consuming. That's why experts are calling for a more sustainable solution today, especially since climate change means more drought periods are expected.

The Zamolyi and Patkai reservoirs could, for instance, be renovated so that water could be stored there during periods of heavy rainfall. During dry spells, this water could then be diverted into Lake Valance.

Yet little has happened so far. In 2021, the government at the time, led by Prime Minister Viktor Orban, rejected a broad investment program for the lake on the grounds that it was too costly. Other projects, however, went ahead.

Although it has long been clear that water levels drop to a critical level in summer and fall, authorities built a brand-new canoeing center on the north shore between 2021 and 2024, suitable for international competitions. The project cost about 140 million euros in government funds.

Lanes are marked off in the lake with buoys in front of the newly built spectator tower. It's very quiet, like elsewhere along the body of water. Floating docks sit low in the greenish-brown water.

The World University Canoe Championships were supposed to be held here in August, the first major event to be staged at the newly built center. Yet due to persistently low water levels, the event was moved to Szeged, southern Hungary, instead.

This means that for the time being, the Lake Velence facility remains nothing more than an expensive training center.

Hungary's ongoing heat wave is being felt all over the country. Water levels of the Danube River have dropped significantly, exposing stretches of dry riverbed around Budapest's Margaret Island. Tourists and locals alike are taking in the unusual sight, snapping photos on a sandbar that has emerged off the island. The low water level has also attracted scrap-metal collectors, who use magnets to pull rusty metal objects from parts of the river that are normally submerged.

The low water level has dramatic consequences. With the exception of a few sightseeing boats, boat traffic has almost ceased on the Danube River. Not only that. Paks nuclear power plant, located about 100 kilometers downstream from Budapest, can no longer be cooled with Danube water. The site's electricity output, which covers about half of Hungary's power consumption, has been gradually reduced over the past few days, and it is set to be shut down later this week for the first time ever.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"We are facing a crisis that is beyond our control and putting us to the test," Prime Minister Peter Magyar said at a joint press conference with Interim President Agnes Forsthoffer on Monday. He added that the next five days would be the most critical of the summer of 2026.

Magyar has asked the Hungarian public to conserve electricity. Many companies have agreed to voluntarily reduce their power consumption. Some public buildings and bridges are no longer illuminated at night, and rail freight traffic is suspended between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m.

Hungary faces a very challenging time, with temperatures over 40 degrees Celsius expected over the next days.

This article was translated from German

https://www.dw.com/en/ai-ecosystem-s-cir.title: AI ecosystem's 'circular' investment: risk or advantage?
https://www.dw.com/en/ai-ecosystem-s-cir.text:
Amid talk of an AI sector bubble, one aspect is under scrutiny. Many big AI players are invested in smaller ones, who then buy the bigger firm's products. This brings risks and advantages.

Reports that Nvidia is in talks to give financial guarantees of almost $250 billion (€217 billion) to OpenAI for a massive data center project show two sides of the artificial intelligence boom.

On one level, it shows the monumental scale of AI's financial muscle and potential. On another, it shows the risks of a so-called "circular" financing system at the core of the AI ecosystem. If one domino falls, would others fall with it?

"The interconnected nature of the AI ecosystem is real," Gary Tan, portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments, told DW. "But near term risks are mitigated by the strong balance sheets, cash flows and credit quality of the major providers funding the buildout."

Jan Frederik Slijkerman, a tech sector strategist at ING, agrees that the exceptionally strong financial positions of big tech companies such as Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet (Google parent company) mitigate against the risks.

He says the degree of collaboration regarding AI is "fascinating" but does not see a "a systemic industry-wide risk arising from the observed interdependencies".

Circular financing typically works as follows: A company pays another for a product or deal, or invests in that company or provides a loan or lease. Then that company purchases the first company's products or services.

It can be seen across the spectrum of AI deals.

For many, the moment the AI revolution began was when ChatGPT, developed by OpenAI, was launched in November 2022. The chatbot's capabilities brought AI into the mainstream. Its success quickly attracted a massive $10 billion investment from software giant Microsoft, enabling it to develop more powerful models.

In return, OpenAI became a key customer for Microsoft's cloud services, which it is investing ever more heavily into as the AI boom gathers momentum.

It set the template for future deals. Amazon and Alphabet began investing billions into OpenAI's rival Anthropic, which has built the hugely successful Claude chatbot. In return, Anthropic uses Amazon's web services and Google's cloud services as well as buying its chips.

Yet that is all relatively small potatoes compared with what AI computing giant Nvidia has brought to the table.

"Nvidia sits at the center of the AI ecosystem, acting not only as a technology supplier but also as a strategic investor helping accelerate adoption of its platform," says Tan.

Slijkerman says Nvidia plays a vital role, as it contributes to the development of a variety of new businesses, from healthcare to autonomous driving. "Its investments help support the growth of the broader AI ecosystem while also facilitating the deployment of AI infrastructure," he says.

The story that Nvidia is in talks to provide $250 billion to OpenAI, first reported by The Wall Street Journal, would be just the latest megadeal the $4.6 trillion company has bankrolled.

Jensen Huang's company is at the center of the artificial intelligence boom thanks to its industry-leading chips. Since 2024, it has invested heavily in multiple AI start-ups, including OpenAI, Mistral and Elon Musk's SpaceX. In turn, these companies are all committed users of Nvidia's chips.

It has also begun to invest heavily in so-called neocloud providers, such as CoreWeave and Nebius. These start-ups rent out cloud space for AI computing. As well as investing, Nvidia itself is also purchasing cloud space from the firms.

Nvidia is stepping up its spending and dealmaking in 2026 too. It struck a partnership with South Korean conglomerate SK Group recently, worth potentially $500 billion in business.

Throughout 2026, such circular dealmaking has become even more pronounced across the sector. OpenAI has struck close to $1 trillion worth of deals with the likes of Microsoft and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) agreeing to become one of AMD's biggest shareholders.

Microsoft and Nvidia have also invested heavily in Anthropic, with Anthropic in turn agreeing to step up its purchases of cloud capacity and chips from both.

The scale of the cross-pollination can bring advantages. "Interconnected ecosystems can accelerate innovation by aligning incentives across infrastructure providers, model developers, application companies and end users, helping new technologies scale faster," says Gary Tan.

Slijkerman says he does not see the circular trend as a form of "financial engineering". "These relationships make strategic sense because they help participants expand their market reach and accelerate adoption," he says. "They can also create mutual financial benefits."

Yet there are risks. Fears of an AI 'bubble' continue to stalk global markets. Tech and semiconductor stocks fell sharply last week amid doubts over profitability in the sector, relative to the vast sums being invested in data centers and other AI-related spending.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If AI revenues do not grow sufficiently, companies that have received funding from bigger players might face financial challenges. In turn, they may stop buying the bigger company's products and their valuations will fall.

Some analysts have drawn comparisons to the dot-com bubble and subsequent crash, which happened after valuations surged in the early days of the internet. Circular financing was a factor in that crisis, too, but many observers reckon the AI boom is ultimately built on more solid foundations.

"While some individual companies or business models may ultimately disappoint, the broader investment cycle appears to be supported by genuine demand and real economic value creation," says Slijkerman.

Tan agrees and says a bigger risk in future problems is interest rates. He thinks if interest rates rise, it could have a significant impact on many AI companies as they will be penalized by the time they become profitable.

"AI cash flows are long dated, so the direction of the yield curve may ultimately matter more than the availability of capital," he says.

Edited by: Kristie Pladson

https://www.dw.com/en/italy-garbage-work.title: Italy: Garbage workers help woman find €1 million jackpot
https://www.dw.com/en/italy-garbage-work.text:
A woman who won €1 million mistakenly threw her lottery ticket in a trash bin in Bitonto, southern Italy — prompting her local sanitation company to launch an hourslong search.

Garbage workers in the city of Bitonto, Italy recovered a €1 million ($1.15 million) lottery ticket, after having to search through an entire truck full of trash. Waste management company SANB administrator Roberto Nicola Toscano told AFP news agency that the ticket was found "miraculously still in one piece."

Toscano received the panicked call from the woman who had won the big prize and lost it.

The unnamed woman entered the Saturday lottery and on Sunday she went to check her ticket's result at her local shop.

But the machine read "non-payable," a common message indicating the prize was too large for the small retailer to redeem. She mistook the message to say that there were no winnings.

"The winner always played the same numbers, as they were associated with a loved one," Toscano said. According to Italian newspaper Corriere Della Sera, the woman's winning combination was 2, 4, 8, 10, and 51. A family member of the woman noticed the combination was the winning one and informed her, but she had already discarded the ticket.

By the time they returned to the shop, a garbage truck had already collected the trash bin that held her ticket.

After SANB was contacted by the woman, the garbage company moved quickly to reconstruct the journey of the ticket, Toscano told AFP. They were able to identify the correct truck and stopped it.

Combing through collected trash would pose the risk of potentially dangerous material in the waste, so the vehicle was taken to a special site equipped to do the search, Toscano said.

It took the workers one day of "working in conditions that were anything but pleasant" to find the ticket, Toscano told Corriere Della Sera.

Toscano said the woman cried when she found out, over the phone, that the ticket was found.

He told the paper that professionalism, organization, and a great deal of luck made the moment happen, saying the impossible result could not have happened without the garbage workers.

As a SANB is a public entity, the cost of the search would be covered by taxpayers, but Toscano told AFP that the woman had promised to "cover all of the additional costs."

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

https://www.dw.com/en/south-sudan-how-cl.title: South Sudan: How climate change can result in toxic water
https://www.dw.com/en/south-sudan-how-cl.text:
Years of flooding have resulted in disastrous water pollution in South Sudan's main oil region. As communities, scientists and health workers scramble for solutions, the long-term impacts of the crisis is yet to emerge.

The village of Bentiu has seen it all: Located in the north of South Sudan near the border with Sudan, the capital of Unity State used to have a population of merely several thousand people.

But war, violence and other crisis have resulted in an additional 140,000 displaced persons seeking shelter there since 2013, resulting in the establishment of a massive camp for internally displaced persons (IDPs).

Several UN bodies including the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) are active on the ground, running what is known as the Protection of Civilians (POC) camp, which by now feels more like a permanent structure.

At a makeshift pier, children are seen playing, countless canoes bring in fish to feed scores of people at the camp, where food insecurity remains a chief concern.

Immediately, each day's yield is separated into two categories: One stock with fresh, healthy fish, and another for those believed to be contaminated.

Simon Gatkuoth, a camp resident in his early forties, lifts a fish from a wheelbarrow, explaining that fish that are caught near the oil fields are contaminated: "When we cook them, the soup sometimes smells like penicillin," he says.

"But there is no option. We have to eat. We cannot stop eating because there is no alternative."

Viewed from the sky, the POC Camp resembles an artificial island in the midst of a region that has been transformed into what appears to be a gigantic lake.

Here, the largely nomadic communities of South Sudan's Unity State have long adapted their lives to the seasonal floods that shape life in what is one of the world's largest wetlands known as the Sudd.

But in 2021, and unprecedented deluge of floods linked to climate change submerged farmland across the region, destroying livelihoods and killing thousands of cattle.

Just one year earlier, authorities in neighboring Uganda had issued a warning that rising levels in Lake Victoria, situated roughly 1,000 kilometers (650 miles) to the south, would require the release of large volumes of water into the White Nile river, which flows past Bentiu.

But South Sudan, one of the poorest countries, lacked the dams, flood-control systems and water-management infrastructure needed to cope with the flooding, leaving many communities highly vulnerable to flooding.

To this day, the waters from that flood are yet to recede.

Maintained by the IOM, a simple levee is all that separates the POC Camp from the flooded plain; without constant maintenance, it would give way to the water.

The people here appear weary: First displaced by war and later hit by floods, most now depend on humanitarian aid, trapped somewhere between continuously rising water levels and unresolved conflict.

Yet in recent years, another disaster has slowly emerged, linking the devastating 2021 flooding to a major environmental hazard: Unity State, where the Bentiu POC Camp is located, is the South Sudan's biggest oil producing region.

Oil makes up more than 90% of state revenue, and accounts for nearly all of the country's exports. It is a vital sector for the country's battling economy, which has been severely limited in recent years by the war in Sudan to its north, with pipelines limited to a trickle, and many reserves sitting untapped or unused.

A geospatial analysis found that during the devastating 2021 floods, 159 out of over 400 oil wells in the region were submerged under water, amounting to around 41% of oil extraction infrastructure in the area.

In a joint effort with PlaceMarks Africa — an organization which makes of satellite imagery to help "design solutions for contemporary challenges" on the continent, DW has found that more than 50 of these wells continue to be submerged to this day — a growing cause for concern.

The rivers and lakes that hundreds of thousands depend on for drinking water, cooking and fishing appear to have been contaminated by the oil fields, with could carry potentially long-term consequences for both local ecosystems and human health.

"Many animals are dying because of this pollution, and people are also suffering from symptoms they attribute to it. All of this is visible, but we do not yet have sufficient evidence or epidemiological studies to state it with certainty," explains researcher Marko Gatkuoth, who is attached to the Rift Valley Institute — an independent research organization operating primarily in Central and Eastern Africa.

"The flood that began more than four years ago has become a vector of pollution. It has made the contaminants mobile."

Bul Duot Kuer, a South Sudanese researcher at Kenyatta University in Kenya, has conducted extensive research on the environmental impact of oil production in Unity State.

In a recent study, he identified lead concentrations of up to 18 micrograms per liter in the rivers around Bentiu and nearby Rotriak — nearly double the guideline value set by the World Health Organization (WHO). He also found hydrocarbon concentrations in the water at more than five times above the recommended limits.

"Water is the most polluted element," says Kuer. "There is no control. The environmental laws are there on paper, but they are simply not being enforced. This is negligence. The government and the oil companies do not care about people's health."

Waters around the settlement of Rotriak are particularly affect by this oil contamination: Satellite imagery analysed by PlaceMarks exposed pipelines, wells and abandoned facilities scattered across the settlement.

This is an area were children play among rusty pipes and women wash laundry at a former retention pond for oil production wastewater — albeit typically not by choice: Local resident Anna Nyashing Bul told DW that she and her family had to evacuate to Rotriak "because it was the only place that remained dry" after the 2021 flooding.

The untreated water they rely on often has "black film on the surface," she explains, which has repeatedly made her family fall sick.

"But we had nothing else to drink."

Meanwhile at Bentiu State Hospital, staff have noticed an increase of children born with deformities and other birth defects.

Midwives interviewed by DW also describe an apparent increase in miscarriages, complicated deliveries and congenital anomalies in recent years — especially with mothers who come from areas located in and around the oil fields.

19-year-old Nyapuka Nios from Rotriak just gave birth days ago; her newborn presents visible malformations to the hands and upper lip.

"I don't know what will happen to him," she whispers. "It is God's will. God gave him to me this way."

In another room, Nyekal Nuok watches over her baby girl, who was born with spina bifida five days earlier. She also lived in Rotriak during most of her pregnancy.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Research has shown that women living near oil wells are more likely to give birth to children with congenital anomalies.

Dorgan Patai, Director of Health Services in Rubkona County agrees that "since the floods, we are seeing more miscarriages and more children born with malformations," adding that "in the long term, this could even lead to infertility."

However, there has been no comprehensive investigation to establish whether these cases are indeed linked to environmental contamination.

The WHO says that a review of routine health surveillance data failed to present any statistically relevant increase in miscarriages, complications or other anomalies in Unity State, stressing that anecdotal reports should be interpreted cautiously.

There are few people who have done more to hold South Sudanese authorities accountable for the environmental consequences of oil production than Ayen Mijok Kiir, First Deputy Speaker of the Council of States, which is South Sudan's upper house of parliament.

She believes that years of conflict and insecurity have pushed issues like environmental protection and public health down the list of national priorities.

"We are not a stable country," Kiir highlights. "There are challenges in allocating resources to different sectors. We are under pressure to prioritise security. But yes, even with these challenges, we should have done more."

With her tireless campaigning, she succeeded in encouraging President Salva Kiir to further investigate the potential link between deformities at birth and oil-related pollution in 2024 despite many other ongoing crises in the region.

But despite numerous ministerial meetings being held, nothing seems to change.

"What difference will it make if I talk about this yet again?" she s ays quietly. "I have spoken about it so much, given so many interviews, and nothing has happened."

Ultimately, South Sudan still lacks effective environmental monitoring and public health standard in its oil producing areas — 15 years after gaining independence.

With conflict and suffering remaining rife throughout the region, addressing the affects of global warming might remain an elusive goal, as South Sudan struggles on many fronts to keep its head above water.

https://www.dw.com/en/tennis-star-sabale.title: Tennis star Sabalenka supports sport's new sex test policy
https://www.dw.com/en/tennis-star-sabale.text:
The world number one women's tennis player supports the WTA's new sex testing rules. Others are more critical of the policy.

"I think it's really important to keep the fairness in our tour," said Sabalenka on Monday. "Obviously, biologically, men are way stronger than women, so I feel like it would not be really fair for a woman to compete against a biological man.

"I believe it took them a little while to make this decision and I support it," the Belarussian continued. "If they want to test us all, I'm happy to do that; it's pretty fair, and let's keep it that way."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In July 2026, the WTA (Women's Tennis Association) introduced a one-time, mandatory genetic test for all players. As part of the protocol, players will be tested for the SRY gene, a segment of DNA typically found on the Y chromosome. The test can be conducted by a cheek swab or a blood test.

The new policy also includes a document players must sign highlighting disciplinary action is possible if testing is refused.

The previous WTA policy allowed transgender women to compete if their testosterone levels had been lowered to below 2.5 nmol/L continuously for the previous two years. There are no known transgender women currently playing on the WTA Tour.

Sabalenka is currently the best female tennis player in the world, and has been ranked number 1 for 92 consecutive weeks, so her endorsement carries a lot of weight.

On top of that, she competed in the modern edition of Battle of the Sexes in Dubai in 2025 — a match she lost to Nick Kyrgios, a male Australian player. While billed as a way to generate interest in tennis, some were critical of the match-up.

World Boxing introduced it in May 2025 after a lengthy and controversial debate around gold medal winner Imane Khelif at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

World Athletics did similarly in September 2025. Then, in the decision likely to have the most far-reaching impacts, the International Olympic Committee updated their guidelines in early 2026.

Trans athletes have long been politicized.

Riley Gaines, a former swimmer at the US collegiate level, has become a conservative political activist who is known for campaigning against the participation of trans women in women's sports. Recently, Gaines was seen supporting WNBA star Sophie Cunningham, who had said in an ESPN feature that "biological men" should not compete in female sports in order to protect young girls.

Maria Jose Martinez-Patino, whose personal experience with gender verification dramatically impacted sporting policy on the matter in the 1980s, believes new genetic testing for women at elite level is "a setback of several decades."

"It takes me back to the 1950s and 1960s, when women practically had to go through a series of controls, had to undress in front of a panel of doctors," Martinez-Patino told DW in an interview in 2025. "I get the impression that we haven't advanced from a scientific point of view. We've made practically no progress if it's now categorically said that women with X and Y chromosomes are not women."

World Athletics argues that the SRY gene — present in people with a Y chromosome, usually men — "is a reliable indicator for determining biological sex." Martinez-Patino believes, though, that determining someone's sex is not as simple as that.

"It's not black or white. There are more than 60 genetic mutations which I think are not all that complicated to study. Something that I've always said is that it should be done case by case," the Spanish former hurdler said.

Edited by: Matt Pearson

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-hedge.title: Germany news: Hedgehog triggers police alert
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-hedge.text:
Police responding to a supermarket burglar alarm in central Germany found it was caused by an unlikely culprit. Germany's flag carrier, Lufthansa, has turned in poor quarterly results.

This blog has now closed. Read below for a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, August 4, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google

BioNTech made a net loss of €1.35 billion ($1.55 billion) for the first six months of 2026, the company said on Tuesday, following a loss of €802.4 million during the same period last year.

Existing vaccine stocks in Germany can be used during the 2026 vaccination season. lowering demand for the company's main product, the COVID-19 vaccine.

BioNTech also expects lower revenue for the remainder of this year.

In May, the firm announced it would close three sites in Germany, with its Singapore operations expected to cease in the first quarter of 2027.

But the company still believes it will float on with developing new products, particularly in the field of oncology.

BioNTech is also undergoing significant leadership changes, with co-founder Ugur Sahin to be succeeded at the helm of BioNTech by Guido Oelkers by early February next year.

Oelkers had been the leader of Swedish biopharmaceutical company Swedish Orphan Biovitrum (Sobi) since 2017.

Sahin and his wife, BioNTech co-founder Özlem Türeci, plan to embark on a new venture while remaining BioNTech shareholders.

A farmer in Selm, north of Dortmund in western Germany, has taken aim at the US and Russian presidents Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in his annual tradition of creating a maze in one of his corn fields, which also forms an image when seen from above.

This year, Benedikt Lünemann's maize maze depicts Trump and Putin as infants wearing diapers and sitting on the grass, as the tiny Trump holds and plays with a ball reminiscent of a globe.

Lünemann has been carving giant mazes into one of his corn fields every year since 2009, often with political motifs.

The maze is also dotted with smaller scale decorations for people who visit in person rather than taking a photograph from above. Various quiz questions await visitors, one of which roughly translates as:

"What guidelines must even the US president follow? a) The rule of law, b) Noise and commotion, c) His momma's rules."

Lünemann recently told regional public broadcaster WDR that he wanted the exhibition to serve as a reminder of "how good we have it and how happy we can be to live in a functioning democracy."

Two driverless subway trains have collided during a shunting maneuver near the city of Nuremberg, derailing several carriages and forcing the closure of a station in the town of Röthenbach.

The city's VAG transport operator said the accident happened on Sunday and that the derailed cars now need to be lifted back onto the tracks.

Röthenbach station is expected to remain closed until Wednesday.

The trains operate on a line that has run without drivers since 2008 and is controlled from a central operations center.

VAG said the system has an extremely strong safety record and that nothing comparable had happened before.

Investigators are now examining whether an error occurred in the control center.

Shunting movements in subway depots have been suspended until the cause is fully established.

An independent expert and the regional government authority for Middle Franconia are also involved in the investigation.

A former mayor in Bavaria has been fined €7,200 (nearly $8,300) after secretly monitoring his secretary with a hidden camera for about a year.

The Landsberg district court issued the penalty just below the threshold at which a conviction is normally entered on a criminal record.

Court director Alexander Kessler called the case an "incredible incident" and said the relatively limited sentence was only possible because the former mayor had reached a compensation agreement with the victim shortly before the ruling.

He has agreed to pay his former employee €10,000 in compensation.

The then-mayor of Reichling had installed a camera beneath a desk in his employee's office, allowing him to monitor her, visitors and phone calls.

He could stream both video and audio to his phone and sometimes made recordings.

The surveillance was discovered in October 2025, after which police searched both the town hall and the mayor's home.

The scandal later prompted him not to seek another term in local elections in March.

The former mayor confessed and said he had distrusted the employee because she supported a political rival.

He told the court he had come to see his outer office as a "meeting point for the opposition" and installed the camera for that reason.

"That was wrong," he said.

He added that his conduct had been unworthy of a mayor and apologized both to his former secretary and to residents of the town of around 1,700 people.

The German government is mulling whether to join with the French state to take complete control of tank maker KNDS, the daily Handelsblatt reported on Tuesday.

The paper cited German government sources in its report.

In July, the Franco-German defense contractor postponed a planned stock market flotation, casting its ownership into uncertainty.

Currently, the family owners and the French state each hold 50% of shares and, under the plan, would have sold 10% each to investors, while the family intended to sell its remaining 40% to the German government.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has previously said that ​he wanted to ‌secure German influence over KNDS and that Berlin was going to talk to French partners "on an equal footing."

KNDS was created in 2015 when Germany's family-owned Krauss-Maffei Wegmann (KMW) and France's state-owned Nexter merged. The company's name stands for KMW Nexter Defence Systems.

The company, which employs more than 11,000 people and generated €4.4 billion ($50 billion) in revenue during the 2025 financial year, produces German Leopard-2 and French Leclerc battle tanks, among other weapons systems.

The Rhine River has sunk to new record low levels at some points in its course amid a series of heat waves, forcing cargo vessels to greatly lessen their loads and driving up transport costs.

The inland navigation agency WSV said the gauge point at Kaub, 32 km (20 miles) from Koblenz, measured just 24 cm (9.44 inches) on Tuesday, one centimeter below the previous record low from October 2018, which was again reached on Friday.

The mean values measured at the gauge point between 2010 and 2020 was 208 cm and the highest level since measurements began was 825 cm in January 1883.

The gauge point measurement, which is taken close to the riverbank, is used as an indication of the river's navigable depth, which is currently about a meter more.

Even that means that ships using the key waterway to transport goods are currently ​able ‌to sail at only around 20% loaded, causing supply delays and surcharges to companies that rely on them.

Traders have told the Reuters news agency that the cost of river transport from Rotterdam in the Netherlands ⁠to Karlsruhe rose to ​around €150-€160 ($173-$184) a ton on Tuesday, up from €45 at the end of June.

The WSV ‌has forecast that the gauge measurement at Kaub will fall to new record lows of around 21 cm on Thursday.

Scientists say the hot and dry weather now increasingly being experienced by Germany and much of Europe is a result partly of human-induced climate change brought about mostly by the use of fossil fuels.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Emergency personnel sprang into action on the Ruhr River on Monday evening after being alerted by passersby who saw a drifting dinghy carrying a motionless man and giving no signs of life despite calls from the bank.

Several boats and divers from the fire service's water rescue unit and the German Livesaving Association (DLRG) all took to the water ready to bring help, the Mülheim fire brigade said.

But their aid proved unnecessary: The man had just fallen asleep in the current warm weather and, awakened by the rescuers' calls, made his own way back to the riverbank. Life is but a dream!

The number of beer breweries in Germany is continuing to sink, a trend possibly reinforced by the falling numbers of people who consume the beverage, new statistics have shown.

In figures released on Tuesday following Friday's International Day of Beer, the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) said there were still 1,415 existing breweries in 2025.

That is 53 fewer than in 2024 and a whole 137 fewer than in 2019, the year in which the most breweries in three decades were registered.

Destatis said declining beer sales were a factor in this development.

They said beer sales had gone down by 15.7% in comparison with 2019.

In 2025, some 7.8 billion liters (2.06 billion US gallons) were sold, down from 8.3 billion liters in 2024 and 9.6 billion liters in 2016.

Of the German states, Bavaria had the most breweries (588), followed by Baden-Württemberg (190) and North Rhine-Westphalia (131).

However, with the exception of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Saxony-Anhalt, all states have seen the number of breweries decline.

Germany's flag carrier, Lufthansa, says its profits have fallen sharply in the second quarter, citing higher fuel costs, geopolitical instability and employee strikes as reasons for the plunge.

Core profit fell almost 56% to €383 million ($440 million) in comparison with the same period last year, Lufthansa said.

The fall came despite sales rising 10% to €11.1 billion in the three months to the end of June.

Lufthansa said higher fuel prices had increased costs by about €750 million.

"The second quarter was characterized by exceptionally high fuel costs and heightened geopolitical uncertainty," Lufthansa chief financial officer Till Streichert said.

The airline group said it now expects its adjusted earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) to come in at €1.7 billion and €2.2 billion this year.

It had previously predicted that adjusted EBIT would surpass last year's €1.96 billion in spite of the rising cost of fuel amid the Iran war.

Officers who deployed to a supermarket in the town of Mühlheim am Main in the central state of Hesse after a burglar alarm went off in the early hours of the morning did not have to deal with a dangerous criminal but a rather confused animal, police said on Tuesday.

"In the entrance area of the supermarket, the police discovered who had set off the alarm: four-legged, small, round and obviously lacking any criminal energy," they wrote in a statement.

"The suspected 'burglar,' caught in the act, turned out to be a hedgehog that had probably already snuck into the supermarket the day before," they said.

They said the animal was shut into the store by accident at closing time and had ended up "triggering the alarm while off exploring the place."

The hedgehog was briefly examined and found to be unharmed before being set free to continue its nocturnal wanderings, they said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A schönen guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn!

We are deep into what in Germany is known as the Sommerloch (summer hole), or "silly season," but we will still be doing our best to bring you some interesting and entertaining reading.

At a time when wars and wildfires are dominating the headlines, news of a hedgehog-triggered police deployment in central Germany could, for example, provide some welcome relief.

But is relief in sight for Germany's best-known airline? The latest news on its finances shows that it is facing some major challenges.

https://www.dw.com/en/more-cancer-prone-.title: More cancer-prone? Why younger generations may be at risk
https://www.dw.com/en/more-cancer-prone-.text:
Researchers are observing certain age-related types of cancer more frequently in younger people. A new study suggests this could be because younger generations are aging faster than their parents or grandparents.

Susanna was just 28 years old when she was diagnosed with bowel cancer. Andre developed lung cancer when he was only 34. Both of them have turned to social media to talk about their fight against the disease. Neither of them are medical outliers — not anymore.

The German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) has reported a sharp increase in gastrointestinal cancer cases for patients between the ages of 20 and 39. In the US, researchers have observed a similar development, with an even higher disease ratio than in Germany. Younger people are also increasingly being diagnosed with other types of cancers, including those that affect patients' bone marrow or uterus.

Cancer is usually regarded as an age-related disease. According to the German Cancer Aid non-profit, the average age for men and women with cancer is around 69. Cancer cells form when certain sections of the genetic sequence mutate and can no longer be repaired. The older we get, the less reliable our repair system becomes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A study by researchers at Washington University School of Medicine, US, has now found a link that could help explain why an increasing number of people under 50 are developing early-onset cancer. The reason, they suggest, is that younger generations are displaying a wider gap between their biological and their chronological ages. In short, they are aging faster.

While the chronological age counts how many years have passed since a person's birth, their biological age describes how much their body has aged, based on the cellular damage accumulated. Individual organs and tissues can age at varying speeds.

In other words, the same person's liver, heart and brain could each have different biological ages, all of which could differ still from the person's actual age.

The recent study has now for the first time established a link between the increasing gap between biological and chronological ages in younger generations on the one hand, and the risk of early-onset cancer on the other, Ron Jachimowicz explains. He's an attending physician and hematologist at the University Hospital Cologne, as well as head of the Max Planck Research Group for Biology of Aging.

"Don't forget, this is a correlative study," Jachomowicz cautions.

Correlation refers to two things appearing in concert, so it looks like they are related. It does not prove causation, which we speak of when one factor causes another.

While results can provide certain indications that seem quite plausible, researchers were already well aware of the fact "that there is an association between biological age and the risk of developing cancer," Jachomowicz says.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

It's not easy to determine a person's biological age. Calculating it requires a number of parameters — there is no single, precise test. Instead, epigenetic tests are used to determine chemical alterations of DNA sequences, evaluating certain blood values and measuring the length of so-called telomeres — that is, the repetitive DNA sequence located at the end of chromosomes that function as protective caps.

There are also physiological tests, to monitor various body and organ functions, as well as cognitive evaluations.

Researchers in the study at hand applied a combination of these various measurement techniques to analyze the data of more than 150,000 individuals drawn from the UK Biobank, a British biometric dataset.

They found that people born between 1965 and 1974 had a significantly higher gap between their chronological and biological ages than people born between 1950 and 1954. The younger the cohort examined, the wider that gap appeared to grow.

An investigation involving  more than 10,000 US individuals revealed an even higher deviation for participants born between 1990 and 1999, compared to a cohort born between 1965 and 1969.

"In Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom (UK) and the US, people born in the 1990s face at least fourfold higher risk of early-onset colorectal cancer compared with those in the 1960s," the authors write in the study.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

We used to assume that a healthy lifestyle could make up 75% to 90% of one's biological age. Now we know that's not true, Jachimowicz explains.

"We can influence about 50% of it," he says, "while the other 50% are genetically predetermined."

To help slow the aging process, he recommends "typical lifestyle interventions," such as working out regularly, eating a balanced diet, getting enough sleep, and avoiding drugs and alcohol.

And the value of social contacts should not be underestimated, he adds.

It's not easy to say why, on a biological level, younger generations are aging faster than their parents and grandparents. But there are a few hypotheses.

"Younger people are being exposed to earlier and longer obesity," says Tanwei Yuan, an epidemiologist in the Department of Clinical Epidemiology and Aging Research of the DKFZ in Heidelberg.

Other contributing factors are a sedentary lifestyle, and poor sleep quality due to extended periods of time in front of a screen, Yuan adds. She says the current study delivers valuable insights that confirm hypotheses long held by cancer researchers.

She also stresses the value of a healthy lifestyle to help reduce the risk of early-onset cancer.

"If you feel unwell, go to a doctor and ask for the screening," Yuan recommends.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yuan knows what she's talking about. The 32-year-old researcher says she had felt unwell for quite some time before being diagnosed with intestinal polyps last year. While these can start out benign, if left untreated, polyps can become cancerous. That's why it's important to listen closely to your body and take measures early, she says.

In a word: no, says Jachimowicz.

Determining an individual's biological age is the "subject of current scientific research, but in no way a practical routine or part of everyday clinical work."

However, he believes it should be, especially when it comes to initiating early cancer interventions. He believes this current study is particularly valuable because it highlights this path forward for future studies.

"It's still far off in the future," he says, "but it's very exciting."

This article was originally published in German.

https://www.dw.com/en/dry-danube-river-t.title: Dry Danube River threatens nuclear power in Romania, Hungary
https://www.dw.com/en/dry-danube-river-t.text:
Hungary's Paks nuclear power plant was operating at about 10% of capacity because of a lack of cooling river water. In Romania, the military blew up a rock outcrop in a bid to improve water flow to the Cernavoda plant.

Several central and eastern European countries are facing power shortages and impacts on industry amid prolonged hot and dry weather and record low levels on the Danube River and other waterways.

Hungary narrowly averted switching off its lone nuclear plant, but had still powered it down to a fraction of capacity. In Romania, the navy demolished a rocky outcrop exposed in the Danube's riverbed, trying to improve the water flow.

And in Serbia, hydroelectric power output was severely impacted by the dry conditions.

Continued hot and dry weather is forecast during the week, providing little sign of relief.

Romania's military detonated a rocky outcrop exposed by the low water levels on a branch of the Danube, seeking to improve the flow of cooling water to the Cernavoda nuclear plant, which typically supplies about one-fifth of the country's power.

The plant draws all of its cooling water from the Danube.

Soldiers detonated a rock some 50 kilometers (roughly 30 miles) upstream. The debris would be taken to a strategic spot and sunk to help raise the water level.

Defense Minister Radu Miruta said the operation was a success and the military had been waiting for a chance to access and demolish the rocks for decades.

If the partial diversion of the water fails, Miruta said, the plant would likely have to shut down entirely by Thursday.

Caretaker Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan said that carmakers Dacia and Ford had agreed to suspend production in Romania until August 19, following a crisis meeting with representatives of the energy-intensive industry. He said that other companies would be taking similar steps.

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said it was possible to avoid the unprecedented total shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant on Monday that was originally announced last week.

But the four-reactor station that typically generates almost half of Hungary's electricity production and around a third of its consumption was running at little more than 10% capacity on Monday.

Hungary had asked industrial users to curb consumption and households to make voluntary savings. Electric-powered freight trains were also stopped on Monday to reduce the load on the grid.

Magyar thanked people for their restraint on Monday evening.

"We have entered the critical period. The network is stable, consumption is currently well below planned levels, thanks to self-restraint. The last Paks turbine is operational. I will report back shortly from the (grid operator) MAVIR control room," he said.

Magyar also said slightly earlier on Monday that "water management forecasts for the coming days have become slightly more optimistic."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Serbia, the vast Iron Gate hydroelectric plant on the Danube was operating at only around one-fifth capacity on Monday.

Prime Minister Djuro Macut convened an emergency meeting on Monday to discuss the energy problems.

He appealed to residents to "minimize the use of big consumers of electricity in their homes, such as air conditioners," having described the situation as "serious and demanding" late on Sunday.

Far upstream in Bavaria, the Danube's levels were also affecting freight transport.

New German Transport Minister Steffen Bilger said the historic low levels on the Danube, and particularly the Rhine to the west — Europe's busiest inland freight waterway — were providing a first challenge for his tenure.

"It is indeed a very tense situation with the low waters," Bilger told Reuters TV on Monday, saying he would chair a crisis meeting on Thursday. "We are used to repeated low water situations, but this is really a very early point in the calendar year for problems of the kind we're currently experiencing."

Typically European rivers reach their lowest levels slightly later in the summer — it's entirely possible that several more weeks of predominantly hot and dry weather are yet to come.

https://www.dw.com/en/ceuta-eu-calls-bor.title: Ceuta: EU calls borders a 'shared European responsibility'
https://www.dw.com/en/ceuta-eu-calls-bor.text:
The European Commission has offered Morocco more support at the border to Ceuta and Melilla, and called for "united action" from the bloc on border security. Its interior ministers will discuss the issue on Tuesday.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has told Spain's prime minister that border security is a "shared European responsibility" and suggested the European Union could provide more assistance to Morocco.

This comes as Spain tries to return the last of tens of thousands of people who swam around or otherwise breached the border to the North African exclave of Ceuta last week.

EU interior ministers will convene for an emergency video meeting on Tuesday to discuss potential responses. The scenes had led to friction between EU members and to Italy and France implementing temporary border controls, even though it's not possible to travel from Ceuta to the mainland without providing identification.

Von der Leyen wrote to Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday, which was soon seen by several news agencies, calling for "united action" on border security within the bloc.

"From this incident it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points," she wrote.

"The protection of all our external borders is a shared European responsibility," von der Leyen said, calling for vigilant monitoring and the use of physical barriers where needed.

She commended Sanchez on his "swift handling" of the situation, with the vast majority of the roughly 50,000 people having already returned across the border to Morocco.

Ceuta's top government official Juan Jesus Vivas estimated that between 3,000 and 5,000 people remained in the city, with the Spanish government's delegate offering a slightly lower estimate.

Von der Leyen also raised the prospect of intensified cooperation with and assistance for Morocco if necessary when it came to the Spanish coastal exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla.

"Morocco is an important strategic partner, particularly in our efforts to combat migrant smuggling and illegal migration," von der Leyen wrote. "In cooperation with Spain, especially on anything related to Ceuta and Melilla, we could enhance border management early-warning systems and improve our technical and financial support to Morocco.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The sudden large-scale rush across Ceuta's border starting on Thursday triggered sharp tensions among the EU's member states, with France announcing temporary border checks.

Migration-averse governments or ministers in Italy, Denmark and Finland even called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-travel area, while right-wing opposition politicians around the bloc were often even more vocal.

Spain responded critically to what it called a "selfish" response from some partners, and called for emergency talks among European interior ministers to chart a way forward.

Von der Leyen said Tuesday's talks would be a "first step," promising the issue would also feature in October's EU leaders' summit.

The EU has significantly tightened its migration rules in recent months, in steps that have led to a marked reduction in irregular migration into the bloc more generally.

It's also agreed on the option of sending failed asylum seekers to partner third countries deemed safe outside its borders, calling these destinations "return hubs." So far, though, no such deals have been set up even though legislation enabling them has been ushered in.

Migration expert Gerald Knaus, the director of the European Stability Initiative think tank, told DW it was clear that last week's developments were not based on "anything structural," given no meaningful changes either in Morocco's social situation or in Spain's migration policy.

Instead, he said, there "was a lot of false information" online wrongly spreading rumors like "Spain was opening its borders" and "there was an opportunity to get through."

He said the lower numbers of people swimming around the border checks earlier in the week fueled the fire and led to the vastly increased numbers by Thursday.

Knaus said the current situation was in no way comparable with the crisis in 2015 when thousands of migrants were arriving on a daily basis, many fleeing civil war in Syria.

"In this crisis, there were very, very few asylum seekers. Most of them were young Moroccan men. So, no, this is not a sudden increase in structural pressure from a big displacement crisis," he said.

But Knaus said that the political reaction throughout Europe and the way it generated similar panic and far-right calls to close the Schengen zone demonstrated that the difference in scale and the event being an outlier rather than a pattern didn't really matter.

"What we see is that politically, even two days of an event in North Africa create fear in Finland and Denmark and Germany," Knaus said. "And so clearly, all countries in Europe have an interest in helping the countries in the Mediterranean find a policy. And the policy has to be signaling clearly: Don't do this. Don't climb across the fence. Don't take to the boats. Don't swim across the sea. Because when you do, we will treat you humanely, but we will return you and if necessary, to a safe third country."

Knaus said that this message, if conveyed and shown to be true, would stop dangerous sea crossings almost completely and overnight. And he said that the new EU rules could make it possible to achieve.

However, he said he did not hold out much hope for the events in Ceuta leading to concerted action or cooperation among EU members.

"What is most likely is that there will be some grandstanding — that different governments will accuse each other. Spain will respond and will say it is not to blame and there will be bad feelings and no solution," Knaus predicted.
