https://www.dw.com/en/binging-on-cringe-.title: Binging on cringe: It's as addictive as 'eating junk food'
https://www.dw.com/en/binging-on-cringe-.text:
Flexing achievements? Cringe. Expressing genuine emotions? Cringe. You want to look away, but you can’t. Cringe. It's so addictive, people have built social media careers by monetizing other people's worst moments.

I feel it. You probably do, too. Someone posts a crying selfie, proposes at a wedding, or confidently sings off-key at karaoke and we cringe.

We cringe when we see something so awkward, embarrassing, or painfully lacking in self-awareness that it makes us recoil.

But we're attracted to it at the same time because — perhaps — we've experienced similar situations ourselves or we know and care about people who have embarrassed themselves and we felt empathy.

And that's why cringe is also known in psychology as secondhand or vicarious embarrassment. We feel it on behalf of other people as well as their feeling it themselves. And sometimes we just enjoy watching other people suffer in a socially awkward situation.

Cringe has an online community: There are cringe compilations, reaction channels on cringe, comedy and other formats built on people's most cringeworthy moments. And people appear to be hooked.

Stefan Hofmann, a clinical psychologist specializing in social anxiety disorder at Marburg University, Germany, says cringe videos are as addictive as junk food: "If you eat junk food, you want more of it [or] even more outrageous stuff," Hofmann said.

Embarrassment is subjective. A bad grade won't embarrass a person who doesn't care about school, but it can trigger real embarrassment in a person for whom academic success is central to their sense of self, their identity.

"If you see a complete stranger misbehaving in public, you might get angry," said Frieder Paulus, a psychologist and neuroscientist at the University of Lübeck, Germany.

"But if your kid is doing the same stuff, you might feel embarrassed, not only for the kid, but also for yourself," said Paulus, "because [you feel] the behavior of the kid reflects [on] you."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Embarrassment belongs to a class of emotions psychologists call 'self-conscious emotions,' alongside shame, pride, and guilt. Within that class, embarrassment functions as a kind of emotional barometer that signals how well you're living up to social norms, and whether you're presenting yourself the way you want to be seen.

For people to feel embarrassment, they need a sense of self, as in some capacity for self-reflection, plus awareness of the social norms and context involved, and to be aware that there is an audience.

Our reactions to embarrassing situations are visible on a brain scan.

"We see failure ... the arousal region [lights] up because something is not okay," said Paulus.

Matthew Feinberg, a social psychologist at the University of Toronto in Canada, has found that people understand displays of embarrassment as a signal of prosocial behavior.

And that prosocial behavior creates a feeling of trust in the observer — they see that the person who is embarrassed knows they have done something socially awkward or wrong.

The message is: "I did something silly and I want to signal that it wasn't intentional and that I am a good member of society," said Feinberg.

On whether the same logic applies to the person observing someone else's mishap, Feinberg said witnessing embarrassment "triggers a natural response. My mind tells me to respond to that person with sympathy."

Feinberg said vicarious embarrassment may even be a stronger trust signal than being embarrassed yourself: "Possibly … because you're experiencing it even though you didn't do anything. It's an interesting research question that as far as I know hasn't been explored."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Embarrassment is also an expression of our fear that we may be excluded from a group when we do something embarrassing. For a social species such as that of humans and other animals, that can be dangerous.

"Fear of exclusion and fear of negative evaluation by others is painful psychologically as well as physically," said Hofmann. "It is certainly not the same quality of pain [as physical pain], but it's pain nonetheless."

In Hofmann's clinical work, he has tested so-called "social mishap exposures" in which patients embarrass themselves in an intentional and engineered way in an attempt to disprove the beliefs driving their fear or anxiety.

But cringe isn't something we can simply stop feeling. The emotion, researchers suggest, is involuntary and develops from an early age. And that also goes for associated emotions, such as empathy and trust, but also schadenfreude — not all of our addiction to cringe can be explained as an expression of positive emotion.

Hofmann says some people do experience pleasure when they see other people in embarrassing situations. And this distinction between empathy and schadenfreude also matters. If the pull toward cringe content was only about empathy, watching more of it would make us feel worse over time. But people keep watching cringe videos online.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany
https://www.dw.com/en/binging-on-cringe-.summary: Cringe is an online community of people who feel embarrassed by others' embarrassing moments. Cringe has an online audience of people's most cringeworthy moments. Psychologists say it's addictive as junk food, and it's also an expression of our fear of being excluded from a group.

https://www.dw.com/en/what-happens-next-.title: What happens next for Infantino and FIFA?
https://www.dw.com/en/what-happens-next-.text:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino is under pressure after the failure of his plan to create a commercial subsidiary for the World Cup. But will he be ousted? And what is needed for that to happen?

Now that Gianno Infantino has shelved his plans to create a commercial subsidiary for the World Cup and other FIFA events, UEFA's boycott of FIFA events is over and matches now appear less in danger. Nevertheless, the European governing body says it is now "rebuilding trust" with FIFA — and the story continues to develop rapidly.

As a result, increased focus will be put on women's football when the U20 World Cup starts on September 5 in Poland, and when the U17 World Cup starts in October in Morocco. There are also matches around the world that will decide the qualifiers for next summer's World Cup in Brazil in the same month. Despite there being scant mention in FIFA's subsidiary proposal of the women's game, it will be the first test of life after it.

While a boycott is now off the table, the games will be harder to navigate given the current chaos around the sport's governing body. This is far from ideal for the teams competing, particularly given the tournament's importance.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With UEFA, Europe's football governors, forming a united front, it is assumed that most, if not all, football associations on the continent will withdraw their support in the coming days.

The first nation to publicly drop their support for Gianni Infantino was Finland, last week. Wales followed on Monday, saying in a statement that "failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept," before England followed suit later in the day.

On Tuesday, Jordan FA President Ali bin Hussein accused Infantino of "blackmail", claiming FIFA offered to help solve the kingdom's problems in exchange for his endorsement. This is in stark contrast to some of the other Asian associations, such as Qatar, the UAE and Sri Lanka, who have publicly supported Infantino.

Germany's FA (DFB) is the biggest sports association in the world, but has yet to officially withdraw its support. It is expected to though, especially when considering the recent words of DFB Director Andreas Rettig. The 63-year-old recently told Stern magazine in an interview that Infantino's recent actions have led to "an irreparable loss of trust" and that football needs to "hit the reset button. We need a different culture. Because trust is the hardest currency."

"From my perspective, Mr. Infantino has invested a great deal of time, money, and energy into maintaining his power structure. Clearly, many decisions served primarily to consolidate his own position," added Retting.

The election for Infantino's post is on March 18, 2027, at the 77th FIFA Congress in Rabat, Morocco.

He will run for re-election as president for a final four-year term, looking to gain 106 votes from FIFA's 211 member states (Uefa has 55 votes, Africa 54, Asia 46, Concacaf 35, Oceania 11 and Conmebol 10) to win. Each state gets a vote and voting is done in a secret ballot, which takes time.

However, it seems as though Infantino is increasingly under pressure. Following the resignation of Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro last week, reports indicate that the FIFA President has called an emergency meeting on Wednesday.

If 19 of the 37 members of the FIFA Council, the organization's main executive body, vote in favor of his resignation then Infantino may well be out of office sooner rather than later. Several members of the council, including Germany's Bernd Neuendorf, have publicly crititcized Infantino for failing to consult them about his latest plans.

There might also be an Extraordinary FIFA Congress if 43 associations formally request it. Given that UEFA has 55 members, it holds the power to request it at any time. For Infantino to be voted out through a vote of no confidence, 106 votes would be required.

Before his venture to sell stakes in FIFA competitions to private investors ended in chaos after widespread condemnation, Infantino looked almost certain to win re-election. The reported revenues from this summer's World Cup were $15 billion (€13 billion), a significantly higher number than expected and one that would have strengthened his position in the organization, given that much of it would be redistibuted among the member organizations.

There has been a lot of speculation about who might succeed Infantino since his position has come under threat in the last week, but it is too soon to really know the legitimacy of any claims. In any case, any potential challengers must declare their candidacy by 18 November.

Nasser Al-Khelaifi, the Paris Saint-Germain chairman, had been touted as a potential candidate given his increasingly influential position in world football. However, the Qatari recently ruled himself out, with a representative for the executive reportedly saying via Politico: "Nasser has absolutely no ambition, no intention, no interest in the Fifa role." Qatar is one of the few federations to have publicly backed Infantino in recent days.

The most obvious candidate is the current UEFA President, Alexander Ceferin, but the Slovenian lawyer is reportedly also not interested in the role.

Concacaf (the confederation of North and Central America and the Caribbean) president Victor Montagliani is one of the few candidates who has expressed interest in the role in the past, but it is unclear whether the man who speaks English, French, Italian and Spanish is ready to challenge now.

Outspoken Norwegian FA President Lise Klaveness has supporters, and, after an initial failure, reached the UEFA Executive Committee in 2025. But the outspoken style that has won her admirers is thought not to have the broad appeal needed in a FIFA candidate. Some also believe her gender may count against her.

Finally, AFC chief, Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who lost out to Infantino in the 2016 election, could be a contender if the AFC breaks ranks from FIFA in the way UEFA have. A member of Bahrain’s ruling House of Khalifa,  the 60-year-old called Infantino's actions "totally unacceptable" and may be tempted to go against him again, though human rights questions contributed to his previous defeat.

Edited by: Matt Pearson
https://www.dw.com/en/what-happens-next-.summary: FIFA President Gianni Infantino shelved plans to create a commercial subsidiary for World Cup and other FIFA events. UEFA says it is now "rebuilding trust" with FIFA and the story continues to develop rapidly.

https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-russian.title: Fact check: Russian disinformation targets German elections
https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-russian.text:
Ahead of four elections in Germany this fall, dozens of fake posts are circulating online aimed at discrediting candidates and portraying Germany as divided. Analysts warn that Russia is now targeting local candidates.

Eric Stehr was unsure what to think when he first saw fake videos about himself.

He describes his reaction as "mixed feelings," somewhere between amusement and concern, laughter, and helplessness. "I don't want something like that online," he told DW. "But at the same time, I know there's nothing I can do about it."

A German student, Stehr is running for the state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt as a candidate for the socialist Left party. Being second on the party list, he has a good chance of winning a seat in the election on September 6.

But social media posts about him have falsely claimed that:

The false reports have been cleverly designed so that they appear to come from major German media outlets, including the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, Stern TV, ARD and Spiegel TV. But the videos are as false as the allegations they make.

A spokesperson for the police confirmed to DW that Stehr is not under investigation and has not been suspected of murder. Meanwhile, a Bauhaus University Weimar spokesperson confirmed to DW that there are no reports of alleged university sex parties or an alleged grading scandal.

According to DW Fact Check findings, the videos are part of the Russian influence operation known as Matryoshka, also referred to as Operation Overload. DW Fact Check has identified more than 180 fake posts on X, Bluesky and TikTok ahead of the upcoming elections.

The data comes from a detailed archive maintained by the anonymous investigative collective Antibot4Navalny, which was originally founded to expose disinformation targeting late Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny and now tracks Russian influence operations online.

DW reviewed several fake posts published since June 24. Notably, the campaign operates only on weekdays, with disinformation activity dropping off on weekends.

Many of the posts target candidates running in the upcoming German elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Lower Saxony and Berlin, all scheduled for September. The votes are seen as an indicator of Germany's political mood and a test for the country's recently reshuffled federal government.

Observers were not surprised to see Germany become a target of the campaign, but the scale of the operation has raised concerns.

"This influence campaign has been active across multiple platforms since September 2023," said Julia Smirnova, researcher at the Berlin-based Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy (CeMAS). "Its targets have included Germany's federal election, elections in Moldova and Armenia, and the Olympic Games in France."

What is new, Smirnova said, is the focus on relatively obscure individual candidates in local elections. "It is unusual for Russian influence campaigns to target specific candidates in regional elections." According to her observations, candidates from all parties have been targeted, except for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).

"What we're seeing now ahead of the state elections is a continuation of Russia's long-term strategy: Supporting parties perceived as more Russia-friendly while discrediting other parties and candidates," said Smirnova.

Pablo Maristany de las Casas, a specialist in foreign information manipulation and interference campaigns at the London-based Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD), sees similar patterns. Like Smirnova, he says the narratives mirror earlier Russian influence operations. The messages, he argues, are once again "pro-Russian, anti-German and anti-EU."

While no definitive link to the Russian state has yet been established, there is evidence that Russian-speakers are behind some of the posts, according to Maristany de las Casas. For example, a Spanish-language post on X was found to contain a revealing clue: The post, which targeted candidates Lydia Hüskens and Andreas Silbersack of the Free Democratic Party (FDP), abbreviated their party's name as "SvDP," which would be the Russian version: Svobodnaya Demokraticheskaya Partiya.

In a report, the Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD) describes Operation Matryoshka as "a Russian-aligned operation" and links the campaign to the group Storm-1679.

The OSINT research group Gnida Project, which investigates Russian disinformation campaigns, has previously found, that fake media campaigns similar to them of Matryoshka are directly linked, both technically and in terms of content, to the notorious Storm-1516 unit, which is controlled by Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU. This was also active in the lead-up to Germany's federal election in 2025. And both the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) and the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) of Germany have attributed this unit to Russia.

For Smirnova, the evidence points strongly in one direction. "With a very high degree of probability, this is a Russian campaign ," she said. The campaign, for her, was likely carried out on behalf of the Russian state, typically by "private companies with expertise in digital marketing and political influence operations."

The fake videos are professionally produced, but small inconsistencies often reveal that they are imitating established media brands.

Key questions can help identify manipulated content:

In the current wave of fakes, these questions quickly expose a familiar pattern: Fabricated stories, stolen footage, cloned logos, and imperfect copies of genuine video formats. Many of the discrepancies become apparent only upon closer inspection.

The campaign's messaging broadly falls into two categories.

Discrediting candidates: In one case DW spotted a video about Berlin Mayor Kai Wegner (archived video on archive.org) of the Christian Democrats (CDU), in which he is falsely accused of murdering a professional tennis player. The voice of the video is AI-generated and no evidence is provided. Berlin police confirmed to DW that no professional tennis player had recently been killed in the city and that there are no investigations involving Wegner.

Candidates from the CDU, the Social Democrats (SPD), Greens, the Left Party, and the FDP have also been targeted with false allegations of corruption, drug use, and, in dozens of cases, fabricated sex scandals.

Deepening divisions between eastern and western Germans: One fake video masquerading as a Eurostat report (archived video on archive.org) claims that a large majority of western Germans consider reunification — the 1990 unification of the former East Germany and West Germany — a "historic mistake." The supposed survey is not described in any detail, and no evidence of its existence can be found.

In a statement to DW, Eurostat said: "This is a fake video. Eurostat did not produce it. Eurostat did not conduct the "survey" mentioned in the video." In fact, genuine polling paints a different picture of western Germans sentiments: According to an ARD DeutschlandTrend survey from October 2025, 64% of respondents in western Germany said they were satisfied with the state of German reunification.

Numerous other posts claim that eastern Germans face systematic discrimination, that eastern Germany receives less investment in security and infrastructure, or even that experts predict a new division of Germany by 2030. One video goes so far as to claim there are plans to build a new Berlin Wall. None of these claims are true. Some posts even use the hashtag #TimeToDivideGermany.

"The goal is to pit eastern and western Germans against one another, or to suggest that people in eastern Germany are despised, hated, or discriminated against by western Germans," Smirnova said. "It is also about harming specific politicians through false accusations."

The operation remains active, with new fake content appearing regularly, but experts interviewed by DW say the campaign's impact appears limited so far. "The impact is really not that significant, as we can see from this artificial amplification of content," Maristany de las Casas said.

Many posts receive tens of thousands of views, sometimes more than 100,000, yet generate little genuine engagement. Comments, shares, and other interactions remain relatively low, and previous research suggests that disinformation campaigns such as Matryoshka/Overload have achieved only modest influence.

Another reason may be platform moderation. Unlike X, platforms such as Bluesky and TikTok often remove the content relatively quickly.

Eric Stehr, however, does not want to rely on that. He plans to file a criminal complaint over the fake videos. His attempt to have one of the videos removed from X was unsuccessful, he said, because the platform said it "saw no reason to take it down," and for now, the disinformation campaign targeting German politicians continues.

Additional reporting by Asya Lokina, Aldo Sanchez Vera and Anwar Ashraf.

Editor's Note: This article was originally published and updated on August 3, 2026, to clarify that German reunification refers to the 1990 unification of East and West Germany. On Aug. 5 this article was updated to reflect a slightly revised statement by Julia Smirnova regarding the campaign’s origin and to clarify the attribution of the operation to Russia by the ISD, the Gnida Project, and Germany’s BfV and BND.
https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-russian.summary: Fake videos are circulating online aimed at discrediting candidates in German elections. The fake videos are part of a Russian influence campaign known as Matryoshka. The campaign is aimed at targeting candidates in the upcoming elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Lower Saxony and Berlin

https://www.dw.com/en/the-economic-toll-.title: The economic toll of Spain's wildfires
https://www.dw.com/en/the-economic-toll-.text:
Devastating wildfires are ravaging Spain's tourism, economy and nature. Could the country have done more to prevent them?

Charred tree stumps, melted asphalt, burned-out cars and destroyed buildings: The wildfires in southern Europe are leaving a trail of devastation and causing billions of euros in damage.

Spain's economy in particular is at risk of being choked by clouds of ash. According to the EU's Copernicus Earth observation system, around 206,000 hectares of forest in Spain have already gone up in flames this year.

"According to the European Commission, the economic impact of wildfires in Spain in 2022 amounted to approximately €7.1 billion ($8.1 billion), representing around 4.5% of the country's GDP. This figure reflects not only the direct costs of firefighting but also the long-term economic consequences of recovering the affected areas," Emilio Vizuete Luciano, an economist at the University of Barcelona, told DW.

The fires often devastate the local economy and disrupt trade in the affected regions, Luciano says. "Tourism is also severely affected. Given Spain's strong dependence on tourism, the disappearance of this activity in fire-affected regions has particularly significant economic repercussions."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Climate economist Sarah Meier of Swiss public research university ETH Zurich has taken a closer look at the economic losses caused by wildfires in southern Europe. Her findings show that in regions affected by at least one wildfire, the growth rate fell by between 0.11% and 0.18%.

According to a 2023 study she co-authored, the decline in growth was even greater when several wildfires occurred simultaneously, rising to as much as 4.5% depending on the extent of the fires. "Our calculations are an average for the period from 2011 to 2018," she explains.

And she issues a stark warning: "The costs become particularly high when wildfires reach larger cities, something that has so far been very rare in southern Europe."

The European Environment Agency (EEA) has also calculated the economic losses caused by wildfires in previous years. In 2017, when nearly 990,000 hectares burned across southern Europe, the losses amounted to almost €10 billion.

According to the European Commission, the EU loses around 500,000 hectares of land to wildfires every year. Spain, Greece and France are among the countries where wildfires are most widespread.

The economic damage goes far beyond losses to tourism. It also includes the loss of biodiversity, declining forestry revenues, soil erosion, destroyed infrastructure and property, as well as the costs of fighting the fires.

A heated debate has erupted in Spain over the cost of fighting wildfires. Since 2009, investment in prevention has actually been declining — even though the number and scale of wildfires have reached alarming levels over the past decade.

According to official figures, spending on wildfire prevention in Spain fell from €364 million in 2009 to €144 million in 2024. Over the same period, annual spending on actually fighting and extinguishing fires remained stable at around €417 million.

For economist Luciano, there is "a certain irony" to this because prevention has been proven to be the best long-term investment. "It is far cheaper than fighting wildfires once they have already broken out."

The Spanish forestry services company Forescat has estimated that fighting and extinguishing wildfires costs around €19,000 per hectare. Nearly 400,000 hectares of forest went up in flames in Spain in 2025, amounting to costs of around €7.6 billion.

It's still too early to say how much fighting this year's fires will cost Spain; however, Maria Inmaculada Marmol Tardaguila of MATS, a social organization representing public-sector healthcare workers, says things cannot continue this way.

"Continuing to rely on the heroic efforts of firefighting crews to keep our forests safe is both ecological recklessness and fiscal irresponsibility," she notes on the organization's platform, which has also warned of an increase in respiratory illnesses caused by wildfire smoke.

"The solution is not to keep buying more and more firefighting aircraft, but, for example, to remove combustible material such as deadwood from forests before the first spark catches," she points out.

Unless public officials understand this, she warns, Spain will continue to "burn through its budget at the same rate as its forests burn."

This piece was originally published in German.

https://www.dw.com/en/man-arrested-over-.title: Man arrested over death of British woman found in suitcase in Athens
https://www.dw.com/en/man-arrested-over-.text:
The body of Scottish national Elisabeth-Jane Ross was discovered last month in a suitcase in a derelict building in Athens.

A 26-year-old man has been arrested by Greek police in connection with the death of a British woman whose body was found in a suitcase in Athens last month.

"Officers of the Directorate for Combating Organized Crime have solved the homicide of a 38-year-old UK national, whose body was found inside a suitcase in an abandoned building in the Kypseli area on July 18," the Hellenic Police said on Sunday.

The victim, identified in British and Greek media reports as 38-year-old Elisabeth-Jane Ross from Scotland, arrived in Greece in late June and was last known to be in the Athens area on July 10. She was later reported missing.

Police said the suspect, a foreign national, confessed on Thursday and now faces charges including intentional homicide, robbery and firearms-related offenses.

"It emerged that the [suspect] placed the body in a suitcase and transported it to the abandoned premises. Furthermore, in the days that followed, the 26-year-old used the victim's bank cards to withdraw sums of money," police said.

According to reports, the suspect said the victim was already dead when he found her, although police made no mention of this in their statement.

A replica pistol and a knife were recovered from the suspect's home.

Greek police said international cooperation, including support from Interpol authorities in the US and UK law enforcement agencies, helped identify the victim despite advanced decomposition.

https://www.dw.com/en/ceuta-most-who-bre.title: Ceuta: Most who breached border have left, Spain says
https://www.dw.com/en/ceuta-most-who-bre.text:
Nearly all of the more than 50,000 migrants who breached the border this week have returned to Morocco, according to Spanish officials. At least 72 people died in the border rush. DW has more.

We've closed the blog. Read here for updates on the situation in Ceuta, Spain's North African territory on the weekend of August 1-2.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Most of the 60,000 migrants who crossed into Spain's North African exclave of Ceuta had walked back to Morocco by Sunday, but some stayed on in the hills surrounding the city.

Spanish authorities continued searching for bodies in the waters near the stretch of urban beach that tens of thousands of migrants had breached days earlier.

We'll have more on the news about what exactly happened and why this many people decided to swim to Ceuta in the coming days.

Morocco's Interior Ministry said on Sunday that the recent border surge in Ceuta was fueled by misinformation on social media, human trafficking networks and a Spain court ruling banning the immediate return of migrants arriving by sea.

The statement was the first from the Moroccan government since the mass border breach on Thursday and Friday, during which Spain says between 50,000 and 60,000 migrants entered Ceuta.

Morocco said around 40,000 people were involved in the mass crossing at Ceuta, while 1,135 were stopped while trying to enter Melilla, Spain's other North African exclave.

The ministry also said 11 people had died. Ten of them died by drowning while attempting to cross the border, the ministry said, with one person dying after falling from a rocky area.

The ministry added that Moroccan officials were checking reports from their Spanish counterparts that 72 people died.

The border crisis in Ceuta has sparked debates in Spain and across Europe about the Spanish government's migration policy.

Many governments in Europe have sought to curb immigration, but Spain has pursued a different approach, recently announcing a plan to provide legal status to up to 500,000 undocumented migrants.

Pedro Sanchez and his Socialist government have been heavily criticized this week by politicians from Spain's right and far-right parties.

The leader of the opposition, the conservative People's Party's Alberto Nunez Feijoo, has traveled to the exclave, where he slammed Sanchez for failing to prevent the border rush.

The leader of the far-right Vox party, Santiago Abascal, who was also in Ceuta on Sunday, blamed the Socialist government for the migrant surge, which he described as "an invasion."

He said the surge was an "act of war" and an "attack on the sovereignty and security of Spaniards."

Abascal also said Sanchez was "a danger" to the country, and called for the EU-Morocco agreement, which functions as a partial free trade area, to be scrapped.

Far-right influencer and Member of the European Parliament Alvise Perez called for migrants to be expelled during a confrontation with a crowd of rival protesters in Ceuta. Much of the city's population is of Moroccan descent.

Perez had to shelter in a bar before being escorted away by police.

Sanchez and his government have also been criticized by other right-wing politicians in Europe, most notably Italy's Interior Minister Antonio Tajani.

Italy has suspended free movement with Spain, even though both are part of the Schengen Area.

Relative calm had returned to Ceuta on Sunday, but the city remained on edge following the deadly border rush.

Local officials have warned that the city's recovery has just begun, while right-wing politicians are blaming the Socialist government in Madrid for chaotic scenes that unfolded this week in the Spanish North African exclave.

Spanish Civil Guard ships were searching the waters around the city on Sunday for more bodies after between 50,000 and 60,000 migrants breached the border with Morocco.

Nearly all of them had walked back to the Moroccan side of the border by Sunday, according to officials in Ceuta, normally home to around 84,000 people.

At least 72 people died during the crush on Thursday and Friday, the Spanish government representative in Ceuta, Miguel Angel Perez, said.

Some drowned, while others were killed in a stampede at a breakwater barrier and a border fence.

Perez added that medical services have treated more than 1,000 people.

He said while the situation in the exclave had improved significantly, work remained to be done for the city to return to normal.

On Saturday, authorities installed a 500-meter (1,600-foot) floating barrier in the waters off Ceuta to boost border security, as well as reinforcing police and army patrols.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez criticised Italy's decision to suspend Schengen travel with Spain for one month.

Spain has reinforced police and military deployments in Ceuta. Authorities stressed that migrants entering the territory irregularly cannot travel onward to mainland Spain or elsewhere in the Schengen area.

An emergency video meeting of European Union interior ministers is to be held on Tuesday, according to Ireland's prime minister, Micheal Martin.

"As Presidency holders, Ireland will convene a meeting on Tuesday of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council... to discuss developments in Ceuta," the Irish leader wrote on Saturday.

The Republic of Ireland currently holds the EU's rotating presidency and Irish Justice, ​Home ⁠Affairs and Migration Minister ⁠Jim O'Callaghan has been tapped by Martin to lead the call.

In a social media post on X, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she had "offered support to Spain from the first moment" and that most of those who stormed the Spanish North African territory of Ceuta this week had been returned to Morocco.

"Not a single person reached mainland Spain or the rest of Europe," she said.

The head of the EU's executive said, however, that the bloc's "strong system" of border protections "needs to be further strengthened."

While emphasizing coordination, she said lessons must be learned "to improve our European resilience."
 
Calling for vigilance and coordination, von der Leyen ended her statement by saying, "Fighting illegal migration requires solidarity and a united European response."

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez on Saturday was cited by news agency AFP as saying that despite France's own increased security along its shared border with Spain, "We are not asking for Spain's suspension from Schengen."

Addressing calls by European politicians for Spain to be temporarily booted from the freedom of travel agreement, Nunez said: "Spain does not need to leave the Schengen zone. It's absolutely not on the table. We have great cooperation with Spain."

Italy announced a one-month suspension of visa-free movement with Spain on Friday after tens of thousands of migrants stormed the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, overwhelming authorities.

Spain has assured EU partners that irregular entry into Ceuta does not confer a right to remain in Spain, travel to the mainland, or move freely throughout Europe.

DW correspondent Jan-Philipp Scholz reported high tensions in Ceuta on Saturday morning, despite the claims by the Spanish authorities that the situation in the exclave was back under control.

"I've still seen clashes between police, military and migrants, also between locals and some migrants this morning," he said.

While the overwhelming majority of irregular migrants has already left the area, Scholz pointed out that thousands were still in Ceuta and Spanish authorities were growing "increasingly robust" in their efforts to get the rest to leave. Most migrants did not receive any food or water, and all the shops in the area are closed, Scholz pointed out.

"They are pushing the people away from the beaches or from overwhelmed reception centers that cannot take any more people in," he said.

He also said that locals were feeling "a mix of fear and anger" in the wake of the incursion.

"Most people did not want to come out of their houses yesterday. And most people are still staying inside today."

Donald Trump has called the migrant crossings into Spain an "invasion." US political analyst Michael Yaki unpacks the political strategy behind the rhetoric.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Ceuta, Spanish authorities started laying a new pneumatic barrier on the sea border with Morocco.

The 500-meter (1,640-feet) long barrier is designed to stand 30 to 70 centimeters (12-28 ​inches) above the water line and up to one meter (3.3 feet) below it. It will run parallel to a line of anchored buoys, forming a channel that would be patrolled by Spanish law enforcement.

Many of the migrants that entered the Spanish territory of Ceuta in recent days achieved that by simply swimming around the existing barrier with Morocco and gaining access to the Spanish-controlled beach.

Spain's El Mundo daily published a video online of a Guardia Civil boat installing the barrier.

In an open letter, 22 out of the EU's 27 members demanded a video meeting of the bloc's interior ministers on Saturday.

The meeting should be convened "as a matter of urgency" to coordinate a joint response to the situation in Ceuta, and "prevent further uncontrolled crossings."

Earlier on Saturday, Spain's Pedro Sanchez also called for a meeting of interior ministers.

In less than 48 hours following the border incursion in Ceuta, the Spanish government has managed to "fully restore control of the border, provide extensive humanitarian aid, repatriate virtually all migrants who crossed irregularly, and prevent any unauthorized movement toward continental Europe," according to Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.

"This has been achieved in close coordination with Moroccan authorities and with very little support from other European states," he added in the letter addressed to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and other top EU officials.

He also pointedly noted that Spain was "one of the European Union's least porous external borders, with a number of irregular entries that is half of that recorded in Italy in recent years (2021–2026), for example."

The Spanish leader also expressed confidence that a meeting of EU interior ministers would help "establish a common response to situations of this kind and reaffirm that the security of our external borders is a responsibility shared by all member states, and not just by those on the Union's front lines."

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-db-ha.title: Germany news: DB hampered by 'organized irresponsibility'
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-db-ha.text:
DB chief Evelyn Palla wants to overcome the culture of ''organized irresponsibility" by empowering new decision-makers within the railway operator. Bavarian brass musicians have wrapped up a 72-hour concert. DW has more.

We've ended coverage. Below is a round-up of some of the main stories from and about Germany hitting the headlines on the weekend of August 1-2.

Thanks for reading the weekend edition of the Germany blog. We'll be back with the latest headlines on the morning of August 3.

The audience at the annual Richard Wagner festival in Bayreuth booed after a performance of "Götterdämmerung" that was staged on a set that was designed with the help of artificial intelligence (AI).

The staging featured a collage of images which appeared to confuse members of the audience, who booed when curator Marcus Lobbes and his team took the stage at the end of the performance on Saturday evening.

The audience, however, warmly applauded the singers and musicians, as well as conductor Christian Thielemann.

Ahead of the performance, organizers had said AI would be used on stage for the first time as "an image-generating force."

The singers of Wagner's epic drama would be "the fixed point within a visually seething cosmos of light, texture, history, and association, amidst projections that erupt, constantly shift, and merge into one another," the festival's organizers said.

The AI-generated projections were drawn from images that Lobbes and his team had pre-selected, which included scenes from previous performances of Wagner's "Ring" cycle of four music dramas and from historical themes.

The collage, which included a commemorative stamp marking German reunification, images of former chancellor Helmut Kohl and the World Trade Center towers after the September 11 terror attacks, appeared to confuse the audience, according to German news agency dpa.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is in a "very, very stable and strong" position, according to Bavarian Premier Markus Söder, who said on Sunday that he is "totally convinced" that Merz will "remain chancellor."

Söder, of the Christian Social Union (CSU), the conservative Bavarian sister party of Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), made the comments in an interview with public broadcaster ZDF amid falling poll ratings for the chancellor.

With some party members fearing a poor performance in upcoming state elections in autumn, speculation has grown that Merz could be replaced as head of the government.

Söder dismissed such suggestions and warned that such a scenario could lead to demands for an early federal election "which would only promote one thing: extremists gaining power."

Instead, Söder urged party members and supporters to "concentrate on the work which needs to be done" and called for "togetherness" and "unity."

Water levels in the Rhine river reached historic lows in Cologne, Düsseldorf, Bonn, Duisburg and other cities this weekend due to continuing high temperatures and a lack of rain.

In Cologne, the Rhine fell to just 67 centimeters (26 inches), two centimeters lower than the previous record set in 2018. By Sunday, the water level (or Pegel in German) had risen back up to 69 centimeters.

In Düsseldorf, however, the water level dropped to just 21 centimeters on Sunday, also two centimeters lower than the previous low point.

Low water levels are driving up transport costs for the business sector and placing a particular burden on industries that rely on the transport of bulk goods. Inland vessels are forced to carry significantly less cargo or suspend operations entirely.

In addition to freight shipping, the exceptionally low water levels on the Rhine are also causing difficulties for tourism and passenger shipping.

According to one company, the Köln-Düsseldorfer Deutsche Rheinschiffahrt GmbH, numerous trips have had to be canceled, and certain vessels have been unable to dock at specific piers along the Rhine due to the receding waters.

"Freight traffic on the Rhine is already reacting to the falling water levels," warned Thilo Schaefer from the German Economy Institute (IW), telling the Rheinische Post newspaper that the reduced loads on river barges force transport costs upwards and also puts motorways and railways under more pressure.

Christoph Ploss, a conservative (CDU) politician who acts as the German government's maritime coordinator, warned that "low water levels must not become a ball and chain for the German economy."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A 41-year-old man was found drunk and asleep next to a German motorway in the early hours of Sunday.

Police said they received several calls from drivers who had spotted the inebriated pedestrian stumbling around on the A96 Autobahn near Memmingen in the southern state of Bavaria.

When officers arrived on the scene, they found the man asleep under a crash barrier.

The man, who was said be "absolutely dunk" was taken to a cell to sober up.

Around 1,850 brass musicians finished an unprecedented, 72-hour live performance with a church service In St. Jacob's church in Nürnberg, Bavaria on Sunday.

The event involved over 140 bands from across the German state, with them swapping roughly every 90 minutes to ensure there are no interruptions longer than 10 seconds.

The record is now to be confirmed by Germany's Record Institute.

Bavaria's Premier Markus Söder agreed to act as patron for the event.

In a statement, he conservative politician praised the "enthusiasm" and "passion" displayed by the musicians, and said that music creates "a strong sense of community — not only inside the circle of brass musicians, but also between them and their listeners."

German cereal producer Kölln is expanding its contamination warning for its cereals with chocolate over fear that "foreign objects" might have gotten into the packages.

"We would like to emphasize that, to date, there has been only one known case in which a hard plastic part from our production process was found in a package. The foreign object was not baked into the product," they said in a statement online.

The warning now applies to cereal packages of 375 grams with batch numbers L6165, L6164 and L6235. The packages are also marked with "best before" dates  of 17.04.2027, 16.04.2027 and 05.06.2027.

Kölln urged customers to return their product to supermarkets, promising a full refund regardless of having a receipt.

The culture inside Germany's Deutsche Bahn (DB) is already shifting but the current crisis will take years to overcome, the head of the national railway company told Germany's Welt am Sonntag.

CEO Evelyn Palla criticized the old decision-making process in DB, saying that the central management often made big decisions on the operative level.

"The people in the headquarters, who made those decisions, don't have any responsibility for implementing them in the field," Palla said. "They have to be implemented by colleagues who are out there. But they say 'I didn't make this call, and it also doesn't work for me.' Then the headquarters says 'I have no operational responsibility, those people in the field did not implement [the decision] properly.' In the end it was something like organized irresponsibility."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

She told the paper that much has been "reformed" and "slimmed down" since she took the reins of the state-owned firm last October, and that multiple administration levels inside DB had been cut.

"But all of that does not make for a better (Deutsche) Bahn," she added. "Things will only change when the management changes, when decentralized units take responsibility and live with it."

In the interview published on Sunday, she also said that the German railway network was "run into the ground by 25 years of saving money" and that tangible improvements will take time.

She pointed to DB's 200-year anniversary coming in 2035, saying that "this should be the year when the worst is behind us."

Welcome back to our coverage of top news stories from Germany on this early August weekend.

On Sunday, Berlin is preparing for an anti-Islamist march in response to the deadly terror attack which shook Germany to the core a week ago.

In Bavaria, over1,800 brass musicians are hoping to break the record for the world's longest concert as they near the end of the unprecedented 72-hour live performance.

And Evelyn Palla, the head of Germany Deutsche Bahn, is decrying "organized irresponsibility" inside the troubled railway company.

We will be bringing you more on these and other stories from Germany in this live blog.

Thank you for reading the weekend edition of our blog about Germany and be sure to check in on Sunday morning to stay up to date with the latest headlines out of the country.

Hamburg's Pride parade went ahead under heightened security, one week after a 21-year-old drove a van into crowds at Berlin Pride. The attack killed one person and injured 29 others.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Earlier this week, Germany for the first time deported a man with no criminal record to Kabul.

This set a precedent that sparked vociferous protests:  260 people heeded the call of an anti-racism alliance and came to demonstrate inside the airport's departure hall, accompanied by a police escort.

Read more about Germany's policy on deportations to Afghanistan.

German Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil on Saturday called on Europeans to stand by Spain amid the debate over the surge of migrants into Ceuta.

Footage showing tens of thousands of migrants crossing into Spain's North African exclave of Ceuta raised concerns across the European Union.

"Migrants were used in an attempt to divide Europe," Klingbeil said.

He noted that Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez had restored control quickly and that most migrants who entered Ceuta had already returned to Morocco.

"Especially in situations like these, Europe must not allow itself to be divided," Klingbeil said.

Klingbeil's comments come after Italy officially suspended the Schengen agreement with Spain for one month in response to the mass crossing in Ceuta.

A popular park in eastern Germany was closed to visitors on Saturday after a storm caused damage and left one person dead overnight.

A 38-year-old man was killed on Friday evening near the Felsenbühne open-air theater in Rathen when he was struck by a falling tree.

Ten other people were injured, three of them seriously, while 40 people were evacuated.

Emergency crews resumed clean-up operations on Saturday.

Authorities closed the area between the Bastei rock formation, the villages of Rathen and Hohnstein, and the Polenztal valley, citing ongoing safety risks for visitors.

The story of the region's success dates back some 200 years: two Swiss artists were teaching at the Dresden Academy of Art when they went on an excursion out of the city. The majestic rocks of the Elbe Valley Sandstone Mountains reminded them of the mountains of their home. They promptly renamed the area Saxon Switzerland.

Dresden continues to be the best starting point for a trip to Saxon Switzerland. In front of the city's Baroque skyline of splendid buildings, which are incidentally made of sandstone, the steamboats cast off and set a course on the Elbe River.

Just two hours cruise up the Elbe towards the Czech border brings you to your destination. If you disembark at Wehlen, Rathen, Königstein or Bad Schandau, the mountain-world is only a few steps away.

Wind and weather had millions of years to shape the soft sandstone into extraordinary formations. Over the years, people have given them imaginary names like hell hound, locomotive, valley-guard. Pictured here are the Herkulessäulen - or Hercules' Pillars - in the Bieltal valley.

The region has an extensive path network offering routes for beginners as well as experienced hikers. You don't need to go far to see new things - rocks, flat mesas shaped hills, plateaus and gorges are all on the path. Should you have to climb uphill rest assured that your hard work will eventually be rewarded with a fabulous view.

Many of the region's hiking trails lead to the Bastei - or bastion - which is probably the most famous rock formation in Saxon Switzerland. Long ago it housed marauding knights, later the romanticists flocked here and today it's tourists. Solitude is something you rarely get to enjoy as the view of the surrounding area from here 200 meters (656 feet) above the Elbe is just too good.

With over 1,100 summits, Saxon Switzerland is Germany's largest rock climbing area. In 1874, a summit was reached for the first time without the use of climbing aids. Saxon free-climbing means it has to be accomplished without the help of any artificial device attached to the rock. Only ropes, bolts and quick-draws may be used to protect the climbers in case of a fall.

It is one of Europe's largest fortresses, which in its 800-year history was never conquered, mostly because of its thick walls and heavy canons. Saxon King Augustus II the Strong used this fortress as a state prison but also for splendid receptions. His wine cellar can still be viewed today.

From the Königstein Fortress the view reaches as far as Lilienstein, one of Saxon Switzerland's most distinct mesa mountains. The Elbe River keeps a respectful distance and even makes a turn. All in all, a picture perfect view.

Those who still have energy reserves after hiking and climbing can bike back to Dresden on the Elbe cycle path. This flat route offers some last fabulous views of the mountains and rock formations along the Elbe.

When Anahita Abdollahi starts her shift, she first checks her emails to make sure she's up to date on all the library requests.

The 26-year-old master's student from Iran describes her job as a "part-time librarian" — she helps people find books they need for their studies, answers phone calls, and waters the plants.

This type of employment is known in Germany as a "minijob," a system that allows millions of workers, including students, to avoid paying income tax or social security contributions.

Read more on why Germany's government is considering eliminating the minijob system in its current form.

https://www.dw.com/en/moscow-restaurant-.title: Moscow restaurant blast a 'brutal terror attack,' mayor says
https://www.dw.com/en/moscow-restaurant-.text:
The deadly explosion outside an upscale Moscow restaurant at Kudrinskaya Square was a "brutal terror attack," Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said, promising the perpetrators would be punished. But many questions remain.

An explosion at a restaurant in central Moscow killed at least three people, including the suspected bomber on Saturday night, authorities said.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin described it as a "brutal terrorist attack."

"Law enforcement agencies are investigating the circumstances of the incident. Those responsible for this crime will certainly be found and face the punishment they deserve," he said in an online post on Sunday.

Russia's Anti-Terrorism Committee said a woman carrying  "a homemade explosive device" tried to enter the restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square but was stopped by a security guard.

The device exploded at the entrance, killing the woman, the guard and a restaurant patron.

State news agency RIA Novosti reported that at least 21 other people were injured in the blast, which occurred shortly before 8 p.m. local time (5 p.m. UTC).

The restaurant's website said the venue had been closed on Saturday for a private event.

Heavily armed law enforcement officers sealed off the area and launched an investigation.

Authorities did not immediately identify those they believed to be behind the attack.

Russia has faced several attacks since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. They blamed a ‌series of assassinations and attempted killings on Kyiv. Russian officials have yet to comment on any possible Ukrainian involvement into the Kudrinskaya Square blast.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, Ukraine used drones to attack other parts of Russia on Saturday evening and early on Sunday, including a bombing which targeted an apartment block and killed two in the city Engels, some 900 kilometers (560 miles) southeast of Moscow.

Russia's Defense Ministry also said Kyiv struck a warehouse belonging to Wildberries, a major online retailer in Russia, with the Ukrainian drones hitting a site in the Samara Oblast, deep inside Russian territory. Regional Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said it was not immediately clear if there were any casualties.

Russian officials also reported over a 100 Ukrainian strikes in the Belgorod Oblast, which borders Ukraine. They said Kyiv forces used artillery, rocket launchers, and drones, leaving 14 people injured.

Over 200 Ukrainian drones have allegedly been shot down during the wave of attacks.

Overall, Russia claimed 635 downed Ukrainian drones overnight.

Meanwhile, at least one person was killed and seven wounded in the Russian attack on Ukraine's Kherson, with the attack involving artillery fire.

In Dnipro, seven passengers were wounded in a drone strike on a minibus, with the regional military administrator Oleksandr Hanzha describing it as a "deliberate and cynical attack on civilians."

At least nine people were killed and 33 injured in Russian strikes on Kyiv earlier this weekend.

https://www.dw.com/en/poland-prime-minis.title: Poland: Prime Minister Tusk defies anti-Ukrainian violence
https://www.dw.com/en/poland-prime-minis.text:
Anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland is on the rise, with numerous attacks against refugees from the war in Ukraine. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has spoken out against the violence and warned of the danger from Russia.

The Polish leader didn't mince his words. "We must wage a resolute fight against this violence, because thugs, hooligans, and this culture of violence are becoming increasingly brazen and insolent — and also because they have received political support," Donald Tusk said on Tuesday, before a Polish cabinet meeting in Warsaw. The liberal-conservative prime minister said he deplored the fact that "more and more such incidents" are taking place all over Poland.

Tusk's comments came in response to an incident in Wroclaw two days earlier, in which three Polish men brutally beat up a young Ukrainian man and his girlfriend on the street. Cellphone videos show the attackers kicking the Ukrainian man as he lies on the ground. The woman was also hit, sustaining injuries to her neck and ear.

The attack came after an argument in a shop; the attackers took exception to the couple's Ukrainian accents. Polish police acted swiftly: Two of the attackers, both of whom have previous convictions, are already in custody, and a third is being sought.

Tusk warned that such incidents negatively impact Poland's image abroad. The country's reputation was greatly enhanced by its willingness to provide assistanceafter the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine. This could be destroyed, said Tusk, "if we allow thugs, hooligans and common criminals to beat and humiliate people just because they have a slightly different accent."

Poland provided military and humanitarian assistance to its neighbor from the very beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It took in more than one million refugees from the war, and around 1.5 million Ukrainians are currently living in Poland. The majority of them work, pay taxes, and contribute to the Polish economy.

But four and a half years after the start of the war, the mood in Poland has changed. More and more often, Ukrainians are being verbally and physically attacked in public. Last Wednesday a Polish manager on a construction site in Skawina, near Krakow, was filmed aggressively insulting Ukrainian workers. In another incident on a local train near Warsaw, two drunken men shouted verbal abuse at a Ukrainian passenger. On July 11, a man on a bus in Bielsko-Biala insulted and threatened two Ukrainian girls who were trying to take a selfie. Even schoolchildren, including teenagers at a playground, have fallen victim to the new climate of hate.

According to the police, 180 hate crimes against Ukrainians were recorded in the first six months of this year — a third more than in 2025. And on Friday (31.07.2026) the newspaper Gazeta Wyborcza warned that the internet is full of fake news about crimes Ukrainians are supposed to have committed against Poles.

Anti-Ukrainian slogans were already apparent during the presidential election campaign last year. But this May was a big turning point. The Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy prompted outrage in Poland with his decision to award a special unit of the Ukrainian army the honorary title of "Heroes of the UPA."

Poland holds the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) responsible for the mass murder of tens of thousands of Polish civilians in Volhynia between 1943 and 1945. Ukrainians, on the other hand, revere the soldiers of the UPA as heroes in the fight against the Sovietization of their country. Individual UPA units continued to fight against Soviet rule well into the 1950s.

Along with Polish opposition politicians, Tusk is also critical of Zelenskyy in the row about the UPA. However, he believes that the reactions on both sides are exaggerated and counterproductive. Poland's president Karol Nawrocki revoked the award of Poland's highest order to his Ukrainian counterpart, which had been made in 2023. Zelenskyy returned the award by courier to Warsaw.

These demonstrative gestures by both leaders have set off an avalanche. The Polish internet is flooded with hatred for Ukraine. Przemyslaw Czarnek, the prime ministerial candidate of the leading opposition Law and Justice party (PiS), demanded that all military aid for Ukraine be stopped until Kyiv backs down in the row over the interpretation of history.

Current opinion polls speak for themselves. According to a survey by the CBOS institute, for the first time since the start of the war a majority of respondents (54%) were opposed to taking in more Ukrainian refugees. Only 42% supported maintaining the policy to date. In 2022, at the start of the war, 94% of Poles wanted to offer sanctuary to refugees.

Another poll, by the Opinia24 institute for the weekly newspaper Polityka, found that 44% were against providing further aid to Ukraine, and 41% in favor. 54% of respondents opposed Ukraine joining the EU. Only 33% supported Kyiv's desire to become part of the European Union.

The Ukrainians who were attacked in Wroclaw spoke to the NEXTA Polska news service and urged their fellow countrymen to be careful while in Poland. They advised them to avoid any kind of conflict and to "speak less Ukrainian" in public, as a precaution.

Poland's center-left government under prime minister Donald Tusk has emphatically condemned the anti-Ukrainian attacks. The Polish police and judiciary have also acted swiftly and decisively. After the incident in Wroclaw, Tusk urged President Nawrocki to "break his silence" and condemn the violence. So far, Poland's head of state still has not commented. During the presidential election campaign, Nawrocki, a former boxer, admitted that in his youth he took part in an organized brawl between fans of rival football clubs, violence he described as a form of "noble, masculine combat."

Tusk agrees with the opposition's criticism in the row about the UPA. All the same, he is trying to pour oil on troubled waters. On Wednesday, he met with the Ukrainian president Zelenskyy in private for the first time since the UPA crisis. "We also talked about the security challenges that, unfortunately, affect our people as well: it is important that Ukrainians who have left their homes because of the war and found refuge in Poland feel safe," Zelenskyy wrote afterwards on social media, and thanked Tusk.

Polish-Ukrainian cooperation is vital for both countries, as demonstrated by an incident in eastern Poland in the early hours of Thursday (30.07.2026). During a massive Russian attack on Ukraine, a Russian rocket crossed into Polish airspace, landing in a field near a village around 90 kilometers inside the Polish border. The explosion left a crater ten meters wide.

"I know it's not very popular these days to speak well of Ukraine," Tusk said after visiting the scene. Nonetheless, the Polish leader continued: "Poland's security directly depends on the effective actions of Ukrainian forces, including in the air." Tusk stated: "I know where the enemy stands," and added that, despite protests by the Polish opposition, he remains committed to supplying weapons to Ukraine.

This article has been translated from German.
https://www.dw.com/en/poland-prime-minis.summary: Polish PM Donald Tusk says violence is becoming more brazen and insolent. Tusk warns of danger from Russia and rise of anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland. Tuski: "We must wage a resolute fight against this violence"

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-islamism-a.title: Germany: Islamism and right-wing extremism — a story of mutual radicalization
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-islamism-a.text:
Following the attack on Berlin's Pride parade, Germany is focusing on the threat of Islamist terrorism. But experts say Islamists and right-wing extremists have more in common than many assume.

The terror attack on Berlin's Pride parade has shocked Germany. The perpetrator, 21-year-old Abdul Ballout, was a German national and known to German security forces as an Islamist who had tried to join the "Islamic State" group. He had already been convicted of criminal offences twice, and was awaiting a decision about a possible prison sentence at the time of the attack.

The LGBTQ+ community is not a surprising target, according to Jakob Guhl, a director of policy and research at the London-basedInstitute for Strategic Dialoguewho has studied Islamist extremism for many years. "The ideology is deeply homophobic and hostile to the queer community. The 'Islamic State' terror group, when it held territory in its so-called caliphate, executed people it accused of homosexuality," Guhl told DW.

In recent years, there have been several attacks on Pride events, Guhl said: In London, Oslo, Zurich and Vienna.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Guhl has also noticed that Islamist extremism has a close relationship with far-right extremist movements. Both ideologies strengthen each other and profit from one another, he argues: "Both are of the view that peaceful coexistence between Muslims and non-Muslims is impossible."

Young Muslims' experiences of discrimination in Germany, being marginalized, and negative reporting about Islam are cited as proof of the German state's hostility towards Islam, according to Guhl.

"In the view of the Islamist extremists, right-wing extremists are representative of Germans as a whole, and on the other hand the right-wing extremists say that Islamist extremists essentially represent Muslims," Guhl says. "There is an attempt to split society into two camps."

Both ideologies overlap in numerous attitudes: contempt for Western liberal society, the propensity toward conspiracy ideas, mistrust of government institutions, anti-feminist attitudes, and hate of the LGBTQ+ community.

"Their reasons for disliking the LGBTQ+ community do vary. On the one hand, from the religious ideological perspective, they believe it goes against the instructions of God," Guhl explained. "On the far-right extremist side, it mostly stems from a biological-racist perspective that it lowers the birthrate and weakens the health of the nation."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Germany, security authorities have for years observed the formation of a new generation of young, violence-prone, far-right extremists who are mobilizing against Pride parades.

In a 2018 study entitled, "Loving hate. Anti-Muslim extremism, radical Islam and the spiral of polarization," Guhl and other authors described the common interest of both ideologies: Social division, itself a breeding ground for extremism.

To combat the proliferation of such ideologies, the authors recommended a tougher approach toward hate speech on social media. They also call upon traditional media to avoid one-sided reporting and finger-pointing, which only fuels the polarization spiral.

According to Guhl, one example of this is the current discussion about the background of the attacker of the Berlin Pride event. "I find the question of the nationality of the perpetrator problematic: You quickly run into the danger of creating a two-tier society between different affiliations. That is counterproductive when it comes to the dynamics of radicalization."

For Guhl, it is also important to keep pointing to what Muslim and non-Muslim communities have in common: "We share many more things than those which divide us."
