Both ideologies overlap in attitudes: contempt for Western liberal society, mistrust of government institutions, anti-feminist attitudes, and hate of the LGBTQ+ community.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-as-tempera.title: Germany: As temperatures rise, so does climate skepticism
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-as-tempera.text:
Some 98% of active climate scientists say climate change is happening, and is man-made. Nonetheless, a new study shows the number of climate-change skeptics in Germany has increased. Why is that?

Climate skeptics are no longer a small but noisy minority. They are now "a mass phenomenon," according to researchers at Flensburg University.

In a study published in the scientific journal Global Environmental Change, authors Katharina Gies and Emanuel Deutschmann reported that between 2022 and 2023 there was a big jump in skeptical attitudes to climate change among the majority of the 3,074 people surveyed. Some 59% said they had more doubts about climate change in 2023 than they had had in the previous year.

The researchers wrote that the respondents' individual economic situations could not be considered the primary explanation for the increase in skepticism. Other factors, they said, were much more decisive: A right-leaning political orientation, distrust of state institutions, and dissatisfaction with democracy.

Social psychologist Marlene Altenmüller said the Flensburg publication is important and fascinating, though she has doubts about its alarming tone. Other studies show that "the number of people who have doubts is still very small," she says. Altenmüller, a junior professor at the Leibniz Institute for Psychology in Trier, conducts research into science reception: How people perceive scientific evidence, and what they think about the scientific system and its researchers.

Altenmüller's research indicates that people in Germany do not have fundamental doubts about scientific evidence. Rather, it varies depending on the topic, and the view the group to which people feel they belong has of the topic.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Her work, and that of many other researchers, also shows that politically right-leaning people express more skepticism about climate change.

"If right-wing parties were suddenly to discover that we should in fact take action against climate change, my assumption is that the followers of these parties would also believe in climate change and would support political measures," Altenmüller said.

Nor does she believe that climate skeptics have a different personality structure. Instead, climate skepticism is more likely to be down to the fact that "people orientate themselves according to their group and its identity." The credo for most people is that content is secondary, or, as Altenmüller calls it, "Party over policy."

Underlying this is something psychologists call motivated reception. People always see the world through the lens of their own desires, ideas, values, and political ideologies, and anything that cannot be squared with their own ideas and values tends to be disparaged. Altenmüller's research demonstrates that all of us are predisposed to seeing the world through our own filters.

Both Altenmüller and the Flensburg researchers emphasize that climate change skepticism comes in different guises. One form is the rejection of climate policy measures. The basis for this may be the assumption that it won't be all that bad, or doubt that human activity is the cause. Another is the belief that all the talk about climate change is simply a con, a conspiracy.

This is the focus of research of Stephan Lewandowsky, a professor of cognitive science at the universities of Bristol and Potsdam. Among other things, he examines the persistence of misinformation and conspiracy theories, and is interested in the parameters that determine whether people reject or accept scientific proofs, especially in connection with vaccines and climate change. "Certain people are more susceptible to conspiracy theories than others," he said.

The COVID-19 pandemic made this very apparent. Lewandowsky argues that for some people, conspiracy theories that apportion blame for a particular situation provide a welcome opportunity to escape from feelings like fear and loss of control. "That offers some brief psychological comfort to people," Lewandowsky says.

However, he goes on to explain that the comfort they derive from assigning blame does not last long. "There's good evidence to suggest that people who do fall into that rabbit hole over time are suffering," he said. "They're less likely to hold their jobs. They lose social contacts. They become mentally challenged."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Climate skepticism and conspiracy theories are mostly a Western phenomenon. Researchers observe them the most in the US, Europe, and Australia. In India and other countries of the global south, climate change is already a question of daily survival, and has been for some time. "In India, a lot of people still suffer from [not] getting access to clean drinking water," says Jagadish Thaker, senior lecturer at the University of Queensland, Australia, and an expert in climate change communication.

For years now, he says, people in the global south have been experiencing first-hand the ways that climate change is exacerbating problems through rising temperatures and extreme weather events.

Consequently, measures to reduce emissions and adapt to changing living conditions are not seen as a matter of political ideology. According to Thaker, people in India are trying to counteract their own vulnerability to climate change while still trying to develop economically.

Heatwaves and other extreme weather events are a direct threat to human life in Germany, as has become apparent during this summer's heatwaves, which are reported to have killed as many as 10,000 people already.

This is why the authors of the Flensburg study are urging people to take climate change skepticism seriously if they are to successfully anchor climate protection measures in society.

Thaker believes the media plays a decisive role. He believes there is still a general lack of information and understanding of the effects of climate change. "The media coverage of extreme weather events, while it's a lot, it is dramatic, and unfortunately doesn't mention climate change."

Altenmüller says it's important to keep emphasizing that there is a scientific consensus that climate change is anthropogenic, or, caused by human activity. Sometimes, she says, it does matter who says it. Research shows that some scientific disciplines are perceived as more biased than others. Consequently, economists have a better chance of their message reaching a wide audience than sociologists.

Taking the values of people who express skepticism into account could also help to communicate a different point of view to them, says Altenmüller. Communication must emphasize not only the restrictions that need to be imposed through political measures, but also the opportunities arising from this.

People who have themselves experienced extreme weather events probably find it easier to shift their perspective. This is why Lewandowsky is hopeful that the this year's heatwaves and wildfires will make a difference. "At some point, people's personal experiences matter," he says.

This article has been translated from German.
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-as-tempera.summary: 59% of people surveyed said they had more doubts about climate change in 2023 than they had in previous year. Other factors, including a right-leaning political orientation, distrust of state institutions, and dissatisfaction with democracy, were more decisive.

https://www.dw.com/en/on-the-front-line-.title: On the front line of Europe's battle against wildfires
https://www.dw.com/en/on-the-front-line-.text:
French firefighters have won out over a massive blaze, with almost 200,000 evacuees returning home. But Europe's climate-fueled wildfire season is far from over.

The signal to move comes suddenly — and within a minute or so the fire truck is full and speeding off into the distance, a cloud of orange dust swirling in its wake. "There's always a bit of adrenaline when you get the call," marine firefighter Julien says. "But we're trained; we're prepared."

Maitre Julien — whom DW can only identity by rank and first name — is part of Marseille-based battalion deployed to France's Gironde region to tackle a wildfire which prompted the largest evacuations in the country since World War II.

Some 264 firefighters were injured in the fight against the Gironde fire, four of whom lost their lives. In nearby towns, French flags still fly at half mast to mark the loss. "It's always on our mind," Lieutenant Damien, another marine firefighter, explains as his team members haul the firehose out behind him.

Letitia, a firefighter and medic, said she tries to ask how colleagues are feeling "without being too intrusive."

"It's the fatigue above all," she says when asked about the most common problem affecting her colleagues. "They're sleeping very little."

"Do you see all all of that?" Maitre Julien asks, gesturing out the car window as he drives past rows of blackened trees and swathes of scorched earth at the roadside. "All of that's already burned. But you can see small peels of smoke here and there. We absolutely have to extinguish those so fires don't restart."

When Julien pulls up at another hotspot, the risk of flare-ups comes sharply into focus: The air smells burned and a cloud of white smoke fills the sky. Within about 20 minutes, the smoke turns thick and black, and the fire — previously under control — was visible burning bright again through the trees.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Here by the firefighters' side are improvised teams of local volunteers — farmers and tradesmen and women who took it upon themselves to use their tractors or vans or four-by-fours to transport water to firefighters on the front line, and often head into the blazes themselves without proper protective gear or training.

"We're here because we're needed. And because we want to help," Steven Page, one volunteer, told DW. Maitre Julien said they played a "primordial" role, saving firefighters "precious time" in the fight.

At times, firefighters said, this felt like a "David and Goliath" battle. But they came out on top. By Saturday, France's Interior Ministry declared the fire was no longer progressing. Most of the 220,000 evacuees were allowed to return home.

Elsewhere in Europe, the heat of battle is far from over: Wildfires have also been raging in Greece and Spain — other countries are likely to face fires in the coming months too.

That's keeping EU crisis management chief Hadja Lahbib busy. She visited Bordeaux on Thursday, meeting local officials in Ornano fire station's crisis room and learning how they felled trees and vegetation across 150 kilometers (93 miles) of land to create tactical firebreaks and prevent the flames from reaching the city.

Dotted around the green lines on the map representing firebreaks are different European flags: Germany, Slovakia, Portugal, Spain, Belgium, Sweden, Czechia, Switzerland, Turkey — some of the countries that sent firefighting aircraft, firefighting crews, and technical teams through the EU's crisis management mechanism.

"Climate change isn't knocking at our door. It's here," Lahbib told DW on Thursday. Last year, her team laid out an EU crisis preparedness plan designed to better anticipate and prevent wildfires and other disasters through EU cooperation. "For that we need the means," she said.

"We proposed a budget of €10.7 billion ($12.3 billion), which is an important amount of money, but at the same time, it pays back," she said. "It's better to prevent —  to anticipate — then to recover. So I hope that member states will follow our proposal."

EU states pay into a communal seven-year budget for the bloc. Some national governments facing their own financial woes — including Germany — are skeptical about the EU Commission's bid to lock in its biggest-ever global budget.

Climate campaigners also accuse the EU of walking back on big green promises as the bloc pursues a red-tape-cutting agenda to better compete with the likes of China and the US.

"This isn't 'just nature.'⁣ Decades of burning coal, oil and gas are making wildfires more frequent and more destructive," Greenpeace wrote in a statement last week.

But ⁣Lahbib gave a cautious response when asked about allegations that EU states were dragging their feet on climate action. "This is not the moment for controversy and so on. This is a moment of solidarity," she said. "We will have the time to draw on the lessons learned."

In Brussels, where a small monitoring and decision team runs a bloc-wide crisis response center, unit chief Maria Zuber is already busy planning.

"We need to think of informing the population," she said. "We need to think of evacuation plans. We need to invest in early warning tools. So all this is something that we we are mapping. I think that is the main challenge — that we need to change our mindset."

Back in Gironde, Maitre Julien is all too aware of what's ahead. "We know we'll have more intense fires like this one more frequently," he said. Even this year's wildfire season isn't over yet — Julien and his team still have all of August and September to get through.

But for now, there's a moment of reprieve. At a hastily setup command center in Lège-Cap-Ferret, firefighters can get a meal and some rest before heading back home, or out on their next shift. There's little privacy — just rows of camp beds in a sports hall full of people. Outside, some firefighters prefer to lie on the ground in the shade of empty firetrucks.

"It's a little moment of cohesion," Maitre Julien explains as he sips coffee and jokes with volunteers. "We're not with our family, so we make this sort of temporary bubble to stay well. So that it's more like home."

Tessa Walther contributed to this article.
https://www.dw.com/en/on-the-front-line-.summary: The fire is the largest in France since World War II. Nearly 200,000 evacuees have been evacuated from the country's Girondes region. The fire was no longer progressing, the French Interior Ministry declared.

https://www.dw.com/en/hungary-to-shut-so.title: Hungary to shut sole nuclear plant for first time on Sunday
https://www.dw.com/en/hungary-to-shut-so.text:
Record-low water levels on the Danube forced the Paks plant offline, leaving Hungary facing a potential power crunch. In neighboring Serbia, energy production at two hydroelectric plants has also been reduced.

Hungary will shut down the Paks nuclear power plant on Sunday for the first time in its 44-year history, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said.

"We are facing the most critical five days ahead," Magyar said. "Tomorrow, ​the Paks power plant will not be generating, while the hottest days are ahead."

He made the announcement on social media late Saturday night, saying the decision was taken after a further drop in the Danube's water level.

The plant, located 120 kilometers (74.5 miles) south of the capital, Budapest, uses water from the Danube to cool its reactors. It provides more than 40% of Hungary's electricity generation.

"The power grid, our public services and ourselves will all come under enormous ⁠strain," ​said Magyar, who has warned that the Paks plant could remain idle ​for weeks.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Danube has fallen to record-low levels in some areas after months of below-average rainfall and successive heat waves since May.

Hungary's water authority projected that the Danube, which flows from Germany to the Black Sea, would fall further in the coming days.

It measured the Danube's water level in Budapest at 23 centimeters (9 inches) on Wednesday morning, well below the previous record low of 33 centimeters (13 inches) set in 2018.

As a result, output at the Paks nuclear power plant had already been cut earlier in the week and some reactors shut down.

"Due to a further decline in the Danube's water level, the second-to-last generating unit at the Paks nuclear power plant will be shut down at 1:30 a.m. (2330 GMT)," the prime minister said.

"As a result, the plant is now producing only 240 megawatts (of electricity), and tomorrow (on Sunday), for the first time in 44 years, it will be completely shut down," Magyar added.

The surge in imported electricity prices could cost Hungary between 120 billion and 240 billion forints ($315 million to $630 million, €273 million to €546 million), Tisza Party Vice Chairman Mark Radnai said on Facebook.

Magyar warned the Paks plant could remain offline for weeks and said his government would seek voluntary power cuts from large users, in addition to the 240 megawatts already pledged, with penalties for noncompliance.

A decree would also allow grid operator MAVIR to mandate consumption cuts and temporarily disconnect large users if necessary.

"Households will be the last to face restrictions," Magyar said, reiterating a call for companies, public institutions, local governments and households ​to significantly reduce or reschedule ⁠electricity use during evening peak hours between 5 p.m. and 10 p.m.

He said the government would decide later ⁠Sunday whether to apply mandatory ​electricity restrictions on large companies from Monday.

Meanwhile, the ongoing heatwave has forced neighboring Serbia to greatly reduce power generation from hydroelectric plants, the country's energy minister said on Sunday.

The two biggest plants, Djerdap I and Djerdap II, provide around 18% of Serbia's electricity generation, have been reduced to an output just 20% and 30% of their respective capacities.

Hydroelectric power accounts for nearly a third of Serbia's energy, with thermal plants making up the rest. But with the Danube, which flows through the Serbian capital, Belgrade, hitting historic lows in some areas, their operations have suffered.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

https://www.dw.com/en/how-does-eastern-e.title: How does eastern Europe commemorate the Roma Holocaust?
https://www.dw.com/en/how-does-eastern-e.text:
In 2015, the EU designated August 2 as the European Roma Holocaust Memorial Day. In Germany, the day is marked with memorial services, educational activites and public addresses. And in eastern Europe?

It took decades before Germany recognized the Romani Holocaust — the Nazi genocide of 500,000 European Roma and Sinti during World War II. Several more decades passed before the European Holocaust Memorial Day for Sinti and Roma became an official German and European day of remembrance, celebrated each year on August 2.

Based on initiatives by Polish Roma groups, the Nazi liquidation of the so-called "Gypsy Family Camp" in the Auschwitz-Birkenau Concentration and Extermination Camp on the evening of August 2-3, 1944, was first commemorated half a century later, in 1994.

Thousands of deported Roma and Sinti had already been killed as a result of malnutrition and disease. That evening, thousands more were forced into gas chambers, shot and beaten to death by Nazi henchmen.

In 2015, the European Parliament declared this date the European Roma Holocaust Memorial Day. In Germany and other European countries, the genocide is commemorated by officials with the participation of government representatives. In some cases, representatives of European governments travel to the memorial site in Auschwitz.

In most cases, however, countries hold their own memorial services — particularly in central and southeastern Europe, where Nazi extermination commonly targeted Romani peoples. These days, such memorial days also take the opportunity to raise awareness for ongoing Antiziganism and the consequences it has.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Poland, home to an estimated 30,000 Roma, has been observing August 2 since 2011. The ceremony routinely includes a visit by parliamentary and governmental representatives to the Auschwitz Memorial.

Another important day of remembrance is observed each year in the village of Szczurowa, east of Krakow, on July 3. It honors the memory of Polish Roma massacred by German troops in 1943. In 1956, Szczurowa became the first site of a European memorial for victims of the Romani Holocaust.

Other small towns and villages across southeastern Poland also commemorate the killing of Polish Roma during Nazi German occupation.

In the Czech Republic, where nearly 250,000 Roma live, August 2 has been an official day of remembrance since 2015. The most important ceremony is held in Lety, south of Prague, where Roma organizations have been commemorating the genocide for decades. This is the site where German Nazis established a concentration camp in 1940, and began deporting and imprisoning Romani families from occupied Bohemia from 1942 onward.

After the war, the site was used as a pig farm. It was closed in 2018, following a long controversy, and transformed into a place of remembrance.

Czech President Petr Pavel and then-Prime Minister Petr Fiala both attended the opening ceremony in April 2024.

Another memorial site is located in Hodonin north of Brno, at the location of a further Nazi concentration camp which imprisoned Romani people from Bohemia and Moravia. Here, one of the atrocities commemorated includes the mass deportation of Roma and Sinti to Auschwitz on August 21, 1943.

Around half a million Roma live in Slovakia. Here, the Romani Holocaust Memorial Day has been observed on August 2 since 2005. The main ceremony is held at the Slovak National Uprising (SNU) museum in Banska Bystrica in central Slovakia.

The museum honors the 1944 armed uprising against Nazi occupation. It was one of the largest anti-fascist movements in Europe during World War II.

The memorial ceremony is organized by the government's Plenipotentiary for Romani Communities and non-governmental Roma initiatives. Other representatives of the state or the presidential office also take part.

Around 600,000 Roma call Hungary home. Here, since 2005, various sites have been observing the Romani Holocaust Memorial Day on August 2, following a parliamentary resolution. In Budapest alone, there are three places of remembering for the Roma murdered during the Holocaust where commemorative events are held. The reason for these and numerous other memorial sites is that Hungarian Roma were the target of deportations and killings particularly following German occupation in 1944 and under the rule of the Arrow Cross, Hungary's fascist regime.

Historical remembrance in Hungary is also deeply intertwined with the racist murdering spree directed at Roma people between 2008 and 2009. In this time, four Hungarian neo-Nazis killed a total of six people and injured 55 others, some of them severely. They planned their final hate crime for the night of August 2, in the eastern village of Kisleta.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Romania, where around 2 million Roma live, Roma Holocaust Memorial Day has officially been observed since 2020. The main event is held at the Holocaust Memorial in Bucharest, which was inaugurated in 2009. Under the dictator Ion Antonescu, who was allied with Nazi Germany, Romania independently organized the mass deportation of Jews and Roma to Transnistria, where about 380,000 Jews and 11,000 Roma were murdered in camps or died from hunger and disease. In 2025, President Nicusor Dan became the first Romanian head of state to personally attend the memorial service.

In 2004, Romania designated October 9 as its official Holocaust Remembrance Day. It was on that day that Jewish citizens were first deported from the Bukovina region to Transnistria. The day also explicitly honors the memory of Roma who were deported and murdered by Antonescu's regime.

About 700,000 Roma call Bulgaria home. Here, August 2 has yet to be declared an official day of remembrance, but it is still marked with commemorative events organized by Roma organizations. Government and state representatives also take the occasion to issue commemorative statements. Although Bulgaria was allied with Nazi Germany, it resisted German demands to deport Jews and Roma. But groups were discriminated against through a wide range of racist laws, and effectively made second-class citizens.

Croatia has a population of about 25,000 Roma. Its parliament only declared August 2 a day of remembrance in 2014. The main commemorative ceremony is held at the site of the former concentration and extermination camp Jasenovac, where the fascist Ustashe movement imprisoned Serbs, Jews, Croats and Roma.

Between 15,000 and 20,000 were murdered there. High-ranking politicians regularly take part in commemorative ceremonies. More broadly, remembrance events in Jasenovac primarily highlight April 22, when prisoners attempted to escape the extermination camp in 1945.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Around 100,000 Roma live in North Macedonia, where the Roma Holocaust Memorial Day has officially been observed on August 2 since 2017. A key remembrance ceremony is held in Skopje at the Holocaust Memorial Center for the Jews of Macedonia. In North Macedonia is also a national and religious holiday: Republic Day and St Elijah Day, respectively. because of this, public remembrance of the Roma genocide tends to receive less attention.

In Serbia, home to around 130,000 Roma, August 2 is not an official memorial day for the Roma genocide. But there are other days of remembering the genocidal policies of the Nazi and Ustase regimes which also honor the memory of the Roma killed in the genocide.

This article was translated from German.
https://www.dw.com/en/how-does-eastern-e.summary: August 2 is the European Roma Holocaust Memorial Day. In Germany, the day is marked with memorial services, educational activites and public addresses. In Poland, the European Parliament declared this date the European Holocaust Memorial day.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-long-roa.title: Germany's long road to equality for same-sex couples
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-long-roa.text:
In 2001, same-sex couples in Germany were able to register a civil partnership for the first time. The Civil Partnership Act was a crucial step toward "marriage for all," which was introduced in 2017.

August 1, 2001, marked a turning point: with the Civil Partnership Act, same-sex couples in Germany gained a legal framework for the registration of their partnerships. However, another 16 years would pass before marriage itself became an option.

"The Civil Partnership Act was a milestone for the legal recognition of same-sex couples in Germany and laid the foundation for opening up marriage," Alexander Vogt of the national board of "Queere Vielfalt e.V." (Queer diversity) told DW.

"It introduced a legally secure partnership with rights similar to those of marriage — such as inheritance, maintenance, and residency rights — though it remained discriminatory in many areas – like adoption or tax law. Nevertheless, it gave us a foot in the door — a solid base from which further rights could be secured, usually by appealing to the Federal Constitutional Court."

The legislation was preceded by a fierce political debate. The opposition bloc of conservative parties, the Christian Democratic Union and the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), denounced it as an "unconstitutional attack on marriage and the family." Lawmakers from the ruling center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), however, described the law as "a long-overdue act of redress."

"There was strong conservative opposition, for instance from churches and civic groups," Alexander Vogt noted. "The debate reflected the classic culture war between traditional and progressive values."

Backed by the governing coalition of Social Democrats and Greens, the majority of Bundestag lawmakers voted in favor of the Civil Partnership Act in November 2000, despite opposition from the CDU/CSU and the neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP).

German public opinion was already a step ahead: A 1999 survey showed that 55% of respondents were already in favor of the Civil Partnership Act.

However, Germany was by no means a pioneer. Denmark was the first country in the world to introduce civil partnerships for same-sex couples, doing so as early as 1989. Norway, Sweden, and Iceland followed in the mid-1990s, with France following in 1999.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Twenty-five years ago, Reinhard Lüschow and his husband Heinz-Friedrich Harre — who has since passed away — became the first same-sex couple in Germany to tie the knot at a registry office under the new Civil Partnership Act. They had spent the preceding decade fighting for legal recognition as a couple.

As early as 1992, they had made a public statement by applying to register their marriage — in a coordinated move by 250 male and female same-sex couples across Germany. When their application was rejected, they took the case all the way to the Federal Constitutional Court. "We simply wanted to be treated equally," Lüschow recently told the Protestant Press Service (epd).

Although the court ruled at the time that marriage was a union between a man and a woman, it also mandated that the legislature ensure same-sex partnerships were not discriminated against. When the Bundestag implemented this requirement through the Civil Partnership Act, Lüschow and Harre reacted immediately.

The Civil Partnership Act regulates matters such as the use of surnames, mutual financial support, and inheritance rights. In the years that followed, the scope of civil partnerships was gradually expanded — first in 2004 to include stepchild adoption, and later to achieve tax equality following several rulings by the Federal Constitutional Court.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Civil Partnership Act was merely the first step toward equality. The decisive step did not come until October 1, 2017, with legislation that introduced so-called "marriage for all."

This, too, was a hard-won victory. The conservative parties had come to power again in 2005. They blocked the legislation until Chancellor Angela Merkel authorized a vote free from party-line constraints, meaning lawmakers were to follow only their consciences; this is how the majority was secured in 2017. Angela Merkel and current Chancellor Friedrich Merz voted against the legislation.

Bodo Mende and Karl Kreile were the first same-sex couple to marry. Reflecting on the 2001 Civil Partnership Act, Mende later told DW: "It was a second-class partnership." Although there were few legal restrictions, the status lacked the standing of a conventional marriage.

Married partners enjoy more rights — for instance, regarding naming laws, child adoption, and the equalization of pension rights. Marriage also carries greater recognition internationally.

According to the Federal Statistical Office, around 108,000 couples had availed themselves of this new option by 2025. At the same time, approximately 24,000 registered civil partnerships remain in existence; these can be converted into marriages upon application.

Differences remain between same-sex and opposite-sex couples. Alexander Vogt of the association Queere Vielfalt cites an example regarding the law of parentage: "If a child is born into a family with two mothers, the non-biological mother must first go through an adoption process to establish legal parenthood. This is not the case for heterosexual couples."

Reflecting on societal developments, Vogt observes: "Acceptance of same-sex marriage has clearly increased."

However, he adds: "We have become more visible in recent years, but not safer; violence and hate crimes — particularly against queer people — have risen sharply. The figures have increased tenfold since 2010! The attack in Berlin represents a tragic peak in this trend, one that has garnered significant public attention."

This article has been translated from German.

The Civil Partnership Act was introduced in 2017, with legislation that introduced so-called "marriage For all" increased tenfold since 2010. The attack in Berlin represents a tragic peak in this trend, one that has garnered significant public attention

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-widens-dep.title: Germany widens deportations to Afghanistan
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-widens-dep.text:
Earlier this week, Germany for the first time deported a man with no criminal record to Kabul. Faridoon Tofan, who is currently in deportation detention, fears the same fate.

Things would likely have turned out very differently had Faridoon Tofan not taken the bus to Italy. He had intended to go on a short trip to Rome. The 46-year-old — who had fled the Taliban to Germany just under four years ago and had since been working and learning the language — was detained during a border check in mid-April and taken directly to a deportation detention center in Munich.

The reason: Tofan did not have the legal right to leave Germany. His asylum application had been rejected; he held only a temporary residence permit, which does not protect against deportation. He could now be sent back to Kabul, even though he is neither a convicted criminal nor has he been classified as a security threat. His asylum application appeal was definitively rejected in July, and he is now to be deported.

Tofan's wife and six children are still living in Kabul. They were recently paid a visit by Taliban officials and say they've been living in constant fear ever since and the sons no longer dare attend school, Nina Alizadeh Marandi told DW. She is an asylum law expert at the human rights organization Amnesty International in Germany and in close contact with Tofan's lawyer.

The Taliban officials' interest in the Tofan family in Kabul came after Faridoon Tofan's meeting with Afghan consulate staff in Berlin. Both the embassy in the German capital and the Afghan Consulate General in Bonn are now under Taliban control — a state of affairs for which the German government has faced heavy criticism from the opposition and human rights organizations.

While the German government does not officially recognize the Taliban administration as the legitimate government of Afghanistan, it points to contacts maintained at a purely "technical level."

This week, another Afghan national with no criminal record was deported.

The flight — operated by Freebird Airlines using an Airbus A320-214 — departed Leipzig/Halle Airport in Eastern Germany at 1:43 a.m. on Tuesday, bound for Trabzon, Turkey, before continuing to Kabul, Afghanistan. The Afghan national with no criminal record was on the plane alongside 30 convicted offenders.

This set a precedent that sparked vociferous protests:  260 people heeded the call of an anti-racism alliance and came to demonstrate inside the airport's departure hall, accompanied by a police escort.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Luca Müller, spokesperson for the anti-racism group, also referenced the deadly terror attack on the Pride event in Berlin over the weekend: "While Islamist violence targeting Berlin's Pride celebration is being condemned from all sides, the federal government is supporting the Islamist Taliban through its deals," Müller said.

By "deals," Müller is referring to accusations leveled by many human rights organizations and the political opposition that the German government is de facto legitimizing the Taliban regime in Afghanistan in order to facilitate more deportations.

What critics view as a breach of fundamental taboo, others see as nothing more than the swift enforcement of existing law. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt again told journalists this week, that anyone who has gone through an asylum process resulting in a rejection is therefore required to leave the country and must expect deportation if they do not depart voluntarily. Dobrindt, who is a member of Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), stated that the federal government is simply pursuing its goals in migration policy, driving forward this "shift in migration policy" with "control, a clear course, and a firm stance," Dobrindt added.

Since the resumption of deportations to Afghanistan in 2024, Germany has returned more than 200 individuals. According to Amnesty International, at least one of them was killed following his arrival in Kabul.

However, the German government points to assessments by the UN migration agency (IOM), which considers the return of men to Afghanistan to be feasible again — in principle.

"The security situation in Afghanistan has improved significantly; that is simply an objective fact," Mihyung Park, the IOM's country chief in Kabul, told the media outlet Redaktionsnetzwerk Deutschland. Park added one caveat: "Under current circumstances, we would strongly advise women against returning to Afghanistan."

In general, however, UN agencies warn against involuntary returns, noting that the returnees heavily depend on support to settle again in their country of origin.

Amnesty International condemns the German government for increasingly toughening its deportation practices without regard for the catastrophic human rights situation in Afghanistan. Nina Alizadeh Marandi pointed out that the very day of this week's historical deportation happened to coincide with the 75th anniversary of the adoption of the Geneva Refugee Convention.

"Human rights standards must not be eroded simply because upholding them is politically inconvenient," Alizadeh Marandi said. "Amnesty calls on the federal government to refrain from further deportations and to monitor whether Afghans who have already been deported are able to live in Afghanistan without persecution or danger to life and limb," she added.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's political opposition has also sharply criticized the first deportation of an Afghan national with no criminal record. "It is irresponsible that Alexander Dobrindt is now deporting people to Afghanistan who have done absolutely nothing wrong here," said Marcel Emmerich, the Green Party's parliamentary spokesperson on interior policy.

Emmerich said that Dobrindt's "dirty deal" regarding deportations strengthens the Taliban, "makes us vulnerable to blackmail, and undermines Germany's own security." He added that the federal government is taking a "dangerous wrong turn" with this Afghanistan policy.

Juliane Nagel, a lawmaker for the socialist Left Party in the parliament of the eastern state of Saxony, called the flight "shameful" and demanded that Saxony's Leipzig/Halle Airport — which is largely state-owned — no longer be used for deportations to Afghanistan.

This article was translated from German.

https://www.dw.com/en/more-women-die-in-.title: More women die in heatwaves, but biology 'isn't main cause'
https://www.dw.com/en/more-women-die-in-.text:
In country after country, more women are dying from the heat than men. But researchers say biology isn't the main reason. Age, working conditions, and unequal access to rest may drive the gap.

Observing recent heatwaves in Europe, one pattern has often been remarked on: More women appear to be dying than men. During Europe's then-record summer of 2022, a study found 56% more heat-related deaths among women than men, drawing on mortality data from 35 countries.

Germany, which has just logged its deadliest heat season since 2016, with close to 9,800 heat-related deaths by mid-July, according to the Robert Koch Institute, is seeing the same pattern again this year.

Some of the recent coverage has leaned on the hormonal reading that women's bodies simply aren't equipped for heat. They sweat less, carry more body fat, and progesterone nudges core temperature up.

But scientists who study the effect of heat on the human body say that's largely incorrect. "Overall, studies usually show only slightly more vulnerability to heat in women compared to men," saidAlexandra Schneider, an environmental epidemiologist and deputy director of the Institute of Epidemiology at Helmholtz Munich. "It's not really a very strong signal."

The small differences that do exist are real: Women do have a lower sweat rate, less skin area relative to body size, and fat distribution that affects thermoregulation. Hormones play a role too, but unevenly across a lifetime.

Schneider points to one group in particular: Women past menopause, when cardiovascular risk climbs. Older women with existing heart disease, she says, are probably at the highest risk of all.

But even in those cases, she doesn't think biology is the main cause for the extra deaths during a heatwave. "The living conditions, the social environment where women live, makes probably even more of a risk than just the differences in hormone status."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Toby Mündel, a kinesiology professor at Brock University in Canada, who studies extreme human environments, says that the impact is "overstated," when asked whether there's a real biological basis for the claim that women are more likely to die in heatwaves.

The factors that most determine how a person copes with a heatwave, Mündel says, are age, body size, fitness and habitual activity, and not biological sex.

Sweating is one example. Even though women do sweat less, that doesn't make them more vulnerable, because they compensate in another way. "They send blood flow to the skin, vasodilation, much better than males do," Mündel says, meaning their blood vessels widen more efficiently, moving heat to the surface where it can escape.

Pregnancy, which many assume must be dangerous, is another example. "As a woman progresses through pregnancy, she actually becomes better at handling heat," Mündel says. He draws a clear line between physiology and circumstance: There are good reasons not to have pregnant women doing heavy outdoor labor in extreme heat. But their bodies aren't the reason.

Partly, Mündel's argument is based on what gets measured. Studies often count hospital and emergency admissions, and women are far more likely than men to seek medical help. "That is not a physiological thing," he says. "Are they actually struggling, or have they just sought help earlier?"

Underneath it all sits a research gap. "We have about a hundred times as much data and evidence on men. We have nearly zero on women," Mündel says. "It's like comparing cats and dogs."

Numbers from Germany point in the same direction. The Robert Koch Institute attributes the higher female death toll to the fact that women make up a larger share of the oldest age groups. Its estimates also break down deaths per 100,000 people, and by that measure, the picture flips.

In every older age band this summer, the male death rate is higher than the female one. In other words, more women are dying in heatwaves only because more very old women are alive.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If the gap isn't physiological, where does it come from?

Laurie Parsons, a researcher at Royal Holloway, University of London, studies how heat stress moves through the global economy in construction, garment factories, farming, driving, street vending.

Across the board, he says, women spend 30% to 50% more of their working time above heat-stress thresholds than men. In construction, when comparing men and women doing the same job, the figure rises to around 50%.

The reasons, he says, are structural. Women often wear more clothing for the same job. Men are more confident asking for breaks. And where men's work is visibly strenuous, it's recognized as a heat risk and rewarded with rest. But women's work is steadier, less obviously punishing, and gets no such relief.

Parsons compares it to the difference between a plane crash and asbestos exposure: One is a sudden, visible catastrophe, the other a slow, constant harm that's easy to miss. "Male heat stress tends to be this taller risk, where you get relatively visible moments of physical distress that can be managed," he says. "Female heat stress is constantly there, but much less visible, because it doesn't have those same obvious peaks in the working day."

Then the shift ends, he says. Men rest, but women cook, clean and care for children.

Heat also cuts into pay. Parsons says workers under heat stress are around 30% less productive in the garment sector, which he says is the easiest to quantify.

In formal jobs, workers make up for it with longer hours during the hottest part of the day, feeding what he calls "a vicious cycle" of worsening health and falling output. The self-employed have no such buffer. For them, heat stress just means less income, which ripples the wider family over time.

For Parsons, the starting premise is flawed. "Heat stress is not an atmospheric condition," he says. "It is a social condition, which happens within particular atmospheric circumstances."
https://www.dw.com/en/more-women-die-in-.summary: More women are dying in heatwaves in Europe this year than men, according to a study. Age, working conditions, and unequal access to rest may drive the gap. Workers under heat stress are 30% less productive in the garment sector, says Parsons.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-weighs-the.title: Germany weighs the future of minijobs
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-weighs-the.text:
Germany's popular minijob system allows millions of workers, including students, to avoid paying income tax or social security contributions. But a reform is on the cards that may soon end this advantage.

When Anahita Abdollahi starts her shift, she first checks her emails to make sure she's up to date on all the library requests. The 26-year-old master's student from Iran describes her job as a "part-time librarian" — she helps people find books they need for their studies, answers phone calls, and waters the plants.

Abdollahi says she likes "almost everything" about her job at the University of Cologne's physics library — the only exception is the occasional tedious task, such as taking inventory of the library's collection. But even that doesn't bother her too much — after all, she only works twice a week for around five hours at a time.

This type of employment is known in Germany as a "minijob", whichthe country's government is considering eliminating in its current form.

A minijob is a form of part-time employment in Germany which pays a maximum of €603 (around $685) per month. As long as employees don't earn more than this amount, they don't have to pay social insurance contributions or income tax.

Minijobbers can also opt out of paying their share of pension contributions — and most of them do just that.

A minijobber typically works around 10 hours per week to reach the €603 cap, making it an ideal job for those with other commitments, such as students or stay-at-home parents. Women make up around 57% of all minijobbers, according to Germany's central agency for minijobs.

The agency also estimates that nearly 7 million of Germany's 45 million employees have a minijob. Some of them have it in addition to another job, while others have a minijob as their only form of employment.

Minijobs were introduced in the 1960s to facilitate low-level employment with little bureaucracy and to combat moonlighting. In 2003, they were redesigned as part of a comprehensive labor market reform.

They have long been criticized for reinforcing gender inequality in the job market, as minijobs are held disproportionately often by women, preventing them from building up substantial pensions.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Employers typically pay a flat tax of 2% on minijobbers' wages, as well as social contributions amounting to around 30% of gross pay. Despite these additional costs, many businesses rely on minijobbers because they offer flexibility.

"There are operational situations where hiring someone only makes sense if the number of hours is truly minimal," Holger Schäfer, a senior economist specializing in labor market economics at the German Economic Institute (IW), told DW.

Supermarkets, for example, need more cashiers on Saturday afternoons than they do on Monday mornings, making minijobs an easy way to fill the staffing gap. The extra weekend work is also why retail and hospitality are the two industries that employ the most minijobbers.

In early July, Germany's governing coalition announced its plans to raise the flat tax rate for minijobs from 2% to 5%. The government also stated its intention to fully implement the Pension Commission's proposals, which were presented in late June and aim to ensure the sustainability of Germany's pension system in the future.

One of these proposals focuses specifically on minijobs, and would eliminate the opt-out option for pension contributions and abolish the special status of minijobs. This would make minijobbers subject to regular social security contributions, effectively bringing an end to minijobs in their current form. According to the commission, this would strengthen social security systems, reduce the risk of poverty in old age, and address gender inequalities.

For Abdollahi, it could mean earning up to €130 less per month. The 26-year-old says she would probably try to increase her work hours to make up for the loss.

She could also get a research job that would require her to work for up to 20 hours per week, but this would considerably slow down the pace of her studies. "Even with my admittedly very chill job here, on the days I work, I usually don't study," Abdollahi explained.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Many labor unions have welcomed the proposal, including Nahrung-Genuss-Gaststätten (NGG), a trade union representing workers in the food, beverage, catering, and hospitality industries.

"Minijobs have not proven to be a bridge to good employment; rather, they cement precarious working conditions for millions of people," the NGG cited their chairman Guido Zeitler in a press statement.

Enzo Weber, a labor market expert from the Institute for Employment Research (IAB), believes the reform may encourage people to work more or pursue different career paths. It would "prevent people from getting stuck in the minijob trap" and "ensure that women's career development doesn't stall during child-rearing years, since they simply remain in low-paying jobs due to misguided tax incentives," Weber told DW.

Business representatives, however, have pushed back against the proposed changes. "Abolishing minijobs would be a mistake," argued Rainer Dulger, president of the Federal Association of German Employers' Organizations, adding that minijobs help businesses remain flexible and tap into additional labor potential.

IW economist Schäfer, meanwhile, doubts that abolishing minijobs would encourage people to work significantly more hours. He also notes that a €600 job fully subject to social security contributions would generate rather small additional benefits. "It's simply not worth it to set the entire social security machinery in motion for such employment relationships," Schäfer said.

Still, he sees room for reform when it comes to people who take on a minijob alongside their primary employment. "We have an economic misallocation of resources when a skilled worker would rather deliver pizza after work than work overtime in their actual main job," he explained. "But that doesn't mean we have to abolish minijobs altogether."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Pension Commission's proposals also include an exemption for school students, which would allow them to continue working minijobs in their current form. Now, the Social Democratic Party (SPD) is considering whether this exemption could be extended to university students.

Abdollahi believes that would be the right decision. "They are one of the groups that need it the most, especially students from outside the EU," she said.

Abdollahi's own minijob at the library allowed her to enter the German labor market more easily and helped her improve her language skills. "It gives me a chance to practice German in a low-pressure environment," she noted.

But Abdollahi and other students in Germany now have to wait to learn what will happen to minijobs, as the government is expected to debate the proposed changes later this year.

Edited by Rina Goldenberg

Sami Behbehani contributed to this report.
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-weighs-the.summary: Germany's popular minijob system allows millions of workers to avoid paying income tax or social security contributions. A minijobs are a form of part-time employment in Germany which pays a maximum of €603 per month. The government is considering eliminating the special status of minijOBs in its current form.

https://www.dw.com/en/what-s-really-caus.title: What's really causing Europe's wildfires
https://www.dw.com/en/what-s-really-caus.text:
From Greece to France, Europe is burning. But what's the real reason for the historic blazes ripping through the continent and why are they getting harder to stop?

Wildfires almost always need a spark to ignite, whether it's lightning, arson, or a car's hot exhaust pipe touching dry vegetation.

In France's historic summer wildfires, authorities blamed a brush-clearing machine being operated around a high-voltage power line. Spanish investigators concluded that sparks from heavy machinery were behind major blazes there.

But scientists say those findings only explain how Europe's historic wildfires began, not why they grew into the megafires that have devastated the continent this summer.

Across Europe, a combination of human-caused climate change, insufficient planning and forests planted in ways that allow flames to spread quickly are fueling fires, say experts.

"It's not that wildfires are magic and just start. You have to have the right climatic conditions," said Silvia Abruscato, coordinator of FoRISK, a pan-European forest risk management hub.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Scientists point to three ingredients that determine whether a wildfire will spread rapidly: the amount of vegetation available to burn, how dry that vegetation is, and the weather conditions around a fire.

"When all three of these conditions are very much fire-prone and they align, then you have this kind of fire event," said Francesca Di Giuseppe, a fire forecast project coordinator at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.

Climate change is making these conditions more common and intense. A rapid analysisfrom World Weather Attribution found global warming made the extreme weather behind Spain and France's summer wildfires much more likely.

One reason is a phenomenon called hydroclimatic whiplash, where ecosystems suddenly swing between wet and dry conditions.

Essentially, as the planet warms, the atmosphere holds more moisture, intensifying rainfall that fuels plant growth.

"This has created an abundance of biomass that then has rapidly dried during a sequence of heat waves," Di Giuseppe said.

In spring, a warmer atmosphere draws water from soil and plants. Drought worsens, vegetation dries out, and landscapes become far easier to ignite. In simple terms, wet winters grow fuel, and dry springs turn that fuel into perfect kindling.

This summer, that's meant fires breaking out almost simultaneously in France, Spain, Greece, and Turkey — all driven by the same broad pattern of heat and drought.

Making matters worse, the fires themselves add to the problem. This year's blazes have already emitted nearly 18 million tons of planet-warming CO2, according to EU figures.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Once a fire begins, it can take thousands of firefighters days or weeks of effort to contain the flames. That's partly due to the way forests have been managed over decades. Across parts of Europe, large areas have been planted as monocultures, dominated by a single species grown for quick timber.

"Some of the fires we've been seeing in France and Spain are in places where you have these very flammable trees which are quite fine and they often are growing close together so fire spreads really easily," Doug Kelley, a land surface modeler at the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology, told DW.

More than three-quarters of the Landes de Gascogne forest in southwestern France, which is currently ablaze, contains maritime pine. Created after Napoleon III ordered the region's marshes to be drained and planted with pine in 1857, it became Europe's largest man-made forest.

But the pine species sheds coarse needles that blanket the forest floor, providing bountiful fuel for fires. Because the trees are of similar age and height across vast areas, they are particularly vulnerable to fast-moving fire.

Another fast-growing timber tree is the eucalyptus. In Portugal the oily species — which represents more than a quarter of the country's forestland — burned far and wide in 2017's deadly wildfire season.

"In some regions of Europe, farmland and lower-biomass shrubland were replaced by fire-prone conifer or eucalyptus species of higher economic profitability, increasing the risk of fire," the European Commission wrote in a case study reporton the 2017 Portuguese wildfires.

That includes Spain, where some 3 million hectares (7.4 million acres) of former farmland and pasture were planted with pine and eucalyptus during and after the Franco dictatorship, which lasted from 1939 to 1975.

Firefighters will always play a crucial role in suppressing wildfires. But experts say reducing risk before fires start is just as important. That starts with tackling the greenhouse gas emissions driving climate change and intensifying weather extremes.

"Trying to prevent in the first place the landscape becoming so flammable is one of the most effective ways to try to avoid this kind of extreme fire behavior," said Di Giuseppe.

Replacing monocultures with mixed forests would also go a long way. Forests with a wider variety of species are generally better able to withstand drought, windstorms, insect outbreaks, and fires, because different trees respond differently to environmental stresses.

Germany offers an instructive case for forest management. Demand for timber after World War II led to spruce being planted across mountain ranges like the Harz in former East Germany. But these monocultures proved vulnerable to drought and bark beetle infestation. Foresters are now working to convert them into mixed forests to improve resilience.

Planting broadleaf, deciduous trees — such as oak, beech, or maple — can help, as they typically store more moisture than conifers. Trees with thick bark, fewer low-hanging branches, and a higher moisture content tend to be more fire-resistant.

A post-event simulation studyof Portugal's 2017 blazes found fires that overwhelmed firefighters in pine and eucalyptus stands, with flames over four meters tall, could be contained in broadleaf forest, where flame heights dropped to under a meter and a half.

Forestry experts also recommend creating breaks between rows of trees to slow fire spread as well as pruning lower branches so flames can't jump quickly to the canopy. Clearing the forest floor of incendiary leaf litter and dead wood, and using controlled burns to reduce underbrush prior to wildfire season helps too.

"We need to manage our forest well in order to avoid such big disasters from happening. So prevention, prevention, prevention," Abruscato said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Edited by: Jennifer Collins
https://www.dw.com/en/what-s-really-caus.summary: Portugal's 2017 blazes were the most severe wildfires in Portugal. Scientists say climate change is making these conditions more common and intense. Forestry experts recommend creating breaks between rows of trees to slow fire spread. Clearing the forest floor of incendiary leaf litter and dead wood helps too.

https://www.dw.com/en/from-petitions-to-.title: From petitions to memes: How students made dissent visible
https://www.dw.com/en/from-petitions-to-.text:
From imperial China to present-day India, student movements have repeatedly adapted the tools and symbols of their age to challenge authority.

It was a clip destined to go viral.

On July 22, 2026, in rainy Mumbai, India, a casually dressed young woman stepped in front of a slow-moving police van carrying detained students. She placed her palm on the hood, forcing the vehicle to stop.

Mobile phones captured the moment from every angle. She too, raised her own phone and recorded the encounter. Within hours, the clip spread across India and beyond.

It became one of the defining visuals of the Cockroach Janta Party protests, a movement in which students demanded transparency and accountability, following leaks in India's medical entrance exams.

But the power of the moment lay not only in what she did, but in how quickly it was seen. A single gesture, a young woman confronting authority, became a symbol shared across millions of screens.

While the clip belongs to a generation raised on social media, the impulse behind it is much older.

From court petitions and revolutionary posters to photographs, umbrellas and memes, student movements have repeatedly adapted the tools and symbols available to them, turning them into vehicles for dissent.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Long before television or social media carried dissent across borders, students still found ways to make their grievances heard.

In Eastern Han China, for instance, scholars at the Imperial Academy (Taixue) aligned with reform-minded officials in opposing powerful eunuchs at court, whom many viewed as corrupt and politically overbearing.

They voiced their objections through public criticism, political networks and petitions.

In an era when political communication moved through official channels, petitions were among the established ways of bringing grievances before the throne. Written in formal language and delivered through the bureaucracy, they carried student concerns directly into the state's communication system.

Centuries later, communication and protest mechanisms evolved.

In Paris in 1968, students challenged university authorities and a conservative postwar social order. As demonstrations spread across the French capital and drew in workers, one of the movement's most enduring contributions emerged from a basement workshop at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts.

The Atelier Populaire ("People's Workshop") printed thousands of posters during the protests, many of them overnight. Their bold graphics, silhouettes and slogans became the visual language of the movement. Produced collectively, many carried no individual author's name, helping transform protest into a shared public voice.

The posters and their messages could appear in dozens of places overnight, giving the protest a wide local visual presence.

Protests also became more impactful when images could be transmitted across borders.

In Soweto in June 1976, Black South African students marched against the apartheid system's education policies, rejecting Afrikaans as a compulsory medium of instruction in Black schools. Many saw it as the language of an oppressive state and a barrier to equal education.

As thousands of students took to the streets, police opened fire. Amid the chaos, South African photographer Sam Nzima captured the image that would travel the world: 13-year-old Hector Pieterson being carried away from the scene after he was fatally shot.

The photograph became one of the defining images of apartheid. For many outside South Africa, it served as the lens through which the students' protest was seen and understood, helping build international awareness of and opposition to apartheid.

In the spring of 1989, students gathered in Beijing's Tiananmen Square demanding democratic reforms, freedom of expression and an end to corruption. As the protests grew, so did the need for symbols that could communicate their message beyond the square.

In the final weeks of the occupation of Tiananmen Square, students built the Goddess of Democracy. Facing Mao Zedong's portrait, the 10-meter statue became a powerful symbol of the movement.

But while the students created one icon, history would produce another. After the brutal military crackdown on the protesters, a photograph of a lone man, later known as "Tank Man," standing facing a column of tanks traveled around the world.

Global media did not create these symbols, but amplified them. Cameras, newspapers and broadcasters transformed these local acts of defiance into enduring images of resistance.

As the sun rises at Tiananmen Square, protesters build a 10-meter (33-foot) Goddess of Democracy statue out of foam and paper-mache over a metal armature. In the early morning of June 4, soldiers backed by tanks and armored cars toppled the statue, which had stood directly facing the Mao portrait at the Forbidden City.

In the often tense days leading up to the Chinese government crackdown, local citizens often gave gifts to soldiers and police officials. Sometimes troops would sing patriotic songs with demonstrators. In this picture, a policewoman sings out loud in Tiananmen Square a few days before troops retook control of the area and crushed the democratic movement.

A woman is caught in the middle of a scuffle between pro-democracy protesters and People's Liberation Army soldiers near the Great Hall of The People on June 3, 1989, the day before one of the bloodiest military crackdowns of the 20th century. Later that night, the 38th Army would open fire on unarmed civilians overtaking the occupied Tiananmen Square.

Thousands of protesters surround a bus with a display of captured weapons just days prior to the crackdown. During the government's enforcement of martial law, soldiers and the public performed a delicate dance of give and take. Sometimes protesters offered gifts to soldiers and sometimes troops withdrew.

In the late evening of June 3, a group of protesters cornered an armored personnel carrier at the gates of the Great Hall of The People. It had just crashed through barricades of street dividers, which the crowds had put up to stop the advance of military vehicles. At the same time, soldiers were preparing to open fire on the demonstrators a short distance away.

On the late evening of June 3, protestors set fire to an armored personnel carrier on the Chang'an Avenue near Tiananmen Square. The picture was the last image before photographer Jeff Widener was struck in the face by a stray protestor brick. Though he sustained a serious concussion, The Nikon F3 titanium camera absorbed the blow sparing his life.

On June 4, a truck manned by People's Liberation Army troops patrol down the Chang'an Avenue in front of the Beijing Hotel the day after the bloody crackdown on student-led pro-democracy supporters. A similar truck full of soldiers had shot tourists standing in the lobby of the Beijing Hotel that day.

A lone man with shopping bags walks to the center of Beijing's Chang'an Avenue and temporarily stops the advance of Chinese tanks a day after the crackdown. Over two decades later, the fate of the man is still a mystery. The incident has come to symbolize the events at Tiananmen Square and is considered one of the most iconic images ever taken.

On June 5, a group of people at the Chang’an Avenue show a picture of protesters lying dead at a local morgue after having been shot by Chinese soldiers of the 38th Army during the recapture of Tiananmen Square. The troops used expanding bullets which created larger wounds. At least 300 civilians were killed, according to Amnesty International.

The remains of a burned-out bus on Beijing’s Chang’an Avenue as two women sweep up debris following the massacre. The demonstrations led to widespread burning of buses and military vehicles, which left several soldiers dead or injured.

Soldiers and a tank stand guard in front of the Forbidden City and across from the occupied Tiananmen Square a few days after the riots.

Associated Press photographers Jeff Widener (left) and Liu Heung Shing pose in front of Beijing's Forbidden City in late May 1989 just days before the Chinese government's military crackdown at Tiananmen Square.

Over time, protest communication no longer flowed only from organizers outward. Crowds and bystanders increasingly helped shape it.

In Chile in 2011, students demanding education reform used flash mobs, performances and public spectacle to draw attention to their cause. Protest was no longer just something people watched. It became something they could join.

In Hong Kong in 2014, students protesting Beijing's plans for electoral reform transformed everyday objects into political symbols. And what began as a practical response to pepper spray and tear gas soon became the defining image of the Umbrella Movement.

Modeled on Prague's original John Lennon Wall that was created after his murder in 1988 and went on to provide a space for people to express irritation with the communist regime, Lennon Walls in Hong Kong also became hubs of public expression, attracting thousands of people who left messages of support and protest on sticky notes attached to walls around the city.

And then there are the political platforms that shape which symbols become widely seen, as is the case in India recently.

Students protesting exam irregularities took an insult aimed at them and made it their own: "Cockroach" quickly became one of the movement's most recognizable symbols online.

Memes and reels often spread faster than official statements, with students using them to respond to criticism, mock their opponents and rally support.

Like posters in Paris or umbrellas in Hong Kong, this particular instance shows how memes can transform a disparaging label into a powerful protest symbol.

https://www.dw.com/en/humanoid-robots-tr.title: Humanoid robots: Trump's latest China trade battle?
https://www.dw.com/en/humanoid-robots-tr.text:
The US has banned foreign-made humanoid robots, a market Chinese tech firms dominate. Although Washington cited national security risks, analysts think Donald Trump is buying time for US robot makers to catch up.

In the latest sign of China's threat to the United States's tech dominance, the Trump administration on Tuesday banned new foreign-made humanoid and four-legged robotsfrom entering the country.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) cited "unacceptable risks" to national security for the decision.

The FCC noted how the robots "collect data that could be leveraged by malign actors to surveil Americans, enhance the capabilities of foreign intelligence services, or to remotely commandeer the robots."

The move is widely seen as aimed squarely at China, which accounted for 85% of humanoid robot deployments last year, according to British bank Barclays.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US officials warn that Chinese humanoid and quadruped (four-legged) robots can collect detailed location and personal data, be controlled remotely and pose risks for critical US infrastructure. Specific concerns center on the robots' potential dual-use — civilian and military purposes.

Unitree Robotics, a leading Chinese robot maker, appears on the Pentagon's list of firms with links to the Chinese military. Its robots have been used in army exercises.

Researchers have also shown that Unitree robots have security flaws that let attackers take control with a voice command and then use one robot to control others.

Washington is also concerned that a large cohort of low-cost Chinese robots could feed real-world data back to Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) systems, which are fast catching up with their US rivals.

The threat, however, is largely theoretical as most commercial humanoid robots are in early stages of development.

China has rejected the accusations, insisting the US is using national security as a pretext for protectionism to suppress Chinese technology. Beijing is expected to impose countermeasures, which could include curbs on the raw materials US robotics firms urgently need to scale up production.

The Trump administration has made no secret of its desire to help the domestic US robotics industry, which in turn supports the country's nearly trillion-dollar AI buildout. According to industry watchers, US President Donald Trump wants to ensure the likes of Figure AI, Tesla Optimus and Agility Robotics are protected from high-volume Chinese producers, whose robots often cost half the price or less of their US rivals.

Washington has put similar curbs on Chinese drones and solar panels and now levies a 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles.

The ban is widely seen as Trump's attempt to buy time, having been caught off guard by how quickly China scaled robotics production.

According to Omdia, a tech research house, China has six firms in the Top 10 robotics rankings. Those firms shipped nearly 11,600 humanoids last year, versus a few hundred by US firms.

In March, Bank of America forecast around 90,000 shipments by the end of this year.

The US is widely seen as stronger at making a robot's brain smart through advanced AI, while China leads at mass-producing cheaper robots with bodies that move better thanks to high-performance actuators or robotic muscles.

Rush Doshi, director of the Initiative on China Strategy at the Council on Foreign Relations, described the ban as "one of the most significant actions taken so far in support of the US robotics ecosystem."

Evan Beard, CEO of Standard Bots, a maker of robot arms, thinks the Trump administration is sending an "unambiguous" message to China.

"Robotics is a technology America must lead and own — and foreign-subsidized robots will not be allowed to unfairly dominate US robotics..." Beard wrote on X.

Critics, however, think the ban could slow US AI innovation as researchers currently benefit from being able to run tests on budget-friendly Chinese robots.

"Restrictions can reduce security exposure, but they do not by themselves create a competitive domestic ecosystem," Georg Stieler, an advisor to the robotics industry, wrote on X.

CNBC, a US business television channel, cited Marc Einstein, a research director at Counterpoint Research, as saying the ban was "bad news for Chinese humanoid producers planning their IPOs in the coming months."

Einstein warned that Beijing could now "further restrict rare earth sales to American companies and … Chinese market access for American companies like Tesla and Nvidia."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Barclays estimates the market, currently worth just $2 to 3 billion (€1.7 to 2.6 billion), could reach $200 billion by 2035 in the most optimistic scenario, if the robot's brains, brawn and batteries can be improved.

Elon Musk is even more bullish, saying Tesla's Optimus could become "the biggest product ever" with long-term sales potentially reaching $10 trillion.

At scale, he believes the robots, which currently sell for about $100,000, could eventually cost $20,000 to $30,000 each — cheap enough for factories, warehouses and later homes.

Combining Barclays' forecast with Musk's target price points to roughly 7 to 10 million humanoid robots being sold each year by 2035.

In the near term, humanoids are expected to take on repetitive and physically demanding jobs in warehouses and factories. Later, they could expand into health, elderly care and household chores.

https://www.dw.com/en/eco-wins-from-deat.title: Eco wins: From death strip to nature haven and other green surprises
https://www.dw.com/en/eco-wins-from-deat.text:
A Cold War relic becomes a biodiversity haven, a Pokemon Go for trees and seagrass gets a second life. This week's eco wins come from some unexpected places.

After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the border zone that divided West and East Germany was left largely untouched. Today, the nearly 1,400-kilometer (870 miles) stretch, once known as the death strip, is a "green belt." It's home to around 7,500 species of insects and spiders, hundreds of them endangered, as well as otters, wildcats and birds on the brink of extinction.

Because the military zone was sealed off for decades, species that have vanished elsewhere in Germany were able to take hold here. Now 88% of the area is under protection, and cycle paths and information panels allow visitors to explore what was once completely off-limits.

Read the full story here: East-West border death zone now Germany's biodiversity oasis

Not all heroes wear capes, but some do form a canopy. Urban trees quietly cool neighborhoods, reduce flooding and improve our wellbeing. But in many cities, trees are under pressure from heat, drought, traffic and too much concrete.

Now, a citizen-science project in Germany is helping people map and monitor the trees around them. Think Pokemon Go, but for urban nature and with real-world benefits for the climate.

On Poel, a German island in the Baltic Sea, washed-up seagrass is being turned into sustainable insulation for homes, while helping clean local beaches in the process.

As demand for eco-friendly construction materials grows, the project is attracting interest from across Europe and could give new value to a resource that was previously viewed as waste.
