https://www.dw.com/en/fifa-plans-infanti.title: FIFA plans: Infantino under pressure as senior advisor quits
https://www.dw.com/en/fifa-plans-infanti.text:
After regional football federations condemned FIFA plans for private investment, Carlos Cordeiro, senior advisor to FIFA President Gianni Infantino, tendered his resignation.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino was under increasing pressure on Friday as global opposition grew to his controversial private investment plans and one of his senior advisors resigned in protest.

The football world was rocked earlier this week when it was reported that FIFA, the sport's global governing body, was planning to sell a stake in a new commercial subsidiary to private equity investors close to US President Donald Trump, prompting widespread outrage.

European football's governing body, UEFA, quickly condemned the plans with its 55 member associations voting unanimously to boycott future FIFA competitions — including the next men's World Cup in 2030 but potentially starting with the under-20 Women's World Cup on September 5 — were the plans to be implemented.

The Europeans soon received backing from CONCACAF, the regional body representing 41 North American and Caribbean football federations, and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) with its 47 members, technically robbing Infantino of majority support among FIFA's 211 member associations (MAs).

On Friday, the pressure on FIFA grew even more when Carlos Cordeiro, former head of the United States Soccer Federation (USSF) and more recently a senior advisor to both Infantino and President Trump during this year's men's World Cup, resigned in protest at the plans, which he described as a "bad deal for football."

In statement, Cordeiro, 69-year-old former partner at Goldman Sachs, questioned why FIFA needed to seek private equity investment at all given its unprecedented World Cup profits, and criticized a lack of transparancy, oversight and due process surrounding the plans.

"FIFA already has access to extraordinary financial resources," he said. "The organization sits on billions of dollars in reserves and no debt. The FIFA president himself has highlighted the $15 billion in revenue generated [during FIFA's last four-year World Cup cycle] between 2022 and 2026.

"If member associations believe additional investment is needed to develop the game, FIFA already has the financial capacity to provide that support from its existing resources. Against that backdrop, selling a permanent stake in football's most valuable asset to raise $4.2 billion makes little sense. It is mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification."

Despite the opposition voiced by UEFA, CONCACAF, AFC and individual national associations including the German Football Federation (DFB), FIFA had earlier doubled down on its plans to establish "FIFA Forward Enterprise" (FFE).

The subsidiary, valued by FIFA at around $20 billion (€17.5 billion), would be responsible for FIFA's commercial rights like broadcast, sponsorship, ticketing and licensing contracts for its competitions, including the World Cup, but would sell a non-controling minority stake worth $4.2 billion to private equity investors.

The proposed investor consortium is expected to be led by "Thrive Eternal," a fund run by "Thrive Capital," in turn founded by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US ​President Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

"Nobody is selling football. ‌This is not something FIFA would ever entertain," FIFA said in statement earlier on Friday, slamming "incorrect media reports" without issuing clarification and what precisely was wrongly reported, and insisting that it would proceed with its "consultation process" — with member associations obliged to make a decision by September 19.

"FIFA [member associations are] now being asked to believe that outside investors are needed to unlock greater value. I do not accept that proposition," said Cordeiro.

"Most troubling of all is the absence of answers to fundamental questions: Why this deal? Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football?"

European football's governing body UEFA, which has been at loggerheads with FIFA and Infantino for years and criticized the global body throughout the recent World Cup over expensive ticket prices and the Folarin Balogun red card affair, had come out publicly in opposition to the plan within an hour of it first being reported by the Financial Times and Times on Tuesday.

"No UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership," UEFA said in a statement after a unanimous vote by its 55 member associations at a hastily convened emergency meeting on Thursday.

"The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product ... No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale," the statement added.

Meanwhile, political criticism came from new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, a keen football supporter and one of the first European leaders to criticize the FIFA plans earlier in the week,

"My view is strengthening [that] this was an outrageous suggestion," said Burnham on Friday. "The idea that it could even be brought forward, in my view, shows that the FIFA general secretary [Infantino] is the wrong man to lead the organization."

Shortly after, North America's soccer body CONCACAF also unanimously rejected the FIFA plan, though it stopped short of threatening a boycott by its 41 members.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) also issued a scathing letter to its 47 member associations and warned the FIFA proposal would never succeed without the support of all six regional blocs.

"While the immediate debate centres on FFE, the AFC considers this issue extends far beyond a single proposal. Rather, it has exposed fundamental weaknesses in FIFA's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed," read an AFC statement.

"This is not the first occasion where major stakeholders have been confronted with significant initiatives after the direction of travel appears to have already been determined. Such an approach undermines confidence in FIFA's governance framework and diminishes the authority of its statutory bodies."

African body CAF said it would convene an executive committee meeting next week to look into the proposal, saying in a statement:

"CAF is committed to continue consulting and working together with its Member Associations, FIFA, other Football Confederations and stakeholders in support of increasing financial and other resources for the development and growth of football in Africa and worldwide," it said.

South America's CONMEBOL, whose president Alejandro Dominguez is seen as a close ally of Infantino, said late on Friday that it had requested "additional information and clarifications from FIFA" on the FFE project.

Unlike its counterparts from Europe, Asia and North America, CONMEBOL and its 10 member associations were considerably more measured in their response to Infantino's plans.

In a statement, the South American federation acknowledged that commercial and financial decisions are needed to develop the sport.

"However, those decisions must always be at the service of football and never take precedence over its essence," a statement said. "Football always comes first."

CONMEBOL president Dominguez recently spoke out in favor of a further expansion of the men's World Cup to 64 teams in 2030 — which would effectively result in all but one South American nations qualifying automatically.

Amid the outrage over the investment plans, the Press Association reported on Friday that FIFA was indeed pursuing precisely such an expansion, with a decision expected by August 14.

Germany's mass-circulation Bild paper reported that key UEFA officials including German Football Federation (DFB) President Bernd Neuendorf had already discussed the FIFA plans via a video call on Wednesday.

"We must not lose the fans' support, but we are well on the way to squandering that," Neuendorf told public broadcaster ZDF, adding:

"I consider this to be extremely problematic and unacceptable. If UEFA rejects this request [for approval of the plan], then it is dead, because I believe that you won't be able to find any investor who would be willing to go ahead with this project if UEFA is out."

It's not the first time that the DFB has crossed swords with FIFA. At the Qatar World Cup in 2022, Germany's men's team covered their mouths before a game in protest at not being allowed to wear a "One Love" rainbow armband to support LGBT+ rights.

German football also has recent experience of similar private equity investment proposals.

In 2024, the Bundesliga was forced to abandon plans to sell a share of its TV rights to foreign investors due to fan protests that included tennis balls and remote control cars with smoke bombs being thrown onto pitch during matches.

Such actions are commonplace in German football, where the so-called 50+1 ownership model bars single investors owning a majority stake in a club and ensures fans retain more power than elsewhere in the world.

Read more on Germany's response to the FIFA plans here.

https://www.dw.com/en/german-court-rules.title: German court rules that AI music firm Suno violated copyrights
https://www.dw.com/en/german-court-rules.text:
Germany's state-mandated licensing agency, GEMA, says the verdict has "global significance," as Suno is also directed to pay yet-to-be-quantified damages.

The Munich Regional Court ruled on Friday that Suno AI, a US-based company, which generates songs from text prompts. has violated copyrights and has to disclose illicit revenues.

The lawsuit initiated in January 2025 by GEMA, Germany's state-mandated licensing agency, argued that Suno trained its AI models on copyrighted music without obtaining licences or compensating its rights holders.

According to the ‌verdict, Suno will have to pay damages that have yet to be quantified. Suno has disagreed with the ruling and said it would evaluate all available options, including an appeal.

"This is a verdict of global significance," Gema CEO Tobias Holzmueller told Reuters.

The lawsuit has been closely watched, as it is one of the first major cases anywhere in the world to test how traditional copyright law applies to AI music training and AI-generated music outputs. Among Suno's arguments was the fact that the German court does not have proper jurisdiction to rule on AI model training activities that occurred exclusively inside the United States.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The proceedings could help determine whether AI music companies must obtain licenses before training their models on copyrighted songs, and whether AI-generated music that closely resembles existing songs constitutes copyright infringement.

"Our goal is not to clear Suno from the face of the earth, but obviously to get into licensing negotiations on an eye-to-eye level, which was not possible with Suno so far," explains GEMA CEO Tobias Holzmüller, who describes the company as "by far the largest and commercially most successful of all AI music models." He believes Suno pursues a much more aggressive business strategy than its competitors.

The outcome of this case is also linked to another central question: How should creators be compensated when their music is used to train generative AI systems?

Last year, GEMA won a related case against OpenAI before the same court. It found that OpenAI unlawfully trained its AI models on copyrighted song lyrics and reproduced them via ChatGPT without authorization.

OpenAI was ordered to cease and desist from reproducing the works in the model, to disclose information and pay damages. But as the company pursues an appeal, the ruling remains non-final.

In contrast to that decision, the current lawsuit does not focus on song lyrics, but on entire music pieces.

One of the aspects that makes this lawsuit important is that it has not been initiated by a private company or record label, but rather by a music collecting society, notes Martin Senftleben, professor of intellectual property law at the Amsterdam Law School.

Such initiatives "are particularly important because, by definition, you could say that they're more inclusive," Senftleben tells DW. "You can become a GEMA member even if you're not a very well-known high-profile artist or composer. And that means there's a chance of bringing remuneration for AI users to a much broader group of rights holders."

GEMA represents more than 95,000 composers, songwriters and music publishers in Germany, along with over 2 million rights holders worldwide.

GEMA claims that Suno trained its AI on copyrighted music without permission or payment to songwriters, composers and publishers represented by the German music collecting society. GEMA also says that the US-based company is commercially benefiting from those works without compensating the artists.

Suno's music creation platform generates songs through simple text prompts. Users can describe the mood, style or genre they desire and the system synthesizes a structured track — complete with lyrics, vocals and instrumentation — in under a minute.

The songs that are produced by the AI system can be very similar to copyrighted songs.

During the court proceedings, GEMA demonstrated this by prompting Suno AI to create tracks with the original lyrics of different popular songs in its repertoire, including "Forever Young" by Alphaville, "Mambo No. 5" by Lou Bega, "Daddy Cool" by Boney M., "Cheri Cheri Lady" by Modern Talking and "Atemlos durch die Nacht," written by Kristina Bach and popularized by Helene Fischer.

Along with the lyrics, the plaintiffs prompted the desired musical style and the title of the work, without specifying any melody, rhythm, harmony or arrangement.

Yet the resulting AI songs are very similar to the original works.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Suno admits that the original songs at the center of GEMA's lawsuit are among the numerous pieces that were used to train the AI model.

AI companies such as Suno claim that the ingestion of data for AI training can be done freely on the basis of what is known as "fair use" in the US and the "text and data mining exception" rule in the EU.

But whether such licence-free AI training is allowed under copyright law remains heavily contested globally. In different lawsuits around the world, courts are now examining whether such uses harm the economic market of the original creators through unfair competition.

"The novelty in the lawsuit is that GEMA does not focus on the AI training stage," explains Senftleben. By basing their claim on tests that demonstrate that these AI systems generate songs that have similarities with copyright-protected works from their repertoire, "they bridge this gap between relevant use now taking place in AI training, and the market harm done at AI output level," he adds.

Anyone who wants to become a good musician needs to listen to and learn from existing music.

Similarly, the AI industry claims this analogy applies to how their models are trained — by absorbing countless creative works in order to generate new ones.

But from the rights holders' perspective, AI models are rather copying and commercially exploiting their works.

This argument that an AI learns from music and is inspired by it like a human being is "completely ridiculous," notes Tobias Holzmüller. "These are concepts that come from the human brain and have been designed for the human brain, and not for a machine that is able to digest millions of sound files in split seconds. I mean, just the amount of sheer data — they say it's data; for us, it's music — that these machines have swallowed up and then digested and are now spitting out, this is completely incomparable to what's happening in a human brain.

"To humanize these machines by using these concepts is not logical — and it's certainly not moral."

Across Suno's platform globally, users collectively generate roughly 7 million songs per day. Around 75,000 of them end up on streaming services daily, adds Holzmüller. "This is definitely where it's not sustainable anymore, but really toxic for the music ecosystem."

"If you want to create a sustainable model where you accept that AI music is here to stay, but at the same time, that it shouldn't push human-created music out of the market, the only way to tackle this is to put a price tag on the output," says the CEO of GEMA. "Because otherwise you will have free-of-charge AI sounds that will outcompete human music in a lot of circumstances."

For example, music in movie scores or social media has until recently allowed various songwriters to make a living. For Holzmüller, if licences lead to an increase in costs in AI-created sounds to a point that they are as expensive as human-created songs, it could provide a level playing field. "Then — it's my firm belief — people will continue to use human music, because it has this additional element."

This article was originally published on July 30, 2026 and was updated on July 31, 2026 to reflect the court's ruling.

Edited by: Brenda Haas
https://www.dw.com/en/german-court-rules.summary: Suno AI generates songs from text prompts. German court rules that Suno AI violated copyrights and has to disclose illicit revenues. Suno has disagreed with the ruling and said it would evaluate all available options.

https://www.dw.com/en/berlin-pride-attac.title: Berlin Pride attack: Are German juvenile courts too lenient?
https://www.dw.com/en/berlin-pride-attac.text:
The terror attack on Berlin Pride has put the work of juvenile courts into the spotlight. Many argue the 21-year-old perpetrator should have been in prison at the time of the attack.

Could the terrorist attack on Berlin's Pride celebrations, allegedly by a 21-year-old Islamist, have been prevented? This question has been the subject of debate driven largely by the fact that the young German man — born in Germany in 2005 to parents of Lebanese origin — had been convicted and released just weeks before the attack.

Abdul Ballout, who drove his car into a crowd in Berlin's Tiergarten park — killing one woman and injuring 31 people, some seriously — had set out last year intending to join the so-called "Islamic State" (IS) terrorist group in Syria. However, he was arrested en route in Lebanon, detained there and subsequently deported to Germany.

Back in Germany, he stood trial on charges of preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state. He was found guilty and sentenced in mid-May to 22 months in prison, but this sentence was initially suspended. He was released — and attacked Berlin Pride just weeks later. The day after the incident, he was shot dead by police while they were attempting to arrest him.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Since then, juvenile criminal law in Germany has been the focus of criticism. Terrorism expert Peter Neumann from King's College London told the news portal T-Online: "This is a real problem. The sentences are too lenient. In my view, juvenile criminal law is sometimes interpreted too broadly. The protection of the public is not given sufficient consideration."

Juvenile criminal law serves special purposes, says Frieder Dünkel, a criminologist and criminal law expert from Greifswald. "It's primarily about education, about the reintegration of the young person," he told DW.

Judges have considerable leeway and can hand out admonitions or prison sentences.

In Germany, a perpetrator is criminally responsible from age 14 and juvenile criminal law applies. From the age of 18, regular criminal law generally applies, with higher minimum sentences.  But juvenile criminal law can also be applied to young adults aged 18 to 20 if they show "developmental delays."

"This is because overall, one can still recognize significant developmental potential in 18- to 20-year-olds," Dünkel said.

This is backed by neuroscientific findings, according to Dünkel, showing that the brain areas responsible for behavioral control do not fully develop until the middle of the third decade of life. This implies that a young offender can still change for the better.

In May, Abdul Ballout was sentenced by the Berlin court under juvenile criminal law, even though he was already 21 at the time of his sentencing. However, he was only 20 years old when he committed the crimes he was found guilty of.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ballout was able to leave the courthouse because he had been granted six months of "preliminary probation," after which the court would have had to make a final decision on whether he needed to go to prison. He was initially placed under intermittent police surveillance until the police officers concluded that he was behaving unobtrusively.

He was ordered to participate in an exit program for extremists, where he attended two preliminary meetings to determine whether he was indeed willing to critically examine his behavior and distance himself from extremism.

Preliminary probation is a relatively new concept in Germany's criminal law and was introduced in 2012. Frieder Dünkel believes that the mechanism has been successful in many cases.

"Specifically, when a juvenile court judge is unsure whether a sentence can or should be suspended in favor of probation, the judge orders a period of up to six months during which the young person is guided toward a law-abiding lifestyle through strict directives and monitoring measures," Dünkel explained.

In the aftermath of the Berlin Pride attack, there have been calls to stop applying the more lenient juvenile criminal law to Islamist or right-wing extremist perpetrators.

But criminologist Dünkel disagrees: "It is not the role of juvenile criminal law to provide preventive protection for society before a crime has even been committed. Juvenile criminal law responds to crimes once they have been committed," he says.

Juvenile criminal law does allow for severe penalties; for instance, a murder conviction can result in a 15-year prison sentence for offenders aged 18 to 20.

Dünkel adds that recidivism rates among perpetrators sentenced under juvenile criminal law are no higher than among those sentenced under adult criminal law.

"Harsher penalties do not lead to greater security," he said.

Nevertheless, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) has announced his intention to examine ways to reform juvenile criminal law.

Konstantin von Notz, the opposition Green Party's expert on internal affairs disagrees with that approach.

"We... note that virtually all experts consulted on this matter so far point out that long prison sentences — especially for young adults — can have a counterproductive effect and may even accelerate existing radicalization," von Notz said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ballout had been classified as a dangerous individual by Germany's Joint Counter-Terrorism Center (GTAZ). The GTAZ is a coordination and communication platform established in 2004, after the 9/11 terror attacks in the United States, to combat Islamist terrorism through inter-agency information sharing.

However, the assessment of Ballout did not reach the Berlin court that handed down the lenient sentence earlier this year. If the information had been shared, Ballout may have remained incarcerated.

This article has been translated from German.
https://www.dw.com/en/berlin-pride-attac.summary: Abdul Ballout was convicted and released just weeks before the attack. He was arrested en route to Lebanon, detained there and deported to Germany. Ballout may have remained incarcerated if the information had been shared.

https://www.dw.com/en/bmw-to-volkswagen-.title: BMW to Volkswagen: How deep is Germany's auto industry cull?
https://www.dw.com/en/bmw-to-volkswagen-.text:
BMW joins VW, Porsche and Mercedes-Benz in cutting thousands of jobs, as Chinese rivals erode their market share. DW recaps the major reforms German automakers are pursuing to safeguard their future.

BMW on Wednesday became the fifth German carmaker to announce major job cuts, as the country's auto sector seeks to tackle rising competition from China.

The Munich-based firm said it would cut up to 8,000 jobs globally, representing about 5% of its 154,000-strong workforce.

BMW, which also owns the Mini and Rolls-Royce brands, said the job losses would primarily affect operations in Germany and be achieved through natural staff turnover and a voluntary redundancy program.

Although BMW was seen as more resilient to Chinese competition, the company warned last month that its sales in China were falling sharply.

Chinese rivals have intensified competition for electric vehicles (EV), which has crushed BMW's sales volumes and pricing power.

Last year, BMW's vehicle deliveries in China dropped to their lowest level since 2017 and in the three months to June, they fell 30% year-on-year.

US PresidentDonald Trump's tariffs have also contributed to BMW's woes, along with higher energy prices from the Iran war and the growth of Chinese EV-makers in other major markets, including Europe, Asia Pacific and Latin America.

On Thursday, the company disclosed that second-quarter net profit dropped 35% to €1.2 billion ($1.4 billion), while revenue fell to €31 billion from €34 billion.

BMW has adjusted its guidance for the rest of the year, warning of a "significant decline" in profit.

Two days earlier, Porsche announced plans to cut an additional 5,000 jobs in Germany by the end of 2035. The figure represents about 1 in 5 workers

The sports performance brand said the new measures would hit Porsche's main production plant in Stuttgart-Zuffenhausen and its research and development (R&D) center in nearby Weissach.

Last year, Porsche announced a restructuring program to cut 1,900 jobs in the Stuttgart region by 2029 and allow 2,000 fixed-term contracts to expire.

The company will also defer wage increases, while performance bonuses will be more closely linked to profits.

Porsche, which is owned by Volkswagen Group but run with a high degree of independence, has also reduced jobs at its Leipzig plant and is closing three subsidiaries that employ about 500 people.

At the end of last year, Porsche employed nearly 41,800 people, with about 85% of them in Germany.

Volkswagen, Europe’s largest carmaker, last month doubled its job-cull program, announcing plans to slash up to 100,000 jobs.

The company also wants to close four German factories.

Unions and the German state of Lower Saxony, which holds a 20% voting stake and can veto major decisions, have rejected the latest plans. VW had originally stated it would cut 50,000 positions.

VW is well-known for its oversized headcount of 630,000 globally — 680,000 including Chinese joint ventures.

The Wolfsburg-based giant employs around 60% more workers than Toyota, despite producing a similar number of vehicles.

Once a sign of German industrial strength, the huge workforce has become a costly burden amid intensifying competition from Chinese EV-makers.

VW controls more stages of production in-house than rivals, driving up labor demand, while German factory costs are often twice those of rivals.

Slow progress on electric vehicles further eroded sales in China, which once accounted for a third of VW’s total, as well as Europe.

In March last year, Mercedes-Benz agreed with its works council plans to deliver €5 billion in savings by 2027.

However, the company ruled out compulsory redundancies at German plants, insisting that voluntary departures could achieve the reforms.

Until March this year, around 5,500 administration, R&D and IT workers accepted severance packages and left. Production workers remained protected.

Additional headcount reductions have been reported in the firm's China operations.

Last month, Mercedes postponed a bonus payment for nearly three-quarters of its German workforce until 2027 and proposed extending the work week from 35 to 40 hours without extra pay.

Mercedes bosses also indicated that some jobs could be moved abroad.

On Tuesday (July 28), Mercedes said it had written off more than €700 million due to fierce competition in China.

Although second-quarter net profit grew 13.5% to €1.09 billion, core earnings at its key cars division fell by a quarter to €909 million.

VW-owned Audi last year announced plans to cut up to 7,500 jobs in Germany by the end of 2029.

The company has ruled out compulsory redundancies and said the job losses in administration and R&D would be achieved through voluntary schemes and early retirement.

Last month, however, Audi's Neckarsulm plant was listed for possible closure in 2030 by parent company VW. This could impact about 15,000 workers.

The site, which makes the A5, A6 and A8, has already cut production from 300,000 to 225,000 vehicles a year.

https://www.dw.com/en/why-germany-may-st.title: Why Germany may stand up against FIFA's World Cup sell-off
https://www.dw.com/en/why-germany-may-st.text:
Leading figures in German football have lined up to criticize Gianni Infantino’s plans to sell a stake in the World Cup. Germany is showing signs that they may be ready to oppose Infantino's re-election.

"We must not let it become a pawn in the hands of investors. We must not lose the fans' support, but we are well on our way to squandering that support. I consider this extremely problematic and unacceptable."

Those were the words of the head of Germany's football association, the DFB, in response to FIFA's plan to form a commercial subsidiary to sell to private investors. Bernd Neuendorf, the DFB president, is on the FIFA Council, which FIFA describes as its "main decision making body" but was blindsided by Tuesday's proposal.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Neuendorf said he "had to learn the news from the newspaper. That's no way to treat people." He said Infantino's method was "extremely troubling. When you sit on the committee, you want to be able to actively participate in decisions and express your opinion. That has to be a process, but none of that is happening at FIFA — not on important issues, and especially not now with the investor issue."

As well as widespread fan discontent, expressed via social media, leading German clubs have voiced their dissatisfaction with the plans.

"I am ashamed that we even discuss such ideas in football. Football does not belong to us," Bayern Munich's board member for sport Max Eberl told Sky.

"I have the feeling that FIFA exists solely to make a profit. It disgusts me," he added.

"Why does FIFA feel it needs to reinvent the wheel? In my view, this initiative is not a good idea at all," said Borussia Dortmund's CEO Carsten Cramer, while his equivalent at Stuttgart, Alexander Wehrle, lent his support to the DFB and European football governor UEFA's stance against the proposal.

"Driving the commercialization of football in this direction without even a semblance of a common, sensible goal would send a disastrous message," he said.

Earlier this year, Germany declined to sign a document recommending Infantino's re-election and Neuendorf was also critical of FIFA's suspension of a World Cup red-card ban for US striker Folarin Balogun following an intervention from US President Donald Trump.

New Germany manager Jürgen Klopp, working as a TV pundit during the tournament, criticized that decision too.

"Let's just say: this is our game, not theirs. These two people (Infantino and Trump), who both have no idea about football, should have nothing to do with that," he said.

Despite falling behind on the pitch in recent times, Germany still holds plenty of sway in European football's governing body and will likely be a key voice when that organization meets, reportedly on Thursday. Neundorf added that: "If UEFA rejects this request (for approval of the plan), then it is dead, because I believe that you won't be able to find any investor who would be willing to go ahead with this project if UEFA is out."

This is not the first time that Germany has protested against a FIFA decision. At the Qatar World Cup in 2022, the men's team covered their mouths before a game against Japan in protest at not being allowed to wear the rainbow armband to support LGBT+ rights. The lack of support from other federations for that action made Germany hesitant to repeat it in World Cup 2026 despite widespread concerns about ticket prices, the failure to issue visas to fans and officials from certain countries and Infantino's relationship with Trump.

But the Balogun case, and the new sell off proposal may have been beyond the pale. The DFB know that they must toe a particularly careful line on these issues due to the country's football culture.

In 2024, the DFL, the organization that operate the Bundesliga, was forced to climb down from plans to sell a share of its TV rights to foreign investors due to fan protests that included tennis balls and remote control cars with smoke bombs being thrown on the pitch during matches.

However, the DFL confirmed on Sunday that it had received an "unsolicited proposal for a debt financing model at the league association level" and have "begun a general, preliminary review of the proposal and its legal feasibility." German newspaper Bild reported that finance firm Apollo is looking to loan the Bundesliga at least €1 billion ($1.14 billion), with the domestic media rights serving as collateral in the deal. Any notion the DFL will accept this would likely be strenuously opposed by fan groups.

In May, fans of Bayern and Stuttgart unfurled a huge banner featuring a crossed out DFB logo at this year's German Cup final in protest at high ticket prices.

Such actions are commonplace in German football, with the 50+1 ownership model, that bars single investors owning a majority stake in a club, ensuring fans retain more power than in most other European nations.

Even if Germany and UEFA continue to protest Infantino's decisions and presidency, the Swiss executive will likely retain control unless other confederations, particularly Africa and Asia, follow suit. Although UEFA only has 55 of 211 votes, it remains the most powerful confederation within FIFA and with leadership from a powerful nation like Germany, Infantino may start to feel the heat.

https://www.dw.com/en/rienzi-why-this-wa.title: 'Rienzi': Why this Wagner opera is so relevant today
https://www.dw.com/en/rienzi-why-this-wa.text:
The opera sparked controversy long before its Bayreuth Festival premiere, and the debate hasn't died down since it came to the stage. Now, another controversy surrounds the new AI-generated Ring cycle.

Even before opening night, expectations of how the themes of Richard Wagner's "Rienzi" would be handled were running high — not least because the opera had never been staged at the Bayreuth Festival. Now it has opened the festival's 150th anniversary. One aspect that fueled the debate: The close relationship between Wagner's descendants and Adolf Hitler — "Rienzi" was one of Hitler's favorite operas.

"It's a piece that's highly contaminated," director Alexandra Szemerédy told DW. "When Katharina Wagner [the festival's director] first approached us, my initial excitement was definitely a bit dampened." Nonetheless, the production received enthusiastic applause at its premiere — conductor Nathalie Stutzmann and the Bayreuth Festival Orchestra were given standing ovations, and Hungarian directors Alexandra Szemerédy and Magdolna Parditka were warmly celebrated for their interpretation of the work.

The directors tell the tale of the rise and fall of the 14th-century Roman tribune Rienzi in the present day. Rienzi, who initially seeks to free the people of Rome from aristocratic rule, is ultimately consumed by power and becomes a dictator himself.

The production opens with a stark landscape of identical concrete apartment blocks that later break off into individual units. Through the windows, neighbors watch each other's lives unfold. Every apartment contains screens broadcasting the same news. Whatever can't be seen through the windows is shared through smartphones, social media and omnipresent screens.

In this new production, Rienzi initially doesn't defeat the aristocracy with violence. He calls for democratic elections — and wins. Afterward, he lavishly celebrates with the elites. But that changes when the same aristocrats attempt to assassinate him. Rienzi survives, imposes a military dictatorship and begins executing his enemies in the streets. Increasingly consumed by paranoia and delusion, he loses his grip on power and ultimately dies.

The directors said they were particularly interested in how someone can inspire the masses and, fueled by populism, become an authoritarian ruler. "He's considered a reference figure in the study of populism because of this first major citizens' uprising in Rome," Szemerédy said. The charisma of the real historical figure Cola di Rienzo, who lived in the 14th century, had also fascinated Adolf Hitler.

Musicologist and theater scholar Anno Mungen criticized the decision to stage "Rienzi" for the first time during the Bayreuth Festival's 150th anniversary, calling it "historically tone-deaf." Wagner himself chose not to include "Rienzi" in the repertoire of his new Festspielhaus in Bayreuth in the 1870s, citing musical considerations.

In his book on the intersections between the festival and the Holocaust, Mungen writes about the deportations from Bayreuth to Auschwitz, which included Jewish members of the Bayreuth Festival Orchestra. "When we look at 'Rienzi,' it would have been both meaningful and necessary to place the production within the context of a major academic conference," Mungen said. "The University of Bayreuth would have been very willing to participate."

From 1940 to 1944, in what are now known as the "Wartime Festivals," Bayreuth kept running thanks to Hitler's financial support. Performances were held for selected audiences only, including wounded soldiers and workers from the arms industry. History students are currently exploring that period in an exhibition at the Steingraeber piano factory in Bayreuth. "These wartime festivals became a cultural showcase, intended to project the message that 'things aren't really so bad in Germany'," Mungen said. He chose not to attend the "Rienzi" premiere because the subject remains too personal.

The opera's dramaturge Markus Kiesel also believes it's essential to confront the controvery surrounding the piece. "Not performing the opera — or even banning it — would achieve nothing," Kiesel said. "On the contrary, we need to face these issues openly, creatively and honestly, and discuss them critically. If not in Bayreuth, then where?" Szemerédy added: "We have to build a bridge from the past to the future, especially at a time when right-wing populism is once again gaining strength and becoming a threat. That's exactly why this work needs to be performed today."

At the end of the opera, Rienzi dies, new elections are held, and two candidates emerge victorious.

Throughout Richard Wagner's operas, power, greed, cruelty, love until death and the destruction of the world are recurring themes. His 16-hour cycle "The Ring of the Nibelung," written for the Bayreuth Festspielhaus that he built specifically for it, explores these human impulses. The Rhine gold guarded by the Rhinemaidens becomes an object of universal desire — and ultimately brings catastrophe.

The piece has been reinterpreted in Bayreuth many times. Patrice Chéreau's landmark 1976 production presented "The Ring" as a parable about greed and the decline of capitalism. Frank Castorf later replaced the symbolism of gold with oil as the true source of capitalist power.

Richard Wagner opened his festival theater 150 years ago in Bayreuth, in a hall built specifically for his monumental masterpiece, "The Ring of the Nibelung" — a 16-hour opera cycle performed over four days. But the first festival was a financial failure. Wagner was forced to sell the stage sets and costumes, and the theater remained closed for the next eight years.

A real horse onstage at the first Bayreuth Festival in 1876? Not quite — though it looks convincing. Amalie Materna played Brünnhilde in Wagner's "The Valkyrie," part of "The Ring of the Nibelung." Wagner drew heavily on Norse mythology, something reflected in the costumes. The "Ride of the Valkyries" remains one of his best-known musical passages.

Franz Betz appeared as Wotan, king of the gods, in full Viking-inspired costume during the 1876 production of "The Ring of the Nibelung." The epic tells a story of greed, betrayal and the pursuit of power. Whoever possesses the Rhinegold gains dominion over others — but in Wagner's world, power brings anything but happiness.

The festival's hall still looks much as Wagner envisioned it. Its wood-paneled interior and simple wooden seats contribute to the theater's distinctive acoustics. Once the performance begins, the auditorium is plunged into complete darkness, focusing every eye on the stage.

Audiences were stunned when a giant balloon expanded into a grotesque face bearing features associated with Nazi antisemitic racial stereotypes. Wagner was an antisemite, and scholars continue to debate whether his character of Beckmesser was designed as an antisemitic caricature. Director Barrie Kosky confronted that question head-on, in one of the festival's most acclaimed recent productions.

"The Master-Singers of Nuremberg" centers on a singing competition. Hitler, who admired Wagner both for his music and his antisemitic views, made the opera a fixture of the annual Nazi Party rallies in Nuremberg. That influence was reflected in Benno von Arent's 1938 stage design, which echoed the monumental architecture of the Nazi Party rally grounds.

Wieland Wagner's production of "Tristan and Isolde" exemplified his break with realistic stage design in favor of minimalist sets and abstract lighting. The approach became known as the "New Bayreuth" style after World War II. When Richard Wagner's grandson first introduced it in the 1950s, many traditionalists were outraged.

Patrice Chereau's groundbreaking reinterpretation of "The Ring" was booed at its 1976 premiere before eventually becoming one of Bayreuth's most celebrated productions. His staging transformed Wagner's epic into an allegory about greed and the decline of industrial capitalism, moving far beyond its original world of gods and heroes. The premiere even sparked fistfights among audience members.

Instead of following Parsifal on his quest for the Holy Grail, director Christoph Schlingensief presented a fragmented journey through cultures, life, death and rebirth. Blending esoteric and shamanistic imagery with video installations, the production bewildered audiences and ultimately achieved cult status.

Katharina Wagner, Richard Wagner's great-granddaughter, abandoned the traditional cobbler's workshop and festival meadow, replacing them with the dark world of an art mafia. Some critics found the concept overly intellectual, while others praised its bold vision. The premiere drew both prolonged boos and enthusiastic applause.

For the 2018 production of "Lohengrin," artistic director Katharina Wagner enlisted celebrated artists Neo Rauch and Rosa Loy to design the sets and costumes. Rauch, one of Germany's best-known contemporary painters, filled the stage with vivid colors and dreamlike imagery. Critics praised the visual concept.

How do we treat our children? That question lay at the heart of Austrian director Valentin Schwarz's 2022 production of "The Ring." Reimagined as a contemporary family saga with dystopian settings and cliffhangers reminiscent of a Netflix series, the production failed to win over many traditional Bayreuth audiences and critics.

Using augmented reality, American director Jay Scheib offered a preview of his 2022 Parsifal project in 2021. During the pandemic-era "Ring" production, audience members wearing 3D glasses could virtually step into the role of dragon slayer Siegfried and battle the monster themselves. In the festival's 150th anniversary season in 2026, AI will be used for the first time in the stage design.

The festival's interpretation curated by Marcus Lobbes, has no stage director. Instead, Lobbes and his team developed a new AI-based imaging system in which the singers perform inside a holographic three-dimensional environment. "What appears on stage is a unified audiovisual image," Lobbes explained. "We create a visual landscape for both the singers and the orchestral performance." To generate the projections, the team trained the AI using archival material from previous Ring productions spanning from 1876 to 2024.

In "Das Rheingold," the first installment of the cycle, viewers see Rhinemaidens in bathtubs, lakes and streams, along with forests of trees, vines and vegetation alternating with wood and metal structures, creating shifting worlds between nature and industrial romanticism. Images crack apart, dissolve into one another and morph continuously. At times, the visuals are mesmerizing; at others, human faces become distorted beyond recognition.

Whether the technology can sustain audience interest over the entire 16-hour cycle remains to be seen. While the imagery is constantly in motion, the singers often stand almost motionless so as not to disrupt the projections. "The singers' positions are predetermined, but they can still interact with one another," Lobbes said. After the performance, one audience member joked that perhaps Siegfried and Sieglinde would eventually be blowing kisses at each other. Musically, however, the production boasts an outstanding cast, including Klaus Florian Vogt, Jochen Schmeckenbecher and Evelin Novak, with Christian Thielemann conducting. As one audience member put it: "If the AI becomes too much for me, I'll simply close my eyes and enjoy the music."

This article was originally written in German and edited by Tenzin Sekhon.
https://www.dw.com/en/rienzi-why-this-wa.summary: "Rienzi" was one of Hitler's favorite operas. The opera was never staged at the Bayreuth Festival. The director says the piece is "highly contaminated"

https://www.dw.com/en/k-pop-s-bts-opt-ou.title: K-pop's BTS opt out of new Asian music Grammy consideration
https://www.dw.com/en/k-pop-s-bts-opt-ou.text:
The K-pop sensation BTS, snubbed when nominated for Grammys in the past, say they're not interested in winning a new Asian music category.

K-pop powerhouse BTS said on Wednesday that they would not submit songs for consideration for the 2027 Grammys next February.

The seven band members issued the same Korean-language note online in concert.

They said they did not want to be included in the new Grammy category, best Asian pop music performance, that's seen as a way to categorize releases across K-pop or J-pop and C-pop from Japan and China, respectively.

Newly reformed BTS, touring to promote a new album after returning from a military service hiatus, would seem to be among the frontrunners in the category.

"We hope our music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language," the band's message read. "We thank Army [the band's colloquial term for the BTS fan base] and everyone who has always stood by us."

Critics of the new Grammy argued it could serve as an exclusionary barrier stopping Asian pop music from winning other awards. Proponents argued it was just the latest of numerous genres added to the list of more than 90 Grammy categories.

No. But the band had been nominated for a total of five.

Three times they made the shortlist as the best pop duo or group performance, once they shared a nomination for best album of the year because of their contributions to Coldplay's "Music of Spheres," and also for their music video "Yet to Come."

Up until this year's ceremonies, no K-Pop act had ever won a Grammy Award.

"Golden" from the Netflix animated film "KPop Demon Hunters" won the best song for visual media, a decision that prompted elation in South Korea, despite the song's US roots and fictional performing artists.

BTS reformed and returned to frontline performance this year after a four-year hiatus.

They have released and are now promoting a 14-track album, "ARIRANG" — named after Korea's most renowned traditional folk song and unofficial national anthem, roughly translating as "My Beloved One."

The band has spent most of the summer in the Americas amid the World Cup and its world tour, including performing at the controversial halftime show of the World Cup final this month.

This fifth studio album follows a four-year break as the band members completed South Korea's mandatory military service and pursued solo projects.

https://www.dw.com/en/german-muslims-are.title: German Muslims are alarmed by the Islamist terror attack in Berlin
https://www.dw.com/en/german-muslims-are.text:
Germany's Muslim organizations condemn the Islamist terrorist attack targeting Berlin's Pride celebrations and fear repercussions.

The terrorist attack that struck Berlin's Pride celebration, or Christopher Street Day (CSD), late on Saturday evening has heightened fears and concerns about further Islamist attacks. Until Sunday evening, when security forces confronted 21-year-old Abdul B. and fatally shot him, most media outlets and the politicians responsible referred to a "suspected perpetrator" and "alleged motives".

Investigators are now relatively certain that the perpetrator was an Islamist, a radicalized Muslim with links to the "Islamic State" terror group. Politicians and security agencies are debating stricter laws and expanded surveillance powers. Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) is politically responsible for this area.

"With shock and profound dismay, we learned of yesterday's inhumane attack on the CSD," the Council of Berlin Imams stated across various channels just over twelve hours after the attack. The Council expressed its solidarity with the victims, their relatives, and the bereaved, and thanked the emergency responders. "This act, which we condemn in the strongest possible terms, demonstrates the terrible consequences to which hatred and hostility toward others can lead. Hatred leads to nothing good."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Two days later, once the perpetrator's Islamist background had been confirmed, the Council of Berlin Imams issued a second statement, this time in greater detail. It stated that the terrorist attack once again demonstrated that "religiously motivated extremism ... poses a real threat to our society."

"As imams, we cannot emphasize often enough that terror, hatred and violence have no religious legitimacy whatsoever. Anyone who uses the religion of Islam to commit violence against people because of their identity, their beliefs or their way of life, or even to kill them, is acting in direct contradiction to the ethical principles of our religion." The term "Islamism" does not appear anywhere in the 30-line statement.

The Council of Berlin Imams explicitly condemns "all violence against queer people and members of other minorities in our society". Such direct references to queer people are relatively uncommon in comparable statements.

The Council has repeatedly faced criticism. Some politicians of the ruling center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and several experts argue that it promotes views that are at odds with Germany's liberal democratic constitutional system. Others dispute that assessment.

The Council's latest statement suggests that the imams are keenly aware of the challenges involved. They note that "radicalization rarely happens overnight". More often, it is the result of a gradual process that unfolds online and across social media platforms. The priority, they argue, must be to reach young people at an early stage and "provide them with guidance, a sense of belonging and future prospects".

No single institution, they emphasize, can shoulder this responsibility alone.

A few months earlier, one imam had told DW that, for many young people, the internet had long since become the real mosque.

"Some Muslims reject the term 'Islamism' because they fear that even the linguistic association with the word 'Islam' harms their religion," sociologist and religious education scholar Mouhanad Khorchide told DW.

The 54-year-old is the founding dean of the Centre for Islamic Theology at the University of Münster. He does not regard this concern as helpful: "If we categorically deny any connection between Islam and Islamism, we make the necessary substantive engagement with the issue all the more difficult."

After all, Khorchide argued, Islamists base their arguments on Islamic sources. They claim to speak in the name of Islam. In his view, it is therefore not enough simply to say that Islamist perpetrators have "nothing to do with Islam". What is needed instead is a nuanced engagement with the issue in order to "deprive Islamist ideologies of their credibility in the long term".

The members of Berlin's Ahmadiyya Muslim community are devout Muslims belonging to a reform movement founded more than a century ago, whose teachings have led many Muslims to reject them as non-Islamic. As a result, they have also been persecuted by Islamists.

In the days following the attack, the Ahmadiyya mosque community in Berlin-Charlottenburg invited the public to a series of dialogue events scheduled for the coming days, as well as to an "open Friday prayer service on the topic of Islamism."

Burhan Kesici, chairman of the Islamic Council for the Federal Republic of Germany, condemned the attack "in the strongest possible terms" and expressed his sympathy. He concluded with the words: "Muslims in Germany stand for peace."

Similarly, the much longer statement issued by the Central Council of Muslims in Germany (KRM) describes the organization as "deeply shaken" by the attack. "As Muslim religious communities in Germany, we condemn all forms of violence, extremism, terrorism, and contempt for humanity in the strongest possible terms," it states.

Like the Council of Berlin Imams, the Central Council of Muslims in Germany avoids using the term "queer", and states: "No one should become the target of violence because of their sexual orientation...". Addressing the perpetrator's "Islamist" motive, the Central Council describes the attack as yet another case "in which an extremist ideology misuses religious references to justify hatred and violence."

According to Professor Khorchide of the University of Münster, many mosque communities, imams and Muslim organizations remain "stuck in an apologetic posture."

Their main concern, he says, is often "to defend Islam against sweeping accusations and to emphasize that violence and terrorism have nothing to do with Islam". Although this is "understandable in light of widespread anti-Muslim hostility", it does not go far enough, Khorchide said: "Anyone who wants to solve problems must first be willing to name them openly."

Khorchide also points to the conspicuous reluctance to mention the event itself, the "CSD," and the queer context in which it took place.

Some imams, he argues, avoid a "clear distancing from Islamism" because "on certain socio-political issues, such as attitudes toward sexual diversity or gender roles, they share conservative convictions, even though they naturally reject violence."

Precisely for that reason, he says, they must be willing to engage in self-critical reflection. "A credible Muslim voice is not one that relativizes problems," the academic says.

Eren Güvercin, deputy chairman of the relatively small Alhambra Society, is even more outspoken. Founded in 2017, the organization advocates a pluralistic Islam and has drawn criticism from established Muslim umbrella groups because of its broadly liberal orientation.

Güvercin speaks of a "deliberate decision" by many not to name "the motive behind the attack, namely Islamist hostility toward queer people," nor "the target of the attack, namely queer people and the CSD."

According to Güvercin, speaking openly about these issues would inevitably raise the question of what their own religious stance toward queer lives actually is, he told DW.

While people are generally able to clearly identify the motives behind far-right attacks, he argues that this willingness is completely absent when it comes to Islamist attacks. There is no serious or self-critical debate within Muslim communities about Islamism as an ideology, nor about hostility toward queer people or antisemitism, Güvercin says.

Muslim organizations that are unable to name problems openly will, in Güvercin's view, be unable to provide meaningful guidance. "Instead, young people find that guidance from Islamist influencers online."

This article has been translated from German.

https://www.dw.com/en/world-cup-sell-off.title: World Cup sell-off: Has FIFA finally gone too far?
https://www.dw.com/en/world-cup-sell-off.text:
A new FIFA proposal to sell off a stake in the World Cup has been met with fury in the football world. Under Gianni Infantino’s presidency, FIFA has become increasingly profit-driven, but is this too much?

"While you divide, we unite," Gianni Infantino wrote on social media on Monday, in a long missive aimed at his detractors. By Tuesday, he had united the football world — albeit in opposition to his latest scheme.

Shortly after reports emerged in UK newspapers The Times and the Financial Times on Tuesday, FIFA confirmed its plans to create a new subsidiary, named FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE). This would enable it to sell a minority stake in the World Cup's operations to private investors for billions of dollars.

Chief among FIFA's proposed investors is the investment vehicle, Thrive Eternal, headed by Joshua Kushner — younger brother of Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

Other than the potential conflict of interest connection to Trump, with whom Infantino has grown close, there are significant concerns about transparency, corruption and whether FIFA has the remit to make such a move unilaterally.

"The World Cup is one of the few truly global sporting events, and that comes with a responsibility beyond maximizing revenue," Bret Myers, a professor of sports business practices at Villanova University in Pennsylvania, USA, told DW.

The US connection is important, with the model echoing the way that many US sports operate. Formula 1 too went through a similar process when it was bought by Liberty Media in 2017. Greg Maffei, a former Liberty CEO, has been a "key commercial adviser" to FIFA on the FFE plan.

"North American sports have long operated within a more commercial framework, where private ownership, franchise valuations, and investor involvement are widely accepted," Myers added.

"Football, particularly in Europe, has a much stronger tradition of clubs and competitions being viewed as cultural institutions rather than purely commercial assets."

More fundamentally, the concern is that this is the first step towards the World Cup, football's biggest prize, becoming privately owned.

"A minority investment is very different from relinquishing control," Myers said. However, it does represent a significant shift in how the World Cup is financed and managed commercially."

World football's global governors are a nonprofit organization but sit on cash reserves of an estimated $8 billion (€7.02 billion) after a World Cup that saw ticket prices skyrocket.

Given FIFA's remit lies in developing football, rather than purely profiting from it, there is a sense that this is a move designed to shore up Infantino's power and, perhaps, encroach on the turf of the continental football federations he failed to include in the planning.

FIFA has promised to invest profits back into the game, mostly by offering all 211 member associations a flat fee of $20 million in 2027, rising to $24 million by 2035. Associations must decide whether to accept those payments by September 19 or risk them being reduced or retracted.

"The president controls this huge pot of money and uses it to reward those that are loyal to him, that support him, and punish those that are not supportive of him," Miguel Maduro a former chairman of FIFA's Governance, Audit and Compliance Committee, told DW.

"FIFA could do lots of good things with money. But there is no system of checks and balances and accountability to make us sure that the money is actually going to be well spent by all national football associations.  Everything that that's happened in the past makes me suspicious of how this money will end up being spent."

Almost universally negative. National federations, world leaders and fan groups have all come out against the idea, with federations particularly peeved about the lack of consultation.

But perhaps the most surprising reaction came from the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), who released a statement confirming it was "not consulted on the proposal and is disappointed" by the way in which it was released. Asia  and Africa, are where Infantino's main power base lies, as together they have 101 of the 211 national associations — with each getting a vote on the president.

Similar misgivings were expressed by a number of powerful national football associations, including Germany's DFB.

"A line is being crossed here. There is a strong consensus among the member associations on this matter, as evidenced by several conversations I have had in recent days with Aleksander Ceferin [president of Europe's football governors UEFA] and other colleagues," said Hans-Joachim Watzke, a DFB vice president.

"If European football stands united in opposing these plans, it carries significant weight."

UEFA seems in the best position to lead any revolt  and has hit out at the plans, saying football is "not FIFA's to sell." It was a strongly worded statement of the type UEFA has released several times in recent months as its battle with FIFA plays out in public. Reports suggest UEFA will meet as soon as Wednesday to discuss their options.

Maduro backs UEFA's stance but said he'd like the current climate to serve as an opportunity for broader reform.

"I don't think UEFA has the same severity of problems that we find in FIFA, but I do think it also suffers from serious governance problems and that they need to be addressed," he said.

"Simply getting rid of Mr. Infantino but leaving the entire structure and model of governance of sports will be removing a couple of bad apples but leaving the tree that produced them in place."

That the AFC and the CONCACAF (which governs North, Central America and Caribbean football) have criticized the way the latest plans were released, may have strengthened UEFA's hand in any thoughts of breakaway or boycott.

It may also lead to the continental federations uniting to find someone to oppose Infantino in next year's presidential election or in threats of boycotting next year's Women's World Cup.

But Maduro thinks such talk is often designed to appease the public before intentions are quietly shelved.

"What we've seen so far for the most part is that these statements, where they distance themselves from these kinds of initiatives of FIFA, are made under the pressure of public opinions. But then they actually never follow through."

Maduro went on to say that UEFA's increasingly strident opposition to FIFA is, at least in part, a reaction to an increased threat to its own highly lucrative Champions League. Should the proposed changes go through, Maduro expects World Cups to be more frequent and a further expansion of FIFA's recently expanded Club World Cup.

"They will want to transform that into the big international football competition of clubs instead of the Champions League. That's what they will try to do because it will be in their commercial interest," he said.

FIFA has promised to invest profits back into the game by offering all 211 member associations a flat fee of $20 million in 2027. FIFA's remit lies in developing football, rather than purely profiting from it.

https://www.dw.com/en/bayreuth-festival-.title: Bayreuth Festival opens with celebration and commemoration
https://www.dw.com/en/bayreuth-festival-.text:
To mark its 150th anniversary, the Bayreuth Festival remembers victims of the Holocaust — and confronts its founder's antisemitism.

"I would like to state explicitly that Katharina Wagner is changing the culture of remembrance in Bayreuth." With these words, spoken from the stage of the Bayreuth Festival, German-Jewish author Michel Friedman encapsulated the central message of the festival's two-day opening celebration.

Friedman spoke during a commemorative event titled "Silenced Voices," dedicated to Jewish artists who worked at the Bayreuth Festival and were later murdered or oppressed under the Nazi regime. Despite initial organizational turbulence, his talk became one of the key events of the opening celebrations on July 26, alongside the concert on the eve of the festival and the premiere of a new production of the opera "Rienzi."

Friedman also visited the exhibition with Bayreuth Festival director Katharina Wagner and several members of the local Jewish community. In the park surrounding the Bayreuth Festival grounds, directly beside the bust of Richard Wagner, a series of gray memorial steles stands as a powerful reminder of the Jewish artists whose lives were lost. A cantor from the Jewish community recited a prayer for the victims, and their names were read aloud.

Friedman's speech in the Festspielhaus, which lasted more than an hour, encompassed far more than the omissions and blind spots of Germany's culture of remembrance. For the 70-year-old, whose family was almost entirely murdered during the Holocaust, the focus was on something more fundamental — the mechanisms that foster hatred and injustice, and the passivity of society that allows them to flourish. His message was about the present as much as the past.

Friedman criticized what he called a "bored, decadent democracy" and urged everyone present and everyone listening — as well as those outside the hall who remain "silent and grumbling”— to become active witnesses to their own time, before it is too late once again.

"My country, Germany, is a community. This community is defined by diversity, and diversity has once again become a concept that is under heavy attack. Yet this community and this diversity are the only future we have," he said.

Few places in Germany bring together history, culture and politics as strikingly as Bayreuth. The opening of this year's festival demonstrated that once again. To mark the festival's 150th anniversary, the red carpet was rolled out and graced by many of Germany's celebrities and politicians, including Chancellor Friedrich Merz, former chancellor Angela Merkel, as well as many international guests.

Inside the Festspielhaus, visitors were greeted by Bayreuth figures from the past century and a half, represented in a large mural by Hungarian street artist Adam Heat that dominates the auditorium.

At the center is King Ludwig II of Bavaria presenting Richard Wagner with a grail overflowing with money — a vivid metaphor for the founding of the festival. Surrounding him is an illustrious cast of Bayreuth figures from the past 150 years — members of the Wagner family, who have guided the festival for generations; conductors ranging from Wilhelm Furtwängler and Arturo Toscanini to Oksana Lyniv and Nathalie Stutzmann. Also depicted is Wagner admirer and longtime Bayreuth guest Adolf Hitler, portrayed in elegant attire and holding a small glass.

Nike Wagner, the composer's great-granddaughter, summed up the message behind the work in her festival address: As visitors to the festival's grand hall, we become part of "Wagner's artistic ritual. Whoever takes a seat here now, sits with all those who have sat here before."

Katharina Wagner, Richard Wagner's descendant and the festival's artistic director spoke candidly about her family's Nazi ties. "Given my family's close and, in some cases, deeply personal ties to the Nazi regime, and given the role of the festival as a cultural showcase of the Third Reich, but also bearing in mind that our German democracy today is once again threatened by forces seeking to make antisemitism, racism, chauvinism, and nationalism part of the foundations of the state, there is no better place than this Festspielhaus to say: No."

In his speech, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz explained why, for him personally, Wagner's legacy and music represent the contradictions of German intellectual history:

"Richard Wagner's person and work are exemplary of both the greatness and the darker depths of Germany's artistic and historical legacy. They represent the uniquely German combination of the most admirable and the most questionable aspects of our past. When we engage with Wagner, we have the opportunity to see and hear so much of ourselves across the centuries in a single body of work."

And nowhere, Merz said, is this opportunity felt more profoundly than in Bayreuth.

With such direct statements during the anniversary event, the Bayreuth Festival has opened a new chapter in its culture of remembrance. In doing so, the festival seeks to make a broader social statement and take a firm stand against antisemitism.

This article was translated from German and edited by Teresa O'Connell.
https://www.dw.com/en/bayreuth-festival-.summary: Bayreuth Festival celebrates its 150th anniversary with a new exhibition and concert. The festival's director and its artistic director spoke candidly about her family's Nazi ties. The event was held at the Festspielhaus in the Fest spielhaus, where the festival's founder was almost entirely murdered during the Holocaust.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-how-effect.title: Germany: How effective are exit programs for Islamists?
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-how-effect.text:
Germany has set up many programs to help individuals break away from the radical Islamist scene. Following the Islamist terror attack on Berlin's Pride event, critics say the programs are ineffective.

Following Saturday's deadly attack by suspected Islamist assailant Abdul B. against Berlin's Pride event, a debate has erupted in Germany over what lessons the country should draw from the incident. The 21-year-old, who was later shot and killed by police while he was on the run, had had two intake interviews in June and July as part of a deradicalization program in Berlin.

However, according to Thomas Mücke, executive director of the Violence Prevention Network, it did not appear that Abdul B. genuinely wanted to turn his back on the Islamist scene — and it is unlikely that he would have been accepted into the program.

Similar cases have also occurred periodically in the Islamism Exit Program (API).

"We then have to conclude that assistance in exiting is not possible at that point because we have no reason to believe the individual actually wants to distance themselves." API exit program counselor and social worker Stefanie Adler* tells DW.

The Islamism Exit Program API is based in Germany's most populous state of North Rhine-Westphalia. It was established in 2014 to support people who want to break away from Islamist circles, including many who are considered potential threats by security services.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"What we've seen over the past two years is that we're dealing with younger and younger individuals. In the past, we saw people traveling to Syria, and it was more or less clear that they went there and joined the Islamic State, became radicalized in the real world," Adler explains.

Today, she says, they are younger, and they are often radicalized through digital media.

"Social media acts as an amplifier for radicalization — and it happens much faster," Adler adds.

Some individuals approach the API on their own initiative, while other potential candidates are reported to the police or youth court services by contact persons in correctional facilities.

"We then take a closer look at the person," said API deradicalization counselor and psychologist Viola Geiger*, "gather information, and begin the counseling process — initially on a weekly basis and toward the end sometimes every few months. It's definitely a lengthy process."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Once an individual has credibly distanced themself from violence as a legitimate course of action and learned to cope with crisis situations on their own, they are considered successfully deradicalized and their cases are closed. But achieving this requires patience and persistence.

In one case, API exit program counselors worked with one individual for as long as seven years. In spite of these challenges, says Adler, deradicalization programs are absolutely essential.

"What would be the alternative if these programs didn't exist? Many people who are released from prison after serving a sentence need such programs to reintegrate into society," said Adler. And the public is largely unaware of the many success stories. "People forget that those who have successfully left the movement then fly under the radar and no longer appear in public because they simply want to live their lives."

Forty organizations and initiatives working on prevention, disengagement or deradicalization in the area of religiously motivated extremism are organized under the umbrella association the Federal Working Group on Religiously Motivated Extremism, or BAG RelEx for short. Its executive director, Jamuna Oehlmann, was just as shocked as many others after the attack in Berlin.

She told DW that the problem of radical Islamism in Germany remains significant.

"There are more and more young women who are becoming radicalized. But still, it is above all young men in Germany who are becoming radicalized, who commit acts of violence and who act out their violent fantasies," Oehlmann says.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Radicalization is a process with many contributing factors, she explains, where various elements converge and, in the worst-case scenario, lead to radicalization. "Society and external factors play an important role in this, but so does the responsibility of each individual who becomes radicalized."

Oehlmann identified specific crisis situations, or "push factors," that can cause people to become alienated from society. These include the loss of a beloved parent, failing an exam, a housing crisis, job loss, experiences of discrimination, exclusion and bullying. Additionally, the global increase in political instability is also driving people to despair.

"Then there are Islamist groups who know how to take advantage of these life crises and target young people by giving them the feeling: 'You will be heard with us, you belong with us, you can be someone with us.' And in addition, they simplify the complexity of the world by breaking it down into good and evil, black and white."

That's why it's all the more important that funding for organizations working to prevent or deradicalize Islamists not be cut. However, Federal Minister of Education Karin Prien has announced exactly that.

Minister Prien plans to restructure the Live Democracy! funding program. Funding for approximately 200 projects is set to expire at the end of the year. Twenty-three of the 40 member organizations of the Federal Working Group on Religiously Motivated Extremism are affected by this.

Jamuna Oehlmann is critical of this decision.

"The problem is that even projects that are doing good work are affected by this. And so now they're having to focus on fundraising — that is, finding new sources of funding — instead of concentrating on the actual work of preventing Islamism. We need reliability and a long-term approach."

*Name has been changed to protect privacy

This article was translated from German.
