https://www.dw.com/en/how-two-wars-and-e.title: How two wars and El Nino could fuel world hunger
https://www.dw.com/en/how-two-wars-and-e.text:
The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East haven't yet crippled global food supplies. Add a powerful weather pattern like El Nino, however, and the risks multiply.

A potentially record-strength El Nino is now intensifying across the Pacific, bringing either drought or flooding to the world's key farming regions.

Earlier this month, the US National Oceanic & Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) predicted a 63% chance that the unusual weather pattern could be "very strong" this year.

JP Morgan, meanwhile, warned last week that El Nino, combined with $100 (€88) oil prices, could spike food inflation by up to 1.5%.

The arrival of El Nino follows two major conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, during which global food supplies have held up remarkably well.

So, could this third crisis bring the perfect storm that tips the balance?

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russia's war in Ukraine still hangs over one of the world's major grain-exporting regions, where repeated attacks on ports and farmland continue to threaten one of the planet's key breadbaskets.

The Iran war has driven up energy and fertilizer prices, raising the cost of growing food worldwide and causing temporary supply disruptions for key soil nutrients.

El Nino, which shifts rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide, is expected to be so strong that the World Bank warned recently it could cut rice output by 20% to 50% in affected regions.

Maximo Torero, chief economist of the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), warned of a "compound effect" that could create "a very complex situation" by the end of the year.

"We are very concerned about El Nino and the delay of the monsoon ... in India," Torero told DW.

El Nino is expected to slow down and weaken India’s monsoon season, a vital time for rice planting. June already saw around 40% less rainfall than normal, according to local media.

India produces nearly a third of the world’s rice, the vast majority of which is consumed domestically.

Aside from South Asia, the FAO thinks the El Nino risks are highest in Africa's Sahel region, southern Africa, Southeast Asia and in the Dry Corridor of Central America.

The UN food agency warned this month that some of these regions face a more than 50% chance of drought in the next few months.

Despite the geopolitical strife, food prices remain nearly 20% below their 2022 peak, according to the FAO Food Price Index.

The world brought in the biggest grain harvest in history last year. This is because farmers planted more land, the weather has been favorable and the crops produced more per acre.

While this year is expected to be slightly smaller, the harvest will still be the second-largest ever.

“We are seeing improvements in agricultural productivity," Simone Bunse, senior researcher at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), told DW, citing India and Latin America as notable examples.

"These have helped sustain food production and reduce undernourishment. And this is balancing some of the localized impacts of conflict.”

War is a major barrier to getting hunger under control globally. The UN says 266 million people are still facing acute hunger, more than half of them due to conflict.

The worst of it is concentrated in just a handful of conflict-hit countries, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sudan and Yemen, where supplies cannot reach the people who need them.

"We have enough calories produced in the world to feed everybody," Torero said. "Those calories are not distributed in the same way across the world, and that's the challenge."

War often destroys local food sources, displaces millions of people, damages infrastructure and severely cuts humanitarian access. In some hotspots such as Sudan and Gaza, experts say hunger is increasingly being used as a weapon.

"Parties deliberately destroy farmland, livestock, water systems, food storage facilities, and transport routes. They jeopardize access to markets and obstruct humanitarian assistance," SIPRI's Bunse told DW.

Another risk to global food supplies is fertilizer, around a third of which normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz. The strait remains heavily disrupted after a failed ceasefire between the US and Iran, along with attacks on shipping in the Red Sea.

Some farmers have been paying substantially more for fertilizer, delaying purchases or switching to crops that require less fertiliser. If they ultimately apply less, yields could suffer in the next harvest.

Food security experts believe the Middle East conflict alone could leave millions more people hungry by 2030 — and that projection does not yet account for the effects of El Nino.

With temperatures in the Pacific Ocean expected to rise by 3.6 degrees Celsius (38.4 degrees Fahrenheit) — almost double the 2015/6 El Nino — climate think tank Berkeley Earth now predicts this year's weather pattern will be strongest on record.

If oil prices leap past $120 a barrel again, if grain exports from Ukraine are successfully blocked, or if El Nino bites harder into next year’s crops as farmers plant less, then the world could face a spike in hunger, experts predict.

If all of those happen at once, the impact would be far worse, with JP Morgan predicting that food inflation will surpass 5% in 2027 and that emerging markets would take the biggest hit.

Additional reporting by Daniel Winter.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-how-weathe.title: Germany: How weather extremes impact local agriculture
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-how-weathe.text:
Heat, drought, heavy rain and late frosts are taking a toll on German farmers. They increasingly respond with adapted varieties, new crops, modern breeding techniques and modified farming methods.

For many German farmers, the heat wave in late June couldn't have come at a worse time. While barley was already ready for harvest across much of Germany, the drought struck other crops during a particularly vulnerable stage of development.

"This year is another difficult one for farms," Horst Gömann of Germany's North Rhine-Westphalia Chamber of Agriculture told DW.

Corn has been particularly hard hit, as the extreme heat coincided with the flowering period, he said. "We're already seeing some corn plants failing to form cobs. That, of course, essentially amounts to a total crop failure," Gömann said.

In corn, the energy is concentrated in the cobs. If they're missing, yields plummet dramatically.

The heat wave in June, with peak temperatures exceeding 40 degrees Celsius, hit other European growing regions even harder. According to a recent analysis by Coceral, the European association of grain traders, this reduced the value of the grain harvest in Europe by more than €2 billion ($2.3 billion), with France and Hungary suffering the greatest losses.

Due to the heat wave, Coceral lowered its expectations for grain production in the European Union and the United Kingdom by just under 9 million metric tons, a decline of 3%. The London-based research institute Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) even expects a 5% decline. Corn accounts for the largest share of the downward revision in Europe's grain forecast, representing about half of the adjustment.

The weather also took its toll on wheat and barley. In some cases, barley was harvested several weeks earlier than usual.

According to Gömann, this year's barley harvest is likely to be slightly below average. For wheat, he expects losses of about 10%.

Risk diversification is therefore an important adaptation strategy. Instead of growing just one kind of grain, many farms are relying on different kinds with varying maturity rates.

"You never know when such extreme heat will strike," Gömann said. He explained that farmers who grow multiple varieties spread the risk across different stages of development.

Barley has a natural advantage in this regard. It matures earlier than wheat and often completes grain formation before the major early-summer drought sets in.

While drought threatens crops in the fields, late frost is a major concern in fruit farming. Due to climate change and mild winter temperatures, flower buds, from which the fruit will eventually develop, form earlier. However, frosty nights can occur well into spring.

Many fruit growers, therefore, protect their blossoms with frost-protection sprinklers. Water is sprayed over the blossoms, forming a layer of ice. "This traps enough heat inside so that temperatures don't drop as low as they would without frost-protection sprinklers," explains Gömann. These systems can also be used for irrigation during long dry spells in summer.

There are also technical solutions for combating heat. Today, hail protection nets serve more than just protection against severe weather, as they also shade the fruit and prevent sunburn.

In addition, experiments are already underway in fruit and wine growing with semi-transparent photovoltaic films. They generate electricity and protect the plants from excessive sunlight while allowing enough light to pass through.

However, while irrigation is an important tool, Gömann believes it is not always economically viable. He said vegetables, potatoes and fruit generate high returns and justify the investment. He added that for grains or corn, irrigation is not worthwhile. "The costs are simply too high," he said.

The water comes primarily from groundwater. Despite frequent periods of drought, Germany is not a water-scarce country. "We basically still have enough water in Germany," the Gömann emphasized. The problem, he said, is rather the uneven distribution. Heavy rainfall occurs in winter, while dry spells are becoming more frequent in summer.

Plant breeding plays a central role. Varieties whose genetic origins lie in warmer regions of Europe are already being cultivated in North Rhine-Westphalia.

"With wheat, for example, we're already making extensive use of genetics from France," said Gömann. The climatic conditions there have, in some respects, already shifted to Germany.

Grains with shorter stalks, known as semi-dwarfs, have been around for many years. Short stalks can bear significantly heavier ears, are less likely to snap during heavy rain, hail, or wind and require less water.

In addition, research is being conducted on wheat varieties with deeper roots. Current research at the German Julius Kühn Institute, the Federal Research Centre for Cultivated Plants, aims to develop wheat whose roots respond dynamically to drought by growing deeper only when water becomes scarce in the topsoil.

The agricultural sector is also experimenting with new crops. Soybeans are now being grown in parts of Germany, albeit on a very small scale. Experiments are even being conducted with millet, a crop known from arid regions around the world, also only on a very small scale. Even winegrowing is slowly expanding further north, which is a visible sign of the shifting vegetation zones.

For Gömann, the condition of the soil is at least as important as new crop varieties. He said it is crucial to avoid soil compaction so that roots can penetrate deep into the ground.

Farmers have always had to adapt to changing conditions, said Gömann. What's new, however, is the pace. While climate change used to take place over generations, now it is noticeable within just a few decades.

"The whole thing is happening quite quickly now," he said.

At the same time, modern agriculture has significantly better options than previous generations. New varieties are developed within a few years, and international breeding companies are continuously working on plants that are more tolerant of drought and heat.

For the agricultural expert, one thing is certain: the increase in extreme weather conditions in the past years is no coincidence. He sees the severe droughts of 2018 and 2019, as well as the recent heat waves, as part of a trend.

"This can certainly be attributed to the emerging climate change," Gömann told DW.

Agriculture must therefore continue to adapt, just as it has done for centuries, he noted, adding that it must do so much faster than before.

https://www.dw.com/en/fifa-plans-to-form.title: FIFA plans to form new commercial subsidiary and sell stake
https://www.dw.com/en/fifa-plans-to-form.text:
FIFA has announced plans to form a commercial subsidiary and to sell a non-controlling interest to private investors. It needs approval from member associations, but is claiming that it will benefit them financially.

FIFA plans to create a new commercial subsidiary valued at $20 billion (roughly €17.5 billion) and sell non-controlling minority stakes to investors, world football's governing body announced on Tuesday.

It called on its 211 member associations to back the plan, saying that if they voted in favor they "would benefit immediately from increased funding."

As soon as the news emerged, European football federation UEFA issued fierce criticism of the plan, saying it "crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross."

The push comes immediately after this summer's World Cup hosted primarily in the US, with FIFA listing a series of potential investors and advisors from the country. Infantino's close relationship with US President Donald Trump had already prompted criticism in some corners prior to Tuesday's announcement, which came a day after Infantino issued a fiery statement defending the tournament in the US and the controversies that accompanied it.

FIFA said that it planned to set up a "new FIFA-owned and controlled subsidiary consolidating FIFA's commercial and event operations" that it would call the FIFA Forward Enterprise, or FFE.

It said this company would be valued at $20 billion and that FFE would aim to raise up to $4.2 billion "this year" by "carefully selecting long-term investors who will purchase minority, non-controlling interests in FFE."

FIFA claimed that "all net benefits of FFE will be reinvested back into football worldwide," without clarifying what constituted "net benefits," or what gains investors then stood to make.

FFE would be responsible for FIFA's commercial rights like broadcast, sponsorship, ticketing and licensing contracts, the statement said. By far the most valuable of these for FIFA are those connected to the World Cup, although other competitions like the recently and controversially relaunched FIFA Club World Cup also apply.

Ahead of this month's World Cup final in New York, FIFA President Gianni Infantino had told member associations that he wanted to "unleash the commercial potential and opportunity" of the organization.

Infantino tried to portray the changes as seeking to more evenly spread out football funding and to "democratize" the game, seemingly in a pitch aimed at less wealthy (and more numerous) football associations in particular.

"As its global governing body, FIFA is responsible for making sure the game reaches every corner of the world, and that the value it creates supports federations and communities everywhere. Our next stage of growth needs a structure built for it, one where the commercial side of the game operates as a focused, dedicated business, with its value shared more and better all around the world," Infantino said in FIFA's press release.

"We intend to invest heavily even in the smallest or most remote parts of the footballing world, places that are too often passed over," Infantino said, championing the new investment scheme dubbed the FIFA Fast Forward Programme, or FFFP.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

FIFA's press release was published soon after an article on the website of UK newspaper The Times — followed soon after by the Financial Times, Bloomberg and others — began attracting international attention.

The European football federation UEFA issued a scathing response online soon after the news broke.

"This crosses a line that football's governing insitutions should never cross," it said. "UEFA takes it extremely seriously. So should every National Football Association. So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments, and everyone who cares about the future of the game."

UEFA said that the "soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially."

UEFA and FIFA have clashed repeated in recent months and years under Infantino's stewardship, including during the World Cup this summer.

"None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA's to sell," UEFA argued.

UEFA, however, only represents around one quarter of FIFA's member associations, so its opposition is by no means guaranteed to halt the plan.

FIFA said its structure would be similar to "other sports governing bodies with dedicated commercial subsidiaries," and said that investors would be selected "against clear long-term, governance and strategic criteria."

It described ideal investors as long-term partners who could contribute capital and commercial expertise to help FIFA's goal of growing the game.

"Subject to these final agreements and required approvals, Thrive Eternal, a permanent capital holding company, is expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE," FIFA said, referring to the holding company set up this year by Joshua Kushner, brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law and senior negotiator Jared Kushner.

Infantino's relations with Trump came under scrutiny more than once amid the World Cup process — perhaps most notably when FIFA overturned the red card suspension of US striker Folarin Balogun ahead of defeat against Belgium, and when Donald Trump was given the inaugural "FIFA Peace Prize" in a much-mocked event last December. This came weeks before the abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and then the war with Iran.

FIFA also said that Greg Maffei, the CEO of BANN Ventures and formerly "the CEO of Liberty Media during its acquisition and ownership of Formula 1" motor racing, "has been a key commercial advisor and will remain involved in the establishment of FFE in this next phase."

It said that investment bank JP Morgan was engaged to work alongside FIFA, and Rome-based economic consulting firm OpenEconomic were also "engaging with prospective long-term investors."

FIFA said that it was trying to set up a geographically diversified investor group and said it had received expressions of interest from every major region in the world.

https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-berlin-.title: Fact check: Berlin Pride attack claims debunked
https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-berlin-.text:
Following the Islamist terrorist attack at Berlin Pride, rumors, false claims and misleading videos have been spreading on social media. DW Fact check examines some of the most widely shared claims.

In the aftermath of Saturday's attack at Berlin's Christopher Street Day, which is how the city's LGBTQ+ Pride celebrations are known, more and more details have emerged about the alleged perpetrator and the attack itself.

But as it is often the case in the aftermath of such events, verified information can be hard to come by, while rumors and false claims spread rapidly on social media.

DW Fact check takes a look at several of such viral posts.

Claim: A videoshared on TikTok shows a crowd of people fleeing from something happening off screen. Text overlaid on the video in the style of a location tag suggests that it shows Christopher Street Day (CSD) celebrations in Berlin. The video is circulating on various platforms and in multiple languages.

The video does not show the attack on Berlin's Pride event that German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has classified as an "Islamist terrorist attack."

A reverse image search leads to an older video on YouTubethat was published on July 13, 2026, well before the Berlin Pride celebrations.

The footage actually shows a shooting at a salsa festival in Toronto, Canada, on July 11. At least two people reportedly exchanged gunfire during the Salsa on St. Clair festival.

According to statements by Canadian police,two people were killed. At least five others were injured. So far, Canadian police have not released any information about the motive behind the shooting.

The video has no connection to the attack in Berlin.

Claim: Shaky nighttime footage shows a person in a white T-shirt lying on the ground with hands bound behind their back, while people in police uniforms stand nearby. According to some posts, such as this one on X,this six-second clip allegedly shows police arresting the suspected perpetrator at the scene of the attack. The claim is also circulating in Arabic, Hebrew and Russian.

The video does not show the arrest of the suspected perpetrator. It was already circulating on social media shortly after the attack during the night from Saturday to Sunday.

At that time, however, the suspect was still on the run. The first reports that police had shot the alleged perpetrator did not emerge until more than 20 hours after the attack.

The media outlet Junge Freiheit initially shared the video on its social media channels, from where it was picked up by other accounts. The red-and-white "JF" logo is clearly visible in the video. Junge Freiheit is a right-wing German weekly newspaper.

In its Facebook post,Junge Freiheit initially wrote: "Arrest at the scene of the Berlin attack. It is still unclear whether this is the perpetrator."

The outlet later updated the post with the clarification: "According to police, this is not the suspect. The suspect remains at large."

On X, Junge Freiheit originally wrote:"According to eyewitnesses, the man lying on the ground is the rampage driver arrested at CSD Berlin."

The newspaper later deleted the post and disclosed that, according to police, the footage showed a different arrest on the sidelines of the CSD.

Whether the video was actually recorded in connection with the CSD in Berlin remains unclear. So far, there is no indication that the footage is older and therefore being taken out of context.

When asked whether the video showed a police operation related to the CSD, Berlin police neither confirmed nor denied that such an operation had taken place and referred inquiries to Germany's federal public prosecutor's office.

What is clear, however, is that the video does not show the arrest of the suspect.

Claim:  A numberof videoshave popped up on TikTok, allegedly showing genuine reactions to the Islamist terror attack in Berlin.

The videos were generated using artificial intelligence. Their visual style makes this clear, and the platforms on which they appear also label them as AI-generated. Nevertheless, they are being widely shared in connection with Berlin Pride.

In one video, styled as a street interview, an AI-generated young woman draped in a rainbow flag says: "We just want to celebrate in peace." A voice from behind responds: "Enjoy what you voted for."

Another videostatement claims that the German government can no longer cope with Islamist terrorism.

The videos do not show real statements from CSD attendees. Instead, they present staged political messages designed to create the impression of authentic reactions to a real event.

Although clearly labeled as AI, such videos can still contribute to the spread of disinformation by associating real groups of people with political statements.

Users are also reacting to the AI-generated videos. Comments show people sharing blue heart emojis, a symbol associated with the far-right party Alternative for Germany (AfD), or writing comments such as: "Then you should have voted for the decent party."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The accountsharing these fake CSD reactions regularly shares AI-generated videos, some of them featuring political messages.

Another clip even imitates an official police statement,featuring an AI-generated police officer that claims that the suspected attacker was known to authorities but was repeatedly released because prisons were overcrowded.

Labels indicating AI-generated content are often small and can easily be overlooked while scrolling on mobile phone screens.

Note: This article is part of a collaboration between Germany's public broadcasting fact-checking teams ARD-Faktenfinder and DW Fact check.

The article was originally published in German.

https://www.dw.com/en/why-is-germany-bui.title: Why is Germany building roads for yesterday's climate?
https://www.dw.com/en/why-is-germany-bui.text:
As the Autobahn buckles under heat waves, Germany is still paving roads for a past climate. Engineers know how to fix that — so what's the holdup?

Multi-day European heat waves with temperatures topping 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit)  are increasingly leaving their mark on Germany's famed Autobahn — buckling concrete slabs, deforming asphalt and forcing temporary speed limits.

In early July alone, seven stretches of the country's highways had to be shut down completely for a time.

"The cause often lies in the bitumen — the petroleum-derived binder in asphalt. It's elastic and can soften at high temperatures, from around 60 degrees Celsius," a spokesperson from Autobahn GmbH, the company that manages Germany's highways, told DW.

Bitumen is a component in most of the country's roads.

When outdoor temperatures climb above 30 degrees Celsius, the surface of dark asphalt can quickly heat to double that or more in the sun and then deform. Using modern, bitumen-free asphalt mixes lowers the risk of such damage, according to Autobahn GmbH.

So, as heat waves intensify and traffic volumes rise, are Germany's roads built to last?

German roads are "not designed for these stresses at all," said Nina Stelzenmüller. The engineer heads the road construction technology division at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) in southwestern Germany.

"The composition of the road surface is based on experience from the last 30 or 50 years," and not on the increasingly noticeable shifts in the climate, explained Stelzenmüller.

At present, road surfaces have to be designed for a temperature range of minus 30 degrees Celsius to plus 45 degrees Celsius, according to Autobahn GmbH. They are built, the company said, to withstand "the climatic stresses from heat and cold to be expected in Germany."

Yet in some regions of eastern Germany, temperatures could exceed that 45C maximum on certain days by the year 2040. That's according to climate models from Germany's National Meteorological Service (DWD), which assume emissions will remain high in the coming years and that global warming will continue to intensify.

A studyinvolving the research institute of Germany's federal transport ministry (BASt) likewise concludes that climate change is already pushing existing road materials to their limits, and that action is needed. But these findings have not yet translated into binding requirements for updating street surfaces.

Every road resurfaced today needs to withstand temperatures that may only become reality decades from now. But there are plenty of ways to make Germany's vital road infrastructure heat-resistant for the medium to long-term.

A 2019 study, also involving BASt, found that dark asphalt heated up by 7C less when light-colored quartzite was mixed in. The researchers recommended applying reflective surface layers to roads and building in other cooling materials as quickly as possible. The study did not examine the cost or durability of such heat adaptations.

According to Autobahn GmbH, lighter-colored stone is already being used in construction in some cases. The regional availability and cost of such stone also play a role in its use, said the company.

Individual states and cities are also testing and planning light-colored road surfaces, including in the western German cities of Oberhausen and Stuttgart, as well as the eastern state of Brandenburg.

Just scattering light-colored quartzite over the asphalt surface could also help, according to Stelzenmüller, and would be a short-term, feasible approach.

Germany isn't alone in facing increasingly hot roads. Infrastructure needs to be adapted worldwide.

Tokyo, for example, already uses reflective, water-retaining road surfaces as standard when resurfacing streets. These can lower the surface temperature by 8 to 10 degrees Celsius. By 2030, some 245 kilometers (152 miles) of roads in the Japanese capital are to be fitted with them.

In Phoenix, in the US state of Arizona, light-colored coatings have also already been applied to numerous streets. They reflect more sunlight, so absorb less heat. During the day, they were around 6.7 degrees Celsius cooler than conventional surfaces. But at the same time, this noticeably warmed the ambient air for passersby.

But Germany, like many other countries, is still a long way from the systematic use of suitable road surfaces to combat heat damage. And even as average temperatures keep rising, the challenge remains that the road surface also has to stay stable in freezing winter conditions.

As an alternative to bitumen, high-performance binders that can survive both extremes — frost and heat — are currently being developed, said Stelzenmüller.

"For one thing, they're especially elastic, so that at low temperatures they can still bear the stresses caused by the cold. But at the same time they also have a very high strength, which allows them to withstand deformation at high temperatures," explained the engineer.

A great deal of research on climate-adapted road construction already exists, according to Stelzenmüller.

"But by the time these findings are actually written into regulation and roads are routinely built with them — that's a process that will take years if not decades. I don't expect it can be implemented in the next two or three years," she added.

The heat-ready overhaul of the infrastructure could happen faster if the transport ministry and the road-construction authorities pushed the issue. That's what happened with the tightening of pollutant limits in the development of asphalt mixes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2025, Germany's transport ministry ordered that less-toxic surfaces be adopted "as quickly as possible," even before a new directive on the issue officially took effect.

"There was a real sense of urgency to meet those limits. And here it worked out [quickly], establishing new regulations within a few years," she said.

For road construction that is adapted to climate change and fit for the future, authorities need to take a similar approach, said Stelzenmüller.

"If you put a stronger focus on it, you could certainly have new types of asphalt within a few years," Stelzenmüller added.

By the time of publication, Germany's transport ministry had not responded to DW's request for comment.

This article was translated from German by Josh Axelrod.

https://www.dw.com/en/bernadette-amani-l.title: Bernadette Amani 'living her dream' at Bayern and WAFCON
https://www.dw.com/en/bernadette-amani-l.text:
Bernadette Amani joined Bayern Munich in January and is now captaining Ivory Coast in their first WAFCON in 12 years. Getting to the top hasn't been a straight path for the newly crowned German double winner.

Seven months after moving to Germany, Bernadette Amani is clearly where she wants to be, having won both the Bundesliga and the German Cup in her first half-season since joining Bayern Munich.

"It's a dream come true for me to be here, and I'm living my dream to the full," the 28-year-old midfielder told DW in an exclusive interview shortly before the Women's Africa Cup of Nations kicked off in Morocco this month.

"Munich is a very, very big club. Beyond just making me happy, it's a real achievement, a dream come true to be here, to play for such a prestigious club."

Amani added that playing for Bayern's women has been a major step up from what she had come to know playing for CD Tenerife Femenino of Liga F, Spain's topflight.

"I was already professional when I was in Spain, but let's just say it wasn't quite the same level of professionalism," she explained.

"In Spain or the Ivory Coast, the coaching staff might have consisted of no more than five or six people. But here there are eight or 10 people. And that enables them (the players) to perform at that high level for a long time."

This structure, and the experience of the players around her, she said, make it virtually impossible for a new player not to improve on their own game.

"I've learned a great deal about aspects I wasn't already aware of; how to position myself, how to position my body, how to interact with the ball and how to think. Really understanding the game is something I'm gradually learning alongside (the players) and the coaching staff."

Getting to the Bundesliga champions was anything but a straight, plotted path for Amani, who, when she began kicking a ball with the boys in her local village as a youngster, had no idea that football could be a career option.

Her parents were anything but encouraging of her passion. They just wanted their daughter to get a good education. To this end, she wound up moving from the village of Dougbafla, where she grew up, to the capital, Abidjan — a move that turned out to be pivotal to her career as a footballer.

"I discovered the women's football league. I went to a match and, as luck would have it, it was the top team against the second-placed team," she recalled.

"I saw the intensity, I saw the technique, and then I heard that so-and-so isn't here today because she's playing in Serbia, another isn't here today because she's playing in Turkey. And that was a real eye-opener for me; it made me realize that I could make a living from what I love."

One of the clubs she watched on that day in 2019, Onze Soeurs de Gagnoa, offered her a trial – and she made it. Within a year, she was in Spain's third tier, and five years later, she found herself in Liga F with Eibar. Always looking to take that next step, she quickly moved on to Tenerife, her launching pad for Bayern, which she describes as "the top." Still, there's no question of complacency.

"Someone on the outside will say to you: 'You've put in the effort, you've made it to Bayern, a club that wins titles, that's professional and renowned all over the world," she said.

"But someone who's involved in football will tell you that's where the hard part begins. Staying there is even better. And it's hard not to let your guard down."

For the next couple of weeks though, her focus will be on her role as captain of Ivory Coast at the Women's Africa Cup of Nations. WAFCON 2026, for which Ivory Coast were one of four late additions after the tournament was expanded from 12 to 16 teams at the last minute, marks the country's return to the continental competition after an absence of 12 years.

"The target that has been set for us is, of course, to do no worse than we did at the last Africa Cup of Nations we took part in — that is, to finish third," she said.

Amani noted that while Ivory Coast now have more players in top leagues in Europe than in 2014, almost half the squad will stand to make their first appearance at a WAFCON. Still, she appeared quietly optimistic.

"We're going to focus on our own game, and we know that we've got qualities that could give (our opponents) a run for their money," she said.

The Lady Elephants did more than that in Casablanca on Monday, cruising past Burkina Faso 4-1 in their opening match, putting them top of Group B. Their second match, on Friday against South Africa, ranked second on the continent, could provide Amani's side with a sterner test – despite South Africa having been upset 2-1 by lowly Tanzania in their opener.

Ali Farhat contributed to this article.

Edited by: Matt Pearson

https://www.dw.com/en/loneliness-influen.title: 'Loneliness influencers': Being alone brings in the clicks
https://www.dw.com/en/loneliness-influen.text:
No friends, no dating, no problem? Many influencers are presenting social isolation as a lifestyle. But experts warn of the consequences.

A young woman in business attire comes home, cuddles with her cat, cleans her high heels, takes a shower and settles down on the couch to watch TV in her pajamas with pizza and a soft drink. Afterward, she tidies up, takes out the trash ("no clutter in this apartment ever") and spends the rest of the evening on the sofa with her cat.

The title of the video: "POV: You live alone in NYC and have no friends so this is how you spend your Friday night." It has already raked in over 11 million views on Instagram.

This reel is the most successful clip to date by Paulina Cee, who boasts over 320,000 followers on Instagram.

Her account features numerous videos of this kind, always emphasizing her friend-free life.

And Paulina Cee is just one influencer amid a broader trend: Social media is full of young women presenting their solitude as a lifestyle. Sometimes they have a dog, sometimes one or two cats, but otherwise the videos share a similar aesthetic: an apartment so clean and so sparsely furnished, it verges on sterility.

One of the pioneers of this trend is Lana Isa from Toronto. Her videos bear such titles as "just an introvert in her natural habitat (home alone with yummy food)" or "what a weekend looks like as a friendless girl with NO interest in men or dating."

Lana Isa always ends her reels with the positive message, "Enjoy your life." She appears to be at peace with her largely solitary lifestyle. Apart from FaceTime calls with her mother and contact with her sister, her clips mainly revolve around consumption: usually unhealthy food, new clothes or movies.

The Canadian says her content has no purpose other than sharing her real life, which, according to her, has been shaped by generalized anxiety disorder and the loss of her relationship and all of her friendships several years ago.

It was never supposed to be just an 'aesthetic vlog,' or to romanticize having no friends. ... I just happened to start filming and show the current chapter of my life, which was the peace that came after I dealt with my feelings."

Mareike Ernst, an assistant professor of psychoanalytically-oriented psychotherapy research at the University of Klagenfurt, has mixed feelings about such reels.

Ernst, whose research focuses on psychotherapy and loneliness, says that on the one hand, it is positive when young women show that being alone, even in public, is good and normal: "That can help destigmatize it and provides a counterpoint to the content of many other influencers, who often portray almost constant social interaction."

On the other hand, young people in similar life situations might view these "loneliness influencers" as role models, "so that it becomes increasingly normalized to spend most of your time alone and convince yourself that 'this is perfectly fine.'"

Whether these loneliness influencers are all truly authentic is difficult to verify. What matters, however, is that many followers believe them and respond positively to the solitary lifestyle shown in the videos. The fact remains: Prolonged social isolation can make people ill. Studies show that it increases the risk of heart disease, mental illness and premature death.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

More and more young people are exposed to these risks. In a 2025 World Health Organization (WHO) study, between 17% and 21% of respondents aged 13 to 29 said they felt lonely, with the highest rates observed among teenagers. The WHO estimates that around one quarter of them are affected by social isolation. According to a Nivea study conducted in 13 countries, 24% of young people aged 16 to 24 feel socially isolated, compared with 19% across all age groups.

"Loneliness influencers" are almost exclusively women. Ernst suspects this has to do with gender stereotypes: Women are expected to build relationships and be there for others. This countertrend may therefore constitute a form of emancipation.

"Or perhaps it simply fits better with the female influencer aesthetic, which often focuses on self-care, cooking, tidying up and similar activities."

Because of this aesthetic, US psychotherapist Phil Lane recently addressed these influencers in an Instagram post. "Loneliness influencers, stop trying to make loneliness as an aesthetic happen; it is not going to happen. It is important that we are around our fellow human beings. It's one of our basic human needs."

Lane stressed that there is nothing wrong with spending time alone. "Sometimes, I really enjoy my own company, and I enjoy solitude, but we can't overapply this because it can have significant health risks."

So far, however, his message has gained little traction: His post has garnered only around 900 views.

This article was originally written in German.
https://www.dw.com/en/loneliness-influen.summary: Many influencers are presenting social isolation as a lifestyle. Experts warn of the consequences of the trend. One expert says it is positive when young women show that being alone, even in public, is good and normal.

https://www.dw.com/en/as-us-iran-war-rag.title: As US-Iran war rages, who's risking the Strait of Hormuz?
https://www.dw.com/en/as-us-iran-war-rag.text:
Though Iran continues to attack vessels as leverage in its war with the United States, data show that several shippers continue to transit the waterway.

The Strait of Hormuz has become one of the world's most dangerous waterways since March, when Iran began attacking shipping vessels as a pressure tactic in its ceasefire talks with the United States. Still, though a significant proportion of the global oil trade bottlenecks at the strait, shipping traffic never completely halted.

With the United States and Iran issuing conflicting statements as to whether the Strait of Hormuz is open, DW analyzed public data sources to track how shipping traffic has changed during the course of the war and which vessels are still taking the risk of transiting the maritime choke point, which connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman.

As Iran's strikes on and interception of vessels in the Strait of Hormuz continue, mines have also been reported in the prewar shipping lanes.

The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC), a project of the US-led Combined Maritime Forces, assesses the threat to shippers as "severe," its second-highest warning level. However, according to one of JMIC's latest advisory notes, issued after attacks resumed on July 6 and 7, "commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained at reduced levels, with vessels transiting via both the southern Omani corridor and the northern Iranian-controlled route."

JMIC added that shippers remained cautious of transiting the strait amid the attacks on vessels in recent weeks.

DW's analysis of data from the open-source platform Global Fishing Watch showed that, nevertheless, several shipping companies have navigated their vessels through the Strait of Hormuz throughout the war. Though the platform's primary purpose is to monitor fishing efforts, it also collects data on all other vessels using satellite imagery and relying on signals transmitted by ships' automatic identification systems (AIS).

As ships can switch off their AIS transponders — and have reportedly repeatedly chosen to while transiting the Strait of Hormuz — the number of vessels is likely higher than shown.

Based on AIS signals, a combined total of at least 84 ships crossed the Strait of Hormuz in two periods of the conflict: from the start of the war on February 28 until the announcement of a ceasefire on April 7 and following the renewed attacks on July 6 and 7. This aligns with reports of the United States saying it gave passage to about 70 ships and adding that not all of them transmitted signals.

For comparison: In the same periods of 2025, more than 900 ships crossed the strait.

Of these 84 ships, 34 moved from east to west into the Persian Gulf and 50 crossed the strait in the opposite direction, moving out of the gulf.

As part of the AIS signal, ships transmit which flag they are sailing under, but this information is entered manually aboard the vessels. In only a few cases investigated for this story did the flag reflect the actual country of origin of the registered owner or the ship manager of a vessel. This information can still be looked up manually in different databases using the ship's international ID number and its name.

Only nine Iranian- and two Pakistani-owned ships transited under their respective national flags. All of the other 73 ships hoisted a flag different from the vessel owner's country.

Analysis of this data shows that a wide variety of companies operating in the region continue to cross the Strait of Hormuz.

At the top of the list is the United Arab Emirates, which neighbors the strait. The UAE's Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline (ADCOP) runs overland parallel to the waterway in the south. 13 cargo ships registered in the United Arab Emirates transited the strait during the shutdown, as well as two liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) tankers and three support vessels.

Most of the UAE-based ship owners in the dataset appear to have only one to five vessels in their fleet. One of the UAE-registered vessels that was detected passing into the Persian Gulf on July 11 is managed by Lubeck Shipping LLC, a company associated with an Iranian oil tycoon that has been sanctioned by the United States.

Also sanctioned by the United States is Salina Ship Management PvT Ltd., a company from the Indian state of Maharashtra that US officials accuse of helping Iran move petrol. The company manages one of the four Indian oil and LPG tankers that Global Fishing Watch recorded transiting the strait.

India, like many Asian countries, is heavily reliant on the Strait of Hormuz for energy supply. China, Pakistan and Vietnam, too, had oil and LPG tankers in the Persian Gulf that they moved out of the Strait of Hormuz before a ceasefire was announced on April 7.

All seven vessels owned and managed by companies from Greece, the world's biggest shipping power, were freighters, typically carrying unpackaged dried goods such as iron, coal and grains.

The primary motive for continuing to move oil and other goods via the Strait of Hormuz despite the threat of attacks by Iran is financial — "simply because the reward seems higher than the risk," said Matt Smith, director of commodity research at Kpler, a business intelligence company headquartered in Belgium that specializes in analyzing global commodity flows.

"The key point is that producers of oil (or gas, aluminum, and other products) within the Strait of Hormuz essentially have only two options," economist David Wech wrote in an email. Wech monitors the flow of energy commodities such as oil and refined products for the British company Vortexa.

"Option 1: to halt production and earn no money at all — or even incur losses due to operating expenditures," Wech wrote. "And option 2: accept the risk of transiting the strait and thereby earn 90% or more of their normal revenue. With an oil price of currently more than $80 per barrel, we're talking about billions of USD."

With hostilities hot again as of July, the Brent Crude oil price is on yet another upward trend, perhaps one of the most perceivable global effects of the war and the near shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz.

In prewar times, roughly 25% of the global maritime oil trade passed through the Strait of Hormuz. Alternative routes have limited capacity to compensate for the loss of oil flow through the strait, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).

Two pipelines are currently used to bypass the Strait of Hormuz: the UAE's ADCOP and another in Saudi Arabia.

The ADCOP in the United Arab Emirates would allow ships to land and load in the northeastern port of Fujairah and transport oil out of the Persian Gulf without transiting the Strait of Hormuz.

The Abqaiq-Yanbu crude oil pipeline system (East-West Crude Pipeline or Petroline) in Saudi Arabia has some capacity left, the IEA reported in February. Publicly available shipping data for Yanbu show an increase in oil-related ship traffic from May through June, compared with previous years.

"Combined, Yanbu and Fujairah have been able to reroute over 4 million barrels a day of crude from having to pass through the Strait of Hormuz," Smith said. "This has been able to act as a release valve to keep barrels flowing to key customers in Asia — but only offsetting 4 of the total 15 million barrels per day that typically passes through the strait."

The alternative routes have their own risks. Reports are increasing of piracy and attacks on ships by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow choke point between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. "Bab al-Mandeb has the potential to add further supply woes to a global supply picture that is already severely constrained," Smith said.

So, the release valve to the Strait of Hormuz might soon become a maritime choke point of its own.

Edited by Milan Gagnon and Andreas Becker.

https://www.dw.com/en/german-chancellor-.title: German Chancellor Merz completes cabinet reshuffle
https://www.dw.com/en/german-chancellor-.text:
After days of confusion, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has reshuffled his cabinet. Conservative politicians fear that this will not help with the prospects in the upcoming state elections.

On Monday, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) was finally able to announce the name of the new Federal Minister of Transport in Berlin, following a weekend of speculation and debate. Steffen Bilger (CDU), aged 47 — who previously served as a state secretary in the transport ministry from 2018 to 2021 — is stepping up to lead the ministry.

The Chancellor had criticized the outgoing Transport Minister, Patrick Schnieder (CDU), for doing too little to address the chronic chaos and frequent delays plaguing the Deutsche Bahn railway system. Merz also faulted him for initiating too few projects to improve Germany's ailing infrastructure.

On Monday, Merz said he expected the new minister to ensure that "we become faster and better at driving a new era of progress in Germany."

Bilger's appointment marks the latest step in a cabinet reshuffle of the conservative wing of the government. This chain reaction of personnel changes was triggered by the resignation of Jens Spahn — the powerful leader of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group in the Bundestag — who was forced to step down following allegations of hypocrisy over his decision to have a child via surrogacy in the United States, circumventing German law and in violation of his party's principles.

Thorsten Frei, previously the head of the chancellery, is now set to become the new leader of the conservative parliamentary group on Wednesday, which involves the CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU). The 208 CDU and CSU lawmakers must cut their summer holidays short to vote on this appointment.

The 52-year-old Frei, currently serving as head of the chancellery and considered a close confidant of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is now set to take over one of the most important positions in German politics. His task will be to explain his party's positions in speeches in the Bundestag and interviews with the media. Above all, he will have to secure majorities for the government's policies and negotiate with the conservatives' coalition partner, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD).

Merz has a reputation for trusting only men within his inner circle. Now, 47-year-old Nina Warken — a politician from the wealthy southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg — is taking over from Frei and will manage the chancellery and be responsible for aligning the government's overall policy agenda.

Warken is a member of the women's organization of the Christian Democratic Union. As health minister, she had recently pushed through a cost-cutting program for statutory health insurance funds.

The chancellor considers Warken to be assertive and well-versed in security policy issues — an important quality, given that the head of the chancellery also coordinates oversight of Germany's intelligence agencies.

With Warken now leaving the health portfolio, Carsten Linnemann — previously the CDU general secretary — is set to take over.

Pundits argue that the chancellor certainly has a clear vision of how Linnemann should lead the department. Until now, Linnemann has been known primarily as an economics expert — a background that Friedrich Merz believes will serve him well in the new role: "Carsten Linnemann is taking over a ministry that represents the fastest-growing sector of our economy. The entire sector — which, unfortunately, we all too often view merely as a cost factor — is a vital part of our social fabric."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The incumbent CDU treasurer and Bundestag lawmaker Franziska Hoppermann will take over as party general secretary.* She is thus stepping up to take on one of the party's most high-profile roles.

Approval of the government's performance is at an all-time low. State elections are scheduled for September in three eastern states where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to see significant gains.

It is against this backdrop that Merz is demonstrating decisiveness.

"I assume that things will have calmed down somewhat by September," Merz said.

Sven Schulze (CDU), a minister in the Saxony-Anhalt state government, takes a very different view. Speaking to public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk on Monday, Schulze said the past few days had dominated political discussions and "not exactly gone well."

He added that it was almost impossible to focus on state-level issues during door-to-door campaigning in his state.

This article was translated from German.

*An earlier version of this article mistakenly stated that Franziska Hoppermann would be the first woman to take over the post as CDU general secretary. There have, in fact, been two before her: Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer and Angela Merkel.

The new Transport Minister, Steffen Bilger, is stepping up to lead the ministry. Merz had criticized the outgoing Transport Minister for doing too little to address the chronic chaos and frequent delays plaguing the Deutsche Bahn railway system.

https://www.dw.com/en/jürgen-klopp-and-g.title: Jürgen Klopp and Germany: A partnership long in the making
https://www.dw.com/en/jürgen-klopp-and-g.text:
In one of the worst-kept secrets in football, the former Dortmund and Liverpool boss has been named head coach of the German men's national team.

Jürgen Klopp had long been the overwhelming favorite to become the new head coach of Germany's national football team. On Friday, the German Football Association (DFB) made his appointment official.

DFB President Bernd Neuendorf announced at a press conference in Frankfurt that Klopp had signed a contract that would see him remain Germany coach through the 2030 World Cup. He is to officially take up the post on August 15.

"It is a great honor to sit here," Klopp said. "I had an idea how big the job is, but when you are directly involved, you feel the responsibility even more. It is a very special day for me."

At the same time, the new Germany coach, who often appears light-hearted in public, appeared to issue a stern warning to the gathered reporters.

"On the day you don't want me anymore, tell me and I'm gone," he said. "If you misbehave and don't leave my family alone, I'm gone."

Rudi Völler stays on as sporting director, but there are changes to the coaching staff. Two former Klopp colleagues in Peter Krawietz, who was Klopp's assistant manager at Borussia Dortmund and Liverpool, and Pep Lijnders, who was with Klopp at Liverpool, have joined the 59-year-old head coach. Former Bundesliga player and Germany international Sven Bender is also part of the staff.

Unsusual is that Klopp's agent, Marc Kosicke, has been handed a position in the new Germany set-up. The 55-year-old is to be responsible "for strategy, development and innovation." Klopp said he needed his close confidant because although playing good football is the priority, "we must also change lots of other things. We need people who can do this alongside me."

Technically, Kosicke will be an "an external consultant," not a DFB employee.

Former Germany defender Per Mertesacker, who spent eight years running Arsenal's youth academy, is to succeed Andreas Rettig as the DFB's managing director for sport in January. Rettig had previously announced that he would be stepping down at the end of the year.

For years, the charismatic Klopp had been seen as the ideal candidate. In recent weeks, he had been the boss-in-waiting, following Julian Nagelsmann's departure after Germany's disappointing performance at this summer's World Cup in North America.

This was the third consecutive World Cup that has ended in disappointment for Germany, with two group-stage exits and the knockout defeat to Paraguay in the round of 32 on June 29. Euro 2024 was more positive, but generally Germany have not enjoyed a successful tournament since Euro 2016. For a four-time World Cup winner and a three-time European champion, a decade-long span of disappointment sits far below expectation.

Klopp's approach to the Germany job has been a long time coming. Even as far back as late October 2024 when he took the job as "Head of Global Soccer" for Red Bull, there were reports that either his contract included a clause allowing him to become Germany head coach in the future or he had a gentleman's agreement to do the same.

And during this summer's World Cup, his role as a pundit for MagentaTV seems to have moved him ever closer to the job. His analysis was seen as on point, but Klopp caused a stir when he said, "Luckily, it's Julian Nagelsmann who's picking the team. For now." Those two words hung over Nagelsmann, and even though Klopp apologized, it almost felt like he knew his time was fast approaching.

After the loss to Paraguay, Klopp continued to distance himself from the job, saying it wasn't time to talk about that.

"When the next tournament comes around and whoever is head coach is asked, what is your goal? If they don't say 'European champion,' then people will say, 'Have you got no ambition? We are Germany!' No, we were football Germany. In order to become that force again, we've really got to give it our all," Klopp said on MagentaTV.

Klopp had been providing "strategic vision and support" as well as helping "coaches develop" in his job at Red Bull. However, his role in the dismissal of RB Leipzig head coach Ole Werner after just one season has been seen critically in the media. Werner guided RB Leipzig to third place in the Bundesliga and returned the club to the Champions League.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

His success in the dugout combined with his warm, funny character has made him a fan favorite in most places in Germany. After playing in Mainz, he guided the club to the Bundesliga for the first time. His departure was emotional, as both Klopp and many of the crowd shed tears.

At Borussia Dortmund, he won back-to-back Bundesliga titles, and took the club to the Champions League final in 2013. More recently, he spent nine years with Liverpool, where he delivered a first league title in more than a quarter of a century, as well as glory in the 2019 Champions League final. He has a history of leading clubs with strong working-class roots to success, allowing him to maintain a bond to the core values of the clubs in question. In combination with his holistic style of coaching, Klopp is seen as one of the best coaches in the world.

During his break from coaching, Klopp was awarded the highest civic award in Germany as a result of his outstanding contribution to democracy and his impact on the football world. He was credited with becoming a role model, a football ambassador and someone who has improved the image of Germany around the world, particularly  in the United Kingdom.

Recently, his face has been hard to miss. Famous for being in a raft of adverts, Klopp has cemented his status as one of the most famous Germans rather than just a great football coach from Germany.

With Euro 2028 in the United Kingdom and Ireland, Klopp will be familiar with many of the stadiums and the way football works in the country. He will have a long run-up at the title, though.

His first game in charge of Germany will be in Amsterdam on September 24 against the Netherlands in the Nations League. This will mark the start of a new format of international break. Unlike in previous years where there have three two-week international breaks in September, October and November, the 2026-27 season will see September and October's breaks merge into one. November's will be the same.

This means Klopp's first time in charge of the team would be for a three-week break in late September, which will see Germany play Greece in Augsburg three days after the Amsterdam game. Four days after that, Germany will play Serbia in Munich before closing out the international break in Thessaloniki against Greece on October 4. This longer break will offer Klopp a chance to hit the ground running and generate a real clarity over his playing style and who the core of his Germany team will be.

With Klopp in charge, there will be no stopping Germany fans daydreaming of what their team will look like in the not-too-distant future. Heavy metal football, as Klopp once famously described his style of play, might well be on the way for a team that is currently out of tune.

This article was originally published on July 3, 2026. It was updated on July 24, 2026 with the official announcement of Jürgen Klopp's appointment as Germany coach.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

Former Dortmund and Liverpool boss has been the overwhelming favorite to become the new head manager. Former Germany defender Per Mertesacker is to succeed Andreas Rettig as the DFB's managing director for Jürger Klopp.

https://www.dw.com/en/are-german-compani.title: Are German companies leaving the country?
https://www.dw.com/en/are-german-compani.text:
Should I stay or should I go? Given Germany's high cost and sluggish growth, some business leaders are mulling relocating, or at least investing abroad. DW has a look at the numbers.

German companies are continuing to move abroad — and that applies to businesses of every size. According to press reports, Gardena, the Ulm-based garden tools specialist, plans to cut 250 jobs in Germanyand partially relocate operations to the Czech Republic. That amounts to a reduction of 10% of its domestic workforce.

Major global players such as BASF are also continuing to invest abroad. Earlier this year, it become known that the chemical company intends to relocate service positions to India, with many jobs at its Berlin site coming under particular pressure.

Last year, the situation was described in even more dramatic terms.

"Germany's industrial crisis is running at full speed," wrote the online magazine Finanzmarktwelt in November, citing figures from the Federal Statistical Office from 2018 to 2023. More recent figures have yet to be published by the office.

According to the data, around 1,300 German companies with more than 50 employees relocated business functions abroad between 2021 and 2023. That's equivalent to 2.2% of all companies of that size based in Germany in 2023.

These relocations are said to have cost approximately 50,800 domestic jobs. Many feared this trend would continue or even accelerate, given Germany's high energy and labor costs.

However, Germany's state-owned development bank KfW is already observing a different trend. In June, its research department announced that: "Many medium-sized companies are withdrawing from international business." According to the bank's findings, the number of German medium-sized companies who were active abroad dropped from around 880,000 in 2022 to some 760,000 a year later.

"The general conditions for foreign trade have deteriorated significantly," said Dirk Schumacher, KfW's chief economist, attributing this to "geopolitical tensions in Ukraine and the Middle East, growing export competition from China in key industries and the protectionist trade policy of the United States."

A rather different picture is painted by the Association of German Chambers of Commerce and Industry (DIHK).

Referring to its business climate survey from early 2026, DIHK spokesman Sven Ehling said cost pressures on German industry had reached a record high, prompting many companies to plan greater investments abroad.

According to DIHK, 43% of industrial companies are planning foreign investments this year, three percentage points higher than the previous year. "The reasons are clear: rising costs, structural problems and weak economic conditions in Germany as a business location," said DIHK's head of international trade, Volker Treier.

In the past, foreign investment tended to strengthen domestic operations, leading to greater employment at home. This was particularly true of investments aimed at opening new markets or expanding sales and customer service. However, the share of German companies investing abroad primarily for market development is falling, according to the DIHK survey, from 30% to 28%.

"Companies are now being forced to invest abroad primarily for cost reasons. This frequently leads to significant cutbacks at domestic sites," said Treier. Foreign investment is now helping to cut costs, rather than drive expansion.

Overall, the trend in foreign investment is far from clear-cut. The current situation resembles more of a sideways move. According to Professor Steffen Müller of the Leibniz Institute for Economic Research Halle (IWH), direct investments abroad by German companies are "well below peak levels."

The Bundesbank statistics, Müller told DW, show annual transaction values of €120 billion between 2017 and 2022. By contrast, the figures for 2024 stand at €80 billion, and for 2025 at under €100 billion. These numbers give "little reason to assume that significantly more capital is flowing out than in previous years."

The survey reveals significant shifts in the target regions for German foreign investment. North America in particular is losing appeal, with the share of German companies planning investments there falling from 48% to 44%.

At the same time, engagement in Asia is growing. According to the DIHK, the share of industrial companies investing in China is rising from 31% to 34%. The Asia-Pacific region (excluding China) is also gaining in importance, growing from 21% to 26%.

"The tariff dispute with the United States is fueling uncertainty and causing companies to postpone decisions," said Treier.

With 64%, the eurozone remains the most important region for German companies to invest in. Stability, the common single market and the shared currency offer reliable framework conditions — a particularly important factor in investment decisions during times of geopolitical uncertainty, the DIHK representative noted.

This piece was originally published in German.

The number of German medium-sized companies who were active abroad dropped from 880,000 in 2022 to some 760,000 a year later.

https://www.dw.com/en/california-s-large.title: California's largest lake is turning to dust
https://www.dw.com/en/california-s-large.text:
The Salton Sea is drying up, worsening air pollution for nearby communities. Officials are racing to contain it, but for some families, it's already too late.

Michelle Dugan-Delgado has had asthma for as long as she can remember. It's why she always takes an inhaler and face mask with her when she leaves the house — just in case the wind picks up and a dust storm hits.

"I know that it's not safe for me to go outside,” she told DW. "It's like I live in a bubble. I have to really protect myself.”

If dust enters her lungs, it could trigger an asthma attack. Invisible bacteria, fungal spores and viruses carried by dust could also cause a life-threatening infection.

"If I'm outside and a dust storm hits, there's a very high chance I'm going to catch something, which means I will end up in the hospital," the 35-year-old said.

Dugan-Delgado knows the dangers well enough. She's been hospitalized multiple times. Asthma has also taken a deadly toll on her family. In 2009, her younger sister Marie died of an asthma attack at the age of 16.

"It wasn't anything that we thought would take her life away," she said. "It's painful to talk about it because I have a lot of survivor's guilt."

Dugan-Delgado lives in the Coachella Valley, an agricultural hub in California's far south that's surrounded by desert. She believes the poor air quality there is to blame for making her and Marie sick.

Dust storms are common in the region, which is home to around 500,000 people.

A major source of that dust is a huge lake that's steadily drying up. Spanning some 343 square miles (888 square kilometers), the Salton Sea is California's largest lake. But it's rapidly shrinking. When winds sweep over the exposed lakebed, they pick up the parched sediment, producing harmful dust storms.

Children living near the lake have been found to have disproportionately high rates of asthma. One study that followed more than 700 primary-school aged children over a number of years found that 24% reported having the condition — far higher than the national rate of about 7% for boys and 5.5% for girls. Over 70% had allergies — more than three times the national average.

"The majority of families that I know will have at least one child with respiratory illnesses," said Dugan-Delgado. "That's really heartbreaking."

Her own 13-year-old daughter has asthma, and her 11-year-old son has allergies.

The Salton Sea was formed by accident in 1905 when the Colorado River burst an irrigation canal gate and flooded the area. Since then, the waterbody has been maintained by continuous agricultural runoff, irrigation wastewaters and local rivers.

It became a popular holiday spot in the 1950s, with trendy lakeside resorts drawing tourists and celebrities. But then the water levels started to drop, partly due to a hotter climate and policies that diverted water away. In the last 30 years, the lake has shrunk by around 20%, or 70 square miles.

The exposed lakebed holds more than just dust, though. Pesticides and other toxic chemicals from farms are also left behind to be picked up by the wind, only worsening air quality in the region.

Climate change driven by the continued burning of fossil fuels is leading to hotter temperatures and prolonged drought that's making desert regions around the world more arid. That makes it considerably harder for plants to grow and stresses water resources, according to Amato Evan, a professor of climate science at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California, San Diego.

"Dust storms are definitely becoming more frequent over time," he said.

Globally, at least a quarter of the dust in the air comes from human activities, including off-roading, deforestation, and unsustainable agricultural practices like tilling and overgrazing.

Lakes that are drying up are also major producers of dust — from California's Salton Sea to Iran's Lake Urmia. The shrinking Aral Sea, for instance, has made Central Asia 7% dustier over the last 30 years.

More than half of the world's dust emissions come from the Sahara Desert in North Africa. If the wind is strong enough, that dust can rise up to 5 miles into the sky and travel over vast distances — across the Atlantic toward the Americas, or over the Mediterranean to Europe.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The World Meteorological Organization says sand and dust storms impact about 330 million people every year. They can engulf entire cities, ground flights, decimate crops and cause deadly traffic accidents.

And then there's the toll on human health.

"This is the number one adverse impact: it's humans breathing in dust," Evan says.

Dust particulate matter can get lodged deep in the lungs and is linked to serious respiratory illnesses and heart disease. It accounts for about 721,000 deaths worldwide each year, with children, the elderly and people with lung conditions most at risk.

Dugan-Delgado says her lungs are continuing to deteriorate. Meanwhile, the Salton Sea is predicted to continue shrinking.

State and local authorities have launched a series of projects as part of a plan to restore 30,000 acres of the lake's dusty shoreline by 2028. Thousands of hay bales have been laid out along the shore to hold down dust. They've also planted native vegetation in an attempt to stabilize the soil and pumped in water to make artificial wetlands for wildlife.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Evan says initiatives such as planting native vegetation can work well at some sites to combat desertification. But he points out that it needs a lot of investment, water, and time.

"All of those things are resources that are not in infinite supply," he says. He and his team are currently developing an early warning system to alert communities when a dust storm is approaching.

"Just like you get a weather forecast, you should be able to get a forecast for dust," he says.

Dugan-Delgado says she'd welcome a warning system for dust storms. She'd also like to see more attempts to raise awareness about the risks of living with dust pollution, so that others know how to protect themselves and their kids.

"I think families need more education about the respiratory illnesses here in the valley and what it could do to your health," she said. "One death is too many and we just got to find a way to stop that."

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

This article was adapted from a DW Living Planet podcast. To listen to the full episode, click here.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yw.title: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yw.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no military pull-out will happen until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.

Trump's Board of Peace said last month it had reached an agreement for the "complete disarmament" of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.

But Hamas said handing over its heavy weapons was contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.

Israel has continued to carry out strikes on Gaza since agreeing to an initial ceasefire in the territory last October.

"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday.

The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens", he added.

A Hamas official told the BBC on Sunday the group "reaffirms it commitment" to the agreement and it was ready "to engage seriously and responsibly in implementing" the 15-point plan.

They called on mediators to ensure "that all parties comply with what has been agreed".

Netanyahu's statement does not come as a surprise.

But he has taken some time to make it, perhaps reflecting the difficult position the Israeli leader is in.

He clearly is unhappy with Trump's plan but at the same time he will not want to upset his closest ally.

It's just over a week since Trump announced what he called a "monumental step toward lasting peace and security" - that Hamas for the first time had agreed to disarm, on condition that Israel withdraws its forces from Gaza.

On Sunday, Netanyahu was clear that was not going to happen under his watch. He said Hamas had to disarm first, adding that it couldn't be some "fictitious disarmament" - it had to be real.

The reality is any disarmament and withdrawal of Israeli forces would likely need need to be phased.

Netanyahu said he was now in discussion with US officials about how to go forward.

"They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," he said.

But just months before Israeli elections and under pressure from members of his right-wing coalition to take a tough stance on Gaza, he is unlikely to want to make concessions.

He has faced calls from his far-right allies to hold a new cabinet vote and end the Gaza plan, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir who dismissed the draft as "not acceptable".

It signals another blow for Trump's Gaza peace plan which was announced in September last year.

The plan included the creation of the Board of Peace to oversee the agreement's implementation, as well as the disarmament of Hamas, withdrawal of Israeli troops and reconstruction of Gaza.

According to the UN, about 1.9 million people - 90% of Gaza's population - have been displaced in the territory since the war in Gaza started.

The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Israel responded to the attack by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
