The US must pressure Israel to accept the next phase of the Gaza plan, a Hamas official told AFP, after Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he rejected the US-backed agreement.

“We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons,” Hamas political bureau member Bassem Naim told AFP.

Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian met the country’s supreme ⁠leader Mojtaba Khamenei around the start of the president’s third year in office in late July, state ⁠media said on Sunday, ⁠and ​a paramilitary leader promised footage of Khamenei in the future, Reuters reports.

Pezeshkian has given differing accounts in recent ⁠weeks about his access to Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since he succeeded his father in the ⁠role in March.

On 21 July, the president said interactions with ​the supreme leader were “increasing day by ‌day”, but in ‌early August he said communicating with Khamenei was “very difficult”.

The late July ‌meeting covered military affairs and the economy, including securing resources, managing foreign exchange and energy use, as well as economic ties with foreign partners, according to state media.

Khamenei was reportedly seriously injured in the ​February strike that killed his father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei on the first day of the US-Israeli war on Iran. The promise to release footage of the leader by paramilitary Basij ⁠Organisation deputy Qasem Qoraishi appeared to be aimed ​at quashing speculation about his health. Senior Iranian sources have said he suffered ⁠facial disfigurement and other injuries ​in the ​strike.

Attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen killed at least four troops from the internationally-recognised government forces and injured 20 more personnel, two military sources told AFP.

The initial toll came from strikes on the Yemeni city of Mokha and surrounding areas, as well as Khokha, south of the port city of Hodeida, the sources said on condition of anonymity, after the Houthis announced they had targeted military forces and equipment on the Red Sea coast.

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected a Gaza plan hailed by US president Donald Trump, vowing no military pullout of Gaza until Hamas is “genuinely” disarmed.

“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said, referring to a plan endorsed in late July by Hamas.

The Israeli military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens,” Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting, Reuters reports.

The document, the latest stage in a US-led ceasefire announced in October that has reduced but not ended Israeli operations in Gaza, said Hamas would surrender weapons to a nascent Palestinian governing body.

The plan said Israel would begin pulling out forces in tandem with the disarmament, an idea adamantly rejected by Israel which also wants Hamas to destroy its weapons.

Netanyahu said that Israel was speaking with the US about its objections. “They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters,” he said.

Netanyahu said that Hamas must give up all of its weapons, a goal that Board of Peace members say is not realistically achievable. “We are talking about real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament,” Netanyahu said.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corp said they will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the United States meets Tehran’s conditions, including compensation for war damages.

The IRGC said their strategy was to maintain the closure “until the enemy accepts all our conditions ... the strait is now actually a theatre of war for us and not just a waterway”.

Iran’s security chief Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr on Saturday laid out a list of demands for reopening the strait, including an end to the “war and aggression against Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen and Iraq”.

He also demanded the lifting of a US counterblockade of Iranian ports, the end of sanctions, the release of frozen assets and compensation for wartime damage, according to remarks reported by the Tasnim news agency.

Iran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait since the US and Israel attacked in late February, and wants to charge tolls for passage, striking ships it accuses of attempting to circumvent its preferred route.

Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said discussions with Oman over transit and management of the strait were “approaching the final stages”, but added that the reopening of Hormuz “is subject to other conditions and compensation for the violation” of an interim June agreement with the US.

Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian has said he believes now is the best time for an agreement with the US. “There is cohesion, strength, and unity in the country, and as far as I know, Iran is considered victorious and powerful in this war,” Iranian news agencies quoted him as saying.

Oman condemned what it described as repeated attacks on vessels while transiting the strait, without assigning blame, and said that ​negotiations with Iran on arrangements for shipping through Hormuz were “positive and constructive”.

The UAE said on Saturday that Iran had attacked a carrier affiliated with the UAE’s state oil company with a missile as it transited the strait of Hormuz. No injuries were reported. The UK maritime trade monitor UKMTO said a ‌vessel had caught fire after being hit by an unknown projectile but the fire was put out and there was no reported environmental impact. There was no immediate comment from Iranian authorities.

US Central Command said on Saturday it had allowed more than 30 ships through for humanitarian aid since the current blockade started. US forces have turned away 53 ships, disabled two vessels and boarded two others, Central Command said in a statement on social media.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Guardian staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Drone strike comes after Riyadh signs defence pact and Iran issues tough demands to reopen strait of Hormuz

Middle East crisis live – latest updates

Yemen’s Tehran-aligned Houthis have claimed responsibility for an attack on a refinery in Saudi Arabia, two days after the kingdom signed ⁠a defence pact with Turkey ⁠and Pakistan in response to ​growing regional instability caused by the US-Israel war on Iran.

The attack early on Sunday came after Iran issued tough new demands to reopen the strait of Hormuz, and the United Arab Emirates said one of its ships had been targeted by an Iranian missile, as a deal to open the strategic waterway remained out of reach.

Iran’s supreme national security council said the strait would not open until the US corrected its “behaviour”. The US must never threaten Iran again and permanently end the war with Tehran and its armed allies in the region, said the statement from the council’s secretary, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, a former commander in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

He added that the US must also end the naval blockade of Iranian ports and withdraw its military from the area, “completely compensate” Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and “unconditionally” release frozen assets.

There was no immediate comment from the US. According to the memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed by the US and Iran in June, a timetable to end sanctions and a plan for compensation would be part of a final peace deal, and negotiations would address frozen assets.

The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said on Saturday that Iran and Oman were close to reaching an agreement on navigation through the strait of Hormuz, “specifically the determination of a transit route”. But the waterway’s reopening was contingent on other conditions, Araghchi said, in remarks shared on social media. He blamed the situation on what he called the US violation of the June MoU.

Oman, which is mediating and has made relatively few comments on the Hormuz talks, said on Saturday that the discussions were continuing “in a positive and constructive atmosphere”. It condemned attacks on ships in the strait.

With Iran and the US still arguing over the parameters for peace, the Houthis last month declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, citing what they said was a Saudi siege on them, an allegation Riyadh denies.

The Saudi energy ministry said a fire had broken out at Aramco’s Jazan refinery early on Sunday but was later extinguished with no injuries and authorities were dealing with the ⁠incident, without giving a cause.

The Houthis used a drone to target the refinery in south-west Saudi Arabia, Yahya Saree, a military spokesperson for the rebel group, said in a post on X. They had struck Aramco sites before in ​Jazan, which processes 400,000 barrels of crude oil a day. They had also hit Yanbu, an oil export hub ‌on the Red Sea.

In a separate statement, Saree said the Houthis had carried out missile and drone strikes on the Yemeni Red Sea port city of Mocha, which is controlled by the country’s internationally recognised, Saudi-backed governing body in Aden.

Tehran and its allied Shia armed groups have been striking Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states and blockading their ‌energy shipments since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on 28 February.

The escalation of the conflict, which has disrupted global energy supplies and rattled the world’s economy, prompted Saudi Arabia on Friday to form an alliance with US allies Turkey and Pakistan.

The accord is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three would be regarded as ⁠an attack on all.

The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, said the alliance was not directed against Iran or ​any other country, but rather served as a general ​pledge to support the security of Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. It was ​not clear whether or how either Pakistan or Turkey would join in any Saudi response to the latest attacks.

Saudi energy ministry says fire broke out at Aramco's Jazan refinery early on Sunday. Iran issues tough demands to reopen strait of Hormuz, and the United Arab Emirates says one of its ships had been targeted by an Iranian missile.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: A pretty penny: three Banksy artworks cost taxpayers £150,000 in upkeep
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
Shadow justice secretary says artist should foot bill, while others say his murals make art accessible

Three Banksy artworks have cost taxpayers almost £150,000 in cleaning, security and other costs, with the bill expected to rise.

The largest bill relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in London in September 2025, where efforts to remove it and provide security have so far cost more than £85,000, according to the BBC.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The mural depicted a judge in a wig beating a protester with his gavel. Banksy confirmed the work was his by posting an image on his website and Instagram account.

The Ministry of Justice told the BBC, after a freedom of information request, that £50,000 had been spent trying to remove the paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building on Carey Street. A further £35,000 had been spent on overtime and security.

“The Royal Courts of Justice is a listed building and HMCTS are obliged to maintain its original character,” the HM Courts and Tribunals Service said.

The costs have reignited a debate over whether Banksy’s work constitutes vandalism or valuable public art, particularly when it appears on historic buildings. The artist, who emerged from Bristol’s graffiti scene in the 1990s, is one of the world’s most famous street artists. His work has sold at auction for upwards of £18m.

The shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, said it was “outrageous” that taxpayers’ money was being spent cleaning up after the artist. “Our courts are a national symbol of justice and the rule of law,” he said. “Banksy’s vandalism should be stopped and he should foot the bill for the costs he imposes on others.”

But the art critic Estelle Lovatt defended Banksy’s work and highlighted the benefits for tourism. “Some people visit Buckingham Palace and others visit Banksy’s art,” she told the BBC. “His work brings people together in a way that politics can divide us. He’s like the Pied Piper or a town crier.

“It can be intimidating if a mural appears on your building, in terms of the crowds, but he makes art accessible because there’s no gallery fee.”

Initial attempts to remove the mural were unsuccessful and contractors have since been using laser technology. If Westminster city council considers the result inadequate, another cleaning method will be required. As a final option, the affected stonework could be removed and replaced.

A listed building consent application has also been submitted for railings to be installed across the wall where the mural appeared. The cost of the installation is not yet known.

Another Banksy work has generated almost £60,000 in costs for Westminster city council.

A statue of a man carrying a flag appeared in Waterloo Place, near Trafalgar Square, in April. Banksy claimed responsibility by posting a video of the overnight installation on Instagram.

The council said it had spent almost £60,000 on safety barriers, administration and a security guard to monitor the statue.

“Ownership of the statue now sits with the council as landowner,” it said. “The council has notified the artist’s agent that it is reviewing options for the short, medium and long term.”

In August 2024, a third Banksy work appeared on a City of London police sentry box. The artist painted a shoal of piranha fish over the box, which had been installed in the 1990s as part of security measures against the IRA.

The box was subsequently removed at a cost of £2,200 and was never replaced. It is due to go on display at the London Museum when it reopens in November.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Most X accounts posting about Belfast and Southampton unrest were based outside UK
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Carmen Aguilar García, Michael Goodier, Pamela Duncan and Dan Sabbagh
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Exclusive: Analysis shows 55% of accounts were located overseas – and seven of 12 most-read posts came from US

More than half the accounts that posted on Elon Musk’s X about the rioting in Belfast and the civil disorder in Southampton in June were based outside the UK, an analysis by the Guardian can reveal.

Of the 8,672 accounts whose combined posts about the events exceeded 1,000 views, just 45.3% were shown as from the UK, according to the social media platform’s own location function.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

One in six (16.8%) came from the US, 4.5% from Ireland, and about a quarter from all European countries other than the UK.

Seven of the 12 most-read tweets about Belfast and Southampton came from the US – including one from Musk himself and two other US “alt-right” commentators – while an eighth was linked to North America.

The analysis underlines that US rightwing actors are seeking to influence the UK and boost their position on X in moments of disorder – an exploitation of flashpoint events that has only intermittently attracted political attention in Britain.

The Guardian collected 43,000 tweets mentioning Belfast, Southampton, Henry Nowak or Vickrum Digwa posted on X during the period of the unrest in both cities.

This covered the period from 2 June to the end of 3 June for Southampton and from the evening of 8 June to the end of 9 June for Belfast.

For X accounts whose combined tweets reached more than 1,000 views, we extracted their location and the number of times they have changed their username as shown in the “about this account” tab.

Using a large language model (LLM), the team first classified which posts were directly related to the protests in Belfast and Southampton, and then categorised them as containing explicit or implicit racist language or anti-immigration comments. For those about Belfast, we also classified tweets as containing calls inciting to violence.

A team of three people manually verified more than 5,500 posts, statistically testing the accuracy of the model to be robust and in line with academic standards.

Nearly a third of all 43,000 posts on X relating to the two incidents contained racist or anti-immigration comments. Almost one in 10 relating to Belfast contained calls for violence or paramilitary or vigilante action.

Imran Ahmed, the chief executive of the Centre for Countering Digital Hate, said the data demonstrated that X had become “a weapon of choice” for hostile foreign actors seeking to manipulate shocking and divisive content.

Their goal, he added, was “to amplify local tragedies and crises, intensify racist narratives, and incite violence in communities they have never set foot in and to whom they have no real connection.”

A post from Musk after the life sentencing of the killer of 18-year-old Henry Nowak, who had been falsely accused of racism by police after being stabbed in Southampton, has been viewed more than 28m times.

“Legacy mainstream media, same ones who wrote about George Floyd millions of times, are dead silent about Nowak,” Musk posted shortly before 3pm on 2 June, in effect promoting his own platform at a time of heightened tension and disorder in the Hampshire port.

Eleven police officers were injured on the night of 2 June in Southampton as people claiming to protest over Nowak’s murder marched to the site of his death. This followed a rally, addressed by the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, outside the city’s main police station.

Musk is based in the US and has not visited the UK since November 2023. A Guardian analysis last month found he posted about race and immigration in the UK twice as often as he did about SpaceX in the run-up to the aerospace company’s initial public offering in June.

Security experts including Fiona Hill, a former adviser to the US and UK governments, have warned that the UK is a soft target for online manipulation by overseas actors because it does not take the idea of civil, or “psychological”, defence seriously.

Dr Julia Ebner, a researcher at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue and the University of Oxford, said flashpoint episodes such as in Southampton and Belfast had become “strategic events” for far-right actors seeking to amplify and exploit them.

“They are using the UK as a negative example, smearing the UK to promote their own narratives of western civilisational decay or social collapse,” Ebner said. “But the other purpose is to influence UK politics, and European politics more widely,” using crisis moments to “promote a strong, strengthened far-right wave across the world”.

Four of the top 12 most-seen tweets came from UK accounts: two were by the leader of the Restore Britain party, Rupert Lowe, whom Musk has endorsed; another was from GB News, while the most popular, with 37.6m views, was written by the “anti-woke” rightwing political commentator Konstantin Kisin.

Other accounts located in the US were anonymous, though familiar. @EndWokeness posted a blurry still image of a black man attacking a white man in Belfast on 8 June, saying the full video was “too graphic” to post. It attracted 16.3m views.

The assault, a stabbing in which the victim, Stephen Ogilvie, lost an eye, prompted three nights of racially motivated rioting targeting non-white people in Belfast. An asylum seeker from Sudan was charged with attempted murder and at least 23 people were arrested.

The @EndWokeness account, which has 3.9m followers, was cited by a parliamentary committee after it amplified a false claim that the 2024 attack in Southport, in which three girls were killed, was carried out by a Muslim man.

The account has been linked by an open source analyst to Jack Posobiec, a rightwing influencer who promoted the Pizzagate conspiracy, a false accusation that leading US Democrats were engaged in satanic child abuse at a child-friendly pizza restaurant in Washington DC.

Another leading poster was the US rightwing influencer Benny Johnson, who accused the New York Times of writing nothing about Nowak and thousands of pieces about the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020 – though Nowak was murdered in the UK.

The analysis of the most-viewed accounts did not reveal any posts from Russia or China – both countries that have been behind online disinformation campaigns – though it is possible that posters successfully disguised their locations using virtual private networks (VPNs).

X shows location data for most profiles, inferred by the platform from user IP addresses, though government accounts are excluded. Last November, after the feature was introduced, X’s then head of product, Nikita Bier, said it was more than 99% accurate. When it was launched, it revealed that some pro-Scottish-independence accounts were based in Iran.

But there were signs of inauthenticity in popular posts. Two of the top most-seen tweets came from the US-based C3 (@C_3C_3) account, accusing “legacy media” of not reporting about the Nowak case. Its profile picture is a baby wearing a Make America Great Again cap; the username has changed 14 times previously.

One UK account, which tweeted at least six times about the murder of Nowak, with almost 3,800 combined views, had changed its name more than 400 times. NewsSceneUK – subsequently changed to BritifyFooty – wrote in one tweet about the “huge crowd of patriots outside #Southampton Police Station”.

Accounts posting from overseas that changed their usernames more than 20 times included one in Kenya that wrote after the Belfast stabbing: “When the state fails to protect people, the streets find their own language.” Another, from Europe, described the Nowak case as “a globalized, calculated and malicious evil” affecting “every White person and every White nation”.

Close to a third – about 13,000 – of the Belfast and Southampton tweets, whether from the UK or abroad, were racist or anti-immigrant, according to the Guardian analysis. When analysed separately, a quarter of the posts that were only about Southampton were racist or anti-immigrant, compared with a third of those that were only about Belfast.

One UK-based poster, writing a day after the Belfast stabbing, claimed they hoped the attacker was British-born because “race is the issue, not immigration status”. The post registered 2m views.

Valerie Wirtschafter, an expert on online foreign influence operations from the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank, said she believed violent events such as those in Belfast and Southampton were “a point of exploitation” in which “outside agitators” had an opportunity to make a disproportionate impact.

Their position was helped by X and other social media companies cutting content moderation, she said, but in particular by “algorithms and how they collide with the basic cognitive processes of humans. We are more attracted to things that are shocking.”
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.summary: Analysis shows 55% of accounts were located overseas. Seven of 12 most-read posts came from US. @EndWokeness account cited by parliamentary committee after it amplified false claim that Southport attack was carried out by Muslim man.

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.title: Parents of baby girl killed at nursery fear unsafe sleeping ‘rife’ in sector across England
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Josh Halliday North of England editor
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
Katie and John Meehan say responses to campaign they launched after death of daughter Genevieve must be ‘wake-up call’

The parents of a nine-month-old girl who died after being placed in an unsafe sleeping position at nursery said they feared poor practice may be “rife” across England.

Genevieve Meehan suffocated when she was strapped face down to a beanbag for an hour and 37 minutes at a nursery in Cheadle Hulme, Stockport, in May 2022.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Kate Roughley, the nursery’s deputy manager, was jailed for 14 years in 2024 after being found guilty of manslaughter. One of Roughley’s colleagues was later jailed for the “deplorable” treatment of other babies in her care.

Genevieve’s parents, Katie and John Meehan, have led a campaign with the charity the Lullaby Trust to strengthen safety and regulation of nurseries after a series of high-profile abuses.

The sector has come under intense scrutiny in recent months after the cases of Vincent Chan and Nathan Bennett, nursery workers who sexually assaulted children in their care.

Chan was jailed in February for 18 years for molesting young children in a campaign of sexual abuse that was described as “every parent’s worst nightmare”, while Bennett was jailed in March for 24 years for raping and abusing young children in his care.

Another nursery worker, Kimberley Cookson, was jailed in April over the death of 14-month-old Noah Sibanda, who had been physically restrained face-down with a blanket over his head while being put to sleep.

As a result of Genevieve’s parents’ campaign, childcare settings in England will be banned from September from putting babies under 12 months to sleep in anything other than a cot.

Ofsted, the regulator, will triple the number of unannounced inspections – adding an extra 3,000 visits a year, boosted by an additional £8m from the government – and inspect nurseries every four years instead of six. Each visit will scrutinise sleeping policies.

Katie Meehan, 42, said she was “really shocked” by the extent of unsafe sleeping practice that had been revealed when nurseries wrote privately to the government about the planned changes this year.

Some reported leaving babies to sleep in pushchairs “due to space limitations”, according to details shared with the Department for Education (DfE). Others put infants to sleep outside, adopting “forest school models or Scandinavian practices”.

By law, nurseries are required to follow NHS safer sleep guidance – which includes laying the baby on their back in a cot or Moses basket – however, in the rules from September, the government will state: “Babies aged one year and under must only be placed to sleep in a cot.”

Katie Meehan, who is working closely with the government and Ofsted, said the responses suggested unsafe sleeping may be “rife” across England and that they were a “wake-up call” for the regulator and officials.

Some nursery owners said they would be forced to reduce the number of infants they take as a result of the new rules. Several raised concerns that this will ban smaller beds, such as dream coracles, which take up less space than a cot and have been widely adopted in recent years.

John Meehan, 40, said he was concerned some nursery owners – many of whom are backed by private equity firms – were potentially putting profit before safety.

Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning

after newsletter promotion

“There are lots and lots of people out there who just want to do their absolute best and they go into that industry because they want to look after children,” he said. “But my impression from some of the responses is that they are taking too many children and there is a money incentive for them to do so, and that is a real concern.”

Ministers are now considering whether to introduce mandatory CCTV to all nurseries in England, one of the key aims of the campaign. Olivia Bailey, the former early years minister who spearheaded the latest reforms, is understood to have been very persuaded by the arguments for mandatory CCTV.

Katie Meehan said she was disappointed that Bailey lost her role in the reshuffle when Andy Burnham became prime minister. However, she is hopeful Burnham will take up the reforms, having met Genevieve’s family this year when he was mayor of Greater Manchester.

She said Burnham was particularly supportive of their call for mandatory CCTV – which was crucial in securing Genevieve’s killer’s conviction – and that he had told them: “Genevieve was a child of Manchester and she was failed. We’ve got to make sure it doesn’t happen again.”

The DfE said: “What happened to Genevieve was a tragedy, and her parents’ campaigning has already changed practice across the country. We will keep going until no family goes through what theirs has.

“The vast majority of settings do a brilliant job, and the response to our updated guidance showed a sector that wants to get this right. But settings have long been legally required to follow NHS safer sleep guidance, and that is why we are working with the Lullaby Trust to make those expectations unambiguous, so there can be no excuses for unsafe practice.”

Sir Martyn Oliver, the chief inspector at Ofsted, said: “No parent should have to endure what Katie and John have been through. They have shown remarkable bravery in pursuing change following their daughter’s tragic death.

“We welcome the DfE’s additional funding for more frequent inspections, including thousands more without notice visits. We’re also strengthening our inspection practice so that safe sleeping in nurseries and with childminders is now a mandatory part of every inspection and will be reported on for parents to read.”
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.summary: Parents of nine-month-old girl say they feared poor practice may be 'rife' across England. Ofsted chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver said there was no excuse for unsafe practice.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Taylor Swift songs removed from Trump and White House’s social media posts
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Eric Berger
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Rage-baiting efforts of Trump accounts silenced after posts such as a video linking her Red album to Republicans

Some of Taylor Swift’s songs have been removed from videos posted on social media by Donald Trump’s campaign and the White House, silencing efforts to mock the pop star.

A video posted 3 August featuring the US president and the first lady, Melania Trump, watching fireworks was posted this month on TikTok with Swift’s song August.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“I’m sure @Taylor Swift is going to be super excited we used her song! #taylorswift #maga #august,” the accompanying text states.

Trump’s campaign later published another post, needling Swift over the title of her 2012 album, Red. “Did you know Taylor Swift wrote a whole album about the color of the Republican party?” it said, suggesting parody track titles.

Both videos are now silent.

Trump-related social media accounts have used Swift’s music in other campaign videos, too, but several of those also no longer have sound.

As the text with the August video suggests, Trump’s social media accounts have used pop stars’ songs as rage bait. They have featured music from artists including Ariana Grande, Katy Perry, Sabrina Carpenter, Olivia Rodrigo and Kenny Loggins, all of whom publicly objected to the use of their music.

“Please do not use my music in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense,” Grande posted after the White House posted her music over a montage of ICE agents handcuffing and detaining people.

When Trump’s White House used one of Carpenter’s songs to soundtrack a video of immigration raids in 2025, the singer wrote: “this video is evil and disgusting. Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda.”

In this latest case, Swift has not commented.

Trump had previously attacked Swift, who endorsed then Democratic vice-president Kamala Harris during the 2024 election. “I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!” Trump declared at the time.

Last year he ​wrote: “Has anyone noticed that, since I said ‘I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT,’ she’s no longer ‘HOT?’”

Swift’s Eras tour was the the highest-grossing tour of all time, according to Pollstar, generating about $2.2bn worldwide. Her album The Life of a Showgirl became the most pre-saved album ever on Spotify ahead of its October 2025 release.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Trump's campaign and White House have used pop stars' songs as rage bait. They have featured music from artists including Ariana Grande, Katy Perry, Sabrina Carpenter, Olivia Rodrigo and Kenny Loggins.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Top Democrats simulate election threats as Trump continues assault on voting
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: George Chidi
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Chuck Schumer and other senators took part in exercises in which legal experts laid out election disruption scenarios

In a Washington DC conference room last month, some of the most senior Democrats in the US Senate gathered to plan for a prospect that only recently would have felt more akin to science fiction: they started to wargame democracy.

Chuck Schumer, the US Senate minority leader, and senators including Alex Padilla, Adam Schiff, Mark Warner, Elissa Slotkin and Raphael Warnock were among those in the room as a team of legal experts offered scenarios.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The first: realistic deepfake videos, created with artificial intelligence, showing “evidence” of widespread election fraud, spreading through social media a few weeks before voting begins.

Forensic experts discredit the videos quickly as synthetic in the given scenario, but rightwing media – and the US president – amplify the claims, nonetheless. Election workers begin receiving death threats. Armed men start appearing at polls.

If you’re a Democratic senator, what would you do?

“These tabletop exercises are a standard planning tool for experts and stakeholders to prepare for potential scenarios. We’re not predicting exactly what would happen,” said Justin Vail, who leads the DC office of the non-partisan advocacy group Protect Democracy. “But we do want to create a realistic context that can help us identify gaps, test our assumptions, and strengthen coordination, and then ultimately develop some recommendations to increase our preparedness.”

Senate Democrats have held two election disruption exercises this year. Voting rights and legal groups like Protect Democracy have also participated, along with election attorney Marc Elias, former attorney general Eric Holder, election law expert Norman Eisen and members of the left-leaning non-profit Democracy Forward.

Skye Perryman, CEO of Democracy Forward, expressed confidence in the resilience of the foundations of US democracy, pointing to the legal system and the distributed nature of American elections, which she said builds a defense against crass political interference, even from the US president.

“The president can try to imagine whatever he may wish to imagine,” Perryman said. “He can’t imagine a new constitution, and the constitution, frankly, is quite clear in no uncertain terms; there’s not a role for the president in election administration in this country.”

Nonetheless, Donald Trump’s continuous false claims about a stolen election in 2020, and his increasingly strident demand for the US Congress to pass a package of federalized oversights of elections, have raised concerns among progressive voters that the administration may mar November’s midterms with misinformation, or worse.

The administration billed Trump’s primetime TV address last month as a presentation of new evidence that the 2020 election was illegitimate, and that his administration had uncovered new findings about vulnerabilities in the US election system. Instead, Trump claimed China had illicitly acquired voter information on 220 million Americans, and that China had undermined his 2020 campaign in other unspecified ways, arguing that intelligence officials had suppressed this information.

Trump’s claims fell apart under scrutiny. His own intelligence officials had already concluded that China refrained from interfering in the US election out of concern for potential political blowback if caught.

Trump threatened the broadcast licenses of networks that refused to carry the address live. In his speech, he again implored Congress to pass the Save America Act, which would ban mail-in ballots nationwide and impose new identification requirements on voters when they register and report to polls. Republican senators refuse to dispense with the 60-vote filibuster threshold to pass the law.

Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, representing a swing state that is a favored rhetorical target of the president, described Trump’s address as “signaling his unmistakable intent to attack these elections and our voting rights, just as he tried to throw out our votes and seize the presidency in 2020”.

Voting rights advocates pointed toward Trump’s July primetime address as indicative of the president’s intentions – rhetorical attacks on the integrity of voting machines and elections offices, potentially escalating into more direct interference.

Trump’s public commentary, and the actions of agencies under his supervision, shaped the scenario building as Democratic leaders plan their possible responses.

Senators were asked at their recent session to contemplate how to react to a threat to withhold Office of Management and Budget (OMB) funding for states that don’t submit their voter rolls for federal oversight. They also considered a threat of Federal Communications Commission (FCC) action against news outlets covering deepfakes.

“The development of AI will only add to the complexity and could create confusion among voters in our fragmented media landscape,” said Vail. “Unfortunately, that confusion can be to the benefit of the administration’s strategy.”

FCC enforcement actions seem relatively mild compared to more extreme scenarios, like planning a response to armed vigilantes in tactical gear at ballot drop boxes – which was not a hypothetical problem in Arizona during the 2022 midterms. Senators were asked to plan responses for online license-plate doxxing, a midnight firebombing of an early voting site and a last-minute unilateral deployment of Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agents and the national guard to polling stations.

The main lesson of the exercise “is that this is an all-hands-on-deck moment, and it is an all-hands-on-deck response”, said Perryman. “And so what that means is that, we’re not looking at any one silver bullet to be able to fully protect elections. It’s going to take all of us.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Deepfake videos created with artificial intelligence show 'evidence' of widespread election fraud. The exercise is an all-hands-on-deck response, says Perryman.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Press access spat adds to fears of circus around Luigi Mangione murder trial
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Victoria Bekiempis in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Lawyers for man accused of killing healthcare CEO Brian Thompson raise red flags about limits on reporters

Weeks before Luigi Mangione faces a jury over the killing of the UnitedHealthcare executive Brian Thompson, the hugely anticipated proceedings already have potential to reach trial-of-the-century status.

Intense global interest in Mangione’s case is unfolding against a media landscape where news consumers expect minute-by-minute updates, a mise-en-scène now made all the more complicated by social media influencers who managed to get press credentials and often flock to major US criminal cases in search of clicks and money.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The Mangione trial is certainly ripe for the headlines. He is accused of gunning down Thompson on the streets of Manhattan, triggering an intense manhunt that ended with his arrest in a Pennsylvania fast-food restaurant. But it also sparked an outpouring of public anger over America’s widely reviled for-profit healthcare firms and their practices. While awaiting trial, Mangione has attracted a small but vociferous group of supporters who almost see him as a political prisoner.

The present media access plan for the trial, which does not include an overflow room to accommodate outsize press and public interest, only adds to fears that Mangione’s trial will become a circus. Mangione’s team and prosecutors are trading barbs over this issue and the defense moves suggest media chaos might be exactly what they want.

Indeed, Mangione’s defense lodged sensational allegations about press access in a letter to Judge Gregory Carro late last week.

Mangione’s team objected to “partial exclusion” of the public and press. They said court administrators and prosecutors engaged in “hand-choosing the reporters permitted to attend the proceeding”. They alleged that only six journalists will be permitted to cover jury selection, “in a dramatic break from customary practice”. These machinations took place, they claimed, without defense knowledge or participation.

They demanded lists of names, for the six journalists covering jury selection, scheduled for 8 September, and for 68 reporters on a reserved seating list – and asked for a hearing about which journalists were “granted general access” to the 8 September trial. Whatever collusion and exclusion might be happening, they argued, threatened Mangione’s sixth amendment right to an open trial.

But news coverage of this letter to Carro swiftly debunked the claims about the court coverage processes, including false accusations of prosecutor involvement in journalist selection. Over the next few days, this narrative lost still more steam.

Manhattan prosecutors told Carro in a 3 August letter they had “no role in developing” court administrators’ media access plan and “will have no role in selecting which news reporters attend the trial”.

Mangione’s team responded with a letter “to clarify their position”, saying they had “no personal knowledge” about whether court administrators and prosecutors discussed press access issues in his case, but wanted to know whether there was any discussion between them and court administrators.

This defense and prosecution barb-trading over media access presages how Mangione’s trial is primed to spiral into feverish disinformation. .

“I was as surprised as anyone by the defense claim that prosecutors were even indirectly hand-picking reporters,” said Laura Italiano, a freelance journalist who is covering the Mangione trial. “This is in no way true.”

Experts say that Mangione’s trial could proceed more smoothly – if steps were taken to improve access.

As for jury selection, there would be a limit on reporters in the courtroom – given that Mangione’s case has the same logistical constraints of all high-profile proceedings. With nearly all courtroom seats filled by prospective jurors, there is limited space for the media in this process.

“That is where the pool comes in,” Italiano said, later explaining, “We let the rest of the journalists know what’s going on.”

Italiano pointed to two prominent examples of this pool system in jury selection: Donald Trump’s 2024 hush-money trial, and Sean “Diddy” Combs’s 2001 nightclub shooting trial. The media organizes its pool for those limited seats; this rotating group distributes notes to all journalists present who, due to the space constraints, cannot be in the courtroom.

“It’s usually chosen by agreement of the veteran reporters who have covered that court. It’s never acrimonious,” Italiano said. “It’s because everyone knows they’re going to get the information.”

As for the defense claim that a pool breaks from “customary practice” and excludes certain media, Italiano said: “No, that is absolutely false.”

The defense has requested a video feed to an overflow courtroom.

Experts believe an overflow room could lessen this acrimony.

“There was universal shock when the state court system announced that the press plan was not to have an overflow room,” Italiano said. “Every big trial where there is this kind of demand for coverage has had overflow courtrooms.”

“It seems like the whole problem could be solved by having an overflow courtroom, which is routinely done,” said Ron Kuby, a defense attorney whose practice focuses on civil rights.

“I don’t understand what’s going on here, but it doesn’t seem to make any sense, hence this sort of sniping back and forth between the prosecution and the defense,” Kuby said, again pointing out: “It’s not difficult. It is done, not uncommonly, in high-profile trials.”

Court administrators did not respond to requests for comment. Lawyers for Mangione, who maintains his innocence, declined to comment.

Asked for comment, the Manhattan district attorney’s office referred to their letter that rejected claims of working with court administrators. A spokesperson said they do not have a say in selecting reporters.

“New York state courts do not allow streaming of the proceedings outside of the courthouse. That’s why you’ll never see New York state trials on TV, as there is no streaming allowed under New York state rules,” Seth Zuckerman, founder of Zuckerman Legal Group and a former New York prosecutor, said. “What they’ve done in prior cases is they set up an overflow room for reporters who there is not enough room for in the courtroom, so that they could follow along in real time.”

For Erik S Groothuis, a partner with Schlam Stone & Dolan, the defense letters seemed “a bit dramatic”.

“It seems to me they’re trying to do everything they can, as careful lawyers, to create appellate issues,” Groothuis said. “Whether these six journalists versus some other six are in there, I’m not sure it matters a whole lot, but they’re just trying to grab for every piece of leverage they can, and create issues that they might be able to leverage for appeal.”

As for the defense request for a list of reporters, he said, “I’ve never heard of that.”

“This is some interesting posturing,” Roy S Gutterman, director of the Newhouse School’s Tully Center for Free Speech at Syracuse University, said. “I do not think an overflow room for media should be a concern for any of the litigants, defense or prosecution, as long as there are media present to cover the trial.”

“Perhaps, there might be a bigger, more accommodating courtroom to hold the trial in,” he said. “But if the court granted access to every interested reporter or member of the public, they would have to move the trial uptown to Madison Square Garden.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Luigi Mangione faces a jury over the killing of UnitedHealthcare executive Brian Thompson. The trial is expected to reach trial-of-the-century status.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Moderate Democrat Ed Case defies progressive challenge in Hawaii primary
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Guardian staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Case, who has represented island state’s first district in US Congress since 2019, beat state senator Jarrett Keohokalole

The moderate Democratic representative Ed Case has seen off a progressive challenge to retain his party’s nomination for the US House of Representatives election in Hawaii’s first congressional district.

Case, who has represented the district in Washington DC since 2019, prevailed in Saturday’s primary over Jarrett Keohokalole, the state senator.

A wave of leftwing candidates has swept through a series of high-profile Democratic primaries in recent months, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan this week. Focus will turn next week to Wisconsin, where Democratic socialist Francesca Hong is leading the party’s chaotic gubernatorial primary.

Keohokalole, 43, had argued during the campaign in Hawaii that the time had come for a new generation of political leadership in the state.

With 91% of votes counted, Case had won 60% of the vote, according to the Associated Press. Keohokalole, in second place, had 36.1%.

“I feel very grateful that the voters want me to continue in office,” Case, 73, told Hawaii Public Radio on Saturday. He will now face Adriel Lam, the Republican who ran unopposed in the party’s primary, in the general election.

“The voters decided, and we respect the results,” Keohokalole told KHON2. “The seats don’t belong to any individual. You have to earn them, and so the voters spoke.”

Case had faced criticism from Democrats including Keohokalole after voting last year for Donald Trump’s Save Act, which would require US voters to prove their citizenship when registering for federal elections.

More recently, Case stressed that he no longer supported the legislation, after an option for voters to attest in writing that they are a citizen was removed. But he used his former vote as an example of his independence.

“I’m not 100% voter with my party,” Case told HawaiiNewsNow. “Never have been, never will be.”

Case holds a senior position on a ​key spending committee and had argued that Hawaii would attract fewer federal dollars if he was not re-elected.

Keohokalole highlighted Case’s campaign donations from businesses to argue he has lost touch with voters.

Hawaii is divided into two US congressional districts. The first, represented by Case, covers the urban center of Honolulu. The second, represented by Jill Tokuda, covers the rest of the state.

Tokuda also won the Democratic primary for the second congressional district. According to AP, with 90% of votes counted, she had won 91.6%.

Josh Green, the Hawaii governor who has led the state since 2022, also defeated several challengers for the Democratic nomination.

Reuters contributed reporting
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Ed Case, 73, has represented Hawaii's first congressional district since 2019. He beat state senator Jarrett Keohokalole, 43, in Saturday's primary. Keohkalole had argued that the time had come for a new generation of political leadership in Hawaii.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘America’s saddest murder trial’: mental health in focus in Lindsay Clancy case
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Edward Helmore
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Jurors hear from host of medical experts as defence says postpartum psychosis caused young mother to kill children

I
t’s been called “America’s saddest murder trial” and last week jurors in the Lindsay Clancy case listened to mental health professionals, counsellors, psychiatrists, and medication experts explain the circumstances in which the young mother killed her three children.

It has been a spectacle that has gripped America, not least because Clancy’s legal defense has been supported by her now divorced husband.

The evidence last week bolstered the contention that Clancy was over-medicated and underserved as she tried to get help before she suffered a psychotic mental break – exacerbated by undiagnosed postpartum depression – that led to her kill her young family. It has also backed up the defense argument that Clancy’s medical team failed in its duty of care towards her.

The court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, heard Clancy described as a “very loving mother who cared about her children” but also that she was in a “difficult mental place”, feeling “tired and anxious”.

On Friday, three psychiatrists who saw Clancy in the months leading up to the January 2023 murders explained why they did not diagnose Clancy with postpartum psychosis.

Dr Alia Goodheart said she considered Clancy a “low-risk” patient. Clancy told her she was experiencing insomnia and numbness and having suicidal thoughts but did not have a plan to act on them.

Another, Dr Jennifer Tufts, said Clancy reported feeling worried about possibly “one day having suicidal thoughts” if she continued “to feel poorly”, but exhibited no signs of mania. She advised Clancy to stop taking Zoloft (sertraline), a medication used to treat panic and obsessive-compulsive disorders, try natural remedies such as fish oil, and take lorazepam in instances of “severe anxiety”.

The court has heard that Clancy was prescribed 13 different psychiatric medications in the months leading up to the killings.

Tufts and Goodheart are named in a medical malpractice lawsuit Clancy and her former husband have filed. Clancy does not deny killing her children, but her defense argues postpartum psychosis warped her sense of reality and that she is not criminally liable for their deaths.

After she killed her three children – eight-month old Callan, five-year-old Cora and three-year-old Dawson – Clancy, then 32, slashed her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-story window in a suicide attempt. The fall paralyzed her from the waist down.

The trial has often made for difficult listening – presiding judge William Sullivan has reminded jurors they cannot decide the case on emotion – and prosecutors have come perilously close to arguing that Clancy’s because suicide attempt failed, it lends credence to the contention that she aimed to kill her children.

Friday’s proceeding broke dramatically when defense attorney Kevin Reddington said in open court that a prosecutor had said “shut her up” while Clancy sobbed after the court was shown autopsy photos of her baby while a medical examiner testified on the stand.

The court also heard from a state police investigator that authorities found no evidence that Clancy had ever been abusive toward her children. Her former father-in-law, Christopher Clancy, said Clancy was a “very good” mother. The picture the couple created, he said, was of “the all-American family”.

Childhood friend Amy Bevins said Clancy was “a good person, a good friend, a good mom” and had been open about her struggles with her mental health and told her that a medication she was taking was causing her to have “dark thoughts”.

Bethany DeCollibus, a family therapist, said Clancy’s demeanor appeared normal but that she had said she could not sleep and felt “like a zombie”. A teacher from the elder children’s school said Clancy was a “very loving mother who cared about her children”.

Even on the day of the murders, the court heard, Clancy took Cora for a regular pediatric check-up. The pediatrician, Dr Lindsay Rosshirt, testified that “as far as I can recall, it was a very normal visit”.

Dr Nicole Kumi, an expert in postpartum mental health, said the Clancy trial raises a host of issues about the diagnosis of postpartum mental health disorders and how the healthcare system recognizes and responds to them.

The trial, she said, highlights “a significant gap in care for moms in the postpartum period”. Professionals who work in the field see that postpartum psychosis, while appearing to be rare to the outside world, is in fact readily apparent.

“We see it frequently and we see it escalate to unfortunate outcomes, because of a lack of education and awareness for moms, their partners and for members of the community that could potentially intervene before it gets to the state it got to with Lindsay Clancy,” she said.

Clancy, Kumi said, was actively seeking help. “She knew something was wrong, but she didn’t know what was wrong,” she said. The fact that she had had three children did not protect her from the condition, and may have made people around her assume she was able to cope.

“They start to normalize the stressors of motherhood,” Kumi said.

If the medical community overlooked Clancy, or failed to take her symptoms seriously, it may be because there is a focus on first-time mothers, Kumi said.

‘She was crying out for help within her home and within the healthcare system, and all she was met with was medication and redirection,” Kumi said. “That’s not how we solve problems in maternal healthcare.”

Clancy had told medical professionals and those around her that she was unable to sleep, a condition that can worsen mental health. “Every journey is different and a lack of sleep is an indicator for postpartum moms,” Kumi said.

The Clancy trial exposes what Kumi said was “a maternal healthcare crisis in this country”.

That Clancy appeared to be functioning as a mother, Kumi added, was not itself a measure of her mental health.

“In my opinion, she was influenced by delusions and hallucinations which are part of psychosis. She had moments when she it looked like she was functioning well from the outside. But we don’t know what was going on internally for her,” she said.

In the US, call or text Mental Health America at 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. You can also reach Crisis Text Line by texting MHA to 741741. In the UK, the charity Mind is available on 0300 123 3393 and Childline on 0800 1111. In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Lindsay Clancy, 32, killed her three children in January 2023 after she slashed her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-story window. Defense says postpartum psychosis caused her to kill her children. Clancy had told medical professionals she was unable to sleep, a condition that can worsen mental health.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump loyalist Todd Blanche confirmed by Senate as US attorney general
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sam Levine
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Major win for president as former personal lawyer wins approval despite outcry over $1.8bn slush fund

The US Senate voted to narrowly confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general in a major win for Donald Trump, who will now have his one-time personal attorney sitting atop the nation’s law enforcement apparatus.

Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana cast the deciding vote in Blanche’s favor after two other Republicans – Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska – voted against him. Every Democrat rejected Blanche’s nomination as the Republican-led Senate voted 50-49.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Blanche had already been leading the department in an acting capacity, and the vote came after his nomination had been in limbo for weeks. He faced pushback from Republican senators over the department’s deal to create a $1.8bn so-called “anti-weaponization fund” and to give the president, his sons and his businesses tax immunity.

“Mr Blanche is not perfect, and he will tell you this, but the choice is not between perfection and Mr Blanche,” Cassidy said Friday on the Senate floor announcing his decision. “It is between Mr Blanche and another acting attorney general who may not run the department effectively under President Trump and who indeed may not be as good as Mr Blanche.”

The Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, said Senate Republicans have “handed Trump an excuse on a silver platter” to continue his “pervasive, breathtaking corruption” by confirming Todd Blanche as attorney general.

“If you want to wipe out corruption, you can’t have the president’s personal attorney as the attorney general. You don’t need a PhD in political science to know that,” he wrote in a post on X.

“Todd Blanche has no intention of stopping Trump’s corruption. He advanced his career enabling it. Every senator who voted to confirm him has now branded themselves as an enabler, too.”

Blanche said on social media that he was “deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me”, adding that he was “grateful” to senators for working late to confirm him.

Concern around the “anti-weaponization fund” appears to have cost Blanche among at least some GOP senators who opposed his nomination, including Murkowski.

“I am also keenly aware that the Department’s nearly $2-billion dollar slush fund – which likely would have rewarded January 6 protesters – is only off the table because this nomination is pending and the Senate has leverage. Once we vote, that will end, and there is no telling what the future holds,” Murkowski said in a post on X on Friday, announcing she was voting against Blanche.

But John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina successfully pushed Blanche to put in writing that the fund was not moving forward and to clarify the scope of the IRS deal. Even though experts said the assurances were far from ironclad, Cornyn and Tillis wound up supporting Blanche, allowing his nomination to narrowly clear the Senate judiciary committee.

Blanche also faced heavy criticism for the department’s sloppy rollout of files related to Jeffrey Epstein, which redacted information that should not have been redacted and left unredacted the names of victims that should have been kept private. During his confirmation hearing, Blanche refused to personally meet with Epstein victims, then agreed to do so. The survivors said they received few answers from Blanche during the meeting.

Blanche, who left a lucrative partnership to represent Trump in 2023, has been at the center of the president’s attempt to bend the federal government to his will. Scores of career justice department attorneys have left the agency under his leadership. Department lawyers have been rebuked by judges across the US for making misrepresentations to the court.

Blanche has also been at the center of Trump’s efforts to use the justice department to punish political rivals. During his tenure as both the deputy attorney general and acting attorney general, the department has indicted former FBI director James Comey twice; the New York attorney general, Letitia James; and the non-profit Southern Poverty Law Center – all in cases that exerts see as thin. It has also tried to bring criminal charges against two Democratic senators, Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and Mark Kelly of Arizona, and used its investigative powers to try and get leverage over Jerome Powell, the former chairman of the Federal Reserve.

“The Attorney General should serve the American people, not the president’s wish list,” Kelly said in a statement on Saturday in which he also noted that Blanche “met with Ghislane Maxwell in secret” before the convicted Epstein accomplice was transferred to a minimum-security prison camp. Blanche, Kelly added “is defined by his loyalty to Trump”.

As his nomination was pending, Blanche also promised anti-abortion advocates the department would make the Dobbs decision permanent in every state, according to Politico.

“While I believe Mr Blanche is a capable lawyer, the Department of Justice has become increasingly political,” Collins, who is running for re-election in Maine, said earlier this week. “Mr Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the department’s independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation.”

Earlier this year, Blanche spoke about how he would feel if someone else was named attorney general.

“As to whether or not I want this job, I did not ask for this job. I love working for President Trump, it’s the greatest honor of a lifetime,” he said in April, shortly after being named the acting attorney general.

“If he chooses to nominate somebody else and asks me to go do something else, I will say, ‘Thank you very much. I love you, sir.’ I don’t have any goals or aspirations beyond that.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The Senate voted 50-49 to confirm Blanche as attorney general. Blanche had already been leading the department in an acting capacity. He said he didn't ask for the job, but he did not want it.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: ‘I’ve definitely lost followers’: influencers face backlash over Meta ‘pervert glasses’ content
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Sammy Gecsoyler
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Using ‘spy glasses’ made by Facebook owner leads to floods of negative comments, say content creators

I
t was hardly an offensive video. Amid the buzz of the Tour de France finale, Oliver Hooson filmed himself whipping up a delicious-looking flat white for a fellow cycling enthusiast. But after posting the footage on social media, the comments that soon rolled in were a real shock. “PERV,” read one. “Out here pushing creep glasses,” said another. His mistake? Documenting the moment with Meta’s “spy glasses”.

Despite being marketed as the latest must-have gadget, Meta’s smartglasses, which can record video footage while being worn, have faced a vicious backlash, particularly relating to concerns about surveillance. There are widespread fears about the glasses being used to film people, especially women, without their consent, and the resultant footage being posted on social media. This has earned them the label of “pervert glasses”, and content creators, no matter how they are used, have faced a flood of negative comments for deploying them.

Things reached a peak this summer when Kylie Jenner collaborated with Meta to launch a pair, leading to a flurry of influencers showing off their trendy, Kardashian-approved goggles. Some content creators have been forced to apologise for plugging the specs. Rida Tharana, a content creator with 1.6 million followers on Instagram, “took accountability” for taking part in a Meta campaign to promote the glasses, criticising men who misuse them to “record and harass women”. Self-described pickup artists have used the glasses to film themselves trying to chat up women in public without their knowledge, sometimes making disparaging, misogynistic comments afterwards.

Hooson says that, while some of the comments left on his video were “savage”, he is fully in support of their message. “It definitely caught me off guard. It was a real ignorant move,” he says, adding that he hates that the glasses are being used against “women mainly being filmed against their knowledge”. The backlash was even coming from those close to home. “Funnily enough, my wife predicted it. She was going to post a banterous comment in a similar tone to the others but she didn’t press send.”

After posting the video, Hooson, who shares his passion for home design and cycling to his 224,000 Instagram followers, says he lost a “good 50 to 100” followers. He called the term “pervert glasses” a “defence mechanism” to dissuade people from using them. “If everybody gets round that they are pervert glasses, which evidently they have, then it’s a really easy way of limiting sales and the usage of them,” he says. “People do not need any more of their privacy stripped away. I’m fully in support of that.”

His interest in the glasses, which he received at a PR event, was far more innocent. “I saw [chefs at] high-end restaurants filming themselves with the glasses on, showing off their process. It was stupid, poetic and beautiful to watch. I wanted to have a play about and show people the things that I enjoy doing,” he says, adding that it is very hard to capture a point of view (POV) angle otherwise. “It was intended as a simple way of capturing a human POV of my morning coffee routine or my fast cycling descents. I think that’s vastly different from somebody going into the centre of Soho and asking somebody a divisive question and clipping them up for views without their knowledge,” he says.

But, for now, it’s not worth using the glasses. “Would I rather just not have that little fun point-of-view shot for the greater good? Yes, I would definitely get rid of them,” he says.

While the glasses have proved unpopular with some online, they sold 7m pairs in 2025 alone. Meta says the tiny, flashing LED light that activates on the glasses will let people know when they are being filmed, but there have been multiple instances of people complaining they have been videoed without prior knowledge.

In one instance, a woman told the BBC a man had recorded her, and then demanded money to remove the videos from social media. Another woman described being recorded during sexual encounters without her consent. Last month, police in Scotland said they were investigating a far-right TikToker who allegedly filmed himself making sexualised comments to young women and telling a Sikh shopkeeper about a plan to “breed out the white race” without their knowledge.

Restaurants, theatres and pubs in the UK, including Wetherspoons, have even joined in on the backlash, banning the Meta glasses over privacy fears.
