A severe bout of COVID-19 can wake up an army of dormant viruses hiding inside the body.

That’s according to a study of more than 1,000 people hospitalized with the disease that is published today in Nature1. The analysis finds that this reactivation of pathogens is linked to especially intense bouts of COVID-19 and to the development of long COVID.

If further research reveals that reactivated viruses can cause people to become seriously ill, it could open the door to new treatments for COVID-19 and even long COVID, says Esther Melamed, a physician-scientist who studies neuroimmunology at the University of Texas at Austin and is a co-author of the analysis.

Although the study didn’t dive into how COVID-19 prompts viruses to reawaken, Melamed says that the disease “probably induces the stress that triggers the reactivations, and then these reactivations further amplify the inflammation” caused by COVID-19. In these cases, she adds, “COVID is not really acting on its own.”

Nearly everyone is infected by a variety of viruses throughout their childhood and adolescence. A handful of these pathogens are never fully cleared from the body. Instead, they hide quietly inside cells for a lifetime, kept in check by a healthy immune system.

Four lessons COVID taught us about the immune system

Researchers have seen hints that these bystander viruses are reactivated in people with long COVID. So Melamed and her colleagues studied the situation systematically, collecting blood, nasal swabs and lung fluids from individuals hospitalized with COVID-19 in 2020 and early 2021. Nearly half of the participants experienced a reactivation of common viruses lurking in their bodies, the researchers found.

These pathogens included herpesviruses such as cytomegalovirus and Epstein–Barr virus, which causes glandular fever (mononucleosis), as well as anelloviruses, which are typically harmless and don’t cause symptoms. More than 90% of the global adult population has been infected with at least one of these pathogens2.

The team found that these viruses do not reawaken all at once after a person contracts the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, which causes COVID-19. Instead, different viral families reactivate on their own timelines. Epstein–Barr virus and anelloviruses tend to surge early during a bout of COVID-19, peaking shortly after hospital admission. By contrast, cytomegaloviruses and herpes simplex viruses emerge around three weeks later, mainly in the respiratory system.

Could long COVID be linked to herpes viruses? Early data offer a hint

The “most striking” result is that this reactivation happens even in people with otherwise healthy immune systems, says Resia Pretorius, a physiologist at Stellenbosch University in South Africa. Some scientists had thought that a reawakening of viruses could happen only in people with a weakened immune system, such as those with HIV. But this study “overturns” that assumption, she adds.

Some people included in the study were receiving immunosuppressive drugs during their hospital stay for various conditions. However, this didn’t make them any more likely to experience virus awakenings than those who were not taking such medication. This suggests that the stress of a coronavirus infection alone can overload the immune system.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Gemma Church once studied at the Cavendish Laboratory and now works at a quantum-computing company in Cambridge. Her short stories appear in numerous publications, and she owns a Countdown teapot.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

It started off as a silly simulation. I fed the quantum computer everything I knew about the process: how heat pulls flavour from the leaves, how tiny currents move through the cup, how our taste buds respond accordingly.

I included one additional control. It was a bit of a joke at first: what if I could change the cup’s gravity just a little around the rim to avoid the dreaded slurp?

The patterns the computer returned were no joke.

The machine revealed that those tiny changes in gravity at the micrometre scale could steady the swirl of the near-boiling water, holding delicate compounds in contact with the leaves for longer and making the flavour cleaner. No slurps and maximum flavour to boot. Magnificent.

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

I decided to build a device that could bring those simulations to life. The resulting machine was a complex configuration of pre-existing systems that could nudge the way mass and energy behaved inside a teacup-sized region. I called the device Thomson. It felt fitting. After all, J. J. Thomson not only presided over the Cavendish from 1884 to 1918 but also instilled the twice-daily tea break that still takes place here in the laboratory, almost 200 years later. And I could only imagine my colleagues’ faces when they tasted my results!

Thomson’s first brews were incredible. The liquid moved in calm, repeating cells instead of chaotic eddies. The tea tasted impossibly balanced: sweet notes without bitterness, texture as smooth as melted ice cream. But warm. Warm melted ice cream with a tannin tang that could have been taken from the recipe books of the gods. I know these notes are not making sense. But the results were intoxicating … the chai equivalent of ambrosia.

But the quantum computer was not.

It refused to stop simulating until it had reached its primary objective: to brew the perfect cup of tea. It was my fault. A quantum computer should not be capable of such independent thought. But I had taken some of the guard rails off to run the simulations faster, letting the machine extrapolate in a way not usually allowed. I saw no harm in doing this. After all, how unethical could making a cup of tea get?

At the quantum computer’s suggestion, I introduced special regions of microgravity, encoded with tiny, deliberate irregularities. The computer’s simulation suggested that those defects would change how the forces behaved inside the little regions in subtle ways, unifying them until Thomson wouldn’t just shape the flow of the tea any more; it would change the gravitational rules inside that patch of space.

I know I should have stopped there. I should have turned the quantum computer and Thomson off, returning to my actual research. But the computer’s simulations just looked so … tantalizing.

With shaking hands, I keyed the instructions into Thomson and executed the program.

Thomson whirred and clicked with a rhythm both deadly and alive. The other instruments in the lab recorded odd things: small mismatches in energy, clocks slipping out of sync with one another, and molecules that seemed to disappear from the spectral readings without explanation. Thomson’s output no longer read like that of a simple optimization experiment. It read like a recipe for making a self-contained region with its own physical behaviour.

And so it was. Because when I peered into the cup as the brewing process continued, a tiny, temporal universe appeared, trapped inside the porcelain. I watched as granules of sugar fell and burst into tiny stars, swirling in the brownness of something evolving into its own little cosmos.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:

Neanderthals are known to have had physiological differences from Homo sapiens, including thicker bones and defined brow ridges, as in this model.Credit: Mike Kemp/In Pictures via Getty

Two genetic changes in the genomes of Neanderthals contributed to the extinct hominin’s characteristic robust physique — and the differences persist in modern humans. The variants make carriers taller and more muscular than non-carriers, according to a study1 published in Current Biology.

Neanderthals, who lived across Europe and western Asia from about 300,000 years ago to around 40,000 years ago, interbred with Homo sapiens before going extinct. Previous studies have shown that modern humans with ancestors from outside Africa inherited roughly 1–4% of their DNA from Neanderthals2.

Fossil evidence shows that Neanderthals had broader chests3, thicker bones4 and larger muscles than most modern humans do. The latest study provides a plausible molecular pathway that contributed to the Neanderthals’ robust traits, says Bastien Llamas, a human geneticist at Adelaide University in Australia.

Well-preserved Neanderthal remains are extremely rare and, so far, scientists have recovered only about five genetic samples of sufficient quality to reconstruct a full or near-complete genome. Most Neanderthal DNA samples are fragmented and yield only partial sequences.

The researchers focused on the growth hormone receptor, which helps to regulate bone and muscle growth. The team used three high-coverage and two medium-coverage Neanderthal genomes to identify two amino-acid changes unique to the growth hormone receptor in these hominins.

They found that the receptor variant entered modern populations through interbreeding around 47,000 years ago. Today, about 20% of the population in South Asia and 15% in East Asia carry it. By contrast, these genetic differences are present in just around 0.5% of Europeans, and are absent in people from sub-Saharan Africa.

To test whether these ancient changes altered the receptor’s function, the team engineered mouse cells to produce either the Neanderthal or the modern human version of the receptor. Cells carrying the Neanderthal receptor proliferated around 39% more over five days than did cells carrying the variant that is dominant in modern humans.

The team also looked at population data sets from five biobanks, analysing health and genetic data from more than 1.1 million adults. On average, people carrying the Neanderthal-derived variant were around 0.3 centimetres taller than those who did not have it.

People who carry this variant also have 0.25 kilograms more muscle mass than those who don’t, says co-author Philipp Kanis, a genetics researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany.

The most interesting aspect of the study is the convergence of ancient genomics, experimental cellular biology and present-day biobank traits, says Llamas. It provides an unusually detailed example of how DNA inherited from Neanderthals can affect a defined molecular pathway and contribute to measurable variation in present-day humans, he adds.

The ancient variant was also associated with several craniofacial features. Modern humans with the gene variant tended to have a shorter ramus — the rear portion of the lower jaw — as well as a greater chance of an overbite and shorter tooth roots than non-carriers.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Peter Gluckman
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Peter Gluckman is president of the International Science Council and director of the think tank Koi Tū Centre for Informed Futures, Auckland, New Zealand.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Public funding for science relies on a social contract: in return for support, science demonstrates its value to society. Until now, the scientific community has enjoyed a great deal of autonomy in deciding where to focus its research. But some governments are intruding on that self-regulation and narrowing how science budgets are spent — away from contested areas such as social sciences and climate change, for example.

Although governments, as patrons of science, are entitled to set broad priorities and expectations, there is a risk to societal progress if policy-driven management of science becomes excessive or intrusive. To keep the balance, the scientific community needs to keep emphasizing the societal benefits of science. Scientists must build compelling narratives and allies across business and civil society.

Scientists should recognize their own political biases to build public trust

Helping researchers to do this is a priority of the International Science Council (ISC) — a non-governmental organization that unites more than 250 international scientific unions, academies and research councils. In the past five years, under my presidency, the ISC has reoriented to focus on helping scientists to serve society better.

We’re supporting training to improve communication with policymakers, for example, and looking at the broader dimensions of ethics and responsibilities in science. We’re examining the challenges of artificial intelligence, transdisciplinary research, data governance and sharing.

Public trust in science is being tested in a fast-changing world. Overall, science remains highly trusted and scientists are seen, for the most part, as members of a trusted profession. But in countries with polarized politics, extreme voices shout loudest and can weaponize disinformation. Surveys suggest a link between political identity and attitudes to science, including total distrust on the part of extreme populists and rejection of science when it comes to areas, such as vaccines, in which the evidence conflicts with someone’s values, interests or political stance.

Six ways to put the public at the heart of science and policy

Researchers must navigate these tensions without allowing science itself to become politicized. Yet, too often, they can come across as entitled and self-serving, more interested in securing funding than in explaining what their science can do for society. Uncertainties are often swept aside, and hyperbolic claims lead to public cynicism. Acknowledging what scientists don’t know, and that many people also turn to other systems of thought — including religion and Indigenous knowledge — helps to engender trust.

AI-based technologies are also creating opportunities and risks for science’s trustworthiness. Generative AI has led to an overwhelming flood of grant applications and an increase in papers of questionable quality. There are growing concerns about what AI use means for the integrity of the scientific record, undermining trust in science itself.

Stronger sanctions are needed against paper mills, tokenistic or non-existent peer review and fraudulent content. The ISC and academic publishers have initiated a project to identify how trust markers might be developed to label journals that have trustworthy practices.

Every year, millions of people take the drugs etoposide and teniposide, which are used to treat cancers of the lung, blood and other organs. But the process of manufacturing both drugs is low-yield and complicated. It also relies on precursors from plants in the subfamily Podophylloideae, including the endangered plant Sinopodophyllum hexandrum (also known as Podophyllum hexandrum), which is native to high-altitude Himalayan regions. Now, researchers have detailed a new pathway for making the drugs — with help from baker’s yeast1.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Mariana Lenharo is a reporter for Nature in New York City.

Search author on:

A juvenile female of the mantid species Choeradodis rhomboidea was collected as part of an effort to catalogue insects in the Amazon.Credit: Bernardo Ferraz/BioInsecta

The Amazon’s lush rainforest harbours a hidden world of tiny creatures, nearly all of them unknown to science. But now hundreds of scientists in Brazil are collaborating on a quest to count every species of insect in one expanse of the Amazon — the largest insect-biodiversity study ever to explore the forest from the ground to the canopy.

Preliminary data suggest that the number of insect species could surpass 40,000, which is almost 0.7% of the widely accepted estimate of six million living insect species worldwide. And that 40,000 figure is for a single location in the Amazon. “If we start sampling other parts of the forest, the number of new species will likely increase almost exponentially,” says José Rafael, an entomologist at the National Institute for Amazonian Research (INPA) in Manaus, Brazil, and one of the scientists leading the megaproject.

Unpicking the rhythms of the Amazon rainforest

The project is unique, says Rudolf Meier, an entomologist at the Museum of Natural History in Berlin, because it is collecting insects high above the ground, in layers that have remained largely unexplored. He adds that the megaproject is also one of the largest to use DNA barcoding in insects, a method which identifies a species on the basis of a short fragment of its DNA, enabling researchers to sequence parts of the genome of thousands of specimens in a small amount of time.

An overview of the campaign was presented in a video poster as part of the online programme of the annual meeting of the Brazilian Society for the Advancement of Science in Niterói last week.

To collect insects, project scientists have deployed three arrays of traps. Each array consists of five mesh traps arranged in a vertical stack: one on the forest floor, one suspended about 30 metres (roughly the height of a ten-storey building) above it and three more in between. Insects that fly into each trap are funnelled into a collecting bottle at the top. There, they fall into ethanol, which kills the insects while preserving their DNA for analysis.

Researchers are deploying five-level trap systems to find insects from the forest floor, the treetops and everywhere in between.Credit: Larissa Queiroz/BioInsecta

The trap systems, which are installed in a 10,000-hectare area of the central Amazon in northern Brazil, have collected insects continuously for 14 months. To catch species that would otherwise be missed by this kind of trap, the team organized an insect-collecting ‘blitz’ last November that used around 50 extra collection methods. For example, researchers used rotting meat to attract carrion-feeding flies and beetles, as well as light traps to sample nocturnal insects.

The result was a sample of 5.5 million specimens, of which around 600,000 will ultimately have sections of their DNA sequenced. A network of nearly 400 taxonomists will combine genetic data with analyses of the insects’ physical traits to identify them. And, in the case of new species, they will describe and name them.

“Coming up with names for all of the new species is going to be a lot of work,” says Dalton Amorim, an entomologist at the University of São Paulo in Ribeirão Preto and one of the leaders of the project. Researchers might draw inspiration from words in the languages of Amazonian Indigenous groups, as well as the names of local rivers and regional historical figures, he says.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus is director-general of the World Health Organization based in Geneva, Switzerland.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

This July marked 80 years since representatives of 61 states signed the constitution of the World Health Organization (WHO) in New York City. The founders understood that diseases do not respect borders, and that progress depends on countries working towards a common goal.

Africa’s response to this Ebola outbreak shows how to shape global health

Over the past eight decades, working with more than 190 member states and other partners, the WHO has helped to eradicate smallpox, driven progress towards wiping out polio, expanded access to life-saving vaccines and led the global fight against HIV. It has strengthened health-care systems, set health standards and helped to save millions of lives through efforts to improve tobacco control, water and air quality and sanitation.

As a result, people today live more than 25 years longer, on average, than they did 80 years ago. Far fewer women die during pregnancy and childbirth, and many more children survive and thrive past their fifth birthday.

These health gains come down to one choice: cooperation over isolation. Events this year show that the vision behind the WHO constitution is just as necessary today.

When physicians and AI work together, who is accountable? How to lay out medical liability

The current Ebola epidemic in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, cases of measles surging across the Americas and the now-ended hantavirus outbreak are reminders that health threats can emerge anywhere and affect anyone. The COVID-19 pandemic, the most severe health crisis in a century, showed that no country can tackle such health threats alone.

The WHO’s strength lies in its ability to bring together health leaders, scientists and the global health community to tackle shared challenges and find solutions, to set global standards and coordinate action in times of crisis. That value was demonstrated again last year, when member states adopted the WHO Pandemic Agreement. This treaty applies the lessons of COVID-19 to make the world more equitable and better prepared for future pandemics.

But cooperation isn’t enough: countries also need greater capacity to respond to health crises. The WHO’s Universal Health and Preparedness Review helps countries to identify gaps in their ability to respond to health emergencies. Through the Pandemic Fund, the WHO and the World Bank have supported projects in 70 countries to strengthen disease surveillance, laboratory networks, health workforces and coordination across sectors.

Last year also tested global multilateralism, science and solidarity like never before. Sudden, severe cuts to international aid disrupted essential health services in many countries, threatening to reverse decades of progress.

Health of people who are displaced in their own countries is a neglected global crisis

The WHO is supporting these nations to build more sustainable, self-reliant health-care systems. In the short term, we are helping them to design affordable packages of essential health services, introducing or raising health taxes on tobacco, alcohol and sugary drinks, and investing in domestic manufacturing. In the long term, countries can strengthen risk-sharing mechanisms, such as publicly funded health insurance, to better protect people financially.

In 2025, the United States gave notice of its intent to leave WHO. For years, the organization leant too heavily on voluntary funding from a few donors. In 2017, it began a finance reform to broaden its sources of revenue. In 2022, member states agreed to raise their membership fees from 16% to 50% of the core budget over time, a key step towards financial independence. Two increases have been approved since then, with three more due over the next five years.

The reform of the WHO’s financing was part of a wider institutional transformation to sharpen the WHO’s focus on what it does best: providing high-quality science, data and standards to help countries deliver health for all. Before 2019, the way that the WHO developed its guidance and standards was fragmented. We created a science division to modernize how we develop guidelines, expand global research networks and increase investment in digital technology and data systems, including artificial intelligence. In 2015, 85 member states had a national digital health strategy; today, 129 do. The WHO also serves as a hub for health data and digital services, through platforms such as the World Health Data Hub, the Global Health Observatory and the Global Digital Health Certification Network.

Should nicotine be regulated like a narcotic? A Pacific nation makes the case

As the organization enters its ninth decade, digital technologies will be crucial as we adapt to meet the world’s fast-changing needs. The world’s population has more than tripled in 80 years, placing strain on natural and urban environments with consequences for people’s health. Outbreaks and epidemics keep emerging. The health effects of conflict, climate change and displacement are growing. Non-communicable diseases, such as heart disease and cancer, are causing more illness and premature death in every country. Antimicrobial resistance threatens to undo a century of medical progress. Technological advances are creating both opportunities and risks for health.

In short, the need for a science-led, evidence-based, impartial and globally representative health organization has never been greater. Eighty years on, the WHO constitution remains a living promise, and a reminder of why the world still needs a strong WHO.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.title: What’s missing from the White House plan for the future of US science
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
A 1945 report by Vannevar Bush, director of the US Office of Scientific Research and Development, was seminal to the growth of US research.Credit: AP/Alamy

Last month, Michael Kratsios, head of the US Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP), released a report called Science: A New Golden Age. The 123-page document is a response to a letter from US President Donald Trump tasking Kratsios with ushering in “a new golden age of American innovation” (see go.nature.com/8tyfk4k). But how likely is it that the report will help the country to achieve this aim?

White House rolls out AI funding — and signals a new era for US science

Such a letter from the president to the OSTP head is not uncommon. It is a signal of the government’s interests and priorities. However, Trump’s letter and the response come amid a systematic effort to reshape US research.

There’s a lot to take in. The report asks hard questions about the future of US science, including about how to support the research that provides the foundations for technological advances and how to enhance crucial scientific infrastructure. There are timely questions about the role of artificial intelligence in science and around the process of issuing research grants. The report proposes changes, too, to how the US federal research-funding portfolio is balanced, for instance. It addresses the persistent concern that grant managers and reviewers are too cautious, and proposes fresh ways to fund people who are willing to take risks and to individuals outside universities. The details need time for reflection and we plan to return to some of the report’s themes in greater depth in future articles.

Before diving deeper into the report’s content, it’s important to consider its precedents and the context in which it was produced. A key predecessor is a 1945 report called Science: The Endless Frontier, which was submitted to then-president Harry Truman by Vannevar Bush, director of the Office of Scientific Research and Development at the time (see go.nature.com/4g7nufa). Produced in the aftermath of the Second World War, this fundamental document in US science policy led to the establishment of a new public funding agency for basic research: the National Science Foundation. The report and its implementation took several years and was a highly inclusive exercise with inputs from academia, industry and policymakers.

White House proposes vast overhaul of US science funding: what you need to know

Science: A New Golden Age has also been written during a tumultuous period, but of a different kind. It was released after 18 months of executive orders, rule changes, abrupt funding cuts, delays to grants being awarded and political interference in many scientific matters that should be the domain of experts, ranging from vaccine safety to climate change. However, unlike the 1945 report, the current one does not name the members of scientific and technical communities who were consulted. This follows a pattern: Trump’s administration has substantially reduced the flow of advice from independent specialists to the federal government, as we documented in an April News Feature (Nature 652, 1106–1109; 2026).

Science: A New Golden Age, at its core, is a set of priorities from Trump’s administration for scientific leaders to focus on. The fields named include “AI, quantum information science, semiconductors, advanced communications, robotics, advanced manufacturing, nuclear fission and fusion, and space systems”. Such large-scale instructions to the research community, without transparent consultation with its stakeholders, is rare for a democratic country — let alone for a powerhouse of research and the home of many globally respected universities and science-based corporations.

But the details of these instructions are not straightforward to find. They are included in an annex in the main document. This part contains a memorandum for the heads of departments and executive agencies co-signed by Kratsios and Russell Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget. The annex includes a list of what the document calls “foundational research to drive scientific breakthroughs for emerging technologies”.

The priorities focus mainly on research in physics, materials science, chemistry, computer science, engineering, space science and mathematics, and especially on “national security-relevant research portfolios”. Federal agencies with annual research budgets of at least US$3 billion have 90 days to tell the White House how they will “prioritize both the absolute level and the relative share of funding”. Furthermore, to support the administration’s priorities in biotechnology and biomanufacturing, agencies are being asked to “prioritize foundational research in the biological sciences over the life sciences, a broader category not focused on foundational research”. Details on which fields will be prioritized for funding extend over several pages.

Key US science panels are being axed — and others are becoming less open

But the people who can assess foundational science accurately are those closest to it: the researchers and their representative societies. The report says that parties “across the country’s scientific enterprise” have been consulted, but doesn’t specify who has provided input. Which scientists or organizations in fields such as physics, computer science, space science and chemistry were asked for feedback? Who is saying that life sciences does not focus on foundational research?

One glaring omission in this proposal for overhauling science is direct evidence of input from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine and from scholarly societies representing individual disciplines. These communities are the modern equivalents of professional guilds. They organize conferences and publish research in their fields; they act as stewards for their disciplines, by setting quality standards, for instance. They represent the field’s interests to policymakers, and protect and defend scholarly integrity.

Entire NSF science advisory board fired by Trump administration

The report’s outlook for the future of science also does not mention some key research areas, such as climate change and public health. Neither is research in social sciences included, although metascience is mentioned. These are surprising omissions, considering that national security is an objective. Climate change and emerging infectious diseases will have huge consequences, for both the United States and the world. Studies in the social sciences and humanities are just as important as those in science and engineering, and will be necessary to help societies to navigate the transformational impacts of AI.

Other surprising omissions from the report’s annex are phrases such as world, global and international cooperation. This is in keeping with Trump’s decision to withdraw funding for, and the country’s participation in, international scientific networks such as the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and the World Health Organization. There is an assumption that US science will achieve its golden age all by itself — cut off from researchers in other countries. That idea goes against the evidence of the past 75 years or so. Moreover, the broader literature of the history of science shows what can be achieved by civilizations that welcome people from all parts of the world. Science is not restricted to national borders, nor should it be.

The latest report seeks to establish itself as a successor to Science: An Endless Frontier — and mentions the words frontier or frontiers more than 50 times. But the two documents are very different. The 1945 report provided a clear path for the United States to make groundbreaking discoveries and inventions — continuing on from the global flurry of advances, such as radar, nuclear weapons and the mass production of penicillin, that emerged during the Second World War. In the process of producing the report, Bush formed four scientific committees, representing medicine, science and public welfare, scientific talent development and the publication of scientific information. Their advice was included in the final report. Science: An Endless Frontier was an inclusive discussion that offered hope for a better future.

The current White House plan could have spoken to the moment: the world is dealing with both planetary and societal challenges, including ones posed by AI. The report could have been inclusive, spanning borders and disciplines, not to complete a box-ticking exercise, but because a consultative approach provides the best chance for the world to emerge out of crisis. It could have said, let’s learn from the best, regardless of who they are; let’s learn what works, regardless of where the ideas come from; let’s ensure that scientists are valued partners in those conversations. But it doesn’t say any of these things and that’s a missed opportunity.

Bioengineering can produce tools for use in cutting-edge cell therapies, among other applications.Credit: Philippe Lopez/AFP via Getty

Europe is losing ground in one of the most innovation-intensive sectors in biomedicine and health care: bioengineering1. Many advances in biomedicine are technologically driven, for example, the use of artificial intelligence to predict protein structures and rapid genome sequencing for precision medicine.

Bioengineering produces technologies that aim to solve medical problems, by merging methods from mathematics, computation, engineering and biomedicine. Many countries, including the United States1, China, Switzerland and the United Kingdom, understand the power of such research. Yet, the European Union has still not caught on.

The EU’s 27 member states (EU27) host fewer than ten fully autonomous bioengineering departments, compared with more than 100 each in the United States and China. Not one EU27 university made it into the 2025 ShanghaiRanking’s top-30 list of biomedical engineering departments, compared with 18 from Asia.

Investment in medical technologies in the EU27 is low (see ‘Untapped potential’). In 2023, biotechnology companies in Europe attracted US$11.5 billion in funding, compared with about $57 billion in the United States and $21 billion China (see go.nature.com/3twrfgr and ref. 2).

Source: European Commission

Concerned about this widening gap, in March, 25 specialists from around the world — including us and our co-signatories (see Supplementary information) — came together at Europe’s life-sciences organization EMBO in Heidelberg, Germany, to find ways to address it. Here, we call on the European Council and relevant EU directorates to adopt a European bioengineering agenda that focuses on three themes.

The EU can build on its vibrant life-sciences sector, which contributes €1.5 trillion to its economy and supports 29 million jobs (see go.nature.com/4fr475p). The region has a strong culture of collaborative research, academic–industry partnerships and funding programmes that encourage the development of technologies. For decades it has excelled in other engineering disciplines, from civil to computational. And the EU’s open society, social-security systems, health-care and education infrastructures attract global talent.

Science sleuths raise concerns about scores of bioengineering papers

What’s needed now is coordinated European investment in bioengineering education, research and innovation ecosystems, to create the conditions for globally competitive health-care technology and biotech companies to flourish.

The EU should incentivize national governments to establish dedicated bioengineering departments at their leading universities. Funding programmes should be used to promote bioengineering excellence.

Universities should recruit dedicated bioengineering staff members with a range of expertise to establish world-class curricula. This should be done in a similar way to how electrical and computer-engineering faculties were established originally, by bringing together top researchers from physics, mathematics and other engineering and technology fields.

New bioengineering institutions should teach students how to develop a problem-solving mindset3. This skill can be applied across life-sciences research, including to methodologies that advance biomedical discovery and technologies that improve clinical care.

Curricula should also emphasize medical ethics and regulation, to help students embrace the processes involved in developing successful biomedical technologies. This will help future bioengineers to navigate the rules and market forces that are specific to technology acceptance in medicine, which are different from other engineering products and pipelines.

Engineering resilient food systems in a warming world

Having several such top-level departments will build homegrown expertise and attract medical technology and biotechnology companies. Evidence for this can be found in Boston, Massachusetts, and San Francisco, California. These areas are home to biotechnology and medical-technology hubs, the foundations of which were built on a reputation for education and research excellence, including top-ranking bioengineering departments.

Recognition and celebration of high-achieving bioengineers can enhance the visibility and reputation of the field, initiating a virtuous cycle that makes entering the bioengineering industry more desirable. As the number of bioengineers in Europe grows, these researchers could establish dedicated societies that can present scientific awards, elect fellows, recognize early-career achievements and establish distinguished lectureships, as well as inspire established funders, societies and philanthropists to support bioengineering.

The EU invests billions of euros annually in biomedical and life-sciences research, including through research funding from the European Research Council and the European Innovation Council. Yet, dedicated review panels for assessing bioengineering grant proposals are absent, and funding proposals are typically assessed by researchers in neighbouring disciplines, such as biology, medicine, physics and engineering. Although reviewers might have relevant expertise, they are likely to evaluate proposals through the lens of their own disciplines.

The EU should establish dedicated funding schemes and review panels for bioengineering research. Experts in the field should also be involved in shaping future initiatives. These include Framework Programme 10 — the EU’s next research and innovation funding programme, which is currently being developed and is scheduled to run from 2028 to 2034.

Tissue bioengineering techniques could improve treatments for congenital heart conditions.Credit: Christophe Archambault/AFP via Getty

To rapidly translate research into marketable products, Europe needs policies that actively engage industry, venture-capital and investment firms. The region cannot establish global leadership in bioengineering while much of its talent is moving abroad and its innovations are being commercialized elsewhere. Dedicated funding programmes, public–private co-investment schemes, tax incentives for investments in technology and reduced administrative barriers to technology transfer are essential at both the EU and national levels. These efforts should be complemented by regulatory pathways that support safe but efficient early approval of technology for use in clinical settings.

The use of artificial-intelligence tools in medicine has hinged on an implicit bargain. Patients and health systems permit sensitive records to be used for research, usually after de-identification so that names and other pieces of personal information are removed. In return, researchers and developers create tools that could improve health care, for example by enabling earlier diagnoses and new treatments. This bargain relies on the assumption that it is impossible for people who have access to an AI model to infer information about individuals whose data were used to train it. Writing in Nature, Knolle et al.1 show that, in the context of powerful machine-learning models, this assumption is often untrue.

Private firms will host US doctoral students in a scheme announced by the US National Science Foundation.Credit: Getty

The US National Science Foundation (NSF) has kicked off a sweeping effort to deepen the ties between PhD students and industry. The pilot programme will provide participants with hands-on industry research experience and funding from universities, companies and the NSF. It will serve more than 250 students, who will receive funding for four years.

The programme aims to “help graduates better apply their research to real-world challenges”, an NSF spokesperson said. The effort will give companies the chance “to invest directly into how our doctoral researchers are trained”, Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, said in a statement, noting that the majority of US recipients of PhDs in science, technology, engineering and mathematics do not remain in academia.

Researchers expressed a mixture of excitement and concern about the programme, called the Industry-Integrated PhD (I-PhD) Scholars Program, which was announced in July.

Pay, perks and culture shocks: a toolkit for scientists moving to industry

Such training provides benefits for both students and employers, says Wojtek Chodzko-Zajko, dean of the Graduate College at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, which already offers PhDs programmes that partner with industry. “I really like the idea that NSF is moving in that direction,” he says. “It’s one that’s always been possible, but it’s probably been underutilized at most research universities.”

But with industry PhDs already available and graduates flocking to industry jobs, NSF money should be spent to “support basic science that industry won’t support”, wrote chemistry Nobel laureate Carolyn Bertozzi at Stanford University in California, on the social-media platform Bluesky. The pilot announcement comes as the NSF plans to claw back funds from its core science programmes, Nature reported last month.

The NSF declined to comment on internal budget deliberations but said that it “remains committed to supporting curiosity-driven research and our high standards of merit review”.

Students on the programme will receive one year of funding from their universities and three years from the NSF. Industry partners will host at least one year of dissertation research at the company’s site and contribute at least US$100,000 per student. In the final three years, students will receive tuition support and yearly stipends of $37,000.

If students take longer than four years to complete their degree, it is the university’s responsibility to ensure they have funding for the extra time, according to Tony Boccanfuso, president and chief executive of the University–Industry Demonstration Partnership (UIDP), a non-profit organization that supports collaborations between universities and industry and that will lead the programme.

NSF plans cuts to core science programmes to fund White House initiative

Students in the I-PhD programme will “continue to complete all of the academic requirements of a traditional PhD, including a dissertation that meets their university’s standards”, says Gretchen Bollar Fiorenza, programme manager at the UIDP. They will also submit an annual programme report, which will document activities such as industry-based research experiences.

The NSF will spend $47 million over the next five years on the pilot project. More than 30 universities, including Columbia University and New York University in New York City and Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois, have already signed letters of intent to participate, as have industry partners such as Procter & Gamble, BP and Rolls Royce.

Many US universities already have strong industry ties. What’s new is the NSF “being the conduit for the activity and providing some leverage”, says Peter Beling, a data scientist at the University of Virginia in Charlottesville.

The programme is exciting and could help to foster collaborations between academia and industry, says Chodzko-Zajko. But a “four-year guaranteed PhD seems a little unrealistic”, he says. “PhDs depend on faculty committees and the progress of the research, and that’s to some degree unpredictable.” On average, it takes 5.6 years for students in the United States to complete a PhD in science or engineering.

Shaira Berg (left) smiles during a take for her short film, Gaslight.Credit: Dik Ng

Shaira Berg is building a career at the intersection of academic research and creative practice. During her PhD in psychology, which focused on behavioural neuroscience, at the University of Cambridge, UK, Berg collaborated with local video-game studio Ninja Theory. Together, they conducted virtual reality (VR) studies of how threat affects goal-directed learning and maladaptive habit formation in obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD).

Berg is open about how her scientific pathway has been shaped by personal experiences. Surviving a traumatic event during her doctoral studies altered how she thought about the limits of established research methods for studying the brain after trauma. Rather than separating that experience from her academic work, Berg began to explore how science and creative expression could inform one another.

Alongside her studies, she wrote and starred in Gaslight, a play based on her experience. The work was nominated for an award and was later adapted into a short film, which is now in development as a feature film, broadening her exploration of how creative forms can communicate psychological experience in ways that scientific data alone cannot.

Now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Texas at Austin, Berg continues to use immersive technologies to study trauma and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Here, she tells Nature why artistic creativity has a place in science and what researchers can gain from taking unconventional paths.

I’d say I’m a cinematic neuroscientist. My tag line is that I did a PhD in collaboration with a game studio that specializes in immersive horror, looking at maladaptive behaviour. I used a way of testing how people learn, called Pavlovian-instrumental transfer, which examines how environmental cues associated with rewards or threats can influence subsequent behaviours. For example, if someone learns that a blue symbol is associated with a reward, seeing blue while completing a different task might be associated with a ‘positive’ behaviour, such as moving faster or putting in more effort.

For my research, I used custom-built VR scenarios, which allowed us to study how these learnt cues affect behaviour in realistic virtual environments. We published the results this year in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience1, showing that immersion strengthened the more habit-like version of that effect, whereas the goal-directed effect remained constant across different levels of immersion. For OCD, in which habitual responses tend to override goal-directed ones, that result is very important. My current work extends that into fear conditioning and PTSD, for which I still blend neuroscience and film through a collaboration with a film studio.

Creatively, everything I write or direct has a neuroscience grounding. For me, it’s a way of examining human behaviour honestly and portraying it honestly, too. Conditions such as PTSD and OCD are rarely depicted in a way that is both sensitive and faithful to what the conditions actually feel like. I thought I had a way to work on both fronts at once.

I think lived experience matters enormously in neuroscience: a lot of people who end up studying a condition have some personal connection to it. Neuroscience appealed to me because it felt like a way to understand my own brain better. Studying trauma in depth helped me, in part, to process my own experiences while working towards findings that might lead to treatments for others.

As for the clinical vocabulary, at the PhD level it becomes difficult to translate that into something people outside the field can relate to. That gap was part of what motivated me to write Gaslight. I wanted audiences to feel, even vicariously, what it’s like to live through trauma, using art to communicate the human experience behind the science.

A research paper can describe a condition. A play can put an audience inside it. The overall structure isn’t that different: a paper has a beginning, a middle and an end, and so does a play. The difference is whose shoes you’re in. When I write creatively, I’m working in the mind of whoever is going through that experience. I’ve done stage and film acting since I was 12, and what always fascinated me about it was being able to feel things I hadn’t necessarily felt myself and portray that truthfully. It’s a much more human experience than when I write in a scientific context.

Everything she writes or directs has a grounding in neuroscience, says Shaira Berg.Credit: Courtesy of Shaira Berg

It fed back quite a lot, in the end. Throughout my PhD and my current research, I’ve had to creatively produce fictional scenes to simulate threat behaviour. This is a great way to generate experimental results, without triggering symptoms and upsetting participants. The immersive environments can elicit behaviours that are harder to study using conventional laboratory tasks. We actually found there was a more measurable response under immersive conditions1.

Illustration: Gibson Kochanek; Getty

Your DNA is under constant assault. Ultraviolet light, environmental toxins, reactive molecules made during run-of-the-mill metabolism and many other disruptors muck with the instructions that keep life humming along. Thankfully, repair crews are at the ready.

This method to reverse cellular ageing is about to be tested in humans

A typical cell can acquire up to a whopping 100,000 lesions each day. “The vast, vast majority are repaired,” says Morten Scheibye-Knudsen, a translational geroscientist at the University of Copenhagen. “We have very, very efficient repair.”

That’s a good thing for a couple of reasons. First, unrepaired or poorly repaired damage can introduce mutations, which can contribute to cancer. And second, DNA damage seems to be one of the main drivers of ageing.

Researchers are amassing evidence that this type of damage underlies many of the hallmarks of ageing, including chronic inflammation, metabolic malfunctions and protein-folding problems1. Such damage triggers cellular alarm bells that can promote inflammation, force cells into an ‘undead’ state known as senescence and even kill them. These responses help the body to grow and thrive, but they become more problematic as we age. The accumulation of beleaguered cells over time is associated with many age-related conditions, including cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis and Alzheimer’s.

That raises a question: if DNA damage is at the root of ageing, can boosting DNA repair slow the process, keeping people healthy for longer? For the first time, this is starting to look like a promising approach, say researchers who study DNA repair2.

Their new optimism comes from studying relatively long-lived species, such as bowhead whales (Balaena mysticetus)3 and naked mole rats (Heterocephalus glaber)4, and looking at the genetics of human centenarians. These studies are pointing to the existence of a great variety of molecular maintenance workers that make for a long and healthy life. A ‘master regulator’ of repair, discovered in 2023, also suggests that these fix-it systems could be enhanced in unison5.

Such findings come alongside a booming interest in longevity more generally, propelled by biotechnology companies, health influencers and governments overseeing ageing populations.

“If you can reduce DNA damage, you would probably have a dramatic effect on the ageing process,” says Paul Robbins, who directs the Nathan Shock Center on Genome Integrity and Aging, which opened last year at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “There are tricks that we can do. But it’s not simple.”

Despite having such a big job, DNA is remarkably fragile. Left unrepaired, its many breaks, kinks, lost bases and crosslinks can physically block the processes necessary to make proteins or to form new cells. That means that for life to get anywhere with DNA as a blueprint, maintenance is essential.

“DNA damage has been the fundamental problem at the origin of life,” says Björn Schumacher, a geroscientist at the University of Cologne in Germany.

Cells have an ancient and varied toolkit. There are six major DNA-repair systems, a few smaller ones and probably some that haven’t been discovered, Schumacher says. Different systems respond to different forms of damage. If a single DNA base, such as guanine, gets oxidized — an oxygen atom gets added to its structure — then a process known as base-excision repair can make the fix. This removes and replaces one base at a time. Nucleotide-excision repair, by comparison, removes a couple of dozen nucleotides along a single strand at once — a heftier fix often triggered by UV damage.

Scientists are studying centenarians to find out what the secret to a long life is.Credit: freemixer/Getty

The repair systems tend to require several steps. They call on many proteins and overlap with one another, with one system jumping in if another is not active. Some are sloppier than others, prone to introducing errors as they make their fixes. One way to repair a break that spans both strands of the DNA double helix, for example, is homologous recombination. This uses an intact DNA strand to serve as a template and is generally accurate. Nonhomologous end joining, however, another way to fix double-strand breaks, doesn’t require a template and does a more slapdash job by fusing broken ends together. This sometimes introduces errors that can lead to cancer-driving mutations, but a repair with a small risk of mutation is better than no repair at all.

Naked mole rats live for decades — genetic tweaks reveal insights into ageing

Many genes are involved in these repair systems; some researchers suggest that 10% of the genome plays a part in genome maintenance. In searching for ways to enhance repair, “this complexity has always been a limiting factor”, says Shumacher. When researchers have tried to enhance repair directly, by switching on one repair system or overexpressing a repair enzyme, the effect has often been limited — or, worse, it has thrown the whole process out of balance.

One of the big challenges is that there are so many repair pathways, says Agnel Sfeir, a molecular geneticist at the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City who studies DNA repair in the context of cancer. “At the moment, we do not know which DNA repair can be boosted or should be boosted,” she says.

The animal kingdom might provide clues. Scientists are studying species with long, relatively cancer-free lives, including naked mole rats, Greenland sharks (Somniosus microcephalus), elephants, bats and lobsters.

For one of her latest projects, biologist Vera Gorbunova at the University of Rochester, New York, and her team chose bowhead whales. These marine mammals weigh in at more than 80,000 kilograms and glide and dive through frigid Arctic waters year-round. Although the whales can live for more than 200 years and have 1,000 times as many cells growing and dividing as humans do, cancer rarely creeps in.

In a study published last year3, Gorbunova and her colleagues went looking for reasons why bowhead whales are resistant to cancer. They thought they might find extra copies of genes that help to suppress and kill cancers. But instead they found that whale cells had very accurate double-strand break repair. “The whales don’t need to kill the cells; they just don’t let cells mutate as far,” Gorbunova says.

A protein, called CIRBP (cold-inducible RNA-binding protein), that helps cells to survive cold-related stress seems to have a role. When expressed in human cells, the whale protein increased two types of double-strand break repair.

The bowhead whale (Balaena mysticetus) can live for more than 200 years.Credit: Tony Wu/NaturePL

That finding chimes with a study from 2019, in which Gorbunova and her colleagues looked at 18 rodent species with varying lifespans. They found a strong link between the maximum lifespan and the accuracy and efficiency of double-strand break repair in skin and lung cells6. That superior repair was explained in large part by one member of a family of enzymes called sirtuins, which are known to have roles in ageing, metabolism and the stability of the genome. The overexpression of the sirtuin SIRT6 had already been linked to extended lifespan in mice. In the 2019 study, the team identified five amino acids that differ between the beaver and mouse versions of SIRT6 and seem to make the beaver version more effective. Beavers live for 10–12 years in the wild, whereas mice typically live for a few years at most.

Genetic studies suggest that some human centenarians7 might also carry a superior variant of the gene SIRT6, says geneticist Jan Vijg at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York City. Vijg co-leads a multiteam effort to identify important genes and pathways in centenarians, validate them and develop drugs that target them.

The team has identified a group of compounds called fucoidans, which occur naturally in brown seaweed and activate the SIRT6 protein, as potential therapeutics. Studies by Robbins, Gorbunova and others8,9 show that supplementing mouse diets with fucoidans improves the animals’ DNA repair, reduces senescence and extends their healthspan and lifespan.

Clinician-geroscientist Andrea Maier, director of the National University of Singapore’s Academy for Healthy Longevity, is now leading a study that gives fucoidans to men aged 50 to 80. The study is looking at cellular markers of ageing and clinical outcomes, measuring as directly as possible how fucoidans affect biology.

This whale lives for centuries: its secret could help extend human lifespan

The ins and outs of DNA repair don’t just differ from organism to organism; they also differ from cell to cell. Sperm and egg cells seem to accumulate much less DNA damage than other cell types do; DNA repair is energetically costly, so it makes sense that it would be prioritized in cells that must pass genetic information down the generations. “Our germ cells are in a sense immortal,” Schumacher says.

He and his colleagues have identified a possible key to this immortality. In 2023, the team reported from experiments in the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans that a protein complex already known for its role in cell proliferation represses many DNA-repair genes in non-reproductive, or somatic, cells5. This ‘DREAM complex’ is found across species. When the team turned it off in a mouse model of a premature-ageing syndrome, the mice showed less DNA damage. Switching it off in human cells boosted the expression of DNA-repair genes.

In the study, Schumacher’s team suppressed the DREAM complex by inhibiting an enzyme that helps to build it. The enzyme, called DYRK1A, is already a potential drug target: it is overexpressed in people with Down’s syndrome, and is tied to cognitive impairments and neurodegeneration associated with the condition.

Schumacher sees DREAM as a game changer for the field because it seems to act as a master regulator of repair, affecting many systems. “For the first time, we could really boost the overall capacity to repair,” he says.

Robbins agrees that the finding is exciting, calling the study “beautiful work”. But he says that there’s a lot more research to do to work out whether the complex could be targeted and how best to do it.

Studying other types of cell with different apparent levels of repair could inform future strategies. There is evidence, for example, that stem cells, which also need to maintain their genome across many divisions, have lower mutation rates than do other somatic cells. If stem cells are better at DNA repair, then partially reprogramming somatic cells into a stem-like state could, among other advantages, improve their repair.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.title: The three-and-beyond-body problem: juggling kids, travel and careers in academia
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Laura Carter
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Laura Carter is an environmental chemist at the University of Leeds, UK, and a mother of two in a dual‑academic family.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Researcher Laura Carter’s children look out at the tarmac at Heathrow Airport, before the family boards a flight for a research trip to Australia.

A trip in November 2025 brought home just how complex my family life has become. For a moment, my husband and I were in the air at the same time, crossing the Indian Ocean in opposite directions. Two work-related trips, two long-haul flights and one very full calendar. Our children, aged five and eight, were being looked after by a combination of grandparents and close friends.

After landing in Manchester, UK, and making my way home, it struck me how symbolic this was of a much larger reality that we are navigating: the constant negotiation required to sustain two academic careers alongside parenting. I am an environmental chemist and my husband lectures in psychology, meaning that both of us find ourselves in an academic system that assumes a much simpler reality.

Most in academia will be familiar with the ‘two‑body problem’: the challenge of a couple trying to secure positions a commutable distance from each other. But the reality, at least for me, has never felt even that tidy or contained. Once children entered the picture, there was a third body (and a fourth, in fact) that completely reshaped our approach and ability to work.

Because there are two of us juggling conferences, fieldwork, project meetings and deadlines, while coordinating childcare and school routines, it becomes a complex logistical challenge. My husband and I have calendars layered on calendars, travel plans negotiated with military precision and a constant mental tally of who can be where, when and with what kind of back-up plan (see ‘Packed schedule’).

For example, when I was in China for a conference towards the end of 2025, I knew that my husband was managing school drop-offs, evening activities and shifting work commitments, while preparing for his own upcoming conference in Indonesia. Once he left for that meeting, we crossed into entirely uncharted territory, relying on our parents along with carefully choreographed contingency plans to keep everyday life running.

This trip was the first time that we had both been away at the same time. With two school-age children, that’s no small feat. I find that there’s a unique kind of stress that comes with leaving your children behind. It’s not just the emotional weight: it’s the logistical puzzle of school runs, endless activities and bedtime routines. For me, being in a different time zone adds further worry; if something goes wrong, it is not always easy to get home or to make new plans.

Travel is a crucial part of academic life. Conferences, workshops and collaborations are an essential component of our jobs for sharing research, building networks and staying engaged with the latest developments in our fields.

Conference dates are rarely flexible. Meetings happen when they happen, and we’re left to juggle everything around them. Why they always seem to cluster in the spring and summer months, at least here in the Northern Hemisphere, is something I might never understand. Although that might suit academic calendars, it often coincides with school holidays, creating a particular challenge for parents.

How I managed my work and personal life as a sole parent during the pandemic

For us, it can mean back-to-back meetings at precisely the time when our normal childcare disappears. Instead of spreading commitments more evenly throughout the year, these periods become especially intense, with competing demands on our time at work and at home.

Trying to balance it all often leads to some truly absurd scheduling on my part: early flights, late returns and tight turnarounds. My personal record is four connecting flights in a single trip simply because that complicated route got me home two hours earlier than a more direct one, just in time for my children’s bedtime. This is all in the name of being present both professionally and personally.

Whenever possible, I’ve reached out to hosts or collaborators to ask whether there’s any wiggle room with scheduling. In practice, that has sometimes meant shifting a talk by a day to align with childcare, or clustering several commitments into a shorter visit to reduce time away. I’ve been fortunate that, when it comes to people with whom I have a strong working relationship, those conversations have gone well. But that’s the key: you need that trust to even ask. People’s personal circumstances differ, and small adjustments can make a big difference. For many of us, it’s not about doing less; it’s about finding a way to do it all without burning ourselves out in the process.

We have both, at times, turned down opportunities to avoid being away simultaneously, because extended travel quickly exposes how few sustainable options exist for dual-academic households. We’re incredibly fortunate to have family support, but it is neither guaranteed nor simple. Our parents have to travel for more than three hours each time they’re drafted in to help, as well as balancing their own caring responsibilities for older relatives.

This highlights a broader reality: academic mobility rarely rests on individual effort. It is often enabled by a hidden — and complex — network of support. I was never told that an academic career might depend on having parents nearby to care for children. Should that really be an unspoken condition of success?

Collection: Juggling scientific careers and family life

Relocation further complicates this. Moving internationally can mean losing the informal support systems that make family life workable.

Our set-up does offer some comforts: a shared understanding of the pressures, rhythms and emotional demands of an academic career. My partner and I sympathize with each other when it comes to travelling away from home and attending conferences. We both intuitively understand the guilt and pressures that we put on ourselves to be present at home and at work.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Vishva M. Dixit
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

We are providing an unedited version of this manuscript to give early access to its findings. Before final publication, the manuscript will undergo further editing. Please note there may be errors present which affect the content, and all legal disclaimers apply.

Caspase-1, -4, -5, and -11 activate Gasdermin D (GSDMD) pores, causing pyroptotic cell death and the release of interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18 1. Blocking this pathway holds therapeutic promise for the treatment of inflammatory disorders, but cell permeable caspase inhibitors have not been successful in clinical trials 2. Here, we describe covalent caspase inhibitors that selectively block pyroptosis and IL-1β secretion despite being excluded from healthy cells. These inhibitors did not prevent caspase-driven apoptosis, implying that GSDMD pores facilitated their uptake. Membrane-impermeable dyes entered the cells rescued from pyroptosis, consistent with transient membrane permeabilization by GSDMD pores. Caspase inhibition prevented rather than delayed cell death, consistent with membrane repair mechanisms neutralizing the initial GSDMD pores. Inhibiting caspase-1 and -11 suppressed IL-1β and IL-18 production in a mouse model of endotoxic shock, underscoring the therapeutic potential of exploiting GSDMD pores for targeted caspase inhibition in inflammatory diseases.
