Zheng Wan is a professor at and director of the Department of International Shipping in the College of Transportation and Communications at Shanghai Maritime University, Shanghai, China.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

A Russian nuclear-powered icebreaker, Rossiya, operates in Arctic waters. Credit: Patrick Landmann/Science Photo Library

The shipping industry needs low-carbon fuels if it is to reach net-zero greenhouse-gas emissions by 2050. But options are limited. Batteries can power ferries and vessels for use in harbours, but are impractical over long distances1. Methanol is hard to produce sustainably2. Ammonia is toxic and its supply chain is polluting3. Hydrogen is too bulky and difficult to store safely at sea4.

Nuclear reactors are being eyed as a solution. Atomic energy produces no direct carbon dioxide emissions and avoids the need to store several thousand cubic metres of fuel on board, freeing up space for cargo. Using nuclear power could shorten voyage times by eliminating refuelling stops and attaining higher speeds. It could save a ship owner tens of millions of dollars per ship per year in marine fuel costs and carbon taxes (see go.nature.com/4hs7u3r).

China reins in the spiralling construction costs of nuclear power — what can other countries learn?

A new generation of nuclear-powered commercial ships could be ploughing through the waves in the next decade. Interest from industry and governments is growing. In May, the US Maritime Administration sought public input on a commercially viable, scalable small modular reactor system for marine use. In 2028, London-based Core Power plans to open an order book for mass-produced floating nuclear power plants, with full commercialization in the mid-2030s and nuclear civil ships to follow. In China, the state-owned Jiangnan Shipyard, based in Shanghai, plans to build the world’s first thorium-powered container vessel by 2035.

A 2023 US report estimates that several hundred nuclear-powered merchant vessels (mostly container ships,large bulk carriers and oil tankers) could be operating worldwide by 2050, assuming a 2–5% market share5 (see ‘Commercial shipping goes atomic’). But a merchant ship fitted with a reactor is a mobile nuclear facility that needs to be treated with great care. It could be hijacked, run aground or even come under missile attack.

Before nuclear-powered ships reach the seas, the world needs to develop robust regulations around them. Engineers, regulators, ports and shipping companies must make these vessels safe and controllable. But current rules are outdated and fragmented.

Two major efforts are under way. In late August, at a ministerial-level event in Washington DC, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) plans to bring nuclear and maritime regulators together at the launch of its Atomic Technologies Licensed for Applications at Sea (ATLAS) initiative. In June 2025, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) began revising its 1981 Code of Safety for Nuclear Merchant Ships, and expects to adopt a revised code in 2030.

Here we set out what is at stake and call on the IAEA and IMO to link reactor licensing, ship certification, port entry and emergency response into one framework, lest companies, ports and countries implement incompatible systems and a nuclear accident at sea ensues.

Nuclear power has a long history at sea, driving submarines, aircraft carriers and icebreakers. Compact reactors with robust shielding, detailed maintenance plans and regular crew training have operated for at least 70 years in tough maritime environments, even under polar ice.

The US Navy runs one of the world’s largest nuclear fleets. By December 2024, it was operating 77 nuclear-powered warships — 66 submarines and 11 aircraft carriers — making up roughly half of the global fleet. Since 1955, US nuclear-powered vessels have racked up distances of some 300 million kilometres.

China, France, India, Russia and the United Kingdom also operate nuclear submarines and Russia has civil nuclear icebreakers. Today’s global fleet is smaller than it was at the end of the cold war — in 1989, more than 400 nuclear submarines were in operation or being built, compared with around 150 in service today.

Forty years after Chornobyl, more nuclear disasters are inevitable — plan for them

Yet this same record exposes the difficulty of commercial application. Nuclear use in a navy is part of a system of sovereign capabilities: one state (or several in close partnership) can design and construct the reactor, build the infrastructure for maintaining or replacing it, train the crew and assume responsibility for safety.

By contrast, most commercial ships are designed in one nation, built in another, flagged in a third, insured in a fourth, enter a variety of foreign ports, and often recycled at the end of their lives in countries with lax safety procedures6.

Early civil nuclear-powered merchant ships failed to achieve broad commercial success. Just four have been built. Launched in 1959, the NS Savannah was part of US president Dwight Eisenhower’s Atoms for Peace programme. It was able to travel the world and dock in many ports. But the complicated procedure for obtaining permits for visits and berths made it unviable as a cargo ship.

West Germany’s Otto Hahn, launched in 1964, carried ore around the world for 9 years, travelling 1.2 million kilometres and visiting 33 ports in 22 countries, before its reactor was removed and the ship converted to conventional propulsion in 1982.

Launched in 1969, Japan’s Mutsu faced a public-relations disaster in 1974, after a shielding flaw caused neutrons to leak during a reactor test. Although not catastrophic, the incident bred local opposition, which kept the ship out of operation for years.

The fourth, Russia’s Sevmorput, entered service in 1988 and spent decades carrying cargo along the northern sea route in the Arctic. It was the only nuclear-powered merchant ship still operating in the 2020s, having been kept on as a state-owned ice-capable cargo vessel.

Most early ships ran on low-enrichment uranium fuel, much as a civil nuclear power station does. But current propulsion options are more diverse7. They include technologies developed from long experience with icebreakers and small modular reactor programmes, such as light-water, high-temperature gas-cooled, lead-cooled fast, molten-salt and heat-pipe reactors. Other experimental designs are on the table.

However, an expanded technology menu only poses more safety questions. Any reactor-powered ship requires licensing, insurance, crewing, upkeep, port acceptance, emergency preparedness and response and support for decommissioning. Even Savannah’s final disposition remains a regulatory issue, yet to be solved. Some business models assume leased reactor modules and lower operating costs through remote monitoring, centralized refuelling and decommissioning. But those choices do not assure ship safety.

One of two nuclear reactors on board the Russian ship Rossiya. Credit: Patrick Landmann/Science Photo Library

Military records show where stress and poor planning can lead. Soviet nuclear-powered submarines have experienced loss-of-coolant accidents, unexpected power surges and damage to the reactor core. On the K-19 submarine in 1961, emergency repairs to restore cooling exposed sailors to lethal radiation. On K-27 in 1968, a liquid-metal-cooled reactor accident led again to fatal radiation exposures. On K-431 in 1985, a power surge during refuelling at Chazhma Bay, near Vladivostok, caused a steam explosion, killing several workers and contaminating the surrounding area.

Newer reactor designs can reduce some of the hazards, especially when they operate at low pressure and have sealed cores, systems for removing excess heat and robust containment structures8. But advanced approaches mainly shift problems rather than eliminating them. A molten-salt reactor might avoid high-pressure coolant accidents, but regulators still need to know whether salt corrosion can be managed after prolonged exposure to vibration. They will also be concerned about management of tritium and volatile fission products, adequate shielding and reliable removal of heat from radioactive decay after shutdown.

A nuclear-powered ship will require a reactor licence, ship certificates and port authorizations. Each involves separate judgements and permissions.

For the nuclear regulator, the core questions surround reactor safety, radiological protection and nuclear security. For the flag state, they include seaworthiness and crew safety. The port authority is concerned mainly with whether the vessel can enter the harbour, berth, discharge cargo, take refuge or be held in port without risk to the surrounding community.

For a conventional ship, these decisions are standard. For a nuclear-powered vessel, the relationships are more complex. If the harbour master, pilot, terminal operator, underwriter or emergency services are unable to understand the safety assurances provided by the reactor licence, then the document has little practical meaning.

Savannah’s port calls, for example, required extensive negotiations about berthing and transit as well as procedures to deal with emergencies and actions to reassure the public. Mutsu showed that, once confidence is lost, no rational argument is of any use; the ship won’t be welcome.

Threats of war and terrorism also pose risks that must be taken seriously. The cost–benefit analysis for nuclear shipping assumes orderly marine traffic and peacetime cooperation between ports. Current events in the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz since US and Israeli strikes on Iran challenge this assumption. Iranian-supported Houthi militias in Yemen have repeatedly used drones, missiles and unmanned boats against commercial shipping. In the Strait of Hormuz, restrictions and attacks have disrupted traffic and stranded thousands of seafarers.

If a nuclear-powered ship were to transit such waters, it could face the same missiles, drones, terrorist boarding attempts and electronic disruption as do conventional tankers, but with much greater consequences.

A marine reactor cannot explode like a nuclear weapon; the fuel and geometry of a civilian reactor make that impossible. But other risks cannot be ignored: damage to fuel, loss of shielding or coolant, hydrogen fires or steam explosions can release radioactive material and contaminated firefighting water, and create a shipwreck that no port is willing to receive.

Would a missile attack make a maritime reactor unsafe? It depends. A strike that hits the bow or a container stack might not reach a reactor located near the middle of the ship. However, a strike that hits the engine room, switchboard, emergency generator, control cables or cooling-water intakes could disable the systems that support a safe shutdown.

A container fire could burn for days and block rescue attempts. A hole below the waterline could compromise the vessel’s stability and flood compartments that are assumed to stay dry in the reactor design.

Autonomous ships are on the horizon: here’s what we need to know

Follow-up strikes might hit rescuers. A boarding party could evacuate the crew after the reactor is shut down, but decay heat still needs to be managed.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

Search author on:

                                         Google Scholar

Bispecific antibodies (orange and yellow, artist’s illustration) grab two different proteins rather than the standard one.Credit: Thom Leach/Science Photo Library

Cancer-fighting drugs called bispecific antibodies are having a moment. A growing number are making their way into the clinic, and researchers are developing increasingly elaborate molecules with new capabilities.

In the past five years, the number of bispecific antibodies — which can bind to two targets at the same time — approved by global regulators has grown from 3 to more than 20, says Christian Klein, who developed drugs at pharmaceutical company Roche in Basel, Switzerland, and is now launching his own biotechnology firm. The drugs generated US$18 billion in sales in 2025, he says.

Landmark cancer trial shows success against ‘undruggable’ cancer — raising hopes for future treatments

“Bispecifics have really kind of exploded,” says Paul Carter, who develops antibody therapies at Genentech, a biotechnology company in South San Francisco, California. “There are more flavours of bispecifics than Ben and Jerry’s ice cream.”

That success — as well as advances in protein production and artificial intelligence — is spurring efforts to create ‘multispecific’ antibodies that bind to three or more different targets, says Daniel Chen, co-founder and chief executive of Synthetic Design Lab, a biotechnology company in San Carlos, California. At the American Association for Cancer Research Drug Discovery and Development meeting in Boston, Massachusetts, at the end of July, for example, researchers presented multispecific-antibody cancer therapies that could be less toxic to healthy cells, more effective against tumours and better able to counter cancer’s pernicious ability to become resistant to treatment than conventional medicines.

Bispecific antibodies were first described more than 50 years ago, but the first treatment was only approved in 2009.

Part of the delay was due to working out how best to produce the molecules in the laboratory, says Jamie Spangler, a bioengineer at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland. Often, the process led to antibodies that bound to themselves and one another. “They would all come out as aggregated balls of garbage,” Spangler says. “With better tools and resources for protein production, we can dream up these molecules and make them happen.”

Most of the approved bispecific antibodies bind both to a protein expressed by cancer cells and to immune cells called T cells. Known as T-cell engagers, these antibodies seek to bring the two cells close to one another, stimulating the T cell to attack the cancer cell. At least 12 such T-cell engagers have been approved for treating cancers, including leukaemia and myeloma.

But there is still room for improvement, says Carter. Scientists’ growing understanding of tumour proteins and cell types is allowing them to design bispecific and multispecific antibodies that better stimulate an immune response to cancer than do earlier versions, and to create a ‘switch’ that prevents the therapy from acting until it is in the right place.

“We’re getting to this point where we’re starting to understand biology at a completely different level,” Chen says. “For the field of multispecifics, it really comes down to being able to understand biological complexity well enough to engineer them.”

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Nikki Forrester
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Nikki Forrester is a science journalist based in Davis, West Virginia.

Search author on:

Illustration by Claire Welsh/Nature. Adapted from image by Roman Samborskyi/Shutterstock

Smartphones and other digital technologies are a constant potential source of distraction. According to a 2025 survey by Reviews.org, an online resource that reviews mobile services and Internet providers, on average, US adults check their phones 186 times per day, or roughly once every five minutes (see go.nature.com/4b4zgje). They also spend 5 hours each day using smartphones, which amounts to 76 days of screen time per year, with Generation Z (those born between 1997 and 2012) and Millennials (those born between 1981 and 1996) spending the most time scrolling on their phones.

Over the past two decades, these has been increased interest in whether people’s ability to focus on a single task has deteriorated. People often report that they think their attention span has shortened (see go.nature.com/4dfz8yc). But data that definitively show a drop in attention are sparse.

LINK Should I use AI to help draft my science job application?

“Every year that passed, things that are so important to me, like reading books, having proper long conversations, even watching films, were getting harder and harder to do,” says Johann Hari, whose 2022 book Stolen Focus, outlines 12 reasons why people’s attention spans have declined, and offers tips to help people regain their focus. “I felt like I was running up a down escalator that was going faster and faster every year,” adds Hari about his declining ability to pay attention.

Staying focused is crucial for short-term memory, problem solving and creativity, whereas frequent distractions lead to more errors and higher levels of stress and frustration. “Attention is at the heart of all human achievement,” says Hari, who lives in London and Los Angeles, California. “Anything you’ve ever achieved in your life that you’re proud of, whether it’s starting a business, getting a PhD, being a good parent or learning to play the guitar, required a huge amount of sustained focus and attention.”

Nature’s careers team asked six attention researchers and educators for tips on how to mitigate disruptions and improve concentration.

“There are two rather separate attention systems,” says Michael Posner, a psychologist at the University of Oregon in Eugene, whose research career of more than 50 years led to the discovery that there are different forms of attention that are associated with different regions of the brain. One form is called executive attention, which describes the ability to focus on one thing. The other is the orienting system, which is guided by disruptions, including changes in lighting, unexpected sounds and other environmental influences.

My relationship with my PhD supervisor has become toxic — what do I do?

“Powerful external stimuli are pretty hard to resist,” Posner says. “That’s because orienting is important for being aware of potential predators.” If someone is deeply involved in a task, he says, it’s nevertheless helpful to know if a tiger is sneaking up on them.

Today, distractions often come in the form of interruptions such as text messages, e-mails, in-person requests, meetings and sudden noises. But people also actively and frequently interrupt themselves. “The problem is not that we get distracted,” says Gloria Mark, a psychologist and attention researcher at the University of California, Irvine. “The problem is: what do we do about it?”

The human brain isn’t able to consciously pay attention to more than one thing at a time, says Mark. Instead, it switches rapidly between tasks, which comes at a cost. “A lot of people think that multitasking is this badge of honour — it’s not,” says Mark. Generally, people who multitask make more errors and take longer to complete a single task because they have to reformulate a mental plan for completing that task every time their attention switches.

Individuals have their own peaks and valleys for when they focus best, says Mark. These personal rhythms vary depending on factors such as a person’s natural tendency to sleep and wake at certain times and how much sleep they get. In general, people have a period of peak focus mid-morning, then a dip around lunchtime and a second peak in the afternoon. “That’s on average,” Marks adds, noting that some people have focus peaks early in the morning, whereas others focus best later in the day or during the evening.

“For scientists, it’s really important for them to understand that they have these limited cognitive resources,” says Mark. “They should understand when their peak periods are and use those times to do their most important work.” For instance, instead of a researcher using their peak focus times to check their e-mail or attend meetings, they can allot that time to analysing data or writing a grant proposal. If someone isn’t aware of their personal rhythm of attention, Mark recommends keeping a diary and taking notes every half an hour or hour, to record how focused they feel.

How to vibe code in science: early adopters share their tips

One of the most effective ways to stay focused during peak periods is by putting away the major source of distraction — the mobile phone. On average, people in the United States spend 10 seconds looking at their phone each of the 200 or so times they check it daily1. Every interruption breaks focus and can make it harder to complete a task. “People find it difficult to work with their smartphone sitting next to them,” says Stefan van der Stigchel, a cognitive psychologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. “You won’t go on a diet with a pack of cookies next to your laptop, right? There’s one moment where you’re bored or when your will is not as strong, and all of the sudden you’re picking up your phone or you’re eating that cookie.”

Researchers can try putting their phones in a drawer, in another room or in a safe with a timer to keep it locked away for a set time. They can also set digital well-being limits on the phone itself. Apps such as Freedom and Cold Turkey Blocker can be used to block specific websites, apps or Internet access. Nova Corciega, a science instructor and education researcher at Negros Oriental State University Mabinay Campus in the Philippines, uses the digital well-being settings on her phone to limit her use of the social-media site Instagram to 35 minutes per day and the platform YouTube to one hour per day. “This gets me to think that I only have 35 minutes for this application per day, so I need to use it wisely,” she says.

In the moment, it’s easy to press ‘ignore’ on a timer, but over a longer period, setting digital limits can help researchers to establish mental routines that support their ability to focus and become more introspective about their attention. “We do so many things automatically and unconsciously, like picking up our phones, swiping them open, going to check e-mail,” Mark says. If researchers recognize when they feel an urge to check their phone or their e-mail inbox, they can then ask themselves whether they really need to. “It’s a way of counteracting habits and being intentional about what we do,” she adds.

Careers advice from scientists in industry

When scientists start to feel their attention spans waning, it’s time to take a break. “We prefer not to have lunch meetings because those are times when you can recharge your battery,” says van der Stigchel, who often takes walks outside (without his phone) during the working day. It can be difficult to take breaks, especially if someone pops into the laboratory to ask a question, but van der Stigchel says that it’s important to be strict about taking time to recharge. “I always say I’m never late for a meeting, including a meeting with myself,” he says. “Not working is part of what allows me to focus and be productive.”

Goal setting is another way that researchers can improve their attention spans. According to a 2023 study2 of 108 university students in the United States, those who set specific and difficult but achievable goals had shorter lapses in attention and stayed engaged with a task longer than did those who set vague goals.

However, goal setting improves attention only when a person is already committed to that goal: you can’t just write something down and expect that to be enough. Mark recommends that researchers write down their goals the night before work and reaffirm them the next morning. “Create a visualization of where you want to be at the end of the day,” she says. “I want to be sitting on my couch. I want to be reading. I want to be relaxing. I don’t want to be working on that paper.”

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Katarina Zimmer
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Review mills — researchers who write fake referee reports with coercive citation requests — are setting off a war in academic publishing. What happens to those caught in the middle?

Illustration by Andreion De Castro

In April 2023, Michael Börsch received what he describes as the laziest peer review in his 30-year career as a biophysical chemist. Reviewer 1 had given detailed feedback on his manuscript about an enzyme that drives the production of the energy-carrying molecule ATP, but Reviewer 2’s comments were, in Börsch’s view, “stupid”.

Reviewer 2 had pasted sections of Börsch’s abstract before listing a series of generic demands. One was “conclusion part is very long, make it brief”, a second asked him to “improve the English grammar” and a third mentioned measurements that weren’t part of the paper. The reviewer also recommended that Börsch and his co-authors include “some latest literature”, pointing to two unrelated studies about Alzheimer’s disease1,2.

“Really, this was a waste of time for all of us,” recalls Börsch, who is at the Friedrich Schiller University Jena in Germany. After revising the manuscript according to Reviewer 1’s remarks and rejecting Reviewer 2’s requests in a thoughtful, if slightly exasperated letter, his paper was published in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences3, which is part of the portfolio of MDPI, a publisher in Basel, Switzerland. Their work was done and dusted — or so Börsch thought.

Michael Börsch uses a specialized microscope to study signalling processes in cells at high resolution. Credit: Heiko Hellmann/UKJ

Michael Börsch uses a specialized microscope to study signalling processes in cells at high resolution. Credit: Heiko Hellmann/UKJ

In December 2023, marketing researcher Maria Ángeles Oviedo-García at the University of Seville in Spain posted on the post-publication peer-review platform PubPeer that language highly similar to that used by Börsch’s Reviewer 2 was also used in 85 reviewer reports for other papers. Oviedo-García included reviewer reports from Börsch’s study and dozens of others in a 2024 paper4 published in the journal Scientometrics about review mills — a term she coined to describe individual or groups of scientists who duplicate reviewer reports, probably with the goal of increasing the number of times their or their collaborators’ papers are cited.

Oviedo-García’s findings prompted MDPI to add a yellow warning notice at the top of dozens of affected papers, including Börsch’s study. The note expresses concern that the paper hadn’t been vetted adequately by one of the reviewers and that it was being put through additional peer review. Suddenly, in Börsch’s view, the paper he and his team had worked on for 15 months was invalidated for the wider academic community and was seemingly tainted by allegations of wrongdoing. And yet, we did not make any mistakes, Börsch says. “We did solid science. We did the review process,” he adds, visibly angry as he recounts the story on a Zoom call. How, he wondered, could this have happened?

Slapdash reviewer reports and ones that include unnecessary citation requests have long plagued academic publishing, but over the past few years the production of some has become much more sophisticated. Publishers, including Springer Nature and Taylor & Francis, and the journal PLoS ONE have told Nature that they have observed a worrying increase in reviewer reports with boilerplate language being reused for several manuscripts, and that these reports often also contain irrelevant citation requests. (Nature’s journalism is editorially independent from its publisher, Springer Nature.)

For instance, 0.05% of reviews received by Institute of Physics Publishing (IOPP) journals in 2025 were 100% identical and 0.3% had 80% overlap. One analysis of nearly 150,000 reports in MDPI journals, several PeerJ journals, The BMJ and a selection of computer-science venues found that between 0.5% and 1.3% were highly similar to other reviews, according to work5 presented at the 2025 International Congress on Peer Review and Scientific Publication.

Review mills not only threaten to sully the academic record with irrelevant references and compromise the quality of peer review, but are a bane to authors such as Börsch, who are finding themselves caught in the crossfire between review mills, the sleuths that hunt them and the journals scrambling to undo the damage. Understanding review mills requires a deep look at the systemic forces that drive fake reviews and the pressures faced by authors and journals to publish studies as quickly as possible.

Unless solutions are found, review-mill activity will only increase, warns psychologist Dorothy Bishop, an emeritus professor at the University of Oxford, UK, who has been investigating review mills with Oviedo-García. “I think it could be quite a common phenomenon,” she says, “and we’re probably only just [seeing a] tiny bit of it.”

One reason for the rise in reports by review mills is that publishers are increasingly making reviews public and hence accessible to sleuths like Oviedo-García. That’s why much of her evidence for review mills comes from MDPI journals — and PLoS ONE and PeerJ. “There should be more publishing of peer reviews, precisely because it is one way to be aware of this phenomenon,” Bishop says. The growing use of artificial-intelligence tools probably contributes, too, as they make it easy to produce generic review content.

“MDPI is much better at publishing the peer reviews than most other publishers. So there’s a sense in which it would be rather unfair to treat this as something to bang MDPI over the head with,” adds Bishop. An MDPI spokesperson says that improving transparency was a key reason for the publisher’s 2018 decision to give authors across all its journals the option to publish peer-review reports (reviewers can choose whether their name is public). The practice “is a key factor in ensuring openness”, says the spokesperson. “It boosts transparency and can serve as a means of increasing accountability.”

But specialists and sleuths also blame the well-documented publish-or-perish pressure faced by academics that favours the quantity of publications and citations over the quality of the research. Nature reached out to more than 30 writers of similar or duplicated reviews identified by Oviedo-García. Only one agreed to a substantive interview. Abd Dagestani, a sustainability researcher at Central South University in Changsha, China, says that much of the pressure comes from journals. He conveyed the sense that it was the feeling of being unvalued as a reviewer that led him to duplicate sections of his reviewer reports for several studies sent out by MDPI for review. When, during his PhD, journals were asking him to review papers, he recalls feeling honoured, hoping his contribution could somehow help to improve the work. Some journals — such as many published by MDPI — offered discounts on paper submissions in return for reviewing.

Sometimes, he’d spend a week reviewing papers, only to find that some editors would accept papers regardless of whether the authors had addressed his comments. “An editor did this once or twice, and I was like, ‘okay, so why am I spending time to review the paper?’,” he says. He felt that this was especially unfair, given that scientists are asked to review for free while publishers make money through authors’ work. Meanwhile, the review requests kept mounting; sometimes tallying ten a week from multiple publishers, including MDPI. At one point, he decided to provide more-generic comments on the studies rather than scrutinizing them in depth, he says, and ended up using similar phrasing across several reviews.

In a 2025 post on social-media platform X, Oviedo-García wrote that she had identified two identical reviewer reports written by Dagestani, and two others that were nearly identical, submitted by an anonymous reviewer. Dagestani’s reviews — for 2022 papers in the MDPI journals Sustainability and Processes — used some of the same statements, including “the abstract should briefly describe the research background” and “research gaps should be well mentioned in the introduction”.

Dagestani also suggested citing his own sustainability papers, but he says he only did this so that authors could learn from his studies, thus saving him time in evaluating their work in detail. “It was just a friendly suggestion,” he says. Dagestani was shocked when — “unfortunately”, he says — some authors included all requested references in their paper (the authors of the study in Processes included all six of his suggestions). Perhaps the authors thought they’d have an easier time getting their paper accepted if they pleased the reviewer, Dagestani speculates. Ultimately, however, Dagestani began declining many of the requests; he now reviews only for journals that he feels value his work.

When Nature journalists contacted Dagestani to fact-check details of his account, he ceased to meaningfully cooperate but added, “I don’t duplicate anything”.

When contacted for comment about Dagestani’s account, an MDPI spokesperson said that the publisher values reviewers’ time and expertise and “does not expect or encourage the use of duplicated or generic review reports”. Although the spokesperson recognized that researchers face growing demands on their time because of high submission volumes and review requests across publishers, editors are nevertheless expected to consider reviewer comments carefully and ensure that substantive concerns are addressed. By offering discounts to reviewers on article-processing fees, as well as reviewer awards and formal recognition of reviewing activity, MDPI helps to support reviewers and recognize their contributions. The publisher also works to identify reviewer ‘cartels’ and to flag misconduct. “Oviedo-García’s work serves as an important starting point for discussion among both academic communities and publishers, highlighting the need for a deeper understanding of how aspects of the publishing process can be manipulated,” the spokesperson said.

Each square in the left column represents a paper produced by the focal author.

Colours represent the broad research topic of each paper based on the journal the article is published in.

The right column represents all papers that interact with the focal author’s articles or with those of other researchers. Highlighted papers either cite the focal author or are cited by them.

The links represent citations from the focal author’s articles (left) to papers by other researchers (right).

Papers of other researchers (right) also cite articles by the focal author (left).

Sometimes, papers cite articles that have a completely different research topic. This can happen when, for instance, a new material or methodology (published in an applied-sciences journal) is used and cited in a health- or natural-sciences article. But they can also serve as indicators of artificially increased citation counts.

Links on the left indicate self-citations — papers by the focal author that cite another of their articles. Most researchers cite their other papers, because those studies are often relevant to their latest work. But some sleuths argue that excessive self-citation is used to inflate citation counts.

Another way to increase an article’s citation count is for a group of scientists to cite each other’s papers excessively, even when the citation is not especially relevant.

A further way to inflate citation counts is to suggest, during peer review, that the manuscript being assessed should include one or more papers by the reviewer’s collaborators in their reference list. In this example, the focal author cites a collaborator (yellow line), who reviews another scientist’s paper (dashed turquoise line), which then cites the focal author (purple line).

According to Bishop, most people involved in review mills are seeking to boost their citation numbers. These guide university decisions around hiring, promotions and tenure, and influence university rankings and funding decisions. The more that citation numbers are used as a metric of academic success, “the more people will try to game the citations”, she says.

Evidence for this comes from the observation that some people who provide duplicate reports are also habitual self-citers. Fabian Wittmers, a marine biologist and science sleuth at Oregon State University in Corvallis, mentions the engineer Rabiul Awual as one example of this phenomenon. Wittmers says that Awual’s high citation count — his work has been cited nearly 43,000 times according to Google Scholar — is partly due to a long-standing self-citation habit. In a now-retracted study about caesium removal from waste water6, for instance, Awual and his co-authors cited their own research 123 times — Wittmers considers 10–15 self-citations per paper to be the acceptable limit. The retraction notice, issued in October 2025, notes that the citations to Awual’s research, most of which were added at the revision stage, were of “either borderline relevance or no relevance whatsoever to the article”, and calls this practice “a violation of publishing ethics”. The notice also says that the authors disagree with the grounds for the retraction.

When contacted about their reasons for disagreeing with the retraction, co-author Nazmul Hasan asked Nature to refrain from sending them e-mails. Other co-authors, including Awual, did not meaningfully reply to requests for comment, instead responding with hostility and profanity.

Many more citations could stem from Awual’s review practices, too. Public reviews that Awual has written for papers in MDPI journals reveal that he often uses the same statements across reports and includes citation requests to his own research. Wittmers says that he has discovered dozens of studies by other researchers in Elsevier journals that cite large numbers of Awual’s studies. The reviews for those studies aren’t public but Wittmers suspects that these were reviewed by Awual or his collaborators.

One 2022 study7 in the journal Food Chemistry about the structural properties of dough in steamed bread, for instance, cites four of Awual’s papers about wastewater treatment. “This is not a one-off situation. There’s multiple papers in Food Chemistry where papers by Awual were cited that make no sense,” says Wittmers.

Wittmers suspects that for Awual and his collaborators, these kinds of review practice might be necessary to get their studies cited, because he deems many of the papers to be of poor quality. For instance, in a 2025 PubPeer post, Wittmers reported evidence of image duplication in six of Awual’s studies. “No one wants to cite these paper-mill products,” Wittmers says. “So you need to request that they get cited. And that’s why you review a lot.”

When Awual was invited to comment on Wittmers’ allegations of self-citation, review milling and image duplication, he asked Nature to stop sending “foolish” e-mails.

One author of a study in an Elsevier journal — who requested anonymity to avoid possible conflicts with reviewers or publishers — says that they felt coerced into citing Awual’s studies because of the anonymous review that they had received. After generic suggestions that the title be rephrased and that the study’s novelty be explained in the introduction, the review contained numerous reference requests. The reviewer concluded with a request to see the revised manuscript, implying — the author thought — that they might recommend rejecting the paper if the requests weren’t fulfilled. “I felt pressured by the reviewer,” the author says.

They say that they’ve asked the journal to review the irregular references and that they’ll alert journal editors if they encounter similar reviewer reports in the future. In general, the author says, they’ve seen a worrying increase in incoherent reviewer reports that seem to be referring to entirely different manuscripts. “It seems that many journals do not perform even minimal checks on the coherence and relevance of peer reviews, leaving scientists vulnerable to inadequate reviewing practices,” they note.

When asked for comment about Elsevier’s handling of reviewer reports, a spokesperson said that the publisher’s policies address citation manipulation by reviewers and that the publisher has training in place to help editors to recognize such practices. “Reviewers should not suggest citations to the reviewer’s (or their associates’) work unless the suggested citations are for genuine scientific reasons,” note the policies. “Editors may remove citations that, in their view, are inappropriate from reviewer comments.”

Why Awual was invited to review for journals outside his scientific expertise is unclear. In general, Wittmers suspects that review mills often make an editor’s job easier, because they struggle to find reviewers among an increasingly overworked academic workforce. Review mills might respond quickly to review requests, helping journals to reduce the time spent on article reviews.

Nature journalists asked Springer Nature for comment on its processes for dealing with coercive peer-review practices and promoting academic integrity. A spokesperson said that the publisher has been working to identify and prevent review-mill activity by examining peer-review content and investigating networks of compromised individuals.

“For cases where we can document repeated attempts to manipulate citation practices, individuals are suppressed from acting as reviewers in future and may be subject to further sanctions, such as being blocked from publishing in our journals,” the spokesperson says. Authors can report coercive citation requests to a journal’s editor-in-chief or to the publisher, and editors should inform their relevant publishing contact, they added.

Scientists often cite some of their past work, because the papers are relevant to their current research. For example, this is the citation map of immunologist John Tregoning, who has worked as a columnist for Nature.

But some sleuths argue that excessive self-citation (more than, say, 10–15 per paper) and other methods are being used to inflate citation counts. For example, this is Rabiul Awual’s citation map.

Awual’s most-cited paper, for instance, has 748 citations, of which 79 were by his own papers.

In total, roughly 16% of Awual’s citations are self-citations.

One way to detect attempts at inflating citations is to look at a citation’s original paper: if the article seems to have an unusual topic compared with the citing paper, it’s possible that this paper’s authors were asked to cite it by a reviewer, say sleuths. This paper, which focuses on steamed bread7, cites several of Awual’s wastewater papers, for example.

In another example, Awual’s applied-sciences papers were cited 20 times by a now-retracted chemistry study.

Collectively, numerous citations from unusual sources might suggest that coercive reviews have contributed to total citation counts.

All data were collected through Digital Science’s Dimensions database. Digital Science is operated by the Holtzbrinck Publishing Group, which has a share in Nature’s publisher, Springer Nature.

Awual did not meaningfully respond to requests for comment.

Review-mill activity can go unnoticed for years and be tricky to spot, Bishop says. Moreover, many people engaged in such activity use identifiers from the PubMed biomedical-science database, rather than full references to make their citation requests, Bishop adds. This means that overworked editors might not recognize improper requests. People involved in review mills also escape detection by requesting that authors cite their collaborators’ papers rather than their own. This might have been the case with Börsch’s Reviewer 2: chemist Qaiser Mahmood at the Guangdong Laboratory of Chemistry and Fine Chemical Engineering in Shantou, China, who Oviedo-García found to have duplicated reviews. Nature journalists determined that the papers1,2 Mahmood asked Börsch and his colleagues to cite were co-authored by some of Mahmood’s collaborators. Altogether, Oviedo-García has identified 85 similar reviewer reports that Mahmood, his collaborators or anonymous researchers have written for various journals, requesting up to 54 studies to be cited. Mahmood did not respond to requests for comment about his and his collaborators’ review practices.

Suggesting that manuscript authors cite the reviewer’s collaborators’ papers rather than the reviewer’s own could be part of a quid-pro-quo dynamic in which those associates reciprocate in kind when they are reviewers, Bishop says. Such networks can grow into large review cartels. For example, Bishop and Oviedo-García identified a group of at least nine Italian oncologists who used similar review templates to get their work cited in 170 articles8. “In this mill, we’re pretty sure an editor is also involved, which helps them allocate papers to friends who will do this,” Bishop says.

Although journals are getting better at detecting review mills, it’s often thanks to science sleuths that journals — and authors themselves — are made aware of this activity. Börsch only learnt of Mahmood’s behaviour through Oviedo-García’s PubPeer post and her Scientometrics paper4, which lists 263 reviewer reports with evidence of review-mill activity. Börsch feels that by implicating his study in her paper about misconduct, he and his co-authors were being unfairly criticized even though he — and many others whose papers are included in Oviedo-García’s article — had rejected the reviewers’ citation requests.

Börsch asked Oviedo-García to remove any mentions of his study from her paper, but received no response. Oviedo-García, whose paper doesn’t mention Börsch’s study directly, says that she associated only reviewers with fraud or misconduct. “It is crystal clear stated in the article that the authors are not to blame,” she says.

Börsch asked the editor-in-chief of Scientometrics to retract Oviedo-García’s paper, but his request was declined. MDPI’s publishers refused to remove the yellow label plastered above the online version of his paper. Börsch has also contacted Mahmood, but did not hear back. He has e-mailed his funding agency to see whether there was anything they could do — all to no avail. “For my PhD student, it’s a disaster to have his first paper branded like this,” Börsch says.

When MDPI sent Börsch’s study to another group of reviewers — which it did without the authors’ permission — it seems to have sent out the original manuscript rather than the updated version, in which Börsch had responded to the helpful first reviewer, he says. When one of the new reviewers had an entire series of further requests, Börsch decided that enough was enough. In his view, the post-publication peer review unfairly placed the responsibility on him to correct the scientific record when it was the publisher’s responsibility to ensure that studies were vetted properly. He sees the extra peer review as a “smokescreen” to cover up MDPI’s failure to ensure adequate review. “At one point, I decided not to respond to any of their e-mails anymore,” he says.

To his fury, in June, a representative of the International Journal of Molecular Sciences asked Börsch and his colleagues for an update. If the journal didn’t hear from the authors soon, it “may have to withdraw the manuscript due to loss of contact”, they wrote.

When asked about Oviedo-García’s findings, an MDPI spokesperson says that since the Scientometrics paper4 the publisher has introduced measures to prevent similar issues from arising in the future. “We have strengthened oversight of the peer-review process to support robust editorial decision-making, and we are vigilant about monitoring all submissions for potential forms of reviewer misconduct.”

And when asked for comment on Börsch’s views, the MDPI spokesperson acknowledged the broader challenges of assigning blame when correcting the scientific record. “No system is entirely immune to error or systematic forms of misconduct,” they say. Moreover, post-publication actions such as corrections or retractions are crucial for maintaining the integrity of the scientific record, they add. “The purpose of post-publication notices is to inform readers in a clear and transparent manner, rather than to serve as a punitive measure.”

Finally, when asked about the suggestion that MDPI might retract Börsch’s paper, the spokesperson said that “retraction would only be considered in cases where the findings of an article are found to be unreliable, and this has not been the case in any of the investigations undertaken to date”.

“It’s very, very unfortunate for authors who are actually innocent in this,” Bishop acknowledges. “They are really just used as fodder” and “do the dirty work for the reviewers”, who then get citations. But journals face tricky decisions when dealing with such cases. Is a paper’s quality compromised even if the authors did not cite the requested papers, as in Börsch’s case? Renee Hoch, the head of publication ethics at the publisher PLOS in San Francisco, California, says that the fact that a paper didn’t receive proper review can harm a journal’s trust in a particular article. In cases in which PLoS ONE has identified peer-review integrity issues that affect several studies — which can include review-mill activity — the journal will consider retracting affected papers or taking other action, such as publishing an expression of concern, depending on the nature and severity of the concerns. “We don’t use retraction as a form of punishment. It’s just to correct the published literature, but [authors] perceive it sometimes as either a punishment or as an allegation,” Hoch says.

PLoS ONE also removes people involved in review mills from its active reviewer databases and removes any involved editors from editorial boards. But fully stamping out review mills can be a game of whack-a-mole. Awual and one of his colleagues, for instance, seem to have been banned from reviewing for one Elsevier journal, but Wittmers has seen Awual’s studies being cited in other Elsevier journals, suggesting that he or his collaborators continue to review for some of the publisher’s outlets, Wittmers says.

Awual listed the Dhaka Institute for Materials Science (DIMS) in Bangladesh and the Japan Atomic Energy Agency as his most-recent affiliations. In March, Elsevier retracted a 2024 environmental-chemistry paper9 after Wittmers questioned on PubPeer why the paper contained citations to ten of Awual’s studies. According to the retraction notice, “the authors said that these were added in response to the reviewer comments. However, the authors do not appear to have checked or questioned the relevancy of these references to their work.” Elsevier has also retracted some of Awual’s own studies for reasons such as extra affiliations being added for the authors without the editor’s approval.

When asked about actions taken with regard to Awual’s or his collaborators’ review activity, an Elsevier spokesperson said, “this case is currently under investigation, and we cannot disclose further information until the investigation is complete”.

When Nature approached a principal scientist at the Materials Science Research Laboratory at the University of Dhaka, which, according to some of Awual’s papers10, is the parent institution of DIMS, they responded that “there is no existence of any institute named DIMS associated with the University”. The website dims-bd.org — which one of Awual’s e-mail addresses is registered to — is “under construction”. Nature contacted the Japanese Atomic Energy Agency in Funaishikawa about Awual; a spokesperson says that he is not currently affiliated with the agency and that they’ve requested that publishers remove the incorrect affiliation.

Some journals are working on ways to prevent review-mill activity to begin with. IOPP, for instance, has released a duplicate-review checker to help editors to identify reviewer reports that contain language similar to that of reviews for other IOPP journals. Kim Eggleton, IOPP’s head of peer review and research integrity in Bradford, UK, says that because review mills operate across journals, the providers of peer-review submission systems could incorporate such checks into their platforms so that publishers can detect reviewers who have given duplicate reviews at other journals.

Wholly preventing the issue, however, would require funders, institutions and publishers to address the pressures on scientists that lead them to duplicate reviews and to try to game the citation system.

In the meantime, Börsch says he no longer submits papers to MDPI journals. Although he has given up on trying to remove the yellow notice from his ATP enzyme study, he hopes that it will serve as a warning to other scientists and prevent them from falling into a similar trap. However, for him, “it’s not a nice reminder”, he says. “It just recalls the troubles we have, and that they are not solved.”

Katarina Zimmer is a science journalist based in Berlin.

Susan Collins, a Republican senator from Maine, has expressed opposition to a proposal from the White House that would give political appointees control over research grants.Credit: Aaron Schwartz/Getty

US senators from both sides of the political aisle released a draft spending bill on 2 August that, if passed, would temporarily halt a far-reaching and controversial proposal by the White House to overhaul federally funded science. The proposal, which states that its goal is to improve “transparency, accountability, and oversight” for federal funds, contains provisions that would reshape US science, including putting political appointees in charge of federal grant review and restricting collaboration between US and international scientists. If finalized, the White House rule could go into effect on 1 October.

White House proposes vast overhaul of US science funding: what you need to know

The overarching goal of the latest bill from the US Senate Committee on Appropriations, which oversees federal spending, is to prevent a government shutdown. US agencies, including funders such as the National Science Foundation (NSF), might have to furlough workers and shut down certain operations after 1 October — when the 2026 federal fiscal year ends — if Republican and Democratic members of the US Congress haven’t agreed on future spending levels. This bill would instead extend funding for agencies until 11 December, keeping it at existing levels while politicians continue to negotiate. As a condition of keeping the government open with this bill, lawmakers included a section that would prevent the White House proposal on federal grants from taking effect until the December extension date.

Science-advocacy organizations have lauded the Senate committee’s bill. “It would not only keep the government open, but it would safeguard scientific progress,” said Russ Paulsen, president of Research!America, a non-profit health-research advocacy group in Arlington, Virginia, in a statement.

Last year, an impasse between Democrats and Republicans over government spending led to a record 43-day government shutdown, during which science-funding agencies, including the National Institutes of Health, halted operations such as issuing research grants.

Many Democratic members of Congress are strongly opposed to the proposal to overhaul federally funded science, which was issued by the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) on 29 May. In June, 125 Democrats in the US House of Representatives sent a letter to the director of the OMB, Russell Vought, saying that “undoing the peer review process in favor of political grantmaking will delay and disrupt health care research that millions of Americans depend on”.

Inside the new political screening that’s stalling NIH grants

Some Republicans have also shown discontent with the proposal. The OMB rule would “undermine scientific and biomedical research, and conflict with Congress’ control over the federal funding process”, said Susan Collins, a Republican senator from Maine who chairs the appropriations committee, in a statement last month.

For the OMB proposal to be blocked until 11 December, the Senate committee’s bill would have to be approved by the entire Senate and then find support in the US House of Representatives. Both chambers of Congress would need to pass the legislation before it could be signed into law by Republican President Donald Trump.

Although the outcome is not certain, some policy watchers are optimistic that the bill will pass, because many members of Congress are on the ballot in November’s US mid-term elections. Not only do lawmakers want to avoid a government shutdown — which would be viewed poorly by many voters — but the OMB rule has also been unpopular with the public. The OMB’s proposal to put political appointees in charge of research and development is a “disaster for American scientific leadership”, says Asad Ramzanali, director of artificial intelligence and technology policy at Vanderbilt University’s Policy Accelerator in Nashville, Tennessee. The fact that the Senate effort is bipartisan is “promising”, he says. “But nothing is done until a bill passes both chambers and is signed into law.”

Hidden Creatures: Luscious Leeches, Bashful Botflies, and the Wondrous, History-Shaping World of Parasites Dino Martins Knopf (2026)

Togetherness: How Symbiosis Can Change the Way We Understand Our World, Ourselves and Our Future Rowan Hooper Fern (2026)

Humans often fancy that we are independent creatures, living sealed off from other species. Yet, that false sense of separation vanishes when bacteria make us sick or a bear raids the rubbish bin. Whether we like it or not, we are interconnected with the living world. Two books explore the ties that bind all living things.

In Togetherness, biologist and science journalist Rowan Hooper proposes that interspecies cooperation is the key driver of life’s evolutionary journey. Hidden Creatures, by entomologist and evolutionary biologist Dino Martins, takes a darker view. Life lives off life, the author explains. “Half of all living things are mooching off others!”

Take parasites, which, Martins notes, have afflicted humans since the beginning of recorded history. Inscribed in ancient Canaanite on an ivory comb are the words: “May this tusk root out the lice of the hair and the beard.” It is the oldest known sentence written using an alphabet. Lice continue to prey on humans nearly 4,000 years later — as do countless other parasites.

Rights for rivers and ice cream for all: top reads for the summer holid

Martins invites us to take a second look at these oft-villainized creatures that are, nevertheless, integral to life. Many today who profess to ‘love nature’ tend to edit out the less savoury and less inspiring parts. But that is misguided, the author says. You must “seek to understand all of nature”, he insists, or “you will end up loving and understanding none of it”.

His book is not for the squeamish. Martins introduces us to caterpillars that are eaten alive by squirming wasp pupae. He devotes a chapter to a rogues’ gallery of worms; one species (Stephanurus dentatus) lives in the urinary tract of pigs, another (Rhabditis orbitalis) in the eyes of mice and voles, and even more species live in the lungs of birds.

Others dwell in the human body. Today, one-third of the human population is infected with nematode worms, often with grisly consequences. Hookworms, once called the “vampires of the south” owing to their prevalence in the southern United States, live for years in the intestine, sapping millions of their strength and vitality.

Tsetse flies in Africa carry the protozoan parasites that cause sleeping sickness. Brain worms infest moose, deer and elk. Thirty-metre-long tapeworms have been found in the bellies of whales. The list goes on.

Wasps can lay eggs inside caterpillars, which the larvae consume after hatching.Credit: Jim Lane/Education Images/UIG/Getty

Parasites can even drive their hosts to kill themselves, when it is to the parasite’s advantage to do so. Take the Gordian worm, which infects the brain of praying mantises and alters gene expression in a way that makes them jump into a body of water and drown. Only then can the worm fulfil its biological destiny by laying its eggs, which hatch in the water.

But there is a silver lining to the parasitic cloud. Some creatures have come up with ingenious ways to combat their parasites, such as birds that evict itchy parasites from their feathers by rubbing themselves with formic acid secreted by the ants that bite them.

Leech therapy shows promise in treating osteoarthritis. Leeches secrete substances with anti-inflammatory and anaesthetic properties, which relieve pain and reduce swelling. They are sometimes used in specialized microsurgeries and skin grafts: the anti-clotting agent that they secrete prevents the surgeon’s incision from prematurely closing.

Martins’s final verdict on the parasites that he so exuberantly describes? They are crucial actors that clean up Earth by decomposing dead flesh and recycling it. Without this invaluable service, ecosystems could not function.

Hooper’s book focuses on the more harmonious side of life. Symbiotic relationships in which two or more species live in partnerships that benefit all parties have been essential in the evolution of life — yet scientists have taken a long time to fully recognize this. “Cooperation is much harder to see than competition,” Hooper explains. “Fights are easier to measure than favors.”

How AI is revealing the secret lives of animals from hummingbirds to pumas

Lichen, Hooper says, provided the first evidence that individuals are not as delineated as we had once thought. What looks like a single organism is in fact a partnership in which algae feed fungi with photosynthesized sugars, and fungi provide algae with water, minerals and a secure structure in which to live. Lichens have been known since ancient times, but it was not until the nineteenth century that scientists recognized their nature as a composite organism.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.title: Want to get more from AI? Treat every prompt like an experiment
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: James M. Dewar
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
James M. Dewar is an assistant professor of biochemistry at Vanderbilt University School of Medicine in Nashville, Tennessee.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

To get the most out of using AI tools in research, apply the science skills that you already have. Credit: Laurence Dutton/Getty

In late 2024, artificial intelligence reached PhD-level performance on scientific-reasoning benchmarks, and in 2025 it approached the measurement ceiling for one such test. In response, I developed an AI module and taught it to incoming biomedical PhD students at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee, where I direct AI initiatives for the interdisciplinary graduate pathway.

As part of the course, I surveyed the students and found that 81% had used AI tools for science. Yet, only 5% met a baseline level of proficiency in writing prompts for AI; after the module, 48% did. Since then, I have taught classes on AI-assisted grant writing, made AI a core part of the scientific training in my laboratory and shared preprints on scientific AI use1 and teaching methods2 for others to adapt and reuse. All of this taught me that you don’t need a computational background to use AI well — my research focuses on the biochemistry of DNA replication and repair. AI is a tool: to get the most from it, you need to apply the scientific training that you already have.

The single most useful strategy I have developed is to treat each prompt as an experiment and the output as a result. Here are ten tips I’ve learnt for running those experiments effectively.

An AI language model can reason only about what it can reach. Web search is the minimum; for biomedical work, granting the model access to the literature, using PubMed or through literature tools such as Scite and Elicit, grounds outputs in published work. This can be done by using an open standard called the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which provides a standardized way to connect applications to external systems. It appears as ‘connectors’ in Claude, as ‘apps’ in ChatGPT and as MCP servers in other tools. Setting up the right tools is part of designing the experiment, so you can give it the best chance of being successful by arming the model with as much information as possible.

Models parse unstructured text less cleanly than structured text, so sometimes it helps to write prompts in a structured format. For example, Markdown formatting works across all major models and is usually enough for prompting; XML helps to structure more-complex inputs (and is particularly effective with Claude); JSON adds more rigour when you need it. Just as scientists use formatting conventions to navigate complex text, so do models. I’ve built a tool to help teach people how to do this, which is free to use.

When running a new assay, you start from the manufacturer’s protocol. The equivalent for an AI system is built into the model itself: you can describe what you want in plain language and ask the model to write the prompt that will achieve it, then run that prompt in a fresh conversation. This is called meta-prompting, and because the model knows how to construct effective prompts, it is the fastest way to get a model working productively. For instance, to summarize a paper, you might ask the model to: “Generate a prompt optimized for [your AI tool] that asks it to summarize a scientific manuscript provided by the user. The prompt should instruct the AI tool to summarize the introduction, results and discussion separately, identify limitations acknowledged by the authors and critically evaluate whether the manuscript’s conclusions are supported by the evidence.” Alternatively, you can use a general-purpose meta-prompt, or an interactive tool that writes one for you.

Just as researchers lean on published protocols rather than reinventing every method, you can start from prompts that others have validated already. The types of prompt that are effective differ across models and shift over time, so a vetted starting point saves you from having to rediscover what already works. I maintain a set of prompts1 for common scholarly tasks (literature summaries, manuscript critique and feedback on writing) on Zenodo — a general-purpose research repository — and as an online library, which is free to use and adapt.

Like any experimental system, this one has limits that are worth recognizing. The conversational interface exists because it suits humans, but models become less reliable as a conversation grows3, and they cannot forget anything that’s already been said. A useful strategy is to develop a task across a conversation, then get the model to condense the result into a single prompt that you then run in a fresh conversation.

Conversations can also degrade mid-thread: for instance, the model might seem to ignore instructions, or you could have to correct the same error repeatedly. This happens because models prioritize the start and end of a conversation over the middle4. Treat this like troubleshooting a protocol. Branch from a point before the errors appeared by editing a message from earlier in the conversation. Alternatively, summarize the stuff that matters and start afresh.

Outputs vary across runs because AI models sample probabilistically. Running the same prompt several times in separate conversations reveals what is robust and what is an artefact. This is the AI-model equivalent of conducting biological replicates, and it improves completeness: the more times that you run a prompt, the more of the relevant answer space you see. Do not assume completeness until repeated runs stop surfacing new answers.

https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: On this day in space! Aug. 9, 1976: Soviet Luna 24 sample return probe launches to the moon
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Hanneke Weitering
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
Luna 24 was a robotic sample return mission and the third of its kind.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Aug. 9, 1976, the Soviet space program launched its last moon mission.

Luna 24 was a robotic sample return mission and the third of its kind. It lifted off on a Proton-K rocket from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan and safely landed on the lunar surface nine days later.

The probe landed in a dark plain of the moon known as Mare Crisium, or the "Sea of Crises" and collected 6 ounces (170.1 grams) of soil samples, which it brought back to Earth on Aug. 22, 1976. Scientists then found that the samples from Luna 24 contained tiny traces of water — about 0.1% by mass.

The Soviet Union lost the Space Race to land the first humans on the moon, but its Luna program of robotic probes was prolific. The country's Luna 2 was the first spacecraft ever to land on the moon (it slammed into the lunar surface in 1959), with the more advanced Luna 9 making the first-ever soft-landing on the moon in February 1966, beating NASA's Surveyor 1 by about 4 months.

By 1976, 12 NASA astronauts had walked on the moon, the last two on Apollo 17 in 1973 and the Space Race was over. But the Soviet moon program was not, with Luna probes and Lunakhod rovers.

The Luna sample return missions consisted of a lander equipped with a descent stage, ascent stage and Earth return capsule. The probes could collect samples of the moon, place them in the return capsule on the ascent stage, then rocket it from the moon for the trip back to Earth. NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has captured photos of the descent stages of Luna 16, Luna 20 and Luna 24 still on the moon.

The Luna 23 spacecraft remained on the moon entirely, as it was damaged during landing and wasn't able to return a sample. NASA's LRO images later revealed Luna 23 likely fell on its side. But Luna 24, the last of the series, worked as planned, landing on Mare Crisium on Aug. 16, 1976, collecting a sample of the lunar regolith and launching back into space less than 24 hours later.

While Luna 24 was the last Soviet moon sample return mission, it was not the last for Russia.

In August 2023, Russia's Roscosmos space agency launched the Luna 25 mission, its first in 47 years, toward the lunar south pole.

Luna 25 was planned to be the first in a new fleet of moon probes, but ultimately crashed into the moon after an orbital maneuver went wrong.

https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: Exploring 'very low Earth orbit': The world's 1st air-breathing satellite thruster could soon get a test run
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Julian Dossett
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
"By enabling satellites to fly lower, longer and more efficiently, we are enabling higher-resolution Earth observation, much better satellite communications, more responsive and accurate missions and a more sustainable orbital infrastructure."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new way to move around Earth's outer atmosphere could soon get a field test.

The Spanish company Kreios Space plans to launch into orbit the world's first satellite that uses scooped-up air to push it forward, the company announced on Tuesday (Aug. 4).

The technology Kreios Space has been developing is called air-breathing electric propulsion (ABEP). It relies on air sourced from Earth's atmosphere, which is then heated up, ionized and expelled to generate thrust.

This method will allow satellites in very low Earth orbit (VLEO) — the region from roughly 60 miles to 250 miles (100 to 400 kilometers) above our planet — to counteract atmospheric drag without the aid of liquid fuel.

"Kreios is building the satellites that make sustained operations in very low Earth orbit possible," Kreios Space CEO Adrián Senar said in the Aug. 4 announcement.

"By enabling satellites to fly lower, longer and more efficiently, we are enabling higher-resolution Earth observation, much better satellite communications, more responsive and accurate missions and a more sustainable orbital infrastructure," he continued.

Kreios Space chose Lithuanian-based Kongsberg NanoAvionics to provide the satellite bus that will carry the ABEP system into orbit for the test run.

"Kreios is tackling one of the most demanding operating environments in space, and this mission joins a very short list of European VLEO initiatives," Kongsberg NanoAvionics CEO Atle Wøllo said in the same statement.

"Our engineering team has worked closely with Kreios to configure the MP42 satellite bus to the mission's specific requirements and support the integration of Kreios' technology," he added.

Kreios Space did not give a target launch date for the mission in Tuesday's statement, saying that the company will launch it "at a time when interest in and development of VLEO technologies has accelerated." But the company's website identifies 2027 as a notional target for its first space mission.

Satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO) — altitudes of roughly 100 miles to 1,200 miles (160 to 2,000 km) — generally don't need constant propulsion. Usually, a small boost from traditional thrusters here and there is enough to keep a LEO satellite on the right track. To power the thrusters, these satellites usually have some form of fuel built in.

VLEO works differently. It's low enough that there's still some atmosphere present, which generates drag on spacecraft. If you want a satellite to move around VLEO, it'll need to employ propulsion most or all of the time to counteract that drag. Any fuel that the satellite brings with it therefore won't last long.

So, if satellites are going to operate in VLEO, it would be very helpful to have a method of propulsion that doesn't require traditional fuel — a method like ABEP.

Satellites in VLEO have a few advantages over those operating in LEO, like sharper imagery thanks to the closer vantage point. One of the biggest advantages is that VLEO is much less crowded. There are thousands of satellites in LEO — most of them SpaceX's Starlink broadband spacecraft — and the number is growing all the time. But VLEO has plenty of room.

If ABEP technology works and companies start outfitting satellites with this new propulsion method, then we might start seeing satellites operate quite close to Earth, zooming through the atmosphere and using the air around it to stay on course.
