https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqlx.title: Puerto Rico rations water supplies due to intense drought
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqlx.text:
Hundreds of thousands of people are going without running water for two days at a time in Puerto Rico, as authorities in the US territory take drastic measures to combat a severe drought.

Many households on the Caribbean island have been split into two groups - with each having their water supply shut off for 48 hours on a rotating basis.

Residents in the capital, San Juan, where the taps were turned off on Friday, decried the rationing. Officials have not said when the measure will end.

Most of Puerto Rico is facing moderate to severe drought conditions, according to the US Drought Monitor, which has been compounded by long-term issues with the island's infrastructure.

Puerto Rico's water authority says about 65% of the water it produces is lost or goes unbilled, much of it through leaks and ageing pipes, according to the BBC's US news partner CBS.

The island's Governor Jenniffer González has acknowledged these issues, but says rationing was implemented due to the weather, which has left the crucial Carraízo reservoir depleted.

Puerto Rico experienced its driest July on record, with 68% of the island currently facing drought conditions.

Seven regions usually served by the reservoir have been affected, with 180,000 properties subject to rationing, the government said.

González said the decision was taken "after carefully evaluating the current conditions of the Carraízo reservoir in conjunction with weather forecasts".

"This situation is beyond our control," she said in a statement. "It is the result of the weather conditions we have been facing, which experts had warned about weeks ago."

As the mains outages take effect, people have been queuing at water tanker trucks sent to affected regions to fill up large bottles.

"It's unbelievable to live through this today," San Juan resident Gloriany Baba told CBS, describing the conditions as "brutal".

But there is some confusion in the territory as to which households and businesses will be affected and when.

The Morcelo area, south of San Juan, was promised water on Friday, with the supply set to be shut off on Sunday, after the first 48-hour period had ended. But residents have told local media that running water was not available.

"People are uncertain because they know we're in the 48-hour window where we're supposed to have drinking water," community leader Rubén Torres told newspaper El Nuevo Dia on Saturday.

"What's happening? The first 24 hours have already passed and the water hasn't arrived."

As well as degraded infrastructure and a lack of rain, experts have also pointed to too much sediment in resevoirs as a factor in the water crisis.

Water rationing measures have been tried previously in 2020 and 2015, when some 400,000 households only received running water every third day.

Puerto Rico has previously been shaken by the kind of extreme weather events scientists say are more likely due to human-induced climate change.

The island's electricity grid was devastated in 2017 by Hurricane Maria, which caused thousands of deaths. Scientists say the extreme amounts of rainfall it brought was made more likely due to climate change.

González also told CNN there were more than 1,000 wildfires currently burning in Puerto Rico, and that rain could return when a cloud of Saharan dust drifts away from the Caribbean.

"It's a difficult situation," she said, adding that the US federal government was "helping us out", without elaborating.

BBC News has approached the US disaster agency Fema for comment.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c935.title: Man arrested after boat capsizes near Statue of Liberty killing woman and infant
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c935.text:
The operator of a boat that overturned near the Statue of Liberty, killing a woman and a baby, has been arrested and charged with reckless endangerment, New York police said.

Officials said a large search and rescue operation was launched after the incident near New York Harbour on Saturday night. Twelve people who were initially rescued from the water are all reported to be in stable condition.

New York police divers later found a 27-year-old woman and a five-month-old girl, who were transported to a nearby hospital where they later died.

The names of passengers and the specific cause of the incident have not been released.

Around 22:25 local time (03:25 BST), police received a 911 call reporting an overturned boat in the waters near Liberty Island, which houses the iconic statue.

A nearby tour operator Sea the City saw the capsized boat and helped pull 11 people from the water, the company's founder Adam Schwartz said according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

The rescue involved two Coast Guard boats, four fire department boats, two police boats and a police helicopter, the USCG said.

The investigation into the incident is ongoing, officials said. The boat's operator, a 46-year-old Manhattan resident, faces 13 counts of reckless endangerment, officials said.

Coast Guard investigators are also determining whether the boat was illegally chartered. An illegal charter is any passenger-for-hire vessel operation that does not have required credentials, safety equipment, and certificate of inspection.

"We are extremely grateful for the heroic, swift actions of our partner agencies and Good Samaritan vessel who assisted in rescuing survivors from the water," said Capt Doreen McCarthy of the USCG.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c935.summary: Woman and baby died after boat overturned near Statue of Liberty in New York Harbour. Police say boat operator arrested and charged with reckless endangerment. 12 people rescued from water are in stable condition.

War in the Middle East

The appointment of Mohsen Rezaei, a longtime military commander, to a top security post suggests that the country’s establishment is consolidating power.

Iran is replacing its top national security adviser with a longtime military commander whose appointment could represent a further consolidation of power by the country’s old-guard security establishment.

Mohsen Rezaei, who led Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps during the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s, will be the new secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, a spokesman for Iran’s president wrote on social media on Sunday.

He had been serving as an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.

Mr. Rezaei is replacing Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who stepped into the role when the council’s previous secretary, Ali Larijani, was killed in an Israeli strike during the U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran earlier this year.

Seyed Mehdi Tabatabaei, a spokesman for President Masoud Pezeshkian, said on social media that Mr. Zolghadr had resigned, would take up a new position, and that Mr. Rezaei would take his place.

While Mr. Zolghadr is himself a veteran of the Revolutionary Guards, Iran’s most powerful security force, analysts say he does not have the authority of some other current and former senior military commanders.

The council, which includes top civilian and military officials, plays a critical role in deciding Iranian policy on the ongoing conflict with the United States. It agreed in June to a memorandum of understanding that would pause the war, although that agreement quickly fell apart because of disputes between the United States and Iran about control over the Strait of Hormuz.

A photojournalist with The New York Times details the displacement and danger, in words and images, that have come to define his home.

I’m the host of The World.

Gaza under a cease-fire remains an extremely violent place. Israel has continued striking on a near-daily basis, killing more than 1,000 Palestinians since October, according to the Gaza health ministry. Among them are senior Hamas officials, but also civilians, including children, my colleagues report.

More than 60 percent of the Gaza Strip remains occupied by Israel, which says that Hamas is seeking to rearm and that Israeli forces are targeting militants. Yesterday, Israel rejected a 15-point plan backed by the Trump administration that called for Hamas to disarm in exchange for an end to the occupation.

The war in Gaza has been hard to cover because Israel has barred foreign journalists from entering the territory. The cease-fire is hard to cover for the same reason. Which is why I want to introduce you to Saher Alghorra, a Gazan photographer who has been documenting the war for The New York Times and this year received a Pulitzer Prize for his work. Today, he writes about what it’s like living in Gaza now.

Gaza City is my home. I grew up in the Tal al-Hawa neighborhood, and I still live there today. I’ve never left Gaza. I studied journalism at the University of Palestine and began working as a freelance photojournalist in 2021.

https://www.npr.org/2026/08/09/nx-s1-592.title: Netanyahu rejects Trump's Gaza Peace Plan, demands Hamas disarm first
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/09/nx-s1-592.author: Rebecca Rosman
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/09/nx-s1-592.text:
President Donald Trump listens as Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks at President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago club, Dec. 29, 2025, in Palm Beach, Fla.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected President Trump's 15-point peace plan for Gaza, saying Israeli forces will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas is "genuinely disarmed."

"We are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament," he said at a meeting with government ministers Sunday.

Netanyahu's comments come just over a week after President Trump announced that his Board of Peace had reached a deal with the Palestinian militant group to completely give up its weapons.

"Today, the Board of Peace reached a HISTORIC agreement for the COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza. This is a monumental step toward lasting PEACE and SECURITY," Trump wrote on social media in late July.

Under Trump's proposed peace deal, Board of Peace officials said Hamas and other militant groups would hand their arms over to a vetted international policing force.

But a senior Hamas official previously told NPR that the group would only hand over their weapons if Israel withdrew from parts of Gaza first.

The latest dispute follows an initial ceasefire reached between Israel and Hamas in October 2025, alongside Trump's broader 20-point Gaza plan.

That first phase of the peace plan halted major fighting, provided for the release of remaining hostages in exchange for some 2,000 Palestinian prisoners, increased humanitarian aid, and called for a partial Israeli withdrawal. More contentious issues – including Hamas's disarmament and further Israeli withdrawals – were left to later negotiations.

Trump's new 15-point roadmap, published on July 31, sought to move those unresolved issues forward. It envisioned Israel's withdrawal from Gaza and Hamas's disarmament as part of a phased process, rather than requiring Hamas to fully disarm before Israeli forces began pulling back.

The Board of Peace had already backed Netanyahu on that key point, saying on Aug. 3 that Israeli forces would not withdraw beyond the Yellow Line until Hamas's weapons were fully decommissioned. Netanyahu's decision to emphasize his demand again comes less than three months before Israel's Oct. 27 election, with polls showing his coalition is at risk of losing its majority.

The apparent stalemate comes as Israel still controls roughly 70% of Gaza, according to Palestinian officials and aid agencies.

Hamas released a press statement Sunday saying it was still committed "to the roadmap agreed upon" in the agreement.

NPR's Anas Baba contributed to this report from Gaza.

https://www.npr.org/2026/08/08/nx-s1-592.title: Meet the man circumnavigating the Arctic Ocean, alone
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/08/nx-s1-592.author: Henry Larson
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/08/nx-s1-592.text:
Sailor Matt Rutherford at the helm of a sailboat. He hopes to be the first to circumnavigate the Arctic Circle alone.

When sailing alone, even sleep is dangerous.

Matt Rutherford knows this all too well. As he travels the Arctic, far from his home port of Annapolis, Maryland, the moments Rutherford does get to rest are precious.

"It just becomes extremely difficult to get any sleep because if you hit the ice, you essentially die," he said.

Rutherford is attempting a maritime first: to circumnavigate the Arctic Ocean completely alone, some 10,000 nautical miles in total. The 45-year-old veteran sailor's journey takes him across the North Atlantic, along the Russian Arctic coast and eventually through the Northwest Passage in Canada.

In an interview with NPR's Rob Schmitz, he said the level of risk will rise as he travels into seas with denser patches of ice, and with worsening conditions.

"It's also going to get dark soon," he said, speaking via Starlink connection from his 42-foot sailboat in the Barents Sea. "I got 24-hour daylight now. How do you see the ice in the dark?"

Rutherford's boat is armed with some helpful tools: radar can spot the bigger chunks of ice, thermal binoculars help him avoid smaller ones – and he has a life raft if things take a turn for the worst.

But the clock is ticking. If he takes too long on his odyssey, and summer turns to fall, the pack ice will freeze his boat in – dooming the expedition.

The route Rutherford plans to take is some 10,000 nautical miles long. No one has completed it unassisted.

Yet for all this obvious danger, Rutherford is steadfast. His voyage, which began on June 25 on the western coast of Greenland, is partly driven by his love of exploration. It's also meant as a fundraiser for his climate science nonprofit, the Ocean Research Project.

"Normally I'm running a research schooner and we're studying glaciers in Greenland. And this year, because there's no funding … I'm doing a little side trip," he joked.

The federal government has slashed funding for climate science over the past two years. With his "side trip," Rutherford hopes to attract new donors to his arctic research group. The group's vessel needs a new engine, among other repairs.

Climate change, in some ways, has made Rutherford's solo voyage more attainable. Arctic sea ice has shrunk by about a third since the early 1980s, according to figures from the National Snow and Ice Data Center.

"[The ice loss is] not everywhere," he said. "I mean, there's still going to be some really heavy ice I have to deal with down the road that could make or break the trip."

The thick ice above Alaska is of particular concern, he says – and so is the pack around eastern Siberia.

Rutherford's sailboat, the Chimera, on an earlier voyage.

But so far, the voyage has been mild. Rutherford sailed past the Nordic countries of Norway and Sweden just a few days ago, and crossed into waters controlled by the Russian government this weekend.

That presents its own sets of challenges. Rutherford says he had to get a permit from the Russian government to allow a pleasure craft like his into the Northern Sea Route, the path along Russia's northern coast connecting the Barents Sea to the Pacific Ocean.

Upon reaching the route, Rutherford has to check in with Moscow every day. He says he's also expected to report his position to the FSB, Russia's security service, if he gets too close to shore.

"You better believe I'm going to be doing that on time," he said. "I don't want to ruffle any feathers."

Rutherford also expects his Starlink connection to stop working at some point inside Russia waters, meaning he'll lose most of his communication capabilities for weeks.

"I don't know what's going to happen. But look, this wouldn't be an adventure if we knew the ending," Rutherford said.

For now, he's confident and comfortable. When NPR spoke with Rutherford this week, the weather forecasts were encouraging.

It looked like he'd be able to have a restful few days.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Canadian government steps in as ‘out of control’ wildfires force thousands to flee
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Olivia Bowden in Toronto
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
British Columbia battling 102 fires day and night across province, as breakneck speed hampers firefighters’ efforts

Canada’s federal government has announced it will provide urgent assistance to British Columbia after an onslaught of unprecedented fast-moving wildfires forced about 22,000 people to flee their homes in frantic evacuations.

A total of 102 wildfires were raging across the province on Sunday, of which nearly half were categorised as “out of control”, according to the BC Wildfire Service. Of those fires, 78 ignited during the past week.

The entire community of Summerland, about 30 miles south-west of the city of Kelowna and home to about 12,000 people, was evacuated overnight on Saturday, along with a further 8,000 people around nearby Peachland. About 10,000 others have been told to prepare to evacuate at a moment’s notice.

“I approved a request for federal assistance from British Columbia to provide shelter and accommodations for people who have been forced to leave their homes,” said Eleanor Olszewski, Canada’s minister of emergency management and community resilience in a social media post on Sunday.

“I have tasked federal officials, led by the government operations centre at Public Safety ‌Canada, to work with the province to ensure support reaches those who need it most,” she ​said.

Efforts to battle the Bald Range wildfire have been hampered by the breakneck speed of its spread.

The blaze was first detected late on Friday evening, and grew within hours to more than 40 sq miles (100 sq km) – nearly twice the size of the island of Manhattan – as it raced nearly nine miles toward Okanagan Lake.

The province’s premier, David Eby, declared a state of emergency late on Saturday, telling reporters that the blaze had been “like a bomb going off.”

Cliff Chapman, BC Wildfire Service’s director of provincial operations, said the prolonged hot and dry weather the province has faced this summer had resulted in “explosive” fire conditions never seen before. Lightning caused by thunderstorms forecast this week could make the situation still worse, he said.

Residents were shaken awake in the middle of the night to flee their homes. Jennifer Pascoa, who lives in Summerland, told the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that she had begun to pack when she saw flames licking the nearby mountains.

“It happened so quickly. We came home from the beach, we saw the plume of smoke, and then within an hour, the sky was covered in dark, black clouds,” she said.

The British Columbia Wildfire Service said 10 standard helicopters and one night-vision helicopter were involved in the response, but had been hindered by thick smoke, turbulence ​and large fires.

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the country’s federal police force, said they were investigating a possible fatality in the fire near Summerland.

Mike Flannigan, a professor of wildland fire at Thompson Rivers University in Kamloops, BC, said the rapidity of the fires’ spread was indicative of increasingly extreme blazes springing up in Canada and the US.

Southern BC and the pacific north-west in the US had had little to no rain in the past six weeks, leaving the regions “bone dry”, he said. “You walk through the forest, it crunches; if you look sideways, you start a fire.”

These conditions were being driven by human-caused climate change, he said. “We’re seeing higher intensity fires today than the past … the shorter the timeframe, the more challenging it is.”

Before this decade, fire agencies’ policy was that if a blaze was 20km (12 miles) away from a community, there was no cause for immediate concern. The ferocity and speed of these fires meant that such calculations no longer held, said Flannigan, warning that all homes in at-risk regions should have an emergency kit ready to go.

“If a fire can run 60km in a day, you should be worried about it,” he said.

The Bald Range fire was also an example of how fires could metastasise through the night, he said.

Traditional firefighting practices would usually give firefighters a break during nightfall, as the cooler air would slow the burning. “That’s not the case any more. The fire roars through the evening, through the night, and we’re seeing this more and more,” he said.

Drought and the sheer power and size of the fires during the day allow them to keep momentum even in the dark. Fire management agencies in BC and Alberta now fight fires after dark using night-vision helicopters.

Current conditions indicated that the fire season in BC and the US states of Washington and Oregon could extend into the autumn, Flannigan said.

“It looks grim … there’s no rain,” he said, adding that, like California, Canada may begin to have “fire years” instead of a summer fire season.

“I’m scared for the coming weeks,” he said.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.summary: British Columbia battling 102 fires day and night across province, as breakneck speed hampers firefighters. Nearly half of the fires are 'out of control' and 78 ignited during the past week. The province’s premier, David Eby, declared a state of emergency late on Saturday.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Typhoon Dolphin makes landfall in China as its strongest storm this year
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Reuters in Beijing
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Tropical cyclone brings torrential rain and high winds to east coast after hitting Japan’s southern Okinawa province

Typhoon Dolphin, the most powerful tropical cyclone to hit China this year, has made landfall on the country’s east coast, bringing torrential rain and strong ⁠winds and triggering warnings ​of flooding and landslides.

The storm has already swept through Japan’s southern Okinawa prefecture, injuring six people and cutting power to more than 50,000 buildings.

Dolphin made landfall near Yuhuan in Zhejiang province at about ⁠5:30pm (0930 GMT) on Sunday, China’s meteorological authorities said. It brought maximum sustained winds of 94mph (151 km/h) near its centre at landfall, equivalent to a category 1 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson scale.

In addition to evacuating at least 30,300 people, Shanghai has cancelled about 1,500 flights, according to the flight-tracking data provider VariFlight.

Authorities moved offshore ⁠workers to safety, ordered vessels back to port and increased checks at reservoirs, mountain streams, landslide-prone areas, construction sites and tourist locations.

Torrential ​rain is forecast for Monday across Zhejiang, Shanghai, northern Fujian, ‌north-eastern Jiangxi, central and southern Anhui, and ‌much of Jiangsu. Parts of central and eastern Zhejiang could receive 250-500 mm (10-20 inches) of rain, according to forecasters.

Dolphin was forecast to track ‌westward before slowing over central and south-western China and gradually losing strength, the chief forecaster at the National Meteorological Centre, Wang Haiping, told the state broadcaster CCTV.

That could prolong heavy rain and increase the risk of flooding and landslides, especially in mountainous areas and along smaller rivers.

Transport was widely disrupted across the east of the country and more than a million people were evacuated from their homes.

A 42-year-old tourist from Guangdong, surnamed Chen, said he had been stranded in Shanghai ‌after his family’s flight, scheduled to depart on Sunday, was cancelled.

He said the family had been rebooked on a flight at 10pm on Monday, although they were unsure whether it would be able ​to take off.

“To us Guangdong people, this typhoon is as ordinary as having a meal and feeling the wind. It’s just part of everyday life,” he said, adding that the storm did not appear particularly strong by the standards of China’s southern coast.

In neighbouring Zhejiang province, the city of Wenzhou relocated more than 900,000 people and opened more than 1,000 emergency shelters. In Fujian province, authorities evacuated 98,900 people from high-risk areas, according to Xinhua.

Fujian maritime authorities ​said 55 coastal passenger ferry routes had been suspended, ​all 115 offshore construction projects halted and 290 construction ​vessels moved to sheltered waters.

The water resources ministry said the Qiantang, Yong, Jiao and Shuiyang rivers could experience major ​flooding, while smaller rivers in the ‌hardest-hit areas could rise above ​warning levels.

Authorities issued an alert for the risk of geological disasters in parts of Zhejiang. Residents in areas covered by a red mountain-torrent warning were told to follow local evacuation orders.

Shanghai’s Yangshan port had cleared ships from its berths and moved more than 500 small and medium-sized vessels to shelter as Dolphin approached, the city’s maritime safety administration said.

Scientists say global warming has made extreme weather more likely, including more powerful typhoons.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.summary: Typhoon Dolphin has made landfall on China's east coast. It has already swept through Japan's southern Okinawa prefecture, injuring six people. More than a million people were evacuated from their homes.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: China expresses ‘grave concern’ as internal documents reveal suicide warning before death in Melbourne immigration detention
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Christopher Knaus and Ariel Bogle
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Exclusive: Serious questions raised about whether Chinese citizen was properly monitored at centre run by US prison giant

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The US private prison company running Australia’s immigration detention system was warned that a newly detained Chinese citizen expressed suicidal ideation and had a history of self-harm less than 24 hours before she died by suicide in a Melbourne detention centre, internal documents show.

The death has raised serious questions about whether the detainee was properly monitored and whether she was placed in an appropriate room, given her state of mind.

It has also triggered an intervention from Australia’s biggest trading partner, Guardian Australia can reveal.

The Chinese embassy has confirmed it has “lodged solemn representations and expressed grave concern to the Australian side” about the circumstances of the death.

“China will closely follow the case and safeguard the safety and legitimate rights and interests of Chinese citizens,” an embassy spokesperson said.

China’s public intervention creates a fresh headache for the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, who is already furious about a string of security lapses involving the government’s new immigration contractor, Secure Journeys, a local subsidiary of the US-based prison multinational Management and Training Corporation.

In May the Guardian revealed that a series of failures had allowed the escape of high-risk detainees, caused ill-equipped staff to be stabbed and hospitalised and triggered multiple investigations, one of which warned that MTC’s “minimalist staffing model” was putting workers and detainees at risk.

Burke took the extraordinary step of hauling in the global president of MTC for a face-to-face dressing down in September 2025, just six months after the company was awarded the $2.3bn onshore immigration detention contract.

On 10 July Australian Border Force issued a short statement saying a detainee had been found dead in the Melbourne immigration detention centre that morning.

The detainee was a Chinese citizen in her mid-30s who had been picked up the day before for allegedly overstaying an English-language studies visa, internal documents seen by the Guardian show. She had no criminal history.

The ABF transferred her into the custody of Secure Journeys on the afternoon of 9 July.

The ABF made clear to Secure Journeys that she had previously attempted self-harm and had “recently thought about self-harm/suicide”, the documents show.

She was found hanging in her room in the Broadmeadows residential precinct, part of the Melbourne immigration detention centre, early the next morning.

Victoria police are investigating the death, which they described as non-suspicious. The coroner’s court of Victoria said it had directed police to prepare a brief of evidence.

There were 360 reported incidents of threatened and actual self-harm across Australia’s onshore immigration detention network between July 2025 and March 2026, according to parliamentary records. There have been at least two deaths this year.

A Secure Journeys spokesperson said the company offered its “deep condolences to the family and friends of the female detainee” but could not comment further due to the investigation.

“Secure Journeys’ commitment to maintaining safe and secure operations, as well as both staff and detainee welfare remains our top priority,” the spokesperson said.

The Department of Home Affairs offered sincere condolences to the woman’s family and friends. “Due to our privacy obligations to the deceased and the ongoing investigation into this matter, it would not be appropriate to comment further,” a spokesperson said.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

China experts described the embassy’s statement as “firm but not excessive”.

The Australia-China Relations Institute’s director, Prof James Laurenceson, said the fact that representations had been made and the embassy had expressed “grave concerns” showed it was taking the death seriously.

But Laurenceson said he didn’t read the embassy’s statement as “excessively aggressive”.

“It is the case that Australia and China have been trading tersely worded diplomatic statements more frequently in recent months over everything from Taiwan, China’s maritime claims in the South China Sea, its cyber operations, the Jimmy Lai case, Darwin Port, and more,” he said. “But I am not convinced that China’s statement in this case should be interpreted as some sort of diplomatic slap back for Australian complaints about Chinese actions in other contexts.”

MTC’s performance in running Australia’s onshore detention network has triggered multiple investigations, including by the federal work safety regulator Comcare.

Internal documents show Comcare has set up a dedicated inspection program to scrutinise immigration detention, citing an “increase in notifiable incidents, the severity and the profile of the reported incidents involving the [contractor]”.

The regulator privately warned the department this year that it had received numerous reports of “serious injury or illness to both workers and others (detainees)”, “self-harm ideations and death involving detainees” and “detainee on detainee violence”.

One of Comcare’s key concerns is that the risk-assessment system used in the centres is not effective and is putting staff and detainees at serious risk of violence and other harms.

Understaffing has been a key concern since MTC took over.

A March report by the National Preventive Mechanism, an independent monitor of places of detention, reported that “critically” low staffing levels were compromising the centres’ safety.

The understaffing is also causing seriously ill detainees to miss medical appointments because MTC lacks workers to escort them to health centres.

In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Labour seeking ‘deeper relationship’ with EU under Burnham, new minister says
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Jessica Elgot and Lisa O’Carroll
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Exclusive: Hamish Falconer wants ‘sense of renewed pace’ in post-Brexit talks while staying within Labour’s red lines

‘I was on my honeymoon!’: Hamish Falconer’s surprise call-up to Burnham’s cabinet

The UK will move faster and be more ambitious on achieving closer ties with Europe under Andy Burnham’s government, his new chief post-Brexit negotiator has said.

Hamish Falconer, the new cabinet minister in charge of the EU reset talks, said there was “room to be ambitious” within Labour’s red lines on Europe, which exclude reopening discussions on the single market and customs union, and he would look at the “art of the possible”.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

He said greater cooperation on services – which might include visa-free travel for British people working in the EU, or mutual recognition of qualifications – was the next big area where the UK hoped to make progress. “I would want a deeper relationship, a more ambitious relationship with the EU,” Falconer told the Guardian.

“There’s also a whole range of areas in relation to services where I’d really like it to be progressed. Services is obviously an area where the EU itself is less closely integrated and there’s a lot of discussion within the EU about where to take the productivity challenge for them – that’s a challenge we can recognise here in the UK as well. So, particularly on services, I’m really interested in where we can go further.”

Falconer, the son of the Labour grandee Charlie Falconer, is a former Middle East minister and diplomat who has experience as a Foreign Office negotiator. He said he wanted “a sense of renewed pace” in the talks – though there is still no new summit date in sight. The long-awaited reset summit, which had been slated for July, was postponed after Keir Starmer resigned as prime minister in June.

“We’re committed to our manifesto red lines, but all of my experiences as a negotiator and the art of the possible is in part shaped by the nature of the relationship between two people negotiating,” Falconer said.

“I used to be a negotiator with the Taliban. With the EU, this is a negotiation with our friends, with whom we share our values and with whom we feel solidarity.”

Earlier this summer, EU diplomats expressed concern that the talks under Starmer had lost momentum, with the second annual summit of EU and UK leaders repeatedly delayed as talks stalled over a youth mobility scheme.

Falconer, who returned from his honeymoon when he was offered the post of Europe minister by Burnham, has spoken already to the EU trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, and senior bloc figures hope he will bring a new energy to talks.

One said of his predecessor Nick Thomas-Symonds: “I really liked him but the problem was the UK didn’t open up a window, create the political space for a deal.”

They complained that instead of seizing opportunities to get a deal over the line and bank a political win to move on to the next phase, the UK negotiators “kept trying to add things” such as an agreement on services.

A source close to Thomas-Symonds disputed this and said good progress had been made on all areas under discussion ahead of the planned July summit.

It is believed that the next summit may not be held until October to give Falconer time to get across the detail, and for Burnham to flesh out his foreign policy.

Resolving the terms of a youth mobility deal is a key priority, to allow tens of thousands of European and British young people to live and work in each other’s territories.

Talks remained deadlocked due to the UK’s reluctance to allow EU students to pay the lower fees charged to UK students, something opposed by cash-strapped universities.

Falconer said the deal should “work for both sides” and was mindful of financial pressures on the university sector. “In my constituency in Lincoln, there’s two universities. I’ve got those issues very much at the forefront of my mind,” he said. “It is vital that as we go through this, we have real respect on both sides for what some of the constraints are for each of us.”

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

Falconer said he wanted to apply Burnham’s “Makerfield test” to the EU negotiations, ensuring they would deliver tangible change to ordinary people struggling with the cost of living, including in his own very heavily leave voting constituency.

But he said he would continuously emphasise principles of “European solidarity”, which he said went beyond trade and were backed by shared values, including on defence and security and on how countries could tackle growing dangers such as wildfires caused by the climate crisis.

Starmer and Thomas-Symonds had been due to host the second UK-EU summit on 22 July, with progress already announced on a deal easing barriers for food and drink exports expected to come into force before summer 2027.

Though there was a warm relationship between Starmer and the EU’s Ursula von der Leyen, the UK had also faced difficulty in fulfilling some of the promised changes agreed at the last UK-EU summit, including an inability to reach agreement on the UK’s entry into the €150bn Safe fund for defence investment.

Talks over UK participation in Safe collapsed last November with France blamed for setting too high a price for British involvement. Seasoned observers in Brussels say it was also embarrassing for the EU and was “a failure of statecraft” on both sides.

Falconer said: “I think that we have made some real initial progress on resetting but now we’ve got to deliver.”

Having Downing Street support to give Falconer the political space that EU diplomats want created will be key. And he says he has the experience to deliver.

“I used to be a negotiator in the Foreign Office, often doing really hard negotiations. Ultimately, the character of the wider relationship is really important,” he said. “Yes, there are some really important technical questions that we have got to get right.”

“But we also need to put this in the big picture… there is also a massive wider European agenda, which is really important to us, and Britain is really important to that agenda too. Security, defence, tech. We are a big part of those discussions and those dilemmas.”

Falconer said he would use his role – now at cabinet level – to boost the UK’s participation in solving Europe-wide challenges outside the EU. “We are part of Europe and we feel the threats to Europe, whether it’s in eastern Europe from Russia invading Ukraine, or even wildfires and that shared sense of challenge in dealing with that.”
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.summary: Hamish Falconer is new cabinet minister in charge of EU reset talks. He wants to stay within Labour's red lines while staying within Labour’s red lines. Faler says he has the experience to deliver on the issue of security and tech.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Italy condemns Spain’s ‘unacceptable’ border controls as Ceuta fallout intensifies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Ashifa Kassam in Madrid
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Travellers caught up in migration row as Madrid introduces checks on visitors from Italy in retaliation for Rome’s move

Italy’s foreign minister has called Spain’s decision to impose retaliatory checks on travellers from Italy “incomprehensible and completely unacceptable” as people making their way between the two EU countries were left grappling with the effects of the escalating feud.

Spain started carrying out spot checks on visitors from Italy at midnight on Saturday. The tit-for-tat move came after Rome infuriated Madrid by launching checks on 1 August for travellers from Spain in response to the recent influx of about 72,000 people into Ceuta, a Spanish territory in north Africa.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Spanish officials were swift to point out that the Italian checks made little sense, given that by 1 August, the border in Ceuta was back under control and the vast majority of those who had arrived had been returned to Morocco. Ceuta is not part of the Schengen free-movement zone, Madrid has repeatedly stressed, meaning there is little chance of onward travel to continental Europe without EU citizenship or residency.

The checks by Italy had led to “intolerable” scenes at Italian airports, Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, told reporters. “This measure is, first and foremost, an attack on the dignity of the Spanish people, but, secondly, it is a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity,” he said.

In an interview published on Sunday in La Stampa, Italy’s foreign minister defended the move by Rome. “Some order needs to be brought in: we’re not against Spain, but we have a duty to protect our borders,” said Antonio Tajani, voicing concerns about some of the migrants potentially holding jihadist views. “What is incomprehensible and completely unacceptable is Spain’s reaction.”

He pushed back against the suggestion that Rome’s actions were symbolic, given the remote possibility of anyone making it to Italy from Ceuta. “Where do they go after arriving in Spain? Italy, as a destination, is the country most at risk. We’re not Germany or Norway.”

When asked if Italy’s response was proportionate, Tajani pointed to the reports of fresh calls online for a mid-August mass crossing. “We hope to be able to lift the suspension soon, as soon as the risk is no longer present,” he said.

Italy’s interior minister publicly praised Spain last week for its handling of the crisis, but Tajani blasted Spain for not being “as vigilant” as it should have been.

He linked the influx to Spain’s recent regularisation programme, describing the move to provide working migrants with papers as a “negative message that puts everyone’s safety at risk,” despite the EU’s earlier dismissal of any connection between the Ceuta influx and regularisation.

Italy’s government has long criticised Spain’s efforts to regularise undocumented migrants, even as it quietly works on similar plans to give nearly 1.1 million work permits to foreign workers by 2028. Speaking to the Financial Times, one researcher described the Italian government’s efforts as a “disguised amnesty.”

Spain and Italy both have a long history of regularisation programmes. In 2002, Tajani’s party, Forza Italia, carried out one of Italy’s largest such programmes, issuing just over 634,000 permits.

Even so, the perception of differences in their approach to migration has pitted Madrid and Rome against each other, with Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, seeking to position herself as a hardliner on migration while Spain’s Pedro Sánchez – who has defended the need for foreign workers to grow Spain’s economy and stave off demographic collapse – said Italy had registered the highest number of irregular crossings in recent years in the EU, with figures that are double those of Spain.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

In recent days, the row has widened to include people making their way between the two countries, a route used by more than 8 million last year.

“It’s ridiculous that we’re in this situation,” Elisa Fabbri, 41, told Spanish news site Eldiario.es as she left Madrid-Barajas airport on Saturday. Israel Pérez, a Cuban-born Spanish citizen, described it as an “absurd spiral” that risked pulling everyone down. “If we keep imposing checks on each other, in the end we’ll all end up losing,” he said. “This shouldn’t be happening between two European countries.”

In Italy, opposition politicians accused Meloni of unleashing an “unfounded diplomatic crisis” that would ultimately harm Italians. “The cynical propaganda of the Meloni government has produced what was predictable: a boomerang that Italians will pay dearly for,” said Nicola Fratoianni, the leader of the Greens and Left Alliance. “This is a colossal mistake.”

The EU commissioner for migration, Magnus Brunner, said on Saturday that he had been in contact with the interior ministers of the two countries. “Both confirmed that the internal border controls are temporary,” he said on social media. “Spanish authorities assured us the events in Ceuta will have no lasting effect on the Schengen area. That is why there are signals from Italy that controls could be lifted soon.”

The row between Rome and Madrid after the events in Ceuta hints at sensitivities over migration across the EU, particularly as governments in Italy, France and Poland prepare to face off against far-right challengers in upcoming elections.

But the latest Eurobarometer poll, which tracks public opinions every quarter, suggests the focus on migration may be out of step with Europeans’ top priorities. When asked about the topics that should be a priority for the European parliament, migration ranked sixth, behind issues such as the cost of living, the defence and security of the EU and the economy and job creation.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Netanyahu rejects US-led 15-point Gaza peace plan in rare public break with Trump
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Andrew Roth in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Israeli PM says IDF will not withdraw until Hamas is disarmed and rebukes US pressure to end wars without his country’s buy-in

Middle East crisis live – latest updates

Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has rejected a US-backed 15-point peace plan for Gaza in a rare public break with Donald Trump.

In a statement on Sunday, Netanyahu said that he was confronting a “wave of rumours about Israeli weakness and Israeli withdrawals on all fronts” and rebuked US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

On Gaza, he said: “Israel does not accept the 15-point document. The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed. And when I say the disarming of Hamas, it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry. And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament. Right now, we are talking with the Americans about this issue.”

Trump’s Board of Peace in July proposed the 15-point plan, which mandated that Hamas disarm in exchange for providing a full Israeli military withdrawal from the Gaza Strip and an eventual transition of power to an independent Palestinian National Committee. Trump had said that the agreement would be implemented in stages, but Netanyahu on Sunday said that he wanted a full disarmament first in order to implement the deal.

The Israeli leader’s main target in his remarks was the US. Israel has emerged as a key stumbling block in the Trump White House’s plans to broker peace in the region, in Israel’s conflicts in Gaza and Lebanon as well as in the war begun by joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran. And Netanyahu, who is facing tough elections in October and pressure from hardliners in his own government, appears ready to test his relationship with Trump in public in order to shore up his reputation as a defender of Israel at home.

Israel had already signalled that it would reject the US-led plan. Soon after Trump announced it last month, Israel stepped up its bombing campaign in the Palestinian territory – strikes killed 18 people last Sunday. Netanyahu’s office had previously indicated it would not back the plan, saying: “The version that has been made public does not reflect Israel’s positions.”

But Sunday’s rejection was far more forceful and direct, and appeared targeted at the Trump White House, as Trump and Netanyahu both face difficult elections. “Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu said.

The head of Trump’s Board of Peace hit back on Sunday, saying the plan remained the “only way forward”. Nickolay Mladenov, the board’s high representative for Gaza, told Israeli television: “The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again.”

Sign up to First Thing

Our US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

Netanyahu’s rejection is a blow to Trump’s desire to be seen as a broker of peace in foreign conflicts. With midterm elections set for October, the White House is desperate to negotiate a peace in Iran in order to reopen the strait of Hormuz and help bring down oil and petrol prices.

But the conflicts in the Middle East are interconnected and parallel US efforts have continued to bring peace to Lebanon, where Israel has occupied land in what it says is a buffer zone against Hezbollah, and Gaza, where Gulf allies of the US have decried what they say is an ethnic cleansing campaign being carried out by Israel.

Like US presidents before him, Trump has found that Netanyahu can be a difficult ally. Bill Clinton, after meeting Netanyahu for the first time in 1996, is reported to have said: “Who’s the fucking superpower here?”

More recently, the Biden administration found that its concerns about the human toll in Gaza were ignored, but continued to publicly back Netanyahu and did not significantly suspend military aid to the country for fear of the political blowback that Netanyahu and his allies in the US could cause.

In Trump, however, Netanyahu has found a far more unorthodox and unpredictable counterpart in the White House. Netanyahu is a natural ally for Trump, and he has attacked Democrats before the midterm elections for being weak on supporting Israel.

Yet more broadly, support for Israel and its war in Gaza is eroding in the Democratic party, and the Republicans have a presidential frontrunner for 2028 in the vice-president, JD Vance, who is publicly sceptical of Israel and the war in Gaza.

Trump will have to decide whether to increase pressure on Netanyahu, potentially alienating some pro-Israel allies, or to allow his efforts for a Gaza peace plan to stall, perhaps indefinitely.

The answer will depend heavily on the US president’s own political instincts – are US voters hoping to see Trump emerge as a statesman capable of ending one of the world’s bloodiest recent wars in Gaza, or would a public clash with Netanyahu provoke a revolt among his base? With both countries entering tumultuous election cycles and a generational shift in support for Israel among US voters, the result could redraw the alliance between Israel and the US.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: London mayor orders council to drop plan to ban new pubs and bars in Soho and West End
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Helena Horton
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Exclusive: Sadiq Khan urges Westminster council to adopt ‘positive vision of economic growth’ of nightlife

Sadiq Khan has ordered Westminster council to scrap a policy that would ban new pubs and bars from opening in Soho and the West End of London.

This comes after the Guardian revealed the council’s new licensing policy asks pubs to stop customers from standing up while consuming beverages, which it calls “vertical drinking”. The policy is under consultation and also asks pubs to have table service rather than allowing orders at the bar.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

There was widespread anger at the plans to direct those applying to open new bars and restaurants in Westminster to implement the restrictions.

The mayor of London has new powers, granted by the government this year, to intervene in licensing decisions. He is using these for the first time to ask the council to rewrite the draft policy.

The Conservative Westminster councillors decree in the draft policy that newly licensed pubs should have to serve last orders at 10pm, and nightclubs should shut by 11.30pm on weekdays and at midnight on weekends.

It also labels the entirety of Soho and the West End as a “cumulative impact zone”, which means no more pubs, bars or night clubs should be allowed to open unless under exceptional circumstances. This is despite the West End being one of the most popular nightlife areas in Europe.

Khan pointed out that Home Office alcohol licensing data shows that only 41 licence applications were made in the West End cumulative impact area in 2023-24, with only 16 granted.

Data also shows only 3.5% of applications that went to a licensing subcommittee in Westminster were approved exactly as applied for between 2023 and 2026, and pub and wine bar applications were down 80% in 2022-24.

There are also plans to label Mayfair and the Victoria area as special zones where nightlife is restricted due to noise and other “nuisance behaviours”.

Khan is asking the council to scrap all of these zones and allow new bars and pubs to open, in his formal response to the consultation. He is also directing it to get rid of the “core hours” policy and allow venues to be open late into the night.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, waded into the row this week when he said standing up to drink in pubs was “British life” and should not be curtailed by local councillors.

Sign up to First Edition

after newsletter promotion

Khan said: “Licensing decisions that could make or break our city’s nightlife have, in my view, been skewed towards the interests of a handful of highly vocal residents and councillors, without giving enough weight to the effects on London’s wider economy and culture.”

He added that the draft proposals “undermine City Hall’s efforts to make London’s nightlife the best in the world”.

In his formal response he asks the council to “remove this cumulative impact policy altogether, instead setting out a positive vision of the economic growth that is being promoted, rather than the activity that is to be restricted”. This means the ban on opening new bars and pubs in Soho and the West End other than in exceptional circumstances would be lifted.

The mayor said that Manchester city council is an example of a local authority that allows economic growth and supports bars, pubs and restaurants.

Khan said: “Manchester city council’s policy has adopted a more enabling approach, with no core hours policy, no cumulative impact policy and a clear vision for what they are looking to promote across their different local neighbourhoods.

“As envisioned by the Licensing Act 2003, there is a presumption to grant licences for pubs, bars, clubs and other premises where applicants can demonstrate effective management and compliance with the licensing objectives.”

Westminster city council has been contacted for comment.

The Guardian disclosed that Rukhsar Ahmed, a former Pakistan state minister, was arrested at Manchester airport in July 2024 on suspicion of raping and trafficking at least two underage girls from care homes in the city’s Rusholme area during the 1990s.

He was released on bail and flew to Pakistan nearly two months ago, missing an appointment at a police station after telling officers he was too unwell to fly back to the UK.

He was elected an MP for prime minister Shehbaz Sharif’s centre-right Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz party days later.

He did not respond to requests for a comment when approached by the Guardian last week.

It emerged on Sunday that Ahmed, 61, had been located in his office in Khari Sharif, a village in Mirpur district.

The Guardian understands that Greater Manchester police (GMP) had wanted to restrict Ahmed’s ability to travel abroad as part of his bail conditions, but a judge rejected tougher measures in July 2024.

The ongoing investigation relates to allegations from several women about sexual abuse of children at care homes in the early 1990s, when Ahmed was in his late 20s.

He is understood to be expected to answer police bail in the next six weeks. If he does not attend, GMP may issue a warrant for his arrest or take steps to extradite him.

The Guardian has approached Ahmed for comment again.

Richard Scorer, the head of abuse law at Slater and Gordon who has acted in many Manchester grooming gang cases said: “Rusholme has regularly featured in grooming gang investigations over the past 30 years, with many cases involving allegations of children being abused in and around the area.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Eric Berger
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Small cruise ship rescued skiff in south-east Alaska even though Meta billionaire’s $300m megayacht was closer

Mark Zuckerberg has faced questions over why a small cruise ship in south-east Alaska rescued a stranded skiff and its crew when his 387ft superyacht had been closer.

The Silicon Valley billionaire’s yacht, worth a reported $300m, is said to have “repeatedly” declined to assist when a nearby boat called for help last week.

Zuckerberg, CEO of Facebook and Instagram owner Meta Platforms, was not on board at the time, a spokesperson told Forbes.

When a nearby 21ft skiff ran out of fuel between Petersburg and Juneau, the Alaska Beacon reported operators of a cruise ship that was further away than Zuckerberg’s yacht came to the rescue.

“I’m on a small-ship Alaska cruise with my son,” a passenger on the UnCruise Adventures ship Wilderness Legacy posted on Bluesky.

“Our boat rescued a stranded vessel last night and apparently we did that after the Coast Guard radioed Mark Zuckerberg’s yacht – which was closer – and they repeatedly refused to respond. (There was near unanimous booing when the captain announced this).”

But Brian Baker, a spokesperson for Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, told Forbes that the couple were not on board his yacht, named Launchpad. The yacht crew had been operating on a different radio channel, Baker told Forbes. “The assist was already under way” by the time they reviewed the broadcast, he said.

Even if he was not on his ship, the report is unlikely to boost public opinion of Zuckerberg, who has faced criticism over the societal impact of his social media platforms; his new warm relationship with Donald Trump; and his lavish, insular lifestyle.

“I live in Juneau and I’ve been having to look at that excessive eyesore parked up in [Auke Bay] for too long now,” a Reddit user wrote of the yacht in response to the rescue story. “Fuck Zuckerberg.”

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Perseid meteor shower set to dazzle northern hemisphere this week
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Astronomers say viewing conditions promising for this year’s shower, and 50 to 100 meteors an hour may be visible

The Perseid summer light show is back, and viewing conditions are especially promising across the northern hemisphere.

The meteor shower’s is expected to peak on Wednesday night into Thursday morning, and coincides with a total solar eclipse across Spain, Iceland and Greenland and a six-planet parade – though the best time to view the fireballs will come after totality.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

As many as 50 to 100 meteors per hour may be visible under ideal conditions, according to NASA. The American Meteor Society estimates 30 to 50 meteors per hour could be seen from rural regions in the US.

Random meteors are visible in dark skies on any given night. Meteor showers tend to put on dazzling celestial shows and happen at predictable times every year when the Earth plows through trails of debris left behind by comets and, sometimes, asteroids. Those remnants collide with Earth’s atmosphere at extremely high speeds, producing streaks of light known as shooting stars.

The Perseids are debris from comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle, an icy ball that orbits the sun every 133 years and is not scheduled for a return visit until 2125. Observations of this meteor shower date back over 2,000 years.

The Perseids are a perennial favorite because they tend to produce brilliant fireballs. Summer temperatures also make this shower popular.

“We don’t have to suffer through a cold winter night to get a good view of meteors,” said astronomer Zach Vanderbosch with McDonald Observatory in Texas.

The moon will be in its new moon phase during the Perseids’ peak, making viewing conditions even better.

“The moon is beautiful, but it’s such a diva,” said astronomer Aparna Venkatesan with the University of San Francisco. “New moon means we don’t have moonlight flooding the sky, and you tend to see way more meteors as a result.”

To spot the meteors, go outside after dark, away from clouds and city lights. Venkatesan plans to drive to the Sierra Nevada.

The best views will be between midnight and dawn when the constellation Perseus is high in the northern sky. The meteors will appear to radiate from that constellation.

Look up and give your eyes a half hour to adjust to the darkness. Vanderbosch recommends picking a patch of sky to focus on until a quick, bright streak passes by – even in your peripheral vision – and to avoid looking at your phone.

“There’s just something magical about it,” Vanderbosch said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Lake Mead plummets to historic low water level as Colorado River struggles
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Guardian staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Levels at reservoir along Arizona-Nevada border dipped below previous record set in 2022, amid water crisis in west

Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States, has plummeted to its lowest water level since it was filled some 90 years ago, the latest sign of a deepening water crisis in the American west.

Water levels at the reservoir, which straddles the Arizona-Nevada border outside Las Vegas, hit 1,040.4ft (317.1 meters) above sea level on Friday, according to federal data. That’s just below the record set on 28 July 2022, according to the US Bureau of Reclamation.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The reservoir is a critical storage system on Colorado River, a massive waterway that supplies roughly 40 million people across seven US states, tribal nations and Mexico, and irrigates millions of acres of farmland.

But the Colorado River basin is facing enormous pressure due to a combination of overuse, prolonged drought and extreme heat, and a lack of snowmelt to replenish the river. Lake Powell, the second major reservoir on the Colorado River, is also at historic low levels.

“It’s extremely significant and extremely concerning. You have three-quarters of the population of the Colorado River basin, some 30 million people, who are directly impacted by risks to Lake Mead,” said JB Hamby, the chair of the Colorado River board of California and a board member of the Imperial Irrigation District, the largest user of the river’s water. Hamby said it is vital for states that use Colorado River water to reduce water use.

Drought and dry conditions have stretched along the length of the Colorado and are particularly intense at its source in the Rocky Mountains.

Melting snow provides important water for the river. This past winter, however, saw the worst snowpack on record for the Colorado River basin, adding more stress on farmers, industry, wildlife and hydropower producers, as well as the cities and towns that rely on the waterway.

Years of overuse combined with drought and rising temperatures have been depleting Lake Mead and Lake Powell, the country’s second-largest reservoir. Both are the lowest they have been in nearly seven decades.

To protect the strained system’s ability to produce hydropower, federal officials said Thursday that they will not release cool Lake Powell water from Glen Canyon Dam in northern Arizona to protect a threatened native fish, the humpback chub, whose habitat is between the reservoirs.

Federal officials recently announced a short-term proposal to stave off a crisis in the beleaguered waterway, after states that rely on it – California, Colorado, Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico, Wyoming and Utah – failed to reach an agreement on how to share the dwindling resource in the long term.

The federal proposal called for the Lower Basin states of Arizona, California and Nevada to take less water. The Bureau of Reclamation, which released the plan, said it was flexible: deeper cuts could happen in drier times, while states would have more time to collectively agree on how to manage the scarce resources.

The government is expected to release a so-called “record of decision” in the coming weeks offering more details on the plan, but experts have warned it might not be enough to solve the problems facing the imperiled river.

Severe drought in 2022 on Lake Mead, which is held back by Hoover Dam, exposed human remains and forced water officials in Las Vegas to pump water from deeper within the reservoir to continue to supply water to millions of people.

Levels at Lake Powell have dropped so much that it has become difficult to descend far enough to reach the water. Boat ramps have had to move, shut down or be built anew.

Lake Mead and Lake Powell are not alone. Of the 54 western reservoirs tracked by the federal Bureau of Reclamation, nine recently recorded their lowest levels in the last three decades.

Federal officials do not believe the record will stay where it is. According to modeling done in July, Lake Mead is forecast to continue dropping through much of the rest of the year.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Eric Berger
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Michigan nominee, who spoke to Obama after primary win, vows to fight inequality as president ‘makes billions off you’

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in Michigan, embraced Donald Trump’s suggestion that the two represent “VERY DIFFERENT” versions of the US, pledging to fight inequality while the president is “making billions of dollars off of you”.

In a Saturday night post on his Truth Social platform, Trump shared an image of himself and the first lady, Melania Trump, beside a photo of El-Sayed, who is Muslim, and his wife, Sarah Jukaku, wearing a hijab. “Two VERY DIFFERENT America’s [sic],” read the caption.

“Yeah, he’s right,” El-Sayed told CNN, when asked about the post on Sunday.

“One in which your overlords are two people who don’t like each other, but join in the interest of making billions of dollars off of you – or two people who genuinely love each other, enjoyed some pancakes together, want to come together to build the kind of America where they can raise a family and know that that family is going to have the good things.”

“Yes, you’ve got two different visions of America,” said El-Sayed. “Donald Trump’s vision is the one you’re living in right now. Can you afford your gas? Can you afford your groceries?”

El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan this week, setting up a bruising general election campaign against former US representative Mike Rogers, a Republican, in the swing state.

His victory is widely seen as crucial to the Democrats’ hopes of retaking control of the Senate from Republicans.

During a speech on Thursday, Trump called El-Sayed a communist and said he was “full of shit”, which was met with loud cheers. Asked about the president’s expletive remark, El-Sayed told Sky News: “At least I don’t let mine go in the middle of the Oval Office.”

Unlike some other new Democratic candidates, El-Sayed, who ran to the left of his primary opponent, is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, and has said he is a capitalist who wants capitalism to work better.

Former US president Barack Obama spoke with El-Sayed after his primary win, in what is deemed an early sign of support for his campaign.

“It was a really good conversation about what we need to do to be able to win, and obviously this is somebody who knows a lot about winning Michigan,” El-Sayed told NBC News.

Michigan backed both of Obama’s runs for the presidency, in 2008 and 2012, before voting for Trump in 2016, Joe Biden in 2020, and turning back to Trump in 2024.

Obama also called Haley Stevens, the moderate Democrat whom El-Sayed defeated in the primary, Politico reported. Stevens urged the former president to “come to Michigan and campaign for the Democrats”, she told the outlet.

Should he beat Rogers in November’s general election in Michigan, El-Sayed could become the first Muslim US senator.

Republicans have described him as “the most radical Senate candidate in America”, and Trump has repeatedly used his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.

El-Sayed noted the party – and Trump – did the same to Obama, regularly including his middle name “Hussein” when referencing the former president.

“At the end of the day it’s not radical to believe that people should be able to afford their groceries,” he told NBC’s Meet The Press. “It’s not radical to believe that you should have healthcare in this country.

“It’s not radical … that you don’t think the president should be able to deny elections, or make $2.2bn out of his role in office. It’s not radical to believe all of us should be able to breathe clean air and drink clean water. Those are the things that I’ve been fighting for.”

El-Sayed said: “They are going to try to paint me as a certain thing, given my name, but I also think it’s important to recognize that America has a long history of embracing, “America is a lot bigger than very small people like Donald Trump or [Vice President] JD Vance or Mike Rogers want to make it out to be. And so I’m grateful for all that America has given me.”

He is the Democratic candidate for the US Senate, and is a former US president. El- Sayed is the first Muslim US senator in the state.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: How clean air clubs are protecting Americans from wildfire smoke
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Lex McMenamin
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Mutual aid groups that started giving out PPEs during Covid are now loaning air purifiers and distributing masks to fume-addled communities

M
iquette Thompson’s home in rural Mendocino county has been covered in smoke all week. There are the nearby Feliz and Woodside fires in northern California, which have burned more than 1,000 acres, as well as the wildfires devastating Oregon and Washington that are sending smoke their way, too.

“It’s become not unusual,” she said of walking outside and seeing a hazy sky.

The wildfire smoke means dangerous air quality for her under-resourced, “wee rural little area”, Thompson said. Wildfire smoke is potentially unsafe for all populations, but particularly for elderly people and those with respiratory conditions. Hospitalizations for asthma go up 10% on smoke days, according to a recent University of California study.

Having locally organized around safety amid airborne illness for years – distributing free personal protective equipment (PPE) to neighbors and Covid tests at farmers markets – Thompson said she watched as the local health department failed to distinguish which types of masks help with smoke issues (N95 masks are better at filtering out tiny particles; cloth or surgical masks are less effective). So with her fellow organizers at Mendo Clean Air Club, she began partnering with local businesses that offered to distribute masks, too.

Mendo Clean Air Club is one of over 40 clean air clubs around the world. Launched by Emily Dupree, a Chicago resident, the first club lent out air purifiers to touring musicians during Covid. Now, Clean Air Clubs and Mask Blocs – a mutual aid practice for sharing masks – are offering free masks and air purifiers from their “lending libraries” to help their local communities stay safe from wildfire smoke and monitor air quality. Mask Bloc Los Angeles, for example, handed out more than 300,000 masks in two weeks during the catastrophic January 2025 LA fires.

“Covid and climate change are two major pillars of collective denial in the last decade,” said Dupree. “So though our lending library was created in response to one kind of public failure – namely a failure of public health, which is still ongoing – it can serve as a solution in response to this second failure, of governments to adequately address the growing threat of climate change, of worsening wildfires and worsening air quality.”

When wildfire smoke was negatively affecting Chicago air quality in July, Dupree noticed that their lending library of 15 purifiers was not fully booked. “It just didn’t sit right with me,” she said. So they started encouraging people struggling with the smoke to reserve purifiers, which they could retrieve from a storage unit; within hours, the library was fully booked, she said.

“We are able to mobilize clean air resources extremely quickly because we are not dealing with bureaucracy or red tape,” Dupree said. “We just get the purifiers placed where they’re needed as quickly as possible.”

This speed and access are particularly helpful for populations with underlying health conditions. When then-president Joe Biden declared the Covid emergency “over” in 2023, Shannon Durkin, a Mask Bloc Delaware organizer – who is especially vulnerable due to her cystic fibrosis – thought her life was functionally over, too. Since the first US lockdown in March 2020, and the ensuing anti-public health backlash, she’s felt excised from participating in public life. She has faced discrimination when going out in her respirator, surrounded by collective denial that Covid and other viral illnesses are still dangerous.

In 2024, Durkin and her husband Jimmy helped launch Mask Bloc Delaware, distributing KN95 masks at protests and partnering with other organizing groups, such as the local Food Not Bombs and DSA chapters. In July, they walked around Wilmington, Delaware, as wildfire smoke from Canada permeated the east coast to distribute PPE. The Durkins said people were surprisingly enthusiastic about receiving it, not even realizing the possible health risks of the air quality. They were also able to drop masks off at various local businesses for distribution.

Organizers say the work of Clean Air Clubs and Mask Blocs feels more necessary than ever, as the current administration continues to cast doubt on the usefulness of masks and the severity of the Covid pandemic that in 2020 killed more than 350,000 Americans.

Thompson said she navigates any Covid hesitancy by explaining to residents how it can affect their health, their families and their livelihoods. “The big message that’s gotten through in a rural, underfunded region is that we can’t afford to get sick or to get long Covid,” said Thompson. “A lot of us are manual laborers or use our bodies for work in some way. We just don’t have the resources here to manage that.”

Awareness of Clean Air Clubs continues to grow; Dupree even created a Google doc breaking down how others can start their own. Organizers say being part of these mutual aid groups can offer hope in a time of hopelessness.

“A lot of people, when they’re looking at the various horrors of the world, can feel overwhelmed and then stuck regarding what they should do about it,” said Dupree. “But what this shows us is that even if you decide to focus on one problem, it turns out usually what you come up with is going to be able to pivot and solve other problems that you didn’t initially try to address. There’s a kind of freedom in that.”
