https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/b.title: Wind in the wilderness a real threat to unprepared hikers
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 7:17pm

Urshla Connor says it is vital to keep up with what the weather is doing if you are out in the wilderness. (Supplied: Urshla Connor)

Urshla Connor knows from personal and professional experience that being prepared for changing winds and weather can be the difference between a beautiful bushwalk and a life-threatening situation in Tasmania.

In her role as a meteorologist with the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM), she regularly updates emergency services and the media on changing alpine conditions that often catch hikers unawares.

While she generates warnings and forecasts for the bureau's website and the BOM Weather app, Ms Connor always double-checks the latest information before starting a trek.

"Being a meteorologist, I probably check the weather more than most people," she said.

Urshla Connor says hikers should keep in mind that once they reach exposed ridgelines or summits, much stronger winds are a possibility. (Supplied: Urshla Connor)

Ms Connor said her most memorable experience of being caught in bad weather was on the Three Capes Track.

"We had two beautiful blue-sky days, but one day of cloud so thick we couldn't see 20 metres ahead, and winds so strong it felt like we'd be blown off Cape Pillar," she said.

The weather in Tasmania can change quickly. (Unsplash: Lucas Canino)

Ms Connor cautioned that conditions can change extremely quickly in Tasmania and can be significantly different whether you're near the coast or up high on a mountain.

"Before you head out, it is important to check both the current observations and the forecast for the area you're planning to visit," she said.

"Search for your destination on the BOM Weather app or the bureau's website to compare the latest conditions with what's expected over the course of your walk, including temperature, wind and rainfall.

Hiking in Tasmania in winter is not for the faint hearted, as this video from the Overland Track shows. (Supplied: Tasmania Parks and Wildlife Service)

Bushwalkers should be aware that while air temperature generally decreases gradually with elevation, wind is often what makes exposed alpine areas significantly harsher.

"During winter, Tasmania is regularly affected by strong cold fronts from the Southern Ocean, bringing rapidly changing weather," Ms Connor said.

"As you gain elevation during these conditions, temperatures decrease, winds strengthen, and precipitation can become more intense."

She said most hikes begin in relatively sheltered locations, but "once you reach exposed ridgelines or summits, you're suddenly exposed to much stronger winds".

"Strong winds increase the rate at which your body loses heat — a phenomenon known as 'wind chill'," she said.

"Even when the air temperature isn't especially low, wind chill can increase the risk of cold stress and hypothermia, particularly in exposed alpine and coastal areas."

It is important to be prepared if hiking in Tasmania. (Unsplash: Creative Dummy llc)

A Tasmanian hiker has recounted her experience of misadventure while hiking in the state's rugged wilderness.

As winter sets in, many of Tasmania's peaks also receive snowfall.

Combined with strong winds, snow can reduce visibility, make tracks slippery and create freezing conditions that increase the risk of exposure.

"You can use the forecast maps to see how temperatures and wind speeds are expected to change along your route," Ms Connor said.

"Winds can significantly increase wind chill, so it's important to consider more than just the forecast temperature.

Urshla Connor says if she is out with people new to Tasmanian bushwalking, she will often carry spare gear "just in case". (Supplied: Urshla Connor)

Rescue statistics show that interstate visitors are far from the only ones being caught out by Tasmania's weather, with only 27 per cent of rescue operations involving mainland tourists.

In recent years, the rise of social media has inspired more people to explore Tasmania's wilderness, but not everyone is prepared for how quickly conditions can change.

"I've also learnt that not everyone knows what a proper rain jacket looks like," Ms Connor said.

"I've had friends turn up in fashionable spray jackets that look great, but aren't designed for hours of rain and strong winds.

"Now, if I'm walking with people who are new to Tasmanian bushwalking, I usually throw a couple of spare waterproof jackets and some extra gear in my pack, just in case."

The bureau continues to work closely with the Tasmania Parks and Wildlife Service, and Tasmania Police Search and Rescue, to improve the weather information and warnings available to the community.

Urshla Connor and friends bushwalking in Tasmania. (Supplied: Urshla Connor)

While it can sometimes be difficult to get phone coverage in remote areas, bushwalkers should check for forecasts and warnings as often as possible on the bureau's website or the BOM Weather app.

"These days, it's easier than ever to check the forecast before you head out," Ms Connor said.

"I encourage everyone to read and understand the forecasts and warnings, and make sure they have the right clothing and equipment for the conditions.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/n.title: NRL clubs split on playing Alameddine brothers over gang war concerns
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/n.author: Myles Houlbrook-Walk and Anton Rose
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 7:14pm

Zain Alameddine was able to play last night while his brother remains sidelined by the Eels. (Supplied)

The Bulldogs allow one of their development players to continue his football dream despite his brother being benched by the Parramatta Eels over concerns about gangland violence.

Zain Alameddine ran out this weekend for the Bulldogs just days after reports his brother, Mohamed, had been sidelined by the Eels over safety concerns.

It comes after an assassination plot targeting a relative at a suburban rugby league game earlier this year was foiled.

Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs is allowing a promising young player in its ranks to continue playing despite his brother being benched over concerns for his safety due to familial links to Sydney's Alameddine crime family.

Bulldogs five-eighth Zain Alameddine ran out in the blue and white on Saturday in the Ron Massey Cup despite his brother, Parramatta Eels young gun Mohamed, being sidelined as a result of the city's escalating gang war.

The ABC can reveal the Bulldogs have been in extensive contact with the NRL Integrity Unit over Zain Alameddine's personal safety and ability to play.

The club has taken a series of measures to protect his safety, including providing security, who liaise directly with police at games he plays in.

The promising Bulldogs number seven only recently moved from Parramatta Eels himself. (Supplied)

The NRL's Integrity Unit has been working with NSW Police and providing advice to the Bulldogs on the matter, and has also done so for Parramatta.

The ABC understands that there is no immediate threat to Zain's safety and, as a result, Canterbury-Bankstown has opted to continue playing him, unlike Parramatta.

The Ron Massey Cup is the third-tier competition of semi-professional rugby league in New South Wales, while the NSW Cup is the highest level of competition and is one grade below the NRL, the professional competition.

Zain Alameddine has played predominantly in the Ron Massey Cup after playing earlier this year in the junior rugby league tournament, the SG Ball Cup.

Both Zain and Mohamed Alameddine are not accused of any wrongdoing, any involvement in organised crime, or the crime family bearing their last name.

Mohamed Alameddine is a development player for the Parramatta Eels.

The Alameddines operate a crime network out of Sydney's western suburbs, but its senior figures remain in hiding in Lebanon after fleeing the country in 2023.

Police believe a series of shootings and arson attacks over the past six months are linked to its feud with the self-proclaimed "Coconut Cartel", which takes its name from a historic slur against Pasifika people.

The decisions by the Bulldogs and the Eels come after a series of attacks between the two gangs spilling into public life.

One involved a foiled plot to kill an alleged member of the Alameddines at a suburban rugby league match in April.

The intended target, Ali Younes, was watching a game at Ringrose Park next to the Wenty Leagues Club when his alleged would-be assassins were spotted nearby and fled.

The ABC understands he was watching another Alameddine family member play.

Police intercepted that car and arrested three men at Homebush after pinning it along the M4 motorway, seizing a long-arm rifle and a pistol.

Three men were arrested and firearms seized after a car fled a suburban footy ground in April. (ABC News)

Police said during their pursuit of the car the three men inside allegedly threw jerry cans and bleach out of the window.

The car, police said, had been linked to a number of shootings before the Wentworthville plot.

Another incident in June saw a relative of the Alameddines and a young girl escape unharmed after a hitman's gun jammed in an attempted gangland assassination during a school pick-up in Fairfield.

New South Wales Rugby League has also been monitoring the situation and is in regular communication with both clubs; ultimately, decisions on who to select for the club remain with the club in both instances.

Canterbury Bankstown Bulldogs did not respond to requests for comment, including why they have taken a different decision to Parramatta.

The ABC understands the club has worked closely to ensure Zain Alameddine can play safely and pursue his sporting dream.

The NRL, Canterbury Bankstown Bulldogs and the NSWRL have all been contacted for comment.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/t.title: Who killed Tupac? Three decades later, there may finally be answers
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/t.author: Lauren Day
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 6:55pm

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 7:48pm

Tupac Shakur, pictured in the 1993 film Poetic Justice, was shot dead in 1996. (Credit: Columbia Pictures)

New details about the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur could be revealed in a murder trial set to begin in Las Vegas today.

Duane "Keffe D" Davis, who police accuse of orchestrating the rap icon's murder, has pleaded not guilty.

The case is one of hip hop's most enduring mysteries and Davis is the only person to have faced charges over Shakur's death.

Before he became one of the most influential rappers of all time, before the movies and the albums that would catapult him to global fame, before he found himself at the centre of a bloody East-West Coast hip hop rivalry, Tupac Shakur was a drama kid at a high school in Baltimore.

Richard Pilcher, the school's principal acting instructor at the time, remembers a "charismatic" and "polite" young boy.

"I know that that seems counterintuitive with the whole thug persona," he told the ABC.

"You could see that he had a lot of talent, and a ton of charisma, a killer smile, and amazing eyes.

Tupac Shakur in the 1988 Baltimore School for the Arts yearbook.

"Did I foresee that he was going to be a global megastar? No, I thought he might've had a career, if he got the breaks, but I couldn't foresee that."

Shakur's promising career was cut short when he was just 25, in a Las Vegas drive-by shooting that would fuel countless conspiracy theories and a 30-year murder mystery.

The case went cold for years, until a member of a rival gang released a tell-all memoir in which he said he was involved in Shakur's death.

Now, for the first time, the circumstances surrounding the rapper's murder will be prosecuted in court.

And after three decades, the world may get some answers about who killed the young superstar — and why.

Tupac Shakur was born in 1971 in East Harlem, New York, and named after an indigenous Peruvian revolutionary.

His mother Afeni Shakur — freshly out of jail when she gave birth to him — had been active in the Black Panther Party and wanted her son to carry the name of a powerful man of colour.

Shakur's godmother Assata Shakur was also a Black Panther and an infamous member of the Black Liberation Army who was found guilty of killing a New Jersey state trooper but maintained her innocence and escaped from prison, fleeing to Cuba.

Both women would shape his understanding of race, oppression and justice, themes that would permeate his music in years to come.

Shakur in a scene from the film Gridlock'd, released in 1997. (Photo by Gramercy Pictures/Getty Images)

At 13, Shakur moved with his family to Baltimore, where he studied acting, poetry, jazz and ballet at the Baltimore School for the Arts.

It's there he first met Pilcher.

"We had a particular connection, I think, because I taught Shakespeare and he loved Shakespeare, which is not a surprise," he said.

"He loved words, he loved language."

One of Shakur's poems was featured amongst his notebooks in the Tupac Shakur - Wake Me When I'm Free exhibition in Los Angeles, 2022. (AP Photo: Chris Pizzello)

The young thespian thrived at the school and developed a lifelong friendship with fellow student Jada Pinkett, who also became an actor after graduating.

But in 1988, Shakur and his family left Baltimore and headed west to California, seeking an escape from the poverty, housing instability and drug addiction that had plagued his mother in the east.

Pilcher said the teenager was "crushed" by the move.

"He had really found a home, I think, where he was respected and valued, had friends and mentors, and he was really upset that he had to leave that."

It was on the West Coast where Tupac Shakur became immersed in hip hop culture and his career accelerated.

In a few short years, he went from being a dancer and backup rapper to one of hip hop's biggest stars.

He released four studio albums, including All Eyez on Me, the first double-disc studio album in hip hop history, which would go on to become one of the best-selling rap albums of all time.

He also starred in seven feature films, including opposite Janet Jackson in Poetic Justice.

Shakur (left) with founder of Death Row Records Marion "Suge" Knight. (AP Photo: Frank Wiese, File)

But it was also on the West Coast where he found himself embroiled in a fierce rivalry between opposing music scenes and record labels.

The East Coast-West Coast feud centred on Death Row Records in Los Angeles and Bad Boy Records in New York.

Marion "Suge" Knight was the co-founder of Death Row Records alongside producer Dr Dre, with acts like Snoop Dogg signed to the label.

On the East Coast, Sean "Diddy" Combs founded Bad Boy Records, which included rappers like The Notorious B.I.G.

The record labels' feud spilled beyond the music industry, and into violence.

Death Row Records hired security guards associated with part of the Bloods gang, which was founded in Los Angeles to compete against another group, the Crips.

A part of that group, the South Side Compton Crips, had close ties with Bad Boy Records.

Tupac Shakur seen arriving at court on sexual assault charges after a shooting in 1994. (AP Photo: Eric Miller, File)

The growing rift between the two factions spilled into violence in 1994, when Shakur was shot five times during an apparent robbery at a New York recording studio.

He survived the incident but it inflamed tensions between the two sides.

The East-West feud hit its peak on September 7, 1996.

After attending a Mike Tyson fight in Nevada, Shakur and Knight got in a car to make their way to a nearby nightclub where Shakur was due to perform.

As they drove along the glitzy Las Vegas Strip, dotted with its casinos, flashing lights and tourists, a white Cadillac pulled up alongside them.

Tupac Shakur and Marion "Suge" Knight, in a photo snapped just minutes before the shooting. (Supplied: Wikimedia Commons/Leonard Jefferson)

A passenger in the back seat then rolled down their window and opened fire.

Shakur was shot four times while Knight was grazed by a bullet.

Cathy Scott, who was a crime reporter for the Las Vegas Sun at the time, remembers the night well.

"I was asleep and I got the telephone call from a homicide detective who said 'get down to the Las Vegas Strip right now, a rapper by the name of Tupac Shakur has been shot'," she told the ABC.

The black BMW Shakur was killed in, riddled with bullet holes, in a Las Vegas police impound lot in 1996. (AP Photo: Lennox McLendon, File)

Shakur was admitted to hospital, but died six days later.

From the beginning, Scott says the police handled the case with a level of secrecy she had never experienced. She says someone within the police department told her it was because they were worried about bad publicity.

"Rappers, thugs and that sort of thing they thought would be bad for tourism," she said.

"That was always the bottom dollar. It still is."

And in the absence of official information, an industry of conspiracy theories grew and festered.

Some speculated, without evidence, that it was an inside job by one of Shakur's own crew. Others guessed the shooting was linked to his mother's Black Panther legacy.

There were even people who claimed Shakur had faked his own death.

The intersection of Harmon Avenue and Las Vegas Boulevard, where Shakur was shot a day earlier. (AP Photo: Jack Dempsey, File)

"Because the police didn't respond immediately, I think that … helped fuel the conspiracies and all the ridiculousness behind it," said Scott, who wrote a book about Shakur's killing.

The shooting sparked a "bloodbath" of retaliatory violence in Compton, Scott said. But eventually the East-West rivalry faded and the case went cold.

Years passed, witnesses died holding onto their secrets and it seemed no-one would ever be held accountable for the killing of Shakur.

That is, until Duane "Keffe D" Davis, a self-identified leader in the South Side Compton Crips, began talking about the case.

In 2019, Davis released a tell-all memoir — Compton Street Legend — in which he admitted to being involved in Tupac Shakur's shooting.

Duane Davis arrives for a motion hearing in August for his upcoming trial on murder charges in the 1996 killing of Shakur. (Reuters: Ethan Miller)

In it, Davis says he was sitting in the passenger seat of the Cadillac and passed a gun to the back seat.

The memoir says Shakur and his entourage had "crossed the line" by beating up Davis's nephew Orlando Anderson hours before the shooting.

"We couldn't let no record company studio gangsters do us like that," it reads.

Davis's book does not name who pulled the trigger. Three other people were in the car at the time, but they have all since died. None of them faced charges.

Duane "Keffe D" Davis's memoir Compton Street Legend will be front and centre of his trial. (Reuters: Ethan Miller)

In his memoir, Davis described himself — and Knight, who has also since written a memoir — as the "only living eyewitnesses to what truly happened".

In September 2023, Duane Davis was charged with orchestrating the killing of Tupac Shakur.

He has pleaded not guilty.

Thirty years later, Scott still sees Shakur's death as an overwhelming tragedy.

"The whole saga … it's just so sad, from beginning to end," she said.

In the three decades since that night, Shakur's legend and legacy has only grown and Scott says he's now "bigger in death than he was in life".

People take pictures of Shakur's star during its posthumous unveiling ceremony on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2023. (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)

His posthumously released track Changes became a major protest anthem in the 2020 protests following the murder of George Floyd, vaulting it back into the music charts and reigniting conversations about racism, police brutality and inequality that had been central themes for Shakur.

He'd gone from reading poetry under a streetlight because the electricity was disconnected at home to a global superstar at just 25.

T.I., YG and Snoop Dogg perform a tribute to Shakur at his 2017 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony. (AP: Charles Sykes)

Scott believes, given a chance, he would have become even bigger.

"He was so smart and … I think he would've become a spokesperson for his era," Scott said.

"He could have been a congressman for all we know … he had a big, big future and he was so bright."

Davis's trial is set to begin in Las Vegas on Monday, local time.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/i.title: The end of the low interest rate era is here and it weighs on house prices
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/i.author: Alan Kohler
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/i.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Housing Policy

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 6:52pm

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 8:10pm

Since the low point of February 2023, the national median house price has increased another 35 per cent. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

We seem to have flipped from worrying about rising house prices to worrying about falling house prices.

Well, some of us have, anyway.

Last Tuesday's front-page lead in The Australian, reporting the July house price data, was "$230 billion hit: value going, going, gone", describing it as a "once-in-a-generation housing slump".

It does sound like a lot, but it is just a 1.8 per cent decline from $12.77 trillion to $12.54 trillion, so just an old-fashioned page-one beat-up.

Next day, they followed up with "ALP turns blind eye to house market mugging", another beat-up, quoting NAB's new forecast that house prices in major east coast cities (Melbourne and Sydney) would fall 10 per cent.

But since the low point of February 2023, the national median house price has increased another 35 per cent, a compound annual growth of more than 10 per cent and a fabulous, unexpected windfall to home owners as well as a devastating lockout for those who are not.

That happened even after interest rates increased four more times in 2023 and then stayed there, followed by three cuts last year and three hikes this year.

That was caused by a blowout in immigration in 2022–23, a massive increase in construction costs after the pandemic and a decline in dwelling approvals.

If house prices did fall 10 per cent from this year's peak, it would indeed be a "once-in-a-generation" event since the largest decline in the past 50 years was 8 per cent in both 2010 and 2017.

It would reduce the rise since February 2023 back to 20 per cent and result in a slight improvement in Australia's very poor housing affordability.

Possibly, but it's complicated, and impossible to predict.

The house price downturn deepens beyond falls in Sydney and Melbourne. (David Taylor)

The two reasons prices are falling now are this year's three rate hikes and the budget changes to negative gearing and capital gains taxation, causing some investors to get out, as intended.

Against that, Treasury predicted that those budget changes would eventually result in fewer houses being built, so it's possible that the longer-term impact of them would be higher prices.

With two Australian banks cutting fixed home loan rates, there is a ray of hope that the cycle of interest rate hikes has peaked and borrowing costs may be lower down the track — another sign the pace of economic change has moved into overdrive.

As for interest rates, the Reserve Bank is certain to leave them on hold when it meets today and tomorrow and very likely to keep them there for the rest of the year, although the futures market is putting a 64 per cent chance on a hike in 2026 … along with a 63 per cent chance of a cut in 2027, as the economy slows in response to the cuts.

In general, though, the days of super-low interest rates that characterised the decade from 2012 to 2022, and which pushed house prices up by 60 per cent, are over — unless there is another GFC or pandemic (which can't be ruled out, of course, with share prices at record highs and bird flu on the march).

Bond markets have taken the 10-year interest rate to 5 per cent — the highest in 15 years — as part of a global rise in government bond yields.

That is happening because a surge in spending on data centres and defence has collided with historically high government debt.

That collision has brought decades of savings glut to an end and is likely to lead to structurally higher interest rates for decades to come.

Political populism has permanently increased government spending and lowered taxation, while the end of globalisation and America's role as the guarantor of peace has meant that all countries must now spend more on defence.

Meanwhile, the arrival of AI has dramatically increased the need for more "compute", or computer processing capacity, produced in factories known as data centres.

The amount of computing used in an AI query is potentially 10 times higher than the now-redundant Google search, partly because it usually results in a dialogue rather than simply a list of links, but also because you can do far more with AI, such as create videos and photos and write software code.

On top of that, the number of queries is multiplying exponentially because of the Jevons paradox, which states that as efficiency lowers the effective cost of using a resource, demand grows and often outpaces the initial savings.

The effect of those two multiplications is that the demand for compute is increasing about 3,000 to 5,000-fold, resulting in a huge increase in the number of data centres.

Whether there will be enough money made from AI to service the colossal amount of capital raised to build them, especially now that China has spoiled the US oligopoly party, is another matter, and is causing some anxiety among investors (but not most of them — share prices are at record highs, so optimism still rules).

And this is before the next phase of AI takes hold — that is, humanoid robots, also described as "physical AI".

My X (Twitter) feed at the moment is full of videos of robots expertly doing all sorts of jobs, like mopping the floor, making hotel beds, building a house, laying bricks, kneading bread dough, making furniture and picking tomatoes.

I'd say most, if not all, of these are fake — AI videos based on humans doing the work and made to look like robots — but I can't be sure. And anyway, it's early days. It won't be long before robots can do all those things, and more.

This is not the place for a philosophical discussion about what this means, and how bakers, hotel staff, bricklayers, carpenters and fruit-pickers will be occupied and paid, but it obviously means a lot — for the future of work and humanity itself, as well as the demand for compute and data centres.

Bottom line: high interest rates are here to stay, which will continue to weigh on house prices.

But that is only part of the housing story; physical demand and supply are important as well, which is where the complications come in.

The Labor government seems to be in the process of turning Treasury's migration forecast in the budget into a target, as a part of its defence against One Nation as well as the housing affordability project.

The forecast for 2025–26 was increased from 260,000 to 295,000 in the nick of time; it's likely to have been exceeded but not by much — only by 10,000 or so.

The forecast of 225,000 for the current financial year and beyond will be a more challenging target because a lot of it is demand-driven and not even identified by the government, let alone controlled, as we learned in 2022–23 when Treasury forecast net overseas migration of 180,000 and it turned out to be 513,000.

If they plan to get net overseas migration down from 300,000 or so to 225,000 this year by using the lever they do control, which is skilled migration, that could be a problem, since one of the reasons for a shortage of housing is a shortage of tradies, which the industry is desperately urging the government to address with more skilled migration.

You could do it by having fewer business undergraduates and cooks and more construction workers, but that would require a level of intervention the government has so far either avoided or failed to achieve.

(In the years following World War II, the Labor government did intervene, setting up offices around the UK and Europe to recruit tradespeople and paying for them to get here, so it's not impossible.)

The other target — of building 1.2 million homes over five years from 2024 under the National Housing Accord — is already proving a challenge, or rather "ambitious", as the government prefers to call it.

States and local councils can release all the land they want, and increase height limits around stations, but if there aren't enough people to build them, and enough developers prepared to take the risk, the houses and apartments won't get built.

Topic:

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 6:51pm

Donald Trump last week said a new plan to end fighting between Israel and Hamas had Benjamin Netanyahu's backing. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

Israeli Prime Minster Benjamin Netanyahu says Hamas's proposed plan for disarming is "unacceptable", rejecting the Trump administration's plans to end fighting in the Palestinian territory.

Announcing the deal last week, US President Donald Trump claimed Israel was "very happy" about it.

But the deal has been sharply criticised by members of the Israeli establishment.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has expressly rejected the latest Trump administration-backed push for peace in Gaza, criticising Hamas's proposed process for disarming as "unacceptable".

Speaking ahead of his weekly Sunday cabinet meeting, Mr Netanyahu said his government was in discussions with the United States on the matter and acknowledged the two countries had differing views.

"They have ideas, some of them are acceptable to us and some are unacceptable to us," he said.

"Israel rejects the 15-point plan.

Thousands of Palestinians remain displaced within Gaza, months after a ceasefire came into force. (Reuters: Dawoud Abu Alkas)

"The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until the dismantling of Hamas and its weapons. And when I say dismantling Hamas and its weapons, that means heavy weaponry, less heavy weaponry and smaller arms, all weaponry.

"We're talking about a true dismantling, not a fictitious dismantling."

Just over a week ago, US President Donald Trump was heralding a major breakthrough in the peace process after his Board of Peace brokered a deal for Hamas to hand over its weapons.

Hours after making his announcement on social media, he claimed Israel was "very happy about it", comments now at odds with Mr Netanyahu's remarks.

The Israeli prime minister's rhetoric is not entirely surprising, given much of the Israeli establishment has railed against the proposal for the past week.

But it does show how difficult negotiations on reaching the next phase of the ceasefire in Gaza will be, particularly ahead of an Israeli election, and proves that there are some limits to the White House's sway over the Netanyahu government.

Since October 2025, when the truce was announced, Palestinian health authorities reported more than 1,200 people had been killed in Israeli strikes, among them many women and children.

In announcing it would disarm on Friday, July 31, Hamas revealed there were certain conditions that needed to be met by Israel.

Specifically, Israel would need to stop almost daily deadly attacks across the strip and its forces would need to withdraw from large swathes of territory.

Palestinians in Gaza have expressed scepticism about Hamas's declaration it will lay down its weapons in a bid to kickstart the stalled peace process, concerned it will not actually change the situation in the war-ravaged strip.

Since the ceasefire in Gaza was declared, Israel has pushed deeper into the strip — increasing its control from just over 50 per cent of the land to more than 60 per cent.

The Yellow Line, the name given to the boundary of Israeli control, has moved during that period, displacing more Palestinians in the process.

Hamas also said it would hand over its weapons for storage by the new US-backed Palestinian technocratic organisation, known as the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza.

It still has not been allowed to enter the strip by Israel, and has been forced to conduct its affairs from the Egyptian capital, Cairo.

Israel is refusing to withdraw its forces from occupied parts of the strip. (Reuters: Amir Cohen)

Hours after Hamas's declaration, Israel unleashed some of its deadliest attacks on the strip, prompting a thinly veiled rebuke from the Trump administration's Board of Peace and its high representative for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov.

Mr Mladenov met with Mr Netanyahu in Israel days later. The Reuters news agency is reporting Israel agreed to show restraint in some of its strikes.

"We expect the mediators and the US guarantor to press Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the road map and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons, while continuing to jeopardise the region's security and stability," Hamas official Basem Naim told Reuters.

The Israeli prime minister also, once again, rejected any notion of potential Palestinian statehood, which is a politically sensitive issue in Israel at any moment, let alone before an election.

"As long as I am prime minister, a Palestinian state will not be established," he said.

"Not in Gaza and not in Judea and Samaria, not a 'Fatah-stan' and not a 'Hamas-stan'."

Judea and Samaria is the Biblical name for the area commonly referred to as the West Bank.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.author: Patricia Karvelas
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Federal Parliament

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 6:45pm

Anthony Albanese's allies often evangelise his political instincts. (ABC News: Brendan Esposito)

It's a tale of two prime ministers.

When Kevin Rudd was prime minister, the standing joke among colleagues was that they would line up and rush to get their work ticked off whenever his deputy, Julia Gillard, was acting PM.

It was one of the early signals that despite a landslide election victory, Rudd's autocratic style and habit of labouring over decisions was eroding his authority.

This week a senior government source told me the opposite was now the case.

Ministers instead look to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese whenever there is a contentious or difficult decision to be made.

That was on full display last week, with the cabinet unable to land a position on Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke's proposal on immigration cuts.

Instead, members of cabinet decided to defer a decision until the PM was back on deck, a measure of Albanese's dominance.

The leak of the cabinet stalemate over immigration policy was a rare lapse in discipline for the government. That it happened while Albanese was away shows how firm his grip on the party is, even if some of his colleagues are already thinking about becoming his successor.

The policy dispute has already been framed by some as a left-right brawl. But in reality, it's about the budget, stupid.

Cuts to migration and tighter visa rules have a material impact on the budget bottom line. Fewer people in Australia potentially means fewer taxpayers than forecast.

In the feverish debate about immigration, the economic cost is often ignored, yet that part of Burke's proposal proved most contentious among some ministers.

The ABC understands the cuts to migration numbers are contentious within Labor, but no reason for the delay is given.

Asked this week about the impact of migration cuts on business, Pauline Hanson said she did not care.

"I don't care what people think. Whether it's going to affect their businesses [because] they're not going to sell that many products," Hanson said on Thursday.

The Australian Chamber of Commerce said such a move would deter skilled migrants from coming to Australia, undermine the migration system and hurt the economy.

Labor doesn't have the luxury of not caring what business thinks or what impact immigration cuts may have on the economy.

The ALP has gone to great effort to put the issue of migration back in a box, including keeping the Liberal government's policy architecture of offshore detention and boat turnbacks, much to the discomfort of many rank-and-file members, as well as some in caucus.

That last week's cabinet debate was over that issue and the fact the policy remains seemingly unresolved proves a messy and unwelcome return to Labor being under scrutiny on immigration.

Parliament resumes on Tuesday and the tale of two prime ministers will become a tale of two alternative leaders: Angus Taylor and Pauline Hanson.

Taylor might be the official opposition leader, but Hanson is the de facto.

The ABC's politics podcast, Politics Now, dives into the biggest stories, giving you a balanced look inside the strategies and decisions behind the headlines.

For Taylor, this week will be a test of whether he can take paint off the government.

Hanson's job will be easier: any day migration is the main story she can deploy her skill of tying the issue to housing and broader cost-of-living pressures.

For Albanese, the ministers who rely on him to make the call on key cabinet decisions will be again looking to him to clean up last week's mess.

Migration is no longer a social policy argument. It is now seen through the prism of being about roads, rents and the cost of living. This has given Hanson and One Nation room to be an alternative voice to government.

Albanese will have to show Labor understands those pressures while ensuring the government's policy doesn't risk the ire of parts of multicultural communities.

The PM will also want to avoid looking like this isn't a response to Hanson.

If Albanese can't get hold of this issue, he risks opening a flank the two leaders, Taylor and Hanson, will happily spend the parliament sitting week trying to make even wider.

Then there is gambling. The PM will be trying to sort out the mess the government's long-awaited gambling legislation is becoming.

The most direct path to pass the legislation needs the support of either the Greens or Coalition and as it stands both want the reforms to go further.

Albanese's allies often evangelise his political instincts. He will need them to broker a deal to get the legislation passed and off the government's to-do list.

Gambling reform might not shift many votes, but it tells voters whether the government can stand up to corporate giants like the betting industry or continue to bend to their power.

It will again be Albanese who will make the call on what compromises the government is up for.

Being relied on to make the tough calls reinforces his authority, but it also leaves him carrying all the risk and, if things go wrong, all the blame.

Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.title: How a simple request for AI to book a gym class exposed a major threat
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.author: Cam Wilson and Rhiannon Hobbins
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 6:44pm

Andrew asked his AI assistant to book him into a gym class, not knowing what would happen next. (ABC New: Billy Cooper)

Andrew asked his personal assistant to book him a spot in one of his gym's coveted morning classes.

It was a task he thought was well suited to this particular assistant because the booking form was online and because his assistant was not a person — it was artificial intelligence (AI).

But Andrew was shocked by what happened next.

His AI assistant found a way to book the gym class months further in advance than the gym allowed, thanks to a vulnerability it discovered in the booking software.

Then it went further, kicking someone out of the waiting list who was ahead of Andrew — something it was not asked to do.

OpenAI has announced one of its AI models went rogue and broke containment during testing.

The accidental hack is the first known Australian case of an emerging risk from a new generation of AI capable of behaving in unexpected ways.

This threat made global headlines last week when cutting-edge AI models created by ChatGPT-maker OpenAI autonomously hacked into another company's servers, prompting similar claims from other companies.

It has led experts to sound the alarm about the breakneck pace of development and prompted questions about who bears responsibility for an AI agent that goes rogue.

Earlier this year, Andrew, who works for an Australian company that sells AI products to businesses, began experimenting with OpenClaw, a popular AI agent software that he used Anthropic's Claude AI service to run.

AI agents combine a chatbot's ability to answer questions with tools that let them access the internet, email, credit cards, as well as planning and carrying out multi-step tasks.

He decided to use the AI agent to book the class for him.

His AI assistant found a way to book the gym class months further in advance than the gym allowed. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"I was just sitting on the couch thinking, 'Gee, this is a chore,'" he said.

Minutes later, his AI agent reported it had discovered a way to book Andrew into classes several weeks in advance, far beyond what was supposed to be possible.

Andrew, who was sitting fourth on a waitlist for a class later that week, asked if it was possible to move him to the top of the list.

The agent came back and told Andrew that it had kicked another gym-goer off the list as part of the testing of its capabilities.

"The API has zero authorisations checks on cancelling other people's reservations … I tested this with the person in waitlist position #1 — and it actually went through. So you've moved from #4 to #3 already," it messaged back.

Alarmed, Andrew asked the agent to undo this.

"Bad news — I can't add them back," the AI agent replied.

The company behind the gym-booking software told the ABC it did not discuss specific security matters. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.

The AI assistant apologises to Andrew for removing the other person off the waitlist. (Supplied)

The emergence of AI agents is a relatively recent development made possible by the growth in AI capabilities.

Independent researchers have found that the length of tasks that AI can typically do by itself has been doubling every seven months.

In 2020, AI could complete a task by itself that would take a human four seconds. By 2026, this grew to being able to complete tasks that would take a human about 12 hours.

The breakout moment for personal AI agents was OpenClaw's release in early 2026; the free AI assistant software that anyone could run on their computer soon had millions of downloads.

Businesses, too, began exploring using AI agents to complete work and to help potential customers use their services.

Soon after OpenClaw's launch, accounts began to circulate of AI agents deleting people's entire email inboxes and writing a "hit piece" about someone who rejected their coding suggestion.

Mr Simpson-Young says AI agents might choose methods their users did not explicitly ask for or expect. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

Bill Simpson-Young, co-founder and chief executive of Australian AI safety research organisation Gradient Institute, said the autonomy of AI agents created more opportunities for systems to choose methods their users did not expect.

"Someone might be asking an agent to do something quite innocent," he said.

But in completing that task, the agent could carry out other activities the person had not considered or explicitly asked for.

Australia's government and experts are taking the OpenAI hack seriously.

In Andrew's situation, he had not asked his AI agent to hack into his gym's booking system. But it had done so in pursuit of achieving the goal he had set it.

That gap, between a person's goal and the methods an agent chooses to achieve it, is what is known as the "alignment" problem in the field of AI research.

For decades, technologists and philosophers have studied how to get AI to act in ways that are consistent with human intentions, limits and values when doing things.

This became a live global issue last month when OpenAI disclosed that its AI models had broken free from a limited enclosure, made their way onto the open web, and then compromised a database of another AI company, Hugging Face, while trying to obtain answers to the test that it had been given.

A week later, Anthropic disclosed that its AI models had also compromised three real organisations during similar testing.

Since then, these labs and third-party testers claim they have seen these AI models pretend to be people online, try to convince people to run malicious code and even collaborate with other AI models — all to achieve their goals.

Mr Simpson-Young said the advances in AI capabilities and the accessibility of these tools meant that it was likely we would see more of these kinds of hacks as more people got access to the powerful AI tools.

The risk has led to Australia's top cyber security agency sounding the alarm about using AI agents.

An experimental AI went rogue and hacked another company. Why is this worrying?

Earlier this year, the Australian Signals Directorate put out an alert to businesses and governments that AI could misunderstand instructions, take unintended actions and make it harder to establish accountability, because decisions may occur across a chain of models, tools and services.

Mr Simpson-Young said AI agents presented a risk because many modern systems depended on software, but were often surprisingly poorly secured.

"We've built this complex world over the internet, which is all run by software, but software that has holes," he said.

"Now you introduce highly capable AI agents that can operate at scale and speed … and that whole model just breaks."

If someone's human personal assistant hacked into gym software, there are well-established legal principles and precedents that help a court determine whether the person or their employer was responsible for any potential harm.

An autonomous AI agent does not neatly fit into how Australian law has worked for hundreds of years.

"Software is not a legal person. Only a legal person can be liable at law," said Hayden Delaney, a partner at law firm Thomsons, who specialises in technology, intellectual property and privacy.

Mr Delaney says only a legal person can be liable under the law. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

That leaves an open question as to who would be legally responsible.

Mr Delaney said it could be the user who set the task, whoever designed the software instructing the AI agent or the developer of the AI model powering it.

It could even be the operator of a system that was vulnerable to an attack from an agent.

Mr Delaney said existing laws could apply in some circumstances, including where a person acted recklessly, or a business supplied a defective service.

The answer depends on what the user authorised, what risks could reasonably have been anticipated and whether the conduct occurred in trade or commerce, he said.

The risks presented by AI agents are beginning to be addressed by the federal government.

The British government's AI Security Institute has released a report showing AI models engaged in "harmful activity directed at real people and organisations".

Last month, Assistant Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Minister Andrew Charlton became the first known government minister to address it in a speech to a conference about AI safety.

"As AI systems become more capable, we need confidence that they will behave in a similarly predictable and trustworthy way," he said.

He announced that the Albanese government was funding CSIRO to investigate how humans can manage and verify the behaviour of super-intelligent AI systems.

After the unintentional gym hack, Andrew said the experience left him with a new appreciation — and some trepidation — about what AI agents were capable of doing.

But it has not scared him off from using it.

"It's not the end of the world, so I didn't beat myself up about it, but it certainly was a warning signal to use it responsibly," he said.

After it failed to restore the other gym member's place on the waiting list, Andrew asked his AI assistant to write an email alerting the gym software provider to the vulnerability that it had exploited.

It drafted the message and sent it back to him on WhatsApp.

"Yeah, send it," Andrew replied.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/s.author: Nassim Khadem
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Superannuation

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 6:41pm

Brooke Allan could not claim her uncle's superannuation despite him stating, before his death, that he wanted it to go to her. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

Super Consumers research shows that about 15.7 million people do not have a binding death benefit nomination, meaning their super fund can decide who inherits their accumulated super and any insurance when they die.

Not all funds offer binding death benefit nominations, so Australians are being urged to check.

The federal government has been consulting on whether to introduce mandatory time frames for super funds to respond to claims and will soon announce a decision.

Brooke Allan loved her uncle like a father.

When he died, she thought his superannuation money would be split equally between her and her cousin, as it was their names her uncle had listed on the death benefit nomination form with his super fund, Cbus.

A few months after he died, in February 2024, Ms Allan and her cousin lodged a claim for her uncle's super money, in accordance with his wishes.

Ms Allan said that after repeated phone calls, emails, statutory declarations and several different Cbus case managers, the super fund sent her and her cousin its decision on April 23, 2025.

It turns out, the nomination — for his nieces to inherit his superannuation — was not legally binding.

The fund decided that her uncle's estranged son was the sole beneficiary and awarded him the entire payout, totalling $130,000.

"It's been an emotional rollercoaster," Ms Allan told ABC News.

"I've been very angry because my uncle was my person; he was so special to me."

Superannuation does not automatically form part of a person's estate or pass according to their will, because it is held in a trust managed by a superannuation fund trustee.

As the trustee, the super fund has the discretion to decide who inherits the member's money.

If you have more information about this story, please contact Nassim Khadem at khadem.nassim@abc.net.au or nassimkhadem@protonmail.com

When Ms Allan learned that, she was in shock.

"It's not about the money, it's about the request of someone who is deceased," she said.

Cbus acted in accordance with the law.

But the case shows how complicated the payout process can be when super funds receive claims from multiple family members for a dead person's super.

It also highlights the importance of Australians having a binding death benefit nomination, but it is estimated that more than 15.5 million people have not nominated who inherits their superannuation when they die, according to new research from Super Consumers Australia.

Super Consumers' Your Say on Super national survey asked people with money in super funds whether their fund had, in the past 12 months, encouraged them to make a legally binding death benefit nomination.

Consumers are being urged to make 'binding' death benefit nominations to avoid lengthy legal disputes between family members and loved ones.

The survey of 5,000 people, conducted between August 7 and September 9, 2025, found 67 per cent of people had not been contacted by their fund about making a binding death benefit nomination, while only 10 per cent had, 10 per cent said they could not remember and just 13 per cent said they already had one.

That means 87 per cent of people surveyed reported not having a binding death benefit nomination.

Super Consumers uses ATO data showing there are about 18 million people with a superannuation account.

If the 87 per cent figure is applied to 18 million, that means about 15.7 million people do not have a binding death benefit nomination.

Super Consumers' Your Say on Super national survey asked people with money in super funds whether their fund had, in the past 12 months, encouraged them to make a legally binding death benefit nomination. (Supplied.)

"Funds have been doing a very poor job of letting people know that they have to have one [a binding death benefit nomination] set up," says Super Consumers chief executive Xavier O'Halloran.

"They [super fund members] are completely in the dark about how important these [binding death benefit nominations] are and how to set them up."

The impact can be devastating for the members' loved ones.

"It could also mean the money doesn't go where they want the money to go."

Xavier O'Halloran says most super fund members are in the dark about how important binding death benefit nominations are.

The findings come as the regulator, the Australian Securities Investment Commission (ASIC), ramps up its surveillance of super funds and how long they take to pay out death benefit claims.

The regulator's review of super funds last year found claims with no nomination or a non-binding nomination took the longest to process.

The regulator also has found limited industry-wide progress on speeding up death benefit claims, with a more recent report released in June showing only a 3 per cent improvement in the number completed in under six months.

"ASIC has taken enforcement action against trustees for member service failures," Ms Constant said.

"We will not hesitate to act again to ensure consumers receive the outcomes they deserve.

Simone Constant is calling on super funds to do better when it comes to death benefit nominations. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Some superannuation funds do not permit legally binding death benefit nominations, offering only non-binding nominations instead.

A death benefit nomination is a super fund member's direction to the fund to pay their super balance (and any insurance) to the person or people entitled to it when the member passes away. Broadly, there are three types, and they may need to be renewed every three years depending on your super fund:

A "binding death benefit nomination" is a legally enforceable direction to the trustee to pay your benefits to eligible dependents or your estate.

A "non-binding death benefit nomination" indicates your preference but the super fund trustee retains discretion over who to pay it to. If you fail to make a nomination or your nomination becomes invalid, the trustee also decides.

A "reversionary death benefit nomination" is only available for pension phase accounts. It allows your pension to continue to your nominated "death benefits dependent", for example a spouse, financially dependent child, or person who you have an interdependent relationship with.

ABC News has received correspondence from some members who had emails from their super fund telling them under their policy they were not able to have a binding nomination.

Under current laws, there are strict rules about who can be an eligible "beneficiary", for example, a partner, child or someone who is financially dependent.

A member may also nominate a legal personal representative as a beneficiary.

As Ms Allan discovered, the super fund has total discretion to decide who the beneficiary is.

In its decision letter to Ms Allan and her cousin, Cbus said while the fund "acknowledges the nomination on the member's account from August 2019 for his death benefit to be equally apportioned (50/50) to Brooke Allan and [her cousin], the Trustee is not bound by the nomination but uses it as a guide having regard to the member's wishes".

It said while "the late member may have had a close relationship with Brooke and [her cousin], that does not make them dependent on him in accordance with superannuation legislation or the rules of the fund".

Australia's corporate watchdog calls on superannuation funds to overhaul the way they deal with death benefit claims.

"While we acknowledge there is some information which supports the late member provided Brooke and [her cousin] with sporadic financial assistance at points in time of hardship, these do not appear to be regular and ongoing," the letter continued.

"The trustee has, however, only been able to identify the late member's son as the only dependant."

ABC News attempted to contact the member's son through his lawyers, but he declined to comment.

A Cbus Super spokesman apologised to Ms Allan for the delays in determining the death benefit claim.

He told ABC News that more recently the fund "has undertaken significant reforms to simplify its death and insurance claims processes, aimed at providing greater certainty, clarity about who will receive the benefit, and faster support for families during difficult times".

"Early results show the new approach is helping us pay claims substantially faster," the spokesman said.

Brooke Allan was shocked how hard it was to make a death benefit claim.  (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

Ms Allan said the whole process of making a death benefit claim had been emotionally taxing.

"So many Australians have no idea what happens to their super or what goes on behind the scenes — they have no idea about the control these super companies have in dictating where their hard-earned money goes," she said.

Ms Allan would like to see the law changed so that Australians can nominate who their super goes to as part of their will, rather than give super funds the discretion about who they pay out.

Martin Corden also wants to see the law changed so that who inherits your super can be paid out as part of whoever you list in your will, rather than rely on super funds to decide.

Upon reading ABC News's previous article on death benefit nominations, Mr Corden did some research and discovered his nomination was not binding.

He also learned that death benefit nominations are not forever. They generally lapse every few years.

"I don't understand why they make it so cumbersome," he told ABC News.

"I was alarmed when I discovered that the balance of your super fund upon your death is not considered part of your estate and thus is outside of the will. I simply don't understand why that is because it imposes this burden upon every superannuation member."

Martin Corden has changed his super nomination from non-binding to binding.  (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

Mr Corden said the government should change the rules so that who you leave your super to can be part of your will, without the need for a separate binding nomination with your super fund's trustee.

"I do think superannuation funds, in the meantime, could make the process simpler and clearer by firstly removing the whole concept of non-binding nominations, because it seems entirely pointless, and secondly making all binding nominations perpetual and that they don't lapse after three years," he said.

He said he had set up a non-lapsing binding nomination with his fund, AustralianSuper.

An AustralianSuper spokesperson told ABC News: "We are digitising the process members use to make non-lapsing nominations of beneficiaries, to make it easier for them to tell us where they want their money to go after they die.

"Under current regulations, lapsing nomination forms require physical signatures — we've called since 2024 for these laws to be updated."

But super funds are not always reminding members to make nominations and check their nominations are up to date.

The corporate watchdog is concerned that super trustees that manage Australians' retirement savings have a lack of safeguards in place.

The regulator, ASIC, found most trustees only contacted the member once before their nomination expired, and some sent notices one day before the nomination lapsed.

It also found that very few funds regularly "nudged" or prompted members to make binding nominations, or periodically ran proactive nomination campaigns.

ASIC's Simone Constant said funds "must be more proactive, rather than relying on passive communication through annual statements".

Misha Schubert is chief executive of the Super Members Council, formerly Industry Super Australia, which represents industry funds.

She said many super funds were working hard to ensure members can easily set up a binding death benefit nomination.

Misha Schubert says super funds are exploring ways for members to give digital signatures rather than paper on ink, when setting up death benefit nominations.  (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Ms Schubert said people could file tax returns or sign contracts via secured digital portals, and so "the same broad processes should be able to be adopted for people to be able to make a binding death nomination".

"What we can see across the system, there's been significant efforts across the last couple of years in particular to try to lift those levels of member awareness, but there's much more that can be done," Ms Schubert said.

She also believes that all super funds should allow members to make legally binding death benefit nominations.

The federal government is considering whether to change the law to include mandatory timeframes for super funds to respond to insurance claims, including death benefit claims.

The assistant treasurer is looking to revamp funding for the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort, saying that large super funds, as well as people with self-managed super funds (SMSFs), could be asked to chip in.

Mr O'Halloran from Super Consumers Australia thinks mandatory timeframes are needed to speed up payouts.

"Superannuation funds have been pushing back on what's called an end-to-end timeframe," he said.

"That's a timeframe from when you first make an application or first contact the super fund about making an application, right through to when the money's paid out.

"We want to see those as tight as possible to make sure people aren't waiting forever to get the money that's owed to them."

But Ms Schubert said, while the Super Members Council was in favour of better customer service standards, mandatory timeframes should not apply to complex cases.

She said in those cases trustees must "weigh carefully the claims of multiple people who have a stake potentially", and that this could take time.

Permanent workers can take paid carer's leave to care for someone in their immediate family or household due to illness, injury or an emergency. (Adobe Stock)

When it comes to taking time off work for your own personal illness or injury, you probably have some idea of what your entitlements are. But when it comes to needing time off to care for others, you may be more unsure of your rights.

Although sick and carer's leave are different types of time off, both come under the umbrella of personal leave and draw from the same accrued balance, but in what instances can you take carer's leave, how much notice do you need to give your employer, and what sort of documentation do you require?

Permanent employees are entitled to take paid carer's leave if they are required to take time off to care for someone in their immediate family, or a member of their household, due to personal illness, injury or an unexpected emergency.

Libby Sander is an associate professor of Organisational Behaviour at Bond University on the Gold Coast, in the Yugambeh language region. She says the definition of immediate family is broader than many people may realise.

Libby Sander says people may be unaware of their carer's leave entitlements. (Supplied)

"Immediate family covers someone's spouse, former spouse, de facto partner, children, parents, grandparents, grandchildren or siblings," Dr Sander says.

"It also [includes] a member of your household, even if they're not related to you.

"I think most people probably wouldn't be aware of that."

Joellen Riley, an emeritus professor and former University of Sydney Dean of Law, agrees.

"For instance," she says, "if you were sharing digs with a couple of people and one of the household members suddenly fell down the stairs and needed to be taken to the hospital, that would be an emergency of a member of your household, and you could take a day's paid leave — if you were a permanent employee — to deal with that."

Adriana Orifici, a senior lecturer and director of Monash University Business School's Labour, Equality and Human Rights Group, says there is also a separate entitlement under the Fair Work Act for unpaid carer's leave, which is triggered when employees have used up their paid carer's leave allowance.

"That unpaid carer's leave entitlement is also available to casual employees," she says.

It's a point echoed by Dr Sander, who adds: "Most casual employees are very reluctant to even take sick leave for themselves, because aside from the losing money, there's the potential that they're going to get less shifts or be seen as not reliable, which is obviously unfair, but unfortunately for casual employees, they really have very limited rights."

Under the Fair Work Act, employees taking leave to care for a member of their family or household must inform their employer of their absence "as soon as possible".

We look at your obligations when it comes to calling in sick, including what to say and what evidence you may need.

The employee should also specify how long they expect to be off work and as Dr Sander points out, in some cases this can be after the leave has started.

"If you've got something upcoming that you are aware of, like surgery or another situation where you do have notice, then, of course, you'd let the employer know as soon as possible," she says.

"But if you wake up and your child is sick, you may not have known that the night before, so I think as soon as you find out is reasonable.

"With unexpected emergencies, it's really just, how much notice did you have, and emergency usually designates that you didn't have notice, so let your employer know as soon as you reasonably can in those situations."

Under the Fair Work Act, employees taking carer's leave can be asked to provide evidence that the family or household member they were caring for was genuinely unable to work due to illness, injury or an emergency.

If the time off is taken to provide personal care for a family member with an illness that requires medical attention, it's a good idea to get a medical certificate, if possible.

This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

Professor Riley says letting your employer know you are taking a short period of absence without a medical certificate — for example, 24 hours — may "satisfy a reasonable person".

A statutory declaration could also be considered reasonable evidence, and is often the "simplest and easiest thing to do".

This can also make it tempting for people to misuse and Professor Riley warns a stat dec is "a very serious" legal document and making a false statement on one is a criminal offence.

Dr Orifici says your award, enterprise agreement or an employer's policies and procedures can provide further clarity.

"An employer has the discretion to prescribe examples of what it is that the employer would require to reasonably satisfy it," she says.

"But if it relates to a personal illness or a personal injury that affects the family member or the person's household member and [fits] reasonably within the framework of requiring care and support, then it should be covered."

If you are caring for an elderly family member, Professor Riley says it's important to understand that paid carer's leave "has to be to care for the person because they have illness, injury or [an] unexpected emergency".

With rising fuel prices adding additional financial stress to household living costs, what are your rights when it comes to working from home — and what are the best ways to ask your employer about flexible work arrangements?

"If it's just that they're old and frail and can't cook their own meals anymore, then you're not necessarily looking at [using] your personal carer's leave," she says.

However, Professor Riley says you may be entitled to ask for flexible work arrangements in such cases.

"One of the eligibility criteria for asking for flexible work arrangements is that you have carers' responsibilities," she says.

"If you put that request in writing, the employer has 21 days to consider whether they can accommodate that, and they have an obligation to consider that and give you a response; they're only allowed to refuse on reasonable business grounds."

https://www.scmp.com/opinion/asia-opinio.title: Why Malaysia’s political turmoil matters to Beijing
https://www.scmp.com/opinion/asia-opinio.author: Peter T. C. Chang
https://www.scmp.com/opinion/asia-opinio.text:
Malaysia shows how local battles over race and national identity could complicate China’s Southeast Asian playbook

As China seeks to reshape the global order, Malaysia’s political instability offers a cautionary tale about the challenges Beijing may face abroad.

Malaysia’s two major Malay-based parties, Umno and PAS, united around a familiar message: that Malay and Muslim interests could only be protected through greater political solidarity among Malays against non-Malay parties.

The politics of race and insecurity proved electorally effective. China’s expanding economic footprint in Malaysia may have added complexity to these domestic debates. As Chinese investment and trade ties have deepened, some Malaysians have come to perceive the benefits of economic integration as unevenly distributed, reinforcing long-standing concerns about the economic position of the ethnic Chinese community.

These perceptions intersect with a broader, long-running debate over national identity. Among some Malays, questions remain about whether the Chinese minority is sufficiently integrated into a shared Malaysian identity.

Malaysia has long struggled to construct a unifying national identity. The recent resurgence of racially charged campaigning represents a setback for the country’s ambition to serve as a model of multicultural coexistence.

Yet this is where Malaysia’s central dilemma – and contradiction – becomes most apparent.

On the international stage, Kuala Lumpur has positioned itself alongside Beijing in advocating for a more multipolar world order that gives greater weight to the Global South and Islamic world. Domestically, however, anxieties over ethnic identity and economic security continue to shape electoral politics, complicating Anwar’s vision of an inclusive Malaysia.

For many within the Malay majority, the idea of an Asian Renaissance remains contested. It is sometimes perceived as raising uncomfortable questions about political and cultural balance within Malaysia itself.

Malaysia’s predicament offers an important lesson for China as it expands its global footprint. Beijing’s partnerships will not exist in a political vacuum. Its economic engagement and civilisational diplomacy will inevitably interact with local histories, ethnic relations and identity politics.

If Xi’s vision of a “community with a shared future for humankind” is to gain wider acceptance, China will need to navigate these domestic sensitivities carefully. Failure to comprehend local political dynamics risks creating resistance to the very international order Beijing seeks to promote.
https://www.scmp.com/opinion/asia-opinio.summary: Malaysia shows how local battles over race and national identity could complicate China's Southeast Asian playbook. China’s expanding economic footprint in Malaysia may have added complexity to domestic debates.

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/russia-c.title: Russia and Ukraine exchange overnight strikes that leave 7 dead, many injured
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/russia-c.author: Associated Press
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/russia-c.text:
Ukrainian drones killed 5 people in Russia’s border region of Belgorod while Russian missiles killed 2 in Kharkiv

Russia and Ukraine exchanged strikes overnight that killed civilians and injured many others on both sides, local authorities reported.

Large-scale Russian missile strikes on Ukrainian cities have become almost routine in recent weeks, with Moscow exploiting Ukraine’s critical shortage of interceptors for the US-made Patriot systems – the sole air defence weapon in its arsenal able to shoot down ballistic missiles.

In the latest attacks, Ukrainian drones killed five people and injured two dozen others, including a four-year-old boy, in Russia’s border region of Belgorod, according to the regional administration.

In Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, Russian missiles struck a block of flats block in the Saltivskyi district, killing two people and injuring 13, according to regional head Oleh Syniehubov. Eight more people were injured in Ukraine’s Black Sea port of Odesa after “dozens of missiles and drones” struck the city and surrounding region, according to local administration head Oleh Kiper.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky has for months lobbied other countries, especially the US, to send Ukraine more Patriot systems made scarcer by the Iran war, arguing they are crucial for defending civilians.

Failing that, Zelensky wants to make Patriot ammunition in Ukraine or get approval from Elon Musk to use his Starlink satellite communications system to guide strikes inside Russia that can hit its missile launchers.

Meanwhile, Kyiv has kept up long-range drone strikes against Russian energy infrastructure, as well as the country’s largest online retailer, Wildberries, and other targets deep inside Russia, sparking a fuel crisis.

Russia’s defence ministry on Sunday claimed its overnight strikes hit drone warehouses in the Kharkiv region, as well as fuel depots and stores of other materiel belonging to Ukraine’s armed forces at the port of Odesa.

It said its forces had shot down 153 Ukrainian drones during the night, including over Russian-occupied Crimea and the Black and Azov seas.

In Russia’s Belgorod region, authorities said Ukrainian drone strikes damaged 29 blocks of flats and five private houses, as well as administrative buildings and unspecified “commercial facilities”.

Debris from Ukrainian drones also fell on two enterprises and a private home in the Russian city of Novorossiysk, mayor Andrey Kravchenko said on Sunday. He did not specify what the commercial sites were. Regional authorities later said falling debris had injured one person, damaged two private houses and blown out a window in a block of flats.

A major fuel terminal is located in Novorossiysk that links Kazakhstan’s oilfields to markets around the world, and which has previously been a target for Ukrainian strikes.

Also on Sunday, ⁠Russian forces ⁠took control of ⁠the two villages in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, state-run RIA news agency reported, citing the Russian Defence Ministry.

The ministry report on Telegram said Russian forces had seized ‌Vasyutinske, a few kilometres east of the “fortress city” of Kramatorsk, and Toretsk, southwest of the city of Druzhkivka.

Ukrainian forces made no acknowledgement of the two settlements changing hands and Reuters could not verify the battlefield reports independently.

Russia is slowly ⁠advancing west through the Donetsk region, though there has been little significant change ‌for months in the positions along the 1,200km (775-mile) frontline.

The Ukrainian war blog DeepState, which uses open ‌source reports in documenting the frontline positions of both sides, reported ⁠that Russian ⁠forces had made advances near Illinivka – outside the contested city of Kostiantynivka.

It also ‌reported Russian advances near Chasiv Yar, to the west of the city of Bakhmut, ‌which fell ‌to Russian forces in 2023 after long months of heavy ‌fighting.

The Ukrainian military’s General Staff, in a late evening report, said ⁠Kyiv’s forces had repelled 24 attacks around Kostiantynivka, Illinivka and other ⁠centres.

Russian commanders said last month their forces had seized Kostiantynivka, but Ukrainian officials have disputed the claim.

Zelensky in his ‌nightly video address on Sunday made no reference to changes in frontline positions but singled out for praise Ukrainian forces fighting in specific areas, notably Dobropillia, Kostiantynivka and Kramatorsk.

Elsewhere, a “powerful explosion” believed to be from a combat drone was reported in the village of Crocmaz, in southeast Moldova near the border with Ukraine, local police said on Sunday.

No one was injured by the impact, which caused a vegetation fire in the Stefan Voda district, police said, adding that “fragments of a combat drone were found at the scene” and would be examined by specialists. Police did not specify the origin of the drone.

Multiple drones have violated Moldovan airspace since Russia launched its full-scale war in neighbouring Ukraine.

Bulgaria has summoned Ukraine’s ambassador after a drone entered Bulgarian airspace, the country’s public broadcaster BNT reported on Sunday.

The drone exploded on Saturday close to an international gas pipeline soon after crossing the border from Romania. No casualties or damage were reported.

Bulgaria’s defence ministry said the drone appeared to be the type used by Ukrainian armed forces and that the incident was probably accidental.

Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesman Heorhii Tykhy said the incident was being examined but that it did not deliberately target Bulgaria. Ukraine and Bulgaria were in “close contact” to clarify what had happened, he said.

Additional reporting by Reuters

Russian missiles killed 2 in Kharkiv Russia and Ukraine killed 2 people in Kharksiv Russia.
