https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/heal.title: Calls for system review after lowest alert in force during record-breaking heat
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/heal.author: Ng Kang-chung,Leopold Chen
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/heal.text:
Amber heat-stress warning remained in place despite scorching temperatures

Labour unionists, joined by a leading meteorologist, also proposed relaxing the law to recognise heatstroke as a work-related injury, thus entitling workers to compensation.

A scorching 36.9 degrees Celsius (98.4 Fahrenheit) was recorded at the Hong Kong Observatory in Tsim Sha Tsui on Sunday afternoon, the highest since records began in 1884, sparking a fresh debate over protecting employees working outdoors in the heat.

Chau Sze-kit, chairman of the Hong Kong Construction Industry Employees General Union, said: “The heat stress alert seems to have made a mockery of the record-breaking heat. It has stayed at the lowest amber level throughout the day.

“The requirements for triggering a higher alert are set too rigidly. There were cases when the amber warning was in force but the temperature at a site was already close to 40 degrees.”

The Heat Stress at Work Warning system was formulated by the Labour Department based on a heat index developed by the Observatory and the Chinese University of Hong Kong.

It takes into account air temperature, humidity, wind speed, solar radiation and hospital admission figures to measure heat stress. There are three warning levels – amber, red and black – to tell employers and workers the level of heat stress while working outdoors or in indoor workplaces without air conditioning.

Under the department’s guidelines, employers should arrange additional rest time for affected workers under the amber alert.

Those with “very heavy” workloads should suspend their duties under the red alert, while workers with “heavy” workloads should do so under the black warning.

Appropriate rest breaks should also be arranged every hour “as far as reasonably practicable”, depending on warning levels, to reduce employees’ risk of heatstroke, according to the department.

In practice, the department will issue the heat stress at work warning based on the heat index measured by the Observatory at King’s Park and incorporate additional data from nine other monitoring stations.

If four or more of the other nine stations indicate that the heat stress situation has reached a certain level, the corresponding warning will be issued even if the index at King’s Park has not reached that level.

A search of the department’s notification archive found that more than 200 heat stress at work warnings had been issued since May 2023, when the mechanism was launched, all of which were amber.

Red and black warnings have never been issued.

Under the mechanism, an amber alert is issued when the heat index is a figure from 30 to below 32. Red is issued for a threshold from 32 to below 34. When the index is 34 or above, a black alert will be issued.

Former Observatory director Lam Chiu-ying also called for reform of the system.

“Given the heat today, no one should work outdoors for extended periods,” Lam said, adding that a more comprehensive and internationally accepted measure – the wet-bulb globe temperature – should be used to determine heat stress in direct sunlight.

“The heat index is only suitable for people who spend most of their time indoors,” Lam added.

But Chau said: “Many workers would not dare to take a rest for fear of being regarded as lazy by the contractors. One reason is that heatstroke is in general not regarded as a work-related injury and workers can hardly get compensation if they suffer heatstroke after working under hot weather for too long.”

Fay Siu Sin-man, the chief executive of the Association for the Rights of Industrial Accident Victims, echoed Chau’s views and called for the law to cover heatstroke.

“Sometimes, the cause of death is a heart attack, or some underlying illness of the workers. But they are heat-related,” Siu said.

“But once the death is certified as having been caused by a heart problem or some underlying illness, it will not be regarded as a work-related injury and the victims will not be entitled to any work injury compensation.”

Lawmaker Ray Wong Wing-wai, who represents the Federation of Hong Kong Industries, however argued that classifying heatstroke as a work injury without a clear definition would complicate labour rights issues.

“If a worker collapses because of low blood sugar level, should it be determined as a result of heatstroke? Fainting from low blood sugar is not a work injury,” he said.

“It would be meaningful to review the matter only after we can have a very clear medical definition [for heatstroke].”

Fellow legislator Peter Shiu Ka-fai, chairman of the pro-business Liberal Party, shared Wong’s views but he agreed there was a need to reform the heat stress alert system.

“I can’t see any reason why we still have the amber alert when we are suffering from record heat.”

Unionist legislator Lee Kwong-yu conceded it was sometimes difficult to determine whether a particular incident was a result of the worker’s chronic conditions or heatstroke.

But Lee, of the Federation of Trade Unions, added that it was worth exploring the feasibility of listing heatstroke as a work injury. He said the federation would seek to meet the department to discuss allowing more rest time and hydration breaks for workers during hot days.

A department spokesman said that the temperature was only one of the risk factors for heat stress.

“Although the temperature was exceptionally high [on Sunday], the relative humidity was below the summer average and the wind conditions were good too,” he said.

“The heat index measured at 10 stations was mostly between 30 and 32. Therefore, the department issued an amber warning according to the established mechanism.

“The department will closely monitor the hot weather and the operation of the heat stress at work warning to see if there are needs for further optimisation.”

https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/south-asi.title: Air India pilot undergoes ‘confirmatory’ drug test after flight plunge
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/south-asi.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/south-asi.text:
The incident is the latest in a series of setbacks for the Indian carrier, which appointed a new executive on Wednesday

The Airbus A320, carrying 137 passengers and eight crew, lost around 300 feet (91 metres) on August 4 while flying from Phuket in Thailand to New Delhi, before stabilising and landing safely, the civil aviation ministry said.

Eight passengers and four cabin crew members were admitted to hospitals after landing in the Indian capital, whose conditions were described as “stable”, after which both pilots were given a standard “psychoactive substance screening test”, the statement read.

“The screening test in respect of the Pilot-in-Command (PIC) indicated a result requiring confirmatory testing,” it said.

“Samples have accordingly been sent to the designated laboratory for confirmatory analysis, and the final report is awaited.”

The ministry said the flight has been classified as a “Serious Incident”, and that India’s Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) has launched an investigation.

Both pilots have been removed from the flying roster pending outcomes of the investigation.

“Further action, as appropriate, will be taken based on the outcome of the investigation and confirmatory test results,” it added.

Videos of the incident’s aftermath showed cabin baggage strewn across the aisle. Some of those injured were taken to hospital on stretchers.

Air India, in a statement earlier on Sunday, confirmed that a “post-flight screening test” had been conducted on the flight’s pilots, but it said the results had not been shared with the company.

The incident is the latest in a series of setbacks for the Indian carrier, which appointed a new executive on Wednesday.

Since taking over Air India in 2022, India’s Tata Group has embarked on an ambitious overhaul, ordering hundreds of aircraft and upgrading its ageing fleet.

While the airline has managed to modernise operations and integrate the group’s aviation businesses, it has faced persistent headwinds including aircraft delivery delays and airspace closures caused by the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict.

But the biggest blow to the airline’s image came in June 2025, when Air India Flight 171 – a London-bound Boeing 787 Dreamliner – crashed shortly after take-off from Ahmedabad, killing all but one of the 242 people on board and 19 people on the ground.

The carrier has now turned to former Ethiopian Airlines chief Tewolde Gebremariam, widely seen as an industry veteran capable of righting the ship, as its new CEO as it seeks to execute a turnaround.

https://www.dw.com/en/alleged-irish-crim.title: Alleged Irish crime boss Kinahan charged with directing criminal organisation
https://www.dw.com/en/alleged-irish-crim.text:
Daniel Kinahan is accused of leading the Kinahan organised crime group, an international network linked to drug trafficking and money laundering operations,

Suspected international crime boss Daniel Kinahan landed in Ireland on Sunday after being extradited from the United Arab Emirates.

Following his arrival in Ireland, prosecutors charged Kinahan with directing a criminal organization during a special court sitting.

Kinahan, 49, was arrested in April in Dubai after Ireland issued a warrant for "alleged serious organized crime offenses."

He is accused of being the leader of a cartel linked to drug smuggling and money laundering.

The group is thought to be the most powerful criminal organization in Ireland, with Irish police estimating its wealth at more than €1 billion ($1.15 billion).

The alleged crime boss had lived openly in the UAE for about a decade before his arrest. He moved there from Spain around 2016 after the murder of one of his associates and an attempt on his life.

In 2022, the United States imposed sanctions on Kinahan after linking his organization to some of the world's most notorious crime networks and offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest.

The group is linked to a brutal feud with a smaller Irish syndicate that has resulted in 18 murders.

“Since February 2016, the (Kinahan Organized Crime Group) has been involved in a gang war with another group in Ireland and Spain, resulting in numerous murders, including of two innocent bystanders,” the US Treasury Department said.

Kinahan is the second alleged senior member of the cartel to be extradited to Ireland from Dubai. Sean McGovern was extradited in 2024 and was ultimately sentenced to 24 years in prison after pleading guilty to directing organized crime and attempted murder.

Irish media reported that a special security convoy would be deployed to escort Kinahan to the Special Criminal Court, which handles offenses related to terrorism and organized crime.

In a joint statement, the justice minister of the UAE and Ireland called Kinahan "one of the most high-profile individuals sought for prosecution in connection with transnational organized crime."

Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan called the extradition a "landmark of judicial cooperation with Dubai," adding that it "sends a clear message that suspected perpetrators of serious and organized crime will find no safe haven from justice."

Meanwhile, Foreign Minister Helen McEntee hailed the outcome as "the culmination of years of determined work" by Irish authorities under various governments.

https://www.dw.com/en/syria-says-deal-ag.title: Syria says deal agreed with Russia on future of military bases
https://www.dw.com/en/syria-says-deal-ag.text:
Under the agreement, Syria will take over management of two Russian bases that were used to support ousted leader Bashar Assad during the Syrian civil war.

Syria and Russia have agreed on the future management of Russian bases on the country's Mediterranean coast.

Russia used the bases to provide military support to former Syrian leader Bashar Assad during Syria's 13-year civil war that ended in 2024.

The Syrian Foreign Ministry announced Sunday that the two nations had signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) after 18 months of negotiations.

The deal effectively means Russia will no longer have military outposts in the Arab country.

Syria will take over management of the Hmeimim airport and the commercial berth at Tartus port, Syria's Foreign Ministry said.

State media cited the ministry as saying that the bases would be converted into "joint training and capacity-building centres, within new arrangements that preserve mutual interests."

The facilities will be gradually integrated into the country's civilian administration. The transition is expected to be completed within three months, the ministry said.

Russia has yet to comment on the agreement.

During the civil war in Syria between 2011 and 2024, while Assad was president, Russia was Syria's main ally and military backer.

Assad was overthrown in December 2024, and now lives in exile in Moscow. Current Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa led an alliance of Islamist rebel groups that fought against government forces during the war.

Assad's ouster in 2024 dealt a major blow to Moscow's influence in the region.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has been trying to build ties with Syria's new leadership to protect the future of the only two official Russian military bases located outside the former Soviet Union.

Al-Sharaa has met with Putin in Moscow twice since coming to power in January 2025.

During his last trip, Putin said, "much has been accomplished in terms of restoring our interstate relations."

The Syrian government has been demanding that Moscow extradite Assad.

Police said they believed that the incident was linked to a "settling of scores" within criminal networks.

Three people were wounded on Sunday in a shooting in Denmark.

They do not face life-threatening injuries, the police said.

Police said in a statement they believed that the incident was linked to a "settling of scores" within criminal networks.

"At this time, we cannot provide further information about their condition. The police presumption is that this is a settling of scores within the criminal milieu," the statement read.

Officers had been called to multiple locations in Holbaek, some 70 kilometers (45 miles) west of the capital, Copenhagen.

The incident was reported to police around 3:45 p.m. local time (1345 UTC).

Before the shots were fired, a fight broke out within a larger group in a residential estate, police said

Police said that the perpetrators were seen leaving the scene in a white car, according to preliminary information.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-berli.text:
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Germany is moving to counter the threats posed by drones. Meanwhile, the transport minister said he wants Deutsche Bahn bonuses tied to punctuality targets.

These updates have been closed. Thank you for joining us.

Here is a roundup of the stories from and about Germany that were hitting the headlines on the weekend of August 8-9, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

The co-leader of Die Linke ("The Left") on Sunday said the socialist party would do anything in its power to keep the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) out of office.

Luigi Pantisano's remarks on public broadcaster ZDF come with less than a month to go before elections in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD is polling at over 40% and is poised to win an absolute majority in the state parliament in Magdeburg.

Were the AfD to win in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, it would mark Germany's first far-right state government since World War II.

To prevent that scenario, Pantisano said he would consider supporting the ruling conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, despite Pantisano recently accusing the CDU of implementing "fascist politics."

"We, The Left, have shown in recent years that we take responsibility for this country," Pantisano told ZDF.

If the AfD falls short of an absolute majority, the CDU's incumbent state Premier Sven Schulze would likely have to form a coalition government with The Left.

The AfD has never been in government at either state or federal level, as all other established parties refuse to work with it, under a policy known as the "firewall."

Germany's new transport minister, Steffen Bilger of the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), said on Sunday that he planned to step up pressure on notoriously delayed railway operator Deutsche Bahn.

He told the mass-market Bild newspaper that bonus payments for Bahn managers would be impacted if government-set punctuality targets are not met.

"There will be a concrete impact on the bonus payments of rail managers if the targets set by the federal government are not met," Bilger said. "I think rail customers and taxpayers have a right to have success genuinely measured."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government is preparing a new financing agreement for the state-owned company that is to tie funding to specific targets.

Bilger took his ministerial post after Merz reshuffled his Cabinet last month, a move sparked by the resignation of senior conservative lawmaker Jens Spahn over a surrogacy scandal.

Deutsche Bahn is mired in a major structural crisis around delays and cancellations. In 2025, only 60% arrived on time or experienced delays of under six minutes, not including trains that were canceled or ended their journeys prematurely.

The center-left Social Democrats (SPD), who are junior coalition partners in Merz's government, expressed support for the planned measure.

"I expressly welcome the fact that Transport Minister Bilger wants to link the bonus payments of rail managers to punctuality," the SPD's Isabel Cademartori told the Tagesspiegel newspaper.

"People expect the railway to become more reliable," she said. "As politicians, we are providing record investments in infrastructure and expect this to be reflected in punctuality."

The German capital's first World Naked Bike Ride began in Berlin on Sunday.

Hundreds of people participated in the event, cycling either naked or partially naked through the streets of Berlin.

Organizers said that participants can join "dressed or undressed in whatever way they themselves feel most comfortable."

They said the event was to embody the idea that "naked we are all equal" and the German nudism movement, historically known as Freikörperkultur (meaning "free body culture" in Germany) or by the acronym FKK.

Organizers said they aimed to send a message of "tolerance and self-acceptance, closeness to nature and protection of the environment and for inclusion and diversity."

The German capital was experiencing hot weather of around 30 degrees Celsius (86 degrees Fahrenheit).

The event started in Mauerpark in eastern Berlin and proceeded to the government district.

Organizers said the route was to follow the Berlin Wall Trail to the Schönefeld neighborhood in the southeast of the Berlin metropolitan area. The suburb contains Berlin Brandenburg Airport.

Berlin police are looking into two incidents in which shots were fired, as shooting incidents in the German capital seem on the rise.

In one incident early on Sunday, shots were fired at a hairdressing salon in the Marzahn-Hellersdorf district in the city's northeast, while a gunshot hole was also found at a nearby nightclub, a police spokeswoman said.

She said no one was injured.

That was, however, not the case with another shooting incident in Kreuzberg on Friday evening.

There, a 22-year-old man was shot and injured by an assailant, who fled the scene.

Homicide squad officers are investigating possible links to previous shooting incidents in the area.

Last year, Berlin police set up the Ferrum specialist unit to investigate gun crime.

Algeria said on Saturday that a German citizen kidnapped by an armed criminal group some two weeks ago in neighboring Niger was safe and in the hands of the Algerian military.

The German national was taken in charge by the Algerian army's security services on Friday, according to a statement from the Defense Ministry shared on the official Algerian news agency.

He has now been taken on a special flight from Guezzam in the far south to the Boufarik military base near the capital Algiers, it said, adding that he was in "good health" and would be handed to German authorities "at a later date."

No details were provided on how the German national was freed.

A spokesperson for the German Foreign Ministry told DW it was aware of the case, but added that the government "does not comment on cases involving the abduction of German citizens abroad."

Niger, which has been under military rule since a July 2023 coup, has in the past few years been wracked by violence from jihadis linked to the al-Qaeda or the "Islamic State" (IS) terrorist groups.

Several states have lifted a rule banning most trucks from using motorways on Sundays and public holidays in view of the low river water levels currently hampering cargo vessels.

The DPA news agency reported that a number of trucks have already been sighted on motorways in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW).

The NRW transport minister, Oliver Krischer, said that "this exceptional regulation allows us to ensure that delivery chains are maintained and supply shortages are avoided."

Industrial associations have welcomed the lifting of the truck ban.

But one of Germany's main unions, Verdi, has criticized the move.

"This measure comes at the cost of employees in the transport and logistics branch and calls into question the legal protection of Sundays and public holidays as days of rest and recreation," said Uwe Köpke, who heads the union's postal services, freight forwarding and logistics department.

Lower Saxony, Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland are so far the only other states to have lifted the ban as one of the measures announced by Transport Minister Steffen Bilger last week to mitigate the economic effect of the cargo shipping shortfalls.

In NRW and Lower Saxony, the suspension of the ban is to run initially until August 31, and in Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland until September 30 at the latest.

In NRW, all trucks will also be able to use the motorways on Saturdays during the day in the current summer holidays as an exemption to an existing regulation.

New preliminary data released on Sunday has shown that German exports to China fell more than 12% year-on-year from January through June. German imports from China rose 8.9%.

That raises the trade deficit to about €55 billion ($63.6 billion) from €40 billion for the same period in 2025.

The data from the state-run agency Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI) reflects the decreasing reliance by Chinese firms on European imports.

They show that although China remains Germany's top trading partner, the Asian powerhouse is now only the ninth-biggest market for German goods, with far smaller economies like Austria and Switzerland buying more from Germany in 2026.

As recently as 2021, China was Germany's second-biggest ​export market.

The US remains Germany's single-biggest foreign market, despite a drop in German exports there amid protectionist tariffs introduced under President Donald Trump.

The CEO of arms giant Rheinmetall, Armin Papperger, has said he will not be intimidated despite the many threats that have been made to his safety.

"These jobs must be done, and anyone that can't take the pressure doesn't belong in this job," he told the DPA news agency, saying "chickening out" was no option in his field.

Pappberger, 63, who is believed to be a possible target of Russian murder plots, is under constant police protection at a level similar to that given to Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Rheinmetall is supplying large quantities of weapons to Ukraine amid the Russian invasion, potentially putting the company in Moscow's crosshairs.

Germany's domestic intelligence services recently called on employees in the defense sector to be very vigilant amid the threat of espionage and sabotage by Russian state agencies.

Germany is establishing a new drone security research facility as it seeks to counter a growing threat from UAVs that are possibly under foreign control, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has told Sunday's edition of the Bild tabloid.

"The arms race in drone technology requires dedicated research units to keep pace," he said.

He said the new center, to be established on August 18 at a German Aerospace Center (DLR) test airport in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, would develop and test technologies to protect against drones.

His remarks come after a number of incidents involving drones in the past week raised security concerns.

You can read more on Dobrindt's statements on security here.

The DW newsroom in Bonn says a warm guten Morgen to its readers as we resume our coverage of all things German on Sunday.

Concerns about national security amid a myriad of threats are featuring largely in today's headlines, with, for example, the interior minister warning of hybrid warfare after several drone incidents.

Some of those threats even target particular people, as the CEO of arms giant Rheinmetall, Armin Papperger, is experiencing.

And nature itself is also posing a security challenge, with the lack of water in the Rhine and other rivers having a widening impact on the economy and beyond.

Read on for more on these and other stories.

We are pausing our coverage as the clock is about to strike midnight here in Bonn. Join us again on Sunday, when we will update this blog with the latest news from Germany.

Sven Schulze, state premier and the CDU's candidate in the upcoming regional election in Saxony-Anhalt has slammed the AfD for its xenophobia, and underscored his state's reliance on exports and foreign workers.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's most important river is running low unusually early in the year.

Ships are still moving on the Rhine, but falling water levels are forcing many to carry lighter loads. Professor Kerstin Stahl, a hydrologist at the University of Freiburg, explains what is driving the drought and why the consequences reach far beyond shipping.

Some 10,000 people protested in the eastern German city of Plauen to call for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's resignation and for new elections to be held immediately.

While the "Unity for Germany" protest was officially independent of political parties, a local pro-democracy group warned that some of the rally's organizers are right-wing extremists.

"The event is being promoted by relevant far-right channels; on Facebook, the comments on the demonstration contain hateful remarks, and the calls to action spread antisemitic and ethno-nationalist narratives," the Alliance for Democracy, Tolerance and Civil Courage said.

Apart from the government's resignation and new elections, the protesters' 11 demands also include:

The immediate deportation of 'all convicted, criminal and illegal migrants'

A cheaper nationwide monthly travel pass, for €29 ($33.50)

Reform to public service broadcasting

Scrapping the carbon dioxide tax

Introducing a direct democracy model like in Switzerland

The protesters also chanted "We are the people," the slogan that was used at pro-democracy rallies during the peaceful revolution of 1989 in East Germany that preceded the end of the former German Democratic Republic.

Many German national flags, as well as banners of the historical Kingdom of Saxony — often used by the far-right Free Saxons party — were seen at the rally, as were blue peace flags with white doves, the German news agency dpa reported.

Around 800 people demonstrated in Berlin, calling for the Federal Constitutional Court to review political parties suspected of right-wing extremism.

Eleven such demonstrations were planned across Germany on Saturday. The "Prüf," which translates to "check" or "examine," initiative, founded by activist Nico Semsrott, is behind the rallies.

Citing a legal opinion published in late June by the Society for Civil Rights that declared the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party unconstitutional, speakers called for a corresponding review by the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe.

Many of the demonstrators' posters bore the slogan, "Examine today — protect tomorrow."

However, the Bundestag, the Bundesrat, or the federal government must file a motion to ban the party in order to initiate such a review.

In early May 2025, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution classified the AfD as a "confirmed far-right extremist movement," but suspended the designation after a legal challenge.

In February, a Cologne court said the agency can’t use the designation while the court evaluates the party’s lawsuit.

The AfD vehemently rejects accusations of extremism.

https://www.npr.org/2026/08/09/nx-s1-592.author: Chandelis Duster
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/09/nx-s1-592.text:
This undated photo provided by the U.S. Forest Service on Friday, Aug. 7, 2026, shows the Widemouth 2 wildfire burning near Richfield, Utah.

Evacuation orders are in place across parts of the Western U.S. and Southwest Canada as extremely hot and dry conditions fuel the spread of wildfires in the region.

There were 183 new fires, including eight large ones, across the U.S. since Saturday, the National Interagency Fire Center reported on Sunday. More than 30,000 personnel with over 640 crews were assigned to the fires. Firefighters were battling more than 94 large fires across the country, the agency also said.

Evacuations are in place across Utah, where close to a dozen active wildfires have scorched more than 300,000 acres, as of Sunday evening. The Rocky Canyon Fire, some 30 miles northeast of Salt Lake City, grew to more than 2,800 acres since it began on Friday and is 0% contained, as of Sunday — leading to evacuations in Morgan County.

Two pilots died on Friday after their helicopter crashed while battling the Widemouth 2 Fire in Fishlake National Forest, the U.S. Forest Service confirmed Sunday.

Utah Gov. Spencer Cox mourned their deaths in a social media post: "They put themselves in harm's way to protect our state and gave their lives in that service."

The Widemouth 2 fire has scorched more than 118,000 acres, becoming the largest fire in the state this year, surpassing the Babylon Fire which has burned over 107,000 acres. The fire was 27% contained as of Sunday morning.

In Oregon, a bulldozer operator identified by officials as Jason Ensign, died battling the Wrights Spring Fire, which has spread over 33,000 acres and was 0% contained as of Sunday afternoon.

Large fires are also burning in Washington state, Idaho, Montana and Colorado.

At least 60,000 people were evacuated in the Spokane, Wash., area as firefighters work to contain several fires that have scorched over 10,000 acres. Local fire officials on Sunday said that "crews made exceptional progress" on containing the fires and were working to ensure there are "no remaining heat sources posing threats."

"An abnormally dry and warm winter has led to an extremely difficult fire season," said the U.S. Forest Service Fishlake National Forest.

In Canada, there were more than 100 active wildfires in the country's British Columbia province, according to the British Columbia Wildfire Service. High temperatures and wind gusts are expected to linger across the southeastern parts of the province and the Okanagan region on Sunday.

"We are expecting a high potential for lightning-caused wildfire starts, particularly in the central Interior and the Okanagan which are receiving limited precipitation and dry lightning," the service said in an update on Sunday. "New ignitions occurring during periods of hot and dry weather can establish and spread quickly."

A state of emergency has been declared in the British Columbia province where the Bald Range wildfire has prompted more than 20,000 people to evacuate.

"At every step, we're focused on ensuring that emergency crews have the tools they need to protect people," said British Columbia Premier David Eby on social media.

https://www.npr.org/2026/08/09/g-s1-1379.title: Demi Vollering wins Tour de France for the 2nd time
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/09/g-s1-1379.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/09/g-s1-1379.text:
Netherlands' Demi Vollering celebrates on the podium after winning the Women's Tour de France cycling race in Nice, France, Sunday, Aug. 9, 2026.

After winning the Women's Tour de France for the second time on Sunday, Demi Vollering tried hard to hold back tears while the Dutch national anthem played.

It was her toughest moment of the day after an ultra-dominant performance on the bike from the 2023 champion.

She secured an impressive stage win, and in doing so extended her overall lead over Polish rider Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney to 1 minute, 18 seconds clear of the 2024 champion.

Vollering raised her bike in the air moments after crossing the finish line in Nice. Niewiadoma-Phinney had started Sunday's ninth and final stage only eight seconds behind Vollering, who got a time bonus for winning it.

Finally, as the Dutch anthem ended, a lone tear trickled down the side of Vollering's face. A few more soon followed as her achievement hit home.

"It's not only the dream of winning the Tour de France. It's also the dream of living this life, of working hard along with passionate people," the 29-year-old Vollering said. "It all starts with dreaming. Go chase the dreams and don't let anyone stop you."

Nobody could on Sunday.

Knowing that she was well clear, Vollering began to celebrate as the line approached, raising her arm in triumph and then tapping her head with her finger to show her mental strength.

"I was thinking about a lot of things as I was approaching the finish line. I thought that I had never won in the yellow jersey before," Vollering said. "I thought about how much work has gone into this victory. I thought about the people who have been behind me."

She finished the stage 1 minute, 4 seconds ahead of Spaniard Paula Blasi Cairol and Niewiadoma-Phinney, who looked tired but was all smiles later on the podium.

Former Giro d'Italia champion Elisa Longo Borghini of Italy was third overall in the Tour — 4:29 behind — after Marlen Reusser lost valuable time after crashing going downhill after the second of the day's four climbs.

Reusser ended up 14th overall at nearly 26 minutes behind.

Niewiadoma-Phinney had it all to do on the final climb, especially with her rival sitting on her wheel, and was unable to pressure Vollering.

Vollering attacked about 800 meters from the top and dropped Niewiadoma-Phinney — as she did when winning Saturday's eighth stage to take the overall lead from her rival.

Two years ago, Vollering missed out on Tour victory after finishing an agonizing four seconds behind Niewiadoma-Phinney on the last stage.

She made full amends this time.

Vollering has now won five Grand Tours, including two Spanish Vuelta titles and the Giro d'Italia secured in June to join countrywoman Annemiek van Vleuten as the only other female cyclist to have won all three Grand Tours.

"I still have a lot of dreams," Vollering said. "On and off the bike."

Each of the first three climbs on Sunday was 7.7 kilometers long with a 5.9% average gradient. But the final ascent branched off onto a slightly different route which, even though it was shorter at 6 kilometers, had a steeper average gradient of 7.6% with one portion stretching to a grueling 12%.

It made little difference.

After winning Friday's seventh stage with an impressive solo attack of her own up the iconic Mont Ventoux, Niewiadoma-Phinney seemed short of energy and Vollering's lead was never under threat.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Australia news live: NSW schools may ban take-home tests over AI concerns; minister calls urgent meeting over airport chaos

Prue Car, the NSW deputy premier, has asked the NSW Education Standards Authority (Nesa) to impose a ban on unsupervised take-home assessments during a broad review of AI’s impact on student learning.

Car said she has asked Nesa to “urgently” examine artificial intelligence and move to protect student learning amid growing evidence the technology is affecting student’s cognitive development. Half of students’ HSC result is based on school-based assessments, some of which is finished outside the classroom.

She said in a statement:

Artificial intelligence has enormous potential to support teaching and learning, but it should never replace the thinking, creativity, and hard work that education is designed to develop.

The purpose of schooling extends beyond producing an assessment task. It is to build knowledge, judgment, resilience, and critical thinking over time. If students rely on AI to bypass that learning process, we risk undermining both their education and the integrity of the HSC.

Subject to Nesa’s advice, any interim changes would be applied from the beginning of term 4.

The NSW government is rolling out a new scheme of smart rental bonds, which will allow some renters to transfer their bonds from one rental to the next when they move house.

The scheme will end the need to save up thousands of dollars for a new bond before the old one is returned, and will begin with a phased rollout for renters in Parramatta, the Central Coast or Penrith local government areas.

The scheme will ultimately be rolled out across the state by the end of the year.

Renters will be notified when a new landlord or agent lodges a bond request online. They can then choose to pay their new bond upfront or use a smart rental bond to move it to the new rental for a $25 fee.

Any difference in bond is either paid by the renter, or refunded if it is cheaper and there is no agreed claim on the bond. If the landlord at an original property makes a claim, the NSW government will pay the landlord directly and the renter will then pay the government.

The premier, Chris Minns, said in a statement:

Over two million people in New South Wales are renters – one of the highest proportions of the population ever living in rental accommodation.

For a lot of renters, moving home can mean finding another $3,000 or $4,000 before you’ve even had your old bond returned. That’s a huge financial hurdle for families already doing it tough.

Smart Rental Bonds removes that barrier by letting renters transfer their bond instead of paying for two at once.

The federal government is trumpeting “big benefits” from its Medicare investments, announcing bulk billing rates across the country are up nearly five percentage points since last year.

The health minister, Mark Butler, said the national bulk billing rate for the June quarter had increased to 84.1%, announcing increases in every state and territory.

Bulk billing was up 5.7% in Victoria (to 85.7%), up 6% in South Australia (82.5%), up 4.1% in NSW (87.5%) and up 13% in the Northern Territory to 90.8%.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Burnham vows crackdown on ‘rip-off’ business practices to ease cost of living
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Aletha Adu Political correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
First of PM’s ‘everyday fixes’ to be banning fake discounts and making it easier to cancel unwanted subscriptions

Andy Burnham: I’ll end the rip-offs that people hate

Andy Burnham has promised a series of measures to tackle the cost of living, including a ban on fake discounts and making it easier for people to escape unwanted subscriptions.

The crackdown on “rip-off” business practices is expected to benefit consumers to the tune of £400m a year and will be the first in a range of “everyday fixes” to be implemented in the coming months.

Writing for the Guardian, the prime minister said his government would step in wherever it could as he sought to put the cost of living at the heart of his premiership.

“We won’t be able to solve every frustration overnight,” he wrote. “But where the government can save people money, remove an unnecessary obstacle or simply make something work better, we should and we will.”

The government will ban misleading pricing practices that retailers use to make discounts appear better than they really are, including fake “was” prices, invented reductions and misleading recommended retail prices.

Ministers will consult in the autumn on the precise practices covered and how the ban will work, before introducing the changes through secondary legislation.

Downing Street hopes the measures can be implemented as soon as possible and does not expect a lengthy parliamentary process.

The changes are intended to stop retailers inflating the price of an item before cutting it to give shoppers the false impression they are receiving a bigger discount.

Burnham wrote: “If something is advertised as half price, it should actually be half price. We’ll make sure that when families snatch a deal, they can be confident they’re actually saving. That’s the least they deserve when budgets are so tight.”

The government is also speeding up new protections against subscription traps, bringing forward their introduction from next spring to January. The rules will force businesses to provide clearer information when people sign up, regularly remind customers about their subscriptions and make it easier for them to cancel. Customers will also be given a 14-day cooling-off period after a trial ends or a long-term contract renews.

The average person has about three subscriptions and spends about £500 a year on them, according to government figures. There are about 155m active subscriptions across the UK, and about £1.6bn a year is spent on unwanted ones.

Ministers estimate consumers will save an average of £14 a month for each unwanted subscription they are able to leave early.

“Too many companies want you to sign up in seconds but then make it feel impossible to leave. It’s exhausting,” Burnham wrote.

The challenge for the prime minister will be whether smaller consumer-oriented interventions can provide savings households notice when many are still under pressure.

after newsletter promotion

The two measures will be followed by more over the coming months as he attempts to show voters his government can make a noticeable difference to household finances.

Burnham also promised “bigger plans to make life easier and fairer for people over the longer term”, but Downing Street has yet to set out what those will include.

Burnham wrote: “As far as I’m concerned, whatever the size, big or small, if it’s a problem for you, it’s a problem for us. That’s why I’ve made it clear from day one that creating room to breathe is my number one priority, and the whole of government is united on that.

“Every single unexpected payment, rip-off or hidden catch chips away at hope. That might sound dramatic – but it’s true. Every single one is another message that thiscountry is built to catch people out rather than help them get on.”

Citizens Advice welcomed the changes but said they “can’t be the end of the story”.

The announcement comes as Burnham prepares to spend the rest of his summer travelling around Britain in an attempt to reconnect the government with voters, particularly in areas where Labour has lost support.

“I’ll be asking people what action they want to see on the cost of living,” Burnham wrote. “Because if we want to find the problems that make everyday life harder, we need to listen to the people dealing with them.”

Downing Street has not said whether what Burnham hears on the tour will shape the next round of “everyday fixes”.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump appoints staff secretary Will Scharf as new White House counsel
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Scharf, who helped president win approval for $400m ballroom, to replace David Warrington on 1 September

Donald Trump announced on Sunday that ⁠Will ​Scharf, the staff secretary who helped secure approval for the $400m White House ballroom project, will become ⁠White House counsel and assistant to the president.

Effective 1 September, Scharf will replace David Warrington, who will be leaving the administration to join the private sector. Warrington ​formerly served ​as a ​personal counsel and a ​lawyer ‌for Trump’s ​2024 campaign.

Trump noted that Scharf previously served as a federal prosecutor and represented him in a number of cases, including at the supreme court. Scharf also led the National ‌Capital Planning Commission, which approved the president’s construction ​of the White House ballroom.

“Will is Tough, Strong, and Smart! He also loves our Country, and respects the Law,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Will Scharf will do a great job as White House Counsel!”

The shakeup in the White House counsel’s office comes at a critical juncture – just months ahead of the midterm elections, where Trump’s Republican party will be fighting to hold on to control of Congress.

Democrats have vowed to pursue investigations into Trump and his administration if they are successful in November.

The White House counsel’s job is to advise on legal and policy questions related to the presidency. The office is the primary White House contact for the justice department, and it handles presidential pardons, works on judicial appointments and reviews legislation. The office also helps investigate and manage congressional investigations into the administration and lawsuits against the president when he is sued in his official capacity.

Trump in July 2025 had named Scharf as chair of the National Capital Planning Commission, the executive branch agency with jurisdiction over construction and major renovations to government buildings in the region.

Trump’s ballroom won final approval from the NCPC in April, though a divided federal appeals court ruled Friday that construction on the project must stop because Congress had not approved it. Trump has vowed to appeal to the supreme court.

The project is already well on its way and has begun to rise above ground on the east side of the White House.

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reporting

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Victoria Bekiempis
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
US congresswoman to share journey online as she criticizes Trump administration’s attacks on reproductive care

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has announced she is going to freeze her eggs and will be sharing the process online.

The progressive New York congresswoman, 36, revealed her decision to undergo fertility treatment in a series of Instagram stories this weekend. “This is a choice that I am making to feel more in control of my life,” Ocasio-Cortez said.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Ocasio-Cortez said she had been saving for the procedure for a very long time, and said there was not a lot of information for women interested in doing so.

“As women in general, we are not taught about our bodies, we are not prepared for our own lives, whether that is in puberty, whether that is in pregnancy, whether that is in perimenopause, menopause, whether that is in so many different aspects of our lives,” she said in one of the stories.

Ocasio-Cortez recognized the balancing act that comes with undergoing fertility treatment with her work as a congresswoman. Ocasio-Cortez told viewers that she would be taking her shots in the dressing room before a scheduled ABC interview on Sunday.

“I want you all to see that,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “Because women can do anything. And I think it’s badass that I’m gonna be giving myself shots in the green room, get my glam on, roll out, talk international events, domestic policy, elections, pop out, live my life, do my thing.”

Ocasio-Cortez also showed the medicines and tools, such as syringes and alcohol wipes, used in the process, which involves injecting multiple forms of medication over a period of time that typically lasts around 10 days or more. She joked she would not be injecting herself on a live feed, quipping: “Maybe I should start an ASMR egg-freezing channel.”

“Don’t be weird about this, even I know though all of you will be,” she said with a slight smile moments before finding an injection site on her abdomen.

She exhaled, injected the medication, and then remarked: “That wasn’t so bad!”

During her Sunday interview on ABC, Ocasio-Cortez discussed her decision further.

“In this political environment where this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country, from abortion rights to the ability to carry out a healthy pregnancy, I think it’s important for us as leaders to have these conversations and share these processes, especially for working women across the country and normalize them,” she said.

Ocasio-Cortez’s announcement drew praise.

Amanda Litman, co-founder and president of Run for Something, a political action committee that supports young progressive candidates, said on X: “I’m just so grateful for her honesty & vulnerability.”

Xochitl Hinojosa, a Democratic strategist, responded to Litman’s post by saying: “THIS. We don’t talk about women freezing their eggs or what women have to go through to start a family. Thank you @AOC for your bravery.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Subscriptions you can’t easily cancel, sales that aren’t sales – I’ll end the rip-offs that British people hate | Andy Burnham
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Andy Burnham
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
These everyday hassles are small, but they add up – especially in a cost of living crisis. That’s why my government will tackle them head-on

Andy Burnham is the UK prime minister

Burnham vows crackdown on ‘rip-off’ business practices

I
t’s remarkable how much of modern life can seem designed to wear us down. Every “sale” seems to come with an asterisk. Consumer contracts often find a way of costing more than you expected. And too many companies want you to sign up in seconds, but then make it feel impossible to leave. It’s exhausting.

They might not be the issues that keep you up at night. But they’re often the reason you go to bed ticked off. Westminster has got used to telling people that these everyday hassles are just part of life. The response has too often been a shrug of the shoulders or just calling it bad luck.

I don’t think that’s right. Because these everyday hassles affect millions of people. And they add up. Every single one is an unnecessary cost. And when the cost of living continues to weigh heavily on so many people’s lives, we need to be pulling every single lever we can to help ease that.

But they add up in another way too. Every single unexpected payment, rip off or hidden catch chips away at hope. That might sound dramatic – but it’s true. Every single one is another message that this country is built to catch people out rather than help them get on.

I want people to start believing in Britain again. But we’ll only get there by building a country that feels fair. And that means getting a grip on those issues that get people’s backs up day in, day out. So we are going to do things differently. We are going to get on with the everyday fixes that make life easier and more affordable. As far as I’m concerned, whatever the size, big or small, if it’s a problem for you, it’s a problem for us.

That’s why I’ve made it clear from day one that creating room to breathe is my number one priority, and the whole of this government is united on that. We won’t be able to solve every frustration overnight. But where the government can save people money, remove an unnecessary obstacle or simply make something work better, we should – and we will.

We are kicking off with a couple of first steps on those everyday hassles that people tell me about time and time again.

First, we are putting an end to phoney bargains. We are taking on poor practices that make people’s lives harder. If something is advertised as half price, it should actually be half price. We will make sure that when families snatch a deal, they can be confident they’re actually saving. That’s the least they deserve when budgets are so tight.

Second, we are making it as easy to leave a subscription as it is to join, and businesses won’t be able to renew a subscription without notifying you. New rules will come into force in January 2027, in time for when people often start new subscriptions, or cancel the ones they have, for the year ahead.

There are about 155m active subscriptions in the UK, with consumers spending an estimated £1.6bn a year on ones they don’t actually want – a direct hit to family budgets. The changes we are introducing will save an average of £14 a month for every unwanted subscription.

These are just a couple of our everyday fixes. There will be more to come over the next few months and bigger plans to make life easier and fairer for people over the longer term.

Each everyday fix will be designed to put a bit more money back into people’s pockets, to make daily life a little fairer and to give people a bit more hope that politics really can work for them again.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

I will also be asking people what action they want to see on the cost of living. Because if we want to find the problems that make everyday life harder, we need to listen to the people dealing with them.

So over the summer, I will be getting out to regions across country to hear directly from people about the challenges they face and the changes they want to see.

Westminster has spent too long asking people to wait for life to get better. This government is determined to make it better and to bring back hope. My message to people is simple: this will be a cost-of-living government and we will be on your side to prevent you being overcharged, trapped or misled.

Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United Kingdom

https://fortune.com/2026/08/09/dollar-do.title: By propping up the yen, the U.S. and Japan are actually admitting dollar dominance isn’t what it used to be, top economist warns
https://fortune.com/2026/08/09/dollar-do.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/08/09/dollar-do.text:
Last week’s attempt to boost the sagging yen wasn’t the first time the U.S. and Japan took such joint action, but the way they did it revealed weakness in the dollar’s global status, according to a top currency expert.

In a Financial Times op-ed on Tuesday, University of California at Berkeley economist Barry Eichengreen pointed to both sides of the currency intervention, which he said reflected concern about long-term yields going up.

On the U.S. end, the New York Fed sold euros instead of dollar-denominated assets to buy yen. Eichengreen said that allowed the U.S. to avoid calling on financial markets to absorb more Treasury securities.

That’s as the federal government must finance a $2 trillion budget deficit this fiscal year, meaning it’s already issuing a flood of Treasury debt. Meanwhile, it’s also competing against AI hyperscalers who are selling a mountain of their own bonds.

The tsunami of public and private debt as well as the competition for investor demand have put upward pressure on yields, which adds to interest costs and the federal deficit.

On the Japanese side of the intervention, Tokyo also refrained from selling Treasuries and instead tapped an obscure Federal Reserve tool called the Foreign and International Monetary Authorities Repo Facility.

This mechanism allowed Japan, which is the world’s largest holder of U.S. debt, to borrow dollars against its Treasury stockpile, obtaining a limited form of liquidity.

“Both moves are an indication that the dollar’s status as a reserve currency is not what it used to be,” Eichengreen wrote. “Central banks are accustomed to holding foreign reserves in dollars because markets in U.S. Treasury securities are liquid. Central banks hold U.S. Treasuries because they can be freely bought and sold and used in interventions. But not now, at least not in unlimited quantities.”

That’s strikes at the heart of dollar dominance, which is in part derived from the immense size and depth of the U.S. debt market.

But by signaling that Treasuries can’t be used anytime and anywhere, the U.S. gives investors less of a reason to own them.

“The bottom line is that Washington, fearing the consequences for U.S. financial markets, is reluctant to see foreign central banks use their dollar reserves,” Eichengreen concluded. “This is telling us that the dollar is not the attractive reserve currency it once was. When this message sinks in, other countries will redouble their search for more attractive, readily usable alternatives.”

Kieran Tompkins, senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, echoed that sentiment, saying in a note on Friday that the U.S. is raising the relative appeal of holding assets like gold because it pressured Japan to not sell dollar assets.

To be sure, central banks have been filling up their reserves with more gold for years while relying less on dollars. Some of that is unrelated to de-dollarization, such as concerns about fiscal, inflation and geopolitical risks.

But it’s also due to a desire to reduce vulnerability to U.S. sanctions that leverage the dollar’s ubiquity, eroding another pillar of its dominance—namely, as the top currency for international transactions.

“Central bank gold buying has slowed this year, but that is likely in response to soaring gold prices caused by speculative momentum. However, the ability of central banks to conduct FX operations without triggering concerns from U.S. administrations about the impact on U.S. bond markets could provide fresh impetus to central banks’ demand for gold,” Tompkins predicted.

But strategists at Goldman Sachs made the opposite argument about dollar dominance. In another note, they downplayed the fear that the U.S. might try to prevent other debt holders from selling Treasuries in the future.

And Japan’s use of the Fed’s Foreign and International Monetary Authorities Repo Facility is actually a sign of dollar strength rather than weakness.

“We believe Treasury’s actions and the availability and utility of the FIMA facility help demonstrate that no one else can come close to competing with the U.S. dollar’s usefulness, network effects, and supporting infrastructure right now,” Goldman added.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/t.author: Katie Spain
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Extreme Weather Events

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:40pm

Broadview Oval was among the locations across South Australia that experienced flooding over the weekend. (Bobby Macumber)

Three people who drove through flood waters have been rescued, following a weekend of heavy rainfall and storm activity across South Australia.

Several South Australian towns recorded record breaking August rainfall totals across Saturday and Sunday, including 110 millimetres at Lenswood and 101mm at Coromandel East.

The State Emergency Service said it had received more than 530 requests for assistance during the weather event, mostly responding to flood-related incidents in the northern suburbs of Adelaide.

Meanwhile SA Police said three people have been rescued after driving into flood waters at the intersection of Wingate and Winzor Roads at Hillier.

Police said emergency services were called just after 4.50am on Monday, following reports that a car had driven into a flooded area.

Police said two occupants of the vehicle, a man and a woman, managed to get themselves out through the windows and safely to the side of the road.

While police were assisting the two people, another car drove into the water and also became stuck.

The male driver was able to exit the vehicle and was also helped by police to safety.

Both of the vehicles were washed away by the floodwaters, but police said there were no injuries as a result.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/d.title: Carlton fans chant 'we want Fraser', talks on coaching future imminent
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/d.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:06pm

Josh Fraser has guided the Blues up the ladder, sitting inside the AFL top 10. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Interim Carlton coach Josh Fraser has continued the club's mid-season revival with a 10th win from 12 matches, defeating St Kilda on Sunday.

Fans were chanting for Fraser at Docklands Stadium on Sunday, but the 43-year-old has still not formally thrown his hat into the ring \to be full-time coach.

The Blues sit eight points clear in 10th with games against the Western Bulldogs and Fremantle to come.

Carlton fans are chanting Josh Fraser's name and a similar endorsement from the club's hierarchy for the Blues' interim coach to take the reins full time could follow as soon as this week.

Fraser has mounted an irrepressible case to take on the vacant head coach role, having delivered 10 wins and just two losses since stepping up when Michael Voss was sacked in mid-May, with the Blues at 1-8.

Fraser, who earned "we want Fraser" chants from Carlton fans after Sunday night's 44-point win, is yet to officially throw his hat in the ring — but that conversation is imminent.

‘We want Fraser’: Carlton fans make their voices heard

"At some stage this week there'll be an opportunity to have some conversations with the club," Fraser said.

"It'll be sometime this week."

Half-back Adam Cerra joked whether the interim boss should take the reins was the hardest question at the club at the moment.

"Obviously the club's got their processes. We've got full faith in that process and their decision and we'll support whatever they pick. 'Frase' has been great," he said.

"The boys obviously love playing with him. We'll leave that to the club."

Cerra put Carlton's turnaround down to a combination of Fraser's influence and how the playing group lifted him — with experienced players leading from the front and young players expressing themselves.

"Frase has probably allowed a bit of freedom for us to do that, a bit of simplicity in the way we're trying to play," Cerra said.

"It hasn't set too many boundaries on us. It's more trying to explore what our best football looks like and building that week to week.

"These last couple of weeks we've been getting more confidence in our process and our trust and executing."

Fraser was asked whether part of his thinking in holding off on nominating was around managing if he missed out on the job while preparing the team for a potential wildcard match.

Carlton plants one foot in the AFL finals series with a statement victory over the Saints at Docklands.

"It's a fair question, but no, I haven't thought too deeply about that," the 43-year-old said.

"I've just tried to stay as narrow as I can and it's been challenging with a lot of the questioning and different things, but I still feel such a responsibility to this role as interim coach.

"That's what I needed to and have focused all of my energy on — because I would be doing a disservice, not only to our players, but our staff and everyone, if I started to stray away from that.

"Clearly I've had to think through some things, but that hasn't occupied a lot of my thinking and all the hypotheticals haven't either. Most of my energy has been focused on this playing group and footy club."

The Blues sit eight points clear in 10th with games against the Western Bulldogs and Fremantle to come.

"[It's] not about daring to dream, I think the thing that's taking us forward is we are just attaching ourselves to the work that we need to do," Fraser said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/g.title: Gold hunters fear World Heritage bid could undermine prospecting
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/g.author: Alice Walker
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/g.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:01pm

Victoria's gold rush began 175 years ago. (Supplied: State Library of Victoria)

Proponents of the Victorian goldfields' bid for UNESCO World Heritage status continue to battle concerns it could lead to land use restrictions.

Prospectors say a significant section of the community remains unconvinced by assurances a listing would not impact local regulations.

Next month the federal government will select which site on its tentative list to submit to UNESCO for consideration.

As Victoria continues to build its case for UNESCO World Heritage status for selected goldfields sites, modern-day prospectors are concerned a successful bid could undermine the very activity that sparked it.

The state's gold rush continues to inspire more than 115,000 prospectors who hold a Victorian miner's right, a permit dating back to the 1850s.

How the gold rush shaped Victoria, episode 6.

But Prospectors and Miners Association of Victoria (PMAV) executive president Jason Cornish said he had been fielding two-hour phone calls from gold hunters anxious about the implications of World Heritage status.

A UNESCO listing has no bearing on local laws, but Mr Cornish said apprehensions it could open the door to further land use restrictions remained widespread.

"Prospectors and miners have always had a distrust of government and over-regulation and bureaucracy," he said.

Jason Cornish says much of the criticism on social media is misinformed. (Supplied: Jason Cornish)

The World Heritage bid for the Victorian goldfields proposes listing a group of selected sites of significance across regional Victoria, such as Castlemaine, Walhalla, and the Great Nuggets landscape.

The proposal is currently on Australia's tentative list, and is spearheaded by 15 local councils, the state government and Heritage Victoria.

Next month, the team will submit its preliminary assessment making the case for "outstanding universal value" to the federal government.

Each year, the federal government can choose just one proposal from its tentative list to put forward to UNESCO.

An Australian government spokesperson said progress was being made on the nomination.

"The Australian government has been working closely with the Victorian government on the Victorian goldfields World Heritage nomination," the spokesperson said.

"The next step in the process is to submit a preliminary assessment request to UNESCO to seek advice on the likelihood of the property to contain outstanding universal value."

Selected Victorian goldfields sites for potential World Heritage listing submitted to Australia's tentative list. (Supplied: Heritage Victoria)

Mr Cornish said open dialogue with the World Heritage bid team had overcome his initial concerns, but some questions remained unanswered.

He said his "optimistic" views were not shared by a significant number of prospectors vehemently opposed to the project.

"There's a lot of people out there that are concerned [about] what's going to happen in the future if the bid is successful, but that's the future," he said.

"If something happens down the track and they actually do start blocking access, well that's just a fight for another day … but so far I haven't seen that."

Chris Bogusis says he is concerned land use is gradually being more restricted. (Supplied: Chris Bogusis)

Wodonga-based prospector Chris Bogusis is one of the PMAV members concerned that platforming the story of the gold rush could have results contrary to its spirit.

"I think World Heritage can be a fantastic thing to have in place for certain areas that certainly show historic significance," he said.

He said he felt a strong connection to Victoria's gold rush miners who left traces in historic tunnels.

The Malmsbury viaduct is one of the sites under investigation for World Heritage status. (Supplied: Barry Gamble)

"The scars of their picks and their chisels are still in the walls," he said.

"Then you'll hit a point where modern mining picked up with pneumatic drills and more effective explosives … and you can literally see the boundary line of where the two different workings meet, and they change."

Barry Gamble, a strategic adviser to the heritage bid, said the preservation of early mining activity was part of what made Victoria's gold rush stand out above its North American equivalents.

"The fact that … no large corporations were allowed to come in subsequently to mass mine the land through large-scale dredging, large-scale hydraulic mining left the signature of the individual prospectors in their tens of thousands," he said.

A deep lead gold mine in Bright, 1880. (Supplied: State Library Victoria)

Mr Gamble has a 100 per cent success rate on 22 UNESCO World Heritage nominations around the world, including his native mining landscape of Cornwall-West Devon.

He said western Victoria's distinctive volcanic landscape also made the local gold rush unique.

"The lava flows that flowed over the landscape that produced the fertile farmland … also covered ancient rivers of gold," he said.

"For about another 20 years, these ancient lava flows concealed a further hidden treasure which then perpetuated that gold rush for another … two decades."

Barry Gamble can trace seven ancestors to Victoria's gold rush. (Supplied: City of Ballarat)

He said he was confident the Victorian goldfields would get over the line with UNESCO.

"This is a winning horse."

Former Victorian premier John Brumby has been pushing for World Heritage status for the goldfields since he was a federal MP in the 1980s.

He said the process for World Heritage had "no impact whatsoever" on land use.

John Brumby (right) is co-patron of the World Heritage bid alongside Dennis Napthine. (ABC Ballarat: Lexie Jeuniewic)

"Those nominations would have no legal status within the Australian, Victorian or relevant local government laws," he said.

"It won't impact any provisions in existing planning schemes… and importantly, there's no impact on the exercise of legal rights under a miner's right."

Mr Brumby said prospectors were an important stakeholder in the process.

"The nomination itself highlights the important historic role of the miner's right and that actually it's a reason why World Heritage inscription is justified," he said.

"It demonstrates the path to democracy and the recognition of the role that diggers played."

The World Heritage bid proposes listing about 10 sites of significance across regional Victoria. (Supplied: Barry Gamble)

Mr Brumby is co-patron of the World Heritage bid alongside former Liberal premier Dennis Napthine.

He said it was a "much more sophisticated proposal" than what was launched in the 1980s, and had brought together an unlikely coalition.

"[It's] almost unprecedented to get 15 councils all united and all supporting this," he said.

The earliest the Victorian goldfields could gain World Heritage status is 2030.

If successful, a World Heritage management plan would then be developed for the goldfields.

A Department of Transport and Planning spokesperson said the World Heritage bid would not affect prospectors.

"The proposed World Heritage listing of the Victorian goldfields will not affect prospecting activities," the spokesperson said.

"As the nomination progresses, we'll continue working with councils and communities to plan for the future, so these places can welcome more visitors while protecting what makes them unique."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/s.title: Aviation bosses summoned, airport workers stood down after Sydney near-miss
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/s.author: Jean Kennedy
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 9:56pm

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 9:59pm

Jetstar and Qatar Airways near miss at Sydney Airport.

Two airport workers have been stood down amid investigations into how two planes almost collided at Sydney Airport on Sunday.

It comes as the head Civil Air Association, the union representing air traffic controllers, said staffing shortages were taking a toll on those on the frontline.

Federal Transport Catherine King is set to meet with Airservices Australia CEO Rob Sharp in Canberra today after the second incident in recent weeks.

Emergency meetings will be held in Canberra as an investigation gets underway into a near-miss involving two passenger planes at Sydney Airport following days of flight disruptions and delays.

Two airport workers were stood down pending the outcome of an official investigation into the near collision, which left a Jetstar crew member injured yesterday.

Jetstar flight JQ402 was preparing to take off for the Gold Coast and was taxiing to the runway when it was forced to slam on the brakes.

Its flight crew noticed a Qatar Airways plane that was being towed along the tarmac by an aircraft tug and in close proximity.

Both aircraft stopped abruptly, avoiding crashing by mere metres.

Two airport workers involved in Sunday's near-miss have since been stood down. (Supplied)

Describing it as "extremely concerning", federal Transport Minister Catherine King vowed any "systemic issues" to come out of the investigation by the aviation safety watchdog would be addressed.

She also said Airservices Australia "needs to do better" to manage disruptions at the airport, which has grappled with a shortage of air traffic controllers.

Thousands of passengers were affected by lengthy delays over recent days, with some missing flight connections as a result.

"They caused significant challenges to passengers, staff and airlines," Ms King said.

It was understood the organisation's CEO Rob Sharp will meet with her this morning in Canberra.

Airservices Australia, the government-owned body responsible for safely and efficiently managing air traffic, said yesterday in a statement that Air Traffic Flow Management measures had been put in place following the incident, including departure spacing "to safely manage projected airborne and departure demands".

"Airservices is reviewing the incident and will assist with any safety investigation," it said

Australian Transport Safety Bureau's Chief Commissioner Angus Mitchell is heading the investigation into yesterday's near collision.

A Jetstar spokesperson said the aircraft had been following air traffic control instructions before its pilots brought the plane to a sudden stop. (ABC News: Peter Garnish)

He said it was too early to confirm the cause with investigators examining all possibilities, including one line of inquiry that the tug pulling the aircraft did not follow Air Traffic Control instructions.

"Now exactly why they came so close is I guess really what we're trying to understand at the moment so we're gathering the evidence we need to make that determination," he said.

"So that will be from both the pilots on board the Jetstar aircraft, those that were controlling the Qatar plane, as well as those in the coordination of air traffic control, to understand what potentially broke down in the coordination or communication.

A shortage of air traffic controllers at Sydney Airport is affecting services, the Civil Air boss says. (ABC News)

It was the second near-miss at the airport in recent weeks, with two Qantas planes narrowly avoiding crashing late last month.

Commissioner Mitchell said in both instances the pilots were able to act quickly to avoid a collision.

He said the probe would be wide-ranging and also scrutinise whether the understaffing issues within the airport's air traffic control fleet had any role to play.

Commissioner Mitchell says the investigation will look into whether any individual errors were made. (Supplied: ATSB)

Commissioner Mitchell said the investigation needed to uncover whether systemic changes were needed to ensure that if individual errors are made, that there are other mechanisms in place to avoid serious problems.

The government confirmed the air traffic control ground worker and the tug operator involved in yesterday's near collision have both been stood down, pending the outcome of the investigation.

A Jetstar spokesperson said the aircraft had been following air traffic control instructions during the incident and its captain acted "quickly and decisively".

The crew member sustained a minor injury after falling when the pilot hit the brakes.

The boss of the union representing air traffic controllers declined to publicly comment what he believed was the cause of the two near collisions, saying it was "premature" while investigations were underway.

Mr Nugent said resourcing for air traffic controllers has been a long-running issue. (Supplied)

But Civil Air president Scott Nugent, who is a trained air traffic controller, said staffing shortages took a heavy toll on those working on the frontline.

"What I can say is that air traffic controllers in Australia are working very hard, and for a long time they have not necessarily had the resources they need to do their jobs properly," he told the ABC.

"There aren't enough controllers in Australia."

He said the air traffic control system at Sydney Airport relied on workers doing excessive overtime, with some potentially doing more than 20 extra hours a week.

"We've seen in the past few days what happened when you don't have enough air traffic controllers, the impact on industry," he said.

"Civil Air has been saying to Airservices over the past four or five years you don't have enough air traffic controllers in Sydney airport tower.

"No matter why they occurred, people no longer want to work the overtime because they're very stressed and upset, and the whole system is propped up on overtime."

Mr Nugent said he would also be meeting with Mr Sharp later today to discuss his concerns in the wake of the weekend disruption.
