https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/h.author: Shiloh Payne
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 9:55pm

In Nepal, Elliot had his head shaved when he signed up for an army-style bootcamp. (ABC iview/Race Around The World: Elliot Constable)

Elliot Constable was wandering through a park in Chisinau, Moldova, when he met Tatiana.

A Race Around the World contestant tasked with making short documentaries on tight deadlines, he was looking for a story.

He had only 10 days to shoot and edit a film, but he spent two of those just listening to her.

Tatiana had fled Ukraine when Russia attacked her home in 2022, but when she met Constable, she was trying to get back into the war-torn country for cancer treatment.

Since then, Constable has been crowned the winner of ABC iview's Race Around the World, a reboot of the 1990s classic TV competition.

Now back home in Sydney, Constable tells me Tatiana's back in Kyiv, and their families remain in touch.

Elliot says his mother has sent Tatiana's family a care package. (ABC iview/Race Around The World: Elliot Constable)

The filmmaker credits his success on the show to his character-driven approach.

"It's those people that have stories where you think, 'Where are they going to end up?' that, I think, really hit home," Constable says.

When I catch him on the phone the day after filming the finale (and the subsequent celebrations), he hasn't even had the chance to return to his apartment yet.

Constable's journey took him across South Africa, Norway, Azerbaijan, the Bahamas and eventually Brazil. He's battling the whirr of jet lag as he admits his success is yet to sink in.

In week four, Elliot travelled to Svalbard, Norway, where he was guided through polar bear territory in the Arctic mountains. (ABC iview/Race Around The World: Elliot Constable)

Winning means Constable receives funding to produce his own project, produced by the ABC.

"I thought I'd won already because I was on the show, and I think that's the consensus with all the other racers. It's an opportunity of a lifetime; we all won, right?" he says.

"But the fact that I now have an opportunity to tell another story or maybe go back and do something a bit bigger … maybe it is going back to Moldova, maybe it's going back to Brazil, I don't know, maybe it's doing something in Australia."

It was Brazil, the destination he was allowed to select for the show's finale, where he entered the favelas in Rio de Janeiro and met a father determined to shield his son from a future of crime.

"I didn't want to do a story about the gangs, but I wanted the film to be more about hope and this boy who is going to have a challenging decision to make one day," he says.

"Do you take an honest path? Often in places like Brazil in the favelas, it's going to mean a tough life.

"Or you take this path that is more of the gang route. You see them walking around with gold chains and weapons; they look like action stars, and they're feared and respected, and young boys see that and think, 'I want that life.'"

Elliot says he's still in touch with the family he profiled in Brazil. (ABC iview/Race Around The World: Elliot Constable)

Constable's main hope is that people watch his films and care for the people and their complex situations.

This sentiment is shared by the competition's People's Choice Award winner, Jayden O'Neill, who took out the top spot in the ABC's audience poll.

"The reason you make content is because you want the audience to take it in," O'Neill says.

Jayden spent time in India, Jordan, Timor-Leste and the Philippines. (ABC iview/Race Around The World: Jayden O'Neill)

On the show, the six contestants were judged each week by a panel of industry experts.

"The judging panel is only made up of three people, and they'll all have their own views," he says.

"If you can get the popular vote, I think it's really cool that it resonates with so many people, and that's what we're here for."

Jayden's favourite films to make were the same ones the audience loved, including his week one entry from the Philippines, which detailed fishers using illegal methods to feed their families.

"The connection I made with the people there is what made the film what it was, and you don't have that connection with every single film," O'Neill says.

If you're wondering whether the six contestants were really showing up to a new country every 10 days and making a film on their own, host Zan Rowe confirms as much.

"They have to find the story, shoot it, edit it, record the sound and deliver it. It's all a completely solo venture," she says.

Zan Rowe says the show took a new approach. (ABC)

The show is a reboot of the original series broadcast in 1997 and 1998, but with all of the technological advancements, Rowe says it's barely recognisable.

"It is basically launching a new show, and the beauty of that is you can try new things," she says.

"In week three we noticed [the contestants] were doing these character pieces that were a bit slow and reflective; we needed to get them more in the field to see them immerse themselves in the country. So we threw them a challenge in that regard and really shook it up."

Destinations were also changed at the last minute.

"Things were changed, both for safety reasons, geopolitical reasons, but also just to see variety, how the filmmakers were reacting to certain places, what sort of ways the producers could challenge them or take them somewhere where they thought they'd probably do something interesting," Rowe says.

In week five, all of the contestants were sent to Japan. (ABC iview/Race Around The World)

In the original series, there was no feedback on the road and no way for the contestants to communicate with each other.

Constable says having access to feedback early on helped him refine his approach.

"Ultimately, they're looking for a narrative that makes sense. And I think I really took on the feedback. I struggled at the start with having too much going on," he says.

"You don't have the luxury of being able to step away from it or have a day off from it, which I think always helps in the real world."

In the Bahamas, Elliot prepared a meal with a local family's catch of the day. (ABC iview/Race Around The World: Elliot Constable)

For Constable, the clock was always the biggest challenge.

"You're constantly up against it with time; you turn up to a country, and you don't know what you're doing. Things fall through, and ideas don't come together, and you sometimes have to pivot," he says.

Catch up on every week 10 film from Race Around the World.

"And then at the end of the episode, they're like, all right, you're going to this place and two hours later you're on a flight."

Constable is still very much running on "autopilot", having come back from Brazil only one day before the finale.

So, after 100 days across the globe, 10 new films and a shiny prize of an ABC-funded project up his sleeve, he's got one thing on his mind: sleep.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/t.title: Flights cancelled, evacuations as Typhoon Dolphin hits China
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 9:49pm

Typhoon Dolphin made landfall in Yuhuan, Taizhou, in eastern China's Zhejiang Province. (AP: Huang Zongzhi/Xinhua)

Typhoon Dolphin has crossed over China's coastline near Yuhuan City in Zhejiang Province.

Thousands of flights have been cancelled and hundreds of thousands of people have been evacuated.

Forecasters in China predicted that areas could see 200–400 millimetres of rainfall over the next few days.

Typhoon Dolphin made landfall in densely populated eastern China on Sunday, meteorological authorities said, after the storm triggered more than 1,000 flight cancellations, evacuations and a top-level alert.

China's east coast has been preparing for the storm's arrival in recent days, with work and transport services suspended in some areas along its predicted path.

The centre of the typhoon moved over the coastline near Yuhuan City in Zhejiang Province at about 5:30 pm (7:30pm AEST), China's National Meteorological Centre said in an online post.

Heavy rains have created a risk of severe flooding in Zhejiang, and authorities have warned of severe landslide risks.

Forecasters predict between 200 and 400 millimetres of rainfall in some areas over the next few days. (Reuters: cnsphoto)

Forecasters in China predicted that areas could see 200–400 millimetres of rainfall over the next few days.

Maximum wind speeds near the centre were more than 150 kilometres per hour at the time it made landfall, the NMC said.

Nearly 1,400 flights in and out of Shanghai's two main passenger airports were cancelled on Sunday, state broadcaster CCTV reported.

Hangzhou's airport in nearby Zhejiang province saw 270 inbound and outbound flights cancelled, the report said.

On Saturday evening, authorities in Zhejiang evacuated 390,000 people in the city of Taizhou. Authorities in Shanghai evacuated more than 30,000 people from riskier areas.

The effects were felt as far away as Hong Kong on China's southern coast, where the weather observatory posted a record high temperature of 36.9 Celsius, caused by warm air pushed over the city by Typhoon Dolphin.

With the storm "moving towards the vicinity of Zhejiang and moving inland, its outer subsiding air will persistently bring extremely hot weather to the territory today to Tuesday", the Hong Kong Observatory said.

Typhoon Dolphin brought heavy rain and strong winds to Japan's Okinawa before reaching China.

Seven people in Okinawa suffered minor injuries, including a man aged over 100 who was blown over by gusts, fell on the ground and hit his head, according to the island's government.

Strong winds and rain led to thousands of flight cancellations. (AP: Wang Xiang/Xinhua)

By Sunday afternoon, 5,290 households in Okinawa were without electricity, according to regional utility Okinawa Electric Power.

In Taiwan, dozens of ferry services were suspended and more than 180 flights were cancelled as the storm brought downpours and strong winds to the island's north on Sunday.

In the Philippines, five people were rescued and seven remained missing after a landslide that hit three houses in the northern mountain resort city of Baguio on Sunday.

China's NMC issued a red typhoon alert — its most severe warning — on Sunday morning, forecasting "extraordinary torrential rain" in some areas of central and eastern Zhejiang.

Heavy precipitation is also expected to fall in Shanghai and parts of Fujian, Anhui and Jiangsu provinces through Monday afternoon, it said.

Typhoon Dolphin was expected to weaken after making landfall while moving in a north-westerly direction over eastern China.

Residents struggled against the strong wind gusts. (AP: Wang Xiang/Xinhua)

In Fujian, nearly 99,000 people were relocated from "risky areas" on Saturday evening ahead of the storm's arrival, state news agency Xinhua reported.

Services on more than 200 ferry routes were suspended in Zhejiang and Fujian, Xinhua said, while work at offshore projects was halted and 474 construction vessels had been called to port by Friday morning.

Some train services in affected areas were also suspended on Sunday to ensure passenger safety, state media reported.

Scientists say human-driven climate change is making extreme heat events more frequent and more intense worldwide.

Typhoon Dolphin's arrival in China comes two weeks after Typhoon Noul lashed southern Guangdong province, declared by authorities at the time as the strongest storm to hit China this year.

Three people were killed and hundreds of homes were damaged by Typhoon Noul in the Philippines before it reached China.

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.title: Trump announces staff secretary Will Scharf will be his new White House counsel
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.author: Associated Press
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.text:
Scharf, who as staff secretary helped Trump secure approval for his US$400 million ballroom, will replace David Warrington on September 1

US President Donald Trump announced Sunday that his new White House counsel will be Will Scharf, the staff secretary who as the Trump-appointed head of the National Capital Planning Commission helped secure approval for the US$400 million ballroom project.

Trump said that, beginning on September 1, Scharf will be replacing David Warrington, who will be leaving the administration to join the private sector. Trump noted that Scharf previously served as a federal prosecutor and represented him in a number of cases, including at the Supreme Court.

“Will is Tough, Strong, and Smart! He also loves our Country, and respects the Law,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Will Scharf will do a great job as White House Counsel!”

The shake-up in the White House counsel’s office comes at a critical juncture – just months ahead of the midterm elections, where Trump’s Republican Party will be fighting to hold on to control of Congress. Democrats have vowed to pursue investigations into Trump and his administration if they are successful in November.

The White House counsel’s job is to advise on legal and policy questions related to the presidency. The office is the primary White House contact for the Justice Department and it handles presidential pardons, works on judicial appointments and reviews legislation. The office also helps investigate and manage congressional investigations into the administration and lawsuits against the president when he is sued in his official capacity.

Trump in July 2025 had named Scharf as chairman of the National Capital Planning Commission, the executive branch agency with jurisdiction over construction and major renovations to government buildings in the region.

Trump’s ballroom won final approval from the NCPC in April, though a divided federal appeal court ruled on Friday that construction on the project must stop because Congress had not approved it. Trump has vowed to appeal to the US Supreme Court.

The project is already well on its way and has begun to rise above ground on the east side of the White House.

The Bald Range wildfire has prompted British Columbia to declare a provincial state of emergency and evacuate about 18,000 people

The Canadian federal government said on ⁠Sunday it would ⁠help British Columbia ⁠as raging wildfires forced thousands of people to evacuate by providing shelter and accommodation for residents displaced in regions around Summerland and Peachland.

The Bald Range wildfire, which prompted British ‌Columbia to declare a provincial state of emergency and evacuate about 18,000 people, had spread to more than 10,300 hectares by at the weekend as firefighters continued to battle the blaze.

“Last night, I approved a request for Federal Assistance from British ⁠Columbia to provide shelter and accommodations for people who have been forced ‌to leave their homes due to wildfires across the province,” Eleanor Olszewski, Canada’s minister of emergency management and ‌community resilience, said in a social media post.

“I have tasked ⁠federal officials, ⁠led by the Government Operations Centre at Public Safety Canada, to work with ‌the province to ensure support reaches those who need it most,” the minister said.

Over the past ‌24 hours, ‌southern British Columbia continued to see fires spreading due to ‌hot and dry weather, the province’s Wildfire Service said.

Poor visibility and ⁠increasing fires created new challenges to aviation and the ground crew ⁠response, it said.

Ten helicopters and a night-vision helicopter were operating but were hindered by thick smoke, turbulence and large ‌fires.

The province had ‌34 staff from Australia, five from New Zealand, and 214 from Mexico supporting hundreds of provincial firefighters and expects additional international resources to arrive over the coming days, it said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/9/.title: Union reports 108 attacks on Palestinian journalists in July
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/9/.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/9/.text:
The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate has documented 108 attacks by Israeli forces and settlers against Palestinian journalists and media workers in the occupied West Bank last month.

The syndicate’s Freedoms Committee said in a statement on Sunday that the violations ranged from detention and beating to interrogation, obstruction of coverage and the seizure or destruction of press equipment, describing a pattern that has made it increasingly difficult for journalists to document Israeli military raids and settler violence on the ground.

Brief detentions and restrictions on reporting were the most common violations, with 58 cases recorded.

The committee also documented 11 settler attacks on journalists, including physical assaults, shoving and threats, mostly while crews covered settler attacks and military raids elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, along with 12 cases in which Israeli forces fired stun grenades or tear gas at journalists, causing some to suffocate.

Six journalists were beaten, and four sustained bleeding injuries while covering developments in Gaza, including from shrapnel. Two others were detained and four interrogated about their reporting.

The committee recorded four raids on journalists’ homes or media offices, including the closure of one outlet, three cases of equipment being confiscated or destroyed, two instances of deleted footage, and two expulsions of journalists from the vicinity of Al-Aqsa Mosque.

The syndicate called for journalists to be allowed to work “free from threats, attacks and pursuit”, and demanded accountability for those responsible.

The July toll adds to a surging record already considered the deadliest in history for journalists.

Rights groups have documented that Israeli attacks have killed more than 270 journalists amid a sweeping campaign of arbitrary press detentions since October 2023.

Al Jazeera has confirmed that 12 of its own journalists have been killed in Gaza since the start of Israel’s campaign in 2023, more than any other media outlet.

https://www.statnews.com/pharmalot/2026/.author: Ed Silverman
https://www.statnews.com/pharmalot/2026/.text:
Sanofi is experiencing shortages of two medicines used to treat Pompe disease, and the problem emerged shortly after the Food and Drug Administration warned the company over manufacturing issues at the Irish facility where the drugs are made.

In recent days, the drugmaker has alerted patient groups and physicians in both the U.S. and Europe that supplies of Myozyme, an older standard of care, and Nexviazyme, a newer treatment, are dwindling due to what has been described as a bottleneck in the final manufacturing phase, as well as quality control issues at its Waterford plant.

The site is responsible for what is known as batch release, which refers to the final quality assurance and regulatory process where a manufactured amount of medicine is formally certified, approved, and cleared for distribution and use by patients. This step is supposed to verify the batch of medicine meets safety and potency requirements.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/07/south-ko.title: From birth to brokerage: Why South Korea is seeing a surge in infant investment accounts
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/07/south-ko.author: Justina Lee,Lisa Kim
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/07/south-ko.text:
Brokerage accounts of kids under the age of one have nearly tripled from a year ago: Mirae Asset Securities.

Those aged 0 to 9 recorded a jump in new accounts of nearly 60% to around 185,000.

Despite the wild swings, South Korea’s market rally has helped spark parents’ interest in investing.

South Korean parents are ramping up efforts to give their children a head start in building long-term wealth by opening investment accounts even before they learn to crawl out of their cribs.

Brokerage accounts of kids under the age of one have nearly tripled from a year ago to about 15,000 in June at Mirae Asset Securities, the country’s largest brokerage by market cap.

New accounts openings for those under 9 have soared nearly 60% to around 185,000, the brokerage said, excluding duplicate accounts.

That enthusiasm, triggered by Korea’s AI-powered market rally, has sparked a trend toward generational wealth-planning, though the volatility in the domestic stock market has prompted investors to look for value beyond the border as well.

Lee Hye-won, who works as a nurse, told CNBC that she and her spouse believed investing long term was a better choice than keeping money in savings or deposit accounts.

“We felt that, when it comes to managing our children’s accounts, the length of time invested matters more than the investment amount, so we opened an account for our first child at age 4, and for our second child right after birth,” she said. The family invests about 300,000 won ($210) to 400,000 won per month in U.S. exchange-traded funds, mainly those tracking the S&P 500.

Other parents are doing similar things.

“I wanted to give my child the gift of time and the power of compounding during those years — that’s why I opened the account right after her birth,” said Lee Jun-hyeok, an office worker.

“I’m also making small, regular investments in the Korean semiconductor sector and U.S. physical AI–related stocks, both of which I see as having high growth potential,” he said.

Jae-joon Woo, professor of economics at DePaul University, told CNBC that parents will continue to open investment accounts for their children even if markets become more volatile. The phenomenon is here to stay “as long as equity investing—whether in Korea or overseas markets—is viewed as a reliable way to build long-term wealth,” Woo said.

“This could represent a gradual but meaningful shift from the traditional preference for real estate, which has long been the dominant form of household wealth in Korea,” he added.

Households held around three-quarters of their wealth in physical assets, primarily real estate, and the rest in financial assets, according to a survey by Ministry of Data and Statistics.

The relatively high capital gains tax on property, particularly for short holding periods or multiple-home ownership, is another factor attracting more Koreans to the stock market, said Jeong-woo Park, senior economist for South Korea at financial services firm Nomura.

Korea applies a progressive tax rate of 6% to 45% on capital gains from properties owned for two years or longer, according to the National Tax Service. The tax rate jumps to 40% to 70% for properties owned for less than two years.

By contrast, most retail investors are not subject to capital gains tax when selling Korea-listed shares, unless they are a major shareholder.

Gift tax is another reason parents are flocking to the stock market. Gifts of up to 20 million won from parents to a minor child are tax-exempt within once in a 10-year period, according to the Ministry of Government Legislation. So parents use that tax-exempt cash gift to invest in stocks.

“At first, our bigger concern wasn’t which stocks to buy via our children’s accounts, but rather how to handle gift tax. We looked into the relevant details ourselves and consulted with a tax accountant,” said “leecoach_mom.”

However, for most middle-income households, the main motivation to invest in stocks for their children would be to save up for education or financial security, rather than reduce taxes, Woo of DePaul University said.

Kakaopay Securities, an online brokerage linked to the Korean internet conglomerate Kakao Corp., said last month that it plans to hand out stocks worth 100,000 won per infant born next year in an effort to expand its customer base.

The government is also doing its part to make the stock market more accessible.

In 2023, financial authorities revised guidelines to allow guardians to open accounts for their children remotely from their smartphones, without having to visit a branch. “Allowing parents to open accounts remotely has removed a significant practical barrier,” Nomura’s Park said.

“Further simplification would probably increase the number of minors’ accounts, especially among households making small and regular investments,” he said.

“However, it would mainly affect participation rather than the total amount invested, which will continue to depend more heavily on household wealth, market conditions and tax considerations.”

The unprecedented U.S.-Japan intervention to support the yen may end up shaping market behavior.

“When increasingly scarce national assets are spent in unison on the same target by two major sovereigns, markets will have to listen,” said Monex’s Jesper Koll.

The unprecedented U.S.-Japan intervention to support the yen may end up shaping market behavior.

Japan has intervened in currency markets before, but this episode was bigger than usual. It was backed by Washington, reportedly executed using the euro-yen cross rather than directly in dollar-yen, and accompanied by explicit political support.

Some investors consider this a major step.

“Japan’s Ministry of Finance and the U.S. Treasury have successfully weaponized the yen,” said Jesper Koll, expert director for Monex Group, referring to market deterrence. The intervention went beyond conventional foreign exchange management because the countries deployed public balance sheets in concert to influence market psychology, he said.

“When increasingly scarce national assets are spent in unison on the same target by two major sovereigns, markets will have to listen,” he added.

The coordinated intervention was the first U.S.-Japan joint operation to buy yen since 1998, and the first coordinated intervention involving the two countries since the G7 acted to weaken the yen after the 2011 earthquake.

Koll also pointed to what he sees as unprecedented political signaling. By combining political backing and financial firepower, Washington and Tokyo sought to raise the cost of betting against the yen by putting two sovereign balance sheets on the other side of the trade.

Cornell University professor Eswar Prasad sees it as more of a defensive move, saying the operation nevertheless signals that foreign exchange policy has become increasingly intertwined with geopolitics.

“Currency market intervention has clearly taken on a geopolitical tinge,” Prasad said, with Donald Trump’s administration appearing more willing to support central banks of countries it views as aligned with U.S. priorities.

Some analysts drew parallels with Washington’s support for Argentina’s peso under President Javier Milei, when the country was battling currency instability ahead of key midterm elections. In September and October 2025, the Trump administration stepped in with a support package, using the Treasury’s Exchange Stabilization Fund to provide a $20 billion currency swap with Argentina’s central bank while also purchasing pesos in the open market.

“Bessent is the common thread. Same Treasury, same ESF, same playbook of using foreign-currency operations as an instrument of statecraft,” said Michael Gayed, chief investment strategist at Tactical Rotation Management. “Argentina was about propping up a friend.”

Similarly, Quantum Strategy’s strategist David Roche said Washington’s motives likely extended beyond financial stability or Treasury markets, and that political considerations could also have played a role.

“He might just want to do nice things for his buddy Takaichi.”

The U.S. Treasury Department did not respond to CNBC’s request for comment.

The intervention has altered the way investors will think about the currency, strategists said.

“It changes the calculus for funding trades specifically,” said Billy Leung, investment strategist at Global X ETFs. “If investors now see intervention risk as a live and coordinated threat, they will likely become more cautious running large short-yen positions and rotate toward alternative funding currencies.”

The yen has long been the world’s preferred funding currency for carry trades, where investors borrow cheaply in yen to invest in higher-yielding assets elsewhere.

Leung added that the broader consequence is that “currency policy itself” has returned as a source of market risk after fading into the background over the past decade. If investors increasingly migrate to other funding currencies such as the euro, that could reshape positioning across major FX markets.

Masahiko Loo, senior fixed income strategist at State Street Investment, agreed the episode means traders must increasingly price in geopolitical developments.

“The biggest shift is that traders now have a new variable to price: policy reaction functions, not just macro fundamentals,” he said.

S. intervention to help the yen could be a major step, analysts said. The intervention was the first U.N. joint operation to buy yen since 1998.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/07/meta-ind.title: The 72-hour crisis that could upend Meta’s business in India as firm risks losing legal protection
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/07/meta-ind.author: Priyanka Salve
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/07/meta-ind.text:
An Indian parliamentary panel has threatened to remove Meta’s safe harbor immunity, demanding an apology from Mark Zuckerberg for a dispute over a post by PM Modi.

Meta’s chief global affairs officer, Joel Kaplan, has apologized “for the error restricting PM Modi’s post.”

Experts told CNBC it would be almost impossible for Meta to operate in India without harbor protection immunity, but the withdrawal would require existing laws to be amended.

Tensions are high between Meta Platforms
 and Indian regulators after the company came under fire in the country twice in short succession.

The tech behemoth briefly restricted a Facebook post by Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressing students during the Gen Z protests in July, just days after regulators summoned the company over concerns about child-abuse content. While it later said the restriction was due to an “error,” initially the post reportedly indicated the content was blocked due to a “legal request.”

A parliamentary panel on Wednesday demanded an apology from Mark Zuckerberg within three days for the restriction on Modi’s post — failing which it recommends revoking the social media giant’s safe harbor immunity in the country. This would make Meta liable for the user-generated content on its platform.

India is a key market for Meta, with the largest user bases for WhatsApp, Instagram, and Facebook, and legal experts told CNBC that it would become almost impossible for Meta to operate in the country if the safe harbor protection is withdrawn.

They added, however, that India would need to amend the broader legal framework to remove the safe harbor rights of the platform.

Meta, though, is keen to assuage concerns of the regulators, especially those around Modi’s post.

Joel Kaplan, Meta’s chief global affairs officer, who was in a meeting with India’s Information Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw on Wednesday, said he “apologized” to the minister “for the error restricting PM Modi’s post,” the company said in a press statement.

But local media reports the same day, quoting government sources, said that it was Meta’s founder and CEO Zuckerberg who made the apology for the presence of child abuse content, deepfake material and errors in operating the platform.

Meta did not comment on the authenticity of these claims in the official statement shared with CNBC.

In an interview with ANI on Wednesday, Nishikant Dubey, the chair of a parliamentary panel on communications and information technology, wrote to India’s information technology and home ministry, demanding an apology from Zuckerberg himself.

“Zuckerberg must apologize within three days” for deleting Modi’s video addressing students, Dubey said, saying the platform was misusing the privilege of safe harbor protection -- adding that if it is revoked “there could be a nationwide flood” of formal police complaints against Meta, he added.

During the Gen Z protests in India last month, Instagram, Meta’s short video app, became a popular platform for public discourse in the country. Modi started to make reels to appeal to the young protesters.

But this growing influence is also exposing the U.S. company to intense government scrutiny over lapses in content moderation and concerns over user privacy. The Indian government last month issued a stern warning to Instagram to remove child abuse ads on its platform that followed a warning to WhatsApp over the rollout of a username feature.

Meta’s global team will remain in India to conduct “three to four” additional meetings with the ministry that will assess whether the social media company is complying with Indian laws, Indian news agency ANI reported on Thursday.

Meanwhile, Saurav Das, spokesperson of the Cockroach Janta Party which steered the Gen Z protest in India, said that Meta was restricting access to his content and claimed it was succumbing to “high-handed pressure from the government.”

India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology didn’t respond to CNBC’s calls and emails seeking comment on the proposal to withdraw Meta’s safe harbor immunity.

Safe harbor protection grants conditional immunity to social media companies, explained Udit Mendiratta, technology and disputes partner at Argus Partners.

He added that this immunity can be removed if a social media platform has abetted an unlawful action, if it has failed to remove content “expeditiously” after a court or government order, and if it fails “due diligence obligations” in removing child sexual abuse material, deepfakes and hate speech.

However, he said that under the existing Indian law, “loss of immunity is content specific,” and the law would need to be amended to remove the safe harbor immunity of an entire platform.

While the Indian government is yet to take any official action, experts said any decision affecting safe harbor would be monitored by the technology industry because it will alter the liability framework.

“Safe harbor protection is the cornerstone of digital regulation dating back to the earliest days of the internet,” Vikram Jeet Singh, partner at law firm BTG Advaya, told CNBC, adding that the loss of this immunity might expose social media companies to further civil and regulatory actions.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/f.title: Mining cities concerned census fails to count FIFO 'ghost population'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/f.author: Jarrod Lucas, Ivo da Silva, Mikki Cusack, and Kimberley Putland
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 11:03pm

Fly-in, fly-out workers arrive at Kalgoorlie-Boulder Airport. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

A lobby group representing some of Australia's most historic mining regions has been pushing for the census to better capture data around fly-in fly-out workers.

The Australian Mining Cities Alliance comprises six local governments, including councils from Kalgoorlie-Boulder, Mount Isa and Broken Hill.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics is expected to begin releasing the data gathered on census night next year.

As households across Australia begin filling out their forms for the 2026 Census, mining communities fear the count will fail to capture the nation's growing fly-in fly-out (FIFO) workforce.

The historic mining city of Kalgoorlie-Boulder, about 600 kilometres east of Perth, is experiencing one of the biggest booms in its history.

An aerial view of Kalgoorlie's Super Pit gold mine. (ABC Goldfields: Ivo Da Silva)

The rise in FIFO work practices has been so dramatic that Kalgoorlie-Boulder Airport is now among the busiest in regional WA, with more than half a million passenger movements.

Mayor Glenn Wilson has made regular use of the airport travelling to Canberra to lobby for changes to the Census while casting doubt on the accuracy of previous data.

"What we've continually done through lobbying of the ABS (Australian Bureau of Statistics) is to make sure our ghost populations are included," he said.

"We have got a baseline population, and then with the mining activities, those populations increase and put added strain on our infrastructure and our services."

He chairs the Australian Mining Cities Alliance which counts the City of Broken Hill, City of Karratha, Mount Isa City Council, Isaac Regional Council and the Shire of East Pilbara among its members.

Glenn Wilson is concerned "ghost populations" are not being included in the data. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

When the first national census was held in 1911, the population of Kalgoorlie and Boulder, then separate towns, was estimated at a combined 19,605.

That grew to 29,306 as of the 2021 Census, with 20 per cent of the population employed in gold mining.

According to the latest ABS data, Kalgoorlie-Boulder's population was 31,268 at June 30 last year.

An aerial view of the Kalgoorlie CBD.   (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Mr Wilson estimates there could be as many as 10,000 FIFO workers in Kalgoorlie-Boulder due to the current boom.

"We know since the last census there's been more dwellings built in Kalgoorlie-Boulder, there are less rentals available, less houses for sale, so if this data comes back and tells us our population is going south, there is an issue with how the census is done," he said.

"Why is it important? Because funding opportunities at a state and federal level rely on up-to-date population figures.

"An increase in population gives us more opportunity to get more funding. It's as simple as that, because many of the grant mechanisms take your population into account."

Passengers line up for security screening at Kalgoorlie-Boulder Airport.   (Supplied: Cass Be)

Kalgoorlie-Boulder Airport was built for 100,000 passenger movements a year back in the early 1990s.

City of Kalgoorlie-Boulder figures show there were 562,710 passenger movements in the 12 months to June 30, eclipsing the previous year's record of 458,876 passengers.

"Based on the airport figures, I am very optimistic we're going to see a population increase," Mr Wilson said.

FIFO workers on the tarmac at Karratha Airport.   (ABC News: Cody Fenner)

The FIFO workforce has been a long-term feature of the iron ore heartland of WA's Pilbara, where the 2021 census put the population at 82,000.

But Regional Development Australia's Pilbara chief executive Daiva Gillam said infrastructure was struggling to meet the needs of the local and FIFO population.

"I'm going to give you a real world example," she said.

"The Shire of East Pilbara in Newman are spending over $50 million of their own money to upgrade the wastewater treatment plant because it can't cope.

"For every person in Newman that lives there, there are up to three FIFOs all flushing the toilet in the East Pilbara.

"The infrastructure is not built to cope, but those workers aren't usually counted in the Pilbara as being residents."

Newman sits in WA's east Pilbara region.     (ABC Pilbara: Charlie McLean)

Robert Powell is on a two and one roster, working two weeks in Port Hedland as a grounds person at a camp and spending the week off in Perth.

Despite spending more time up north, he will list his Perth home as his primary residence.

"Home is home, work is work, and it needs to be reflected that way in the census," he said.

"It's, to me, no different to saying I live in Armadale and work in Welshpool. It's where I live, it's where I want the services provided."

He suggested adding more questions to the census would help properly account for the FIFO workforce.

Workers leave a FIFO flight at Karratha Airport. (ABC News: Cody Fenner)

Census spokesperson Emily Walter said FIFO workers were similar to seasonal farm workers who can be a challenging demographic to collect data on.

She said the ABS had employed a dedicated team to coordinate with mine sites to enable workers to complete the census in the most accurate way.

"The census creates a snapshot at a point in time, like taking a photograph," she said.

"FIFO workers are often in a location for several days or weeks at a time, and the concept of a usual residence is one that we use to capture where someone is for more than six months of the year.

"If they are spending more than six months of the year at the location where they work, then they need to use that as their usual residence.

"That 'usual residence' concept is something that is really important for how we understand the data, and an internationally comparable definition."

Organisational psychiatrist Cheryl Yam said the question ran deeper than data for affected FIFO workers.

"The question isn't simply 'where do I sleep most nights?' It's more where do I belong?" she said.

Cities like Kalgoorlie previously relied on a chiefly residential workforce, but the FIFO population is growing. (ABC News: Erin Parke)

"The camp really isn't necessarily home, but it's also more than just a workplace; because it's where they spend much of their day-to-day life."

Dr Yam said workers often felt the remote camp was where they stayed and home being where they lived.

Officials understand the sentiment, but say the workforce and infrastructure pressures across regional Australia meant every worker needed to be accurately counted.

In keeping with that growth theme, Ms Gillam said it was vital for regional areas that every worker was counted.

"Nobody wants to say that they live where they work," she said.

"But for the purpose of the census only, if you're here for six months, yeah, this is where you live."

The census data is scheduled to be released in June 2027.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 10:54pm

The man was found unconscious with critical head injuries on a Bahrs Scrub street by police on July 26 after reports of an out-of-control house party nearby.   (Supplied)

Four more teenagers have been charged with murder after a 21-year-old died days after an alleged assault in Logan, south of Brisbane, late last month.

Eight people have now been charged with murdering the Redbank Plains man.

He was found unconscious with critical head injuries on Orchard Avenue at Bahrs Scrub by police on July 26 after reports of an out-of-control house party on Discovery Boulevard.

He was taken to hospital but died on August 1 from his injuries.

Four teenagers — three 18-year-olds and a 17-year-old — were arrested at Morayfield on Sunday and are due to face court today.

A total of nine people have now been charged in relation to the death.

On Thursday, three teenagers — Joshua Jackson John Jirima, 18, Amnaud Nduwayo, 19 and Kandour Khalil Tagelsir, 18 — were charged with murder.

A fourth — Sunday Obol, 19 — was charged with murder, intimidation, harassing or abuse, unlawful stalking, robbery, extortion, and deprivation of liberty.

A 22-year-old was charged with contravening an order to provide information necessary to access electronically stored information.

Police thanked the community for "significant cooperation" with the investigation, particularly "residents, community leaders and representatives who have worked with investigators and encouraged members of the community to come forward with information".

https://www.dw.com/en/netanyahu-says-isr.title: Netanyahu says Israel rejects Trump’s Gaza peace plan
https://www.dw.com/en/netanyahu-says-isr.text:
The Israeli prime minister says his country will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas fully disarms, putting him at odds with a US-backed roadmap endorsed by the group.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday rejected US President Donald Trump's plan for Gaza, saying Israeli troops would not withdraw from the territory until Hamas was fully disarmed.

"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu told a Cabinet meeting, referring to the US-backed roadmap agreed to by Hamas in late July.

The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed," Netanyahu said, adding that this included "heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Netanyahu said Israel remained in talks with Washington despite its objections. He described Trump as "our greatest friend in the White House," but added: "They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters."

The White House did not immediately comment.

Trump announced last month that there had been a breakthrough on a 15-point roadmap aimed at ending the war in the Gaza Strip.

The plan drawn up by his Board of Peace calls for Israeli troops to withdraw as Hamas gives up its weapons. An International Stabilization Force would then work alongside a new Palestinian police force to secure Gaza.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hamas is designated as a terrorist organization by Israel, the United States, the European Union and several other countries.

The group has avoided using the term "disarmament." It says it agreed to hand over its weapons for storage under a US-backed Palestinian technocratic administration that would govern Gaza under the supervision of the Board of Peace.

Hamas has said implementation also depends on Israel meeting its obligations, including withdrawing troops and halting attacks.

"We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap, and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons," Hamas political bureau member Bassem Naim said.

Hamas said Sunday it remained committed to the roadmap.

Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace's high representative for Gaza, said Israel would face no obligations until Hamas had surrendered all its weapons, including assault rifles.

However, Mladenov told Israel's Channel 12 that Israeli troops would eventually have to withdraw "sector by sector" once Hamas' weapons had been collected and rendered unusable.

"The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again," he said, referring to the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, which triggered the war against Hamas in the Gaza Strip.

Mladenov said discussions with Israel were continuing and that he hoped for a "positive outcome."

The disagreement comes at a politically sensitive moment for Netanyahu ahead of elections scheduled for October 27, Israel's first national vote since the Hamas led attacks that sparked an ongoing Israeli military campaign in Gaza.

The prime minister is running level with or behind rivals in some polls and faces pressure from far-right members of his government who oppose concessions to Hamas.

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich welcomed Netanyahu's position.

"We went to war with a central goal: the destruction of Hamas," he said. "The [military] cannot withdraw even a millimetre from the Gaza Strip."

The dispute is the latest sign of differences between Netanyahu and Trump. The two leaders are considered as close allies, but have recently disagreed over how to deal with the conflicts in Iran, Lebanon and Gaza.

The Gaza roadmap builds on a US-mediated ceasefire reached in October 2025.

Gaza health officials say more than 1,250 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since then. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed during the same period.

Despite the ongoing negotiations over the roadmap, Israeli forces continue to control large parts of Gaza, while most of the enclave's more than 2 million residents have been displaced and are living in a much smaller coastal area, many in tents or damaged buildings.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c20d.title: 'Not afraid to stay': The Canadians taking fighting wildfires into their own hands
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c20d.text:
When a wildfire broke out near his First Nation community in northern Ontario, Hubert Wigwas decided to stay put.

He put sprinklers on his roof to extinguish falling embers. He checked on elders in his community who also stayed behind, and he fuelled up four boats down on the lake in case they needed a quick escape.

"This is everything I've built in my 58 years," Wigwas, a councillor from Gull Bay First Nation, told the BBC. "I'm just not going to run away and let it burn."

Canada has seen some of its worst fire seasons in recent years, and experienced its most destructive on record in 2023, when blazes tore through forest land roughly the size of Syria. As of this August, more than 750 wildfires are actively burning across the country.

The impact has been felt as far as the US Midwest, where smoke had choked the air in cities. Even President Donald Trump has taken note, threatening to further tariff Canada for allowing "filthy, polluted" air to waft south of the border.

The intensifying wildfires have sparked a national conversation: Are there enough firefighters to battle these more challenging fire seasons? What happens when resources are stretched too thin? And how can remote communities, often closest to danger because of their proximity to Canada's vast boreal forest, learn to live with this new reality?

Wigwas asked himself these questions when he decided to stay, even as he faces a fine of around C$800 ($570; £425) for defying evacuation orders.

Leaders of Gull Bay First Nation, also known as Kiashke Zaaging Anishinaabek, have been urging residents to stay away since mid-July as more than 150 wildfires burn across Ontario's northwest.

Its chief penned a letter on 29 July pleading with those who have remained to leave immediately, saying that Ontario firefighters cannot do their jobs safely with people still in their homes.

It is the same message officials across the country have been conveying in British Columbia, where around 115 fires are currently burning.

But with a wildfire 24km outside his community, Wigwas, speaking in late July, said he had yet to see fire personnel from out of town there to help fireproof properties or keep an eye out on the elders who remained.

He said it made him realise that his First Nation would benefit from setting up its own wildfire emergency response and teaching residents how to protect their own homes.

"Everybody talks about climate change, but nobody is doing something to unite the (First Nations) reserves and have a system like that set up," Wigwas said.

Dave Bradley, a spokesperson for Ontario's ministry of natural resources, did not address Wigwas' claim directly, but said the province has been in "constant contact" with First Nations leaders.

He added that fire fighting resources are directed based on "fire behaviour, weather conditions and risks to communities."

In the west-coast province of British Columbia - long the front line of Canada's wildfire response - people are doing just what Wigwas is envisioning for his First Nation, with efforts underway to train residents of rural and remote communities how to safely respond to wildfires before out-of-town crews can arrive.

Sonja Leverkus, a wildfire researcher and specialist, said she has helped train more than 400 people in and around her community of Fort Nelson over the last three years through a firefighting group she helped start called the Northeast BC Rural Incident Management Team.

She told the BBC that her efforts are inspired by a realisation that Canada needs to change how it fights wildfires as climate change increases their frequency and intensity.

"There are not enough human beings in Canada," she said, with the appropriate training, "to fight the fires that we have currently, especially over the last five years".

Remote communities, where the nearest town might be hundreds of kilometres away, can sometimes be bumped down the priority list for BC firefighting crews if there are blazes threatening more populated areas, she said.

Her crew, who are primarily indigenous, have carried out prescribed burns, also known as a hazard reduction burns – a practice of setting planned, controlled blazes to remove fuels that could contribute to wildfires.

They have also helped put out smaller fires before they grow out of control using fire wagons that they purchased through fundraising and grants, sometimes arriving ahead of provincial firecrews and then working in tandem with them, Leverkus said.

When a major wildfire tore through Fort Nelson in 2024, she said she and 40 of her team members stayed behind and were hired by the province to clear flammables and support fire suppression activities.

Leverkus also organised a structural protection training course for locals to learn how to shield buildings from embers that can quickly spur fires that engulf entire towns.

"We have mechanics, we have carpenters, we have real good problem solvers," Leverkus said. "We're all not afraid to stay."

Cam Allen, a 70-year-old former helicopter pilot in Fort Nelson who has previously fought fires from the air, said he recently took Leverkus' course to learn about ground fire suppression techniques, and, more broadly, how to help if a blaze reaches his town.

He mentioned John Carr, a California man who went viral last year for staying behind and warding off flames with a garden hose during the Palisades fire, ultimately saving his home even when others around it burned down.

"It makes you wonder, if 100 people had stayed or 1,000 people had stayed behind and actually did what he did, how much more could have been saved?" Allen asked.

But not all were as fortunate as Carr during the Los Angeles fires, which killed a total of 29 people – a few of whom had, too, defied evacuation orders in order to protect their homes, even as officials urged thousands in the area to leave.

Leverkus' group is not officially recognised by BC's government, and what it is trying to achieve highlights simmering tensions in fire-prone regions between those who enforce evacuation orders and those who defy them.

Last week, wildfire crews in BC were forced to rescue a man when his home in the Village of Clinton was surrounded by flames, after he had refused to evacuate.

In a wildfire update on Tuesday, BC's minister responsible for emergency management reiterated that all those who are under evacuation orders should leave.

"We may not be able to get back to you if an emergency happens," warned Minister Kelly Greene, adding that evacuation orders are made as "a last resort to keep people and communities safe".

Paul Kovacs, a researcher at the University of Western Ontario and director of its Catastrophic Loss Reduction Institute, said that Canada has had a lower fatality rate from wildfires despite their frequency in part because of its evacuation approach.

The stay and defend mindset, he said, "is aggressively opposed" by the academic community in Canada, as opposed to other fire-prone countries like Australia.

"In the hierarchy of what is it that you do to manage a wildfire, preservation of life is first," Kovacs said.

Rural and remote communities can and should play an outsized role in informing officials of how best to protect their town, he said, and can do a lot of work to fire proof homes and structures. But that work, he argued, should not be done "while the fire is burning."

A spokesperson for BC's Ministry of Forests told the BBC that self-organised groups in rural areas can be hired temporarily by the province during an active wildfire, but only when there are no more available provincial firefighters in the area.

The ministry added that BC Wildfire's full-time staff has increased by 56% in recent years to respond to the growing frequency of fires, in addition to seasonal staff.

Leverkus said she has been exploring ways to have her programme recognised by BC officials so that those trained through it can also help without being penalised for staying behind.

She added that safety precautions are engrained in her courses, including training on how to predict fire behaviour and mapping out at least two safe escape routes.

Not all of those who are trained want to stay back, she said, but those that do receive orders from trained crew commanders, including on when it's time to leave.

"If people want to stay and defend, they need to understand what that means for themselves, what that means for their family," Leverkus said.

Her goal is for the programme to one day become a blueprint that can be adopted by rural and remote communities across Canada, creating teams that can be relied on across the country.

As for Wigwas, he will be fighting his evacuation fine in court.

"If the chief and council want to charge me for saving my house, and I end up with nowhere to live, I might as well be in jail," he said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c20d.summary: More than 750 wildfires are burning across Canada this summer, with more than 750 burning. Canada has seen some of its worst fire seasons in recent years, and experienced its most destructive on record in 2023. The impact has been felt as far as the US Midwest, where smoke had choked the air in cities.

https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/a.title: Cut £175 from energy bills for low-income homes, says thinktank
https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/a.author: Heather Stewart Economics editor
https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/a.text:
Resolution Foundation proposes £2bn emergency scheme to help people facing higher costs this winter

Labour should draw up an emergency plan to cut energy prices for low-income families by up to £175 this winter, the Resolution Foundation has said.

One of Andy Burnham’s first policy announcements as prime minister was to remove VAT temporarily from electricity bills, saving households about £45 a year.

But with wholesale gas prices higher since the resumption of hostilities in the Middle East, the thinktank says costs are likely to rise through the winter.

In a report, the Resolution Foundation recommends a scheme that would cut annual bills by up to £175 for poorer consumers, at a cost of £2bn to the taxpayer. Support would be restricted to households where the highest earner is taking home £24,000 a year or less.

By helping 40% of households, the proposal would be more generous – but harder to implement – than one that targeted only those in receipt of means-tested benefits.

Jonathan Marshall, principal economist at the foundation and co-author of the report, said: “The government can get ahead of this, if it acts now. A targeted energy discount could save eligible households £175 a year and reach more than four-fifths of the poorest families, while expanding support beyond just those on means-tested benefits.”

He suggested ministers should have a plan ready to be “switched on” in January next year, when the quarterly energy cap is adjusted. It could either offer a flat rate £175 discount or additional help to the lowest-income households.

Burnham begins a tour of Britain on Monday, pledging to provide “everyday fixes” for rising bills. Officials say he intends to spend much of the rest of August travelling the country asking the public how the government can improve their lives with a focus on weekly bills and the decline of high streets.

A survey by the charity Carnegie UK has found that 28% of UK households say they cannot afford an emergency £850 payment. Another 6% say they cannot afford enough food for everyone in their home and 12% say they cannot afford to socialise at least once a month.

Thinktanks have long called for better coordination between Whitehall and energy companies to deliver targeted help with energy costs. “Successive governments have failed to build a robust system for dealing with household energy prices,” Marshall said.

The government spent £44bn during the 2022 energy crisis on subsidising bills for all households, including the wealthiest.

The foundation’s report shows that households in the poorest areas cut back on their energy use by 15% more than those in wealthier postcodes over that period. It says that only one-sixth of this fall in consumption had been reversed, suggesting that these households are still heating their homes less than is comfortable.

A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “The energy secretary’s focus is bringing bills down for good. We will tackle the cost of living to make life’s essentials affordable again and bring back hope.”

Sign up to Headlines UK

Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning

after newsletter promotion

The chancellor, John Healey, has said tackling the cost of living would be a priority ahead of his first budget, scheduled for 25 October.

As well as setting out how the government plans to fund Burnham’s policies, including cutting VAT on energy, the budget is expected to detail how tax revenues will be distributed to regional mayors.

Healey resigned as defence secretary in June in protest at the failure of Keir Starmer and his chancellor, Rachel Reeves, to fund a significant uplift in his department’s budget.

He is likely to face pressure to explain how he hopes to fund a promise to spend 3% of GDP on defence over the next parliament – let alone the Nato target of 3.5%, which Starmer said would be reached by 2035.

Burnham has suggested he would like to exploit “flexibilities” in the fiscal rules set out by Reeves, to allow for additional borrowing to invest in infrastructure projects, to pursue his goal of “good growth in every postcode”.

Reeves, who was Britain’s first female chancellor, returned to the backbenches last month when Burnham arrived in No 10.

Support would be restricted to households where highest earner is taking home £24,000 a year or less.

https://fortune.com/2026/08/09/porter-ai.title: An airline had to cancel a flight and rebook passengers for the next day because a child refused to sit down and buckle up
https://fortune.com/2026/08/09/porter-ai.author: The Associated Press
https://fortune.com/2026/08/09/porter-ai.text:
A Porter Airlines flight in Canada was canceled last week after a young child refused to sit down and buckle up, forcing the plane back to the terminal and delaying it past the airport’s runway closure.

The Toronto-based airline said Sunday the parent and crew repeatedly tried unsuccessfully to secure the child in the seat before returning the plane to the terminal in Victoria International Airport in British Columbia to remove the parent and child.

Porter said removing the parent and child and their baggage delayed the Toronto-bound flight on Thursday past the airport’s 12:30 a.m. runway closure, forcing the remaining passengers to disembark.

Porter apologized to the other passengers, who were rebooked on a flight the following day.

https://fortune.com/2026/08/09/trump-whi.title: Trump’s new White House counsel headed the commission that secured his $400 million ballroom project
https://fortune.com/2026/08/09/trump-whi.author: The Associated Press
https://fortune.com/2026/08/09/trump-whi.text:
President Donald Trump announced Sunday that his new White House counsel will be Will Scharf, the staff secretary who as the Trump-appointed head of the National Capital Planning Commission helped secure approval for the $400 million ballroom project.

Trump said that, beginning Sept. 1, Scharf will be replacing David Warrington, who will be leaving the administration to join the private sector. Trump noted that Scharf previously served as a federal prosecutor and represented him in a number of cases, including at the Supreme Court.

“Will is Tough, Strong, and Smart! He also loves our Country, and respects the Law,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Will Scharf will do a great job as White House Counsel!”

The shakeup in the White House counsel’s office comes at a critical juncture — just months ahead of the midterm elections, where Trump’s Republican Party will be fighting to hold on to control of Congress. Democrats have vowed to pursue investigations into Trump and his administration if they are successful in November.

The White House counsel’s job is to advise on legal and policy questions related to the presidency. The office is the primary White House contact for the Justice Department, and it handles presidential pardons, works on judicial appointments and reviews legislation. The office also helps investigate and manage congressional investigations into the administration and lawsuits against the president when he is sued in his official capacity.

Trump in July 2025 had named Scharf as chair of the National Capital Planning Commission, the executive branch agency with jurisdiction over construction and major renovations to government buildings in the region.

Trump’s ballroom won final approval from the NCPC in April, though a divided federal appeals court ruled Friday that construction on the project must stop because Congress had not approved it. Trump has vowed to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.

The project is already well on its way and has begun to rise above ground on the east side of the White House.

The Blue Heeler Hotel is the only pub in the town of Kynuna, with a population of 50 people. (Supplied: The Blue Heeler Hotel)

Police have arrested a man following reports of a shot fired in Kynuna last night.

At 7:50pm, police were called to the Landsborough Highway to reports a shot had been fired at a passing vehicle.

Prior to police arrival, a motorist located a stationary Toyota Hilux in the centre of the highway and a firearm.

The motorist collected the firearm and continued on the highway to meet attending officers, where it was passed over.

Officers then attended the vehicle and located a 19-year-old man near the highway.

He was taken into custody and is assisting police with inquiries.

No-one was physically injured during the incident.

The town of Kynuna is 300 kilometres south of Mount Isa and has a population of just over 50 people.

Officers are appealing to anyone with relevant information or dash cam footage to contact police.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.title: The AFLW season opener was a double-header. Here's what fans thought
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.author: Marnie Vinall
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 11:14pm

Carlton starts its season well with a comfortable win over St Kilda at Docklands. (Getty: Morgan Hancock)

As young Carlton star Poppy Scholz launched the ball into the stands at Docklands Stadium to kick the first goal of the 2026 AFLW season, fans were asking each other: "What do you think this crowd is?'"

The Blues were playing against St Kilda in the season opener in one of five double-headers between the men's and women's competitions this season.

Players, clubs and fans have been calling for regular double-headers to be introduced by the AFL to help grow the women's game.

This was in a bid to increase exposure of the women's game, try to adopt more fans across, give a unified club identity (one club, two teams approach) and allow the women to play on better conditions to allow for a better product.

St Kilda puts up a late challenge against Carlton but the Blues never give up their lead. (Getty: Morgan Hancock)

By half-time on Sunday evening there were 11,000 people in the crowd, 2,000 more than the sold-out Australia vs Ireland game at North Sydney Oval a week earlier.

Halfway through the final quarter, that number had ballooned to 20,455.

For St Kilda veteran and former captain Hannah Priest, they gave "a nice unity for an all-club approach".

"I look at the idea of all of your teams playing on the same day and celebrating each other," she told ABC Sport, acknowledging that a lot of club staff worked across both the men's and women's programs.

"To open the season at [Docklands] is a testament to every single AFLW supporter who has advocated for this sort of growth, and everyone who's been on board since the start. It's a celebration for all of us."

Carlton has held off a St Kilda fightback to claim the opening win of the new AFLW season by 26 points in an entertaining game that made a case for more double header fixtures.

Across the stadium and fan sections, fans enjoyed the pizzazz of the bigger stadium, crowd noise and being sheltered from the rain.

However, there were also some who missed the community element of the suburban grounds and felt like AFLW was the main event.

Carlton AFLW fan Asha Ziffer, who has a membership for the women's team but not the men's, said she probably wouldn't have gone to the double-header had it not been the opener.

"I've got a lot of mixed feelings about it, but I don't think that this showcases it as it should be," Ziffer told ABC Sport.

"I think that it is presenting it as second to the men's game, and certainly for a season opener, W should be the focus."

There were 20,455 in the last quarter of the AFLW opener between St Kilda and Carlton. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

Ziffer said her 14-year-old daughter, Lily, said "it's like when you go to a concert and there's a support act that only half the people come to and then there's the main event".

"I think even if a 14-year-old can identify that, then it does say something more broadly to the community about where the women's game sits," Ziffer said, during the third quarter.

"Look, it's great and the game is going our way, which is great, even better. But it does feel, because it's such a big venue, I think 11,000 turnout is great but it just doesn't feel like a big crowd because the venue is so big. And you know, I'm sure it's a great ground for them to play on. And you know, it's nice to have a roof over our heads, given the weather's average."

Long time AFLW St Kilda fan Shae Williams said although her side didn't come away with the win, she hoped the team left the evening with a few more fans.

"It was exciting walking in and the thought of W starting … [although it] felt weird not being in a more intimate setting like Moorabbin.

"Twenty thousand attendance was a great result [and a] good experience for the players to play on a bigger stage," Williams told ABC Sport.

"The idea of double-headers are great, [although] I understand the need for W to have its own space as well."

Carlton won its opening match against St Kilda at Docklands. (Getty: Morgan Hancock)

Another Saints supporter, Dylan Cross, who got into both the games with his men's and women's membership, was pleased with the early turnout for the women's game.

"I heard a few people comment around me that haven't watched much women's footy that it was better than they expected," Cross told ABC Sport.

"So, hopefully it [double-headers] grow the game.

"I will say personally I still prefer the AFLW games at smaller grounds like Ikon or Moorabbin due to the more local footy vibes and that it's so family friendly. The crowd felt a bit reserved tonight.

"But all in all, I think it was a success and hopefully we see more double-headers in the future."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
Iran said it was nearing a final pact with Oman defining new shipping lanes between them through the Strait of Hormuz but repeated that the U.S. must meet other conditions, including compensation and an end to sanctions and military threats, before the strategic waterway is reopened.

A U.S. official said on Friday that Iran and Oman were close to a deal that could pave the way for restoring safe passage through the strait, a ​major conduit for oil and gas shipping before Iran blocked Hormuz in response to U.S. and Israeli attacks on Tehran that began in late February. Iranian ‌Foreign Minister ‌Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday an agreement with Oman on the strait was in its “final stages” but reiterated comments made ​on Saturday that Tehran would not reopen the channel unless the U.S. met certain demands made by Tehran.

The deal with Iran would set out the new shipping lanes to be used once the U.S. fulfills those conditions and the strait is reopened, Iran’s Mehr news agency quoted him as saying.

Iran and ⁠the U.S. are not engaged in direct talks, and Tehran will not start them as long as Washington breaches an interim deal signed in June, Araqchi said, adding ⁠that messages were being exchanged through intermediaries.

U.S. President Donald Trump said in an interview with Axios that the U.S. was “low-keying” it with Iran. “We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money.”

Araqchi said reopening the strait would depend in part ⁠on the U.S. paying compensation for damage it caused in widespread attacks on Iran. The secretary of Iran’s top national security body, Mohammad Baqer Zolqadr, also listed ending further U.S. threats against Iran; halting aggression toward Iran and its ⁠Lebanese, Palestinian, Yemeni and Iraqi allies; removing ​a U.S. naval blockade in the Gulf; lifting sanctions on Iran; and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

The United ​States and Israel launched air strikes on Iran more than five months ago. Trump has said the attacks were aimed at keeping ​the Islamic Republic ‌from developing nuclear weapons and degrading its ability to threaten the region. Washington and Tehran agreed to a ceasefire in June, but the U.S. reimposed a blockade on Iranian shipping in the Gulf in July, a move that Tehran said violated the truce, which by then had already broken down.

“Once the deal is announced to restore commercial shipping without impediments, the United States will lift the blockade of Iranian ports,” the U.S. ‌official said on condition of anonymity.

U.S. actions would be tied to Iran’s implementation of its commitments, the official said. The U.S. comments indicated delicate sequencing toward a deal that sources said appeared to be set to give Tehran control over vessel traffic entering the Gulf through the strait, which shippers have said was not easily workable. The United Arab Emirates said on Saturday that Iran had attacked a ship affiliated with its state oil company. There was no immediate comment from Iran, whose ​Revolutionary ​Guard Corps previously has attacked ships that it said tried to cross the strait without Iranian permission.

Iranian ​strikes on Strait of Hormuz shipping have been coupled with increased attacks by its Yemen-based allies, the Houthi rebels, who have targeted ships at another oil chokepoint on ⁠the other side of the Arabian Peninsula between the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

The Houthis also declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea last month in response to what they said was a Saudi siege on them in Yemen, an allegation denied by Riyadh, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognized government. The Yemeni rebel group said they had attacked Saudi Aramco’s Jazan refinery on Sunday, two days after the ​kingdom signed a defense pact with Sunni Muslim allies Turkey and Pakistan in response to growing regional instability from the U.S.-Israeli war on Shi’ite Iran. The Saudi energy ministry said a fire had broken out at the refinery but was later extinguished with no injuries and authorities were dealing with the incident, without giving a cause.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said the new alliance was not directed against Iran or any other country, but rather served as a general pledge to support security.
