https://www.dw.com/en/netanyahu-rejects-.text:
The Israeli prime minister says his country will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas fully disarms, putting him at odds with a US-backed roadmap endorsed by the group.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday rejected US President Donald Trump's plan for Gaza, saying Israeli troops would not withdraw from the territory until Hamas was fully disarmed.

"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu told a Cabinet meeting, referring to the US-backed roadmap agreed to by Hamas in late July.

The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed," Netanyahu said, adding that this included "heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Netanyahu said Israel remained in talks with Washington despite its objections. He described Trump as "our greatest friend in the White House," but added: "They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters."

The White House did not immediately comment.

Trump announced last month that there had been a breakthrough on a 15-point roadmap aimed at ending the war in the Gaza Strip.

The plan drawn up by his Board of Peace calls for Israeli troops to withdraw as Hamas gives up its weapons. An International Stabilization Force would then work alongside a new Palestinian police force to secure Gaza.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hamas is designated as a terrorist organization by Israel, the United States, the European Union and several other countries.

The group has avoided using the term "disarmament." It says it agreed to hand over its weapons for storage under a US-backed Palestinian technocratic administration that would govern Gaza under the supervision of the Board of Peace.

Hamas has said implementation also depends on Israel meeting its obligations, including withdrawing troops and halting attacks.

"We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap, and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons," Hamas political bureau member Bassem Naim said.

Hamas said Sunday it remained committed to the roadmap.

Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace's high representative for Gaza, said Israel would face no obligations until Hamas had surrendered all its weapons, including assault rifles.

However, Mladenov told Israel's Channel 12 that Israeli troops would eventually have to withdraw "sector by sector" once Hamas' weapons had been collected and rendered unusable.

"The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again," he said, referring to the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, which triggered the war against Hamas in the Gaza Strip.

Mladenov said discussions with Israel were continuing and that he hoped for a "positive outcome."

The disagreement comes at a politically sensitive moment for Netanyahu ahead of elections scheduled for October 27, Israel's first national vote since the Hamas led attacks that sparked an ongoing Israeli military campaign in Gaza.

The prime minister is running level with or behind rivals in some polls and faces pressure from far-right members of his government who oppose concessions to Hamas.

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich welcomed Netanyahu's position.

"We went to war with a central goal: the destruction of Hamas," he said. "The [military] cannot withdraw even a millimetre from the Gaza Strip."

The dispute is the latest sign of differences between Netanyahu and Trump. The two leaders are considered as close allies, but have recently disagreed over how to deal with the conflicts in Iran, Lebanon and Gaza.

The Gaza roadmap builds on a US-mediated ceasefire reached in October 2025.

Gaza health officials say more than 1,250 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since then. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed during the same period.

Despite the ongoing negotiations over the roadmap, Israeli forces continue to control large parts of Gaza, while most of the enclave's more than 2 million residents have been displaced and are living in a much smaller coastal area, many in tents or damaged buildings.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czjl.title: You could be missing out on £150 off your energy bill - here's how to check
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czjl.text:
One call to your energy supplier to ensure your name is on the electricity bill may mean you are in line for a £150 discount this winter – but you need to get in before the deadline.

While the cost of heating your home might not be at the forefront of your mind during the long, hot summer prices are set to rise again this winter.

Suppliers use customers' records as of Sunday 23 August to check who is eligible for the Warm Home Discount.

The government scheme knocks £150 off bills if you are on means-tested benefits such as universal credit.

Millions of people will learn of the level of winter energy prices later this month, when Ofgem announces the quarterly price cap for the three months from October.

To help those who might struggle to pay, energy companies distribute the £150 Warm Home Discount to about six million households in the winter. Households in receipt of housing benefit, income-related Employment and Support Allowance, Pension Credit and universal credit qualify.

Households who are eligible should get the discount automatically, provided their supplier has over 1,000 customers.

However, that only happens if your name is on the bill and you are receiving one of these benefits. It can also help suppliers offer better support, such as repayment plans, to those who have energy debt.

Someone might not be named on their electricity bill if they have recently moved house.

Eligible customers on pre-payment meters who use a key or card to top up will also need to ensure that their household's account is registered in their name.

"If you know someone who might benefit, please start spreading the word and encourage them to check they are named on their energy bill," said Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

The government also said that 345,000 Scottish low-income households would now automatically receive the rebate in the winter, bringing Scotland's policy in line with England and Wales.

Previously, eligible Scottish households have had to apply for the scheme.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/s.title: NSW Police forced to reopen investigation into Sydney gay club drug raids
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/s.author: Alexander Lewis
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Mon 10 Aug 2026 at 12:06am

Mon 10 Aug 2026 at 12:11am

Police were accused of aggression and carrying out "humiliating" searches on club-goers at LGBTQIA+ venues. (Supplied)

The police watchdog has forced NSW Police to reopen a misconduct investigation into drug dog raids in Sydney LGBTQIA+ venues.

Sydney Lord Mayor Clover Moore and Sydney MP Alex Greenwich say they have been inundated with reports that police shoved patrons.

An initial internal police review did not find any evidence of misconduct or policy breaches by officers involved.

Police have been forced to reopen a misconduct investigation over drug dog raids on several Sydney LGBTQIA+ venues after an initial probe cleared officers of wrongdoing, the ABC can reveal.

Club-goers were allegedly pushed against walls and forced to strip in public as police led sniffer dogs through venues on and near Oxford Street on June 13 in the middle of Pride Month.

Complaints by Sydney MP Alex Greenwich and Sydney Lord Mayor Clover Moore prompted an internal police review, which last month concluded "no further investigation was warranted".

"The assessment did not identify any evidence of misconduct, unlawful conduct, or breaches of NSW Police Force policy by the officers involved," professional standards manager Inspector Michael Butcher said in a letter.

Club-goers reported being shoved, pushed against walls, and forced to remove clothing in full public view. (ABC News: Jak Rowland)

In the correspondence to Mr Greenwich and Cr Moore, Inspector Butcher said police had reviewed body-worn video footage, CCTV footage, police records and witness accounts.

"The operation was conducted in accordance with applicable NSW Police Force policies and procedures," he said.

"As a result, no further action will be taken in relation to this matter."

But the police watchdog, the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission (LECC), has decided to pull rank and use its power to force a probe.

"The [LECC] has conducted its own assessment and disagrees with the NSW Police Force's decision not to investigate your complaint," LECC Commissioner Anina Johnson said in a letter last week.

"The commission has invoked our statutory powers and directed the NSW Police Force to investigate the matter."

The incidents occurred in the middle of Pride Month. (ABC News: Jak Rowland)

The LECC would review the police investigation, Ms Johnson said, and consider whether any further action was needed.

Mr Greenwich told the ABC he welcomed the LECC's decision to overrule the police assessment and require a full investigation.

"This investigation is an important step towards transparency, accountability and rebuilding trust between police and our community."

The NSW Police Force has been contacted for comment, while the LECC said it was unable to comment.

Mr Greewich has welcomed the LECC investigation, saying it is about transparency. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

In his letter, Inspector Butcher said the decision to target the Oxford Street entertainment precinct "formed part of broader strategies aimed at reducing risks to public safety associated with possession, supply and use of prohibited drugs".

He said deployments were informed by intelligence, emerging drug trends, overdoses and fatalities, patterns of drug and alcohol-related offending, and offending within and near licensed premises.

In the aftermath of the operation, police said 93 people were searched, 42 drug detections made, and one person charged with supply.

Police said 93 people were searched. (Supplied)

In their complaint to the LECC, Mr Greenwich and Cr Moore said they had been inundated with reports from locals, many of whom were out celebrating Pride Month.

"Large groups of between six and 12 officers with drug detection dogs descended on the precinct, saturating venues and intimidating people trying to enjoy their night," they said in a letter.

78er Rebbell Barnes, who witnessed a raid at Kinselas, said it brought back memories of the first Mardi Gras parade, which ended in violence at the hands of police.

The raids sparked debate in state parliament, with Greens MLC Cate Faehrmann accusing the police of "killing Sydney's nightlife".

The furore also led to 78er and historian Garry Wotherspoon quitting the LGBTQIA+ Consultative Committee, which was set up to promote a better relationship between police and the rainbow community.

Sun 9 Aug 2026 at 11:53pm

Cairns community mourns Savannah Spence Paige. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

Dozens of people gathered at Fogarty Park in memory of  Savannah Spence Paige on Sunday night.

Ms Spence Paige died when her car was hit on the Smithfield Bypass on Wednesday, August 5 by a ute allegedly stolen from Palm Cove minutes earlier.

Community is calling for more action to make roads safer for everyone.

A 25-year-old woman who was killed in a multi-vehicle crash, allegedly caused by a man driving a stolen car, has been remembered at a community vigil held in Cairns in Far North Queensland.

Savannah Spece Paige died when her car was hit on the Smithfield Bypass on Wednesday, August 5 by a ute allegedly stolen from Palm Cove minutes earlier.

The late Savannah Spence and her husband Lachie Paige. (Supplied)

Yesterday night, dozens of people gathered at Fogarty Park in memory of Ms Spence Paige, a Kewarra Beach resident.

Community members have came together to light candles for Savannah Spence Paige. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

As the sun set, family and friends sat at the front of the crowd as candles were lit around a photo of the woman.

Shinae West organised the vigil after feeling the community needed to come together. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

Vigil organiser Shinae West said she wanted to give the community a place to grieve together after the Ms Spence Paige's death.

"In honour of her life, and Cairns getting together and grieving together with the family, is really what it's about," Ms West said.

She said Ms Spence Paige's death "hit home" because her own family had experienced a similar tragedy almost a decade ago.

"My brother was killed in a car accident in 2007. It could've been avoided really," Ms West said.

Jake Edward Warn, 36, has been charged with manslaughter and four other offences over the crash.

He remains in custody ahead of his next hearing in October.

But police prosecutors have flagged they may ask for the charge to be upgraded to murder.

Ms Spence Paige's husband Lachlan attended the vigil alongside other family and friends. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

In the days after the crash, police described Ms Spence Paige's death as devastating for the whole community.

The crash happened on a newer section of the Captain Cook Highway. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

In a statement, her family has since thanked locals for the outpouring of support, saying they were touched by plans for the vigil.

They described Ms Spence Paige as someone with an incredible sense of humour and a kind and caring heart.

Forensic marks remained on the northbound lane of the Smithfield Bypass the day following the fatal multiple-vehicle crash. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

The statement said she had only recently started a new life with her husband in Cairns.

Jenna Shingles said the crash had shaken her, and she attended to show support for the family.

"Our daughter is 17, and driving, and she just drove [the Smithfield Bypass] to have lunch with me half an hour beforehand," she said.

"It could have been anyone."

The road and verge of the Smithfield Bypass are still littered with debris following the fatal crash. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

Alicia Clark said the crash was "close to our hearts".

Leonie and Mark Bowen say they came down to support the family. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

Leonie Bowen said she felt compelled to attend the vigil.

"I think there's a lot of people here that are just here to say we care — there's not ... much else we can say," she said.

"Just to let the husband and the family know that the whole Cairns community is supporting them.

"They're not alone. It's so very sad."

Savannah Spence Paige and her husband Lachlan lived in the Cairns northern beaches. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

An online fundraising attempt set up since the crash has so far raised more than $60,000, from hundreds of donors, toward helping Ms Spence Paige's husband Lachlan cover expenses.

Flowers on the verge adjacent to the northbound lane of the Smithfield Bypass where Savannnah Spence Paige died last week. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Yemen’s Houthis attack Saudi refinery after kingdom signs defense pact
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis have attacked Saudi Aramco’s Jazan refinery, they said on Sunday, two days after the kingdom signed a defense pact with Turkey and Pakistan in response to growing regional instability from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.

The alliance with Sunni Muslim U.S. allies, Turkey and Pakistan, is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three would ​be regarded as an attack on all.

It was not clear whether or how either Pakistan or Turkey would join in any Saudi ‌response ‌to the latest attacks.

The Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea last month, ​citing what they said was a Saudi siege on them, an allegation Riyadh denies.

The Saudi energy ministry said a fire had broken out at the refinery but was later extinguished with no injuries and authorities were dealing with the incident, without giving a cause.

The Houthis used a drone ⁠to target the refinery, military spokesperson Yahya Saree posted on X. They had struck Aramco sites before in Jazan, which processes 400,000 barrels of crude oil per ⁠day in southwestern Saudi Arabia. They had also hit Yanbu on the Red Sea.

In a separate statement, Saree said the Houthis carried out missile and drone strikes on the Yemeni Red Sea port city of Mocha.

The port, controlled by the Aden-based ​government, is close to the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait, ⁠which links the southern Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. Should it be closed, Saudi Arabia would be deprived of an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

Three Yemeni government ​sources told Reuters that air defenses were engaging drones launched by the Houthis towards the commercial quay ​and storage in the port.

Saree said the Houthi strikes targeted Saudi troops and weapons arsenal in the area. There ​was no Saudi ‌comment on the attacks in Yemen.

Rashad al-Alimi, head of Yemen’s Saudi-backed presidential council, on Sunday briefed U.S. Mission to Yemen Chargé d’Affaires Neil Hop on the developments, according to a statement.

He said the Houthis’ attack put a responsibility on the international community, foremost among them the U.S., to “move beyond only containing the Houthi threat to addressing its sources and instruments.”

The Yemeni military ‌spokesperson said the attack on the port killed seven people.

The Yemeni transportation ministry said in a statement that the attack caused severe damage to the port’s infrastructure.

“This marks yet another assault on a vital civilian facility that serves citizens and contributes to boosting commercial and maritime activity in the Red Sea,” the ministry said.

Iran and its allied Shi’ite Muslim armed groups have been firing on Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states and blockading their energy shipments since the ​U.S. ​and Israel attacked the country on February 28 in a major escalation after years of regional tumult. Talks have ​dragged on between the U.S. and Iran in pursuit of a peace deal, with access to the Strait of Hormuz, a major conduit for energy supplies, ⁠proving a major stumbling block.

Houthi attacks in the Red Sea have aggravated the disruptions of supplies to global markets.

Pakistan’s military, air force, prime minister’s office and information and foreign ministries did not respond to requests for comment and the Turkish government did not respond to a request on Sunday for comment on the implications of the refinery attack.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Friday, as ​the alliance was announced, that it was not directed against Iran or any other country, but rather served as a general pledge to support the three allies’ security.

Fidan said the allies would decide through consultations what degree, form, and format of support they would ask for in the event of an attack on any of them.

https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/economics.title: Indonesia’s strong GDP data prompts ‘resilient but uneven’ growth forecasts
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/economics.author: Resty Woro Yuniar
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/economics.text:
While manufacturing and household spending rose in Q2, growth expectations are tempered by a decline in the mining and trade sectors

Analysts, however, urged caution about the country’s economic outlook in the coming quarters, saying the latest data also revealed uneven sectoral performance and a reliance on government spending.

Southeast Asia’s largest economy grew 5.29 per cent year on year in the April-June period, slower than the 5.61 per cent recorded in the first quarter but above a 5.1 per cent forecast by economists polled by Reuters.

In its economic report published on Tuesday – a day before the official data’s release – the Institute for Economic and Social Research at University Indonesia estimated second-quarter growth of 4.8 per cent.

Mohammad Edy Mahmud, deputy for national accounts and statistical analysis at statistics agency BPS, told reporters on Wednesday that the quarterly expansion was largely supported by manufacturing and household spending.

Manufacturing, agriculture, trade, construction and mining accounted for 63.73 per cent of gross domestic product on the production side, Mohammad said.

All industries expanded in the second quarter except mining, which contracted 1.64 per cent because of quota restrictions on coal, bauxite, tin and nickel ore, he said.

Household consumption grew 5.06 per cent, contributing to 53.52 per cent of GDP.

Officials welcomed the better-than-expected growth, with Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa saying on Wednesday that the “suboptimal” growth was mostly caused by skyrocketing global oil prices between April and June.

“We were able to grow by 5.29 per cent, which is quite good under these circumstances,” Purbaya said.

“I’m confident that in the third and fourth quarters, we will push for a faster growth rate towards 6 per cent by maximising all existing growth engines in the economy.”

Airlangga Hartarto, coordinating minister for economic affairs, said the latest growth figure was more meaningful because “there were no big events such as Eid al-Fitr in the second quarter, which fell in the first quarter, so this [growth] is quite good”.

The rupiah rose to 17,933 per US dollar at the close of trading on Wednesday following the GDP data’s release, from 18,027 per US dollar on Tuesday.

Josua Pardede, chief economist at Permata Bank, said that forecasters who anticipated a deeper growth slump understated the key engines driving expansion.

“The main surprise was not household consumption. Instead, the upside surprise came from the combined strength of government expenditure and fixed investment,” Pardede said.

“The consensus error was principally an underestimation of fiscal execution, construction activity and government-linked capital expenditure, rather than an underestimation of a broad consumer boom.”

Yusuf Rendy Manilet, an economist with the Centre of Reform on Economics Indonesia, said the increased domestic spending was “quite surprising” as there were no big religious holidays in the second quarter.

“When household consumption grows to above 5 per cent, it means that the general condition of society is improving,” Yusuf said.

However, Pardede noted that the figures contained “an important warning about the quality of growth”. He pointed to the main contributors to fixed investment growth in the second quarter, which were all linked to “government-related procurement, infrastructure programmes, and purchases of ships and tankers”.

“Machinery and equipment investment grew by only 1.32 per cent, suggesting that the investment recovery was not yet centred on expanding industrial production capacity,” Pardede said.

“The underlying fundamentals are therefore best described as resilient but uneven. Indonesia continues to benefit from a large domestic market, diversified economic activities, active fiscal support, adequate banking intermediation and relatively stable macroeconomic institutions.”

Nonetheless, economists warned against external pressures building up in the next quarters, particularly through foreign exchange and trade channels.

BPS said on Monday last week that Indonesia recorded a narrower trade deficit of US$450 million in June following a US$1.61 billion deficit in May, the country’s first since April 2020.

Yusuf said the deficit was likely to “worsen” in the next few months with a weak rupiah continuing to weigh on industries dependent on imported raw materials, such as plastics and food and beverages.

“At the same time, our exports remain under pressure due to market access issues related to changes to the trade agreement between Indonesia and the United States,” Yusuf said.

“Industries such as textiles and their derivatives, as well as footwear, which rely on the US for their markets, will be affected as they must adapt to these changes.”

Bhima Yudhistira, an executive director at the Centre of Economic and Law Studies think tank, said household spending might decline in the next few quarters due to El Nino, as the weather phenomenon could lead to lower food production and water supply.

Pardede and Yusuf agreed that Indonesia remained a bright spot among developing economies.

But they highlighted that the country was not the best economic performer in the region, citing Vietnam’s whopping 8.39 per cent growth in the second quarter, fuelled by expansion in its manufacturing industry.

“The central conclusion is that the second-quarter result confirms Indonesia’s capacity to absorb external shocks, but it does not yet demonstrate a structural acceleration,” Pardede said.

“Indonesia will remain a bright spot only if temporary fiscal support is converted into stronger manufacturing, higher productivity, better quality employment and greater export capacity.”
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/economics.summary: Indonesia's economy grew 5.29 per cent year on year in the April-June period. But growth expectations are tempered by a decline in the mining and trade sectors. Analysts urged caution about the country's economic outlook in the coming quarters.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly8.title: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly8.text:
Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on. Finally, he was told, it was going to come his way.

But he feared his pursuit of it could cost him his life.

Two days later, his car was found overturned - he had been shot dead while driving.

Now seven members of South Africa's special forces, and one military police officer, have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa, a highly respected officer, in August 2023. They deny the charges.

There has been no date scheduled for their trial, and there are concerns it will never go ahead, because three of the men charged with his murder have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. They are still working for the army's special forces, and one of them has been promoted.

The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men.

The case has caused consternation in one of Africa's most robust democracies, with fears the country's military is significantly overreaching its mandate.

We asked the South African army whether it was responsible for Mathipa's killing. It did not respond.

Several hundred pages of secret police and court documents, shared with the BBC, set out the evidence suggesting special forces killed Mathipa - who worked for an elite police unit known as "The Hawks".

We have also interviewed key sources in the police investigation - South Africa's former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks; Mathipa's commanding officer; and Mathipa's family - to build the most comprehensive public account of the events leading up to the detective's death.

It presents a compelling case that South Africa's special forces are responsible for his murder.

In particular, police documents show that the vehicle that trailed Mathipa just before he was shot was registered to a front company for the special forces. And that tracking data found in that vehicle puts it at the scene of the shooting.

One of the men in the car, Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, the documents show, was also spotted at the scene of an alleged abduction carried out by special forces soldiers - the case that Mathipa had been investigating.

After Mathipa's death, special forces issued a chilling warning to The Hawks, the police documents say. "You can appoint 10 investigating officers; we will kill all of them," said the warning, according to police.

The case Mathipa had been investigating was sensitive.

It centred on an Ethiopian man called Abdella Abadigga, an alleged so-called Islamic State [IS] militant. He had been granted temporary asylum in South Africa in 2008, but was arrested abroad in 2017.

Abadigga had then been smuggled back into the country, by the South African military and Department of Home Affairs, to be used as an intelligence asset - but had "gone rogue", according to Col Tollie Vreugdenburg, former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks.

Abadigga had gone on to extort Johannesburg's Ethiopian neighbourhood, sources in the community told us. This money was used to fund IS, says the US government.

We asked the South African army if it had facilitated Abadigga's return to South Africa. And we asked the Department of Home Affairs if it had lied about a planned deportation of him to Ethiopia, and had instead smuggled him back into South Africa on an expired passport and refugee permit. They did not respond.

Specifically, Mathipa was investigating the allegation that special forces had then gone on to abduct and kill Abadigga in December 2022 - who the United States, earlier that year, had put under sanctions, designating him an IS recruiter and fundraiser, as well as a trusted supporter of Bilal al-Sudani, a top IS figure in Somalia.

Court documents show that after Abadigga's abduction, his phone connected to a mast near a military base. Police sources say it was used to call a number in Somalia.

The Pentagon did not respond to the BBC's question on whether Abadigga's phone helped locate al-Sudani, who was killed by US special forces in Somalia in January 2023, only a few weeks after Abadigga's alleged abduction.

We also asked South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa whether Abadigga had been kidnapped at the behest of the US. He declined to comment.

When Mathipa was assigned the case, four months before his own death, he already knew special forces were implicated, but he was trying to secure more evidence.

He was building on information already gathered by Abadigga's brother, Ameen - who had opened a missing person's case soon after the disappearance, and had been assigned an investigating officer (IO) from local police.

He and the IO had obtained CCTV footage showing the last known movements of Abadigga and his bodyguard Kadir Abotese at the Mall of Africa, a shopping centre on the outskirts of Johannesburg.

The footage, clips of which the BBC has seen, shows a man in a blue top following Abadigga and his bodyguard as they leave the food court to head back to the car park, and paying for parking three seconds after Abadigga and Abotese do.

The mall CCTV footage contains another vital clue. The licence plates of the suspected kidnappers' vehicles are clearly visible.

The vehicles were all registered to a company called Peters Communications Trust (PCT), a front company for South African special forces - Ameen and the IO were to discover.

At the time of Abadigga's disappearance, PCT's directors included Maj Gen Herbert Mashego, the then commanding officer of 5 Special Forces Regiment.

Police documents say a meeting was arranged between the IO and high ranks of the military, including Brig Gen Yalo, the then head of special forces, at which the IO was instructed to tell Ameen there was no link between PCT and the military.

So, with the investigation seemingly at a standstill, Abadigga's brother took his case to the Johannesburg High Court.

Responding to Ameen's legal action, special forces denied all knowledge of Abadigga or his whereabouts. They did, however, admit their soldiers had been at the Mall of Africa on the date in question, but said they had been there for a training exercise.

They named the man seen wearing blue on CCTV as Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, and said he had been the exercise commander. They also admitted all the suspect vehicles seen at the mall belonged to them.

Domestic operations by South Africa's military need to be authorised by both the government and the presidency.

We asked South African former Defence Minister Thandi Modise, and President Ramaphosa, if they had authorised a training exercise in the Mall of Africa - Modise did not respond and Ramaphosa declined to comment.

When Mathipa was assigned to the case a month later, he issued a subpoena to special forces to force them to hand over full details of this alleged training exercise and all the personnel involved.

When access to these documents was finally promised, three months later, Mathipa had a premonition that he would be murdered - according to Brig Paulina Sekgobela, his commanding officer.

"When [Mathipa] left my office he said: 'Brigadier, you know, these people - they are going to kill me. I'm going to die'," she told the BBC.

On the day Mathipa was killed, he was phoned by a man calling himself Tebogo, who claimed he had information on the case for the detective - according to Mathipa's daughter Basetsana, who was home with him at the time.

Mathipa and Tebogo arranged to meet at a petrol station in Pretoria.

When Tebogo failed to show, Mathipa drove away again, along the highway.

He was killed while driving, by rounds fired from high-velocity weapons which special forces would have had access to, according to South African police.

And footage from motorway toll gantries, police say, shows one of the occupants of the black BMW, which tailed Mathipa moments before his murder, was Maj Sunnybooi Wambi.

This car, like the three vehicles connected with Abadigga's disappearance at the mall, was registered to PCT, they add.

New detectives were assigned to the case after Mathipa's death, triggering a chilling message from special forces, that made its way to the police's Criminal Intelligence division.

Police say it warned that, however many investigating officers were assigned to the case, "we will kill all of them".

Twelve members of the South African military have been arrested in total, including Lt Col Sunnybooi Wambi, and the current head of South Africa's special forces, Brig Gen Solomon Lechoenyo - both promoted to these positions since police first started investigating their roles in the case.

The 12 have been variously charged with the abduction and murder of Abadigga and Abotese, the murder of Mathipa, fraud, and obstruction.

All deny all charges and they were initially released on bail. But six of them later had their bail revoked, and were ordered to turn themselves in to custody.

Three of the six, including Wambi, have been charged with both Mathipa's murder, and Abotese's abduction and murder.

The military has refused to hand them over.

In July, their lawyers cited mental health treatment for their absence. Three years after Mathipa's killing, no trial date has been set.

Meanwhile, Abadigga's body has never been found.

"[Mathipa] was barking up the right tree. He was taking on the right lion," Vreugdenburg says of the late detective.

Mathipa's daughter Basetsana puts it starkly: "We need justice. I'm never going to see my dad anymore... Why my dad? Because he was doing his job."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly8.summary: Seven members of South Africa's special forces and one military police officer have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa. They deny the charges and have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cly5zp.text:
Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan appeared in court in Dublin on Sunday after being extradited from Dubai following his arrest there in April.

Kinahan has been charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between October 2015 and April 2017.

The 49-year-old was remanded in custody after appearing at the non-jury Special Criminal Court in Dublin, telling the court: " I think we all know I won't be getting bail."

The Kinahan cartel has been responsible for trafficking tonnes of drugs and firearms around the world for more than 20 years, according to the UK's National Crime Agency.

The BBC's Ireland correspondent, Chris Page, was inside the court during the hearing.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2r.title: China evacuates one million from homes as massive storm arrives
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2r.text:
More than a million people have been evacuated from their homes in eastern China including Shanghai, as Typhoon Dolphin made landfall on Sunday evening.

It packed maximum wind speeds of 150km/h (94mph) when it first slammed into Yuhuan in the Zhejiang province at 17:30 (09:30 GMT) before making a second landfall in the city of Wenzhou about an hour later, meteorological authorities said.

The typhoon halted transportation across the region – 1,400 flights were cancelled in Shanghai alone.

Chinese authorities had earlier issued their highest-level red alert on Dolphin, but by Monday morning they downgraded it to a tropical storm.

The storm is continuing to move further inland, and authorities are still warning of torrential rains, severe flooding and the risk of landslides through to Wednesday.

Heavy rain was forecast on Monday for the provinces of Shandong, Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and the city of Shanghai.

Local governments have urged people to avoid outdoor activities, while several top tourist attractions remain closed, including parts of Disneyland and Legoland, and several viewing platforms along the Bund in Shanghai.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crrv.title: How much parents could save from September's new school uniform rules
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crrv.text:
A new law coming into force in September means parents in England should have to buy fewer branded items of school uniform, which the government says will save them money.

From September, uniforms will be limited to three items with a school logo, like a blazer, jumper or sportswear – plus a tie for secondary schools.

Schools are already advised to keep these items to a minimum, meaning many are already within the rules, but about a quarter of schools will need to make changes by the time the law comes into effect.

The government says the changes will save some families "up to £50 per child", but schoolwear suppliers say they now face uncertainty in demand for this year's uniforms.

Co-op Academy Belle Vue, in Manchester, is planning to drop the number of its compulsory branded items from seven to three, plus a tie.

It estimates the average cost of the branded parts of the uniform last year was £101.94 with a pinafore, and £83.95 without – but this year it will cost families an average of £53.97.

Next year, when the school switches to a new supplier, it says it will fall further.

The school has decided to get rid of its branded blazer, the branded pinafore, branded shorts and PE jogging bottoms.

The school's branded jumper currently has a coloured stripe, which is different for every year group, but this will switch to a plain one so parents will not have to buy a new jumper every year.

Parents must now buy a branded jumper, a tie, and two branded PE tops for summer and winter.

Linda Ubawike, who has three children at the school, says her uniform bill has dropped by £70 this year.

"It has honestly saved me so much," she says.

"I can now get more of the uniform in the local supermarket, and my son who is starting in September is getting the whole uniform for free – it works so much better."

Because every school sets its own uniform policy, parents can still face very different expectations and costs.

Lorraine, who lives in London, has two children in secondary schools and is frustrated that her school has not changed any of its uniform policy this year.

She says several items are still compulsory, including the branded blazer, tie, branded polo shirt, branded shorts and two-toned PE socks.

Even the plain grey trousers or skirt have to be purchased from one of the school's suppliers, she says.

Both her sons have been through a growth spurt this summer, so she is expecting to spend more than £200 on their branded items alone.

"I'm just frustrated, for me it's not even about the money," she says.

"I feel these inconsistencies do not make a difference to education and are really blinkered."

But mum-of-five Carol, from Stockport, welcomes the changes at her children's school. She says her son's secondary school only requires a branded blazer, a branded jumper and tie, with everything else available from a range of shops.

She tries to get most of her children's uniforms second-hand anyway, but always buys the blazer, which costs around £30, as she likes them to have a new one.

She says anything that makes it more affordable for parents is a good thing.

But others are not seeing the changes they would like.

One father from Oxfordshire, who did not want to be named, says his daughter still has to have seven branded items - three for the uniform, three for PE and a summer polo shirt - as there are no alternatives allowed.

"It's ridiculous and unfair. We are paying £200 which we can't afford," he says.

Most primary schools already have very few branded items.

At Broadhurst Primary, in North Manchester, only the school jumper – and, from 2027, the PE T-shirt – are branded, which the school says brings the total cost of its uniform to £13 per child.

Around 23% of secondary schools will have to change their uniform lists for September to comply with the new rules, according to the latest government survey.

The education secretary has legal powers to direct schools to comply if they are not sticking to the new rules.

One head teachers' union, the Association of School and College Leaders, says the actual difference in cost is likely to be marginal for most families.

Its general secretary Pepe Di'Iasio says schools are already trying to balance the cost to parents with maintaining a sense of identity. He says it's also important to keep expensive fashion brands out so no one feels excluded.

Some schools have been phasing their changes in over the last few years.

King's Oak Academy, in Bristol, has one compulsory item left on its uniform list - a branded PE T-shirt.

The school, which goes from reception right through to Year 11, used to have a branded jumper, tie and a shirt, which together cost about £41.

Students are now asked to wear a plain polo shirt - which changes colour for the lower, middle and upper school - a sweatshirt or cardigan, and grey skirt or trousers, with all pupils also wearing black trainers. The school says it now costs about £10 to £25, depending on where parents buy the uniform.

Principal Katherine Ogden, a former PE teacher, wanted to make the uniform practical and comfortable, but says parents can buy other optional items with the school logo on if they wish.

Some of England's largest academy trusts have told the BBC they are also keeping a number of optional branded items on the uniform list, which the new law allows.

Uniform retailers have long argued the changes might increase costs for families.

The Schoolwear Association says the plans could mean parents spend more on replacing lower-quality generic garments, which might not last as long as branded ones.

Chair Matthew Easter says it will also create "division" in schools, because branded uniforms help to reduce inequality and improve behaviour.

He says some suppliers are also finding it harder to plan this year as it is not clear how many parents will want the optional branded items.

Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland do not have a cap on branded school uniform items, but guidance in each nation encourages schools to keep uniforms affordable for families.

A spokesperson for the Department for Education said some families would save "up to £50 per child" due to the changes, and that it is supporting schools to take more steps to bring down the cost of individual items.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crrv.summary: New law comes into force in September means parents must buy fewer branded items of school uniform. Government says the changes will save some families up to £50 per child. Schoolwear suppliers say they now face uncertainty in demand for this year's uniforms.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/09/busin.title: Taylor Farms Voluntarily Recalls Fresh Jalapeños Over Salmonella Concerns
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/09/busin.author: Alexandra E. Petri
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/09/busin.text:
The company said it was unaware of any reported illnesses linked to its products containing jalapeños, which were distributed to major retailers across 26 states.

By Alexandra E. Petri

Taylor Farms, which has been linked to a large outbreak of cyclosporiasis associated with iceberg lettuce in the United States, said on Sunday that it was voluntarily recalling several of its products made with fresh jalapeños that have been tied to a multistate salmonella outbreak.

The recalled products include spicy guacamole, mango pico de gallo, taco dip and more than a dozen other Taylor Farms branded and unbranded products, the company said in a statement on its website. They were distributed across 26 states to major retailers — including Whole Foods, Trader Joe’s, Hannaford and Kroger’s — and have a “Best If Used By” date up to and including Aug. 16, 2026.

Taylor Farms said it was recalling finished products containing jalapeños that were voluntarily recalled by Coast Citrus Distributors earlier this month.

Taylor Farms said it is “no longer sourcing products from this farmer,” and that the company “is not aware of any reported illnesses linked to its products containing jalapeños.”

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said imported recalled fresh jalapeños traced back to a grower in Sinaloa, Mexico, appear to be the source of the salmonella outbreak in the United States.

At least 345 people across more than two dozen states have gotten sick with the same strain of salmonella that has now been linked to jalapeños, the C.D.C. said in a statement. It said no deaths have been reported in connection to the outbreak.

According to the C.D.C., most people infected with salmonella develop diarrhea, fever and stomach cramps six hours to six days after being exposed to the bacteria.

The voluntary recall for Taylor Farms, one of the nation’s largest producers of leafy greens and fresh vegetables, comes as the company has been linked to a large outbreak of cyclosporiasis associated with iceberg lettuce in the United States, which causes severe diarrhea.

Infants, older adults and those who are pregnant or immunocompromised are the most vulnerable.

On Monday, health officials in Michigan reported the first two deaths associated with the outbreak. The two people who died had significant underlying health issues, according to the Michigan Health Department.

In July, the C.D.C. linked cases in Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia to the outbreak.

The iceberg lettuce was sourced from central Mexico and distributed by Taylor Farms, which has issued a recall of bagged iceberg lettuce in 27 states.

https://www.npr.org/2026/08/09/nx-s1-592.title: Nearly 30 years after Tupac's death, the trial over his murder will finally begin
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/09/nx-s1-592.author: Rob Schmitz
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/09/nx-s1-592.text:
Alejandra Marquez Janse

In 2023, police charged Duane Davis, also known as "Keefe D," with organizing Tupac Shakur's murder in 1996. Author Ben Westhoff discusses Davis' trial that begins Monday.

Next month will mark 30 years of the death of a rap legend.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "HIT 'EM UP")

TUPAC SHAKUR: (Rapping) Grab your Glocks when you see 2Pac. Call the cops when you see 2Pac.

SCHMITZ: In September of 1996, Tupac Shakur died following a drive-by shooting near the Las Vegas strip. For decades, the mystery of who was behind his killing plagued the public, but no one had ever been charged, that is, until just a few years ago. In 2023, police charged Duane Davis, also known as Keffe D, with organizing Shakur's murder. The trial begins tomorrow. Joining us now is journalist Ben Westhoff. He's also the author of "Original Gangstas," where he writes about the Tupac Shakur murder investigation. Welcome.

BEN WESTHOFF: Thank you for having me.

SCHMITZ: So let's be specific here. Davis is not charged with pulling the trigger. The actual person police suspected as the gunman, Orlando Anderson, was killed in an unrelated shooting in 1998. So what exactly is Duane Davis charged with here?

WESTHOFF: He's charged with providing the murder weapon and basically orchestrating the killing.

SCHMITZ: And bring us back to that night in Las Vegas when Tupac Shakur was killed. Who was involved? What was happening?

WESTHOFF: Tupac was in Las Vegas for the Mike Tyson fight, actually. And so after the fight, Tupac and his group got into an altercation with a guy named Baby Lane, who was a member of the South Side Crips from Compton. And they got in a fight, and Tupac is actually seen on camera stomping this guy and beating him. And it wasn't too much longer after that when this group of people affiliated with the guy who got stomped allegedly came and killed him right on the Las Vegas Strip.

SCHMITZ: And now Duane Davis has been arrested for this. What led to Duane Davis' arrest and now the trial?

WESTHOFF: Well, he has kind of been talking about this case for a long time, and he was originally charged with drug dealing, with PCP-related charges. And so as part of a plea bargain, he talked to a LAPD cop named Greg Kading and basically laid out what actually happened, according to him and, you know, said he didn't pull the trigger himself, but his nephew did, the one who got stomped. Keffe D also later published a book, seemingly admitting to the crime.

SCHMITZ: So he actually wrote a book in which he said, hey, I did this.

WESTHOFF: Well, it was kind of in the OJ style, you know? If I did it...

SCHMITZ: If I did it, yeah.

WESTHOFF: ...Sort of thing, except that it was very self-incriminating. But the defense is now arguing that since he had a coauthor for the book, it can't always be clear if it's him talking or the coauthor talking.

SCHMITZ: Is this a slam dunk case, in your mind?

WESTHOFF: I think so. I mean, we've known about these details for so long. He seems to have admitted so much of it, that I would think so. The only aspect is that a lot of what he's being charged with can't really be corroborated otherwise. There were three other men with him in the car that night, but all three of them are dead. And so it's just sort of his own story is all we really have to go on.

SCHMITZ: And he, of course, is facing life in prison if convicted. What have we heard from people who are close to Tupac Shakur - his friends, his family?

WESTHOFF: I think the main thing we've heard is - why have we not had resolution in this case?

WESTHOFF: It's been 30 years, and it's not like there haven't been leads. There have been, in fact, you know, multiple LAPD investigations.

SCHMITZ: So after his death, Tupac Shakur became sort of a mythical figure in many ways. You know, there's so many theories about his killing. Some even believed that he was still alive. Why do you think his story became such a kind of a pop culture legend?

WESTHOFF: Tupac really captured, you know, not just the zeitgeist of his time - he was really popular while he was alive. But in death, he almost became more popular and not just as a musician and not even really just as a cultural figure, but as a sort of almost political prophet. You know, his words, his lyrics and also the things that he said in interviews still resonate today. He was very much for, you know, empowerment for African American people. And a lot of what he said kind of predicted the Black Lives Matter movement in a way.

SCHMITZ: That is Ben Westhoff, a journalist and author of "Original Gangstas." He's been speaking about the Tupac Shakur trial that begins tomorrow. Thanks.

WESTHOFF: Great to talk with you.

(SOUNDBITE OF 2PAC SONG, "CALIFORNIA LOVE")

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Hong Kong records hottest day ever as Typhoon Dolphin fuels heatwave
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Observatory says 36.9C posted on Sunday is city’s highest official temperature since its records began 142 years ago, with storm driving intense heat in region

Hong Kong has officially recorded its highest ever temperature as Typhoon Dolphin swept warm air over the city, the meteorological service said.

The city’s weather observatory posted a temperature of 36.9C on Sunday, the highest recorded since records began in 1884, the Hong Kong Observatory said in the afternoon.

The approaching storm has fuelled intense heat in the region over the weekend and triggered mass flight cancellations and evacuations along China’s east coast before making landfall there on Sunday evening.

The previous record for Hong Kong was set at 36.6C on 22 August 2017, before Typhoon Hato hit.

Figures recorded at the observatory’s headquarters are the official reference point for the city’s records, but temperatures elsewhere in the densely built Chinese finance hub topped 39C.

A weather station in Sheung Shui, in the city’s north, recorded 39.8C, the highest temperature logged in Hong Kong since automatic weather stations were introduced in the 1980s, the observatory said.

“With Tropical Cyclone Dolphin moving towards the vicinity of Zhejiang and moving inland, its outer subsiding air will persistently bring extremely hot weather to the territory today to Tuesday,” the forecaster said.

The observatory issued a “very hot weather warning” on Sunday, advising citizens to drink water and avoid vigorous outdoor physical activities.

Typhoon Dolphin has made landfall in the Chinese mainland, about 1,000km (620 miles) north-east of Hong Kong.

Dolphin made landfall near Yuhuan in Zhejiang province at about ⁠5:30pm (0930 GMT) on Sunday, China’s meteorological authorities said. It brought maximum sustained winds of 94mph (151 km/h) near its centre at landfall, equivalent to a category 1 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson scale.

Scientists say human-driven climate change is making extreme heat events more frequent and more intense worldwide.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.summary: Hong Kong Observatory says 36.9C is city's highest temperature since records began in 1884. Typhoon Dolphin has made landfall in the Chinese mainland. It brought maximum sustained winds of 94mph (151 km/h) near its centre at landfall.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: World’s seas have hit hottest temperature on record for July, say scientists
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Ajit Niranjan
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Average sea surface temperature outside polar regions was highest on record for July, beating previous high in 2023

The world’s seas were hotter last month than in any July on record, scientists have said, as devastating heat struck western Europe.

Sea surface temperatures hit record highs for July on the Atlantic coast and western Mediterranean, the EU’s Copernicus climate change service found, with severe marine heatwaves roiling Europe’s seas. Globally, the average sea surface temperature outside the cold polar regions was the highest on record for the month, beating the previous July record set in 2023.

Surface air temperatures around the world in July 2026 were marginally cooler than July 2024 – by just 0.01C – leading scientists to consider the two months as the joint-second warmest Julys on record.

Western Europe has experienced its hottest June-July period on record, data shows, with “exceptional” heat driving wildfires that devastated swathes of the Mediterranean.

The first two summer months of 2026 were 2.79C hotter than usual, the Copernicus said on Monday, beating the previous record set four years ago and reflecting the “exceptional persistence of heat” since the season began.

Central Europe is reeling from a heatwave in which national temperature records fell in a handful of countries including Austria and Slovakia. It is the latest in a scorching summer that has dried out vegetation and primed the continent to burn.

Samantha Burgess, a climate scientist at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, said this summer had been “a clear example” of climate breakdown intensifying extremes that reinforce each other.

“[As] persistent high-pressure systems trapped heat over western Europe, the extreme temperatures also amplified widespread drought,” she said. “As soils dry out, they lose their ability to provide natural cooling, allowing heat to build more readily.”

Supercharged by fossil fuel pollution, a string of heatwaves have hit Europe since the end of spring, with particularly brutal heat at the end of June expected to have resulted in more than 10,000 deaths.

Copernicus said widespread dryness observed in May and June intensified last month, with exceptionally low rainfall and soil moisture in much of western Europe. Across the dry regions, which include France, Spain, and parts of Germany and the UK, low river flows hit water supply, irrigation and power plants, including in countries downstream. Short of cooling water, two coal-fired power plants were forced to shut in Poland last week, as well as Hungary’s sole nuclear power plant, for the first time in its 44-year history.

Heat and drought are among the biggest environmental threats to Europe’s economy. Early estimates for this summer suggest the June heat cost grain farmers €2bn in lost crops.

The longer-term damage can eclipse short-term losses, economists warn, particularly if droughts persist over many years. The mega-drought of 2015-18 cost Europe €439bn, a new working paper led by the CMCC European Institute on Economics found, with high but short-lived hits to agriculture and low but persistent impacts on manufacturing and construction. The researchers argue that conventional methods substantially underestimate drought-related economic losses as they fail to capture the years after.

Marta Mastropietro, a researcher at CMCC and the Polytechnic University of Milan, and lead author of the study, said: “Even a single dry year causes real economic damage, but a persistent drought is different: its effects can compound across sectors and keep accumulating for years afterward.

“That intersection between compounding and long-lasting impacts is what conventional impact estimates tend to miss.”

About half a million hectares have burned across the EU since the start of the year, data published by the European Forest Fire Information System shows, accompanied by above-average pollution as burning vegetation spews thick smoke. The hot, dry and windy conditions that make it harder to battle blazes has set new records for severity for this time of year.

Víctor Resco de Dios, a professor of forestry engineering at the University of Lleida, said: “Climate change is creating increasingly favourable conditions for the development of mega-wildfires.

“The good news is that through vegetation management and urban planning we can largely mitigate the problem,” he said. “However, we must be clear about one thing: what seems extreme to us today will be remarkably benign in a few decades if we continue to fail to take the necessary adaptive measures.”

Western Europe has experienced its hottest June-July period on record. Average sea surface temperature outside polar regions was highest on record for the month.

Israel has confirmed, nearly two years after the fact, that a Palestinian detainee from Gaza died in detention, according to the Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs.

The Israeli Prison Service informed the commission on Sunday that Ihab Mohammed Abdel Qader Diab, 36, had died while detained. Palestinian officials say the case fits a broader pattern of Israel concealing the fate of detainees held since its genocidal war on Gaza began.

Diab was detained on December 12, 2023, and the commission believes he died around September 18, 2024, after roughly nine months in custody that it alleges involved torture.

Israeli authorities said Diab had an underlying health condition, but his family has rejected this, saying he was healthy and had no illnesses at the time of his detention.

Diab’s death brings the number of Palestinian detainees who have died in Israeli custody since 1967 to 328, including 91 since October 7, 2023 – 53 of them from Gaza, according to the commission.

Gaza’s Prisoners’ Ministry said it holds the Israeli government and prison administration fully responsible, citing evidence of torture, medical neglect and brutal detention conditions.

It called for an international investigation, accountability for those responsible, the return of Diab’s body to his family and disclosure of the fate of all Gaza detainees it says Israel continues to conceal.

Diab’s case surfaces amid growing scrutiny of Israel’s detention system, under which thousands of Palestinians are held without charge or trial.

As of August, Israeli rights group HaMoked said Israel was holding nearly 8,000 “security” prisoners, including 3,198 people in administrative detention – held on secret evidence without formal charges, under orders that can be renewed indefinitely.

Those figures exclude the additional Palestinians detained from Gaza and classified separately by Israel as “unlawful combatants”.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.text:
The Malaysian government has announced that Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim is undergoing medical checks and a procedure and is expected to remain under observation for two days.

On Monday, Senior Press Secretary Tunku Nashrul Abaidah said Anwar was undergoing examinations and procedures on the advice of a team of medical specialists. No details about the procedure were shared.

“Let us pray that all matters relating to YAB Prime Minister’s examinations and procedures are made easier and that he is blessed with lasting good health so that he can return to carrying out his duties as usual in the near future, God willing,” Tunku Nashrul said.

The announcement came on Anwar’s 79th birthday. He was born on August 10, 1947, and has served as prime minister since November 2022.

Anwar underwent a routine medical examination in January, when doctors said he was in good health and able to continue his official duties as scheduled.

Anwar has previously received treatment for back and shoulder problems. In June 2018, he was hospitalised after experiencing shoulder and back pain, according to the Reuters news agency. The following month, he underwent spinal surgery in Istanbul and was scheduled for surgery on his right shoulder for a rotator cuff injury.

There is no indication that Monday’s procedure is connected to those earlier conditions.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.title: Could Morocco’s football chief Fouzi Lekjaa become its next prime minister?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.text:
Rabat, Morocco – As Morocco prepares for parliamentary elections on September 23, political debate is centred less on ideology and party programmes than on the decision of one of the country’s most influential public officials to enter partisan politics.

The decision by Fouzi Lekjaa, Morocco’s minister delegate for the budget and president of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF), to join the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) has prompted intense debate across the political class and social media.

Best known for his role in public finance and the transformation of Moroccan football, Lekjaa built his reputation in public administration rather than electoral politics.

His move represents more than a simple party affiliation. It reflects a broader shift in Moroccan politics, where managerial competence, state-led development and national prestige are becoming increasingly important sources of political legitimacy.

Mustafa Ahdar, a researcher in constitutional law and political science at Ibn Zohr University in Agadir, told Al Jazeera that Lekjaa joined PAM less than three months before the elections, making the timing politically significant.

“From a constitutional perspective, every Moroccan citizen is free to join any political party under the 2011 Constitution,” Ahdar said, noting that former PAM secretary-general Abdellatif Ouahbi has publicly reaffirmed this principle.

“However, someone who simultaneously heads the national football federation and occupies a senior ministerial position cannot realistically be viewed in the same way as an ordinary citizen entering politics.”

The timing matters for another reason: the government formed after the election will oversee Morocco’s preparations for the 2030 FIFA World Cup, which it will cohost with Spain and Portugal.

With billions expected to be invested in infrastructure, transport and tourism, commentators have increasingly described the next administration as Morocco’s “World Cup government”, one likely to be judged as much by its ability to deliver the tournament as by traditional economic indicators.

Lekjaa’s rise reflects a broader trend in Morocco and beyond, where successful public officials are increasingly becoming political assets in their own right.

As budget minister, he became closely associated with major infrastructure and investment projects while emerging as a central figure in Morocco’s football renaissance.

The Atlas Lions’ historic run to the semifinals of the 2022 FIFA World Cup transformed Morocco’s international image, strengthened its soft power across Africa and the Arab world, and made football a symbol of national ambition and institutional effectiveness.

For Ahdar, however, the trend raises deeper questions about the role of political parties.

“Political parties are supposed to create spaces where citizens become politically engaged and future leaders emerge,” he said. “When parties increasingly recruit influential personalities who have built their popularity outside politics, they risk abandoning that mission.”

Morocco’s political evolution also reflects changing voter behaviour.

Turnout exceeded 50 percent in the 2021 parliamentary elections, yet nearly half of eligible voters still abstained.

Many analysts argue that this reflects scepticism towards political parties rather than a lack of political interest, particularly among younger Moroccans, who increasingly express their concerns through social media activism and protests over unemployment, rising living costs and public services.

According to Ahdar, the debate surrounding Lekjaa illustrates this shift.

“PAM is part of the current governing coalition and faces criticism over its governmental record,” he said. “Yet the debate today is centred far more on Lekjaa’s arrival than on the party’s political programme or achievements.”

He noted that some social media users had even joked that “Lekjaa attracted PAM rather than PAM attracting Lekjaa”, reflecting what he described as the growing personification of politics.

Morocco’s 2011 Constitution expanded the powers of parliament while maintaining the monarchy’s central role in government formation. Under Article 47, the king appoints the head of government from the party winning the largest number of parliamentary seats.

Morocco’s proportional electoral system almost always produces coalition governments, making post-election negotiations nearly as important as the vote itself.

Speculation over Lekjaa’s future political role has intensified, despite no official indication that he is being considered for head of government.

Ahdar also sees parallels with Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch, who entered partisan politics after establishing himself outside traditional party structures.

“This inevitably raises questions about internal party democracy,” he said. “Many party activists spend years progressing through party ranks, while outsiders sometimes reach senior positions very quickly.”

He added that observers will naturally ask whether such moves reflect genuine political conviction or primarily pragmatic political calculation.

Founded in 2008, PAM presents itself as a modernising political force focused on institutional reform, regional development and economic modernisation. The party has also faced corruption and abuse-of-office controversies involving some of its elected officials.

For PAM, recruiting a figure associated with effective governance and football success may reinforce its image as a party of competence while helping shift attention from criticism of the governing coalition’s economic record.

Administrative competence can strengthen political credibility, but governing requires more than managerial efficiency. Morocco continues to face major challenges, including unemployment, education, healthcare, regional inequalities and rising living costs.

Nouh El Harmouzi, head of the Arab Center for Research, believes Lekjaa’s administrative profile nevertheless explains the attention surrounding his political move.

“Few senior officials combine his experience in public finance, institutional management and strategic planning,” he told Al Jazeera.

“The next government will face enormous budgetary pressures alongside growing geopolitical and economic risks while simultaneously delivering one of the largest projects in Morocco’s modern history: the 2030 World Cup.”

The debate has also attracted attention among Moroccans abroad.

Touria Guerraoui, a Moroccan-French technology expert, said the diaspora has followed Lekjaa’s political move with particular interest because of his popularity through football.

“Many Moroccans living abroad closely followed the national team’s achievements and feel connected to that success,” she told Al Jazeera. “His decision to join PAM has made many in the diaspora more attentive to this election.”

She argued that Morocco is not unique in seeing influential senior state officials enter politics, pointing to French President Emmanuel Macron, who entered national politics after a career in the private sector and public administration.

“A large part of Morocco’s football team comes from the diaspora, and their achievements have generated enormous pride,” she said. “But many people are now asking whether the effectiveness demonstrated in football administration can also be translated into the economic and social progress that Moroccans expect.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.summary: Fouzi Lekjaa joined Authenticity and Modernity Party in September. Move reflects a broader shift in Moroccan politics, where managerial competence, state-led development and national prestige are becoming increasingly important sources of political legitimacy.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.title: Houthis renew missile and drone attacks on Yemen’s port of al-Makha
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.text:
Yemen’s Houthis have launched a new wave of missile and drone attacks on the Red Sea port city of al-Makha (Mocha), extending an assault on government-held areas along Yemen’s western coast and killing at least 11 people.

The latest attacks came on Sunday evening, less than 24 hours after an earlier barrage struck al-Makha and its commercial port. Yemeni government forces said air defences intercepted six drones during the renewed assault, while two ballistic missiles fell into the sea without hitting their targets.

Footage broadcast by the Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV showed several ballistic missiles and drones being launched. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the operation targeted Saudi troop concentrations and weapon depots in the area, according to the Reuters news agency.

Earlier on Sunday, Attacks on al-Makha killed at least 11 people, including eight military personnel and three civilians, and wounded 32 others, according to the latest toll cited by the AFP news agency.

The strikes also caused extensive damage at al-Makha’s port. Government authorities said buildings and commercial facilities were hit, while The Associated Press reported damage to port infrastructure, commercial goods and food supplies.

Government forces also said they intercepted and destroyed an unmanned explosive boat approaching the commercial port.

During the renewed attacks later on Sunday, the National Resistance Forces, which are aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government, urged residents of al-Makha to remain indoors, accusing the Houthis of carrying out indiscriminate shelling.

The Houthis said the operation involved a large number of ballistic missiles and drones and was launched in response to an alleged continued Saudi military buildup, including the reinforcement of allied forces with weapons and equipment along Yemen’s western coast and in Taiz province.

Houthi political council member Hizam al-Assad separately claimed that continuing explosions, fires and columns of smoke from the port were caused by large quantities of weapons and military equipment stored there.

The escalation was not limited to al-Makha, but also targeted the al-Khokha district, south of the coastal city of Hodeidah.

Al-Jumhuriya television, which is affiliated with the National Resistance Forces led by Presidential Leadership Council member Tareq Saleh, said the government-appointed governor of Hodeidah, al-Hassan Taher, survived an assassination attempt on Sunday after a Houthi ballistic missile struck his residence in the district.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.title: Iran war live: US ‘semi-negotiating’ with Tehran; Israel rejects Gaza plan
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.author: Adam Hancock,Zsombor Peter
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.text:
Phyllis Bennis, a Middle East specialist and fellow at the Institute for Policy Studies, says Netanyahu’s rejection of the plan for Hamas’s disarmament and Israel’s withdrawal in Gaza undermines the framework that Trump himself laid out.

She noted that Trump, in a Truth Social post, said the agreement was going to be carried out in “carefully structured phases”, under which the disarmament of Hamas and the withdrawal of Israeli forces would proceed simultaneously. But now, Netanyahu has said he would not follow the plan.

Bennis said the leader’s stance is driven by domestic politics in Israel, “where Netanyahu is under enormous pressure, both from his electoral coalition in the Knesset and public opinion, which is very much in support of his very hardline position”.

But the other factor is that US pressure on Israel remains largely rhetorical.

“The so-called pressure from the United States is simply in the arena of words. It’s only statements, and we’ve seen this from the beginning of the genocide in Gaza back in 2023,” Bennis said.

She argued concrete pressure would mean ending arms transfers and aid to Israel.

“This is what makes the genocide, which is still going on in Gaza, possible. It’s also the diplomatic support from the United States, [including] in the United Nations and protection from the International Criminal Court.”

I don’t think you’ll be able to remember a time when US President Donald Trump liked to be told no by pretty much anyone, including members of his own party, members of Congress, members of his cabinet, and definitely not foreign leaders.

This is a potentially dangerous move for Netanyahu and for Israel, because right now, they’re losing support among the Democratic Party, and American support for Israel has been completely held together by the Republican Party, and this is something that Trump often boasts about.

In a couple of recent interviews, he has said things like, “The Israelis respect me and do what I say”, “I call the shots, Netanyahu doesn’t call the shots”.

So, what Trump could do is act and tell his supporters that they no longer need to support Israel. He has maintained almost complete control over that MAGA base and the Republicans in Congress.

That said, we have seen Netanyahu defy the president in the past. For example, in Lebanon and during the MoU with Iran. And there were no repercussions.

We have more on the Houthi attack on the port of al-Makha.

Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili, the spokesman for Yemeni government forces, said in a statement on X that the seven victims of the attacks included four soldiers and three civilians.

He said 30 others were wounded.

The Houthis fired drones and missiles in the attacks, targeting both military and civilian sites, including power-generating stations, he said.

Yemeni government forces shot down 11 of the drones, he added.

Yemen’s Saba news agency, meanwhile, reported that the intercepted drones were targeting a solar power station supplying the port city, citing a military source.

The Houthis say they were targeting Saudi Arabian troops and weapons depots at the port.

Israel has formally rejected a 15-point Gaza peace plan championed by its closest ally, the United States.

The plan called for Hamas to disarm and for Israeli forces to withdraw from Gaza in stages. But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says there will be no Israeli pull-out until Hamas is fully disarmed.
