This port that holds strategic weight. It was under the control of the Ansar Allah Houthi movement from 2015 to 2017.

After that, Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognised Yemeni government launched a military operation to regain control of the port, and it has remained under their control ever since.

Experts believe that this latest attack is an indication that the Houthis are attempting to regain control of the port of al-Makha, which would give them control of two ports and a strategic advantage, including the ability to monitor shipping coming in from the Gulf of Aden and the Arabian Sea.

Experts also believe that these latest attacks are in direct defiance against the new Mecca defence pact signed between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye.

On Saturday, after the agreement was signed, the Houthi spokesperson, Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, said that Pakistan and Turkiye will be dealt with severely and will pay the price if they engage with Saudi Arabia in any military operations or in any military hostile actions against Yemen.

The Yemeni group has been attacking in Saudi Arabia, including Aramco oil facilities in Najran and in Jazan. And they continue to threaten to escalate their military operations not just against Yemeni government forces scattered around the country but also against Saudi Arabia, and according to this agreement, an attack on Saudi Arabia would be an attack on Pakistan and Turkiye.

Oil prices have climbed as markets reopened in Asia after the weekend amid continued uncertainty over the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, according to Reuters.

Brent crude futures rose 91 cents or 1.09 percent, to $84.46 a barrel by 00:56 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose 61 cents, or 0.78 percent, to $78.79 a barrel.

Both benchmarks had fallen more than 7 percent last week on hopes that Iran and Oman were close to reaching a deal that would result in a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil transited before the war.

Tehran says a deal with Oman is in its final stages, but insisted the US must still meet several conditions.

Windward says Iran’s crude export pipeline on Kharg Island remains at a “complete halt” amid the US military’s blockade of Iranian ports.

In a post on X, the maritime intelligence firm said all three of the island’s terminals are currently empty, and that 17 “dark” tankers, which have their transponders turned off, have remained stationary around it.

“The pattern is consistent with a blockade-driven export halt: no loadings, no departures, and a dark queue that isn’t moving,” it said.

Located 15 nautical miles (about 28km) from the Iranian mainland, Kharg Island is the economic backbone of Iran and typically processes about 90 percent of Iran’s crude exports.

As we’ve been reporting, Iran’s Supreme Leader Khamenei has appointed Mohsen Rezaei as his representative to the country’s Supreme National Security Council.

Rezaei, 71, is a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), a role he held for 16 years. That period included the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s, referred to in Iran as the “Sacred Defence”.

He went on to serve on Iran’s Expediency Discernment Council, which advises the supreme leader and resolves differences between parliament and the Guardian Council, a body that reviews all legislation and vets candidates for office.

Rezaei has placed high importance on Iran maintaining control of the Strait of Hormuz. In July, he said control of the waterway was worth more than “dozens of atomic bombs”. Last week, he warned the US it will “face serious risks and casualties” if its blockade of Iranian ports continues.

The US has spent decades presenting itself as the defender of a rules-based order, but Gaza has tested that claim to breaking point.

Congressman Ro Khanna joins journalist Sreenivasan Jain to examine Washington’s support for Israel, the failures of US foreign policy, and the widening gap between what the US says and what it does.

Can a superpower that has lost the world’s trust win it back – and what would that take?

Trita Parsi, executive vice president of The Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, says Iran’s recently released conditions for opening the Strait of Hormuz, as well as Trump’s wait-and-see position, are both common negotiation tactics and do not preclude the possibility of a deal.

“It is not unusual, particularly in negotiations between the US and Iran – which ultimately this is – that at certain moments, particularly close towards reaching a deal, there is some sort of an escalation by either side, or both sides, [including] putting forward some very hawkish demands,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Trump’s comments should also be seen in this context, in which he’s saying, I’ve got time on my side, your economy is really suffering,” he said.

Parsi said both Iran and US are under pressure to make a deal, though Washington likely faces more pressure.

“Iran is under a tremendous amount of pressure because of, essentially, the blockade of the blockade, and because of all kinds of other difficulties that are emerging with this war. But they are not facing the same political limitations as Trump is,” he said.

“Trump is facing midterm election coming up in just a month and a half or so. So, there are a lot of other challenges that Trump faces that I think leaves the Iranians with the impression, right or wrong, that they have more time on their side. And right now, it does appear that it is the Iranians that are playing for time, prolonging the negotiations, not Trump.”

https://spacenews.com/katalyst-space-mak.title: Katalyst Space makes progress in restoring control of Swift servicing spacecraft
https://spacenews.com/katalyst-space-mak.author: Jeff Foust
https://spacenews.com/katalyst-space-mak.text:
WASHINGTON — The company that developed a spacecraft to boost the orbit of a NASA observatory says it is making progress in recovering from its own spacecraft’s problems.

In a social media post last week, Katalyst Space Technologies said it had slowed the spin of its Link spacecraft, which had entered what the company said on July 28 was a “multi-axis spin” because of technical issues encountered during post-launch commissioning.

“LINK was spinning at approximately 9 degrees per second when recovery operations began,” the company stated. “The team has since reduced the spacecraft’s body rate to 1.47 degrees per second, where it will remain while the team prepares for the next phase of the mission.”

Controllers used one of the spacecraft’s electric thrusters to slow the spin, a process the company said consumed less than 100 grams of fuel. The company has not disclosed how much fuel remains on the spacecraft, but it said it was conserving propellant for later phases of the mission.

Katalyst said it was planning to upload a “significant flight software update” in the coming days to allow for attitude control in the spacecraft’s current configuration. That will allow the company’s engineers to restore full attitude control of the spacecraft and resume plans to head toward NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory.

The company has not said more about what caused Link to lose attitude control weeks after its July 3 launch on a Pegasus rocket. Two of the three reaction wheels on the spacecraft were not functioning after the incident, and its reaction control system thrusters were only partially working.

Current plans call for Katalyst to reach Swift in late August, a few weeks later than planned. Link will attempt to grapple Swift and use its thrusters to raise the observatory’s decaying orbit.

The $30 million mission is the first attempt by Katalyst, a satellite servicing company, to grapple another satellite and boost it. NASA has acknowledged the mission is a high-risk one, but offers benefits to both the agency and the broader space industry.

Without Link, Swift is expected to deorbit late this year or early next year, as the 22-year-old spacecraft lacks the ability to raise its own orbit. The reboost must start before Swift reaches an altitude of about 300 kilometers, a threshold it is expected to cross no earlier than October. Its altitude was just below 350 kilometers as of Aug. 9.

Jeff Foust writes about space policy, commercial space, and related topics for SpaceNews. He earned a Ph.D. in planetary sciences from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and a bachelor’s degree with honors in geophysics and planetary science...

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/10/oil-pric.title: Oil rises amid uncertainty over U.S.-Iran Strait of Hormuz deal
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/10/oil-pric.author: Justina Lee
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/10/oil-pric.text:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that Tehran is not currently in direct talks with the U.S. to end the war with Iran and open the Strait of Hormuz.

Risks remain elevated outside Hormuz too, with Houthi groups in Yemen continuing attacks and threats, according to Citi.

“Uncertainty remains high as we go into the sixth month of the Iran war,” Westpac noted.

Oil rose Monday, as traders continue to assess mixed signals from the U.S. and Iran amid worries that a deal between both countries to open the Strait of Hormuz may not be anytime soon.

Futures for international benchmark Brent crude
 for October delivery gained 1.09% to $84.46 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures
 for September advanced 0.84% to $78.84 per barrel.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that Tehran is not currently in direct talks with the U.S. to end the war with Iran and open the Strait of Hormuz, while Washington earlier asserted that a deal is near.

In addition, Iran has asked the U.S. for compensation as a condition to reopen the crucial waterway, according to a report by media outlet Independent. The Strait of Hormuz will remain shut until the U.S. meets six conditions, including ending the war and aggression against Iran and its allies, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, the head of Iran’s supreme national security council, reportedly said.

However, the U.S. maintains that any reopening must preserve unrestricted freedom of navigation without Iranian approvals, tolls, or controls, disputing key elements of the reported arranged, according to Citi. “Risks remain elevated outside Hormuz too, with Houthi groups in Yemen continuing attacks and threats against Saudi-linked shipping in the Red Sea and around Bab el Mandeb,” it added.

“Uncertainty remains high as we go into the sixth month of the Iran war,” Westpac said in a note. “The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed and the entry of the Yemen Houthis into the fray is interrupting alternative Red Sea supply routes,” it added.

“As of Aug. 9, CENTCOM has redirected 55 commercial vessels, disabled 2, and boarded 2 to ensure compliance,” according to a post on X by U.S. Central Command.

—CNBC’s Garrett Downs contributed to the report.

https://thehill.com/homenews/administrat.author: Ryan Mancini

President Trump on Sunday said there was “some contractor error” with the renovations to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool while still accusing a former Olympian canoeist of vandalizing the Washington, D.C., landmark despite charges against the athlete being dropped.

“There was substantial damage to the Reflecting Pool, also but, unfortunately, there is no video or proof, other than the damage, itself,” he wrote on Truth Social. “We are working on the Pool, and it will reopen shortly. As with many jobs, there was also some contractor error done by rushing the job for a July 4th opening, but it was a very small area of this massive Pool, and was relatively inconsequential.”

Trump claimed that a National Park Service “career employee, a highly credible witness,” saw Olympian David Hearn “in broad daylight vandalize the Reflecting Pool by ‘violently’ ripping and tugging at the Pool’s somewhat delicate coating.” He added that this employee’s testimony was provided to U.S. Attorney of the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro.

The president concluded his post by saying that security cameras “have been, and are being, installed.”

The remarks went up on Truth Social the day after Trump posted photos of alleged vandalism amid a push for Pirro to revisit the decision to drop the charges against multiple people also accused of vandalizing the pool.

This other post on Truth Social included two photos of what appeared to be graffiti and some peeling of the coating of the pool. Both photos were labeled with the word “Vandalism.”

Trump is pushing for the Justice Department to backtrack on its move to drop criminal charges against people accused of damaging the site. On Friday, the president pressed for Pirro to revisit “her hastily made decision.”

D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman formally dropped the charges against Hearn and will later decide whether prosecutors can try to charge Hearn in the future.

The president last week accused Pirro of having “choked” in response to the decision.

Pieces of “American flag blue” paint floated to the Reflecting Pool’s surface following renovations to the pool leading up to the country’s 250th anniversary. Trump claimed this, and green algae blooms that appeared in the pool’s waters, were perpetuated by vandals.

Pirro’s office blamed the contractor for overspraying and delamination after the charges against Hearn were dropped.

“The rush to complete the project led to hasty and botched work that was not remediated before the project was finished and the fencing removed,” prosecutors wrote.

https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/60.title: Sanders: 'Ban super PACs from Democratic primaries now'
https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/60.author: Ryan Mancini
https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/60.text:
This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) on Sunday called for Democratic leaders to ban the involvement of super PACs in Democratic primary elections.

Sanders’s ask was part of a letter written to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin.

The Vermont senator’s call for a ban stems from campaign donations made by the pro-Israel lobbying group American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) to ensure that Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) — whom Sanders supports — loses his race in November.

Sanders wrote that AIPAC, which backed Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) before she lost to El-Sayed, will reportedly back the Republican nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.), in his Senate campaign against El-Sayed. Sanders has been a staunch supporter of El-Sayed, stumping and campaigning for the physician.

“What is particularly obscene is not only the outrageous amount of money coming into Democratic primaries from billionaire-funded super PACs, but the reality that these special interests have no particular desire to see Democrats win,” Sanders wrote. “It is absurd that they spend tens of millions of dollars to try to determine who the Democratic nominee is and, if they fail, then proceed to support the Republican candidate in the general election.”

“That is not democracy,” he added. “That is not what Democratic voters want.”

The Vermont senator reiterated his calls to repeal the Supreme Court’s 2010 decision in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, which protects corporations and labor unions from political campaign spending. Sanders has been a longtime opponent of the decision and urged Democratic leaders to pass legislation to “move toward the public funding of elections.”

“While there are ideological differences of opinion within the big tent of the party, I would hope that we can all agree that Republican special interests should not play a role in determining the outcome of Democratic primaries,” Sanders’s letter concludes. “The time to act is now.”

Progressive Democrats like Sanders have pushed back against AIPAC’s involvement in the Democratic Party, which has seen an ideological split over support for Israel in response to the country’s war in Gaza.

El-Sayed, who is Muslim and has been critical of Israel’s government and the leadership of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu by accusing him of committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, has pushed back against the criticism of his views. He used the AIPAC issue against Stevens in a debate last month to point out her vote in Congress to send $3.3 billion in aid to Israel, a vote that 100 House Democrats voted against.

“That is the pro quo that comes with a quid of $30 million spent by AIPAC,” El-Sayed said during the debate.

Following the results of the Michigan Democratic Senate primary, AIPAC wrote that its “members remain determined to ensure that voters reject Dr. El-Sayed and his radical anti-Israel agenda in November.”

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/k.title: A golden mic, a 'clunky start' but Sandilands returns to the air
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/k.author: Tony Ibrahim
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/k.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Kyle Sandilands's new show opens with a "clunky start". (Supplied: Kyle Sandilands Live)

NSW Premier Chris Minns has dropped into radio shock jock Kyle Sandilands's first show since being sacked from his radio program earlier this year.

The subscription-based show went to air on Monday morning amid a few minor technical hiccups.

It comes just weeks after Sandilands accepted a multi-million-dollar out-of-court settlement from a wrongful termination case he brought against KIIS FM owners ARN Media.

"The golden microphone is on" were the five words that heralded a new era for Kyle Sandilands, but not everything went to plan.

When he moved his lips after the introduction, the audience tuning in for his new digital program heard nothing, with dead air lingering for five seconds.

The moment was emblematic of the teething issues that plagued the beginning of Kyle Sandilands Live, the subscription-only podcast looking to reinvent the controversial shock jock after his decades on commercial radio came to an end earlier this year.

As the seasoned presenter ploughed on to introduce the show's new personalities, audio played loudly and for a touch too long, briefly drowning Sandilands's commentary.

"The brand new Kyle Sandilands Live program, it is a new invention, it is live, we're all here," Sandilands said.

"And it's a digital mess behind the scenes."

His longtime friend and manager Bruno Bouchet chimed in.

He had skipped sleep over the course of a week to help develop the show.

"If everything went smoothly, it would've been worse, not sleeping … and everything like that," Mr Bouchet said.

"But you know, it all went to shit."

Sandilands pushed back: "It didn't go to shit, I just can't hear, I can't hear any audio.

"I would imagine … the man speaking behind the microphone should be the main one that hears what's going on."

The show's first few minutes acknowledged the efforts that come with building a podcast quickly, as Sandilands tried to capitalise on media interest from a settled court dispute, and popularity from his radio and TV career.

New South Wales Premier Chris Minns visited the show as the inaugural guest, bringing with him "golden" scissors for a ribbon cutting.

But subscribers barely got to witness the moment, as it took place in the background and was obscured by a pylon and staff member.

Sandilands praised Mr Minns for being a Labor politician with appeal beyond his party, and brought up a recent chance meeting in the Blue Mountains.

Premier Chris Minns on Kyle Sandilands Live's first episode. (Supplied)

He also asked the premier for his opinion on his old show's cancellation.

"I was worried for you, I was worried about the show," Mr Minns said.

"There's not many shows in radio or TV or ratings history that don't keep going when they're number one.

Sandilands described the program as a work in progress.

"Well would you call it up and running? I feel it's half up and running."

It is Kyle's first day on air after being sacked by ARN from his show co-hosted with Jackie O Henderson in February. (Supplied)

Six months have passed since an on-air dispute with Sandilands's longtime radio co-host Jackie 'O' Henderson led to the eventual demise of his breakfast show on Kiss FM.

In February, owner ARN Media told the Australian Stock Exchange Jackie O had "given notice that she cannot continue to work with Mr Sandilands".

It signalled the ending of radio contracts with the duo paid a combined $200 million.

Sandilands launched the new show after negotiating a multi-million-dollar out of court settlement over his termination from ARN. (ABC News: Jamie McKinnell)

Separate wrongful termination cases were launched by Sandilands and Jackie O against ARN Media in the Federal Court.

Sandilands settled his dispute with his former employer in June for $12.09 million, well under the $85 million he initially sought.

The deal also included a provision where ARN Media would receive 19.9 per cent of the revenue from Kyle Sandilands Live for three years, in exchange for providing $1.5 million in advertising.

Jackie O has not settled her dispute and was seeking $82 million in compensation for wrongful termination.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/w.title: Phones across western Cape York down again
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/w.author: Brendan Mounter, Sophie Johnson, and Charlie McKillop
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Telecommunications Services Industry

Telstra says its cabling was damaged in a bushfire near Weipa on Saturday evening. (Supplied: Chad King)

Phones across western Cape York were down again this morning just hours after services were restored following a bushfire which crippled the network over the weekend.

Businesses and community leaders are calling for better solutions for telecommunications in the bush.

Telecommunications across western Cape York have suffered another outage this morning just hours after services were restored following a bushfire which crippled the network over the weekend.

Rachel Cliffe, Telstra's northern Queensland general manager, said the latest outage was the result of a "secondary power-related fault" at one of the telco's sites.

"Some of our bigger sites have more power backups and some of our smaller sites don't, it's all engineered for the power reserves that are needed.

"Typically it's the power reserves needed before we can get a technician to that site before it goes down."

"We again apologise … this is a secondary fault to the one we had related to the bushfire on Saturday through Sunday."

That outage saw mobile phone reception affected in the towns of Weipa, Mapoon and Aurukun as well as Mission River, Napranum and Rocky Point, with services down for almost 30 hours.

Customers were unable to make any calls, including to Triple Zero (000), from around 5pm on Saturday evening until 10pm last night.

Ms Cliffe has defended the time it took to restore services, saying crews needed to be deployed from Cairns to repair significant damage to infrastructure.

"Unfortunately, a bushfire burnt our pit and burnt our optic fibre that was in the pit," she said.

"It doesn't take two minutes to do [fix] this … we needed to replace large lengths of optic fibre and connect them in.

"Of course, we never, ever want this type of incident to occur and we do apologise to the customers impacted."

Local businesses including the Weipa Campground were thrown into chaos when the initial outage hit over the weekend.

Campground manager Angela Burr said losing access to internet services had the biggest impact on the business.

At the time of the outage, guests were arriving and Ms Burr was unable to confirm who had booked, who had paid, and which sites were available for walk-ins.

She said the business had to go back to basics to get through.

The Weipa Campground was impacted by the initial Telstra outage. (Supplied: Weipa Camping Ground)

"[We took] down very detailed information of our guests, trying to have a pretty good memory on which sites have been booked and which sites are available," she said.

"We did have to set up Starlink, which did take some time to get active, but thankfully we were back fully operational by the following day, so Sunday, although slower, it still worked well."

She said all guests who hadn't been able to pay before the Starlink was set up did the right thing the following morning.

"Luckily enough, we weren't affected financially by this," she said.

"It hit us hard, the realisation of how much we truly rely on this system."

The community of Mapoon, about 80 kilometres north of Weipa, was affected by both outages.

The shire's CEO Chad King said council had set up additional free wi-fi yesterday but the inability for residents to make Triple Zero calls made for an anxious weekend.

The western Cape York community of Mapoon in far north Queensland is home to around 500 people. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

Mr King said Telstra removed fixed lines to the community during the NBN rollout and were now reliant on a single phone tower which the outage highlighted as a "single point of failure".

He said better services in the bush were needed.

"We need to think about how we make these telecommunications more resilient given that we're so reliant on them now," Mr King said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/w.title: WNBA player claims 'white privilege' saw her ejected after foul
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

DiJonai Carrington, left, was ejected for whacking Sophie Cunningham around the head. (Getty Images: Michael Reaves)

DiJonai Carrington was ejected for a foul, deemed "Flagrant" by officials, on Indiana Fever's Sophie Cunningham where she hit her head and neck, knocking her to the ground.

Carrington posted "white privilege" on social media minutes after being booted from the game, tagging the Fever.

Carrington's coach said the club would "handle" her post, while Cunningham said "there's no reason even to play that card".

DiJonai Carrington of the Chicago Sky has been ejected after being called for a Flagrant 2 foul on Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever.

Minutes after the eviction on Saturday (local time), Carrington posted on social media the words "WHITE PRIVILEGE" and tagged the Fever.

Cunningham, who is white, was shooting a fast-break lay-up in the first quarter when Carrington, who is black, came from behind and hit her in the head and neck, knocking her to the court as the shot went in.

Cunningham said she thought the foul in the 90–86 Indiana win was "absolutely" intentional.

"Clearly I think it was unnecessary," Cunningham said.

"I've never really spoken to her and I have no beef with her, but I guess she has some pent-up stuff."

DiJonai Carrington had little to complain about, most suggested. (Getty Images: Michael Reaves)

Fever coach Stephanie White had a different view of the play.

"It was a hard foul," White said.

"I don't think that DiJonai intentionally came out to get her across the neck like she did, but it did happen, and I thought it was the right call."

Cunningham got up immediately, charged toward Carrington and pushed her as she was held back by a teammate.

"I popped up," Cunningham said.

"I'm not going to let anyone just do that to me. I think everyone knows that. I think that's why she did it, because she wants attention."

Sophie Cunningham had to be held back after popping up after the foul. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/Melissa Tamez)

The play was reviewed and upgraded to a Flagrant 2 after the referee said there was wind-up, impact and follow-through on the foul.

Sky coach Tyler Marsh said he had not seen a replay of the play, but that seeing it live, he thought Carrington was making a play on the ball and that he did not believe it warranted a Flagrant 2 foul.

"I haven't looked at that play since, so I really don't know if it was justified or not," he said.

"But, that's what I thought in the moment."

Marsh was then asked about Carrington's social media post.

"I have to get back to you on that because I'm just now hearing about that," he said.

"So yeah, we'll handle that."

But Cunningham had plenty to say about the post.

"I think the league is taking care of that," she said.

"This has nothing to do with race. Last year, I did the same thing and I got kicked out. And I deserved to be kicked out. There's no reason even to play that card."

In the third quarter, Fever star Caitlin Clark was assessed a technical foul after she made contact with a referee when she was forced out of bounds.

The outsized spotlight on Caitlin Clark has prompted some to suggest others in the WNBA are jealous of her, but two champions of the league say that is nonsense.

The technical was Clark's eighth of the season, triggering a one-game suspension for Indiana's next game if not rescinded by the league.

"She said I ran into her," Clark said in a post-game television interview.

"I've already watched it on the tape, so we'll let the league decide. But it wasn't intentional or anything, so I'm hoping it's getting rescinded,"

A few hours after the game, Clark got her way. The WNBA rescinded the technical foul.

Cunningham has frequently come to Clark's defence after physical play by opponents and has become one of the higher-profile players in the league this season.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/b.title: Brazilian footballer falls in tunnel after scoring disallowed goal
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/b.author: Ahmed Yussuf
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Jacy Maranhão falls into a tunnel during a goal celebration.

Brazilian footballer Jacy Maranhão was rushing to meet a sea of his supporters, ball in hand and jumping with joy, before he fell down a dark tunnel.

The Corbita defender had just put his club 2-0 up against Chapecoense in the first half of a game in the Brazilian Serie A.

But just as he found his footing again and dusted himself off from the fall, the referee halted the game.

On review, the Video Assistant Referee (VAR) found the 29-year-old's goal was offside.

Jacy managed to continue playing into the first few minutes of the second half before being substituted with an injury.

The incident was not the first time a footballer had fallen foul of the tunnel at the Estádio Major Antônio Couto Pereira.

Cameroonian forward Joel falls into the tunnel during goal celebration in 2014.

Almost a decade earlier, Cameroonian forward Diederrick Joel Tagueu-Tadjo ran to the same end of the pitch, jumping over the same advertising hoardings before falling into the now-infamous Corbita tunnel.

But unlike Jacy, his goal was not ruled out, and he managed to finish the game against São Paulo.

But according to Brazilian journalist Leonardo Mendes Jr, there was a striking similarity to the two incidents.

"There's one detail that makes it even more unbelievable," he posted on social media.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/c.title: Man accused of Coles Bay home invasion, arson pleads not guilty
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/c.author: Hayden Smith
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Law, Crime and Justice

Grant Whelan spent six days in hospital following the alleged assault. (Supplied)

Jason Robert Burns, 33, has pleaded not guilty to charges stemming from an alleged violent home invasion at Coles Bay.

Police allege he is among a group of three men who attacked and robbed a 76-year-old last month.

He is set to front the Supreme Court on September 25.

One of the three men accused of attacking a 76-year-old on Tasmania's east coast last month has pleaded not guilty.

Jason Robert Burns appeared in the Launceston Magistrates Court today on multiple charges, including aggravated armed robbery, aggravated assault, motor vehicle stealing and arson.

The 33-year-old from the Launceston suburb of Invermay is one of three men allegedly behind a violent attack on a Coles Bay man on the morning of Saturday, July 11.

Police allege 76-year-old Grant Whelan was tied up at his home, having firearms stolen, his car stolen and his house set alight.

Mr Whelan spent six days in the Royal Hobart Hospital after the incident.

Appearing via video link from prison this morning, Mr Burns pleaded not guilty through his lawyer.

The destroyed remains of Grant Whelan's Coles Bay house. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

He is due to appear in the Supreme Court in Launceston on September 25.

Magistrate Simon Brown remanded him in custody.

Mr Burns was arrested alongside two other men — Charlie Hills, 29, and Hayden Morrison, 33.

They all face similar charges.

Mr Hills's lawyer previously indicated his client would plead not guilty. Mr Hills was granted bail on July 31, and is due to return to court on September 8.

Mr Morrison is due to reappear in court tomorrow.

There has been an outpouring in support from the Tasmanian community for Mr Whelan since the incident, with more than $100,000 raised in an online fundraiser and volunteers working to help clean up the burnt remains of his home.

Mr Whelan was released from the Royal Hobart Hospital on July 16 after six days.

The missing firearms remain missing, with Tasmanian Police calling for information.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/b.title: Chiefs sign premiership winger To'o away from Panthers
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/b.author: Michael Doyle
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Brian To'o (centre) will leave the Penrith Panthers at the end of 2027. (Getty Images: Jeremy Ng)

Brian To'o will join the PNG Chiefs for their inaugural NRL season in 2028, signing a three-year deal.

To'o has won four premierships with the Penrith Panthers, and 2027 will be his final year with the club.

To'o is the sixth player signed by the Chiefs as the new club builds its roster for 2028.

Four-time premiership-winning winger Brian To'o has become the sixth player to sign with the PNG Chiefs for their inaugural NRL season in 2028.

The signing of the Penrith Panthers flyer, who has represented NSW in State of Origin and Samoa in Test matches, was announced by the Chiefs on Monday.

To'o has signed a three-year deal to join the Chiefs, with 2027 to be his final year with the Panthers.

Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

"Brian is an exceptional rugby league player, but this signing is about much more than football," PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson said.

"The PNG Chiefs will be a club proudly built in Papua New Guinea but with a strong Pacific identity.

"Across our region, family, culture, community and rugby league are deeply connected, and Brian represents those values every time he takes the field.

"He is fiercely proud of his Samoan heritage, incredibly close to his family and understands what it means to represent something bigger than yourself.

"That is exactly the kind of person we want wearing the Chiefs jersey."

To'o has been a key component of the Penrith Panthers dynasty, which won four consecutive premierships from 2021–2024, were grand finalists in 2020 and made last year's preliminary final.

The Panthers are on top of the NRL ladder in 2026, seeking a fifth title in six years.

To'o has played 151 matches for the Panthers since making his debut in 2019, scoring 99 tries to date.

He has played 17 Origins for the Blues, and 11 Tests for Samoa.

"Brian is an exceptional player, but he's an even better person. He's a great teammate, a devoted family man and someone who brings so much energy and positivity to our club every day," Penrith coach Ivan Cleary said.

"He's been a huge part of what we've built here and we're looking forward to sharing one more season with him before he begins his next chapter."

The Chiefs have now signed six players to its maiden roster, but have already secured key talent.

Former Penrith five-eighth Jarome Luai, who won four premierships with To'o, was the club's marquee signing earlier this year.

Alex Johnston, the all-time leading try scorer in Australian premiership rugby league, was a key outside back signed along with NSW Origin representative Zac Lomax.

Sydney Roosters utility Connor Watson and Englishman Matty Lees have also been signed.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Road Accidents and Incidents

Mount Buller is a popular ski resort in Victoria's High Country. (ABC News: Margaret Burin)

One person has died and another is recovering in hospital after a tree fell on a car at the Victorian snow resort town of Mount Buller.

Victoria Police say emergency services responded to the single-vehicle incident about 9:15am on Monday.

Police say a report will be prepared for the coroner.

A man has died after a tree fell onto a car at Mount Buller in Victoria's north-east.

Emergency services, including Victoria Police and Advanced Life Support paramedics, responded to the single-vehicle incident about 9:15am today.

Police believe the vehicle was travelling along Mount Buller Road when a tree fell onto the car.

The female driver was taken to Wangaratta Hospital by road in a serious condition with an upper body injury.

A male passenger, who is yet to be formally identified, died at the scene.

Police said the investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident remained ongoing and a report would be prepared for the coroner.

Mount Buller Road is closed in both directions, with significant delays expected.

Alpine Resorts Victoria (ARV) said it was working closely with authorities to support the emergency services response, but said Mount Buller Road was expected be closed for an extended period.

Overnight resort visitors are being advised to contact their accommodation providers, and ARV said the Mount Buller Sports Hall had been opened for resort visitors to shelter from the conditions.

State Emergency Service (SES) crews in the state's north-east had 80 requests for assistance overnight.

SES Hume regional duty officer Michael Isbister told ABC Goulburn Murray Breakfast that crews had already completed five water rescues.

"We had one member of the public wake up and be completely surrounded by water," he said.

With record-breaking rainfall totals across the region, the SES is warning residents to stay alert as more rain comes through.

"The ground is extremely wet, so it's going to [make] these rivers flow and rise really quickly," he said.

A driver and passenger were rescued after their vehicle became stuck in floodwater at Lexton in Victoria's west, early this morning.

The incident occurred along the Sunraysia Highway north-west of Ballarat.

Flooding has forced the closure of a number of roads across the Pyrenees Shire, including at Avoca, Lexton and Beaufort.

More than 135 millimetres of rain has fallen over parts of Ballarat and surrounds since midnight.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/p.title: Up to 30 vehicles suffer tyre damage due to freeway pothole 'carnage'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/p.author: Madeleine Stuchbery and Zaida Glibanovic
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Road Accidents and Incidents

Potholes damage dozens of cars on the Princes Freeway at Bunyip

Up to 30 vehicles have suffered pothole damage on the Princes Freeway at Bunyip due to potholes.

The Bureau of Meteorology has recorded about 15 millimetres of rain in the area since last night.

The Victorian government and opposition have made repairing potholes central to their election campaigns.

Up to 30 vehicles have been forced off the road due to large potholes that have opened along the Princes Freeway at Bunyip in Victoria's east.

The Victorian transport department has warned of Melbourne-bound delays on the freeway as a result of the road damage just before Hope Street.

Garry, who was driving through the area, has told ABC Melbourne it was carnage, with more than two dozen cars damaged as a result.

"For about 15 kilometres thereafter, cars were pulled over with damaged rims," he said.

"We were shocked, and as you approach, I thought there was a major accident.

"The highway has just fallen apart. I reckon there was probably 30 cars pulled over."

Road crews have had a busy morning after potholes forced up to 30 vehicles off the road at Bunyip, east of Melbourne. (ABC Gippsland: Danielle Kutchel)

Admiral Towing operator David Gridley said he knew of at least 30 vehicles that had suffered flat or blown tyres.

"There's just multiple very large potholes that when they're full of water, they're just impossible to see," he said.

"The holes are that deep that they're just destroying the tyres.

"It's happened once before where we've had a series of potholes that have caused a major issue for weeks, and it's just happening again."

He blamed the problem on a failure to properly maintain roads.

"The roads, they're not getting repaired properly. We're getting patch jobs and the patches are just removing themselves in the weather," Mr Gridley said.

The department issued its warnings shortly after 7am and by 10am, most vehicles had been repaired or towed.

At nearby Warragul, the Bureau of Meteorology has recorded about 15 millimetres of rain since last night.

In November, more than 20 cars were damaged when they struck a large pothole on the Princes Freeway at Nar Nar Goon.

Potholes have become a major state political issue, with the government promising $1 billion for pothole repairs in this year's budget.

The Coalition has also pledged $5 billion to repair and rebuild the state's roads if it wins the November state election.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/p.title: Yeo learns fate on pec in seismic moment for Panthers
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Isaah Yeo will not need surgery, in a boost to his hopes of playing again in 2026. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Penrith Panthers captain Isaah Yeo has avoided serious injury and is a chance to play again this NRL season.

Yeo came off the field during Penrith's loss last week to the New Zealand Warriors in Auckland.

Yeo will begin rehabilitation in a bid to play again in 2026.

Penrith's premiership charge has received a massive boost, with Isaah Yeo a chance to play again this year after avoiding surgery on his pectoral injury.

Yeo had been at risk of missing the rest of the NRL season after he left the field in Friday's loss to the Warriors, in what shaped as a major blow for the Panthers.

But Penrith medical staff confirmed on Monday the club's co-captain would not go under the knife following scans, and could begin rehabilitation in a bid to play again in 2026.

The news will also likely come as a relief to Australia coach Kevin Walters, with Yeo expected to again lead the Kangaroos at the World Cup if he avoids later surgery.

Former Panther Apisai Koroisau missed just one week with a pectoral injury early this year, as opposed to the 10 weeks usually out if surgery is required.

Penrith has made a habit of having players play through injury to be part of premiership wins throughout their dynasty.

Almost half of their squad were walking wounded through the first title of their four-peat in 2021, which the club compared to climbing Mount Everest.

Halves Jarome Luai and Nathan Cleary both played through persistent shoulder issues in 2023 and 2024 respectively, with both requiring surgery afterwards.

Had Yeo been sidelined, it would have been a monumental blow to the first-placed Panthers, given the role he plays in both attack and defence at lock.

Ex-Panther Spencer Leniu described Yeo as the "heartbeat" of Penrith's team over the weekend, declaring his injury would be a "massive loss" for the club.

Penrith faces Leniu's Sydney Roosters in a blockbuster top-of-the-table clash on Thursday night, which Yeo would not be expected to play in.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/m.title: After decades of pleas, fallen miners from a historic mine will be memorialised
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/m.author: Abbey Halter and Tim Little
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Mining Accidents and Incidents

Steve Trevor (left) lost his brother at Mount Isa Mines about 30 years ago. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

The North West Queensland town of Mount Isa will soon have a memorial put up to honour miners who have died at its flagship mine.

The state government, Glencore, and Mount Isa City Council are funding the $4.7 million landmark.

The memorial is set to be built by the end of 2027.

After almost 30 years of advocacy, a multimillion dollar memorial honouring 151 fallen workers who died at a historic mine will be built in outback Queensland.

The $4.7 million Mount Isa Miners Memorial will be jointly funded by the state government, the mine's current owner Glencore, and the Mount Isa City Council.

Overlooking Mount Isa Mines, which sits directly across from the North West Queensland town, the landmark set to be erected at Frank Aston Hill is expected to be completed by late 2027.

Designs for a proposed miners' memorial were drafted in 2023 and paid for by the Mount Isa City Council.  (Supplied)

Former Mount Isa resident Steve Trevor lost his brother Tony in a mining accident in 1995 and said he has spent decades waiting for a formal memorial site.

"The memories are still sharp in my mind," Mr Trevor said.

Operations at the Mount Isa underground copper mine officially ceased last year. (Supplied)

"[The memorial] will bring recognition of a life lost. What they gave to their community is the ultimate sacrifice.

Steve Trevor (left) and John Moran have been advocating for a miners memorial to be built in Mount Isa for decades. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Mr Trevor said his brother's death was still a haunting memory.

"I remember I got my call about my brother's passing at midnight, and it was terrible not just for myself but my family, my mother, my father," he said.

"It means not just a lot to myself, but there's the 151 families as well."

Former local John Moran, who first called for a memorial in 1998, said it was a historic day for Mount Isa.

"[The fallen miners] were residents of Mount Isa. They never flew in or flew out," Mr Moran said.

"Let's hope that there's never another one.

"As I've said for a long, long time, those 151 workers deserve to be remembered, but more importantly they deserve to be memorialised."

Mount Isa Mines underground copper mine closed in July of last year. (Supplied: Mount Isa Mines Photographic Collection/ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

Mount Isa Mayor Peta MacRae said she was proud the long called-for memorial was finally becoming a reality.

"We are hoping to get the sod turned and get underway as soon as we possibly can," Mayor MacRae said.

Peta MacRae says the memorial plans will go to tender as soon as possible. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

She said $700,000 of the funding would be provided by council for the construction of the memorial.

Despite plans and costings being drawn up in 2023, support for the project ultimately stalled without the backing of the previous state government.

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said the Crisafulli government would be injecting $2 million into the memorial through repurposed funds from the Mount Isa Transition Fund.

Jarrod Bleijie and mines minister Dale Last say the Queensland government is injecting $2 million into building the miners memorial. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Mr Bleijie said re-allocating the funds for a memorial site still honoured its original plan of supporting the region's economy after the closure of the Mount Isa underground copper mine in 2025.

"When people are coming to towns like Mount Isa, that's heart and soul is the mining community, they can reflect and be educated on how important the mining industry is in the great state of Queensland," he said.

While there had been no deaths at Mount Isa Mines since Glencore took ownership in 2013, the mining giant is also putting $2 million into the site.

Glencore's Troy WIlson and Maryann Wipaki say bringing the memorial into existence is important for Mount Isa. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Glencore Metals chief operating officer Troy Wilson began his career at the famed mine in the 1990s and said the mine and local community had been connected for over a century.

"But that history has suffered some profound loss and we must remember every day that there's people that went to work here and didn't get to come home," Mr Wilson said.

"This memorial will create a permanent place where we can honour all those that have gone before.

"It also will stand as an opportunity for us to remember what our responsibility is and that's to learn from the past, to continuously improve, and to ensure we do everything we can every day to make sure all of our workers go home safe at the end of the day."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/t.title: Walker announces retirement after one last shot at AFL premiership
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/t.author: Michael Doyle and Daniel Keane
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Taylor Walker has played more than 300 AFL matches. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/James Elsby)

Adelaide Crows great Taylor Walker has announced he will retire from the AFL at the end of the season.

Walker, who debuted in 2009, has played 316 matches and kicked 706 goals to date.

Adelaide travels to Perth for a Friday night blockbuster against ladder-leaders Fremantle, then hosts GWS in the final round of the home and away season at Adelaide Oval.

Adelaide Crows great Taylor Walker has announced the 2026 AFL season will be his last, saying he hopes to end his career as a premiership winner.

The Crows today announced the veteran of 316 games would bring an end to his playing career, where he has kicked a club-record 706 goals to date.

Affectionately known as Tex, the 36-year-old told media after the announcement that the decision to step away had been "probably the hardest one of my life".

"I knew it was the right time for me and the football club that I retire at the end of the year, hopefully with a premiership cup or a medallion around my neck," he said.

"I don't want to be that player that goes that extra year or probably outstays their welcome.

"The closer I've got to the end, it's probably become a little bit more evident that it might be this year, but I've sort of treated it like my last year for the past six years."

Walker was drafted by the Crows in 2007 and made his AFL debut during the 2009 season.

He captained the club from 2015-2019, where he was twice named the AFL Players Association Best Captain in 2016 and 2017. He also led the Crows to the 2017 grand final, the club's most recent appearance in the sport's biggest game.

Today Walker was asked about one of the low points in his career — when he was fined and suspended for using a racial slur in 2021.

The Crows great described the incident as the "one thing I wish never happened".

"That was an incredibly difficult time for my family and I, and I suppose the biggest thing I learnt was that words don't just hurt one person, they can hurt so many different people, and I feel like I'm a better person for that mistake that I made," he said.

While Walker's sights remain firmly fixed on the remainder of the season, he said his hometown of Broken Hill had been very much in his thoughts as he looked both back and forward.

"I grew up barracking for the Adelaide footy club. It was my dream. I had Crows posters all through my room as a little kid," he said.

"I've said to my two best mates that are still playing back in Broken Hill that I want to go and try and win a premiership back there, so we'll try and do that next year."

The Crows currently sit fifth on the AFL ladder, level on points with fourth-placed Brisbane on percentage.

Adelaide travels to Perth for a Friday night blockbuster against ladder-leaders Fremantle, then hosts GWS in the final round of the home and away season at Adelaide Oval.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Burnham begins U.K. cost-of-living tour amid row over prisoners
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: Alex Wickham
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is embarking on a nationwide tour to promote new policies aimed at reducing the cost of living, just as controversy over his prisons policy threatens to end the honeymoon he’s enjoyed since taking office.

Burnham will on Monday announce a consultation to determine whether companies should be banned from advertising misleading recommended retail prices that exaggerate discount offers. He will also bring forward plans to crack down on expensive subscriptions that are difficult to cancel, a policy his predecessor, Keir Starmer, had been due to implement in spring 2027.

Burnham is rolling out what he’s calling “everyday fixes” for smaller problems that contribute to the cost of living, part of a slew of announcements he will make as he tours the U.K. in August.

The new premier, who replaced Starmer three weeks ago, is trying to build momentum after achieving an early boost that has put his governing Labour Party ahead of Nigel Farage’s Reform U.K. in some recent polls. He has said he’s working on a more detailed 10-year plan for the country that will be informed by the tour and unveiled in the coming months.

“These are just two of the everyday fixes we’re going to be rolling out — today is just the start,” Burnham said in remarks emailed by his office. “We want to put more money in people’s pockets and give people hope that politics really can work for them and their everyday lives.”

The new administration’s first budget is due Oct. 28, when Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey is expected to announce more radical policies to deliver on Burnham’s promise to be the most transformational British leader in four decades, even as pressure on Britain’s public finances and economy is exacerbated by the Iran war.

Burnham’s summer tour and his early polling success are in danger of being overshadowed this week by growing scrutiny of his approach to reducing prison overcrowding, which poses his first major political test since he entered 10 Downing Street.

An early-release program drawn up by the Starmer government to address an overcrowding crisis inherited from the previous Conservative administration is due to begin in the fall.

Public anger at the prospect of releasing of some dangerous criminals earlier in their sentences led Burnham to announce last week that he was restricting the program to exclude the release of serious sex offenders.

That provoked questions about other criminals who are still set for potential early release, including the high-profile and emotive case of two men convicted of the 2019 manslaughter of a police officer, Andrew Harper, who would be eligible for release halfway through their sentences.

Burnham is under pressure from police and Harper’s family to stop the two men from being released and is considering options for doing so. Still, a U-turn would only raise further questions about other criminals being let out under the program.

Some 5,000 offenders are expected to be released early over the next 10 months, down from 6,000 before Burnham’s intervention. The premier had said he wanted to impose further restrictions but was unable to do so.

The government’s plan to relieve overcrowding while seeking tougher release conditions depends on a probation service that’s suffering from an acute shortfall in staff.

Groups representing probation staff said the government will struggle to safely implement the changes without spending more to address a retention crisis.

Mel Stride, the Conservative shadow chancellor, said Labour’s own policies, such as tax increases on businesses, are increasing the cost of living, and warned proposals to release criminals were “disastrous.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: North Korean hacking group builds AI tools for cyberattacks, report says
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
SEOUL – A North Korean hacking group built large ⁠language model tools and collected software that could help automate cyberattacks, analyze stolen material and produce more convincing phishing campaigns, a South Korean cybersecurity firm said on ​Monday.

The cybersecurity firm, Genians, said it found evidence ‌that ‌the North Korean-linked group Kimsuky had ​set up tools for running and managing AI models locally, including Ollama, GPT4All and Msty, alongside document ⁠search technology known as retrieval augmented generation.

According to the company, ⁠the tools could allow operators to process documents without sending sensitive information to outside ​AI services.

Genians also ⁠found AI agent development frameworks, speech-to-text software and Cursor, an AI-assisted coding ⁠tool, on infrastructure it ​linked to the campaign.

The findings ​suggest Kimsuky is moving beyond using generative AI ​to ‌create phishing lures and is building capacity to integrate existing AI models into malware development, data analysis and attack automation, Genians said in ‌a report.

Genians also said it found finance and cryptocurrency-themed decoy documents that appeared to have been generated with AI. The materials were designed to resemble ​legitimate ​investment reports and other workplace documents, it ​said.

The company’s findings could not be independently ⁠verified.

North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue generation, according to U.S. and South Korean authorities, as ​well as cybersecurity experts.

The U.S. Treasury in 2023 sanctioned Kimsuky as a North Korean government-controlled cyber-espionage group, saying it gathered intelligence in support of Pyongyang’s strategic objectives.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Naomi Osaka and Elena Rybakina win to set up clash in Canadian Open quarterfinals
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
TORONTO – World No. 2 Elena Rybakina survived a huge scare to battle into the Canadian Open quarterfinals on Sunday in Toronto, while fourth-ranked Coco Gauff cruised through.

Kazakhstan’s Rybakina recovered from being 0-3 and two breaks down in the final set to beat Liudmila Samsonova 6-4, 4-6, 6-4 before American Gauff swept aside another Russian, teenage qualifier Alina Korneeva, 6-3, 6-1 in Toronto.

Rybakina will face a quarterfinal against four-time Grand Slam champion Naomi Osaka, who eliminated home hero Leylah Fernandez 6-4, 6-4.

Gauff reached the last eight in Canada for the first time since 2023 and will come up against Swiss 12th seed Belinda Bencic, who won 6-4, 6-0 in 73 minutes over 20th-ranked Alexandra Eala, a Filipina who won her first WTA title last Monday in Washington.

“My main focus today was let me try and close it out,” said Gauff, who has not dropped a set in Canada.

“Probably not the way I should be thinking, but it worked today.

“I’m proud of how the last three matches have gone and just knowing if I have to go the distance I’m ready but obviously would prefer to cut it short if I can.”

Osaka broke in the seventh game of each set to advance in 82 minutes.

“It was all pretty good for me,” the 13th-ranked Osaka said. “She has a great attitude. She’s consistent and she will fight. She’s kind of like a bulldog.”

The Japanese star, who has never faced Rybakina, said sound groundstrokes were key.

“When I feel comfortable or at least confident in myself knowing I can run things down, I loosen up a lot,” Osaka said.

“I was catching my service toss a couple times. Hopefully in the next match I don’t do that as often.

“I need to be confident in myself, execute what I can and at the end of the day just try my best and whatever happens happens.”

Bencic connected on 64.4% of her first serves and won 72.4% of those points in a 73-minute victory, her 10th win in a row over left-handed opponents.

“I hate to play against lefties so I’m surprised by this statistic,” Bencic said. “Very tricky.

“Maybe helped me I played a lefty the round before against Taylor Townsend. I got used to the serve a little bit. I wish I was a lefty too.”

Japan’s public and private sectors are stepping up joint efforts to revive the nation’s struggling shipbuilding industry.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: U.S. Forces airlift water for Kumamoto earthquake victims
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
The U.S. Forces Japan on Sunday airlifted a total of about 33,000 bottles of drinking water for victims of the recent powerful earthquake that struck Kumamoto Prefecture.

A KC-130 aircraft of the U.S. military transported the water, weighing about 16 tons, from the U.S. Air Force’s Yokota Air Base in Tokyo to the Japanese Ground Self-Defense Force’s Vice Camp Takayubaru in the Kumamoto town of Mashiki.

The water will be conveyed to relief goods management stations by land by the Self-Defense Forces and then delivered to people affected by the temblor, which struck on July 28.

U.S. Ambassador to Japan George Glass inspected the operation at Vice Camp Takayubaru.

Glass later visited Kumamoto Gov. Takashi Kimura at the prefectural government office with Lt. Gen. Stephen Jost, commander of the U.S. Forces Japan.

The ambassador told Kimura that it was an honor for his country to provide assistance for Japan, and that the U.S. was glad to respond to a Japanese government request for support.

The U.S. Forces Japan conducted Operation Tomodachi to provide support after Japan’s Tohoku region was hit hard by a strong earthquake and tsunami in March 2011. Tomodachi means friend in Japanese.

The U.S. military also delivered relief goods using its transport aircraft after major earthquakes in Kumamoto in April 2016 and a powerful quake in the Noto Peninsula in Ishikawa Prefecture in January 2024.

Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told reporters Sunday that the U.S. military’s assistance shows the strength of the bond between the two countries and that their cooperative relationship is working well in the support of disaster victims.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Indonesia closes national park as wildfire spreads
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
JAKARTA – Indonesian authorities have closed access to a national park on Java Island as firefighters battle a wildfire raging there for about a week.

The blaze has razed 176 hectares since it broke out last Monday in the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park, near the popular East Java tourist destination of Mount Bromo, a disaster official said.

Authorities barred access to visitors late Saturday until further notice.

No injuries or property destruction have been reported, said National Disaster Mitigation Agency spokesman Abdul Muhari.

Two water-bombing helicopters have been deployed to douse the flames in areas difficult for firefighters to reach due to steep slopes and strong winds, he said in a statement Sunday.

“These conditions make air operations important to reach areas that cannot be accessed optimally by land,” the official said.

A blaze destroyed more than 500 hectares of land on Mount Bromo in 2023 when a couple lit a flare during a pre-wedding photo shoot.

Indonesia is projected to experience a more intense and prolonged dry season this year, raising the risk of wildfires and drought, due in part to the El Nino weather phenomenon, weather agency BMKG said.

More than 107,000 hectares of land burned in Indonesia in the first half of this year, over twice the area destroyed in wildfires in 2023.

El Nino is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon that brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns. It usually causes drier conditions in Southeast Asia and India.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
A mutual defense pact between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan could be expanded to include other regional states including Egypt, Turkey’s foreign minister said.

Several countries are interested in joining the trilateral security agreement that was signed in Mecca on Friday, Hakan Fidan told state-run Anadolu Agency in an interview late Saturday.

“I believe that in the next stage, Egypt will also be among us,” he said. “There are a few technical matters there. Once those are implemented, there is no reason for Egypt not to be included as well.”

Egypt’s accession would add one of the biggest militaries in the Middle East to the alliance and another key Sunni Muslim-majority state in the region.

Officials at Egypt’s Foreign Ministry weren’t immediately available for comment.

The grouping, which Fidan said is provisionally called the “Mecca Alliance” or “Mecca Defense Alliance,” was formed against the backdrop of the war in Iran and commits members to jointly retaliate against attacks on allies.

Pakistan’s participation shows the alliance’s scope is regional and “much broader” than the Middle East, Fidan said.

“In our president’s vision, we are not meant to remain limited to three countries anyway; we are meant to grow further,” he added.

Pakistan Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar said the accord “remains open to any country in the region willing to uphold its fundamental principles and resolve differences through mutual respect, cooperation and peaceful means,” in a post on X on Sunday.

https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.title: China is using AI facial ID to track migrating fish in Tibet’s largest river
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.author: Victoria Bela
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.text:
Round-the-clock tracking system helps to identify and monitor species travelling through a dam fishway on the Yarlung Tsangpo River

Monitoring the route once relied on labour-intensive manual counts, but it now uses an AI-based “fish facial recognition” system to identify species unique to the Tibet autonomous region, according to a report published by Global Times on Tuesday.

“On the contrary, the aquatic ecology and animal-plant life in the entire middle gorge section of the Yarlung Tsangpo River have shown positive changes,” Yang added.

Hydropower facilities offer flood protection and a reliable renewable energy source to offset intermittent renewables such as solar and wind. But they also pose significant environmental challenges due to the restructuring of natural water bodies.

Hydropower dams can block fish from moving along their natural migratory pathways between feeding and spawning grounds, limiting their ability to reproduce, according to Stanford University.

But there are ways to reduce the impact of dams on aquatic species, such as the development of man-made structures that help migrating fish swim across dams.

They typically feature a series of low steps or pools that slow down rushing water to allow the fish to gradually travel across the dam, according to the US Department of Energy.

The Zangmu Hydropower Station is a 400-metre (1,300ft), 510-megawatt hydroelectric project. To design the dam’s fishway, team members travelled to Canada and the United States to learn from other projects.

The Zangmu fishway was built with a gentle incline to accommodate local cold-water species with weaker swimming abilities than species in North America, and it uses an optimal flow speed to entice fish to swim upstream, Zhang Lianming, a design engineer at the dam, told the Global Times.

Seven fish species unique to the river pass through the fishway at the hydropower station. This includes protected species such as Glyptosternon maculatum, a catfish found at high altitudes.

Zhang said that when the fishway was completed, it was the largest and highest-altitude project of its kind in China and showed that it was possible to build them for dams that were over 40 metres in height.

The fishway initially used manual monitoring at an observation room window to count and verify fish, but the process was slow and could not give accurate figures as the volume of migrating species grew.

Instead, an AI-based fish identification system trained on historical footage was used to track migrating species passing through and improve efficiency.

Using sonar and optical technologies, the system identifies species, counts passing fish and analyses features such as swimming posture and fin characteristics with 95 per cent accuracy.

It also collects data on migration timing and water temperature to evaluate the fishway’s effectiveness, sharing it with research institutes and other hydropower facilities in China.

Advanced fish recognition technology – including drones, AI and 3D stereo cameras – is also used in the US by the Alaska Fisheries Science Centre to monitor species such as walleye pollock, according to fishing industry publication, the National Fisherman.

Innovasea, a Canadian provider of aquatic technologies, has also partnered with Nova Scotia Power to develop technology to detect, classify and count fish that pass through hydroelectric dams in the Canadian province.

To help ensure the stability of rare fish populations in the Yarlung Tsangpo River, a breeding and release programme at the Zangmu plant has returned just under 2 million fish to the wild since the facility opened, according to Global Times.

The project – which will have a capacity three times larger than the Three Gorges Dam, the current largest hydropower facility in the world – has drawn concern over the potential environmental impact both locally and downriver in India, where the river is known as the Brahmaputra, and Bangladesh.

https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.title: China experts explain why hugging winter melons for cooling in summer can cause explosions
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.author: Alice Yan
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.text:
The tradition of hugging winter melons to cool off dates back over 650 years to the late Ming dynasty in China

While many people have embraced the trend of hugging a giant winter melon to sleep as a means of cooling down during summer, some have shared their “painful” experiences, recounting instances where the fruit exploded, releasing a foul-smelling and putrid liquid that soiled their beds and floors.

They detailed this “disastrous scene” on social media, noting that the winter melons exploded after several nights of being held, as reported by the Sichuan Daily.

“It exploded. The stench was unbearable. It was like a burst sewer,” one internet user remembered.

A woman from central Hubei province recounted her experience, advising others against this method of cooling down. “The rotten melon pulp and fluid ruined my bedsheet. It was disgusting. I had to dispose of both the bedsheet and the winter melon,” she said

“I initially sought relief from the summer heat, but it only caused me great discomfort,” she added.

Hugging winter melons to sleep in summer is a traditional practice that dates back to ancient China.

In the late Ming dynasty (1368–1644), an encyclopaedia called Wu Li Xiao Shi, or Some Tips in Physics in English, mentioned the remedy of using winter melon to cool off on warm nights.

The renowned wellness book Xian Qing Ou Ji, known as Daily Jottings for Health in English, from the Qing dynasty (1644–1912), describes the custom of residents in southern China clutching winter melons while sleeping in the summer.

The rationale behind this practice is that the fruit contains 95 per cent water, which helps absorb heat through skin contact. Essentially, it is akin to holding a cold water bag, experts explain.

Since last year, many have adopted this trend as a natural alternative to air conditioning, which can lead to colds, finding the winter melon method more economical.

However, this remedy carries a risk: the melon can potentially explode after being held for several days.

According to Ao Qingyan, a senior agricultural specialist from the Chengdu Academy of Agriculture and Forestry Sciences, microbes enter the winter melons when the white wax on their skin is compromised through frequent skin contact.

These microbes ferment inside the melon as they decompose sugars and organic matter, producing carbon dioxide in the process.

As gas accumulates, an explosion can occur, Ao explained.

“When people hug the melon all night, especially when covered with a quilt, it creates a warm, incubating environment for fermentation,” Ao informed the media.

She recommended changing the melon once a week.

“It’s wise to touch and inspect it regularly. If you notice any part of it is soft, swollen, or emits a sour odour, you should discard it immediately,” Ao advised.

“Hugging winter melons is merely a low-cost, temporary method for alleviating summer heat. Due to the risk of explosion and mould growth, it is not an ideal solution. Air conditioners, cold mats, and cold pillows are more reliable alternatives with lower risks,” she concluded.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Typhoon Dolphin: more than a million people evacuated in China as record rainfall dumped on Shanghai
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Yu-chen Li in Taipei
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Authorities warn that days of intense rain could trigger widespread flooding and landslides as storm moves north and further inland

More than a million people were moved to safety across eastern China by Sunday evening as powerful Typhoon Dolphin made landfall amid fears torrential rain would cause flooding and landslides.

Wenzhou, a coastal city in Zhejiang province, said it relocated more than 900,000 people and opened more than 1,500 emergency shelters. In neighbouring Fujian, 98,900 people were moved from high-risk areas.

In Shanghai, 215,600 people were moved from areas considered at risk by Sunday evening, substantially higher than an earlier figure of 30,300. A weather station in the city centre recorded its highest 24-hour rainfall in more than 150 years.

Forecasters in China predicted some areas could see 200-400mm (7.9–15.7 inches) of rainfall over the coming days.

Dolphin weakened rapidly to a tropical storm by 5am on Monday. But as the storm continued to move northwards and farther inland, heavy rain was forecast across large parts of eastern and central China, extending north into Shandong and affecting Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Shanghai. Authorities warned that days of intense rain could trigger widespread flooding and landslides through Wednesday, urging people to stay indoors during the heavy downpours.

The storm forced Shanghai’s two airports to cancel more than 1,300 flights.

Dolphin earlier swept through Japan’s southern Okinawa prefecture, injuring six people and ⁠cutting power to more than 50,000 buildings.

In the Philippines, the typhoon did not make landfall in the country’s north but intensified the seasonal monsoon rains, which flooded many areas of the main northern Luzon region, including around Manila.

Scientists say global warming has made extreme weather more likely, including more powerful typhoons.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/8.title: Oil prices climb as Iranian demands cloud outlook for Strait of Hormuz
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/8.author: John Power
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/8.text:
Oil prices are climbing higher as Iran’s latest demands for reopening the Strait of Hormuz dampen hopes for a return to stability in global energy markets.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose more than 1 percent on Monday as Tehran’s insistence that the critical waterway will not reopen without major concessions from the United States stoked market anxiety.

Brent futures for October stood at $83.77 a barrel at 2:30 GMT, up about 16 percent compared with before the start of the US and Israel’s war on Iran.

“The lack of concrete movement, together with lingering questions about the practical details of any agreement, is keeping a risk premium in the price,” Tim Waterer, chief market ‌analyst at ⁠Sydney, Australia-based KCM Trade, told Al Jazeera.

“Each day that passes without a breakthrough is making traders a little more cautious.”

Iranian Minister of Foreign Affairs Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that while Iran and Oman were close to an agreement on the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway would not reopen until Washington met certain conditions, including easing sanctions and paying war reparations.

Shipping in the strait, a conduit for about one-fifth of global oil supplies before the war, has effectively collapsed since the conflict began in late February, prompting the largest energy disruption in recorded history.

Between eight and 15 vessels crossed the strait on August 4, August 5 and August 6, according to ship-tracking platform MarineTraffic, a fraction of the roughly 130 transits before the conflict.

Iran has repeatedly insisted on the right to control shipping in the strait despite freedom of navigation being a cornerstone of international maritime law, threatening to attack commercial vessels that attempt passage on unapproved routes.

On Saturday, the United Arab Emirates condemned Tehran over what it said was an Iranian missile attack on a vessel owned by the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company.

At least 64 violent incidents and 17 deaths involving commercial vessels have occurred in the region since the war began, according to the International Maritime Organization, most of which have been blamed on Iran.

Despite renewed volatility in energy markets, Asian stocks rose on Monday morning, with benchmark indices in Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong all making substantial gains.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s Kospi were up 2.1 percent and 0.7 percent, respectively, while the Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong was 0.6 percent higher.
