https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/iri.title: Irinotecan Fails to Boost Rectal Cancer Outcomes
https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/iri.text:
Edited by Victoria Stern

Adding irinotecan to standard capecitabine chemoradiotherapy for MRI-defined, locally advanced rectal cancer did not improve disease-free survival (DFS) or pathologic complete response (pCR) rates. At 36 months, DFS was 68% in the irinotecan group vs 67% in the standard-of-care group, and pCR occurred in 19% of patients receiving irinotecan vs 17% in the standard-of-care group. However, patients receiving irinotecan experienced more grade 3 or worse adverse events (AEs) (78% vs 52%).

"For MRI-defined, high-risk, locally advanced rectal cancer, the addition of irinotecan to standard of care did not improve outcomes and should not be used in combination with radiotherapy plus capecitabine," the study authors wrote.

The study was led by David Sebag-Montefiore, FRCR, Leeds Institute of Medical Research, University of Leeds, Leeds, UK. It was published online on August 1 in The Lancet Oncology.

The study observed a lower number of disease-related events than initially assumed, suggesting the target effect size might have been overestimated and the study may be underpowered to detect smaller but clinically relevant differences. Ethnicity data were not collected, limiting the ability to assess ethnic differences in outcomes. The trial did not evaluate UGT1A1 or DPYD status to inform irinotecan or capecitabine dosing, which might have affected toxicity profiles and treatment efficacy.

The study was supported by grants from Cancer Research UK. The chief investigator received a study grant from Cancer Research UK to conduct the ARISTOTLE trial. Several authors reported institutional support from Cancer Research UK, Yorkshire Cancer Research, and the National Institute of Health Research. Multiple authors disclosed consulting fees, honoraria, or research support from pharmaceutical companies including Amgen, Bristol-Myers Squibb, GSK, Incyte Biosciences, Nanobiotix, Pfizer, Servier, and Takeda. Additional author disclosures are reported in the original article.

https://thehill.com/homenews/house/60196.author: Ryan Mancini
https://thehill.com/homenews/house/60196.text:
This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) on Sunday said she will undergo physical rehabilitation after she was injured in what Toledo, Ohio, first responders said was a hit-and-run crash.

Kaptur shared a video on the social platform X thanking “you so very, very much for the thousands of good wishes that are coming from our community, across our region, our state, our country and even around the world” toward her “rapid recovery.”

“We will not return to Washington until next month, so I’m blessed to have time to recover fully,” she said, referring to herself and her staff, including one staffer who was also injured in the crash.

In thanking the first responders, Kaptur described the crash as “not a pleasant experience, and there were wounds that resulted. But let me tell you, we have to be very grateful, in this region, to have the kind of dedicated medical staff that exists at Mercy St. Vincent [Medical Center].”

Kaptur concluded the video by sharing a card she received “from a young gentleman named Avery.” The card, written by a child, read on the front of it: “For Marcy Kaptur: Get well soon with Charlie.” Beside the words was a drawing of a brown dog that Kaptur said was Charlie.

“[Avery] and I happen to be friends and he was worried about me,” Kaptur said before reading the card. “So he did this card for me …These are wonderful people, and they uplift your spirits, and each of you uplift my spirit as we move forward.”

The 80-year-old congresswoman was a passenger in a vehicle heading to church service last Sunday when her car was struck, her office previously said. Toledo police learned of a “hit-skip” crash at around 10:48 a.m. EST in the area of Detroit Avenue and Central Avenue, Toledo Police Sgt. Mohamad Nasser previously told The Hill.

Ohio law treats a hit-skip the same as a hit-and-run, with both signifying the failure to stop after an accident.

Kaptur has served in Congress representing Ohio’s 9th Congressional District since 1983 and is actively seeking an 18th term this November, making her the longest-serving member of Ohio’s 17-member congressional delegation by more than 20 years.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/q.title: Child safety worker union alarmed by possible removal of key reporting tool
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/q.author: Laura Lavelle
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
State and Territory Government

The Department of Child Safety has come under fire from the union representing child safety workers for proposing to remove a key reporting tool. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

The union for child safety workers in Queensland says the state department has proposed removing a tool that shows how many youths workers are responsible for at any given time.

When questioned about the removal of the reporting tool, Premier David Crisafulli seemingly contradicted his own department and said he didn't think it should be withdrawn.

The Together Union says all options are on the table as part of the bargaining process, including walking off the job.

The Queensland government has been accused of attempting to remove a key reporting tool depicting just how under-pressure child safety workers are.

The Together Union, which represents child safety officers, said the Department of Child Safety has proposed removing the workload management tool in its latest bargaining agreement offer.

The union's assistant secretary, Dee Spink said the tool shows how many children workers are responsible for at any given time.

"We're actually seeking to expand the workload management tool as part of this bargaining process, and the department has told us they want to remove it," Ms Spink said.

Together Union assistant secretary Dee Spink. (ABC News)

Child safety and youth justice workers have been under protected industrial action as part of their bargaining period since August 3.

The union said Child Safety Minister, Amanda Camm and the Director-General Belinda Drew had not attended any bargaining sessions.

Ms Spink said she did not expect either to appear at every meeting.

"But what we do expect is that they will back up their words about wanting to fix the crisis in child safety with actions," she said.

Child Safety Minister Amanda Camm has been under pressure after recent statistics showed the number of children in residential care had soared. (ABC News)

Ms Spink said all options are on the table as part of the bargaining process, including walking off the job.

When questioned about the removal of the reporting tool, Premier David Crisafulli seemingly contradicted his own department and said he didn't think it should be withdrawn.

"I think it makes complete sense to keep it the same," he said.

The premier did not commit to making a directive ordering the reporting tool remain.

Opposition leader Steven Miles accused the government of trying to hide data from Queenslanders.

He was also scathing of Minister Camm, calling for the premier to sack her and condemned her failure to attend union bargaining agreement meetings.

"That's not good enough for Crisafulli government ministers to continue to say that it's not their job to work with their workforces, to meet with their unions and to get positive outcomes," Mr Miles said.

Opposition leader Steven Miles called on the premier to sack Child Safety Minister Amanda Camm. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

The latest stoush between the union and the government comes after it tabled its response into a landmark child safety inquiry.

As part of its response, the government released new data which showed a record number of children were in residential care, at almost 3,000 in March.

It accepted 32 out of 52 recommendations and accepted in principle a further 16.

Ms Spink said the proposal to remove the workload management tool strips the public of its ability to see if the changes are working.

The Queensland government has handed down its response to the Child Safety Inquiry.

"[This] offer proposes removing one of the few mechanisms that allows workers — and ultimately Queenslanders — to see whether the system is actually improving, while failing to address the excessive workloads, unpaid overtime and retention issues identified by the Commission of Inquiry," she said.

The union also raised concerns about the number of vacancies for child safety officers.

Ms Spink said she's been told there are over 100 jobs that have not been filled across the state.

"And there is nothing in the [bargaining offer] that would address that," she said.

When asked for comment, the Minister for Child Safety referred to the premier's statement.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/t.title: Head aims to maintain opening spot ahead of busy 12 months
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Travis Head says he believes he is here to stay as an opener. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Morgan Hancock)

Travis Head says he is comfortable opening the batting on a variety of different surfaces ahead of a potential 20-Test year.

Head was promoted from the middle order during the Ashes series and hit three centuries as opener.

Follow all the action on ABC Radio and ABC Sport's live blog as Australia faces Bangladesh in the first of two Tests, starting Thursday in Darwin.

Travis Head can envisage himself continuing to open the batting for Australia at the end of next year's Ashes.

The positive mindset of the back-to-back Allan Border Medal winner is no surprise.

Head was a revelation in home conditions in last year's Ashes series with three centuries after moving up from the middle order.

Ahead of the opening Test against Bangladesh in Darwin, the 32-year-old was asked if his order switch was short-term or whether it could work across the 20 or more Tests Australia will play in the next 12 months.

There was a sense that Head's move up the order against England was intended to counter their ultra-aggressive "Bazball".

It worked so well that the term "Travball" was coined.

Prior to the home Ashes, his stints as an opener had been short-lived.

Travis Head scored three centuries as an opener in the last Ashes series. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

Head was unstoppable on home tracks in the Ashes series, but he will face a variety of surfaces in Australia, South Africa, England and India in the next 12 months.

He says he is not worried about playing in different conditions.

"I feel like I have been adaptable in the places that I have played," Head said.

"In India and England I have opened the batting, which is a slightly different to Australia.

"Everything is going to be different, but what I have been able to do over my career is problem solve the best that I can and work through challenges — whether they are green wickets or flat wickets.

"It will look different in every Test match or every series. I am trying to be as calm and consistent as I can."

Whether Head stays an opener will depend largely on how he performs and also on the displays of the middle order.

Tweaks may be made but right now Head plans to be opening in the final Test of next year's away Ashes series.

"I think it will work," he said.

"If I have done it for [another] 20 Tests and I am sitting there in a few years and I have opened the batting the whole time … I would have done an OK job and been consistent, contributed and had a good partnership with Jake [Weatherald].

"It is a new challenge coming here and a new challenge in South Africa in a month's time and I am looking forward to the challenge."

International cricket coach Joe Gatting has posted videos of how Head plans for a variety of scenarios and surfaces and he is expected to continue to find the best approach in all conditions.

"We have a lot of footage and we couldn't be more resourced in that space. I'll continue to do that," Head said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/n.title: ICAC questions lobbyist's role with 'toxic' Reformers
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Anti Corruption Agencies

Lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood says he encouraged friends to leave The Reformers, a right-wing Liberal Party factional group. (ABC News)

Lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood said a right-wing Liberal Party factional group at the centre of a corruption watchdog inquiry became so "toxic" he encouraged his friends to leave it.

The NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) is examining allegations prohibited donations were funnelled through third parties to support conservative Christian group, the NSW Reformers, and advance the interests of fugitive property developer Jean Nassif.

The inquiry is also examining allegations involving Mr Greenwood's former company, Beckington, which is alleged to have been used to conceal political donations as payments for lobbying and government relations work.

The inquiry had previously heard money from Mr Nassif's company, Toplace, was allegedly channelled through companies linked to Mr Greenwood before being distributed to some Reformers members.

Mr Greenwood fronted ICAC for the first time on Monday. (Supplied)

During his first day of evidence, Mr Greenwood said the Reformers eventually became a source of professional trouble for him and that the group was causing him "a lot of grief personally".

During his evidence, Mr Greenwood became combative at times and disagreed with suggestions he wanted the group to continue to advocate for matters he personally supported or "thrive as a movement".

"I privately told all of them to not keep going … it became so toxic so no, I disagree with that," Mr Greenwood replied.

Mr Greenwood downplayed his involvement with the group, telling the inquiry he was more interested in policy than factional politics.

He told the commission he was working with Nationals senator Matt Canavan in 2018, while his friends and Reformers co-founders, Christian Ellis and Robert Assaf, were becoming increasingly involved in efforts to recruit conservative Liberal Party members.

Mr Greenwood said he considered himself "all about the Nationals" at the time and did not regard himself as a member of the Reformers or involved in the group's recruitment activities.

Mr Greenwood said he was interested in the group's conservative social policies and would have attended some events featuring speakers, including one with former broadcaster Alan Jones.

"If Alan was going and speaking, I would have wanted to go. Yeah, I like Alan. He's great," Mr Greenwood told the inquiry.

Dr Dwyer questioned Mr Greenwood's level of involvement with The Reformers. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Counsel Assisting Peggy Dwyer SC argued it was clear that Mr Greenwood was supporting the group's activities and events.

Dr Dwyer said: "Can I suggest this to you ... You are at pains to try to distance yourself from the Reformers, but in fact, it's abundantly clear that you were supporting their work in 2019."

Mr Greenwood replied: "I counted 30 times a witness in here said, 'I'm not a member of the Reformers'. I am at pains because how many people have to say I'm not a member of the Reformers? Nobody has said I'm a member of the Reformers."

"I've told you that from time to time in social settings, I would give advice and yes, I supported their issues."

Mr Greenwood also told the inquiry Mr Ellis wanted to give evidence to ICAC, despite declining to appear before the commission.

Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

In her opening statement, Dr Dwyer said Mr Ellis, who now lives in the UK, went to "significant lengths to avoid process servers".

Dr Dwyer said he had cited family commitments and the timezone difference for not participating in the inquiry.

Mr Greenwood said he remained in contact with Mr Ellis and recently visited him in the UK, but was not sure of any plans for him to return to Australia.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.author: Conor Byrne
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Law, Crime and Justice

Hao Wang, 30, has been denied bail in Cairns Magistrates Court. (ABC News: Paula Broughton)

Hao Wang has been denied bail on people-smuggling charges.

It is alleged he was involved in the arrival of 10 Chinese citizens, who travelled from Indonesia to Far North Queensland.

Mr Wang has been remanded in custody and his case will be back in court on October 1.

An alleged people smuggler has been denied bail after his fishing-trip alibi was dismissed because he had 10 illegal migrants in his hotel room and no evidence of an interest in fishing.

Sydney-based Chinese national Hao Wang has been charged with smuggling Chinese citizens, after being arrested in Weipa on western Cape York Peninsula on June 30.

Cairns Magistrates Court today heard Mr Wang had driven a rental car from Cairns three days earlier, a distance of more than 800km that can take more than 10 hours.

It is alleged that early on June 30, a group of people without visas came ashore at Pennefather River, about 50 kilometres north-west of Weipa.

Magistrate Michael Dalton said Mr Wang was arrested by AFP and Border Force officers at Weipa's Heritage Shopping Centre that afternoon on the grounds that he himself was an unlawful non-citizen.

The 10 migrants were then found in a room at the Albatross Hotel.

Magistrate Dalton disagreed with defence lawyer Aaron Dunkerton's comments that the prosecution case was weak.

"I have an unlawful non-citizen painter who lives in Sydney, who is in Weipa — a very, very long way from home — and you wouldn't Adam-and-Eve it, but the unlawful non-citizens have been found in his hotel room booked by him," Magistrate Dalton told the court.

"That's a remarkable coincidence."

To which Mr Dunkerton replied: "I accept how it appears."

Magistrate Dalton also rejected Mr Dunkerton's reasoning that Mr Wang had been on a fishing trip, saying fishing off Weipa was "not for novices", and there was no evidence of an interest in the activity.

"Weipa is not for people who might be beginning dropping a line in the ocean," Magistrate Dalton said.

Mr Dunkerton said evidence that WhatsApp messages to a phone in Indonesia — the country the migrants had come from by boat — were circumstantial.

"It's entirely unremarkable in my submission that there's a text message to an Indonesian number on the same day. We live in a global world," Mr Dunkerton told the court.

But Magistrate Dalton refused bail, saying Mr Wang was a flight risk.

"Given that he has connection to the people-smuggling offence, I do hold concerns that he may be able to use those connections to leave this country," he said.

But Commonwealth prosecutor Chris Moore said that even if Mr Wang had been granted bail, the attorney-general would have acted quickly to take Mr Wang to an immigration detention centre.

Hao Wang's case will return to court in Cairns on October 1. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

Mr Moore said the immigration minister had been notified about Mr Wang's case.

"Whether he takes that into account or whether there's some other factors at play in determining what should be done with him," he said.

The offence Mr Wang has been charged with has a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, with a mandatory non-parole period of at least three years.

The court heard Mr Wang arrived in Adelaide in 2012 to study at St George's College, but had not had a valid visa for at least two years.

He has a three-year-old daughter with his ex-partner in Sydney.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/g.title: Geelong Cats board holds crisis meeting over concussion deal
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/g.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

News of Geelong's secret concussion deal with defender Jake Kolodjashnij has rocked the AFL. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

Geelong's board has held a crisis meeting as the fallout from the secret concussion deal with Jake Kolodjashni continues.

Geelong captain Patrick Dangerfield said the club had "buggered up", but strongly defended club CEO Steve Hocking.

A statement from the Cats said the club will respond to the AFL's 'please explain' letter on Tuesday.

Geelong is about to reply to the AFL's "please explain" as the Cats brace for a potential massive penalty over the secret concussion deal with Jake Kolodjashnij.

Amid speculation over the futures of Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking and AFL chairman Craig Drummond, the club board held a crisis meeting on Monday to work out its response to the league.

Also on Monday, Geelong captain Patrick Dangerfield said the club had "buggered up", but strongly defended Hocking.

Pressure has been mounting on Geelong and the AFL since it emerged last Thursday that the Cats struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij, who had a history of concussion.

AFL chair Craig Drummond issues a statement apologising for his part in the Jake Kolodjashnij concussion contract saga.

"We acknowledge this has been a challenging time for Jake, our club and Geelong supporters," Cats president Grant McCabe said in a statement on Monday.

"The board has met this morning to discuss our response to the AFL's letter. That will be submitted by end of day Tuesday, 11 August.

"This will provide the club with the chance to detail the actions it took in navigating this complex matter. We welcome this opportunity.

"The club remains committed to providing our players with the highest standard of care and support."

Hocking was Cats chief executive and Drummond was the club president when the deal was struck two years ago with Koladjashnij.

The Geelong defender signed a waiver that meant he effectively took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to indemnify the club and its medical staff from potential court action.

On the weekend Hocking defended the club in a radio interview and argued there was not a lot they would do differently.

"As a leader it's really important to take ownership and just lead through this. It's not easy to do, but I wouldn't change too much — we are a really good football club," he said.

"I know there are people out there who say culturally we are maybe not as strong as we have been, but we do so much right and occasionally there might be one or two per cent we don't get right.

"In this case that will be proven, I would suggest, that will be proven with the 'please explain'. We don't get everything right."

Drummond also released a statement in which he apologised over the deal. He added he would not be involved in the AFL's assessment and deliberation of the Kolodjashnij situation.

On Monday, Dangerfield told Fox Footy that Hocking was one of the most "placid" people he had met and gave him his full support.

"He's a man of the highest integrity … we're lucky to have him," Dangerfield said.

But he acknowledged mistakes had been made.

"Clearly there were some parts that we buggered up as a club. We can be better," he said.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: Italy’s record-low Po River forces farmers to weigh crop switch
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: Alberto Brambilla
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
Massimo Salvagnin has the seeds ready. He just isn’t sure whether to put them in the ground.

Next week, the farmer plans to sow green beans in the sandy soil of his family’s 600-hectare farm near Italy’s Po River delta. But this summer’s extreme heat has made the ground so hot that he worries the seeds could die before they have a chance to germinate.

“The sand gets so hot that the risk of cooking — boiling — the seed when it touches the soil is extremely high,” he said.

Across northern Italy, farms, factories and power plants reliant on abundant and predictable water are confronting a new reality. Climate change is making the Po River, the engine of Italy’s industrial economy, swing violently between flood and drought.

It’s forcing farmers to rethink what they grow, engineers to reconsider how water is stored and moved, and industries to compete for a resource they once took for granted. With Italy in the grip of another major heat wave, the challenge is to adapt decades-old businesses that were built on the assumption the water would always be there.

Salvagnin, 59, made sure before planting that his irrigation consortium could guarantee water for the next month to six weeks. The anxiety is spreading across northern Italy as the Po sinks to historic lows.

At Cremona, the river fell to 8.59 meters below the hydrometric zero on July 30, 1 centimeter below the previous record low set during the severe drought of 2022. Flow was reduced to less than a third of the historical norm for this time of year, according to the Po River Basin District Authority.

The 652-kilometer Po is Italy’s longest river, rising in the Alps near the French border and emptying into the Adriatic Sea south of Venice. While much shorter than the Rhine or the Danube — two of Europe’s other great economic waterways — it carries an exceptionally large volume of water.

Each spring, snowmelt is channeled to Europe’s largest rice-growing region, flooding fields near Milan for planting varieties used in risotto and working its way east. The river and its tributaries also support nearly 900 hydropower plants, helping to drive the country’s manufacturing economy.

The Po River district accounts for about 41% of Italy’s gross domestic product and 32% of its agricultural production, according to the basin authority.

Climate change is testing the economy near Ferrara, where much of the farmland was created by draining delta marshes and lagoons. From the 1950s, the vast Mezzano wetlands were converted into farmland for crops from strawberries to tomatoes, maize and sugar-beets, much of it below sea level.

Pumps and canals are used to continually manage the boundary between land and water, draining fresh water when there’s too much and bringing it back when there’s too little.

Increasingly, the water arrives at the wrong time, said Stefano Calderoni, chairman of the Consorzio di Bonifica Pianura di Ferrara, which operates roughly 4,200 kilometers of canals and 160 pumping facilities.

At peak spring flows, he estimates that roughly 10 billion cubic meters can pass Pontelagoscuro near Ferrara in less than two weeks. Months later, the same region can be scrambling for water. The Po increasingly seems like a torrent, continually filling and emptying, he said.

“We have two great challenges: managing too much water and too little water,” Calderoni said. “We relied on nature when we should have relied on planning.”

Even rainfall increasingly offers only temporary relief. Intense, localized storms do little to rebuild water reserves, according to Alessandro Delpiano, chairman of the basin authority. Higher temperatures melt Alpine snow earlier, while urbanization and soil sealing diminish groundwater replenishment.

Salvagnin is hardly a farmer who resisted modernization.

His father founded Porto Felloni farm about 50 years ago. After traveling to the U.S. in the 1990s to study how American farmers used technology, Salvagnin introduced precision agriculture at the family business, including yield mapping and variable-rate farming.

Today, buried sensors measure soil moisture, while weather stations, satellite data and crop models estimate how much water plants are consuming. Irrigation can be adjusted by individual sections of a field.

Some of the techniques were developed in Italy’s hotter, drier south.

Nicola Gherardi, a national executive board member of Confagricoltura, one of Italy’s main farming associations, learned about drip irrigation for tomatoes from farmers in the Puglian area of Foggia. The systems water directly around the plants, unlike the large sprinklers common in the Po Valley.

“I went to those who had faced these problems before us and developed techniques and know-how that we simply didn’t have,” Gherardi said. He points to France’s Rhone as another model for the Po, where water-management interventions have allowed agriculture to coexist with hydropower and the delta.

Farmers have also shifted crops. Maize, a cornerstone of northern Italy’s livestock and dairy industries, has contracted sharply. It needs large amounts of water and is vulnerable to salinity. Gherardi said Italian production is around half what it was two decades ago, while more tolerant crops such as sorghum are increasingly appearing in rotations.

Switching can have an economic downside. A hectare of industrial tomatoes can yield up to double the income of barley, Salvagnin estimates. High-value crops sustain processing plants, logistics companies and seasonal jobs.

“If farms have to grow barley because it doesn’t consume water, they can’t make a living,” he said.

Energy providers are also feeling the pinch. At Enel Green Power’s Isola Serafini hydroelectric station, all four generating units have been idle since July 30 because river flows are too low.

During periods of scarcity, drinking water takes priority, followed by irrigation and food production. Energy and other uses come afterward.

Rivers are also normally required to retain an ecological flow to protect ecosystems, though regions and provinces are asking for exemptions to allow more water to be withdrawn, Delpiano said.

The basin authority has also asked hydroelectric operators to release additional water stored in Alpine reservoirs to support the Po downstream. This year, authorities changed a roughly 80-year-old rule governing the regulated water level at Lake Maggiore, allowing it to hold an additional 15 centimeters of water.

At Pontelagoscuro, the last major measuring station before the delta, the Po is flowing at roughly one-third of historical volumes, according to the basin authority, signaling heightened risk of saltwater intrusion. Seawater is penetrating more than 25 kilometers inland, affecting irrigation withdrawals and ecosystems.

It also worsens a longstanding problem for the reclaimed countryside, which sits atop saline groundwater left from the original marshes and lagoons. Fresh water near the surface helps hold it down, but prolonged dry periods can allow salt to rise through the soil, burning the land and making it difficult for crops to grow.

While engineers originally removed water to turn wetlands into farmland, preserving it now depends on keeping freshwater in.

Farmer Salvagnin says agricultural economy that has defined this part of Italy for generations is under threat. Across the region, farms are closing and younger generations are moving into other professions.

He’s worried that extreme heat will trigger an abandonment, similar to the kind that’s emptied parts of Italy’s mountain regions.

“I’ll keep doing my job,” Salvagnin said. “But around me there could be a desert.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Sony and TSMC to invest ¥1 trillion in joint chip plant in Japan
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Takashi Mochizuki
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Sony Group and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. are in talks to spend a combined ¥1 trillion ($6.4 billion) on their planned joint factory in Japan, according to a person familiar with the plans.

The Japanese company’s chip arm Sony Semiconductor Solutions  and TSMC are partnering on next-generation image sensors for robots and cars. The factory will begin production in 2029, the person said, asking not to be named because the talks are private. Representatives of Sony and TSMC did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The investment under discussion, which was earlier reported by the Nikkei, is the latest in Sony’s transition toward a more asset-light approach with its image sensor operations. The company has been focusing more of its resources on intellectual property like music distribution rights, film and video game franchises.

Sony’s shares rose as much as 2.2%, while TSMC’s gained 1.7% Monday morning.

The project will get its launch in Kumamoto Prefecture, where TSMC has set up its own chip fabrication plant, and may expand if the Japanese government provides backing, the companies have said.

Sony, which is a minority shareholder in TSMC’s chipmaking site in the region, will be the controlling shareholder of the new joint venture.

The Tokyo-based company has supplied premium image sensors to the likes of Apple, Huawei Technologies and Samsung Electronics. It has in recent times sought to expand its sensing business into applications in cars and robotics.

https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.title: China releases powerful DNA-screening AI tool for free to help fight rare diseases
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.author: Holly Chik
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.text:
The team hopes the open-source AI framework will help decode rare diseases and provide equitable access to precision medicine

Patients can spend years visiting specialists and undergoing inconclusive tests, while the underlying cause of their condition remains hidden within three billion base pairs of DNA in the human genome.

Rather than reading DNA sequences, OneGenome is trained to reason. It uses accumulated human medical logic to interpret the clinical consequences of gene mutations.

It was developed by integrating Genos – a genomic foundational model released last year that was trained on human genomes to represent diverse global populations – with large language model capabilities.

“Unlike common diseases, rare conditions suffer from a lack of knowledge, making an accurate diagnosis very challenging,” Liu Shiping, chief scientist in brain science at BGI-Research, said in an interview.

“This is our attempt to accelerate that timeline. After building a comprehensive database constructed from rare diseases, patients’ gene sequencing data and clinical manifestations, we can deploy AI to analyse these findings,” he said of OpenRare, an open-source genetic analysis system for rare disease diagnosis.

“In the future, AI can support doctors in identifying potential disease-causing mutations so that they no longer have to rely only on their experience to investigate each possibility one by one.”

The automation of screening and clinical reasoning enables the model to compress a process that used to take years into just a few hours, while also generating a traceable analysis.

The goal is to provide doctors with leads that will be further verified and eventually help establish a diagnosis, Liu said.

The team also applied the AI model to treat rare types of cancer by identifying therapeutic targets for developing personalised immunotherapy.

At the United Nations’ AI for Good Global Summit 2026 in July, where the team received the ITU Innovate for Impact Use Case Award, the team demonstrated the model with one case of a desmoplastic small round cell tumour, a type of rare and aggressive soft-tissue cancer.

The OneGenome process pinpointed 11 therapeutic targets that standard clinical testing had overlooked in a late-stage patient.

Liu said the traditional approach of treating each mutation as an isolated actor failed to capture how these mutations interacted with each other.

“Genomic sequences are connected instead of independent. When a sequence is removed, the whole network could change,” Liu explained.

Liu’s vision for the technology was to turn it into a global public good, especially for developing countries where medical resources were limited.

He said he hoped that in the future, “AI tools will be able to help individuals analyse their health data so patients can communicate more effectively with doctors to confirm diagnosis”.
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.summary: OpenRare is an open-source genetic analysis system for rare disease diagnosis. It uses accumulated human logic to interpret the clinical consequences of gene mutations. The team hopes the system will provide access to precision medicine.

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.title: Hong Kong heatwave to persist before showers bring relief later this week
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.author: Matthew Cheng
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.text:
Very hot weather warning remains in force as Tropical Cyclone Dolphin brings extreme heat, with thundery showers forecast later this week

More frequent showers expected later this week should bring relief from Hong Kong’s extreme heat, the city’s weather forecaster has said, although scorching conditions will persist in the coming days, with temperatures in some areas forecast to reach at least 37 degrees Celsius (99 Fahrenheit).

The Hong Kong Observatory said on Monday that outer subsiding airflow associated with Tropical Cyclone Dolphin continued to bring extremely hot weather to Guangdong and Hong Kong. The heat is expected to persist until Wednesday or Thursday, with high temperatures increasing the likelihood of thundery showers.

Upper-air disturbances will bring unsettled weather later in the week, with increasing showers potentially easing the intense heat, it said.

Temperatures rose above 32 degrees across much of the city on Monday morning.

Wong Tai Sin recorded the highest reading, at 35.1 degrees at 10am, followed by Happy Valley at 35 degrees. Yuen Long Park, Sheung Shui, Tai Po, Sha Tin, Sai Kung, Kowloon City, Clear Water Bay and Tsuen Wan Shing Mun Valley all recorded temperatures above 34 degrees.

A very hot weather warning remains in force, while the Labour Department has issued an amber heat stress at work warning.

Cheung Ping, a senior scientific officer at the Observatory, said that although Dolphin had made landfall in Zhejiang, its extensive circulation meant its outer subsiding airflow was still affecting Guangdong’s coastline.

“Subsiding airflow is usually warmer and drier. It suppresses cloud formation and makes rain less likely. As a result, areas under its influence typically enjoy fine weather and continuous sunshine,” he said.

“Under the influence of this circulation, Hong Kong tends to have northerly or northwesterly winds, bringing hotter inland air towards the coastal areas.”

On Sunday afternoon, the Observatory recorded a maximum temperature of 36.9 degrees Celsius, the highest since records began in 1884.

Sheung Shui recorded 39.8 degrees, its highest temperature since the forecaster installed automatic weather stations in the 1980s.

Cheung said temperatures in inland areas, such as the New Territories, rose more sharply under daytime solar heating than those in coastal districts.

“Seawater absorbs heat more slowly … It helps prevent temperatures from rising too quickly, and sea breezes also help moderate the increase in temperatures,” he said.

“Coastal areas therefore usually have lower temperatures than inland regions. In the New Territories, such as Sheung Shui and Ta Kwu Ling, daytime temperatures tend to be higher.”

The Observatory urged the public to monitor their health closely and avoid vigorous outdoor physical activity.

“Drink more water and take all necessary protective measures against the heat,” it said.

“If symptoms such as dizziness, headache, nausea, shortness of breath or confusion develop, take rest and seek help immediately, and seek medical advice as soon as possible.”

A man in his sixties was found collapsed on the Plover Cove Reservoir Country Trail in Tai Po on Sunday and was later pronounced dead. The cause of death is under investigation.

Dr Yang Siu-ming, a council member of the Hong Kong College of Emergency Medicine, said the recent hot weather posed significant health risks during outdoor activities, including heatstroke and heat exhaustion. He advised residents to avoid outdoor activities or keep them brief.

“In cases of heat exhaustion, a person may feel very tired, sweat heavily, and experience a body cold,” he said.

“If we notice these signs of discomfort, it means the body is already sending out warnings. The person should quickly move to a shaded place and reduce outdoor activity.”

He added that children, pregnant women, elderly people and obese individuals were among the high-risk groups. He also urged outdoor workers to wear loose-fitting white clothing to reduce heat absorption and to drink water regularly.

https://www.dw.com/en/western-europe-rec.title: Western Europe records hottest June and July on record
https://www.dw.com/en/western-europe-rec.text:
Drought is gripping large parts of Europe, with soils unusually dry and major rivers running low. A strengthening El Nino could push global temperatures even higher later this year.

Western Europe experienced its hottest June and July on record, according to data released Monday by the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service.

The average temperature across the region for the two-month period reached 21.62 degrees Celsius (70.92 Fahrenheit), breaking the previous record set in 2022.

Copernicus said the figure reflected the "exceptional persistence of heat" in western Europe, where four heatwaveshave occurred since May.

The extreme temperatures have contributed to prolonged drought, major wildfires and new national temperature records across the region, as well as thousands of projected heat-related deaths.

Europe is the fastest-warming continent in the world, though temperatures varied considerably, with eastern Europe and Scandinavia experiencing much cooler conditions. For Europe as a whole, July was only the 11th warmest on record, with an average temperature of 20.49 degrees Celsius (68.88 Fahrenheit).

Conditions were drier than average across large parts of Europe in July, including Spain and other areas of the Iberian Peninsula, France, Germany, Austria, Hungary and the United Kingdom.

Ireland and parts of Iceland also experienced unusually dry conditions. Soil moisture in western Europe was significantly lower than in July 2022, when the region last experienced a severe drought.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Persistent high-pressure systems trapped heat over western Europe, the extreme temperatures also amplified widespread drought," said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which operates Copernicus.

"As soils dry out, they lose their ability to provide natural cooling, allowing heat to build more readily," she added.

"This is a clear example of how climate change is intensifying heat extremes, with heat and drought increasingly reinforcing one another."

River flows were also unusually low, with the Seine, Rhine and Danube among the hardest-hit waterways. Low water levels have disrupted transport, irrigation and energy production in several European countries.

The hot and dry conditions have also increased the risk of wildfires. France and Spain have battled particularly severe fires this summer, while serious blazes have also hit other parts of Europe, the northwestern United States and Canada.

Copernicus also reported a record for global sea surface temperatures in July.

The average temperature across oceans outside the polar regions reached 20.96 degrees Celsius (69.73 Fahrenheit), surpassing the previous July record of 20.89 degrees (69.60 Fahrenheit) set in 2023.

Record temperatures were measured along parts of the Atlantic coast and in the western Mediterranean, accompanied by intense marine heatwaves.

A developing El Niño in the equatorial Pacific also contributed to the record. Copernicus director Carlo Buontempo described the emerging El Niño as "very large" and potentially unprecedented in its strength.

El Nino is the warm phase of a natural climate cycle in the Pacific Ocean that can temporarily raise global temperatures and alter weather patterns around the world.

Globally, July was the joint second-warmest on record, tied with July 2024.

The average global surface air temperature was 16.90 degrees Celsius (62.42 Fahrenheit), around 1.47 degrees (2.65 Fahrenheit) above the 1850-1900 pre-industrial average for July. July 2023 remains the hottest on record, with an average temperature of 16.95 degrees (62.51 Fahrenheit).

So far, 2026 is the third-hottest year recorded globally, behind 2024 and 2025. Scientists say the strengthening El Niño could push temperatures higher later this year.

Buontempo said scientists expect a new global average temperature record to be set either later this year or in early 2027.

The past 11 years have been the hottest on record. "We have not seen a climate that warm during our lifetime, and very possibly our civilisation," Buontempo said.

"And the main driver for this warming — as we know — are the greenhouse gases," he added.

Oceans absorb most of the excess heat caused by human greenhouse gas emissions. Higher ocean temperatures can contribute to heavier rainfall and stronger storms and damage marine ecosystems, including coral reefs.

Copernicus bases its climate analyses on billions of measurements from satellites, ships, aircraft and weather stations around the world.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/world.title: Malaysia Was Confident in Its Social Media Ban, but Kids Are Still Logged In
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/world.author: Zunaira Saieed
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/world.text:
Officials told platforms to verify children’s ages using government-issued documents, like identity cards. But the companies have balked, apparently over privacy concerns.

Reporting from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia

Fathin Farhana was expecting respite from the daily arguments she has with her preteen sons about putting away their phones. Both gave a fake age to sign up for TikTok, she said, and spend too much time watching livestreams of the game Mobile Legends or playing games themselves.

Her country, Malaysia, had barred children under 16 from social media starting on June 1, and Ms. Fathin was hoping the rule would forcibly reduce the boys’ screen time.

But months later, that has not been the case.

“It is the best thing ever that I can still log on to TikTok,” said Kayden Malik, 12, Ms. Fathin’s older son. “It cures my boredom every day.”

Malaysia is not alone in struggling to implement and enforce restrictions on social media use. But the authorities there had suggested the rollout would be smoother than in countries like Australia and Indonesia, because they had told companies to rely on government-issued documents like identity cards to verify users’ ages. Now they have suggested that the social media companies are wary of storing government data.

The ban applies to platforms with more than 8 million users in Malaysia, which are TikTok, Facebook, Instagram and YouTube. The platforms either declined to comment or did not address why they had not established new age-verification systems. Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, has argued social media bans for children could be counterproductive and push them toward less safe online spaces. Google, which owns YouTube, said it was committed to working with the Malaysian authorities.

For now, nothing has changed for users.

“This delay for the ban is not good,” said Ms. Fathin, whose younger son is 10. “Children’s mental health is being affected by watching TikTok for hours.”

https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-588.title: The view from the proving grounds for next-generation nuclear reactors, Atomic City, Idaho
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-588.author: Hanna Merzbach
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-588.text:
Arco, Idaho is among the small towns near Idaho National Laboratory with a decades-long nuclear energy legacy.

People still smoke indoors at the bar in Atomic City, Idaho, population 52. The walls are plastered with one dollar bills and a Don't Tread On Me flag.

"Where were you Monday?" bar and nearby race track owner Vickie O'Haro asks one of her regulars.

O'Haro knows her customers orders without asking: cold beers or shots called atomic bombs — fitting since most of her customers work down the road at Idaho National Laboratory, or INL, America's nuclear energy testgrounds since 1949.

A March Gallup poll shows a majority of Americans still oppose a nuclear energy plant in their area, but that's not the case here

" I live 10 miles away, and I'm fine," O'Haro said. "I'm not glowing in the dark, you know? There's nothing to be scared of."

Vickie O'Haro stands behind the bar at Atomic City Bar & Store, which she owns, along with Atomic Motor Raceway, on June 8, 2026. The businesses are located near Idaho National Laboratory.

After stalling out for decades, nuclear power is having a moment. President Donald Trump fast-tracked new projects, and now a new generation of small nuclear reactors is poised to come online in the next few years.

Three companies at INL — and one in central Utah — switched on new types of reactors this summer.

" I think it's actually pretty cool to be happening in my backyard," O'Haro said.

Zoom out and INL is a pretty big backyard. It's 900 square miles of remote, sagebrush-filled high desert, almost the size of Rhode Island.

And it's in an unassuming building here that one startup, Deployable Energy, recently took its test reactor "critical." That means it had a sustained chain reaction for the first time, proving the design works and could someday generate electricity.

Lance Maul, chief operating officer at Deployable Energy, described this as a "real moment in history for the nation."

"This could be a real turning point for the energy future," said Maul, who has an Australian accent and was sporting a scraggly beard and a man bun.

He said the goal isn't your 20th century reactor: massive, expensive nuclear plants. It's micro reactors, which could power a thousand homes versus a million.

"It's something deployable," Maul said. "it's something that you can put on the back of a truck. It is a fundamentally different proposition."

Nuclear optimists like Maul see a future where these reactors are mass produced and power remote communities, military bases and AI data centers. They see them as a solution to meet America's rising energy demand without emitting carbon.

Trump is also a fan. Last year, the Department of Energy sped up reactor permitting. NPR reporting has shown that means getting rid of hundreds of pages of regulations, without telling the public.

"I have no confidence in the Department of Energy and its oversight of this at all." said Edwin Lyman, Nuclear Power Safety Director at the Union of Concerned Scientists.

He said he worries about reduced standards around radiation, security and environmental contamination.

Plus, according to ProPublica reporting, the federal commission that oversees commercial nuclear development has lost hundreds of staff, especially safety experts, due to cuts by the Trump administration and resignations. Companies now testing their reactors will seek approval from that commission.

"I don't think cutting corners when you're talking about nuclear safety is a good idea," Lyman said. "I'm concerned about its impact on the communities around INL"

White House staff secretary Will Scharf hands President Donald Trump an executive order to sign regarding nuclear energy in the Oval Office of the White House, Friday, May 23, 2025, in Washington.

But at the bar in Atomic City, where lab workers drink after a long day, O'Haro said she's not worried.

" If we weren't safe, my guys would tell me that we weren't safe." she said, before turning up the country music playing in the background.

A majority of Americans oppose new nuclear plants near them, but polling also shows growing support for the U.S. "emphasizing" nuclear power more broadly.
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-588.summary: Idaho is among the small towns near Idaho National Laboratory with a decades-long nuclear energy legacy. A new generation of small nuclear reactors is poised to come online in the next few years. A majority of Americans still oppose a nuclear energy plant in their area, but polling shows a majority of people still oppose it.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Lobbyist tells Icac there’s not a ‘shred of evidence’ he was involved with conservative Liberal group
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Penry Buckley
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Jeremy Greenwood tells inquiry he instructed the factional group ‘not to keep going’ because ‘it became so toxic’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A Liberal figure under investigation for allegedly accepting illegal donations has told the corruption watchdog that it does not have a “shred of evidence” that he was part of a conservative factional group, saying he told members “not to keep going” after it became “toxic”.

Consultant and lobbyist, Jeremy Greenwood, 37, who is named in two of the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s (Icac) allegations as part of Operation Rosny, gave evidence on Monday.

Icac is investigating whether conservative Liberal figures including Greenwood “solicited or accepted” donations, including from prohibited donors, in amounts which were undeclared or exceeded caps, for the recruitment or renewal of members to the Liberal party. The practice, known as branch-stacking, is not itself illegal.

Members of the group, known as the Reformers, wanted more conservative policies on same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia.

Reformers witnesses Robert Assaf and Jean-Claude Perrottet have disputed whether Greenwood was part of the core factional group. On Monday, Greenwood admitted his political views were aligned with members of the Reformers, but downplayed his involvement.

Counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, suggested to Greenwood that he was “at pains” to distance himself from the Reformers, but that intercepted messages showed he supported their activities and events in 2019.

Greenwood said evidence showed he “assisted on one event under heavy pressure”.

“But I’ve yet to see another shred of evidence that shows me for the entire history of the Reformers that I was ever involved,” he said.

In a tense exchange, after he was asked if he had supported anti-abortion and anti-euthanasia petitions by the group, Greenwood said: “Sorry, you’re asking me if I’m anti-abortion?”

Presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, asking Greenwood to pause, said: “You’re not being criticised for any views you hold on any moral issue whatsoever, and I would not allow that to occur. Do you understand?”

Greenwood described meeting Ellis when both were staffers in the office of Nationals senator Matt Canavan in 2018. He recalled attending a Reformers event in that year in a professional capacity, but said he did not listen to speeches by Canavan or Dominic Perrottet. Asked about another event where former broadcaster Alan Jones spoke, he said was not sure if he had attended.

“If Alan was going and speaking, I would have wanted to go, but it would have depended on my availability,” he said. “I like Alan, he’s great”.

He said his involvement with former lobbying company Beckington, set up by Reformer Christian Ellis and himself in 2019, which the commission has heard received payments for factional work under bogus arrangements for financial and consulting advice, “started to cause me a lot of grief professionally”.

Greenwood said he “privately told all of them [the Reformers] to not keep going”. “I don’t know what date, but it became so toxic,” he said. The commission heard that Greenwood’s lobbying firm JGP Advisory had lost clients after the announcement of Icac’s inquiry.

Greenwood, who was a groomsman at Ellis’s wedding, said he remained close friends with him, as well as Charles Perrottet, and Reformers Robert Assaf and Jean-Claude Perrottet, with whom he attended independent Catholic school Redfield College. He said he considered Dominic Perrottet a friend, but said he had not spent “not a lot of time” with the former premier.

He said he had visited Ellis, who moved to the UK at the start of the year, and who Icac says has declined to give oral evidence to the inquiry and is yet to respond to alternative proposals, in June. Greenwood insisted Ellis did want to give evidence.

The inquiry has previously heard allegations that Greenwood, Ellis, Charles and Jean-Claude Perrottet avoided summons to appear at a parliamentary inquiry in 2023 which preceded Icac’s investigation.

Dominic Perrottet is not accused of any wrongdoing, while Jean-Claude and Charles Perrottet have previously denied any wrongdoing.

Catholic Schools NSW CEO, Dallas McInerney is expected to appear on Wednesday and Thursday this week.

Icac is investigating an allegation that prohibited donations were made by the schools’ governing body, arranged and approved by McInerney, including through Beckington and JPG Advisory.

Icac’s inquiry continues.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: ‘Babies will be born in laybys’: maternity cuts leave women with stark choices in Devon
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Steven Morris
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Concerns about feeling pressure to have caesarean section, or paying for hotel in Exeter after hospital in Barnstaple suspends birthing services

For mother-to-be Harriet Knight, the suspension of maternity services at one of England’s most remote hospitals means having to face horribly stark choices.

“The next closest maternity unit is a full two hours away and we have a family history of labour taking under two hours from start to finish,” said Knight.

“So we have the option of potentially giving birth in a layby on the north Devon link road as we try to get there or opting for free-birthing at home with no access to maternity care.”

Sunday was the last day that North Devon district hospital in Barnstaple will accept women in spontaneous labour. From Tuesday, births at the hospital will be suspended because of “unsafe levels of medical staffing”.

Mothers in labour will have to trek to Exeter or Taunton, at least an hour and a half away, but usually more, especially at this time of year when the roads are thick with holiday traffic.

“It feels there is no safe option at the moment,” said Knight, who is 34 weeks pregnant. “We live in one of the most rural places in the country and this has left pregnant mothers in north Devon in a really scary situation. It feels like a complete failure by the hospital trust.”

One option she and her partner are considering is spending all their savings on temporary accommodation in Exeter as her due day approaches. “Moving out may be the only thing we can do to keep us safe,” Knight said.

Hannah Rulton, who is expecting her third baby in November, is to undergo a caesarean section because during her second labour she and her child suffered severe shoulder dystocia, an obstetric emergency in which the baby’s head is delivered, but the shoulder gets stuck behind the mother’s pubic bone.

“He was stuck for 11 minutes. Both my son and I very nearly died. The trauma of that birth has never left us. Every appointment during this pregnancy has brought back memories,” she said.

“I have been told there is a significant chance of shoulder dystocia occurring again and what now keeps me awake at night is the fear of going into labour before my planned surgery. The thought of making that journey knowing I have a history of one of the most time-critical obstetric emergencies imaginable is absolutely terrifying.

“Instead of looking forward to meeting our baby, I am worrying about whether I will go into labour early, whether I will make it to another hospital in time and whether I could be forced to relive the worst day of my life.”

Carolyn Mills, the chief nursing officer at Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust, said suspending services had been an “exceptionally difficult” decision.

She said: “Unfortunately, we have now reached the point where we cannot safely provide the level of medical cover required to continue births at North Devon district hospital.

“While we recognise the additional travel this will mean for some families, we believe that concentrating services where safe medical staffing can be guaranteed is the safest option.”

The trust said its projected consultant maternity rotas were at times 50% short, and tier 2 (registrar) doctors 40% short because of staff departures, maternity leave, absences through sickness and a scarcity of locums on short notice. It said it was continuing to work to recruit more staff.

Births and face-to-face triage will be suspended. Other services including community midwifery, scans and antenatal outpatient clinics are continuing. The trust said it would restart birthing services when it was safe but could not estimate a timeframe.

Almost 15,000 people have signed a petition started by Ian Roome, the local Liberal Democrat MP, expressing concern. He said he felt the trust had taken its eye off the ball on recruitment. “Babies are going to be born in laybys,” he said. “There may be deaths.”

after newsletter promotion

Louise Pamment, a local resident who mentors women, has set up a campaign on Instagram calling for medical staff to apply for positions in north Devon. “I’ve seen genuine fear and distress in the women in my life who are pregnant,” she said.

Dr Alison Wright, the president of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG), said: “Maternity services are currently under huge pressure, and we are aware of staffing gaps on almost every obstetric rota in the country. The RCOG is calling for urgent investment in the maternity workforce – to ensure safe staffing levels, so that we can provide the compassionate care that women and families deserve.”

Chloe Ross, who is due to have her second child in October, described the situation as “utterly dangerous”. She said she had a previous bad birthing experience in Exeter and only decided to have another baby having moved to north Devon, thinking she would be able to give birth locally.

“The idea of Exeter dealing with the additional pressures of women coming from our catchment is terrifying. Any way you look at it, women will have to labour in cars on overcrowded roads for nearly two hours,” Ross said.

“The loss of triage will prevent women seeking support for things such as low movement, HG [extreme sickness] and much more.”

Hannah, another expectant mother, is due to have her baby in January. “But I’ve already been told to prepare for travelling to Exeter to give birth,” she said.

“As a first-time mum, it’s inevitable that questions are running through my mind. Will I make it to the hospital in time, or could I end up giving birth on the A361? At the moment, I’m feeling positive about labour and birth, but having to factor in such a long journey adds an extra source of anxiety that shouldn’t have to be there.

“Many expectant parents are already talking about booking Airbnbs or hotels near their due dates to reduce the risk of not reaching Exeter in time. My partner and I are fortunate: we have access to cars, can afford temporary accommodation if necessary and have a strong support network around us.

“But the closure of the unit will have the greatest impact on those who don’t have those advantages. How will people without reliable transport, financial flexibility or family support get to Exeter, particularly if an ambulance isn’t available?”

She is also concerned some women may feel pressure to have planned caesarean sections, “simply because it offers certainty about when and where they will give birth. A caesarean is major surgery and should be a clinical choice, not something women feel forced to consider because local maternity services are unavailable.”

Hospital has been suspended from Tuesday because of ‘unsafe levels of medical staffing’ Exeter hospital to close after maternity services are closed.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: ‘I’ve sat at the very precipice of life’: Clarke Carlisle on gambling, depression – and survival
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Simon Hattenstone
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
The former professional footballer has struggled with his mental health for most of his life. But it took five suicide attempts for him to admit how badly he wanted to end it. He talks about how he turned the corner – and his hopes for his new post with the charity Mind

‘H
ow are you?” I ask Clarke Carlisle. Usually when you meet people it’s a nicety. Not with Carlisle. He smiles ecstatically. “I’m incredibly well, thank you. Yeah, really, really good,” says the former footballer and incoming chair of the mental health charity Mind. “I have been consistently well – not just stable, but well – for three or four years now.”

Few people understand what it is to be mentally unwell quite like Carlisle does. And few understand what recovery means like he does. “It doesn’t happen by accident. Once you get stable that’s not the end of the journey. And that seems to be the MO of our society these days. You do something, you go into hospital and they patch you up, then send you on your way. And that’s the same with mental health. You might get some pills, have a counselling session, you might have a hug and a chat with someone, and they think that’s the end of the journey. And it’s not.”

It has taken him a lot of work to get to the stage where he holds down a senior day job with the gambling support charity Betknowmore, believes in himself again, enjoys family life and truly wants to live.

In his 20s, Carlisle looked as if he had it all. He was a handsome centre-back playing for clubs including Blackpool, Queens Park Rangers and, at his peak, in the Premier League for Watford and Burnley. He was also the chair of the Professional Footballers’ Association (PFA), hugely respected by his fellow players. Clarke appeared on the BBC’s Question Time, more than holding his own with MPs on the hot political topics of the day. In 2002, he beat 11 other players to win a TV quizshow hosted by Carol Vorderman called Britain’s Brainiest Footballer.

After making more than 500 appearances for nine clubs in a 17-year career, he hung up his boots in 2013. Carlisle was one of the last footballers you would have expected to struggle on retiring. There were so many opportunities for him – in business, media, coaching, you name it. But struggle he did. In December 2014 came the shocking news that Carlisle had tried to kill himself by jumping in front of a lorry. It wasn’t his first attempted suicide. Nor was it to be his last. There have been five in total, Carlisle says.

For most of his life, he has suffered with depression. Despite Carlisle’s success, he believed he was a failure. Retirement exacerbated this. After his experience with the PFA, he thought he would walk into a senior executive role. But, he says, he was patronised by the corporate world. “The condescending nature of business to sports people is off the scale. They said things to me like: ‘You’re very intelligent, aren’t you?’ For what? ‘You’re very well spoken, aren’t you?’ For what? Is it for a black man, or is it for a footballer, or for both?”

Fortunately, he got himself a £100,000-a-year contract as a TV pundit for ITV. But he was still finding it hard to adapt from his footballer lifestyle. He and his first wife were due to make a down payment on a £675,000 house when Carlisle heard that ITV wasn’t renewing his contract. Yet again, he told himself he had failed. He tried to gamble his way out of it, as he had done many times before. So many athletes are attracted to gambling, he says, because their life is predicated on win or lose. “When I went in the doors of the casino, I was coming out with half a million pounds or nothing.” He came out with nothing. Two days later, he jumped in front of the lorry.

Astonishingly, Carlisle survived. But he was a mess. He was airlifted to Leeds general infirmary, where he was stitched back together over the next two days. “I remember being in the air ambulance and the paramedic said: ‘This guy is DOA.’ Dead on Arrival. And I remember thinking: ‘Happy days!’ But I wasn’t.” He pauses. “Thank … God,” he says fiercely. A short while later, the crew asked him his name and what year it was. “‘Clarke Carlisle, 2014,’ I said. Then I went: ‘Fucking hell! I’ve not even got amnesia!’”

Carlisle, 46, has always had a good sense of humour. He talks incredibly movingly and perceptively about depression, but you sense he could just as easily turn his hand to mental health standup.

Today, he lives in Newcastle, where his wife comes from, but we meet at the Guardian’s office in London. He’s dressed in shorts and a polo shirt on another fizzing summer day. Carlisle is little changed from his footballing days: now bearder with a few extra scars. He always had plenty of scars – the souvenirs of a defender’s life. But these are more painful reminders. The most dramatic slices are from his crown to his left eyebrow, like a steep contour – a result of his 2014 suicide attempt. He’s got a dog-tag tattoo on his upper arm to mark the date of it. “Small steps,” it says.

The young Carlisle was gifted. He left school with 10 grade A GCSEs (five of them A*s), then went into his football apprenticeship. But nothing he did seemed good enough for his father, a former semi-professional player and God-fearing old-school disciplinarian. All the young Carlisle wanted was approval, and he rarely got it.

In professional football, he found it much the same. But now it was machismo rather than God that dictated the terms. He appeared hard as nails, bantered with the best of them, but the culture was eating away at his insecurities. After his first training session at Leeds United, he returned to the changing room to find his new shirt and shoes shredded – a practical joke, an initiation ceremony, call it what you will; he drove home in tears. In professional team sport, he says, your best friend can also be your greatest rival – an injury for you is an opportunity for them. The football narrative “You’re only as good as your last game” invites insecurity. And if you show vulnerability, it’s pounced on. Despite his success (three appearances for England under-21s and an £8,000-a-week salary at Burnley) he was struggling. His drinking and gambling spiralled.

Carlisle has often been labelled an alcoholic and gambling addict. He says it’s up to others how they see him, but he doesn’t accept those terms. If you do, he says, you render yourself powerless. Today, he doesn’t gamble. He says he could happily drink and leave it at one or two pints, but he chooses not to. Alcohol was not really the cause of his problems, he insists, just the symptom. He had to deal with the motivation behind his drinking. “Once you address your motivation and put positive coping strategies in place, the action is largely irrelevant.” He used alcohol to obliterate his fears and to escape.

After the suicide attempt in 2014, Carlisle was diagnosed with recurrent complex depression disorder and borderline personality disorder. He left hospital with a cocktail of meds, dismantled what was left of his life and began to rebuild it. He and his wife, with whom he had two children, separated. In 2016, he met Carrie Armstrong. They married the following year, and now have two children aged eight and six.

It felt as if his life was falling back into place. But there was a terrible fallout from what happened in 2014. The lorry driver, who suffered PTSD, successfully sued Carlisle. Seven months after the incident, a 24-year-old van driver who had swerved to avoid the prone Carlisle, and then went to his rescue, took his own life. He had spoken publicly about being traumatised by the incident. While many people were sympathetic to Carlisle, some were less so. His former friend and ex-housemate, the actor Ralf Little, tweeted that Carlisle was going to “get away with it – AGAIN”. In his memoir, Carlisle admitted he took Little’s bank card to buy petrol and then used it to fund a two-day drinking and gambling bender.

I ask him if he ever made up with Little. “I’ve not spoken to Ralf for a long time. I apologised to him and he heard that apology, but it didn’t reconcile the relationship.” And that’s fair enough, he says. “I undertook behaviours and actions that had huge impacts on other people’s lives. I can be as contrite as I want, but those actions hurt people, Simon. There’s no getting away from that, whether it’s Ralf or my ex-wife, my children, my parents, whether it’s the lorry driver and his family. My actions impacted other people’s lives. That’s why I’m so passionate about the work I do now. Because it’s never just about the person experiencing adverse mental health; it’s the affecting others around them and the butterfly effect. The factors of multiplication are so far-reaching.”

In September 2017, four months after and he and Carrie had married, Carlisle went missing. He was spotted by a stranger 12 hours later in Liverpool, sitting on a bench. The man sat down with him, told him that he had just lost a close friend to suicide, and begged him to phone home. Carlisle agreed to let him call Carrie, who was pregnant with their first child. “I’d thrown my wallet away, thrown my phone away,” he says today. “I was trying to find the most suitable location and manner in which to take my own life.”

I ask if this is because of what had happened in 2014, and mention the van driver. He gulps. “One of the first people on the scene took their own life, yeah,” he says quietly. “Yes, I was looking for a responsible way to take my own life. Where would the first responders be happy to find me? Where would my wife like to find me? Where would nobody find me? These were the measurements I was taking with that unwell mind; trying to factor in the human impact of the choice, but still from an incredibly illogical base.”

The crux of that illogical base was his conviction that the world would be better off without him; that he would always be a drain on loved ones. Was he glad that the stranger stopped him? “Not immediately, no. That first week in psych hospital I decided to be brutally and unapologetically honest with what was going on in here.” He points to his head. “So when my mum and dad and Carrie came to see me and said how are you, I said: ‘I want to die.’” Had he never said that to them before? “No, never. No. From 2010 to 2017 I’d been very honest about my depression, but I’d never been honest about my suicidal ideation.”

This is when he started to turn his life around, with the help of his family. He says he doesn’t want to go on too much about Carrie because he’s aware that plenty of struggling people don’t have a Carrie for support. But he can’t help himself. “My wife, my human, is the most incredible woman I’ve ever met.” He beams from cheek to cheek.

During that time in hospital, he started doing the work he should have been doing for decades. He looked back to 2014 and realised all he had done was medicate himself out of the immediate crisis.

For all he had believed he was a mental health expert, he now realised he wasn’t. And for all that he thought he understood himself, he didn’t. He was introduced to cognitive analytic therapy. “You mind-map all your thoughts, beliefs and values. It was so enlightening for me.” Ever since getting back to a good place, he’s worked hard to stay there: healthy diet, early nights, exercise, therapy and, of course, plenty of talking.

Having got through the worst, though, he was left broke. The exec jobs he dreamed of never materialised, so he went to work for Amazon as a van driver. “Those shifts are brutal,” he says. But he loved it. “I went from training to training other drivers within 10 days.” He applied himself with the same rigour he did to football. “You’ve got to do it as efficiently as possible. Can you imagine how much that played into me? Elite athlete mindset perfection. I had my nine-hours shift done in about five hours, then I was going around sweeping other people’s shifts up.”

He gave it up after six months when he was appointed business development executive at Betknowmore – a job he’s every bit as invested in as the voluntary office of chair at Mind, which he takes up in September. He already has a firm grip of his agenda at the mental health charity. “First of all, we need open access to mental health services, and a single point of access.” In other words, when people are in crisis they need to know where to go. “Then we need to break up the system into crisis, recovery, wellness. Distinct parts that everybody understands. It’s a traffic light system, and if people know where they are then we can give a clearer understanding of the services that are needed at each point. That. Must. Happen.” Crisis means the NHS; recovery takes place in community hubs, which should help with everything from complementary therapies to social clubs and financial advice; and finally, wellness is up to the individual to actively maintain, with help when needed.

Carlisle says he needs a wee. “Remind me when I come back to talk about young people and mental health.” The 2014 lorry incident affected his bladder for a while, he tells me on his return. “OK, young people. When it comes to children and young people, we’ve got people of our generation trying to create and impose systems for our young people. What do I know about what it is to be a young person these days? We don’t know what it’s like to have grown up through Covid and the digital age.” Young people are so much more emotionally literate than his generation, he says, and we’ve got to respect this. “We need to have our children and young people inform the services we construct and deliver.”

It’s wonderful to see Carlisle back, and so determined to use his experiences to help others. And, as he says, who could be in a better position, having survived all he has? “I genuinely believe I can convey a message,” he says. “I’m a man who has sat at the very precipice of life.” His voice is getting more fervent by the second. Now he sounds like an evangelical preacher – not for God, not even for good mental health, but for life itself. “I have been in end-of-life care, I have been in crisis care, I have been in psychiatric hospitals, I have been in multiple therapeutic services; not only have I been through them, I live them every day, Simon, and I live them now to a point where I am so well.” And finally he takes a breath. “So well.”

Long may it stay that way.
