https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.title: Netanyahu rejects 15-point Gaza peace plan in new break with Trump
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday rejected a US-led Gaza plan endorsed by Hamas, putting distance between himself and President Donald Trump as he tries to shore up his base ahead of close elections.

After more than a week of gradually escalating criticism of the plan, and despite receiving assurances that Israel would not need to start withdrawing in Gaza immediately, Netanyahu explicitly opposed the deal following pushback from his right-wing allies.

"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said, referring to the plan Hamas agreed to in late July.

The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed, and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens", he told a cabinet meeting.

Netanyahu described Trump, who had hailed the Gaza deal as a milestone for peace, as "our greatest friend in the White House" – but quickly made clear he was willing to challenge him, saying Israel was raising its objections with the United States.

READ MORE
Gaza faces ongoing food crisis despite ceasefire

"They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," he said.

Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader, is running even or trailing in some polls ahead of October 27 elections, the country's first since the devastating October 7, 2023 attack by Hamas that sparked the Gaza war.

Polls show that the Gaza plan is unpopular with Netanyahu's right-wing base, and far-right members of his cabinet have urged him to kill it.

The head of Trump's body implementing the plan, dubbed the Board of Peace, defended the plan as a way to prevent a repeat of October 7.

"The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again," Nickolay Mladenov, the board's high representative for Gaza, told Israel's Channel 12 television.

He said he hoped for a "positive outcome" from follow-up discussions with Israel, and characterised the latest stage of the deal as a commitment involving the United States, Hamas and the Board of Peace – notably leaving out Israel.

Mladenov again promised that Israel would not face any obligations until Hamas gave up all its weapons, down to Kalashnikov rifles – but said Israel would eventually need to pull out.

Hamas, which publicly backed the plan days after selecting a new leader, Khalil al-Hayya, called on Washington to push Netanyahu.

"We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap, and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons," Bassem Naim, a member of Hamas's political bureau, told AFP.

Hamas in a statement said it was still committed to the plan.

Netanyahu until recently campaigned on the strength of his relationship with Trump, who has taken unprecedented steps to back Israel, including moving the US embassy to Jerusalem.

Trump joined Netanyahu in late February in launching a war against Iran, but the two diverged when Trump sought a ceasefire and subsequent settlement to the conflict as it sapped his popularity and sent oil prices soaring.

Netanyahu told his cabinet that "with an agreement or without an agreement, as long as I am prime minister, Iran will not have nuclear weapons", a goal he has long alleged Tehran is pursuing.

Netanyahu last week also ordered fresh strikes on Lebanon in response to what Israel called a ceasefire violation by Iran-backed Hezbollah, just as Israel and Lebanon were holding US-mediated talks.

READ MORE
Trump's Board of Peace reassures Israel after objections on Gaza pullout plan

The Gaza plan was the latest stage in a US-brokered ceasefire announced in October that has reduced, but not ended, Israeli operations there.

Despite Netanyahu's stance, Israel appears to have decreased operations in Gaza since the deal was announced, without halting them completely.

Israeli gunfire on Sunday injured several people including a child who was taken to hospital in Khan Younis, civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Bassal told AFP.

Israeli operations in Gaza have killed 1,258 Palestinians since the ceasefire, according to the territory's health ministry, which operates under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

The Israeli army has reported five deaths in its ranks during the same period.

Topic:
Public Housing

Jonny Warren wants to repair and redevelop 20 properties to provide housing for some homeless Canberrans by Christmas. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

Jonny Warren, a Canberra real estate agent, wants to renovate or repair 20 properties in the ACT after experiencing homelessness himself earlier in his life.

He is calling on the ACT government to support the pro bono project, alongside MLA Thomas Emerson and local homelessness organisations.

The idea has been put to the ACT government, but experts say broader change is needed across the public housing sector.

Canberra real estate agent Jonny Warren remembers all too well what it's like to be homeless.

Falling in with the "wrong crowd" as a teenager, he found himself addicted to ice and living on the streets.

But with help from his family, he managed to kick his addiction and in 2014, began working in real estate.

As his career grew, he became involved with a number of charities to raise funds for homelessness, and one evening headed out with the Vinnies Night Patrol in Canberra's city centre.

That encounter, and his own experience with homelessness, has prompted him to spearhead a campaign to renovate 20 of the ACT government's vacant public housing dwellings pro bono.

And, he wants to do it all by Christmas.

Mr Warren said the project has been inindated with support. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

There are currently more than 580 vacant public housing dwellings in the ACT, 285 of which need upgrades or maintenance before they can be tenanted.

That is despite some 3,650 approved applicants being on Canberra's public housing waitlist.

The average wait time for priority housing is more than five months; for standard housing, it's more than five years.

Mr Warren wants the government to choose and approve 20 of these vacant homes to be renovated, with the aim to have tenants in them by Christmas.

And there is already an army of tradespeople volunteering to help him.

"We've got plenty of people helping, but you can never have enough hands," he said.

The Vinnies Night Patrol van provided more than 19,000 instances of support in Canberra and Queanbeyan last financial year — a 38 per cent jump on the previous year. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

Mr Warren said some of the properties required deep cleaning, while others needed new paint, carpets and tap fittings.

Housing All Australians ACT Chair Jo Farrell welcomed the initiative, but said fixing some properties would not be as simple as "running down to Bunnings and buying 20 litres of paint".

"There's a level of dignity and there's a level of quality that needs to be implemented with this," she said.

Jo Farrell said some properties would need significant repair to be ready for inhabitants.

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson is backing Mr Warren's plan to have 20 homes renovated by Christmas, and is calling on the government to do the same.

"The government's obviously struggling on its own to meet the level of demand we're seeing in our community for safe, secure, subsidised housing," Mr Emerson said.

Mr Emerson said he believed the housing crisis required "a whole of community response" but that the ACT government also needed to "come to the table".

"It's insane that we have 588 public housing properties that are vacant right now, while we have thousands of Canberrans in desperate need of public housing," he said.

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson is campaiging for more public housing to meet rising demand in the ACT. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

"Almost 300 of the properties that are vacant need maintenance or upgrades in order to be made liveable.

Ms Farrell said Mr Warren's project was just one element of a wider conversation we need to have about the ACT's ageing stock of public housing.

"The big conversation with ACT government is how can we actually work together collaboratively between community and industry and not have vacant properties and then have someone sleeping out in weather like this," Ms Farrell said.

"It's a society issue, so we can't just keep laying blame at politicians' feet or particular community sectors.

"We all have to step up and understand our accountability and responsibility with these issues that are affecting us and then that way we can all do our part."

Ms Farrell also rejected the notion that Canberra's building industry could not keep up with the level of work that was needed.

"We have a lot of tradespeople who are willing [and] ready," she said.

"So if there's going to be a rhetoric around 'we don't have the skill set', we're not looking in the right place and you're not talking to the right people."

ACT Shelter CEO Corinne Dobson says the project will make a difference but is no substitute for broader solutions. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

Corinne Dobson from ACT Shelter said the project would provide hope for the Canberrans waiting "for years" to access housing.

"We think this is a really welcome initiative and something that we would hope the government can make happen," she said.

Mr Warren said he and his team "have got a meeting [with the government] tomorrow morning, which I hope is the final step".

"We'll start small and get those 20 numbers and the 20 houses and then if we achieve that and do it with ease and with all the support that we do have, then we can shoot a little bit higher," he said.

"Our goal is hopefully next year to get 100 homes and 100 people off the streets."

The ACT government has been contacted for comment.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.title: Breaking: SA launches royal commission into artificial intelligence
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

SA will hold a royal commission into AI technologies and industries. (Igor Omilaev, Unsplash)

South Australia will hold a royal commission into "artificial intelligence and the policy development around it".

Premier Peter Malinauskas said AI, if unchecked, presented a "material risk to the way society operates".

He said the inquiry was intended to maximise benefits and minimise unwanted impacts from the growth of AI.

The royal commission is expected to commence in October and report by mid next year.

"We are at a really important fork in the road where we can choose to allow this industry to come to our country and evolve in a way that is unregulated and unchecked," Mr Malinauskas said.

"Or we can choose to set the agenda. We can choose to set the guard rails and the policy frameworks to ensure that we use AI in a way that puts people first.

"The use of artificial intelligence is an exciting opportunity to advance the cause of humanity but it is also true that unchecked artificial intelligence does represent a material risk to the way our society operates and a risk to the future of work if not thought through carefully."

Mr Malinauskas said the royal commission would follow his recent trip to the United States where he met with representatives from AI heavyweights OpenAI, Anthropic and Apple.

Some wild mushrooms have poisons that can make you sick, so it is recommended to only eat varieties you get from a reliable supermarket, grocer or market.

You can also use store-bought red curry paste as a shortcut.

https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/east-asia.title: Malaysia seeks to deepen trade ties with South Korea in chips, AI, halal sector
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/east-asia.author: The Korea Times
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/east-asia.text:
South Korea’s biotechnology and pharmaceutical sectors can complement Malaysia’s halal certification system, a Malaysian official says

In an interview with The Korea Times, Malaysian Investment Development Authority (MIDA) director Redzuan Abd Rahman and Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE) trade commissioner Mohamad Termizi HJ Piee said the two countries’ economic relationship had entered a new phase, with growing opportunities for South Korean companies to leverage Malaysia as both an investment destination and a gateway to the wider Asean market.

“Malaysia and South Korea have built a strong and enduring economic partnership over the past several decades,” Redzuan said. “We believe the greatest opportunities lie in deepening collaboration in industries that are shaping the future of our economies.”

According to MIDA, South Korean companies have implemented investments totalling US$11.7 billion across more than 400 projects in Malaysia as of 2025, creating nearly 50,000 jobs. Those investments span chemicals, transport equipment, electrical and electronic products, petroleum products and basic metals.

Redzuan highlighted that the two countries’ respective national development strategies were highly complementary, explaining that while South Korea continued to advance its leadership in semiconductors, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, mobility, batteries and green technologies, Malaysia was implementing the New Industrial Master Plan 2030, the National Semiconductor Strategy and the National Energy Transition Roadmap “to accelerate industrial transformation towards higher-value, innovation-driven and sustainable industries”.

This strong strategic alignment presents significant opportunities for deeper Malaysia-South Korea collaboration in investment, technology and industrial partnerships, reinforcing Malaysia’s position as a strategic destination for South Korean companies seeking regional growth.

Termizi echoed that assessment from the trade perspective, pointing to rapidly expanding bilateral commerce between both countries.

“Malaysia and the Republic of Korea have built a strong and resilient economic partnership, supported by growing trade, complementary industries and close cooperation through Asean and regional trade agreements,” he said.

From January through June this year, bilateral trade increased a whopping 52.3 per cent year on year to US$19 billion, with Malaysia’s exports to South Korea rising 44.2 per cent and imports from South Korea climbing 58.9 per cent.

“From MATRADE’s perspective, the next phase should focus on diversifying trade into emerging sectors such as AI, robotics, medical devices, green technology, digital services and the halal economy, while helping more Malaysian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) participate in South Korean supply chains,” he said. “Ultimately, our priority is to transform conventional buyer-seller relationships into long-term partnerships involving technology, innovation, joint product development and access to wider regional and global markets.”

As South Korean companies continue diversifying their supply chains across Southeast Asia, both officials highlighted Malaysia’s advantages beyond competitive production costs. Redzuan said Malaysia combined “industrial maturity, strategic location and policy stability” with more than five decades of experience in electrical and electronics manufacturing.

“Malaysia handles roughly 13 per cent of global semiconductor packaging and testing, providing an established supplier ecosystem that significantly lowers market entry risks,” he said.

He also stressed the country’s multilingual, English-proficient workforce, strong intellectual property protection and long-term industrial policy frameworks.

“Unlike markets that compete solely on low labour costs, Malaysia offers South Korean investors an ecosystem capable of supporting capital-intensive, hi-tech and ESG-compliant manufacturing from day 1,” Redzuan said.

Termizi similarly described Malaysia as “a strategic gateway to Asean,” citing its participation in major trade agreements including the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the free trade agreement between South Korea and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, in addition to its multilingual business environment. He added that the coming Malaysia-South Korea FTA was expected to further strengthen bilateral trade and investment, enhance market access and create new opportunities for businesses in both countries.

“These strengths make Malaysia an ideal sourcing partner for South Korean companies seeking to build resilient and diversified supply chains,” Termizi said.

Asked where bilateral cooperation could expand most significantly over the coming years, both officials identified advanced technology industries as priority areas. Redzuan said Malaysia aimed to deepen collaboration with South Korea in advanced electronics, electric vehicles (EV), renewable energy and digital infrastructure, in tandem with the Southeast Asian country’s acceleration of its dual transition towards a hi-tech and low-carbon economy.

“We see South Korean firms not merely as foreign investors, but as long-term strategic partners that co-develop intellectual property, upskill local engineering talent and integrate Malaysian suppliers into global value chains,” Redzuan said.

Termizi likewise pointed to opportunities in semiconductors, AI, robotics, smart manufacturing, medical devices, green technology and digital services.

“Malaysia is already a key player in the global semiconductor ecosystem, while South Korea is recognised for its leadership in advanced technologies and industrial innovation,” he said. “These complementary strengths create opportunities for greater collaboration in supply chains, technology partnerships and regional market expansion.”

Redzuan cited South Korean conglomerates including SK Nexilis, Samsung, POSCO, OCI and Lotte as examples of successful investments in Malaysia, highlighting SK Nexilis’ US$540 million EV copper foil manufacturing facility in Sabah as the company’s largest overseas investment.

He said MIDA supported investors through end-to-end facilitation, including manufacturing licences, tax incentives and expatriate services, while MATRADE connected South Korean companies with Malaysian suppliers through business-matching programmes.

“Together, MIDA Seoul and MATRADE Seoul handhold investors from the initial site selection and regulatory approvals all the way through to commercial operations and supply chain localisation,” he said.

Both officials reaffirmed their commitment to supporting South Korean companies seeking opportunities in Malaysia, noting that MIDA Seoul and MATRADE Seoul were conveniently co-located at the Malaysian Trade and Investment Centre near Jonggak station in central Seoul. That arrangement, they said, gave South Korean businesses a single point of contact for investment- and trade-related inquiries, reflecting Malaysia’s commitment to delivering seamless support throughout every stage of the investment journey.

On sustainability, Redzuan said both countries’ shared commitment to net-zero emissions by 2050 would create significant room for collaboration in renewable energy, hydrogen, carbon capture and storage, solar manufacturing and the circular economy.

Termizi noted that MATRADE launched its Sustainability Action Values for Exporters (SAVE) initiative back in 2019 to help Malaysian exporters strengthen environmental, social and corporate governance practices and remain competitive in global supply chains.

“By combining South Korean technology with Malaysian manufacturing, engineering and market-access capabilities, companies from both countries can jointly develop and commercialise sustainable solutions for Malaysia, Asean and wider global markets,” he said.

Both officials also highlighted the halal economy as an area with particularly strong growth potential.

Redzuan said combining South Korea’s advanced biotechnology and pharmaceutical capabilities with Malaysia’s internationally recognised halal certification system could unlock major opportunities in halal pharmaceuticals, functional foods and cosmetics.

Termizi emphasised that halal had evolved well beyond food: “Another misconception is that halal is only relevant to food,” he said. “In reality, the halal economy now covers cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, healthcare, logistics, tourism and many other sectors, representing one of the world’s fastest-growing consumer markets.”

He encouraged South Korean businesses to leverage Malaysia’s well-established halal ecosystem to expand into Muslim markets across Asean, the Middle East, South Asia and Africa, while also pointing to the MIHAS as a platform for building international partnerships.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c235.title: Woman questions hosepipe ban while leak not fixed
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c235.text:
A woman has criticised Anglian Water for imposing a hosepipe ban while not fixing a water leak that she had reported "weeks ago".

Linda Kirby, a receptionist at Polly's Field Village in Deanery Hill in Braintree, Essex, said in June she reported a leak that tickles down Church Lane and forms a puddle next to Chantry Close.

She added a hosepipe ban amid a drought while the leak remained made her "very annoyed".

Anglian Water said its teams were "working hard" through the hot weather to "prioritise repairs that are having the greatest impact on customers' water supplies".

Kirby, who lives in Halstead, Essex, said she goes past the leak every time she drives to work.

She said: "Why are we paying all of this money when there is water being wasted down a drain?"

"It started as a small trickle and over the weeks it has got bigger - they need to get their act together."

Residents who live next to the leak have also expressed their disappointment with the company.

One woman, who the BBC has agreed not to name, said she had reported the leak to Anglian Water.

"The leak has been there for two to three months and no-one seems to be doing anything about it," she said.

"There's a hosepipe ban and we are wasting water and it's causing a huge puddle in the street that cars splash through," she added.

In a statement, Anglian Water said the current weather "can cause ground movement that results in an increase of burst water mains or leaks".

"We'd like to thank our customers for their patience while we respond to the challenges created by this period of exceptionally dry weather," it added.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq89.title: Forest funding boost as two million trees planted
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq89.text:
A tree planting scheme has received £8.7m of government funding to expand the project as organisers celebrate planting more than two million trees.

The Forest for Cornwall scheme started in 2019 in a bid to help the county respond to climate change.

Cornwall Council said the money should help the authority reach its target of 8,000 hectares (19,768 acres) of "new tree canopy by 2035".

The project has included tree planting in communities, farms, schools and streets across Cornwall. Bosses said the scheme was designed to help England reach the target of 16.5% canopy and woodland cover by 2050.

Loic Rich, Cornwall's cabinet member for environment and climate change, said the Forest for Cornwall "enhances our local landscape, towns and villages, bringing the beauty and benefits of trees to our doorsteps to improve our health and happiness, providing much-needed shade during this prolonged period of heat".

He said it helped farmers increase farm resilience and helped wildlife "by providing homes for birds, mammals and insects, helping keep our rivers and streams clean and cool, reducing run-off, and improving the health of our soils".

He added increased tree cover helped "reduce flooding in coastal towns and building resilience to a changing climate".

The latest grant from Defra's Trees Programme comes after hundreds of trees were destroyed in January when Storm Goretti brought gusts of up to 100mph (160km/h).

It brought down mature trees at St Michael's Mount near Penzance and Trewithen in Truro.

Ben Thomas, from Treveddoe Farm near Cardinham, has planted 2,500 trees.

He said: "Without the knowledge, contacts and funding it would have been hard to find the time to get the project started.

"In the end we have ended up with a brilliant agroforestry network on the farm which is already delivering."

Cornwall Council said the money should help the authority reach its target of 8,000 hectares of "new tree canopy by 2035" The project has included tree planting in communities, farms, schools and streets across Cornwall.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0km.title: Work at National Trust site to prevent flooding
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0km.text:
A National Trust site in Shropshire are working to try and slow down water, to prevent the catchment from getting flooded.

Rangers and volunteers at Attingham Park, in Atcham, have been building dams, restoring ponds and planting trees, in a bid to use their land as a sponge for the River Severn and River Tern.

It is one of eight projects being supported through the Severn Valley Water Management Scheme and Shropshire Council.

They say this project will help "understand how nature-based solutions" can be used to improve water management and make the Severn catchment resilient to future climate change.

Dams have been made with willow wood from pond restoration projects on the Attingham estate.

Park ranger, Emilia Fahlstromova, said that wood is the best material possible to restore the wetland habitats.

"By putting these dams in, we are hoping to wet in the area up," she added.

"Over the years the area has dried up a lot, which we do not want to see in this area, so we are hoping to see some more wetland species come through."

"Hopefully, it will make the land act like a sponge and hold all that water."

Project manager, Jane Birch, has been working on more solutions to restore the habitats, like planting hedgerows and making barriers out of wood that trap debris.

She added it is important for landowners to adapt.

"Post World War Two, there was a big emphasis on food production and how can we make as much of the land [as] productive as possible," Birch said.

"That means draining it to create that dry land. But I think we [now] need to look at how we can hold more water on the land, so that we can reduce that flooding risk downstream."

Flooding has become more common across the United Kingdom because of extreme weathers caused by climate change.

BBC Midlands Today's environmental correspondent, David Gregory Kumar, said using natural methods can make a huge difference.

"It solves a lot of problems, even if it is just a simple idea like sticking a few logs into a stream," Gregory Kumar added.

"Places in the West Midlands are trying this out in rivers and tributaries, but not in the massive rivers like the Severn.

"There is this thinking now that if we slow down the water and it does flood a bit into land, that's not necessarily a problem."

The project is one of eight supported by the Severn Valley Water Management Scheme and Shropping Council. The aim is to use the land as a sponge for the River Severn and River Tern.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62e.title: Ospreys hatch at nature reserve for first time
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62e.text:
The RSPB is celebrating conservation success after ospreys bred at one of the bird charity's nature reserves in England for the first time.

A pair of the rare birds of prey successfully hatched three chicks at Campfield Marsh, a wetland on the shores of Solway Firth, in Cumbria, it said.

The reserve has an osprey platform to attract the raptors and the adults who have nested there are also believed to be first-time parents. The female is unringed while the male was ringed in Dumfries in 2021.

Site manager Mhairi Maclauchlan said staff had been "on tenterhooks" until the chicks hatched and very relieved when they did.

Ospreys are migratory birds which journey from wintering grounds in west Africa to Europe in the spring to breed.

The chicks have now been ringed and are expected to fledge in August, but are likely to remain in the area learning to fish and fend for themselves before starting the weeks-long migration to Africa from September.

The rings will allow the chicks' future movements to be recorded and monitored.

Maclauchlan said: "We were on tenterhooks after the eggs were laid and throughout the incubation period until they hatched.

"There was a huge collective sigh of relief when they did."

The species were persecuted to extinction as a breeding bird in the early 20th Century but returned to Scotland in the 1950s and have now recolonised other parts of the UK.

"Osprey parents are surprisingly tender despite their large size and sharp talons," Maclauchlan said.

"They can also offer good comedic value with nest tidying exploits and antics.

"Ospreys are frequently site- and partner-faithful, so we're hoping to see more of them and their offspring in the future."

The eggs were laid between 30 April and 6 May and, once the chicks hatched in June, a local primary school helped name them Ash, Bowness Bobbi and Beau.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly5.title: Burnham brings forward ban on 'subscription traps' to ease cost of living
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly5.text:
Consumers will benefit from an end to so-called subscription traps and a crackdown on "pretend prices", Andy Burnham has said.

The prime minister is bringing forward a package of changes announced under his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, to make it easier to cancel subscriptions.

Burnham is also planning to outlaw shops using fake "was" prices, which he said trick shoppers into thinking they are getting better value on purchases.

Shadow chancellor Mel Stride branded the measures "reheated" and said the prime minister "has already run out of ideas".

The plans were announced under Sir Keir in April, but are being brought forward by Burnham's government in a bid to give families "room to breathe" amid the high cost of living.

Burnham, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, has promised a series of "everyday fixes" to help people with the cost of living.

He said: "I'm determined to pull every single lever we can to provide people with some room to breathe on the cost of living."

The measures being brought forward are aimed at making it easier for consumers to cancel unwanted subscriptions and stopping people being rolled onto expensive contracts without their knowledge.

They were expected to come into force next spring, but Burnham's government has promised they will now be implemented by January 2027.

When they were announced in April, the government said the plans would save consumers £400m a year in total, or up to £170 per person.

On top of the already planned changes, Burnham is also vowing to end shops' use of "pretend prices". This will stop retailers using "was" prices, made-up discounts or misleading recommended retail prices (RRPs) to highlight deals.

The government will launch a consultation this autumn to decide how the new measures should be implemented.

Consumer group Which? said it has "repeatedly exposed businesses, including trusted household brands, ripping off customers with dodgy deals that aren't what they seem".

Its head of consumer rights policy, Sue Davies, welcomed the announcement and called for the government to bring the rules in "swiftly".

But Stride said: "The cost of living didn't become a problem last week, so you have to ask why it has taken Labour so long to enact legislation passed by the previous government."

The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumer Act, passed under the Conservatives in 2024, cracked down on hidden fees, fake reviews online and made it easier for customers to cancel subscriptions.

The announcement is Burnham's latest intervention aimed at easing the cost of living, following a £2 bus fare cap in England and a VAT cut on household electricity bills.

But he is likely to come under pressure to make more significant changes in the Budget, which will be delivered by Chancellor John Healey on 28 October.

But Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" – which will limit how much the government has to spend.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly5.summary: Andy Burnham is bringing forward a package of changes to make it easier to cancel subscriptions. The changes will stop shops using fake "was" prices, made-up discounts or misleading retail prices. The measures were announced under Sir Keir Starmer in April but are being brought forward by Burnham's government.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62e.title: Risk of patient safety 'bonfire' with Health Bill changes, Lib Dems say
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62e.text:
The Liberal Democrats have urged Andy Burnham to stop the "bonfire of patient safety" as part of the government's plans to modernise the NHS.

Healthwatch England (HWE), an independent body which represents the views of patients at their local health and social care providers, is set to be scrapped under the NHS Modernisation Bill.

The Health Service Safety Investigation Bureau (HSSIB), which carries out patient safety investigations, is also being abolished.

The government says its changes will strip back bureaucracy and improve patient safety.

The Lib Dems warned it risks another Stafford Hospital scandal – where years of abuse and neglect led to hundreds of unnecessary patient deaths.

A Healthcare Commission report found the scandal – one of the biggest in NHS history – involved at least 400 more deaths than expected between 2005 and 2008.

Under the government proposals, Healthwatch's responsibilities will be transferred to integrated care boards (ICBs) and local authorities, meaning they would have to respond to feedback about their own services, rather than being challenged by an independent body.

Separately, HSSIB's functions will be transferred to the government-run Care Quality Commission (CQC), which the Lib Dems argue raises concerns there is no guarantee that staff who raise safety concerns are given anonymity.

Other measures include the abolition of NHS England in a bid to centralise the running of health and social care services under the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC).

The government says this will reduce bureaucracy and allow more resources to be delivered to frontline healthcare services.

The NHS Modernisation Bill is currently at the report stage and due for a third reading on 7 September.

Liberal Democrat health spokesperson Helen Morgan said this was "a catastrophic step backwards" and described it as the "greatest backward step in patient safety in a generation".

"Andy Burnham must urgently put an end to this, and fix the Health Bill so that modernising the NHS doesn't come at the expense of accountability, transparency or patient safety," Morgan added.

In a speech on NHS reform in January, then-Health Secretary Wes Streeting said "there are many decent people working at Healthwatch who care, but the job of listening to patients can't be farmed out to an arm's length body".

"It must be core business for the NHS. That is why we're taking it back in-house and I won't back down on that either."

The Lib Dems also said the current bill removes the duty for the NHS to cooperate with the Care Quality Commission in providing key safety data and removes automatic "safe space" protections for whistleblowers.

Amendments tabled by the Liberal Democrats would cancel the changes and the party is "urging the new Burnham administration to adopt them".

The party vowed to robustly fight the government in the House of Lords, where Labour doesn't have a majority.

A DHSC spokesperson said NHS Modernisation Bill "explicitly preserves safe space provisions and staff will continue to be protected".

"The reforms we are introducing will give patients a stronger, clearer voice at the heart of health and social care."

Burnham was health secretary in 2009, when the Healthcare Commission's report was released on the Stafford Hospital scandal. Burnham then launched an independent inquiry in 2010.

In May, the Local Government Association (LGA) told the BBC disbanding Healthwatch would be a "significant step back" in accountability.

"Without an independent, locally rooted voice to challenge and represent communities, there is a risk of duplication and gaps in accountability," the LGA said.

There are currently more than 150 local Healthwatch organisations in England.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy8m.title: Harry Potter fans force diversion of UK-Ireland power link to avoid 'Dobby's grave'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy8m.text:
Harry Potter fans succeeded in diverting a multimillion-pound power link between the UK and Ireland after they complained it would disturb a "memorial" to Dobby the House Elf.

The £430m Greenlink interconnector links the National Grid to Ireland via 125-mile cable between County Wexford and Freshwater West, a beach in Pembrokeshire where the death of fictional character Dobby was filmed in the Potter films.

Project manager Simon Ludlam told the Energy Revolution podcast the cable was originally "going to go straight through" the tribute, before fans began leaving his firm "hundreds of calls".

"Actually we went quite close to some real Bronze Age remains, but we avoided Dobby's grave," he said.

Ludlam, founder of Etchea Energy, said a BBC News interview about the project had turned into a public relations nightmare after fans got wind of what was to happen.

He told the podcast that during the filmed interview he had pointed out where the cable would go underground, saying: "We did the shot, we finished I went back to London, and they then aired it a couple of weeks later.

"And we got hundreds of calls, I mean hundreds of calls."

He said a colleague told him the nature of the calls, and that "apparently we're going to go straight through Dobby's grave".

"I said 'Dobby, who's Dobby? I don't know Dobby?'

"I said 'he's a fictitious character in a fictitious book, the whole thing is fictitious what are you talking about?'

"[The colleague] said 'no it's very, very serious'."

Ludlam said he then discussed with planners "exactly how to reroute the cable so we wouldn't go anywhere close to Dobby's grave".

He added: "A lot of people were very happy about that, and the project is now going [ahead] and Dobby's happy."

The Bronze Age remains the cable went close to were mentioned in Pembrokeshire council planning documents about the power link.

It said archaeological trenches dug near the route of the underground cable "contained the rim of an inverted pottery vessel whose fabric suggests a Bronze Age collared urn circa 1700-1500BC, typically associated with human burial".

The cable diversion is not the first time Dobby's grave has been saved.

In 2022 the National Trust agreed it could remain in place following a consultation, but urged visitors not to leave souvenirs.

Fans were asked not to leave socks on the mock grave, made of pebbles with messages written on them, because the beach was environmentally sensitive.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy8m.summary: £430m Greenlink interconnector links the National Grid to Ireland via 125-mile cable. The cable was originally "going to go straight through" the tribute, says project manager. But fans began leaving firm after they complained it would disturb a "memorial" to Dobby the House Elf.

https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.text:
Iran’s national security chief on Sunday outlined a list of demands for the US to meet before Tehran reopens the Strait of Hormuz.

They include lifting the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, compensation for war damages and the release of frozen Iranian assets.

The Yemeni military said seven people including military personnel and civilians were killed ​and ‌30 others wounded in ⁠a Houthi attack on the Red Sea ‌port city of Mocha, civilian infrastructure and ⁠armed forces.

"Four members of the armed forces and three civilians ​have been killed, and 30 others ‌injured," the Yemeni military said in a statement early on Monday.

Air defences ‌intercepted and shot down 11 Houthi drones ​that participated in the attack, the military said.

Footage shown by Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV ​showed the launch of several ballistic ​missiles and drones, which ​Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a post ​on Telegram targeted Saudi troop concentrations and weapons depots.

The Yemeni military said the Houthi attacks had also targeted residential ⁠neighbourhoods in Mocha.

Iran said it was nearing a final ​pact with Oman defining new shipping lanes between them through the Strait of Hormuz but repeated that the US must meet other conditions, including compensation and an end to sanctions and military threats, before the strategic waterway is reopened.

A US official told Reuters on Friday that Iran and Oman were close to a deal that could pave the way for restoring safe passage through the strait, a major ​conduit for oil and ‌gas shipping before Iran blocked Hormuz in response to US and Israeli attacks on Tehran that began in late February.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said ⁠on Sunday an agreement with Oman on the strait was in its "final stages" but reiterated comments made on Saturday that Tehran would not reopen the channel unless the US met certain demands made by Tehran.

Araqchi said reopening the strait would depend in part on the US paying compensation ‌for damage it caused in widespread attacks on Iran.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/c.title: 'Modern-day pirates': Calls to protect foreign cruise ship workers
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Australia's Anti-Slavery Commissioner Chris Evans says change is "long overdue". (ABC News: Jasper Wells)

Australia's Anti-Slavery Commissioner says crew on foreign cruise ships should receive the same treatment as local workers.

A decades-old exemption to Australian labour laws for cruise ships leaves crew with far fewer protections than onshore workers covered by the Fair Work Act.

The government is reviewing the findings of a review into the exemption, which is due to expire at the end of the year.

Australia's Anti-Slavery Commissioner says crew on foreign cruise ships need greater protections and that they should be treated on par with Australian workers.

An ABC News investigation last week uncovered allegations from crew onboard Carnival cruise ships of paltry pay and shocking living conditions.

Workers alleged extreme working hours, medical neglect and that they were forced to eat rotten buffet leftovers. Carnival denies the allegations.

Chris Evans says change is needed in the legal protections for workers on foreign-flagged cruise ships in Australia. (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

Currently, foreign-flagged cruise ships do not need to comply with the Fair Work Act when travelling between Australian ports, due to an exemption from licensing requirements.

It was introduced as a "temporary" measure in 1998, and has been renewed every few years since.

"Fundamentally the situation ought to be that ships that are working through Australian ports ought to be applying conditions that are on a par with Australian conditions," Anti-Slavery Commissioner Chris Evans said.

Asked if the exemption should be rolled back, Mr Evans said, "I think some change in this area is long overdue."

Mr Evans was appointed the inaugural Anti-Slavery Commissioner by the Albanese government in 2024 after serving as immigration minister and workplace relations minister in the Rudd and Gillard Labor governments.

One contract seen by the ABC shows that some workers are paid $US23.26 ($AU33) a day.   (ABC News: Jasper Wells)

Several crew members working on Carnival's Australian ships told the ABC they worked 12 hours a day, seven days a week for almost all of their nine-month contracts.

A contract seen by the ABC from 2025 showed one worker being paid just $33 a day.

According to the maritime union, most staff are contract workers from Africa and South East Asia.

Passengers boarding a Carnival cruise ship are promised a world of endless food, relaxation and oceanic luxury. But for the crew, life is vastly different.

"Fundamentally, they are employing people from countries with very low wages rates and they're getting people prepared to work for conditions that we regard as unacceptable," Mr Evans said.

Labor Senator Tony Sheldon went onboard a Carnival ship last month to investigate similar claims.

He said his conversations with dozens of crew backed up the allegations reported by the ABC, including wages less than $3 an hour, crew paying for bottled water and long working days.

Tony Sheldon says he spoke to dozens of crew members onboard a Carnival ship. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

"These are guys operating like modern day pirates, but instead of raiding other ships, they're plundering their own crew," Senator Sheldon said.

Carnival rejected the allegations made by crew about working conditions and treatment.

"AMSA, Australia's maritime compliance regulator, has carried out surprise inspections of our three ships in recent weeks — and cleared Carnival on each occasion," Carnival said in a statement.

The company also said it followed the Maritime Labour Convention, and referred the ABC to a statement provided in February, which said, "Carnival has nothing to hide."

Senator Sheldon said the company needed to respect the crew's right to collective bargaining under the Maritime Labour Convention, to which Australia was a signatory.

Carnival has accused the maritime union of using crew as "props" to increase its membership.

Australia's Anti-Slavery Commissioner Chris Evans says change is "long overdue". (ABC News: Jasper Wells)

"It looks like Carnival has a floating holiday for passengers whilst having a floating sweatshop for the crew with no voice," Senator Sheldon, formerly secretary of the Transport Workers Union, said.

The Anti-Slavery Commissioner said there was no reason that foreign-flagged cruises should be able to undercut the costs of worker wages through the exemption, which he said gave them an advantage over competitors that could not use it.

Chris Evans says worker exploitation is a systemic issue. (Alicia Barry)

"If they're working out of Australian ports they ought to be meeting those Australian conditions, and they certainly should be meeting those international conditions that are expected," Mr Evans said.

The findings of a review into the Coastal Trading Act, which facilitates the exemption, were handed to the government at the end of last year and are not yet public.

The exemption is due to expire at the end of December, and a spokesperson for Transport Minister Catherine King, who is responsible for the exemption, said the minister would decide whether to renew the exemption before then.

The spokesperson said the exemption recognised "the importance to Australians and our economy of the cruise sector".

They said it recognised the difference in labour laws in the global cruise industry, but that it did not undermine international labour rights conventions.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2.title: ‘Total whiplash’: Foreign residents react to Japan’s changing permanent residency rules
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2.author: Jessica Speed
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2.text:
Foreign residents who have spent years working toward permanent residency in Japan say the government’s proposed new requirements have left them angry, anxious and unable to plan for the future, with some reconsidering whether they can remain in the country at all.

The changes, which could affect income assessments for applications submitted as early as April, have been particularly unsettling for residents approaching the end of the standard 10-year pathway to permanent residency.

“Many like myself have been diligently working based on the current rules, but are now suddenly feeling derailed from that trajectory,” said Leshe Scott, who lives in the city of Kasai, Hyogo Prefecture.

Scott, who is entering her ninth year in Japan, works in academia. In her free time, she farms and is working to create a community studio focused on science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics.

Her 10th year in Japan will coincide with the implementation of the new requirements.

“I may meet the new salary requirement for now, but I’m on contract, not a permanent employee, so that and the new projected 30-year pension requirement based on that salary may negatively impact my chances,” she said.

“To say my anxiety about everything is through the roof would be an understatement.”

Scott’s uncertainty reflects a broader frustration among residents who say the conditions for permanent residency have shifted after they spent years organizing their careers and finances around the existing system.

Under changes announced earlier this year, starting April 2027, applicants will need to hold the maximum period of stay available under their visa status — generally five years for many work-related categories — before applying for permanent residency.

But immigration authorities do not publish concrete criteria explaining why one resident receives a one-, three- or five-year visa.

American J.R., who works in regional revitalization in northern Japan and asked to go by his initials for privacy reasons, said the lack of transparency leaves residents unable to identify a realistic path toward permanent residency.

“If I cannot get a five-year visa, I cannot apply for PR after 10 years,” he said. “The government is placing me in a strange chicken-and-egg situation: Do I put down roots first and then obtain PR, or do I obtain PR and then put down roots? There’s no clear explanation.”

L., an adjunct university instructor in Shimane Prefecture from the U.S. who also asked to go by an initial, has repeatedly received only a one-year professor visa, despite having worked in Japan since 2017 and being connected to the country through study and sister-city activities since around 2010.

Her workplace has consistently expressed a desire to continue employing her, she said, but as a part-time instructor she receives contracts on a semester-by-semester basis.

That means she cannot satisfy the maximum-period requirement, regardless of whether she meets other conditions.

She had hoped permanent residency would allow her to contribute more freely in Shimane through education and tourism work, without repeatedly seeking permission from immigration authorities for activities outside her main job.

“Step by step, with all of the changes that have been made, I’ve kind of given up on the idea,” she said.

The proposed income and pension requirements have added another layer of uncertainty, particularly for contract workers, older applicants and those whose income may fluctuate.

For American Nick Woolsey, founder and CEO of relocation advisory company Japan Remotely, the pension provisions have created particular concern for experienced professionals who want to use their savings and expertise in Japan later in their careers.

Some of his clients are leaving corporate jobs and hope to reinvest their money in rural communities, but might not have enough years remaining in their working lives to build the pension record contemplated under the new guidelines.

“It’s unfortunate that those so passionate about Japan are affected by politics targeted toward bad actors,” Woolsey said. “Just like the business manager visa, it seems we are collateral damage.”

“It seems like the income requirements are meant to deter the young and pension requirements are meant to deter the old. Who does Japan want then as a permanent resident? It’s a paradox that ultimately may mean ‘no one,’” he added.

Scott also questioned whether the government’s new required level of financial contribution adequately reflects the people already supporting local communities and public services, such as caregivers, construction workers or those under the Specified Skilled Worker visa.

“Many who are actively holding society up aren’t in the high-income brackets they want,” she said.

The proposed financial requirements have also raised concerns that Japan could undermine its own efforts to revive rural regions and address labor shortages outside major cities.

L. said salaries in Shimane tend to be lower than those in urban areas, even as the prefecture struggles to retain young people and attract workers.

She described watching students leave because of limited career and educational opportunities, even when they would prefer to remain in the region.

“If rural areas have to bring in foreign workers to make up for the fact that many young Japanese people don’t want to be here, I feel this new salary requirement could make it even more difficult to retain the foreign workers who are needed,” she said.

A national income benchmark could encourage foreign residents seeking permanent residency to move to Tokyo or another major city, rather than remain in communities where they may be more urgently needed.

For some residents, the tightening measures have become one factor in a broader calculation over whether remaining in Japan makes financial sense over the long term.

L. said that if she eventually returns to the United States, leaving sooner would allow her to build retirement savings in dollars rather than yen. Staying in Japan for many more years while the yen remains weak could reduce the overseas value of the savings she accumulates.

At the same time, leaving would mean giving up a community in which she has spent much of her adult life.

She said the policy changes had created a sense of “total whiplash” between the acceptance she experiences locally and decisions made by officials with no knowledge of her life.

“The people who know me are always offering me opportunities to get involved and really become part of the community,” she said. “But people who don’t know me decide whether I can live here or not.”

However, not all foreign residents reject the government’s reasoning.

Jake Nalton, a British education consultant who obtained permanent residency in 2021, said the income and pension requirements could be understood as an attempt to ensure that people settling indefinitely in Japan can support themselves in retirement.

“The pension requirements appear intended to make sure people can support themselves after retirement and that the country does not have to pay out too much,” he said. “I’ve tried to interpret the changes not simply as ‘we only want wealthy foreigners,’ but as an effort to ensure people can support themselves after retirement.”

“The language requirements also suggest the government wants people to be able to communicate without placing the entire burden on Japanese people,” he said.

A single person earning the previous benchmark of ¥3 million ($18,960) or ¥3.5 million a year may struggle to buy a home, accumulate significant savings and retire securely without a spouse’s income, Nalton said.

He also argued that Japan’s immigration system had been relatively accessible for many foreign residents over a long period.

Still, Nalton said he sympathized with people who were only months away from applying and “suddenly had the rug pulled out from under them.”

He also warned against allowing the issue to become a dispute between higher- and lower-earning foreign residents. Rather than telling lower-paid residents to find better jobs or leave the country, the discussion should focus on encouraging companies to improve salaries and expand the range of careers available to foreign workers, particularly outside Tokyo, he said.

Rich Young, an American lawyer and founder of product-safety consultancy LegalKaizen, likewise said Japan has the sovereign authority to decide who may remain in the country and under what conditions.

He said the proposed changes were not inherently unfair, but questioned whether they addressed the underlying problem.

Young supports Japanese-language requirements and higher application fees if the additional revenue is used to employ more immigration officers and conduct individualized assessments.

But he said rigid income thresholds are unlikely to identify the people who would make the greatest contribution to the country.

“Clever people will find ways around a numerical system,” he said. “I would rather the government focus on whether people genuinely love the country and want to be part of it.”

Young, who participates in shrine activities, local neighborhood administration, cat rescues and local patrols, said immigration officials should consider applicants’ involvement in their communities rather than relying primarily on numerical criteria.

Local immigration offices may be better placed to assess whether an applicant has established a genuine life in the community, he said, including through interviews and discussions with people who know them.

Japan needs immigration, Young added, but must create a system that helps foreign residents integrate and establish lasting connections with their communities.

However, for those who had viewed permanent residency as the final step toward buying a home, changing careers, opening a business or retiring in Japan, the government’s proposed measures may become the trigger that causes them to stop seeing the country as a place where they can build a permanent future.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2.summary: Residents say they are worried about the new requirements for permanent residency. The changes could affect income assessments for applications submitted as early as April. L. L. says the policy changes have created a sense of ‘total whiplash’ between acceptance and decisions made by officials with no knowledge of her life.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g3.title: Sophia Laforteza steps away from Katseye, the second member to depart this year
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g3.text:
Katseye vocalist Sophia Laforteza has announced she will temporarily step away from the popular girl group over mental health concerns.

The departure comes less than six months after fellow bandmate Manon Bannerman said she would go on hiatus from the ensemble, known for its global hits Gnarly, Pinky Up and Gabriela.

Laforteza "will be temporarily unable to participate in upcoming promotional activities", HYBE x Geffen Records said in a statement.

"We understand how much EYEKONS were looking forward to seeing Sophia on stage, but it is imperative that her mental health and wellness are prioritised," the label said of the Filipino-American superstar.

The label said Laforteza had been receiving "the utmost support" and consulting medical professionals, and had been advised to dedicate time to "extended rest and ongoing care to ensure a full recovery".

"While Sophia herself is eager to perform alongside her members, the health, safety and long-term wellbeing of our artists will always remain our highest priority," the statement said, noting that her condition will be reassessed in September.

Laforteza wrote separately on Instagram: "Making this decision wasn't easy, but I'm learning that health has to come first. I'm realising that if I don't take care of my mind and body now, I won't be able to keep doing what I love the most for so long."

She added: "It means more to me than I could ever say. I promise I'm going to work as hard as I can to get through this, heal properly, and come back stronger."

The girl group formed with six members in 2023 and was nominated for two Grammy Awards last year. It now will continue to appear at events with four members.

The group has previously said its members have received multiple online death threats since they made their debut.

The label announced in February that Katseye member Bannerman would take a temporary break to focus on her health and wellbeing, as well. She has not returned but their label has said the door will always be open.

The 23-year-old Swiss singer told fans she was "healthy" and "taking care of myself".

The group said the decision had been made following "open and thoughtful conversations together".

The departure comes less than six months after fellow bandmate Manon Bannerman said she would go on hiatus. The group has previously said its members have received multiple online death threats.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Victorian Liberals promise weekly red bin garbage collections for all, calling fortnightly system ‘disgusting’
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Benita Kolovos Victorian state correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
If opposition wins November’s state election, leader Jess Wilson vows households will not pay more under the change

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Victorian Liberals have vowed to restore weekly rubbish collections if they win November’s state election, with leader Jess Wilson describing the current fortnightly system in her local area as “disgusting”.

Thirty-three Victorian councils have switched general rubbish collections from weekly to fortnightly, with a similar shift occurring in other states.

In metropolitan Melbourne they include Banyule, Bayside, Boroondara, Glen Eira, Knox, Manningham, Monash, Nillumbik and Yarra Ranges.

Merri-bek is also expected to follow from mid-2027, in a move it has said would save ratepayers $16m over 10 years, help keep food waste out of landfill and reduce pollution.

Under Merri-bek’s proposal, the standard red-lid rubbish bin would increase from 80 litres to 120 litres, while certain households, such as those with multiple children in nappies, could get bigger bins for free.

But Wilson said if elected in November, a Liberal-National government would require councils to collect general rubbish every week.

She said her government would also apply the council rate cap – which now limits annual rate increases to inflation – to waste charges, so households would not pay more as a result of the change.

The opposition leader, whose electorate of Kew falls within the Boroondara local government area, said reverting to weekly general rubbish collections was “common sense”.

“To be perfectly honest – it’s disgusting. The bins are overflowing. I have a toddler, we have nappies and we have many little kids on our street with large families,” Wilson told 3AW radio on Monday.

“You know what it’s like on bin night, when you have two or three extra bags and you’re trying to find somewhere to put them. They end up in council parks in the bins there overflowing.”

In a statement, she added that weekly rubbish collection was an “essential service that shouldn’t depend on your postcode”.

Most councils that have switched to fortnightly collection have cited the introduction of weekly food organics and garden organics (Fogo) collection as the main reason for the change.

They have said the shift encourages residents to place food scraps in a green bin, which can then be turned into compost rather than sent to landfill, where they break down and produce methane.

after newsletter promotion

Whitehorse council has considered making the change but decided to keep weekly collection. In material sent to residents as part of its consultation, the council said food waste was accounting for 40% of the weight of rubbish bins.

It said Boroondara, Knox, Manningham and Monash had “reduced the amount of waste sent to landfill by an average of 19%” in the first year after switching to weekly Fogo collections and fortnightly general rubbish collections.

Other councils, however, have blamed the state government’s landfill levy, which has increased significantly in recent years.

It is not the first time rubbish has made headlines this year, with several Victorian councils in April pushing back against a mandated deadline to introduce a fourth, purple-lidded bin for glass by 1 July 2027 as part of a shift to a statewide four-bin system.

The government first announced the overhaul of the state’s rubbish collection in 2020, following the collapse of the state’s largest recycling company SKM a year earlier, which resulted in thousands of tonnes of recycling being sent to landfill.

The Liberals have committed to reviewing the landfill levy, if elected, as well as make the purple bin option.

In Western Australia, the One Nation candidate Luke Herdegen is using a state byelection to campaign for Rockingham council to restore weekly rubbish collection.

Boroondara council has been contacted for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Monday briefing: How the new phase of confrontation at al-Aqsa signals a challenge to the status quo
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Hettie O'Brien
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
In today’s newsletter: ​Jerusalem’s most volatile site has again become a flashpoint, with Arab states and former Israeli officials sounding the alarm over Benjamin Netanyahu’s complicity

Good morning. In late July, Itamar Ben-Gvir, West Bank settler and far-right extremist minister of security in Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, joined a group of more than 2,000 Jewish extremists to storm al-Aqsa mosque compound, Jerusalem’s most sensitive holy site. The far-right group has been doing this for years. Ben-Gvir has made series of visits to the site over the last three years, eroding norms and inflaming tensions. Jordanian officials have recently warned that it could be at risk of an “imminent” Israeli takeover.

With national elections scheduled in October, and many eyes still firmly on Gaza (this weekend, Netanyahu rejected a US-backed 15 point plan for peace), the Israeli government appears to be racing to expand Israeli settlements and accelerate ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem before its mandate expires.

For this morning’s First Edition, I spoke to our senior international correspondent, Julian Borger, about the latest incursions, and how Israeli extremists are trying to create a new reality in Jerusalem. That’s after the weekend roundup.

UK politics | Sadiq Khan has called on the government to commit to revamped climate action and to reduce the UK’s reliance on oil and gas, as the UK endures a summer of drought, wildfires and heatwaves.

US politics | The US Senate voted to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general in a win for Donald Trump, who will now have his one-time personal attorney sitting atop the nation’s law enforcement apparatus.

US-Israel war on Iran | Iran has issued tough new demands for reopening the strait of Hormuz, as a deal to open the strategic waterway remained out of reach on Saturday.

Russia-Ukraine | Up to 50,000 North Korean soldiers will be deployed in Russia, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said. On Saturday, Turkey called for a “moratorium” on attacks by Russia and Ukraine in the Black Sea after a series of strikes on civilian ships there

World news | The alleged leader of the Kinahan organised crime group was extradited from Dubai on Sunday and met by a huge security operation in Dublin, marking the end of a global game of cat and mouse with European, US and Gulf authorities.

The al-Haram al-Sharif site in Jerusalem’s old city, known to Jews as the Temple Mount, is one of the most contentious places on earth. It’s governed by a fragile agreement that gives Muslims exclusive rights to pray and worship there, while Jews pray at the Western Wall below. But Israel’s messianic right, which has gained a powerful foothold in Netanyahu’s coalition government, is fixated on the site as a symbol of its political project. Their vision of building a new Jewish temple on one of Islam’s holiest sites – once a fringe idea – has become increasingly widespread.

Since 2023, Jewish religious extremists have made numerous visits to the 35-acre compound which is home to both al-Aqsa mosque and Dome of the Rock, the holiest sites for Muslims in Jerusalem and one of holiest sites for Muslims in the world. “At first, you had groups of perhaps 20 Jews, mostly settlers, who were escorted by the police to the far wall of the compound to pray discreetly,” Julian tells me. “If you were just a casual visitor, you wouldn’t necessarily see them”. Over the last two years, however, the groups have grown bigger and more audacious. On 23 July, they sang the national anthem, and prayed and performed rituals in the centre of the compound, while Israeli police – who report to Ben-Gvir, who was in attendance – set up tents to provide shade to the worshippers.

“To erect structures, even if they’re temporary, is a red rag to a bull,” Julian says. “The longstanding fear is that Israelis would knock down the Dome of the Rock or the mosque, or rebuild a [Jewish] temple on the site. And these tents were part of a gradual attempt to push the boundaries.” Eight Arab nations swiftly issued a joint statement condemning “mass incursions by settlers led by extremist Israeli ministers”. Last Wednesday, the Jordanian authorities, who administer the site, held an emergency meeting of Arab and Islamic nations to discuss these risks, and afterwards, the Jordanian authorities condemned Israeli violations and warned that they constituted a “blatant provocation” to Muslims worldwide.

“All they can do is issue strong statements, saying, ‘don’t do this’,” says Julian. The Waqf, the Jordanian-appointed foundation that manages the site, is “defenceless”, he explains. In the run-up to Ramadan this year, Waqf sources told the Guardian that five of its staff had been detained by the Shin Bet, Israel’s counterintelligence service. Meanwhile, Israeli police have begun actively recruiting extremist activists to serve in the Temple Mount Unit, the force responsible for policing the compound. According to Haaretz, the deputy commander of the police’s Temple Mount Unit published a callout to officers on social media and in WhatsApp groups associated with West Bank settlers. “Anyone who wants to take part in implementing sovereignty is welcome to contact me,” he wrote.

Why is the site so significant?

The site’s history is constantly enlisted in attempts to justify the present. Muslims know the raised compound in the south-east of Jerusalem as al-Haram al-Sharif (the Noble Sanctuary), or simply al-Aqsa, after the mosque located at its southern edge. Next to the mosque, at the centre of the compound, is the Dome of the Rock, one of the oldest surviving Islamic places of worship. It’s on this site the prophet Muhammad is said to have ascended to heaven.

At the base of the compound is the Western Wall, a section of retaining wall that survived the destruction of the second Jewish temple in 70CE. The Temple Mount is also the holiest site in Judaism, the site of two temples which were built and then destroyed by invaders in ancient times.

Access to the site has been delicately managed for centuries. After the six-day war in 1967, when Israel captured East Jerusalem from Jordan, the Israeli government agreed that Jordan would continue to be the site’s custodian. Since then, the “status quo”, as it is known, has sought to prevent violent conflict by circumscribing the rights of Muslims and Jews to access the compound. While Jews are permitted to visit the site at specific times, they cannot pray there. Many Jews opt not to visit the site, out of fear of treading on holy ground while ritually impure.

“The status quo represented a historic compromise. Jews got the Western Wall. Muslims got Haram al-Sharif,” Julian says. “But the site has always been a detonator, sitting right there in the centre of the old city, with strong religious beliefs crammed together in a small area.”

How has this erupted in the past?

It’s not uncommon in the region for holy sites to be carefully managed with intricate arrangements. Elsewhere in the Old City, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre is divided up between six Christian denominations, with its keys held by two Muslim families. At the Cave of the Patriarchs in the occupied city of Hebron, a mosque and synagogue share one building.

Past Israeli moves to challenge the status quo at al-Haram al-Sharif have been incendiary, sparking deadly violence. In 2000, then Israeli opposition leader and future prime minister Ariel Sharon made a visit to the site in an attempt to demonstrate Israeli sovereignty, sparking a chain of events that helped ignite the second intifada. More recently, Hamas gave the name “al-Aqsa flood” to its attack on Israel in October 2023 that killed 1,200 Israelis and triggered the war on Gaza, claiming it was provoked by Israeli violations at the Jerusalem mosque.

What’s the end goal of these incursions?

Some Jewish extremists have begun marching under the temple flag – a star of David overlaid with a picture of the (as yet nonexistent) third temple they hope to build. “You see these flags on the bulldozers that are flattening neighbourhoods in Gaza, and soldiers wearing patches with a picture of the third temple on them,” Julian says.

The rise of the third temple movement comes at a time of surging attacks on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, with the scale of violence prompting urgent calls for intervention from the heart of the Israeli establishment.

Earlier this year, dozens of Israelis, including two former prime ministers, former heads of its security services and former judges, signed a “final warning” threatening legal action against their government over its support for “Jewish terrorism” in the occupied West Bank. They argued the actions of the government had isolated Israel internationally and put its security at risk.

“There’s a feeling that the far-right side of Netanyahu’s government is now creating unnecessary, long-term security problems for Israel,” Julian says. That extends to attempts to change the status quo at al-Aqsa.

Netanyahu has publicly backed Jewish prayer at the site, claiming that changes pushed by Ben-Gvir were coordinated with him. “This isn’t the stuff of radicals any more,” Julian says. “It has government approval.”
