Novel squat Android opens to an iPad-like screen for video or multitasking, with plenty of power and battery life

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

S
amsung’s latest folding phone breaks the mould with a squat, passport-like shape reminiscent of the Blackberry, which opens up to become a tablet similar to an iPad mini. It is certainly a better shape for a tablet than other designs, but is a short and wide phone when closed a compromise too far?

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is an entirely new variant in Samsung’s foldable family for this year launched alongside the Z Fold 8 Ultra with a more familiar candy bar shape. Both folders are extremely expensive, with the Fold 8 starting at £1,699 (€1,999/$1,899.99/A$2,699) and the Fold 8 Ultra at £1,899 (€2,199/$2,099.99/A$2,999), with RAMageddon driving up prices even at the top of the market.

While Samsung’s first folding phone adopted a candy bar shape that opened up like a book to a square tablet, others began with more squat and wide forms including the original Google Pixel Fold and Microsoft Surface Duo. But as the technology matured most folders adopted the narrower closed form, which proved a better shape for performing phone-type duties such as messaging.

The Fold 8 is 9.7mm thick when closed, which is about the same as a regular phone in a case, but its short and wide design looks more like a mini tablet or notepad in your hand. Its width also makes it hard to reach the other side of the screen one-handed, making it a two-handed affair most of the time, similar to huge superphones such as the Galaxy S26 Ultra.

Photos, apps, games and websites look and work great on the crisp and super-bright outside screen. That is until you open the keyboard, which then takes up just over half the screen, leaving you very little space to see the content you are trying to type into. Apps that include a bar at the top, such as WhatsApp, shrink that space even further.

Open the Fold 8 like a book to reveal a beautiful 7.6in OLED display, which is crisp, smooth and super-bright, making it easy to see in direct sunlight. Like all folders the necessarily softer screen material is fragile and a fingerprint magnet, so needs regular gentle cleaning.

The tablet screen’s 4:3 ratio matches that of Apple’s iPads or Microsoft’s Surfaces, which makes it a better fit for video with smaller black bars top and bottom when held in landscape compared to squarer foldables.

Portrait orientation is great for websites and the keyboard only takes up about two-fifths of the screen giving you plenty of space with which to work. Most apps will present a dual-pane tablet interface in either orientation.

But when you directly compare the Fold 8’s internal screen with last year’s Fold 7 or the new Fold 8 Ultra’s squarer display, you realise that landscape video is almost the same size on both tablets; only the thickness of the letterboxing black bars differs significantly.

The speakers of the Fold 8 are pretty good for a phone, but they are only stereo when the tablet is held in portrait, not landscape when watching video which is unfortunate.

Main screen: 7.6in QXGA+ 120Hz (403ppi) AMOLED flexible display

Cover screen: 5.5in WUXGA+ 120Hz (428ppi) AMOLED

Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy

Storage: 256, 512GB or 1TB

Operating system: One UI 9 based on Android 17

Camera: 50+50MP rear; 10MP+10MP selfie cameras

Connectivity: 5G, dual sim, e-sim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, UWB, GNSS

Water resistance: IP48 (1.5 metres for 30 minutes)

Dimensions folded: 123.9 x 81.9 x 9.7mm

Dimensions unfolded: 123.9 x 161.4 x 4.5mm

The Fold 8 has the same Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip and memory as Samsung’s top S26 Ultra and performs very similarly, making it one of the fastest Android phones available with plenty of power for multitasking, gaming or anything else.

The battery lasts a solid 40 hours between charge, using an even split of both screens for a total of eight hours on a mix of 5G and wifi for browsing, messaging, shooting photos and making notes. Gaming and other more intensive tasks drained the battery faster, but the Fold 8 should comfortably see out even the heaviest of days without needing a top up.

Samsung has the best, most adaptable software for making the most of folding phones, allowing multiple split-windowing configurations with up to three apps in a grid on screen and more in floating windows. One UI 9 is based on the latest Android 17 with Samsung providing Android and security updates until 31 July 2033.

The great Now Bar remains from last year’s version for live sports scores, music, timers and other ongoing tasks at the bottom of the lock screen or in the status bar. The improved Now Nudge, Samsung’s AI suggestion tool from the S26, can surface information from a greater number of sources in a wider range of apps. The Now Brief AI box remains a weak point, however, rarely suggesting anything useful beyond the weather or your calendar events.

Google’s Gemini is baked in along with plenty of other AI tools that can occasionally be useful. One oddity is that if you choose not to have the same home screen on the outside and inside displays, the tablet screen ends up with two separate home screen layouts, one for portrait and one for landscape orientation. That means you have three separate home screens to customise with their own configuration of apps and widgets.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

The Fold 8 has two 10-megapixel selfie cameras but only two 50MP cameras on the back with no telephoto camera.

The main 50MP camera is the best of the bunch and similar in performance to the main camera of the standard S26, shooting good photos across a range of conditions. The 50MP ultrawide is also solid, with consistent colour across both cameras. The 2x crop zoom on the main camera works fairly well, but magnifying beyond to 4x or 10x digital zoom rapidly becomes poor.

The Fold 8’s selfie cameras are decent and handy for video calls, but you get better results using the main camera for selfies with the outside screen as a viewfinder, even if it is a bit ungainly.

The camera app has plenty of modes and shoots decent video, with some fancy auto-tracking features that make it easy to set the camera up partly folded and keep a subject in frame.

The battery has expected lifespan of at least 1,200 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is generally repairable. Inside screen repairs cost about £600. Samsung offers a self-repair programme, as well as Care+ accidental damage insurance that reduces the cost of repairs to £50.

The Fold 8 is made from 14.9% recycled material by weight, which Samsung breaks down in its environmental report. The company offers trade-in and recycling schemes for old devices.

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 costs from £1,699 (€1,999/$1,899.99/A$2,699).

For comparison, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs £1,899, the S26 Ultra costs £1,279, the Honor Magic V6 costs £1,999.99 and the Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold costs £1,299.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a bit of a curio from Samsung. Having forged the way with narrower book-style foldables, suddenly offering a squat, passport-shaped version seems like an odd step.

On paper, the inside screen’s more conventional iPad-like shape makes it better suited to websites, video and apps. But because the Fold 8’s internal screen isn’t any wider than that of the Fold 7 or Fold 8 Ultra, apps have less screen space to work with while landscape videos are practically the same size, just with slimmer black bars at the top and bottom on the Fold 8.

Meanwhile, the short and fat form of the closed Fold 8 makes for a worse phone experience. It is much harder to use one-handed and the keyboard takes up far too much of the screen. I didn’t find it any easier to fit in a pocket than narrower rivals, either.

Shape aside, the Fold 8 is another stunning piece of technology from Samsung with excellent software to make the best of its folding form, plenty of processing power and surprisingly good battery life. But it only has two cameras on the back with no telephoto option, which is poor for this kind of money.

The Fold 8 is better than some of the original attempts at the passport folder shapes, but there are many good a reasons book-style folding phones evolved into candy bar shapes over the last eight years.

Pros: a phone and tablet in one, thin and light, powerful multitasking abilities, great tablet screen, top performance, solid battery life, water resistance.

Cons: extremely expensive, passport-shape not ideal for phone duties, no dust resistance, more fragile than a regular device and costly to repair, no telephoto camera.

https://www.wired.com/story/space-agenci.title: Space Agencies Are Trying to Keep Astronauts From Losing Their Sight
https://www.wired.com/story/space-agenci.author: Isabella Ward
https://www.wired.com/story/space-agenci.text:
THE EUROPEAN SPACE Agency is trying to understand why astronauts lose their eyesight in space, in the hope they can figure out how to treat—or even prevent—the condition as looming longer spaceflights heighten the risk of permanent vision damage.

The agency has commissioned British eye-scanning startup Siloton to develop a solution ahead of the international Artemis flights to the moon and other deep space missions. The health tech uses quantum technology to shrink core components used in eye-testing equipment found at optometrists to fit on a photonic chip smaller than a coin.

Founded by physicists in 2020, Siloton is currently working with the UK’s National Health Service to enable patients with retinal conditions to self-scan at home. “The ESA pretty much has the same requirements,” says cofounder and chief technology officer Euan Allen. “It's just in a totally different environment.”

Spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) is a collection of eye and brain changes caused by spending prolonged periods in a low-gravity environment, and it impacts around 70 percent of astronauts on the International Space Station, according to NASA. One of the starkest cases is that of NASA astronaut John Phillips, who launched to the ISS in 2005 with 20/20 vision, and splashed down six months later with his vision at 20/100—what’s considered a moderate visual impairment. While he was in space, bodily fluid, uninhibited by gravity, built up in his head, squashing his eyeballs, swelling his optic nerve, and pushing his retina forward.

While returning to Earth can reverse some of the damage, space agencies are concerned by both the operational risk of astronauts losing their vision mid-mission, as well as the longer-term health impacts. “The eye condition SANS is a serious health risk facing astronauts on long missions,” says Rebecca Evernden, director of the UK Space Agency. Medical engineers want to develop their understanding of the condition and the factors causing it so that they can manage any ocular damage, and eventually treat it or even stop it from becoming a problem.

Scientists are already monitoring how spaceflight impacts the human eye on the ISS using a modified version of the device found in optometry offices that measures the thickness of layers at the back of the eye. However, the device is bulky and requires real-time remote guidance from experts on the ground. As astronauts journey further into deep space, lengthening communication delays with Earth will mean this is no longer feasible.

Siloton’s device would allow astronauts to scan their retinas more frequently by automating some of the process so that examinations do not need ground support. The ESA hopes that will generate more data on any ocular degeneration, and possibly provide early warning signs that changes in the eye may be occurring—even before they result in vision change.

Other technical challenges include getting around using batteries to power the device because they pose such a big fire risk. In spacecraft, where space is at a premium, designers will also have to decide where the binocular-sized equipment would live and how to position and keep an astronaut’s head in place without gravity (typically, that’s done by having a chin rest).

But that’s a walk-in-the-park compared with getting a retiree whose sight is failing to cooperate, says Allen. “We're very confident, because we're trying to do that with 80-year-old patients who already have some level of visual imparity,” says Allen, “whereas these will be highly trained astronauts who are much younger and have full function of their eyes.”

”I think lots of the stuff that we're doing for space will bleed through and make our home device better, and vice versa as well,” he adds. “All this research and development work, in principle, is making our products that are going to go into the NHS much better.”
https://www.wired.com/story/space-agenci.summary: Spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) is a collection of eye and brain changes caused by prolonged periods in a low-gravity environment. Spaceflight is a serious health risk facing astronauts on long missions. The UK Space Agency has commissioned British eye-scanning startup Siloton to develop a solution.

https://www.space.com/stargazing/solar-e.author: Daisy Dobrijevic

Here are key timings for some of the eclipse's most popular viewing destinations.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you're planning to watch the total solar eclipse on Aug. 12, knowing exactly when to look up is crucial.

While totality will be visible from parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain, millions more people across Europe will experience a dramatic partial solar eclipse. Whether you're chasing the moon's shadow in Reykjavik or watching the moon take a 'bite' out of the sun from London, Paris, or Berlin, timing is everything.

You can keep up with the latest total solar eclipse news and coverage with our total solar eclipse live blog.

Totality begins (local time)

Scoresby Sund, Greenland

Snæfellsjökull, Iceland

Local time (maximum coverage)

% of sun's disk covered

Looking for your own eclipse time? The interactive map and resources from Time and Date let you search by city and view detailed timing information for every stage of the eclipse.

A total solar eclipse occurs when the moon moves directly between Earth and the sun, completely blocking the sun's disk from view.

During totality, the sky darkens significantly, temperatures drop and bright stars and planets can even become visible. Observers can also catch a glimpse of the sun's outer atmosphere, known as the corona, glowing around the silhouetted moon.

Totality — when the sun is completely obscured — is only visible within the narrow path of the moon's shadow. Outside that path, observers may see a partial solar eclipse, whereby only a portion of the sun is covered.

REMEMBER to NEVER look directly at the sun. To view this solar eclipse safely, you must use solar filters. Only during the brief period of totality when the moon completely covers the sun, is it safe to look at the sun without protection. Observers will need to wear solar eclipse glasses, and cameras, telescopes and binoculars must have solar filters placed in front of their lenses at all other times.

Our how to observe the sun safely guide tells you everything you need to know about safe solar observations.

After the total solar eclipse on Aug. 12, 2026, the next solar eclipse will be an annular solar eclipse on Feb. 6, 2027 visible across parts of Africa and South America. The next total solar eclipse will be a spectacular event on Aug. 2, 2027. Visible across North Africa, it will be the longest totality on land since 1991.

https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/china-us-.title: Forget DeepSeek. China’s real ‘Sputnik moment’ is happening on campus as American universities lose their advantage
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/china-us-.author: Mia Osmonbekov
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/china-us-.text:
When DeepSeek unveiled an AI model last year that rivaled America’s best at a fraction of the cost, or when a Chinese hypersonic missile test caught U.S. intelligence off guard to the point where a top U.S. general called it “very close” to a “Sputnik moment”, the reaction each time was the same: that a handful of Chinese firms had suddenly pulled ahead.

But a sweeping new National Bureau of Economic Research study of nearly 14 million Chinese patents suggests that framing misses the real story—and it’s a more unsettling one for the United States.

Harvard Business School’s Josh Lerner and his co-authors dug into who is actually filing the patents behind the 14 technology areas the Pentagon deems critical—advanced computing, space technology, AI, hypersonics and biotech. The answer: Chinese universities account for more than a quarter of the country’s inventions in those fields, 8x the U.S. rate at 3.3%, with state-owned enterprises and the government accounting for just 4%.  Fewer than one in 10 Chinese critical technology patents involve an inventor with U.S. work experience, undercutting the assumption that Beijing relies on returning U.S. talent for innovation.

Lerner told Fortune his team was “programmed” to expect a few large corporations like Huawei and Tencent to lead the charge on Chinese innovation through patents similarly to IBM and Samsung in the U.S. Instead, they found Chinese innovation in critical technologies “much more diverse—spread out across the parties,” with universities “more represented” there than anywhere else in the country’s patent system. That’s a reversal of the U.S. pattern, where academic patenting is “more of a sideshow.”

“We’ve clearly seen this dramatic boom in terms of research funding and patenting in China,” Lerner said, “and the natural question being is this bearing fruit? In the software side, Deepseek was certainly something that was really not anticipated, and clearly these open-source Chinese models are getting an enormous amount of traction.”

The findings arrive as the quality gap many assumed would protect American tech leadership seems to be closing, with DeepSeek, Moonshot and Z.AI going toe-to-toe with U.S. frontier labs and beating them on cost.

Using four text-based measures of patent novelty and scientific relevance, the authors found no evidence China’s patent boom came at the cost of quality—Chinese patents have converged with, and in some technologies overtaken, their U.S. counterparts. The share of Chinese critical-technology patents containing “disruptive” technical language jumped from under 2% in the early 1990s to 16% by 2022, closing in on the American share of roughly 20%.

There’s also a seeming difference in dynamics between China and the U.S. with their respective universities, especially as the Trump administration’s international student crackdown strained campuses and raised questions about the future of STEM talent.

The paper describes Beijing’s role as “coordinative rather than directly productive”—steering research through funding and priorities rather than owning the institutions that produce it. Lerner drew a contrast with his own university Harvard’s public standoff with Washington over research funding.

“When you think about the dynamics between our university and the administration, which has been a lot of back and forth in the courts,” he said, “one doesn’t suspect the same kind of interactions would characterize those between a major Chinese university and the state.”

The U.S. has scaled back its federal research grant pipeline. Last year, the Trump administration moved to cut $4 billion from NIH’s reimbursement of universities’ research overhead costs, capping a rate that had typically run 50-60% at just 15%. By April, the administration had formally terminated 1,392 NIH grants worth $539 million in unspent obligations, while the National Science Foundation had cancelled or suspended nearly 2,000 awards of its own: the Brennan Center for Justice puts total NIH and NSF cuts and freezes at more than $3 billion since 2025, with roughly $1.4 billion still frozen or unresolved. Some of the terminations have been reversed by courts, but the fights continue on a grant-by-grant basis.

The potential lag in innovation might not be seen immediately, but it could have a sizable effect on competition with China as the Trump administration has proposed steep cuts to federal science funding and a rewrite of federal grant rules that critics — including groups well outside academia, from farm cooperatives to bankers—warn would let agencies cancel research awards midstream.

“You don’t really see the consequences until perhaps years or even decades afterwards, just given the very long‑run nature of this process,” Lerner told Fortune.

While Lerner’s paper highlights the asymmetry in critical technology patent production between the U.S. and China, Dan Wang, a China analyst at Eurasia Group, is skeptical of how far the patent numbers should be trusted: commercialization rates for Chinese university patents remain low, Wang told Fortune over email, and few are filed overseas, while companies like Nvidia and Google drive “exceptionally strong” R&D in the United States.

The rankings are catching up to the money. In June, Harvard lost the top spot in the Nature Index Research Leaders—a closely watched measure of high-quality research output—for the first time since the index began tracking universities in 2015. Among academic institutions, Zhejiang University (the alma mater of DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng), moved into first place, with Harvard falling to second. Including the Chinese Academy of Sciences, a government research body rather than a university, Harvard falls to third place. Nine of the top 10 academic institutions globally are now Chinese; five years ago, eight of the top 10 were American.

“China is likely to narrow the gap in patent-related indicators, but not in overall technological leadership,” Wang said. “The university innovation system is heavily influenced by administrative process and political mandate, and thus does not leave enough room for self driven research.”

But Wang cautioned that Washington’s fixation on sanctioning a handful of “national champions” in China like Huawei and Tencent overlooks “the real base for China’s technological upgrading”—decentralized networks of universities, suppliers and state-owned enterprises. Wang estimates there are 18,000 state-designated “little giant” firms working on components and materials alone.

“Sanctioning a few major firms alone is unlikely to halt the broader ecosystem,” Wang added.

China surpassed the U.S. in total R&D spending for the first time in 2024, investing $1.03 trillion to America’s $1.01 trillion, and has reached via R&D growth topping 14% annually since 2004, more than double the U.S. pace.
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/china-us-.summary: Study of nearly 14 million Chinese patents shows that framing misses the real story. The findings arrive as the quality gap many assumed would protect American tech leadership seems to be closing. China is likely to narrow the gap in patent-related indicators, says Wang.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/m.title: Adelaide waterfalls roar to life as reservoirs receive decade-high deluge
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/m.author: Malcolm Sutton
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Water cascades over Morialta Conservation Park's Second Falls. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

SA Water's metro reservoirs received about 18 billion litres of water in the 24 hours to 8am.

It is the highest 24-hour deluge since September 2016.

SA Water is monitoring forecast rain and water levels to guide any potential releases from Mt Bold.

Waterfalls in the Adelaide Hills have roared to life as reservoirs in the region received their highest inflows over a 24-hour-period in nearly 10 years.

Lightning, heavy rain and small hail swept over Morialta Conservation Park east of the city at about 2:30pm yesterday, turning its usually gentle waterway into a raging torrent reminiscent of tropical Queensland.

Across the Mount Lofty Ranges, about 18 billion litres was injected into the state's metro reservoir system in the 24 hours to 8am today, according to SA Water, lifting their combined level by 9 per cent to 73 per cent of capacity.

Morialta Conservation Park's First and Second Falls were spectacular on Sunday. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

He said Mount Bold, the largest reservoir with a capacity of 46.4 gigalitres, received more than 5 billion litres of water, lifting its storage level by 13 per cent to 82 per cent of capacity, with Kangaroo Creek increasing by 19 per cent.

"Relative to the size of their catchments, Little Para and South Para reservoirs were some of the main beneficiaries of this rainfall, with their storage levels increasing by 7 per cent and 10 per cent respectively," Dr Kingsborough said.

More than 71 billion litres of water has flowed into the metro reservoirs since the beginning of winter, leaving them well over the storage holding of 55 per cent at this time last year.

"A wet start to winter laid the groundwork by helping increase soil moisture across our catchments, and we're now seeing the benefit of this on our reservoirs, through the cumulative impact of rainfall events like yesterday," Dr Kingsborough said.

Mount Bold is the biggest of SA Water's primary reservoirs and can hold 46.2 gigalitres. (Supplied: SA Water)

The last time SA Water needed to release water at Mt Bold, which is typically triggered when storages reach above 95 per cent of capacity, was in November 2022.

"We will continue working in partnership with the Bureau of Meteorology [BOM] to monitor forecast rain and water levels in our reservoirs, to guide any potential releases of water from Mt Bold," Dr Kingsborough said.

"Our reservoirs are in a healthy position heading into spring, and we will keep a close eye on our storage levels to ensure a secure water supply for our customers in advance of what the BOM is forecasting to be a dry late winter and spring."

The Kaurna name for Morialta Conservation Park's Fourth Creek is Moriatta, which means "ever flowing", although that is no longer the case due to upstream dams and agriculture.

Three people were rescued after attempting to drive through floodwaters, following a weekend of heavy rainfall and storms across South Australia.

Its water flows through Morialta and into the River Torrens system, but occurs below reservoir catchments so does not impact upon storage levels.

Bushwalkers visiting the site are urged to stick to trails and stay behind guardrails as it has been the site of several rescues and fatal accidents.

"Visitors are responsible for their own safety and should follow advice from park rangers, comply with all warnings and other park signage, stay on marked trails, and remain behind safety barriers that are installed to protect the public," a Department for Environment and Water spokesperson said last month.

Several South Australian towns recorded record-breaking August rainfall totals across Saturday and yesterday, including 110 millimetres at Lenswood, 101mm at Coromandel East and150mm in some parts of the state's far north.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/w.title: Premier defends candidate after comments on Labor's 'culture of silence'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/w.author: Keane Bourke
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Roger Cook has backed Labor candidate Georgia Tree over remarks she made about the party five years ago. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

The WA premier has staunchly defended Labor's candidate for the Secret Harbour by-election over comments she made five years ago criticising her party's response to sexual harassment.

Roger Cook has described Georgia Tree as someone who "doesn't take bull crap" and says he is "sure" she does not still hold the same views of the party.

Ms Tree has released a statement saying she stands by her comments, but adding that politics and the party have changed in the past five years.

Western Australian Premier Roger Cook has described Labor's Secret Harbour by-election candidate as someone who "doesn't take bull crap", after old comments she made about her own party’s culture of silence on sexual harassment in the workplace resurfaced.

In July 2021, Labor candidate Georgia Tree spoke on a political podcast about the actions of the federal Australian Labor Party (ALP) amid allegations from former Liberal staffer Brittany Higgins that she was raped by her colleague Bruce Lehrmann.

Two Federal Court judgements later found Mr Lehrmann did, on the balance of probabilities, rape Ms Higgins at Parliament House in 2019, after a night out with other Liberal staffers.

It was a saga that gripped the national conversation after Ms Higgins went public in February 2021, leading to a national reckoning over women's safety in the workplace.

In her podcast appearance months later, Ms Tree described instances of Labor members erring on the side of caution when attacking political opponents to avoid drawing attention to Labor’s own faults.

Georgia Tree told the podcast Labor would deal with things "in-house" so it did not "taint the brand". (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"You would have people offhand say, 'Oh God, like we probably shouldn't go too hard on X because what about like, the skeletons in our closet?'" she said.

"It's like the Catholic Church, right, like we don't want to taint the brand, so let's deal with everything in-house, and everyone just shut up."

Asked about the comments this morning, Mr Cook was staunch in his defence of Ms Tree.

"What it shows is that Georgia Tree stands up for her community," he said.

The premier said he was "sure" Ms Tree did not still hold the same views about the ALP, and denied WA Labor had any "skeletons" in its closet.

Premier Roger Cook and Georgia Tree walking and talking in Rockingham prior to a press conference. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

"The context in which she was speaking was five years ago, in the context of the accusations by Britney Higgins against a Liberal member of parliament," he said.

"Things have changed significantly over the last decade in relation to the way people conduct politics."

Here's everything you need to know about the Secret Harbour by-election, which is shaping up as one of the most closely-watched political contests in WA for some time.

Ms Tree said she stood by her 2021 comments, but added that her party had changed since then.

"I've always been outspoken, and I will always fight for what is right — particularly when it comes to women," she said in a statement.

"Both the federal and WA Caucus is now made up of more than 50 per cent women.

"This is one of the reasons why I am running, we need to see more young women entering politics to fight for change and not be afraid to stand up, speak out and take their seat at the table."

The Secret Harbour by-election is shaping up to be one of the most closely-watched political contests in WA for some time.

The battle for the outer suburban seat in Perth's south is expected to be a major test of One Nation's popularity in the state, and the ability of the Labor and Liberal parties to fight back.

Secret Harbour has long been considered a safe Labor seat, with the by-election triggered by last month's retirement of high-profile minister Paul Papalia, who represented the electorate for almost two decades.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/u.author: Kimberley Putland and Alistair Bates
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/u.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Industrial Action

BHP says vessels were loaded and departed as scheduled despite the weekend strike action. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)

Unionised staff have resumed work after 48 hours of industrial action at BHP's facilities in Port Hedland, Western Australia.

BHP has indicated the action caused minimal disruption to its operations, but unions say the strike had the desired effect.

The two parties will return to the Fair Work Commission for another meeting on August 18.

As unionised BHP staff return to work after 48 hours of industrial action, the strike's full impact on the mining giant and Australia's largest export port remains contested.

Members of the Electrical Trades Union (ETU), the Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union (AMWU), and the Australian Workers' Union (AWU) downed tools over the weekend at the miner's operations in Port Hedland, 1600km north of Perth in WA's Pilbara.

It represented the latest escalation of the combined port unions' dispute with the miner, which has dragged on for months.

Workers from three unions took strike action over the weekend at BHP's operations in Port Hedland. (ABC News: Glyn Jones)

While the unions claimed the weekend's dispute caused more disruption than last month's eight-hour stoppage, BHP and official sources indicated minimal impact overall.

Unlike the July strike, there was no demonstration or picket line, with unions telling their members to simply stay home.

Union sources said all but three eligible staff at BHP's port facility took part in the actions over Saturday and yesterday, with three of the miner's iron ore loaders operating at significantly reduced capacity.

But BHP said about 20 staff participated in protected industrial action on Saturday and 90 yesterday.

Four vessels still departed the port on Saturday and four yesterday.

A further three bulk carriers were expected to depart Port Hedland today.

A spokesperson for port operator Pilbara Ports said it had not anticipated any broader disruption.

"The industrial action is not expected to have any impact on Pilbara Ports operations," the spokesperson said.

"As this is a matter involving BHP and its workforce, questions relating to the industrial action are best directed to BHP."

Negotiations between unions and BHP have been going on for months. (ABC News: Glyn Jones)

Despite the low-key nature of the weekend's strike action, unions insist it had a substantial impact.

The ETU, whose members involved in high voltage electrical work at Newman also took separate industrial action over the weekend, is also claiming increased membership since the dispute began.

But BHP is adamant it was business as usual.

"Our focus remains on reaching a fair and reasonable agreement."

BHP and unions will return to the Fair Work Commission next week. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

Premier Roger Cook said he encouraged both parties to work towards an agreement.

"We want those workers to get the best wages and conditions they can," Mr Cook said today.

"We want them to work with their union, and we want the union to work with their employers.

"We want their employers to be productive, profitable and sustainable, and the way they do that is coming together and reaching an agreement."

WA's Chamber of Minerals and Energy (CMEWA) said the strike would be felt beyond the weekend's operation and ship movements.

"It appears that the company was able to maintain its production and, most importantly, was able to keep everyone involved safe," chief executive Aaron Morey said.

"A significant amount of resources had to be dedicated to that, so there was undoubtedly a productivity impact, and the more that productivity is harmed, the harder it is to continue to grow the sector.

"The other concerning impact is that this sends a signal to the world that the Pilbara is a conflict-ridden environment, which makes it more difficult to attract investments into the sector."

The miner and unions will return to the Fair Work Commission next week, for the 12th meeting between the parties since the dispute began.

BHP has committed to tabling an updated offer, labelling the ongoing industrial action as unnecessary and disruptive.

"Our approach will deliver greater pay consistency across the workforce while locking in industry-leading pay and conditions," a BHP spokesperson said.

"With another meeting scheduled and an updated proposal to come, we have made significant progress with the commission's assistance."

Berths were empty at the usually bustling port of Port Hedland for parts of yesterday. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

Unions said that movement was the direct result of the strike action, with ETU state secretary Adam Woodage arguing it was beginning to achieve recognition of "uneven" and "extreme" conditions.

"Prior to the notification of industrial action they were stonewalled for month after month," he said.

"Our most recent meeting was productive and identified a path forward."

"We look forward pursuing this path and negotiating an agreement for a safe, fair and productive iron ore industry."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: 12-year-old Kumamoto violinist performs at New York’s Carnegie Hall
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
NEW YORK – Twelve-year-old violinist Sora Iwai from earthquake-hit Kumamoto Prefecture, has performed at Carnegie Hall in New York after winning the top prize in the under-18 division of an international music competition.

Iwai, a sixth grader who lives in the city of Kumamoto, played Franz Waxman’s “Carmen Fantasie” before an audience of about 250 on Aug. 1.

“I felt I had to do my part, too,” Iwai said as his home prefecture works toward recovering from a July 28 quake that registered the maximum 7 on Japan’s seismic intensity scale.

Unfazed by the crowd, Iwai completed his performance, drawing loud applause.

“The acoustics at Carnegie Hall were very good,” he said.

Iwai’s dream is to become a violinist who performs around the world.

“I think performing here brought me closer to my dream,” he said.

Spanish-born musician Felix Ardanaz, who accompanied Iwai on piano, praised his interpretation of the piece.

“He really understands the emotion of Carmen Fantasie,” he said. Iwai is “so extremely talented, extremely musical, and of course, for his age, that’s incredible.”

He added, “I really hope that Sora could play afterwards in many, many concert halls after this competition because this is the main goal of the Manhattan competition.”

Iwai first picked up a violin at age 2 under the guidance of his parents, Hiroshi and Fumi Iwai, both string musicians, and began practicing seriously at 4.

He regularly hones his skills through performances at events including concerts at Tsuruya Department Store in Kumamoto.

His parents submitted a video of him playing to the Manhattan International Music Competition, which seeks outstanding musicians from around the world.

Judges selected Iwai for the First Grand Award in the Junior division. He was invited to perform alongside winners in other divisions.

On July 17, Iwai visited Kumamoto Mayor Kazufumi Onishi, who offered him words of encouragement.

But on July 28, the day before he was due to leave for the United States, the temblor struck while he was practicing at home.

Iwai’s home suffered no major damage, but he left Kumamoto with the disaster weighing on his mind.

After completing his performance on the stage he dreamed of, Iwai said he wanted to return home to check on the safety of his grandparents and friends.

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/law-.title: Hong Kong police arrest 8 over HK$6.2 million ‘sugar baby’ dating scam
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/law-.author: Lo Hoi-ying
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/law-.text:
Fraudsters posed as wealthy clients to extract bogus legal fees from victims, including teachers and healthcare workers, seeking compensated dates

Hong Kong police have arrested eight people over an alleged compensated-dating scam syndicate that cheated victims, including teachers and healthcare workers, out of HK$6.2 million (US$790,000) by telling them they had to pay a “legal fee” to formalise contracts to become “sugar babies”.

Police said on Monday that they had investigated 80 cases involving scammers who used compensated dating as a pretext to lure victims between February and July this year. The largest individual loss was HK$480,000.

The four men and four women, aged between 23 and 57, were arrested last week on suspicion of conspiracy to defraud, money laundering and possession of dangerous drugs, according to the force’s cybersecurity and technology crime bureau.

Chief Inspector Chan Lai-yu of the technology crime division said the scammers advertised compensated dating arrangements on social media, offering victims between HK$50,000 and HK$70,000 a month to become “sugar babies”.

“They required them to sign non-disclosure agreements and added them to a chat group with scammers posing as lawyers and wealthy clients, displaying forged name cards to gain their trust,” he said.

“When discussing the terms of the contract, they asked victims to transfer what they claimed were legal fees, High Court fees and termination fees to different accounts, which would be refunded to them when the contract was over.”

In a chat-group conversation obtained by police, the “client” proposed a list of terms for the agreement. These included using protection, keeping their relationship confidential, not taking photos or videos during meetings, and paying HK$50,000 a month.

The “lawyer” presented his forged name card and mediated the discussion before asking both parties to transfer him HK$15,500 in “legal fees”.

After victims realised the dating scheme was fraudulent and could no longer contact the scammers, the syndicate targeted them again.

“They claimed to be able to retrieve their lost funds and tricked them into paying a handling fee,” Chan said.

Women accounted for 65 per cent of the victims, who were aged between 19 and 41.

Those aged 19 to 29 made up nearly 70 per cent of victims, Chan added.

More than half of the victims worked in the service, retail and administrative sectors, while 20 per cent were students and another 15 per cent were professionals, including teachers and healthcare workers, she said.

Police clinical psychologist Fung Ho-kin warned that residents should not underestimate the psychological manipulation skills of fraudsters.

“They used personalised scenarios on the victims, posing as successful men who have been hurt and lost trust in love to make female victims feel pity or attraction to them,” he said.

“When targeting the male victims, they pretended to be pitiful women who have been neglected or mistreated by their boyfriends.”

During discussions of the “sugar baby” dating scheme, victims could negotiate the compensation offered and the acts to which they consented, making them feel respected, Fung added.

“The turning point was the role of the lawyer during contract discussion, which made them feel safe. A third-party professional would oversee the transaction, and they were paying legal fees to protect themselves,” he said.

Fung added that, after realising they had been scammed, victims were often willing to invest more resources to recover their money because of the sunk-cost effect.

“If you suspect that you have been scammed, find the police at once. Do not trust anyone who claims to be able to help you,” he said.

https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.title: Chinese researchers use microbubbles to shrink aggressive liver tumours: paper
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.author: Victoria Bela
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.text:
Cancer patients who received the experimental treatment in combination with standard therapies saw improvement, study finds

Chinese researchers have found a safe way to shrink advanced tumours from an aggressive form of liver cancer, an advance that could see microbubbles used to enhance current treatments.

The tiny gas-filled bubbles, typically a few micrometres in diameter, were originally designed as contrast agents in ultrasound imaging, but scientists have recently been exploring their therapeutic potential.

According to a paper published by the peer-reviewed Scientific Reports on July 19, the study compared cancer patients who received the standard therapy with a group that also received the experimental ultrasound and microbubble treatment.

The researchers, from the Affiliated Hospital of Guangdong Medical University and Huzhou Central Hospital, found that tumours in the second group of patients grew smaller than in those who only received the standard therapy.

“This technology shows [promise] for enhancing localised treatment approaches in cancer patients,” they wrote in the reviewed but unedited manuscript, which was provided with legal disclaimers to give early access to the findings, according to the journal.

Microbubbles are used in various fields, including engineering, environmental clean-up, and medicine. When injected into the bloodstream and hit by ultrasound waves, these bubbles can expand or contract.

According to the research team, previous studies have shown that ultrasound and microbubble treatment can enhance perfusion, or the delivery of oxygen-rich blood to tissue.

Research has also indicated that the movement of microbubbles can enhance drug delivery, suggesting the potential of the treatment to complement tumour immunotherapy, the team said.

The scientists said that previous research on a combined therapy of standard treatments and ultrasound with microbubbles had mostly been performed in laboratory settings or animal models.

“Therefore, the function of diagnostic ultrasound cavitation in the management of advanced liver cancer in humans remains ambiguous,” they noted.

In their study, the researchers tested whether the combined treatment could improve tumour response in patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma, a common type of liver cancer.

All of the 40 patients enrolled in the study had tumours which could not be removed safely with surgery and were receiving conversion therapy – a treatment strategy that includes chemotherapy, immunotherapy and targeted therapy to shrink advanced tumours initially deemed inoperable or incurable.

The researchers described conversion therapy as a “pivotal strategy” for unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma, as its aim is to make tumours smaller which could allow for their eventual removal.

A reduction in tumour size is a “clinically relevant imaging biomarker for assessing treatment response”, according to the team. Changes were evaluated in the maximum viable tumour diameter, or the widest straight-line measurement across.

In the 16 patients who received the ultrasound and microbubble treatment after the conversion therapy, researchers recorded maximum viable tumour diameters that were “significantly smaller” than the control group. The reduction rate was also greater.

Ultrasound combined with microbubbles “can improve local blood flow perfusion in advanced liver cancer and may enhance the efficacy of conversion therapy without increasing treatment-related adverse effects”, they wrote.

According to the paper, the improved perfusion reduces tumour hypoxia, a low-oxygen state that can drive aggressive growth and resistance to treatment. It also helps alleviate an acidic micro-environment, a factor in helping cancer spread.

While the microbubble treatment helped to shrink tumours, the study showed no statistically significant difference in the overall response rate, or in the proportion of patients whose tumours completely or partially shrank, between the treatment and control groups.

Adverse effects experienced by patients during the study were related to the conversion therapy, with none reported that could be directly associated with the ultrasound treatment, the team said.

Limitations of the study included the sample size. Researchers suggested that subsequent trials should be conducted to establish standardised protocols for the treatment.

https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.title: Chinese neighbours trapped in mountains ignore rescue calls over spiritual fears
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.author: Fran Lu
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.text:
According to Chinese folklore, it is believed that mountain demons can imitate familiar voices to lure lost individuals

Two individuals in Beijing found themselves trapped in a mountain but refused rescue due to a superstition that responding to strangers brings bad luck.

The police and firefighters in the Huairou district received a call on the evening of July 29, reporting that two neighbours from a nearby village had gone missing while foraging for herbs in a wild mountain area.

The pair, a 73-year-old man and a 58-year-old woman, frequently foraged together. Both had hearing impairments.

They did not carry mobile phones since there was no signal in the mountainous region. Rescuers were informed that they also lacked food and water.

Rescue teams were quickly formed and began searching through the night. After 17 hours of effort, they successfully located the two extremely exhausted individuals, who had been trapped for nearly 30 hours.

Upon discovery, the rescuers learned that the pair had heard their calls long before being found.

However, they chose not to respond due to their belief in the superstition that “if you hear your name called in the mountains, do not respond, and do not express that you are thirsty or hungry.”

In Chinese folklore, it is believed that demons in the mountains can mimic the voices of familiar people, calling out to the lost person.

Responding to such calls is thought to lure their soul, further leading to disorientation and danger.

Additionally, some believe that wandering spirits exist in the wilderness, calling out to the lost. Responding to such voices may lead to possession.

This superstition also extends to other situations, such as hearing one’s name called while walking down an empty street or outside one’s front door at midnight – one is advised not to respond.

In the case of the trapped pair, not only did they refrain from responding to the rescuers’ calls, but they also walked in the opposite direction to distance themselves from the voices, thereby missing several opportunities for rescue.

Moreover, the challenging terrain and slippery paths complicated the search efforts.

They reportedly only responded to the rescuers when the teams reached the rear of the mountain.

News of their ordeal attracted a flurry of curious comments online after being shared on social media.

“From the perspective of the elderly, those 17 hours must have been quite painful. They might have thought the king of hell had sent many devils to claim their lives,” commented an online observer.

“If I were lost in the mountains for more than half a day and heard people calling my name, I would be frightened too,” joked another person.

“I couldn’t laugh at them, considering my dad also believes in this superstition, and I’m in Huairou,” noted a third commentator.

The Huairou firefighters urged citizens to avoid venturing into wild mountains alone. They also advised that if encountering danger in the wilderness, one should not succumb to superstitious beliefs but instead call for help.
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.summary: Two people in Beijing found themselves trapped in a mountain but refused rescue due to superstition. In Chinese folklore, it is believed that demons can mimic the voices of familiar people. Rescuers were informed that they also lacked food and water. After 17 hours of effort, they successfully located the two extremely exhausted individuals.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-low-w.title: Germany news: Low water on Rhine could sever freight route
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-low-w.text:
Germany's inland shipping association has warned that the Rhine could soon become effectively split in two as water levels continue to fall. In Berlin, a man was shot dead near a busy central transport hub. DW has more.

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Monday, August 10, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

A 30-year-old man has been shot dead following a dispute involving several people near Berlin's busy Zoologischer Garten station.

Paramedics tried to resuscitate the victim, but he died at the scene, police said.

The suspected attackers fled and remain at large.

Police did not say how many shots were fired shortly before midnight, and the circumstances surrounding the dispute remain unclear.

A homicide unit has taken over the investigation.

The shooting took place at one of western Berlin's busiest transport hubs, close to the Kurfürstendamm shopping boulevard and the Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church.

The case comes amid a marked rise in firearms incidents in the German capital.

Berlin police recorded 1,119 cases involving firearms in 2025, up 68% from 2024. Shots were actually fired in more than 500 of those cases.

Police chief Barbara Slowik Meisel said earlier this year that disputes once settled with fists were now increasingly involving guns.

Other recent cases include shots fired at a restaurant window in Neukölln early on Sunday and the shooting of a 38-year-old man in the city's Schöneberg district the previous weekend.

The Rhine River could soon become effectively split in two for commercial shipping as water levels continue to fall amid persistent dry weather, Germany's inland shipping association has warned.

Jens Schwanen, managing director of the Federal Association of German Inland Navigation, said the gauge at Kaub, a crucial point for freight traffic, was forecast to fall into single digits for the first time this week.

"Commercial shipping will no longer be able to transport goods in the region at such low water levels," Schwanen told the Rheinische Post newspaper.

He said excursion boats and river cruises would also be affected.

"In principle, the Rhine would then no longer be continuously navigable and would be divided into two," Schwanen said.

Shipping would still be possible between the ports of Amsterdam, Rotterdam and Antwerp and parts of North Rhine-Westphalia, roughly as far as Cologne.

Further south, traffic could continue on tributaries and connected waterways including the Neckar, Moselle, Main and Main-Danube Canal.

Historic low-water levels were recorded at several points on the Rhine in North Rhine-Westphalia over the weekend after weeks of dry weather and too little rainfall across the river's catchment area.

The falling river is already forcing freight vessels to carry much lighter loads, pushing up transport costs for industries that depend on bulk cargo.

At such low levels, commercial vessels would no longer be able to transport goods through that stretch of the river.

https://www.dw.com/en/type-2-diabetes-in.title: Type 2 diabetes in young women increasingly common
https://www.dw.com/en/type-2-diabetes-in.text:
British researchers say rates of type 2 diabetes are growing most in women under 40. The disease is often underdiagnosed in women or it's diagnosed too late to reverse the condition's progression.

There used to be a clear-cut way to distinguish diabetes type 1 and type 2. Medical jargon aside:

Type 1 diabetes was a genetic autoimmune disease that presented in young people.

And type 2 diabetes was a disease that presented in older patients in their fifties or sixties due to an unhealthy lifestyle.

But that distinction of young and old doesn't work anymore.

More and more, younger people are being diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. In England, for example, the biggest increase in new diagnoses of type 2 diabetes is among young women.

This was revealed when a team of researchers from Imperial College London evaluated data from an English National Diabetes Audit between 2011 and 2024. They found that while the prevalence of type 2 diabetes was decreasing in adults between 60 and 79 years of age, it was rising in under-40-year-olds.

The results, published in The Lancet Regional Health Europe journal, showed the sharpest increase was among white, Asian and Black women in their 20s, and in white women in their 30s.

"Much of the discussion around rising type 2 diabetes in younger people has focused on ethnic minority groups," said Shivani Misra, the lead author of the study and a clinical associate professor for diabetes at Imperial College London.

"While these ethnic groups are disproportionately affected with early-onset type 2 diabetes, we now see that incidence is […] increasing in white populations too, showing that this public health challenge is broadening across the generation," said Misra.

In Germany, the situation is similar to the UK, said Baptist Gallwitz, an endocrinologist and spokesperson for the German Diabetes Society (DDG).

"Type 2 diabetes is on the rise in many countries," Gallwitz told DW. "It's basically a pandemic. In Germany, we're also seeing an increase in children and teenagers diagnosed with the disease."

From 2014 to 2023, there was an increase in type 2 diabetes cases of 5.8% a year among youth aged 11 to 17 years, according to a 2026 health report on diabetes released by the DDG.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

While genetic disposition can play a role in the development of type 2 diabetes, the biggest factor is lifestyle.

"We live in a world where we don't move enough and where our nutrition contains too much sugar and too many calories," Gallwitz said. "That leads to more obesity among young people, and that in turn greatly increases the risk of type 2 diabetes."

In people with type 2 diabetes, reduced insulin secretion or a weaker effect of insulin on its receptors lead to a higher glucose content in the blood.

Type 1 diabetes is characterized by a full loss of insulin-producing cells, leading to severe insulin deficiency.

The increase is particularly concerning because in young patients, the progression of the disease can be more serious than in older patients.

"Any diagnosis of type 2 diabetes is serious, but it can be more aggressive in younger people, increasing the risk of devastating complications and cutting lives short," said Helen Kirrane from Diabetes UK, a charity that campaigns on the issue.

That's why it's important to intervene early. Gallwitz said the DDG welcomed the introduction of a tax on sugary sodas in Germany, but added that it wasn't enough.

DDG is calling for a tiered value-added tax (VAT) system, with fresh fruit and vegetables being sold with no tax, and the VAT increasing the more the products contain saturated fats and sugars.

The organization also wants healthier food in kindergarten and school cafeterias and one hour of mandatory movement per day to be incorporated into class schedules.

Asking for more exercise during the school day is one thing. But conditions in the general environment also need to be improved to stop the increase of type 2 diabetes in young women, said Alexandra Kautzky-Willer, head of the division for endocrinology and metabolism at the Medical University of Vienna.

"More movement is important, so we need to ensure conditions in which it's safe for women to move," Kautzky-Willer, who is also a professor of gender medicine, told DW.

For example, a woman who fears being catcalled, ridiculed for her weight or even attacked in the dark is less likely to go running after work or join a gym.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The number of women with type 2 diabetes might be even higher than what current data show. In 2025, Kautzky-Willer and a colleague wrote a report for the Deutsches Ärzteblatt, a German medical journal, saying that the disease is underdiagnosed in women.

"Men are usually diagnosed with [type 2 diabetes] at a younger age," they wrote in the the article. "At the point of diagnosis, more women are obese, they have hypertension more often and have gained more weight" than men when they are diagnosed.

Those factors contributed to an increased risk of stroke and heart attacks as well.

So, why is it that diabetes type 2 is often only diagnosed in women when they are already this sick?

"For one, the value often tested in initial diabetes diagnosis is fasting blood sugar," Kautzky-Willer said.

Your fasting blood sugar is your blood sugar level when you haven't eaten for eight hours. It's just a single snapshot in time, however, and misses blood sugar spikes after a meal.

Fasting blood sugar "is generally lower in women than it is in men," Kautzky-Willer said. "It would make more sense to do a glucose tolerance test, but that is more work."

A glucose tolerance test involves taking blood several times in the span of two hours during which patients need to stay at the doctor's.

Kautzky-Willer says it would be good if HbA1c levels were tested as well. Tests for HbA1c levels show a person's average blood sugar level over a two or three month period.

HbA1c refers to glycated haemoglobin, which is when glucose in your body sticks to red blood cells. This prevents the body from using the sugar properly.

A high HbA1c means you have too much sugar in your blood and are more likely to develop diabetes complications. But testing HbA1c levels requires specialized lab equipment and is more expensive than testing the fasting blood sugar.

The glucose tolerance- and the HbA1c tests are not covered by health insurance in Germany and Austria, only the fasting blood sugar one is covered, and that may be influencing the options for people in those countries.

But the experts DW spoke to agreed that to bring type 2 diabetes numbers down among young people, it's important to know when their blood values get close to the line for the disease, a condition known as being "pre-diabetic".

People who find out they have a problem at this early stage still have a chance to turn the ship around. With lifestyle and nutrition changes, diabetes progression can be stopped in some cases, saving you from a host of health problems later on, like having to take medication regularly and a reduced life expectancy.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany
https://www.dw.com/en/type-2-diabetes-in.summary: British researchers say rates of type 2 diabetes are growing most in women under 40. Fasting blood sugar is generally lower in women than it is in men, says Kautzky-Willer.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cpq8.title: Could your tattoo stop you from getting a job?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cpq8.text:
Tattoos have been in the cultural mainstream for years. Even the prime minister has got one (a bee, on his bicep).

And there are no signs the trend is starting to fade. More people than ever are going under the needle as a form of self-expression: 40% of British 25-49 year-olds have at least one tattoo, according to a 2024 YouGov poll.

The most popular body part to be inked? The upper arm, says YouGov.

But has that acceptance carried over into the workplace?

Sociologist Dr Michael Rees says a big gulf in social acceptability remains between visible and non-visible tattoos, particularly those on hands, neck and face as opposed to the rest of the body.

"I don't think it's completely accepted, and I think there's probably limits to that."

While Rees himself has his hands and neck inked, he didn't get either done until he got his first permanent job as an academic.

"Even working in the career I work in, I was concerned that it may harm my job prospects.

"I think people getting tattooed in those areas are potentially restricting the careers that they go into."

This is borne out by 2022 YouGov research, which found that while about two-thirds of people consider visible tattoos on the face or neck unprofessional, a similar proportion would think other visible tattoos are professional.

Dr Alyssa Grocutt, who is herself heavily tattooed, explored perceptions of tattoos in the workplace for her PhD at the University of Calgary in Canada, and found many stereotypes around tattooed people still exist today, both positive and negative.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, people with intimidating tattoos – in this study, a skull and a knife – were perceived as risky, while those with "friendly" tattoos of a rose and some leaves were perceived as more creative and artistic.

Overall, job applicants with visible tattoos are still slightly less likely to be hired than those without, she says.

But for entrepreneurs, or those working in creative industries, Grocutt suggests they may be viewed as an extension of someone's personal brand.

"Even 11 years ago, when I started getting tattooed, the hands, neck and face were called 'job stoppers', and a lot of artists wouldn't tattoo people in those areas," she says.

"I think it's shifting a bit or maybe tattoo artists don't want to be gatekeepers. There's more positive perceptions now, [but] you still get a lot more attention, and that's an adjustment to get used to."

For centuries, tattoos were firmly linked to criminal gangs and sailors and, more recently, counter-cultural movements such as punk and motorbike clubs.

But since the early 2000s, tattoos have been steadily "demystified" through a combination of celebrities and popular TV shows such as Tattoo Fixers and London Ink, says Rees.

"When I got my first tattoos in the late '90s... they were outside of the mainstream. But they are everywhere now."

Every tattooed person he interviewed in the 2000s for his research cited David Beckham as their inspiration; the footballer made a statement when he got his first inking in 1999. Now, celebs like Harry Styles and Ed Sheeran are covered in tattoos, with more than 50 each.

Tattoo artist Martha Smith thinks stigma has "changed massively", with tattoos no longer seen as associated with criminality or class discrimination.

And new trends are emerging too. Smith, who is based in Broadstairs, Kent, specialises in fine line and dot work tattoos. The hashtag #finelinetattoo has racked up 10.3m searches on Instagram, while #dotworktattoo boasts 4.8m searches.

"Probably until the early noughties, there was a very specific person who thought they could be tattooed. But in the 13 years I've been tattooing, clients have certainly become more diverse," Smith says, adding that she quite often tattoos NHS workers, social workers or teachers.

Catherine Hibbert, 44, waited almost 20 years to get her first tattoo. She now plans to get one every year of her forties.

"I was a bit nervous when I went for my first one," she says. "I was scared of it being painful, or that I was making the wrong decision.

But as soon as the tattoo template was on, Hibbert says she "instantly loved it".

"I guess it's an adrenaline rush, but I'm on a high for days after."

Her forearm tattoo comprises geometric shapes symbolising different members and aspects of her family.

"They've all got meaning, and I like the fact that I can design them myself," says Hibbert, who works in an art gallery.

Smith thinks tattooists themselves now come from a much broader artistic background.

"You now often go to a tattooist because of their artwork. This massively opens up the kind of person that would want a tattoo and what a tattoo can mean. It also is a more affordable way of becoming an art collector."

This chimes with how Hibbert feels.

"Everybody loves my arm tattoo," she says. "I think it's because it's quite unusual from what lots of people expect a tattoo to look like… this is very delicate."

Of all the factors behind tattoos' popularity, authenticity is the one Rees thinks trumps them all – because, he says, it is something we really value culturally.

"A lot of my respondents thought that was something that a tattoo gave them, a commitment to a band or to a person, to [addiction] recovery, just to kind of [being] who they really were."

Of course, the elephant in the room is regret. Tattoos are permanent, and critics suggest that as these generations age they may no longer like the inkings they chose decades previously.

But Hibbert says that is not a concern for her.

"They're like a story, so it's memories and it's stories about me and my life."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cpq8.summary: 40% of British 25-49 year-olds have at least one tattoo, YouGov poll says. Sociologist Dr Michael Rees says a big gulf in social acceptability remains between visible and non-visible tattoos.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Two workers were temporarily stood down after near-miss collision at Sydney Airport
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Catie McLeod
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Transport minister says improved staff rostering will be in place from next month after ‘unacceptable’ delays and incident involving Qatar Airways and Jetstar planes

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The transport minister, Catherine King, has said improved staff rostering will be in place at Sydney airport from next month after “unacceptable” delays and a near-miss collision that resulted in two workers being stood down.

King called in the Airservices Australia chief executive officer, Rob Sharp, for a meeting in Canberra on Monday, the day after a Jetstar plane narrowly avoided hitting a Qatar Airways plane that was pulled across the runway in front of it.

Two staff involved in the incident – an Airservices Australia air traffic controller and the tug driver who was towing the Qatar plane – were stood down while they completed standard post-incident drug and alcohol testing.

The temporary loss of an air traffic controller only exacerbated delays at Australia’s biggest airport, where staff shortages had already resulted in days of disruption.

Additionally, a cabin crew member aboard the Jetstar plane was injured when the planes stopped abruptly, and some equipment was damaged.

The incident occurred less than two weeks after another near-miss relating to air traffic control on the tarmac at Sydney. On 27 July, a Qantas flight was cleared to cross a runway in front of one of the airline’s other planes that had just landed.

King on Monday said the delays and disruptions were unacceptable, but she was “confident” that Airservices Australia was “doing everything they can to get on top of this”.

“Airservices have committed to implementing improved rostering practices for Sydney’s Air Traffic Controllers that will be implemented from early September,” she said.

King said the situation would be “carefully” managed for the rest of August.

A new Sydney Tower simulator had also been installed to increase training capacity and enable more air traffic controllers to be trained, she said.

“It has been a big focus of ours to encourage more people to enter the profession, and 95 people are expected to be endorsed as air traffic controllers by the end of the year,” King said.

“Six controllers are currently training in Sydney Tower, with another 15 expected to commence before the end of 2027.”

King said she wanted to “give a shout out” to the air traffic controllers, who
are dealing with a really stressful and difficult job” and “did a very good job over the weekend to try to manage the disruptions as best they could”.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) is investigating both the Sunday incident and the 27 July near-miss involving Qantas aircraft.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

The head of the ATSB, Angus Mitchell, on Monday said the two incidents were unacceptable.

“Planes should not be getting that close and we should never have to rely on, as has happened in both these instances, pilots at the last minute, making an emergency decision to prevent them coming together,” he told ABC radio.

Investigators would interview flight crew, tug operators and air traffic controllers, plus other witnesses, and review any CCTV footage, the ATSB said.

A source told Guardian Australia on Sunday that initial inquiries suggested the tug vehicle pulling the Qatar aircraft may not have followed instructions.

Michael Kaine, the national secretary of the Transport Workers’ Union, which represents air traffic controllers and airport ground crews, said the aviation industry was in “crisis” due to staff shortages and poor conditions.

“Across the industry, this revolving-door workforce is understaffed and exhausted,” he said.

“We’ve seen another worker hurt from this incident after a horrific string of injuries and a worker killed at Qantas Freight last year.”

Qatar Airways was contacted for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Albanese gives ground on gambling inducements as Labor and Coalition inch towards deal
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Tom McIlroy and Josh Butler
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Prime minister and opposition leader meet in Canberra to advance agreement on gambling advertising

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Anthony Albanese has bowed to pressure and will limit gambling inducements as part of a deal between Labor and Angus Taylor, even as some Liberals warn it might not do enough to help vulnerable people.

The prime minister and the opposition leader met in Canberra on Monday to negotiate the deal, a week after sensational revelations about illegal drugs, sex workers and alcohol being provided to high-spending gamblers.

A deal to strengthen Labor’s bill, which has been criticised for falling short of the ambition of a parliamentary inquiry led by the late Labor MP Peta Murphy, is necessary to get the legislation through parliament this week.

Speaking to a meeting of Labor’s caucus in Canberra on Monday afternoon, Albanese promised some limits on inducements – which are designed to keep punters losing money – as well as touting new, but as-yet-unknown, rules on gambling advertising.

Communications minister Anika Wells’ office was contacted for specifics of potential amendments. Coalition sources said Taylor’s meeting with Albanese was “very positive” but stopped short of confirming any deal had been struck.

“This will be the strongest anti-gambling legislation that Australia has ever seen,” Albanese told the Labor caucus on Monday afternoon.

“I’m confident that later in the week we will have the legislation in the House of Representatives with some really practical amendments, dealing with the targeting of advertising, dealing with reducing children’s exposure, and dealing with as well, the full suite of measures in a really practical way.”

He said action on inducements would “get the balance right between people who want to go along and have a punt on a Saturday at the races, but also, that problem gambling is actually dealt with”.

Albanese also told his party room the government was seeking agreement with the Coalition on Labor’s plans to cut spending in the National Disability Insurance Scheme, as well as on the news bargaining incentive.

A deal on gambling looks set to be finalised as soon as Tuesday’s Coalition joint party room meeting. Any such deal will infuriate the Greens and crossbench, who had demanded much stronger action; Senator Sarah Hanson-Young had earlier urged Taylor not to fold, sending a message to the opposition leader at a press conference: “don’t roll over and let the prime minister tickle you on the belly”.

Earlier, Taylor said action on “predatory inducements” needed to be added to the government’s bill.

“We will approach these discussions with goodwill. We want to get a good outcome,” he said.

“We want to get the right outcome for younger, vulnerable Australians. We want to get the right outcomes for those who have gambling addictions and are trying to deal with them.

“We do need to make sure we get the balance right. We understand that personal responsibility is also an important part of this so it’s key to get this right and we will work with the government to do that in so far as that’s possible.”

But some Liberal MPs want the opposition to go further, even potentially shifting from an opt-out model for gambling ads on streaming platforms to an opt-in system. That proposal would be fiercely opposed by the industry.

The gambling industry was increasingly resigned to the paring back of inducements ahead of parliament resuming on Tuesday, but wagering sources warned MPs that restricting inducements could send gamblers to offshore operators.

Labor sources said the government was willing to deal with either the Coalition or Greens on the bill. But the Greens want even further-reaching changes, meaning the more likely pathway to passing the bill is with Taylor.

Debate on the bill was supercharged by sensational evidence from former NRL player Luke Bateman and veteran anti-gambling campaigner Tim Costello last week.

They alleged problem gamblers had been supplied with cocaine, alcohol and sex workers, part of efforts from gambling company VIP managers to keep big-spending punters betting as long as possible.

Betting giants who appeared before the inquiry said there was no evidence to support the allegations.

In June 2023, Murphy’s committee recommended the government “prohibit all online gambling inducements and inducement advertising, and that it do so without delay”.
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.summary: Prime Minister and opposition leader meet in Canberra to advance agreement on gambling advertising. Labor and opposition leaders meet in Sydney to advance deal on gambling. A deal to strengthen Labor's bill is necessary to get legislation through parliament this week.
