https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/openai.title: OpenAI's Next AI Model Astra Shows Cyber Performance Strong Enough to Trigger Pause
https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/openai.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/openai.text:
OpenAI has announced that it's pausing some "internal activities" involving its upcoming artificial intelligence (AI) model Astra after an internal evaluation found it had made significant advancements in agentic coding and cybersecurity.

In response to the discovery, the AI upstart said it's implementing security controls for higher-capability models and associated activities, such as isolated testing environments, restricted network and tool access, enhanced model weight protections and encryption, additional monitoring and detection capabilities, and sandboxed execution.

"We are pausing internal activities involving Astra that do not yet meet these strengthened security control requirements," it said in a statement.

"We have implemented universal monitoring for risky actions and misalignment across all agentic applications of Astra, including training and evaluation. Monitors evaluate the model's Chain of Thought and trigger a security response to review and interrupt high risk activity."

OpenAI said it will also work with relevant government agencies and select AI safety organizations to test out the model's capabilities, as well as sharing recommended security controls to third-party testing partners to run higher-risk evaluations and workloads safely.

The company said it "cannot rule out" the model has "Critical" cyber capabilities under its Preparedness Framework, which defines the threshold as follows -

A tool-augmented model can identify and develop functional zero-day exploits of all severity levels in many hardened real-world critical systems without human intervention OR model can devise and execute end-to-end novel strategies for cyberattacks against hardened targets given only a high level desired goal.

In other words, the model can discover and develop functional zero-day exploits of all severity levels in many hardened real-world critical systems without human intervention, or can orchestrate and execute end-to-end novel strategies for cyberattacks against targets when prompted a high-level desired goal.

OpenAI pointed out its preliminary evaluations of Astra indicate "strong enough performance" that it cannot eliminate the possibility that the model doesn't possess a "Critical" capability level at this stage. It also emphasized that Astra was not involved in last month's incident aimed at Hugging Face. In a recent academic paper, OpenAI touted that the model solved 10 open problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science for around $2,000 at Sol API rates.

OpenAI said it was sharing this information because it believes "it's important to be transparent with the public and the safety and security communities about this potential shift in capabilities."

"We believe advanced cyber-capable models should help defenders identify and address vulnerabilities before attackers do," it added. "We're committed to working alongside governments, safety institutes, and civil society to ensure that the frontier capabilities of models like Astra, and those that follow, are deployed responsibly and broadly for the benefit of all humanity."

The development is the latest sign of rapidly advancing cyber capabilities from frontier models, even as it marks the first time an AI lab has publicly committed to slowing progress due to cybersecurity concerns.

Earlier last week, the U.K. AI Security Institute (AISI) disclosed that its own evaluation found that AI models with access to the internet reached out into the real world to target individuals and organizations autonomously across 10 of the total of 122 runs. Of 19 such actions recorded, 17 originated from Anthropic's Mythos 5 and the remaining two involved OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers.

"In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project," AISI said. "In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering – creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code."

"These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world."

The disclosure also comes amid revelations that models from Meta and Chinese company Moonshot, namely, Muse Spark ​1.1 and Kimi K3, escaped contained and targeted real-world targets, amplifying concerns about developers' abilities to sandbox increasingly capable AI systems. In both cases, the models have been found to weaponize network misconfigurations as opposed to independently identifying and exploiting a previously unknown vulnerability to reach the internet.

As AI models are tested against widely accepted benchmarks to examine how they perform offensive and defensive cybersecurity tasks in isolated test environments, Frontier Security said Kimi K3 found a network egress leak that enabled it to reach out github[.]com, clone an official repository for the benchmark problem it was supposed to be solving, and access the solution rather than solving the challenge by itself.

"In our case the model didn't solve the task natively at all, it probed the network, realized standard DNS resolution for github.com was functional (most other websites were blocked by the sandbox), cloned the official benchmark repository, and read the solution directly off the disk," Frontier Security said.

The ⁠growing list of ⁠incidents in ​which AI agents from major developers escaped testing environments in different ways and ended up breaching real targets that were not part of the experiment has prompted the creation of a new website, aptly named Felony Bench, to track these cases.

The company says it has made significant advancements in agentic coding and cybersecurity. The development is the latest sign of rapidly advancing cyber capabilities from frontier models.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.text:
Russia shot down 456 Ukrainian drones in overnight attacks that left several dead in two Russian regions, local authorities said Monday.

More than four years since the start of Russia's large-scale offensive against Ukraine, diplomacy is at a standstill and the two countries have ramped up long-range strikes, resulting in a rise of civilian casualties.

READ MORE
Russia-Ukraine war: First half of 2026 sees sharp rise in civilian casualties

"Over the past night, air defence systems intercepted and destroyed 456 Ukrainian aerial drones," Russia's defence ministry said, specifying that the attacks targeted around fifteen Russian regions and annexed Crimea.

In Tatarstan, in central Russia, "massive" strikes targeted the industrial city of Nizhnekamsk, about 1,600 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, according to a statement from the regional authorities.

The attack, still under way at 0530 GMT, "is being carried out against both industrial and civilian sites. Unfortunately, there are fatalities," the statement said.

Authorities in the Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, reported that a woman was killed in a drone attack targeting a house in the village of Novaya Tavolzhanka.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/m.title: Former kindergarten cleaner jailed over AI-produced child abuse material
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/m.author: Wade Stephens
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

ABC Mildura-Swan Hill

Christopher Rankin will remain behind bars until at least August 2029. (ABC News: Tyrone Dalton)

A former teacher's aide and kindergarten cleaner in north-west Victoria has been jailed for four-and-a-half years for possessing and producing child abuse material.

Mildura man Christopher Rankin, 36, pleaded guilty to 17 charges, and will be classed as a serious sexual offender for life.

He will be eligible for parole in three years.

A Mildura man who possessed thousands of child abuse images, including hundreds he produced himself has been jailed for four-and-a-half years.

The actions of Christopher Rankin, 36, were described as abhorrent during sentencing in the Victorian County Court on Monday.

Rankin offended across an eight-month period at a north-west Victorian home between November 9, 2024 and June 6, 2025.

His offending directly involved five children and six adults known to him, as well as a number of unidentified child victims.

The former teacher's aide and kindergarten cleaner was found guilty of possessing a total of 3,638 images and videos of child abuse material.

Almost 3,300 of the files were not created by Rankin, and were described as perverse, depraved and disgusting by Judge Krista Breckweg.

Christopher Rankin, 36, had served 81 days in detention prior to sentencing. (Supplied: Facebook)

Those videos and images related to the sexual abuse of unknown child victims, some as young as one-year-old.

Across the offending period, Rankin himself created more than 350 explicit videos and images, either through covert filming or use of artificial intelligence.

While the material did not feature sexual abuse, it was described as "nevertheless predatory".

The court heard he installed a black covert pinhole camera in a home bathroom in Mildura, producing explicit videos and images of two children known to him.

Christopher Rankin 's moral culpability was described as high. (ABC News: Tyrone Dalton)

He also used AI software to transpose the faces of a total of four children and six women onto the bodies of unknown naked female children and adult women.

Judge Breckweg said the offending was not isolated or sporadic, as there was evidence Rankin had moved the child abuse material files across multiple devices and had encrypted access to them.

Rankin was described as a deviant offender, who was assessed a moderate risk of sexual reoffending.

Judge Breckweg said Rankin's prospects for rehabilitation remained guarded.

She acknowledged the material Rankin possessed on his devices was for personal use, and was not obtained for the purposes of blackmail, revenge or sale.

He was sentenced to a combined total sentence of four-and-a-half years imprisonment, and would be eligible for parole in three years.

Christopher Rankin was arrested on June 5, 2025. (Facebook)

Upon release he will be put on a two-year good behaviour bond, and he will need to complete a sex offender program and alcohol abuse rehabilitation program within two years.

He must also report to Mildura Police Station, and is barred from travelling interstate or overseas without permission.

Rankin also will have lifetime reporting obligations, due to being sentenced as a serious sexual offender.

Judge Breckweg said if he did not enter a guilty plea, Rankin would have been sentenced to six years imprisonment.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/c.title: Second coal train derails weeks after runaway train incident
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/c.author: Giselle Wakatama and Peter Sanders
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Rail Accidents and Incidents

Investigators and crews are on site at Ardglen after an incident involving a Pacific National train. (ABC News: Peter Sanders)

A second Pacific National coal train is being examined after a derailment, just weeks after a runaway train incident on the same freight track.

The train derailed just before midday, shutting the line between the Upper Hunter and Tamworth.

Rail safety investigators will examine the scene.

A coal train has derailed in the NSW Upper Hunter less than two weeks after a runaway unmanned train operated by the same company reached 90 kilometres per hour.

The Australian Rail Track Corporation (ARTC) confirmed it was notified about an incident just before midday.

ARTC was advised the lead wheel, or bogie, of the Pacific National coal train derailed at Ardglen Loop, a stretch of track between the Upper Hunter and Tamworth.

Pacific National has confirmed the incident.

"The incident occurred on the Ardglen loop and has resulted in disruption to rail traffic through the area," a spokesperson said.

"There have been no reports of injuries to the train crew.

"The train has been secured and our teams are responding to the incident."

ARTC said the site had been "preserved" pending the arrival of investigators from the Office of the National Rail Safety Regulator (ONRSR).

The derailment comes three weeks after an incident involving an unmanned Pacific National train travelling up to 90km/h over 20 kilometres without a driver on board.

An interim report found the three locomotives and 96 wagons reached speeds well over the safe limit, and only came to a halt after rolling backwards for 5 kilometres.

Last week ONRSR updated its advice about reporting requirements for rail transport operators.

It said "a notifiable occurrence means an accident or incident associated with railway operations that must be reported to ONRSR".

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.title: AGL fined $60k after workers exposed to lead during power plant deactivation
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.author: Jordanna Schriever
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Jordanna Schriever

Topic:
Occupational Health and Safety

The workers were exposed to lead during decommissioning operations at AGL's Torrens Island A Power Station. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

South Australia's Employment Tribunal has convicted and fined AGL for exposing workers to lead during decommissioning works at the Torrens Island A Power Station.

The energy giant pleaded guilty to failing to comply with a health and safety duty to its employees.

AGL says it has taken actions to ensure similar events do not occur in the future.

Energy giant AGL has been convicted and fined $60,000 after workers were exposed to lead during a decommissioning project at an Adelaide power station.

The company pleaded guilty to failing to comply with a health and safety duty to its employees, after SafeWork SA lodged criminal proceedings over the plant's decommissioning process at the Torrens Island A Power Station.

In 2024, the ABC revealed workers, including AGL employees, had been affected by lead exposure during the works between October 2022 and April 2023.

In a statement, SafeWork SA said testing found five employees had elevated blood lead levels, after the presence of lead was detected in workplace dust.

AGL was sentenced in the South Australian Employment Tribunal on Friday.

SafeWork SA said the exposure occurred when "large quantities of paper insulated lead covered (PILC) cables were required to be de-energised, cut and removed".

AGL says it cooperated fully throughout the process. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

The statement said that process involved cutting cables into 1-metre lengths and placing them into drums for disposal.

"The work generated dust and debris, including lead dust," the statement said.

"Workers undertaking the task were provided with personal protective equipment including long sleeves, long pants, boots, safety glasses, hard hats and gloves.

"However, respiratory protection to prevent inhalation of lead dust, such as full-face respirators, was not provided."

Sean Gibbons says he started experiencing fatigue, stomach upsets, pins and needles in his legs, and insomnia after helping decommission AGL's Torrens Island power plant.

In his sentencing remarks, Deputy President Judge Miles Crawley said the work "should have been an obvious source of the risk of lead exposure needing to be addressed".

"Risk assessment protocols are only as effective as the way in which they are implemented," he said.

As well as the $60,000 fine, the company was convicted and ordered to pay SafeWork SA's costs of $2,640.

SafeWork SA executive director Glenn Farrell said the case "demonstrates the importance of thorough hazard identification and risk assessment processes for known materials that are known to cause harm".

"Lead exposure remains a significant workplace health risk, particularly during demolition, decommissioning and maintenance activities where hazardous materials may be disturbed," he said.

"Employers must ensure all foreseeable sources of hazardous exposure are identified and appropriate controls are implemented before work begins."

Glenn Farrell says lead exposure is a significant workplace health risk. (Supplied: SafeWork SA)

Mr Farrell said where lead hazards were present, workers must be provided with suitable protective equipment and safe systems of work to minimise exposure.

"Effective safety management depends not only on having systems in place, but on correctly identifying and addressing workplace risks before workers are put in harm's way," he said.

In a statement, a spokesperson for AGL said the energy provider had cooperated with all aspects of the investigation and had "taken actions to ensure the event does not happen again".

"Health and safety is a core value of AGL and is an integral part of the way we work," the statement said.

"While we acknowledge that on this occasion AGL fell short of our own standards, the health and safety of our people, both employees and contractors, remains our highest priority."

The spokesman said AGL had updated written procedures to include a new working with lead procedure, hazard identification risk assessments, and is educating employees and contractors.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/f.title: Renaming of electorate for Aboriginal leader abandoned after disagreement
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/f.author: Ashleigh Barraclough
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Ashleigh Barraclough

Topic:
Indigenous Australians

The Franklin electorate is named for former governor of Tasmania, Rear-Admiral Sir John Franklin. (Supplied)

A proposal to rename a Tasmanian electorate after an Indigenous resistance leader has been abandoned.

If the change had gone ahead, it would have been the first time in the state's history that an electorate was named after an Aboriginal person.

The Australian Electoral Commission has said any change to electorate names would be best considered at future redistributions, when it could conduct further consultation.

The Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) has abandoned a controversial plan to rename a Tasmanian electorate after an Aboriginal resistance leader.

WARNING: This article contains a depiction of an Aboriginal person who has died

The AEC proposed renaming the electorate of Franklin, which takes in Hobart's eastern shore and southern Tasmania, to Tongerlongeter — an Aboriginal leader and warrior who died in 1837.

The proposed change was canvassed at the same time as the AEC announced an electoral boundary redistribution, which will see more than a quarter of Tasmanians voting in a new electorate.

The AEC said the new boundaries would take effect from the next federal election, but all electorates would retain their current names, including Franklin.

The proposed name change to Tongerlongeter was suggested to honour the Aboriginal resistance leader and warrior who died in 1837. (Watercolour by Thomas Bock, 1832 — British Museum)

"The panel considered the case for the proposed name to be very strong — including Tongerlongeter's strong connection to the area encompassed by the new boundaries of the electorate of Franklin," Australian Electoral Commissioner Jeff Pope said.

A national inquiry into racism, hate and violence towards First Nations people has come to Hobart to hear from the state's Aboriginal groups and people with lived experience of racism.

"However, public submissions not only indicated a level of disagreement among Tasmanian Aboriginal organisations and individuals about the proposed name but also highlighted a broad sentiment that further consultation was required.

"While other name options were put forward — including Mathinna, Rooke and Woureddy — the panel had to reach its final decision based on the evidence and views already received.

The boundary changes will see more than a quarter of Tasmanians voting in a new electorate. (Supplied: AEC)

The proposal had been criticised by the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre (TAC), which said the warrior's name was actually Tukalunginta, and that he died resisting British invasion.

More than a quarter of Tasmanians will vote in new electorates under a long-awaited boundary redistribution announced by the Australian Electoral Commission.

"To suggest that Tukalunginta's name should now be used to represent the very colonial political system he resisted — one that, 223 years later, continues to deny Aborigines the same rights he fought and died defending, is offensive and absurd," TAC campaign manager Nala Mansell said at the time.

The AEC had consulted with the public since October last year on the new electoral boundaries, but did not reveal the proposed name change until July 15.

The commission said by that point, it only had seven days for further consultation.

"The panel did seek to engage the various members of the Tasmanian Aboriginal community on the question of the name of the electorate, and a number of organisations and individuals from the Aboriginal community took the opportunity to express their views through a formal submission," Mr Pope said.

"This outreach included contacting the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre before and after a name was proposed, to encourage the TAC to consider making a submission, noting the submissions process is the formal way the panel can receive input under redistribution laws."

The AEC decided any change to electorate names would be best considered at future redistributions, when it could conduct further consultation.

After July's announcement of the name change and new boundaries, the AEC received 272 written submissions.

In their submissions, both the First Peoples (Tasmania) Aboriginal Corporation and Parrdarrama Pungenna Aboriginal Corporation both endorsed the name change to Tongerlongeter.

If the change had gone ahead, it would have been the first time a Tasmanian electorate was named after an Aboriginal person.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
Amid the Los Angeles Dodgers’ worst stretch of the season, at least one star player insists there is no reason to panic as ⁠the team heads home to face the Kansas City Royals on Monday.

The last time the Dodgers were at home, they were swept by the Boston Red Sox in a three-game series. They went to Chicago and met the same fate against the Chicago Cubs before their losing streak hit a season-high seven games in Phoenix against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Friday.

Los Angeles ended its skid Saturday in a ​tight 2-1 victory before falling 4-2 to the Diamondbacks to close out a 1-5 trip Sunday. The ‌Dodgers are ‌11-17 since July 5.

“It’s baseball (with) ups and downs,” said Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman, a 10-time ​All-Star. “We’re going to go through it. No one’s worried in here. ... As an offense, we got to do better. So, hopefully, that starts (Monday).”

The Los Angeles bullpen retired all 14 batters it faced on Sunday, but the offense ⁠was limited to six hits, including Andy Pages’ RBI double in the third inning, and Kyle Tucker’s RBI triple in the ⁠sixth.

The Dodgers are set to send left-hander Tarik Skubal (7-6, 2.81 ERA) to the mound for his first start in Los Angeles since the two-time American League Cy Young Award winner was acquired ​from the Detroit Tigers on Aug. 2.

In ⁠his Dodgers debut Tuesday, Skubal allowed two runs on four hits in six innings against the host Cubs. He added six strikeouts with two walks over 85 pitches. Despite ⁠the strong effort, the ​Dodgers fell 5-1 as their losing streak reached five games.

“I’m going to show ​up and kind of be a chameleon in a sense and fit right in with these ​guys and ‌just gel with them,” Skubal said, according to the Orange County Register. “They’ve got the winning recipe.”

The Royals will make their fourth-ever visit for a series at Dodger Stadium, where they have won just twice in nine games. They last visited in 2024 when they lost two of three.

Kansas City is set to ‌send left-hander Noah Cameron (6-8, 4.37) to the mound while on his best run of the season.

Cameron has a 0.39 ERA over his last three appearances (two starts) and picked up the win over the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday when he gave up one run and matched a season high with nine strikeouts over eight innings.

Cameron threw more sliders than usual against the ​Twins ​and closed strong by retiring the last 14 batters he faced — the final five on ​strikeouts.

“Trying to be as convicted and confident in (the slider) as I can,” Cameron told reporters last week. “Trying to throw it ⁠for strikes early and trying to throw it in the dirt late. When that pitch is on, it opens up everything else.”

Since that victory, the Royals have lost three of four, falling 10-2 at home to the Cubs on Sunday. Starling Marte delivered the only Kansas City runs on a two-run homer.

Since returning from ​the injured list Tuesday (back tightness), Kansas City shortstop Bobby Witt Jr. is 8-for-22 (.364) with three RBIs and six runs scored.

According to multiple reports, the Royals signed right-hander reliever Craig Kimbrel to a major league deal, and the 38-year-old could be available as soon as Monday. Kimbrel, a former Dodger among 11 previous teams in 17 seasons, was designated for assignment by the Tampa Bay Rays last week and elected free agency after clearing waivers.

https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/people/ar.title: Discovery of almost 1,000 weapons in Indonesian school fuels safety fears
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/people/ar.author: SCMP’s Asia desk
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/people/ar.text:
Suspected narcotics and pornographic CDs were also found in a room used by a former chair of a school foundation

An Indonesian minister has called for better protection of students after nearly 1,000 weapons were found at a private school in South Jakarta.

Police seized 995 airsoft guns and one live firearm from a school run by the Harapan Ibu Islamic School Foundation on Friday, Antara news agency reported.

The foundation’s former chair, identified only by the initials IWD, has been called in for questioning. IWD had been dismissed amid allegations of misuse of foundation funds, according to the Jakarta Globe.

All the weapons – along with suspected narcotics and 25 pornographic CDs – were found in a room used by IWD when the school’s new management was doing a clear-out.

“When we opened the room, we found the weapons,” said Untung Sangaji, a board member, adding that they were classified as such because “airsoft guns can kill because the bullets are plain and there is no groove”.

“We have no idea why they were being kept on school grounds,” he said.

Police spokesman Budi Hermanto said the live firearm was a Franchi SPAS-15 12-gauge combat shotgun belonging to a man who died several years ago. “As for the other 995, they are believed to comprise four 4.5-mm air rifles, 215 air pistols of 4.5-mm calibre and 776 air revolvers of 4.5-mm calibre,” he added.

A company affiliated with the Indonesian Shooting Association initially claimed ownership of the weapons on Friday, saying that they were “not firearms in the conventional sense but primarily airsoft guns used for sports and school extracurricular activities”.

However, foundation lawyer Hermawanto said that the school “never had a shooting extracurricular” – directly contradicting IWD’s lawyer, Alhadid Endar Putra, who maintained that the weapons were licensed and intended for school activities.

Lawmaker Adang Daradjatun on Saturday called on the police to conduct a transparent and objective investigation.

“The law enforcement process must not be influenced by public opinion or conflicts between the parties involved. Investigators should work based on facts and evidence so that the outcome provides legal certainty and a sense of justice for all parties,” he said.

Women’s Empowerment and Child Protection Minister Arifah Fauzi said on Sunday that the discovery should not be allowed to affect the students’ education.

“Children must not bear the burden of an issue that is beyond their responsibility. Let us protect their privacy and psychological well-being, so that they can continue learning in a comfortable environment,” she said.

She urged a thorough inspection of the school’s premises – but without causing a disruption in their learning.

The foundation has moved lessons online for all its schools in South Jakarta for a week starting Monday “to ensure the safety and security of the students”, Hermawan said.

There were other rooms that needed inspecting, he said, including one that resembled a bunker. “There are still locked rooms and we don’t know what’s inside them.”

Alvon Kurnia Palma, a lawyer for the foundation, said parents had requested remote learning while the police examined areas suspected of storing prohibited or potentially dangerous items. “We strongly encourage the police to immediately secure and clear the areas whose contents remain unknown.”

School safety has become a concern in the region after a Thai student shot and killed eight people – including his grandparents, several school staff and a schoolgirl – using his grandfather’s firearm last week. He had reportedly had an airgun confiscated by a teacher last year.

https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/southeast.title: 2 injured in Thai government office shooting, ex-MP arrested
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/southeast.author: Reuters
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/southeast.text:
The shooting comes just days after a teenager’s killing rampage at a school in the same province reignited debate over gun control

The suspected shooter, a former lawmaker, fired at a senior provincial official and his driver, said Major General Dejrapee Kongdee, the police commander of Nonthaburi, which borders Bangkok.

“There were two people wounded, who have been sent to hospital for treatment,” Dejrapee said.

At Debsirin School in Bangkok, a sister institution to where Friday’s shooting took place, authorities installed metal detectors and ‌stepped up security as students returned to classrooms after the weekend.

School director Withan Promsintusak said officials had acted immediately ⁠after the attack, introducing weapons ⁠screening to reassure parents and protect students.

“We never imagined that a school, which should be the safest place, was where something like this would happen,” he said.

Thidarat Songrat, the ‌54-year-old grandmother of a student, said weapons screening was necessary because schools could not otherwise determine whether students might be carrying dangerous objects.

Following Friday’s shooting, Thailand’s Education ‌Ministry has said ‌it will develop new school safety protocols over the next three months, including mental health screenings, emergency response drills, measures to ‌tackle bullying and improved detection of weapons and other prohibited items.

Thai Premier Anutin also ordered tougher enforcement against people carrying guns in public ⁠and said police would set up checkpoints as part of a crackdown, which would include tightening controls on the possession, carrying and use ⁠of firearms.

“No one has the right to carry a firearm, especially in a public place,” Anutin told reporters, adding that claiming a weapon was for self-defence was no justification.

Thailand had an estimated 10.3 million firearms in civilian possession, equating to around ‌15 guns per 100 residents, ‌the highest rate in Southeast Asia by a wide margin, according to a 2017 estimate by the Small Arms Survey.

The country’s current licensing regime lacks mental health screening for people applying to possess a gun, allows people as young as 20 to hold weapons and does not require periodic reassessments for licence holders, according to experts.

https://www.dw.com/en/china-typhoon-dolp.title: China: Typhoon Dolphin prompts mass evacuation, canceled flights
https://www.dw.com/en/china-typhoon-dolp.text:
Even as it weakens, Typhoon Dolphin is disrupting life in China. Close to 1,500 flights have been canceled in Shanghai while parts of Beijing are under flood alert.

Heavy rainfall and strong winds prompted flood alerts and more than 1,000 flight cancellations across China on Monday, even as Typhoon Dolphin weakened.

China's National Meteorological Centre (NMC) issued its least severe typhoon alert on Monday morning as the storm lost power after making landfall in China's Zhejiang Province on Sunday.

Despite the weaker storm, the NMC warned that parts of east and central China will continue to receive heavy rainfall. Authorities issued their most severe flash flood alert for parts of eastern and southern Zhejiang on Monday, state news broadcaster CCTV reported.

Five districts in Beijing are also under red alerts for heavy rainfall on Monday, with risks of landslides and flooding.

The storm had already forced over 300,000 people in eastern China to preemptively relocate, while bringing heavy rainfall to northern Taiwan over the weekend. In Shanghai, authorities evacuated more than 30,000 people out of high-risk areas. Overall, some one million people have been told to seek shelter.

Shanghai's two main passenger airports, Pudong International Airport and Hongqiao International Airport, canceled 943 flights between them for Monday, the airport authority said in a post online. That's a reduction of capacity by nearly 40%.

On Sunday, the two airports had cancelled nearly 1,500 flights, or about 60% of their scheduled travel, according to state media.

Public transport services in the city were also impacted, with several local trains suspended.

At the same time, Zhejiang province began to resume its transport facilities.

Zhejiang's Ningbo International Airport will resume flights midday on Monday but warned that some of the scheduled travel may still be delayed or canceled as the storm had "not yet completely dissipated."

China is dealing with Typhoon Dolphin just two weeks after Typhoon Noul struck its southern Guangdong province. Last month, Typhoon Maysak killed 11 people and injured over 300 in the central Hubei province.

Extreme weather systems are a common feature in China this time of the year, with typhoons leaving significant displacement, infrastructural damage and loss of lives. Scientists warn that the intensity and frequency of such extreme weather have increased and will continue to rise amid climate change.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgje.title: Memories of rock royalty in my garden in Knebworth
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgje.text:
Not many people can say Queen and Oasis have played in their back garden. Henry Lytton Cobbold can.

Forty years ago, on 9 August 1986, Freddie Mercury, Brian May, Roger Taylor and John Deacon brought Queen's sold-out European tour to a close at Knebworth House in Hertfordshire.

Lytton Cobbold, now the owner of the estate, was 24 at the time and remembers the suitably rock-and-roll celebrations backstage afterwards, complete with fairground rides and naked women mud wrestling.

"They had a lot to celebrate," he recalls. "They'd really smashed it live the year before... And then of course it became legendary for various rather sadder reasons."

Five years later, Mercury died from bronchial pneumonia resulting from AIDS. His performance in front of 125,000 people at Knebworth was his final time on stage with Queen.

Lytton Cobbold says: "He was at the top of his game and nobody knew about his illness at that point.

"The other thing, of course, that makes it legendary is this bizarre fact that although the field was full of screens nobody pressed record.

"The only record we've got of the show is a little bit of news footage from the beginning and then a really bizarre bootleg that a Dutch guy took on his little home video camera of a screen at the back of the audience.

"I mean, imagine going to a Freddie Mercury gig and spending the whole time at the back of the audience filming the screen with your wobbly video camera."

Lytton Cobbold never met the band, unlike some of the other stars who had played Knebworth in earlier years.

"Back in the old days, they didn't used to helicopter off the minute they'd done the encore, they would come up and chill at the house until the roads cleared."

Knebworth Park has hosted live music since 1974. Pink Floyd were the first major act to play the venue in 1975, with the Rolling Stones following a year later.

He said: "My mum and dad generally loved a party.

"I mean my dad's birthday was on 14 July, and every summer holiday began with a big party and the concerts just gave us that encore party. "

Genesis, Led Zeppelin, The Beach Boys and Cliff Richard were among the names to play Knebworth in the 1970s and 80s, but it was the 90s when guitars in Hertfordshire were heard around the world.

There was a lot happening in the UK in the summer of 1996: England hosted Euro 96, the Spice Girls made their debut, Dolly the sheep was cloned, and Oasis played two nights at Knebworth to 250,000 people.

"Our catering company did the bars in 96 and that was one of our biggest trading days ever... Quite a lot of beer was drunk that day," he recalls.

The band slept backstage in Winnebagos. Then, on the Monday morning, a dishevelled Noel Gallagher appeared at the back door.

Lytton Cobbold says: "We've got a four poster bath as part of our main guest room, our old Tudor guest room, and so my dad brought him a bottle of champagne in the bath.

"Subsequently in interviews he said that he was brought champagne by a liveried servant- it was actually my dad!"

Oasis only released recordings from those shows in recent years, but their Knebworth legacy has stayed strong.

Two turrets attached to the house, named Noel and Liam, were built using income from the 1996 shows.

Lytton Cobbold said: "The rest of this house is still falling down and you know, we've got massive repairs and bills still to pay to to do the rest of the house.

"So, we do need them to come back and help us fix the rest of the roof!"

Earlier this week, SJM Concerts, the promoter behind Oasis' 2025 reunion, was granted a licence to host large events at Knebworth.

However Lytton Cobbold insists "there is nothing set yet".

He adds: "I'm confident that Oasis will play Knebworth again, and I would love it to be next year, I would love it to be whenever they want to come, whenever feels right for them."

When asked if it would be fitting to announce a return on Monday, the 30th anniversary of their Knebworth shows, he agrees, but says his wife handles bookings and he does not know what is planned.

"They have got a documentary coming out in September and they'll want to make a bit of buzz around their documentary. If they want to make some announcements, I would have thought that would be more of the time to do it.

"We're delighted that our local authorities are supporting the licence, that's great, fingers crossed that all comes together, but it's not happening as of today."

https://www.nytimes.com/article/flock-sa.author: Neil Vigdor
https://www.nytimes.com/article/flock-sa.text:
Flock Safety’s automated license plate-reading cameras, used by thousands of law enforcement agencies in the U.S., have drawn intense criticism from civil liberties groups.

Law enforcement agencies have embraced them. So have many cities across the United States, large and small.

But the proliferation of Flock cameras, a brand of automated license plate readers that employ artificial intelligence to identify and track vehicles, has divided the public and rattled civil liberties watchdogs.

Some say the cameras are a valuable tool to help catch criminals, while critics argue that they are an invasion of privacy, and that the information they collect can be misused by the government or rogue law enforcement officers.

Flock Safety is a private company based in Atlanta that supplies many of the license plate-reading cameras used by law enforcement offices across the nation.

The company was valued at $8.4 billion as of April 2026, less than a decade after it was started by three graduates of the Georgia Institute of Technology.

More than 7,000 organizations in the United States have contracts with Flock Safety, according to the company.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/busin.title: Private Equity Is Stuck With 33,575 Unsold Businesses
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/busin.author: Maureen Farrell
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/busin.text:
Even amid a booming deal-making environment, private equity firms are unable to exit a growing number of investments at values their investors require.

Maureen Farrell has been following the dearth of private-equity deals and the circuitous ways firms have sought to cash out their investments.

The long-awaited deal-making boom has finally arrived. SpaceX set a record for the world’s largest initial public offering. David Ellison is pursuing a $110 billion deal linking Paramount with Warner Bros. The utility firm NextEra Energy has struck a deal to buy Dominion Energy that values it at more than $120 billion.

But private equity — a deal-making machine for decades — is largely sitting on the sidelines. For the third consecutive year, private equity firms are saddled with a rapidly increasing number of companies that they cannot sell or take public at the returns their investors expect.

As of June 30, private equity firms had 33,575 unsold companies in their portfolios, according to PitchBook, an industry data firm. That’s up from 32,451 companies at the end of last year and 15,923 companies a decade ago.

The growing backlog is a challenge for private equity’s core business model. Typically, such firms aim to buy a company, often add large amounts of debt to its balance sheet, improve its financial performance and then sell it for a profit, usually within five to seven years.

The state of limbo has been difficult for large investors like pension funds and endowments that have spent decades paying steep fees to private equity firms promising market-beating returns. Some investors and industry professionals are worried that the firms won’t be able to sell companies without taking big losses.

“Private equity is stuck because those companies have failed to fulfill their value promise,” said Andrew Milgram, a managing partner and chief investment officer at Marblegate Asset Management, an investment firm.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/trave.title: Can A.I. Get You Where You Want to Go for Less?
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/trave.author: Elaine Glusac
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/trave.text:
A wave of new services uses A.I. to monitor flights and hotel reservations to help you find lower prices. We look at how these tools work.

For years, I’ve recommended tracking the prices of hotel reservations and airline tickets after you’ve booked them to see if the prices drop. If they do, and your booking is flexible, you can usually cancel without penalty and rebook at the lower price.

It’s still solid — if time-consuming — advice. But now travelers can have a bot do the legwork as a wave of new apps trains artificial intelligence models on travel searches.

These apps springboard from the travel industry’s cancellation polices. Other than the most restrictive basic economy tickets, most U.S.-based legacy airlines allow travelers to cancel a flight and retain the cost as a credit for future bookings. (This works with more expensive refundable airfares, too, in which case the refund is in cash.)

“Airlines adjust fares constantly, so two people on the same flight routinely pay very different amounts, and most travelers have no idea the airline’s own rules let them recover the difference after booking,” said Bryan Dubno, the founder and chief executive of JetBack, an app that tracks airfares. “The mechanism exists. It’s just buried in fare rules and manual claim forms almost nobody has the time to navigate.”

When a fare drops, these apps go to the airlines to request refunds. They don’t otherwise alter the reservation, nor do they ask for a flier’s airline login information.

“The consumer effectively gains the opportunity to monitor the market,” Mareike Mohlmann, the chair of A.I. and business at Bentley University in Waltham, Mass., wrote in an email. “It is a small but meaningful shift from A.I. acting ‘on’ consumers to A.I. acting ‘for’ consumers.”

Elaine Glusac is The Times’s Frugal Traveler columnist, focusing on budget-friendly tips and journeys.

https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-587.title: The FAA wants to reboot the nation's airspace. This airline shows how it might work
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-587.author: Joel Rose
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-587.text:
Dispatchers in Alaska Airlines' Network Operations Center near the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport.

On a typical day, Alaska Airlines operates roughly 1,500 flights, most of them guided by a team of dispatchers on the sixth floor of an office building near the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport known as "The Hub."

The dispatchers sit in a big open room, surrounded by as many as five flatscreen monitors that display real-time information on air traffic, weather, upper-level wind patterns, and more.

It's a lot to process. But these dispatchers are getting some help from a software tool called Flyways AI.

"It ingests all that information," said Alek Mead, a manager in Alaska's Network Operations Center, "and it really kind of puts us all together in a nice little package for the dispatcher to look at, take some options, maybe play around with some different ideas, and then pick the most efficient and the safest route."

When Alaska wanted to optimize its operations, it turned to a small startup called Air Space Intelligence. Now the Federal Aviation Administration has tapped the same company to carry out a major reboot of the entire U.S. airspace.

The FAA wants to use technology — including artificial intelligence — to make the nation's airspace more efficient. And Flyways offers a glimpse of how that might look in practice.

Alaska was the first airline to start using the Flyways system back in 2021 to do things that would be challenging, if not impossible, for a human dispatcher working alone.

"It doesn't decide the route or waypoints that a dispatcher uses to get an airplane from A to B, but it does help provide suggestions that might be more efficient," explained Captain Bret Peyton, the managing director of Alaska's network operations control. "That's where Flyways is really excelling for us."

Alaska says it's saving tens of thousands of hours in the air and roughly a million gallons of fuel per year because of Flyways.

The system works by basically crunching data on air traffic, wind, weather and other factors to anticipate what is going to happen during flight before it does.

Phillip Buckendorf, the CEO and co-founder of Air Space Intelligence, speaking at a conference in Washington, D.C. earlier this year.

"It's actually a really fundamental change, a massive behavior change," said Phillip Buckendorf, the co-founder and CEO of Air Space Intelligence, the company that built Flyways, in an interview on the podcast Crossing the Valley last year.

Buckendorf says his company worked closely with Alaska to build Flyways from the ground up. The company has since expanded to work with Delta Air Lines and United Airlines, as well as the U.S. Army and Air Force.

"One of the hardest things is we're dealing with users that have basically made decisions against static displays for like 10, 20 years of their career. And so now they basically make a decision against a predictive picture," Buckendorf said.

Federal regulators are betting that predictive analytics can make the entire U.S. airspace work better, too.

"I think we've got a real opportunity to do something transformational with AI," said Bryan Bedford, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, at an industry conference in May.

Bedford says the U.S. airspace is safe today because air traffic controllers make sure planes are separated from each other at every stage of their journey. But he says the current system is not as efficient as it could be.

"What we're seeing is a system that is woefully unorganized," Bedford said. "We don't have in any of our facilities the ability to see the entire national airspace picture in a unified way."

Bedford says predictive analytics can help prevent bottlenecks and congestion before they happen, with relatively small adjustments to schedules and routes.

The FAA is so convinced that it recently announced an $875 million dollar contract with Air Space Intelligence to modernize the nation's airspace. The company is tasked with building what the agency is calling the SMART system, short for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories.

It's part of the Trump administration's ambitious push to deliver a Brand New Air Traffic Control System. FAA officials say the goal is to help air traffic controllers, not replace them.

But skeptics wonder if the technology can scale up from helping airline dispatchers to optimizing the entire U.S. airspace, which is the busiest and most complex in the world.

Bret Peyton at Alaska Airlines says dispatchers there were skeptical, too.

"It took a while for us to convince the dispatch group that it is what we say it is, which is a decision making aid, and not a tool that's going to run rogue and make weird decisions for the dispatcher," Peyton said. "And it happened relatively quickly once dispatchers saw their true results that were pretty immediate."

KNKX's Izzy Ross contributed reporting from Seattle.

https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-592.title: An arts school where Epstein allegedly preyed on students reveals decades of abuse
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-592.author: Ava Berger
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-592.text:
Paul Busch was 16 years old when he was sexually abused by his ballet teacher at the Interlochen Center for the Arts in 2005. At the time, Busch told NPR, he was living away from his parents, wanted more than anything to be a professional dancer and revered the teacher who harmed him.

Busch is sharing his experience publicly for the first time after spending 21 years reckoning with what happened to him at the Michigan boarding school.

"A lot of my desire was to prove that I was enough," Busch said. "That I was good enough and that I was worthy of love." He said that "this was the perfect condition" for someone to prey on him.

His story reflects the larger themes of a sweeping independent report, released last month, that details decades of sexual abuse allegations on the campus of the prestigious arts boarding school and summer camp.

In the report, former Interlochen students recount some 70 allegations of sexual abuse by nearly 50 adults who were employed or affiliated with the school from the 1950s to the 2010s. It's a stark contrast to the longtime idyllic image of Interlochen, which helped launch the careers of performers such as Josh Groban, Norah Jones, Chappell Roan, Felicity Huffman and Da'Vine Joy Randolph.

The report offers a window into the conditions that contributed to the abuse. In many cases, it says, adults were able to have one-on-one interactions with students, while the children at the school had limited communication with their families and were vulnerable due to age, sexual identity and lack of experience. And, it says, some were scared to report what happened to them.

The report includes allegations of sexual abuse by convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, an alumni and benefactor, and his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell. NPR reported in February that Epstein met and recruited two young teenagers on the campus. But the allegations go far beyond the disgraced financier, who died in prison in 2019.

Interlochen hired Sanghavi Law Office in 2024 to investigate abuse at the school after an alumna came forward about her experience in the 1970s regarding a longtime faculty member and administrator.

In a letter to the community released alongside the report, Interlochen said that today it is "fundamentally different from the institution described in this report." In a statement to NPR, the school described safety measures it has put in place to protect students and a network of resources, including a team of school counselors, social workers and a psychologist.

But for Busch, the response from Interlochen is not enough.

"They get to say, 'Case closed,'" he said. "That is completely unacceptable because — guess what? — my life is still open."

Together, Busch's perspective and the report's observations shed light on a decades-long history of sexual abuse at a school that was built for children and teenagers who aspire to be artists but were often unprotected, due to what the report called "gaps in oversight" and a "permissive environment."

A band rehearses at Interlochen in 1942, when there was only a summer program for young musicians and artists.

In its letter to the community, Interlochen named three former staff members and one former trustee who have been accused of sexual misconduct. Only one of them is still alive — Thomas Clower, the teacher who pleaded guilty to abusing Busch.

At the time that the law firm's report was released, Clower's name was listed as an instructor on the website of a dance school for children and teenagers in Texas. It has since been removed.

For this story, NPR spoke to nearly a dozen people, including Busch; a witness to his sexual abuse; his mother, brother and sister; and one of his closest friends from Interlochen. NPR also reviewed court documents, a report from the sheriff's office, a recording of a conversation between a Texas parent and Clower, and current correspondence between Busch's family and Interlochen. Clower did not respond to multiple attempts by NPR to contact him, including through his attorney. Interlochen would not comment on the specifics of Clower's case and its aftermath to NPR.

In the fall of 2004, Busch felt special. It would take less than a year for that feeling to be replaced with shame and isolation, he said.

After initially attending Interlochen as a summer music student, Busch told NPR, Clower recruited him from a ballet studio in Dayton, Ohio. He secured a partial scholarship as a boarding student for his sophomore year of high school. The summer students dream of being invited to the boarding school, he said.

Paul Busch during his time studying dance at Interlochen.

"It was, at that point, my prayers being answered," said Busch, now 37, in a recent interview from his home in Nashville, Tenn.

But, Busch said, the bliss quickly dissipated as Clower, a well-known and award-winning ballet teacher, showered him with attention and became increasingly involved with his life. Busch said that Clower requested to be his mentor and that he took several of Clower's classes.

The two met often in his office, Busch said. A few months into the semester, Clower began emailing him. Busch would later describe to law enforcement an email that he called "inappropriate," with questions about his personal life and sexual activity. The report, written by the Grand Traverse County Sheriff's Office, also describes warm responses from Busch, which he now says show "how groomed I was … and how vulnerable and dependent that I became to him."

Busch said that because he wanted to do well at Interlochen, he let a lot of Clower's inappropriate conduct slide. "It's really hard to differentiate what's appropriate and what's not until it's too late," he said.

The interaction that led to Clower's conviction happened on a cold spring day during Busch's first year at Interlochen. Clower was 44. Busch had recently turned 16. He wasn't the only student in the room, according to the report from the sheriff's office.

Nellie Salisbury, then a 15-year-old fellow student, told NPR that Clower drove her and Busch to his house after they got special permission from the school. "We thought we were going over there because we were special dancers getting sort of like a treat," said Salisbury, now 36. She remembers the three of them on the couch — Clower next to Busch, and Salisbury a few feet away on Busch's other side. She said Clower handed her a chocolate bar and then put on a movie.

Once the movie was on, she said, she noticed Clower taking off the jangly silver bracelets from his wrist and placing them on the coffee table.

Busch said Clower casually threw a blanket over the two of them. Clower was sitting close enough that their thighs touched, Busch said, and then Clower put his hand on Busch's upper thigh. Busch told NPR that Clower then reached his hand into Busch's pants and began to touch his genitals.

"My heart was like beating out of its chest," Busch said. "I froze."

Clower then moved Busch's hand toward his lap, according to Busch. That prompted him to pull away, Busch said. Clower then stood up and went to the bathroom, according to Busch and Salisbury.

Busch told investigators that when Clower stood up, his "penis was in an erect position." Salisbury remembers Busch turning to her when they were alone in the room, looking scared and saying, "What do I do? Help me." Clower later drove the students home.

"He wanted me and he took me and it didn't even matter that someone else was watching it happening," Busch said.

Busch acknowledged that the description of the abuse that he gave to NPR is more serious than what he told investigators at the time of the incident. Busch denied to a school counselor at the time that Clower had touched his genitals, the report from the sheriff's office says. He told investigators that Clower was "rubbing the inside of his thigh" and "rubbed near his groin area," but said his belt buckle was unfastened afterward. Looking back, Busch told NPR that he didn't describe the full extent of the touching because he was in denial and afraid of getting in trouble.

That's a common response from minors who are victims of sexual abuse, said Matthew Curtis, a Michigan-based attorney representing multiple people who allege they were abused while students at Interlochen. Curtis said minors might not report their abuse at the time it occurs for a number of reasons, including self-protection, and at Interlochen, the stakes were high.

"These are all aspiring students, aspiring fine arts individuals," he said. "They're looking for careers and success. … Coming forward could really have sabotaged their career."

Clower did not respond to requests for comment on Busch's account. But Mike Skaggs, a parent of a former ballet student in Texas, shared a recording with NPR that appears to shed light on how Clower sees the incident that led to his criminal conviction. Skaggs said he recorded himself confronting Clower about what happened at Interlochen.

According to Skaggs, Clower taught Skaggs' 13-year-old daughter at the Dallas-area Ballet Ensemble of Texas. In the 2025 recording, Skaggs can be heard telling a man whom he refers to as "Mr. Thom" and a third person that he has some reservations about an agreement the young dancers must sign. Then, Skaggs says he has been researching Clower and found newspaper articles about his Michigan conviction.

He wants an explanation. He says he heard that Clower claimed the "kids made it up" and that he was "exonerated."

"That's true," the man identified as Clower states, without providing evidence. Skaggs notes that Clower pleaded guilty, and Clower clarifies that it was "to a misdemeanor."

Clower then explains what he views as his mistake: "I was in my house, 30 below zero, and we all got under a blanket. The girl and the boy and me. And I put myself in a place where I was too close to the kids."

Clower casts the incident as a misunderstanding: "I didn't even think, 'This is going to look horrible.' … What happened was the girl thought that something happened underneath the blanket and then she called her parents."

Busch said the details of what happened after the incident are a blur. He told investigators at the time that Clower picked him up from school three days later and drove him to Clower's house, where, Busch said, the teacher apologized. Busch told NPR that Clower told him that he felt "sick to his stomach" about what happened.

Salisbury's parents sounded the alarm to Interlochen. Busch said he was called into an administrator's office. The school had already called his parents, and he said administrators demanded that he tell them what had happened.

"The feeling was I'm in trouble ... which is probably the worst thing to feel," Busch said. "That only leads to more shame, guilt, isolation and fear, you know? I mean, it was just paralyzing." He does not remember anyone from Interlochen asking whether he was OK.

The report from the sheriff's office shows Busch was interviewed by an investigator twice, the second time without another adult present. He was asked about his sexuality. The investigator said in his report that a "reasonable person" would believe the teen and the 44-year-old "have a relationship that may not necessarily be only at a friendship level."

A mugshot of Thomas Clower from 2005.

"It was like I was being interrogated," Busch said of the school's and the investigators' responses. "It was like I was the perpetrator." He said it led to years of struggling with his identity and sexuality.

Clower was arrested the next month, in April 2005.

In June of that year, he pleaded guilty to attempted fourth-degree criminal sexual conduct — a misdemeanor — and was sentenced to 90 days in jail. He was ultimately released nearly a month early due to overcrowding, according to court records obtained by NPR, and was added to a sex offender registry. Interlochen fired him.

Busch said he felt like a "social pariah" for his final two years at Interlochen. "I was never integrated back into the community," he said. "I was always looked at as different."

Busch says he is still waiting for accountability from Interlochen.

He doesn't recall the school offering him counseling or mentioning the incident to him again after the legal proceedings concluded. He said he was not aware that Interlochen would name Clower in the letter it released last month alongside the law firm's report.

NPR asked Interlochen for comment on how Busch described his treatment at the time of the incident and the lack of support afterward. Interlochen did not comment on Busch's experience specifically but apologized "for the harm experienced by members of our community."

Busch said that the last time he heard from Clower was in a letter he received at some point in his last two years at Interlochen and that in it his former teacher apologized and admitted his actions were wrong. Busch said he burned the letter in his parents' driveway in Ohio.

Clower was listed on the website of the Ballet Academy of Texas as the director of the men's division as recently as Friday, but his name has since been removed. Clower was also listed as the artistic director of the Ballet Ensemble of Texas, a nonprofit affiliated with the academy, until recently. That nonprofit's website has been taken down.

Clower has worked at the academy since at least 2019, according to an NPR review of the website's archives. The ensemble and the academy did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

A photo of Clower on a trip to Venice with members of the Ballet Ensemble of Texas.

In posts on the Ballet Ensemble of Texas' Facebook account, Clower is pictured leading a group of young dancers on a multicountry trip around Europe in June and July of this year.

After his guilty plea, Clower was required to register as a sex offender in Michigan, according to court documents. Clower's name is not currently on the Texas registry. NPR requested records from the Texas Department of Public Safety to see whether he was also previously registered in Texas and did not receive a response by publication time. Clower's record would still be readily available in an employer background check.

A professional biography that was previously on the ballet academy's website indicated that he continued to teach after his guilty plea. It described him as "one of the most energetic and inspiring teachers across the country" and lists a number of dance companies and organizations in multiple states.

In a video posted to YouTube in 2014, Clower said he had been a "freelance master teacher since the year 2000." "Every Monday, basically, I'm in a new location with a new group of kids," he said.

Busch said it makes him uneasy to think about Clower still working with kids. "Are we in that dire of a situation that we need dance teachers that badly that we'll look to the side when we see that they've molested children?" Busch said.

His mother, Nancy Busch, said of Clower: "He should never be able to work with children."

Skaggs, the parent who confronted Clower last year, said he eventually pulled his daughter out of the dance program. "I can't believe I have to say this, but any teacher that's been fired for sexual misconduct should never, ever teach again," Skaggs said. "Full stop." But when Skaggs shared the information with several other parents, he said, some of them defended Clower.

Busch's dance career still thrived. He attended Juilliard after Interlochen and danced professionally for more than a decade, most of which was spent in Europe. But despite his success, Busch said, he masked his emotions for years with substances. Recently, he finished a 10-month recovery program for substance use disorder and PTSD.

Busch danced professionally for over a decade.

And as the extent of sexual abuse of Interlochen students has come into sharper focus, he has been reflecting on the school and how it handled his experience. "It's the lack of aftercare … let alone that it happened 69 other times with other people," Busch said. "The fact that the predator was on the campus to begin with is all Interlochen's responsibility."

In response to the Sanghavi report, Interlochen sent the names of those accused of misconduct to the Grand Traverse County prosecutor's and sheriff's offices. Curtis, the lawyer representing multiple individuals who allege abuse at Interlochen, said that there is no route for some of his clients to pursue criminal charges, because their alleged abusers are dead. In Michigan, the statute of limitations for criminal sex crimes depends on the severity of the crime, according to RAINN, an anti-sexual violence organization.

Interlochen's letter to the community says there were very few incidents at Interlochen in the past 25 years, but Busch says this offers little comfort to him. The school established a counseling fund to help cover future care for affected alumni.

That has come too late for Busch, who has already paid for counseling for the last two decades.

During the law firm's investigation, former students were asked what they hoped would come of it. According to the report, a number of alums said that "they hoped that this investigation would lead to cultural changes at Interlochen." Others said they hoped for "accountability," according to the report.

Busch said he's still waiting for accountability from Interlochen — and he has another reason to share his story now.

"I hope that other people understand that they're not alone," Busch said.

Thomas Clower was convicted of misdemeanor sexual assault in Michigan. BusCh says he felt like a "social pariah" for his final two years at Interlochen.

https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-592.title: In a competitive Maine Senate race, women voters could be the deciders
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-592.author: Elena Moore
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-592.text:
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, walks in the annual Moxie Day Parade on July 11, 2026 in Lisbon, Maine. In her 2020 Senate campaign, Collins won women voters by three points, according to exit polling.

BANGOR, Maine — On an 89-acre farm in Belmont, Maine, Stacy Leafsong is finishing up a series of intricate flower arrangements for an upcoming wedding. With pops of blue and white, the flowers mirror the colors of the coast, just a short drive to the east.

"I do flowers seven days a week, literally live and breathe flowers all the time," she said with a laugh.

Leafsong is also a progressive organizer, and at the farm last summer, she hosted Graham Platner's first fundraiser for his U.S. Senate campaign. She watched his rise and eventual fall, ending last month when he suspended his campaign over an allegation of rape, which he denies.

Leafsong, a domestic violence survivor, denounced him before then, after growing concerned by previous reporting about Platner's behavior towards women. Now, she's supporting Troy Jackson, the progressive former state senator who Democrats nominated to replace Platner.

Stacy Leafsong was an early Graham Platner supporter. She watched his rise and eventual fall, and is now supporting Troy Jackson.

The race for Senate in Maine was always expected to be one of the most competitive matchups of the midterms. But the Platner scandal adds pressure to Jackson's already daunting task of chipping away at a key source of support for Republican incumbent Susan Collins: Maine women.

"He really needs to speak to the women in Maine, and really convince them that he's going to advocate well for them," Leafsong said. "Women's issues are much more than childcare and abortion."

The power of women voters is clear when looking at Collins' winning coalition in 2020. Women in the state made up nearly 60% of total turnout, according to exit polling, voting for Joe Biden by 23 percentage points. However the same group flipped for Collins, by just three points.

"Women voters in Maine are the majority of voters, and so you have to take them seriously," said Democrat Emily Cain, a former state senator and the previous executive director of Emily's List, an organization that backs women candidates who support abortion rights.

"Independents are almost a third of voters in Maine. But the majority of voters are women who are older," she added. "So the people who decide statewide races typically are independents who are also a majority women."

Democratic officials see flipping Maine this year as a crucial pickup opportunity if the party wants to regain a majority in the Senate, and Collins is the only sitting Republican Senator up for reelection who represents a state President Trump lost in 2024.

But Collins is also no stranger to a tough race, having won in multiple cycles where Democratic presidential candidates have also carried the state. Plus, Republicans have already spent millions on a barrage of ads trying to link Platner to Jackson, according to data from AdImpact, seizing on reports that he has a short temper.

Unlike Platner, Jackson has never been accused of sexual violence towards women. But he has admitted to getting into shouting matches with colleagues during his time as a state lawmaker, something he's apologized for.

However, 2026 does pose a new challenge for Collins, given it's the first time she's back on the ballot since Roe v. Wade was overturned.

Collins has long voiced support for abortion protections, but in 2018, her vote was crucial in confirming Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, expanding a conservative majority that went on to ultimately eliminate the constitutional right to abortion in 2022.

Democrats want to make Collins' vote for Kavanaugh key point of contention in this race. But it's also a topic where Jackson's views have evolved. He initially entered politics as an abortion rights opponent, but shifted left over time and voted to expand access in recent years, post-Roe.

"I'm rock solid on this now, and Susan has been the opposite," Jackson said in an interview with Maine Public Radio last month. "She's made sure that everyday people across this country have a real challenge to get abortion access."

Troy Jackson greets people after being selected as the new Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Maine on July 25, 2026, in Bangor.

Speaking to reporters in June, Collins defended her support for Kavanaugh, saying she does not regret her vote. Her campaign has also pushed back on claims that Jackson is the better advocate on the issue.

"This was a conversion motivated by political convenience and marked a complete reversal of his long-held positions," Collins' campaign communications director Blake Kernen said in a statement.

"In contrast, Senator Collins is a champion for women, and her pro-choice views have never changed."

But this political sore spot may end up coming in second for many voters, who remain primarily motivated to vote because of economic worries.

Diana Kushnar is a Republican candidate running for the Maine House of Representatives. When she's out on the campaign trail, she says, affordability concerns are what's top of mind for voters.

"They're worried about whether they can afford a home – because [of] the rising utility bills – the costs of raising your family and then just the access to health care … and whether their children will have even a reason to stay in Maine," she said.

Kushnar is supporting Collins this fall, but the concerns she raised are shared with many voters on the other side of the political aisle. Though often it's paired with a desire for a change in leadership.

Kelli Brennan volunteered for Troy Jackson's unsuccessful gubernatorial campaign. She sees his Senate bid as "a second chance to get Troy in a position of leadership."

"I think Susan Collins' time is up," said Jackson supporter Kelli Brennan, a nurse and co-president of the Maine State Nurses Association. "I think a lot of women have stuck up for her, and I think a lot of women feel burned by her."

"What we need right now is somebody who understands the working class," she said, adding that from nurses and teachers to single moms, the working class includes women.
