https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/m.title: My Brilliant Career cast reflects on 'defiant' Netflix adaptation
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/m.author: Mawunyo Gbogbo
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Philippa Northeast is the newest Sybylla in Netflix's My Brilliant Career adaptation. (Supplied: Netflix)

My Brilliant Career is a story that has stayed with actress Philippa Northeast for years.

Northeast rediscovered the 1901 Miles Franklin novel as a teenager, after her mother first read it to her when she was a child.

"I was [about] 10, and illiterate," Northeast told ABC News.

"[I was] way too young to be having this book read to [me] … but what it did establish in me from a young age is this is a really important book to my mum."

Northeast says her mother was overcome with emotion when she got the role. (Supplied: Netflix)

Northeast (Territory, The Newsreader) plays Sybylla in the upcoming Netflix series, a young woman who wants to be a writer, while her family is determined to marry her off.

She breaks every convention as she looks for a story that will allow her to write her way to independence.

The tension comes when she falls in love. Will she marry, or risk it all for a creative life?

"And that's been more than iconic; it's so incredibly essential, and that was the case with my mum."

Northeast was speaking to ABC News at an intimate luncheon celebrating the series, which is out on Thursday.

She says when she landed the role of Sybylla, there was one person she knew she had to call straight away.

"And then she rang back later to say that she just had to cry in the car and have her own moment with the information I'd given her."

My Brilliant Career has been adapted for stage and screen before, including Gillian Armstrong's 1979 film starring Judy Davis as Sybylla and Sam Neill as suitor Harry Beecham.

There was an outpouring of tributes when Neill died suddenly last month. He was 78.

In the Netflix adaptation, Harry is played by Christopher Chung (Slow Horses, Blitz).

Christopher Chung takes on the role of Harry Beecham. (Supplied: Netflix)

Kate Mulvany (Hunters, Elvis) takes on the role of Augusta, Harry's aunt, who brings him up when he is orphaned as a boy.

"Sam was a dear friend of mine," Mulvany told ABC News.

"And I had the enormous privilege of calling him when I got the role and saying, 'Hey, I'm playing your aunt, can you believe that?'

Kate Mulvany says she relayed messages between "the two Harrys". (Supplied: Netflix)

Mulvany says the two would send messages to each other, often via her.

"I was the very happy middle person in the Chris Chung/Sam Neill sandwich, getting to relay the messages between the two Harrys, between the two eras," Mulvany said.

"And I'm so sad that Sam won't get to see this iteration of My Brilliant Career, but he was very present in the shooting.

"He was texting constantly and wanting to know all the gossip, and I think he'd be really proud of what Chris brings to Harry Beecham."

Mulvany says the series is "a celebration of rebellion".

"It's got a real rebel heart to it," she says.

"It's got a feminist rebel heart, but every single person has a bit of Sybylla in them, no matter who you are.

Mulvany says in the era of AI, the series tells the story of an artist standing up for her craft. (Supplied: Netflix)

"And in the era of AI, and jobs being taken from artists, this is a pure artist standing up for her craft and saying, 'I want to do this; let me do this.'

Miah Madden (Paper Dolls, The Clearing) plays Betty, a young First Nations woman who is new to the story in this iteration of the narrative.

Miah Madden's character Betty is introduced in the Netflix adaptation. (Supplied: Netflix)

"I think that this series has a lot of potential to be able to reflect a period of Australian history that has been told before, but we are broadening that perspective to include a true reflection of that time," Madden told ABC News.

"And I think that Australian audiences and the Australian population are ready for a story like this.

"I think it's definitely a correction of the original text because I think these perspectives — these First Nations, Chinese, queer perspectives — have always been there and it's wonderful for us to be defiant and showcase those stories."

Shari Sebbens, a stage director and actress (The Sapphires, The Office), is an associate producer on the show and says Liz Doran, who adapted the story for the small screen as a writer and one of the executive producers, was determined to include other cultures and stories.

Shari Sebbens says there's a defiance in the Netflix production. (Supplied: STC/Prudence Upton)

"Liz wanted to make sure there was First Nations representation because I think it's really odd when we tell Australian stories, especially this early — this is set around Federation — and you can't tell that story without First Nations presence or at least acknowledging First Nations absence," Sebbens told ABC News.

"So, in that way I think the defiance in this production lives in the expansion of Miles Franklin's world, which I know when you read the book, people will say there was racism that was of its time, but it's still of this time.

"That racism that existed then is the racism that exists today; it hasn't evolved."

Sybylla is described as a "shockingly modern" young woman. (Supplied: Netflix)

Sebbens says My Brilliant Career still resonates 125 years on because women are still coming up against glass ceilings, no matter their cultural background.

"One hundred and twenty-five years is a long time," Sebbens says.

"It's also a blip in the long line of societies and cultures that have existed, and women's roles have changed so much because the patriarchy decided to take over, but I think that's what it is.

My Brilliant Career will stream on Netflix globally from this Thursday, August 13.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.author: Briana Shepherd
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Cassius Turvey, 15, died after a brutal assault in Perth's north-eastern suburbs in October 2022.  (ABC News: Cason Ho)

Aleesha Gilmore, found not guilty of murdering Perth school boy Cassius Turvey, has avoided an immediate prison term for breaching the terms of her suspended sentence.

Gilmore was convicted of offences she committed in the days leading up to the assault on Cassius Turvey.

She breached the terms of that sentence by driving without a licence, but the Supreme Court said she did not have to immediately go to jail to give her a chance at rehabilitation.

A woman found not guilty of murdering Perth school boy Cassius Turvey has avoided being sent to jail for driving without a licence.

WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains an image of a person who has died, used with the permission of their family.

Cassius Turvey was chased down and beaten with a metal pole while walking with friends after school in Perth's east in October 2022. He died in hospital ten days later.

Aleesha Gilmore stood trial for the 15-year-old's murder along with three other men. She was found not guilty, but was convicted of assaulting a teenager and unlawfully detaining two others in the days before the attack.

Court sketch shows Aleesha Gilmore, in a blue jacket, at the sentencing trial for the murder of Cassius Turvey.  (Supplied: Anne Barnetson)

She was handed a 15-month prison sentence for those offences in June 2025, suspended for two years with strict community conditions.

On Monday, Gilmore appeared before the Supreme Court via video link from a secure location for driving without a licence, an alleged breach of her conditional suspended imprisonment order.

State prosecutor Benjamin Stanwix told the court Gilmore lost her licence in December 2025 after police found she was driving under the influence of alcohol.

The court was told Gilmore blew over 0.08 — with a blood test showing her alcohol level at 0.098.

She was fined and disqualified from holding a licence for seven months at the time, but was convicted in June of driving without a licence and given a further nine-month disqualification.

Warren Pearce says the court ruling went against the intentions of the Act. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

Mr Stanwix told the court even though driving without a licence breaches the terms of a suspended sentence, the state was not asking for an immediate term of imprisonment as that would not give Gilmore the opportunity for rehabilitation.

He said the state did not take that position lightly and told the court he did not want Gilmore to leave with the impression the state was "a soft touch".

Gilmore's lawyer, Simon Freitag, said Gilmore had been following the terms of her suspended sentence, which include attending counselling and taking part in programs.

Mr Freitag said his client had managed to get some cleaning work until they asked for a police check, and was now actively looking for FIFO work.

A memorial plaque for Cassius Turvey in his community of Midland, east of Perth, sits as an enduring reminder of the legacy he left behind: "gentle giant", "huggable teddy bear", and a "young leader".

Chief Justice Peter Quinlan said he was satisfied it would be unjust to order a term of immediate imprisonment, considering Gilmore was half way through her suspended sentence, but that she needed to stay on the "straight and narrow".

He told Gilmore she was not responsible for the death of Cassius Turvey but said her notoriety meant her name would probably always be associated with that.

"I appreciate given your notoriety it makes it more difficult for you to obtain work," he told Gilmore.

"But that's not a reason to give up."

Gilmore was fined $500, to be paid on top of the $1,000 she was already fined for driving without a licence.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Victoria's health watchdog has warned the public to avoid engaging a Melbourne woman for health services, who is charged with trafficking steroids. (ABC Kimberley: Vanessa Mills, file photo)

The Victorian Health Complaints Commissioner has issued a public warning about a Melbourne woman who is alleged to have charged $20,000 for unapproved treatments while pretending to be a doctor.

Assma Samadi was charged by police in July with trafficking steroids, possessing drugs and common assault.

Ms Samadi will next face court on October 19.

Victoria's health watchdog has issued a warning about a Melbourne woman accused of pretending to be a doctor and charging $20,000 to use unapproved medicines to treat a man with a chronic illness.

The state's Health Complaints Commissioner has issued an interim prohibition order against Assma (Sarah) Samadi, banning her from providing any health service in Victoria, alleging she may have contravened the code of conduct under the Health Complaints Act.

The Victorian Health Complaints Commissioner also made a public warning about the case, after an investigation was launched on August 5.

Commissioner Bernice Redley said it was alleged that Ms Samadi, an unregistered health practitioner, offered treatment to an individual she was not qualified to provide and unlawfully supplied unapproved medications to treat a chronic illness.

It's alleged Ms Samadi charged more than $20,000 for the treatments and represented herself as a medical practitioner, the commissioner said.

"The Commissioner reasonably believes that Ms Samadi may have contravened the Code of Conduct as set out in Schedule 2 of the Health Complaints Act 2016, and that it is necessary to publish this warning statement to avoid an imminent and serious risk to the life, health, safety or welfare of a person or the public," a statement from Ms Redley said.

"Members of the public are encouraged not to engage with Ms Samadi in relation to the provision of any general health service."

The interim prohibition order against Ms Samadi will also remain in place.

The Victorian Health Complaints Commissioner has issued an official warning after a woman allegedly provided unapproved medication to a man. (Health Complaints Comissioner)

The health watchdog urged anyone with concerns about the matter to contact the Health Complaints Commissioner on 1300 582 113 or online.

Police charged Ms Samadi last month with trafficking steroids, possessing drugs and common assault in Melbourne's Bayside.

After executing two search warrants, police allege they found a stash of cocaine and significant quantities of prescription medicines including testosterone, synthetic anabolic steroids, painkillers and human growth hormone.

She was granted bail and is set to appear in Moorabbin Magistrates Court on October 19.

Police also arrested a 39-year-old man from Brighton East and he was also charged for the same offences, including two counts of trafficking steroids along with possessing cocaine, a drug of dependence and a schedule 4 poison.

He was granted bail to appear in court on the same date.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/n.title: Nine boys charged with 70 offences over alleged Kimberley crime spree
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/n.author: Ruby Littler
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Police allege a group of nine teenagers were responsible for a string of burglaries and car thefts across Derby. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

Nine boys are facing a total of 70 charges after a string of vehicle thefts in WA's Kimberley.

Derby Police say seven cars were stolen from multiple properties across the town in the early hours of August 7.

Seven boys will face the Derby, Broome and Perth Children's Court at various dates across August, while two others were issued juvenile cautions.

Police have charged nine boys with a combined 70 offences over a string of vehicle thefts in Western Australia's far north.

Police allege the boys trespassed several houses across Derby, 2,200 kilometres north of Perth, between 1am and 4:30am on Friday last week.

The boys allegedly stole a tray-top ute, a Toyota LandCruiser, a quad bike and four motorcycles over the course of the morning.

The group were arrested and all vehicles recovered and returned to the owners.

There were no reports of injuries.

Derby Police arrested the boys after the string of break-ins and thefts in the early hours of August 7. (ABC Kimberley: Erin Parke)

The 70 charges include several counts of stealing and attempting to steal a motor vehicle, as well as trespassing.

Seven of the boys are due to face the Derby, Broome and Perth Children's courts at various dates this month, while two teenagers were issued with cautions.

Derby Police officer-in-charge Nathan Smith said the group had allegedly been the driving force behind a recent spike in offending around the town.

"Every sub-district has certainly bubbles where there's increases in crime and this is just one that's happened in Derby," Senior Sergeant Smith said.

Senior Sergeant Nathan Smith thanked the community for help in reporting and resolving the incidents.  (ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson)

He said the close-knit nature of Derby's community, including residents looking out for each other and being mindful of suspicious behaviour, had played a key role in resolving the incident.

"It's a safe place to live, it's a safe place to come and visit and travel through," Senior Sergeant Smith said.

"We take this very seriously."

Youth crime in the Kimberley has been in the spotlight across the past week, after a viral video of a separate alleged car theft in Kununurra.

A long-awaited on-country youth facility in the Kimberley welcomed its first cohort of young men earlier this year.

The Wala Kooral-bi Centre, 120km south of Derby, offers an on-country diversion program for boys aged 14 to 17.

Eight teenagers have been housed at the facility since May, with the Marlamanu Project offering an alternative to sending juveniles south to Perth's controversy-plagued Banksia Hill Detention Centre.

The Wala Kooral-bi Centre opened this year. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)

"Those community led solutions are the ones that increase our ability to distract and prevent this cohort from continuing this behaviour," Senior Sergeant Smith said.

"We're really supportive of Marlumanu and the work they are doing.

"We want to make sure that's a program that continues to operate because I think it's a needs basis in community."

Shire of Derby-West Kimberley chief executive Tamara Clarkson said the incident was a disappointing one for the town.

"Community safety is obviously a priority of the shire, but it is a police matter," she said.

Tamara Clarkson says incidents like the one last week are not common.  (ABC Kimberley: Anthony Pancia)

"Always ensure that you are locking vehicles, your windows and doors, hiding keys never leaving them available."

Ms Clarkson urged people to report anything concerning to police.

"This is definitely a rarity for Derby," Ms Clarkson said.

"We've worked hard with our community to ensure that safety in priority."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/t.author: Ewa Staszewska and Stephen Dziedzic
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Federal Government

Anthony Albanese on the Bush Deep podcast with host Nikki Osborne.

Anthony Albanese is facing backlash over a gesture involving two melons, amid claims it was in reference to Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's body.

The opposition has called for Mr Albanese to apologise, with cabinet ministers once again defending his track record.

It remains unclear if the prime minister will publicly apologise, with his team issuing a statement to a limited number of outlets.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is facing pressure to apologise to his Japanese counterpart over a gesture he made about two melons she gifted him, which his office insists was not a crude joke.

In an interview last month, Mr Albanese gestured to his chest when recalling the melons during an exchange with Bush Deep podcast host Nikki Osborne, who asked how the fruit had been smuggled into the country.

The incident resurfaced this morning after former Australian ambassador Shingo Yamagami criticised the exchange in The Australian, labelling it "insulting", ignorant and a betrayal of the "close relationship" between Australia and Japan.

Anthony Albanese is facing backlash from another gaffe during his appearance on the Bush Deep podcast last month. (Supplied: YouTube)

The former Ambassador suggested Mr Albanese was making a quip about Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's body, but a spokesperson for Mr Albanese told The Australian, "this assertion is wrong".

The comment has not been supplied to the ABC despite multiple requests.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said it was beneath the office of the prime minister, and demanded Mr Albanese apologise.

"They were insulting, and the prime minister should make a personal apology. He's done it through a statement. I mean, the hypocrisy of Labor and the foreign minister on this topic," Mr Taylor said.

Angus Taylor has called on Anthony Albanese to apologise. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

The gaffe occurred during the same podcast that landed Mr Albanese in hot water when he said he would shag Kylie Minogue during a game of "shag, marry, date". He later apologised for those comments.

While Mr Albanese was condemned by several female parliamentarians at the time, including Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson, the main focus was on Minogue and not Ms Takaichi.

Liberal Deputy Leader Jane Hume added to the criticism, calling the comments "grubby" and "inappropriate".

Senior cabinet ministers have again been forced to defend Mr Albanese's appearance on the podcast.

Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek today deflected criticisms and disagreed with Mr Yamagami's interpretation.

Anthony Albanese made the comments during a game of "shag, marry, date" on the Bush Deep podcast.

"We have an excellent relationship with Japan. Japan is a very important strategic and economic partner … and I think the former ambassador is wrong in his interpretation," she told Sunrise.

Health Minister Mark Butler reiterated Australia's strong economic and security ties with Japan.

"It's very close. It involves constant communication between our two countries, two at the highest level. I know Prime Minister Albanese feels the deepest respect for that relationship," he told reporters.

The federal Transport Minister Catherine King argued the comments were being blown up by the opposition.

While officials may have winced in private, nobody in the Japanese government has publicly commented about Mr Albanese's gaffe.

Ms Takaichi's first visit in May solidified Australia's place as a critical energy partner for Japan, and an increasingly important security partner as well.

When the episode first came out, officials in the Japanese government told the ABC they were not focused on the exchange and that Tokyo would not comment on a minor episode, particularly given the scale of cooperation between the two countries.

The episode has also drawn little attention so far in the Japanese press, aside from one scathing opinion piece in the English-language Japan Times which lambasted Mr Albanese and accused him of rank sexism.

Shingo Yamagami says it shows cultural ignorance and is insulting to the partnership between Japan and Australia. (Perth USAsia Centre: Kelly Pilgrim-Byrne)

But one member of the Australian business community with close links to Japan said the exchange "had absolutely not gone unnoticed" among Japanese elites, even if they were publicly silent about it.

In his criticism, Mr Yamagami pointed out that Ms Takaichi has already copped sexist and derogatory attacks from Chinese state media, but it was not expected from Japan's strategic partner.

Innuendo aside, the former diplomat also highlights that Mr Albanese's comments ignore the cultural significance of crown melons, which are intensely cultivated luxury fruits in Japan.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and his Japanese counterpart Takaichi Sanae agreed to bolster cooperation on energy, defence and critical minerals.

In the face of an "increasingly dangerous" geopolitical climate, he urged the prime minister to show greater focus.

"So, prime minister, please enjoy Japan's sweet and juicy melons without thinking about a woman's anatomy, and instead focus on what our two countries must do together," he said.

Mr Yamagami had a fraught relationship with Labor when he was in Canberra and was particularly angry when Foreign Minister Penny Wong urged him, while she was still in opposition, to pull back his public criticisms of China.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.title: What have we learnt from Origin Energy's data breach?
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.author: Zena Chamas and Dannielle Maguire
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/a.text:
Topic:
Cyber Security

Cybersecurity threats have been increasing lately, but 2025 was the biggest year. (Supplied: Aloshin Evgeniy/Adobe stock)

Three weeks ago, Origin Energy told 900,000 former and current customers that their information had been exposed in a data breach.

The major cybersecurity data leak made headlines and raised the alarm that the threats were becoming more prevalent.

It also showed that anyone with their information online could be vulnerable, according to Curtin University Associate Professor in AI and Cybersecurity, Mihai Lazarescu.

Associate Professor Lazarescu, who has worked in cybersecurity for over 16 years, said whenever anyone put information online, there was a chance it could be compromised.

That included commonly used details, such as email addresses and first and last names.

"Never give your full name and date of birth because that is identifiable evidence," he said.

Origin's breach affected hundreds of thousands of customers, but it wasn't technically the largest.

Australian companies such as Canva, Optus, and Qantas had data breaches that affected millions of customers.

Australian online design tool Canva suffered a data breach impacting 137 million of its users in 2019.

In March 2023, Latitude, the Australian personal loan and financial service provider, was affected by a data breach that impacted more than 14 million people from Australia and New Zealand.

In September 2022, the Optus data breach impacted 9.8 million customers.

In December 2022, Medibank, the Australian health insurance giant, was the victim of a data breach affecting the personal details of 9.7 million customers.

In July 2025, up to 6 million Qantas customers were affected when the Australian airline confirmed a data theft incident that impacted a significant portion of its customer base.

In July 2026, Origin Energy, Australia's largest energy retailer with more than 4.8 million customers, announced that the information of 900,000 current and former customers was accessed during a data security breach.

The information included names, dates of birth, phone numbers, home addresses and email addresses, as well as the last four digits of some credit cards and the last three digits of some bank account numbers.

Associate Professor Lazarescu said the fact that a power company was potentially breached should have been expected, given how easy data could be accessed online.

"It will get worse," he said.

"99 per cent of people have no understanding of how difficult it is to protect data.

"It requires both the technical and administrative aspects of security to be perfect."

He said the only way to be fully protected online was to be "checking all the time", from bank statements to which information was given online.

Recent data from the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) showed most of the leaked customer information in data breaches included contact details, financial details and identity information.

Associate Professor Lazarescu said social media was also one of the easiest ways for criminals to access data.

"You see people posting online with photos with specific locations, timing. These are not secure," he said.

"When you have criminal groups that are very well organised and make a lot of money out of what they do, these are not beginners.

Associate Professor Lazarescu said having data leaked could not only put people at risk of being hacked but, in worst-case scenarios, their data could be sold on the dark web to criminal groups.

"It could create a situation that's expensive and complicated to fix," he said.

He said serious discussion should be taking place that outlined to customers what the risks of data leaking could entail and the potential consequences if security measures failed.

The severity of a data breach depends on the sensitivity of the data and the nature of the exposure, rather than just the total number of people affected.

Charles Sturt University computing professor Yeslam Al-Saggaf said the Origin data breach was "more concerning" than the Canva breach, despite fewer customers being affected.

"The value of data is low as these students don't have credit cards, don't have car loans, mortgages, and don't have driver's licences," Professor Al-Saggaf said.

Energy company Origin has confirmed that there has been unauthorised access and disclosure of some customers' data, a day after it announced it was investigating a "potential" breach.

"Whereas in the Origin data breach financial details of individuals and businesses have been compromised."

He said when individuals' and businesses' financial details were published online, it exposed them to a range of risks, such as losing money through payment redirection attacks and identity theft.

He said businesses and individuals could also face a situation with additional costs and an increase in insurance premiums.

Cyber insurance providers have noted the increase in cyber attacks and, in turn, are raising premiums.

The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) received 1,205 data breach notifications in the 2025 calendar year, representing an 8 per cent increase from 2024, according to OAIC data.

Cyber hacking remains the primary cause of data breaches reported to the OAIC.

Of the data breaches notified in 2025, the majority were attributable to malicious or criminal activity.

Health service providers were the most commonly affected, accounting for 19 per cent of the total.

The Australian government said it had revised its cybersecurity policies to strengthen resilience against nation-state threat actors amid the rise in cyber attacks.

In 2025, the OAIC launched a new Notifiable Data Breaches (NDB) statistics dashboard to keep the public informed on the volume and type of data breaches occurring.

Professor Al-Saggaf said "people are becoming numb to the drama of data breaches", and people who remained naive to cybersecurity were most at risk.

"They happen every day in Australia because Australians are trusting, affluent, speak English, and some are not technically savvy," he said.

"We need to improve our literacy with respect to cybersecurity hygiene practices."

The theft of names, addresses and phone numbers may seem less serious than stolen bank details, but cyber experts say AI is changing what criminals can do with that information.

He advised using a strong, unique password that differed for each account, or using a password manager, to help protect individuals.

He said enabling multi-factor authentication could provide an additional layer of verification, and using secure payment methods on secure websites could also help avoid potential security risks.

But as scammers started to integrate artificial intelligence into their operations, he warned regular security measures would need to be strengthened.

"AI is going to make impersonation more sophisticated, so use more than one method to communicate with your close contacts if they ask for financial assistance, and keep an eye on bank balances and credit card statements," he said.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Battle of Okinawa survivor conveys message of peace through the classroom
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
As U.S. forces advanced across Okinawa’s main island in late May 1945, Kohei Nohara — who was 14 years old at the time — fled his hometown of Haebaru with his relatives, moving ever farther south in a desperate bid to get to safety.

In June this year, 81 years after the end of the Battle of Okinawa in the closing stages of World War II, Nohara visited Haebaru’s Shonan Elementary School, which was built after the war. The now 95-year-old Nohara told his story about how he experienced the fierce ground battle to some 90 fifth graders at the school.

To help students follow Nohara’s journey, teacher Naoya Arakaki projected Google Maps onto a classroom screen.

Arakaki, the fifth grade head teacher, zoomed in on the present-day municipalities of Yaese and Itoman to show the locations where Nohara’s family had fled to.

“This is where Mr. Nohara was,” he told the students, while displaying wartime photographs showing landscapes scarred by relentless shelling.

Arakaki guided the session by turning it into the form of an interview with Nohara, starting off with a question: “What was it like on the battlefield?”

Nohara said the most vivid scene in his memories was when he and his relatives were discovered by American soldiers near Cape Kyan at the southern tip of Okinawa’s main island in June 1945.

“I thought they were about to shoot me to kill,” he said, recalling hearing a sharp metallic click.

The sound, however, was not of a rifle being cocked: It was of a lighter igniting a cigarette that an American soldier had given to one of his uncles.

“At that moment, I realized I had survived,” Nohara said. “I thought, ‘The Americans aren’t going to do anything to us.’”

Before Nohara and his relatives surrendered that day, however, they endured a grueling journey as they made their way south, fleeing through shelling, seeing countless bodies and losing some members of their family.

Nohara’s father was not with them as he had been mobilized into a local defense unit before the ground fighting began in Okinawa. Nohara’s mother and three younger sisters had also evacuated to the northern part of the island, so Nohara stayed behind with his older brother and relatives, sheltering in caves in their community in Haebaru.

Around April 1945, he watched as nearby villages went up in flames.

“So, this is war,” he remembered thinking. “What are we going to do?”

The sound of incoming mortar rounds became a constant source of fear.

By late May, the 32nd Army of the Imperial Japanese Army had decided to withdraw from their headquarters in Shuri — in present-day Naha — to southern Okinawa. The Japanese military moved into areas where civilians had already sought refuge, which drew devastating American attacks that resulted in more civilian casualties.

One rainy day near the end of May, word spread in Nohara’s community that U.S. troops were approaching, so he and his relatives left their hometown and headed south.

Along the way, they passed a large number of corpses.

“I thought that if I was going to die, I’d rather be killed instantly,” Nohara said.

He remembers seeing a small child wandering, crying out for their mother, but no one had the capacity to lend a helping hand. All he could think of was to escape, Nohara said.

In June, the family eventually reached Mabuni, an area in present-day Itoman where some of the war’s bloodiest final battles were fought. There, tragedy struck one after another.

One day, an aunt suffered a severe leg wound from shell fragments and could no longer walk.

“You all go on without me,” the aunt told the rest of them. They had no choice but to leave her behind and never learned what became of her.

Two days later, another shell exploded right in front of the family, causing smoke to engulf the area. A cousin was struck by shrapnel that tore into his abdomen. He died almost instantly, without even a scream.

The following day, Nohara and his relatives were found by American soldiers, and they surrendered.

Nohara later found out about more losses among the people close to him.

One of his younger sisters, who had been evacuated to northern Okinawa, died, possibly from malnutrition. All seven members of a neighboring relative’s household also perished.

As Nohara’s story drew to a close, Arakaki reminded students that war remains a reality in certain parts of the world today.

“Wars are still going on, aren’t they?” the teacher asked the students.

“I know about Gaza,” one child called out.

“War is not somebody else’s matter,” Arakaki said. “I want you to study these things and pass them on so that we can build a more peaceful world.”

At the end of the interview, Arakaki asked Nohara once again for his thoughts on the Battle of Okinawa.

After a pause, Nohara said quietly, “I saw pieces of human flesh caught in trees. I saw countless bodies. War is a terrible thing.”

More than eight decades after the war, Nohara continues to visit the Cornerstone of Peace monument in Itoman with his family to pray for the victims. Every year, he makes his visit around June 23, Okinawa Memorial Day, which marks the end of the Battle of Okinawa.

“I want to pray for those who died and ask them to watch over us as we strive for a peaceful world,” he said softly at his home in Haebaru.

Asked what he thought of Okinawa’s current situation, Nohara said he is concerned about the massive presence of U.S. military facilities on the island.

“If the bases remain concentrated here, Okinawa could become the first target if something happens. I’m against the bases,” he said.

For Arakaki, 46, who leads the peace education program at the school and is a graduate there himself, opportunities such as Nohara’s visit are a reminder of the importance of hearing war experiences firsthand.

Arakaki told his students again that they were listening to “a very precious story” from Nohara.

Since childhood, Arakaki has listened to testimonies of numerous war survivors, including his own grandfather. Those older people — many of whom spoke through tears — have left a lasting impression on the teacher.

Hearing directly from survivors matters, he said, because their choice of words, the tone of their voice and their facial expressions tell their stories.

Even though the clock is ticking, there is still time to hear their stories, he said.

“I want to create these opportunities for children while we can.”

Arakaki also believes that teaching about the Battle of Okinawa requires broad perspectives, including explaining about historical events that led to the war.

Rather than reducing history to simple narratives of blame on either the American or the Japanese military, he tries to convey different perspectives to children so that they will be able to make their own judgment as they grow.

The ultimate goal of peace education, he added, is not only to teach that war is wrong.

“Of course, it is important,” he said. “But I also hope children won’t be trapped in hatred. I want them to love the place where they were born, to appreciate their own country, and to respect other countries as well.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.summary: Kohei Nohara, now 95, fled his hometown of Haebaru with his relatives, moving ever farther south. Nohar's family fled through shelling, seeing countless bodies and losing some members of their family. NOHara says he is concerned about the massive presence of U.S. military facilities on Okinawa.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: Saudi Arabia can break the Houthis’ grip on the Red Sea
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: James Stavridis
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
The Strait of Hormuz isn’t the only Middle Eastern naval choke point under threat: In the Red Sea, vital shipping is being disrupted by an Iranian proxy, the Houthis of Yemen. Now Saudi Arabia, the nation most affected by the Houthis’ threats to commercial traffic, is forming a naval coalition to restore order in the waterway.

What will this new group look like and what are its likely capabilities? Can it be more effective in keeping the Red Sea open than the U.S. has been in protecting shipping through Hormuz? And will America and its European allies inevitably have to play a role?

The civil war in Yemen has been raging for over a decade and Saudi Arabia (as well as the United Arab Emirates) has been intermittently involved in combat against the Houthi rebels. Now Iran wants to put greater pressure on the Saudis, the U.S. and Israel, so it has encouraged the Houthis to blockade and threaten attacks on Saudi supertankers carrying crude oil south through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait or north through the Suez Canal. These ships carry a significant percentage of the world’s petroleum products, up to as much as 15% since the Strait of Hormuz crisis began, and the route handles up to 30% of containerized shipping.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.summary: Saudi Arabia is forming a naval coalition to restore order in the Red Sea. The Houthis of Yemen are threatening to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. has been in the role of protecting shipping through Hormz since the crisis began.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: How the hard reality of climate change hit Europe’s economy this summer
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Balazs Koranyi
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
FRANKFURT, GERMANY – For anyone in Europe who still thought climate change was a problem for future generations, this summer’s sweltering heat waves have brought home the reality that its costly and life-altering economic impacts have already arrived. Record heat and droughts this summer — which scientists say are exacerbated by global warming — have wreaked havoc in power production, shipping and public health systems, while this wildfire season is on track to be Europe’s biggest ever.

Together, the hit to the region’s economy can already be measured in the hundreds of billions of euros, economists and academics estimate. But they warn this is just the beginning, as costs are set to rise ​faster than temperatures.

Climate is changing more rapidly in Europe than on any other continent and the damage is already stretching public finances, setting off wild swings in inflation, redrawing the tourism map, and ‌forcing the ‌bloc to rethink how power is produced and how goods are transported.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: Ben Blanchard
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
TAICHUNG/PENGHU, TAIWAN – Taiwan slowed the mobile internet in a large swathe of the central part of the island on Monday for the first time ​during annual war games, simulating communication disruption in the event of a Chinese attack or ‌natural disaster.

Democratically ‌governed Taiwan, which China claims as its own territory, has long ​lived with the threat of a Chinese invasion and holds air raid drills along with its war games every year, clearing people from the streets for 30 minutes.

During the internet “throttling” ⁠drill, centered on Monday on the major central metropolis of Taichung, only basic mobile phone services worked, though ⁠key services, from ATMs and traffic signals, were not affected, and neither were landlines nor fixed internet services.

Air raid sirens rang out in Taichung and people ​cleared the streets from 2:30 p.m. The government has ⁠widely flagged the drill, sending on Friday afternoon a text message alert to mobile phones across Taiwan in both Chinese and English ⁠and posting details on ​social media.

Northern Taiwan, including the capital Taipei, will see the same ​exercise on Thursday.

Taiwan’s government rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims, saying only ​the island’s ‌people can decide their future.

Earlier on Monday, Taiwan’s military simulated repelling a Chinese air landing assault on the strategically vital Penghu Islands. The 10-day Han Kuang exercise kicked off last week, rehearsing various scenarios should China, which views democratically governed Taiwan as its own ‌territory, ever make good on threats to try and seize the island by force.

Reuters was given rare access to the exercise, observing ground troops loading tank ammunition and taking up firing positions in darkness before the drill began.

Troops from the First Theatre Command opened fire in the pre-dawn hours on ​a ​beach in Penghu, which sits in the Taiwan Strait, with M60A3 tanks, ​various artillery pieces and anti-aircraft guns.

The troops were combining to form what the military called ⁠a “multi-layered” defense against a simulated enemy attempting a rapid coastal landing.

Penghu, which sits closer to the coast of the main island of Taiwan than to China, is seen by Taiwanese strategists as a potential first target for Beijing, which could try and take ​the islands and use them as a base to attack Taiwan with missiles and drones. Reservists from Penghu took part in the exercise, part of their 14-day training program as Taiwan’s military works to better integrate reserve forces into its operational planning and make its preparations more realistic.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.summary: Taiwan slowed the mobile internet in a large swathe of the central part of the island on Monday for the first time during annual war games. Only basic mobile phone services worked, though ⁠key services, from ATMs and traffic signals, were not affected.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: How disinformation on X imperils Japan’s democracy
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: Stephen R. Nagy
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
Today’s Indo-Pacific is hyperconnected. Information is no longer merely a medium for public discourse. It has become a strategic battlespace between authoritarian and democratic states. Across democratic societies, the weaponization of false narratives threatens the fundamental consensus required for self-governance. Arguably, nowhere is this vulnerability more acute and yet so dangerously underappreciated than in Japan.

To understand the scope of the threat, one must first establish conceptual clarity. As Kyoko Kuwahara, a leading scholar on foreign interference and information warfare at the Japan Institute of International Affairs, has argued, we must distinguish between “fake news” and “disinformation.” Fake news often refers to inaccurate or sensationalized reporting, sometimes born of carelessness or commercial clickbait. Disinformation, by contrast, is a deliberate, coordinated and covert effort to propagate falsehoods with the intent to deceive, polarize and manipulate public perception. It is not an accident of the digital age; it is a weapon of political warfare.

On X (formerly Twitter), this weapon is deployed against the Japanese public daily. Consider three recent, illustrative examples that reveal the mechanics of modern digital manipulation.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.summary: Today's Indo-Pacific is hyperconnected, says author Kyoko Kuwahara. It has become a strategic battlespace between authoritarian and democratic states, she says.

Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola said his side is unable to ⁠sustain the required level of performance after it lost 3-2 to Monaco in a friendly at Anfield on Sunday.

Liverpool squandered a two-goal advantage for the second straight game after losing 4-2 to Leeds ​United earlier this month, raising concerns about its readiness ‌ahead ‌of its Premier League opener against Newcastle United ​on Aug. 23.

“We played really good (in the) first half, especially the first 30 minutes, but right now probably we don’t ⁠have much more in terms of the level required to play like ⁠this,” Iraola told the club’s TV channel.

“We won the first two games but the last two, ​we cannot sustain the level ⁠that we want for all the game. As soon as we have made some changes ⁠they start ​to get tired, we cannot sustain that level, ​so we have work to do.”

Captain Virgil van ​Dijk, goalkeeper ‌Alisson Becker and winger Cody Gakpo were all making their first appearances since the World Cup.

“The problem is right now probably they don’t have the energy for 90 ‌minutes, and they start to get tired,” said Iraola, who joined Liverpool in June after Arne Slot was sacked.

“It will take time with them, we need more training with them. But we ​can ​take a lot of positives, but also a ​lot of negatives from today.”

Iraola also said they were taking ⁠a cautious approach with new signing Jeremy Jacquet, who suffered a shoulder injury in February and has recently been troubled by a knee issue.

“We were in doubt whether ​to put him (in the squad) today, we decided not but he should be fine for the next one. It is taking a little bit more time than we expected,” he said.

AYASE, KANAGAWA PREF. – The Maritime Self-Defense Force’s P-1 patrol aircraft has left the Atsugi air base in Kanagawa Prefecture for deployment to Djibouti to take part in an anti-piracy mission.

This is the first time the P-1, Japan’s first domestically built patrol aircraft, has taken part in an overseas mission. It will replace the P-3C patrol aircraft.

The MSDF has been deploying personnel for the anti-piracy mission in the Gulf of Aden off the coast of Somalia since 2009, and the latest dispatch marks the 60th such deployment.

About 50 personnel are scheduled to serve on a three-month mission to conduct surveillance and monitoring activities using the P-1 in place of the aging P-3C aircraft.

The P-1 entered service in 2013. Unlike the propeller-driven P-3C, it is equipped with four turbofan jet engines. As of the end of March this year, the MSDF had taken delivery of 40 P-1s.

After leaving Japan on Monday via the Naha air base in Okinawa Prefecture, the P-1 will arrive in Djibouti on Wednesday.

In a speech at a departure ceremony Sunday, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said he is confident that the new personnel will steadily carry out their duties.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Post-quake crime and scams compound misery for Kumamoto residents
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
Crimes and unscrupulous business practices taking advantage of the powerful earthquake that struck Kumamoto Prefecture are adding to the hardships faced by residents reeling from the disaster.

Suspicious individuals have been spotted repeatedly around damaged homes and evacuation shelters, prompting police forces around the country to send more than 300 officers in special units to patrol affected areas. The Kumamoto Prefectural Police department has also stepped up security, including by installing additional surveillance cameras.

In the town of Hikawa, which saw shaking at the highest level of 7 on Japan’s seismic intensity scale, a woman in her 70s returned home from an evacuation site to find that the window frames of her house, which had been completely destroyed, appeared to have been deliberately removed.

“I wonder if someone got into the house looking for valuables. Some people in the neighborhood have even pitched tents so they can keep watch over their homes and prevent burglaries,” she said.

In the city of Kamiamakusa, police arrested a 47-year-old unemployed man from the city of Amakusa on Saturday on suspicion of stealing an outdoor air-conditioning unit from the home of a 44-year-old company employee who had evacuated the house and was sleeping in his vehicle.

The suspect has admitted to the allegation, telling investigators, “I was short of money and intended to sell it.”

Municipalities in disaster-hit areas have also received multiple reports of suspicious people visiting damaged homes and evacuation centers while claiming to be water utility workers, psychological counselors and other professionals.

A 48-year-old female company employee in Hikawa said a suspicious man and woman came to her home claiming to represent a water-heater company. They left after a male relative answered the door.

“The woman was wearing heavy makeup and didn’t look like someone from a legitimate company. If this was a fraudulent sales scheme, it’s unforgivable,” she said.

After the 2016 Kumamoto earthquakes, inspection scams became widespread, with operators offering to inspect damaged homes before pressuring residents into expensive repair contracts.

Authorities are again receiving complaints from disaster-stricken areas about problems involving home repairs following the latest earthquake.

“If something seems suspicious, contact the Consumer Hotline at 188 as soon as possible,” the Consumer Affairs Agency said.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.summary: Police have stepped up security in areas of Kumamoto Prefecture. Suspicious individuals have been spotted around damaged homes and evacuation shelters. Police have sent more than 300 officers in special units to patrol affected areas.

Tropical Storm Chan-hom, currently located in the Pacific, is expected to make landfall in the northern Kanto region sometime from late Tuesday through early Wednesday, bringing strong wind and heavy rain to the area.

The storm is heading northwest at 25 kilometers per hour and is forecast to make landfall in Ibaraki and Fukushima prefectures, which would be the first storm to make landfall in either prefecture.

The Japan Meteorological Agency said Monday that it is highly likely to issue warnings for heavy rain, strong winds and landslides in Fukushima Prefecture for Tuesday, urging local residents and tourists heading to the region during the Bon holiday to be on alert.

The storm is expected to cause up to 40 millimeters of rain per hour on Tuesday in the Tohoku region, the JMA said, adding that it will cause maximum gust wind of 30 meters per second, or 108 kilometers per hour.

According to the JMA, between 30 and 50 millimeters per hour will make it feel as if it were raining “buckets.”

Chan-hom, the season’s 15th storm, is expected to pass through the mainland and to the Sea of Japan, where it is likely to be downgraded to a tropical depression.

All Nippon Airways said that its flights in and out of Haneda, Narita, Fukushima and Sendai airports might be affected due to the weather, while Japan Airlines did not announce any potential impacts on operations. No scheduling changes were announced by operator East Japan Railway for the Tohoku Shinkansen or the Yamagata Shinkansen lines, both of which pass through Fukushima Prefecture.

Ferries operating between Oarai in Ibaraki Prefecture and Tomakomai, Hokkaido, will be canceled on Tuesday and Wednesday, operator MOL Sunflower said.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Sony and TSMC to invest ¥1 trillion in joint chip plant in Japan
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Takashi Mochizuki
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Sony Group and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. are in talks to spend a combined ¥1 trillion ($6.4 billion) on their planned joint factory in Japan, according to a person familiar with the plans.

The Japanese company’s chip arm Sony Semiconductor Solutions and TSMC are partnering on next-generation image sensors for robots and cars. The factory will begin production in 2029, the person said, asking not to be named because the talks are private. No time frame was given for the investment under discussion, they said.

Representatives of Sony and TSMC did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In May, the two partners announced preliminary talks to build new production lines and development facilities within Sony’s existing image sensor factory in Kumamoto Prefecture.

“This is a virtually risk-free investment for Sony and TSMC,” Toyo Research Advice analyst Hideki Yasuda said. The joint venture lowers Sony’s burden in an arena that requires big capital spending to stay relevant, while securing steady revenue for TSMC, he said.

The Japanese company’s shares rose as much as 2.2%, while TSMC’s gained 1.7% on Monday.

The investment under discussion, which was earlier reported by the Nikkei, is the latest in Sony’s transition toward a more asset-light approach with its image sensor operations. The company has been focusing more of its resources on intellectual property like music distribution rights, film and video game franchises.

Sony, which is a minority shareholder in TSMC’s chipmaking site in the region, will be the controlling shareholder of the new joint venture.

The Tokyo-based company has supplied premium image sensors to the likes of Apple, Huawei Technologies and Samsung Electronics. It has in recent times sought to expand its sensing business into applications in cars and robotics.

Japan’s government will consider providing financial support to the venture, Trade Minister Ryosei Akazawa said.

The company's chip arm Sony Semiconduct Solutions and TSMC are partnering on next-generation image sensors for robots and cars. The factory will begin production in 2029

https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/southeast.title: Philippines floods, landslides, kill at least 12, 8 missing
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/southeast.author: Bloomberg
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/southeast.text:
Over 500,000 people are affected across 33 provinces as monsoon rains batter the main island, Luzon, including the nation’s capital, Manila

Landslides and floods caused by non-stop monsoon rains have killed at least 12 people in the Philippines, while eight more were missing and thirteen injured, authorities said.

More than half a million people in 33 provinces have been affected by the southwest monsoon that has been enhanced by two tropical cyclones, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council.

The agency also reported hundreds of damaged homes and infrastructure, with about 98,000 displaced from their homes.

Tens of thousands were evacuated to hundreds of government-run emergency shelters, Laurence Mina of the government’s Office of Civil Defence said.

The deaths were primarily recorded in the provinces of Benguet, Rizal and Batangas, on the nation’s main island, Luzon.

In its mountainous city of Baguio, four people died and six others were missing after a landslide buried several houses, its public information office said in a Facebook post.

A frantic search for the missing was continuing on Monday despite intermittent rain.

Three people were dug out alive by rescuers and taken to hospital, Baguio officials said.

Around 150 rescuers were working on rotation as search and retrieval operation continues, it said, adding that a dozen other landslide incidents were monitored in Baguio amid continued heavy rain.

Other causes of death included electrocution and drowning.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr on Monday ordered government workers to work from home, and officials to implement alternative learning modes for schools in Metro Manila and more than a dozen provinces as heavy rainfall flooded towns and major thoroughfares.

Water reached waist height in some parts. Ferry services were disrupted in affected regions. The coastguard said operations had been suspended at 20 ports in the central and eastern Philippines.

The country’s weather service forecast further heavy rainfall.

Tropical Storm Dolphin, which dumped heavy rain in eastern China, did not directly hit the Philippines but helped to intensify seasonal monsoon rains that set off flooding and landslides.

Additional reporting by dpa, Associated Press

More than 500,000 people are affected across 33 provinces as monsoon rains batter the main island, Luzon. The floods and landslides have killed at least 12 people in the Philippines.

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/heal.title: Hong Kong eyes licensing for livestock in New Territories amid urban push
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/heal.author: Leopold Chen
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/heal.text:
Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department seeks to extend licensing requirement for goats, sheep and cattle to entire city

Hong Kong residents raising goats, sheep and cattle in the New Territories will need a licence under a proposed regulation which aims to reduce nuisance and hygiene problems affecting neighbours, amid the acceleration of urban development under projects such as the Northern Metropolis.

The plan was revealed in an Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) document, scheduled to be discussed at the Yuen Long District Council on Tuesday, in which the department sought to extend the licensing requirement for raising goats, sheep and cattle to the entire city.

“Currently, the New Territories accounts for over half of Hong Kong’s total population, and many areas within the region have become highly urbanised, leaving no distinct boundary with urban areas. Treating the New Territories purely as a rural area without regulating animal-keeping activities is no longer appropriate,” the department said.

Under current regulations, residents must obtain a licence from the department to keep these animals in Kowloon and Hong Kong Island, but this requirement does not apply in the New Territories.

“The department frequently receives complaints from the public regarding goat-keeping in the New Territories. These include nuisance caused to nearby residents during grazing, environmental hygiene issues arising from animal waste, and even suspected illegal slaughtering and sale of goat meat, posing environmental hygiene and food safety risks,” it said.

It added that tighter regulation was also necessary in light of increasing rural-urban interaction driven by the government’s Northern Metropolis megaproject, which aims to transform 30,000 hectares of land bordering mainland China into a technology and housing hub.

According to the department’s 2025 survey, the New Territories was home to 2,500 to 3,000 raised goats, mostly concentrated in Yuen Long, Tuen Mun and North districts, while over 130 cattle were raised in the North district.

Under the proposed regime, residents applying for licences to raise these animals in the New Territories would have to meet a range of requirements covering buildings, minimum living space for each animal, waste disposal and farming activities.

The department may also impose additional conditions on public health, biosecurity measures, professional veterinary supervision and animal welfare on each licence, according to the paper.

Separately, some volunteers and charities proactively monitor the condition of buffaloes living in the New Territories and, in some cases, provide them with food.

https://www.scmp.com/plus/news/china/dip.title: ‘Islamic Nato’ may create China opening in Middle East
https://www.scmp.com/plus/news/china/dip.author: Brian Rhoads,Raymond Ma
https://www.scmp.com/plus/news/china/dip.text:
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement stipulates that “any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all”, the three countries said in a joint statement. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the deal in Mecca on Friday.

Named after Islam’s holiest city, the pact brings together Turkey’s military – the second-largest in Nato – Saudi Arabia’s financial muscle and Pakistan’s nuclear capabilities at a time when US President Donald Trump’s war on Iran and “America First” policies have upended long-standing confidence in US security guarantees. It also unites three majority Sunni Muslim countries, two of which border majority-Shia Muslim Iran.

Other states could join the alliance, potentially starting with Egypt, according to Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan.

Untested pact: None of this guarantees the agreement will hold under real pressure. Mutual-defence clauses are tested only when war actually spreads, and how Riyadh, Ankara, and Islamabad would interpret their obligations if one of them comes under attack directly remains, for now, untested. What is not in doubt is that three of the Muslim world’s most consequential states have decided the moment called for more than statements of solidarity. They wanted something written down. (TRT World, Turkey)

Cohesion shortage: The best the US and its allies can do is fortify military capabilities and bonds of cooperation. Yet while military spending is rising throughout the democratic world, strategic cohesion is plummeting – along with faith in American competence and leadership. The costs of that decline only rise as autocratic convergence becomes more pronounced. (Bloomberg Opinion)

In tension: But its founding premise, hedging against waning confidence in US protection, is itself an implicit vote of no confidence that Washington cannot ignore, particularly given Turkey’s simultaneous Nato membership. Beijing and Moscow … have structural reasons to welcome any dilution of sole US centrality in Gulf security – China through its deep Saudi energy ties and [China-Pakistan Economic Corridor] relationship with Pakistan, Russia through its own Turkey and Gulf-adjacent diplomatic investments. Neither needs to lift a finger to benefit from a more multipolar Gulf security order. (Eurasia Review)

Burden-sharing: I would resist reading this as evidence of a post-American Middle East, just as I would caution against premature claims of an emerging “Muslim Nato”. If anything, it fits the broader US preference for greater regional burden-sharing, regional powers assuming more responsibility for deterrence and security while remaining embedded, to different degrees, within a US-centred security architecture. At the same time, it aligns with the ‘regional solutions to regional problems’ approach long advocated by Ankara. (Burcu Ozcelik, Royal United Services Institute, on x.com)

Policy divergence: Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad may coordinate policies that diverge from Washington’s preferences on Iran, Israel, China or the use of force. Turkey’s membership in Nato also raises practical questions about intelligence protection, interoperability and competing consultation obligations. The United States should engage the pact rather than dismiss it, while pressing for clear deconfliction procedures and transparency about command structures, weapons integration and possible expansion. (Lowy Institute)

The US war on Iran is creating unexpected diplomatic dividends for China, with the Mecca security pact being a case in point.

New defence cooperation between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey reflects growing concerns about the reliability of US military commitments around the world, particularly in the Middle East. It also creates a chance for China to strengthen ties, raise its global influence and boost defence exports, especially as the new group includes Pakistan. The South Asian country is already a major buyer of Chinese equipment, such as J-10 fighter jets.

A shift from a US-dominated Middle East towards a more multipolar one is something that China will welcome. The country has been building ties in the region for years in search of oil supplies and trade opportunities. President Xi Jinping visited Riyadh in December 2022, and hosted Arab nations in a cooperation forum in Beijing in May 2024. More recently, Vice-Premier Han Zheng met Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud at the end of June.

The new Mecca agreement potentially lessens US influence in the Middle East by giving Saudi Arabia alternative defence guarantees. The energy giant seemingly now has commitments from nuclear-armed Pakistan and Turkey, which boasts Nato’s largest military behind that of the US. That suggests that the kingdom is no longer quite so reliant on the US.

There is also some weight behind these defence pledges. All three of the Mecca group are leading middleweight nations in defence terms, even if they trail far behind global leaders the US, China and Russia. Turkey has about 355,000 active duty troops, 378,000 reservists, 237 F-16 Fighting Falcon aircraft, a fleet of UH-60 Black Hawk helicopters, and a sizeable navy including 13 submarines, according to open-source database GlobalMilitary.net. It ranks Turkey’s military as the ninth-strongest worldwide, with Saudi Arabia 14th and Pakistan in 16th. Much of Pakistan’s strength is focused on deterring India.

The Mecca deal sounds a bit like Nato, with a declaration that an attack on one member is an attack on all of them. Comparisons quickly dwindle after that. Nato has an integrated military headquarters, unified command systems and joint forces assigned to the alliance. The Mecca pact lacks all those. Its members’ resources are also a pale shadow of those available to Nato, which boasts 32 members, including the huge US military. That’s understandable given the Mecca group’s so far limited membership and Nato’s 80-year head start.

Still, the fledgling arrangement counts for something – if not simply because three major Muslim powers are bolstering their own security in the face of angst about the fraying American defence umbrella. President Trump has pursued an “America first” agenda and demanded US partners ante up defence spending since returning to office in 2025.

Trump’s war on Iran has added further tensions, with Gulf states complaining about a lack of consultation. Saudi Arabia, other Middle East nations and Turkey have also come under direct attack by Iranian missiles. Still, efforts at security cooperation predate the war. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a mutual defence agreement in September. This led to Pakistan deploying fighters and support jets to Saudi Arabia’s King Abdulaziz Air Base in April.

Questions about the new Mecca pact start with what it really entails, particularly given the lack of a published text. What commitments have the countries actually made if one of them is attacked militarily? Are they obliged to deploy troops, for instance, or can they respond in other ways? What about a non-military attack, such as a cyber strike or an airspace incursion? These are issues that Nato wrestles with, and are sure to affect the new grouping as well.

Another question is the response to attacks by non-state actors. This is particularly pertinent with Saudi Arabia confronting Houthi forces in Yemen that menace shipping in the Red Sea. It’s also unclear whether Pakistan will extend its nuclear umbrella to cover its new allies.

Furthermore, the new alliance doesn’t mark a full break with the US. Turkey remains part of Nato and Saudi Arabia will continue to host major US bases. Indeed, arguably, the grouping represents exactly the sort of self-reliance and burden-sharing that the Trump administration has been calling for.

Still, optimists in Beijing will see any gap between the US and allies, particularly in a key region such as the Middle East, as an opportunity to exploit.

https://www.dw.com/en/ukrainian-drone-at.text:
Ukraine launched hundreds of drones at targets inside Russia, according to Russian officials. The strikes killed at least 12 people in one of Kyiv's deadliest attacks since the Russian invasion began over four years ago.

A Ukrainian drone attack on the city of Nizhnekamsk, located in an energy-rich Tatarstan region of central Russia, killed at least a dozen people and wounded 39 more, according to a local press service statement issued Monday.

Over 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) from the Russian-Ukrainian border, the region has many major oil refineries that Kyiv has targeted in recent strikes as both sides increase long-range attacks on infrastructure.

The United Nations said such attacks have led to a jump in civilian casualties in Russia and Ukraine.

Unspecified industrial and civilian targets had been hit in Monday's strike, Radmir Belyayev, the mayor of Nizhnekamsk, said in a statement on Telegram.

The Ukrainian strikes on refineries have led to some fuel shortages and reduced Russia's oil-refining capacity.

Russia has also regularly fired missiles, glide bombs and drones hitting civilian areas in Ukraine and causing thousands of civilian casualties, according to the United Nations.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the campaign aims to force Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiations to end the more than 4-year-old full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"We do deliver entirely justified responses, and every Russian strike will be met with our response. Russia's war will be felt more and more at their own home — in Russia," Zelenskyy said late Sunday in a social media post.

Ukraine's air force said Russia fired 126 drones in its overnight attack.

The Russian Defense Ministry said it shot down 456 Ukrainian drones fired overnight. The ministry, however, does not include how many drones or missiles reach their targets or how many were intercepted in the Tatarstan region.

Near the front line in Ukraine, a Russian artillery strike killed five people in a village in the northeastern Kharkiv region, Ukrainian officials said.

"On August 10, Russian forces carried out a massive artillery strike on the residential area of the village of Bugaivka in the Chuguiv district. Various houses were destroyed as a result of the enemy attack. Five people were killed," the regional prosecutor's office said in a statement on Telegram.

The suspected shooter is reportedly a former lawmaker who fired several shots at a senior official at a government office. The incident came just days after Thailand's deadliest shooting in nearly four years.

Thai Police arrested a suspected gunman — a former lawmaker — after he allegedly fired shots at a local government office at the outskirts of Bangkok, on Monday morning.

The shooter fired shots at a senior provincial officer and his driver, Nonthaburi police chief Major Dejrapee Kongdee told Reuters news agency.

Meanwhile, the Bangkok Post reported that the provincial administration's president, Thongchai Yenprasert, had died in the shooting.

As per the report, the suspected shooter forced his way into the government office at about 11 a.m. local time (0400 GMT) and fired several shots at Thongchai. The official was given cardiopulmonary resuscitation at the scene befoe being rushed to a local hospital where he was declared dead.

This comes just days after a 14-year-old's shooting rampage, first at his home and then at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, left nine people dead and over 20 injured. That incident was Thailand's deadliest mass shooting in nearly four years.

Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul had reiterated his intention to tighten gun control laws in the wake of the shooting. The southeast Asian country's current gun laws do not include mental health screenings and allows people as young as 20 to hold guns.

Thailand had around 15 guns per 100 ⁠residents, the highest rate in Southeast Asia ​by a wide margin, according to a 2017 estimate by the Small Arms Survey.

https://www.dw.com/en/india-news-kerala-.title: India news: Kerala arrest highlights online harassment of women at CJP protest
https://www.dw.com/en/india-news-kerala-.text:
A right-wing activist was arrested over alleged remarks that women attending the CJP protests "enjoy" sexual assault as female demonstrators face a wider online harassment campaign. DW has more.

Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Monday, August 10:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Mumbai-based model Rhiya Ahir, who gained attention after standing in front of a police van carrying protesters during last month's Cockroach Janta Party-led demonstrations, has spoken about facing online abuse and threats following the protest.

In an interview with DW's Shalu Yadav, Ahir said the attention had come at a "heavy price" of online trolling and harassment, adding that women should be able to express their views without being targeted.

She referred to comments made about women protesters, including comments that they "should be raped" and would "enjoy it," saying such remarks could influence others and should not be allowed to go unchallenged.

"I read one comment saying 'we are going to rip you apart from the middle. And nobody's going to come to lay flowers on your grave,'" she said.

Ahir described the attacks as "criminal."

"I will not let it slide," she said. "I will not let them feel that they can sit behind their blank screens and feel so powerful by belittling other people.

Her comments come amid a wider online campaign targeting women who took part in the CJP-led protests, with reports of fake and AI-manipulated images, doxxing and threats against participants.

An activist who considers himself a right-wing "political commentator" was arrested in the southern state of Kerala on Sunday over remarks he allegedly made about the women at the Cockroach Janta Party-led student protests last month, media reports said.

The case was registered following a complaint alleging that videos on TG Mohandas' YouTube channel, Pathrika, were intended to disturb public order and create fear and unrest.

According to reports, in the videos, Mohandas allegedly said the Delhi protests could lead to gang rape and claimed that women attending it "like rape" and that some "enjoy being raped."

He also called for police to open fire at protesters.

News channel NDTV reported that Mohandas is a former member of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). However, the RSS has denied any association with the commentator.

The BJP on Monday criticized the arrest as "discriminatory" and accused the Kerala government of attempting to divert attention from other issues, reports said.

The development comes amid an online campaign targeting women who took part in CJP-led student protests. The countrywide stir ended last month with the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Multiple reports indicate that young women involved in the movement are facing severe online harassment. They have been targeted with fake and AI-manipulated images, as well as a barrage of online abuse, including assault threats.

Additionally, their phone numbers and home addresses have been leaked online alongside targeted attacks against their family members.

Hello! This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi Studio bringing you the latest updates from across India.

Female protesters who took part in Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) demonstrations against the government are facing harassment and doxxing. In the latest development, a right-wing activist was arrested in the southern state of Kerala for allegedly posting a video saying that those attending the protests "like rape."
