On Wednesday, at the end of the day in London, Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis had some news for employees.

Hassabis, DeepMind’s co-founder and the lab’s longtime steward, was giving up the CEO title and moving to a chairman role, they said. Minutes later, the news broke that long-time chief scientist Jeff Dean and several other prominent researchers were leaving the company.

Staff in DeepMind’s London office were shocked. They had questions. Was the move a promotion or a demotion? Would Hassabis retain real influence over DeepMind’s direction? And was Google finalizing a power shift from the London lab to its Mountain View headquarters?

One DeepMind engineer familiar with internal reaction told Fortune employees were “very mixed” on what the reshuffle meant, with some wondering whether the chairman role would ultimately end with Hassabis phased entirely out of the company.

In reality, the shock exit was just the tip of the iceberg of what has been a difficult year for Google DeepMind. Within the lab, three current and one former employee told Fortune tensions were already simmering. Delayed models, high-profile exits of talent, and a very public fight with its own staff over controversial defense contracts had left insiders wondering if Google had lost its way in the AI race.

Once a frontrunner, the company has recently ceded ground to rivals, especially OpenAI and Anthropic. This was most evident in delays around the release of the company’s Gemini 3.5 Pro model, which has missed three release deadlines in recent months. Three of the DeepMind engineers who talked to Fortune blamed the delays on the company failing to prioritize AI coding abilities.

And now, for the second time in just four years, the company is again playing catch-up.

Google DeepMind is struggling to retain its technical edge, keep hold of top researchers, and contain an employee revolt over its defense work. Pichai’s reshuffle—which employees say shifts power back to Mountain View and pulls DeepMind closer to Google proper—arrives at a critical moment for the company. But it’s also a gamble. Will new leadership restore Google’s AI momentum, or worsen internal tensions at crucial moments in the AI race?

In his note to staff on Wednesday, Hassabis said that he was handing over day-to-day operational responsibilities for the lab to allow him the “time and space to focus on the big picture and help influence what is to come to the best of my ability.”

Instead of selecting a new CEO for DeepMind, however, Pichai announced that DeepMind’s chief technology officer, Koray Kavukcuoglu, was taking over day-to-day operations as senior vice president, reporting directly to him rather than holding a standalone DeepMind CEO title. Kavukcuoglu, unlike London-based Hassabis, works 6,000 miles away, in the California offices in Mountain View. A Google spokesperson said that Hassabis was moving into an expanded role to focus on advancing science and long-term strategy.

Three DeepMind engineers, who asked for anonymity to discuss company matters, told Fortune this represents a broader structural change and a shifting of power to Mountain View, where Google is headquartered, and away from London, where DeepMind was originally founded.

Losing Hassabis as a CEO and not getting a new one, they said, also means the lab is being somewhat absorbed into the rest of the company and losing some of its independence. The first engineer called it a “small step, but gradually continuing the trend.”

“A lot of people are quite upset by it,” they said. “Both Demis exiting, and losing some of the separation from Alphabet and identity as DeepMind.”

For months, there had been rumors of a significant power shift to California, and concerns about the message that change would send to the London-based staff. Workers describe an ongoing “background pressure” of things moving to Mountain View and several prominent London-based engineers, including AlphaFold veterans John Jumper, Jonas Adler, and Alexander Pritzel, recently exited the company to join Anthropic.

The company had also been slowly moving reporting lines away from Hassabis for a while, according to the second engineer.

A Google spokesperson disputed the characterization that power was shifting to Mountain View and said Google DeepMind remained committed to its London presence. The spokesperson said Hassabis, along with much of Google DeepMind’s leadership, would remain based in the London office. They added that DeepMind would retain separate leadership and research autonomy under Kavukcuoglu.

From a commercial perspective, there may be an argument that things need to change, especially if the company is having issues shipping models in an increasingly competitive environment. Mountain View may well have run out of patience and want a tighter grip on its AI crown jewel.

“It’s very clear that they’re having a big internal debacle,” the second engineer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said. “This might have also contributed to speeding up some of these power shifts. Generally in Google, when something is significantly underperforming or not working, their solution is to just do a huge reorg, a reallocation of compute and priorities to try and fix it.”

This isn’t the first time Google has hit a stumbling block on its AI journey.

Back in late 2022, the company famously declared a “code-red” following the launch of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, fearing the impact on its core search business. Since then, its race to catch up has been somewhat successful. Its Gemini 3 model outperformed all its rivals and pushed OpenAI to declare its own “code-red” in late 2025, as Gemini’s benchmark gains and rapid user growth put pressure on ChatGPT’s lead.

But since then, things appear to have gone in the wrong direction.

Google’s models are currently not competitive with the bleeding edge of the U.S. frontier on intelligence and coding benchmarks. Even some open-source Chinese efforts are also outshining the tech giant.

Gemini 3.5 Pro was supposed to be Google’s next big answer to advanced models such as Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT 5.6. Unveiled at the company’s flagship I/O conference in May with a promise to ship “next month,” it missed that June target and another mid-July date. The company headed into August with the model still unreleased, even as Google shipped a trio of smaller Flash models around it and claimed it had already begun training Gemini 4.

Micah Hill-Smith, co-founder and CEO of independent benchmarking company Artificial Analysis, told Fortune that Gemini 3.6 Flash, the strongest model Google has shipped, now sits behind models from Anthropic, OpenAI, one or two leading Chinese labs, xAI, and Meta on his firm’s intelligence index, which measures overall performance of AI models.

“For a brief moment, we actually did have [Google’s] model on top as the smartest model in the world. Right now, it’s fair to say that [model] from Google is less compelling,” he said.

Many of the mistakes that led to this started last summer, when the company failed to prioritize the development of Gemini’s coding abilities, according to a third engineer. Google, they said, was preoccupied with protecting its search traffic and beating OpenAI on chat, while rivals were running ahead on agentic and coding capabilities. Google models now significantly lag rivals on coding agent benchmarks, according to Hill-Smith.

A Google spokesperson said Gemini 3.5 Pro was currently in testing and that the DeepMind team was already working on its next generation of models. The spokesperson acknowledged that the company needed to improve in coding and agentic capabilities, but said its teams were focused on that work.

Google perhaps failed to predict that coding abilities would play such a major role in consumer products just a year later. Developer tools such as Claude Code or OpenAI’s Codex, are now underpinning a new wave of consumer and general-use products. They include Anthropic’s Cowork—an agentic tool built on the same underlying technology as Claude Code that lets non-developers hand off multi-step knowledge work, like organizing files or drafting documents, rather than writing code—and OpenAI’s superapp, positioned as a one-stop entry point for AI tools.

“They dropped the ball a little bit [on coding],” the third DeepMind engineer said. “By the time you realize something like that…a number of months have passed, and now you have to play catch-up. Then it also becomes political.” Coding is now in “big focus” inside the lab, the second engineer added.

However, not winning on pure model performance doesn’t mean Google is down and out of the AI race. The company has other advantages such as vertical integration—at the application, cloud, and chip layers—that are structural advantages that can offset weaker performance at the cutting edge of raw model intelligence.

“For OpenAI and Anthropic, because the model layer is so important to what they do, it’s pretty existential for them to win there,” Hill-Smith said. “Google could end up doing very well in the AI race overall, even if they’re not at the frontier of the model layer,” he said, adding that the company’s unusually deep vertical integration is a structural advantage that could well offset weaker performance at the cutting edge of raw model intelligence.

The technical difficulties and feeling of playing catch-up twice in less than five years have been a knock to morale, all the current and former DeepMind workers who spoke to Fortune say.

That internal frustration has coincided with one of the most damaging stretches of departures in DeepMind’s history. In a single week in June, Google lost Gemini co-lead Noam Shazeer to OpenAI and Nobel laureate and AlphaFold co-inventor John Jumper to Anthropic.

The employees who spoke to Fortune describe the exits as driven by overlapping forces: aggressive poaching from cash-flush rivals, frustration at being behind in the AI race, and engineers racing to get into a pre-IPO lab before they go public, hoping the equity compensation will make them fabulously rich. “There’s a lot of just hopping over to pre-IPO labs,” one employee said.

A Google spokesperson said talent moved regularly between technology companies and that Google remained focused on attracting people aligned with DeepMind’s mission.

Google has tried to combat some of the exodus, with the second engineer describing big retention and equity bonuses being deployed for some staff, and a prior round of enhanced compensation during a period when Meta was making aggressive counteroffers to AI researchers.

However, employees say, it hasn’t been enough to offset a deeper problem of burnout.

“I’ve been pushing 60-hour weeks for quite a long time because there is so much to do,” the third engineer said. “People are pushing themselves really hard because it is a race, and you have this feeling that you need to catch up… [but] telling people to work 60-hour weeks constantly and that it is constant crunch time usually doesn’t work that well, and people do burn out.”

Google said AI was an intensely competitive field and pointed to researchers who had publicly expressed excitement about their work and the company’s direction.

Employees had issues with leadership too. Even before his exit, workers described Hassabis as absent, especially compared to Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who came out of retirement to help the company’s AI efforts.

“You will see Sergey being incredibly hands-on, working hard on stuff and being involved,” the third DeepMind engineer said. “I can’t say that I’ve ever seen Demis walk around the office in the Gemini area.”

“Demis isn’t a very inspiring leader,” the former employee added. “Certainly not the way people talk about Dario [Amodei] … Demis is more of a guy who is known but not seen.”

Frustration over the leadership and talent exodus has collided with a separate, more politically charged fight over Google’s defense work.

In April 2026, Google signed a deal with the Pentagon allowing the Department of Defense to use Gemini models on classified networks for any lawful government purpose. More than 580 Google employees, including senior DeepMind researchers, later signed an open letter urging Pichai to reconsider the deal, citing concerns around autonomous weapons and mass surveillance.

Google was not alone in making the controversial deal: OpenAI, xAI, Microsoft, Amazon, and others signed similar classified-use deals. Anthropic was the only outlier, declining to drop its own restrictions on autonomous weapons and mass surveillance—a stance that led the Pentagon to designate the company a supply-chain risk and order the military to stop using its products.

At Google, the Pentagon deal reopened a longer-running fight over the company’s defense and intelligence contracts. Employees have also taken issue with Project Nimbus, a roughly $1.2 billion cloud-computing agreement Google and Amazon struck with the Israeli government in 2021.

For many employees, the Pentagon deal slipped largely under the radar. But for others it was existential.

Alex Turner, who spent more than two years on DeepMind’s AI safety team, resigned in June citing the Pentagon deal as the trigger.

In a public post, he said that his decision followed months of internal advocacy that went nowhere: he even tried to enlist Google chief scientist Dean as an ally. Andreas Kirsch, another DeepMind research scientist, was also a vocal public critic of the deal. Kirsch posted publicly at the time that the contract’s restrictions amounted to little more than “meaningless weasel words” for PR purposes, and said he felt “incredibly ashamed” to be associated with the lab over the decision.

The Pentagon deal was the final straw for a group of London-based DeepMinders, who launched a union bid in May in an attempt to win back some of their waning leverage. The action is the first formal attempt by a frontier AI lab to unionize.

The union drive really traces back to February 2025, when Google removed language from its public AI Principles committing not to build AI for weapons or surveillance that violates international norms. The decision angered many engineers who felt Google was backtracking on its ethical assurances. The company adopted that pledge in 2018 after the intense backlash over Project Maven—a separate defense contract.

Google has declined to voluntarily recognize the union, instead offering talks through the UK’s conciliation service, ACAS. The two sides have already clashed over basic questions, like which staff should be included in the bargaining unit, a person familiar with the situation said. Now employees worry that American leadership may be less inclined to play nice in negotiations.

A Google spokesperson said the company was still in the early stages of the union process and would continue to engage in negotiations in good faith.

With Hassabis stepping back and Dean gone, DeepMind appears to be entering a new phase at precisely the moment it can least afford further disruption.

While the lab still has advantages few rivals can match—distribution, cloud business, custom chips, vast research bench, and the ability to embed AI across products used by billions—the reorganization seems to remove a layer between DeepMind and a parent company increasingly focused on turning AI research into commercial—and government—deployments.

For employees, the question is whether new leadership and tighter integration will bring the urgency and clearer direction DeepMind needs to close the gap in coding and agents, or deepen the problems already driving people out: burnout, weakened autonomy, and concerns over how the company will use its technology. Just four years after Google’s first AI “code red,” DeepMind is again trying to prove it can move fast enough to keep pace. But this time, it will be doing so without the two figures most closely associated with its scientific identity.

The news was the tip of the iceberg of what has been a difficult year for Google DeepMind. The company is struggling to retain its technical edge, keep hold of top researchers and contain an employee revolt over its defense work

https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/student-d.title: My $80,000 in student debt changed the next 10 years of my life — and that was in 1988. Imagine what it’s like now
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/student-d.author: Verna L. Williams
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/student-d.text:
In 1988, I graduated from law school $80,000 in debt and wanted nothing more than to work in civil rights. Instead, the math pulled me toward the private sector. It took years of payments and strategic spending before I could afford to do the work I actually wanted to do.

That choice — dream job or debt-free — is one I made nearly four decades ago. Today, it’s even harder, and the federal government is making it more difficult.

One in five student loan borrowers are in default — a record-breaking 9.5 million people who are nine or more months behind on payments, up from 5.3 million just a year ago. At the same time, the Trump administration has eliminated the SAVE repayment plan and continues to fight for sweeping changes to Public Service Loan Forgiveness, the program that has helped thousands eventually afford the work they’re called to do.

Each move jeopardizes America’s ability to build and sustain the public service workforce our communities depend on. Preserving a stable, predictable PSLF program is essential to that mission.

PSLF is one of the federal government’s primary tools for recruiting and retaining public servants. By making careers in teaching, nursing, public safety and public interest law financially viable, PSLF ensures those seeking to give back to their communities through public service may do so without the rising cost of higher education getting in the way.

In the legal field, I see the repercussions of this situation play out daily. Families facing eviction, people navigating immigration proceedings, survivors seeking protection, and countless others are often left to navigate complex legal systems on their own simply because they cannot afford legal representation.

The result is a justice gap that leaves millions without meaningful legal assistance. According to the Legal Services Corporation’s latest Justice Gap Report, 92% of the civil legal problems experienced by low-income Americans receive inadequate or no legal help. In 27 states, there are fewer than one civil legal aid attorney for every 10,000 people living below 200% of the federal poverty level, leaving far too few lawyers to meet overwhelming demand. Legal aid organizations from California to Maryland struggle to recruit and retain attorneys, largely because public service salaries cannot compete with the private sector.

Public interest attorneys help close this gap. They educate people about their rights, resolve legal problems before they become life-altering crises, and ensure that legal help is not contingent upon zip code or connections. But when careers in public interest law become less financially sustainable – or less financially predictable – recruiting the attorneys communities desperately need becomes even harder.

Public interest attorneys routinely graduate with more than $150,000 in student loan debt while entering careers where median starting salaries are less than one-third of that amount. They are just one example of a broader student debt crisis. Four years of undergraduate education averages $35,210 in federal loans per borrower – and more than 1 million Americans are carrying $200,000 or more in student loan debt.

Without workable repayment options, many young lawyers who are in situations like mine will forgo such service because they simply cannot afford to do the work.

When fewer attorneys can afford to choose public service, fewer people get the legal help they need, reinforcing the belief that our legal system is unfair and justice is out of reach. In a recent survey, nearly 80% of respondents reported mistrust of the legal system, with fully 61% believing a person’s income affects whether courts provide fair outcomes. Our nation needs more justice, not less.

PSLF gives aspiring public servants confidence that the government values their commitment to filling community needs and will offer concrete assistance to support their vital occupations. This principle extends far beyond the legal profession. The PSLF program helps communities recruit teachers who educate our children, nurses who care for patients, social workers who protect vulnerable families and countless other professionals who choose service over higher-paying private-sector careers.

These professions differ in their missions, but reflect a common reality: public service often requires choosing purpose over higher pay. That choice is only possible when people can trust that the commitments supporting those careers will remain reliable.

As policymakers consider the future of student loan repayment and civil legal aid funding, they should remember that policy decisions today will shape who chooses public service tomorrow. Protecting the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program is essential to ensuring America can continue recruiting and retaining the public servants our communities depend on.

Verna L. Williams is the CEO of Equal Justice Works, which works to mobilize the next generation of public-interest lawyers.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/n.author: Holly Tregenza

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Melissa Donnelly wants the union movement to appeal to younger workers most at risk of losing work to AI. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

Public Sector Union boss Melissa Donnelly will take the helm of the Australian Council of Trade Unions at the end of August.

It comes after former peak union body secretary Sally McManus and president Michele O'Neil announced their resignation late last month.

Ms Donnelly says the cost of living and the AI boom will be her priorities when she starts at the end of August.

The new boss of Australia's biggest union is confronting a question that is increasingly worrying workers: not just whether AI will take their jobs, but if any jobs will be left for their children.

Public Sector Union boss Melissa Donnelly will take the helm of the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU), inheriting a movement at the height of its political influence but facing a long-term decline in membership and a fight over the impact of AI on the workforce.

"Lots of workers aren't just worried about what it means for their jobs, they're worried about what it means for their teenage kids," Ms Donnelly said.

"Are there going to be jobs for them in the future?"

Melissa Donnelly will first focus on cost of living when she takes over as head of the ACTU. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

Things are very different from when Ms Donnelly was a 15-year-old union member clocking in to shifts at her local Target.

Today the average union member is 44 years old and, like her, a working mum.

Trade union membership has been in general decline since 1992, but under outgoing secretary Sally McManus it increased for the first time since 2011.

Despite that gain, less than 4 per cent of members were aged 15 to 19, while about 7 per cent were aged 20 to 24.

Sally McManus was ACTU secretary from 2017 to 2026. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Ms McManus said her replacement represented generational change.

"With two school-aged children and having led a large union, she well knows the pressures working people are under," she said.

The cost of living will be Ms Donnelly's first focus when she takes the helm at the end of August.

"Every time you go to the checkout it costs more and more," she said.

"It will continue to be a key focus for our movement."

Ms Donnelly inherits the long-held challenge to bring more workers into the base.

She will also have to deal with a series of reputational hits to the union movement in recent years, particularly in Victoria with the CFMEU forced into administration and a looming royal commission into the state's Big Build program.

Despite those headwinds, trade unions have had an exceptional run under the current federal Labor government, with wins including Same Job Same Pay and the Right to Disconnect.

Ms Donnelly said these real gains were the way the union movement must continue to appeal to younger workers most at risk of losing work to AI.

The heads of the Australian Council of Trade Unions have announced that they are making way for the next generation.

"We're already making good progress," she said.

"We've got to continue that work, we've got to remain relevant, and that's the way I believe we will continue to have young people join our movement."

Beyond real wage growth and a push for better working conditions, there remains unanswered questions and an inherent tension around the ability to raise living standards through productivity gains without ultimately replacing workers with AI.

"[AI] obviously has the capacity to bring fundamental change to workers, and our job is to make sure there are strong guardrails in place," Ms Donnelly said.

Ms Donnelly has trotted a very Labor path.

She worked for left-leaning think tank The McKell Institute, and started her union career as a 25-year-old lawyer fighting the Howard government's bid to stop unionised public sector workers participating in protest action against WorkChoices laws.

"For me, that was a galvanising experience," she said.

"It really motivated me in my career on behalf of working people to advance the interests of union members."

BHP's Port Hedland operations just faced 48 hours of industrial action, how much of an impact did it have?

Ms Donnelly went on to spend seven years at the helm of the Community and Public Sector Union as secretary.

Her major wins during her tenure include the reversal of the outsourcing of government work to big consultancy firms, and securing work-from-home rights for public service employees.

Ms McManus said Ms Donnelly had "overwhelming support" from all unions.

The ACTU will announce a replacement for outgoing president Michele O'Neil later this year.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/v.author: Olivia Mason
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/v.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Hospitality Industry

Mia Anfiteatro and Chrit Atkinson say they had to find a new wedding venue after Ondeen closed. (Supplied: JakeyVass Media)

Adelaide Hills venue Ondeen says it has been forced to close, leaving engaged couples out of pocket and scrambling to find alternative locations.

The landlord said the tenants had been "served with four notices of default" but Ondeen said the rent had been paid in full last week.

The business said it will work with couples and customers who have events booked to find a solution.

Many Adelaide couples are scrambling to find a new venue for their weddings after a popular restaurant and cellar door announced its "unexpected" closure.

Ondeen, which opened in Adelaide Hills' Verdun two years ago, posted to social media last week announcing it had been forced to close.

"It is with incredibly heavy hearts that we share that Ondeen has unexpectedly received notice of the termination of its lease and has been forced to close for now," the post read.

Adelaide bride Mia Anfiteatro told 891 ABC Adelaide she was now $15,000 to $20,000 out of pocket after having to change her wedding venue.

"We've got two young girls who were really excited to get photos with the highland cows," she said.

Ms Anfiteatro said the couple had purchased 700 golf balls for guests to use on the driving range and had selected Ondeen's culinary expertise as "the art and centrepiece" of their wedding.

Ondeen is also home to four highland cows and two calves. (Supplied)

She said it was disappointing to have to find a new venue but the Adelaide community had rallied around her in helping to secure a spot on her original date.

"We put a post up on the Adelaide wedding chitchat page and we had some outstanding responses," she said.

Ondeen is a popular choice for weddings. (Supplied)

Riverland bride Nicola Thiele said she had managed to secure another venue in nearby Hahndorf for her upcoming wedding next month — but said the change had been stressful.

"I'm a busy mum — I've got three children under six, and then I'm trying to get married," she said.

"It did really throw me off because I picked somewhere like Ondeen because they had everything there … they do the food, they do the drinks, they supply most of the crockery, cutlery, chairs and everything.

"Leaving it this late to try to find somewhere that's got all of that — I think I was in the deep end."

Scott Edwards and Nicola Thiele had been looking forward to celebrating their wedding at Ondeen. (Supplied)

Ms Thiele said the venue closure had other flow-on effects, including that she was unable to get her money back from other vendors.

Both brides were also disappointed that they had been notified of Ondeen's closure via email, and had struggled to get in contact with the business via other channels

In the email, Ondeen co-founder Deborah Kingsbury told couples the business was "pursuing our legal options" and they would work with customers to find another suitable venue.

In a statement from its legal representative, the landlord said Ondeen had "been served with four notices of default".

"The tenant remains in default under the lease and the landlord has taken steps to protect its position," the statement read.

"Our client preference is to see the matter resolved promptly and appropriately and as the matter is currently the subject of ongoing communications and it would not be appropriate to comment further on the detail."

Deborah Kingsbury says Ondeen has numerous events booked for the months ahead. (ABC News: Katie Spain)

In a statement, Ms Kingsbury disputed this — saying the rent had been paid in full last week.

"On Tuesday we made the requested payments, covering the period right through to the end of August," she said.

"After that payment was made, we were advised the termination would remain in place."

Ms Kingsbury said the lease was due for a two-year renewal at the end of November.

"We have invested hundreds of thousands of dollars in this property over the last two and a half years, and we have numerous functions, weddings and events booked in the months ahead.

"Like everyone in regional hospitality, we have traded through a tough winter and faced the real pressures of rising business costs.

"Through it all Ondeen has continued to grow, celebrating our first two award-winning years and achieving our strongest ever forward bookings."

Ondeen has been at the Verdun site for more than two years. (ABC News: Duy Dash)

Ondeen staff said they had not been allowed on the property at all, including to feed the highland cows.

The landlord's representative said the animals on the property were being looked after.

Another pay offer will be put to Victorian teachers for a vote which may head off next week's third statewide strike. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

A new pay offer for Victoria's state school teachers and staff will be put to a vote ahead of a third planned statewide strike.

Among the new offers are a $2,000 lump-sum payment if union members sign the deal and a 1 per cent annual payment for teachers and staff who are stuck at the top of their pay bands.

The offer will open immediately, with an outcome to be known before the strike.

Victorian teachers and education staff are being asked to vote on a new pay offer which could avert a third statewide strike and end a protracted pay dispute.

An extraordinary Australian Education Union (AEU) council meeting was held this evening to discuss the Victorian government's latest pay offer to the state's public school teachers and education staff.

The new deal maintains the previous 28 to 32 per cent pay rise depending on an educator's role but adds in a $2,000 lump-sum payment for signing the agreement, a limit on the number of face-to-face teaching hours and a one-hour reduction in the time spent attending meetings.

There would also be a 1 per cent annual lump-sum payment for teachers, learning specialists, assistant principals and education support employees who had reached the top of their pay scale.

New Premier Ben Carroll says Victoria will fulfil the state’s funding obligations to public schools under the once-called Gonski plan

The offer comes ahead of another planned statewide 24-hour strike on Wednesday, August 19.

The council meeting has resolved to put the offer to a vote of all union members, with the ballot opening tonight and running until August 17, two days before the planned strike.

If a majority of union members accept the government's offer, the strike will be called off.

The offer comes a day after Premier Ben Carroll promised Victoria would increase funding to state schools in accordance with its obligations under the former Gonski plan.

The government and union said signing the full funding agreement with the federal government would mean Victoria's schools were no longer the lowest-funded in Australia.

The union has not said whether it recommended its members accept the deal.

The last time the AEU recommended its members accept a government pay offer, it was voted down by 58 per cent of teachers and education staff who were concerned about workloads and school funding.

The latest government offer comes a little more than a week out from another planned 24-hour statewide teacher strike. (Supplied: Emily Pinney Brown)

But earlier today, AEU Victorian branch president Justin Mullaly said the new offer was a significant step towards recognising and rewarding experienced teachers while achieving sought-after funding improvements for schools.

"It is a significant offer that has been built upon over a period of time," he said.

However, he could not guarantee that teachers and education staff would accept it.

"Our union is a proudly democratic union. Members get to have a say about their terms and conditions."

Justin Mullaly says the deal builds on previous offers made by the state government. (ABC News)

Gabrielle Williams was sworn in as the new education minister in Mr Carroll's cabinet.

She said she spoke to Mr Mullaly over the phone on the day she was appointed to the ministry and met face-to-face with the union the next day.

She said getting the $5 billion agreement across the line remained her first priority in the new portfolio.

"We, of course, hope that our teachers and education support staff will have a close look at this offer and understand that we come to this in good faith and wanting to genuinely ensure that we respect the incredibly important work that they do," she said.

"We believe it's a good offer. In fact, we believe it's an excellent offer."

She said the government was doing all it could to minimise disruptions for Victorian students and their families.

She said active discussions were underway with the Commonwealth about school funding.

Gabrielle Williams took over from Ben Carroll as education minister last week.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/t.title: Thailand rocked by second shooting tragedy in three days
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Monday's shootings were at Nonthaburi province, just north of Bangkok. (Facebook)

Thailand has suffered its second major shooting in just three days after a former member of parliament opened fire at a government building near Bangkok.

Thongchai Yenprasert, a former police colonel who was shot through the neck, died in hospital, while his driver was badly injured.

Police are investigating the motive for the shooting, with a dispute over money being the possible cause.

A gunman has killed a Thai official inside a local government office on the capital Bangkok's outskirts, authorities said, days after a teenager's shooting spree at a school in the same province reignited debate over gun control.

Police said the shooting came after a disagreement over borrowed money.

The suspect, former politician Chalong Riewrang, fired at Thongchai Yenprasert, the chairman of the Provincial Administrative Organisation in Nonthaburi, which borders Bangkok.

"The motive was personal," Police Lieutenant General Wattana Yijin said, adding that the provincial official's driver was also wounded but is not in a critical state.

Thongchai Yenprasert died in hospital after being shot in the neck. (Facebook)

After being shot in the neck, Mr Thongchai died of his wounds at Nonthaburi's Phra Nang Klao Hospital, its director Dr Sakol Sookprome said.

In a statement to reporters while in police custody, Chalong said he had gone to confront the victim over a long-standing dispute but the latter declined to talk things out.

"But when he was driving away, he pulled a gun," Chalong said, referring to Mr Thongchai.

Police did not provide any information on whether the slain official was armed.

His driver was hit in the arm and hand.

The Thai Prime Minister has vowed to introduce a new firearms control law after a teenager killed nine people at a high school and a home outside Bangkok.

Earlier, Chalong declared he had carried out the attack on a phone call to a well-known political commentator, the BBC reported, with the commentator livestreaming the incident on YouTube.

He was formerly a member of Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul's party.

The attack in Nonthaburi province, north of Bangkok, came just three days after a school shooting in the same region that raised questions over gun control in Thailand.

There does not appear to be any link between the two attacks.

Friday's rampage began at the teenager's home and continued at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, leaving nine people dead, including the shooter, and more than 20 wounded in the country's deadliest mass shooting in nearly four years.

Thai school children returned to their classrooms on Monday, some going through metal detectors and other checks, as Prime Minister Charnvirakul reiterated his intention to tighten gun controls in the wake of the shooting.

Shoes left behind by evacuated students at Debsirin Nonthaburi School. (Reuters: Chalinee Thirasupa)

School director Withan Promsintusak said officials had acted immediately after the attack, introducing weapons screening to reassure parents and protect students.

"We never imagined that a school, which should be the safest place, is where something like this would happen," he said.

Following Friday's shooting, Thailand's Education Ministry has said it would develop new school safety protocols over the next three months, including mental health screenings, emergency response drills, measures to tackle bullying and improved detection of weapons and other prohibited items.

The prime minister also ordered tougher enforcement against people carrying guns in public and said police would set up checkpoints as part of a crack down, which would include tightening controls on the possession, carrying and use of firearms.

Thailand had ​an estimated 10.3 million firearms in civilian possession, equating to around 15 guns per 100 residents, the highest rate in South-East Asia by a wide margin, according to a 2017 estimate by the Small Arms Survey.

https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomac.title: Why India’s new Himalayan border map threatens a fragile thaw in China ties
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomac.author: Shi Jiangtao
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomac.text:
New Delhi’s list of names for Arunachal Pradesh locations includes sensitive sites near its disputed frontier with China

The Indian government announced the move on Friday, just a day after officials from the two countries held a working-level consultation in New Delhi to discuss border management and reaffirm the need for peace along the Line of Actual Control.

In a statement, India’s Ministry of Home Affairs said the Survey of India had issued standard names for the locations to ensure “accurate recognition” and improve public awareness of their geographical and historical significance.

The list includes 21 land areas, four mountain passes, a high-altitude lake and a memorial. The names have been added to official Survey of India maps.

The list also includes the Sher-e-Thapa Memorial, which commemorates an Indian soldier who fought in that conflict, and Sambho Sarovar, a high-altitude lake.

Indian media described the step as a response to Beijing’s own mapping campaign since 2017 to assign standardised names to places in Arunachal Pradesh.

According to the state-owned Global Times, China’s Ministry of Civil Affairs has issued six lists of names covering 112 locations, including villages, mountain passes, rivers and peaks.

New Delhi has consistently rejected China’s renaming exercises, with Indian Ministry of External Affairs spokesman Randhir Jaiswal on Saturday describing them as “vain and preposterous”.

“Arunachal Pradesh was, is, and will always remain an integral and inalienable part of India. Assigning invented names will not alter this reality,” he said.

Beijing rejects Indian sovereignty over Arunachal Pradesh, which borders China’s Tibet autonomous region, and claims the area as historically part of China. Three of the areas included in India’s list of names – Longju, Maja and Bisa – are under Chinese control.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun defended Beijing’s naming campaign in April, saying the “Zangnan region is China’s territory” and that China did not recognise the “so-called Arunachal Pradesh illegally set up by India”. He said issuing standard names for locations in the region fell within China’s sovereign rights.

Liu Zongyi, a senior fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said India’s latest move was “primarily aimed at reinforcing its territorial claims” and creating the impression that its sovereignty over Arunachal Pradesh was already settled.

He said the naming exercise was based on what Beijing considered the “illegal McMahon Line” and built on India’s 1987 establishment of the “so-called Arunachal Pradesh”.

According to Liu, the move served both external and domestic purposes.

“By issuing these names, New Delhi seeks both to declare sovereignty externally, including over some sites under China’s actual control, to demonstrate continuity of its claims, and to foster a domestic perception that the territory is beyond dispute,” he said.

He said several of the chosen locations carried “clear military and strategic significance”, such as mountain passes and logistical hubs that could support future Indian deployments and infrastructure projects in the region.

He added that the inclusion of a war memorial reflected an element of “political education and nationalist messaging”.

“In essence, India is using maps and place names to construct a narrative of expansion, relying on its own mythology rather than established international norms,” Liu said.

He contrasted this with China’s approach, which he argued was rooted in sovereignty and historical legitimacy, and in Beijing’s rejection of the British colonial-era McMahon Line, which India regards as the basis of its eastern boundary with China.

“By publishing standardised names, China reaffirms its sovereignty over Zangnan to the international community and underscores its right to exercise lawful authority there in the future,” Liu said.

Pending a comprehensive border settlement, the two countries have fought a war and several deadly clashes over their competing perceptions of the Line of Actual Control.

Liu described the latest naming controversy as evidence that New Delhi’s position on the territorial dispute remained entrenched despite recent efforts to improve relations.

“Rather than seeking resolution through negotiation, it attempts to legitimise its occupation by asserting ‘possession itself equals sovereignty’. This shows that, despite outward gestures of easing relations, India’s stance on fundamental questions remains unchanged,” Liu said.

New Delhi and Beijing have been trying to sustain a cautious improvement in ties after years of tension along the Himalayan frontier.

India is preparing to host next month’s summit for Brics, the bloc of emerging economies that also includes China. Meanwhile, special representatives from the two countries are expected to hold their 25th round of boundary talks in Beijing in the coming months.

There have also been limited signs of practical engagement. Border trade through Nathu La resumed on August 1 after a six-year suspension, while Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Indian Minister of External Affairs Subrahmanyam Jaishankar pledged at a July 22 meeting in Manila to consolidate positive momentum in bilateral ties.

On Thursday, senior diplomats co-chaired the 36th meeting of the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on China-India Border Affairs in New Delhi, joined by representatives from defence, home affairs and immigration agencies.

According to China’s foreign ministry, the two sides discussed border management, cross-border cooperation and official demarcation. They agreed to prepare for the next round of special representative talks and to maintain communication through diplomatic and military channels.

The list includes 21 land areas, four mountain passes, a high-altitude lake and a memorial. The names have been added to official Survey of India maps.

https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.title: ‘Happiest person’: Chinese husband dedicates 25 years to caring for severely paraplegic wife
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.author: Alice Yan
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.text:
Jia playfully remarks that Li’s tireless dedication and concern for their family have turned his hair grey, while much of hers remains black

The story of a devoted couple from central China, where the husband has lovingly cared for his severely paraplegic wife for 25 years, has touched the hearts of millions on social media throughout mainland China.

The couple live in Pingdingshan, Henan province. In 2001, 36-year-old Jia Fang suffered a horrific fall from a cliff while riding a pedicab, resulting in paralysis from the chest down, as reported by Henan TV.

Since that life-altering moment, her husband, Li Junliang, who is one year older than Jia, has been her constant carer, dedicated to looking after her around the clock while also raising their son and daughter, who were just 10 and 13 years old at the time of the accident.

Li takes on all responsibilities for Jia, who is unable to care for herself.

In the initial years, Li would turn Jia’s body every two hours to prevent bedsores. Over time, he adjusted this to every four hours, meaning he has gone without a full night’s sleep for the past two decades.

He often carries Jia to a wheelchair and takes her outside to bask in the sun and enjoy the fresh air, according to the report.

Li regularly massages Jia’s limbs to prevent muscular atrophy.

It remains unclear what profession Li pursues to support his family.

Their children have since grown up and started their own families. The walls of Li’s home are adorned with certificates of achievement from when his children were students, hinting at the care and dedication he provided during their upbringing.

“My husband works tirelessly and worries about every aspect of our family. His hair has turned completely grey, while most of mine is still black,” Jia shared with the media.

“Junliang, thank you for taking care of me for 25 years!” Jia expressed gratefully.

Li responded, saying: “You are my wife. You have given birth to our son and daughter and contributed so much to our family. No matter the challenges we face or how tired I become, I will care for you for another 25, 35, or even 45 years.”

He emphasised that his actions are a fulfilment of the promise he made to Jia on their wedding day: “Home is complete only with your presence,” Li told her then.

“I believe I am the happiest person in the world; I’ve married the right man,” said Jia.

A neighbour, who was unnamed in the report, expressed admiration for Li’s unwavering devotion to his wife.

“Many men would find it difficult to endure caring for a paraplegic wife for long. Few exhibit such commitment as Li has for all these years. Moreover, their home is clean and tidy – he truly is a remarkable man!” praised the neighbour.

“His loyalty and kindness will surely touch the heart of God, and his family will be blessed for a long time,” commented one online observer.

Another person remarked: “I am moved by this kind-hearted man. Very few would do what he has done. This woman is truly fortunate!”
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.summary: Li Junliang has cared for his paraplegic wife for 25 years. Jia Fang suffered a horrific fall from a cliff while riding a pedicab. She is unable to care for herself and has been her constant carer. Li regularly massages Jia’s limbs to prevent muscular atrophy.

https://www.scmp.com/business/china-evs/.title: Can CATL’s battery breakthrough push flying cars closer to a commercial reality in China?
https://www.scmp.com/business/china-evs/.author: Daniel Ren
https://www.scmp.com/business/china-evs/.text:
World’s top EV battery maker says aviation pack is ready for mass production after clearing a major safety test

A successful roll-out of passenger-carrying drone batteries, backed by CATL’s innovation drive and manufacturing heft, would bolster China’s leading position in the renewable energy sector and the future of mobility, according to analysts.

“The aviation battery system is ready for mass production and will be first applied to our Autoflight flying vehicles,” CATL said in a statement on Sunday. “We will work with our partners and relevant research institutions to continuously overcome technical challenges and build safe and reliable products for drone makers and users.”

During a plant visit by Hong Kong media outlets last week, CATL, based in Ningde, in China’s southeast province of Fujian, said it was determined to expand energy solutions across transport modes from cars and trucks to ships and aircraft.

Davis Zhang, a senior executive at Suzhou Hazardtex, a supplier of specialised batteries, said CATL was not just a battery manufacturer, but a pioneer in decarbonising the global economy.

“The test is yet another example of how its innovations redraw the business landscapes,” Zhang said.

The aviation battery packs used prismatic cells with technology that isolated individual cells to prevent heat from spreading, which was verified by officials from the Civil Aviation Administration of China, CATL said in the statement. The batteries had an energy density of 350 watt-hours per kilogram – 50 per cent higher than the average counterparts powering an electric car.

Batteries with higher energy density can store more power, giving vehicles longer ranges between charges.

Current rules permit passenger-carrying vehicles to operate below 1,000 metres.

Seven eVTOL manufacturers were expected to start delivering products before the end of this year, CCID Consulting said in a report in January.

In November, CATL’s subsidiary Autoflight, a drone maker, launched a waterborne vertiport to support the eVTOL sector.

CATL officials told Hong Kong reporters that its advanced production lines had an automation rate of 95 per cent, with thousands of checkpoints to ensure quality.

They added that the company was striving to be a world-class technology innovator, delivering superior contributions to green energy.

CATL led the global EV battery market with a 40.2 per cent share in the first five months of 2026, according to Seoul-based SNE Research. It also commanded 30 per cent of the world’s energy-storage market share last year.

Goldman Sachs said in July that CATL’s scale, cost and technology leadership, reinforced by strategic ecosystem ­investments, provided a strong foundation for its transition to an integrated battery energy-storage system provider.

Ningde-based Skeqi, which supplies production equipment such as robotic arms and machinery to CATL and other leading Chinese EV battery makers, said last week its 2026 orders were set to jump more than 50 per cent from a year earlier, spurred by demand for renewable energy.

“We are quite confident about the growth trajectory and will invest heavily in production and human resource in line with the trend,” said Zheng Ting, Skeqi’s general sales manager. “We believe that over the next five years, it will be an upwards trend. We are determined to invest and get ready for more orders from the market.”

Between January and May, the Chinese companies commanded a 72.6 per cent share of the global EV battery market, its data showed.

https://www.dw.com/en/thai-ex-lawmaker-s.title: Thai ex-lawmaker shoots local official dead over loan
https://www.dw.com/en/thai-ex-lawmaker-s.text:
A former lawmaker confessed to shooting a senior official at a government office over a money dispute, police have said. The incident came just days after Thailand's deadliest shooting in nearly four years.

Thai police arrested a suspected gunman — identified as former lawmaker Chalong Riewraeng — after he allegedly fired shots that killed a local politician on Monday at a government office on the outskirts of Bangkok.

Authorities said the former MP confessed to the shooting.

Surrounded by police, Chalong told reporters he attempted to speak with Thongchai Yenprasert about money.

"I followed him to his car and hit his car's window, saying I want to talk," the suspect said. "He said he will not talk, so I pulled my gun. I did not aim to shoot, but his driver pulled a gun and pointed it at me so I fired."

Thongchai, who was chairman of the Nonthaburi Provincial Administrative Organization, died of his wounds, according to Sakon Sukprom, director of Phra Nang Klao hospital.

Thongchai's driver was also shot and successfully underwent surgery, Sakon added.

Nonthaburi Governor Chestha Mosikarat told reporters the suspect and victim were "friends for a long time" and the incident likely stemmed from a misunderstanding.

Police said the motive for the shooting was a "personal issue."

"According to his confession, it was about money that the ... chairman borrowed from him for several years, and he asked for the return of the money several times," regional Police Commander Wattana Yeechin told reporters, adding that the dispute was over several million baht (1 million baht is about €26,220 or $30,300).

This comes just days after a 14-year-old's shooting rampage, first at his home and then at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, left nine people dead and over 20 injured. That incident was Thailand's deadliest mass shooting in nearly four years.

Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul had reiterated his intention to tighten gun control laws in the wake of the shooting. The Southeast Asian country's current gun laws do not include mental health screenings and allow people as young as 20 to have guns.

Thailand had around 15 guns per 100 ⁠residents, the highest rate in Southeast Asia ​by a wide margin, according to a 2017 estimate by the Small Arms Survey.

https://www.dw.com/en/netanyahu-at-odds-.title: Netanyahu, at odds with Trump, rejects Gaza peace plan
https://www.dw.com/en/netanyahu-at-odds-.text:
The Israeli prime minister says his country will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas fully disarms, putting him at odds with a US-backed roadmap endorsed by the group.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday rejected US President Donald Trump's plan for Gaza, saying Israeli troops would not withdraw from the territory until Hamas was fully disarmed.

"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu told a Cabinet meeting, referring to the US-backed roadmap agreed to by Hamas in late July.

The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed," Netanyahu said, adding that this included "heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Netanyahu said Israel remained in talks with Washington despite its objections. He described Trump as "our greatest friend in the White House," but added: "They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters."

The White House did not immediately comment.

Trump announced last month that there had been a breakthrough on a 15-point roadmap aimed at ending the war in the Gaza Strip.

The plan drawn up by his Board of Peace calls for Israeli troops to withdraw as Hamas gives up its weapons. An International Stabilization Force would then work alongside a new Palestinian police force to secure Gaza.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hamas is designated as a terrorist organization by Israel, the United States, the European Union and several other countries.

The group has avoided using the term "disarmament." It says it agreed to hand over its weapons for storage under a US-backed Palestinian technocratic administration that would govern Gaza under the supervision of the Board of Peace.

Hamas has said implementation also depends on Israel meeting its obligations, including withdrawing troops and halting attacks.

"We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap, and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons," Hamas political bureau member Bassem Naim said.

Hamas said Sunday it remained committed to the roadmap.

Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace's high representative for Gaza, said Israel would face no obligations until Hamas had surrendered all its weapons, including assault rifles.

However, Mladenov told Israel's Channel 12 that Israeli troops would eventually have to withdraw "sector by sector" once Hamas' weapons had been collected and rendered unusable.

"The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again," he said, referring to the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, which triggered the war against Hamas in the Gaza Strip.

Mladenov said discussions with Israel were continuing and that he hoped for a "positive outcome."

The disagreement comes at a politically sensitive moment for Netanyahu ahead of elections scheduled for October 27, Israel's first national vote since the Hamas led attacks that sparked an ongoing Israeli military campaign in Gaza.

The prime minister is running level with or behind rivals in some polls and faces pressure from far-right members of his government who oppose concessions to Hamas.

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich welcomed Netanyahu's position.

"We went to war with a central goal: the destruction of Hamas," he said. "The [military] cannot withdraw even a millimetre from the Gaza Strip."

The dispute is the latest sign of differences between Netanyahu and Trump. The two leaders are considered as close allies, but have recently disagreed over how to deal with the conflicts in Iran, Lebanon and Gaza.

The Gaza roadmap builds on a US-mediated ceasefire reached in October 2025.

Gaza health officials say more than 1,250 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since then. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed during the same period.

Despite the ongoing negotiations over the roadmap, Israeli forces continue to control large parts of Gaza, while most of the enclave's more than 2 million residents have been displaced and are living in a much smaller coastal area, many in tents or damaged buildings.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx7.title: Former Thai MP allegedly kills official and confesses on YouTube
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx7.text:
A former Thai MP allegedly shot dead a local official in the southern province of Nonthaburi, then dialled into a YouTube livestream to inform the host - a political pundit - of what he had done.

Former Nonthaburi MP Chalong Reawraeng told the shocked host, Anchalee Paireerak, that he had shot Thongchai Yenprasert, a former police official, outside Thongchai's office.

Thongchai, who was hit in the neck, died in hospital. His driver was shot in the arm and hand.

Chalong was arrested but then allowed to hold a press conference at a police station where he attempted to explain what had happened while smoking a cigarette.

He told the reporters there that Thongchai was "angry" at him, but did not explain why. He also said he did not intend to shoot Thongchai, whom he described as a "good friend".

Chalong said he told Thongchai that he wanted to talk to him. According to local media reports, the two were involved in a personal dispute.

"He [Thongchai] then pushed me, saying 'I don't want to talk, I don't want to talk.'"

Chalong said he then followed Thongchai towards his car.

"When I pulled the gun out, I didn't intend to shoot him. But then [Thongchai's driver] pulled his gun out and pointed it at me, so I fired."

Thongchai, a retired police colonel, was president of the Nonthaburi Provincial Administrative Organisation or PAO, a local government body.

Earlier, Chalong had called political commentator Anchalee Paireerak, who was livestreaming on YouTube at the time, to confess to the incident.

Anchalee was filmed picking up a call midway through her programme. "I'll call you back... Oh, something big [happened]? Go ahead, what's that?" she said.

Viewers could not hear what the caller said next, but Anchalee was seen reacting in shock.

"Did he die? Did he die? You shot him in the head? You need to wait there for the cops," she said on the video, which was seen by the BBC. "Don't go anywhere."

Monday's shooting came three days after a 14-year-old boy shot dead eight people at his home and school, then killed himself, in Thailand's worst mass shooting since 2022. The two attacks are not related.

The latest shooting will further spur debate about gun control in Thailand, which has the highest rate of gun ownership in South East Asia by a wide margin.

After Friday's school shooting, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul ordered tougher enforcement of gun laws and said police would set up checkpoints as part of a crackdown.

Other measures would include tightening controls on the possession, carrying and use of firearms.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyq.title: 'Body in suitcase' found in Australia turns out to be lifelike doll
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyq.text:
Australian police called in to investigate a body found in a suitcase have concluded that the "victim" was in fact a lifelike doll.

The suitcase was discovered by two men on the side of a road near the small village of Oallen, about 230km (143 miles) south-west of Sydney.

On Monday, police announced a murder investigation, sparking intense interest in the case but backtracked hours later, saying forensic testing had proved the contents were not human.

The contents in the suitcase were "mistaken for a human originally, so they are very realistic in terms of looking like human remains," said Supt Linda Bradbury from the Hume Police District.

"But we've confirmed by other means that they are not."

The doll was wearing clothing, had hair and a nose piercing," police said, adding that "the item also had markings that resembled bruises and grazes".

Supt Bradbury said forensic teams and investigators had attended the scene on Sunday and that all processes had been followed.

"The idea is to not disturb crime scenes as much as possible, to maintain the integrity of our investigation," Bradbury said, adding she had "no regrets" about how the case was handled.

Hours earlier, Bradbury had told media that it has been "quite a shocking discovery" for the two men who found the suitcase.

"Unfortunately, they were on a weekend drive as a lot of people do over the weekend and stopped for a break," she said.

She said the pair had made the "right decision" to report the find.

"They were affected yesterday and we will be in touch to let them know that it was not human remains," Bradbury said.

Police have now closed their investigations.
