https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Shoved the tube so hard it tore my nose’: Kurdish film-maker recounts ‘inhumane’ ICE force-feeding
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: José Olivares
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Gabar Choli tells of how, for months, he was shackled, pinned and forcibly fed – and the physical and emotional scars the ordeal has left

In June 2025, a sluggish and thin Gabar Choli, with sunken temples and bones visible under his skin, braced himself for the immigration detention center guards to charge into his cell once again.

Choli was in a solitary confinement medical cell inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility in south Texas where immigrants arrested in Donald Trump’s anti-immigration crackdown are detained.

Choli, a 40-year-old Kurdish asylum seeker with a thick beard and long dark hair, had been on hunger strike for over two months, demanding improved conditions for detained immigrants and to be released or deported. That day in June 2025, Choli’s nose was swollen, his throat hurt and he could still taste blood from previous days of treatment for which he never gave his consent, he said.

The film-maker and activist for an independent Kurdistan has spoken out for the first time, talking exclusively to the Guardian last week from Canada about the ordeal in the United States that he said “broke him”.

He recounted the vile routine as the detention center guards would rush towards him and wrestle him to the concrete cell floor, shackle his wrists and ankles, and drag him to the detention center infirmary. There, the guards pinned Choli on a bed while medical staff forcibly inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach. Choli was being force-fed by ICE.

“Two guards would hold my feet; two hold my hands; one hold my head – and they would shove tubes in my nose,” Choli said. “It’s not easy to be wrestled to the ground twice a day by men that are stronger than you. And you just take it. You have 60cm of tube going through you and you just feel every centimeter of it.”

An investigation by the Guardian, based on dozens of pages of court records and interviews with medical and legal experts, found that Choli was quietly and intermittently force-fed by ICE for nearly eight months – from late May 2025 until he was deported in January.

He was not alone – he even met a fellow hunger striker, an Afghan man the Guardian also learned about, as they were both forcibly fed in the same ICE facility.

Force-feeding is an excruciating and traumatizing process that has been widely condemned by human rights organizations as torture. For Choli and others, refusing food is a last resort to protest against harsh conditions and lack of progress in their immigration cases, but sometimes brings only harsher conditions.

“I understood the necessity of making a stand for what was right,” Choli said, speaking by phone with the Guardian, talking in a very matter-of-fact way about his recent experience. At various times, Choli would sarcastically chuckle, almost incredulous now when remembering the officials’ actions. “I was respectful. I just told them I am protesting for humane treatment, nothing else. But they were determined to break me,” he said.

Choli suffered swollen sinuses, a damaged esophagus, stomach problems and psychological torment, according to court records and his own account.

“It just broke me, mentally broke me,” Choli said gravely. After sometimes twice-daily sessions “they would take me to [a] solitary cell and I would just choke on my blood and drink the blood from inside [my throat],” he said, describing how the feeding tube would scrape him inside. Many of his court records remain sealed and he did not have a lawyer – and medical staff there did not respond to the Guardian’s reporting – so some details in Choli’s account remain uncorroborated.

The Trump administration has not officially acknowledged force-feeding anyone in immigration jails. But an investigation by the Guardian found that since January 2025, the administration used court orders in plans to subject at least 10 hunger strikers in ICE detention to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding.

However, it has since emerged that the number is even higher. Sources with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), ICE’s parent agency, later told the Guardian that between January 2025 and 4 August 2026, ICE received “a court order for involuntary treatment for 18 hunger strikers”.

DHS did not respond to questions concerning Choli’s specific case, but a spokesperson said in a statement: “ICE respects an individual’s right to refuse medical treatment where appropriate. However, when an individual’s medical condition presents a serious risk of death or permanent harm, or when other compelling legal or operational interests are implicated, ICE may seek judicial authorization for appropriate medical interventions consistent with applicable law.”

“Any involuntary medical treatment is undertaken only pursuant to legal authority and under the direction of qualified medical professionals,” the spokesperson added.

The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas did not respond to a detailed request for comment.

“This likely amounts to torture,” said Dr Chanelle Diaz, an assistant professor of medicine at Columbia University’s medical center, in New York. Diaz has medically evaluated other ICE force-feeding cases and advocated for hunger strikers’ release. She reviewed the limited court records available for Choli’s case, at the Guardian’s request. “I would say that it’s even difficult to capture the degree of risk that he was being put at, long-term,” she said.

Choli, a deeply religious Muslim, had been living in Vancouver, where he was a film-maker and activist campaigning for an independent nation of Kurdistan, having come to Canada in 2007 from what he considers occupied territory in Iran. His life was and is complicated. He said he had previously served nine months in prison in Canada following a 2012 drug-smuggling charge and court records show the case was related to receiving just over one kilogram of opium in the mail from Turkey.

Then his activism for Kurdish independence drew death threats and in 2022 he crossed the border into the US in Blaine, Washington and requested asylum. He was quickly released by the authorities and made his way to Los Angeles to try to pursue his ambitions in film while his asylum case played out, attending regular mandatory check-ins with ICE and qualifying for a work permit. Court records say a judge denied his asylum claim in 2024 but granted him protection from deportation to Iran.

Then Donald Trump returned to the White House after campaigning on a promise of mass deportation and, at a 25 February 2025 check-in with ICE, Choli was arrested. He was first sent to the Desert View Annex in California, an immigration detention center that has been repeatedly criticized for substandard conditions. While in detention, Choli says he was pressured by ICE officials to sign a deportation order to be sent to Iran. He refused and after demanding better conditions and a fairer resolution to his immigration case, he began his hunger strike on 24 March, court records show.

“I am not suicidal,” Choli would later write in a declaration to a federal judge. “I am using hunger strike as the only available option to protest the abuse and mistreatment.”

Choli was then transferred to the privately-run Port Isabel facility in Texas for a “higher level of medical care”, an ICE court declaration says. There, Choli refused to end his strike and was placed in a solitary medical cell, which ICE describes as administrative segregation, meaning he was under frequent observation by medical staff. It features a perpetually illuminated cell, alongside other cells in that unit with suicidal or other medically vulnerable detainees.

Almost 10 days later, ICE sought their first court order to force-feed Choli. He broke his strike, believing the federal court’s involvement could help his immigration case move along. “God opened a door for me,” he said he was thinking, and wrote a letter to the federal judge requesting assistance.

But three weeks later, Choli said he learned the case was closed and no one had responded to his letter. Furious, he stopped accepting meals again. On 23 May 2025, ICE and the US attorney’s office for the southern district of Texas filed a second request for a court order to conduct involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding. According to ICE’s request, a social worker at the detention facility evaluated Choli and found he was “operating under his own free will”.

The World Health Organization and other medical organizations “have said that it is an individual’s right to decide to go on hunger strike, as long as they are of sound mind – which he was”, Dr Parveen Parmar said about Choli after reviewing some of his records shared by the Guardian. Parmar is a doctor and expert with Physicians for Human Rights, a New York-based advocacy group. Like Diaz, she has provided expert medical testimony in other ICE force-feeding cases and also reviewed the limited court records available for Choli’s case.

“Patient autonomy is one of the core tenets of medicine,” Parmar added.

But as Choli’s hunger strike went on, it threatened his health and also, in the government’s opinion, posed “a serious threat to the security and good order” of the facility, ICE argued in court filings. “The public interest is served by not allowing [Choli’s] attempts to manipulate the immigration system and by maintaining prison and inmate safety and security,” the case documents say.

Such filings not only contradict federal silenceor denials about hunger strikes going on intermittently in various ICE detention facilities, but they appear to speak to a desire by authorities to limit such protests from spreading.

In Choli’s case, doctors working for ICE, Dr Benjamin Salinas and Dr Shauna Kincheloe, also submitted declarations to the court last May requesting the procedures take place – and continue. One day later, the federal judge, Rolando Olvera, ordered Choli to be force-fed, without hearing from Choli himself.

When contacted, Salinas told the Guardian: “Thanks for reaching out, but I’m not interested.” Kincheloe did not respond to requests from the Guardian for comment. Olvera’s assistant declined to make the judge available for comment.

“Immigration detention is civil, it is not necessary,” Diaz said, referring to the fact that many alleged immigration violations, such as remaining in the US without legal status, involve civil, not criminal law. She said that ICE’s court arguments “feel like a false dichotomy”, adding that detained immigrants “could be released, that is always a choice. And that should be the default, not force-feeding.”

In most cases seen by the Guardian, federal judges will often approve ICE’s requests without hearing from the hunger strikers first, or their lawyers – those that have one.

Choli did not have an attorney during his detention and the entire force-feeding proceedings, records show, and was not provided with one by the government.

“In my view, those proceedings shouldn’t continue without the person having legal representation if they don’t have it already,” said Rebecca Sharpless, the founding director of University of Miami’s immigration clinic. Sharpless is not familiar with Choli’s case but represented an ICE hunger striker in 2021 who was ordered force-fed. “It makes a big difference when people understand that there are people who are fighting for them – both in terms of their legal case but also their right to make choices about their body.”

The very first time Choli was force-fed, he had voluntarily gone with the guards to the detention center’s infirmary. But after experiencing the painful and traumatic process for the first time, he began to resist.

“First I did not resist. But after I saw they were torturing me, I started protesting: ‘I’m not coming with you people,’” he said.

Then the guards, employees of the private prison company Akima Global Services, “started wrestling”, he said. Many ICE detention centers are run by private US contractors. Akima and its parent company did not respond to detailed requests for comment.

During the first days of Choli’s force-feeding, his nose and throat were swollen from the repeated tube insertions and removals, according to Choli and court records. He recalled an occasion in which, while being restrained, an ICE nurse “shoved the tube so hard” that “he tore my nose from the inside”. His nose bled for days, Choli wrote in a declaration to the court recounting the incident.

Parma of Physicians for Human Rights said repeated force-feeding can produce such symptoms and is “just inhumane from beginning to end”.

The rapid administration of nutrients after Choli had been starving himself also triggered stomach problems. During one early session last June, Choli said he immediately had diarrhea. He was then taken to a cell with no toilet, he said, where he further defecated on himself.

“I kept looking at my soiled body and clothing and went on crying,” Choli wrote in the declaration to the judge. “I cried for being objectified and inhumanely treated, for seeking a humane treatment.”

Weeks passed and Olvera, the judge, continued to extend the force-feeding order. Choli, with swollen sinuses, presented his declaration to the court at one hearing in mid June, telling Olvera he could not afford a lawyer and requested a court-appointed attorney.

Olvera denied Choli’s request, writing in his court order that attorneys are not guaranteed in civil proceedings and that, even if Choli had one, it would be of no use – he would continue to grant force-feeding orders.

The twice daily process became a grim routine.

Weeks turned to months. At one point, Choli recalled a guard’s rough treatment injuring his ribs, making breathing painful for weeks. At another, guards who were restraining him “pressed so hard on my shoulder, I thought my chest was going to break in half”.

“I lost my breath” and he heard the doctor say, “‘Take him to the hospital, he’s dead.’ [Then] I completely went ‘out’,” Choli said in an interview.

Another time he recalls that despite his warnings a medical staffer incorrectly inserted the tube and it entered his lung, causing him to choke and then cough that end of the tube up into his mouth.

Choli remembers that as he was passing out, he “lost [his] senses” and vaguely remembers “reaching for [the guard’s] hand with my mouth”. DHS, ICE and Akima did not respond to this specific allegation.

Choli said that at one point he made a deal with the facility staff: on Fridays, he agreed to drink the nutritional liquids if they allowed him to pray with other detainees. “That was my opportunity to socialize,” Choli said, calling those Fridays his “peace days”.

Late October rolled around. It was Choli’s birthday and, incredibly, he recalls that Kincheloe, one of the facility doctors, and other nurses sang “Happy Birthday” to him in Spanish. The Guardian has not been able to verify thisdetail. Choli does not remember whether he drank the nutritional liquids that day or was force-fed.

“In Choli’s case, where he was force-fed for eight months, you’re looking at easily over 100 NG tube placements, possibly over 200… that is just not medical care, that is torture,” Diaz said, referring to nasogastric tubing.

ICE finally deported Choli to Canada on 6 January this year, where he reunited with his siblings who also live in Canada.

He told the Guardian how, the next day, he nervously ate his first solid meal in months, a small, simple salad. He was fine, but his jaw hurt for days.

“It may sound strange, but I had to learn how to eat [again],” Choli said. He is still struggling today, physically and mentally, but hopes that speaking out may help others in ICE detention.

“The price of [the hunger strike] was my life,” Choli said in an angry but level and determined tone. “The price of it was my kidneys, my gallbladder. My intestines. My being. My bladder, you know, is damaged. Every time I twist and turn, I feel pain. But this is the price you pay for making a stand for what is right.”

“Trump is just one person,” he said, indicating his problem is with the broader treatment of immigrants and refugees by the US. “Trump is not here torturing me.”

ICE and the US attorney’s office requested Choli’s force-feeding court case be dismissed in January, saying he was no longer in their custody. An envelope addressed to Choli, containing the dismissal notice, was sent to the Port Isabel detention center. The envelope was returned to the court.

“Return to sender”, “Not here,” the envelope read.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Gabar Choli, 40, was forced to be forcibly fed by ICE in a Texas detention center in June 2025. He was on hunger strike for over two months, demanding improved conditions for detained immigrants. He had been living in Vancouver, where he was a film-maker and activist campaigning for an independent nation of Kurdistan.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Kurdish hunger striker says ICE force-feeding ‘mentally broke me’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: José Olivares in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Exclusive: Film-maker Gabar Choli describes how he endured coercive treatment over eight months in detention in Texas

A Kurdish man who was force fed over the course of eight months while on hunger strike in US immigration detention has spoken out about it for the first time, describing how much the process harmed him physically and psychologically.

Gabar Choli, a film-maker and activist now living in Canada after being deported, described how he endured the coercive treatment – a practice widely considered torture by international human rights groups – often twice a day after being detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) when his asylum application was denied.

“It just broke me, mentally broke me,” Choli said in an exclusive interview with the Guardian. “It came to a point that I decided to write my body an apology letter.”

ICE officials force-fed Choli at the Port Isabel federal detention center in Los Fresnos, south Texas, from late May 2025 until he was deported in January of this year, a Guardian investigation found. Choli had resorted to a hunger strike to protest conditions at the facility and to push for a resolution to his immigration case.

He described how a team of detention center guards would physically restrain him while ICE medical staff forcibly inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his esophagus and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach.

“I was respectful. I just told them I am protesting for humane treatment, nothing else,” Choli said. “But they were determined to break me.”

Much of what happens in ICE detention has been hidden from public view over successive administrations.

An investigation by the Guardian last week found that the second Trump administration used court orders in plans to subject at least 10 hunger strikers in ICE detention to involuntary medical procedures.

However, it has since emerged that the number is even higher. DHS sources told the Guardian over the weekend that between January 2025 and 4 August, 2026 ICE obtained court orders for involuntary medical treatment for 18 hunger strikers. The Guardian has previously found that while some people are force-fed, some give in and eat at the last minute when presented with a court order.

DHS sources also said that ICE “provides involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death”.

In court records reviewed by the Guardian in relation to Choli’s case and other hunger strikers, “involuntary medical treatment” is used as an umbrella term that includes the option of force-feeding.

According to court records related to Choli, ICE requested the court give the agency permission “to conduct routine physical examinations and routine laboratory testing, administer hydration, and if necessary, use restraints to accomplish this involuntary monitoring, treatment and administration of nutrients, fluids and medication(s), by way of intravenous measures and/or a nasogastric tube”.

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), its parent agency, did not respond to specific questions about Choli’s case and had not responded to questions about force-feeding for the prior articles in the investigative series, but on Friday night sent a statement by email in response to the Guardian’s reporting and requests for comment.

“ICE respects an individual’s right to refuse medical treatment where appropriate,” an unnamed DHS spokesperson said. “However, when an individual’s medical condition presents a serious risk of death or permanent harm, or when other compelling legal or operational interests are implicated, ICE may seek judicial authorization for appropriate medical interventions consistent with applicable law. Any involuntary medical treatment is undertaken only pursuant to legal authority and under the direction of qualified medical professionals.”

“ICE is committed to ensuring the safety, security, and well-being of all individuals in its custody,” the spokesperson added.

Dozens of pages of federal court records verify that Choli was subjected to force-feeding, including declarations by ICE doctors and officers. Combined with interviews with medical and legal experts and an interview by phone with Choli himself , much of the secretive process is revealed. His case could be the longest documented case of force-feeding in ICE detention to date.

Choli arrived in Blaine, Washington state, in 2022. He had been living in Vancouver where he was a film-maker and activist campaigning for an independent nation of Kurdistan, having come to Canada from what he considers occupied territory in Iran. He said he requested asylum in the US due to death threats for his political activism while in Canada, and lived in Los Angeles with a work permit while his case was in process. But he was arrested during an ICE check-in on 25 February 2025 – the month after Donald Trump returned to the White House – after his asylum case failed.

He began a hunger strike in detention in California and was transferred to Texas. DHS and ICE then requested an emergency court order from a federal judge to force-feed him and perform other medical procedures, such as involuntary intravenous hydration, involuntary blood draws and urine analysis tests through forced catheterization, documents from the southern district of Texas federal court seen by the Guardian show.

“I am not suicidal,” Choli wrote in a letter to the federal judge overseeing his proceedings. “I am using hunger strike as the only available option to protest the abuse and mistreatment.”

DHS and ICE said in court records that force-feeding Choli was necessary for his health, but also that his prolonged hunger strike posed “a serious threat to the security and good order” of the detention center. They further accused Choli of attempting to “manipulate the immigration system” by striking.

During his first force feeding sessions, he recalled in an interview occasions where a nurse working for ICE “shoved the tube so hard” that “he tore my nose from the inside.” After such sessions “they would take me to solitary cell and I would just choke on my blood and drink the blood from inside [my throat],” he added. Many of his court records are sealed, so the Guardian is not able to corroborate some details in Choli’s account.

He did not have legal representation throughout the eight month ordeal. The federal judge presiding over his case, Rolando Olvera, denied Choli’s request for legal assistance and extended the force-feeding order several times at ICE’s request, according to records filed in the southern district of Texas federal court.

Choli suffered injuries and medical complications, including swollen sinuses, damage to his esophagus and stomach problems, court records show.

“That is just not medical care, that is torture,” Dr Chanelle Diaz, an assistant professor of medicine at Columbia University’s medical center, told the Guardian. Diaz has reviewed cases of other detained immigrants subjected to force-feeding and advocated for their release.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Gabar Choli was arrested during an ICE check-in on 25 February 2025. He was forced into a feeding tube through his nose and down his esophagus. Judge denied Choli's request for legal assistance and extended the force-feeding order several times.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Cait Kelly  Inequality reporter
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Melissa Donnelly, the national secretary of the Community and Public Sector Union, will replace the outgoing ACTU head

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Melissa Donnelly, the national secretary of the Community and Public Sector Union, will take on the role as the next head of the trade movement in Australia, after the resignation of Sally McManus.

The Australian Council of Trade Unions’ secretary and its president, Michele O’Neil, revealed last month they would be stepping down after eight years together as the first all-female leadership team in the ACTU’s 99-year history, playing a major role in shaping the Albanese government’s workplace agenda.

On Monday, the ACTU executive met to elect 44-year-old Donnelly, who will be among the peak body’s youngest secretaries.

In a statement, Donnelly said it was a “tremendous honour” to take on the “important role”.

“Following in the footsteps of Sally is no easy task,” she said. “She has dedicated her life to fighting for fairer, safer and more secure workplaces.

“I am eager to get to work delivering real outcomes for working people and advancing the interests of workers across the country.

“Most of all, I am looking forward to meeting union members from every corner of Australia and serving alongside you as we work to lift living standards and secure a better future for all.”

Donnelly, who started her career as a lawyer in private practice, has led the CPSU for seven years, rising through the ranks after spearheading the union’s federal court case enabling public servants to participate in the nationwide “Your Rights at Work” campaign, which opposed the Howard government’s WorkChoices legislation.

In a statement, the CPSU said membership had grown by 23% during her tenure, with Donnelly pursuing flexible working arrangements, including a removal of caps on the number of days staff can work from home, delivering 18 weeks’ paid parental leave for both parents and leading the campaign to reverse the government outsourcing work to private consultancy firms.

Under her leadership, the CPSU has recently taken the tax office to the Fair Work Commission over alleged violations of the Albanese government’s “same job same pay” laws.

In a statement, the public service minister, Katy Gallagher, congratulated Donnelly and said the pair had worked “closely together” to rebuild “the public service and strengthened its capacity and capability to deliver for Australians”.

“Melissa has been a tireless advocate for public servants,” Gallagher said. “I know she’ll bring that same determination and experience to standing up for workers across Australia.”

McManus said Donnelly had “overwhelming support” across the union movement, describing her as “smart, strategic and completely focused on the needs of working people”.

“The average union member is a 44-year-old working mother and so is Melissa. She’s a year younger than I was when I took up the office and represents generational change,” she said.

“With two school-age children and having led a large union, she well knows the pressures working people are under. She has my full support, and I look forward to assisting her as she steps into the role.”

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Mother of Briton fatally shot by father in Texas urges Miliband to press US for new inquiry
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Josh Halliday North of England editor
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Jane Coates says foreign secretary should draw attention to coroner’s finding that Lucy Harrison was unlawfully killed

The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is being urged to push US authorities to reopen an investigation into a man who shot dead his 23-year-old British daughter while she was visiting him in Texas.

Lucy Harrison, from Warrington in Cheshire, was fatally shot on 10 January 2025, the day before she was due to fly home to the UK.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Her father, Kris Harrison, who admitted holding the pistol at the time, has never been arrested.

A Texas grand jury decided not to prosecute the telecoms executive, originally from Liverpool, last year after what Lucy’s family described as an “inadequate” police investigation.

Earlier this year, the senior coroner for Cheshire ruled that Lucy had been unlawfully killed and that Harrison’s actions amounted to gross negligence manslaughter.

Lucy’s mother, Jane Coates, on Monday wrote to Miliband urging him to press the US authorities to reopen the investigation into her former husband, in light of the coroner’s findings.

She wrote: “I understand that the British government cannot interfere in the American justice system or direct US prosecutors to take a particular course of action.

“However, the Foreign Office can use appropriate diplomatic channels to draw attention to the coroner’s conclusion, raise the serious concerns surrounding the original investigation and ask the relevant US authorities to review the case.”

A number of UK politicians, including the former justice secretary Robert Buckland, are also urging Miliband to intervene.

Buckland said on Monday: “This is such a terrible situation for Lucy’s family and there are serious questions here that must be answered. This case must be reopened in the US.

“The new foreign secretary, lord chancellor and, indeed, prime minister should pursue this for those grieving for someone who left us at such a young age and in the most appalling of circumstances.”

Harrison, a telecoms executive, had bought a pistol for $500 (£370) from a colleague two years before Lucy’s death. Gun owners over the age of 21 are not required to obtain training or a licence in Texas, one of the most firearms-friendly US states.

An inquest in Cheshire was told that Lucy had expressed concern to friends about her two younger siblings being in the house with her father’s Glock 9mm semi-automatic pistol.

It also heard that the pair had an argument about Donald Trump in the hours before the fatal shooting, although Lucy’s family say this is not why she was shot.

Despite an officer smelling alcohol on Harrison’s breath, he was not breathalysed. During his police interview, a Texas ranger explained to Harrison that the “gun would only discharge if the trigger was pressed”, according to a report released to the UK inquest. “Kris said ‘OK’,” it noted. Yet authorities said they were unable to arrest Harrison because they could not prove intent.

Sarah Hall, the Labour MP for Warrington South who has raised the case in parliament, said the Foreign Office should also address why the family was not given “adequate support” from the UK government after Lucy’s death.

In her letter to Miliband, Coates said: “I must also express my disappointment at the response we received from the previous administration. There was no meaningful action to help us seek justice.

“The formation of the new government under Andy Burnham has given us renewed hope. We have been struck by the prime minister’s determined tone, and by his emphasis on taking action and getting things done. We sincerely hope that this approach will extend to Lucy’s case.”

The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.

Lucy Harrison, from Warrington in Cheshire, was fatally shot on 10 January 2025. Her father, Kris Harrison, who admitted holding the pistol at the time, has never been arrested.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Harvey Nichols warns it could collapse without rescue deal, as bidders circle
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Jasper Jolly
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group is frontrunner to buy Knightsbridge-headquartered department store chain

Can Harvey Nichols find its way back to being Ab Fab again?

Business live – latest updates

Harvey Nichols has warned that it will not be able to survive another year without new investment, as bidders for the Knightsbridge-headquartered department store chain circle.

The retailer’s Hong Kong-based owner, Dickson Poon, put it up for sale in June, with Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group aiming to buy it for about £40m.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Harvey Nichols used to attract a high-profile clientele, including the late Diana, Princess of Wales, and its place in popular culture was confirmed in its 1990s heyday by the TV sitcom Absolutely Fabulous, which used the store as a symbol for luxury retail. Yet “Harvey Nicks” has struggled to adjust to increased competition from other shopping destinations, as well as the rise of online retail.

The company has not made a profit since the coronavirus pandemic locked out big-spending foreign tourists, and it reported a loss after tax of £105m after writing off inter-company loans for the year to 29 March 2025, according to accounts published over the weekend.

The directors warned that the company was not a going concern, because it would run out of money within the next year and that it had no agreements for new funding.

The accounts said that the company had received “a number of bids” to buy it, and that it was hoping to complete a deal within the next year.

FTSE 100 retailer Next had been interested in taking over the business, although it has withdrawn its interest, according to more recent reports.

That has left Ashley, the founder of the Sports Direct retail empire, as one of the frontrunners. Ashley, the controlling shareholder in Frasers, on Friday told the Financial Times that Harvey Nichols was in a “death spiral” and that it would be a “huge challenge” to turn it around.

Ashley has bought a series of struggling premium brands in recent years after starting out with a single sports shop. He said he would keep the Knightsbridge and Edinburgh stores, but rebrand other stores as House of Fraser or Flannels under his Frasers Group.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

Harvey Nichols was founded in 1831, as a linen shop. Its department store headquarters in Knightsbridge opened in 1889. In the last century it has been owned by Debenhams and the Burton Group, before Poon bought it in 1991 for £53m.

Poon oversaw an expansion outside London, with a Leeds branch opening in 1996. The chain has shops in Birmingham, Bristol, Dublin, Edinburgh and Manchester, as well as a series of restaurants including the one in London’s riverside Oxo Tower. Outside the UK it has a store in Riyadh, one in Dubai, two in Hong Kong and one in Kuwait.

Poon retired as a director in May. Harvey Nichols is led by Julia Goddard, who joined in 2024 from Alexander McQueen.

Israeli PM is insisting on a full Hamas disarmament before the deal can be implemented. Plus, what it feels like to get locked into an opera performance that lasts nearly 24 hours

Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected a US-backed 15-point peace plan for Gaza in a rare public break with Donald Trump. In a statement, Israel’s prime minister said he was confronting a “wave of rumours about Israeli weakness and Israeli withdrawals on all fronts” and rebuked US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Trump’s Board of Peace in July proposed the 15-point plan, which mandated that Hamas disarm in exchange for providing a full Israeli military withdrawal from the Gaza Strip and an eventual transition of power to an independent Palestinian national committee. Trump had said the agreement would be implemented in stages, but Netanyahu on Sunday said he wanted a full Hamas disarmament first in order to implement the deal.

What other developments have happened in the region? Iran has issued tough new demands for reopening the strait of Hormuz, while the United Arab Emirates said one of its ships was targeted by an Iranian missile over the weekend. Tehran said the strait of Hormuz would not open until the US “corrects its behaviour”. Yemen’s Tehran-aligned Houthis have claimed responsibility for an attack on a refinery in Saudi Arabia on Sunday morning.

What impact is the conflict having on seafarers in Hormuz? The US-Iran war has stranded up to 20,000 seafarers, mostly Indian and Filipino crews, with none knowing when the nightmare will end. Seventeen seafarers have died since hostilities began, the majority following Iranian strikes.

Chuck Schumer, the US Senate minority leader, and senators including Alex Padilla, Adam Schiff, Mark Warner, Elissa Slotkin and Raphael Warnock were among those in the room as a team of legal experts offered scenarios they might face in the coming months: an assault in real-time on the integrity of November’s election results from the right-wing and their Republican opponents.

What sort of exercises did they take part in? Justin Vail, who leads the DC office of the non-partisan advocacy group Protect Democracy, said: “These tabletop exercises are a standard planning tool for experts and stakeholders to prepare for potential scenarios. We’re not predicting exactly what would happen. But we do want to create a realistic context that can help us identify gaps, test our assumptions, and strengthen coordination, and then ultimately develop some recommendations to increase our preparedness.”

How has Trump been working to undermine confidence in US elections? Voting rights advocates pointed toward Trump’s July primetime address as indicative of the president’s intentions – rhetorical attacks on the integrity of voting machines and elections offices, potentially escalating into more direct interference. Trump threatened the broadcast licenses of networks that refused to carry that address live, and in his speech, he again implored Congress to pass the Save America Act, which would ban mail-in ballots nationwide and impose new identification requirements on voters when they register and report to polls.

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in Michigan, embraced Donald Trump’s suggestion that the two represent “VERY DIFFERENT” versions of the US, pledging to fight inequality while the president is “making billions of dollars off of you”.

“Yeah, he’s right,” El-Sayed told CNN when asked about a post by the US president that depicted an image of Trump and the first lady, Melania Trump, beside a photo of El-Sayed, who is Muslim, and his wife, Sarah Jukaku, wearing a hijab.

What did El-Sayed say? “One in which your overlords are two people who don’t like each other, but join in the interest of making billions of dollars off of you – or two people who genuinely love each other, enjoyed some pancakes together, want to come together to build the kind of America where they can raise a family and know that that family is going to have the good things. Donald Trump’s vision is the one you’re living in right now. Can you afford your gas? Can you afford your groceries?”

Donald Trump has appointed his staff secretary, Will Scharf, as the new White House counsel. Scharf, who helped the president win approval for his $400m ballroom, will replace David Warrington on 1 September.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has announced she is going to freeze her eggs and will be sharing the process online. The progressive New York congresswoman, 36, revealed her decision to undergo fertility treatment in a series of Instagram stories

Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States, has plummeted to its lowest water level since it was filled some 90 years ago, the latest sign of a deepening water crisis in the American west.

Mark Zuckerberg faces questions over why his superyacht reportedly declined to help a stranded boat. The Meta CEO was not personally on board at the time.

Some of Taylor Swift’s songs have been removed from videos posted on social media by Donald Trump’s campaign and the White House, silencing efforts to mock the pop star.

A weather station in central Shanghai recorded over 12 inches of rain in 24 hours, its highest 24-hour rainfall in more than 150 years of records, as more than a million people were moved to safety across eastern China as powerful Typhoon Dolphin made landfall.

Mutual aid groups that started giving out PPEs during Covid are now loaning air purifiers and distributing masks to fume-addled communities.

Spanning generations and multiple Indigenous societies and nations, Sarah Gilbert has picked highlights from In Light and Shadow, a new book tracing the visual importance of Indigenous photographers.

Flora Willson explains how she was swept up in his mad, miraculous marathon of a score as she enjoys – endures? – a 23-hour Richard Wagner marathon on a rock-hard seat in a heatwave at the Bayreuth festival in Germany. It sounds like … a challenge.

The world’s seas were hotter last month than in any July on record. Sea surface temperatures hit record highs for July on the Atlantic coast and western Mediterranean. Globally, the average sea surface temperature outside the cold polar regions was the highest on record for the month, beating the previous July record set in 2023.

The Perseid summer light show is back. Up to 100 meteors an hour may be visible under ideal conditions, according to Nasa. The American Meteor Society estimates 30 to 50 meteors an hour could be seen from rural regions in the US.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump officials offer cities tens of millions for Memphis-style police surges – with conditions
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: George Chidi
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
DoJ to give $300m for enforcement surges in four cities, as long as they abandon progressive ideologies on policing

The Trump administration is offering grants of tens of millions of dollars to cities across the US to create more Memphis-style enforcement surges – on the condition that they abandon progressive ideologies on policing.

The US Department of Justice says it will announce up to four finalist cities which will split $300m in grant funding under a federal “Model Cities” policing initiative (MCI) next month, setting the stage for some of the largest federal policing grants ever awarded to individual US cities.

In exchange for the funding, cities are required to comply with federal immigration enforcement requests, enact conservative policies on anti-homelessness rules, and potentially repay millions of dollars in the event of a surge in violent crime or “civil unrest”, according to a grant document.

The document cites Washington DC and Memphis, Tennessee – two cities with national guard troops patrolling the streets – as a model to emulate. The administration has so far defied calls to suspend its controversial taskforce in Memphis, following four officer-involved deaths since its launch last September.

“That’s not a model I’d be looking for,” said Steven Reed, the mayor of Montgomery, Alabama. Reed said he had seen the grant and passed on applying. “Everybody wants a quick fix, and no one wants to invest in the root cause of the issue,” he said.

Despite the significant funding boost on offer, Reed is one of several leaders of large municipalities with Democratic majorities who have signaled they will not even consider applying for the grant.

The justice department has offered policing grants to cities through programs of the office of community oriented policing services (Cops) since 1994, disbursing more than $20bn since then. The Cops office of the justice department offered city governments about $700m this fiscal year to supplement hiring, training and equipment.

The MCI, a product of funding from Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill, offers another $300m to two to four municipalities with more than 100,000 residents. Grant funding will last three years under the program.

Unlike most previous grants, awards will be seemingly be awarded after evaluation by senior political appointees in the justice department, and not through a more politically neutral recommendation process of peer review, said Amy Solomon, a senior fellow at the Council on Criminal Justice, who previously served as assistant attorney general of the office of justice programs under Joe Biden.

The grant guidelines require applicants to have documented “buy-in and support” across the local government – mayors, sheriff’s offices, city councils and county commissions – as a condition of approval.

The initiative focuses on reducing violent crime, to “surge substantial, targeted federal funding into select cities”, according to a justice department presentation on the grants. City governments can use the money to hire more police and fund substance abuse recovery programs, prisoner re-entry programs, facilities, training and other initiatives.

A justice department spokesperson claimed jurisdictions have “expressed intense interest” in the initiative.

“Senior department leaders have made themselves available in a variety of formats to answer questions about how cities can submit the most competitive application possible,” a spokesperson replied to emailed questions. “[The justice department] looks forward to reviewing applications from across the country that demonstrate how creative solutions and close teamwork between local and federal partners can achieve the same dramatic gains in public safety seen in Washington DC and Memphis. This is the Make America Safe Again mission in action.”

The department did not answer questions about the repayment provision, and declined to say whether it had yet received eligible applications, or whether city governments would be required to accept the activation of the national guard under the grant program.

Sign up to Breaking News US

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

“Awards under this funding opportunity will include a condition (the specific terms of which will govern the award) related to the future reimbursement of the costs associated with federal law enforcement intervention or assistance provided in the event of a surge in violent crime or public disorder,” the grant document states. “The condition will, generally speaking, require an MCI Department of Justice award recipient to fulfill any such future reimbursement obligation(s) incurred in accordance with its terms.”

“To my knowledge, this funding condition is unprecedented,” Solomon said. “It forces applicants to agree – preemptively – to foot the bill for future, unspecified federal interventions in their own back yards.”

It is among the sharpest sticking points for municipal leaders and critics, who view the grant as a $300m enticement to accept a package of Trump’s ideological interests.

The grant requires municipalities to directly support immigration law enforcement operations. It also requires the enforcement of prohibitions on open illicit drug use, urban camping, loitering, squatting, and “standards that address individuals who are a danger to themselves or others and suffer from serious mental illness or substance use”.

It calls for assisted outpatient treatment for people experiencing mental health problems that have led to homelessness, but it repudiates the housing-first model for homelessness relief by requiring compliance with treatment to retain housing.

Few municipalities with populations larger than 100,000 residents also have Republican political majorities. Fewer still are in states with Republican governors, which would be a realistic requirement for a national guard activation.

“In other cities, they have killed American citizens for reasons that turned out to be lies. Do we really need this in Billings?” said Karen Jarussi, speaking to the city council of Billings, Montana, this week.

The Billings city council voted 9-1 against forwarding a grant application for the MCI. The city of San Bernardino, California, withdrew a vote on its agenda on Tuesday after public outcry.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Dr Fauci made mistakes. But his persecution is a travesty | Margaret Sullivan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Margaret Sullivan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
It’s easy to second-guess decisions made during the pandemic. That doesn’t justify the Republicans’ politicized response

L
ike the rest of us, Anthony Fauci is far from perfect. His influential guidance, as the country’s top infectious-disease specialist during the height of the Covid-19 pandemic, certainly didn’t get everything right.

A great deal about the deadly disease – where it came from, how it spread, how best to protect the public – was unknown, or was being learned midstream, during a crisis.

Decisions needed to be made in real time, and those decisions had major consequences.

Now, with the benefit of hindsight, we can see more clearly. It’s easy to second-guess Fauci, and others who guided policy about masks, research and closures of businesses and schools.

But surely, the 85-year-old physician and immunologist doesn’t deserve what’s happening right now, as a highly politicized Republican-led Senate committee attempted to humiliate him, possibly trap him into perjuring himself, and then voted – along party lines – to hold him in contempt of Congress.

No surprise, really, that Fauci, now retired from his public post, invoked the fifth amendment more than 100 times during last week’s Senate committee hearing.

That’s the action that – though reasonable enough given all the circumstances – is the supposed impetus for holding him in contempt. Now the committee has referred the matter to the justice department for possible criminal prosecution.

Fauci could see the writing on the wall as this trumped-up hearing began. In his opening statement, he singled out the Kentucky senator Rand Paul, the Republican committee chairperson.

“The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, ‘behind bars’,” Fauci said. “Any reasonable person who has followed his unhinged obsession with me would readily come to the same conclusion.”

Paul has long held that Fauci funded research in China that began the pandemic, and then lied about it. Fauci strongly denies all of that.

Joe Biden saw something like this coming, which is why he pre-emptively pardoned Fauci before leaving the White House in early 2025. Since then, Senate Republicans, led by Rand Paul, have subpoenaed and released more than a thousand pages of Fauci’s diary, pointing to inconsistencies in his private beliefs and his public guidance.

Biden’s pardon doesn’t cover anything that happened after January of last year, nor does it protect Fauci from state or local prosecution. He remains vulnerable.

Granted, it’s never ideal for someone so influential or prominent to take the fifth. It can’t help but look like he’s hiding something.

But many legal experts understand exactly why he did it.

Fauci “knew the point of the hearing was to find a basis to prosecute him,” Michael Gerhardt, a University of North Carolina law professor, told PBS. “He found the safest way to minimize that from happening.”

Fauci is far from the only public official to invoke the right not to answer potentially incriminating questions, whether during a trial, a hearing or something else.

In fact, Donald Trump did just that – more than 400 times – during a civil deposition in 2022, run by the New York attorney general’s office during its civil fraud investigation into the Trump organization’s business and financial practices. And so have many other prominent public officials for a whole host of reasons.

This politicized persecution of Fauci goes back years, as rightwing commentators and politicians made him into their supervillain.

Latching on to some of Fauci’s emails as early as 2021, Republican senators and members of Congress called for his immediate firing from his high-level governmental post. And for years, Fauci and his family received repeated and, he felt, credible death threats.

Rightwing media joined right in.

Steve Bannon’s podcast was kicked off Twitter/X (before the Musk era) after he called for Fauci’s beheading, saying of Fauci and the former FBI chief Christopher Wray: “I’d put the heads on pikes.” (A Bannon representative claimed the comments were metaphorical.)

So much craziness. So much dangerous rhetoric. An “unhinged obsession”, in Fauci’s own words.

Not all the criticism of Fauci belongs in that category. The respected academic Zeynep Tufekci has posited that the government’s shifting pandemic guidance – and the failures of transparency by government officials, including Fauci – may have harmed public trust at a crucial time.

“Just when it was needed most, some of the officials in charge of our Covid response undermined it,” she wrote in 2024.

Legitimate debate about what went wrong – and even who was at fault – is reasonable. There may well be something to learn from it.

But that’s a far cry from the travesty of what we’ve just seen take place on Capitol Hill.

And, lamentably, there’s little reason to believe that Trump’s weaponized justice department will put an end to it.

Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: I’ve discovered the joys of postcard-writing in middle age | Amanda Uhle
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Amanda Uhle
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
There are profound rewards of handwritten correspondence in our digital age

I sent my first postcard, as a six-year old, to Olympian Mary Lou Retton, who returned an autographed black and white photo of herself in a wide smile and chic haircut. “‘GOOD LUCK USA ‘84” it said.

There followed four relatively fallow decades for me as a postcard sender or receiver until last year, when I became enchanted by the infinite possibilities available in four by six inches.

I received at least five dozen and lost count of how many I stamped and disseminated. Once ubiquitous as correspondence, advertising and more, postcards in 2026 are exceptional: a bite-sized miracle that’s improved my relationships, my attention span, and my art and writing skills. And let me tell you about the surge of dopamine I routinely experience under the fluorescent lights of my local post office lobby.

Around the time I was embarking on my book tour last year, I had amassed several dozen vintage postcards from a lifetime of thrift-store forays: oddball 1960s hotel lobbies, corny Florida beaches, dusty national landmarks. They’re so inexpensive and so charming, I rarely resisted grabbing a few when I saw good ones. I’d occasionally tuck them into gift enclosures for friends but I used postcards sparingly compared to how fast I was accumulating them.

With so many on hand and an imminent plan to travel to 18 states, the only solution was to disburse them widely. It’s taken me until middle age to remember that holding on to things I love is almost never as much fun as sending them out into the world.

I stamped 40 postcards and wrote my own address on the back. Because I wanted to spend part of my time on the road documenting the trip, I also packed some postcard-sized watercolor paper & paint.

At bookstores, I arrayed the cards in front of readers while I signed books and encouraged people to take one and send me a note about anything on their minds. “Or take a card home and if you don’t write to me maybe it will remind you to write someone else in your life,” I always suggested.

People told me they love mail but never send it, that they only get bills in the mailbox, that they kept all of their high-school boyfriend’s letters, that they have three email accounts and all of them are full of garbage. I have five email accounts, I’d tell them, which generate even more garbage.

I’m not naive enough to think I was starting a nationwide handwritten mail revolution, but these short conversations, like the postcards themselves, were satisfying and real. The cards were a tiny way to show my appreciation for the book buyers I met but also a secret way for me to seed meaningful exchanges with strangers. (Even memoirists tire of talking about themselves at some point.)

Interstitial moments on the tour were filled with brief notes to friends, or if I had more time and the right mood, a little watercolor of a great omelet I ate in LA, the facade of a tavern in Cincinnati, or whatever I saw and wanted to remember. A big frameable oil painting on canvas is a commitment, but postcards are practically scrap paper and can be completed in the brief window an impulse lasts.

Early on, I deemed myself as worthy a recipient of these tiny missives as anyone else. I wanted to discover what would happen to these cherished little cards on their journey through bureaucracy. And of course I wondered: who might get a glimpse or read a few lines and how might that change what I write?

Given the current state of the US Postal Service, it takes a real message-in-a-bottle level of blind faith to send any piece of mail these days but my postcards, each of them one-of-a-kind whether they were original paintings or Kodachrome wonders from decades ago, felt risky in a new way.

That little bump of danger was only the beginning. I have never regretted the minute or two I spend composing a note to someone. Half of the back of a postcard is the just-right size for a message, which the writer is free to lengthen or shorten by calibrating the size of their handwriting. Letters are intimidating.

Texts are disposable (and even editable or recallable for those plagued by second thoughts). There’s an improvisational freedom in a dashed off few lines, written by a human hand with a pen and without much rumination. Even in the mere moments it takes to read or write a postcard, the brain is activating in ways it simply can’t with thumb-typing. And how beguiling to see the way a friend or lover loops their vowels or blurs the dots above letters, so much richer than the emoji-punctuated texts I’m guilty of sending a lot more often than I send postcards.

Some proponents of the nouveau analog movement will brag about bricking their smart phones all weekend or raw-dogging a cross-country flight, but that kind of bravado really isn’t necessary. I have a job. I have a teenager. I’d obviously be dead meat without my iPhone, but becoming a postcard person hasn’t made me into a luddite.

Writing, or reading, a postcard is a miniature but significant 60-second connection with someone else. The kind of thing almost everyone on earth urgently needs now more than ever. Call it a meditation or an intention if you frame the world that way. Postcards are just a little flourish you can add into your rotation of texts and Slacks and however else you constantly communicate, and they generate such profound rewards.

Seven months ago I took part in a book festival in Nashville. To pass some time I painted the circus-like tents set up on its capitol mall. The stripes and primary colors felt old-fashioned and pure, much like the festival itself which united thousands of readers and hundreds of writers, and that day was sharing space with a spirited No Kings rally despite some oppressive humidity.

I’m an absolute amateur at painting, long reconciled to accepting my efforts as meditative for me but not gallery material. But this one was good: the red and white and yellow parallel stripes against a sapphire southern sky. It was also a perfect capsule of my really happy afternoon in an unfamiliar city. I couldn’t wait to see it pop up five states away.

I walk into the harshly-lit post office most weekdays with a welcome sense of anticipation. Sometimes my PO box is empty. Sometimes, I find catalogs and invoices and tucked among them are a picture postcard or two.

When my own inept but genuine little pictures show up I get a minute to fondly remember a place or some people from a few weeks back. My paintings are returned to me with a patina of their journey–a subtle orange sorting barcode, a knick off the corner.

On the back of an image of Historic Williamsburg, a guy wrote to me about the best Chinese food in San Antonio. A woman from a Detroit suburb wrote me about something her father had in common with mine, on a card featuring an oversized cactus in a cotton candy sunset.

Maybe it’s a symptom of digital fatigue but I think I could go the rest of my life without ever again interacting with those cartoonish avatars of my friends that emerge in group chats or the realer-than-real AI videos of a shih tzu icing a birthday cake. Isn’t it infinitely better to get lost in the turquoise of an ocean scene from some vacation spot in an era when the world’s water was bluer?

This many months later I should probably write off the Nashville painting as the single anomaly in all these dozens that never made it home. I was sure I mailed it so maybe it’s lodged between something mechanical in a letter-sorting machine in Tennessee. Or maybe that one slipped out of my outgoing pile and wafted into the No Kings crowd or got swept up in the book festival refuse. Or maybe I misaddressed it, or it misdelivered. My little painting could be displayed on some stranger’s bedroom bureau right now or it could show up in tomorrow’s post office haul. I suppose I don’t really need that particular rendering of that Nashville afternoon; I bet there are six thousand pictures of it on Instagram right now. Even so, I’m happy I get to carry that little iota of hope into my next mail run.

Confederations write open letter damning Fifa president

Concacaf president Montagliani seen as top contender

Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf will push for Gianni Infantino to resign after writing an open letter calling for “leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it”.

In a dramatic escalation of the war that has threatened to tear football apart since details emerged of the Fifa president’s failed Football Forward Enterprise scheme, the three governing bodies accused Infantino of “trust broken through deception” and condemned his failure to acknowledge that the proposal should not have been unilaterally launched.

The three confederations are understood to have started preliminary discussions about the organisation of new competitions amid Uefa’s repeated threats to boycott Fifa events. As things stand, next month’s under-20 women’s World Cup could take place without the presence of European teams and alternative options are being sought.

The letter is signed by the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, his AFC counterpart, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, and the Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani. Efforts to unite around a suitable candidate to replace Infantino have stepped up since his privately-backed plan was revealed and Montagliani is believed to be among the leading contenders.

“Leadership in football is not a possession,” part of the letter reads. “It is not about holding – or demanding – power to be held. It is a duty of service to the football family that entrusts it. When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned.”

It strongly criticises Fifa’s response to the crisis, which saw a meeting between a small number of senior staff in Rabat followed by an apology from Infantino that appeared not to show remorse for the scheme itself.

“It treats this as a failure of communication, when what football witnessed was a failure of judgment,” the letter says. “It did not acknowledge that the proposal itself was inherently wrong. There remains no recognition that attempting to sell an interest in the Fifa World Cup was a profound failure of judgment – not just a procedural misstep, but a fundamental breach of trust with the very institutions Fifa exists to serve.”

The three presidents also call for an independent review, conducted by a body outside of football, into the scandal. Fifa had previously committed to presenting a full report to the Fifa Council at its next scheduled meeting. The letter also directly addresses concerns that countries may lose out on financial aid under a different leadership, saying it is “[not] about any member association losing the support it has earned, despite the fearmongering directed at our leadership to suggest otherwise.”

The letter concludes: “There is silence where there should be accountability, distance where there should be openness … Football’s strength has always been its unity. We call for that unity to be honoured now, with leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it.”

Any candidates to run for the Fifa election must announce their bid by 18 November. The confederations are understood to consider all options on the table in their push for Infantino to be replaced, provided they fit within Fifa’s statutes and governance framework.

While the letter outlines the stances of the three confederations, and particularly their leaderships, the story is more complicated within individual member associations. Few outside Europe have been willing to come out publicly against Infantino and only a small minority have been tempted to recall the letters of support they had sent backing his re-election next March. Additionally the influential African and South American confederations, Caf and Conmebol, have both come out backing Infantino in recent days.

A number of larger member associations are understood to have written to Infantino asking for a meeting in which he would be required to explain his actions around the FFE scheme, with no response received so far. Nor has Infantino been in touch personally with federations to address his leading role in the ongoing turmoil.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: I should be happy to have a pigeon for a friend. But she wouldn’t be my first choice | Emma Beddington
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Emma Beddington
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Truman Capote had a ‘crow bro’; Dickens had a raven. And I get standoffish Susan, who has never brought me a present or perched on my shoulder

O
ne of the greatest failures of my life to date (along with my sons’ shameful inability to eat apples correctly, down to the core) is my inability to attract a “crow bro”. That’s a corvid companion, and more and more people apparently have them, including Washington Post journalist Caitlin Gibson, who recently wrote about hers, Cormac, a charismatic fish crow with a taste for cashews.

It’s not a new phenomenon – Charles Dickens had a pet raven, Grip; Truman Capote had a crow called Lola – but thanks to CrowTok (a wholesome online enclave where people post enthusiastically about the exploits of their feathery familiars), there seem to be more corvid whisperers than ever. Yet however many unshelled peanuts (the recommended treat) I scatter, I can never seem to get a shred of attention from a black-feathered beauty.

Corvids are clever and sophisticated. They can spontaneously problem-solve, use tools, are capable of lying (and of working out when they’re being lied to), have complex responses to the deaths of their comrades, hold – and pass on – grudges, even hold down jobs (rooks in the Puy du Fou theme park pick up cigarette butts in return for food). They’re razor-sharp, and they don’t want to hang out with me. That stings.

I might not have a crow bro, but I do have a pigeon pal. Susan – a mysterious ringed white pigeon – arrived three years ago and never left. Does she bring me presents or perch on my shoulder? Absolutely not. Does she let me anywhere near her? Also no. She lives on our roof, shunning the two elaborate homes my husband built for her, shouting at us until I put out the specialist pigeon food I buy from an agricultural merchant a 20-minute drive away. Only then will she deign to descend to eat, under my servile, respectfully distant supervision (I have to stand guard or other pigeons chase her away). She pecks at the food, eyeing me warily, as if I’m about to put her in a pie, then leaves. No one would make a TikTok of this, but it’s a friendship of sorts, I like to think. Maybe we get the bird friends we deserve?

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: A TikTok PM may seem laughable – but reaching young people like me might just keep Labour in office | Lucy O’Brien
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Lucy O’Brien
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Andy Burnham and his social media team know how to connect with us. We’re no fools, though – this has to be backed by serious policies

S
trapped up in his navy suit, blue tie and charmingly nerdy glasses, Andy Burnham entered No 10 newly appointed as our fifth prime minister in four years. I didn’t watch this historic scene live on BBC News. Instead, I saw a 10-second clip on TikTok, with a viral Love Island soundbite: “A hot new bombshell has entered the villa.” Not exactly the introduction you might expect from a world leader – or is it?

The video sent millions of eyes rolling backwards and many flocking to the comments, cringing at the idea of British politics succumbing to ridiculous social media trends. Critics have called his social media strategy “trivial” and a “distraction”. After years of leadership turmoil and a flailing Labour government under Keir Starmer, should we really be making light of yet another transfer of power on a platform designed for teenagers?

More than a month into the job, Burnham’s team has continued the shenanigans on his own accounts (where he has more than a million followers across Instagram and TikTok combined). Scroll down his feed and you will still find a fair amount of silliness, but the tide is starting to change.

One video starts with the PM defending “barms” – the northern-preferred nickname for a bread roll (it’s definitely a bap, sorry Andy) – before seamlessly flowing into a metaphor for his strategy of devolution and handing back power to local councils. It now has more than 850,000 views.

Similarly, when he talked through his education strategy on TikTok, cheekily transitioning between holding a graduation cap and hard hat, his audience listened. That video has 3m views and is flooded with comments of people feeling alarmingly inspired by his plans. “Have we actually maybe finally got a good one?” one user said. Finally, it seems we have a politician who comes across like a real person who knows how to talk to other real people (even if it does remind you of your dad trying to prove he’s down with the kids) – and for gen Z members like me, it’s working.

Social media popularity isn’t the end goal, but it is the first hurdle. If you want young people to vote for you, you have to find a way to make them care. You have to meet them where they are. And in today’s attention-span economy, that is the hardest job of all. Reuters’ 2026 Digital News Report found that, globally, 52% of 18- to 24-year-olds use social media, video networks and AI chatbots as the main way of getting their news.

This article includes content provided by TikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

If you’re over 30, Burnham’s videos may seem clumsy – embarrassing, even. But don’t get it twisted, the PM’s team knows exactly what it’s doing. Burnham has tapped into something I have long understood: if we have any chance of overturning the general sense of misery in this country, we need to get young people to believe in politics again. This is the first time in my adult life I have heard my peers say they actually like what the PM is doing, that they think he’s a decent guy, and that there’s a reason to hope again.

Since the Brexit referendum in 2016, I’ve witnessed my generation become increasingly disillusioned with politics. Faced with crippling student loans, the risk of becoming a Neet, or the seeming impossibility of getting on the property ladder, young people have had little to hope for under previous governments. Rebuilding the PM’s trust among the young is the only way to dismantle more than a decade of political alienation.

What Burnham is doing is nothing new. Labour understood the power of social media to rally younger voters during the 2024 general election, and it paid off. YouGov polling documents that 41% of those aged 18-24 voted Labour, rising to 45% among those aged 25-29. Keir Starmer was the first British PM to launch a personal TikTok profile, where he tried – and failed – to maintain Labour’s initial momentum. Ultimately, his stuffy and ineffective communication style ended up alienating the very voters that handed him his mandate in the first place. Hopefully, Burnham won’t make the same mistake.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

TikTok fame won’t buy Burnham unwavering support. Nor should it. We might be a fickle generation, but we’re not stupid. No one really thinks a few viral videos equates to the PM effecting real and lasting change. But getting young people on side is essential work; work that could keep Labour in government for a generation, if he plays his cards right.

Lucy O’Brien is a deputy audience editor at the Guardian

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/8/.text:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino has come under renewed fire as a joint letter from three confederations – UEFA, CONCACAF and AFC – declared that football “belongs to no individual”.

Infantino has received scathing criticism ever since launching, and then withdrawing within days, a plan to bring in private investment into FIFA competitions, including the World Cup.

FIFA had hit back on Saturday, claiming “a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine” football’s governing body and Infantino.

However, Monday’s letter from the governing bodies of European football (UEFA), North and Central America (CONCACAF) and Asia (AFC), showed his critics were unbowed.

“Leadership in football is not a possession. It is not about holding – or demanding – power to be held,” they wrote.

“When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned,” the confederations added.

The three confederations called for a fully ⁠independent review into the stake sale proposal.

“Football’s strength has ⁠always been its unity,” the statement concluded. “We call for that unity to ‌be honoured now, for leadership that serves football, not ‌seeks ‌to command it.”

They also criticised a FIFA emergency meeting in Morocco last week, saying there was only one elected official present, while also calling for an independent review which FIFA would have ⁠no role in, to determine what led to this “profound failure of judgement”.

On Friday, Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) President ⁠Lise Klaveness, seen by some as a potential candidate to replace Infantino, called on the 56-year-old to step down from the presidency immediately. Klaveness has long been an outspoken critic of Infantino.

After quelling in-house dissent at the emergency meeting on Wednesday, FIFA apologised to the 211 federations and Infantino rallied his support among the six confederations that ⁠make up the world governing body.

Africa’s confederation CAF released a statement on behalf of its 54 members backing Infantino on Thursday, with CONCACAF member Mexico following suit along with South American countries Argentina, Paraguay, Ecuador and Bolivia.

On Friday, as Infantino attended the inauguration of Colombia’s new President Abelardo De La Espriella ⁠in Cali, FIFA released a blistering attack on the president’s critics, saying attempts to challenge his leadership must follow the governing body’s statutes and democratic procedures.

FIFA also echoed the statements of several of the bodies that supported Infantino, as well as one from South American confederation CONMEBOL.

FIFA’s ‌statement came after reports by The Daily Telegraph about payments made by UEFA to a former employee during Infantino’s time as the European governing body’s general secretary, allegations he has denied and that FIFA has rejected as unfounded.

Almost 70 of FIFA’s 211-member associations have said publicly they will ‌vote ‌for Infantino, with about a dozen either withdrawing previously promised support or saying they will not vote for him.

UEFA apart, the confederations that say they have lost confidence in Infantino are not completely united, with several Asian nations backing him as well as Mexico from CONCACAF.
