https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Car owners should challenge insurers on steep price hikes and ‘call their bluff’, Asic says
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Luca Ittimani
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Regulator finds many insurers raising premiums faster than inflation and advises customers to ask for better deals

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Car owners should challenge motor insurers over steep premium hikes, the corporate regulator advises, after finding many companies were raising prices faster than inflation.

In a report released on Tuesday, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (Asic) found that none of the eight insurers it reviewed adequately explained the reasons behind premium calculations to customers or why prices had changed in quote or renewal documents.

“Most insurers gave only generic explanations in supplementary documents, with some providing no explanations at all,” the Asic commissioner Alan Kirkland said.

Insurance premiums have been a major household expense and inflation trigger in recent years, although the industry has not faced the same sort of scrutiny as other consumer sectors, such as supermarkets.

Premiums are an unavoidable cost for most households but are rising faster than most prices in the economy.

Car insurance premiums increased 8% in the 2025 financial year, according to Asic, far outpacing inflation. Consumer group Choice estimates that they rose 3.1% in just the first four months of 2026.

Comprehensive car insurance premiums rose by $111 in the year to June, to $2,460 on average, Canstar has estimated.

Asic’s report uncovered poor price transparency across the sector, although it did not identify the companies in each case.

The regulator found that about one in three customers who contacted their insurer before they renewed got a lower premium without any change to their policy.

“The insurers bank on a lot of their customers not taking any action when they get a premium increase,” Kirkland said.

“You should call their bluff – demand answers, challenge them on the increase and ask for a better deal.”

Five of the insurers surveyed charged consumers 10% to 20% less if they paid their premium annually instead of in instalments, although none made the savings clear in the renewal notices, according to the regulator.

Kirkland said the companies’ disclosure practices stopped customers from understanding, challenging or comparing premium increases.

“There is no excuse why some insurers cannot communicate such a basic benefit to customers,” Kirkland said.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

Five of those surveyed failed to show previous-year comparisons for insured value or excess on renewal notices. Another scattered past and present costs across different pages, making price comparisons difficult.

The Insurance Council of Australia said it was exploring options to explain premiums more clearly to customers.

The representative body said motor vehicle claim costs had risen 47% since 2020 amid higher costs for repairs and parts.

“Insurers recognise the need to support customers to understand what they are paying and why,” a spokesperson said.

“This is a highly competitive market, and we encourage every customer to talk to their insurer and shop around at renewal.”

Customer dissatisfaction with car insurance has been on the rise.

Asic’s internal dispute resolution data shows that general insurance was the most complained about financial product across the financial services industry last financial year.

More than half of general insurance complaints related to motor vehicle products, with premiums the most complained about issue.

AAMI, Suncorp Insurance, Allianz, NRMA, RACV, RAC, Youi and Territory Insurance Office had their comprehensive and third‑party car insurance renewal and disclosure documents reviewed as part of the report.

The insurers were contacted for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Only spending outlet for man accused of helping to control a third of Europe’s cocaine supply will be prison tuck shop

It sounds like the penal equivalent of five stars: a private gym and library, daily outings to the exercise yard and a landing cleared of other prisoners.

Daniel Kinahan’s first full day inside the walls of Portlaoise prison on Monday, however, marked a drastic change from his luxury lifestyle in the United Arab Emirates.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The alleged leader of the Kinahan organised crime group is confined to a cell for about 20 hours a day, and instead of presiding over an empire said to be worth hundreds of millions of euros his only outlet for expenditure is the tuck shop.

The facilities, it turns out, are meagre consolation – a treadmill, some free weights and limited reading material. “The so-called gym and library are nothing much,” one source told the Irish Times. “The gym is probably slightly bigger than a box room in a house.”

That is the reality facing Kinahan, 49, for months until his trial – and possibly decades if convicted.

The Dubliner has not been convicted of any crime and remains innocent before the law, but his extradition on Sunday represents a victory for the Irish state and law enforcement agencies across the world.

Kinahan was named a leader of a cartel said to control about a third of Europe’s cocaine supply, along with running criminal sidelines in firearms and racketeering. From his base in Dubai he had appeared impervious to such allegations for almost a decade, while becoming an influential figure in sport through his boxing management company MTK Global, which arranged championship bouts.

That changed after the US offered a reward of up to $5m (£3.7m) for information that led to his arrest or conviction. The US treasury department said the Kinahan group had engaged in a gang war with another group in Ireland and Spain, “resulting in numerous murders”.

The US bounty helped Ireland to secure an extradition treaty with the UAE last year, paving the way for Kinahan’s arrest in Dubai in April on foot of an Irish warrant.

After failing to block extradition, Kinahan was flown in an Irish government jet to Casement aerodrome on Sunday and taken to the criminal courts of justice in central Dublin where he was charged with directing organised crime.

after newsletter promotion

Told by one of the three judges that a bail application would have to be made to the high court, the prisoner was phlegmatic. “I think we know I won’t be getting bail, but thank you,” he said.

Observers at the hearing noted that Kinahan, wearing a black hoodie, black tracksuit bottoms and white trainers, looked older than the photographs that show a smiling, more youthful figure. He was pale, reflecting his incarceration since April.

Crowds lined part of the route to watch as he was driven in a Garda car – not a blast-proof prison van, as originally expected – to Portlaoise, a high-security prison 50 miles (80km) outside Dublin that used to house republican paramilitaries and is now home to drug gang members and others convicted of serious crimes.

Kinahan is the sole prisoner on a landing in A block that usually hosts eight inmates. During visits to the yard, which has wire netting to prevent contraband being dropped in, he will be alone. He will be served breakfast at 8am, lunch at 12.30pm and supper at 4.30pm and have a tuck shop account to buy personal items from the prison shop.

Video calls will afford contact with his wife and children in Dubai. A glass pane will separate him from in-person visitors. Kinahan is scheduled to return to the non-jury court on 5 October.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: People flocking to Spain to view solar eclipse could spark more ‘devastating’ wildfires
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Stephen Burgen in Tarragona
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Northern Spain will be one of the best places in world to view phenomenon with 460,000 extra visitors expected

Authorities in Spain have warned of an increased risk of fires when hundreds of thousands of people head to the hills and beaches to get a better view of Wednesday’s total solar eclipse.

“The vegetation is extraordinarily dry and the smallest spark or carelessness could lead to devastating forest fires,” the environment minister, Sara Aagesen, said on a visit to Niebla in the south of the country, the site of Spain’s latest fire.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Relentless heat and scarce rainfall have created ideal conditions for wildfires that have scarred swathes of Spain in recent weeks, including a huge blaze west of the capital, Madrid.

Police estimate that about 1.5m additional car journeys will be made on Wednesday, and there are fears that the volume of traffic could block access for emergency vehicles if fires break out in rural areas. Parking on hard shoulders or close to dry vegetation has been banned, as have barbecues and fireworks.

Spain is among the best locations in Europe to view the total solar eclipse. The finance ministry says it expects 460,000 overseas tourists to visit specifically to see the eclipse.

As a precautionary measure, the Valencia region has closed its natural parks and banned walking on rural footpaths.

On Monday, the national weather agency, AEMET, said July was mainland Spain’s joint-hottest month since records began in 1961. Last month was also mainland Spain’s driest July on record with just 4.3mm of rain falling, representing just 26% of the normal precipitation for the time of year.

Human-caused climate breakdown is supercharging extreme weather across the world, and is responsible for a higher likelihood of fire and bigger burned areas in southern Europe.

Hospitals are on alert for possible eye damage to people who do not wear the protective sunglasses that have been handed out free all over the country before the eclipse. Six brands of glasses have been withdrawn after being deemed unsafe by the consumer association FACUA.

People should wear the glasses before, during and after the eclipse, said Jesús Merayo Lloves, head of the Fernández-Vega ophthalmology research institute, warning that looking directly at the sun can cause irreparable damage.

The total eclipse will cross Spain and is best viewed in a band about 200km (124 miles) wide from A Coruña in the Atlantic north-west to Mallorca in the Mediterranean.

Accommodation in small towns and villages in its path, as well as makeshift observatories set up by local enthusiasts, have been booked out for months. There have been reports of people offering house exchanges in Washington DC and elsewhere in the US for a place in villages in Castilla y León, one of the best regions to view the eclipse.

The US space agency Nasa has installed four high-powered telescopes next to the romanesque church in the tiny village of Villalibado in north-west Spain where it will live stream the eclipse to more than 10 million viewers.

Nasa chose the village, which was abandoned for decades before being restored as a holiday destination, after almost a year searching for the perfect site to view the eclipse.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Rush to find solar eclipse glasses as UK high street stocks run short
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Steven Morris
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Some online shoppers may have left it too late to order – but you can view partial eclipse indirectly without specs

A frantic rush is on across the UK to find the right kind of protective eyewear ahead of Wednesday’s partial solar eclipse.

High street stores are running out of eclipse glasses and online shoppers who track down a pair are being told they may not reach them until the end of the week. In other words, in plenty of time for the next comparable UK eclipse – in 2081 – but no good at all for Wednesday’s show.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The Royal Observatory Greenwich said it was aware of a shortage of glasses. A spokesperson said: “We have sold out of solar eclipse glasses, both online and in our shops, due to an unprecedented volume of orders.”

Ordinary sunglasses are not safe to use and over the last few weeks consumer experts have been recommending specialised glasses. But try to get, for example, a pack of Lunt solar eclipse glasses (£14.99) on Amazon and the dispiriting message “free delivery Thursday 13 August” pops up.

The Robert Dyas store was offering Bresser eclipse glasses for £2.99, but there was an “out of stock” message on its website.

Emma, from Tonbridge in Kent, described her mission to find pairs for herself and three relatives. “They were sold out everywhere,” she said. When she called her local opticians, she received short shrift. “They sounded really angry. I said: ‘I’m calling to see if you have any glasses for the …’ The assistant interrupted and said no and hung up.”

Emma managed to get one from a friend whose forward-thinking mum had bought a multipack. “If we can’t get any more, we’ll have to share,” she said.

Neill Sanders, the founder of Go Stargazing and the UK coordinator of Astronomers Without Borders, said there wasn’t a shortage – it was just that people had not planned ahead.

He said: “I’m getting loads of calls, text messages, emails with people asking ‘do you have some glasses?’. Everyone’s suddenly realising we need glasses for Wednesday.”

Sanders said he had imported 300,000 pairs from the US. He had sent out 100,000 pairs in the last few weeks at discount prices to astronomy clubs and community groups but it was too late to get most of the others out.

Another distributor said: “We have good stocks, our issue is everybody has left it until the last minute to order and we only have so many people we can put into packing at a time.”

Jake Foster, an astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich, said: “If you don’t have a pair of eclipse glasses, you can still view the eclipse indirectly. Any household item with small round holes in it, such as a colander or even a piece of paper with a small hole poked in it can project an image of the eclipse on to a flat surface.

“Don’t look at the sun itself but instead at the shadow that’s being produced – you should be able to see the shape of the eclipse within it.”

After the 1999 total solar eclipse, the Royal College of Ophthalmologists reported about 70 cases of people experiencing vision problems from watching it.

The UK Health Security Agency and the royal college have issued detailed advice on their websites on the sort of glasses that are safe and other ways of watching the eclipse.

Ordinary sunglasses are not safe to use and over the last few weeks consumer experts have been recommending specialised glasses.

https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/a.title: Ofcom investigates GB News over guest’s pride and paedophilia remarks
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/a.author: Michael Savage Media editor
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/a.text:
Regulator acts after 12,000 complaints over comments by Caroline Farrow linking parades with bestiality and paedophilia

UK politics live – latest updates

GB News is being investigated by the UK’s media regulator after a guest appeared to link pride parades with bestiality and paedophilia.

The remarks are thought to have set a new record for individual complaints about a GB News programme, with more than 12,000 people raising concerns about comments made by the guest Caroline Farrow.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Those to speak out included the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, and Bimini, the star of RuPaul’s Drag Race UK.

Farrow, who describes herself as a Catholic commentator and is a campaigns manager for the ultra-conservative advocacy group CitizenGO, made the remarks during a discussion after the Pride in London march in July.

Speaking on the Alex Armstrong Tonight show, Farrow said the march was “not about gay rights” and had instead “become about celebrating every single sexuality that isn’t heterosexuality”.

She said this included “some very bizarre and unhealthy kinks and quirks, you know, like furries and bestiality and even minor-attracted, they call themselves minor-attracted people, you know, paedophiles”.

The remarks prompted an open letter signed by Polanski and Bimini calling on Ofcom to deal with the “dangerous” disinformation.

Ofcom confirmed to the Guardian that it was investigating the show over potential breaches of broadcasting standards. The rules dictate that “material which may cause offence is justified by the context”.

The edition of the show containing the remarks has since been removed from YouTube.

Armstrong, the show’s presenter, challenged the comments at the time, saying “the overwhelming amount of people at pride were there for good reasons”.

He added: “I don’t think it was full of paedophiles and everything, I’m sure there are nefarious people.”

He went further on a later show, saying: “Comments made by guests last weekend conflated gay pride with the celebration of paedophilia. This is an age-old gay trope that’s been used over a number of years to demonise and slander gay people. Those comments by guests had no place in that discussion.”

The Green party deputy leader welcomed Ofcom’s latest decision to investigate Farrow’s comments.

“Zack was right to complain about it at the time,” Rachel Millward said. “The suggestion that gay people are somehow a particular threat to children is baseless, irresponsible and deeply harmful.

“GB News is a regulated broadcaster, and broadcasters are supposed to meet basic professional standards. That should include not using their platform to spread hateful lies about a marginalised group.”

GB News has been approached for comment. At the time, it said: “These comments were expressed within a live debate by a contributor. They were her own views, and do not reflect the views or editorial position of GB News.

“Anyone watching the debate would have noted the comments were robustly and repeatedly challenged by two other contributors.”

GB News has previously been criticised by Ofcom for similar remarks on another programme. Last year, the regulator concluded that the channel breached the broadcasting code after a presenter, Josh Howie, said the “full inclusion of LGBTQ+ persons” at a church would “include paedos”.

On that occasion, sanctions were not imposed on GB News because it had already broadcast an apology and a fuller discussion about the context of the comment within weeks of the original broadcast.

The investigation comes amid increased pressure on Ofcom to enforce broadcasting rules.

While the regulator is also investigating a GB News repeat of its interview with Donald Trump, it declined to investigate a claim by a GB News presenter that there had been no riot in Belfast in June, despite cars and houses being set alight, attacks on police and families fleeing their homes.

The previous Ofcom chair, the Conservative peer Michael Grade, who left the post in April, accused GB News’s critics of seeking to restrict free speech to a “liberal, Islington consensus”.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: SpaceX plan for vast rocket launch site on Louisiana coast sparks backlash
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Oliver Milman
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Opponents fear Elon Musk firm’s plan to develop 18-mile strip of Pecan Island will badly damage fragile ecosystem

Plans by Elon Musk’s SpaceX to build a vast rocket launch site on a stretch of Louisiana’s rapidly eroding coastline have stirred a backlash among some local opponents who fear it will badly damage the area’s fragile ecosystem.

A deal for SpaceX to take control of 130,000 acres of coastal Vermilion parish is reported to be close to being finalized, allowing the company to escalate its number of launches, including of its new Starship mega rocket. SpaceX also has ambitions to deploy artificial intelligence datacenters in space, and while some experts have doubts about this, it has submitted regulatory filings to build a constellation of up to a million of them.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The deal with Louisiana’s Republican state leadership will enable SpaceX to build on an 18-mile strip of Pecan Island, a low-lying slice of land with just a few hundred inhabitants that sits south of the city of Lafayette. The land was previously given up via a legal settlement with the oil giant ExxonMobil, which was accused of worsening land loss and pollution through its activities in the area. ExxonMobil has described the lawsuits against it as “meritless”.

Neither SpaceX nor Jeff Landry, Louisiana’s governor, have yet confirmed the plan for the rocket site, although the space company did previously post on X, another Musk company, that thousands of starship launches will “require the ability to launch from many different locations, so we are constantly exploring to find viable sites to expand Starship operations in the future, both domestically and internationally”.

The prospect of a new spaceport spanning an area several times larger than Washington DC has alarmed some opponents in Pecan Island. On Monday a website was launched to rally opposition to the SpaceX plan, with its organizer warning that the huge new facility would imperil critical migratory bird habitat.

Hundreds of millions of birds, including snow geese, whooping cranes and 40% of all North American waterfowl, use Pecan Island as a crucial stop-off in their migratory flights through the Mississippi flyway, a key corridor that birds use in seasonal flights between North and South America.

“We have existed alongside oil and gas for over 100 years, we aren’t against industry, but we haven’t blasted off high-octane rocketry before,” said Gabe Giffin, a Louisiana resident who set up the new website. “I think space is cool, too. But many of these birds need this area and we need to have a proper process in place for this.”

Giffin and other critics have raised concerns about moves by federal and state governments to sweep aside requirements to follow laws such as the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act when approving new rocketry projects like SpaceX.

Musk, the world’s richest person, is a leading donor to Republicans and undertook an unelected reorganization of the federal government last year at the behest of Donald Trump.

“They are throwing out the rulebook to make my home a desolate wasteland for what? Rockets?” said Brooke Broussard, a schoolteacher in nearby Abbeville whose family has long lived on Pecan Island.

“I’m concerned about the already fragile hydrology of Pecan Island and its wetlands, and the quality of life for residents who live there despite the hardships. These are people who want peace, not crowds and traffic. This would set a precedent to allow dirty business without any sort of accountability.”

Some locals do see opportunities arriving through jobs and investment brought by SpaceX, Broussard said, and even some protection from the onward march of the seas.

Perched on the Gulf of Mexico coast, Pecan Island is part of a fraying Louisiana coastline that is quickly eroding away, losing about one football field of land every 100 minutes.

This rapid land loss is caused by rising sea levels from the climate crisis, as well as the subsidence of the state’s coastline. Scientists project that Louisiana faces about 2ft of sea level rise by 2050, a scenario that imperils even New Orleans and will drown almost all of Pecan Island, including its buildings.

“Some people are saying that SpaceX will build up the land here and save us but most of the people I’ve spoken to are against all this,” said Broussard.

“It’s all Trumpers on Pecan Island but people aren’t for this. We are probably doomed, with all the storms coming. But my thing is that we should be allowed to go in peace. The people who continue to live there despite the peril deserve better.”

Neither SpaceX nor Landry’s office responded to a request for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Louisiana warns beachgoers amid surge in flesh-eating bacteria infections
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ed Pilkington and agency
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
State confirms nine cases, including five deaths, from Vibrio vulnificus organism, which thrives in seawater

Health officials in Louisiana are urging beachgoers to take precautions during a summertime surge in infections from a flesh-eating bacterium found in coastal waters.

Louisiana has confirmed nine cases of Vibrio vulnificus infections this year, the state’s health department said last week in a news release. All were hospitalized, and five died. During the same period over the previous decade, Louisiana reported an average of seven cases and one death.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“Seek medical care immediately if a wound exposed to brackish or salt water becomes red, swollen, painful, warm or discolored,” officials said in the release.

Vibrio bacteria thrive in seawater and in the brackish mix of fresh and saltwater found in estuaries and lagoons. Most infections are reported from May to October, and most happen in states along the Gulf coast. Doctors say the Gulf is an ideal environment with the right amounts of salt and heat to let this organism proliferate.

The mostly deadly type is Vibrio vulnificus, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). As many as one in five of those infections are fatal, a much higher rate than other types of Vibrio bacteria.

The rate of infections remain exceptionally rare compared with other infectious diseases. But once the bacterium enters the body it can cause bruising, swelling and decay within hours and bring on septic shock and death unless there is rapid treatment with powerful antibiotics.

Last year Louisiana recorded five deaths from the bacterium among at least 26 people who were infected, all of whom were hospitalized. One of those who died, Basil Kennedy, 77, became sick after he scraped his leg on a boat trailer then entered the water; he died three days later.

Florida has reported 14 Vibrio vulnificus cases and two deaths so far this year, compared with 33 cases and five deaths for all of last year.

Some people become infected by eating raw or undercooked shellfish – particularly oysters. But a large percentage fall ill when the person is in ocean or brackish water and the bacteria enter the body through small breaks in the skin.

Doctors say severe cases are seen more often in elderly patients, people with weakened immune systems, and those with liver disease, diabetes and certain chronic illnesses.

Scientists say the climate crisis is helping the germs proliferate and spread northward. As the oceans warm, the concentration of Vibrio in seawater also rises, increasing the risk of infection.

A 2023 study found that the northernmost case has been shifting by about 30 miles each year, and that cases overall have been rising, and over time the northward proliferation might bring infections within range of population centers around New York.

Vibrio vulnificus can enter the body through unhealed cuts and scrapes, recent piercings and tattoos, and recent surgical incisions. People should immediately wash cuts and scrapes thoroughly with soap and clean running water after coming in contact with coastal waters or raw seafood, the CDC said.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Crew of Zuckerberg yacht did not hear radio call to assist boat, Meta says
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Guardian staff and agency
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Small skiff ran out of fuel off Alaska and was helped by cruise ship even though Meta CEO’s vessel was closer

Zuckerberg faces questions over why superyacht reportedly declined to help stranded boat

The crew of a yacht owned by Mark Zuckerberg did not hear a radio call for a maritime assist from a small skiff that ran out of fuel off the coast of Alaska, and by the time it did, another nearby ship had already rendered assistance, a spokesperson for the Meta CEO said.

The Alaska Beacon news outlet reported that the skiff had issued a call for assistance through the US Coast Guard last week and a nearby small cruise ship, the Wilderness Legacy, towed it into nearby Farragut Bay in south-east Alaska and refueled it.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Although it was closer, Zuckerberg’s yacht, called Launchpad, had not responded to the call.

The Alaska Beacon further reported that the spokesperson told them via email on Sunday that the yacht Launchpad did not initially hear the call for assistance.

“Mark and his family were not on board at the time of the incident. As the Coast Guard noted, the boat was not in distress, and by the time the crew reviewed the Coast Guard contact on a different radio channel from the one they were operating on, the assist was already underway. We’re grateful all parties are safe,” the email to said.

A passenger on the cruise ship had previously described on social media how the vessel he was on went to the skiff’s assistance, while claiming that the authorities had radioed Zuckerberg’s yacht and they “repeatedly refused to respond”.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Francesca Hong, the progressive leading a ‘messy’ race for Wisconsin’s governor: ‘They’re tired of the status quo’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Rachel Leingang in Milwaukee, Wisconsin
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Hong, whose grassroots campaign has made her a frontrunner, aims for primary win after public skepticism from top Democrats and a last-minute shake-up

As Francesca Hong surged ahead in the final weeks of the chaotic Democratic primary to be Wisconsin’s next governor, the democratic socialist has become the internet’s main character.

Donald Trump has mocked her old tweets, while major figures in her own party publicly questioned her ability to win a general election. The man she is vying to succeed even launched a late blitz in support of one of her rivals.

But on the ground in Wisconsin, the enthusiasm for her shines through.

Riding through a 24-hour bike race in Milwaukee’s Riverwest neighborhood in late July, residents passed Hong coloring books on a table of campaign merch; a scrolling sign saying “We love Fran”; and a DJ calling Hong “so fresh and so clean” as he played OutKast.

After the sun went down, Hong hopped on a bike herself after a line of supporters grabbed photos with her. She danced with other racers in a tame mosh pit at one of the race’s side quests, and later that night got a tattoo to commemorate the race, Riverwest 24, on her leg, alongside her Milwaukee Bucks tattoo.

In hundreds of events across Wisconsin – from karaoke nights to ramen pop-ups – Hong, 37, built a grassroots army that pushed her to the cusp of clinching the Democratic nomination for governor in a marquee battleground state.

Her status as frontrunner put Hong on national shows in recent days, summoning a wave of headlines about her past tweets, including one – seized on by Republicans, including Trump – where she called for cancelling Thanksgiving.

After the progressive Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for US Senate in next-door Michigan last week, scrutiny of Hong intensified. In Wisconsin, Democrats face another test of whether voters in a swing state will side with leftwing candidates in primaries – and what that could mean for the party’s chances in a typically close general election in November.

Hong – a chef and former restaurant owner, a single mom and a state lawmaker from Madison – is running on a progressive platform that includes universal childcare and fully funding the state’s public schools. She is also calling for a moratorium on datacenters, a centerpiece that differentiates her from the other Democratic candidates.

“I got into this race because I know that we can win and that Wisconsinites are going to fight for one another and fight to be a part of the change,” she told the Guardian, “because they’re tired of people making decisions that don’t improve lives and they’re tired of the status quo.”

Four candidates are vying for the open governor’s seat on Tuesday, with most polls showing Hong in the lead. Kelda Roys, a state senator, and Joel Brennan, a former head of the state administration department, are still in the race. A previous contender, Sara Rodriguez, left the race after campaign finance irregularities. Mandela Barnes, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in 2022, dropped out on 31 July.

David Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, exited the race and then reentered it – receiving the endorsement of the outgoing Democratic governor, Tony Evers. A memo from the Crowley campaign on 5 August suggested polling may be off, pointing to Michigan polls showing El-Sayed with a much broader lead than he actually achieved. Evers recently claimed Hong’s campaign was “in a tough place”, because she had to spend time dealing with “what’s on the Twitter”.

Hong has pointed to Crowley’s change of heart as evidence of panic by the Democratic establishment. There is a “reluctance to change, and a fear of change” among “a lot of our candidates and some of their consultants”, she suggested after he reentered the race.

Whoever wins the Democratic gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin will face Tom Tiffany, an ardent Trump supporter running unopposed in the Republican primary. He voted against certifying the results of the 2020 election, which Trump lost. Tiffany has more cash than any of the Democratic candidates so far, and Republicans are sure to flood the market to boost him.

“The Wisconsin governor certifies the presidential election results, and Tom Tiffany was part of a plot to overturn the 2020 results,” said Ben Wikler, the former chair of the Wisconsin Democratic party. “This is a very high-stakes seat that will affect not just the lives of every Wisconsinite, but also potentially the future of American democracy.”

Five of the last seven presidential elections in Wisconsin have come down to less than one percentage point, Wikler notes. Most states have trended red or blue over time, but Wisconsin stays “consistently right on the knife’s edge”, he said.

The stakes are greater than Wisconsin’s role in the national elections. Democrats are angling for a governing trifecta in Wisconsin, trying to win back control of both chambers of the state assembly and keep the governor’s office so they can enact a full agenda.

Some want a perceived “safe” candidate, and have expressed doubt that Hong could win a general election, even in a predicted wave year for Democrats. David Axelrod, the Democratic strategist who helped Barack Obama win, has repeatedly panned Hong, whom he has described as “a font of zany liberal, faculty lounge exotica”.

Michael Wagner, the director of the University of Wisconsin-Madison’s journalism school who researches political communication, said that while Republicans have increasingly run more extreme candidates in the past decade, Democrats have instead believed the only way to win statewide in swing states is with moderate candidates. But there’s evidence that’s not true, he said: Wisconsin’s two US senators fall on either edge of their parties, with the progressive Tammy Baldwin, and Ron Johnson rising from the Tea party.

“Sometimes the party establishment can get too cute with what they worry about,” said Wagner. “But it’s not unreasonable that they’re worried, because in an election in Wisconsin, any one of 20 things could shift 10,000 votes, and that could be it.”

Wagner said Hong’s strongest coalition is among young voters, so she needs to make sure they show up and vote for her, while calming any fears from moderates and independents. But in a place like Wisconsin, where voters are willing to take chances on people who speak directly to the issues they are about, Hong has a good shot at winning both the primary and the general, he added. “That doesn’t mean she’ll win either of them, but she’s got a really good chance.”

Hong often counters the electability question with: “The person who wins the most votes is the most electable. And we are fighting harder than any other campaign to win the most votes.”

In one recent conversation on the campaign trail, a voter asked Hong point blank: what are you going to do for me?

“I was like, I’m going to work harder for you than anyone else and make sure that we’re raising wages, taxing the billionaires, and we’re stopping datacenters,” she recounted, sitting outside at the University of Wisconsin-Superior in northern Wisconsin after an education forum with other gubernatorial candidates.

She thinks voters appreciate her firm, bold stances. She doesn’t shy away from the democratic socialist label, but noted that the DSA hasn’t endorsed her, and stressed that she doesn’t agree with the full DSA platform. She previously said she wanted to defund the police but now says she does not.

“The urgency of this moment requires actually meeting the scale and speed in which these different things have become a problem,” she said. “You see the mass income disparities. You have to meet that with a policy that’s going to fix it permanently. And that’s changing a rigged system.”

She wears a stack of beaded bracelets picked up while campaigning – one from a datacenter organizing meeting, another with the ICE watch hotline. Born in Madison, she cut her teeth in restaurants, and was elected to the state assembly in 2020, becoming the first Asian American member. As a lawmaker, she authored a bill that would provide healthy school meals for all kids and a package of bills that would fight back against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) overreach.

Chris Larson, a state senator who recently endorsed Hong, cited her ability to form coalitions at the capitol, including by bringing in outside groups affected by policy ideas. He is friends with multiple people running for governor, but saw the maneuvering against Hong over electability concerns “lacking in imagination”.

“This is where we build hope. This is how we get shit done,” he said during Riverwest 24. “And that for me is what Francesca Hong brings. And if there are folks who are saying that that is too much, I want to be part of the pushback against that.”

On datacenters, Hong’s call for a one-year moratorium on their construction opens the door for voters to wonder why no one else is trying to stop this, Larson said.

Hong said the datacenters piece resonates because people feel the most threat to their own control. The unregulated boom of AI has people feeling a need for quick action, she said. “Just because I’m team human doesn’t mean I’m anti-AI. I just don’t want it to control us. I think that we get to regulate it.”

Riding through the Riverwest neighborhood with bright green Hong signs strapped to his bike, people stopped Larson to ask if Hong would be there. One man, Chris Montezon, asked if he could snag a sign. Larson handed one off as they biked through city streets.

Montezon said he appreciated Hong’s policies, but also that she’s gone all over the state, including rural Wisconsin, to engage with people. He thinks she can win a statewide general election. “I think there’s a lot of disaffected voters in the state.”

At the education forum in Superior, four gubernatorial candidates went deep on funding formulas and spending. They didn’t attack each other; for the most part, the race has remained friendly, with veiled references to electability aimed indirectly at Hong.

Terrence Dahmen, a 73-year-old independent who said he ends up voting for Democrats most of the time, watched the candidates at the forum and found them all “young, enthusiastic, well-read and well-spoken”.

He didn’t think the state could go wrong with any of them, but was leaning toward Hong because of her datacenter moratorium. She was “a little more of a socialist, which doesn’t bother me at all”, he said, adding that Evers’ intervention in the race “doesn’t smell good”.

“I know she could probably get elected in Madison pretty easily and probably in Milwaukee, but I’m a little leery about northern Wisconsin,” Dahmen said. “I live in northern Wisconsin and there’s a lot of racism up here, so that might weigh against her.”

But Robert Edelstein, a 62-year-old who described himself as progressive but isn’t registered with a political party, was concerned that Republicans were boosting Hong. He wants a a Democratic candidate who will prevail in November. “I’m troubled that it could be someone who can’t win.”

Crowley, 40, told the Guardian his decision to reenter the governor’s race and make a last-minute, all-out bid to topple Hong did not have anything to do with the so-called Democratic establishment. While he’s happy to have Evers’ endorsement, he has insisted his reentry didn’t hinge on the governor’s support.

Instead, after Rodriguez, Wisconsin’s lieutenant governor, unexpectedly left the race, Crowley and his wife prayed over whether he should get back in, and the answer was at first a solid no. They had booked a trip to Jamaica. He knew it could be confusing to voters. His wife asked the Lord to send a sign – a red bird – if they should get back in the race. Crowley continued to field calls from supporters. His wife saw a red cardinal on a Friday morning, just minutes before Rodriguez announced she would drop out.

“We knew that the stakes were too high for me to sit on the sideline, and that we need the best candidate – not just with executive leadership, but somebody who has a proven track record of getting things done,” Crowley said. “And that’s what voters want. They want someone that they can trust. And that’s why we got back into this race.”

Crowley said voters have raised concerns about electability in a general election as he’s traveled throughout the state, and he said polls show him beating Tiffany in a head-to-head matchup. “We need to make sure that we build a winning coalition to bring not just Democrats, but those independents and even Republicans who are exhausted by Maga on to this campaign to make sure that we reach our ultimate goal.”

“I know that it has been a little chaotic,” he acknowledged. “It’s a little messy in this primary, but so is our democracy.”

He is “far from” the establishment, he said: he grew up with parents who struggled with mental health and drug addiction. He was evicted three times. He worked hard to get to where he is.

“I don’t want folks to get me being established because of what I’ve worked extremely hard for, for me being a part of any type of establishment,” he said.

Some voters have struggled with his reentry, and Evers’ involvement. William Norman, a Hong supporter who biked in the Riverwest 24 alongside his parents, said the race got hectic in the last few weeks “for all the wrong reasons”.

“I think it’s kind of loser behavior to think that one of your candidates can’t beat somebody who’s running on such a nasty platform across the aisle,” Norman said. “I just feel like you should have faith in your candidate. Whoever the people want should be the person to be sent into battle.”

Others, including Crowley and Evers, point to the haranguing over Hong’s old tweets, most of which have not been deleted, that journalists and Republicans have elevated in recent. Her campaign told the New York Times that a lot of those tweets were written during “peak woke” in the 2020s.

When initially asked by CNN about the since-deleted “cancel Thanksgiving” tweet from November 2020, Hong said “views can evolve” and that Thanksgiving can be “incredibly painful for many people in our communities”. She later joked to Politico that Thanksgiving was her favorite.

Becky Cooper, Hong’s campaign manager, said digging up tweets from more than five years ago is an attempt to distract from voters’ needs, including affordable healthcare and property tax relief, as well as a “huge waste” of time and energy. “But,” she added, “we’re always working to sharpen language and deliver the message.”

Hong told the Guardian she welcomes national interest in her campaign, but does feel the pressure. For a Democratic socialist running on a broad agenda that disrupts the political status quo, winning in a place like Wisconsin could change politics – not just in the state, but across the country, she said.

“We can’t have a more representative democracy unless we have more folks who are willing to fight the way things have been done,” she said. “Because that’s what’s gotten us here.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: An ambitious new project in Florida is giving marine scientists hope: ‘I just see so much potential’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Richard Luscombe in Miami
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Conservationists have created a ‘coastal corridor’ of ocean-based projects designed to preserve and nourish vulnerable marine life

F
rom disappearing manatees to bleached coral reefs, gender-changing turtles and oyster beds destroyed by hurricanes, no other state’s marine life faces the magnitude of climate-related challenges than Florida’s.

Now, wildlife authorities are attempting to bring some cohesion to tackling the diverse slate of issues by borrowing from a playbook that has already proved successful on land.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC), and its charitable arm, the Fish and Wildlife Foundation of Florida (FWFF), have announced the creation of an ambitious “coastal corridor”, an interconnected chain of ocean-based projects and enhancements designed to preserve and nourish vulnerable marine creatures.

It replicates to a significant degree the state’s wildlife corridor, an 18m-acre (7m-hectare) project established in 2021 to provide a safe, contiguous habitat spanning much of Florida where rare or threatened land-based species including birds, reptiles, panthers and bears can flourish.

Featuring projects including habitat restoration, fisheries enhancement and improved public access and coastal resilience along Florida’s Atlantic and Gulf coasts, the project aims to create a connected network of artificial reefs, oyster beds, seagrass and mangroves on which marine life can thrive.

“The goal is to protect and connect all these important habitats for fish and wildlife,” said Nick Wiley, the former head of FWC who was appointed in April as executive director of FWFF.

“Everyone has seen how successful the wildlife corridor initiative has been, rallying everybody around the mission. The wildlife species needed these travel lanes and corridors across the state, but it also highlighted how private landowners contribute to federal, state and county public lands and how all that fits together.

“Our board members were really inspired by that, looking at our coast, our fisheries and the coastal communities, and from the beaches, estuaries, all the way out into the deeper water.”

The coastal corridor is designed to not only protect Florida’s precious marine legacy, but also the economic riches of its waters. Recreational fishing alone brings in $14bn a year, and provides 120,000 jobs, the foundation said. Another $3.1bn and 39,000 jobs come from creating and maintaining artificial reefs.

Additionally, more than 2 million out-of-state anglers visit Florida each year, renting charter boats and plowing plenty of dollars into hotels and restaurants.

“If you had to list what sets Florida apart and makes it such an iconic place for people to go and enjoy the outdoors, and the water and the fish and everything, our coast is our treasure,” Wiley said.

“But we hadn’t really looked at it as a connected corridor all the way around the coastline. It’s like the wildlife corridor’s sister on the coast that shows how you connect our estuaries all the way out through the grass flats into the deeper water.

“We already have a lot of partners from local government, non-profit, federal government, and state that are doing a lot of great work to protect our coastlines and provide habitat for fisheries, but it’s like here and there, scattered along the coastline.

“This pulls us all together under one great umbrella to inspire and provide a vision that we can all celebrate and leverage, and identify where we need to do better, make improvements, where we need to restore places and where we need to add habitat, from coral reefs all the way up to the grass flats.”

FWC and FWFF leaders are partnering with local governments, scientists, reef builders, conservation organizations and coastal communities. One early project, planned for next month, is a collaboration with Collier county to lay a sizable new artificial reef some 13 miles from shore in the Gulf of Mexico.

Mike Norberg, a marine biologist with decades of experience in artificial reefs, who is also the coastal corridor’s project director, said a chain of prefabricated concrete structures 8ft-15ft would be lowered onto the seabed, and would mimic natural reefs to attract fish.

“There’s a number of benefits for artificial reefs,” he said. “It removes pressure from natural reefs, which obviously have a lot of ongoing challenges, especially in south Florida, and also creates habitats in areas where none might have existed.

“In parts of the coastal waters, it’s largely just sand sea floor and not a ton of natural reefs, especially when you look in the northern Gulf or north-eastern side of Florida. So it’s a win-win both for the ecosystem as well as recreational access opportunities, whether that’s fishing and diving or just going out and sightseeing and having fun.”

Norberg said strategic reef deployments were a priority for the first year, with other projects under way in Okaloosa county in the Panhandle, and Duvall county on the northern Atlantic coast.

Future plans, he said, include exploring coastal restoration projects to help address beach erosion, the loss of coastal mangroves that protect against storm surge during tropical events and the reduction in natural food stocks that sustain declining species, such as seagrass for manatees.

“We’ve got a number of different projects that are in various stages of development in different parts of the state,” he said.

“We’re looking at various oyster bed restoration opportunities and how that can help tie in to this network of connected habitats, living shorelines. That’s a huge thing, one that helps improve coastal resiliency from a community perspective.

“It also provides habitat for juvenile fish and adult fish to spend their time within an estuary before they move offshore. So there really is this opportunity to tie both inshore to offshore habitats and use that as a tool for marine resource management.”

To Wiley, the creation of the coastal corridor represents what he says is a peak of his decades-long career in wildlife conservation in Florida.

“I see more excitement and opportunity on this one than anything I’ve touched,” he said. “It speaks to me so well in my heart about bringing people together to do great things for Florida’s environment and Florida’s coast, and I just see so much potential and opportunity for everybody to come in and be a part of it.

“As we’ve seen on the wildlife corridor, it will bring a deeper, richer identity to the state that will enrich and enhance the value of Florida for people that live here, and the people that want to come visit.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) and Fish and wildlife Foundation of Florida have announced the creation of an ambitious ‘coastal corridor’ The project aims to create a connected network of artificial reefs, oyster beds, seagrass and mangroves on which marine life can thrive.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Not your imagination: from backpacks to food, consumer goods are getting worse
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Heather Timmons
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Is it possible to avoid the continuing decline in quality of consumer products brought on by corporate greed?

When Keyana Sapp, 31, went shopping for a new backpack, the brands he remembered as a kid were just not the same.

He researched the companies, from North Face to JanSport and Eastpak, and soon realized they were all owned by the VF Corporation after a wave of acquisitions in the 2000s. After a Reddit post he made about his discovery picked up traction, he started looking at other types of consumer goods – cookware, shoes, tools, clothing.

“It seems like that was a story that just repeated in every industry,” Sapp told the Guardian.

Big conglomerates and private equity were buying up “trusted brands and riding that reputation out until it was a husk of what it was”.

From a zipper jam on a nearly new coat to a casserole dish cracking in the oven on its third use, Americans are finding that the quality of many once-beloved name brands are declining. Three-quarters of Americans had a quality or service issue in 2025, the National Consumer Rage Study found, double the rate since the survey started in 1976. And customer complaints have reached record levels, according to the latest University of Michigan American Customer Satisfaction Index.

Sapp channeled his personal frustration into building a database of hundreds of brands and ranking them “approved” to “avoid” based in part by their corporate ownership. And as part of his publication, Worse on Purpose, he explains the financial transactions that have undercut the quality of some of the biggest name brands.

Sapp sees a structural problem within the consumer retail industry: founders who built brands they love take lucrative offers from big corporations or private equity investors. While they cash in on the decades it took to build their product’s brand, the new corporate owners eventually prove they don’t have the same emotional investment and are distanced from loyal customers.

“When you’re running everything from an office building that has no relation to where the product is manufactured and people who are doing the manufacturing”, quality is going to suffer, Sapp said.

Big US companies haven’t always been associated with lower-quality products, of course. Purchasing a product from a well-known national brand was often associated with guaranteed quality and consistent customer service for much of the last century.

But in recent years, investors have become increasingly “big and powerful” due to the pro-shareholder rights movement and the growth of large institutional investors, explains Dorothy Lund, a law professor at Columbia University. That increased shareholder power can contribute to consumer harm.

Thanks to activist investors, many company executives face what feels like “gun-to-the-head pressure to maximize shareholder returns”, or be fired, she said.

Shareholder activism targeting CEOs has more than quadrupled since 2018, a December 2025 report by the Conference Board found. Consumer-facing industries have seen “particularly large spikes” in shareholder campaigns that focus on making sure investors get more money.

Meanwhile, corporate profits hit an all-time high in the first quarter of 2025, of $3.9tn on an annualized basis.

Some brand owners who have sold their companies to big corporations say it’s this relentless pressure to increase profits that intrinsically erodes product quality.

“I don’t believe in this idea that you take a sliver off the loaf of baloney and nobody realizes it … and then the next year you take another sliver off, nobody realizes it,” Ben & Jerry’s co-founder Ben Cohen told the Guardian in a recent interview. Cohen is fighting to buy his brand back from Magnum, the ice-cream brand sprung out of Unilever, among disagreements over the brand’s social activism.

“You keep on doing that, year after year, and all of a sudden, you don’t have any baloney” any more, he added.

The news industry in the US used to hold corporations more accountable for the quality of their products and service. But consumer-facing business news was decimated when local newspapers disappeared and national news outlets shifted their corporate coverage to focus on investors.

Recently, a fresh crop of apps and websites, like Worse on Purpose, are taking their place.

The progressive non-profit More Perfect Union has detailed the impact on food quality as restaurant supplier Sysco grew through acquisitions, for example, and the Buy’r blog and app tracks the ownership of food and health and beauty brands. Earlier this month, the New York Times’ Wirecutter mapped the changing ingredients, and taste, of Talenti gelato, after its 2012 takeover by Unilever.

Meanwhile, the Reddit group Enshittification, named after tech critic Cory Doctorow’s term for internet decline, has been a clearinghouse for consumers to rant about products and services getting worse since it was started in 2023.

So what’s an irate shopper to do? Buy from small companies where possible, Sapp suggests.

“The easiest thing any consumer can do is just say, ‘Wherever I can, I’m going to buy independent, rather than from a big conglomerate,’” Sapp recommends. When you’re shopping, “just check who owns the company”.

The Guardian is exploring Americans’ frustrations with big companies and how consumer rights have changed in the world’s biggest consumer economy. Disappointed with a product or service, or have a solution to recommend? Get in touch at Consumed@theGuardian.com.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Three-quarters of Americans had a quality or service issue in 2025, the National Consumer Rage Study found. Customer complaints have reached record levels, according to the latest University of Michigan American Customer Satisfaction Index.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The media is infatuated with Gadi Eisenkot, the ‘anti-Netanyahu’. Why? | Mehdi Hasan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Mehdi Hasan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The challenger to Netanyahu is more of the same. His record makes that abundantly clear

Western media outlets cannot seem to get enough of Gadi Eisenkot.

Israel’s former military chief and the leader of the newly formed Yashar party has been embraced by the international press as he and his party take the lead in the polls in the run-up to October’s elections.

“Will Israel embrace the ‘anti-Netanyahu’ who lost a son in Gaza?” asked the Times of London.

“He lost his son in Gaza. Now he’s coming for Netanyahu,” declared the Daily Telegraph.

“How Netanyahu’s Top General Became His Strongest Challenger,” ran the headline on a lengthy David Remnick profile of Eisenkot in the New Yorker.

“Does Gadi Eisenkot offer Israel a new chance?” wondered the Economist.

It’s a fair question. But perhaps British and American commentators aren’t the right people to answer it.

Why not ask the Palestinians of Gaza?

At the height of the genocide, between October 2023 and June 2024, Eisenkot sat in Benjamin Netanyahu’s war cabinet while Israel waged its barbaric military campaign in Gaza. During that period, Israeli airstrikes leveled entire apartment buildings, hit schools, hospitals and refugee camps, and killed more than 30,000 Palestinians.

Eisenkot eventually resigned from the war cabinet in 2024. But not over the horrific death toll. He left over what he regarded as the government’s strategic failures. Even the New Yorker’s Remnick, in his sympathetic profile piece, noted how the general, who lost his own soldier son Gal in the fighting, “remains reluctant to condemn Netanyahu in any detail for the extraordinary severity and duration of the war in Gaza”.

And Eisenkot has form when it comes to killing Gaza’s Palestinians. As Israel’s chief of staff during the “Great March of Return” in 2018 and 2019, he oversaw the armed response to mass Palestinian demonstrations against the siege of Gaza.

Israeli soldiers, mostly snipers, killed more than 200 Palestinians, including dozens of children. “The Israeli security forces killed and maimed Palestinian demonstrators who did not pose an imminent threat,” concluded a UN commission of inquiry, adding that it “found reasonable grounds to believe that demonstrators were shot in violation of their right to life”.

If the Economist wants to know whether Eisenkot represents “a new chance”, perhaps it should also ask Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Yes, Eisenkot may be opposed to the far-right Netanyahu government’s annexation plan, but he is also opposed to Palestinian self-determination and statehood. “I have never said two states for two peoples,” he proudly declaimed in an interview in June, “because I understand the depth of this religious-national-social conflict, and anyone who talks about ‘peace now’ and two states doesn’t understand the conflict.

“I very much believe in settlement in Judea and Samaria,” he continued, using the biblical term for the occupied West Bank.

So much for Eisenkot’s supposed pragmatism and liberalism. He openly rejects a two-state solution and proudly supports Israeli settlements – settlements that the international court of justice and multiple UN resolutions consider illegal under international law.

Or perhaps journalists should ask the residents of Beirut’s southern suburbs, where hundreds of men, women and children were killed in the 2006 Israeli assault on Lebanon, whether Eisenkot represents a fresh start.

As head of Israel’s Northern Command, he became closely associated with what came to be known as the “Dahiya Doctrine”: an Israeli military strategy of deterrence premised on the widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure.

“What happened in the Dahiya quarter of Beirut in 2006 will happen in every village from which Israel is fired on,” Eisenkot explained to an interviewer in 2008. “We will apply disproportionate force on it [village] and cause great damage and destruction there.”

The use of disproportionate force against civilian targets is, of course, an undeniable war crime.

Netanyahu may be a clear villain – but he can also be a cartoon villain. The danger with Eisenkot is that he is a villain who projects the image of a “moderate”. While Netanyahu has become a lightning rod, thanks to his arrogance and belligerence, and his indictment at the international criminal court (ICC) has made Israel an international pariah, Eisenkot cuts a more sober and reasonable figure; a “humble soldier”, to quote Remnick.

By simply not being Netanyahu, a Prime Minister Eisenkot would neutralize a lot of western liberal critics of Israel and restore the country’s standing in western capitals, while allowing the Israeli military and settlers to pursue the same policies of expansion and destruction in both the West Bank and Gaza.

Nor is Eisenkot unique. The Israeli political scene is filled with wolves in sheep’s clothing. There are Eisenkot’s fellow retired “moderate” generals in the Israeli opposition: Benny Gantz, who once bragged about sending parts of Gaza “back to the stone age”, and Yair Golan, who said after 7 October that Israel should prevent humanitarian aid from entering Gaza and the people there could “starve to death – it’s completely legitimate”.

Then there is Naftali Bennett, who has a long history of vile anti-Arab racism, oversaw the deadliest year on record for West Bank Palestinians when he was last prime minister of Israel in 2022, and is currently threatening both Turkey and Qatar.

The point is not that these Israeli politicians are all identical. They are not. They do differ in terms of tactics, personalities and political coalitions.

The point is that replacing Netanyahu with Eisenkot or any other Israeli opposition leader would not be a fundamental change in direction on the key issues of genocide, apartheid and occupation; it would only be a change in branding and messaging. For Palestinians and Lebanese, among many others in the Middle East, the result would be the same.

So come October, Israel’s most notorious prime minister may finally be voted out of office. If that happens, we can and should all celebrate the end of the Netanyahu era – and hope the ICC gets its man.

But then we’ll meet the new boss of Israel, same as the old boss of Israel.

Mehdi Hasan is Guardian US columnist and the editor-in-chief and CEO of Zeteo.

Group including Amazon founder has held talks with FSG

Bhatia and Facebook co-founder Saverin also involved

A consortium including the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, is close to completing a deal for a 30% stake in Liverpool after months of talks with Fenway Sports Group. The investors are led by Amit Bhatia, the son-in-law of the Indian billionaire Lakshmi Mittal and who previously was a shareholder and director at Queens Park Rangers.

The Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin is another member of the group who will pay in the region of £1.35bn. The deal is effectively agreed, but may take up to a month to complete.

Bezos has a personal fortune of around $257bn (£190bn), according to Forbes, making him the fourth-richest person in the world, while Saverin is reportedly worth $32bn. This will be Bezos’s first investment in football, but he has previously looked into bidding for NFL franchises. The 62-year-old will receive equity as part of the deal, which Deloitte has advised on.

Bezos is the executive chair of Amazon having relinquished day-to-day control when he stepped down as chief executive five years ago. Under his leadership, the online retailer has diversified into being an entertainment provider and has bought numerous sports rights for its streaming service.

Amazon had live UK rights for 20 Premier League games each season for six seasons until the end of last year and broadcasts the Champions League in several European countries, as well as some NFL games in the US.

FSG bought Liverpool in 2010 and have overseen two Premier League titles. FSG sold 3% of the club to the US private equity firm Dynasty Equity in 2023.

It has been a summer of change at Anfield, with Andoni Iraola replacing Arne Slot as head coach, Mohamed Salah left on a free transfer and has joined Trabzonspor and Michael Edwards departed his role as chief executive officer at FSG.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Gen Z calls it ‘loud budgeting’ – small business owners have been doing it for decades
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Gene Marks
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
The practice of openly proclaiming to the world what you can’t afford can lead to lower fees, reduced prices and better deals

A
sk any small business owner what has challenged them the most over the past couple of years and you’ll frequently hear about cashflow. It’s no secret that costs have risen dramatically and finding places to save money isn’t easy.

If this describes your situation then I’ve got a solution to your problem. Ever hear of “loud budgeting”? Of course you have! You’ve probably been doing it for years.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Loud budgeting is considered to be a relatively new trend. According to one recent survey from Bank of America, as many as 42% of gen Zers “swear by it”. The concept isn’t hard. It’s basically the practice of openly proclaiming to the world that you can’t afford to do stuff instead of just quietly going along with the crowd and paying for something that you can’t afford. Financial services firm Charles Schwab & Co says it “makes oversharing cool – and effective”. The Economic Times says “it’s the smartest way to build wealth in 2026”.

“Loud budgeting is effectively being upfront about your financial situation and when something doesn’t align with your financial goals, values or capacity,” says Emma Edwards, founder of the Broke Generation who offers millennials financial advice on social media. “We have this belief that our financial situation shouldn’t have to be an inconvenience to others, or we shouldn’t reveal ourselves as being on a budget.”

How does one practice loud budgeting? That’s easy. Just complain a lot about money. Make it clear that you can’t afford to do stuff. Or, to save face among your friends, say that you probably could afford to go to that great restaurant or concert or trip to the lake, but choose not to because you simply don’t want to spend the money. Don’t blame yourself. Blame the economy. Blame the president. Point to the high cost of living and your paltry raise. Just be vocal and transparent about your finances. People like honesty. And they’ll understand. If they don’t – well, that’s their problem not yours.

All of the reports I’ve read about loud budgeting have focused on individuals, particularly younger people grappling with a challenging economic environment. But this strategy certainly isn’t new. In fact, I’ve seen a number of my clients – older, boomer, well-seasoned business owners – practice this behavior for literally decades.

“What? You want $0.02 more per pound for that poly-laminate? I can’t afford that!”

“A 4% price increase? Believe me, I hate doing it, but have you seen what my insurance company is charging me?”

“A 5% raise? Is he crazy? We’re barely able to stay in business and this guy wants a 5% raise. Sheesh!”

“I am certainly not going to pay $200 an hour for your accounting services. You of all people should know we can’t afford that.”

“A holiday party for the staff? Bah. Humbug!”

See what I mean? It’s loud budgeting, but from a business owner’s perspective. For many, this is not easy, because it goes against what we’re taught in business school.

The business gurus want us to be confident. And bold. We’re encouraged to take risks, work hard and relentlessly pursue our goals. “Fail greatly!” they say. “Reach for the stars!” “Push yourself to the limits!” “Be positive!” No one ever says to complain about your costs, gripe about your margins or whine about your money problems.

Loud budgeting turns all that positive-thinking advice on its head. Instead, it’s telling everyone around you – your customers, your employees, your suppliers – that you’re barely holding it together and that the $0.02 increase in poly-laminates is going to put you out of business.

You don’t have to reveal the truth. My clients who complain the most are the ones who are generally sitting on the biggest piles of cash. They’re driving 10-year-old cars, fly economy and eat at Outback Steakhouse. They don’t actually tell anyone that they’ve got enough money to afford more expensive things. That would destroy their ruse. They’re not broke. They just consider paying full price a character defect.

Loud budgeting is part of that ruse. Go ahead, try it. You’ll find that it’s a strategy to constantly remind anyone within earshot of your constrained budget and inevitably people start believing it. You’d be surprised at how many of them offer concessions – lower fees, reduced prices, better deals – out of sympathy or empathy or simply just to stop you from complaining.

You don’t need to be a young adult to understand this. Most successful small business owners do.

And it’s never too late to start. Go ahead: complain about your company’s terrible cashflow. Grumble. Grouse. Moan. Bellyache. Do this in public and do it loud. Make it so any one will think twice before coming to you with something that’s going to cost more than what you’re already paying. People don’t want to get into fights. More than a few will be forced to come up with better ideas, rather than suffer your protests. Others may abandon their price increases altogether just to keep the peace. The ones that pursue their course of action will learn to really think through their case before presenting it to you.

“Loud budgeting helps take an element of shame away from feeling like you don’t have enough money,” said one financial educator.

Shame? I think shrewd is the better word.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Dogs can distinguish between fearful and angry or sad human faces, brain scans suggest
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Researchers analysed activity in regions of brain when dogs were shown images of different facial expressions

While dogs are known to turn the puppy eyes on their owners, it seems our pets are keeping a close eye on us too: research has revealed dog brains can distinguish different types of unhappy human faces.

Dr Laura Cuaya, a co-author of the study from the University of Vienna, said previous behavioural studies had shown dogs could tell apart some human facial expressions, but such studies tended to only test two at a time, one positive and one negative. As a result, it was not clear if dogs could distinguish different types of happy or unhappy faces.

Now Cuaya and colleagues have revealed dog brains can not only distinguish happy faces from other expressions, but can tell apart different negative expressions, distinguishing fearful faces from those that are angry or sad.

“This is the first demonstration that the dog brain can distinguish between emotions from the same valance,” she said.

While the team’s previous research has suggested dogs do not have a particular region of the brain devoted to processing faces, Cuaya noted that did not mean the brain activity pattern was the same for the front and back of the head.

Writing in the journal iScience, Cuaya and colleagues report how they worked with pet dogs that had been trained to voluntarily lie still, awake and unrestrained, within an MRI scanner.

In the first experiment, eight dogs were shown five sets of happy faces and five sets of neutral faces. Each set contained four photos of humans that were unfamiliar to the dog but were of the same gender as their primary caregiver. This was repeated five times for each dog.

The results revealed increased activity in certain parts of the brain when the dogs were shown happy faces compared with neutral ones.

Cuaya said these areas were associated with higher visual processing, social processing and reward processing – suggesting the dog was processing something positive.

Dr Raúl Hernández Pérez, the first author of the study, said the results raised another question, however: “We don’t know if these regions are related just to happy faces or to emotional faces in general.”

The team then carried out a second MRI experiment involving 12 dogs. Each was shown new sets of unfamiliar male and female human faces, this time bearing four different expressions: happiness, sadness, fear and anger.

The researchers used machine learning to analyse activity in the same brain regions identified in the first experiment, revealing such activity could distinguish happy faces from each negative expression – but could not distinguish between different types of unhappy face.

However, when the team analysed activity in the whole dog brain, they found it was possible to distinguish between sad v fearful faces, and angry v fearful faces – with differences in activity in different parts of the brain – but not angry and sad faces.

after newsletter promotion

Hernández said different negative expressions might trigger different responses as they represented a different type of threat.

The authors said it might be harder for dogs to tell apart two human facial expressions if they were both negative or both positive, and dogs might also need additional information – such as body language – to distinguish anger from sadness.

The research has limitations, including small sample size; most of the dogs being border collies, and all were healthy and without behavioural problems.

Cuaya said the study could have practical implications: for example, expressing happiness when training a dog could aid the learning process.

Bridget Waller, a professor of evolution and social behaviour at Nottingham Trent University, who was not involved in the study, described the work as fascinating, saying it showed how dogs have been shaped through domestication to understand human behaviour.

“Smiling is the most commonly used human facial expression, vital to our social interactions, and so it makes sense that dogs have developed a particular ability to distinguish this from other facial movements,” she said. “It seems less clear that they can distinguish between the other facial expressions, and again this would make sense as these are much less commonly produced in human social interaction.”
