An earthquake on Monday caused injuries and significant damage in a province on Colombia’s Pacific Coast as well as the city of Pereira, provincial governors ​said.

The temblor occurred at 7:34 a.m. local time near the town of San José del Palmar, Chocó province, the Colombian Geological Service said in a preliminary bulletin posted to social media. The U.S. Geological Survey said it measured the earthquake’s magnitude at 7.4.

Colombia’s geological ‌service said its depth was 96 km. The country’s unit for disaster risk ​management ​said it was in contact with local authorities ​to verify potential damage.

It was felt in Ecuador and as far away as Panama to the north, and prompted building evacuations in the country’s capital of Bogota.

The governor of Colombia’s Choco province wrote on X that there were injuries and serious damage to buildings in the department’s capital Quibdo.

The mayor of Cali, Colombia’s third largest city, also reported “major damage.”

Footage published by local media showed damage to residential and office buildings in other nearby cities. Blu Radio reported cracks in buildings in Cali, Armenia and Pereira, as well as Medellin

Venezuela was hit by devastating twin earthquakes in June, which killed more than 6,000 people, mostly on the coast near the capital, Caracas.

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/heal.title: Hong Kong to review warning system after record heat triggers lowest alert
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/heal.author: Theodora Yu,Ng Kang-chung,Kristen Cheung
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/heal.text:
Pledge follows calls to adopt international measurement that places greater weight on direct sunlight and to increase monitoring stations

Hong Kong labour authorities have pledged to review the city’s heat stress warning system, a day after the weather forecaster issued the lowest-level alert for outdoor workers despite record-breaking temperatures, prompting questions about the index’s effectiveness.

The pledge on Monday followed calls from experts for the government to adopt an international measurement that gives greater weight to direct sunlight, and to increase the number of heat stress monitoring stations so that all districts are covered and the risks faced by outdoor workers are better reflected.

“We will review the current mechanism while maintaining our close communications with relevant departments,” Undersecretary for Labour and Welfare Ho Kai-ming said on Monday.

“The Labour Department has been working with different departments, including the Observatory, to mitigate the occupational safety risks faced by workers.”

The city reached a scorching 36.9 degrees Celsius (98.4 Fahrenheit) on Sunday, the highest temperature recorded since the Hong Kong Observatory began operating in 1884. Yet the lowest-level amber heat stress alert for outdoor workers remained in place.

The Observatory said the scorching conditions would persist in the coming days, with temperatures in some areas forecast to reach at least 37 degrees, although more frequent showers are expected later this week.

The Heat Stress at Work Warning system was formulated by the department based on a heat index developed by the Observatory and the Chinese University of Hong Kong.

It takes into account air temperature, humidity, wind speed, solar radiation and hospital admission figures to measure heat stress. There are three warning levels – amber, red and black – to alert employers and workers to the heat severity while they work outdoors or indoors without air conditioning.

Under the department’s guidelines, employers should arrange additional rest periods for affected workers when an amber warning is in force.

Workers with “very heavy” workloads should suspend their duties under a red alert, while those with “heavy” workloads should do so under a black warning.

A check by the South China Morning Post found all previous warnings issued regarding the level of heat stress for outdoor workers were at the lowest tier since the system’s launch in May 2023 by the department.

Former Observatory director Lam Chiu-ying described the heat index used by the warning system as “a wrong parameter”.

“The index does not give much weight to heating by sunshine. It therefore does not apply to situations exposed to sunshine, like work sites, street sweepers, open-air hawkers, food and other delivery people,” he said.

Lam said the index had been designed to reflect the broader environment faced by residents rather than outdoor workers.

The Hong Kong Heat Index formula consists of three variables: the air temperature; the wet-bulb temperature, which reflects humidity and wind speed; and the globe temperature, which reflects the heating effect of the sun.

It has the same variables as the wet bulb globe temperature formula (WBGT), an internationally adopted environmental index measuring outdoor heat stress on the human body for outdoor workers and military personnel, yet the variables carry a different weight.

The proportion of the globe temperature accounts for a weight of only 0.05 – four times lower than 0.2 as required under the WBGT formula, he said.

“The current heat parameter does not reflect the heating effect of the sun,” he said.

Lam noted that because most Hong Kong residents stay indoors, the heat index was designed around general local hospital admission rates, placing greater weight on humidity and temperature while assigning a smaller weight to solar radiation.

He urged the government to adopt the WBGT to determine heat stress in direct sunlight for work-related situations.

Lam also suggested lowering the heat stress warning thresholds, arguing the lack of elevated warnings despite record-breaking temperatures indicated that those thresholds were unrealistically high.

He recommended that the government consider Japan’s example, which revised its regulation in 2025 to set a wet bulb globe temperature threshold of 28 degrees – sustained for more than an hour – that mandates hydration protocols and rest cycles to protect outdoor workers.

In Causeway Bay, Ken Kwok, a courier in his forties, told the SCMP on Monday he took a two-hour break from noon to 2pm and received a heat subsidy. But the morning sun remained scorching as he moved between buildings.

“Even if I get to work less under heat stress, the parcels and orders are still there waiting for me to deliver, and the workload just keeps piling up,” he said.

A street cleaner surnamed Lam, 68, said he had been working since 7am and could occasionally take 15 minutes of rest.

The subcontracted cleaner said he did not know how to request cooling equipment from his company.

“I only work part time, so fewer hours in the heat means I earn less,” he said. “I saw some workers wearing cooling vests, but I am not sure if the company will provide them for me.”

Beyond reviewing the heat index, Ren Chao, a professor in the faculty of architecture at the University of Hong Kong, suggested the government increase monitoring stations from the existing 10 sites under the Observatory so that each district has a station to monitor the work situation locally and more accurately.

Measuring stations are set up at construction sites in Japan, using on-site data to more accurately estimate potential health risks for their outdoor workers, she added.

Albert Chan Ping-chuen, professor at Hong Kong Polytechnic University’s faculty of construction and environment, suggested using technological devices to monitor the health conditions and physiological responses of individual workers.

“We need continuous, personalised monitoring – that is the best way to effectively monitor and protect workers,” Chan said.

https://www.scmp.com/economy/global-econ.title: Wave of US tariff refunds flows back to Chinese firms, buoying profits by millions
https://www.scmp.com/economy/global-econ.author: Emma Ma
https://www.scmp.com/economy/global-econ.text:
Five listed firms, operating mainly in automotive and healthcare sectors, disclosed payouts, as reversal of duties strains US customs revenue

The wave of US tariff refunds is reaching Chinese companies. More than US$38 million in tariff rebates, plus accrued interest, from US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has landed in the bank accounts of five listed Chinese firms since last month, providing a windfall that is expected to bolster their earnings.

The five listed firms primarily operate in the automotive and healthcare sectors. Each secured an average tariff refund of US$7.64 million, representing between 13.12 per cent and 53.58 per cent of their 2025 net profit, according to the companies’ annual reports and filings. The funds were disbursed through accounts held by their US subsidiaries.

The largest payout went to the US subsidiary of Zhejiang-based Huahai Pharmaceutical, which has received more than US$14.2 million in tariff refunds. The sum is substantial for the drug maker, equivalent to 36.36 per cent of its full-year 2025 net profit. In its exchange filing, the firm noted that the refunds would “impact its profit in the second half of this year”.

Guizhou Tyre, based in southwest China, generated more than 45 per cent of its annual revenue from overseas markets last year. Its core products sold in the US are trailer and off-road tyres. In an announcement released on Friday, the tyre maker disclosed that its US subsidiary had received more than US$11.98 million in combined tariff refunds and interest, which would be factored into its 2026 financial statements.

And the wave is far from finished. Figures from Chinese data provider Wind show that more than a dozen mainland enterprises had either filed disclosures or responded to investors via online interaction platforms, confirming they had submitted applications.

“The tariff rebates benefit not only firms with US subsidiaries, but also original equipment manufacturers (OEMs),” said Zhou Zheng, an analyst with Shanghai-based Aijian Securities. “The refunds, in theory, will boost US importers’ appetite and financial capacity to restock, while curbing their urge to drive down prices in negotiations. This will ultimately benefit Chinese OEMs.”

Official figures show that CBP had disbursed US$100 billion in tariff refunds by the end of July. The sum accounted for roughly 60 per cent of more than US$166 billion in tariff revenue that the US federal government collected via sweeping duties – imposed last year by President Donald Trump – that the US Supreme Court struck down in February.

Multiple US businesses have also received their tariff reimbursements. Amazon.com, for example, said it had secured US$600 million in tariff refunds by late July.

Though the extra tariffs weighed on American consumers last year, billions in rebates are unlikely to deliver tangible benefits to shoppers at present, according to a KPMG survey.

The firm polled 300 US corporate leaders in February and found that only 18 per cent planned to fully remove the price surcharges they had previously imposed.

Meanwhile, the sweeping wave of tariff refunds is reducing US federal fiscal revenue.

A monthly statement by the US Treasury showed that the US government disbursed US$21.97 billion in tariff refunds in May, completely offsetting tariff collections of US$21.93 billion that month. In June, tariff payouts ballooned to US$49.18 billion, dragging net customs revenue down to negative US$25.56 billion.

“Taking all relevant factors into account – including US tariff rebates and personal income tax refunds – unless the US rolls out additional policies to boost household consumption demand, fiscal support for the US economy is set to weaken in the second half of the year compared with the first six months,” said Lu Zhe, chief economist at Suzhou-based Soochow Securities.

Tao Chuan, an analyst at Shanghai-based Guolian Minsheng Securities, wrote in a late-July research note that “the fiscal strain stemming from tariff rebates is intensifying for US government revenue”.

“Slumping customs receipts could push the US deficit ratio up by 0.3 percentage points,” Tao explained. “Existing tariff policies are insufficient to plug the revenue shortfall created by these repayments.

“We believe the Trump administration is dissatisfied with this outcome and is likely to roll out additional tariff measures.”

https://www.dw.com/en/india-news-jharkha.title: India news: Jharkhand police use tear gas, water cannons to disperse student protesters
https://www.dw.com/en/india-news-jharkha.text:
Police used force to disperse students marching towards the Jharkhand assembly, as protests over alleged irregularities in government recruitment exams entered their third week. DW has more.

These updates have been closed. Thank you for joining us.

Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Monday, August 10:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

That's all for today, people!

I will be back tomorrow with more.

The situation in India's northeastern Assam state remained critical on Monday, with the death toll in the floods reaching 100, officials said.

Two more people died overnight on Sunday after weeks of heavy monsoon rain inundated villages, damaged roads and farmland and disrupted livelihoods.

More than 700,000 people have been displaced since the floods began last month, while about 49,000 remain in 125 relief camps and distribution centers, officials said.

Authorities are warning that, several rivers, including the Brahmaputra, remained above danger levels, raising the risk of further flooding in vulnerable areas.

Farukuddin Ahmed, a 47-year-old trader from Nazira town in Assam's worst-hit Sivasagar district, that in a nearby village of 100 houses only a few remain.

"The residents, mainly dairy farmers, have to rebuild their lives from scratch having lost all their cattle," he said, according to the Associated Press.

Authorities are assessing the damage and providing financial assistance to affected residents. According to the government about 50,000 people had already received interim compensation.

While flooding is a recurring problem in Assam during the monsoon, experts warn that climate change is making rainfall increasingly erratic and extreme.

Police used tear gas, batons and water cannons to disperse the crowd of students marching towards the state assembly in Ranchi in the eastern state of Jharkhand on Monday, reports said.

On Sunday, the sixth round of talks between student protesters and the government failed to reach a breakthrough after students alleged irregularities in government recruitment exams.

The sit-in protests in Jharkhand began on July 25.

Student leader Devendra Nath Mahto has been on an indefinite hunger strike since August 2 is demanding action over alleged irregularities in the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC), Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission Combined Graduate Level (JSSC CGL) and other competitive examinations required to qualify for government jobs.

Meanwhile, authorities on Monday arrested former Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) chairperson L Khiangte in connection with alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations, reports said.

Earlier, Chief Minister Hemant Soren has assured the protesting students that his government would take action over alleged exam irregularities and invited them for talks.

A Delhi court called the sexual harassment allegations against former Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) chief Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh "false and fabricated" and part of a "deep conspiracy which seems to be politically motivated," media reports said.

Singh was acquitted last week of the sexual harassment and stalking charges brought by female athletes. The former lawmaker from Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), had denied allegations that he groped wrestlers and demanded sexual favors.

In its detailed judgment, the court cited "material contradictions" in the wrestlers’ accounts, inconsistencies between their allegations and documentary evidence, and the absence of contemporaneous complaints, media reports said.

The court said some allegations appeared "rehearsed, well-practiced and planted."

Lawyer Rebecca John, who represented four of the women, described the acquittal as "deeply, deeply disturbing" on Monday, news channel NDTV reported.

The allegations had triggered months of protests in New Delhi in 2023, led by prominent Indian wrestlers with hundreds joining the sit-in demonstrations accusing authorities of failing to act against Singh.

Delhi police charged Singh in 2023, and a court formally brought charges against him in 2024 over allegations involving five women.

Mumbai-based model Rhiya Ahir, who gained attention after standing in front of a police van carrying protesters during last month's Cockroach Janta Party-led demonstrations, has spoken about facing online abuse and threats following the protest.

In an interview with DW's Shalu Yadav, Ahir said the attention had come at a "heavy price" of online trolling and harassment, adding that women should be able to express their views without being targeted.

She referred to comments made about women protesters, including comments that they "should be raped" and would "enjoy it," saying such remarks could influence others and should not be allowed to go unchallenged.

"I read one comment saying 'we are going to rip you apart from the middle. And nobody's going to come to lay flowers on your grave,'" she said.

Ahir described the attacks as "criminal."

"I will not let it slide," she said. "I will not let them feel that they can sit behind their blank screens and feel so powerful by belittling other people.

Her comments come amid a wider online campaign targeting women who took part in the CJP-led protests, with reports of fake and AI-manipulated images, doxxing and threats against participants.

An activist who considers himself a right-wing "political commentator" was arrested in the southern state of Kerala on Sunday over remarks he allegedly made about the women at the Cockroach Janta Party-led student protests last month, media reports said.

The case was registered following a complaint alleging that videos on TG Mohandas' YouTube channel, Pathrika, were intended to disturb public order and create fear and unrest.

According to reports, in the videos, Mohandas allegedly said the Delhi protests could lead to gang rape and claimed that women attending it "like rape" and that some "enjoy being raped."

He also called for police to open fire at protesters.

News channel NDTV reported that Mohandas is a former member of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). However, the RSS has denied any association with the commentator.

The BJP on Monday criticized the arrest as "discriminatory" and accused the Kerala government of attempting to divert attention from other issues, reports said.

The development comes amid an online campaign targeting women who took part in CJP-led student protests. The countrywide stir ended last month with the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Multiple reports indicate that young women involved in the movement are facing severe online harassment. They have been targeted with fake and AI-manipulated images, as well as a barrage of online abuse, including assault threats.

Additionally, their phone numbers and home addresses have been leaked online alongside targeted attacks against their family members.

Hello! This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi Studio bringing you the latest updates from across India.

Female protesters who took part in Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) demonstrations against the government are facing harassment and doxxing. In the latest development, a right-wing activist was arrested in the southern state of Kerala for allegedly posting a video saying that those attending the protests "like rape."

Meanwhile, a Delhi court has said allegations of sexual harassment made by women wrestlers against former Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) chief Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh were "false" and "fabricated."

For all this and more, stay tuned to our blog.

https://www.dw.com/en/colombia-several-k.title: Colombia: Several killed after large earthquake rocks region
https://www.dw.com/en/colombia-several-k.text:
A powerful earthquake, initially measured at magnitude 7.4, has struck Colombia, killing at least 18 people. Tremors were also felt in neighboring Ecuador, as well as in Panama and Venezuela.

A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning.

Officials said at least 18 people were killed in the city of Pereira. Rescue teams were working to free residents after buildings collapsed in Cali and other cities.

The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast.

The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed, in some cases with people trapped inside.

"Residents of Cali, we currently have at least 20 collapsed structures in the city with people trapped inside; we are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," Eder said on Instagram, posting an accompanying video statement. "I have requested support — specifically rescue personnel — from the mayors of Bogota and Medellin."

The Choco region's governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi was among the first the report the "severe seismic event" in the east of her state.

"Although the epicenter was in San Jose del Palmar, in the capital Quibdo there are injuries and severe damage to buildings. We are already conducting the damage assessment to issue the first official report," Cordoba-Curi said. Quibdo is home to around 150,000 people.

Mauricio Salazar, the mayor of Pereira, the capital of Risaralda to the east of the epicenter, told Caracol Radio that 18 people had died, saying "the situation is critical."

The mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas, said in a radio interview that two people were killed in his city, not far northeast of Pereira.

Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined.

"Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online.

The US Geological Survey (USGS) initially measured the quake at magnitude 7.4. Colombia's national authority at first logged a smaller figure but later revised its reading up to 7.4 as well.

The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border.

The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south.

The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter.

The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors.

Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela.

USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake.

The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake.

https://www.dw.com/en/which-country-is-t.title: Which country is the new Mecca defense pact targeting?
https://www.dw.com/en/which-country-is-t.text:
Observers suggest the new alliance between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan won't result in any of the countries fighting for each other. Instead it's about preventing Iran and Israel from regional dominance, they say.

Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia sealed a historic defense pact on Friday, signing an agreement "intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression."

The so-called "Mecca Joint Defense Agreement" between the three Sunni Muslim-majority states is meant to increase cooperation during regional uncertainty and threats from the Iran war.

The agreement was signed in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

The alliance has been likened to a NATO-style alliance and on Friday, the Pakistani foreign ministry said that an attack on any member would be regarded as an attack on all.

But experts and analysts have been quick to point out that the deal is unlikely to work that way — at least at first.

For example, on the weekend the Houthi rebel group in Yemen fired at Saudi Arabian oil facilities again. The Houthis consider Saudi Arabia their enemy and are also aligned with Iran. The latter has also targeted Saudi Arabia after the US and Israel attacked it, starting a war in late February, because it sees the Saudis as a US ally.

But following the Houthi attack on the weekend, neither Turkey nor Pakistan sprang to the Saudis' defense. Nor are they likely to attack Iran, analysts say. In fact, Pakistan is acting as a mediator between Iran and the US currently.

This arrangement is meant as more of a deterrent and as an "elastic defense pact," Dania Thafer, executive director of the Washington-based think tank the Gulf International Forum, or GIF, told DW late last week.

"If you look at the parties in this agreement, you have Saudi Arabia, which is in the middle of this conflict. But you also have Turkey and Pakistan, who both have relations with Iran and both have relations with the US. So I think it's an extra layer of deterrence, if you will, for Saudi Arabia," Thafer explained. "I think Saudi Arabia is looking at a layered deterrence approach to regional threats as they emerge."

This new alliance is likely to work out in various stages with the short-term goal being a "stabilized region," Kamran Bokhari, a senior fellow at the Middle East Policy Council in Washington, told DW.

Longer term goals will involve defense cooperation rather than fighting, other experts have said.

"The three countries complement each other unusually well," Andreas Krieg, a lecturer in security at King's College London, told news agency Agence France-Presse last week.

Saudi Arabia has oil wealth but limited defense technology and has been reliant on the US up until now. Meanwhile Turkey and Pakistan need investment and have strong armed forces, and in Turkey's case an advanced defense-industrial sector, Krieg explained. Pakistan is the only one with nuclear weapons of the three.

"Turkey has technology and production capacity but needs markets and investment. Pakistan has a workforce, military institutions and nuclear deterrent, but needs financing and industrial capabilities," Krieg noted.

A Turkish official cited by Reuters said the agreement was purely defensive in nature and open to any regional neighbors who might want to sign on. Egypt is thought to be a potential partner but also has other allies to consider, including the United Arab Emirates. The latter have not joined and relations between the UAE and Saudi Arabia are currently strained.

The Turkish official also said the pact does not replace or negate previous bilateral or multilateral agreements between signatories, nor is it directed at any one actor or threat.

Yet there's no doubt the agreement has been understood as a deterrent, mainly against two other nations, Iran and Israel.

The Mecca pact's objectives are not about some kind of military victory, Khalid al-Jaber, director of the Doha-based Middle East Council on Global Affairs wrote in a Sunday op-ed for Qatari news outlet, Al Jazeera. "It is the prevention of hegemony."

"Diminished American weight could leave the region inside an order whose rules are set by two actors alone: Israel and Iran," he continued. "The Mecca pact is best understood as an early attempt to build a third pole — a bloc that does not need to fight either power, but one that has enough weight to deny either a monopoly over the region."

Two of the signatories to the agreement — Pakistan and Saudi Arabia — don't recognize Israel and have no official relations with it, even though at least in Saudi Arabia's case there are likely some covert ties. Turkey does recognize Israel but the relationship is strained at the moment, due to Israel's activity in Gaza that Turkey has called genocide.

Turkish leader Erdogan said last week that Israel's actions in Syria and Lebanon also constitute a threat to Turkish security.

"The development [of the Mecca pact] poses significant challenges for Israel, pushes the prospect of normalization with Riyadh further out of reach and cuts short the vision of a 'new Middle East'," Oshrit Birvadker, a research fellow at the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security, wrote in a Saturday editorial for the outlet Israel Hayom.

Birvadker also believes that the new trilateral alliance will increase the growing rivalry and tensions between Turkey and Israel.

The Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University looked at how the Iranians were reacting.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi did not seem too upset by the agreement. On the social media platform, X (formerly Twitter) he posted that "when Muslims stand together, we can face every challenge by malicious outsiders head-on."

Observers took this to be a positive, part of Iran's argument for pushing the US out of the region.

Some Iranian observers thought that the Saudis might be trying to leverage the better relations that the Turkish and Pakistanis have with the Iranians, to make itself safer from Iranian attacks. But other Iranian politicians were more critical, saying that Saudi Arabia wasn't safe with the US as an ally and wouldn't be safe with Turkey and Pakistan either.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker
https://www.dw.com/en/which-country-is-t.summary: Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed a historic defense pact on Friday. The three Sunni Muslim-majority states are meant to increase cooperation during regional uncertainty. Experts say the agreement is meant to prevent Iran and Israel from regional dominance.

https://www.dw.com/en/how-climate-change.title: How climate change is reshaping Africa's malaria risk
https://www.dw.com/en/how-climate-change.text:
Researchers say warming temperatures are altering malaria transmission patterns across Africa, creating new challenges for health systems and disease control.

For decades, global efforts towards the eradication of malaria, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, have focused essentially on West and Central Africa where the disease is most endemic.

The WHO African Region accounts for about 95% of global malaria cases and deaths. More than half of all malaria deaths in the region occur in Nigeria (31.9%), the Democratic Republic of Congo (11.7%) and Niger (6.1%). Children under 5 years of age account for about 76% of malaria deaths in the region.

To stem the tide of malaria cases across Africa, the global health body has recommended a wider use of the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine among children living in regions with moderate to high malaria transmission by the Plasmodium falciparum — a parasite that causes 95% of all malaria infections in Africa. It's transmitted to humans through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.

The WHO warned in April 2025 that recent funding cuts were jeopardising malaria control efforts, with more than half of malaria-endemic countries surveyed reporting moderate or severe disruptions to malaria services.

A study published in The Lancet found that the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine reduced all-cause mortality among vaccine-eligible children by 13.2% in pilot programmes in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi.

Malaria transmission is most efficient within temperature ranges common across many tropical regions of West and Central Africa, according to a new study by nature.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Malaria transmission by mosquitoes usually peaks at temperatures of around 25 degrees Celsius (77 Fahrenheit) and becomes much less likely when temperatures drop below 16 degrees or rise above 34 degrees Celsius, largely because the malaria parasite must complete part of its life cycle inside the mosquito — a process that is highly temperature-dependent.

Because of this, malaria transmission has historically been most favourable across many tropical parts of West and Central Africa, where temperatures frequently fall within the range most suitable for transmission.

In contrast, some parts of Southern Africa and the highlands of East Africa have historically remained cool enough to keep the spread of malaria at bay, preventing the disease from becoming a major public health burden.

That, however, is beginning to change. The nature study found that rising temperatures are making parts of southern Africa and high-elevation areas of East Africa increasingly suitable for malaria transmission, while parts of West Africa are becoming too hot for optimal transmission.

Climate change is not only heating up the continent, it's redistributing risks, says Olugbenga Mokuolu, professor of pediatrics at Nigeria's University of Ilorin.

Although West African countries like Nigeria fall under areas that are "too hot for malaria to thrive, this is not good news to celebrate either, because a world that's too hot for malaria is not a good world for children's health overall," Mokuolu, who also serves as an advisor to the Nigerian Minister of Health on malaria elimination, told DW.

"The same heat that's inconvenient for mosquitoes is dangerous for people," he added, noting that climate is "not the primary driving factor of malaria. Funding, drug and insecticide resistance, and health system strength still matter more."

Olugbenga continued that the elimination and prevention of malaria on the continent could become "a story of two very different regions: West and Central Africa may get a small, unplanned assist from climate, while East and Southern Africa, historically lower-burden areas, face a growing new threat that could undo hard-won gains."

Climate change is fundamentally changing the geography of disease on the continent, Olumide Idowu, founder of the International Climate Change Development Initiative, told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Idowu added that many African countries have developed adaptation plans but implementation has lagged behind the pace of climate change.

Although Africa is one of the lowest contributors to greenhouse gas emissions, it remains one of the most vulnerable regions to climate change — posing systemic threats to the economy, infrastructure, and even its fragile health systems.

Idowu mentioned that without a significant increase in "investment at home, reinforcement of local institutional capacity and embedding health as a core pillar of climate resilience, many African countries risk being unprepared for the changing epidemiological landscape that climate change is creating."

The regions expected to be hardest hit are also regions less accustomed to fighting malaria today, the study revealed.

"Governments, health systems and communities must adapt to this evolving threat, including getting ready now to run more aggressive anti-malaria programs in cooler areas where risk is rising," Olugbenga said.

He also urged countries in West and Central Africa to sustain malaria elimination efforts, warning that resistance to insecticides and drugs, funding gaps and weak health systems could easily negate any reduction in malaria transmission associated with rising temperatures.

The German government regards US President Donald Trump's plan for ‌Gaza as an opportunity to make progress towards the disarmament of Hamas, a Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on Monday.

Asked about Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's announcement Sunday that Israel rejected the US-led plan, the spokesperson said some disagreement was not surprising.

"With such a ‌complex undertaking, it was perfectly clear there ⁠would be many, many ⁠unanswered questions," he added.

Late last month, Trump hailed a 15-point plan that would see Hamas lay down its weapons and the Israeli military withdraw from the Gaza Strip. It expands on an October 2025 ceasefire agreement that slowed, but did not end, the conflict in the Palestinian territory, about two-thirds of which is under Israeli control.

Despite the truce, Israel continued to carry out airstrikes in Gaza. Health officials there say more than 1,200 Palestinians, most of them civilians, have been killed since October 2025. Five Israeli soldiers were killed in Gaza during that time. Hamas, which is classified as a terrorist organization by Israel, the US, Germany and several countries, does not disclose figures on its war dead.

On Sunday, Netanyahu said Israeli troops would not leave the Gaza Strip until Hamas had been "genuinely" disarmed.

An Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson said Iran will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the United States met its conditions.

"It is up to the US side to stop and make amends for its illegal and destructive actions," Esmail Baghaei said Monday.

In a statement over the weekend, a member of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and Revolutionary Guards commander said Tehran had the following demands of the US:

The impasse over the Strait of Hormuz has led to a global jump in fuel prices.

Iran is holding talks with Oman over transit through the strait, including a possible temporary shipping corridor, but it has said any actual reopening depends on negotiations with the United States.

On Sunday, however, US President Donald Trump said the US not engaged in major talks with Iran.

"We are low-keying it," he said, according to US media outlet Axios. "We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money."

Trump also expressed his optimism that a satisfactory conclusion would eventually be reached.

"It will work out. It always works out. It's like a chess game," he said of the war.

Iran has said it intends to charge commercial vessels for passage through the Strait of Hormuz, according to a statement Monday from the Foreign Ministry.

Iranian media cited spokesperson Esmail Baghaei as saying that Iran was working with Oman on "mechanisms for monitoring security, protecting the environment and combating crime at sea."

Fees would be for maritime services provided to ships, he explained.

The dispute over transit rights in the strait, through which some 20% of the world's oil passed before the war and which is a key route for gas and fertilizer, is regarded as a key reason behind the continuation of the war against Iran.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Before the United States and Israel launched the conflict against Iran at the end of February, shipping through the waterway did no incur tolls nor fees for transit.

The Strait of Hormuz measures only around 39 kilometers (24 miles) at its narrowest point.

Since Iran and Oman each claim the maximum 12 nautical miles allowed under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) as their territorial waters, there are no international waters in the narrowest part of the roughly 21-nautical-mile-wide strait.

The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea guarantees a right of transit passage and prohibits a blockade of commercial vessels. Iran, however, does not accept this legal position.

The US goal is to restore pre-war levels of oil and gas transit through the Strait of Hormuz, US Vice President JD Vance said on Sunday.

https://www.dw.com/en/asean-closing-rank.title: ASEAN closing ranks as cyberscam threat escalates
https://www.dw.com/en/asean-closing-rank.text:
Southeast Asian governments are searching for a joint strategy against cyberscammers, a criminal industry that has grown too big, too connected and too embedded in ASEAN economies to be solved just by policing.

For years, governments across Southeast Asia largely approached the region's online fraudsters as a matter for the police, anti-trafficking agencies and border authorities.

But these bodies have appearently failed to stem the rise of international cyberscam cartels. The illicit industry is increasingly using international banking systems, cryptocurrencies, telecommunications networks, shell companies and trafficking routes, with some of its centers operating under the protection of armed or politically connected groups.

Now, ASEAN governments seem increasingly willing to tackle the threat as a united bloc.

Signs of this shift were visible at the controversial meeting in Bangkok on August 6 between Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and President Min Aung Hlaing, the head of Myanmar's military government.

The two governments agreed to clamp down on scam centres along their shared frontier, exchange information and jointly disrupt criminal financial flows.

Thailand also offered support for Myanmar's participation in the Egmont Group, an international network of financial-intelligence bodies. Myanmar's military-backed parliament had already voted in favour of applying the death penalty on those caught operating online scam centres.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

While visiting Cambodia late last month, Indonesian Deputy Foreign Minister Arif Havas Oegroseno also proposed a joint task force to combat online scam syndicates.

And last week, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto and Thai Prime Minister Charnvirakul held talks in Jakarta where they agreed their two countries must lead the way and strengthen ASEAN's resilience against scam groups.

A UN estimate published last month put the annual losses from cyber scammers — many of whom are located in Southeast Asia — at between $88.3 and $114.1 (between €76 billion and €98 billion) globally in 2025.

Artificial intelligence, cryptocurrencies, encrypted communications and deepfake technology have made their operations cheaper and harder to detect.

"Cyber scams in Southeast Asia have evolved beyond a conventional cybercrime issue and should be viewed as an economic security threat," Hai Luong, a lecturer at Australia's Griffith University's School of Criminology and Criminal Justice, told DW.

Governments in Southeast Asia have already had to respond to pressure from the US, the EU and China as their online cartels drew international attention.

In October 2025, the US designated Cambodia's Prince Group, one of the country's largest conglomerates, as a transnational criminal organisation and imposed sanctions on 146 people and companies connected to it.

US authorities also charged Chinese-born Prince Group chairman Chen Zhi with wire fraud and money laundering conspiracies. Cambodia eventually revoked Chen's citizenship and extradited him to China.

Prince Group's business empire extended across real estate, finance and other sectors in Cambodia. US authorities allege that criminal revenues were mixed with legitimate commercial activities through an international network of companies.

Washington has also sanctioned other Southeast Asian individuals and companies accused of investing in scam compounds and laundering money.

The EU followed last month, imposing sanctions  on Prince Group and Jin Bei Group in Cambodia and the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army in Myanmafor alleged involvement in cyberscams.

In 2024, the United States Institute of Peace estimated that Cambodia's cyber-scam industry generated more than $12.5 billion annually, equivalent to roughly a third of the country's formal economy.

The collapse of several scam-linked conglomerates has raised concerns about how the economic shockwaves will affect the rest of the country. At the same time, other voices say negative publicity around scamming is hurting the country's tourism sector and keeping away foreign investors.

Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet has acknowledged that the illicit scam economy is damaging legitimate businesses and has vowed a systematic crackdown on online scam networks, including greater scrutiny of the financial sector.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The National Bank of Cambodia has shuttered at least six financial institutions since the start of the year. Three commercial banks whose licences were revoked in August had all been sanctioned by the US over alleged links to scam networks.

On August 4, the Singaporean government introduced legislation that would expand information-sharing between police and service providers, allow authorities to disable accounts suspected of facilitating scams and strengthen restrictions on financial, telecommunications and online services supplied to suspected offenders.

As ASEAN nations try to clamp down on cybercriminals, the region's greatest weakness is its fragmentation, Sophal Ear, an associate professor at Arizona State University's Thunderbird School of Global Management, told DW.

"Criminal organizations operate seamlessly across borders while governments continue responding through separate agencies with different mandates and limited coordination," he said.

Ear added that the financial infrastructure used to move and conceal criminal proceeds can often prove more resilient than the law-enforcement architecture designed to dismantle it.

Now, the regional governments seem to be catching on — at least judging by ASEAN's new Plan of Action in Combating Transnational Crime for 2026–2035.

The plan calls for improved intelligence-sharing between national law-enforcement agencies and financial-intelligence units, joint investigations, better cross-border coordination and stronger capacity among anti-money-laundering regulators.

ASEAN has also recently established a joint working group to combat money laundering.

But ASEAN's consensus-based system still heavily relies on national governments implementing those commitments and sharing sensitive financial and law-enforcement information.

"In practice, governments should prioritise disrupting the financial infrastructure, labour supply chains, technological services, and transnational business models that sustain scam operations rather than focusing solely on individual offenders," said Luong from Griffith University's School of Criminology and Criminal Justice.

Asha Hemrajani, senior fellow at  Nanyang Technological University's  S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, agreed that the region needs to take a "holistic, not siloed" approach to attack the entire cyberscam business model.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The shared objective should be to identify and dismantle crime syndicate leadership, financial networks and enabling infrastructure, not just arrest money mules or raid individual scam compounds in Cambodia and Myanmar," Hemrajani said.

This includes official scrutiny of high-risk corporate structures and checking sources of funding, as well as a much tougher stance against money laundering, she added. Hemrajani also recommended ASEAN sanctioning business groups linked to the cyberscam networks, similar to how Washington cut off sanctioned Southeast Asian companies from the entire US economy.

Criminal groups have largely survived previous crackdowns by simply moving workers, technology and money to new places and new compounds. In order to fight the online cartels, ASEAN should do more than just closing scam centres. The real challenge is making the regional economy itself harder for them to exploit.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

The illicit industry is increasingly using international banking systems, cryptocurrencies, telecommunications networks, shell companies and trafficking routes. The two governments agreed to clamp down on scam centres along their shared frontier, exchange information and jointly disrupt criminal financial flows.

https://www.dw.com/en/india-anger-over-e.title: India: Anger over exam irregularities spreads to Jharkhand
https://www.dw.com/en/india-anger-over-e.text:
Inspired by the Cockroach movement, young people in India's eastern state of Jharkhand are marching on the state assembly to demand transparency and a probe into alleged irregularities in civil service recruitment exams.

Thousands of protesters in Jharkhand are marching on the eastern Indian state's parliament to demand a federal inquiry into alleged irregularities in recruitment exams for government jobs, for the tests to be canceled and for a more transparent hiring process.

Police used water cannons against the protesters on Monday as they tried to breach security barricades en route to Jharkhand Legislative Assembly.

The confrontation marked a sharp escalation between the authorities and the protesters.

The movement began on July 25, when demonstrators started camping at Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium in the state capital, Ranchi.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In scenes reminiscent of the youth-led "Cockroach" protests that swept New Delhi last month, some protesters also went on a hunger strike.

Rahul Kranti, a 40-year-old government job aspirant and one of at least six protesters participating in the hunger strike, was moved to intensive care after his health deteriorated.

"The future of Jharkhand's youth will not be allowed to be sold. I will remain on hunger strike, whether I am in hospital or at the protest site," Kranti told DW.

He pledged to continue his protest until the government cancels Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) exams and orders a criminal inquiry by the national Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI).

After hours of negotiations on Sunday, the government agreed to suspend this year's disputed JPSC exam, and three members of the commission resigned.

But the protesters say the concessions fall short of their demands, which include the cancelation of the Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission's Combined Graduate Level (JSSC-CGL) examination, a major recruitment test for state government jobs, and a full federal probe into alleged irregularities across Jharkhand's recruitment system for public sector jobs.

The initial trigger was the latest JPSC civil services examination, which advertised just 103 government posts. More than 2,000 candidates qualified for the next stage when results were announced in early July.

Then, an answer sheet began circulating online, apparently showing a candidate who had passed the exam, despite completing very little of it. The image went viral, prompting allegations that the results had been manipulated.

Police have arrested the candidate at the center of the controversy, along with 10 others, and the commission's chair resigned under pressure.

But the protesters say those steps have not addressed the larger problem.

The Jharkhand protesters want the exam results to be scrapped and for the exam to be repeated.

They are also calling for an independent inquiry, either by retired High Court judges from outside the state, or by federal authorities. The protesters argue that a state police probe cannot adequately examine allegations involving Jharkhand's own recruitment machinery.

The Jharkhand Chhatra Sangh (JCS), one of the student groups involved in the protests, is also demanding greater transparency in answer sheets and test results, biometric verification, tougher safeguards against paper leaks and accountability for officials and private, third-party recruitment agencies.

The JCS also wants alleged tainted examinations from recent years to be investigated and, where necessary, canceled and retaken.

"The government must clean up the entire JPSC and JSSC recruitment system, investigate those responsible, blacklist tainted agencies and make future examinations transparent and fraud-proof," S Ali, national president of the JCS, told DW.

The Ranchi protest began days after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) called off its 36-day protest in Delhi over leaked medical entrance examination papers.

That movement, which saw youths stage hunger strikes and camp outside the Delhi observatory, Jantar Mantar, culminated in the resignation of India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan .

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke has announced plans to travel to Jharkhand, while a delegation has already reached Ranchi to support the protesters.

But Jharkhand's movement is more than a mere copy of the CJP. The JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch has led the protests, alongside the Jharkhand Loktantrik Krantikari Morcha. Student unions, including All-India Students Association (AISA) and All India Students' Federation (AISF), have also joined.

Neha Bora, AISA president, visited the protesters in Ranchi.

"Whether at Jantar Mantar or in Ranchi, these protests symbolize the broken trust young people feel towards the system," Bora told DW.

"They are demanding to be heard, but also asking for changes that can prevent such crises in the future."

Jharkhand has its own history of popular struggles over land, identity and political rights.

Political analyst Radhika Ramaseshan said the students had clearly taken cues from Delhi, but were also drawing on that local tradition.

"Jharkhand has doubtless adopted the CJP playbook to flag a different set of issues that also impinge on the future of young people," Ramaseshan told DW.

"The difference is that the protesters' target is the coalition government in Ranchi, which, like the union government, responded late," she added.

Chief Minister Hemant Soren has said he is open to talks, while authorities have restricted protests within 750 meters (820 yards) of the assembly through August 12.

"The solution to every issue lies in dialogue, not batons and guns," Soren said at Jharkhand's annual tribal festival in Ranchi on Sunday. He sought to assure students that those responsible for the alleged recruitment irregularities would face severe punishment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The protests in Delhi showed that a student movement built around social media, hunger strikes and anger over a compromised examination can force a national government into a major concession.

The protesters in Jharkhand have already secured a win, with the cancelation of this year's disputed JPSC exam and the resignation of three members of the commission.

But India's youth are refusing to stop there.

Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan have all seen major controversies around recruitment examinations. What has been missing in those states is a sustained movement capable of turning those grievances into broader political pressure.

For now, and despite the state government's concession, the students in Ranchi are refusing to call off their protest.

"We are waiting to find out what happens. These fraudulent examinations have to end, but our patience is running thin too," Motilal Mahto, one of the protesters, told DW.

They want tests to be canceled and for a more transparent hiring process. Police used water cannons against the protesters on Monday as they tried to breach security barricades.

https://www.dw.com/en/is-iran-s-middle-c.title: Is Iran's middle class being pushed into poverty?
https://www.dw.com/en/is-iran-s-middle-c.text:
The war has intensified Iran's economic crisis, squeezing household budgets, hurting businesses and raising fears that millions of middle-income families are slipping closer to poverty.

For Mina, a housewife in Iran, the war is no longer measured by air strikes or military statements. It is measured by what has disappeared from her family's dinner table.

"Since the war started last year, we have become poorer every day," she told DW. "I honestly can't remember the last time I bought red meat. We replaced it with chicken, but even chicken has become a luxury. We no longer think about saving money. We only think about paying the rent and buying food."

The International Monetary Fund forecasts Iran's economy will contract by 5.4% this year, while inflation is expected to approach 69%. The World Bank has also warned that conflict, weaker trade and prolonged uncertainty are weighing heavily on the country's economy.

For economist Ahmad Alavi, a Sweden-based researcher, the war did not create Iran's economic crisis, but sharply intensified it.

"Iran entered the conflict with inflation already above 40%, a weakening currency, chronic budget deficits and years of sanctions," he told DW.

"The war acted as an external shock. Damage to infrastructure, disruption of trade through the Strait of Hormuz, internet shutdowns and rising inflation expectations accelerated the collapse in purchasing power," he added.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Alavi points to official figures showing annual inflation reaching 66% and year-over-year inflation nearing 88%. Food prices have risen even faster. Bread and cereals have increased by around 140%, meat and poultry by 135%, dairy products by more than 116%, and edible oils by over 200%.

For many families, those figures have meant buying less meat, postponing medical treatment and abandoning plans to save money.

Economists say households often cut spending on travel and clothing first. As inflation persists, however, the cuts extend to food, healthcare and education, placing growing pressure on middle-income families that once considered themselves financially secure.

Alavi says lower-income households have suffered the most but argues that the middle class is increasingly facing the same pressures: "Many salaried workers and pensioners have fallen below the poverty line for the first time because incomes have failed to keep pace with inflation."

He estimates that between 3.5 and 4.5 million more Iranians have fallen into poverty since the conflict intensified, bringing the total number of people living below the poverty line to more than 40 million.

The pressure is also being felt by Iran's private sector.

Morteza, an Iranian trader, says regional trade routes changed rapidly after shipping through the Strait of Hormuz became more difficult.

"China moved quickly to fill part of the gap left by suppliers in Dubai," he told DW. "Unlike Gulf countries, China can also ship goods through rail links across Central Asia, avoiding many of the risks and delays associated with maritime transport."

He believes the growing importance of these overland routes was one of the reasons the US targeted a railway line near Iran's border with Turkmenistan, although that assessment could not be independently verified.

Even so, Morteza says the shift has brought little benefit to Iranian traders.

"The collapse of the rial and soaring inflation have prevented the market from growing," he says. "Merchants are living with constant uncertainty because exchange rates change almost every day. Goods that we bought and sold at lower prices now have to be replaced at much higher costs, and that's only if customers still have enough purchasing power to buy them."

For Morteza, uncertainty has become the biggest obstacle.

"With tensions continuing, I honestly don't see a clear future for doing business in Iran."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Despite higher global oil prices, Alavi says Iran is unlikely to benefit significantly because sanctions, export restrictions and higher transport costs continue to limit its oil revenues.

He argues that government measures, including subsidies, price controls and intervention in the foreign exchange market may ease some immediate pressure, but are unlikely to address the underlying problems: "Without restoring confidence, reducing sanctions and addressing structural problems, these policies remain short-term responses rather than lasting solutions."

Alavi says uncertainty itself has become one of the biggest barriers to economic recovery.

According to him, many businesses are delaying investment because they have little confidence in future economic conditions. At the same time, households are becoming increasingly cautious about spending as they expect prices to keep rising and the value of their incomes to fall further.

He says rebuilding confidence among investors, businesses and consumers is likely to take much longer than repairing physical damage caused by the war.

Unless inflation eases, the exchange rate stabilizes and trade conditions improve, Alavi believes many households will remain under financial pressure, even if military tensions subside.

Looking ahead, he expects living standards to deteriorate further if current trends continue.

He says more families are likely to cut spending on protein, healthcare and education, while business closures and unemployment may continue to rise.

"We don't talk about the future anymore," Mina says. "We only hope we can afford next month's rent."

Edited by: Kristie Pladson
https://www.dw.com/en/is-iran-s-middle-c.summary: Iran's economy is expected to contract by 5.4% this year, while inflation is expected at 69%. The World Bank has warned that conflict, weaker trade and prolonged uncertainty are weighing heavily on the country's economy. The International Monetary Fund forecasts Iran's economic crisis

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce3q.title: Netanyahu's rejection of Trump's 15-point Gaza plan unlikely to be final word
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce3q.text:
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have categorically rejected the new Board of Peace roadmap to disarm Hamas in Gaza, but that is unlikely to be the final word.

The White House has not officially commented. However, it is reportedly "not bothered" by Netanyahu's statement and views it as campaign rhetoric in the run-up to a heated general election.

"We understand Bibi's political needs" the Israeli journalist, Barak Ravid, quotes a senior US official as saying – using a nickname to refer to the Israeli leader. "We have no problem with it as long as he continues to do what we ask – especially regarding restraining attacks in Gaza."

Recent days have seen an apparent pause in Israel's strikes on Gaza – something Hamas had demanded when signing on to the US-backed, 15-point roadmap.

And there is another suggestion that Israel is ready to advance US President Donald Trump's peace plan for Gaza – getting ready for the deployment of the International Stabilization Force (ISF). The force is made up of international troops, with the plan being for them to work with a new Palestinian police force to secure the territory.

The expected construction of the first ISF base is still scheduled to begin amid the ruins of Rafah in southern Gaza at the end of this month, according to Israeli public radio, Kan News, which would allow reconstruction to begin at last.

In July, after months of delicate negotiations, Trump announced a "major milestone" in the implementation of his plan to end Israel's war in Gaza.

Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump said that the Board of Peace had reached an agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups in the territory.

The deal is meant to be carried out in phases, with all weapons decommissioned and stored by a new Palestinian administration in Gaza – which reports to the Board of Peace - and Israeli forces withdrawing from the more than 60% of Gaza they currently control.

Senior Hamas officials confirmed that they had agreed to the new framework, conditioning it on mutual compliance by Israel. This was widely viewed as a major potential breakthrough in the conflict. The UK welcomed it and the European Union hailed it as a "crucial step".

However, for more than a week, Israel did not give its formal response.

An Israeli spokesman said only that the roadmap did not "reflect Israel's positions." A far-right member of the government, Itamar Ben-Gvir, wrote on X that the deal was "unacceptable."

Increasingly, mainstream Israeli opposition politicians also raised doubts. They questioned whether all small arms would be decommissioned and the sequencing of the plan.

Finally on Sunday, Netanyahu told his cabinet, "I wish to be precise here: Israel does not accept the 15-point document."

He added: "The IDF [Israel Defense Forces] will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed. And when I say the disarming of Hamas, it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry. And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament."

In the same statement, the prime minister described President Trump as "the greatest of our friends in the White House" but said that Israel knew "how to stand firm" against unacceptable ideas.

In Israel, there is widespread scepticism that Hamas intends to follow through on its commitments.

The Islamist movement has long seen "armed struggle" as a core precept, its legitimate response to Israeli occupation of Palestinian lands. In recent months, there had been signs of it reasserting its authority in Gaza.

"Israel can certainly never agree to retreating anywhere where the terrorist group that caused the worst massacres since the Holocaust is still there and is still ruling the Strip," Fleur Hassan-Nahoum, an Israeli commentator and former deputy mayor of Jerusalem told the BBC.

She stressed that the "trauma of the Israeli people" from the deadly Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023, which ignited the devastating Gaza war, should not be underestimated.

Any potential concessions for Netanyahu would come at a politically sensitive moment.

He is facing an uphill contest in the upcoming general election, scheduled for 27 October. It will be Israel's first since the 7 October assault and three years on, Netanyahu has failed to secure what he vowed: "absolute victory" over Hamas.

The former American diplomat and veteran Middle East negotiator, Aaron David Miller, said the Israeli leader is facing "the most consequential election" of his political life.

"He's navigating a very fine line between keeping his constituents happy and not angering or alienating President Trump," he told the BBC.

For now, he believes the White House recognises the situation and is giving Netanyahu "a pass."

Miller added: "It's hard to believe that you're going to see any serious movement before you have another Israeli government."

In the meantime, the Board of Peace has been trying to reassure the Israeli public about the roadmap.

The High Commissioner for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov – who led months of delicate negotiations with Hamas – gave an interview to Israel's Channel 12 just hours after Netanyahu's formal rejection of the roadmap.

"Its goal is to make sure that Gaza is never again a threat to Israeli security and that what happened before, [on] October 7, never happens again," he said.

He said the deal takes "a step-by-step approach" meaning: "If there is verified decommissioning of weapons, that they are taken away from the factions and stored and ultimately rendered unusable, Israel then withdraws from Gaza."

Ultimately, Mladenov said that nothing was being built "on the basis of trust" but on "verification."

Hamas has since indicated that it still remains committed to the roadmap. It called on mediators and the Board of Peace to push for Israel to stick to the terms agreed.

The Israeli prime minister has confirmed that talks with the Americans are continuing.

Meanwhile heavy pressure from Washington is likely to increase.

Trump is also looking at an important election this year – November's midterm elections for the US Congress. His Republican party faces the prospect of heavy losses, with petrol and grocery prices pushed up, in part due to Washington's unpopular five-month-long war in Iran.

The US president's own approval rating has tumbled, and he may well demand positive developments in his peace plan for Gaza in an effort to score a much-needed foreign policy win.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce3q.summary: Netanyahu's statement is reportedly "not bothered" by the statement and views it as campaign rhetoric. Hamas has since indicated that it still remains committed to the roadmap.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyr.title: When and where to see the solar eclipse in Scotland
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyr.text:
People across Scotland will get the best view of a solar eclipse in nearly three decades on Wednesday.

Up to 95% of the Sun will slowly disappear behind the Moon in the most dramatic eclipse visible from the UK since August 1999.

The entire event is set to last about two hours and it is important to never look directly at the Sun.

Here is what you need to know about the partial solar eclipse, including the best places to watch it in Scotland and how to do so safely.

Astronomers say the best place to see the eclipse is an elevated location with unobstructed views to the west.

"People in England are worried about having to find a clear view of the western horizon," said Astronomer Royal for Scotland Prof Catherine Heymans.

"But that is less of a problem for us in Scotland because the Sun sets later."

That means in general the Sun should be higher in the sky in Scotland at the time of the eclipse, and people will be able to see the event more clearly.

And by the time the Sun sets after approximately 21:00, the event will be well and truly over.

According to Heymans, the Moon will start to move in front of the Sun between about 18:01 and 18:10 BST.

The peak of the eclipse will occur about an hour later, with the whole event ending just before 20:00.

"It is so slow moving. So if you go out and the sun is not there you have time to walk down the street to a park or climb up a hill," she added.

"The most important thing is to watch the Met Office cloud cover forecast and plan accordingly from there."

A Met Office spokesperson said: "Weather fronts grazing the west of Scotland may hamper ideal views.

"So although viewers in the south and east of Scotland will see less of the sun covered by the moon, they may get better views because of clearer skies."

There are a number of community events happening across Scotland to mark the occasion:

It is important to never look directly at the sun and follow proper guidance for safely viewing the eclipse.

Eclipse glasses - which will be handed out at events across Scotland hosted by astronomical societies or bought online - can offer protection from harmful rays of sunlight.

Legitimate pairs will have safety certification ISO 12312-2 or ISO 12312-2:2015 printed somewhere on the glasses, according the Royal Observatory Greenwich.

Regular sunglasses do not provide adequate protection.

"Even if you don't feel like it is painful to look at the Sun, it is still really damaging to the retina," Heymans said.

"It is a two-hour extravaganza as the Moon slowly covers the Sun and then moves away again so it is not just one glimpse, and it is really dangerous to keep looking."

She added there is a temptation to look at the Sun through the cloud but even that can harm the eyes.

Following the 1999 total solar eclipse, the Royal College of Ophthalmologists reported about 70 cases of people experiencing vision problems after watching the eclipse.

The college said about 40% of those people had looked at it for less than a minute.

Alternative methods for safely viewing the eclipse, include using a solar telescope or making a pinhole projector.

"The next best thing is a colander," Heymans said - or any household object with small holes.

The holes in the colander project an indirect image of the sun on a surface, such as a wall or the ground.

"Normally the sunlight shines through the holes but during the eclipse, chunks will be eaten out of the Sun, and at the peak, it will just be the arc in the shadow of the colander," she explained.

People should also be careful when photographing the eclipse as the sun can damage the camera on a phone the same way as it can damage the eyes.

Cameras can be protected with eclipse glasses.

Parts of Spain and Portugal will witness the phenomenon of a total eclipse on Wednesday but Heymans said Scotland will be "agonisingly close".

The path of the eclipse shadow means the UK will not see a total eclipse, but in Scotland, up to 95% of the sun will be obscured.

"Solar eclipses happen every couple of years but a total eclipse is very rare and we are a stone's throw away from it," Heymans said.

"Over the course of two hours, the moon will be biting chunks out of the Sun as it moves across in front of it, blocking the light out."

However, the Sun will not be entirely covered.

While there will be smaller solar eclipses over the next few years, the next total eclipse is not expected to take place until 23 September 2090.

"It will be darker and it will feel a little eerie but we're not going to have the sky go completely dark," she said.

At its peak - weather permitting - only an arc of the Sun will be seen.

"It's going to be agonisingly, frustratingly close but if anyone wants to see a full total eclipse, they will have to leave the UK," Heymans added.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyr.summary: The eclipse will be the most dramatic visible from the UK since August 1999. Up to 95% of the Sun will disappear behind the Moon in the most spectacular eclipse since August 1998. The entire event is set to last about two hours and it is important to never look directly at the Sun.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdx7.title: Best places to see partial solar eclipse across England
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdx7.text:
People across England have a rare chance to experience a dramatic partial solar eclipse this week, when the Sun will be almost entirely blocked by the Moon.

The Moon will cover 90 to 96 per cent of the Sun on 12 August - the biggest coverage since the total eclipse in 1999.

There will be dozens of celestial events to mark the occasion across the country and ideal spots where people should be able to watch the moment safely.

People in the South West of England are likely to see the most coverage in England, while people in parts of Greenland, Iceland and northern Spain will experience a total eclipse.

The celestial event will last about one hour and 50 minutes, starting at about 18:20 BST and finishing by 20:10, but exact times will vary depending on where you are.

You can follow the links below for the latest on where - and how - to experience the eclipse in different areas of England.

The government is advising people to either use indirect viewing methods or wear genuine eclipse glasses with specially designed filters that meet international safety standards ISO 12312-2:2015(E).

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c235.title: New weight loss pill approved for use in UK
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c235.text:
A daily weight-loss pill made by the drug firm behind the Mounjaro jab has been approved for use in the UK - the first country in Europe to do so.

Foundayo, made by Eli Lilly, is for treating obesity and type 2 diabetes.

But while people will be able to buy it privately with a prescription, the approval by the Medicines and Healthcare productors Regulatory Agency does not automatically mean it will be made available on the NHS.

Foundayo is a form of GLP-1 medication that blunts appetite, and comes after the MHRA approved a pill version of a similar weight-loss drug, Wegovy, in June.

Eli Lilly said while it could immediately be used by the NHS for type 2 diabetes, it would be making an application to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence in England for it to be recommended as a weight loss treatment as well.

Dr Simon Cork, from Anglia Ruskin University, said while the weight-loss benefits of Foundayo were less than other treatments, patients could still expect to see "significant, clinically meaningful changes to their weight".

And he said a key advantage was that it was likely to be cheaper than other weight-loss treatments, which have tended to be tightly restricted by the NHS.

University of Glasgow expert Prof Naveed Sattar agreed it was "good news".

He said another benefit was its convenience, pointing out that unlike the Wegovy pill, which has to be taken on an empty stomach, this pill could be taken at any time of the day.

"The arrival of another effective oral option is a positive development and should help more people access treatment that best suits their needs and preferences," he added.

Experts belive it could help people coming off weight-loss jabs remain slim.

Trials found that patients given the tablet, called orforglipron, every day for a year avoided regaining much of the weight they had lost - a known risk when coming off GLP-1 injections.

People on weight loss medication are also advised to eat a healthy diet and get enough exercise.

And, like any medication, there can be side effects to using Foundayo, including nausea, diarrhoea, constipation and vomiting.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c235.summary: Foundayo is a daily weight-loss pill made by Eli Lilly. It is for treating obesity and type 2 diabetes. But it does not automatically mean it will be made available on the NHS.
