China's latest rocket launch ended in failure this morning, lighting up the skies with some unwanted fireworks.

The state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) launched a Long March 7A rocket today (Aug. 10) from the Wenchang Space Launch Site, in the country's Hainan province, just after 8:00 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT; 8:02 p.m. local time). Around 85 seconds into the launch, the rocket exploded, generating a massive fireball and a cloud of smoke and debris while still soaring through Earth's atmosphere.

CASC had not yet released a statement about the incident by the time of this story's publication, but video reposted to social media captured the shock of onlookers the moment that the rocket burst into flames. Based on such views, the mission will almost certainly be deemed a complete failure, with total loss of vehicle and payload.

Today's launch was the 18th Long March 7A mission since the rocket's debut in 2020, which, subsequently, also ended with the vehicle's explosion. China traced that mishap to an engine malfunction that occurred shortly after first-stage separation. This morning's launch, however, didn't get that far.

The Long March 7A's four side boosters and core stage detach as a full cluster during first stage separation, which typically occurs just under three minutes after liftoff. As today's incident occurred just 85 seconds into flight, the rocket was still engaged in the main stage's initial engine burn to escape Earth's atmosphere.

The 7A — a variant of China's Long March 7 rocket family — stands just over 197 feet (60 meters) tall and combines the first two Long March 7 stages with a hydrolox (liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen)-powered third stage capable of launching up to 7 tons to geostationary transfer orbit (GTO).

According to China National Radio, today's launch carried China's Zhongxing-4B spacecraft,, a communications satellite presumably bound for GTO. China's Zhongxing satellites provide telecommunications and broadband internet services and are also thought to provide services for China's military.

It is unclear what repercussions today's explosion may have on upcoming launches, including a Chinese Zhuque-3 rocket liftoff scheduled for Monday evening. That mission is scheduled to fly from China's Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, more than 1,500 miles (2,415 kilometers) from Wenchang, at 7:45 p.m. EDT (2345 GMT; 7:45 a.m. local time), and is expected to feature a first-stage landing attempt.

CASC uses the standard Long March 7 rocket, which shares its core stage with the 7A, as its launch vehicle for delivering cargo to the Tiangong space station in low Earth orbit about every eight months. The most recent of those missions launched in May, putting the next resupply launch sometime around January 2027. Depending on the cause of this morning's explosion, that mission and others could face delays as China investigates the incident.

https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/taylor-fr.title: Taylor Fresh Foods recalls jalapeños after supplier discloses potential salmonella contamination
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/taylor-fr.author: The Associated Press, Michelle Chapman
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/taylor-fr.text:
Taylor Fresh Foods, parent company of Taylor Farms, is voluntarily recalling some products that include jalapenos because of worries about a possible salmonella contamination.

The announcement comes a few weeks after Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled its iceberg lettuce products sourced from central Mexico because of a potential link to a multistate cyclospora outbreak that has sickened people across the U.S.

Taylor Fresh Foods said that it was pulling some products including jalapenos from stores shelves after finding out that Coast Citrus Distributors was voluntarily recalling fresh jalapeños due to a potential salmonella contamination.

Guacamole, pico de gallo and taco dip are some of the prepared foods included in the recall. The list of recalled products were distributed by Taylor Farms in multiple states with a “Best If Used By” date up to and including Aug. 16, 2026. The products were sold at stores including Kroger, Stop & Shop, Target, Whole Foods, Trader Joe’s and Walmart.

Taylor Fresh Foods said that the Food and Drug Administration and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention were working with state and local partners to investigate illnesses in a multistate outbreak of salmonella infections linked to fresh jalapeños supplied by Coast Citrus Distributors. The company said that a grower in Sinaloa, Mexico, a supplier to Coast Citrus Distributors, was identified as the potential source in the outbreak.

Taylor Fresh Foods said that it is no longer sourcing products from the farmer and will be filling orders from alternative suppliers. The company is currently not aware of any reported illnesses linked to its products containing jalapeños.

Consumers who have any recalled product are advised to discard it immediately and not eat it. Refunds are available at the location of purchase.

Consumers with any questions can contact Taylor at 855-455-0098 Monday through Friday from 8am-5pm PT.
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/taylor-fr.summary: Taylor Fresh Foods is pulling some products including jalapenos from stores shelves. The company is not aware of any reported illnesses linked to its products. The recall comes a few weeks after Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled its iceberg lettuce products.

https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/mackenzie.title: MacKenzie Scott has given away $26 billion and rarely speaks publicly. Now she’s releasing a novel—but you won’t find it on Amazon
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/mackenzie.author: Sydney Lake
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/mackenzie.text:
MacKenzie Scott is notoriously generous and notoriously quiet. The billionaire philanthropist, novelist, and ex-wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has doled out more than $26 billion to charity during the past few years, but has done so without much fanfare.

Now Scott is going back to her writing roots—she was trained under the acclaimed writer Toni Morrison, after all—and is releasing her new novel, Last Days in Two Nations, chapter by chapter on Substack. Noticeably, she’s opted to publish it on an open platform, and not through a publishing house or distributed by a major bookseller like, say, Amazon.

Scott married Bezos in 1993 before Amazon was officially launched in 1994. She played a critical role in the early days of establishing what is now the No. 1 company on the Fortune Global 500 list, including overseeing early operations, business plans, and contracts. Upon their 2019 divorce, she received roughly a 4% stake in Amazon.

Of course, we may never know whether her intention was to keep her first novel since 2013 off of Amazon, since she never responds to press inquiries and rarely shares her personal thoughts with the masses. (She does, however, sometimes discuss her philanthropic efforts on a blog for her philanthropic organization, Yield Giving). But it’s undeniably interesting that she would opt to publish a book and likely make nothing for it, although she’s got plenty in the bank.

Her current net worth is estimated at more than $38 billion, even though she’s donated more than half of that to charity. But the power of the Amazon shares she received upon her divorce from Bezos is what keeps her net worth and her ability to give high. It’s the classic paradox of how a bull market allows billionaires like Scott to give away tens of billions without getting noticeably poorer. Wealth advisors call this phenomenon “concentrated equity wealth.”

Nearly all of Scott’s fortune is tied up in Amazon stock, and Amazon has been on a historic run. Although Scott reduced her original stake by about 42% by selling or donating some 58 million shares worth around $12.6 billion, the shares she still holds have appreciated faster than she can distribute them. Amazon share prices have jumped nearly 69% in the past five years. Her net worth has only dropped about $2 billion year-to-date, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

While attending Princeton University in the early 1990s, she studied under Morrison, who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1993, the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for Beloved in 1988, and the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012.

Scott has long credited Morrison with shaping her writing and helping her get her footing early in her career. Morrison helped put Scott on a path to publish her first novel, The Testing of Luther Albright, which was published in 2005 and received an American Book Award in 2006.

“This writer that I admired so much also turned out to be such a gifted and devoted teacher,” Scott said of Morrison in a 2017 Princeton University interview. “She has given me a real example of a life of passionate devotion to more than one calling.”

Morrison had the same admiration for Scott, having called her “one of the best students I’ve ever had in my creative-writing classes…really one of the best,” according to Vogue.

Scott is releasing her new novel piece by piece, having dropped the title, epigraph, personae, and contents on Saturday, the prologue on Sunday, and the first chapter called “Monday” on Monday. It appears the entire novel will be out by Aug. 31. That being said, it’s difficult to decipher at this point exactly what the novel is about, but the subtitle of the story is called “A History in Eighteen Minds.”

Based on the prologue she posted, the novel appears to center on a fictional religious community called the Church of the Long Tomorrow, whose members she describes as “trapped by beliefs that were not their own.”

“Such a habit to breathe in those words before we have words, and make them thoughts, a thought worm, decomposing us while we are still alive,” the prologue reads.

Scott married Jeff Bezos in 1993 before Amazon was officially launched in 1994. Scott has been a philanthropist since her divorce from Bezos in 2013.

https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/why-so-ma.title: Global wildfire surge hits U.S., propelled by rising temperatures
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/why-so-ma.author: Bloomberg, Brian K. Sullivan, Leslie Kaufman, Todd Woody
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/why-so-ma.text:
The US is enduring one of its worst wildfire seasons in years, with blazes scorching millions of acres. It’s part of a global pattern of hot, dry conditions that favor fires becoming more common with climate change.

Fires that erupted over the weekend in and around Spokane, Washington, have destroyed hundreds of structures and forced more than 60,000 from their homes — about 10% of the population. Three major fires have burned more than 8,000 acres and have not been contained, according to InciWeb, a federal fire-tracking website. There are 17 total fires currently active across Washington, Public Lands Commissioner Dave Upthegrove said on Monday.

Meanwhile, ongoing fires in Greece have consumed tens of thousands of acres and triggered evacuations. These conflagrations follow the historic fires that raged in France and Spain last month, displacing hundreds of thousands of residents.

All these fires broke out in different regions and ecosystems. But they’re examples of the same underlying shift: Rising temperatures are worsening wildfire risk. It’s happening in two ways at once. First, traditional fire country is becoming hotter and drier in all regions. Second, the range of landscapes that can sustain destructive blazes is growing broader.

“We’re seeing both, in the same moment, in different places, in different ecosystems,” said Daniel Swain, a University of California climate scientist who studies wildfire. “The commonality between all of them is that there has been a substantial period of record-breaking warmth and/or dryness.”

Swain describes the phenomenon as “lifting the flammability veil.”

Some parts of the world have always been susceptible to burning but rarely became hot and dry enough, for long enough, to support large fires. Now global warming is “putting a thumb on the scale, producing severe and unprecedented heat waves,” said Noah Diffenbaugh, a professor of Earth system science at Stanford University.

Trees lose moisture over extended periods of exceptional heat and dryness, becoming progressively more combustible. That has a stronger impact in ecosystems like Canada’s boreal forests, California’s Sierra Nevada mountains and parts of temperate Europe that evolved under relatively cool, moist conditions. Unlike many forests in the American Southwest, where trees are adapted to seasonal drought and frequent fire, these forests can become tinderboxes when subjected to weeks of unusual heat.

Mojtaba Sadegh, a wildfire researcher at Boise State University, compared a heat wave’s effect on a landscape to the toll it takes on the human body. Successive days of high temperatures are much more dangerous than a single day. “The physiology of the human body takes several days to kick in,” Sadegh said. “The same happens with vegetation.”

In research published last month, a team of scientists including Sadegh identified “fire weather waves,” or prolonged episodes of exceptionally hot, dry and often windy weather. Forest regions of the world experienced such a wave on an average of 4% of all days between 1979 and 2024. But the waves coincided with more than a quarter of land area burned and nearly half of the most energetic forest fires. The researchers found these episodes have become more frequent in most regions since 1979 and project that trend will continue.

Across the US, signs pointing to an active fire season were already there in April: Air tanker outfits, which fight blazes from the sky, were busy. By June, the National Interagency Fire Center warned it could be a bad year across the Pacific Northwest and Northern California.

Last winter, the Pacific Northwest, Rocky Mountains and large parts of California experienced a snow drought. Instead of feet of snow covering the landscape, mountaintops remained bare. This robbed the landscape of its natural replenishment that happens every spring and early summer when the snow melts and the waters run, leaving not only the grasses and shrubs dried out, but starving trees of moisture.

But extreme precipitation, not just the lack of it, plays a role in worsening fire conditions too. Deluges promote the growth of vegetation that then becomes fuel. Swain noted that heavy rains battered Spain in February prior to this summer’s heat waves.

“That is the same sequence of events that led up to the Los Angeles fires in 2025,” he said.

With fires now happening everywhere all at once, nations will be constrained in their ability to come to each other’s aid by dispatching firefighters and equipment. Communities that didn’t think they needed evacuation plans or fire mitigation measures will need to reevaluate.

Climate change doesn’t mean every place will become California — which this week is battling multiple wildfires amid a heat wave. It means that more landscapes around the world will occasionally cross a threshold where sustained heat and drought make extreme wildfire possible.

If the planet’s warming is lifting the flammability veil, as Swain says, the question is whether we’re prepared for what lies beneath.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/10/oil-in-s.title: Oil in U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve falls below 300 million barrels, lowest since 1983
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/10/oil-in-s.author: Spencer Kimball
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/10/oil-in-s.text:
Crude oil stocks in the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve have fallen below 300 million barrels, the lowest level in more than four decades, as global inventories are under pressure due to the Iran war.

The SPR fell by 6.1 million barrels to 298.7 million barrels last week, according to data released by the Department of Energy on Monday. The reserve is at its lowest level since January 1983.

President Donald Trump ordered the release of 172 million barrels in March after Iran choked oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, triggering the largest crude supply disruption in history.

The U.S. release is part of a coordinated action by countries in the International Energy Agency to support the global oil market with 400 million barrels, the largest deployment of crude stocks in the organization’s history.

The SPR stood at around 415 million barrels before the U.S and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/10/gold-jus.title: Gold just had its best week in 7 months. Here’s why Mike Khouw is buying more
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/10/gold-jus.author: Michael Khouw
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/10/gold-jus.text:
Gold
 jumped roughly 7% last week, logging its best weekly gain since January, driven by a weaker U.S. dollar, falling Treasury yields, and an unexpected contraction in employment data that reduced fears of aggressive Federal Reserve rate hikes.

(Note: the employment data wasn’t that bad; layoffs were low, private employment climbed by 30,000, and the data was negatively skewed by the seasonal effect of ~50k fewer government education jobs)

Key Drivers for Gold last week:

For the moment, gold remains below the 150-day moving average; the more leveraged way to play it — the gold miner ETFs GDX
 and GDXJ
 — are bumping up against it.

The key indicator is that Newmont Mining, the largest constituent of the gold miners, has broken through the 150-day moving average. To me, that suggests the others (GDX and GLD) will soon follow.

From an options traders perspective, gold has a more symmetric “Volatility Smile” - meaning out-of-the-money calls have higher “implied volatility” than at-the-money calls do, which improves the payoff of a long call spread (debit spread) relative to a similar option strategy in the S&P 500.

For example, a November 400/460 call spread in SPDR Gold Shares (GLD)
 would cost about $16.15, just over 25% of the difference between the strikes (a total of $1,615 as each contract represents 100 shares), providing an upside payoff of almost 3:1 if GLD should rally another 15% over the next 100 days.

https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.title: In Malaysia, wave of hate speech threatens Rohingya refugees
https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.author: The FRANCE 24 Observers
https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.text:
Malaysia has long been considered a safe haven for Rohingya Muslims fleeing persecution in predominantly Buddhist Myanmar. As of the end of February 2026, 126,000 Rohingyas were registered with the UN refugee agency in Malaysia, out of a total of around 215,600 refugees and asylum seekers.

However, they have faced growing hostility since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020, culminating in a wave of online hate and disinformation that began in April 2026. On July 27, around 1 hundred Rohingya refugees were forced to leave their homes in a fishing village after their neighbours put up signs urging them to leave.

Maryam* works for the NGO Article 19, which defends freedom of expression in Malaysia and combats hate speech.

"The latest wave of anti-Rohingya rhetoric has undoubtedly been one of the most intense in terms of both scale and duration. It began towards the end of April and is still continuing today.

It all started with a disinformation campaign claiming that Rohingya refugees were demanding land and special rights. In May, an online petition was launched calling on the Malaysian prime minister to expel Rohingya refugees from Malaysia. Organisations such as UNHCR, the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia (SUHAKAM), and NGOs came under pressure and received threats on social media."

To display this content from Facebook, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

Some Malaysian influencers regularly post anti-Rohingya content and contribute to the spread of hostile hashtags such as  #SaveMalaysiaFromRohingya.

"We reported some of the problematic content to Meta so that action could be taken immediately. However, Meta's content moderation, complaint handling, and reporting mechanisms remain far too slow to deal with harmful content."

She adds that the situation is particularly alarming because refugees are neither officially recognised nor protected under Malaysian law, as the country is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention. Although they are registered with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), they have no legal protection and are not allowed to work, leaving them vulnerable to exploitation and abuse.

This wave of online hatred has had dramatic consequences. On July 27, more than 1 hundred Rohingyas were forced to leave their homes in the village of Kuala Muda, in the state of Penang.

To display this content from Facebook, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

According to the local newspaper Sinar Harian, the Rohingya population in this village has almost quadrupled, rising from 108 people in 2018 to around 400 in 2026. A non-Rohingya resident told the media outlet Bharian: “The locals feel disadvantaged, particularly economically, because many Rohingya have taken up fishing, creating competition with local residents who depend on fishing for their livelihoods."

The refugee families were reportedly escorted to buses bound for Kuala Lumpur. On arrival in the capital, they went to the office of the UNHCR to seek assistance. They then set up tents outside the organisation’s offices while awaiting a response. The Malaysian police then intervened and detained them for a day to check their documents and legal status. They were eventually released and placed in the care of local NGOs.

Children are also being targeted. At least nine community schools for refugees have temporarily closed to protect their students. The exact number of affected schools remains difficult to determine.

Amira* is the founder of an NGO that provides education for refugees in Malaysia. She describes the climate of fear that has forced many refugee schools to shut their doors.

"Many children have been chased and harassed on their way to school. Some of these incidents have been shared on social media. Youth teams from several NGOs are now afraid to go in the field. The content being posted online is extremely radical. It is highly aggressive, using dehumanizing and threatening language. There is a real sense of fear within the Rohingya community."

Ahmad* is a Rohingya teacher and activist in Kuala Lumpur. He teaches at two schools in the capital that decided to close.

"One school remained closed for a month, the other for two weeks because of all this chaos. We have only just reopened. Despite the risks, the staff felt it was essential to resume classes so that the children could continue their education. We advised students not to wear their school uniforms so that they would not attract attention on their way to school."

He also points out that his students come from different refugee communities, but many Malaysians assume they are all Rohingya. According to him, this misconception is reinforced by media coverage that often labels all refugees as Rohingya.

To display this content from Facebook, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

Amira* explains that refugees have no legal right to formal education in Malaysia, as the country is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention.

"Schools like ours operate in a grey area. If someone were to ask, ‘Is this school legal? Do you have the right to be here?’ Of course, the answer is no. Some schools have been closed down by the authorities because they did not have the necessary authorisations.

The lack of the right to work and access to education marginalises the Rohingya and limits their integration in Malaysia. At the same time, disinformation campaigns wrongly portray them as economic migrants or invaders. On social media, many ask why the UNHCR does not send them to other countries, but they are unaware that its ability to organise resettlement depends on the willingness of states to offer places to refugees."

On 23 July, the deputy foreign minister informed Parliament that 5,000 Myanmar nationals currently held in immigration detention centres would be repatriated to Myanmar.

On 28 July, Foreign Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan said that the presence of the UNHCR office had made Malaysia "a magnet" for refugees and warned that the government could reconsider the agency's presence in the country if it refused to resettle more refugees.

Despite allegations of genocide against the Rohingya in Myanamar, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced on 30 July that Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya asylum seekers currently living in Malaysia.

The Myanmar Ethnic Rohingya Human Rights Organization Malaysia (MERHROM) expressed serious concern over the announcement:

"We cannot trust the Myanmar government to guarantee our safety while the massacres continue. Rohingyas will be forced to join the Myanmar military without any training and used as human shields in the army's war against various ethnic armed groups. That is the only reason the Myanmar military has agreed to take the Rohingyas back."

However, the Malaysian government later appeared to reverse its position. On 5 August, Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil announced that the government would not deport refugees if they faced a risk of persecution.

Denied citizenship under Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law, the Rohingya fled the country in large numbers in 2017 following a military campaign marked by massacres, sexual violence, and the systematic destruction of villages. The International Court of Justice is currently examining allegations of genocide against Myanmar over those events, following hearings held in January 2026.

* For security reasons, the people interviewed for this article asked to speak anonymously and their names have been changed.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20260.title: Nearly 70 percent of France under water restrictions amid record heat
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20260.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20260.text:
Nearly 70 percent of France is subject to water-use restrictions as drought conditions worsen amid successive heatwaves, the government said Monday.

A series of heatwaves over the past three months, compounded by drought, have broken temperature records, caused thousands of excess deaths, and fuelled massive wildfires.

"As France is experiencing a particularly severe drought, the effects of climate change continue to increase pressure on water resources," the ministry for ecological transition said, adding that "nearly 70 percent of French territory is subject to restrictions on water use".

As of August 9, the vast majority of mainland France, including Paris, was under at least the first water warning level, with 67 of the country's 101 departments under the highest crisis alert.

In areas subject to the highest alert, water is reserved for priority uses such as healthcare, civil protection, drinking water and sanitation.

Under lower alert levels, restrictions apply to activities such as watering gardens and green spaces, filling swimming pools, washing cars and irrigating crops.

In a further sign of the worsening drought across much of heatwave-pummelled Europe, two thirds of the aquifers that provide most of France's drinking water have dropped below their normal levels, the country's Bureau of Geological and Mining Research (BRGM) said on Monday.

The drawdown of groundwater reserves, common during the summer, is particularly pronounced this year "due to the shortfall in effective rainfall in July and the increase in water demand for various purposes", particularly in agriculture and tourism, the BRGM said.

READ MORE
Western Europe lived through hottest June and July ever recorded

July 2026 was the hottest month ever recorded in France and the third driest July in terms of precipitation, with a nationwide rainfall deficit of nearly 70 percent, according to national weather agency Meteo-France.

Ecology Minister Monique Barbut said on July 27 that drinking water supplies were "under strain in several areas", noting that tap water cuts were already affecting "more than 30,000 people", with drinking water supplied to residents by tanker trucks or bottled water.

The minister will convene a crisis meeting on the drought on Wednesday, which comes as France and swaths of Europe face another heatwave.

Meteo-France warned on Monday the southeast would see temperatures as high as 35°C, spreading further across the country as the week progresses.

https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military.title: China’s Long March 7A rocket explodes after launch, satellite lost
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military.author: Ling Xin
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military.text:
Rare failure ends a run of successful missions for the new-generation rocket, which was carrying the ChinaSat-4B communications satellite

China has suffered a rare failure of one of its newer-generation Long March rockets, losing a communications satellite after the launcher exploded shortly after take-off on Monday night.

Around 8pm Beijing time, the 60-metre (197-foot) Long March 7A blasted off from the Wenchang Space Launch Site on the southern island of Hainan, piercing the night sky as it carried the ChinaSat-4B satellite towards high Earth orbit.

But less than 90 seconds into the flight, the rocket erupted into a fireball engulfed in thick black smoke, according to videos posted on social media by spectators near the launch site.

Space observers suggested a major anomaly may have triggered the rocket’s flight termination system, destroying the vehicle. Both the rocket and satellite were lost over the South China Sea.

State news agency Xinhua confirmed the failure about three hours after the launch.

“The rocket experienced an anomaly during flight and the launch mission failed,” it said. “The specific cause is under further investigation.”

The China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology and its parent company, the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation, reposted the statement on their social media accounts.

ChinaSat-4B was expected to provide radio, television and other communications services to users around the world. Low-numbered ChinaSat satellites are also believed to be used for military communications.

The Long March 7A is one of China’s new-generation rockets and has become a workhorse for sending large satellites to high orbits. It burns mainly kerosene and liquid oxygen.

Monday’s launch had been expected to set a speed record of a different kind. Chinese media reported before lift-off that the roughly 12-day gap since the previous Long March 7A mission would be the shortest turnaround yet for the rocket – and for any of China’s new-generation Long March launchers.

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/africa/a.title: Congo’s Ebola outbreak started months before it was declared, says WHO
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/africa/a.author: Associated Press
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/africa/a.text:
Some cases early on were wrongly attributed to malaria and typhoid ‘so we are chasing the virus, it is ahead of us’

The fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record started in February, months before it was officially declared in mid-May, the World Health Organization said on Monday, as responders in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) struggle to catch up.

The WHO regional director for Africa, Mohamed Yakub Janabi, told a press conference that sequencing indicated the outbreak’s start.

He said some cases early in the outbreak were wrongly attributed to malaria and typhoid.

“So we are chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us,” Janabi said.

Confirmed cases of Ebola in this outbreak have reached 4,200, including over 1,900 deaths, according to the latest government figures.

The outbreak declared on May 15 is unlike most previous ones for Ebola because the Bundibugyo virus responsible for it has no approved vaccines or treatments.

Early testing was conducted for the more common type of Ebola, contributing to delays.

This Ebola outbreak has killed more people at a quicker rate than any other, including the 2014-2016 outbreak that is considered the worst on record with over 11,000 deaths out of at least 28,000 cases.

That outbreak took about eight months to reach 1,000 deaths.

Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted via bodily fluids such as vomit, blood or semen and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing.

The disease it causes is severe and often fatal.

Last week, WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Ebola is spreading faster than efforts to fight it, while some health workers are striking over a lack of pay.

New cases are doubling in some hotspots, Ghebreyesus said on X after meeting with officials in the capital, Kinshasa.

Health authorities have said between 60 and 70 per cent of new cases are recorded outside of contacts being monitored, and that the outbreak is spreading at an “alarming” rate.

Access to healthcare in the region already had been challenged by years of rebel conflict in one of Congo’s most remote and vulnerable areas, near the borders of South Sudan, Uganda and Rwanda.

Several past Ebola outbreaks have also been declared late, including the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak.

That outbreak was declared in March 2014, although the first human case was later found to have occurred in December 2013.

https://www.dw.com/en/why-the-rhine-drou.title: Why the Rhine drought is bad news for Germany’s recovery
https://www.dw.com/en/why-the-rhine-drou.text:
Germany’s inland waterways still move around 5% of the nation’s goods. With the Rhine at a critically low level, DW explores how the drought is hitting the economy where it hurts most.

Water levels on the Rhine River — a small but critical artery for goods vital to Germany’s industry — remain critically low as a result of weeks of drought.

At one of the river's shallowest stretches, Kaub — between Mainz and Koblenz — the water level stood at around 16 centimeters at Monday lunchtime, according to the Federal Waterways and Shipping Administration (WSV).

Although the real navigable channel is roughly a meter deeper, 40 centimeters is regarded as the lowest for standard commercial vessels at Kaub.

Ship operators use the reading at Kaub to decide how much cargo their barges can safely carry and whether a passage is feasible at all.

According to local media, in recent weeks, carriers have significantly cut their cargoes along the Rhine — in many cases to as little as one-fifth of normal capacity.

The problem isn't just limited to the Middle Rhine, the 130-kilometer (80-mile) stretch between Mainz and Bonn that is the narrowest and shallowest section of the river.

Areas around Cologne, Düsseldorf, Duisburg-Ruhrort and Emmerich are also at historic lows.

Jens Schwanen, the head of the BDB association of inland shipping, told the Rheinische Post newspaper on Monday that the Rhine may become impassable at Kaub before the end of the week.

This would effectively split the river in two for commercial traffic.

The drought could not come at a worse time for Germany’s economy, which is already grappling with weak growth, high energy costs and fading industrial competitiveness.

Germany still relies on its long rivers and waterways to transport some 5% of goods around the country, most of them bulk materials, including iron ore, coal, sand and petroleum products.

Out of 3.28 billion tons of goods transported in 2024, 173 million tons were carried by inland water, including the Rhine, according to BDB.

Eurostat, the European Union's statistics agency, calculated in 2023 that the Rhine corridor — from the Port of Rotterdam in the Netherlands to the German-Swiss border — accounts for around 40% of freight by ton-kilometers.

After two previous droughts, the Kiel Institute for the World Economy calculated in 2023 that for every 30 days of low water on the Rhine, Germany's industrial production declines by about 1%.

In an economy that has barely grown for the past two years, even a temporary 1% hit to industrial output is highly damaging.

The German Economic Institute (IW) now predicts a 0.4% drop in gross domestic product, effectively wiping out this year's economic growth, which was expected at 0.5%.

"A prolonged disruption of navigability on the Rhine could completely stifle the tiny seed of growth we have," warned IW economist Thilo Schäfer in an interview with Bild newspaper last week.

Other experts have warned of losses of €1-2 billion in the third quarter alone, with the steel, chemicals and energy sectors hit especially hard.

The BDB's Schwanen warned that "Due to the lack of rainfall, a single-digit reading is forecast for the first time this week at the Kaub gauge."

"In principle, this means the Rhine is no longer navigable along its entire length and is therefore effectively divided in two," he told the Rheinische Post.

This would result in two separate areas. On the one hand, shipping traffic would continue between the North Sea ports of Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and Antwerp and the Cologne region via the Rhine and the Western German canal system.

Further south, shipping would operate on the tributaries of the Neckar, Moselle, and Main, as well as the Main-Danube Canal, which is regarded as a key global link on the route to and from Southeast Europe.

Between the two sections, shipping companies would then try to move as much cargo onto trucks and freight rail services.

However, Germany's roads cannot absorb the typical 50 to 150 truckloads that a single large barge can handle without severe congestion and substantially higher costs.

Baden-Württemberg said Monday it would join four other German states in easing restrictions on truck movements on Sundays to help ease congestion.

Following urgent talks last Thursday, Transport Minister Steffen Bilger announced several other measures to shore up Germany's supply chain.

These include cutting red tape for heavy loads shifted to the road network, stopping unnecessary roadworks and better coordination with DB Cargo, the rail freight arm of Deutsche Bahn.

Extremely low water on the Rhine and other major European rivers used to be rare events.

Yet, many scientists believe climate change is making them now more frequent, longer and more severe.

According to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service, western Europe has just experienced its warmest June and July on record, with exceptionally low rainfall driving much lower than average water levels on the Rhine, Danube and Seine.

The current crisis marks the third major low‑water episode in eight years, after major droughts in 2018 and 2022.

The Rhine has traditionally been supported during dry summer months by meltwater from Alpine snow and glaciers. As those glaciers retreat and snow cover declines, this natural buffer is weakening.

Germany’s Federal Institute of Hydrology (BfG) projected in 2023 that severe low-water events like 2018 could strike every five to 10 years by mid-century.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2l.title: 'Total incinerated destruction': Canada wildfire evacuees wonder if they still have homes
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2l.text:
Earl Kurz and his wife have lived in Peachland, a town overlooking Okanagan Lake in Canada's British Columbia, for 30 years. In the last 10, he said he has grown used to wildfires threatening his community.

But this is the first time he's been forced to flee, and surveying the damage left behind by the Bald Range wildfire, which broke out on Friday and grew in a matter of hours to 53 sq miles (136 sq km) in size, has been difficult.

"It's total incinerated destruction," Kurz said. "The hot spots are just barren areas of nothing except 12 inches of ash."

Officials in British Columbia are still trying to determine how many homes were lost to the fire, which remains out of control as of Monday.

More than 12,000 residents in the area are still under an evacuation order.

One woman, aged 80, died while trying to flee from the wildfire, police said on Sunday.

The Okanagan area of British Columbia, known for its world renowned vineyards and picturesque scenery, has been grappling with extreme drought in recent years. As of July, the level of the Okanagan Lake was at its lowest since 1992, according to the Okanagan Basin Water Board.

The Bald Range wildfire is one of more than 100 burning in British Columbia as of Monday - 70 of which started in the last week alone.

The west coast province's premier, David Eby, declared a state of emergency over the weekend, urging residents to heed evacuation orders and warning that the fires continue to move "incredibly quickly".

Keegan Radomski is one of thousands who have had to flee their homes in Summerland, a town on the Okanagan Lake just south of Peachland. The 18-year-old told the BBC she barely escaped with her mother's ashes before she saw the fire breach her property.

"We've had a lot of close calls before, but it's never been like this," Radomski said. "You always think it's not going to be you, and then it's you."

The home she fled was built by her grandmother 30 years ago, she said. Living in the Okanagan for decades meant that Radomski and her family are familiar with wildfires and evacuation notices, but they were still caught off guard by the speed of this fire.

The family noticed wildfire smoke from the distance while eating dinner on Friday evening. Less than four hours later, Radomski said she was scrambling to get everyone out as she saw a hill on her property begin to burn.

She added she is still unsure if her family's home survived, and when she can return and check for herself.

The Bald Range wildfire comes on the heels of another fire in the Okanagan, called Bradley Creek, which is believed to have destroyed more than 200 homes.

Officials said the Bradley Creek fire is now being held after "tireless work" by wildfire crews to contain it.

Drought conditions have also contributed to fires in the US state of Washington, just south of British Columbia, where more than 65,000 people were forced to flee their homes.

Devastating fires have also burned this summer in Spain and France as Europe grapples with drought and record high temperatures.

France has seen its worst fires in two decades, while officials in the Spanish capital Madrid say theirs are the worst the region has ever experienced.

Fires are part of the natural cycle of Canada's vast boreal forest, but experts say climate change - particularly hotter and dryer weather - has made them more intense and frequent in the last decade. In 2023, the country saw its worst wildfire season in history in terms of the total area burned.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cglj.title: Taylor Farms recalls jalapeno products after salmonella outbreak
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cglj.text:
Food producer Taylor Farms is recalling a swathe of its fresh products containing jalapeno peppers after a salmonella outbreak.

The agricultural giant, which said it made 40% of all salad kits sold in the US last year, said it would recall around 20 products such as dips and sandwiches from retailers including Walmart, Target and Whole Foods.

The company said it was not aware of any illnesses linked to the products but that it was withdrawing them across 26 US states.

It comes after some Taylor Farms' lettuce was recently linked to an outbreak of cyclospora, a parasite that causes explosive diarrhoea, that has affected thousands of people.

The jalapeno recall came after Coast Citrus Distributors, which supplied the company with its peppers, recalled its own fresh jalapeno because of the salmonella concerns.

Taylor Farms said a grower in Sinaloa, Mexico, had been identified as the source of the outbreak and that it "is no longer sourcing products from this farmer and will be filling orders from alternative suppliers".

"Consumers who have any recalled product should discard it immediately and not consume it. Refunds are available at the location of purchase," it added.

Eating food contaminated with salmonella usually leads to illness within 12 to 72 hours. Symptoms include diarrhoea, fever and stomach pain, according to the US Food and Drug Administration.

The recall includes products such as pico de gallo salsa, several types of guacamole, burritos, spicy sandwiches and fresh sliced jalapenos.

Taylor Farms was already under scrutiny after it recently recalled its iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico because of the unusually large cyclosporiasis outbreak.

That had made more than 22,000 people ill since 1 May, as of a 4 August update from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The food-borne illness has spread to 45 states and Michigan health officials confirmed the first two deaths linked to the outbreak last week.

Taylor Farms is one of the largest produce companies in the US and is an important supplier to retail giants Walmart, Costco and Target.

It also supplies restaurant chains including Taco Bell and McDonald's and employs more than 25,000 people.

UK health officials have also warned about the cyclosporiasis outbreak following recent cases contracted by returning travellers.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/po.author: David A. Fahrenthold
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/po.text:
The president had insisted for weeks that the landmarks’ algae-stained waters and peeling lining were the fault of vandals, not the project itself.

By David A. Fahrenthold

President Trump on Sunday said on social media that the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool’s problems were caused in part by “some contractor error done by rushing the job for a July 4th opening.” It was a change in rhetoric for the president, who had spent weeks falsely blaming the pool’s problems on vandals.

The Trump administration’s efforts to rush through repairs to the pool, a national landmark, ended in disaster earlier this year. A hastily installed blue lining began to peel up, and new water-purification systems failed to prevent a huge bloom of algae that turned the pool green.

Mr. Trump responded to the tears in the blue lining with falsehoods, saying that it had been slashed by vandals. The U.S. attorney in Washington, Jeanine Pirro, charged at least seven people with vandalizing the pool, then dropped at least some of the cases after she discovered that the repair job had failed on its own, she said.

In his social media post, Mr. Trump also conceded that there was “no video or proof” to back up the assertions that vandalism damaged the pool. Still, he continued to blame one of the people who had been charged with vandalism, David Hearn, a former U.S. Olympian. Mr. Hearn had been charged with a felony by Ms. Pirro’s office, before his case was dropped.

The pool remains drained for repairs. In his post, Mr. Trump said that “We are working on the Pool, and it will reopen shortly.”

David A. Fahrenthold is a Times investigative reporter writing about nonprofit organizations. He has been a reporter for two decades.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/09/scien.title: Maura L. Gillison, Who Linked Throat Cancers to HPV, Dies at 61
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/09/scien.author: Jeré Longman
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/09/scien.text:
She challenged the conventional view that most head and neck cancers resulted from cigarette smoking and excessive alcohol consumption.

Maura Gillison once told an interviewer that she had wanted to be a doctor and a scientist since childhood. She trained in ballet, but as she grew, reaching a height of 6-foot-2, dance became an unlikely career path because she felt that it would draw too much attention to her height.

Instead, she forged a trailblazing career as a medical oncologist and molecular epidemiologist, studying head and neck cancers. In the early 2000s, she was credited as the first researcher to show definitively that the human papillomavirus, or HPV — the most common sexually transmitted infection — caused the so-called oropharyngeal cancers of the throat, tonsils and base of the tongue.

“No head and neck medical oncologist has had a bigger impact on patients than Maura Gillison,” Dr. John V. Heymach, the chair of thoracic/head and neck oncology at MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, where Dr. Gillison conducted research beginning in 2017, said in an interview.

Dr. Gillison died on June 21 at her childhood family home in Willoughby, Ohio, northeast of Cleveland. She was 61. The cause was a rare cancer of the small intestine, her husband Dr. David E. Symer, an oncologist, said.

For almost a century, a vast majority of throat cancers were attributed to cigarette smoking and excessive alcohol consumption. Then cases of cancer of the tonsils began to rise in the 1970s and 1980s. While HPV was detected in some head and neck cancers, many researchers dismissed the findings as laboratory contamination.

“I couldn’t help but wonder, What if it wasn’t?” Dr. Gillison told the magazine of the Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center at Johns Hopkins University in its 2023-24 issue.

https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/g-s1-1378.title: Despite Mideast wars, 20 million gather in Iraq for Shia pilgrimage
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/g-s1-1378.author: Jane Arraf
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/g-s1-1378.text:
Large crowds of pilgrims fill the area between the two holy shrines in Karbala at sunset, with the illuminated dome and minarets of Imam Hussein's shrine visible in the background during the Arbaeen commemoration.

KARBALA, IRAQ – In the holy city of Karbala during the commemoration of Arbaeen, the story of the killing of Imam Hussein 1,400 years ago, resonates down through the centuries. It's in the plastic containers of cold water handed to sweltering pilgrims, not just for hydration but in remembrance of the water denied to the Imam and his followers before they were killed by a powerful army.

For many of the 20 million pilgrims attending this year, the killing this year of Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and his family by Israel and the United States is a thundering echo of grave injustice against the Shia Muslims. Iran said more than three million of its pilgrims attended Arbaeen ceremonies in Karbala.

A pilgrim raises his hands and chants amid the crowds during mourning rituals inside the Imam Hussein Shrine in Karbala during the Arbaeen commemoration.

A man carries a large banner featuring a portrait of Iran's slain Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei amid crowds of pilgrims on a street in Karbala during Arbaeen.

Some, like Maryam Ghanbari, showed their devotion by walking 200 miles from the Iranian border.

"More people came to Arbaeen this year because they want to avenge Agha's blood," said Ghanbari, using the Persian honorific for the slain Iranian leader. This was the ninth pilgrimage for the municipal worker from Mazandaran province.

Arbaeen commemorates the beheading of Imam Hussein in 680 in the Battle of Karbala, when the grandson of the Prophet Mohammed was killed in a dispute over who should become the heir to the faith's founder. It was the moment that caused the schism between the Shia, who followed Hussein – and the Sunnis, who gathered around his rival.

A pilgrim raises his hands in prayer amid the crowds inside the Imam Hussein Shrine in Karbala during the Arbaeen commemoration.

Pilgrims pass through a historic vaulted passage decorated with religious flags and banners in Karbala during the Arbaeen commemoration.

The festival is commemorated by the world's roughly 200 million mainstream Shia. Iran is the world's most populous predominantly Shia nation.

Suppressed for years under Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein's rule, the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq opened the door for Iraq's Shia majority to take power, including reviving ceremonies central to the Shia faith. Iran, which fought a devastating eight-year-long war with Iraq in the 1980s, turned from an enemy to an ally of the new Iraqi government.

Two decades after the U.S. toppled Saddam and oversaw his execution, Iran has a seemingly unshakeable hold on the Iraqi government and security forces. During the ongoing U.S. war in Iran, Iran-backed militias that are now officially part of Iraqi security forces have launched rockets and drones at the U.S. embassy in Baghdad and military positions in the Kurdistan region of Iraq.

Pilgrim carries a portrait of Iran's Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei, outside the Imam Hussein Shrine in Karbala during the Arbaeen pilgrimage.

Many Iraqis, as well as Iranians, see the U.S. and Israeli war as a war against the Shia Islam.

Ali Aadi Khairi and his cousin Sajjad Haitham Latif, both 18, walked five days from the Iraqi city of Kut to get to Karbala. Two days ago, a stick attached to the large image of Imam Hussein they were carrying broke. They walked the final two days carefully holding the image between them. On the corner of the image portraying the imam with long hair and piercing green eyes were photos of Qassem Soleimani, the former commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and Abdul Mehdi al-Muhandas, the late head of Iraq's Iran-backed forces. The U.S. killed them in an airstrike near Baghdad airport six years ago.

"In Iran the U.S. attacked the schools and the granddaughter of Khamenei," said Khairi, referring to the U.S. Tomahawk missile which hit an Iranian elementary school in southern Iran in February, killing 120 children, according to Iranian health authorities. Khamenei's 14-month-old grandchild was among the family members killed in the U.S.-Israel strike on his home.

A religious procession moves through dense crowds of pilgrims in the area between the two holy shrines in Karbala, carrying flags, banners and portraits of religious figures during the Arbaeen commemoration.

Pilgrims carry religious flags and banners during the Arbaeen pilgrimage near the Imam Hussein Shrine in Karbala, as millions of worshippers from Iraq and abroad continue to gather for the annual religious commemoration.

For weeks before Arbeen, pilgrims set off on foot for Karbala, some carrying flags with images of Imam Hussein in the searing heat. Hospitality tents along the highways and inside cities along the pilgrimage route offer free meals and shelter. Many Iranians arrive on package tours which include bus fare and a week's stay in budget hotels in Karbala.

Inside the Imam Hussein shrine, pilgrims in men's and women's sections press against the gold and silver-encrusted latticework around the spot where he was killed, many striking their foreheads in grief. Millions of mirrored tiles reflect the crystal chandeliers and gilded walls. For Arbaeen, the lights inside the shrine and the flags fluttering from its golden dome are switched to red – the color of vengeance.

A young pilgrim weeps as he takes part in mourning rituals inside the Imam Hussein Shrine in Karbala during the Arbaeen commemoration.

The sound of sobbing underlays chanting in dozens of dialects woven together in a single expression of sorrow for Imam Hussein and his companions and family, killed and taken captive in the defining event of Shia Islam. Many of them call out to Hussein and his slain relatives – seen as part of every Shia's family. In the men's section, some of the Iranian pilgrims add a Persian suffix of endearment as they cry out to Husseinjan.

Outside, processions of young men in 120-degree heat carry images of Khamenei. Some hoist Iraqi and Iranian flags joined together. Some of the religious chants refer to the trip back to Karbala from Damascus by companions and relatives of Imam Hussein to reunite his severed head with his body on the 40th day of mourning in 680 C.E. The battle of Karbala is known to every school Shia child in Iraq and Iran – re-enacted every year by participants in period costumes – often with horses and camels.

Pilgrims hold a large piece of fabric above their heads while taking part in mourning rituals inside the Imam Hussein Shrine in Karbala during the Arbaeen commemoration.

On a covered walkway between the Imam Hussein and Imam Abbas shrines this week, metal fans blow a cooling mist. Shrine guards flick sticks with ostrich feathers at female pilgrims lingering too long in the shade to try to keep the flow of people moving. Medics treat heat stroke and other ailments from trailers while an announcer calls out an endless stream of names of people separated from their families.

While Iraqi Shia in particular still express gratitude to the U.S. for toppling Saddam and helping to fight ISIS militants a decade later, many now believe that the U.S. and its Gulf Arab allies are intent on destroying the region.

Crowds of pilgrims gather in the area between the two holy shrines in Karbala during Arbaeen, as one of them holds up a portrait of Iran's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.

Naser Zadih, 38, a teacher from Tabriz, says Khamenei's killing has hardened support for resistance against the U.S. and Israel.

"It helped this movement get more depth. It got deeper and more targeted. It has helped us flaunt the power of Shia more to the face of the world to show that the Shia are building their own civilization," he says.

Two pilgrims recite prayers amid crowds in Karbala during the Arbaeen commemoration.

Asked about the economic hardship of the war, the schoolteacher says that Iranians have learned to deal with it as part of "the culture of resistance."

Like the Iranian government, he says the U.S. is not interested in negotiations. "We can talk to someone who actually wants to talk," he says.

Iranians on religious pilgrimage are disproportionately supporters of the country's Islamic regime. In upscale hotels in Karbala, a city some 55 miles south of Baghdad, wealthier Iranians dressed in black fill the lobbies. None of those asked will speak to U.S. media. One man says he is afraid of repercussions in Iran.

A pilgrim touches a sticker bearing a portrait of slain Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei affixed to a utility pole on a street in Karbala during the Arbaeen pilgrimage, as millions of pilgrims gather at the Imam Hussein Shrine to commemorate the annual religious occasion.

Near the shrine, Mohammad Yasin Ahmadi, 15, has come from the Iranian city of Qom on his second pilgrimage. He says many Iranians came this year because of Ayatollah Khamenei, who visited Iraq in the 1950s but was never able to come as Iran's supreme leader.

Before Khamenei was buried in July in his hometown in Iran, his body was brought to the Iraqi holy cities of Karbala and Najaf.

"Most people came for him this year," Ahmadi says. "This Arbaeen has the scent and the feeling of the Ayatollah."
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/g-s1-1378.summary: The Battle of Karbala is commemorated by the world's roughly 200 million mainstream Shia. The killing of Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and his family by Israel and the United States is a thundering  Iranians on religious pilgrimage.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: US intelligence ‘believes Russia was behind Leipzig airport drone bomb’
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Deborah Cole in Berlin
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
German government talks of a ‘new level of danger’ but declines to say who it thinks was responsible for device

American intelligence experts believe Russia was behind an attack on a German airport last week with a drone laden with explosives, US media have reported, as Berlin remained silent on the likely culprit.

Last week’s security emergency prompted the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, to break off his summer holiday in Italy and rush to the scene in the eastern city of Leipzig, as he spoke of a “new level of danger” for Germany.

Dobrindt called the incident, in which a quadcopter with semtex plastic explosives attached was found next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at the major shipping and military hub, part of a “professional hybrid threat scenario” by a well-equipped foreign actor.

As the German investigators raced to identify the perpetrators, the tabloid Bild reported that authorities had found DNA traces at the scene that matched a sample from a firebomb, posted via DHL, that exploded at Leipzig airport in July 2024.

Five men suspected in a related series of mailed incendiary devices are on trial in Lithuania, where it emerged in court last week that the plane that was the target of the firebomb only avoided being set on fire in mid-flight because it was delayed. The suspects are alleged by Lithuanian prosecutors to have been employed by Russian intelligence.

Even as MPs and security analysts pointed the finger at the Kremlin over the latest incident in Leipzig, German government officials have not levelled a specific accusation against Moscow.

The Wall Street Journal, however, has quoted US officials familiar with intelligence reports about the incident as saying that the drone probably belongs to the Russian government.

CNN reported that Washington had concluded the drone came from a Russian secret service, citing a US defence official in Europe noting the explosive material found on the drone suggested a military manufacturer.

German officials said the drone managed to fly past Leipzig airport’s defences.

It was only immobilised when an alert airport bus driver ferrying a group of late-night passengers spotted and reported it, an estimated four hours after it breached the facility’s security, averting what authorities have said could have been a multiple casualty event.

The same night, a DHL cargo plane, which had been forced to abort its landing at the airport due to the discovery of the drone, then collided with an unknown object in mid-air as it was climbing away from the airport. It later landed safely elsewhere, with minor damage.

Investigators now believe it hit a second hostile drone being flown that night.

A day later, drones were detected above an army installation in western Germany housing components for US-made Patriot air-defence systems, which Ukraine has often requested to help fend off Russia’s aerial bombardments.

In response to the increased threat, the German interior ministry said on Monday it plans to double its federal team of anti-drone experts to 300, with the number of operational bases for the unit to rise to eight from four.

Germany and other European countries have long reported suspicious unauthorised drone overflights at airports, military facilities, ports and logistics companies, and accused Russian agents of spying as well as a targeted campaign of sabotage, disruption and intimidation.

Moscow has denied this, and late last week its embassy in Berlin called any suggestion it had a hand in the Leipzig case a “rashly contrived provocation” that “serves only the interests of Kyiv and the militarist wing of the European political establishment”.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

Berlin is Ukraine’s biggest national supplier of military aid in its defence against the Russian onslaught.

Next month, Germany will hold three pivotal elections in eastern states, where support for defence assistance for Kyiv is controversial among voters and fears of “provoking” Moscow run high.

The pro-Russian far-right Alternative für Deutschland is poised to perform well in all three races, polls show, amid reports of Russian disinformation targeted at its principal rivals, the mainstream democratic parties.

The opposition Greens have criticised the government for not naming and blaming Russia at this stage of the Leipzig investigation.

Political scientist Wolfgang Schröder of the University of Kassel in western Germany said two factors could be shaping Berlin’s restraint.

Firstly, Russia had been named early on as a prime suspect behind the 2022 sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines, which German prosecutors now say was ordered by Ukrainian “state authorities”.

More important, Schröder said, were the incalculable consequences of accusing Moscow of a botched military attack on German soil amid warnings of an escalation in tensions.

“If it were to be defined as an act of aggression – that is, a military attack by Russia against (Germany’s) critical infrastructure – then we would be on the brink of entering a state of war, and that would have implications not only of a diplomatic nature but also with regard to Nato,” he told local news broadcaster n-tv.

“A cautious approach is being taken here, precisely because the aim is to prevent being drawn in, and that would mean turning this into a matter of European security – a matter of Nato security – and that would certainly take Germany’s involvement in the armed conflict between Russia and Ukraine to a whole new level.”
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.summary: German interior minister Alexander Dobrindt called the incident a 'new level of danger' for Germany. US intelligence experts believe Russia was behind attack on German airport last week.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Arron Banks urged to set out extent of surveillance of journalists
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Daniel Boffey Chief reporter
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Industry body says use of private investigators against reporters is ‘attack on our democracy’ after apparent admission by Reform donor

The businessman and Reform UK donor Arron Banks is facing calls to lay out the extent of his surveillance of journalists, described by an industry body as an “attack on our democracy”.

The News Media Association (NMA), which represents regional and national media, raised concerns after Banks appeared to admit over the weekend to hiring private investigators to spy on a Sunday Times journalist.

The revelation, first reported in the New Statesman, has led to fears that other journalists examining the funding of Reform and Nigel Farage, including those at the Guardian, could have been targeted.

When asked over the weekend whether he had commissioned investigators to surveil reporters at the Guardian, Banks said he was “not really interested in the Guardian” but declined to comment further.

The Guardian, along with the Sunday Times, has broken a series of stories in recent months revealing how cash has been given to Reform and Farage personally from donors and wealthy benefactors.

Theo Bamber, the chief executive of the NMA, said aggressive attempts to deter journalistic inquiry were at risk of becoming normalised.

He said: “Using private investigators to try to deter journalists from making legitimate inquiries about public figures is an attack on our democracy. Sadly, intimidation and abuse of local and national journalists is increasingly used as a weapon to limit scrutiny and deflect attention away from matters of public interest. This must not become normalised.

“Ministers must wake up to this threat to our democracy and do much more to protect the independent journalism which underpins our democratic way of life.”

According to the New Statesman, Banks instructed Precision Risk and Intelligence, a private investigations company he once owned, to examine Gabriel Pogrund, the editor of the Sunday Times’ Insight investigations team.

In response to inquiries, Banks told the magazine: “We believe the Sunday Times used hacked information and that was an area of interest. We do have an investigative arm that’s got advanced capabilities.”

The Sunday Times has strongly rejected Banks’s suggestion.

Banks, when asked directly by the New Statesman whether he had paid investigators to look into Pogrund, responded: “When you live by the sword, you die by the sword.”

Jemimah Steinfeld, the chief executive of Index on Censorship, said Banks should be open and transparent about the extent of his surveillance of journalists.

She said: “I really, really hope that it’s not happening to other journalists. But my fear is that it will be, because Gabriel is not the only one who’s asking the right questions about Reform.

“These tactics are often used to just stop the questions, to stop accountability, and that can have hugely detrimental effects on our democratic structure.”

Reform UK has denied any knowledge of Banks’s alleged use of investigators.

Gawain Towler, a member of Reform’s board and a former head of press for Ukip, said he was uncomfortable with the development but there were legitimate questions as to where journalists were sourcing private information.

“Personally I don’t like it,” he said. “But truly how in the light of the situation does one ask questions with a possibility of getting an answer …

“I think the issue with Banks is that there was actually silence about this possible collusion with the [National Crime Agency and journalists] … It would be ridiculous of us not to ask questions. So how do you ask questions?”

Nicky Morgan, a former Conservative secretary of state for culture, media and sport, said such intrusions in press freedom were “not compatible with an open democracy”. She said: “Investigating a journalist can only be intended to have a chilling effect on free speech.”

Lisa Smart, the Liberal Democrats’ Cabinet Office spokesperson said: “Hiring private investigators to target journalists who are simply doing their jobs is a desperate attempt to dodge accountability.

“Anyone who uses or condones these tactics demonstrates complete contempt for a free press and should have no business in British public life.”

Banks, who helped run the pro-Brexit campaign group Leave.EU, is reported to have previously hired what he described as “ex-MI5 and SAS” operatives to surveil political opponents in the run-up to the EU referendum.

Included among those was Matthew Elliott, a Conservative peer who was the chief executive of the rival Vote Leave campaign. He has warned that such tactics will “drive out the decent people we need in public life”.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/metas-.title: Meta’s new Glimmer AI model offers a hint at Zuckerberg’s personal intelligence vision
https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/metas-.author: Rebecca Bellan
https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/metas-.text:
Meta on Monday released Muse Glimmer, an open-weight model designed to power AI agents locally on consumer hardware, providing the clearest picture yet of what CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s vision of “personal superintelligence” could look like in practice.

The 30-billion parameter model is essentially an open version of Meta’s most powerful closed model, Muse Spark, which the company debuted in April. Glimmer’s weights are available under the permissive Apache 2.0 license, so developers can download them and modify as necessary.

Glimmer is designed to run AI agents that can perform multi-step tasks — like call tools, write and debug code, work with files and screenshots, and execute on a task over an extended workflow — locally on a Mac or PC with a single consumer GPU. It supports text and images, and was trained across more than 100 languages, the company said.

Meta imagines Glimmer being used for things like managing schedules, drafting messages, and organizing files — tasks that would require large amounts of access to personal data. By processing the information on a user’s device instead of sending it to the cloud, Meta is laying the groundwork for a more privacy-sensitive personal agent. Glimmer is also designed to be “always-on” and able to operate “anywhere, anytime, with or without an internet connection.”

That vision mirrors the future Mark Zuckerberg has previously laid out for Meta. Last year, he argued that advanced AI should empower individuals rather than stay concentrated in the hands of a few companies, while also warning that Meta would have to be careful about which of its increasingly powerful models it released openly due to safety concerns.

In a new letter Monday, Zuckerberg reiterated that vision, arguing that distributing superintelligence widely “has the potential to begin a new era of personal empowerment where individuals can use this powerful new capability to reach their full potential, pursue their interests, and improve their lives and the world more than ever before.”

Zuckerberg went on to list the ways Meta’s superintelligence can improve a person’s life, from providing a capable personal agent that “will work 24/7 on your behalf to improve your relationships, health, career, finances, home management, hobbies, and more” to giving people access to tools needed to create a new business or advance scientific progress. The biggest promise of all is that “everyone will have free or affordable access to these tools.”

But access isn’t the same as ownership. Zuckerberg’s promise to distribute superintelligence widely comes as Meta is increasingly distinguishing between models it will release openly and those it will keep under its control. Muse Spark, its more powerful mode, remains closed-weight, while the smaller Glimmer can be downloaded, fine-tuned, and run on a user’s hardware.

As a result, Glimmer offers an early indication of where Meta may draw the line between the AI it wants people to own themselves and the more powerful intelligence that remains under the company’s control.
