https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-592.author: Ken Tucker
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-592.text:
The 1976 film Sparkle wasn't a huge hit, but it has a devoted cult following, and its soundtrack features some of Aretha Franklin's finest performances.

The 1976 movie Sparkle follows the troubles and triumphs of a trio of singers — based loosely on The Supremes — trying to make it in the soul-music world of the 1960s. Sparkle was the film debut of Irene Cara, who'd become a big star four years later in the movie Fame. The movie was only a modest success, and what now seems most impressive about Sparkle are Curtis Mayfield's songs, as sung by Aretha Franklin.

"Look into Your Heart" is a dreamy ballad powered by Franklin's passionate singing. In every song here, she is holding nothing back. She's pouring as much of herself into these Mayfield compositions as she did in the staggeringly great series of hit singles she made for Atlantic Records in the late '60s. Mayfield was, of course, familiar with the ways of Hollywood movie-music, as the man who gave us the theme from the 1970s Blaxploitation film classic Shaft.

For me, Sparkle's high point is Mayfield's five-minute production of "Hooked on Your Love." It begins as a smooth medium-tempo tune, with Franklin's vocal gliding atop a glittering string section and backup vocals by the Kitty Haywood singers.

Then, deeper into it, Franklin gives a demonstration of the song's title — how being hooked, addicted, to love becomes an intense craving. Franklin's gospel-rooted, passionate shouting turns out to be the perfect way to convey this ecstatic obsession.

She gives another fantastic performance on the album's first single, a moody, sexy number called "Something He Can Feel." The song went to No. 1 on the R&B chart, but stalled at 28 on the Billboard pop chart. The album itself barely cracked the Top 20, and only briefly at that. This is what I mean about Sparkle being such an underrated achievement for both Franklin and Mayfield.

The collaboration between Franklin and Mayfield transcends the movie. It stands on its own as a rich, risk-taking collection that deserves a reevaluation in 20th-century pop music history.

Sparkle wasn't a smash in 1976, but it developed an intense cult following that has reverberations. I don't think it's a coincidence, for instance, that Dreamgirls, a far bigger success in 1981, bears a striking resemblance to Sparkle.

Sparkle was remade in 2012, starring Jordin Sparks and Whitney Houston, and was a modest hit. But the collaboration between Franklin and Mayfield transcends the movie. It stands on its own as a rich, risk-taking collection that deserves a reevaluation in 20th-century pop music history.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Indian police use force to disperse youth protesters calling for exam overhaul
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Penelope MacRae in Delhi
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Demonstrators accuse authorities of failing to tackle issues in exams for highly sought-after civil service jobs

Thousands of angry young job-seekers clashed with police in Jharkhand, one of India’s poorest states, on Monday as a weeks-long protest over alleged irregularities in recruitment drives for coveted government jobs escalated into a march on the state legislature.

Police fired water cannon and teargas and swung batons as they tried to stop flag-waving demonstrators from clambering over barricades and surging towards the assembly in Ranchi, the state capital. Some of the protesters responded by dancing and cheering as jets of water drenched the crowd.

The unrest comes just weeks after the self-styled “Cockroach” movement, a youth-led protest campaign that began as an online joke and grew into a nationwide outcry over leaks in a national medical entrance examination, put the BJP-led national government under heavy pressure and led to the resignation of the education minister.

Both protesters and police officers were injured in the Jharkhand clashes, local media reported, although no official figures were released.

“The baton charge was barbaric. We were protesting peacefully, but the government used batons against us,” protester Piyush Kumar Soni told the Press Trust of India.

The demonstrators are demanding an investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), India’s premier investigative force, saying that only an independent inquiry can get to the bottom of alleged wrongdoing in government recruitment examinations.

They accuse authorities of failing to prevent irregularities in public service exams, including test paper leaks and cheating, and say the alleged scandals have deprived young people of a fair chance.

Jharkhand has long struggled with high unemployment, making government jobs highly sought after. Competition for civil service and other public-sector posts, which offer job security, health and pension benefits, is intense.

Government recruitment drives routinely attract hundreds of thousands of applicants, with many young people spending years preparing for examinations. In one recent Jharkhand recruitment exercise, nearly 640,000 applications were received for just 2,025 posts. In another, more than 322,000 candidates competed for only 510 vacancies.

The state government, led by a regional party allied with the opposition Congress, has sought to defuse the crisis through talks. Officials say most of the protesters’ demands have been accepted and that they’re open to more negotiations.

after newsletter promotion

Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, condemned the use of force. “Students have a right to peaceful protest, and only dialogue can yield solutions,” he said.

The row has already claimed senior figures. The former Jharkhand public service commission chair has been arrested over alleged exam irregularities, while three commission members have resigned.

The protests underscore mounting frustration among young Indians over corruption in public examinations and recruitment systems, a shortage of good jobs and fears that opportunities are being lost to cheating and political influence. Nearly two-thirds of Indians are under 35.

Official data shows unemployment fell to 9.9% last year, but a 2026 study by Azim Premji University found that nearly 40% of graduates aged 15 to 25 were unemployed.

https://www.theverge.com/streaming/97747.title: YouTube is making it harder to earn money on YouTube
https://www.theverge.com/streaming/97747.author: Emma Roth
https://www.theverge.com/streaming/97747.text:
Now you’ll need twice as many watch hours on YouTube to start making money from ads and subscriptions.

Now you’ll need twice as many watch hours on YouTube to start making money from ads and subscriptions.

Starting February 1st, 2027, creators who want to monetize their channel through YouTube’s Partner Program (YPP) will need at least 1,000 subscribers and either 8,000 qualified watch hours over the past year, or 20 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days. That’s a sizeable jump from YouTube’s current requirement of 1,000 subscribers with 4,000 watch hours in the past year, or 1,000 subscribers with 10 million Shorts views in the last 90 days. Creators will also need to maintain 10 million Shorts views over 90 days to earn money from the Shorts Creators Pool, though falling below this threshold won’t result in removal from YPP.

Additionally, YouTube says creators will benefit from an expansion of its cheaper Premium Lite subscription, which is coming to all countries where it offers Premium. YouTube splits up subscription revenue to creators based on watch time and views, with 55 percent dedicated to long-form videos and 45 percent for Shorts. “With these additional subscribers, creators can expect higher earnings: when a user signs up for Premium, partners, on average, earn more than when the user was watching ads,” YouTube says.

The requirements are changing as YouTube ramps up efforts to become more like a premium TV service alongside Netflix, HBO Max, and Disney Plus, rather than just an online platform for videos. This year, YouTube struck deals to broadcast shows from big names like Trevor Noah, and broadly rolled out a feature that allows creators to organize their videos into seasons.

Separately, there are some new requirements for creators to keep earning money from ads and subscriptions through the YPP, though.

https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilit.title: Coruna, DarkSword iOS Exploits Proliferate Globally
https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilit.author: Alexander Culafi
https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilit.text:
Sophisticated iPhone exploit chains previously limited to nation-states are spreading far and wide to organized cybercrime groups.

The advanced iPhone exploit chains Coruna and DarkSword continue to escape nation-state and mercenary containment to enter the hands of more conventional cybercriminals.

While nation-state-grade malware will, from time to time, make its way from government use to cybercriminal adoption, it's far more unusual to see whole complex exploit chains — especially those targeting iOS — adopted broadly. Yet that phenomenon, first observed last spring, appears to be shifting into overdrive. iVerify has tracked approximately 17,000 domains hosting second-generation iterations of Coruna and DarkSword so far, and infections have continued months after public disclosure earlier this year.

"In five minutes, you can deploy an iOS exploit chain. ... This is extremely dangerous and extremely easy to proliferate," says Matthias Frielingsdorf, vice president of research at iVerify.

And cybercriminals are making improvements: After iVerify disclosed Coruna, threat actors apparently modified the framework, Frielingsdorf says; iVerify researchers saw new variants with improved jailbreak and virtualization detection functionality, improved encryption, Telegram-focused implants, new persistence mechanisms, and more.

Related:Flaws in Google APK for Python Unlock Agent-to-Agent Attack

Just as interesting, perhaps even more so, iVerify and Palo Alto Networks separately observed threat actors using both chains against targets despite DarkSword and Coruna being very much distinct. In a post, researchers at iVerify said telemetry and third-party reporting suggest some threat actors have adopted both frameworks, and in some cases appear to be combining techniques from the two platforms. iVerify informally named these hybrid variants "Darkuna," and noted they illustrate how operators continue to modify frameworks long after development and disclosure.

"These threat actors are actually changing quite a lot [with] this version," the researcher explains, adding that these newer variants incorporate updated process-injection targets, stronger anti-analysis functionality, and new implants in the modified framework.

Google, iVerify, and Lookout have all detailed DarkSword, a complex exploit chain used since November 2025 against iPhones running iOS versions 18.4 through 18.7. It was used in campaigns linked to multiple commercial surveillance vendors and suspected state-sponsored actors to target users across Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Ukraine. It's very sophisticated, utilizing multiple vulnerabilities: JavaScriptCore memory-corruption flaws CVE-2025-31277 and CVE-2025-43529; dyld user-mode pointer authentication code bypass CVE-2026-20700; ANGLE memory corruption flaw CVE-2025-14174; iOS kernel memory management flaw CVE-2025-43510; and iOS kernel memory corruption bug CVE-2025-43520 — all along with multiple malware families. Attacker aims include achieving remote code execution (RCE), sandbox escape, and privilege escalation, ultimately leading to payload delivery. Apple patched DarkSword in April.

Related:Attackers Exploit N-able Patch Bypass Flaw on RMM Servers

Coruna, meanwhile, is a more mature exploit chain that targets iOS 13 through 17.2.1. Though iVerify first discussed the kit shortly before DarkSword, its toolset is thought to be years older, developed by a government contractor and sold to zero-day brokers for mass iOS device targeting. Coruna deploys 23 vulnerabilities across five exploit chains, and was thought to have cost between $30 million and $40 million to develop. Apple patched the older vulnerabilities behind Coruna in 2023 and 2024.

The framework uses watering-hole attacks, where victims visited compromised websites that deliver browser exploits, sandbox escapes, and privilege-escalation vulnerabilities. Once compromised, according to Frielingsdorf, Coruna injected its code into legitimate system processes such as the power daemon and location daemon rather than running a dedicated spyware process, making detection more difficult. It includes capabilities such as command and control (C2), application launching, process injection, data exfiltration, and cryptocurrency theft.

Related:'Certighost' Flaw Haunts Microsoft Active Directory Certificates

Frielingsdorf hosted a session at Black Hat USA 2026 last week diving deep into both DarkSword and Coruna, offering an analysis into the recent history of both exploit kits, and emphasizing that both represent the first time he's seen nation-state-grade iOS exploitation spill over into organized cybercrime at a meaningful level. For example, he connected Coruna infrastructure use to a Chinese organized crime group, and tied DarkSword deployments to multiple operators across the world (portions of the DarkSword exploit chain later appeared on GitHub). In other words, these don't belong to a single government or spyware operator.

"There is a strong difference between the operator of malware and who is actually authoring it in the first place and selling it," Frielingsdorf explains.

He also says DarkSword is designed to steal "basically everything," including keychain credentials, Wi-Fi passwords, iCloud data, photos and notes, and more. But particularly notable is the fact that DarkSword's data theft capabilities also targeted cryptocurrency wallets, indicating possible intended use by financially motivated cybercriminals from the get-go.

"These technologies are massively proliferating and trying to target as many devices as they can," Frielingsdorf warns, adding, "We're probably going to see more and more mass exploitation."

Senior News Writer, Dark Reading

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/meta-bran.title: Meta brandishes open-source AI models again, as Zuckerberg media blitz emphasizes battle against Chinese rivals
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/meta-bran.author: Beatrice Nolan
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/meta-bran.text:
Meta launched its newest family of AI models—Muse Glimmer, a group of open-source models designed to run on a laptop—on Monday, alongside a 6,500-word essay from Mark Zuckerberg making the argument for American open-source AI.

In the essay, Zuckerberg argues that powerful AI should not be controlled by a handful of companies, a seeming jab at competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic. Zuckerberg positions Meta’s commitment to open-source as critical to challenging Chinese open-source models from DeepSeek and Moonshot which have been getting uncomfortably close to the American frontier. He also urged Washington to support American efforts.

As part of this new commitment, Meta says it plans to open the weights for Muse Spark 1.2—meaning it will publicly release the underlying trained parameters of the model, letting anyone download, inspect, and modify it rather than access it only through Meta’s own products or API—its most advanced AI model on the market.

“I do not believe restricting access to foreign open source models is an effective solution. Our goal should be for American open source models to be the best globally. This requires removing the hurdles that make it harder for American open source models to compete,” Zuckerberg wrote in the essay, part of a coordinated media blitz by Meta that included a Zuckerberg-penned opinion piece on same themes in the Wall Street Journal last month and interviews with select media outlets.

The Muse Glimmer release lands in an American market increasingly dominated by closed-sourced AI companies, those that sell controlled access to their best models.

OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google generally keep their most advanced “frontier” models locked behind closed doors, retaining tight control of the weights and infrastructure. Meta initially sought to differentiate itself by embracing open source, launching the open-weight Llama family of models in February 2023. The Llama family, which expanded through several versions, helped make high-performing models available for outside developers to download and modify, and gave Meta influence over the wider AI ecosystem even as rivals captured more revenue by selling access to their proprietary models. Over the past year however, Meta’s commitment to open-weight has blurred, as the company mixed open releases with proprietary ones.

Meta has spent heavily on its new Superintelligence Labs, including bringing in former Scale AI CEO Alexander Wang. The company has been trying to position the Muse family as the foundation for a more capable Meta AI assistant across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and its Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses, while also being competitive with models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

The shift and refocus on open-source may also reflect an attempt by Meta to try to regain momentum after recent models have fallen short of systems from OpenAI and Anthropic. Meta is also looking to reassure investors that it is still competitive with frontier labs.

Meta said it trained its new Glimmer series using distillation, a process in which a smaller model learns from Muse Spark, its larger proprietary system. In his essay, Zuckerberg wrote that American AI developers face disadvantages against Chinese rivals, including in training data, and argued that policy should reduce those barriers.

With the strategy shift, Meta will likely be hoping its commitment to open-source will set it apart from rivals that keep their most capable systems behind closed doors and give it a political argument for user and government support.
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/meta-bran.summary: Meta launched its new family of AI models, Muse Glimmer, a group of open-source models designed to run on a laptop. Mark Zuckerberg wrote an essay on the issue, saying American AI developers face disadvantages against Chinese rivals.

https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/barnes-no.title: Barnes & Noble CEO James Daunt was a Carnival Cruise ship officer before building his bookstore empire
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/barnes-no.author: Sarah Glodek
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/barnes-no.text:
James Daunt’s favorite book is Leo Tolstoy’s Anna Karenina, though the Barnes & Noble CEO has never finished it. He says he’s returned to the novel several times, but always stops short of its conclusion so he can preserve the feeling of coming back to it.

That may be an unusual habit for the executive leading America’s largest bookstore chain. But Daunt has never had a conventional career. Before he ran Barnes & Noble, Waterstones, and his own Daunt Books chain, he worked as a purser for Carnival Cruise Lines and later as an investment banker at JPMorgan.

Now, Daunt is applying his skills as an independent bookseller to execute a comeback for one of retail’s most recognizable big-box brands. Since becoming CEO of Barnes & Noble in 2019, Daunt has focused on shifting power away from headquarters and into the hands of frontline employees.

“I had been a bookseller for 30 years at this point,” Daunt told Fortune’s Phil Wahba for Behind the Business. “I simply wanted to make these stores really good again. One sets on a series of very slow and incremental processes to do that.”

Daunt’s route to bookselling was anything but direct. After studying history at Pembroke College, Cambridge, he worked as a pursuer for Carnival Cruise Lines, a job that put him in charge of administrative, financial, and guest-relations duties on the ships.

In 1985, he moved to New York to become an investment banker at JPMorgan. While he enjoyed the business trips, Daunt quickly determined that banking was not his calling.

“I decided to give up a good office job for something more vocationally interesting,” he told The Guardian in 2018.

That vocation would ultimately be bookselling, with a specialization in travel books. In 1990, Daunt returned to the UK and opened the first Daunt Books location in London’s Marylebone neighborhood.

“My parents were appalled,” he recalled in a conversation with The Times last year.

To fund his new enterprise, Daunt raised £250,000 through the UK government’s tax incentive program for small businesses, now known as the Enterprise Investment Scheme.

The small bookstore eventually grew into a distinctive London chain known for browsing-friendly stores, knowledgeable booksellers, and shelves intentionally tilted upwards to best catch the light. Today, it’s valued at over $10 million.

The bookstore’s famous Edwardian interior, lined with classic oak shelving, several skylights, and a large arched window is just part of the charm that draws tourists and customers to its storefronts. In 2010, Daunt Books Publishing was founded to produce lost classics and titles inspired by the bookshop specifically.

In 2011, Daunt was tapped to lead the floundering British retailer Waterstones, which returned to profitability under his leadership.

Prior to Daunt’s arrival, Waterstones was struggling to compete with online booksellers including Amazon. Previous CEOs led the book and stationary retailer to the brink of bankruptcy while the store’s physical book sales dwindled.

Daunt led the company to its first year of profits since the 2008 recession by applying a small bookstore mentality. He closed under-performing locations and gave store managers more power to pick which books to sell. The experiences gave Daunt his most enduring management principle: bookselling is local.

“Choose your books well, show them off very nicely and, above all, have nice people working in the shop who are friendly and run the place in an intelligent, dynamic way that reflects where they are,” he told The Times.

His latest challenge has been engineering a turnaround for Barnes & Noble. When Elliot Advisors acquired the company for $683 million in 2019, the retailer was struggling with years of declining sales, store closures, and stiff competition from Amazon and other online sellers.

Barnes & Noble brought in Daunt to revive the chain, but instead of imposing a one-size-fits-all playbook, he gave local booksellers control over the displays so each store could reflect its community’s tastes.

“We’ve abandoned that [prior approach] 100%,” Daunt told Fortune. “Now each store curates its own assortment, reorders its own books, does each to their own and we encourage, develop, promote, and train against how you do that well.”

The result is a more decentralized operation. A Barnes & Noble in Union Square can highlight literary fiction and books by New York authors, while another store can lean into romance, young adult novels, fantasy, or regional history. Stores are encouraged to create their own displays, offer handwritten staff recommendations, and stock titles that reflect local demand.

Daunt said people can come into a bookstore for one title then be inspired to walk out with three. He also noticed a key difference between American and UK customers.

“American consumers are wonderful because they buy enormous amounts of books,” Daunt told Wahba. “Individually, they buy more than the UK customer does.”

The rebound has been dramatic. Today, there are a total of 717 brick-and-mortar stores, almost 100 more than in 2019, and Daunt plans to open more by the end of the year.

There have also been rumors of a possible IPO, however it is unclear when and if the company will go public. Daunt is apprehensive about what this could mean for the individual bookstores’ management, which has been perfected since his arrival as CEO.

“We are trying to run really good bookstores, most of that effort is being done at the local level,” he told Fortune. “We’re really just bringing these principles first: small bookstores to large chains to even larger chains, and it’s all based on the core principle of what makes a great bookstore.”
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/barnes-no.summary: James Daunt is the CEO of Barnes & Noble, the U.S. largest bookstore chain. He has been a bookseller for 30 years.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.title: Tensions in the Arctic: Greenland issues sharp rebuke to Trump-linked oil company
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.author: Sonya CIESNIK
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.text:
A Texas oil company that wants to extract what could amount to billions of barrels of oil from East Greenland’s Arctic basin has crossed a red line before even starting to drill.

In a statement issued on July 30, Greenland’s mineral resources authority said it had become aware that Greenland Energy – a Texas oil company founded last year – had transferred drilling equipment ashore on a remote stretch of the island’s eastern coast.

“All future logistical matters must be advised and approved by the mineral resources authority – before they are carried out,” the government said.

Greenland Energy has claimed that $1 trillion in crude oil may lie beneath the Jameson Land region. The firm thus announced plans to spend $60 million drilling two exploratory wells to find out.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

“The exploration for oil by Greenland Energy is relatively unproblematic,” said Lukas Wahden, an associate fellow of the Russia programme at George Washington University, in an interview on FRANCE 24. “The issue that caused political controversy last week is that the US company Greenland Energy didn’t coordinate with the relevant Greenlandic authorities in its disembarking of equipment for the exploration that is planned in East Greenland.”

The move by the US firm “stepped on a number of toes” given the delicate political context, according to Wahden. Trump flummoxed his NATO allies in January when he announced he must “have” Greenland – even by force, if necessary.

He also threatened tariffs against European countries opposing his conquest of the mineral-rich Arctic territory, an autonomous territory of NATO ally Denmark.

The shock announcement triggered the biggest crisis in transatlantic relations in decades. European NATO members deployed troops in Greenland for a military exercise designed to show the world – and the United States – that they were prepared to defend Danish sovereignty.

To defuse the crisis, Denmark, Greenland and the United States established a working group early this year to find a framework for the future of Greenlandic and US relations.

Greenland’s authorities must now “walk a tightrope”, said Wahden. The main question is whether the behaviour of a private US company will be raised within the negotiation group, “about which we know relatively little”.

READ MORE
Taking over Greenland, a long-standing US obsession

If Trump sides with Greenland Energy, it would disrupt “this very sensitive and very important diplomatic process and undermine some of the gains that the Greenlandic authorities in particular have been making in trying to stabilise the relations with the United States over the last couple of months”, said the expert.

At the height of the transatlantic crisis he sparked in January, Trump suddenly pivoted from military intervention to a NATO-brokered compromise.

The US president announced after a meeting with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte in Davos that he had found “a solution” to Greenland, adding that he was rescinding the tariffs scheduled to go into effect in February.

But Trump’s appetite for Greenland has not subsided after the dramatic climbdown in January, said Mikaa Blugeon-Mered, a Greenland specialist, on FRANCE 24.

READ MORE
Acquire territory, export culture wars: How to make sense of Trump’s ‘new imperialism’

He cited the US president’s July interview with the right-wing Real America’s Voice News host Steve Gruber, during which the president predicted that Greenland would come under US control before the end of his presidential term.

For Blugeon-Mered, the unauthorised movement of equipment by Greenland Energy, which stopped short of actual drilling, could lead to a stand-off between Trump and Greenland’s authorities.

“If Greenland doesn’t give the company permission to drill between now and October, the question that will arise is whether or not Trump [will] send in the army or employ security methods that will allow this company – with collaborators close to him – to go forward,” said Blugeon-Mered.

For the moment, the power struggle remains between the US firm and Greenland’s government. “We have a company that claims to be ready [to drill] after engaging costs and transferring its material. On the other hand, we have a government that responds by saying, ‘You don’t have authorisation to launch the drilling.’”

“It’s a free-for-all situation with political, economic and technical implications,” said Blugeon-Mered.

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/russia-c.text:
The move by the Supreme Court sidelines the liberal Yabloko party, the only officially registered party that opposes the ‌war in Ukraine

Russia’s Supreme Court barred the liberal Yabloko party on Monday from contesting September’s parliamentary elections, sidelining the only officially registered party that opposes Moscow’s ‌war in Ukraine.

More than four years after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the decision highlights the authorities’ intolerance of anti-war views and further narrows the already limited space for dissent in Russian politics.

“The decision will ⁠be appealed. Friends, let’s not despair,” the party said in ‌a statement.

The court ruled in favour of a lawsuit filed by the small pro-Kremlin nationalist ‌party Rodina, which sought Yabloko’s exclusion from the election. ⁠

Rodina alleged ⁠that Yabloko had received undeclared campaign support, including from Western sources, among other ‌accusations.

During the hearing, Yabloko leader Nikolai Rybakov said there was no evidence ‌to support ‌the allegations and described the case as an unconstitutional ‌attack on freedom of thought by political opponents seeking ⁠to clear the field of rivals.

In a rare show of ⁠defiance, a few hundred – mostly young – supporters attended the hearing as police stood by. Some carried apples ‌to display their ‌affiliation to Yabloko, which means apple in Russian. One wore a Russian flag as a cape.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yd.text:
The latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo began at least three months before it was officially declared - meaning the health authorities are still playing catch-up, the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned.

More than 1,900 people have died from the virus since that declaration on 15 May, making this the second-worst Ebola outbreak ever.

Infection rates are still high, adding to the concern that the authorities are struggling to get to grips with the spread of the disease.

The epicentre of this outbreak of the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, is in the east of DR Congo where insecurity has hampered control efforts.

There is also no approved vaccine or any recognised therapeutic drugs, making treating Bundibugyo harder.

"We are chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us," WHO Africa director Dr Mohamed Janabi said at a news conference in the city of Bunia, which is at the heart of this outbreak.

He cited research showing that the virus started spreading in February and was initially misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid.

Janabi also said that, in part because of insecurity, health workers are only reaching about 30% of the cases with the rest dying at home.

Traditional burial practices – where mourners touch the deceased's body - and a suspicion of health authorities in some communities have also made things difficult.

But there are now several dedicated treatment centres in the east of DR Congo and people are getting diagnosed much more quickly.

So far there have been 4,294 confirmed cases and 1,960 deaths, DR Congo's health ministry has said.

The largest recorded outbreak was in West Africa between 2014 and 2016 when 11,325 people died.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgmk.title: 30 years later, a former rival will stand trial for Tupac's murder
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgmk.text:
It's been three decades filled with mystery, conspiracies - and anger.

The drive-by shooting that killed rap superstar Tupac Shakur on 7 September 1996 changed the trajectory of hip-hop and elevated the rapper from the face of the genre to a cultural icon.

His killing became one of popular culture's great mysteries, with countless theories but no arrests until 2023, when Duane "Keffe D" Davis was unexpectedly charged with murdering the famous rapper.

The 63-year-old former gang boss is due to stand trial in Las Vegas, where he is accused of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang. He's pleaded not guilty. If convicted, he faces life in prison without parole.

The trial is likely to unravel the intricacies of the bitter and deadly East Coast vs West Coast rap rivalries AND turf wars between the Bloods and the Crips street gangs that were immortalised in rap lyrics and news reports in the 1990s.

It could also include several celebrity witnesses - including Suge Knight, the former CEO of Death Row Records, who has been thought of as the last surviving witness to Shakur's death.

But the complicated case hinges almost exclusively on one key piece of evidence: a book co-authored by Davis that he has argued is partially a piece of fiction.

Jury selection in the case began on Monday, with opening arguments slated to start on 17 August.

To understand how the case became so mythologised, you have to go back to rivalries that grew larger than the men at its centre.

In the Los Angeles gang landscape of the 1990s, there was a vicious turf war between the Bloods, often represented by the color red, and Crips, who often wore blue. But that territorial dispute spread through the airwaves as part of a bigger national rivalry - East Coast vs West Coast rap. The genre dispute was represented by two rival record companies that defined 1990s hip-hop: Knight's Death Row Records and Sean "Diddy" Combs' Bad Boy Records.

"The funny thing about it is Tupac is actually an East Coast rapper," said Jeff Pearlman, author of Only God Can Judge Me: The Many Lives of Tupac Shakur.

Born in New York City, Tupac moved to northern California as a teenager. He became known as a Southern California rapper after signing with Death Row Records, which included acts like Snoop Dogg and Dr Dre.

Santi Elijah Holley, author of An Amerikan Family: The Shakurs and the Nation They Created, says the Death Row persona never told the whole story.

Tupac's mother Afeni was a Black Panther and he grew up around the Black liberation movement. Holley says his music became his politics: "His activism was his art, his lyrics."

He acted in a number of Hollywood movies, and released hip-hop's first double album, All Eyez on Me, which sold over 5,000,000 copies. That album, which debuted months before his death, cemented his place in the cannon of gangsta rap, a genre that celebrated the violent life of street criminals and drug dealers.

After he was shot in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996, he became immortalised as a kind of martyr for the lifestyle he helped make famous.

That fatal night began when Tupac and Knight attended a boxing match between Mike Tyson and Bruce Seldon at the MGM Grand.

After the match, surveillance footage captured Tupac and members of his entourage, who police have said were associated the Mob Piru Bloods street gang, attacking a man named Orlando Anderson, an alleged member of the South Side Compton Crips.

About three hours after the attack, Tupac was riding in the passenger seat of Knight's BMW driving through Las Vegas when a white Cadillac pulled alongside them and opened fire.

Tupac was hit four times and died six days later.

For nearly three decades, the killing remained one of America's most famous unsolved murders. There is no single explanation why.

Las Vegas police have long said witnesses refused to cooperate. Members of Tupac's entourage said police initially treated them like suspects and failed to follow important leads.

Within weeks of the shooting, investigators had identified Anderson from the MGM footage and questioned him.

He denied involvement and was never charged; he was killed in an unrelated shooting in 1998.

Over the years, police say they pursued thousands of tips, but the case stalled amid disappearing witnesses, many of whom were also killed in gang-related shootings, limited physical evidence, and a street code that forbid cooperation with police.

It was years later when Anderson's uncle, Davis, started talking and according to police, blew the case wide open again.

It was ultimately the death of another legendary rapper that helped unravel Tupac's shooting death.

Months after Shakur was gunned down, Biggie Smalls or the Notorious BIG, was killed in a drive-by shooting in Los Angeles.

Both rappers were the stars of their respective rival record labels - Shakur with Death Row Records and Biggie with Bad Boy Records.

Biggie's case has remained unsolved, with no arrests or suspects.

In the mid 2000's the Los Angeles Police Department reopened the investigation and spoke with Davis, who was at a party with Biggie before the fatal shooting. While Davis said he didn't have information about Biggie's death, he did have knowledge in Tupac's case and shared that he was in the car when the rapper was shot and killed. He told police the information in exchange that he not be charged.

That deal stuck until years later, when Davis went public with his knowledge.

He co-authored a memoir in 2019 titled Compton Street Legend, that claimed he not only was inside the vehicle when Tupac was shot but also he was the person who "tossed" the gun used to kill him into the backseat of the Cadillac. He never claimed to be the person who opened fire.

Davis also elaborated on the shooting to the media, detailing information to reporters in interviews.

Las Vegas police said his public statements had "reinvigorated" the investigation. Over the next couple of years they spent time corroborating Davis' account and then in 2023, searched his home and seized multiple computers, two tubs of photographs and a slew of Tupac-related material, including a Vibe magazine.

He was arrested later that year.

Prosecutors have alleged that Tupac's killing was in retaliation for the beating of Davis' nephew - Orlando Anderson - just hours before the shooting.

They claim that Davis was the architect of the crime, who ordered the shooting and supplied the deadly weapon to further gang criminal conduct.

Nevada prosecutors argued that by publicly talking about what happened on the night of Tupac's death and writing a book where he claimed to have supplied the gun, Davis had broken the agreement he entered with law enforcement. A judge later sided with the prosecutor's argument, opening the door for Davis's arrest.

Davis and his defence team have argued that the book was co-authored and sections were embellished or fictionalised to make a profit, and they should not be viewed as direct admissions. In an interview last week with a local TV news station, Davis denied being in Las Vegas when Tupac was killed and distanced himself from the memoir that lists him as an author.

"I did not write that book," Davis told Fox 5. "A ghost writer wrote that."

He also said he might take the stand and testify at his trial. "If I have to, I will."

"This is what makes this case so fascinating. The two biggest pieces of evidence against Keffe D came from Keffe D," trial attorney Shaun Kent told the BBC. "Keffe D has the right to take the stand and say 'I made all this up. I lied to sell copies of the book. I lied to the police. I'm a liar but I did not murder Tupac.'"

Davis has also publicly stated multiple times that Bad Boy Records head Sean "Diddy" Combs had offered him $1m to kill Death Row Records rivals Tupac and Knight.

Combs is currently serving a 50-month prison sentence after being convicted for two counts of transportation for the purposes of prostitution in New York. He has repeatedly denied allegations that he was involved in Tupac's death.

Prosecutors have released a list of potential witnesses who could be called to testify, with over 200 names, including members of Tupac's family, former mayor of Las Vegas Oscar Goodman and former Los Angeles police Detective Greg Kading.

Prosecutors have also named Knight, although it's unclear if the rap empresario will testify, as he's previously said he would not.

"This would be huge as he has never offered law enforcement any information that would lead to the conviction of anyone," Kent said. "This trial is going to be a legal scholar's Super Bowl."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgmk.summary: Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been charged with murder in the death of Tupac Shakur. He has denied being involved in the shooting of the rapper. He co-authored a memoir in 2019 titled Compton Street Legend.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Benjamin Netanyahu’s rejection of US deal for Gaza is a risky gamble
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
Israeli prime minister’s unexpected move blindsided IDF commanders and risks alienating Trump, his main ally

Benjamin Netanyahu’s public rejection of a US-backed deal for Gaza drew scepticism in Israel, amid reports he was personally hammering out details of a pilot military withdrawal days earlier.

The Israeli prime minister is struggling to balance incompatible demands on Gaza policy from his key domestic and international allies.

The far-right Israeli politicians who prop up Netanyahu’s coalition government want to intensify Israeli attacks on Gaza and establish settlements inside the territory.

Donald Trump, who provides vital diplomatic and military backing for Israel, wants to move toward a permanent settlement and return to Palestinian control in Gaza, brokered by the Board of Peace that he created and chairs.

With an Israeli election looming in just over two months, Netanyahu appears to have opted to publicly placate domestic partners who are already on the campaign trail.

On Sunday he rejected a new 15-point plan for Gaza, which included a Hamas commitment to give up its weapons, meeting a key Israeli demand. He also resisted US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in.

The remarks blindsided Israeli commanders who had been discussing implementation of the plan in meetings with Netanyahu and the Israeli chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, just days earlier, Israel’s Channel 12 television reported.

“We learned about it today from the media,” the station quoted a defence official saying. “At the meetings that were held until now, the prime minister personally gave his consent to this plan and to a withdrawal from the points in Rafah.”

The meetings covered precise boundaries of three pilot areas in southern Gaza where a proposed international force – which has yet to be stood up – could take over from the Israeli military, and the interface between the two forces, the report said.

Netanyhu’s public attack on the Board of Peace plan seemed like a particularly pointed rejection of US goals because it was released soon after a reported visit by Adm Brad Cooper, who heads US Central Command.

He came to deliver in person the message that the Trump administration wants Israel to end its wars in Gaza and Lebanon, Israeli media reported. “The Americans’ message to the IDF was to move in the direction of shutting down all three theatres of operations,” a senior Israeli military officer told Channel 13 Television.

Defying Trump, who is notoriously thin-skinned and intolerant of dissent, is a risky gamble when Israel is internationally isolated and needs US military supplies.

But Netanyahu has a long track record of audacious political manoeuvring, both at home and internationally, undaunted even by ostensible power imbalances. Bill Clinton, after meeting him for the first time in 1996, is reported to have said: “Who’s the fucking superpower here?”

In May 2024 US president Joe Biden announced an Israeli-backed ceasefire and hostage release plan for Gaza, only to have Netanyahu distance himself from the proposal and ultimately reject it.

For now the administration in Washington appears to have largely shrugged off Netanyahu’s comments as electioneering, perhaps encouraged by military decisions that indicate a far more attentive regard for Trump’s wishes.

Last week Netanyahu scaled back Israeli airstrikes on Gaza by raising the threshold for authorising attacks. Targeted killings must now be approved by the chief of staff, rather than the regional commander, unless Israeli forces are in “imminent danger”.

Nor is this the first time he has bowed to US pressure to rein in wars that have the enthusiastic backing of his far-right allies, recently limiting the offensive in Lebanon, and last year ordering fighter jets heading for Iran to turn back at Trump’s demand.

Netanyahu’s combination of fierce domestic rhetoric and some conciliatory steps on the ground in Gaza may have bought him a bit of time but US patience may not last until polling day in late October.

Trump is weighing up election concerns of his own, as the US is holding midterms just a week after Israel votes.

Netanyahu’s visit to the White House last month was notably low profile for a leader who has repeatedly campaigned on his reputation as an international statesman and close relationship with the US president, Haaretz newspaper noted.

It ended without a joint statement, and strains caused by the Israeli prime minister’s competing political priorities have become increasingly evident. “That’s how it is when you try to juggle too many balls; you start dropping them,” the paper said.

The top envoy for the Board of Peace, Nickolay Mladenov, declined to comment on Netanyahu’s rejection of a deal that took months to hammer out. In an interview with Israeli media he said only that “discussions continue”.

Palestinians in Gaza have endured nearly a year of deadly limbo after Trump brokered a nominal ceasefire last October, that he said would halt fighting and pave the way for reconstruction.

Israeli attacks have continued, killing over 1,200 people, and Israel has blocked the entry of equipment, supplies and fuel needed for rebuilding homes, schools and medical infrastructure.

The majority of Gaza’s surviving population live in tent camps with little sanitation, and although hunger has diminished food shortages are still widespread, with over 70,000 children projected to need treatment for acute malnutrition to April 2027, food security experts have warned.

Netanyahu’s office rejected reports that he had discussed detailed withdrawal plans for Gaza.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.summary: Israeli PM's rejection of a US-backed deal for Gaza drew scepticism in Israel. Netanyahu's rejection drew sceptic in Israel amid reports he was personally hammering out details of a pilot military withdrawal days earlier. Netanyahu is struggling to balance incompatible demands on Gaza policy from his key domestic and international allies.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Labour peer urges Badenoch to reverse decision on ex-neo-Nazi’s advisory role
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Aletha Adu
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Luciana Berger, who was subject to abuse from Joshua Bonehill-Paine, said Tory leader should ‘listen to victims’

The Labour peer Luciana Berger has urged Kemi Badenoch to “listen to victims” and reverse her decision to give a national advisory role to a former neo-Nazi.

Joshua Bonehill-Paine was jailed in 2015 for more than three years after posting antisemitic material online before a planned neo-Nazi rally. In 2016, he was found guilty of racially aggravated harassment for abuse directed at Berger, an MP at the time. He was also the founder and leader of the National British Resistance, a far-right group.

Berger said she was still affected by his crimes more than nine years later, and questioned what safeguarding checks Badenoch and the Conservative party had carried out in relation to his appointment to the party’s culture and integration commission.

Berger asked whether Bonehill-Paine’s new role could bring him to Westminster, writing on X: “Can I expect to come face to face with him on the parliamentary estate?”

Badenoch’s spokesperson said Bonehill-Paine would not have a parliamentary pass and would not be on the estate.

Berger’s intervention came after the Conservative party leader published a lengthy defence of Bonehill-Paine in the Times, describing questions over his suitability to stand as a councillor in Somerset as a “pile-on”.

Bonehill-Paine was set to stand as a Tory local councillor but announced last week that he had withdrawn from next year’s local elections after Badenoch offered him the advisory role.

Badenoch said: “People need to understand that the Conservative party under my leadership is now the party of personal responsibility and law and order. That means insisting on consequences by punishing wrongdoing and protecting the public, especially victims.

“We need fewer double standards and instead higher standards in a system that is repeatedly failing to protect the public. We should be tough enough to stand by our beliefs even when politically inconvenient, wise enough to recognise rehabilitation and consistent enough to apply the same principles to friend and foe.”

Berger said she had seen the piece late on Saturday night and “tried to ignore it” but after Badenoch shared the article on Monday, the former MP for Liverpool Wavertree accused her of giving insufficient consideration to Bonehill-Paine’s victims.

“Badenoch makes one passing reference to the ‘victims’,” Berger wrote. “There were many. And I was one of them. Did Badenoch read the judge’s sentencing remarks? In court we heard the victim impact statements from people unable to testify, whose lives he had destroyed.

“His appointment as an adviser to the Conservative party’s culture and integration commission could conceivably bring him to Westminster. Can I expect to come face to face with him on the parliamentary estate?

“It’s still not too late for Badenoch to listen to victims and reverse her decision.”

A spokesperson for Badenoch said Bonehill-Paine had served his time, completed Home Office Prevent (counter-terrorism) courses, and had gone into schools to teach about combatting antisemitism and extremism. But the party did not answer questions about what safeguarding checks it had carried out in relation to his appointment as an adviser, or why Badenoch had not contacted Berger.

The abuse Bonehill-Paine directed at Berger included calling her a “rodent” and an “evil money-grabber”. He also has a conviction for assaulting a police officer and burglary of a police station, and was convicted in 2014 of malicious communications over an anti-Islam hoax that led to death threats against the owners of a pub in Leicester.

Berger challenged Badenoch over what consideration had been given to safeguarding: “Badenoch’s article says she wants to safeguard the public and victims, but what safeguarding checks have she and the Conservative party carried out?”

If Badenoch or her team had reached out to her, Berger said, “I would say, I don’t think it is ‘harder politics’ for this man to be part of Kemi’s operation. I think it’s the wrong politics.”

She added: “I’m all for rehabilitation. But someone convicted of neo-Nazi misogynistic crimes is not suitable for public office less than a decade after his conviction. And neither should he be gifted a national advisory role, even closer to power.”

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Progressive US senator urges Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic to ‘stop building machines that humans cannot control’

Senator Bernie Sanders has called on Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic executives to halt their development of artificial intelligence, warning that the US Senate will implement regulation if the companies continue deploying AI at their current pace.

In a new letter addressed to the CEOs of three of the country’s leading AI companies, Sanders said the capabilities of these AI models have reached a critical risk threshold and that the companies are losing control over the technology.

“Mr. Altman, Mr. Amodei and Mr. Zuckerberg: In the interest of humanity, stand by your words. Pause AI development,” Sanders’s letter, first reported by Axios, read. “It is not too late to avoid disaster. Stop building machines that humans cannot control.”

The Vermont senator cited recent reports that AI was used to develop new viruses, warning that if this technology fell into the “wrong hands” it may “lead to new bioweapons that result in the deaths of tens of millions of people”.

All three companies have also disclosed their models hacked other companies’ servers, a sign that the firms have lost control over their models, Sanders wrote.

“Yoshua Bengio, the most cited living scientist in the world, said these incidents ‘should serve as a wake-up call,’ I agree,” Sanders wrote in the letter.

Experts, however, have cautioned that OpenAI’s claims that its AI model went rogue may be overblown as part of a media campaign to make their technology seem highly dangerous, and thus extremely powerful.

“And yet, at a moment when we have seen human loss of control and the creation of potentially dangerous viruses, your companies are still racing ahead – investing tens of billions of dollars into a technology that nobody can fully understand, predict or control,” he continued.

Sanders’s letter comes after more than 1,300 scientists and developers from across the tech industry published another letter warning that AI development is moving at a pace that makes it difficult to address and identify the risks of the technology. Companies and countries are facing intense competitive pressure to move quickly. In the open letter, the engineers and other staffers called on the US government to help coordinate an international effort to slow down the development of frontier models so that regulators could create safety guardrails around the tech.

The companies have previously committed to pausing their AI development if certain risk thresholds were met – but the companies did not detail exactly what those limits would entail.

Anthropic said it would “commit to pause the scaling and/or delay the deployment of new models whenever our scaling ability outstrips our ability to comply with … safety procedures”.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

OpenAI, which said it would slow down the development of its latest cybersecurity model, Astra, after the autonomous hack of another organization, said it would “halt further development” if AI capabilities met a “critical” threshold until guardrails were implemented.

Sanders said recent hacking incidents were signs that the threshold has been surpassed.

“That moment is here,” his letter reads. “AI capabilities HAVE reached a critical threshold. There is a reason why the head of the CIA says that AI models are ‘akin to digital nuclear weapons’ and ‘almost like a doomsday device.’”

The progressive senator previously called for a moratorium on datacenter construction across the US. He and congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced a bill to pause the building of new datacenters in the US in March. Their rationale was similar to Sanders’s case for pausing the development of AI models: a temporary ban, the lawmakers said, would give the US government time to create strong federal safeguards for AI.

He says the US Senate will implement regulation if the companies continue deploying AI at their current pace. Sanders says the companies are losing control over the technology.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on the failed Gaza peace plan: Trump’s hollow claims are ignored in Jerusalem | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has no interest in agreeing to a deal. For relief to come to Gaza, real US pressure must be exerted

A
t the end of July, Donald Trump announced that a “monumental” US-backed deal had been struck on Gaza, securing the phased disarmament of Hamas in parallel with Israeli military withdrawal. Three days later it was reported that another 18 people had died in Israeli airstrikes. Not for the first time, it appeared that Mr Trump’s rhetoric had only a distant relationship with the reality it purported to describe.

Such suspicions were duly confirmed yesterday. Under pressure from far-right members of his coalition, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, explicitly rejected the sequencing of a 15-point plan from the increasingly hapless Board of Peace – an international body set up by the US president – and poured scorn on “a wave of rumours of … Israeli withdrawals on all fronts”. In a direct message to the White House, Mr Netanyahu stated that “we know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary.”

In practical terms that will mean the continued, brazen violation of the terms of last October’s ceasefire agreement, since when close to 1,300 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli air assaults. Far from envisaging any withdrawal, the Israeli military has expanded its presence and now controls about 65% of the territory. Hemmed in towards the coast in the rest of the strip, much of the population faces an unrelenting daily struggle.

Formal schooling has not restarted, the healthcare system has been largely destroyed and the entry of medical and other humanitarian aid remains severely restricted. Reconstruction work has been blocked, while the first building contract issued by the Board of Peace has been for an outpost to host foreign troops. Meanwhile, the world’s attention has shifted  to Mr Trump’s illegal and reckless war on Iran – a grievous miscalculation in which Israel’s prime minister also played his part.

In calling for complete Hamas disarmament before Israel makes a move, Mr Netanyahu is transparently playing for time. For two years he has relentlessly flattered the US president, and exploited his backing to pursue a scorched earth project of revenge following the Hamas massacre of October 7. But two months out from the first elections held since then, his priority now is appeasing the intransigent far-right forces who can keep him in power. Should Mr Netanyahu lose, he could face jail in relation to corruption charges first laid more than five years ago.

Despairing Palestinians can only hope that growing White House frustration with Mr Netanyahu’s forever wars will lead to a tipping point – one that should have been reached during the Joe Biden presidency. If he opted to use it, Mr Trump has the power to isolate the Israeli prime minister, call time on his temporising and manoeuvring, and compel a different approach. Board of Peace attempts yesterday to reassure the Israeli government over the verification process for disarming Hamas indicate that we are not close to that point.

Nevertheless, ahead of challenging midterm elections for the Republicans, pro-Israel sentiment may not be the political force that it once was. Recent polling suggests that traditionally high levels of US public sympathy with Israel are on the wane. Mr Trump has a choice: he can continue to accept being played by Israel’s prime minister, or he can exert the kind of pressure that could bring genuine relief to Gaza.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/8/.title: Palestinian club football to restart in September after Gaza war suspension
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/8/.text:
The Palestinian Football Association has announced that it will resume activity in September after a nearly three-year pause due to Israel’s genocidal war on Palestinians in Gaza.

“We announce the resumption of sports activities and the football association’s league beginning September 4,” association President Jibril Rajoub said at a Ramallah news conference on Monday.

Palestinian sports leagues, including professional football, came to a halt after the war began on October 7, 2023.

The association has named the first tournament back the “Thousand Martyrs’ Cup”, to honour the 1,014 Palestinian athletes killed by Israel during the war, according to the association’s data.

More than 200 clubs will compete in the tournament, including 146 from the Israeli-occupied West Bank, 44 from Gaza, and 36 from Palestinian refugee camps in Lebanon.

The tournament will kick off simultaneously in the three locations.

Rajoub said the war “created difficult conditions for all Palestinians that led to the suspension of our competitions and activities”.

“But we have not lost our Palestinian national will, nor have we lost our belief that sport will remain a symbol of hope and life,” he said.

Rajoub noted that the association and Palestinian clubs faced tough financial circumstances.

During the news conference, he called on FIFA and other federations to stand by Palestinian sports and to protect the rights of players, clubs and children to enjoy sports in “freedom and dignity”.

The association previously issued a statement regarding FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s now-withdrawn plan to open tournaments to private investors, saying “many today are questioning FIFA’s commercial direction”.

“But for Palestine, the issue is more fundamental … Our question is whether FIFA still has the courage to apply its regulations to everyone equally … without succumbing to political pressures,” Rajoub said.

The association has called on FIFA to impose sanctions on Israeli clubs that operate in occupied West Bank settlements and to suspend Israel’s FIFA membership over the country’s conduct in Gaza.

Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law.

“We are not asking for privileges; we are demanding legitimate rights guaranteed by international sporting laws and charters,” Rajoub said.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/clicks.title: Clicks’ Power Keyboard brings BlackBerry-style typing to any phone — with some compromises
https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/clicks.author: Sarah Perez
https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/clicks.text:
Clicks Technology, the startup determined to bring back physical keyboards to smartphones, began shipping its now-$99 MagSafe-compatible Power Keyboard this summer, after some delays. As of last week, 75% of the pre-orders from the first batch had shipped to customers.

Designed to work with a range of devices, this new, slide-out keyboard with tactile buttons can accommodate different phone sizes and can be used in either portrait or landscape mode, the company says, giving any phone a BlackBerry-like feel.

The device is something of a teaser for what’s to come when Clicks ships its first smartphone, the BlackBerry-like Clicks Communicator, also featuring a physical keyboard, later this year.

Like the upcoming smartphone, the idea behind the Power Keyboard is to provide an alternative to onscreen keyboards for those who miss the speed and reliability that came with typing on a small, physical keyboard.

However, in its current implementation, the Power Keyboard suffers from the same fate as the company’s earlier Clicks keyboard — a smartphone case that included a physical keyboard. It can make the phone feel top-heavy and difficult to hold in portrait mode, especially if you’re using a larger smartphone as I did in tests with the iPhone 17 Pro Max and Pixel 10 XL.

Still, the device itself is crafted with care, and could appeal to those who still desperately long for their BlackBerry.

Unboxing the device, we noticed the Power Keyboard was nicely packaged as a premium device would be, with peel-away cling films to prevent scratches during shipping and a full-color Quick Start guide to using the product.

You may first need to charge the device’s battery via USB-C, though we found ours shipped with a charge already. To pair the device with your phone over Bluetooth, press and hold the power button and slide out the keyboard. We quickly paired the device with our Android phone. We ran into trouble once we switched over to the iPhone. Even after “forgetting” the device on Android, it still refused to pair with our iPhone. Returning to the instructions, it appears this was our mistake. The trick is to press a number key alongside the power button on the keyboard to add a second Bluetooth device. (The only way to actually “forget” a device is by removing it from its slot using the Clicks mobile app.)

The keyboard attaches to your phone via MagSafe or Qi2. If your phone doesn’t support either technology, you could opt to use an adhesive ring or a phone case that adds the magnetic power profile instead.

Once connected, you can then pull the keyboard out when you need to type. Helpfully, the keyboard adjusts to different phone sizes, so it will work with standard models as well as larger “Ultra” or “Pro Max” devices. We appreciated the satisfying clicks as the keyboard locked into place on the various sliders. The keyboard offers an adjustable LED backlight, so you can type in the dark.

The keys themselves have a nice, clicky feel and are well-placed, making them easy to reach. While it takes quite a bit of adjustment after years of on-screen keyboards to return to pressing buttons, the learning curve is less steep than it was on the earlier Clicks keyboard case. It’s clear that the company has been iterating on what it learned with its older device, and those lessons have been channeled into this product.

In addition, while Clicks’ older keyboard case pulled power from the phone by way of its USB-C connection, the Power Keyboard instead includes a built-in 2,150 mAh battery.

The product itself has a slimmer profile than some snap-on battery packs, at 119.7 × 76.6 × 15.2mm, and doesn’t add an unreasonable amount of weight at 180 grams. Nevertheless, this is not something that would fit well in a woman’s pants pocket. The keyboard could get caught on a back pocket as well, as it could slide open if you press against the device while trying to cram the phone and keyboard into your pocket too quickly.

Despite the added heft, there is an advantage to the battery pack that powers the keyboard — it can provide wireless charging to products with MagSafe and Qi2. (You can opt to entirely disable wireless charging in the Clicks companion app, if you prefer to keep all the power reserved for the keyboard itself. Or you can designate a portion of the battery just for the keyboard.)

Another key advantage of the Power Keyboard is that it is highly customizable. Users can enable the Clicks key on the keyboard to function as a Tab button, or turn on “Cursor Mode” (Sym + CMD) to make certain letters on your keypad work as directional keys that move a cursor on the screen.

You can also adjust various settings like the idle timeout, battery reserves for wireless charging, LED backlight, and whether the Return key works as a hard or soft return. You can create your own Number Row shortcuts that allow you to press a number and the Sym button to enable Esc, volume controls, play/pause options, page up/down, and more.

And you can pair Apple Shortcuts with certain keys to do other things like start a call, get a weather forecast, turn on the flashlight, receive an AirDrop, send texts, and much more. (Several popular shortcuts are included in the Clicks app, but you can add your own.)

These, of course, are power user features that you’ll only appreciate if you get comfortable with typing on the keyboard first. That could take some time to learn, and arguably, you’ll be more comfortable using smaller, standard phones or lightweight options, like the iPhone Air. As for larger devices, we found it much easier to get started in landscape mode.

We also struggled to type comfortably with our iPhone case on, although it’s a heftier, protective case, not a slim case. To test the device, we removed the case and used our iPhone bare. While that was much better, it was still somewhat difficult to use because of the larger phone.

The company itself says it has tested the device with a number of phone models, including the iPhone Air, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max, 16 Pro, Pixel 9, Galaxy Fold, and other Android devices.

Whether or not the keyboard is worth the purchase has much to do with how much you really miss your BlackBerry; for the time being, it’s an affordable enough holdover until the company’s smartphone ships, at least. (Prototypes of the phone were much easier to use when we tried them at CES in January. It’s obviously easier to make a comfortable device when Clicks is in control of all the technical specifications, instead of having to create something that works with phones of various weights and sizes.)

While the Power Keyboard works as advertised, for the sake of comfort and portability, I’d prefer to make the switch to physical keys with Clicks’ Communicator smartphone.

If you also decide this keyboard is not for you, all is not lost: There’s still another way to use the product.

Because the Power Keyboard should be able to pair with any device that supports external Bluetooth keyboards, you could use it with tablets, smart TVs like the Apple TV, or AR/VR headsets, like the Apple Vision Pro. This could come in handy when you’re trying to set up new apps and have to type your email address and passwords awkwardly via a remote control or other input method.

TechCrunch tries new devices via review units, which are later returned to the company or donated, depending on the company’s specific return procedures.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/clicks.summary: The Power Keyboard is a slide-out keyboard that can accommodate different phone sizes. It attaches to your phone via MagSafe or Qi2. The keyboard can be used in either portrait or landscape mode.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/china-.title: China-Linked Hackers Deploy New StormEncryptor Ransomware, Likely via N-central Flaw
https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/china-.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/china-.text:
Microsoft has disclosed that Storm-1175, a financially motivated threat actor linked to China, has deployed a previously undocumented ransomware strain called StormEncryptor.

The use of StormEncryptor marks a shift from the adversary's previous use of Medusa ransomware, the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Team said.

"StormEncryptor is written in C++ and appends the file name extension .encrypted to files it encrypts," Microsoft noted in a series of posts on Bluesky. "It then drops a ransom note named !!!README_FIRST!!!.txt to every scanned directory."

Although the exact vulnerability exploited by the threat actor as part of this campaign is unclear, the tech giant said it likely involves the exploitation of CVE-2026-18577, a newly disclosed security flaw in N-able N‑central, to obtain initial access.

The vulnerability is assessed to be a patch bypass for CVE-2026-18556, both of which allow authentication bypass and account takeover in susceptible versions. The vulnerabilities have since been flagged by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) as actively exploited in the wild.

Storm-1175 is the name assigned to a China-based threat actor with a history of deploying Medusa ransomware after exploiting security flaws in Mirth Connect (CVE-2023-37679, CVE-2023-43208), ConnectWise ScreenConnect (CVE-2024-1709, CVE-2024-1708), JetBrains TeamCity (CVE-2024-27198, CVE-2024-27199), and Fortinet FortiClient EMS (CVE-2023-48788).

In an analysis published in October 2025, Microsoft also attributed the threat actor to the exploitation of a critical security vulnerability impacting Fortra GoAnywhere (CVE-2025-10035) to facilitate the deployment of Medusa ransomware.

The group, per the Windows maker, weaponizes a combination of zero-days and N-day vulnerabilities to carry out high-velocity attacks and break into susceptible internet-facing systems by taking advantage of the window between vulnerability disclosure and patch adoption.

"In this new activity, Storm-1175's post-compromise behavior includes abuse of remote monitoring and management tools AnyDesk or SimpleHelp, Advanced IP Scanner for discovery, and LSASS dumping using Mimikatz," it added.

Storm-1175 has also been observed rapidly moving from initial access to data exfiltration and ransomware deployment, mostly within a few days, making it essential that customers apply the patches as soon as possible.
https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/china-.summary: Microsoft says threat actor has deployed previously undocumented ransomware strain called StormEncryptor. The threat actor is linked to a China-based threat actor with a history of deploying Medusa ransomware. The vulnerability is assessed to be a patch bypass for CVE-2026-18556.

https://www.space.com/astronomy/galaxies.author: Rahul Rao
https://www.space.com/astronomy/galaxies.text:
"We can't explicitly say that we are seeing a decrease in star formation because of M32. But it's right there, and it's definitely the most likely suspect."

Thanks to the Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers have shed light on a recent chapter in the history of our Milky Way's neighboring galaxy, Andromeda.

Using Hubble Space Telescope observations of Andromeda's stars, a research team showed that the spiral galaxy's rate of making new stars has dramatically slowed down in the last 40 million years. And they've found more evidence that one of Andromeda's own neighbors — a smaller galaxy called M32 — may be to blame.

"We can't explicitly say that we are seeing a decrease in star formation because of M32. But it's right there, and it's definitely the most likely suspect," said Tobin Wainer, a graduate student at the University of Washington and one of the astronomers, in a statement.

Astronomers like Wainer knew from prior research that Andromeda saw a burst of star formation about 2 billion years ago (possibly as a result of a collision with an unknown galaxy). They also knew that star formation had slowed down since then. What they did not know was how quickly that deceleration had been. If they could find out, they could fill in some of the gaps in Andromeda's history.

At 2.5 million light-years' distance, Andromeda is near enough to Earth that Hubble can measure its stars. In the past several years, Hubble has conducted two surveys of Andromeda. While Hubble can only make out stars in Andromeda that are brighter than our sun, these two surveys still gave Wainer and colleagues a compendium of 200 million stars, covering two-thirds of Andromeda's disk.

Wainer and colleagues parceled out this vast space into a grid of squares, 300 light-years to a side. They reconstructed the history of each square by examining the colors of its stars.

A square with many bright blue stars, for example, probably saw a lot of star formation recently, since blue stars tend to be younger. On the other hand, if a square only contains smaller, redder stars, we know those stars are longer-lived and older, and that square probably hasn't seen a lot of newborn stars.

The astronomers mapped out a story of slowing star formation. Around 500 million years ago, on average, Andromeda turned the equivalent of our sun's mass in gas and dust into newborn stars each year. As millions of years passed, that rate declined. About 40 million years ago, it was about one-half the sun's mass each year. Then, it tilted into a dramatic deceleration. Today, it stands at about one-fifth the sun's mass each year.

Curiously, they found that Andromeda's starmaking slowdown is especially pronounced on one particular side of the galaxy, starting about 60 million years ago. Astronomers know this side of Andromeda is closest to another galaxy: M32.

Astronomers have eyed M32 with suspicion for some time now. M32 is only located about 16,000 light-years from Andromeda (Andromeda is formally called M31) and it looks like the rump core of a spiral galaxy that lost its arms. It's possible that this is actually the aftermath of a collision between M32 and its larger neighbor. It's possible, though not confirmed, that Andromeda's slowing bears the fingerprints of this collision.

We may not need to wait long for more answers. Just as Hubble can see Andromeda's stars, so too will the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, set to launch in late August. In the coming years, Roman will be able to measure even more of Andromeda than Hubble has.
