https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/ost.title: OA Tied to Arthritis AE Risk in ICI-Treated Patients
https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/ost.text:
Edited by Manasi Talwadekar

Osteoarthritis (OA) was associated with the risk of developing inflammatory arthritis immune-related adverse events (IA-irAEs) in patients with cancer receiving immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy. Among ICI-treated patients, 69% of those who developed IA-irAEs had OA, with hand OA being the predominant pattern in those with IA-irAEs.

“[The study] findings suggest that preexisting hand OA may be predisposed to the development of polyarticular IA-irAE rather than reflecting a nonspecific consequence of ICI exposure,” the authors of the study wrote.

The study was led by Shiju Chen, MD, Department of Medicine, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, Minnesota. It was published online on June 01, 2026, in Arthritis Care & Research.

OA identification relied on retrospective documentation rather than systematic joint screening, and variations in imaging availability may have influenced OA detection rates. Site-specific prevalence could have been affected by documentation practices, potentially introducing detection bias. IA-irAE cases managed without specialty referral may have been underrecognized because only patients evaluated by rheumatologists were included. Residual confounding related to treatment selection cannot be ruled out.

The study received support from the National Institutes of Health through grants to an author, along with funding from the Mark E. and Mary A. Davis Initiative in Rheumatoid Arthritis Research and Mayo Foundation for Medical Education and Research. Two authors reported receiving grants or contracts from other organizations.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/10/crowdstr.title: CrowdStrike, Palo Alto hit records after Black Hat cyber conference illuminates rising AI threat
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/10/crowdstr.author: Samantha Subin
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/10/crowdstr.text:
Cybersecurity stocks CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks jumped to new highs following the industry’s Black Hat conference in Las Vegas.

Analysts at BTIG wrote that “AI agents have fundamentally changed the threat landscape.”

Businesses are leaning on more AI tools to fend off more sophisticated cyber attacks.

Cybersecurity stocks CrowdStrike
 and Palo Alto Networks
 jumped more than 5% to new highs on Monday on renewed demand for artificial intelligence security tools following the industry’s annual Black Hat conference in Las Vegas.

“The single most consistent theme across our conversations — partners, vendors, and customers alike — was that AI agents have fundamentally changed the threat landscape,” wrote analysts at BTIG in a note to clients.

While AI agents have become the predominant attack threat and the environment is “meaningfully worse,” deployment and AI security tools are only in the early innings,” they added.

Businesses are turning to cybersecurity companies for new agentic tools to fend off adversaries in a hyper-accelerated threat landscape fueled by new cyber models. Executives and potential customers gathered in Las Vegas last week in search of answers and ways to secure systems from rogue AI agents.

BTIG lifted its price target on Palo Alto to $380 a share, reflecting about 4% upside from Friday’s close. Palo’s identity platform stands to benefit from the proliferation of AI agents, while products such as XSIAM and Chronosphere create a “data moat” for other security verticals.

The firm lifted its price target on CrowdStrike to $237 per share, reflecting 11% upside from Friday’s close, and boosted shares of Rubrik to a $109 per-share target.

“We think AI is creating a new modernization cycle in the endpoint security space, which directly benefits CRWD’s core business,” they wrote.

Other cybersecurity stocks rallied, with Tenable
 and Rubrik
 last up more than 7%. Netskope
 and Zscaler
 jumped about 5% each.

“AI has moved from being a cybersecurity feature to a key pillar of both the attack surface and the attacker/defender infrastructure,” wrote analysts at Cantor.

https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/08/10/rus.title: Ukrainians Are Trying to Help a Traumatized Generation
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/08/10/rus.author: Luke McGee
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/08/10/rus.text:
As Russian strikes pummel Ukrainian cities, a quieter, systemic crisis also threatens Ukraine’s future. For Russia, targeting Ukrainian youth is not merely collateral damage; it is demographic warfare aimed at erasing Ukrainian identity. For the millions of children forced to grow up in a war zone, the trauma extends far beyond the front lines, stretching from occupied reeducation camps to disrupted homes across the country.

Understanding the conflict four years on.

Children kidnapped by Russian forces in the occupied territories have received the most global attention. Since Russia’s invasion of Crimea in 2014, and the full-scale attack on Ukraine in 2022, a huge number, possibly into the millions, of Ukrainian children have found themselves living under Russian rule—either in Ukraine or relocated to Russia. There, they have been forced to attend Russian schools and facilities, where they are bombarded with pro-Russian propaganda and drip-fed stories intended to eventually turn them into soldiers for their kidnappers.

As Russian strikes pummel Ukrainian cities, a quieter, systemic crisis also threatens Ukraine’s future. For Russia, targeting Ukrainian youth is not merely collateral damage; it is demographic warfare aimed at erasing Ukrainian identity. For the millions of children forced to grow up in a war zone, the trauma extends far beyond the front lines, stretching from occupied reeducation camps to disrupted homes across the country.

Understanding the conflict four years on.

Children kidnapped by Russian forces in the occupied territories have received the most global attention. Since Russia’s invasion of Crimea in 2014, and the full-scale attack on Ukraine in 2022, a huge number, possibly into the millions, of Ukrainian children have found themselves living under Russian rule—either in Ukraine or relocated to Russia. There, they have been forced to attend Russian schools and facilities, where they are bombarded with pro-Russian propaganda and drip-fed stories intended to eventually turn them into soldiers for their kidnappers.

“One of the first messages they receive is that they have been abandoned by both their parents and their country,” said Myroslava Kharchenko, chief legal specialist at Save Ukraine, a charity that supports people under Russian occupation. “They are repeatedly told that their parents will never come to take them home.”

Kharchenko explained that over time, this reeducation evolves from anti-Ukraine propaganda to something more overtly aggressive.

“School lessons and textbooks portray Russia as fighting not Ukraine but the collective West, NATO, and Europe while presenting Ukraine merely as a tool used in that broader conflict. We have repeatedly heard from children who have returned … that teachers told them a future war with NATO was inevitable and that they needed to prepare for it. … Some children also reported that individual teachers openly advocated the use of nuclear weapons against Western countries.”

Rescuing children who were kidnapped from this radicalization is essential but dangerous work. Children and their families are contacted on messaging platforms like Telegram by a team in Ukraine using Russian SIM cards. They communicate mostly through voice notes that are immediately deleted after listening—phone calls and typed messages are too traceable and dangerous. The Russian authorities have a particular interest in those trying to rescue Ukrainian children.

The number of Ukrainian children currently living under occupation—either kidnapped or with parents in the territories—is unknown, although there are rough estimates based on prewar population figures. It is impossible to track how many have been born, escaped, become Russian citizens, or died.

But even for Ukrainian children living at home, the war is a constant trauma. Thousands have had their lives turned upside down after losing one or both parents.

Sofiia Hromakova was 15 years old when her father was killed while serving in the territorial defense of Ukraine. She learned of his death after moving from the now-occupied Mariupol to Poland via Zaporizhzhia. Her family ended up living in England, where Hromakova could return to her education.

“When I started at an English school, people would ask questions like, ‘You are here with your mother, where is your father?’ I would cry,” she said. “Most teenagers are thinking about their exams, not ‘oh, god, where is my father’s body?’”

Hromakova said that Children of Heroes, a Ukrainian charity, helped her rebuild her life after suffering such enormous trauma. “They helped us right at the start when we only had a couple of bags and needed clothes,” she said. “They helped me get back to school and pass my exams. They helped me paint and get back to doing hobbies. I felt like I was in a cage and they helped me get out.” She is now back in Ukraine and studying for a university degree.

How Kyiv and Europe can defeat Russia on their own.

Children of Heroes is currently registering around 15 children a day, said Yuliya Sotska, the charity’s head of communications. “Some of them want to tell their story and some don’t, but we collect stories from every family that joins the fund, with their consent, so that those stories exist and the world doesn’t get to forget them. One girl who lost her entire family, everyone except her dog, told me her story the way you’d read aloud from a book, completely flat, and that distance is sometimes what trauma sounds like in a child’s voice.”

Russia’s first modern invasion of Ukraine came in 2014, which means the foundation is already working with a second generation. “We have children whose parents joined the armed forces after losing their own parents in 2014, so the people who enlisted were once the children we exist for, and now, unfortunately, their children are,” Sotska said.

The Ridni Foundation, a charity that helps orphans find new homes, noted that as of March 2025, almost 26,000 children were living full-time in institutions across the country. “What tends to surprise people most is that only 18 percent of them, 4,568 children, are actually orphans or legally without parental care,” Mariana Romaniak, Ridni’s CEO, said. “Roughly four in five children in institutional care have at least one parent alive—they’re there because their family didn’t get the support it needed in time, not because they have no family at all.”

Ridni works with government bodies to reform the system and fix the problems behind this. “Together with the Lviv Regional Military Administration, we initiated the transformation of a former residential institution into the Lviv Regional Centre for Social Support of Children and Families,” Romaniak said. “Instead of long-term institutional care, children now receive temporary protection there while specialists work with their families to overcome the crisis and, whenever it’s safe, reunite them.”

Romaniak explained that some children withdraw and have behavioral problems. Others attach to particular adults and struggle when separated. And, in some cases, children who have lost everything they knew struggle to accept help. “It can look like defiance, but underneath there may simply be a question: ‘Can I trust you, and will you still be here tomorrow?’” she said.

Even if the conflict ends, Ukraine’s war generation will continue to cause problems for the country, Sotska said. “Even if the war ended tomorrow, an entire generation of Ukrainian children will carry it. … As a fund, we can’t erase the loss of a parent,” she said. “What we can do is show them there is a future and support that child until they can see that future for themselves.”

Luke McGee is an Emmy Award-winning journalist covering European diplomacy. He was previously CNN’s European policy editor. X: @lukemcgee

https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20.title: Russia bars only anti-war party from elections
https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20.author: https://www.facebook.com/FRANCE24.English
https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20.text:
The court thereby upheld a suit brought by a pro-Kremlin nationalist party, stripping voters opposed to the four-and-a-half-year war in Ukraine of their last option on the ballot.

"The claims seeking to annul the registration of the federal list of candidates for the State Duma of the ninth convocation, nominated by the Yabloko political party, were granted," judge Vyacheslav Kirillov said.

About a hundred supporters, mostly young people, gathered outside the courthouse, chanting "Shame! Shame!" after the ruling was delivered.

Addressing them after the hearing, Yabloko leader Nikolay Rybakov said the party would appeal the decision.

"We have a long way ahead and we have a big and important task: to stop deaths and bring the peace back," he said.

"Everything we do should be dedicated to that," Rybakov added.

With most of President Vladimir Putin's opponents jailed, exiled or dead, Yabloko is the only liberal party still operating in Russia.

The party has received the backing of several exiled opposition figures, including Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny. Both are listed as "extremists" in Russia.

A poll conducted earlier this year showed Yabloko ("apple" in Russian) at just three percent support -- short of the five-percent threshold needed to enter Russia's lower house.

With the Kremlin tightening its control over elections, Yabloko has failed to win seats in the State Duma since 2003.

Since then, every parliamentary vote has been won by the ruling United Russia party, which backs Putin.

Efforts to end the Ukraine war through diplomacy have so far failed, with Putin pushing hardline territorial demands to end the fighting and ruling out talks with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Independent polls show most Russians favour peace negotiations with Kyiv.

https://www.scmp.com/news/article/336357.title: Nvidia to team with Wall Street on US$500 billion package for AI infrastructure projects
https://www.scmp.com/news/article/336357.author: Bloomberg
https://www.scmp.com/news/article/336357.text:
Apollo Global Management, Blackstone and Goldman Sachs are among the firms in talks with Nvidia on the deal, the Financial Times reported

A group of US investment giants are partnering with Nvidia on US$500 billion in funding for AI infrastructure projects, the Financial Times reported.

Apollo Global Management, Blackstone, BlackRock’s Global Infrastructure Partners, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs and KKR are among the firms in talks with Nvidia on a deal to invest in the AI buildout, the Financial Times reported, citing unidentified sources. The deal may be announced as soon as Monday, the Times said.

The named firms did not respond to requests from the Times for comment. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The company’s shares fell by as much as 3.2 per cent.

Nvidia has already signed hundreds of billions of dollars worth of deals with companies across the AI ecosystem, stoking concerns from some investors that the chips giant is inflating demand and valuations across the industry through the circular nature of such agreements.

The company just last month expanded a partnership with South Korean conglomerate SK Group and said the companies will be doing more than US$500 billion in business with each other. It was also in talks to backstop as much as US$250 billion to help OpenAI lease computing power from a US data centre project in what would be among the chipmaker’s biggest financing deals with a customer.

The Financial Times report did not detail which projects or companies the funding would back, the nature of the funding or whether the US$500 billion represented new commitments or already existing ones.

Nvidia said last month it had made a “substantial” investment in Safe Superintelligence, the AI start-up co-founded by former OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever. And it was in discussions to finance US$350 billion of OpenAI’s purchases of its chips for the US project.

Nvidia said in June it would raise US$25 billion through a US bond issuance, as it ‌taps the debt ‌market to increase liquidity for the first time since 2021.

Additional reporting by Reuters

The deal may be announced as soon as Monday, the Financial Times reported. Nvidia has already signed hundreds of billions of dollars worth of deals with companies across the AI ecosystem.

https://www.dw.com/en/colombia-dozens-ki.title: Colombia: Dozens killed after large earthquake rocks region
https://www.dw.com/en/colombia-dozens-ki.text:
A powerful earthquake, measured at magnitude 7.4, has struck Colombia, killing at least 73 people. Cities including Cali, Pereira and Manizales were among the hardest-hit.

A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning.

Around five hours after the quake struck, officials around the country had reported at least 73 deaths, 67 of them just in two of the worst-hit states. Rescue teams were working to free residents after buildings collapsed in Cali and other cities.

The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast.

The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed, in some cases with people trapped inside.

"Residents of Cali, we currently have at least 20 collapsed structures in the city with people trapped inside; we are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," Eder said on Instagram, posting an accompanying video statement. "I have requested support — specifically rescue personnel — from the mayors of Bogota and Medellin."

Authorities in the Valle del Cauca, whose capital city is Cali, later said that at least 27 people had died in the quake.

Officials in Risaralda said that 40 people had died across the state, at least 18 of them in the capital Pereira based on earlier comments from the mayor.

And the mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas, said in a radio interview that two people were killed in his city, in the Caldas region not far northeast of Pereira.

The governor of the Choco region where the quake's epicenter was located, Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi, said there were four dead and 69 wounded in her district as of late morning local time.

Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined.

"Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online, later adding Cali's airport to this list.

Colombia's newly-inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said that he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency in San Jose del Palmar following the earthquake that struck the country.

"You are not alone. The state is present and taking action," he said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "closely monitoring" the situtation and stood "ready to support the people of Colombia."

The US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake at magnitude 7.4. Colombia's national authority at first logged a smaller figure but later revised its reading up to 7.4 as well.

The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border.

The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south.

The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter.

The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors.

Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela.

USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake.

The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake.

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.
https://www.dw.com/en/colombia-dozens-ki.summary: At least 73 people have died in Colombia, officials say. The quake struck at magnitude 7.4, the USGS says. The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast. The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce3q.title: Trump signs order to limit childhood vaccines and split MMR shots
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce3q.text:
President Donald Trump has signed an order that calls for fewer childhood vaccines and also recommends splitting the mumps, measles and rubella (MMR) shots.

"Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today," Trump said on Monday. "In those times, people were much healthier and of course the high rates of autism now observed did not exist."

The Trump administration has long pushed a discredited link between MMR vaccines and autism, but multiple studies have found no link between the two.

The federal government does not have the authority to implement the new recommendations. Shots that are required for school attendance are set at the state level.

Speaking in the Oval Office, Trump said that his administration "is recognising gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for only 11 core vaccinations against the most serious and dangerous diseases".

The immunisations recommended for all children under the order are for measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus, and varicella or chicken pox.

"We're reducing them," Trump said. "It's not only that you're doing fewer vaccines, or jabs, as they say, but you're doing them in a series of visits to the doctor."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce3q.summary: Trump administration has long pushed a discredited link between MMR vaccines and autism. Multiple studies have found no link between the two. The federal government does not have the authority to implement the new recommendations.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2l.title: New train service connects Finland and Sweden for first time in decades
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2l.text:
A new passenger train linking Finland and Sweden has begun running, creating the first rail connection between northern Finland and southern Europe in nearly 40 years.

Shortly after 05:00 local time (04:00 BST) on Monday, a double-decker train set off from the coastal Finnish city of Oulu, rumbling its way across the border to Sweden.

As the inaugural service crossed the Torne river from Finland and pulled into Sweden's Haparanda station, it was met by crowds of people waving Finnish and Swedish flags.

The route was initially suspended in the late 1980s to the early 1990s, due to low passenger numbers and technical differences in the tracks between Finland and Europe.

Finland uses the same track widths as Russia, which are wider than the European standard - a holdover from when the Nordic nation was part of the Russian Grand Duchy in the 19th and early 20th centuries.

It is currently in the process of updating its track widths to match the European standard.

The new, twice-daily journey to Sweden's Haparanda takes 100-minutes as it hugs the west coast of Finland before crossing the border between the two Nordic neighbours.

Passengers travelling on from Haparanda will need to transfer onto a different train to continue southward.

But the service makes it possible to travel around 5,000km by rail from Portugal's Algarve to Finland's northernmost train station of Kolari - believed to be the longest train route in Europe.

It will also enable a 24-hour train journey between capitals Helsinki and Stockholm.

Finland's transport minister said the return of the cross-border service shows cooperation between the two countries was growing "all the time".

Elisa Markula, chief executive of Finland's state-owned railway operator VR, said she hopes the service will benefit from a "renaissance" in rail travel across Europe.

"Train travelling in all Europe is having a renaissance. Also in Finland, our passenger numbers are increasing a lot," Markula told AFP.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2l.summary: New, twice-daily journey to Sweden's Haparanda takes 100-minutes. The route was initially suspended in the late 1980s to the early 1990s. It will also enable a 24-hour train journey between capitals Helsinki and Stockholm.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy9w.title: Russian court bars only anti-war party from standing in parliamentary elections
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy9w.text:
Russia's only liberal, anti-war party will not be able to take part in next month's parliamentary elections, a Moscow court has ruled.

Yabloko was the only registered party to oppose Russia's war on Ukraine.

The case against it was brought forward by Rodina, a pro-Kremlin nationalist party.

Hundreds of people - mostly very young - on Monday had stood outside the Moscow courthouse where the hearing was taking place in support of Yabloko, singing songs and waving flags.

Videos posted on social media showed that when news of the verdict spread among the crowd, many started chanting: "Shame! Shame!"

The lawsuit by the Rodina party accused Yabloko of publicly supporting an extremist organisation by publishing material on its website in support of the "international LGBT movement", which Russia's Supreme Court designated as extremist in 2023.

Rodina also said Yabloko was guilty of copyright infringement after a senior party member had quoted the lyrics of a Soviet-era song - "Let there always be sunshine" - in an interview.

At the hearing, Russia's financial monitoring service also claimed that Yabloko received money through third parties from foreign countries, including Germany and the US.

The Kremlin-controlled Central Electoral Commission had approved Yabloko's candidate list in late July.

But by then several party members had already been barred from running, including two deputy chairmen and deputy leader Maxim Kruglov, who was sentenced in June to seven years' imprisonment for social media posts about civilian casualties in Bucha, Mariupol and other Ukrainian cities.

And last week, Yabloko had suffered a cyberattack soon after launching a donations appeal for its election campaign fund.

It campaigned under the slogan "For peace and freedom! For a life without fear!" and advocated for a "ceasefire, diplomacy, and peace" and "for a Russia free from fear and political repression".

Hundreds gathered outside the Moscow courthouse, chanting "Russia" and "Yabloko" - the Russian word for "apple" - as the eight-hour hearing dragged on. Many carried apples as a sign of support.

Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, any remaining opposition to the Kremlin has been crushed.

Public shows of dissent have been suppressed by wartime censorship laws and can trigger hefty fines or long prison sentences.

Because protests are no longer permitted, the Yabloko hearing offered a rare chance for likeminded Russians opposing the war to gather publicly. "For Yabloko. For freedom" was scribbled in chalk on the pavement outside the courthouse.

Yabloko has not won Duma seats since 2003 but has contested every election since.

Once led by presidential contender Grigory Yavlinsky, it later fractured with allies - expelling the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny in 2007 and criticising him even after he was eventually imprisoned ahead of his death in 2024.

Still, Yabloko remained Russia's most consistent anti-war voice, opposing Russia's war on Chechnya, the 2014 annexation of Crimea, and the invasion of Ukraine.

With ruling party United Russia's ratings down to 33% amid inflation, internet blackouts and drone strikes, Yabloko's support had been surging.

The Central Electoral Commission could have allowed Yabloko to contest the election and initially appeared to be leaning in that direction, potentially to use the party's marginal result in 2021 - when it won just 1.34% of the vote - to show how that the anti-war stance in Russia does not hold much sway.

But the government has now appeared to have changed its calculations, as signs of growing dissent over the war in Ukraine emerge.

Without a political force that clearly represents the opposition on the ballot, fewer people may be motivated to go to the polls. A low-turnout election, particularly among those who oppose the ruling party, would likely benefit the Kremlin.

All 10 other parties taking part in the election either support the war in Ukraine or do not openly criticise it.

And although United Russia's ratings appear to be in a deep dive, the Kremlin still has the resources to deliver the outcome it wants at the election.

Independent election watchdogs have been deprived of much of their ability to monitor and challenge the process.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy9w.summary: Yabloko was the only registered party to oppose Russia's war on Ukraine. The case against it was brought forward by a pro-Kremlin nationalist party. Hundreds of people - mostly very young - stood outside the Moscow courthouse where the hearing was taking place.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd69.title: Blaze tackled at suspected illegal waste dump
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd69.text:
Firefighters have been tackling a blaze at a suspected illegal waste dump close to the River Mersey in Greater Manchester.

Crews were called to the scene at 11:30 BST on Monday after reports that smoke had been coming from the site in woodland close to the Carrington Spur.

Helen Carr from Flixton, who walks her dogs in woodland nearby, said: "The smell is absolutely acrid and what I really worry about is things like builders' waste setting on fire, then releasing all sorts of chemicals into the air.

"Its criminal. There is just no need for people to be dumping waste like this, in this day and age. This is just sheer greed and laziness."

The 43 year-old added: "The type of rubbish being dumped used to be agricultural waste, but it now involves builders waste alongside household waste, with things like mattresses and fridge freezers.

"The waste has just being growing and growing and getting out of control."

In July, Ms Carr reported the waste to the Environment Agency (EA), which responded by saying they were aware of the site and has referred the case to the Area Enforcement Team.

In an email to Ms Carr, the EA said: "We take illegal waste offences seriously and will use the powers available to us to investigate and, where appropriate, take enforcement action against those responsible."

The burned waste at the site included several old mattresses, a fridge freezer, builders waste, car tyres, a cement mixer and wood panelling.

Parts of the site that were still smouldering reignited.

Firefighters were able to prevent the fire spreading.

Earlier this year, the BBC reported that hundreds of illegal dumps were operating across England, including at least 11 so-called "super sites" containing tens of thousands of tonnes of rubbish.

Most sites are in countryside locations, often hidden, and on what should be agricultural land.

Police say many are run by organised crime gangs, who are making cash by charging much less than legitimate operators to take and bury waste.

Earlier this year, a prolific waste criminal was ordered to pay £1.2m in compensation for illegally dumping more than 4,000 tonnes of waste across England.

Laura Clinton, who walks her dogs close to the River Mersey in Ashton Woods, said: "On several occasions, I've seen lorries coming here and dumping waste.

"Its appalling and something needs to be done about it."

A spokesperson for Trafford Council said: "We are aware of the fire on private land and we are supporting GMFRS in response to this.

"Fire is just one of the risks associated with unauthorised tipping and the council will work actively with partners to protect the environment and keep communities safe."

A spokesperson for the EA said: "We share the public's disgust at this case of illegal waste dumping and will do everything in our power to bring the people responsible to justice.

"A criminal investigation is underway, and we are working with the local council and other organisations on this."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd69.summary: Firefighters called to the scene at 11:30 BST on Monday after reports of smoke coming from the site. The site is close to the River Mersey in Greater Manchester. The Environment Agency has referred the case to the Area Enforcement Team.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c78g.title: Blaze at Full Monty club thought to be arson
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c78g.text:
A fire at a working men's club in Sheffield which famously appeared in the 1997 film The Full Monty is believed to have been started deliberately.

The blaze broke out at Shiregreen Working Men's Club on Shiregreen Lane just before 16:45 BST on Sunday, according to South Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service.

A spokesperson said eight fire engines and a turntable ladder were sent to the scene, with no reports of any injuries. Crews left just after midnight and were due to return later to ensure there were no hotspots remaining.

The building has been closed since 2019 and has become derelict in recent years, with a fire also started there deliberately last year.

A fire service spokesperson said the latest blaze was also believed to have been started deliberately.

In 2020, Sheffield City Council refused an application to bulldoze the building after more than 1,000 people signed a petition to save it.

Ann Bentley, who was behind the petition having worked at the club for 15 years, said she was "absolutely devastated" to learn there had been another fire there.

"It meant so much to me," she said of her time working at the club, where she met her husband Roy.

"Every time I pass it I want to cry. I would have loved to have seen it back on its feet."

Oscar-winning comedy The Full Monty depicted the lives of Sheffield steelworkers who were made redundant and turned to stripping at a club to earn a living.

The movie, starring Robert Carlyle and Mark Addy, ended up as one of the best-loved and highest-grossing British films of the 1990s.

The film's famous final scene was filmed inside Shiregreen Working Men's Club.

The most powerful temblor in a decade struck in a Pacific Coast region, killing over 100 people.

Looking for survivors on Monday in Cali, Colombia.
Credit...
Joaquin Sarmiento/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

By The New York Times

Shortly after 7:30 on Monday morning, the most powerful earthquake to hit Colombia in a decade sent people fleeing for safety as buildings teetered and then fell.

The epicenter was in a less populous rural area off the Pacific Coast, potentially blunting its effect, but even so, by midafternoon, Colombian officials were reporting that at least 111 people had been confirmed dead.

More than 1,500 residential buildings were damaged, they said, some of them irreparably. At least 20 buildings collapsed in the city of Cali, trapping people inside, according to its mayor.

Eighteen health centers and dozens of schools were also damaged, and air service to more than half a dozen cities was suspended.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/po.title: How a Counterintelligence Inquiry Into Trump’s Russia Ties Was Derailed
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/po.author: Michael S. Schmidt
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/po.text:
This story is free to read.

Documents released by the White House shed new light on the demise of an often-overlooked 2017 F.B.I. investigation.

By Michael S. Schmidt

For the last year, the Trump administration’s efforts to seek retribution against intelligence officials and F.B.I. agents who investigated Russia’s 2016 election meddling have been spearheaded by federal prosecutors in South Florida trying to build a criminal case.

But in recent weeks, the White House has added a dimension to its push to rewrite the history of the Russia investigation, releasing a trove of previously classified F.B.I. memos that it says back up President Trump’s claims that a so-called deep state was out to get him.

There is little new of substance in the documents, and nothing that fundamentally undercuts the F.B.I.’s rationale for pursuing the Russia investigation.

But the material does shed new light on an often overlooked aspect of the swirl of events surrounding Mr. Trump in his first months in office in 2017: the bureau’s remarkable decision to open a separate counterintelligence investigation into the president of the United States, and how that inquiry was sidetracked before it had much of a chance to get going.

Mr. Trump has always dismissed as baseless smears suggestions that he was a Russian asset or had extensive financial ties to Russia. And no publicly known investigation into Mr. Trump ever demonstrated that he was acting at the behest of the Russians.

Here is a look at what we know now, based on the new documents and interviews with former federal law enforcement officials, about what happened.

Michael S. Schmidt is an investigative reporter for The Times covering Washington. His work focuses on tracking and explaining high-profile federal investigations.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/po.summary: Documents released by the White House shed new light on the demise of an often-overlooked 2017 F.B.I. investigation. The White House has added a dimension to its push to rewrite the history of the Russia investigation.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/po.title: D.C.-Area Airport to Close for 3 Hours for Grand Prix Event
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/po.author: Karoun Demirjian
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/po.text:
The Federal Aviation Administration has imposed other closures at Reagan National Airport over events for the 250th anniversary of the nation’s founding.

The Federal Aviation Administration announced on Monday that it will close Ronald Reagan National Airport in Washington to flight traffic for three hours later this month, to accommodate the Trump administration’s planned IndyCar grand prix on the National Mall.

The expected ground stop will take place from 10:15 a.m. to 1:15 p.m. on Aug. 23, covering the period leading up to the race’s expected start time.

“The F.A.A. has been planning and coordinating with stakeholders to help ensure the safe and efficient movement of air traffic during Freedom 250 event,” the agency said in a statement. When asked what pre-race festivities were expected to pose a potential risk to passing flights, a spokeswoman from the agency did not elaborate.

The F.A.A. has had to impose a number of closures at Reagan National Airport this summer coinciding with events marking the 250th anniversary of the nation’s founding because of flyovers, parachutists, fireworks and other pyrotechnics that have posed risks either for the physical sanctity of nearby aircraft or to pilots’ ability to navigate safely through the area. Flyovers are a common feature of many IndyCar series races.

In July, the runways at National Airport were closed for 12 hours for Independence Day festivities and fireworks, and for several hours the day before for rehearsals. When the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority announced those plans in June, it noted that the car race would also bring about temporary runway closures.

The F.A.A.’s announcement on Monday noted that the exact timing of the Aug. 23 ground stop could change.

“Travelers should check with their airline for the latest flight status,” it read.

The grand prix event is expected to play out in Washington over two days, culminating with Sunday’s race. The 1.7-mile course, which race cars are expected to circle 147 times, stretches from the shadow of the Capitol to within a few blocks of the White House.

Karoun Demirjian is a breaking news reporter for The Times.

The expected ground stop will take place from 10:15 a.m. to 1:15 p.m., covering the period leading up to the race’s expected start time.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/ja.title: Jackie, Bald Eagle in California Who Became Livestream Star, Is Dead
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/ja.author: Alexandra E. Petri
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/ja.text:
Jackie had been receiving medical treatment since she was attacked by other eagles last month and found unable to fly near Big Bear Lake.

By Alexandra E. Petri

Jackie, the famous bald eagle whose nest in the San Bernardino Mountains in California has been featured on a livestream watched by millions, died on Monday after weeks of intensive care.

The news of Jackie’s death was shared in a Facebook post on Monday by the Ojai Raptor Center, a wildlife rehabilitation center in Ojai, Calif., where the bird had been undergoing treatment since she was injured by other eagles last month.

“We know this news will be deeply felt by the many thousands of people around the world who have followed her journey, hoped alongside us, prayed for her, and supported the people caring for her,” the center said in a Facebook post. “Our team is heartbroken. It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her.”

Jackie’s remains have been transferred into the care of the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, the center said.

The eagle arrived at the raptor center needing critical care in July after she was attacked by other eagles and found unable to fly near Big Bear Lake. Workers at the center then discovered more underlying health issues, including kidney inflammation and severe anemia.

Through a series of Facebook posts over several weeks, the center updated the public on Jackie’s condition, sharing information, pictures and videos of the famous eagle.

While her kidneys improved, Jackie (known as Bald Eagle patient 26-519) remained in critical condition because of her anemia. Chris Eksteen, the executive director of the center, said in an update on July 31 that Jackie had most likely been sick for some time before she was rescued.

Jackie underwent repeated testing during her time at the center, including physical examinations, blood work, advanced imaging, toxicology screening and a blood transfusion. Her care team ruled out some possible causes for the anemia, but her condition remained puzzling to experts.

The bird was also suffering from a possible infection, or inflammation, according to the July 31 update that noted she had an elevated white blood cell count.

Jackie, who hatched in the spring of 2012, has shared a nest with her mate Shadow since he showed up in the summer of 2018 and refused to leave, pushing out her then-partner, named Mr. B. In the wild, bald eagles can live 25 years or longer.

The introduction of a livestream more than a decade ago helped Jackie and her family become online sensations, capturing the nest she shares with Shadow atop a 120-foot-tall Jeffrey pine tree in Big Bear Valley, a lakeside recreation area in Southern California.

Together, Jackie and Shadow have fledged six eaglets, most recently Sandy and Luna. According to Facebook posts from Friends of Big Bear Valley, the nonprofit organization that operates the camera, Sandy and Luna have not been seen on the camera in the area since July 23, a sign they may have fled the nest.

Shadow has still been spotted around the habitat, the Friends of Big Bear Valley said.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/ja.summary: Jackie had been receiving medical treatment since she was attacked by other eagles last month and found unable to fly near Big Bear Lake. The eagle arrived at the Ojai Raptor Center in Ojia, California, needing critical care in July. She had been suffering from kidney inflammation and severe anemia.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/clima.title: Top Science Body Deletes Climate Chapter From Judges’ Manual
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/clima.author: Karen Zraick
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/clima.text:
The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine had been under pressure from Republican leaders, including President Trump.

The nation’s top scientific body has removed a chapter on climate science from a reference manual for judges after an outcry from critics on the right, including President Trump.

The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine said Friday that it had “determined that questions about the processes used to develop the chapter warrant an independent review, and the chapter will not appear on our website while that review is underway.”

The chapter appeared in the fourth edition of the Reference Manual on Scientific Evidence, which was produced in partnership with the Federal Judicial Center and was released last year. The 1,700-page manual covers many different topics and is intended to help judges understand science and technology that might come up in cases. Other subjects covered in the manual include eyewitness identification, toxicology and neuroscience.

Climate change is figuring into a growing number of legal cases, including lawsuits against oil companies over their role in global warming, as well as other cases involving government regulations, natural disasters, insurance claims, land use and the energy industry. The now-deleted chapter was the manual’s first foray into climate science.

The Federal Judicial Center, which is a government agency, removed the chapter from its website in February after criticism from Republican attorneys general and other officials. The National Academies, which operates as a private scientific advisory body under a congressional charter, declined to do so at the time.

In a separate development last month, the National Academies issued a report on a type of research known as attribution science, a growing field that examines whether specific extreme-weather events, such as a particular storm or flood, were intensified or made more likely by climate change. The report concluded that research of this type was getting more sophisticated and yielding better data.

https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-592.title: After his Reflecting Pool vandalism case is dismissed, David Hearn looks for closure
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-592.author: Rachel Treisman
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-592.text:
David Hearn (second from left) and his attorney Norman Eisen (right) addressed reporters after he entered his not guilty plea on July 9 in Washington, D.C.

A judge agreed to drop the federal government's vandalism case against former U.S. Olympian David "Davey" Hearn and three others last week, after months of accusing them of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

But Hearn's legal fight isn't over yet: Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman has yet to weigh in on whether it could potentially be reopened later.

"We feel strongly this case should be dismissed for once and for all," Hearn's lawyer, Norm Eisen, told NPR's All Things Considered on Monday. "Davey is an innocent man. He shouldn't have to go through this a second time."

Prosecutors have sought the dismissal of the case "without prejudice," allowing them to potentially refile in the future. Hearn's lawyers are asking the judge to dismiss his felony charge "with prejudice," to close the case for good.

"From day one, the case against Mr. Hearn was motivated by political considerations and devoid of adequate factual support," his lawyers wrote in a 28-page motion filed last week. "Those political pressures have not dissipated in the mere four weeks since the government saw fit to obtain the indictment."

In the days since federal prosecutors moved to have Hearn's case dismissed, President Trump has railed against Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, accusing her of "folding like an umbrella."

And he has repeated his claims that vandals damaged the lining of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, contradicting evidence from Pirro's 20-page legal filing that blamed the peeling lining on "botched installation."

"A National Park Service career employee, a highly credible witness, saw David Hearn (ActBlue) in broad daylight vandalize the Reflecting Pool by 'violently' ripping and tugging at the Pool's somewhat delicate coating," Trump posted Sunday on Truth Social, wading back into the pool discourse even as he acknowledged "there was also some contractor error."

Speaking to NPR on Monday, Hearn described his ordeal as "Kafkaesque" and "Orwellian."

The experience has taken a toll on the 67-year-old, in terms of added stress and lost sleep. But it's also changed the way he sees the country that he represented in three Olympic Games, as a canoe slalom athlete in 1992, 1996 and 2000.

"My confidence is being tested for sure here, in what our nation can withstand," Hearn said. "But I don't think people are taking this lying down."

Hearn said he's buoyed by the support he's gotten from his lawyers, family and community, which includes "paddling buddies," "biking buddies" and "music and dance friends." His case has become a cause célèbre for people far beyond D.C., as the embattled reflecting pool has become a symbolic referendum on the Trump administration.

"I think that that has really gripped the imagination and the sympathy of the nation," Eisen said. "If it can happen to Davey, it could happen to you or me or anyone."

Supporters have rallied around Hearn in D.C. and beyond, as the reflecting pool saga became a national story.

For Hearn, the fight isn't just about his future, but that of U.S. democracy.

"I feel like I've been practicing democracy my whole life," he said. "And being down at the reflecting pool on Juneteenth was part of that for me."

The lifelong Maryland resident was on a group bike ride through the National Mall on June 19 when he stopped to look at the recently repainted Reflecting Pool.

He said he had heard reports about algae turning the water green and pieces of the new "American flag blue" lining peeling off. The pool recently had been refilled; Pirro's July filing cites Department of the Interior records indicating that personnel first flagged issues with the lining as early as June 11.

Hearn said he was interested in the controversial renovation project in part because of his longtime waterproofing business.

"There's a real sort of an engineering, scientific curiosity for me about what was going on," he explained.

An example of peeling paint as seen on June 22.

Hearn maintains that he dipped a hand into the pool and plucked out one of the floating paint pieces. He was promptly arrested and charged with destroying government property.

Hearn has consistently denied the allegations, which he said sting especially because of his deep-seated respect for national parks. He has been a National Park Service volunteer for the Chesapeake & Ohio Canal National Historical Park, which runs from D.C. to Maryland, for 20 years. His own father was a field geologist in Northern California and Montana.

"You're supposed to leave nothing but footprints. That's all ingrained into my psyche from a very young age," Hearn said. "So to be accused of damaging a national monument like this is completely outrageous for me."

A grand jury indicted Hearn on a single felony count of destruction of property worth $1,000 or more on July 2. He pleaded not guilty a week later, exiting the D.C. courthouse to a sea of sign-wielding supporters chanting "Davey! Davey!"

Hearn was facing a late September trial date, and the possibility of up to 10 years in prison if convicted, before prosecutors moved to have his case dismissed on July 31.

The reflecting pool, seen on Monday, is being partially refilled to flush water supply pipes, according to the National Park Service.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia cited Department of the Interior records that showed damage to the reflecting pool was "the result of botched installation and not vandalism."

"It is difficult to attribute the widespread damage to the Reflecting Pool to vandalism, let alone to establish that fact beyond a reasonable doubt," Pirro wrote.

But just weeks earlier, Pirro — a Trump appointee — had announced at a press conference that "the evidence shows … that Hearn willfully destroyed property at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool."

In an about-face, her filing blamed the Department of the Interior for withholding evidence that proved otherwise.

But Eisen said Hearn's legal time has filed "motion after motion proving that the reflecting pool was the same before and after [he] touched it." He said they entered photographic proof as soon as the day after his first court appearance.

"The Department of Justice finally came to their senses and dismissed the case," Eisen said. "But the justification that they gave — that they didn't figure it out until the Department of the Interior told them — that does not hold water."

Hearn's lawyers want his case dismissed without prejudice, citing the "risk of harassment and bad faith."

If not, they are asking the judge to review and potentially disclose materials from the grand jury proceedings against Hearn.

"The grand-jury record bears further on the question now before the Court: whether the government obtained Mr. Hearn's felony indictment in a manner warranting dismissal with prejudice, that is, through a rushed and misleading presentation that disregarded the absence of evidence supporting any case against Mr. Hearn," they wrote.

Eisen said they are reviewing "all legal remedies." Hearn has a status hearing scheduled for September on the dismissal question, and is feeling optimistic.

"With the power of the law, the power of the courts, the judges and my wonderful team … I feel very well-equipped to contest this, to bring democracy back to me," he said.
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-592.summary: David Hearn has been charged with vandalism in the federal government's case. He has denied the allegations, saying he was not involved in the project. The judge has yet to decide whether the case could be reopened later.

https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-592.title: Trump and RFK Jr. try again to upend vaccines for kids
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-592.author: Rob Stein
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-592.text:
President Trump speaks before signing an executive order that calls for changing the childhood vaccine schedule.

This is a developing story that will be updated.

President Trump signed another executive order aimed at trying to upend the way U.S. children are vaccinated against dangerous infectious diseases.

The new executive order, signed Monday afternoon in the Oval Office, calls for reducing the number of childhood vaccines recommended by the federal government.

It also calls for breaking up the shot known as the MMR, which is now given as a single vaccination for measles, mumps, rubella and chickenpox. The order advises breaking it up into separate shots.

The order also directs the Justice Department to pressure states to reduce the number of vaccines required for school.

The moves will likely be challenged in court, as previous similar attempts to change the childhood vaccination schedule have been.

At the signing ceremony, the president talked about vaccines needing to be studied in light of rising autism rates, a thoroughly studied and debunked theory.

The news was welcomed by vaccine critics and denounced by many public health experts.

https://www.npr.org/2026/08/06/nx-s1-592.title: An AI chatbot is joining the search for art looted by the Nazis
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/06/nx-s1-592.author: Chloe Veltman
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/06/nx-s1-592.text:
U.S. troops found a collection of treasures stolen by the Nazis hidden in a castle near the Austrian border in May 1945.

More than 600,000 artworks and other cultural objects, mostly owned by Jews, were stolen by the Nazis leading up to and during World War II.

Efforts to shine a light on and restore the more than 100,000 as-yet-unclaimed artifacts from this hoard have been on the uptick. In April, President Trump signed the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act into law, which put an end to legal loopholes that advocates of the law said made it tough for people with valid claims to get their looted artworks back. And in May, the Musée D'Orsay in Paris opened a permanent gallery dedicated to paintings and sculptures by the likes of Degas, Rodin and Renoir that are thought to have been looted.

But reclaiming these artifacts is often a long and fraught process.

"There's no central repository, no database that's telling you where that art is," said

Joel Greenberg, founder of Art Ashes, a nonprofit that helps families track down and recover art looted by the Nazis. On top of locating the missing art, the rightful owners need to prove it was stolen from them in the first place. "And then to recreate the historical record of what actually happened to the family and the family's art is also very difficult, because those records, if they exist, are spread among different repositories around the world," Greenberg said.

There are dozens of archives containing information about these missing artworks. Their holdings consist of records in a variety of languages and formats.

"If you could create a system that could scan all the databases that have the Nazi looted art records, that would be very, very useful," Greenberg said.

A team at Santa Clara University in Silicon Valley is aspiring to do just that, with a new AI chatbot that could help streamline the complicated process of getting these works back to their owners. It's part of a broader shift toward digital tools in the field of art provenance and repatriation.

Developed by professors Michael Santoro, Haibing Lu and Michele Samorani, the AI Provenance Assistant is testing how artificial intelligence could eventually make it easier for people to search archives of stolen art.

"We are applying AI tools to make it easier to make the kinds of connections that seasoned researchers would have to spend a long time having to do manually," said Santoro.

Right now, the tool is only scraping records from one database — that of the Jeu de Paume museum in Paris. The Nazis warehoused tens of thousands of looted artworks at the museum during World War II and kept elaborate records — records that are now available for anyone to search online in a database alongside archives from several other institutions around the world, including the German Bundesarchiv, the French Archives of the Ministry of Europe and Foreign Affairs, and the U.S. National Archives.

But Santoro said his team's AI tool is more intuitive than the Jeu de Paume's database because it doesn't require users to deal with drop-down menus and input keywords into boxes.

"It enables ordinary language queries to be made of art databases," he said.

By "ordinary language," Santoro means users can type a question using everyday words into the chatbot's interface. For example, entering the sentence, "What artworks belong to Hugo Simon?" brings up a list of more than 70 belonging to the late Jewish banker and art collector, including stolen works by Picasso and Canaletto.

Santoro admits the tool is currently limited in scope. But some experts in the field of tracking down and restoring artifacts seized by the Nazis are curious about how AI will shape their work in the future.

"This project shows promise," said Carla Shapreau, who teaches cultural property law at the University of California, Berkeley. She said tools like the AI Provenance Assistant will be more useful when they encompass many databases, not just one.

Shapreau also said these chatbots should link to digitized copies of the original archival records such as confiscation and claim files, since the summaries available in online resources like the Jeu de Paume's are susceptible to errors."It's all speculative if you can't look at the evidence," Shapreau said. "And the evidence is in the primary sources."

But others are less optimistic about AI's potential to streamline this complicated field of research and recovery.

"People find looted art without resorting to AI," said Marc Masurovsky, co-founder of the Holocaust Art Restitution Project. He said many archives remain undigitized and subject to data privacy laws. These realities drastically limit the pool of data an AI tool can scrape.

"Even if they are published on the internet, how are you going to interpret all that alphabet soup?" Masurovsky said. "These are really complex cases."

Researchers at Santa Clara University aren't the only ones turning to AI to take on these complex cases.

One example is Legacy Explorer. The Jewish Digital Cultural Recovery Project Foundation's AI-powered platform currently enables users to search documents and photographs of looted cultural property from a handful of databases. (The Jeu de Paume's is among them.)

Meanwhile, the Santa Clara University team said they plan to expand their tool to include more databases and are launching a project to use AI to track down artworks that have not yet been identified as looted.

"This will involve using AI to find patterns in looted art and investigating whether those patterns are replicated in art databases where no looted art has heretofore been identified," Santoro said. "We have only scratched the surface of how AI can assist in provenance research."
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/06/nx-s1-592.summary: The tool is only scraping records from one database in Paris. The tool could help find and restore art looted by the Nazi Nazis. The project is being developed by Santa Clara University in Silicon Valley.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Trump demands Iran pay compensation for decades of US soldier deaths
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Andrew Roth in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
US president’s statement is latest sign that negotations to end war and reopen strait of Hormuz have stalled

Donald Trump has said he will demand that Iran pay compensation for the deaths of thousands of US soldiers and Iran’s own civilians killed in recent decades in the latest sign his negotiations to end the war and reopen the strait of Hormuz have reached an impasse.

The US president is trying to end conflicts in Iran, Gaza and Lebanon, and his additional demands of Iran are likely to provoke anger in Tehran at the same time as Israel has rejected Trump’s terms for a 15-point roadmap to end the war in Gaza.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he was issuing the demand for war reparations in response to Iranian negotiators making similar claims for damages for the five-month war that has killed thousands and devastated Iran’s military and economy.

“Now I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts, for which they are famous, as led initially by Gen Soleimani, including the families of those killed on the USS Cole, and thousands of others killed in combat,” he wrote on Truth Social.

“Additionally, compensation should be paid to the families of the hundreds of thousands of innocent protesters that Iran has killed over the last 50 years, not to mention the 52,000 that have been killed in the last five months.”

The demands are likely to be a nonstarter for Iran’s leaders in the careful peace negotiations aimed at reopening the strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of global oil trade flowed before the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in late February. Trump and other senior negotiators have claimed many times that a deal is imminent, although none has materialised.

The remarks followed a series of setbacks for Trump’s efforts to end several Middle East conflicts before the midterm elections in November, in which high oil prices and inflation will probably hurt fellow Republicans at the polls.

On Sunday, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said he rejected the Trump-backed Board of Peace’s 15-point plan to end Israel’s war in Gaza. Netanyahu had said Hamas must fully disarm before Israel would consider pulling out of Gaza, rather than the phased withdrawal proposed by the Board of Peace.

Netanyahu framed the decision as a rejection of US pressure on Israel to make peace in several wars in the Middle East. “Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu said.

Trump has not replied to Netanyahu’s statement, which was a remarkably public break between the leaders of the US and its closest ally in the Middle East. But in response to a shouted question in the Oval Office on Monday, he said his relationship with Netanyahu was “very good”.

Trump has sought to increase pressure on Iran. An hour after his first post demanding war reparations from Tehran, he broadened their scope to include the victims of recent wars throughout the region.

“Also, with respect to the Iran negotiations, Iran should be responsible for the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza!” he wrote.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: ‘National priority’ to equip UK firefighters amid growing wildfire threat
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Caroline Davies, Matthew Pearce and Pippa Neill
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Exclusive: FBU calls for more funding as ‘unprecedented summer’ puts rising demands on already stretched crews

Firefighters in the UK are under increased pressure as a result of an “unprecedented summer of dangerous and volatile wildfires”, the Fire Brigades Union has said, as many parts of the country brace for a fifth heatwave of the year.

As authorities declared almost three-quarters of England was now in drought, Steve Wright, the FBU general secretary, said the unpredictable environmental challenges the UK was now confronted with meant it was a “national priority” to have enough properly equipped firefighters to “face these threats”.

More than 120 firefighters continued to tackle a blaze in the New Forest national park in Hampshire that began on Sunday. Nottinghamshire fire and rescue service declared a major incident on Sunday as two large fires in woodland near Mansfield put a significant strain on resources there.

Emergency calls to the London fire brigade have increased by almost a third this summer as firefighters have battled a surge in wildfires and flooding in the capital, according to an internal briefing seen by the Guardian.

The document warned that the brigade had come under mounting pressure from extreme weather and predicted the trend would continue because of the climate crisis. Between 1 April and 9 July, the service received 75,652 emergency calls – 31% more than the previous five-year average – while the number of incidents rose by nearly a quarter to 42,943.

London firefighters responded to 392 wildfires during the period, alongside 68 water rescues, the briefing said, as repeated spells of hot weather and heavy thunderstorms stretched the service’s resources.

The climate breakdown has been linked to the increasing frequency of wildfires, burning larger areas, across many parts of the world. The so-called “fire wave” under way in the UK is the most widespread the country has ever seen, with the combination of wet winters and prolonged heatwaves exacerbating the risk.

In recent weeks, there have been large blazes in places including Dunwich Heath in Suffolk, Headon Warren on the Isle of Wight, Llanwonno in the Rhondda valley in south Wales, and the Cairngorms national park in Scotland.

The National Drought Group, which met on Monday, said 71.3% of England was now experiencing a “flash drought”, which develops very quickly brought about by a combination of very low rainfall and higher temperatures. About 45 million people live in a drought area and more than 27 million are now living under water use restrictions.

The group said all regions of the country were experiencing pressure on their water resources, with growing pressure on agriculture, public supplies, navigation and the environment.

Tony Grayling, the chair of the National Drought Group, said: “Drought conditions are worsening and will continue to do so until we see significant and sustained rainfall. We know the hot and dry weather is taking a real toll on farming and there will be long-lasting impacts on our environment.”

He urged everyone to use less water to “make sure our current water reserves last”.

No 10 said the dry conditions were having a “significant impact on communities, farmers and businesses across the country”, adding: “Our climate is changing. Droughts are becoming more common.”

The prime minister’s spokesperson said the government was focused on “both the immediate response and long-term resilience”, including working through the National Drought Group to “protect water supplies and minimise environmental damage”.

The spokesperson did not say what threshold would constitute a national emergency. Ministers were monitoring the situation closely, No 10 said, and the Environment Agency had stepped up monitoring and was working with water companies, farmers and local partners to “manage pressure on water resources”.

Joanne Smith, the LFB’s deputy assistant commissioner for control and mobilising, said the service had responded to thousands of emergency calls and “hundreds of wildfires alongside water rescues and other significant incidents across the capital”.

She said: “We have learned from previous events such as the summer of 2022 and developed our training for firefighters and officers to enhance their knowledge of tactical awareness at wildfires. We’ve invested in new equipment and training to help tackle wildfires, and we will continue to evolve so that we are ready and prepared for future summers.”

after newsletter promotion

The FBU’s Wright called for “increased funding, improved access to the best equipment and better national resilience” to combat rising demands on firefighters. He added: “Our country is facing unpredictable environmental challenges, and it must be a national priority to ensure we have enough properly equipped firefighters ready to face these threats.”

He has previously said fire crews had been stretched by staffing cuts, with 12,000 fewer firefighters in the UK today than in 2010.

In Hampshire, hundreds of people were forced to abandon their vehicles and walk after Sunday’s wildfire caused by a van fire on the A31 near Ringwood spread to nearby New Forest heathland and affected an area the size of 140 football pitches.

Twenty-six fire engines and four water carriers were called to the scene, which was scaled down to 10 engines and 13 off-road vehicles by Monday.

Hampshire fire and rescue said on Monday: “There are more than 120 firefighters on the scene battling the heat and arduous terrain in order to prevent further fire spread. We are monitoring the fire, which is affecting a 1 square kilometre area of heathland off the A31, with police drones.”

Amber heat health alerts have been issued for the East Midlands, West Midlands, east of England, Yorkshire and the Humber, London, the north-west, south-east and the south-west, while a yellow heat health alert has been issued for the north-east, from Tuesday at 9am until Friday at 9pm.

The Met Office said it was expecting temperatures to exceed 36C in some areas later in the week, after a relatively cool day on Monday, with the heat peaking on Thursday. England and Wales have had their driest July in records dating back to 1836, with 19 counties of England seeing no rain for the entire month, provisional statistics show.

Southern England had its hottest July on record, and it was the joint hottest July on record for Wales, while England and the UK as a whole had their second hottest July, Met Office figures show.

A spokesperson for the mayor of London said: “The prolonged, extreme heat is presenting incredible challenges for our emergency services, with a huge rise in demand.” They said the mayor had provided record funding to ensure LFB was better equipped and to improve training.

Additional reporting by Aletha Adu

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Police looking into whether Joshua Kerry linked to alleged attempted burglary last year at Reform leader’s then home

Police are investigating whether Joshua Kerry, the man charged with the murder of the former Reform UK and Conservative politician Ann Widdecombe, had any role in an attempted burglary last year at the then London home of Nigel Farage.

Kerry, 28, from Rotherham, was charged with the murder of Widdecombe, 78, who was killed at her Devon home in July, after an investigation by counter-terrorism police.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

On Friday, police said they were reinvestigating an incident in April 2025 at a London address where Farage was living at the time, which they have said was an attempted burglary. Other sources describe it as an attempted arson.

Police attended the incident, which they initially recorded primarily as a burglary. The Guardian understands detectives are studying fingerprints taken from the scene, as well as video from CCTV cameras in the area and from devices such as video doorbells. They examined the scene to see if an accelerant, such as lighter fluid, was used.

On Friday, Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) said it had referred itself to the police watchdog over the initial investigation of the April 2025 incident.

It said: “As part of the ongoing investigation led by Counter Terrorism Policing South East into the murder of Ann Widdecombe, officers have reopened an investigation into an incident reported to police last year.

“In April 2025, the Metropolitan police received a report of an attempted burglary at an address in the Greater London area. Enquiries were carried out by the Metropolitan police, supported by Counter Terrorism Policing London. No arrests were made and the investigation was subsequently closed, pending any new lines of inquiry.

“Following the reopening of the attempted burglary investigation, Counter Terrorism Policing London identified a line of enquiry which was not identified and pursued by them at the time, which may have been relevant. As a result, to ensure their support to the initial investigation is thoroughly reviewed, Counter Terrorism Policing London made a mandatory conduct referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct today.”

On Monday, Farage said at a press conference: “It’s a great, great tragedy that it took the death of Ann for the security services in Britain to finally take seriously the safety and security of Reform politicians and Reform prominent figures.”

He said he now had confidence in counter-terrorism police and said they were not trying to cover anything up.

The Reform leader said of CTP’s decision to refer itself to the IOPC: “The fact they’ve done that shows you they’re not trying to cover up, they’re not trying to ignore, and I have to say I have met Laurence Taylor [the head of CTP] and I did feel a great, great confidence in it.”

Widdecombe’s body was found with “serious injuries” by paramedics at her home in Haytor Vale, Devon, at 11.40am on Thursday 9 July.

Kerry’s first court appearance in July heard that Widdecombe died after being hit on the head with a hammer 21 times in her home. Police have said they believed the 78-year-old former minister was attacked the day before her body was found.

The attack on Widdecombe has not yet been declared a terrorist incident. CTP took the lead in the investigation because of the possibility there may have been a political motive behind her killing.

CTP’s investigations continue.

Police investigating whether he had any role in attempted burglary at Nigel Farage's home. Police said they were reinvestigating an incident in April 2025 at a London address where Farage was living at the time.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Melody Schreiber
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
President and RFK Jr, the health secretary, repeatedly referred to autism during signing, though studies show no link between it and vaccines

Donald Trump has signed an executive order with plans for sweeping changes to the childhood vaccination schedule that attempts to override the authority of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

It is an attempt to undergird the changes made earlier this year to CDC vaccination recommendations, which were halted by a federal judge. The CDC is the federal agency tasked with recommending vaccines, not the White House.
