https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/w.title: The RBA's big challenge: How to navigate a real estate downturn
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/w.author: Ian Verrender
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Interest Rates

The shoe is now on the other foot when it comes to complaints about house prices. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Is this the beginning of the great unravelling?

Australian real estate and the glorified building societies that back it — sorry, our big banks — are on the turn.

And the blame is being sheeted squarely at the tax changes announced in the May budget, which wound back some of the excesses that had helped drive a 25-year property market boom.

Quite possibly. At the very least it was on the cusp of fundamentally altering the structure of Australian society by creating a permanent class of landowners that would all but exclude anyone not born into it.

For years, a growing band of youthful would-be home owners were baying for change. That generational push was rapidly turning into a political force as waves of younger Australians became voters.

The aggrieved always make the most noise. And now the boot is on the other foot.

Those with property, who have sat idly by and watched real estate values climb to extraordinary levels, are upset by the prospect that the salad days are over.

Many had the quinella going: Go big on property and put the rest of your cash into shares in the banks which profited from fuelling the boom.

We seem to have flipped from worrying about rising house prices to worrying about falling house prices. Well, some of us have, anyway.

Despite all the alarm, and the lurid headlines dominating the financial press, the current downturn is still relatively modest by even recent standards, although it has the potential to become a significant event.

Deflating a property bubble takes quite some skill; something that has escaped almost every government or central bank that has ever attempted it.

Think Japan in the post-80s boom. Or China since 2019. And let's not forget America in 2007.

The RBA watches the cascade of economic effects from house price moves. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

When Michele Bullock steps up to the lectern today, you can expect a repeat of the same message that the Reserve Bank of Australia has broadcast all year.

Inflation is the enemy. The RBA will do whatever it takes to defeat it, and the pain of higher interest rates is far more preferable than the long-term pain of entrenched inflation.

Michele Bullock will likely stay on message about the RBA's inflation focus. (ABC News: John Gunn)

When the RBA talks about inflation, it's talking about the cost of purchasing everyday goods like bread and butter and even petrol.

It is definitely not talking about the cost of keeping a roof over your head, unless of course, you are renting.

But those who own a home and are hocked to the eyeballs with a mortgage aren't counted.

Housing is only counted in the inflation figures if you are building a new one.

Will the RBA hold rates?

As far as the RBA is concerned, real estate and the cost of a mortgage aren't consumer items, even though they have a huge impact on household budgets and spending.

So, publicly, the RBA has no interest in real estate prices.

Privately, however, each of the board members understands the enormous repercussions mortgage repayments and property price movements have on the economy, spending and inflation.

They're acutely aware that when real estate is soaring, wealthy home owners are more likely to borrow and spend on consumer items.

But if housing values drop too sharply, there can be a cascading effect on spending, investment and economic growth.

That's why you won't see a rate hike this month and, if this downturn continues, for the rest of this year.

Westpac was under fire yesterday.

Australia's second-biggest housing lender, after the Commonwealth Bank, released some quarterly figures that highlighted the sudden downturn in its home lending business.

Home loan applications fell off the financing cliff, down 20 per cent.

Bank stocks have come off the boil as home loan applications fall. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Given home loans are the primary business of Australian banks, investors responded by sending Westpac's shares sharply lower, off more than 5 per cent.

It was more ammunition for the aggrieved housing industry in the wake of the federal budget changes that curtailed negative gearing for new dwellings and saw the 50 per cent capital gains discount replaced with an inflation discount.

The changes coincided with three consecutive rate hikes, and there's been an ongoing dispute among economists over which shift has had the biggest impact.

Going by Westpac's numbers, you'd have to conclude that, while both measures have caused potential buyers to hit the brakes, the interest rate hikes are the dominant factor.

While investor loan applications plummeted 26 per cent in the quarter, owner-occupier applications — which were not affected by the budget changes — fell 18 per cent.

If that 18 per cent drop was replicated over both sets of loans, the budget changes clearly have hurt, but by far less than the rate hikes.

The rate increases have had the greatest impact on the two biggest markets of Sydney and Melbourne, which makes sense given they were the biggest beneficiaries of the spectacular boom since 2023.

Nationally, prices have dropped 1.9 per cent in the past quarter. But the rate of decline is gathering pace, with even former runaway markets like Perth, Brisbane and Hobart either barely climbing or in reverse.

Sydney has now fallen more than 4 per cent in the past quarter. But that pales when compared with the pre-pandemic fall, the 20 months from mid-2017 to early 2019.

During that period, Sydney real estate dropped almost 14 per cent, and Melbourne shed close to 10 per cent. And this was at a time when interest rates were steady.

That downturn was deliberately engineered by the banking regulator, the Australian Prudential Regulatory Authority.

Concerned about the pace of growth in new lending, it deliberately targeted investors by placing restrictions on the banks.

If there is anything to learn from that period, it is that market dynamics can change swiftly and sentiment is fragile.

For all the warnings and threats from the RBA over the evils of inflation, central banks have been reluctant to address runaway asset prices until it's too late.

Australia's housing downturn is spreading across the country, with the latest property price data showing previously resilient markets that had recently set record-high prices are now experiencing a decline in values.

At the height of Japan's stupendous property boom in the 80s, the couple of hectares that housed the Imperial Palace was valued at about $US5.1 trillion, worth more than all the real estate in California.

When the Bank of Japan popped the bubble with a punishing series of rate hikes, it took the Japanese economy with it, resulting in decades of recession from which it has never really recovered.

China's president, Xi Jinping, pulled the plug on its runaway real estate market just before the pandemic, wreaking havoc on the domestic economy ever since through weak consumption and investment.

Prices are still falling, forcing the country to rely increasingly upon exports, which is skewing global trade.

When the US property bubble burst in 2007, exposing malfeasance and reckless lending in the banking system, it almost brought the global economy to a halt.

Until now, Australian real estate has been among the world's most expensive, with Australians correspondingly among the world's most indebted.

Taking the steam out of the property market will be tricky, but entirely necessary.

And the RBA knows it.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/a.title: Police mass AI surveillance pilot draws rebuke from privacy experts
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/a.author: Cam Wilson and Andy Burns
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Police in Western Australia have been running a trial using live facial recognition technology in public. (Supplied)

An Australian-first trial of live AI facial recognition technology by a police force has been criticised by privacy experts and legal advocates.

The mass AI surveillance pilot has been rolled out in Western Australia and is being closely watched by law enforcement agencies across the country.

Since the trial began in June, cameras linked to facial recognition software have scanned more than 130,000 people in Perth and Fremantle, comparing their faces against a police watchlist in real time.

Western Australian police say the results are promising but questions have been raised about an opaque watchlist and trial site locations that some say may target First Nations people.

The technology scans faces then compares them to a watchlist held by police in a van nearby. (Supplied)

In June, the Western Australian Police announced it would be the first police force to use live facial recognition technology on the public.

Facial recognition technology has become increasingly commonplace. It includes simpler one-to-one systems that check whether a single face matches a particular identity, like those used to unlock a mobile phone.

It also includes the more complex one-to-many systems like those used in Bunnings to compare faces of customers against a database of people suspected of activity including theft or abuse of staff.

The Privacy Commissioner finds Bunnings Warehouse interfered with the privacy of its customers by using facial recognition without consent in 63 of its stores over a three-year period.

Since June, WA Police have been trialling that more complex type of system.

Using tech company NEC's Neoface m40 product, a pilot program scanned more than 130,000 faces around Perth and Fremantle in the first week of the trial.

It compared their faces against a watchlist of about 4,000 people, including people accused of serious offences, people who are missing, and people who may pose a risk to themselves or others, police said.

WA Police celebrated the early results from the trial, which resulted in 33 alerts and 18 arrests.

Police say images of people not on the database will be deleted almost immediately and will appear pixelated, even for officers monitoring the technology. (ABC News: Callum Liddelow)

Of the faces scanned in the first week, the algorithm falsely identified one person as being on the watchlist — a better result than the 2023 UK trial of the same technology.

Since then, the pilot has continued for several weeks across multiple sites, but WA Police declined to release any more data about the trial saying more would come in a "co-ordinated matter".

There are about 4,000 people on the police watchlist. (Supplied)

Melbourne Law School associate professor Jake Goldenfein said facial recognition technologies have known accuracy issues with particular demographic groups.

"Historically, these systems have performed worse for people of colour and for women, and especially worse for women of colour," he said.

That is because the algorithms used in the systems are trained on a data set of predominantly white and male faces, and an under-representation of other demographics in the training set results in worse accuracy.

Dr Goldenfein says facial recognition technologies have known accuracy issues. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)

Dr Goldenfein said the systems produced both false positives, which could mean incorrectly identifying someone as being on the watchlist, as well as false negatives, which could lead the technology to fail to identify someone being sought.

When choosing the technology for its trial, WA Police pointed to the findings of a 2023 study by the UK's National Physical Laboratory which tested the NEC algorithm and found there were no statistically significant differences in false positives by gender or ethnicity when used under specific conditions.

But the study found accuracy issues increased when the facial recognition system's settings were relaxed and once real-world variables crept in, including changes to picture quality, lighting, skin tone and subject age.

WA Police are monitoring through screens located in a nearby van. (ABC News: Callum Liddelow)

Michael Birtwisle, an associate director of data and AI law and policy at the Ada Lovelace Institute in London, was called to give evidence at a 2023 UK parliamentary inquiry about the Metropolitan Police Service and South Wales Police's use of facial recognition technology.

He said Australian police could not rely on the UK's trial data when applying the technology here, particularly given the lack of testing on First Nations faces.

"It's a snapshot so it can only tell you [about] that version of that system, for that population," Mr Birtwisle told the ABC.

A UK study of the NEC algorithm found no statistically significant differences in false positives by gender or ethnicity. (Supplied)

WA Police did not respond to a question about whether NEC's technology had been tested or trained on First Nations faces prior to the trial.

"WA Police is committed to transparency and is collating statistics throughout the trial," a spokesperson said.

"The trial will assess demographics during the deployments and gauge whether or not there is a disproportionate impact on an ethnicity or group within the community."

Aboriginal Legal Service of Western Australia's (ALSWA) legal services director Peter Collins was on leave in June when he received an email from WA Police.

It was from a police superintendent asking for "20 minutes" to discuss the new pilot.

"This is the extent of the consultation: an email asking to meet two days before it is launched," Mr Collins said.

Mr Collins said he thought that WA Police would want the input of the state's primary legal agency for First Nations people involved in the trial, given WA's high incarceration rates of Aboriginal people and the risks of over-policing on a vulnerable cohort.

But he said the consultation was simply "an exercise in tokenism".

Mr Collins says police did not provide adequate consultation in the lead up to the trial. (ABC News: James Carmody)

Mr Collins said WA Police had not explained whether the technology was being used to identify children.

A WA Police spokesperson told the ABC that the force had made "attempts" to meet with ALSWA.

WA Police completed an assessment of the trial's impact on privacy as part of its preparations.

On a form for the privacy impact assessment released publicly by police, it declared the trial would not "primarily or especially affect Aboriginal people".

Experts say there could be accuracy issues with the technology. (Supplied)

Peter Collins said the trial was one of the growing ways the WA Aboriginal community was being over-surveilled by police.

"It can only have been by design, not chance, that facial recognition technology has been rolled out in those suburbs and places where everyone is aware that significant numbers of Aboriginal people either live or frequent," he said.

"It is easy to understand why many Aboriginal people in WA believe they live in a police state."

A WA Police spokesperson said "the locations are identified ... based on policing need and policing objectives. Locations do not target any group of people or demographic."

Privacy expert at Electronic Frontiers, John Pane, said the consultation was thin but the bigger problem was the law that guides it.

Mr Pane believes the privacy act needs to be amended urgently to keep up with the tech.

WA's privacy watchdog, the Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC), said the state police force did not invite it to take part in any "meaningful" consultation process for the trial.

The watchdog launched an unusually public broadside about the dangers of such a program without appropriate guardrails in July.

A WA Police spokesperson said it had briefed the OIC in April and invited the office to a demonstration of the technology.

WA Police have been displaying a sign letting the public know that live facial recognition is in use. (Supplied)

An OIC spokesperson told the ABC it turned down that invitation because it did not think it was appropriate to attend, given its role as an independent regulator and to avoid appearing as though it was endorsing the trial.

Former Australian Privacy Commissioner Malcolm Crompton said the Information Commissioner's missive was a clear warning from the agency.

"And the Information Commissioner put a warning shot across their bows, very clearly."

Former Australian Privacy Commissioner Malcolm Crompton says the trial's privacy assessment was "feather-light". (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

Mr Crompton, who now works as a privacy consultant, said the trial's privacy assessment was "feather-light" and should have undergone a proper consultation by an independent assessor.

"[The] privacy impact assessment is the cornerstone of this particular thing," he said.

"It's not an 'I'm going to wave this piece of paper in front of you and I've let you know it's happening consultation'," he said.

Associate professor Hannah McGlade is a human rights lawyer and Noongar woman based at Curtin University in Perth.

She said she had deep concerns about the roll out of a program that would impact First Nations people more than other groups.

"This new policing program is looking at people with outstanding warrants. We know Aboriginal people are over-represented here," Dr McGlade said.

"The technology is being set up in well-known Aboriginal areas: Midland, Northbridge."

Dr Hannah McGlade says the program will impact First Nations people more than other groups. (ABC News: Rhiannon Shine)

The human rights law expert said WA Police needed to be more transparent about who it had chosen to put on its watchlist.

"Should this sort of technology be used for people who have engaged in minor offending?" Dr McGlade said.

"Now, if people are at risk to the public, there might be other arguments in favour of it, or more surveillance. But here we just don't know."

Mr Birtwistle said the UK Home Office was currently considering laws that would limit inclusion on facial recognition watchlists to only those who had committed serious offences.

The ABC asked WA Police for more information on the nature of the 16 arrests for outstanding warrants in the first week of the trial. It did not respond.

WA Police say the trial's results have been promising, with 33 alerts and 18 arrests. (Supplied: WA Police)

Dr McGlade said the lack of transparency was unacceptable.

"If they've got nothing to hide then they really should show us who's being charged."

Dr Goldenfein said the WA trial could help shape how the technology was adopted elsewhere in Australia.

"I hope that as Australia starts to look again at the management of AI technologies in a more holistic way, the use of these technologies by law enforcement and intelligence apparatus doesn't escape that regulatory oversight," he said.

Other state police forces are paying close attention to the trial of the technology too, according to WA Police Commissioner Col Blanch.

He told a press conference when the WA trial was announced: "My colleagues, other police commissioners in other jurisdictions, are watching this trial closely to see how it goes."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/t.author: Kellie Scott
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Pet owners spend about $1 billion annually on pet insurance. (Pexels: Harry Tucker)

Pets are like family and when they get sick or injured, you can be faced with vet bills in the thousands.

That's a difficult position to be in when you don't have the funds to treat them, which is why pet insurance can be an attractive option.

"With no pet equivalent of Medicare subsidies, the full cost of treatment falls on the pet owner," says financial educator Lacey Filipich.

"Insurance can help take the stress out of life, as well as help pet owners avoid going into debt if the worst happens."

But pet insurance is a "complex financial product", explains Daniel Graham, insurance analyst at consumer advocacy group Choice, making it difficult to know if it's worthwhile.

And insurance isn't your only option when it comes to planning for pet expenses.

A 2025 survey from Animal Medicines Australia shows Australian pet owners spent about $1 billion annually on pet insurance, but most don't have it.

Eighty-six per of cat owners and 76 per cent of dog owners aren't covered. Responses to the survey include "it's too expensive", "I don't see the value" and "haven't looked into it".

Recent Canstar data shows for accident and illness cover, the average annual premium for a cat is $807, and $1,374 for a medium-sized dog.

Add in routine care cover and the premium typically increases by a couple of hundred dollars.

Costs will also depend on the age and breed of your pet.

Peace of mind is the biggest benefit of pet insurance, says Ms Filipich.

"Spending a few hundred to a couple of thousand dollars a year might be worth it for the certainty, especially when you know you'd pursue expensive treatments for your pet if they fell ill or were injured.

"Gone are the days when the majority of people simply put down their pet when something went drastically wrong."

This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

Mr Graham says veterinary costs in Australia are increasing, with the most significant driver being technological investment.

"Like with human health, the technology to treat different conditions is becoming more widely available, and vet practices are purchasing that technology — that costs money."

The ease of claiming has also improved, says Mr Graham.

Pets can be lifelong companions, but they can also test us in ways we never imagined. We asked you to share your stories.

"Several insurances in recent years have introduced systems where they will process the claim while at the vet clinic, making the payment directly.

"You as the customer simply have to cover the gap, which is a huge difference from a decade ago where the most common practice was to cover the bill up-front, then claw back a cheque from the insurer."

The option to add routine pet cover may appeal to dog and cat owners, which covers things like blood tests, vaccinations and parasite control.

Put simply, pet insurance can be expensive, especially if your pet enjoys a long life.

"You could be forking out tens of thousands of dollars in pet insurance," Ms Filipich says.

A pet's age and breed are also major factors.

"There is decreasing cover for older pets," says Mr Graham.

"[Often] when you purchase the policy for a puppy or kitten, the insurer covers all of your eligible vet costs while young, then it tapers down as they age."

For example, when your pet is eight years old, your insurance provider might cover 80 per cent of the vet bill. But at the age of 10, only 65 per cent is covered.

"But this is the age your pet is most likely to need vet cover," Mr Graham says.

Daniel Graham, with his cat Cyclone, who recently cost him $14,000 in vet care. (Supplied)

And while cat insurance is fairly consistent across breeds, for dogs it varies greatly.

Brachycephalic dog breeds such as French bulldogs, pugs and Boston terriers are flat-faced dogs with shortened skulls that face unique health risks, notably breathing and heat challenges.

"They require a lot of medical treatment throughout their life, which is very costly to insurers," says Mr Graham. He says this makes premiums much higher.

A monthly fee for a Cavoodle might cost you between $60 and $100, whereas a Frenchie will be $230 to $375, he adds.

Other than high costs, the main drawback of pet insurance is the difficultly in switching to a new provider for pets with pre-existing and chronic conditions, says Mr Graham.

All insurers have blanket exclusions for pre-existing conditions, such as an illness or injury your pet had before you first took out the insurance policy.

"Some will agree to cover if you meet certain criteria … which it basically never does," Mr Graham says.

"What ends up happening is that the ability to switch to a new product decreases, so you end up sticking with the same provider, even if they are increasing premiums or the service isn't good."

Even if you can switch, your options are limited with older pets, he says.

"They are usually limited to lower-cover products with lower annual limits."

And policies are complex, Mr Graham says.

"It's a lot for people to get their head around and feel confident they are making a good decision."

He says pet owners are often surprised to find their cover doesn't include dental, for example.

When you don't take out insurance, you're essentially self-insuring, Ms Filipich says.

"You could choose to put what you would have spent on insurance aside for if or when illness or injury happens and use the funds directly instead of via an insurance process."

For example, you could put the equivalent cost of the premium into a dedicated savings account (or demarcated offset account if you have a mortgage) each month or year, then draw on it when needed, she says.

Mr Graham chooses to self-insure, a decision he made after paying $14,000 in vet care for his cat, Cyclone, a couple of years ago.

"Not everyone is financially in that position and insurance makes more sense when you don't have a safety net."

Because there are also many non-monetary benefits of owning a pet, those struggling to pay for their care can also reach out to a financial counsellor.

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.title: US judge dismisses criminal case against Indian billionaire Adani
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.author: Reuters
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.text:
Move comes after the Justice Department said it had decided to abandon the fraud and bribery case in which Adani Group has denied wrongdoing

A US judge on Monday dismissed criminal charges against Indian billionaire Gautam Adani, after the Justice Department said it had decided to abandon the fraud and bribery case.

Brooklyn-based US District Judge Nicholas ‌Garaufis’ decision to grant federal prosecutors’ rare bid to toss the case came after he inquired into their reasons for doing so, including by asking Adani whether anything was promised in exchange for the dropping of the case.

In November 2024, before the charges were unsealed, Adani had promised to invest US$10 billion in the United States.

Adani was charged in 2024 with agreeing to bribe Indian government officials so a subsidiary of his Adani Group could win approval to develop ⁠a solar energy plant, then misleading US investors by providing reassuring information about his company’s anti-corruption practices.

Adani Group has consistently denied wrongdoing. ‌Adani himself has not appeared in court in the US to respond to the charges.

On May 18, the Justice Department announced it would no longer pursue the case. That marked the latest instance in which federal ‌prosecutors had sought to drop a high-profile white-collar criminal prosecution during Republican President Donald Trump’s second term in ⁠the White House.

Legal experts ⁠say US judges have little discretion to compel prosecutors to continue with criminal cases they no longer wish to pursue but the charges cannot be formally dismissed ‌without a judge’s approval.

Garaufis asked the Justice Department to justify its decision to drop the charges, writing that its “bland and conclusory” announcement did not give him enough information.

In ‌a ‌July 4 court filing, Trent McCotter, a senior Justice Department official, said the case was primarily foreign, hard to prove and ‌inconsistent with the agency’s current priorities.

In the filing, McCotter also denied as false what he called media stories suggesting he ⁠sought to dismiss the case in part because of a promise by Adani to invest money in the United States.

In response, ⁠Garaufis asked Adani whether he was “aware of any agreement exchanging anything for the dismissal of the indictment”.

In a sworn declaration filed in court on July 15, Adani said he was not aware of any such agreement. He ‌acknowledged having previously promised to invest US$10 billion ‌in the US and said his lawyers told the Justice Department in meetings that the pledge “might be part of a resolution of these matters”.

Robert Giuffra, a lawyer for Adani, said in a July 15 court filing that the Justice Department had told him that it would not consider the Adani Group’s willingness to invest in the US as part of any resolution.

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.title: Defence lawyer takes aim at psychiatrist’s care before Lindsay Clancy killed her children
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.author: Associated Press
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.text:
The lawyer highlighted Jennifer Tufts’ use of short video calls with little time for therapy, implying the doctor was a box-checking ‘robot’

Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer questioned her psychiatrist’s expertise, prescribing decisions and overall treatment as the defence sought on Monday to suggest that the mental healthcare system overlooked and even accelerated the Massachusetts mother’s decline in the months before she killed her three young children.

In questioning Dr Jennifer Tufts, defence lawyer Kevin Reddington highlighted her use of 25-minute video appointments with limited time for talk therapy, the computerised forms that documented her observations and the series of pharmaceuticals she recommended as Clancy reported various side effects, symptoms and concerns about taking medications.

Reddington portrayed Clancy’s care not as common practice in US mental healthcare, but rather as inadequate and indifferent treatment, at one point implying that the doctor was a box-checking “robot”.

“What did you do? You had a woman who was telling you she felt hopeless,” he asked as they discussed an appointment about two months before the killings.

“I told her that this was something we could address, that there was hope, that there are treatments, that there are different types of programmes, so she knew that she still had options and a reason to hope,” Tufts said.

“Did you ever suggest to her that ‘maybe you should come in and see me, rather than on the computer?’” Reddington asked.

“Talking to her over the video didn’t seem like an issue. It didn’t seem like there was something I was missing,” Tufts replied.

Clancy, 35, has pleaded not guilty to murder charges in the deaths of Callan, Dawson and Cora Clancy, who ranged from 8 months to 5 years old.

They were found in the basement of the family’s home in coastal Duxbury, Massachusetts, and their mother was found lying in the garden. She had jumped out of a second-storey window and remains paralysed from the waist down.

Prosecutors argue that the former labour and delivery nurse was an intentional killer who connived to get her husband out of the house by sending him out on errands, then strangled the children with exercise bands on January 24, 2023.

In an opening statement last month, prosecutor Shannan Buckingham urged jurors not to view the trial as “a public debate about women’s mental health and how the medical system treats women”.

Clancy’s lawyers do not dispute that she killed the children. But they say that she should not be held criminally responsible because she was mentally ill, believing that she heard voices ordering her to take the children’s lives and her own.

The defence contends that she was in the grip of bipolar disorder and post-partum psychosis, a rare post-pregnancy condition that can alter women’s sense of reality. A forensic psychiatrist diagnosed her with those conditions after the killings.

Her lawyers say Clancy did everything she could to seek help: She turned to multiple outpatient providers, tried various drugs they prescribed, called a suicide hotline, went to an accident and emergency department and approached but was not accepted into a hospital-based, full-day treatment programme for women with post-pregnancy mental health problems. Clancy then even checked herself into a psychiatric hospital for several days.

Rather than improving, her condition worsened on the ever-remixed cocktail of psychiatric medications, some of them problematic for bipolar patients, her lawyers and family say.

Tufts saw Clancy, via video, from September 2022 until the day before the killings. Her diagnosis: generalised anxiety disorder and an adjustment disorder with depressed mood.

The psychiatrist testified that Clancy never told her about manic episodes, a criterion for a bipolar diagnosis, nor about hearing voices or having other signs of psychosis.

Clancy at times said she was “close” to feeling suicidal, hopeless or like she was going to die, Tufts said. But she said Clancy denied having a plan to take her own life or harm anyone else and never revealed – as the defence says she did to her husband – that she had thoughts about harming the children.

“I would have been very concerned if I had heard that,” Tufts said.

Clancy is suing Tufts and other practitioners in civil court.

“I do not believe that I’ve been negligent,” Tufts testified in the criminal trial on Monday as Reddington questioned how much experience she had treating post-pregnancy conditions before Clancy came to her. Tufts had finished her psychiatric residency training in July 2022 and joined a private practice the month before Clancy’s first appointment.

If convicted of murder, Clancy faces life in prison without parole. If found not guilty due to a lack of criminal responsibility, she would be committed to a state mental health facility.

https://www.dw.com/en/russia-top-court-b.title: Russia: Top court bans opposition anti-war party from vote
https://www.dw.com/en/russia-top-court-b.text:
Yabloko, Russia's only anti-war party, has been barred from September's parliamentary elections. The motion to bar Yabloko was filed by the nationalist pro-Kremlin party Rodina.

The Supreme Court of Russia on Monday ruled in favor of the nationalist pro-Kremlin Rodina (Motherland) party and barred Yabloko (Apple) — Russia's only anti-war party — from participating in September parliamentary elections.

Rodina accuses Yabloko of receiving undeclared financial support from Western sources, among other things.

Arguing before the court, Yabloko vehemently denied the accusations and railed against Rodina's lack of supporting evidence.

On Monday, Judge Vyacheslav Kirillov said, "The claims seeking to annul the registration of the federal list of candidates for the State Duma of the ninth convocation, nominated by the Yabloko political party, were granted."

The court's decision means citizens opposed to Russia's four-and-a-half-year invasion of Ukraine — or "special military operation" as it has been legally deemed under penalty of imprisonment — have no opportunity to vote for representatives willing to articulate that opposition.

Yabloko leader Nikolay Rybakov told the hundred or so supporters gathered outside the court, "Excluding Yabloko from the election means refusing dialog with people who ask questions that are uncomfortable for the authorities."

"We have a long road ahead and we have a big and important task — to stop deaths and bring back peace. Everything we do should be dedicated to that," Rybakov added, vowing to appeal the decision.

Yabloko — the only liberal party still operating in Russia since most of President Vladimir Putin's opponents have been jailed, exiled or murdered — has received the backing of several exiled opposition figures, including Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny.

Yabloko was once a strong liberal force in Russia but like other opposition outfits it has been systematically sidelined by the Kremlin.

The party is currently only polling around three percent — short of the five percent threshold for entry into parliament — and has not won a seat in the federal State Duma since 2003.

Putin-backing United Russia has won every single election since then and that is expected to again be the case in September.

But despite barring political opposition to the war, public opinion toward the conflict has soured, more so since Ukraine has intensified its attacks on energy and logistics infrastructure inside Russia.

The non-governmental Levada Center — which is on the Kremlin's "foreign agents" list — charts support at around 66%, the lowest since Russia launched its attack against neighboring Ukraine on February 24, 2022.

The Kremlin has cracked down on opposition to the war with strict censorship rules and mass arrests, with many activists and journalists preferring to flee than to face potentially deadly persecution by staying in Russia.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

https://www.dw.com/en/colombia-earthquak.title: Colombia earthquake: Death toll rises to over 100
https://www.dw.com/en/colombia-earthquak.text:
A powerful earthquake, measured at magnitude 7.4, has struck Colombia, killing dozens of people and trapping many under rubble. Cities including Cali, Pereira and Manizales were among the hardest-hit.

A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning.

Around six hours after the quake struck, Colombia's president said that 111 people had been confirmed dead around the country.

Rescue teams were working to free residents after buildings collapsed in Cali and other cities.

The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast.

Colombia's newly-inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said that he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency.

He said that locating anyone still potentially trapped was the highest priority for rescuers and declared a national state of emergency.

"As of 12:30 [local time], the toll stood at 111 dead and 87 injured, with 1,575 homes damaged, 37 completely destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, and 18 health centers and 52 schools damaged," de la Espriella said from Bogota.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU stands "ready to provide more support" to Colombia. The bloc's satellite service, Copernicus, has already been mobilized to aid rescuers.

"Tonight, Europe's heart is with the people of Colombia," she wrote on social media.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "closely monitoring" the situation and stood "ready to support the people of Colombia."

The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed, in some cases with people trapped inside.

"Residents of Cali, we currently have at least 20 collapsed structures in the city with people trapped inside; we are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," Eder said on Instagram, posting an accompanying video statement. "I have requested support — specifically rescue personnel — from the mayors of Bogota and Medellin."

Authorities in the Valle del Cauca, whose capital city is Cali, said that at least 27 people had died in the quake, in numbers issued prior to the president's address.

Officials in Risaralda had said that 40 people had died across the state, at least 18 of them in the capital Pereira based on earlier comments from the mayor.

The governor of the Choco region where the quake's epicenter was located, Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi, said there were 12 dead and 84 wounded in her district as of lunch time local time.

And the mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas, said in a radio interview that two people were killed in his city, in the Caldas region not far northeast of Pereira.

Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined.

"Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online, later adding Cali's airport to this list.

The US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake at magnitude 7.4. Colombia's national authority at first logged a smaller figure but later revised its reading up to 7.4 as well.

The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border.

The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south.

The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter.

The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors.

Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela.

USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake.

The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake.

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/world.author: Julie Turkewitz, Genevieve Glatsky and Michael Levenson
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/world.text:
Rescue crews and regular people searched for survivors, and the death toll was likely to rise. More than 1,500 homes were damaged, the president said.

By Julie TurkewitzGenevieve Glatsky and Michael Levenson

Julie Turkewitz and Genevieve Glatsky reported from Bogotá, Colombia

A powerful earthquake rocked western Colombia on Monday morning, rattling much of the country and setting off a desperate search for survivors in the rubble of collapsed buildings in several major cities.

At least 111 people were killed and 87 others were injured, according to Colombia’s president, Abelardo De La Espriella, who said that at least 1,575 homes, 18 health centers and 52 schools had been damaged. The death toll was likely to rise as rescue crews and residents continued to dig through flattened buildings.

The 7.4-magnitude earthquake, which struck at 7:34 a.m. local time, was the strongest recorded in Colombia in the last decade, according to the Colombian Geological Survey. The agency said that two aftershocks with magnitudes of 2.8 and 4.8 had been recorded and that the quake was felt in neighboring countries, including Panama, Ecuador and Venezuela, which is still recovering from devastating twin quakes just weeks ago that killed more than 6,000 people.

The epicenter, according to the U.S. Geological Survey, was about 3 miles east of San José del Palmar, a town of about 5,000 people in the Chocó region, one of the poorest parts of Colombia.

Videos showed partially collapsed buildings in Cali, Colombia’s third largest city, with about two million residents, as well as in Pereira and Manizales, two cities that are hubs of Colombia’s coffee-growing region.

In the town of Calima El Darién, three children were killed when a wall collapsed, according to the region’s governor, Dilian Francisca Toro. Ms. Toro said that one hospital had also collapsed, another had been overwhelmed with victims and that patients had been evacuated from a third hospital.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/po.author: Anton Troianovski
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/po.text:
War in the Middle East

President Trump is eager to declare success in Iran and Gaza, but he is struggling to impose his will in either conflict.

Reporting from Washington

President Trump may want to let go of the Middle East. But it won’t let go of him.

Over the weekend, Mr. Trump said his new strategy was to be “low-keying it” in Iran, a suggestion that he wants to pressure the country into making a favorable deal without taking major military action. But a stark reminder of the limits of U.S. power in the region came from Israel, where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu declared Sunday he was “ruling out” Mr. Trump’s peace plan for Gaza.

The two Middle East conflicts have underscored Mr. Trump’s eagerness to declare success and his inability to impose his will on them, despite the enormous military firepower that he has been able to deploy.

Mr. Trump is “clearly trying to find a pathway as the midterms approach to downgrade all of this,” said Brian Katulis, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, a Washington think tank. Instead, Mr. Katulis went on, “reality is slapping him in the face.”

Mr. Trump faces depleted weapons stockpiles, an Iranian regime determined to impose pain on the United States, an Israeli prime minister battling for re-election and American voters reeling from high prices induced by the Iran war. The November midterms keep ticking closer, steadily raising the political costs of the turmoil to Mr. Trump and Republicans.

Mr. Trump laid out his low-key approach to Iran in a brief interview with the news website Axios on Sunday. Rather than make new military threats, he said that “we are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money.” He added: “It will work out. It always works out. It’s like a chess game.”

“Now, can they make trouble? Yeah, they can make trouble,” Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office Monday, acknowledging Iran’s ability to keep harassing commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. “But they’re broke.”

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Australia politics live: gambling lobby’s talking points ‘coming out the PM’s mouth’, Chaney says; RBA tipped to hold interest rates
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Krishani Dhanji
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Kate Chaney, who was on the inquiry with the late Labor MP Peta Murphy that handed down the landmark ‘you win some, you lose more’ report on gambling harm, says so far it seems the talks between the Coalition and Labor on a gambling reform package are “disappointing”.

Speaking to the ABC’s RN Breakfast a little earlier, the independent MP says the government has listened to the gambling lobby instead of the evidence.

Part of the government’s proposed reforms limit online gambling ads on television to three per hour between 6am and 8.30pm.

But Chaney says the last time ads were partially banned, the ads didn’t slow down – they just moved to different time slots.

In 2017, when the last round of partial restrictions came in, the money just moved around. And for example, gambling ads after 8.30 more than doubled, increased 131%. And I suspect that that’s what we’re going to see here too: is the money moving around.

I think it is about the government listening to the money and the power, not the people. The gambling companies make big political donations. They are present lobbyists in this building. We’re hearing their talking points coming out of the prime minister’s mouth. And the media companies and the sports codes make a lot of money out of gambling too. Unfortunately, Australians pay the cost for that. And the average Australian household loses more in gambling than they pay for in electricity. So this is our blind spot.

‘He did not mean it’ Gallagher dragged into melon-gate

Katy Gallagher has also been asked to weigh in on the PM’s melon comments – you can see a hint of exasperation in her face as she’s asked on channel nine.

I’m sure you don’t need a recap at this point but just in case you’ve missed it, Anthony Albanese told the Bush Deep podcast last month Sanae Takaichi had given him a gift of two Japanese melons, and appeared to make hand gestures in front of his chest.

Gallagher says Albanese “did not mean it in the way that it’s been reported”.

I accept that he did not intend those comments to be made the way that some media are reporting them, it’s an important relationship. He has a good relationship with the Japanese.

Earlier this morning Michaelia Cash called the comments an embarrassment and a “diplomatic incident”.

To give you a bit of context on how Japan has taken the comments, News.com.au reported the Japanese government said there was “sensationalised reporting” over the incident in a memo sent last month, and that they did not believe there was “ill intention” in Albanese’s comments. They said there would be no action taken over the matter.

Government sticks to Treasury advice on cooling housing market

The finance minister, Katy Gallagher, has been tapped on the shoulder to do the media rounds this morning ahead of the RBA’s rates decision.

She’s asked repeatedly on channel nine whether the government takes some responsibility for the decline in the housing market, but says the advise from the Treasury department in the budget showed house prices would continue to grow but slow by 2%.

Yesterday big four bank Westpac said mortgage applications were down 20% between mid-May and the end of July, the period right after the federal budget was handed down.

Gallagher says there’s a range of factors influencing the housing market, not just the government’s changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount:

There are other factors that influence the housing market, including the interest rate increases that we have seen over the last few months … the Treasury advice to us was that house prices would continue to grow slightly slower. Our focus on the housing market is making those tax changes so that first home buyers can get into the housing market, but also focusing on supply to make sure we’re building enough houses for people to buy.

Monique Ryan weighs in on melon-gate

Independent MP Monique Ryan says Anthony Albanese’s now infamous interview with the Bush Deep podcast was “pretty cringe” and has joined critics who say the PM should apologise over his comments about the Japanese’s prime minister’s gift of melons.

Albanese told the podcast Sanae Takaichi had given him a gift of two Japanese melons, and appeared to make hand gestures in front of his chest.

Ryan told the Today Show this morning that “we can probably expect a bit better” from the PM.

I think that that whole interview was pretty cringe. Let’s face it, the prime minister didn’t really cover himself with glory with that. And it’s disturbing to hear that the Japanese government has expressed some concerns about it.

We’re talking about a really special gift that the Japanese state has given to the country. And if I was the PM, I’d pick up the phone to the Japanese prime minister and apologise to her on this one.

Cabinet ministers have defended the PM and called it an issue “people are trying to blow up”, while Angus Taylor yesterday said Albanese should pick up the phone to Takaichi and apologise.

Joining the panel with Ryan, shadow cabinet minister Michaelia Cash called it a “diplomatic incident”.

When the prime minister’s crude and dirty podcast banter is formally raised by the Japanese government. Anthony Albanese just has embarrassed himself. He’s embarrassed Australia. This is now a diplomatic incident because of the appalling behaviour of the prime minister.

The Reserve Bank’s latest interest rate decision is due at 2.30pm today, and the unanimous prediction is that they will hold the cash rate at 4.35% for a second meeting in a row.

Inflation is still running too hot at 3.8% in the year to June – miles above the RBA’s official 2.5% target.

But recent data shows inflation is not as high as had been expected, while unemployment is a touch higher – two signals for the RBA to sit on its hands for now.

While financial markets see virtually no chance of a hike today, they still see a nearly 50% chance of a move higher this year.

A number of economists see a November hike as the most likely next move; others reckon the next move will be down (although not until the second half of 2027).

That means all the attention will be on the statement the RBA board issues at the time of the decision, and whether the decision to hold rates is unanimous.

RBA watchers will also be listening for what message Michele Bullock, the governor, sends at her 3.30pm press conference.

Today the bank will also release its latest set of economic forecasts in the quarterly statement on monetary policy.

Experts reckon it will still show inflation heading back to target in the next 12 months, but any slippage would be a red flag that the bank might need to hike again.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Burnham to give councils more powers to block vape and betting shops
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Aletha Adu and Alexandra Topping
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Vape shops in England and Wales to be subject to planning permission while betting shop law change will also apply in Scotland

Councils are to be given powers to stop betting and vape shops taking over their high streets under new plans announced by Andy Burnham.

Local authorities will be able to reject new betting shops and adult gaming centres, while vape shops will be subject to planning permission under plans Downing Street says could be in place from the start of next year.

Burnham is promising to scrap the “aim to permit” rule in the Gambling Act 2005, which in effect requires councils to allow new gambling premises where applications meet licensing requirements.

This could mark a big shift from changes introduced by his predecessor, Keir Starmer, in April that gave councils more of an ability to consider the number of gambling premises already in an area but stopped short of scrapping the “aim to permit rule”.

As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham called on Starmer to abolish the rule in January, alongside almost 300 other politicians and campaigners.

Burnham said communities should have much more control over their high streets where traditional shops, pubs and other services have disappeared while vape and gambling shops have expanded.

The push fits into Burnham’s attempt to make the first weeks of his premiership about tangible changes people can see in their everyday lives.

A No 10 source said the government was determined to crack down on vape and betting shops because they were two of the most visible signs of decline on high streets, and local people were genuinely concerned. A fast-tracked consultation on the new measures would take six weeks, with the aim of having the measures in place by the start of 2027.

“Local people will actually have more of an input into whether or not those shops should open in the first place, giving them a proper say about how their high streets should look,” they said.

The move comes after research suggested Labour would be “washed away in a tide of discontent” at the next general election unless it tackled the decline of Britain’s high streets.

Prof Will Jennings, who led the University of Southampton research, said Burnham’s targeting of vape and betting shops was “an important first step”. However, with nearly one in three retail sales in the UK now online, it was clear that the policy would “not solve everything”, he said. “But it is speaking to some real area of concern that impacts how people view their local area.”

Vape shops currently fall into the same planning category as shops, cafes and even banks meaning they can open without needing a new planning application. Ministers will consult on putting them into their own planning category so councils will be able to consider each new vape shop application individually and reject those they deem not appropriate for the area.

The government is also looking at tightening the definition of what a vape shop is, to prevent people saying they were opening a convenience store that had the primary function of selling vapes as well as provisions to specifically stop them opening near schools. Angela Rayner said the move addressed problems that had built up over decades. “That’s why we’re giving local leaders the power to say no to what doesn’t belong on their high street, and the tools to fix it themselves,” the communities secretary said.

Jennings said the government also needed to tackle opaque ownership structures of high street property, which allows some landowners “who aren’t necessarily that motivated to have shops in their property”.

The growth of vape shops is not evenly spread, with research from Health Equity North highlighting the most deprived communities had three times as many vape shops as the most affluent areas.

Burnham said high streets had become “unrecognisable” after decades of decline. “The rise of vape shops, betting shops and rogue operators have replaced the shops, services, and community spaces that people are crying out for.

“That’s not on. I said we would improve Britain’s high streets, and that’s exactly what we are starting to do.”

The measures are seen as a “first step” on a wider beautification of Britain’s high streets, with Westminster setting clearer expectations for the design and appearance of high street shopfronts.

Local leaders will be encouraged to look at blueprints for ideal high streets, and given examples of what works best and how they can improve the look of their own main shopping areas.

Vape shops will be subject of planning permission under plans Downing Street says could be in place from the start of next year. Vapes and betting shops will also be subject. Councils will be given powers to stop betting and vape shops taking over their high streets

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Boat operator faces federal charges after mother and infant killed in New York capsizing
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Sara Sanchez, 27, and her daughter died after a speedboat capsized in the New York Harbor over the weekend

The driver of a speedboat that capsized in New York Harbor over the weekend, killing a 27-year-old woman and her infant daughter, was charged on Monday with causing their deaths through misconduct or neglect.

Manuel Hernandez, 46, wiped his eyes with his hand as he arrived for his initial appearance in Manhattan federal court. He was not required to enter a plea and was released on bail.

Sara Sanchez and her five-month-old daughter, Antonella Garcia, died after the 22-foot Yamaha speedboat overturned late Saturday near the Statue of Liberty. Twelve others were rescued and are in stable condition, authorities said.

The vessel was pulled from the water and taken to the New York police department’s harbor unit facility on Randall’s Island.

After state charges were lodged against Hernandez over the weekend, prosecutors said on Monday that he will be tried in federal court, not state court.

Capt Doreen McCarthy, the coast guard sector New York commander, credited the rescue of survivors to “heroic, swift actions” by those who responded from various agencies, along with a good Samaritan vessel.

Meanwhile, a GoFundMe campaign that began Sunday to help Andres Garcia pay for the funeral and other expenses for his partner, Sanchez, and their daughter had topped $25,000 by Monday afternoon.

Antonio Russo, general manager at Il Punto Ristorante, said Garcia is an “amazing guy” who has been working long hours each week as a waiter, driver and food-runner, to provide for his family here and in Colombia.

Diego Naranjo, a neighbor of Sanchez in Queens, said he first met her last spring when her son threw a ball into their back yard. After recovering the ball, Naranjo invited her son to play on a trampoline with his children.

“They were really nice people. You can see when a person is noble,” Naranjo said.

He said he last saw Sanchez last Tuesday as she brought groceries into her home. He said he was shocked by the deaths.

Manuel Hernandez, 46, was charged with causing their deaths through misconduct or neglect. He was not required to enter a plea and was released on bail.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Nearly 30 pine trees intentionally poisoned in Lake Tahoe’s Nevada side
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Coral Murphy Marcos
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Incidents of damaged trees at Burnt Cedar beach have been reported since 2022 and seem to be linked, officials say

Pine trees near Lake Tahoe are being poisoned in what authorities believe are a series of interconnected incidents in the popular tourist community on border of Nevada and California.

The incidents have damaged nearly 30 trees, some reportedly more than a century old, and caused hundreds of thousands of dollars in losses.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Officials in Nevada said 28 trees were poisoned at Burnt Cedar beach, a restricted-access beach located on the north-east shore of Lake Tahoe. Six trees were also damaged in 2022, another six in 2024, and 16 more were discovered this year. In a statement released on Thursday, authorities said that the incidents appear to be connected, causing an estimated $300,000 in losses.

No suspect has been identified or arrested.

“We take these crimes very seriously and will utilize every available resource to identify and apprehend the person or persons responsible,” said the office of Darin Balaam, the Washoe county sheriff, in a statement. “The destruction of mature trees in the Tahoe Basin and the environmental damage caused by these deliberate acts are unacceptable.”

The most recent incidents were reported in late July and early August. On 24 July, deputies responded to the beach after a strong odor was detected near a large pine tree. Soil samples collected from the area had an odor consistent with other incidents related to the pine trees at the property, according to the county sheriff’s office.

Officials returned on 2 August after more trees were found with a substance around their bases. Authorities believe the most recent incident occurred sometime between 11.30am on 1 August and 5am on 2 August.

Authorities are still investigating the substance used to poison the trees in the residents-only beach in Incline Village. Investigators have collected soil samples for testing to determine which substance was used and whether the same substance was involved in each incident.

In some instances, officials found holes had been drilled near the roots of the pines in Incline Village.

Authorities said that, based on the estimated amount of damage, the person or people responsible could face felony-level charges.

Incline Village is a scenic mountain town that has recently attracted some of the world’s wealthiest, earning it the nickname “Income Village,” as billionaires including Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison and Google co-founder Sergey Brin have reportedly purchased homes in the area.

The incidents have damaged nearly 30 trees, some reportedly more than a century old, and caused hundreds of thousands of dollars in losses.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.title: Europe braces for another heatwave after record-breaking temperatures
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.text:
Many parts of Europe are bracing for another heatwave after record-breaking temperatures in June and July sparked wildfires, dried out rivers and contributed to thousands of deaths.

Parts of Britain and France on Monday were already under extreme heat warnings with forecasts of temperatures around the mid-30 degrees Celsius (mid-90 degrees Fahrenheit).

“We know the hot and dry weather is taking a real toll on farming and there will be long-lasting impacts on our environment,” said the British Environment Agency’s Director of Sustainable Business and Development Tony Grayling.

The British government has imposed irrigation restrictions on farmers and introduced a hosepipe ban in some regions, with more than 27 million people living under water-use restrictions as Britain prepares for its fifth consecutive heatwave this year.

Meanwhile in France, water-use restrictions have been applied on 70 percent of the country as drought conditions worsen amid successive heatwaves, the government said Monday.

Restrictions apply to activities such as watering gardens and green spaces, filling swimming pools, washing cars and irrigating crops.

Spain’s national weather agency AEMET said on Monday Spain recorded the joint-hottest July since records began in 1961, after scorching temperatures fuelled the country’s biggest wildfire in recent history.

Last month was also mainland Spain’s driest July on record as 4.3 millimetres of rain fell, which represented just 26 percent of the normal precipitation for the time of year.

The parched conditions are fuelling wildfires in Greece and Spain, including in Andalusia where firefighters are struggling to put out blazes.

Andalusia’s emergencies chief, Antonio Sanz, told reporters that extinguishing fires around the medieval town of Niebla was akin to a “long-distance obstacle race” and was expected to last several days.

Sanz said nearly 500 people have been evacuated from the area.

Meanwhile, the BDB association, an inland shipping group, warned that vessels will soon not be able to navigate parts of the Rhine river in Germany as water levels drop further due to soaring summer temperatures and low rainfall.

“With water levels this low, commercial shipping will no longer be able to transport goods in the region,” the group’s managing director Jens Schwanen told the Rheinische Post newspaper.

“In principle, this means the Rhine is no longer continuously navigable and thus divided in two.”

Europe is the fastest-warming continent on the planet due to climate change.Soaring temperatures are also forecast in Switzerland, Austria and Hungary.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.title: Wildfires burn across Indonesia as officials cite El Nino as a cause
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.text:
Close to 50,000 firefighters and disaster personnel, backed by dozens of helicopters, are battling wildfires in several parts of Indonesia after an unusually dry season in the sprawling archipelago.

Increased El Nino conditions have raised the risk of more forest and land fires during the peak dry season, said Indonesia’s Coordinating Minister for Political and Security Affairs, Djamari Chaniago, on Monday.

Authorities in East Java say the largest blaze is in Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park, where about 743 hectares (1,836 acres) of land have been scorched. The park is closed to visitors until further notice.

“This closure is a crucial step to ⁠⁠maintain the safety of visitors, staff and ⁠⁠people in the surrounding areas,” the park’s operator said on its Instagram page.

The fire has burned large areas of dry grassland, vegetation and protected Edelweiss flowers. Flames have spread to the Penanjakan area, a popular viewpoint for tourists visiting the volcanic landscape of Mount Bromo, one of Indonesia’s best-known attractions. No injuries or building evacuations have been reported.

Almost 6,000 firefighters have been deployed to battle wildfires in Jambi province. Officials said deep peat soil, limited water supplies, difficult access and strong winds have complicated efforts, even with help from three firefighting helicopters.

Dry weather and strengthening El Nino conditions have raised the risk of fires during the peak dry season, according to Indonesia’s forestry ministry. Indonesia’s BMKG weather agency has warned that the 2026 dry season will be more intense and prolonged than usual, with a higher risk of wildfires and drought due in part to El Nino.

The naturally occurring climate phenomenon brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns and typically causes drier conditions in India and Southeast Asia. The last El Nino helped make 2023 and 2024 the two hottest years on record globally.

Indonesia’s forestry ministry says more than 107,000 hectares of land caught fire nationwide between January and June this year – double the area burned in all of 2023. Indonesia’s meteorological agency warned that August and September are expected to be the most critical months for fire risk.

Weather-modification, or cloud-seeding, operations are considered one of the most effective ways to help firefighters combat wildfires by inducing rainfall through the dispersal of salt particles into suitable clouds.

However, the effort would be difficult to carry out because scientific monitoring “found no rain-bearing clouds suitable for weather-modification operations,” government minister Chaniago said.

With cloud-seeding ruled out because of unfavourable weather conditions, “we are relying solely on water bombing and ground firefighting teams,” said Forestry Minister, Raja Juli Antoni, while visiting Mount Bromo on Sunday. He urged the public to avoid activities that could spark new blazes, including discarding cigarette butts and clearing land by burning.

Wildfires have been reported in several of Indonesia’s most fire-prone regions, including 48,890 hectares of peatland ablaze in the provinces of Riau, Jambi and South Sumatra on Sumatra island, as well as Central Kalimantan and South Kalimantan on Borneo island. The emergency has forced regional authorities to deploy over 48,000 firefighters and disaster personnel, the National Disaster Management Agency said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.title: Turkiye approves pardon-like bill for thousands of PKK fighters
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.text:
Turkish lawmakers have approved legislation offering a conditional pardon for thousands of members of the outlawed Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), a major step towards ending decades of deadly violence.

The text – which passed on Monday with a vote of 468 in favour and 88 against, with six abstentions – envisages a return to civilian life for some of the PKK fighters who lay down their weapons without granting a total amnesty.

The law is Turkiye‘s first legislative step towards ending the conflict and comes 18 months after Abdullah Ocalan, the PKK’s jailed founder, urged his followers to disarm.

The PKK, designated a “terrorist” organisation by Turkiye, the United States and the European Union, launched its rebellion in 1984. The conflict has killed more than 40,000 people, imposed a heavy economic burden on mainly Kurdish southeast Turkiye, and fuelled decades of political and social division.

Backed by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AK Party) and the pro-Kurdish DEM Party, the bill suspends prosecutions and prison sentences for some offences for between five and 10 years.

The move is expected to involve the release of around 3,500 PKK-linked detainees in an initial phase, lawmakers said – around a third of the number held in Turkish prisons.

The law is Turkiye’s first legislative step towards ending the conflict. https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.title: Trump says relationship is good even as Netanyahu rejects Gaza peace plan
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.text:
United States President Donald Trump has briefly commented on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s outright rejection of the 15-point peace plan for Gaza drafted by the US-led Board of Peace.

Trump insisted on Monday that his relationship with Netanyahu is “very good” despite Netanyahu’s dismissal.

“The relationship is very good,” Trump said in response to a shouted question from a journalist at the end of an Oval Office event at the White House in Washington.

After more than a week of gradually escalating criticism, Netanyahu explicitly stated on Sunday that he opposed the Gaza plan, which called for Israel to begin pulling back forces in tandem with disarmament by Hamas.

Polls show that the Gaza plan is unpopular with Netanyahu’s right-wing base, and far-right members of his cabinet had urged him to kill it.

Trump late last month announced a breakthrough in the US-led ceasefire framework, saying that Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza had accepted a phased plan under which they would surrender their weapons to a new Palestinian governing body, and Israel would begin pulling out troops in tandem with disarmament to end the Israel-Palestine conflict that began in October 2023.

When the blueprint was first released by the Board of Peace on July 31, Netanyahu kept quiet for days, only later acknowledging that the Trump administration had “sent us a draft”, and that he did not agree with it. But Sunday was the first time that the Israeli prime minister formally asserted his refusal to endorse it.

The Israeli army “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed … and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens”, Netanyahu said on Sunday, adding that Israel is “talking to the Americans about this issue”, further vowing that “no Palestinian state will arise as long as I am prime minister”.

Netanyahu’s comments signal a growing public policy rift between the US and Israel over Tel Aviv’s hard-power strategy. Reporting from Washington, DC, Al Jazeera’s Patty Culhane said that Netanyahu is playing a “very dangerous game” with Trump. Israel is growing increasingly unpopular in the US, with the Democratic Party “very much sliding towards the Palestinian cause”, said Culhane.

On Monday, a Board of Peace official said the Gaza plan is still operative.

“The process is based on implementation and verification on the ground,” the official told Reuters. “Discussions with Israel are continuing, and the framework is designed so that each stage only moves forward once the required commitments have been met. The roadmap is between the Board of Peace and Hamas and discussions with Israel are continuing. Israel is not being asked to rely on trust or to make irreversible moves before verified steps are taken on the ground.”

Al Jazeera reached out to the White House and US Department of State for comment on Netanyahu’s remarks, but has received no response at the time of this writing.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.summary: Trump said on Monday that his relationship with Netanyahu is ‘very good’ despite Netanyahu’s dismissal of the Gaza plan. Netanyahu explicitly stated on Sunday that he opposed the Gaza plans.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.title: US appeals court says social media addiction lawsuits can proceed
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.text:
A federal appeals court in the United States has permitted thousands of lawsuits to move forward against Meta, Google, TikTok, Snapchat and other social media companies for allegedly designing addictive products that harm children, rejecting the companies’ initial bids to stop litigation before trial.

The San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the appeal came too early – most appeals are only filed after a case concludes with a ruling or verdict. The companies had argued that Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act which generally shields online platforms from liability over user-generated and user-posted content, also protected them from claims that they failed to warn the public about the addictive design of their platforms.

The court disagreed, finding that Section 230 offers a defence to liability rather than blanket immunity from being sued, rendering the appeal premature.

The panel also denied Meta’s request to delay the trial set to begin on Wednesday, brought by 29 state attorneys general who allege the company illegally collected and used children’s data, and engineered its platforms to keep young users hooked, ultimately misleading the public about their safety.

The ruling comes as several countries are penalising social media platforms’ allegedly harmful design that can directly impact children’s and teenagers’ health, including self-harm and eating disorders, according to The Guardian. France plans to ban under-15s from social media sites and prohibit mobile phones in high schools from next month. Australia has also imposed a ban and Britain plans one next year.

The legal moves reflect rising public concern over online harms to minors. President Emmanuel Macron has pointed to social media as a factor in youth violence and has signalled he wants France to follow Australia’s world-first ban on social media for children under 16. The law obliges major social media platforms to block under-16s, with companies that fail to comply facing penalties of up to 49.5 million Australian dollars ($35 million).

In late May, Britain’s then Prime Minister, Keir Starmer, vowed to take “decisive” action to tackle the impact of social media on British youngsters. That was after families, who insist their children died as a result of social media, and campaigners rallied outside Downing Street to hold tech giants accountable.

The US lawsuits, filed by states, municipalities, school districts and individual families, allege that the companies knowingly built addictive products that have fuelled the surge in depression, anxiety and broader youth mental health crises. The cases are centralised before US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers in Oakland, California, where plaintiffs are seeking damages, penalties and restitution.

A jury in Los Angeles has already found Meta and Google negligent in the first such case to reach trial, awarding $6m to a 20-year-old woman who said she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube as a child, according to Reuters.

Meta separately lost both phases of a New Mexico lawsuit, with a jury ordering $375m in damages over misleading safety claims and a judge later imposing an additional $567m penalty after finding the company had created a public nuisance.

Meta and Google have denied wrongdoing and said they plan to appeal.
