Thermal energy systems typically use a network of underground water-filled pipes to move and regulate heat across buildings and other infrastructure. Because temperatures deep underground are relatively stable, these systems can use the Earth as a source for heating and cooling.

The subway pilot will study the use of radiant cooling technology, where a cooling loop runs beneath surfaces in the station, absorbing heat out of the surrounding environment and transferring it into the water.

During the summer, some thermal systems can store heat in underground boreholes until winter. MTA chairman and CEO Janno Lieber hopes the study will find a way to store that excess heat to warm nearby municipal buildings during colder months.

“Bringing down the temperature is a real challenge in a century-old system with open entrances and vents everywhere,” said Lieber, adding that he hopes the system would result in energy savings for the city.

The MTA has been looking for ways to cool subway stations since at least 2023. Not only does the heat impact equipment, such as switches and signals, but the subway operations reinforce the problem, according to a climate resilience report that MTA published in 2024.

When trains brake in the stations, the friction generates heat. The trains’ air-conditioning systems also release heat into the stations. And the electrical equipment generates heat when it’s operating, as do the air conditioning units used to cool it.

Brooklyn Bridge-City Hall, one of the stations involved in the pilot program, reached average temperatures of 96 degrees last summer, Lieber said at a Monday press conference, calling it “one of the sweatiest in our system.” Chambers Street, which serves more than 18,000 riders on an average weekday, is the other station involved in the pilot program.

A statement from Mamdani’s office says that the MTA plans to award the contract for the feasibility study by this fall. If thermal energy networks are deemed viable for these stations, the design phase could begin in early 2027.

If it succeeds, New York would be the first state to use thermal energy networks in its subway system. Interest in thermal energy networks has risen across the state in recent years, with city developers and property owners increasingly exploring the technology. Local utilities often offer incentives for installations.

The state legislature passed a bill in 2022 that allowed gas and electric utilities to own and operate thermal energy networks. Environmental groups, labor unions and utilities supported the legislation. New York’s Public Service Commission, which regulates local utilities, directed the seven largest investor-owned ones to develop at least one pilot geothermal project.

By 2024, there were 12 pilot projects in active development—including three at Con Edison, the main electric utility in downstate New York. One of these projects would use thermal energy networks to store excess heat from the Rockefeller Center’s existing cooling system to heat three commercial buildings in Midtown Manhattan.

Jenille Scott, the climate director for ALIGN, a worker-advocacy organization that has called for the development of more thermal energy systems, said that she was excited by the idea of them in subway stations because they are very efficient and the buildout could bring new construction jobs to the city.

Because of the climate crisis, heat will continue to pose a challenge for subway riders. A 2024 report by the New York City Panel on Climate Change projected that, by the 2080s, the number of days per year with maximum temperatures at or above 82 degrees Fahrenheit in the city will nearly double. Currently, the city reaches or exceeds that temperature 69 days a year.

“Sweltering subway platforms are not just uncomfortable, they are a matter of health and safety,” said Louise Yeung, the city’s chief climate officer. “Amidst one of the hottest summers on record, we need no reminder that our aging infrastructure is not keeping pace with our changing climate.”

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: Trump pushes rethink of school vaccine mandates and MMR shots
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
US President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday pushing for a rethink of school vaccine mandates and repeating calls for the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine to be separated into three individual shots.

Curbing vaccines has been a key priority for Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, who founded an anti-vaccine non-profit and has long promoted a disproven link between immunisation and autism.

The federal government does not have direct control over several areas covered by the order. States, for example, have the authority to require vaccinations for students to attend school.

On these points Trump's move is more of a suggestion than an order.

"States and territories are advised to review" the Trump administration's recommendations on "immunisation requirements for contexts such as school enrolment and attendance," the order states.

In another section, it says the US Health and Human Services department will form a task force to offer the MMR shot as individual vaccines "by working with the private sector and other countries as appropriate, while guaranteeing continued availability of combination vaccines and those vaccines recommended for shared clinical decision-making."

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Years of scientific evidence support the safety of a combined MMR vaccine.

Public health experts have long advised that the combined shot offers children more protection faster, and also decreases the logistical hurdles for parents who may struggle to make multiple appointments.

Yet during the Oval Office signing, Trump made a series of incendiary and unsupported statements, including: "Together, there could be a possibility they are quite lethal."

In a call with reporters, Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), estimated it would take more than a decade to develop approved separated vaccines in the US.

"We're advising that you continue to give children a vaccine that has decades of safety data," added Aaron M. Milstone, a member of the AAP Committee on Infectious Diseases.

In a separate press call, senior White House officials were asked repeatedly why the president wanted to separate the components of the MMR shot, but they did not provide any clear rationale.

Senator Bill Cassidy, a doctor whose deciding vote confirmed Kennedy's controversial appointment as health chief, posted on X that the president's initiative would only serve to "increase hesitancy and make children less safe."

"This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes. Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism," Cassidy said.

The Trump administration's push to overhaul vaccine policy comes as its efforts to implement major changes were blocked by a federal court earlier this year, pending further court proceedings.

The judge's stay preventing the overhaul sided with major medical organisations, which asserted that the Trump administration's actions to push the changes through were unlawful.

The president's latest order also arrives just as children across the country are readying to return to school, and as the US suffers its worst measles outbreak in 35 years.

Trump's health secretary Kennedy is accused of contributing significantly to the crisis by spreading anti-vaccine sentiment and fuelling fears of well-studied and proven immunisations.

READ MORE
US scraps universal child vaccine guidance, drawing expert concern

Polling indicates that most Americans still support vaccination, and in recent months both Kennedy and Trump had backed off anti-vaccination rhetoric which could spell negative repercussions in November's midterm vote.

But Monday's efforts show the issue remains a core component of their health policy agenda, as both men remain committed to the false notion that vaccines can cause autism.

Such a potential link has been debunked by years of research.

"The Trump administration's proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule illustrate the risks of allowing government recommendations to occupy a privileged position in medical decision-making," said Jeffrey Singer of the Cato Institute in a statement.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/b.title: Bird flu drives a 50 per cent cost increase for badminton players
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/b.author: Will Corbett
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Avian Influenza

The professional shuttlecock is made from goose or duck feathers. (ABC Sydney: Amanda Hoh)

Australian badminton clubs are paying a premium for equipment as bird flu drives up the price of goose feathers.

Goose or duck feathers are used to craft shuttlecocks, the projectile central to the game.

Clubs and players are switching to synthetic shuttlecocks to manage costs, but players are adamant they are a poor quality substitute for the real thing.

While bird flu has only landed on Australian shores in the last few months, a group of sportsmen and women have been feeling its impact for years.

The deadly strain of H5 avian influenza has riddled wild and domesticated avian species across the world, with the total number of dead birds in the hundreds of millions.

While the spread of the disease has Australians across science and agriculture increasingly concerned, the nation's badminton players have long counted its costs.

The mass culling of flocks of geese and poultry across east and central Asia in recent years has massively cut the global supply of feathers critical to making the shuttlecocks needed for any game of the racquet sport to go ahead.

Countries across the world have culled birds to manage H5N1 outbreaks. (Reuters: Luc Gnago)

The impact has seen equipment costs skyrocket for badminton clubs across the country.

A high-quality shuttlecock uses 16 feathers from the left wing of either a duck or a goose, though each bird can only supply two to three feathers that meet specifications.

China is home to most of the world's poultry farms where the specific feathers are harvested, leaving the product exposed to major price fluctuations pinned to the health of the birds.

Goose feathers are at a premium as healthy flocks become rarer. (ABC Great Southern: Eliza Kavanagh)

Badminton Australia chief executive Tjitte Weistra says even a mid-range shuttle, such as the Yonex AS-30, has become near-unaffordable for most players and clubs.

"This means the cost of hosting a tournament or even club play can get very, very expensive."

Tjitte Weistra said synthetic shuttles are not yet good enough for most players. (Supplied: Tjitte Weistra)

Great Southern Badminton Association chair Michelle Watson said her organisation spends $3,000 on shuttles every four to six months.

Nightly fees have had to rise to maintain quality equipment with synthetic alternatives not an option.

Michelle Watson (right) says increasing costs have been challenging for local players. (Supplied: Michelle Watson)

"Feathers are what the game should be played with and are far superior," she said.

"Players that understand the game and play more than at a social level expect quality shuttles.

Metamorph Shuttle director Ryan Zengyuan said WA's near-total reliance on imported equipment left local players even more exposed.

"An agricultural supply crash in Asia instantly triggers inventory shortages and doubles prices for local players," Mr Zengyuan said.

"[As a result] local sport retailers have been forced to increase retail prices by 30 to 50 per cent over the last few years to cover the skyrocketing cost of raw feathers and international freight."

Players say you cannot replicate the flight of natural feather shuttles. (ABC Great Southern: Will Corbett)

While bird flu has decimated the global feather market, freight costs, oil prices and competition for the cork used in the head of the shuttle are additional factors in the rising prices.

Mr Weistra said local clubs are starting to look at alternative options to curb the price rise, including players making peace with synthetic shuttles.

"They're trying to get cheaper feather shuttles which don't have the same characteristics," he said.

"I guess they are inclined to look at alternative options and accept that maybe they're not perfect, but it will do for now."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/b.title: Ben Jones, who played Cooter in the Dukes of Hazzard, has died
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Arts, Culture and Entertainment

Ben Jones, who played Cooter in the original Dukes of Hazzard TV series, has died. (AP: Steve Helber)

Ben Jones, who played the good ol' boy mechanic in The Dukes of Hazzard TV series and parlayed his fame into a political career and two terms in the US House of Representatives, has died.

Jones had a heart attack in his home on Sunday in Washington, Virginia, as he was waiting to watch his beloved Atlanta Braves play baseball, his wife, Alma Viator, said on social media.

Jones's fame came from his role as Cooter Davenport, the mechanic who got the Duke boys out of jams as they tried to fight the corrupt Boss Hogg in the fictional Hazzard County, Georgia.

After playing Cooter for all seven seasons of the series from 1979 to 1985, Mr Jones turned to politics and was elected for the Democrats to the US House from a district near Atlanta in 1988.

Ben Jones, second from right, with The Dukes of Hazzard cast, from left, Denver Pyle, Catherine Bach, John Schneider and Tom Wopat.

Jones was born in North Carolina.

While he attended college he became involved in acting and civil rights, he wrote in his autobiography Redneck Boy in the Promised Land: The Confessions of 'Crazy Cooter'.

Acting took over his life.

Jones performed in numerous stage productions and had a few minor TV and movie roles in Atlanta during the 1970s before his life-defining break came on a TV show Jones defended as a modern-day morality tale and a fine example of Southern values.

For seven seasons, Jones was one of a small band of friends and family helping Bo and Luke Duke in The Dukes of Hazzard.

The brothers were on probation for running moonshine and were constantly trying to clear their names and stop the crooked and powerful Boss Hogg from stealing or cheating.

The Duke boys drove a modified 1969 Dodge Charger called the General Lee with a Confederate flag on its roof.

Cooter owned Cooter's Garage in the town square.

Shooter Jennings unearthed a treasure trove of unreleased recordings from his legendary father Waylon.

Nearly every episode involved a car chase with jumps and stunts and a patrol car badly in need of repairs.

Cooter was often on the CB radio in his pickup truck saying: "Breaker one, Breaker one. I might be crazy but I ain't dumb. Crazy Cooter coming at you."

The Dukes of Hazzard was a hit for CBS and its popularity never waned.

It went into syndication and later became a prominent fixture on cable's The Nashville Network.

Jones also credited the series with pulling him out of a self-destructive, alcoholic lifestyle that led to the failure of several marriages.

"It was like being in a Beatles movie," Jones said.

Tom Wopat, who played Luke Duke, said Jones was an integral part of making the series work.

"Ben Jones was a fine friend and a fierce advocate of all the best things we can offer in the entertainment business. He will be sorely missed," Wopat wrote on Instagram.

After The Dukes of Hazzard, Jones went into politics.

He kept his 'aw shucks' personality, but took the issues seriously.

In his four years in Washington, Jones was known as a Democrat who could buck his party.

He was liberal on social issues and conservative on economics.

But even in politics, he made a splash.

Ben Jones was elected for the Democrats but was prepared to vote against party lines. (AP: Joe Holloway Jr)

After losing in 1992 when the boundaries to his district were redrawn, Jones ran for Congress again in 1994.

He lost to Newt Gingrich in the elections that elevated the Republican to the Speaker's office.

Jones would file an ethics complaint that Mr Gingrich used tax-deductible donations to fund his partisan college course leading to a House reprimand and Mr Gingrich's decision to leave the body.

Jones always embraced his role as Cooter.

After moving to Virginia, he opened at least three Cooter's country stores in Nashville and Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, and near his home.

They sold T-shirts, key chains and insulated tumblers and included Dukes of Hazzard memorabilia like one of the 300 or so General Lee cars used and abused in the TV series.

The show and Cooter lived on because it was funny, had plenty of action and car chases and had a good, family-friendly heart, Jones told the Richmond Times-Dispatch at a 2001 car show, when he played in a band, signed autographs and met fans.

"The show reflects the values of the heartland of America. The good guys always win," Jones said.

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.title: Trump extends Jones Act waiver for 90 days, narrows scope
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.author: Reuters
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.text:
The extension ensures the US military and key industries maintain uninterrupted access to critical resources, the White House said

US President Donald Trump has extended for 90 days a waiver allowing foreign-flagged ships to transport oil and other commodities between US ports but imposed new limits after shipbuilders and their allies in ‌Congress argued the policy was undermining the domestic maritime industry, the White House said.

The extension, finalised on Monday, comes as the war with Iran disrupts global crude flows and pushes up fuel costs, increasing pressure on the administration to find ways to ease transport bottlenecks and keep petrol and other energy prices from rising further.

The 90-day extension ensures the US military and key industries maintain uninterrupted access to critical resources, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said on Monday.

“Data shows the waiver has driven ⁠a significant increase in domestic deliveries of essential products such as gasoline, diesel and jet fuel,” Rogers said in a post on social media.

Under the new terms, the administration has narrowed the scope of the relief, requiring individual voyages to undergo case-by-case review rather than allowing foreign ships to receive blanket exemptions from the Jones ‌Act, a White House official confirmed.

The Jones Act requires cargo moving between US ports to be carried on ships ⁠built in the US, owned ⁠by US companies and crewed by American workers, and the waiver aims to lower gas prices by increasing shipping flexibility and reducing transport bottlenecks.

The waiver was set to ‌expire on August 16 without the extension. It is the longest suspension of the more than a century-old law in its history.

Targeted Jones Act waivers provide critical flexibility to move ‌American energy ‌efficiently between US ports and deliver fuels to consumers at a time of continuing global market volatility, industry trade group American ‌Petroleum Institute said.

While the Jones Act waiver increases the availability of tankers to move fuel, it would probably only reduce petrol prices by pennies ⁠per gallon, some analysts and industry experts have said.

The American Maritime Partnership, which is in favour of the Jones Act, said it ⁠was disappointed that the waiver had been extended but that requiring a case-by-case review is an improvement over the previous blanket waiver.

The group urged the Trump administration to conduct a rigorous review of the national defence justification for each ‌waiver request and assess the availability of ‌US vessels before allowing a foreign vessel to move cargo between US ports.

About 208 exemptions to the Jones Act were granted in about four-and-a-half months until August 3, US government data showed.

https://www.scmp.com/news/us/article/336.title: China moves to join Brazil’s WTO fight over Trump’s forced labour tariffs
https://www.scmp.com/news/us/article/336.author: Igor Patrick
https://www.scmp.com/news/us/article/336.text:
Beijing said it held a substantial commercial interest in consultations Brasilia opened over duties of up to 37.5 per cent

China has asked to join World Trade Organization consultations that Brazil opened against US tariffs of up to 37.5 per cent.

Beijing filed the request in Geneva on Monday, telling the trade body it held a substantial commercial interest in the case.

The move was first reported by the Brazilian newspaper Folha de S. Paulo and independently confirmed to the South China Morning Post by a Brazilian government source.

In the request, China said Washington could apply comparable measures to Chinese goods, and that such measures would affect all Chinese exports to the American market, subject to specific exemptions.

It said the additional duties altered the conditions of competition for Chinese products sold in the United States. The document had not yet appeared in the WTO’s public records on Monday.

The grounds Beijing set out concern its own exports rather than the treatment of Brazilian goods. China has challenged Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974 at the WTO since 2018. It argues the statute lets Washington determine violations and impose penalties without multilateral authorisation.

Under WTO rules on dispute settlement, a member claiming a substantial trade interest may notify the parties and the Dispute Settlement Body within 10 days of the circulation of the original complaint. The country being challenged decides whether the claim is well founded, and a member turned away is free to open a case of its own.

A member admitted to the consultations does not become a complainant in the dispute. It takes part in the discussions and sees what is exchanged. It cannot make claims of its own or ask for a panel, and would have to open a separate case to do either.

A Chinese commerce ministry spokesman said in March that the inquiry was “highly unilateral, arbitrary and discriminatory” and noted that the United States has never ratified the Forced Labour Convention of 1930.

Beijing made representations to Washington while the two sides were holding trade talks in Paris, the spokesman said.

Chinese officials have repeatedly invoked a September 2020 WTO panel report that found American tariffs on Chinese goods under Section 301 inconsistent with global trade rules. Washington appealed.

The report has never taken effect, and China has separate consultations pending against American tariff measures adopted last year. The Trump administration extended 178 product exclusions from the Section 301 duties on Chinese goods to November after the president met Xi Jinping in November.

Brazil contends the two measures exceed the tariff ceilings in the American schedule of concessions and breach the most favoured nation rule, which bars a member from giving one trading partner worse terms than it gives the rest.

It also argues that Washington sought redress through unilateral determinations rather than through the dispute settlement system, the same claim China brought in 2018.

The United States has accepted the request for consultations, according to Folha, although no date has been set for the talks to begin.

The Brazilian foreign ministry said the duties reached more than 23 per cent of the country’s exports to the American market.

A Brazilian government source, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the case publicly, said Brasilia read the Chinese request as “a signal of support” and as confirmation that its complaint “reached beyond Brazilian interests”.

But the same source admitted that the dispute would remain “largely political” until the WTO appellate body is restored, because the organisation cannot penalise the United States over the tariffs.

The appellate body is the final stage of WTO litigation and needs at least three members to hear a case.

It lost its quorum in December 2019 after Washington blocked replacements for departing members, and the seats remain empty. A losing party at panel stage can appeal to a body that cannot hear the case, which leaves the ruling unadopted and blocks any authorisation to retaliate.

Should the consultations fail within 60 days, Brazil may ask for a panel of experts to rule on the measures.

The Chinese embassy in Brasilia did not immediately respond to a SCMP request for comment and the commerce ministry in Beijing has not addressed the filing publicly.

The move was first reported by the Brazilian newspaper Folha de S. Paulo. China has challenged Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974 at the WTO since 2018.

https://www.dw.com/en/turkey-mps-back-hi.title: Turkey MPs back historic law on reintegrating PKK militants
https://www.dw.com/en/turkey-mps-back-hi.text:
Turkey's parliament has taken a major step toward ending four decades of conflict with the PKK. The new law sets out how some militants can return to civilian life, but leaves Abdullah Ocalan's future unresolved.

Turkey's parliament on Monday approved legislation offering a conditional pardon and legal protections to thousands of members of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK).

After around 12 hours of debate, lawmakers voted 468 to 88 in favor of the 12-article bill, with six abstentions. It was backed by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's AK Party, its nationalist MHP allies and the pro-Kurdish DEM party.

The law sets out procedures for the PKK's disarmament and dissolution and the reintegration of some members into civilian life. The government has stressed that it is not a general amnesty.

Some prison sentences would be suspended, while investigations and trials could be postponed for five or 10 years depending on the offense.

If those covered commit no terrorism-related crime during that period, cases would be dropped and sentences considered served.

Around 3,500 PKK-linked detainees could initially be released, lawmakers said. Media reports suggest exiled members and fighters in Iraq and Syria could also benefit.

People convicted of intentional killings and some serving life sentences are excluded.

The measures will only come into force once Turkey's National Security Council confirms that the PKK has dissolved and surrendered all weapons.

Those seeking to benefit would then have six months to apply. Ministerial and parliamentary committees are also due to monitor the process.

Turkey’s Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz called the vote a "historic step", saying "the 468 'yes' votes are of the utmost importance in terms of political consensus".

The law does not cover imprisoned PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan, 77, who has been held on Imrali island near Istanbul since 1999.

Yilmaz said Ocalan's case "does not fall within the scope of this law", but added that he could remain "in a position to contribute to the peace process".

Ocalan has been central to the initiative. In February 2025, he urged the PKK to disarm and dissolve and pursue Kurdish rights through democratic means.

The PKK announced its dissolution in May 2025. Two months later, militants symbolically burned weapons at a ceremony in northern Iraq and the group said it was withdrawing fighters from Turkey.

The PKK has called the legislation a "beginning" but said it contains "serious shortcomings and deficiencies."

It has demanded Ocalan's release and said the process can move forward only if he "lives and works freely."

The group also said fighters would not return without guarantees that they could engage in politics without prosecution over their views or organizations.

Pro-Kurdish DEM lawmaker Gulistan Kilic Kocyigit said: "The people of Turkey, who have paid a heavy price for many years, now have an opportunity to consolidate peace and build democracy."

Nationalist opposition lawmakers accuse the government of making concessions to the PKK.

"How can you negotiate with terrorists? You said they would be laying down their weapons unconditionally," said Turhan Comez, a lawmaker with the nationalist opposition Iyi party.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iyi Party leader Musavat Dervisoglu also said the law "would pave the way" for Erdogan to remain in power. Erdogan could run again if parliament calls an early election during his current term.

The PKK launched its insurgency in 1984. More than 40,000 people have been killed, and the conflict has caused major economic damage in Kurdish-majority southeastern Turkey and fueled decades of political and social division.

The PKK initially sought an independent Kurdish state but later shifted toward demands for autonomy and expanded rights.

It is designated a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States and the European Union.

Previous peace efforts failed, most recently in 2015.

The initiative could also have regional effects, including closer Turkish-Iraqi ties and implications for efforts to integrate areas in Syria administered by the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF).

The SDF's dominant militia, the People's Defense Units (YPG), is seen as an offshoot of the PKK, and is considered by Ankara to be a terrorist organization.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Ilhan Omar questions whether Trump administration has used ICE to ‘surveil’ critics
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Congresswoman demands answers after a DHS agent was apparently stationed outside her Minnesota town hall

Donald Trump’s administration is facing questions over whether it is using Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to “surveil political opponents” after after an investigative agent was apparently stationed outside Democratic representative Ilhan Omar’s monthly town hall meeting in Richfield, Minnesota.

After the incident, Omar demanded the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) clarify whether Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents have been used to monitor “any other activity” involving “local, state, or federal officials” in the state.

In a letter to Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), an arm of ICE, the congresswoman said an agent claiming to be conducting an undercover drug operation was parked outside the community center where she was holding an event last Thursday, without prior coordination with local law enforcement.

According to Omar, who represents Minnesota’s fifth congressional district, a Richfield police officer noticed the agent sitting in a Ford Explorer and “became suspicious of the way she was monitoring the building”.

“He proceeded to run the plates attached to the vehicle and discovered they were registered to a different vehicle,” said Omar. “He approached the woman in the vehicle to ask about the purpose for her presence there and why the plates on her vehicle did not match the government’s records. Like any reasonable officer, he was concerned that she harbored ill intentions and may be in a stolen vehicle.”

The woman initially identified herself as security, but later called her supervisor and said she was an HSI agent conducting an undercover drug operation in the area, Omar said. Richfield police had not been informed of the operation beforehand, according the congresswoman.

Omar said that despite a visible sign indicating that a town hall was taking place at the community center, the agent remained parked there until speaking with her supervisor, after which she left the property.

“HSI’s actions yesterday evening put an entire community at risk,” she said. “Instead of monitoring the area for those who might wish harm to me and my constituents, Richfield Police were required to devote time to investigating why an HSI agent was outside of a Congressional event in a vehicle with mismatched plates.”

Omar added: “It also raises serious and uncomfortable questions about the purpose of HSI’s presence outside of my event. At best, your agent was unable to assess that the parking lot of a community center hosting a congressional event wasn’t the best place to conduct a drug operation.

“At worst, it emphasizes many Americans’ growing concern that the Trump administration uses ICE to surveil political opponents and may interfere with our democracy.”

In her letter, Omar is demanding answers about why the agent was at the community center, how the agent and her supervisor knew she was holding a town hall there and what action they took in response to that knowledge.

The Guardian has contacted DHS for comment.

Inside the department, HSI is a federal law enforcement agency and the main investigative branch of ICE. ICE operations in Minnesota have sparked widespread protests across the state this year and have also resulted in the deaths of two Americans, Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, who were killed by federal agents.

In January, a man sprayed Omar with an unidentified substance from a syringe during a town hall where she called for ICE to be abolished “for good”.

The incident drew widespread condemnation from local and state leaders, with Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey calling it “unacceptable” and saying: “We can disagree without putting people at risk.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Ilhan Omar demands answers from Homeland Security Investigations (DHS) after incident. She says agent was parked outside her town hall in Richfield, Minnesota.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/now-ri.title: Now Rippling is counter suing tiny startup Runlayer
https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/now-ri.author: Julie Bort
https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/now-ri.text:
HR startup Rippling filed a lawsuit Monday accusing MCP gateway startup Runlayer of infringing on three of its patents, according to the lawsuit seen by TechCrunch.

The filing comes after Runlayer sued the HR startup last month, accusing it of breach of contract and stealing its product ideas.

It’s the latest saga between the two companies after Rippling spent nearly a year testing the startup’s MCP product. The two companies never agreed on a price, and the trial never turned into a paid contract. Instead, Rippling built its own MCP server, and will soon offer it as a product that competes with Runlayer. (Rippling often turns its internally used tech into products, like its recently released AI Spend Console.)

Their battle serves as a warning of how the relationship between customers and startups can devolve in this AI-powered age of fast product building.

Runlayer, which launched its product about a year ago, bundles an MCP gateway with cybersecurity features like threat detection. MCP is an open standard that allows AI agents to connect with data and software systems needed to work independently.

Runlayer has raised a total of $42 million and was founded by third-time founder Andrew Berman. (His previous companies were baby-monitor maker Nanit and an AI video conferencing tool, Vowel, that sold to Zapier in 2024). Rippling became one of Runlayer’s earliest potential customers trialing its software.

The most dramatic detail in the lawsuit is Runlayer’s claim that a Rippling employee reached out to Berman to warn him that his employer was building a “copy” of Runlayer’s product. A Rippling spokesperson tells TechCrunch that its employee has since revised that view.

On Rippling’s side, perhaps the most dramatic claim is that it informed Runlayer of the patents it believed Runlayer had infringed soon after the startup filed its lawsuit.

One might infer that the suit is intended as leverage to bring Runlayer to the settlement table. Indeed, that’s how Runlayer views it.

“This is a desperate, retaliatory ploy to distract from the fact Rippling misappropriated our proprietary technology. We clearly have a standout AI product that has nothing to do with these patents. No attempt to bully or distract will prevent us from protecting our IP and continuing to innovate and create the best product for our fast-growing customer base,” Berman said in a written statement.

Rippling loves a good fighting-words statement too. Its spokesperson told TechCrunch: “It takes a certain boldness to accuse a competitor of violating intellectual property laws while infringing on that competitor’s inventions. But that’s exactly what Runlayer has done here. Rippling’s lawsuit calls out Runlayer’s hypocrisy. Having manufactured claims against Rippling to distract from its business failures, it now has to face a lawsuit for repeatedly copying Rippling’s inventions in building its own products.”

Now it’s up to the courts to unwind who did what to whom, unless the parties settle. But these dueling cases still serve as a buyer- and seller-beware warning. With AI advances, enterprises have never before been more empowered to build tech in-house. Yet they still may put a startup through its paces before choosing that option.

https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: 'Launching anywhere, anytime and without compromise': Rocket Lab unveils new 'GHOST' portable spaceport system
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Mike Wall
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
"We've mastered the art of building launch sites. Now we're making them deployable worldwide."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rocket Lab plans to start launching even more frequently and flexibly, thanks to a new portable spaceport system called "GHOST."

GHOST — short for "Global Hypersonic & Orbital Spaceport Technology" — turns the company's "Electron and HASTE rockets into a launch-anywhere, launch-anytime capability for multi-launch flight campaigns and critical national security missions," Rocket Lab representatives said in a statement today (Aug. 10).

"Packaged entirely within standard shipping containers, GHOST deploys complete rockets, launch infrastructure, ground support and range control systems anywhere in the world," they added.

Electron is Rocket Lab's workhorse orbital rocket, giving small satellites dedicated rides to the final frontier. The expendable 59-foot-tall (18-meter-tall) launcher debuted with a test flight in 2017 and has 83 missions under its belt to date.

As its full name suggests, HASTE ("Hypersonic Accelerator Suborbital Test Electron") is a suborbital version of Electron that customers use to test various technologies in the hypersonic flight environment. HASTE first flew in June 2023 and has flown nine times to date, most recently in June of this year.

Rocket Lab currently flies from two different launch sites — one on the North Island of company founder and CEO Peter Beck's native New Zealand and one at Wallops Island in Virginia. But the company recently announced plans to fly out of Alaska's Pacific Spaceport Complex as well, and GHOST will expand its launch footprint even further.

"Electron and HASTE revolutionized small orbital launch and hypersonic testing. Now we're making it easier to deploy them wherever they're needed most, whether that's for missile defense testing or sovereign orbital launch capability," Beck said this afternoon during Rocket Lab's second-quarter 2026 earnings call.

"We've mastered the art of building launch sites," he added. "Now we're making them deployable worldwide."

Rocket Lab intends to deploy its two planned pads at the Pacific Spaceport Complex using GHOST, Beck said during the call. The company was inspired to develop the portable spaceport system, he added, to meet the needs of a HASTE customer, who expressed a desire for Rocket Lab to be "a little bit more mobile than we are."

Rocket Lab currently flies out of two pads at its New Zealand site and one at Wallops, though it has built a second pad at the Virginia facility to accommodate launches of its coming Neutron rocket.

Neutron will be bigger and more powerful than Electron, and partially reusable as well; its first stage is designed to come back to Earth for recovery and reflight, like SpaceX's Falcon 9.

Rocket Lab originally wanted to fly Neutron for the first time in 2024, but the new launcher has yet to leave the ground. Such delays aren't uncommon in the case of new rockets, and the company is making considerable progress with Neutron, according to Beck.

"Every part of the vehicle has now seen significant testing," he said during today's call. "As with any complex development program, we've had to tweak a few things along the way, but we're moving now into final checkout and assembly of all of our flight hardware before integrating them at the pad."

The company is on target to deliver the first Neutron to that Wallops pad in the fourth quarter of this year, Beck added.

https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/elon-musk.title: Everything’s bigger in Texas: Musk’s planned $16.8 billion chip factory is five times bigger than the world’s current largest building
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/elon-musk.author: Joshua Hong
https://fortune.com/2026/08/10/elon-musk.text:
Elon Musk is betting that the next phase of his sprawling technology empire will require a building on a scale that has never existed before. SpaceX and Tesla are building Terafab, a 100-million-square-foot semiconductor manufacturing facility in Grimes County, Texas, more than five times the size of the world’s largest building.

“Terafab Texas will be the largest and most valuable building on Earth by far. And it will be stunningly beautiful,” Musk wrote on X.

With about 18.9 million square feet of floor space, the New Century Global Center in Chengdu, China, currently holds the record for the world’s largest building. But Terafab is expected to exceed that quickly: “The first phase of the Terafab project represents a capital investment of more than $16.8 billion and will create 3,000 new jobs,” Texas Gov. Greg Abbott wrote in a press release.

The accompanying vision is even more ambitious than the building itself. The Terafab website describes the project as a vertically integrated chip factory that will combine logic, memory, and advanced packaging under one roof. Both SpaceX and Tesla will benefit from the facility, which is designed to produce more than 1 terawatt of compute annually.

“We’re now embarking on the most epic chip-building effort—combining logic, memory, and advanced packaging all under one roof,” said Musk in a press release. The project seeks to “close the gap” between the chip production necessary for today and the demand for future production when humanity, according to Musk, eventually embarks on space travel.

“Terafab is bringing cutting-edge manufacturing to America, creating thousands of high-paying jobs,” he continued, “and enabling us to produce AI chips at scale for use on Earth and in space.”

Terafab is less of a conventional semiconductor factory rather than an attempt by Musk to build an enormous piece of his own technology supply chain. Both companies expect their combined demand for computing power to eventually exceed 1 terawatt. Terafab will bring chip manufacturing, packaging, and testing into one singular operation. The project aspires to launch a galactic civilization by harnessing “all of the energy on a planet,” echoing Musk’s sci-fi dreams.

Terafab’s website ties the factory to Musk’s longer-term vision of AI infrastructure. According to the site, the project is intended to produce AI chips at scale, supporting a vision that includes  as many as 1 million Tesla Optimus robots, 10 million tons of mass launched into orbit annually, and more than 1 terawatt of solar power.

SpaceX went public in June, raising $75 billion by selling 555.56 million shares at $135 apiece.  While the company had an initial valuation of about $1.77 trillion at the time, the public markets have already forced investors to confront the costs behind Musk’s ambitions. SpaceX reported a $541 million loss in its first quarterly earnings report as a public company, despite generating $7.8 billion in revenue. The $16.8 billion announced for Terafab is only the initial investment.

Musk hopes to use taxpayer dollars to offset some of the costs associated with building the largest single property in the world. The project has filed eight tax incentive applications with the two local school districts, asking to freeze school maintenance and operations property taxes at roughly 48% of appraised value for 10 years per phase. Terafab is asking the state to cover the difference of the maintenance and operations (M&0) and interest and sinking (I&S) taxes using the Texas Jobs, Energy, Technology, and Innovation, or JETI, program.

The company’s explanation for the tax breaks centered on the cost differential between Texas and “competing jurisdictions,” it wrote in the applications.

“Absent the limitation, the project IRR would fall below the minimum investment threshold, and competing jurisdictions (e.g., Arizona) would present a more favorable after-tax return,” the application read, “in which case the project would likely be relocated outside Texas.”

To Abbott, Texas is willing to take the hit. Texas extended SpaceX a $30 million Texas Enterprise Fund grant according to Abbott’s press release. SpaceX is already headquartered in Texas, as well as both Starbase’s launch facility and its manufacturing plant. Terafab is just another testament to Musk’s Texas footprint, Abbott said.

“Texas is where big ideas grow even bigger,” the governor said in the release. He called Terafab a “first-of-its-kind” facility that would accelerate chip production and create thousands of jobs.

The Terafab website compares the planned 100 million square feet with Tesla’s roughly 10-million-square-foot Gigafactory Texas and says the facility is designed around production at “terawatt scale.”

SpaceX and the office of Gov. Abbott both did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The 100-million-square-foot facility is more than five times the size of the world’s largest building. The project is designed to produce more than 1 terawatt of compute annually.

At 5:20 a.m. Eastern Time, oil was priced at $86.04 per barrel with Brent serving as the benchmark (we’ll explain different benchmarks later in this article). That’s a gain of $2.40 compared with yesterday morning and around $19 higher than the price one year ago.

Check Out Our Daily Rates Reports

It’s impossible to forecast oil prices with detailed precision. Many different elements affect the market, but ultimately it boils down to supply and demand. When worries about economic recession, war, and other large-scale disruptions increase, oil’s path can shift fast.

Gas prices at the pump don’t only track crude oil. They also include what it takes to refine and move that fuel, the taxes layered on top, and the extra markup your local station adds to stay in business.

Since crude oil generally makes up a majority of the per-gallon cost, changes in its price have an outsized impact. When oil surges, gas prices typically rise in tandem. But when oil retreats, gas prices often lag on the way down, a trend sometimes described as “rockets and feathers.”

In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks.

It’s not a long-term answer and is more meant to provide temporary relief, assisting consumers and keeping critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc.

Both oil and natural gas are key sources of the energy we use every day. Because of this, a big change in oil prices can affect natural gas. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which increases demand for natural gas.

To gauge oil’s performance, we often turn to two benchmarks:

Between these two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/s.title: Federal police urged to investigate 'concerning' subsea cable fault
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/s.author: Rachel Stowers and Emma Wynne
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Information and Communication

High voltage undersea cable being laid into water.  (Prysmian Group)

Two separate cables in the Submarine Cable Protection Zone off Perth had both experienced faults in short succession over the weekend.

The cables are vital for international communications between Australia and the rest of the world.

The cables' owner, Subco, is urging the Australian Federal Police to investigate.

Two subsea cables off the coast of Perth, vital for international communications, suffered a fault over the weekend, and the company that owns them urgently wants to know what happened.

The chief executive of the cable company Subco, Bevan Slattery, wrote on LinkedIn yesterday that two separate cables in the Submarine Cable Protection Zone off Perth had both experienced faults "straight after each other and in close proximity to each other".

His post further said that it was a concerning development and called for the Australian Federal Police to investigate urgently.

David Brewster, senior research fellow at the National Security College at the Australian National University, told Nadia Mitsopoulos on 102.5 ABC Perth that the international cables that link Australia to the world are vital.

"Australia has 16 subsea cables that carry 99 per cent of our international communications," Dr Brewster said.

"It's really fundamental to the Australian economy and our daily life, and if they were to be disrupted or cease, it would have a massive impact on our country.

Undersea cables lie on the ocean floor, are about the width of a garden hose and can be easily cut by accident, by ship's anchors.

They can also be cut deliberately.

"We've seen numerous incidents in Europe and around Taiwan over the last, say, three or four years of cables being cut," he said.

"It's difficult to be absolutely certain of the reasons in some of these cases, but in a great number of cases, it's fairly obvious that they were done by state actors, Russia and China."

A network of subsea cables link world communications. (Wikimedia Commons)

In this case, the cables that were damaged inside the Perth Cable Protection Zone, which extends 60 nautical miles off City Beach, to a depth of 2,000 metres and one nautical mile each side of the cables.

Dr Brewster said the best protection strategy would be to lay more cables.

"We've put many of the cables in what's called a cable protection zones, but it is extremely difficult to stop a determined adversary from cutting the cables. It's extremely difficult to stop cyber attacks on the cables," he said.

He said we also needed to consider who owned the cables.

"They are all privately owned, and increasingly, they are being owned by US tech companies such as Meta or Google or Amazon," he said.

"That does create other risks as well, because it means that not only are these cables privately owned, but they're also privately owned by, in many cases, foreign companies.

"The government has very limited power to actually influence what is being done into how these cables are operated or repaired."

He said a further complicating issue was that no single government department or agency was responsible for the cables. Rather, multiple departments had jurisdiction over some aspects of the subsea cable sector.

"We need to nominate an agency to take responsibility for protecting the cables and any response," he said.

"Who do you call when a cable is being cut or disrupted? For many private operators, it's really not clear to them who takes responsibility within government."

Mr Slattery was unavailable to be interviewed.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2.title: Where do foreign residents in Japan want to die?
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2.author: Yumi Wijers-hasegawa
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2.text:
Across Japan, people are preparing to return to their hometowns to honor the spirits of their ancestors with traditional dances and grave visits during the annual Bon summer holiday period.

But as the native Japanese population plummets and the number of foreign residents continues to rise — topping 4 million for the first time in 2025 — a morbid question emerges: Where do foreign nationals want to die?

The question can be a difficult one for many, particularly those with religious beliefs that might not conform with how death is traditionally handled in Japan.

Although burial is the norm in many countries, it is extremely rare in Japan — over 99.97％ of all bodies in the country are cremated, primarily due to limited space for large burial plots and out of concern that buried bodies could have a negative impact on soil and groundwater.

There are about 10 cemeteries that allow burial scattered around Japan. But in practice, the number of plots is very limited, and burial permission, which is necessary from both the local government and temple or cemetery that conducts it, is difficult to obtain, according to several funeral service providers interviewed for this article.

That means some simply have to compromise.

Maria, a Brazilian Portuguese woman who has lived here for 28 years, says there’s no other place she wants to die.

“It’s my place in the world and I wish to be buried here,” she said. Maria, like the other foreign residents quoted in this story, asked that her full real name not be published in order to protect their privacy while discussing personal matters.

“I see no reason to live out my days anywhere else than where I’ve spent most of my life and where my family actually are,” she said of her daughter and Japanese husband. “I’m Catholic and although it’s not part of our custom to be cremated, I’ve made my peace with that since this is how it is usually done here.”

But many are not as willing to follow local customs, and stories centering on foreign groups attempting to conduct illegal burials have made headlines in recent years.

In 2019, 14 bodies of Muslim people were discovered to have been buried at a cemetery in Saitama Prefecture, one of the rare cemeteries that allow burials under certain conditions. But in this case, permission was not granted by the cemetery. A burial conducted without permission constitutes the crime of abandonment of a corpse under the Penal Code.

Because Islam forbids cremation, some adherents in Japan have attempted to purchase land for the purpose of burials, a practice that has been met with protests from local communities.

Ryoko Takagi, a cultural anthropological expert at the Institute of Science Tokyo whose research focuses on mourning and technology, highlighted a case in Hiji, Oita Prefecture, in which the Beppu Muslim Association purchased a plot of land in a mountainous area in 2018, with the purpose of using it as a burial site.

But a petition signed by 100 residents opposing the plan due to concerns over “water source contamination” prompted Mayor Hirofumi Honda to propose an alternative plot owned by the town as the site for a Muslim cemetery. The decision was again met with protests, this time by residents of the neighboring village of Yamaga, as the proposed plot was near their water source.

While the municipalities’ water sources were cited as reasons, it’s likely that residents also had concerns due to their unfamiliarity with burials in Japan.

Hiroyuki Tanaka, director of funeral services provider Cosumo Sousai in Saitama Prefecture, said he feels for the Muslim communities of Japan, as he understands that it is very difficult for them to make end-of-life plans that adhere to their religious beliefs.

“If cremation was accepted among them, tree burial, where ashes are scattered around trees, could be an alternative to burial, as it is also a natural means where the body comes close to the soil. But that’s probably also not a choice for them,” he said.

Tanaka said he has heard of Muslim funeral services companies that operate in Japan, but added that, among Japanese operators, little is known about them or how they operate.

That’s not to say that burial plots don’t exist.

The Yokohama Foreign General Cemetery in a leafy area of the city’s Naka Ward had about 40 to 50 plots available, according to manager Sei Higuchi. There are conditions to fulfill in order to be buried there, however. The deceased must have had a foreign nationality and been a permanent resident living in Kanagawa Prefecture.

“In earlier days, one could book a burial spot in advance with us, but now we can only grant a spot after the person has passed away,” Higuchi said. “And this is also after receiving a permit to bury from the city of Yokohama, either in person or through a funeral provider.

“It’s indeed getting more and more difficult to be buried in Japan.”

While many people may wish to have the bodies of their loved ones transported to their home countries after death, Tanaka notes that cost is often a high hurdle.

“We receive many inquiries, but we have actually only taken care of one such case — of a successful Thai businessman in his 70s who ran a company here.”

Tanaka said that for this assignment, he had to arrange every procedure separately, finding specialized companies for the embalming, the coffin, and road and air transportation. The process also involved huge amounts of paperwork and required permission from the Thai Embassy to send the body to Thailand.

All told, the process cost the family ¥2 million ($12,700).

Maria, the Brazilian Portuguese woman, believes that logistical hurdles are a huge reason most long-term residents wish to remain here after death.

“All of the long-term foreign residents I know wish the same,” she said. “The wish to be buried in their home country would put a terrible burden on the remaining family here, both financially and in terms of logistics.” If cremation is an acceptable choice for the deceased and the family, people may choose to have their ashes scattered at sea or in a remote area.

According to Sea Ceremony, which provides services for scattering ashes, the cost of such services differs significantly depending on the location.

Scattering at sea is quite reasonable at ¥150,000 to ¥300,000 depending on the type and size of the boat that is rented. If scattering is entrusted to Sea Ceremony staff, the cost can be as little as ¥80,000.

Scattering in forests or woodlands can involve dispersing ashes on private land, therefore it can only be conducted by Sea Ceremony staff for about ¥100,000.

For something even more adventurous, and expensive, companies such as Space NTK and Space Memorial offer services that scatter a person’s ashes in the atmosphere. This can run up to anywhere from ¥500,000 to ¥10 million depending on the given plan, with the operation subcontracted to aerospace companies such as SpaceX.

Other foreign residents take a more practical approach when it comes to planning for death, with family and philosophy helping shape their decisions.

Mio, who is originally from China and first came to study in Japan in 1991, is determined to be cremated and have her ashes kept next to those of her Japanese husband.

She met her husband through a friend, but despite the fondness for Japan she had held since childhood, it took her a long time to fully trust the love of a man from “a different country.”

That feeling soon faded, but it wasn’t until their wedding in China, when Mio’s father-in-law went out of his way to give a speech in Chinese, that she felt truly welcomed.

Mio, now in her 50s, had already assumed by then that she would be part of the family’s Japanese grave when the time comes, but the speech pushed her to naturalize and change her surname to her husband’s.

“I saw that all names engraved in the back of the tombstone were Japanese. I didn’t want to become a nuisance to the family with my Chinese name,” she said. When she expresses anxiety about dying in a foreign country, her husband always reassures her. “Please do not worry,” he said. “I will die at least one day later than you.”

For Marc, a 67-year-old from western Europe, funeral rites are more important for those who survive the deceased.

The recently retired physicist cycles 250 kilometers a week, but his doctors have urged him to avoid long-distance travel due to a heart condition, meaning he may never return to his homeland.

“I want to see my friends in France, Netherlands, Belgium and other countries, so I do want to go there, but not because I want to die there,” he said.

Marc is also known as a philosopher among his friends.

“For me, death is mainly about molecules moving into some different organization. But the families of the deceased need a set of rituals to help them cope with the loss, say their farewell and make them feel they are doing the right thing for the deceased.”

At Marc’s retirement party last month, colleagues performed an original song about him during a celebration that highlighted both his humorous side and his achievements, including research inventions he made during his long career.

After the party, his team members came to tell him that the party gave them an opportunity to come to terms with the fact that he is gone and how to cope with the loss of his leadership.

“In that sense, I must say that the party was like a funeral, with the rather significant difference being that I was still there to also enjoy it,” he said with a laugh.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c78g.title: Nvidia gets $500bn from major banks to develop AI data centres
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c78g.text:
Nvidia has teamed up with some of Wall Street's largest banks to help raise $500bn (£370bn) in capital to develop artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

The chipmaker said it had struck deals with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR, and that the banks were for the first time treating AI hardware and infrastructure, often referred to as "compute", as a separate asset class.

"In AI, compute is revenue", Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, said. "We are bringing the world's leading long-term capital providers together to independently underwrite AI infrastructure."

The financing will go towards Nvidia's own projects and those being built by its partners.

Infrastructure projects backed by this fund will include the construction of new data centres to house, operate, and cool miles of stacked computer chips that process AI data and actions.

This will also back new factories to manufacture the AI chips needed to power these systems.

"Compute has become a critical infrastructure asset", Joe Bae and Scott Nuttall, co-chief executives of KKR, said in a joint statement. "As we've scaled our approach to digital infrastructure, we've learned that delivery, not ambition, is the hard part."

Essentially every major technology and AI company uses Nvidia's computer chips, or graphics processing units (GPUs), to power their services, AI platforms and AI chatbots.

Companies using Nvidia's popular chips or GPUs include Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic.

Such companies have collectively spent over $1tn in just three years on AI projects and infrastructure, with much more spending expected. And their demand for Nvidia's chips and services has driven the stock market value of the company up five fold in three years.

In a statement on Monday, Huang referred to Nvidia's role as a chip-maker as the company's beginning.

"Today, we are helping create a new class of productive, investable infrastructure: AI factories," he said.

With a new ability to tap some funding from the banks partnering with Nvidia, such banks will be able to finance more of the AI boom.

Jim Zelter, president of Apollo, a lender which manages more than $800m in assets, said: "Modern compute has emerged as a scarce, mission-critical asset class."

It is also "positioned to drive significant long-term economic growth and productivity gains", Zelter added.

BlackRock last month entered into an individual deal with Meta to finance and take a majority ownership stake in one data centre in Texas.

Anthropic also recently entered into a deal with Macquarie Asset Management and GIC, an investment bank in Singapore, for its own investment in AI infrastructure.

The company did not specify the size of the deal, but said more financing was needed as its popular chatbot Claude had become so popular that the "demand requires significant new compute".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62v.title: Jackie, the famous California bald eagle, dies after weeks of intensive care
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62v.text:
Jackie, a bald eagle in California who became an online star, died on Monday after receiving weeks of veterinary treatment.

Jackie was being cared for by Ojai Raptor Center, a wildlife rehabilitation organisation, after she was attacked by other eagles. The bird had underlying health issues that caused anaemia and weight loss.

"Over the past several days, her condition continued to deteriorate despite intensive treatment and the combined efforts of our veterinary team and consulting specialists," Ojai Raptor Center said in a statement.

A livestream featuring the Big Bear Valley nest of Jackie and her partner, Shadow, has hundreds of thousands of subscribers.

The Big Bear Eagle Nest Cam, run by the nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley in California, amassed a loyal following and Jackie was frequently spotted in the area since she hatched in the spring of 2012.

Jackie and Shadow had been mates since 2018, the Friends of Big Bear Valley website said.

"Our team is heartbroken. It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her," the Ojai Raptor Center said.

"We know this news will be deeply felt by the many thousands of people around the world who have followed her journey, hoped alongside us, prayed for her, and supported the people caring for her.

"We are working closely with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and will provide a more comprehensive statement including additional information on her treatments and test results."

Jackie's remains have been transferred to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, the Ojai Raptor Center said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maanvi Singh
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Thousands mourn the death of the eagle at California’s Big Bear Lake, whose life was closely followed via livestream

Jackie – the beloved bald eagle at California’s Big Bear Lake whose livestream was followed by millions of viewers as she birthed and raised chicks – died on Monday due to a mysterious illness. She was 14.

Jackie had been receiving treatment at the Ojai Raptor Center since mid-July when she was found weak and unable to fly after a scuffle with two younger eagles. Experts at the center had discovered that she was suffering from severe anemia, and suspected she had been sick for weeks before the fight grounded her.

“We know this news will be deeply felt by the many thousands of people around the world who have followed her journey, hoped alongside us, prayed for her, and supported the people caring for her,” the raptor center staff wrote in an Instagram post announcing Jackie’s death. “Our team is heartbroken. It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her. “

Despite administering a number of tests including a CT scan and bone marrow biopsy, experts at the center said they could not determine what had sickened Jackie.

The center is in consultation with the US and California fish and wildlife services about Jackie’s condition, and “will provide a more comprehensive statement including additional information on her treatments and test results” at a later date, it said.

The public had been watching Jackie’s nest since a livestream was first set up in October 2015 – it was then inhabited by her parents Ricky and Lucy. In 2018, the public watched as Jackie defended her nest against an intruder, dubbed Mr B. Then, Shadow – the male eagle who became her mate – moved in. Greater and greater numbers of viewers tuned in during the pandemic to watch the couple build their lives together and welcome several clutches of fluffy hatchlings.

In January, the couple’s clutch of two eggs was eaten by ravens. Jackie laid two more eggs in February, and thousands watched as the couple hatched their two youngest – Luna and Sandy. The latter was named after Sandy Steers, the executive director of Friends of Big Bear Valley, who had recently died from cancer.

The couple inspired the public to fight for the environment they inhabited. The Friends of Big Bear Lake launched a $10m effort to buy land near the eagles’ nest which had been slated for development – drawing support from the local elementary school, as well as from OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna. The non-profit will now steward 63 acres of the land.

Fans of Jackie shared messages of grief following the news of her death – and celebrated her legacy of inspiring a massive public campaign for preserving natural habitat.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Jackie was found weak and unable to fly after a scuffle with two younger eagles. Experts at the Ojai Raptor Center discovered she was suffering from severe anemia. The public had been watching her nest since a livestream was first set up in October 2015.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.title: Ceuta mayor calls for migrant detention amid mass influx crisis
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/10.text:
Ceuta’s leader has demanded the detention and expulsion of thousands of asylum seekers and undocumented migrants roaming the streets in the Spanish North African territory after last month’s mass crossing from Morocco.

“A space that acts as an internment centre for foreigners must be set up, where these people can be held and remain confined,” Ceuta’s Mayor-President Juan Jesus Vivas of the conservative Popular Party told reporters.

He said the measure “must be achieved urgently” so that the migrants “are not in our streets and that expulsion proceedings can be handled with greater speed and ease”.

A surge of asylum seekers and migrants swam or used inflatable rafts to cross from Morocco to Ceuta at the end of July, sparking a debate about the external borders of the European Union and controversy between Spain and other EU members.

Spanish authorities on Monday updated the estimated number of irregular migrants who made the journey to 80,000.

The Spanish government says 70,000 migrants and asylum seekers returned to Morocco within two days.

But the thousands who remained, including hundreds of unaccompanied children who cannot be summarily deported under Spanish law, are struggling to access food, water, shelter and sanitation, putting a strain on Ceuta’s resources.

Their future has sparked a political battle between Spain’s leftist central government and regions governed by the main conservative Popular Party and far-right Vox, which oppose taking in unaccompanied children under existing legal provisions.

Ceuta Mayor Vivas estimates that between 8,000 and 11,000 migrants are still in the Spanish territory and says the situation is “unsustainable”. He disputes the government’s statistics that only 2,500 asylum seekers and undocumented migrants remain.

Police said that 5,000 Ceuta residents gathered to protest on Sunday over the handling of the migration crisis that they say has left the enclave unsafe.

The Spanish government minister responsible for relations with the regions, Angel Victor Torres, assured Ceuta’s population that police and troop numbers had been ramped up, including 40 percent more civil guards.

The number of migrants and asylum seekers who made the journey to Ceuta has risen to 80,000. The thousands who remain are struggling to access food, water, shelter and sanitation.

https://arstechnica.com/gaming/2026/08/a.title: Ars Live: Ross Scott discusses the Stop Killing Games movement
https://arstechnica.com/gaming/2026/08/a.author: Kyle Orland
https://arstechnica.com/gaming/2026/08/a.text:
Our discussion takes place live on August 11 at 3 pm ET.

By now, any serious gamer is familiar with a favorite title becoming unplayable after a centralized online server gets shut down, or being unable to purchase and download a digitally delisted, critically acclaimed title from yesteryear. Can anything be done about this video game preservation problem?

To help answer that question, we’ll be hosting a live conversation with Ross Scott, the founder of the Stop Killing Games campaign, on August 11 at 2:30 pm ET as part of the Ars Live series. As Ars’ Senior Gaming Editor, I’ve documented countless examples of once vibrant games being left for dead by their creators.

You can watch the discussion live on YouTube when the time comes.

Scott founded the Stop Killing Games movement in 2024 after Ubisoft decided to shut down the servers for The Crew. Since then, he’s helped gather millions of gamers’ signatures on government petitions demanding legislative action to provide some form of perpetual access for games people purchase—either via continuing centralized server support or an option for players to maintain their own servers. The movement has already led to an official parliamentary debate and response from the European Commission and proposed legislation that is working its way through the California legislature.

I’ll be talking to Scott about how the movement came together, what’s animating gamers’ interest in long-term game preservation, and whether or not this problem can really be legislated away. We’ll also discuss how recent moves like Sony’s decision to stop selling PlayStation discs are impacting the debate over long-term game access.

Please join us for what should be a lively conversation.
