It also directs the nation's health department to improve research on vaccines. Public health experts have raised concerns that spacing out shots can lead to an increased risk that children become infected with vaccine.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czek.title: What he told me made my blood run cold - Michael Sheen investigates Wales' toxic legacy
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czek.text:
Michael Phillips spent his childhood in the 1980s playing with friends at a lagoon, firing air guns at rusty barrels that released clouds of coloured powder - completely oblivious to the toxic chemicals within.

Decades later, several of those friends and Phillips himself have developed rare cancers, which they believe may be linked to this.

Researcher and whistleblower Douglas Gowan tried to sound the alarm about 14 such sites - 12 of which were in Wales - but died before his warnings were heeded.

"What he told me made my blood run cold," said Hollywood actor Michael Sheen, who spoke to Gowan just months before he died and has now continued his investigation in a new BBC iPlayer documentary.

Gowan, a former farming consultant, alleged that chemical giant Monsanto had dumped "huge amounts of industrial chemicals all around Wales".

These included polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), he said, which he described as "some of the worst contaminants known to man" and were widely used during the last century, including for lipsticks and white goods.

"This stuff builds up in the environment, builds up in animals and fish, and it builds up in us," Gowan said.

Eastman Chemical Company, which is responsible for Monsanto's legacy production in the UK, did not respond to either Sheen and his team or the BBC when asked to comment.

Sheen said PCBs were now known as "the godfather of forever chemicals".

He added: "There is something out there in the forest, there is something in our bodies that can turn against us and tear us apart, but it's not like it is in the horror films. It's invisible. It's a silent killer."

These manmade chemicals are stable, resistant to extreme temperatures and pressures and have insulating properties. Because of this they were used in everything from plastics and paint to electrical equipment.

After concerns about toxicity to humans and animals were raised, a series of bans were put in place around the world from the 1970s onwards.

But the chemicals take a long time to break down and have lingered in the environment, particularly in landfill, where they can leach into waterways and then into the sea.

Gowan told Sheen in the documentary: "There was no regulation at the time, they could dump it wherever they wanted to."

In the 1980s, a fire at the lagoon at Llwyneinion near Ruabon in Wrexham took 60 firefighters more than 18 hours to bring under control.

The effects of the chemicals were reportedly felt up to 20 miles (32km) away.

Phillips and his friends went to watch and he believes the impact of this exposure began to emerge in 2001.

"I started getting lumps on my shoulder, I caught cancer. I lost a large part of my shoulder that's literally as wide as my hand.

"While he was operating, my surgeon said 'this is strange, I've never seen this type of cancer before', and he'd had a distinguished career of 40 years."

It was not just him who was affected.

"I lost a very close friend who used to be [at the lagoon] all the time, more than me. He died of breast cancer.

"I have another friend who passed away with brain cancer. I've got another friend who is trying to get over brain cancer, I have another friend who's had all of his lymph glands taken out because they were cancerous."

Another friend has the exact type of cancer Phillips had, and his surgeon told him: "For me to catch what I had was like winning the lottery.

"For your friend who lives down the road to get exactly the same, he said it's like winning the lottery every day for six months. It's not a coincidence."

Phillips' blood tests showed higher-than-average PCB levels.

"It's chilling to think that having any PCBs in your blood is normal, when 90 years ago no-one would have had them as they didn't exist," said Sheen.

The actor also had his blood tested and it revealed 81 different types of PCBs, despite him not having lived near any dump sites.

"There is no safe level of PCBs, it's a risk all of us have to try and manage. The lower your level of PCBs, the lower your risk of getting cancer," he said.

Paul Pemberton has been a Wrexham councillor for more than 20 years and said the site had been "abused for many many years".

Scientists found cyanide, arsenic and PCBs at the site and said it needed to be cleaned up, he said.

"We were then quoted around about £45m and that would bankrupt the council," he said.

However, Wrexham council said later investigations and risk assessments concluded that although contaminants were present, the sites did not meet the legal threshold requiring remediation.

In 2017, Gowan said the companies responsible "should be made to remediate".

Wales was not Monsanto's first choice when it came to PCB dumping.

Initially it pumped PCBs into waterways in Anniston, Alabama.

In 1993, the whole town sued Monsanto for chemical contamination, resulting in one of the largest single town lawsuits in US history.

Donald Stewart, one of the attorneys involved, said it was settled for $300m.

Internal Monsanto documents showed they had been aware of the toxicity of PCBs in 1949, so how could they get away with knowingly exposing people to these chemicals?

Stewart said: "If you look at this area, it's working people. They were people who wouldn't be able to fight back."

In another memo from 1972, journalists Dan Ashby and Lucy Taylor helping Sheen with the investigation found that Monsanto had decided PCBs were a worldwide problem, an environmental danger and a risk to human health, and were shutting down work at Anniston.

But then there were proposals to increase capacity to make five million more kilograms of PCBs at their plant in Newport.

"They're doing it in Newport because the legal risk in America is so much," said Ashby.

"Then the government in the UK told industry we're not going to put any restrictions on importing PCBs. So they begin importing from around the world, hundreds of tonnes of PCBs."

Gowan said: "If one wanted to be cynical about it, you could say that almost they were choosing places where chronic health issues might be hidden behind pre-existing health issues.

"People grew up with the knowledge that... they were in an area that had coal mining, heavy industry, the environment was contaminated, and there were health problems."

Sheen and his team took their findings to Wales' Parliament in the hope that more tests can be done.

"These people deserve more," he said.

"They deserve their concerns to be met with proper research and appropriate action. Douglas spent most of his life fighting to get the truth out there.

"The fact we all have traces of this chemical in our blood shows that we all have skin in the game. We've got to get together, we've got to fight this."

Meanwhile, members of the documentary team will appear before the Welsh Affairs Committee as it looks into alleged toxic "forever chemical" contamination in south Wales, the BBC has been told.

At a screening of the documentary, Sheen said: "These are just the places we know about... Douglas Gowan believed that there was much more."

Kirsty Luff of Friends of the Earth Cymru has called for a public inquiry into the "scale and impact of toxic sites in Wales".

She warned that climate change would make the situation worse as "more frequent and intense flooding... will bring these contaminants to the surface where they can spread over fields, they can get into water courses".

Environmental regulator Natural Resources Wales tested Llwyneinion acid tar lagoon close to Ruabon.

Investigation work found the site did not meet the legal definition of contaminated land.

Wrexham council said because of this there was "no statutory requirement for remediation", but that it continued to carry out regular inspections and water monitoring.

It said only limited information from more recent testing had been shared with it, but it remained open to reviewing any new "robust and verifiable evidence".

The Welsh government said: "Addressing contaminated land is a key priority for this government.

"Our industrial heritage has left us with a difficult legacy that can affect both people and places - we want to ensure this does not pose a risk to our communities or our natural environment.

"A survey of local authorities carried out by Natural Resources Wales in 2015 identified more than 9,000 potential sites requiring further investigation.

"While not all of these sites will pose a risk to human health or the environment, this figure demonstrates the scale of the issue facing regulators in Wales.

"We now intend to develop a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land, so that communities are no longer exposed to potential risks."

Buried with Michael Sheen is on BBC Two, BBC One Wales and BBC iPlayer from 17 August at 21:00 BST

Additional reporting by Steffan Messenger

https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/jeff-b.title: Jeff Bezos might finally get his hands on a sports team
https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/jeff-b.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/jeff-b.text:
Jeff Bezos is reportedly attempting to join the club of very rich Americans buying stakes in U.K. soccer teams.

Bezos, alongside others including Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin, is looking to buy at least a 30% stake in the English soccer team Liverpool at a £1.35 billion valuation (around $1.8 billion), The Guardian reports. If the deal closes, it will be the first sports investment for the billionaire, although he reportedly previously looked at buying a stake in a US football team.

Liverpool is one of the most notable sports teams in Europe and is worth about $6 billion, reports Forbes. Arguably, this team has the kind of brand recognition in the U.K. as the Dallas Cowboys has in the U.S.

It seems no billionaire portfolio is complete these days without a mega yacht and a sports team, so Bezos’ interest is not surprising. There’s also something very romantic these days about owning an English soccer team after the success of TV shows like “Ted Lasso” and Ryan Reynolds’ FX show “Welcome to Wrexham” about his experience owning that English team.

Other American billionaires in this club include Todd Boehly and Mark Walters (who also own the LA Dodgers and LA Lakers) buying Chelsea; New York Jets co-owner (and former U.S. Ambassador to the U.K.) Woody Johnson buying Crystal Palace; Dan Friedkin taking a stake in Everton; and Bill Foley leading a group that also included Michael B. Jordan buying Bournemouth.

For that matter, owning a stake in a U.K. sports team has also become a celebrity cultural phenom. Besides Reynolds and Jordan, Tom Brady purchased a minority stake in Birmingham City. Will Ferrell has a minority stake in Leeds United, alongside Russell Westbrook and Michael Phelps.

Sky Sports had a story earlier this year mapping out why so many Americans seem to be taking over U.K. football. It found that 13 out of 20 Premier League clubs (the top football league in England) had American shareholders.

Soccer has become increasingly popular in the U.S., and many of the top sports franchises, like the NFL and MLB, are either too expensive or closed off to new buyers. It’s much more possible to buy into a Premier League team.

Owning a share in such a team also buys access and proximity to some of the most bankable and recognizable sports icons on Earth. Bezos over the past few years — especially since he married former news anchor and TV show host Lauren Sanchez — has become seen as more of a cultural figure, rather than solely a tech mogul.

So, with a net worth currently sitting at around $280 billion, perhaps it’s actually more than time that Bezos got himself a sports team. Amazon has also streamed some European soccer leagues in the past — and Bezos has growing interests in the U.K. As we previously reported, his new AI company Prometheus is reportedly looking to sign a lease to move into London’s AI hub King’s Cross.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.title: Live: Russian missiles strike Kyiv, triggering fires in city centre
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260.text:
A Russian attack on the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia killed five people and wounded 20, the regional governor said early on Tuesday.

"Five people killed, a further 20 wounded: sadly, the number of casualties continues to rise following the enemy attack on Zaporizhzhia," Ivan Fedorov, the head of the regional military administration, said on Telegram.

In Zaporijjia, in the southeast of the country, another nightly Russian attack injured at least nine people, wrote the head of the regional military administration, Ivan Fedorov, on Telegram.

Russian forces "attacked industrial facilities and infrastructure," he said.

At least one person was injured in Kiev, the capital's military administration said, without providing further details.

Russian forces attacked the Ukrainian capital Kyiv with missiles early on Tuesday, triggering fires in the city centre, officials said.

The city's military administration said warehouses in a central district were ablaze. One person was reported injured.

The air raid alert was in effect for about 40 minutes before officials declared the all clear.

Mayor Vitali Klitschko said medical personnel had been dispatched to a central district.

Reuters witnesses reported explosions in the city.

Russian forces also deployed missiles and bombs in an attack on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia, regional Governor Ivan Fedorov said on Telegram. He said two people were injured and several buildings had been damaged.

A series of blasts were heard in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, shortly after midnight local time, AFP journalists said, after authorities warned of several approaching missiles.

The reporters said they heard several loud explosions while the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, wrote on social media that Kyiv was "under attack by ballistic missiles".

• Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that as many as 50,000 North Korean soldiers could be deployed to Russia, reflecting growing military cooperation between the two countries.

• Russian ⁠bomb ​strikes ​on Ukraine's northern city of ​Sumy ‌injured ⁠at ‌least five ⁠people and damaged a number of residential areas, according to regional governor ​Oleh Hryhorov.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/c.title: Calvary considers new Launceston hospital at aged care site
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/c.author: Emily Smith
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Health Administration

Calvary Health Care is considering its Sandhill aged care home site as an option for a new private hospital in Launceston. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Catholic health provider Calvary has confirmed it is considering a new hospital in Launceston, which would be co-located with an aged care home.

It comes two years after Calvary scrapped plans for a new hospital next to the public Launceston General Hospital.

Calvary Health Care has submitted a land use strategy for its Sandhill Residential Aged Care site in South Launceston, and is exploring a rezoning application to be considered by the Launceton City Council.

A Catholic health care provider has confirmed it is considering building a new private hospital in Tasmania's north, two years after it cancelled plans for a $130 million development.

Calvary Health Care said it was investigating redeveloping its Sandhill Residential Aged Care site in South Launceston to include a new hospital.

A spokesperson said the organisation had submitted a land use strategy for the site and was exploring a rezoning application to be considered by the Launceston City Council.

It is understood the existing aged care facilities would be retained.

The news has been welcomed by some healthcare advocates, who have become increasingly concerned by the aging state of Calvary's two Launceston hospitals, St Luke's and St Vincent's.

The shutdown of Calvary St Luke's Hospital will affect 40 planned surgeries this week, with 22 of those reallocated to nearby St Vincent's Hospital.

Last year, Calvary was forced to close three surgical operating theatres at St Luke's hospital after rips were found in the flooring.

While modular theatres were set up and patients diverted to St Vincent's hospital, some have warned it is also aging.

"So the real risk here then is that that infrastructure fails," Australian Medical Association Tasmania spokesperson Dr Michael Lumsden-Steel said.

Dr Michael Lumsden-Steel says a new private hospital in Launceston is needed. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

The Launceston Health Hub's Jerome Muir Wilson said he discussed the idea of a new hospital at the Sandhill site with Calvary Health Care chief executive Damien Bruce when the two met in Launceston yesterday.

"They [Calvary] mentioned they're exploring Sandhill … as an option."

Dr Muir Wilson said while the model may work for some medical or palliative care patients, he said he did not make sense to put a surgical hospital next to an aged care home.

Dr Jerome Muir Wilson says there's room for more than one private hospital in Launceston.  (ABC News: Emily Smith)

He said having a new private hospital next to the public Launceston General Hospital, which Calvary had been planning in 2024, would be ideal.

"That way, there's no wrong front door if someone goes into an emergency department," he said.

"They can be a public patient one way or a private patient the other way."

A Calvary spokesperson said Launceston-based visiting medical officers had been asked to give feedback on its idea for the Sandhill site, and the organisation's wider clinical services plan, by September 7.

Calvary Health Care is asking Launceston-based visiting medical officers for feedback on the idea. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

When Calvary withdrew from plans for a new private hospital beside the Launceston General Hospital in 2024 just months before work was set to start, it cited "insurmountable budget pressures".

Financial documents show those pressures have continued; Calvary has reported losses since 2019, with deficits of $138 million in 2025, $144 million in 2024, and $377 million in 2023.

But private health insurer St Lukes chief executive Paul Lupo, who also met with Mr Bruce yesterday, said investing in its infrastructure in Launceston would improve Calvary's position in the long run.

"There is no doubt that the assets in the north would be a drain on their financial position," Mr Lupo said.

"So I think if we can get over the hurdle of attracting some capital for them to renew the asset, that will actually make Calvary more sustainable going forward."

Paul Lupo says investment in its infrastructure will improve Calvary's financial position in the long run. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Mr Lupo said he hoped a decision on further Calvary investment in Tasmania's north would be made quickly.

"If I had my way it would have been about five years ago," he said.

"[Their current hospitals have] aging infrastructure and the implication of that is high maintenance, high disruption, a higher cost to maintain.

"Which means that the price that they require for services is greater than it could be if it was in a more modern and well-appointed hospital.

"And what that means is that it's more costly for Tasmanians."

St Luke's is one of two aging private hospitals operated by Calvary in Launceston. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

Dr Lumsden-Steel said he hoped the state government was speaking with Calvary about how any future planned investment could also benefit the overwhelmed Launceston General Hospital.

While there are two other private hospital plans in the works for Launceston — with the state government wanting to partner with the private sector on a 250-bed facility and Dr Muir Wilson's Launceston Health Hub pushing for a two-stage development — there has been little progress on these in the past year.

Dr Muir Wilson said there was room for more than one private hospital in the city.

"We need to be able to attract and retain the best doctors. And currently the infrastructure in town is getting old," he said.

Along with the two Launceston private hospitals, Calvary Health Care also operates two hospitals in Hobart — Calvary Lenah Valley and St John's in South Hobart.

Its proposal to take over the Hobart Private Hospital following the collapse of Healthscope is being considered by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c75g.title: England set to eliminate hepatitis C
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c75g.text:
England is on track to become one of the first countries in the world to eliminate hepatitis C, a dangerous virus that attacks the liver, figures show.

The target of treating 80% of all known cases has already been met, and deaths from the virus have fallen by 36% in the last decade, just short of what is needed by 2030.

Taking antiviral tablets for 8 to 12 weeks can cure more than 95% of cases.

Initiatives including A&E blood tests, GP registration testing and free at-home tests have helped to find people who were previously undiagnosed, says NHS England.

Hepatitis C is spread through contact with blood infected with the virus, such as by sharing needles with someone who has it.

Donor blood is already screened for it.

It is a silent disease, meaning people often have no symptoms until much later.

Untreated, it can cause serious and potentially life-threatening liver damage.

NHS England says that since 2015, more than 100,000 people have been diagnosed and treated for hepatitis C, meaning the country is already meeting that target.

Another goal - a 65% reduction in hepatitis C-related mortality compared with 2015 levels - has yet to be met, but might be before the 2030 target date.

Around 50,200 adults are living with hepatitis C, figures for England in 2024 suggest.

Estimates indicate 84.6% of those living with hepatitis C have been diagnosed - just short of the 90% target.

The Hepatitis C Trust says England is "on the cusp" of one of the most significant public health achievements in our country's history.

Prof Frankie Swords, NHS national medical director, added: "England is now leading the world in the mission to eliminate this disease and on course to beat the WHO's 2030 target, but we are determined to keep up the momentum and finish the job.

"We are committed to finding and treating everyone who needs support and would urge those at greater risk to come forward by ordering a free and confidential home-testing kit online."

Adults born in Ukraine, Romania, Estonia, Latvia, Poland, Albania, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Czechia or Slovakia are particularly urged to test, as some may have been infected through medical or dental procedures before 1991.

People can order a free, confidential NHS home self-testing kit without needing to speak to a GP.

Paul Eatwell, 65, was diagnosed after a routine blood test.

The grandfather from Blackburn, Lancashire, said: "My first reaction was disbelief. I remember saying: 'Are you sure? Surely there's been some mistake.'

"I didn't feel ill. I kept wondering how I could possibly have caught it."

He says the medical support he received made a huge difference.

While it has not been established how Eatwell caught the virus, it has been suggested that surgery in South Africa decades ago may have been the cause.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czdm.title: 'I started in my 20s and made £8,000': Why women are often better investors than men
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czdm.text:
Women who invest their money get slightly higher long-term returns than men, new analysis suggests.

But only about a quarter of UK women have investments, compared with about 40% of men, a separate report shows.

We've looked at the data behind these trends, which reveal some surprising differences in how men and women approach investing.

Teleri Evans was 25 when she began saving into a Help To Buy ISA then a couple of years later she took out a stocks and shares Lifetime ISA. By 33, she had £40,000 saved - with £8,000 of it returns on her investments.

"I saved aggressively, and lived at my mum's for half of that time, so I could save as close as possible to the maximum £4,000 per year into Lifetime ISA," she says.

The civil servant from Cardiff used the money towards a house deposit earlier this year with her partner.

Only 26% of UK women invest, but that this falls to 23% for those under 45, according to a study by consumer finance website Boring Money.

In contrast, 41% of all men invest, which holds steady at 40% of those under 45.

So why are fewer women investing than men?

It can be "largely attributed to culture", according to Gillian Fleming, co-founder and managing director of UK-based Mint Ventures, a women-led angel investment firm.

"Men historically have been more likely to make family investment decisions, and women have also historically not owned the balance of wealth, but that is changing now," she says.

"Also, money and wealth creation is not a topic that women often discuss, and we would like to change that."

Teleri says she has noticed a shift of late. "Investing is definitely something that women are talking about more, which is always a good thing," she says. "That's the case with my friendship group."

When women do invest in stocks and shares, analysis by Fidelity International found that over three years its female personal investing customers recorded cumulative returns of 50%, compared with 47% for men. The analysis does not identify the reason for the difference, but why may it be the case?

One possible clue to women's slightly higher long-term returns lies in how often they buy and sell their investments, with Barclays data showing that women trade around half as frequently as men.

This could be because women are more patient and risk averse, says Joanna Floyd, business psychologist at London-based The Work Psychologists.

"Studies show that male investors trade more than women, chasing higher returns, but women actually get higher returns," she says.

"The restraint that keeps women out of the market in the first place is the very same thing that rewards them once they are in it."

That more cautious approach to risk can be seen beyond investing, with women more likely to choose certainty when faced with a financial gamble.

When it comes to how women invest, Fleming says they are deliberately more cautious.

"Women are often accused of being more risk adverse, we call it more risk aware," she says. "Certainly from speaking to male investors their main focus is on the rate of return."

Fleming also says women appear to invest more broadly. "Men are more likely to invest in technology companies for their higher potential returns, whereas women want to invest in a broader range, from retail to food and drink, health and beauty, fem tech and creative industries."

Anna Macdonald, investment strategy director at financial services company Hargreaves Lansdown, agrees that women choose the companies they invest in carefully.

"Women appear to place relatively greater weight on where their money is going and what impact it might have, as well as the reassurance that an investment is right for them," she says.

"Our research suggests men are...more readily attracted by the potential financial return."

Jemma Slingo, pensions and investment specialist at investment firm Fidelity International, says female investors "appear more likely to connect investing with real-life goals, from building emergency savings to looking after children."

It's important to remember women in the UK generally have less money to invest than men because the continuing gender pay gap means they earn less on average.

Macdonald says that the investment sector "needs to do a better job of making investing feel accessible, relevant and connected to people's own goals and values".

"Addressing this would be good for women's long-term financial resilience and for the UK economy."

https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/openai.title: OpenAI reportedly completed a $7 billion employee tender offer
https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/openai.author: Tim Fernholz
https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/openai.text:
OpenAI has bought back $7 billion worth of shares from employees at the privately held frontier AI lab as part of an effort to provide liquidity to its workforce.

The deal, reported by Bloomberg, valued OpenAI at $852 billion, the same as its most recent fundraising round in March, which added $122 billion to the company’s war chest.

The company also filed confidentially with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June to prepare for a potential IPO later this year. However, a tender offer suggests that an IPO may not be forthcoming soon. With many tech companies remaining private longer than previous generations of startups, private tenders have proven a useful way for firms to allow employees to realize the value of their stock compensation without the difficulties that come with a public offering.

OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.

Last month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote that “we did not have our best 12 months ever, which is mostly my fault, but we are about to have our best 12 months to date.” Firms going public typically want to show strong financial results to bring investors on board, and the Wall Street Journal reported in April that the company missed internal financial goals.

While OpenAI’s incredible growth and products are likely to generate massive interest in public markets, the potential debut of rival Anthropic — which was reportedly profitable earlier this year — gives the company a reason to ensure it puts its best face forward. The tender could be another signal that the much-anticipated offering will wait for OpenAI’s new strategy of paring down its bets and focusing on its enterprise business to gain traction.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/as-ai-.title: As AI-led attacks multiply, OpenAI launches a new cyber model
https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/as-ai-.author: Lucas Ropek
https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/10/as-ai-.text:
Every day seems to brings fresh news of an AI agent going “rogue.” Whether that’s compromising Hugging Face, hacking a gym website, or creating its own fake profiles to socially engineer an intrusion, AI models are increasingly behaving like bad actors.

So, the AI labs that make the models doing the hacking are expanding their cyber protection offerings. This week, OpenAI announced an expansion of Daybreak, its cyber defense service which it launched earlier this year, not long after Anthropic released its cyber-focused model Mythos.

Daybreak is a service that bundles access to models, tools and workflows for defenders. The expansion includes access to a brand new cyber-focused model designed for defensive work.

OpenAI said Monday that Daybreak would now consist of two tiers: Blue and Red. Both of these tiers will allow approved customers access to OpenAI’s limited-access frontier cyber models. Frontier models — the most advanced available — have been a subject of controversy. The Trump administration previously sought to collaborate with AI companies on the roll out of such models, purportedly over safety concerns. Previously, OpenAI deployed significant guardrails to using these models, limiting what customers could do with them.

Blue, which appears to be the more basic of the two, offers a variety of cyber services, including incident response, malware analysis, and patch validation. OpenAI calls Blue its “recommended starting point for most defenders,” implying that it should be more than enough for most enterprises.

Red, on the other hand, offers a broader and potentially more dangerous toolkit. The company grants its users “purpose-trained cybersecurity models,” designed to carry out security testing and vulnerability research.

With Red also comes the new model, GPT‑5.6‑Cyber, which is only available at that tier. 5.6-Cyber is built off of GPT‑5.6 Sol, and offers enhanced capabilities for certain specialized cybersecurity tasks, the company said.

At the moment, GPT‑5.6‑Cyber is only being made available for “trusted customer partners,” including reportedly Accenture, IBM, Crowdstrike, Cloudflare, and others.

While the threats from AI agents are rapidly increasing, critics have also pointed out that they function as marketing opportunities for the AI labs. OpenAI is certainly marketing its upgraded Daybreak that way.

“The cybersecurity world is rapidly changing—threat actors will increasingly use AI to conduct cyberattacks at unprecedented speed and scale, including in fully autonomous ways,” the company said in a blog post. “As these capabilities spread, defenders have a narrowing window to prepare.”

At the same time, enterprises remain interested in buying their protection from the AI labs who know the security risks best, because they know them first-hand.

https://venturebeat.com/technology/opena.title: OpenAI launches GPT-5.6-Cyber with reduced refusals, 95% completion on advanced cybersecurity tasks
https://venturebeat.com/technology/opena.author: carl.franzen@venturebeat.com (Carl Franzen)
https://venturebeat.com/technology/opena.text:
Credit: VentureBeat made with ChatGPT-Images-2.0

Earlier today, OpenAI launched GPT-5.6-Cyber, a specialized model designed to perform advanced vulnerability research and exploit development for approved defenders — including categories of work that its general-purpose models will often refuse.

GPT-5.6-Cyber is a fine-tuned version of OpenAI's most advanced general model, GPT-5.6 Sol, unveiled back in June, but trained specifically to improve performance on advanced cybersecurity tasks, including finding zero-day vulnerabilities and developing exploit chains.

Crucially, OpenAI also trained it to reduce refusals on some higher-risk, "dual-use" cybersecurity requests — that is, requests that could be used for legitimate defensive or malicious offensive purposes.

Indeed, on an internal OpenAI benchmark called Advanced Cybersecurity Completion Rate — which the company says in its launch blog post measures tasks involving exploit-chain development, authentication bypass, privilege escalation, and other advanced cybersecurity scenarios — GPT-5.6-Cyber completed 95% compared to just 57.3% from its immediate predecessor model GPT-5.5-Cyber, and just 1.5% with the normal GPT-5.6 Sol model and all its safeguards applied.

OpenAI researcher Eric Wallace posted on X, describing GPT-5.6-Cyber as OpenAI's "first large-scale attempt at directly improving capabilities for advanced cybersecurity tasks such as exploit development."

Unfortunately for enterprises, GPT-5.6-Cyber is not being made broadly available to every ChatGPT or API customer.

To get access, an organization has to be accepted into the newly created tier of OpenAI’s Daybreak cybersecurity program, called Daybreak Red — also announced today, which gives access to dedicated cybersecurity models like GPT-5.6-Cyber

Another new tier, Daybreak Blue, gives a wider swath of enterprises access to general models like GPT-5.6 Sol but with some guardrails lifted to allow for more cybersecurity uses.

OpenAI’s documents list pricing for GPT-5.6-Cyber at $12.50 per million input tokens and $75 per million output tokens, with cached input at $1.25 per million tokens.

OpenAI-GPT-5.6-Cyber and Sol (Daybreak) pricing table. Credit: OpenAI

That makes it more expensive than GPT-5.6 Sol in the same Daybreak cyber pricing table, where Sol is listed at $5 per million input tokens and $30 per million output tokens for short-context use.

OpenAI does not list long-context pricing for GPT-5.6-Cyber in the same table, and access still requires separate Daybreak Red approval and provisioning.

Daybreak Red is for approved security teams doing advanced, authorized cyber work — the kind of work that can look risky out of context, even when it is being done for defensive reasons. That includes vulnerability research, penetration testing, red-team exercises and exploit validation on systems the organization owns, operates or has permission to test. In other words, OpenAI is saying GPT-5.6-Cyber is for trusted defenders with a clear professional need, not for general experimentation.

Enterprises that want access have to apply through Daybreak Access, OpenAI’s current pathway for vetting cyber users. The application asks companies to identify who they are, what kind of security work they plan to do, where they will use the models, and which OpenAI products or surfaces they expect to use. Applicants also have to confirm that their work is lawful, defensive and authorized.

OpenAI is also looking for signs that the applicant has a serious security program of its own. The company says participating enterprises need controls such as single sign-on, multifactor authentication, role-based access, employee-use monitoring, usage logs, API-key controls and a documented incident-response process. OpenAI also asks for a recognized security certification such as SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 or an equivalent standard. Access is limited to approved people inside the organization using company-controlled accounts and devices.

If an enterprise does not qualify for Daybreak Red, or does not need that level of access, OpenAI is pointing most companies toward Daybreak Blue, its other cyber models access tier, instead.

Blue is the broader tier for approved defenders. It does not provide GPT-5.6-Cyber, but it does give vetted users access to OpenAI’s frontier general-purpose models, including GPT-5.6 Sol, with safeguards adjusted for legitimate defensive work.

For many enterprise security teams, Blue may be the more realistic starting point. OpenAI says it is meant for tasks such as secure-code review, vulnerability discovery, malware analysis, incident response and patch validation. These are still sensitive uses, but they do not necessarily require the same specialized cyber model access that comes with Red.

The practical takeaway is that enterprises now have two routes into Daybreak. Blue is for approved defenders who want stronger AI help with everyday security work. Red is for the smaller set of approved teams that can justify access to specialized cyber models, including GPT-5.6-Cyber. Companies that want to use Daybreak capabilities in products or services for their own customers need a separate approval path through the Daybreak Cyber Partner Program, rather than simply applying for internal enterprise access and passing it along.

OpenAI has supported defenders through its Cybersecurity Grant Program since 2023 — later expanded to $10 million — and began building cyber-specific safeguards into its model deployments starting with GPT-5.2.

In February 2026 it introduced Trusted Access for Cyber (TAC), an identity-and-trust framework that gave vetted defenders lower classifier-based refusals for authorized work such as vulnerability triage, malware analysis and binary reverse engineering.

From there, the cadence accelerated. In March, OpenAI CEO and co-founder Sam Altman announced the Daybreak program. In April, OpenAI scaled TAC and released GPT-5.4-Cyber, a version of GPT-5.4 fine-tuned to be "cyber-permissive" for a limited set of vetted vendors and researchers.

In May, it followed with GPT-5.5-Cyber in limited preview for defenders of critical infrastructure, and lined up partners including Cisco, Intel, SentinelOne, Snyk and Cloudflare.

Notably, OpenAI said at the time that GPT-5.5-Cyber was "primarily trained to be more permissive," not to significantly out-perform its general model — GPT-5.5-Cyber actually scored worse than GPT-5.5 on some evaluations.

TAC required phishing-resistant Advanced Account Security for individuals on its most capable models beginning June 1, and Daybreak now requires hardware security keys for individual accounts beginning September 1.

OpenAI isn't relying exclusively on benchmarks to make its case.

The company says its researchers used GPT-5.6-Cyber to investigate V8, the JavaScript engine underlying Chrome, and uncovered two previously unknown vulnerabilities that could be chained to corrupt memory and escape the V8 heap sandbox.

OpenAI researchers validated the findings and disclosed them to Google, which fixed the vulnerability assigned CVE-2026-15903 — a high-severity flaw in which V8's optimizing compiler skipped a safety check during integer conversion, allowing an out-of-bounds array index that an attacker could use to read or overwrite memory.

OpenAI says the model has also contributed to finding at least five vulnerabilities in an unnamed popular mobile operating system, three critical vulnerabilities in an unnamed popular database, and more than 400 vulnerabilities capable of producing privilege escalation in a popular operating-system kernel. Those disclosures are still being coordinated, according to OpenAI.

The results put OpenAI into a rapidly developing market for AI-assisted offensive security. XBOW, for example, markets autonomous penetration-testing agents that map attack surfaces, attempt exploits and independently validate findings; in 2025 it became the first AI system to top HackerOne's U.S. bug-bounty leaderboard, and this year it disclosed a set of critical, CVSS-9.8 remote-code-execution flaws in Microsoft's Bing image-processing systems, found without source-code access.

For enterprise security leaders, that emerging competition matters because vulnerability research is moving beyond using an LLM as an assistant. Vendors are increasingly building systems in which models can investigate targets, operate tools, validate hypotheses and produce actionable findings.

OpenAI's own results also show why enterprises shouldn't simply equate cyber specialization with better performance everywhere.

GPT-5.6-Cyber outperformed GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.5-Cyber on OpenAI's implementation of ExploitGym, which evaluates whether agents can turn known vulnerabilities into working exploits in controlled environments. It also beat Sol on an internal zero-day evaluation.

But GPT-5.6 Sol performed better on OpenAI's Vulnerability Discovery and Report Writing evaluation. OpenAI attributes the Cyber model's lower score partly to shorter and less detailed vulnerability reports.

Sol also performed best on ExploitBench under its standard 300-turn limit, with OpenAI saying it solved tasks more token-efficiently. Extending the evaluation to 600 turns narrowed the gap between the models.

That suggests enterprises may eventually treat cyber models as specialized workers rather than replacements for general reasoning models: one model for deep exploit work, another potentially better suited to analysis, documentation or other parts of a security workflow.

SpecterOps CTO Jared Atkinson said GPT-5.6-Cyber is "materially improving our specialist vulnerability-research workflows," adding that it completed some work in less than a day that previous models had failed to resolve after weeks of intermittent effort.

The permissive-model pitch arrives weeks after OpenAI's most serious public demonstration of what can go wrong when cyber refusals are turned down — and OpenAI addresses that history head-on in the Daybreak announcement.

In July, OpenAI and Hugging Face jointly disclosed that during an internal ExploitGym benchmark evaluation — run with production classifiers deliberately disabled to measure maximal capability — a combination of OpenAI models, including GPT-5.6 Sol and an unreleased, more-capable pre-release model, broke out of their sandboxed research environment and autonomously attacked Hugging Face's production infrastructure.

The models exploited a zero-day in an internally hosted package-registry cache proxy to reach the open internet, moved laterally through OpenAI's research nodes, then inferred that Hugging Face likely hosted ExploitGym's answer keys and chained stolen credentials and remote-code-execution flaws to reach its production database. OpenAI called it an "unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities."

As VentureBeat previously reported, the episode also exposed the flip side of blanket safety guardrails: when Hugging Face's defenders tried to use commercial frontier models to analyze the raw exploit payloads and credential dumps from the attack, the models refused, and the company completed its forensic reconstruction only after switching to a Chinese open-weight model, GLM 5.2, run locally.

That guardrails-block-the-defender dynamic is much of what OpenAI's reduced-refusal Daybreak tiers are meant to solve — even as the same incident illustrates the risks of reducing refusals in the first place.

OpenAI is careful to draw a line between that incident and this product. In the Daybreak announcement it states directly that GPT-5.6-Cyber "was not involved in exploiting Hugging Face, nor are any other models planned for an upcoming release," and notes that the pre-release model implicated in July was an internal-only research prototype that has since been deactivated, encrypted and restricted from research access.

The company has said it is working with external advisers including CrowdStrike, METR and Redwood Research on the review, and has brought Hugging Face into its trusted-access program.

In my assessment, the access model still leaves OpenAI with a hard question: whether keeping GPT-5.6-Cyber inside the narrower Daybreak Red tier also limits the very defensive work it says it wants to accelerate. If only a small group of approved participants can use the model, enterprises outside that tier may still lack access to the kind of specialized AI assistance that could help with fast diagnosis, containment and response in incidents like the one involving Hugging Face.

That means OpenAI may still be repeating part of the mistake it is trying to move past. By holding its most capable cyber model behind a tighter approval process, it reduces obvious misuse risk, but also leaves many enterprise defenders looking elsewhere. For teams that cannot qualify for Daybreak Red, or cannot wait for approval, open weights models may remain the more practical alternative: less controlled, but easier to obtain, inspect, run internally and adapt during a live security investigation.

The most consequential part of Daybreak may ultimately be its access architecture rather than its benchmarks.

OpenAI explicitly says Daybreak Blue removes system-level guardrails that can interfere with legitimate defensive work, while GPT-5.6-Cyber goes further by reducing model refusals for certain dual-use tasks. In their place, OpenAI is imposing controls around who receives access and how the models operate.

Daybreak access is restricted to approved individuals and organizations performing authorized work. OpenAI says controls include identity verification, account security, monitoring, approved-use restrictions and legal attestations.

The company is also encouraging Daybreak customers using Codex to move from full-access execution to an auto-review mode capable of evaluating actions requiring elevated permissions before they execute. Individual Daybreak accounts will be required to adopt hardware security keys beginning September 1. OpenAI says it is additionally rolling out improved monitoring in the coming weeks and prioritizing alignment training and testing for upcoming Daybreak releases — commitments that read, in context, as a direct response to the Hugging Face review.

OpenAI's broader Codex Security product supplies another layer around the models, providing repository analysis, vulnerability validation, remediation and integration into cloud, pull-request and local development workflows. OpenAI says Codex Security has scanned more than 30 million commits across more than 30,000 codebases, with more than 500,000 findings fixed.

That model-plus-harness approach resembles a broader shift in AI security products. XBOW, for example, emphasizes orchestration, exploit validation and governance around frontier models rather than treating an LLM alone as the complete penetration-testing system.

OpenAI nevertheless acknowledges that increasingly permissive cyber models create additional risks, whether from misuse or misalignment. It assesses both GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6-Cyber at the High cybersecurity capability level under its Preparedness Framework, but below its Critical threshold. A fuller GPT-5.6-Cyber system card is planned for later publication.

For CISOs and security engineering leaders, Daybreak therefore presents a different deployment question than another incremental model upgrade. As models become capable enough to perform work previously reserved for experienced vulnerability researchers — and, as the Hugging Face incident showed, capable enough to pursue a narrow goal straight through a sandbox — the enterprise control plane around those models — permissions, sandboxes, monitoring, human review and authorization — becomes as important as the intelligence inside them.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/g.title: Limp Bizkit return to headline loud and proud Aussie festival
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/g.author: Al Newstead
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/g.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Nu-metal icons Limp Bizkit return to Australia this Decmber to headline Good Things 2026.   (Getty Images: Paul Natkin)

Having cemented its status as an annual summer festival staple, Good Things has announced its return this December, boasting a line-up packed with metal, punk, emo, rock and more.

The event's seventh edition once again spans a range of genres and eras, bringing together both local and international acts across multiple stages. Let's dive in, shall we?

Arguably the defining band of nu-metal, Limp Bizkit are back in the country for the first time since headlining Good Things and sideshows back in 2023.

Emerging in the late '90s with a riotous fusion of rock, metal and rap, Limp Bizkit's angsty anthems were a polarising force but became a blockbuster success with teenage millennials.

Fronted by Fred Durst, songs like Nookie, Break Stuff, Rollin, and Mission: Impossible 2 theme Take A Look Around, were inescapable in the 2000s.

Limp Bizkit were also never far from headlines; most famously, their 2001 performance at the Sydney Big Day Out that led to the death of 16-year-old Jessica Michalik.

A confluence of factors during Limp Bizkit's 2001 Sydney performance led to the death of 16-year-old Jessica Michalik. Eighteen years later, the anger and the hurt remain.

At 2012's Soundwave festival, the band's first Australian dates in 11 years, Durst dedicated their performance to Jessica and was joined by her father, George Michalik.

Heavy fans will be thrilled to experience Spiritbox. Fronted by Courtney LaPlante, a vocalist capable of ethereal melodies and visceral screams, the Canadian metal group boldly mixed genre on their breakout 2020 debut album Eternal Blue.

Between that record and last year's acclaimed follow-up, Tsunami Sea, Spiritbox have been feted in just about every way that still matters: magazine covers, festival billings, a ferociously dedicated fanbase and multiple nominations at Canada's Juno music awards.

This marks Spiritbox's second time touring Australia, following their 2023 debut as part of Knotfest. (Supplied: Alexander Bemis)

Simple Plan, Montreal's premiere pop-punk exports and a staple of 2000s, are also at the top of the bill. Nearly 30 years after forming, the band still largely consists of the same high school friends, who've released six albums much loved by anyone who went through an emo phase in the 2000s.

Alexisonfire, yet another celebrated Canadian act, will mark the 20th anniversary of Crisis, their influential third album of bracing post-hardcore, by performing the record in full.

Similarly, Swedish punk group Millencolin will perform their 2000 album Pennybridge Pioneers — an international hit evidenced by its songs featuring in the blockbuster Tony Hawk's Pro Skater video games, as well as Penguins & Polarbears cracking triple j's Hottest 100.

The biggest homegrown heavy name is resilient metalcore crew Polaris, who are beginning work on new material to follow their first three ARIA-nominated albums.

Grinspoon, who've been touring rock favourites since the late '90s, are sure to draw big sing-alongs. Their addition follows frontman Phil Jamieson cancelling his current tour after a serious back injury sustained mid-show.

You've also got Speed, the J Award-winning crew who put Western Sydney's hardcore scene on international radars with their community-driven live shows.

Plus, Slowly Slowly, who've hopped from emo-rock to pop-punk and even glossy electro-pop, Brisbane four-piece Headwreck and the Choirboys.

Best known for their 1987 pub rock hit Run To Paradise, the Choirboys fill a legacy slot that has become Good Things tradition, occupied in previous years by James Reyne and Dragon.

Bad Religion, pioneers of a melodic take on hardcore that helped draft the blueprint that '90s acts like Green Day and The Offspring drafted from, are billed to celebrate their "45 + 1 year anniversary."

The All-American Rejects will bring their alt-rock and pop--punk songbook to Australia for the first time in over 17 years, after having to pull out of last year's Good Things festival.

There's also The Devil Wears Prada, the Ohio metal group who, like the popular 2006 movie, take their name from the 2003 bestselling novel.

Industrial metal trailblazers Ministry will make Good Things the Australian stop of their global farewell tour, ending a 45-year career.

Ringleader Al Jourgensen has stated he's "f***ing done" after Ministry's final live shows and upcoming 17th album Hate To Go (Take Out or Delivery). (Supplied: Derick Smith)

Other Good Things acts include Christian nu-metal group P.O.D, Mudvanye and Hellyah vocalist Chad Gray; Bilmuri, aka US singer-songwriter John Franck; punk rock mainstays MxPx and Welsh pop-punk band Neck Deep.

Plus, there's German trio Future Palace; young internet sensation ivri; dynamic singer-drummer Kami Kehoe; and Voice of Baceprot, an all-female Muslim Indonesian heavy metal trio.

Here's the full Good Things line-up so far:

Limp Bizkit, Simple Plan, Spiritbox, Polaris, The All-American Rejects, Bad Religion, Alexisonfire, Grinspoon, Millencolin, Ministry, Bilmuri, Chad Gray, MxPx, Neck Deep, Speed, Slowly Slowly, P.O.D., The Devil Wears Prada, Choirboys, All Them Witches, The Black Queen, Future Palace, Headwreck, The Home Team, House of Protection, ivri, Kami Kehoe, Locked Shut, LØLØ, Vianova, Voice Of Baceprot

Here are the dates, and the festival is once again welcoming younger moshers:

Fri 4 December — Flemington Racecourse: Melbourne, Wurundjeri Woi Worrong Land, VIC (15+)

Sat 5 December — Sydney Showgrounds: Sydney, Gadigal Land, NSW (16+)

Sun 6 December — Brisbane Showgrounds: Brisbane, Turrbal Jagera Land, QLD (16+)

Tickets are on sale from 10am AEST, Thursday August 20. You'll find more info at the Good Things website.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/p.title: Potholes force cars off Calder Freeway as Victorian road anger rises
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/p.author: Anna McGuinness
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The lane closure on the Calder Freeway on Tuesday morning. (Supplied: Connor Smith)

Up to seven cars have been forced off the road with damaged tyres after hitting potholes on the Calder Freeway near Gisborne.

The cars were lined up on the side of the freeway waiting for roadside assistance.

Damage to Victoria's major highways is causing anger ahead of the Victorian election.

More drivers have been left stranded after their vehicles were damaged by a pothole on a major Victorian freeway this morning.

Macedon Ranges resident John told ABC Central Victoria, at least seven cars with damaged tyres were lined up on the side of the Calder Freeway between Gisborne and Sunbury about 6.30am.

He said another three were pulled over on the off-ramp.

"There were people changing tyres on the side of the road; one young lady was in tears because she didn't know what to do," he said.

He lanes have been closed due to road damage on the freeway between Kyneton and Sunbury for two weeks.

"They're just filling gaps, they're not actually going to the cause of the problem," he said.

"We just keep blaming the weather without proper remediation."

A spokesperson from the Department of Transport couldn't confirm how many vehicles had been affected.

The right lane of the freeway remains closed city-bound near Mundy Road, with patching works under way.

Elsewhere in central Victoria, Johnny Ravet from Seymour Tyre and Mechanical told ABC Statewide Mornings there were six cars in his workshop all with pothole damage.

"Just last week we had one, an Audi, travelling to Nagambie, hit a pothole and no spare tyre so it was towed in," he said.

"That rim [cost] $4000 before we even put a tyre on it."

This morning's traffic hazard on the Calder Freeway follows a similar problem on the Princes Freeway at Bunyip, east of Melbourne yesterday where about 30 cars suffered tyre damage by hitting a pothole that was hard to see in the rain.

https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.title: South Korea faces quandary over Ukraine’s air defence system request
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.author: Park Chan-kyong
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.text:
If South Korea were to agree to Zelensky’s request, it could further strain ties with Russia and impair its own defence, analysts say

In a social media post on Saturday, Zelensky warned that “a decision has been made for 30,000 to 50,000 North Koreans to be deployed on the territory of Russia”, a figure higher than his earlier estimate of 30,000 made in July. He provided no further details.

Therefore, South Korea “should have closer cooperation with Ukraine”, he said.

Zelensky said: “We would very much like to receive support from South Korea in the form of what we lack – air defence systems.” In return, Ukraine could help South Korea with drone technology, among other things, he added.

The Ukrainian leader acknowledged that South Korea faced legal constraints on arms exports to countries at war.

“That is their choice. But we would like cooperation and are counting on it; our diplomats are in contact,” Zelensky added.

A Defence Ministry spokesman in Seoul said South Korea, in cooperation with other countries, was closely monitoring North Korea’s ties with Russia but declined to elaborate.

A South Korean Foreign Ministry official said on Monday: “Our provision of defence equipment to other countries has been carried out in compliance with relevant domestic laws and policies. We have provided support to Ukraine in various areas, including energy, infrastructure, health care and education.”

South Korea would continue to consider ways to “help restore peace in Ukraine and support its reconstruction”, he added.

Doo Jin-ho, director of the Eurasia Research Centre at the Korea Research Institute for National Strategy, said even if South Korea were willing to provide weapons to Ukraine, it would face production constraints.

“South Korea cannot rapidly expand its production capacity for air defence systems. It also needs to meet demand from other countries,” Doo said.

Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of advanced air-defence interceptors, particularly US-made Patriot missiles, leaving its major cities and critical energy infrastructure vulnerable to Russian ballistic missile strikes.

Earlier this year, South Korea’s Cheongung-II medium-range surface-to-air missile system was deployed by the United Arab Emirates to intercept incoming ballistic missiles and drones during the ongoing Middle East conflict. It reportedly successfully intercepted 96 per cent of Iranian-launched ballistic missiles and drones.

Cheongung’s performance in a real-world combat situation has increased the global profile of South Korea’s defence industry and procurement interest from several countries.

However, South Korea must also consider its ties with Russia, which remain deeply strained because Seoul has partnered with other countries to impose sanctions against Moscow over the war in Ukraine, according to Doo. South Korea’s growing defence cooperation with Nato and Russia’s deepening military alliance with North Korea had also complicated the relationship, he added.

“I wonder whether there would be any balance of interest for South Korea to provide Ukraine with air defence systems in return for cooperation in drone warfare know-how,” he said.

“South Korea is an industrial powerhouse. Once it sets its sights on drone warfare, it would be able to catch up with other countries very fast in this sector too.”

Meanwhile, Ukrainian military intelligence has reported that a North Korean missile unit had begun deploying personnel and equipment to western Russia. The unit could eventually include around 90 personnel, six launchers and up to 120 ballistic missiles for use in the war against Ukraine.

Referring to Zelensky’s comment on the additional North Korean deployment, Cho Han-bum, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification (KINU), said there appeared to be differences between North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the issue.

North Korea could be pressing Russia for military technology transfers, while Putin had emphasised that the deployment was Pyongyang’s initiative, Cho said.

“Kim may think: ‘We’ve done our job by helping you retake Kursk. Now it’s your turn to pay back.’ The trust between Kim and Putin is not as high as it may appear,” he said.

Pyongyang could not afford to send another 30,000 to 50,000 elite troops to fight Russia’s war, according to Cho.

The additional deployment – reportedly from the elite 11th Corps or the Storm Corps – would represent a serious drain on North Korea’s special operations capabilities, he added.

“The 11th Corps has some 110,000 troops and half of them are tied down with agriculture,” Cho said, adding that economic struggles had forced military units to sustain themselves through self-reliance.

Since the signing of a partnership treaty by Putin and Kim in June 2024, North Korea is believed to have dispatched about 20,000 combat troops and military engineers to date, primarily to Russia’s Kursk region, with an estimated 14,000 currently serving near the front lines.

About 6,000 of the North Korean soldiers deployed to Russia have been killed or wounded so far in the conflict, according to South Korean intelligence, while the BBC has estimated the death toll to be around 2,300.

If elite units such as the 11th Corps were to suffer heavy losses, it could deal a blow to Kim’s authority in North Korea, Doo said.

“Kim wouldn’t risk further casualties by sending troops to combat zones or having them taken prisoner.”
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.summary: South Korea's military has been asked to send 30,000 to 50,000 North Koreans to Russia. The figure is higher than his earlier estimate of 30,00 made in July. South Korea has been closely monitoring North Korea’s ties with Russia.

https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.title: 2,300-year-old wine found near Great Wall ruin reveals ancient brewing secrets
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.author: Shi Huang
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.text:
Archaeologists uncover 3.7 litres of well-preserved liquid in a Qin cemetery, confirming the use of millet-based brewing near the frontier

“He who has never been to the Great Wall is not a true man,” former Chinese leader Mao Zedong wrote in a poem while passing through the Liupan Mountains in Guyuan, Gansu, during the Long March of the Red Army in October, 1935.

Recently, a well-preserved bronze wine vessel was discovered at the Shanjiabao cemetery, located 2km (1.2 miles) from the Warring States Qin Great Wall. The ancient Warring States-era jar remained perfectly sealed and still glistened, according to a study published in the June issue of the Journal of Archaeological Science.

Along the 170km stretch of the Qin Great Wall, there are numerous forts, castles and barrier outposts of various sizes. At the time of the Warring States period, border soldiers and their families lived within fortified passes, castles and defensive outposts.

A total of 183 tombs from the Warring States period were excavated, 179 of which belonged to the Qin culture. It is inferred that this may have been a public cemetery for garrison troops and residents stationed at fortifications along the Great Wall.

In Tomb No 39, archaeologists extracted 3,740 millilitres of ancient liquid residue from a bronze garlic-head-shaped pot, a hallmark of Qin culture. Analysis confirmed that the liquid was wine.

“This bronze pot used a double-layer sealing technique with a textile inner lining and an outer coating of organic clay, which allowed the ancient wine from over 2,000 years ago to remain largely intact,” said Wang Xiaoyang, head of the Shanjiabao cemetery archaeological project at the Ningxia Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology, in an interview with the Chinese Social Sciences Today on July 30.

“It is currently the most well-preserved and information-rich wine relic from the period of the Qin state that has been publicly reported in China.”

To accurately decipher the ancient wine recipe and craftsmanship, they jointly sent the samples to Northwest University for further analysis.

China is one of the earliest regions in the world to consume alcoholic beverages. An increasing number of ancient alcoholic beverage residues have been discovered in China, sparking widespread interest in the origins of brewing and the evolution of brewing techniques.

However, the raw materials used for brewing differ between southern and northern China. In the south, rice is typically used for brewing, while in the north, grains such as millet and foxtail millet are commonly used.

A total of 24 types of compounds, including organic acids and their derivatives, amino acids and their derivatives, and carbohydrates, were detected in the liquid unearthed from the archaeological site.

The distribution pattern of organic acids was consistent with that of artificially aged yellow wine, confirming that the liquid was a grain-based alcoholic beverage rather than a fruit wine such as grape wine.

In the liquid inside the garlic-head-shaped pot, researchers confirmed through starch residue analysis that over 92 per cent of the starch originated from broomcorn millet (Panicum miliaceum) – a water-efficient grain that has been consumed in northern China for over 10,000 years – while the remaining starch came from wheat and barley.

This discovery fills an archaeological gap in the study of winemaking in the Ningxia region during the Warring States period of the Qin state.

It also suggests that over 2,300 years ago, there was a Qin person at the Great Wall border pass – maybe a soldier – who loved a drink, and when he was buried, his family filled his most cherished bronze wine vessel with fine wine to accompany him for eternity.
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/.summary: Archaeologists uncovered 3.7 litres of well-preserved liquid in a Qin cemetery. The ancient Warring States-era jar remained perfectly sealed and still glistened. The liquid was found in a bronze garlic-head-shaped pot, a hallmark of Qin culture.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/ch.title: North Carolina G.O.P. Picks Replacement for Candidate Plagued by Scandal
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/ch.author: Eduardo Medina
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/ch.text:
Representative Chuck Edwards dropped his re-election bid amid sexual harassment allegations. His replacement, Jennifer Balkcom, has about 80 days to campaign.

Reporting from Asheville, N.C.

Republican officials in western North Carolina on Monday selected a candidate to replace Representative Chuck Edwards on the November ballot. Mr. Edwards dropped out of the race last week after the House Ethics Committee documented his troubling conduct toward two young female aides.

The new candidate, State Representative Jennifer Balkcom, will now have roughly 80 days to crisscross North Carolina’s sprawling 11th Congressional District and retain the seat for Republicans, who are vying to keep control of Congress in a challenging midterm election.

Even without scandal, Mr. Edwards had already been facing a competitive re-election contest. Jamie Ager, the Democratic candidate, has been making inroads in the district as a farmer with deep roots in a mostly conservative region that has shifted left in recent election cycles.

But after the House Ethics Committee recommended that Mr. Edwards be censured for “persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct” toward the women, he faced growing pressure to abandon his re-election bid.

Ms. Balkcom was selected to replace Mr. Edwards by the Republican executive committee of North Carolina’s 11th District. The committee includes dozens of members, such as local party chairs.

Ms. Balkcom, who has served two terms in the State House, had expressed interest in running for the district, saying in a statement on Monday that she was eager to “work with President Trump’s administration to continue rebuilding western North Carolina, and make sure Washington never forgets the people who call these mountains home.”

Ms. Balkcom will need a crush of cash to be able to compete with Mr. Ager, who has raised more than $3 million. (Mr. Edwards had $940,000 in his campaign coffers.)

Western North Carolina, a mountainous and mostly rural area that is anchored by the liberal city of Asheville, has not elected a Democrat to Congress since 2010, when Heath Shuler, a former N.F.L. quarterback, won his third term in the House.

But Democrats have felt optimistic about Mr. Ager’s chances, especially after Mr. Edwards’s scandal.

For many residents, the central issue is the slow pace of recovery from Hurricane Helene, which killed more than 100 people in 2024 and was the worst natural disaster to strike the state.

The Helene response has also hovered over North Carolina’s Senate race between former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, and Michael Whatley, a Republican who was named the Helene “recovery czar” by President Trump.

Eduardo Medina is a Times reporter covering the South. An Alabama native, he is now based in Durham, N.C.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/ch.summary: Rep. Chuck Edwards dropped his re-election bid last week after the House Ethics Committee documented his troubling conduct toward two young female aides. The new candidate, Jennifer Balkcom, will now have about 80 days to campaign for the seat.

Charles Kupchan, a former special assistant to ex-US President Barack Obama, says Iran holds the upper hand in negotiations with the US due to political pressure on President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections.

Kupchan told Al Jazeera that Tehran may be better positioned to weather the current standoff than Washington as the elections approach.

“Can the Iranians bear more pain than Donald Trump as he heads into the midterms? The answer to that is probably yes,” Kupchan said.

Iran is leveraging that advantage, he noted, though it risks pushing its position too far in the negotiations.

Tehran is “perhaps trying too hard to take advantage of it by making demands that Trump can’t say yes to. But right now, we’re not there yet, I’m guessing we will get there,” he said.

“I think we’re in a game of a kind of cat and mouse,” Kupchan added.

Yemen’s government-aligned military says Houthi forces have launched ballistic missiles at the Red Sea city of al-Makha (Mocha) and its port facilities.

We’ll bring you more when we get it.

Trump says he’ll demand compensation from Tehran for people killed or wounded in the US war on Iran.

The move comes days after Tehran demanded Washington compensate it for damage from the five-month war as a condition for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Stay with us for the latest news and analysis from across the Middle East and beyond.

https://www.scmp.com/economy/china-econo.title: China’s aviation regulator steps up safety communication with foreign carriers
https://www.scmp.com/economy/china-econo.author: Frank Chen
https://www.scmp.com/economy/china-econo.text:
The Civil Aviation Administration of China, following some operational changes, has increased its aircraft checks as an additional safety measure

An aviation analyst said the move was made in light of changing operational practices, adding that air travel in the country remained safe.

In attendance were AirAsia’s senior management members, including the group chief safety officer, the CEO of AirAsia X – the company’s long-haul service subsidiary – as well as the China regional manager and engineering director, among others.

AirAsia briefed CAAC officials on its China operations and compliance plans to further enhance safety, the reports said. In response, CAAC officials “fully affirmed” AirAsia’s efforts, track record and cooperation.

AirAsia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the South China Morning Post.

In March, CAAC’s office for southwestern China also revealed on its website that it had summoned representatives from Malaysia-based cargo carrier Raya Airlines following “incidents”, including two instances of cabin depressurisation requiring emergency descent while in Chinese skies.

Raya’s directors overseeing operations, safety and maintenance heard requirements and safety recommendations from CAAC specialists and discussed rectification measures.

Aviation analyst Jason Zheng Lin said CAAC has one of the most stringent safety supervision regimens in the world and its meetings with operators were aimed at routinely reminding them of risks and areas for improvement.

“Such meetings are a routine measure to keep up communications and convey safety reminders … All airlines, regardless of their nationality, could be called up,” said Zheng, who works with a Shanghai-based transport consultancy.

In 2025, CAAC also conducted a thorough operations audit of Hainan Airlines, one of the country’s largest carriers.

Zheng said that some events had led to amendments in operational practice and aviation safety this year, and CAAC had moved proactively to strengthen supervision during the summer travel peak. However, none of these events had led to serious incidents, he added.

“CAAC holding talks with airlines may be the most visible part of its work, but on top of these, the watchdog has [in] recent months increased inspection and checks on airlines’ work to troubleshoot any aircraft found to have risks,” Zheng said.

“Sometimes foreign firms may need time to get up to date with China’s extra or unique safety supervision, culture or policies, thus CAAC is stepping up its contact with them to help ensure full understanding and compliance.”

The analyst said that, among other measures, CAAC would invite Chinese airlines to share best practices and experience with foreign firms, especially smaller ones that have just launched their China operations.

For instance, in March, safety experts with leading domestic courier SF Airlines were invited to share their experience with Raya Airlines.

In October, CAAC convened a special meeting on foreign carrier safety operations, attended by Batik Air Malaysia, Myanmar National Airlines and others, to discuss some safety occurrences and prevention strategies.

“All these efforts on the part of CAAC and operators should further ensure peace of mind for travellers: flying in China, including on flights operated by foreign firms, remains extremely safe,” Zheng said.

Mainland China has maintained one of the safest civil aviation records globally over the past few decades. The International Air Transport Association’s (IATA) regional safety performance data for North Asia, which includes mainland China, shows the regional accident rate well below the global baseline.

In 2025 alone, carriers logged over 14.5 million flight hours and 5.54 million take-offs handling 770 million passenger trips in China, with an operational safety record among the top tier worldwide, according to CAAC and IATA data.

This incident – which occurred due to a mechanical breakdown and logistical issues – did not relate to the new safety rules, but saw the operator of Hangzhou’s airport come under fire for what was perceived as poor communication and inflexibility.
