https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.title: Zuckerberg envisions 'superintelligence' for everyone in AI manifesto
https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/technology/2.text:
Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg laid out a vision Monday of what he said artificial intelligence can do for the world, imagining a future where everyone has their own, all-knowing AI agent that strives to improve all aspects of their lives.

Zuckerberg detailed his ambitions for the technology in a 6,500-word essay published online where he also outlined why he favours open-source AI technology, in which developers make key components accessible for anyone to examine, modify and build upon.

In a document derided by critics as fantastical, Zuckerberg said his company is working towards an era where everyone will have the tools to create new businesses, receive PhD-level tutoring and receive personalised lifestyle tips. His 8-year-old daughter, he wrote, can already code her ideas and quickly produce videos.

"Everyone will soon have invention superpowers," Zuckerberg wrote.

Zuckerberg warned of risks if control of advanced AI is concentrated with a select few companies, institutions or governments. On Monday, Meta also announced the release of a new open-source AI model, Muse Glimmer, which can run on a personal computer, and Zuckerberg said the company would also provide a way for developers to access a more powerful AI model, Muse Spark 1.2.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Meta makes AI models, like several other tech companies, and uses them to power platforms such as Instagram and Facebook. The Menlo Park, California, company also makes them available to developers who can create their own apps and features.

Critics said Zuckerberg was not reckoning fully with the risks inherent in AI's rapid development.

Noting recent incidents where AI models, including Meta's own, hacked other companies on at least three separate occasions, Anthony Aguirre, president and CEO of the AI safety non-profit Future of Life Institute, asked "what on Earth makes Meta think they – or anyone – could control something exponentially smarter, faster, and more capable?"

"Meta's chosen path is ultimately one of human replacement and disempowerment, but there is an alternate, pro-human path – one that brings about individual flourishing and scientific breakthroughs with controllable AI tools. What's urgently needed now is for governments to facilitate a pause on advanced AI development and steer us onto the pro-human path – before it's too late," Aguirre said.

In his essay, Zuckerberg outlined why he thought open source is a better path for fair development of AI. He warned that if control of AI "superintelligence" is too concentrated, it will lead to less favourable outcomes for everyone else. The key, he wrote, is finding a balance that ensures advanced AI is "broadly distributed" to empower billions of people equitably.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Meta has long been a proponent of open-sourcing its AI models, but has struggled to keep up with rivals such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google that have not taken the same approach.

Zuckerberg made what could be a veiled reference to Meta's rivals without naming specific companies.

"Most other labs are focused on building AI for companies, governments, or other institutions, so if those labs lead, then the balance of power will favour larger institutions over individuals," he wrote.

Zuckerberg also included policy recommendations for keeping the US ahead of rivals, including China. The United States and its allies need to speed up building energy capacity and infrastructure to stay competitive, he said.

Zuckerberg called for authorities to reconsider their position on "distillation", which involves training a less capable model on the outputs of a stronger one. The Trump administration has vowed to crack down on Chinese AI companies using distillation to extract technical features from US AI models. Anthropic earlier this year accused China's DeepSeek of using distillation.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

"Some have tried to frame distillation as harmful, but I think it is important to protect the principle that you can learn from anything you can observe," Zuckerberg said. "This is how the world works, and the US will not be able to lead if we restrict ourselves on this front."

Matt Lane, senior policy counsel at the non-profit digital rights advocacy group Fight for the Future, called Zuckerberg "annoyingly out of touch on his best day", but said the CEO is right about the importance of open-source AI.

Shared access to open-source AI systems is important for protection in a world where AI can be used to hack into electronic systems, like voting systems and benefits infrastructure, he said.

But he said only Meta will benefit if everyone were to use Meta-designed AI systems, even if they are fully open-source. "Open-source AI needs to be supported beyond these corporate interests. We, unlike Zuckerberg, hope for as much competition as possible," he said.

Australia's world champion Moesha Johnson has continued her season of complete dominance in open water swimming, winning the Pan Pacific Championships 10-kilometre title off Long Beach, California.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/g.title: How Gianni Infantino's FIFA leadership imploded over two weeks
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/g.author: Luke Cooper
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/g.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Gianni Infantino has been embroiled in a scandal that has endured for more than two weeks. (Reuters: Dylan Martinez)

After weeks of pressure, three of the world's largest continental football confederations have issued a joint open letter attacking the leadership of FIFA President Gianni Infantino over his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup.

The presidents and general secretaries of the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA), Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF) said the saga showed Mr Infantino "places himself above the collection that entrusted him with authority".

The letter marked the latest development in more than two weeks of turmoil surrounding Mr Infantino following this year's World Cup.

This is the timeline to date of how Mr Infantino became embroiled in controversy.

Gianni's message to 'haters'

Seven days after the final ball was kicked at the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Mr Infantino posted a lengthy, 15-picture slide show message on Instagram that celebrated the tournament's success.

In the statement, the FIFA president targeted people who "were so consumed by hate and criticism" in their opposition to some of how the tournament unfolded.

The message came after intense scrutiny of Mr Infantino, who has been repeatedly accused of attempting to align FIFA with the Trump administration, both before and during the World Cup.

In December 2025, he faced widespread international criticism for awarding the inaugural FIFA Peace Prize to United States President Donald Trump.

Mr Infantino has sought to closely align FIFA with the Trump administration. (Reuters: Dylan Martinez)

Four weeks into the tournament, questions about his proximity to Mr Trump resurfaced when the US president claimed he had successfully lobbied FIFA's bosses to overturn a World Cup red card ban handed to American forward Folarin Balogun.

FIFA later reversed Balogun's ban after Mr Trump asked for a review of the decision.

The closeness was also evident at the World Cup final when Mr Trump was the sole political leader allowed onto a stage alongside Mr Infantino for the all-important moment when tournament winners Spain were handed the trophy, despite the event being co-hosted by Mexico and Canada.

Mr Infantino's latest scandal came after he announced a plan to form a commercial subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) that would grant private buyers control over competitions including the World Cup and Club World Cup.

The $US20 billion ($28.7 billion) proposal was first revealed by British newspaper The Times, and FIFA later described the FFE as "a new FIFA-owned and controlled subsidiary consolidating FIFA's commercial and event operations".

The governing body said it would retain control of the subsidiary and authority over football governance, competitions, match calendars and regulatory decisions.

The FIFA Forward Enterprise would have granted corporate buyers access to commercial control over the governing body's events and tournaments. (Reuters: Mark J Rebilas)

Mr Infantino said FIFA's hope was that the FFE could generate enough commercial revenue to raise $US20 million in additional funding by 2030 for the further development of "infrastructure, coaching, national teams, competitions, grassroots football and the women's game" in member nations worldwide.

The effort was initially being bankrolled by Joshua Kushner — the brother of Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law — via the Thrive Eternal investment firm.

UEFA was the first to condemn the plan, issuing a strongly-worded statement on the same day FIFA announced the idea.

Joshua Kushner's Thrive Eternal was named by FIFA as the frontrunner to buy the FFE rights. (Reuters: Brendan McDermid)

"This crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross," UEFA said.

"The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially.

As immediate criticism of the FFE plan grew, it was revealed Mr Infantino had written to each of FIFA's 211 member nations with a one-off offer aimed at enticing them into approving the deal.

The FIFA president set out a single $US20 million ($28.7m) funding boost for each member nation that chose to vote to approve the FFE bid.

He also gave those nations a deadline of mid-September to choose whether they would accept the offer.

UEFA issued an additional statement addressing the offer.

"UEFA knows there is significant and growing opposition to FIFA's scheme," the statement said.

"FIFA cannot continue to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends. We can grow the game correctly. It's time to prioritise associations, clubs, leagues, players and fans."

In the first significant move by a continental football confederation against the FFE, UEFA announced each of its 55 member nations would refuse to participate in FIFA-commissioned events and tournaments until the proposal was removed.

"The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product," UEFA's statement said.

"It is both irresponsible and indefensible that a proposal of such significance for football was conceived in secret and brought to the brink of approval without any meaningful consultation with those entrusted with stewarding the game.

"This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of FIFA's duty as the custodian of world football.

"Some things are simply too important to sell. The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale."

CONCACAF released its own statement on the same day, confirming it had held a meeting with representatives from each of its 41 member nations and that the confederation had rejected the FFE proposal.

Football Australia Football only confirmed it had received notice from FIFA detailing the proposal.

"As this is the first time we have been made aware of the initiative, we are now working to understand the proposal in full," a statement said.

"We have requested further information from FIFA to properly assess the strategic, commercial, and governance implications of such a significant step."

The AFC became the third continental confederation to join the revolt against the FFE plan, issuing a statement that said it joined UEFA and CONCACAF "in expressing serious concerns" about the idea.

The Asian football organisation did not go as far as UEFA as to commit to boycotts of FIFA events, but demanded the global body "undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework".

"While the immediate debate centres on FFE, the AFC considers this issue extends far beyond a single proposal," the statement said.

"Rather, it has exposed fundamental weaknesses in FIFA's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed."

On the same day, FIFA and Mr Infantino a statement that sought to address the increasing criticism.

"FFE has been proposed solely to ensure that all FIFA Member Associations have the opportunity to take meaningful ownership of the commercial opportunity of football in their respective countries," FIFA said.

From within the organisation, FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour also attacked the bid, telling The Associated Press that he believed the body's staff were "deceived" by how the FFE idea was conceived.

"It is the project of one person," he said in a statement.

FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour claimed the governing body's staff had been deceived by Mr Infantino's secrecy around the FFE bid. (AP: Alessandra Tarantino)

"Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions."

Mr Lamour's statement also followed the extraordinary resignation of Mr Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro.

Mr Cordeiro claimed he had no involvement in planning the FFE, and described it as "a bad deal for football".

Four days after FIFA first confirmed the FFE plan, Mr Infantino announced it would not proceed.

"Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place," a statement said.

"Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support."

The uproar from UEFA and CONCACAF continued to arrive

While UEFA welcomed the FFE proposal's withdrawal, it also said those responsible should be held to account and that Mr Infantino was failing in his leadership of FIFA.

David Gallop was Football Australia CEO when Gianni Infantino took over the FIFA presidency from the corruption-stained run of Sepp Blatter, he says Infantino's World Cup proposal stank.

"We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game," it said.

"No option should be off the table. The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA's confidence but also that of many other members of the football family."

CONCACAF echoed those calls.

"A proposal of this magnitude does not reach that stage by accident. It is a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first," it said in a statement.

"This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour.

The legal threats and support pulled

After its initial threat to boycott FIFA-led events and tournaments, UEFA's action against the FFE proposal went further.

UEFA's lawyers informed FIFA that the European body was "actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints".

A letter named 18 FIFA executives who UEFA said should retain data, documents and electronic messages as potential evidence.

They included Mr Infantino, Zurich-based chief finance officer Thomas Peyer and Arsène Wenger, the coaching great who is FIFA's head of global football development.

"UEFA puts you on formal notice that any destruction, deletion, alteration, concealment, or loss of relevant materials following receipt of this notice — or following any earlier date on which you were, or reasonably should have been, aware that proceedings were anticipated — may constitute spoliation of evidence," the letter said.

Legal proceedings were "reasonably anticipated," UEFA's lawyer Andrew J Levander wrote, citing the belief of football stakeholders that the plan was "fundamentally incompatible with the proper governance of football".

European football body UEFA threatens FIFA with legal action over Gianni Infantino's failed plan to sell a stake in future World Cup profits to private investors.

At the same time, the Swedish football federation confirmed UEFA was actively looking "to come up with an alternative candidate" as FIFA president.

In England, the Football Association confirmed it would withdraw its support for Mr Infantino as FIFA president in the wake of the FFE scandal.

That decision followed the football governing bodies of both Wales and Serbia, which also issued statements against Mr Infantino.

Amid what had become a multinational furore, the FIFA executive called an emergency meeting to be held in Rabat, Morocco.

At that meeting, FIFA Secretary General Mattias Grafström and members of the organisation's board confirmed they would continue to support Mr Infantino as president.

In its statement after the meeting, the executive team said "mistakes" surrounding the FFE proposal "were acknowledged" and "that the process should have been handled differently".

The governing body also said that a separate letter to the FIFA Council and its 211 member nations included an apology for the scandal, although it did not explicitly say the apology had come from Mr Infantino.

"A review will now be conducted, and a report will be presented to the FIFA Council at its next scheduled meeting," the statement said.

"There are always lessons to be learned, and FIFA will continue to improve its processes in light of this experience."

The move also came on the same day Portuguese football legend Luis Figo issued his own scathing statement about Mr Infantino and demanded he resign.

"Infantino has debased the office that he promised to elevate. He has lied, deceived and tried to feather his own nest at the expense of the game he is supposed to serve," the statement posted to X said.

The divided confederations

A week after it first threatened to boycott FIFA-commissioned events and tournaments, UEFA doubled down on the announcement.

European football's governing body said that despite FIFA apologising, it had lost confidence in Mr Infantino and the conditions it had set to withdraw its boycott threat had not been met.

"UEFA's associations were very clear about the conditions attached to the non participation in FIFA competitions," it said in a statement.

"First, the proposals to sell off the major competitions had to be withdrawn and secondly, assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again.

"These conditions have not been met. In addition, UEFA made it abundantly clear in its statement on Saturday that it has lost confidence in Gianni Infantino's presidency. That position holds."

The statement joined the increasingly mounting pressure placed on Mr Infantino, after global football players union FIFPRO also accused him of "a profound abuse of presidential power".

"No institution can restore confidence in a presidency that has itself dismantled the conditions upon which confidence depends," the FIFPRO statement read.

Argentina was one high-profile footballing nation that threw its support behind Mr Infantino. (AP: Tony Gutierrez)

While most of the opposition to Mr Infantino's leadership appeared to originate in Europe, Asia and North America, on other continents the message was different.

In South America, the Confederación Sudamericana de Fútbol — known as CONMEBOL — released a statement promising to reject any attempt to unseat Mr Infantino outside of FIFA's usual election processes.

"[FIFA's] future can only be built on the basis of respect for the institutions, governance and democratic procedures that represent the 211 FIFA Member Associations," it said.

The show of support was backed by the Argentine Football Association, the body that governs the World Cup runners-up, and also by the Confederation of African Football.

The fallout continues

In a break with the standing of CONCACAF, joint world cup host Mexico threw its support behind Mr Infantino.

"The FMF will neither recognise nor approve any process convened outside of that institutional framework, and it joins the call made … by President Infantino to collectively continue developing football for the benefit of the 211 member associations," it said in a statement.

"The FMF supports President Infantino's leadership in continuing to promote the development of football through institutional strengthening."

The Mexican position was also at odds with the Norwegian Football Federation, whose President Lise Klaveness said Mr Infantino no longer had the confidence of the football community and that the sport needed to move beyond "Game of Thrones" power struggles.

"He does not have the institutional trust required to govern FIFA stably in the times we are in," Ms Klaveness said,

In continuing their assault against Mr Infantino, UEFA, the AFC and CONCACAF released a joint open letter that took aim at FIFA for not conceding the FFE proposal was "inherently wrong".

"When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned," the letter said.

"There remains no recognition that attempting to sell an interest in the FIFA World Cup was a profound failure of judgment — not just a procedural misstep, but a fundamental breach of trust with the very institutions FIFA exists to serve."

The confederations also demanded an independent review of the FFE scandal take place over an internal, FIFA-commissioned investigation.

"FIFA's own letter also confirms that only one elected official was present at the leadership meeting in Morocco. No FIFA Council members or Member Associations were invited to participate," the letter said.

"Only the management committee, composed of FIFA-employed senior staff, was present.

Gianni Infantino's future as the head of FIFA will ultimately be decided by each of the organisation's 211 member nations.

Unless an emergency election — known as an Extraordinary Congress — is called, his leadership will be determined at the next Presidential Election at the FIFA Congress to be held in Morrocco on March 17, next year.

An Extraordinary Congress can only be called by the 37-member FIFA Council, or if 20 per cent of the 211 nations — 43 members — issue a written request that that one be held.

If that does not happen, presidential candidates expecting to run against Mr Infantino in March will need to be named by November 18.

According to FIFA's rules, each member nation has a single vote — regardless of size, population or influence and success in football.

FIFA presidents are allowed to remain as leader for three terms consecutively, but no longer.

Mr Infantino has already been re-elected twice consecutively after he ran unopposed in 2019 and 2023.

He also led for three years before that after he replaced Sepp Blatter amid FIFA's notorious corruption scandal, but those years were not considered as a complete presidential term.

Candidates who could run against Mr Infantino would need to be endorsed by at least five member nations.

If there is just a single opponent against Mr Infantino, the eventual victor would need to be elected with 50 per cent of the 211 votes.

If there are more than two candidates in the race, run-off votes are held to reduce the number to a final duo.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/a.title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is freezing her eggs to feel 'in control'. How does it work?
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/a.author: Nelli Saarinen
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Fertility and Infertility

US Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has shared she has started the process of freezing her eggs. (Supplied: Instagram)

US Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has shared in a series of Instagram posts that she is in the process of freezing her eggs.

She said she was not ruling out a presidential run in an interview with US broadcaster ABC.

Ocasio-Cortez said the Trump administration had made pregnancy "more dangerous" than at any point in the last three decades, and that "we're going to have to talk about it".

US congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is freezing her eggs and says she will be documenting the process on her social media.

"It has taken me time to consider, weigh and save up for, and it is of a sensitive matter and a personal matter and usually I keep my private life quite private, but I have made the decision to start freezing my eggs," Ms Ocasio-Cortez said in a video posted to her Instagram stories over the weekend.

Ms Ocasio-Cortez shared a video showing her medications laid out on a table before filming herself doing what she said was the first injection in her egg freezing cycle.

"Don't be weird about this, even though I know all of you will be," she said while sanitising a patch of skin on her stomach to use as an injection site.

Being elected at a young age to represent New York's 14th district came with the flip side of having to "grow up in the public eye", Ms Ocasio-Cortez said.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez shared a video of herself injecting medications at a TV studio where she was being interviewed. (Supplied: Instagram)

The now 36-year-old was sworn into the US House of Representatives in 2019 when she was 29, making her the youngest woman ever to serve in the US Congress.

"This is a choice that I am making to feel more in control of my life and if people want to make assumptions about my decision, let them make those assumptions.

"I feel empowered to make this choice, I think it's a very privileged position that I've been able to make."

In an interview with US broadcaster ABC's program This Week, Ms Ocasio-Cortez said she was not ruling out a presidential run.

"I'm focused on winning the mid-terms. I'm running for Congress right now," Ms Ocasio-Cortez said in the interview on Sunday.

In the wake of widespread abortion bans, US prosecutors launch hundreds of cases charging people with crimes related to their pregnancy, miscarriage, stillbirth or birth.

"I haven't ruled out the possibility. And I'm very humbled to the tremendous amount of support out there."

In her earlier Instagram posts, Ms Ocasio-Cortez said she was aware her choice to share her egg-freezing process came with "political risk".

"I'm also aware that in all of this kind of swirling conversation that happens, I am now kind of now opening the door to this being part of that discussion," she said.

"This is just not something that men deal with."

"Men run for office or frankly they interview for jobs and people don't think in the back of their mind, 'okay, this guy's running for office, how old is he? Oh well, is he going to want to start a family?'"

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said she felt "empowered" by the decision to freeze her eggs. (Reuters: Al Drago, file)

She said US President Donald Trump's administration was "dedicated to politicising women's bodies and taking our choices away from us and punishing us around decision to be pregnant or not be pregnant."

Mr Trump's first-term appointees to the US Supreme Court provided the margins that struck down the Roe v Wade decision in a 2022 ruling. Roe v Wade had established a constitutional right to terminate a pregnancy.

Mr Trump has dubbed himself the "father of IVF" and even vowed to make IVF cost-free, although his measures fell short of imposing a mandate on employers and insurance companies to cover IVF.

His support of IVF has been contentious for his voter base.

While the majority of Americans support IVF, some conservative Christians oppose it because it often involves the destruction of unused embryos.

An egg freezing cycle typically takes around two weeks, and involves daily medical injections and ultrasound monitoring to determine how the patient's body is responding to the medications and when to collect the eggs.

The patient will take a trigger injection to initiate the release of the eggs, and 36 hours later the eggs will be collected in a procedure under anaesthetic.

The eggs can be frozen indefinitely, although different legal limits apply across the Australian states and internationally, and used to create embryos for in vitro fertilisation (IVF) in the future.

Retrieved eggs are frozen in liquid nitrogen, with patients paying annual storage costs to clinics. (ABC News: Hugh Sando)

A woman's likelihood of having a baby using frozen eggs largely depends on how old she was when they were frozen, said Alex Polyakov, Associate Professor at the University of Melbourne and a fertility specialist.

"In younger women, if you freeze eggs, you sort of stop the timing in a sense. So, every egg would have the same potential as a fresh egg in an IVF cycle, but at the age of freezing," he said.

While women's fertility begins to decline after the age of 35, the physical ability to carry a pregnancy can remain much longer provided there were no other health issues, Dr Polyakov said.

"As women get older, more and more of the eggs are genetically abnormal, and that reduces the chance of pregnancy, and it reduces the chance of a live birth."

But freezing eggs, even if it's done at a young age, never guarantees a baby, Dr Polyakov noted.

"No matter how many eggs you freeze, it doesn't give you 100 per cent chance that you would actually have a baby," he says.

"It's possible to freeze 20 eggs and then when you try to use them none of them survive the thaw. Or you thaw them and they survive, but none of them fertilise and become embryos. Or they become embryos but none of them become good embryos. So, there is attrition at every step," he explained.

Data from the Australian and New Zealand Assisted Reproduction Database in 2024 showed that the number of women freezing their eggs to preserve fertility had almost doubled in the previous three years.

A meta-analysis of 10 studies conducted between 1999 and 2020 showed only one in 10 patients returned to use eggs that they had frozen.

Celebrity endorsements and social media influencers are helping drive more women to freeze their eggs. But one doctor is warning young women to seriously consider the financial, physical and emotional toll.

The analysis found that when using eggs that were frozen before age 35, more than half the women achieved a live birth, while for women who froze their eggs over the age of 40, the likelihood of a live birth was about one in five.

But the data also showed that women who freeze their eggs when younger are less likely to return to use them, while those who freeze their eggs when they are older are more likely to want to use them — but have a lower chance of pregnancy.

It's a dichotomy Dr Polyakov is familiar with.

"The younger age of freezing makes you less likely to actually need those eggs, because younger women, when they freeze their eggs … there is a decent chance that they will find a partner and have babies naturally, so they won't need them," he said.

"On the other hand, if you do it when you're older, the success rate is much less, but you're more likely to use them."

In IVF treatment, embryos are created and grown in a petri dish from sperm and eggs. (AP Photo: Michael Wyke, file)

Some people don't return to use their eggs because they decide to forgo having children altogether for a variety of reasons.

An egg freezing cycle in Australia typically costs between $3000 and $6000, depending on the clinic and the medications used.

Some people need to undergo multiple cycles to get a number of eggs they are satisfied with.

On top of the cost of the cycle, there is the ongoing cost of storing the frozen eggs.

When speaking of the cost of egg freezing, Ms Ocasio-Cortez indicated fertility checks were "a great small step" for those who are "on the fence" or "not sure about costs".

Women like Libby French are using the egg-timer test to make high-stakes decisions about their fertility, but experts say it's not a reliable predictor of reproduction potential.

"A great small step you can take that can really empower you is to get your fertility checked," she said.

"It's a little bit of blood work and an ultrasound, they will give you your follicle count and then some short time after that they will give you something known as an AMH level in your blood which … it's a general kind of ballpark around your fertility and it is so empowering to receive that information because you can make a choice based on you."

The AMH test measures the anti- Müllerian hormone, which gives an indication of a woman's ovarian reserves— but many experts stress the test is misleading and not accurate for measuring fertility.

The test could help a doctor estimate how many eggs could be collected in an IVF or egg retrieval cycle, Dr Polyakov said.

"It does not tell you what your chance of natural pregnancy is at any given time. It does not tell you when you will run out of eggs. It does not tell you how long you've got," Dr Polyakov says.

"There are plenty of women in their late 20s who have low AMH and get pregnant with no issues."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/n.title: 'Seismic shift': Māori set to invest in First Nations projects under new deal
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/n.author: Stephanie Boltje
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Business, Economics and Finance

The deal will open up new sources for capital for First Nations-led projects. (Supplied: Joseph Mayers/ IBA)

A new partnership will open the door for one of New Zealand's wealthiest Māori iwi to invest in large-scale First Nations projects in Australia.

The Waikato-Tainui will look to invest in Indigenous-led projects in renewable energy, mining, infrastructure, agriculture and more.

The agreement will be signed again in New Zealand at the annual celebration of the Māori Queen's coronation next month.

Indigenous business groups hope an historic deal with one of the largest and wealthiest tribal authorities in Aotearoa New Zealand will bring much-needed investment in large-scale First Nations projects.

The investment partnership between federal government agency Indigenous Business Australia (IBA) and the Waikato-Tainui iwi (nation) was signed today in Sydney.

Under the deal, IBA will help Waikato-Tainui, which holds around $AU2 billion in assets, invest in projects developed with Traditional Owners, including in the resources and agriculture sectors.

IBA chair Darren Godwell, a proud descendant of the Kokoberren peoples, said the signing of the "letter of intent" between two Indigenous investment institutions was a "seismic shift" for self-determination in Australia.

"We've got Indigenous institutional capacity that's willing to mobilise investment at scale so that TOs [Traditional Owners] can participate in the biggest projects that are happening on their Country," he said.

"Once we ... extend this invitation out to Indigenous Australia, we think we're going to be swamped with demand and opportunities."

Darren Godwell and Tuku Morgan signed the agreement Tuesday morning. (Supplied: Joseph Mayers/IBA)

Waikato-Tainui Chairman Tuku Morgan was in Sydney for the signing and said it represented a "watershed moment".

"This is about trying to build a new era of relationships that promises cohesion, better synergy on the basis of shared values, shared cultural values, shared environmental values, and the ability to do business with each other," he said.

Mr Godwell said the Waikato-Tainui, already a big investor in New Zealand retail, residential, ports and agriculture projects, is looking to generate long-term commercial returns.

He said the iwi is also concerned about being too exposed to the New Zealand economy.

"They need to offset that risk by investing in other places, and what better place to invest than Australia."

IBA's Darren Godwell says the deal is a 'watershed moment' for economic self-determination. (Supplied: Indigenous Business Australia)

The IBA will work closely with the Waikato-Tainui to help ease the transition into Australia, he said.

"We're going to share our information, our market intelligence, and then our relationships directly with TOs."

While the successful projects are yet to be decided, early beneficiaries could be Indigenous stakes in ports or large-scale renewable projects, as well as industries such as mining, agriculture and botanicals.

Mr Godwell said Yindjibarndi WaterCo's recent agreement to acquire the Dampier Seawater Desalination Plant in the Pilbara from Rio Tinto and the WA government is one contender.

"A large-scale project like that is something that's a very serious proposition for an investment partnership like the one we're announcing."

Michael Woodley hopes the deal will prompt broader interest in First Nations investment opportunities. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

CEO of the Yindjibarndi Group Michael Woodley said the new partnership was an example of First Nations people empowering each other across borders.

"It hasn't been something that First Nations have generally been successful (at) in the past," he said.

"The market as well … will obviously see this as a stepping-stone towards supporting First Nations with capital investment for our ideas."

Mr Woodley said he hoped it would open doors for more global First Nations institutions to do the same.

"Australia is one of the establishing frontiers for First Nations in terms of economic development, economic investment," he said.

"That could lead to something bigger and better in terms of how we unite around the globe."

Many Maori tribal authorities in New Zealand hold investment portfolios funded by historical Treaty of Waitangi settlements, with proceeds distributed to community projects such as social housing, health, environment and education.

"At the heart of what we do is, how do we build and ensure the ongoing prosperity of our people and at the same time, achieve the preservation and ongoing sustenance of the environment [and] keeping our culture alive, our language alive," Mr Morgan said.

The Waikato-Tainui is made up of 100,000 people, including around 15,000 who live in Australia, he said.

"They married into First Nations mobs across Australia. They are part of our family.

"Connecting and doing this high-level agreement is more than just doing business. This is family."

The agreement will be signed again in New Zealand at the annual celebration of the Māori Queen's coronation, expected to be attended by thousands of people next month.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/a.title: Perhaps the answer to my dating woes is to simply tell people who I am
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/a.author: Vanessa Mbeve
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Vanessa Mbeve would like to believe she is being authentic on dating apps, but knows she is self-editing in an effort to make herself "palatable". (Supplied: Vanessa Mbeve)

Every time I rejoin Tinder or another dating site, I am faced with the dreaded questions of whether to include my disability in my profile.

Often, I omit the fact and only disclose it after a potential match gets to know me a little.

I would like to say I am still being authentic, but in truth I am not.

I am performing an edited version of myself; the socially acceptable one that platonic and romantic prospects seem to connect with.

It is as if, by only mentioning my interests and goals — l am a foodie, history and art buff, and lover of long conversations — I am using my dating app descriptions to scream: "Look, I am just like you. Don't put me in a box."

I was tired of trying to live up to an idealised version of myself. So, I decided to do something I had learnt from Marie Kondo: sort my wardrobe into what brought me joy and what didn't.

At other times, I do include it, a disclosure coming from a place of acceptance and tiredness. Tiredness from pretending that I don't have a disability, and after a long time desperately trying to follow the rules of what is "normal" in dating, that in hindsight were not actually written anywhere and enforced by no-one but me.

With this disclosure comes the dreaded, unspoken "please still like me" and the questioning of whether I have characterised my disability in an abled-body-friendly way (not too off-putting?). At the same time the alarm bells are ringing in the back of my mind: "Why am I self-editing to make myself palatable?"

I never get around to answering that question.

My disability is a part of who I am, but it's not the entirety of who I am. (Supplied: Vanessa Mbeve)

Instead, I start swiping away at potential matches with the alarms still ringing in the background. For every 20 l swipe on l come across a profile of a person with disability and recognise something of myself in their profiles, in their choice of words.

Within 30 minutes I have matches, and right out of the gate I am performing a version of myself while getting to know the other person. Presenting my positives and downplaying my disability as a minor thing. As if to say the essence of who I am is not enough, and that my disability is a point of shame.

Disclosure during the chatting phase is met with a few instant unmatches, dead-end conversations, and the odd forward question: "Does your disability prevent you from being sexually active?"

This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

But the vast majority of potential matches I encounter largely seem OK with my disability.

And yet when I meet them in person, the performance continues. I show up in character — not as myself — trying to prove I am "normal" and more than my disability. Instead of saying, "this is who I am and this is where I am at."

Do you have a dating story you would like to share? We'd love to hear from you

I am so busy trying to make potential partners comfortable with my disability that I almost forget the more important questions, like "do I even like this person?".

I am brutally reminded of that reality by my sister. When I described a date as "OK," she answered bluntly, "I don't think you like that guy. Otherwise, you would say he's hot, cute, or something."

In an instant, I get that ugly sinking feeling that I have set myself up for failure again because somewhere along the way, I turned dating into a chore. I stopped asking whether I actually wanted someone, or what my end goal was (marriage, a one-night stand, or something else?) and instead became focused on whether I could convince them to want me.

As a result, I end up doing the exact thing I am trying to avoid: harming others and, above all, myself. I disrespect myself, and in turn I disrespect others by not allowing people to see me and make their own informed decision.

And at end of it all, I am exhausted.

For me, dating apps have, in theory, made dating easier and more accessible in terms of being able to meet people. But of all the people I met, I was genuinely attracted to and compatible with only a handful. So do I really need to appeal to everyone?

Vanessa Mbeve spent more than a decade hiding away from the world, unhappy with the way cerebral palsy affected her. Now, at 26, she's breaking free from self-imposed shackles.

The best date I've had so far this year was with someone who did show up as themselves.

We talked for hours until we were the only people left in the bar, and the staff were desperately waiting for us to leave so they could go home.

Maybe trying to find the perfect words to explain myself is a futile endeavour. My disability is a fixture of who I am, but it is not the entirety of who I am, just like all the other things I include in my dating profile.

Perhaps the answer is not to find a better explanation, but to simply tell people who I am.

My name is Vanessa Mbeve, I am 27 I have cerebral palsy. I am addicted to Cheetos and my laptop. On a weekend you will find me out or blasting music in my house while scrolling on Reddit.

PS;  Did I mention I'm single?

Vanessa Mbeve is a New South Wales-based writer with cerebral palsy. She is passionate about exploring social dynamics and sharing her unique perspectives through her writing.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/v.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Remote Working

The Victorian government says work-from-home legislation will still pass before the state election, despite debate being delayed amid concerns from the business community. (Unsplash: Nubelson Fernandes)

Proposed work-from-home laws in Victoria have been pushed back nearly 12 months, as the government seeks further consultation with business.

It comes as new premier Ben Carroll vows to reset his relationship with the business community.

The premier says the legislation is still scheduled to pass before the coming state election in November.

The Victorian government's proposed work-from-home laws will be delayed for nearly 12 months, as premier Ben Carroll allows more time for consultation and amendments to the legislation.

The laws were first flagged by former premier Jacinta Allan last year, when she outlined plans to develop legal protections for employees who want to work at least two days a week from home.

Mr Carroll said he had informed both Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Sally Curtain and Australian Industry Group head Tim Piper that the implementation of the laws would be delayed by almost a year.

"I've spoken with Sally Curtain this morning, and Tim Piper, and I've informed them that work-from-home will not proceed on the 1st of September," he said.

"It will proceed on the 1st of July, 2027."

Ben Carroll says debate on work-from-home legislation will be delayed to allow more time for consultation. (ABC News)

Mr Carroll said he supported working-from-home laws, but said the benefits had to be balanced against other priorities.

"It is good for working families," he said.

"Equally though, we need to make sure that our economy — everyone knows its a partnership between working families and the business community and the government."

He said he would listen to and consult on any "common-sense" amendments, but promised the legislation would pass before the November state election.

The Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry welcomed the delay, warning the legislation posed a "profound risk" to the state's economy.

"The Victorian Chamber maintains that the Bill must be scrapped, as it is completely unnecessary, costly and burdensome for Victorian businesses," chamber chief executive Sally Curtain said.

"The premier has been in touch with us directly and has indicated he is willing to meet with us. We hope to persuade him to abandon this destructive course."

In an exclusive interview with the ABC last week, the premier said resetting his relationship with Victoria's businesses was one of his biggest priorities.

"I'll roll the red carpet out for them. I want to grow our economy. We've got the best workforce in the nation, the most skilled. This is my focus," he said.

"I think it's about a rhetorical reset, making sure that business knows I'm in their corner."

Business Council of Australia chief executive Bran Black said the government was taking "the first steps" in listening to the business community, but still argued for scrapping the legislation altogether.

"Already, Victoria has the highest unemployment rate in the country and the Victorian economy cannot afford another policy that drives investment and jobs away, which only hurts Victorians through lower living standards," Mr Black said.

Business leaders have called for work-from-home legislation to be scrapped altogether. (Adobe Stock)

Shadow Attorney-General James Newbury said the opposition had announced their proposed amendments to the work-from-home legislation.

Mr Newbury said while the opposition supported work-from-home laws, it wanted to see amendments made to ease a transition period.

"Rolling out a change of this nature within three weeks across an entire economy is difficult," he said.

"I think it's only reasonable that there's some understandable delay."

He said the opposition was also asking for amendments to remove the right of unions to enter the property of a person working from home.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/r.title: Dying woman urges PM to overturn 'cruel' law to save others suffering
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/r.author: Lucy Barbour
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Death and Dying

Sandra Sarantou is using her last days to lobby for better access to voluntary assisted dying for regional patients. (Supplied: Marcel Sarantou)

An Adelaide woman who is preparing to end her life using voluntary assisted dying (VAD) is calling for changes to the criminal code to make it easier for regional residents to access the care.

Delegates at the Labor Party's national conference voted to amend federal law to allow telehealth for VAD consultations, but Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is personally opposed.

Independent MP Kate Chaney and Greens Senator Sarah Hanson Young are pushing for changes to allow telehealth for VAD care.

As she prepares to die tomorrow using voluntary assisted dying (VAD), Sandra Sarantou has one final request for the prime minister.

She is urging the nation's leaders to change a law that is limiting some Australians' access to VAD.

Despite voluntary assisted dying being legal in Victoria, many regional patients are not getting the same end-of-life care.

Nine weeks ago, the 58-year-old Adelaide woman was diagnosed with the same aggressive lung cancer her father died from.

Medication is no longer effective for her nerve pain, nausea and dizziness. Having watched her father endure a long and painful death, before VAD was legal around the country, Ms Sarantou is "grateful" to be ending her life on her terms.

But she said she was shocked to learn a provision in the Commonwealth Criminal Code means some Australians are effectively denied access because of where they live.

"It's even a struggle just to move from one end from the house to another … for those people to travel hours to possibly see a doctor and not get the chance for VAD is just horrific," she told ABC News.

VAD is legal in every Australian jurisdiction except the Northern Territory, which is expected to pass legislation allowing it this month.

Other state laws do allow the use of telehealth for some discussions about VAD, particularly where patients are too ill to travel or live remotely.

But a provision in the Commonwealth Criminal Code, intended to outlaw the use of "carriage services" to "incite suicide", has been interpreted to apply to doctors advising patients about VAD and has overridden those state provisions.

That means doctors cannot use phone, email, internet or video to advise patients about accessing VAD medication.

Workforce shortages in rural and remote areas have meant some dying people have been forced to travel long distances to make those appointments. For some that has not been possible and they have missed out.

Families of people who wanted to access VAD but died before completing the process say telehealth consultations could have spared them unnecessary suffering.

Federal Independent Kate Chaney will today attempt to bring on debate of her private members bill, which would see the Commonwealth Criminal Code amended.

Greens Senator Sarah Hanson Young will introduce a similar bill to the Upper House this month. Without government support, both bills may languish.

WA MP Kate Chaney has a private member's bill to allow the use of telehealth for VAD consultations. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

There is also a push within Labor's rank and file for change. Last month, delegates to Labor's National Conference voted to amend the party's platform, supporting the use of telehealth for end-of-life care.

Delegates also enshrined a commitment to give Labor MPs and senators a conscience vote on all VAD issues.

At the recent Labor conference, only one issue was contested on the floor: support for the use of telehealth in voluntary assisted dying care.

Labor sources have said Prime Minister Anthony Albanese remains personally opposed to allowing telehealth for VAD, and his opposition may prove crucial to the fate of any legislative change.

He supports voluntary assisted dying but has argued face-to-face consultations are an important way to ensure vulnerable patients are not taken advantage of.

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has also expressed reservations and raised concerns about the risk of elder abuse if telehealth was allowed.

Several Labor MPs have told the ABC they are confident the law will eventually change but that it will require more time and conversations to convince the prime minister.

Sandra Sarantou had a career as a paramedic, often working in rural areas of South Australia. (Supplied: Sandra Sarantou)

Ms Sarantou, who worked as a paramedic for 13 years and treated patients in rural areas, felt "guilty" she could access VAD while others could not.

She is pleading with the Albanese government to amend the criminal code.

"Please change these laws, make it fair and available for everyone despite where they are living."

Advocacy group, Go Gentle's latest "State of VAD report" suggested there was strong demand for the care outside cities, with 39 per cent of applicants in 2024-25 living in rural, regional and remote areas.

General practitioner Scott Lewis has travelled 3,000 kilometres across South Australia in the past fortnight alone to see people seeking voluntary assisted dying.

South Australian GP Dr Scott Lewis flies to regional areas of the state to see patients, including those who want to access voluntary assisted dying.  (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Dr Lewis, who flies his own plane to reach rural patients, said he saw about two new VAD patients a week.

He said workforce shortages and the lack of Medicare funding were preventing more rural doctors from offering VAD care.

"I don't make much money from it, to be blunt."

He told ABC News he had experienced "a sense of failure" knowing patients have missed out on VAD due to their isolation.

"To see the hurt in family members who've had to see their loved ones suffer and … come so close to being approved for voluntary assisted dying but not quite get there … it's hard at times."

Sydney University Law Health expert Dr Christopher Rudge said he believed telehealth could be allowed without weakening overall protections.

"Across the country the states have very rigorous and documented process for permitting someone to undergo a VAD procedure, and all of those would apply whether it's by telehealth or any other circumstance," he said.

Dr Christopher Rudge, of the University of Sydney Law School. (Supplied)

"My understanding is that the telehealth communications would occur at an early stage of the process but that at some stage, the witnessing and some other processes, would presumably need to occur in an environment where doctors are present."

Generally, under state laws, people applying for VAD must have been diagnosed with a terminal illness and facing death within a year.

They must attend face-to-face medical appointments so that two independent, trained practitioners can assess whether they are eligible, acting voluntarily and capable of making their own decisions.

The patient must provide a written request for VAD, which has to be witnessed by independent adults — not family members.

A co-ordinating practitioner makes a final declaration and a state board — or oversight body — provides final approval.

Dr Rudge said he was "sympathetic" with concerns that telehealth could replace face-to-face consults, but did not think that would be a consequence of changes to the Commonwealth Criminal Code.

"In circumstances where informed consent is not clear, the in-person consultation is the best place for those questions to be answered. And so, I can understand why people could be concerned," he said.

For Sandra Sarantou, the hardest part of preparing for VAD is knowing that she has to say goodbye to her son.

But, she said they had been "completely open" about the VAD process and had found comfort in black humour.

Sandra Sarantou held a party with friends before her planned death through voluntary assisted dying. (Supplied: Sandra Sarantou)

"We had the idea to put my ashes into a big party cracker … and then everybody has got a bit of my ashes," Ms Sarantou laughed.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Ukrainian prisoners recount torture, sexual abuse while in Russian detention
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: David Brunnstrom
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
Former Ukrainian detainees and Ukrainian officials accused Russia on Monday of systematically torturing prisoners of war and civilian detainees, holding captives incommunicado and subjecting them to beatings, electric shocks and sexual abuse, with thousands still in captivity.

Russia rejected the allegations made at an informal U.N. Security Council meeting, with its Deputy U.N. Representative Maria Zabolotskaya calling ​it “a disinformation campaign” and alleging that Russian prisoners in Ukraine were subjected to “torture and degradation and moral and physical abuse.”

Khuan ‌Alberto ‌Levya Garsiya, still an active member of the Ukrainian military, said his Russian captors subjected him ​to every imaginable form of torture during 1,183 days in captivity.

“Yes ... I was tortured,” he told reporters after the U.N. meeting. “Anything you can think of that can be done hurtful, humiliating to a man, unwillingly. Anything that comes to your mind, not only ⁠verbal, physical abuse, daily beatings, electrocution, excessive, excessive exercises in freezing cold when it’s minus degrees ... sexual abuse. Everything that can be applied to ⁠a person into making a person break mentally. It was all applied to me and most of my comrades.”

Garsiya said he was lucky to survive but two of his friends were beaten to death in ​detention centers in the Donetsk region. Prisoners were held ⁠in “overcrowded barracks without adequate conditions,” where “almost all POWs were ill with dysentery” and many were starving, he told the U.N. meeting.

A Ukrainian with a Cuban father, he said guards targeted ⁠him particularly because of his Latino ​name, accusing him of being “a mercenary and an American spy.”

Crimean Tatar activist ​Leniie Umerova, released in a prisoner exchange in 2024, said she was detained while trying to visit her seriously ​ill father ‌in Crimea.

She described being moved through “seven detention facilities” in what she called “a carousel of repression” and accused Russia of using torture against Ukrainians in captivity. Oleg Gushin of the Ukrainian government’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said Ukrainian prisoners were “killed and tortured” in detention.

He said Kyiv had identified “more than 300 places of detention” in Russia ‌and occupied Ukrainian territory and that while more than 9,000 Ukrainians had been returned through exchanges, “thousands” remained in Russian captivity.

Ukraine’s Chargé d’Affaires Volodymyr Pavlichenko called for greater international pressure and accountability for Russia’s treatment of prisoners.

U.N. Assistant Secretary-General for Human Rights Claudia Fuentes Julio said U.N. monitoring showed that “widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment of Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees by the Russian Federation authorities continues,” including ​sexual ​violence.

Since February 2022, the U.N. Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights had ​documented the execution of 129 Ukrainian prisoners of war at the beginning of their captivity and the deaths of 48 in custody, ⁠resulting from torture, denial of medical care, or other inhumane conditions of detention, she said.

She said more than 95% of Ukrainian prisoners of war interviewed reported experiencing torture or ill-treatment.

She said more than half also reported sexual violence, including “rape, gang rape, beating while nude, beatings to the genitals, electric shocks to the genitals and nipples, and degrading treatment of a ​sexualized nature.”

She said the U.N. had received “consistent accounts of severe beatings with objects such as batons, heavy belts, and wood, electric shocks, dog attacks, mock executions, and other forms of torture.”

Fuentes Julio said the OHCHR had also documented torture and ill-treatment of Russian and third-country national prisoners of war held by Ukraine, but “on a fundamentally different scale.”

She said about half of Russian and third-country prisoners interviewed reported abuse during initial stages of captivity.

The effort has included attracting outside investments from the U.S. government and even chip rivals such as Nvidia Corp.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Japan shares data on foreign nationals facing deportation with local governments
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
The Immigration Services Agency has started sharing personal information on foreign nationals subject to deportation proceedings with local governments, as part of a review of policies concerning foreign nationals pursued by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

Previously, such information was shared only when there was consent from affected individuals, sometimes leaving local governments unsure of the whereabouts of foreign nationals subject to deportation proceedings.

The latest move is aimed at promoting appropriate responses through cooperation between the central and local governments.

In July, the agency informed local governments of the number, names, addresses, nationalities and dates of birth of foreign nationals who were subject to deportation proceedings and living outside immigration facilities as of the end of June.

Going forward, the agency plans to provide monthly updates on such foreign nationals’ relocations or deportations to their home countries. Information will also be made available upon request from local governments.

Under the immigration control law, foreign nationals who overstay their authorized periods of stay or commit certain crimes are subject to deportation.

In such cases, foreign nationals are not immediately deported, however. They are allowed to remain in Japan while investigations into violations and hearings are conducted.

In addition to those staying at immigration facilities, some individuals subject to deportation procedures may be granted provisional release due to health or humanitarian issues. Others may be placed under a supervision system, which allows them to live outside immigration facilities under the oversight of a supervisor, such as a relative or friend.

Those on provisional release or under the supervision system are subject to certain restrictions on their residences and movements.

Meanwhile, local governments are often left in the dark because those subject to deportation proceedings lose their residence records, and some people’s whereabouts become unknown. This has created challenges in providing public services, such as education and healthcare.

According to the agency, 18,442 foreign nationals were subjected to deportation procedures in 2025. As of the end of last year, 2,429 individuals were on provisional release and 1,546 were under supervisory measures.

The agency plans to provide monthly updates on such foreign nationals’ relocations or deportations to their home countries.

https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomac.title: Why did US defence official Colby avoid mention of Scarborough Shoal in Manila speech?
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomac.author: Nayan Seth
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomac.text:
Some analysts attribute the restraint to a desire to avoid antagonising Beijing ahead of next month’s expected Xi-Trump summit

Instead, he sought to reassure regional allies that the United States was “definitely not disengaging from Asia”.

“We are not leaving; in fact, we are digging in, to ensure a favourable balance of power where it matters most,” Colby said during an event at a Manila think tank.

His omissions were particularly notable because two days earlier Washington had criticised Beijing for its actions over what it called a “destabilising” nature reserve at the reef and denying Filipino fishermen access to their traditional fishing grounds.

“With the Trump-Xi summit six weeks away, Colby likely thought it best to avoid commenting on China, lest he upset the fragile stability reached by the two leaders in Busan and Beijing,” said Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the Indo-Pacific programme at the German Marshall Fund.

Another possible consideration was Colby’s long-standing interest in visiting Beijing, Glaser noted. “Harsh criticism of Chinese activities in the region would have angered Beijing; mild criticism would have made Manila unhappy,” she added.

People familiar with the matter told the South China Morning Post that Colby’s long-awaited visit to Beijing was unlikely to take place before Xi’s expected visit to the United States next month.

But other analysts cautioned against interpreting Colby’s language as evidence of any substantive easing in Washington’s approach towards China.

Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, argued that while Colby did not mention China by name, “almost everything he discussed was about China”.

Moriyasu added that it would be a “mistake to take up diplomatic language leading up to the summit as some sort of softening of strategy towards China”.

“There is a difference between tone management towards Beijing and the underlying defence strategy,” he said. “Colby’s Manila speech was hard-edged in strategic terms.”

The Philippines is the first stop on Colby’s Southeast Asian tour, which will also take him to Indonesia, Thailand and Cambodia. The visit comes amid renewed friction around Scarborough Shoal, which is claimed by both China and the Philippines but has been under Beijing’s effective control since 2012.

In a statement on Saturday, the US State Department criticised China for attempting to “enforce its destabilising ‘national nature reserve’ at Scarborough Reef and deny Filipino fishermen access to their traditional fishing ground”.

“This is yet another unilateral attempt by China to use dubious environmental and legal pretexts, backed by coercion, to advance its sweeping territorial and maritime claims in the South China Sea at the expense of its neighbours,” spokesman Tommy Pigott said.

“The United States stands with our ally, the Philippines, in support of a free and open Indo-Pacific.”

The US remarks were in response to China’s introduction of new management measures for the nature reserve it established around the shoal last year.

Tensions have escalated in the South China Sea in recent weeks, with multiple skirmishes between Filipino and Chinese forces.

In July, the Philippine coastguard said its Chinese counterpart had fired water cannons at Filipino vessels near the Scarborough Shoal and condemned what it called Beijing’s “dangerous and unprofessional actions”.

In a statement, China’s coastguard said it had imposed “control measures” and accused Manila’s vessels of “illegally” gathering in the waters.

Sourabh Gupta, a resident senior fellow at the Institute for China-America Studies, noted that Colby had “little or nothing to say about his host’s top priority” which is “keeping China at bay in the South China Sea”.

“By Colby’s philosophy though, that is an interest for Manila’s policymakers to elaborate on; it is not an issue for an American policymaker to dwell on. Realist and pragmatic,” he added.

The Philippine embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomac.summary: Colby said the U.S. was not disengaging from Asia and is digging in to ensure a favourable balance of power. He was speaking at a Manila think tank on his Southeast Asian tour. The Philippines is the first stop on Colby’s Southeast Asian trip.

https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/lifestyle.title: Why are South Korean football fans choosing European clubs over the K League?
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/lifestyle.author: David D. Lee
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/lifestyle.text:
Observers say the K League has fallen short of the standards European clubs have set for quality, spectacle and emotional connection

But on Sunday night, he made the pilgrimage from the suburbs of Gimpo to see Manchester City and Atletico Madrid, two European clubs whose pull in South Korea rivals, and often overwhelms, interest in the domestic game.

The 21-year-old and his friends were among 50,000 fans who filled the stadium with City’s light blue and Atletico’s red-and-blue shirts, turning a pre-season friendly into a vivid display of where much of South Korean football passion now flows.

Yoon and his friends sounded like broadcast announcers, calling out every player’s name and reacting excitedly to every dribble and shot.

“I first became a fan in 2022 to cheer on Kevin De Bruyne. I’m his biggest fan,” he said, pointing to the former City midfielder whose jersey he was wearing.

Many fans had arrived hours early to buy merchandise, take photos and catch a glimpse of players they usually watched on screens after midnight.

The match, organised by Coupang Play, the streaming service of South Korean e-commerce giant Coupang, also marked South Korean star Lee Kang-in’s debut for Atletico, giving the occasion an added emotional pull for local fans.

City beat Atletico 3-1, but the broader winner was European football itself.

The night captured a deeper problem for South Korea’s domestic game: the K League struggles to convert the country’s love of football into regular support, while European clubs increasingly set the standard for quality, spectacle and emotional connection.

Against the backdrop of South Korea’s disappointing World Cup exit and mounting scrutiny of the Korea Football Association, the country’s so-called national sport is facing one of its deepest periods of unease in years.

The K League, South Korea’s top professional football league, briefly enjoyed a renaissance in 2024 when former England midfielder and Premier League star Jesse Lingard signed with FC Seoul.

His arrival brought record crowds and rare international attention, but the surge did not resolve the deeper problems facing the domestic game.

Average K League attendance per match, which had remained above 10,000 since 2023 and previously hit a peak of 11,003 in 2024, has dipped to 9,008 so far this season, according to data from the league. Meanwhile, professional baseball continues to draw record crowds and dominate the country’s sporting conversation.

The contrast has been difficult to miss: the Korea Baseball Organisation League now averages about 18,000 fans per game, while the K League remains far behind in total attendance and media attention.

During Lingard’s final press conference with FC Seoul in December, the former captain highlighted pitch conditions, club infrastructure and refereeing as three areas for improvement.

Lee Jong-sung, a professor of sports management at Hanyang University, said Lingard’s comments reflected the “deeply rooted perception that the K League is simply too backward or underdeveloped compared with European football”.

“When you watch professional football in European leagues, the flow of passing and even the pitch itself gives you this overwhelming impression,” he told This Week in Asia. “K League stadiums simply haven’t been able to create that same feeling.”

The former football journalist said part of the gap stemmed from how South Korean stadiums were run.

“European club stadiums are often operated by the clubs themselves or by third parties affiliated with them. In Korea, by contrast, very few K League clubs actually own or operate their stadiums,” Lee Jong-sung said.

“Local governments have traditionally managed football stadiums in Korea, and that has meant there hasn’t been much investment or serious consideration given to professionally managing the pitches, whether in terms of personnel or financial resources.”

That also limited the commercial ecosystem around clubs, he said, as football offered far fewer home games than baseball, resulting in fewer opportunities to turn stadiums into year-round destinations.

“In legacy media and major media outlets, the K League has rarely been treated as a major news topic. Almost all of the headlines among professional sports are effectively dominated by professional baseball.”

The 2002 World Cup was one of the most transformative moments in modern South Korean society that helped change the country’s sporting gaze.

South Korea’s historic run to the semi-finals as co-hosts turned players including Park Ji-sung, Lee Young-pyo and Ahn Jung-hwan into national heroes and global names as they were recruited by top European clubs.

“The world view of Korean sports fans shifted from the United States towards Europe, and people often refer to this as the era of overseas football,” Lee Jong-sung said.

“Fans call it haechuk for short, and this culture has become so big today that among peer groups, particularly among boys, not being familiar with European football could make it somewhat difficult to be part of conversations.”

The rise of European football was reinforced by a new generation of Korean stars whose careers unfolded on the continent.

Son Heung-min became one of the Premier League’s most popular players, while Lee Kang-in’s move to Paris Saint-Germain, before his latest transfer to Atletico, gave South Korean fans another reason to follow the European game.

“When young Koreans travel to Europe, it’s almost become a ritual for them to attend at least one or two football matches, whether that’s a Premier League game or a match in Spain,” Lee Jong-sung said.

“Even if they travel during the off season when there are no matches, they’ll often make a point of visiting a big club’s museum or stadium tour and spending money on souvenirs.”

Kim Se-hoon, content executive for Wolverhampton Wanderers, said European clubs were also far more conscious of keeping overseas fans engaged beyond matchdays.

The English Football League Championship club is best known in South Korea as the home of forward Hwang Hee-chan.

“Football leagues in the UK set global standards not only in terms of players’ performances, but also in content creation and distribution”, such as footage from training sessions and interviews, he told This Week in Asia.

Clubs there put “considerable thought” into maintaining relationships with fans and keeping them engaged through informal channels such as fan groups and online communities, he added.

“For us, we offer fans the opportunity to directly meet club officials to voice their concerns about the club’s activities.”

In the K League, by contrast, fan frustration has often taken more confrontational forms, with supporters sending protest trucks to club offices or stadiums and, in some cases, blocking team buses after unpopular decisions over managers, players or club management.

Lee Jong-sung said South Korean football needed to rethink what kind of sporting culture it wanted to build.

“Football in our country shouldn’t only be concentrated on World Cup results. We need to set goals for what we want to achieve in other areas as well, and have a broader discussion about those ambitions,” he said.

“Only then can Korean football become a team and a footballing nation that can continue to grow and remain competitive over the long term, rather than simply having a one-off successful World Cup.”

The match was organised by Coupang Play, the streaming service of South Korean e-commerce giant Coupang. The K League has fallen short of the standards European clubs have set for quality, spectacle and emotional connection.
