https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/08/11/mor.title: What Morocco Was Saying to Spain in Ceuta
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/08/11/mor.author: Albert Guasch Rafael
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/08/11/mor.text:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has built a brand as one of Europe’s most vocal critics of the United States and Israel, recognizing Palestinian statehood over Gaza and denying the U.S. military the use of its Rota and Morón bases during the war against Iran. And while he seems perfectly comfortable playing hardball with governments worlds apart from his own ideology, when it comes to Spain’s fraught relations with Morocco, Sánchez has folded far more than his reputation suggests.

Nowhere was that clearer than in his handling of the recent crisis in Ceuta. On July 30, around 70,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, the small Spanish exclave in North Africa, a city of little more than 80,000 inhabitants. The sudden increase in arrivals caught security forces off guard, and local shelters and social services were soon overwhelmed. Lacking food, shelter, or a clear legal path in Spain, most of the migrants headed back to Morocco within a day, their disappointment standing in stark contrast with the joy and chants of “Viva España” upon their arrival. At least 88 migrants have died, and more bodies might be recovered from the water.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has built a brand as one of Europe’s most vocal critics of the United States and Israel, recognizing Palestinian statehood over Gaza and denying the U.S. military the use of its Rota and Morón bases during the war against Iran. And while he seems perfectly comfortable playing hardball with governments worlds apart from his own ideology, when it comes to Spain’s fraught relations with Morocco, Sánchez has folded far more than his reputation suggests.

Nowhere was that clearer than in his handling of the recent crisis in Ceuta. On July 30, around 70,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, the small Spanish exclave in North Africa, a city of little more than 80,000 inhabitants. The sudden increase in arrivals caught security forces off guard, and local shelters and social services were soon overwhelmed. Lacking food, shelter, or a clear legal path in Spain, most of the migrants headed back to Morocco within a day, their disappointment standing in stark contrast with the joy and chants of “Viva España” upon their arrival. At least 88 migrants have died, and more bodies might be recovered from the water.

Sánchez deployed the military and traveled to Ceuta, where he called the crossings “a violation and attack of Spain’s territorial integrity.” Yet he never mentioned who had attacked Spain. For decades, Morocco has claimed sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla, Spain’s second exclave in North Africa. It’s been the biggest friction point between Madrid and Rabat. But in this case, Sánchez instead highlighted the collaboration with Moroccan authorities in sending the migrants back.

It is not clear why Sánchez is absolving Morocco. Evidence collected by the New York Times and other outlets shows that, shortly before the crossings on July 30, Moroccan guards had ceased to control the crowds that had been building up in the border town of Fnideq for weeks prior. News from a recent ruling from the Spanish Supreme Court saying that migrants arriving by sea could not be returned on the spot prompted thousands of people, many of them young, to travel to the border and eventually cross into Ceuta. This was accompanied by numerous posts and videos on social media that said the border was open and could be crossed easily.

Morocco’s use of migrants as tools of leverage fits tactics of hybrid warfare that have been previously used by Europe’s autocratic border neighbors, such as Turkey and Belarus. Sánchez should know the playbook. After all, he was Spain’s prime minister when Morocco helped around 8,000 migrants cross into Ceuta in 2021, triggering a crisis that looks remarkably similar to this one.

At the time, Morocco used migration as reprisal for Spain allowing the leader of the Polisario Front, Western Sahara’s independence movement, to receive treatment for COVID-19 on Spanish soil. This plunged relations with Morocco into a crisis, and mending ties took more than diplomatic pleasantries. Sánchez only restored full relations with Morocco in 2022 by abandoning a decades-old policy of supporting self-determination for Western Sahara and backing Rabat’s plan for autonomy over the region instead. Spaniards learned about this massive pivot in foreign policy after a letter sent to King Mohammed VI leaked in the Moroccan press.

A former colony of Spain, Western Sahara was occupied by Morocco as Madrid withdrew from the territory in 1975. The International Court of Justice and, until recently, most of the international community do not recognize Moroccan claims of sovereignty over the territory, which is why Spain, until recently, backed a plan for Western Sahara’s self-determination. The pivot also tanked relations with Algeria, Morocco’s regional rival and a guarantor of the Sahrawi peoples’ independence movement. In retaliation, Algeria cut off its natural gas supply to Spain just as Europe needed it most.

This new era of rapprochement with Morocco allowed Sánchez to put bitter chapters such as the Ceuta crisis from 2021 behind him and enter an era of cooperation with Morocco on several matters, including migration. Or so he thought.

This isn’t the first time that Sánchez has turned a blind eye to Morocco’s actions. In 2022, the government disclosed that the mobile phones of Sánchez and Defense Minister Margarita Robles had been tapped with Pegasus, an Israeli-made spying software. Despite investigations by the European Parliament and journalistic reports pointing in that direction, no Spanish official—including either Robles or Sánchez himself—has acknowledged that Morocco could be behind the hacking. In fact, just a year ago, Spain’s interior minister awarded a medal to Morocco’s intelligence chief, Abdellatif Hammouchi, a man who has been linked to the Moroccan security services’ use of Pegasus.

No one knows for sure why Morocco let the crossings happen this time around. One explanation could just be that it wished to show Madrid its power to wreak havoc in Ceuta. This is in line with what the Moroccan press has published on the issue. According to outlet Le 360, the crisis shows “the untenable status of the occupied enclaves of Sebta [the Arabic name for Ceuta] and Melilla,” which they consider to be “geographic, political, and security anomalies.”

Spain’s sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla, which dates back centuries, is not questioned by international law or any other country beyond Morocco, although there are signs that this might change. Just a few weeks ago, the U.S. House of Representatives approved a bill directing $40 million to Morocco in security funding. Attached to the bill was a report by Republican Rep. Mario Díaz-Balart which describes Ceuta and Melilla as “located in Moroccan territory” and asks Secretary of State Marco Rubio to mediate their future.

The history of the disputed exclave should inform what Spain does next.

In their willingness to blame Spain, European leaders have shown they cannot be trusted on collective security.

The United States has already acknowledged Morocco’s sovereignty over Western Sahara. It did so in 2020, in exchange for Morocco normalizing ties with Israel under the Abraham Accords. Since then, Morocco has been one of Israel’s most reliable partners in the Muslim world.

There is also evidence of at least one high-ranking Israeli official questioning Spain’s control over Ceuta and Melilla. Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, said in the wake of the crisis that it was time that Spain “explained to the world why it still maintains colonial enclaves in Africa,”—though Israel’s ambassador to Spain, Dana Erlich, made it clear that this was not Israel’s official position.

Another possible explanation behind Morocco’s motivations is that Spain is starting to mend its ties with Algeria after they were strained over the Western Sahara pivot. On July 20, Sánchez made his first visit to Algeria in four years, meeting with President Abdelmadjid Tebboune to discuss cooperation on energy, investment, and migration.

Other analysts point to a law granting Spanish citizenship to Sahrawis born under Spanish colonial rule and their direct descendants, which has been introduced in the Spanish parliament and could pass soon.

We may never know exactly what message Morocco was sending, but the tragedy which resulted reveals that Spain is in an increasingly tenuous position geopolitically. Sánchez’s rapprochement with Morocco failed to prevent a crisis even larger than the one in 2021. European states can no longer count on U.S. support. And furthermore, while Spain issued an arms embargo against Israel over Gaza, Morocco has been signing lucrative arms deals with Israel.

Rather than treating the crossings as a security emergency, the U.S. State Department posted on X blaming the crossing of migrants on “the direct result of the Spanish Government’s deliberate efforts to enable and facilitate mass illegal migration into Europe.” The crisis also saw some European allies snap at Spain. Italy, led by far-right Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, temporarily suspended Schengen, the EU’s free border agreement. Finland and Denmark backed the move.

Could this “triple entente” between Morocco, Israel, and the United States threaten Spain’s control of Ceuta and Melilla? Only time will tell. Yet Sánchez is known to always have some ace up his sleeve. Following an invitation from Madrid in 2023, Morocco joined Spain and Portugal’s bid to host the 2030 FIFA Men’s World Cup, which ultimately proved to be successful. Morocco has greeted the prospect with genuine excitement, investing more than $20 billion in preparation. Sánchez may have bought himself some temporary breathing room. Once again, soccer brings Spain some joy.

Albert Guasch Rafael is a freelance journalist from Spain who writes about global and European affairs. He is also a communications coordinator at the nongovernmental organization Democracy Reporting International. X: @albertguaschr

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/r.title: Breaking: Reserve Bank keeps interest rate at 4.35pc
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/r.author: Gareth Hutchens
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Interest Rates

The RBA Monetary Policy Board has voted to keep the cash rate at 4.35 per cent. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

The RBA has kept interest rates at 4.35 per cent.

Headline inflation cooled a bit in June, and property prices have declined by a little more than anticipated, but underlying inflation pressures remain elevated.

The monetary policy board's next interest rate meeting will be held on September 28-29.

The Reserve Bank has kept interest rates on hold at 4.35 per cent, in a unanimous decision.

The move comes after headline inflation cooled a bit in June, and property prices declined by a little more than anticipated in recent months.

But it also comes as economists warn that underlying inflation is still too high, with some saying that they expect interest rates to have to rise again, at some point, to squeeze inflation out of the economy.

Following today's decision, the cash rate target will remain at 4.35 per cent for the next seven weeks, until the RBA Board's next meeting in late September.

In a statement, the RBA's Monetary Policy Board said inflation was likely to remain high for some time.

"The disruption to global oil supply is adding directly to inflation and there are indications that higher fuel prices are being passed through to prices of other goods and services," it said.

Australia's economy grew at an annual rate of 2.5 per cent in the March quarter, the same as in the previous quarter.

"This inflation impulse is in addition to the effect of capacity pressures in the economy.

"Following three increases in the cash rate target since the beginning of the year, financial conditions are now tighter than they were, and the economy appears to be slowing as expected.

"But inflation is still too high. It is not expected to return to around the midpoint of the target range until late 2027 and there are upside risks to this projection.

"With monetary policy judged to be somewhat restrictive, the board decided to leave the cash rate target unchanged while it assesses how the economy is evolving," it said.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Concerns persist over salaries of lawmaker secretaries in Japan
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
Questions surrounding the salaries of publicly funded secretaries to members of parliament, Japan’s Diet, continue to surface, underscoring persistent concerns about oversight within the country’s political system.

Recent cases have renewed scrutiny of allegations that some lawmakers improperly received government funds by registering individuals as secretaries despite little or no evidence that they actually performed duties associated with the positions.

The recurrence of such cases has fueled concerns about weaknesses in accountability mechanisms and the adequacy of existing safeguards against misuse of public funds.

Experts argue that stronger governance and oversight by political parties are essential to preventing similar abuses. “The most important thing is for political parties to exercise effective governance,” one expert said.

A state-paid secretary is employed under the Diet law to assist a lawmaker. The position is classified as a special-service national public servant, and each lawmaker may employ up to three such secretaries: a first secretary, a second secretary and a policy secretary. Monthly salaries range from about ¥340,000 to about ¥660,000.

Lawmakers are required to submit two documents to the Diet — a “notification of employment,” which contains the information necessary for salary payments, and a “current status report,” which lists the secretary’s name and workplace.

The position of policy secretary was introduced in 1994 to strengthen lawmakers’ legislative activities. To be hired as a policy secretary, an individual must pass a qualifying examination or be certified through a selection review. There are no comparable requirements for first and second secretaries.

Fraud involving the salaries of secretaries to lawmakers came to light during a succession of cases from the 1990s through the early 2000s. Five lawmakers faced criminal charges and all were convicted.

In response, a revised law on the salaries of lawmakers’ secretaries was enacted in 2004. The revisions included measures such as prohibiting lawmakers from demanding donations from their secretaries and requiring salaries to be paid directly to the secretaries, rather than via lawmakers.

Under an agreement among parliamentary groups, submission of current status reports to the Diet was also made mandatory. For about 20 years, no lawmaker was charged with fraud linked to secretaries’ salaries.

In 2024, however, the special investigation squad of the Tokyo District Public Prosecutors Office indicted Megumi Hirose, a former House of Councillors member from the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, without arrest on fraud charges. She was accused of swindling the state out of about ¥3.58 million by falsely claiming that the wife of her first government-paid secretary had been hired as her second state-funded secretary.

Through her first aide, Hirose received in cash the salary that had been paid into the bank account of the purported second secretary. During a hearing at Tokyo District Court, she said, “Political activities cost money, and I was unable to manage my office unless I put in my own funds.” Handing down a guilty verdict, a judge at the court described her actions as “far too thoughtless.”

In 2025, the special investigation squad indicted former Upper House lawmaker Akira Ishii of the Japan Innovation Party and a female member of his office staff, without arrest. They were charged with fraudulently obtaining about ¥8.28 million in public funds by misrepresenting one of Ishii’s relatives as having been hired as a government-paid second secretary.

According to sources, the salary transferred to a bank account in the relative’s name was managed by the female staff member and used for office expenses and other purposes.

A senior prosecutor said that even if the law is revised, “in the end, it comes down to lawmakers’ good sense.”

In March 2026, the weekly magazine Shukan Shincho reported that Reiwa Shinsengumi, an opposition party, had registered party staff members as publicly funded secretaries of party lawmakers, while in practice assigning them primarily to party-related work.

At a news conference, Takashi Takai, the party’s deputy secretary-general, defended the arrangement, saying that party activities also fall within the scope of a secretary’s duties. “There is absolutely no illegality,” he said.

Masaki Taniguchi, a professor of political science at the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Public Policy and an expert on political funding, said a series of problems involving the salaries of state-funded secretaries may reflect “a lack of awareness on legal compliance among many lawmakers.”

As a measure to prevent similar cases, Taniguchi emphasized the need to “educate, monitor and guide new lawmakers thoroughly on managing secretaries and handling their salaries.

Recent cases have renewed scrutiny of allegations that some lawmakers improperly received government funds by registering individuals as secretaries. Recurrence of such cases has fueled concerns about weaknesses in accountability mechanisms and the adequacy of existing safeguards against misuse of public funds.

https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.title: South Korea aims to criminalise fictional AI pornography after man’s acquittal
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.author: SCMP’s Asia desk
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.text:
Lawmakers move to close a legal loophole by proposing a bill criminalising virtual porn of fictional characters

The move by lawmakers came after a court in Goyang, Gyeonggi province, acquitted a man accused of distributing deepfake images of nude women in a Telegram chat room.

Despite prosecutors presenting the evidence under a law carrying up to seven years in prison or a maximum fine of 50 million won (US$35,341), a judge last August ruled that the victims were virtual, not human.

“There is no material confirming the origin or synthesis method of the image, making it difficult to conclude that a real person was depicted,” Lee Jung-hoon of the Uijeongbu District Court said in the case, as reported by the Dong-A Ilbo.

That verdict prompted representative Huh Young and nine other lawmakers of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea to propose a bill criminalising the creation, distribution and possession of sexually explicit material made using artificial intelligence, even when it does not depict a real person.

“Rapid advances in AI have made it easy for anyone to create images of virtual people that are difficult to distinguish from real individuals,” the legislators said in the proposal referred to detailed review by the subcommittee of the National Assembly’s Legislation and Judiciary Committee, according to The Korea Times.

“However, the technology has also been misused to produce and distribute manipulated sexual content that causes sexual humiliation or disgust, which is emerging as a serious social problem.”

If the bill is passed, sexually explicit deepfakes featuring a virtual person that could be mistaken for human will be considered similar to those using manipulated images of real individuals. The penalties will be in line with the ones in the existing Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment of Sexual Crimes.

Legal experts said the bill was problematic and could infringe on individual freedom.

“The reason deepfake composites can be punished is that images or videos are created against the will of actual victims,” Moon Hye-jeong, a spokeswoman for the Korean Women Lawyers Association, told the Chosun Biz. “To punish virtual people where there is no victim, more discussion is needed on the targets and scope of punishment.”

Another issue is applying the same level of punishment as when a real person is harmed.

“On the grounds of protecting sexual morality, criminally punishing not only the production of AI photos and videos using virtual people, but also possession and viewing, could excessively restrict individual freedom,” said Kim Yeong-mi, a lawyer at Soongin Law Firm.

Digital sex crimes rose 66 per cent over nine years – from 9,385 cases in 2015 to 15,612 in 2024, according to a report released last month by state-funded Korean Women’s Development Institute.

The increase was particularly significant in deepfake sex crimes, which jumped more than 17 times from only 31 cases, or 0.3 per cent of all reported digital sex crimes, in 2020 to 550 in 2024.

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/law-.text:
Wholesale food supplier posted personal details of restaurant owner and consultant after dealings turned sour, Hong Kong privacy watchdog says

Hong Kong’s privacy watchdog has arrested a man on suspicion of doxxing a former restaurant owner and a business consultant following a financial dispute over unpaid bills.

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data (PCPD) said on Tuesday that the suspect, a 37-year-old wholesale food businessman, allegedly disclosed the personal data of two victims without their consent.

The PCPD’s investigation revealed that the suspect became acquainted with the male victim, a restaurant operator at the time, through the female victim’s consultancy in March 2025.

The suspect subsequently supplied frozen meat to the restaurant between March and May that same year. However, a monetary dispute later arose between the suspect and the operator following a payment default, and the two parties were unable to reach an agreement.

A year after the business collapsed, a post surfaced on a social media platform via a personal account accusing the male victim of defaulting on his debts and appealing to internet users to track him down.

The post disclosed sensitive personal details, including the man’s English name, former school names, vehicle registration number, and the registered name and address of his former company, alongside photos of him and his family and a screengrab of the registration record of his defunct company.

A day later, a second post from the same social media account targeted the female consultant, making similar allegations of unpaid debt. The post disclosed her English alias, phone number and the name of her consultancy firm.

The suspect has been granted bail while the PCPD continues its investigation.

The watchdog warned that doxxing is a severe criminal offence with a maximum penalty of five years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to HK$1 million (US$127,500) upon conviction.

“The PCPD reminds members of the public that they should not dox others because of monetary disputes. Doxxing is not a means to resolve disputes as it would only escalate conflicts.”

https://www.dw.com/en/trump-pushes-overh.title: Trump pushes overhaul of US policy on vaccines for children
https://www.dw.com/en/trump-pushes-overh.text:
In an executive order, President Trump calls for fewer recommended childhood vaccinations and more spacing between shots. Medical experts say the changes lack scientific backing and could leave children less protected.

On Monday, President Donald Trump signed an executive order seeking sweeping changes to the US's childhood vaccine policy, including fewer recommended immunizations and more separate appointments for children to receive them.

The order calls for the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, to be separated into three single-disease shots. It also advocates administering childhood immunizations at separate medical visits whenever possible.

Trump described the move as a "major victory for parents rights, religious and constitutional rights, and for the gold standard science."

The order says the federal government will support 11 core childhood vaccinations and advises states and territories to review vaccine requirements for school enrollment.

However, Washington cannot directly determine most school vaccine mandates, which are largely set by individual states. On those requirements, Trump's order is therefore primarily a recommendation.

The order also directs the Health and Human Services Department to improve vaccine research and develop a plan to make separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines available in the US. Such single-antigen vaccines are not currently licensed there.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. had already sought in January to remove vaccines against six of 17 diseases from the childhood schedule. A federal judge later blocked those changes while legal proceedings continue. Monday's order reaffirms much of that overhaul.

Public health experts say childhood vaccination schedules are based on extensive research into when and how vaccines can safely be administered together. Safety monitoring continues after vaccines are introduced.

They warn that spreading shots across more appointments can leave children vulnerable to preventable diseases for longer and increase the risk that later doses are delayed or missed.

Vaccine maker Merck said there was no published scientific evidence showing any benefit from splitting the MMR vaccine. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, estimated that developing and approving separate vaccines in the US could take more than a decade.

"We're advising that you continue to give children a vaccine that has decades of safety data," said Aaron M. Milstone, a member of the AAP Committee on Infectious Diseases.

Speaking in the Oval Office, Trump repeatedly suggested that the number or timing of childhood vaccines could be linked to rising rates of autism spectrum disorder.

Scientific consensus and decades of studies have found no link between vaccination and autism.

Kennedy has also repeatedly promoted the disproven connection. He founded an anti-vaccine nonprofit before joining the administration.

Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a physician and chairman of the Senate health committee, condemned the move.

"I'm a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The president does not have the expertise to make these changes," Cassidy said, adding that splitting combination vaccines "will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots."

Cassidy cast the decisive vote to confirm Kennedy as health secretary in 2025 despite concerns over his vaccine skepticism. He lost his Republican primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger and is due to leave office in January.

New York City Health Commissioner Alister Martin said the order was based "in politics and conspiracy theories."

"Fortunately, vaccination recommendations are not set by the president, nor should they be," Martin said.

The policy shift comes as the United States experiences its worst measles outbreak in 35 years and children prepare to return to school.

Critics have accused Kennedy of contributing to vaccine hesitancy through years of questioning established immunizations.

The renewed focus on vaccines also marks a shift from the administration's recent emphasis on less divisive health policies, including healthy eating, drug price negotiations and efforts to combat medical fraud ahead of November's midterm elections.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdx7.title: Where to enjoy the partial eclipse spectacle
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdx7.text:
Stargazers keen to see the partial eclipse of the sun will get help from the experts to watch it safely across the South West and the Channel Islands.

There are a range of free and ticketed events to help people enjoy the spectacle, with venues including a spectacular beachside spot, an observatory and even a pub with its own observatory.

Charlie Payne, who has been helping to organise an event on the Isles of Scilly, advised people who plan to go it alone to "pick your favourite place to watch the sunset."

She said an ideal spot was "somewhere where you've got really clear views and a clear line of sight to the horizon" and stressed people should not look directly at the sun as it could seriously damage their eyesight.

In Devon and Cornwall, the eclipse will start at about 18:18 BST, peak at 19:15 and finish at about 20:10.

In Guernsey and Jersey, those timings will be about 18:21, 19:17 and 20:10.

The Cosmos Community Observatory on the Isles of Scilly is hosting a free event between 18:00 and 20:00 on the lawns of the Karma Hotel on St Martin's.

People would be able to view the partial eclipse through telescopes with solar filters and eclipse glasses at the event on Scilly, which is only open to those who live or are holidaying on St Martin's.

Payne said: "It's a really big deal. These kind of eclipses don't happen very often and one almost this deep, almost near to totality is pretty rare".

In Cornwall, Kernow Astronomers have stocked with 420 eclipse glasses to give out at their event at the National Trust car park at Carnewas, at the Bedruthan Steps near Newquay, on the county's north coast.

Frank Johns, of the club, said: "We really have got a good view to the west and you can see right towards the ocean."

The Smugglers Rest is Talland Bay, near Looe, is holding a paid ticket event.

Bosses said they planned to use proceeds to help pay for an access ramp at the venue on Cornwall's south coast.

Like the other paid-for eclipse events, organisers have advised checking for ticket availability before travelling.

In Devon, stargazers from Plymouth Astronomical Society are also to help people enjoy the spectacle safely and said they were planning to give out a number of eclipse glasses at Lowery Cross near Yelverton.

Organisers said they would be there from 17:00 with their telescopes and would help people view the eclipse at the free event.

Members were also due to be there when it started to get dark to view the Perseids meteor shower, they added.

The Norman Lockyer Observatory in Sidmouth is hosting a paid-for ticketed event from 17:00 for people to see the partial eclipse and also the Perseids meteor shower later when the sky got dark, from about 21:30.

There will also be storytelling from 20:30 and astronomers will help people see the partial eclipse safely, with a live stream of the event from a venue in Spain which is expecting a full eclipse.

The Poltimore Inn, at North Molton on the edge of Exmoor, has its own observatory and is hosting a paid-for event.

Landlord Alan Boddington said, even though this is not a full eclipse, "it is still going to be quiet and dark and the birds will think it is night time".

Boddington said the pub, which is in a dark sky reserve, is believed to be one of just a handful in England with their own observatories.

In Guernsey, Dr Jean Dean, from La Société Guernesiaise's astronomy section, advised people to head to the west coast of the Channel Island to enjoy the spectacle.

She said people needed to use eclipse glasses or have their back to the sun and project it onto a piece of card.

Eclipse glasses have been given out are Les Bourgs Hospice charity shops in St Martins and St Sampsons.

Dean warned that if anyone looked directly at the sun they would "burn your retina in your eye and you will be permanently blind".

She stressed people should not use the eclipse glasses with other optical equipment such as binoculars, but could put them over spectacles.

Jersey Astronomy Club said it was setting up several solar telescopes by the slip at Le Braye on St Ouens Bay and it planned to have a supply of solar glasses for people to wear.

The club warned people not to attempt to look through binoculars or telescopes which did not have proper solar filters as they could collect more light than the human eye could cope with, risking blindness.

It said, without proper solar filters, "the only safe way to observe an eclipse is to use the telescope or binoculars to project an image, not into your eye but onto a piece of white paper or card", and removing or taping over the front of the finder scope "to prevent any accidents".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0rd.title: 'Day turned into dusk' in 1999 total solar eclipse
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0rd.text:
As the countdown begins to a partial solar eclipse, people have been sharing memories of the total eclipse in 1999 in parts of the South West and Channel Islands.

On 11 August 1999 a few minutes of the day turned to night as the Moon blocked out the sun's light.

It was the last total solar eclipse of the 20th Century, with only Cornwall and the Channel Islands the only parts of the British Isles to witness totality, the full blacking out of the sun by the Moon.

Barbara Logan, who watched the eclipse in Shortlanesend, near Truro, said the experience was a "weird sensation".

In Devon and Cornwall, the partial solar eclipse will start at about 18:18, peak at 19:15 and finish at about 20:09.

In Guernsey and Jersey the timings will be about 18:21, 19:17 and 20:10.

Recalling the 1999 eclipse in Cornwall, Logan said: "One minute it was light then it began to get dark and I could hear all the birds singing and getting ready to go to roost.

"We were all gathered down in the square with our glasses ready.

"It was a weird feeling, you didn't know if it was night-time or daytime."

Nigel Brown, from Horsham, who was visiting Truro for the day, said the eclipse in 1999 had felt peculiar.

"Once the eclipse started it was a wonderful but really eerie experience," he said.

"I couldn't believe how day turned into dusk and the birds stopped making a noise.

"I was on my own and I didn't feel frightened, but you were aware something really big was happening."

Anne Le Cheminant said hundreds of people lined the seafront in St Peter Port, Guernsey, to watch the total eclipse.

"I'm still quite emotional about it, it was just such a gigantic, awesome event," she said.

"It was eerie, it was very strange, you can imagine the ancients had a supernatural feel about it.

"The light wasn't quite the same as evening lights, it was very grey.

"All the birds flew around and went back to their nests.

"As the Moon cleared the sun, you could feel the collective awe of everyone watching it."

Former BBC News correspondent Simon Hall reported from Alderney during the 1999 eclipse.

The third-largest Channel Island had some of the best views of the eclipse in the British Isles, despite some cloud cover.

More than 250 astronomers had gathered with islanders to watch the event.

Hall said: "Eclipse day in Alderney was a tease.

"From the start there was cloud and uncertainty about what we would see."

He said the first half of the event was obscured by cloud which had helped to reduce the sun's dazzle.

"At 11:00 the temperature dropped sharply when totality was approaching," he said.

"The odds had been 50/50 but at 11:16, the moment of totality, the cloud cleared."

The UK's next total solar eclipse will not happen until 2090, according to Royal Museums Greenwich.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crrv.title: PM asks justice secretary to find way to keep PC Harper's killers in jail
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crrv.text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told his justice secretary to find a way to exclude PC Andrew Harper's killers from an early release scheme designed to ease prison overcrowding.

Burnham is confident a solution can be found to remove Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in 2020, from the government plan, the BBC has been told.

Downing Street had earlier warned that it would not be possible to exclude "one or two offenders" convicted of manslaughter from the early release of prisoners.

PC Harper, 28, from Wallingford, Oxfordshire, died in 2019 when he was dragged behind the getaway car of three teenagers who had fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

Under changes to the Sentencing Act made this year, Cole and Bowers, who were found not guilty of murder, will become eligible for release from custody next January after serving half of their sentences.

They are in a category of prisoners - those who have committed certain serious violent or sexual crimes - who until now would have had to serve at least two-thirds of their sentence in jail before being considered for release.

It is not yet clear how the government will prevent Cole and Bowers from being treated the same as other prisoners with similar sentences.

If ministers said, for example, that prisoners with manslaughter convictions could not be considered for the scheme, that would have an instant impact on many other inmates.

A government spokesperson told the BBC: "The prime minister has asked the Justice Secretary to work through further options to keep a greater number of the most serious offenders in prison, including the killers of PC Harper."

A source said the Justice Secretary Alex Norris would set out "in due course" how the government would exclude Cole and Bowers from early release.

The prime minister has been making daily calls while on holiday to find a solution, sources told the BBC.

Around 5,000 people are expected to be released under the sentencing changes, down from 6,000 after exemptions were previously announced for those convicted of the most serious crimes including rape, child sex offences and grooming.

The third man jailed for the manslaughter of PC Harper - the vehicle driver Henry Long - was given a longer 16-year jail term. Because he received what is called an extended determinate sentence at the time, he cannot be considered for this early release scheme.

PC Harper's widow, Lissie Harper, has been among a growing number calling for Cole and Bowers to be denied early release. She and PC Harper had been married for just a month when he was killed in the line of duty.

Lissie Harper previously led a successful campaign for Harper's Law, which introduced mandatory life sentences for anyone convicted of killing an emergency worker whilst committing a crime.

Former police dog handler Chris Bushnell, who was at the scene of PC Harper's death, said he was "shaking" when he heard that two of the officer's killers might be released early from prison.

Bushnell was waiting in a lay-by near Sulhamstead, west Berkshire, in August 2019 when the teenagers' vehicle appeared, dragging PC Harper along the ground.

The former constable gave chase until he was ordered to stop and remain where he was. He said: "I've seen people die before. I've seen suicides. This was beyond brutal. It was awful."

"To think they could be released early is absolutely outrageous," Bushnell said.

"I'm angry with them, but I'm also angry with the government. They're spitting in the face of police officers."

Aileen O'Connor, chairwoman of Thames Valley Police Federation, added: "The public are speaking loudly and clearly. They agree with us that the government are firmly on the wrong side of this."

About 900,000 people have signed O'Connor's petition to stop the killers' early release.

But ministers have said prison spaces might run out as soon as October.

Dame Vera Baird, a former victims' commissioner, told BBC Two's Newsnight that one "good thing" the government has done is invest money in victim support services, as there would be many people currenty concerned that their attackers will be walking the streets sooner than they had expected.

She said the government "need to look at the right people to be letting out more carefully than they've managed so far".

Dame Vera added that women and people jailed under controversial Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences could also be considered for early release to alleviate pressure on prisons.

IPP sentences were introduced in 2005 and allowed judges to give out sentences with no maximum tariff to perpetrators of serious crimes or repeat offenders.

The sentences were scrapped in 2012, but were not retrospectively applied. As of this year, more than 2,000 people are still in prison on IPP sentences according to the United Nations (UN), who have called for the end of IPP sentences.

"I think somebody has to just seize the thing and get it sorted," Dame Vera said. "There has to be a wholesale resentencing attempt, I think, and really that does need thinking through."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crrv.summary: Andy Burnham confident a solution can be found to remove killers from scheme. Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in 2020. Downing Street had earlier warned it would not be possible to exclude "one or two offenders" from early release.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/ng-i.title: Matilda in pieces: what one mother’s suicide reveals about the carers broken by the system
https://www.theguardian.com/society/ng-i.author: Josh Halliday
https://www.theguardian.com/society/ng-i.text:
Parent-carers of disabled children are exposed to chronic levels of extreme stress and often reach crisis point before help is available – then they face a ‘fight for basic support’, experts say. This is Matilda Davis’s story

Two days before she died, Matilda Davis issued a plea on Facebook. Sharing a study that found more than 40% of parent-carers had considered suicide, she called for “greater awareness, action and change” in Britain’s broken social care system. “This speaks the words I can’t,” she wrote.

Matilda, known as Tilly to her family and friends, had spent years battling for support in a regime that close observers and those who rely on it often say is increasingly confusing, fragmented and difficult to navigate.

Her seven-year-old son, Jude – not his real name – has significant disabilities. She was, her friends said, an “absolutely inspirational” mother, juggling care for Jude’s five-year-old sister Lilly – also a pseudonym – alongside his appointments at therapy, physio, hospital and two schools, as well as the significant financial and administrative burden.

She cherished every moment with her children. “Tilly cared more than anyone I know,” said her sister Georgina Davis, 35. “It was what she lived for.”

On 3 October last year, Matilda, 36, was found dead in the bathroom of their home in Stratford-upon-Avon in the West Midlands.

She had killed herself a day after saying she felt “completely exhausted” by her responsibilities, and “paralysed with anxiety” about the prospect of her looming divorce from her estranged husband, who the Guardian has chosen not to name.

After Andy Burnham promised the biggest reforms to social care in a generation, experts said Matilda’s death showed how carers were being “pushed to breaking point” by a broken system.

“Health and social care services in England are failing disabled children and their parents are being left to pick up the pieces,” said Dr Siobhan O’Dwyer, one of Britain’s leading experts on family carers.

“In his speech, the prime minister acknowledged that without support unpaid carers can break. But what does it mean to break? For Matilda it meant death by suicide, it meant dying alone and in pain because services failed to fully appreciate the impact of the caring role and the troubled marriage, and it meant leaving behind the children she loved more than anything else in the world.

“That is a break that can never be healed, but it was entirely preventable. If the government really wants to stop other carers breaking, it’s going to need more than a heartfelt speech. It’s going to need real action.”

Evidence heard at Matilda’s inquest earlier this year, including GP records and disclosures to professionals, showed a person engulfed by stress in the final weeks of her life.

Last August, she told her GP she was worried about her “ability to cope emotionally with the daily demands as a parent-carer living with a home environment, which is becoming increasingly stressful, full of anxiety and worry … My absolute focus is to ensure [Jude and Lilly] are spared the turmoil of the unrest and upset in the house.”

Matilda had struggled with her mental health since Jude became critically unwell shortly after his birth. But two days before she died, she was in the “slight depths of ruin”, she told a friend in a voice note.

“I’m just in pieces and I’m trying to hold it together with the children, but it’s so physically taxing and emotional with what I’m dealing with [Jude] alone,” she said. “I’m just breaking really. I’m just completely broken. I haven’t really got any physical strength in me.”

Matilda had given up work as an art teacher to care for Jude full time. Social workers had not carried out a family care assessment, where professionals assess what support they might need, for almost four years by the time she died. They were due to visit the following week to carry out an updated plan.

On 2 October, Matilda told her divorce solicitor the worry was “overwhelming”. “My capacity to earn is basically nothing and will be long term,” she said.

Her day-to-day life was packed with “appointments, rehabilitation, admin, emails, phone calls, transporting/commuting”, she said, which would become more complex over the coming years with Jude’s schooling and health needs.

With her marriage coming to an end, Matilda said she was “desperately fearful” about the future of the family home, as she had sacrificed years of earnings to care for Jude full time. “The estate agents will not accept me as a non-earning single occupant and I have absolutely no where else suitable to go,” she said the day before she died, the inquest heard. She said she felt “financially trapped” and that it was “both physically and emotionally relentless at times”.

That morning, her husband called social services to say he was concerned about Matilda’s mental health. He said she had expressed suicidal thoughts that morning by saying: “I won’t be here much longer and then you will all have to look after yourselves.”

Social workers are obliged to act on welfare concerns within 24 hours and visited Matilda at home at 2pm the following day, a Friday.

A note of the meeting, shared at the inquest, detailed how Matilda was “visibly upset and tearful” when they arrived and “expressed significant anxiety” about the visit.

The coroner, Deborah Sewell, noted that Matilda spoke of the “emotional and psychological strain arising from relationship conflict, financial pressures, and the ongoing divorce proceedings”. Matilda told the social workers she had hit her head on the door in front of the children that morning “as a manifestation of emotional frustration”.

Before they left the meeting, social workers suggested her husband look after the children that weekend and that Matilda stayed with her parents. She was reluctant to leave, having already expressed concern about how Jude would manage without her.

When the social workers left at 2.30pm, Matilda “appeared calm” and there was “no indication of any suicidal ideation”, the note of the meeting recorded. Minutes later, she was dead.

At the inquest in March, social workers admitted they did not ask Matilda whether she had thoughts of suicide despite knowing she was in significant distress. Nor was she directed to crisis organisations.

Neither social worker who visited her that day had undertaken suicide prevention training. When told it is best practice to ask someone directly whether they have plans to kill themselves if they have expressed suicidal thoughts, one said: “Well, I’ve not done the training.”

Asked whether they were concerned that Matilda had said a day earlier she “won’t be here much longer”, which they were told by her husband was a suicidal thought, the social worker added: “Obviously it is concerning she said that but she wasn’t using the word ‘suicide’.”

Sewell issued a rare prevention of future deaths report in April to direct Warwickshire council to make suicide prevention training mandatory for 600 members of staff.

The council said: “We extend our deepest sympathies to the family and all those affected by this tragic loss. Following Matilda’s death and the subsequent coroner’s inquest, we have implemented enhanced suicide prevention training for all social workers to equip staff with skills to identify when parents and carers need additional support and to help them to access it.

“In addition, all agencies involved with this case will participate in a review to look closely at all the circumstances leading up to Matilda’s death. The purpose of the review will be to make recommendations for improving services and support.”

In research published in 2024 – and shared by Matilda two days before her death – the University of Birmingham found 42% of parent-carers had thought about suicide, many times higher than the general population.

Those caring for significantly disabled children are exposed to chronic levels of extreme stress that are “compounded by other factors like poverty, domestic abuse, or social isolation”, said O’Dwyer, who led the research.

She said social workers often had an “excess of professional optimism” about parents’ ability to cope with the pressures of caring for children with complex needs, particularly when they saw a devoted, loving mother – and it was often women who took on primary care responsibilities – and would think she would never act on thoughts of self-harm because she loved her children so much.

“But it is possible to love your children and be pushed to the point of suicide,” O’Dwyer said. “Love does not mitigate the overwhelming pressure of caring for a disabled child in a broken system.”

Contact, a charity for families with disabled children, said parents often reach crisis point before help was available and had to “fight for basic support”. Anna Bird, its chief executive, said parent-carers were being “squeezed from every direction: by the cost of living crisis, reduced services; and a support system that is increasingly confusing, fragmented and difficult to navigate”.

In the garden of Jude’s primary school in Birmingham, two apple trees and a rose bush have been planted in Matilda’s memory. Twenty miles away in Stratford, her friends at a family club have raised money for a bench engraved with her name and a number for the Samaritans suicide helpline.

Her sister Georgina described Matilda as “the most incredibly devoted mother”, draining her savings and driving hundreds of miles a week to get Jude the support he needed.

“She would tell me how she had to really fight to get what she wanted and needed for [Jude],” she said. “[Often talking about] how exhausting it is having to continually have to battle to get the provision he so needs.”

Matilda’s friend Francesca Roberts, a nursery manager, said she was constantly in awe of her ability to go “far beyond what any parent should have to do simply to access proper care and support”.

“She absolutely adored her children and dedicated every part of herself to them,” she said. Matilda was “one of the most caring, devoted, and selfless people I have ever known,” she added. “She was the village that everybody dreams of having around them.”

In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123, or email jo@samaritans.org or jo@samaritans.ie. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org, or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Nimra Shahid and Damien Gayle
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Supply in nine blocks in Tower Hamlets affected with some residents suspecting nearby building developments

They cannot even flush their toilets: life in east London blocks where taps often run dry

Hundreds of residents in blocks of flats in east London have been left without regular running water for more than seven months after development in the area may have left it without an adequate supply.

Taps have been running dry in nine blocks in Tower Hamlets, where residents have been forced to use bottled water while their landlord, the housing association Poplar Harca, delayed works to solve the problem.

In the meantime, hundreds of families have been unable to properly cook, clean, wash or even flush their toilets. Residents, who are bracing for a fifth heatwave this week, say they are still in the dark about why their water suddenly stopped – although some suspect it is because of new housing developments built nearby.

“I’m appalled at the situation my constituents find themselves in,” said Uma Kumaran, the area’s Labour MP. “Access to water is a basic right, yet residents of Devons Road estate have been denied that right for far too long. It’s a gross failure of one of the most fundamental duties a landlord owes to their tenants – especially during record-breaking heatwaves.

“I have repeatedly pushed Poplar Harca to take urgent action, full accountability, and set out a clear and swift timetable for repairs, for all buildings. Residents deserve nothing less than an urgent and permanent fix.”

Poplar Harca acknowledges “pressure levels can fluctuate” but denies the water supply has ever stopped completely.

Residents who spoke to the Guardian said they first began experiencing water shortages last summer. By December, the problems had become widespread, with at least nine blocks affected.

In correspondence with residents, seen by the Guardian, Poplar Harca initially claimed the problem lay with the water supplier. The housing association claimed Thames Water was supplying “lower flow pressures than in previous years”.

But at the same time, Poplar Harca was also telling other residents that their flats needed “extensive works” to create a new pump room in their block to increase water pressure. The landlord said these works could not begin until a formal process – called section 20 – was carried out to determine what share of the cost should be borne by leaseholders.

In common with social housing blocks around the UK, some flats have been purchased by their residents under the right to buy. Those homeowners must share the costs of the blocks’ upkeep. When major works are planned the freeholder must carry out a consultation to determine how much leaseholders should contribute.

Poplar Harca suggested there was no need for emergency action from a judge but a property solicitor the Guardian spoke to said that may not be the case.

Clair Phillips, a senior associate at the law firm Moore Barlow, said: “In circumstances where works are urgent, such as a prolonged loss of water supply, one would ordinarily expect the landlord to undertake the necessary works without delay and then apply to the first-tier tribunal for [urgent] dispensation from the section 20 consultation requirements.”

In the meantime, Poplar Harca told residents – including families and those classed as vulnerable – to access public shower facilities at Poplar Baths and by expensing day passes at Mile End leisure centre. Residents, many of whom are parents with young children, or are elderly or disabled, said this was not an acceptable solution.

As a landlord, Poplar Harca was obliged to provide water to its tenants whose taps had run dry. Residents said they often ended up waiting on the housing association’s phone line for more than an hour at a time, often not getting through at all on weekends or during July’s unprecedented heatwaves.

When they did get through, deliveries were limited to 15 litres per household, regardless of how many people lived there. Some residents said they only received their first delivery last week – more than eight months after the shortages began.

Residents suspect their water has been diverted to new developments in their neighbourhood. Water shortages began for many last autumn, around the time of the completion of Stroudley Walk, a Poplar Harca commercial housing development.

Water engineers were divided on the cause. Paul Kent of Kent Group Services said: “As a boom in construction has emerged over the past few decades, [Thames Water’s] infrastructure is still decades and centuries old, with lots of leaks on the systems due to the number of new housing developments in east London. Thames Water has had to lower water pressure to be able to supply everyone.”

Dale Joseph, a gas and plumbing engineer with Under Pressure Plumbing London, visited some of the affected blocks with the Guardian. He said that given Thames Water said it was meeting its responsibility to provide adequate pressure to the properties, it was up to the landlord to ensure each flat had enough to keep the taps flowing.

Towards the end of last month, Poplar Harca told some residents they could expect the issue to be fixed in six affected blocks between 5 August and 8 September. Work at three blocks is not due to begin until 27 August. That means some residents will have been left without adequate water for up to a year.

A Thames Water spokesperson said that after investigating a number of complaints, the company believed the low pressure was “due to extensive new development in the area, as well as some problems related to customers’ internal plumbing.

“We are looking into remodelling the wider area, which could raise the water pressure to take account for increased localised development. This requires extensive testing and any plans are at a very early stage.”

Sadaf Moosvi, an organiser with the community organisation Acorn, who helped some residents to come together to make a complaint, said: “There are genuinely no words to describe the scale of this scandal. I’ve been organising communities for several years and have seen a great deal, but never anything like this.”

A Poplar Harca spokesperson said: “Residents continue to receive water, although pressure levels can fluctuate and, at times, may be insufficient for some households’ needs. As soon as we became aware of the issue in December, we worked with Thames Water to investigate the cause who confirmed that pressure to the affected buildings remains above the minimum level required under Ofwat’s guaranteed standards scheme.

“The permanent solution requires the installation of new pump systems within the affected buildings. While we were keen to move forward as quickly as possible, because the water supply has remained available, albeit with temporary interruptions, we did not need to pursue an emergency route to fit the pumps. As a result, we’ve followed the statutory section 20 consultation process with leaseholders before major works can proceed.”

The spokesperson added: “We appreciate that residents would have liked a faster resolution. Our focus has been on maintaining support for affected residents – including supplying bottled water on request as quickly as possible, providing alternative washing facilities and offering additional assistance to residents with support needs – while progressing the permanent solution as quickly as the statutory process and technical works allow. We have kept residents updated throughout by text message, online, drop-in sessions, door-knocking and regular written updates.”
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.summary: Residents say they are still in the dark about why their water suddenly stopped. Thames Water said pressure was due to extensive new development in the area.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Could you predict which children will be Neets? No – and it’s unfair to ask that of teachers | Daisy Christodoulou
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Daisy Christodoulou
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The idea of government adviser Alan Milburn sounds laudable. But it’s asking too much of a system already struggling to meet society’s demands

W
hen you go to the dentist, what do you expect? That they will check your teeth, see if you need any fillings, give you some advice on oral hygiene? You probably don’t expect that they will teach your child to read, tackle youth unemployment or solve poverty.

But when it comes to education, politicians are remarkably relaxed about loading wider social responsibilities on to schools. The suggestion from Alan Milburn, a former minister and now a senior government adviser, is that primary schools – that is, schools that educate children aged four to 11 – should identify children who might not be in education, employment or training at the age of 16. “The warning signs are there from a very early, early age. You know, frankly from preschool,” he said. “So, definitely primary schools should be identifying children who are at risk of being Neet. And secondary schools and other services should be intercepting, intervening, supporting and helping those young people to get on a different path.”

Laudable in theory, but we need a bit of realism about what it is fair to make schools responsible for, and if making them responsible for so many things is going to cause more problems than it solves.

Defenders of this approach will argue that big problems have many causes, so we need a holistic response that breaks down institutional silos. I’d argue that by making people responsible for outcomes they have very little control over, you risk demoralising them and distracting them from what they can control.

Of course, it is true that primaries, and secondaries as well, have some influence over students’ later career prospects. There are numerous studies showing the importance of numeracy and literacy to economic outcomes. Getting GCSE English and maths means a student will be much less likely to be Neet. In fact, if a primary did want to create a “Neet risk register”, the simplest thing to do would be to list the pupils struggling to read.

But that just shows the futility of this kind of policy. The main way a primary school can contribute to a pupil’s future work success is by teaching them maths and English. Requiring a separate Neet strategy would add another layer of bureaucracy to a system that is already too full of them. A boy who is struggling to read shouldn’t need a “potentially unemployed in 2034” database tag before a school can act.

We also need to recognise that while schools have influence over students’ later success, they are just one small part of a wider system. Having better basic skills and more qualifications will help individuals succeed in the labour market. But if there are persistent structural problems with the labour market, improving individuals’ skills will not necessarily create more or better opportunities overall.

Our new government disagrees. They see rising youth unemployment rates as largely education’s problem. It isn’t just Alan Milburn: the new education secretary, Lucy Powell, has suggested a causal link between schools policy and Neet rates, and this analysis is being used to justify radical reform, or as she puts it “rewiring the entire education system to give young people from all backgrounds the chance to thrive”. But is that link true? Neet rates have risen in England and Wales, despite them having very different education systems. The tax and regulatory burden of employing young people has increased in the past few years, and this may have contributed to the sudden rise in Neets over and above what goes on in schools.

More broadly, we need to look at systemic issues with the British economy. A recent analysis by John Burn-Murdoch in the Financial Times showed that US workers who are functionally illiterate earn as much as the average British worker. “The same proportion of US workers who score stunningly low on literacy earn an average of almost $30 per hour, and two-thirds of them are in work,” he said. “Their British counterparts make the equivalent of $20 and fewer than half are employed.”

Schools can make sure students have the skills they need to thrive in a modern economy, but the economy has to be set up to take advantage of those skills. Increasingly, ours is not. We need to look at all the factors other than skills that might be contributing to this: housing, energy, transport, tax, regulation, health.

And we need to be careful: if we keep improving skills without increasing opportunities, we risk creating a generation of smart but disillusioned young people, youngsters who worked hard at school and university but still ended up with worse living standards than their parents and their peers in other countries.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Over the past 20 years, the UK has barely seen any per capita GDP growth, or any growth in median wages. In the same period, primary schools in England have risen up the rankings on international tests: according to the most recent rankings in 2021, England is one of the best-performing countries in the west on Pirls, a test of primary literacy. Primaries are a rare example of an English public policy success. We risk undermining that success by making them compensate for state failures elsewhere.

More broadly, why is it that a holistic approach to a social problem generally requires schools to take on extra responsibilities? “Joined-up government” always seems to involve schools helping the Treasury and Home Office achieve their objectives, not Treasury officials and police officers teaching eight-year-olds to read and count.

Schools are already doing a good job. Some other parts of the British state need to get better at doing theirs.

Daisy Christodoulou is an education writer and director of education at No More Marking, an educational technology startup

He says schools must intercept, intervening, supporting and helping those young people to get on a different path. But he says we need realism about what it is fair to make schools responsible for schools responsible.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/11.title: Trump’s media company reports $238m loss
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/11.author: Erin Hale
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/11.text:
US President Donald Trump’s media conglomerate has reported a net loss of $238m in the second quarter of 2026, against revenue of $1.7m.

In its latest filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Monday, Trump Media & Technology Group (TMTG) attributed most of the shortfall to $190.4m in unrealised losses on digital assets, digital assets pledged and equity securities.

Other losses included $11.7m in “accreted interest” – unpaid interest on a loan that is added to the principal – and $8.1m in “stock-based compensation”.

TMTG said revenue for the April-June quarter rose 89 percent compared with the same period last year, though losses continued to outpace earnings.

Almost all of TMTG’s revenue came from “media segments”, including $1.43m from advertising and $179,500 from subscriptions, according to the SEC filings.

The financial results bring TMTG’s net losses for the first half of 2026 to $644m, against revenue of $2.5m.

Shares of TMTG, which trades under the NASDAQ symbol “DJT”, were down 8 percent at market closing on Monday.

TMTG’s portfolio includes the social media platform Truth Social, the video streaming service Truth+ and the fintech brand Truth.Fi.

Over the past year, the company has also branched into other areas, including cryptocurrency and, as of August 1, market intelligence through the controversial subscription service Truth API.

Truth API provides investors faster access to posts on Truth Social, where Trump regularly makes market-moving announcements on policy issues such as tariffs and the US-Israel war on Iran.

TMTG interim CEO Kevin McGurn said during an earnings call on Monday that 10 companies had already signed up for the service, which has raised conflict of interest concerns, paying $60,000 to $100,000 per month in fees.

Despite the influence of Trump’s posts, Truth Social has lagged behind rival platforms such as X and Facebook in terms of users since its launch in 2022.

The New York Times reported on Monday that visitors to Truth Social in July were down by more than a third compared with the same period last year, citing data from the online tracking firm Similarweb.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/11.title: Huge fire breaks out at Libya’s Zawiya refinery after drone attack
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/11.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/11.text:
Firefighters in Libya are battling a massive blaze at the Zawiya refinery following a drone attack, with the country’s national oil company warning it may declare a force majeure and shut down operations if attacks continue.

Libya’s Ambulance and Emergency Service said in a statement on Tuesday there were no “serious injuries” from the fire, with most patients treated for smoke inhalation.

Footage verified by Al Jazeera showed huge flames and thick black ‌smoke billowing over the facility, the largest operating refinery in Libya with a refining capacity of 120,000 barrels per day.

It is located about 40km (25 miles) west of the capital, Tripoli.

The National Oil Corporation (NOC) said in a statement on Facebook that the fire broke out on Monday evening at tank number 402-T, belonging to the Brega Oil Company.

It said the tank, which contained about 4.5 million litres (1.2 million gallons) of gasoline, was “directly targeted, resulting in a severe fire before the tank completely collapsed”.

The NOC said the attack followed drone strikes on a water desalination plant at the refinery on Sunday and on a naphtha reservoir on Saturday.

The company declared a “maximum emergency” in the region and urged authorities to launch an investigation and bring the perpetrators to justice.

There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attacks, and the company did ‌not say who they believed was behind them.

In a statement hours later, the NOC said the refinery was “still being subject to sabotage attacks” with a drone targeting an oil blending and filling ⁠plant operated by the Zawiya Oil Refining Company.

It said the drone fell near its main oil tank and a pipeline network used to produce oils for the domestic market, without causing any casualties or damage.

“The company’s board of directors also confirms that if these attacks continue, it will have to declare a state of force majeure and suspend operations at the refinery,” it warned.

The Brega Oil Company, meanwhile, appealed to “all parties to stop the fighting and stay away from oil facilities and depots”. It said “oil facilities are vital infrastructure and owned by all Libyans” and that “protecting them is a national responsibility that does not tolerate any negligence”.

The attacks highlight the continuing security challenges in Libya, where rival administrations and armed groups have retained influence despite a ‌2020 ⁠ceasefire that halted major warfare. The country split in 2014 after a NATO-backed uprising that toppled longtime leader Muammar ⁠Gaddafi in 2011.

Two governments are currently vying for power: the United Nations-recognised administration in Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, and a rival in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.

In a statement, the Tripoli-based government said Dbeibah held a meeting earlier in the day with key officials, including the interior minister and the chiefs of some armed groups in the capital, “to follow up on the latest security developments”.

Dbeibah “stressed the need to deal firmly with any transgressions or actions that threaten security or harm vital facilities and installations”, the statement said.

Separately, a Libyan parliamentary panel condemned the attack and called for stronger protection of oil installations.

“The House of Representatives’ Energy and Natural Resources Committee condemns in the strongest terms the criminal attack targeting the Zawiya Refinery, one of the most vital facilities in the oil and gas sector that is a cornerstone of the national economy,” it said in a statement.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/11.summary: Firefighters battling massive blaze at Zawiya refinery after drone attack. META IS THE go-to brand for best-in class smart glasses and virtual reality headsets. Meta Glasses in particular helped popularize the new wave of face computers we’re seeing now—largely stylish sunglasses that also have built-in speakers, microphones, cameras, and AI assistants. (They’re so subtle that they’ve sparked a new wave of issues around smart glasses and privacy.) If you’re looking to try Meta Glasses or Meta Quest for yourself, here’s where to find Meta promo codes and other Meta discounts on this high-tech gear.

BEST BUY (WALKING DEAD BUNDLE)

There are two virtual reality headset models to choose from: Quest 3 and Quest 3S. The more budget-friendly of the two is the Meta Quest 3S (8/10, WIRED Review). It has a slightly lower resolution screen, and the pass-through isn’t as sharp, but most people will be happy with it. It’s currently marked down by up to $50, taking the price as low as $250. If you want to spend those savings accessorizing, some of the extra add-ons are marked down by 20%. I’d recommend picking up the Elite Strap with a battery, which will improve the comfort and make up for the limited battery life.

If you're looking for an extra game to go with your new headset, you can also use our links to score $30 in Quest Cash with the purchase of a new Quest 3 or Quest 3S headset. You can use that Quest Cash in the store to buy games or apps, and it’s good for DLC as well, if you want to pick up some extra courses for Walkabout Mini Golf, for example, one of my favorite games. You’ll get the cash for your account once you’ve activated the device—make sure to click here to buy the Quest 3, or use this link for the Quest 3S.

As a frequent Quest 3 user, a Quest+ subscription has been well worth the price. You typically get access to at least two free games every month, yours to play as long as you claim them during the month and keep your subscription active. There are a ton of games in the included library too, and regular discounts on DLC and big releases. If you pick up a Quest 3 bundle, you can score three months of Quest+, plus Batman: Arkham Shadow, one of the best single player immersive story games for the platform. That gives you a chance to try tons of games and titles, and is a great place to start diving into virtual reality head first.

While “refurbished” might be a dirty word to some folks, to me it sounds like savings. Particularly when a product is coming from the manufacturer refurbished, you can usually trust that it’s been properly cleaned, checked for any issues, and reset to factory settings. Scuffs and dings can happen, but generally if they go back to manufacturers, they can replace cosmetic parts easily, and you’ll get warranty support if any problems arise.

If you’re looking to pick up the more powerful Quest 3, and still want to save some cash, there are refurbished units available for just $380. That’s a $50 discount from a new model, and you get the same great hardware, cleaned and checked by Meta directly. The refurbished units have one year of warranty support, a pair of Touch Plus controllers, plus a charging cable and power adapter.

Alongside the Quest virtual reality headsets, refurbished pairs of the Ray-Ban Meta glasses are also discounted as low as $239. There are various styles and colors available of the Gen 1 glasses (6/10, WIRED Review), including the classic Wayfarer. If you pick up any of the refurbished smart glasses, you’ll get free shipping and a 30 day return window, in case you don’t end up liking the fit or style.

If you already have a headset, and you're looking to pick up some games, we spotted some great discounts on new and classic titles. The excellent Batman: Arkham Shadow is marked down by 10% when you purchase through our link, and you can also grab Metro Awakening for 10% off, both of which are dark and immersive single player experiences. Perennial VR favorite Beat Saber is also marked down by 10% when you use our link, and really should be in every headset owner’s library.

For the more competitive gamer, we found some special discounts when buying add-ons for some popular multiplayer games. You can redeem an offer for 50% off your first add-on purchase in Gorilla Tag, to make sure you stand out while swinging from tree to tree. Similarly, you can score 50% off your first add-on purchase in the serious shooter VAIL.

Students or teachers in higher education can also qualify for an extra meta discount code. You’ll have to verify your information with Meta on the Education Purchase Program (EPP) page first using your .edu email, and then you’ll get a link for a 10% off at checkout, no actual code required. The discount is good for Quest products like headsets, the Ray-Ban Meta glasses, and some accessories. While that program is meant for personal use folks in education, there’s a separate program called Meta for Education you can check out if you’re interested in using Meta to educate, with programs for manufacturing and non-profit sectors.

For existing headset owners looking to draw friends into their virtual worlds, Meta has a program for personal referral links that will score you both store credit. In the Meta Horizon app on your phone, tap the “Menu” button, and then go down to “Referrals” in the “Payment and Subscriptions” section, and you’ll be able to copy your code to share with friends. If they use that code to purchase and activate a Quest 3 or Quest 3s headset, you’ll both get $30 added to your Quest Cash account. Check out the Meta official page on referrals for more info, or the help page for sending and redeeming codes.

Meta teamed up with Xbox to bring the Meta Quest 3S Xbox Edition. This is a limited edition bundle with a custom 128GB Meta Quest 3S in signature Xbox Carbon Black and Velocity Green with matching Touch Plus controllers, a limited edition Xbox controller, an Elite Strap, and a 3-month Xbox Game Pass Ultimate membership.

With this, you’ll put your Meta Quest on 3S Xbox Edition, where you'll be able to play hundreds of Xbox games on a huge screen, thanks to the combination of Meta Quest and Xbox Cloud Gaming (Beta) with Xbox Game Pass Ultimate, as well as a bevy of other immersive experiences from the Meta Horizon Store.

For many of the above products, particularly the Meta Quest headsets and Ray-Ban smart glasses, there are financing options available as low as $19.99 per month. Meta works with Affirm, Shop Pay, PayPal, and Klarna, in case you want to split that big upfront cost into smaller monthly payments.
https://www.wired.com/story/meta-quest-p.summary: Meta Horizon app allows users to send and redeem codes to their Quest 3 or Quest 3s headsets. The Meta Horizon program is available for both headset owners and users.
