AS THE PET tech writer here on the WIRED Reviews team, I’ve tested over 100 pet-related products, including automatic pet feeders, pet water fountains, and pet cameras. The one brand I keep buying for myself—and recommending to friends and family with pets—is Petlibro.

Petlibro dominates the game when it comes to high-tech, seamlessly designed automatic feeders and pet fountains. Most of their products have a connected app to make pet parenting easier, whether you’re near or far. Where most pet tech falls flat, with poorly translated or confusing directions and over-crowded, buggy apps, Petlibro shines. Petlibro makes it easy to monitor your pets: with real-time updates, scheduled feedings, activity logs, and reminders so you can always keep tabs on them and their needs. Although Petlibro products aren’t the cheapest, I still consider them a great value for how well-designed and reliable they are. But you’re in luck. We love the brand so much, we’ve gathered the best Petlibro discount codes and coupons to make spoiling your pet easier (and cheaper) than ever.

I could go on and on (and I have) about the importance of pet hydration, especially with cats. Cats sometimes struggle to consume enough water, which can lead to potentially lethal UTIs and blockages, especially in male cats. Unlike dogs, cats are generally quite particular in their likes and dislikes, and cats can see stagnant water as potentially harmful. If the cat was in the wild, stagnant water has more potential for harmful bacteria. Cats are more drawn to moving water in nature, and a pet fountain (like those from Petlibro) helps encourage them to drink more by emulating what they’re naturally drawn to. Read my whole spiel here for more information about pet fountains.

This month is pet hydration month at Petlibro, which means huge discounts of over 30% on the best pet health products, including bundles, discounts on automatic litter boxes, and heavily-discounted food and water solutions. Plus, many are FSA/HSA eligible for even more financial help.

If you're already in the market for a new feeder and fountain, one of the easiest ways to save is by buying this essential pet tech in bundles. One of the best Petlibro bundles I’ve seen are for the RFID Smart Dining Bundle (now $10 off), which gives you two RFID Feeders, and an RFID Fountain, which helps to more closely monitor how much each pet is drinking or eating, and ensures no selfish pet gets more than their fair share of kibble. Plus, my ultimate favorite two Petlibro products, the Polar Wet Food Feeder (which is essentially a mini-fridge for your cats canned wet food) and Granary Camera Feeder (my #1 pick feeder with a crystal clear video feed) are on sale in a bundle, for $10 off.

Once you've tried (and loved) your Petlibro products, you can give a 15% off discount to a friend and get 30% off when they buy. When you refer a friend, you’ll both save. Plus, if you refer three friends, you’ll get a $50 gift card. Those are huge savings you could use on a cat water fountain, automatic cat feeder, and more!

This brand-new AI-enabled pet camera is sleek, and the app is intuitive and easy to use. (Read my full review here.) The Scout Smart camera has 1080p HD video, color night vision, two-way audio, and an option to mount. As the Scout camera captures footage, the built-in AI quickly learns which pet is which, and it uploads taken photos for the human to review to continually get smarter. You probably didn’t realize PlayStation had its own Visa Credit Card, but if you’re a hardcore fan, it can offer some really impressive perks. If you sign up and spend $500 within the first 60 days, you immediately get $100 back in the form of a statement credit applied directly to your account.

The PlayStation Visa Credit Card has no annual fees and comes with a variety of gamer perks. These include a 12-month membership to PlayStation Plus if you spend at least $6,000 within a calendar year and 5% back in points when you shop at the PlayStation Store or Sony Store. There’s also some more standard perks such as pay-per-use roadside assistance and emergency card replacement. Plus, you can save $100 with this credit card without needing a PlayStation promo code.

Speaking of becoming a member, that’s another easy way to get PS5 game discounts without a PlayStation discount coupon. There are three tiers to choose from, starting at $11 per month for the “Essential” tier. Being subscribed to this tier (or any of the higher ones) gets you access to loads of freebies, such as free exclusive add-ons, in-game items, or content packs for some of your favorite games. Check out all the available exclusive content to see what you’re in for.

Being subscribed to PlayStation Plus also grants you access to exclusive discounts on games, which are new each month. PlayStation Plus members can receive up to an additional 30% off on both PS5 or PS4 titles with these PlayStation deals . There’s a lot more content here than you probably even realize.

A few years back, we rounded up every “essential” PS4 game you should try. It’s definitely worth checking out if there’s some hits you missed out on over the years.

As I mentioned above, finding discounts on a PS5 isn’t easy. But one way to save on a new console is by using a PlayStation gift card. You can save up to $100 on PlayStation by applying your accumulated gift card balance toward one of these items—so long as you are buying through an official channel.

Unfortunately, PlayStation Store gift cards can only be used on digital products at PlayStation Store. Physical products from PlayStation Direct and merchandise from PlayStation Gear can’t be purchased with a gift card.

One of the only ways to actually get a deal on a PlayStation is by buying a certified model. You don’t want to just go and buy through any retailer though, as some have different certifications and define the term “refurbished” differently. Fortunately, Sony has its certified refurbished program to get you PS5 discounts that you won’t regret buying later. These undergo a rigorous recertification process to ensure that they function as well as a brand new PlayStation. In other words, they should work like they’re new.

This includes up to $100 off consoles, such as the PlayStation 5 Digital Edition or the PlayStation 5 Slim. Sony also has refurbished DualShock controllers for sale.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/11/hormuz-o.title: Hormuz Deadlock: Where oil prices could head next as prospects for an imminent deal fade
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/11/hormuz-o.author: Jenni Reid
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/11/hormuz-o.text:
Oil price gains remained in check on Monday, even after Washington’s latest hints of an imminent U.S.-Iran deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz failed to deliver.

Market moves won’t be so “benign” if the current deadlock runs into next week, Jefferies economist Modupe Adegbembo told CNBC.

Factors such as China’s rising crude imports and Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure could also push prices higher if the Strait remains closed.

Oil prices remain below their recent peaks even as prospects for a quick reopening of the Strait of Hormuz fade, a disconnect analysts warn may not last.

Brent crude futures ended last week down more than 7% following signals from Washington that an agreement with Tehran to unblock the vital maritime chokepoint was in sight.

An agreement is yet to materialize, with prospects for a deal appearing to deteriorate over the weekend.

Tehran is now adamant that Washington must adhere to several conditions before the strait can reopen. U.S. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has signaled a shift in strategy, telling news outlet Axios on Sunday that Washington was “low-keying it” and hinting the administration would rely on mounting economic pressure on Tehran rather than immediate fresh military strikes.

International benchmark Brent crude was closing in on $88 a barrel in early trading on Tuesday, up from around $83 at the end of last week. That rise still leaves prices well below last month’s surge above $100 a barrel and the peak above $110 recorded in May.

Energy markets drew short-term confidence from indications that negotiations between Iran and Oman over a temporary shipping route through the strait are continuing, alongside expectations that near-term military escalation between the U.S. and Iran may be held in check.

For now, traders are “confident that we can get to some sort of agreement, even if it may be a fudge,” Modupe Adegbembo, an economist at Jefferies, told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Europe” on Monday. “It may not be a great agreement, but it may be something that allows more oil and more things to flow through the Strait of Hormuz.”

However, that reaction will be “time-sensitive,” Adegbembo added. “If we see things remain as they are right now, I don’t think we’ll still see oil prices move in such a benign way if this continues over the end of this week or into next week.”

Kieran Tompkins, senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, said the relatively “low” level of oil prices reflects that investors have continued to factor in two opposing scenarios — a quick and imminent resumption in energy flows, and a prolonged Hormuz closure.

If the deadlock rumbles on in its current form for much longer, traders will be forced to ratchet up the implied chance of a prolonged closure, Tompkins told CNBC by email.

“I would naturally expect front-month oil futures prices to increase, especially if attention on a so-called ‘tipping point’ in the oil market is renewed,” he said. “This is the point at which the market’s ability to absorb the supply shock through inventory drawdowns is exhausted and demand will have to adjust downwards to match supply through much higher prices.”

“If the strait remains closed and oil inventories in OECD countries continue to be depleted quickly, the oil market could reach a tipping point around the start of Q4. This would be consistent with much higher prices, possibly in the region of $120-140 per barrel based on historical form.”

There are mounting questions over how long wider market factors — such as alternative export routes bypassing the strait, lower demand, a surge in production and a temporary slump in Chinese oil imports — can continue to cushion against supply shortfalls.

China “singlehandedly balanced the market in May with its cut-back in [oil] imports,” Amrita Sen, founder and director of research at consultancy Energy Aspects, told CNBC’s “Morning Call” on Friday. However, with Chinese crude imports recovering in July and set to rise further in August, Sen warned that “crude can’t stay down forever.”

Markets have recently been quick to price in the prospective normalization of shipping flows on any hint of a deal, rather than the full reality of ongoing physical supply constraints, Sen said. That also includes continued Houthi strikes on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, a key source of market stability.

“The crude set-up is more bullish on a fundamental basis,” Sen said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/11/us-judge.title: U.S. judge ends graft case against Indian billionaire Gautam Adani
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/11/us-judge.author: Priyanka Salve
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/11/us-judge.text:
A U.S. judge dismissed the bribery case against Indian billionaire Gautam Adani, ending the businessman’s legal woes in the U.S.

However, the judge said “irregularities” in the DOJ’s move to dismiss the indictment were “concerning.”

Court documents showed that the Adani Group’s offer to invest $10 billion in the U.S. had no bearing on the DOJ’s decision to drop the indictment.

A US judge on Monday dismissed the bribery case against Indian billionaire Gautam Adani, while also rebuking a senior Department of Justice official’s conduct related to the case as “concerning.”

Adani and seven others had been indicted in November 2024 in a New York federal court on criminal charges related to an alleged bribery and fraud scheme. Adani Group
 is one of the biggest Indian conglomerates, with a significant presence in crucial sectors of the country’s economy—from ports to cement, from energy to media.

The prosecutors had alleged that the defendants paid more than $250 million in bribes to Indian government officials to secure solar energy supply contracts, misled U.S. investors and banks to raise billions of dollars, and obstructed justice.

Adani in a post on X said he welcomed the U.S. court’s decision with “humility and deep respect for the judicial process” and added that his faith in “the rule of law remained unwavering.”

In the 47-page ruling, Judge Nicholas Garaufis slammed the conduct of Trent McCotter, the principal associate deputy Attorney General, saying he “eschewed the professional opinions of innumerable officials from various federal offices and replaced them with his singular judgment.”

Judge Garaufis also said it was “highly unusual” that McCotter’s decision to drop the indictment against the Indian tycoon was made “largely in collaboration with defense counsel,” and “seemingly without input” from agencies that investigated the bribery and fraud charges.

McCotter filed a request to dismiss the indictment against Adani with prejudice on May 18, stating that the Department of Justice had reviewed this case and decided “not to devote further resources to these criminal charges against individual defendants.”

Robert Giuffra, Adani’s lawyer who also serves as the personal attorney for U.S. President Donald Trump, and his team from Sullivan & Cromwell had submitted a 600-page document to help familiarize McCotter with the case, according to court documents.

The New York Times in May reported that Giuffra, in a meeting at the Justice Department’s headquarters in Washington, had argued that the prosecutors lacked “basic evidence” to pursue the investigation into alleged bribery by Adani.

Adani had offered to invest $10 billion in the U.S. economy and create 15,000 jobs as part of the settlement, the NYT reported. However, that was found not to be a part of the DOJ’s decision-making, according to the latest court documents.

Earlier this year, the Securities and Exchange Commission settled its civil case over bribery charges against Adani and his nephew, Sagar Adani, directing the two to pay a total of $18 million in fines.

In June, after Adani’s legal woes in the U.S. almost ended, the Indian businessman’s wealth swelled by $2 billion, as per Forbes, making him Asia’s richest man, surpassing Reliance Industries
 Chairman Mukesh Ambani and SoftBank
’s chief executive Masayoshi Son.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/t.author: Jordanna Schriever
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Jordanna Schriever

Former Beauty and the Geek contestant Tamika Chesser has been accused of murder. (Supplied: Facebook)

Tamika Chesser is accused of murdering Julian Story and dismembering his body, which was found in the couple's unit at Port Lincoln.

Ms Chesser today pleaded not guilty to murdering Mr Story and destroying his remains to pervert the course of justice.

She will next appear in the Supreme Court later this year.

A former Beauty and the Geek contestant accused of murdering her partner has denied the allegation and has flagged a potential mental health defence, a court has heard.

Warning: This story contains content some readers may find distressing.

Tamika Chesser today appeared in the Adelaide Magistrates Court and entered not guilty pleas to murdering Julian Story and destroying his remains to pervert the course of justice.

A lawyer for Ms Chesser told the court that investigations were underway into the 35-year-old's mental competence.

Mr Story's dismembered body was found in the couple's unit at Port Lincoln, on Eyre Peninsula, in June last year after emergency services responded to reports of a fire.

The body of Julian Story, who was allegedly murdered, was found last year. (Supplied: SAPOL)

The 39-year-old's head was found by a member of the public in scrubland east of the town in July, and was confirmed to belong to Mr Story in September.

Ms Chesser was a contestant on the television show Beauty and the Geek in 2010.

She has been housed in secure forensic mental health facility James Nash House since her arrest.

Ms Chesser will next appear in the Supreme Court for arraignment later this year.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/n.title: NT Police claim they can't trigger curfew in Katherine amid crime fears
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/n.author: Matt Garrick
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Police in Katherine have charged three boys after an allegedly stolen car was driven recklessly around the town for several hours before eventually crashing. (ABC News: James Elton)

Three children have been charged over a dangerous driving spree in the regional town of Katherine last week that shocked the local community.

Federal Member for Lingiari and Special Envoy for Remote Communities, Marion Scrymgour, has joined calls from residents for a curfew to help restore calm to the town.

NT Police Assistant Commissioner Travis Wurst says the situation does not reach the legal threshold required to trigger a "public disorder" response.

Northern Territory Police have claimed they cannot trigger a youth curfew in Katherine, after the community was left shocked by a dangerous driving spree in the regional outback town last week.

A car was allegedly stolen from outside a business on Thursday and taken on an hours-long joy-ride around the town, with occupants seen hanging out of the windows and putting residents at risk.

The 13-year-old boy who was allegedly behind the wheel and a 15-year-old boy have been charged over the incident, while police today said an 11-year-old boy had also been summonsed to appear before court.

Footage posted to social media shows a black Volkswagen being driven dangerously for hours.

Police said they were continuing to work to identify four other alleged offenders.

Dozens of residents of the town about 300 kilometres south of Darwin took to the streets last week to express their fear and frustration over ongoing youth crime in the town.

At the time, some urged police to declare a youth curfew — a call that was backed last night by Marion Scrymgour, the Labor Member for the seat of Lingiari, which includes Katherine.

"I support calls from the community and Katherine Town Council for the NT government to urgently intervene and stop the spike in youth crime that is having a devastating effect on the town and its residents," she said in a statement.

Under laws introduced in 2024, the NT police commissioner can trigger a snap order banning people from a certain area, including a town centre.

Marion Scrymgour says curfews can act as a "much-needed, short-term circuit breaker". (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

NT Police Assistant Commissioner Travis Wurst told Darwin radio station Mix 104.9 today the recent behaviour in Katherine was "unacceptable", but ruled out declaring a curfew in response.

"That's not applicable to this scenario," he said.

Assistant Commissioner Wurst said the dangerous driving spree did not reach the "public disorder" threshold under the act and it would take a "riot" to trigger such a response.

"It does not fit the definition as the legislation is constructed," he said.

Travis Wurst says the situation in Katherine does not meet the legal threshold to declare a "public disorder" response. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Police have said their response will instead be based around surging resources into the town, and having a higher visibility on its streets during the period of unrest.

Assistant Commissioner Wurst said he would be meeting with Katherine Mayor Joanna Holden today.

The public disorder laws were used to calm a wave of violence and crime in Alice Springs in 2024, which Ms Scrymgour said acted as a "much-needed, short-term circuit breaker" and restored town safety.

Member for Katherine and NT Education Minister Jo Hersey has not backed community calls for a curfew, citing the possibility of reputational damage to the region.

"We just need to be very careful that we don't go down that same road that Alice Springs did, where we do detrimental damage to our community, where people don't want to come to Katherine," she told Mix 104.9 today.

Jo Hersey says the court system is "where sometimes it falls down" in regards to youth crime. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"We just need to make sure that these children are not repeatedly out on the streets, breaking into cars, stealing from people, and that they are dealt with in a manner that the law is there for them, and that they are not getting bailed and out on the streets."

Mrs Hersey blamed the ongoing incidents on "the judiciary, that's where sometimes it falls down".

Some Katherine residents are calling for a youth curfew to be imposed after a group of joy-riding youths nearly collided with a mother and her 2-year-old daughter while they were driving home.

She also called for the parents of the children and teenagers involved in the recent crime wave in the township to take more responsibility.

"Parents need to be responsible," she said.

"Know where your young person is at night-time, and if you can't know where that young person is, well, maybe that's where someone else needs to step in."

The NT's Country Liberal Party government came to power in late 2024 on a tough-on-crime platform, but has not yet made any firm announcements about new plans to tackle the issue in Katherine.

The ABC has requested an interview with Mrs Hersey and Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/v.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
A-League Women

Cortnee Vine is back in A-League Women with Melbourne City after a challenging couple of years with NSWL's North Carolina Courage.    (Getty Images: NWSL/Matt Kelley)

Triple ALW premiership winner and Matildas star Cortnee Vine is heading back to Australia to spearhead Melbourne City's title tilt.

Vine is leaving NWSL side North Carolina Courage to join City, while Brisbane veteran Tameka Yallop is leaving the Roar to link up with grand finalists Wellington Phoenix.

The new ALW season begins on Friday October 16.

Cortnee Vine has returned to A-League Women with champions Melbourne City in a move that could help the Matildas' penalty shootout hero push for a second Women's World Cup berth.

Elsewhere, Matildas great and Brisbane captain Tameka Yallop has joined Wellington in a huge recruiting coup for the grand finalists.

Vine, 28, starred for Sydney FC as an explosive and tricky winger, winning three premierships and two championships.

Vine catapulted to stardom when she scored the winning spot-kick in the Matildas' famous penalty shootout against France that secured a maiden Women's World Cup semi-final berth in 2023.

The winger joined North Carolina Courage in 2024 but made just 23 appearances in two years, scoring twice, while also taking time away from football to prioritise her mental health.

With golden boot winner Holly McNamara leaving City for Super League club Everton, Vine is instantly the club's biggest name.

"I'm really excited to be coming home and joining Melbourne City," Vine said in a statement.

"I've watched what City has achieved over the last few seasons and the standards this group continues to set, so the opportunity to come into that environment and be part of a team competing for trophies was really exciting to me.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport?

Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

"My time in the NWSL has helped me grow both as a player and a person, and I'm looking forward to bringing those experiences back to Australia."

Vine will have the opportunity to impress and push for three trophies across the ALW and the Women's Asian Champions League.

Tameka Yallop has left Brisbane Roar after 158 games and 66 goals in various stints since 2008. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Attacking midfielder Yallop looms as the missing piece for Bev Priestman's Phoenix.

Yallop's wife Kirsty Yallop is a former New Zealand international and the move allows the couple and their two young daughters to be closer to family.

The 35-year-old, who missed this year's Asian Cup through injury, can also press her Women's World Cup case with the ambitious Phoenix.

Bev Priestman took Wellington Phoenix to the grand final in her first season at the helm. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

"I'm chasing that trophy and so is Wellington, so we're aligned," Yallop said.

"Getting the opportunity to work under Bev was a massive drawcard, not to mention the facilities at NZCIS. They're second to none.

"It's a high performance environment in Wellington and that's something that I love being a part of.

"And the Phoenix have shown they're dedicated to their women's program. That was a major pull for me too."

Brisbane is retiring the former Julie Dolan Medallist's number 13 jersey — the first time the club has done so for a men's or women's player.

Yallop, who has attended four World Cups and three Olympics and played overseas in several top leagues, spent the majority of her decorated A-League Women career at the Roar, bar a one-season stint at City in 2018-19.

An inaugural Queensland Roar player at the age of 17 in 2008, Yallop won three premierships at Brisbane and scored in two grand final wins.

Yallop scored 66 goals in 158 games in three separate stints at the Roar.

The new season is due to start on Friday October 16.

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/heal.title: Hong Kong considers lowering heat-stress warning thresholds amid criticism
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/heal.author: Emily Hung
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/heal.text:
Commissioner for Labour Sam Hui says thresholds could be adjusted after the heat-stress warning failed to rise during city’s hottest day on record

Hong Kong authorities are considering lowering the threshold for activating higher-tier heat stress warnings during abnormally hot weather, following public criticism that the system failed to escalate as the city sweltered through its hottest day on record.

Commissioner for Labour Sam Hui Chark-sam said on Tuesday that the warning system was currently more responsive to “muggy weather” than conditions of purely high temperature and strong solar radiation, but the government would seek to improve its sensitivity during periods of extreme heat.

Hui explained that the heat stress at work warning system took into account factors such as air temperature, humidity, wind speed and solar radiation, but that their weighting was “localised” to suit Hong Kong’s climate.

“In Hong Kong, the heat stress does not always track actual temperature change. When the humidity is high and the wind speed is slow, our cooling efficiency would drop sharply even if the temperature is not that high, and the associated health risk could be higher than in a well-ventilated open space with a higher temperature,” he said.

“Our system is more sensitive to this muggy situation, and the weighting of direct solar radiation is relatively smaller.”

The Labour Department recently came under criticism after its Heat Stress at Work Warning System remained at the lowest level while the city’s forecaster recorded a scorching 36.9 degrees Celsius on Sunday afternoon – the highest temperature since records began in 1884.

The temperature in Sheung Shui climbed above 39 degrees, the highest recorded there since the forecaster installed automatic weather stations in the 1980s.

Developed by the Hong Kong Observatory and Chinese University of Hong Kong, the system has three warning levels – amber, red and black – to alert employers and workers to heat severity when working outdoors or indoors without air conditioning.

Under the department’s guidelines, employers should arrange additional rest periods for affected workers when an amber warning is in force. Workers should suspend their duties when a higher-level alert is issued, depending on their workload.

Hui said the situation was beyond expectations, as they had anticipated that a higher-level alert would be issued after the heat stress monitoring system was expanded in April.

The expansion added eight monitoring stations and enabled an alert to be issued when the heat stress level was triggered at four of the nine stations.

“We are considering adjusting the activation threshold under high temperatures. By lowering the thresholds for temperature and solar radiation, it would be easier to meet the conditions of issuing a higher-level alert,” Hui said, adding that the government aimed to complete the review by the end of the summer holidays.

“Should we adjust the numerical values, the number of monitoring stations required [to report extremely high temperatures], or use another method? We are working closely with the Hong Kong Observatory to find a data-backed and scientifically sound approach that is easy to implement and boosts sensitivity, to address the previously underweighted factor based on our original design.”

However, Hui said the authorities were taking a cautious approach to suggestions that localised heat stress alerts should be issued.

He said working conditions could vary even within the same location, with some areas having poorer ventilation and posing greater health risks than places with higher temperatures but better airflow.

“We need to be vigilant against adopting localised indicators and causing a false sense of security, which causes oversight of the risks in certain working environments – that would defeat the purpose of the warning system,” he said.

Separately, former politician Emily Lau Wai-hing urged Correctional Services Department chief Wong Kwok-hing to review existing heat-prevention policies at correctional facilities.

“Given Hong Kong’s increasingly extreme and scorching weather in recent years, the relatively enclosed prison environment inevitably turns cell blocks into something like a ‘steamer’, creating a high risk of heatstroke or heat exhaustion for both inmates and duty correctional officers,” she wrote in a letter.

Lau asked whether any new heat-prevention strategies had been deployed this year and requested data on whether any inmates – particularly elderly ones – had been hospitalised because of heat-related illnesses.

“It is hoped that your department will adhere to the principles of humane and safe custody, attach importance to the concerns of the public, actively review the situation, and publish corresponding new measures as soon as possible,” she said.

The South China Morning Post reached out to the department for comment.

Some Yuen Long residents also spent part of the early morning without electricity after an underground cable fault at around 4am caused a power outage affecting about 2,400 households in Shui Pin Wai Estate and nearby areas.

CLP Power said emergency repair work was completed and power supply resumed at 10.45am.

Wu Chung House in Wan Chai, which houses several government departments, including the Department of Health and the Social Welfare Department, also experienced an air-conditioning system breakdown.

A management office staff member said that about half of the air-conditioning system remained operational and that emergency repair work was under way.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ceqe.title: Royal Golden Guernsey Goats join conservation herd
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ceqe.text:
Three Royal Golden Guernsey goats have joined the island's conservation herd, which was previously made up of only Guernsey cattle.

The herd was established by La Société Guernesiaise in 2014 to graze areas around the island, removing the need for mechanical cutting while improving biodiversity.

Herd manager Will Harford-Fox said the goats would eat species cattle missed, including gorse, blackthorn and brambles.

The goats were welcomed on their release by Governor of Guernsey Lt Gen Sir Richard Cripwell, who said: "They can make a really valuable contribution to how Guernsey manages its own environment in the future."

He added that the milestone also provided an important step in the conservation of the goat species, which received its royal title from King Charles III in July 2024.

He said: "Many people for a number of years have been working to see how we can preserve but also promote the breed.

"Today is the first step really in seeing how we can broaden the way in which the goats live and are perceived by others."

Harford-Fox said the introduction of the goats followed well established conservation principles around mixed animal grazing.

He said: "They will strip bark and leaves from trees and they will eat spiky plants without issue, get in and around places that the cows wouldn't be able to.

"We're targeting the south coast cliffs and places like Icart Headland and Pleinmont... And we're hoping they're going to make a real difference in knocking back some of the scrub."

The goats are currently grazing separately from the existing cattle herd, but Hartford-Fox said he hoped to graze them together on certain sites once introductions were made.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ceqe.summary: The goats were introduced to the island's conservation herd in 2014. They will graze areas around the island to improve biodiversity and protect the environment. The goats will eat species cattle missed, including gorse, blackthorn and brambles.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c89n.title: Isle of Man 'very well placed' for solar eclipse
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c89n.text:
People on the Isle of Man are set to enjoy one of the best vantage points in the British Isles to witness Wednesday's solar eclipse, with the moon expected to cover about 93% of the sun at its peak.

The island is particularly well placed to see the partial eclipse, sitting just outside the path of totality, making it one of the best places in the British Isles to see it.

The event is unique in the solar system because the moon is 400 times smaller than the sun, but 400 times closer to it, making them appear the same size.

Astronomer Howard Parkin said the island was "very well placed" to see the latest eclipse of this magnitude, with another total solar eclipse not due to be visible in this part of the world until 2151.

Parkin described eclipses as "nature at its absolute best" and said having now witnessed four of them, they always left him "awestruck".

The eclipse will begin shortly after 18:10 BST on Wednesday, reaching its peak at about 19:09, when around 93% of the sun will be obscured, before ending shortly after 20:00.

Parkin said the island was well placed to experience a dramatic change in daylight, even though it would not enter the path of totality.

The weather is set to be dry and bright on Wednesday, making conditions ideal for observing it.

Parkin said while "it won't go pitch black", it would "go semi-dark, it'll be like dusk", leaving only a thin crescent of sunlight visible.

Despite the high degree of coverage, "even 7% of the sun will still give quite a degree of illumination," he explained.

Parkin encouraged people to watch the phenomenon, himself profoundly affected by seeing his first eclipse that had left him "smitten".

For those watching from the Isle of Man on Wednesday, Parkin suggested locations along the west coast for the best view, particularly Peel or Niarbyl.

And he said it was "extremely important" anyone watching used appropriate solar eclipse eyewear.

The eclipse will be total in parts of the world including Iceland, northern Spain, northern Portugal, and parts of the Atlantic and North America, with totality lasting for a maximum of about a minute and a half.

The west coast of Ireland will see an even greater partial eclipse, at around 95-96%, he said.

The coverage experienced from the island on Wednesday is the most significant since the total solar eclipse in 1999, without another to match or surpass it until 2151.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2lq.title: School uniform rules must go further, charity says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2lq.text:
A limit on the number branded items schools can force pupils to wear "are a start", but the government "needs to go further", a charity says.

From September, uniforms will be limited to three items requiring a school logo, like a blazer, jumper or sportswear – plus a tie for secondary schools.

In the run-up to the rules being introduced, Clothing Coventry have opened a three-week long school uniform pop-up, as some families saying uniforms are costing them hundreds of pounds.

Zia Lee, from the charity, says the law needs to go further: "To have three compulsory logo items I mean you're still looking at a lot of money, you know, one to two hundred pounds for one child."

Around 23% of secondary schools will have to change their uniform lists for September to comply with the new rules, according to the latest government data.

The government says the changes will save some families "up to £50 per child", but schoolwear suppliers say they now face uncertainty in demand for this year's uniforms.

Mum of three, Eniole Okwuosa, said secondary school uniform was particularly expensive: "Uniforms are usually over £200 because the blazers alone are about £40 or £45.

"Two of my girls, the schools they do go to, their clothes have to be logoed, the blazer and the jumpers. So, they can't really wear the regular ones.

However, she welcomed the limits on logoed items.

"It's a brilliant idea if it works," she added.

Angelica Jaros' son is starting school this year, on top of buying uniform for her six-year-old daughter too.

She said there was pressure to get new clothes, bags and shoes.

"It's about £300 per kid.... because you remember when you were a child, you wanted to go to school with brand new things, you want the same thing for your kids as well," Jaros explained.

Meme Horner, 21, volunteers at the charity and said it's a way of giving back.

"As a child I got hand-me-downs, my mum got quite a lot of help, so it's kind of like just giving back to the community in a way, I feel good doing it," she said.

Schools having three branded items is still too many, she added.

"The crisis of money nowadays, the inflation has gone up so dramatically, and parents are struggling to do the basic necessities, let alone get children three pairs of logoed clothing for school," she explained.

Seyedeh Naseriniaki also volunteers at the uniform bank and says the cost of branded secondary school uniforms remains a problem for her family too.

"Last year we had to change twice", she said. "And going for a specific uniform cost a lot for us.

"With the help of charities we had a better chance, but we could choose the newer uniform if it was not logoed."

The education secretary has legal powers to direct schools to comply if they are not sticking to the new rules.

One head teachers' union, the Association of School and College Leaders, says the actual difference in cost is likely to be marginal for most families.

The Schoolwear Association says the plans could mean parents spend more on replacing lower-quality generic garments, which might not last as long as branded ones.

Clothing Coventry's school uniform pop-up is open by appointment only until 28 August.

From September, uniforms will be limited to three items requiring a school logo. 23% of secondary schools will have to change their uniform lists for September to comply with new rules.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0m7.title: Families under pressure to find food in summer
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0m7.text:
With the school holidays in full swing, a charity is running 'family fun days' to help those struggling with the cost of food over the summer break.

YMCA Cheltenham is hosting park-based events, which allow children to play outside and enjoy free, healthy food with their family.

Rob Charsley, head of communities, health and wellbeing at the charity, said 67 children and their families had attended an event in one week alone.

Meanwhile, in Somerset, Radstock Food Club said the increased cost of living had seen a rise in the number of people requiring their service, with more than 100 families now receiving food from the facility.

Charsley said 18% of children in Cheltenham and 17% of Gloucester children experience very low food security.

"Summertime is a great and fun time for children, but it's also a difficult time for parents [dealing] with financial pressures and food poverty," he said.

"There can be real pressures for families to find those positive activities and be providing healthy food for children, and it all comes at a cost."

Charsley said the 'family fun day' events were proving "a real help for our community".

"It's great fun and really satisfying when you've managed to feed all those families as well."

Atlanta, who attended the event with her two children, raised concerns about the quality and price of food.

"It just goes off really quickly," she said.

"It is quite difficult because it's so pricey to get all the healthy stuff, whereas the cheap stuff - the junk food - is just cheap, so it's easier to buy that."

In Somerset, Sofia Perkins manages Radstock Food Club, which provides food from supermarkets and supplier-surplus to families and older people in need.

She said there "definitely" seems to be less stigma when it comes to food banks than previously.

"There's more people [going to food banks] - people are less worried about accessing it."

But Perkins said the increased demand for food among families was concerning, claiming Radstock was "one of the lowest income places in the country".

"People can't afford your standard healthy food, which means people are eating quick, convenient food, which is no good for them," she said.

"Being able to provide this for everybody really does make a big difference."

The charity says 67 children and their families have attended an event in one week alone. Radstock Food Club in Somerset says more than 100 families are receiving food from the facility.

https://www.npr.org/2026/08/11/g-s1-1381.title: Trump pivots back to sanctions for Iran as other strategies to end his war fizzle
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/11/g-s1-1381.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/11/g-s1-1381.text:
President Donald Trump walks to board Air Force One at Morristown Airport, Sunday, Aug. 9, 2026, in Morristown, N.J.

WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump likes to say that he started his war with Iran after 50 years of economic pressure had failed to stop its nuclear weapons ambitions — but he's now betting that another financial squeeze can bring an end to that war.

The Trump administration is hoping that months of bombing have pushed Iran's economy to a breaking point that will force its leadership to cave to demands to end its nuclear program and fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to oil and natural gas tankers.

The president on Monday said that since Iran is seeking compensation as part of any peace talks, he now intends to demand the same for the U.S. side. It's part of a larger pivot this weekend by Trump to argue that Iran is now on the cusp of financially collapsing, even though it has already endured decades of financial sanctions, which are often a longer-term strategy rather than an immediate tool of warfare that can halt a conflict.

The shift comes as U.S. stockpiles of key weapons have dwindled and as stop-start talks seem again to have stalled. But Trump insists the pressure can lead to a breakthrough.

"Yeah, they can make trouble, but they're broke," Trump told reporters. "They have no money. You know, Iran is broke, totally broke. And, they're not paying their soldiers. They have inflation of 300%."

Inflation is running high in Iran, although Trump's estimates were higher than what administration officials have been citing to reporters. But the prospect of a longer war also carries inflation risks for other nations, including the U.S. — where the war and higher gasoline prices are unpopular.

Crude oil prices climbed on Monday as investors interpreted Trump's comments as a sign that fewer ships would be traversing the Strait of Hormuz, continuing to limit global supplies of gasoline, jet fuel, natural gas and other forms of energy. The Iran war largely closed the waterway involved in shipping roughly 20% of global oil supplies before the conflict — and attempts to reopen the strait have been short-lived as it has become a source of leverage for the Iranians in negotiations.

Iran does not appear to be publicly intimidated by the prospect of more financial sanctions.

"Whenever Washington proves itself incapable of pursuing diplomacy, it retreats into sanctions; and whenever those sanctions fail to produce results, it simply increases the dose," said Esmaeil Baqaei, spokesman for Iran's Foreign Ministry, on social media. "The real risk is that American politicians, clinging to this bad habit, will instead strangle their own remaining chances of a less humiliating exit from a crisis of their own making."

The president didn't say what additional financial pressure would be applied, but the administration has since April 16 been engaged in what it calls " Operation Economic Fury " against Iran. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called this component the "financial equivalent" of a bombing campaign as the countries that buy oil from Iran or bank with it could be sanctioned.

But one problem with this pivot is that the sanctions are unable to bite as quickly as the impact of the largely shuttered strait, said Richard Nephew, a senior research scholar at Columbia University who helped direct Iran sanctions strategy in the Obama administration.

Nephew stressed that the value of sanctions as a tool is limited because Trump has not articulated clear strategic goals for the war, at times stressing that it can't have a nuclear weapon, then emphasizing the strait and then talking about ballistic missiles. Instead, Trump has engaged in a massive series of aerial assaults and a level of destruction that has not produced the quick end that he initially promised.

"Economic pressure is a possible element in his strategy, but he's yet to explain the purpose," Nephew said. "Trump has systematically weakened his own hand through his inadequate use of force, inarticulate elucidation of an objective, and vacillation on negotiations."

Still, the sanctions and the ongoing U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports give the U.S. economic and financial leverage, said Juan Zarate, a deputy national security adviser in the George W. Bush administration. Zarate said the U.S. sanctions threatening third-party countries doing business with Iran also have an impact. But these things take time, he noted.

"The ultimate question will be how far the United States is willing to go to constrict Iran's oil trade and threaten third countries with severe sanctions -- and whether it has the patience to test whether the economic pain will change the regime's behavior," Zarate said.

Trump's latest pivot to economic issues with Iran is something of a flip-flop. Trump has long derided past presidents who used sanctions to limit Iran's economic ability to pay for its military and nuclear development. In a speech last week in Las Vegas, he defended the bombing, missiles and drone attacks that began on Feb. 28 by indicating that the sanctions from previous administrations that date back to November 1979 had failed to succeed.

"It's been 47 years, but really, it's been 50 years because they've been saying 47 for three years, it's been 50 years," Trump said. "And no other president has done what you should have done a long time ago, because Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, can't have it."

The Iranian economy has suffered gravely because of the war, with the International Monetary Fund estimating the overall economy shrinks by 5.4% and the Iranian government recently reporting an annual inflation rate of 88.6%. The U.S. Treasury Department said average loadings of Iranian oil have decreased from 1.8 million barrels per day before the war to less than 500,000 barrels per day over the past month.

The U.S. economy — the world's largest — has continued to grow, but inflation is elevated and borrowing costs have risen in ways that have hurt Trump's popularity and led to disapproval of the Iran war.

A senior U.S. official, insisting on anonymity to discuss strategy, said the U.S. military has set back Iran's ability to produce, sell and ship oil and other energy resources. The administration sees the naval blockade of the strait and sanctions as effective and views Trump as having additional options that can be cranked harder in the weeks and months ahead.

Trump is essentially arguing that U.S. voters are better able to tolerate any economic inconveniences than Iranians, who have been in a state of economic hardship for years.

"It's not just what the military can do — we've got the most powerful economy in the world as well," Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Monday in a joint appearance with Bessent. "And when you've got a motivated treasury secretary who can pull a lot of levers because he knows how to do it, you can put a lot of pressure on adversaries."

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Lobbying firm linked to Reformers created fake administrative assistant named ‘Jessica’, Icac hears
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Penry Buckley
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Consultant Jeremy Greenwood gives evidence to Independent Commission Against Corruption as it investigates allegations linked to Christian Liberal group

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A former lobbying firm which allegedly accepted illegal donations to fund factional Liberal party work created a fake administrative assistant called “Jessica”, an inquiry has heard.

Consultant and lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood gave his second day of evidence to the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s (Icac) Operation Rosny on Tuesday.

Icac is investigating whether a Christian Liberal factional group known as the Reformers – who wanted more conservative policies on issues such as same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia – solicited or accepted prohibited donations for the recruitment or renewal of members to the party. The practice, known as branch stacking, is not itself illegal.

Icac is investigating whether the former registered lobbying company Beckington, set up by Greenwood and Reformer Christian Ellis in 2019, accepted payments for factional work through fake invoices to Michael O’Hara, a prohibited donor, and the schools governing body Catholic Schools NSW. Greenwood has said he cannot recall either arrangement.

On Tuesday, counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, read out 2020 correspondence from Beckington to Catholic Schools NSW with invoices, signed “Kind regards, Jessica”. “Who’s Jessica?” she asked.

“Sorry, I’m not laughing,” said Greenwood. “Jessica was a fake admin name Christian created. He just thought it was funny.”

After Dwyer said she was “not getting the joke”, Greenwood said: “We have silly humour. Sorry.”

Greenwood, a founding director of Beckington, said he could not recall if the company paid Reformers members to do factional work. He said he believed the company had made payments to Jean-Claude Perrottet, the younger brother of Dominic Perrottet. Dominic Perrottet is not named in Icac’s allegations.

“If he wanted money, we looked after him,” said Greenwood, who later admitted to a payment of $12,000 to Jean-Claude Perrottet, who he described as his “favourite friend”. Dwyer put it to him that the money was for Reformers recruitment work.

Greenwood said: “I didn’t care about the recruitment work. I felt for him. He wanted to get married. He didn’t have a job.”

He was shown an invoice to Beckington for consulting fees from Jean Claude Perrottet for $5,500. Under repeated questioning from Dwyer, he said “to the best of my knowledge”, he was not aware of Jean-Claude Perrottet ever carrying out consulting work for the company.

Ellis moved to the UK at the start of this year, and the inquiry has heard he declined to give oral evidence, but on Monday Greenwood insisted his friend did want to give evidence.

On Tuesday, the inquiry heard Ellis rang Greenwood at 6am on encrypted messaging app Signal.

Greenwood said Ellis had asked him, “‘What was the reaction to you saying I wanted to appear?’ And I said, ‘Just noted.’” He said he could not recall if he had discussed payments to Jean-Claude Perrottet with Ellis.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

Greenwood defended saying in a compulsory examination prior to public hearings that he had not heard of O’Hara before Icac’s inquiry was announced. O’Hara has admitted to making payments to Beckington for factional Liberal work under fake invoices, but disputed whether they counted as political donations.

On Tuesday, Greenwood admitted to having first heard O’Hara’s name mentioned in 2019 or 2020. He said the compulsory examination had taken place immediately after a return flight following a trip to the UK in June, during which he met with Ellis at least four times, and the men had been drinking.

“We were at a pub every single time we caught up from about midday to 9pm on my days off from a conference,” he said.

Greenwood, who is named in two of the watchdog’s allegations, has repeatedly disputed being a member of the Reformers. On Monday he said there was not a “shred of evidence” that showed he was involved in the group.

On Tuesday, he told the commission that “hearing things when you’re having a beer at a pub is not actively engaging in the [Reformers] work”.

He was asked about being privy to and responding to messages in which the Reformers discussed recruitment work. Greenwood repeatedly said he was not an “active participant” in group chats.

Icac’s inquiry continues.
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.summary: Consultant Jeremy Greenwood gives evidence to Independent Commission Against Corruption’s (Icac) Operation Rosny. The Independent Commission against Corruption is investigating allegations linked to Christian Liberal group. The practice, known as branch stacking, is not itself illegal.

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: Trump warns FIFA would make 'terrible mistake' by replacing Infantino
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
US President Donald Trump on Monday backed FIFA president Gianni Infantino, who is in hot water over allegations of a workplace affair and criticism of a failed private investment scheme.

READ MORE
Infantino denies affair allegation, FIFA slams ‘concerted’ effort to weaken him

"FIFA would be making a terrible mistake if, for any reason, they even considered replacing President Gianni Infantino," Trump said in a Truth Social post, calling the Italian-Swiss lawyer "fantastic" and saying he "presided over the most successful World Cup, by four times, ever presented".

"If he is gone, it will never be as successful or profitable again!"

Trump's backing of Infantino contrasts with the response of US Soccer, which issued a statement critiquing the FIFA leader alongside Canada Soccer and football organisations in Central America and the Caribbean.

READ MORE
UEFA, CONCACAF and AFC accuse Infantino of 'fundamental breach of trust'

Infantino, who faces re-election next March, has denied allegations of wrongdoing, and FIFA for their part has backed its besieged president, calling the backlash "a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine" the organisation.

Other football organisations, including the Confederation of African Football and South American governing body CONMEBOL, share Trump's position in supporting Infantino.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/h.title: The medics offering healthcare to homeless people 'no questions asked'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/h.author: Niki Burnside and Caitlin Maloney
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Dr Sarah Peters is among the volunteers working with the team at Street Side Medics. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Street Side Medics is expanding to the ACT after opening in Sydney and Melbourne, offering healthcare to people who are homeless or in danger of being so.

The team of volunteers provides medical services like any GP, including supporting mental health and developing relationships with individuals.

Chief executive Nic Brown hopes to expand to other locations beyond Civic and is asking for other services to reach out if they want to partner with them.

For the team behind Street Side Medics, the service comes down to an "exceptionally simple idea".

Founder Daniel Nour wanted to provide healthcare to people in insecure housing situations who are often too preoccupied with basic daily struggles to seek out medical attention.

But there are still barriers.

"I think that there's some distrust that will still take us time to work on," Dr Nour told ABC Radio Canberra.

Street Side Medics will operate weekly in Canberra to provide medical care primarily to people who are homeless or in insecure housing. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Dr Nour said there were many reasons for people's reluctance to seek out healthcare, including financial barriers, Medicare status, previous negative experiences, stigma and embarrassment.

"Inevitably at times they're more concerned about where they're sleeping, what they're eating, shelter, companionship, and not why they're short of breath or not why their stools might be brown or black."

Street Side Medics has already been providing care in Sydney and Melbourne and is starting to expand to other jurisdictions.

It partners with other organisations, including those addressing the need for food and shelter.

The team includes a general practitioner, nurses, allied health professionals and volunteers.

Anyone can access the service, regardless of name, status or living arrangements.

Street Side Medics was started on the understanding that accessing healthcare can be challenging for a variety of reasons. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Dr Nour said they had soft-launched in Canberra, prior to their official opening this week, and he had already seen some positive impacts.

He said the fact that they were made up of volunteers was key to the success of the enterprise.

"Every doctor that is there on any given night or nurse or health professional is doing it because they truly care," he said.

"They want to see an improvement in the lives of some of our most vulnerable Australians."

After successfully running in Sydney and Melbourne, the team has expanded to the ACT. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

The service has received unanimous support from governments, and Dr Nour said many Australians were "doing it a little bit tougher in the current climate".

"Accessing health care services can be challenging for any one person, let alone really if you have some barriers that limit you."

Sarah Peters is a doctor with the mobile clinic and said she saw it as a "great opportunity".

"I'm someone that's volunteered overseas in the Australian Aid Volunteer Program and I think it's really important to remember that there's need in our own backyard and there's an invisible population here that really need access to care," she said.

Dr Peters said the program was not only free, but took a "no questions asked" approach to patient care.

The team hopes people will develop relationships with them as they seek medical care. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

"Particularly for those in homeless or insecure housing situations, we will attend to any medical need," she said.

Canberra's medical services are at a "saturation point", according to Dr Peters, and a difficult environment in which to get care, particularly without a fixed address to enable Medicare.

Expressions of interest are being sought to find organisations who are interested in establishing three bulk billed clinics in Canberra.

In June, it was announced three new bulk-billing clinics would open in the ACT thanks to federal funding, but it is unclear how they will be financed long-term.

With this in mind, Street Side Medics is also focused on providing continuity of care.

Dr Peters said this aspect, and the positive connections she could make with individuals, was rewarding.

"We don't force people to disclose anything they don't want to. And doing that, we hope that they will continue to come back to us and we make continuity plans, follow them up.

"They know us and we know them."

Street Side Medics chief executive Nic Brown said they would run the service in one location but intended to expand to others over time.

He said 50 per cent of people they saw did not have a Medicare card.

Nic Brown is the chief executive of Street Side Medics, which started out in Sydney and then Melbourne. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

"And so there's a whole variety of factors, notwithstanding a focus on just trying to ... get their next meal.

The van currently operates once a week in Civic, in partnership with Vinnies Roadhouse at the Griffin Centre on Genge Street.

Mr Brown said they were keen to hear from other services that might want to work with them at other locations.

"Please reach out, because we'd love to partner."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: U.S. Treasury chief’s ‘whatever-it-takes’ vow to help the yen masks limited firepower
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Daniel Flatley
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s suggestion of a no-limits approach toward helping Japan rescue the yen risks getting called out by market participants flagging his limited firepower to do the job.

Japan’s currency slid as much as 1% Monday to past ¥159 per dollar, wiping out half the rally triggered by the July 31 U.S.-Japan intervention. The exercise, the first coordinated effort since 1998, had lifted the currency near ¥155 before the retreat resumed.

In the wake of that unusual operation, Bessent said “we will do whatever it takes to support them in a way that helps the American economy, the American taxpayer, stabilizes the global economy.”

Trouble is, as far as currency-intervention ammunition goes, the Treasury chief is seen limited by his main dedicated instrument — the Exchange Stabilization Fund, with holdings of less than $220 billion. As a gauge of comparison, Japan on its own is estimated to have spent $53 billion on yen operations on July 30, the day before the coordinated move.

“The U.S. can influence the narrative by coordinating with Japan on intervention, but can’t rewrite the fundamentals,” said Nathan Thooft, a senior portfolio manager at Manulife Investment Management. With regard to American authorities’ capacity, “the pockets are deep but not limitless,” he said.

In the U.S., the Federal Reserve is the agency with — in principle — unlimited firepower for foreign-exchange intervention to drive down the dollar, as it’s effectively able to manufacture greenbacks. In the case of last month’s operation, however, its role was limited to the actual conduct of the yen purchases, done on behalf of the Treasury.

Historically, the Fed has sometimes joined in with the Treasury with its own funds to show its support for interventions. Back in 1998, the yen intervention at that time was done 50-50 with Fed and Treasury funds. A 2011 joint intervention to sell yen and a 2000 one to buy euros similarly involved even splits.

This time, media reporting on the intervention suggests the Fed “did not stump up” for the U.S. intervention, Derek Tang, an economist at Monetary Policy Analytics wrote in a note Monday. Official data are unlikely to be available to confirm that until later this year.

“Its intervention capacity is theoretically limited only by its willingness,” Tang noted of the U.S. central bank.

The Fed on Monday declined to comment about the U.S. intervention. The Treasury didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Bessent has put a spotlight on a separate way the Fed could prove helpful: via its Foreign and International Monetary Authorities Repo Facility. That program would allow Japan to swap a portion of its $1 trillion-plus stockpile of Treasuries for dollar cash. Two days after the intervention, Bessent recommended the program be “upsized.”

Fed data published Thursday suggested Japan hasn’t used the tool, however. Earlier this month, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama signaled it could be used at some point.

Pressure for either Japan or the two allies together to step in again could rise should the yen sink past ¥160 per dollar, a level seen earlier this year as a key psychological threshold. Authorities intervened to support the currency when it crossed that level in the summer of 2024.

“If the U.S. and Japan let the yen go back to trading durably above ¥160, markets could interpret the absence of FX intervention” as a sign of U.S. reluctance toward selling dollars, Marco Casiraghi and Gang Lyu at Evercore ISI wrote in a note Monday. “The result could invite additional market pressure that would test the commitment to a stronger yen.”

Bessent’s key likely motivation for propping up the yen, according to economists and market participants, has been to halt any contagion into Treasuries. Japanese government bond selloffs have occasionally spilled over to U.S. securities, and if Tokyo offloads its dollars, that could send American yields higher. Benchmark 10-year Treasury yields recently hit their highest since Bessent took office.

“If Bessent is concerned about the impact of yen trading exerting possible upward pressure on U.S. Treasury and longer-term U.S. yields, the best way to tackle the problem is to counter U.S. fiscal profligacy,” said Mark Sobel, who served at the Treasury for over three decades. “FX intervention and FIMA usage is a Band-Aid.”

“Renewed yen weakness alongside higher Treasury yields could draw Washington back in. If the U.S. eventually sells dollars, rather than euros as it did in July, that would be a much stronger deterrent to still short yen positioning,” said Skylar Montgomery Koning, macro strategist at Bloomberg.

With Japan observing a holiday on Tuesday, traders are wary that thinner liquidity could create conditions for another bout of intervention — as officials could get bigger bang for the buck.

Still, Monday’s currency moves highlight the limits of that mechanism in changing the yen’s broader trajectory when the forces behind its decline remain largely intact.

Those forces include wide interest-rate differentials between Japan and the U.S., concerns over Japan’s fiscal outlook and geopolitical uncertainty. The yen’s retreat on Monday came alongside a rise in the price of oil amid continuing tensions over Iran. Japan imports most of its energy, leaving it vulnerable to higher prices.

As for policy rates, the Bank of Japan’s benchmark is currently 1%, versus the Fed’s 3.5% to 3.75% target range for its own key rate.

A summary of the BOJ’s most recent policy meeting flagged rising risks of inflation heating up, with one board member pointing to the possibility of an acceleration in the pace of rate hikes. Swaps show traders pricing about a 63% chance of an increase by September, with an October move almost fully priced.

“We think the relatively muted response to the intervention reflects the fundamental reasons for the currency’s weakness,” Goldman Sachs Group Inc. strategists including Kamakshya Trivedi wrote in a note. The team expects “depreciation pressures to reemerge over time absent a shift in global conditions or a policy surprise.”

https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.title: Brics’ ‘stiffest test’: can India, China rally bloc to resolve Strait of Hormuz crisis?
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.author: Biman Mukherji
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.text:
Analysts say a unified Brics could support Oman-led talks for a resolution and provide an alternative to US diplomacy

Analysts say the forum from September 12 to 13 amid the global energy crisis wrought by the Middle East conflict could see parallel diplomacy, given the 11-member grouping’s economic clout accounts for about 40 per cent of the world’s gross domestic product.

“I see a convergence of interests between India and China, though not necessarily a convergence in geopolitical positions,” said Uday Chandra, a political-science professor at India’s Ashoka University.

“Both countries would like the Iran and Ukraine wars contained, energy supplies secured, the Strait of Hormuz fully reopened, and the global economy stabilised in the medium run.”

“But China is closer to Russia and Iran than India is. India, in turn, has vital strategic partnerships with the US, Europe, Israel, the UAE and Ukraine,” Chandra said. “Paradoxically, these differences may make India-China cooperation more worthwhile.”

Brazil, seen as a major voice and bridge for the Global South, could help smooth out internal divides within Brics, he added.

The bloc, originally comprising Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, has expanded to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates, Indonesia and Saudi Arabia.

The Brics foreign ministers’ meeting in New Delhi in May concluded without a joint statement because of differing views among members regarding the Middle East conflict.

Deep divisions surfaced between newer members Iran and the UAE over the regional conflict. Iranian officials pushed the bloc to explicitly condemn US and Israeli actions, while other member states objected to the language.

“If Delhi and Beijing agree on certain basic principles for de-escalation, they may be able to bring very different parties towards them. Strategic cooperation and economic competition may be perfectly compatible in the medium to long run,” Chandra said.

China and India have cautiously improved ties in recent months, resuming direct flights last October after a five-year suspension and restarting cross-border trade through the Lipulekh Pass in the Himalayas earlier this month.

A military stand-off along their disputed border remains a point of strain, though both nations have moved towards a diplomatic thaw.

“There could be some convergence albeit limited on moving ahead with the diplomatic and dialogue process [at the Brics summit], and perhaps even proposing a definitive road map towards a lasting ceasefire [between US and Iran, and Ukraine and Russia] to end the conflicts,” said Srikumar Menon, a former Indian diplomat.

“Both India and China are unlikely to get involved or position themselves deeply in the process. In fact the two may rather focus on seeking support for multipolarity, leveraging the Global South card and finding ways to not give in to sanctions imposed by the West.”

Western nations – led primarily by the US – have actively imposed punitive secondary sanctions and tariff threats against third-country companies, financial institutions and individuals to discourage them from trading with Russia and Iran.

The US Senate recently passed legislation that could once again see tariffs of up to 100 per cent levied on countries – including India and China – that continue to buy Russian oil.

The convergence of common economic interests in helping resolve geopolitical conflicts such as the Strait of Hormuz disruption “may even goad both sides [India and China] to act with more caution and care than has been in the past decade”, Chandra said.

“Whether it leads to durable peace around geopolitical focal points remains to be seen,” he added. “Hormuz is probably where Brics faces its stiffest test. Iran may view restrictions on American shipping as legitimate strategic leverage, but India, China and the Gulf states need the waterway to function normally.”

Iran and Oman have progressed towards reaching a deal on Hormuz, which carried a fifth of the world’s oil before the conflict. Tehran has said reopening the waterway would be subject to Washington meeting conditions, including American reparations for attacks on Iran.

Brics could focus on a narrower objective such as uninterrupted commercial shipping, no attacks on merchant vessels, and a negotiated mechanism for de-escalation, Chandra said. “It should support, not supplant, Oman-led negotiations.”

Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that Iran and the US were not engaged in talks and Tehran would not start them as long as Washington breached an interim agreement signed in June.

Meanwhile, in a further threat to supply, the Iran-aligned Houthis said they had hit Saudi Aramco’s Jazan refinery on Sunday.

The attack came two days after Saudi Arabia signed a defence pact with Turkey and Pakistan in response to growing regional instability that has undermined confidence among nations about Washington’s ability to secure peace and stability.

Srinivaasan Balakrishnan, director of strategic engagements and partnerships at the Delhi-based think tank Indic Researchers Forum, said Brics could provide “precisely the kind of inclusive, multipolar platform that can offer a credible alternative to US-centric approaches in resolving conflicts”.

The US being a “direct party” to the conflict in the Middle East “limits Washington’s ability to act as a neutral broker”, but Brics brought together players with “shared stakes in energy security, maritime commerce and a less zero-sum global order”, Balakrishnan said.

“It is not a military alliance or an anti-Western bloc, it is a forum where differences can be managed without forcing alignment.”

https://www.npr.org/2026/08/11/g-s1-1381.title: Turkey's parliament approves a pardon-like bill for thousands of PKK militants
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/11/g-s1-1381.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/08/11/g-s1-1381.text:
FILE - Youngsters hold a photograph of Abdullah Ocalan, the jailed leader of the militant Kurdish group, or PKK, in Diyarbakir, Turkey, Feb. 27, 2025.

ANKARA, Turkey — Turkey's parliament on Monday approved legislation that would introduce a conditional pardon for thousands of Kurdish militants in a bid to advance the government's peace initiative with their insurgent group.

Legislators voted 468-88 in favor of the measure that would only come into effect after Turkish authorities have verified that the Kurdistan Workers' Party, or PKK, has fully disarmed.

The PKK announced last year that it is ending its decades-long armed campaign against the Turkish state, declaring a decision to dissolve itself as part of the peace effort. The move came in response to a call from its imprisoned leader, Abdullah Ocalan.

The group then staged a symbolic disarmament ceremony in northern Iraq, where it is based, and announced that it was withdrawing fighters from key locations in Turkey to Iraq.

The measure, which is a step toward ending a conflict that has killed tens of thousands of people, could have implications beyond Turkey's borders, leading to closer Turkish-Iraqi ties. It could also support the Syrian government's efforts to integrate areas that were under the control of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, affiliated with the PKK.

It also offers Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan the opportunity to court the support of the pro-Kurdish DEM party to help him remain in office beyond the presidential two-term limit. Erdogan could run again if parliament calls an early election during his current term.

The 12-article legislation outlines the procedures for the group's disarmament and the rehabilitation of thousands of PKK members.

It will suspend some prison sentences for convicted PKK members and postpone ongoing investigations and trials against others for five or 10 years, depending on the severity of the alleged offenses. If no terror-related crime is committed within the time frame, the cases will be dropped.

Militants convicted of intentional killings and those sentenced to life terms before 2005 are excluded from the bill's provisions. This applies to Ocalan and other senior PKK figures.

The proposal also sets up ministerial and parliamentary committees to monitor the disarmament process. The measures will come into effect only after Turkey's National Security Council confirms that the group has disbanded and surrendered all weapons.

Those wanting to benefit from the law will have six months to apply after the National Security Council's decision is published in the official gazette.

Media reports have said exiled PKK members and those in Iraq and Syria are expected to benefit.

"With the armed organization laying down its arms and dissolving itself, we will build a new era in which peace, brotherhood, and solidarity will prevail," Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus told reporters following the vote.

The PKK-linked ANF news outlet carried a statement from the group in which it said that the Turkish legislation is a "beginning" to resolving the outstanding issues but has "serious shortcomings and deficiencies." It called for Ocalan's release from prison, saying that the peace process can move forward only if he "lives and works freely."

It also said that the legislation failed to address demands for democratic reforms and Kurdish rights, adding that PKK fighters would not give up their weapons and return to Turkey "if, upon returning to Turkey, they are unable to engage in democratic politics on the basis of freedom of thought and freedom of association, and if they are prosecuted and imprisoned because of their views or the organizations they establish."

"The people of Turkey, who have paid a heavy price for many years, now have an opportunity to consolidate peace and build democracy," Gulistan Kilic Kocyigit, of the pro-Kurdish Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party, or DEM, told parliament.

"Of course, the proposal has shortcomings, and we now have a responsibility to address these shortcomings," she added, in an apparent reference to demands for greater rights for Kurds and for democratic reforms.

Musavat Dervisoglu, the leader of the center-right nationalist Good Party, which opposes the bill, said it "would pave the way" for Erdogan to stay in power.

DEM has lobbied for Ocalan, who has been imprisoned since 1999, to be granted official status to coordinate the transition process, leading to his release.

The current proposal, however, makes no mention of Ocalan's status or possible release.

Media reports have suggested, however, that Ocalan's conditions in his island prison off Istanbul will likely be improved, giving him broader visiting conditions and communication with the outside world.

The PKK has waged an armed insurgency since 1984 that has claimed tens of thousands of lives and spilled into Iraq and Syria. It has been designated a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States and the European Union.

The group initially sought an independent Kurdish state but later shifted to demands for autonomy and expanded rights in Turkey.

Previous peace efforts between Turkey and the PKK have failed, most recently in 2015.
