https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Coalition divided over tougher gambling laws - with MPs warning Angus Taylor against overreach
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Josh Butler and Tom McIlroy
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Some Liberal and National MPs warned against over-regulation in party room discussion, while others argued for more stringent rules

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Coalition MPs have warned the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, not to overreach in talks with Anthony Albanese on Labor’s gambling advertising crackdown, insisting rules that are too stringent would not strike the right balance on personal responsibility.

The prime minister and the opposition leader continued talks on Tuesday over a deal to advance Labor’s legislation to limit online gambling advertising, with betting inducements and more restrictions on advertising hours among possible avenues for movement.

Debate over the issue dominated a meeting of the joint Coalition party room in Canberra on Tuesday, with nine Liberal and Nationals MPs making their views known to colleagues.

Among the contributions were five MPs pushing for tougher restrictions and four arguing the Coalition needed “to get the balance right” and not go too far in limiting advertising. Some warned overly restrictive rules for Australian gambling companies could push some punters to illegal overseas operators, citing comparisons with the rise of illegal tobacco amid rising government excises pushing up retail prices.

Taylor himself raised the question of personal responsibility in a media conference on Monday, an issue that was also raised in Tuesday’s meeting alongside concerns about “over-regulation”.

Coalition MPs used the meeting to raise concerns about “perceived behaviour of gambling preying on the vulnerable”, but the possibility of a deal remained “a moving feast” as parliament resumed after the winter break.

The gambling industry is increasingly resigned to the paring back of inducements, but it says that such restrictions could send gamblers to unregulated offshore operators and particularly impinge the earnings of smaller wagering operators.

Industry sources said they were seeking to warn Coalition MPs about the impact of further changes to inducements or ad rules, but rejected claims from the Greens that they were intimately involved in negotiations.

While Labor sources say they are still confident Taylor will get on board, the Greens are also still talking with the government, signalling a deal with the Coalition is not yet done. Albanese on Monday said publicly he would “later this week” have progress on inducements and advertising rules.

Labor has been criticised for falling short of the ambition of a parliamentary inquiry led by the late Labor MP Peta Murphy three years ago, and is talking with the Coalition and the Greens to find a pathway through the Senate. Murphy’s 2023 committee recommended the government “prohibit all online gambling inducements and inducement advertising, and that it do so without delay”.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

Guardian Australia understands some small tweaks to the timing of TV advertising, specifically to lessen the impact on children, could be among the things being considered.

Labor’s proposed changes would see gambling ads restricted to three an hour on broadcast TV between 6am and 8.30pm. But further tweaks to that may be part of the discussions. Other reforms potentially in the frame could be around the discrepancy in ad rules on broadcast TV versus streaming services.

Opt-in provisions for advertising on streaming platforms are also being discussed.

Simon Kennedy, one of the Liberal MPs helping drive tougher action, used a speech in parliament to call for an independent review of the rules after the next election. That plan would help make any newly introduced protections even stronger within three years.

Kennedy said there were “two glaring gaps” in the existing laws: inducements to keep punters gambling longer and unlimited advertising online.

“There should be an independent review of wherever we land after the next election, so we can do more,” Kennedy said.

The government is expected to make amendments to the bill in the lower house, where the bill is listed for debate on Wednesday.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.title: Tuesday briefing: To drill or not to drill – Burnham’s first big climate test
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.author: Michael Segalov
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text:
In today’s newsletter: As we enter our fifth summer heatwave, Andy Burnham’s government is looking at what the UK should do with its remaining North Sea oil and gas

Good morning. What a difference a new job can make. “To have a shot at staying within 1.5C global warming, we can’t have any new oil or gasfields … It’s irresponsible and shortsighted to be funding new #fossilfuels when we need to be getting to #NetZero.”

This was the 2022 message from Miatta Fahnbulleh, now the secretary of state for energy security and net zero. It’s a testament to her remarkable rise that Fahnbulleh wasn’t even an MP when she posted it four years ago. Today, she is in the cabinet, facing (or is the face of, at least) one of the most challenging, and potentially controversial questions looming for the new government: to drill or not to drill, baby?

Two sites are the focus of fierce debate. Yesterday, a public consultation on whether to greenlight extraction at one of them – Jackdaw – closed. Next Monday, it’ll be the same for the other, Rosebank. Andy Burnham has been silent about the climate crisis since taking office. As we enter yet another heatwave, what his government does next will be a defining signal of intent on the issue.

But what would extraction actually mean, and how many options are open to Fahnbulleh? That’s the subject of today’s First Edition, after a roundup of this morning’s headlines.

Colombia | More than 100 people have died after a powerful earthquake struck western Colombia, collapsing and severely damaging scores of buildings in major cities including Cali and Pereira.

UK weather | Almost three-quarters of England is now in drought, with four more regions officially declared, and as much of Europe braces for its fifth climate crisis-driven heatwave this summer.

Crime | Police are investigating whether Joshua Kerry, the man charged with the murder of the former Reform UK and Conservative politician Ann Widdecombe, had any role in an attempted burglary last year at the then London home of Nigel Farage.

China | More than a million people were moved to safety across eastern China by Sunday evening as powerful Typhoon Dolphin made landfall amid fears torrential rain would cause flooding and landslides.

Ukraine | Russia has banned voting against the war in September’s elections, after the supreme court upheld a suit brought by a small pro-Kremlin nationalist party, and stripped voters of their last option on the ballot: Yabloko, the country’s only remaining anti-war party.

While often lumped together, Rosebank and Jackdaw are two separate sites, hundreds of miles apart.

Rosebank is a proposed new oilfield 80 miles off the Shetland coast, containing 300 to 500m barrels of oil. It’s the UK’s last major undeveloped oil site. There is also gas at Rosebank, equating to roughly 1% of current demand.

Jackdaw is a gasfield 150 miles east of Aberdeen. If operational, it could probably produce approximately 40,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (bpd), which at peak is equivalent to 6% of the UK’s North Sea gas supply. Jackdaw could displace 2% of the UK’s imports of gas over its nine- to 12-year lifetime.

Under UK law, all oil and gas under the ground or seabed is owned by the state. It’s our collective asset. The government then dishes out licences for exploration and extraction of these fossil fuels to business. Often, these have complicated structures.

Shell holds the licence to extract at Jackdaw. Rosebank is majority owned by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Equinor (mostly owned by the Norwegian state). A minority stake of Rosebank is owned by UK-based Ithaca Energy, a subsidiary of the Israeli energy conglomerate Delek Group. Delek operates in Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories.

The case for drilling – and the holes in it

Unsurprisingly, the PR from fossil fuel companies on Rosebank and Jackdaw is full of optimism. It will bring down bills! Energy security! Jobs! These are all claims that have been repeatedly debunked.

The UK Energy Research Centre is scathing in its assessment: “Assertions that drilling the North Sea will provide energy resilience and affordability in the face of current fuel price shocks are a delusion.”

Jackdaw would create only 27 direct full-time jobs, according to its owner. Across both sites, there would be 880 jobs created during production, and 2,700 temporary construction roles. That’s no fix for structural decline. At least 70,000 jobs in the industry were lost in the decade to 2024, despite the Tories granting hundreds of licences. BP is now shutting down its North Sea operations. As our environment editor, Fiona Harvey tells me: “Whatever government does, jobs will decline. It’s unavoidable.”

Because, the UK’s gas and oil is running out. Even if extraction is minimised, supplies are depleting: 90% has already been drained dry. Experts point to this as proof that new drilling won’t bolster long-term energy security.

Who benefits from oil and gas?

Drill or not, our household energy prices will unlikely be affected. Anything extracted wouldn’t be funnelled to UK residents at a knock-down rate: oil and gas are sold by private companies on international markets, which set the price. The scale of output from UK production is negligible in this global context. As we’ve seen, it takes one unreliable actor in charge of the world’s largest military to send global prices spiralling.

Of course, there’s money to be made from tax – though these companies aren’t famed for coughing up when HMRC comes knocking. In 2024, Shell reported a negative UK tax figure of £12.5m while posting global post-tax profits of £18bn. In the same year, Equinor’s record was no better.

Even if North Sea tax revenues were collected and somehow funnelled directly into energy bill subsidies, the impact would be limited. For context, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Conservatives spent up to £80bn across two years shielding households and businesses from energy price hikes. Even by the oil and gas industry’s own estimates, the Rosebank and Jackdaw tax take would pale in comparison.

And given the scale of tax subsidies available, campaigners suggest Rosebank could actually cost taxpayers money. That means underwriting the very businesses who help to cause the climate crisis we’re experiencing.

This, of course, would be exacerbated by any fossil fuels extracted by Jackdaw and Rosebank. Burning just Rosebank’s oil and gas would produce about 250m tonnes of CO2 over its lifetime. As Areeba Hamid, co-executive director of Greenpeace UK, put it to me: “Sections of the media just keep repeating myths and lies. We are expecting a fifth summer heatwave, wild fires are burning the country, oil and gas companies are posting billions in profits, while the rightwing press and fossil fuel companies are pushing for Rosebank and Jackdaw approval. It’s pure cognitive dissonance.”

Under the Conservatives, Rosebank and Jackdaw were approved, but a court ruled these permits unlawful after a legal challenge from Greenpeace and Uplift. New approval needed to be sought – the results of which are impending.

Labour’s 2024 manifesto ruled out new licences for North Sea exploration, while stating existing ones would not be revoked. Insiders say a compromise might be struck, with only Jackdaw OK-ed. Gas is needed for home heating and electricity generation, though in what should be diminishing quantities, and its extraction is less carbon intensive than oil. “Allowing it to go ahead is far less harmful than Rosebank,” Fiona tells me. And Jackdaw is a tieback, so can be connected to existing infrastructure. “It could therefore come online quicker.”

Fahnbulleh is on holiday for the next couple of weeks. In the absence of answers, the briefing wars are in full swing. Reports that oil and gas execs are “near certain” that Rosebank and Jackdaw will get the go-ahead should be treated with caution, given their incentive to will this into fruition. Remember how Shabana Mahmood was definitely going to be Burnham’s chancellor?

For all his flip-floppery, Starmer was generally steadfast in his climate commitments while PM, even if rightwing backlash tempered his ambitions. Burnham had a strong environmental track record as Manchester mayor. But he’s an unknown entity in Downing Street. Until last month, Ed Miliband held the energy brief, driving the last government’s decarbonisation agenda. An experienced Westminster operator with decades of experience and press attacks, Miliband was resolute enough to stick with climate plans, however often he was heralded the “MOST DANGEROUS MAN IN BRITAIN”.

Fahnbulleh looks like continuity. She has Miliband’s backing and before entering parliament, she held top jobs at left-leaning thinktanks, including as CEO of the New Economics Foundation (NEF), which expressed opposition to further fossil fuel extraction. But she’s a parliamentary newbie. How she’ll respond to power and significant external pressure remains uncertain.

In an interview last weekend, she struck a vague but cautious note: “We’ve always been clear that oil and gas are part of the mix … We are doing the hard trade-offs to make sure that we are doing this transition in a way that still delivers affordability.”

“It’s going to be tough,” Hamid says, “but Miatta has to stick to her position. Otherwise, it’s a slippery slope: the pressure won’t stop at Rosebank and Jackdaw.”

European championships | Britain’s Amy Hunt sprinted to women’s 100m glory in 11.00sec in Birmingham, with Ewa Swoboda claiming silver and Delphine Nkansa a bronze.

Fifa | US president Donald Trump has warned Fifa would be making a “terrible mistake” if they get rid of Gianni Infantino as the head of world football’s governing body.

Football | A consortium including the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, is close to completing a deal for a 30% stake in Liverpool after months of talks with Fenway Sports Group.

“Firefighters raise alarm over surge in ‘unprecedented’ summer blazes”, is the Guardian’s front page today, while the i Paper writes “45 million people in the UK now living in drought”, the Mirror says “High & dry”, and Metro has “It never rains … but it pours”.

On politics, the Times has “Burnham demands plan to keep PC’s killers in jail” and the Express writes “Kemi: Rule out new taxes to prevent more hardship”. The Mail’s headline is “Day small boats crisis became a BIG boats crisis”, the Telegraph says “‘No limit’ to migrant mega dinghies”, and the Sun’s take is “Not-so-small boats crisis”. Finally, the FT splashes “Wall Street big names join Nvidia to build $500bn AI financing package”.

Why did Saudi Arabia just spend billions on a video games company?

Last week Saudi Arabia’s wealth fund and a group of investors spent $55bn (£41bn) on Electronic Arts, the video games company behind the Sims, Madden NFL and Battlefield. But why would such a powerful government take a risk with video games? As Keith Stuart and George Osborn tell Annie Kelly, it’s part of a pattern of superpowers and authoritarian regimes seeing games as handy propaganda tools.

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

At 60, Darren Miles is about to represent Great Britain at the world championships in slalom skateboarding – a sport he took up only in his late 50s. After a lifetime on a skateboard, he noticed his flexibility fading and his old tricks becoming increasingly difficult to do. Then, during lockdown, a stranger praised him for performing a simple 180 manoeuvre. It was a life-changing inflection point.

Rather than give up, Miles found a new challenge in slalom, racing downhill between cones and learning to move his body in a different way. Now, after years of skating for the joy of it, he is discovering what he can still achieve – and seeing how far he can push himself.

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: ‘Drops take seconds but change a life for ever’: the women saving India’s remotest people from polio
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Kamran Yousuf in Pulwama, Kashmir
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
Shameema and Tanzeela must trek for miles in summer heat to vaccinate children in Kashmir’s highlands as part of a vast national programme

B
efore sunrise, Shameema slips on her worn rubber sandals and checks the insulated box – the ice packs inside must maintain the crucial cold chain at between 2C and 8C (35.6-46.4F). She hoists the container on one shoulder and steps out into the dark.

Tanzeela follows with her own pack, after quickly retying the laces of her canvas shoes. Both women live in Pulwama, a district where summer temperatures climb to 37C. Their destination lies higher, out of the valley where asphalt turns to dirt track and then to a barely distinguishable footpath along the floor of the mountain pine forests.

Shameema, 45, has worked as a vaccinator for more than a decade, while Tanzeela, 28, joined the programme three years ago. They form part of India’s army of 2.5 million frontline health workers – the human machinery behind the world’s largest immunisation campaign.

Shameema estimates she has administered polio drops to more than 3,000 children during her years as a vaccinator. She remembers a boy in her village who limped with a deformed leg, the legacy of a polio infection before India had fully eradicated it. It is this memory that keeps her going.

“I saw that child struggle to walk to school,” Shameema says during a pause near a stream. “His mother held him on her back until he grew too heavy. [People in] these mountains need protection too – the children here deserve the same health as those in the cities.”

This morning, they are walking towards Namblan, a meadow ringed by pine trees where nearly 50 dhokas, the seasonal mud-and-stone homes of Gujjar and Bakarwal nomadic families, are scattered over the hillsides.

Even before the paved roads end, the electricity lines stop far below these settlements. Horses are the primary transport for the families who spend the summer months with their livestock in these highlands.

The women climb more than 12 miles (20km) with the heavy insulated cool boxes, which hold vials of the oral vaccines, ice packs and the thick paper registers that document the day.

Tanzeela has given polio drops to about 800 children since she joined the programme. She wears the same shoes she uses for farm work. The soles have worn thin, but they grip the rocky paths better than the sandals of some colleagues, she says. One fellow worker walks barefoot for parts of the trail.

“The payment is small and the paths are steep,” Tanzeela says. “I think about my own nephews when I climb. The drops take seconds, but they change a life for ever.”

Their compensation is 125 rupees a day – about £1 – from the state government for the two-day vaccination campaigns, which happen four to six times a year during the national immunisation drives that target all children under five.

India’s polio programme represents a triumph of planning, vigilance and human endurance. The country has been certified polio-free since 2014 – with the final confirmed case in January 2011 in West Bengal – largely thanks to a surveillance network of 60,000 health workers, who monitor 40,000 reporting sites for acute flaccid paralysis, the signature symptom of wild poliovirus.

The oral polio vaccine uses a live but weakened form of the virus developed by a Polish scientist, Albert Sabin, in the late 1950s. The two drops placed on a child’s tongue stimulate antibodies in the intestinal lining that destroy the virus before it can enter the bloodstream and attack the nervous system.

The same gut immunity reduces viral shedding in infected children, ending the chain of transmission in communities where clean water comes from streams and springs. The oral formula creates communal immunity, protecting whole clusters of children who share courtyards and water sources.

This biological shield proves especially vital in the disputed region of Indian-administered Kashmir, where 73% of the 14 million population live in rural areas, with hundreds of thousands of children under six living in far-flung villages and mountain settlements.

Sign up to Global Dispatch

Get a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development team

after newsletter promotion

Seasonal migration routes take the Gujjar and Bakarwal pastoral communities of about 1.2 million people far from clinics and hospitals during the summer. Reaching them requires coordination between state health departments, local panchayats (village councils) and the frontline workers who know the mountain trails.

The national immunisation effort targets 27 million children under five, and up to 1.7 million vaccinators can be deployed during a single day of a national immunisation drive. Those workers staff 750,000 booths, then fan out with mobile teams into forests, deserts and urban slums.

The scale of this operation dwarfs most military logistics exercises. Insulated boxes travel by foot, bicycle, boat and bus, but in regions such as Kashmir, the final leg of this journey is always down to women travelling on foot.

The dhokas sit miles apart, sometimes separated by ravines and streams that swell with melted snow. A mother might walk two hours to meet the vaccinators halfway, her baby strapped to her back. The workers record these encounters in their paper registers, marking the child’s name, age and the date of the dose.

Shameema and Tanzeela know the terrain and the communities, and time their ascent to reach the first dhokas as the families finish their morning prayers.

“The families welcome us with tea and bread,” Shameema says. “They know the value of these drops. Some remember the days prior to full eradication, when children in neighbouring villages fell ill.”

India’s greatest public health victory still depends on these health workers willing to make such critical journeys for little reward, dedicated to maintaining the country’s protection against the devastating disease.

By late afternoon, the final dhoka receives the vaccinators. A child opens their mouth, gets two drops on their tongue, another name goes on the register and the insulated box is a bit lighter as the women begin their descent down the same tracks they climbed hours earlier. It will be dark by the time they reach home.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/bdthem.title: BdThemes Supply Chain Attack Poisons JSON to Create Rogue WordPress Admins
https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/bdthem.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/bdthem.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have warned of a supply chain compromise impacting WordPress plugin vendor BdThemes, prompting the content management systems (CMS) platform's plugins team to temporarily disable their downloads.

"Unlike traditional software supply chain attacks, zero source code files were modified within the official WordPress.org repository," Wordfence researcher Paolo Tresso said. "Instead, threat actors poisoned a static remote JSON data stream fetched by an administrative promotional banner component."

The list of affected plugins is below -

Users visiting the listings for each of the aforementioned plugins on the WordPress plugins directory are displayed the message that they have been closed as of either August 7 or 8, 2026, and are not available for download pending a "full review."

The issue, per the WordPress security company, is rooted in an internal component called Biggopti that's shipped along with the plugins. The system is designed to pull promotional banners from their API server and render them in the WordPress admin dashboard by fetching relevant JSON files from a DigitalOcean Spaces bucket.

The library has been found vulnerable to a cross-site scripting (XSS) flaw in the JSON response parsing code via the "display_id" parameter from the Sigmative API due to insufficient client-side escaping. As a result, an attacker who can compromise the API can inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that get executed every time a user accesses those pages.

Because the script runs on every "wp-admin" page load, the injected code gets activated silently in the browser of any logged-in administrator. The vulnerability is rated 5.4 on the CVSS scoring system, indicating medium severity.

The change is said to have been first introduced on March 1, 2026, in "bdthemes-prime-slider-lite" before being applied to others. The attack is notable because it's entirely driven via the API and requires no plugin updates or files to be modified on disk.

"Rogue actors obtained write access to that bucket, replacing the legitimate JSON responses with crafted payloads to exploit that vulnerability," Wordfence said. "The XSS fires inside every logged-in admin's browser, silently, on every wp-admin page load. From there, the injected script creates rogue administrator accounts, uploads a web shell plugin, and phones home to a command-and-control (C2) server."

The main payload is delivered to the plugins using the "api-data-all-records" API endpoint. A JavaScript file named "w2.js," the payload performs the following actions -

An alternate payload ("x.js") found hosted on the plugin developer's infrastructure is served to victims using the "api-data-records" API endpoint. It's designed to generate "deterministic" administrative credentials that are mathematically derived from the victim website's hostname.

"This algorithm produces predictable usernames (bd_ followed by a 6-character base36 hash) and passwords (Bd@26! followed by the hash and x), pairing them with an @wordpress.org email address," Wordfence said. "Because the credentials are deterministic, threat actors do not need to store compromised site lists centrally, and incident responders can compute the exact username and password to hunt for on suspected domains."

The generated credentials are then leveraged to create a malicious administrator user, and the results of the attack are then exfiltrated back to the C2 server.

The C2 server used in the campaign is assessed to be related to two other software supply chain attacks involving Advanced Responsive Video Embedder (CVE-2026-18072) and OptinMonster in recent months. In the two cases, the WordPress plugins were backdoored to grant full administrative access to unauthenticated attackers either via a single hard-coded token or a hidden administrator account and a concealed plugin that were created and installed only when a site admin logged in.

This indicates that the end goal of the campaign is to establish covert administrative persistence and remote code execution across WordPress environments.

"The fact that malicious JSON records and the secondary x.js payload were uploaded directly into the vendor's own bucket indicates a severe upstream compromise of BdThemes' cloud storage credentials or internal infrastructure," Wordfence said.

The development comes days after WordPress addressed a pre-authentication reflected XSS flaw (CVE-2026-64638 aka XSS2Shell, CVSS score: 8.9) that can be exploited to achieve PHP code execution on the server when a logged-in administrator interacts with an attacker-controlled page.

https://www.space.com/stargazing/solar-e.author: Anthony Wood
https://www.space.com/stargazing/solar-e.text:
Here's how to watch the Aug. 12 total solar eclipse live online for free.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Aug. 12 total solar eclipse is just one day away! Here's how you can watch the entire show live online from the comfort of your home

Millions of people across Spain, Iceland and Greenland will see the moon completely hide the sun during the climactic phase of totality on Aug. 12. Countless more skywatchers across Europe will witness a deep partial solar eclipse, as the moon's curved silhouette covers a swathe of the sun's surface, while failing to cover it entirely.

Thankfully, we live in modern times. So there's no need for you to miss out on the solar spectacle if you find yourself outside of the path of totality, or if clouds conspire to ruin your view. Here's where to watch every phase of the 2026 total solar eclipse live online.

NASA will be hosting its own livestream of the event starting at 1:15 p.m. EDT on Aug. 12, featuring live views of totality from cameras spread throughout the path of the eclipse. The visuals will be accompanied by information on the science of the incredible event and details on how the agency is working to learn more about our sun.

The NASA coverage will be hosted here on Space.com, but can also be streamed through YouTube, Twitch, NASA+, Facebook, Instagram and Amazon Prime.

Time and Date's YouTube livestream kicks off at 12 p.m. EDT (1700 GMT) on Aug. 12, bringing live views of the eclipse from Leon in northwestern Spain and the island of Mallorca, along with live commentary from journalist Anne Buckle and astrophysicist Graham Jones.

An official European Space Agency (ESA) livestream will begin at 1:30 p.m. EDT (1730 GMT) on Aug. 12. The stream will feature expert commentary on the science of the eclipse along with live views from telescopes at the Observatorio Astrofisco de Javalambre, which is located close to the Spanish city of Teruel directly in the path of totality.

London's historic Royal Observatory Greenwich will host two simultaneous YouTube streams featuring live views of the partial solar eclipse starting at 1:15 p.m EDT (1815 GMT) on Aug. 12. The first livestream will be presented by Royal Observatory astronomer Greg Brown, who will discuss the science of the sun while providing expert commentary on the eclipse, while the second will offer a silent livestream, featuring visuals of the eclipse with no accompanying audio.

The Virtual Telescope Project livestream begins at 1:20 p.m. EDT (1720 GMT) on Aug. 12, bringing real-time views from the organization's robotic telescopes in Manciano, Italy, where a partial eclipse will be visible and from the path of totality in Spain. The Virtual Telescope Project will host a separate livestream a few hours later featuring views of the Perseid meteor shower peak, which occurs overnight on Aug. 12-13.

Be sure to check out our live blog for all of the latest news on the Aug. 12 total solar eclipse. We'll also have reports from Skywatching Writer Anthony Wood as he watches the eclipse unfold low in the horizon in central Spain, and also from Skywatching Editor Daisy Dobrijevic as she witnesses the spectacle during a voyage with HX Expeditions to Greenland!

Editor's Note: If you would like to share your eclipse photos with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.title: Five years on, Afghanistan's Taliban build foreign ties despite rights concerns
https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.text:
Five years after returning to power, Afghanistan's Taliban authorities have built working relationships with a slate of countries, despite a lack of formal recognition.

Russia remains the only nation to officially recognise the Taliban government, and many Western countries have demanded to see domestic reforms on human rights before considering doing the same.

READ MORE
Four years after the fall of Kabul, Taliban succeeds in near-total exclusion of women

But many states are nevertheless engaging with Afghanistan's leaders – including Britain and European Union members – driven largely by practical considerations.

Beyond the high walls of the foreign ministry in central Kabul stand embassies, rows of travel agencies, and an airline billboard promising: "We're all connected."

While few Afghans have the means to go abroad, their government "seeks relations with all countries", according to Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid.

The authorities' diplomatic strategy has involved hosting envoys in Kabul – and frequently publishing the photos – including those from China, Japan, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Britain.

"The countries of the region and our neighbouring states have particular importance, because our economic ties and interests are closely linked," Mujahid said last month.

This year officials from Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan gathered in Kabul, as landlocked Central Asia seeks trade routes through Afghanistan to access the sea beyond.

Erica Gaston, who was part of a team mandated by the UN Security Council to identify strategies for addressing the challenges in Afghanistan, said regional nations were "always more pragmatic" in dealing with the Taliban authorities.

"You had much more receptivity among regional member states to say, 'this is the reality that we have in our region and engagement is inevitable'," said Gaston, who heads the Conflict Prevention and Sustaining Peace Programme at the United Nations University Centre for Policy Research.

As well as coordinating on security, Taliban officials have been touting cross-border infrastructure projects to boost the country's fragile economy while Afghans are hit hard by international aid cuts.

Seeing potential in untapped natural resources, the government has expanded the mining sector, attracting firms from neighbouring China and elsewhere.

But foreign funds have been scarce as investors remain wary of the Taliban government's limited official recognition, with rumours that Iran would follow Russia falling flat.

Despite this, many Taliban officials travel abroad, including a delegation that flew to Brussels in June for talks with 15 EU nations about returning failed asylum-seekers to Afghanistan.

READ MORE
EU hosts Afghan Taliban for migration talks slammed by rights groups

A spokesperson for the bloc told AFP: "Those who have no legal right to stay in Europe must be returned."

Germany has been at the forefront, and deported an Afghan not convicted of any crime for the first time since the Taliban's 2021 return to power, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said in July.

For Gaston, the passage of time has meant "more and more countries accept that this is the reality, even if it's a reality that they don't like or condone".

But many have restricted further ties until they see changes in Afghanistan, particularly on rules that stop girls' education at age 12. Yet no policy shift is expected.

Accusing Supreme Leader Hibatullah Akhundzada and chief justice Abdul Hakim Haqqani of crimes against humanity over the persecution of women and girls, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for them last year.

READ MORE
ICC issues arrest warrants for Taliban leaders over persecution of Afghan women

Afghan women remain banned from a host of places including UN premises, a rule still in force despite a visit last month by the heads of two of its agencies.

A UN source in Kabul, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the subject, said the ability to exert influence on the authorities remains "highly issue-dependent".

"Some of these issues are kind of fairly impenetrable, but then you have other issues on which you are able to make progress," they told AFP, citing positive relations in some parts of Afghanistan on counternarcotics and humanitarian access.

Multiple nations stepped in this year when Afghanistan and Pakistan went to war, with China hosting talks after hundreds of civilians were killed.

Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Iran, Turkey, Uzbekistan and Malaysia were also engaged in trying to stop the fighting, according to the UN.

Pakistan's arch-foe India has strengthened its ties with the Taliban government, with New Delhi securing a sanctions waiver last year so that Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi could travel there.

In June, India's UN envoy suggested a rethink was necessary on sanctions – a travel ban, asset freeze and arms embargo – that target dozens of Taliban members.

"The political reality of Afghanistan has changed in the last five years, and the current UN sanctions regime must take that into account," said Harish Parvathaneni.

The diplomat stopped short of detailing what the new approach should be but, as the UN source told AFP, engagement with the Afghan government is "the current state of play".

"Everybody recognises the fact that, essentially, Afghanistan is fully controlled by the de facto (Taliban) authorities and, essentially, there are multiple issues on which the world, the region, has to deal with them," they said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/t.title: Trump signs order to reduce childhood vaccines and break up MMR shots
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/t.author: Elissa Fitzgerald
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Vaccines and Immunity

An executive order signed by Donald Trump calls for fewer childhood vaccinations. (Reuters: Kylie Cooper)

US President Donald Trump has issued an executive order calling for American children to be immunised against fewer diseases.

The vaccination schedule put forward by his administration recommends immunising children against 11 diseases, six fewer than what is currently recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Doctors say the order is based on pseudoscience, and will harm children.

Here's what to know about the order.

In short, the revised schedule called for by Mr Trump seeks to reduce the number of diseases and viruses American parents are advised to vaccinate their children against.

The six vaccinations the Trump administration would drop from the routine childhood immunisation schedule are:

The order advocates separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three separate, single-disease shots, despite scientific consensus that the combined shot is safe and effective.

It also directs the nation's health department to improve research on vaccines, which are already extensively studied.

The changes appear to be motivated by misinformation, public health experts say.

In signing the order, Mr Trump promoted his long-held but discredited theory that childhood shots should be spaced out into separate medical visits.

That's despite public health experts raising concerns that spacing out shots in such a way could lead to an increased risk that children become infected with a vaccine-preventable disease before returning for another visit.

The decline in childhood vaccination rates should alarm governments and the health sector, according to the peak body for doctors.

Childhood vaccines (and how and when to give them in combination) go through rigorous studies, and safety tracking continues for years as the shots are used.

Kush Desai, a spokesperson for the president, told the Associated Press the plan to develop single-disease vaccines would "give parents more options on timing and frequency for their children", and increase vaccine uptake.

Mr Trump also repeatedly suggested the number or timing of vaccines could play a role in rising rates of autism spectrum disorder.

But scientific consensus based on decades of studies firmly concludes that there is no link.

Secretary of Health Robert F Kennedy Jr, a longtime vaccine critic, also said American children get 72 shots under the current schedule.

But that number includes vaccines administered during pregnancy and individual components of combined shots that inoculate against several diseases.

The schedule currently recommended by the CDC is similar to those in Australia, the UK and Canada.

The Trump administration erroneously said American children receive 72 shots under the current immunisation schedule. (AP: Jacquelyn Martin)

The Royal Australian College of GPs Specific Interests Child and Young Person's Health chair, Tim Jones, said the announcement would increase harm to children.

He disputed Mr Trump's recommendations, which he told the ABC were informed by pseudoscience and would "muddy the waters on the safety and effectiveness of childhood immunisation".

Senator Bill Cassidy, the Republican chair of the Senate health committee, also slammed the executive order in a social media post, saying vaccines are safe and do not cause autism.

"I'm a doctor. This executive order is wrong," the Louisiana senator wrote.

"Breaking up vaccines will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe.

"The president does not have the expertise to make these changes."

It's not exactly clear.

In the US, vaccination recommendations are approved by the CDC director on the advice of a committee of experts.

US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr's anti-vaccination agenda is gaining ground, but resistance is coming from all sides.

Mr Trump ordered the Department of Health and Human Services in December to review how peer nations approach vaccine recommendations and consider revising US guidelines.

The department responded by cutting the number of vaccines it recommends for every child, but that move was later blocked in court.

That ruling was part of an ongoing lawsuit brought by medical organisations that argued the Trump administration did not follow standard legal procedure.

But Lawrence Gostin, a public health law expert at Georgetown University, said the Supreme Court's interpretation of Mr Trump's power may allow him to supersede CDC director Erica Schwartz if she does not agree to the new recommendations.

"This is clearly the first test for Dr Erica Schwartz," he said.

"The president is placing her in an untenable position."

In most US states, children must be immunised against certain diseases to attend day care or enrol in school.

That's not something the president has the authority to change.

In fact, the executive order only advises states with school vaccine mandates to consider updating their laws to reflect the administration's preferred schedule, according to a White House fact sheet.

The president does not have the power to scrap vaccine mandates in schools. (Reuters: Jim Young)

Doctors have raised concerns that the Trump administration's misinformation around vaccines could stoke vaccine hesitancy.

Mr Trump's executive order comes as students are returning to classrooms after their summer breaks.

Federal data shows US kindergarten vaccination rates have been dropping, with the share of children with exemptions rising to an all-time high in the 2024-25 school year.

The nation is contending with a measles outbreak so severe, experts say it could result in the US losing its measles elimination status.

Dr Jones said the outbreak has so far impacted more than 2,400 Americans, almost all of whom were unvaccinated, and caused three deaths.

Medical experts have linked the rise to slumping vaccination rates, a trend many attribute in part to vaccine scepticism espoused by Mr Kennedy.

Just this month, Mr Kennedy urged parents to vaccinate their children against measles, though he took no responsibility for the surge.

Mr Trump's executive order would needlessly contribute to increased fear and avoidance of vaccination both in the US and around the world, Dr Jones added.

"Without confidence in the lifesaving properties of widespread vaccination of children further children are going to die of preventable diseases — a travesty."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/m.author: James Tugwell
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The mother of a 17-year-old who allegedly watched on while the teenager was tortured has had her bid for bail rejected. (ABC North Queensland: Rachael Merritt)

The mother of a teenager with an intellectual disability who was allegedly tortured, zip tied, wrapped in plastic and dumped in bushland allegedly "laughed" as she watched her son being beaten, a court has heard.

Warning: This story contains details that some readers may find disturbing.

Eleven people have been charged, including six minors, after the 17-year-old was found by joggers in bushland at Pallarenda, Townsville, on July 18.

During a bail application for the boy's mother in Townsville Magistrate's Court on August 11, police prosecutor Lescha Lawson said the alleged assault started after the mother of the boy made "false allegations against the child" that he was a paedophile.

The court earlier heard that the teenager was allegedly assaulted at a residence, and when he crawled away to escape, the alleged assault continued in the street with a horse whip and metal rods.

One of the co-accused allegedly made a phone call which led to more people arriving at the scene before the teenager was wrapped in plastic, zip tied and transported in the boot of a car and dumped in bushland, the proceedings previously heard.

On Tuesday, Ms Lawson said the mother allegedly "actively participated in the assault and encouraged" others.

The victim required surgery after sustaining multiple injuries. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

She said the mother allegedly watched on while her son was bashed with metal rods, "joking" about the assault, "tormenting" him and saying, "he deserved it".

Ms Lawson said the teenager allegedly told police: "His mother laughed as she watched him be beaten by a number of people with metal bars."

The court heard the boy has undergone two surgeries for injuries that include a broken nose, two lacerations to the scalp, a spinal fracture, a tibia fracture and substantial bruising.

Defence lawyer Mikaila Ward told the court there was a "lack of particularisation" about which of the alleged offenders were involved and to what degree.

She said there was "no forensic evidence linking my client to the offence".

The victim was allegedly dumped in bushland near Pallarenda in Townsville. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

She said the boy's mother said she asked her son to leave and watched him walk out the door before she headed to bed.

Ms Ward said the co-accused all provided different versions of events to police and flagged potential issues with finding separate legal representation for all the co-accused.

"There are 11 charged so, finding representation could be an ongoing issue," she said.

Magistrate Steven Mosch said the alleged offending was "incomprehensible".

"It is reprehensible that the biological mother of the defendant was said to be present — if not actively engaged and encouraging others to do so," he said.

He read from documents tendered by the police which alleged methamphetamine had been smoked at the residence before the alleged assault.

The mother was refused bail and her case was adjourned to September.

Meanwhile, when another co-accused applied for bail in Townsville Magistrates Court on August 11, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Legal Service lawyer Matt Morton said his client "strongly" contested the allegations, and allegedly "put herself in the firing line to protect the child".

However, Ms Lawson argued the woman did not call police at the time of the alleged offending and had been identified by the 17-year-old as an alleged perpetrator.

The court heard the woman was not at the initial social gathering at the house but allegedly arrived at the house after an alleged phone call from another co-accused.

Police have charged 11 people over the incident. (ABC North Qld: James Tugwell)

Ms Lawson said the woman allegedly sent text messages to another co-accused saying: "I'm coming now, sorry. I was a little scared. I'm sorry. I thought jail time for me lol".

The woman allegedly texted another person later in the night saying she was "just dealing with this sick f**k".

Ms Lawson said those text messages suggested the woman was "more than a mere bystander".

Magistrate Mosch said the texts suggested "some proactive involvement".

He rejected that woman's bail application. Her case was also adjourned to September.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/i.title: Inside Donald Trump's 'Hunger Games'-style athletics contest
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/i.author: Fergus Gregg
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/i.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Student athletes at the Spire Institute and Academy in Ohio (Freedom 250 via Facebook)

120 students from the US, its territories and some tribal nations will compete against each other to win a $US125,000 ($177,449) college scholarship in the Patriot Games 2026.

Competitors were selected after submitting 5-minute video applications and personal essays.

At least one athlete has revealed they do not actually live in the state or territory they represent.

Anderson Reid, representing Puerto Rico, sprinted onto a military-style bootcamp course to the cheers of supporting families and friends.

Thrift Shop by Macklemore & Ryan Lewis played as he crawled, sprinted and carried jerry cans, vying to top the times of 119 other teenagers between the ages of 14 and 17 for a chance to win a university scholarship.

Anderson Reid says contestants did not have to currently live in the state or territory they represented, but did not clarify what ties he had to Puerto Rico. (Instagram: andersonreid88)

The Patriot Games 2026 were announced in December 2025 by US President Donald Trump, who billed it as "an unprecedented four-day athletic event featuring the greatest high school athletes".

"One young man and one young women from each state and territory, but I promise there will be no men playing in women's sports," he said.

One hundred and twenty competitors made it to Ohio to compete in the three-day-long athletic competition, commemorating the United States 250th anniversary.

The ABC has identified participants from Puerto Rico, Guam, the Shawnee Tribe and the US Virgin Islands, but not from American Samoa or other Native American groups.

However, there has been speculation some athletes might not live in the state or territory they represent.

Reid is representing Puerto Rico, but does not appear to live there, with one Instagram commenter asking, "Isn't he from Texas?"

Videos on Reid's YouTube channel show clips from Daikin Park stadium in Houston, Texas.

Responding to another comment on Instagram, Reid said "[Contestants] don't have to be currently living in the state or territory they are representing".

"They do have to have some sort of association with it such as living there or having social [family] ties to it," Reid said.

Little is known about the Freedom 250 Patriot Games selection committee, which chose the athletes based on video applications and personal essays. (AP: Nate Manley)

The idea behind the Patriot Games drew immediate comparison to The Hunger Games, a series of books by Suzanne Collins, which were later adapted into a multi-billion-dollar film franchise.

Patriot Games organisers Freedom250 said the event would "bring together outstanding young Americans from across the nation to compete, inspire, and showcase the values that have shaped the United States for nearly 250 years".

It's a unique qualification process, as unlike the Junior Olympics or national sports competitions, the pre-selection method did not involve qualifying rounds, but rather a video application process.

Chris Brennan is representing North Carolina at the Patriot Games, and has been sharing each step of the experience on his social media.

In an interview with Trump-aligned influencer Adam Francisco Brennan said he stumbled across the Patriot Games online.

US President Donald Trump promoted the event as a showcase of the nation's best student athletes. (Supplied: X/Freedom250)

"I was just on Instagram one day, scrolling, scrolling and I saw an advertisement and I was like, 'Hey, I heard Trump talking about that,'" Mr Brennan said.

"I clicked, submitted, I made a quick 5-minute video application.

"Honestly I think it was a little bit of luck and a little bit of my personality."

Chris Brennan posts conservative content on Instagram and, in an interview, said women couldn't compete with men athletically.  (Instagram: notchris71)

Brennan then made it into the next round, and was asked to write an essay and answer "personal questions".

He later interviewed several of his fellow competitors in Baltimore, and they described stumbling on the Patriot Games like he did.

"I think it was on TikTok and I did it as a joke with my friend," Owen Carter of South Carolina said.

"I didn't think I'd get on."

The youth from North Carolina also runs a social media page called Club America, which features Christian content and Charlie Kirk quotes.

Some competitors said they prepared for the Patriot Games with cardio and pre-existing fitness routines.

Campbell Remus of Minnesota also participates in "Ninja Warrior" contests and other athletic competitions. (AP: Nate Manley)

Campbell Remus from Minnesota said she trains year round for track, cross country and the "Ninja Warrior" obstacle and fitness challenge, while Mr Carter said he went for "a lot of runs" despite not having much time to prepare.

On August 9 the athletes completed the presidential physical fitness test, a former national benchmark of core, upper body and cardio fitness retired in 2013. They also competed in team games of dodgeball and kick ball.

Joshua Chechile of Vermont participated in the 55-metre hurdles during day one of the Patriot Games, one of many different athletic events. (AP: Nate Manley)

The next day, competitors completed a multi-sport skill challenge called the varsity circuit, along with a military style bootcamp obstacle course.

The games will conclude at 7pm on August 11, local time, with semi-finals, finals and team competitions like tug of war.

In her application video, incoming freshman Sophie Skidmore of West Virginia appeared with her neck adorned in sports medals.

"I'm always looking for my next challenge," she said.

"As for the scholarship it would help me follow my dreams without financial burden."

Skidmore was eliminated in day two of the qualifiers.

The occasion was complicated by severe storms that gathered near Washington, forcing event organisers to order an earlier evacuation.

The top male and female athlete will each receive a $US125,000  university scholarship, but according to a report by the Education Data Initiative, the average cost of attending an out-of-state, public school in the US is more than $US182,000.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Eleven-time WSL champion Kelly Slater turned back the clock in Tahiti, producing a huge heat to beat Gabriel Medina. (Getty Images: World Surf League/Matt Dunbar)

Surfing legend Kelly Slater has turned the clock back at the Tahiti Pro, producing a brilliant performance to beat three-time world champion Gabriel Medina.

The 54-year-old Slater, who retired from full-time competition in 2024, survived having his board snapped in heavy swell to beat Medina with a score of 19.06 out of 20.

Slater is into the third round where he will face Australian defending champion Jack Robinson, who beat compatriot Callum Robson.

Kelly Slater has advanced to the third round of the Tahiti Pro after the 54-year-old American overcame Brazil's Gabriel Medina and ​some heavy wipeouts at the 2024 Paris Olympics venue of Teahupo'o.

Surfing legend Kelly Slater holds back tears as his career effectively ends at Western Australia's Margaret River Pro, although the 11-time world champion is hoping for one last wildcard in Fiji.

Slater, who recently underwent hip surgery, retired from full-time competition in 2024 and welcomed a third child earlier this year ​but showed he had ‌lost none of his competitive edge against three-times world champion Medina.

In dangerous, challenging waves, Slater got smashed on his first attempt and was hit even harder on ‌his second wave, breaking his board in two.

But the Floridian recovered ⁠and threaded a long, deep tube that scored a 9.73 ‌out of 10 to take ​the lead.

He ‌then backed it up with another excellent score to advance over Medina, who beat Slater in an epic final at the same venue in 2014.

"I don't know if I'll ever have another heat with him, and ​he ‌got me last time," said Slater, who dominated the first day of competition.

He said he had been motivated by criticism of the ⁠decision to award him a wildcard ‌to compete.

ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"You see those comments, ‌a lot of people doubting me or saying [the opportunity] should have gone to ‌a local wildcard," he said. "Even after all this time, I have something to prove."

Slater finished with an excellent two-wave ‌total ​of 19.06 out of ⁠20 to set up a third-round meeting with reigning champion Jack Robinson of Australia, who was pushed hard by countryman Callum Robson in round two.

California's Griffin Colapinto, who was born six years after ⁠Slater won the first of his 11 world titles, was the only man to better Slater's ‌performance in ‌the second round, racking up a perfect 10-point ride ​on his way to a season-high heat total of 19.6 out of 20.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Takaichi to forgo foreign trips this summer following Kumamoto quake
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will refrain from making overseas trips this summer, with the exception of a possible trip to New York for a U.N. General Assembly session in late September, informed sources said Monday.

Takaichi will stay at home to prioritize the response to a powerful earthquake that struck Kumamoto Prefecture last month.

Prime ministers often travel abroad from July to September, a period that falls in-between Diet sessions.

Among recent former prime ministers, Fumio Kishida visited the United States and Germany in July 2024 and South Korea that September, and Shigeru Ishiba, Takaichi’s immediate predecessor, traveled to South Korea in September 2025.

This year, a special session of parliament was convened in place of the ordinary session because an election for the Lower House was held in February. The special session ran until July 25, including an eight-day extension.

The Kumamoto earthquake struck three days later, so Takaichi, who took office last October, will not travel abroad this summer, multiple government officials said.

At Monday’s meeting of the government’s disaster response headquarters, the prime minister instructed her staff to proactively move ahead with necessary relief measures.

Apart from the quake response, the Takaichi administration plans to adopt a tax system reform package next month that would pave the way for realizing her goal of lowering the consumption tax rate on food.

In addition, Takaichi is considering reshuffling her Cabinet and the leadership team of her ruling Liberal Democratic Party in September.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.summary: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will not travel abroad this summer, sources say. She will stay at home to prioritize the response to a powerful earthquake that struck Kumamoto Prefecture last month. The Kumamoto earthquake struck three days later, so Takaich will not go abroad this year.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: What Japan’s language rules for permanent residency should look like
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: Midori Inagaki
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
Early this month, the Immigration Services Agency proposed a nationwide guideline concerning Japanese language and daily life orientation for foreign residents, suggesting that these items could become requirements for permanent residency.

For decades, Japan has left migrant language education to municipalities, volunteers, private schools — or migrants themselves. The government’s willingness to finally assume public responsibility is a welcome development. A state-funded system could mark a shift from treating foreign residents as temporary labor to recognizing them as members of Japanese society.

However, if this program becomes a prerequisite for permanent residency, its design will determine whether it supports integration or simply erects another barrier.

The main question is how Japanese language ability will be assessed. Japan must avoid turning the Japanese Language Proficiency Test into a de facto national filter.

The JLPT measures vocabulary, grammar, reading and listening. It does not assess speaking, writing or interaction. Yet these are the skills people rely on in workplaces, clinics, schools and local communities. Its heavy emphasis on literacy also creates unequal burdens for applicants from nonkanji backgrounds or those with limited formal education.

Japanese is used differently depending on occupation and setting. Care workers supporting the elderly rely on sustained daily conversation and construction workers need clear on-site communication for safety. In these fields, functional Japanese is indispensable.

But not all residents work in Japanese dominant settings. Tech professionals at multinational firms, researchers in international programs or some faculty at universities may conduct most of their work in English. Parents interacting with schools face yet another set of linguistic demands.

Language proficiency cannot be separated from occupation, living environment or societal roles.

Applicants for permanent residency should not be expected to speak like native speakers or decipher specialized kanji. What matters is whether they can obtain essential information, explain a problem and request clarification or interpretation when needed. Using plain Japanese, translation tools or support services is part of real communicative competence.

The JLPT can remain an option, but it should not be the only one. Japan should accept diverse forms of evidence of language proficiency such as course records, interviews, practical tasks, portfolios and proof of communication at work. Alternatives must be available for older applicants, people with disabilities and those with limited access to formal schooling.

Japan’s own Framework of Reference for Japanese Language Education defines proficiency by what a person can do with the language. That principle should guide any residency requirement. Otherwise, Japanese risks becoming a tool of exclusion rather than participation.

Providing clear information about taxes, pension, health care, disaster preparedness and public services is valuable. Many residents struggle with administrative procedures simply because information is inaccessible, and those misunderstandings can later jeopardize their visa status.

But the program must not become a test of whether newcomers have absorbed “Japanese values” or conformed to implicit cultural expectations. Instead, it should focus on civil rights and civic responsibilities. For sure, participants should learn how to pay taxes and sort the trash, but they must also know where to seek help if they face labor exploitation, discrimination or domestic violence. They need access to legal, medical and social support. Integration is not a one-way process. If Japan expects foreign residents to adapt, public institutions should also adapt to accommodate linguistic and cultural diversity.

Cost will determine whether the program becomes a bridge or a barrier. If the government makes language and daily life education mandatory for permanent residency, it must guarantee free access nationwide.

Germany and Denmark both link language proficiency to long-term or permanent residence while providing publicly supported language education. Their systems are not without its flaws, but they reflect an important principle: If a government makes language learning a condition of secure residence, it must also ensure that people have a realistic and affordable opportunity to meet that condition.

Japan must avoid creating a system in which permanent residency is effectively available only to those who can afford private tuition. Instruction, materials and assessments should be publicly funded. Evening, weekend and online options must be available for shift workers, parents and rural residents. And the government cannot rely, once again, on unpaid volunteers. A national requirement demands qualified professionals, including certified Japanese language teachers, working under fair conditions.

Expecting long-term residents to learn Japanese and understand public institutions is reasonable. But permanent residency is meant to stabilize the lives of people who have already built families, careers and community ties in Japan.

Those who have lived and contributed here for years should not be excluded by a rigid, one-size-fits-all test. The new program should offer a genuine pathway to participation, supported by accessible education and fair evaluation. Whether language becomes a bridge or a barrier will depend on how Japan chooses to design this system.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.summary: Immigration Services Agency proposes new guidelines for Japanese language and daily life orientation for foreign residents. The JLPT measures vocabulary, grammar, reading and listening, but it does not assess speaking, writing or interaction. Japan must avoid turning the Japanese Language Proficiency Test into a de facto national filter, says author.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Fireworks event in Shiga abruptly canceled
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
OTSU, SHIGA PREF. – The organizers of a large fireworks festival planned for Aug. 22 in three cities in Shiga Prefecture have announced that the even has been cancelled.

According to local fire authorities, fireworks event organizers must apply to use explosives about a month in advance for such events.

But the executive committee of the canceled event did not submit an application to or consult with authorities by the deadline.

For the event, the organizers had been planning to launch a total of more than 10,000 fireworks in the cities of Nagahama, Hikone and Takashima, all located along the coast of Lake Biwa, the largest lake in Japan.

The three cities and the Shiga prefectural government said that an official from the organizing committee had visited them between last December and this April with a plan to hold a fireworks festival, but they were not given explanations about specifics such as venues.

The organizers billed the fireworks festival as an event with reserved seating only and sold tickets ranging from ¥7,000 to ¥19,000 online. They said that purchasers would receive an email about the specific locations approximately a week before the event.

On Sunday, however, the executive committee announced on its official website that it had “determined that it would be difficult to make the necessary preparations and management system by the date of the event.”

The committee said that it is confirming and sorting out its next moves while consulting with legal experts, and urged ticket buyers and vendors who had planned to take part in the event to check its website and social media for updates.

After receiving multiple inquiries about whether the festival would actually be held, the Nagahama, Hikone and Takashima city governments released a statement online Thursday explaining that they were not involved in the event.

The committee told Jiji Press in an email that it would officially provide necessary information after clearing up issues such as details on coordination with related organizations and various procedures. It declined to provide contact information for individuals associated with the event.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.summary: Organizers had planned to launch 10,000 fireworks in three cities in Shiga Prefecture. Organizers did not submit application to or consult with authorities by deadline. Organizer says it will officially provide necessary information after clearing up issues.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.title: Japan shares data on foreign nationals facing deportation with local governments
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
The Immigration Services Agency has started sharing personal information on foreign nationals subject to deportation proceedings with local governments, as part of a review of policies concerning foreign nationals pursued by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

Previously, such information was shared only when there was consent from affected individuals, sometimes leaving local governments unsure of the whereabouts of foreign nationals subject to deportation proceedings.

The latest move is aimed at promoting appropriate responses through cooperation between the central and local governments.

In July, the agency informed local governments of the number, names, addresses, nationalities and dates of birth of foreign nationals who were subject to deportation proceedings and living outside immigration facilities as of the end of June.

Going forward, the agency plans to provide monthly updates on such foreign nationals’ relocations or deportations to their home countries. Information will also be made available upon request from local governments.

Under the immigration control law, foreign nationals who overstay their authorized periods of stay or commit certain crimes are subject to deportation.

In such cases, foreign nationals are not immediately deported, however. They are allowed to remain in Japan while investigations into violations and hearings are conducted.

In addition to those staying at immigration facilities, some individuals subject to deportation procedures may be granted provisional release due to health or humanitarian issues. Others may be placed under a supervision system, which allows them to live outside immigration facilities under the oversight of a supervisor, such as a relative or friend.

Those on provisional release or under the supervision system are subject to certain restrictions on their residences and movements.

Meanwhile, local governments are often left in the dark because those subject to deportation proceedings lose their residence records, and some people’s whereabouts become unknown. This has created challenges in providing public services, such as education and healthcare.

According to the agency, 18,442 foreign nationals were subjected to deportation procedures in 2025. As of the end of last year, 2,429 individuals were on provisional release and 1,546 were under supervisory measures.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.summary: Immigration Services Agency has started sharing personal information on foreign nationals subject to deportation proceedings with local governments. Previously, such information was shared only when there was consent from affected individuals. The agency plans to provide monthly updates on such foreign nationals’ relocations or deportations to their home countries.

https://www.scmp.com/business/banking-fi.title: Shein set to take orders for Hong Kong IPO next week, eyeing US$35b valuation: sources
https://www.scmp.com/business/banking-fi.author: Zoe SL Chan
https://www.scmp.com/business/banking-fi.text:
Singapore-based company, which was founded in China, aims to raise as much as US$2.8 billion and began gauging investor demand last week

The Singapore-headquartered company, which was founded in China, aims to raise as much as US$2.8 billion and began gauging investor demand last week, said sources who asked not to be identified while discussing confidential information.

The timing and size of the deal could still change, but the company aimed to complete the process by the end of the month, a source said.

A source said that the valuation “won’t be less than US$30 billion, as the company works hard to achieve its target of US$35 billion”.

Either outcome would represent a steep drop from its peak expected valuation of US$100 billion in 2022 and a decline from earlier private targets of US$40 billion to US$50 billion.

Shein previously sought to go public in New York or London, according to earlier reports by the South China Morning Post and other media outlets. However, those ambitions were derailed by intense regulatory scrutiny in the US and Europe over the company’s supply chain practices and tax structures.

The company generated revenues of more than US$40 billion in 2025, with a net profit of nearly US$2 billion. But the company said in its listing prospectus that a new European Union rule charging extra fees on low-value imports could dampen its growth this year.

Last month, the EU began collecting €3 (US$3.40) for each parcel valued below €150 sent from outside the bloc, affecting fast-growing online shopping platforms like Shein and Temu. A similar rule was imposed by the US last year on imported goods valued at US$800 or less.

A representative for Shein did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The joint sponsors leading Shein’s Hong Kong IPO are Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan. Haitong International and UBS have also been named as overall coordinators.
