https://fortune.com/2026/08/11/arianna-h.title: Arianna Huffington says even high-flying CEOs are unhappy and feel stuck in their multimillion-dollar jobs: ‘It’s a trap’
https://fortune.com/2026/08/11/arianna-h.author: Orianna Rosa Royle
https://fortune.com/2026/08/11/arianna-h.text:
It’s every worker’s dream: You work hard and climb the ladder until eventually you’re rewarded with an executive title and cushy salary to go with it. But according to Huffington Post founder Arianna Huffington, the reality isn’t quite as glamorous as it looks—and plenty of CEOs, she says, are desperate to quit, despite seemingly having it all.

“Success can be a trap,” Huffington told Fortune, adding that once you’ve dedicated years of your life to honing your craft and gaining recognition, it can feel impossible to leave it all behind and start something new. Even if you’re miserable where you’re at.

“It’s a trap because a lot of very successful people have a hard time leaving,” she explained. “I have CEO friends who’ve stopped loving their jobs, but they’re afraid to leave.”

And it’s not just the huge mortgages, private school fees and luxury first-class vacations they’ve become accustomed to bankrolling with their multi-million dollar pay packages keeping them stuck.

“The financial trap is much easier to see, while the identity trap is less tangible but no less real,” Huffington added. “They’re so identified with the CEO role, or the anchor of an evening show, or whatever big job comes with a lot of recognition—it’s become their identity.”

Huffington spent a grueling 11 years building Huffington Post into one of the biggest names in digital media, growing its newsroom to more than 850 journalists and becoming the first digital-native outlet to win a Pulitzer Prize. She graced the covers of magazines, made Time’s list of most influential people and was a regular at the likes of Davos.

By any measure, she’d made it. Walking away from that to start over would have made no sense to many people—and yet that’s exactly what she did in 2016 to found her new wellness venture, Thrive Global.

“There are no guarantees anytime you start a new company,” the 76-year-old multimillionaire said. “But I was ready to throw myself into health, and if I hadn’t done it, I would have kind of betrayed myself.”

At the time, when she was weighing up whether to hold onto what she had built or walk away, Huffington said that her mother’s voice was in her head.

“She brought me up not to be afraid of failing,” she said, adding that women in particular are hit harder by perfectionism and therefore more likely to remain stuck and not take that leap of faith in case it doesn’t work out. “My mother used to say failure is not the opposite of success, it’s a stepping stone to success.”

It’s why, for Huffington, how a role makes you feel matters more than what it looks like from the outside.

“I’ve always believed that there is no job that defines us, no success that defines us,” she added. “If we are able to follow our heart, it means we can keep growing and evolving.”

Huffington’s far from the first person to admit that reaching the top can leave you feeling empty rather than fulfilled. After cofounding Wingstop UK and selling a majority stake for £400 million (around $540 million), Tom Grogan should have been ecstatic. Instead, he felt hollow.

“For seven years, your whole mind is occupied on making a success of this business,” Grogan told Fortune.  “It’s all you think about. And then when you get there, it’s just a bit surreal. It’s like, Okay, it’s done now. Now what? And money doesn’t necessarily fill that void either.”

Growing up, Brian Chesky, the cofounder and CEO of Airbnb, said he “desperately wanted to be successful” because he thought it would bring him adoration. Plus, having social worker parents who were by no standards rich, he also thought a large sum of money could “solve every problem.” But actually, he said the company’s blockbuster 2020 IPO—despite making him a billionaire—was “one of the saddest periods” of his life.

Loom cofounder Vinay Hiremath hit a similar wall after selling his company to Atlassian for $975 million. In a blog post candidly titled “I am rich and have no idea what to do with my life,” he described the identity collapse that followed the company’s rapid rise and eventual sale. “I lost myself,” he wrote, adding that the windfall left him with “infinite freedom” but no idea what to do with it.

It’s why, despite having no current plans to step down, TIAA’s CEO Thasunda Duckett is already thinking about who she is outside of her job.

“I rent my title. I own my character,” Duckett recently told Fortune, noting that a job title is never permanent—and therefore shouldn’t be mistaken for who you actually are. “I own my intellectual curiosity. I own my grit. I own my perseverance. I own my compass.”

https://fortune.com/2026/08/11/carescout.title: CareScout CEO: the hidden economic cost of an aging baby Boomer generation
https://fortune.com/2026/08/11/carescout.author: Samir Shah
https://fortune.com/2026/08/11/carescout.text:
America is getting older. That much is obvious.

What’s less obvious—and far more consequential—is that we have failed to build the infrastructure families need to navigate aging. As a result, growing old in America is becoming an invisible tax, one paid not just in dollars, but in time, productivity, opportunity and financial security.

The burden touches nearly every family differently. But one thing is becoming increasingly clear: those with the fewest resources often bear the greatest cost.

Recent reporting from The Washington Post highlighted a troubling reality. As the Baby Boomer generation ages, the financial burden of caregiving widens wealth disparities. Families with greater financial resources are often better positioned to purchase care, access expert guidance and preserve assets for future generations. Families with fewer resources are far more likely to shoulder the burden themselves, often sacrificing income, career progression and retirement savings in the process.

That observation is important. But it points to an even larger problem.

For too long, we’ve treated aging as a private family challenge—or simply as a healthcare issue. It is neither.

Aging has become a consumer issue and an economic one.

America has built sophisticated systems to help people buy homes, save for retirement, finance education and invest for the future. Yet when a parent develops dementia, can no longer live independently or suddenly needs care, millions of families are forced to navigate one of life’s most complex transitions largely on their own.

As CareScout’s Cost of Care data show, the median cost of assisted living now exceeds $74,000 annually, while a private room in a nursing home approaches $130,000 a year. Specialized settings such as memory care reach even higher. Understanding those costs is difficult enough. Figuring out where to turn, what options exist and how to coordinate care is often even harder.

Families find themselves piecing together healthcare providers, home care agencies, senior living communities, legal advice, insurance benefits, financing options and family responsibilities while under enormous emotional pressure. They aren’t failing. They’re being asked to navigate a fragmented system that was never designed to guide them through one of the most important chapters of life.

No American family should have to invent its own aging strategy in the middle of a crisis.

The consequences extend well beyond individual households.

The visible costs of aging are easy to identify: paying for home care, assisted living, transportation, medications or home modifications.

The invisible costs are often much larger.

Millions of family caregivers reduce work hours, delay promotions, leave the workforce entirely or sacrifice retirement savings to care for aging parents. Employers absorb lost productivity and increased absenteeism. Governments face mounting pressure on healthcare and social programs. Communities struggle to meet growing demand for services.

These costs ripple throughout the economy.

They also help explain why the financial burden of aging falls disproportionately on lower-wealth households. Families with financial means can often purchase expertise, coordination and time. Families without those resources frequently provide those things themselves, paying with their income, careers and future financial security instead.

The widening wealth gap is therefore not simply the problem. It is one of the clearest symptoms of a much larger structural failure.

America has not built the infrastructure required for an aging society.

As longevity increases and millions more Americans enter their later years, that infrastructure gap will become increasingly expensive—not just for families, but for employers, governments and the broader economy.

Building that infrastructure will require action across sectors. Public policy matters. Private innovation matters. Employers have a role. Healthcare organizations have a role. Financial institutions have a role. Entrepreneurs have a role.

Most importantly, we must stop thinking about aging as someone else’s problem.

Every American is a future consumer of the systems we build—or fail to build.

The generations that helped build this country deserve more than a fragmented maze of decisions during the final chapters of their lives. And future generations deserve better than inheriting the same broken system.

The real question isn’t whether America can afford to build better infrastructure for aging.

It’s whether we can afford not to.

Samir Shah leads CareScout’s efforts to expand access to high-quality care and drive new solutions to the long-term care crisis. He has more than 20 years of experience spanning financial services, strategy, and digital transformation, including senior roles at JPMorgan Chase, McKinsey, and Goldman Sachs.

https://fortune.com/2026/08/11/record-be.title: Record beef prices are minting fortunes for ranchers—but straining the American farmers who fatten their cattle
https://fortune.com/2026/08/11/record-be.author: Sasha Rogelberg
https://fortune.com/2026/08/11/record-be.text:
Last week, Tyson Foods CEO Donnie King offered investors a sobering report on beef prices: “Beef hasn’t performed the way we expected,” King said during an earnings presentation, “and we’re not pretending otherwise.”

These soaring prices have not just left meatpacking giants like Tyson looking for answers—they’ve impacted the entire cattle industry. And while some sectors like feedlot farmers are beginning to reel from dwindling inventories, others like ranchers are being minted as the major winners.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics latest consumer price index data indicates beef prices have soared 11.8% in the last year, including 1.2% on a monthly basis in June. Ground beef prices are up 12.4% year-over-year, and beef roast prices have increased even higher, up 13.8% from a year ago. While a natural cattle cycle shifts inventories roughly every decade, leading to ebbs and flows in beef prices, the current herd sizes are the smallest they’ve been since 1951 as a result of severe droughts drying up pastures, as well as the spread of flesh-eating screwworms limiting cattle imports from Mexico.

The tight supply means those at the foundation of the cattle industry are seeing profits grow. Cow-calf ranchers, who raise permanent herds of mother calves to sell for beef, produce the supply of cows for the entire industry and have been able to hike prices.

Prices for feeder calves are expected to increase from $437.44 per hundredweight today to up to $467 per hundredweight in 2027’s second quarter, according to David Anderson, a Texas A&M professor of agricultural economics.

“At that primary level, cow-calf production, they are making more money,” Derrell Peel, a professor of agribusiness specializing in livestock at Oklahoma State University, told Fortune. “They’re making record returns, by and large.”

Most other parts of the industry, however, are under greater pressure, having to buy more expensive cattle while facing slimming margins, including rising input costs for fertilizers, chemicals, and equipment as a result of tariffs, Peel explained. Most economists expect those costs to remain elevated or continue to increase.

“Pretty much everybody above [cow-calf producers] is a margin operation, and most of those margins are under some sort of adverse pressure,” Peel said. “The farther we go with this, the squeeze on cattle numbers is getting tighter.”

Among those sectors are feedlot farmers, who ration grain to cattle in the last few months of their lives to have the animals quickly gain weight before they are processed. For a while, the feedlot sector could maintain profitability because there’s about a six-month time lag between when farmers buy the calves and when they are again sold to be processed, Peel noted. Feedlots have been able to stay full by keeping turnover down, even as their own incoming supply of cattle also slows.

But that’s likely to change as the shortage continues. According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Cattle on Feed report for June, while the number of cattle and calves on feed increased year-over-year for the month, there’s been a year-over-year decrease in both cattle being placed on feed and fed cattle being marketed.

“Feedlots are having trouble,” Peel said. “They’re going to have more and more trouble in the coming months of maintaining that volume and keeping their feedlots full.”

Other parts of the industry are also struggling, including meatpackers like Tyson Foods. Last week, the Arkansas-based food producer saw a $138 million operating loss on its beef segment, and sales volumes in the segment dropped 15.9%, while prices rose 12.1%.

The bifurcated fortunes of the cow-calf ranchers and the feedlot farmers is reflective of the challenges the cattle industry faces today, Peel said, but it’s not necessarily unique to this shortage. The boom-bust cycle of herd inventory is a natural part of the industry. When herd inventories are high, cow-calf ranchers struggle with a glut of cattle to sell; meanwhile, feedlots, meatpackers, and other parts of the industry enjoy greater profits.

“It’s oftentimes the case that when one sector is doing well, another part of the industry is struggling,” Peel said. “Over time, they all tend to average out.”

What makes this cattle cycle different is that it’s been exaggerated by external factors, primarily the droughts, Peel said. Rebuilding herd inventories takes some time to begin with, and is even more challenging when there’s a deeper shortage, as there’s an even smaller population of females.

The beef industry may be familiar with the up-and-down dynamics of the cattle cycle, but the prolonged shortage means the sectors struggling will have to flounder a little longer than what is typical.

“It’s been a slower than usual process,” Peel said. “It could have started two years ago…but it hasn’t for various reasons, and so we’re still kind of waiting for that to happen. It’s going to prolong this period of tight supplies and the margin structure that we have today.”

https://fortune.com/2026/08/11/data-cent.title: AI’s biggest buildout is here. These stocks offer a way to invest in the data center boom
https://fortune.com/2026/08/11/data-cent.author: Camila Grigera Naón
https://fortune.com/2026/08/11/data-cent.text: The AI revolution is leading to a massive boom in data centers. Major cloud service providers like Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon are engaged in a frenzied bid to keep up with the demand for AI services, and are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to compete. The money taps remain turned on full-blast even in the face of a choppy stock market and persistent fears over whether AI stocks are in a bubble. “Hyperscalers are going to spend maybe between $750 and $800 billion [a year]. Some forecasts even have it up to a trillion, and that would put it at 2.5 to 3% of U.S. GDP, which is just extraordinary for a capital market,” John Mowrey, chief investment officer at NFJ Investment Group, said. A considerable portion of this spending will go to data centers, which offer a pick-and-shovels options for investors looking to ride the AI wave. Fortune has identified four distinct entry points into the data center economy: semiconductor chips, real estate, energy, and cooling. Experts weighed in on which stocks stand out in each category. The AI data center buildout requires several components to work, but none of it matters without a brain, and that’s exactly what semiconductors provide. Even as companies focus on constructing the actual buildings to house these facilities, the chips that power them can’t be produced fast enough. Demand for these specialized processors that run AI workloads has outpaced the industry’s ability to manufacture them, making semiconductors one of the most acute bottlenecks in the entire buildout, according to Craig Ellis, research director and senior semiconductor analyst at B. Riley Securities. For investors, that shortage isn’t necessarily bad news. “We’re at a point where undersupply is so severe that there needs to be a multi-year period of unusually strong capex growth in front of us, and that capex growth is something that is very investable because it has the potential to continue to lift expectations for revenues and earnings,” Ellis said. To capture that opportunity, he recommends investors shift their attention away from chip giants like Nvidia, AMD, or TSMC, and instead toward the companies that actually supply the equipment used to make the chips themselves. Applied Materials (AMAT), the largest semiconductor equipment company in the world, is a key example. Its core Semiconductor Systems division makes up about 73% of the company’s revenue, according to its most recent annual filing, selling to the companies that manufacture chips for computing, logic, and memory. Its benefit is breadth: nearly every advanced chip and display passes through Applied’s tools at some point, spreading its exposure across the whole chipmaking ecosystem instead of betting on one type of chip. Ellis also flagged Lam Research (LRCX) as a worthy alternative. The company makes equipment for memory and storage chips, and while its product range is narrower than Applied Materials’, he sees Lam as especially well positioned to benefit from a surge in new capacity investment over the next two years, and B. Riley Securities has raised its earnings estimates for the company by 25% to reflect that outlook. Marvell Technology (MRVL) is another strong contender, particularly excelling at networking, or the plumbing that lets thousands of chips inside a data center talk to each other fast enough to work as one giant machine. Despite being less of a household name, Marvell captures roughly $195 billion in market value, according to analytics company FactSet, putting it in the same weight class as Nvidia and AMD, even drawing a direct investment from Nvidia as part of a partnership on next-generation networking technology. Right now, the bulk of Marvell’s business comes from Amazon Web Services, the cloud computing arm of Amazon. Though that relationship has been lucrative, it also means Marvell’s fortunes are somewhat tied to a single client. But Ellis sees this concentration as an opportunity rather than a red flag. If Marvell can land more of these customers and scale up its network products, he believes it could produce meaningfully more profit than it does today. These investments don’t come without risks, however. Chip stocks are known for big price swings and can be rattled by geopolitical tensions or shifts in how hyperscalers choose to fund their spending. Still, Ellis believes the industry is shifting from a boom-and-bust cycle into more durable, long-term growth. Even after the SOX, the main index that tracks AI-linked chip stocks, fell 26% on worries that all this spending won’t pay off, Ellis argues the drop already reflected most of that risk, making now a reasonable time to buy in. The numbers back him up: since the July 28 sell-off, Applied Materials, Lam Research, and Marvell have climbed back between roughly 22% and 30%. A brain without a body doesn’t get far. Chips need physical space to operate, and that’s where real estate investment trusts, or REITs, step in. These trusts rent out climate-controlled spaces equipped with the generators and high-speed connectivity required for around-the-clock operations. Patrick Wilson, a portfolio manager on the real estate securities team at CenterSquare Investment Management, spoke of REITs as a sound investment, given the industry’s shift from the AI training phase to the inference phase, or the stage where models move from being taught to being actively used for daily queries. While the initial training of AI models happened in large rural data centers built for cheap land and power, running those models day to day works best in facilities close to major cities, where shorter distances help cut latency, or the time delay between a request and a response. Because established REITs already control the limited, “carrier-dense” real estate in these urban centers, they stand to capture this next wave of demand better than anyone else. REITs are also built to be tax efficient for ordinary investors. As Wilson put it, “REITs are only taxed once, provided that they satisfy IRS tax rules. So, if they pay out 90% of their taxable net income into a dividend, there’s no corporate level tax that they pay,” Wilson explained. To capture this opportunity, he pointed to two REIT behemoths, Equinix (EQIX) and Digital Realty (DLR). Equinix is a large landlord for internet and cloud computing, running data centers that host servers for thousands of companies, from Fortune 500 firms to major cloud providers such as AWS and Google Cloud. Digital Realty has spent more than two decades buying and building similar facilities, benefiting from demand for secure, climate‑controlled server space that still exceeds supply. Wilson notes that this imbalance has allowed the REIT to raise rents, and that its thousands of tenants make it more stable than newer names that depend on only a few big contracts. However, Wilson clarified that investment risks remain. Data center REITs can be hit hard by rising interest rates, which push up borrowing costs and weigh on property values. They also depend on maintaining premium rents, so a flood of new competitors could erode their pricing power. Meanwhile, there are also geographic restraints to consider. Though data centers closer to metropolitan areas are more beneficial, they are also more scarce. “They need a lot of land, and that’s not necessarily found in midtown Manhattan,” he said. That said, Wilson still sees REITs as a safer bid compared to newer AI infrastructure firms that are heavily in debt. If AI demand slows or their short‑term customers walk away, these firms are still stuck with long‑term bills and big interest payments, which makes them much more fragile than the REITs. Given the enormous amounts of electricity needed to power AI data centers, the boom has fundamentally rewired the energy sector. Andrew Bischof, utilities analyst at financial services firm Morningstar, noted how, for decades, annual electricity demand in the U.S. remained stagnant, growing at a mere 0% to 0.5%. However, AI’s power-hungry nature has supercharged this forecast and transformed the sector’s investment profile, turning what were historically low-growth yield stocks into upside vehicles. “You’re now seeing more growth-oriented investors coming to utilities because they can provide that six to eight and sometimes 10% annualized growth over the five-year forecast,” Bischof said. One company positioned to benefit is American Electric Power (AEP), a major public utility holding company headquartered in Ohio that, according to its website, distributes electricity to more than five million customers across 11 states. Anticipating a massive increase in data center-driven electricity demand, AEP plans to invest $78 billion between 2026 and 2030 to build out the infrastructure needed to keep pace. Morningstar is optimistic about this buildout, citing AEP’s strong track record of completing the projects it commits to, and expects the investment to translate into 9% average annual earnings growth through 2030—a strong figure for a utility. However, not all utility stocks are created equal. Bischof explained that in certain regions, particularly the Mid-Atlantic, the transition to supporting data centers has led to higher power prices and concerns that these increased costs flow directly down to the retail customer. As a result, Bischof recommended utilities, beyond AEP, like DTE Energy (DTE), Alliant Energy (LNT), and Evergy (EVRG), as companies situated in regions where there is a strong alignment between regulators and communities over the data center boom. For a more contrarian way to play the power side of the AI buildout, David Trainer, CEO of investment research firm New Constructs, suggests looking beyond just utilities. He argues that while alternative and green energy are growing, they still cannot deliver the high-intensity power needed for massive AI data centers, leaving fossil fuels essential for meeting this demand. Because of that, Trainer sees “cheap” traditional energy stocks as a rare chance to capture the infrastructure boom at value prices, pointing to refiners like Valero (VLO) and HF Sinclair (DINO), which he believes the market is treating as if their profits are destined for a permanent 30% to 40% decline. If energy stocks are one way to profit from powering the boom, another lies in the hardware that keeps those AI factories from melting down. Data centers’ massive electricity consumption generates intense heat that standard air cooling can’t handle. Nick Lieb, industrials analyst at Morningstar, argues that this makes cooling and power equipment a very different kind of AI trade. While companies like Nvidia roll out new flagship GPUs every year or two, the core technology behind data center infrastructure evolves far more slowly, offering investors a more stable alternative. Vertiv (VRT), a long-time provider of precision cooling and power systems, is his prime example of a company built to benefit from this shift. “Vertiv owns the original data center cooling brand called Liebert, which actually invented the original computer room air handling unit… in the 1960s. That base technology is still quite relevant today [and] sells a lot of computer room air handling units,” Lieb explained. Lieb noted, however, that this stability is balanced by a high degree of concentration risk, given that over 80% of Vertiv’s revenue is generated directly within the data center market. Any slowdown or hiccup in spending from the major hyperscalers could also make Vertiv investors vulnerable. For those looking for more limited exposure to the infrastructure boom, Lieb points to power management company Eaton (ETN). Only a quarter of its sales tie directly to data centers, while the rest comes from commercial structures and other segments of the broader electrical grid. This diversification gives Eaton a stronger hedge if data center growth slows. Lieb added that Eaton is uniquely positioned to benefit from a U.S. electrical grid that he describes as “old and decrepit” and long overdue for a replacement. The company produces essential hardware—specifically transformers and switchgear—required to support both new data center demand and this critical national infrastructure upgrade. Despite the AI narrative’s success, some observers are wary this surge in capital spending may not ultimately deliver the payoff many expect. Lieb views the sheer magnitude of current spending as a potential source of long-term risk, citing how hyperscalers have reached a point where the cost of building new data centers is starting to “exceed the cash that they generate,” forcing tech giants to increasingly dip into the debt market and issue equity to fundraise. Trainer described the current market as a “crowded trade,” making it nearly impossible to find an obvious stock that isn’t already overpriced. He warns that many of the large firms like Amazon and Microsoft currently “bragging” about their massive capital expenditures “can’t afford to stay in the race” at their current spending rates. It’s a competitive contest he contends many of the current firms lack the balance sheets to survive. Yet the scale and potential impact of the buildout are hard to ignore. Mowrey stressed that the data center boom isn’t just big in dollar terms. For him, it’s laying the backbone for a technology shift that could touch nearly every corner of the economy. “AI adoption is still in its early innings… I think we’re just scratching the surface,” he said. “The broad enterprise application across healthcare, manufacturing, and financials—that’s going to take years to filter in.”

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/g.title: Small but promising signs of recovery on Great Barrier Reef
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/g.author: Holly Richardson and Michael Clarke
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/g.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Great Barrier Reef

More than 120 reefs were surveyed by AIMS, up and down the Great Barrier Reef. (ABC News: Holly Richardson)

Hard coral cover surveys by the Australian Institute of Marine Science show increases in cover in northern and central parts of the Great Barrier Reef and a slight drop in the south.

Experts say monsoons gave the reef some relief after significant bleaching in 2024.

Previous El Niños have meant more events of significant heat stress but scientists say it's still too early to say what this season may mean for the Great Barrier Reef.

Monsoons spared the Great Barrier Reef from the worst heat during the 2025-26 summer allowing some coral to recover, according to a new report from the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS).

"We have to place this in the context that these are small, [but] it's promising signs of recovery from the really large declines we saw from the 2024 bleaching event," said lead researcher on the long-term monitoring program, Mike Emslie.

Surveys also looked for evidence of crown-of-thorns starfish infestation as well as bleaching prevalence. (ABC News: Holly Richardson)

Dr Emslie said there was a smaller bleaching event in 2025 when temperatures increased in the early part of the summer, but the onset of a monsoon brought some relief to the corals.

"It managed to produce a lot of cloud cover and rain and brought the sea surface temperatures down," he said.

He said this provided some relief for the corals and gave an opportunity for the organisms to start growing again.

Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority chief scientist Roger Beeden said it was an encouraging sign and showed the reef was close to the long-term average coral cover.

"But the counterpoint to that is that it's under increasing pressure."

Dr Emslie said while it was positive showing that the reef had capacity to recover, more frequent and severe heat stress events were a growing concern.

And the forecast El El Niño could mean further stress to the reef, he said.

Scientists say the results are positive, showing the reef still has the capacity for resilience. (ABC News: Holly Richardson)

"We know from the past that El Niño events have led to widespread severe bleaching, so I guess it's a case of wait, watch and see what happens over the upcoming summer.

"We've really got to be taking very strong measures to reduce global greenhouse emissions to continue the prospects of the reef into the future."

Dr Beeden agreed it was too early to speculate on the potential impact of the El Niño event on the reef.

"It's important to note where that warmer water is concentrated at the moment is actually over the other side of the Pacific right now," he said.

He said multiple climate drivers determined outcomes in Australia's waters.

"The reality of climate change is that these kinds of events are becoming more likely: the risk of marine heat waves that can lead to coral bleaching events, coral bleaching events are a modern phenomenon," said Dr Beeden.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/d.title: Inside Donald Trump's 'Hunger Games'-style athletics contest
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/d.author: Fergus Gregg
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/d.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Higher Education

Student athletes at the Spire Institute and Academy in Ohio (Freedom 250 via Facebook)

120 students from the US, its territories and some tribal nations will compete against each other to win a $US125,000 ($177,449) college scholarship in the Patriot Games 2026.

Competitors were selected after submitting five-minute video applications and personal essays.

At least one athlete has revealed they do not actually live in the state or territory they represent.

Anderson Reid, representing Puerto Rico, sprinted onto a military-style bootcamp course to the cheers of supporting families and friends.

Thrift Shop by Macklemore & Ryan Lewis played as he crawled, sprinted and carried jerry cans, vying to top the times of 119 other teenagers between the ages of 14 and 17 for a chance to win a university scholarship.

Anderson Reid says contestants did not have to currently live in the state or territory they represented, but did not clarify what ties he had to Puerto Rico. (Instagram: andersonreid88)

The Patriot Games 2026 were announced in December 2025 by US President Donald Trump, who billed it as "an unprecedented four-day athletic event featuring the greatest high school athletes".

"One young man and one young women from each state and territory, but I promise there will be no men playing in women's sports," he said.

One hundred and twenty competitors made it to Ohio to compete in the three-day-long athletic competition, commemorating the 250th anniversary of the United States.

The ABC has identified participants from Puerto Rico, Guam, the Shawnee Tribe and the US Virgin Islands, but not from American Samoa or other Native American groups.

However, there has been speculation some athletes might not live in the state or territory they represent.

Reid is representing Puerto Rico, but does not appear to live there, with one Instagram commenter asking, "Isn't he from Texas?".

Videos on Reid's YouTube channel show clips from Daikin Park stadium in Houston, Texas.

Responding to another comment on Instagram, Reid said "[Contestants] don't have to be currently living in the state or territory they are representing".

"They do have to have some sort of association with it such as living there or having social [family] ties to it," Reid said.

Little is known about the Freedom 250 Patriot Games selection committee, which chose the athletes based on video applications and personal essays. (AP: Nate Manley)

The idea behind the Patriot Games drew immediate comparison to The Hunger Games, a series of books by Suzanne Collins, which were later adapted into a multi-billion-dollar film franchise.

Patriot Games organisers Freedom250 said the event would "bring together outstanding young Americans from across the nation to compete, inspire, and showcase the values that have shaped the United States for nearly 250 years".

It's a unique qualification process, as unlike the Junior Olympics or national sports competitions, the pre-selection method did not involve qualifying rounds, but rather a video application process.

Chris Brennan is representing North Carolina at the Patriot Games, and has been sharing each step of the experience on his social media.

In an interview with Trump-aligned influencer Adam Francisco Brennan said he stumbled across the Patriot Games online.

US President Donald Trump promoted the event as a showcase of the nation's best student athletes. (Supplied: X/Freedom250)

"I was just on Instagram one day, scrolling, scrolling and I saw an advertisement and I was like, 'Hey, I heard Trump talking about that,'" Mr Brennan said.

"I clicked, submitted, I made a quick 5-minute video application.

"Honestly I think it was a little bit of luck and a little bit of my personality."

Chris Brennan posts conservative content on Instagram and, in an interview, said women couldn't compete with men athletically.  (Instagram: notchris71)

Brennan then made it into the next round, and was asked to write an essay and answer "personal questions".

He later interviewed several of his fellow competitors in Baltimore, and they described stumbling on the Patriot Games like he did.

"I think it was on TikTok and I did it as a joke with my friend," Owen Carter of South Carolina said.

"I didn't think I'd get on."

The youth from North Carolina also runs a social media page called Club America, which features Christian content and Charlie Kirk quotes.

Some competitors said they prepared for the Patriot Games with cardio and pre-existing fitness routines.

Campbell Remus of Minnesota also participates in "Ninja Warrior" contests and other athletic competitions. (AP: Nate Manley)

Campbell Remus from Minnesota said she trains year round for track, cross country and the "Ninja Warrior" obstacle and fitness challenge, while Mr Carter said he went for "a lot of runs" despite not having much time to prepare.

On August 9 the athletes completed the presidential physical fitness test, a former national benchmark of core, upper body and cardio fitness retired in 2013. They also competed in team games of dodgeball and kick ball.

Joshua Chechile of Vermont participated in the 55-metre hurdles during day one of the Patriot Games, one of many different athletic events. (AP: Nate Manley)

The next day, competitors completed a multi-sport skill challenge called the varsity circuit, along with a military style bootcamp obstacle course.

The games will conclude at 7pm on August 11, local time, with semi-finals, finals and team competitions like tug of war.

In her application video, incoming freshman Sophie Skidmore of West Virginia appeared with her neck adorned in sports medals.

"I'm always looking for my next challenge," she said.

"As for the scholarship it would help me follow my dreams without financial burden."

Skidmore was eliminated in day two of the qualifiers.

The occasion was complicated by severe storms that gathered near Washington, forcing event organisers to order an earlier evacuation.

The top male and female athlete will each receive a $US125,000  university scholarship, but according to a report by the Education Data Initiative, the average cost of attending an out-of-state, public school in the US is more than $US182,000.

Opposition lawmakers had asked for the special session on the pilgrimage savings fund to be postponed until the prime minister’s return

Tabung Haji manages haj savings for Malaysian Muslims, making the inquiry into its governance, accounting practices and investment losses particularly sensitive in a Muslim-majority country where a pilgrimage to Mecca carries deep religious and political weight.

Anwar was absent from Tuesday’s sitting as he was recovering from an elective laparoscopic surgery for a para-umbilical hernia. The opposition had called for the inquiry to be postponed until the prime minister’s return.

“Do you want to debate me, or do you want to debate Tabung Haji? Do you want to know about me, or do you want to know about the betrayal of Tabung Haji?” Anwar asked.

https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/australas.title: Albanese refuses to say sorry for ‘insulting’ melon joke about Takaichi
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/australas.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/australas.text:
The Australian leader made the remarks about his Japanese counterpart last month, sparking backlash over perceived disrespect

Albanese had already faced a backlash and apologised over comments made during an interview last month with the Bush Deep podcast in which he said he would “shag” singer Kylie Minogue.

During the conversation with host Nikki Osborne at his official residence, the Australian leader joked that he’d received a “strange” present of a Japanese royal melon from Takaichi.

When the host asked if she had smuggled the fruit through Australian customs, Albanese held his hands up and said “got a couple of melons”.

“She came in looking like Pamela Anderson,” the host replied.

Australia’s opposition leader has called for Albanese to apologise over the “insulting” joke.

Asked whether he would say sorry for his “disrespectful behaviour” in parliament on Tuesday, the Australian leader said: “I reject the assertion in the question.”

Australia’s Foreign Minister Penny Wong also rejected accusations Albanese’s comments were intended to be an insult.

“The prime minister has been clear that he did not mean for those comments to be interpreted in the way they have been by those opposite,” she said, referring to the opposition.

https://www.dw.com/en/how-do-we-prepare-.title: How do we prepare for climate change that's already here?
https://www.dw.com/en/how-do-we-prepare-.text:
Western Europe has recorded its hottest-ever June and July, and extreme weather is here to stay. How can we adapt to what seems to be the new normal? Cities like Kiel in Germany are trying.

In October 2023, the worst storm surge in more than 150 years hit the Baltic Sea coast.It destroyed dikes, collapsed coastal cliffs and devastated marinas in the northern German state of Schleswig-Holstein and parts of southern Denmark.

The catastrophic surge wiped away 2.68 meters (8.79 feet) of coastal bluff in Kiel, a port city and Schleswig-Holstein's capital. That was more than four times the yearly average lost over the previous two decades.

Human-made climate change is supercharging extreme weather such as storms. And in coastal cities like Kiel, the consequences are already impossible to ignore.

"The impacts of climate change are hardly abstract in Kiel," said Martina Baum, who heads the city's climate adaptation division. "Since at least the 2023 storm surge, we have all been reminded of the profound effects it can have on us, on our daily lives, and on the environment around us."

Those effects are forcing Kiel — among the first cities to declare a climate emergency back in 2019 — to rethink how it works and is designed. It has since become a frontrunner in adapting to the realities of a changing climate, establishing Baum's division in 2025 to help make the city more resilient to weather extremes and adopting an adaptation plan in February 2026 to step up those measures.

For city officials like Baum, adaptation is not a substitute for cutting the fossil fuel emissions heating the planet. Climate protection remains the first line of defense, because limiting warming will reduce future damage.

"For a long time, there was hesitation to engage officially with the issue of climate change adaptation. I also felt uneasy about it at first, because it felt as though it would somehow take the pressure off climate protection efforts," Baum told DW.

But the move to adaptation in Kiel reflects what's happening in other cities around the world from Santa Cruz in the USto Quezon City in the Philippines, as governments increasingly prepare for the impacts of heat, heavier rainfall and stronger storm surges that are already here.

That doesn't mean climate protection and adaptation always align. Installing power-hungry air-conditioning in housing, daycare or senior centers, for instance, protects vulnerable people in heat waves. But it increases energy consumption, "which would run counter to climate protection goals," Baum said.

"Even if we use renewable energy, demand is not yet covered by renewable sources 100% of the time, so any additional energy we consume will ultimately result in the emission of climate-damaging greenhouse gases," added Baum.

While AC will sometimes be necessary, Kiel is working on solutions that cool the city naturally. It's adding vegetation to building facades, redesigning a park to channel cooler air into the city center, and making it easier for residents to access permits, information, and grants for adaptation projects.

The city is also testing which tree species can survive future conditions. A decade ago, Kiel planted five specimens each of 20 different species to find out which can best withstand heat, drought and salt spray from the nearby Baltic Sea.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trees provide shade, cool streets by roughly 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) and improve air quality, but not every species will thrive as the climate changes.

"There is no one-size-fits-all climate tree; different sites require different tree species," said Nicole Holz, who works in the department responsible for the city's green spaces.

The research requires patience.

"It's going to take some 20, 30 years until you get some real results," said Petra Holtappel, head of the same department.

Adapting to climate change will also require changes to daily life, said Baum. Children, for example, may no longer be able to play soccer tournaments at 3 p.m. because it's too hot.

Although Kiel is getting warmer, it is expected to fare better than much hotter Southern or Central Europe when it comes to heat. Still, the city is vulnerable to more storm surges and heavy rain and needs more retention areas to manage all that excess water. The city is dredging the park's pond to store stormwater during heavy rainfall but is also exploring other ideas.

"One idea is what's known as multi-use design, meaning that in future, a soccer pitch could be built slightly lower than the surrounding area. During periods of heavy rain, water could then be directed there and allowed to gradually infiltrate into the ground or evaporate," Baum said.

The downside is the pitch might be unusable for up to 60 days a year, she added. But residents would need accept that, said Baum, who emphasized the need for greater public debate about adaptation measures.

Helping residents understand those trade-offs and what's at stake is part of Annafried Stürmer's work. Stürmer organizes educational events, leads public excursions with scientists and attends neighborhood fairs to meet people who might not otherwise engage with climate issues.

At Kiel Week, the world's biggest annual sailing event, Stürmer displayed a map showing city flood risk from extreme rainfall.

"People often find that interesting, because it doesn't immediately seem like it's connected to climate change. Instead, the initial reaction is , 'Wow, if we get one of those intense heavy rainfall events, my house could be in serious trouble,' or 'My backyard could end up flooded,'" Stürmer said.

Stürmer has often found it easier to talk about climate adaptation than about climate change because the former is more tangible.

"It's easier to talk about the need for a better-developed sewer system to handle heavy rainfall, or about planting different types of trees and vegetation, than it is to talk about reducing CO2 emissions," Stürmer told DW.

Recent record heat waves have made the adaptation conservation more urgent too.

"People noticed that it hadn't been as hot before," she said, adding residents increasingly recognize the need to protect children, the elderly, pregnant women and outdoor workers.

Even with growing public awareness of the need for adaptation, funding remains a problem in cash-strapped Kiel. Still seen as optional, climate action can quickly come under pressure when budgets tighten.

"I disagree with the idea that climate adaptation and climate action are optional responsibilities. I keep asking myself: what are the alternatives?" Baum said. "After all, it has been demonstrated time and again that investing in climate adaptation and climate mitigation will simply pay off."

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

Whether in Europe, Asia, or North America — the same is evident everywhere. Rivers are shrinking, lakes are receding, and parched soil is cracking. People are seeking relief from the heat, and animals are searching for water. The persistent heat is transforming landscapes and the daily lives of millions. Drought has long since become a global challenge.

The Rhine — which flows for about 1,230 kilometers (765 miles) through six countries — has reached historic lows. Sandbars are blocking navigation, and freighters are sailing with reduced cargo. Steel production in Duisburg, western Germany, is being slowed because important raw materials are no longer arriving in sufficient quantities.

What had been hidden beneath the surface for decades is now resurfacing. In Prahovo, in eastern Serbia, the extremely low water level of the Danube has exposed the remains of a German warship from World War II. A drone shot shows people swimming in the immediate vicinity of the wreck.

France experienced its hottest July since weather records began in 1900. At the same time, rainfall is nearly 70% below normal. Parched soil is turning forests into powder kegs. The largest fire since 1949 has destroyed more than 42,000 hectares of land — an area four times the size of Paris.

An explosion echoes through the Danube as the Romanian Navy blasts underwater rocks. Drought and extreme heat have lowered the river to critical levels, threatening water supply for the Cernavoda nuclear power plant. The operation highlights the extraordinary measures countries are taking to protect vital infrastructure from the impacts of climate change.

From the air, Lake Palas Tuzla in central Turkey looks like a work of art created by nature. In the Turkish province of Kayseri, dried-up watercourses form bizarre patterns that, from the air, resemble tree canopies. The landscape is visibly changing — and at an ever-faster pace.

An aerial photograph shows the mosque and the abandoned buildings of the village of Somang in the Indonesian province of Banten. The settlement was flooded to make way for the Karian Dam, but is now reemerging from the water as a result of drought and El Nino. This unusual image illustrates the consequences of extreme weather events, as Indonesia fears water shortages and food security risks.

In London, cricket teams play on small green islands surrounded by parched grass. Around the world, people are trying to adapt their daily lives to extreme temperatures. But in many places, water is already becoming the scarcest resource.

Tourists visit Badwater Basin, the lowest point in North America, during an extreme heat wave in Death Valley National Park in California. The surreal-looking salt flat is located in one of the hottest regions on Earth. Death Valley in the US holds the official temperature record of 56.7 degrees Celsius (137 Fahrenheit), set in 1913, although some experts today doubt the historical measurement.

The images from Germany, France, Romania, Indonesia, the United Kingdom, and the United States all tell the same story. Where water disappears, agriculture, energy supply, shipping, and nature are thrown out of balance. Drought is no longer a regional problem. It has long since become a global warning sign — and shows just how vulnerable our planet has become.
https://www.dw.com/en/how-do-we-prepare-.summary: Kiel, Germany, is one of the first cities to declare a climate emergency back in 2019. Drought and extreme heat have lowered the Rhine to critical levels, threatening water supply for the Cernavoda nuclear power plant.

Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Tuesday, August 11:

Protesting student leader Devendra Nath Mahto was admitted to a hospital in the eastern state of Jharkhand after taking part in a protest march to the state legislature on Monday while on a nine-day hunger strike.

Police used tear gas, batons and water cannons to disperse the crowd of students marching towards the state assembly on Monday in state capital Ranchi.

The students are alleging irregularities in government recruitment exams.

Mahto said his health deteriorated after police used batons to disperse protesters outside the Legislative Assembly.

Earlier on Sunday, the sixth round of talks between student protesters and the government failed to reach a breakthrough following which the protesters announced a march to the state Assembly.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Amber heat health alerts to kick in across England ahead of fifth summer heatwave – latest news
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Yohannes Lowe
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
As we mentioned in the opening post, amber heat health alerts come into force across most of England from 9am today and will last until 9am on Friday.

As well as a rise in deaths and likely “significant” impacts across health and social care services, here are some of the other risks associated with the amber category, as outlined by the UK Health Security Agency:

internal temperatures in hospitals and care homes may exceed the recommended threshold for clinical risk assessment

the heat affecting the ability of the workforce to deliver services

indoor environments overheating increasing the risk to some vulnerable people

issues managing medicines

increased demand for power exceeding capacity

possible travel delays

water‑related incidents may increase, including risks from cold‑water shock and drowning

Health alerts are set to come into force across England this morning as parts of the UK brace for fifth climate crisis-driven heatwave this summer.

Amber heat health alerts have been issued for all regions in England, except the north-east, which mean significant impacts are likely across health and social care services due to the high temperatures, according to the UK’s Health Security Agency (UKHSA). The alerts stretch from 9am on Tuesday until 9am on Friday.

The north-east will be under a yellow health alert, which is less intense than the amber category but is still linked to a rise in deaths, particularly among those aged 65 and over or with health conditions, and a likely increase in demand for health services.

The alerts come a day after four more regions of England were officially declared to be in drought: the East Midlands, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Kent and East Sussex, and Solent and the South Downs.

They joined seven English regions, alongside the whole of Wales, already under drought status since last month: East Anglia, Hertfordshire and London, Thames Valley, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, Devon and Cornwall, the West Midlands, and Wessex (covering Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire and south Gloucestershire).

The Environment Agency said 71.3% of England is experiencing “flash drought”, as a dry start to August followed the country’s driest July on record.

On Tuesday, highs of 29C in Cardiff, 28C in Manchester and 25C in London are forecast before temperatures soar to the mid-30s in some areas on Thursday, according to the Met Office, with temperatures possibly exceeding 36C in some places.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Guardian moderators (now); Jillian Ambrose and Damian Carrington (later)
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Last week Jillian Ambrose and Damian Carrington published a front-page story that revealed the vast scale of the profits that eight of the biggest oil firms made in three months as the Iran conflict sent energy prices soaring and the emissions-fuelled climate crisis caused deadly heatwaves.

They will be online at 2pm to answer your questions about their reporting – and any others you might have about how the oil markets work – and how many of these companies have withdrawn from their commitments to a clean energy transition.

As the Guardian’s energy correspondent, Jillian’s recent reporting has also included the spike in demand for solar power in the UK; the political row surrounding how Great Britain’s grid operator was managed during recent heatwaves and what is holding back a British green energy transformation.

Damian’s recent work as environment editor has included looking at how the climate crisis has accelerated the scale of Europe’s summer heatwaves; an audacious plan to refreeze the Arctic and a fascinating piece looking at how nature can help treat mental illness.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/11.title: Mass grave with 25 bodies found in Sudan’s Kurmuk after army retakes town
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/11.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/11.text:
Sudanese armed forces have discovered at least 25 bodies in a mass grave in the southeastern Blue Nile State, with local officials accusing the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of carrying out the killings.

The grave was found in the town of Kurmuk, a month after the Sudanese army regained control of the area after weeks of heavy fighting.

Abdel Aty Mohamed al-Faki, the commissioner of Kurmuk, announced the discovery on Sunday, according to The Sudan Tribune, saying the Sudanese armed forces found the grave during sweeping operations in the northeastern part of the town.

The grave included the remains of children, women and hospital staff.

Al-Faki said the victims had been executed near Jebel Fankat, a hilltop position the RSF had used to launch drone attacks during its assault on the area.

There was no comment from RSF.

The RSF, which has been fighting the Sudanese army since April 2023, has been accused of carrying out mass killings, including in the capital, Khartoum, the city of el-Fasher and the central Gezeira state.

Al Jazeera’s Almigdad al-Ruhaid, reporting from Khartoum, called the discovery in Kurmuk “significant and disturbing”.

“The local authorities have accused the Rapid Support Forces of executing them during its occupation of the town of Kurmuk,” he said, adding that the discovery comes as RSF attacks also continue in Blue Nile State.

“In the city of Kurmuk, the Rapid Support Forces have launched explosive drone attacks for the second consecutive day,” al-Ruhaid said. “So while the map of control between both sides may be changing”, fighting between the two sides continues, creating “mass displacement”.

Intense fighting also continues in West Darfur, the main stronghold for the RSF, with Sudanese armed forces reportedly repelling the paramilitary force’s attacks in Bir Saliba, located about 40km from the city of el-Geneina, he added.

The conflict has killed an estimated 40,000 people, according to the World Health Organization, and forced more than 14 million people to flee their homes.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/t.title: Trump reportedly hid in catering truck to board secret flight out of Türkiye
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
World Politics

Catering truck parked at Air Force One before Donald Trump's departure after NATO summit at Ankara international airport in July 2026. (AP Photo: Alex Brandon)

Donald Trump departed on a secret military flight from Türkiye last month when the White House said he was flying aboard Air Force One, US media report.

The elaborate ruse, which involved hiding the US president in a catering truck, took place when Mr Trump was in Ankara for a NATO summit in July.

The operation was triggered by an Iranian assassination threat to Mr Trump, the Post reports.

US President Donald Trump departed on a secret military flight from Türkiye last month when the White House said he was flying aboard Air Force One, in an extraordinary move that involved hiding him in an airport catering truck, the Washington Post reports.

Mr Trump had taken the newly renovated Qatari-donated jet to Ankara for the NATO summit but he unexpectedly used an older Air Force One when departing the country, a move that prompted questions about the newer plane's security.

The trip to NATO was the first international travel for the new plane, whose speedy upgrades triggered questions over its cost and security, and took place as hostilities escalated with Iran, which borders Türkiye.

Officials reportedly urged the US president to swap out his Qatari-donated luxury jet as a security precaution.

Before departing Ankara, Mr Trump said on Truth Social that he would use an older baby blue Air Force One plane "for old time's sake" ⁠to RAF Mildenhall in Britain, while the new plane stopped at the same base so US service members stationed there could tour the aircraft.

After Mr Trump boarded the old Air Force One in front of cameras in Ankara, he was secretly shuttled by an airport catering truck to a smaller plane, an Air Force C-32A, the Post reported, citing a US official familiar with the operation and corroborating material it reviewed.

The deception operation was triggered by a credible Iranian assassination threat to Mr Trump, the Post reported.

A US official with knowledge of the deception plan also confirmed the operation to the New York Times.

A similar operation had taken place in 2000, when President Bill Clinton used an unmarked executive jet to fly into Pakistan while sending his formal Air Force One as decoy.

On this occasion, the journalists who thought they were travelling with Mr Trump on the older Air Force One, which was effectively used as a decoy, reported being advised to keep their window shades in the press cabin closed.

Donald Trump boards the new, Qatari-gifted Air Force One to return to Washington at RAF Mildenhall in July 2026. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

The Post said aside from reporters, some White House staff also believed that the president was on board.

When asked later by reporters why they had to keep their shades shut during the flight, Mr Trump said it was because they were "probably on a dangerous flight".

He went on to say: "But if I go, you go. Right?"

The C-32A carrying Mr Trump flew to Britain and arrived at around 10:20pm while the older Air Force One and media arrived minutes later, the Post reported.

It was not clear, the paper said, how Mr Trump was moved from the C-32A back to Air Force One.

Mr Trump's travelling press pool reported he climbed down the stairs of the old Air Force One at 10:56pm UK local time.

He gave press a peace sign but didn't walk over to talk to them. He then spent some time greeting service members before walking to the new, Qatari-donated plane.

The jet, gifted to the US government by Qatar, has been retrofitted, with Trump shaking off concerns over the cost.

When asked for comment on the revelation of a secret flight on a third plane, the White House provided a statement from Communications Director Steve Cheung.

He said the Qatari-donated jet has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the president and his staff.

"As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats," Mr Cheung said.

It was the same statement provided to the Post.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The new plane, with red, white, dark blue and gold livery chosen by Mr Trump, is a Boeing 747 gifted to the United States by Qatar last year and refitted by defence contractor L3Harris Technologies.

It was intended to serve as a temporary replacement while Boeing struggled to deliver long-delayed next-generation Air Force One planes.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/b.title: Boy, 10, clotheslined by wire on remote dirt bike track
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/b.author: Bella Munro
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Accidents and Emergency Incidents

Braymond Pyke riding a motorcycle in Cunnamulla. (Supplied: Bronwyn Wood)

Ten year old Braymond Pyke had to be airlifted to hospital after injuring his neck when he rode his motorbike into a piece of rope that had been strung up across an outback Queensland dirt bike track.

His mum, Bronwyn Wood, said they were getting ready to head home late on Friday when he begged her to go for one last ride around the track just outside Cunnamulla, about 790km west of Brisbane.

Aerial of Cunnamulla, a small outback Queensland town about 790km west of Brisbane. (Supplied: Peninsula Hot Springs)

“He's like 'please mum', so of course I let him go for one more lap,” she said.

But she said she soon heard Braymond’s scream for help.

"My son was just bleeding from the throat," she said.

"It's the worst thing … you never want to imagine.

"I've never seen him in so much pain. It was horrifying.”

Braymond Pyke boarding a Royal Flying Doctor plane, and transported from Cunnamulla to Toowoomba. (Supplied: Bronwyn Wood)

She said she drove her son straight to the Cunnamulla hospital before he flown to Roma and on to Toowoomba Hospital for treatment.

Braymond returned home to Cunnamulla on Monday nursing severe rope burn, scratches on his neck, and some internal bruising after the clotheslining incident.

"The relief, knowing that the outcome could have been so much worse. He is one very lucky boy," Ms Wood said.

Braymond Pyke riding a motorcycle on a Cunnamulla dirt bike track. (Supplied: Bronwyn Wood)

Police said they are investigating the crash and have patrolled the track for any further risks.

Braymond’s dad, Brendon Pyke, said the area along Old Charleville Road had been used by drovers recently and suggested it was possible that the ropes had mistakenly been left up.

"It's electric fence wire designed to hold cattle in," he said.

"I can't say for sure but I'm thinking maybe they have left it behind."

An electric fence wire was tied up across the Bandy motorcycle track in Cunnamulla with no visible marking. (Supplied: Bronwyn Wood)

Mr Pyke said it was drovers' responsibility to mark any ropes or wires and take them down when they were done.

He said they couldn’t confirm how the wire was left up, but also didn’t rule out that it could have been tied up by someone intentionally.

He warned families to be cautious.

Braymond Pyke's parents Bronwyn Wood and Brendon Pyke. (Supplied: Bronwyn Wood)

"Double check where your kids are going to be riding," he said.

Cunnamulla resident Troy Nelson started to maintain the motorbike track when his own two boys started riding several years ago.

Mr Nelson and his sons found about 10 similar ropes in the area following Braymond’s injury and cut them all down.

Braymond Pyke riding a motorcycle in Cunnamulla. (Supplied: Bronwyn Wood)

He said Braymond’s injury was not the first case he had heard of recently.

“Only a couple of weeks ago, another kid actually got caught as well on a rope,” he said.

Mr Nelson said the boy had not been severely injured and decided not to report it.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/s.title: Service stations nationwide raided over illegal tobacco, vapes
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/s.author: Nabil Al-Nashar
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Dozens of petrol stations across the country were raided simultaenously on Tuesday. (Supplied: Australian Border Force)

Dozens of service stations have been targeted in a multi agency campaign against "suspected criminal activity".

The Australian Border Force says some are allegedly selling illegal tobacco products, including vapes.

The ABF says some service stations targeted may be closed temporarily.

More than 100 service stations across the country have been raided in a coordinated blitz targeting "suspected criminal activity" and the alleged sale of illicit tobacco and vapes.

The Australian Border Force (ABF) said nearly 300 personnel were deployed to every state and territory except Tasmania and the Northern Territory on Tuesday as part of the coordinated campaign.

Fifteen federal and state agencies were involved in Operation Shorthand, including NSW Police, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) and the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission, operating under the Illicit Tobacco National Disruption Group (NDG), established by the federal government in 2025.

Australian Federal Police officers at a petrol station.  (Supplied: Australian Border Force)

Footage of one raid showed officers entering a service station, seizing packets of imported tobacco boxes and cash.

ABF Assistant Commissioner Customs Compliance and Enforcement Tony Smith said all agencies had a shared goal of disrupting an evolving illegal tobacco trade.

"Criminal actors are continuing to adapt their business models and diversify their activities by moving away from traditional tobacconists and in to selling their products out of convenience stores, milk bars and even service stations," he said.

"This diversification demonstrates an enforcement pressure from border agencies and our partners across the country and internationally is forcing criminal enablers to adapt their tactics to evade detection and enforcement."

The raids were nationwide except Tasmania and the NT. (Supplied: Australian Border Force)

AFP Superintendent Crime Command Jim Rowe said their intelligence suggested the illegal tobacco trade was connected to organised crime.

"We have seen organised crime groups use the sales of illicit tobacco to fund further criminal activity," he said.

"The aim of today's enforcement activity for the AFP is to obtain information to help us identify the potential importation of illicit tobacco, distribution networks and how the proceeds of sales are collected and then distributed."

NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said that NSW Health was were part of the multi-agency effort.

"We work closely with our federal enforcement agencies to share intelligence around people who are doing the wrong thing," he said.

"It's not fair on legitimate small business owners, it's not fair on the community or young children that these stores are popping up and are selling illegal products across the board."

The ABF said the operation remained active as NDG agencies assessed evidence gathered during the raids.

Some of the targeted service stations may be closed temporarily.

The ABC has reached out to the Australian Service Station and Convenience Store Association for comment.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: She is Russia’s richest woman. Her business empire is going up in flames.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Paul Sonne
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
She built Russia’s answer to Amazon. She navigated wartime Kremlin politics. And she outmaneuvered her ex-husband — the father of her seven children — in a rancorous business feud that involved a deadly shooting near Red Square.

But Tatyana Kim, billionaire co-founder of the online marketplace Wildberries and the richest woman in Russia, is now facing a far greater challenge. Ukrainian airstrikes are decimating her company’s facilities and threatening her business empire’s survival.

After months of attacks on Russian oil refineries that caused nationwide gas shortages, Ukraine has expanded its air campaign to Wildberries warehouses across Russia. Kyiv has targeted at least 23 Wildberries facilities so far, hitting them night after night since mid-July, with billions of dollars in merchandise going up in smoke. Nine of the company’s workers have been killed.

The attacks mark a new stage in the conflict, with Kyiv aggressively targeting a single private business for the first time. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is attempting to bring the war home for more Russians, hoping that rising discontent and inconvenience in Russian society will increase the pressure on President Vladimir Putin to end the war.

Kyiv has argued that Wildberries, which accounts for about 10% of all Russian retail sales, is a legitimate target because it provides goods to Russian soldiers.

Kim, speaking in a video address late last month, condemned what she described as “terrorist attacks.” She said the goods Wildberries was selling were no different from what was on offer by platforms like Amazon or the Chinese giant Alibaba.

“There is no logic, common sense or rationality in the actions of the terrorists, nor can there be,” Kim said, referring to the Ukrainians. She said the “enemy” was trying to “apply pressure, destabilize and provoke panic and shock among a large number of people.”

The strikes are hurting Wildberries, and the Russian retail market in general, at a time when the country’s economy is already facing difficulties, though the damage pales in comparison to the destruction Russia has caused in Ukraine.

Consumer spending in Russia for nonfood items on marketplaces like Wildberries has plummeted in recent weeks, amid the airstrikes, according to a research note by SberIndex, a research arm of state-owned Sberbank.

Wildberries has lost up to one-third of its warehouse space and as much as 480 billion rubles’ worth of goods ($5.9 billion) in the Ukrainian attacks, according to Moscow-based Data Insight, an e-commerce consultancy.

Wildberries “has almost run out of its biggest warehouses,” said Sergei Semko, an analyst at Data Insight.

“Every single day, one warehouse after another is getting methodically destroyed,” he added.

What ultimately happens to Wildberries will depend in part on how long Ukraine’s strikes continue and how effectively and quickly Kim adapts the company’s logistics. It will also depend on what sort of redress she is able to win from the Russian state.

Born into a Russian family that is ethnically Korean, Kim is a former English teacher who launched Wildberries in 2004 along with her husband, Vladislav Bakalchuk, as a website that sold clothes from European catalogs.

Over the years, Wildberries grew into a linchpin of the Russian consumer economy, with nearly 95,000 pickup points opening across the country and more than half the nation’s population making purchases at least once a month. Putin’s invasion of Ukraine made the platform all the more important, as Western companies retreated from the market.

In 2024, Kim navigated a merger with a Russian outdoor advertising firm that was reportedly mediated by the Kremlin. The deal was denounced as a corporate raid by her husband. At one point, he showed up at the Wildberries office in Moscow with a retinue of armed Chechens, leading to a shootout that left two people dead and seven wounded. Kim and Bakalchuk finalized their divorce the following year.

Faced with a new, broader crisis, Kim, 50, is scrambling to adapt.

In her video address, she said Wildberries was moving to decentralize its distribution and redoing its logistics infrastructure as quickly as possible. In an online post Thursday, she said the company was holding meetings with regional governments and sellers, adding that “broad support measures at the federal level are also being actively developed.”

The company has made two rounds of voluntary payouts to more than 80,000 small and medium-size sellers and rolled out limited insurance that sellers can buy for drone attacks. The Russian government is also working on an aid package for Wildberries’ sellers that will involve tax breaks and grace periods, Alexei Sazanov, the deputy finance minister, said this past week.

But while sellers are finding some relief, Kim’s staff is now worried about their safety. One 24-year-old Wildberries warehouse worker from St. Petersburg, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of security concerns, said she had felt a terrible inner fear as Ukrainian drones blew up Wildberries facilities in the region.

After the one where she worked and another near her house were hit, she decided to stop working there, even though she had liked the job.

The independent entrepreneurs who sell goods through Wildberries are also feeling anxiety.

Katerina Kordik, 44, had built a business selling boho jewelry from Asia that grew successful enough to support her family of five.

She lost about a third of her inventory, including her most expensive artisan pieces, in the first Ukrainian strike on a Wildberries warehouse, near Moscow, last month. She still had many items stored elsewhere, but as more Wildberries warehouses were blown up by the day, she was unable to retrieve her merchandise.

Then, an attack this past week on a Wildberries warehouse in Tula, south of Moscow, took out half her merchandise. Today, only about 100 of her roughly 2,000 items are available for sale, she said.

For the first time in her life, she has sought the help of a psychiatrist, she said.

“If you live in a country that is at war, it would be strange to expect that it wouldn’t get you at some point,” Kordik said. She added that she was trying to take it as a lesson, “to learn to cope with situations where nothing depends on you, where you can’t do anything and you just hang out in this uncertainty.”

Kim is also facing pressure from the competition. Industry watchers are already seeing signs that sellers are fleeing to Ozon, Russia’s second-largest e-commerce platform, which has a more decentralized logistics setup and has not been singled out by Kyiv.

In many places, Wildberries is still functioning normally. The company has such a sophisticated logistics and information technology infrastructure that it is not going to fold simply because a number of its warehouses have been damaged or destroyed, said a former Wildberries executive who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of previous contractual obligations.

While Ukraine has accused Wildberries of selling military-related goods, including replacement parts for drones and navigation equipment, Kim has denounced the strikes as “attacks on peaceful people.”

Wildberries explicitly says in its rules that sales of weapons and armaments are prohibited.

Still, many supporters and family members of Russian soldiers have been known to buy equipment such as body armor and helmets from the site. Drones and other items that can be used on the front are available.

A review by The New York Times found that first-person-view drones were for sale on the site in early August, as were spools of fiber-optic cable, which can be attached to drones to guide them.

One listing — marked as “out of stock” — offered a drone with a dropping system for explosives. In the “questions” section, some users expressed legal concerns. Others inquired about bulk discounts, naming the Russian military unit for which they intended to buy the drones.

One review, using a Russian slang term for Ukrainian soldiers, said: “Drone is good, chops the Ukrops:)))))” The Times was unable to verify whether any of the drones were purchased or shipped.

One potential buyer asked in the questions section whether the drone could be used for the special military operation, the Kremlin’s term for the war. The seller replied, “Hello, yes.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.author: Chris Buckley
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/0.text:
TAICHUNG, TAIWAN – For half an hour Monday, mobile data was throttled across central Taiwan, leaving millions of people unable to stream videos, share photos or make video calls on their cellphones.

The interruption was deliberate: Taiwan was testing, for the first time on a mass scale, how the island might cope if a Chinese attack disrupted its communications.

The activity was part of Taiwan’s annual civil defense exercise, when the government tries to give citizens a sense, albeit a fleeting one, of how they should respond if China tried to seize the self-governed island by force.
