https://www.dw.com/en/why-a-soccer-field.title: Why a soccer field in one German city may become a flood zone
https://www.dw.com/en/why-a-soccer-field.text:
Western Europe has recorded its hottest-ever June and July, and extreme weather from wildfires to storms are here to stay. How can we adapt to what seems to be the new normal? Cities like Kiel in Germany are trying.

In October 2023, the worst storm surge in more than 150 years hit the Baltic Sea coast.It destroyed dikes, collapsed coastal cliffs and devastated marinas in the northern German state of Schleswig-Holstein and parts of southern Denmark.

The catastrophic surge wiped away 2.68 meters (8.79 feet) of coastal bluff in Kiel, a port city and Schleswig-Holstein's capital. That was more than four times the yearly average lost over the previous two decades.

Human-made climate change is supercharging extreme weather such as storms. And in coastal cities like Kiel, the consequences are already impossible to ignore.

"The impacts of climate change are hardly abstract in Kiel," said Martina Baum, who heads the city's climate adaptation division. "Since at least the 2023 storm surge, we have all been reminded of the profound effects it can have on us, on our daily lives, and on the environment around us."

Those effects are forcing Kiel — among the first cities to declare a climate emergency back in 2019 — to rethink how it works and is designed. It has since become a frontrunner in adapting to the realities of a changing climate, establishing Baum's division in 2025 to help make the city more resilient to weather extremes and adopting an adaptation plan in February 2026 to step up those measures.

For city officials like Baum, adaptation is not a substitute for cutting the fossil fuel emissions heating the planet. Climate protection remains the first line of defense, because limiting warming will reduce future damage.

"For a long time, there was hesitation to engage officially with the issue of climate change adaptation. I also felt uneasy about it at first, because it felt as though it would somehow take the pressure off climate protection efforts," Baum told DW.

But the move to adaptation in Kiel reflects what's happening in other cities around the world from Santa Cruz in the USto Quezon City in the Philippines, as governments increasingly prepare for the impacts of heat, heavier rainfall and stronger storm surges that are already here.

That doesn't mean climate protection and adaptation always align. Installing power-hungry air-conditioning in housing, daycare or senior centers, for instance, protects vulnerable people in heat waves. But it increases energy consumption, "which would run counter to climate protection goals," Baum said.

"Even if we use renewable energy, demand is not yet covered by renewable sources 100% of the time, so any additional energy we consume will ultimately result in the emission of climate-damaging greenhouse gases," added Baum.

While AC will sometimes be necessary, Kiel is working on solutions that cool the city naturally. It's adding vegetation to building facades, redesigning a park to channel cooler air into the city center, and making it easier for residents to access permits, information, and grants for adaptation projects.

The city is also testing which tree species can survive future conditions. A decade ago, Kiel planted five specimens each of 20 different species to find out which can best withstand heat, drought and salt spray from the nearby Baltic Sea.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trees provide shade, cool streets by roughly 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) and improve air quality, but not every species will thrive as the climate changes.

"There is no one-size-fits-all climate tree; different sites require different tree species," said Nicole Holz, who works in the department responsible for the city's green spaces.

The research requires patience.

"It's going to take some 20, 30 years until you get some real results," said Petra Holtappel, head of the same department.

Adapting to climate change will also require changes to daily life, said Baum. Children, for example, may no longer be able to play soccer tournaments at 3 p.m. because it's too hot.

Although Kiel is getting warmer, it is expected to fare better than much hotter Southern or Central Europe when it comes to heat. Still, the city is vulnerable to more storm surges and heavy rain and needs more retention areas to manage all that excess water. The city is dredging the park's pond to store stormwater during heavy rainfall but is also exploring other ideas.

"One idea is what's known as multi-use design, meaning that in future, a soccer pitch could be built slightly lower than the surrounding area. During periods of heavy rain, water could then be directed there and allowed to gradually infiltrate into the ground or evaporate," Baum said.

The downside is the pitch might be unusable for up to 60 days a year, she added. But residents would need accept that, said Baum, who emphasized the need for greater public debate about adaptation measures.

Helping residents understand those trade-offs and what's at stake is part of Annafried Stürmer's work. Stürmer organizes educational events, leads public excursions with scientists and attends neighborhood fairs to meet people who might not otherwise engage with climate issues.

At Kiel Week, the world's biggest annual sailing event, Stürmer displayed a map showing city flood risk from extreme rainfall.

"People often find that interesting, because it doesn't immediately seem like it's connected to climate change. Instead, the initial reaction is , 'Wow, if we get one of those intense heavy rainfall events, my house could be in serious trouble,' or 'My backyard could end up flooded,'" Stürmer said.

Stürmer has often found it easier to talk about climate adaptation than about climate change because the former is more tangible.

"It's easier to talk about the need for a better-developed sewer system to handle heavy rainfall, or about planting different types of trees and vegetation, than it is to talk about reducing CO2 emissions," Stürmer told DW.

Recent record heat waves have made the adaptation conservation more urgent too.

"People noticed that it hadn't been as hot before," she said, adding residents increasingly recognize the need to protect children, the elderly, pregnant women and outdoor workers.

Even with growing public awareness of the need for adaptation, funding remains a problem in cash-strapped Kiel. Still seen as optional, climate action can quickly come under pressure when budgets tighten.

"I disagree with the idea that climate adaptation and climate action are optional responsibilities. I keep asking myself: what are the alternatives?" Baum said. "After all, it has been demonstrated time and again that investing in climate adaptation and climate mitigation will simply pay off."

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

Whether in Europe, Asia, or North America — the same is evident everywhere. Rivers are shrinking, lakes are receding, and parched soil is cracking. People are seeking relief from the heat, and animals are searching for water. The persistent heat is transforming landscapes and the daily lives of millions. Drought has long since become a global challenge.

The Rhine — which flows for about 1,230 kilometers (765 miles) through six countries — has reached historic lows. Sandbars are blocking navigation, and freighters are sailing with reduced cargo. Steel production in Duisburg, western Germany, is being slowed because important raw materials are no longer arriving in sufficient quantities.

What had been hidden beneath the surface for decades is now resurfacing. In Prahovo, in eastern Serbia, the extremely low water level of the Danube has exposed the remains of a German warship from World War II. A drone shot shows people swimming in the immediate vicinity of the wreck.

France experienced its hottest July since weather records began in 1900. At the same time, rainfall is nearly 70% below normal. Parched soil is turning forests into powder kegs. The largest fire since 1949 has destroyed more than 42,000 hectares of land — an area four times the size of Paris.

An explosion echoes through the Danube as the Romanian Navy blasts underwater rocks. Drought and extreme heat have lowered the river to critical levels, threatening water supply for the Cernavoda nuclear power plant. The operation highlights the extraordinary measures countries are taking to protect vital infrastructure from the impacts of climate change.

From the air, Lake Palas Tuzla in central Turkey looks like a work of art created by nature. In the Turkish province of Kayseri, dried-up watercourses form bizarre patterns that, from the air, resemble tree canopies. The landscape is visibly changing — and at an ever-faster pace.

An aerial photograph shows the mosque and the abandoned buildings of the village of Somang in the Indonesian province of Banten. The settlement was flooded to make way for the Karian Dam, but is now reemerging from the water as a result of drought and El Nino. This unusual image illustrates the consequences of extreme weather events, as Indonesia fears water shortages and food security risks.

In London, cricket teams play on small green islands surrounded by parched grass. Around the world, people are trying to adapt their daily lives to extreme temperatures. But in many places, water is already becoming the scarcest resource.

Tourists visit Badwater Basin, the lowest point in North America, during an extreme heat wave in Death Valley National Park in California. The surreal-looking salt flat is located in one of the hottest regions on Earth. Death Valley in the US holds the official temperature record of 56.7 degrees Celsius (137 Fahrenheit), set in 1913, although some experts today doubt the historical measurement.

The images from Germany, France, Romania, Indonesia, the United Kingdom, and the United States all tell the same story. Where water disappears, agriculture, energy supply, shipping, and nature are thrown out of balance. Drought is no longer a regional problem. It has long since become a global warning sign — and shows just how vulnerable our planet has become.

Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Zaporizhzhia “was struck with North Korean ballistic missiles, Zircons, and guided aerial bombs.”

“It was a vicious attack, calculated to inflict maximum damage specifically on civilian infrastructure,” he said.

“Every step Russia takes – increasing ballistic missile production, bringing in North Korean equipment, preparing for mobilisation – all of this shows that Moscow is preparing not for peace, but for escalation. And the world needs to respond now, not wait.”

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Heathrow says need for expansion ‘clear’ as it loses title of Europe’s busiest airport
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: PA Media
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
West London airport reports 7.86 million passengers in July, compared with 8.15 million for Istanbul

Business live – latest updates

Heathrow airport has argued “the case for expansion has never been clearer” after it lost its position as Europe’s busiest airport to Istanbul.

Figures published on Tuesday showed 7.86 million passengers passed through Heathrow’s four terminals in July,whereas its Turkish counterpart recorded 8.15 million passengers over the same period.

Annual figures from the trade body Airports Council International show Heathrow was Europe’s busiest airport from 1996 to 2019.

The UK’s biggest airport, located west of central London, lost that position in 2020 amid coronavirus travel restrictions before regaining it in 2023 and holding the title since then.

Heathrow’s July passenger total was 1.5% down compared with the same month last year, whereas Istanbul saw a 2.3% boost.

The US-Israel war on Iran has had an impact on Heathrow’s passenger traffic.

Its passenger numbers on Middle East routes in July were down 20.2% year on year.

Despite this, Heathrow continues to operate its two runways at near full capacity, and is seeking government permission to build a third.

An expansion proposal by the airport’s owners would enable it to accommodate 150 million passengers per year. It recorded 84.46 million passengers in 2025.

Heathrow said: “Heathrow is operating at capacity. The case for expansion has never been clearer, as Heathrow was overtaken in July by Istanbul airport as the busiest hub in Europe.

“Our plans will ensure the country gets the infrastructure it needs to stay competitive and will deliver all-important economic growth.”

The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, launched a consultation on the renamed Heathrow expansion national policy statement in June, setting out the conditions needed if the project is to be given the go-ahead.

The then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, said at the time she was determined to get “spades in the ground” for the third runway in the current parliament, and for it to be built by 2035.

after newsletter promotion

Andy Burnham, who sacked Reeves, has previously expressed concerns over Heathrow expansion, stating the plans divert infrastructure investment “away from the north and traps it in London”.

Heathrow said 19 July was its busiest day of the year so far after many schools broke up for summer, with 267,000 passengers recorded.

It added that several new airlines began serving the airport last month, which demonstrates “clear demand for access to Heathrow”.

They include ITA Airways from Italy, Alaska Airlines from the US and Riyadh Air from Saudi Arabia.

The Heathrow chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, said summer was “off to a flying start” but “we want to go further” by “growing our route network and passenger offering”.

He continued: “Expanding Heathrow will help ensure the UK remains home to Europe’s leading hub and continues to benefit from the trade, investment and tourism that increased connectivity will bring.”

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Gangs using Airbnb-type rentals as drug stash houses, top Belgian official says
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Flexible short-term bookings used to store and pack drugs and stash weapons and cash, says Ine Van Wymersch

Airbnb-type short-term rentals are being used as stash houses by criminal gangs, as booming e-commerce aids organised crime “enormously”, Belgium’s lead official in charge of countering drugs has said.

More criminal organisations are using “these Airbnb platforms etc” as a stash place for money, drugs, weapons or people, Belgium’s national drug commissioner, Ine Van Wymersch, said.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Speaking to the Guardian, she said authorities did not have a precise idea of the scale of the problem but criminals were taking advantage of the flexibility offered by short-term booking platforms.

“You need someone to pick up a cargo from the harbour. You don’t know exactly when the boat will arrive. Well, you can hire an Airbnb apartment or studio for three days. It’s very flexible. If the boat is not coming to Antwerp but going to Marseille, there is free cancellation.”

She said short-term rental companies had “a very good legal purpose” but needed to be more resilient to avoid abuse by criminals.

One weekend at the beginning of August, police seized 3.3kg of cocaine and €4,845 (£4,140) in cash from an Airbnb-rented apartment in central Brussels, which was believed to have been used for storing and packing drugs, the news agency Belga reported. In 2024 when 11 people were sentenced for their role in a vast drug trafficking operation between Belgium and the UK, it was revealed that drugs worth €21m were seized from an Airbnb rental in Staden, West Flanders.

A representative for Airbnb in Belgium declined to comment but directed the Guardian to recent remarks by Clément Eulry, Airbnb’s country manager for France and the Benelux.

He told De Staandard that such criminal bookings represented an extreme minority among the millions the company processes annually. He said every case was one too many and the company undertook various measures, including using artificial intelligence to identify suspicious bookings. He said reports of problematic renters were always notified to police and local authorities.

Short-term rentals are only one facet of the modern economy making life easier for organised crime.

Van Wymersch cited the ease of setting up anonymous email accounts, encrypted communications, cryptocurrency and the ubiquity of parcel delivery. “The fact that e-commerce is booming business is facilitating enormously organised crime.”

Without naming specific companies, she said delivery firms were also “very at risk” of being instrumentalised by organised crime, because “it is not a suspicious situation any more when you see that there is a white van stopping at your neighbour’s house and … a small box handed over”.

Van Wymersch became Belgium’s first-ever national drug commissioner in 2023 after Antwerp became firmly established as one of Europe’s main gateways for cocaine.

Her appointment followed a wave of drug-fuelled violence and threats.

In 2022 the then Belgian justice minister had to live under police protection after an alleged plot to kidnap him was uncovered. Antwerp endured a spate of grenade attacks and the fatal shooting of an 11-year old girl, the victim of a conflict between rival drug gangs.

Last year an anonymous investigative judge – who was forced to live in a safe house for four months – warned that Belgium risked becoming a narco state in an excoriating critique of the government’s response.

The narco state warning originated with Van Wymersch. She agreed, she said, with her earlier opinion that “if we don’t do anything, we are at risk to become a narco state … where you don’t know any more who are the good guys and who are the bad guys”.

But she is hopeful of change for the better, as she prioritises going after criminal money: “This multi-headed monster only has one heart and that’s the money.”

Her strategy means targeting small businesses – hairdressers, nail bars or night shops – used for laundering money. Her message to local authorities was that they needed to inspect and investigate “the dodgy shop” in their neighbourhood: “It matters because all these small businesses are one big network.”

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

She said criminal gangs had changed their modus operandi, exploiting small business, rather than using the “big money-laundering constructions” of the past.

At the same time organised crime had changed, she said, morphing from top-down pyramid hierarchies bonded by trust into looser anonymous networks where criminals “don’t know to which network they are belonging any more”.

Illicit activities are outsourced to different gangs, who specialise in money laundering, procuring or using weapons. “It is really crime as a service and it’s very opportunistic,” she said.

After a rapid rise through Belgium’s judicial system, Van Wymersch is known for articulating an “iceberg strategy” to combat organised drug crime.

The shootings and explosions are the visible part of the iceberg, she said, while below the waterline are harms not always linked to organised crime, from people killed by drivers under the influence, to victims of drug-fuelled domestic violence and sexual offences.

While stressing the importance of the police, she said society needed to guarantee young people a stake to prevent them being drawn into drug gangs – essentially melting the iceberg. “We need to invest in warming up the temperature of the water,” she said citing education, anti-poverty strategies, housing and adequate pay for delivery workers.

Crime is under scrutiny in Brussels, where police recorded 101 shootings in 2025, reported by local media to be a record high, often resulting from turf wars between rival gangs. Van Wymersch sees a link between the increase in shootings in the EU capital and social problems, “because the people that are shooting are people without any perspective”.

In Brussels 12.8% of people aged 15-29 are not in education, employment or training, above the national average, although numbers have been on a downward trend since the millennium.

“It is naive to believe that a purely repressive approach will reduce the number of shootings,” Van Wymersch said. “We will see fewer shootings only when there are fewer vulnerable people. In fact, we need to strengthen the resilience of society as a whole.”

The European Holiday Home Association, which represents Airbnb and other platforms, was contacted but a representative said the companies were best placed to respond.

Van Wymersch said her team planned to be in touch with online booking platforms: “What we want to know now is what are the criteria for suspicious booking, what can we learn from that, how can we help you to be more resilient.”

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: PM asks justice secretary to find way to exclude PC Harper’s killers from early release scheme
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Caroline Davies
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Andy Burnham said to be ‘determined’ to work out solution after increasing pressure from family and police

Andy Burnham has told the justice secretary to find a way to exclude PC Andrew Harper’s killers from the early release scheme aimed at easing prison overcrowding.

The prime minister is said to be “determined” that a solution can be found after increasing pressure from Harper’s family and police not to allow Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter, to be freed in January under the existing plans.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

On Monday, Downing Street said it was “not possible” to exempt “one or two offenders” convicted of manslaughter from the early release scheme, and it is not clear how the government could prevent Cole and Bowers from being treated the same as other prisoners with similar sentences.

But later it said the justice secretary, Alex Norris, would “work through further options” and look at ways to keep “a greater number of the most serious offenders” behind bars, it said.

A government spokesperson said: “The prime minister has asked the justice secretary to work through further options to keep a greater number of the most serious offenders in prison, including the killers of PC Harper.”

Harper, 28, was fatally injured when he got caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and was dragged down a country road as the killers fled the scene of a quad-bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire, in 2019.

Cole and Bowers, two of three sentenced over the police officer’s death, are due to be released halfway through their 13-year sentences, after being convicted of manslaughter in 2020. A petition demanding an intervention has nearly 900,000 signatures.

The communities secretary, Angela Rayner, said:“The prime minister is determined to ensure that there is a solution to this and I think he’s made that really clear. He’s tasked the justice secretary to come to parliament in September with that solution.”

About 5,000 people are expected to be released early under sentencing changes, down from 6,000 after some exemptions were announced as part of an urgent review of the scheme to tackle jail overcrowding. Exemptions were made for those convicted of rape, serious child sex offences and grooming offences.

Prison Service officials have warned Burnham that changing the terms of the prisoners’ early release scheme so that those convicted of manslaughter, such as Cole and Bowers, remain in jail would mean further early releases would be needed within 18 months.

Sign up to First Edition

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

Governors told the Guardian the prime minister’s decision last week to exempt rapists and serious child sex offenders would force thousands of sentences to be recalculated in haste and could lead to the mistaken early release of some prisoners.

Rayner told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that potential options to stop prisons reaching capacity could include speeding up the deportation of foreign criminals, reviewing indefinite sentences, and looking at female prisoners’ jail terms. “So there is a lot of work that’s going on,” she said.

“And the prime minister has made it clear he will not just accept that the system says no. He understands the anger and the trauma that PC Harper’s family are going through and others, and other victims who are seeing this prison crisis unfold and they feel that they’re not getting the justice and it’s reopening the trauma that they have been through.”

The early release changes were part of the Sentencing Act passed earlier this year that cut the minimum amount of time many offenders would have to spend in prison.

The third man jailed for the manslaughter of Harper – the vehicle driver, Henry Long – was given a longer jail term of 16 years. Because he received what is called an extended determinate sentence at the time, he cannot be considered for this early release scheme.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Zuckerberg pushes ‘superintelligent’ AI for all as Meta drops open-source model
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Nick Robins-Early
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Meta CEO presents utopian vision of AI in 6,000-word essay amid Silicon Valley debate over government regulation

Mark Zuckerberg published a lengthy essay on Monday detailing his views on artificial intelligence and announced several plans for how Meta would develop the technology in the future. The CEO’s essay went online the same day as Meta released a new, open-source AI model that seeks to rival Anthropic and OpenAI’s products called Muse Glimmer.

Over the course of more than 6,000 words in a post titled “The Future is for Everyone,” Zuckerberg addressed a range of topics related to AI that included datacenters, government regulation, cybersecurity, the creation of bioweapons, labor market disruption, surveillance powers and more. The essay presented a utopian vision of AI as a personalized “superintelligence” – using the word 60 times.

“Some argue that superintelligence itself or a small set of experts who control it should decide what is best for humanity. We disagree,” Zuckerberg wrote.

Central to Zuckerberg’s post was an argument for free-to-download, open-weight AI models – like the kind Meta develops – and a lack of government regulation of artificial intelligence. Zuckerberg’s stance sets him and Meta apart from industry leaders OpenAI and Anthropic, which have argued that open-source AI is dangerous. The two frontier labs have released proprietary AI products and argued that cutting-edge models should remain tightly controlled by the companies that build them.

Zuckerberg’s post comes as Silicon Valley is engaged in a heated debate over how to regulate AI development, which has involved the creation of a secret White House framework for testing new models and an ongoing debate over whether to restrict the use of Chinese-made open-source AI. As Anthropic and OpenAI have surged ahead in the AI industry, competitors such as Meta have also grown wary of their dominance and sought to position their open models as alternatives.

Zuckerberg framed Meta’s pursuit of open-weight AI as a more democratic version of the technology and one that will create a “balance of power” between users, whether that involves states, companies or individuals. His plans also called for letting users decide what “values” an AI model should have, as opposed to a company encoding it with rigid guardrails and beliefs.

“If the power of superintelligence is held by a small number of individuals, businesses, governments, or AI itself, then that will naturally lead to outcomes that are less favorable for everyone else,” Zuckerberg wrote.

Tech leaders have made a cottage industry out of releasing broad, vaguely philosophical treatises on artificial intelligence, which tend to double as marketing materials for their own companies and products. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Palantir’s Alex Karp and the venture capitalist Marc Andreessen have all written long manifestos on the virtues and dangers of the technology.

In addition to weighing in on open source models, Zuckerberg also called for accelerating the buildout of AI infrastructure such as datacenters. The massive development of resource-hungry datacenters has become a divisive issue in the US, with rapidly growing public opposition and calls from politicians to issue moratoriums on their construction. Zuckerberg wrote in the essay that Meta would create a fund to invest more in local communities near datacenters, as well as cited an example from Louisiana where some teachers received a $50,000 bonus check as a result of increased sales tax revenue from the company’s infrastructure investment.

On government testing of AI models for cybersecurity risks, a tangible concern after rogue models have hacked outside organizations in recent months, Zuckerberg agreed that companies should share “intermediate training checkpoints and technical staff” but provided few details. He broadly warned that regulation would cause China to overtake the US in the AI race, where he claimed it already has an advantage in terms of building infrastructure.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

“Any policy that slows American model releases – even by a month – could add significant risk to American leadership while letting foreign models race ahead,” Zuckerberg.

Many of Zuckerberg’s policy plans in his essay lacked detail or reiterated previous claims about the abundant wealth and prosperity that AI would create, such as touting that everyone would have “invention superpowers” to create new businesses. His version of the future also is inherently tied to Meta products, such as the company’s AI-enabled smart glasses.

“Everyone will have an exceptionally capable personal agent that understands you, your goals, and everything you care about,” Zuckerberg said. “You’ll be able to interact with your agent through any device, including your glasses to keep you present in the moment with the people you care about.”

On thornier issues such as loss of jobs from AI, autonomous weapons and government surveillance, Zuckerberg mostly brushed them aside. Law enforcement and the military already possess greater intelligence-gathering powers than the average person, Zuckerberg argued, and this would continue with access to AI. Companies may shrink in size due to AI, he conceded, but the technology would create new economic opportunities.

“People will have to adapt, and this will be challenging,” Zuckerberg said about labor disruption from new technology. “But the more that everyone has a personal agent that is superintelligent at teaching us new skills and helping us adapt to change, the smoother this will be.”

Have you ever wondered whether we strictly need all of the particles in the standard model of particle physics? If I were making a fundamental particle ingredients list for the most common forms of visible matter in the universe, I’d say we primarily need electrons, up quarks and down quarks. But this list completely ignores important elements of how matter works: how it sticks together, what happens when it gains or loses energy and whether particle identities are stable.

https://grist.org/health/floods-can-leav.title: Floods can leave communities facing higher overdose deaths for years
https://grist.org/health/floods-can-leav.author: Katie Myers
https://grist.org/health/floods-can-leav.text:
This coverage is made possible through a partnership between Grist and BPR, a public radio station serving western North Carolina.

Hush Sinn delivers needles, naloxone, and other medical supplies to people in the mostly rural mountain communities of Madison County, North Carolina. Sinn does this through Holler Harm Reduction, a grassroots organization that strives to minimize the risk of overdose and infection in a region where many residents are still recovering from the devastation of Hurricane Helene.

Sinn, who uses the pronoun they, believes the nonprofit, often known simply as “Holler,” has prevented a lot of tragedy. But nearly two years after the storm they and other harm reductionists have noticed a troubling pattern.

“While overdose rates are still trending down, we get these weird spikes,” Sinn said. “And the spikes we get, we kind of consistently are able to relate back to Helene.” Financial stress, ongoing trauma, and unstable housing have disrupted some people’s recovery and thrust others into dangerous, even deadly, patterns of substance use.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Sinn’s observations reflect a broader pattern across the region. A Pennsylvania State University study published last month found that severe flooding was associated with higher overdose death rates in economically distressed Appalachian counties — increases that can persist for at least a decade after the water recedes.

Kristina Brant, the study’s lead author, began the research after watching healthcare providers struggle to maintain addiction treatment and harm reduction services during catastrophic floods in eastern Kentucky in 2021 and 2022.

“After such a huge disaster, especially in a small community where so many people wear so many hats, the same person that provides one public health service is also going to be asked to jump in on flood recovery, right?” she said. Brant began to understand services could be interrupted for a long, long time, and wondered what that might mean for both those in long-term recovery and those actively using opioids.

Brant’s team analyzed federal records of opioid overdose deaths and severe floods in rural Appalachia, comparing 118 counties that experienced major flooding between 2000 and 2017 with 101 that did not.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The researchers found that overdose deaths began rising in the years after an inundation and remained elevated for at least a decade. Over that period, annual overdose deaths in flooded counties increased by about 28 percent, while overdose mortality rates rose by 26 percent compared with the year before the flood. These changes were most pronounced in economically distressed and lower-income counties.

The findings prompted Brant’s team to ask why the effects endured for so long. Interviews with healthcare providers, harm reduction workers, and others involved in the response to Kentucky’s 2022 disaster identified several factors, including disrupted treatment and harm reduction services, prolonged housing and economic instability, and the lasting effects of trauma.

“It’s important to have a number of important ingredients in your life, like access to a safe home, like access to a well-paid, meaningful job, like access to social support,” Brant said. “And for many people, the flood upended those things.”

One clinic Brant spoke with closed after the flood because the costs of reopening were simply too great. Flood-related disruptions can also interrupt treatments like methadone, forcing some people to return to illicit opioids to stave off the unpleasant and often dangerous effects of withdrawal. After weeks or months in treatment or recovery, that return to use can be especially dangerous because people may not realize how much their tolerance has changed.

Losing a job, stable housing, or reliable access to food can take a heavy toll on people’s mental health and increase the risk of an overdose, said Cassie York. She works in behavioral health at Mountain Community Health Partnership in Yancey County, North Carolina. The flooding that followed Helene killed at least 10 people in the county and caused landslides that destroyed 1,400 homes. Another 2,300 were heavily damaged.

“I think the main issue here, and probably not just here, is a lack of resources in general,” York said. “Housing, which has always been a shortage here, is even more so since the hurricane.”

Addressing the instability that so many people are still dealing with two years after Helene is what harm reduction is all about, Sinn said. “We’re also seeing so many people still living in trailers,” they added. “These things that were supposed to be temporary are now permanent, you know?”

Brant believes people like Sinn and York who work directly with affected communities should be involved in disaster planning and recovery from the start. That’s something healthcare providers have also begun to publicly support.

“When it comes to things like flood preparedness conversations or flood recovery conversations, it’s not the case that often a substance use service provider might have a seat at that table,” she said. “Anything that could make care easier to access generally, every day, for rural people, would also help to limit disruptions after disaster.”

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: Trump secretly swapped planes in Turkey over Iran threat, report says
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
US President Donald Trump secretly flew out of last month's NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, on an alternate military aircraft while the White House made it appear that the Republican president was flying on Air Force One, according to a report published by The Washington Post on Monday.

The Post said the operation was prompted by an Iranian assassination threat against Trump. The ruse was carried out as journalists and some White House staff members were led to believe they were on the same plane as the president as he began his journey back to Washington from the annual gathering of NATO country leaders.

READ MORE
Trump tempers fury at NATO summit after lashing out at key allies in Ankara

The Post cited material reviewed by the newspaper, a US official familiar with the operation and another person with knowledge of the president’s travel.

The Associated Press has not independently confirmed the report.

Trump had flown to the summit in a new Qatari-gifted and retrofitted red, white and navy blue jet. But ahead of departing Turkey, he said he would fly partway home on an older-model baby blue Air Force One plane instead.

The president at the time said the new luxury jet was being flown out ahead of his departure from Ankara to give some US troops based in eastern England a chance to check out the new Air Force One.

In Ankara, Trump boarded the old Air Force One jumbo jet in view of television cameras ahead of the plane flying to Royal Air Force Mildenhall in the United Kingdom.

However, according to the Post report, after boarding the legacy Air Force One jet, he was secretly shuttled minutes later to a smaller plane – an Air Force C-32A – via an airport catering truck typically used to load meals and other supplies. Trump flew to Mildenhall on that smaller jet.

The White House did not respond directly to questions about the Post report of the secret operation to whisk Trump out of the country on a third aircraft, or the reported elaborate ruse to make it appear he was on the baby blue Air Force One jet flying to Mildenhall.

“As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement.

The US Secret Service declined to comment. The Air Force, which maintains the fleet of executive travel aircraft, referred questions to the White House.

While Trump was in Turkey, the US military conducted a series of large strikes in Iran in retaliation for its attacks on merchant shipping in the region.

The New York Times and CBS News reported last month that intelligence officials had raised concerns about a potential attack on the president or his jet, triggering additional precautions and the decision not to use the newly inaugurated aircraft gifted to Trump by Qatar for the first leg of Trump’s trip home from Ankara.

The swap had spurred questions about the security of the Qatar-provided aircraft, and Trump said last month after the trip that it would undergo additional upgrades.

Cheung on Monday maintained that the new, Qatari-gifted plane was “a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff".

The new Post report on clandestinely putting Trump on a third aircraft and quietly whisking him out of the country adds a fresh layer to just how seriously concerned US security officials were about the threat against Trump during the ongoing war with Iran.

Paul Eckloff, a former special agent with the Secret Service, said such an unusual move could either reflect actionable intelligence or an abundance of caution given volatility in the region with the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

“I would not say unprecedented, but it is an unusual occurrence,” Eckloff told The Associated Press.

The Post reported that to exit that plane without being seen by those uninvolved in the operation, Trump and several aides stepped aboard an airport catering truck, which was elevated planeside using hydraulics and positioned at a door on the opposite side of Air Force One’s entrance.

The small group of reporters who thought they were traveling with Trump were advised to lower their window shades ahead of takeoff.

After arriving at Mildenhall, news photographers captured images of Trump getting off the presidential plane – suggesting he reboarded Air Force One out of sight of the pack of journalists who thought they were traveling with him.

Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal called for a congressional investigation.

“It is unprecedented and it is surreal,” he said Monday on CNN, calling the incident “downright scary".

After the brief visit to the base at Mildenhall, Trump boarded the new Air Force One aircraft to fly the rest of the way to Washington.

During a gaggle with reporters aboard the aircraft, Trump was asked directly if there was any credible threats on Air Force One by Iran.

“Well, I have a threat all the time. I’m number one on their list before you,” Trump said. He added to the traveling reporters, “But if I go, you go.”

Russian attacks struck Kyiv, triggering fires in the capital, officials said. (Reuters: Gleb Garanich)

Russian attacks killed six people and wounded 20 in the south-eastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Tuesday, local time, officials said.

Elsewhere in Ukraine, local authorities reported another six people were killed and 16 wounded in the regions of Dnipropetrovsk and Donetsk.

A drone attack also killed one person and injured two others in Russia's Voronezh region, while falling debris triggered fires at a Wildberries warehouse, regional governor Alexander Gusev and the company said.

Thirteen people have been killed and a Wildberries warehouse set ablaze as Russia and Ukraine traded attacks on Tuesday, local time.

Russian attacks killed six people and wounded 20 in the south-eastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia and also struck Kyiv, triggering fires in the capital, officials said.

Zaporizhzhia regional governor Ivan Fedorov said Russian troops launched missiles and aerial bombs at the city. He posted pictures showing buildings and vehicles ablaze.

Air raid alerts were sounded in both Zaporizhzhia and in Kyiv, where the capital's military administration said warehouses in a central district were ablaze. One person was reported injured.

Elsewhere in Ukraine, local authorities reported another six people were killed and 16 wounded in the regions of Dnipropetrovsk and Donetsk.

A drone attack killed one person and injured two others in Russia's Voronezh region, while falling debris triggered fires at a Wildberries warehouse, regional governor Alexander Gusev and the company said.

Almost two weeks ago, what is believed to be a North Korean missile was fired in an attack that killed a Ukrainian family. It could be part of a major escalation in North Korea's involvement in the war in Ukraine.

Russia's air defence units destroyed 15 drones over the city of Voronezh and five districts of the region, Mr Gusev said on Telegram.

"A drone crash caused fires at two warehouses of a large company. At one facility, the fire has been contained to an area of 16,000 square metres, while at the other, a blaze covering 20,000 square metres is being extinguished. Emergency services are on scene," the governor said.

Earlier on Tuesday, Russian online retailer Wildberries said its logistics facilities in the Voronezh region had been evacuated in accordance with safety requirements.

It later said that the fire at the facility had been extinguished, that goods had not been damaged and that deliveries had been rerouted to other warehouses.

An industrial enterprise was on fire in Russia's Orenburg region after an attack by "enemy drones", the local governor said on Tuesday.

There had been no reports of casualties, Yevgeny Solntsev said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/s.title: Luxury cruise ship passengers ferried to shore after strike closes port
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/s.author: Rachel Jackson, Vanessa Mills, and Ruby Littler
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Industrial Action

Operations at both Broome port terminals are quiet, after stevedores and maintenance workers began two week's protected industrial action last Friday. (ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson)

Strike action is set to continue for two weeks at the Port of Broome, affecting cruise ship arrivals to the popular tourist town.

Workers walked off the job after failing to reach an agreement with the Kimberley Ports Authority over wages and conditions.

The KPA says it will continue to meet with employees and the union to resolve the outstanding terms.

Cruise boat passengers on luxury tours of Western Australia’s remote north have been ferried to shore using tenders and provisions loaded by hand onto ships as work stoppages at Broome’s port begin to take effect.

Stevedoring and maintenance employees walked off the job last Friday after failing to reach an agreement with the Kimberley Ports Authority (KPA) over wages and conditions.

Cruise ship crew have been forced to hand load cargo and transfer passengers in small boats. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

The strike action is set to impact both of the port’s terminals for two weeks.

It's the second major industrial action in the state's north in less than a week, following unrelated work stoppages at BHP's facilities in Port Hedland over the weekend.

Two livestock ships and seven cruise boats were due to berth at KPA port this week, while another 12 vessels were due alongside the adjacent, privately owned floating jetty.

Discovery One Cruises owner Erie Astrup said her crews had been forced to load provisions from the slipway near the wharf, instead of relying on stevedores and cranes.

"I support the negotiations that are going on but it really does have a huge knock-on effect for the whole community, all the tourism industry, the small businesses," she said.

"And that can feel a bit unfair and challenging for many because it's a short tourism season in the Kimberley."

Discovery One has operated cruises in the Kimberley region for 26 years. (Supplied: Erle Astrup)

It is unclear how larger cruise boats, due alongside this week with up to 300 people on board, will manage the massive amount of food and fuel required for voyages.

The luxury cruiser Le Jacques Cartier had been scheduled to dock at KPA's main wharf on Tuesday morning, but remained offshore.

Passengers were seen being ferried to the slipway using the ship's tenders.

Ponant Explorations CEO Deb Corbett said the company was making the necessary arrangements to manage Le Jacques Cartier's schedule and would update its guests directly.

The luxury cruise boat Le Jacques Cartier moored offshore instead of being alongside as scheduled the Broome wharf during the strike action. (ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson)

Shayne Murray, who runs a bus company which regularly services visiting cruise boats, said the transfers using the slipway were "not ideal".

"But it's working well — the tide's in our favour and the easterlies aren't in today," he said.

Mr Murray is also the president of Cruise Broome, an association of industry and volunteers who help promote and manage cruise groups to the town.

"It [the strike action] affects everyone, from the hotels to planes, the people who pay a lot of money for these cruises," he said.

The tourism and livestock industries are concerned about the impact of a protracted strike at Broome port. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

In an online post, Liberal MLC Neil Thomson said it was "so embarrassing for our state to have people disembarking via the slipway rather than on the new multi-million dollar port facility".

KPA port workers and their union, the Maritime Union of Australia (MUA), have been trying to negotiate a new enterprise agreement since October last year.

MUA WA branch secretary Will Tracey said the strike action was justified.

“Broome tradesmen are paid the lowest rates for tradesmen at port authorities in the state,” he said.

“The cost of living has only increased since the last agreement was done and there should be a reflection of that within the Broome area allowance, which compensates for the excessive cost of living across the Kimberley.”

The union said strike action at the port came as a last resort. (ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson)

In a statement, the KPA said it would continue to meet with employees and the union and "bargain in good faith" to resolve the outstanding items, with the Fair Work Commission now assisting in conciliation.

The parties are due to meet again tomorrow.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/o.title: Why police took 20 hours to identify 'body' in suitcase as lifelike doll
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/o.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A forensic expert says the Oallen case highlights why investigators must resist disturbing suspected human remains. (ABC News.)

Police took the suitcase found at Oallen to a mortuary for examination rather than risk destroying fragile evidence at a potential homicide scene.

Forensic expert Xanthe Weston says the 20-hour time frame was not extraordinary and highly realistic dolls can be mistaken for human remains

NSW Police have closed the investigation.

The more than 20 hours it took to establish suspected human remains found in a suitcase near Goulburn were actually a life-like doll highlights the painstaking process required to preserve a potential crime scene, according to a forensic expert.

NSW Police have revealed investigators deliberately decided to examine the bag and its contents at a mortuary rather than at the remote Oallen crime scene, to avoid potentially losing fragile forensic evidence.

Forensic expert Xanthe Weston says while it might seem extraordinary that a doll could be mistaken for a woman's body, she can understand how it happened.

"So whilst it seems that it is ridiculous almost that a doll could be mistaken for a human, I can totally see how that could have happened and the police did absolutely the right thing," Dr Weston said.

Forensic expert Dr Xanthe Weston says some modern life-like dolls can be extraordinarily realistic. (Supplied: University of Newcastle)

"Not disturbing that scene and making sure that it was not forensically relevant rather than destroying the scene, suspecting it could be a doll. So they actually followed protocol."

In a statement, police said there was "no typical time frame" for determining whether unknown remains are human because no two crime scenes are the same.

They said the Oallen discovery was treated as a suspicious death, with investigators believing a potentially decomposed body was inside a bag in remote bushland, with light and weather conditions deteriorating.

"A forensic and operational decision was made that the examination of the bag and its contents should be conducted at a mortuary with sophisticated medical and scientific equipment, to mitigate any risk of fragile forensic evidence being lost."

Dr Weston said the roughly 20-hour time frame was not extraordinary from a forensic perspective.

"I know that people will probably want to be quite critical, but from a forensic perspective, an identification perspective, this is exactly as I would have expected it to go," she said.

She said investigators faced a fundamental problem, if the suitcase did contain a homicide victim, disturbing it simply to establish what was inside could destroy evidence.

"If there is a body in there, you cannot afford to contaminate it or damage any of that evidence. So it has to be done in a very controlled, methodical way."

That could include first examining the surrounding scene and the outside of the suitcase before opening it, with Dr Weston saying fibres, hair, skin cells or DNA transfer could otherwise be lost.

"Once it's gone, all compromised, it's gone. There's no coming back from that."

Dr Weston said mistakes involving suspected human remains were not unprecedented.

She recalled working in Scotland when police were concerned remains found in an area where authorities were searching for a missing young woman were human.

She said a dog walker had gone home, returned with a plastic bag and dug up the remains before they were examined.

"They were brought in a plastic bag and it was a sheep. I was so relieved because imagine that scene was totally destroyed if they had been human remains," Dr Weston said.

Dr Weston said modern lifelike dolls could also be extraordinarily convincing and she had professionally examined both adult and childlike dolls.

"Some of them are not at all lifelike, but some, they are becoming more and more realistic because obviously that's what the market is requesting. They want realism," she said.

She cautioned against assuming markings on the Oallen doll, which police said resembled bruises and grazes, had been deliberately designed to depict injuries.

Dr Weston said intentionally replicated bruising was not something she had encountered and the marks could have been dirt or damage interpreted as injuries, because investigators believed they were looking at human remains.

Police said the markings gave further weight to the initial belief the suitcase contained a deceased person.

But with the contents now established as non-human, police said there would be no further investigation.

NSW Police also said the response to the incident was appropriate and reports of this nature were expected to be taken seriously and managed professionally.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/a.author: Blake Kagi
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-11/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Law, Crime and Justice

Andrew Forrest is suing Meta over scam ads that use his likeness without permission. (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

A US Federal Court has ruled against Meta in an ongoing legal dispute with Australian billionaire Andrew Forrest, who is suing the social media giant over scam ads that feature his likeness without his permission.

A judge ruled Meta had "spoliated" evidence, resulting in "prejudice against" Mr Forrest and imposed sanctions on the company.

Mr Forrest has welcomed the ruling and said Meta "must not be allowed to outrun responsibility or the full weight of the law."

A US Federal court has ruled that Meta failed to preserve key evidence in an ongoing legal battle with Andrew Forrest, an outcome the Australian billionaire said could help make sure the social media giant did not "outrun responsibility".

Mr Forrest is suing Meta over scam ads on its platforms that use his likeness without permission.

His legal team said the adverts, which show him endorsing fraudulent cryptocurrency and other investment products on Facebook, have "plagued" the mining magnate for years and duped thousands of victims.

Meta has countered that the offending marketing messages were not its doing.

Meta has said that it did not produce the scam ads, which according to the law suit, racked up thousands of victims.  (Reuters: Daniel Cole/File)

The hearing also looked into whether Meta had wrongly ditched evidence, forfeiting its ability to take shelter behind the act.

On Tuesday, the judge has found Meta had "spoliated evidence … resulting in prejudice to Forrest".

The ruling also stated the company had failed to take reasonable steps to preserve electronically stored information that should have been kept in anticipation of litigation, including the final scam ads that were shown to victims.

Under US law, spoliation is the intentional, reckless, or negligent withholding, hiding, altering, or destroying of evidence relevant to a legal proceeding.

The ruling said in this case Meta should have foreseen the need to preserve any data relevant to the case.

The words emblazoned across the ads are dramatic, and they're usually accompanied by a photoshopped or AI-generated image of an Australian celebrity being arrested. It's an attempt to take your money.

The ruling said if the jury found at trial that Meta acted with the intent to deprive Mr Forrest of the information, they should also assume the evidence in question was unfavourable to Meta.

Mr Forrest welcomed the ruling, saying: "We now have a glimmer of hope of correcting a huge injustice inflicted on society".

Forrest's legal team has argued that Meta's artificial intelligence tools optimised and personalised fraudulent ads before distributing them. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

"Meta's conduct in this litigation so far has been evasive, duplicitous and deeply revealing. It exposes a corporate culture that disregards proper and fair process with little restraint.

"The Court's sanctions send a clear message. Meta cannot destroy or lose evidence and then use that missing evidence as a shield. The penalties for these wrongdoings must fall on Meta, not on the victims of scam advertising."

The court said Mr Forrest was entitled to fees and costs incurred as of the ruling, and that he and Meta must meet to discuss how much should be awarded.

Financial advertisers on Facebook and Instagram will be required to reveal who is paying for the ads and who benefits from them.

Mr Forrest had previously launched criminal charges against Meta in 2022 in an Australian court, but they were discontinued in 2024.

Since 2019, thousands of deceptive advertisements on Facebook have used the likeness of the highly prominent businessman to promote scams, racking up thousands of victims, according to the suit.

The billionaire's legal team argues that Meta's artificial intelligence tools optimised and personalised fraudulent ads before distributing them, thereby making Meta an active participant, rather than a mere intermediary.
